# Neural Project Institute

> Neural Project Institute (neuralprojectinstitute.com) is an independent project management education site. It publishes free, in-depth guides on project management, Agile, Scrum and Kanban; free Excel, Google Sheets and PDF templates; independent reviews and comparisons of project management software; and the PMAI (Project Management Artificial Intelligence) certification. Contact: support@neuralprojectinstitute.com.

Guides are written in British English, cite primary sources (PMI, the Scrum Guide 2020, the Kanban Guide, vendor documentation) and label worked examples as illustrative. Most pages are also available in German, Spanish, French, Italian, Japanese, Russian and Chinese under /de/, /es/, /fr/, /it/, /ja/, /ru/ and /zh/. This file contains the full text of every English page; the index is in [llms.txt](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/llms.txt).

### What is project management?
Project management is the practice of applying knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to deliver a specific result within agreed limits of time, cost, scope and quality. Every project moves through five phases: **initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure**. [Read the full introduction](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/).

### Project management guide: frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project management guide?**
A project management guide explains how to plan, run and close projects: the phases, processes, tools and methodologies that help teams deliver results on time and on budget. This free guide from the Neural Project Institute covers all of them, from fundamentals to Agile, Scrum and Kanban.

**Q: How do I learn project management from scratch?**
Start with the fundamentals (what a project is, the five phases and the main methodologies), then learn planning, scheduling, cost and risk techniques, and practise them on a small real project. Our learning path below lists the guides to read in order.

**Q: What are the 5 phases of project management?**
Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure.

**Q: Which project management methodology should I use?**
Use a predictive (Waterfall) approach when requirements are stable, an Agile approach such as Scrum or Kanban when they are uncertain, and a hybrid when you need both governance and flexibility.

**Q: Do I need a certification to be a project manager?**
Not always, but certifications such as PMP, PRINCE2, Scrum certifications or PMAI help you show your knowledge, especially when changing careers.

**Q: Is this project management guide free?**
Yes. Every guide on this site is free to read. The optional PMAI certification adds assessed courses and a verifiable certificate.

# 35 Contact Hours for PMP: What Counts and the 2026 Rules

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/35-contact-hours-pmp/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: 35 contact hours for PMP explained: what counts, the 1 December 2026 live-training rule, the CAPM waiver and how to count and record hours, with examples.


## 35 Contact Hours for PMP: What Counts and the 2026 Rules
The 35 contact hours for the PMP are the 35 hours of formal project management training you must complete before you apply for the exam, unless you hold an active CAPM, which waives the requirement. From 1 December 2026, live instructor-led training only counts if it comes from a PMI Authorized Training Partner or an eligible accredited academic programme, while self-paced courses can still come from any provider. This guide explains what counts, how to count and record your hours, and how the new rule affects training you have already done.
- Published 3 October 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 22 min read

### Key takeaways
- You need at least 35 hours of project management training aligned to the PMP Examination Content Outline, completed before you submit your application. An active CAPM waives the requirement.
- From 1 December 2026, live instructor-led training only counts if delivered by a PMI Authorized Training Partner (ATP), a China Registered Education Provider or an eligible accredited higher-education programme, including GAC-accredited programmes.
- Courses completed before 1 December 2026 remain eligible under the old rules, and self-paced courses from any organisation still count if they meet PMI's quality checks.
- Training hours do not expire and can be combined from several courses. Count only time spent receiving project management instruction.
- You do not upload certificates when you apply, but PMI asks for proof if you are audited, so keep a record of every course.
- The training is separate from experience: you also need 3, 4 or 5 years of project leadership within the last 10 years depending on your education, or 2 years with a GAC-accredited degree.

### What are the 35 contact hours for the PMP?
**The 35 contact hours are the formal project management education PMI requires before you can apply for the Project Management Professional (PMP) exam.** One contact hour is one hour of instruction in project management topics aligned to the PMP Examination Content Outline. The hours must be completed before you submit your application, and an active CAPM certification can be used instead.
PMI now usually calls them **training hours** or the **35-hour training requirement**, but candidates, course providers and older PMI handbooks still say "contact hours". They mean the same thing.
The training requirement sits alongside two other parts of PMP eligibility: your **education** (the highest qualification you hold) and your **professional project experience**. PMI is clear that training and experience do different jobs. Training shows you have studied project management; experience shows you have actually led and directed project work. One cannot replace the other.
| Rule | What PMI says (checked 25 October 2026) |
| --- | --- |
| Amount | At least 35 hours of qualifying project management training |
| Content | Must align with the current PMP Examination Content Outline (People, Process, Business Environment) |
| Timing | Completed before you submit your application |
| Live training from 1 December 2026 | Only from a PMI Authorized Training Partner, a China Registered Education Provider or an eligible accredited higher-education programme, including GAC programmes |
| Self-paced training | Can come from any organisation if it aligns with the current outline |
| Expiry | Training hours do not expire |
| Combining courses | Allowed; hours do not have to come from one course or provider |
| Waiver | An active CAPM waives the training requirement |
| Proof | Not uploaded at submission; required if your application is audited |
For the wider picture of the exam itself, read our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

### PMP eligibility in 2026: where the 35 hours fit
Before you spend money on training, check that you meet the experience requirement, because that is usually what decides when you can apply. PMI's PMP page sets out four routes, all of which need the 35 hours (or an active CAPM).
| Highest education | Project experience needed | Training |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Secondary diploma (high school, GED or equivalent) | 5 years (60 months) | 35 hours or active CAPM |
| Associate degree or vocational/trade school diploma | 4 years (48 months) | 35 hours or active CAPM |
| Bachelor's degree or higher | 3 years (36 months) | 35 hours or active CAPM |
| Bachelor's or postgraduate degree from a PMI GAC-accredited programme | 2 years (24 months) | 35 hours or active CAPM |
Three details matter when you add up experience:
- **The 10-year window.** All the experience you claim must fall within the last 10 years.
- **Leadership, not just participation.** PMI describes qualifying experience as taking responsibility for planning, decisions, delivery and outcomes in a professional setting. Your job title does not have to be "project manager", and predictive, Agile and hybrid projects all count.
- **No double counting.** Overlapping project time is counted once, and each project is listed separately on the application.

#### Worked example: checking experience with overlapping projects
**Daniel** has a vocational diploma, so he needs 48 months. He plans to apply in January 2027, which means only experience from January 2017 onwards counts.
| Project | Dates | Months in the 10-year window | Overlap | Months counted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A: Warehouse relocation | Mar 2015 to Feb 2017 | 2 (Jan to Feb 2017) | None | 2 |
| B: ERP rollout | Jan 2019 to Jun 2020 | 18 | None | 18 |
| C: New distribution centre | Apr 2020 to Mar 2022 | 24 | 3 months with project B (Apr to Jun 2020) | 21 |
| D: Fleet tracking system | Sep 2023 to Aug 2024 | 12 | None | 12 |
| **Total** |  | 56 |  | **53 months** |
Daniel has 53 unique months against 48 needed, so he meets the experience rule. Project A barely contributes because most of it falls outside the window. His remaining task is the 35 hours, which is what the rest of this guide covers.
Tip
Draft your project descriptions while you plan your training. A one-paragraph summary per project, using terms such as [scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/), [risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) and [stakeholders](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/), makes the application faster and is easier to support if you are audited.

### The 1 December 2026 rule for live training
In September 2026 PMI confirmed a change to which live courses can be used for the 35 hours. In PMI's words: "Beginning 1 December 2026, live training will qualify only when delivered by a PMI Authorized Training Partner or an eligible accredited academic program, including GAC-accredited programs." PMI's PMP page adds that a separate **China Registered Education Provider (REP)** pathway applies in China.
From that date, live hours count only if your provider is one of these:
- **A PMI Authorized Training Partner (ATP).** PMI describes ATPs as organisations it has vetted and approved to deliver official instructor-led PMP training using PMI-developed course content, taught by PMP-certified instructors who have completed a PMI trainer course. PMI publishes a searchable ATP directory on pmi.org.
- **A China Registered Education Provider**, for candidates in China.
- **An eligible accredited higher-education programme**, including programmes accredited by PMI's Global Accreditation Center (GAC).
Several things have **not** changed:
- The requirement is still 35 hours (or an active CAPM).
- Self-paced, on-demand courses can still come from any organisation, provided they align with the current content outline.
- Training hours still do not expire, and you can still combine courses.
- Courses completed before 1 December 2026 remain eligible under the rules in place at the time, even if you apply after the change.

#### What counts as live and what counts as self-paced
The rule turns on the format of the course, so it helps to be precise. PMI's application asks you to say, for each course, whether it was live instructor-led or self-paced/on-demand.
| Format | Typical examples | Provider rule from 1 December 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Live instructor-led | Classroom courses, scheduled virtual classes with a trainer, bootcamps, in-house workshops led by a trainer | ATP, China REP or eligible accredited academic programme only |
| Self-paced, on-demand | Recorded video courses you complete in your own time with an end-of-course assessment, including PMI's own PMP Exam Prep Course | Any organisation, if the course meets PMI's checks |
A virtual class with a live trainer at a fixed time is live training, even though you attend online. "Online" does not mean self-paced.

#### Timing scenarios: does my training count?
| Your situation | Counts? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Live course from a non-ATP provider, completed in October 2026 | Yes | Completed before 1 December 2026, so the old rules apply |
| Live non-ATP course that starts in late November 2026 and finishes in December 2026 | Very likely not | PMI's protection covers courses completed before 1 December 2026; check with PMI before relying on it |
| Live course from an ATP, any date | Yes | ATPs meet the new rule |
| Self-paced course from any provider, taken in 2027 | Yes, if it meets PMI's checks | The provider rule applies to live training only |
| Employer's in-house live workshop, run in 2027 by a non-ATP trainer | No | Live training after 1 December 2026 must come from an approved provider |
| Employer's in-house live workshop run by an ATP | Yes | The provider, not the venue, is what matters |
| Project management modules in a GAC-accredited degree | Yes | Eligible accredited academic programmes are named in the rule |
| Active CAPM | Waives the requirement | No training hours needed |
| Expired CAPM | No | Only an active CAPM waives the requirement |
Tip
What matters is the date you **finish** the course, not the date you book or pay. If you are part-way through a live non-ATP course, finish it before 1 December 2026 and keep the completion certificate, or plan to make up the hours with an ATP or self-paced course.
If you are weighing up training providers more generally, our [project management certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) compares the main routes.

### What counts towards the 35 hours
PMI's guidance is that qualifying training is formal project management instruction aligned to the current PMP Examination Content Outline. In practice, these sources usually qualify:
- **PMI Authorized Training Partner courses**, live or self-paced.
- **PMI's own PMP Exam Prep Course**, which is self-paced. PMI says the training details can be applied to your application automatically once you finish.
- **Self-paced courses from other organisations** that state their hours, include an end-of-course assessment and issue a completion record.
- **College or university courses** on project management. If project management was only part of a broader course, count only the hours spent on those topics. From 1 December 2026, live university teaching needs to be part of an eligible accredited programme.
- **Employer-sponsored project management training**, if it was completed before 1 December 2026 or, after that date, if it is self-paced or delivered by an approved provider.
- **Older PMP prep courses**. PMI says training taken for an earlier version of the exam can still count, but compare it with the current outline so you know what to revise.
The content matters as much as the source. The current outline groups the exam into three domains, so qualifying training typically covers topics such as:
| Exam domain (weight) | Example topics a qualifying course covers | Related guides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| People (33%) | Leading teams, conflict, stakeholder engagement, servant leadership, building shared understanding | [Stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/), [project manager responsibilities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-roles-and-responsibilities/) |
| Process (41%) | Scope, schedule, cost, risk, quality, procurement, choosing predictive, Agile or hybrid approaches | [Work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/), [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/), [earned value](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) |
| Business Environment (26%) | Governance, benefits and value, compliance, organisational change, project context such as AI and sustainability | [Project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/), [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) |
Agile and hybrid training counts as long as it is project management instruction aligned to the outline. PMI's outline treats Agile and predictive approaches as equally valid, so a good course covers both.

### What does not count
These are the most common reasons hours are rejected or have to be removed during an audit:
- **Books, practice exams and other self-study on their own.** PMI says these "do not count by themselves". Reading the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) is useful revision, but it is not training.
- **Marketing labels.** PMI warns that a course advertised as "35 hours" or "35 PDUs" does not automatically qualify. The course itself has to meet the requirements.
- **Time that is not instruction.** Lunch, breaks, registration, networking and travel do not count. Only time spent receiving project management instruction does.
- **Non-project-management content.** In a general business, leadership or technical course, only the project management portion counts.
- **Live training from a non-approved provider completed on or after 1 December 2026.**
- **Project experience.** Leading projects counts towards the experience requirement, not the training hours.
- **Training you plan to do.** Hours must be complete before you submit the application.
Be cautious, too, with any provider that guarantees you will pass. PMI specifically advises care with such claims.

### How to count contact hours correctly
PMI's rule is simple: one hour of project management instruction equals one training hour. For example, PMI says a college course that meets for three hours a week for 15 weeks gives 45 hours. The worked examples below show how this applies to less tidy situations.

#### Worked example 1: a one-day classroom course
A course runs from 09:00 to 17:00. It includes a 60-minute lunch and two 15-minute breaks.
| Item | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Scheduled day | 8 hours |
| Less lunch | −1 hour |
| Less two breaks | −0.5 hours |
| **Instruction time to claim** | **6.5 hours** |
A three-day course with the same timetable gives 19.5 hours, not 24. Good providers state the instruction hours on the certificate; if yours shows only dates, work out the figure from the timetable and keep the timetable with your records.

#### Worked example 2: a university module with partial project management content
A module called Operations and Project Management meets for three hours a week for 12 weeks (36 hours). The syllabus shows that five of the 12 weeks covered project planning, scheduling, risk and project governance; the rest covered supply chain and operations.
| Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Total module time | 3 hours × 12 weeks = 36 hours |
| Weeks on project management | 5 |
| **Hours to claim** | **3 hours × 5 weeks = 15 hours** |
Keep the syllabus, because it is the document that shows which weeks were project management. A transcript alone usually shows only the module title.

#### Worked example 3: combining three sources to reach 35
**Priya** wants to apply in February 2027. She lists the training she already has, then fills the gap.
| Source | Format | Completed | Counts? | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Employer's two-day project management course (non-ATP) | Live | September 2026 | Yes, completed before 1 December 2026 | 13 |
| University module (project management weeks only) | Live, accredited university | 2021 | Yes, training does not expire | 15 |
| Self-paced online PMP course with end-of-course assessment | Self-paced | January 2027 | Yes, any provider for self-paced | 10 |
| **Total** |  |  |  | **38 hours** |
Priya now has 38 hours, comfortably above 35. Had she filled the gap with a live weekend workshop from a non-ATP provider in January 2027, those hours would not count. Building in a small margin above 35 protects you if an auditor decides part of a course was not project management.
Tip
Use a simple [training plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) or [project tracker](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) to log each course, its format, completion date, hours and where you saved the evidence.

### How to get your 35 contact hours: step by step
If you are starting from scratch or topping up existing training, follow this sequence.
1. **Confirm you meet the experience rule first.** Count your unique months of project leadership within the last 10 years against the 36, 48, 60 or 24 months your education requires. There is no point finishing training a year before you are eligible to apply, although the hours will not expire.
2. **Check whether you hold an active CAPM.** If you do, you do not need the 35 hours. If it has lapsed into its suspension period, renew it before you apply.
3. **Audit the training you already have.** List every project management course, university module and employer programme you have completed, with the hours of instruction and any evidence. Remember that live courses completed before 1 December 2026 keep their eligibility.
4. **Work out the gap.** Subtract your qualifying hours from 35, then add a small margin.
5. **Choose a format for the remaining hours.** For live training after 1 December 2026, choose a PMI Authorized Training Partner (use PMI's directory to check) or an eligible accredited programme. For self-paced training, check the course against PMI's criteria in the next section.
6. **Complete the course, including the final assessment, and download the certificate.** Save the course outline or syllabus with it.
7. **Record each course on your application.** Enter the provider, course title, hours and format, then submit once the total reaches 35. Keep all evidence until well after you pass, in case of audit.
Our guide on [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/) covers how the PMP fits into a wider career plan.

### Choosing a course format
Each route has different strengths. The right choice depends on how you learn, your budget, your deadline and whether your employer is paying. The table below is our summary; PMI's rules are as stated earlier.
| Format | Counts after 1 December 2026? | Strengths | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ATP live course (classroom or virtual) | Yes | PMI-developed content, PMP-certified instructors, structure and accountability, chance to ask questions | Fixed dates; usually the most expensive option |
| PMI PMP Exam Prep Course (self-paced) | Yes | Built by PMI around the outline; PMI says completion details can be applied to your application automatically | Needs self-discipline |
| Other self-paced online course | Yes, if it meets PMI's checks | Flexible and often low cost; wide choice | Quality varies; check the hours, assessment and certificate |
| Accredited university or GAC programme | Yes, for eligible programmes | Deep learning; a GAC degree also reduces the experience requirement to two years | Long and costly if taken only for the hours |
| Employer in-house live training | Only if delivered by an approved provider | Often free to you and tailored to your organisation | Non-ATP live sessions after 1 December 2026 do not count |

#### Questions to ask a provider before you pay
PMI's guidance on self-paced courses translates into a short checklist. A reputable provider can answer every question in writing.
1. Does the course give **formal project management instruction**, not just practice questions?
2. Is it **aligned to the current PMP Examination Content Outline** (the 2026 version, with People, Process and Business Environment domains)?
3. Does it **state the number of training hours** clearly?
4. Does it include an **end-of-course assessment**?
5. Will I receive a **certificate or completion record** showing my name, the provider, the course title, the hours and the completion date?
6. For live courses after 1 December 2026: **are you a PMI Authorized Training Partner?** Check the answer in PMI's ATP directory rather than relying on a logo.

#### Can you get the 35 hours free?
Sometimes. The most common no-cost routes are training you have already completed (old university modules or employer courses), employer-funded courses, and free self-paced courses that meet every point on the checklist above. Free webinars and chapter talks are useful for learning and for PDUs once certified, but they are rarely formal, assessed courses, so do not rely on them for the 35 hours. If budget is tight, compare the cost of a self-paced course with the value of having the hours properly documented.

### Using the CAPM instead of 35 hours
PMI states that an **active** Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM) certification waives the PMP training requirement. This is one reason many people take the CAPM early in their career and the PMP later.
- **Active CAPM:** waives the 35 hours.
- **Expired CAPM:** does not waive them.
- **CAPM in its suspension period:** renew it before you apply if you want to use the waiver.
- **You still need the experience.** The CAPM replaces the training only, not the 36 to 60 months of project leadership.
The CAPM itself needs 23 hours of project management education and no project experience. Our [CAPM certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) covers the exam and study plan.

#### Worked example: a CAPM holder moving to the PMP
**Sam** passed the CAPM in March 2024, holds a bachelor's degree and has led projects since January 2023. By March 2026 he has 38 months of qualifying experience, above the 36 he needs. His CAPM is active until March 2027, so he applies in late 2026, selects the CAPM option for training and needs no further course. Had he waited until his CAPM lapsed, he would have had to renew it or complete 35 hours first.
Tip
Even with the waiver, consider a PMP prep course. The CAPM covers fundamentals; the PMP tests judgement in scenario questions, so most candidates still benefit from structured preparation.

### Recording training on your application and passing an audit
PMI's online application asks you to list each course with its provider, title and number of hours, and to say whether it was live instructor-led or self-paced. You do **not** upload certificates or transcripts when you submit. PMI selects some applications for audit, and all training is subject to audit, so keep evidence for every course you list.
| Evidence to keep | Best for | What it should show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Completion certificate | Courses from training providers and ATPs | Your name, provider, course title, hours, completion date |
| Transcript plus syllabus | University and college courses | The module, dates and which topics were project management |
| Employer training record | In-house programmes | Course name, dates, hours and the trainer or provider |
| Course description or timetable | Any course where the certificate lacks hours | Instruction time, so you can justify the hours claimed |
If you are audited, the process described on PMI's site and in our [PMI guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/) works like this:
1. You are told your application has been selected before you pay the exam fee.
2. You have 90 days to send copies of your education certificate, signed confirmation of your project experience and your training certificates.
3. PMI reviews the documents, which it says takes about five to seven business days once everything is received.
4. If the audit is approved, you pay the exam fee and schedule your exam.
Audits are far easier when your records match what you entered. Store everything in one folder, named by course, and keep it until your certification is well established.

### Contact hours vs PDUs
Contact hours and PDUs are both measured in hours of learning, which is why they are often confused. They serve different purposes at different stages.
|  | Contact (training) hours | PDUs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Qualify you to apply for the exam | Maintain your certification after you pass |
| When earned | Before you submit your application | During each three-year certification cycle |
| How many | 35 for the PMP; 23 for the CAPM | 60 every three years for the PMP; 15 for the CAPM |
| What counts | Formal training aligned to the exam content outline | Education plus giving back to the profession, split across the Talent Triangle |
| Expiry | Do not expire | Count only towards the cycle in which they are earned (with limited carry-over) |
A course marketed as "35 PDUs" may or may not meet the training requirement; judge it against PMI's criteria.

### Common mistakes to avoid
- **Booking a live course from a non-approved provider that finishes after 1 December 2026.** Check ATP status in PMI's directory before you pay.
- **Claiming scheduled time instead of instruction time.** Remove breaks, lunch and admin from your count.
- **Claiming a whole module when only part was project management.** Keep the syllabus and claim only the relevant hours.
- **Relying on an expired CAPM.** Only an active CAPM waives the requirement.
- **Applying before the training is finished.** All 35 hours must be complete when you submit.
- **Assuming a "35 hours" label means the course qualifies.** PMI says it does not automatically.
- **Keeping no evidence.** You do not upload certificates, but you will need them if audited.
- **Treating the 35 hours as exam preparation.** Completing the hours does not mean you are ready to pass. Plan practice questions and revision on top.
Tip
Collect experience evidence at the same time. A [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/), [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) or [lessons learned log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) you produced helps you describe your projects accurately and supports an audit.

### After the 35 hours: next steps
Once your training and experience are in place, the rest of the process moves quickly:
- **Submit your application.** Complete the education, experience and training sections and submit.
- **Pay and schedule.** After approval, pay the exam fee. PMI says you then have one year from approval to take the exam, with up to three attempts in that year.
- **Know the exam.** The current exam has 180 questions in 240 minutes, with two 10-minute breaks, weighted People 33%, Process 41% and Business Environment 26%. You can sit it at a Pearson VUE test centre or online.
- **Plan for renewal.** After you pass, earn 60 PDUs every three years to keep the PMP active.
If you are also considering Agile credentials, compare them in our guide to [learning Agile and getting certified](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/). For the exam itself, see our [PMP study plan and exam guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the 35 contact hours for the PMP?**
They are the 35 hours of formal project management training PMI requires before you can apply for the PMP exam. The training must align with the current PMP Examination Content Outline and be completed before you submit your application. An active CAPM waives the requirement.

**Q: Do the 35 contact hours have to come from a PMI Authorized Training Partner?**
Only for live training completed from 1 December 2026, which must come from an ATP, a China Registered Education Provider or an eligible accredited higher-education programme, including GAC programmes. Self-paced courses can come from any organisation if they align with the current outline.

**Q: Does training I completed before 1 December 2026 still count?**
Yes. PMI says courses completed before 1 December 2026 remain eligible under the rules in place at the time, even if you apply after the change. Keep the completion certificate as evidence.

**Q: What if my live course finishes after 1 December 2026?**
PMI's protection applies to courses completed before 1 December 2026, so a live course from a non-approved provider that finishes on or after that date is unlikely to count. Finish before the date, choose an ATP, or make up the hours with a qualifying self-paced course.

**Q: Do PMP contact hours expire?**
No. PMI says qualifying project management training does not expire, so a course from several years ago can still count. Check it against the current outline so you know which topics to revise.

**Q: Can I get the 35 contact hours online?**
Yes. Self-paced online courses from any provider count if they give formal instruction aligned to the outline, state their hours, include an end-of-course assessment and issue a completion record. Live virtual classes count too, but from 1 December 2026 only from an approved provider.

**Q: Can I get the 35 contact hours for free?**
Sometimes, through training you have already completed, employer-funded courses or free self-paced courses that meet PMI's criteria. Webinars and chapter talks rarely qualify because they are not formal, assessed courses.

**Q: Does my degree count towards the 35 hours?**
Project management courses within a degree can count, but only the hours spent on project management topics. A degree does not count as 35 hours automatically. A degree from a GAC-accredited programme also reduces the experience requirement to two years.

**Q: Does the CAPM replace the 35 contact hours?**
An active CAPM waives the PMP training requirement. An expired CAPM does not, and a CAPM in its suspension period must be renewed first. You still need the project experience.

**Q: Can I combine several courses to reach 35 hours?**
Yes. PMI says training does not have to come from one course or provider. List each course separately on the application and keep evidence for each.

**Q: Do I need to upload certificates with my application?**
No. You list each course's provider, title, hours and format, but you only send certificates or transcripts if your application is selected for audit.

**Q: Can project experience replace the 35 hours?**
No. Training and experience are separate requirements. Only an active CAPM can replace the training hours.

**Q: Are contact hours the same as PDUs?**
No. Contact hours qualify you to apply for the exam; PDUs maintain your certification afterwards. The PMP needs 60 PDUs every three years.

**Q: Does Agile training count towards the 35 hours?**
Yes, if it is formal project management instruction aligned to the current PMP Examination Content Outline, which covers predictive, Agile and hybrid approaches.

# Assistant Project Manager: Duties, Skills and Career Path

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/assistant-project-manager/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What an assistant project manager does: duties, skills, salary factors, a sample job description, a worked example and a step-by-step path to PM.


## Assistant Project Manager: Duties, Skills and Career Path
An assistant project manager supports a project manager in planning and delivering a project and takes ownership of parts of it, such as the schedule, risk and issue logs, supplier follow-up, reporting or a whole workstream. The role sits between project coordinator and project manager and is one of the most common routes into project management. This guide covers the duties, skills, qualifications, pay, a sample job description, a worked example and a step-by-step plan to become a project manager.
- Published 4 October 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- An assistant project manager owns parts of a project's delivery under a project manager's direction, which goes further than the administrative focus of a coordinator.
- Core duties are schedule upkeep, progress tracking, risk and issue logs, reporting, supplier and team follow-up, budget support and, increasingly, a workstream of your own.
- The title is especially common in construction, engineering and large IT programmes, and duties vary by sector.
- Employers look for organisation, communication, scheduling and budgeting basics and comfort with project software. An entry-level certification such as the CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation or PMAI helps.
- To step up, own a workstream end to end, keep an evidence log of what you led and practise the decisions a project manager makes.
- Pay depends on country, sector and project size; compare current job adverts and official salary data rather than relying on one average.

### What is an assistant project manager?
**An assistant project manager (APM) is a project professional who helps a project manager plan, track and deliver a project, and who is responsible for defined parts of it, such as the schedule, risk log, procurement follow-up or a workstream.** They make decisions within agreed limits and escalate anything that affects scope, cost, time or quality beyond those limits.
Organisations usually add an assistant project manager when a project is too large or busy for one person to manage alone: several workstreams, many suppliers, a busy site or a demanding reporting cycle. It is also a deliberate development role, giving someone a structured way to learn from an experienced project manager before running projects themselves.

#### Assistant project manager vs project manager assistant
The two titles sound alike but usually mean different jobs. A **project manager assistant** (or project administrator) provides administrative support: diaries, minutes, document control and travel. An **assistant project manager** does part of the management work: tracking progress, managing risks and issues, coordinating suppliers and sometimes leading a workstream. Always read the duties in the job advert rather than relying on the title.

### Assistant project manager vs project coordinator vs project manager
The three roles overlap, and employers draw the lines differently. This table shows the typical pattern.
|  | Project coordinator | Assistant project manager | Project manager |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main focus | Administration, scheduling and communication | Supporting delivery and owning parts of the project | Accountable for the whole project |
| Owns | Trackers, minutes, document control | Schedule upkeep, logs, a workstream or sub-project | Scope, budget, schedule, risks and stakeholders |
| Decision-making | Limited | Some, within agreed limits | Full, within the charter and tolerances |
| Typical reports to | Project manager or PMO | Project manager | Sponsor, programme manager or PMO |
| Typical next step | Assistant or junior project manager | Project manager | Senior project manager or programme manager |
Our guide to the [project coordinator](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-coordinator/) role covers the level below in detail, and [project manager roles and responsibilities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-roles-and-responsibilities/) covers the level above.

#### Assistant, junior and associate project managers
Junior project manager and associate project manager are often used for a similar level. The usual difference is that a junior or associate PM runs small projects of their own with light oversight, while an assistant PM works inside a larger project under one project manager. In practice the titles overlap heavily, and pay bands are often the same, so judge a role by its duties and decision rights.

#### Decision rights: what an assistant PM decides, recommends or escalates
The clearest difference between the roles is decision rights. Agree them with your project manager in the first week; the examples below are illustrative.
| Decide alone | Recommend to the project manager | Escalate immediately |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Updating task dates within the workstream's float | Moving a milestone | Any slip to a key milestone or contractual date |
| Chasing suppliers and booking meetings | Approving a change request | Safety, legal or data protection concerns |
| Logging and assigning low-impact issues | Spending contingency | Forecast overspend beyond tolerance |
| Formatting and issuing the status report | Changing a red/amber/green rating | Stakeholder complaints at senior level |

### Assistant project manager duties and responsibilities
Duties vary by employer, but most fall into seven areas.

#### Planning and scheduling
- Maintain the [project schedule](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/), update progress and flag slipped tasks.
- Help build work breakdowns and estimates with the team.
- Track milestones and dependencies, and check the impact of late tasks.

#### Tracking and reporting
- Collect progress updates and draft the weekly [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
- Prepare packs for progress meetings and steering groups.
- Keep dashboards and trackers current.

#### Risks, issues and changes
- Maintain the [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) or [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/): record items, chase owners and update ratings.
- Log change requests and assess their impact for the project manager; see [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).

#### Budget and procurement
- Raise purchase orders, track invoices and reconcile actual costs against the budget.
- Follow up supplier deliveries and support tendering; see [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/).

#### Stakeholders and meetings
- Run routine progress meetings for a workstream, issue agendas and record actions.
- Act as day-to-day contact for suppliers and team members.

#### Owning a workstream
As you gain experience, the project manager will hand you a workstream or small sub-project to run end to end, such as fit-out of one floor, a data migration or a supplier contract. This is the duty that does most to prepare you for promotion.

#### Documentation and closure
- Keep project records and document control in order.
- Help with handover, snagging or acceptance and [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/), including lessons learned.

### How the role differs by sector
The title is used in many industries, but the emphasis changes.
| Sector | Typical emphasis | Common extra requirements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Construction | Procurement packages, subcontractor coordination, programme updates, RFIs, site meetings, cost reports, snagging | Site safety training; knowledge of contracts and drawings |
| IT and software | Release plans, test and cut-over plans, vendor follow-up, RAID logs, Agile ceremonies support | Familiarity with Jira or similar tools and with Agile ways of working |
| Engineering and manufacturing | Technical documentation, supplier quality, change control, test schedules | Engineering background is often preferred |
| Agencies and creative | Briefs, timelines, client approvals, resource booking | Strong client communication |
| Public sector | Governance papers, risk reporting, procurement rules, benefits tracking | Knowledge of formal methods such as PRINCE2 |

#### Assistant project managers in construction
On construction projects the assistant project manager usually works for the contractor or the client's project manager, focusing on the commercial and coordination side: procurement packages, subcontractor programmes, information requests, cost reports and handover. That makes it different from a site manager, who runs day-to-day work and safety on site, and from a project engineer, a title used by many contractors for a technical coordination role at a similar level. Titles vary by country and company, so compare the duties.
Construction is where the title is most common. If that is your route, read our guide to the [construction project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/construction-project-manager/) role. For technology projects, see [IT project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/it-project-manager/).

### A typical week
This illustrative week is for an assistant project manager on a medium-sized office refurbishment with five suppliers.
| Day | Main activities |
| --- | --- |
| Monday | Update the schedule from Friday's progress; flag two slipped tasks to the PM; issue this week's look-ahead to suppliers |
| Tuesday | Chase the flooring supplier's delivery date; update the procurement tracker; check three invoices against purchase orders |
| Wednesday | Run the weekly progress meeting for the mechanical and electrical workstream; record actions and update the RAID log |
| Thursday | Draft the status report; review risk ratings with owners; prepare a change request impact note for the PM |
| Friday | Walk the site or review the latest outputs; agree next week's priorities with the PM; note lessons and update your evidence log |
A [meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/) and a [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) cover most of the paperwork in a week like this.
Tip
Build a 20-minute daily routine: check overnight emails for anything that changes a date, update the tracker, then decide the three follow-ups that matter most today. Small, regular updates beat a Friday afternoon scramble.

### Skills an assistant project manager needs
Employers hire assistant project managers for reliability first and potential second. These are the skills that matter most and how to build them.
| Skill | Why it matters | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organisation and follow-through | Most of the job is keeping many small commitments moving | Use one task system and review it daily |
| Written communication | Status reports, minutes and emails shape how others see the project | Draft the status report every week and ask for feedback |
| Scheduling basics | You will update plans and test the impact of delays | Learn dependencies, float and the critical path |
| Budget basics | You track costs, invoices and forecasts | Reconcile actuals to budget monthly; learn simple variance |
| Risk awareness | Spotting problems early is what makes an APM valuable | Ask "what could stop this?" in every meeting |
| Stakeholder handling | Suppliers and team members respond to clear, polite persistence | Agree how and when each person wants updates |
| Tool fluency | Most teams run projects in work management software | Learn your employer's tool deeply, plus spreadsheets |
| Judgement about escalation | Knowing what to raise, when, is how you earn more responsibility | Use the decision rights table and review misses with your PM |
See our full guide to [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/) for a wider view.

### Qualifications and certifications
There is no single required qualification. Many employers ask for a degree, often in a related field such as construction management, engineering, business or IT, but experience as a coordinator, in a trade or in operations is often accepted instead. An entry-level certification shows you understand the fundamentals and are serious about the career.
| Certification | Body | Experience needed | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CAPM | PMI | None (secondary diploma plus 23 hours of project management education) | A broad, internationally recognised foundation |
| PRINCE2 Foundation | PeopleCert (AXELOS) | None | UK, European and public-sector employers |
| APM Project Fundamentals Qualification (PFQ) | Association for Project Management | None | UK employers that use APM's body of knowledge |
| Scrum certifications (CSM, PSM I) | Scrum Alliance, Scrum.org | None | Agile and software teams |
| PMAI | Neural Project Institute | None | An affordable, modern grounding including AI in project management |
| PMP (later) | PMI | 3–5 years leading projects plus 35 contact hours or CAPM | The next step once you lead projects |
Our [CAPM certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) covers the exam (150 questions in 180 minutes) and a study plan. For a comparison of all the main options, see [project management certifications](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/).

### Assistant project manager salary
Pay varies widely, so treat any single average with care. The main factors are:
- **Country and region.** Large cities usually pay more, with higher living costs.
- **Sector.** Construction, engineering, energy and technology often pay more than non-profit or public-sector roles.
- **Project size and complexity.** Larger budgets and more suppliers usually mean higher pay.
- **Experience and credentials.** Moving from coordinator-level duties to owning workstreams makes the biggest difference.
For context in the US, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median annual wage of $102,320 for project management specialists in May 2025, with employment projected to grow 7% from 2025 to 2035. That category includes experienced project managers, so it is not a figure for assistant roles, which sit lower on the ladder. PMI's Earning Power salary survey (14th edition, November 2025, 21 countries) found that PMP holders reported median salaries 17% higher than those without it, which is relevant once you step up.
For a realistic figure, compare 15–20 current job adverts in your area and sector, and check national salary surveys from professional bodies and official statistics.

### Sample assistant project manager job description
Use this illustrative job description as a starting point if you are hiring, or as a checklist of what to evidence if you are applying.

#### Role summary
The assistant project manager supports the project manager in delivering [project type] on time, within budget and to the required quality. You will maintain the schedule and project controls, coordinate suppliers and team members, and lead a workstream under the project manager's direction.

#### Responsibilities
- Maintain the project schedule and report progress against milestones.
- Maintain the RAID log, chase owners and escalate issues in line with agreed tolerances.
- Prepare weekly status reports and meeting packs.
- Coordinate suppliers and subcontractors, track deliveries and support procurement.
- Track costs, purchase orders and invoices against the budget.
- Lead a defined workstream, including its meetings, actions and reporting.
- Support handover, closure and lessons learned.

#### Requirements
- Experience as a project coordinator or in a related project, technical or operational role.
- Working knowledge of scheduling, budgeting and risk management.
- Strong written and verbal communication; confident with suppliers and stakeholders.
- Proficiency with project management software and spreadsheets.
- A degree or relevant experience; CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation or similar is an advantage.

### Worked example: handling a supplier delay
This illustrative example shows the judgement that separates an assistant project manager from a coordinator. You are the APM on an office refurbishment. On Tuesday the flooring supplier tells you its delivery will be eight working days late.
1. **Confirm the facts.** Get the new date in writing and ask what is causing the delay and how confident the supplier is.
2. **Check the schedule impact.** Flooring precedes furniture installation, which has two days of float. An eight-day delay therefore pushes the furniture milestone by six days and the client move-in date is at risk.
3. **Look for options within your authority.** Ask whether part of the order can be delivered on time for the first two floors, and whether the furniture supplier can start on those floors first.
4. **Escalate with a recommendation.** Because a key milestone is affected, you escalate the same day. Your note gives the facts, the impact (six days on the furniture milestone, move-in at risk) and two options: phased delivery and floor-by-floor installation at no extra cost, or an alternative supplier at an estimated extra £4,000 with a four-day saving.
5. **Record it.** Log the issue in the RAID log, raise a change request if the PM chooses the second option and update the schedule once a decision is made.
6. **Close the loop.** Tell the affected suppliers and the team, confirm the new plan in the next status report and note the lesson: confirm delivery dates in writing two weeks before need.
The PM approves the phased option. Move-in is protected, and you have evidence for your log: "identified a supplier delay, assessed schedule impact and proposed a phased delivery that protected the move-in date at no extra cost".

### How to become an assistant project manager
Most people reach the role from one of four starting points.
| Starting point | Typical route |
| --- | --- |
| Project coordinator or administrator | Take on more ownership (a workstream, the RAID log, supplier management), then apply internally or externally |
| Graduate | Graduate scheme or junior role in construction, engineering or IT, often with a related degree |
| Trade or technical specialist | Move from site, engineering or technical work into project support, using your technical knowledge as an advantage |
| Career changer | Use transferable experience from operations, events, marketing or administration, plus an entry-level certification |
1. Learn the fundamentals: project phases, scheduling, budgeting, risk and stakeholder management.
2. Take an entry-level certification such as the CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation, APM PFQ or PMAI.
3. Get hands-on with a work management tool and spreadsheets.
4. Build evidence: volunteer to run small projects at work or in the community and record what you delivered.
5. Rewrite your CV around outcomes, using project language.
6. Apply for assistant, junior or associate project manager roles, and ask about internal moves.
Read [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/) for the full career route.

### How to step up from assistant project manager to project manager
Promotion usually comes from showing you can already do the job. This illustrative 12-month plan works in most organisations.
| Months | Focus | Evidence to collect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–3 | Agree decision rights; master the schedule, RAID log and reporting | Status reports issued; issues caught early |
| 4–6 | Own a workstream end to end, including its meetings and budget | Workstream delivered on time; costs reconciled |
| 7–9 | Lead a supplier or stakeholder relationship; present at a steering meeting | Decisions you shaped; feedback from stakeholders |
| 10–12 | Run a small project or cover for the PM during leave | A complete project, from plan to closure |
Keep an evidence log throughout: project, your role, what you led, the outcome and the lesson. It feeds your promotion case and, later, a PMP application. PMP eligibility requires 3, 4 or 5 years of project experience within the last 10 years depending on your education (2 years with a GAC-accredited degree), plus 35 contact hours or the CAPM. Experience counts when you led and directed project work, so describe what you led, not what you assisted with. From 1 December 2026, live PMP training must come from a PMI Authorized Training Partner.
Tip
Shadow your project manager in steering meetings. Seeing how decisions are framed and escalated is one of the fastest ways to learn the judgement the next role needs.
See our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) for the current exam and application process.

### Your first 30 days as an assistant project manager
The first month sets how much responsibility you are given. Use it to understand the project, agree your role and become reliable.
1. **Week 1: Learn the project.** Read the business case or charter, schedule, budget, RAID log and the last three status reports. List what you do not understand and ask.
2. **Week 1: Agree your role.** Sit down with your project manager and agree your duties, decision rights, reporting routine and how they want to be updated.
3. **Week 2: Meet the people.** Introduce yourself to suppliers, team leads and key stakeholders. Ask each what they need from the project team and what usually goes wrong.
4. **Week 2: Take over the routines.** Start running the schedule update, RAID log and status report draft, with the PM reviewing your work.
5. **Week 3: Find one improvement.** Fix something small but visible, such as an out-of-date tracker, a confusing report or missing action owners.
6. **Week 4: Review.** Ask your PM what is going well and what to change, and agree what you will own next, ideally a workstream.

### CV bullets that show impact
Hiring managers want to see what changed because of you. Turn duties into outcomes.
| Weak (duty) | Strong (outcome) |
| --- | --- |
| Responsible for the RAID log | Maintained the RAID log for a £3m fit-out; flagged a supplier risk six weeks early, avoiding a two-week delay |
| Prepared status reports | Issued weekly status reports to a 12-person steering group; introduced a one-page format adopted across the PMO |
| Liaised with suppliers | Coordinated five suppliers and tracked 40 purchase orders with no late payments |
| Helped with the project | Led the data migration workstream (3 people, 10 weeks), delivered on schedule |
The figures above are illustrative; use your own, and be ready to explain each one in an interview.

### Assistant project manager interview questions
Expect a mix of practical and behavioural questions. Prepare a specific example for each.
| Question | What a good answer shows |
| --- | --- |
| Tell me about a time you spotted a problem early. | Risk awareness, initiative and clear escalation |
| How do you keep a schedule up to date? | A routine, an understanding of dependencies and float |
| A supplier misses a date. What do you do? | Facts first, impact assessment, options, escalation with a recommendation |
| How do you decide what to escalate? | Agreed tolerances and good judgement about impact |
| How do you handle a team member who keeps missing deadlines? | A direct but respectful conversation, support and follow-up |
| Which project tools have you used, and how? | Practical fluency, not just a list of names |
| Walk me through a status report you wrote. | Ability to summarise, highlight risks and ask for decisions |
| How would you reconcile invoices against a budget? | Basic cost control and attention to detail |
| Why do you want to be a project manager? | Motivation and a realistic view of the role |

### Common mistakes new assistant project managers make
- **Being a messenger, not a manager.** Passing on problems without impact or options. Always bring a recommendation.
- **Escalating too late.** Hoping a slip will recover. Raise it as soon as a key date is at risk.
- **Escalating everything.** Agree decision rights so you can act within them.
- **Updating documents without reading them.** The RAID log is a management tool; ask what each item means for the project.
- **Staying in the background.** Ask to run meetings and present updates.
- **Not recording achievements.** Without an evidence log, promotion cases and PMP applications are much harder.
- **Copying last week's status report.** If the report never changes, people stop reading it. Lead with what changed, what is at risk and what decision is needed.
- **Owning tasks instead of outcomes.** Closing actions is good; making sure they achieved their purpose is better. Check that a chased delivery actually arrived and was right.
- **Neglecting relationships with suppliers and site or delivery teams.** Persistence works best when people trust you. Be clear, polite and consistent, and thank people when they deliver.

### Tools assistant project managers use
You will spend much of your day in project software, so fluency is a real advantage.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated work management platform, is a strong all-round choice for schedules, Gantt charts, dashboards, request forms and cross-team reporting.
- **[Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/)** suits organisations that like spreadsheet-style planning and reporting.
- **[Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/)** works well in Microsoft 365 organisations.
- **Asana** and **monday.com** are popular for cross-team task tracking and visual workflows.
- **Spreadsheets** remain essential for cost tracking, procurement logs and quick analysis.
If your employer lets you choose, start with ready-made structures such as a [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) and a [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/), then move them into your team's tool.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does an assistant project manager do?**
Supports the project manager by maintaining the schedule, RAID log and reports, coordinating suppliers and team members, tracking costs and, increasingly, leading a workstream within agreed limits.

**Q: Is assistant project manager an entry-level job?**
Often it is a step above entry level, after a coordinator, administrator or technical role, but some employers hire graduates directly, especially in construction and engineering.

**Q: Is an assistant project manager higher than a project coordinator?**
Usually, yes. Coordinators focus on administration and communication; assistant project managers own parts of delivery and make more decisions. Titles vary, so compare the duties.

**Q: What is the difference between an assistant project manager and a project manager assistant?**
A project manager assistant provides administrative support. An assistant project manager does part of the management work, such as tracking, risk management and leading a workstream.

**Q: What qualifications does an assistant project manager need?**
Employers often ask for a degree or relevant experience. An entry-level certification such as the CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation, APM PFQ or PMAI strengthens an application.

**Q: Do you need a degree to be an assistant project manager?**
Not always. Many employers accept coordinator, trade or operational experience instead, although some sectors, such as engineering, prefer a related degree.

**Q: How much does an assistant project manager earn?**
It depends on country, sector, project size and experience. Compare current job adverts and salary surveys for your market; broad official figures for project management include experienced project managers.

**Q: How long does it take to go from assistant project manager to project manager?**
It varies by employer, often one to three years. Owning a workstream, running a small project and keeping an evidence log speed it up.

**Q: Does assistant project manager experience count towards the PMP?**
Experience counts when you led and directed project work, such as running a workstream. Describe what you led, and check PMI's current rules before applying.

**Q: What skills does an assistant project manager need?**
Organisation, written communication, scheduling and budgeting basics, risk awareness, stakeholder handling, tool fluency and good judgement about what to escalate.

**Q: What does an assistant project manager do in construction?**
Supports the project manager with procurement packages, subcontractor coordination, programme updates, information requests, site meetings, cost reports and snagging.

**Q: What certification is best for an assistant project manager?**
The CAPM is a widely recognised starting point; PRINCE2 Foundation or APM PFQ suit UK and public-sector employers; Scrum certifications suit Agile teams. The PMP comes later.

**Q: What tools should an assistant project manager learn?**
A work management platform such as Wrike, Smartsheet, Asana or monday.com, plus spreadsheets and the reporting tools your employer uses.

**Q: Is assistant project manager a good job?**
For people who want to manage projects, it is one of the best learning roles: you see the whole project, build evidence and learn from an experienced PM. The trade-off is that you have responsibility without full authority, so agree your decision rights early.

**Q: What comes after assistant project manager?**
Usually project manager, then [senior project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/senior-project-manager/) or programme manager. Some move into PMO, [technical project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/technical-project-manager/) or product roles.

# Budget at Completion (BAC): Definition, Formula and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/budget-at-completion/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What budget at completion (BAC) means in earned value management, how it is calculated, how it differs from EAC and the project budget, with examples.


## Budget at Completion (BAC): Definition, Formula and Example
Budget at completion (BAC) is the total planned budget for all the work in a project, or in a control account or work package. It equals the cost baseline and is the figure that earned value, forecasts and variances are measured against.
- Published 28 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- BAC is the cost baseline: the total planned budget for the work.
- It includes contingency but excludes management reserve.
- EV, EAC, VAC and TCPI are all calculated from BAC.
- BAC changes only through formal change control.

### How BAC is calculated
BAC is the sum of the budgets for all work packages plus the contingency reserve. It does **not** include management reserve.
| Component | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Design | $40,000 |
| Build | $90,000 |
| Test | $30,000 |
| Deploy and train | $20,000 |
| Contingency reserve | $20,000 |
| **BAC (cost baseline)** | **$200,000** |
| Management reserve (excluded) | $15,000 |
| Total project budget | $215,000 |

### How BAC is used
- **Earned value:** EV = percent complete x BAC. At 35% complete, EV = 0.35 x 200,000 = $70,000.
- **Forecasts:** EAC = BAC / CPI. With CPI 0.8235, EAC = $242,857.
- **Variance at completion:** VAC = BAC - EAC = 200,000 - 242,857 = -$42,857.
- **TCPI:** (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) shows the efficiency needed to finish within BAC.
- **Percent spent:** AC / BAC = 85,000 / 200,000 = 42.5%, compared with 35% complete.

### BAC vs related terms
| Term | Meaning | Changes when? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BAC | Planned total budget for the work | Only through approved changes |
| [EAC](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/) | Forecast total cost | Every reporting period |
| ETC | Forecast cost of remaining work | Every reporting period |
| [Project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) | BAC plus management reserve | Through approved changes |

### When BAC changes
BAC is a baseline, so it should only change through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/): for example, when approved scope is added, or when management reserve is released for new in-scope work. Changing BAC simply because costs are running high hides the real performance.

### Tips
- Make sure the sum of control account budgets equals BAC.
- Keep BAC fixed between approved changes so trends are meaningful.
- Report BAC and EAC side by side so the forecast gap is obvious.
- Record every baseline change with its reason and date.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is budget at completion?**
The total budget planned for all the project's work, equal to the cost baseline. It is written BAC.

**Q: How do you calculate BAC?**
Add up the budgets for all work packages and the contingency reserve. Management reserve is excluded.

**Q: Does BAC include management reserve?**
No. Management reserve is outside the cost baseline; adding it to BAC gives the total project budget.

**Q: What is the difference between BAC and EAC?**
BAC is what the work was planned to cost. EAC is the current forecast of what it will actually cost.

**Q: Can BAC change during a project?**
Only through approved changes, such as added scope. It should not be changed just to hide an overrun.

**Q: How is BAC used to calculate earned value?**
EV = percent of work complete x BAC. If BAC is $200,000 and the work is 35% done, EV is $70,000.

**Q: How is BAC used to calculate VAC?**
Variance at completion, BAC - EAC. A negative value is the expected overrun at the end.

**Q: Is BAC the same as the project budget?**
Not quite. BAC is the cost baseline; the project budget adds management reserve.

**Q: Does BAC include contingency reserve?**
Yes. Contingency for identified risks is part of the cost baseline and therefore of BAC.

**Q: Can BAC be calculated for part of a project?**
Yes. Each control account and work package has its own BAC, and they add up to the project BAC.
