# Capacity Planning in Project Management: Steps and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Capacity planning in project management explained: formulas, step-by-step process, worked examples, lead/lag/match strategies, tools and common mistakes.


## Capacity Planning in Project Management: Steps and Example
Capacity planning in project management is the process of comparing the work your projects and day-to-day operations will demand with the productive time and skills your people can actually supply, so you can spot shortfalls before they delay delivery. This guide gives you the formulas, a step-by-step process, three worked examples and the decisions to make when demand and capacity do not match.
- Published 30 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Capacity planning compares demand (hours of work needed) with productive capacity (hours people can really give) for a team, skill or portfolio over a set period.
- Productive capacity = people x hours x weeks, minus leave and holidays, multiplied by a productive-time factor for meetings, admin and support.
- Plan by skill or role, not by headcount: a surplus of testers does not cancel out a shortage of developers.
- Include business-as-usual work and weight pipeline projects by their likelihood, or the plan will look better than reality.
- Do not plan to 100%. Keep a buffer, often 10-15% of productive capacity, for urgent work and estimating error.
- Review the plan on a fixed cadence: monthly for portfolios, every sprint or fortnight for teams.

### What is capacity planning in project management?
**Capacity planning** is the process of estimating how much productive work a team, department or organisation can deliver in a period, comparing it with the work requested, and acting on the difference. It answers one question before work starts: do we have enough of the right people, at the right time, to deliver what we have promised?
It works on two sides of a balance:
- **Supply (capacity):** the hours of productive time available, by person, role or skill, after leave, holidays and non-project work are taken out.
- **Demand:** the hours of work required by approved projects, likely future projects and the business-as-usual work that never goes away.
It looks weeks, months or years ahead and works with teams, roles and portfolios rather than individual tasks. Typical questions: can we start this project next month, which skill runs out first, and do we need to hire, contract or say no? Once capacity planning confirms the work fits, [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) assigns named people to specific tasks and [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) sets the dates.

### Capacity, demand, allocation and utilisation
These terms are often used loosely. Agreeing what each one means is the first step to a capacity plan people trust.
| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gross capacity | Total contracted hours for the period | 5 people x 40 hours x 4 weeks = 800 hours |
| Availability | Gross capacity minus leave, public holidays and training | 800 - 40 hours of leave = 760 hours |
| Productive capacity | The part of available time that can go on planned work, after meetings, admin and support | 760 x 80% = 608 hours |
| Demand | Hours of work requested by projects and business-as-usual activity | 680 hours across two projects and routine requests |
| Allocation | Which work is assigned to which person or team | Ana: 24 hours a week on Project A |
| Utilisation | Allocated or demanded hours divided by capacity, as a percentage | 680 / 608 = 112% |
| Capacity gap | Demand minus productive capacity; positive means a shortfall | 680 - 608 = 72 hours short |

#### Capacity planning vs resource planning vs resource allocation
The three activities overlap and the names vary between organisations, but the distinction below is the most useful in practice.
|  | Capacity planning | Resource planning | Resource allocation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main question | Do we have enough of each skill for all the work we want to do? | What resources does this project need, and when? | Who exactly does which task? |
| Scope | Team, department or portfolio | One project or programme | One project or team |
| Horizon | Months to years | Life of the project | Days to weeks |
| Unit | Hours or FTE by role or skill | Roles, people, equipment, materials | Named people and hours per task |
| Typical owner | PMO, resource manager, functional heads | Project manager | Project manager or team lead |
| Output | Gap analysis and decisions: start, delay, hire, cut | Resource plan and requirements | Assignments in the schedule |
When individual people are overloaded inside an approved plan, the fix is [resource levelling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/), which moves tasks within float or extends the schedule. Capacity planning works one level up and decides how much work should enter the system in the first place. For a wider view of people, equipment and materials, see our guide to [project resources](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-resources/).

#### Capacity planning and Agile teams
Agile teams turn the problem round: the team is fixed, so they ask how much work fits into its capacity each sprint, using availability and past velocity. Portfolio-level planning still decides which teams work on which initiatives. See our guide to [agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) for the sprint-level formula.

### Why capacity planning matters
Most organisations approve projects one at a time, each with a plausible plan. Trouble starts when those plans all draw on the same specialists in the same months. Capacity planning helps you:
- **Set realistic dates**, checked against the hours actually available.
- **Protect people from overload**, which shows up as long hours, then mistakes and resignations.
- **Find skill shortages early**, while there is time to recruit, train or contract.
- **Make portfolio decisions on evidence**: what can start now and what must wait.
- **Reduce multitasking and budget accurately**, since capacity converts directly into cost.
Skipping it rarely causes a single dramatic failure. Instead, projects all run a little late and shared experts become bottlenecks. Our guide to [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) covers the day-to-day side.

### Strategic, tactical and operational capacity planning
Capacity planning happens at three levels. Each has a different horizon, level of detail and owner, and they should feed each other.
| Level | Horizon | Unit of planning | Typical decisions | Usual owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strategic | 1-3 years | FTE by role or capability | Hiring plans, new teams, outsourcing, building a capability | Leadership, HR, portfolio board |
| Tactical | 1-12 months, usually a quarter | Hours or FTE by skill, per month | Which projects start, sequencing, contractors, training | PMO, resource managers |
| Operational | 1-6 weeks | Hours by person, per week or sprint | Who works on what, rebalancing, short-term overtime | Project managers, team leads |
This guide concentrates on the tactical level, but the same method scales up and down.

### Capacity planning formulas
You need only a handful of formulas. Use the same period (week, month or quarter) for every figure in the calculation.
| Measure | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Gross capacity | Number of people x contracted hours per week x weeks in the period |
| Available capacity | Gross capacity - (leave + public holidays + planned training) |
| Productive capacity | Available capacity x productive-time factor |
| Total demand | Committed project hours + business-as-usual hours + (pipeline hours x probability) |
| Capacity gap | Total demand - productive capacity |
| Utilisation | Total demand / productive capacity x 100 |
| Gap in FTE | Capacity gap / productive hours one FTE supplies in the period |
Tip
**Productive capacity = (people x hours x weeks - leave and holidays) x productive-time factor.** Compare demand with this figure, never with contracted hours.
Calculate separately for each role that matters; decisions are made skill by skill. Converting gaps into [full-time equivalents (FTE)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/full-time-equivalent-fte/) makes them easier to discuss: "1.3 developers short" is clearer than "378 hours short".

### How to do capacity planning step by step
This process works for a single team or a whole portfolio. The first cycle takes longest; after that it is a regular update.
1. **Set the scope and horizon**, for example one department for the next quarter in monthly buckets.
2. **Define the roles or skills to plan**, such as developers, testers and analysts. A [skills matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) shows who can cover more than one role.
3. **Calculate gross capacity** by role from actual contracts, so part-timers count at their real hours.
4. **Subtract known absence**: leave, public holidays, training and long-term absence.
5. **Apply a productive-time factor**, derived from timesheets where you have them.
6. **Collect demand from every source**, by role and month: committed projects, business-as-usual and weighted pipeline projects.
7. **Compare demand with capacity** and flag every role and period above your target utilisation.
8. **Decide how to close gaps** and record the decision and who made it.
9. **Publish a one-page view** for project managers, functional heads and the portfolio board, with assumptions.
10. **Review on a fixed cadence** and compare planned with actual utilisation to improve your factors.

#### Estimating demand
Demand is where most capacity plans go wrong, because it is easy to count projects and forget everything else. Build it from four sources:
| Demand source | How to estimate it | Common trap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Committed projects | Remaining effort by role and month from each project's estimate or schedule | Using the original estimate instead of the remaining work |
| Pipeline projects | Rough effort by role x probability of approval | Leaving them out until they are approved, then discovering there is no room |
| Business-as-usual | Average hours from the last 3-6 months of timesheets or ticket data | Assuming it is zero because it is not in a project plan |
| Support and incidents | Historical average plus a margin for peaks | Ignoring on-call rotas and release support |
Remaining effort should come from the people closest to the work; see [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/) for three-point and bottom-up techniques.

#### Choosing a productive-time factor
Meetings, email, admin, line management, support and context switching all take a share of contracted time. The best source for your factor is your own timesheets: hours booked to planned work divided by hours available over a few months. Without data, many teams start around 70-80% for specialists and lower for leads and managers, then adjust. Treat these as starting assumptions, not benchmarks.

### Worked example 1: one month for a team of five
This is an illustrative example. A design team has five people working 40-hour weeks. The month has four working weeks. Planned leave totals 40 hours, and timesheets show about 20% of time goes on meetings, admin and support, so the productive-time factor is 80%.
| Step | Calculation | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gross capacity | 5 people x 40 h x 4 weeks | 800 |
| Less leave | 800 - 40 | 760 |
| Productive capacity | 760 x 80% | 608 |
| Demand source | Hours |
| --- | --- |
| Project A (website redesign) | 320 |
| Project B (brand refresh) | 240 |
| Business-as-usual requests | 120 |
| **Total demand** | **680** |
Demand of 680 hours exceeds productive capacity of 608 hours by **72 hours**, so utilisation is 680 / 608 = 112%, roughly 12% over. Expressed in FTE, one designer supplies 160 x 80% = 128 productive hours a month, so the gap is 72 / 128 = **0.56 FTE**.
The team lead takes three options to the head of marketing:
- Move 72 hours of Project B into next month, delaying the brand refresh by about two weeks.
- Bring in a freelance designer for about two weeks to cover the shortfall.
- Pause lower-priority business-as-usual requests for the month, with an agreed list of what waits.
Without the numbers the team would simply have worked late and missed some dates. With them, the business chooses the trade-off.

### Worked example 2: a quarterly skill-based capacity plan
This example is also illustrative. A PMO is planning the next quarter for an IT delivery team of 11 people: 6 developers, 3 testers and 2 business analysts. The quarter has 12 working weeks after public holidays, the standard week is 37.5 hours, and each person averages 1.5 weeks of planned leave, leaving 10.5 available weeks each. Timesheets give different productive-time factors by role.

#### Step 1: productive capacity by role
| Role | People | Available hours (people x 37.5 x 10.5) | Productive factor | Productive capacity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Developers | 6 | 2,362.5 | 75% | 1,772 |
| Testers | 3 | 1,181.3 | 80% | 945 |
| Business analysts | 2 | 787.5 | 70% | 551 |
| **Total** | **11** | **4,331.3** |  | **3,268** |

#### Step 2: demand by role
Two projects are approved. A third, Project Gamma, is in the pipeline and the portfolio board puts its chance of approval at 60%, so its hours are weighted by 0.6.
| Demand source | Developers | Testers | Business analysts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project Alpha (CRM upgrade, committed) | 900 | 300 | 150 |
| Project Beta (mobile app, committed) | 700 | 250 | 200 |
| Business-as-usual and support | 250 | 100 | 50 |
| Project Gamma (500 / 200 / 150 hours x 60%) | 300 | 120 | 90 |
| **Total demand** | **2,150** | **770** | **490** |

#### Step 3: compare and calculate the gaps
| Role | Productive capacity | Demand | Gap (hours) | Utilisation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Developers | 1,772 | 2,150 | 378 short | 121% |
| Testers | 945 | 770 | 175 spare | 81% |
| Business analysts | 551 | 490 | 61 spare | 89% |
| **Whole team** | **3,268** | **3,410** | **142 short** | **104%** |
Looked at as a whole, the team is only 4% over capacity, which might pass as "tight but manageable". By role, developers are 21% over while testers have spare time. One developer supplies 37.5 x 10.5 x 75% = about 295 productive hours a quarter, so the developer gap is 378 / 295 = **1.3 FTE**. Even without Project Gamma, developers would be 78 hours short (about 0.26 FTE), so the shortage is real and not just a pipeline risk.
This is why planning by headcount fails: "11 people, 104% loaded" invites "work a bit harder", while "1.3 developers short from week one" invites a decision.

### What to do when demand exceeds capacity
You have a limited set of levers, each with a cost. The right mix depends on priorities, budget and how long the gap lasts.
| Option | How it works | Best when | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reprioritise | Stop, pause or defer lower-value work | The portfolio has more ideas than capacity, which is common | Someone's project waits; needs a clear decision-maker |
| Reschedule | Move the start or phases to a period with spare capacity | Dates are flexible or the peak is short | Benefits arrive later |
| Reduce scope | Cut or postpone lower-priority features | Some requirements are nice to have | Less delivered in this release |
| Rebalance skills | Move work to roles with spare time or cross-trained staff | Skills overlap, for example testers automating tests | Lower productivity at first; needs training |
| Contractors or partners | Buy capacity for a fixed period | The gap is temporary and the skill is available in the market | Day rates, onboarding time, knowledge leaving at the end |
| Hire | Add permanent capacity | The gap is lasting and strategic | Recruitment lead time; ongoing cost |
| Overtime | Ask people to work extra hours | Short, genuine peaks only | Fatigue, errors and attrition if it becomes normal |
Inside individual projects, [resource levelling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) and techniques from [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) help once the portfolio decision has been made. Watch for [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/): unmanaged additions quietly increase demand after the capacity plan has been agreed.

#### Worked example 3: closing the developer gap
Continuing the illustrative example, the PMO models the options for the 378-hour developer shortfall.
| Option | Effect on developers | Cost or consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Defer Project Gamma's start to next quarter | Demand falls by 300 hours | Gamma's benefits arrive about three months later |
| B. Testers take on 80 hours of test-automation scripting estimated as developer work | Demand falls by 80 hours | Uses tester surplus; small learning curve |
| C. Contract developer at 0.5 FTE for 10 weeks | Capacity rises by about 159 hours (187.5 hours x 85% productive) | Contractor cost for 10 weeks |
| D. Cut 120 hours of lower-priority Beta features | Demand falls by 120 hours | Features move to a later release |
| E. Two hours' overtime a week for all developers | Capacity rises by about 126 hours | Unsustainable over a quarter; not recommended |
Options A and B together remove 380 hours, bringing developer demand to 1,770 hours against 1,772 hours of capacity. On paper the gap is closed, but utilisation is 100%, with nothing left for urgent defects or estimating error. The portfolio board therefore also approves option C. Developer capacity becomes about 1,931 hours against 1,770 hours of demand, a utilisation of about **92%**, leaving roughly 160 hours of buffer. Option D is held in reserve if Gamma is approved early.
Tip
Closing the gap to exactly zero is not the goal. Aim for a plan that leaves a buffer, because real work always contains surprises.

### What to do with surplus capacity
In example 2 the testers had about 175 spare hours. Decide how to use spare capacity rather than letting it fill with low-value work:
- **Pull forward** approved work waiting on that skill, or absorb work from a constrained role.
- **Invest in improvement**: automation, documentation or technical debt that frees capacity later.
- **Train and cross-skill**, using a [training plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/).
- **Lend capacity** to another team, or reduce contractor use.
A surplus that persists for several cycles suggests the skill mix no longer matches the work.

### Capacity planning strategies: lead, lag and match
When demand is growing, there are three classic strategies for adding capacity. They come from operations management but apply equally to project teams.
| Strategy | What it means | When to use it | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lead | Add capacity before demand arrives | Growth is near certain and delay is costly, for example a signed programme of work | Paying for idle capacity if demand does not appear |
| Lag | Add capacity only once demand is confirmed | Budgets are tight or demand is uncertain | Overload and delays while you recruit |
| Match | Add capacity in small steps as demand grows | Most project organisations; balances cost and risk | Needs frequent reviews to time each step |
| Fixed-team (Agile) | Keep stable teams and prioritise work into their capacity | Product teams with continuous demand | Low-priority work may wait a long time |
Many organisations combine them: a permanent core for steady demand, contractors for confirmed peaks and early recruitment for strategic skills.

### Utilisation targets and buffers
It is tempting to plan everyone at 100% of productive capacity. In practice, a fully loaded team has no room to absorb urgent work, estimating error or sickness, so queues form and every item waits longer. The same idea underpins [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) in Kanban and the shared buffers in [critical chain project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-chain-project-management/).
- Keep a buffer of unallocated productive capacity, often 10-15%, and protect it.
- Plan shared specialists more lightly than generalists, because they are pulled in many directions.
- In agencies, keep planned project utilisation separate from billable utilisation.
- Watch the trend: planned at 90% but running at 110% every month means your estimates or factors are wrong.
There is no universal correct rate. Set a target per role and compare it with actuals each cycle.

### Who owns capacity planning and how often to review it
Capacity planning works when ownership is clear and everyone knows when the numbers will be refreshed.
| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Portfolio board or sponsor | Makes the priority calls when demand exceeds capacity |
| PMO or resource manager | Owns the capacity model, consolidates demand, runs the review and reports gaps |
| Functional or line managers | Provide capacity by role: headcount, leave, skills, recruitment plans |
| Project managers | Provide remaining demand by role and month, and flag changes early |
| Team leads | Keep operational allocation and actual utilisation up to date |
| Finance and HR | Turn gaps into budgets, hiring plans and contractor approvals |
In many organisations the [project management office](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) is the natural owner because it already sees the whole portfolio. Decisions about which projects to start belong to portfolio management; see [program vs project vs portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/program-vs-project-vs-portfolio-management/) for how the levels fit together.
| Plan level | Typical review cadence |
| --- | --- |
| Strategic | Annually, refreshed quarterly |
| Tactical (portfolio) | Monthly |
| Operational (team) | Weekly, fortnightly or every sprint |
| Any level | Immediately after a major change: a large project approved, cancelled or re-scoped, or a key person leaving |
Comparing forecast with actual at each review improves your factors, estimates and [project forecasting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/).

### Capacity planning tools and templates
A spreadsheet is enough for one team or a small portfolio: a tab for capacity by role, a tab for demand by project and a summary of gaps and utilisation. Keep demand aligned with each project's [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) or [project tracker](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/).
Once several projects share people, [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) saves manual consolidation. Workload features often sit on higher plans:
- [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, shows team workload and capacity, accounts for working hours and holidays, and includes time tracking. Advanced resource and capacity planning, including role-based planning, is among its Pinnacle capabilities, which suits PMOs.
- [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) has a visual workload view on Pro, with resource management on Enterprise.
- [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) includes workload, portfolios and time tracking on Advanced.
- [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) has workload tracking on Business and above, plus a Resource Management add-on.
- [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) Premium adds Plans for cross-team roadmaps and capacity.
Whatever the tool, the inputs matter most: honest remaining estimates, real leave data and an evidence-based productive-time factor.

### Common capacity planning mistakes
- **Counting contracted hours as capacity.** Plans built on 40 productive hours a week are short before they start.
- **Planning by headcount instead of skill.** Totals hide the bottleneck role, as example 2 shows.
- **Ignoring business-as-usual and support.** Routine work is real demand even if no project plan lists it.
- **Leaving out the pipeline.** Unapproved projects become approved projects; weight them by probability.
- **Using original estimates instead of remaining work.** Late projects need more hours than their plans say.
- **Planning to 100%.** There is no room for surprises, so planned work slips when they arrive.
- **Treating it as a one-off exercise.** An unreviewed plan is out of date within weeks.
- **Hiding the gap.** Absorbing shortfalls with overtime protects today's dates at the expense of next quarter's.
Read our guide to [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) for the next step: turning an approved capacity plan into named assignments.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is capacity planning in project management?**
It is the process of comparing the work demanded by projects and day-to-day operations with the productive time and skills available, for a team or portfolio over a set period, so that gaps can be fixed before they delay delivery.

**Q: How do you calculate capacity for capacity planning?**
Multiply the number of people by their contracted hours and the weeks in the period, subtract leave, holidays and training, then multiply by a productive-time factor, such as 75-80%, to allow for meetings, admin and support. Do this separately for each role or skill.

**Q: What is an example of capacity planning?**
Five designers have 800 contracted hours in a month; after leave and an 80% productive factor that is 608 hours. Demand is 680 hours, so the team is 72 hours (0.56 FTE) short and must defer work, add a freelancer or pause requests.

**Q: What is the difference between capacity planning and resource planning?**
Capacity planning compares total supply with total demand across a team or portfolio, usually by role and over months. Resource planning works out what one project needs, and resource allocation assigns named people to specific tasks.

**Q: What is a good utilisation rate in capacity planning?**
There is no single correct figure. Many teams plan productive capacity at roughly 85-90% so that a buffer of 10-15% remains for urgent work and estimating error. Set targets per role and compare them with actuals.

**Q: What are the three capacity planning strategies?**
Lead adds capacity before demand arrives, lag waits until demand is confirmed, and match adds capacity in small steps as demand grows. Agile organisations often use a fourth approach: fixed teams with work prioritised into their capacity.

**Q: What is the difference between capacity and availability?**
Availability is the time someone is at work and not on leave. Capacity, in the productive sense, is the part of that available time that can go on planned work once meetings, admin and support are taken out.

**Q: How often should capacity plans be updated?**
Monthly is common for portfolio plans, weekly or every sprint for team plans, and annually with quarterly refreshes for strategic workforce plans. Update immediately after a major change in projects or people.

**Q: Who is responsible for capacity planning?**
Usually the PMO or a resource manager owns the model, line managers supply capacity, project managers supply demand, and a portfolio board or sponsor makes the priority decisions when demand exceeds capacity.

**Q: How do you include projects that are not yet approved?**
Estimate their effort by role and multiply it by the probability of approval. A 500-hour project with a 60% chance adds 300 hours of weighted demand. Replace the weighted figure with the full estimate once it is approved.

**Q: How does capacity planning work in Agile?**
Agile teams estimate how much work fits each sprint from team availability, a focus factor and past velocity, then commit only to that. See our [agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) guide for the formula.

**Q: What tools are used for capacity planning?**
Spreadsheets work for small teams. Larger portfolios use the workload and resource features of tools such as Wrike, monday.com, Asana, Smartsheet or Jira, which often sit on higher-tier plans or add-ons.

**Q: How does FTE relate to capacity planning?**
FTE expresses capacity and demand in full-time-person units, which makes gaps easy to communicate, for example "1.3 developers short next quarter". See our guide to [full-time equivalent](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/full-time-equivalent-fte/).

# CAPM Certification: Requirements, Exam, Cost and Study Plan

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: CAPM certification guide: eligibility, the 23 contact hours, exam domains and fees, a 6-week study plan, worked examples, CAPM vs PMP and renewal.


## CAPM Certification: Requirements, Exam, Cost and Study Plan
The CAPM certification (Certified Associate in Project Management) is the Project Management Institute's entry-level credential, showing that you understand project management fundamentals, predictive and Agile methods, and business analysis. You need a secondary diploma and 23 hours of project management education, and no project experience. This guide explains the requirements, exam, fees, a step-by-step route to certification, a six-week study plan with worked examples and sample questions, how the CAPM compares with the PMP, and how to keep it active.
- Published 3 October 2026
- Last updated 18 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- The CAPM is PMI's entry-level certification and needs no project experience: a secondary diploma and 23 hours of project management education are enough.
- The exam has 150 questions (135 scored) in 180 minutes, across four domains: fundamentals 36%, predictive 17%, Agile 20% and business analysis 27%.
- Exam fees are widely reported as US$225 for PMI members and US$300 for non-members; check PMI's site before you pay.
- Most candidates prepare in four to eight weeks; practise calculations such as schedule variance and the critical path, not only definitions.
- An active CAPM meets the PMP training requirement, which makes it a natural first step towards the PMP.
- Keep it active by earning 15 PDUs every three years.

### What is the CAPM certification?
The **Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM)** is a professional certification awarded by the [Project Management Institute (PMI)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/) to people who pass an exam on project management fundamentals. It shows employers that you understand core terms, processes and approaches, including predictive, Agile and business analysis practices, before you have led projects yourself.
The CAPM sits below the [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) in PMI's range. The PMP tests experienced judgement and requires years of project leadership; the CAPM tests knowledge and is open to anyone who meets the education rules.

#### What the CAPM shows, and what it does not
- **It shows** that you know the language of project management: scope, schedules, risk, stakeholders, iterations, backlogs and requirements.
- **It shows** commitment to the profession, which helps when you have little experience on your CV.
- **It does not show** that you have led projects. Employers will still ask for examples of what you have organised, coordinated or delivered.
If you are still comparing options, our overview of [project management certifications](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) sets the CAPM alongside PRINCE2, Scrum and other credentials.

### CAPM requirements
According to PMI's CAPM page (checked 18 October 2026), you need:
| Requirement | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Education | A secondary degree, such as a high school diploma, GED or global equivalent |
| Project management education | At least 23 hours, completed before you sit the exam |
| Experience | None required |
| Age | PMI's page lists a minimum age of 18 |

#### What counts as the 23 contact hours
A contact hour is one hour of structured learning about project management. PMI lists its own on-demand CAPM Exam Prep Course and instructor-led CAPM courses from training providers as options. University or college modules in project management can also qualify. The learning must cover project management topics, and you should keep the certificate or transcript in case your application is audited.
- **Usually counts:** project management courses (online or in person) with a certificate showing the hours, academic project management modules, and courses run by PMI chapters or training providers.
- **Usually does not count:** networking meetings, general business or software courses without project management content, and reading a book on your own without a course.
- **Courses you have already done:** earlier courses can count if you can prove the hours and the content. Check PMI's current handbook if you are unsure.
The CAPM's 23 hours are separate from the PMP's training requirement. Our guide to [35 contact hours for the PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/35-contact-hours-pmp/) explains that rule.
Tip
Choose a course built on PMI's current CAPM Exam Content Outline. Courses written before the 2023 exam update cover an older structure and leave gaps in Agile and business analysis.

### CAPM exam format
| Item | Detail (PMI, checked 18 October 2026) |
| --- | --- |
| Questions | 150 in total: 135 scored and 15 unscored pretest questions |
| Time | 180 minutes |
| Delivery | Pearson VUE test centre (PMI recommends this) or online proctored exam |
| Languages | English plus several translations, including Arabic, French, German, Japanese, Spanish and Chinese |
| Attempts | Up to three attempts within a one-year eligibility period |
| Rescheduling | Free more than 30 days before; US$70 within 30 days; not possible within 48 hours (PMI certification handbook) |

#### Question types
Most questions are multiple choice with one correct answer. Training providers report that the current exam can also include multiple-response, matching and hotspot items, so practise with a simulator that includes these formats. The 15 pretest questions are mixed in and look like the rest, so treat every question as if it counts.

#### Scoring and results
PMI does not publish a passing percentage. It sets the pass standard through psychometric analysis, and your result report shows pass or fail plus a performance rating for each domain. Many training providers suggest aiming for 75% to 80% or more on full-length practice exams before you book, but that is a rule of thumb, not a PMI figure.

### What the CAPM exam covers
The exam follows PMI's **CAPM Exam Content Outline (ECO)**, last updated in 2023. It has four domains. The approximate counts below assume the weights apply to the 135 scored questions.
| Domain | Weight | Approximate scored questions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Project management fundamentals and core concepts | 36% | About 49 |
| 2. Predictive, plan-based methodologies | 17% | About 23 |
| 3. Agile frameworks and methodologies | 20% | About 27 |
| 4. Business analysis frameworks | 27% | About 36 |

#### Domain 1: fundamentals and core concepts (36%)
- Project life cycles; projects vs programmes, portfolios and operations; predictive vs adaptive approaches.
- The difference between issues, risks, assumptions and constraints.
- The purpose of cost, quality, risk and schedule plans; milestones; using a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) and stakeholder register.
- Roles of the project manager, sponsor and team; leadership vs management; emotional intelligence.
- The PMI Code of Ethics, project initiation, benefits planning, closure and common problem-solving techniques.

#### Domain 2: predictive, plan-based methodologies (17%)
- When a plan-based approach suits the organisation and the work.
- [Work breakdown structures](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) and work packages.
- The [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) and schedule management.
- Calculating schedule and cost variance; quality and integration management plans; artefacts used in predictive projects.

#### Domain 3: Agile frameworks and methodologies (20%)
- When an adaptive approach suits the project; pros and cons compared with predictive work.
- Planning iterations, translating a WBS into iterations, and adaptive tracking.
- Components of methods such as [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/), XP, SAFe and Kanban.
- Artefacts used in adaptive projects, success criteria and prioritising tasks.

#### Domain 4: business analysis frameworks (27%)
- Business analysis roles such as process owner, product manager and product owner, and stakeholder identification.
- Choosing communication channels for different audiences; see [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/).
- Gathering [requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/) with interviews, workshops, surveys, user stories and use cases.
- Requirements traceability matrices, product backlogs, product roadmaps and release planning.
- Acceptance criteria and deciding whether a product is ready for delivery.

#### Which references to study
PMI's [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) is the main reference, but the exam is based on the content outline rather than any single book. The eighth edition of the PMBOK Guide was published in November 2025, while the CAPM outline dates from 2023, so use a prep course aligned to the outline and check PMI's current reference list. Add an Agile primer, because a fifth of the exam is Agile; our guide to [Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) is a good starting point.

### How much the CAPM costs
PMI's CAPM page does not list the fee, and PMI says prices vary by membership status and region. The figures below are those widely reported by training providers and education sites in 2025 and 2026 (checked 18 October 2026). Confirm the current price on pmi.org before you pay.
| Cost item | PMI member | Non-member |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CAPM exam | US$225 | US$300 |
| Re-examination (each retake) | US$150 | US$200 |
| Rescheduling within 30 days | US$70 | US$70 |
| 23-hour course | Varies by provider | Varies by provider |
| PMI membership | Annual fee plus a one-time joining fee (check pmi.org) | Not applicable |

#### Worked example: total cost
Suppose you take a low-cost online course for US$100 and buy a practice exam simulator for US$50. As a non-member you pay US$300 for the exam, so your total is US$450. If you fail once and retake, add US$200, giving US$650.
As a member the exam costs US$225, a saving of US$75, and a retake costs US$150, a saving of another US$50. Because a year's membership costs more than the US$75 exam saving on its own, membership pays off mainly if you also use other benefits, such as cheaper PMI courses, member access to PMI standards, local chapter events and lower renewal fees.
Tip
Ask your employer before paying. Many organisations fund entry-level certifications for coordinators and project team members, especially if you link the CAPM to a development plan.

### How to get the CAPM certification step by step
1. **Check you are eligible.** Confirm you have a secondary diploma or equivalent, and that you meet PMI's other conditions.
2. **Complete 23 hours of project management education.** Pick a course aligned to the current CAPM content outline and keep the completion certificate.
3. **Decide on PMI membership.** Join before you pay the exam fee if you want the member price; PMI applies the member rate only if your membership is active when you pay.
4. **Create a PMI account and apply online.** Enter your education and course details. PMI keeps an application open for 90 days while you complete it.
5. **Wait for review, and respond to any audit.** PMI reviews most applications quickly. A percentage are randomly audited; if yours is, send copies of your diploma and course certificate within the time PMI gives you.
6. **Pay the exam fee.** Once your application is approved, payment opens your one-year eligibility period.
7. **Book the exam with Pearson VUE.** Choose a test centre or online proctoring. For online exams, run the system check on the computer you will use.
8. **Prepare and sit the exam.** Follow the study plan below and take full-length practice exams under timed conditions.
9. **Receive your result and certificate.** You see pass or fail when you finish. Your three-year certification cycle starts, and you can add the credential to your CV and LinkedIn profile.
PMI's handbook allows up to three attempts within the one-year eligibility period. If you do not pass in three attempts, you must wait a year from your last attempt before you can apply again.

### A 6-week CAPM study plan
This plan assumes you have finished your 23-hour course and can study for six to eight hours a week. Stretch it to eight weeks if you are new to project work or studying part-time.
| Week | Focus | Activities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Fundamentals (part 1) | Life cycles, projects vs operations, predictive vs adaptive, roles, ethics. Make flashcards for key terms. |
| 2 | Fundamentals (part 2) | Planning, risk and stakeholder registers, issues vs risks, closure. Do 50 topic questions and review every mistake. |
| 3 | Predictive methods | WBS, critical path, schedule and cost variance, quality and integration plans. Practise calculations until they are quick. |
| 4 | Agile methods | Scrum roles, events and artefacts; Kanban; XP; SAFe basics; iteration planning and prioritisation. |
| 5 | Business analysis | Requirements gathering, traceability, backlogs, roadmaps, acceptance criteria. First full-length timed practice exam. |
| 6 | Review and exam practice | Second and third full-length exams. Re-study your two weakest domains. Book the exam once you score consistently well. |
Tip
Keep an error log: for each practice question you get wrong, write down the concept, why your answer was wrong and why the right answer is right. Re-read it the day before the exam.

### Worked examples of CAPM calculations
The content outline asks you to calculate schedule and cost variance and apply the critical path method, so expect some arithmetic. These examples show the level of calculation to expect.

#### Example 1: earned value, schedule and cost variance
A project has a budget at completion (BAC) of US$100,000. At the end of month 3, the plan says 50% of the work should be done. In fact 40% is complete, and US$45,000 has been spent.
| Measure | Formula | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Planned value (PV) | Planned % complete × BAC | 50% × 100,000 | US$50,000 |
| Earned value (EV) | Actual % complete × BAC | 40% × 100,000 | US$40,000 |
| Actual cost (AC) | Money spent so far | Given | US$45,000 |
| Schedule variance (SV) | EV − PV | 40,000 − 50,000 | −US$10,000 (behind schedule) |
| Cost variance (CV) | EV − AC | 40,000 − 45,000 | −US$5,000 (over budget) |
| Schedule performance index (SPI) | EV ÷ PV | 40,000 ÷ 50,000 | 0.80 |
| Cost performance index (CPI) | EV ÷ AC | 40,000 ÷ 45,000 | 0.89 |
Negative variances and indices below 1.0 mean the project is behind schedule and over budget. Our guides to [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/), [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) and [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/) go further.

#### Example 2: finding the critical path
A small project has five activities. B and C can start when A finishes; D needs both B and C; E follows D.
| Activity | Duration (days) | Depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 3 | None |
| B | 5 | A |
| C | 2 | A |
| D | 4 | B and C |
| E | 1 | D |
1. List the paths through the network: A-B-D-E and A-C-D-E.
2. Add the durations: A-B-D-E = 3 + 5 + 4 + 1 = 13 days; A-C-D-E = 3 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 10 days.
3. The longest path, A-B-D-E, is the critical path, so the project takes 13 days.
4. Activity C has 13 − 10 = 3 days of float: it can slip by up to three days without delaying the project.
A delay to any activity on the critical path delays the whole project, which is why exam questions often ask which activity a project manager should watch most closely.

### Sample CAPM-style questions
These are our own practice questions written in the style of the exam. They are not taken from PMI's question bank.

#### Question 1
A team is building a new mobile app. Users are unsure what they need and the sponsor wants feedback every two weeks. Which approach is most appropriate? (a) Predictive (b) Adaptive (c) No formal approach (d) Phase-gate with a single final release.
**Answer: (b).** Uncertain requirements and frequent feedback favour an adaptive approach.

#### Question 2
A key supplier might go out of business before delivering a component. This is best described as: (a) an issue (b) a risk (c) an assumption (d) a constraint.
**Answer: (b).** It is an uncertain future event that would affect the project. It becomes an issue only if it actually happens.

#### Question 3
Which document links each requirement to its source and to the deliverables and tests that satisfy it? (a) Product roadmap (b) Stakeholder register (c) Requirements traceability matrix (d) Burndown chart.
**Answer: (c).** A traceability matrix tracks requirements from origin to delivery and testing.

#### Question 4
In Scrum, who is accountable for ordering the product backlog? (a) Scrum master (b) Project sponsor (c) Developers (d) Product owner.
**Answer: (d).** The Scrum Guide makes the product owner accountable for product backlog management, including ordering items.

### Exam-day tips
- **Read the last line of the question first.** Questions often ask for the "best", "first" or "most appropriate" action; identify what is asked before reading the scenario.
- **Watch for the approach.** Decide whether the scenario is predictive, Agile or hybrid; the right answer often depends on it.
- **Eliminate wrong answers.** You can usually remove two options quickly, which turns a guess into a 50% chance.
- **Pace yourself.** 150 questions in 180 minutes is 72 seconds each. Flag hard questions and come back to them.
- **Answer every question.** There is no penalty for wrong answers, so never leave one blank.
- **Check break rules in advance.** Rules differ between test centres and online exams, so read PMI's and Pearson VUE's current instructions before exam day.
- **For online exams,** clear your desk, test your webcam and connection, and log in early.

### CAPM vs PMP
|  | CAPM | PMP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level | Entry level | Experienced practitioner |
| Experience | None required | Roughly 3 to 5 years leading projects, depending on education (see PMI's current rules) |
| Training | 23 hours of project management education | 35 hours, or an active CAPM |
| Exam | 150 questions, 180 minutes | 180 questions, 240 minutes on the exam introduced in July 2026, as reported by training providers |
| What it tests | Knowledge of concepts, terms and methods | Judgement in realistic, experience-based scenarios |
| Renewal | 15 PDUs every 3 years | 60 PDUs every 3 years |
| Typical holder | Students, coordinators, career changers | Project managers and senior project staff |
PMI states that CAPM holders already meet the PMP training requirement, so the CAPM can save you from taking a separate 35-hour course later. PMI also changed the PMP exam in July 2026 and is updating the rules for live training hours from 1 December 2026; check PMI's PMP page if you plan to move on soon.

#### Which should you take?
- **Take the CAPM** if you have little or no experience leading projects, or want a recognised credential while you build experience.
- **Go straight for the PMP** if you already meet its experience requirement. The CAPM adds little once you are eligible for the PMP.

### CAPM vs other entry-level certifications
| Certification | Body | Best for | Experience needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CAPM | PMI | A broad foundation recognised internationally, especially where PMI credentials are common | None |
| [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) Foundation | PeopleCert (AXELOS) | UK, European and public-sector roles that use PRINCE2 | None |
| Scrum certifications (CSM, PSM I) | Scrum Alliance, Scrum.org | Agile teams and Scrum master roles | None |
| PMAI | Neural Project Institute | An affordable, modern foundation including AI for project managers | None |
The PMAI is our own programme of assessed online courses; it is a certificate of completion rather than a PMI or PeopleCert credential, so many learners use it alongside or before the CAPM. See the [PMAI certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/#cert-pmai). For Agile roles, compare options in our [Scrum certification and training guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/).

### Is the CAPM worth it?
For most people starting out, yes, provided employers in your market recognise PMI credentials. Check job adverts for coordinator and junior project roles in your area to see how often the CAPM or PMP is mentioned.

#### Benefits
- A recognised credential with no experience requirement.
- A structured way to learn predictive, Agile and business analysis basics in one go.
- It meets the PMP training requirement for later.
- It signals commitment when your CV is light on project experience.

#### Limitations
- It does not replace experience; you will still need examples of work you have organised.
- It is better known in markets where PMI is strong; in some UK and European public-sector roles, PRINCE2 is asked for more often.
- It needs 15 PDUs and a renewal fee every three years.

#### Jobs that suit CAPM holders
- [Project coordinator](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-coordinator/)
- Assistant or junior project manager
- Project administrator or PMO analyst
- Business analyst or junior product roles
- Team members who want to move into project roles
PMI's CAPM page cites an average US salary for CAPM-certified project managers of US$100,750, from Forbes. Pay depends far more on role, location and experience than on the certificate alone, so treat any average with care. For the wider career route, read [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/).

### Maintaining your CAPM
The CAPM is valid for three years. To renew, you earn **15 professional development units (PDUs)** during each three-year cycle and pay PMI's renewal fee. One PDU equals one hour of learning or giving back to the profession.
| Category | CAPM rule |
| --- | --- |
| Total PDUs per cycle | 15 |
| Education | At least 9, with at least 2 in each Talent Triangle area (Ways of Working, Power Skills, Business Acumen) |
| Giving back | Up to 6, including up to 2 for working as a practitioner |

#### Example renewal plan
- A 6-hour Agile course: 6 PDUs (Ways of Working).
- Two 1.5-hour webinars on communication and negotiation: 3 PDUs (Power Skills).
- A 3-hour course on project finance: 3 PDUs (Business Acumen).
- Working as a practitioner: 2 PDUs; volunteering at a PMI chapter event: 1 PDU.
That gives 12 education PDUs and 3 giving-back PDUs, 15 in total. If you earn the PMP during the cycle, the CAPM is no longer needed. Our [PDU guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pdu-professional-development-units/) explains how to claim and report PDUs.

### Common CAPM mistakes to avoid
- **Studying from out-of-date material.** Prep books and courses written before the 2023 update miss much of the Agile and business analysis content.
- **Memorising without practising.** The exam asks you to apply concepts to scenarios; use practice questions from week 2 onwards.
- **Skipping the calculations.** Variance and critical path questions are easy marks once you have practised them.
- **Under-weighting business analysis.** At 27% it is the second-largest domain, larger than predictive methods.
- **Booking too early.** Wait until you score consistently well on full-length timed practice exams.
- **Joining PMI only for the exam discount.** Work out whether you will use the other benefits first.
- **Losing your course certificate.** Keep evidence of your 23 hours in case of an audit, even after you pass.
- **Forgetting renewal.** Log PDUs as you earn them rather than at the end of the cycle.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the CAPM certification?**
The Certified Associate in Project Management is PMI's entry-level certification. It shows you understand project management fundamentals, predictive and Agile approaches, and business analysis, and it needs no project experience.

**Q: What are the CAPM requirements?**
A secondary diploma or equivalent and at least 23 hours of project management education completed before the exam. PMI's page also lists a minimum age of 18.

**Q: Can I take the CAPM without experience?**
Yes. The CAPM has no project experience requirement, which is why it suits students, career changers and coordinators.

**Q: How much does the CAPM cost?**
The exam fee is widely reported as US$225 for PMI members and US$300 for non-members, with retakes at US$150 and US$200. Add the cost of your 23-hour course and check PMI's site for current prices.

**Q: How hard is the CAPM exam?**
It is easier than the PMP because it tests knowledge rather than experienced judgement, but it covers a broad range of topics, including Agile, business analysis and some calculations. Most candidates who study consistently for four to eight weeks are well prepared.

**Q: What is the CAPM passing score?**
PMI does not publish a passing percentage. It sets the standard through psychometric analysis and reports pass or fail with a performance rating for each domain.

**Q: How long should I study for the CAPM?**
Many people prepare in four to eight weeks alongside work, studying six to eight hours a week after their 23-hour course.

**Q: Can I take the CAPM exam online?**
Yes. You can take it at a Pearson VUE test centre or as an online proctored exam.

**Q: How many times can I take the CAPM exam?**
Up to three times within your one-year eligibility period. After three unsuccessful attempts you must wait a year before reapplying.

**Q: Is the CAPM worth it?**
For beginners in markets that value PMI credentials, it is a recognised way to show your knowledge and prepare for the PMP. It does not replace experience, so pair it with practical project work.

**Q: Should I take the CAPM or the PMP?**
Take the CAPM if you do not yet meet the PMP's experience requirement. If you already have several years of project leadership, go straight for the PMP.

**Q: Does the CAPM count towards the PMP?**
Yes. PMI states that CAPM holders already meet the PMP training requirement, so you do not need a separate 35-hour course. You still need the PMP's project experience.

**Q: Does the CAPM expire?**
It lasts for three years. To renew, earn 15 PDUs in each cycle and pay the renewal fee.

**Q: Which PMBOK Guide edition should I study for the CAPM?**
The exam follows PMI's CAPM Exam Content Outline, not a single edition of the PMBOK Guide. The eighth edition was published in November 2025; use a prep course aligned to the current outline and check PMI's reference list.

**Q: Should I take the CAPM or PRINCE2 Foundation?**
The CAPM suits markets where PMI credentials are common and gives a broad grounding, including Agile and business analysis. PRINCE2 Foundation is more often requested in the UK, Europe and the public sector.

# Change Control in Project Management: Process and Template

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: How the change control process works, from change request to impact analysis and approval, with a change request template, change log, worked example and tips.


## Change Control in Project Management: Process and Template
Change control is the formal process for proposing, assessing, approving or rejecting, and recording changes to a project's agreed baselines, such as scope, schedule, cost and deliverables. It lets a project adapt to new needs without losing control of what it has committed to.
- Published 1 October 2026
- 4 min read

### Key takeaways
- Change control makes the impact of changes visible before they are accepted.
- Every request is logged, analysed, decided by the right person and recorded.
- Delegate authority by change size so small changes move quickly.
- Update baselines and communicate after each approved change.

### Why change control matters
- Prevents [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/): unapproved additions that consume time and budget.
- Makes the impact of each change visible before it is accepted.
- Ensures the right people decide, at the right level of authority.
- Keeps plans, [baselines](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) and documents consistent.
- Creates an audit trail of what changed, when and why.

### The change control process
1. **Raise a change request:** anyone can submit one, using a standard form.
2. **Log it:** record it in the change log with an ID and status.
3. **Initial review:** the project manager checks it is complete and not a duplicate.
4. **Impact analysis:** assess the effect on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources and benefits, and consider options.
5. **Decide:** the project manager, sponsor or a change control board (CCB) approves, rejects or defers it, depending on delegated authority.
6. **Update baselines and plans:** if approved, update the schedule, budget, requirements and any affected documents under [configuration management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/configuration-management/).
7. **Implement and verify:** carry out the change and confirm it delivers what was approved.
8. **Communicate and close:** tell affected stakeholders and close the log entry.

### Change request template
| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Change ID and date | Unique reference and date raised |
| Requested by | Name and role |
| Description | What change is requested |
| Reason | Why it is needed and the benefit |
| Priority | Urgency and consequence of not making it |
| Impact: scope | Deliverables or requirements affected |
| Impact: schedule | Effect on milestones and critical path |
| Impact: cost | Additional or saved cost |
| Impact: quality and risk | New risks, testing needs |
| Options considered | Including 'do nothing' |
| Recommendation | Project manager's recommendation |
| Decision | Approved, rejected or deferred; by whom and when |

### Change log example
| ID | Change | Cost | Schedule | Decision | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CR-04 | Add single sign-on to the portal | +£18,000 | +2 weeks | Approved by CCB | Implemented |
| CR-05 | Change report colours to new brand palette | +£1,200 | None | Approved by PM | Closed |
| CR-06 | Add mobile app to scope | +£120,000 | +4 months | Deferred to phase 2 | Closed |
| CR-07 | Remove legacy data export | -£6,000 | -1 week | Pending impact analysis | Open |

### Authority levels
Agree delegation in the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) so small changes do not clog the board. For example:
| Change size | Who decides |
| --- | --- |
| Under £5,000 and no milestone impact | Project manager |
| £5,000 to £50,000 or a milestone moves by up to 2 weeks | Change control board |
| Over £50,000, a milestone moves by more than 2 weeks, or benefits change | Sponsor or steering committee |
Tip
Thresholds should match your organisation's [governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) and the project's tolerances. These figures are only an illustration.

### Change control in Agile
In Agile approaches, changing requirements are expected. New ideas go into the product backlog, and the product owner reorders it, so most change is handled through backlog prioritisation rather than formal requests. Formal change control is still used for changes to contracts, budgets, fixed dates or the overall product goal. See [change management vs change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-management-vs-change-control/) for how this differs from the people side of change.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is change control in project management?**
The formal process for submitting, assessing, approving or rejecting and recording changes to a project's baselines.

**Q: What are the steps in the change control process?**
Raise a request, log it, review it, analyse impact, decide, update plans, implement and verify, then communicate and close.

**Q: What is a change control board?**
A group with authority to approve or reject changes above a set threshold, often including the sponsor, key users and technical leads.

**Q: What is a change request in change control?**
A formal proposal to change scope, schedule, cost, deliverables, processes or documents.

**Q: What is a change log in change control?**
A record of all change requests, their impacts, decisions and status.

**Q: What is integrated change control?**
The PMBOK term for reviewing all change requests and managing changes to deliverables, documents and plans across the whole project; see [integration management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-integration-management/).

**Q: Who can raise a change request under change control?**
Usually any stakeholder, though it is best submitted through the project manager using a standard form.

**Q: What is the difference between change control and configuration management?**
Change control decides whether a change is made; configuration management tracks versions of items and makes sure the approved change is reflected accurately.

**Q: Should change control record rejected change requests?**
Yes. Recording rejected and deferred requests prevents the same request being raised repeatedly and supports audits.

**Q: How do you stop scope creep with change control?**
Agree clear scope and acceptance criteria, route every change through change control, and make the cost and time impact of each request visible.

**Q: Do Agile projects use change control?**
They manage most change through backlog prioritisation, but still apply formal control to contracts, budgets and fixed commitments.
