# Construction Project Manager: Duties, Skills and Career

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/construction-project-manager/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a construction project manager does at each stage, key skills, qualifications (CCM, PMP, MCIOB), career path, pay data and a worked example.


## Construction Project Manager: Duties, Skills and Career
A construction project manager plans, coordinates and controls a building or infrastructure project from the first feasibility study to handover, managing cost, programme, quality, contracts and safety on behalf of the client or the contractor. This guide explains what the role involves at each stage, how a typical day runs, the skills and qualifications employers look for, how to get into the job and how it differs from site managers and construction managers.
- Published 4 October 2026
- Last updated 16 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- A construction project manager owns the whole project (brief, design coordination, procurement, construction and handover), not just the site.
- Duties differ depending on whether you work client-side, for a contractor or for a project management consultancy.
- The programme, cost plan, risk register and change (variation) register are the four controls you will use every week.
- Long-lead items, permissions, ground conditions and late design information drive most delays.
- Employers value site and commercial experience plus professional membership (such as MCIOB or RICS) or certification (such as CCM or PMP).
- Most people reach the role through site engineering, assistant project manager or quantity surveying posts.

### What is a construction project manager?
A **construction project manager** is the person responsible for delivering a construction project to the agreed scope, cost, time and quality. They turn the client's needs into a brief and budget, coordinate designers and contractors, manage contracts and change, oversee safety arrangements and hand over a finished, compliant building. They lead the whole project, not just the site.
The title covers three slightly different jobs, depending on who employs you:
- **Client-side project manager.** Works for the owner or developer (or for a consultancy appointed by them). Manages the brief, the design team, procurement and the contractor, and protects the client's budget and programme.
- **Contractor-side project manager.** Works for the main contractor. Delivers the works under the building contract, managing subcontractors, site teams, buying, cost and the contractor's programme, while protecting the contractor's margin.
- **Project management consultant.** An independent professional appointed to act as the client's project manager, common on public sector and larger private projects.
If you want the discipline rather than the job (methods, phases and tools for running construction projects), read our guide to [construction project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/construction-project-management/).

### What does a construction project manager do?
The core duties are broadly the same on a house extension or a hospital. What changes is the scale, the contract and how much is delegated.
- **Develop the brief and business case** with the client, including scope, quality expectations, budget and the target completion date, often supported by a [feasibility study](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/feasibility-study/).
- **Build and manage the construction programme**: the project schedule, usually a Gantt chart with dependencies and the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).
- **Coordinate the design team**: architects, structural, civil and building services engineers, cost consultants and specialist designers.
- **Run procurement**: choose the procurement route and form of contract, prepare tender documents, evaluate bids and appoint contractors (see [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/)).
- **Secure permissions and approvals**: planning or zoning consent, building control or permits, utility connections and third-party agreements.
- **Control cost**: cost plans, budgets, monthly valuations, cash flow forecasts and final account.
- **Manage change**: log, value and agree variations (change orders) and their effect on time.
- **Oversee health and safety arrangements**, making sure legal duty holders are appointed and doing their jobs.
- **Manage risk**: keep a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) and a contingency, and act on early warnings.
- **Report** progress, cost and risk to the client or board.
- **Lead handover and close-out**: commissioning, snagging, as-built information, operation and maintenance manuals, defects period and lessons learned.

#### Duties by project stage
| Stage | What the project manager does | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feasibility and brief | Site appraisal, options, outline budget and programme, risk review, appoint the design team | Project brief, feasibility report, budget |
| Design | Coordinate designers, chair design meetings, manage design programme, obtain planning consent, review cost plans | Approved design, planning consent, cost plan |
| Procurement | Agree procurement route, prepare tender package, run tender, evaluate and negotiate, award contract | Signed contract, contract programme |
| Construction | Progress meetings, monitor programme and cost, manage RFIs and variations, inspections, client reporting | Monthly reports, valuations, variation register |
| Handover and close-out | Commissioning, snagging, training the occupier, collect O&M manuals, release retention, final account, lessons learned | Practical completion, handover pack, final account |

#### How this maps to the RIBA Plan of Work
In the UK, many teams describe stages using the RIBA Plan of Work 2020: 0 Strategic Definition, 1 Preparation and Briefing, 2 Concept Design, 3 Spatial Coordination, 4 Technical Design, 5 Manufacturing and Construction, 6 Handover and 7 Use. A client-side project manager is usually most involved from stage 0 to stage 6; a contractor-side project manager typically joins at stage 4 or 5, depending on the procurement route.

### Client-side vs contractor-side project managers
Job adverts often say "construction project manager" without saying which side of the contract the role sits on. Check, because the day-to-day work is quite different.
| Aspect | Client-side project manager | Contractor-side project manager |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main goal | Deliver the client's project within budget, time and quality | Deliver the works profitably under the contract |
| Manages | Design team, contractor, client stakeholders, approvals | Subcontractors, site managers, buyers, commercial team |
| Money focus | Client budget, contingency and value for money | Contractor cost, margin, cash flow and claims |
| Change | Instructs and approves variations | Prices variations and notifies delays |
| When involved | From feasibility to the end of the defects period | From tender or contract award to final account |
| Typical background | Surveying, architecture, engineering or client estates teams | Site engineering, site management or quantity surveying |
Tip
Under many standard contracts, only a named person (for example the contract administrator, employer's agent or, under NEC4, the Project Manager) can issue instructions. Know exactly what authority your appointment gives you before you instruct anything.

### A typical day and week
No two days are identical, but most construction project managers settle into a rhythm built around site visits, meetings and paperwork. The example below is for a contractor-side project manager on a mid-sized building.
| Time | Activity |
| --- | --- |
| 07:30 | Walk the site with the site manager: progress, safety, quality, logistics |
| 08:30 | Review the look-ahead programme and today's deliveries; chase a late steel delivery |
| 09:30 | Respond to requests for information (RFIs) and review subcontractor drawings and submittals |
| 11:00 | Design coordination meeting on the mechanical and electrical services layout |
| 13:30 | Cost review with the quantity surveyor: valuations, committed costs, forecast final cost |
| 15:00 | Price a client variation and draft the notification of its time effect |
| 16:30 | Update the risk register and plan tomorrow's priorities |
Across a week, expect these fixed points:
- **Weekly progress meeting** with subcontractors, comparing actual progress against the programme.
- **Client or design team meeting**, usually fortnightly or monthly on larger projects.
- **Programme update** with a two- to six-week look-ahead for the site team.
- **Cost and change review**: variations, early warnings and the forecast final cost.
- **Health and safety inspection** and review of incidents and near misses.

### Worked example: a four-classroom school extension
The figures below are illustrative, but the steps are the ones a client-side project manager would follow.

#### 1. Back-schedule from the fixed date
A council needs four new classrooms open for the start of the school year. The opening date cannot move, so the project manager works backwards:
| Phase | Duration | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fit-out, commissioning and handover | 12 weeks | Includes furniture, IT and fire alarm testing |
| Main construction | 24 weeks | Steel frame, envelope and services |
| Tender and contract award | 8 weeks | Two-stage tender to bring the contractor in early |
| Design and planning permission | 16 weeks | Planning decision is the main uncertainty |
| Total | 60 weeks | Approval was given 64 weeks before opening |
That leaves only four weeks of [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) on the whole project. Every activity is on, or very close to, the critical path.

#### 2. Protect the critical path
1. Submit the planning application as early as the design allows and hold a pre-application meeting with the planning authority.
2. Bring the contractor in through a two-stage tender so they can advise on buildability and order long-lead items early.
3. Place the structural steel and electrical switchgear orders as soon as the contract is signed, and track them on a separate long-lead items list.
4. Schedule noisy and disruptive work (piling, steel erection) for school holidays.
5. Agree a phased handover: classrooms first, external works can finish during the first weeks of term.

#### 3. Set the budget and contingency
The construction cost plan is £2,400,000. The project manager recommends a client contingency of 10% (£240,000) because the site investigation shows variable ground conditions next to the existing building. The contingency sits in the client's budget, not in the contractor's price, and drawing on it needs the sponsor's approval.

#### 4. Value a variation
During construction the school asks for a covered canopy between the extension and the main building. The project manager handles it like this:
1. Records the request in the variation register and confirms whether it is essential (it is: it shelters the main route between buildings).
2. Asks the contractor for a quotation covering both price and time.
3. The contractor quotes £38,000 and one extra week. The cost consultant checks it against the contract rates: measured work of £31,500 plus one week of site overheads (preliminaries) of £6,000, a total of £37,500.
4. The project manager agrees £37,500 and confirms the canopy can be built during fit-out without delaying the classrooms, so the one-week extension applies to the external works only.
5. Issues a formal instruction under the contract and updates the budget: contingency remaining is £240,000 − £37,500 = £202,500, and project float on the classrooms stays at four weeks.
Tip
Track long-lead items on their own list with order date, lead time and required-on-site date. A late lift, switchgear panel or steel order can delay a whole building.

### Key documents a construction project manager owns
| Document | Purpose | Useful template or guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project brief and execution plan | Scope, objectives, roles, governance and procedures | [Project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) |
| Construction programme | Activities, durations, dependencies and critical path | [Critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) |
| Cost plan and budget | Estimated cost by element, contingency and cash flow | [Project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) |
| Tender documents | Specification, drawings, pricing schedule and contract conditions | [RFQ template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/rfq-template/) |
| Risk register | Risks, owners, responses and contingency | [Risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) |
| RFI and variation registers | Design queries and changes with cost and time effects | [Change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) |
| Monthly progress report | Progress, cost, change, risk and safety for the client | [Project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) |
| Health and safety file and handover pack | As-built information, O&M manuals and certificates for the building's owner | Collected throughout and handed over at completion |

### Skills a construction project manager needs

#### Technical skills
- Reading drawings, specifications and survey information.
- Understanding construction methods, sequencing, temporary works and logistics.
- Building programmes with dependencies, [Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) and critical path analysis.
- Knowing building regulations, codes and the permits your projects need.

#### Commercial and contract skills
- Cost plans, valuations, cash flow and forecast final cost.
- Procurement routes (traditional, design and build, management contracting, two-stage) and standard forms of contract such as JCT and NEC in the UK, or AIA and ConsensusDocs in the US.
- Valuing variations and assessing delay, and using earned value or similar measures on larger jobs.
- Negotiation and dispute avoidance.

#### People and leadership skills
- Leading teams you do not directly employ: designers, subcontractors and client staff.
- Clear written records: instructions, meeting minutes and early warnings.
- Calm decision-making when weather, suppliers or ground conditions upset the plan.
- Visible health and safety leadership on site.
Soft skills often decide whether a technically strong candidate becomes a good project manager, so build them deliberately, for example by chairing meetings and leading client presentations early in your career.

### Qualifications and certifications
Most employers look for a degree or equivalent in construction management, civil or structural engineering, building surveying, quantity surveying or architecture. Experienced site staff without a degree do reach the role, especially on the contractor side, usually with professional membership gained through a work-based route.
| Credential | Body | Who it suits | Requirements (summary) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chartered Member (MCIOB) | Chartered Institute of Building (UK and international) | Construction managers and project managers | A degree plus 3 years' construction management experience (5 with a non-construction degree), then a Professional Review; work-based routes exist for people without a degree |
| Chartered surveyor (MRICS) | RICS | Project managers from a surveying or cost background | Assessment of Professional Competence in a pathway such as project management |
| Certified Construction Manager (CCM) | CMCI / CMAA (US) | Experienced client-side and agency construction managers | At least four years of responsible-in-charge experience across project phases, plus a degree or extra experience, and an exam |
| Certified Associate Construction Manager (CACM) | CMCI / CMAA (US) | Earlier-career construction managers | Four years of general design or construction experience or one year in charge, plus a degree or extra experience, and an exam |
| Project Management Professional (PMP) | PMI (global) | Project managers wanting a cross-industry credential | Typically three years leading projects with a four-year degree (five years without), 35 hours of project management education and an exam |
Requirements change, so check the awarding body's current handbook before you apply. Our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) and [project management certification overview](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) compare general credentials in more detail.

#### Safety training
Site safety training is expected in most countries. Examples include a site management safety course and a CSCS card for site access in the UK, and OSHA 30-hour construction training in the US. These are usually expected rather than optional for anyone who regularly visits site.

### How to become a construction project manager
1. **Get a relevant qualification** such as a degree, degree apprenticeship or higher technical qualification in construction management, engineering or surveying.
2. **Start in an entry role**: site engineer, assistant site manager, trainee quantity surveyor, project coordinator or [assistant project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/assistant-project-manager/).
3. **Build site experience.** Learn sequencing, temporary works, logistics and how trades interact. Field credibility matters.
4. **Build commercial experience.** Spend time on valuations, variations and subcontract packages, even if you start on the technical side.
5. **Take ownership of a package** (for example the envelope or the mechanical and electrical services) and then a small project.
6. **Work towards professional membership** (for example MCIOB or MRICS) or a certification such as CCM or PMP.
7. **Step up to project manager** on a single project, then to [senior project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/senior-project-manager/) running larger or multiple projects.

#### Typical career ladder
| Level | Typical titles | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry | Site engineer, assistant QS, project coordinator | Supports a package or project team |
| Developing | Assistant project manager, package manager, site manager | Owns a package or a small project with supervision |
| Project manager | Construction project manager | Delivers a whole project |
| Senior | Senior project manager, project director | Large or multiple projects, client relationships, team leadership |
| Executive | Operations director, director of projects | Portfolio, business performance and strategy |
For a broader view of entry routes, read [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/).

### Construction project manager vs related roles
The titles overlap and vary between countries and companies. The table shows the usual split.
| Role | Main focus | Where they work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Construction project manager | The whole project: brief, design, procurement, construction, handover | Office and site |
| Construction manager | In the US, often used for the same role or for a construction management firm acting for the owner; in the UK, usually the senior person running construction on site | Mainly site |
| Site manager or superintendent | Day-to-day site operations, trades, safety and quality | Site |
| Quantity surveyor or cost manager | Cost plans, valuations, variations and final account | Office and site |
| Contract administrator or employer's agent | Administers the building contract for the client | Office |
| Architect or lead designer | Design and, on some contracts, contract administration | Office |
On smaller projects one person may combine several of these roles. On large projects the project manager leads a team that includes all of them.

### Health, safety and legal duties
Safety duties are set by national law and the project manager must know who holds them on each project.
- **Great Britain:** the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 (CDM) place duties on the client, principal designer, designers, principal contractor and contractors. According to HSE, a project must be notified to HSE if construction work will last longer than 30 working days with more than 20 workers on site at the same time, or exceed 500 person-days.
- **England, higher-risk buildings:** under the Building Safety Act 2022, higher-risk residential buildings need approval from the Building Safety Regulator before construction starts (Gateway 2) and before occupation (Gateway 3), so build these approvals into the programme.
- **United States:** OSHA standards for construction apply, alongside state and local building codes and permits.
Whatever the jurisdiction, the project manager's role is to make sure the right duty holders are appointed early, that safety is considered in design and that site arrangements are checked regularly. Take specialist advice where you are not the legal duty holder.

### Construction project manager salary
Pay depends on country, sector, project value and whether you work client-side or for a contractor. For the US, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median annual wage of $114,990 for construction managers in May 2025, with employment projected to grow 9% from 2025 to 2035. That category includes construction project managers as well as other construction management roles.
In other countries, use professional body salary surveys (for example from the CIOB or RICS), recruitment agency reports and current job adverts for your region and sector. Compare like with like: a project manager on a large infrastructure scheme and one on residential refurbishments can earn very different amounts.

### Common mistakes new construction project managers make
- **Trusting the programme over the site.** Walk the site often; the programme is only as good as its last update.
- **Weak records.** Undocumented instructions and verbal agreements become disputes later. Confirm everything in writing.
- **Late notification.** Most contracts set time limits for notifying delays and changes. Miss them and you can lose entitlement.
- **Ignoring long-lead items** until the design is complete.
- **Spending contingency quietly.** Report every drawdown so the client always knows what is left.
- **Treating handover as an afterthought.** Plan commissioning, training and O&M information from the start.
- **Not asking for help.** Use experienced site managers and surveyors; they have seen most problems before.
Structured [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) solves several of these at once.

### Software and tools for construction project managers
Construction project managers usually combine several types of tool:
- **Scheduling software** for detailed critical path programmes.
- **Cost and commercial systems** for budgets, valuations and variations.
- **Common data environments and document control** for drawings, RFIs and submittals.
- **Work management platforms** for coordinating design, procurement and client tasks, approvals and reporting across several projects.
For the work management layer, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) suits teams that need Gantt charts with dependencies, resource views and approvals across many projects, and [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) suits teams who prefer a spreadsheet-style interface.

### How construction differs from other projects
| Aspect | Construction | Typical office or IT project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contracts | Formal standard forms, retentions and defined notice periods | Often internal or simpler |
| Safety | Legal duties and serious physical risks | Lower physical risk |
| Changes | Variations priced and instructed under the contract | Change requests through internal control |
| Constraints | Weather, ground conditions, permits, long-lead items | Mainly people, budget and technology |
| Approach | Mostly predictive, with Lean and some Agile practices | Often Agile or hybrid |
Lean tools such as the Last Planner System and short planning cycles are increasingly used in design and pre-construction.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does a construction project manager do?**
A construction project manager plans and controls a building or infrastructure project from feasibility to handover. They coordinate designers and contractors and manage cost, programme, quality, contracts, change, risk and safety arrangements.

**Q: Is a construction project manager the same as a construction manager?**
Not always. In the US the terms are often used interchangeably, and construction management firms may act for the owner. In the UK a construction manager usually runs construction on site, while the project manager oversees the whole project including design, procurement and handover.

**Q: Is a construction project manager the same as a site manager?**
No. A site manager runs day-to-day work on site: trades, safety, quality and logistics. The project manager oversees the whole project, including design, procurement, budget, contracts and client relations.

**Q: What qualifications does a construction project manager need?**
Commonly a degree in construction management, engineering, surveying or architecture, or equivalent experience, plus professional membership such as MCIOB or MRICS, or a certification such as CCM or PMP. Site safety training is also expected.

**Q: Do you need a degree to become a construction project manager?**
A degree is the most common route, but not the only one. Many people progress from site or trade roles, and bodies such as the CIOB offer work-based routes to chartered membership for experienced practitioners without a degree.

**Q: Which certification is best for construction project managers?**
It depends on your market. In the UK, chartered membership of the CIOB or RICS is widely recognised. In the US, the CCM from CMCI (CMAA) is construction-specific. The PMP is a recognised cross-industry credential that complements either.

**Q: Is the PMP useful for a construction project manager?**
Yes. It is recognised in many markets and covers planning, risk and stakeholder management. Construction employers often value industry-specific credentials and chartered status as much or more, so many people hold both.

**Q: How long does it take to become a construction project manager?**
It varies. A common path is a degree followed by several years as a site engineer, assistant project manager or quantity surveyor. Chartered membership routes, for example, typically expect three to five years of relevant experience after a degree.

**Q: How much do construction project managers earn?**
Pay depends on country, sector and experience. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median annual wage of $114,990 for construction managers in May 2025. Elsewhere, check professional body surveys and current job adverts.

**Q: Is construction project management stressful?**
It can be, because of fixed deadlines, cost pressure, weather and many parties to coordinate. Good records, early warnings, realistic programmes and a strong site team reduce the pressure considerably.

**Q: How does a construction project manager handle variations?**
They log the change, get a quotation for price and time, check it against the contract rates, agree it, issue a formal instruction under the contract and update the budget, contingency and programme.

**Q: What is a construction programme?**
The construction programme is the project schedule, usually a Gantt chart showing activities, durations, dependencies, milestones and the critical path. The project manager uses it to plan, coordinate and track progress.

**Q: What software do construction project managers use?**
Scheduling software for programmes, cost and document control systems, and work management platforms such as Wrike or Smartsheet for coordination and reporting. See our [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) rankings.

**Q: Can a construction project manager use Agile?**
Mostly in design and pre-construction, through short planning cycles, visual boards and Lean methods such as the Last Planner System. Construction itself remains largely predictive because of contracts and sequencing.

# Contingency Plan in Project Management: Steps and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Contingency plan in project management explained: triggers, a free template, a 9-step method, worked examples and how to size the contingency reserve.


## Contingency Plan in Project Management: Steps and Examples
A contingency plan in project management is a pre-agreed set of actions the team will take if a specific risk occurs, activated by a clear trigger and funded in advance. Because the decisions are made calmly beforehand, people can act within minutes instead of improvising under pressure. This guide shows you how to write one step by step, with a template, two fully worked examples and a method for sizing the contingency reserve.
- Published 1 October 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- A contingency plan is a response prepared in advance for one identified risk, used only if that risk occurs.
- Every plan needs a measurable trigger, a named decision maker, ordered actions with owners, a reserve, a fallback and a stand-down rule.
- Mitigation acts before a risk occurs; a contingency plan acts when it occurs; a fallback plan acts if the contingency plan fails.
- Write plans for high-impact or time-critical risks, not for every line in the risk register.
- Contingency reserve sits inside the cost baseline for identified risks; management reserve sits outside it for unknown ones.
- Rehearse critical plans and record how each activated plan performed in lessons learned.

### What is a contingency plan in project management?
A **contingency plan** is a documented set of actions that a project will carry out only if a specific, identified risk occurs. It names the trigger that activates it, who decides, what each person does, the time and money set aside, and what happens if the plan itself fails. It is prepared and approved before it is needed.
Five features separate a real contingency plan from a vague intention to "deal with it if it happens":
- **It is tied to one risk.** Each plan responds to a named entry in the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/), not to bad luck in general.
- **It has a trigger.** An observable condition, such as a date, a measurement or an event, tells you the plan is now live.
- **It is pre-approved.** The sponsor or governance body agrees the actions and spending in advance, so nobody waits for sign-off on the day.
- **It is owned.** One person monitors the trigger and one person (often the same) leads the response.
- **It is funded.** The time and money it needs are covered by the contingency reserve.
In PMI terminology, these are **contingent response strategies**: responses designed for use only if certain events occur (the term used in the PMBOK Guide 6th edition). They deal with known-unknowns, risks you have identified but cannot be sure will happen. Contingency plans are one part of wider [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/), which also covers identifying, analysing and reducing risks before they occur.

### Contingency plan vs mitigation, fallback plan and workaround
These terms are often mixed up, including in exam questions. The difference is timing: when the response is used and whether it was planned.
| Response | When it is used | Planned in advance? | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mitigation | Before the risk occurs, to reduce its probability or impact | Yes | Run a load test eight weeks before go-live |
| Contingency plan | When a trigger shows the risk is occurring | Yes | If response times exceed 3 seconds under load, add two application servers |
| Fallback plan | When the contingency plan does not work | Yes | Roll back to the old system and process orders manually |
| Workaround | When an unplanned problem occurs, or a risk with no plan | No | Staff re-key orders by hand while the fault is investigated |
| Business continuity plan | When the organisation's operations are disrupted | Yes, at organisation level | Move the call centre to a second site after a building fire |

#### Contingency plan vs mitigation
Mitigation is proactive: you spend effort now to make a risk less likely or less damaging. A contingency plan is reactive but prepared: you spend nothing (or very little) unless the trigger fires. Many risks need both. You might mitigate a supplier risk by approving a second supplier, and still hold a contingency plan for switching volume to that supplier if the first one misses a delivery.

#### Contingency plan vs fallback plan
A fallback plan exists because contingency plans can fail too: the marquee company is fully booked, or the rollback script errors. Write one where failure of the contingency would be serious.

#### Contingency plan vs workaround
A workaround is improvised for a problem nobody planned for. If you keep needing the same one, the underlying risk belongs in the register with a proper plan. Once a risk has occurred, track it in the [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/).

#### Contingency plan vs business continuity plan
A business continuity plan keeps the whole organisation running through a disruption such as a fire, cyber attack or loss of a key site; ISO 22301 is the international standard for business continuity management systems. A project contingency plan is narrower: it protects one project's objectives against one identified risk.

### When does a risk need a contingency plan?
Not every risk deserves a plan; plans for low risks bury the important ones. Use these rules:
| Situation | Contingency plan? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High score (for example 15+ on a 5x5 matrix) after mitigation | Yes | Residual exposure is still serious |
| Accepted risk with a severe impact | Yes | Acceptance without a plan is hope, not a response |
| Low probability but catastrophic impact (safety, legal, go-live failure) | Yes | Scores understate these risks |
| Time-critical risk where hours matter (events, cutovers, launches) | Yes | No time to decide on the day |
| Medium risk with good mitigation in place | Optional: a short note is enough | Proportionate effort |
| Low risk | No | Monitor at review; write a workaround if it occurs |
The score bands above are an example; use the thresholds from your own risk management plan. Look at the [residual risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/residual-risk/), not the inherent risk: a contingency plan covers what is left after mitigation. If you are unsure how to score risks consistently, see our guide to [project risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk/).

### What a contingency plan contains
A good contingency plan fits on one page. People use it under pressure, so it must be quick to read and unambiguous. Use these fields as your template:
| Field | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| Risk ID and title | Link to the risk register entry |
| Plan owner | Who monitors the trigger and keeps the plan current |
| Decision maker | Who confirms activation, plus a named deputy |
| Warning sign | An early signal that puts the team on alert |
| Activation trigger | The measurable condition that activates the plan, with a decision deadline |
| Actions | Numbered steps, each with an owner and a deadline |
| Resources and reserve | People, budget and time pre-approved, with the spending limit |
| Communication | Who is told, in what order, through which channel |
| Fallback plan | What to do if the contingency fails |
| Stand-down rule | How and when the plan is closed |
Keep the plan with the risk it supports. A small project can hold contingency plans as extra columns in the free [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/), or in a [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) that also tracks assumptions, issues and dependencies. Larger projects usually keep a short plan document per major risk and link to it from the register.

### How to write a contingency plan in 9 steps
1. **Select the risks.** Filter your register for the risks that meet the criteria above. On most projects that is a handful, not dozens.
2. **Describe the scenario.** For each risk, write what it looks like when it happens: what fails, when, and what the first effects are.
3. **Set the trigger and decision deadline.** Choose an observable threshold and the latest time a decision can be made while the response will still work. Add an earlier warning sign if one exists.
4. **List the actions in order.** Write each action as a verb with an owner and a deadline: who does what, by when. Put the actions that buy time first.
5. **Estimate cost and time.** Price each action, including any cancellation fees, overtime or expedited delivery. Estimate the schedule effect and check it against [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) on the affected path.
6. **Agree the reserve and authority.** Agree with the sponsor how much contingency reserve the plan may draw on and who can authorise it. Record the limit in the plan.
7. **Plan communication.** List who must be told when the plan activates, in what order and by which channel, using your [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/communication-plan/).
8. **Write the fallback and stand-down rules.** Decide what happens if the response fails and how you will know the plan is finished.
9. **Approve, store and rehearse.** Get formal approval, store the plan where the team can reach it at any hour (including offline if needed) and rehearse the critical ones.
Tip
Write the actions so that someone who has never seen the plan could carry them out. The person who wrote it may be on leave on the day it is needed.
Assign responsibilities with a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) if several teams are involved, so there is no doubt about who decides and who acts.

### How to write good triggers
The trigger is the most important line in the plan, and the one most often written badly. A weak trigger leads to late activation, arguments about whether the plan applies, or false alarms.
| Weak trigger | Strong trigger | Why it is better |
| --- | --- | --- |
| If the supplier is late | If the supplier misses the 12 March sample date by more than 2 working days | Specific date and tolerance |
| If performance is poor | If p95 page response time exceeds 3 seconds for 15 minutes under test load | Measurable, with a duration to avoid noise |
| If a key person leaves | If the lead engineer gives notice or is absent for more than 5 consecutive working days | Observable event and threshold |
| If it rains | If the forecast at 08:00 two days before shows more than a 60% chance of rain | Named source, time and threshold |
| If the budget is under pressure | If the cost performance index falls below 0.90 for two consecutive months | Uses an existing metric |

#### Warning signs and activation triggers
Many risks give you notice. Use two levels: a **warning sign** that puts the plan owner on alert and starts low-cost preparation (checking supplier availability, briefing the team), and an **activation trigger** that starts the full plan. This avoids both late reactions and expensive false starts.

#### Decision deadlines
Some responses only work if they start early enough. A replacement marquee needs 48 hours; a rollback must start before the old system's data becomes out of date. Work backwards from the response lead time to set a decision deadline, and write it into the trigger: "if X by 08:00 on Thursday".

### Worked example 1: outdoor product launch
This illustrative example shows a complete plan for a risk on an outdoor launch event for 300 guests. The risk register rates heavy rain as probability 3 (possible) and impact 5 (severe) on a 5x5 matrix, a score of 15. Mitigation has already been done: a marquee supplier has been pre-booked on a provisional basis, with a £2,000 cancellation fee if the marquee is not used.
| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Risk | R-07: Because the launch is outdoors, heavy rain could force cancellation or a poor guest experience, damaging press coverage. |
| Owner / decision maker | Events lead owns the plan; project manager decides (deputy: marketing director). |
| Warning sign | Five days before: Met Office forecast shows more than a 40% chance of rain. Events lead confirms marquee and crew availability. |
| Activation trigger | 08:00 two days before: forecast shows more than a 60% chance of rain. Decision by 10:00 the same day. |
| Actions | 1. Events lead confirms marquee with supplier by 10:30. 2. Venue manager approves revised layout by 12:00. 3. Communications lead updates the invitation page and emails guests by 15:00. 4. Catering lead confirms covered serving area by 16:00. 5. Health and safety lead checks marquee sign-off on arrival. |
| Reserve | £6,500 marquee hire plus £800 extra crew, from contingency reserve. Authority: project manager up to £8,000. |
| Communication | Guests (email), press contacts (phone), venue and suppliers (phone, then written confirmation). |
| Fallback | If the marquee is unavailable or fails its safety check: move to the indoor conference room with a reduced guest list of 150, prioritising press and key customers. |
| Stand-down | Plan closes after the event. Record actual cost, guest feedback and decision timing in lessons learned. |

#### How the plan runs
1. **Monday (five days out):** the forecast shows a 45% chance of rain. Warning sign reached. The events lead confirms the marquee and crew are still available. No spend yet.
2. **Wednesday 08:00 (two days out):** forecast at 70%. Trigger reached. The events lead calls the project manager, who confirms activation at 08:40.
3. **Wednesday 08:45 to 16:00:** actions 1 to 4 completed in order. The project manager logs the activation in the issue log and records a reserve drawdown of £7,300.
4. **Friday:** the event goes ahead in the marquee. The plan is stood down that evening.
The plan costs £2,000 if it is not needed (the cancellation fee, a mitigation cost) and £7,300 if it is, far less than cancelling the event. For more on planning events, see our guide to [event project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/event-project-management/).

### Worked example 2: system go-live with a rollback plan
Technology cutovers are classic contingency planning territory: the risk is clear, the window is short and a wrong call is expensive. In this illustrative example, a distribution company is replacing its order management system over a weekend. The old system is switched off at 18:00 on Friday, data is migrated overnight and the new system must be ready for the warehouse at 06:00 on Monday.
| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Risk | R-12: Because data migration is complex, migrated order and stock data may be incomplete or wrong, stopping warehouse operations on Monday. |
| Go/no-go checkpoint | Sunday 12:00: cutover lead presents results to the steering group. |
| Activation trigger | At the checkpoint, any of: stock balance reconciliation variance above 0.5%; fewer than 95% of critical test scripts passed; any open severity 1 defect. |
| Decision maker | Sponsor (operations director), advised by the cutover lead and IT service owner. |
| Actions if triggered | 1. Freeze the new system (IT lead, 12:15). 2. Run the tested rollback script to restore the old system from the Friday 18:00 snapshot (database lead, by 16:00). 3. Run smoke tests on the old system (test lead, by 18:00). 4. Notify warehouse, customer service and key customers (communications lead, by 19:00). 5. Rebook the cutover for a later weekend through change control (project manager). |
| Reserve | Rollback team on standby all weekend (£4,200 overtime, pre-approved). Schedule: a second cutover weekend four weeks later is already held in the plan. |
| Fallback | If the rollback fails: restore from the Friday 20:00 full backup and run manual order processing on Monday using printed pick lists, which have been rehearsed with the warehouse team. |
| Stand-down | If go-live succeeds, the plan closes after five days of stable operation. If triggered, it closes once the old system is confirmed live. |
The plan works because the go/no-go criteria were agreed weeks earlier, the 12:00 decision deadline leaves time for the rollback to finish before Monday, and the rollback was rehearsed, so the team knows how long it takes.
Treat the rescheduled cutover as a formal change: raise it through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) using a [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) so the baseline, budget and stakeholders are updated together. Our guide to [IT project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/it-project-management/) covers cutover planning in more depth.

### More contingency plan examples
Short, illustrative plans for common risks. Add owners, deadlines and costs from your own project.
| Project | Risk | Trigger | Contingency actions | Fallback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Construction | Steel delivery delay | Supplier misses the fabrication milestone by 5 working days | Resequence the groundworks; book a crane for later dates; approve overtime for erection | Source standard sections from a stockist and accept design substitution |
| Software | Third-party API not ready | Provider misses the sandbox release date | Release behind a feature toggle with a mock service; ship other features first | Descope the integration to the next release |
| Any project | Loss of a key specialist | Notice given or absence beyond 5 working days | Bring in the named backup; activate the contractor framework call-off | Reschedule dependent work and use float |

### Contingency reserve: funding your plans
A contingency plan without money or time behind it is a wish. The **contingency reserve** is the budget and schedule allowance for identified risks, held inside the cost and schedule baselines. It differs from **management reserve**, which covers unknown risks and sits outside the baseline.
|  | Contingency reserve | Management reserve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Covers | Identified risks (known-unknowns) | Unidentified risks (unknown-unknowns) |
| Part of the cost baseline? | Yes | No; it is part of the overall project budget |
| Who controls it | Usually the project manager, within agreed limits | Usually the sponsor or governance body |
| How it is sized | From risk analysis: expected monetary value or simulation | Often a percentage set by organisational policy |
| How it is used | Drawn down when a contingency plan activates | Released through change control, which changes the baseline |
See our guide to the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) for how both reserves fit into the overall budget and the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).

#### Worked example: sizing the reserve with expected monetary value
Expected monetary value (EMV) is probability multiplied by impact. For an illustrative product launch programme with four risks that each have a contingency plan:
| Risk | Probability | Cost if the plan is used | EMV |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rain on launch day | 25% | £7,300 | £1,825 |
| Rollback at system cutover | 15% | £18,000 | £2,700 |
| Late delivery of display stands | 30% | £12,000 | £3,600 |
| Loss of key specialist | 20% | £9,500 | £1,900 |
| **Total** |  | £46,800 | **£10,025** |
An EMV-based contingency reserve of around £10,000 works as a **pool**: you would not expect all four risks to occur, so the pool covers the likely total. Two cautions apply:
- If a single large risk occurs, its plan may cost more than the whole pool (the rollback alone is £18,000). For high-impact risks, check that the sponsor will fund the full plan cost, from management reserve if necessary, and record that agreement in the plan.
- EMV is a simple average. For larger projects, a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) gives a range of outcomes and lets you set the reserve at a chosen confidence level, such as P80.

#### Schedule contingency
Time works the same way. Hold schedule contingency as a visible buffer before key milestones rather than padding every task, and check how much [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) the affected path already has. If a plan's actions would push the critical path, note which [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) options you would use to recover.
Log every drawdown against the risk it served, release the share for risks that close without occurring, and report the remaining reserve alongside the top risks.

### Activating and standing down a contingency plan
When a trigger fires, follow a short, repeatable routine:
1. **Confirm the trigger.** The plan owner checks the data and contacts the decision maker. If the decision maker is unavailable, the named deputy decides.
2. **Decide and record** the decision, time and reason, including any decision not to activate.
3. **Execute the actions** in order; each owner confirms completion.
4. **Log it.** Move the risk to the issue log as an occurred risk, record the reserve drawdown and note any new risks the response creates (secondary risks).
5. **Communicate** to the people listed in the plan, then update the [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
6. **Watch for failure.** Agree in advance what would show the contingency is not working, and switch to the fallback plan if it happens.
7. **Stand down.** Close the plan when the stand-down condition is met, confirm the final cost and schedule effect, and update the baseline through change control if needed.
8. **Learn.** Record what worked and what did not in [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/): was the trigger early enough, were the actions in the right order, was the reserve right?

### Testing and reviewing contingency plans
An untested plan is an assumption. Match the testing effort to the stakes: desk-check every plan at each risk review (contacts, costs, lead times), hold a tabletop walkthrough for plans that involve several teams, and physically rehearse technical responses such as rollbacks, data restores and failovers, ideally in a full dress rehearsal before a go-live.
Review each plan whenever its risk is reviewed or something changes, such as a new supplier, a moved date or a new person in a key role, and check the contact details every time.

### Contingency planning in agile projects
Agile teams handle many risks by working in short cycles and delivering the riskiest work early, but contingency plans still matter for risks that short cycles cannot absorb, such as release dates, regulatory deadlines, vendor dependencies and production incidents.
- **Release planning:** agree in [agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) which features would be dropped first if a date is at risk. That ranked list is your contingency plan for schedule risk.
- **Feature toggles:** release unfinished or risky features switched off, so the contingency is simply to keep them off.
- **Retrospectives:** discuss risks that nearly occurred and decide whether they need a plan.

### Tools for managing contingency plans
Most teams start with a spreadsheet: a risk register with extra columns for the trigger, plan owner, actions summary and fallback, plus a link to the full plan. That works well for small projects.
As projects grow, a work management tool puts risk items next to the schedule they affect. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, suits date-driven projects well: its Gantt charts (from the Team plan) show dependencies, the critical path, float and baselines, so you can see what a triggered plan would do to the schedule. [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) makes it easy to build a risk board with custom columns and dashboards, and [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) suits teams that like a spreadsheet-style register linked to a Gantt chart.
Whichever tool you use, keep critical plans available offline as well. If the contingency is "the system is down", the plan should not live only in that system.

### Common contingency planning mistakes
- **Vague triggers.** "If the supplier is late" invites debate. Use a date, a number or an event.
- **No decision maker.** Plans stall while people look for authority. Name a deputy too.
- **No money behind the plan.** If the reserve has not been agreed, the first hour is spent asking for budget.
- **Confusing mitigation with contingency.** "Monitor the supplier" is neither; it is part of managing the risk. A contingency plan is what you do when monitoring shows trouble.
- **No fallback for critical risks.** Contingency plans fail too, especially under pressure.
- **Never testing.** The rollback that has never been run is the one that fails.
- **Not learning.** Each activation is evidence about your risk estimates. Feed it back.
Read our guide to the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) to see how contingency plans fit alongside probability, impact, owners and review dates.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a contingency plan in project management?**
A documented set of actions, prepared and approved in advance, that the project carries out only if a specific identified risk occurs, activated by a trigger and funded from the contingency reserve.

**Q: What is an example of a contingency plan?**
For an outdoor event: if the forecast two days before shows more than a 60% chance of rain, confirm a pre-booked marquee, update the layout and email guests, funded from a pre-approved reserve, with an indoor venue as the fallback.

**Q: What is the difference between a contingency plan and a fallback plan?**
The contingency plan is used when a risk occurs. The fallback plan is used if the contingency plan itself does not work.

**Q: What is the difference between mitigation and a contingency plan?**
Mitigation acts before a risk occurs to reduce its probability or impact. A contingency plan is prepared in advance but only carried out if the risk occurs.

**Q: What is the difference between a workaround and a contingency plan?**
A contingency plan is prepared in advance for an identified risk. A workaround is an unplanned response to a problem that was not anticipated or had no plan.

**Q: What is a trigger in a contingency plan?**
A specific, observable condition, such as a missed date, a measurement crossing a threshold or an event, that signals the plan should be activated. Good triggers include a decision deadline.

**Q: Does every risk need a contingency plan?**
No. Write plans for high-scoring residual risks, accepted risks with severe impacts, low-probability catastrophic risks and time-critical risks. Monitor the rest.

**Q: Who approves a contingency plan?**
Usually the sponsor or governance body approves plans for major risks, together with the reserve the project manager may use, so the plan can be activated without further sign-off.

**Q: How much contingency reserve should a project have?**
There is no universal percentage. Base it on your analysed risks, for example the total expected monetary value of risks with contingency plans, or a Monte Carlo simulation at a chosen confidence level.

**Q: What is the difference between contingency reserve and management reserve?**
Contingency reserve covers identified risks and is part of the cost baseline. Management reserve covers unidentified risks, sits outside the baseline and is usually controlled by the sponsor.

**Q: Is a contingency plan the same as a business continuity plan?**
No. A business continuity plan keeps the whole organisation operating through a disruption. A project contingency plan protects one project's objectives against one identified risk.

**Q: Should contingency plans be tested?**
Yes, in proportion to the stakes: desk-check every plan, walk through multi-team plans and rehearse technical responses such as rollbacks before go-live.

# Cost-Benefit Analysis for Projects: Steps and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: How to do a cost-benefit analysis for a project: identifying costs and benefits, discounting, benefit-cost ratio, NPV, a worked example and pitfalls.


## Cost-Benefit Analysis for Projects: Steps and Example
Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) compares the total expected costs of a project with its total expected benefits to decide whether it is worth doing, or which of several options is best. Good CBAs put money values on costs and benefits over time and discount future amounts to today's value.
- Published 29 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- CBA compares all costs and benefits in money terms.
- Discount future amounts and include a do-nothing option.
- NPV above zero and BCR above 1 suggest a worthwhile project.
- Test key assumptions with sensitivity analysis.

### When to use cost-benefit analysis
- Building a business case or [feasibility study](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/feasibility-study/).
- Choosing between alternative solutions or suppliers.
- Deciding whether to approve a major [change request](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
- Prioritising projects in a portfolio.

### Costs and benefits to include
| Costs | Benefits |
| --- | --- |
| Initial investment: labour, hardware, software, fees | Extra revenue |
| Running costs: support, licences, maintenance | Cost savings |
| Training and change management | Avoided costs, such as fines or downtime |
| Disruption during the change | Faster delivery or better quality |
| Decommissioning | Intangibles: satisfaction, reputation, morale |

### How to do a cost-benefit analysis
1. Define the decision and the options, including doing nothing.
2. List all costs and benefits for each option over an agreed period.
3. Put a money value on each, and note intangibles separately.
4. Discount future amounts using an agreed discount rate; see [net present value](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/net-present-value/).
5. Calculate net benefit (PV benefits - PV costs) and the benefit-cost ratio (PV benefits / PV costs).
6. Test key assumptions with [sensitivity analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/sensitivity-analysis/).
7. Recommend an option, stating assumptions and risks.

### Worked example
A new booking system costs $120,000 up front plus $10,000 a year to run. It saves $60,000 a year. The analysis uses three years and an 8% discount rate (three-year annuity factor 2.5771).
|  | Undiscounted | Present value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Costs | 120,000 + 3 x 10,000 = $150,000 | 120,000 + 10,000 x 2.5771 = $145,771 |
| Benefits | 3 x 60,000 = $180,000 | 60,000 x 2.5771 = $154,626 |
| Net benefit (NPV) | $30,000 | $8,855 |
| Benefit-cost ratio | 1.20 | 154,626 / 145,771 = 1.06 |
The project is worthwhile because the BCR is above 1 and NPV is positive, but the margin after discounting is thin, so a sensitivity test on the savings estimate is essential.

### Decision rules
| Measure | Accept if |
| --- | --- |
| Net present value | Greater than zero |
| Benefit-cost ratio | Greater than 1 |
| [Return on investment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/return-on-investment/) | Above the organisation's target |
| Payback period | Shorter than the maximum allowed |

### Common pitfalls
- Counting benefits that would happen anyway.
- Leaving out running, training or disruption costs.
- Ignoring the time value of money over multi-year periods.
- Double-counting the same benefit under different names.
- Presenting a single number without testing the assumptions.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a cost-benefit analysis?**
A comparison of a project's total expected costs with its total expected benefits, in money terms, to decide whether it is worthwhile.

**Q: What is the benefit-cost ratio in a cost-benefit analysis?**
Present value of benefits divided by present value of costs. A ratio above 1 means benefits exceed costs.

**Q: How do you calculate net benefit in a cost-benefit analysis?**
Net benefit = total benefits - total costs, ideally using present values, which gives the NPV.

**Q: Why discount future costs and benefits in a cost-benefit analysis?**
Money received in the future is worth less than money today, so discounting makes amounts at different times comparable.

**Q: What discount rate should I use in a cost-benefit analysis?**
Usually the rate set by your finance team, often based on the organisation's cost of capital or a required rate of return.

**Q: How do you handle intangible benefits in a cost-benefit analysis?**
Estimate a money value where reasonable, otherwise list them separately and describe them clearly alongside the figures.

**Q: What is the difference between cost-benefit analysis and ROI?**
CBA weighs all costs and benefits, often as NPV or BCR. ROI expresses net gain as a percentage of cost.

**Q: Should a cost-benefit analysis include a do-nothing option?**
Yes. It gives a baseline, and doing nothing often has its own costs.

**Q: Who prepares a cost-benefit analysis?**
Often the project manager or business analyst with finance, for review by the sponsor.

**Q: Where does CBA fit in a project?**
In the business case and feasibility stage, and again when major changes are considered.

**Q: What are the limitations of cost-benefit analysis?**
It depends heavily on estimates of future benefits, which can be uncertain or optimistic.
