# Cost Control in Project Management: Process and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-control/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Cost control in project management explained: the monthly process, EVM and variance analysis, committed costs, forecasting and a full worked example.


## Cost Control in Project Management: Process and Example
Cost control in project management is the regular cycle of measuring what the work done has really cost, comparing it with the approved cost baseline, forecasting the final cost and acting early enough to change the outcome. It is not the same as cutting costs or checking spend against budget. This guide sets out a ten-step monthly process and the techniques behind it, then works through a complete month-end cost review with real numbers.
- Published 28 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 23 min read

### Key takeaways
- Cost control compares actual cost with the value of work completed (earned value), not just spend with budget.
- Run it as a fixed monthly (or sprint) cycle: collect, measure, analyse, forecast, decide, record.
- Track committed costs as well as actuals: purchase orders can lock in an overrun before any invoice arrives.
- Split a variance into price and quantity effects to find out what you can actually change.
- Use reserves only for what they were set up for, and change the baseline only through change control.
- The forecast (EAC) matters more than the variance to date, because it is the number you can still influence.

### What is cost control in project management?
**Cost control** is the process of monitoring project costs against the approved cost baseline, analysing variances, forecasting the final cost and taking corrective or preventive action so the project finishes within its authorised budget. Good cost control measures cost against the work actually completed, and it manages changes to the baseline through formal change control.
Cost control is the monitoring part of [project cost management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-cost-management/). Planning, [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/) and building the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) happen first and produce the cost baseline. Cost control then runs from the first day of work until the final invoice is paid.
In PMI's *PMBOK Guide* sixth edition this was a named process, **Control Costs**, whose tools included earned value analysis, forecasting, the to-complete performance index and reserve analysis. The seventh edition (2021) replaced processes with principles and performance domains. The eighth edition, published in November 2025, has seven performance domains including **Finance**, and brings back process guidance in a non-prescriptive form; the Finance domain includes a process for monitoring and controlling finances. The names have changed, but the work is the same. Our [PMBOK Guide overview](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) explains the editions.

#### What cost control is not
- **It is not cost cutting.** Cost control can lead to savings, but its job is to make the final cost predictable and agreed, not as low as possible.
- **It is not comparing spend with the budget to date.** A project can be "under budget" simply because it is behind schedule. Cost control asks what the completed work should have cost.
- **It is not an accounting report.** Finance systems record what has been paid. Cost control also needs accruals, commitments, progress and a forecast.
Tip
A quick test: if your cost report has no measure of progress and no forecast of the final cost, it is a spending report, not a cost control report.

### Cost control vs cost management, budgeting and cost reduction
These terms are often used as if they mean the same thing. They do not, and mixing them up leads to the wrong conversations with sponsors.
| Term | Question it answers | When it happens | Main outputs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cost management** | How will we plan, fund and control costs on this project? | Whole life cycle | Cost management plan, estimates, budget, baseline, reports |
| **Cost estimating** | What will each piece of work cost? | Planning, then re-estimating | Cost estimates and their basis |
| **Budgeting** | How much money is authorised, and when is it needed? | Planning | Cost baseline, funding profile, reserves |
| **Cost control** | Are we getting the value we planned for the money spent, and where will we finish? | Execution, every period | Variances, forecasts (EAC), actions, change requests |
| **Cost reduction** | How can we make this cheaper? | Any time, often after an overrun | Savings options, value engineering, scope trade-offs |
In short, cost management is the umbrella, the budget is the yardstick and cost control is the regular act of measuring against it. Your [cost management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-management-plan/) should say how cost control will be done: the reporting cycle, the progress rules, the thresholds and who can approve what.

### What you need before you can control costs
Cost control fails most often because the groundwork was never laid. Before the first status date, make sure you have:
- **An approved cost baseline**: the time-phased budget, broken down to control accounts or work packages. See [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).
- **A [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/)** with every cost assigned to a [work package](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/), so there is nowhere for costs to hide.
- **Progress measurement rules** agreed in advance: 0/100 for short tasks, 50/50 or weighted milestones for longer ones, units completed for repetitive work.
- **Cost data feeds** at the same level of detail: timesheets with rates, supplier invoices, purchase orders and accruals.
- **Reserves defined**: a contingency reserve for identified risks (usually held by the project manager) and a management reserve for unknown risks (usually held by the sponsor).
- **Thresholds and authority levels**: what size of variance triggers a report, an escalation or a change request.
- **A change control process** so that approved scope changes update the baseline and unapproved ones do not slip in. See [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
Earned value figures built on vague progress rules or incomplete cost data look precise but tell you very little, so fix any gaps first.

### The cost control process step by step
The cycle below suits most projects reporting monthly. Short or fast-moving projects can run it every fortnight or every sprint. Each step has a clear output, so the cycle is easy to audit.
1. **Fix the status date.** Everyone reports progress and cost as at the same cut-off, such as the last working day of the month. *Output: status date.*
2. **Collect actual costs.** Pull labour from timesheets at the agreed rates, invoices from suppliers, and **accruals** for work done but not yet invoiced. *Output: actual cost (AC) per work package.*
3. **Record commitments.** List open purchase orders and contract balances that are signed but not yet incurred. *Output: commitments register.*
4. **Measure progress.** Apply the agreed rules to each work package and convert progress into earned value: EV = % complete x budget. *Output: EV per work package.*
5. **Calculate the indicators.** [Cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/) (CV = EV - AC), [cost performance index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/) (CPI = EV / AC), [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) and SPI, for each package and in total. *Output: variance table.*
6. **Compare with thresholds.** Flag packages and totals outside the agreed limits. *Output: exceptions list.*
7. **Analyse the exceptions.** For each one, find the root cause and split price effects from quantity effects. Decide whether the cause will continue. *Output: variance explanations.*
8. **Forecast the final cost.** Recalculate the [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/) using more than one method, check it against commitments, and work out the TCPI. *Output: EAC, VAC, TCPI.*
9. **Decide and act.** Agree corrective or preventive actions with owners and dates, draw on reserves where the rules allow, and raise change requests where the baseline can no longer be met. *Output: action log, reserve log, change requests.*
10. **Report and follow up.** Publish the results in the [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) and check at the next cycle whether the actions worked. *Output: cost report.*
Steps 2 to 4 are data collection, steps 5 to 8 are analysis, and steps 9 and 10 are where the value lies. Automate the data collection wherever you can so the review meeting is spent on decisions.

### Worked example: month-end cost review for an office fit-out
A company is refurbishing two floors of an office for 180 staff. The work is planned over ten months. The budget is set up as follows:
| Budget element | Amount | Held by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work package budgets (budget at completion, BAC) | $600,000 | Control account managers |
| Contingency reserve for identified risks | $45,000 | Project manager |
| Management reserve for unknown risks | $30,000 | Sponsor |
| **Total authorised funding** | **$675,000** |  |
The control thresholds in the cost management plan are: report any work package with a CPI below 0.95 or a CV worse than -$5,000, and escalate to the sponsor if the project CPI falls below 0.90 or the forecast exceeds the work package budgets by more than the remaining contingency.

#### The status table at the end of month five
Planned value (PV) at month five is **$290,000**: the budget for the work scheduled to be done by now.
| Work package | BAC | % complete | EV | AC | CV | CPI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Design and permits | $60,000 | 100% | $60,000 | $57,000 | +$3,000 | 1.05 |
| 2. Strip-out and demolition | $45,000 | 100% | $45,000 | $53,000 | -$8,000 | 0.85 |
| 3. Mechanical and electrical (M&E) | $180,000 | 50% | $90,000 | $101,000 | -$11,000 | 0.89 |
| 4. Partitions and finishes | $150,000 | 30% | $45,000 | $51,000 | -$6,000 | 0.88 |
| 5. IT and AV installation | $95,000 | 10% | $9,500 | $9,000 | +$500 | 1.06 |
| 6. Furniture and move | $70,000 | 0% | $0 | $0 | $0 | - |
| **Total** | **$600,000** | **42%** | **$249,500** | **$271,000** | **-$21,500** | **0.92** |

#### Reading the figures
- **CV = 249,500 - 271,000 = -$21,500**, or -8.6% of the work done. The completed work has cost $21,500 more than it was budgeted to cost.
- **CPI = 249,500 / 271,000 = 0.92**: about 92 cents of planned work for every dollar spent. This is below the 0.95 reporting threshold but above the 0.90 escalation threshold.
- **SV = 249,500 - 290,000 = -$40,500** and **SPI = 0.86**: the project is also behind schedule.
- Packages 2, 3 and 4 breach the package threshold. Package 5 looks healthy on CPI, but see the commitments check below.
- A simple budget-versus-spend view would say: "We planned to spend $290,000 and have spent $271,000, so we are $19,000 under budget." That is wrong. The project is spending less only because it is doing less.

#### Variance analysis: what is driving each overrun
The project manager meets each package owner and finds three different causes:
| Package | CV | Root cause | Type | Will it continue? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strip-out and demolition | -$8,000 | Asbestos found behind old ceiling panels; specialist removal needed | Identified risk that occurred (on the risk register with a $10,000 allowance) | No: package complete |
| Mechanical and electrical | -$11,000 | Ductwork clashed with structural beams on floor one; rework needed | Performance issue: design coordination | Yes, on floor two, unless fixed |
| Partitions and finishes | -$6,000 | Plasterboard price rise, plus slower installation | Mixed: price and productivity | Price yes; productivity can be fixed |
For partitions, the variance is split into its price and quantity parts. The package covers 3,000 square metres at a budget of $50 per square metre: $20 for materials and $30 for labour (0.75 hours at $40 per hour). By month five, 900 square metres are complete.
| Component | Budget for 900 m2 | Actual | Variance | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Materials | 900 x $20 = $18,000 | 900 x $24 = $21,600 | -$3,600 | **Price**: supplier raised the board price by $4 per m2 |
| Labour | 675 hours x $40 = $27,000 | 735 hours x $40 = $29,400 | -$2,400 | **Quantity**: 60 extra hours, mostly waiting for M&E to clear areas |
| **Total** | **$45,000** | **$51,000** | **-$6,000** |  |
This matters because the two halves need different responses. The price rise will continue for the remaining 2,100 square metres (another $8,400) and was a known risk. The lost hours are caused by poor sequencing with the M&E contractor, which the team can fix.

#### Checking commitments
Earned value only looks backwards. The commitments register shows money that is already promised:
| Package | BAC | AC to date | Open commitments | AC + commitments | Uncommitted budget |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M&E | $180,000 | $101,000 | $46,000 | $147,000 | $33,000 |
| Partitions and finishes | $150,000 | $51,000 | $62,000 | $113,000 | $37,000 |
| IT and AV installation | $95,000 | $9,000 | $92,000 | **$101,000** | **-$6,000** |
| Furniture and move | $70,000 | $0 | $38,000 | $38,000 | $32,000 |
| **Whole project** | **$600,000** | **$271,000** | **$238,000** | **$509,000** | **$91,000** |
Two findings stand out. First, **IT and AV is already overcommitted by $6,000**, even though its CPI is 1.06. The facilities manager asked the supplier for extra meeting-room screens, and the purchase order was amended without a change request. Earned value would not have shown this for months. Second, the project has committed or spent **85% of its budget** while completing only **42% of the work**, so only $91,000 of the budget is still free to redirect.

#### Forecasting the final cost
The project manager calculates three forecasts and compares them:
| Forecast method | Calculation | EAC | Assumption |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Remaining work at budgeted rates | AC + (BAC - EV) = 271,000 + 350,500 | $621,500 | The overruns were one-offs |
| Current efficiency continues | BAC / CPI = 600,000 / 0.921 | $651,700 | The month-five CPI holds to the end |
| Bottom-up re-estimate by package | Sum of package owners' forecasts (below) | $639,400 | Specific causes, specific fixes |
The bottom-up forecast is built package by package: design $57,000 (complete), demolition $53,000 (complete), M&E $196,000 (another $5,000 of rework expected on floor two even after the fix), partitions $164,400 ($8,400 more price impact, labour back to plan), IT and AV $101,000 (committed) and furniture and move $68,000 (purchase order plus a removals quote).
The **to-complete performance index** to finish within the original $600,000 is (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = 350,500 / 329,000 = **1.07**. The project would need to become 7% more efficient than planned on the remaining work, while it is currently running at 0.92. That is not credible, so the conversation moves to reserves and decisions.

#### Reserves and decisions
| Item | Decision | Funded from | Effect on BAC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Asbestos removal ($8,000) | Approved: identified risk R-07 occurred | Contingency reserve | +$8,000 to demolition |
| Plasterboard price rise ($12,000 total) | Approved: identified risk R-11 occurred | Contingency reserve | +$12,000 to partitions |
| Extra meeting-room screens ($6,000) | Retrospective change request raised and approved by the sponsor | Management reserve | +$6,000 to IT and AV |
| M&E rework ($16,000 forecast) | Not funded from reserves: coordination workshop and clash check of floor-two drawings before work starts | Absorbed as a variance | None |
| Partitions labour (-$2,400) | Resequence work so partitions follow M&E by floor zone | Absorbed as a variance | None |
After the transfers, the work package budgets total **$626,000**. The bottom-up forecast of $639,400 gives a **variance at completion of -$13,400**, made up of M&E (-$16,000) and partitions labour (-$2,400), partly offset by design (+$3,000) and furniture (+$2,000). Contingency of $25,000 and management reserve of $24,000 remain. The project is still expected to finish within its total authorised funding, but the sponsor now knows exactly why, and which risk is left: M&E performance on floor two.
Tip
Notice that the M&E overrun was not paid for from contingency. Contingency exists for the risks it was calculated for. Using it to cover poor performance hides the problem and leaves nothing for the risks that are still ahead. Record the variance honestly and fix the cause.
Our [earned value management guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) explains each of these measures in more depth.

### Tracking the trend month by month
A single month's figures tell you where you are. The trend tells you whether things are getting better or worse, and when they changed. Here are the cumulative figures for the office fit-out, with the period CPI (that month's EV divided by that month's AC).
| Month | PV | EV | AC | Cumulative CV | Cumulative CPI | Period CPI | SPI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | $30,000 | $28,000 | $27,000 | +$1,000 | 1.04 | 1.04 | 0.93 |
| 2 | $75,000 | $70,000 | $68,000 | +$2,000 | 1.03 | 1.02 | 0.93 |
| 3 | $140,000 | $120,000 | $125,000 | -$5,000 | 0.96 | 0.88 | 0.86 |
| 4 | $215,000 | $185,000 | $199,000 | -$14,000 | 0.93 | 0.88 | 0.86 |
| 5 | $290,000 | $249,500 | $271,000 | -$21,500 | 0.92 | 0.90 | 0.86 |
The period CPI dropped sharply in month three, when demolition and M&E started. The cumulative CPI drifted down more slowly, because it carries the good early months with it. That is why you should watch both: the period figure shows a problem quickly, and the cumulative figure is the better basis for forecasts. The slight rise in the month-five period CPI (0.90) is the first sign that the resequencing is helping.
Plot cumulative PV, EV and AC on one chart and the story is visible at a glance.

### Cost control techniques and when to use them
Many articles on this topic list estimating methods such as analogous or three-point estimating. Those belong to planning. The techniques below are the ones you use to control costs once work has started.
| Technique | What it tells you | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Earned value management (EVM)** | Cost and schedule performance against the value of work done | Any project with a budget and measurable progress |
| **Variance analysis** | Why a variance happened, split into price and quantity | A package breaches a threshold |
| **Trend analysis** | Whether performance is improving or getting worse | Every period, using CPI and SPI over time |
| **Forecasting (EAC, ETC, VAC)** | Where the project is likely to finish | Every period; re-estimate bottom-up when something changes |
| **To-complete performance index (TCPI)** | How efficient the remaining work must be to hit a target | Testing whether a budget is still achievable |
| **Commitment tracking** | Money already promised but not yet spent | Projects with significant purchasing or subcontracting |
| **Reserve analysis** | Whether remaining contingency matches remaining risk | After each risk review and each drawdown |
| **Change control** | Whether a cost change is approved and funded | Any change to scope, specification or baseline |
| **Value engineering** | Ways to deliver the same function for less | Before committing major spend, or to recover an overrun |
| **Procurement controls** | Prices, terms and approvals on bought-in costs | Before purchase orders are raised or amended |
| **Timesheet and rate controls** | Accurate labour cost by work package | Labour-heavy projects such as IT and consulting |
On small projects, EVM can be done in a spreadsheet at work package level. On large or government projects, it is often a contractual requirement with a formal earned value management system. Either way, the techniques work as a set: EVM finds the problem, variance analysis explains it, forecasting sizes it and change control deals with it.

### Setting cost control thresholds
Thresholds stop the project manager from reporting every small variance while making sure significant ones are never missed. They belong in the cost management plan and should be agreed with the sponsor before work starts.
There is no industry-wide standard. The right levels depend on estimate accuracy, contract type and the organisation's tolerance for risk. The table below is an **illustration** to adapt:
| Level | Example trigger | Required response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Green | CPI 0.95 to 1.05 and package CV within plus or minus $5,000 | Report figures only |
| Amber | CPI 0.90 to 0.95 or 1.05 to 1.10, or package CV beyond $5,000 | Written variance explanation and action plan |
| Red | CPI below 0.90 or above 1.10, or forecast overrun greater than remaining contingency | Escalate to the sponsor; revised EAC; consider a change request |
- **Use both a ratio and a money amount.** A ratio alone flags tiny packages; a money amount alone misses steady drift on large ones.
- **Set favourable thresholds too.** A CPI well above 1 often means missing costs, overstated progress or padded estimates.
- **Tighten thresholds as the project matures.** Early on, estimates are less reliable and there is time to recover; late on, there is not.
- **Include a forecast threshold.** A forecast that exceeds the remaining reserves should always be escalated, whatever today's CPI says.

### How to bring an over-budget project back on track
When the forecast is worse than the budget, work through the options roughly in this order, starting with those that do not need anyone else's approval.
| Option | Effect | Trade-off or approval needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fix the root cause** | Improves efficiency on remaining work | None, but it needs a real diagnosis, not a guess |
| **Resequence or re-plan the work** | Removes waiting time and rework | May affect the schedule |
| **Change the resource mix** | Lower rates, or more experienced people who work faster | Check the effect on quality and on other projects |
| **Renegotiate supplier terms** | Lowers bought-in costs | Depends on the contract; can strain relationships |
| **Value engineering** | Same function for less | Needs design and stakeholder agreement |
| **Use contingency reserve** | Funds identified risks that have occurred | Only for the risks it was set up for |
| **Reduce or defer scope** | Lowers the remaining cost | Change request; sponsor and customer approval |
| **Request more budget** | Changes the baseline | Change request; sponsor or board approval |
To find the root cause, ask the people doing the work, not just the reports. A [fishbone diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/) helps when the cause is not obvious. Whatever you decide, record it, assign an owner and check the result at the next cycle.

#### When to change the cost baseline
Change the baseline only when an approved change alters the scope or the funding, or when the existing baseline is so far from reality that it no longer helps anyone measure performance (a re-baseline). Both go through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/). Never move the baseline quietly to make a variance disappear: you lose the history and the sponsor loses trust in every number that follows. Unmanaged [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) is the most common reason a baseline drifts out of date.

### Who is responsible for cost control?
| Role | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| **Project manager** | Runs the cycle, owns the forecast and contingency, proposes actions and change requests, reports to the sponsor |
| **Control account or work package managers** | Report progress and forecasts for their packages, explain variances, carry out actions |
| **Project controller or PMO** | Collects data, calculates EVM measures, checks consistency, maintains the change and reserve logs |
| **Finance** | Provides actual costs, accruals and commitments, and reconciles project and company records |
| **Procurement** | Controls purchase orders, contract changes and supplier claims |
| **Sponsor** | Approves baseline changes and use of management reserve; decides when forecasts exceed tolerance |
| **Team members** | Book time accurately and raise issues early |
Make package owners responsible for their own forecasts: when the person closest to the work has to say what it will cost to finish, problems surface earlier.

### Cost control in Agile projects
Agile teams usually work with a fairly fixed cost per sprint and flexible scope, so cost control focuses on the **cost of value delivered** rather than the cost of individual tasks. The same ideas apply at release level.
**Example.** A team of six costs $48,000 per two-week sprint. The release has a budget of $480,000 (ten sprints) and a backlog of 400 story points. A contractor was added in sprints three and four at $3,000 per sprint. After four sprints:
| Measure | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Actual cost (AC) | 4 x 48,000 + 2 x 3,000 | $198,000 |
| Planned value (PV) | 4 / 10 x 480,000 | $192,000 |
| Earned value (EV) | 136 of 400 points done = 34% x 480,000 | $163,200 |
| CPI | 163,200 / 198,000 | 0.82 |
| SPI | 163,200 / 192,000 | 0.85 |
| Cost per point | 198,000 / 136 (planned 1,200) | $1,456 |
| EAC if nothing changes | 480,000 / 0.824 | about $582,400 |
Instead of asking for $100,000 more, the product owner reviews the backlog with stakeholders and removes 60 points of low-value items, leaving 340 points. At the current cost per point, the remaining 204 points cost about $297,000, giving a forecast of **$495,000**: within $15,000 of budget and a decision the sponsor can make with full information.
Points only work as a progress measure if the team sizes the backlog consistently and the total is updated when the backlog changes. Our guide to [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) covers how to use velocity for forecasting.

### Common cost control mistakes
- **Comparing spend with budget without measuring progress.** It hides overruns on projects that are behind schedule.
- **Waiting for month-end finance figures** that arrive two or three weeks late. Use timesheets, accruals and commitments to get a current view.
- **Ignoring committed costs.** Purchase orders and contract changes can lock in an overrun long before invoices arrive.
- **Subjective percent complete**, such as tasks stuck at 90% for weeks. Agree objective progress rules.
- **Spending contingency on performance problems.** It leaves nothing for the risks still ahead.
- **Moving the baseline to hide overruns.** Change it only through change control, and keep the history.
- **Reporting variances without a forecast.** The sponsor needs to know where the project will finish, not just where it is.
- **Treating symptoms instead of causes.** Overtime to recover a schedule often makes the cost position worse.

### Tools and templates for cost control
For small and medium projects, a well-built spreadsheet is enough: one row per work package with BAC, percent complete, EV, AC, commitments, CV, CPI and EAC. Start your baseline from our [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/), track monthly planned and actual spend in the [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/), log realised risks in the [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) and use the [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) for baseline changes. Buying-heavy projects should also follow the controls in [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/).
For larger portfolios, look for project management software that links timesheets, budgets and progress, so actual cost and earned value are captured as the work happens rather than rebuilt each month.
To choose the right forecasting formula for your situation, see our [estimate at completion guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/).
For more on reading the main cost efficiency ratio, read our guide to the [cost performance index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is cost control in project management?**
Cost control is the process of monitoring project costs against the approved cost baseline, analysing variances, forecasting the final cost and taking action so the project finishes within its authorised budget. It measures cost against the work actually completed, not just against the budget to date.

**Q: What are the steps in the cost control process?**
Fix the status date, collect actual costs and accruals, record commitments, measure progress as earned value, calculate CV and CPI, compare with thresholds, analyse the causes of exceptions, forecast the final cost, agree actions and change requests, then report and follow up.

**Q: What is the difference between cost control and cost management?**
Cost management is the whole discipline: planning, estimating, budgeting and controlling costs. Cost control is the part that happens during execution, where actual performance is measured against the baseline and corrected.

**Q: Is cost control the same as cost reduction?**
No. Cost reduction aims to make something cheaper. Cost control aims to make the final cost predictable and within the agreed budget. Cost control may lead to cost reduction when a project needs to recover from an overrun.

**Q: What is the main technique used for project cost control?**
Earned value management is the most widely used, because it compares actual cost with the value of work completed and separates cost performance from schedule performance. It works best alongside variance analysis, forecasting and commitment tracking.

**Q: What are committed costs and why do they matter?**
Committed costs are amounts promised through signed purchase orders or contracts but not yet incurred or invoiced. They matter because they can lock in an overrun before it appears in actual costs, as in the IT and AV package in our example.

**Q: What are control thresholds?**
Agreed limits on variances, such as a CPI below 0.95 or a package overrun above a set amount, that trigger a written explanation, escalation or a change request. They are set in the cost management plan; there is no universal standard.

**Q: How often should project costs be reviewed?**
At every reporting period, which is usually monthly. Short or high-risk projects benefit from fortnightly or per-sprint reviews. The key is a fixed status date so that progress and costs relate to the same point in time.

**Q: How do you bring an over-budget project back on track?**
Validate the data, find the root cause, then consider fixing that cause, resequencing work, changing the resource mix, renegotiating with suppliers or value engineering. If those are not enough, use contingency for identified risks, reduce scope or request more budget through change control.

**Q: When should the cost baseline be changed?**
Only when an approved change alters scope or funding, or when the baseline is so unrealistic that a formal re-baseline is needed. Both go through change control, and the original baseline and the reasons for the change are kept.

**Q: Who is responsible for cost control?**
The project manager runs the process and owns the forecast. Work package owners report progress and explain variances, finance and procurement supply cost and commitment data, and the sponsor approves baseline changes and the use of management reserve.

**Q: What is the difference between contingency reserve and management reserve?**
Contingency reserve covers identified risks and is usually controlled by the project manager as part of the cost baseline. Management reserve covers unforeseen work within scope, sits outside the baseline and needs sponsor approval to use.

**Q: How does cost control work in Agile projects?**
Agile teams usually have a known cost per sprint, so they track cost per story point and release-level earned value, then control cost mainly by reprioritising the backlog. Release EV is the share of planned points completed multiplied by the release budget.

# Cost Estimation in Project Management: Methods and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: How to estimate project costs: analogous, parametric, bottom-up and three-point methods, accuracy ranges, a worked example and tips for better estimates.


## Cost Estimation in Project Management: Methods and Examples
Cost estimation is the process of predicting how much money a project's work will need. A good estimate states not just a number but its range of accuracy, the assumptions behind it and how it was produced.
- Published 27 September 2026
- 4 min read

### Key takeaways
- Choose the estimating method to match how much you know about the work.
- Always quote a range and document the basis of estimate.
- Three-point and PERT estimates make uncertainty visible.
- Re-estimate as the project progresses and knowledge improves.

### Main estimating methods
| Method | How it works | Best used when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analogous (top-down) | Uses the actual cost of a similar past project, adjusted for differences | Early on, with little detail |
| Parametric | Multiplies a unit rate by a quantity, such as cost per square metre | Work is repeatable and good historical rates exist |
| Bottom-up | Estimates each work package and adds them up | The [WBS](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) is well defined |
| Three-point | Uses optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values | Uncertainty is significant |
| Vendor bid analysis | Compares supplier quotes | Work will be bought in |
| [Expert judgment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/expert-judgment/) | Draws on people who have done similar work | Alongside any other method |

### Estimate accuracy ranges
Estimates become more accurate as the project is better understood. Commonly quoted ranges are:
| Estimate class | Typical range | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rough order of magnitude (ROM) | -25% to +75% | Initiation, ideas and feasibility |
| Budget estimate | Around -10% to +25% | Planning, once scope is outlined |
| Definitive estimate | Around -5% to +10% | Detailed planning, once the WBS is complete |
Always quote the range, not just a single figure, so decision makers understand the uncertainty.

### How to estimate project costs
1. Confirm the scope and break it down into work packages.
2. Identify the resources each package needs: people, equipment, materials, services.
3. Choose a method for each package and apply current rates.
4. Add the cost of risk responses and a contingency reserve based on the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/).
5. Include indirect costs, licences, travel, training and inflation for long projects.
6. Document the basis of estimate: assumptions, sources, exclusions and the accuracy range.
7. Review with the people who will do the work and with finance.

### Worked examples
**Parametric:** an office fit-out costs about $1,200 per square metre. For 250 square metres: 1,200 x 250 = **$300,000**.
**Analogous:** a previous 40-screen app cost $80,000, or $2,000 per screen. A new 50-screen app of similar complexity: 50 x 2,000 = **$100,000**, before adjusting for differences.
**Three-point (PERT):** optimistic $8,000, most likely $12,000, pessimistic $22,000. PERT estimate = (8,000 + 4 x 12,000 + 22,000) / 6 = 78,000 / 6 = **$13,000**. The triangular average would be (8,000 + 12,000 + 22,000) / 3 = $14,000.
**Bottom-up:** design $18,000 + build $54,000 + testing $16,000 + training $7,000 = **$95,000**, plus a contingency reserve of $9,500 (10%) = $104,500.

### Tips for better estimates
- Estimate effort first, then convert to cost; see [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/).
- Have the people who will do the work estimate it.
- Keep a library of actual costs from past projects.
- Separate contingency from the base estimate so it can be managed openly.
- Re-estimate at each phase as knowledge improves (progressive elaboration).
- Watch for optimism bias and pressure to hit a target number.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is cost estimation in project management?**
It is predicting the money needed to complete the project's work, stated with a range of accuracy and the assumptions behind it.

**Q: What are the four main cost estimating techniques?**
Analogous, parametric, bottom-up and three-point estimating are the most widely used.

**Q: What is the most accurate cost estimating method?**
Bottom-up estimating is usually the most accurate because it is based on detailed work packages, but it takes the most time.

**Q: What is a rough order of magnitude cost estimate?**
A very early estimate, commonly quoted as -25% to +75% accurate, used to decide whether an idea is worth pursuing.

**Q: What is the PERT formula for cost estimating?**
PERT estimate = (optimistic + 4 x most likely + pessimistic) / 6. It weights the most likely value most heavily.

**Q: What is the difference between analogous and parametric cost estimating?**
Analogous estimating scales the total from a similar past project. Parametric estimating multiplies a unit rate by a quantity, such as cost per metre.

**Q: What is a basis of estimate in cost estimation?**
Supporting documentation explaining how an estimate was produced: assumptions, sources, rates, exclusions, risks and the accuracy range.

**Q: Should contingency be included in the cost estimate?**
Contingency for identified risks is added to the estimate to form the cost baseline, but it should be shown separately rather than hidden in task estimates.

**Q: Who should prepare cost estimates?**
The people doing the work, supported by the project manager, cost specialists and finance, ideally reviewed against historical data.

**Q: How does cost estimation work for Agile projects?**
Agile teams often estimate cost per sprint (team cost x number of sprints) and combine it with relative estimates of scope; see [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/).

**Q: Why is cost estimation on projects often wrong?**
Common reasons are unclear scope, optimism, missing items such as indirect costs, unmanaged risks and pressure to quote a low number.

# Cost Management Plan: What to Include, Example and Template

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-management-plan/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a cost management plan is, the 12 sections to include, a complete filled-in example, a copyable template outline and steps to write your own.


## Cost Management Plan: What to Include, Example and Template
A cost management plan sets out how a project's costs will be estimated, budgeted, recorded, measured and controlled, and who can make which financial decisions. It is part of the project management plan and is agreed before the budget is set. This guide explains what to include, gives a 12-section template outline and shows a complete example for a $1.2 million system rollout.
- Published 28 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- The cost management plan sets the rules for money on the project; the budget and cost baseline are the numbers produced by following those rules.
- PMBOK 6 lists the core contents: units of measure, precision, accuracy, links to organisational procedures, control thresholds, rules of performance measurement and reporting formats.
- Write down financial authority: who can spend, who can release contingency and who can approve baseline changes, with money limits.
- Set thresholds with a ratio (such as CPI) and a money floor, so small packages do not cause noise and large ones do not drift unnoticed.
- Choose earned value rules of credit by type of work, and avoid subjective percent complete.
- Scale the plan to the project: two pages can be enough for a small internal project.

### What is a cost management plan?
A **cost management plan** is the part of the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) that describes how project costs will be planned, structured, estimated, budgeted, recorded and controlled. It defines units, precision, thresholds, earned value rules, reporting, reserves and approval authority, so everyone handles project money the same way.
In the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) 6th edition, the plan is the output of the **Plan Cost Management** process, the first of the four [project cost management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-cost-management/) processes. The 8th edition, published in November 2025, moves cost into a Finance performance domain whose first process is called **Plan Financial Management**. The name has changed, but the job is the same: agree the rules before you produce the numbers.
A good plan answers a handful of practical questions:
- In what currency and units will we estimate and report, and how precisely?
- How will costs be structured so actuals from the finance system match the work breakdown?
- How will we estimate, and how accurate must the baseline estimate be?
- How will progress be measured, and how will we calculate earned value?
- What size of variance triggers an explanation, and what triggers escalation?
- Who can approve spending, release contingency or change the budget?
- What reports will be produced, for whom and how often?

### Cost management plan vs budget, baseline and estimate
These four terms are often used interchangeably, but they are different things produced at different points.
| Item | What it is | Produced in | Changes how? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost management plan | The rules and procedures for managing project costs | Plan cost management | Updated when the approach changes, with sponsor agreement |
| Cost estimate | A prediction of what each piece of work will cost, with a range | Estimate costs | Refined as the project is better understood |
| [Cost baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) | Approved, time-phased work package estimates plus contingency reserve | Determine budget | Only through formal change control |
| [Project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) | Cost baseline plus management reserve | Determine budget | Only through formal change control |
A simple way to remember it: the plan is the rulebook, the estimate is the prediction, the baseline is the commitment you measure against, and the budget is all the money set aside for the project.

### Why you need a cost management plan
- **It prevents arguments later.** If the threshold for escalation is agreed in advance, a CPI of 0.92 triggers a known response instead of a debate.
- **It makes reports comparable.** When everyone uses the same units, rounding and earned value rules, figures can be rolled up across work packages and projects.
- **It connects the project to finance.** Mapping work packages to cost codes means actual costs land in the right place without manual re-coding.
- **It controls reserves.** Clear rules on who can release contingency and management reserve stop reserves being spent quietly or not at all.
- **It supports audits and contracts.** Clients, funders and auditors often expect to see how costs are controlled, not just what was spent.
Even on small projects, a one- or two-page version that covers units, thresholds, authority and reporting avoids most of the common disputes.

### What to include: the PMBOK components
The PMBOK Guide 6th edition lists the typical contents of a cost management plan. The table translates each formal term into plain English with an example entry.
| Component | What it means | Example entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Units of measure | The currency and the units for effort and quantities | US dollars; effort in person-hours; materials in units |
| Level of precision | How far estimates are rounded | Work packages to the nearest $100; reports to the nearest $1,000 |
| Level of accuracy | The acceptable range for estimates, which may include contingency | Baseline estimate within -5% to +10% |
| Organisational procedures links | How the WBS maps to control accounts and finance cost codes | Control accounts at WBS level 2; code format PRJ-CA-WP |
| Control thresholds | Variances that trigger analysis or escalation | Cumulative CPI below 0.95 needs a written explanation |
| Rules of performance measurement | Earned value methods, how progress is credited and the EAC formulas to use | Tasks under one month use 0/100; longer tasks use weighted milestones |
| Reporting formats | What cost reports are produced, for whom and how often | Monthly EVM report to the steering group |
| Additional details | Funding choices, exchange rates, inflation and how costs are recorded | Supplier invoices in euros converted at the budget rate |
Most organisations add three more sections that PMBOK treats as part of the wider plan: **roles and financial authority**, **reserve management** and **cost change control**. Without them the plan describes how to measure costs but not who acts on the results.
Tip
A control account is the management point where scope, budget, actual cost and schedule are brought together and compared with earned value. Each control account has one manager and contains one or more [work packages](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/).

### Earned value rules of credit
The rules of performance measurement decide how much earned value a task earns as it progresses. Choosing them well is one of the most useful things the plan does, because overstated progress makes every cost measure look better than it is.
| Method | How earned value is credited | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0/100 | Nothing until complete, then 100% | Short tasks, within one reporting period |
| 50/50 | 50% at start, 50% at finish | Tasks spanning two reporting periods |
| 25/75 or 20/80 | A small share at start, the rest at finish | Tasks over two periods where a cautious view is wanted |
| Weighted milestones | A set share at each objective milestone | Longer tasks with clear interim outputs, such as design drafts |
| Physical percent complete | Measured quantity done, such as metres laid or units installed | Repetitive, measurable work |
| Level of effort | Earned in line with time passing | Support work with no discrete output, such as project management |
| Apportioned effort | A fixed share of a related task's earned value | Work tied to other work, such as quality inspection |
Avoid subjective percent complete ("about 70% done") for anything significant. Tasks reported at 90% for weeks are a familiar sign that progress is being overstated. Our [earned value management guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) explains how earned value feeds the cost and schedule measures.

### How to write a cost management plan step by step
1. **Check organisational requirements.** Find the PMO or finance policies on reserves, capitalisation, approval limits and reporting. Your plan should apply them, not reinvent them.
2. **Agree units, precision and accuracy.** Decide the currency, effort units and rounding, and the accuracy expected of the baseline estimate.
3. **Structure the costs.** Using the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/), set control accounts and agree cost codes with finance.
4. **Choose the estimating approach.** Say which [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/) methods will be used at which stage, which rates apply and how the basis of estimate is documented.
5. **Define the budget build-up.** State how estimates, contingency and management reserve combine into the cost baseline and budget, and how funding will be released.
6. **Set reserve rules.** Say how contingency is sized (for example, from the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/)) and who can release each reserve.
7. **Define how actuals are recorded.** Cover timesheets, invoices, accruals and committed costs, and the status date used each period.
8. **Set performance measurement rules.** Choose rules of credit by type of work and the default EAC method.
9. **Agree thresholds and reporting.** Set variance thresholds, escalation routes and report formats with the sponsor.
10. **Agree change control and approve the plan.** Define how cost baseline changes are requested and approved, then get the sponsor's sign-off and record the version.
Steps 1 to 3 need finance in the room. Steps 6, 9 and 10 need the sponsor, because they define the sponsor's own authority and what they will be told.

### Cost management plan template (12 sections)
Copy this outline into your project management plan or a standalone document. Delete prompts that do not apply.
1. **Purpose, scope and references.** What the plan covers, links to the project charter, organisational policies and contract terms.
2. **Roles and financial authority.** Who prepares, approves, spends and reports, with money limits for each role.
3. **Units, precision and accuracy.** Currency, effort units, rounding rules and target estimate accuracy.
4. **Cost structure.** Control accounts, work packages, cost codes and how indirect costs are allocated.
5. **Estimating approach.** Methods by stage, rate tables, the basis of estimate and review steps.
6. **Budget, cost baseline and funding.** Build-up from estimates to budget, time-phasing, funding tranches and cash flow.
7. **Reserve management.** How contingency and management reserve are sized, held, released and recorded.
8. **Recording actual costs.** Timesheets, invoices, accruals, committed costs, status dates and the system of record.
9. **Performance measurement.** Earned value rules of credit, EAC methods and measurement frequency.
10. **Control thresholds and escalation.** Green, amber and red limits, the response to each and timescales.
11. **Reporting.** Reports, audience, frequency, content and owner.
12. **Cost change control and plan maintenance.** How baseline changes are requested and approved, review triggers, approval and version history.
To build the numbers that sit under this plan, start with our [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) and track planned against actual spend in the [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/).

### Cost management plan example: warehouse system rollout
The extracts below show the 12 sections completed for a nine-month project to implement a warehouse management system (WMS) across two distribution centres. Adapt the values to your organisation; they are an example, not a standard.

#### 1. Purpose, scope and references
This plan defines how costs for the WMS implementation will be estimated, budgeted, recorded and controlled from approval to closure. It applies the company's capital project policy and the PMO reporting standard. Ongoing support costs after handover are out of scope.

#### 2. Roles and financial authority
| Role | Responsibilities | Authority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sponsor (Operations Director) | Approves budget and plan, holds management reserve | Approves baseline changes up to $50,000 and contingency releases over $10,000 |
| Steering group | Reviews monthly performance and major changes | Approves changes over $50,000 and any use of management reserve |
| Project manager | Owns the plan, baseline, forecasts and reports | Approves spend within the baseline; releases contingency up to $10,000 per listed risk |
| Control account managers | Manage budget and variances for their accounts | Approve spend within their control account |
| Finance business partner | Cost codes, actuals, accruals, capitalisation | Confirms capital and operating split |

#### 3. Units, precision and accuracy
- Currency: US dollars. Effort: person-hours. Internal labour costed at a blended rate of $95 per hour; contractors at contract rates.
- Precision: work package estimates to the nearest $100; control accounts and reports to the nearest $1,000.
- Accuracy: the baseline estimate is expected to be within -5% to +10% of the final cost.

#### 4. Cost structure
| Control account | Manager | Budget (BAC) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CA1 Project management | Project manager | $90,000 |
| CA2 Process design | Operations lead | $150,000 |
| CA3 Software and licences | IT procurement lead | $320,000 |
| CA4 Configuration and integration | Solution architect | $260,000 |
| CA5 Hardware and site readiness | Site engineering lead | $140,000 |
| CA6 Testing and training | Test and training lead | $90,000 |
| **Total work package budgets** |  | **$1,050,000** |
Cost codes follow the format WMS-CA-WP, for example WMS-04-03 for the carrier integration work package. Indirect costs are not allocated to the project.

#### 5. Estimating approach
Initiation used a rough order of magnitude estimate from a similar past project. The baseline uses bottom-up estimates for labour, supplier quotes for software and hardware, and three-point estimates for integration work. Each work package has a basis of estimate listing assumptions, sources, exclusions and the estimator.

#### 6. Budget, cost baseline and funding
| Layer | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Work package budgets | $1,050,000 |
| + Contingency reserve (from the risk register) | $90,000 |
| = Cost baseline | **$1,140,000** |
| + Management reserve (PMO policy, about 5%) | $60,000 |
| = Total project budget | **$1,200,000** |
The baseline is time-phased by month from the schedule. Funding is released in two tranches: $700,000 at approval and $500,000 at the month-5 stage gate.

#### 7. Reserve management
- Contingency is held at project level and linked to named risks. When released, it is moved into the relevant work package budget and recorded in the change log.
- The project manager may release up to $10,000 per listed risk; larger releases need the sponsor.
- Management reserve can only be used through a change request approved by the steering group.
- Unused contingency is reported monthly and returned at closure, not spent on new scope.

#### 8. Recording actual costs
Timesheets are submitted weekly. Supplier invoices are matched to purchase orders and coded by work package. Finance posts accruals at month end for work done but not invoiced. Committed costs (orders placed but not delivered) are reported separately. The status date is the last working day of each month. Hardware priced in euros is converted at the exchange rate fixed when the budget was approved; any exchange difference is reported as its own line.

#### 9. Performance measurement
- Work packages under one month: 0/100. One to two months: 50/50. Longer packages: weighted milestones agreed in the basis of estimate.
- Hardware installation: physical percent complete (scanners and access points installed against plan). Project management: level of effort.
- Default forecast: EAC = BAC / CPI. The project manager may use a bottom-up estimate to complete when the cause of a variance is known to be one-off, and must say so in the report.

#### 10. Control thresholds and escalation
| Status | Cumulative CPI or SPI | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Green | 0.95 to 1.10 | Report as normal |
| Amber | 0.90 to 0.95, or 1.10 to 1.15 | Written cause and recovery action in the monthly report |
| Red | Below 0.90, or above 1.15 | Escalate to the sponsor within five working days with options and a revised EAC |
- Control account variances under $10,000 are reported but not escalated, whatever the ratio.
- If the forecast variance at completion is larger than the remaining contingency, the project is escalated to the steering group regardless of CPI.
- Favourable variances outside the band are investigated too, because they often mean missing actuals or overstated progress.

#### 11. Reporting
| Report | Audience | Frequency | Content |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost snapshot | Project team, control account managers | Weekly | Hours booked, spend and commitments by control account |
| Earned value report | Sponsor, steering group | Monthly | PV, EV, AC, CV, SV, CPI, SPI, EAC, VAC, reserve status, threshold breaches |
| Finance forecast | Finance | Quarterly | Forecast spend by month, capital and operating split |
| Closure cost report | Sponsor, PMO | At closure | Final cost against baseline, reserve use, lessons for estimating |
The monthly cost section is included in the project's [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).

#### 12. Cost change control and plan maintenance
Any change to the cost baseline needs a change request with the cost, schedule and benefit impact, routed through the project's [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) process using the authority limits in section 2. The plan is reviewed at each stage gate and whenever the budget changes by more than 10%. Version 1.0 approved by the sponsor at project approval.

### Applying the thresholds: a month-4 check
Here is how the example plan's rules work at the end of month four, when the project has earned 50% of its work package budgets.
| Control account | EV | AC | CV | CPI | Status under the plan |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CA1 Project management | $40,000 | $41,000 | -$1,000 | 0.98 | Green |
| CA2 Process design | $150,000 | $148,000 | +$2,000 | 1.01 | Green |
| CA3 Software and licences | $160,000 | $176,000 | -$16,000 | 0.91 | Amber: written explanation |
| CA4 Configuration and integration | $78,000 | $87,000 | -$9,000 | 0.90 | Red by ratio, but under $10,000: reported, not escalated |
| CA5 Hardware and site readiness | $70,000 | $74,000 | -$4,000 | 0.95 | Amber by ratio (0.946), but under $10,000: reported |
| CA6 Testing and training | $22,000 | $22,000 | $0 | 1.00 | Green |
| **Project total** | **$520,000** | **$548,000** | **-$28,000** | **0.95 (0.949)** | **Amber** |
- **Project status.** CPI = 520,000 / 548,000 = 0.949, just inside the amber band, so the monthly report must include a cause and recovery action.
- **Forecast.** EAC = BAC / CPI = 1,050,000 / 0.949 = about **$1,107,000**, a variance at completion of about -$57,000. That is less than the $90,000 of contingency, so the steering group trigger is not met.
- **Contingency release.** The CA3 overrun comes from a supplier price increase on additional licences, which was a listed risk. The release needed is $16,000, over the project manager's $10,000 limit, so it goes to the sponsor for approval.
- **Watch item.** CA4 has the worst ratio but a small money variance. The plan keeps it out of escalation, but the project manager notes it as a trend to watch next month.
Without the money floor, CA4 and CA5 would both have been escalated, taking sponsor time for $13,000 of combined variance. Without the ratio, CA3's drift would have been hidden inside the project total. Using both is what makes the thresholds work. For the formulas, see [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/), the [cost performance index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/) and the [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/).

### Tailoring the plan to your project
| Situation | What to emphasise | What to simplify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small internal project | Units, budget, simple thresholds (for example, more than 10% over), who approves extra spend | Skip control accounts and formal earned value; a planned vs actual tracker may be enough |
| Capital or construction project | Cost codes, commitments, retentions, inflation and exchange rates, capitalisation rules | Little; these projects usually need the full plan |
| Agile delivery | Cost per sprint, release budgets, how scope changes affect forecasts | Task-level estimates and rules of credit; measure value at release level |
| Fixed-price contract (as supplier) | Margin protection, change orders and claims, internal cost tracking | Client reporting may be limited to milestones |
| Time-and-materials contract | Rate cards, approval of hours, not-to-exceed limits | Earned value may be replaced by burn against a cap |
| Programmes with formal EVM requirements | Compliance with the client's earned value system requirements, such as the EIA-748 standard | Nothing; follow the contract requirements |
For Agile work, the plan typically fixes the team's cost per sprint and the release budget, then states how forecasts are updated from velocity. Our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) covers the measures most teams pair with cost. If much of the budget is bought in, align the plan with your [procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) approach.

### Who writes and approves the plan, and when
The **project manager** writes the plan, with input from finance, the sponsor, the PMO and the people who will manage control accounts. The **sponsor** approves it, usually alongside the rest of the project management plan.
It is written during planning, **before** the detailed estimates and budget are produced, because it sets the rules those estimates must follow. In practice the first draft is often prepared in parallel with the [WBS](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) and refined once the cost structure is clear.
Review it at each stage gate, when the budget changes significantly, when the contract or funding model changes, and when thresholds are breached repeatedly, which can mean they were set at the wrong level. Record every change in the version history. Clear ownership of these decisions is part of good [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/).

### Common cost management plan mistakes
- **Copying a template without tailoring it.** A 20-page plan that nobody reads is worse than a two-page plan that everyone follows.
- **No financial authority limits.** Without them, every spend decision becomes an email chain to the sponsor, or nobody checks spend at all.
- **Thresholds with only a percentage.** Small work packages trigger constant false alarms.
- **Subjective progress measurement.** Without rules of credit, earned value depends on optimism.
- **Not involving finance.** If the cost codes do not match the WBS, actuals cannot be compared with the baseline.
- **Ignoring accruals and commitments.** The project looks cheaper than it is until the invoices arrive.
- **Reserves without release rules.** Contingency is either spent quietly or never used when it should be.
- **Writing it once and never reviewing it.** The plan should change when the project's size, risk or funding changes.

### Cost management plan review checklist
Before you ask the sponsor to approve the plan, check that you can answer yes to each question.
- Are the currency, effort units and rounding rules stated?
- Is the expected accuracy of the baseline estimate stated?
- Does every work package have a cost code that finance recognises?
- Is it clear how contingency and management reserve are sized and who can release them?
- Are timesheets, invoices, accruals and commitments covered, with a fixed status date?
- Are rules of credit defined for each type of work?
- Do thresholds use both a ratio and a money amount, with a response for each level?
- Are reports, audiences and frequencies listed?
- Are authority limits for spend and baseline changes written down?
- Is there a version number, approval and review schedule?

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a cost management plan?**
A component of the project management plan that describes how project costs will be estimated, budgeted, recorded, measured and controlled, including thresholds, reporting, reserves and approval authority.

**Q: What are the components of a cost management plan?**
PMBOK 6 lists units of measure, level of precision, level of accuracy, organisational procedures links, control thresholds, rules of performance measurement, reporting formats and additional details. Most plans also cover roles and authority, reserves and change control.

**Q: Who prepares the cost management plan?**
The project manager, with input from finance, the PMO, the sponsor and control account managers. The sponsor approves it.

**Q: When is the cost management plan created?**
During planning, before detailed estimates and the budget are produced, because it sets the rules they follow.

**Q: Is the cost management plan the same as the budget?**
No. The plan describes how costs are managed. The budget is the approved amount of money: the cost baseline plus management reserve.

**Q: What is the difference between the cost management plan and the cost baseline?**
The plan is the set of rules. The cost baseline is the approved, time-phased budget, including contingency, that performance is measured against.

**Q: What is a control threshold?**
An agreed variance level, such as a cumulative CPI below 0.95, that triggers a defined response such as a written explanation or escalation.

**Q: What is a control account?**
A management point where scope, budget, actual cost and schedule are integrated and compared with earned value. It contains one or more work packages and has a single manager.

**Q: What are earned value rules of credit?**
Rules for how much earned value a task earns as it progresses, such as 0/100, 50/50, weighted milestones, physical percent complete or level of effort.

**Q: What is the level of precision in a cost management plan?**
How far estimates and reports are rounded, for example to the nearest $100 for work packages and $1,000 for reports.

**Q: What is the level of accuracy in a cost management plan?**
The acceptable range for cost estimates, such as -5% to +10% for the baseline estimate, which may include an allowance for contingency.

**Q: Do small or Agile projects need a cost management plan?**
Yes, but a short one. A small project may need only units, budget, thresholds, authority and reporting. Agile plans usually fix cost per sprint and forecast from velocity.

**Q: How long should a cost management plan be?**
Long enough to answer the key questions and no longer. Two pages can work for a small project; a large capital project may need ten or more.

**Q: What is the PMBOK 8 equivalent of Plan Cost Management?**
The 8th edition places cost in the Finance performance domain, and its first process is called Plan Financial Management.
