# Cost Performance Index (CPI): Formula, Examples, Meaning

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Cost performance index (CPI) explained: the CPI = EV / AC formula, what values mean, cumulative vs period CPI, forecasting EAC, and worked examples.


## Cost Performance Index (CPI): Formula, Examples, Meaning
The cost performance index (CPI) measures a project's cost efficiency: how much budgeted work you get for each unit of money you spend. It is calculated as CPI = EV / AC, so a CPI of 0.90 means you are getting 90 cents of planned work for every dollar spent. This guide covers the formula, how to read the result, cumulative and period CPI, forecasting with CPI and a worked example in which a healthy-looking project CPI hides a real problem.
- Published 29 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- CPI = EV / AC. Below 1 means over budget for the work done; above 1 means under budget.
- A CPI of 0.85 means each unit of work costs about 18% more than planned (1 / 0.85), not 15%.
- Calculate the project CPI as total EV divided by total AC. Never average the CPIs of work packages.
- Watch period CPI to spot changes quickly; use cumulative CPI for forecasts such as EAC = BAC / CPI.
- A good project CPI can hide poor packages, so check CPI by work package and by cost type.
- Compare CPI with the TCPI to judge whether a budget is still achievable.

### What is the cost performance index (CPI)?
The **cost performance index (CPI)** is an earned value management measure of cost efficiency. It divides the earned value of work completed (EV) by the actual cost of that work (AC). A CPI of 1.0 means the work has cost exactly what was budgeted; below 1.0 means it has cost more, and above 1.0 means it has cost less.
CPI is one of the core indicators in [earned value management (EVM)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/), alongside [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/), [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) and the schedule performance index (SPI). Because it is a ratio rather than a money amount, it lets you compare the efficiency of work packages and projects of very different sizes.
In older EVM material and many government contracts, the inputs have different names. Earned value is the **budgeted cost of work performed (BCWP)** and actual cost is the **actual cost of work performed (ACWP)**, so you will also see the formula written as CPI = BCWP / ACWP.
Tip
The project cost performance index has nothing to do with the consumer price index, the inflation measure that shares the CPI abbreviation. If a report mixes inflation and cost efficiency, spell out both names.

### The CPI formula
| Formula | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **CPI = EV / AC** | Cost efficiency of the work done to date |
| **EV = % complete x BAC** | Earned value: the budget for the work actually completed |
| **Cumulative CPI = total EV to date / total AC to date** | Efficiency since the project started; used for forecasting |
| **Period CPI = EV this period / AC this period** | Efficiency in one month or sprint; shows recent change |
| **Project CPI = sum of package EVs / sum of package ACs** | The correct way to roll package figures up |
| **1 / CPI** | Actual cost per unit of planned cost, for example 1 / 0.85 = 1.18 |
**BAC** is the [budget at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/budget-at-completion/), the total approved budget for the work. **AC** must cover the same work and the same period as EV, including accruals for work done but not yet invoiced.

### How to calculate CPI step by step
1. **Choose the status date** and use it for both progress and costs.
2. **Take the BAC** for each [work package](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/) from the current approved [cost baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/), including approved changes but excluding management reserve.
3. **Measure percent complete** using agreed rules (0/100, 50/50, weighted milestones or units completed), not personal judgement.
4. **Calculate EV** for each package: % complete x BAC.
5. **Collect AC** for each package, including accrued labour and supplier costs.
6. **Divide EV by AC** for each package to get the package CPI.
7. **Add up EV and AC** across all packages and divide the totals to get the project CPI.
8. **Compare with last period** and with your thresholds, and note any package that is moving the total.
**Quick example.** A website rebuild has a BAC of $120,000. It is 40% complete, so EV = 0.40 x 120,000 = $48,000. Actual cost to date is $54,000. CPI = 48,000 / 54,000 = **0.89**. The team is getting about 89 cents of planned work for every dollar spent.

### How to interpret CPI values
| CPI | Meaning | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Above 1.0** | Work is costing less than budgeted: under budget for the work done | Are all costs recorded? Is progress overstated? Were the estimates generous? |
| **1.0** | Work is costing exactly its budget | Keep monitoring the trend |
| **Below 1.0** | Work is costing more than budgeted: over budget for the work done | Which packages are driving it, why, and will the cause continue? |

#### Converting CPI into an overrun percentage
A common shortcut is to read a CPI of 0.85 as a "15% overrun". That is not quite right. A CPI of 0.85 means you get 0.85 units of planned work per unit of money, so each unit of planned work costs 1 / 0.85 = **1.176**, a 17.6% overrun. The gap grows as CPI falls. The table shows the effect on a $500,000 budget if each CPI held to the end of the project:
| CPI | Cost per $1 of planned work (1 / CPI) | Overrun if it continues | EAC on a $500,000 BAC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.10 | $0.91 | -9.1% (under budget) | $454,545 |
| 1.00 | $1.00 | 0% | $500,000 |
| 0.95 | $1.05 | +5.3% | $526,316 |
| 0.90 | $1.11 | +11.1% | $555,556 |
| 0.85 | $1.18 | +17.6% | $588,235 |
| 0.80 | $1.25 | +25.0% | $625,000 |
| 0.75 | $1.33 | +33.3% | $666,667 |
This is why small changes in CPI matter more than they appear to. A drop from 0.90 to 0.80 adds nearly $70,000 to the forecast on a $500,000 project.

### Worked example: packaging line upgrade
A food manufacturer is upgrading a packaging line. The BAC is **$500,000** across five work packages. At the end of month six, planned value (PV) is $345,000. Here is the status:
| Work package | BAC | % complete | EV | AC | CV | CPI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Engineering design | $80,000 | 100% | $80,000 | $76,000 | +$4,000 | 1.05 |
| 2. Equipment purchase | $220,000 | 80% | $176,000 | $171,000 | +$5,000 | 1.03 |
| 3. Installation | $120,000 | 35% | $42,000 | $56,000 | -$14,000 | 0.75 |
| 4. Controls software | $50,000 | 40% | $20,000 | $26,000 | -$6,000 | 0.77 |
| 5. Commissioning and training | $30,000 | 0% | $0 | $0 | $0 | - |
| **Total** | **$500,000** | **64%** | **$318,000** | **$329,000** | **-$11,000** | **0.97** |

#### The project-level reading
- **CPI = 318,000 / 329,000 = 0.97.** On its own, this looks close to plan.
- **SPI = 318,000 / 345,000 = 0.92.** The project is somewhat behind schedule.
- **EAC = BAC / CPI = 500,000 / 0.967 = about $517,300**, a forecast overrun of around $17,300 (3.5%).
A sponsor reading only the headline would conclude the project is slightly over budget and nothing more.

#### What the packages reveal
The good CPIs come from design and equipment purchase, which are mostly finished and made up of fixed-price purchases. The work that is still ahead is labour-heavy: installation (CPI 0.75) and controls software (CPI 0.77), plus commissioning, which uses the same installation crews. The early, efficient packages are flattering the total.
Forecasting each package separately, using its own CPI for the remaining work:
| Package | AC to date | Remaining budget (BAC - EV) | Package CPI | Forecast to complete | Package EAC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Engineering design | $76,000 | $0 | 1.05 | $0 | $76,000 |
| Equipment purchase | $171,000 | $44,000 | 1.03 | $42,750 | $213,750 |
| Installation | $56,000 | $78,000 | 0.75 | $104,000 | $160,000 |
| Controls software | $26,000 | $30,000 | 0.77 | $39,000 | $65,000 |
| Commissioning and training | $0 | $30,000 | 1.00 (assumed) | $30,000 | $30,000 |
| **Total** | **$329,000** | **$182,000** |  | **$215,750** | **$544,750** |
The package-level forecast is **$544,750**, an overrun of nearly $45,000 (9%), compared with about $17,300 from the project-level formula. If commissioning runs at the same 0.75 as installation, the forecast rises to $554,750. The project CPI was not wrong, but it was averaging good past work with poor future work.
Tip
When the remaining work is different in kind from the completed work, forecast by package or by cost type (labour, materials, subcontract), not with a single project CPI.

#### Why you must never average package CPIs
A simple average of the four package CPIs is (1.05 + 1.03 + 0.75 + 0.77) / 4 = **0.90**. The correct project CPI is total EV divided by total AC: 318,000 / 329,000 = **0.97**. The simple average gives a small package such as controls software the same weight as a large one such as equipment purchase. Always add up EV and AC first, then divide. The same rule applies when rolling projects up to a programme or portfolio.

### Cumulative vs period CPI
The cumulative CPI includes everything since the project started. The period CPI looks at one month on its own. Here are both for the packaging line:
| Month | EV this month | AC this month | Period CPI | Cumulative EV | Cumulative AC | Cumulative CPI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | $30,000 | $29,000 | 1.03 | $30,000 | $29,000 | 1.03 |
| 2 | $40,000 | $38,000 | 1.05 | $70,000 | $67,000 | 1.04 |
| 3 | $95,000 | $90,000 | 1.06 | $165,000 | $157,000 | 1.05 |
| 4 | $70,000 | $70,000 | 1.00 | $235,000 | $227,000 | 1.04 |
| 5 | $45,000 | $51,000 | 0.88 | $280,000 | $278,000 | 1.01 |
| 6 | $38,000 | $51,000 | 0.75 | $318,000 | $329,000 | 0.97 |
Installation started in month five. The period CPI fell to 0.88 and then 0.75, while the cumulative CPI was still above 1.0 in month five. Anyone watching only the cumulative figure would have seen "slightly under budget" one month and "slightly over" the next, and missed how fast the current work was deteriorating.
- **Use period CPI** to spot changes early and to check whether corrective actions are working.
- **Use cumulative CPI** for forecasts, because a single month is easily distorted by a large invoice or a late accrual.
- **Plot both**, or plot cumulative EV and AC as an [S-curve](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/s-curve/), where a widening gap between the lines shows the same story.

### Using CPI to forecast the final cost
CPI is the main input to the [estimate at completion (EAC)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/). Which formula you use depends on what you believe about future performance.
| EAC formula | Packaging line result | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **EAC = BAC / CPI** | 500,000 / 0.967 = $517,300 | Current cost efficiency is expected to continue |
| **EAC = AC + (BAC - EV)** | 329,000 + 182,000 = $511,000 | The variance so far was a one-off; the rest will go to plan |
| **EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI)** | 329,000 + 182,000 / 0.891 = $533,300 | Schedule pressure will also push costs up |
| **Bottom-up by package** | $544,750 | Remaining work differs from completed work, as here |
Present a range rather than a single number when the methods disagree, and explain which one you believe and why. Our guide to [project forecasting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/) covers how to present forecasts to sponsors.

#### CPI and the to-complete performance index (TCPI)
The **TCPI** is the cost efficiency you would need on the remaining work to hit a target: TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC). For the packaging line, (500,000 - 318,000) / (500,000 - 329,000) = 182,000 / 171,000 = **1.06**.
To finish on budget, the remaining work would need a CPI of 1.06, while the work in progress is running at about 0.75. Unless something changes fundamentally, the original budget is not achievable, and the sponsor should hear that now. Our working rule: whenever the TCPI is noticeably above the current cumulative CPI (by 0.05 or more), the report should explain what will make the remaining work more efficient, or the target should be revisited.

### CPI and SPI together
CPI tells you about cost; the schedule performance index (SPI = EV / PV) tells you about progress. Read them together.
|  | SPI above 1 | SPI below 1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **CPI above 1** | Ahead of schedule and under budget. Check the data is right | Under budget but behind schedule. Is work being delayed rather than done cheaply? |
| **CPI below 1** | Ahead of schedule but over budget. Are you paying for speed? | Behind schedule and over budget. The most serious position: recovering time usually costs more |
Some organisations multiply the two: **CPI x SPI**, sometimes called the critical ratio. For the packaging line, 0.967 x 0.922 = 0.89. A value well below 1 suggests both cost and schedule are under pressure, and it is the divisor in the third EAC formula above.
Bear in mind that SPI based on money drifts back towards 1.0 at the end of a project whether or not it is late, because all planned work is eventually earned. CPI does not have this problem.

### CPI vs cost variance, SPI and TCPI
| Measure | Formula | Type | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cost performance index (CPI)** | EV / AC | Ratio, to date | How efficiently are we spending? |
| **Cost variance (CV)** | EV - AC | Money, to date | How much over or under budget is the work done? |
| **Schedule performance index (SPI)** | EV / PV | Ratio, to date | How efficiently are we progressing against the plan? |
| **To-complete performance index (TCPI)** | (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) | Ratio, future | How efficient must the rest of the work be? |
| **Estimate at completion (EAC)** | For example BAC / CPI | Money, forecast | What will the project cost in total? |
CPI and CV always point in the same direction: a negative CV means a CPI below 1. Report both. CV shows the amount at stake and CPI shows the efficiency, which is easier to compare between projects.

### What is a good CPI?
A CPI close to 1.0 is the goal. There is no universal standard for acceptable limits; they depend on estimate accuracy, contract type and the organisation's appetite for risk, and they should be set in the [cost management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-management-plan/). As an **illustration** only:
| Status | Example CPI range | Typical response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Green | 0.95 to 1.05 | Report as normal |
| Amber | 0.90 to 0.95, or 1.05 to 1.10 | Explain the variance and set out an action plan |
| Red | Below 0.90, or above 1.10 | Escalate, revise the EAC and consider a change request |
Whatever bands you choose, show the CPI trend and a one-line explanation in every [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/), so readers see the direction as well as the number.
Note the upper band. A CPI well above 1 is not automatically good news. It can mean that invoices or timesheets are missing, that progress is overstated, that the estimates were padded, or that cheap work has been done first and the expensive work is still ahead. Persistent high CPIs also tie up budget that the wider portfolio could use.

### Does CPI stabilise early? The 20% rule
You may hear that "once a project is 20% complete, the CPI will not change much". This comes from research on large US defence contracts. Christensen and Heise (1993) studied 155 Department of Defense contracts and concluded that the cumulative CPI was stable from the 20% completion point on most of them, where stability meant the CPI stayed within a range of less than 0.20. In their data, 134 of the 155 contracts met that test at 20% complete. Where the CPI did change, it tended to get worse rather than better.
The rule has since been widely over-applied. Later commentary, such as Mosaic Projects' paper on the "CPI stability myth" citing Henderson and Zwikael (2008), argues that stability is not something to rely on, especially on smaller commercial projects. Part of the effect is also arithmetic: as more work is completed, each new month moves the cumulative ratio less.
The practical lessons are:
- **An early low CPI is a serious warning.** Do not assume it will recover on its own.
- **Act early.** The further a project progresses, the less any action can move the cumulative CPI.
- **Do not stop managing after 20%.** A change in the CPI trend usually means something on the project has changed.
- **Use the TCPI** to judge whether recovery is realistic, rather than hoping the CPI will drift back.

### How to improve a low CPI
1. **Validate the data.** Check progress claims and make sure AC includes accruals and nothing from other projects.
2. **Find the packages and cost types driving the result.** A detailed [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) makes this possible. Look at package CPIs and, where possible, labour versus materials versus subcontract.
3. **Separate price from quantity.** Are you paying more per hour or unit, or using more hours or units than planned?
4. **Identify the root cause** with the people doing the work. A [fishbone diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/) helps when causes are mixed.
5. **Decide whether the cause will continue,** and update the EAC on that basis.
6. **Act on the remaining work:** fix sequencing and rework, change the resource mix, renegotiate rates or use value engineering.
7. **Raise a change request** if scope or the baseline must change, through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
8. **Watch the period CPI** over the next one or two cycles to confirm the actions are working.
For the full monthly routine around these steps, see our guide to [cost control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-control/).

### CPI in Agile projects
Agile teams can calculate CPI at release level. Use the release budget as BAC, the share of planned story points completed as percent complete, and the team's cost to date as AC.
**Example.** A team costs $25,000 per sprint, and a 12-sprint release has a budget of $300,000 and 240 story points. After five sprints, the team has completed 110 points and spent $125,000.
- EV = 110 / 240 x 300,000 = **$137,500**.
- CPI = 137,500 / 125,000 = **1.10**: the team is delivering more points per dollar than planned.
- Now the product owner adds 30 points of new scope without changing the budget. Percent complete becomes 110 / 270, so EV falls to $122,222 and CPI to **0.98**, even though nothing about the team's efficiency has changed.
The lesson is that in Agile, scope changes to the backlog must be matched by a decision about the release budget, or the CPI stops measuring efficiency. Pair it with velocity; see our guides to [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) and [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).

### How to calculate CPI in Excel or Google Sheets
Set up one row per work package with these columns:
| Column | Heading | Formula (row 2) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Work package | Text |
| B | BAC | Value from the baseline |
| C | % complete | Value, for example 35% |
| D | EV | =B2*C2 |
| E | AC | Value from timesheets and invoices |
| F | CV | =D2-E2 |
| G | CPI | =IFERROR(D2/E2,"-") |
For the project total, use **=SUM(D2:D6)/SUM(E2:E6)**, not =AVERAGE(G2:G6). For the period CPI, keep last month's cumulative EV and AC in two extra columns and divide the differences. Conditional formatting on column G against your thresholds turns the sheet into a simple traffic-light report. Our [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) and [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) give you a starting point, and the [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) helps you build the BAC by work package.

### Common CPI mistakes
- **Averaging package CPIs** instead of dividing total EV by total AC.
- **Mismatched data**: EV at one status date and AC at another, or AC missing accruals.
- **Subjective percent complete**, which inflates EV and the CPI with it.
- **Reading 1 - CPI as the overrun.** Use 1 / CPI - 1 instead.
- **Relying on one month's figure.** Look at the trend over several periods.
- **Trusting a good project CPI** without checking packages and cost types.
- **Ignoring committed costs**, such as purchase orders that will overrun a package with a healthy CPI today.
- **Including management reserve in BAC**, which blurs the measure of performance against the baseline.

### Related measures and templates
CPI is most useful as part of a full earned value report. If you are preparing for an exam, these calculations appear regularly in the [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) and [CAPM certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) syllabuses.
To see how CPI combines with PV, EV and AC in one worked example, read our guide to [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).
To choose between EAC formulas and explain a forecast to a sponsor, see our guide to the [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/).
For the money-amount version of the same measure, read [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the cost performance index?**
The cost performance index (CPI) is an earned value measure of cost efficiency. It compares the budgeted value of the work completed with what that work actually cost: CPI = EV / AC.

**Q: What is the formula for CPI?**
CPI = EV / AC, where EV is earned value (percent complete x budget at completion) and AC is the actual cost of the work completed. In older terms, CPI = BCWP / ACWP.

**Q: What does a CPI of 1 mean?**
The work completed has cost exactly what was budgeted for it, so the project is on budget for the work done.

**Q: What does a CPI below 1 mean?**
The work completed has cost more than its budget. For example, a CPI of 0.90 means the project is getting 90 cents of planned work for every dollar spent.

**Q: What does a CPI of 0.8 mean?**
Each dollar is buying 80 cents of planned work, so each unit of work costs 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 times its budget. If that continues, the project will finish 25% over budget: a $500,000 budget becomes $625,000.

**Q: Is a CPI above 1 always good?**
No. It can mean genuine efficiency, but it can also mean missing costs, overstated progress, padded estimates or expensive work still to come. Investigate high CPIs as well as low ones.

**Q: What is a good CPI?**
A CPI close to 1.0. Organisations set their own limits in the cost management plan, for example treating 0.95 to 1.05 as acceptable and escalating below 0.90. There is no universal standard.

**Q: What is the difference between CPI and SPI?**
CPI = EV / AC measures cost efficiency. SPI = EV / PV measures schedule efficiency: how much of the planned work has been done. Both use earned value, and they should be read together.

**Q: What is the difference between CPI and cost variance?**
Both use EV and AC. Cost variance is the difference in money (EV - AC); CPI is the ratio (EV / AC). A negative cost variance always means a CPI below 1.

**Q: How do you forecast EAC using CPI?**
The most common formula is EAC = BAC / CPI, which assumes current cost efficiency continues. With a BAC of $500,000 and a CPI of 0.967, EAC is about $517,300. Other formulas use CPI x SPI or a bottom-up re-estimate.

**Q: Should I use cumulative or period CPI?**
Use both. Cumulative CPI is more stable and is used for forecasts. Period CPI shows recent performance and reveals problems, or improvements, much sooner.

**Q: What is TCPI and how is it different from CPI?**
CPI looks back at efficiency achieved so far. TCPI looks forward: the efficiency needed on the remaining work to meet a target, TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC). If TCPI is well above CPI, the target is unlikely to be met.

**Q: Does CPI stabilise after 20% complete?**
Research on large US defence contracts (Christensen and Heise, 1993) found that cumulative CPI was usually stable from about 20% complete. Later work questions how far this applies to other projects, so treat it as a warning to act early, not a guarantee.

**Q: Is the cost performance index the same as the consumer price index?**
No. Both are abbreviated to CPI, but the consumer price index measures inflation in an economy, while the cost performance index measures cost efficiency on a project.

# Cost Variance (CV): Formula, Examples and Analysis

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Cost variance (CV) explained: the CV = EV - AC formula, CV%, worked examples by work package, thresholds, causes, VAC and how to act on a negative CV.


## Cost Variance (CV): Formula, Examples and Analysis
Cost variance (CV) tells you whether the work completed on a project has cost more or less than was budgeted for it. In earned value management it is calculated as CV = EV - AC: a negative result means you are over budget for the work done, and a positive result means you are under. This guide covers the formula, a worked example across five work packages, how to set thresholds and what to do when the number turns red.
- Published 29 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- CV = EV - AC. Negative means over budget for the work done; positive means under budget.
- CV% = CV / EV x 100 lets you compare work packages and projects of different sizes.
- Compare actual cost with earned value, not with planned spend; otherwise schedule and cost effects get mixed up.
- Break CV down by work package to find what is driving it, and track the cumulative trend month by month.
- Set thresholds with both a percentage and a money amount, and agree in advance what happens when they are breached.
- Always read CV alongside schedule variance, CPI and the estimate at completion.

### What is cost variance (CV)?
**Cost variance (CV)** is the difference between the budgeted cost of the work actually completed (earned value, EV) and the actual cost of that work (AC) at a given status date. It shows, in money, whether completed work has cost more or less than planned. A negative CV means the project is over budget for the work done.
Cost variance is one of the core measures in [earned value management (EVM)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/), alongside [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/), the [cost performance index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/) and the [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/). It is calculated for the project as a whole and, more usefully, for each [work package](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/) or control account.
In older EVM material and in some government contracts, you will see different names for the same inputs:
| Current term | Older term | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Earned value (EV) | BCWP: budgeted cost of work performed | The budget for the work actually done |
| Actual cost (AC) | ACWP: actual cost of work performed | What that work really cost |
| Planned value (PV) | BCWS: budgeted cost of work scheduled | The budget for the work that should have been done by now |
So **CV = BCWP - ACWP** is exactly the same formula as CV = EV - AC.
Tip
In general finance, "cost variance" or "budget variance" often just means actual spend compared with budget. In project management with EVM, cost variance always compares actual cost with the **value of work completed**. That distinction is the whole point of the measure, and it is covered in detail below.

### The cost variance formula
| Formula | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **CV = EV - AC** | Cost variance in money, for the work done to date |
| **CV% = (CV / EV) x 100** | Cost variance as a percentage of the work done |
| **EV = % complete x BAC** | Earned value for a work package or project |
| **VAC = BAC - EAC** | Variance at completion: the cost variance expected at the end |
Where **BAC** is the [budget at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/budget-at-completion/), the total approved budget, and **EAC** is the estimate at completion, the current forecast of the final cost.

#### How to read the result
| Result | Meaning | Typical response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CV > 0 (positive) | Completed work cost less than budgeted: under budget | Check the data is complete, then look for lessons or release contingency |
| CV = 0 | Completed work cost exactly its budget | Keep monitoring |
| CV < 0 (negative) | Completed work cost more than budgeted: over budget | Find the cause, forecast the impact and agree action |
The sign convention in EVM is simple to remember: **negative is bad** for both cost variance and schedule variance. Some finance teams use the opposite convention for budget variances (actual minus budget), so check which one a report uses before you read it.

### How to calculate cost variance step by step
1. **Fix the status date.** All figures must relate to the same cut-off, such as the last working day of the month.
2. **Confirm the BAC for each work package.** Use the current approved [cost baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/), including approved changes, and exclude management reserve.
3. **Measure progress.** Apply your agreed percent-complete rules, such as 0/100 for short tasks, 50/50, or weighted milestones for longer ones, to each work package.
4. **Calculate EV** for each work package: % complete x BAC. Add them up for the project total.
5. **Collect AC** for the same work, including accruals for work done but not yet invoiced, and timesheet hours at the right rates.
6. **Calculate CV and CV%** for each work package and for the total.
7. **Calculate CPI** (EV / AC) and compare with the previous period to see the trend.
8. **Compare with your thresholds** and write a variance explanation for anything outside them.
9. **Update the forecast**: recalculate EAC and VAC, and report the result in your [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
Steps 3 and 5 are where most errors come from. If progress is overstated, EV is too high and CV looks better than it is. If costs are missing because invoices lag the work, AC is too low with the same effect. Both problems make the project look healthier than it is, so the bad news arrives late.

### Worked example: CRM implementation by work package
A company is implementing a new customer relationship management (CRM) system. The budget at completion is **$400,000**, split across five work packages. Here is the position at the end of month five.
| Work package | BAC | % complete | EV | AC | CV | CV% | CPI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Requirements and design | $60,000 | 100% | $60,000 | $58,000 | +$2,000 | +3.3% | 1.03 |
| 2. Configuration and build | $140,000 | 60% | $84,000 | $103,000 | -$19,000 | -22.6% | 0.82 |
| 3. Data migration | $70,000 | 40% | $28,000 | $26,500 | +$1,500 | +5.4% | 1.06 |
| 4. Testing | $80,000 | 10% | $8,000 | $9,500 | -$1,500 | -18.8% | 0.84 |
| 5. Training and go-live | $50,000 | 0% | $0 | $0 | $0 | - | - |
| **Project total** | **$400,000** | **45%** | **$180,000** | **$197,000** | **-$17,000** | **-9.4%** | **0.91** |

#### Calculating the totals
- EV = 60,000 + 84,000 + 28,000 + 8,000 + 0 = **$180,000** (45% of the BAC).
- CV = 180,000 - 197,000 = **-$17,000**.
- CV% = -17,000 / 180,000 x 100 = **-9.4%**.
- CPI = 180,000 / 197,000 = **0.914**: the project is getting about 91 cents of planned work for every dollar spent.

#### What the breakdown tells you
- The whole overrun is explained by **configuration and build**: -$19,000, or 22.6% over for the work done. The other packages net to +$2,000.
- **Testing** has a large percentage variance (-18.8%) but only -$1,500 in money, because it has barely started. Watch it, but it is not yet the priority.
- Requirements came in slightly under budget, and data migration is running efficiently so far.
Without the breakdown, the project total (-9.4%) suggests a general problem. With it, you know where to look: in this case, the build team's productivity, the supplier's rates or unplanned customisation.

#### Turning CV into a forecast
CV tells you where you are; the forecast tells you where you are heading.
- If the current efficiency continues: **EAC = BAC / CPI** = 400,000 / 0.914 = about **$437,800**.
- **VAC = BAC - EAC** = 400,000 - 437,800 = about **-$37,800**. The project is heading for a 9.4% overrun.
- If the overrun was a one-off and the remaining work goes to plan: EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) = 197,000 + 220,000 = **$417,000**, a VAC of -$17,000.
- To finish on the original budget, the remaining work would need a **TCPI** of (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = 220,000 / 203,000 = **1.08**, which is better efficiency than any work package has achieved so far.
The honest message to the sponsor is that the project is likely to need between $17,000 and $38,000 more than budgeted unless the build issue is fixed. Our [estimate at completion guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/) explains how to choose between the formulas.

### Cumulative and period cost variance
Most reports show **cumulative** CV: everything from the start of the project to the status date. **Period** CV looks at one month (or week) on its own and shows when a problem started. Here are both for the CRM project.
| Month | EV this month | AC this month | Period CV | Cumulative CV | Cumulative CV% | Cumulative CPI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | $20,000 | $19,000 | +$1,000 | +$1,000 | +5.0% | 1.05 |
| 2 | $25,000 | $25,000 | $0 | +$1,000 | +2.2% | 1.02 |
| 3 | $40,000 | $44,000 | -$4,000 | -$3,000 | -3.5% | 0.97 |
| 4 | $45,000 | $51,000 | -$6,000 | -$9,000 | -6.9% | 0.94 |
| 5 | $50,000 | $58,000 | -$8,000 | -$17,000 | -9.4% | 0.91 |
The period figures show the variance getting worse every month since month three, when the build started. This is a **trend**, not a blip, which supports the more pessimistic EAC. If month five had shown a positive period CV, you would have evidence that corrective action was working, even though the cumulative figure was still negative.
Tip
Plot cumulative EV, AC and PV on one chart. The gap between the AC and EV lines is your cost variance; the gap between the PV and EV lines is your schedule variance. See our guide to the [S-curve](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/s-curve/).

### Why cost variance uses EV, not planned spend
The most common misreading of project costs is to compare actual cost with the planned spend to date (PV). In the CRM example at month five:
| Comparison | Calculation | Result | What it seems to say |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Actual vs planned spend | PV - AC = 205,000 - 197,000 | +$8,000 | "We are $8,000 under budget" |
| Cost variance (EVM) | EV - AC = 180,000 - 197,000 | -$17,000 | "The work we have done cost $17,000 more than budgeted" |
| Schedule variance (EVM) | EV - PV = 180,000 - 205,000 | -$25,000 | "We are $25,000 of work behind plan" |
The project has spent less than planned only because it has done less work than planned. Comparing AC with PV mixes up two different questions, "are we spending efficiently?" and "are we on time?", and here it hides a real overrun. EVM separates them: **CV for cost, SV for schedule**, both measured against the value of work actually earned.
This is why a simple budget-versus-actual spreadsheet is not enough for anything but the smallest projects. You need a measure of progress, not just spend.

### Reading cost variance with schedule variance
CV on its own only tells half the story. Read it alongside SV to understand the project's real position.
| CV | SV | What it usually means | Questions to ask |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Positive | Positive | Ahead of schedule and under budget | Is progress reported accurately? Can contingency be released? |
| Positive | Negative | Under budget but behind schedule | Is work being delayed rather than done cheaply? Are resources missing? |
| Negative | Positive | Ahead of schedule but over budget | Are we paying for speed (overtime, extra staff)? Was that agreed? |
| Negative | Negative | Behind schedule and over budget | What is the root cause? Is a re-plan or change request needed? |
The CRM project is in the bottom row: negative CV and negative SV (SPI = 180,000 / 205,000 = 0.88). That is the most serious combination, because catching up on schedule will usually cost more money, making the cost variance worse.

### Cost variance vs CPI, VAC and budget variance
| Measure | Formula | Type | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cost variance (CV)** | EV - AC | Money amount, to date | Showing the size of the overrun or saving so far |
| **CV%** | CV / EV x 100 | Percentage, to date | Comparing work packages and projects; thresholds |
| **Cost performance index (CPI)** | EV / AC | Ratio, to date | Efficiency trend; forecasting EAC |
| **Variance at completion (VAC)** | BAC - EAC | Money amount, forecast | Showing the expected overrun at the end |
| **Schedule variance (SV)** | EV - PV | Money amount, to date | Showing how far ahead or behind plan the work is |
| **Budget variance (finance)** | Budget - actual, or actual - budget | Money amount, by cost line | Accounting control by period and cost code |
CV and CPI use the same inputs and always point the same way: a negative CV means CPI is below 1. CV shows the money at stake; CPI shows efficiency and travels well between projects of different sizes. Report both.

#### Accounting cost variances
You may also see **material, labour and overhead variances**. These come from standard costing in management accounting rather than from EVM. They split a variance into its price and quantity (or rate and efficiency) components. For example, a labour variance can be divided into a rate variance (paying more per hour than planned) and an efficiency variance (using more hours than planned).
They are useful for explaining a project cost variance. If configuration and build is $19,000 over, finding that $4,000 is due to higher contractor rates and $15,000 to extra hours tells you where to act. But they are a diagnostic tool, not a replacement for EVM's comparison with earned value.

### Variance thresholds and when to act
Not every variance needs a meeting. Most organisations set **variance thresholds** in the [cost management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-management-plan/): limits beyond which the project manager must explain the variance, forecast its impact and propose action. Thresholds are usually set for both CV and SV, and often tighten as the project matures, because there is less time to recover.
There is no universal standard for the right threshold. It depends on the industry, the contract type, the accuracy of the estimates and the organisation's tolerance for risk. The table below is an **example** to adapt, not a rule:
| Status | Example threshold (cumulative) | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Green | CV% within plus or minus 5%, and under $10,000 | Report as normal |
| Amber | CV% between 5% and 10%, or $10,000 to $25,000 | Written variance explanation and recovery plan in the next report |
| Red | CV% beyond 10%, or over $25,000 | Escalate to the sponsor or board; revised EAC; consider a change request |
Using both a percentage and a money amount avoids two problems. A percentage alone flags small packages, like testing in the CRM example (-18.8% but only -$1,500), and creates noise. A money amount alone misses meaningful drift on large packages. Many teams also set a favourable threshold, because a large positive variance often signals a data or estimating problem.
Under the example thresholds, the CRM project as a whole (-9.4%, -$17,000) is **amber**, and the configuration and build package (-22.6%, -$19,000) is **red** at the package level.

### Common causes of cost variance

#### Causes of a negative cost variance
- **Optimistic or incomplete estimates.** Missing tasks, low productivity assumptions or no allowance for risk. See [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/).
- **Higher rates or prices than planned.** Labour rates, contractor day rates, materials, currency movements or inflation.
- **Rework.** Defects, unclear requirements or late design changes that mean work is done twice.
- **Unapproved scope changes.** [Scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) absorbed without going through change control, so cost rises but the budget does not.
- **Lower productivity.** Inexperienced staff, interruptions, context switching or tools that do not work.
- **Schedule pressure.** Overtime, expediting fees or extra resources added to recover lost time.
- **Realised risks.** Ground conditions, supplier failure, regulatory changes, outages.

#### When a positive cost variance is a warning
An underspend is not automatically good news. Check for these before celebrating:
- **Missing actual costs**: invoices not yet received, timesheets not submitted or accruals not posted.
- **Overstated progress**: tasks claimed as further along than they are, which inflates EV.
- **Padded estimates**: a large, persistent positive CV suggests the budget was too generous and could have been used elsewhere in the portfolio.
- **Deferred work**: cheaper work done first while the expensive, risky work is still ahead.
- **Quality shortcuts**: lower cost now, higher cost later in testing or support.
To find the real cause of a significant variance, a structured technique such as a [fishbone diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/) or five whys works well with the team that did the work.

### How to respond to a negative cost variance
1. **Validate the data.** Confirm progress measurement and actual costs, including accruals, before anyone draws conclusions.
2. **Locate the variance.** Drill down from the project to the control account, work package and cost line until you find what is driving it.
3. **Find the root cause.** Separate price from quantity: are you paying more per unit, or using more units?
4. **Decide whether it is typical or atypical.** Will the cause continue (a structural productivity issue) or was it a one-off (a single supplier failure)? This decides which EAC formula to use.
5. **Forecast the impact.** Recalculate EAC and VAC, and check the effect on contingency.
6. **Agree corrective or preventive actions.** Assign owners and dates.
7. **Raise a change request if the baseline is no longer realistic,** and route it through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
8. **Record the decision** and monitor the next period's CV to check the actions are working.

#### Corrective action options
| Option | When it helps | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fix the root cause (training, tooling, clearer requirements) | Productivity or rework problems | Takes time to show in the numbers |
| Renegotiate rates or change suppliers | Price-driven variances | Contract terms and switching costs |
| Re-sequence or simplify the remaining work | When there is flexibility in the design or approach | Quality and stakeholder expectations |
| Reduce scope, with sponsor approval | When the budget is fixed | Benefits may fall; check the business case |
| Draw on contingency reserve | When the cause was an identified risk | Contingency is finite; track the burn rate |
| Request extra budget through change control | When the original baseline is no longer achievable | Needs a strong explanation and revised forecast |
For the identified risks behind a variance, your [contingency plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) should already say which reserve to use and who can release it.

#### What to write in a variance explanation
- The variance: CV, CV% and CPI, cumulative and for the period.
- The cause, in one or two sentences, with evidence.
- Whether the cause is expected to continue.
- The impact on EAC, VAC, contingency and any milestones.
- The actions, owners and dates.
- Any decision needed from the sponsor or board.
Example: "Configuration and build is $19,000 over for the work done (CV% -22.6%, CPI 0.82). The cause is 210 extra hours of custom development for the sales pipeline, requested by users without a change request. This is expected to continue unless scope is controlled. Forecast EAC is $437,800 (VAC -$37,800). Actions: freeze customisation requests through change control from 1 November (PM); re-estimate the remaining build (lead developer, by 8 November). Decision needed: approve or reject the outstanding pipeline changes."

### Cost variance in Agile projects
EVM was designed for plan-driven projects with a detailed baseline, but the idea behind cost variance still works in Agile delivery if you measure progress in a way that fits.
- **Measure EV at release level.** Treat the release budget as BAC and the proportion of planned story points completed as percent complete. If 120 of 300 points are done on a $300,000 release, EV is $120,000.
- **Use team cost per sprint for AC.** Agile team costs are fairly stable, so AC is often the number of sprints multiplied by the cost of the team per sprint, plus any other spend.
- **Re-baseline when the backlog changes.** If the product owner adds or removes scope, adjust the planned points so CV reflects efficiency rather than scope change.
- **Read it with velocity.** A falling [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) will show up as a worsening CV, because the same cost buys fewer points.
Approaches of this kind are often called AgileEVM. They work best as a conversation starter with the sponsor rather than as a precise control tool. Our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) covers the measures most Agile teams rely on day to day.

### Common cost variance mistakes
- **Comparing actual cost with planned value** instead of earned value.
- **Reporting only the project total**, which hides which work package is driving the problem.
- **Subjective percent complete**, such as tasks stuck at 90% for weeks, which inflates EV.
- **Ignoring accruals and committed costs**, which makes AC too low.
- **Including management reserve in BAC**, which blurs the performance baseline.
- **Treating every variance as a problem**, without thresholds, so real issues get lost in noise.
- **Explaining the variance without forecasting it**: always update EAC and VAC.
- **Assuming a positive CV is good news** without checking the data.
- **Letting scope changes in without change control**, so the baseline no longer matches the work.

### Tools and templates
For a small project, a spreadsheet with BAC, percent complete, EV, AC, CV, CV% and CPI for each work package is enough. Build it from a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) so every cost has a home, starting from our [WBS template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/), and track spend in the [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/). Our [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) helps with progress, and the [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) helps when a variance needs a baseline change.
For larger portfolios, look for project management software with budgets, timesheets and custom fields, so EV and AC are captured as the work happens.
Cost variance is one part of keeping a project on budget.
To forecast the final cost from today's figures, read [project forecasting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is cost variance in project management?**
Cost variance is the difference between the earned value of the work completed and its actual cost, CV = EV - AC. It shows whether completed work has cost more or less than its budget.

**Q: What is the cost variance formula?**
CV = EV - AC, where EV is earned value (the budget for the work completed) and AC is the actual cost of that work. As a percentage, CV% = CV / EV x 100.

**Q: What does a negative cost variance mean?**
The work completed so far has cost more than its budget, so the project is over budget for the work done. In the CRM example, EV of $180,000 and AC of $197,000 give a CV of -$17,000.

**Q: What does a positive cost variance mean?**
The work completed has cost less than budgeted, so the project is under budget for the work done. Check the data before treating it as good news.

**Q: Can a positive cost variance be bad?**
Yes. It can be caused by missing invoices or accruals, overstated progress, padded estimates or expensive work still to come. A large, persistent positive variance also suggests budget that could have been used elsewhere.

**Q: How do you calculate cost variance percentage?**
Divide the cost variance by earned value and multiply by 100. A CV of -$17,000 on EV of $180,000 is -9.4%.

**Q: What is an acceptable cost variance?**
There is no universal figure. Acceptable limits are set in the project's cost management plan and depend on the industry, contract and estimate accuracy. Many teams use a percentage band plus a money amount, and tighten them as the project progresses.

**Q: How often should you calculate cost variance?**
At every reporting period, usually monthly for most projects and weekly or fortnightly for short, fast-moving ones. Use the same status date for progress and costs.

**Q: What is the difference between cost variance and schedule variance?**
Cost variance (EV - AC) measures cost performance: are we spending efficiently? Schedule variance (EV - PV) measures schedule performance in money terms: have we done as much work as planned? Both use earned value.

**Q: What is the difference between cost variance and CPI?**
Both use EV and AC. CV is the difference (EV - AC) in money; CPI is the ratio (EV / AC). A negative CV always means a CPI below 1.

**Q: What is variance at completion?**
Variance at completion (VAC) is the cost variance expected when the project finishes: VAC = BAC - EAC. A negative VAC means a forecast overrun.

**Q: Is cost variance the same as budget variance?**
Not quite. Budget variance usually compares actual spend with the budget for a period. EVM cost variance compares actual cost with the earned value of the work completed, which separates cost efficiency from schedule progress.

**Q: What are BCWP and ACWP?**
They are the older names for earned value (budgeted cost of work performed) and actual cost (actual cost of work performed). Cost variance is BCWP - ACWP.

**Q: Can cost variance be used in Agile projects?**
Yes, at release level. Use the release budget as BAC, the share of planned story points completed as percent complete, and team cost per sprint for actual cost. Adjust the baseline when the backlog changes.

# Critical Chain Project Management (CCPM) Explained

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-chain-project-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: How Critical Chain Project Management works: resource-constrained scheduling, aggressive estimates, project and feeding buffers, and buffer management.


## Critical Chain Project Management (CCPM) Explained
Critical Chain Project Management (CCPM) is a scheduling method developed by Eliyahu Goldratt, based on his Theory of Constraints. It focuses on resource constraints and protects the project deadline with shared buffers rather than padding every task.
- Published 12 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- CCPM schedules around resource constraints.
- Safety time is pooled into project and feeding buffers.
- Progress is tracked through buffer consumption.

### The problem it addresses
- **Padded estimates:** people add safety time to each task.
- **Student syndrome:** work starts late because there seems to be plenty of time.
- **Parkinson's law:** work expands to fill the time available.
- **Multitasking:** switching between projects delays all of them.
Together, these mean individual safety margins are wasted while projects still finish late.

### How CCPM works
1. Estimate tasks aggressively, without individual safety margins.
2. Identify the critical chain: the longest chain of dependent tasks, taking resource availability into account.
3. Add a **project buffer** at the end of the critical chain.
4. Add **feeding buffers** where non-critical chains join the critical chain.
5. Use **resource buffers** or alerts to make sure key people are ready.
6. Avoid multitasking; work on one task at a time and pass it on as soon as it's done.

### Buffer management
Progress is tracked by how much buffer has been consumed relative to how much of the chain is complete, often on a fever chart with green, yellow and red zones. Managers act only when buffer consumption gets ahead of progress.

### Critical chain vs critical path
|  | Critical path | Critical chain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Considers | Task dependencies | Dependencies and resource constraints |
| Safety time | In each task estimate | Pooled in shared buffers |
| Tracking | Task dates and float | Buffer consumption |
See [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Who created CCPM?**
Eliyahu M. Goldratt, who introduced it in his 1997 book Critical Chain.

**Q: Where is CCPM used?**
In engineering, manufacturing, construction and organisations managing many resource-constrained projects.

**Q: What is Critical Chain Project Management?**
A scheduling method that accounts for resource limits as well as task dependencies, removes safety time from individual tasks and pools it into shared buffers.

**Q: What is the critical chain?**
The longest chain of dependent tasks in a project, taking resource availability into account.

**Q: What is the difference between critical chain and critical path?**
Critical path considers task dependencies and keeps safety time in each estimate; critical chain also considers resource constraints and pools safety time into buffers. See [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).

**Q: What is a project buffer in CCPM?**
Pooled safety time added at the end of the critical chain to protect the project's finish date.

**Q: What is a feeding buffer in CCPM?**
A buffer placed where a non-critical chain joins the critical chain, so delays on the feeding chain do not delay the critical chain.

**Q: What is a fever chart in CCPM?**
A chart that tracks buffer consumption against chain completion, with green, yellow and red zones that tell managers when to act.

**Q: What is student syndrome in critical chain project management?**
The tendency to start work late because there seems to be plenty of time, which wastes the safety margin built into estimates.

**Q: What is Parkinson's law in critical chain project management?**
The observation that work expands to fill the time available, so padded estimates rarely lead to early finishes.

**Q: How is CCPM related to the Theory of Constraints?**
CCPM applies Goldratt's [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/) to projects, treating the critical chain as the constraint to protect.
