# Effort Estimation: Techniques, Formula and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Effort estimation explained: effort vs duration, 8 techniques, the PERT formula, a step-by-step method and a worked example from hours to days and cost.


## Effort Estimation: Techniques, Formula and Examples
Effort estimation is the process of predicting how much work, measured in person-hours or person-days, a task or project will need. It is the foundation of both the schedule (how long it will take) and the budget (how much it will cost), so getting it roughly right matters more than almost any other planning step. This guide explains the main techniques, the formulas, a step-by-step method and a full worked example from task estimates to duration and cost.
- Published 27 September 2026
- Last updated 15 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Effort is the amount of work in person-hours or person-days; duration and cost are calculated from it, not the other way round.
- Choose the technique to match what you know: analogous or top-down early on, bottom-up and three-point once the work is broken down.
- Three-point (PERT) estimates give a range and a measure of uncertainty, which is more honest than a single number.
- Convert effort to duration using realistic productive hours and availability, not a full working day.
- Estimates should get more accurate as the project progresses; state the accuracy range you are working to.
- Comparing actual effort with estimates gives you a calibration factor that improves every future estimate.

### What is effort estimation?
**Effort estimation** is the process of forecasting the total amount of work needed to complete a task, deliverable or project, usually expressed in person-hours, person-days or person-months. It is based on the scope of the work, the skills of the people doing it and data from similar past work, and it is the main input for the project schedule and labour budget.
In a typical planning sequence, you first define the [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) and break it into a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/). You then estimate the effort for each piece of work, and only after that do you build the schedule and budget. Estimating effort before the work is broken down is possible, but the result is a rough order of magnitude rather than a plan.
An effort estimate answers "how much work is this?" It does not, on its own, answer "when will it be finished?" or "how much will it cost?" Those depend on who is available, for how many hours, and at what rate.

### Effort vs duration vs cost
Mixing up effort and duration is the most common estimating error. The table shows the difference.
| Measure | What it means | Unit | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Effort | Total amount of work | Person-hours or person-days | 120 person-hours of development |
| Duration | Working time from start to finish | Working days or weeks | 10 working days |
| Elapsed time | Calendar time, including weekends and holidays | Calendar days | 14 calendar days |
| Cost | Money needed to pay for the effort | Currency | 120 hours × £55 = £6,600 |
The relationships are simple:
- **Duration** = effort ÷ (number of people × productive hours per person per day)
- **Labour cost** = effort × hourly rate (or effort in days × day rate)
Forty person-hours of effort could be one week for one person, half a week for two, or two weeks for one person who is only available half the time. The effort is the same in each case; the duration is not. For the money side, see our guide to [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/).

### Units of effort
Use the smallest unit that suits the level of detail. State the conventions you use, because "a person-month" means different things in different organisations.
| Unit | Typical use | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Person-hour | Task-level estimates, time tracking | The most precise and least ambiguous unit |
| Person-day | Work packages and small projects | State the hours in a day (for example 7.5 or 8) |
| Person-week | Phases and resource plans | Usually 5 person-days |
| Person-month | Large projects and early estimates | Conventions vary; the COCOMO II cost model, for example, uses 152 hours |
| Full-time equivalent (FTE) | Staffing and capacity plans | A rate of effort over time, such as 2.5 FTE for six months |
| Story points | Agile teams | Relative size, not time; converted to dates through velocity |
To convert effort into staffing, divide it by the hours one full-time person works in the period. For example, 900 person-hours over three months, at about 150 hours per person-month, needs 2 FTE.

### Why effort estimation matters
- **Realistic schedules.** Durations and the critical path are calculated from effort and availability.
- **Accurate budgets.** On most service, IT and knowledge-work projects, labour is the largest cost.
- **Resource planning.** Effort shows how many people with which skills you need and when.
- **Go/no-go decisions.** An early estimate tells sponsors whether an idea is worth pursuing.
- **Baselines for control.** Once approved, effort estimates become part of the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) used to measure progress, for example with [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).
- **Stakeholder trust.** Transparent estimates with stated assumptions make later conversations about change easier.

### Effort estimation techniques
There is no single best technique. Most experienced estimators use two or more and compare the results. The table summarises eight common techniques; each is explained below with a short example.
| Technique | How it works | Best used when | Effort to produce |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expert judgment | Experienced people estimate from their knowledge | Any stage; quick checks | Low |
| Analogous | Scale the actual effort of a similar past project | Early, with little detail | Low |
| Parametric | Multiply a unit rate by a quantity | Work is repetitive and measurable | Low to medium |
| Top-down | Split a total across phases using historical ratios | Early budget-setting | Low |
| Bottom-up | Estimate each task and add them up | Scope is broken down | High |
| Three-point (PERT) | Optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values | Tasks are uncertain | Medium |
| Wideband Delphi | Anonymous group estimates in rounds until they converge | High-stakes or unfamiliar work | Medium to high |
| Relative (Agile) | Story points or T-shirt sizes compared with each other | Agile teams with a backlog | Low per item |

#### Expert judgment
People who have done similar work estimate it directly. A senior developer might say an integration is "about two weeks for one person", which you would record as roughly 60 to 75 person-hours. It is fast but depends on who you ask, so record the assumptions and, where possible, get more than one opinion.

#### Analogous estimation
You take the actual effort from a similar past project and adjust it for differences. Last year's intranet redesign took 400 person-hours. The new one has about 25% more pages but reuses an existing design system, which you judge saves 10%: 400 × 1.25 × 0.9 = 450 person-hours. Analogous estimates are only as good as the similarity and your records of actual effort.

#### Parametric estimation
You multiply a measured unit rate by the quantity of work. If your team averages 1.5 hours to write and run a test case and there are 40 test cases, the effort is 40 × 1.5 = 60 person-hours. Parametric estimates are accurate when the rate comes from reliable historical data and the work really is similar each time.

#### Top-down estimation
You start from a total, often from an analogous estimate or a fixed budget, and divide it across phases using historical proportions. A 1,000-hour project might be split 15% analysis, 45% build, 25% testing and 15% deployment. Top-down is useful for early budgets and for checking whether a fixed budget is realistic, but it can hide missing work.

#### Bottom-up estimation
You break the work into small tasks or [work packages](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/), estimate each one with the people who will do it, and add them up. It is the most accurate approach for a well-defined scope and the most time-consuming. Its main risk is forgetting work that is not on the list, such as reviews, rework and coordination.

#### Three-point and PERT estimation
For each task you estimate three values: optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P). Two formulas are used:
- **Triangular mean:** E = (O + M + P) ÷ 3
- **PERT (beta) mean:** E = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6, with standard deviation SD = (P − O) ÷ 6
For a task estimated at O = 24, M = 40 and P = 80 hours, the triangular mean is 48 hours and the PERT mean is 44 hours, with an SD of about 9.3 hours. PERT weights the most likely value more heavily, so it is less pulled by the pessimistic tail. For the network diagram technique that shares the name, see our guide to [PERT charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/).

#### Wideband Delphi
A facilitator gives a group of experts the scope, and each estimates anonymously. The facilitator shares the spread of results, the group discusses the reasons for the differences (usually different assumptions), and everyone re-estimates. For example, a first round of 90, 120, 180 and 200 hours might converge to 140 to 170 hours once the group agrees that data migration is in scope. Anonymity reduces anchoring on the most senior voice.

#### Relative estimation in Agile
Agile teams usually estimate in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/) or T-shirt sizes, comparing items with each other rather than with the clock, often using planning poker. Story points become a time forecast through the team's measured [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/). This is covered in more detail below.

### Choosing a technique by project stage
Estimates should become more accurate as you learn more. A useful idea here is the **cone of uncertainty**: Construx, Steve McConnell's consultancy, describes estimates at the initial concept stage as potentially ranging from 0.25 times to 4 times the actual result, narrowing only as decisions remove variability. In other words, the cone does not narrow by itself; it narrows because you make decisions about scope and design.
The PMBOK Guide gives typical accuracy ranges for estimates: a rough order of magnitude (ROM) estimate of −25% to +75%, and a definitive estimate of −5% to +10%. Organisations often set their own ranges for each stage gate. The table is a practical guide based on those ideas.
| Stage | What you know | Suitable techniques | Typical accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Idea or business case | A goal and a rough scope | Analogous, top-down, expert judgment | Rough order of magnitude (for example −25% to +75%) |
| Initiation and planning | Main deliverables and a high-level WBS | Analogous plus parametric, Wideband Delphi | Budget estimate (narrower range) |
| Detailed planning | WBS down to work packages and tasks | Bottom-up with three-point estimates | Definitive (for example −5% to +10%) |
| Execution | Actual progress and productivity | Re-estimate remaining work; forecasting | Improves as work completes |
Tip
Always quote an estimate with its accuracy range and its key assumptions. "About 900 hours, −10% to +25%, assuming the client supplies content by March" is far more useful, and safer, than "900 hours".

### How to estimate effort step by step
The method below works for most projects. On a small piece of work you can do it in an hour; on a large project it may take several workshops.
1. **Define the scope.** Agree what is in and out, the deliverables and the acceptance criteria. Unclear scope is the main cause of bad estimates.
2. **Break the work down.** Decompose the scope into a WBS until each task is small enough to estimate with confidence; as a rule of thumb, roughly 8 to 80 hours of effort per task.
3. **Define "done" for each task.** Include design, review, testing, documentation and handover, so nobody estimates only the "doing" part.
4. **Choose the technique.** Use parametric where you have reliable unit rates, three-point where tasks are uncertain, and analogous as a cross-check.
5. **Ask the people who will do the work.** They know the hidden steps. The project manager facilitates and challenges; they should not impose numbers.
6. **Use historical data.** Compare with actual effort on similar tasks, from your [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) records or time tracking.
7. **Record assumptions and risks.** Skills, availability, tools, client inputs and anything you have excluded.
8. **Add management effort and contingency once, openly.** Include project management and coordination as tasks, and hold contingency as a visible reserve rather than padding every task.
9. **Review, approve and revisit.** Have a peer or the team review the estimate, baseline it, and re-estimate remaining work as you learn.

### Worked example: bottom-up three-point estimate
A team is building a small online booking feature: a specification, a database change, a payment integration, eight new screens, testing, documentation and coordination. Each task has been estimated by the people who will do it, in person-hours.
| Task | O | M | P | PERT mean | SD |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements workshops and specification | 16 | 24 | 40 | 25.3 | 4.0 |
| Database changes | 20 | 32 | 56 | 34.0 | 6.0 |
| Payment provider integration | 24 | 40 | 80 | 44.0 | 9.3 |
| Eight screens (parametric: 8 × 6 h most likely) | 36 | 48 | 72 | 50.0 | 6.0 |
| Testing and fixes | 24 | 36 | 60 | 38.0 | 6.0 |
| Documentation and handover | 8 | 12 | 20 | 12.7 | 2.0 |
| Coordination, reviews and meetings | 14 | 20 | 32 | 21.0 | 3.0 |
| Total | 142 | 212 | 360 | 225.0 | about 15 |

#### How the totals are calculated
1. **Expected effort.** Add the PERT means: 25.3 + 34 + 44 + 50 + 38 + 12.7 + 21 = **225 person-hours**.
2. **Combined uncertainty.** Standard deviations do not add up directly. Square each SD to get its variance, add the variances (16 + 36 + 87.1 + 36 + 36 + 4 + 9 = 224.1) and take the square root: √224.1 ≈ **15 hours**.
3. **Range.** Assuming the tasks are independent and the total is roughly normally distributed, there is about a 68% chance the effort falls between 210 and 240 hours (±1 SD), and about a 95% chance it is under 225 + 1.645 × 15 ≈ **250 hours**.
Notice that simply adding the most likely values gives 212 hours, 13 hours less than the PERT total. Because the pessimistic values are further from the most likely than the optimistic ones, single-point estimates tend to be biased low. This is one reason projects using only "most likely" estimates often overrun.
Tip
The range calculation assumes tasks are independent. In reality, one shared problem (an unclear requirement, a difficult supplier) can push many tasks late together, so treat the range as optimistic and keep a separate risk reserve. For a more realistic picture on larger projects, use [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/).
You can build this kind of estimate in our free [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/), starting from a [work breakdown structure template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/).

### Converting effort to duration and cost

#### From effort to duration
Duration depends on how many people work on the task and how many productive hours they have each day. Nobody does eight hours of project work in an eight-hour day: meetings, email, support and context switching all take time. Many planners assume about five to six productive hours per person per day, but this is a planning assumption, not a standard; measure it for your own team.
In the example, two developers each have six productive hours a day, giving 12 hours a day between them:
- Expected duration = 225 ÷ 12 = 18.75, so about **19 working days**.
- At the 95% figure, 250 ÷ 12 ≈ 21 working days.
- Allow for dependencies: the specification must be finished before most of the build starts, so the real schedule is usually longer than effort ÷ people suggests. Sequence the tasks in a [project schedule](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) to find the true duration.
Adding people does not shorten duration in proportion. Fred Brooks observed in The Mythical Man-Month (1975) that adding people to a late software project makes it later, because new people need onboarding and every extra person adds communication. Treat extra people as extra effort for coordination, not just extra capacity.

#### From effort to cost
At a blended rate of £55 per hour:
| Basis | Effort (hours) | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Expected (PERT mean) | 225 | £12,375 |
| About 95% confidence | 250 | £13,750 |
| Contingency (difference) | 25 | £1,375 |
A common approach is to budget the expected cost for the planned work and hold the difference as a visible contingency reserve, controlled by the project manager.

### Effort estimation in Agile projects
Agile teams usually avoid estimating every task in hours up front. Instead, they size backlog items relative to each other in story points and let the team's measured velocity convert size into a forecast. This has three advantages: relative sizing is quicker, it is less affected by who does the work, and velocity automatically absorbs meetings, interruptions and other overheads.
- **Sizing:** the team compares a new item with items it has already completed and gives it a point value, often using planning poker so everyone estimates independently before discussing.
- **Forecasting:** if the team completes 30 to 36 points per sprint and the release backlog is 180 points, it needs roughly 5 to 6 sprints.
- **Hours still help** for sprint-level task planning on some teams, for fixed-price contracts and when a budget must be expressed in money. Convert using the team's cost per sprint rather than an assumed hours-per-point ratio.

### Factors that affect estimate accuracy
| Factor | Effect on the estimate | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unclear requirements | Estimates cover the wrong work | Clarify scope and acceptance criteria first; estimate ranges |
| New technology or domain | Wider spread, optimism | Run a spike or prototype; widen the pessimistic value |
| Team experience | Productivity varies between people | Estimate with the people who will do the work |
| Dependencies on others | Waiting and rework | List them; add coordination tasks |
| Availability and multitasking | Fewer productive hours | Plan with measured availability |
| Scope changes | Estimate becomes obsolete | Re-estimate through change control; watch for [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) |
| Pressure to hit a number | Estimates bend to the target | Separate the estimate from the target and the commitment |

### Common effort estimation mistakes
- **Confusing effort with duration** and promising a date from an effort figure.
- **Assuming a full productive day** of seven or eight hours per person.
- **Estimating only the build,** and forgetting analysis, review, testing, documentation, deployment and handover.
- **Padding every task** instead of holding one visible contingency, which hides risk and tends to be used up (Parkinson's law).
- **Giving a single number** without a range or assumptions, which is then treated as a commitment.
- **Letting the manager estimate for the team,** or anchoring the team with a number before they estimate.
- **Ignoring history.** Not checking how long similar work actually took.
- **Never re-estimating,** even after the scope or team changes.
- **Adding people to recover a late task** without accounting for onboarding and coordination effort.

### How to improve your estimates over time
The single most useful improvement is to track actual effort and compare it with estimates. Over time, this gives you a calibration factor for your team and type of work.

#### Worked example: calibration ratio
Over the last ten completed tasks, a team estimated a total of 180 person-hours and actually spent 225. The ratio of actual to estimate is 225 ÷ 180 = **1.25**. Until the ratio improves, the project manager multiplies new bottom-up estimates by 1.25 as a cross-check, and the team discusses which kinds of tasks are underestimated most, usually testing and integration.
- **Keep a simple estimating database:** task type, size, estimate, actual and notes.
- **Hold short estimation retrospectives** at milestones: which estimates were furthest out, and why?
- **Use more than one technique** on important estimates, and investigate big differences.
- **Track variances during the project** with tools such as earned value and [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/), so you learn early, not at the end.
- **Record assumptions** with every estimate so you can see which ones proved wrong.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is effort estimation in project management?**
Predicting the total amount of work, in person-hours, person-days or person-months, needed to complete a task or project. It is the basis for the schedule and the labour budget.

**Q: What is the formula for effort estimation?**
There is no single formula. Common ones are parametric (effort = quantity × unit rate) and PERT (expected effort = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6). Duration = effort ÷ (people × productive hours per day), and cost = effort × rate.

**Q: What is the difference between effort and duration?**
Effort is the amount of work; duration is how long it takes in working time. Forty hours of effort is one week for one full-time person or half a week for two.

**Q: What are the main types of estimating?**
Analogous, parametric, bottom-up and three-point are the four most commonly cited, alongside expert judgment, top-down, Wideband Delphi and Agile relative estimation.

**Q: How do you calculate person-hours?**
Multiply the number of people by the hours each works on the task. Three people working 20 hours each is 60 person-hours. To estimate, add the person-hours of every task in the work breakdown structure.

**Q: How many productive hours a day should I assume?**
It varies by organisation and role. Many planners assume around five to six productive hours per person per day rather than the full working day, but you should measure your own team's actual figure.

**Q: What is the difference between three-point and PERT estimation?**
Both use optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values. The simple three-point (triangular) mean is (O + M + P) ÷ 3; PERT weights the most likely value four times: (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6.

**Q: What is Wideband Delphi?**
A group technique in which experts estimate anonymously, discuss the reasons for differences and re-estimate in rounds until the estimates converge.

**Q: How accurate should an effort estimate be?**
It depends on the stage. The PMBOK Guide gives −25% to +75% for a rough order of magnitude estimate and −5% to +10% for a definitive estimate. Always state the range you are working to.

**Q: What is FTE in effort estimation?**
Full-time equivalent expresses effort as a number of full-time people over a period. 900 person-hours over three months, at about 150 hours per person-month, is 2 FTE.

**Q: Who should estimate effort?**
The people who will do the work, facilitated by the project manager and checked against historical data. Estimates imposed from above are usually optimistic and weakly owned.

**Q: Do Agile teams estimate effort in hours?**
Usually not at backlog level. They size items in story points and use velocity to forecast. Some teams still break sprint items into tasks estimated in hours.

**Q: Why do effort estimates go wrong?**
Unclear scope, missing tasks, optimism, pressure to hit a target, interruptions, multitasking and changes that are not re-estimated are the usual causes.

# Estimate at Completion (EAC): Formulas and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Estimate at completion (EAC) explained: the four EAC formulas, when to use each, ETC, VAC and TCPI, worked examples and common mistakes.


## Estimate at Completion (EAC): Formulas and Examples
Estimate at completion (EAC) is the forecast of what a project will cost in total once all the work is finished. It equals the actual cost spent so far plus the estimated cost of the remaining work, and the most widely used shortcut is EAC = BAC / CPI.
- Published 29 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- EAC is the forecast total cost of the project: EAC = AC + ETC.
- There are four standard formulas; pick the one that matches the cause of the variance.
- BAC / CPI assumes current cost efficiency continues; AC + (BAC - EV) assumes the rest goes to plan.
- VAC = BAC - EAC shows the expected overrun; TCPI shows the efficiency needed to hit a target.
- Report a range of EACs with the reason behind your preferred figure, not a single number.
- Update EAC every reporting period and act early when it moves away from the budget.

### What is estimate at completion (EAC)?
**Estimate at completion (EAC)** is the expected total cost of a project, or of a work package or control account, when all of its work is complete. It is calculated as the actual cost to date plus the estimate to complete (EAC = AC + ETC). EAC is compared with the budget at completion (BAC) to show whether the project is heading for an overrun or an underrun.
EAC is one of the forecasting measures in [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/). The other measures tell you where the project stands today: the [cost performance index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/) shows cost efficiency, and [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/) and [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) show how far you are from plan. EAC turns that history into a forecast of the final bill.
The key distinction is between **EAC and BAC**. The [budget at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/budget-at-completion/) is the approved budget for all the work and only changes through formal change control. EAC is your current best forecast and can change every reporting period. When EAC drifts above BAC, the gap is a warning that needs a decision, not just a note in the report.
In PMI's PMBOK Guide, forecasting sits within cost control. In the eighth edition (published late 2025), cost work falls under the **Finance** performance domain, whose processes include monitoring and controlling finances. The formulas themselves are the long-established earned value formulas used across PMI's standards and most project controls guidance.

### The inputs you need
Every EAC formula is built from a small set of earned value figures. Get these right first; a precise formula applied to poor data gives a precise-looking wrong answer.
| Term | Meaning | How it is calculated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **BAC**: budget at completion | Total approved budget for the work | Sum of the cost baseline |
| **PV**: planned value | Budgeted cost of work scheduled to date | From the time-phased baseline |
| **EV**: earned value | Budgeted cost of work actually completed | Percent complete x BAC |
| **AC**: actual cost | What the completed work has really cost | From timesheets, invoices and accruals |
| **CPI**: cost performance index | Cost efficiency so far | EV / AC |
| **SPI**: schedule performance index | Schedule efficiency so far | EV / PV |
| **ETC**: estimate to complete | Expected cost of the remaining work | EAC - AC, or a fresh estimate |
Two data points matter most. **EV depends on honest progress measurement**: if tasks are reported as 80% done for weeks, EV is inflated and every forecast looks better than it should. Agree objective rules, such as 0/100 or 50/50 for short tasks and milestones for longer ones, at [work package](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/) level. **AC must include costs incurred but not yet invoiced**, such as accrued contractor hours, or the project will look cheaper than it is.
The time-phased baseline behind PV is usually plotted as an [S-curve](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/s-curve/).

### The four EAC formulas
PMI's earned value guidance describes four standard ways to forecast EAC. Each makes a different assumption about how the remaining work will perform.
| Formula | Assumption | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EAC = BAC / CPI | Current cost efficiency will continue | The cause of the variance is ongoing (typical variance) |
| EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) | Remaining work will be done at the budgeted rate | The variance was a one-off (atypical variance) |
| EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) | Both cost and schedule performance affect the rest | You are behind schedule and must still hit a fixed date |
| EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC | The original estimates are no longer valid | Scope, rates or approach have changed significantly |

#### 1. EAC = BAC / CPI (typical variance)
This is the most common formula and the default in many tools. It assumes the project will keep spending at the same efficiency for the rest of its life. If the team is delivering 82 cents of value for every dollar spent, the formula assumes that will continue. It is mathematically the same as EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / CPI.
Use it when the cause of the overrun is structural: labour rates higher than planned, productivity lower than estimated, or a complexity that affects all the remaining work. Once a good share of the work is done, the cumulative CPI tends to move slowly, because each new period adds only a little to the total. That is why many project controllers treat this formula as the realistic baseline forecast.

#### 2. EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) (atypical variance)
This formula adds the original budget for the remaining work to what has already been spent. It assumes the past variance was a one-off and will not repeat: a supplier failure, a single piece of rework or a one-time price spike.
It is the most optimistic of the four when a project is over budget, so use it only when you can explain why the cause has gone away. Defaulting to it because it gives the smallest number is one of the most common forecasting mistakes.

#### 3. EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI)
This version adjusts the remaining work for both cost and schedule performance. It suits projects that are behind schedule and have a fixed end date, where catching up will mean overtime, extra people or expedited delivery, all of which cost more.
Because CPI x SPI is smaller than CPI when the project is late, this usually gives the highest EAC when both indices are below 1. Some organisations use a **weighted version**, such as AC + (BAC - EV) / (0.8 x CPI + 0.2 x SPI), to give schedule pressure some influence without letting it dominate. The weights are a local convention, not a standard, so state them in your [cost management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-management-plan/).

#### 4. EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC
Here you ignore the indices and re-estimate the remaining work from the bottom up, task by task, using current knowledge of scope, rates and risks. It is the most effort but often the most credible when the plan has changed: a redesign, a new supplier, approved scope changes or a fundamentally different delivery approach.
A bottom-up ETC uses the same techniques as the original estimate; see [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/) and [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/).

### How to calculate EAC step by step
1. **Confirm BAC.** Use the current approved budget, including any approved changes. Exclude management reserve, which sits outside the performance baseline.
2. **Measure EV.** Apply your agreed percent-complete rules to each work package and add them up.
3. **Collect AC.** Include all costs incurred for the work done, including accruals and committed costs that relate to completed work.
4. **Find PV.** Read the planned value for the status date from the baseline.
5. **Calculate CPI and SPI.** CPI = EV / AC; SPI = EV / PV.
6. **Calculate the formula EACs.** Work out all three index-based formulas; they take seconds once the inputs are known.
7. **Ask why the variance happened.** This determines which formula is most realistic.
8. **Prepare a bottom-up ETC if the plan has changed** or if the formulas disagree widely.
9. **Derive ETC, VAC and TCPI** from your chosen EAC.
10. **Report** a preferred EAC, the range, the reasons and the actions you recommend.
Tip
Calculate EAC at the level where you manage cost, usually the control account or work package, and roll it up. A healthy project total can hide one work package that is badly overrunning.

### Worked example: an over-budget project
A website rebuild has a budget of **$200,000** over eight months. At the end of month four:
- Planned value (PV) = $80,000
- Earned value (EV) = $70,000 (35% of the work is done)
- Actual cost (AC) = $85,000
So **CPI = 70,000 / 85,000 = 0.8235**, **SPI = 70,000 / 80,000 = 0.875**, and the budgeted value of the remaining work is BAC - EV = **$130,000**. The project is both over budget and behind schedule.
| Formula | Calculation | EAC | VAC (BAC - EAC) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BAC / CPI | 200,000 / 0.8235 | $242,857 | -$42,857 |
| AC + (BAC - EV) | 85,000 + 130,000 | $215,000 | -$15,000 |
| AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) | 85,000 + 130,000 / 0.7206 | $265,408 | -$65,408 |
| Weighted 0.8 CPI / 0.2 SPI | 85,000 + 130,000 / 0.8338 | $240,908 | -$40,908 |
| AC + bottom-up ETC | 85,000 + 140,000 | $225,000 | -$25,000 |
The forecasts range from $215,000 to $265,408. Which one to report depends on the cause. Suppose the investigation shows that the main driver is a senior developer day rate 15% above the estimate, and that developer is staying to the end. The cause is ongoing, so **BAC / CPI = $242,857** is the most defensible forecast. The bottom-up figure of $225,000 would need a credible explanation of why efficiency will improve.
From the chosen EAC:
- **ETC** = EAC - AC = 242,857 - 85,000 = **$157,857** still needed.
- **VAC** = BAC - EAC = **-$42,857**, a forecast overrun of about 21%.
- **TCPI to meet BAC** = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = 130,000 / 115,000 = **1.13**. The remaining work would need to be 13% more efficient than planned, while the team is currently running 18% less efficient. That is not realistic without a change in scope or approach.
- **TCPI to meet the EAC** = (BAC - EV) / (EAC - AC) = 130,000 / 157,857 = **0.82**, which equals the current CPI, as you would expect for this formula.
The same project data is used in our guides to [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/), [CPI](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/) and [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/), so you can follow the numbers across all of them.

### Worked example: an under-budget project
EAC can also be lower than BAC. A small office move has a budget of **$50,000**. At the status date PV = $22,000, EV = $20,000 and AC = $18,000.
- CPI = 20,000 / 18,000 = **1.11** (under budget)
- SPI = 20,000 / 22,000 = **0.91** (slightly behind schedule)
- BAC - EV = **$30,000** of work remaining
| Formula | EAC | VAC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BAC / CPI | $45,000 | +$5,000 |
| AC + (BAC - EV) | $48,000 | +$2,000 |
| AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) | $47,700 | +$2,300 |
Here BAC / CPI is the most optimistic figure. A cautious project manager might report $48,000, because early savings often come from easier tasks and may not continue. A positive VAC is good news, but it may also mean the original estimate was padded; record the reason in your [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) so future estimates improve.

### EAC, ETC, VAC and TCPI compared
These four forecasting measures are closely linked and often confused, especially in exam questions.
| Measure | Question it answers | Formula | Good result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **EAC** | What will the whole project cost? | AC + ETC (or one of the four formulas) | At or below BAC |
| **ETC** | How much more will we spend? | EAC - AC, or a bottom-up estimate | Within remaining budget (BAC - AC) |
| **VAC** | How far over or under budget will we finish? | BAC - EAC | Zero or positive |
| **TCPI** | How efficient must the remaining work be? | (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) or (BAC - EV) / (EAC - AC) | Close to or below the current CPI |

#### Reading the TCPI
The to-complete performance index is a reality check on any target. If TCPI to meet BAC is 1.13 and the current CPI is 0.82, the budget is very unlikely to be met by working harder. As a rough rule of thumb (our guidance, not a formal standard):
- **TCPI below or close to the current CPI:** the target is achievable at current performance.
- **TCPI a little above CPI (up to about 0.05 to 0.10):** achievable only with specific improvement actions.
- **TCPI well above CPI:** unrealistic; a re-plan, scope change or budget change is needed.
TCPI rises sharply late in a project because there is less work left over which to recover. If actual cost already exceeds BAC, the BAC-based TCPI becomes meaningless or negative, and only the EAC-based version is useful.

### Which EAC formula should you use?
The right formula depends on why performance differs from plan, not on which answer looks best. Use this as a starting point:
| Situation | Preferred EAC | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rates, productivity or complexity are worse than estimated and will stay that way | BAC / CPI | The cause affects all remaining work |
| A single event caused the overrun and has been resolved | AC + (BAC - EV) | Remaining work should go to plan |
| Behind schedule with a fixed end date that must be met | AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) | Recovery will cost extra |
| Scope, design, supplier or approach has changed | AC + bottom-up ETC | The original estimates no longer apply |
| Early in the project (under about 15 to 20% complete) | Bottom-up ETC, with formulas as a cross-check | Early indices are volatile |
| Formulas give a wide spread | Bottom-up ETC plus a range | Uncertainty needs to be visible |

#### Independent and management EACs
In formal earned value systems you will see two kinds of forecast. An **independent EAC (IEAC)** is calculated from the formulas, without anyone's judgement, and acts as a statistical check. A **management EAC** (sometimes called the estimate at completion of record) is the project manager's own forecast, usually built bottom-up. If the management EAC is much lower than the independent EACs, sponsors will expect a clear explanation of what will change.

#### Report a range, not a point
Showing the best case (AC + (BAC - EV)), the most likely case and the worst case (CPI x SPI) gives decision-makers a realistic picture. For high-uncertainty projects, a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) of the remaining work can produce a probability-based range, for example an 80% confidence EAC.

### Calculating EAC in a spreadsheet
You do not need specialist software. With BAC in cell B1, PV in B2, EV in B3 and AC in B4, these formulas work in Excel and Google Sheets:
| Cell | Measure | Formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B5 | CPI | =B3/B4 |
| B6 | SPI | =B3/B2 |
| B7 | EAC (typical) | =B1/B5 |
| B8 | EAC (atypical) | =B4+(B1-B3) |
| B9 | EAC (CPI x SPI) | =B4+(B1-B3)/(B5*B6) |
| B10 | ETC | =B7-B4 |
| B11 | VAC | =B1-B7 |
| B12 | TCPI to BAC | =(B1-B3)/(B1-B4) |
Track these each period in a row per status date so you can chart the trend. A rising EAC line is more informative than any single value. Our free [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) and [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) give you a structure for BAC and bottom-up estimates.
Most project management tools with budgeting features record planned and actual cost; check that yours can export the figures you need. Our [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) reviews cover which tools include budgeting and financial tracking.

### Reporting EAC to sponsors
An EAC on its own invites the question "so what?". A useful forecast in a [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) includes:
- The **preferred EAC** and the range from the other methods.
- **VAC** in money and as a percentage of BAC.
- The **trend**: how EAC has moved over the last few periods.
- The **main causes** of the variance and whether they will continue.
- **TCPI** to show whether the budget is still achievable.
- **Recommended actions**: corrective measures, use of contingency, or a change request to rebaseline.
Agree thresholds in advance, such as escalating when VAC exceeds 5% or 10% of BAC, so a forecast overrun triggers a decision rather than a debate. If the overrun cannot be absorbed, it goes through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) for a revised budget. Keeping EAC visible every period is one of the core habits of [cost control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-control/).
For the wider picture of forecasting finish dates and benefits as well as cost, read [project forecasting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/).

### Common mistakes
- **Defaulting to AC + (BAC - EV)** because it gives the smallest overrun, without evidence that the cause has gone away.
- **Relying on one early CPI reading.** Wait for a trend; early indices swing widely.
- **Using poor progress data.** Subjective percent complete inflates EV and flatters every forecast.
- **Leaving out accruals and committed costs**, so AC and EAC are understated.
- **Confusing EAC with BAC or the funding limit.** EAC is a forecast; BAC is the approved budget; funding may include management reserve.
- **Including management reserve in BAC.** Reserve sits outside the performance measurement baseline.
- **Forecasting only at project level**, which hides overrunning work packages.
- **Reporting one number without the reasoning**, which makes the forecast hard to trust or challenge.
- **Not updating BAC after approved changes**, so variance includes scope that was formally added.

### EAC on the PMP exam
EAC questions appear regularly in PMP and CAPM preparation material. A few conventions help:
- If the question says the variance is **typical** or performance will **continue**, use BAC / CPI.
- If it says the variance is **atypical**, a **one-off** or will **not recur**, use AC + (BAC - EV).
- If it mentions both cost and schedule affecting the remaining work, or a **firm deadline**, use AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI).
- If it says the **original estimate is flawed** or a new estimate has been made, use AC + ETC.
- Remember ETC = EAC - AC and VAC = BAC - EAC; a negative VAC means over budget.
- TCPI above 1 means the remaining work must be more efficient than planned.

### Related guides
EAC is the forecasting end of a connected set of cost tools. [Project cost management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-cost-management/) covers the full cycle from estimating to control, and the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) guide shows how BAC is built.
To understand the measures EAC is built on, read our guide to [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is estimate at completion in project management?**
Estimate at completion (EAC) is the forecast total cost of a project when all its work is done. It equals the actual cost to date plus the estimated cost of the remaining work, and is compared with the budget at completion to show an expected overrun or underrun.

**Q: What is the formula for EAC?**
There are four standard formulas: BAC / CPI; AC + (BAC - EV); AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI); and AC + a bottom-up estimate to complete. The general relationship is always EAC = AC + ETC.

**Q: Which EAC formula is used most often?**
EAC = BAC / CPI. It assumes current cost efficiency will continue, which is often realistic once a project is well under way, and it is the default in many tools and exam questions.

**Q: What is the difference between EAC and ETC?**
EAC is the forecast total cost of the project. ETC (estimate to complete) is the forecast cost of the work still to do. EAC = AC + ETC, so ETC = EAC - AC.

**Q: What is the difference between EAC and BAC?**
BAC is the approved budget for all the work and changes only through change control. EAC is the current forecast of the final cost and can change every reporting period. VAC = BAC - EAC shows the gap.

**Q: When should I use EAC = AC + (BAC - EV)?**
When the variance so far was caused by a one-off event that has been resolved, so the remaining work is expected to be done at the budgeted rate. It is the most optimistic formula for an over-budget project.

**Q: When should I use the CPI x SPI formula?**
When the project is behind schedule and must still meet a fixed date, so catching up will add cost through overtime, extra resources or expediting. It usually gives the highest EAC when both indices are below 1.

**Q: Can EAC be lower than BAC?**
Yes. If the CPI is above 1 the project is spending less than budgeted for the work done, and EAC will be below BAC. VAC will then be positive, showing a forecast underrun.

**Q: What does a negative VAC mean?**
Variance at completion = BAC - EAC. A negative VAC means the project is forecast to finish over budget by that amount. For example, BAC $200,000 and EAC $242,857 gives VAC of -$42,857.

**Q: What is TCPI and how does it relate to EAC?**
The to-complete performance index is the cost efficiency the remaining work must achieve to meet a target. TCPI to BAC = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC); TCPI to EAC = (BAC - EV) / (EAC - AC). A TCPI well above the current CPI means the target is unrealistic.

**Q: How often should EAC be updated?**
Every reporting period, usually monthly or at the end of each sprint or phase, alongside the other earned value measures. Also update it after major events such as approved changes or significant risks occurring.

**Q: Is a bottom-up EAC better than a formula?**
When the plan has changed significantly it is usually more credible, because it reflects current scope, rates and risks. Formulas are faster and work well as an independent cross-check on the bottom-up figure.

**Q: What is an independent EAC?**
An independent EAC (IEAC) is a forecast calculated purely from earned value formulas, without management judgement. It is used to test the project manager's own forecast; a large gap between the two needs explaining.

**Q: Is EAC the same as a project forecast?**
EAC is the cost part of a project forecast. A full forecast also covers the expected finish date and, often, benefits. See our guide to [project forecasting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/).

# Expert Judgment in Project Management: Guide and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/expert-judgment/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Expert judgment in project management explained: who counts as an expert, Delphi and other techniques, a 7-step process, worked examples and bias fixes.


## Expert Judgment in Project Management: Guide and Examples
Expert judgment in project management is advice based on the specialist knowledge, skills or experience of people who understand the work, used to support estimates, plans, risk assessments and decisions. This guide explains where it fits, who counts as an expert, the main techniques, a seven-step process and two worked examples, plus how to keep bias out of the result.
- Published 2 October 2026
- Last updated 18 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Expert judgment is structured advice from people with relevant expertise; it is a tool and technique across almost every area of project management.
- Expertise is specific: choose experts for the exact question, and use more than one where the stakes are high.
- Structured methods such as Delphi, nominal group technique and planning poker reduce anchoring, groupthink and the pull of senior voices.
- Ask for ranges and reasons, not single numbers, then combine expert views with historical data wherever it exists.
- Record who gave the judgment, their assumptions and their reasoning, so it can be checked against actual results.
- The project manager does not have to be the expert, but stays accountable for how the advice is used.

### What is expert judgment in project management?
**Expert judgment** is guidance based on the expertise of people with relevant education, knowledge, skill, experience or training, applied to a specific project question. It is used when you need an estimate, an assessment or a decision and the answer depends on knowledge that sits in people's heads rather than in a formula or a database.
The PMBOK Guide describes it as judgment based on expertise appropriate to the activity being performed, and notes that the expertise can come from any group or person with specialised education, knowledge, skill, experience or training. In other words, the definition is about the fit between the person and the question, not about job titles.

#### Expert judgment or expert judgement?
Both spellings are correct. PMI publications use **judgment**, so that is the form you will see in the PMBOK Guide, in PMP exam material and in most search results. British English often uses **judgement** outside legal contexts. We use "judgment" on this page because it matches the term readers search for and the standard they are studying.

#### Is expert judgment a tool or a technique?
In the PMBOK Guide Sixth Edition, which organised project management into 49 processes, expert judgment is listed as a tool and technique in many of those processes, from developing the project charter to closing the project. The Seventh Edition (2021) moved away from process detail towards principles and performance domains. The Eighth Edition, which PMI published in November 2025, brings back process guidance alongside its principles and domains and includes a separate section of tools and techniques. Whatever edition you study, the idea is the same: expert input is a technique you plan and manage, not an informal chat.

### Why expert judgment matters
Most project methods need inputs that cannot be calculated from first principles. A [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) needs someone who knows what the work actually involves. A risk register needs people who have seen similar projects go wrong. A supplier evaluation needs someone who can tell a sound technical proposal from a polished one.
Expert judgment earns its place in four situations:
- **New or unusual work**, where there is little historical data to draw on.
- **Early stages**, such as a [feasibility study](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/feasibility-study/), when decisions are needed before details exist.
- **Time pressure**, where a structured conversation with two specialists is quicker than building a model.
- **Tacit knowledge**, such as how a regulator tends to interpret a rule or why a legacy system behaves the way it does, which rarely appears in documents.
The **project manager does not need to be the expert**, but is accountable for finding the right expertise, asking good questions and deciding well with the answers. It is part of how [project integration management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-integration-management/) brings specialist knowledge into joined-up plans.

### Where expert judgment is used across the project
Expert judgment is not limited to estimating. The table shows typical questions at each stage.
| Stage or area | Typical question for experts | Example | Related guide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initiation | Is this objective achievable with the proposed budget and time? | A delivery lead reviews a business case before approval | Project charter |
| Scope | What has been missed or misunderstood? | A tester spots that data migration is absent from the WBS | Project scope |
| Schedule | How long will this take, and what does it depend on? | An integration engineer estimates API work and flags a dependency on the vendor | [Project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) |
| Cost | What will it cost, and which assumptions drive the cost? | A quantity surveyor prices a fit-out | Cost estimation |
| Risk | What could go wrong, how likely is it and how bad would it be? | Security specialists rate threats for a new customer portal | [Project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) |
| Quality | Which standards and tests apply? | A compliance officer confirms accessibility requirements | [Project quality management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/) |
| Procurement | Is this bid technically sound and fairly priced? | An architect scores supplier proposals | [Procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) |
| Change control | What is the real impact of this change request? | A lead developer sizes a late feature request | [Change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) |
| Closure | What should we repeat or avoid next time? | Team leads review estimates against actuals | [Lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) |

### Who counts as an expert
An expert is anyone whose knowledge is relevant to the specific question. Common sources include:
- **Project team members** who have done similar work before.
- **Subject matter experts** in other departments, such as finance, legal, security, procurement or operations.
- **The PMO**, which may hold estimating data and lessons from past projects.
- **Experienced project managers** who have delivered similar projects.
- **Suppliers and consultants**, who know their own products and markets.
- **Professional bodies and industry groups**, which publish standards and guidance.
- **Users, customers and sponsors**, who are experts in how the work is actually done and what value looks like (see [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/)).
Expertise is narrow: a strong solution architect is not automatically an expert on software licensing. Use simple criteria when you choose people:
| Criterion | Question to ask | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relevance | Has this person done this specific kind of work recently? | Experience is from a different technology, sector or decade |
| Track record | How did their past estimates or forecasts compare with what happened? | No one has ever checked |
| Independence | Do they gain or lose from a particular answer? | A supplier estimating its own work, or a team keen to win approval |
| Diversity of view | Does the group cover technical, commercial and user angles? | Every expert comes from the same team |
| Availability | Can they give the question proper time? | A five-minute answer in a corridor |
Tip
Keep a short expert directory for your organisation or PMO: names, areas of expertise and past projects. It saves time on every new project and makes it easier to find a second opinion.

### Expert judgment techniques
How you collect expert views matters as much as whom you ask. The main techniques are summarised below, followed by notes on when to use each.
| Technique | How it works | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One-to-one interviews | Structured questions with one expert at a time | Detailed, technical or sensitive topics | Interviewer leading the answer |
| Facilitated workshops | A group session with a clear agenda and facilitator | Risk identification, planning, design reviews | Groupthink and dominant voices |
| Delphi technique | Anonymous rounds of estimates with shared summaries and reasons until views converge | Estimates and forecasts where seniority could sway the group | Takes several days; needs a neutral facilitator |
| Nominal group technique | Silent individual ideas, round-robin sharing, discussion, then a private vote | Generating and prioritising options | Can feel formal for small teams |
| Planning poker / wideband Delphi | Simultaneous reveal of estimates, discuss outliers, re-estimate | Agile estimation and quick team estimates | Becomes routine if outliers are not discussed |
| Peer review | Independent experts review a plan, design or estimate | Quality assurance and stage gates | Reviewers lacking time or context |
| Structured elicitation with ranges | Experts give a low, most likely and high value with reasons | Inputs to three-point estimates and simulation | Ranges that are too narrow (overconfidence) |

#### Delphi technique
The Delphi technique was developed at the RAND Corporation in the 1950s for forecasting. A facilitator sends the same question to each expert, collects answers anonymously, then shares a summary of the range and the reasons given. Experts revise their answers in the light of the summary, and the process repeats, usually for two or three rounds. Anonymity stops a senior or confident person from setting the answer for everyone else, while the shared reasons still let the group learn from each other.

#### Interviews, workshops and nominal group technique
Interviews give depth: prepare questions, ask for the reasoning behind every number and finish with "what would make you change this view?" Workshops give breadth but need a facilitator who draws out quieter people and keeps estimates hidden until everyone has committed. The nominal group technique adds structure by having people write ideas silently, share them in turn and vote privately.

#### Planning poker
Planning poker is a team version of wideband Delphi used in Agile estimation. Everyone chooses an estimate card privately and reveals it at the same time. The people with the highest and lowest estimates explain their thinking, and the team estimates again.

#### Structured elicitation with ranges
Instead of asking "how long?", ask for a low, most likely and high value, and for the assumptions behind each. Ranges carry more information than a single number and feed directly into a [PERT three-point estimate](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/) or a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/).

### How to use expert judgment: a 7-step process
Good expert judgment follows a repeatable process. The steps below draw on the practices in PMI's book *Expert Judgment in Project Management: Narrowing the Theory-Practice Gap* (Paul S. Szwed, 2016), expressed as our own practical checklist.
1. **Frame the problem.** Write down exactly what you need to know, why and by when. "Estimate the effort to migrate 40 reports to the new platform, including testing, to the nearest week" is far better than "how long will the migration take?"
2. **Plan the elicitation.** Choose the technique (interviews, Delphi, workshop), the number of experts, the format of answers (single value, range, rating scale) and how you will combine them.
3. **Select the experts.** Use the criteria above. For important questions, aim for three to five people with different viewpoints rather than one authority.
4. **Brief the experts.** Share the same background pack with everyone: scope, assumptions, constraints, relevant data and definitions. Explain the answer format and remind them about common biases, such as anchoring on a target date.
5. **Elicit the judgments.** Collect answers independently before any group discussion. Ask for reasons and key assumptions as well as the number or rating.
6. **Analyse and combine.** Look at the spread. Where views differ widely, find out why: often one expert knows something the others do not. Combine using an agreed method, such as a three-point estimate, an average of the second Delphi round, or a consensus discussion.
7. **Document and communicate.** Record the result, the range, the experts consulted, the assumptions and any risks raised. Share it with stakeholders and feed it into the plan, the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) or the estimate.
Tip
If the experts disagree strongly and you cannot resolve it, do not average the difference away. Treat the disagreement as a risk or an assumption to test, and plan a quick spike, prototype or supplier check to find out who is right.

### Worked example 1: Delphi estimate for a data migration
A finance team is moving 40 management reports from an old reporting tool to a new analytics platform. The project manager needs an effort estimate for the business case and has no historical data for this platform.

#### Setting up
The project manager frames the question as "working days of effort to rebuild, test and sign off all 40 reports", selects four experts (two report developers, a data engineer and a business analyst) and sends each the report inventory, the target platform's documentation and the definition of "signed off".

#### Round 1
| Expert | Estimate (days) | Main reason given |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 15 | Most reports are simple tables |
| B | 25 | Allow time for user testing |
| C | 30 | Data model needs to be rebuilt first |
| D | 60 | 12 reports use custom scripts that the new platform does not support |
The facilitator shares the range (15 to 60 days), the median (27.5 days) and all four reasons without names. Expert D's point about custom scripts is new information to the others.

#### Round 2
| Expert | Estimate (days) | Change and reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 30 | Up 15: had not known about the custom scripts |
| B | 35 | Up 10: scripts need rewriting and testing |
| C | 35 | Up 5: agrees with the script concern |
| D | 45 | Down 15: data model work can run alongside |
The range has narrowed from 45 days to 15 days, so the facilitator stops after two rounds.

#### Turning the result into an estimate
The team uses the round 2 views as a three-point estimate: optimistic 30, most likely 35 and pessimistic 45 days.
- **PERT estimate** = (O + 4M + P) / 6 = (30 + 4 x 35 + 45) / 6 = 215 / 6 = **35.8 days**.
- **Standard deviation** = (P − O) / 6 = (45 − 30) / 6 = **2.5 days**.
- Roughly 95% of outcomes would fall within two standard deviations, so about **31 to 41 days**, if the assumptions hold.
The custom-script issue is logged in the risk register with an owner, and the business case states the estimate as "36 days, likely range 31 to 41 days" with the assumptions attached. Compare this with the first-round median of 27.5 days: without the structured rounds, the estimate would probably have been too low.

### Worked example 2: expert risk assessment
A project is integrating a new payments supplier. The project manager asks three experts to rate one risk independently on a 1 to 5 scale for probability and impact: "The supplier's test environment is not ready by the start of integration testing, delaying go-live."
| Expert | Role | Probability (1–5) | Impact (1–5) | Score (P x I) | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E1 | Integration lead | 4 | 4 | 16 | The supplier has missed two environment dates on other projects |
| E2 | Test manager | 3 | 5 | 15 | Integration testing is on the critical path |
| E3 | Supplier manager | 2 | 4 | 8 | The supplier has committed a named environment manager this time |
The scores range from 8 to 16. Rather than averaging, the project manager brings the three together for 20 minutes to compare reasons. E3's information is new and credible, but E1's history is also real. They agree on probability 3 and impact 4, a score of **12 (high on the project's scale)**, and two actions:
- Ask the supplier to confirm the environment date in writing, with a check-in two weeks before.
- Prepare a contingency: build and test against the supplier's sandbox so work can start even if the full environment is late (see [contingency planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/)).
The assessment, the three original ratings and the reasons are stored with the risk, so the team can see later whether the experts were right.

### Choosing your role: decide, delegate, consult or facilitate
Not every question needs a Delphi study. A practical way to choose, discussed by several practitioners including Mosaic Projects, is to consider how much the decision matters and whether you have the expertise yourself.
|  | You have the relevant expertise | You lack the relevant expertise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low consequence, needs a quick answer | **Decide** yourself and note the reasoning | **Delegate** to someone who has the expertise |
| High consequence or plenty of time | **Consult**: seek independent views, then decide | **Facilitate**: run a structured process with several experts and make the decision with the sponsor if needed |
This keeps effort proportionate. A five-day task estimate inside a team does not need four rounds of anonymous voting; a contract value, a safety risk or a go-live date usually does deserve more structure.

### Common biases and how to reduce them
Experts are human. The biases below are well documented in decision research, and each has a practical counter.
| Bias | What it looks like | How to reduce it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Optimism bias / planning fallacy | Estimates assume everything goes well | Ask for ranges; compare with actuals from past projects; ask "what went wrong last time?" |
| Anchoring | Everyone converges on the first number mentioned, or on a target date | Collect estimates independently before sharing any number, including the sponsor's target |
| Overconfidence | Ranges are far too narrow | Ask for a value you would be surprised to beat, and one you would be surprised to exceed; check past ranges |
| Groupthink and seniority | The group follows the most senior or loudest person | Use anonymous rounds (Delphi), silent writing or simultaneous reveal |
| Availability bias | Recent or vivid events dominate | Use checklists and historical data alongside memory |
| Motivational bias | The expert benefits from a high or low answer | Use independent experts; declare interests; seek a second opinion |
| Narrow expertise | One discipline's view dominates | Mix technical, commercial and user perspectives |
| Curse of knowledge | The expert cannot explain the reasoning to non-specialists | Ask for assumptions in plain language; ask "what would a newcomer get wrong?" |

### Expert judgment vs other estimating methods
Expert judgment is often described as an estimating method in its own right, but in practice it sits underneath most other methods. The table shows how it relates to them.
| Method | How it works | Role of expert judgment | Best when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expert judgment | Specialists estimate directly from experience | The whole method | Work is new or data is scarce |
| Analogous estimating | Uses the actual cost or duration of a similar past project | Experts choose the analogy and adjust for differences | Early stages, with a good comparable project |
| Parametric estimating | Applies a unit rate or model, such as cost per square metre | Experts check the model fits and the parameters are right | Repeatable work with reliable data |
| Bottom-up estimating | Estimates each work package and adds them up | Each package is estimated by the people who will do it | Scope is well defined |
| Three-point estimating (PERT) | Combines optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values | Experts supply the three values | Uncertainty matters and needs to be shown |
| Monte Carlo simulation | Runs thousands of scenarios from input ranges | Experts supply ranges and correlations | Large, uncertain projects with many risks |
Our advice: use **data as the starting point and experts to adjust for what is different this time**. Where you have historical data, use it; where you do not, structured expert judgment is far better than a single guess. You can test how sensitive your plan is to each expert assumption with [sensitivity analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/sensitivity-analysis/).

### Advantages and disadvantages of expert judgment

#### Advantages
- Fast and inexpensive compared with building models or collecting data.
- Works when there is no historical data, such as new technology or one-off projects.
- Captures tacit knowledge and context that formulas miss.
- Flexible: works for estimates, risks, design choices and supplier evaluation.

#### Disadvantages
- Prone to bias, especially optimism, anchoring and group pressure.
- Hard to verify or repeat unless the reasoning is recorded.
- Depends on finding the right experts and on their availability.
- Can give false confidence when an opinion is presented as a fact.
Most of the disadvantages are reduced by structure: independent answers, ranges, several experts, recorded reasoning and later comparison with actual results.

### How to document expert judgment
A short record makes expert judgment auditable and helps you learn which experts and methods give good results. Capture these fields wherever the judgment is used, for example in the estimate, the risk register or the decision log.
| Field | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Question | Effort to migrate and sign off 40 reports |
| Date and method | 3 to 10 March, two-round Delphi |
| Experts consulted | Two report developers, a data engineer, a business analyst |
| Result | 36 days (range 31 to 41) |
| Key assumptions | Data model can be built in parallel; users available for testing in weeks 4 to 6 |
| Disagreements and risks | Custom scripts may need more rework; logged as a risk |
| Review date | Compare with actual effort at project closure |
Our free [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) has space for estimating basis and assumptions, and the [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) holds the risks experts raise. At closure, compare estimates with actuals and record the findings in a [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) so the next project starts with better data.

### Expert judgment in Agile teams
Agile teams use expert judgment constantly, though they rarely call it that. The team doing the work is treated as the expert on its own estimates, which is why Agile practices emphasise whole-team estimation.
- **Planning poker and affinity estimation** gather the team's expertise quickly while avoiding anchoring.
- **Backlog refinement** brings in specialists, such as security or UX, to judge feasibility and acceptance criteria before work starts.
- **Sprint planning** relies on the team's judgment of what it can complete, balanced by velocity data (see [sprint planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/)).
- **Retrospectives** turn experience into improvements, closing the loop between judgment and results.
The same rules apply: independent estimates first, then discussion of outliers.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is expert judgment in project management?**
It is advice based on the specialist knowledge, skills or experience of people who understand the work, used to support estimates, plans, risk assessments and decisions. The PMBOK Guide treats it as a tool and technique used across many processes.

**Q: What is an example of expert judgment?**
Asking three experienced developers to estimate the effort for an integration, collecting their low, likely and high values independently, discussing the differences and combining them into a three-point estimate is a typical example. Asking a security specialist to rate a risk is another.

**Q: Is it spelled expert judgment or expert judgement?**
Both are correct. PMI and the PMBOK Guide use 'judgment', which is also the more common search term. 'Judgement' is common in British English outside legal writing.

**Q: What are the main expert judgment techniques?**
Interviews, facilitated workshops, the Delphi technique, nominal group technique, planning poker (a form of wideband Delphi), peer review and structured elicitation using ranges.

**Q: Is the Delphi technique a form of expert judgment?**
Yes. It is one of the best-known ways to gather expert judgment. Experts answer anonymously over several rounds and see a summary of the group's views and reasons each time, which reduces the influence of dominant individuals.

**Q: What are the disadvantages of expert judgment?**
It can be biased, inconsistent between experts, hard to verify and dependent on finding the right people. Structure, ranges, several experts and recorded reasoning reduce these problems.

**Q: What is the difference between expert judgment and analogous estimating?**
Analogous estimating uses actual data from a similar past project, scaled for size or complexity. Expert judgment is broader: experts often choose the analogy and adjust it, but they also add opinion and interpretation where no comparable data exists.

**Q: Is expert judgment qualitative or quantitative?**
It can be either. Experts may give a number, such as a duration or cost, or a qualitative view, such as whether a design meets a standard. Asking for ranges and ratings makes judgments easier to combine and compare.

**Q: How many experts should you consult?**
For routine questions, one relevant expert may be enough. For high-stakes estimates or risks, three to five experts with different perspectives usually give a more reliable view without becoming hard to manage.

**Q: How should expert judgment be documented?**
Record the question, the date and method, who was consulted, the result and range, the key assumptions, any disagreements or risks raised, and when you will compare the judgment with actual results.

**Q: Can AI tools provide expert judgment?**
AI assistants can help you prepare questions, summarise past project data and suggest risks to consider, but they are not accountable experts. Treat their output as an input for qualified people to review, and follow your organisation's rules on sharing project data.

**Q: Is expert judgment on the PMP exam?**
Yes. Scenario questions often test whether you consult subject matter experts before committing to an estimate, prefer structured methods when opinions conflict and remember that the project manager stays accountable. See our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

**Q: Does the project manager have to be the expert?**
No. The project manager's role is to find the right expertise, structure how it is gathered and make a sound decision with it. The project manager remains accountable for that decision.
