# Extreme Project Management (XPM): Guide and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/extreme-project-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Extreme project management (XPM) explained: what makes a project extreme, the Flexible Project Model, XPM vs Agile, a worked example and how to run one.


## Extreme Project Management (XPM): Guide and Examples
Extreme project management (XPM) is an approach for projects with high speed, high change and high uncertainty, where the goal, the solution or both are unclear at the start and a detailed upfront plan would be out of date within weeks. Instead of controlling the project against a fixed plan, XPM treats it as a self-correcting process: the team works in short cycles, learns from each one and keeps asking whether the project is still worth doing. This guide covers what makes a project extreme, the two best-known XPM models, a step-by-step process, a full worked example and the mistakes to avoid.
- Published 12 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- XPM is for projects where the goal, the solution or both are unclear and conditions change quickly: innovation, R&D and new ventures.
- Doug DeCarlo's Flexible Project Model runs in cycles: Visionate, Speculate, Innovate, Reevaluate and, when the result is right, Disseminate.
- Four business questions drive every decision: Who needs what and why? What will it take to do it? Can we get what it takes? Is it worth it?
- Success is measured by business value and stakeholder satisfaction, not by conformance to the original plan.
- XPM still needs control: time boxes, funding released in tranches, clear kill criteria and an engaged sponsor.
- Use it selectively. Predictable, regulated or fixed-price work is better served by traditional or Agile approaches.

### What is extreme project management?
Extreme project management (XPM) is an adaptive approach for managing highly uncertain, fast-moving projects in which the requirements, the solution or even the goal are expected to change. It replaces a fixed upfront plan with short cycles of planning, doing and reassessing, and judges success by the business value delivered rather than conformance to the original plan.
The term is most closely associated with Doug DeCarlo, whose book eXtreme Project Management: Using Leadership, Principles, and Tools to Deliver Value in the Face of Volatility was published by Wiley in 2004. DeCarlo describes XPM as the art and science of facilitating and managing the flow of thoughts, emotions and interactions so that a project produces valued outcomes in turbulent conditions. XPM is first about people, conversations and decisions, and only second about schedules.
Robert K. Wysocki also uses "extreme" as one of his project categories in his book Effective Project Management, alongside traditional and agile (earlier editions said adaptive). Both authors reach a similar conclusion: you cannot manage the unknown the way you manage the known.
Tip
Extreme project management is not the same as Extreme Programming (XP). XP is an Agile software development method with specific engineering practices such as pair programming and test-driven development. XPM is a broader way of managing any highly uncertain project, software or not.
XPM sits at the far end of the spectrum of [project management methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-methodologies/), beyond Agile, with the least upfront structure and the most frequent replanning.

### What makes a project extreme?
DeCarlo's publisher summarises extreme projects as having high speed, high change, high complexity, high risk and high stress. A project is a candidate for XPM when several of these hold at once:
| Characteristic | What it looks like in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Unclear or moving goal | The sponsor can describe the opportunity but not the finished deliverable; the target shifts as the market or the science changes |
| Unknown solution | Nobody has built this before, at least not here; the technical or operational path must be discovered |
| High speed | A window of opportunity or a competitor sets the pace, so waiting for a full plan costs more than replanning |
| High change | New information arrives weekly and regularly overturns earlier assumptions |
| High risk and experimentation | Some approaches will fail by design; the question is how quickly and cheaply |
| Many stakeholders with different views | Agreement on what "done" means has to be built during the project, not before it |
A review of DeCarlo's book by the Product Development and Management Association (PDMA) notes his rule of thumb that a project is extreme when it shows at least two of: high stakes, short deadlines, a requirement for innovation, a bottom-line measure of success, no tolerance for bureaucracy and an emphasis on quality of life for the team.

#### The goal and solution clarity grid
Wysocki's way of classifying projects is the quickest test of whether XPM is appropriate. Ask two questions: is the goal clear, and is the solution clear?
| Project type | Goal | Solution | Typical approach | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Traditional | Clear | Clear | Plan-driven, such as [waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) | Moving an office to a new building |
| Agile (adaptive) | Clear | Unclear | Iterative delivery, such as Scrum or Kanban | Building a customer portal with an agreed purpose |
| Extreme | Unclear | Unclear | XPM: cycles of vision, speculation, learning and reassessment | Creating a new product category or business line |
| Emertxe ("extreme" backwards) | Unclear | Clear | Exploratory: find the problem a solution can solve | Finding uses for a new technology or patent |

#### Quick self-assessment
If you answer yes to three or more of these questions, consider XPM or at least an XPM-style governance wrapper around your normal method:
- Would a detailed plan written today be largely wrong within a month?
- Could the final deliverable look substantially different from what the sponsor first imagined?
- Is speed to a first result more valuable than predictability of cost and date?
- Are you willing to stop the project early if the evidence says it is not worth continuing?
- Is there a sponsor who can make funding and direction decisions quickly?

### Core principles of extreme project management
XPM is less a set of templates than a set of beliefs about how to work under uncertainty. The principles below appear, in different words, in both DeCarlo's and Wysocki's work:
- **The project is a self-correcting process, not a fixed plan.** Plans are hypotheses that each cycle tests and updates.
- **Value beats conformance.** A project that delivers the right thing late is more successful than one that delivers the wrong thing on time.
- **Plan to replan.** Plan the next short cycle in detail and everything beyond it only roughly.
- **Fail fast and cheaply.** Design early cycles to kill bad ideas before they absorb the budget.
- **Stakeholders are inside the project.** The sponsor and key users take part in planning and review, not just sign-off.
- **People first.** Motivation, trust and fast, honest communication matter more than documentation.
- **Keep asking whether it is worth it.** Continuation is a decision made at every cycle boundary, not an assumption.
These ideas echo the [Agile mindset](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-mindset/) and the [empiricism behind Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/). XPM pushes them further by putting the goal itself, not just the solution, up for revision.

### The Flexible Project Model: DeCarlo's five cycles
DeCarlo calls his life cycle the Flexible Project Model. It has five elements, which he calls cycles because the first four repeat as often as needed until the deliverable is right. Only then does the project move to Disseminate.
| Cycle | Purpose | Key outputs | Business question in focus |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Visionate | Capture the sponsor's vision and build a shared one | Vision statement, project scope boundaries, stakeholder map | 1. Who needs what and why? |
| Speculate | Plan the next stretch of work and the bets to test | Ideas, priorities, rough plan, next cycle's goals and budget | 2. What will it take to do it? |
| Innovate | Build, test and learn by doing | Working results, prototypes, test data, lessons | 3. Can we get what it takes? |
| Reevaluate | Decide the project's future | Continue, redirect, pause or stop decision | 4. Is it worth it? |
| Disseminate | Release the deliverable and start harvesting benefits | Deliverable in use, stabilisation, project review, benefits tracking | Are the benefits being realised? |

#### Visionate
Visionate turns the sponsor's idea into a collective vision the whole team and key stakeholders can act on. The aim is a short statement of who the deliverable is for, what problem it solves, why it matters now and how success will be judged, plus clear boundaries. A one-page [project brief](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-brief-template/) is usually enough.

#### Speculate
In Speculate the team brainstorms options, picks the most promising bets and plans only the next cycle in detail; any plan made now is an informed guess. The output is a short list of experiments or features, the question each should answer, a time box and a budget.

#### Innovate
Innovate is where the work happens: prototypes, pilots, user tests and data collection. Learning is a deliverable in its own right, so the team records what it found as well as what it built.

#### Reevaluate
At the end of each cycle the sponsor, the project manager and the team decide whether this is still the right project: can it still win, should it change direction or be put on hold? Stopping here is a valid and often valuable outcome, not a failure.

#### Disseminate
Disseminate releases the finished deliverable, stabilises it in use, reviews how it is performing and begins benefits realisation. DeCarlo stresses that it is premature to declare victory until the customer is using the result and benefits are starting to flow.

#### Wysocki's INSPIRE model
Robert Wysocki describes a similar extreme life cycle called INSPIRE: Initiate, Speculate, Incubate and Review, the four phases also used in Wrike's guide to XPM. Initiate corresponds to Visionate, Incubate to Innovate and Review to Reevaluate. Most teams borrow the cycle structure and business questions from either model and keep their existing delivery practices inside each cycle.

### The four business questions
The four business questions are the decision spine of DeCarlo's model. They are asked first during Visionate and Speculate and then again at every Reevaluate, because the answers change as the team learns.
| Question | What it tests | Evidence you would look at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Who needs what and why? | Whether there is a real customer and need | Interviews, usage data, sponsor priorities, problem statements |
| 2. What will it take to do it? | Scope, effort, skills and cost of the next stage and of the whole | Cycle results, revised estimates, technical findings |
| 3. Can we get what it takes? | Whether people, money, technology and support are available | Resource commitments, budget, sponsor backing |
| 4. Is it worth it? | Whether expected benefits still justify the remaining investment | Updated business case, [return on investment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/return-on-investment/), strategic fit |
A useful habit is to write the current answer to each question on a single page and update it at every cycle boundary. If an answer has worsened for two cycles running, it should trigger a serious redirect-or-stop conversation.

### How to run an extreme project step by step
This process combines the two models into a practical sequence. Outputs are deliberately light: enough to make decisions, no more.
1. **Confirm the project really is extreme.** Use the goal and solution clarity grid and the self-assessment above. If the goal and solution are both clear, a traditional plan will serve you better. Output: a short rationale for the approach.
2. **Secure an active sponsor.** Agree who can approve funding and change direction within days, not weeks, and how often they will attend reviews. Output: named sponsor and decision rights.
3. **Write the vision.** Capture who needs what and why, the outcomes that would count as success and the boundaries of the project. Output: a one-page vision or [project brief](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-brief-template/).
4. **Map stakeholders and bring the key ones inside.** Identify users, funders and blockers, and invite the most important to planning and review sessions. See [project stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/). Output: stakeholder map and review invitees.
5. **Agree cycle length, funding tranches and kill criteria.** Typical cycles run from one to four weeks. Release money one tranche at a time and agree in advance what evidence would stop the project. Output: governance rules on a page.
6. **Speculate: choose the next bets.** Brainstorm options, pick the few with the highest learning or value per unit of effort, and write the question each should answer. Output: prioritised list for the next cycle.
7. **Innovate: build, test and learn.** Run the time-boxed work, keep the board visible and capture findings daily. Output: working results and evidence.
8. **Reevaluate: answer the four business questions.** Review results with the sponsor and stakeholders, update the business case and decide to continue, redirect, pause or stop. Output: recorded decision and next tranche released (or not).
9. **Repeat until the deliverable is right.** Each loop should narrow the uncertainty; if it does not, redirect or stop.
10. **Disseminate and capture lessons.** Release the deliverable, stabilise it, start tracking benefits and record [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) for the next extreme project. Output: handover, benefits measures and a retrospective.
Tip
In an extreme project most risks are untested assumptions. Log them from day one in a simple [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) and test the riskiest first.

### Worked example: a 12-week service pilot
The following example is illustrative. The organisation, figures and results are invented to show how XPM works in practice.
A regional energy supplier wants to know whether it can offer a home-battery subscription to existing customers. The sponsor, the director of new services, has a 12-week window before the annual budget round and an initial allocation of £150,000. Nobody knows yet which customers would pay, how installation would be handled or whether the margins work. Goal and solution are both unclear, so the team chooses XPM with three-week cycles and funding released in four tranches.

#### Visionate (week 1)
The sponsor, a product lead, an operations manager, a finance analyst and two customer-service advisers agree a one-page vision: "Help homeowners with solar panels store and use more of their own energy, through a subscription that is profitable within three years." They set three kill criteria: fewer than 5% of surveyed solar customers expressing serious interest, no installation partner able to meet a two-week lead time, or a modelled payback beyond five years.

#### Cycles 1 to 3
| Cycle | Bets tested | What the team learned | Reevaluate decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (weeks 2–4) | Customer survey; three installer conversations; first margin model | Interest strong among solar owners, weak among others; one installer can meet lead times | Continue, but narrow target to solar owners only; release tranche 2 |
| 2 (weeks 5–7) | Landing-page test with two price points; installer pilot contract draft | Higher price point converts almost as well as the lower one; installer wants volume commitment | Redirect: test a lower-commitment pilot of 20 homes instead of 100; release tranche 3 |
| 3 (weeks 8–10) | Install in the first 8 pilot homes; measure customer effort and support calls | Installation works; support calls mostly about app set-up | Continue: fix onboarding, prepare business case; release final tranche |

#### Final Reevaluate (week 11)
At the last cycle boundary the sponsor scores the project against the four business questions, using a simple 1–5 scale agreed in week 1:
| Business question | Score (1–5) | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who needs what and why? | 4 | Clear segment (solar owners); repeat themes in interviews |
| What will it take to do it? | 3 | Installer capacity, app onboarding fix, two extra support staff |
| Can we get what it takes? | 4 | Installer pilot signed; budget available within the new services line |
| Is it worth it? | 3 | Modelled payback just under four years; sensitive to battery prices |
The decision is to proceed to a controlled launch for solar customers only, with the business case going into the budget round and a [sensitivity analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/sensitivity-analysis/) on battery prices. In week 12 the team disseminates: the pilot is handed to operations, benefits measures are agreed and a retrospective is held.
Notice what happened: the scope changed twice and the pilot shrank from 100 homes to 20. Under a traditional plan those would be variances to explain; under XPM they are the project working as intended, because each change came from evidence and was approved at a planned decision point.

### Extreme vs traditional vs Agile project management
The clearest way to understand XPM is to compare it with the approaches on either side of it.
| Dimension | Traditional (predictive) | Agile | Extreme |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Goal | Clear and fixed | Clear | Unclear and expected to change |
| Solution | Known | Emerges iteratively | Unknown; discovered by experiment |
| Plan | Detailed and baselined upfront | Rolling: release and iteration plans | Next cycle only; everything else is speculation |
| Change | Controlled through formal change control | Welcomed within the product goal | Expected, including changes to the goal itself |
| Success measure | On time, on budget, to scope | Valuable increments delivered | Business value and stakeholder satisfaction |
| Documentation | Comprehensive | Just enough | Minimal |
| Stakeholder role | Approve at gates | Review increments regularly | Take part in planning and decisions |
| Continuation | Assumed once approved | Usually assumed within a product | Decided at every cycle |
| Best for | Predictable, repeatable work | Evolving products with a clear purpose | Innovation, R&D, new ventures |
For a deeper look at the first two columns, see our guide to [Agile vs waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/). Many organisations end up running XPM-style governance (vision, cycles, decision points) around an Agile delivery method such as [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) or [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/).

#### XPM vs Extreme Programming (XP)
|  | Extreme project management (XPM) | Extreme Programming (XP) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A management approach for highly uncertain projects | An Agile software development method |
| Scope | Any industry: products, services, research, ventures | Software teams |
| Focus | Vision, decisions, stakeholders, whether to continue | Engineering practices and code quality |
| Typical practices | Cycles, business questions, tranche funding, kill criteria | Pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases |
The two can work together: an extreme software project might use XP practices inside each Innovate cycle. Our overview of [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/) covers XP in more detail.

### Roles and skills in an extreme project
| Role | Responsibilities in XPM |
| --- | --- |
| Sponsor | Owns the vision and the money; attends Reevaluate sessions; makes continue, redirect or stop decisions quickly |
| Extreme project manager | Facilitates cycles, keeps stakeholders engaged, surfaces evidence and risks, protects the team from bureaucracy |
| Core team | Small, multi-skilled and largely self-organising; plans and runs each Innovate cycle |
| Key stakeholders and users | Take part in visioning, planning and review; test outputs and give fast feedback |
The extreme project manager is closer to a facilitator and coach than a controller; DeCarlo devotes a large part of his book to self-mastery and leadership. The most useful [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/) for this role are:
- Comfort with ambiguity and the ability to make decisions on incomplete information.
- Facilitation: running short, productive planning and review sessions with people who disagree.
- Stakeholder management and plain, frequent communication.
- Commercial judgement: reading a business case and knowing when the numbers no longer add up.
- The confidence to recommend stopping a project.

### Planning, budgeting and control without a fixed plan
A common misunderstanding is that XPM has no control. It has different controls: instead of comparing progress with a baseline, it limits exposure and forces regular decisions.
- **Time boxes.** Every cycle has a fixed length. Work that does not fit is reprioritised, not allowed to overrun.
- **Tranche funding.** Money is released one cycle or stage at a time, so the maximum loss is always known.
- **Kill criteria.** Agreed in advance and written down, so stopping is a rule being applied rather than a personal judgement under pressure.
- **Decision log.** A short record of each Reevaluate decision and its evidence, which supports [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) and audit.
- **Assumption testing.** The riskiest assumptions are tested first, which is how XPM handles [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/).
Measures also change. Earned value and baseline variance make little sense when the scope is meant to move. Use measures of learning and value instead:
| Measure | What it tells you | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assumptions validated or killed per cycle | Whether the project is reducing uncertainty | 4 of 6 critical assumptions tested by cycle 3 |
| Stakeholder satisfaction at review | Whether the people who matter still back the work | Average sponsor and user score of 4 out of 5 |
| Business-case trend | Whether "Is it worth it?" is improving or worsening | Payback estimate moving from 6 to 4 years |
| Burn rate against tranche | Whether the cycle will finish within its funding | 70% of tranche spent at 60% of the time box |

### Advantages and disadvantages of extreme project management
| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Responds quickly to new information and market change | Cost and finish date are hard to predict at the start |
| Kills weak ideas early, limiting wasted spend | Can feel chaotic without strong leadership and clear decision rights |
| Keeps the sponsor and users closely involved, so the result fits real needs | Demands a lot of the sponsor's time |
| Encourages innovation and learning from failure | Constant change can create pressure and burnout |
| Measures success by value, not by conformance to an outdated plan | Light documentation can be a problem for audit, regulation or handover |
| Suits small, experienced, motivated teams | Relies on experienced, self-directed people; hard for new teams |

### When not to use extreme project management
XPM is a specialist tool. It is a poor match when:
- The goal and solution are both well understood, as in many construction, relocation or system upgrade projects.
- The work is safety-critical or heavily regulated and needs full documentation and formal approvals at defined gates.
- The contract is fixed-price and fixed-scope, so the customer expects a predictable deliverable.
- The organisation cannot commit an engaged sponsor or release funding in stages.
- The team is new, large or spread across many suppliers who need detailed coordination.
In these cases a predictive or [iterative and incremental](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/iterative-and-incremental-development/) approach will usually serve better. A practical middle path is to run an extreme discovery phase of a few cycles, then switch to Agile or traditional delivery once the goal and solution are clear. See our guide to [project management methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-methodologies/).

### Common extreme project management mistakes
- **Using XPM as an excuse for no planning.** XPM plans constantly; it just plans in shorter horizons.
- **Labelling a messy project as extreme.** Poor requirements on a well-understood project need better analysis, not XPM.
- **An absent sponsor.** Without fast decisions, cycles end with nobody able to continue, redirect or stop.
- **No kill criteria.** Teams drift for months because nobody agreed what failure would look like.
- **Treating every change as progress.** Changes should come from evidence, not from the loudest stakeholder; otherwise it is simply [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).
- **Skipping Disseminate.** Delivering the result without stabilisation, handover and benefits tracking throws away much of the value.
- **Never holding retrospectives.** Learning about how the team works is as important as learning about the product. A [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) adapts well to XPM cycles.

### Tools and templates for extreme projects
Extreme projects need tools that make work visible and are quick to reshape, rather than tools built around a fixed baseline. Look for boards for each cycle, lightweight request intake, dashboards for the sponsor and easy restructuring when the plan changes. A [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) is enough for a small team's first cycles.
As the project grows, work management software helps. Wrike, our top-rated tool, combines boards (available on its Free plan), custom workflows, request forms and dashboards, which suits running cycles and reporting decisions to a sponsor; see our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/). monday.com and Asana are also strong choices for visual, fast-changing work. Our guide to [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-tools/) compares the options.
Read our guide to [Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is extreme project management?**
Extreme project management (XPM) is an approach for highly uncertain, fast-changing projects. It replaces a fixed plan with short cycles of planning, doing and reassessing, and measures success by business value and stakeholder satisfaction rather than conformance to the plan.

**Q: Who created extreme project management?**
The term is most closely associated with Doug DeCarlo, whose book eXtreme Project Management was published by Wiley in 2004. Robert K. Wysocki also uses extreme as a project category in his book Effective Project Management.

**Q: What are the phases of extreme project management?**
In DeCarlo's Flexible Project Model they are Visionate, Speculate, Innovate, Reevaluate and Disseminate, with the first four repeating as needed. Wysocki's INSPIRE model uses Initiate, Speculate, Incubate and Review.

**Q: What is the difference between extreme project management and Agile?**
Agile usually assumes a clear goal and lets the solution emerge. XPM is for projects where the goal itself is unclear, so it revisits both the goal and whether to continue at every cycle, with even less upfront structure.

**Q: Is extreme project management the same as Extreme Programming?**
No. Extreme Programming (XP) is an Agile software development method with engineering practices such as pair programming. XPM is a broader management approach for any highly uncertain project.

**Q: When should you use extreme project management?**
When the goal and solution are both unclear, conditions change quickly, speed matters more than predictability, and you have an engaged sponsor and an experienced team willing to stop if the evidence says so.

**Q: What are the four business questions in XPM?**
Who needs what and why? What will it take to do it? Can we get what it takes? Is it worth it? DeCarlo's model asks them at the start and again at every Reevaluate.

**Q: How long is an XPM cycle?**
There is no fixed length. Cycles of one to four weeks are common, short enough to learn quickly and long enough to produce meaningful evidence.

**Q: Can XPM be combined with Scrum or Kanban?**
Yes. Many teams use XPM's vision, cycles and decision points as a governance wrapper and run Scrum sprints or a Kanban flow inside each Innovate cycle.

**Q: Is there an extreme project management certification?**
There is no widely recognised standalone XPM certification. Its ideas are usually learned through Agile training, adaptive approaches in general project management study, and the original books.

**Q: How is XPM controlled if there is no fixed plan?**
Through time boxes, funding released in tranches, kill criteria agreed in advance, a decision log and measures of learning and value reviewed at every cycle boundary.

# Fast Tracking vs Crashing: Differences and Worked Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: The difference between fast tracking and crashing a schedule, crash cost slope formula, a worked example, risks, and how to choose between them.


## Fast Tracking vs Crashing: Differences and Worked Example
Fast tracking and crashing are the two main [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) techniques. Fast tracking overlaps activities that would normally run one after another, which adds risk. Crashing adds resources to critical activities to finish them sooner, which adds cost.
- Published 26 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Fast tracking overlaps work and adds risk; crashing adds resources and cost.
- Use crash cost slope to choose the cheapest days to buy.
- Only compress critical activities and recheck the path after each step.
- Record the extra risk and cost through change control.

### Side-by-side comparison
|  | Fast tracking | Crashing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How | Run activities in parallel or overlap them | Add people, overtime, equipment or faster suppliers |
| Main cost | Risk of rework | Extra money |
| Works on | Discretionary dependencies | Activities that respond to more resources |
| Typical example | Start building before design is fully finished | Add a second installation crew |
| Effect on budget | Little direct effect unless rework occurs | Increases cost |
| Best when | Dependencies are soft and requirements are stable | Money is available and work can be divided |

### Crash cost slope
Crash cost slope = (crash cost - normal cost) / (normal duration - crash duration). It is the extra cost of each day saved and lets you compare activities fairly.
| Activity | Normal | Crash | Max days saved | Slope per day |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A Plan move | 3 days, $6,000 | 2 days, $9,000 | 1 | $3,000 |
| B Order furniture | 4 days, $8,000 | 3 days, $10,000 | 1 | $2,000 |
| D Install furniture | 5 days, $10,000 | 3 days, $13,000 | 2 | $1,500 |
| F Move and unpack | 2 days, $4,000 | Cannot crash | 0 | - |

### Worked crashing example
The critical path A-B-D-F is 14 days; the other path A-C-E-F is 10 days.
1. Target 13 days: crash the cheapest critical activity, D, by 1 day. Cost $1,500.
2. Target 12 days: crash D by another day (now at its 3-day limit). Total $3,000. Paths: 12 and 10.
3. Target 11 days: next cheapest is B at $2,000. Total $5,000. Paths: 11 and 10.
4. Target 10 days: crash A by 1 day for $3,000, which shortens both paths because A is on both. Total $8,000. Paths: 10 and 9.
5. No further crashing is possible on A-B-D-F, so the minimum is 10 days for $8,000 extra.

### Worked fast-tracking example
Instead of waiting for all furniture to arrive, the team starts installing as the first deliveries come in: B to D becomes FS-2 days (a [lead](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/)). D now starts on day 5 instead of day 7, and the project finishes on day 12 with no direct cost. The risk is that installers may need to return if late deliveries do not fit the layout.

### How to choose
- Fast track first when dependencies are discretionary and the risk of rework is low.
- Crash when money is available and adding people genuinely speeds up the work.
- Combine both on long projects, but recheck the critical path after each change.
- Record the extra risks in the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) and the extra cost in the [budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/).
Tip
Some work cannot be sped up by adding people: one person can paint a small room, but four people in the same room just get in each other's way.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between fast tracking and crashing?**
Fast tracking overlaps activities and increases risk; crashing adds resources and increases cost.

**Q: Which is better, crashing or fast tracking?**
Neither is always better. Fast tracking is cheaper but riskier; crashing is more predictable but costs more.

**Q: What is an example of fast tracking?**
Starting construction on the foundations while the upper floors are still being designed.

**Q: What is an example of crashing?**
Paying for overtime or adding a second team to finish a critical activity sooner.

**Q: How do you calculate the cost per day of crashing?**
(Crash cost - normal cost) / (normal duration - crash duration).

**Q: Does fast tracking increase cost?**
Not directly, but rework caused by overlapping work can add cost later.

**Q: Is crashing a non-critical activity worthwhile?**
It is possible, but it will not shorten the project, so it wastes money.

**Q: What is the crash point when crashing a schedule?**
The shortest duration an activity can reach no matter how many resources are added.

**Q: Which dependencies are suitable for fast tracking?**
Discretionary (soft) dependencies. Mandatory dependencies, such as physical constraints, usually cannot.

**Q: Are fast tracking and crashing on the PMP exam?**
Schedule compression techniques are a standard topic in PMP study materials; see [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

# Feasibility Study in Project Management: Types and Steps

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/feasibility-study/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a feasibility study is, the five types of feasibility (technical, economic, legal, operational, schedule), how to run one and what the report covers.


## Feasibility Study in Project Management: Types and Steps
A feasibility study assesses whether a proposed project is practical and worthwhile before significant resources are committed. It helps decision-makers choose to proceed, change direction or stop.
- Published 14 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- A feasibility study tests whether a project is practical and worthwhile.
- It covers technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule feasibility.
- It should compare options, including doing nothing.

### The five types of feasibility
| Type | Key question |
| --- | --- |
| Technical | Do we have, or can we get, the technology and skills? |
| Economic | Do the benefits justify the costs? See [cost-benefit analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/). |
| Legal | Does it comply with laws and regulations? |
| Operational | Will the organisation and users adopt and run it? |
| Schedule | Can it be delivered in the time available? |
A common memory aid is TELOS: technical, economic, legal, operational and scheduling.

### How to conduct a feasibility study
1. Define the project scope and objectives at a high level.
2. Describe the current situation and the problem.
3. Identify options, including doing nothing.
4. Assess each option against the five feasibility types.
5. Estimate costs, benefits and risks.
6. Recommend an option.
7. Present findings to decision-makers.

### What the report includes
- Executive summary and recommendation.
- Description of options.
- Findings for each type of feasibility.
- Financial analysis such as [NPV](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/net-present-value/).
- Key risks and assumptions.
- Next steps.

Beginner · Advanced · Expert

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: When is a feasibility study done?**
Before or during initiation, before committing to the project.

**Q: Who conducts a feasibility study?**
Business analysts, project managers or external consultants, with input from experts.

**Q: How long does a feasibility study take?**
From days for small projects to months for major investments.

**Q: Is a feasibility study the same as a business case?**
No. A feasibility study tests whether options are viable; the business case justifies the chosen option.

**Q: What is TELOS in a feasibility study?**
An acronym for technical, economic, legal, operational and scheduling feasibility.

**Q: Can a feasibility study recommend not proceeding?**
Yes. Stopping an unviable project early is a valuable outcome.

**Q: What tools support feasibility analysis?**
Cost-benefit analysis, NPV, SWOT, risk assessment and [sensitivity analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/sensitivity-analysis/).

**Q: Do small projects need a feasibility study?**
A brief, informal assessment is usually enough.

**Q: What is a pre-feasibility study?**
A quicker, high-level screening of options before a full feasibility study.

**Q: Who approves the feasibility study?**
The sponsor or an investment committee, depending on the organisation.

# Fishbone Diagram: Steps, Categories and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram is, which categories to use, how to build one step by step, worked project examples and how to confirm root causes.


## Fishbone Diagram: Steps, Categories and Examples
A fishbone diagram, also called an Ishikawa or cause-and-effect diagram, is a visual tool that helps a team list and organise the possible causes of a problem so it can find the root causes rather than the first obvious one. This guide explains the categories to use, an eight-step method, two worked project examples, a workshop agenda and how to confirm causes with data before you act.
- Published 1 October 2026
- Last updated 18 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- A fishbone diagram puts the problem at the head and groups possible causes on bones by category, such as people, methods, tools and inputs.
- Start with a specific, measurable problem statement; a vague or solution-shaped statement produces a vague diagram.
- Ask "why does this happen?" repeatedly to move from symptoms to causes you can actually change.
- Everything on the diagram is a hypothesis until data supports it: prioritise, then check with a check sheet or Pareto chart.
- Choose categories that fit the work. The 6Ms suit manufacturing; projects and services often need categories such as requirements, communication and suppliers.
- Finish with owned, dated actions in your issue log or action plan, and measure whether the problem actually improves.

### What is a fishbone diagram?
A **fishbone diagram** is a cause-and-effect diagram that shows the possible causes of a single problem, grouped into categories. The problem is written at the "head" of the fish, a horizontal line forms the spine, and each major bone represents a category of causes, with smaller bones for more detailed sub-causes. Its purpose is to help a team explore causes widely and systematically before deciding what to fix.
| Part | What it holds | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head | The problem or effect, stated specifically | User-reported defects per release have more than doubled |
| Spine | The line linking causes to the effect |  |
| Major bones | Categories of causes | People, process, tools, requirements |
| Minor bones | Individual causes within a category | Acceptance criteria are unclear |
| Sub-bones | Deeper causes found by asking why | Product owner has no time to review stories |

#### Other names for a fishbone diagram
- **Ishikawa diagram**, after Kaoru Ishikawa, the Japanese quality expert who popularised it.
- **Cause-and-effect diagram**, the descriptive name used in many quality standards and textbooks.
- **Herringbone diagram**, another reference to its shape.

#### A short history
Ishikawa popularised the diagram in the 1960s while developing quality management practices, including at the Kawasaki shipyards, and included it in his book *Guide to Quality Control*, first published in Japan in 1968. It became one of the **seven basic quality tools**, alongside the check sheet, control chart, histogram, Pareto chart, scatter diagram and stratification (some lists include a flowchart instead). Today it is used well beyond manufacturing, in software, healthcare, services, construction and project management.

### When to use a fishbone diagram (and when not to)
A fishbone diagram is most useful when a problem keeps coming back and nobody is sure why. Typical project situations include:
- A recurring defect, delay or complaint, such as late deliverables or repeated rework.
- Several entries in the [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/) that seem to share a cause.
- A post-incident review after an outage, a failed release or a missed milestone.
- A [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) session at a phase end or at [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/).
- A team that disagrees about the cause and needs to see all the possibilities before collecting data.
- Risk identification, when you want to ask "what could cause this threat to happen?"
It is less useful in some cases:
- **The cause is already known and proven.** Go straight to fixing it.
- **The problem is very simple.** A quick 5 whys conversation may be enough.
- **You need to rank causes by frequency or cost.** Use a Pareto chart, ideally after the fishbone has suggested what to count.
- **There are several unrelated problems.** Draw one diagram per problem, not one diagram for everything.
Tip
A fishbone diagram generates hypotheses; it does not prove them. Plan time after the session to check the most likely causes with data.

### Fishbone diagram categories
The categories (the major bones) are prompts that stop the team focusing on one area. Pick a set that suits your work, rename bones freely and use four to seven of them. Too few and you miss areas; too many and the diagram becomes hard to read.

#### The 6Ms (manufacturing and operations)
| Category | Prompts | Example causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Man / people | Skills, training, workload, handovers, staffing | New operators not trained on the changeover |
| Machine | Equipment, software, maintenance, capacity | Calibration overdue on a filling machine |
| Method | Procedures, work instructions, sequence | Two shifts follow different set-up steps |
| Material | Raw materials, parts, information received | New supplier's packaging film is thinner |
| Measurement | Gauges, inspection, data accuracy | Weight check uses an unverified scale |
| Mother nature / environment | Temperature, humidity, location, culture | Line runs hotter in summer |
Some teams add **management** and **money** (budget, priorities, investment), or **maintenance**, giving 7Ms or 8Ms. Many people now use neutral terms such as "people" and "environment" rather than "man" and "mother nature".

#### The 4Ss and 8Ps (services and marketing)
Service and marketing teams often prefer categories that fit their work:
- **4Ss:** surroundings, suppliers, systems and skills.
- **8Ps:** product (or service), price, place, promotion, people, process, physical evidence and performance (sometimes productivity and quality).

#### Categories for project teams
Project problems often come from requirements, communication, planning and suppliers rather than machines and materials. These sets work well as a starting point:
| Project type | Suggested categories |
| --- | --- |
| Software and IT | People, process, tools and environments, requirements, code and architecture, measurement, suppliers |
| Construction | Labour, plant and equipment, materials, design, methods and sequencing, site conditions, subcontractors |
| Marketing and creative | Brief, people, process and approvals, tools, data, channels, external factors |
| Events | Venue, suppliers, people, planning and timeline, communication, budget, external factors |
| General projects | People, process, tools, inputs and information, planning, communication, management, environment |
If a problem relates to scope, for example repeated unplanned work, consider bones such as [requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/), [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) and stakeholder expectations. Our guide to [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) lists common causes worth prompting for.

### How to make a fishbone diagram in 8 steps
You need a whiteboard, sticky notes or a digital whiteboard, the right people and about 60 to 90 minutes. The steps below follow the widely used procedure described by quality bodies such as ASQ, with our additions on prioritising and validation.
1. **Agree the problem statement.** Write a specific, measurable description of the effect in the head of the fish, such as "User-reported defects rose from an average of 6 to 14 per release over the last four releases". See the next section for how to write a good one.
2. **Draw the spine.** Draw a horizontal arrow pointing to the head.
3. **Add the major bones.** Choose four to seven categories and draw them as diagonal lines off the spine, each labelled.
4. **Brainstorm causes.** Ask "why does this happen?" and place each idea on the bone it fits best. A cause can appear on more than one bone if it genuinely fits several. Have people write ideas silently first so everyone contributes.
5. **Ask why again.** For each cause, ask why it happens and add the answers as smaller bones. Stop when you reach something the team can act on or measure. This is where the 5 whys technique fits in.
6. **Fill the gaps.** Look for bones with few ideas and prompt for them deliberately, for example "what about measurement?" Thin bones often hide causes the group has not thought about.
7. **Prioritise likely root causes.** Use multi-voting: give each person three votes to place on the causes they think contribute most. Circle the top three to five.
8. **Validate and act.** Check the top causes with data, then agree actions with owners and dates and record them in your [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/), [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) or an action plan. Measure the problem again after the actions to confirm it improved.
Tip
Keep the diagram visible and dated. Taking a photo or exporting the digital board and attaching it to the issue gives you a record of the reasoning for later reviews.

### How to write a good problem statement
The problem statement drives everything else. A good one describes the effect, not a cause or a solution, and includes a measure, a scope and a time frame.
| Weak statement | Why it is weak | Better statement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Testing is rubbish" | Blames a team and assumes the cause | "User-reported defects rose from 6 to 14 per release between releases 4 and 8" |
| "We need a new reporting tool" | A solution in disguise | "Monthly client reports are delivered an average of four working days late" |
| "Communication problems" | Too vague to analyse | "In Q3, 9 of 12 design changes reached the site team after work had started" |
| "The project is over budget" | Too broad; many separate problems | "Subcontractor variations added 8% to phase 2 costs against the baseline" |
If you are not sure how to phrase it, ask: what is happening, where, since when, how often and compared with what? Our free [problem statement template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/problem-statement-template/) walks through these questions.

### Worked example: rising release defects on a software project
A product team ships a release every two weeks. Over the last four releases, defects reported by users have risen from an average of 6 per release to 14, and the support team is struggling. The project manager runs a 75-minute fishbone session with eight people: developers, testers, the product owner, a support analyst and the release manager.

#### Step 1: the diagram
**Head:** "User-reported defects rose from an average of 6 to 14 per release over releases 5 to 8." The team chose seven bones. The main causes and sub-causes were:
| Bone | Causes | Sub-causes found by asking why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| People | Two new developers joined; testers stretched across two teams | No onboarding guide for the legacy billing module |
| Process | Code reviews skipped near release day | Release date fixed regardless of readiness |
| Requirements | Acceptance criteria unclear or missing | Product owner has little time to refine stories |
| Tools and environments | Test environment differs from production | Configuration copied manually |
| Code and architecture | Legacy billing module has few automated tests | Regression tests never written when module was built |
| Measurement | Defects not tagged by component or cause | Support tool has no cause field |
| Management | Release frequency doubled without extra test capacity | Decision made to hit a marketing date |

#### Step 2: prioritise
Each of the eight participants placed three votes (24 in total):
| Cause | Votes |
| --- | --- |
| Unclear acceptance criteria | 7 |
| Few automated regression tests on billing module | 6 |
| Test environment differs from production | 4 |
| Code reviews skipped near release day | 3 |
| New developers not onboarded on billing module | 2 |
| Release frequency doubled without extra test capacity | 2 |

#### Step 3: check with data
Because defects were not tagged by cause, a tester and the support analyst reviewed all 56 user-reported defects from releases 5 to 8 and classified each one. The result, shown as a Pareto table:
| Cause | Defects | Share | Cumulative |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unclear or missing acceptance criteria | 21 | 37.5% | 37.5% |
| No regression tests on billing module | 16 | 28.6% | 66.1% |
| Environment configuration differences | 9 | 16.1% | 82.1% |
| Code review skipped | 6 | 10.7% | 92.9% |
| Other | 4 | 7.1% | 100% |
| Total | 56 | 100% |  |
The data broadly confirmed the vote, and showed that the top two causes explained about two thirds of the defects. It also gave the team a baseline to measure against.

#### Step 4: actions
| Action | Root cause addressed | Owner | Due |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Add a definition of ready: no story enters a sprint without testable acceptance criteria | Unclear acceptance criteria | Product owner | Next sprint |
| Write regression tests for the 20 most-used billing scenarios | No regression tests | Lead developer | Within 3 sprints |
| Automate environment configuration from production settings | Environment differences | Release manager | Within 2 sprints |
| Add a cause field to the support tool and tag every defect | Measurement gap | Support analyst | This week |
The team tracked user-reported defects per release on its dashboard and in the [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/), and agreed to repeat the Pareto check after four more releases to confirm whether the actions worked. Note how the fishbone widened the discussion (the measurement gap would otherwise have been missed), while the data narrowed it to the causes that mattered most.

### Worked example 2: late monthly client reports
A shorter example from a service project. **Problem:** "Monthly client reports are delivered an average of four working days late." The team's diagram included these causes:
| Bone | Causes found |
| --- | --- |
| People | One analyst produces all reports; no cover during leave |
| Methods | No agreed cut-off for data; reviews done one after another rather than in parallel |
| Tools | Report template rebuilt by hand each month |
| Inputs | Finance data arrives on working day 5 instead of day 2 |
| Measurement | Nobody tracks how long each step takes |
| Management | Report deadline not shown in team planning |
Two months of timing data showed that late finance data and manual template work explained most of the delay. The team agreed a day-2 data cut-off with finance and automated the template, and trained a second analyst as cover. The remaining causes were logged as smaller improvements.

### How to read a fishbone diagram
If someone hands you a finished diagram, read it in this order:
1. **Start at the head.** Make sure you understand the problem, its measure and its time frame.
2. **Scan the major bones.** See which categories were considered and whether any obvious area is missing.
3. **Look at the depth.** Causes with several levels of sub-bones have been explored; single words on a bone may be symptoms rather than causes.
4. **Look for repeats.** A cause that appears on several bones, or that sits behind several others, is often a strong root-cause candidate.
5. **Check what is marked.** Circled or voted causes show what the team thinks matters most; check whether data supports them.
A dense bone shows where the team had most to say, which is not the same as where the biggest cause lies. Treat the shape of the diagram as a guide to discussion, not as evidence.

### Running a fishbone workshop: agenda and facilitation tips
A fishbone session works best with five to ten people who are close to the work, plus at least one person from outside the immediate team for a fresh view. This 75-minute agenda works for most project problems:
| Time | Activity | Facilitator notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–10 min | Purpose, ground rules and problem statement | Agree the wording of the head; remind people it is about the system, not individuals |
| 10–15 min | Agree categories | Propose a set and let the group rename or add bones |
| 15–35 min | Silent brainstorming, then place notes on bones | One idea per note; everyone writes before anyone speaks |
| 35–55 min | Ask why on each cause and fill thin bones | Push for causes the team can act on; prompt empty categories |
| 55–65 min | Multi-vote on likely root causes | Three votes each, placed at the same time |
| 65–75 min | Agree how to check top causes and who will do it | Assign owners and a date to report back with data |
- **Keep it blame-free.** "Why did the process allow this?" gets better answers than "who did this?"
- **Separate facts from opinions.** Mark causes backed by data differently, for example with a tick.
- **Draw out quieter voices.** Silent writing and round-robin sharing stop a few people dominating. These are the same techniques that improve [expert judgment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/expert-judgment/).
- **Park solutions.** People will suggest fixes early; capture them on a separate "ideas" area for later.
- **Run it remotely if needed.** Digital whiteboards with a fishbone template work well; ask people to add notes before the call to save time.

### Fishbone diagram vs 5 whys, Pareto and other tools
The fishbone diagram is one of several root-cause and quality tools. They work best together.
| Tool | What it does | Strength | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fishbone diagram | Maps many possible causes of one problem by category | Breadth; involves the whole team | The cause is unclear and many factors may contribute |
| 5 whys | Asks why repeatedly down one chain of cause | Depth; quick and simple | The problem is fairly simple, or to drill into a cause on the fishbone |
| Pareto chart | Ranks causes by frequency, cost or impact | Focus on the vital few | You have data, or the fishbone has suggested what to count |
| Check sheet | A simple form for counting occurrences | Easy data collection | Validating causes from the fishbone |
| Scatter diagram | Tests whether two variables are related | Shows correlation | Checking whether a suspected cause moves with the problem |
| FMEA | Rates potential failure modes by severity, occurrence and detection | Prevention before problems happen | Designing a new process or product |
| Fault tree analysis | Logic diagram of events that combine to cause a failure | Rigour for safety-critical systems | Complex technical failures with AND/OR logic |
A common sequence is: **fishbone** to list possible causes, **5 whys** to dig into the most likely ones, a **check sheet** to collect data, and a **Pareto chart** to decide where to act. Our [root cause analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) gives you a structured 5 whys record to use alongside your fishbone diagram.

### Fishbone diagrams in Lean, Six Sigma and quality management
In [Six Sigma](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/six-sigma/), the fishbone diagram is commonly used in the **Analyse** phase of DMAIC to list potential causes (often called Xs) that might drive the problem (the Y). The most likely causes are then tested statistically, for example with hypothesis tests or regression.
In [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/), fishbone diagrams support problem-solving on the shop floor and in A3 reports, often combined with the 5 whys. The emphasis is on going to where the work happens and seeing the problem directly before drawing the diagram.
In [project quality management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/), PMI and other bodies list cause-and-effect diagrams among the data representation and quality tools used to find the sources of defects and non-conformance. Use it when quality control finds a pattern of problems, then feed the agreed corrective actions back into the quality management plan.

### Using fishbone diagrams for project risks and retrospectives

#### Risk identification
Turn the diagram around: put a potential threat at the head, such as "Go-live slips past the contract date", and ask what could cause it. Each bone then produces risk causes that you can write in cause-event-effect form and add to the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/). This often finds risks that a simple checklist misses, such as dependencies on another team's release calendar.

#### Retrospectives and lessons learned
When a retrospective keeps surfacing the same problem, a fishbone diagram is a good way to break the cycle. Spend one [sprint retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) on it: agree the problem, draw the bones, vote, then pick one or two improvement actions for the next sprint. Our [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) has space to record them. At phase end or closure, use it to explain the biggest variances and record findings in a [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/).

### Advantages and limitations of fishbone diagrams
| Advantages | Limitations |
| --- | --- |
| Simple to learn and needs no software | Can become cluttered when the problem is too broad |
| Encourages the team to look beyond the first explanation | Shows possible causes, not proven ones |
| Involves people who do the work, which builds ownership of fixes | Does not show how causes interact or which matters most |
| Gives structure to brainstorming through categories | Quality depends on who is in the room |
| Creates a visual record of the reasoning | Can drift into blame if not well facilitated |
| Works with other tools such as the 5 whys and Pareto charts | Less suited to complex, interacting technical failures than fault tree analysis |
Most limitations are handled by a tight problem statement, good facilitation and a data check before action.

### Fishbone diagram templates and tools
You do not need special software. Options include:
- **A whiteboard or flip chart with sticky notes**, which is often best for in-person sessions.
- **Digital whiteboards**, many of which include ready-made fishbone templates for remote teams.
- **Diagramming and presentation tools**, useful for a tidy final version to share.
- **Spreadsheets**: a simple table with columns for category, cause, sub-cause, votes, evidence and action works well for tracking, even if you draw the picture elsewhere.
To turn your analysis into action, use our free [action plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/action-plan-template/) to track owners and dates, and the [root cause analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) for the 5 whys follow-up.

### Common fishbone diagram mistakes
- **A vague or solution-shaped problem statement**, such as "we need more testers".
- **Stopping at symptoms**, such as "bugs" or "delays", instead of asking why until you reach something actionable.
- **Blaming people** instead of looking at the process, tools and conditions that let the problem happen.
- **Only managers in the room**, missing the knowledge of people who do the work.
- **Treating the diagram as the answer** and acting on causes without checking the data.
- **Trying to fix everything** instead of focusing on the few causes that explain most of the problem.
- **No follow-up**: actions without owners, dates or a measure of whether the problem improved.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a fishbone diagram used for?**
It is used to identify and organise the possible causes of a specific problem, such as recurring defects, delays or complaints, so a team can find and fix root causes rather than symptoms.

**Q: Why is it called an Ishikawa diagram?**
It is named after Kaoru Ishikawa, the Japanese quality expert who popularised it in the 1960s. It is called a fishbone diagram because the finished drawing looks like a fish skeleton.

**Q: What are the 6Ms of a fishbone diagram?**
Man (people), machine, method, material, measurement and mother nature (environment). Some teams add management, money or maintenance.

**Q: What categories should I use for a project?**
Common project categories are people, process, tools, inputs and information, requirements, communication, planning, suppliers, management and environment. Pick four to seven that fit the problem.

**Q: How do you make a fishbone diagram?**
Agree a specific problem statement, draw the spine and head, add four to seven category bones, brainstorm causes, ask why to add sub-causes, fill thin bones, vote on likely root causes, then check them with data and agree actions.

**Q: What is the difference between a fishbone diagram and the 5 whys?**
A fishbone diagram maps many possible causes across categories, giving breadth. The 5 whys follows one chain of cause downwards, giving depth. They are often used together.

**Q: Is a fishbone diagram one of the seven basic quality tools?**
Yes. The cause-and-effect diagram is one of the seven basic quality tools, alongside the check sheet, control chart, histogram, Pareto chart, scatter diagram and stratification (or flowchart in some lists).

**Q: How many causes should a fishbone diagram have?**
There is no fixed number. A typical session produces 20 to 50 ideas. What matters is reaching actionable causes and then focusing on the three to five that seem most important.

**Q: Who should take part in a fishbone session?**
Five to ten people who are close to the work, including those who experience the problem, plus a facilitator and ideally one person from outside the team for a fresh perspective.

**Q: How long does a fishbone analysis take?**
The workshop usually takes 60 to 90 minutes. Allow extra time afterwards, often a few days, to collect data that confirms or rules out the main causes.

**Q: Can a fishbone diagram be used for project risks?**
Yes. Put a potential threat at the head and ask what could cause it. Each cause can then be written as a risk and added to the risk register.

**Q: Can I make a fishbone diagram in Excel or Word?**
Yes. You can draw one with shapes and connectors, or keep a simple table of category, cause, sub-cause, votes and evidence. Many diagramming and whiteboard tools also offer ready-made templates.

**Q: What are the disadvantages of a fishbone diagram?**
It shows possible rather than proven causes, can become cluttered for broad problems, does not show how causes interact and depends on who takes part. Validating with data and good facilitation address most of these.

**Q: Is a fishbone diagram used in Six Sigma?**
Yes. It is commonly used in the Analyse phase of DMAIC to list potential causes, which are then tested with data.
