# Float and Slack in Project Management: Types and Formulas

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Float and slack in project management explained: total, free, project and negative float, formulas, a step-by-step worked example and how to manage float.


## Float and Slack in Project Management: Types and Formulas
Float in project management, also called slack, is the amount of time an activity can be delayed without delaying something else: its successors (free float) or the project finish date (total float). Activities with zero total float form the critical path. This guide gives the formulas for every type of float, two fully worked examples and practical rules for managing float on a live schedule.
- Published 24 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Float and slack mean the same thing: how long an activity can slip before it causes a delay.
- Total float = LS - ES (or LF - EF) and protects the project finish; free float = earliest ES of successors - EF and protects the next activity.
- Float is shared along a path, so using it early leaves less for activities later on the same path.
- Negative float means the schedule cannot meet a required date; its size is the time you must recover.
- Unusually high float usually signals missing logic, not genuine flexibility.
- Agree who owns float before the project starts; contracts and standards take different positions.

### What is float in project management?
**Float**, or **slack**, is the amount of time a schedule activity can be delayed without delaying either the early start of its successors (free float) or the project finish date (total float). It is calculated from the network of activities, durations and dependencies. Activities with zero total float are critical: any delay to them delays the project.
Three points follow from that definition:
- **Float is calculated, not entered.** It comes out of the [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) once you have activities, durations and [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/). If the logic is wrong, the float is wrong.
- **Float belongs to a path, not just an activity.** Two activities in a chain often show the same total float because they share it. Use it on the first and the second has less.
- **Float changes every time the schedule is updated.** Progress, delays, new dependencies and changed deadlines all move it.
Float is what tells you where you have room to manoeuvre and where you have none. It is the basis of the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/), resource levelling and most schedule recovery decisions.

### Float vs slack: is there a difference?
No. In scheduling, float and slack are interchangeable terms for the same calculation. The choice of word is mostly a matter of tradition and software:
| Where you see it | Term usually used |
| --- | --- |
| PMI publications and PMP exam material | Float (total float, free float) |
| PERT literature | Slack |
| Microsoft Project | Slack (Total Slack and Free Slack fields) |
| Construction and engineering planning tools | Float |
| Some Gantt chart tools, such as ClickUp | Slack time |
Do not confuse schedule slack with the general idea of spare capacity, or with the Slack messaging app. Slack in this guide always means scheduling float.

### Types of float
| Type | What it measures | Formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total float | How long an activity can slip without delaying the project finish (or a constraint) | LS - ES, or LF - EF |
| Free float | How long an activity can slip without delaying the early start of any successor | Earliest ES of successors - EF |
| Project float | How much the whole project can slip before missing an imposed deadline | Required finish - calculated early finish |
| Negative float | How far the schedule is behind a required date or constraint | Total float below zero |
| Independent float | Slip available even if predecessors finish late and successors start early | Earliest ES of successors - latest LF of predecessors - duration (if positive) |
| Interfering float | The part of total float that, if used, takes float away from successors | Total float - free float |

#### Total float
Total float is the figure most people mean when they say "float". It is measured against the project finish, or against a date constraint if one applies. Zero total float marks the critical path. Total float is shared by all activities on the same chain of non-critical work.

#### Free float
Free float is more local. It tells you how long an activity can slip before the next team or activity is affected. Only the last activity in a chain of non-critical work usually has free float; the earlier ones pass any slip straight to their successors. Free float is always less than or equal to total float.

#### Project float
Project float compares the calculated finish with an imposed deadline from the sponsor, customer or contract. If the network finishes on day 27 and the contract requires day 30, the project has 3 days of project float. Some planners call this terminal float, particularly in construction contracts.

#### Independent and interfering float
These two are mainly used in exam questions and detailed schedule analysis. **Independent float** is the most conservative measure: the slip an activity can absorb even in the worst case, when its predecessors finish as late as possible and its successors need to start as early as possible. **Interfering float** is the part of total float that is not free float, so using it interferes with the float of later activities.

### Float formulas at a glance
| Measure | Formula | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Early finish | EF = ES + duration | Forward pass |
| Early start | ES = largest EF of all predecessors | Add any lag; subtract any lead |
| Late start | LS = LF - duration | Backward pass |
| Late finish | LF = smallest LS of all successors | Allow for lags on the links |
| Total float | TF = LS - ES = LF - EF | Both give the same answer |
| Free float | FF = min(ES of successors) - EF | Subtract any lag on the link |
| Interfering float | IF = TF - FF |  |
| Project float | Required finish - project EF | Negative if the deadline is earlier |
This guide uses the day-0 convention: the first activity starts at 0 and each successor starts at its predecessor's early finish. Some textbooks use a day-1 convention where ES = previous EF + 1. The float values and the critical path are the same either way, so stick to one convention throughout. If your network uses [leads and lags](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/), include them in every calculation: a 3-day lag on a link reduces the free float of the predecessor by 3 days.

### How to calculate float step by step
1. **List the activities** with durations and predecessors. A [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) is the usual source.
2. **Draw the network** so every activity, except the start and finish, has at least one predecessor and one successor. See our guide to the [project network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/).
3. **Forward pass.** Work from left to right: ES = largest EF of predecessors, EF = ES + duration. The largest EF is the project duration.
4. **Backward pass.** Work from right to left: LF of the last activity = project finish (or the required date), LS = LF - duration, and LF of other activities = smallest LS of successors.
5. **Total float** for each activity: LS - ES.
6. **Free float** for each activity: earliest ES of its successors - its EF.
7. **Identify the critical path**: the chain of activities with zero total float (or the lowest float, if it is negative).
8. **Sanity-check the results.** Look for activities with surprisingly high float; they often have a missing successor.
Free template: the [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) calculates early and late dates, float and the critical path for you, in Google Sheets, Excel and PDF.

### Worked example 1: the six-activity network
This illustrative network is the same one used in our [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) guide, so you can follow the calculation from start to finish.
| Activity | Duration (days) | Predecessors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 3 | - |
| B | 4 | A |
| C | 2 | A |
| D | 5 | B |
| E | 3 | C |
| F | 2 | D, E |
The forward and backward passes give these dates and floats:
| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Total float | Free float | Interfering float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | 3 | 0 | 3 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| B | 3 | 7 | 3 | 7 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| C | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9 | 4 | 0 | 4 |
| D | 7 | 12 | 7 | 12 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| E | 5 | 8 | 9 | 12 | 4 | 4 | 0 |
| F | 12 | 14 | 12 | 14 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
- **Critical path:** A-B-D-F, 14 days. Every activity on it has zero total float.
- **C:** total float 7 - 3 = 4 days. Free float = ES of E (5) - EF of C (5) = 0, so any slip in C pushes E.
- **E:** total float 9 - 5 = 4 days. Free float = ES of F (12) - EF of E (8) = 4 days.
- **Shared float:** the 4 days belong to the path C-E. If C slips 3 days, E has only 1 day left.
- **Independent float** of C = ES of E (5) - LF of A (3) - 2 = 0, and of E = ES of F (12) - LF of C (9) - 3 = 0.
- **Project float:** if the sponsor requires completion by day 16, project float is 16 - 14 = 2 days. If the deadline is day 12, the critical activities have -2 days of float.
See our guide to the [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) for each step of the date calculation.

### Worked example 2: a website relaunch
This larger illustrative example shows how float behaves when things change. A marketing team is relaunching its website. Durations are in working days.
| ID | Activity | Duration | Predecessors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Requirements and kick-off | 4 | - |
| B | Visual design | 6 | A |
| C | Content writing | 7 | A |
| D | Content sign-off | 2 | C |
| E | Front-end build | 8 | B |
| F | Back-end integration | 10 | A |
| G | Content load | 3 | D, E |
| H | Testing | 5 | F, G |
| I | Launch | 1 | H |

#### Step 1: calculate dates and float
| ID | ES | EF | LS | LF | Total float | Free float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | 4 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| B | 4 | 10 | 4 | 10 | 0 | 0 |
| C | 4 | 11 | 9 | 16 | 5 | 0 |
| D | 11 | 13 | 16 | 18 | 5 | 5 |
| E | 10 | 18 | 10 | 18 | 0 | 0 |
| F | 4 | 14 | 11 | 21 | 7 | 7 |
| G | 18 | 21 | 18 | 21 | 0 | 0 |
| H | 21 | 26 | 21 | 26 | 0 | 0 |
| I | 26 | 27 | 26 | 27 | 0 | 0 |
The critical path is A-B-E-G-H-I (4 + 6 + 8 + 3 + 5 + 1 = 27 days). The content path C-D shares 5 days of float, and back-end integration (F) has 7 days, all of it free float. If the sponsor's launch date is day 30, the project has 3 days of project float.

#### Step 2: content writing slips 3 days
The copywriter is ill and C takes 10 days instead of 7. C now finishes on day 14 and D on day 16. G cannot start until E finishes on day 18 anyway, so the launch date does not move. But the C-D path now has only 2 days of float left, and D's free float has dropped from 5 to 2. Tell the content team: one more slip of 3 days and the launch moves.

#### Step 3: content writing slips 6 days
Suppose instead C takes 13 days. It finishes on day 17, D on day 19, and G cannot start until day 19. The project now finishes on day 28, one day later than planned. The critical path has switched to A-C-D-G-H-I, and the old critical activities B and E now have 1 day of float. This is why near-critical paths need watching: a path with 5 days of float can become critical after a single bad week.

#### Step 4: the deadline moves to day 25
Back to the original plan. Marketing brings the launch forward to day 25 to coincide with an event. Run the backward pass from day 25 instead of day 27 and every float value falls by 2:
| Path | Total float before | Total float with day-25 deadline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A-B-E-G-H-I | 0 | -2 |
| C-D | 5 | 3 |
| F | 7 | 5 |
The -2 tells you exactly how much time must be recovered on the critical path.

#### Step 5: recover the time and recheck float
The team adds a second front-end developer and crashes E from 8 days to 6. Recalculating:
- E now finishes on day 16, G runs from 16 to 19, H from 19 to 24 and I from 24 to 25. The launch meets day 25.
- The critical path is still A-B-E-G-H-I, now with zero float.
- The C-D path keeps 3 days of float, and F's float has dropped from 7 to 5 days.
Notice that the recovery used up float elsewhere in the network. Every compression decision should be followed by a fresh float check, because a parallel path may now be close to critical. See our guide to [fast tracking vs crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/) for the two main recovery techniques and their costs.

### Negative float: what it means and how to fix it
Negative float appears when the calculated dates are later than a required date or constraint. It is not an error in the maths: it is the schedule telling you that the plan, as it stands, cannot meet the date. The size of the negative number is the time you must recover on that path.
Common causes:
- A deadline or "finish no later than" constraint earlier than the network can achieve.
- Delays on critical activities that have not been offset.
- Added scope or new dependencies after the baseline was set.
- Over-optimistic durations that are now being corrected with actual progress.
| Response | How it removes negative float | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crashing | Adds resources to shorten critical activities | Higher cost; not every task can be shortened |
| Fast tracking | Overlaps activities that were planned in sequence | More rework risk |
| Reducing scope | Removes or defers work on the critical path | Needs sponsor and customer agreement |
| Changing logic | Removes dependencies that were preferences, not necessities | Only valid if the original logic was unnecessary |
| Moving the date | Agrees a new deadline | Requires formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) |
See [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) for a step-by-step method for choosing between these options. Never hide negative float by deleting links or adding constraints; it only postpones the conversation.

### Float and the critical path
The critical path is the longest path through the network, and in a schedule without date constraints its activities have zero total float. In practice there are a few complications:
- **Constraints and deadlines** can give the critical path negative float, or leave it with positive float if the deadline is later than the calculated finish. The critical path is then the path with the lowest float.
- **Different calendars** (for example a 5-day calendar for most work and a 7-day calendar for curing) can make float values on the same path look uneven.
- **Near-critical paths** have a small amount of float. Many teams set a threshold, such as 5 or 10 days, and monitor every path below it as closely as the critical path itself.
- **Several critical paths** can exist at once, which makes the schedule riskier: a delay on any of them delays the project.
For a schedule with significant uncertainty, a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) shows how often each activity ends up on the critical path, which is a better guide to risk than a single float value. The [critical chain](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-chain-project-management/) approach goes further and replaces activity float with managed buffers.

### How to manage float on a live project
1. **Recalculate float after every schedule update.** Float from last month's plan is out of date as soon as progress is entered.
2. **Use free float first.** When you need to delay an activity, choose one with free float, because nobody else is affected.
3. **Use float to level resources.** [Resource levelling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) moves non-critical work within its float to smooth peaks in demand without moving the end date.
4. **Protect shared float.** When an early activity in a chain uses float, tell the owners of later activities how much is left.
5. **Watch near-critical paths.** Report paths below your threshold alongside the critical path.
6. **Do not treat float as a buffer for estimates.** If an estimate is uncertain, fix the estimate or add an explicit contingency activity or buffer, so the risk is visible.
7. **Report trends, not just values.** Float that shrinks every week is an early warning even if it is still positive. Compare with the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).
Tip
A simple float report works well in steering meetings: critical path end date, project float against the deadline, the three paths with the least float, and how each of those numbers has moved since the last report.

### Who owns float?
When a delay uses up float, someone has benefited from it. If the contract or project rules say nothing, the person who uses it first effectively takes it, which can lead to disputes. Positions vary:
| Source | Position on float ownership |
| --- | --- |
| Common project practice | Float is a shared project resource, managed by the project manager for the benefit of the project |
| SCL Delay and Disruption Protocol (2nd edition, UK) | Unless the contract says otherwise, float is not for the exclusive use or benefit of either the employer or the contractor |
| NEC4 contracts | Extensions of time are assessed against planned completion, so terminal float between planned completion and the completion date is protected, which is why it is often said to belong to the contractor |
| JCT and FIDIC contracts | Do not expressly define float or its ownership; float generally has to be used up before an extension of time can be claimed |
The contract positions above follow a 2026 summary by law firm Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer; always check the exact terms of your own contract and take advice on disputes. Inside an organisation, the practical answer is to agree the rule at the start, record it in the schedule management plan and make sure team leads know they cannot spend float without telling the project manager. This matters most in [construction project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/construction-project-management/), where float often decides who pays for a delay.

### Checking float as a schedule quality test
Float values are a quick health check on the schedule itself. Two widely used references:
- **GAO Schedule Assessment Guide.** Its best practice on ensuring reasonable total float warns that unreasonably high total float on an activity or path suggests that schedule logic may be missing or invalid, and that incomplete logic, unrealistic durations and unstatused work all distort float. It also expects managers on both the customer and contractor side to manage total float actively as work is completed.
- **DCMA 14-point assessment.** Its high float check flags incomplete activities with total float greater than 44 working days, with a benchmark that they should not exceed 5% of incomplete activities. Its negative float check has a threshold of zero: every activity with negative float should have an explanation and a corrective plan.
You do not need to work on a government contract to use these tests. Filter your schedule for activities with very high float and check each one has a real successor; it takes minutes and catches most logic gaps.

### Float in scheduling software
You rarely calculate float by hand on a real project. Most scheduling tools do it automatically once dependencies are in place:
- **Microsoft Project** calls it slack. Switch to the Detail Gantt view and the Schedule table to see the Free Slack and Total Slack fields. A task with zero slack is critical by default, and you can change that threshold with the option "Tasks are critical if slack is less than or equal to".
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)** (our top-rated tool) shows the critical path and float in its interactive [Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), from the Team plan upwards, together with all four dependency types, lead and lag time and baselines.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** Gantt charts show the critical path and slack time, with automatic rescheduling of downstream tasks when a date moves.
- **[Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/)** premium plans include dependencies, and Plan 3 adds baselines and the critical path.
- **Spreadsheets** work for small networks. Our [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) and [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) are good starting points.

### Common mistakes with float
- **Treating float as spare time.** It is shared along a path and disappears quickly once used.
- **Trusting high float without checking logic.** Missing successors inflate float; an activity with 60 days of float usually has a missing link, not 60 days of freedom.
- **Hiding float with constraints.** "Must start on" dates and other hard constraints distort float. Use logic wherever you can.
- **Reporting only total float.** Free float shows the immediate impact on the next team.
- **Letting teams consume float silently.** Agree who can use float and require a heads-up when they do.
- **Ignoring float when assigning people.** A low-priority task with float can take a resource needed on the critical path.
- **Mixing day conventions.** Combining day-0 and day-1 calculations creates off-by-one errors.
- **Forgetting lags.** A lag on a link reduces the free float of the predecessor.
Read our guide to the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) to see how float fits into the full scheduling process.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is float in project management?**
The amount of time an activity can be delayed without delaying its successors (free float) or the project finish date (total float). It is also called slack.

**Q: Is slack the same as float?**
Yes. The terms are interchangeable. Slack is more common in PERT literature and Microsoft Project; float is more common in PMI material and construction planning.

**Q: How do you calculate total float?**
Total float = late start - early start, or late finish - early finish. Both give the same answer.

**Q: How do you calculate free float?**
Free float = the earliest early start of the activity's successors minus its own early finish, after allowing for any lags on the links.

**Q: What does zero float mean?**
The activity is on the critical path, so any delay to it delays the project finish, unless time is recovered later.

**Q: What is negative float?**
Float below zero. It shows that the schedule cannot meet a required date or constraint, and by how much. It needs recovery through crashing, fast tracking, scope changes or a new agreed date.

**Q: Can free float be greater than total float?**
No. Free float is always less than or equal to total float.

**Q: What is project float?**
The difference between the project's calculated finish and an imposed deadline. A network finishing on day 27 with a deadline of day 30 has 3 days of project float.

**Q: What is the difference between total float and free float?**
Total float protects the project finish date; free float protects the next activity. An activity can have total float but no free float when it shares float with later activities on the same path.

**Q: Who owns float in a project?**
It depends on the contract. Many organisations treat float as a shared project resource. In the UK, the SCL Delay and Disruption Protocol says float is not for the exclusive benefit of either party unless the contract says otherwise.

**Q: Does float change during a project?**
Yes. As activities finish early or late, or as logic and deadlines change, float is recalculated and can grow, shrink or become negative.

**Q: What is a good amount of float?**
There is no single figure. Low float means risk, and very high float often means missing logic. The DCMA 14-point assessment flags activities with more than 44 working days of total float.

**Q: What is interfering float?**
Total float minus free float. It is the part of an activity's float that, if used, reduces the float available to activities later on the same path.

# Forward and Backward Pass: Step-by-Step Worked Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Forward and backward pass explained step by step: formulas, day 0 vs day 1, a full worked example, lags, SS and FF links, deadlines and negative float.


## Forward and Backward Pass: Step-by-Step Worked Example
The forward and backward pass are the two calculations at the heart of the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/): the forward pass works from start to finish to find each activity's earliest start and finish dates, and the backward pass works from finish to start to find the latest dates. The gap between the two is the float, and activities with zero float form the critical path. This guide gives the formulas, three fully worked examples and a checklist for checking your answer.
- Published 24 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Forward pass: EF = ES + duration, and at a merge point take the largest EF of the predecessors.
- Backward pass: LS = LF - duration, and at a burst point take the smallest LS of the successors.
- Total float = LS - ES = LF - EF; activities with zero total float form the critical path.
- Day 0 and day 1 conventions give different dates but the same float and critical path; never mix them.
- Start the backward pass from a required date, not the calculated finish, to reveal project float or negative float.
- Lags and SS, FF or SF links change the formulas: always apply the lag to the date the link refers to.

### What is the forward and backward pass?
The **forward pass** is a calculation that moves through a project network from the first activity to the last, finding each activity's early start (ES) and early finish (EF). The **backward pass** moves from the last activity to the first, finding each activity's late finish (LF) and late start (LS). Together they give the project duration, the float of every activity and the critical path.
Both passes need the same inputs: a list of activities, a duration for each and the [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) between them. The terms you will meet:
| Term | Abbreviation | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Early start | ES | The earliest an activity can start, once its predecessors allow it |
| Early finish | EF | The earliest it can finish: ES + duration |
| Late finish | LF | The latest it can finish without delaying the project finish (or a required date) |
| Late start | LS | The latest it can start without delaying the project: LF - duration |
| Total float | TF | How long it can slip without delaying the project: LS - ES |
| Free float | FF | How long it can slip without delaying any successor |
| Merge point |  | An activity with two or more predecessors; matters in the forward pass |
| Burst point |  | An activity with two or more successors; matters in the backward pass |
On an activity-on-node diagram, each box usually shows ES, duration and EF along the top and LS, total float and LF along the bottom. Our guide to the [project network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/) shows the layout.

### Forward and backward pass formulas
This guide uses the **day-0 convention**: the first activity starts at time 0, and a successor starts at the same number as its predecessor's finish. Read the numbers as the end of a day: EF 3 means the end of day 3, so a successor with ES 3 starts on day 4.
| Pass | Formula | Rule when there are several links |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Forward | EF = ES + duration | ES = the **largest** EF of all predecessors (plus any lag) |
| Backward | LS = LF - duration | LF = the **smallest** LS of all successors (minus any lag) |
| Float | Total float = LS - ES = LF - EF | Free float = smallest ES of successors - EF |
| Start and end | ES of the first activity = 0 | LF of the last activity = project EF, or a required finish date |
An activity cannot start until **all** its predecessors have finished, so the latest one controls it. And it must finish in time for **every** successor, so the one needed earliest controls it.

### Day 0 vs day 1 convention
Many textbooks, exam courses and the US GAO Schedule Assessment Guide use a **day-1 convention** instead, where the first activity starts on day 1 and both start and finish dates refer to whole working days. The formulas change slightly:
|  | Day-0 convention | Day-1 convention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First activity ES | 0 | 1 |
| Early finish | EF = ES + duration | EF = ES + duration - 1 |
| Successor's ES (FS link) | ES = predecessor EF | ES = predecessor EF + 1 |
| Late start | LS = LF - duration | LS = LF - duration + 1 |
| Predecessor's LF (FS link) | LF = successor LS | LF = successor LS - 1 |
| Total float | LS - ES | LS - ES (same result) |
Under day 1, every ES and LS is one higher than under day 0, while EF and LF stay the same. Float and the critical path do not change. Day 0 is quicker for hand calculation; day 1 maps more naturally onto a calendar, because "starts on day 4" means the fourth working day. Pick one and use it consistently: mixing them is the most common source of off-by-one errors.

### How to do a forward pass step by step
1. **Prepare the inputs.** List every activity with its duration and predecessors. A [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) is the usual source of the activity list, and your estimates give the durations.
2. **Order the activities** so that every activity comes after all its predecessors. Drawing the network first makes this easy.
3. **Set the first activity's ES to 0** (or 1 under the day-1 convention). If there are several start activities, each starts at 0 unless a constraint says otherwise.
4. **Calculate EF = ES + duration** for that activity.
5. **Move to the next activity.** If it has one predecessor, its ES is that predecessor's EF. If it has several (a merge point), its ES is the **largest** of their EFs. Add any lag on the link.
6. **Repeat** until every activity has an ES and EF.
7. **Read the project duration.** It is the largest EF in the network, normally the EF of the last activity.

### How to do a backward pass step by step
1. **Choose the finish point.** Set the LF of the last activity (or activities) to the project EF from the forward pass, or to a required finish date if one has been imposed.
2. **Calculate LS = LF - duration** for that activity.
3. **Move backwards to its predecessors.** If an activity has one successor, its LF is that successor's LS. If it has several (a burst point), its LF is the **smallest** of their LSs. Subtract any lag on the link.
4. **Repeat** until you reach the first activity.
5. **Check the start.** If you started from the calculated finish, the first activity's LS should be 0. If it is positive or negative, you either used a required date or made an error.
6. **Calculate float** for every activity: total float = LS - ES, free float = smallest ES of successors - EF.
7. **Identify the critical path**: the chain of activities with zero total float (or the lowest float, if a required date has been used).

### Worked example: the six-activity network
This illustrative network is the same one used in our [float and slack](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) guide, so you can follow the numbers from one guide to the other. Durations are in working days and all links are finish-to-start with no lag.
| Activity | Duration (days) | Predecessors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 3 | - |
| B | 4 | A |
| C | 2 | A |
| D | 5 | B |
| E | 3 | C |
| F | 2 | D, E |

#### Step 1: forward pass
| Activity | Predecessor EFs | ES | Working | EF |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | None (start) | 0 | 0 + 3 | 3 |
| B | A = 3 | 3 | 3 + 4 | 7 |
| C | A = 3 | 3 | 3 + 2 | 5 |
| D | B = 7 | 7 | 7 + 5 | 12 |
| E | C = 5 | 5 | 5 + 3 | 8 |
| F | D = 12, E = 8: take the largest | 12 | 12 + 2 | 14 |
F is a merge point: it cannot start until both D and E are finished, so it waits for D on day 12. The project duration is **14 days**.

#### Step 2: backward pass
| Activity | Successor LSs | LF | Working | LS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F | None (finish) | 14 | 14 - 2 | 12 |
| E | F = 12 | 12 | 12 - 3 | 9 |
| D | F = 12 | 12 | 12 - 5 | 7 |
| C | E = 9 | 9 | 9 - 2 | 7 |
| B | D = 7 | 7 | 7 - 4 | 3 |
| A | B = 3, C = 7: take the smallest | 3 | 3 - 3 | 0 |
A is a burst point: it must finish in time for B, which is needed on day 3, even though C could wait until day 7. A's LS comes out as 0, which confirms the arithmetic.

#### Step 3: float and the critical path
| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Total float | Free float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | 3 | 0 | 3 | 0 | 0 |
| B | 3 | 7 | 3 | 7 | 0 | 0 |
| C | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9 | 4 | 0 |
| D | 7 | 12 | 7 | 12 | 0 | 0 |
| E | 5 | 8 | 9 | 12 | 4 | 4 |
| F | 12 | 14 | 12 | 14 | 0 | 0 |
- **Critical path: A-B-D-F**, 14 days. Every activity on it has ES = LS and EF = LF.
- **C** has 4 days of total float (7 - 3) but no free float (ES of E 5 - EF of C 5 = 0): any slip in C pushes E later.
- **E** has 4 days of total float (9 - 5) and 4 days of free float (ES of F 12 - EF of E 8), because F does not need it until day 12.
- **The 4 days are shared** by C and E. If C uses 3 of them, E has only 1 left.

#### Step 4: the same network under the day-1 convention
| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Total float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1 | 3 | 1 | 3 | 0 |
| B | 4 | 7 | 4 | 7 | 0 |
| C | 4 | 5 | 8 | 9 | 4 |
| D | 8 | 12 | 8 | 12 | 0 |
| E | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 4 |
| F | 13 | 14 | 13 | 14 | 0 |
Every start is one day later, every finish is identical, and the float is unchanged.

#### Step 5: check your answer
- The first activity's LS is 0 (day 0) or 1 (day 1) when the backward pass starts from the calculated finish.
- The last activity's EF equals its LF.
- Every critical activity has ES = LS and EF = LF.
- No activity has free float greater than its total float.
- The critical path length equals the sum of its durations (3 + 4 + 5 + 2 = 14).
Free template: the [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) does these calculations for you in Google Sheets or Excel.

### Backward pass from a required finish date
So far the backward pass started from the calculated finish (day 14). In practice a sponsor, customer or contract often sets a required date. Start the backward pass from that date instead, and every late date moves by the difference.

#### Required finish on day 16
Set LF of F = 16 and repeat the backward pass. Every LS and LF rises by 2:
| Activity | ES | LS | LF | Total float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | 2 | 5 | 2 |
| B | 3 | 5 | 9 | 2 |
| C | 3 | 9 | 11 | 6 |
| D | 7 | 9 | 14 | 2 |
| E | 5 | 11 | 14 | 6 |
| F | 12 | 14 | 16 | 2 |
The critical path is still A-B-D-F, but it now has 2 days of float: the project float between the calculated finish (14) and the required date (16). The critical path is now the path with the **lowest** float, not zero float.

#### Required finish on day 12
Now set LF of F = 12, two days earlier than the network can achieve:
| Activity | ES | LS | LF | Total float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | -2 | 1 | -2 |
| B | 3 | 1 | 5 | -2 |
| C | 3 | 5 | 7 | 2 |
| D | 7 | 5 | 10 | -2 |
| E | 5 | 7 | 10 | 2 |
| F | 12 | 10 | 12 | -2 |
A late start of -2 means A should have started two days before the project began, which is impossible. The negative float is not a mistake: it tells you that the plan, as it stands, misses the date by 2 days, and that the time must be recovered on A-B-D-F. The C-E path still has 2 days of float, so shortening C or E would not help.
To recover the 2 days you can crash a critical activity, overlap activities, reduce scope or agree a new date. See our guide to [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) for a step-by-step method.

### Forward and backward pass with leads and lags
A **lag** is a delay added to a link; a **lead** is an overlap, written as a negative lag. Both enter the calculation on the link itself, not on the activity duration. For a finish-to-start link:
- **Forward pass:** ES of successor = EF of predecessor + lag (a lead is a negative lag).
- **Backward pass:** LF of predecessor = LS of successor - lag.
- **Free float:** ES of successor - lag - EF of predecessor.

#### Example: a 3-day lag between E and F
Suppose E is pouring a concrete base and F cannot start until it has cured for 3 days (E to F, FS+3). In the forward pass, E's link now gives F an ES of 8 + 3 = 11. D still gives 12, so F starts on 12 and the project still takes 14 days. In the backward pass, E's LF = LS of F (12) - 3 = 9.
| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Total float without lag | Total float with lag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C | 3 | 5 | 4 | 6 | 4 | 1 |
| E | 5 | 8 | 6 | 9 | 4 | 1 |
The critical path is unchanged, but the lag has used 3 of the 4 days of float on C-E.

#### Example: a 2-day lead between D and F
Now suppose F can start 2 days before D finishes (D to F, FS-2). F's ES = max(12 - 2, 8) = 10, so F finishes on day 12 and the project shortens from 14 to 12 days. A-B-D-F is still critical, and C-E's float falls from 4 to 2. Using leads in this way is the basis of [fast tracking](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/), and it carries rework risk.
Read our guide to [leads and lags](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/) for when each is justified and how to record them.

### SS, FF and SF relationships
Finish-to-start is the most common link, but networks built with the precedence diagramming method can use all four types. The rule is always the same: apply the lag to the date the link refers to.
| Link | Forward pass (successor) | Backward pass (predecessor) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finish-to-start (FS) | ES ≥ EF of predecessor + lag | LF ≤ LS of successor - lag |
| Start-to-start (SS) | ES ≥ ES of predecessor + lag | LS ≤ LS of successor - lag, then LF = LS + duration |
| Finish-to-finish (FF) | EF ≥ EF of predecessor + lag, then ES = EF - duration | LF ≤ LF of successor - lag |
| Start-to-finish (SF) | EF ≥ ES of predecessor + lag, then ES = EF - duration | LS ≤ LF of successor - lag, then LF = LS + duration |
When an activity has several incoming links, work out the date each link implies and take the latest (forward pass). When it has several outgoing links, work out each implied late date and take the earliest (backward pass). The link that sets the date is called the **driving** relationship.

#### Worked example: an office fit-out
This illustrative network for an office fit-out uses an SS link, an FF link and an FS link with a drying lag. Durations are in working days.
| ID | Activity | Duration | Links from predecessors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Strip-out | 4 | - |
| B | Build partition walls | 6 | A (FS) |
| C | Electrical first fix | 3 | B (SS+2) and B (FF+1) |
| D | Plastering | 4 | B (FS), C (FS) |
| E | Painting | 3 | D (FS+2, drying) |
| F | Order and deliver furniture | 10 | A (FS) |
| G | Install furniture | 2 | E (FS), F (FS) |
| H | Handover | 1 | G (FS) |
The electricians can start 2 days after the partitions start (SS+2), but cannot finish until a day after the partitions are complete (FF+1).
**Forward pass:**
- A: ES 0, EF 4. B: ES 4, EF 10. F: ES 4, EF 14.
- C: the SS+2 link gives ES ≥ 4 + 2 = 6. The FF+1 link gives EF ≥ 10 + 1 = 11, so ES ≥ 11 - 3 = 8. Take the later: **ES 8, EF 11**. The FF link is driving.
- D: predecessors B (EF 10) and C (EF 11), so ES 11, EF 15.
- E: ES = 15 + 2 = 17, EF 20.
- G: predecessors E (EF 20) and F (EF 14), so ES 20, EF 22.
- H: ES 22, EF 23. The project takes **23 days**.
**Backward pass:**
- H: LF 23, LS 22. G: LF 22, LS 20.
- E: LF 20, LS 17. F: LF 20, LS 10.
- D: LF = LS of E - 2 = 15, LS 11.
- C: LF = LS of D = 11, LS 8.
- B has three outgoing links. To D (FS): LF ≤ 11. To C (SS+2): LS ≤ 8 - 2 = 6, so LF ≤ 12. To C (FF+1): LF ≤ 11 - 1 = 10. Take the earliest: **LF 10, LS 4**.
- A: successors B (LS 4) and F (LS 10), so LF 4, LS 0.
| ID | ES | EF | LS | LF | Total float | Free float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | 4 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| B | 4 | 10 | 4 | 10 | 0 | 0 |
| C | 8 | 11 | 8 | 11 | 0 | 0 |
| D | 11 | 15 | 11 | 15 | 0 | 0 |
| E | 17 | 20 | 17 | 20 | 0 | 0 |
| F | 4 | 14 | 10 | 20 | 6 | 6 |
| G | 20 | 22 | 20 | 22 | 0 | 0 |
| H | 22 | 23 | 22 | 23 | 0 | 0 |
The critical path is A-B-C-D-E-G-H, and it runs through the FF link and the drying lag. Furniture (F) has 6 days of float. **What if the supplier quotes 17 days instead of 10?** F would finish on day 21, G would start on 21 and the project would take 24 days. The critical path would switch to A-F-G-H, and the fit-out work (B, C, D and E) would gain 1 day of float.

### Forward pass vs backward pass
|  | Forward pass | Backward pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direction | Start to finish | Finish to start |
| Calculates | Early start and early finish | Late finish and late start |
| Starting value | ES of first activity = 0 (or 1) | LF of last activity = project EF or a required date |
| Rule at junctions | Largest EF at a merge point | Smallest LS at a burst point |
| Answers | How soon can we finish? | How late can each activity be without delaying the finish? |

### Real-world complications
Textbook networks have one start, one finish and only finish-to-start links. Real schedules add a few complications that change how the passes behave:
- **Date constraints.** A "start no earlier than" constraint can push an ES later in the forward pass; a "finish no later than" constraint can pull an LF earlier in the backward pass and create negative float. Use logic wherever you can and keep constraints to genuine external dates.
- **Calendars.** Software counts working time on each activity's calendar, so a 5-day activity that spans a weekend or holiday takes longer in calendar days. Activities on different calendars, such as a 7-day calendar for curing, can make float look uneven along a path.
- **Open ends.** An activity with no successor gets its LF from the project finish, which gives it inflated float. Every activity except the last should have a successor.
- **Progress.** Once work has started, the forward pass for remaining work begins from the status (data) date rather than day 0, using actual dates for completed work and remaining durations for work in progress.
- **Uncertain durations.** The passes treat every duration as fixed. For a range of outcomes, use three-point estimates with a [PERT chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/) or a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/).
- **Resources.** The passes assume unlimited resources; [resource levelling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) can move work and change the critical path.

### Forward and backward pass in scheduling software
Scheduling software recalculates both passes every time a date, duration or link changes. Knowing the method lets you check and explain the output.
- **Microsoft Project** runs both passes automatically and shows the results as Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, Free Slack and Total Slack fields. You can schedule from the project start date (the usual forward approach) or from a finish date.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, highlights the critical path in its interactive [Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) from the Team plan upwards, with all four dependency types and lead and lag time.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** Gantt charts support all four dependency types and show the critical path and slack time, rescheduling downstream tasks automatically.
- **[Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/)** combines a grid with Gantt dependencies and can identify the critical path, which suits date-driven projects.
- **Spreadsheets** work for small networks. Our [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) and [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) are good starting points.
Whatever the tool, save a [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) once the schedule is approved, so you can compare later passes against it.

### Common mistakes
- **Taking the smallest EF at a merge point** in the forward pass. Always take the largest.
- **Taking the largest LS at a burst point** in the backward pass. Always take the smallest.
- **Mixing day-0 and day-1 formulas** in the same calculation.
- **Forgetting lags**, or applying an SS or FF lag to the wrong date.
- **Starting the backward pass from the wrong date.** Use the calculated finish or the required date, and say which.
- **Reading the critical path off durations alone.** In networks with lags, constraints or SS and FF links, the longest-looking chain of durations may not be critical; trust the float.
- **Not recalculating after a change.** A new duration, link or deadline can switch the critical path.
Read our guide to the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) to see how the passes fit into the full scheduling process.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a forward pass in project management?**
A calculation from the start of the network to the end that finds each activity's early start and early finish, and so the shortest possible project duration.

**Q: What is a backward pass?**
A calculation from the end of the network to the start that finds each activity's late finish and late start, which shows how much each activity can slip.

**Q: Why take the largest EF in a forward pass?**
Because an activity cannot start until all its predecessors have finished, so the latest-finishing one controls its start.

**Q: Why take the smallest LS in a backward pass?**
Because an activity must finish in time for every successor, so the successor needed earliest controls its late finish.

**Q: Should the forward pass start at day 0 or day 1?**
Either, if you are consistent. Day 0 is simpler for hand calculation; day 1 matches calendar days more naturally. Float and the critical path are the same either way.

**Q: How do you calculate float from the forward and backward pass?**
Total float = LS - ES, or LF - EF. Free float = the smallest ES of the activity's successors minus its own EF, allowing for any lag.

**Q: Which comes first, the forward or backward pass?**
The forward pass, because the backward pass normally starts from the project finish it calculates. The exception is when you start the backward pass from an imposed date.

**Q: What if the required finish date is earlier than the forward pass finish?**
Start the backward pass from the required date. Critical activities will show negative float equal to the time that must be recovered.

**Q: Do I need to do the forward and backward pass by hand?**
Scheduling software does it automatically, but working a small network by hand helps you understand and check the results, and it is a common exam topic.

**Q: Is the forward and backward pass on the PMP exam?**
Network calculations such as float and the critical path are commonly covered in PMP preparation. See our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) for the current exam content.

**Q: Is this the same as the forward and backward pass in neural networks?**
No. In machine learning the terms describe computing a network's output and its gradients. In project management they are schedule calculations.

# Full-Time Equivalent (FTE): Meaning, Formula and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/full-time-equivalent-fte/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Full-time equivalent (FTE) explained: the formula, conversion tables, worked examples for teams and projects, FTE vs headcount and common mistakes.


## Full-Time Equivalent (FTE): Meaning, Formula and Examples
A full-time equivalent (FTE) is a unit that expresses how much working time a person, team or piece of work represents compared with one full-time employee: 1.0 FTE is one full-time schedule, and someone working half that schedule is 0.5 FTE. This guide gives you the FTE formula, a conversion table, four worked examples and a step-by-step method for using FTE to staff, cost and track a project.
- Published 30 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- FTE = hours worked or planned / full-time hours for the same period.
- Always state your full-time basis (for example 37.5 or 40 hours a week), because the same hours give different FTE figures under different bases.
- Contracted FTE is what someone is paid for; allocated FTE is what your project gets. Plan against productive hours, not the full contract.
- To staff a project, divide the estimated effort hours by the productive hours one FTE supplies in that period.
- FTE measures capacity; headcount counts people. Five part-time people can be fewer than four FTE.
- FTE converts directly into cost: FTE x hours per FTE x hourly rate.

### What is a full-time equivalent (FTE)?
A **full-time equivalent (FTE)** is a standard unit of working time equal to one person working a full-time schedule for a given period. Part-time or shared work is expressed as a fraction of that unit, so a person on 20 hours in a 40-hour organisation is 0.5 FTE. FTE measures time and capacity, not the number of people.
Because it converts every working pattern into the same unit, FTE lets you add up and compare effort that would otherwise be hard to compare: a full-time developer, a part-time analyst on three days a week, a designer shared with two other projects and a contractor booked for 15 hours a week can all be expressed in FTE and summed.
FTE turns up in two main places:
- **HR and finance**, where it describes the size of the workforce, drives salary budgets and is used in some legal and reporting tests.
- **Project and resource management**, where it describes how much capacity a project needs (demand), how much is available (supply) and what that capacity costs. This guide concentrates on the project use, which most HR-focused explanations skip.
FTE is also used as a noun for a role: "we need two more FTEs" means two full-time people's worth of time, which could be filled by two full-time hires, four people at 0.5 FTE, or a mix.

### The FTE formula
The basic formula is the same whatever period you use:
Tip
**FTE = hours worked (or planned) / hours in a full-time schedule for the same period**
The only things that change are the period and the full-time hours that go with it.
| Version | Formula | Example (40-hour basis) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weekly | Hours per week / standard weekly hours | 30 / 40 = 0.75 FTE |
| Monthly | Hours in the month / standard monthly hours | 120 / 160 = 0.75 FTE (using four 40-hour weeks) |
| Annual | Hours in the year / standard annual hours | 1,560 / 2,080 = 0.75 FTE |
| Project period | Total effort hours / (standard weekly hours x weeks in the period) | 600 / (40 x 20) = 0.75 FTE |
| Team or organisation | Sum of everyone's hours / standard hours for one person | 1,000 weekly hours / 40 = 25 FTE |

#### Choosing the full-time basis
The organisation, not the formula, defines what full time means. Common bases are 35, 37.5 and 40 hours a week. In the UK there is no legal number of hours that makes someone full time; the government's nidirect guidance says a full-time worker usually works 35 hours or more a week. Many US organisations use 40 hours, which gives the familiar annual figure of 40 x 52 = **2,080 hours**. A 37.5-hour week gives 37.5 x 52 = **1,950 hours**.
Pick the basis your organisation uses for contracts and write it next to every FTE figure, for example "2.5 FTE (37.5-hour basis)". The same 30 hours a week is 0.86 FTE on a 35-hour basis, 0.80 on 37.5 hours and 0.75 on 40 hours, so an unstated basis is the most common source of FTE confusion between teams, countries and suppliers.

#### Converting FTE back to hours
Reverse the formula when you need hours, for example to book people or estimate cost:
Tip
**Hours = FTE x full-time hours for the period**
0.6 FTE on a 37.5-hour basis is 0.6 x 37.5 = 22.5 hours a week. 2.5 FTE for 12 weeks on a 40-hour basis is 2.5 x 40 x 12 = 1,200 hours.

### FTE conversion table
Use this table to convert weekly hours into FTE under the three most common full-time bases. Values are rounded to two decimal places.
| Hours per week | 35-hour basis | 37.5-hour basis | 40-hour basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 (one day) | 0.23 | 0.21 | 0.20 |
| 15 | 0.43 | 0.40 | 0.38 |
| 16 (two days) | 0.46 | 0.43 | 0.40 |
| 20 | 0.57 | 0.53 | 0.50 |
| 22.5 | 0.64 | 0.60 | 0.56 |
| 24 (three days) | 0.69 | 0.64 | 0.60 |
| 28 | 0.80 | 0.75 | 0.70 |
| 30 | 0.86 | 0.80 | 0.75 |
| 32 (four days) | 0.91 | 0.85 | 0.80 |
| 35 | 1.00 | 0.93 | 0.88 |
| 37.5 | 1.07 | 1.00 | 0.94 |
| 40 | 1.14 | 1.07 | 1.00 |
Figures above 1.0 mean someone is working more than the organisation's full-time schedule. That is possible in a calculation, but a plan that relies on it is a warning sign, as explained under common mistakes.

### How to calculate FTE step by step
Whether you are sizing a team, a department or a project, the method is the same.
1. **Confirm the full-time basis.** Find the standard weekly hours in your organisation's contracts, such as 37.5 hours.
2. **Choose the period.** Week, month, year or the project period. Use the same period for the hours and for the full-time standard.
3. **Work out full-time hours for that period.** For example 37.5 x 52 = 1,950 hours a year, or 40 x 10 = 400 hours for a 10-week phase.
4. **Collect the hours.** For an existing team use contracted, timesheet or payroll hours. For a project use estimated effort hours from your estimates.
5. **Add the hours together** for everyone or everything you want to measure.
6. **Divide** the total hours by the full-time hours for the period.
7. **Round sensibly.** Two decimal places for people (0.75), one decimal place for plans (2.5 FTE). Spurious precision such as 3.137 FTE implies certainty you do not have.
8. **Record the basis and the source** next to the result, for example "4.25 FTE, 37.5-hour basis, 2026 payroll hours".

### Worked example 1: FTE of a mixed team
This is an illustrative example. Full time in this organisation is 40 hours a week.
| Person | Hours per week | FTE |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project manager | 40 | 1.0 |
| Developer 1 | 40 | 1.0 |
| Developer 2 | 40 | 1.0 |
| Analyst (part time) | 24 | 0.6 |
| Designer (shared with another team) | 16 | 0.4 |
| **Total** | **160** | **4.0** |
Five people provide 4.0 FTE, because 160 / 40 = 4.0. Headcount is 5, but the capacity is that of four full-time people. If you estimated the work assuming five full-time people, the plan would be 25% short before a single task started.

### Worked example 2: annual FTE with joiners, part-timers and contractors
Annual FTE is useful for budgets and year-end reporting, and it handles people who were only present for part of the year. In this illustrative example the organisation uses a 37.5-hour week, so one FTE year is 37.5 x 52 = 1,950 hours.
| Who | Pattern | Hours in the year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 full-time staff | 37.5 hours x 52 weeks each | 5,850 |
| 1 part-time analyst | 22.5 hours x 52 weeks | 1,170 |
| 1 joiner | 37.5 hours x 26 weeks (joined mid-year) | 975 |
| 1 contractor | 15 hours x 20 weeks | 300 |
| **Total** |  | **8,295** |
Annual FTE = 8,295 / 1,950 = **4.25 FTE**, from a headcount of six people. Whether the contractor is included depends on why you are counting: include them when you measure the capacity the team actually used or the cost of delivery, and exclude them when you report employee FTE to HR or finance. Say which you did.

### Worked example 3: converting project effort into FTE
This is the calculation project managers use most. Suppose an illustrative project needs 1,200 hours of development effort over 10 weeks, and the organisation's standard week is 40 hours.
1. Hours one FTE supplies in 10 weeks: 40 x 10 = 400 hours.
2. Nominal FTE needed: 1,200 / 400 = 3.0 FTE.
3. Adjust for productive time. If about 80% of a developer's hours go on project work once meetings, support and admin are taken out, each FTE supplies 400 x 0.8 = 320 project hours.
4. FTE to staff against: 1,200 / 320 = **3.75 FTE**.
The second figure is the one to request. Planning with 3.0 FTE would leave the team 240 hours short, which is three weeks of one developer's productive time. The 80% figure is an assumption; use your own timesheet data where you have it, and record the assumption in the plan.
See our guide to [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/) for how the 1,200 hours might be estimated.

#### Building an FTE profile by month
Real projects rarely need a flat level of effort. Converting estimated hours per role per month into FTE gives you a profile you can compare with what each team can supply. In this illustrative six-month website project, one FTE month is taken as 160 hours (four 40-hour weeks) for simplicity.
| Role | Month 1 | Month 2 | Month 3 | Month 4 | Month 5 | Month 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project manager | 0.5 | 0.5 | 0.5 | 0.5 | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| Designer | 1.0 | 1.5 | 0.5 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Developers | 0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 3.0 | 2.0 | 0.5 |
| Tester | 0 | 0 | 0.5 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 0.5 |
| **Total FTE** | **1.5** | **4.0** | **4.5** | **4.5** | **4.0** | **1.5** |
Each cell is hours divided by 160; for example 480 developer hours in month 3 is 3.0 FTE. The profile shows at a glance that the project peaks at 4.5 FTE in months 3 and 4, that design needs 1.5 FTE in month 2 (so one designer is not enough that month), and that testing ramps up as development winds down. Build the hours from your [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) and [project schedule](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/), and record the profile in a [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) or resource plan.

### Worked example 4: turning FTE into project cost
FTE converts directly into labour cost, which is why it is so useful for [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/). The formula is:
Tip
**Labour cost = FTE x hours per FTE in the period x hourly rate**
Using example 3, 3.75 developer FTE for 10 weeks at 40 hours, with an illustrative fully loaded rate of $90 an hour: 3.75 x 40 x 10 x $90 = **$135,000**. A fully loaded rate includes salary plus on-costs such as employer taxes, pension and overheads; ask finance which rate to use, because salary alone understates cost.
Most teams have several rates, so build the estimate by role:
| Role | FTE | Hours (10 weeks x 40) | Rate (illustrative) | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project manager | 0.5 | 200 | $95 | $19,000 |
| Developers | 3.75 | 1,500 | $90 | $135,000 |
| Tester | 1.0 | 400 | $70 | $28,000 |
| **Total** | **5.25** | **2,100** |  | **$182,000** |
The total labour cost then feeds your [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) and [budget at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/budget-at-completion/). Our [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) and [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) have the columns to do this by role.
See our guide to the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) for how labour, contingency and reserves fit together.

### Contracted, available and allocated FTE
Most FTE mistakes in projects come from mixing up three different figures. Keep them separate in your plans.
| Term | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contracted FTE | The working time someone is employed and paid for | Priya is contracted for 32 of 40 hours: 0.8 FTE |
| Available (productive) FTE | Contracted time minus leave, public holidays, training, admin and meetings | About 0.55 FTE after leave and overheads (assumptions below) |
| Allocated FTE | The share assigned to a specific project or activity | 0.5 FTE to Project A, 0.2 FTE to Project B |

#### How many productive hours is 1 FTE?
On a 40-hour basis, one FTE year is 2,080 hours, but nobody works all of them on a project. This illustrative calculation shows why. Substitute your organisation's own leave entitlement and figures.
| Step | Hours | Running total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contracted hours (40 x 52) | 2,080 | 2,080 |
| Less annual leave (assume 25 days x 8 hours) | -200 | 1,880 |
| Less public holidays (assume 8 days) | -64 | 1,816 |
| Less sickness and training allowance (assume 5 days) | -40 | 1,776 |
| Available hours |  | 1,776 |
| Less meetings, admin and support (assume 20%) | -355 | 1,421 |
| **Productive project hours per FTE** |  | **about 1,421** |
Under these assumptions one FTE supplies about 1,421 project hours a year, roughly 68% of the contracted 2,080. Planning against 2,080 would overstate capacity by almost half.

#### Allocation example
Priya (0.8 FTE contracted) is allocated 0.5 FTE to Project A, 0.2 FTE to Project B and 0.1 FTE to team duties, which adds up to her 0.8. If Project C now asks for 0.5 FTE of her time, her total allocation becomes 1.3 FTE against a 0.8 FTE contract. Showing contracted and allocated FTE side by side in the resource plan makes that over-allocation visible before it becomes overtime or missed dates. Our guides to [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) and [resource levelling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) explain how to resolve it.

### FTE vs headcount
FTE and headcount both describe the size of a team, but they answer different questions.
|  | FTE | Headcount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Measures | Working time supplied | Number of people |
| Part-time worker on 20 of 40 hours | 0.5 | 1 |
| Two job-sharers covering one role | 1.0 | 2 |
| Can be fractional? | Yes | No |
| Useful for | Capacity, effort, cost and budget planning | HR records, licences, equipment, desk space, onboarding, management span |
| Main risk if used alone | Hides the overhead of many part-time or shared people | Overstates capacity when many people are part time |

#### When to use each
- Use **FTE** for anything driven by working time: estimating, staffing requests, budgets, capacity and utilisation reporting.
- Use **headcount** for anything driven by the number of people: software seats, laptops, onboarding, communication and team size.
- Report **both** when they differ a lot. A team of 12 people providing 7.5 FTE has more coordination overhead than a team of 8 full-time people providing 8.0 FTE, even though the FTE figures are similar.

### How project managers use FTE
FTE gives project managers a common language with resource managers, finance and the [PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/). Typical uses include:
- **Resource plans:** each role with the FTE needed per period, for example "2.0 FTE developers, months 2 to 5". See [project resources](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-resources/) for what a resource plan contains.
- **Capacity planning:** comparing the FTE a team can supply with the FTE projects demand.
- **Estimating:** converting effort hours into team size and duration, and checking whether a deadline is realistic.
- **Budgeting:** converting FTE into labour cost for the [cost management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-management-plan/).
- **Staffing requests and business cases:** asking for "1.5 FTE business analyst for six months" is clearer than asking for "some BA help".
- **Tracking:** comparing planned FTE with actual FTE from timesheets in the [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).

#### Portfolio example: FTE supply vs demand
In this illustrative example, a delivery team has six full-time people and two people at 0.6 FTE on a 40-hour basis, so contracted capacity is 6 + 1.2 = **7.2 FTE**. After leave, training and team overheads, the team leader assumes 85% is available for project work: 7.2 x 0.85 = **6.1 FTE** (rounded).
| Demand next quarter | FTE |
| --- | --- |
| Project A (in delivery) | 3.0 |
| Project B (starting) | 2.5 |
| Project C (proposed) | 1.0 |
| **Total demand** | **6.5** |
| **Available supply** | **6.1** |
| **Gap** | **-0.4** |
The team is about 0.4 FTE short, or roughly 16 hours a week on a 40-hour basis. Expressing the gap in FTE turns a vague sense of being busy into a decision the sponsor can make: delay Project C, bring in a contractor for 0.4 FTE, reduce scope, or accept a later finish. This kind of comparison is the core of [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/).
See our guide to [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) for a full supply-and-demand method.

### FTE in HR and employment rules
In project planning, FTE is simply a unit of capacity. In HR it can also have legal or contractual meaning, and the definitions differ from country to country, so check with HR or legal advisers before using an FTE figure for anything other than planning.
- **United States (Affordable Care Act):** the IRS treats a full-time employee as someone averaging at least 30 hours of service a week, or 130 hours in a calendar month. For the applicable large employer test, you add the monthly hours of employees who are not full time, counting no more than 120 hours per person, and divide by 120 to get full-time equivalent employees. An employer with 50 or more full-time plus full-time equivalent employees on average in the previous year is an applicable large employer.
- **United Kingdom:** there is no legal definition of full-time hours; the government's nidirect guidance says full-time workers usually work 35 hours or more a week, and employers set their own standard.
- **Elsewhere:** standard working weeks and statutory rules vary, so international projects should agree one planning basis and convert local hours into it.
Tip
A legal FTE test (such as the US 30-hour rule) and your planning basis (such as 40 hours) can give different figures for the same person. Keep them apart: use the legal test only for compliance and your contracted standard for project plans.

### Tracking FTE in templates and software
For a single project, a spreadsheet works well: list each person or role, their contracted FTE, their allocated FTE per week or month and the resulting hours. Our [skills matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) helps you see who has the skills a role needs before you allocate FTE to them, and the [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) holds dates and owners.
Once you run several projects with shared people, spreadsheets become hard to keep consistent, and [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) with workload views helps:
- [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) (our top-rated tool) shows team workload and capacity, accounts for working hours, non-working days and holidays, and supports time tracking. Advanced, role-based resource and capacity planning is part of its Pinnacle plan, which suits PMOs and professional services firms that plan in FTE across a portfolio.
- [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) offers workload views on its Pro plan, which is often enough for basic capacity planning in small and mid-sized teams.
- [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) includes workload on its Advanced plan, alongside portfolios and goals for cross-team work.
- [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) provides workload tracking on Business and above, with a Resource Management add-on for capacity planning, time tracking and project budgets.
Whichever tool you use, set each person's working hours and leave correctly first. Workload views are only as accurate as the capacity behind them.

### Common FTE mistakes
- **Not stating the full-time basis.** 2.0 FTE on a 35-hour basis is 70 hours a week; on a 40-hour basis it is 80.
- **Treating 1.0 FTE as 40 productive project hours.** Leave, meetings, support and admin reduce it, often to two-thirds or less.
- **Allocating one person to several projects at 1.0 FTE each.** Add up every allocation per person and compare it with their contracted FTE.
- **Mixing contracted and allocated FTE** in the same column, so nobody can tell what the project actually gets.
- **Assuming FTE is interchangeable.** Two 0.5 FTE people rarely deliver the same as one 1.0 FTE person; handovers and context switching cost time, and skills differ.
- **Splitting people into many small fractions.** Someone on five projects at 0.2 FTE each loses time to switching between them. Prefer fewer, larger allocations.
- **Planning above 1.0 FTE.** It may balance the spreadsheet, but it relies on overtime and increases burnout and quality risk.
- **Using salary instead of a fully loaded rate** when converting FTE into cost.
- **Never comparing plan with actuals.** Check planned FTE against timesheet hours each month and adjust future estimates.
Tip
In every resource plan, show contracted FTE, allocated FTE and the difference for each person. The difference shows what they owe to other work and is the quickest way to spot over-allocation.
See our guide to [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) for how to assign people once you know the FTE you need.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does FTE stand for?**
FTE stands for full-time equivalent: a unit that expresses working time relative to one full-time employee. 1.0 FTE is one full-time schedule.

**Q: How do you calculate FTE?**
Divide the hours worked or planned by the hours in a full-time schedule for the same period. For example, 30 hours in a 40-hour week is 30 / 40 = 0.75 FTE.

**Q: How many hours is 1 FTE per year?**
It depends on the organisation's full-time standard. On a 40-hour week it is 40 x 52 = 2,080 hours; on 37.5 hours it is 1,950 hours. Productive project hours are lower once leave, holidays and overheads are removed.

**Q: What is 0.5 FTE?**
Half of a full-time schedule: 20 hours a week when full time is 40 hours, or 18.75 hours when full time is 37.5 hours.

**Q: What is 0.8 FTE?**
Four-fifths of a full-time schedule, usually four days a week. That is 32 hours on a 40-hour basis or 30 hours on a 37.5-hour basis.

**Q: What is the difference between FTE and headcount?**
Headcount counts people; FTE measures the working time they provide. Two half-time people are a headcount of 2 but 1.0 FTE.

**Q: How do you convert project hours to FTE?**
Divide total effort hours by the hours one FTE supplies in the project period. 1,200 hours over 10 weeks at 40 hours a week is 1,200 / 400 = 3.0 FTE, or 3.75 FTE if only 80% of each person's time is productive project time.

**Q: Can FTE be more than 1 for one person?**
In a calculation it can, if someone regularly works more than the standard week. In a plan, allocating anyone above 1.0 FTE is a warning sign of overtime, burnout and quality risk.

**Q: Is 37.5 hours a week 1 FTE?**
It is if the organisation defines full time as 37.5 hours. FTE is always relative to the organisation's own standard.

**Q: Do contractors count in FTE?**
For project capacity and cost, yes: include their hours, because they supply working time. For employee FTE reported by HR or finance they are usually excluded. State which approach you used.

**Q: Does overtime count towards FTE?**
If you measure actual capacity used, overtime hours count and can push FTE above contracted levels. For planning, base FTE on standard hours and treat overtime as a risk response, not as capacity.

**Q: Does 1 FTE mean 100% project time?**
No. 1 FTE means a full-time schedule. The share actually spent on the project is usually lower once leave, meetings, support and other duties are counted.

**Q: How is FTE used in resource plans?**
Resource plans list each role with the FTE needed per period, such as 2.0 FTE developers in months 2 to 6, so they can be compared with available capacity and costed. See our guide to [project resources](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-resources/).
