# Gantt Chart: What It Is, How to Make One, Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a Gantt chart is, its parts, how to read one and how to make one step by step, with a worked example, dependency types, tracking and mistakes.


## Gantt Chart: What It Is, How to Make One, Examples
A Gantt chart is a bar chart that shows a project's activities against a timeline, so you can see at a glance what happens when, in what order and who is doing it. This guide explains every part of the chart, how to read one, how to build one in eight steps and how to use it to track progress, with a fully dated worked example.
- Published 22 September 2026
- Last updated 18 October 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- A Gantt chart shows each activity as a horizontal bar on a timeline, with arrows for dependencies and diamonds for milestones.
- Build it from activities, durations and dependencies so the dates calculate themselves, rather than typing dates in by hand.
- The critical path and float show which bars can move without delaying the finish and which cannot.
- Save a baseline before work starts and compare progress against it at least weekly.
- Keep stakeholder views short (20 to 40 lines) and hold the detail underneath in collapsible summary rows.
- Spreadsheets are fine for simple charts; move to software when you need linked dependencies, rescheduling and resource views.

### What is a Gantt chart?
A **Gantt chart** is a horizontal bar chart used to plan and track a project schedule. Activities are listed down the left-hand side and time runs across the top. Each activity is drawn as a bar whose position shows when it starts and finishes and whose length shows its duration. Arrows link dependent activities and diamonds mark milestones.
A well-built Gantt chart answers five questions that a plain task list cannot:
- **What** work has to be done, grouped into phases or deliverables.
- **When** each piece of work starts and finishes.
- **In what order** the work must happen, and what is waiting on what.
- **Who** is responsible for each activity.
- **Are we on track?** How actual progress compares with the plan.
The Gantt chart is the most common way of presenting a schedule, but it is a view of the schedule rather than the schedule itself. The underlying model is the list of activities, durations and dependencies that you build during [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/). Get that model right and the chart draws itself; get it wrong and the chart is just a picture.

### Parts of a Gantt chart
Most Gantt charts, whether drawn in a spreadsheet or in software, share the same building blocks.
| Element | What it shows | Tip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task list | Activities down the left side, often numbered | Use verb-noun names such as "Install furniture" |
| Summary rows | Phases or [WBS](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) levels that roll up their child tasks | Collapse them for executive views |
| Timescale | Days, weeks, months or quarters across the top | Pick the scale that fits on one screen or page |
| Bars | Start, finish and duration of each activity | Colour by phase, owner or status, not all three |
| Dependency arrows | Which activities must finish (or start) before others; see [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) | Link everything except the first and last activity |
| Milestones | Diamonds marking zero-duration events such as approvals; see [project milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) | Use them for decision points and handovers |
| Progress shading | The percentage of each bar that is complete | Update from real progress, not hope |
| Owners and resources | Who does the work, shown in a column or beside the bar | Name one accountable owner per activity |
| Today line | A vertical line at the status date | Anything left of the line should be shaded |
| Baseline bars | The original planned dates, usually shown as thin grey bars | Save the baseline before work starts |
| Critical path | Bars, often red, where any delay delays the project; see [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) | Check it after every update |
You do not need every element on every chart. A one-page plan for a board meeting may show only summary bars and milestones, while the working schedule for the project team shows every activity, link and owner.

### How to read a Gantt chart
If someone hands you a Gantt chart, read it in this order.

#### Bars and the timescale
Start with the timescale at the top so you know whether each column is a day, a week or a month. Then read each bar from left to right: the left edge is the start date, the right edge is the finish date and the length is the duration. Bars that overlap vertically happen at the same time; bars that sit end to end happen in sequence.

#### Arrows
An arrow from the end of one bar to the start of another is a **finish-to-start** dependency: the second activity cannot start until the first finishes. Arrows from start to start or finish to finish show the other dependency types explained further down. A bar with no arrow coming in, other than the first activity, is a warning sign that a dependency may be missing.

#### Diamonds
A diamond is a **milestone**: a point in time with no duration, such as "design approved" or "go-live". Milestones are often the dates stakeholders care about most, so look along the diamonds first if you only have a minute.

#### Shading and the today line
Darker shading inside a bar shows how much of the activity is complete. Compare it with the today line: if the shading on a bar stops to the left of the line, that activity is behind where it should be. If it reaches beyond the line, it is ahead.

#### Summary bars, baselines and colours
Summary bars, often drawn as black brackets, span all the activities beneath them. Thin bars under the main bars are usually the **baseline**, so a gap between the two shows slippage. Red bars normally mark the critical path. Always check the legend, because colour conventions differ between tools and organisations.
Tip
A quick five-question check for any Gantt chart: When does it finish? Which milestones are next? What is on the critical path? Is anything to the left of the today line unfinished? Has the finish moved since the baseline?

### A short history of the Gantt chart
The chart is named after **Henry Gantt** (1861–1919), an American engineer and management consultant who designed his charts around 1910 to 1915. His early charts were used to compare planned and actual output in factories, so that managers could see where work was ahead of or behind schedule.
He was not the first to draw schedules this way. According to Wikipedia's history of the Gantt chart, the Polish engineer **Karol Adamiecki** devised a similar chart, which he called a harmonogram, in 1896, but published only in Polish and Russian, so it was little known in the West. The Swiss engineer Hermann Schürch also published comparable bar charts for construction work in the 1910s.
Gantt charts were used by the US Army during the First World War, and Wallace Clark's 1922 book *The Gantt Chart: A Working Tool of Management* helped spread the technique internationally. For decades the charts were drawn by hand on paper or wall boards, which made changes slow. Computer scheduling, and network techniques such as the critical path method and the [PERT chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/) from the late 1950s, made it possible to link activities and recalculate dates automatically. Modern Gantt chart software combines both ideas: the network logic underneath and the familiar bars on top.

### How to make a Gantt chart step by step
These eight steps work in any tool, from a spreadsheet to enterprise scheduling software.

#### 1. Define the scope and break it down
Start from the agreed scope and break it into deliverables and work packages with a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/). The WBS becomes the summary rows of your chart, so the chart is organised around what you are delivering rather than a random list of jobs.

#### 2. List the activities
Break each work package into activities that one person or team can own and that last somewhere between a day and a few weeks. Name each with a verb and a noun. Add milestones for approvals, handovers and deadlines.

#### 3. Estimate durations
Estimate the working time each activity needs, in one unit (usually working days). Ask the people who will do the work, and use a three-point estimate where the work is uncertain.

#### 4. Identify dependencies
For each activity, record its [predecessors](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/predecessors-and-successors/): the activities that must finish (or start) before it can begin. Most links are finish-to-start. Note any waiting time as a lag, such as concrete curing or a supplier lead time.

#### 5. Choose a tool and set the calendar
Enter the activities into a spreadsheet template or scheduling tool. Set the project start date and the working calendar: working days, weekends, public holidays and any shutdown periods. A missing holiday is one of the most common reasons a chart's dates are wrong.

#### 6. Link the activities and let the dates calculate
Enter the dependencies rather than typing start dates. The tool then calculates every date from the start date, durations and links. Add milestones as zero-duration activities at the points they depend on.

#### 7. Assign owners and check workload
Assign an owner, and resources if you track them, to every activity. Check that nobody is booked on several full-time activities at once. If they are, move non-critical work using its float or level the resources.

#### 8. Review, baseline and share
Check the critical path and float, confirm the finish date meets the business need, and walk the team through the chart. When everyone agrees, save a **baseline** (see [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/)) and share the chart in the format each audience needs.
Tip
If most of your activities have a start date typed in, the chart is a picture, not a schedule. Replace fixed dates with dependency links wherever you can, and keep date constraints for genuine external deadlines.

### Gantt chart example: an office move
A 40-person team is moving to a new office. The project starts on **Monday 2 November 2026**, the team works Monday to Friday and there are no holidays in the period. Durations are in working days.
| ID | Activity | Duration | Predecessor | Start | Finish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Confirm requirements and budget | 3 days | - | Mon 2 Nov | Wed 4 Nov |
| B | Select and order furniture | 5 days | A | Thu 5 Nov | Wed 11 Nov |
| C | Book removal firm | 2 days | A | Thu 5 Nov | Fri 6 Nov |
| D | Install network and phones | 6 days | A | Thu 5 Nov | Thu 12 Nov |
| E | Deliver and install furniture | 5 days | B | Thu 12 Nov | Wed 18 Nov |
| F | Pack and label | 3 days | C | Mon 9 Nov | Wed 11 Nov |
| G | Move and unpack | 2 days | D, E, F | Thu 19 Nov | Fri 20 Nov |
| M | Milestone: new office open | 0 days | G | Fri 20 Nov | Fri 20 Nov |
Drawn on a weekly timescale, the bars look like this (■ = the activity runs that week, ◆ = milestone):
| Activity | w/c 2 Nov | w/c 9 Nov | w/c 16 Nov |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A Confirm requirements | ■ Mon–Wed |  |  |
| B Order furniture (critical) | ■ Thu–Fri | ■ Mon–Wed |  |
| C Book removals | ■ Thu–Fri |  |  |
| D Network and phones | ■ Thu–Fri | ■ Mon–Thu |  |
| E Install furniture (critical) |  | ■ Thu–Fri | ■ Mon–Wed |
| F Pack and label |  | ■ Mon–Wed |  |
| G Move and unpack (critical) |  |  | ■ Thu–Fri |
| M Office open |  |  | ◆ Fri 20 Nov |

#### Reading the example
There are three paths from A to G. The longest, **A-B-E-G**, takes 3 + 5 + 5 + 2 = 15 working days, so it is the critical path and sets the opening date of Friday 20 November. A software tool would show those bars in red.
| Path | Length | Total float on the path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A-B-E-G | 15 days | 0 (critical) |
| A-D-G | 11 days | 4 days on D |
| A-C-F-G | 10 days | 5 days shared by C and F |
- **D (network and phones)** has 4 days of total float and 4 days of free float. It could finish as late as Wednesday 18 November without moving the opening.
- **C and F** share 5 days of total float. C has no free float of its own, because any slip in C pushes F straight away, but F can slip 5 days before it touches G. If C uses some of the float, there is less left for F. See [float and slack](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) for the difference between total and free float.
- **B and E** are where the project manager should spend most attention. A late furniture order moves the opening date day for day.
You can reproduce this example in our free [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/), or in the [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) if you want the float calculated for you.

### Dependencies, leads and lags on a Gantt chart
The arrows on a Gantt chart represent four possible dependency types. Finish-to-start covers most links, but the others let you model overlapping work realistically.
| Type | Rule | Example | How it looks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Finish-to-start (FS) | B cannot start until A finishes | Furniture is installed after it is ordered | Arrow from end of A to start of B |
| Start-to-start (SS) | B cannot start until A starts | Packing can start once the removal firm starts work | Arrow from start of A to start of B |
| Finish-to-finish (FF) | B cannot finish until A finishes | Snagging cannot finish until installation finishes | Arrow from end of A to end of B |
| Start-to-finish (SF) | B cannot finish until A starts | The old phone system stays live until the new one starts | Arrow from start of A to end of B (rare) |
Two adjustments refine any link:
- A **lag** adds waiting time. "Paint walls, then lay carpet FS + 2 days" leaves two days for the paint to dry.
- A **lead** is a negative lag that allows overlap. "Start testing FS − 3 days" lets testing start three days before the build finishes.
Our guide to [leads and lags](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/) has worked examples. Use date constraints such as "must start on" only for genuine external fixes like a booked venue, because each one stops the chart from rescheduling naturally. Some charts also use a [hammock activity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/hammock-activity/), a bar whose length is set by other activities, to show support work such as supervision or equipment hire.

### Tracking progress with a Gantt chart
A Gantt chart earns its keep during delivery, when it shows what has changed and what that means for the finish date.

#### Worked tracking example
Back to the office move. At the end of **Friday 13 November** (working day 10), the project manager updates the chart:
| Activity | Baseline finish | Status at 13 Nov | Forecast finish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A Confirm requirements | Wed 4 Nov | Complete | Wed 4 Nov |
| B Order furniture | Wed 11 Nov | Complete, one day late | Thu 12 Nov (actual) |
| C Book removals | Fri 6 Nov | Complete | Fri 6 Nov |
| D Network and phones | Thu 12 Nov | Complete | Thu 12 Nov |
| E Install furniture | Wed 18 Nov | 20% complete (planned 40%) | Thu 19 Nov |
| F Pack and label | Wed 11 Nov | Complete | Wed 11 Nov |
| G Move and unpack | Fri 20 Nov | Not started | Mon 23 Nov |
| M Office open | Fri 20 Nov | - | Mon 23 Nov |
Because B is on the critical path, its one-day slip pushes E, G and the opening milestone back by one working day. On the chart, the current bars for E and G now sit one day to the right of their grey baseline bars, and the shading on E stops short of the today line. In schedule terms the project has a **one-day variance** against the baseline; see [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) for the earned value version of the same idea.
The project manager now has clear options:
- **Crash** the critical activity: pay for a second installation crew so E finishes a day earlier. See [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/).
- **Fast track**: move the IT equipment on Thursday 19 November while the last furniture is still going in, overlapping E and G.
- **Accept** the new date and tell stakeholders through the project status report.
Note that slips on D, C or F would not have mattered on this scale, because those activities had float. That is the main value of the critical path on a Gantt chart: it tells you which delays deserve action.

#### A weekly update routine
1. Pick a status date (for example, close of business every Friday).
2. Record actual start and finish dates for anything that started or finished.
3. Update percent complete or remaining duration for activities in progress.
4. Let the tool reschedule unfinished work from the status date.
5. Compare the forecast finish and milestones with the baseline.
6. Check whether the critical path has moved and note any near-critical activities.
7. Agree actions for any slip, and record approved changes through change control before re-baselining.

### Types of Gantt chart
The same basic chart is used in several forms, depending on what you need to see.
| Type | What it adds | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simple timeline Gantt | Bars and milestones only, no links | Small projects, one-page plans, spreadsheets |
| Dependency-linked Gantt | Arrows between activities; dates recalculate | Most project schedules |
| Tracking (baseline) Gantt | Baseline bars, percent complete and today line | Reporting progress and slippage |
| Resource-loaded Gantt | People or equipment assigned to bars, with workload views | Teams sharing people across activities |
| Multi-project or portfolio Gantt | Summary bars for several projects on one timeline | PMOs and programme managers |
| Release-level Agile Gantt | Sprints, releases and milestones rather than tasks | Hybrid and Agile teams; see [agile Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-gantt-charts/) |

### Gantt chart vs PERT chart, timeline, Kanban and roadmap
Gantt charts are often confused with other planning visuals. Each answers a different question.
| Tool | Shows | Strength | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gantt chart | Activities as bars on a timeline, with links | Easy to read dates, overlaps and progress | You need a dated, trackable schedule |
| [PERT chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/) | Activities and dependencies as a network, with three-point estimates | Shows logic and uncertainty clearly | Durations are uncertain or logic is complex |
| [Network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/) | Boxes and arrows with early and late dates | Makes the critical path calculation visible | You are building or checking the logic |
| [Project timeline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-timeline/) | Key phases and milestones only | Very simple for executives | Stakeholders need the big picture |
| Project roadmap | Goals and themes over months or quarters | Strategic, outcome-focused | Communicating direction, not tasks |
| [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) | Work items by status in columns | Shows flow and bottlenecks | Work arrives continuously and is not tightly scheduled |
They combine well. Many teams build the logic in a network view, present it as a Gantt chart, summarise it for executives as a timeline and manage day-to-day work on a Kanban board.

### When to use a Gantt chart (and when not to)

#### A Gantt chart works well when
- The work has a clear sequence and real dependencies, as in construction, events, office moves, migrations and product launches.
- Several teams or suppliers have to hand work over to each other.
- There is a fixed deadline and you need to know whether you can meet it.
- Stakeholders need to see dates and milestones.
- You report progress against an approved baseline, as in most [Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) and hybrid projects.

#### Consider something lighter when
- The work is a stream of small, independent requests, where a Kanban board shows flow better.
- Scope changes every sprint, so detailed bars would need rebuilding every fortnight. Plan releases and milestones on the chart and leave the detail to the backlog.
- The project is a handful of tasks for one person, where a to-do list is enough.

### Advantages and limitations of Gantt charts
| Advantages | Limitations |
| --- | --- |
| Easy for anyone to read, with little training | Large charts become cluttered and hard to follow |
| Shows sequence, overlap and duration at a glance | Does not show effort, cost or risk unless you add them |
| Makes the critical path and float visible | Can give false precision when work is uncertain |
| Shows progress against a baseline clearly | Needs regular updating to stay useful |
| Highlights handovers between teams | Dependencies are hard to maintain in a spreadsheet |
| Works for almost any project type | Encourages detailed up-front planning that may not suit highly iterative work |
Most of the limitations come from how the chart is maintained rather than the chart itself. Linked dependencies, a sensible level of detail and a weekly update routine deal with nearly all of them.

### Common Gantt chart mistakes
- **Typing dates instead of linking activities.** The chart cannot reschedule itself, so it goes out of date the first time anything moves.
- **Too much detail.** Hundreds of one-hour tasks make the chart unreadable and impossible to maintain. Keep activities between about a day and a few weeks.
- **Dangling activities.** An activity with no successor can finish late without moving anything on the chart, which hides the real critical path.
- **Ignoring calendars.** Weekends, public holidays and part-time resources change the real dates even when the logic is right.
- **No baseline.** Without one, you can see where you are but not how far you have drifted.
- **Over-allocated people.** Bars can look fine while one person is booked on three full-time activities at once. Check workload, not just dates.
- **Showing everyone everything.** Executives want milestones and summary bars; the team wants the detail. Build one schedule and filter it for each audience.
- **Updating only when asked.** A chart updated once a month is a history book. Update it on a fixed cadence.

### How to make a Gantt chart in Excel or Google Sheets
Spreadsheets do not have a built-in Gantt chart type, but there are two common methods.

#### Method 1: the stacked bar chart
1. Create columns for Task, Start date and Duration (in days).
2. Select the Task and Start date columns and insert a stacked bar chart.
3. Add the Duration column as a second data series on the same chart.
4. Format the Start date series with no fill and no border, so only the duration bars remain visible.
5. Reverse the order of the vertical (category) axis so the first task appears at the top.
6. Set the horizontal axis minimum to your project start date and adjust the date format and gridlines.

#### Method 2: the shaded grid
List tasks in rows and put days or weeks across the columns, then shade the cells each task covers, manually or with conditional formatting that compares each column's date with the task's start and finish. This is how our [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) works: enter owners and start and end dates, and the day count calculates for you.
Both methods show timing well but do not calculate dependencies, float or the critical path, and bars do not move when a predecessor slips. For linked logic in a spreadsheet, use the [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/); for anything larger, use software.

### Gantt chart software and templates
For small projects, a free [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) in Google Sheets or Excel is often enough. Move to Gantt chart software when you need any of the following:
- Dependencies that reschedule bars automatically when something slips.
- Critical path highlighting and baselines.
- Resource and workload views across several projects.
- Real-time collaboration, comments and progress updates from the team.
- Portfolio views that roll several project charts into one.
Most of the tools in our [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) ranking include a Gantt or timeline view, although on several it sits on paid plans. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, offers interactive Gantt charts with dependencies, and on paid plans critical path and baselines, which suits teams running several linked projects. [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) suits planners who like a spreadsheet grid with a Gantt chart beside it, while monday.com, Asana and ClickUp offer Gantt or timeline views alongside boards and lists. Check which plan includes dependencies, baselines and critical path before you buy.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a Gantt chart used for?**
A Gantt chart is used to plan, communicate and track a project schedule. It shows what work needs doing, when each activity starts and finishes, the order of the work, who is responsible and how progress compares with the plan.

**Q: What are the main elements of a Gantt chart?**
The main elements are the task list, a timescale, bars for each activity, dependency arrows, milestones, progress shading, owners, a today line and, on more advanced charts, baseline bars and critical path highlighting.

**Q: Who invented the Gantt chart?**
It is named after Henry Gantt, who designed his charts around 1910 to 1915. The Polish engineer Karol Adamiecki had devised a similar chart, the harmonogram, in 1896, but it was published only in Polish and Russian and was little known outside Eastern Europe.

**Q: How do I make a Gantt chart?**
Break the scope into a work breakdown structure, list the activities, estimate durations, identify dependencies, enter everything into a template or tool with a start date and calendar, link the activities so dates calculate, assign owners, then review the critical path and save a baseline.

**Q: What is the difference between a Gantt chart and a timeline?**
A [project timeline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-timeline/) shows key phases and milestones in a simple form, usually for stakeholders. A Gantt chart shows every activity with its duration, dependencies and progress, so it is the working tool for managing the schedule.

**Q: Can I make a Gantt chart in Excel?**
Yes. Use a stacked bar chart with the start date series hidden, or a grid of shaded cells. Excel will not calculate dependencies or the critical path, so bars do not move when a predecessor slips. A ready-made [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) saves setup time.

**Q: What does a diamond mean on a Gantt chart?**
A diamond is a milestone: a significant point in time with zero duration, such as an approval, a handover or a go-live date.

**Q: What do the arrows on a Gantt chart mean?**
Arrows show dependencies between activities. Most are finish-to-start, meaning the next activity cannot start until the previous one finishes. Start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish links are also possible.

**Q: Is a Gantt chart Agile or Waterfall?**
It is most associated with Waterfall and other plan-driven approaches, but many Agile and hybrid teams use simplified Gantt charts for releases, milestones and dependencies between teams. See [agile Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-gantt-charts/).

**Q: What is the difference between a Gantt chart and a PERT chart?**
A Gantt chart shows activities as bars on a timeline, which makes dates and progress easy to read. A [PERT chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/) shows activities as a network of boxes and arrows with three-point estimates, which makes logic and uncertainty easier to analyse.

**Q: What is a baseline in a Gantt chart?**
A baseline is a saved copy of the approved planned dates, usually shown as thin bars under the current bars. The gap between the two shows how far each activity has slipped or moved ahead.

**Q: How many tasks should a Gantt chart have?**
There is no fixed limit, but a view of 20 to 40 lines is readable on one screen or page. Hold larger schedules in collapsible summary rows and filter the view for each audience.

**Q: How often should I update a Gantt chart?**
At least weekly on most projects, on a fixed status date. Fast-moving projects or the final weeks before a deadline may need updates every day or two.

**Q: Which tools have Gantt charts?**
Most project management tools offer a Gantt or timeline view, including [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/), monday.com, Asana and ClickUp, though features such as dependencies, baselines and critical path often depend on the plan. Compare them in our [Gantt chart software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/) guide.

# Hammock Activity: Definition, Example and How to Use It

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/hammock-activity/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a hammock activity is, how its duration is calculated, a costed example, hammock vs summary task vs LOE, and how to build one in P6 or MS Project.


## Hammock Activity: Definition, Example and How to Use It
A hammock activity is a schedule activity whose start and finish are tied to other activities, so its duration is calculated from them rather than estimated. It stretches or shrinks as the work it spans moves, which makes it ideal for time-based support such as supervision, equipment hire or project management. This guide shows how the duration is worked out, a costed example, how hammocks differ from summary tasks and level-of-effort activities, and how to build one in common tools.
- Published 26 September 2026
- Last updated 18 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- A hammock activity spans a group of activities and takes its dates from them: start from the first, finish from the last.
- Its duration is calculated, never estimated: latest linked finish minus earliest linked start.
- Use hammocks for time-dependent support, costs and reporting spans, such as supervision, hire and overheads.
- A hammock should follow the network, not drive it, and should not appear on the critical path.
- Primavera P6 has a Level of Effort activity type for this; Microsoft Project needs a workaround.
- Spread resources evenly across the hammock so costs are not front-loaded.

### What is a hammock activity?
A **hammock activity** (or hammock task) is a summary-type schedule activity that spans a group of other activities. It has no duration of its own. Instead, it starts when the first activity it is linked to starts and finishes when the last one finishes, so its duration is calculated automatically and changes whenever those activities move.
The name comes from the image of a hammock slung between two trees. Move either tree and the hammock stretches or shortens, but it never holds the trees in place. In the same way, a hammock activity hangs between two points in the schedule and follows them.
You may also see it called a **summary duration task** or **frame activity**. Older editions of the PMBOK Guide grouped hammock activities with summary activities in their glossary, and many scheduling tools implement the idea as a **level-of-effort (LOE)** activity. The terms overlap, and the differences are explained in the comparison further down.
Hammocks belong to the detailed side of [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/). You build them once the activity network is in place, because they depend on its dates.

### How a hammock activity works
A hammock activity has four defining features:
- **It is linked, not estimated.** Its start is tied to the start of one activity (typically with a start-to-start link) and its finish to the finish of another (typically finish-to-finish). See [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) for the link types.
- **It can span any activities.** Unlike a summary task, it is not limited to children in one branch of the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/). It can begin in one phase and end in another.
- **It follows the network.** When the activities in between slip or speed up, the hammock lengthens or shortens. It should never push other work.
- **It often carries resources and costs.** Anything that is paid for by time, such as a supervisor, a crane or a site cabin, can be assigned to the hammock so its cost updates with the schedule.

#### The duration formula
Using the day 0 convention from the [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/):
- **Hammock start** = the early start of the first linked activity.
- **Hammock finish** = the early finish of the last linked activity.
- **Hammock duration** = hammock finish − hammock start, in working days on the hammock's calendar.
If the hammock spans several activities that could start or finish first, use the earliest start and the latest finish among them. Some tools let you link several predecessors and successors to a hammock and do this for you.

#### What happens when the schedule changes
Because the hammock reads its dates from other activities, it reacts to every change between them:
| Change in the schedule | Effect on the hammock |
| --- | --- |
| An activity it spans slips but stays within its float | No change, because the first start and last finish do not move |
| A critical activity it spans slips | The hammock lengthens by the same amount |
| Critical work is crashed or fast tracked | The hammock shortens |
| The first linked activity starts late | The hammock starts late; its length may also change |
| Work after the hammock's end activity changes | No change, because it is outside the span |
This is exactly what you want for time-based costs, and it is why hammocks are popular on construction, engineering and government schedules.

### Hammock activity example: an office fit-out
A contractor is fitting out an office floor. The six construction activities, with durations in working days, form this network:
| ID | Activity | Duration | Predecessor | Early start | Early finish | Total float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Strip out | 4 | - | 0 | 4 | 0 |
| B | First-fix electrics | 5 | A | 4 | 9 | 1 |
| C | Partitioning | 6 | A | 4 | 10 | 0 |
| D | Second-fix electrics | 3 | B, C | 10 | 13 | 0 |
| E | Decorating | 4 | D | 13 | 17 | 0 |
| F | Snagging and handover | 2 | E | 17 | 19 | 0 |
The critical path is A-C-D-E-F at 19 working days. B has 1 day of float. (If you want to check the numbers, our [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) guide explains the calculation.)

#### Step 1: add the hammocks
The contractor has two costs that depend on time rather than on any single activity:
- **H1 Site supervision**, at $450 a day, needed from the start of strip-out until handover. It is linked start-to-start from A and finish-to-finish from F.
- **H2 Skip and welfare unit hire**, at $60 a day, needed from the start of strip-out until second-fix electrics are complete, when the noisy, dirty work ends. It is linked start-to-start from A and finish-to-finish from D.

#### Step 2: calculate the durations and costs
- H1 starts at A's early start (0) and finishes at F's early finish (19), so it lasts **19 days** and costs 19 × $450 = **$8,550**.
- H2 starts at 0 and finishes at D's early finish (13), so it lasts **13 days** and costs 13 × $60 = **$780**.

#### Step 3: see what happens when the schedule moves
| Scenario | Project finish | H1 duration and cost | H2 duration and cost | Total hammock cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plan | Day 19 | 19 days, $8,550 | 13 days, $780 | $9,330 |
| B slips 1 day (within float) | Day 19 | 19 days, $8,550 | 13 days, $780 | $9,330 |
| C slips 3 days (critical) | Day 22 | 22 days, $9,900 | 16 days, $960 | $10,860 |
| E crashed by 1 day | Day 18 | 18 days, $8,100 | 13 days, $780 | $8,880 |

#### What the example shows
- **Float protects the hammock.** B's one-day slip is absorbed by its float, so neither hammock changes.
- **Critical slips cost money twice.** A three-day slip in partitioning delays the finish and adds $1,530 of support costs, which would be easy to miss if supervision and hire were entered as fixed-duration tasks.
- **Each hammock only sees its own span.** Crashing the decorating shortens H1 by a day but leaves H2 untouched, because H2 ends at D.
- **The cost of time is visible.** When you evaluate [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/), the hammock costs saved by finishing earlier are part of the business case. Here, crashing E is worth up to $450 a day before it costs more than it saves.
Tip
Never make a hammock a predecessor of other real work. If H1 drove F and F drove H1, the tool would either report circular logic or produce dates that make no sense. Hammocks should hang from the network, not hold it up.

### Hammock activity vs summary task vs level of effort
These terms are often used interchangeably, but they are not quite the same thing.
|  | Hammock activity | Summary task | Level-of-effort (LOE) activity | Milestone |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | An activity whose dates come from linked activities | A parent row that rolls up its child tasks | Ongoing support work with no specific output | A point in time |
| How dates are set | By dependency links to chosen activities | By the outline (WBS) hierarchy | By the work it supports, often via hammock links | By its predecessors or a constraint |
| Can span different WBS branches | Yes | No, only its own children | Yes | Not applicable |
| Duration | Calculated | Calculated from children | Calculated, or sometimes fixed | Zero |
| Holds resources and costs | Yes, commonly | Usually avoided | Yes, that is its main purpose | No |
| Typical example | Crane hire from erection to dismantling | Phase 2: Fit-out | Project management, QA, site security | Practical completion |
In practice: **level of effort** describes the *kind of work* (support that lasts as long as the work it supports), while a **hammock** describes the *scheduling technique* (taking dates from other activities). Hammocks are the usual way to schedule LOE work, which is why tools such as Primavera P6 implement hammocks as a Level of Effort activity type.
A **summary task** follows the WBS outline. Oracle's P6 documentation describes a separate **WBS Summary** activity type whose dates run from the earliest start to the latest finish of activities sharing a WBS code, which is the summary-task idea rather than a hammock. If your support cost spans several branches of the WBS, a hammock is the better fit. Our guide to [project tasks and activities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-tasks-and-activities/) covers the other activity types, and [project milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) covers zero-duration events.

### When to use a hammock activity
Use a hammock whenever something lasts exactly as long as a stretch of the schedule and you want it to update itself.
| Use | Example | Industry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Supervision and management | Site manager from mobilisation to handover | Construction |
| Equipment or facility hire | Tower crane from erection to dismantling | Construction, engineering |
| Quality and safety cover | QA inspector during the build and test phases | Engineering, manufacturing |
| Project management effort | PM and PMO support from kick-off to closure | Any |
| Environment and licence costs | Test environment from build start to user acceptance sign-off | IT and software |
| Reporting spans | "Phase 2 delivery" spanning activities from several work packages | Programmes and government projects |
| Event support | Security and venue staff from load-in to load-out | Events |
Hammocks are also useful in large programme schedules, such as an [integrated master plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/integrated-master-plan/) and its schedule, where managers want summary bars that cut across the WBS without restructuring it.

#### When not to use one
- **When the work produces a deliverable.** Real work with an output should be an ordinary activity with its own estimate and links.
- **To represent buffer or float.** A hammock that spans a gap is not contingency. Plan buffers explicitly.
- **To force dates.** If you want an activity to start on a set date, use a constraint, sparingly, not a hammock.
- **When a summary task already does the job.** If the support only covers one branch of the WBS, a summary row may be simpler.
- **On very small projects.** If nothing costs money by time, a hammock adds complexity without benefit.

### How to create a hammock activity step by step
The method is the same in any tool; only the menus differ.
1. **Build and check the network first.** Every real activity needs its durations and [predecessors and successors](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/predecessors-and-successors/) before you add hammocks.
2. **Decide what the hammock represents** and which activity marks its start and which marks its finish. Write this in the activity name or notes, for example "Site supervision (hammock: A start to F finish)".
3. **Create the activity** with no fixed duration, or as a Level of Effort type if your tool has one.
4. **Link the start** to the first activity, usually start-to-start with no lag.
5. **Link the finish** to the last activity, usually finish-to-finish with no lag.
6. **Assign resources or costs** for the whole period, spread evenly (or on a curve) across the duration.
7. **Test it.** Change a critical duration upstream and check that the hammock and its cost move. Change a non-critical duration within its float and check that they do not.
Keep hammocks together, for example under a "Support and overheads" heading, so they are easy to find and exclude from critical path reports.

### Hammock activities in Primavera P6
Oracle's Primavera P6 offers five activity types: Task Dependent, Resource Dependent, Level of Effort, Start or Finish Milestone and WBS Summary. According to Oracle's P6 help, a **Level of Effort** activity has a duration determined by its dependent activities and is typically used for ongoing work such as project management, clerical work or change management. This is P6's hammock.
1. Add the activity and set its **Activity Type** to Level of Effort on the General tab.
2. Add relationships to the first and last activities it should span. A common convention, described by Primavera trainers, is a start-to-start relationship with the first activity and a finish-to-finish relationship with the last.
3. Schedule the project and check that the LOE runs from the start of the first activity to the finish of the last.
4. Assign resources or expenses. If you add a resource, apply a resource curve so the units spread across the duration rather than bunching at the start.
Follow your organisation's linking convention and check that the LOE is not driving any real work. If you only need a roll-up for one WBS element, the **WBS Summary** type may be the better choice.

### Hammock tasks in Microsoft Project
Microsoft Project does not have a hammock task type, but a long-standing workaround, described in Microsoft's TechNet wiki, uses linked cells:
1. Create the task that will act as the hammock.
2. Select the **Start** cell of the task that should drive the hammock's start and copy it.
3. Select the hammock task's **Start** cell and choose **Task > Paste > Paste Special > Paste Link**.
4. Copy the **Finish** cell of the task that should drive the hammock's finish.
5. Select the hammock task's **Finish** cell and paste link it in the same way.
The hammock's dates now update when the source tasks move. Be aware of the caveats the wiki lists:
- The links use older DDE technology and can be fragile. Only the hammock shows a small indicator; the source tasks show nothing.
- To remove a hammock, break the links first rather than just deleting the task, to avoid leaving orphaned link fragments.
- Name the task clearly, for example "Provide management support (hammock)", and record the source tasks in its notes.
Because of these limits, many Microsoft Project users keep hammocks to a handful of important support costs, or use a summary task where the support covers one branch of the outline.

### Hammocks in spreadsheets and other tools
If your tool has no hammock or level-of-effort type, you can still get the same result:
- **Spreadsheet formula.** Set the hammock's start to the start of the first linked row and its finish to the finish of the last linked row, or use MIN() of the start dates and MAX() of the finish dates across the range it spans. Duration is then finish minus start (or NETWORKDAYS() for working days).
- **Parent or summary rows.** Many project management tools calculate a parent row's dates from its children. Group the activities under a parent and assign the cost there, accepting that it only covers that group.
- **Cost columns.** Multiply the calculated duration by the daily rate so the support cost updates when dates change.
Our free [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) has columns for durations and predecessors, and the [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) is a good place to hold the daily rates. If you show the result on a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), give hammocks a distinct colour so readers do not mistake them for real work.

### Hammock activities and the critical path
A hammock spans critical activities, so its total float may look like zero, but it is not itself critical. Nothing depends on it, and shortening it is impossible without shortening the activities it hangs from.
The US Government Accountability Office's Schedule Assessment Guide is clear on the point: it states that LOE activities should not drive the schedule, and warns that if LOE is critical, management has no indication of which activities can slip or which would respond to extra resources. In practice that means:
- Exclude hammocks and LOE activities from critical path reports and filters.
- If a hammock appears on the critical path, check for a link where it acts as a predecessor of real work and remove it.
- Do not count hammock float when you look at [float and slack](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) for risk; look at the real activities instead.
- Review hammocks after major re-planning, because new activities may fall outside the span they were meant to cover.

### Hammock activities, costs and earned value
Hammocks matter most to cost control, because many project overheads are paid by time.
- **Budgeting.** When you build the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/), price time-based costs on hammocks so the baseline cost matches the baseline schedule.
- **Forecasting.** When the schedule slips, the hammock lengthens and the forecast cost rises automatically, which gives early warning through [cost control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-control/).
- **Earned value.** In [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/), level-of-effort work is normally measured with the LOE method: value is earned as time passes, so earned value equals planned value and LOE shows no schedule variance. It can still show a cost variance if you spend more per day than planned.
Because LOE earns value with time, a schedule with a large share of its budget on hammocks can make overall performance look better than it is. Keep LOE budgets proportionate and report them separately from discrete work.

### Common hammock activity mistakes
- **Typing a fixed duration.** A hammock with a hard-coded duration is just an ordinary task and will not update.
- **Making the hammock a predecessor of real work.** This can create circular logic or let support activities drive the finish date.
- **Linking to the wrong activities.** A hammock tied to a non-critical activity at its end may stop early while the work continues.
- **Front-loaded resources.** In some tools, resources on an LOE bunch at the start unless you apply a curve or even spread.
- **Using hammocks to hide gaps or buffers.** Contingency should be visible and managed, not buried in a support bar.
- **Too many hammocks.** A schedule full of hammocks is harder to read and to audit. Keep them for genuine time-based support and reporting.
- **Fragile links in Microsoft Project.** Deleting a task with paste links, without breaking them first, can leave orphaned link fragments.

### Hammock activity for the PMP exam
Hammock activities appear occasionally in [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) study material as part of schedule management terminology. The points worth remembering are:
- A hammock is a summary-type activity whose duration is set by the activities it spans.
- It is linked from the start of one activity to the finish of another.
- It is commonly used for level-of-effort and support work.
- It does not drive other activities and is not part of the critical path.
Exam questions are more likely to test the critical path, float and dependency types than hammocks themselves, so make sure those foundations are solid.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a hammock activity in project management?**
A hammock activity is a summary-type schedule activity that spans a group of activities and takes its dates from them. It starts when the first linked activity starts and finishes when the last linked activity finishes, so its duration changes automatically when they move.

**Q: Why is it called a hammock activity?**
Because it hangs between two points in the schedule, like a hammock between two trees, and stretches or shrinks as those points move.

**Q: How is the duration of a hammock activity calculated?**
Duration equals the finish of the last linked activity minus the start of the first linked activity, in working days on the hammock's calendar. If it spans several possible start or end activities, use the earliest start and the latest finish.

**Q: What is an example of a hammock activity?**
Site supervision on a construction project, linked from the start of the first site activity to the finish of handover. If any critical work slips, the supervision activity, and its cost, lengthens automatically.

**Q: Is a hammock activity on the critical path?**
No. It spans critical activities but does not drive any work, so it should be excluded from the critical path. The GAO Schedule Assessment Guide states that LOE activities should not drive the schedule.

**Q: What is the difference between a hammock activity and a summary task?**
A summary task groups its child tasks in the WBS outline. A hammock is linked by dependencies and can span activities from different branches of the WBS, and it commonly carries resources and costs.

**Q: Is a hammock activity the same as level of effort?**
Not exactly. Level of effort is support work with no specific output, such as project management. A hammock is the scheduling technique of taking dates from other activities. Hammocks are the usual way to schedule LOE work, and Primavera P6 implements hammocks as a Level of Effort activity type.

**Q: How do I create a hammock activity?**
Create an activity with no fixed duration, link its start to the start of the first activity it should span and its finish to the finish of the last, then assign the time-based resources or costs. Test it by changing an upstream critical duration.

**Q: Can a hammock activity have resources?**
Yes. Assigning time-based resources and costs, such as supervisors, equipment hire or management time, is one of the main reasons to use a hammock. Spread them evenly or on a curve across its duration.

**Q: Does Microsoft Project have hammock tasks?**
Not as a built-in type. You can create one by copying the start date of one task and the finish date of another and using Paste Special > Paste Link into the hammock's Start and Finish fields, though these links can be fragile.

**Q: How do you create a hammock in Primavera P6?**
Set the activity type to Level of Effort and add relationships to the first and last activities it should span, commonly start-to-start with the first and finish-to-finish with the last. Apply a resource curve if it carries resources.

**Q: Should a hammock activity drive other activities?**
No. A hammock should follow the network and never act as a predecessor of real work, otherwise you risk circular logic and a misleading critical path.

**Q: How does a hammock activity help with cost control?**
Time-based costs update automatically when the schedule moves, so a slip shows up straight away as a higher forecast cost. See [cost control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-control/).

**Q: How does earned value treat hammock or LOE activities?**
LOE work normally earns value as time passes, so earned value equals planned value and it shows no schedule variance, though it can still show a cost variance. See [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).

# How to Become a Project Manager: Step-by-Step Career Guide

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: A practical route into project management: building experience, learning the basics, choosing a certification, getting your first role and growing your career.


## How to Become a Project Manager: Step-by-Step Career Guide
You become a project manager by combining practical experience of coordinating work with a grounding in project management methods, usually supported by a recognised certification. Many people move in from another role rather than starting in project management directly.
- Published 3 October 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Most project managers move in from another role or start as coordinators.
- Keep a detailed log of every project you run.
- Combine practical evidence with a certification that matches your experience.

### Common entry routes
| Route | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| Accidental PM | You already coordinate projects in your current job and formalise it |
| Coordinator first | Start as a [project coordinator](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-coordinator/) or [assistant project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/assistant-project-manager/) and step up |
| Specialist to PM | Engineers, analysts or designers move into leading projects in their field |
| Graduate scheme | Some employers run project management trainee programmes |
| Career change | Transferable skills from teaching, hospitality, the military or operations |

### Step-by-step plan
1. Learn the fundamentals: [what project management is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/), the [phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/) and core documents.
2. Volunteer to run small projects at work or in the community to build evidence.
3. Keep a log of projects: goal, size, your role, outcome and lessons.
4. Pick an entry-level certification such as the [CAPM](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/), or the PMAI from the Neural Project Institute.
5. Learn a mainstream [project management tool](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-tools/).
6. Rewrite your CV around outcomes delivered, using project language.
7. Apply for coordinator, junior or assistant PM roles, or an internal move.
8. Once you meet the experience requirement, consider the [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

### Worked example: building an experience log
Suppose you are an operations analyst. Over 18 months you lead a supplier switch (4 months, 6 people), a new reporting dashboard (3 months, 3 people) and an office move (2 months, 10 people). Logging each with objectives, budget, risks handled and results gives you strong interview stories and a record you can later use for certification applications.

### Skills employers look for
- Planning and scheduling.
- Clear written and spoken communication.
- Stakeholder management and negotiation.
- Risk and issue management.
- Comfort with budgets and numbers.
- Familiarity with Agile as well as traditional methods; see [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).
See [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/) for detail.

### Mistakes to avoid
- Waiting for a job title before calling yourself experienced: count the projects you have already run.
- Collecting certificates without practical examples to back them up.
- Listing duties on your CV instead of results.
- Ignoring the soft skills that make or break projects.
Tip
To compare pay, look at current job adverts in your area and sector, recent salary surveys from professional bodies such as PMI, and official labour statistics. Figures vary by location and change every year.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Can I become a project manager without a degree?**
Yes. Many project managers do not have a degree. Experience and certification matter more to most employers, though the PMP requires more experience if you do not hold a four-year degree.

**Q: Can I become a project manager with no experience?**
You will usually start in a coordinator or assistant role, or by running small projects in your current job, then step up.

**Q: Which certification should I get first to become a project manager?**
Beginners often start with the CAPM or an entry-level course; experienced practitioners aim for the PMP. See [project management certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/).

**Q: How long does it take to become a project manager?**
It depends on your starting point. People moving from a related role sometimes step up within a year or two; others take longer to build experience.

**Q: Is it worth becoming a project manager?**
It offers transferable skills used in almost every industry and clear progression to senior, programme and portfolio roles.

**Q: How much can you earn once you become a project manager?**
Pay varies by country, industry and seniority. Check current job adverts, PMI salary surveys and government labour statistics for up-to-date figures.

**Q: What does it mean to become a project manager by accident?**
It describes an accidental project manager: someone who ends up running projects as part of another job without formal training.

**Q: Do I need to learn Agile to become a project manager?**
It helps. Many employers expect familiarity with Agile and Scrum alongside traditional methods; see [how to learn Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/).

**Q: What entry-level jobs help you become a project manager?**
Project coordinator, project administrator, PMO analyst, project support officer and assistant project manager.

**Q: Is becoming a project manager a stressful career choice?**
It can be, because you are accountable for outcomes you do not fully control. Good planning, early escalation and clear boundaries help.

# How to Choose Project Management Software: 8 Steps

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: How to choose project management software in 8 steps, with a requirements checklist, weighted scoring matrix, cost worked example and trial plan.


## How to Choose Project Management Software: 8 Steps
To choose project management software, define the problems you need to solve, turn them into prioritised requirements, shortlist three tools, score them with a weighted matrix, trial them on real work and compare the full cost before you commit. This guide walks through each step with worked examples, a requirements checklist, a trial plan and the questions to ask vendors.
- Published 5 October 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Start from today's problems and must-have requirements, not from vendor demos or feature lists.
- Count full users, light users and guests separately: licence types change the price more than the headline rate.
- Score a shortlist of three with a weighted matrix, then trial the top two on a real project for two to four weeks.
- Compare total cost of ownership, including the plan tier that holds your must-haves, set-up, training and admin time.
- In our independent rankings, Wrike is the strongest all-in-one choice for teams that need planning, resources and reporting in one place; lighter tools can suit simpler needs.

### What does choosing project management software involve?
**Choosing project management software** is a structured selection process: you identify what your team needs a tool to do, compare options against those needs, test the best candidates on real work and confirm the total cost before buying. The goal is the best fit for how your team works, not the tool with the longest feature list or the best demo.
It is worth doing properly. Once a team has moved its projects, templates, history and habits into a platform, switching again is slow and disruptive. A tool people find awkward is used half-heartedly, and plans drift back into spreadsheets.
If you are still getting to grips with what these tools do, start with our overview of [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) and the main [types of project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-tools/).

#### How deep should your selection go?
The process below scales. A five-person team can work through it in a fortnight; a regulated enterprise may need a formal procurement with legal and security review.
| Organisation | Typical selection effort | Who is involved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Freelancer or team of 2–10 | 1–2 weeks; free plans and trials, light scoring | Team lead plus one or two users |
| Team or small business of 10–50 | 3–6 weeks; written requirements, weighted scoring, a real trial | Project lead, a few users from each role, whoever pays |
| Department or mid-sized company of 50–500 | 1–3 months; formal requirements, vendor demos, security review | PMO or operations lead, IT, finance, user representatives |
| Enterprise or regulated organisation | 3+ months; RFP, security and legal review, pilot | Procurement, IT security, legal, PMO, executive sponsor |

### How to choose project management software in 8 steps
1. **Define the problems** you need the tool to solve.
2. **Turn them into requirements**, sorted into must-haves, should-haves and could-haves.
3. **Count your users** and the type of access each one needs.
4. **Check integrations, security and IT requirements.**
5. **Build a shortlist of three tools** that meet every must-have.
6. **Score the shortlist** with a weighted matrix.
7. **Run a structured trial** of the top two on real work.
8. **Calculate the total cost**, make the decision and plan the rollout.
Each step is explained below, with a running example: a 25-person marketing and creative team that currently manages work in spreadsheets, email and a shared drive.

### Step 1: Define the problems you need to solve
Begin with what is going wrong today, in plain language. Problems are more useful than features at this stage.
Run a 45-minute session with a few people from each role and ask:
- Where do deadlines slip, and why?
- How do new requests reach the team, and what gets lost?
- How do people know what they should work on next?
- How does the manager see who is overloaded and who has capacity?
- How long does it take to produce a status report?
- Where do reviews and approvals get stuck?
For our example team, the answers point to four core problems: missed launch dates because dependencies are invisible, overloaded designers, approvals buried in email, and requests arriving through every channel at once.
Tip
Write each problem with a measure attached, such as "status reporting takes about four hours a week". You can check the same measures three months after rollout to see whether the tool helped.
A [gap analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gap-analysis-template/) is a simple way to record the current state, the desired state and the gap for each problem.

### Step 2: Turn problems into prioritised requirements
Next, translate each problem into requirements the software must meet. Sort them with a simple **MoSCoW** split: must have, should have, could have (and won't have this time). Keep must-haves short and strict: if a tool fails one, it is out.
| Problem | Requirement | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Launch dates slip because dependencies are invisible | Gantt or timeline view with task dependencies that reschedule automatically | Must |
| Designers are overloaded | Workload view showing each person's assigned effort against capacity | Must |
| Approvals are buried in email | Proofing and approval workflow on files, with comments on the asset | Must |
| Requests arrive through every channel | Request forms that create tasks automatically | Must |
| Status reports take hours | Shareable dashboards that update in real time | Should |
| Work sits in many tools | Integrations with email, chat and file storage | Should |
| Repetitive admin | No-code automations | Could |

#### Typical must-haves by team type
Requirements vary by the kind of work you do. These are common starting points, not a substitute for your own list:
| Team type | Usually must-have | Often should-have |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marketing and creative | Request forms, proofing and approvals, calendar or timeline | Workload, dashboards, asset storage integrations |
| Software development | Scrum or Kanban boards, backlog, sprints, Git integration | Roadmaps, release tracking, bug workflows |
| PMO or professional services | Gantt with dependencies and baselines, resource planning, portfolio views | Time tracking, budgets, advanced reporting |
| Agency or client work | Guest or client access, time tracking, per-client spaces | Proofing, budgets, flat or predictable pricing |
| Operations and internal teams | Task lists, recurring work, simple boards | Forms, automations, Microsoft 365 or Google integration |
Our [project management software features checklist](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software-features/) explains each feature in more depth, and the guide to [project requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/) covers how to write requirements that can be tested.

### Step 3: Count users and licence types
Most project management software is priced per user, so the number and type of users drives cost more than any other factor. List three groups:
- **Full users**: people who create and manage work every day, such as project managers, designers and developers.
- **Light users or collaborators**: people who update their own tasks or comment but do not build projects.
- **Viewers and guests**: executives who only read dashboards, and clients or freelancers outside your organisation.
Vendors handle these groups differently. Some offer cheaper collaborator roles or free viewers; others charge everyone the same seat price; a few, such as Basecamp, charge a flat monthly price rather than per user. Some sell seats in fixed bundles, and some plans have minimum or maximum user counts: Wrike's Team plan, for example, is for 2 to 15 users and its Business plan for 5 to 200 (according to our review data, checked 5 October 2026).
Also estimate growth over the next two years. A plan that fits 12 people today may not fit 20 next year.
Tip
Ask every vendor exactly what a viewer, collaborator or guest can and cannot do. The definitions differ, and they decide how many full licences you really need.

### Step 4: Check integrations, security and IT requirements
A project management tool sits in the middle of your other systems, so check early whether it connects to them and whether your IT team can approve it.

#### Integrations
- Email and calendar (Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace)
- Chat (Slack or Microsoft Teams)
- File storage (OneDrive, SharePoint, Google Drive, Dropbox, Box)
- Development tools (Jira, GitHub, GitLab) if engineers are involved
- CRM, finance or time-tracking systems, if projects are billed to clients
- BI tools, such as Power BI or Tableau, if you report across the business
- An open API or automation platform connector for anything else
Check whether each integration is native, works through a third-party connector or needs a higher plan. For example, our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) notes that its two-way sync and cross-system integration products are included on the top Apex plan and sold as add-ons on other plans.

#### Security and administration checklist
- Single sign-on (SAML SSO) and automatic user provisioning (SCIM), which are often on enterprise tiers only
- Granular permissions, user roles and the ability to lock sensitive projects
- Independent security certifications or audit reports (for example SOC 2 or ISO/IEC 27001) and their scope
- Data residency options and GDPR support, if you hold personal data
- Audit logs and admin controls
- Data export in usable formats if you ever leave
Ask for the vendor's trust or security documentation rather than relying on badges on a marketing page, and let IT review it before the trial, not after you have chosen.

### Step 5: Build a shortlist of three tools
With requirements in hand, filter the market down to three tools that meet every must-have. Three is enough to compare fairly without turning selection into a project of its own.
Use independent rankings and side-by-side comparisons to save time. Our [top 10 project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) are scored on ease of use, feature depth, planning and resource management, collaboration, Agile support, value and scalability. The table below summarises where each tool fits best; prices are starting list prices from our review data (checked 5 October 2026), so confirm current pricing on each vendor's site.
| Our rank | Tool | Best for | Starting price |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (9.4) | [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) | One platform for projects, resources, portfolios, approvals and reporting | Free plan; paid from $10/user/month |
| 2 (9.1) | [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) | Ease of use and visual, flexible workflows | Free for 2 seats; paid from $9/seat/month |
| 3 (9.0) | [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) | Cross-team task and goal management | Free plan; paid from $10.99/user/month |
| 4 (8.9) | [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) | Many features at a lower price | Free plan; paid from $7/user/month |
| 5 (8.6) | [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) | Spreadsheet-style enterprise planning | From $9/member/month (no free plan) |
| 6 (8.6) | [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) | Software and Agile teams | Free for up to 10 users |
| 7 (8.1) | [Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/) | Organisations standardised on Microsoft 365 | Basic Planner included in Microsoft 365 |
