| 10 (7.6) | [Basecamp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/basecamp/) | Calm team and client communication with flat pricing | Free for 1 project; paid from $25/month flat |

#### Shortlist shortcuts by situation
- **You need planning, resource management, approvals and reporting in one system:** start with Wrike, then compare it with monday.com and Asana.
- **Fast adoption by a non-technical team matters most:** monday.com and Asana are the easiest of the full platforms to roll out.
- **Budget is tight but you want many features:** ClickUp offers the most features per dollar in our rankings.
- **You run Scrum or Kanban for software:** Jira is the specialist; see also our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/).
- **Everyone already lives in Microsoft 365:** Microsoft Planner is the natural first look.
For our example team, the must-haves of proofing, workload management, request forms and Gantt dependencies point to a shortlist of **Wrike, monday.com and Asana**. Our head-to-head comparisons of [Wrike vs monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/wrike-vs-monday/), [Wrike vs Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/wrike-vs-asana/) and [monday.com vs Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/monday-vs-asana/) set out the differences in detail, and the [comparison index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/) covers every pair in our top 10.

### Step 6: Score your shortlist with a weighted matrix
A **weighted scoring matrix** stops the loudest opinion or the slickest demo from deciding. You give each criterion a weight that reflects its importance, score each tool against each criterion, multiply and add up.
1. List 6–8 criteria drawn from your must-haves and should-haves, plus ease of use and cost.
2. Give each criterion a weight so that the weights add up to 100.
3. Score each tool from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion, ideally after demos and a first look at the trial.
4. Multiply each score by its weight, add the results and divide by 5 to get a total out of 100.
5. Use the totals to pick the top two for a full trial, not to make the final decision on their own.

#### Worked example: the 25-person marketing team
The scores below are illustrative scores the example team might give after demos; your own will differ. Weighted points = score × weight ÷ 5.
| Criterion | Weight | Wrike | monday.com | Asana |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gantt with dependencies | 20 | 5 (20) | 4 (16) | 4 (16) |
| Workload and resource management | 20 | 5 (20) | 3 (12) | 4 (16) |
| Proofing and approvals | 15 | 5 (15) | 3 (9) | 4 (12) |
| Ease of use and adoption | 15 | 3 (9) | 5 (15) | 5 (15) |
| Integrations | 10 | 4 (8) | 4 (8) | 4 (8) |
| Reporting and dashboards | 10 | 5 (10) | 4 (8) | 4 (8) |
| Cost for 25 users | 10 | 3 (6) | 4 (8) | 3 (6) |
| **Total (out of 100)** | 100 | **88** | **76** | **81** |
Wrike leads because it scores highest on the three heaviest must-have criteria, even though it scores lower on ease of use. monday.com wins ease of use and cost, and Asana sits between the two. The team takes **Wrike and Asana** into the trial. If ease of use had carried a weight of 30 instead of 15, the result would be much closer, which is why agreeing the weights before scoring matters.
Tip
Agree the weights with the team and the budget holder before anyone sees a demo. Changing weights after scoring is the most common way selection processes are quietly bent towards a favourite.

### Step 7: Run a structured trial
A trial is where most selection decisions are really made. Most of the tools in our rankings offer a free plan or a free trial; for example, Wrike offers a 14-day trial without a credit card, and Smartsheet a 30-day trial (from our review data, checked 5 October 2026). Plan the trial so you test real work, not just features.

#### A four-week trial plan
| Week | What to do | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before you start | Pick one live project and 5–8 testers across roles, including one or two sceptics. Ask the vendor for onboarding help. | Trial plan and test scenarios |
| Week 1 | Set up the workspace, import or create the project, build the request form and the workload view. | A realistic set-up, not a demo account |
| Week 2 | Run daily work in the tool: assign tasks, run an approval, handle new requests. | Notes on friction and missing features |
| Week 3 | Test reporting, integrations, mobile, permissions and guest access; produce a real status report from the tool. | Evidence for each must-have |
| Week 4 | Collect scores and feedback; confirm pricing and contract terms. | Completed trial scorecard |

#### Trial scorecard
Ask each tester to rate the tool on the same short set of questions, from 1 to 5:
- How easy was it to find what you needed to work on?
- How easy was it to update your work?
- Did the tool save you time compared with the current way of working?
- Did each must-have work for your real tasks?
- Would you be happy to use it every day?
Combine the testers' average with your matrix scores. If a tool wins on features but testers would not use it every day, take that seriously: adoption is part of fit.
In the example, Wrike's request forms, proofing and workload view handled the team's real campaign well; testers found the interface dense in week one but comfortable by week three once templates were in place. Asana was quicker to learn, but the team needed its Advanced plan for proofing and workload. The team chose Wrike and planned extra onboarding for the first month.

### Step 8: Calculate total cost and make the case
The headline price per user is only part of the cost. **Total cost of ownership (TCO)** includes the plan tier that holds all your must-haves, add-ons, set-up time, training, ongoing administration and any migration help.

#### Worked example: year-one cost for 25 users
Licence prices below are annual-billing list prices from our review data (checked 5 October 2026) for the tier each tool needs to meet the example team's must-haves. Internal time is costed at an assumed $50 an hour; the hours are illustrative estimates.
| Cost item | Wrike Business | monday.com Pro | Asana Advanced |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Licence price | $25/user/month | $19/seat/month | $24.99/user/month |
| Licences: 25 users × 12 months | $7,500 | $5,700 | $7,497 |
| Set-up and configuration (internal time) | 60 hours: $3,000 | 40 hours: $2,000 | 40 hours: $2,000 |
| Training: 25 people × 3 hours | $3,750 | $3,750 | $3,750 |
| Ongoing admin: 2 hours/week × 48 weeks | $4,800 | $4,800 | $4,800 |
| **Year-one total** | **$19,050** | **$16,250** | **$18,047** |
Three lessons come out of this kind of calculation:
- **Internal time often costs more than licences.** In the example, set-up, training and admin are well over half of the year-one total for every tool.
- **The right tier matters more than the entry price.** monday.com's lowest list price is $9 per seat, but the example team priced its Pro plan, and monday.com's fuller resource and portfolio management sits on its quote-based Enterprise plan. Price the tier that includes every must-have.
- **Price differences need context.** Wrike costs about $2,800 more than monday.com in year one in this example. The team judged that worth it for stronger workload management and built-in proofing, which were two of its four must-have problems. Another team could reasonably decide the other way.
Also check add-ons (such as extra AI capacity, whiteboards or integration products), monthly versus annual billing, price increases at renewal, and whether you can reduce seats mid-contract.

#### Making the case to your budget holder
Keep the business case short: the problems from Step 1 with their measures, the weighted scores, the trial feedback, the three-year cost and the rollout plan. Our [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) gives you a ready-made structure.

### Free vs paid project management software
Free plans are useful, but they are designed to let you start, not to run a growing team indefinitely.
|  | Free plans | Paid plans |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Good for | Individuals, very small teams, simple task lists, trying a tool | Teams that need planning, reporting and control |
| Typical limits | Few users, projects, boards or storage; basic views only | Higher or no limits, depending on tier |
| Usually missing | Gantt charts, dashboards, workload, automations, admin controls | Enterprise security and advanced resource or financial features may still need top tiers |
Examples from our review data (checked 5 October 2026): Jira's free plan covers up to 10 users, Trello's up to 10 collaborators per workspace, monday.com's up to 2 seats and Basecamp's one project. If your must-haves include Gantt dependencies, workload views or dashboards, you will almost certainly need a paid plan, so trial that tier rather than judging the tool by its free version.

### Questions to ask vendors
Use demos and sales calls to fill gaps your trial cannot answer. Ask for answers in writing, especially on pricing and contract terms. For a formal process, a [request for quote (RFQ) template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/rfq-template/) keeps vendor responses comparable.
- Which plan includes each of our must-have features, and which are add-ons?
- How are full users, collaborators, viewers and guests defined and priced?
- Are there minimum or maximum user numbers, or seat bundles, on each plan?
- What limits apply to automations, storage and AI usage on each plan?
- Which integrations are native, and which need a third-party connector?
- What security certifications and audit reports can you share, and where is our data stored?
- What onboarding, training and support are included, and what costs extra?
- How do price increases at renewal work, and can we reduce seats mid-term?
- How can we export all our data, including attachments and history, if we leave?

### Rolling out your new project management tool
Selection is only half the job. A careful rollout is what turns a good choice into a tool people actually use.
1. **Appoint an owner and champions.** One person owns the set-up and standards; a champion in each team answers day-to-day questions.
2. **Design a simple structure.** Agree spaces or workspaces, project templates, statuses and a handful of custom fields before importing anything.
3. **Migrate selectively.** Move active projects and templates; archive finished work in the old system or as exports rather than migrating everything.
4. **Pilot with one team.** Run two to four weeks with a single team, fix what does not work, then roll out in waves.
5. **Train by role.** Short, role-specific sessions work better than one long general demo. A [training plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) helps you schedule them.
6. **Switch off the old way.** Set a date after which status reports, requests and approvals happen only in the new tool.
7. **Review after 90 days.** Re-measure the problems from Step 1 and adjust templates, automations and permissions.

### Common mistakes and red flags

#### Common mistakes
- **Choosing on demos.** A demo shows the vendor's best case; a trial with your real work shows yours.
- **Buying for the most advanced user.** A tool configured for the most demanding person can overwhelm everyone else; use templates and permissions to keep views simple.
- **Comparing entry prices instead of the right tier.** Must-have features often sit one or two tiers above the headline price.
- **No owner after go-live.** Without someone maintaining templates and standards, every team sets the tool up differently.

#### Red flags during selection
- Testers keep returning to spreadsheets or chat during the trial.
- The vendor cannot say clearly which plan includes a must-have feature.
- Exporting your data is difficult or incomplete.
- Pricing depends on bundles or limits you only discover late in the process.

### Next steps
Write down your problems and must-haves this week, then use our rankings to build a shortlist. Start with our [top 10 project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/), where Wrike ranks first as the strongest all-in-one platform.
To check the differences between two shortlisted tools, use our [project management tool comparisons](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/).
If AI features are on your requirements list, see our guide to [AI project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/ai-project-management-tools/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: How do I choose the right project management software?**
Define the problems you need to solve, turn them into must-have and nice-to-have requirements, shortlist three tools, score them with a weighted matrix, trial the top two on real work, then compare total cost and plan the rollout.

**Q: What are the most important features to look for?**
It depends on your work, but most teams need task management, several views (list, board, timeline or Gantt), collaboration on tasks, dashboards, integrations and sensible permissions. Resource management, proofing and time tracking matter for specific teams.

**Q: What is the best project management software?**
There is no single best tool for everyone. In our independent rankings, Wrike scores highest overall (9.4/10) as the strongest all-in-one platform, followed by monday.com and Asana. The best choice for you is the one that meets your must-haves and passes a real trial.

**Q: How much does project management software cost?**
Paid plans from the tools in our rankings typically range from about $5 to $30 per user per month on annual billing, with enterprise plans priced on quote. Basecamp is an exception with flat monthly pricing. Always add set-up, training and admin time.

**Q: Is free project management software good enough?**
For individuals, small teams and simple task lists, often yes. Free plans usually limit users, projects or storage and leave out Gantt charts, dashboards, workload views and admin controls that growing teams need.

**Q: How long should a project management software trial last?**
Long enough to run real work through the tool, typically two to four weeks. Many vendors offer 14- or 30-day trials; ask for an extension if your project needs longer.

**Q: What is a weighted scoring matrix?**
A table that lists your selection criteria, gives each one a weight reflecting its importance, scores each tool against each criterion and multiplies the scores by the weights to produce a comparable total.

**Q: Which project management software suits Agile teams?**
Jira is the specialist choice for software teams running Scrum or Kanban. ClickUp and Wrike suit teams that mix Agile work with other kinds of projects.

**Q: Which project management software suits small businesses?**
Small businesses often start with an easy tool and a free or low-cost plan, such as Trello, Asana, monday.com or ClickUp, or Basecamp for flat pricing. If you expect to need resource planning and reporting as you grow, include Wrike in the trial.

**Q: Should IT be involved in choosing project management software?**
Yes, from the start. IT should check single sign-on, security certifications, data storage, integrations and data export before the trial, so a late objection does not overturn your choice.

**Q: How do I get my team to adopt new project management software?**
Involve users in the trial, start with simple templates, train by role, appoint champions in each team and set a date after which work is managed only in the new tool.

# Integrated Master Plan (IMP): IMS, Structure and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/integrated-master-plan/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Integrated master plan (IMP) explained: events, accomplishments and criteria, IMP vs IMS, numbering, a step-by-step method and a worked example.


## Integrated Master Plan (IMP): IMS, Structure and Example
An integrated master plan (IMP) is an event-based plan that defines a programme's major events, the accomplishments each event needs and the criteria that prove each accomplishment is complete. Its time-based companion, the integrated master schedule (IMS), adds the detailed tasks, durations and logic. This guide explains how both work, how to write and number an IMP, and walks through a worked example from plan to schedule.
- Published 21 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- An IMP has three levels: events, accomplishments and criteria. It describes what "done" looks like, not when each task happens.
- The IMS adds a fourth level, tasks, with durations, dependencies and dates, so it can show the critical path.
- On US defence contracts the approved IMP generally becomes part of the contract; the IMS usually does not, because its dates change.
- IMP items are written in the past tense ("Design review completed"); IMS tasks start with an action verb ("Develop", "Test").
- The IMP and IMS trace to the work breakdown structure, the statement of work and earned value control accounts.
- The event-based idea is useful on any large, multi-team project, even without a formal IMP.

### What is an integrated master plan?
An **integrated master plan (IMP)** is an event-based, hierarchical plan made up of programme events, the accomplishments that must be achieved by each event, and the criteria that provide objective evidence each accomplishment is complete. It answers "what does done look like at each review?" and forms the framework for the integrated master schedule.
The IMP is deliberately not a schedule. It contains no task durations or dependencies, and any dates in it are usually for information only. That is its strength: it fixes the logic of progress (you cannot hold the critical design review until the detailed design is finished and its evidence exists) independently of the dates, which will move.
Three ideas sum it up:
- **Event-driven, not calendar-driven.** A review happens when its entry criteria are met, not because a date has arrived.
- **Evidence-based.** Each accomplishment has measurable criteria, such as an approved document or a passed test, rather than a percentage complete.
- **Integrated.** It brings engineering, manufacturing, test, logistics and management work into one plan, traced to the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) and contract requirements.

### Where IMPs are used and the guidance behind them
The IMP and IMS come from US Department of Defense (DoD) acquisition, where they are used on major development and production contracts, often alongside earned value management. They also appear on other government, aerospace and large engineering programmes, especially those with several contractors.
The current reference is the *Integrated Master Plan and Integrated Master Schedule Preparation and Use Guide* published by the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering (OUSD(R&E)) in May 2023, with Change 1 dated 1 October 2024. It replaced the DoD guide of October 2005, which many older articles still cite. This page follows the 2023 guide; if your contract names a specific version or customer guidance, that takes precedence.
Tip
"Integrated master plan" is also used by city and regional governments for long-term public works plans (water, wastewater, transport). Those are strategic infrastructure plans, not the event-based programme plan described here.
If you work in the public sector, see our guide to [government project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/government-project-management/) for the wider context of contracts, oversight and reporting.

### The three levels of an IMP
| Level | What it is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Event | A programme assessment point at the end of significant activities, usually a major review or decision | Critical design review (CDR) completed |
| Accomplishment | A result that must be achieved before or at the event, showing progress | Software design completed |
| Criteria | Definitive, measurable evidence that the accomplishment is complete | Software design description baselined |
Older guidance and many contracts call accomplishments **significant accomplishments (SAs)** and criteria **accomplishment criteria (ACs)**. The 2023 guide uses the shorter names; the meaning is the same.

#### Events
Events are the big checkpoints: design reviews, test readiness reviews, production readiness reviews, first deliveries and acceptance. An event is achieved only when all its accomplishments are complete. There is no required number of events; choose the points where the customer and contractor genuinely need to assess progress and decide whether to proceed. These are often the programme's key [project milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/).

#### Accomplishments
Accomplishments describe the state the programme must reach for the event to succeed: a design finished, a test facility ready, a supplier qualified, risks assessed. The guide says an event normally has two or more accomplishments. Accomplishments often cut across teams, which is what makes the plan integrated.

#### Criteria
Criteria are the proof. Each one should be a yes/no test that an independent reviewer could check: a document approved, an analysis delivered, a test passed. The guide says there are generally at least two criteria per accomplishment, though one may be enough. Criteria can be:
- **Entry criteria:** what must be ready before a review, test or demonstration can start.
- **Exit criteria:** what shows the event itself has succeeded, such as review actions closed.

### IMP numbering and wording rules
A consistent numbering scheme lets every IMS task trace back to the criterion, accomplishment and event it supports. The 2023 guide's examples use a hierarchical alphanumeric scheme:
| Level | Format | Example ID | Example name |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Event | Letter | C | Critical design review completed |
| Accomplishment | Event letter + two digits | C02 | Software design completed |
| Criterion | Accomplishment + lower-case letter | C02a | Software design description baselined |
| IMS task | Criterion + two digits | C02a01 | Develop software architecture |
Some programmes use separators (C.02.a); either way, keep one scheme across the whole programme, give each sub-plan a unique sequence and let the scheduling tool generate the numbers where possible.

#### How to word IMP items and IMS tasks
The guide sets a simple grammar. IMP items describe a finished state, so they use **past participles**: completed, approved, conducted, delivered. IMS tasks describe work, so they **start with an imperative verb**: develop, perform, test, deliver. Define each verb once in an **Event and Action Dictionary** so that "approved" or "verified" means the same thing to everyone.
| Item | Weak wording | Better wording |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Event | CDR | Critical design review completed |
| Accomplishment | Work on hardware design | Detailed hardware design completed |
| Criterion | Thermal analysis 90% done | Thermal analysis report approved by chief engineer |
| IMS task | Thermal analysis | Perform thermal analysis of display unit |

### IMP vs IMS
The IMP and IMS are two views of the same plan. The IMP is the top-down, event-based framework; the IMS is the bottom-up, time-based schedule that shows how and when the work behind each criterion gets done.
|  | Integrated master plan (IMP) | Integrated master schedule (IMS) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basis | Events and the evidence needed for them | Tasks with durations and dependencies |
| Levels | Events, accomplishments, criteria | The same three, plus tasks (and often work packages) |
| Question answered | What must be achieved, and how will we prove it? | When will it happen, and what drives the date? |
| Dates | None, or for information only | Calculated from logic; baselined and updated |
| Contract status (DoD) | Generally part of the contract once approved | Usually a data deliverable, not contractually binding |
| Changes | Rarely; through contract change | Every status update |
| Main users | Programme leadership, customer, contract managers | Planners, control account managers, team leads |
In the IMS, every event, accomplishment and criterion appears as a milestone, worded exactly as in the IMP. Tasks sit beneath the criteria, linked by finish-to-start logic, so the schedule shows which criterion is late and which event it threatens. Read our guide to [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) for the general scheduling process.

### How the IMP and IMS connect to the WBS, SOW and EVM
Traceability is what makes the IMP "integrated". Each element links to the documents that define and measure the work:
| Document | What it defines | How it links to the IMP/IMS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Statement of work (SOW) | The work the contractor must do | Every SOW task should be covered by at least one IMS task |
| Work breakdown structure (WBS) | The product-oriented breakdown of the deliverables | Accomplishments, criteria and tasks carry WBS codes; WBS is the foundation of both |
| Organisation breakdown structure (OBS) | Who is responsible | Assigns each task and control account to a team |
| Control accounts and work packages | Where budget and progress are managed | IMS tasks roll up to work packages and control accounts |
| Earned value management (EVM) | Cost and schedule performance | The IMS provides the time-phasing and status for earned value |
| Risk register | Threats and opportunities | Risk responses appear as IMS tasks; risks are reviewed at events |
The WBS and IMP give two complementary views: the WBS shows **what** is being produced, the IMP shows **how maturity is proven** over time. Work packages are where they meet; see our guide to the [work package](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/) and the [statement of work](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/).
See our guide to [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) for how the IMS time-phasing feeds cost and schedule performance indices.

### What an IMP document contains
The 2023 guide describes four main parts:
1. **Introduction:** a short programme description, assumptions and ground rules, the Event and Action Dictionary, the programme organisation and reference documents.
2. **IMP table:** the numbering scheme, event descriptions and the full hierarchy of events, accomplishments and criteria, usually as a table.
3. **Narratives:** brief descriptions of key processes, such as systems engineering, risk management or configuration management, where the customer needs them.
4. **Glossary:** terms and abbreviations.
Because the approved IMP generally becomes contractual, the guide advises keeping narratives concise: anything written there can bind the contractor and reduce flexibility. Put detailed process descriptions in management plans that can be updated without a contract change.

### How to create an integrated master plan step by step
The guide's steps for an IMP fit inside a wider sequence that ends with a baselined IMS. In practice:
1. **Read the requirements.** Start from the statement of work or statement of objectives, the contract data requirements and any customer IMP guidance.
2. **Build or adopt the WBS.** Agree the product-oriented [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) first; the IMP will be coded to it.
3. **Select the events.** Choose the major reviews and decision points, usually from the programme's life cycle (requirements, preliminary design, critical design, test readiness, production, delivery).
4. **Define accomplishments for each event.** Ask each team what must be true for the event to succeed. Aim for two or more per event, covering every discipline involved.
5. **Write criteria for each accomplishment.** Make each one measurable and evidence-based; include entry criteria for reviews and exit criteria where needed.
6. **Write the introduction, dictionary and any narratives.** Define every action verb you use.
7. **Apply the numbering scheme** and check every item has a WBS code and an owner.
8. **Iterate with the IMS.** As teams build tasks beneath each criterion, gaps and overlaps appear. Adjust the IMP until every SOW requirement traces to a task and every task traces to a criterion.
9. **Review and approve.** The customer reviews the IMP, often as part of proposal evaluation, and the agreed version is incorporated into the contract.
Tip
Write accomplishments with the people who will do the work. An IMP drafted by planners alone tends to describe documents rather than the engineering maturity that the customer actually needs to see.

### Worked example: IMP for an avionics display upgrade
This illustrative example follows a contractor upgrading the cockpit display units on a fleet of transport aircraft. The programme has five events:
| ID | Event |
| --- | --- |
| A | System requirements review completed |
| B | Preliminary design review completed |
| C | Critical design review completed |
| D | Test readiness review completed |
| E | First production units delivered |

#### Event C in detail
Here is the IMP for event C, showing four accomplishments and their criteria:
| ID | IMP item | WBS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C | **Critical design review completed** | 1.0 |
| C01 | Detailed hardware design completed | 1.1 |
| C01a | Circuit card assembly drawings released | 1.1.2 |
| C01b | Thermal analysis report approved | 1.1.3 |
| C02 | Software design completed | 1.2 |
| C02a | Software design description baselined | 1.2.1 |
| C02b | Interface control documents signed | 1.2.2 |
| C03 | Verification planning completed | 1.4 |
| C03a | System test plan approved | 1.4.1 |
| C03b | Test equipment requirements defined | 1.4.2 |
| C04 | Programme risks and estimates updated | 1.6 |
| C04a | Risk register updated with design risks | 1.6.3 |
| C04b | Estimate to complete updated and reviewed | 1.6.1 |
Notice that the accomplishments span hardware, software, test and management. Event C cannot be declared complete because the hardware team is ready; all four accomplishments, and all eight criteria, must be met.

#### From IMP to IMS: tasks under accomplishment C02
The software team now plans the tasks behind C02. Durations are in working days and day 0 is the day after event B completes.
| ID | Task or milestone | Duration | Predecessor | Start | Finish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C02a01 | Develop software architecture | 15 | B | 0 | 15 |
| C02a02 | Draft software design description | 20 | C02a01 | 15 | 35 |
| C02a03 | Conduct software design peer review | 5 | C02a02 | 35 | 40 |
| C02a04 | Incorporate comments and baseline design description | 5 | C02a03 | 40 | 45 |
| C02a | Software design description baselined (milestone) | 0 | C02a04 | 45 | 45 |
| C02b01 | Draft interface control documents | 20 | C02a01 | 15 | 35 |
| C02b02 | Hold interface working group with hardware team | 3 | C02b01 | 35 | 38 |
| C02b03 | Obtain interface control document signatures | 5 | C02b02 | 38 | 43 |
| C02b | Interface control documents signed (milestone) | 0 | C02b03 | 43 | 43 |
| C02 | Software design completed (milestone) | 0 | C02a, C02b | 45 | 45 |
Working through the result:
- Accomplishment C02 is achieved on day 45, driven by the design description path (C02a01, C02a02, C02a03, C02a04).
- The interface path finishes on day 43, so it has 2 days of [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) relative to C02.
- Every task is under 44 days, so none would be flagged as a long-duration task in a DCMA-style check.
- If the peer review (C02a03) slips by 3 days, C02 moves to day 48, and the planner can see immediately that event C is threatened, not just a software task.
The same pattern repeats for every criterion. Once all tasks are linked, the IMS calculates the date for event C and the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) through the whole programme.

### Building the IMS from the IMP
The 2023 guide sets out the IMS steps: determine objectives from the SOW, create the WBS, develop the IMP, define the OBS, then develop the IMS by defining tasks, resources and milestones, building and validating the network logic, setting the baseline, identifying the critical path and planning status reporting. The scheduling practices it recommends are the same ones that make any schedule reliable:
| Practice | Guidance |
| --- | --- |
| Relationships | Prefer finish-to-start; use finish-to-finish sparingly; never use start-to-finish |
| Leads | Avoid leads (negative lags); see our guide to [leads and lags](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/) |
| Constraints | Hard constraints are highly discouraged; document any constraint other than as soon as possible |
| Durations | Review tasks longer than 44 days, which DCMA treats as long-duration, and break them down where practical |
| Critical path | Only one critical path at a time; validate tool-generated paths for gaps caused by lags, constraints or calendars |
| Dates | IMS dates are forecasts, not due dates; events happen when their criteria are met |
| Analysis | Support filtering by WBS, team or control account, and allow what-if analysis without changing the master schedule |
Every task needs at least one predecessor and one successor, using sound [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/). Once the logic is validated, set the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) and change it only through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).

### Tracking progress with the IMP and IMS
During delivery the two documents do different jobs:
- **Event reviews use the IMP.** At each event the customer checks every criterion. If the evidence is not there, the event is not complete, whatever the schedule says.
- **Status updates use the IMS.** Teams report actual starts, finishes and remaining durations, and the IMS recalculates forecast dates, float and the critical path.
- **Earned value uses both.** The IMS time-phases the budget; completed criteria provide objective evidence for earned value claims.
- **Schedule risk analysis uses the IMS.** Adding three-point durations lets you run a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) to estimate the confidence of meeting each event. The guide warns that without accurate logic, the critical path and any statistical analysis are suspect.
On US defence contracts, IMS data is usually delivered under the Integrated Program Management Data and Analysis Report (IPMDAR) data item, DI-MGMT-81861. According to Humphreys & Associates, this superseded the stand-alone IMS data item, DI-MGMT-81650. Check your contract data requirements list for the exact version and format required. Risks found at reviews feed your wider [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) process.

### Using an IMP outside defence
You do not need a government contract to benefit from event-based planning. On any large project with several teams or suppliers, a light version of the IMP gives sponsors a clear answer to "how will we know we are ready?". This illustrative example is for a hospital replacing its patient records system:
| ID | Event, accomplishment or criterion |
| --- | --- |
| A | Design approved |
| A01 | Clinical workflows agreed |
| A01a | Workflow designs signed off by clinical leads for all wards in scope |
| A02 | Data migration approach agreed |
| A02a | Migration test 1 completed with reconciliation report approved |
| B | Go-live readiness confirmed |
| B01 | Staff trained |
| B01a | Training completion at or above the agreed threshold for every ward |
| B02 | Cutover rehearsed |
| B02a | Full dress rehearsal completed and rollback timed |
Use the events as stage gates in your [project roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-roadmap/) and the criteria as go/no-go checklists. The tasks can live in an ordinary schedule; the free [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) and [work breakdown structure template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) are enough for a first version.

#### Software for IMP-style planning
Formal defence IMSs are normally built in dedicated scheduling software and delivered in the format the contract specifies. For lighter use, a work management tool with proper scheduling works well. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, is a strong option for multi-team, date-driven programmes: its Gantt charts (from the Team plan) support all four dependency types, the critical path, float and baselines, and milestones can carry the IMP numbering in their names. [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) offers dependencies and the critical path on a familiar grid, and [Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/) Plan 3 adds baselines and the critical path for teams already using Microsoft 365.

### Who does what on an IMP and IMS
Because the IMP and IMS span the whole programme, responsibilities need to be clear from the start. A typical split on a large contract looks like this:
| Role | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Customer programme office | Sets requirements and IMP guidance, evaluates the IMP in the proposal, approves it and runs event reviews |
| Contractor programme manager | Owns the IMP, agrees events with the customer and decides when the programme is ready for each event |
| Integrated product team (IPT) leads | Write the accomplishments and criteria for their area and plan the tasks beneath them |
| Planners and schedulers | Maintain numbering, build and validate the IMS logic, run critical path and schedule risk analysis |
| Control account managers | Link IMS tasks to work packages and budgets, and report earned value |
| Systems engineering lead | Checks that events and criteria reflect real technical maturity and trace to requirements |
This is a programme-level way of working. If you are unsure where project management ends and programme management begins, see our comparison of [programme, project and portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/program-vs-project-vs-portfolio-management/). Our guide to [engineering project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/engineering-project-management/) covers the design review cycle that most IMP events are built around.

### IMP review checklist
Before you submit an IMP, or approve one as the customer, work through these checks:
1. **Coverage:** every SOW requirement and WBS element is covered by at least one criterion.
2. **Events:** each event is a real decision point, with two or more accomplishments spanning the disciplines involved.
3. **Criteria:** each criterion is a yes/no test with named evidence (a document, approval, test result or delivery) and is not expressed as a percentage.
4. **Wording:** IMP items use past participles, every verb is defined in the Event and Action Dictionary, and the IMS milestones repeat the IMP wording exactly.
5. **Numbering:** IDs follow one scheme, are unique and carry WBS codes.
6. **Dates:** any dates in the IMP are marked as information only.
7. **Narratives:** process narratives are short and do not commit the contractor to more than the contract requires.
8. **Schedule link:** every criterion has tasks beneath it in the IMS, and the IMS logic produces a credible date for every event.

### Benefits and limitations
| Benefits | Limitations |
| --- | --- |
| Defines progress by evidence, not by elapsed time or percentage complete | Takes significant effort to build and maintain on large programmes |
| Gives customer and contractor a shared, contractual view of what each event requires | Contractual status makes changes slow; over-detailed IMPs reduce flexibility |
| Integrates all disciplines, so no team can declare an event complete alone | Can become a documentation exercise if criteria describe paperwork rather than maturity |
| Traces every task to a requirement and every requirement to a task | Needs disciplined numbering and tooling to keep traceability intact |
| Provides a solid structure for earned value and schedule risk analysis | Adds little value on small or single-team projects |

### Common IMP and IMS mistakes
- **Treating the IMP as a schedule.** Putting firm dates in the IMP invites contract changes every time the schedule moves. Keep dates in the IMS.
- **Vague criteria.** "Design 90% complete" cannot be verified. Use approvals, releases, test results and signed documents.
- **Activity-based accomplishments.** "Work on software" describes effort, not a result. Write the state you will reach.
- **Broken traceability.** Tasks with no criterion, or SOW requirements with no task, mean the plan is incomplete.
- **Inconsistent wording.** IMS milestones must match IMP wording exactly, or reviewers cannot trace them.
- **Poor schedule logic.** Missing links, hard constraints and leads distort float and the critical path.
- **Over-long narratives.** Detailed process text in a contractual document limits how you can improve the process later.
- **Declaring events on date.** Holding a review because the date arrived, with criteria unmet, defeats the purpose of event-based planning.
Read our guide to the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) to check that the IMS logic behind your events is sound.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an integrated master plan (IMP)?**
An event-based plan made up of programme events, the accomplishments needed for each event and the criteria that prove each accomplishment is complete. It provides the framework for the integrated master schedule.

**Q: What is an integrated master schedule (IMS)?**
A networked, time-based schedule that adds detailed tasks, durations and dependencies beneath the IMP's events, accomplishments and criteria, so forecast dates and the critical path can be calculated.

**Q: What is the difference between an IMP and an IMS?**
The IMP defines what must be achieved and how it will be proven; the IMS shows how and when the work will be done. The IMP rarely changes, while the IMS is updated at every status cycle.

**Q: What are the three elements of an IMP?**
Events, accomplishments (formerly called significant accomplishments) and criteria (formerly called accomplishment criteria).

**Q: Is the IMP a contractual document?**
On US defence contracts, the approved contractor IMP generally becomes part of the contract. The IMS is usually delivered as data and is not contractually binding, because its dates change.

**Q: Does an IMP include dates?**
Usually not, or only for information. Dates, durations and logic belong in the IMS.

**Q: How is an IMP numbered?**
Typically hierarchically: events use a letter (C), accomplishments add two digits (C02), criteria add a lower-case letter (C02a) and IMS tasks add two more digits (C02a01).

**Q: How should IMP items be worded?**
IMP items use past participles to describe a finished state, such as "Design review completed". IMS tasks start with an imperative verb, such as "Develop" or "Test".

**Q: How does the IMP relate to the WBS?**
The WBS is the foundation. IMP items and IMS tasks carry WBS codes, and IMS tasks roll up to work packages and control accounts.

**Q: Who prepares the IMP and IMS?**
Usually the contractor, often as part of the proposal, with the customer reviewing and approving the IMP before it is incorporated into the contract.

**Q: Is the IMS used for earned value management?**
Yes. The IMS time-phases the work and budget, and completed criteria provide objective evidence for earned value.

**Q: Which guide covers IMP and IMS preparation?**
The OUSD(R&E) Integrated Master Plan and Integrated Master Schedule Preparation and Use Guide, May 2023, with Change 1 dated 1 October 2024. It replaced the 2005 DoD guide.

**Q: Can I use an IMP on a non-defence project?**
Yes, in a lighter form. Event-based milestones with evidence-based criteria work well on any large, multi-team project, even without the full contractual apparatus.

# Issue Log: Template, Examples and How to Manage Issues

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What an issue log is, the columns to include, a worked example, priority and escalation rules, and how it differs from a risk register and RAID log.


## Issue Log: Template, Examples and How to Manage Issues
An issue log is the single record a project keeps of problems, concerns and requests that are affecting it now, with a priority, an owner, agreed actions and a status for each one. Kept well, it means nothing raised is forgotten and every issue is resolved, escalated or closed on purpose. This guide covers the columns to use, how to prioritise and escalate, a worked example from capture to closure and a full sample log.
- Published 1 October 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- An issue is something that is happening now or is certain to happen; a risk is something that might happen. Keep them in different places, or clearly typed in one RAID log.
- Every entry needs a factual description, an impact, a priority, one named owner, a next action with a date and a status.
- Define priority levels in plain terms (for example, 'critical' means critical-path work has stopped) so two people would rate the same issue the same way.
- Escalate by rule, not by feel: when resolving the issue would breach an agreed time, cost or scope tolerance, or needs a decision above your authority.
- If fixing an issue would change the scope, schedule or cost baseline, raise a change request and link it to the issue.
- Review the log every week, report the high-priority items and their age, and mine closed issues for lessons learned.

### What is an issue log?
An **issue log** is a project document that records every current issue (a problem, concern, query or request already affecting the project) together with its impact, priority, owner, agreed actions, target date and status. Its purpose is to make sure each issue is visible, has someone responsible for it and reaches a deliberate outcome: resolved, escalated or closed.
The log is usually a table: one row per issue, one column per piece of information. It can live in a spreadsheet, a shared document or a project management tool. What matters is that there is only one log for the project and that everyone knows where it is.
The term is used in the PMBOK Guide, where the issue log is one of the project documents updated throughout execution. PRINCE2 uses the name **issue register** for formally managed issues. Both mean essentially the same thing. Some organisations call it an issue tracker or issues list.

#### What counts as an issue
An issue is anything that is already affecting the project, or is certain to, and needs someone to act or decide. PRINCE2 7 describes issues very broadly, as anything that could affect the project, and groups them into a few types that are useful on any project:
| Type | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem | Something has gone wrong or is blocking work | The test environment has been down for two days |
| Concern | A stakeholder is worried about something and wants it addressed | The finance director doubts the new invoice layout meets audit rules |
| Off-specification | A deliverable does not meet, or will not meet, its agreed requirements | 2,000 printed labels carry the old logo |
| Request for change | Someone wants a baseline (scope, requirements, dates) changed | Marketing asks for a second language on the website |
| Opportunity | Something certain and beneficial that was not in the plan | A supplier offers to deliver a week early at no extra cost |
Many teams record requests for change in a separate change log and handle them through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/). That is fine, as long as the issue log points to the change request when an issue leads to one.

#### What does not belong in the issue log
- **Risks:** uncertain future events belong in the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) until they happen.
- **Routine tasks:** "Send the weekly report" is a task, not an issue. Put it in the plan or an action list.
- **Every individual bug:** product defects are normally tracked in a defect or bug tracker. Log a defect as a project issue only when it threatens a milestone, the budget or acceptance.
- **Decisions already made:** record these in a decision log. The issue log can reference the decision that resolved an issue.

### Why keep an issue log?
Problems surface on every project. Whether a project recovers usually depends on whether they are written down, owned and followed up. An issue log gives you:
- **Visibility:** one place where the project manager, team and sponsor can see what is going wrong and how serious it is.
- **Accountability:** each issue has a single owner and a date, so issues do not sit unanswered in email threads.
- **Faster decisions:** with impact and options recorded, the person who needs to decide can do so quickly.
- **Patterns:** several issues with the same cause point to a deeper problem worth analysing with a [fishbone diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/) or root cause analysis.
- **Lessons learned:** closed issues are the most honest record of what went wrong and are a strong input to [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).

### Issue log vs risk register, change log and other logs
Most confusion about issue logs comes from mixing up issues with the other things a project tracks. Use this table to decide where an item belongs.
| Item | Definition | Question it answers | Where it is recorded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Issue | A current problem, concern or request that needs action | What is wrong now and who is fixing it? | Issue log |
| Risk | An uncertain event that might affect objectives | What might happen and what will we do about it? | [Risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) |
| Change request | A formal proposal to change an agreed baseline | Should we change scope, time or cost? | Change log, through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) |
| Defect | A fault in a product or deliverable | What does not work as specified? | Defect or bug tracker |
| Action | A task agreed in a meeting | Who will do what by when? | Action log or meeting notes |
| Decision | A choice made by someone with authority | What was decided, by whom and why? | Decision log |

#### When a risk becomes an issue
If a risk occurs, it is no longer uncertain, so it becomes an issue. Close the risk in the register with a status such as "occurred", open a new entry in the issue log, and put each ID in the other entry so the link is clear. If a [contingency plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) was prepared for that risk, the first action on the issue is usually to trigger it.

#### When an issue becomes a change request
Some issues can only be fixed by changing what was agreed: extra scope, a later date or more money. At that point the issue owner (often with the project manager) raises a change request and the decision moves into change control. The issue stays open, with status "escalated" or "awaiting decision", until the change is approved or rejected. This keeps the trail from problem to decision intact. A useful test from PRINCE2 7 guidance is that an issue only becomes a change once you know it will affect a baseline.

#### Issue log vs RAID log
A [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) combines Risks, Assumptions, Issues and Dependencies in one table, with a type column. It suits small and medium projects where one view is easier to review. Larger projects, or projects with many issues, usually keep a dedicated issue log with more columns and report a RAID summary to the sponsor.

### What to include in an issue log (columns)
Start with the core columns below. They are enough for most projects, and adding more before you need them only makes the log harder to keep current.
| Column | What to record | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ID | A unique reference that never changes or gets reused | I-014 |
| Title | A short label, five to eight words | Refund tests blocked by sandbox error |
| Date raised | When the issue was logged | 3 March 2026 |
| Raised by | Who reported it, so you can confirm closure with them | Test lead |
| Type | Problem, concern, off-specification, request for change, opportunity | Problem |
| Description | What is wrong, where, the evidence and the consequence | Payment sandbox returns error 500 on all refund calls since 2 March; 14 of 60 test cases blocked |
| Impact | Effect on time, cost, scope, quality or benefits | System testing finish date at risk by up to 5 days |
| Priority | Critical, high, medium or low, using agreed definitions | High |
| Owner | One named person responsible for resolving it | Integration lead |
| Next action and date | The next concrete step and when it is due | Raise ticket with provider; follow up 5 March |
| Target resolution date | When it should be resolved | 7 March 2026 |
| Status | Open, in progress, escalated, on hold, resolved, closed | In progress |
| Resolution and date closed | What was done and when it was confirmed closed | Provider fixed config; all 14 tests passed 6 March |

#### Optional columns for larger projects
- **Category or workstream:** technical, supplier, people, environment, stakeholder; useful for spotting patterns.
- **Severity and urgency** as separate fields, if you calculate priority from them (see below).
- **Escalated to and date:** who now holds the decision.
- **Linked items:** risk ID, change request ID, defect ID, affected milestone or work package.
- **Root cause:** completed on closure; this is what makes the log useful for lessons learned.

#### How to write a good issue description
A good description lets someone who was not in the room understand the issue and judge its priority. Use three parts: the **condition** (what is happening), the **evidence** (how you know) and the **consequence** (what it is doing to the project).
| Weak | Strong |
| --- | --- |
| Supplier problems | Supplier has delivered 300 of 1,000 chairs due on 10 June; remaining 700 now promised for 24 June, after the office opening on 17 June |
| Testing delayed | UAT cannot start: 6 of 9 test users have not received system access; access requests raised 28 May, still pending with IT security |
Tip
Keep descriptions factual and free of blame. Write about the situation, not the person. People stop raising issues quickly if the log becomes a record of who to blame.

### How to prioritise issues
Priority decides what gets attention first, so it is worth agreeing the definitions at the start of the project and writing them at the top of the log. A practical approach is to rate two things separately and combine them:
- **Severity:** how much damage the issue does, or will do, to objectives if nothing changes.
- **Urgency:** how soon that damage happens, or how soon a decision is needed.
|  | Urgency: needs action within days | Urgency: needs action within weeks | Urgency: can wait |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Severity: high** (milestone, budget or acceptance threatened) | Critical | High | Medium |
| **Severity: medium** (workaround exists, some delay or extra cost) | High | Medium | Low |
| **Severity: low** (minor inconvenience) | Medium | Low | Low |
Then define what each priority means in practice, and how quickly it should be handled. The response times below are our suggestions; adjust them to your project's length and governance.
| Priority | Plain-language definition | First response | Review |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Critical | Critical-path work has stopped, a key milestone or legal requirement will be missed, or cost overrun exceeds tolerance | Same day; sponsor informed | Daily until resolved |
| High | A milestone or the budget is threatened, or a major deliverable will fail acceptance without action | Within 2 working days | At least twice a week |
| Medium | Work is slowed or extra effort is needed, but a workaround exists and no milestone is at risk yet | Within 1 week | Weekly |
| Low | Minor inconvenience; can be fixed when convenient | When capacity allows | Weekly or fortnightly |

#### Priority vs severity
Severity describes how bad the effect is; priority describes the order in which you will deal with it. A severe issue that will not bite for two months can be lower priority than a medium issue blocking today's work. Recording both helps explain your choices to stakeholders.

### Issue statuses and what they mean
Statuses only help if everyone uses them the same way. Agree a short list with clear entry and exit rules:
| Status | Means | Moves on when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open | Logged, not yet assessed or assigned | Priority and owner are agreed |
| In progress | Owner is working on actions | Fix is delivered, or escalation is needed |
| Escalated | Decision or resources needed from above the project manager | The decision is made and actions are agreed |
| On hold | Deliberately parked, with a reason and a review date | The review date arrives or circumstances change |
| Resolved | The fix is in place | The person who raised it confirms the problem has gone |
| Closed | Confirmed resolved, or formally accepted with no further action | Final; reopen as a new linked issue if it returns |
The difference between **resolved** and **closed** is important. Resolved means the owner believes it is fixed; closed means the fix has been checked, the person who raised it agrees, and the resolution has been written up. Skipping the check is how the same issue comes back a fortnight later.

### How to manage issues step by step
The process below works for most projects. It mirrors the capture, assess, decide and implement pattern used in PRINCE2 and most organisational issue procedures.
1. **Capture:** log the issue as soon as it is raised, even if it seems small. Anyone on the project should be able to raise one, either directly in the log or by telling the project manager.
2. **Triage:** within the agreed response time, confirm it really is an issue (not a risk, task or defect), check it is not a duplicate, and set type and priority.
3. **Assign:** give the issue one owner. The owner is accountable for driving it to resolution, even if other people do the work.
4. **Analyse:** the owner confirms the impact and identifies options. For anything significant, find the cause, not just the symptom.
5. **Act:** agree the next action and a date. Check whether a contingency plan already covers it.
6. **Escalate if needed:** if the fix needs authority, money or decisions beyond the project manager's tolerances, escalate (see the next section). If it changes a baseline, raise a change request.
7. **Monitor:** update the next action and status at least as often as the priority requires; review the whole log weekly.
8. **Close:** confirm the fix with the person who raised it, record the resolution and root cause, and note any lesson worth sharing.
The project manager owns the log and the review; each issue owner keeps their own entries current; the sponsor or board decides escalated issues. If those roles are unclear on your project, a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) for the issue process takes ten minutes and prevents a lot of argument.

### When and how to escalate an issue
Escalation is not failure. It is the mechanism that gets a decision made by the person with the authority to make it. The problem is usually escalating too late. Agree escalation rules with the sponsor at the start, ideally as part of your [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/), and tie them to tolerances:
| Trigger | Example rule | Escalate to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time | Resolution would delay a key milestone by more than 5 working days | Sponsor |
| Cost | Resolution needs more than the project manager's contingency, e.g. above 2,000 | Sponsor or board |
| Scope or quality | Resolution means dropping or changing an agreed deliverable or acceptance criterion | Board, through change control |
| Authority | Needs a decision from another department, a supplier's management or a contract change | Sponsor |
| Ageing | A high-priority issue has had no progress for 5 working days | Next level up from the owner |
| Reputation, safety or legal | Any issue with safety, legal or regulatory exposure | Sponsor immediately |
The figures above are illustrative; set your own. When you escalate, send a short note that the decision-maker can act on without a meeting:
- The issue in one sentence, and its ID.
- The impact if nothing is done, in days, money or scope.
- What has already been tried.
- Two or three options with their consequences, and your recommendation.
- The decision you need and the date you need it by.
Record the escalation in the log (status "escalated", escalated to, date) and keep chasing until there is a decision.

### Worked example: one issue from capture to closure
Here is how a single issue moves through the log on an office relocation project. The project moves 120 staff to a new building, with the move weekend fixed for 14 June because the old lease ends that month.
| Date | Event | Log update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 20 May | The furniture supplier emails that 700 of 1,000 desks will arrive on 24 June, not 10 June | I-021 logged by the facilities coordinator. Type: problem. Status: open |
| 20 May | Project manager triages the same afternoon | Impact: 70 per cent of staff without desks on day one; move date at risk. Severity high, urgency within days, so priority **critical**. Owner: procurement lead |
| 21 May | Owner contacts the supplier and two alternatives | Next action: get quotes for hiring 700 temporary desks; due 23 May. Status: in progress |
| 23 May | Hire costs 6,500; project manager's contingency is 4,000 | Cost tolerance would be breached, so the issue is escalated to the sponsor with three options: hire desks, phase the move, or delay the move a week |
| 24 May | Sponsor approves hiring desks for 300 staff and moving one department a week later | Decision recorded and linked to change request CR-006 (phased move). Status: in progress |
| 14 June | Move completes; hired desks in place | Status: resolved |
| 26 June | Permanent desks installed; facilities coordinator confirms no outstanding problems | Status: closed. Root cause: supplier capacity not checked at contract stage. Lesson: add capacity confirmation to supplier onboarding |
Three points from the example. First, triage was the same day, which is what a critical rating demands. Second, the escalation was triggered by a pre-agreed cost tolerance, so nobody had to argue about whether to involve the sponsor. Third, the closed entry captures a root cause and a lesson, which is where most of the long-term value of an issue log comes from.

### Issue log example: a full sample log
The sample below shows seven entries from a website relaunch project mid-way through delivery. It is shortened to the most useful columns.
| ID | Title and description | Priority | Owner | Next action (due) | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I-007 | Refund tests blocked: payment sandbox errors on refund calls since 2 March; 14 test cases blocked | High | Integration lead | Chase provider ticket; run other test cases first (5 Mar) | In progress |
| I-008 | Budget sign-off delayed: finance approver away 3 weeks; phase 2 purchase order waiting | Medium | Project manager | Ask sponsor to name deputy approver (6 Mar) | Escalated |
| I-009 | Copy late: 40 of 120 product descriptions not delivered by content agency | High | Content lead | Agree revised delivery plan with agency (4 Mar) | In progress |
| I-010 | Brand concern: head of brand unhappy with homepage imagery | Medium | Design lead | Present two alternatives at design review (8 Mar) | Open |
| I-011 | Off-spec: mobile page speed below agreed acceptance target on product pages | High | Tech lead | Image compression fix in next build (7 Mar) | In progress |
| I-012 | Request: sales want live chat added before launch | Medium | Product owner | Raised as CR-004; awaiting board (12 Mar) | Escalated |
| I-006 | Training room double-booked for launch week | Low | Training coordinator | Rebooked alternative room | Closed |
At a glance, a sponsor can see two items waiting for decisions from above and two separate issues (I-009 and I-011) that both threaten the launch date: exactly the pattern a weekly review should pick up.
If you want a ready-made format, our [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) includes an issue type with owner, action, due date and status columns, and the [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) covers issues that turn into changes.

### Reviewing the issue log and reporting it
An issue log is only useful while it is current. Put a review on the agenda of your weekly project meeting, and keep it short by following the same order each time:
1. New issues since last week: confirm type, priority and owner.
2. Critical and high issues: progress, next action, any escalation needed.
3. Overdue actions: why, and a new date or an escalation.
4. Issues on hold: is the review date due?
5. Resolved issues: confirm and close.
6. Patterns: any repeated causes, categories or owners?

#### Issue log health measures
A few simple counts tell you, and your sponsor, whether issues are under control. Our suggestions:
| Measure | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| Open issues by priority | Current exposure; a growing count of high and critical items is an early warning |
| Average age of open high and critical issues | Whether serious issues are actually being resolved |
| Issues with overdue next actions | Whether owners are following through |
| Issues opened vs closed this period | Whether the project is catching up or falling behind |
| Issues with no update in two weeks | Stale entries that need challenging |
In the [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/), list critical and high issues with their impact and next step, state any decisions you need, and give the counts above. Do not paste the whole log into the report.

### Issue logs in Agile teams
Agile teams deal with most day-to-day issues as **impediments** or **blockers**. They are flagged on the board, raised at the [daily scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) and removed quickly, often by the Scrum Master. A heavyweight log for these would slow the team down.
A light issue log is still useful for issues the team cannot remove on its own, such as other-team dependencies, supplier problems or anything needing escalation. An impediment list with an owner and date is an issue log by another name.
One terminology trap: in Jira, everything tracked used to be called an "issue", including stories, tasks and bugs. During 2025 Atlassian began using "work item" as the collective term in Jira Cloud. Either way, a Jira issue or work item is not necessarily a project issue in the sense used here. If you track project issues in Jira, create a dedicated type or label for them.

### Issue log in PMBOK and PRINCE2
If you are studying for an exam, the vocabulary differs slightly between the two main bodies of guidance.
|  | PMBOK Guide (PMI) | PRINCE2 7 (PeopleCert / AXELOS) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name | Issue log | Issue register for formal issues; informal issues are noted in the daily log |
| Issue types | Not formally typed | Request for change, off-specification, problem or concern, and business opportunity |
| Process | Issues are managed as part of directing and monitoring the work | Capture, assess, propose, decide, implement |
| Who decides | Project manager, escalating via governance | Project manager within tolerance; a change authority or the project board beyond it |
Whichever method you follow, the practice is the same: log it, own it, assess it, decide, act and close. For more on each method, see our guides to the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) and [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/).

### Tools for keeping an issue log
A spreadsheet is enough for most single projects. It is quick to set up, everyone can open it and filtering by owner or priority is easy. Move to a project management tool when you need automatic reminders, issues linked to tasks and milestones, request forms for raising issues, or a portfolio view across many projects.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, handles this well through custom item types, request forms and dashboards, and is a good fit for PMOs tracking issues across several projects. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) suits software teams that already track work there, and [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) is a natural step up for teams who like the spreadsheet format.

### Common issue log mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Logging risks as issues (or the reverse) | Real problems get lost among possibilities; risks get no response plan | Apply the test: has it happened, or is it certain? If not, it is a risk |
| Vague descriptions | Nobody can judge priority or check the fix | Condition, evidence, consequence |
| No owner, or a team as owner | Everyone assumes someone else is dealing with it | One named person per issue |
| Undefined priorities | Everything is 'high'; nothing stands out | Write definitions and response times at the top of the log |
| Next actions without dates | Issues sit for weeks | Every open issue has a next action and a due date |
| Escalating too late | Options narrow and costs rise | Agree tolerance-based escalation rules at the start |
| Closing without confirmation | The same issue returns | Use resolved and closed as separate statuses |
| Deleting closed issues | You lose the audit trail and the lessons | Filter them out of the working view; never delete |
| Using the log to assign blame | People stop raising issues | Factual language; discuss causes, not culprits |
| Too many columns | Nobody keeps it up to date | Start with the core columns; add fields only when needed |
When you see the same cause behind several issues, run a structured analysis using our [root cause analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) and feed the outcome into your [lessons learned log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an issue log in project management?**
An issue log is a project document that lists every current problem, concern or request affecting the project, with its impact, priority, owner, actions, target date and status, so that each one is resolved, escalated or closed deliberately.

**Q: What should an issue log include?**
At minimum: ID, date raised, raised by, description, impact, priority, owner, next action with a date, target resolution date, status and resolution. Larger projects often add type, category, escalation details, linked risk or change IDs and root cause.

**Q: What is the difference between an issue log and a risk register?**
An issue log tracks problems that are happening now or are certain; a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) tracks uncertain events that might happen. When a risk occurs, close it in the register and open a linked issue.

**Q: Who is responsible for the issue log?**
The project manager (or a project coordinator) owns and maintains the log. Each issue owner keeps their own entries up to date, and the sponsor or board decides escalated issues.

**Q: How do you create an issue log?**
Agree the columns, priority definitions and status list; set up a shared spreadsheet or tool; explain to the team how to raise issues; then log, triage and review issues weekly. Starting from a template such as our [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) saves time.

**Q: How often should an issue log be updated?**
Update entries whenever something changes, and review the whole log at least weekly. Critical issues may need a daily update until they are resolved.

**Q: What priority levels should an issue log use?**
Four levels (critical, high, medium, low) work for most projects, provided each has a plain-language definition and a target response time. Many teams derive priority from severity and urgency.

**Q: When should an issue be escalated?**
When resolving it would breach an agreed time, cost, scope or quality tolerance, needs a decision outside the project manager's authority, involves safety or legal exposure, or a high-priority issue has stalled.

**Q: What is the difference between an issue log and a RAID log?**
A [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) tracks risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies in one table. An issue log covers issues only, usually in more detail. Smaller projects often use just a RAID log.

**Q: Is an issue log the same as a change log?**
No. An issue log records problems and requests; a change log records formal change requests and their decisions. An issue that needs a baseline change leads to a change request, and the two entries should be linked.

**Q: What is an issue log in PMP?**
In the PMBOK Guide, which underpins the PMP exam, the issue log is a project document used to record and monitor issues, their owners and their resolution, and it is updated throughout execution.

**Q: What is an issue register in PRINCE2?**
It is PRINCE2's name for the log of formally managed issues. Each formal issue gets an ID and may have an issue report with impact analysis and options. Informal issues are handled by the project manager and noted in the daily log.

**Q: Can I keep an issue log in Excel or Google Sheets?**
Yes. A spreadsheet works well for most projects. Use dropdowns for type, priority and status, freeze the header row and filter by owner. Move to a [project management tool](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) when you need reminders, forms or cross-project reporting.

**Q: Should closed issues be deleted from the log?**
No. Filter them out of the working view but keep them. Closed issues provide the audit trail and are a valuable input to lessons learned.
