# IT Project Manager: Role, Skills, Career Path and Certs

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/it-project-manager/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What an IT project manager does, key skills, certifications, career path and pay, with a typical week, a cut-over example and how to get into the role.


## IT Project Manager: Role, Skills, Career Path and Certs
An IT project manager plans and delivers technology projects such as software releases, system implementations, cloud migrations and infrastructure upgrades, coordinating developers, engineers, vendors and business users so the new system goes live safely and is adopted. This guide explains what the role involves at each stage, a typical week, a worked cut-over example, the skills and certifications employers look for, how it compares with related roles and how to get into it.
- Published 3 October 2026
- Last updated 18 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- IT project managers deliver technology change by joining up technical teams, suppliers and the business.
- You do not usually need to code, but you do need to understand environments, testing, releases, data migration and security well enough to spot risk.
- Cut-over, rollback and go/no-go decisions are where IT projects differ most from other projects.
- Most IT projects now use Agile or hybrid delivery, often alongside formal IT change management.
- PMP, CAPM, PRINCE2, Scrum, PMI-ACP, ITIL and CompTIA Project+ are the certifications seen most often in job adverts.
- Common routes in are from developer, analyst, tester, infrastructure, service desk or project coordinator roles.

### What is an IT project manager?
An **IT project manager** is a project manager who specialises in information technology projects. They turn a business need into a technical scope and plan, coordinate the people who build, test and run the system, manage risk, budget and suppliers, and lead the release or cut-over so that the business can use the new technology with minimal disruption.
IT project managers work in three main settings:
- **In-house IT departments**, delivering projects for the organisation's own business units (for example a new HR system or a network refresh).
- **Technology suppliers and consultancies**, delivering implementations for clients under a contract, often with commercial targets.
- **Software product companies**, coordinating releases and platform work across engineering teams.
Whatever the setting, an IT project manager is accountable for delivery: the agreed scope, on time, within budget, at the right quality, with the business ready to use it. For the general duties shared by every project manager, see [project manager roles and responsibilities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-roles-and-responsibilities/).

### What does an IT project manager do?
- Turns a business need and its requirements into a clear technical [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) and plan.
- Builds the schedule, including technical [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/), environment availability, test cycles and release windows.
- Coordinates developers, architects, infrastructure engineers, testers, security, data and service management teams, and external vendors.
- Manages the budget, including licences, cloud costs, contractors and supplier milestones.
- Tracks [risks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) such as data loss, downtime, security weaknesses and integration failures.
- Runs [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) for scope and works with the organisation's IT change process for releases into live systems.
- Plans testing, user acceptance, training, cut-over and go-live with the business.
- Hands the system over to operations and support teams with agreed service levels, documentation and knowledge transfer.
- Reports progress, risks and decisions to the sponsor and steering group.

#### Responsibilities across the project life cycle
| Stage | What the IT project manager does | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiation | Clarify the business problem, options and benefits; agree sponsor, budget and constraints | Business case input, project charter |
| Discovery and design | Run requirements workshops, coordinate solution architecture, security and data reviews, select vendors | Requirements, solution design, delivery plan |
| Build and configure | Plan sprints or build phases, manage environments, track progress, handle scope changes | Working increments, test plans, change log |
| Test | Coordinate system, integration, performance, security and user acceptance testing; manage defects | Test reports, defect log, acceptance sign-off |
| Deploy and cut over | Plan the runbook, rehearse, chair go/no-go, coordinate the release and hypercare | Cut-over plan, rollback plan, go-live decision |
| Handover and close | Transfer to support, confirm service levels, close contracts, capture lessons | Support handover pack, closure report |
If you want the discipline rather than the job (methods, phases and practices for running technology projects), read our guide to [IT project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/it-project-management/).

### Types of IT projects
The title covers a wide range of work. The type of project shapes the skills you need most.
| Project type | What makes it distinctive | Typical approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Software development | Frequent releases, backlogs, technical debt, close work with product managers | Scrum or Kanban, often with DevOps practices |
| System implementation (ERP, CRM, HR) | Heavy configuration, business process change, data migration and user training | Hybrid: phased plan with iterative configuration |
| Infrastructure and cloud migration | Cut-over plans, downtime windows, rollback options, network and security dependencies | Wave-based plan, predictive or hybrid |
| Security and compliance | Fixed regulatory deadlines, audit evidence, controls testing | Predictive with clear milestones |
| Data and analytics | Data quality, governance, integration of many sources | Iterative, with early prototypes |
| Service transition | Moving a system into live support with agreed service levels and processes | Predictive checklist with acceptance criteria |
| Hardware and end-user rollout | Logistics, scheduling across sites, user disruption | Repeatable rollout waves |
For projects that are mainly software, see our guide to [software project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/software-project-management/).

### A typical week as an IT project manager
No two weeks are the same, and the balance shifts as a project moves from design to go-live. The pattern below is typical for a mid-sized implementation in its build and test phase.
| When | Activity | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily, 15 minutes | Stand-up or check-in with the delivery team | Spot blockers and dependency problems early |
| Monday | Plan the week: review the schedule, risks and environment bookings | Keeps test and release windows protected |
| Tuesday | Vendor progress meeting | Holds suppliers to milestones and surfaces their risks |
| Wednesday | IT change advisory board (CAB) submission or meeting | Releases into live systems need approval |
| Wednesday | Requirements or design clarification with business leads | Prevents rework and scope drift |
| Thursday | Defect triage with testers and developers | Agrees which defects block go-live |
| Thursday | Budget review: actuals, cloud spend, contractor time | Catches cost drift early |
| Friday | Status report and steering group preparation | Gives decision-makers one clear view |
| Ad hoc | Incident or escalation from a pilot or earlier release | Protects live service and user trust |
Expect some evening or weekend work around go-live, because cut-overs are usually scheduled when the fewest users are affected. Good IT project managers plan this well ahead and agree time off in lieu with the team.

### Worked example: migrating 40 applications to the cloud
The figures in this example are illustrative, but the approach reflects how many organisations run migrations.

#### 1. Plan the migration in waves
An IT project manager is asked to move 40 internal applications from an ageing data centre to a cloud platform within nine months, before the data centre contract ends. Moving everything at once is too risky, so the applications are grouped into four waves, starting with the least critical:
| Wave | Applications | Risk level | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (pilot) | 6 internal tools with few users | Low | Months 3 to 4 |
| 2 | 12 departmental applications | Medium | Months 4 to 6 |
| 3 | 14 business applications with integrations | Medium to high | Months 6 to 8 |
| 4 | 8 critical systems including finance and payroll | High | Month 8, with month 9 as contingency |

#### 2. Find the critical path
Months 1 and 2 are spent on foundations: network connectivity, identity and access, the security review and the landing zone (the baseline cloud environment). Nothing can migrate until these are done, so the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) runs through them. The project manager starts the security review in week 1 rather than waiting for the design to be finished, because the security team has a six-week queue.

#### 3. Write a repeatable cut-over runbook
Each application follows the same sequence, which the team rehearses on a test copy before the real weekend:
1. Freeze changes to the application five working days before cut-over.
2. Take a full backup and confirm it can be restored.
3. Replicate data to the cloud environment and check record counts and checksums.
4. Run smoke tests and key user journeys in the new environment.
5. Switch DNS and integrations to the new environment.
6. Business users verify agreed test scripts.
7. Go/no-go checkpoint at a fixed time; if criteria are not met, run the rollback plan.
8. Two weeks of hypercare with extra support cover, then hand over to business-as-usual support.

#### 4. Agree go/no-go criteria in advance
| Criterion | Threshold for go |
| --- | --- |
| Data reconciliation | 100% of record counts match; no critical differences |
| Smoke tests | All passed |
| Business verification | All priority scripts passed and signed by the business owner |
| Open defects | No critical or high defects without an agreed workaround |
| Support readiness | Support team trained, contacts and escalation paths confirmed |
| Rollback window | Decision made by 02:00 so a rollback can finish before 07:00 |
Tip
Write the rollback plan and agree the decision time before the cut-over weekend. Deciding under pressure at 3 a.m. is how outages get longer. The question is not whether you can fix the problem, but whether you can fix it before the rollback window closes.

#### 5. Outcome and lessons
Wave 1 overruns by a week because firewall rules for two tools were missing from the design. The project manager adds a firewall-rule checklist to the runbook and a dependency discovery step to each wave's planning. Waves 2 to 4 each take less time than planned, and wave 4 completes in month 8, leaving the contingency month unused. Recording the lesson after wave 1 and changing the process was worth more than any amount of schedule pressure.

### IT project risks and how to manage them
Technology projects share a familiar set of risks. Put them in your risk register at the start and review them every week.
| Risk | Early warning sign | Typical response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unclear or changing requirements | Business users disagree in workshops; many clarification requests | Prioritise requirements, prototype early, use iterative delivery |
| Data migration errors | Poor data quality found in profiling | Data cleansing workstream, trial migrations, reconciliation checks |
| Integration failures | Interfaces untested until late | Test integrations early with stubs and contract tests |
| Security and compliance gaps | Security review not booked; unclear data classification | Involve security in design, schedule reviews early |
| Vendor delays | Missed supplier milestones, staff changes | Milestone-based payments, weekly vendor reviews, escalation route |
| Environment shortages | Teams queueing for test environments | Environment booking plan, automated provisioning where possible |
| Under-estimated testing | Test phase squeezed by late build | Protect test time, automate regression tests, track defect trends |
| Low adoption | Few users attend training or demos | Early user involvement, champions, training close to go-live |
Our [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) tracks risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies in one place, which suits IT projects with many technical dependencies.

### Skills IT project managers need

#### Project management skills
- Planning, scheduling and estimating, including dependency and critical path analysis.
- Budgeting and cost control, including licence and cloud consumption costs.
- Risk, issue and change management.
- Vendor and contract management, including statements of work and milestone acceptance.
- Reporting to sponsors and steering groups in plain language.

#### Technical knowledge
You do not need to be the most technical person in the room, but you need enough understanding to ask good questions and judge risk.
| Concept | What you should know enough to do |
| --- | --- |
| Software development life cycle | Understand how work moves from backlog to code, test and release |
| Environments (development, test, staging, production) | Plan which work happens where and book environments in advance |
| Testing types | Plan unit, integration, performance, security and user acceptance testing |
| Release and IT change management | Work with change advisory boards and release calendars |
| Cloud and infrastructure basics | Follow discussions about networks, identity, hosting and costs |
| Data migration | Plan extraction, cleansing, loading and reconciliation |
| Security and privacy | Know when security and data protection reviews are needed |
| APIs and integrations | Understand dependencies between systems and how they are tested |

#### People skills
- Translating between technical and business language without losing accuracy.
- Facilitating workshops and decisions with people who disagree.
- Negotiating scope, priorities and resources.
- Staying calm and structured during incidents and go-live weekends.
- Building trust with engineers by protecting their time and removing blockers.

### Delivery approaches: Agile, Waterfall and hybrid
Most software work now runs in iterations using Scrum or Kanban, while infrastructure, compliance and large system implementations often use a predictive or hybrid plan. Many IT project managers work in hybrid mode: a fixed outer plan for budget, contracts and go-live, with iterative delivery inside it.
- **Agile** suits work where requirements will evolve and value can be released in increments. The IT project manager often acts as a delivery lead, working alongside the Product Owner and Scrum Master; see [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/).
- **Waterfall or predictive** suits work with fixed scope, hard dependencies or regulatory deadlines, such as a data centre exit.
- **Hybrid** suits system implementations, where design and data migration are planned up front and configuration is done in sprints.
IT projects also interact with IT service management. Releases into live systems usually need approval through the organisation's change process, and the project must hand over to support teams in a way they accept. In organisations that practise DevOps, many releases are automated and small, and the IT project manager focuses more on dependencies, readiness and stakeholder change than on release mechanics. Our [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) guide compares the approaches in detail.

### IT project manager vs related roles
Job titles overlap, and organisations use them differently. The table shows the usual distinctions.
| Role | Main focus | Owns | Technical depth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IT project manager | Delivering a defined technology project | Plan, budget, risks, delivery | Working knowledge |
| Technical project manager | Delivering technically complex work, often engineering-led | Delivery plus technical coordination | Deep, often hands-on background |
| IT manager | Running IT services and teams day to day | Ongoing operations, staff, IT budget | Broad |
| Product manager | Deciding what to build and why | Product strategy, roadmap, priorities | Varies |
| Scrum Master | Helping a Scrum team work effectively | Scrum practice and team improvement | Varies |
| Programme manager | Coordinating several related projects for benefits | Programme plan, benefits, interdependencies | Working knowledge |
For the closest comparison, see our guide to the [technical project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/technical-project-manager/).

### Certifications for IT project managers
Certification is rarely required by law, but it often appears in job adverts and can help you move from a technical role into project management. The facts below were checked on 18 October 2026; always confirm requirements with the awarding body.
| Certification | Awarding body | Best for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) | PMI | Experienced project managers | Widely recognised; updated exam in effect from 9 July 2026, with roughly 60% Agile and hybrid content |
| [CAPM](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) | PMI | People new to project management | No project experience required |
| PMI-ACP | PMI | Project managers working in Agile teams | Covers several Agile approaches, not only Scrum |
| [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) | PeopleCert (AXELOS) | UK, Europe, Australia and public sector roles | Foundation and Practitioner levels |
| [Scrum certifications](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/) | Scrum.org, Scrum Alliance and others | Software delivery roles | Scrum Master and Product Owner tracks |
| ITIL Foundation | PeopleCert | Roles close to IT service management | ITIL (Version 5) Foundation is available in 2026; ITIL 4 remains available alongside it |
| CompTIA Project+ | CompTIA | Entry-level IT project roles | Suggested for people with around 6 to 12 months of project experience |
A practical sequence for someone moving from a technical role is CAPM or CompTIA Project+ first, then a Scrum certification if you work in software, then PMP once you meet the experience requirement.

### How to become an IT project manager
1. **Build technical credibility.** Work in, or closely with, development, testing, infrastructure, analysis or the service desk so you understand how systems are built and run.
2. **Take on project tasks in your current role.** Volunteer to plan a small release, coordinate a rollout or run a test cycle.
3. **Learn the fundamentals.** Scope, scheduling, budgeting, risk, change control and stakeholder management, plus at least one Agile framework.
4. **Get an entry-level certification.** CAPM, CompTIA Project+ or a Scrum certification show commitment while you build experience.
5. **Move into a coordination role.** [Project coordinator](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-coordinator/), PMO analyst or junior project manager roles give structured experience.
6. **Keep a delivery portfolio.** For each project, note the goal, your role, constraints, decisions and results. It makes interviews much easier.
7. **Step up and certify.** Apply for IT project manager roles and, once eligible, take the PMP or PRINCE2 Practitioner.

#### Common routes in
| Starting role | Strength you bring | Gap to close |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Developer or engineer | Technical credibility, estimating | Budgeting, stakeholder management, letting go of hands-on work |
| Business or systems analyst | Requirements, process knowledge | Scheduling, vendor management, technical release knowledge |
| Tester | Quality mindset, defect management | Planning, budgeting, wider stakeholder management |
| Service desk or infrastructure | Operations and support view | Formal planning, business case and requirements |
| General project manager | Project discipline | Technical vocabulary, SDLC and release management |
For the general route into project roles, see [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/).

### Career path and salary
| Level | Typical titles | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry | Project coordinator, PMO analyst, junior IT project manager | Supports projects or runs small ones |
| Mid | IT project manager | Runs projects end to end |
| Senior | [Senior project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/senior-project-manager/), technical programme lead | Large or high-risk projects, mentoring |
| Leadership | Programme manager, head of delivery, PMO lead, IT director | Portfolios, teams and delivery strategy |

#### How to research IT project manager pay
Pay varies widely by country, city, sector, seniority, contract type and the size of projects you run, so any single figure is misleading. Some published figures also group IT project managers with broader or more senior occupations such as IT managers. To get a reliable picture:
- Compare current job adverts for the same title and seniority in your city.
- Check official labour statistics for your country, noting which occupation code the figures cover.
- Use PMI's salary survey, which breaks pay down by country and certification.
- Ask recruiters who specialise in technology delivery roles for a range.
- Compare permanent salaries with contract day rates separately; they are not like for like.
Tip
Specialist knowledge of a platform (for example a major ERP or cloud provider) or a regulated sector such as finance or healthcare often matters as much to pay as a general certification.

### Sample IT project manager job description
Use this as a starting point for a job advert or to check your own experience against a typical role.
**Role summary:** Plan and deliver technology projects of up to [size] across software, infrastructure and system implementations, working with internal teams, vendors and business stakeholders.
- Define scope, plans, budgets and success measures with sponsors.
- Lead cross-functional teams and suppliers through design, build, test and deployment.
- Manage risks, issues, dependencies and changes, and report to steering groups.
- Plan and run cut-overs and go-lives, including rollback and hypercare.
- Hand over to support teams and capture lessons learned.
**Typical requirements:** experience delivering IT projects; working knowledge of the software development life cycle and Agile delivery; strong communication with technical and non-technical people; a project management certification such as PMP, PRINCE2 or a Scrum qualification is often preferred.

### Common mistakes new IT project managers make
- **Taking estimates as commitments.** Ask for ranges and assumptions, and track them.
- **Squeezing testing to protect the date.** Defects found after go-live cost far more to fix.
- **Leaving security, data and support teams until late.** Book their reviews in the first weeks.
- **Treating go-live as the finish line.** Plan hypercare, adoption and handover as real work.
- **Doing the technical work yourself.** It feels productive but leaves nobody steering the project.
- **Reporting technical detail to sponsors.** Report outcomes, decisions needed and risks in business terms.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does an IT project manager do?**
They plan and deliver technology projects, coordinating developers, engineers, vendors and business users to deliver working systems on time, within budget and ready for the business to use.

**Q: Does an IT project manager need to code?**
Usually not. They need to understand how software and infrastructure are built, tested and released so they can plan realistically, spot risks and ask good questions.

**Q: What qualifications do you need to be an IT project manager?**
Many employers ask for a degree in a technology or business subject, but relevant experience and certification can often substitute. Experience in a technical or coordination role matters most.

**Q: Which certification is best for IT project managers?**
The PMP is the most widely recognised for experienced project managers. CAPM or CompTIA Project+ suit beginners, Scrum certifications help in software teams, PRINCE2 is common in the UK and Europe, and ITIL helps where service management matters.

**Q: How much does an IT project manager earn?**
It depends on country, city, sector, seniority and contract type. Compare current job adverts, official labour statistics for the right occupation and PMI's salary survey for up-to-date figures.

**Q: What is the difference between an IT project manager and a technical project manager?**
An IT project manager focuses on delivery and coordination across technical and business teams; a technical project manager typically brings deeper hands-on technical expertise and is more involved in technical decisions.

**Q: Is an IT project manager the same as an IT manager?**
No. An IT project manager runs temporary projects with a defined end. An IT manager runs ongoing IT services, staff and budgets.

**Q: How do I become an IT project manager with no experience?**
Start in a technical, analyst, service desk or project coordinator role, take on small project tasks, earn an entry-level certification such as CAPM or CompTIA Project+, and build a record of what you delivered.

**Q: Do IT project managers use Agile?**
Many do, especially for software. Infrastructure, compliance and large system implementations often use predictive or hybrid approaches.

**Q: What tools do IT project managers use?**
Work management tools such as Wrike or Smartsheet, Agile tools such as Jira, documentation tools such as Confluence, IT service management tools for change requests, and collaboration tools.

**Q: Is IT project management a stressful job?**
It can be, especially around go-live and incidents. Clear plans, protected testing time, agreed rollback decisions and realistic estimates reduce the pressure considerably.

**Q: Is IT project management a good career?**
Technology projects happen in almost every industry, so the skills transfer widely, and there is a clear path to senior project, programme and delivery leadership roles.

**Q: Will AI replace IT project managers?**
AI tools can draft plans, summarise status and flag risks, which removes some administrative work. Decisions, trade-offs, negotiation and leadership during go-live still need a person, so the role is changing rather than disappearing.

# Iterative and Incremental Development: Examples and Steps

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/iterative-and-incremental-development/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Iterative and incremental development explained: the difference, worked examples, how to plan increments, models, history, pros, cons and when to use it.


## Iterative and Incremental Development: Examples and Steps
Iterative and incremental development is a way of delivering a project in small, usable pieces (increments) while improving the product through repeated cycles of building, getting feedback and adjusting (iterations). It is the delivery pattern behind Agile frameworks such as Scrum, but it is much older than Agile and works well beyond software. This guide explains the difference between the two ideas, shows how they combine, works through two examples, gives a step-by-step planning process and helps you decide when to use the approach.
- Published 7 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Iterative means improving the same thing through repeated cycles of feedback. Incremental means delivering the solution in usable pieces that add up over time.
- Used together, they give users something valuable early and let the team learn and correct course with every cycle. Agile and Scrum are built on this combination.
- PMI's Agile Practice Guide describes four life cycles: predictive, iterative, incremental and agile. Agile combines iterative and incremental working.
- Plan by slicing work into thin, end-to-end increments ordered by value and risk, then run short, fixed-length cycles that each end with a review and a decision.
- The approach suits uncertain requirements and work that can be used in parts. It needs available stakeholders, a clear definition of done and active control of scope.
- It is not new: Larman and Basili trace iterative and incremental development to engineering programmes of the 1950s and 1960s.

### What is iterative and incremental development?
**Iterative and incremental development** is a delivery approach in which a team builds a solution in a series of short cycles. Each cycle adds a usable piece of the solution (the increment) and uses feedback on what already exists to refine and correct it (the iteration). The aim is early value, fast learning and lower risk.
The two words describe different things, and it helps to separate them:
- **Iterative development** means repeating a cycle of building, reviewing and improving the same piece of work until it is good enough. Each pass makes it more correct. PMI's Agile Practice Guide (2017) describes an iterative life cycle as one that uses feedback on unfinished work to improve and modify it.
- **Incremental development** means delivering the solution in parts, each of which works on its own and adds to what came before. Users get something they can use before the whole solution is complete. The same guide describes an incremental life cycle as one that provides finished deliverables the customer may be able to use immediately.
A simple analogy: writing a long report. Working **iteratively**, you draft the whole report roughly, ask for comments, then redraft it several times. Working **incrementally**, you finish and publish the executive summary first, then each chapter in turn. Working **iteratively and incrementally**, you publish a useful first chapter, collect reactions, improve it, and use what you learned to shape the next chapter.

### Iterative vs incremental: the key differences
|  | Iterative | Incremental |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core idea | Refine the same thing through repeated cycles | Add new, usable pieces one at a time |
| What each cycle produces | A better version of existing work | Additional working functionality or deliverables |
| When users get value | Often only at the end, unless combined with increments | After the first increment |
| Feedback focus | Is this right? How can we improve it? | Is this useful? What should come next? |
| Main benefit | Quality and fit improve as the team learns | Earlier value and visible progress |
| Main risk | Endless refinement without delivering | Building the wrong pieces well, or pieces that do not fit together |
| Example | A prototype checkout redesigned after three rounds of user testing | Release login, then search, then payments |
The two answer different questions. Iteration asks **how do we make this right?** Increments ask **how do we deliver this in pieces?** You can do either without the other, but each covers the other's weakness: increments get value out early, and iteration stops those increments being built on wrong assumptions.

### Predictive, iterative, incremental and agile life cycles
PMI's Agile Practice Guide (2017), published with the Agile Alliance, compares four types of project life cycle. The table below summarises its comparison in plain English:
| Life cycle | Requirements | Activities | Delivery | Main goal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Predictive | Fixed early | Each performed once for the whole project | Single delivery at the end | Manage cost |
| Iterative | Dynamic | Repeated until the solution is right | Single delivery | Correctness of the solution |
| Incremental | Dynamic | Performed once for each increment | Frequent smaller deliveries | Speed |
| Agile | Dynamic | Repeated until right, within each increment | Frequent small deliveries | Customer value through frequent delivery and feedback |
Agile, in other words, is iterative **and** incremental. PMI's guidance also treats these as points on a continuum from predictive to adaptive, with **hybrid** approaches in between: for example, a fixed-scope construction phase run predictively alongside an iteratively designed software component. Our guides to [waterfall project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) and [Agile vs waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) cover the predictive end in detail.

### How iterative and incremental development work together
In practice, most teams combine both in one repeating cycle:
1. **Plan** the next small increment, choosing the most valuable or riskiest piece.
2. **Build** it to a finished, usable standard.
3. **Review** it with users and stakeholders.
4. **Adapt**: refine the increment and update the plan for what comes next.
5. **Release** when there is enough value, then repeat.

#### In Scrum
[Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) makes this cycle explicit. Each [Sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/), a fixed timebox of one month or less, produces at least one **Increment**. The 2020 Scrum Guide describes an Increment as a concrete stepping stone towards the Product Goal: it adds to all previous Increments, must be usable and must meet the Definition of Done. Several Increments can be created within one Sprint.
The [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) is the iterative part: the team and stakeholders inspect the outcome and adapt the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/), so the next Sprint builds on what was learned. The Sprint Retrospective applies the same idea to the way the team works, improving the process as well as the product.
Note that the Sprint is the iteration and the Increment is the output. A team can release Increments to users during a Sprint; the Sprint Review is a point to inspect progress, not a gate that holds back releases. See our guide to the [Increment in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/increment-in-scrum/).

#### Increment then iterate, or iterate then increment
Teams combine the two in different orders depending on uncertainty:
- **Increment, then iterate:** split the product into pieces, deliver the first and improve it based on feedback while building the next. This is the usual pattern when the overall direction is clear.
- **Iterate, then increment:** run a few rapid iterations on a prototype or spike to settle the direction, then deliver in increments. This suits work where even the shape of the solution is uncertain.

### What changes for the project manager
Iterative and incremental delivery does not remove project management; it changes when and how planning, control and reporting happen. The table compares the main activities:
| Activity | Predictive project | Iterative and incremental project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planning | Detailed plan for the whole project at the start | Outline roadmap for the whole project; detailed plans for the next one or two cycles only |
| Scope | Fixed and controlled through change requests | Prioritised backlog; scope is the main variable within a fixed time and budget |
| Budget | Estimated bottom-up and approved once | Often funded per release or per period, with a review before each new tranche |
| Progress reporting | Percent complete against the baseline | Working increments delivered, plus burnup or throughput trends |
| Risk management | Risk register reviewed at milestones | Riskiest assumptions tested in early increments; risks reviewed every cycle |
| Governance | Stage gates between phases | Release or funding decisions informed by what has been delivered |
| Quality | Testing phase near the end | Testing and acceptance in every cycle, against a definition of done |
The project manager's job shifts from protecting a baseline to keeping the outcome, budget and backlog aligned, removing obstacles and making sure stakeholders turn up to reviews. In a hybrid project you may do both: run fixed contracts and milestones predictively while the team delivers increments within them.
Tip
Report progress in delivered value, not activity. 'Releases 1 and 2 are live and phone bookings are down 20%' tells a sponsor far more than '45% complete'. (Illustrative figures.)

### Worked example: an online booking system
This illustrative example follows a team building an online booking system for a chain of physiotherapy clinics, using two-week iterations and releasing every second iteration.
| Release | Added (incremental) | Refined from feedback (iterative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (weeks 1–4) | View available slots and book one clinic, one practitioner; confirmation email | Booking form cut from 12 fields to 6 after test users abandoned it |
| 2 (weeks 5–8) | All clinics and practitioners; cancel and rebook | Slot display changed from a list to a calendar after reception staff feedback |
| 3 (weeks 9–12) | Online payment of deposits; SMS reminders | Reminder timing moved from 48 to 24 hours before, based on no-show data |
| 4 (weeks 13–16) | Practitioner diary sync and reporting for clinic managers | Payment flow simplified after a spike in failed card payments |
Each release is usable on its own, and each one also improves what was released before. Compare when users first get something they can use under four approaches to the same 16-week project:
| Approach | First usable delivery | What happens to the booking form problem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Big bang (predictive) | Week 16 | Found after launch, when it is expensive to fix |
| Purely iterative | Week 16, after several internal prototypes | Found in a prototype review, but no one benefits until the end |
| Purely incremental | Week 4 | Found in release 1 but not revisited, because the plan moves on to the next piece |
| Iterative and incremental | Week 4 | Found in release 1 and fixed before most users ever see it |
The combined approach is not faster at building everything. Its advantage is that value starts sooner and mistakes are caught when they are cheap.

### Worked example outside software: a staff training programme
Iterative and incremental development works for any deliverable that can be used in parts. In this illustrative example, an HR team must deliver a six-module management training programme to 200 new line managers over six months.
| Cycle | Increment delivered | What was learned and changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Month 1 | Module 1 (giving feedback) piloted with 12 managers | Sessions shortened from a full day to two half-days; more role-play |
| Month 2 | Module 1 for all; module 2 (one-to-ones) piloted | Pre-reading replaced with a short video after low completion |
| Months 3–4 | Modules 2–4 rolled out | Module 4 split in two after attendees asked for more on absence management |
| Months 5–6 | Modules 5–6 and a refreshed module 1 | Module 1 updated with examples drawn from earlier cohorts |
Managers started benefiting in month one, the expensive mistake of a full-day format was found with 12 people rather than 200, and the programme ended up closer to what managers needed than the original design. The same pattern suits marketing campaigns, policy rollouts, research projects and the design stages of construction projects.

### How to plan iterative and incremental delivery, step by step
1. **Define the outcome and a measure of success**, not just a list of features. For example: 'Clients can book online, and phone bookings fall by half.'
2. **Identify the biggest uncertainties and risks**: technical, user, commercial and regulatory. These shape what you build first.
3. **Break the work into thin, end-to-end increments.** Each should be usable and deliver something of value, not a layer such as 'the database'.
4. **Order the increments by value and risk.** Early increments should either deliver the most value or retire the biggest risk, ideally both.
5. **Choose a fixed cycle length** and a release rhythm, and agree when stakeholders will review each cycle.
6. **Agree a definition of done** so every increment is genuinely finished: tested, documented and ready to use.
7. **Run the cycle**: build, review with real users, refine and update the plan.
8. **Release as soon as an increment is worth releasing**, rather than waiting for a big launch. [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) helps you group increments into meaningful releases.
9. **Re-plan after every review.** Keep a longer-term roadmap, but treat everything beyond the next few cycles as a forecast.
Our [Agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/) and [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) give you a structure for steps 3 to 8.

#### Ways to slice work into increments
| Slicing approach | Example (booking system) |
| --- | --- |
| By user journey step | Find a slot, then book, then pay, then get reminded |
| By user group | Existing clients first, then new clients, then clinic managers |
| By location or segment | One clinic first, then all clinics |
| Simple case before complex | Single appointment before repeat course bookings |
| Happy path before exceptions | Successful booking before cancellations and refunds |
| Manual first, automated later | Staff confirm bookings by hand until automatic confirmation is built |
Each slice still crosses every layer needed to work end to end. Writing them as [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) keeps the focus on what the user can do.

#### Choosing an iteration length
| Iteration length | Suits | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 week | Fast-changing products, small teams, support work | Planning and review overhead feel heavy |
| 2 weeks | Most product and project teams; a common default | Large items that do not fit must be split |
| 3–4 weeks | Work with longer lead times, such as hardware or regulated content | Slower feedback; mistakes run longer |
Shorter is usually better while requirements are uncertain. Keep the length fixed once chosen so that the team's rhythm and forecasts stay stable.

### Iterative and incremental models and frameworks
Many named methods put the idea into practice, with different emphasis:
| Model or framework | Iterative | Incremental | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spiral model | Yes | Often | Barry Boehm's risk-driven model, published in IEEE Computer in 1988: each loop plans, analyses risk, builds and evaluates |
| Evolutionary delivery (Evo) | Yes | Yes | Tom Gilb's method of frequent, small, measured deliveries |
| Rational Unified Process (RUP) | Yes | Yes | Iterations within four phases: inception, elaboration, construction and transition |
| Staged or incremental waterfall | Little | Yes | Fixed requirements delivered in planned stages |
| Scrum | Yes | Yes | Sprints of one month or less, each producing a usable Increment |
| Extreme Programming (XP) | Yes | Yes | Short iterations, small releases and strong engineering practices |
| Kanban | Yes | Yes | Continuous flow rather than fixed iterations; items are delivered one at a time, often through continuous delivery |
| SAFe | Yes | Yes | Team iterations rolled up into a Planning Interval, typically 8 to 12 weeks |
Read more in our guides to [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/) and [what is Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/).

### A short history of iterative and incremental development
Iterative and incremental development is often presented as a product of the Agile movement, but Craig Larman and Victor Basili's paper 'Iterative and Incremental Development: A Brief History' (IEEE Computer, 2003) traces it back to the mid-1950s. Highlights from their account:
- **1950s:** the X-15 hypersonic aircraft programme used iterative and incremental development. It was not a software project, but some of its people later worked on NASA's Project Mercury.
- **Late 1950s to early 1960s:** Project Mercury's software team used half-day, time-boxed iterations and wrote tests before each small increment.
- **1970:** Winston Royce's paper, often cited as the origin of waterfall, actually recommended building a pilot version first and doing the job twice.
- **1970s:** IBM's Federal Systems Division built the command and control system for the US Navy's Trident submarine in four roughly six-month iterations, and the LAMPS helicopter system in 45 one-month iterations.
- **1976 and 1988:** Tom Gilb introduced 'evolutionary' delivery in 1976 and set out his Evo method in a 1988 book.
- **1988:** Barry Boehm's spiral model was published in IEEE Computer.
- **2001:** the [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/) brought these ideas together under one name. One of its principles is to deliver working software frequently, from every couple of weeks to every couple of months, preferring the shorter timescale.
See our guide to [the history of Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/history-of-agile/) for what happened next.

### Advantages of iterative and incremental development
| Advantage | Why it happens |
| --- | --- |
| Earlier value | Users can use the first increment months before the full solution is finished |
| Lower risk | Big uncertainties are tested early, in small and cheap experiments |
| Better fit to real needs | Each review lets users correct misunderstandings before they are built on |
| Visible progress | Working increments are harder to misreport than percent-complete estimates |
| Easier change | New information changes the next increment, not a signed-off master plan |
| Better quality | Integration and testing happen every cycle rather than in one late phase |
| Option to stop early | If enough value has been delivered, the sponsor can end the project with something useful |
The last point is easy to overlook. On a predictive project, stopping halfway usually leaves nothing usable. On an iterative and incremental project, every completed increment works, so the sponsor can stop, pause or change direction at any release with value already in hand.

### Disadvantages and risks, and how to manage them
| Risk | How to manage it |
| --- | --- |
| Scope keeps growing because every review generates new ideas | Keep a clear outcome, a prioritised backlog and an agreed budget or end date; see [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) |
| Early shortcuts make the design hard to extend | Invest in architecture and refactoring in every cycle, not only at the start |
| Endless refinement of one feature | Timebox iterations and agree in advance what good enough means |
| Fixed-price, fixed-scope contracts sit awkwardly with changing scope | Fix time and cost, and make scope the variable; or contract per increment |
| Stakeholders are not available to review | Book reviews at the start of the project and make them short and regular |
| Overhead of repeated planning, testing and release | Automate testing and deployment, and keep ceremonies proportionate |
| Some work cannot be usefully split, such as pouring a foundation | Use a hybrid: predictive for indivisible work, iterative for design and fit-out |
Treat these as project risks and track them like any other. See our guide to [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/).

### When to use iterative and incremental development
| Factor | Favours iterative and incremental | Favours a predictive approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | Uncertain or likely to change | Clear, stable and agreed |
| Can the work be used in parts? | Yes | No; value only exists when everything is complete |
| Cost of change late on | Low or moderate | Very high, as with physical construction |
| Stakeholder availability | Can review regularly | Available only at set milestones |
| Regulation and contracts | Allow staged approval | Require full upfront specification |
| Team experience | Familiar with short cycles | Familiar with phased delivery only |
A quick test: for each row, mark which column describes your project. If most marks fall on the left, plan iterative and incremental delivery from the start. If most fall on the right, a predictive plan is likely to be simpler, though you may still prototype the riskiest parts. If they are mixed, consider a hybrid that runs each part of the project in the way that suits it.
Most real projects score on both sides, which is why hybrid approaches are common. Our guide to [project management methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-methodologies/) helps you choose and tailor an approach.

### Common mistakes
- **Calling it iterative when nothing changes.** If reviews never alter the plan, you are running mini-waterfalls.
- **Delivering layers instead of slices.** 'Build the database' is not an increment; nobody can use it.
- **Increments that are not really finished.** Without a [definition of done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), unfinished work piles up for later.
- **Reviewing without users.** Feedback from the project team alone misses what matters to customers.
- **No long-term direction.** Short cycles still need a roadmap and an outcome to aim for.
- **Never releasing.** Increments that sit unreleased deliver no value and no real feedback.
- **Changing the iteration length constantly**, which makes planning and forecasting unreliable.
- **Ignoring technical debt** until it slows every later cycle.

### Tools and templates for iterative delivery
Most project management tools support short cycles, backlogs and boards. A few notes from our reviews:
- **Wrike**, our top-rated tool, combines boards and custom workflows with interactive Gantt charts, which suits hybrid projects that mix iterative delivery with fixed milestones. See our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).
- **Jira** is built around backlogs, sprints, boards and releases, and is the most common choice for software teams. See our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/).
- **ClickUp** includes sprints with burndown, velocity and cumulative flow reporting alongside general project features.
- **monday.com** and **Asana** offer boards, timelines and dashboards that work well for non-software teams running staged delivery.
For planning, use our [product roadmap template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-roadmap-template/) to set direction, a release plan to group increments, and a [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) for each cycle. For the full Agile life cycle around these steps, see our guide to the [Agile development life cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-development-life-cycle/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between iterative and incremental development?**
Iterative development improves the same thing through repeated cycles of feedback. Incremental development delivers a solution in usable pieces that add up over time. Agile frameworks combine both.

**Q: What is an example of iterative development?**
Building a prototype checkout page, testing it with users, redesigning it and testing again until it works well. Each cycle improves the same feature.

**Q: What is an example of incremental development?**
Releasing a booking system in stages: first booking at one clinic, then all clinics, then payments, then reminders. Users can use each piece as soon as it is released.

**Q: Is Agile iterative or incremental?**
Both. Agile delivers in small usable increments and uses feedback from each cycle to refine the product and the plan. PMI's Agile Practice Guide describes agile life cycles as both iterative and incremental.

**Q: Is iterative development the same as Agile?**
No. Agile uses iterative and incremental development, but it also rests on values and principles such as customer collaboration, responding to change and self-organising teams. A team can iterate without working in an Agile way, for example by iterating on a design inside a predictive project.

**Q: What is a vertical slice?**
A vertical slice is an increment that cuts through every layer needed to work end to end, such as screen, logic and data, so users can actually use it. It is the opposite of building one layer, such as the database, for everything first.

**Q: Is Scrum iterative or incremental?**
Both. Each Sprint of one month or less produces at least one usable Increment, and the Sprint Review and Retrospective feed what is learned into the next Sprint.

**Q: Is waterfall iterative or incremental?**
Classic waterfall is neither: it completes each phase once and delivers at the end. Some predictive projects add iterations within design phases or deliver in planned stages.

**Q: Is an MVP iterative or incremental?**
A minimum viable product is the first increment: the smallest usable version that lets you learn from real users. What you do with that learning is iterative.

**Q: What is the incremental model in software engineering?**
A model in which requirements are divided into builds, and each build is designed, developed and tested before being added to the system. It is incremental, and may be more or less iterative depending on how much each build is revisited.

**Q: What is the spiral model?**
A risk-driven iterative model described by Barry Boehm and published in IEEE Computer in 1988. Each loop of the spiral sets objectives, analyses and reduces risk, develops and tests, and plans the next loop.

**Q: How long should an iteration be?**
Usually one to four weeks, with two weeks a common default. Scrum limits Sprints to one month or less. Shorter iterations give faster feedback but add planning overhead.

**Q: Can iterative and incremental development be used outside software?**
Yes. Training programmes, marketing campaigns, policy rollouts, research and the design stages of construction can all be delivered in usable stages and improved from feedback.

**Q: How old is iterative and incremental development?**
Larman and Basili (2003) trace it to the mid-1950s, including the X-15 programme and NASA's Project Mercury, long before the Agile Manifesto of 2001.

**Q: Can waterfall projects use iterative development?**
Yes. Many predictive projects use iterations within design or prototyping, or run iterative parts alongside predictive ones in a hybrid approach.

# Leads and Lags in Project Management: Guide with Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Leads and lags in project management explained: lead vs lag, notation, date formulas, worked examples, critical path effects and scheduling rules.


## Leads and Lags in Project Management: Guide with Examples
Leads and lags in project management are adjustments to the link between two dependent activities: a lag adds a deliberate wait before the successor can start or finish, and a lead lets the successor start early so the two activities overlap. This guide explains the notation, the date formulas for every dependency type, worked examples with the critical path, and the rules experienced schedulers follow.
- Published 23 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- A lag adds waiting time to a dependency (FS+3d); a lead overlaps activities and is entered as a negative lag (FS-2d).
- Lags are not activities: no one works during them and they use no resources, but they still add time to any path they sit on.
- Leads shorten the schedule but are a form of fast tracking, so they add rework risk.
- Never use a lag to hide real work, supplier lead time or contingency; model those as activities or buffers.
- State whether each lag is in working days or calendar days and record why it exists.
- Schedule quality checks such as the DCMA 14-point assessment aim for no leads and lags on no more than 5% of links.

### What are leads and lags?
**Leads and lags** are time adjustments applied to a dependency between a predecessor and a successor activity. A **lag** delays the successor, for example waiting three days for concrete to cure before building walls. A **lead** advances the successor so it starts before the predecessor finishes, for example starting testing two days before development ends.
PMI's glossary describes them in the same way: a lag is the amount of time a successor activity is delayed with respect to its predecessor, and a lead is the amount of time a successor can be advanced. In other words, they modify a logical relationship rather than add new work.
Three points follow from that definition:
- **A lag is not an activity.** Nobody is assigned to it, it has no cost and it uses no resources. It is pure waiting time built into the link.
- **A lead is a negative lag.** Most scheduling tools have only one field, usually called Lag, and you enter a lead as a negative value, such as -2 days.
- **Both only exist on a dependency.** You cannot add a lead or lag to an activity on its own. If the links are wrong, the leads and lags will be too, so start with sound [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/).
See our guide to [predecessors and successors](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/predecessors-and-successors/) for how activities are linked before you add leads or lags.

### Lead vs lag at a glance
|  | Lag | Lead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it does | Adds waiting time between linked activities | Overlaps linked activities |
| Notation | Positive value, e.g. FS+3d | Negative value, e.g. FS-2d (a negative lag) |
| Typical reasons | Curing, drying, settling, notice or consultation periods, mandatory waiting times | Starting work on partial output to save time |
| Effect on the path | Lengthens it | Shortens it |
| Uses resources? | No | No (but the overlapped work does) |
| Risk | Low, if the wait is genuine | Higher: the successor starts on incomplete inputs and may need rework |
| Related technique | Physical or contractual constraints | Fast tracking |
A simple way to remember the difference: a lag is a gap on the [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), and a lead is an overlap.

### Leads and lags vs similar terms
The words lead and lag are used in several other ways, and some articles mix them up. In scheduling they have the narrow meaning above. This table separates them from terms they are often confused with.
| Term | What it means | How it differs from a schedule lead or lag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Float (slack) | How long an activity can slip without delaying a successor or the project | Float is calculated from the network; a lag is an input you put into it. See [float and slack](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/). |
| Lead time (supply chain, Lean) | Time from order or request to delivery | A duration of a process, not an overlap. Supplier lead time should be modelled as an activity, not a lag. |
| Leading and lagging indicators | Metrics that predict (leading) or confirm (lagging) performance | Performance measurement, unrelated to dependencies. |
| Buffer or contingency | Time reserved to absorb risk | A buffer is managed and consumed deliberately; hiding it in a lag makes it invisible. See [critical chain](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-chain-project-management/). |
| Duration | Working time an activity takes | Duration belongs to an activity and uses resources; lag belongs to a link and does not. |
| Constraint (e.g. start no earlier than) | A fixed date imposed on an activity | Use a constraint, not a lag, when an external date drives the start. |

### Notation and the four dependency types
Leads and lags can be applied to any of the four dependency types. Schedulers usually write them as the link type followed by the lead or lag, for example FS+3d or SS-1d. Tools often show the predecessor's ID first, such as 4FS+3d.
| Dependency | Meaning | Lag example | Lead example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Finish-to-start (FS) | B starts after A finishes | FS+3d: walls start 3 days after the slab is poured (curing) | FS-2d: testing starts 2 days before development finishes |
| Start-to-start (SS) | B starts after A starts | SS+2d: cable laying starts 2 days after trench digging starts | SS-1d: set-up starts 1 day before training starts (rare; usually remodelled) |
| Finish-to-finish (FF) | B finishes after A finishes | FF+1d: documentation finishes 1 day after the software is finished | FF-1d: a review finishes 1 day before the drafting finishes |
| Start-to-finish (SF) | B finishes after A starts | SF+1d: old system support ends 1 day after the new system goes live | Rarely used |
Some tools also accept leads and lags as a **percentage of the predecessor's duration**. Microsoft's own guidance for Project gives -50% on a finish-to-start link as the way to start the second task when the first is half complete. Percentage lags adjust automatically if the predecessor's duration changes, which can be useful but also makes the logic harder to read.
The link types themselves, and when to use each, are covered in our guide to [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/).

### How to calculate dates with leads and lags
In a forward pass you calculate each activity's early start (ES) and early finish (EF). Leads and lags slot into the standard rules as an extra term. In these formulas a lead is simply a negative lag.
| Link from A to B | Forward pass rule | Then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FS + lag | ES(B) = EF(A) + lag | EF(B) = ES(B) + duration(B) |
| SS + lag | ES(B) = ES(A) + lag | EF(B) = ES(B) + duration(B) |
| FF + lag | EF(B) = EF(A) + lag | ES(B) = EF(B) - duration(B) |
| SF + lag | EF(B) = ES(A) + lag | ES(B) = EF(B) - duration(B) |
If B has several predecessors, work out the date each link requires and take the **latest**. The backward pass mirrors these rules: for an FS link, the late finish of A = late start of B - lag, and so on. Our guide to the [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) covers the full method.

#### Mini calculations
Dates in this guide are counted as elapsed working days from the project start: an activity that starts at day 0 and lasts 10 days finishes at day 10, and a successor with no lag can start at day 10. Take activity A (10 days, day 0 to day 10) and a successor B lasting 4 days:
| Link | B starts | B finishes | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FS (no lag) | Day 10 | Day 14 | Baseline |
| FS+2d | Day 12 | Day 16 | 2-day gap |
| FS-2d (lead) | Day 8 | Day 12 | 2-day overlap |
| SS+3d | Day 3 | Day 7 | B runs alongside A |
| FF+1d | Day 7 | Day 11 | B finishes 1 day after A |

### Worked example: a lag (curing concrete)
In this illustrative example, A **Pour concrete slab** takes 2 days. B **Build walls** takes 5 days and, according to the project's (hypothetical) specification, cannot start until the slab has cured for 3 days.
| Activity | Link | Start | Finish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A Pour slab | - | Day 0 | Day 2 |
| B Build walls | FS+3d from A | Day 5 | Day 10 |
The total is 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 days. Nobody works during days 2 to 5 and the lag carries no cost, but it still sits on the path. If this path is critical, every day of lag is a day on the project end date.

#### Working days or calendar days?
Curing continues over a weekend; most crews do not work one. That is why many tools let you specify a lag in elapsed (calendar) time as well as working time. Suppose the slab is finished at the end of a Wednesday on a Monday-to-Friday calendar:
| Lag type | Lag runs over | Walls can start |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 working days | Thursday, Friday, Monday | Tuesday |
| 3 calendar (elapsed) days | Thursday, Friday, Saturday | Monday (next working day) |
Using the correct unit saves one working day here. The wrong unit either wastes time or, worse, schedules work before a physical process is complete. Always write the unit next to the lag, for example FS+3ed (elapsed days) or FS+3d (working days), and agree with the engineer or supplier which one the requirement means.

### Worked example: a lead (development and testing)
In this illustrative example, C **Develop module** takes 10 days and D **Test module** takes 6 days. The testers agree they can start on features that are already finished 2 days before development ends.
| Link | D starts | D finishes | Time saved |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FS (no lead) | Day 10 | Day 16 | - |
| FS-2d (lead) | Day 8 | Day 14 | 2 days |
Using the lead saves 2 days, but testing now starts on an incomplete module. If a late change in development affects features already tested, some testing must be repeated. Before agreeing a lead, ask what the successor needs to start, whether that partial output will really exist on the day, and what rework would cost if it changes.
There are often clearer ways to model the same overlap. FS-2d on a 10-day predecessor gives the same start date as SS+8d. Better still, split development into two deliverables (for example features 1 to 4 and features 5 to 6) and link testing of the first batch to the first deliverable with a plain FS link. The schedule then shows exactly what testing depends on.

### Worked example: leads and lags in a network and the critical path
This illustrative office fit-out shows how several leads and lags interact and how they affect the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) and float.
| ID | Activity | Duration | Predecessors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Strip out and survey | 4 days | - |
| B | Install partitions | 6 days | A (FS) |
| C | Plaster walls | 5 days | B (SS+2d), B (FF+1d) |
| D | Paint | 3 days | C (FS+2d drying lag) |
| E | Furniture made and delivered (supplier) | 10 days | A (FS) |
| F | Install furniture | 2 days | D (FS), E (FS) |
Plastering can start 2 days after partitions start (SS+2d), because the first rooms are ready, but cannot finish until 1 day after the last partition is in (FF+1d). Paint needs 2 days of drying time after plastering (FS+2d).

#### Forward and backward pass
| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Total float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | 4 | 0 | 4 | 0 |
| B | 4 | 10 | 4 | 10 | 0 |
| C | 6 | 11 | 6 | 11 | 0 |
| D | 13 | 16 | 13 | 16 | 0 |
| E | 4 | 14 | 6 | 16 | 2 |
| F | 16 | 18 | 16 | 18 | 0 |
How the dates were worked out:
1. C: the SS+2d link gives ES = 4 + 2 = 6, so EF = 6 + 5 = 11. The FF+1d link requires EF of at least 10 + 1 = 11, which is met.
2. D: FS+2d gives ES = 11 + 2 = 13, EF = 16.
3. E: FS from A gives ES = 4, EF = 14.
4. F: two predecessors require day 16 (D) and day 14 (E); take the later, so ES = 16 and the project finishes on day 18.
5. Backward pass: F's late start of 16 gives D and E a late finish of 16. C's late finish is D's late start minus the lag: 13 - 2 = 11. E has 16 - 14 = 2 days of float.
The critical path is **A-B-C-D-F**, and it includes the SS+2d overlap and the 2-day drying lag. E has 2 days of float.

#### What-if analysis
| Change | New finish | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drying lag increases from 2 to 3 days | Day 19 (+1) | The lag is on the critical path, so it adds directly to the end date |
| Plastering waits for partitions to finish (plain FS, no overlap) | Day 22 (+4) | C runs day 10 to 15, D day 17 to 20, F day 20 to 22 |
| Supplier needs a 1-day order confirmation period before starting E (FS+1d) | Day 18 (no change) | E now finishes on day 15; its float falls from 2 days to 1 |
The example shows the two rules that matter most: a lag on the critical path moves the end date day for day, and an overlap (a lead, or an SS link with a positive lag) is often what makes a deadline achievable. Our [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) lets you practise this calculation.
See our guide to the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) for the full forward and backward pass procedure.

### How to apply leads and lags step by step
1. **Build the logic first.** Identify every activity and link them with the right dependency types, with no leads or lags yet. Draw a [project network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/) if the logic is complex.
2. **Look for genuine waiting time.** Curing, drying, settling, statutory notice or consultation periods, regulator response times. These are lag candidates.
3. **Check whether the wait is really work.** If someone does something during it (a supplier manufactures, a reviewer reviews), create an activity instead, so it can be resourced and tracked.
4. **Look for safe overlaps.** Where a successor can start on partial output, decide whether a lead, an SS link with a positive lag, or splitting the predecessor models it most clearly.
5. **Agree the value and unit** with the person who knows: the engineer, supplier or team lead. Decide on working or calendar days.
6. **Enter the lead or lag** on the link in your scheduling tool and check the resulting dates on the Gantt chart.
7. **Document the reason** in the activity notes or schedule basis document, for example "FS+7ed: minimum 7-day consultation period".
8. **Recalculate and check the critical path.** Note which leads and lags are on it, because they drive the end date.
9. **Review them at every update.** Leads and lags are static; when actual progress differs from the plan, check they still make sense.

### Entering leads and lags in scheduling software
Most scheduling tools handle leads and lags in a similar way.
- **Microsoft Project:** open the task's Task Information box, go to the Predecessors tab and type a value in the Lag column. Microsoft's guidance is to enter a positive number or percentage for lag (such as 2d) and a negative number or percentage for lead (such as -50%).
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/):** its interactive Gantt charts, available from the Team plan upwards, support all four dependency types with lead and lag time, reschedule successors automatically when a predecessor moves, and show the critical path, float and baselines. That combination makes it a good fit for teams who schedule with real dependency logic rather than simple task lists.
- **[Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/):** premium plans include timeline (Gantt) views and dependencies, and Planner and Project Plan 3 adds the critical path and the Project desktop application for full scheduling.
- **Spreadsheets:** you can model lags with formulas (start = predecessor finish + lag), as in our [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) and [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/), but there is no automatic critical path, so check the logic by hand.
Our guide to [Gantt chart software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/) compares dependency and scheduling features across tools.
Tip
Check how your tool treats lag units. Some default to working days on the task's calendar, and some let you enter elapsed days with a different suffix. A 7-day lag can mean 7 or 9 calendar days depending on the setting.

### Good practice rules for leads and lags
Leads and lags are easy to misuse, which is why formal schedule assessments look at them closely. Two widely used references in project controls are the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) Schedule Assessment Guide and the DCMA 14-point schedule assessment.

#### GAO guidance on lags
- Each lag should be justified by a real reason outside the schedule, and that reason documented.
- Lags should not represent work. Because a lag uses no resources, effort belongs in an activity.
- Procurement and work by external parties should be shown as activities, not lags.
- A lag should not be used to force a fixed start date; use a date constraint such as start no earlier than instead.
- A lag should not be used as a risk buffer, because it stays in the schedule even after the risk it was meant to cover has passed.
- Misused lags can distort float and the critical path.

#### GAO guidance on leads
- Leads should generally be avoided: a lead implies that a future event dictates the timing of an earlier one.
- A lead longer than its successor can produce out-of-sequence logic, where the successor finishes before its predecessor.
- Leads are static, so schedules that rely on them need more manual updating and become less reliable as management tools.
- Instead, use a start-to-start link with a positive lag, or split the predecessor into smaller activities linked finish-to-start.

#### DCMA 14-point thresholds
The DCMA 14-point assessment, as described in schedule analysis tools that implement it, sets two simple targets: **no leads** (negative lags) at all, because they distort total float, and **lags on no more than 5% of relationships**. Even if your project is not subject to these checks, they are useful benchmarks for a schedule review.
See our guide to [float and slack](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) to understand why distorted float misleads decisions.

### Leads, lags and schedule compression
When a project is running late, removing lags and adding leads are among the first options people look at. They belong to two different categories:
- **Adding a lead** (or converting FS links into overlapping SS links) is a form of [fast tracking](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/): doing in parallel what was planned in sequence. It costs little up front but increases rework risk.
- **Removing or shortening a lag** is only valid if the lag was not genuine in the first place, or if you can change the underlying condition, for example using a faster-curing material or agreeing a shorter review period with a regulator. Simply deleting a curing lag does not make concrete cure faster.
- **Crashing**, adding resources to shorten activities, does not change leads or lags at all, because they use no resources.
Only compress activities and links on the critical path; shortening a lag on a path with float saves nothing. Our guide to [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) walks through the options in order of cost and risk.
See our guide to [fast tracking vs crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/) to choose between the two techniques.

### Leads and lags in the PMBOK Guide and exams
Earlier, process-based editions of the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/), such as the 6th edition, listed leads and lags as a tool and technique in the Sequence Activities and Develop Schedule processes. The current 8th edition, published in November 2025, is organised around 6 principles and 7 performance domains rather than detailed processes, but leads and lags remain standard scheduling vocabulary.
For the [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/), whose exam content outline was updated in July 2026, scheduling questions sit mainly in the Process domain (41% of the exam). Expect to:
- Tell a lead from a lag and recognise that a lead is a negative lag.
- Calculate early and late dates on a network that includes lags.
- Distinguish lag (an input) from float (a calculated result).
- Recognise that applying a lead is fast tracking and carries rework risk.
Our [project time management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-time-management/) guide puts leads and lags in the wider context of planning, estimating and controlling the schedule.

### Common mistakes with leads and lags
- **Using lags to represent work**, such as a supplier's manufacturing time or a client's review. Model it as an activity so it can be owned, tracked and reported.
- **Hiding contingency inside lags.** The buffer becomes invisible and is never released. Use a visible buffer or a [contingency plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) instead.
- **Using a lag to hit a date.** If a start is fixed by an external date, use a date constraint or a [milestone](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/).
- **Large leads** that make the logic hard to follow or produce out-of-sequence results. Split the predecessor instead.
- **Forgetting the unit.** Working days and calendar days give different dates, especially around weekends and holidays.
- **Not documenting the reason.** Six months later nobody remembers why there is a 10-day gap, and it is either wrongly removed or wrongly kept.
- **Ignoring leads and lags in progress updates.** A lead assumes partial output will exist by a certain date; if the predecessor is late, the lead may no longer be valid.
- **Confusing lag with float**, for example "using up" lag as if it were spare time. Lag is a requirement; float is flexibility.
- **Changing leads and lags after baselining without change control**, which makes [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) against the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) meaningless.
Tip
Add a notes column to your schedule and write the reason and unit for every lead and lag, for example "FS+3ed: slab curing per structural engineer". It takes seconds and makes every later review faster.
