# PMBOK Guide 8th Edition: Principles, Domains and Processes

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: The PMBOK Guide 8th edition explained: 6 principles, 7 performance domains, 5 focus areas, 40 processes, what changed and how it links to the PMP.


## PMBOK Guide 8th Edition: Principles, Domains and Processes
The PMBOK Guide (A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge) is the Project Management Institute's standard and guide to good practice in project management, and its current edition is the eighth, published in November 2025. It combines six principles, seven performance domains and 40 processes grouped into five focus areas. This guide explains the full structure, what changed from the 6th and 7th editions, and how the book relates to the PMP exam.
- Published 8 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- The PMBOK Guide 8th edition (November 2025) is the current edition; it replaces the 7th edition published in 2021.
- It has six principles, seven performance domains (governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources, risk) and five focus areas containing 40 processes.
- The 8th edition brings back process guidance that the 7th removed, but presents it as non-prescriptive guidance you tailor, not steps you must follow.
- New appendices cover project management offices, artificial intelligence and procurement.
- The PMP exam is built on PMI's July 2026 exam content outline, not on the PMBOK Guide alone; use the book as a reference alongside it.
- PMBOK is a standard, not a methodology: pair it with a way of working such as predictive, Agile, hybrid or PRINCE2.

### What is the PMBOK Guide?
The **PMBOK Guide** is the Project Management Institute's foundational publication on project management. It sets out the principles, performance domains, processes and vocabulary that PMI regards as good practice for most projects, most of the time. It is a standard and reference, not a step-by-step methodology, so you tailor it to each project.
PMBOK stands for **Project Management Body of Knowledge**. The body of knowledge itself is the whole collection of practice in the profession; the Guide is PMI's summary of the generally recognised part of it. The book is published by [PMI, the Project Management Institute](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/), and it is the best-known reference behind PMI's certifications.
Since the 7th edition, one volume contains two documents:
- **The Standard for Project Management**, the formal standard: what a project is, how projects create value, the six principles and project life cycles.
- **The PMBOK Guide** itself: the seven performance domains and their processes, tailoring, and reference chapters on inputs, outputs, tools and techniques, plus appendices.
What it is not: it is not a method that tells you which meeting to hold on which day. Methods such as [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/), Scrum or your organisation's own lifecycle supply that detail. Think of the PMBOK Guide as the map of what a well-run project must cover, and the method as the route you choose.

### The PMBOK Guide 8th edition at a glance
| Item | PMBOK Guide 8th edition |
| --- | --- |
| Full title | A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide), Eighth Edition, and The Standard for Project Management |
| Publisher | Project Management Institute (PMI) |
| Published | November 2025 (digital); the print edition became widely available from January 2026 |
| Length | 408 pages, according to PMI |
| Principles | 6 |
| Performance domains | 7: governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources, risk |
| Focus areas | 5: initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, closing |
| Processes | 40, presented as non-prescriptive guidance |
| Appendices | Contributors, project management offices, artificial intelligence, procurement, evolution of the guide |
| Access | Free digital copy for PMI members; on sale to non-members through PMI and booksellers |
PMI describes the update as refreshing key terms and concepts, consolidating the principles, reintroducing the old process groups as focus areas and bringing technical "how to" guidance back into the performance domains. In short, it keeps the principle-based thinking of the 7th edition and restores much of the practical structure that readers of the 6th edition missed.

### Inside The Standard for Project Management
The Standard is the shorter, more formal half of the book. Its four chapters set the foundations that the rest of the Guide builds on.
| Chapter | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Introduction | Purpose of the Standard, key terms, characteristics of a project, how organisational and project governance connect, and how portfolios, programmes, projects and operations relate |
| 2. A System for Value Delivery | How projects create value, how to assess project success, the project environment (enterprise environmental factors, organisational process assets, structures), product management and project roles |
| 3. Project Management Principles | The project management mindset and the six principles, each with its impact, the principle in action and the performance domains it connects to |
| 4. Project Life Cycles | Phases, predictive, adaptive and hybrid development approaches, how to choose one, delivery cadence, and the five focus areas |
Two ideas from the Standard run through everything else. Projects exist to deliver **value**, judged by benefits as well as time and cost. And the **development approach** is a choice: predictive, as in [waterfall project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/), adaptive, as in [Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/), or a hybrid.

### The six project management principles
The 7th edition had twelve principles. The 8th consolidates them into six, which describe the mindset behind good project management rather than the mechanics. The titles below are the chapter headings in the Standard; some summaries shorten them (for example "embed quality" or "lead accountably").
| Principle | What it means | What it looks like on a project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adopt a holistic view | See the project as a system of interacting parts inside a wider organisation | Checking how a scope change affects cost, risk, people and other projects before approving it |
| Focus on value | Judge work by the benefits it delivers, not only by outputs | Re-testing the business case at each phase gate and stopping work that no longer pays back |
| Embed quality into processes and deliverables | Build quality into how work is done, not just inspect it at the end | Agreeing acceptance criteria before work starts and reviewing early drafts |
| Be an accountable leader | Take ownership of outcomes and lead with integrity, whatever your formal role | Owning a missed milestone openly and setting out the recovery plan |
| Integrate sustainability within all project areas | Weigh environmental, social and economic effects in decisions | Including energy use, supplier practices or long-term running costs in option appraisal |
| Build an empowered culture | Create a team and stakeholder environment where people can collaborate and decide | Delegating decisions to the people closest to the work, with clear boundaries |
Sustainability is the most visible new emphasis; the rest will feel familiar from the 7th edition. Our guide to [project management principles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-principles/) explains the wider set of principles in plain English.

### The seven performance domains
A performance domain is a group of related activities that are critical to delivering project outcomes. In the 8th edition the domains are practical subject areas again, much closer to the old knowledge areas than the 7th edition's more abstract domains. Each domain chapter covers key concepts, its processes, tailoring considerations, interactions with other domains and how to check results.
| Domain | What it covers | Processes | Closest 6th-edition knowledge areas |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Governance | Oversight, decision-making, integrated planning, sourcing strategy, quality assurance, knowledge, change and closure | 9 | Integration; parts of quality and procurement |
| Scope | Requirements, scope definition, the scope structure (such as a WBS), validation and control | 6 | Scope |
| Schedule | Planning, developing and controlling the schedule, whichever approach you use | 3 | Schedule |
| Finance | Cost estimates, budget, funding, reserves and financial control | 4 | Cost |
| Stakeholders | Identifying and engaging stakeholders, and planning and managing communications | 7 | Stakeholder; communications |
| Resources | People and physical resources: planning, estimating, acquiring, leading the team and control | 5 | Resource |
| Risk | Threats and opportunities: planning, identification, analysis, responses and monitoring | 6 | Risk |
Notice what has gone as a separate heading: communications now sits inside stakeholders, quality is both a principle and a governance process, and procurement is a governance process plus a full appendix. Integration has become governance, which is broader: it covers how decisions are made and who makes them, not only how plans fit together. See our guide to [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) for how this works in practice.

### The five focus areas and 40 processes

#### What the focus areas are
The focus areas reuse the names of the old process groups: **initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing**. They describe the type of management attention a project needs at a given moment. They are not phases: on a multi-phase project you initiate, plan, execute, monitor and close within every phase, and monitoring and controlling runs throughout. On an adaptive project the same cycle repeats inside each iteration.

#### The 40 processes by domain and focus area
The table places each process by domain and focus area. Process names follow published summaries of the guide; the allocation to focus areas is our reading of the names, so check the guide itself if you need the exact wording.
| Domain | Initiating | Planning | Executing | Monitoring and controlling | Closing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Governance | Initiate Project or Phase | Integrate and Align Project Plans; Plan Sourcing Strategy | Manage Project Execution; Manage Quality Assurance; Manage Project Knowledge | Monitor and Control Project Performance; Assess and Implement Changes | Close Project or Phase |
| Scope |  | Plan Scope Management; Elicit and Analyze Requirements; Define Scope; Develop Scope Structure |  | Validate Scope; Monitor and Control Scope |  |
| Schedule |  | Plan Schedule Management; Develop Schedule |  | Monitor and Control Schedule |  |
| Finance |  | Plan Financial Management; Estimate Costs; Develop Budget |  | Monitor and Control Finances |  |
| Stakeholders | Identify Stakeholders | Plan Stakeholder Engagement; Plan Communications Management | Manage Stakeholder Engagement; Manage Communications | Monitor Stakeholder Engagement; Monitor Communications |  |
| Resources |  | Plan Resource Management; Estimate Resources | Acquire Resources; Lead the Team | Monitor and Control Resources |  |
| Risk |  | Plan Risk Management; Identify Risks; Perform Risk Analysis; Plan Risk Responses | Implement Risk Responses | Monitor Risks |  |
| **Total** | **2** | **19** | **8** | **10** | **1** |
Planning holds almost half of the processes, as it did in the 6th edition, which reflects the number of subjects that need thinking through, not the share of time planning should take. Compared with the 6th edition's 49 processes, several have been merged: schedule work now has three processes instead of six, and qualitative and quantitative risk analysis have become one Perform Risk Analysis process. Our guide to [project management processes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-processes/) shows the classic 49-process matrix if you need to compare the two.
Tip
Treat the 40 processes as a checklist of decisions, not a list of documents. A two-month internal project might cover Plan Risk Management, Identify Risks and Plan Risk Responses in one hour-long workshop and a [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).

### Tailoring, inputs and outputs, tools and techniques
Three further chapters turn the domains into something you can use.
- **Tailoring (chapter 3)** explains why to tailor, what to tailor (life cycle and development approach, processes, and engagement) and a four-step tailoring process: select the initial development approach, tailor for the organisation, tailor for the project, and implement ongoing improvement. It also covers tailoring each performance domain and diagnostics for spotting where tailoring is needed.
- **Inputs and outputs (chapter 4)** describes the documents and artefacts that processes use and produce, such as the charter, plans, registers and logs.
- **Tools and techniques (chapter 5)** describes the methods used to carry out the processes, from estimating and analysis techniques to meetings and data representation.
This is a middle path between the 6th edition, which attached inputs, tools and techniques and outputs (ITTOs) to every process, and the 7th, which replaced them with a looser section on models, methods and artefacts.

### The appendices: PMOs, AI and procurement
The appendices are where much of the genuinely new material sits.
| Appendix | Topic | What it covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| X1 | Contributors and reviewers | The people who developed and reviewed the edition |
| X2 | Project management offices | The PMO value proposition, customer centricity, PMO types, models and structures, and PMO maturity models |
| X3 | Artificial intelligence | AI in the project context, strategies for AI adoption, the state of the market, common use cases, and responsible use and ethical concerns |
| X4 | Procurement | Buyer and seller roles, make-or-buy decisions, procurement strategy, bid documents, source selection, contract types and claims |
| X5 | Evolution of the PMBOK Guide | The evidence base and research behind the edition, the changes it makes, its sources and how the principles were refined |
The PMO appendix reflects a shift PMI describes from PMOs that enforce process to PMOs that act as customer-focused partners delivering value. If you run or are setting up one, read it with our guide to the [project management office (PMO)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/). The procurement appendix restores much of the contract material that was a full knowledge area in the 6th edition; our guide to [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) covers the same ground step by step.

### What changed: 6th vs 7th vs 8th edition
Many study guides, courses and job adverts still refer to older editions, so it helps to know how they line up.
|  | 6th edition (2017) | 7th edition (2021) | 8th edition (November 2025) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Organised around | Processes | Principles and outcomes | Principles, domains and non-prescriptive processes |
| Principles | None as a list | 12 | 6 |
| Main structure | 10 knowledge areas, 5 process groups | 8 performance domains | 7 performance domains, 5 focus areas |
| Processes | 49, each with ITTOs | Removed from the guide (moved to Process Groups: A Practice Guide, 2022) | 40, as guidance |
| Approaches | Mainly predictive, with Agile considerations | Predictive, adaptive and hybrid | Predictive, adaptive and hybrid |
| Notable additions | Agile content per knowledge area; Agile Practice Guide published alongside | Value delivery system, tailoring, models, methods and artefacts | Sustainability principle, governance and finance domains, appendices on PMOs, AI and procurement |

#### From the 7th to the 8th edition
- **Fewer principles:** twelve became six, with sustainability added as a principle of its own.
- **Different domains:** the 7th edition's domains (stakeholders, team, development approach and life cycle, planning, project work, delivery, measurement, uncertainty) gave way to seven subject-based domains.
- **Processes are back:** 40 processes within five focus areas, after the 7th edition removed process detail from the guide.
- **More practical content:** domain chapters include processes, tailoring and checks, and the reference chapters restore inputs, outputs, tools and techniques.
- **New topics:** PMOs, artificial intelligence and procurement get dedicated appendices.

#### Where the ten knowledge areas went
| 6th-edition knowledge area | Where it sits in the 8th edition |
| --- | --- |
| [Integration](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-integration-management/) | Governance domain (planning, execution, knowledge, change and closure processes) |
| [Scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) | Scope domain |
| [Schedule](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) | Schedule domain |
| [Cost](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-cost-management/) | Finance domain |
| [Quality](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/) | Principle (embed quality) and Manage Quality Assurance in governance |
| [Resource](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-resources/) | Resources domain |
| Communications | Stakeholders domain |
| [Risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) | Risk domain |
| Procurement | Plan Sourcing Strategy in governance, plus Appendix X4 |
| [Stakeholder](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) | Stakeholders domain |

### PMBOK Guide editions history
The body of knowledge grew out of a 1983 PMI report on ethics, standards and accreditation, and PMI dates the body of knowledge itself to 1987. The first edition of the Guide followed in 1996.
| Year | Edition | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1996 | 1st edition | First publication as A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge |
| 2000 | 2nd edition | Updated to reflect growth in practice |
| 2004 | 3rd edition | Inclusion standard moved from "generally accepted" to "generally recognised as good practice" |
| 2008 | 4th edition | Refinements to processes and terminology |
| 2013 | 5th edition | Stakeholder management added as the tenth knowledge area |
| 2017 | 6th edition | 49 processes; Agile considerations added to each knowledge area |
| 2021 | 7th edition | Twelve principles and eight performance domains replace process groups and knowledge areas |
| November 2025 | 8th edition | Six principles, seven domains, five focus areas and 40 processes; appendices on PMOs, AI and procurement |
PMI also publishes companion titles. The most relevant are *Process Groups: A Practice Guide* (2022), which preserved the 49-process model after the 7th edition, and the *Agile Practice Guide*. Our guide to [what PMI is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/) lists PMI's other standards.

### The PMBOK Guide and the PMP exam
The most common question about the PMBOK Guide is whether you need it to pass the [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/). The short answer: it is a key reference, but it is not the syllabus. PMI builds the exam from its **Examination Content Outline (ECO)**, and the current outline took effect in July 2026.
|  | PMBOK Guide 8th edition | PMP exam (from July 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A standard and guide to good practice | A test of how you would act in realistic situations |
| Structure | 6 principles, 7 domains, 5 focus areas, 40 processes | 3 domains: People 33%, Process 41%, Business Environment 26% |
| Approaches | Predictive, adaptive and hybrid | Predictive, Agile and hybrid scenarios across all domains |
| Role in study | Background, vocabulary and concepts | Defines what you are tested on |
The 8th edition fits the new exam well: its governance, finance and sustainability material overlaps with the much larger Business Environment domain, and its stakeholder and resources domains support People questions. But the exam rewards judgement, so reading the Guide cover to cover is far less useful than practising scenario questions.

#### How to study the PMBOK Guide for the PMP
1. Download the current PMP Examination Content Outline from pmi.org and read it first.
2. Check eligibility: 35 contact hours or an active CAPM, plus three, four or five years of experience within the last 10 years depending on your education (two with a GAC-accredited degree).
3. Book training from a PMI Authorized Training Partner if you need live hours: from 1 December 2026 only approved providers count. See our guide to [35 contact hours for the PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/35-contact-hours-pmp/).
4. Read the Standard's principles and life cycle chapters and the seven domain chapters; skim the reference chapters and appendices.
5. Map each ECO task to the domains and processes that support it, and note any gaps your course covers.
6. Spend most of your time on full-length, timed practice exams built on the 2026 outline.
If you are earlier in your career, the [CAPM certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) tests foundational knowledge and is a common first step.

### Worked example: applying PMBOK 8 to a project
This illustrative example shows how the principles, domains and focus areas work together on one project. The organisation and figures are invented.
A regional insurer is replacing its customer relationship management (CRM) system. The project has a budget of £300,000, six months to go-live and about 85 users in sales and customer service. The project manager chooses a **hybrid approach**: a predictive plan for the contract, data migration and cut-over, and two-week iterations for configuring screens and workflows with users.

#### Step 1: apply the principles
- **Holistic view:** the CRM touches billing and the call-centre telephony, so both teams join the design reviews.
- **Value:** success is defined as cutting average call handling time and giving sales a single customer view, not just "system live by 30 June".
- **Quality:** acceptance criteria for each workflow are agreed before configuration starts.
- **Sustainability:** the option appraisal compares hosting energy use and the supplier's support commitments alongside price.

#### Step 2: work through the domains
| Domain | Key question | What the project manager did |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Governance | Who decides, and how do changes get approved? | Signed [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/), steering group every four weeks, change threshold of £10,000 or two weeks |
| Scope | What exactly is in and out? | Requirements workshops, scope statement, WBS for migration and cut-over, product backlog for configuration |
| Schedule | When will it be done? | Milestone plan for the predictive work, iteration calendar for configuration |
| Finance | What will it cost and how is it funded? | Budget with a 10% contingency reserve held by the sponsor |
| Stakeholders | Who is affected and how will we engage them? | Stakeholder map, fortnightly demos, communications plan for go-live |
| Resources | Who and what do we need? | Two super-users seconded from each department, supplier consultants for eight weeks |
| Risk | What could go wrong or better? | Risk register; top threat is poor data quality, so a trial migration is scheduled in month two |

#### Step 3: tailor the processes by focus area
| Focus area | Processes used in full | Processes kept light |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiating | Initiate Project or Phase; Identify Stakeholders | None |
| Planning | Plan Sourcing Strategy; Develop Budget; Identify Risks; Plan Risk Responses | Plan Schedule Management (one page); Plan Communications Management (folded into the stakeholder plan) |
| Executing | Manage Project Execution; Lead the Team; Implement Risk Responses | Manage Project Knowledge (a shared lessons log) |
| Monitoring and controlling | Assess and Implement Changes; Monitor and Control Finances; Validate Scope | Monitor Communications (checked at steering group) |
| Closing | Close Project or Phase, including supplier contract closure and lessons learned | None |
The result covers every domain without 40 documents. Work management platforms such as [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) can hold the predictive milestones and the iteration boards in one place, with dependencies and dashboards for the steering group.

### How to use the PMBOK Guide step by step
Whether or not you are studying for an exam, the Guide is most useful as a checklist and shared vocabulary. A practical routine:
1. **Choose the development approach** using the Standard's life cycle chapter: predictive, adaptive or hybrid.
2. **Check what is mandatory** in your organisation: governance gates, PMO standards, contract or regulatory requirements.
3. **Walk the seven domains** and write down, for each, the key decisions this project needs.
4. **Pick the processes** from the 40 that each decision needs, and decide how formal each one should be.
5. **Record your tailoring** in the project management plan so the sponsor and team know what to expect.
6. **Use the principles as a test** at each phase gate: are we still delivering value, leading accountably and building quality in?
7. **Review and adjust** the process set when risk, size or stakeholders change.
Read our overview of [project management methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-methodologies/) to choose the way of working that sits on top of the PMBOK Guide.

### PMBOK, PRINCE2 and Agile
The PMBOK Guide is often compared with methods, but it does a different job. PRINCE2 is a process-based method that tells you how to direct and manage a project in stages; Scrum is an Agile framework for delivering in short iterations; the PMBOK Guide describes what a well-run project must address, whatever method you use. Many organisations use PRINCE2 or an Agile framework as the method and the PMBOK Guide as the wider body of knowledge. See our guide to [PMBOK vs PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-vs-prince2/) for a detailed comparison.

### How to get the PMBOK Guide
PMI members can download a free digital copy of the PMBOK Guide and PMI's other standards as a membership benefit, and PMIstandards+ offers searchable online access. Non-members can buy print or digital copies from PMI's store and major booksellers, and translations are available in several languages. Check that you are buying the eighth edition: listings for the 6th and 7th editions are still common.

### Common mistakes with the PMBOK Guide
- **Studying from an old edition only.** The 6th edition's 49 processes and the 7th edition's domains are both out of date. Use the 8th edition with materials built on the 2026 exam outline.
- **Treating it as a methodology.** It tells you what to cover, not how to run your Monday stand-up. You still need to choose and tailor an approach.
- **Running every process.** The 40 processes are options. Using all of them on a small project wastes time and frustrates the team.
- **Confusing focus areas with phases.** Initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing repeat within each phase or iteration.
- **Memorising instead of applying.** Exams and real projects both reward judgement. Practise using the domains on a real or illustrative project.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does PMBOK stand for?**
Project Management Body of Knowledge. The full title of PMI's book is A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide).

**Q: What is the latest edition of the PMBOK Guide?**
The eighth edition, published by PMI in November 2025. It replaced the seventh edition from 2021.

**Q: What are the six principles in PMBOK 8?**
Adopt a holistic view; focus on value; embed quality into processes and deliverables; be an accountable leader; integrate sustainability within all project areas; and build an empowered culture.

**Q: What are the seven performance domains in the PMBOK Guide 8th edition?**
Governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources and risk.

**Q: How many processes are in the PMBOK Guide 8th edition?**
40, presented as non-prescriptive guidance and grouped into five focus areas: initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing. Planning holds 19 of them.

**Q: Are the process groups back in PMBOK 8?**
In effect, yes. The five process groups return as five focus areas with the same names, after the 7th edition removed process detail from the guide.

**Q: What happened to the ten knowledge areas?**
They were replaced by seven performance domains. Most map directly; integration became governance, communications moved into stakeholders, cost became finance, and quality and procurement are covered by governance processes, a principle and an appendix.

**Q: Is PMBOK a methodology?**
No. It is a standard and guide to good practice. Methodologies such as PRINCE2 or Scrum describe how to do the work; the PMBOK Guide describes what good practice covers.

**Q: Is the PMP exam based on the PMBOK Guide 8th edition?**
The exam is based on PMI's Examination Content Outline, updated in July 2026. The PMBOK Guide is one of several references, so study it alongside the outline and scenario-based practice questions.

**Q: Is the PMBOK Guide free?**
PMI members get a free digital copy as a membership benefit. Non-members usually buy it from PMI or a bookseller.

**Q: Does the PMBOK Guide cover Agile?**
Yes. The 8th edition covers predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches and includes tailoring guidance for each. PMI also publishes a separate Agile Practice Guide.

**Q: What is the difference between PMBOK and PMP?**
PMBOK is the body of knowledge and PMI's guide to it; the PMP is a certification awarded by PMI to people who meet the experience and training requirements and pass the exam.

**Q: Is the PMBOK Guide used outside the US?**
Yes. It is used worldwide, particularly in the Americas, the Middle East and Asia. In the UK it is often used alongside PRINCE2 or the APM Body of Knowledge.

# PMBOK vs PRINCE2: Key Differences and Which to Choose

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-vs-prince2/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: PMBOK vs PRINCE2 compared for 2026: standard vs method, PMBOK 8 vs PRINCE2 7, roles, processes, documents, PMP vs PRINCE2 certification and how to choose.


## PMBOK vs PRINCE2: Key Differences and Which to Choose
PMBOK vs PRINCE2 is less a contest than a comparison of two different kinds of guidance: the PMBOK Guide is a standard that describes what good project management covers, while PRINCE2 is a method that tells you how to direct, manage and deliver a project. This guide compares the current editions (the PMBOK Guide eighth edition and PRINCE2 7), shows how they map to each other, and helps you choose between the PMP and PRINCE2 certifications.
- Published 10 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 15 min read

### Key takeaways
- The PMBOK Guide (PMI) is a non-prescriptive standard; PRINCE2 (PeopleCert) is a prescriptive, stage-based method.
- PMBOK explains what to consider; PRINCE2 defines who decides what, when, and with which documents.
- The current editions are the PMBOK Guide eighth edition (November 2025) and PRINCE2 7 (2023).
- They complement each other: many teams run PRINCE2 governance and use PMBOK techniques inside it.
- Choose a certification by region, sector and experience: the PMP needs years of experience, PRINCE2 Foundation does not.

### What is the difference between PMBOK and PRINCE2?
**The main difference between PMBOK and PRINCE2 is that the PMBOK Guide is a standard and body of knowledge, while PRINCE2 is a project management method.** PMBOK describes the principles, performance domains and practices that good project management should cover, without telling you exactly how to run a project. PRINCE2 gives you a defined set of roles, stages, processes and management products to follow and tailor.
A simple way to remember it: PMBOK is the reference book that explains the whole subject, and PRINCE2 is the operating manual for running one project in a controlled way. That is why they are not really competitors. A project manager can use PRINCE2 to organise governance and decision-making, and draw on PMBOK guidance for scheduling, cost, risk and stakeholder work inside each stage.
Both are owned by different organisations: the [Project Management Institute (PMI)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/) publishes the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/), and PeopleCert owns [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) (it acquired AXELOS, the previous owner, in 2021).

### PMBOK vs PRINCE2 at a glance
|  | PMBOK Guide | PRINCE2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | Standard and body of knowledge | Project management method |
| Owner | Project Management Institute (PMI), USA | PeopleCert (originally UK government) |
| Current edition | Eighth edition, published November 2025 | PRINCE2 7, published 2023 |
| Core structure | Six principles and seven performance domains, plus process guidance | Five integrated elements: 7 principles, people, 7 practices, 7 processes, project context |
| Prescriptive? | No: describes what to consider | Yes: defines roles, processes and products, which you tailor |
| Lifecycle | Not fixed; predictive, adaptive or hybrid | Managed in stages with formal decision points |
| Governance | Assumes governance is set by the organisation | Defines a project board and management by exception |
| Main focus | Breadth of knowledge, value delivery, leadership | Business justification, control, accountability |
| Documents | Examples given; not mandated | Defined management products (business case, PID, logs, registers, reports) |
| Certifications | PMP, CAPM and other PMI credentials | PRINCE2 7 Foundation and Practitioner |
| Often seen in | North America, Middle East, Asia, multinationals | UK, Europe, Australia, public sector |
Regional patterns are general tendencies, not rules. Many employers, especially multinationals and consultancies, list both qualifications in the same job advert.

### What is the PMBOK Guide?
*A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge* (the PMBOK Guide) is PMI's flagship standard. It collects generally recognised good practice so that project professionals share a common vocabulary and understanding. It deliberately avoids prescribing one way of working: you are expected to tailor its guidance to your project, organisation and delivery approach.

#### The PMBOK Guide eighth edition
PMI published the eighth edition in November 2025. According to PMI, it keeps the principle-based structure introduced in the seventh edition but simplifies it, and it reintroduces process guidance in what PMI calls an evolved, non-prescriptive way. It also expands coverage of AI, project management offices and procurement.
| Six principles (8th edition) | Seven performance domains (8th edition) |
| --- | --- |
| Adopt a holistic view | Governance |
| Focus on value | Scope |
| Embed quality into processes and deliverables | Schedule |
| Be an accountable leader | Finance |
| Integrate sustainability | Stakeholders |
| Build an empowered culture | Resources |
|  | Risk |

#### How the PMBOK Guide has changed
Study guides and older articles still describe earlier editions, which is a common source of confusion when comparing PMBOK with PRINCE2.
| Edition | Year | Structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sixth | 2017 | Five process groups, ten knowledge areas and 49 processes, each with inputs, tools and techniques, and outputs |
| Seventh | 2021 | Twelve principles and eight performance domains; processes removed from the main standard |
| Eighth | 2025 | Six principles and seven performance domains, with process guidance reintroduced in a non-prescriptive form |
If you are comparing knowledge areas with PRINCE2 themes, you are comparing the PMBOK sixth edition with PRINCE2 2017. Both have since been replaced. Our [project management processes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-processes/) guide explains the classic process groups if your course still uses them.

### What is PRINCE2?
PRINCE2 (PRojects IN Controlled Environments) is a structured method for directing, managing and delivering projects. It was first published in 1996 by the UK government's CCTA and is now owned by PeopleCert. It is used across many sectors, and it remains particularly common in UK [government project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/government-project-management/).
PRINCE2 splits a project into management stages. A project board authorises each stage, sets tolerances, and steps in only when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. The project manager runs the project day to day, and team managers deliver the specialist products.

#### The five integrated elements of PRINCE2 7
- **Principles:** seven guiding obligations. A project is only a PRINCE2 project if all seven are applied.
- **People:** leadership, culture, communication and relationships, which PRINCE2 7 brought to the centre of the method.
- **Practices:** aspects of project management applied throughout the project.
- **Processes:** the activities from start-up to closure, and who does them.
- **Project context:** how you tailor the method to the project's environment, scale and delivery approach.

#### PRINCE2 principles, practices and processes
| 7 principles | 7 practices | 7 processes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ensure continued business justification | Business case | Starting up a project |
| Learn from experience | Organising | Directing a project |
| Define roles, responsibilities and relationships | Plans | Initiating a project |
| Manage by stages | Quality | Controlling a stage |
| Manage by exception | Risk | Managing product delivery |
| Focus on products | Issues | Managing a stage boundary |
| Tailor to suit the project | Progress | Closing a project |
PRINCE2 lets you tailor processes, practices, roles and management products, but not the principles.

### Key differences between PMBOK and PRINCE2

#### 1. Standard versus method
PMBOK tells you what areas of project work need attention and what good practice looks like. PRINCE2 tells you how to organise and control a specific project. This is why PMBOK covers more techniques (for example estimating, earned value or the critical path) while PRINCE2 focuses on decisions, responsibilities and controls.

#### 2. Governance and roles
PMBOK places the project manager at the centre and treats [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) as something the organisation provides, now covered in its own governance performance domain. PRINCE2 defines the governance itself: a **project board** made up of the project executive (who owns the business case), the senior user (who represents those who will use the outputs) and the senior supplier (who represents those building them). It also defines project assurance, change authority, project support and team manager roles.

#### 3. Lifecycle and stages
PMBOK does not impose a lifecycle; it discusses predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches and leaves the choice to you. PRINCE2 always works in management stages: the board approves one stage at a time, using the end-stage report and the next stage plan. This gives sponsors regular go/no-go points and limits how much money is committed at once.

#### 4. Documentation
PMBOK gives examples of artefacts, such as the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/), [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) and project management plan, but does not mandate them. PRINCE2 defines management products, including the business case, [project initiation documentation (PID)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-initiation-document/), issue and risk registers, the daily log, lessons log and highlight reports. In PRINCE2 7 these can be held in whatever form suits the project, including a digital tool rather than separate documents.

#### 5. The project manager's authority
In PMBOK the project manager's authority depends on the organisation and the project. In PRINCE2 the project manager has clear but bounded authority: they act within the time, cost, scope, quality, benefit and risk tolerances the board sets, and escalate an exception report if a tolerance is threatened.

#### 6. Business justification and value
Both care about value, but they express it differently. The PMBOK Guide makes 'focus on value' a principle and covers benefits in its finance and governance domains. PRINCE2 turns it into a rule: the project must stay justified by its business case at every stage, or it should be stopped.

#### 7. Agile and tailoring
Since the seventh edition, PMBOK has treated predictive and adaptive approaches as equals. PRINCE2 7 includes guidance on using the method with agile delivery, and PeopleCert also offers PRINCE2 Agile as a separate qualification.
Tip
When someone says a project is 'run using PMBOK', they usually mean it follows PMI's processes and terminology, often in a predictive way. PMBOK itself does not require any particular process or lifecycle.

### Similarities between PMBOK and PRINCE2
The two have more in common than the debate suggests:
- Both are **principle-based** and expect you to tailor them rather than apply them mechanically.
- Both support **predictive, agile and hybrid** delivery in their current editions.
- Both emphasise **value and benefits**, not just delivering on time and budget.
- Both cover **risk, quality, planning, stakeholders and change control** in depth. Our guide to [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) applies to either.
- Both expect you to **learn from experience** and capture [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).
- Both are maintained by **global bodies** with certification schemes and are updated regularly.
Neither guarantees success. Results depend on how well the project manager applies the guidance, engages stakeholders and adapts to the situation, which both bodies acknowledge.

### How PMBOK and PRINCE2 map to each other
There is no official one-to-one mapping, but the following tables show where each topic is mainly covered. Use them as an approximate guide when you are translating between the two vocabularies.

#### PMBOK performance domains and PRINCE2 practices
| PMBOK 8th edition domain | Closest PRINCE2 7 coverage |
| --- | --- |
| Governance | Organising practice, project board, management by exception, Directing a project |
| Scope | Plans practice (product-based planning), Quality practice (product descriptions) |
| Schedule | Plans practice, Progress practice |
| Finance | Business case practice, cost tolerances |
| Stakeholders | Organising practice (communication management approach), People element |
| Resources | Plans practice, team managers and work packages |
| Risk | Risk practice; issues and change in the Issues practice |

#### Classic PMBOK process groups and PRINCE2 processes
| PMBOK process group (6th edition) | PRINCE2 processes |
| --- | --- |
| Initiating | Starting up a project; Directing a project (authorise initiation) |
| Planning | Initiating a project; Managing a stage boundary |
| Executing | Managing product delivery |
| Monitoring and controlling | Controlling a stage; Directing a project |
| Closing | Closing a project |
The biggest gap in the mapping is the board level. PMBOK has no direct equivalent of the Directing a project process, which runs across the whole PRINCE2 lifecycle.

### Using PMBOK and PRINCE2 together
Because they answer different questions, the two combine well. A common pattern is to use PRINCE2 for structure and governance and PMBOK for the techniques inside each stage.
**Example: a council replacing its case management system.** The council uses PRINCE2 for governance. The project board (a director as executive, a service manager as senior user and the supplier's account director as senior supplier) approves the business case and the project initiation documentation, then authorises the project stage by stage. Inside each stage, the project manager uses PMBOK-style techniques: a work breakdown structure and critical path schedule, cost estimating, a stakeholder engagement plan and quantitative risk analysis. The supplier's development team works in sprints within each stage.
1. Agree the governance model: board roles, stage boundaries and tolerances (PRINCE2).
2. Write a business case the board can review at each stage boundary (PRINCE2, supported by PMBOK finance guidance).
3. Plan each stage with PMBOK techniques for scope, schedule, resources and cost.
4. Manage risks, issues and changes with registers and agreed thresholds (both).
5. Report progress with highlight reports and escalate exceptions (PRINCE2).
6. Close the project, hand over and record lessons (both).
Free templates help here: start with our [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/), [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) and [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).

### PMP vs PRINCE2 certification
Most people searching for PMBOK vs PRINCE2 are really choosing a qualification. The PMBOK Guide is one of the references behind PMI's [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) and [CAPM certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/); PRINCE2 has its own Foundation and Practitioner exams.
|  | PMP (PMI) | PRINCE2 7 Foundation | PRINCE2 7 Practitioner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tests | Experience-based project management across people, process and business environment | Knowledge of the PRINCE2 method | Applying and tailoring PRINCE2 to a scenario |
| Experience needed | 3 years with a bachelor's degree, 4 with an associate's degree, 5 with a secondary diploma (2 with a PMI-accredited degree) | None | None, but you need a prerequisite qualification |
| Training or prerequisite | 35 hours of project management education, or an active CAPM | None required (most people take a course) | PRINCE2 Foundation, or a recognised qualification such as PMP, CAPM or IPMA Levels A–D |
| Exam | 180 questions in 240 minutes | Multiple-choice, closed book | Open book (official manual only), scenario-based |
| Keeping it | 60 PDUs every three years | Check PeopleCert's current rules | Valid three years; renew by exam or CPD |
PMI introduced an updated PMP exam on 9 July 2026. It is based on the 2026 Examination Content Outline, which gives more weight to the business environment domain. Training providers note that the exam is built from that outline, not from any single edition of the PMBOK Guide, so you will study several references.
PRINCE2 Foundation is the faster route to a recognised credential: no experience is required and many people complete a course and the exam within a week. The PMP takes longer to qualify for and prepare for, but it signals several years of real project experience. Our [project management certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) compares these with other options.

### PMBOK or PRINCE2: which should you choose?
There is no universally better choice. Use your situation to decide.
| Your situation | Our suggestion |
| --- | --- |
| You are new to project management and want a quick, recognised qualification in the UK or Europe | PRINCE2 7 Foundation, then add the CAPM or PMP as you gain experience |
| You have three or more years leading projects and want a globally recognised credential | PMP |
| You work in UK central or local government, or for its suppliers | PRINCE2 Foundation and Practitioner are frequently requested |
| You work in North America, the Middle East or for a US-headquartered company | PMP is usually the stronger signal |
| You work in agile software teams | Either, plus an agile qualification; consider PRINCE2 Agile if your organisation uses PRINCE2 governance |
| You already hold the PMP and move to a PRINCE2 organisation | You can go straight to PRINCE2 Practitioner, as PeopleCert accepts the PMP as a prerequisite |

#### Choosing for your organisation
If you are setting standards for a team or [PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/), the question changes. PRINCE2 gives you a ready-made governance model, consistent roles and document set, which suits organisations with many similar projects, external suppliers or public accountability. The PMBOK Guide gives you a broad reference for building your own method and developing project managers' skills. Many organisations adopt PRINCE2-style stage gates and roles and train their people against PMI's standards. Our guide to [project management methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-methodologies/) compares the wider options.
Tip
Before you pay for a course, search job adverts for your target role and region. Count how often each qualification appears. That evidence is more useful than any general comparison.

### Common misconceptions about PMBOK and PRINCE2
- **'PMBOK is a methodology.'** It is a standard and guide. PMI says it should be tailored and does not prescribe a lifecycle.
- **'PRINCE2 is only for waterfall projects.'** Stages are management stages, not technical phases, and PRINCE2 7 covers agile delivery. Read our [Waterfall guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) for the difference.
- **'PRINCE2 means lots of paperwork.'** Management products can be combined, simplified or held in a tool, as long as the principles are applied.
- **'PMBOK still has ten knowledge areas.'** That was the sixth edition (2017). The current edition uses principles and seven performance domains.
- **'You must pick one.'** Many project managers hold both qualifications and use both bodies of guidance.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the main difference between PMBOK and PRINCE2?**
The PMBOK Guide is a standard that describes what good project management covers, while PRINCE2 is a method that defines roles, stages, processes and documents for running a project. PMBOK is descriptive; PRINCE2 is prescriptive, though it must be tailored.

**Q: Is PMBOK a methodology?**
No. PMI describes the PMBOK Guide as a standard and guide, not a methodology. It sets out principles, performance domains and practices that you tailor to build or improve your own way of working.

**Q: Is PRINCE2 better than PMP?**
Neither is better in general. PRINCE2 certifies knowledge of one method and is widely requested in the UK, Europe and the public sector. The PMP certifies experienced project managers against PMI's standards and is widely recognised internationally. Choose based on your region, sector and experience.

**Q: Which is easier, PMP or PRINCE2?**
PRINCE2 Foundation is generally quicker: there is no experience requirement and many people pass after a short course. The PMP requires several years of project experience, 35 hours of training and a 180-question exam, so it takes longer to prepare for.

**Q: Can you use PMBOK and PRINCE2 together?**
Yes. A common approach is to use PRINCE2 for governance (the project board, stages, tolerances and reports) and PMBOK guidance for techniques such as scheduling, estimating, stakeholder engagement and risk analysis within each stage.

**Q: What is the latest version of PMBOK and PRINCE2?**
The PMBOK Guide eighth edition, published by PMI in November 2025, and PRINCE2 7, published by PeopleCert in 2023.

**Q: Do I need experience for PRINCE2 or the PMP?**
PRINCE2 Foundation needs no experience. PRINCE2 Practitioner needs a prerequisite qualification such as PRINCE2 Foundation or the PMP. The PMP needs three to five years of project experience depending on your education, plus 35 hours of training or an active CAPM.

**Q: Should I get PRINCE2 if I already have the PMP?**
It can help if you work in the UK, Europe or the public sector, or for organisations that use PRINCE2 governance. PMP holders can usually take the PRINCE2 Practitioner exam without first passing Foundation, because PeopleCert accepts the PMP as a prerequisite.

**Q: Is PRINCE2 Agile?**
PRINCE2 is not an agile framework in itself, but PRINCE2 7 explains how to apply it with agile delivery, and PRINCE2 Agile is a separate qualification that combines PRINCE2 governance with agile ways of working. See [PRINCE2 vs Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/prince2-vs-agile/).

**Q: Who owns PMBOK and PRINCE2?**
The Project Management Institute (PMI) owns the PMBOK Guide. PeopleCert owns PRINCE2, having acquired AXELOS, which previously managed it on behalf of the UK government, in 2021.

**Q: Is PRINCE2 still relevant?**
Yes. It was updated to PRINCE2 7 in 2023 with more emphasis on people, tailoring and digital working, and it remains widely used, particularly in UK government and organisations that need clear governance and accountability.

**Q: Is the PMP exam based on the PMBOK Guide eighth edition?**
Not directly. The PMP exam is built from PMI's Examination Content Outline; a new version based on the 2026 outline started on 9 July 2026. The PMBOK Guide is one important reference among several.

**Q: Which is more popular in the UK, PMP or PRINCE2?**
PRINCE2 has long been one of the most widely requested project management qualifications in the UK, especially in the public sector. The PMP and APM qualifications are also common, so check job adverts in your sector.

### Related guides
