# PMP Certification: Requirements, 2026 Exam, Cost and Prep

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: PMP certification guide for 2026: eligibility, the 35 hours and new training rule, the July 2026 exam, fees, how to apply, a study plan and renewal.


## PMP Certification: Requirements, 2026 Exam, Cost and Prep
PMP certification (Project Management Professional) is the Project Management Institute's flagship credential for experienced project managers: you need three to five years of project leadership within the last 10 years, depending on your education, plus 35 hours of project management training, and you must pass a 180-question exam. PMI launched a new version of the exam on 9 July 2026, and from 1 December 2026 live training only counts if it comes from an approved provider. This guide explains the requirements, the new exam, the costs, the application step by step, a 12-week study plan with sample questions, and how to keep the PMP active.
- Published 3 October 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- You need project leadership experience within the last 10 years: five years with a secondary diploma, four with an associate's degree, three with a bachelor's degree, or two with a degree from a PMI GAC-accredited programme.
- You also need 35 hours of project management training or an active CAPM. From 1 December 2026, live instructor-led training only counts if it comes from a PMI Authorized Training Partner or an eligible accredited programme.
- The exam launched on 9 July 2026 has 180 questions in 240 minutes, weighted People 33%, Process 41% and Business Environment 26%.
- Fees are widely reported as US$425 for PMI members and US$675 for non-members in the US (checked 25 October 2026); confirm the price at checkout.
- Most candidates study for two to three months; practise scenario questions and full timed exams, not only definitions.
- The PMP lasts three years. Renew it by earning 60 PDUs and paying the renewal fee.

### What is PMP certification?
**PMP certification is a professional credential awarded by the Project Management Institute (PMI) to project managers who meet its education and experience rules and pass the PMP exam.** It shows that you can lead projects using predictive, Agile and hybrid approaches, manage people and stakeholders, and connect project work to business outcomes. It is valid for three years and renewed through continuing education.
PMI is a not-for-profit professional association rather than a regulator, so the PMP is voluntary. It is, however, one of the credentials most often named in project manager job adverts. Our guide to [what PMI is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/) explains the organisation behind it and its other 12 certifications.

#### Who the PMP suits, and who should wait
- **Good fit:** you have led projects for at least three years and want a credential recognised across industries and countries, or you hold the CAPM and now have the experience to step up.
- **Wait or choose another route:** you are new to project work (consider the [CAPM certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/)), your target employers mainly ask for [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/), or your role is purely Scrum-based.
If you are still comparing options, our overview of [project management certifications](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) sets the PMP alongside PRINCE2, APM, Scrum and Agile credentials.

### PMP certification requirements
According to PMI's PMP page (checked 25 October 2026), you need one combination of education and experience from the table, plus the training requirement. The experience must be professional, gained within the last 10 years, and overlapping projects cannot be counted twice.
| Your highest education | Project management experience (within 10 years) | Training |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Secondary diploma (high school, GED or global equivalent) | 5 years (60 months) | 35 hours, or an active CAPM |
| Associate's degree or vocational/trade school diploma | 4 years (48 months) | 35 hours, or an active CAPM |
| Bachelor's degree or higher | 3 years (36 months) | 35 hours, or an active CAPM |
| Bachelor's or postgraduate degree from a PMI GAC-accredited programme | 2 years (24 months) | 35 hours, or an active CAPM |
GAC is PMI's Global Accreditation Center, which accredits university project management degrees.

#### What counts as project management experience
PMI is looking for time spent **leading and directing** projects, not simply working on them. You do not need the job title "project manager", but your role must involve responsibility for parts of the project life cycle. Activities that usually count include:
- Defining scope and objectives, or writing a [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/).
- Managing schedules, budgets, risks and resources.
- Leading a team, engaging stakeholders and managing changes.
- Leading Agile delivery or closing a project with handover and lessons learned.
Pure technical work with no coordination role, and routine operations, usually do not count on their own.

#### Worked example: counting non-overlapping months
**Ben** has a vocational diploma, so he needs 48 months of experience gained between October 2016 and his application date in October 2026. He lists four projects:
| Project | Dates | Months | Counted months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Office move (lead coordinator) | Mar 2015 to Feb 2016 | 12 | 0 (outside the 10-year window) |
| CRM roll-out (project lead) | Jan 2018 to Dec 2019 | 24 | 24 |
| Data migration (project lead) | Jun 2019 to Mar 2021 | 22 | 15 (Jun to Dec 2019 overlaps the CRM project) |
| New site opening (project manager) | Sep 2022 to Aug 2024 | 24 | 24 |
| **Total** |  | 82 | **63** |
Ben has 63 qualifying months, comfortably above 48. The key points are that the office move is too old, and the seven months in 2019 when he ran two projects at once count only once.

#### The 35 hours of training
You need 35 hours (often called contact hours) of project management education, completed before you apply. An active CAPM meets this requirement on its own. Qualifying routes include PMI's own on-demand PMP Exam Prep course, a self-paced course from any organisation, a live course from an approved provider, or relevant modules in an accredited academic programme. Our guide to [35 contact hours for the PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/35-contact-hours-pmp/) explains what counts and how to document it.

### The 1 December 2026 training rule
PMI has changed which live training counts towards the 35 hours. From **1 December 2026**, live instructor-led classes (in person or virtual) only count if they are delivered by a **PMI Authorized Training Partner (ATP)**, a China Registered Education Provider (REP) or an eligible accredited higher education programme, including PMI GAC programmes. Self-paced, on-demand courses can still come from any organisation, and PMI says training completed before 1 December 2026 remains eligible under the previous rules.
| Your situation | Does it count? |
| --- | --- |
| Self-paced online course from any provider, any date | Yes |
| Live course from any provider, completed before 1 December 2026 | Yes, under the previous rules; keep the certificate |
| Live course from a PMI Authorized Training Partner, any date | Yes |
| Live course from a non-ATP provider, taken on or after 1 December 2026 | No |
| Project management modules in a GAC-accredited or other eligible accredited degree | Yes |
| An active CAPM certification | Yes, it replaces the 35 hours |
Tip
If you are booking a live boot camp that starts in late November and finishes in December, ask the provider whether it is a PMI Authorized Training Partner before you pay. PMI's ATP directory on pmi.org lets you check.
The rule does not change the experience rules, the exam or renewal.

### The PMP exam in 2026
The current exam is based on PMI's 2026 PMP Examination Content Outline (ECO). The format, as described by PMI and the ECO:
| Item | Current PMP exam (from 9 July 2026) |
| --- | --- |
| Questions | 180: 170 scored and 10 unscored pretest questions mixed in |
| Time | 240 minutes, with two 10-minute breaks |
| Domains | People 33%, Process 41%, Business Environment 26% |
| Approaches | About 40% predictive; the rest Agile/adaptive and hybrid, spread across all domains |
| Delivery | Pearson VUE test centre (PMI recommends this) or online proctored |
| Languages | 15, including English, Arabic, French, German and Spanish |
| Attempts | Up to three within your one-year eligibility period |

#### What changed on 9 July 2026
The last date to sit the previous (2021) version was 8 July 2026. The biggest change is the weight given to the business context of projects.
| Domain | 2021 exam | 2026 exam | Approximate scored questions (2026) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| People | 42% | 33% | About 56 |
| Process | 50% | 41% | About 70 |
| Business Environment | 8% | 26% | About 44 |
The approximate counts apply the weights to the 170 scored questions; PMI notes that exact numbers vary by exam form. The exam is also 10 minutes longer and has two breaks instead of one. PMI says the update puts more emphasis on outcomes, value and business impact. If you studied from 2021 materials, add governance, compliance, change and organisational change topics.

#### Question types
The 2026 ECO lists two new formats: **case or scenario** questions (a longer scenario followed by several questions) and **graphic-based** questions (interpreting charts, dashboards or artefacts). These sit alongside multiple choice, multiple response, matching, point and click (hotspot) and pull-down list items.
According to the ECO, the first break comes after the case-study section and the second roughly half way through the remaining questions. Once you start a break you cannot go back to earlier questions, so review flagged items before each break.

### What the exam covers: the 2026 content outline
The ECO organises the exam into three domains and 26 tasks, each with enablers (examples of the work involved).

#### Domain I: People (33%)
| Task | Related topic |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Develop a common vision | Project objectives and charter |
| 2. Manage conflicts | Team leadership and negotiation |
| 3. Lead the project team | Project manager roles and responsibilities |
| 4. Engage stakeholders | [Stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) |
| 5. Align stakeholder expectations | Stakeholder analysis and engagement plans |
| 6. Manage stakeholder expectations | Ongoing engagement and feedback |
| 7. Help ensure knowledge transfer | Lessons learned |
| 8. Plan and manage communication | [Project communication management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-communication-management/) |

#### Domain II: Process (41%)
| Task | Related topic |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery | Project management plan |
| 2. Develop and manage project scope | [Project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) and the work breakdown structure |
| 3. Help ensure value-based delivery | Incremental delivery and benefits |
| 4. Plan and manage resources | Resource allocation |
| 5. Plan and manage procurement | [Procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) |
| 6. Plan and manage finance | Budgets and [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) |
| 7. Plan and optimise quality of products/deliverables | Quality management |
| 8. Plan and manage schedule | [Critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) and Agile release planning |
| 9. Evaluate project status | Status reports, metrics and forecasts |
| 10. Manage project closure | Project closure |

#### Domain III: Business Environment (26%)
| Task | Related topic |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Define and establish project governance | Project governance |
| 2. Plan and manage project compliance | Regulatory, contractual and sustainability requirements |
| 3. Manage and control changes | [Change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) |
| 4. Remove impediments and manage issues | Issue logs and escalation |
| 5. Plan and manage risk | [Project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) |
| 6. Continuous improvement | Retrospectives and process improvement |
| 7. Support organisational change | Change management and adoption |
| 8. Evaluate external business environment changes | Market, regulatory and technology changes |

#### AI and sustainability on the exam
The ECO names AI as an emerging trend PMI considered in its job analysis, but no task is dedicated to it. Expect AI to appear as project context, for example a team adopting AI tools or a stakeholder worried about data. Sustainability appears in enablers on cost of quality, compliance and risk responses. Apply normal judgement on risk, governance and stakeholders to these scenarios.
The exam is not a test of the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) alone. PMI lists the PMBOK Guide among its references, but questions test how you would act in a situation, drawing on predictive, Agile and hybrid practice.

### How much does PMP certification cost?
PMI does not list exam prices on its public PMP page; they appear when you pay and can vary by country. The figures below are the US prices reported by independent training providers in 2026 (Simplilearn, updated August 2026, and Training Camp, June 2026), checked 25 October 2026. Treat them as indicative.
| Fee | PMI member | Non-member |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PMP exam (application review and one attempt) | US$425 | US$675 |
| Re-examination (each retake) | US$275 | US$375 |
| Certification renewal (every three years) | US$60 | US$150 |
| Rescheduling within 30 days of the exam | US$70 | US$70 |
| PMI membership (optional, per year) | About US$129 to US$139 plus a one-off US$10 application fee | Not applicable |
Rescheduling more than 30 days before your appointment is free, and you cannot reschedule within 48 hours of it, according to PMI's certification handbook as reported by training providers. Membership prices come from our [guide to PMI](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/), which explains what membership includes.

#### Worked example: total budget, member vs non-member
**Priya** plans to self-study with a self-paced course costing US$250 and a practice exam simulator costing US$100. She compares two routes.
| Cost | Non-member route | Member route |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Membership and application fee | US$0 | US$149 (US$139 + US$10) |
| 35-hour self-paced course | US$250 | US$250 |
| Practice exam simulator | US$100 | US$100 |
| PMP exam fee | US$675 | US$425 |
| **Total if she passes first time** | **US$1,025** | **US$924** |
| Extra cost if she needs one retake | + US$375 | + US$275 |
Joining PMI saves Priya about US$100 on a first-time pass and about US$200 if she needs a retake, before counting the free digital PMBOK Guide and member eLearning. Member pricing only applies if membership is active before you pay. A live boot camp usually costs more than a self-paced course, and many employers will fund it if you ask.

### How to get PMP certification step by step
The process below follows PMI's PMP page and certification handbook. Allow two to four months from starting your training to sitting the exam.
1. **Check your eligibility.** Use the requirements table and count your non-overlapping months within the last 10 years. Download the current PMP Examination Content Outline from pmi.org.
2. **Complete the 35 hours (or confirm your CAPM is active).** If you choose live training starting on or after 1 December 2026, use a PMI Authorized Training Partner. Save the certificate.
3. **Decide whether to join PMI.** Join before you pay the exam fee if you want the member price.
4. **Create a PMI account and start the online application.** Enter your education, training and each project separately, with dates, your role and a short description.
5. **Submit the application.** PMI reviews it and emails you. Training providers commonly report a review of about five business days.
6. **Pay the exam fee.** After payment you receive your eligibility details; some applications are selected for audit at this stage.
7. **Schedule the exam with Pearson VUE.** Choose a test centre or online proctoring. You have one year from approval to take the exam, with up to three attempts.
8. **Study and sit the exam.** Follow a study plan, take full-length practice exams and book a date that gives you a deadline.
9. **Maintain your PMP.** Your three-year cycle starts on the day you pass. Earn and report 60 PDUs and pay the renewal fee before it ends.

#### Writing your project descriptions
Each project needs a short summary in your own words. A good structure is one sentence each for the objective, your role, your responsibilities and the outcome:
- **Objective:** "Replace the regional CRM system for 120 sales staff within a budget of 400,000."
- **Your role:** "Project lead reporting to the sales director, managing a team of six."
- **Responsibilities:** "Defined scope with stakeholders, built the schedule and risk register, ran fortnightly sprint reviews with the vendor and managed change requests."
- **Outcome:** "Went live on schedule; adoption reached the agreed target within three months; closed the project with a lessons-learned review."

#### If your application is audited
PMI selects some applications for audit at random. If yours is chosen, you cannot schedule the exam until you have sent copies of your diploma or degree, your training certificates (not needed with an active CAPM) and supervisor signatures confirming each project.
Training providers report a 90-day window to respond. Keep your evidence together from the start so you can reply quickly.

### How to prepare: a 12-week PMP study plan
Most candidates study for two to three months alongside work, at roughly 8 to 10 hours a week. This plan is our suggestion, built around the 2026 domain weights; adjust it to your experience.
| Week |  |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Read the 2026 ECO; take a diagnostic practice test; review project life cycles and predictive vs [Agile approaches](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) |
| 2 | Process: integrated planning, scope and the work breakdown structure |
| 3 | Process: schedule, critical path, Agile release and iteration planning |
| 4 | Process: finance, budgets and earned value; resources and procurement |
| 5 | Process: quality, value-based delivery, status and closure |
| 6 | People: vision, team leadership, conflict, servant leadership |
| 7 | People: stakeholders, expectations, communication and knowledge transfer |
| 8 | Business Environment: governance, compliance, change control |
| 9 | Business Environment: risk, issues, continuous improvement, organisational and external change |
| 10 | Full-length timed exam 1 (180 questions, 240 minutes, two breaks); review every wrong answer |
| 11 | Revise weak tasks; full-length timed exam 2 and review |
| 12 | Light review, rest, check exam-day logistics |

#### Choosing study materials
- **PMI's resources:** the free Examination Content Outline, PMI's PMP Exam Prep course and practice exam, and PMI Study Hall. Members get the PMBOK Guide free.
- **A course and simulator built on the 2026 ECO:** check they cover the larger Business Environment domain and the new question formats, with full-length timed exams and explanations.
- **Background reading:** our guides to [Agile methodology](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-methodology/) and [risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) cover topics many candidates find hardest.

#### How to know you are ready
PMI does not publish a pass mark. It sets the standard through psychometric analysis, and your result shows pass or fail with a performance rating for each domain. Many training providers suggest booking when you consistently score around 75% to 80% or more on full-length practice exams from a reputable simulator. That is a rule of thumb, not a PMI figure, but it is a sensible signal that you can sustain performance over four hours.

### Sample PMP exam questions with explanations
These questions are our own, written in the style of the 2026 exam. The explanations matter more than the answers: the exam rewards the action a well-informed project manager would take first.

#### Question 1 (People)
Two senior developers on your hybrid project disagree strongly about the architecture for a new feature, and the disagreement is slowing the team. What should you do first?
- A. Make the decision yourself so the team can move on.
- B. Escalate the issue to the sponsor.
- C. Meet the two developers to understand both positions and help them reach an agreed solution.
- D. Ask the team to vote at the next stand-up.
**Answer: C.** The exam favours collaborative problem-solving as the first step in conflict, because it addresses the cause and keeps ownership with the team. Escalation (B) comes later if the team cannot resolve it; deciding alone (A) or voting (D) may leave the underlying disagreement unresolved.

#### Question 2 (Process, with a calculation)
Your project has a planned value of 200,000, an earned value of 180,000 and an actual cost of 200,000. Which statement is correct?
- A. The project is ahead of schedule and under budget.
- B. The project is behind schedule and over budget.
- C. The project is on schedule and over budget.
- D. The project is behind schedule and on budget.
**Answer: B.** Schedule variance is EV minus PV, so 180,000 minus 200,000 = minus 20,000 (behind schedule). Cost variance is EV minus AC, so 180,000 minus 200,000 = minus 20,000 (over budget).

### Exam day: what to expect
- **At a test centre:** arrive early with the identification named in your confirmation email; personal items go in a locker.
- **Online:** run Pearson VUE's system test first and clear your room. A proctor watches throughout, and leaving the camera view outside scheduled breaks can end your exam.
- **Timing and breaks:** you have about 80 seconds per question. Take both breaks, and review flagged questions before each one.
- **Results:** a provisional pass or fail appears on screen, followed by a report rating your performance in each domain.
PMI recommends the test centre where possible.

### Is PMP certification worth it?
For most experienced project managers, the PMP is worth it if employers in your market ask for it. Evidence from PMI's own research is positive: a PMI blog post from April 2026 reports that, in PMI's most recent salary survey covering 21 countries, PMP holders reported median salaries 17% higher than those without it. In the United States the gap was 24%, with a median of US$135,000 for PMP holders against US$109,157 for non-holders. The figures show association, not proof that the certificate alone causes the difference.
It is most likely to pay off when job adverts you want list it as required or preferred, when you work internationally or lead mixed predictive and Agile projects, and when your employer funds the costs. If target employers mostly ask for PRINCE2 or APM, or you have less than three years of leadership experience, another credential may serve you better first.
Preparing also fills gaps in areas you have not led before, such as procurement or governance. Our guide on [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/) shows where the PMP fits in a typical career path.

### PMP vs CAPM and other certifications
|  | PMP | CAPM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level | Experienced practitioner | Entry level |
| Experience needed | 2 to 5 years leading projects, within 10 years | None |
| Training | 35 hours or an active CAPM | 23 hours |
| Exam | 180 questions, 240 minutes | 150 questions, 180 minutes |
| Renewal | 60 PDUs every 3 years | 15 PDUs every 3 years |
In the UK and much of Europe, PRINCE2 (from PeopleCert) is the main alternative, and many project managers hold both. Our comparison of [PMBOK vs PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-vs-prince2/) explains how the two approaches differ.

### Keeping your PMP: renewal and PDUs
The PMP is valid for three years from the day you pass. To renew, you earn 60 Professional Development Units (PDUs), where one PDU equals one hour of learning or giving back, report them in PMI's Continuing Certification Requirements System (CCRS), agree to PMI's code of ethics and pay the renewal fee.
| Rule | PMP requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Total PDUs per three-year cycle | 60 |
| Education PDUs | At least 35 |
| Giving back PDUs (volunteering, creating content, working as a practitioner) | No more than 25 |
| Talent Triangle minimum | At least 8 PDUs in each of Ways of Working, Power Skills and Business Acumen |
| Renewal fee (reported) | US$60 for members, US$150 for non-members |
A simple approach is to earn about 20 PDUs a year from webinars, courses, chapter events and some volunteering. If you miss the deadline, training providers report that the certification is suspended for a year, during which you can still complete the requirements; after that it expires and you would need to requalify.

### Common PMP mistakes to avoid
- **Counting overlapping months twice.** PMI counts calendar months once, however many projects ran at the same time.
- **Listing experience older than 10 years.** It will not count towards the requirement.
- **Booking an ineligible live course.** From 1 December 2026, live training must come from an Authorized Training Partner or an eligible accredited programme.
- **Joining PMI after paying the exam fee.** You will pay the non-member price.
- **Studying only from 2021-era materials.** The Business Environment domain is now more than three times its old weight.
- **Choosing what your organisation would do.** The exam asks what a well-informed project manager should do, often the first step, following good practice.
If you are building evidence of your experience, the documents you create on real projects help with both the application and the exam. Our free [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/), [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) and [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) are good places to start.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the PMP certification requirements?**
Project leadership experience gained within the last 10 years (five years with a secondary diploma, four with an associate's or vocational diploma, three with a bachelor's degree, or two with a degree from a PMI GAC-accredited programme), plus 35 hours of project management training or an active CAPM.

**Q: How much does PMP certification cost?**
Independent providers report US exam fees of US$425 for PMI members and US$675 for non-members in 2026, plus your training costs. Check the price at checkout, as fees vary by country.

**Q: How many questions are on the PMP exam and how long is it?**
180 questions (170 scored and 10 unscored) in 240 minutes, with two 10-minute breaks.

**Q: What changed in the PMP exam in July 2026?**
The domains are now People 33%, Process 41% and Business Environment 26% (previously 42%, 50% and 8%). The exam adds case-study and graphic-based questions, 10 extra minutes and a second break.

**Q: Can I get the PMP without a degree?**
Yes. With a secondary diploma you need five years of project leadership experience within the last 10 years, plus the 35 hours of training.

**Q: Does my CAPM count towards the PMP?**
Yes. An active CAPM meets the PMP's 35-hour training requirement. You still need the full experience requirement.

**Q: Does my 35-hour course still count after 1 December 2026?**
Yes if you completed it before that date, or if it is self-paced. Live courses taken from that date must come from a PMI Authorized Training Partner, a China REP or an eligible accredited programme.

**Q: Is the PMP exam hard? What is the passing score?**
It is demanding because most questions are long scenarios that test judgement over four hours. PMI does not publish a passing score; it uses psychometric analysis and reports performance by domain.

**Q: How long does it take to get PMP certified?**
Most candidates take two to four months from starting training to passing, including about 8 to 12 weeks of study. Your eligibility period lasts one year from approval.

**Q: Can I take the PMP exam online?**
Yes. You can sit it online with a remote proctor or at a Pearson VUE test centre, which PMI recommends.

**Q: What happens if my application is audited?**
PMI asks for copies of your education and training certificates and supervisor confirmation of your experience, and you cannot schedule the exam until the audit is complete.

**Q: Do I need to be a PMI member to take the PMP?**
No. Membership is optional, but members pay less for the exam, retakes and renewal and get the PMBOK Guide free, so it usually pays for itself in the year you sit the exam.

**Q: How do I maintain my PMP?**
Earn 60 PDUs every three years (at least 35 from education and at least 8 in each Talent Triangle area), report them in PMI's CCRS and pay the renewal fee.

**Q: Is the PMP worth it in 2026?**
For experienced project managers in markets where employers ask for it, usually yes. PMI reports PMP holders earn a 17% higher median salary across 21 countries.

# Predecessors and Successors in Project Management

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/predecessors-and-successors/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Predecessors and successors in project management explained: definitions, the four link types, a worked example, MS Project notation and common mistakes.


## Predecessors and Successors in Project Management
In project management, a predecessor is an activity that must start or finish before another activity can start or finish, and a successor is the activity that depends on it. Every link in a schedule joins one predecessor to one successor, and together those links decide the order of work, the critical path and how far a delay will spread.
- Published 23 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 16 min read

### Key takeaways
- A predecessor comes first and controls its successor; the successor follows and depends on it.
- Every dependency has exactly one predecessor and one successor, and most activities are both.
- When an activity has several predecessors, the one that finishes latest (the driving predecessor) sets its start date.
- Record only immediate predecessors, with the link type and any lead or lag.
- Every activity except the project start and finish should have at least one predecessor and one successor.
- Good predecessor logic is what makes the critical path, float and delay forecasts trustworthy.

### What are predecessors and successors?
A **predecessor** is an activity that logically comes before another activity and controls when that activity can start or finish. A **successor** is the activity that comes after it and depends on it. The relationship between them is a dependency, and the predecessor is always the activity the arrow leads out of.
A simple example: you cannot install software on a laptop until the hardware has been set up. "Set up hardware" is the predecessor and "Install software" is the successor. If the hardware arrives three days late, the software installation moves three days too, unless you change the plan.
PMI's terminology talks about the **predecessor activity** and the **successor activity**, and the method most schedules use to draw them is the precedence diagramming method (PDM), where activities are boxes (nodes) and dependencies are arrows. A few points follow from the definition:
- Each dependency has exactly one predecessor and one successor.
- Most activities are both: a successor to the work before them and a predecessor to the work after them.
- An activity can have several predecessors and several successors.
- Only the very first activity has no predecessor and only the last has no successor. In practice these are usually a start milestone and a finish milestone; see [project milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/).
Predecessors and successors describe the two ends of a link. The link itself, and its type, is covered in our guide to [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/).

### Predecessor vs successor at a glance
|  | Predecessor | Successor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Position in the logic | Comes first | Comes after and depends on the predecessor |
| Question it answers | What must happen before this? | What is waiting for this? |
| If it is delayed | Can push every successor later | Delays only its own successors |
| In a Gantt chart | The bar the arrow starts from | The bar the arrow points to |
| In a network diagram | Node with an arrow leading out | Node with an arrow leading in |
| In a scheduling tool | Listed in the successor's Predecessors column | Listed in the predecessor's Successors column |
The words are relative. "Design pages" is a successor of "Agree requirements" and, at the same time, a predecessor of "Build pages". Whether you call an activity a predecessor or a successor depends on which link you are looking at.

### The four relationship types in predecessor terms
A predecessor does not always have to finish before its successor starts. There are four logical relationship types, and each one describes which end of the predecessor controls which end of the successor.
| Type | Rule | Example | How common |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Finish-to-start (FS) | The successor cannot start until the predecessor finishes | Pour the foundations, then build the walls | By far the most common; the default in most tools |
| Start-to-start (SS) | The successor cannot start until the predecessor starts | Start proofreading once writing has started | Common for overlapping work |
| Finish-to-finish (FF) | The successor cannot finish until the predecessor finishes | Testing cannot finish until development finishes | Common for parallel work that must end together |
| Start-to-finish (SF) | The successor cannot finish until the predecessor starts | The old system keeps running until the new one goes live | Rare; usually a sign the logic should be rethought |
Any of these links can carry a **lag** (a deliberate wait, such as FS+3 days for paint to dry) or a **lead** (an overlap, written as a negative lag such as FS-2 days). Leads and lags change the timing of the link but not which activity is the predecessor.

### Types of predecessor you will hear about

#### Immediate and indirect predecessors
An **immediate predecessor** is linked directly to the activity. Activities further back in the chain are indirect predecessors: they still affect the activity, but only through the links in between. Record only immediate predecessors. Linking an activity to every earlier activity creates redundant links that make the schedule hard to read and harder to change.

#### Driving and non-driving predecessors
When an activity has several predecessors, only one of them usually controls its start date at any time. That is the **driving predecessor**. The others are non-driving: they finish earlier and have some float before they would affect the successor.
|  | Driving predecessor | Non-driving predecessor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Effect on the successor | Sets its earliest start (or finish) date | No effect at the moment |
| If it slips by one day | The successor slips by one day | Nothing happens until its float is used up |
| Where to focus | Monitor closely; it is often on the critical path | Watch the float rather than the date |
The driving predecessor can change as work progresses. A non-driving predecessor that runs late can overtake the driving one and become the new driver.

#### Multiple predecessors and multiple successors
An activity with several predecessors is where paths meet; PMI calls this **path convergence**. An activity with several successors is where paths split, known as **path divergence**. Convergence points are risky because the successor waits for the latest of all its inputs, so a delay on any one path can hold everything up. Divergence points are risky because a delay to one activity spreads to every path that leaves it.

#### Mandatory, discretionary and external predecessors
Predecessors also differ in why the link exists. A mandatory (hard logic) predecessor reflects physical or contractual necessity. A discretionary (soft logic) predecessor reflects a preferred way of working that you could change, which makes it the first place to look when you need to [fast-track](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/) a schedule. An external predecessor sits outside the project, such as a supplier delivery or a regulator's approval. These categories are explained in [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/).

### How to identify predecessors and successors step by step
1. **Start from the activity list.** Break the scope down with a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) and turn each work package into activities; see [project tasks and activities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-tasks-and-activities/).
2. **Ask one question per activity:** what must be finished (or started) before this can begin? The answers are its candidate predecessors.
3. **Keep only the immediate predecessors.** If A drives B and B drives C, do not also link A to C.
4. **Choose the relationship type.** Use finish-to-start unless the work genuinely overlaps or must finish together.
5. **Add a lead or lag only when there is a real reason**, such as curing time or a notice period, and write that reason down.
6. **Check successors.** For each activity, ask what is waiting for it. An activity that nothing depends on is either the finish milestone or a missing link.
7. **Draw or generate a network diagram** to spot loops, dangling activities and parallel paths; see [project network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/).
8. **Review the logic with the people doing the work.** They know which dependencies are real and which are habits.
Tip
Identify predecessors with the team in the room, not alone at a desk. A 30-minute walkthrough of the activity list usually finds missing hand-offs that nobody would have spotted on paper.

### Worked example: a website launch schedule
A small team is launching a new website. The table lists each activity with its duration, immediate predecessors and successors. All links are finish-to-start with no lag.
| ID | Activity | Duration | Predecessors | Successors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Agree requirements | 3 days | None (start) | B, C |
| B | Design pages | 5 days | A | D |
| C | Write content | 4 days | A | E |
| D | Build pages | 6 days | B | E |
| E | Load content | 2 days | C, D | F |
| F | Test and launch | 3 days | E | None (finish) |
A is a burst point (path divergence) because it has two successors. E is a merge point (path convergence) because it has two predecessors. Working forward from day 0 gives these earliest dates:
| ID | Earliest start | Earliest finish | Total float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Day 0 | Day 3 | 0 |
| B | Day 3 | Day 8 | 0 |
| C | Day 3 | Day 7 | 7 days |
| D | Day 8 | Day 14 | 0 |
| E | Day 14 | Day 16 | 0 |
| F | Day 16 | Day 19 | 0 |
E cannot start until **both** predecessors have finished. C finishes on day 7 but D does not finish until day 14, so **D is the driving predecessor of E** and C is non-driving, with 7 days of float. The critical path is A, B, D, E, F and the project takes 19 days.
- If **C slips by 3 days**, it finishes on day 10. E still starts on day 14, so the launch date does not move; C's float drops to 4 days.
- If **D slips by 3 days**, E starts on day 17 and the launch moves to day 22.
- If **C slips by 9 days**, it finishes on day 16, overtakes D as the driving predecessor and pushes the launch out by 2 days (9 days of delay minus 7 days of float).
This is why you monitor driving predecessors closely and watch the float on the others. The calculation method is explained step by step in [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/).

### How predecessors appear in Gantt charts, network diagrams and tools

#### Gantt charts
In a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), a dependency is drawn as an arrow from the predecessor's bar to the successor's bar. For a finish-to-start link the arrow runs from the end of the predecessor to the start of the successor. When you move a predecessor in most [Gantt chart software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/), its successors move with it automatically.

#### Network diagrams
In an activity-on-node [network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/), each activity is a box and each arrow runs from predecessor to successor. Network diagrams make convergence and divergence points easy to see, which is why they are useful for checking logic even if you manage day to day in a Gantt view. A [PERT chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/) uses the same idea with three-point estimates.

#### Predecessor notation in scheduling tools
Most desktop scheduling tools let you type predecessors into a column using the predecessor's row ID, the link type and any lead or lag. In Microsoft Project, according to Microsoft's documentation, entering just an ID creates a finish-to-start link with no lag, a positive number adds lag and a negative number adds lead. Several predecessors are separated by the list separator (a comma or semicolon, depending on regional settings).
| Entry | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 3 | Task 3 must finish before this task starts (FS, no lag) |
| 3FS+2d | Starts 2 days after task 3 finishes |
| 3SS | Can start once task 3 has started |
| 3FF-1d | Must finish no earlier than 1 day before task 3 finishes |
| 2,5 | Waits for both task 2 and task 5 to finish |
In the website example, E (Load content) would show "3,4" if C and D were rows 3 and 4. Cloud tools such as [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) and [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) let you create the same links by dragging between bars in the Gantt view or by filling in a predecessors column, and both support dependencies and critical path views on paid plans.

#### Tracing logic
Many tools can highlight a task's predecessors and successors. Microsoft Project's Task Path feature, for example, can highlight predecessors, driving predecessors, successors and driven successors in the Gantt chart. When a milestone slips, tracing its driving predecessors backwards is usually the fastest way to find the real cause.

### Why predecessors matter for the critical path and float
The [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) is built entirely on predecessor and successor links. The forward pass pushes earliest dates from predecessors to successors; the backward pass pulls latest dates from successors back to predecessors. The difference between the two is [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/), and the chain of activities with zero (or the least) float is the critical path.
That has some practical consequences:
- **An activity with no successor has misleading float.** Its float is measured against the project end, so it can slip a long way before the schedule shows any impact, even if something else really depends on it.
- **An activity with no predecessor can start on day one.** Unless that is true, the schedule will show work starting before it realistically can.
- **Missing links make the critical path wrong.** If the logic is incomplete, the path your tool highlights may not be the one that actually controls the finish date.
- **Resource limits are not predecessors.** CPM assumes unlimited resources. If two activities cannot run together because the same person does both, that is handled by [resource leveling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/), not by inventing a logic link.

### Common mistakes with predecessors (and how to fix them)
| Mistake | Why it causes problems | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open ends (no predecessor or no successor) | Delays do not flow through, so float and the finish date look better than they are | Link every activity into the network, ending at the finish milestone |
| Linking to summary tasks | The logic becomes hard to follow and some tools calculate it unexpectedly | Link the detailed activities, not the summary rows |
| Redundant links | Clutter that hides the real driving logic | Keep immediate predecessors only |
| Circular logic (A before B before A) | The schedule cannot calculate; most tools reject it | Break the loop by splitting an activity or rethinking the order |
| Date constraints instead of links | Dates stop moving when predecessors slip | Use logic links and keep constraints for genuine fixed dates |
| Lags used to represent work | Work hidden in a lag cannot be tracked or resourced | Model the work as its own activity |
| Overusing SS and SF links | Logic becomes hard to explain and easy to break | Default to FS; split activities if they overlap |
| Stale links after replanning | The schedule forecasts dates for a plan nobody is following | Review links whenever scope or approach changes |
If the same overlap keeps needing a start-to-start link with a long lag, it is often clearer to split the predecessor into two activities and link the successor to the first part.

### Checking the quality of your schedule logic
Large projects often test schedule logic against published health checks. A widely used example is the US Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) 14-point assessment, which includes these logic checks:
| Check | DCMA threshold |
| --- | --- |
| Incomplete activities missing a predecessor or successor | No more than 5% |
| Links that are finish-to-start | At least 90% |
| Leads (negative lags) | None |
| Links with lags | No more than 5% |
| Incomplete activities with hard date constraints | No more than 5% |
These thresholds come from a defence-contracting context, but they make a useful sanity check for any schedule. Our own advice for smaller projects is simpler:
- Filter for activities with an empty Predecessors or Successors column and fix each one.
- Move one early activity by a week and check that the finish date moves as you expect.
- Read the critical path aloud from start to finish; if any step sounds illogical, check its links.
- Re-run the checks before you set the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) and after any major replan.

### Best practices for managing predecessors
- Build the logic before you add dates. Let the links calculate the dates rather than typing them in.
- Give every activity a clear owner so someone is accountable when a predecessor runs late.
- Agree cross-team and external predecessors early, with a named contact on the other side.
- Treat convergence points (activities with many predecessors) as risks and monitor them.
- Note why each discretionary link exists so you know which ones can be changed to recover time; see [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/).
- Keep the network tidy with start and finish milestones, and use a [hammock activity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/hammock-activity/) for support work that spans a group of activities.
- Update links as part of your regular schedule review, not only when something goes wrong.
Tip
When a successor's owner asks "why can't I start yet?", show them the driving predecessor in the Gantt chart. It turns an argument about dates into a conversation about the work that is holding things up.
If you are building a schedule from scratch, the free [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/), [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) and [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) all include predecessor columns, and the [work breakdown structure template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) helps you build the activity list first. For the wider process, read our guide to [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a predecessor in project management?**
A predecessor is an activity that must start or finish before another activity can start or finish. It controls the timing of the activity that depends on it.

**Q: What is a successor in project management?**
A successor is an activity that depends on another activity (its predecessor) and comes after it in the schedule. Its start or finish date is driven by that predecessor.

**Q: What is the difference between a predecessor and a successor?**
The predecessor comes first and controls the timing; the successor follows and depends on it. They are the two ends of the same dependency, and most activities are a predecessor in one link and a successor in another.

**Q: Can a task have multiple predecessors?**
Yes. With finish-to-start links it cannot start until all of its predecessors have finished, so the latest-finishing one, the driving predecessor, sets its start date.

**Q: Can a task have multiple successors?**
Yes. A delay to that task then affects every one of its successors, which is why activities with many successors deserve close attention.

**Q: What is an immediate predecessor?**
An immediate predecessor is linked directly to the activity. Earlier activities in the chain are indirect predecessors and should not be linked again.

**Q: What is a driving predecessor?**
The predecessor that actually determines a successor's earliest start or finish date at the moment. A delay to it delays the successor straight away.

**Q: What does 3FS+2d mean in MS Project?**
It means task 3 is a finish-to-start predecessor with a 2-day lag: this task can start 2 days after task 3 finishes. Entering just "3" would mean finish-to-start with no lag.

**Q: What happens if a task has no predecessor?**
The scheduling tool will let it start on the project start date. That is fine for the first activity, but for anything else it usually means a link is missing.

**Q: What happens if a task has no successor?**
It becomes an open end, so a delay to it will not show any effect on later work or the finish date. Link it to the activity that needs its output, or to the finish milestone.

**Q: Are predecessors the same as dependencies?**
Not quite. A dependency is the link between two activities; the predecessor and successor are the activities at each end. See [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/).

**Q: Can a successor start before its predecessor finishes?**
Yes, if the link is start-to-start or finish-to-finish, or if a lead (negative lag) is applied to a finish-to-start link. Overlapping work like this saves time but increases the risk of rework.

**Q: Do predecessors affect float?**
Yes. Float is calculated by comparing an activity's dates with those of its successors, so missing or wrong links give wrong float. See [float and slack](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/).

**Q: How are predecessors shown in a network diagram?**
As arrows. The predecessor is the node the arrow leaves and the successor is the node it points to; see [project network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/).

# What Is PRINCE2? Principles, Practices and Processes

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: PRINCE2 explained: its seven principles, seven practices and seven processes, key roles, management by exception, benefits and certifications.


## What Is PRINCE2? Principles, Practices and Processes
PRINCE2 (PRojects IN Controlled Environments) is a structured, process-based project management method. Originating with the UK government and now owned by PeopleCert, it is widely used in the UK, Europe, Australia and the public sector worldwide.
- Published 9 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- PRINCE2 is a stage-based method focused on governance.
- It has seven principles, seven practices and seven processes.
- Management by exception keeps the board focused on key decisions.

### Seven principles
- **Ensure continued business justification:** the project must remain worthwhile.
- **Learn from experience.**
- **Define roles, responsibilities and relationships.**
- **Manage by stages:** plan, monitor and control stage by stage.
- **Manage by exception:** set tolerances and escalate only when they will be exceeded.
- **Focus on products:** define and deliver products that meet quality criteria.
- **Tailor to suit the project.**

### Seven practices
Called themes in earlier editions, these are aspects to manage continually: business case, organising, plans, quality, risk, issues and progress.

### Seven processes
| Process | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Starting up a project | Check the project is viable and worthwhile |
| Directing a project | Project board makes key decisions |
| Initiating a project | Establish solid foundations and plans |
| Controlling a stage | Day-to-day management by the project manager |
| Managing product delivery | Team managers deliver work packages |
| Managing a stage boundary | Review the stage and plan the next |
| Closing a project | Confirm acceptance and close |

### Key roles
- **Project board:** executive, senior user and senior supplier; accountable for success.
- **Project manager:** runs the project day to day within tolerances.
- **Team manager:** leads delivery of specialist products.
- **Project assurance** and **project support.**

### Certifications
PeopleCert offers PRINCE2 Foundation and Practitioner certifications, and PRINCE2 Agile for combining PRINCE2 with Agile delivery. See [PRINCE2 vs Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/prince2-vs-agile/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is PRINCE2 better than PMP?**
They are different: PRINCE2 is a methodology; PMP certifies knowledge of PMI's standard and broader practice. Choice depends on your region and industry.

**Q: What is management by exception in PRINCE2?**
The project board sets tolerances; the project manager handles everything within them and escalates only when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.

**Q: What does PRINCE2 stand for?**
PRojects IN Controlled Environments.

**Q: Who owns PRINCE2?**
PRINCE2 originated with the UK government and is now owned by PeopleCert, which runs its certifications.

**Q: What are the seven processes of PRINCE2?**
Starting up a project, directing a project, initiating a project, controlling a stage, managing product delivery, managing a stage boundary and closing a project.

**Q: What are the PRINCE2 practices?**
Business case, organising, plans, quality, risk, issues and progress. Earlier editions called them themes.

**Q: What is a PRINCE2 project board?**
The group accountable for the project's success, made up of the executive, senior user and senior supplier.

**Q: What is the difference between PRINCE2 Foundation and Practitioner?**
Foundation tests knowledge of the method; Practitioner tests the ability to apply and tailor it to a project scenario.

**Q: Is PRINCE2 Agile?**
Classic PRINCE2 is not Agile, but PRINCE2 Agile shows how to run Agile delivery within PRINCE2 governance. See [PRINCE2 vs Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/prince2-vs-agile/).

**Q: What is a PRINCE2 stage?**
A section of the project with its own plan, approved by the project board before it starts. The project is managed stage by stage.

**Q: Where is PRINCE2 most used?**
In the UK, Europe, Australia and the public sector, where clear governance and accountability are valued.

# Project vs Program vs Portfolio Management: Key Differences

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/program-vs-project-vs-portfolio-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project vs program vs portfolio management explained: definitions, a side-by-side table, roles, examples and how the three levels work together.


## Project vs Program vs Portfolio Management: Key Differences
The difference between project vs program vs portfolio management comes down to what each level delivers: projects deliver outputs, programmes deliver benefits, and portfolios deliver strategy by choosing which work to fund. A project manager focuses on getting one result done well, a programme manager coordinates related projects so their combined benefits are realised, and a portfolio manager makes sure the organisation invests in the right mix of work. This guide explains each level, compares them side by side and shows how they fit together.
- Published 8 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 15 min read

### Key takeaways
- A project is a temporary effort to create a unique result; a programme groups related projects to achieve shared benefits; a portfolio is all the work an organisation funds to meet its strategy.
- Projects are judged on delivery (time, cost, scope, quality), programmes on benefits realised, portfolios on strategic value and return.
- Programme components are related to each other; portfolio components do not have to be, and a portfolio can include operations.
- Decisions flow down (strategy, funding, priorities) and information flows up (progress, risks, benefits).
- Not every organisation needs all three levels, but any organisation running several projects benefits from basic portfolio thinking.

### Project, programme and portfolio: the short answer
A **project** is a temporary effort to create a unique product, service or result. A **programme** is a group of related projects and activities managed together to achieve benefits that none could deliver alone. A **portfolio** is the full collection of projects, programmes and other work an organisation selects, prioritises and funds to meet its strategic objectives.
Think of it as three questions. Project management asks "are we doing this piece of work right?" Programme management asks "are these related pieces of work adding up to the change we need?" Portfolio management asks "are we doing the right work at all?"

#### Official definitions
The Project Management Institute (PMI) publishes a separate standard for each level: the PMBOK Guide for projects, The Standard for Program Management (fifth edition, 2024) and The Standard for Portfolio Management. Its definitions, summarised:
| Level | PMI definition (summarised) |
| --- | --- |
| Project | A temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result |
| Program | Related projects, subsidiary programs and program activities managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually |
| Portfolio | Projects, programs, subsidiary portfolios and operations managed as a group to achieve strategic objectives |
In the UK and many Commonwealth countries the same three levels are often called **P3M** (portfolio, programme and project management), and the programme level is covered by the MSP (Managing Successful Programmes) method alongside PRINCE2 for projects.
Tip
Program or programme? Both are correct. "Program" is the American spelling and the one PMI uses; "programme" is the usual British spelling for a set of related projects. This guide uses programme in the text but the meaning is identical.

### Key differences at a glance
|  | Project | Programme | Portfolio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Deliver a specific output | Achieve benefits through related projects | Achieve strategic objectives by selecting and balancing work |
| Scope | Defined and controlled | Wider; changes as benefits become clearer | Organisation-wide or divisional; changes with strategy |
| Components | Tasks and work packages | Related projects and programme activities | Projects, programmes and operations, related or not |
| Focus | Deliverables | Benefits and outcomes | Investment choices and value |
| Success measure | On time, on budget, to scope and quality | Benefits realised | Strategic value, return on investment and balance |
| Time frame | Defined start and end | Longer, often several years, ends when benefits are secured | Ongoing |
| Approach to change | Controls change to protect the baseline | Expects and manages change between projects | Rebalances continuously as priorities change |
| Leader | Project manager | Programme manager | Portfolio manager or portfolio board |
| Planning | Detailed plans for the work | High-level plans that guide project plans | Strategic plans, roadmaps and funding cycles |
| Risk focus | Risks to the project's objectives | Risks across projects and to benefits | Aggregate risk and the balance of the portfolio |
| Key documents | Charter, plan, schedule, status report | Programme brief, benefits map, roadmap | Portfolio strategy, prioritised list, dashboards |

### What is project management?
Project management is the application of knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities to meet project requirements. A project manager plans the work, leads the team, manages risks, issues and changes, keeps stakeholders informed and hands over the finished result. Success is usually judged on delivering the agreed scope within time, cost and quality limits.
Projects can stand alone. A small company refurbishing its reception area has a project, not a programme, and probably no formal portfolio. Projects can also sit inside a programme, or directly inside a portfolio when they are not related to other work.
For the basics, see [what is a project](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-a-project/) and [what is project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/).

### What is programme management?
Programme management is the coordinated management of a group of related projects and activities to achieve benefits and outcomes that the projects could not achieve separately. A programme exists because the projects depend on each other: they share resources, deliver parts of the same change, or only create value when they come together.

#### Why group projects into a programme?
- **Dependencies:** one project's output is another's input, so schedules and changes need coordinating.
- **Shared resources:** the same specialists, budget or suppliers are needed across projects.
- **Combined benefits:** the benefit only appears when several outputs are in use together, such as a new system plus new processes plus trained staff.
- **Consistent governance:** one sponsor and one board can direct related work instead of several competing ones.
- **Managing change in the business:** programmes typically include business change and transition activities, not just project deliverables.

#### Benefits management
Benefits are what set programmes apart. A programme team identifies the benefits it expects (for example, faster processing times or higher customer retention), maps which project outputs enable them, assigns owners in the business, and tracks them during and after delivery. Because many benefits appear only once the new ways of working are embedded, programmes often continue after their last project has closed.

#### The programme life cycle
PMI's Standard for Program Management describes a life cycle of programme definition, programme delivery (where component projects are started, delivered and closed) and programme closure. In practice that means: define the vision and benefits, design the set of projects, deliver them in tranches or waves, embed the changes and confirm the benefits, then close. The fifth edition (2024) also sets out eight principles and adds a Collaboration performance domain.

#### What a programme manager does
A programme manager rarely manages tasks directly. They coordinate project managers, resolve conflicts over resources and priorities, manage dependencies and risks that cross project boundaries, keep the roadmap aligned with the benefits, and report to the programme sponsor or board.
Tip
A very large project is not automatically a programme. If the work has a single, clear output and one plan, it is a big project. It becomes a programme when several distinct projects, often with different teams and life cycles, are needed to achieve a wider outcome.

### What is portfolio management?
Portfolio management, often called **project portfolio management (PPM)**, is the centralised selection, prioritisation and oversight of an organisation's projects, programmes and related operational work to achieve its strategic objectives. Where programme management asks how to deliver a set of related changes, portfolio management asks which changes the organisation should invest in at all, and in what order.
Two points cause the most confusion. First, the work in a portfolio does not need to be related: a portfolio may contain an IT upgrade, a new product and a training initiative. Second, PMI's definition includes operations, because ongoing work competes for the same money and people as change work.

#### The portfolio management process
1. **Identify** candidate initiatives from strategy, business units and demand.
2. **Evaluate** each one using a business case: costs, benefits, risks and strategic fit. Measures such as [return on investment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/return-on-investment/) help compare options.
3. **Prioritise and select** using agreed criteria, and decide what to start, defer or reject.
4. **Balance** the portfolio across risk, time horizon, business area and available capacity. See [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/).
5. **Authorise** the chosen work and allocate funding and resources.
6. **Monitor and review** performance regularly, and rebalance: accelerate, change, pause or stop work as conditions change.

#### Common prioritisation criteria
- Strategic alignment: how directly the work supports stated objectives or OKRs.
- Value: financial return, cost savings, revenue or customer impact.
- Risk and urgency: regulatory deadlines, safety, or the cost of delay.
- Feasibility: whether the organisation has the skills, capacity and budget now.
- Dependencies: whether other work relies on it.
Portfolio decisions are usually made by a portfolio board or investment committee, supported by a portfolio manager and often a [PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/). Tools such as our [OKR template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/okr-template/) and [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) help connect strategy to the work being proposed.

### How the three levels work together
The three levels form a hierarchy of decisions, not just of size. Strategy shapes the portfolio, the portfolio authorises programmes and projects, and programmes coordinate their component projects.
| Direction | What flows | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Top down | Strategy, priorities, funding and constraints | Approved budgets, priority rankings, target dates, policies |
| Bottom up | Performance, risks, issues and benefits data | Status reports, forecasts, escalated risks, change requests, benefits tracking |
When this works well, a project manager knows why their project matters and what to escalate, a programme manager can move resources between projects, and the portfolio board can stop work that no longer earns its place. Good [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) defines who makes each of these decisions.

#### Worked example: a hospital
- **Portfolio:** all of the hospital's change initiatives, managed by a portfolio board that balances clinical, digital, estates and workforce investment against its strategy and budget.
- **Programme:** a digital health programme within that portfolio, aiming to cut outpatient waiting times and improve patient experience. Its programme manager coordinates the projects below and tracks benefits such as appointment waiting times.
- **Projects:** a patient app, an upgrade to electronic patient records, integration between the two, and staff training. Each has its own project manager, plan and deliverables.
- **Standalone project in the same portfolio:** a car park resurfacing project. It is unrelated to the programme, so it sits directly in the portfolio.
If the app is delayed, the programme manager decides how that affects the records upgrade and training and whether benefits will slip. If a new regulatory requirement appears, the portfolio board may pause the car park project to free up budget.

#### More examples
| Organisation | Portfolio | Programme | Project |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Retailer | All change initiatives across stores, online and supply chain | Omnichannel programme to unify online and in-store shopping | Launch click-and-collect in 50 stores |
| Software company | Product and platform investments for the year | Platform modernisation programme | Migrate the billing service to the new platform |
| Local council | Capital and service-improvement investments | Housing regeneration programme | Build a new community centre |
| Manufacturer | Operational and growth investments | Net-zero programme | Install solar panels at one plant |
| University | Strategic initiatives across faculties | Digital learning programme | Replace the virtual learning environment |

### Roles and responsibilities at each level
| Role | Level | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Executive leadership or portfolio board | Portfolio | Set strategy, approve investment, decide priorities, stop or start work |
| Portfolio manager | Portfolio | Run the selection and prioritisation process, monitor portfolio performance, balance capacity and risk, advise the board |
| Programme sponsor or senior responsible owner | Programme | Own the programme's vision and benefits, chair the programme board, secure funding |
| Programme manager | Programme | Coordinate projects, manage dependencies, shared resources and cross-project risks, track benefits |
| Business change manager | Programme | Prepare the business to adopt new ways of working so benefits are realised |
| Project sponsor | Project | Authorise the project, own its business case, make decisions above the project manager's authority |
| Project manager | Project | Plan and deliver the project within agreed tolerances, lead the team, report progress |
| PMO (project, programme or portfolio office) | Any | Set standards, consolidate reporting, support planning and assurance |
On smaller programmes some of these roles are combined; on the largest each may be a full-time team. For the project level in detail, see [project manager roles and responsibilities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-roles-and-responsibilities/).

### Project, programme or portfolio: which do you need?
Start from the work, not the label. These questions help you decide how to organise it:
1. Is there one clear output that a single team and plan can deliver? Run it as a **project**.
2. Do several projects depend on each other, share scarce resources or only create value together? Group them into a **programme**.
3. Does the organisation run more projects than it has people or money for, or struggle to say which work matters most? Introduce **portfolio management**.

#### Signs you need a programme
- Project managers keep negotiating with each other over the same people or dates.
- Nobody owns the overall outcome, only individual deliverables.
- Benefits depend on business change as well as new systems or products.

#### Signs you need portfolio management
- Too many projects start and too few finish.
- Teams are spread across many projects and everything is "top priority".
- Leaders cannot see all current work, its cost or its status in one place.
- Projects carry on after their business case has stopped making sense.
Portfolio management does not have to be heavy. A single prioritised list of all work, reviewed monthly by the people who control budgets, is a good start. If you personally juggle several projects, see [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/).

### Programme and portfolio management in Agile organisations
Agile organisations use the same three levels with different mechanics. Instead of approving fixed-scope projects one by one, they often fund long-lived teams or value streams and adjust priorities in short cycles.
- **Lean portfolio management** funds value streams rather than individual projects and reviews priorities regularly. See [Agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/).
- **Agile Release Trains** in the [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) play a role similar to a programme: several teams plan and deliver together. See [Agile Release Train](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/).
- **PI planning** works like a programme-level planning event, aligning teams on objectives for the next increment.
- **Roadmaps** replace detailed long-range plans at portfolio and programme level. See [project roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-roadmap/).
The questions stay the same: are we investing in the right work, are related pieces of work coming together, and is each team delivering well?

### Careers and certifications
A common career path runs from project coordinator to project manager, then senior project manager, programme manager and portfolio manager or head of a PMO. The skills shift from planning and delivery towards stakeholder influence, benefits, finance and strategy.
| Level | PMI certification | Other options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project | PMP (and CAPM for those starting out) | PRINCE2 Foundation and Practitioner |
| Programme | PgMP (Program Management Professional) | MSP Foundation and Practitioner |
| Portfolio | PfMP (Portfolio Management Professional) | Portfolio-level qualifications from other bodies |
PgMP and PfMP require several years of programme or portfolio experience on top of project experience, so most people earn them later in their career. Check the current eligibility rules on pmi.org before you apply.

### Tools for managing projects, programmes and portfolios
Managing a single project needs tasks, a timeline and collaboration. Programme and portfolio work adds requirements: roll-up dashboards across many projects, cross-project dependencies, resource and capacity views, intake and approval workflows, and reporting on budgets and benefits.
Many work management platforms now cover all three levels to some degree. Our #1-ranked tool, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), is a good fit for organisations that need cross-project dashboards, resource planning and custom request workflows.

### Common mistakes
- **Calling a big project a programme.** The label adds governance overhead without adding coordination value if the work has one output.
- **Treating the portfolio as a list.** A portfolio needs active decisions: selecting, balancing and stopping work, not just recording it.
- **Measuring programmes like projects.** A programme that is on time and on budget but delivers no benefits has failed.
- **Starting everything at once.** Approving more work than the organisation has capacity for slows everything down. See [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/).
- **Ignoring operations.** Business-as-usual work uses the same people as change work; leaving it out of portfolio decisions gives a false picture of capacity.
- **No link to strategy.** If nobody can explain how a project supports an objective, question whether it belongs in the portfolio.
