### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between project, programme and portfolio management?**
Project management delivers a specific result within time, cost and scope limits. Programme management coordinates related projects to realise shared benefits. Portfolio management selects, prioritises and balances all of an organisation's initiatives to meet its strategic goals.

**Q: What is the difference between program and portfolio management?**
A programme contains related projects working towards common benefits and is led by a programme manager. A portfolio contains all the work an organisation funds, related or not, including operations, and focuses on choosing and balancing that work against strategy.

**Q: Is a program bigger than a portfolio?**
Usually not. A portfolio sits above programmes and can contain several programmes, standalone projects and operational work. A small organisation's portfolio might be smaller than a large organisation's programme, but in the hierarchy the portfolio is the higher level.

**Q: Which comes first: portfolio, program or project?**
Strategy and the portfolio come first: the portfolio decides which programmes and projects to fund. Programmes then define and coordinate their component projects, and projects deliver the outputs.

**Q: Can a project exist without a program or portfolio?**
Yes. Many projects stand alone, especially in small organisations. Even so, someone should decide that the project is worth funding, which is a simple form of portfolio decision.

**Q: What does a program manager do that a project manager doesn't?**
A programme manager manages dependencies, shared resources and risks across several projects, and is accountable for the benefits those projects deliver together. A project manager focuses on delivering one project's scope. See [project manager vs program manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-vs-program-manager/).

**Q: What is project portfolio management (PPM)?**
The practice of identifying, evaluating, prioritising, selecting and monitoring projects and programmes against strategy, capacity and risk, and deciding what to start, stop or change.

**Q: Does a portfolio include operations?**
In PMI's definition, yes. A portfolio can include operational work as well as projects and programmes, because they compete for the same budget and people.

**Q: Is it program management or programme management?**
Both are correct. Program is the American spelling and the one PMI uses; programme is the usual British spelling. They mean the same thing.

**Q: What is P3M?**
P3M stands for portfolio, programme and project management. It is a term used mainly in the UK to describe the three levels and how they work together.

**Q: What certifications exist for program and portfolio management?**
PMI offers PgMP for programme managers and PfMP for portfolio managers, alongside PMP for project managers. MSP is a widely used programme management certification in the UK and Europe.

**Q: How does a PMO relate to portfolio management?**
A PMO supports governance by setting standards, consolidating reporting and providing analysis. A portfolio-level or enterprise PMO often runs the portfolio management process, but investment decisions usually sit with a portfolio board. See [PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/).

**Q: What is enterprise project management?**
Enterprise project management (EPM) applies consistent project, programme and portfolio practices, tools and reporting across a whole organisation, often supported by an enterprise PMO.

**Q: When should related projects become a programme?**
When they depend on each other, compete for the same resources, or only deliver their intended benefits together. Grouping them lets one sponsor and programme manager coordinate the work and track benefits.

# What Is a Project Baseline? Scope, Schedule and Cost

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a project baseline is, the scope, schedule and cost baselines, how to set and re-baseline, and how baselines are used to measure performance.


## What Is a Project Baseline? Scope, Schedule and Cost
A baseline is the approved version of a plan, frozen so that actual performance can be compared against it. Projects usually have three: scope, schedule and cost.
- Published 21 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Baselines are approved plans used to measure performance.
- Projects have scope, schedule and cost baselines.
- Change them only through change control.

### The three baselines
| Baseline | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Scope baseline | Scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary |
| Schedule baseline | Approved start and finish dates for activities and milestones |
| Cost baseline | Time-phased budget, excluding management reserve |
Together they form the performance measurement baseline, used for [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).

### Setting a baseline
1. Complete planning and get the plan approved.
2. Save the baseline in your scheduling tool.
3. Communicate it to the team and stakeholders.

### Using the baseline
- Compare actual progress with baseline dates.
- Calculate schedule and cost variance; see [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) and [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/).
- Show baseline bars on Gantt charts.
- Plot planned vs actual on an [S-curve](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/s-curve/).

### Re-baselining
Change the baseline only through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/), for example after a major approved scope change. Keep earlier baselines so the history remains visible.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a baseline in project management?**
The approved version of the scope, schedule or cost plan used to measure performance.

**Q: Why is a project baseline important?**
Without it you cannot measure variance or progress objectively.

**Q: When is the project baseline set?**
At the end of planning, once the plan is approved.

**Q: What does re-baselining mean for a project baseline?**
Formally changing the project baseline after an approved change.

**Q: Should you change the project baseline often?**
No. Frequent re-baselining hides performance problems.

**Q: How does the performance measurement baseline relate to the project baseline?**
It is the integrated scope, schedule and cost baselines, the part of the project baseline used to measure performance.

**Q: Is management reserve part of the project baseline?**
No. It sits outside the cost baseline, in the overall budget.

**Q: How is a project baseline shown on a Gantt chart?**
As a second, usually grey, bar beneath each task.

**Q: Do Agile projects use a project baseline?**
Not in the classic sense; release plans and burnup charts play a similar role.

**Q: What tools support project baselines?**
Most scheduling tools such as Wrike, Smartsheet and Microsoft Planner premium plans.

# Project Budget: How to Create One, With an Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a project budget is, what it includes, how to build it step by step from estimates and reserves, a worked example and tips for managing it.


## Project Budget: How to Create One, With an Example
A project budget is the total approved funding for a project, broken down by work and time. It is built from cost estimates, plus contingency reserves for known risks and a management reserve for unknown ones.
- Published 28 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- The budget is built from work estimates, contingency and management reserve.
- The cost baseline (BAC) is what performance is measured against.
- Time-phase the budget so cash flow and progress can be tracked.
- Change the baseline only through formal change control.

### What a project budget includes
- Labour: internal staff time and contractors.
- Materials, equipment, software and licences.
- Facilities, travel and training.
- Supplier and subcontract costs; see [procurement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/).
- Indirect costs or overheads, if the organisation allocates them.
- Contingency reserve for identified risks.
- Management reserve for unforeseen work within scope.

### How the budget builds up
| Layer | What it contains | Who controls it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Activity estimates | Cost of each activity | Team |
| Work package estimates | Activities rolled up | Control account manager |
| Contingency reserve | Money for identified risks (known unknowns) | Project manager |
| Cost baseline | Work packages + contingency, time-phased | Project manager |
| Management reserve | Money for unknown unknowns | Sponsor |
| Project budget | Cost baseline + management reserve | Sponsor / organisation |
The cost baseline is also the [budget at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/budget-at-completion/) used in earned value.

### How to create a project budget
1. Start from a clear [scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) and [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/).
2. Estimate the cost of each work package; see [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/).
3. Add contingency based on risk analysis.
4. Spread the costs over time using the schedule to create a time-phased baseline and [S-curve](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/s-curve/).
5. Add management reserve and check funding limits and cash flow.
6. Get the budget approved and baselined.
7. Track actuals against it and change it only through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).

### Worked example
| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Work packages (design, build, test, deploy) | $180,000 |
| Contingency reserve for identified risks | $20,000 |
| **Cost baseline (BAC)** | **$200,000** |
| Management reserve | $15,000 |
| **Total project budget** | **$215,000** |
If an identified risk occurs, the project manager draws on the $20,000 contingency. If unforeseen in-scope work appears, the sponsor may release management reserve, which then raises the cost baseline through a change request.

### Tips for managing a budget
- Review actuals weekly, not only at month-end.
- Use [earned value](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/), not spend alone, to judge performance.
- Agree control thresholds, for example a CPI below 0.95 triggers a review.
- Record why reserves were used, for [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).
- Check the funding schedule so money is available when it is needed.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project budget?**
The total approved funding for a project, built from cost estimates plus contingency and management reserves, and spread over time.

**Q: What is the difference between the cost baseline and the project budget?**
The cost baseline includes work estimates and contingency reserve. The project budget adds the management reserve on top.

**Q: What is a contingency reserve in a project budget?**
Money set aside for identified risks, held within the cost baseline and usually controlled by the project manager.

**Q: What is a management reserve in a project budget?**
Money for unforeseen work within scope. It sits outside the cost baseline and is controlled by the sponsor or management.

**Q: How do you create a project budget?**
Estimate each work package, add contingency, time-phase it with the schedule, add management reserve and get it approved.

**Q: How much contingency should a project budget have?**
It should come from risk analysis rather than a fixed rule. Riskier, less well-defined projects need more.

**Q: What is a time-phased project budget?**
A budget showing how much is planned to be spent in each period. Plotted cumulatively it forms an [S-curve](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/s-curve/).

**Q: Who approves the project budget?**
Usually the project sponsor or a governance board, in line with the organisation's financial authority levels.

**Q: Can a project budget change?**
Yes, but only through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/), with the baseline updated once the change is approved.

**Q: What is budget at completion in a project budget?**
The total cost baseline for the work, written BAC. It excludes management reserve.

**Q: What tools help manage a project budget?**
Spreadsheets work for small projects; larger ones use [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) or finance systems with timesheets and budget tracking.

# What Is a Project Charter? Template, Examples and Tips

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a project charter is, why it matters, what to include, a ready-to-use template outline, an example, and tips for getting it approved.


## What Is a Project Charter? Template, Examples and Tips
A project charter is the short document that formally authorises a project. It names the sponsor and project manager, states why the project exists and what it must achieve, and gives the project manager authority to use organisational resources.
- Published 13 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- A project charter formally authorises a project and the project manager.
- It covers purpose, objectives, scope, milestones, budget, risks and roles.
- Keep it short and get it signed before detailed planning.

### Why the charter matters
- Creates formal authorisation and a clear starting point.
- Aligns the sponsor, project manager and stakeholders on purpose and scope.
- Gives the project manager authority to act.
- Becomes the reference point when scope or priorities are questioned later.

### What to include
| Section | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and business case | Why the project is needed and the benefits expected |
| Objectives | Measurable [SMART objectives](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-objectives/) |
| High-level scope | What is in and out of scope; see [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) |
| Key deliverables | Main outputs; see [deliverables](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/) |
| Milestones | Major dates |
| Budget | Summary budget or funding range |
| Stakeholders | Key people and groups; see [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) |
| Risks, assumptions and constraints | Top items known at the start; see [constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/) |
| Roles | Sponsor, project manager and authority levels |
| Approval | Signatures and date |

### Example (summary)
**Project:** New customer portal. **Purpose:** reduce support calls by letting customers manage accounts online. **Objective:** cut account-related calls by 30% within six months of launch. **Scope:** account view, invoices, password reset; excludes mobile app. **Budget:** $150,000. **Sponsor:** Head of Customer Service. **Project manager:** A. Rossi. **Key risk:** integration with billing system.

### Tips
- Keep it short: two to four pages.
- Write objectives that can be measured at the end.
- List exclusions explicitly to prevent [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).
- Get the sponsor's signature before planning in detail.
- Revisit it at major milestones.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Who writes the project charter?**
Usually the project manager or sponsor drafts it; the sponsor approves and signs it.

**Q: Who signs the project charter?**
The project sponsor, and sometimes other key stakeholders such as the customer.

**Q: When is the project charter created?**
During initiation, before detailed planning begins.

**Q: How long should a project charter be?**
Typically two to four pages. Detail belongs in the project management plan.

**Q: What is the difference between a project charter and a project plan?**
The charter authorises the project at a high level; the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) explains in detail how it will be delivered.

**Q: Is a project charter the same as a business case?**
No. The business case justifies the investment; the charter authorises the project and summarises the business case.

**Q: Can a project charter change?**
It should be stable, but major changes in purpose or scope may require a revised charter approved by the sponsor.

**Q: Do Agile projects need a project charter?**
Many Agile teams use a lightweight charter or product vision to align on purpose, goals and boundaries.

**Q: How does a project charter compare with a project initiation document?**
A project initiation document (PID) is a more detailed PRINCE2 document that serves a similar purpose to a charter; see [project initiation document](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-initiation-document/).

**Q: What happens if there is no project charter?**
Projects without a charter often suffer from unclear authority, disputed scope and weak sponsor support.

# Project Closure: Steps, Checklist and Report Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project closure explained: steps to close a project, a full checklist, closure report template and worked example, handover, cancelled projects and FAQs.


## Project Closure: Steps, Checklist and Report Example
Project closure is the final phase of a project, in which deliverables are formally accepted and handed over, contracts and finances are closed, people are released, lessons are recorded and the sponsor signs the project off. This guide gives you a 10-step closure process, a checklist with owners, a closure report template with a worked example, a closure meeting agenda and a method for closing projects that are cancelled early.
- Published 2 October 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project closure formally ends the project: the customer accepts the deliverables, ownership passes to operations and the sponsor confirms in writing that the project can stop.
- Completion and closure are different. Completion means the work is done; closure means acceptance, handover, contracts, finances, people, lessons and records are all dealt with too.
- Plan closure from the start, with time and budget in the schedule. Closure that is left until the last week is usually rushed or skipped.
- A closure report compares results with the objectives, schedule and budget, lists every open item with a new owner and records the main lessons.
- Cancelled projects need formal closure as much as successful ones: record why they stopped, salvage what is useful and close contracts and costs.
- PMBOK, PRINCE2 and agile approaches all include closure; they differ mainly in who authorises it and how often it happens.

### What is project closure?
**Project closure is the last phase of the project life cycle, in which the project manager confirms that all work is complete, obtains formal acceptance, hands deliverables to their long-term owners, closes contracts and budgets, releases resources, captures lessons learned and obtains sign-off that the project has ended.** It turns a temporary project into business as usual.
Closure ends the project, not the product. The new system, building or process carries on under an operational owner; what stops is the temporary team, budget and governance that were set up to create it. That is why handover is at the heart of closure: someone else must be ready, willing and equipped to take responsibility.
Closure can also happen at the end of each phase or stage, not only at the end of the whole project. A phase closure confirms that the phase's outputs are complete and gives the sponsor a decision point on whether to continue. For the full life cycle, see our guide to the [five phases of project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/).

### Why formal project closure matters
Closure is often cut short because the team is tired and new work is waiting. A few days of disciplined closure protect the value the project has just created.
- **Confirms acceptance.** Written sign-off from the sponsor or customer settles the question of whether the work is finished.
- **Transfers ownership.** Operations or support teams take responsibility, so the project team can stop answering calls about the deliverable.
- **Stops spending.** Cost codes, purchase orders and contracts are closed, so no more charges land on the project.
- **Frees people and equipment** for other work, with feedback on each person's contribution.
- **Keeps the learning.** [Lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) are captured while memories are fresh and shared with future projects.
- **Creates a complete record** for audits, disputes, warranty claims and similar projects in the future.
Projects that drift to an end leave open purchase orders, support arrangements nobody agreed and customers who keep asking for small changes.

### Project closure vs project completion
The two terms are often used interchangeably, but they describe different moments. Completion is about the product; closure is about the project as a whole.
| Aspect | Project completion | Project closure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Question answered | Is the work finished? | Is the project finished, handed over and signed off? |
| Focus | Deliverables built and tested | Acceptance, handover, contracts, finance, people, lessons and records |
| Main evidence | Test results, inspection or demo | Signed acceptance and closure report |
| Who confirms it | Project team and quality checks | Sponsor or governance board |
| What happens next | Closure activities start | Operations own the product; the project organisation is disbanded |
A project can be complete but not closed for weeks if handover drags on, so track closure tasks in the plan.

### Types of project closure
How you close depends on why the project or phase is ending. The steps are similar, but the emphasis changes.
| Type | When it happens | What is different |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal closure | Objectives achieved and deliverables accepted | Full handover, closure report and celebration |
| Phase or stage closure | End of a phase, stage or release | Formal review of the phase and a decision to continue, change course or stop |
| Premature closure | Project cancelled, for example because the business case no longer holds | Record the reasons, the work done and what can be salvaged; close costs quickly |
| Contract closure | A supplier contract ends | Verify the supplier's deliverables, settle payments and formally close the agreement |
| Suspension | Project paused, for example for funding or a regulatory decision | Document status so the work can restart; keep minimum governance in place |

### When project closure starts
Closure is the last phase, but the preparation starts at initiation. The [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) and project management plan should state the acceptance criteria, who signs off and who will own the deliverables afterwards. If those are vague at the start, closure becomes a negotiation at the end.
Build closure tasks into the schedule as a work package with its own effort and budget. A simple timeline for a medium-sized project looks like this:
| When | Closure activities |
| --- | --- |
| At initiation | Agree acceptance criteria, sign-off authority and the future operational owner |
| 4–6 weeks before go-live | Confirm the handover plan, training dates and support model; warn suppliers about contract close-out; book the closure meeting |
| 2 weeks before | Draft the closure report; start reconciling costs; list open issues and risks for transfer |
| Closure week | Formal acceptance, handover, closure meeting and lessons session |
| 2–6 weeks after | Final invoices paid, cost codes closed, records archived, closure report signed |
| Later | Benefits reviewed by the business owner, usually months after closure |

### How to close a project: 10 steps
The steps below follow the order most projects need. Some run in parallel, but acceptance should come before release of the team, and the closure report should come last because it summarises everything else.

#### 1. Confirm the work is complete
Check every deliverable against the [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) and the acceptance criteria. Use the scope statement or deliverables list as a checklist and record the evidence for each item: test results, inspection reports, user acceptance testing or a demonstration. Include approved changes from the [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) log, and mark descoped items explicitly so nobody expects them later.

#### 2. Obtain formal acceptance
Ask the sponsor or customer to sign an acceptance form or approve the acceptance in your governance tool. Acceptance with conditions is common: list each condition, such as a minor defect to be fixed, with an owner and a date. Avoid verbal acceptance. Without a written record, the question of whether the work is finished can reopen months later.

#### 3. Hand over the deliverables
Transfer the deliverables to the people who will run, use or support them, together with documentation, training, access and warranty information. The receiving team should confirm in writing that it accepts ownership. The section on handover below covers what to include.

#### 4. Transfer open issues and risks
Go through the [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/) and [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/). Close what is resolved. For anything still open, agree a new owner in operations and record the transfer. Risks that only made sense during the project, such as a supplier delay, can be closed with a note.

#### 5. Close contracts
For each supplier, confirm that the statement of work has been met, resolve any claims or disputes, pay final invoices and send formal notice that the contract is complete. Retention payments and warranty periods may continue after closure, so record their end dates and who will manage them. Our guide to [procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) covers contract close-out in more detail.

#### 6. Close the finances
Reconcile actual cost against the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/), explain the [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/), accrue any costs still to be invoiced and ask finance to close the cost codes. Cancel open purchase orders and remove project credit cards or approvals so nothing new can be charged.

#### 7. Release resources
Release people in a planned way, keeping the few needed for handover and the closure report. Give each person written feedback for their line manager and remove temporary access and licences.

#### 8. Capture lessons learned
Run a final lessons session with the team and key stakeholders. Focus on causes and recommendations rather than blame, and give each recommendation an owner. Move the lessons into the organisation's repository or PMO knowledge base. The [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) gives you a ready-made structure.

#### 9. Write the closure report and obtain sign-off
Summarise performance against the objectives, schedule, budget and quality targets; list outstanding items and their new owners; record the main lessons; and ask the sponsor to sign. The template and worked example below show what to include.

#### 10. Archive, communicate and celebrate
Store final versions of key documents in the agreed location, following retention rules. Tell stakeholders the project is closed and who to contact from now on. Then thank the team properly.
See our guide to [project integration management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-integration-management/) for how closure connects to the other processes that hold a project together.

### Project handover to operations
Handover is where many closures stall, because the receiving team will not inherit something it cannot support. Agree the handover contents early, ideally during planning.
| Handover item | Typical contents | Received by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deliverable and configuration | The product, final versions, configuration and asset records | Operations or asset owner |
| Documentation | User guides, technical manuals, process maps, as-built drawings | Support team and users |
| Training | Completed training, materials and a list of trained people | Line managers |
| Support model | Who handles questions and faults, service levels and escalation routes | Service desk or support team |
| Warranties and contracts | Warranty terms, support contracts and supplier contacts | Procurement or operations |
| Open items | Known defects, open risks and issues with owners and dates | Operations lead |
| Benefits plan | Benefit measures, baselines and review dates | Business owner |
For larger changes, agree a short period of extra support after go-live, sometimes called hypercare, with an end date and exit criteria so it does not quietly become permanent.

### Project closure checklist
Use this checklist to confirm that nothing has been missed before you ask for sign-off. Adjust the owners to your organisation; on small projects, the project manager may own most rows.
| Area | Checklist item | Owner | Done |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deliverables | All deliverables completed and verified against acceptance criteria | Project manager | [ ] |
| Scope | Approved changes reflected; descoped items recorded | Project manager | [ ] |
| Acceptance | Formal sign-off received from sponsor or customer | Sponsor | [ ] |
| Handover | Operations or support team trained and has accepted ownership | Operations lead | [ ] |
| Handover | User guides, technical documents and warranties handed over | Project manager | [ ] |
| Issues | Open issues and defects closed or transferred with an owner | Project manager | [ ] |
| Risks | Risk register closed; ongoing risks handed to operations | Project manager | [ ] |
| Contracts | Supplier deliverables confirmed and contracts formally closed | Procurement | [ ] |
| Finance | Final costs reconciled, invoices paid, purchase orders cancelled, cost codes closed | Finance | [ ] |
| Resources | Team members released with written feedback | Project manager | [ ] |
| Access | Temporary system access, licences and building passes removed | IT and facilities | [ ] |
| Knowledge | Lessons learned session held and register updated | Project manager | [ ] |
| Benefits | Benefits measurement plan handed to the business owner | Sponsor | [ ] |
| Records | Project files archived in the agreed location under retention rules | Project coordinator | [ ] |
| Report | Closure report written and signed | Project manager and sponsor | [ ] |
| Communication | Closure announced to stakeholders with future contacts | Project manager | [ ] |
If you track the project in a [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/), filter it for open items on the day you start closure. It is the fastest way to find the issues, risks and actions that need a new home.

### Project closure report template
The closure report, sometimes called an end project report or project completion report, is the formal record of how the project performed and what has been left for others. Keep it short: two to six pages is enough for most projects, with links to detailed records.
| Section | What to include |
| --- | --- |
| Project summary | Purpose, sponsor, project manager, start and end dates, approach used |
| Objectives and results | Each objective, its target and the actual result |
| Scope | Delivered, changed and descoped items, with approved change requests |
| Schedule performance | Planned and actual dates for key milestones, with reasons for variance |
| Cost performance | Budget, actual cost and variance, with an explanation |
| Quality | Acceptance results and outstanding defects |
| Benefits | Benefits achieved so far and how the rest will be measured, by whom |
| Outstanding items | Open issues, risks and actions, each with a new owner and date |
| Lessons learned | The three to five most important lessons and recommendations |
| Approval | Sponsor sign-off and date |
Write for someone who was not involved, such as a future project manager or an auditor. Give numbers, not adjectives. An [executive summary template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/executive-summary-template/) is useful for the first page.

### Worked example: a closure report
The example below is **illustrative**. It shows how the template looks when filled in for a payroll system upgrade at a mid-sized organisation.
**Project summary.** Upgrade of the payroll system to the supplier's current version, with a new pension interface added by approved change. Sponsor: finance director. Planned dates 6 January to 30 June; actual finish 14 July.
| Objective | Target | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Upgrade payroll to the supported version | Live before support for the old version ends | Achieved: live on 1 July |
| Run two parallel payrolls with no unexplained differences | Zero unexplained differences | Achieved: two parallel runs reconciled |
| Automate the pension interface (approved change) | Manual pension uploads stopped | Achieved |
| Train payroll staff | All 9 payroll staff trained | Achieved |
| Reduce manual processing time | Measured after three pay cycles | Handed to the finance director to measure |
| Measure | Baseline | Actual | Variance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Finish date | 30 June | 14 July | 14 days late |
| Cost | $320,000 | $334,000 | $14,000 over (4.4%) |
**Variance explanation.** The pension interface change was approved in March, adding $16,000 and two weeks. Excluding the change, the project finished $2,000 under budget and on schedule.
**Outstanding items.** Two minor defects in the payslip layout transferred to the payroll support team, fix due 15 August. One supplier invoice of $4,000 accrued, payment due 31 July. Benefit tracking passed to the finance director, first review after three pay cycles.
**Lessons.** (1) Involve the pension provider at the requirements stage; the interface was identified late. (2) Two parallel runs were enough to build confidence and should become the standard. (3) Book payroll staff for training before the busy year-end period.
**Approval.** Signed by the sponsor, 4 August.
Every number has a baseline, the variance is explained by an approved change and each open item has an owner and a date. For the arithmetic, see our guides to [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/) and [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/).

### The project closure meeting
A closure meeting, or closeout meeting, brings the sponsor, key stakeholders and team leads together to confirm acceptance, agree how open items will be handled and mark the end of the project. It is different from a team retrospective, which focuses on how the team worked; many projects hold both, with the retrospective first so its findings can feed the closure report.
A 60-minute agenda that works for most projects:
| Time | Item | Led by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 min | Purpose of the meeting and what will be decided | Project manager |
| 10 min | Results against objectives, schedule and budget | Project manager |
| 10 min | Acceptance status and any conditions | Sponsor or customer |
| 10 min | Handover: confirmation from the receiving owners | Operations lead |
| 10 min | Open issues, risks and actions: agree owners | Project manager |
| 10 min | Top lessons and recommendations | Team leads |
| 5 min | Formal closure decision and thanks | Sponsor |
Send the draft closure report beforehand so the meeting is spent on decisions rather than reading. A written agenda and clear minutes, ideally with each action's owner and date, make the outcome easy to record.

### How to close a cancelled project
Stopping a project that no longer makes sense, for example after a change of strategy, is a good decision, not a failure. Close it formally so the organisation gets the most from what it has spent.
1. **Confirm the decision in writing.** Get the cancellation decision and its reasons from the sponsor or board, with an effective date.
2. **Stop work and spending quickly.** Tell the team and suppliers, stop new orders and check the notice periods and termination terms in each contract.
3. **Record the status of the work.** List what was completed, what was partly done and what was not started, with the cost to date.
4. **Salvage useful outputs.** Requirements, designs, data, code, purchased equipment and supplier relationships may be reused; give each one an owner.
5. **Close contracts and finances.** Agree termination costs, pay what is owed and close cost codes.
6. **Release people with care.** Explain the reasons openly and recognise the work done; people who feel their effort was wasted are slower to commit next time.
7. **Capture lessons.** Focus on what could have shown the problem earlier, such as clearer stage gates or benefits checks.
8. **Write a short closure report** that records the reasons, work done, money spent, items salvaged and lessons, and get it signed.
Tip
Avoid the word failure in the communication. Say what changed and why stopping is the right decision. Good [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) makes stopping a normal outcome of a stage gate rather than an embarrassment.

### Who does what at project closure
The table uses R for responsible, A for accountable and C for consulted. Adapt it in a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) for your project.
| Activity | Sponsor | Project manager | Project coordinator | Operations | Finance and procurement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Confirm deliverables complete | C | A/R | R | C |  |
| Formal acceptance | A | R |  | C |  |
| Handover | C | A | R | R |  |
| Close contracts |  | A | C |  | R |
| Close finances | C | A | R |  | R |
| Lessons learned | C | A/R | R | C | C |
| Closure report | A | R | R | C | C |
| Archive records |  | A | R |  |  |
On many projects, a [project coordinator](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-coordinator/) runs much of the closure administration: chasing sign-offs, collecting documents, updating logs and archiving files. The project manager remains accountable for the result.

### Closure in PMBOK, PRINCE2 and agile
Every major framework includes closure; they differ in terminology and in who authorises it.
| Approach | How closure is handled |
| --- | --- |
| PMBOK Guide 6th edition | Close Project or Phase, a process in project integration management and the only process in the closing process group. It also covers closing procurements. |
| PMBOK Guide 8th edition (November 2025) | Brings back Closing as one of five focus areas, alongside six principles and seven performance domains, with processes described in a non-prescriptive way. |
| PRINCE2 7 | The Closing a project process prepares planned or premature closure, hands over products, evaluates the project and recommends closure. The project board authorises closure through Directing a project. |
| Agile and Scrum | Each sprint ends with a review and retrospective; a release or product effort is closed when the product owner and stakeholders agree the goal is met or funding ends. The product usually continues with a support or product team. |
For background on the standards themselves, see our guides to the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/), [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) and the [five process groups](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-processes/). If you are preparing for the [PMP exam](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/), expect scenario questions about obtaining acceptance before releasing the team and about closing a project that has been cancelled.

### Common project closure mistakes
| Mistake | What happens | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Releasing the team before handover | Nobody is left to answer questions or fix defects | Keep a small closure team until acceptance and handover are signed |
| No written acceptance | The customer keeps asking for small changes | Agree acceptance criteria at initiation and get written sign-off |
| Leaving contracts and orders open | Late invoices land on closed or other budgets | Reconcile with procurement and finance; cancel open orders |
| Skipping lessons learned | The same problems recur on the next project | Book the session in advance and keep it to 90 minutes |
| Losing open risks and issues | Known problems surprise operations later | Transfer each open item with a named owner |
| Not closing cancelled projects | Money keeps leaking and learning is lost | Use the cancelled-project steps above |
| Unplanned, unfunded closure | Closure is rushed or forgotten | Include closure as a work package with time and budget |

### Tools and templates for project closure
You do not need special software to close a project, but a shared tool helps because the evidence already sits in one place.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, works well for closure on larger or multi-project portfolios: custom workflows can add an acceptance step, dashboards show open tasks and issues across a project, and completed projects can be archived while staying searchable. monday.com, Asana and Smartsheet also support closure checklists and templates. Our overview of [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) compares the options.

- [Lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) for the final lessons session and register.

- [Executive summary template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/executive-summary-template/) for the first page of the closure report.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project closure?**
Project closure is the final phase of a project, in which deliverables are formally accepted and handed over, contracts and finances are closed, resources are released, lessons are recorded and the sponsor signs the project off.

**Q: What are the steps to close a project?**
Confirm completion, obtain acceptance, hand over, transfer open issues and risks, close contracts and finances, release resources, capture lessons, write and sign the closure report, then archive and communicate.

**Q: What is a project closure report?**
A short document that records how the project performed against its objectives, schedule, budget and quality targets, lists outstanding items with new owners, summarises the main lessons and carries the sponsor's sign-off. PRINCE2 calls it the end project report.

**Q: Who is responsible for project closure?**
The project manager is responsible for running closure. The sponsor or governance board is accountable for approving it, and coordinators, finance, procurement and operations each handle part of the work.

**Q: Who approves project closure?**
Usually the project sponsor or the board that authorised the project. In PRINCE2, the project board authorises closure after the project manager recommends it.

**Q: How long does project closure take?**
It depends on the size of the project and its contracts. A small internal project may close in a few days; a large project with several suppliers can take weeks, mainly because of final invoices, contract close-out and handover.

**Q: What is the difference between project closure and contract closure?**
Contract closure ends one agreement with a supplier: deliverables are verified, payments are settled and the contract is formally closed. Project closure ends the whole project, which may include several contracts.

**Q: What is administrative closure?**
Administrative closure covers the paperwork side of closing a project or phase: collecting records, reconciling costs, closing accounts, archiving documents and recording acceptance. It is part of project closure rather than a separate phase.

**Q: How do you close a cancelled project?**
Close it formally: confirm the decision in writing, stop spending, record what was done, salvage useful outputs, close contracts, capture lessons and write a short closure report.

**Q: What is the difference between phase closure and project closure?**
Phase closure is a formal review at the end of a phase or stage, confirming its outputs and deciding whether to continue. Project closure happens once, at the end of the whole project, and includes handover and disbanding the project team.

**Q: What happens after project closure?**
The operational owner runs and supports the deliverable, the business owner tracks benefits that appear later, and the archived records and lessons are available to future projects.

**Q: How does the PMBOK Guide handle project closure?**
The sixth edition describes Close Project or Phase as part of integration management and the closing process group. The eighth edition, published in November 2025, brings back Closing as one of five focus areas.

**Q: How does PRINCE2 handle project closure?**
PRINCE2 has a Closing a project process, in which the project manager prepares planned or premature closure, hands over products, evaluates the project and recommends closure to the project board.

**Q: Should benefits be measured at project closure?**
Measure the benefits that are already visible, but many appear months later. Hand a benefits measurement plan, with baselines and review dates, to the business owner so tracking continues after the project ends.

# Project Communication Management: Processes and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-communication-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project communication management explained: the three processes, push, pull and interactive methods, the channels formula, a worked example and steps.


## Project Communication Management: Processes and Examples
Project communication management is the work of making sure the right people get the right project information, in the right format and at the right time, and that they understand it and act on it. It has three parts: planning communication, delivering it and monitoring whether it works. This guide explains each process, the methods and formulas you need, and a full worked example you can adapt.
- Published 2 October 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Communication management has three processes: plan communications management, manage communications and monitor communications.
- In the PMBOK Guide 8th edition the three communication processes sit inside the Stakeholders performance domain, according to published summaries.
- Match the method to the message: interactive for decisions and sensitive topics, push for things people must receive, pull for reference material.
- Communication channels grow quickly with team size: n(n - 1) / 2, so 10 people have 45 channels and 12 people have 66.
- Sending is not communicating. Build in feedback, measure whether messages land and adjust the plan.
- Keep one source of truth for status, decisions and documents so people are not chasing information across tools.

### What is project communication management?
**Project communication management** is the set of processes a project uses to plan, create, distribute, store and monitor project information. Its aim is simple: every stakeholder gets the information they need, in a form they can use, when they need it, and the project team can confirm that messages have been understood and acted on.
In practice it covers all the information that flows around a project: status reports, steering committee papers, meeting notes, change decisions, risk escalations, team updates, supplier correspondence and announcements to end users. It covers formal and informal communication, and people inside and outside the organisation.
Two related documents are often confused:
- **The communication management plan** is the part of the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) that sets the rules: audiences, information needs, methods, frequency, owners, escalation routes, templates, storage and how the plan will be reviewed.
- **The communication plan** (or communication matrix) is the working schedule that comes out of it: a table of who receives what, how, when and from whom. On smaller projects the two are usually one short document.
The project manager sits at the centre of this flow. You will often see the claim that project managers spend 90% of their time communicating; it is widely repeated, but we could not trace it to a solid study, so treat it as a figure of speech. What is clear is that most project management work, from running meetings to negotiating scope and reporting to the sponsor, is communication.
See our step-by-step guide to writing a [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/communication-plan/) for the document itself.

### Why communication management matters
Many project problems that look technical start as communication problems. A sponsor is surprised by a delay the team knew about for weeks. A supplier delivers to the old specification because a change decision never reached them. Scope is disputed because an agreement was never recorded.
Good communication management prevents these failures. It:
- Keeps stakeholders informed and engaged, so support does not quietly fade.
- Gets decisions made on time, because the people who decide have what they need in a form they can act on.
- Reduces misunderstanding about scope, priorities and responsibilities.
- Makes risks and issues visible while they are still cheap to fix.
- Creates a record of decisions and agreements that protects everyone when memories differ.
The best-known evidence comes from PMI's Pulse of the Profession in-depth report on communications, published in May 2013. It found that US$135 million was at risk for every US$1 billion spent on projects, and that 56% of that amount (US$75 million) was at risk because of ineffective communications. The same report found that one in five projects was unsuccessful because of ineffective communications, and that 55% of project managers agreed effective communication with all stakeholders was the most critical success factor. The data is more than a decade old, so treat it as an indication, not a current measure.

### The three communication management processes
The PMBOK Guide sixth edition defines Project Communications Management as one of ten knowledge areas, with three processes. They form a cycle that repeats throughout the project: you plan, you deliver, you check, and you feed what you learn back into the plan.
| Process | Key question | Main inputs | Main outputs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plan communications management | Who needs what information, why, when, how and from whom? | Project charter, stakeholder register, organisational standards | Communication management plan |
| Manage communications | Are we creating, sending and storing information as planned? | Communication plan, work performance reports, issue and change logs | Project communications (reports, presentations, notes), updated records |
| Monitor communications | Is communication working, and what should change? | Communications sent, feedback, stakeholder engagement | Work performance information, change requests, plan updates |

#### Plan communications management
Planning starts from your stakeholder analysis. For each person or group you work out their information needs, how much detail they want, how they prefer to receive it, how often, and who on the team is responsible. You also set the rules that apply to everyone: where documents live, which template a status report uses, how quickly urgent issues are escalated, and any constraints such as confidentiality, language or time zones. Planning happens early, but it is revisited at every phase.

#### Manage communications
This is the delivery process: writing and sending reports, running meetings, publishing updates, answering questions and storing records so people can find them later. Managing communications is not only about pushing information out. It includes choosing words carefully, checking understanding during conversations and making sure the record of decisions is complete.

#### Monitor communications
Monitoring checks whether communication is achieving its purpose. Are decisions being made on time? Are people asking the same questions repeatedly? Are stakeholders surprised by things that were reported? When the answer shows a gap, you adjust the plan: a different method, a different frequency, a different messenger or a different level of detail.

### Communication management in PMBOK 7 and PMBOK 8
If you are studying for an exam or working with an organisation that follows PMI standards, it helps to know how the topic has moved between editions of the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/).
| Edition | Structure | Where communication sits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6th edition (2017) | Ten knowledge areas, five process groups | Its own knowledge area, Project Communications Management, with three processes |
| 7th edition (2021) | Twelve principles, eight performance domains, no processes | No separate area; communication runs through the Stakeholders and Team performance domains |
| 8th edition (November 2025) | Six principles, seven performance domains, processes reintroduced in a non-prescriptive form | Inside the Stakeholders performance domain, alongside the stakeholder engagement processes |
According to published summaries of the 8th edition, the Stakeholders performance domain contains seven processes: identify stakeholders, plan stakeholder engagement, plan communications management, manage stakeholder engagement, manage communications, monitor stakeholder engagement and monitor communications. The practical message is that communication is treated as one of the main tools of [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/), not as a separate discipline.

### Communication methods: interactive, push and pull
The PMBOK Guide groups communication methods into three types. Choosing the right one for each message is one of the simplest ways to improve communication on a project.
| Method | How it works | Examples | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Interactive | Two-way, real-time exchange between two or more people | Meetings, phone and video calls, workshops, instant messaging conversations | Decisions, complex or sensitive topics, conflict, building relationships | Costly in people's time; decisions need recording afterwards |
| Push | Sent to specific recipients, who do not have to ask for it | Emails, status reports, memos, newsletters, notifications | Information people must receive, such as decisions, deadlines and warnings | Sending does not prove it was read or understood |
| Pull | Stored centrally for people to access when they choose | Intranet pages, shared drives, project dashboards, knowledge bases, recorded briefings | Reference material, large audiences, detail some people want and others do not | People may never look; needs signposting |

#### Which method for which message?
Use this rule of thumb when you are unsure:
| Message | Recommended method | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A decision is needed from the sponsor | Interactive, followed by a short written record (push) | Discussion surfaces concerns; the record prevents later disputes |
| Weekly progress | Push (status report) plus pull (live dashboard) | Regular rhythm for those who must know; detail for those who want it |
| Bad news, such as a missed milestone | Interactive first, then push | People should hear bad news from you directly, with options |
| Policy, process or training material | Pull, announced by push | Large audience, used when needed |
| Changes affecting end users | Push and interactive briefings through line managers | People trust messages from their own manager |

### Types of project communication
Beyond the three methods, it is useful to think about the type of communication, because each has its own expectations about tone, formality and record-keeping.
| Type | Description | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Formal | Structured, planned and usually recorded | Steering committee papers, contracts, change requests, sign-offs |
| Informal | Unplanned, conversational | Corridor chats, quick calls, chat messages |
| Written | Permanent and easy to share | Reports, emails, meeting notes, documentation |
| Verbal | Faster, with tone and immediate feedback | Stand-ups, presentations, phone calls |
| Internal | Within the project or organisation | Team updates, briefings to department heads |
| External | With customers, suppliers, regulators or the public | Supplier progress meetings, client reports, press statements |
A useful habit is to **follow informal communication with a formal record when it matters**. If a decision is agreed in a hallway conversation, send a two-line note confirming it, and log it in the decision or [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/).

### The sender-receiver communication model
The basic communication model in project management texts describes how a message travels from one person to another, and where it can go wrong.
1. **Encode.** The sender turns an idea into words, numbers or images.
2. **Transmit.** The message is sent through a channel: email, meeting, report, call.
3. **Decode.** The receiver interprets the message, through their own knowledge and assumptions.
4. **Acknowledge.** The receiver confirms they have received it. This is not the same as agreeing or understanding.
5. **Feedback.** The receiver responds, showing whether the meaning came across as intended.
Anything that distorts the message along the way is called **noise**: jargon, a poor connection, a distracted reader, cultural differences, or a 40-page report when the reader wanted one page. The interactive version of the model stresses the last two steps: communication is only complete when the sender has checked that the receiver understood.

### Communication channels formula
Every pair of people on a project is a potential communication channel. The number of channels grows much faster than the number of people, which is why communication gets harder as projects grow.
The formula is **n(n - 1) / 2**, where n is the number of people (including the project manager).
| People (n) | Calculation | Channels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | 5 x 4 / 2 | 10 |
| 8 | 8 x 7 / 2 | 28 |
| 10 | 10 x 9 / 2 | 45 |
| 12 | 12 x 11 / 2 | 66 |
| 20 | 20 x 19 / 2 | 190 |

#### Worked example: channels added
Exam questions often ask how many channels are **added** when people join. Calculate both totals and subtract:
1. A team has 10 people: 10 x 9 / 2 = 45 channels.
2. Two people join, so n = 12: 12 x 11 / 2 = 66 channels.
3. Channels added = 66 - 45 = 21.
Read the question carefully: "a project manager and 9 team members" means n = 10.
The number is not a target. Its practical lesson is that you cannot rely on everyone talking to everyone. As teams grow you need structure: clear roles (a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) helps), a predictable meeting rhythm, team leads who pass information on, and one place where status and decisions are published.

### How to manage project communication step by step
This process works for most projects, whether you follow a predictive, agile or hybrid approach. On a small project it can take an hour; on a large programme it is a workshop and a formal document.
1. **Identify stakeholders.** Start from the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) and list everyone affected or able to influence the project. Record them in a stakeholder register.
2. **Analyse their information needs.** For each group, ask what decisions they make, what they need to know to make them, how much detail they want and how they prefer to receive it.
3. **Set communication objectives.** Decide what each communication must achieve: inform, consult, gain approval, build support or prompt action. The objective drives the method.
4. **Choose methods, frequency and owners.** Match interactive, push or pull to each message, set a rhythm and name the person responsible for every item.
5. **Agree rules and escalation routes.** Decide where documents live, which templates to use, response times for questions, and how issues move up to the sponsor or [governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) board.
6. **Write the plan and agree it with the sponsor.** Keep it short. A one-page matrix plus a few rules is usually enough.
7. **Deliver consistently.** Send reports on the agreed day, using the same format each time, so people know where to look and can spot changes quickly.
8. **Monitor and adjust.** Gather feedback, watch the indicators in the measurement section below and update the plan at each phase or when stakeholders change.

#### Questions to ask in a communication requirements analysis
- What decisions does this person or group make, and when?
- What happens if they find out late?
- How much detail do they want: headline, summary or full data?
- Which format do they actually read: email, dashboard, meeting, phone call?
- Who do they trust to deliver bad news?
Free template: our [communication plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/) has columns for audience, information, method, frequency, owner and feedback, and comes in beginner, advanced and expert versions. Pair it with the [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) to show who is informed and who is consulted.

### Worked example: communication management on an ERP rollout
This example is illustrative. A 9-month ERP rollout has a steering committee, 4 department heads, a 12-person project team, an external implementation partner and 600 end users across two sites.

#### Step 1: the communication matrix
| Audience | What they need | Method | Frequency | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Steering committee | Progress against milestones, top risks, decisions needed | Meeting plus one-page RAG report (push) | Monthly, plus by exception | Project manager |
| Sponsor | Early warning, decisions, political issues | One-to-one (interactive) | Weekly, 30 minutes | Project manager |
| Department heads | Impact on their teams, readiness actions, training dates | Briefing call (interactive) and action list (push) | Fortnightly | Change lead |
| Project team | Tasks, blockers, priorities | Stand-up and task board (interactive and pull) | Daily | Workstream leads |
| Implementation partner | Deliverables, issues, acceptance status | Joint progress meeting (interactive), shared RAID log (pull) | Weekly | Project manager |
| End users | What is changing, when, what they must do, training | Newsletter (push), intranet page (pull), team briefings | Monthly, weekly in the last 6 weeks | Change lead |

#### Step 2: rules and escalation
- All decisions are recorded in the decision log within one working day of being made.
- Status, risks and issues live in one [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) in the project tool; email attachments are not the record.
- Red issues are escalated to the sponsor the same day by phone, then in writing.
- Questions from department heads receive a reply within two working days, even if the reply is "we are checking".

#### Step 3: monitor and adjust
Three months in, the project manager reviews the indicators. Newsletter open rates are low, the service desk is already fielding questions about go-live, and a readiness survey shows that only a minority of end users can say what is changing for them.
| Signal | Diagnosis | Change to the plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Newsletter rarely opened | Wrong channel for end users; email overload | Department heads deliver a 5-minute briefing in existing team meetings, using a script and FAQ from the project |
| Repeated questions to the service desk | Information exists but is hard to find | Single intranet page with a search-friendly FAQ, linked from every message |
| Steering committee asks for more detail on data migration | One-page report too thin for the highest risk | Add a monthly data migration annex with trend charts |
| Partner surprised by a scope decision | Decision log not shared with partner | Give the partner read access to the decision log and add a weekly decisions summary |
The next readiness survey shows a clear improvement, and repeated service desk questions fall. That is the monitor process doing its job: the plan changed because the evidence showed it was not working.

### Status reports, meetings and escalation
Most project communication runs through three routines. Getting them right covers a large share of what stakeholders need.

#### Status reports
A good [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) is short and leads with what the reader must know or do. A reliable structure:
1. **Overall status** (RAG) and a one-sentence summary.
2. **Decisions or help needed**, with a date by which they are needed.
3. **Progress since last report** against milestones, not a list of activities.
4. **Top risks and issues**, with owner and next action.
5. **Forecast**: are the end date and budget still achievable?
6. **Next period**: the main things that will happen.

#### Meetings
Meetings are the most expensive communication method, so each one needs a clear purpose, an agenda and a record. Use a [meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/) and capture decisions and actions with a [meeting notes template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-notes-template/). On agile teams, the regular events described in our guide to [agile meetings and ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-meetings-and-ceremonies/) replace many traditional status meetings; the [daily scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/), for example, is for the developers to inspect progress and adapt their plan, not a report to a manager.

#### Escalation
| Level | Who decides | Typical trigger | Response time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Team | Workstream lead | Task blocked, small slip within float | Same day |
| 2. Project | Project manager | Milestone at risk, cross-team conflict | Within 2 working days |
| 3. Sponsor | Sponsor | Tolerance breach on time, cost or scope | Within 1 week, or same day if urgent |
| 4. Governance board | Steering committee | Change to business case, major scope change | Next meeting or extraordinary session |
Write your tolerances into the plan so everyone knows when an issue must move up a level. Changes to baselines should follow your [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) process, and the decision should be communicated to everyone affected.

### How to measure whether communication is working
The monitor process needs evidence, not impressions. Pick a handful of indicators that fit your project and review them at each phase gate or monthly.
| Indicator | What it tells you | How to collect it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decision turnaround | Whether decision makers get what they need in time | Days from request to decision in the decision log |
| Repeated questions | Whether information is clear and easy to find | Service desk tickets, inbox, FAQ page searches |
| Surprises | Whether bad news travels early | Count of issues stakeholders say they heard about late |
| Attendance and engagement | Whether meetings and briefings are valued | Attendance, questions asked, actions completed on time |
| Stakeholder feedback | Whether people feel informed | Short pulse survey: two or three questions each phase |
| Readiness | Whether end users understand what is changing | Readiness survey or quiz before go-live |
Tip
Keep the feedback survey short. Two questions work well: "How well informed do you feel about the project?" (1 to 5) and "What one thing would make our communication more useful to you?"

### Communication barriers and how to overcome them
| Barrier | What it looks like | How to reduce it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Information overload | People stop reading updates; important messages are missed | Fewer, shorter messages; put the action in the subject line; use dashboards for detail |
| Jargon and acronyms | Business users nod along but do not understand | Plain language; a project glossary; test messages on someone outside the team |
| Distance and time zones | Delays, people left out of decisions | Agreed core hours, written decision records, recorded briefings; see [remote project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/remote-project-management/) |
| Language and culture | Silence mistaken for agreement; directness mistaken for rudeness | Check understanding explicitly; written follow-ups; agree team norms |
| Tool sprawl | Decisions spread across email, chat and documents | Agree one source of truth for status and decisions; define what each channel is for |
| Unclear ownership | Everyone assumes someone else told the supplier | Name an owner for each communication in the plan |
Many of these are skills as much as processes. Our guide to [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/) covers listening, writing and negotiation in more depth.

### Tools for project communication
Tools do not fix communication on their own, but good [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) keeps conversations attached to the work and status in one place. Agree what each tool is for before the project starts.
- [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) (our top-rated tool) keeps comments, @mentions, approvals and files on each task, offers dashboards across projects and includes AI comment summaries. Agree notification habits early, as reviewers mention notification volume.
- [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) gives every item an updates thread with comments, @mentions and files, plus dashboards and guest access, and is quick for teams to pick up.
- [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) lets project owners publish status updates, and its portfolios give leaders one view of the health of many projects.
- [Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/) lives inside Teams and Outlook, which suits organisations that already communicate there.

### Common mistakes in project communication
- **One message for everyone.** Executives need decisions and exceptions; teams need detail. Tailor the same facts for each audience.
- **Reporting activity, not outcomes.** "We held six workshops" says little. Say what has changed, what is at risk and what you need.
- **Hiding or softening bad news.** Raise problems early, with options and a recommendation. Late bad news damages trust far more than early bad news.
- **No feedback loop.** Sending is not communicating. Check understanding and measure whether messages land.
- **Too many channels.** Decisions in chat, documents in email and status in a spreadsheet leave everyone hunting. Agree one source of truth.
- **Plan written once and forgotten.** Stakeholders change between phases. Review the plan at every phase gate and when key people change.
- **Forgetting the end.** At closure, tell people what was delivered, thank contributors and share [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/), including lessons about communication.
Read our guide to [project stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) to connect your communication plan with how you engage each group.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project communication management?**
It is the planning, delivery and monitoring of project information so that stakeholders receive what they need, when they need it, in a useful format, and understand it.

**Q: What are the three processes of project communication management?**
Plan communications management, manage communications and monitor communications. They come from the PMBOK Guide sixth edition and, according to published summaries, also appear in the 8th edition's Stakeholders performance domain.

**Q: What is the difference between a communication plan and a communication management plan?**
The communication management plan sets the approach and rules: audiences, methods, owners, escalation and storage. The communication plan, or matrix, is the working schedule of who receives what, how and when. Small projects often combine them.

**Q: How do you calculate communication channels?**
Use n(n - 1) / 2, where n is the number of people. A team of 8 has 8 x 7 / 2 = 28 channels. To find channels added when people join, calculate both totals and subtract.

**Q: What is the difference between push and pull communication?**
Push communication is sent to specific recipients, such as an email or status report. Pull communication is stored centrally for people to access when they need it, such as an intranet page or dashboard.

**Q: What is interactive communication?**
Real-time, two-way exchange such as meetings, calls and workshops. It is best for decisions and for complex or sensitive topics, and should be followed by a written record of what was agreed.

**Q: How much of a project manager's time is spent communicating?**
A large share. The often-quoted figure of 90% could not be traced to a solid study, but most project management work, including meetings, reporting, negotiating and coordinating, is communication.

**Q: What should a communication management plan include?**
Stakeholder groups and their information needs, the information to be shared, methods, frequency, owners, escalation routes and timescales, templates, where information is stored, constraints such as confidentiality, and how the plan will be reviewed.

**Q: How do I write a good project status report?**
Keep it short and lead with overall status and any decisions needed. Then cover progress against milestones, top risks and issues, the forecast and what happens next, using the same format every time.

**Q: What are common communication barriers in projects?**
Information overload, jargon, time zones and distance, language and cultural differences, unclear ownership, too many tools and a culture where bad news is delayed.

**Q: How do you monitor project communication?**
Track a few indicators, such as decision turnaround, repeated questions, surprises and short survey scores, ask for feedback, and adjust the plan when the evidence shows something is not working.

**Q: Where is communications management in the PMBOK Guide 8th edition?**
There is no separate knowledge area. Published summaries place plan, manage and monitor communications in the Stakeholders performance domain, one of the edition's seven performance domains.

**Q: What is the role of the kick-off meeting in communication?**
It sets a shared starting point. The kick-off should explain the project purpose, objectives, scope, key milestones, roles and how the team will communicate, so everyone starts with the same understanding.

# Project Constraints: The Triple Constraint and Beyond

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What project constraints are, the triple constraint and its modern extensions, examples of constraints, and how to manage trade-offs.


## Project Constraints: The Triple Constraint and Beyond
Constraints are limits that a project must work within. Understanding them, and how they interact, is essential to making good trade-offs.
- Published 19 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scope, time and cost form the triple constraint, with quality at the centre.
- Other constraints include resources, risk and regulation.
- Agree which constraint is most fixed and manage trade-offs openly.

### The triple constraint
Scope, time and cost are linked: change one and at least one other usually changes. Quality sits at the centre and suffers if the three are squeezed together.

### Six common constraints
| Constraint | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | Must include a payment feature |
| Time | Must launch before the trade show |
| Cost | Budget capped at $200,000 |
| Quality | Must meet accessibility standards |
| Resources | Only two developers available |
| Risk | Low risk tolerance for regulatory issues |
Other constraints include regulation, technology, contracts and stakeholder expectations.

### Managing trade-offs
- Agree with the sponsor which constraint is most fixed.
- Show options and their impact when something changes.
- Use techniques such as [fast-tracking and crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) for time constraints.
- In Agile, fix time and cost and let scope flex.

### Constraints vs assumptions
Constraints are known limits; assumptions are things believed true but not proven. Both should be documented and reviewed.
