### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are project constraints?**
Limits within which a project must operate, such as time, cost and scope.

**Q: What is the triple constraint?**
The relationship between scope, time and cost.

**Q: Is the project management triangle the same as the triple constraint?**
Yes. It is another name for the triple constraint.

**Q: Which project constraint is most important?**
It depends on the project; agree it with the sponsor.

**Q: How do project constraints affect quality?**
Squeezing scope, time and cost together typically lowers quality.

**Q: Which project constraint covers resources?**
The resource constraint: limited availability of people, equipment or materials.

**Q: Where are project constraints documented?**
In the charter, scope statement and project plan.

**Q: What is the difference between a project constraint and a risk?**
A constraint is a known limit; a risk is an uncertain event.

**Q: How does Agile handle the triple constraint?**
It typically fixes time and cost per iteration and lets scope vary.

**Q: Can project constraints change?**
Yes, but changes should be approved and their impact assessed.

# Project Coordinator: Role, Duties, Skills and Career Path

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-coordinator/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a project coordinator does: responsibilities, skills, a sample job description, worked examples, how to become one, salary factors and the path to PM.


## Project Coordinator: Role, Duties, Skills and Career Path
A project coordinator keeps a project organised by handling its scheduling, tracking, documentation and communication, so the project manager and team can focus on delivery. It is one of the most common ways into a project management career. This guide covers what coordinators do in each phase, the skills employers look for, worked examples of a coordinator's work, a sample job description, how to get your first role and how to step up to project manager.
- Published 4 October 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project coordinators run the administration and communication that keep projects moving: schedules, trackers, logs, meetings, reports and follow-ups.
- The project manager is accountable for the outcome; the coordinator supports delivery and makes few decisions beyond administrative ones.
- Organisation, clear writing, persistence with follow-ups and confidence with spreadsheets and work management tools matter more to employers than a specific degree.
- You can get a coordinator job without direct project experience by showing transferable work, such as organising events, rotas, moves or system roll-outs.
- The CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation and PMAI are good first certifications; the PMP comes later, once you have led projects.
- Coordinators who learn why each process exists, and ask to own small pieces of work, move fastest into assistant PM and project manager roles.

### What is a project coordinator?
**A project coordinator is a member of the project team who organises the day-to-day administration of a project: maintaining the schedule and trackers, arranging meetings and recording actions, keeping documents and logs up to date, preparing reports and acting as a first point of contact.** They work under the project manager, who remains accountable for the project's results.
The title varies by organisation and country. Similar roles are called project administrator, project support officer, project assistant or PMO coordinator. Some coordinators support one large project; others support several smaller ones or sit in a [project management office](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) serving many project managers. Judge a job by its duties rather than its title.
To see the role in context, compare it with the full set of [project manager roles and responsibilities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-roles-and-responsibilities/).

### What does a project coordinator do?
Job descriptions differ by sector, but most coordinator work falls into six groups.

#### Scheduling and planning support
- Entering tasks, dates and owners into the project schedule and keeping it current.
- Flagging tasks that are late or at risk to the project manager.
- Booking resources, rooms, equipment and supplier visits.

#### Tracking and reporting
- Maintaining the action tracker and chasing owners before deadlines.
- Collecting updates from workstreams and drafting the [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
- Keeping dashboards in the project tool accurate.

#### Documentation and logs
- Managing document storage, version control and naming conventions.
- Updating the [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) of risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, and the change log.
- Preparing templates and packs for governance meetings.

#### Communication and meetings
- Scheduling meetings, sending agendas, taking notes and circulating actions.
- Sending updates in line with the [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/communication-plan/).
- Answering routine questions from the team and stakeholders.

#### Finance and procurement administration
- Raising purchase orders and tracking invoices against the budget.
- Collecting timesheets and expense claims.
- Keeping supplier contact lists and contract dates.

#### Onboarding and logistics
- Arranging access, equipment and inductions for new team members.
- Organising workshops, site visits, training sessions and travel.

### Project coordinator responsibilities by phase
The balance of work shifts as the project moves through its [life cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/). This table shows typical coordinator tasks in each phase.
| Phase | Typical coordinator tasks |
| --- | --- |
| Initiation | Set up the project folder and tool workspace; arrange the kick-off; draft the stakeholder contact list |
| Planning | Enter tasks into the schedule; book planning workshops; format the project plan and logs; collect estimates from team leads |
| Execution | Run the action tracker; arrange meetings; raise purchase orders; onboard new team members; chase deliverables |
| Monitoring and controlling | Collect progress updates; draft status reports; update the RAID and change logs; prepare governance packs |
| Closure | Collect sign-offs; gather handover documents; organise the lessons learned session; archive records |
Closure is often where coordinators add the most visible value, because the project manager is under pressure and many closure tasks are administrative. See our guide to [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/) for the full checklist.

### A day in the life of a project coordinator
The day below is **illustrative**, based on a coordinator supporting a six-month office relocation with about 20 people involved. Your day will differ, but the mix of tracking, chasing and communicating is typical.
| Time | Activity |
| --- | --- |
| 8:45 | Check email and the project tool for overnight updates; note anything urgent for the project manager |
| 9:15 | Daily 15-minute stand-up: record blockers and new actions |
| 9:45 | Update the schedule: two furniture tasks have slipped; flag the knock-on effect on IT installation |
| 10:30 | Chase three overdue actions by message, then by phone for the one blocking the IT team |
| 11:30 | Raise a purchase order for removal crates; check it against the budget tracker |
| 13:30 | Facilities meeting: take notes and circulate actions within the hour |
| 14:30 | Arrange building access passes for contractors starting next week |
| 15:30 | Collect workstream updates and draft the weekly status report |
| 16:30 | Review the draft with the project manager; update the RAID log with a new risk about lift availability |

### Project coordinator vs project manager
Both roles work on the same projects, but they carry different levels of accountability and authority.
| Aspect | Project coordinator | Project manager |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accountability | Supports delivery | Accountable for outcomes |
| Planning | Maintains the plan and schedule | Creates and owns the plan |
| Decisions | Few, mostly administrative | Scope, schedule, cost and risk decisions |
| Budget | Tracks spend and raises orders | Owns the budget and forecasts |
| Stakeholders | Day-to-day communication | Negotiation, escalation and expectations |
| Risks and issues | Records and chases | Assesses, decides responses and escalates |
| Team | Coordinates people's tasks | Leads and motivates the team |

#### Coordinator vs administrator vs assistant project manager
These titles overlap, and employers draw the lines differently. As a rough guide:
| Role | Main focus | Decision-making | Typical next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project administrator | Documents, bookings, records and finance admin | Very limited | Project coordinator |
| Project coordinator | Administration plus tracking, reporting and communication | Limited | Assistant or junior project manager |
| Assistant project manager | Supporting delivery and owning parts of the project | Some, within agreed limits | Project manager |
| Project manager | Accountable for the whole project | Full, within the charter | Senior project manager |
Read our guide to the [assistant project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/assistant-project-manager/) role for the next step up.

### Essential project coordinator skills
Employers hire coordinators mainly for reliability. The skills below are the ones that show up most in job adverts and interviews, with practical ways to build each. For the wider skill set, see [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/).
| Skill | What it looks like in the role | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organisation | Nothing slips through the gaps; files and trackers are easy to find | Run your own work from a single task list for a month |
| Attention to detail | Dates, names and figures in reports are right first time | Proofread every report against its source before sending |
| Written communication | Short, clear updates and minutes with actions, owners and dates | Rewrite a long email as five bullet points |
| Follow-up | Polite but persistent chasing before deadlines, not after | Set reminders two days before each action is due |
| Spreadsheets | Filters, sorting, simple formulas and conditional formatting | Build a budget tracker that totals spend by category |
| Work management tools | Comfortable setting up tasks, views and dashboards | Use the free plan of a mainstream tool for a personal project |
| Basic PM knowledge | Understands schedules, risks, budgets and change control | Study for an entry-level certification |
| Problem spotting | Notices early warning signs and raises them | In each meeting, write down one thing that could go wrong |
Tip
Learn the reason behind each process, not only how to fill in the form. A coordinator who knows why the risk log exists asks better questions, and that is what gets noticed.

### Worked examples of a coordinator's work
Duty lists say what coordinators do; these examples show what good work looks like. All three are **illustrative** and come from the same office relocation project.

#### Example 1: an action tracker
| Action | Owner | Due | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Send revised floor plan to facilities | J. Patel | 12 March | Done |
| Confirm furniture delivery date | Supplier | 14 March | Chased twice |
| Book IT for desk set-up | Coordinator | 15 March | Open |
| Agree parking allocation | HR lead | 18 March | Open |
A simple tracker like this, reviewed at every meeting, stops actions being forgotten and gives the project manager early warning. The [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) gives you a ready-made version with priorities and progress.

#### Example 2: a weekly status update
**Overall status: Amber.** The move date of 4 April is still achievable, but furniture delivery is at risk.
- **Done this week:** floor plan approved; IT cabling survey complete; staff briefing sent.
- **Next week:** confirm furniture delivery; book removal crew; start desk allocation.
- **Risk:** furniture supplier has not confirmed 28 March delivery. If it slips beyond 1 April, the move date is at risk. Action: project manager to escalate to the supplier's account manager by 15 March.
- **Decision needed:** approve $2,400 for weekend IT installation (within contingency).
Notice the structure: status first, then progress, then risks with an action and owner, then any decision needed. Project managers value a coordinator who can draft this without being asked.

#### Example 3: a meeting follow-up
Within an hour of a meeting, send a short note with three headings: decisions made, actions (each with an owner and date) and items carried forward. Keep it under 150 words. A [meeting notes template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-notes-template/) makes this quick and consistent.

#### Example 4: handling a slipping task, step by step
On 13 March the furniture supplier still had not confirmed delivery. A good coordinator handles this as a short, repeatable process rather than a string of reminders:
1. **Check the facts.** Confirm the due date, the agreed delivery date in the order and who last spoke to the supplier.
2. **Assess the impact.** Using the schedule, work out what depends on the task: here, IT installation and the move date of 4 April.
3. **Chase with a specific request.** Ask the supplier for a confirmed date by a set time, for example by noon on 14 March.
4. **Record it.** Update the tracker status to Chased and add the risk to the RAID log with its impact.
5. **Escalate with options.** If there is no answer by the deadline, brief the project manager with the facts, the impact and two or three options, such as a temporary furniture hire or moving the IT work first.
6. **Close the loop.** Once a date is confirmed, update the schedule, tell the teams affected and close or downgrade the risk.
The project manager makes the decision; the coordinator makes sure it is made early, with the right information. Our guide to [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) explains how dependencies carry delays through a plan.

### Project coordinator job description (sample)
Hiring managers can adapt this outline, and candidates can use it to check how their experience matches a typical advert.
**Role summary.** We are looking for a project coordinator to support our project managers in delivering projects on time and within budget. You will maintain schedules and trackers, coordinate meetings and communications, keep project documents in order and prepare progress reports.
**Key responsibilities**
- Maintain project schedules, action trackers and RAID logs in our work management tool.
- Organise meetings, prepare agendas, take notes and follow up actions.
- Collect progress updates and draft weekly status reports.
- Raise purchase orders, track invoices and update the budget tracker.
- Manage project documentation, version control and archiving.
- Act as the first point of contact for team and stakeholder queries.
**Skills and experience**
- Strong organisation and attention to detail.
- Clear written and spoken communication.
- Confidence with spreadsheets and project management software.
- Some experience of coordinating work, events or administration (project experience desirable).
- An entry-level project management certification such as the CAPM (desirable).

### How to become a project coordinator
Most coordinators come from administration, customer service, operations, events, teaching or graduate roles. These steps work whether you are starting out or changing careers.
1. **Learn the fundamentals.** Understand the [project phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/), schedules, risks, budgets and status reporting.
2. **List your transferable experience.** Anything you organised with a goal, a deadline and other people counts.
3. **Get practical with a tool and templates.** Set up a small project in a free plan of a work management tool, with a schedule, tracker and status report.
4. **Take an entry-level certification.** The [CAPM](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) or PMAI shows commitment and gives you the vocabulary.
5. **Rewrite your CV around outcomes,** using project language: scope, deadline, stakeholders, budget, result.
6. **Look inside your organisation first.** Internal moves are often easier than external applications because people already know your reliability.
7. **Apply widely,** including roles titled project administrator, project support officer and PMO assistant.

#### Getting in with no project experience
Employers look for evidence that you can organise work and people. Translate what you have done into project terms:
| Experience you may have | How to describe it |
| --- | --- |
| Organised an event or conference | Coordinated a 150-person event: venue, suppliers, budget and run sheet |
| Managed rotas or schedules | Maintained a weekly schedule for 25 staff and resolved conflicts |
| Supported an office move or system roll-out | Tracked actions and communicated updates for a 40-person move |
| Handled customer complaints | Logged, prioritised and followed up issues to resolution within agreed times |
| Coordinated a volunteer group | Recruited and coordinated 12 volunteers across 3 workstreams |

#### Project coordinator CV: example bullet points
Recruiters scan for scope, tools and results. Each bullet below starts with an action verb, gives a sense of scale and ends with an outcome. They are illustrative; replace the numbers with your own.
- Coordinated schedules, trackers and reporting for 4 concurrent IT projects with a combined team of 30.
- Introduced a shared action tracker that cut overdue actions at weekly meetings from around 12 to 3 within two months.
- Drafted weekly status reports for the steering group, praised by the sponsor for clarity.
- Raised and tracked 60+ purchase orders against a $250,000 budget with no unreconciled invoices at closure.
- Organised the lessons learned session and archived 400 project records during closure.
Our guide on [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/) covers the longer route and how to keep an experience log from the start.

### Qualifications and certifications
Many coordinator roles do not require a degree; organisation, communication and tool skills often matter more. Some employers, especially in engineering, construction, public sector and healthcare, do ask for a degree or sector knowledge.
A certification is not mandatory, but it helps you pass CV screening when you have little direct experience.
| Certification | Who it suits | Key facts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CAPM (PMI) | New coordinators who want a widely recognised credential | Needs a secondary diploma and 23 hours of project management education; no experience required |
| PRINCE2 Foundation | Coordinators in the UK, Europe, Australia and organisations that use PRINCE2 | Tests knowledge of the PRINCE2 method; no prerequisites |
| PMAI (Neural Project Institute) | Coordinators who want practical project skills, including AI in project work | Assessed online chapters with a verifiable certificate |
| Agile or Scrum foundation credentials | Coordinators in software, digital or product teams | Short courses on agile values and Scrum roles, events and artifacts |
Compare the options in our guide to [project management certifications](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/). An active CAPM also meets the training requirement for the PMP later on.

### Project coordinator interview questions
Interviewers want evidence that you are organised, reliable and calm when things change. Prepare a short example for each of these.
| Question | What a good answer shows |
| --- | --- |
| Tell me about a time you kept several tasks on track at once. | How you prioritise and what system you use |
| How do you chase someone who keeps missing deadlines? | Persistence with tact, escalation when needed |
| Describe a mistake you made in a report or schedule. | Honesty, how you fixed it and what you changed |
| How would you set up a tracker for a new project? | Practical tool knowledge: owners, dates, status, filters |
| What would you do if two managers gave you conflicting priorities? | Clarifying with the project manager instead of guessing |
| What does a RAID log contain? | Basic project management knowledge |
| How do you keep stakeholders informed? | Regular, concise updates matched to the audience |
Use the situation, task, action and result structure, and finish each answer with a measurable result where you can.

### Project coordinator salary
Pay varies widely, so we do not quote a single figure. The main factors are:
- **Country and city:** large cities usually pay more, with higher living costs.
- **Sector:** construction, engineering, IT, pharmaceuticals and finance often pay more than non-profit or education.
- **Scope:** coordinating several projects, a large budget or external clients usually raises pay.
- **Experience and certifications:** a CAPM or PRINCE2 credential can help at the margin; proven experience matters more.
- **Contract type:** contract and temporary roles often pay a higher day rate without employment benefits.
For reliable figures, compare several current job adverts for the same title and location, national salary statistics and PMI's project management salary survey. Treat single-source online averages with caution because their samples and definitions differ.

### Tools project coordinators use
Coordinators spend much of the day in a work management tool, so confidence with one or two mainstream platforms is a real advantage. Our guide to [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) explains the main features.
| Tool | Why coordinators use it |
| --- | --- |
| [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) | Our top-rated tool; request forms, custom workflows and dashboards suit coordinators supporting several projects or a PMO |
| [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) | Visual boards and automations that are quick to set up for trackers and request intake |
| [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) | Clear task ownership, timelines and status updates, with a gentle learning curve |
| [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) | Spreadsheet-style project tracking for teams used to Excel |
| Spreadsheets | Budget trackers, contact lists and quick analysis |
| Email, chat and video calls | Day-to-day communication and meetings |
If your organisation has no tool yet, free templates are a good start: the [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/), the [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) and the [meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/) cover most coordinator needs.

### Common mistakes new coordinators make
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chasing only after deadlines pass | Delays are already locked in | Remind owners two days before due dates |
| Reporting tasks as done without evidence | Status reports lose credibility | Ask for the deliverable or confirmation |
| Keeping problems to yourself | The project manager hears about them too late | Flag risks early, with facts and a suggested action |
| Letting trackers go stale | People stop trusting and using them | Update after every meeting; archive closed items |
| Saying yes to every request | Your own core tasks slip | Check priorities with the project manager |
| Long, unstructured updates | Busy readers miss the key point | Lead with status, then risks and decisions needed |

### From project coordinator to project manager
Many project managers started as coordinators. The move usually takes a deliberate plan rather than waiting to be noticed.
1. **Months 1–3:** master your current duties so they run smoothly, and learn why each process exists.
2. **Months 3–6:** offer to draft the status report and the risk review; shadow the project manager in steering meetings.
3. **Months 6–9:** ask to own a small workstream or project end to end, with your own plan, budget and stakeholders.
4. **Months 9–12:** take an entry-level certification if you have not already, and keep a log of every project you lead.
5. **Then:** apply for assistant or junior project manager roles, internally first.
| Stage | Typical role | What changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Project administrator or coordinator | Supporting projects; learning the processes |
| 2 | Assistant or junior project manager | Owning workstreams and small projects |
| 3 | Project manager | Accountable for whole projects |
| 4 | [Senior project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/senior-project-manager/) | Larger, riskier projects and mentoring others |
| 5 | Programme manager, portfolio manager or head of PMO | Several projects and organisational strategy |

#### Is project coordinator a good career?
For many people it is a strong start. You see how projects work from the inside, meet people across the organisation and build a record that leads to more senior roles. The trade-offs are real too: much of the work is routine, you have responsibility without much authority, and in some organisations the role is treated as purely administrative. If you want to progress, choose employers that give coordinators ownership of small pieces of work and that have a visible path to project manager.
Your coordinator years can help with a future [PMP application](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/), which requires experience leading projects within the last 10 years (three to five years depending on education) plus 35 contact hours or an active CAPM. Time spent purely on administration may not count, so record the project work you led or directed, such as owning a workstream.
Tip
Offer to draft the status report. Writing it forces you to understand the whole project, and project managers are usually glad of the help.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does a project coordinator do?**
A project coordinator handles a project's scheduling, tracking, documentation and communication: maintaining trackers and logs, arranging meetings and following up actions, drafting reports and acting as a first point of contact, so the project manager and team can focus on delivery.

**Q: Is project coordinator an entry-level job?**
Often, yes. It is one of the most common entry-level roles in project management, although some employers ask for a year or two of administrative or coordination experience.

**Q: Can I become a project coordinator with no experience?**
Yes, if you can show transferable experience such as organising events, managing rotas, supporting an office move or coordinating volunteers. Describe it in project terms and consider an entry-level certification.

**Q: Do I need a degree to be a project coordinator?**
Not always. Many employers value organisation, communication and tool skills more than a degree, though some sectors ask for one.

**Q: What certification is good for a project coordinator?**
The CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation and PMAI are all good starting points. The CAPM needs 23 hours of project management education and no experience.

**Q: What is the difference between a project coordinator and a project manager?**
The project manager is accountable for the project's outcome and makes scope, schedule, cost and risk decisions. The coordinator supports delivery through administration, tracking and communication.

**Q: What is the difference between a project coordinator and a project administrator?**
The titles overlap. Administrators usually focus on documents, bookings and finance admin; coordinators also track progress, chase actions and communicate with the team.

**Q: Is project coordinator a stressful job?**
It can be busy, especially near deadlines, because coordinators juggle many small tasks and people. Good systems, early reminders and clear priorities from the project manager make it much more manageable.

**Q: How much does a project coordinator earn?**
It depends on country, city, sector, scope and experience. Compare several current job adverts for your location, national salary statistics and PMI's salary survey rather than relying on a single online average.

**Q: What software do project coordinators use?**
Work management tools such as Wrike, monday.com, Asana or Smartsheet, plus spreadsheets, email, chat and video calls.

**Q: How long do people stay project coordinators?**
It varies. Many move to assistant or junior project manager roles once they can show they have led small projects or workstreams.

**Q: Does project coordinator experience count towards the PMP?**
It can, but only the time you spent leading and directing project work, such as owning a workstream. Purely administrative time may not count, so keep a detailed log.

**Q: What makes a great project coordinator?**
Reliability, attention to detail, persistent but polite follow-up, clear writing and the habit of spotting problems early and raising them.

**Q: Can a project coordinator become a project manager?**
Yes. It is one of the most common routes. Ask to own small projects, learn the reasons behind each process and build an experience log.

# Project Cost Management: Processes, Steps and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-cost-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project cost management explained: the four processes, cost types, reserves, a worked example from estimate to forecast, EVM, Agile and common mistakes.


## Project Cost Management: Processes, Steps and Examples
Project cost management is the work of planning, estimating, budgeting and controlling a project's costs so it delivers its scope within an approved budget. It runs through four connected processes: plan cost management, estimate costs, determine budget and control costs. This guide explains each one, shows how the PMBOK editions describe them, and follows a single project through all four with real numbers.
- Published 27 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project cost management has four processes: plan cost management, estimate costs, determine budget and control costs.
- PMBOK 8 places this work in a Finance performance domain, but the underlying work is the same as in earlier editions.
- The cost baseline is the work package estimates plus contingency reserve; adding management reserve gives the total project budget.
- Earned value compares the value of work done with what it cost, which shows overruns long before the money runs out.
- Forecast the final cost every reporting period and act while the variance is still small.
- In Agile delivery, team cost per sprint is fairly fixed, so scope becomes the main lever for staying on budget.

### What is project cost management?
**Project cost management** is the set of processes used to plan, estimate, budget, fund, monitor and control the costs of a project so that it can be completed within its approved budget. It turns scope and schedule into money, sets a cost baseline, and then compares actual spending and progress against that baseline so problems are found early.
Cost is one side of the classic [triple constraint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/): change the scope or the schedule and the cost usually changes too. That is why cost management cannot be done in isolation. It depends on a clear project scope, a realistic schedule and the resource plan, and it is pulled together through project integration management.
A [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) is one output of cost management, not the same thing: an estimate predicts cost, the budget is the approved money, and cost accounting records what was actually spent. Good cost management also covers how the budget was built, how it will be tracked and what happens when reality differs from the plan.

### Why project cost management matters
Most projects are approved on the basis of a business case that compares costs with expected benefits. If the costs drift and nobody notices, the business case can quietly stop making sense. Cost management protects that decision. In practice it gives you:
- **Early warning.** Earned value and regular forecasting show an overrun when it is a few per cent, not when the money has gone.
- **Better decisions about scope.** When the sponsor can see what each piece of work costs, trade-offs become explicit rather than political.
- **Reliable funding.** Finance teams need to know how much money is needed and when, especially for capital projects funded in tranches.
- **Better estimates next time.** Recorded actual costs become the historical data that makes future estimates more accurate.

### The four project cost management processes
The [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) 6th edition, still the most widely taught description, sets out four processes. They follow each other in planning and then repeat during delivery.
| Process | Key question | Main inputs | Main outputs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Plan cost management | How will we estimate, budget, track and control costs? | Project charter, organisational policies, finance rules | [Cost management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-management-plan/) |
| 2. Estimate costs | What will each piece of work cost? | Scope baseline (WBS), schedule, resource needs, risk register, rates | Cost estimates and their basis of estimate |
| 3. Determine budget | How much money do we need, and when? | Cost estimates, schedule, risk register, contracts | Cost baseline and project funding requirements |
| 4. Control costs | Are we on budget, and where will we finish? | Cost baseline, actual costs, progress data | Performance measures, forecasts, change requests |

#### 1. Plan cost management
This process sets the rules before any numbers are produced. The output, the cost management plan, records the currency and units, how precise estimates should be, how progress will be measured, which variances trigger action, who can approve spending and how reserves are released. It is a component of the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/). Our [cost management plan guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-management-plan/) has a full example.

#### 2. Estimate costs
Here the team predicts the cost of every work package in the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/): labour, materials, equipment, services, licences, travel and any other cost. Common methods are analogous, parametric, bottom-up and three-point estimating. A good estimate states a range of accuracy and is backed by a **basis of estimate** that records assumptions, sources and exclusions.

#### 3. Determine budget
The estimates are added up, contingency reserves are added for identified risks, and the result is spread over time to form the **cost baseline**: the approved, time-phased budget that performance is measured against. Adding management reserve gives the total project budget. The **funding requirements** then show how much money is needed in each period, which may be released in tranches at stage gates.

#### 4. Control costs
During delivery, the project manager records actual costs, measures progress, compares both with the baseline and forecasts the final cost. [Earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) is the standard technique. When variances breach the agreed thresholds, the project manager investigates, takes corrective action and, if the baseline itself must change, raises a change request through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/). Our guide to [cost control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-control/) covers this in depth.

### Cost management in PMBOK 6, 7 and 8
PMI has described the same work in different ways across recent editions of the PMBOK Guide. If you are studying, or your organisation uses an older template, this mapping helps.
| Edition | How cost is organised | Process or area names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6th edition (2017) | Project Cost Management is one of ten knowledge areas, with four processes | Plan Cost Management, Estimate Costs, Determine Budget, Control Costs |
| 7th edition (2021) | Principles-based. No process chapters; cost content sits mainly in the Planning and Measurement performance domains | Estimating, budgeting and earned value appear as concepts and methods |
| 8th edition (published November 2025) | Six principles, seven performance domains and 40 processes. Cost sits in the **Finance** performance domain | Plan Financial Management, Estimate Costs, Develop Budget, Monitor and Control Finances |
The 8th edition's Finance domain widens the view slightly: as well as costs, it covers funding sources, financing and the value the project creates for the organisation. The core steps of planning, estimating, budgeting and controlling are recognisably the same as in the 6th edition, which is why this guide uses the familiar four-process structure.
Tip
If you are preparing for an exam, check which edition and exam content outline your exam is based on, and learn the process names it uses. The concepts in this guide apply to all of them.

### Types of project costs
Classifying costs helps you make sure nothing is missed in the estimate and that actual costs are recorded in the right place.
| Cost type | Meaning | Project example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct | Can be traced to the project | Contractor fees, project-specific software licences, materials |
| Indirect | Shared costs allocated to the project | Office space, IT support, finance and HR time |
| Fixed | Does not change with the amount of work | A one-off equipment purchase, a fixed-price supplier contract |
| Variable | Rises or falls with the amount of work | Hourly labour, materials per unit, cloud usage |
| Sunk | Already spent and cannot be recovered | Money spent on a design that was later abandoned |
| Opportunity | The value of the best alternative given up | Benefits from a project you chose not to run |
| Capital (CapEx) | Spend on assets with a life beyond the current year | Servers, buildings, capitalised software development |
| Operating (OpEx) | Day-to-day spend charged in the year it occurs | Training, subscriptions, maintenance |
The CapEx and OpEx split matters because many organisations fund and approve the two differently. Agree with finance early which project costs can be capitalised.
Tip
Sunk costs should not drive decisions about the future. When a project is in trouble, ask what it will cost from today to finish and whether the remaining benefits justify that amount.

### Contingency reserve vs management reserve
Reserves are where many budgets go wrong, either because they are hidden inside task estimates or because nobody agreed who can spend them.
|  | Contingency reserve | Management reserve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Covers | Identified risks (known unknowns) | Unforeseen work within scope (unknown unknowns) |
| How it is sized | Risk analysis, such as expected monetary value or Monte Carlo simulation | Often a percentage set by organisational policy |
| Part of the cost baseline? | Yes | No |
| Who controls it | Usually the project manager, within agreed rules | Usually the sponsor or management |
| Used in earned value? | Moved into work package budgets when released | Added to the baseline only through change control |
The budget is built up in layers:
| Layer | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Work package estimates | Sum of activity cost estimates |
| + Contingency reserve | = **Cost baseline** |
| + Management reserve | = **Total project budget** |
Each contingency amount should trace back to a risk in the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/), and the response to each risk should be described in your [contingency plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/).

### How to manage project costs step by step
1. **Write the cost management plan.** Agree units, precision, thresholds, earned value rules, reporting and approval limits with the sponsor and finance.
2. **Break down the scope.** Build a WBS so every cost has a home, and map work packages to finance cost codes.
3. **Estimate effort and resources.** Estimate hours first, then convert to cost using agreed rates; see [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/).
4. **Estimate other costs.** Add materials, equipment, licences, travel, training and procurement costs, including supplier quotes for anything bought in.
5. **Analyse risks and size the contingency.** Quantify identified risks and add contingency reserve, shown separately from the base estimate.
6. **Build the time-phased cost baseline.** Spread costs across the schedule so you know how much should be spent by each date.
7. **Agree the budget and funding.** Add management reserve, confirm funding tranches and get formal approval.
8. **Track actual costs and progress.** Record actuals, including accruals for work done but not yet invoiced, at the same status date as progress.
9. **Analyse performance and forecast.** Calculate CV, CPI, SV and SPI, update the estimate at completion and compare with thresholds.
10. **Act and close.** Take corrective action, raise change requests where the baseline is no longer realistic, and at closure record final costs and lessons learned.

### Worked example: one project through all four processes
A company is rebuilding its customer self-service portal over six months. Here is how the four processes work on this one project, with the numbers carried from step to step.

#### Process 1: the rules in the cost management plan
- Costs in US dollars, rounded to the nearest $1,000 in reports. Internal and contractor labour costed at blended rates.
- Progress measured monthly by work package using agreed percent-complete milestones.
- Thresholds: a CPI or SPI below 0.95 needs a written explanation; below 0.90 is escalated to the sponsor.
- The project manager may release contingency for risks listed in the risk register. Management reserve needs sponsor approval through change control.

#### Process 2: estimate the work packages
| Work package | Basis of estimate | Estimate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Discovery and design | 320 hours x $125 | $40,000 |
| 2. Build | 960 hours x $125 | $120,000 |
| 3. Integration with core systems | 400 hours x $125 + $10,000 middleware licence | $60,000 |
| 4. Testing | 240 hours x $100 + $11,000 test tools and devices | $35,000 |
| 5. Deployment and training | 120 hours x $125 + $10,000 venue and materials | $25,000 |
| **Base estimate** | 2,040 labour hours plus other costs | **$280,000** |

#### Size the contingency from the risk register
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Expected monetary value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1. Core system supplier changes its API | 40% | $30,000 | $12,000 |
| R2. Key developer leaves mid-build | 20% | $25,000 | $5,000 |
| R3. Accessibility audit finds extra fixes | 30% | $10,000 | $3,000 |
| **Contingency reserve** |  |  | **$20,000** |
Expected monetary value (probability x impact) gives a pooled reserve. It will not cover the full impact of every risk if several occur at once, which is one reason a management reserve is also held.

#### Process 3: determine the budget
| Layer | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Base estimate (work packages) | $280,000 |
| + Contingency reserve | $20,000 |
| = Cost baseline | **$300,000** |
| + Management reserve (5%, company policy) | $15,000 |
| = Total project budget | **$315,000** |
The $280,000 of work package budgets is spread across the schedule to give planned value (PV) for each month. Contingency is held at project level and moved into a work package budget only when it is released.
| Month | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Planned value this month | $30,000 | $45,000 | $55,000 | $60,000 | $55,000 | $35,000 |
| Cumulative planned value | $30,000 | $75,000 | $130,000 | $190,000 | $245,000 | $280,000 |
Finance agrees to release funding in two tranches: **$150,000** at approval, covering the first three months plus some contingency, and **$165,000** at a month-3 stage gate, which includes the management reserve. Plotted cumulatively, the planned value forms the project's S-curve.

#### Process 4: control costs at the end of month 3
| Work package | Budget (BAC) | % complete | Earned value (EV) | Actual cost (AC) | Cost variance (CV) | CPI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Discovery and design | $40,000 | 100% | $40,000 | $42,000 | -$2,000 | 0.95 |
| 2. Build | $120,000 | 50% | $60,000 | $68,000 | -$8,000 | 0.88 |
| 3. Integration | $60,000 | 20% | $12,000 | $14,000 | -$2,000 | 0.86 |
| 4. Testing | $35,000 | 0% | $0 | $0 | $0 | - |
| 5. Deployment and training | $25,000 | 0% | $0 | $0 | $0 | - |
| **Total** | **$280,000** | **40%** | **$112,000** | **$124,000** | **-$12,000** | **0.90** |
- **Cost variance:** CV = EV - AC = 112,000 - 124,000 = **-$12,000**. The work done has cost $12,000 more than budgeted.
- **Cost performance index:** CPI = EV / AC = 112,000 / 124,000 = **0.90**. Each dollar is buying about 90 cents of planned work.
- **Schedule variance:** SV = EV - PV = 112,000 - 130,000 = **-$18,000**, and SPI = 112,000 / 130,000 = **0.86**. The project is also behind schedule.
- **Forecast if current efficiency continues:** EAC = BAC / CPI = 280,000 / 0.903 = **$310,000**, a variance at completion of -$30,000.
- **Forecast if the overrun was a one-off:** EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) = 124,000 + 168,000 = **$292,000**.
- **Efficiency needed to finish on $280,000:** TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = 168,000 / 156,000 = **1.08**, better than any work package has achieved so far.
A spend-only report would have said the project had spent $124,000 against a plan of $130,000 and was "$6,000 under budget". Earned value shows the opposite: less work has been done than planned, and the work that has been done cost more than budgeted. Our guides to [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/), the [cost performance index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/) and the [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/) explain each measure.

#### The decisions that follow
1. **Release contingency for a risk that has occurred.** The core system supplier has announced the API change (risk R1). The integration package is re-estimated at $15,000 extra. Under the plan's rules, the project manager moves $15,000 of contingency into work package 3, leaving $5,000 of contingency.
2. **Fix the build overrun at its cause.** The build package is below the 0.90 escalation threshold for work packages. Analysis shows rework caused by unclear acceptance criteria, which is not a listed risk. The team agrees to add acceptance criteria to every story before development starts.
3. **Give the sponsor an honest range.** Adding the $15,000 integration change to the two forecasts gives a likely final cost of **$307,000 to $325,000**, against a cost baseline of $300,000 and a total budget of $315,000.
4. **Agree a trigger for the next decision.** If the cumulative CPI has not improved to at least 0.95 by month 4, the project manager will bring a change request to the steering group to either use the management reserve or defer a lower-value feature.
Notice that the four processes are connected: the rules from process 1 decided who could release contingency, the risk analysis in process 2 created the reserve, the time-phased baseline from process 3 made the schedule variance visible, and process 4 turned the data into decisions.
To see how each earned value formula is calculated, read our [earned value management guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).

### Estimate accuracy through the project life cycle
Estimates get more accurate as the project is better understood. That is normal and should be planned for, not treated as a failure. The PMBOK Guide 6th edition quotes these typical ranges:
| Estimate | Typical accuracy range | When it is produced | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rough order of magnitude (ROM) | -25% to +75% | Initiation, before scope is detailed | Deciding whether the idea is worth pursuing |
| Definitive estimate | -5% to +10% | Detailed planning, once the WBS is complete | Setting the cost baseline |
Many organisations also use an intermediate budget estimate between the two. In engineering and construction, AACE International's recommended practices define a five-level estimate classification, from Class 5 (concept screening) to Class 1 (check estimate), with the expected range narrowing as project definition improves.
Two practical rules follow. First, always quote an estimate with its range, so a sponsor does not treat an early figure as a promise. Second, re-estimate at each stage gate and update the business case if the cost moves materially. A feasibility study usually works with ROM figures; the baseline should not.

### Project cost management tools and techniques
| Technique | Process | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analogous, parametric, bottom-up and three-point estimating | Estimate costs | Predicting the cost of work packages; see [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/) |
| Expert judgment | All | Checking estimates and assumptions with people who have done the work before |
| Reserve analysis | Estimate costs, determine budget | Sizing contingency and management reserves from risk data |
| Cost aggregation | Determine budget | Rolling activity estimates up to work packages, control accounts and the project |
| [Earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) | Control costs | Measuring cost and schedule performance against the baseline |
| Project forecasting | Control costs | Predicting the final cost (EAC) and the cost to finish (ETC) |
| Variance analysis | Control costs | Finding the cause of differences from the plan |
| [Cost-benefit analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/), NPV and ROI | Business case and stage gates | Deciding whether the project is still worth its cost |
For most projects, the software side is a spreadsheet or a project management tool with budgets, timesheets and custom fields, linked to the finance system for actual costs.

### Key project cost metrics
| Metric | Formula | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Budget at completion (BAC) | Total of the baseline budgets | What did we plan to spend? |
| Cost variance (CV) | EV - AC | Has the work done so far cost more or less than budgeted? |
| Cost performance index (CPI) | EV / AC | How much work are we getting for each unit of money? |
| Schedule variance (SV) | EV - PV | Have we done as much work as planned, in money terms? |
| Schedule performance index (SPI) | EV / PV | How fast are we progressing against plan? |
| Estimate at completion (EAC) | BAC / CPI, or AC + (BAC - EV), or AC + bottom-up ETC | What do we now expect to spend in total? |
| Estimate to complete (ETC) | EAC - AC | How much more will we spend? |
| Variance at completion (VAC) | BAC - EAC | How far over or under budget will we finish? |
| To-complete performance index (TCPI) | (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) | How efficient must the remaining work be to hit the budget? |
| Burn rate | Spend per period | How quickly are we using the budget? |
Report CPI and SPI with their trend: a steady decline matters more than one noisy month.

### Who is responsible for project costs?
| Role | Typical cost responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Sponsor | Approves the budget and business case, holds the management reserve, decides on major changes |
| Project manager | Writes the cost management plan, builds the baseline, tracks and forecasts costs, manages contingency within agreed limits |
| Control account or work package managers | Estimate and manage the budget for their part of the work, explain variances |
| Project team | Provide effort estimates, record time accurately, flag issues that will affect cost |
| Finance or project controls | Set cost codes, record actuals and accruals, check capitalisation and support forecasting |
| Steering group or change control board | Approve baseline changes and use of management reserve above the project manager's authority |
Write the approval limits down in the cost management plan, including the value above which a change must go to the sponsor or board.

### Project cost management in Agile
Agile teams still manage costs, but the emphasis shifts. A stable, dedicated team costs roughly the same every sprint, so cost is close to fixed and **scope becomes the main variable**.

#### Example: costing an Agile release
- A team of seven at an average of $800 per person per day, over a two-week sprint of ten working days, costs 7 x 10 x 800 = **$56,000 per sprint**. Add $4,000 per sprint for licences and cloud services: **$60,000 per sprint**.
- The release is planned at eight sprints for a backlog of 400 story points: a budget of 8 x 60,000 = **$480,000**.
- After four sprints the team has completed 160 points, 40% of the backlog, against a plan of 50%. Actual cost is 4 x 60,000 = $240,000.
- Release-level earned value is 40% x 480,000 = $192,000, so CPI = 192,000 / 240,000 = **0.80**.
- At the current velocity of 40 points per sprint, the full backlog needs ten sprints, or $600,000. Within the $480,000 budget, the team can expect to deliver about 320 points.
The decision is a product one: the product owner prioritises the backlog so that the most valuable 320 points are delivered within budget, or the sponsor agrees extra sprints. Either way, the conversation happens at sprint four rather than at the end. Track this alongside the measures in our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).

### Common project cost management mistakes
- **Treating an early estimate as a commitment.** Quote ranges and re-estimate at each stage.
- **Hiding contingency in task estimates.** Padding cannot be managed or released; show reserves openly.
- **Tracking spend only.** Spend against plan says nothing about how much work the money bought. Use earned value.
- **Not linking the WBS to finance codes.** Actual costs then land in the wrong place or in a single project bucket.
- **Leaving out accruals.** Work done but not yet invoiced makes the project look cheaper than it is.
- **No agreed thresholds.** Without them, either every small variance becomes a crisis or real problems are ignored.
- **Reporting variances without forecasts.** Always say where the project is likely to finish, not just where it is.
- **Absorbing [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).** Extra work accepted without change control raises cost but not the budget.
- **Changing the baseline informally.** Every change to the cost baseline should go through change control so performance remains measurable.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project cost management?**
The processes used to plan, estimate, budget and control a project's costs so it is completed within its approved budget.

**Q: What are the four processes of project cost management?**
In the PMBOK Guide 6th edition: plan cost management, estimate costs, determine budget and control costs.

**Q: How does PMBOK 8 describe cost management?**
It places cost in the Finance performance domain, with four processes: Plan Financial Management, Estimate Costs, Develop Budget, and Monitor and Control Finances.

**Q: What is the difference between a cost baseline and a project budget?**
The cost baseline is the time-phased work package estimates plus contingency reserve. The project budget adds management reserve on top.

**Q: What is the difference between contingency reserve and management reserve?**
Contingency reserve covers identified risks, sits inside the cost baseline and is usually managed by the project manager. Management reserve covers unforeseen work, sits outside the baseline and is controlled by the sponsor.

**Q: What are direct and indirect project costs?**
Direct costs can be traced to the project, such as contractor fees. Indirect costs are shared overheads allocated to it, such as office space.

**Q: Why is project cost management important?**
It gives early warning of overruns, supports decisions on scope, makes sure funding is available when needed and protects the business case.

**Q: Who is responsible for project cost management?**
The project manager day to day, with work package managers, finance and the sponsor, who approves the budget and holds the management reserve.

**Q: What tools are used in project cost management?**
Estimating methods, reserve analysis, earned value management, forecasting, variance analysis and cost-benefit analysis, supported by spreadsheets or project management software.

**Q: How does earned value help with cost management?**
It compares the budget for work done with its actual cost and with planned work, separating cost efficiency (CPI) from schedule progress (SPI) and giving a forecast of the final cost.

**Q: What causes project cost overruns?**
Unclear or changing scope, optimistic estimates, missing cost categories, rework, delays, price increases and unfunded risks.

**Q: How is cost managed in Agile projects?**
Team cost per sprint is treated as roughly fixed and scope varies. Cost is tracked at release level with spend per sprint, velocity and the share of the backlog delivered.

**Q: How does cost management relate to the triple constraint?**
Cost is one of the three constraints with scope and time. Changing either of the others usually changes cost.

**Q: What is the difference between cost management and cost control?**
Cost control is the fourth process within cost management, which also includes planning, estimating and budgeting.

# Project Deliverables: Definition, Types and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What project deliverables are, internal vs external and tangible vs intangible deliverables, examples, and how to define and accept them.


## Project Deliverables: Definition, Types and Examples
A deliverable is any unique, verifiable product, result or capability produced to complete a process, phase or project. Deliverables are what the project hands over.
- Published 17 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Deliverables are verifiable outputs of a project.
- They can be internal or external, tangible or intangible.
- Define acceptance criteria and record formal acceptance.

### Types of deliverables
| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| External (to customer) | Software release, building, report, trained staff |
| Internal (for the project) | Project plan, design documents, test results |
| Tangible | Equipment, printed materials, a physical space |
| Intangible | Training, a new process, improved capability |

### Deliverables vs milestones vs objectives
| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deliverable | An output | Approved website design |
| [Milestone](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) | A significant point in time | Design approved |
| [Objective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-objectives/) | The outcome sought | Increase online bookings by 25% |

### Defining deliverables well
- Describe each deliverable clearly.
- Set acceptance criteria.
- Assign an owner.
- Link it to the WBS.
- Agree how it will be reviewed and accepted.

### Accepting deliverables
Formal acceptance, sometimes called scope validation, confirms the deliverable meets its criteria. Record acceptance in writing to avoid disputes later.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project deliverable?**
A unique, verifiable output produced by a project.

**Q: What is the difference between a project deliverable and an outcome?**
A deliverable is an output; an outcome is the change or benefit it enables.

**Q: Are documents project deliverables?**
Yes, if they are required outputs, such as a design specification.

**Q: What are acceptance criteria for project deliverables?**
Conditions a deliverable must meet to be accepted.

**Q: Who accepts project deliverables?**
The customer, sponsor or designated stakeholders.

**Q: What is a key project deliverable?**
A major output listed in the charter or contract.

**Q: How are project deliverables tracked?**
Through the WBS, schedule and status reports.

**Q: Are project deliverables the same as milestones?**
No. Milestones mark points in time; deliverables are outputs.

**Q: What is a project deliverables list?**
A list of all deliverables with owners, dates and acceptance criteria.

**Q: Can project deliverables change?**
Yes, through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
