# Project Forecasting: Methods, Examples and Steps

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project forecasting explained: methods to predict final cost and completion date (EAC, earned schedule, Monte Carlo, velocity), worked examples and steps.


## Project Forecasting: Methods, Examples and Steps
Project forecasting is predicting where a project will finish, mainly its final cost and completion date, from its performance so far and the work still to do. A good forecast gives the sponsor an honest, early warning while there is still time to act, and it is usually best stated as a range with a level of confidence rather than a single number.
- Published 30 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Forecast both the final cost (EAC) and the completion date; one without the other gives a misleading picture.
- Earned value formulas such as EAC = BAC / CPI are a quick, objective starting point, not the final answer.
- Earned schedule (forecast duration = planned duration / SPI(t)) gives a time forecast that stays reliable late in the project.
- Monte Carlo simulation and Agile velocity ranges turn forecasts into probabilities and date ranges.
- Validate formula results with the team's re-estimate of remaining work, open risks and pending changes.
- Update forecasts every reporting period, track their accuracy and report them honestly.

### What is project forecasting?
**Project forecasting** is the process of predicting a project's future outcomes, chiefly its final cost, completion date and resource needs, using actual performance to date, the remaining work and known risks. Unlike the original estimate, a forecast is updated throughout delivery, so decision makers always see the most likely end point compared with the approved baseline.
Forecasting is part of monitoring and controlling. In PMI's PMBOK Guide, eighth edition (November 2025), it sits within processes such as monitoring and controlling finances and the schedule.

#### Forecast, estimate, budget and target compared
These four words are often used loosely, which causes confusion in steering meetings.
| Term | What it is | When it is set | Can it change? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Estimate** | A prediction of cost or duration made before the work is done | During planning, from the scope and assumptions | Refined during planning |
| **Budget** | The approved amount of money (the [budget at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/budget-at-completion/), BAC) | When the cost baseline is approved | Only through formal change control |
| **Forecast** | The current best prediction of the final outcome, using actual performance | Every reporting period during delivery | Yes, every time it is updated |
| **Target** | A desired result, often a stretch goal set by management | Any time | At management's discretion |
The budget is a commitment; the forecast is a prediction. When the forecast moves away from the budget, the gap is a signal that needs a decision, such as a change in scope, extra funding or recovery actions. A forecast that is quietly adjusted to match the budget is no longer a forecast.

### What to forecast
Most attention goes on cost and dates, but a complete forecast covers everything the sponsor needs to make decisions.
| Forecast item | Typical measure | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Final cost | [Estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/) (EAC) | What will the project cost in total? |
| Cost to finish | Estimate to complete (ETC = EAC - AC) | How much more money do we need? |
| Variance at completion | VAC = BAC - EAC | How far over or under budget will we finish? |
| Completion date | Forecast finish date or duration | When will the last deliverable be done? |
| Resource needs | People, skills or FTEs by month | Do we have the people for the remaining work? |
| Risk and contingency | Expected value of open risks; contingency remaining | Is the remaining contingency enough? |
| Benefits | Expected benefits and their timing | Is the project still worth doing? |
On large projects the forecast is usually produced at work package or control account level and then rolled up.

### Project forecasting methods
Forecasting methods fall into two broad families. **Qualitative methods** rely on judgement and are used when there is little data, for example early in a project or for novel work. **Quantitative methods** use performance data and models and become more reliable as the project progresses.
| Method | Type | Data needed | Output | Best used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expert judgement and team re-estimates | Qualitative | Knowledge of remaining work | Point or range estimate | Any time, especially after changes |
| Delphi technique | Qualitative | A panel of experts | Consensus range | Early, for uncertain work |
| Analogy and reference class forecasting | Qualitative / data-based | Outcomes of similar past projects | Adjusted estimate based on history | Business case and early planning |
| Earned value formulas | Quantitative | BAC, PV, EV, AC | EAC, ETC, VAC, TCPI | Once enough work is done for indices to settle |
| Earned schedule | Quantitative | PV curve, EV, actual time | Forecast duration | Throughout, including late in the project |
| Critical path update | Quantitative | Updated schedule network | Forecast finish and milestone dates | Every update on scheduled projects |
| Three-point estimates (PERT) | Quantitative | Optimistic, most likely, pessimistic durations | Expected value and spread | Re-estimating remaining tasks |
| [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) | Quantitative | Ranges for durations, costs and risks | Probability of meeting dates and budgets | Large or high-risk projects |
| Velocity or throughput | Quantitative | Recent iteration data, remaining backlog | Date or scope range | Agile and flow-based work |

#### Qualitative methods
**Expert judgement** is the most used method of all, because someone has to decide whether the formula results make sense. The most valuable form is a structured **re-estimate of the remaining work** by the people doing it. The **Delphi technique** gathers anonymous estimates from a panel over several rounds, sharing the results between rounds until the range narrows.
**Reference class forecasting** starts from the actual outcomes of a group of similar past projects rather than from the details of this one. The idea comes from Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's work on the planning fallacy and has been applied to projects by Bent Flyvbjerg and others. It is a strong check on optimism bias, especially in business cases.

#### Quantitative methods
Quantitative methods use the project's own data: earned value and earned schedule project indices forward, a schedule update recalculates the critical path, and Monte Carlo simulation and velocity ranges add a measure of uncertainty. The sections below work through each with numbers.

### Forecasting cost with earned value
[Earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) (EVM) is the most widely used quantitative method for cost forecasting. It compares three numbers at each status date: planned value (PV), earned value (EV) and actual cost (AC), and derives the [cost performance index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/) (CPI = EV / AC) and the schedule performance index (SPI = EV / PV).
| Formula | Assumption | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EAC = BAC / CPI | Current cost efficiency continues | The cause of the overrun affects the remaining work |
| EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) | Remaining work goes to the original budget | The variance was a one-off and the cause has gone |
| EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) | Cost and schedule performance both affect the remaining work | You are late and must still meet a fixed end date |
| EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC | The original estimates no longer apply | Scope, rates or approach have changed |
| ETC = EAC - AC |  | Cost of the remaining work |
| VAC = BAC - EAC |  | Expected overrun (negative) or underrun |
| TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) |  | Efficiency needed on the rest of the work to finish on budget |

#### Worked example: forecasting final cost
A software implementation has a budget (BAC) of $200,000 and a planned duration of eight months. At the end of month four the figures are: **PV = $80,000, EV = $70,000, AC = $85,000**. So CPI = 70,000 / 85,000 = **0.824** and SPI = 70,000 / 80,000 = **0.875**. The project is over budget and behind schedule.
| Forecast | Calculation | EAC | VAC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EAC (CPI continues) | 200,000 / 0.824 | $242,857 | -$42,857 |
| EAC (one-off variance) | 85,000 + (200,000 - 70,000) | $215,000 | -$15,000 |
| EAC (CPI x SPI) | 85,000 + 130,000 / (0.824 x 0.875) | $265,408 | -$65,408 |
| EAC (bottom-up) | 85,000 + team's ETC of $150,000 | $235,000 | -$35,000 |
The formulas give a range of roughly $215,000 to $265,000. To pick a figure, the project manager asks why the overrun happened. Here, the team found that integration work was harder than estimated and that this will affect the remaining interfaces, so the one-off formula is too optimistic. The team's bottom-up re-estimate ($235,000) sits close to the CPI-based figure ($242,857), which gives confidence. The forecast reported to the sponsor is **$235,000 to $245,000, most likely around $240,000**, with ETC of about $155,000.
The to-complete performance index adds a reality check: TCPI = (200,000 - 70,000) / (200,000 - 85,000) = **1.13**. To finish on budget, the team would have to deliver $1.13 of value for every dollar spent from now on, while it has managed $0.82 so far. That gap is too large to close by working harder, so the sponsor must choose between extra funding and reduced scope. For more detail on every formula, see our guide to [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/).

### Forecasting the completion date
Cost formulas say nothing directly about dates. There are three common ways to forecast completion; use at least two.

#### 1. Update the schedule and critical path
Enter actual start and finish dates and the remaining duration of each in-progress task, then let the scheduling tool recalculate. The new finish date comes from the updated [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/), which shows which tasks are actually driving the end date. This is the most direct method and the one most sponsors understand. Its weakness is that it depends on honest remaining durations, ideally from [three-point estimates](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/).

#### 2. Use SPI to scale the planned duration
A quick check is forecast duration = planned duration / SPI. In the example, 8 / 0.875 = **9.1 months**. It is simple but has a known flaw: SPI is calculated in money, and it always drifts back to 1.0 as the project nears completion, because eventually all planned value is earned, even if the project is months late. Late in a project it stops being useful.

#### 3. Use earned schedule
**Earned schedule** (ES), developed by Walt Lipke in 2003 and extended by Kym Henderson, fixes that flaw by measuring schedule performance in time rather than money. ES is the point in time at which the current EV *should* have been earned according to the baseline. The key formulas are:
- **ES** = C + (EV - PV at C) / (PV at C+1 - PV at C), where C is the last whole period in which planned value is less than or equal to EV.
- **SPI(t)** = ES / AT, where AT is the actual time elapsed.
- **SV(t)** = ES - AT, the schedule variance in time units.
- **Forecast duration (IEAC(t))** = planned duration / SPI(t).
Continuing the example, the cumulative planned value by month is shown below.
| Month | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cumulative PV ($000) | 10 | 28 | 50 | 80 | 112 | 145 | 175 | 200 |
1. EV at month four is $70,000. Planned value passed $50,000 at the end of month three and reached $80,000 at the end of month four, so C = 3.
2. ES = 3 + (70,000 - 50,000) / (80,000 - 50,000) = 3 + 0.67 = **3.67 months**.
3. SPI(t) = 3.67 / 4 = **0.917**, and SV(t) = 3.67 - 4 = **-0.33 months** (about a week and a half behind).
4. Forecast duration = 8 / 0.917 = **8.7 months**.
So the date forecasts range from 8.7 months (earned schedule) to 9.1 months (simple SPI). The project manager then checks the critical path: if the delayed integration tasks are on it, the later figure is more realistic; if they have float, the earlier one may be. The reported forecast is a finish **between mid-month nine and early month ten**, alongside the cost range.
Tip
Earned schedule is not yet a built-in feature in every scheduling tool, but it is easy to calculate in a spreadsheet from the time-phased baseline, the same data used to draw an [S-curve](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/s-curve/).

### Probabilistic forecasting with Monte Carlo simulation
**Monte Carlo simulation** makes uncertainty visible. Instead of one duration or cost for each remaining task, you enter a range (optimistic, most likely and pessimistic), plus the probability and impact of key risks. The software recalculates the schedule and cost thousands of times, picking random values from each range, and plots the spread of results.
The output is a set of **confidence levels**, often called P-values. P50 means there is a 50% chance of finishing on or before that date or cost; P80 means an 80% chance. The table shows an illustrative result for the remaining work in the example project.
| Confidence level | Forecast finish (illustrative) | Forecast final cost (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P10 | 8.6 months | $226,000 |
| P50 | 9.1 months | $239,000 |
| P80 | 9.6 months | $251,000 |
| P90 | 9.9 months | $258,000 |
Reading it: the most likely outcome is close to the deterministic forecast, but if the sponsor wants 80% confidence they should plan for 9.6 months and about $251,000. The difference between P50 and P80 is a reasoned basis for schedule and cost contingency. It also shows which tasks and risks drive the spread most.
Monte Carlo is only as good as its ranges: if they are too narrow, which is common, the results look precise and are wrong. Use historical data where you can, and link the model to the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) so known risks are modelled explicitly.

### Forecasting in Agile projects
Agile teams usually fix time and cost per iteration and forecast how much scope will be delivered by a date, or when a given scope will be done. The inputs are the remaining backlog and the team's recent delivery rate: [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) in story points or [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) in items per week.

#### Worked example: a release forecast from velocity
A Scrum team has 240 story points left in the release backlog and works in two-week sprints. Its velocity over the last six sprints was 28, 32, 25, 30, 35 and 30 points (average 30).
| Scenario | Velocity used | Sprints needed (240 / velocity) | Weeks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Optimistic (average of best three sprints) | 32.3 | 7.4, so 8 sprints | 16 |
| Average | 30 | 8 sprints | 16 |
| Pessimistic (average of worst three sprints) | 27.7 | 8.7, so 9 sprints | 18 |
| Worst observed sprint repeated | 25 | 9.6, so 10 sprints | 20 |
The team reports a forecast of **8 to 10 sprints (16 to 20 weeks)**, most likely 8 or 9. The forecast is updated after every sprint, and the release burn-up chart shows both the completed work and any growth in scope, so the sponsor can see whether a slipping date is caused by slower delivery or by new backlog items.

#### Throughput and Monte Carlo for flow-based teams
Kanban teams often forecast from throughput instead. A simple Monte Carlo approach samples from the team's actual weekly throughput history to simulate thousands of possible futures, producing statements such as "85% chance of finishing these 60 items within 11 weeks". It needs no item estimates, only a reasonable history of completed work.

### Resource and benefits forecasting
**Resource forecasting** predicts the people, skills and equipment the remaining work will need and when. Start from the updated schedule and ETC, convert the remaining effort into hours or FTEs by month for each role, and compare it with what is available. Gaps show where you need to hire, borrow or re-sequence work; see [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/).
**Benefits forecasting** asks whether the project will still deliver the value in its business case: a later finish delays benefits, an overrun reduces the return and scope cuts may remove benefits altogether. Revisit it at each phase gate.

### How to produce a project forecast step by step
1. **Set the status date.** Use the same cut-off date for progress, costs and risks so the figures are consistent.
2. **Check the data.** Make sure actual costs include accruals and committed costs for completed work, and that progress is measured with agreed rules rather than optimistic percentages.
3. **Calculate the indicators.** Work out CPI, SPI, SPI(t) and the formula-based EACs and durations. These take minutes in a spreadsheet.
4. **Update the schedule.** Enter actuals and remaining durations and recalculate the critical path.
5. **Re-estimate the remaining work.** Ask the people doing the work for a bottom-up ETC on work packages that have changed or are performing differently from plan.
6. **Add risks and changes.** Include the expected cost of open risks, the remaining contingency, approved changes and change requests likely to be approved.
7. **Compare and choose.** Put the formula results, the schedule update and the bottom-up estimate side by side, decide which is most credible and explain why.
8. **Express a range.** State a most likely value and a range, with a confidence level where you have run a simulation.
9. **Report and act.** Present the forecast, its drivers and the options to improve it, and record the forecast so you can compare it with the actual outcome later.
Steps 1 to 4 can largely be automated, leaving time for the judgement in steps 5 to 9, which is where forecasts become credible.

### Choosing the right forecasting method
| Situation | Recommended methods |
| --- | --- |
| Business case or early planning, little project data | Reference class forecasting, analogy, expert judgement, three-point estimates |
| Less than about 15-20% complete | Bottom-up re-estimate and schedule update; treat earned value indices as early indicators only |
| Mid-project with stable performance | Earned value EACs and earned schedule, cross-checked with the critical path |
| After a major change or replan | Bottom-up ETC from the new plan; earned value from the new baseline |
| Late in the project | Earned schedule and critical path for dates (not simple SPI); bottom-up ETC for remaining items |
| Large, high-risk or contractual projects | Monte Carlo simulation on cost and schedule, alongside earned value |
| Agile or flow-based delivery | Velocity or throughput ranges, burn-up charts, throughput Monte Carlo |
Whatever the situation, use at least two independent methods. When they disagree, the difference tells you something important.

### How to present a forecast
A forecast only helps if the sponsor understands it and can act on it. A clear forecast section in the [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) usually includes:
- **Headline:** the most likely final cost and finish date, compared with the baseline.
- **Range and confidence:** for example "$235,000 to $245,000; finish between mid-month nine and early month ten".
- **Change since last report:** what moved and why.
- **Drivers:** the two or three main causes of variance.
- **Options:** actions that would improve the outcome, with their cost and effect, such as reducing scope, adding people or using contingency.
- **Decision needed:** what you are asking the sponsor to decide, and by when.
Agree thresholds in advance, for example escalate if EAC exceeds BAC by more than 5% or the forecast finish slips past a key milestone, so a worsening forecast triggers a decision rather than a discussion. Our [contingency plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) guide explains how to set and release reserves when a forecast shows they are needed.

### How accurate are project forecasts?
Forecasts become more accurate as the project progresses, because more of the cost is actual rather than estimated. There is some research evidence on how quickly earned value forecasts settle. In a 1993 study of 155 US Department of Defense contracts, David Christensen and Scott Heise found that once a contract was more than 50% complete, the cumulative CPI did not change by more than 10%. Later research, such as Henderson and Zwikael's work on performance stability, has questioned how far this applies to other kinds of project, so treat it as a useful guide rather than a rule.
The practical lesson: a project over budget at the halfway point rarely recovers without a specific change in how the remaining work is done.

#### Track your own forecast accuracy
Record each period's forecast of final cost and finish date, then compare them with the actual outcome at closure. A simple chart of forecast EAC over time shows whether forecasts were stable, drifted steadily upwards (a sign of optimism) or jumped late (a sign that problems were hidden). Capture the findings in your [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) so the next project's estimates and forecasts improve.

### Common forecasting mistakes
- **Forecasting what the sponsor wants to hear.** Political pressure is the biggest single threat to an honest forecast.
- **Assuming the project will recover** without a concrete reason, such as a changed approach or added resources.
- **Defaulting to the most optimistic formula.** AC + (BAC - EV) gives the smallest number when you are over budget, but it assumes the problem has gone away.
- **Forecasting cost without dates, or dates without cost.** A late project nearly always costs more.
- **Ignoring committed costs and accruals,** which makes the project look cheaper than it is.
- **Relying on inflated progress.** If tasks sit at 90% complete for weeks, EV is overstated and every forecast is too rosy.
- **Using simple SPI late in the project,** when it drifts to 1.0 regardless of actual delay. Use earned schedule or the critical path.
- **Reporting a single precise figure** such as $242,857, which implies false certainty.
- **Updating too rarely,** so the forecast jumps near the end.
- **Leaving out risks and pending changes** that everyone on the team knows about.

### Forecasting tools and templates
A spreadsheet is enough for earned value and earned schedule forecasting on most projects: you need the time-phased baseline, actual costs, progress by work package and a few formulas. Our free [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) tracks budget against actuals and forecast, and the [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) supports velocity-based release forecasting for Agile teams. For the estimates behind your ETC, use the [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/).
Scheduling tools update forecast finish dates automatically, and Monte Carlo analysis can be run with a risk-analysis add-in or a spreadsheet simulation. Our comparison of [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) shows which platforms offer Gantt charts, workload and reporting features.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project forecasting?**
Predicting a project's final cost, completion date, resource needs and other outcomes from its performance to date and the work remaining, and updating that prediction throughout delivery.

**Q: What are the main project forecasting methods?**
Expert judgement and bottom-up re-estimates, reference class forecasting, earned value formulas, earned schedule, critical path updates, three-point estimates, Monte Carlo simulation, and velocity or throughput forecasting for Agile teams.

**Q: How do you forecast the final cost of a project?**
Calculate estimate at completion with earned value formulas such as EAC = BAC / CPI, then cross-check with a bottom-up estimate of the remaining work plus open risks and pending changes.

**Q: How do you forecast a project's completion date?**
Update the schedule and critical path with actual progress, and cross-check with earned schedule: forecast duration = planned duration / SPI(t).

**Q: What is the difference between a forecast and an estimate?**
An estimate is made before the work starts, from the scope and assumptions. A forecast updates the prediction during delivery using actual performance.

**Q: What is the difference between a forecast and a budget?**
The budget is the approved amount and changes only through change control. The forecast is the current best prediction of the final cost and can change every period.

**Q: What is ETC in project forecasting?**
Estimate to complete: the expected cost of the remaining work. ETC = EAC - AC, or a fresh bottom-up estimate of the remaining work.

**Q: What is earned schedule?**
A method, developed by Walt Lipke, that measures schedule performance in time rather than money. It gives SPI(t) = ES / AT and a forecast duration of planned duration / SPI(t), and stays reliable late in a project.

**Q: What is a Monte Carlo project forecast?**
A simulation that recalculates the schedule and cost thousands of times using ranges for each estimate and risk, showing the probability of finishing by a date or within a cost, such as P50 and P80.

**Q: How do Agile teams forecast?**
By dividing the remaining backlog by a range of recent velocities or throughput, giving a date range, and updating it every iteration with a burn-up chart.

**Q: How often should project forecasts be updated?**
Every reporting period, often monthly or every sprint, and whenever a significant change, issue or risk occurs.

**Q: Why should a forecast be a range rather than a single figure?**
Because the future is uncertain. A range with a confidence level is more honest and helps sponsors set sensible contingency.

**Q: When are earned value forecasts reliable?**
They become more reliable as the project progresses. Christensen and Heise's 1993 study of US defence contracts found the cumulative CPI changed by no more than 10% once contracts were over 50% complete, though later research questions how widely that applies.

# Project Governance: Framework, Structure and Roles

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project governance explained: framework, structure, roles, decision rights, stage gates and tolerances, with a template, worked example and Agile tips.


## Project Governance: Framework, Structure and Roles
Project governance is the framework of roles, decision rights and controls that directs a project and holds it to account. It answers three questions: who can decide what, how those decisions are made, and how the organisation knows the project is still worth doing. This guide explains the structure, the key mechanisms and how to set up governance that is proportionate to your project.
- Published 2 October 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 16 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project governance decides direction and holds the project to account; project management plans and delivers the work.
- A typical structure has a sponsor, a steering committee or project board, a project manager, a PMO and some form of independent assurance.
- Clear decision rights, tolerances and escalation routes let senior people manage by exception instead of approving everything.
- Stage gates and a regularly re-checked business case stop projects drifting on after they stop being worthwhile.
- Good governance is proportionate: a small internal project needs a one-page framework, a major programme needs much more.

### What is project governance?
**Project governance** is the set of roles, responsibilities, decision rights, processes and controls that directs and oversees a project on behalf of the organisation that funds it. It defines who is accountable, who can approve what, how progress is reported and how the project is checked against its business case.
Governance sits above day-to-day delivery. Its job is to make sure the organisation is doing the right project, doing it in the right way, and stopping or changing course when the case for the project changes. Done well, it speeds decisions up, because everyone knows who decides and on what information.
Many practitioners describe governance with a simple three-pillar model. It is a useful way to check a framework is complete, though it is a teaching model rather than a formal standard:
- **Structure:** the decision-making bodies and how they relate, such as the sponsor, steering committee, project board and PMO.
- **People:** the named individuals in those roles, with the authority, time and skills to fill them.
- **Information:** the reports, logs and reviews that give decision-makers an honest view of progress, risks and benefits.

### Project governance vs project management
The two are closely linked but they are not the same. Governance directs and oversees; management plans and delivers. A project manager works within the authority that governance delegates.
|  | Project governance | Project management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Direct, authorise and hold to account | Plan, organise and deliver |
| Key question | Is this still the right project, run the right way, and is it worth continuing? | How do we deliver the agreed outcomes within the agreed limits? |
| Who | Sponsor, steering committee or project board, PMO, assurance | Project manager, team leads and the project team |
| Typical decisions | Approve funding and stage progression, accept major risks, approve significant changes, stop or close the project | Assign work, manage day-to-day issues, approve changes within tolerance |
| Time horizon | Whole life of the project and the benefits after it | Current stage, sprint or work package |

#### Project governance vs PMO
A [project management office (PMO)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) supports governance but is not the governing body. It typically sets standards and templates, consolidates reporting and may carry out assurance reviews. Decisions such as approving funding or stopping a project normally sit with the sponsor, the board or a portfolio committee, not with the PMO itself.

#### Project governance vs corporate and portfolio governance
Corporate governance is how the whole organisation is directed and controlled by its board. Portfolio governance decides which projects and programmes to fund and how to balance them. Project governance applies those rules to a single project. The three should connect: a project's tolerances, reporting and stage gates should reflect the organisation's wider policies.

### Project governance structure and roles
Titles vary between organisations and methods, but most governance structures contain the same roles. On a small project one person may hold several; on a large one each may be a group.

#### Project sponsor
The sponsor owns the business case and is ultimately accountable for the project delivering its benefits. They secure funding, chair or sit on the steering committee, make or escalate the big decisions, and champion the project with senior stakeholders. An absent sponsor is one of the most common causes of weak governance.

#### Steering committee or project board
A small group of senior people who give direction, approve each stage and resolve issues the project manager cannot. In [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) the project board has three roles: the **executive** (who represents the business and owns the business case), the **senior user** (who represents the people who will use the outputs) and the **senior supplier** (who represents those designing and building them). Keep it small; a board of 12 rarely decides anything quickly.

#### Project manager
Runs the project day to day within delegated authority: planning, coordinating the team, managing risks and issues, and reporting honestly upwards. When a forecast breaches tolerance, the project manager escalates with options rather than solving it alone.

#### PMO
Sets methods and templates, supports planning and reporting, maintains the portfolio view and often runs health checks. In some organisations a portfolio PMO also prepares information for investment committees.

#### Project assurance
Independent checks that the project is being run properly and that reports reflect reality. Assurance may come from the PMO, internal audit, an external reviewer or, in PRINCE2, from assurance roles appointed by the board. It should be independent of the project manager.

#### Change control board
On larger projects a change control board, or the steering committee itself, decides on changes above the project manager's authority.
Write the roles down. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) is the simplest way to show who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each key decision; our free [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) gives you a ready-made layout.

### Decision rights: who decides what
The most practical governance document is a short table of decision rights. It removes the question 'can I approve this?' and stops small decisions travelling to the board. The thresholds below are an illustration only; set your own to match your organisation's financial delegations and the project's risk.
| Decision | Project manager | Sponsor | Steering committee / board |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Re-plan tasks within a stage | Decides | Informed | - |
| Change within tolerance (for example up to £10,000 or 1 week) | Decides and logs | Informed | - |
| Change beyond PM tolerance but within stage tolerance | Recommends | Decides | Informed |
| Forecast breach of stage tolerance | Raises exception report | Recommends | Decides |
| Approve the next stage | Prepares end-stage report | Recommends | Decides |
| Accept a high residual risk | Recommends | Decides or escalates | Decides if above sponsor's limit |
| Stop or close the project | Recommends | Recommends | Decides |
Record every significant decision in a **decision log**: what was decided, by whom, when, which options were considered and why. It protects the project manager, helps new team members understand history and feeds [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) at the end.

### Key components of a project governance framework
A governance framework is the documented set of rules for one project, usually agreed at initiation and recorded in the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) or project initiation document. These are the components most frameworks include:
| Component | What it does | Typical document |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business case | Justifies the investment and is re-checked at each stage gate | Business case |
| Roles and terms of reference | Defines who sits on each body, what it decides and how often it meets | Charter, terms of reference, RACI |
| Decision rights | Sets who can approve what, with financial and time thresholds | Delegation table |
| Stage gates | Formal go / no-go points between phases | End-stage report, gate checklist |
| Tolerances | Agreed limits for time, cost, scope, quality, risk and benefits | Charter or project plan |
| Escalation routes | How and when issues move up a level | Escalation path, exception report |
| Reporting | Regular, honest information for decision-makers | [Status reports](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/), dashboards |
| Risk, issue and change control | How threats, problems and changes are logged and decided | [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/), change log |
| Assurance | Independent checks on health and compliance | Health check or gateway review |
| Benefits review | Confirms whether the expected value arrives | Benefits plan, post-project review |
If you are starting from scratch, our free [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) and [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) cover two of the documents governance relies on most.

### Project governance in PMBOK and PRINCE2
Both major standards treat governance as central, though they describe it differently.
- **PMBOK Guide, eighth edition:** PMI published the eighth edition in November 2025. It organises the guide around seven performance domains, and **governance** is the first of them, alongside scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources and risk. One of its six principles is to **lead accountably**. See our [PMBOK Guide overview](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/).
- **PRINCE2 (7th edition):** governance runs through its seven principles, several of which are governance rules: ensure continued business justification, define roles, responsibilities and relationships, manage by stages and manage by exception. The organising practice sets out the project board and assurance roles, and tolerances can be set for time, cost, scope, quality, benefits, risk and sustainability.
- **Agile frameworks:** the Scrum Guide does not describe project governance, but it gives the product owner clear accountability for maximising value and makes progress visible every sprint, which governance bodies can use directly.
Our own view: take the vocabulary from whichever method your organisation uses, but judge your framework by whether decisions are fast, well informed and recorded.

### How to set up project governance step by step
1. **Check what already exists.** Ask the PMO or finance team for the organisation's delegation limits, stage-gate rules and reporting standards. Do not invent a parallel system.
2. **Confirm the sponsor.** Agree one accountable sponsor with the authority and time to do the job.
3. **Size the governance.** Decide how much control the project needs based on cost, risk, complexity and visibility (see the scaling table below).
4. **Form the decision-making body.** Name the steering committee or project board members, write short terms of reference and set a meeting rhythm.
5. **Agree decision rights and tolerances.** Fill in a delegation table and set tolerances for time, cost and scope at project and stage level.
6. **Define stage gates.** Choose the decision points, usually at the end of each [project phase](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/), and what evidence each gate needs.
7. **Set up reporting and logs.** Agree the status report format and frequency, the escalation path and where the RAID log, change log and decision log live.
8. **Plan assurance.** Decide who will run independent health checks and when.
9. **Record and communicate it.** Put the framework in the charter, share it with everyone involved and include it in the [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/communication-plan/).
10. **Review it at each gate.** Tighten or lighten governance as the risk profile changes.
Tip
Agree governance before the first major decision, not after the first crisis. It is much easier to set tolerances when nothing has gone wrong yet.

### Project governance framework template
Copy this table into your charter and replace the example content. The figures are illustrative.
| Element | Example content |
| --- | --- |
| Sponsor | Operations director: owns business case and benefits |
| Steering committee | Sponsor (chair), finance business partner, head of customer service, IT supplier lead; meets monthly and at each stage gate |
| Decision rights | PM approves changes up to £10,000 and 1 week; sponsor up to £50,000 and 4 weeks; board above that |
| Project tolerances | Cost ±10%; end date +6 weeks; mandatory scope fixed |
| Stage tolerances | Cost ±5%; stage end date +2 weeks |
| Stage gates | End of initiation, design, build and test; go / no-go recorded in the decision log |
| Reporting | Weekly status to sponsor; monthly highlight report to board; exception report within 2 working days of a forecast breach |
| Escalation path | Issue owner → project manager → sponsor → steering committee |
| Risk and change | RAID log reviewed weekly; change requests via the change log |
| Assurance | PMO health check at the end of each stage; independent review before go-live |
| Key documents | Charter, business case, project plan, RAID log, change log, decision log |
Our [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) and [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) give you a starting point for the charter and the change log.

### Tolerances, escalation and management by exception
**Tolerances** are the agreed amount a project or stage can deviate from plan before the next level of authority must be involved. **Management by exception**, a core PRINCE2 principle, means senior people do not review every decision; they set tolerances, receive regular reports and step in only when a forecast breaches those limits. This keeps the board focused on decisions only it can make.
When a forecast goes beyond tolerance, the project manager raises an **exception report** that explains the cause, the impact and the options, with a recommendation. The board then chooses an option, and the result is recorded in the decision log.

#### Worked example
A £2 million office relocation sets a cost tolerance of ±5% (£100,000). In month four the project manager forecasts an overrun of £140,000 because of extra electrical work. As this is outside tolerance, she sends an exception report to the board with three options: absorb the cost from contingency, reduce the scope of meeting-room technology, or delay the move by six weeks to retender the electrical work.
The board approves £90,000 from contingency and trims £50,000 of scope, which brings the forecast back within tolerance. The decision is logged, the plan is re-baselined and the tolerance for the remaining stages is confirmed. The whole exchange took a week, because everyone knew the threshold, the format and who decided.

### Scaling governance to the size of the project
Too little governance lets projects drift; too much slows every decision. Match the weight of governance to the project's cost, risk and visibility.
| Project type | Typical governance |
| --- | --- |
| Small internal project | Named sponsor, one-page charter with decision rights, fortnightly status note, simple issue and risk log |
| Medium project | Sponsor plus small steering group, stage gates at major phases, weekly status, RAID and change logs, PMO check at go-live |
| Large or high-risk project | Formal project board, full delegation table and tolerances, monthly board and exception reporting, independent assurance at each gate |
| Programme or portfolio | Programme board above project boards, benefits management, portfolio prioritisation and consolidated reporting through a PMO |
Tip
A useful test: if a decision routinely takes longer to approve than the work it governs, your governance is too heavy for that level.

### Governance in Agile projects
Agile teams still need governance, but it looks different. Instead of approving detailed plans up front, governance bodies review working product often and fund outcomes over time.
- **Fund products or value streams, not fixed scope.** Agree a budget and a goal, then review value delivered at regular intervals.
- **Use the product owner's accountability.** The [product owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) makes most scope decisions; governance sets the boundaries.
- **Make reviews the evidence.** A [sprint review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) or quarterly planning event shows real progress, which is better evidence than a written status report.
- **Keep gates light and frequent.** Short, regular decision points replace long phase gates.
- **Set guardrails, not approvals.** Agree security, architecture and spending rules the team can apply themselves.
- **Adapt the PMO.** An [agile PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-pmo/) supports teams with metrics and coaching rather than document checks.
Hybrid projects often keep formal stage gates for funding and contracts while running delivery in sprints. That works well as long as the gate criteria use the same evidence the team already produces.

### Signs of weak governance and common mistakes
| Warning sign | What to do about it |
| --- | --- |
| Nobody can say who can approve a particular change | Publish a delegation table and a RACI for key decisions |
| The sponsor is absent or delegates everything | Agree the sponsor's time commitment up front; escalate to the portfolio owner if it is not met |
| The project continues after the business case has failed | Re-check the business case at every gate, and treat stopping as a valid outcome |
| Reports stay green until a sudden crisis | Define RAG ratings against tolerances and reward early bad news |
| The board discusses detail and avoids decisions | Send papers in advance with a clear decision requested and options |
| Small decisions take weeks | Raise the project manager's tolerances and use management by exception |
| Decisions are made in corridors and forgotten | Keep a decision log and confirm decisions in writing |
Most of these problems are cultural as much as procedural. A framework only works if the sponsor and board take part, and if the project manager feels safe reporting problems early. Good stakeholder management helps with both.

### Tools that support project governance
Governance mostly depends on people and clear rules, but software makes the information side easier. Look for portfolio dashboards, approval workflows, audit trails, permission controls and a single place for the RAID, change and decision logs.
Among the tools we review, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is a strong fit for organisations that want cross-project dashboards, request forms and approval flows in one place, and [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) suits teams that prefer a spreadsheet-style approach with portfolio reporting.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project governance?**
Project governance is the framework of roles, decision rights, processes and controls that directs and oversees a project, so the organisation knows who decides what and whether the project is still worth doing.

**Q: What are the three pillars of project governance?**
A widely used model describes three pillars: structure (the decision-making bodies), people (who fills each role) and information (the reports and reviews that inform decisions). It is a helpful checklist rather than a formal standard.

**Q: What is the difference between project governance and project management?**
Governance sets direction, authorises funding and stages, and holds the project to account. Project management plans and delivers the work within the authority that governance delegates.

**Q: Who is responsible for project governance?**
The sponsor is ultimately accountable, supported by a steering committee or project board. The PMO and assurance functions support governance, and the project manager works within it.

**Q: What is a project governance framework?**
The documented rules for a specific project: roles, decision rights, tolerances, stage gates, escalation routes, reporting, logs and assurance. It is usually recorded in the project charter or initiation document.

**Q: What does a steering committee do in project governance?**
It gives direction, approves stages and significant changes, resolves escalated issues and decides whether the project should continue. It should be small enough to make decisions quickly.

**Q: What is the difference between a PMO and project governance?**
Governance is the decision-making framework. A PMO is a team that supports it by setting standards, consolidating reports and often running assurance, but it does not normally own the major decisions.

**Q: What is a stage gate?**
A formal decision point at the end of a phase where the board reviews progress, risks and the business case before approving the next phase, changing direction or stopping.

**Q: What are tolerances in project governance?**
Permitted deviations from plan, for example ±5% on cost or two weeks on a stage end date, within which the project manager can act without escalating. PRINCE2 also allows tolerances for scope, quality, benefits, risk and sustainability.

**Q: What is management by exception?**
A principle, central to PRINCE2, where senior managers set tolerances and step in only when a forecast breaches them. It saves their time and speeds up routine decisions.

**Q: How does project governance work in Agile?**
Agile governance funds outcomes over time, relies on the product owner for scope decisions, uses frequent reviews of working product as evidence and replaces long phase gates with lighter, more frequent decision points.

**Q: What is a decision log?**
A record of significant decisions showing what was decided, by whom, when, which options were considered and why. It supports accountability, audits and lessons learned.

**Q: How much governance does a small project need?**
Usually a named sponsor, a one-page charter with decision rights and tolerances, a short regular status update and a simple risk and issue log. Add more only if cost, risk or visibility justify it.

**Q: What happens to a project without governance?**
Decisions stall or are made by the wrong people, risks go unescalated, scope grows without approval and projects can continue long after they have stopped being worthwhile.

# Project Initiation Document (PID): Contents and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-initiation-document/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a project initiation document (PID) is, what it contains in PRINCE2 7, how to write one step by step, an example and PID vs charter.


## Project Initiation Document (PID): Contents and Example
A project initiation document (PID) is the set of information that defines a project, explains how it will be managed and forms the baseline the project board approves before delivery starts. It comes from PRINCE2, where the project manager assembles it during initiation, but many organisations use PIDs whatever their method. This guide explains what a PID contains, how to write one, a worked example and how it differs from a charter.
- Published 13 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 14 min read

### Key takeaways
- A PID defines what the project will deliver, why, how it will be managed and within which limits.
- In PRINCE2 the project manager assembles it during Initiating a Project and the project board approves it.
- Once approved, the PID is baselined and changes go through change control, often reviewed at stage boundaries.
- Tolerances in the PID let the project manager act without escalating every small deviation (management by exception).
- Scale it to the project: a small or Agile project needs a short PID, a large programme much more.

### What is a project initiation document?
A **project initiation document (PID)** is a collection of information that defines a project and sets out how it will be managed. It brings together the project definition, business case, team structure, project plan, management approaches, controls and tailoring. Once the project board approves it, the PID becomes the baseline for running and judging the project.
PRINCE2 formally calls it **project initiation documentation**, because it does not have to be one file. It can be a single document, a set of linked documents or a page in a project management tool, as long as everything is approved and controlled together.
The PID answers the questions a decision-maker needs to answer before committing money and people:
- What exactly are we doing, and what are we not doing?
- Why is it worth doing, and what benefits do we expect?
- Who is responsible for what, and who decides?
- How long will it take and how much will it cost?
- How will we manage quality, risk, issues, change and communication?
- How much can things move before the project manager must escalate?
Although the term comes from [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/), PIDs are widely used in UK public-sector bodies, health services and companies that do not follow PRINCE2 strictly.

### Why the PID matters
PRINCE2 describes the PID as a contract between the project manager and the project board: it records what the board has agreed to and what the project manager has committed to deliver. In practice, a good PID gives you:
- **A clear go or no-go decision:** the board authorises the project on the basis of a complete picture, not a rough idea.
- **A baseline:** progress, cost, scope and benefits are measured against what was approved.
- **Management by exception:** agreed tolerances let the project manager run the project day to day and escalate only when limits are forecast to be exceeded.
- **Clear governance:** roles, decision rights and reporting lines are agreed before problems arise; see [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/).
- **Continuity:** new team members, suppliers and board members can understand the project from one place.
- **A reference at closure:** at the end, the board compares what was delivered with what the PID promised.

### Where the PID fits in PRINCE2
The PID is produced in the second stage of a PRINCE2 project, the initiation stage, and is then used throughout. The table follows it through the PRINCE2 processes.
| PRINCE2 process | What happens to the PID |
| --- | --- |
| Starting up a project | Before the PID exists, a short project brief and outline business case are prepared so the board can decide whether initiation is worthwhile. |
| Directing a project (authorise initiation) | The project board agrees to invest in the initiation stage. |
| Initiating a project | The project manager develops the management approaches, project plan, controls and detailed business case and assembles them into the PID. |
| Directing a project (authorise the project) | The project board reviews and approves the PID. It is then baselined. |
| Managing a stage boundary | The project manager updates the PID where needed (for example the business case and project plan) for the board to review before the next stage. |
| Closing a project | The PID is used to compare the final outcome with the original baseline and approved changes. |
**PRINCE2 7**, published by PeopleCert in 2023, renamed the seven themes as **practices**: business case, organising, plans, quality, risk, issues and progress. It also added management approaches for commercial, sustainability, and digital and data, and introduced a new chapter on people. The PID still sits at the centre of initiation.
If you are comparing frameworks, see [PMBOK vs PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-vs-prince2/).

### What a project initiation document contains
PRINCE2 guidance describes the PID as bringing together the following parts. Outside PRINCE2, most PID templates follow a similar structure under different headings.
| PID section | What it contains |
| --- | --- |
| Project definition | Background, objectives, desired outcomes, scope and exclusions, deliverables, constraints, assumptions, users and interfaces |
| Business case | Reasons, options considered, expected benefits and dis-benefits, costs, timescales, investment appraisal and major risks |
| Project management team structure | The project board, project manager, assurance and support roles, often as an organisation chart |
| Role descriptions | Responsibilities and authority for each role |
| Management approaches | How quality, risk, issues and change, communication and other areas will be managed |
| Project plan | Stages, major products, milestones, resources, costs and timescales |
| Project controls | Stage boundaries, tolerances, reporting (for example highlight reports) and escalation |
| Tailoring | How the method has been adapted to suit the project and why |

#### Project definition
This is the heart of the PID. Write measurable [project objectives](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-objectives/), a scope statement with explicit exclusions, a list of [deliverables](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/) with acceptance criteria, and the [constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/) and assumptions you are working within. Many disputes later in a project trace back to a vague definition here.

#### Management approaches in PRINCE2 7
Management approaches (called strategies in older editions) explain how a particular area will be handled on this project. PRINCE2 7 describes approaches for areas such as:
- **Quality:** standards, quality methods, responsibilities and records.
- **Risk:** how risks are identified, assessed and managed, with scales, owners and review frequency. See [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/).
- **Issues and change control:** how issues and change requests are captured, assessed and decided.
- **Communication:** what information goes to whom, when and how. See [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/communication-plan/).
- **Commercial:** how suppliers and contracts are managed (new in PRINCE2 7).
- **Sustainability:** how the project will meet its sustainability targets (new in PRINCE2 7).
- **Digital and data:** how data and digital technology will be handled (new in PRINCE2 7).
PRINCE2 also uses a benefits management approach, which describes how and when benefits will be measured, often after the project has closed.

#### Project controls and tolerances
Controls explain how the board will stay in charge without managing the detail: how the project is divided into management stages, what tolerances apply, what reports the project manager produces and how often, and when an exception must be raised. Tolerances are covered in more detail below.

### PID vs project charter, business case and plan
Several start-up documents overlap. The table shows where each one fits.
| Document | Purpose | When | Approved by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project brief (PRINCE2) | Short outline used to decide whether to start initiation | Starting up | Project board |
| Business case | Justifies the investment; kept up to date throughout | Outline at start-up, detailed in initiation | Executive or sponsor |
| [Project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) | Formally authorises the project and the project manager (PMBOK-style) | Initiation | Sponsor |
| Project initiation document | Complete baseline for authorising and managing the project (PRINCE2) | Initiation | Project board |
| [Project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) | How the project will be executed, monitored, controlled and closed (PMBOK-style) | Planning | Sponsor |
| Statement of work | Contractual description of work a supplier will do | Procurement | Buyer and supplier |
The simplest way to remember the difference: a **charter** is short and says the project is authorised; a **PID** is longer and says exactly what has been authorised and how it will be run. The PID contains the project plan, but it also includes the business case, team structure and management approaches, which a plan alone does not.
A [statement of work](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/) is different again: it governs a contract with an external supplier, while the PID governs the project internally.

### How to write a project initiation document in 9 steps
The order below works for most projects. In PRINCE2 these steps happen in the Initiating a Project process; outside PRINCE2 they form your initiation phase.
1. **Review the project brief or mandate.** Confirm the background, objectives, outline business case and any decisions the sponsor has already made. Check that any [feasibility study](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/feasibility-study/) findings are reflected.
2. **Agree the tailoring.** Decide how formal the project needs to be given its size, risk and complexity, and record those decisions.
3. **Write the project definition.** Set objectives, scope, exclusions, deliverables, acceptance criteria, constraints, assumptions and interfaces with other projects or systems.
4. **Define the management approaches.** Agree how quality, risk, issues and change, communication and any other relevant areas will be managed. Start the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) at this point.
5. **Set up the project management team.** Name the executive or sponsor, senior user, senior supplier and project manager, with role descriptions. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) makes responsibilities clear.
6. **Build the project plan.** Break the work into products or deliverables, define stages, estimate effort, cost and duration, and identify milestones and dependencies.
7. **Refine the business case.** Update costs, timescales, benefits and risks using the detailed plan. Use [cost-benefit analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/) where it helps.
8. **Set controls and tolerances.** Agree stage boundaries, reporting frequency, tolerances for time, cost, scope and other areas, and how exceptions will be escalated.
9. **Assemble, review and submit for approval.** Check the parts are consistent, ask project assurance to review, then submit the PID to the project board with a plan for the next stage.
Tip
Do not write the PID alone and present it as a finished document. Short workshops with the sponsor, users and suppliers on scope, risks and the plan produce a better PID and make approval much faster.

### Project initiation document example
The example below is illustrative and simplified. It shows how each part of a PID might read for a mid-sized organisation replacing its customer relationship management (CRM) system.
| PID section | Example entry |
| --- | --- |
| Background | The current CRM is no longer supported by its vendor and cannot integrate with the new finance system. |
| Objectives | Replace the CRM by 30 June; migrate all active customer records; train all 85 sales and service staff before go-live. |
| Scope | Includes selection support, configuration, data migration, finance integration and training. Excludes the website and marketing automation. |
| Deliverables | Configured CRM; migrated and validated data; finance integration; training materials; support handover. |
| Constraints and assumptions | Budget fixed at £250,000; go-live must avoid the year-end period. Assumes the finance system API is available by March. |
| Business case summary | Avoids the risk of running unsupported software; expected benefits are less manual re-keying and better reporting for sales managers. |
| Project management team | Executive: Sales Director. Senior user: Head of Customer Service. Senior supplier: CRM vendor account lead. Project manager: internal. |
| Management approaches | Quality: user acceptance testing signed off by the senior user. Risk: monthly risk review. Change: changes over £5,000 go to the board. |
| Project plan | Four stages: initiation; configuration and integration; migration and testing; training and go-live. |
| Tolerances | Time: plus or minus two weeks. Cost: plus or minus 5%. Scope: must-have requirements cannot be dropped without board approval. |
| Reporting | Fortnightly highlight report to the board; end stage report at each stage boundary. |
| Tailoring | Board meets monthly rather than at every decision; a single combined risk and issue log is used. |
Each entry is specific enough for the board to approve or challenge. Vague entries such as "improve customer data" give the board nothing to hold the project to.

### Tolerances and management by exception
Tolerances are one of the most useful parts of a PID and one of the most often skipped. They are the agreed limits within which the project manager can make decisions without going back to the board.
PRINCE2 sets tolerances for areas such as time, cost, scope, quality, risk and benefits. Typical examples:
| Area | Example tolerance |
| --- | --- |
| Time | Plus or minus two weeks on the go-live date |
| Cost | Plus or minus 5% of the approved budget |
| Scope | Could-have features may be dropped; must-haves may not |
| Quality | Defined defect levels allowed at go-live |
| Risk | No single risk above an agreed impact score without board review |
| Benefits | Expected benefits may vary by an agreed percentage |
When the project manager forecasts that a tolerance will be exceeded, they raise an exception to the board rather than waiting for it to happen. This keeps board meetings focused on decisions that need them, and gives the project manager clear authority for everything else. Our [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) guide shows how to report against these limits.

### Tailoring the PID for small and Agile projects
PRINCE2 expects the method to be tailored, and that applies to the PID too. A short internal project does not need a 40-page document.
- **Small projects:** combine sections, use a single page for the definition and plan, and reference standard organisational approaches for quality, risk and communication rather than rewriting them.
- **Agile projects:** PRINCE2 Agile still uses a PID, but it focuses on goals, outcomes, tolerances and ways of working. Detailed scope sits in a prioritised backlog, and tolerances usually allow scope to flex while time and cost stay fixed.
- **Large or high-risk projects:** keep the PID as the controlling summary and link to separate documents for the detailed plan, registers and approaches.
For more on combining PRINCE2 governance with Agile delivery, read [PRINCE2 vs Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/prince2-vs-agile/).

### Common PID mistakes and how to avoid them
| Mistake | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Copying a long template and filling every section | Tailor the structure and record why sections were shortened or removed |
| Vague objectives and scope | Use measurable objectives and list exclusions explicitly |
| No tolerances, or tolerances of zero | Agree realistic limits so management by exception can work |
| Business case written once and forgotten | Update it at each stage boundary and check the project is still worthwhile |
| Roles named but not explained | Write short role descriptions with decision rights |
| Treating the PID as paperwork for approval only | Use it in board meetings, highlight reports and stage reviews |
| Changing it informally | Change the baselined PID only through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) |
| Duplicating content from other documents | Reference the risk register, plan or contracts rather than copying them |

### Templates to build your PID
We do not offer a single PID template, because most of the content already lives in documents you will create anyway. These free templates cover the main sections, and you can assemble or link them into your PID:
- [Project brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-brief-template/) for the starting-up summary.
- [Business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) for the reasons, options, costs and benefits.
- [Project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) for objectives, scope, milestones and roles in one place.
- [Project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) for stages, tasks and milestones.

Once your PID is approved, the next step is running the first delivery stage against it.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project initiation document?**
A project initiation document (PID) is the collection of information that defines a project and how it will be managed: project definition, business case, team structure, plan, management approaches, controls and tailoring. In PRINCE2 it is approved by the project board and becomes the baseline for the project.

**Q: What does PID stand for in project management?**
PID stands for project initiation document. PRINCE2 calls it project initiation documentation, because it can be one document or a set of linked documents.

**Q: Who writes the PID?**
The project manager assembles it, with input from the team, users, suppliers and specialists. The executive or sponsor is responsible for the business case, and project assurance often reviews the PID before it goes to the board.

**Q: Who approves the PID?**
In PRINCE2, the project board approves the PID when it authorises the project in the Directing a Project process. Outside PRINCE2, approval usually comes from the sponsor or a steering committee.

**Q: When is a PID written?**
During the initiation stage, after the board has agreed to invest in initiation and before the main delivery work begins.

**Q: Is a PID only used in PRINCE2?**
No. The term comes from PRINCE2, but many organisations, especially in the UK public sector, use PIDs regardless of the method they follow.

**Q: What is the difference between a PID and a project charter?**
A [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) is a short, high-level document that authorises a project and its project manager. A PID is more detailed: it adds the business case, management approaches, controls, tolerances and the project plan, and acts as the full baseline for the project.

**Q: What is the difference between a PID and a project plan?**
The project plan covers stages, products, milestones, resources, costs and timescales. The PID contains the project plan, plus the project definition, business case, team structure, management approaches and controls.

**Q: How long should a PID be?**
There is no set length. A small, low-risk project may need a few pages, while a large programme may need a substantial document that links to separate plans and registers. Tailor it to the project's size and risk.

**Q: Can the PID change after approval?**
Yes, but only through change control. In PRINCE2, the project manager typically updates the PID at stage boundaries for the board to review, and any change to the baseline needs board approval.

**Q: Do Agile projects need a PID?**
PRINCE2 Agile still uses a PID, usually shorter and focused on goals, tolerances and ways of working. Detailed scope lives in a prioritised backlog rather than in the PID itself.

**Q: What are tolerances in a PID?**
Tolerances are agreed limits for areas such as time, cost, scope, quality, risk and benefits. Within them, the project manager can act without escalating; if a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, they raise an exception to the project board.

**Q: How is a PID different from a statement of work?**
A PID governs a project internally and is approved by the project board or sponsor. A [statement of work](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/) describes work an external supplier will deliver under a contract.
