# Project Integration Management: Processes and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-integration-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project integration management explained: the 7 PMBOK processes, inputs and outputs, integrated change control steps, worked examples and Agile tips.


## Project Integration Management: Processes and Examples
Project integration management is the work of coordinating every part of a project (scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources, communications and stakeholders) so that the plans and decisions in each area fit together and serve the same objectives. It is the project manager's own job. This guide explains the seven PMBOK processes, how newer editions of the PMBOK Guide treat integration, a step-by-step method, integrated change control and a fully worked example.
- Published 2 October 2026
- Last updated 18 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Integration management joins up every other area of the project: one plan, one set of baselines, one change process and one view of performance.
- The PMBOK Guide sixth edition defines seven integration processes, from Develop Project Charter to Close Project or Phase.
- The seventh and eighth editions drop knowledge areas, but integration still runs through them, mainly through systems thinking and the Governance performance domain.
- Integrated change control means assessing every change for its effect on all areas before anyone approves it.
- Accountability for integration stays with the project manager, even though specialists own their own plans.
- In Agile teams much of the integration happens through the backlog and short iterations, while a delivery lead integrates across teams, funding and governance.

### What is project integration management?
**Project integration management** is the set of processes and activities that identify, combine, unify and coordinate the work of a project. It turns separate plans for scope, time, cost, quality, risk and resources into one consistent plan, keeps them aligned during delivery, manages changes as a whole and closes the project in an orderly way.
Most project management activities focus on one area. Integration looks across all of them. A decision in one area almost always affects another: adding scope changes cost and time, cutting testing raises quality risk, and moving a milestone changes who is needed when. Integration is how the project manager sees those links and makes balanced decisions. In practice it comes down to four verbs:
- **Unify.** Combine the subsidiary plans into a single [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) that uses the same assumptions, dates and priorities.
- **Coordinate.** Make sure teams, suppliers and workstreams hand work to each other smoothly and on time.
- **Decide.** Weigh competing objectives and agree trade-offs with the sponsor when they conflict.
- **Control.** Track performance against the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) and manage changes as one system rather than area by area.

#### Integration at three levels
The PMBOK Guide sixth edition describes the project manager as performing integration at three levels. It is a useful way to see that integration is more than paperwork:
| Level | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Process level | Making the project management processes work together, so outputs of one feed inputs of another | The approved change log updates the schedule, budget and risk register on the same day |
| Cognitive level | Using judgement, experience and leadership to make sense of the whole project | Spotting that a supplier delay and a new compliance rule together threaten the go-live date |
| Context level | Taking account of the organisation, technology and environment the project sits in | Adjusting reporting for a new portfolio governance process or a move to Agile delivery |
Tip
Team members and specialists can own the risk plan, the schedule or the budget. The project manager is the person accountable for integrating them, and that accountability cannot be delegated away.

### Why integration management matters
Projects rarely fail because one plan is poor. They struggle because good plans do not fit together: the schedule assumes people the resource plan does not provide, the budget ignores risk contingency, or a change is approved on cost alone and quietly breaks the testing window. Integration management exists to catch those gaps.
| Without integration | With integration |
| --- | --- |
| Each workstream reports in its own format, so nobody sees the whole picture | One status report draws on a single set of baselines and metrics |
| Changes are approved by whoever is asked first | Every change goes through one process and is assessed across all areas |
| Plans are written once and filed | Plans are kept aligned and re-baselined only through approved change |
| Trade-offs are made implicitly, often by the team under pressure | Trade-offs are made explicitly, with the sponsor, and recorded |
| Lessons are gathered at the end, if at all | Knowledge is captured and reused throughout the project |
| Closure is an email saying the project is done | Formal acceptance, handover, release of resources and archived records |
Integration is also where the classic project constraints meet. When scope, time, cost and quality pull against each other, the integration role is to show the options and their consequences, not to absorb the pressure silently.

### The 7 project integration management processes
The sixth edition of the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) treats integration as one of ten knowledge areas and gives it seven processes. Later editions reorganised the content (see the next section), but these processes are still the clearest map of the work and they remain common in training and exam preparation.
| Process | Process group | Purpose | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Develop Project Charter | Initiating | Formally authorise the project and give the project manager authority | Project charter, assumption log |
| 2. Develop Project Management Plan | Planning | Define, prepare and coordinate all plan components into one plan | Project management plan, baselines |
| 3. Direct and Manage Project Work | Executing | Lead the work and implement approved changes | Deliverables, work performance data, issue log, change requests |
| 4. Manage Project Knowledge | Executing | Use existing knowledge and create new knowledge | Lessons learned register |
| 5. Monitor and Control Project Work | Monitoring and Controlling | Track, review and report overall progress against the plan | Work performance reports, change requests |
| 6. Perform Integrated Change Control | Monitoring and Controlling | Review, approve or reject and manage all change requests | Approved change requests, change log |
| 7. Close Project or Phase | Closing | Finalise all activities and hand over | Final report, transitioned product, archived records |

#### 1. Develop Project Charter
The [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) authorises the project, names the project manager and sets out the purpose, objectives, high-level scope, milestones, budget, key risks and success criteria. Its main inputs are business documents such as the business case and benefits plan, plus any agreements. The charter is the reference point for every later trade-off: if a change does not serve the charter's objectives, that is a strong reason to reject it.

#### 2. Develop Project Management Plan
Here you bring the subsidiary plans together: scope, requirements, schedule, cost, quality, resource, communications, risk, procurement and stakeholder engagement plans, plus the change and configuration management plans. The output is one integrated plan with three baselines (scope, schedule and cost). Integration in this process means checking that the plans agree, for example that the schedule includes the review cycles in the quality plan and the budget includes the contingency in the risk plan.

#### 3. Direct and Manage Project Work
This is the execution engine: assigning work, removing blockers, managing suppliers and implementing approved changes, corrective actions, preventive actions and defect repairs. It produces the deliverables and the raw work performance data (hours, dates, costs, defects). Problems that need action go into the [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/).

#### 4. Manage Project Knowledge
This process covers both explicit knowledge (documents, data) and tacit knowledge (what people know but rarely write down). Typical activities are short reviews after milestones, pairing experienced and new staff, and keeping a [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) register that is used during the project, not just filed at the end.

#### 5. Monitor and Control Project Work
You compare actual performance with the baselines, forecast where the project will finish and decide whether action is needed. Techniques include variance analysis, trend analysis and [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/). The output is a set of work performance reports, often a [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/), and any change requests needed to bring the project back on track.

#### 6. Perform Integrated Change Control
Every change request, whatever its source, is logged, assessed for its effect on all areas and decided by the person or board with the authority to do so. Approved changes update the plan and baselines; every decision is recorded in the change log. This process links closely to [configuration management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/configuration-management/), which controls versions of the deliverables and documents themselves.

#### 7. Close Project or Phase
Closure confirms that the work is complete and accepted, transfers the product to its owners, closes contracts, releases people, finalises the lessons learned and archives records. Phase closure follows the same steps at the end of each phase.

### Integration management in PMBOK 7 and PMBOK 8
If you studied the sixth edition, the newer editions can look as if integration has vanished. It has not; it has been reorganised.
- **Seventh edition (2021).** PMI replaced the knowledge areas and process groups with twelve principles and eight performance domains. There is no integration knowledge area. Integration shows up as a way of working: one principle asks project teams to recognise, evaluate and respond to system interactions (systems thinking), and the performance domains are designed to be used together rather than in isolation.
- **Eighth edition (published by PMI in November 2025).** The eighth edition brings processes back in a non-prescriptive form. According to published summaries, it has six principles, seven performance domains (Governance, Scope, Schedule, Finance, Stakeholders, Resources and Risk), five focus areas that mirror the old process groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, Closing) and 40 processes. Much of the former integration work, such as integrating and aligning project plans, sits within the Governance domain, and one of the six principles is to adopt a holistic view.
| Edition | Structure | Where integration lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6th (2017) | 10 knowledge areas, 5 process groups, 49 processes | Integration knowledge area with 7 processes |
| 7th (2021) | 12 principles, 8 performance domains, no processes | Systems thinking principle; the domains working together |
| 8th (2025) | 6 principles, 7 performance domains, 5 focus areas, 40 processes | Mainly the Governance domain, plus the holistic view principle |
The practical conclusion is the same whichever edition you use: someone has to join up the plans, decisions and changes, and that someone is the project manager.
Tip
For the exam, check the current PMP Examination Content Outline rather than any single edition of the PMBOK Guide. The updated PMP exam that took effect on 9 July 2026 is organised into three domains (People 33%, Process 41%, Business Environment 26%), and integration topics such as planning, change and closure appear across them. See our [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) guide.

### How to manage project integration step by step
The processes describe what has to happen. The steps below describe how most project managers actually do it, with the artefact you should have at each stage.
1. **Agree the charter.** Confirm purpose, objectives, success criteria, high-level scope, budget and your authority with the sponsor. Artefact: signed charter (start from our [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/)).
2. **Map the interfaces.** List workstreams, suppliers and other projects that depend on yours, and the hand-offs between them. Artefact: dependency list or [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/).
3. **Build one integrated plan.** Have each owner draft their plan, then reconcile them in a planning workshop: same dates, same assumptions, same priorities. Artefact: project management plan.
4. **Set and approve baselines.** Fix scope, schedule and cost baselines and agree tolerances (for example, plus or minus 5% on cost before escalation). Artefact: baselined schedule and budget.
5. **Set up one change process.** Define who can raise changes, who assesses them, who decides at which threshold and how decisions are communicated. Artefact: change management plan and change log.
6. **Run a regular control cycle.** Weekly or fortnightly, collect performance data, compare with baselines, forecast, and decide on action. Artefact: status report and updated forecasts.
7. **Keep risks, issues and changes connected.** When a risk becomes an issue, or an issue needs a change, move it between logs explicitly so nothing is lost. Artefact: linked risk register, issue log and change log.
8. **Capture knowledge as you go.** Hold short reviews after each milestone and act on them in the next phase. Artefact: lessons learned register.
9. **Close formally.** Obtain acceptance, hand over, close contracts, release people and archive. Artefact: closure report.
Steps 6 and 7 are where integration either works or fails. A project with a tidy plan and no real control cycle drifts; a project with a control cycle but separate, unconnected logs makes decisions on partial information.

### Integrated change control step by step
Integrated change control is the most visible part of integration management. The word integrated matters: a change is assessed across every area, not only the one that raised it. Our [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) guide covers the wider process; this is the integrated core.
1. **Log the request.** Record who raised it, what is requested, why and by when. Give it a unique ID in the change log.
2. **Check it is a change.** Some requests are clarifications of agreed scope or defects. Route those correctly rather than through the board.
3. **Assess the impact across all areas.** Scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources, procurement and stakeholders. Ask each owner for their part and consolidate.
4. **Identify options.** Usually at least three: approve as requested, approve a reduced or phased version, or reject. Include the effect of doing nothing.
5. **Decide at the right level.** Changes inside the project manager's tolerances can be decided by the project manager; larger ones go to the change control board or sponsor.
6. **Update the plan and baselines.** For approved changes, re-baseline only the elements affected and record the version.
7. **Communicate the decision.** Tell the requester, the team and affected stakeholders, using the [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/communication-plan/).
8. **Implement and verify.** Track the change as work, then confirm it delivered what was approved.
| Decision | When it fits | What happens next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approve | Benefit clearly outweighs impact and funding is available | Update baselines, schedule the work, communicate |
| Approve with conditions | Worthwhile but only if scope, timing or cost is adjusted | Agree the conditions, then update baselines |
| Defer | Valuable but not now, for example after go-live | Add to a later release or phase backlog |
| Reject | Does not serve the charter objectives or costs too much | Record the reason and tell the requester |
| Escalate | Exceeds the board's authority or affects other projects | Refer to the sponsor, programme or portfolio board |
Tip
Agree change thresholds before the project starts. A common pattern is that the project manager can approve changes under a set cost and with no effect on milestones, the change board handles the rest, and anything that breaches the project's overall tolerances goes to the sponsor. Our [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) includes an impact assessment and a change log.

### Worked example: integrating a CRM replacement project
The figures in this example are illustrative, but the steps are the ones you would follow on a real project.

#### 1. The charter and integrated plan
A distribution company is replacing its customer relationship management (CRM) system. The charter sets a budget of £480,000, a go-live date of 2 March and a success measure of all 120 sales and service users working in the new system within four weeks of launch. Planning reconciles five subsidiary plans into one:
| Baseline or plan | Key content | Integration check made |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | Configure CRM, migrate 8 years of customer data, integrate with the finance system, train 120 users | Data migration and integration both appear in the WBS with owners |
| Schedule | Design 8 weeks, build 12 weeks, test 6 weeks, train and cut over 4 weeks | Training dates fit the sales team's quiet period in February |
| Cost | £440,000 planned work plus £40,000 contingency | Contingency matches the top risks in the risk register |
| Quality | Two test cycles and a user acceptance sign-off | Both test cycles have time and testers in the resource plan |
| Risk | Top risks: poor data quality, finance integration delays, low adoption | Each risk has an owner and a response task in the schedule |

#### 2. A change request arrives
In week 14 the sales director asks for a mobile app for field sales staff to be included at launch. The project manager logs it as CR-07 and gathers an impact assessment from each owner:
| Area | Impact of adding the mobile app at launch |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | New deliverable: configure and test the vendor's mobile app for 45 field users |
| Schedule | About 3 weeks of extra build and test; go-live moves from 2 March to 23 March if nothing else changes |
| Cost | £36,000 for configuration, testing and device management setup |
| Quality | If the date is held, the second test cycle shrinks from 3 weeks to 1 |
| Risk | New risk: device security policy not yet approved by IT security (rated high) |
| Resources | Lead CRM consultant already at full capacity in weeks 15 to 20 |
| Stakeholders | Sales strongly in favour; finance concerned about using most of the contingency |

#### 3. Options and decision
| Option | Cost | Go-live | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A. Add now, move go-live | £36,000 | 23 March | Misses the quiet period for training; year-end data migration clashes |
| B. Add now, hold the date | £36,000 plus overtime | 2 March | Reduced testing; high chance of defects at launch |
| C. Go live on 2 March, mobile app as release 2 in April | £38,000 (small re-planning cost) | 2 March, app in April | Field users wait six weeks for mobile access |
The change board chooses option C. The scope, schedule and cost baselines for release 1 stay intact. The mobile app becomes a separate, funded release with its own small plan, and the security policy risk is assigned to IT security with a due date before release 2 starts. That is integration management in one decision: the request was judged across every area, the options were explicit and the sponsor made an informed choice.

#### 4. Closing the loop
- The change log records CR-07 as approved with conditions, with the decision date and approver.
- The schedule gains a release 2 phase; the release 1 baseline is unchanged.
- The budget is increased by £38,000 from a separate change budget, leaving the original contingency for release 1 risks.
- The risk register adds the device security risk; the communication plan adds a field-sales update.
- The lessons learned register notes that mobile needs were missed in requirements and should be asked about earlier on future CRM projects.

### Tools and documents that support integration
Integration relies on a small set of linked documents. If these are consistent, most integration problems become visible early.
| Document | Integration role | Free template |

| Project management plan | Unifies all subsidiary plans and baselines | [Project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) |
| Change request and change log | Records every change and decision | [Change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) |
| RAID log or risk register | Links risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies | [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) |
| Lessons learned register | Captures knowledge during and after the project | [Lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) |
| Status report | Shows performance across all areas in one view | See our [status report guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) |
Work management software helps by keeping plans, tasks, requests and reports in one place, so a change to a date or a task is visible everywhere it matters. Wrike, our top-ranked tool, suits this well for teams that run many linked projects, with request forms, cross-project dashboards and workload views; see our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).

### Integration in Agile and hybrid projects
In [Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) much of the detailed integration happens inside the team. Short iterations, a single ordered backlog and a shared definition of done keep scope, quality and schedule aligned by design. The Product Owner makes most scope trade-offs through backlog ordering, so many changes never need a formal change request.
| Integration need | Predictive approach | Agile approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One plan | Integrated project management plan | Product goal, roadmap and ordered backlog |
| Change handling | Change requests and change board | Backlog refinement and reordering by the Product Owner |
| Performance view | Baselines, variances, earned value | Increments, velocity or throughput, burn-up charts |
| Cross-team coordination | Integrated schedule and interface management | Release planning, [PI planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/), dependency boards |
| Knowledge | Lessons learned register | Retrospectives every iteration |
Integration at the project and programme level does not disappear. A delivery lead or project manager still integrates funding and contracts, dependencies between teams, governance and reporting, release and deployment planning, and communication with stakeholders who do not work in sprints. In hybrid projects, a common pattern is a predictive outer plan (budget, milestones, contracts) with Agile delivery inside it, joined by a lightweight change process for anything that affects the outer baselines.

### Common integration management mistakes
- **Plans that never reference each other.** Fix: hold one reconciliation workshop and keep shared assumptions in a single log.
- **Approving changes on cost alone.** Fix: require an impact assessment covering schedule, quality, risk and resources for every change above the threshold.
- **Several change routes.** Fix: one entry point, even if small changes are fast-tracked.
- **Re-baselining to hide variance.** Fix: re-baseline only through approved changes and keep the original baseline for comparison.
- **Different reporting formats for each workstream.** Fix: one status template and one set of metrics.
- **Leaving knowledge and closure to the end.** Fix: review after each milestone and close each phase formally.
- **Confusing integration with doing everything.** Fix: specialists own their plans; the project manager owns how they fit together.
- **Ignoring other projects.** Fix: check shared resources and dependencies with the PMO or programme regularly.

### Integration management checklist
Use this checklist at the start of a project and at each phase gate:
- The charter is signed and states objectives, success criteria and your authority.
- Every subsidiary plan uses the same dates, assumptions and priorities.
- Scope, schedule and cost baselines are approved, with tolerances agreed.
- There is one documented change process with clear decision thresholds.
- Risks, issues, assumptions and dependencies are logged and linked.
- Performance is reported in one format against the baselines.
- Lessons are being captured and used during the project.
- Closure criteria and the handover owner are known.
Integration management sits within a wider framework of decision rights and approvals.
For how integration fits with the other process groups and knowledge areas, see [project management processes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-processes/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project integration management?**
It is the coordination of all project management areas and activities (scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources, communications and stakeholders) so that the project works as one system and meets its objectives.

**Q: What are the 7 processes of project integration management?**
In the PMBOK Guide sixth edition they are Develop Project Charter, Develop Project Management Plan, Direct and Manage Project Work, Manage Project Knowledge, Monitor and Control Project Work, Perform Integrated Change Control, and Close Project or Phase.

**Q: Why is project integration management important?**
Because decisions in one area affect others. Without integration, each team optimises its own part, changes are assessed in isolation and the project as a whole suffers.

**Q: Who is responsible for project integration management?**
The project manager. Team members and specialists contribute and own their own plans, but accountability for integrating the project sits with the project manager.

**Q: What is the first process in integration management?**
Develop Project Charter, which formally authorises the project and gives the project manager authority to apply resources.

**Q: What is integrated change control?**
A single process for reviewing every change request, assessing its effect on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and other areas, deciding on it and recording the decision before the plan and baselines are updated.

**Q: What is a change control board?**
A group with authority to approve or reject change requests above an agreed threshold. It usually includes the sponsor or their delegate, the project manager and representatives of the main affected areas.

**Q: What is the difference between integration management and scope management?**
Scope management defines and controls what work is included. Integration management coordinates scope with every other area, so a scope change is assessed for its effect on time, cost, quality and risk too.

**Q: Does PMBOK 7 or PMBOK 8 still include integration management?**
Neither has an integration knowledge area. The seventh edition covers integration through principles such as systems thinking and performance domains used together; the eighth edition, published in November 2025, places much of the work, such as integrating and aligning plans, in the Governance performance domain.

**Q: Is integration management on the PMP exam?**
Yes, although not as a separate section. The exam is organised by the People, Process and Business Environment domains, and integration topics such as planning, change, knowledge and closure appear throughout.

**Q: What are the main outputs of integration management?**
The project charter, the project management plan and baselines, deliverables, work performance reports, the issue log, the change log, the lessons learned register and the final report.

**Q: How does integration management work in Agile?**
Teams integrate continuously through a single backlog, short iterations and a shared definition of done, while a delivery lead integrates cross-team dependencies, funding, governance and release planning.

**Q: What tools help with project integration management?**
A work management tool that holds plans, tasks, requests and dashboards in one place, plus linked documents such as the charter, plan, change log, RAID log and lessons learned register.

# Project Management Certification: Which One to Choose

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Compare the main project management certifications (PMP, CAPM, PRINCE2, PMI-ACP, Scrum, APM and AI options) with requirements, renewal and how to choose.


## Project Management Certification: Which One to Choose
A project management certification is a credential that shows you have met a defined standard of project management knowledge and, for some credentials, experience. In short: the PMP suits experienced project managers, the CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation or APM PFQ suit beginners, and Scrum or PMI-ACP credentials suit Agile roles. This guide compares the main options, their requirements and renewal rules, and shows you how to choose.
- Published 3 October 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 14 min read

### Key takeaways
- Choose by experience, country and way of working, not by fame alone.
- The PMP is the best-known credential for experienced project managers; PMI launched a new PMP exam in July 2026.
- Beginners can start with the CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation, APM PFQ, CompTIA Project+ or a structured course such as the PMAI.
- Agile roles usually start with a Scrum certification; the PMI-ACP suits practitioners with Agile experience.
- Many credentials must be renewed, for example 60 PDUs every three years for the PMP.
- Always check current fees and eligibility on the awarding body's official website before you book.

### What is a project management certification?
A **project management certification** is a credential awarded by a professional body after you pass an exam or assessment against a published standard. Some, such as the PMP, also require verified project experience and ongoing learning to stay valid. Employers use certifications as evidence that you understand a shared vocabulary and recognised methods.

#### Certification vs certificate
The words are often used interchangeably, but they are not the same thing. A **professional certification** usually involves eligibility checks, a proctored exam and renewal rules. A **certificate of completion** shows you finished and passed a course or programme. Both can be valuable: a course certificate is often the quickest way to build knowledge, while a professional certification carries more weight in job adverts that name a specific credential.

#### Who awards project management certifications?
- **PMI (Project Management Institute):** PMP, CAPM, PMI-ACP, PgMP, PfMP and specialist credentials. See [what is PMI](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/).
- **PeopleCert (owner of AXELOS):** PRINCE2 Foundation and Practitioner, PRINCE2 Agile.
- **APM (Association for Project Management, UK):** Project Fundamentals Qualification (PFQ) and Project Management Qualification (PMQ).
- **IPMA (International Project Management Association):** a four-level certification scheme delivered through national associations.
- **Scrum.org and Scrum Alliance:** Professional Scrum Master (PSM) and Certified ScrumMaster (CSM), among others.
- **CompTIA:** Project+, popular in IT.
- **Course providers and universities:** for example the Google Project Management Certificate on Coursera, and our own PMAI certification.

### The main project management certifications compared
The table summarises the credentials most readers consider. Requirements are simplified; check the official body for full rules.
| Certification | Awarding body | Level | Experience needed | Renewal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) | PMI | Experienced | Yes: 3 to 5 years leading projects, depending on education | 60 PDUs every 3 years |
| [CAPM](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) | PMI | Entry | No: 23 hours of project management education | 15 PDUs every 3 years |
| PMI-ACP | PMI | Intermediate (Agile) | Yes: Agile experience, plus 21 hours of Agile training | 30 PDUs every 3 years |
| PRINCE2 Foundation | PeopleCert | Entry | No | Renew after 3 years (check PeopleCert rules) |
| PRINCE2 Practitioner | PeopleCert | Intermediate | No formal experience; PRINCE2 Foundation or another qualifying credential first | Renew after 3 years (check PeopleCert rules) |
| APM PFQ / PMQ | APM | Entry / intermediate | PFQ: no; PMQ: some experience recommended | Check APM |
| CSM / PSM I | Scrum Alliance / Scrum.org | Entry (Agile) | No | CSM: every 2 years; PSM I: does not expire |
| CompTIA Project+ | CompTIA | Entry | No formal requirement; some experience recommended | Check CompTIA |
| PgMP / PfMP | PMI | Senior | Yes, extensive programme or portfolio experience | 60 PDUs every 3 years |
| PMAI | Neural Project Institute | Foundation to practitioner | No | Certificate of completion |
Tip
Requirements and fees change. The figures above reflect the awarding bodies' published rules when we checked on 9 October 2026; confirm them before you apply.

### Certifications for experienced project managers

#### PMP (Project Management Professional)
The PMP is PMI's flagship credential and the one most often named in project manager job adverts worldwide. According to PMI's certification page, you need 35 hours of project management education (or an active CAPM) and, depending on your education, between three and five years of experience leading projects within the last ten years: five years with a secondary diploma, four with an associate's degree or vocational diploma, three with a bachelor's degree, and two if your degree is from a PMI-accredited programme.
The exam has 180 questions in 240 minutes. PMI launched a new version of the PMP exam in July 2026. PMI states that the domain weightings changed from People 42%, Process 50% and Business Environment 8% to **People 33%, Process 41% and Business Environment 26%**, and that scenarios now include AI, sustainability and stakeholder engagement, with a stronger focus on outcomes and value. Our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) covers the application and study plan, and [35 contact hours](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/35-contact-hours-pmp/) explains the education requirement.

#### PRINCE2 Practitioner
PRINCE2 Practitioner tests whether you can apply and tailor the PRINCE2 method to a real project scenario. It is widely requested in the UK, parts of Europe, Australia and the public sector. You need PRINCE2 Foundation or another qualifying credential accepted by PeopleCert first.

#### APM Project Management Qualification (PMQ)
The PMQ from the UK's Association for Project Management covers the breadth of project management knowledge and suits people with some project experience. It is a common step for UK professionals working towards APM's higher qualifications and Chartered Project Professional status.

#### PgMP and PfMP
PMI's Program Management Professional (PgMP) and Portfolio Management Professional (PfMP) are for senior practitioners who manage groups of related projects or whole portfolios. Both require extensive experience. If you are unsure which level you work at, read [program vs project vs portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/program-vs-project-vs-portfolio-management/).

### Entry-level certifications for beginners
If you have little formal project experience, choose a credential with no experience requirement, then aim for an experienced-level certification later.

#### CAPM (Certified Associate in Project Management)
PMI's entry-level credential. PMI lists a secondary education, 23 hours of project management education and a 150-question, 180-minute exam. It is a natural stepping stone to the PMP, and an active CAPM also satisfies the PMP's education requirement.

#### PRINCE2 Foundation
Tests your understanding of PRINCE2's principles, practices and processes. There are no prerequisites, and it is often the first credential for project support roles in the UK and Europe.

#### APM Project Fundamentals Qualification (PFQ)
A UK entry-level qualification covering the fundamentals of project management. It is a good fit for team members and new coordinators who want a recognised starting point.

#### CompTIA Project+
A vendor-neutral credential that covers the project life cycle, roles, tools and basic Agile concepts. It is popular with IT professionals who manage smaller projects alongside technical work.

#### Google Project Management Certificate
A self-paced online programme delivered through Coursera. It is a structured introduction for career changers and covers traditional and Agile project management. It is a course certificate rather than a professional certification with an eligibility check, so many learners use it as preparation for the CAPM or a first coordinator role.

#### PMAI certification
The PMAI (Project Management Artificial Intelligence) certification from the Neural Project Institute is our own programme of six assessed online courses: project management foundations, scope, schedule and cost control, Agile and Scrum, risk and quality, leadership and stakeholder communication, and AI for project managers. Each course gives a verifiable certificate, and the PMAI certificate is awarded when you pass every chapter of all six. It is a certificate of completion, not an accreditation by PMI, PeopleCert or any other organisation, so it works best as an affordable, modern foundation alongside or before a professional certification.

### Agile and Scrum certifications
If you work in software, product or any team that runs sprints, an Agile credential may be more useful than a traditional one.
- **Certified ScrumMaster (CSM)** from Scrum Alliance: requires a live course with an approved trainer, followed by an online test. Renewal is every two years.
- **Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I)** from Scrum.org: an online assessment with no mandatory course, and the credential does not expire.
- **PMI-ACP** from PMI: for practitioners with Agile experience. PMI currently lists 21 hours of Agile training plus one of several experience routes, for example two years of Agile experience in the past five years, or one year with a relevant degree or another Agile certification; an active PMP also qualifies. Renewal is 30 PDUs every three years.
- **PRINCE2 Agile:** combines PRINCE2 governance with Agile delivery; useful in organisations that already use PRINCE2.
- **SAFe certifications:** for organisations scaling Agile across many teams; see [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/).
Our [Scrum certification and training](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/) guide compares CSM and PSM in detail, and [how to learn Agile and get certified](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/) suggests a learning path.

### AI project management certifications
AI is now part of mainstream project management. PMI's July 2026 PMP exam includes AI in its scenarios, and PMI also offers a dedicated credential, the PMI Certified Professional in Managing AI (PMI-CPMAI), based on the CPMAI methodology for running AI and data projects.
There are two different needs here. If you manage projects that build AI systems, a specialist credential such as PMI-CPMAI focuses on data, model development and deployment phases. If you want to use AI tools to plan, report and communicate better as a project manager, a broader course is usually more practical. The Foresight course in the PMAI certification covers that second need. For the tools themselves, see our guide to [AI project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/ai-project-management-tools/).

### How to choose the right certification
1. **Check job adverts in your target market.** Search for the roles you want in your country and sector, and note which credentials appear most often.
2. **Match the credential to your experience.** If you cannot yet meet the PMP's experience rules, start with an entry-level option.
3. **Match it to how your organisation works.** Predictive, Agile or hybrid? See [project management methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-methodologies/) if you are unsure.
4. **Consider cost, study time and renewal.** Include training, exam, membership and ongoing learning in your budget.
5. **Check the official rules.** Eligibility, exam formats and fees change; confirm them with the awarding body before you pay.
| If you are… | Consider first | Then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New to project management | CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation, APM PFQ or PMAI | PMP or PRINCE2 Practitioner once you have experience |
| A project coordinator or assistant PM | CAPM or PRINCE2 Foundation | PMP when eligible |
| An experienced PM in North America or global firms | PMP | PgMP, PMI-ACP or a specialist credential |
| An experienced PM in UK or European public sector | PRINCE2 Practitioner or APM PMQ | PMP if you work internationally |
| In an Agile or software team | CSM or PSM I | PMI-ACP or a scaling framework |
| In IT with project duties | CompTIA Project+ | PMP or an Agile credential |
| Managing AI or data projects | PMI-CPMAI or an AI-focused course | PMP for broader leadership roles |

### Example decisions
- **A career changer with no project experience** in the US takes a structured introductory course, then the CAPM, and applies for project coordinator roles. Our [project coordinator](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-coordinator/) guide describes the role.
- **A UK local government analyst** who supports projects chooses PRINCE2 Foundation because job adverts in that sector name it, then plans for Practitioner.
- **A software team lead** with three years of Scrum experience takes the PSM I, then the PMI-ACP to show broader Agile knowledge.
- **An operations manager** with a bachelor's degree and four years of leading projects goes straight for the PMP.

### Costs, study time and renewal
Costs change often and vary by country, so we do not publish fee figures that may go out of date. Plan for these components:
| Cost element | What to expect |
| --- | --- |
| Exam fee | Set by the awarding body; PMI charges members less than non-members |
| Membership (optional) | PMI membership reduces PMI exam fees, which can make it worthwhile |
| Training | Required for some credentials (for example the PMP's 35 hours or CSM's live course) and optional for others |
| Study materials and practice exams | Books, simulators and mock exams |
| Renewal | Continuing education, renewal fees or retaking an exam |
Study time depends on the credential and your background. Entry-level exams such as PRINCE2 Foundation or PSM I can be prepared for in days or a few weeks; the PMP usually takes a few months of part-time study.
PMI credentials are maintained with professional development units: 60 PDUs every three years for the PMP, 30 for the PMI-ACP and 15 for the CAPM. Our [PDU guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pdu-professional-development-units/) explains how to earn them.
Tip
Ask your employer whether they fund certification. Many training budgets cover exam fees and preparation courses, especially when the credential is linked to your development plan.

### Are project management certifications worth it?
For most people, yes, if the credential matches the jobs you want. The benefits are practical:
- **More interviews.** Many job adverts list a specific certification, and some recruiters filter on it.
- **A shared language.** You learn the terms and frameworks used in standards such as the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) and PRINCE2.
- **Structured knowledge.** Studying fills gaps you may not notice on the job, such as risk, procurement or earned value.
- **Credibility with clients and sponsors**, particularly in consulting, government and regulated sectors.
A certification does not replace experience. Employers still want evidence that you have planned work, managed stakeholders and delivered results. The strongest applications combine a relevant credential with concrete examples.

### How to prepare and pass
1. Download the official exam outline or syllabus and use it as your checklist.
2. Complete any required training with an approved provider.
3. Build a study plan with fixed weekly hours and a booked exam date.
4. Use the official guide or standard as your main reference and add one good prep book.
5. Take timed practice exams and review every wrong answer.
6. Relate topics to your own projects; scenario questions reward practical understanding.
7. Rest the day before the exam and check the technical requirements if you test online.

### Mistakes to avoid
- Choosing a certification you are not yet eligible for.
- Picking the most famous credential when your market prefers another.
- Relying on outdated exam information; the PMP changed in July 2026.
- Buying unofficial training that does not count towards eligibility requirements.
- Forgetting renewal requirements and letting a credential lapse.
- Relying on certification alone without practical experience.
Once you are certified, keep building the [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/) employers look for. A [skills matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) is a simple way to track your progress.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the best project management certification?**
For experienced practitioners, the PMP is the most widely recognised globally. For beginners, the CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation or APM PFQ are better starting points. The best choice is the one employers in your market ask for and that matches your experience.

**Q: Which project management certification is best for beginners?**
The CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation, APM PFQ, CompTIA Project+ and Scrum certifications have no experience requirement. Structured courses such as the Google Project Management Certificate or the PMAI are also good starting points.

**Q: Can I get a project management certification without experience?**
Yes. The CAPM, PRINCE2 Foundation, APM PFQ, CSM and PSM I do not require project experience. The PMP, PMI-ACP, PgMP and PfMP do.

**Q: Is PMP or PRINCE2 the better certification?**
Neither is better overall. The PMP is popular globally and especially in North America; PRINCE2 is common in the UK, Europe and the public sector. Many experienced PMs eventually hold both. See [PMBOK vs PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-vs-prince2/).

**Q: What changed in the PMP exam in 2026?**
PMI launched a new PMP exam in July 2026. Domain weights moved to People 33%, Process 41% and Business Environment 26%, and scenarios now include AI, sustainability and stakeholder engagement. PMI also lists eligibility based on experience within the last ten years.

**Q: How much does a project management certification cost?**
It varies by credential, country and whether you are a member of the awarding body. Budget for the exam fee, any required training, study materials and renewal, and check the official website for current fees.

**Q: How long does it take to get a project management certification?**
Entry-level credentials can take a few days to a few weeks of study. The PMP usually takes a few months of part-time preparation, plus the time to complete the application.

**Q: Do project management certifications expire?**
Many do. PMI credentials require PDUs every three years (60 for the PMP, 30 for the PMI-ACP, 15 for the CAPM), PRINCE2 certifications must be renewed after three years, and the CSM renews every two years. PSM I does not expire.

**Q: Which project management certification is best for Agile?**
CSM or PSM I for Scrum team roles, PMI-ACP for experienced Agile practitioners, and SAFe credentials for organisations scaling Agile.

**Q: Is there a project management certification for AI?**
Yes. PMI offers the PMI-CPMAI for managing AI projects, and the new PMP exam includes AI in its scenarios. Our PMAI certification includes a course on using AI as a project manager.

**Q: Is the Google Project Management Certificate worth it?**
It is a well-structured introduction for career changers. It is a course certificate rather than a professional certification, so many learners follow it with the CAPM or another recognised credential.

**Q: Can I get a project manager job with only a certification?**
A certification helps you get interviews, but employers also want evidence that you have coordinated real work. Volunteer projects, coordinator roles and project tasks in your current job all count.

**Q: Are online project management certifications respected?**
It depends on the awarding body, not the delivery format. PMI, PeopleCert and Scrum.org exams can all be taken online with remote proctoring. Recognised bodies and clear standards matter most.
