# Project Management Methodologies: Types and How to Choose

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-methodologies/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project management methodologies compared: Waterfall, Agile, Scrum, Kanban, PRINCE2, Lean and more, with a step-by-step guide to choosing the right one.


## Project Management Methodologies: Types and How to Choose
Project management methodologies are defined systems of principles, processes, roles and practices for planning and delivering projects, such as Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban and PRINCE2. No single methodology is best for every project: the right choice depends on how stable your requirements are, whether the work can be delivered in pieces and how much governance applies. This guide compares the main methodologies, explains where standards such as the PMBOK Guide fit, and gives you a step-by-step way to choose, with a worked example.
- Published 6 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Approach, framework, methodology and standard mean different things: predictive and Agile are approaches, Scrum is a framework, PRINCE2 is a methodology and the PMBOK Guide is a standard.
- Predictive methods such as Waterfall suit stable, well-understood work; adaptive methods such as Scrum and Kanban suit uncertain or evolving work.
- Choose by scoring requirement stability, incremental delivery, customer availability, cost of change, governance and team experience.
- Hybrid approaches, typically predictive governance with Agile delivery, are common and often the most practical.
- Lean, Six Sigma, critical path and critical chain are usually combined with a main methodology rather than used alone.
- Whatever you choose, tailor it, pilot it and review it after a few cycles.

### What is a project management methodology?
A project management methodology is a defined set of principles, processes, roles, tools and rules that a team follows to plan, deliver and control a project. It sets out how work is organised, who decides what, which artefacts are produced and how changes are handled, so the team works in a consistent, predictable way.
In practice a methodology gives you five things:
- **A life cycle:** the phases, stages or iterations the project moves through.
- **Roles and responsibilities:** who sponsors, manages, decides and delivers.
- **Processes and events:** how planning, reviews, approvals and reporting happen.
- **Artefacts:** the plans, backlogs, logs and reports the team keeps.
- **Rules for change:** how scope, schedule and budget changes are requested and agreed.
A shared methodology means less time arguing about how to work and more time doing it. It also makes projects easier to compare, govern and staff. But every methodology needs tailoring to the size, risk and context of the project. Our guide to [what project management is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) gives the broader picture.

### Approach, framework, methodology and standard
These words are often used interchangeably, which causes confusion when teams say they are "doing Agile" or "using PMBOK". The distinctions are worth knowing:
| Term | What it means | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approach | The overall philosophy for delivering work | Predictive, adaptive (Agile), hybrid |
| Framework | A light structure with a few rules, leaving room to add your own practices | Scrum, SAFe, the Kanban Method |
| Methodology | A more complete, defined system of processes, roles and artefacts | PRINCE2, Waterfall, DSDM |
| Technique | A specific tool used within any approach | Critical path method, earned value, user stories |
| Standard | A description of recognised good practice, not a step-by-step method | PMBOK Guide, ISO 21502 |
In everyday use, "methodology" covers all of these, and this guide follows that convention. The distinction matters when you choose: a framework such as Scrum gives you less out of the box than a methodology such as PRINCE2, so you will need to add practices for things like budgeting or contracts.

#### Predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches
Every methodology leans towards one of three broad approaches.
|  | Predictive | Adaptive (Agile) | Hybrid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Planning | Detailed plan up front | Plan a little, often | High-level plan up front, detail per iteration |
| Scope | Fixed early; changes go through change control | Expected to evolve | Fixed for some parts, flexible for others |
| Delivery | Mostly at the end | Frequent working increments | Increments within planned stages |
| Customer involvement | At the start and at sign-off | Continuous | At stage gates and reviews |
| Examples | Waterfall, critical path scheduling | Scrum, Kanban, XP | PRINCE2 with Scrum delivery |
See our comparison of [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).

### Project management methodologies compared
Use this table to shortlist. Each method is explained in more detail below.
| Methodology | Core idea | Approach | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Waterfall | Sequential phases, each finished before the next | Predictive | Stable, well-defined projects | Late discovery of problems |
| Agile | Short iterations, continuous feedback | Adaptive | Uncertain or evolving requirements | Weak planning disguised as agility |
| Scrum | Sprints, three accountabilities, five events, three artifacts | Adaptive | Product development teams | Needs an engaged Product Owner |
| Kanban | Visualise flow, limit work in progress | Adaptive | Continuous work and service teams | Can drift without cadence |
| Scrumban | Scrum events with Kanban flow | Adaptive | Teams with mixed planned and unplanned work | Unclear rules if not agreed |
| Lean | Maximise value, remove waste | Either | Process improvement, construction, operations | Cost-cutting without value focus |
| Six Sigma | Reduce variation with data (DMAIC) | Predictive | Quality and process problems | Overkill for one-off work |
| PRINCE2 | Stages, business case, management by exception | Predictive or hybrid | Governance-heavy and public sector projects | Documentation overhead |
| Critical path method | Schedule around the longest chain of dependent tasks | Predictive | Date-driven projects with many dependencies | Ignores resource limits |
| Critical chain | Schedule around resources, pool buffers | Predictive | Resource-constrained portfolios | Requires culture change |
| Extreme Programming (XP) | Engineering practices for quality code | Adaptive | Software teams | Software-specific |
| Extreme project management | Rapid cycles for highly uncertain goals | Adaptive | Innovation and R&D | Hard to govern conventionally |

### The main methodologies explained

#### Waterfall
Waterfall moves through fixed phases, typically requirements, design, build, test and deployment, each signed off before the next starts. Winston Royce described this sequence in a 1970 paper, while also warning that a purely sequential process is risky. It works well when requirements are clear and changes are expensive, as in construction or hardware. The risk is that problems surface late, at testing or handover. Our guide to [Waterfall project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) covers the phases in detail.

#### Agile
Agile is an approach based on the values and principles of the Agile Manifesto (2001): deliver working results in short cycles, collaborate closely with customers and respond to change. It is not one method but a family that includes Scrum, Kanban and XP. It suits work where requirements are uncertain and early feedback is valuable. Its main risk is losing sight of budgets, dates and dependencies if the organisation treats "Agile" as a reason not to plan. See our guide to the [Agile methodology](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-methodology/) and the [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/).

#### Scrum
Scrum is the most widely known Agile framework. Under the 2020 Scrum Guide, a Scrum Team of usually ten or fewer people (a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and Developers) works in sprints of one month or less, with five events (the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective) and three artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment). It suits product development where a usable increment can be produced every sprint. Our guide to [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) explains each element.

#### Kanban
Kanban manages work as a continuous flow. Work items move across a visual board, work-in-progress (WIP) limits stop the team starting more than it can finish, and flow metrics such as cycle time and throughput drive improvement. There are no prescribed roles or sprints, so it fits support, operations, marketing and any team with a steady stream of requests. You can start by visualising how you already work and improve from there, which makes it one of the least disruptive methods to introduce. See [what Kanban is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/).

#### Scrumban
Scrumban combines Scrum's planning and review cadence with Kanban's flow and WIP limits. It is popular with teams that handle planned feature work alongside unplanned requests, or teams moving from Scrum to Kanban. Compare the options in [Kanban vs Scrumban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrumban/).

#### Lean
Lean comes from the Toyota Production System. It focuses on delivering customer value with the least waste, using ideas such as value stream mapping, pull and continuous improvement. In projects it is used in construction (for example the Last Planner System), operations and alongside Agile. It works best as a mindset applied within another method rather than as a stand-alone project life cycle. See [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/).

#### Six Sigma
Six Sigma is a data-driven method for reducing defects and variation, run as projects that follow the DMAIC cycle (Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control). It is strongest on repeatable processes with measurable output and is often combined with Lean as Lean Six Sigma. Our [Six Sigma guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/six-sigma/) includes a worked DMAIC example.

#### PRINCE2
PRINCE2 (PRojects IN Controlled Environments) is a process-based method that originated with the UK government and is now owned by PeopleCert, which launched the current version, PRINCE2 7, in October 2023. It has seven principles, seven practices and seven processes. Projects are divided into management stages, a project board makes key decisions, a business case must remain valid throughout, and the project manager works within agreed tolerances (management by exception). It is widely used in the UK, Europe, Australia and the public sector, and can be combined with Agile delivery inside its stages. See our [PRINCE2 guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/).

#### Critical path method
The critical path method, developed in the late 1950s, is a scheduling technique rather than a full methodology. You list activities, durations and dependencies, then find the longest chain of dependent tasks, which sets the earliest finish date. It is used inside predictive and hybrid projects. Our guide to the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) shows how to calculate it.

#### Critical chain project management
Critical chain, developed by Eliyahu Goldratt from his theory of constraints, schedules around resource availability as well as dependencies. Safety time is removed from individual tasks and pooled into shared buffers, and progress is tracked by buffer consumption. It suits organisations where scarce specialists are shared across projects. Our guide to [critical chain project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-chain-project-management/) explains buffer management.

#### Extreme Programming (XP)
XP is an Agile software development method created by Kent Beck in the late 1990s. It centres on engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration and small, frequent releases. Many teams use XP practices inside Scrum or Kanban.

#### Extreme project management (XPM)
Extreme project management, described by Doug DeCarlo in 2004, is for projects where the goal, the solution or both are unclear and conditions change quickly, such as innovation and R&D. It works in rapid cycles and treats the plan as a hypothesis. Our guide to [extreme project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/extreme-project-management/) covers DeCarlo's model.

#### Scaled Agile frameworks
When many Agile teams work on one product, scaling frameworks such as SAFe, LeSS and Scrum@Scale add coordination: shared planning events, roles across teams and portfolio management. Our guide to the [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) covers the most widely adopted option.

### Where the PMBOK Guide and ISO 21502 fit
The PMBOK Guide and ISO 21502 are often listed as methodologies, but they are standards: they describe what good project management involves, not a step-by-step process to follow.
- **The PMBOK Guide** is published by the Project Management Institute (PMI). The eighth edition, published in November 2025, is organised around six principles and seven performance domains, and covers predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches. It underpins the PMP and CAPM exams.
- **ISO 21502:2020** is the international standard giving guidance on project management, published by the International Organization for Standardization.
Use a standard as a reference for what to cover, and a methodology or framework for how to do it. Most organisations tailor a methodology so that it meets the standard their sponsors or clients expect. Read our guide to the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) and the comparison of [PMBOK vs PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-vs-prince2/).

### How methodologies map to the project life cycle
Every project, whatever the method, needs to be started, planned, delivered, controlled and closed. Methodologies differ in how often they repeat those activities and what they call them. This mapping helps when you translate between methods or report to stakeholders used to a different one; see our guide to [project management phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/).
| Life cycle activity | Waterfall | PRINCE2 | Scrum | Kanban |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initiating | Project charter, requirements | Starting up and initiating a project; business case | Product goal, initial Product Backlog | Agree the workflow, policies and WIP limits |
| Planning | Full plan and schedule up front | Project plan plus a detailed plan for each stage | Sprint Planning every sprint; backlog refinement | Continuous replenishment of the board |
| Executing | Design, build, test in sequence | Managing product delivery within each stage | Developers build a usable Increment each sprint | Items pulled through the workflow as capacity allows |
| Monitoring and controlling | Progress against baseline, change control | Controlling a stage; tolerances and exception reports | Daily Scrum, Sprint Review | Flow metrics, daily review of the board |
| Closing | Handover and sign-off | Closing a project; lessons and benefits review | Sprint Retrospective each sprint; release | Delivery of each item; regular retrospectives |
The pattern is clear: predictive methods run each activity once, in sequence, while adaptive methods repeat planning, delivery and review every few weeks or continuously.

### How to choose a project management methodology
There is no universally best methodology, only the best fit for a particular project, team and organisation. Work through these steps:
1. **Define what the project must deliver.** Is the end product well understood, or will it be discovered along the way? Are there fixed dates, contracts or regulatory approvals?
2. **Assess requirement stability.** Stable, well-documented requirements point to predictive methods; vague or changing requirements point to adaptive ones.
3. **Check whether the work can be delivered in pieces.** Software, marketing campaigns and services can usually be released incrementally; a bridge or an office move mostly cannot.
4. **Consider the customer.** Agile methods need a customer or product owner who can review work and make decisions every few weeks.
5. **Map governance and compliance needs.** Regulated, contracted or publicly funded work may require stage gates, formal approvals and audit trails; see our guide to [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/).
6. **Look at your team and organisation.** Consider team size, location, experience with each method and what the rest of the organisation already uses. Switching method on a critical project is risky.
7. **Score, decide and tailor.** Score the shortlist against these factors, choose the closest fit, then document how you will tailor it: which roles, events, documents and approval points you will use.

#### Selection criteria at a glance
| Factor | Points towards predictive | Points towards adaptive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | Clear, stable, documented | Uncertain, expected to change |
| Delivery | Only valuable when complete | Usable in increments |
| Customer availability | Limited; sign-off at milestones | Regular, engaged reviewer |
| Cost of late change | High (physical work, contracts) | Low (software, content) |
| Governance | Formal approvals, audit trails | Light, outcome-focused |
| Team | Specialists in sequence, distributed | Small, cross-functional, collaborative |
Tip
If your factors split roughly evenly between the two columns, that is a strong sign a hybrid approach will work best.

### Worked example: choosing a methodology for three projects
In this illustrative example, a PMO scores three projects from 1 to 5 on each factor, where 1 points strongly towards a predictive approach and 5 strongly towards an adaptive one. The thresholds are a rule of thumb for discussion, not a formal standard: 6 to 13 suggests predictive, 14 to 22 hybrid and 23 to 30 adaptive.
| Factor | Office relocation | Customer mobile app | Regulated system upgrade |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement uncertainty | 1 | 5 | 3 |
| Can deliver usable increments | 1 | 5 | 4 |
| Customer available for feedback | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| Low cost of late change | 1 | 5 | 2 |
| Light governance needs | 3 | 4 | 1 |
| Team experience with Agile | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| **Total (out of 30)** | **10** | **27** | **16** |
| Suggested approach | Predictive | Adaptive | Hybrid |
- **Office relocation (10): predictive.** The scope is clear, the move happens on fixed dates and nothing is useful half-finished. The PM uses a Waterfall life cycle with a [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/), critical path scheduling and formal sign-off from facilities and IT.
- **Customer mobile app (27): adaptive.** The team does not yet know which features users value most and can release every two weeks. It runs Scrum with two-week sprints and a dedicated Product Owner, then moves to Kanban for maintenance after launch.
- **Regulated system upgrade (16): hybrid.** An auditor requires approved stages and documented validation, but the configuration work benefits from short feedback cycles. The project uses PRINCE2-style stages, a project board and stage gates, with Scrum sprints inside each delivery stage and validation evidence produced every sprint.
The scores matter less than the conversation they prompt. If two people score the same factor very differently, that usually reveals a risk or assumption to resolve before the project starts.

### Hybrid project management in practice
Hybrid project management combines predictive and adaptive elements in one project. It is common because most organisations need some fixed commitments (budgets, contracts, launch dates) and also benefit from short feedback loops. These are the patterns you will see most often:
| Pattern | How it works | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predictive governance, Agile delivery | Business case, budget and milestones fixed up front; teams deliver in sprints within each stage | Corporate IT, digital transformation |
| Phased by component | Fixed elements (hardware, building works) run predictively; software or content runs in iterations | Product launches, fit-outs with technology |
| Agile discovery, predictive build | Iterate to define requirements, then plan and deliver the rest sequentially | Construction design, engineering |
| Kanban within milestones | A milestone plan sets dates; a Kanban board manages the flow of tasks between them | Marketing campaigns, events |

#### Hybrid example: a website relaunch
In this illustrative example, a company relaunches its website for a fixed trade-show date. The sponsor approves a business case, budget and three milestones: design approved, content migrated, site live. Within those dates, the web team runs two-week sprints from a prioritised backlog and demonstrates working pages at each sprint review. Content migration, which is repetitive, runs on a Kanban board with a WIP limit per editor. Hosting, legal review and launch communications follow a simple Gantt schedule because they have fixed lead times. The project manager reports progress against the milestones, using sprint and flow data as evidence.
To make hybrid work, agree which parts of the project are fixed and which are flexible, align reporting so sprint progress rolls up into milestone reports, and make one person clearly accountable for each decision. The main risk is a mix that keeps the overhead of both approaches and the benefits of neither. Our [Agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/) shows how sprints can sit inside a milestone plan.

### Methodologies by industry
Industry is a useful starting point, though the project's own characteristics should decide.
| Industry | Common approach | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Construction and engineering | Predictive with critical path scheduling; Lean construction techniques | Physical work, high cost of change, contracts |
| Software and digital products | Scrum, Kanban, XP practices; scaled frameworks for large programmes | Requirements evolve; frequent releases are possible |
| Government and public sector | PRINCE2 or other stage-gated methods, increasingly hybrid | Accountability, audit and funding approvals |
| Manufacturing and operations | Lean, Six Sigma, critical chain | Repeatable processes and shared resources |
| Marketing and creative | Kanban or Scrumban, often within a campaign plan | Steady flow of requests with fixed launch dates |
| Research and innovation | Agile or extreme project management | Outcome unknown at the start |

### How to introduce a new methodology
1. **Explain the reason.** Link the change to a problem people recognise, such as late delivery or unclear priorities.
2. **Start with a pilot.** Choose one project or team with a supportive sponsor, not the most critical project in the portfolio.
3. **Train the people involved,** including sponsors and stakeholders, not only the delivery team.
4. **Use the method as written first,** then tailor it once the team understands why each element exists.
5. **Set up templates and tools** that match the method, such as a [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) for predictive work or a [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) for flow.
6. **Agree how you will measure success,** for example on-time delivery, cycle time or stakeholder satisfaction.
7. **Review after a few cycles or stages,** adjust, then roll out more widely with lessons learned.

### Common mistakes when choosing a methodology
- **Following fashion.** Choosing Agile because it is popular, or Waterfall because it is familiar, without checking the project's characteristics.
- **Using one method for everything.** Different projects in the same portfolio may need different approaches.
- **Adopting the vocabulary but not the practice.** Calling meetings stand-ups or phases sprints changes nothing on its own.
- **Over-tailoring too early.** Removing the uncomfortable parts of a method, such as retrospectives or stage reviews, before seeing their value.
- **Ignoring governance.** Agile teams still need budget control, risk management and stakeholder reporting.
- **Forgetting the customer.** Adaptive methods fail without someone available to review work and make decisions.
- **Letting the tool decide.** Software should support the chosen method, not dictate it.

### Tools and templates for any methodology
Most modern project management software supports several methodologies through different views of the same work, which is useful for hybrid teams.
- **Wrike**, our top-rated tool, combines interactive Gantt charts with dependencies and the critical path (from the Team plan) with board views, dashboards and custom workflows, so predictive and Agile teams can work in one place. See our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).
- **monday.com** and **Asana** let the same work be shown as a table or list, a Kanban board, a timeline or a Gantt chart, which suits teams mixing approaches.
- **Jira** is built around Scrum and Kanban boards and Agile reports, and is a strong choice for software teams.
- **ClickUp** covers sprints, WIP limits and Gantt charts in one platform at a competitive price.
Choose the methodology first, then the tool. Our guide on [how to choose project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/) explains what to look for.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the main project management methodologies?**
The most widely used are Waterfall, Agile (including Scrum, Kanban, Scrumban and XP), PRINCE2, Lean and Six Sigma, together with scheduling techniques such as the critical path method and critical chain.

**Q: What is the most popular project management methodology?**
Agile approaches, especially Scrum and Kanban, are the most common in software and digital work, while predictive and hybrid approaches remain the norm in construction, engineering and government. Many organisations use more than one.

**Q: What is the difference between a methodology and a framework?**
A methodology prescribes a fuller set of processes, roles and documents, as PRINCE2 does. A framework gives a lighter structure and leaves you to add your own practices, as Scrum does.

**Q: Is Agile a methodology?**
Strictly, Agile is an approach or mindset based on the Agile Manifesto. Scrum, Kanban and XP are the frameworks and methods that put it into practice, though people commonly call Agile a methodology.

**Q: Is the PMBOK Guide a methodology?**
No. The PMBOK Guide is PMI's standard describing good project management practice. You use it alongside a methodology rather than instead of one.

**Q: How do I choose the right project management methodology?**
Assess requirement stability, whether the work can be delivered in pieces, customer availability, the cost of late change, governance needs and team experience, then choose and tailor the closest fit.

**Q: Can you combine project management methodologies?**
Yes. Hybrid approaches are common, for example a milestone plan and stage gates for governance with Scrum sprints or a Kanban board for delivery.

**Q: What is a hybrid project management methodology?**
One that combines predictive and adaptive elements, such as fixing budget and key dates up front while delivering the work in short iterations with regular feedback.

**Q: What is the difference between Agile and Waterfall?**
Waterfall plans everything up front and delivers in sequence at the end; Agile plans in short cycles, delivers working increments and adapts as it learns.

**Q: What is the difference between Agile and Scrum?**
Agile is the broad approach; Scrum is one specific framework for applying it, with defined accountabilities, events and artifacts.

**Q: Which methodology is best for construction?**
Predictive methods with critical path scheduling remain the norm, often combined with Lean construction techniques such as the Last Planner System, and Agile practices in design.

**Q: Which methodology is best for software development?**
Usually an Agile framework such as Scrum or Kanban, often with XP engineering practices. Large or regulated programmes may add a scaling framework or hybrid governance.

**Q: Which methodology is best for small teams?**
Kanban is often the easiest to start with because it adds few rules. Scrum suits small teams building a product that can be released in increments.

**Q: Do I need a methodology for a small project?**
You need some structure, even if it is light: a clear goal, a simple plan or board, agreed roles and a way to handle changes. A small project can use a slimmed-down version of any method.

# Project Management Office (PMO): Types, Roles and Setup

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: A project management office (PMO) sets standards and supports projects. Learn PMO types, services, roles, KPIs and a step-by-step plan to set one up.


## Project Management Office (PMO): Types, Roles and Setup
A project management office (PMO) is a team or function that sets the standards for how projects are run and supports, monitors or directly manages them, so that an organisation delivers its projects more consistently and can see all of them in one place. This guide explains the types and levels of PMO, the services and roles inside one, how to set a PMO up step by step, and how to prove it is worth the cost.
- Published 4 October 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- A PMO standardises, supports and oversees project delivery across a department or a whole organisation.
- Supportive, controlling and directive PMOs differ in how much authority they hold over projects.
- PMOs also differ by level: project or programme office, departmental PMO, enterprise PMO and centre of excellence.
- Start with a short list of services that solve a real problem, prove their value, then expand.
- Measure the PMO by delivery outcomes, such as forecast accuracy and benefits, not by the number of reports it collects.
- Most PMO failures come from adding bureaucracy without giving project managers anything useful back.

### What is a project management office (PMO)?
A **project management office (PMO)** is a team or organisational function that defines how projects are managed and supports, monitors or directly runs them. It provides common methods, templates, reporting, governance and expertise, so projects are delivered more consistently and leaders can see the health of all project work in one place.
The letters PMO can also stand for a **programme management office** (supporting one large programme) or a **portfolio management office** (supporting decisions about which projects to fund). The functions overlap, and many organisations simply call all of them "the PMO". The differences are covered in the levels section below and in our guide to [programme vs project vs portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/program-vs-project-vs-portfolio-management/).
PMOs are common in medium and large organisations. CIO.com, citing PM Solutions' 2022 State of the PMO research, reports that nearly three-quarters of midsize and large companies have one. The [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) 8th edition, published by PMI in November 2025, includes an appendix on project management offices that covers PMO types, models, structure and maturity, and describes the PMO moving from a process-focused unit that standardises methods and tools towards a partner tailored to the organisation's strategy.

### What does a PMO do?
What a PMO does depends on the problem it was set up to solve, but most PMO services fall into eight areas. Few PMOs offer all of them, and a new PMO should not try to.
| Service area | Typical activities | What good looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Governance | Stage gates, approval workflows, assurance reviews, decision logs | Decisions are made at the right level, quickly, with clear criteria. See [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) |
| Standards and methods | Lifecycle, templates, tailoring rules, guidance | A light, documented method that teams actually follow |
| Reporting | Status reports, portfolio dashboards, RAG ratings, executive packs | One version of the truth, produced from live data, not retyped |
| Portfolio support | Intake, prioritisation, business case review, roadmap | Leaders can see what is running, what is queued and why |
| Resources and capacity | Capacity plans, allocation across projects, conflict resolution | Clashes for key people spotted weeks before they cause delays |
| Capability | Training, coaching, onboarding, community of practice | Project managers improve and new starters ramp up quickly |
| Tools | Administering the project management platform, templates, integrations | Data is entered once and reused for every report |
| Knowledge | Lessons learned, estimating data, risk libraries | Lessons from one project change how the next one is planned |

#### A typical month in a PMO
To make this concrete, here is what an illustrative month looks like for a three-person PMO supporting around 30 projects:
| Week | Main activities |
| --- | --- |
| Week 1 | Collect status updates, check data quality, publish the portfolio dashboard, flag projects with red or worsening ratings |
| Week 2 | Portfolio review meeting with executives; prepare decision papers for new requests and change requests; update the capacity plan |
| Week 3 | Stage gate reviews for projects reaching a decision point; coaching sessions; one assurance health check |
| Week 4 | Lessons learned workshop for a closing project; improve one template or process; plan next month's priorities |
The PMO also answers ad hoc questions, maintains the [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) for cross-project risks and dependencies, and keeps the tool configuration tidy.

### Types of PMO: supportive, controlling and directive
The best-known classification groups PMOs by how much control they have over projects. It was popularised by earlier editions of the PMBOK Guide and remains the standard answer in exams and job interviews.
|  | Supportive | Controlling | Directive |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Level of control | Low | Medium | High |
| Main role | Advise and provide resources | Set standards and check compliance | Manage projects directly |
| Who project managers report to | Their business unit | Their business unit, with PMO oversight | The PMO |
| Typical services | Templates, training, lessons learned, coaching | Mandatory methods, reviews, reporting, stage gates | Staffing, running and closing projects |
| Best for | Organisations with capable teams that want consistency without central control | Regulated or high-risk work, or organisations with uneven delivery | Strategic, high-value portfolios where central accountability is needed |
| Main risk | Being ignored because nothing is required | Being seen as bureaucracy | Cost, and becoming a bottleneck |

#### Supportive PMO
A supportive PMO acts as a consultant and library. It offers templates, training, expertise and lessons from previous projects, but does not insist that anyone use them. It works well where project managers are experienced and the main problem is inconsistency, or as a first step in an organisation wary of central control. Its weakness is that its influence depends entirely on being useful.

#### Controlling PMO
A controlling PMO requires compliance. Projects must use agreed methods, templates and tools, submit regular reports and pass reviews or stage gates. It suits regulated industries, organisations with repeated delivery problems and portfolios where executives need reliable data. To avoid becoming pure overhead, a controlling PMO should tailor its rules to project size and risk.

#### Directive PMO
A directive PMO manages projects itself. Project managers are employed by, or report to, the PMO and are assigned to projects as needed. This gives the most consistency and the clearest accountability, and suits organisations where projects are the main way strategy is delivered. It is also the most expensive model and needs strong leadership to avoid becoming a bottleneck.

#### How to choose the right type
Answer these questions honestly before you decide:
1. **What problem are we solving?** Poor visibility usually needs a reporting-led supportive or controlling PMO; repeated failure of strategic projects may need a directive one.
2. **How mature is project delivery today?** Teams with little experience need more support and more structure.
3. **How much regulation or risk is involved?** Audit, safety and financial controls push towards a controlling model.
4. **What will executives actually back?** A directive PMO without visible executive support will fail.
5. **What can we afford?** Each step up in control adds people and process.
Many PMOs are hybrids: directive for a handful of strategic projects, controlling for large ones and supportive for everything else.

### PMO levels and structures
A second way to classify PMOs is by the scope of work they cover. An organisation can have several of these at once.
| Level | Scope | Typical focus | Lifespan |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project office | One large project | Planning, scheduling, reporting, document control | Temporary |
| Programme office | One programme of related projects | Dependencies, benefits, programme reporting | Temporary |
| Departmental PMO | All projects in a function, such as IT, engineering or marketing | Standards, reporting and resourcing for that function | Permanent |
| Enterprise PMO (EPMO) | All projects across the organisation | Strategic alignment, portfolio decisions, enterprise reporting | Permanent |
| Portfolio office | The investment portfolio | Prioritisation, funding, capacity, benefits tracking | Permanent |
| Centre of excellence | Methods and capability across all levels | Standards, training, tools, continuous improvement | Permanent |
The P3O (Portfolio, Programme and Project Offices) guidance, now owned by the PeopleCert group, uses a similar model: portfolio, programme and project offices, supported by a centre of excellence that owns standards and capability.

#### Centralised, federated and virtual PMOs
| Structure | How it works | Strengths | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Centralised | One PMO serves the whole organisation | Consistency, one data set, economies of scale | Distance from the front line |
| Federated (hub and spoke) | A central PMO sets standards; departmental PMOs apply them locally | Local knowledge with common reporting | Duplicated effort and local variations |
| Virtual | PMO roles are part-time duties held by people in delivery teams | Low cost, close to the work | Work slips when delivery is busy |
Organisations that deliver mainly through Agile teams often reshape the PMO around flow, outcomes and portfolio funding rather than project plans. See our guides to the [Agile PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-pmo/) and [Agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/).

### PMO roles and responsibilities
Job titles vary, but most PMOs are built from the roles below. A small PMO may combine several of them in one person.
| Role | Typical responsibilities | Useful background |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head of PMO or PMO director | Sets the PMO's direction, reports to executives, owns the PMO's value and budget | Senior delivery or programme management, stakeholder skills |
| PMO manager | Runs PMO services day to day, manages PMO staff, improves processes | Project management, process design |
| Portfolio manager | Runs intake and prioritisation, balances the portfolio against capacity and strategy | Business analysis, finance, strategy |
| PMO analyst | Collects and checks data, builds dashboards and reports, supports governance | Data and spreadsheet skills, attention to detail |
| Planner or scheduler | Builds and maintains integrated schedules, critical path and dependency analysis | Scheduling tools and techniques |
| PMO coordinator or support officer | Administration, document control, meeting support, onboarding | Organisation and communication; a common entry role |
| Project and programme managers | In a directive PMO, deliver projects and report to the PMO | Delivery experience and certification |
The PMO coordinator role overlaps with the [project coordinator](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-coordinator/) role, and many people move between them.

#### How big should a PMO be?
There is no reliable universal ratio of PMO staff to projects; it depends on the services offered and how much is automated. Size the PMO from its service catalogue instead: estimate the hours each service needs per month, add time for improvement work and convert to people using full-time equivalents (FTE). A reporting-only PMO with good tooling can be very lean; a directive PMO that employs the project managers is much larger.

### PMO vs project manager vs programme manager
|  | Project manager | Programme manager | PMO |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | One project | A group of related projects and their combined benefits | Many projects, and how they are run |
| Main question | How do we deliver this project? | How do these projects together deliver the benefits? | How do we deliver all our projects well, and can we see them? |
| Authority | Over the project team and plan | Over the programme and its projects | From advisory to directive, depending on type |
| Lifespan | Temporary | Temporary, often several years | Usually permanent |
| Typical outputs | Plan, schedule, status report, deliverables | Roadmap, benefits plan, programme reports | Standards, dashboards, governance, capacity plans |
Read our comparison of [project manager vs programme manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-vs-program-manager/) for a closer look at the first two roles.

### How to set up a PMO step by step
1. **Define the problem.** Interview executives, sponsors and project managers. Write down the two or three problems the PMO must solve, such as "we cannot see which projects are late" or "the same specialists are booked on four projects at once".
2. **Find a sponsor.** A senior executive must own the PMO, defend its mandate and attend its key forums. Without one, a PMO cannot enforce anything.
3. **Agree the type, level and scope.** Decide whether the PMO is supportive, controlling or directive, which projects it covers, and which it does not. Many start with projects above a size or risk threshold.
4. **Design a short service catalogue.** Choose three to five services that address the problems from step 1. Write what each service provides, who it is for and how often.
5. **Write a PMO charter.** Record purpose, scope, services, authority, roles, funding and success measures, and have the sponsor approve it. Our [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) is a good starting structure.
6. **Set minimum standards.** Agree a light lifecycle, a one-page [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/), a risk register format and a change control route. Scale them by project size so small projects are not overloaded.
7. **Choose one shared tool.** Put all in-scope projects in one platform so data is entered once. See [how to choose project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/).
8. **Set the reporting and governance rhythm.** Fix dates for status updates, the portfolio review and stage gates, and publish them for the year.
9. **Pilot with friendly projects.** Test templates and reports with two or three willing project managers, then fix what does not work.
10. **Roll out and support.** Train project managers, offer drop-in help and show them what they get back.
11. **Measure and publish results.** Track the KPIs agreed in the charter and report them to the sponsor every quarter.
12. **Expand deliberately.** Add services only when the current ones run well and there is demand.

#### A 90-day plan for a new PMO
| Period | Goals | Outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Days 1-30: understand | Interview stakeholders, list all projects, assess current practice | Project inventory, problem statement, draft charter |
| Days 31-60: design and pilot | Agree services, standards and tool; pilot reporting | Approved charter, status template, first draft dashboard |
| Days 61-90: launch | Roll out to all in-scope projects; first portfolio review | Live dashboard, governance calendar, first quick wins reported |

#### What to include in a PMO charter
- Purpose and the problems the PMO will solve
- Sponsor and reporting line
- Type (supportive, controlling or directive) and scope: which projects, departments and thresholds
- Service catalogue with service levels, such as "dashboard published by the fifth working day"
- Authority: what the PMO can require, approve or stop
- Roles, staffing and budget
- Success measures and how often they are reported
- Review date for the charter itself
Tip
Write the charter in the language of the problem, not of process. "Executives will see the status of every project over £100,000 on one page by the fifth working day of each month" wins more support than "implement portfolio reporting standards".

### Worked example: a new PMO in a 40-project organisation
This example is illustrative. A professional services firm runs about 40 internal and client projects at any time. There is no shared tool, status reports arrive in five different formats, and the leadership team learns about problems only when a client complains.

#### Quarter 1: visibility
- The operations director sponsors a two-person supportive PMO: a PMO manager and a PMO analyst.
- The charter names two problems: no single view of project health, and specialists double-booked across projects.
- The PMO builds a project inventory (it finds 46 projects, not 40) and introduces a one-page status template with RAG ratings, forecast finish date and top three risks.
- All projects move into one work management platform; the analyst builds a portfolio dashboard from live data.
- The first monthly portfolio review takes place in week 10.

#### Quarter 2: capacity and decisions
- A simple [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) sheet shows that two senior engineers are allocated at about 180% of their time over the next eight weeks.
- The leadership team delays one internal project by six weeks to free them, and records the decision.
- Two projects with overlapping scope are merged into one.
- A light stage gate is introduced for new projects above an agreed budget, using a short [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/).

#### Results after two quarters
| Measure | Start | After 6 months |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Projects with a current status report | Unknown (no central list) | All 46 |
| Time to produce the executive portfolio pack | About 3 days of manual collation | Half a day, mostly review |
| Resource conflicts identified in advance | None tracked | 7, of which 5 resolved before they caused delay |
| Projects stopped or merged after review | 0 | 3 |
The figures are illustrative, but the pattern is typical: the first wins come from simply seeing all the work in one place. Only after that does the PMO earn the authority to introduce stage gates and move towards a controlling model for larger projects.

### PMO KPIs and how to measure value
A PMO costs money, so it must show what it returns. Choose a few measures linked to the problems in the charter, set a baseline and report the trend.
| KPI | How to measure it | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On-time delivery | % of projects finishing within an agreed tolerance of the baselined date | The most visible sign of delivery reliability |
| Forecast accuracy | Gap between forecast and actual finish dates or costs | Shows whether reports can be trusted |
| Schedule and cost performance | SPI and CPI from [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) | Objective view of progress against plan |
| Benefits realised | Benefits achieved vs the business case | Links projects to business value |
| Portfolio alignment | % of spend on projects linked to a strategic objective | Shows the PMO is steering, not just counting |
| Decision speed | Days from request to approval or rejection | Slow governance is a common complaint |
| Resource conflicts resolved early | Number of clashes flagged and resolved before causing delay | Direct evidence of preventive value |
| Stakeholder satisfaction | Short survey of executives and project managers | Captures whether the PMO is seen as useful |
Avoid vanity measures such as the number of templates published or reports collected: they show activity, not value.

### PMO maturity: from administrator to strategic partner
PMOs usually grow through recognisable stages. Several PMO maturity models exist, and the PMBOK Guide 8th edition appendix on PMOs discusses maturity models; the simplified view below is a practical summary rather than any one official model.
| Stage | What the PMO does | Typical evidence | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Administrative | Collects reports and maintains templates | Status reports exist but are inconsistent | Standardise reporting and data |
| 2. Standardising | Sets common methods and reporting | One status format, one tool, regular portfolio review | Add governance and capacity planning |
| 3. Controlling | Runs governance, stage gates and assurance | Decisions documented; struggling projects spotted early | Link projects to strategy and benefits |
| 4. Portfolio-driven | Supports prioritisation and funding decisions | Projects stopped or reprioritised based on data | Track benefits and improve continuously |
| 5. Strategic partner | Shapes strategy execution with leadership | PMO leader part of planning and investment forums | Sustain, adapt to new ways of working |
Do not try to jump stages. A PMO that introduces portfolio prioritisation before it has reliable project data will base decisions on guesses.

### Why PMOs fail and how to avoid it
| Failure mode | What it looks like | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bureaucracy without value | Project managers fill in forms and get nothing back | Give something back for every request: help with risks, resources or escalations |
| No executive sponsor | Rules are ignored with no consequence | Secure a named sponsor before launch and involve them in portfolio reviews |
| Unclear purpose | The PMO tries to do everything at once | Limit the service catalogue to the problems in the charter |
| One-size-fits-all process | Small projects buried in paperwork | Tailor standards by project size, risk and delivery approach |
| Reporting the past | Reports explain what went wrong last month | Report forecasts, trends and decisions needed |
| Tool before process | An expensive platform nobody uses consistently | Agree the minimum data and process first, then configure the tool |
| Not measuring itself | The PMO cannot answer "what have you done for us?" | Baseline KPIs at launch and report quarterly |
Most of these share one root cause: the PMO was set up to control rather than to help. Effective PMOs behave like a service, with project managers as their main customers.

### PMO tools and software
A PMO needs one place where project data lives, so reports can be generated rather than assembled by hand. Most PMOs use a work or portfolio management platform plus a reporting tool. Options from our reviews:
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool (9.4/10), combines projects, request intake, workflows, resource planning and dashboards that pull data from across projects; its top plans add deeper portfolio, financial and resource analysis aimed at PMO-level insight.
- **[Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/)** offers a spreadsheet-style grid with Gantt charts, dependencies and roll-up reporting, and its scheduling depth is a key reason PMOs choose it.
- **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)** is easy to adopt, with dashboards across boards and prebuilt AI agents for PMO tasks such as project intake, status reporting and portfolio health; portfolio and resource management arrive on the Pro and Enterprise plans.
- **[Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/)** connects projects to portfolios and goals on its Advanced plan, which suits organisations coordinating work across many teams.

Compare them side by side on our [tool comparison page](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/). If you are not ready for a platform, start with a shared spreadsheet based on our [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) and [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/).

### PMO careers and certification
PMO work suits people who like organisation, data and seeing the bigger picture. A common path is PMO coordinator or support officer, then PMO analyst, then PMO manager or portfolio manager. Many PMO leaders also have project or programme management experience.
| Certification | Body | Relevance to PMO work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PMI Project Management Office Certified Professional (PMI-PMOCP) | PMI | Dedicated PMO credential. Requires a secondary degree, 3 years of project-related experience in the last 8 years or a current PMP, and 10 hours of PMO education; the exam has 120 questions in 165 minutes |
| P3O Foundation and Practitioner | PeopleCert | Designing and running portfolio, programme and project offices, popular in the UK |
| [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) | PMI | Broad project management credential, often expected for PMO manager roles |
The PMI-PMOCP builds on the PMO-CP certification that PMI acquired from the PMO Global Alliance in 2023. Check the current requirements on PMI's site before you apply. For a wider view of the options, see our guide to [project management certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/).
Read our guide to [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) for the techniques PMO staff and project managers use to keep a portfolio on track.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a PMO in project management?**
A project management office: a team or function that sets standards for how projects are run and supports, monitors or directly manages them across a department or organisation.

**Q: What does PMO stand for?**
Usually project management office. It can also mean programme management office or portfolio management office, depending on what the office supports.

**Q: What are the three types of PMO?**
Supportive (low control: templates, training and advice), controlling (medium control: required methods, reporting and reviews) and directive (high control: the PMO manages projects directly).

**Q: What does a PMO do day to day?**
Collects and checks project data, publishes dashboards, supports portfolio and stage gate reviews, resolves resource conflicts, coaches project managers and maintains templates and tools.

**Q: What is the difference between a PMO and a project manager?**
A project manager delivers one project. A PMO supports and oversees many projects, sets common standards and gives leaders a consolidated view.

**Q: What is an enterprise PMO?**
An enterprise PMO (EPMO) works at organisation level. It links projects to strategy, supports portfolio decisions and provides enterprise-wide reporting and standards.

**Q: How many people does a PMO need?**
It depends on its services. Estimate the effort for each service in your catalogue and convert it to FTE; a reporting-focused PMO with good tooling can start with one or two people.

**Q: How long does it take to set up a PMO?**
A basic PMO with reporting and a governance rhythm can be running in about three months. Reaching a mature, portfolio-driven PMO usually takes a few years.

**Q: What are good PMO KPIs?**
On-time delivery, forecast accuracy, schedule and cost performance, benefits realised, portfolio alignment, decision speed, resource conflicts resolved early and stakeholder satisfaction.

**Q: Why do PMOs fail?**
Mostly through adding bureaucracy without value, lacking executive sponsorship, trying to do too much at once and failing to measure and show their own value.

**Q: Does an Agile organisation need a PMO?**
Many still have one, reshaped as an Agile PMO or value management office that supports portfolio funding, flow, dependencies and outcomes rather than detailed plans.

**Q: Is there a PMO certification?**
Yes. PMI offers the PMI Project Management Office Certified Professional (PMI-PMOCP), and PeopleCert offers P3O Foundation and Practitioner. The PMP is also common among PMO managers.

**Q: Is a PMO the same as a portfolio office?**
Not quite. A portfolio office focuses on choosing and balancing the investments; a PMO focuses on how projects are delivered. In practice many PMOs do both.
