# The 5 Phases of Project Management: Steps and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: The 5 phases of project management explained: what happens in each, key documents, a worked example, phase gates, Agile phases and common mistakes.


## The 5 Phases of Project Management: Steps and Example
The five phases of project management are initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure. Together they form the project life cycle: you decide whether the project is worth doing, plan how to deliver it, do the work while tracking it against the plan, then close it formally. This guide explains what happens in each phase, the documents and decisions involved, and follows one example project from start to finish.
- Published 5 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- The five phases are initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure.
- Monitoring and controlling is not a separate stretch of time: it runs alongside execution and checks the work against the baseline.
- Each phase ends with outputs and a decision, such as an approved charter, an approved baseline or formal acceptance.
- Phase gates stop weak projects early and make sure the next phase starts with what it needs.
- Agile projects repeat planning, delivery and review in short cycles, but still need a start-up and a close.
- Scale the phases to the project: a two-week project needs a one-page version of each, not a stack of documents.

### What are the phases of project management?
The **phases of project management** are the stages a project passes through from idea to completion. The most widely used model has five: **initiation** (decide and authorise), **planning** (define how), **execution** (do the work), **monitoring and controlling** (track and correct) and **closure** (finish formally). Together these phases are called the **project life cycle**.
Each phase has a purpose, a set of activities, outputs you can point to and a decision at the end.
| Phase | Key question | Main activities | Key outputs | Decision at the end |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Initiation | Should we do this, and why? | Define the need, test feasibility, write the business case, identify stakeholders | Business case, [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/), stakeholder register | Authorise the project |
| 2. Planning | How will we deliver it? | Define scope, break down the work, schedule, budget, plan risk, quality and communication | [Project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) and baselines | Approve the baseline |
| 3. Execution | Are we doing the work well? | Lead the team, produce deliverables, manage suppliers and stakeholders | Deliverables, performance data, change requests | Deliverables ready for acceptance |
| 4. Monitoring and controlling | Are we on track, and what must change? | Measure progress, manage changes, risks and issues, report status | Status reports, approved changes, forecasts | Continue, correct or escalate |
| 5. Closure | Is it finished and what did we learn? | Gain acceptance, hand over, close contracts, capture lessons | Acceptance sign-off, closure report, lessons learned | Formally close the project |
The model describes a **predictive** project, where scope is fixed early and the work is planned in detail before it starts. It is the basis of [Waterfall project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/), but the same five concerns appear in every approach, including Agile.
Tip
Phases describe the order of the project. They do not mean you finish one completely before touching the next. Planning continues during execution as details emerge, and monitoring runs from the first day of delivery to the last.

### Why break a project into phases?
Phases turn one large, uncertain undertaking into a series of smaller commitments:
- **Control points.** A review at the end of each phase lets the sponsor confirm the project is still worth doing before more money is committed.
- **Funding in stages.** A project that stops after initiation costs very little.
- **Earlier visibility of risk.** Feasibility work and planning surface problems while they are still cheap to fix.
- **Clear roles and reporting.** Everyone knows who decides what and when, and "the baseline goes to the board on 14 March" is easier to follow than a percentage complete.

### Phase 1: Initiation
Initiation answers one question: **should this project go ahead?** It turns an idea, problem or opportunity into an authorised project with a clear objective, a sponsor and a project manager. It is the shortest phase on most projects, but decisions made here shape everything that follows.

#### Steps in the initiation phase
1. **Define the need.** Write down the problem or opportunity in plain language and who it affects.
2. **Set objectives.** Agree what success looks like, ideally in measurable terms linked to business goals.
3. **Test feasibility.** For larger or riskier ideas, run a [feasibility study](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/feasibility-study/) covering technical, financial, legal, operational and schedule feasibility.
4. **Build the business case.** Compare options, including doing nothing, with costs, benefits, risks and a recommendation.
5. **Identify stakeholders.** List the people and groups affected, their interest and influence, and how you will engage them. See [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/).
6. **Draft the charter.** Summarise purpose, objectives, high-level scope, key milestones, budget estimate, main risks and the project manager's authority. A [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) speeds this up.
7. **Get approval.** The sponsor or project board signs the charter, which formally authorises the project and the use of resources.

#### Outputs and exit criteria
- Approved business case (or a short justification for small projects).
- Signed project charter, or a project initiation document in PRINCE2 environments.
- Initial stakeholder register, named sponsor and project manager.
- High-level assumptions, constraints and risks.
You are ready to leave initiation when the charter is approved, the objective is clear enough to plan against and funding for at least the planning phase is in place.

### Phase 2: Planning
Planning answers **how the project will be delivered**: what exactly will be produced, by whom, in what order, at what cost and with what controls. The result is the project management plan and its baselines, which become the yardstick for the rest of the project.

#### Steps in the planning phase
1. **Collect requirements.** Work with stakeholders to capture what the deliverables must do.
2. **Define scope.** Write a scope statement that says what is in, what is out and the acceptance criteria.
3. **Break down the work.** Create a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) that splits deliverables into manageable work packages.
4. **Sequence and schedule.** Turn work packages into activities, set dependencies and durations, and use the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) to find the activities that drive the end date.
5. **Estimate costs and set the budget.** Estimate each work package and add contingency for known risks.
6. **Plan resources and roles.** Confirm who is needed and when, and clarify responsibilities with a RACI matrix.
7. **Plan for risk.** Identify risks, assess them and agree responses in a risk register. See [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/).
8. **Plan quality, communication and procurement.** Decide how quality will be checked, who receives which reports and what will be bought from suppliers.
9. **Set the baselines.** Approve the scope, schedule and cost baselines.
10. **Hold a kickoff.** Walk the team and key stakeholders through the plan so everyone starts from the same understanding.
The plan should be as detailed as the project needs and no more. A [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) gives you the structure.

### Phase 3: Execution
Execution is where the team **does the work** and produces the deliverables. It usually takes the most time and money, so most of the project manager's effort goes into coordinating people, removing obstacles and keeping stakeholders informed.

#### Steps in the execution phase
1. **Mobilise the team.** Confirm availability, onboard new members and agree ways of working, tools and meetings.
2. **Assign and sequence work.** Release work packages to owners in line with the schedule, using a board or tracker so everyone can see what is in progress.
3. **Lead and support.** Hold short regular check-ins, resolve blockers and manage conflict.
4. **Manage suppliers.** Place orders and contracts in line with the procurement plan.
5. **Assure quality.** Apply the agreed reviews and tests as work is produced, not at the end.
6. **Engage stakeholders.** Follow the communication plan and run demos or walk-throughs.
7. **Record performance data.** Capture actual dates, hours, costs and completed deliverables for monitoring.
8. **Raise change requests.** When someone asks for something outside the baseline, log it rather than absorbing it quietly. Unmanaged requests are the usual cause of scope creep.

### Phase 4: Monitoring and controlling
Monitoring and controlling **compares actual progress with the plan and acts on the differences**. Although it is listed fourth, it starts as soon as execution starts and continues until closure. Think of execution and monitoring as two sides of the same period of work.

#### Steps in a monitoring and controlling cycle
1. **Collect actuals** for dates, costs, effort and completed work at a fixed interval, often weekly.
2. **Compare with the baseline** to find variances in scope, schedule and cost.
3. **Analyse causes and trends.** Is the variance a one-off or a pattern? Will it affect a milestone or the end date?
4. **Review risks and issues.** A [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) keeps risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies together.
5. **Decide on action.** Choose corrective or preventive actions, or raise a change request if the baseline itself must change.
6. **Process changes formally** through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/): assess impact, get a decision and update the plan if approved.
7. **Report status.** Share a concise [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) with RAG ratings, variances, decisions needed and next steps.

#### Common control measures
| Measure | Formula | How to read it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule variance (SV) | EV − PV | Negative means behind schedule |
| Cost variance (CV) | EV − AC | Negative means over budget |
| Schedule performance index (SPI) | EV ÷ PV | Below 1.0 means less work done than planned |
| Cost performance index (CPI) | EV ÷ AC | Below 1.0 means each pound buys less than a pound of planned work |
| Milestone slippage | Forecast date − baseline date | Positive values show late milestones |
PV is planned value, EV is earned value and AC is actual cost. These measures come from [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/); you do not need full EVM on every project, but the questions it asks are always useful.

### Phase 5: Closure
Closure **formally finishes the project** or a phase of it. It confirms the deliverables are accepted, hands them over, releases resources and records what the organisation should learn. Skipping closure is common, and it leaves open contracts, unclear ownership and repeated mistakes.

#### Steps in the closure phase
1. **Confirm completion** of every deliverable against the acceptance criteria.
2. **Obtain formal acceptance** in writing from the sponsor or customer.
3. **Hand over** deliverables, documentation, training and support arrangements to operations or the client.
4. **Close contracts and finances.** Settle final invoices and close cost codes.
5. **Release the team** with feedback and recognition.
6. **Run a lessons-learned review.** Capture what worked and what to do differently. See [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).
7. **Write the closure report** covering results against objectives, budget and schedule, open items and benefits still to be realised.
8. **Archive** final documents where future projects can find them.
Closure also applies to **cancelled** projects. Stopping a project that no longer makes sense is a sound decision, and closing it properly protects the organisation.

### Worked example: an office relocation in five phases
To show how the phases fit together, here is a hypothetical example: a 60-person company moving to a new office when its lease ends. The figures are illustrative.

#### 1. Initiation (weeks 1–3)
The current lease ends in nine months. The operations director prepares a short business case comparing three options: renew at a higher rent, move to a similar-sized office nearby, or move to a smaller office with hybrid working. It recommends the smaller office, because the fit-out cost pays back through lower rent within the lease term. The managing director, as sponsor, signs a one-page charter: **move all staff into the new office by 30 June with no more than one working day of disruption, within a budget of £180,000**. A project manager is appointed and stakeholders listed (staff, IT, facilities, landlord, removal firm, visiting clients).

#### 2. Planning (weeks 4–8)
The WBS has six branches: fit-out, IT and telecoms, furniture, move logistics, communications, and exit from the old office. The critical path runs through the fit-out contract and IT cabling, because desks cannot go in until cabling is done. The budget is £165,000 of estimated costs plus £15,000 contingency. The risk register includes fit-out delay, data loss during the server move and staff resistance to hot-desking. A RACI matrix makes the IT manager accountable for the network cut-over. The sponsor approves the baseline at a gate review in week 8.

#### 3. Execution (weeks 9–24)
The contractor starts on site, IT orders equipment and the team runs two staff workshops on the new seating plan. Weekly 30-minute check-ins cover progress, blockers and decisions. Halfway through, the sales team asks for video-conferencing kit in two meeting rooms. It was not in scope, so the project manager logs a change request.

#### 4. Monitoring and controlling (weeks 9–26)
At the end of week 16, planned value is £90,000. The work completed is worth £81,000 at budgeted rates (earned value) and £88,000 has been spent (actual cost).
| Measure | Calculation | Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule variance | £81,000 − £90,000 | −£9,000 | Behind schedule |
| Cost variance | £81,000 − £88,000 | −£7,000 | Over budget for the work done |
| SPI | 81,000 ÷ 90,000 | 0.90 | 90% of the planned work done |
| CPI | 81,000 ÷ 88,000 | 0.92 | 92p of planned work per £1 spent |
The cause is a two-week cabling delay after a late landlord approval. Because cabling is on the critical path, the move date is at risk. The project manager agrees with the contractor to run cabling and decorating in parallel in different zones, recovering ten days. The sponsor approves the video-conferencing change at £6,500 from contingency, leaving £8,500 for remaining risks. Two weeks later the status returns from amber to green.

#### 5. Closure (weeks 25–28)
Staff move over a weekend and start in the new office on Monday 29 June, a day early. The sponsor signs acceptance once the snagging list is cleared. Warranties pass to facilities, the old office is returned to the landlord and the final cost is £176,400. Lessons learned: secure landlord approvals before signing the fit-out contract, and add meeting-room technology to the standard requirements list. The closure report notes that finance will track the rent savings over the next year.
Tip
Notice how the phases overlap: planning detail kept emerging during execution, and monitoring started in week 9, not after the work was done. That is normal.

### Documents and deliverables by phase
Not every project needs every document, but this table shows what is typically produced in each phase.
| Phase | Typical documents |
| --- | --- |
| Initiation | Business case, feasibility study, project charter or PID, stakeholder register, project proposal |
| Planning | Project management plan, scope statement, WBS, schedule or Gantt chart, budget, risk register, RACI matrix, communication plan |
| Execution | Task tracker, meeting notes, supplier contracts, quality records, deliverables |
| Monitoring and controlling | Status reports, change requests and change log, RAID log, updated forecasts |
| Closure | Acceptance sign-off, handover documents, closure report, lessons learned register |
Free starting points include our [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) for planning and our [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) for closure.

### Who does what in each phase
Roles shift through the life cycle. The sponsor is most active at the start and at phase gates; the team is most active during execution.
| Phase | Sponsor | Project manager | Team and stakeholders |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initiation | Owns the business case, approves the charter | Drafts charter, identifies stakeholders | Describe needs; experts support feasibility |
| Planning | Approves baselines | Leads planning with the team | Estimate work, identify risks, confirm requirements |
| Execution | Removes organisational obstacles | Coordinates work, manages suppliers | Produce deliverables; review interim results |
| Monitoring and controlling | Decides escalated changes and risks | Tracks performance, runs change control, reports | Report progress honestly; request changes formally |
| Closure | Accepts the result, owns benefits | Leads handover, lessons and closure report | Hand over knowledge; formally accept |

### Phase gates: how to move from one phase to the next
A **phase gate** (also called a stage gate or decision point) is a formal checkpoint at the end of a phase where a decision-maker reviews the results and decides whether the project may continue. Gates stop projects drifting into the next phase without the inputs they need.

#### How to run a phase gate review
1. **Agree the gate criteria in advance**, ideally in the charter or plan, so everyone knows what "ready" means.
2. **Prepare a short gate pack**: phase outputs, status against objectives, updated business case, top risks and the plan for the next phase.
3. **Circulate it** to decision-makers a few days before the meeting.
4. **Hold the review**, focusing on risks, open questions and whether the business case still holds.
5. **Record the decision**: go, go with conditions, hold and rework, or stop.
6. **Release funding and resources** for the next phase if approved.
Tip
A gate that has never said "stop" or "hold" is probably just a meeting. Its value comes from being willing to pause or end a project when the evidence says so.

### Phases vs process groups
Project **phases** and **process groups** are often confused because they share the same five names:
- A **phase** is a period of the project with its own deliverables, such as design or construction. Phases are specific to the type of project and are usually sequential.
- A **process group** is a family of management activities (initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, closing) that can happen **within every phase**. A design phase has its own start-up, planning, execution, control and close.
The five-phase model in this guide treats the process groups as phases. That works well for small and medium projects. On a large project you usually define industry-specific phases (for example concept, design, build, commission) and apply the five process groups inside each.

#### What the main standards say
| Standard | How it describes the life cycle |
| --- | --- |
| PMBOK Guide (PMI) | Up to the sixth edition, PMI organised the work into five process groups and ten knowledge areas. The seventh edition (2021) replaced them with principles and performance domains. The eighth edition, released in late 2025, brings Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling and Closing back as five "focus areas", alongside six principles and seven performance domains. |
| PRINCE2 | Divides the project into management stages separated by decision points and uses seven processes: starting up, directing, initiating, controlling a stage, managing product delivery, managing a stage boundary and closing a project. |
| APM Body of Knowledge (UK) | Describes linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles, plus an extended life cycle that adds adoption and benefits realisation after handover. For linear projects APM names concept, definition, deployment and transition. |
For more detail, see our [PMBOK Guide overview](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/), [PRINCE2 guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) and [project management processes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-processes/).

### Types of project life cycle
The phases can be arranged in different ways depending on how certain the requirements are. Choosing the life cycle is one of the most important tailoring decisions you make.
| Life cycle | How the phases run | Best suited to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predictive (Waterfall) | Each phase happens once, in order; scope is fixed early | Stable requirements, regulated or contract-heavy work, construction |
| Iterative | The product is refined through repeated cycles of planning, building and feedback | Requirements that become clearer as people see early versions |
| Incremental | The product is delivered in usable pieces, each passing through the phases | Projects where early partial value is worth having |
| Adaptive (Agile) | Short iterations combine iterative and incremental delivery with continuous planning | High uncertainty and frequent change, such as software |
| Hybrid | Predictive for some parts, adaptive for others | Mixed projects, such as a hardware rollout with Agile software development |
Our advice: choose the life cycle project by project, based on how stable the requirements are, rather than applying one approach to everything.

### Project phases in Agile and hybrid projects
In Agile projects the five concerns still exist, but planning, execution, monitoring and a small close happen **in every iteration** rather than once. A short start-up and a final close usually wrap around the iterations.
| Classic phase | Agile or Scrum equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| Initiation | Product vision, initial product backlog, release goal, team formation |
| Planning | Release planning, then sprint planning every sprint; backlog refinement throughout |
| Execution | The sprint: building and testing increments that meet the Definition of Done |
| Monitoring and controlling | Daily Scrum, burndown and velocity, sprint review with stakeholders |
| Closure | Sprint retrospective each sprint; final release, handover and retrospective at the end |
Hybrid projects often keep a predictive initiation and closure with phase gates for governance, and run execution in sprints. See [the Scrum process and phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-process-and-phases/).

### How to scale the phases for small projects
The five phases apply to a two-week website update as much as to a two-year programme; only the weight changes. For a small project, initiation can be a one-paragraph objective and a yes from whoever pays; planning a task list with owners, dates and main risks; execution a simple board and a weekly check-in; monitoring a weekly comparison with the plan; and closure an acceptance email and a 15-minute lessons conversation.
The test is proportionality: each phase should cost much less than the problems it prevents.

### Common mistakes in each phase
| Phase | Common mistake | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiation | Starting without a clear objective or sponsor | Do not start planning until the charter is signed and the sponsor is named |
| Initiation | Skipping the "do nothing" option | Always compare against doing nothing in the business case |
| Planning | Planning without the people doing the work | Build the WBS and estimates with the team |
| Planning | No contingency | Base contingency on the risk register |
| Execution | Absorbing "small" requests informally | Log every request and route it through change control |
| Monitoring and controlling | Keeping the status green to avoid difficult conversations | Agree RAG definitions in advance and apply them honestly |
| Closure | Moving the team on before handover and lessons | Put closure activities in the schedule from the start |

### Tools that support the project phases
You can run all five phases with documents and spreadsheets, but project management software makes planning, execution and monitoring easier: schedules update automatically, status is visible to everyone and changes leave an audit trail. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), for example, combines request forms, Gantt charts with baselines, workload views and dashboards, which suits teams running several projects at once.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the 5 phases of project management?**
Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure. Initiation decides whether to do the project, planning defines how, execution produces the deliverables, monitoring and controlling tracks progress and manages change, and closure formally finishes the project.

**Q: What are the 4 phases of project management?**
Some models merge monitoring and controlling into execution, giving initiation, planning, execution and closure. The activities are the same; tracking is treated as part of doing the work.

**Q: Which phase of project management is the most important?**
Initiation and planning have the most influence on success because changes are cheap early and expensive later. Monitoring and controlling is what keeps a well-planned project on track once work starts.

**Q: Are the project management phases sequential?**
Initiation and closure normally happen once. Planning, execution and monitoring overlap, and in Agile projects they repeat in every iteration.

**Q: What is the difference between project phases and process groups?**
A phase is a period of the project with its own deliverables, such as design or build. Process groups are types of management activity that can happen within every phase. The five-phase model treats the process groups as phases for simplicity.

**Q: What is the project life cycle?**
The series of phases a project goes through from start to finish. The common model is initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure, but industries often define their own phases.

**Q: What happens in the initiation phase?**
You define the need, set objectives, test feasibility, build a business case, identify stakeholders and get a project charter approved.

**Q: What documents are produced in the planning phase?**
The project management plan, typically with a scope statement, WBS, schedule, budget, resource plan, risk register, communication plan, change control process and approved baselines.

**Q: What is a phase gate in project management?**
A formal review at the end of a phase where a sponsor or board decides whether the project continues, continues with conditions, reworks the phase or stops.

**Q: How long should each project phase take?**
There is no fixed rule. Execution usually takes the most time and budget. Initiation and planning should be long enough to make sound decisions: hours for a small project, months for a major programme.

**Q: Do Agile projects have phases?**
Yes, in a different shape: a short start-up, repeated iterations that each include planning, delivery and review, then a final release and close.

**Q: What is the difference between the project life cycle and the product life cycle?**
The project life cycle ends when the deliverables are accepted and handed over. The product life cycle covers the product from concept to retirement and can contain several projects.

# Project Management Plan: Components, Steps and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a project management plan is, its subsidiary plans and baselines, how to create one in 10 steps, a worked example and an outline.


## Project Management Plan: Components, Steps and Example
A project management plan is the approved document that explains how a project will be carried out, monitored, controlled and closed. It brings the scope, schedule, cost, risk, quality, communication and other plans together with the baselines you measure progress against. This guide covers its components, a 10-step method, a worked example and an outline you can copy.
- Published 15 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- A project management plan explains how the project will be run, not just what it will deliver.
- It combines subsidiary management plans (scope, schedule, cost, risk and more) with the scope, schedule and cost baselines.
- Build it from the approved charter: requirements and scope first, then schedule and budget, then the supporting plans.
- Scale the level of detail to the project's size, risk and complexity; a small project may need only a few pages.
- Treat it as a living document: update it through change control and re-baseline only when changes are approved.

### What is a project management plan?
A **project management plan** is a formal, approved document that defines how a project will be executed, monitored and controlled, and closed. It integrates the subsidiary management plans for scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communication, risk, procurement and stakeholders, together with the baselines used to measure performance.
The wording comes from PMI's *PMBOK Guide*, which defines the project management plan as the document that describes how the project will be executed, monitored and controlled, and closed. In practice, it is the rulebook for the project: the place the team, sponsor and stakeholders go to find out how decisions are made, how progress is reported and what happens when something changes.
A good plan answers a handful of practical questions:
- **What** are we delivering, and what is out of scope?
- **When** will the main deliverables and milestones be complete?
- **How much** will it cost, and how will spending be controlled?
- **Who** is doing the work, and who makes which decisions?
- **How** will we manage quality, risks, issues, suppliers and communication?
- **What happens** when someone asks for a change?
It is usually written by the project manager with input from the team, subject-matter experts and key stakeholders, and approved by the sponsor or project board. Developing it is a core activity of [project integration management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-integration-management/), because it ties all the other knowledge areas together.

### Project management plan vs other project documents
People often use "project plan", "project management plan" and "schedule" interchangeably. They overlap, but they are not the same thing. The table below shows how the main start-up documents relate to each other.
| Document | Main purpose | Level of detail | Typical owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) | Authorises the project and names the project manager | High level, 2–4 pages | Sponsor |
| [Project initiation document (PID)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-initiation-document/) | PRINCE2 baseline for authorising and running the project | Detailed | Project manager, approved by the project board |
| Project management plan | Explains how the project will be executed, monitored, controlled and closed | Detailed, scaled to the project | Project manager, approved by the sponsor |
| Project schedule | Sequenced activities, durations, dependencies and dates | Detailed for timing only | Project manager or scheduler |
| Statement of work | Describes work a supplier will deliver under a contract | Detailed for the contracted work | Buyer and supplier |
| "Project plan" (informal) | Often used to mean the schedule or a short summary plan | Varies | Project manager |
The key distinction is that the **charter says the project exists and why**, while the **project management plan says how it will be delivered**. The schedule is only one part of the plan. If you work in a PRINCE2 environment, the PID plays a similar role to the project management plan but also contains the business case and the project management team structure.

### Why a project management plan matters
Writing a plan takes time, so it is fair to ask what it gives you. In our experience the benefits come less from the document itself than from the thinking and agreements it forces early on.
- **Shared understanding:** the sponsor, team and stakeholders agree on scope, priorities and ways of working before money is spent.
- **A basis for measuring progress:** without approved [baselines](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) for scope, schedule and cost, you cannot say whether the project is ahead, behind or over budget.
- **Faster decisions:** roles, approval limits and escalation routes are agreed in advance, so issues do not stall while people work out who decides.
- **Control of change:** a defined [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) process protects the project from scope creep.
- **Fewer surprises:** planning for risk, quality and procurement up front exposes problems while they are still cheap to fix.
- **Easier onboarding:** new team members and suppliers can read one document instead of piecing together emails and meeting notes.

### Components of a project management plan
The most widely used checklist of components comes from the *PMBOK Guide* 6th edition, which describes three groups: subsidiary management plans, baselines and additional components. Later editions moved to a principles-and-performance-domains structure and put more weight on tailoring, but the 6th edition list remains a practical reference for deciding what your plan should cover.

#### Subsidiary management plans
Each subsidiary plan explains how one area of the project will be managed. On a small project several can be a paragraph each; on a large project each may be a separate document referenced from the main plan.
| Subsidiary plan | What it explains |
| --- | --- |
| Scope management plan | How scope will be defined, validated and controlled; see [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) |
| Requirements management plan | How requirements will be gathered, prioritised, traced and changed |
| Schedule management plan | The scheduling method, tool, units, update frequency and thresholds for schedule variance |
| Cost management plan | How costs are estimated, budgeted and controlled; see [cost management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-management-plan/) |
| Quality management plan | Quality standards, metrics, reviews, acceptance checks and responsibilities |
| Resource management plan | How people, equipment and materials are acquired, assigned and released |
| Communications management plan | Who receives which information, when, in what format and from whom; see [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/communication-plan/) |
| Risk management plan | How risks are identified, assessed, owned and reviewed; see [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) |
| Procurement management plan | What will be bought, contract types and how suppliers are selected and managed |
| Stakeholder engagement plan | How each stakeholder group will be involved and kept informed |

#### Baselines
Baselines are the approved versions of scope, schedule and cost. They change only through formal change control, and actual performance is compared against them.
| Baseline | Made up of | Used to measure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope baseline | Scope statement, [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) and WBS dictionary | Whether the right work is being delivered |
| Schedule baseline | The approved schedule with start and finish dates | Schedule variance and slippage |
| Cost baseline | The approved, time-phased budget, excluding management reserve | Cost variance and spending trends |
Together, the three form the **performance measurement baseline**, which is what earned value management compares against.

#### Additional components
The *PMBOK Guide* 6th edition also lists components that describe how the project as a whole is run:
- **Change management plan:** how changes are requested, assessed, approved and recorded.
- **Configuration management plan:** how versions of deliverables and documents are identified and controlled.
- **Project life cycle description:** the phases the project will pass through.
- **Development approach:** predictive, adaptive (Agile) or hybrid, and why.
- **Management reviews:** when the sponsor or steering group will review progress and make go or no-go decisions.
Tip
You do not need a separate document for every component. Our advice: list every component in the plan's contents, then either write a short section or link to the separate document. That way nothing is forgotten and nothing is duplicated.

### How to create a project management plan in 10 steps
The order below follows the logic most practitioners use: agree what you are delivering, then when and for how much, then how you will manage everything around it. In reality you will loop back as later steps expose problems with earlier ones, which is normal.

#### 1. Start from the approved charter and business case
Read the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) and business case closely. Note the objectives, high-level scope, fixed dates, budget range, known risks and any constraints. Everything in the plan must be consistent with these. If something in the charter is unrealistic, raise it with the sponsor now rather than burying it in the plan.

#### 2. Identify stakeholders and gather requirements
List everyone affected by or able to influence the project, then gather and prioritise their requirements. Interviews, workshops and reviews of existing processes all help. Record requirements so you can trace each one to a deliverable later.

#### 3. Define scope and build the work breakdown structure
Write a scope statement with clear inclusions, exclusions, deliverables and acceptance criteria. Then break the deliverables down into a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) until each work package is small enough to estimate and assign. Our free [WBS template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) gives you a starting structure.

#### 4. Choose the life cycle and tailor your approach
Decide whether the project will be predictive, Agile or hybrid, which phases it will have and how much formality each area needs. A two-month internal project and a two-year regulated programme should not use the same level of documentation.

#### 5. Build the schedule
Turn work packages into activities, sequence them with dependencies, estimate durations and identify the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/). Add milestones for key decisions and handovers. Our guide to [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) walks through each step.

#### 6. Estimate costs and set the budget
Estimate the cost of each work package using techniques such as analogous, parametric or bottom-up estimating, then add contingency for identified risks. Aggregate the estimates into a time-phased [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) and agree any management reserve with the sponsor.

#### 7. Plan resources, roles and responsibilities
Confirm who will do the work, when they are available and what equipment or materials are needed. Use a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) to show who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each major deliverable and decision.

#### 8. Plan quality, risk, communication, procurement and stakeholder engagement
Write the supporting plans. Set quality standards and acceptance checks, run a risk workshop and start a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/), agree reporting rhythms and channels, decide what to buy and how, and plan how you will engage each stakeholder group.

#### 9. Define change control, baselines and reporting
Describe how changes are requested and approved, who can approve what (for example, the project manager up to a set cost, the sponsor above it) and how decisions are recorded. Set the scope, schedule and cost baselines and agree how progress will be reported, for example in a weekly status report.

#### 10. Review, approve and kick off
Walk the sponsor and key stakeholders through the plan, resolve comments and obtain formal approval. Then hold a kickoff meeting so the whole team understands the objectives, the plan and their part in it. A plan that only the project manager has read will not guide anyone.

### Project management plan example
The example below is illustrative and simplified. It shows how each part of a plan might read for a mid-sized internal project: moving a 120-person team to a new office.
| Section | Example entry |
| --- | --- |
| Objective | Move all staff and equipment to the new office by 28 February with no more than one working day of disruption per team. |
| Scope | Includes space planning, IT and network set-up, furniture, removals and staff communication. Excludes the building fit-out, which the landlord delivers. |
| Deliverables | Approved floor plan; working network and phones; furniture installed; staff moved; old office cleared. |
| Schedule | Planning Oct–Nov; IT installation Jan; moves over three weekends in Feb. Critical path runs through network installation. |
| Budget | Cost baseline of £180,000 plus £15,000 contingency held by the project manager; management reserve held by the sponsor. |
| Resources and roles | Project manager, facilities lead, IT lead, removals supplier. Sponsor: Operations Director. RACI for each deliverable. |
| Quality | Network tested and signed off by IT before any team moves; snagging list closed within 10 working days. |
| Risks | Late network installation (high): weekly supplier check-ins and a fallback date. Staff resistance (medium): early floor-plan previews. |
| Communications | Fortnightly email to all staff; weekly steering update to the sponsor; team briefings two weeks before each move. |
| Procurement | Removals and furniture through competitive quotes from three suppliers; fixed-price contracts. |
| Change control | Project manager approves changes up to £2,000 and two days; above that, the sponsor decides. |
| Closure | Handover to facilities, final cost report and a lessons-learned session within a month of the last move. |
Notice that each entry is specific and measurable. "Minimal disruption" becomes "no more than one working day per team", and "keep people informed" becomes a named channel and frequency.

### Project management plan outline
Use this outline as the contents page for your document. Remove or merge sections that do not apply, and link to separate documents where they already exist.
1. Document control: version, date, author, approvers and change history.
2. Project overview: background, objectives and success criteria from the charter.
3. Scope: scope statement, exclusions, deliverables, acceptance criteria and WBS.
4. Development approach and life cycle: phases, methods and tailoring decisions.
5. Schedule: milestone list, summary Gantt chart and schedule management rules.
6. Budget: cost baseline, contingency, funding and cost control rules.
7. Organisation: roles, responsibilities, RACI and decision rights.
8. Resource management: staffing, equipment and materials.
9. Quality management: standards, reviews and acceptance.
10. Risk management: approach, scales, owners and review cycle; link to the risk register.
11. Communications: stakeholders, messages, channels and frequency.
12. Procurement: what will be bought and how suppliers are managed.
13. Stakeholder engagement: approach for each key group.
14. Change and configuration control: process, thresholds and records.
15. Monitoring and reporting: status reports, reviews and key metrics.
16. Closure: acceptance, handover and lessons learned.
17. Appendices: detailed schedule, estimates, registers and templates.
Our free [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) gives you a ready-made structure in Sheets, Excel and PDF. Pair it with the [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/), [communication plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/) and [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) for the supporting sections.

### How detailed should the plan be?
There is no fixed length. The right amount of detail is whatever lets the team work without constantly asking how things should be done, and lets the sponsor see what they are approving. As a rough guide:
| Project type | Typical plan | What to keep short |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small, low-risk (weeks, a few people) | A few pages or a single shared workspace page: objectives, scope, milestones, budget, roles, top risks | Procurement, configuration and detailed quality plans |
| Medium (months, one team or supplier) | A main document of moderate length with the schedule, budget and risk register as attachments | Subsidiary plans can be a section each |
| Large or regulated (a year or more, many suppliers) | A main plan that references separate subsidiary plans and registers | Repetition: link rather than copy |
Ask two questions about every section: would anyone notice if it were missing, and would they make a different decision because of it? If the answer to both is no, cut it.

### Project management plans in Agile and hybrid projects
Agile teams still plan, but they plan differently. Instead of fixing detailed scope up front, they fix the vision, time and budget boundaries and the ways of working, then plan in detail one release or sprint at a time. This is sometimes called rolling-wave planning.
- **Keep firm:** objectives, governance, budget limits, release milestones, roles, definition of done and how stakeholders are involved.
- **Keep flexible:** detailed scope, which lives in the prioritised product backlog rather than a fixed scope baseline.
- **Replace:** the detailed Gantt chart with a product roadmap and release plan; formal change requests for scope with backlog prioritisation by the product owner.
Hybrid projects often combine both: a predictive plan for hardware, contracts or regulatory milestones, and Agile delivery for software or content.

### Keeping the plan up to date
An approved plan is a baseline, not a final answer. Projects change, and the plan should change with them in a controlled way.
- **Use change control:** assess the impact of each change on scope, time, cost, quality and risk before approving it, then update the affected sections.
- **Re-baseline only when a change is approved:** do not quietly move the baseline to hide slippage; the variance is useful information.
- **Review at set points:** at each phase gate, after major changes and at least monthly on longer projects.
- **Keep version control:** record what changed, when, why and who approved it in the document control section.
- **Tell people:** a changed plan that nobody knows about causes as many problems as no plan.

### Common project management plan mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treating the schedule as the whole plan | Risk, quality, communication and change are left unmanaged | Cover every component, even briefly |
| Copying a template without tailoring | Long documents nobody reads, with sections that do not apply | Scale each section to the project's size and risk |
| Writing it alone | Estimates are unrealistic and the team does not feel ownership | Plan with the people who will do the work |
| Vague objectives and scope | Disputes about what "done" means | Use measurable objectives and explicit exclusions |
| No contingency | The first risk that occurs breaks the budget or deadline | Add contingency based on the risk register |
| No change thresholds | Every small change escalates, or large ones slip through | Set clear approval limits |
| Filing it after approval | The plan drifts away from reality | Review and update it at set intervals |
| Not getting formal sign-off | Stakeholders later deny agreeing to scope or budget | Record approval with names and dates |

### Tools for building and maintaining the plan
Many teams write the narrative parts of the plan in a document and manage the schedule, tasks, risks and budget in project management software. Software makes it easier to keep the plan live: dependencies update automatically, dashboards show progress against the baseline, and everyone sees the same version.
When comparing tools for planning work, look for Gantt charts with dependencies and baselines, resource or workload views, custom fields for risks and issues, and reporting dashboards. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, offers interactive Gantt charts with dependencies, and shareable dashboards from its Team plan upwards, which suits teams running several projects at once, while lighter tools suit simpler plans. Our guide to [Gantt chart software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/) and the full [project management tools ranking](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) can help you choose.
Once the plan is approved, the next job is turning it into a schedule the team can follow.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project management plan?**
A project management plan is a formal, approved document that describes how a project will be executed, monitored and controlled, and closed. It brings together subsidiary plans for areas such as scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and communication, plus the scope, schedule and cost baselines.

**Q: What are the main components of a project management plan?**
Following the *PMBOK Guide* 6th edition, the plan has subsidiary management plans (scope, requirements, schedule, cost, quality, resource, communications, risk, procurement and stakeholder engagement), baselines (scope, schedule and cost) and additional components such as change and configuration management plans, the life cycle and the development approach.

**Q: What is the difference between a project plan and a project management plan?**
In everyday use, "project plan" often means the schedule or a short summary of what will be delivered. The project management plan is broader: it explains how the whole project will be run, including control processes for scope, cost, quality, risk, communication and change.

**Q: Is the project schedule the same as the project management plan?**
No. The schedule shows activities, durations, dependencies and dates. It is one component of the project management plan, which also covers scope, cost, quality, resources, risk, communication, procurement and change.

**Q: What are the three baselines in a project management plan?**
The scope baseline, the schedule baseline and the cost baseline. Together they make up the performance measurement baseline, which actual progress is compared against. See our guide to the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).

**Q: What are subsidiary plans?**
Subsidiary plans are the parts of the project management plan that explain how a specific area is managed, such as the risk management plan, communications management plan or cost management plan. On small projects they can be short sections; on large projects they are often separate documents.

**Q: Who creates the project management plan?**
The project manager leads its development, working with the team, subject-matter experts and key stakeholders. Estimates and plans are more realistic when the people doing the work help build them.

**Q: Who approves the project management plan?**
Usually the project sponsor, sometimes together with a steering committee or other key stakeholders. Formal approval turns the plan and its baselines into the reference point for measuring performance.

**Q: How long should a project management plan be?**
As long as the project needs and no longer. A small, low-risk project may need only a few pages, while a large or regulated project usually needs a main document that refers to separate subsidiary plans and registers.

**Q: How often should the project management plan be updated?**
Whenever an approved change affects it, and at planned reviews such as phase gates. On longer projects, review it at least monthly so it stays aligned with how the project is actually being run.

**Q: Do Agile projects need a project management plan?**
Agile projects still need agreed objectives, governance, budget limits, roles and ways of working, but detailed scope lives in the product backlog and is planned release by release. The plan is lighter and more adaptive rather than absent.

**Q: What is the difference between a project charter and a project management plan?**
The [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) formally authorises the project and sets out its purpose, high-level scope and the project manager's authority. The project management plan is created afterwards and explains in detail how the project will be delivered and controlled.

**Q: What tools can I use to create a project management plan?**
A word processor or shared document works for the narrative sections, and project management software with Gantt charts, dashboards and registers helps keep the schedule, risks and budget current. Our free [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) is a good starting point.
