# Project Management Principles: The 6 PMBOK 8 Principles

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-principles/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project management principles explained: PMBOK 8's six principles with examples, where the 7th edition's 12 went, and PRINCE2 7's seven compared.


## Project Management Principles: The 6 PMBOK 8 Principles
Project management principles are the guiding ideas that shape decisions on any project, whatever method you use, and PMI's current set is the six principles in the PMBOK Guide 8th edition, published in November 2025. They replace the twelve principles of the 7th edition, which many articles still present as current. This guide explains all six with examples, shows where the twelve went and compares them with the seven principles of PRINCE2 7.
- Published 5 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- The PMBOK Guide 8th edition (November 2025) has six principles: adopt a holistic view, focus on value, embed quality, be an accountable leader, integrate sustainability and build an empowered culture.
- The 7th edition (2021) had twelve principles. Their ideas have not disappeared: most were merged into the six, and tailoring and risk now sit elsewhere in the guide.
- PRINCE2 7 (2023) has seven principles, and a project only counts as PRINCE2 if all seven are applied; you can tailor almost everything else, but not the principles.
- Principles tell you what good looks like when no process covers the situation; processes tell you how to do a specific piece of work.
- Use principles at real decision points: kick-off, phase gates, change requests and retrospectives, not as a poster on the wall.
- For the PMP exam, PMI's July 2026 exam content outline defines what is tested; the principles are useful background for situational questions.

### What are project management principles?
**Project management principles** are short, broadly applicable statements of how good project work should be approached. They guide behaviour and decisions rather than prescribing steps, so they apply to predictive, Agile and hybrid projects alike. In PMI's PMBOK Guide 8th edition there are six; PRINCE2 7 has seven.
Principles sit above the detail of any method. A Scrum team and a PRINCE2 project board can follow very different processes and still agree that work should deliver value, that quality should be built in and that someone must own outcomes. Principles hold when your process runs out.
| Term | What it is | Example | Can you tailor it? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Principle | A guiding idea about how to behave and decide | Focus on value | You apply it in proportion, but you do not drop it |
| Process | A defined set of activities with inputs and outputs | Perform integrated change control | Yes: combine, simplify or skip as the project needs |
| Practice or technique | A specific way of doing part of the work | Daily stand-up, earned value, RACI chart | Yes: choose what fits |
| Method or framework | A packaged way of running projects | PRINCE2, Scrum, Kanban | Yes, within the method's own rules |
The main principle sets you will meet come from different owners. PMI publishes the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/); PeopleCert owns [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/); the [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/) has twelve principles of its own; Scrum rests on three pillars and five values; and the Kanban Method has its own principles and practices. This page focuses on PMI and PRINCE2 and points you to the others.

### The six PMBOK 8 principles at a glance
The PMBOK Guide 8th edition includes *The Standard for Project Management*, and its principles chapter sets out the project management mindset and six principles. For each principle the Standard describes its impact, what the principle looks like in action and how it connects to the seven performance domains (governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources and risk).
| # | Principle (Standard title) | Core idea | The question it makes you ask |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Adopt a holistic view | A project is a system of connected parts inside a wider organisation | What else does this decision affect? |
| 2 | Focus on value | Success is judged by the benefits delivered, not only by outputs | Is this still worth doing, and is it the most valuable thing to do next? |
| 3 | Embed quality into processes and deliverables | Build quality in from the start rather than inspecting it in at the end | How will we know it is good enough, and how do we prevent defects? |
| 4 | Be an accountable leader | Own outcomes and lead with integrity, whatever your formal role | Who owns this, and am I acting in the project's and stakeholders' best interest? |
| 5 | Integrate sustainability within all project areas | Weigh environmental, social and economic effects throughout | What does this leave behind for the organisation, community and environment? |
| 6 | Build an empowered culture | Create conditions in which people collaborate, decide and recover from setbacks | Do the people closest to the work have the information and authority to act? |
Some summaries shorten the titles, for example "embed quality", "integrate sustainability" or "lead accountably". The meaning is the same. For the full structure of the book, including the 40 processes and five focus areas, see our [guide to the PMBOK Guide 8th edition](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/).

### The six principles explained

#### 1. Adopt a holistic view
A project is not a set of independent tasks. Scope, schedule, cost, risk and people interact, and the project itself interacts with operations, other projects and the wider organisation. A holistic view means looking at those connections before you act. Commentators link it to the 7th edition's systems-thinking principle, and it also absorbs much of what the 7th edition said about complexity.
- **In practice:** assess every significant change for knock-on effects on cost, schedule, risk, people and neighbouring projects before approving it, using a formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) process where the stakes justify it.
- **In practice:** map dependencies with other teams and suppliers early, and revisit the map at each phase.
- **Warning signs:** teams optimising their own work at the expense of the whole; surprises from departments nobody consulted; risks that "belong to someone else".

#### 2. Focus on value
Value is the reason the project exists. It may be financial, social, regulatory or strategic, and it can change during delivery as markets, priorities or technology move. Focusing on value means checking the business case regularly, prioritising work that delivers the most benefit soonest, and being willing to stop work that no longer pays back.
- **In practice:** state the expected benefits and how they will be measured in the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/), then test them at each phase gate.
- **In practice:** use a [cost-benefit analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/) when options compete, and record value assumptions so you can see when they change.
- **Warning signs:** reporting only on time and budget; a business case written once and never reopened; features delivered that nobody uses.

#### 3. Embed quality into processes and deliverables
Quality is a design decision made early, not an inspection made late. This principle covers both the deliverables (do they meet agreed acceptance criteria?) and the way the work is done (does the process prevent defects?). It also means not gold-plating: delivering what is needed, to the standard agreed, rather than everything that is possible.
- **In practice:** agree acceptance criteria before work starts, review early drafts and prototypes, and automate checks where you can.
- **In practice:** treat recurring defects as process problems; see our guide to [project quality management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/).
- **Warning signs:** testing squeezed into the last week; rework accepted as normal; arguments at handover about what "done" meant.

#### 4. Be an accountable leader
Leadership on a project is not limited to the project manager, and it is not the same as administration. An accountable leader takes ownership of outcomes, acts with integrity and transparency, and makes sure accountability is clear across the team. Some commentators note that this principle combines the 7th edition's separate stewardship and leadership principles.
- **In practice:** make decision rights and accountability explicit, for example with a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/), and report bad news early with a recovery plan.
- **In practice:** model the behaviour you expect: keep commitments, admit mistakes, give credit.
- **Warning signs:** "I just follow the process"; missed milestones explained away; decisions that nobody admits to having made.

#### 5. Integrate sustainability within all project areas
Sustainability is the most visible new emphasis in the 8th edition. It asks you to consider what the project leaves behind: environmental effects such as energy use and waste, social effects on people and communities, and economic effects such as long-term running costs. It belongs in every area, from supplier choice and design to operations and closure, not in a separate report.
- **In practice:** include whole-life cost, energy and supplier practices in option appraisal and [procurement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) criteria.
- **In practice:** add sustainability risks and opportunities to the risk register and track them like any other.
- **Warning signs:** sustainability mentioned in the charter and nowhere else; the cheapest option chosen without considering running costs or disposal.

#### 6. Build an empowered culture
Projects are delivered by people, and people do their best work when they trust each other, understand the goal and have the authority to act. An empowered culture covers collaboration within the team, genuine engagement with stakeholders, psychological safety and resilience when things go wrong. It carries forward much of the 7th edition's team, stakeholder and resiliency principles.
- **In practice:** delegate decisions to the people closest to the work, with clear boundaries and escalation routes.
- **In practice:** involve stakeholders early and often; our guide to [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) shows how to plan it.
- **Warning signs:** every decision waits for the project manager; people hide problems; the same few voices dominate meetings.

### From twelve principles to six
The PMBOK Guide 7th edition, published in 2021, replaced the old process groups and knowledge areas with twelve principles and eight performance domains. The twelve are still widely taught and quoted, but they are no longer PMI's current set, even though the thinking behind them is still sound.
PMI describes the 8th edition as consolidating the principles. The table below lists the twelve with their 7th edition titles and shows where each idea now sits. PMI has not published a simple one-to-one mapping that we could find, so the right-hand column is **our reading**, based on the 8th edition's principle titles and structure.
| 7th edition principle | Short name | Where the idea sits in the 8th edition (our reading) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Be a diligent, respectful and caring steward | Stewardship | Be an accountable leader; care for the environment and society now has its own sustainability principle |
| Create a collaborative project team environment | Team | Build an empowered culture |
| Effectively engage with stakeholders | Stakeholders | Build an empowered culture, plus the stakeholders performance domain |
| Focus on value | Value | Focus on value |
| Recognise, evaluate and respond to system interactions | Systems thinking | Adopt a holistic view |
| Demonstrate leadership behaviours | Leadership | Be an accountable leader |
| Tailor based on context | Tailoring | A full tailoring chapter in the guide rather than a principle |
| Build quality into processes and deliverables | Quality | Embed quality into processes and deliverables |
| Navigate complexity | Complexity | Adopt a holistic view |
| Optimise risk responses | Risk | The risk performance domain and its processes |
| Embrace adaptability and resiliency | Adaptability and resiliency | Build an empowered culture, and the choice of life cycle and development approach |
| Enable change to achieve the envisioned future state | Change | Focus on value (benefits depend on people adopting the output) and build an empowered culture |

#### Why PMI consolidated the principles
Twelve principles overlapped considerably: stewardship and leadership, team and stakeholders, systems thinking and complexity all describe related behaviours. Six are easier to remember and apply. The 8th edition also moved practical material back into the book, so ideas such as tailoring and risk response, which the 7th edition could only express as principles, now have their own chapters, domains and processes.
Tip
If you studied the 7th edition, you do not need to unlearn anything. Group what you know under the six new headings, add sustainability, and read the 8th edition's tailoring chapter and risk domain for the material that moved.

### PRINCE2 7's seven principles
PRINCE2 is a process-based method owned by PeopleCert. Its current edition, PRINCE2 7, was published in 2023 and is built from five integrated elements: principles, people, practices, processes and the project context. The seven principles are the foundation. A project is only being run as PRINCE2 if all seven are applied; you can tailor processes, practices, roles and management products, but not the principles.
| PRINCE2 7 principle | What it means | How it shows up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ensure continued business justification | The project must remain desirable, viable and achievable throughout | The business case is reviewed at every stage boundary; the project is closed early if it stops being worthwhile |
| Learn from experience | Seek, record and act on lessons from previous and current work | Lessons are gathered at start-up and captured throughout, not only at closure |
| Define roles, responsibilities and relationships | Everyone knows who decides, who does and how people work together | A project board representing business, user and supplier interests |
| Manage by stages | Plan, monitor and control the project one management stage at a time | Detailed stage plans; authorisation to continue at each stage boundary |
| Manage by exception | Set tolerances so each level of management only escalates when they are forecast to be exceeded | Tolerances for time, cost, quality, scope, benefits, risk and sustainability |
| Focus on products | Define and agree the outputs and their quality before doing the work | Product descriptions with quality criteria |
| Tailor to suit the project | Adapt the method to the project's environment, size, complexity, importance, capability and risk | Tailoring decisions recorded in the project initiation documentation |
PRINCE2 7 renamed the roles principle. The 2017 edition called it "defined roles and responsibilities"; the 7th edition adds **relationships**, reflecting the new people element. The 7th edition also added sustainability as a performance target alongside time, cost, quality, scope, benefits and risk.
See our [PRINCE2 guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) for the practices and processes, and our [PMBOK vs PRINCE2 comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-vs-prince2/) for how the two fit together.

### PMBOK 8 vs PMBOK 7 vs PRINCE2 7 principles
The three sets are often confused, especially in exam preparation. They differ in purpose as well as number.
|  | PMBOK Guide 8th edition | PMBOK Guide 7th edition | PRINCE2 7 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Owner | PMI | PMI | PeopleCert |
| Published | November 2025 | 2021 | 2023 |
| Number of principles | 6 | 12 | 7 |
| Status | Current | Superseded by the 8th edition | Current |
| Nature | Mindset that underpins a non-prescriptive standard | Mindset that underpins a non-prescriptive standard | Mandatory foundations of a prescriptive method |
| Must all be applied? | Applied in proportion to the project | Applied in proportion to the project | Yes, all seven, or it is not PRINCE2 |
| Distinctive emphasis | Sustainability, accountable leadership, empowered culture | Stewardship, systems thinking, tailoring, change | Business justification, stages, exception, products |

#### Where the themes overlap
| Theme | PMBOK 8 principle | PRINCE2 7 principle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Value and justification | Focus on value | Ensure continued business justification |
| Accountability and roles | Be an accountable leader | Define roles, responsibilities and relationships |
| Quality of outputs | Embed quality into processes and deliverables | Focus on products |
| Learning and improvement | Build an empowered culture; embed quality | Learn from experience |
| Fitting the approach to the project | Tailoring chapter of the guide | Tailor to suit the project |
| Sustainability | Integrate sustainability within all project areas | Sustainability performance target and tolerance (not a principle) |
| Control structure | Governance performance domain | Manage by stages; manage by exception |
| Whole-system thinking | Adopt a holistic view | Implicit in the project context element |
The practical lesson: if you run PRINCE2 projects, the PMBOK principles add little that conflicts and a good deal that complements, especially around leadership and culture. If you follow PMI, PRINCE2's stage and exception principles are a useful model for [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/).

### Other principle sets you will meet
Many teams combine a project management standard with an Agile or Lean way of working. Each comes with its own principles, and they sit comfortably alongside PMI's six.
| Source | What it contains | Our guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agile Manifesto (2001) | Four values and twelve principles for adaptive, collaborative delivery | [Agile Manifesto values and principles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/) |
| Scrum Guide (2020) | Three pillars of empiricism and five Scrum values; no list called principles | [Scrum principles and values](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-principles-and-values/) |
| Kanban Method | Change management and service delivery principles plus six general practices | [Kanban principles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-principles/) |
| Lean thinking | Value, value stream, flow, pull and continuous improvement | [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/) |
If you see a list of "5", "8" or "10" project management principles that matches none of these, it is usually an author's own summary of good practice. Such lists can be useful, but they are not a standard.

### Worked example: the six principles on one project
This illustrative example shows how the principles change real decisions. The organisation, figures and outcomes are invented.
A housing association plans to replace gas boilers with heat pumps in 120 homes over nine months, with a budget of £1.2 million. Tenants stay in their homes during the work. The project uses a predictive plan for procurement and installation, with short weekly cycles for scheduling visits.
| Principle | Decision point | What the team did | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Adopt a holistic view | Installation plan | Checked the plan with the repairs team, the call centre and the electricity network operator before fixing dates | Found that 30 homes needed electrical upgrades first and resequenced them, avoiding wasted visits |
| Focus on value | Month 4 review | Re-tested the business case against new tariff data and tenant fuel bills | Kept the project, but moved the oldest, least efficient homes to the front of the queue |
| Embed quality | First 10 installations | Treated them as a pilot with a checklist, photo evidence and a tenant walkthrough | Fixed a recurring commissioning fault before it reached the remaining 110 homes |
| Be an accountable leader | Supplier delay | The project manager told the board about a six-week delay in the week it was known, with two recovery options | The board approved a second installer within its tolerance; trust held |
| Integrate sustainability | Procurement | Scored bids on whole-life cost, refrigerant type, waste handling and local employment as well as price | Chose a supplier that was not the cheapest but had lower running and disposal costs |
| Build an empowered culture | Daily scheduling | Let installation leads rebook visits directly with tenants within agreed rules | Fewer missed appointments and faster rebooking without waiting for the office |

#### The same project through a PRINCE2 lens
- **Continued business justification:** the month 4 review was a stage boundary with a formal go or stop decision.
- **Manage by exception:** the board set tolerances of plus or minus four weeks and 5% of cost, so the second-installer decision stayed within delegated limits.
- **Focus on products:** the pilot produced a product description for a "completed installation", with quality criteria every crew used.
- **Learn from experience:** lessons from another landlord's pilot shaped the checklist before work began.

### How to apply project management principles, step by step
Principles only help if they influence decisions. This process works on predictive, Agile and hybrid projects.
1. **Choose your set.** Use the PMBOK 8 six as a default, add PRINCE2's seven if you run PRINCE2, and add your delivery framework's principles if you use Scrum or Kanban.
2. **Translate each principle into a project-specific rule.** For example, "focus on value" might become "no feature enters the plan without a named benefit owner".
3. **Build them into the charter.** Record the benefits, quality expectations, sustainability goals and decision rights in the charter; our [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) has sections for each.
4. **Make accountability visible.** Agree who decides what, using our free [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/).
5. **Use them at decision points.** At each phase gate, change request and major risk response, ask the six questions from the table above before you decide.
6. **Keep the value case live.** Revisit the [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) at every gate, not just at approval.
7. **Review them in retrospectives and lessons-learned sessions.** Ask which principle was weakest this period and what you will change. Our [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) gives a simple structure.
8. **Adjust as the project changes.** When risk, size or stakeholders shift, revisit how strongly each principle needs to be applied.

### Principles health check
Use this check at kick-off, at each phase gate or quarterly on long projects. Score each line from 1 (rarely true) to 5 (consistently true). Any score of 2 or below is worth a conversation; a total below 18 suggests the principles are not yet shaping decisions.
| Principle | Question to score | Evidence to look for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adopt a holistic view | Do we assess the knock-on effects of changes before approving them? | Impact assessments on change requests; a dependency map that is up to date |
| Focus on value | Have we re-tested the benefits since the last gate? | Updated business case; benefits with owners and measures |
| Embed quality | Are acceptance criteria agreed before work starts? | Criteria on work items; falling rework over time |
| Be an accountable leader | Is it clear who owns each decision, and is bad news raised early? | Decision log; issues raised before they become crises |
| Integrate sustainability | Do our option appraisals include environmental, social and whole-life costs? | Sustainability criteria in procurement and design decisions |
| Build an empowered culture | Can team members make routine decisions without waiting for approval? | Delegated authority written down; problems raised openly in meetings |

### Common mistakes with project management principles
- **Teaching the twelve as current.** The 7th edition's principles are superseded. Use the six, and explain the twelve as background.
- **Treating principles as a poster.** Principles that never appear in a decision, a gate review or a retrospective have no effect.
- **Confusing principles with processes.** Principles do not tell you which documents to produce. Use the [project management processes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-processes/) for that.
- **Applying everything at full strength.** A two-week internal project needs a light touch; a regulated infrastructure programme needs much more. Proportion is part of applying principles well.
- **Leaving sustainability to someone else.** It is now a core principle, not a corporate report.
- **Using accountability to blame.** Accountable leadership is about ownership and transparency, not finding someone to fault when things go wrong.

### Project management principles and the PMP exam
The [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) exam is built on PMI's exam content outline, which was updated in July 2026 and weights three domains: People 33%, Process 41% and Business Environment 26%. The PMBOK Guide is one of several references, not the syllabus itself.
The principles still matter for the exam because many situational questions test judgement: whether you re-check value before continuing, involve the people affected, take ownership of a problem or build quality in rather than inspecting it later. If you know the six principles well, the best answer in those questions is often easier to spot. The same applies to the [CAPM](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) at a more foundational level. For background on the organisation behind both exams, see [what is PMI](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/).
Read our overview of [project management methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-methodologies/) next to see how these principles sit under predictive, Agile and hybrid ways of working.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the principles of project management?**
They are guiding ideas that shape decisions on any project, whatever method you use. PMI's current set, in the PMBOK Guide 8th edition, has six: adopt a holistic view, focus on value, embed quality into processes and deliverables, be an accountable leader, integrate sustainability within all project areas, and build an empowered culture.

**Q: How many project management principles are there?**
It depends on the source. The PMBOK Guide 8th edition has six, the 7th edition had twelve, PRINCE2 7 has seven and the Agile Manifesto has twelve of its own. Lists of five, eight or ten are usually an author's own summary.

**Q: What are the six principles in PMBOK 8?**
Adopt a holistic view; focus on value; embed quality into processes and deliverables; be an accountable leader; integrate sustainability within all project areas; and build an empowered culture.

**Q: What were the 12 principles of project management in PMBOK 7?**
Stewardship, team, stakeholders, value, systems thinking, leadership, tailoring, quality, complexity, risk, adaptability and resiliency, and change. They come from the 7th edition (2021), which the 8th edition replaced in November 2025.

**Q: Are the 7th edition's 12 principles still valid?**
Their ideas are still sound, but they are no longer PMI's current list. Most were merged into the six principles of the 8th edition, while tailoring and risk now have their own chapter and performance domain.

**Q: Which principle is new in the PMBOK Guide 8th edition?**
Integrate sustainability within all project areas. The 7th edition touched on care for the environment under stewardship, but the 8th edition makes sustainability a principle in its own right.

**Q: What are the seven principles of PRINCE2 7?**
Ensure continued business justification, learn from experience, define roles, responsibilities and relationships, manage by stages, manage by exception, focus on products, and tailor to suit the project. All seven must be applied for a project to count as PRINCE2.

**Q: What is the difference between principles and processes?**
Principles are guiding ideas about how to behave and decide; processes are defined activities with inputs and outputs. You tailor processes heavily, but you keep the principles and apply them in proportion.

**Q: Can you tailor project management principles?**
You apply them with more or less rigour depending on the project, but you do not drop them. PRINCE2 is explicit: processes, practices and products can be tailored, the principles cannot.

**Q: Do project management principles apply to Agile projects?**
Yes. PMI's principles are written for predictive, adaptive and hybrid work. Agile teams usually combine them with the Agile Manifesto's principles and their framework's own values, such as the Scrum values.

**Q: What is the most important project management principle?**
No source ranks them, and they work as a set. If you need one starting point, focus on value is the reason the project exists, and the other principles help you deliver that value well.

**Q: Are project management principles tested on the PMP exam?**
Not as a list to memorise. The PMP exam follows PMI's July 2026 exam content outline, but the principles inform many situational questions about judgement, leadership and value.

**Q: Why are project management principles important?**
They guide decisions when no process covers the situation, let teams using different methods work to the same standards and keep attention on outcomes rather than paperwork.

# Project Management Processes: The 5 Groups Explained

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-processes/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project management processes explained: the 5 process groups, 10 knowledge areas, all 49 PMBOK processes, PMBOK 8 changes, a worked example and tailoring.


## Project Management Processes: The 5 Groups Explained
Project management processes are the repeatable sets of activities a project manager uses to start, plan, deliver, control and close a project. PMI groups them into five process groups (initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing) and, in its classic model, ten knowledge areas, giving 49 processes in all. You rarely need every one of them, so the real skill is choosing the right ones for each project.
- Published 6 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- The five process groups are initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing.
- Process groups describe the type of management activity; the ten knowledge areas describe the subject being managed.
- The classic PMBOK model has 49 processes; PMBOK 8 (November 2025) has 40, grouped into five focus areas.
- Process groups are not phases: they repeat within every phase and overlap.
- Monitoring and controlling runs from start to finish, not just at the end.
- Tailor the processes to the project's size, risk and context rather than applying all of them by default.

### What are project management processes?
**Project management processes** are defined sets of activities that turn inputs, such as a business case or a progress report, into outputs, such as a charter, a schedule or an approved change. Each process has a clear purpose, uses particular tools and techniques, and produces something the next process needs. Together they form the management system around the project's work.
It helps to separate two kinds of process on any project. **Project management processes** organise and control the work: planning, tracking, reporting and change control. **Product-oriented processes** create the deliverable itself: designing a building, writing code or running a marketing campaign. This guide covers the first kind, which are broadly the same whatever the industry.
The most widely used model comes from PMI (the Project Management Institute). Its [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) arranged processes in two directions: by **process group**, which says when and why a process is used, and by **knowledge area**, which says what subject it deals with. Every process sits in exactly one of each. Even though PMI's newer standards are organised differently, this two-way structure is still the clearest way to see what a complete approach to a project needs.
Processes are different from project management principles, which guide behaviour and judgement, and from methodologies, which package processes, roles and rules into a complete way of working such as PRINCE2.

### The five project management process groups
A **process group** is a logical grouping of processes by the type of management activity. The five groups apply to any project, of any size, using any method.
| Process group | Purpose | Key outputs | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Initiating** | Define a new project or phase and obtain authorisation to start | Project charter, stakeholder register | Should we do this, and who is involved? |
| **Planning** | Establish the total scope, refine objectives and define the course of action | Project management plan, scope baseline, schedule, budget, risk register | How will we deliver it? |
| **Executing** | Complete the work defined in the plan to meet the requirements | Deliverables, work performance data, change requests, issue log | Are we doing the work? |
| **Monitoring and controlling** | Track, review and regulate progress and performance; manage changes | Work performance reports, approved changes, forecasts | Are we on track, and what must change? |
| **Closing** | Formally complete the project, phase or contract | Final report, accepted deliverables, lessons learned, archived records | Is it finished and handed over? |

#### Initiating
Initiating processes give the project a formal start. The sponsor confirms the business need, the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) is written and approved, and the project manager is named and given authority. Stakeholders are identified early so their interests shape the plan. In a multi-phase project, a short initiating step at the start of each phase checks that the project is still worth continuing.

#### Planning
Planning processes work out what will be delivered and how. They produce the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) and its subsidiary plans, the scope statement and [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/), the schedule, the budget, the quality and resource plans, and the risk register. Planning is iterative: as you learn more, you return and refine the plan, which is often called progressive elaboration.

#### Executing
Executing processes do the work and manage the people doing it. The project manager directs the team, acquires and develops resources, runs quality assurance, communicates with stakeholders, carries out procurements and implements agreed risk responses. Most of the project's time and money is spent here.

#### Monitoring and controlling
Monitoring and controlling processes compare actual performance with the plan, analyse variances, forecast the outcome and decide on corrective action. They include scope validation, schedule and cost control, quality control and [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/). Unlike the other groups, monitoring and controlling runs throughout the project, from the moment the charter is signed.

#### Closing
Closing processes finish the project or phase properly: deliverables are accepted, contracts are closed, the team is released, records are archived and [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) are captured. Projects that are cancelled early still need closing, so the organisation keeps the knowledge and closes the accounts.

### How the process groups interact
The process groups are often drawn as five boxes in a row, which suggests that you finish initiating, then plan, then execute. In practice they overlap heavily. Planning continues while execution starts; monitoring and controlling runs from day one; and an approved change can send you back to planning in the middle of delivery.
PMI has long linked the process groups to the **plan-do-check-act** cycle: planning is "plan", executing is "do", and monitoring and controlling covers "check" and "act". Initiating starts the cycle and closing ends it. The cycle repeats many times on a real project, often every reporting period.

#### Process groups vs project phases
The most common confusion is between process groups and phases. A **phase** is a time-bound part of the project life cycle, such as feasibility, design, build and handover. A **process group** is a type of management activity. All five process groups are used within each phase.
|  | Process groups | Project phases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What they describe | Types of management activity | Stages of the project's life over time |
| Number | Always five | Varies by project and industry |
| Sequence | Overlap and repeat | Usually sequential, ending in a gate or review |
| Example | Monitoring and controlling | Detailed design |
| Defined by | PMI's standards | Your organisation, industry or method |
For example, a construction project's design phase has its own short initiation (confirm the brief and authorise design), planning (design programme and budget), execution (produce drawings), monitoring and controlling (design reviews and cost checks) and closing (sign-off at the design gate).

### The ten knowledge areas
A **knowledge area** is a field of project management defined by its required knowledge and described by its processes. The PMBOK Guide used ten from its fifth edition (2013) onwards.
| Knowledge area | What it covers | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Integration | Coordinating all parts of the project: charter, plan, direction, change control and closure | [Integration management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-integration-management/) |
| Scope | Defining and controlling what is and is not included | [Project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) |
| Schedule | Activities, sequence, durations and the schedule model | [Project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) |
| Cost | Estimating, budgeting and controlling costs | [Project cost management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-cost-management/) |
| Quality | Planning, assuring and controlling quality | [Quality management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/) |
| Resources | Identifying, acquiring and managing people, equipment and materials | [Project resources](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-resources/) |
| Communications | Planning and managing project information | [Communication management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-communication-management/) |
| Risk | Identifying, analysing and responding to uncertainty | [Risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) |
| Procurement | Buying goods and services from outside the project team | [Procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) |
| Stakeholders | Identifying and engaging the people affected by the project | [Stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) |
Integration is the odd one out: it is less a subject than the job of holding the others together. When you change the scope, integration is what makes sure the schedule, budget, risks and communications change with it.

### All 49 processes: the process group and knowledge area matrix
This matrix shows the 49 processes from the PMBOK Guide sixth edition (2017), which PMI also publishes in *Process Groups: A Practice Guide* (2022). Read across a row to see a knowledge area's processes in order; read down a column to see everything in one process group.
| Knowledge area | Initiating | Planning | Executing | Monitoring and controlling | Closing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Integration | Develop Project Charter | Develop Project Management Plan | Direct and Manage Project Work; Manage Project Knowledge | Monitor and Control Project Work; Perform Integrated Change Control | Close Project or Phase |
| Scope |  | Plan Scope Management; Collect Requirements; Define Scope; Create WBS |  | Validate Scope; Control Scope |  |
| Schedule |  | Plan Schedule Management; Define Activities; Sequence Activities; Estimate Activity Durations; Develop Schedule |  | Control Schedule |  |
| Cost |  | Plan Cost Management; Estimate Costs; Determine Budget |  | Control Costs |  |
| Quality |  | Plan Quality Management | Manage Quality | Control Quality |  |
| Resources |  | Plan Resource Management; Estimate Activity Resources | Acquire Resources; Develop Team; Manage Team | Control Resources |  |
| Communications |  | Plan Communications Management | Manage Communications | Monitor Communications |  |
| Risk |  | Plan Risk Management; Identify Risks; Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis; Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis; Plan Risk Responses | Implement Risk Responses | Monitor Risks |  |
| Procurement |  | Plan Procurement Management | Conduct Procurements | Control Procurements |  |
| Stakeholders | Identify Stakeholders | Plan Stakeholder Engagement | Manage Stakeholder Engagement | Monitor Stakeholder Engagement |  |

#### How many processes are in each group?
| Process group | Number of processes | Share of the 49 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiating | 2 | 4% |
| Planning | 24 | 49% |
| Executing | 10 | 20% |
| Monitoring and controlling | 12 | 24% |
| Closing | 1 | 2% |
Planning holds almost half of the processes. That does not mean planning should take half the project's time: on most projects execution takes far longer. It reflects the fact that each knowledge area needs its own planning thinking, even if much of it can be done in a single workshop.
Three patterns make the matrix easier to remember. Every knowledge area starts with a **Plan ... Management** process. Most have one **control or monitor** process. And only integration has a closing process, because closing the project or phase happens once, for everything.
Tip
If you are studying for the [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) or CAPM, learn the logic of the matrix rather than memorising every input and output. Current PMI exams are based on exam content outlines that draw on several sources, not on a single edition of the PMBOK Guide.

### Inputs, tools and techniques, and outputs (ITTOs)
In the classic model, each process is described by its **ITTOs**: the inputs it needs, the tools and techniques used to carry it out, and the outputs it produces. Outputs from one process become inputs to others, which is what links the 49 processes into a system.
| Element | Example: Develop Project Charter |
| --- | --- |
| Inputs | Business documents (business case, benefits management plan), agreements, organisational policies and templates |
| Tools and techniques | Expert judgement, data gathering such as interviews and brainstorming, meetings, conflict management and facilitation |
| Outputs | Project charter, assumption log |
The charter then becomes an input to Develop Project Management Plan, Identify Stakeholders and several planning processes. If the charter is weak, every process downstream inherits the problem, which is why experienced project managers spend time getting it right.
Treat ITTOs as a checklist of what good practice looks like, not as paperwork you must produce. A small internal project might combine the charter and the plan into a single page; the thinking still happens even if the documents are lighter.

### How PMI's processes have changed: PMBOK 6, 7 and 8
If you have seen different numbers of processes in different places, it is because PMI's standard has changed shape twice since 2017.
| Edition | Published | How processes are treated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PMBOK Guide 6th edition | 2017 | 49 processes in 5 process groups and 10 knowledge areas, each described with ITTOs |
| PMBOK Guide 7th edition | 2021 | Replaced processes with 12 principles and 8 performance domains; the 49 processes moved to *Process Groups: A Practice Guide* (November 2022) for predictive projects |
| PMBOK Guide 8th edition | November 2025 | Six principles, seven performance domains and 40 processes, presented as non-prescriptive guidance within five focus areas |
According to PMI and published summaries, the eighth edition's seven performance domains are **governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources and risk**, and its five **focus areas** are initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing, the same names as the old process groups. In effect, the domains have taken over the role of the knowledge areas and the focus areas the role of the process groups.
Published summaries list processes such as these for some of the domains (names may differ slightly from the guide itself):
| Performance domain | Example processes in PMBOK 8 |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | Plan Scope Management, Elicit and Analyze Requirements, Define Scope, Develop Scope Structure, Validate Scope, Monitor and Control Scope |
| Finance | Plan Financial Management, Estimate Costs, Develop Budget, Monitor and Control Finances |
| Risk | Plan Risk Management, Identify Risks, Perform Risk Analysis, Plan Risk Responses, Implement Risk Responses, Monitor Risks |
| Resources | Plan Resource Management, Estimate Resources, Acquire Resources, Lead the Team, Monitor and Control Resources |
The practical message is the same in every edition: these are processes you **select and tailor**, not a sequence you must follow in full. The classic 49-process matrix above remains the best-known reference, which is why we use it in this guide. For more on the editions, see our [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) overview.

### Worked example: one project through the five process groups
Here is how the processes play out on a typical mid-sized project: a company moving 120 staff to a new office within six months, with a budget of £450,000. The project has three phases (planning and fit-out design, fit-out works, move and settle in), and each phase uses all five process groups. The table summarises the project as a whole.
| Process group | What the project manager does | Main outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiating | Confirms the business case with the operations director (sponsor), agrees objectives (move by 30 June, no more than one day of lost working time) and identifies stakeholders: staff, IT, facilities, landlord, fit-out contractor | Signed charter, stakeholder register |
| Planning | Breaks the work into a WBS (fit-out, IT and telecoms, furniture, move logistics, communications), builds the schedule and critical path, estimates costs, plans procurement for the fit-out and removals, and runs a risk workshop | Project plan, schedule, £450,000 budget with £30,000 contingency, risk register, procurement plan, communication plan |
| Executing | Tenders and appoints the contractor and removals firm, holds weekly site meetings, runs staff briefings, orders IT equipment, implements risk responses such as booking a backup removals date | Contracts, fit-out progress, issue log, change requests |
| Monitoring and controlling | Tracks progress against the schedule and spend against the budget each fortnight, reviews risks, assesses a change request for extra meeting rooms (£18,000, approved from contingency), and forecasts the final cost and date | Status reports, approved and rejected changes, updated forecasts |
| Closing | Confirms that the fit-out snags are cleared, closes the contracts, releases the team, runs a lessons-learned session and hands the building over to facilities | Acceptance certificate, final report, lessons learned |
Notice how the groups overlap. The removals firm is procured (executing) while the detailed move plan is still being written (planning). The extra meeting rooms send the project back through planning (update the scope, schedule and budget) after change control approves them. And monitoring starts in week one, when the first schedule milestone is checked.
The same project in knowledge-area terms: integration is the charter, plan and change control; scope is the WBS; schedule and cost are the programme and budget; quality is the snagging standard; resources are the internal move team; communications is the staff briefing plan; risk is the register; procurement is the two contracts; and stakeholders covers staff, the landlord and the IT department.

### How to tailor project management processes
PMI's guidance has always said that not every process is needed on every project, and that the project manager and team decide which processes are appropriate and how rigorously to apply them. That decision is called **tailoring**. The table shows a typical starting point at three scales; adjust it for your context.
| Process area | Small project (weeks, low risk) | Medium project (months) | Large or regulated project |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initiating | One-page brief agreed by email | Signed charter | Business case, charter and formal gate approval |
| Scope | Bullet list of deliverables and exclusions | Scope statement and WBS | Requirements specification, WBS and WBS dictionary |
| Schedule | Task list with dates | Gantt chart with dependencies | Integrated schedule with critical path and baseline |
| Cost | Budget line | Estimate and budget by work package | Cost baseline with earned value |
| Risk | Top five risks in the status update | Risk register reviewed fortnightly | Risk management plan, quantitative analysis, contingency reserves |
| Change control | Sponsor agrees changes by email | Change log and request form | Change control board |
| Communications | Weekly update | Communication plan and status reports | Communication plan, dashboards and governance reporting |
| Closing | Short wrap-up note | Closure report and lessons learned | Formal acceptance, audit and benefits handover |

#### Step by step: build the process set for your project
1. **Assess the project.** Note its size, duration, budget, risk, complexity, regulatory requirements, number of suppliers and how stable the requirements are.
2. **Check what is mandatory.** Your organisation's governance, PMO standards, contracts or regulators may require certain processes and documents. These are not optional.
3. **Walk through the five process groups.** For each, decide which processes you need and how formally. Use the matrix above as a checklist so nothing is forgotten by accident.
4. **Decide the documents.** For each chosen process, decide whether it needs a separate document, a section in the plan, or just a conversation and a note in the log.
5. **Set the control rhythm.** Agree how often you will report, review risks and forecast, and what thresholds trigger escalation.
6. **Record the decisions.** Write the tailoring choices into the project management plan so the team and sponsor know what to expect.
7. **Review at each phase gate.** Add rigour if risks grow; remove processes that are not adding value.
The aim is enough process to keep control and keep stakeholders informed, and no more. Too little and problems surface late; too much and the team spends its time feeding the method instead of delivering.

### Processes in Agile and PRINCE2
The five process groups are method-neutral, so they map onto other ways of working.

#### PRINCE2 processes
[PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) has its own seven processes, which are the same in PRINCE2 7 (2023). They are built around management stages and the project board rather than knowledge areas.
| PRINCE2 process | Closest PMI process groups |
| --- | --- |
| Starting up a project | Initiating (pre-project checks and project brief) |
| Directing a project | Runs throughout: the project board's decisions and authorisations |
| Initiating a project | Initiating and planning (project initiation documentation) |
| Controlling a stage | Executing and monitoring and controlling |
| Managing product delivery | Executing (team managers deliver work packages) |
| Managing a stage boundary | Planning and monitoring and controlling (stage plan, end-stage report) |
| Closing a project | Closing |

#### Agile projects
Agile teams use the same management activities in a shorter loop. Product vision and initial backlog creation play the role of initiating; release and sprint planning are planning; the sprint itself is executing; daily scrums, reviews and burn-down charts are monitoring and controlling; and the retrospective and release are a form of closing, repeated every iteration. The difference is that planning happens just in time and change is expected rather than controlled through a formal board.

### Common mistakes with project management processes
- **Treating process groups as phases.** Planning does not stop when execution starts, and monitoring is not a final step.
- **Applying all 49 processes to a small project.** The result is documents nobody reads. Tailor first.
- **Skipping initiating.** Without a charter and named sponsor, the project has no clear authority, and scope disputes start early.
- **Planning once and never again.** The plan should be updated as you learn; an out-of-date plan is worse than none because people trust it.
- **Weak change control.** Accepting changes informally is the main route to scope creep.
- **Monitoring without controlling.** Reporting a variance is not enough; someone has to decide what to do about it.
- **Closing badly.** Unclosed contracts, unrecorded lessons and a team that drifts away cost the organisation more than a short closure meeting.
- **Confusing documents with management.** A perfect risk register does not reduce risk; acting on it does.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the five project management process groups?**
Initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing. They describe the types of management activity used in every project and every phase.

**Q: What are the 49 project management processes?**
The 49 processes defined in the PMBOK Guide sixth edition and PMI's Process Groups: A Practice Guide, arranged in five process groups and ten knowledge areas. The full matrix is shown above.

**Q: What are the ten knowledge areas of project management?**
Integration, scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risk, procurement and stakeholders.

**Q: What is the difference between a process group and a knowledge area?**
A process group describes the type of activity, such as planning or controlling; a knowledge area describes the subject, such as cost or risk. Every process belongs to one of each.

**Q: Which process group has the most processes?**
Planning, with 24 of the 49 processes in the classic model, followed by monitoring and controlling with 12.

**Q: Are the project management process groups sequential?**
No. They overlap and repeat. Planning continues during execution, and monitoring and controlling runs throughout the project.

**Q: Are process groups the same as project phases?**
No. Phases divide the project life cycle over time, such as design and build. All five process groups are used within each phase.

**Q: Does the PMBOK Guide still use process groups?**
The seventh edition dropped them in favour of principles and performance domains and moved the 49 processes to a separate practice guide. The eighth edition, published in November 2025, brings back 40 processes within five focus areas with the same names as the process groups.

**Q: How many processes are in the PMBOK Guide 8th edition?**
According to PMI and published summaries, 40 processes, presented as non-prescriptive guidance alongside six principles and seven performance domains.

**Q: What are ITTOs in project management?**
Inputs, tools and techniques, and outputs: the way the classic PMBOK model describes each process. They show what a process needs, how it is done and what it produces.

**Q: What does tailoring project management processes mean?**
Choosing which processes to use and how formally to apply them, based on the project's size, risk, complexity and any mandatory requirements.

**Q: What is the most important project management process group?**
None works alone, but many practitioners see planning and monitoring and controlling as the groups that most often decide success, because they set the baseline and catch problems early.

**Q: Do Agile projects use the project management process groups?**
Yes, in a shorter, repeating loop: backlog creation, sprint planning, the sprint, reviews and retrospectives cover the same activities each iteration.

**Q: What are the seven PRINCE2 processes?**
Starting up a project, directing a project, initiating a project, controlling a stage, managing product delivery, managing a stage boundary and closing a project.
