# Project Management Skills: Hard, Soft and How to Build Them

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project management skills explained: the hard and soft skills PMs need, proficiency levels, a self-assessment, a 90-day plan and CV examples.


## Project Management Skills: Hard, Soft and How to Build Them
Project management skills are the technical, interpersonal and business abilities you need to plan work, lead people and deliver a project's intended outcome. This guide lists the hard and soft skills that matter most, shows what each looks like at beginner, practitioner and expert level, and walks you through a scored self-assessment, a 90-day development plan and how to prove your skills to employers.
- Published 3 October 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project management skills fall into three groups: hard (technical) skills, soft (interpersonal) skills and business acumen.
- PMI's Talent Triangle groups the same ideas as Ways of Working, Power Skills and Business Acumen.
- Rate yourself against clear proficiency levels, not a vague 1–5 gut feeling, and weight each skill by how much your role needs it.
- Close one or two gaps at a time with real practice, feedback and structured learning over about 90 days.
- Employers believe evidence, not adjectives: describe outcomes, numbers and the methods and tools you used.

### What are project management skills?
**Project management skills** are the abilities a person needs to start, plan, run and close a project successfully. They combine **hard skills**, such as scoping, scheduling, budgeting and risk management; **soft skills**, such as communication, leadership and negotiation; and **business acumen**, the ability to connect project work to an organisation's goals, money and strategy.
The three groups depend on each other. Hard skills let you build a credible plan. Soft skills get that plan delivered through people who often do not report to you. Business acumen makes sure the plan is worth delivering at all. A project manager with a perfect Gantt chart but poor stakeholder relationships struggles just as much as a charismatic one who cannot estimate.
It also helps to separate three related words:
- **Skill**: something you can do and improve with practice, such as building a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/).
- **Competency**: a skill plus the knowledge and behaviour to apply it reliably at work, usually described in a framework with levels.
- **Trait**: a personal tendency, such as curiosity or calm under pressure. Traits help, but you are hired and promoted on skills you can demonstrate.
If you are new to the discipline, start with what project management is and the [project manager's roles and responsibilities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-roles-and-responsibilities/), then come back to this guide to plan how you build the skills behind them.

### Project management skills list at a glance
The table summarises the core skills covered in this guide, what each looks like in practice and the point in a project where it matters most.
| Skill | Type | What it looks like in practice | Matters most during |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scope and requirements | Hard | Agreeing what is in and out, and writing testable acceptance criteria | Initiation and planning |
| Planning and scheduling | Hard | Breaking work down, sequencing it and finding the critical path | Planning, then every update |
| Budgeting and cost control | Hard | Estimating costs, setting a baseline and tracking variance | Planning and execution |
| Risk management | Hard | Running risk workshops, keeping a live risk register and acting early | Throughout |
| Quality management | Hard | Defining standards and checking deliverables against them | Execution and closure |
| Resource management | Hard | Matching people and capacity to work without overloading anyone | Planning and execution |
| Reporting and data | Hard | Clear status reports, honest RAG ratings and useful metrics | Execution |
| Methods and tools | Hard | Choosing predictive, Agile or hybrid ways of working and using software well | Throughout |
| Communication | Soft | The right message, to the right people, in the right format and frequency | Throughout |
| Leadership and influence | Soft | Setting direction and motivating people without formal authority | Throughout |
| Stakeholder management | Soft | Identifying, analysing and engaging everyone affected by the project | Initiation onwards |
| Negotiation and conflict resolution | Soft | Trading scope, time and cost; resolving disagreements constructively | Planning and execution |
| Problem solving and decision making | Soft | Framing issues, weighing options and committing on incomplete data | Execution |
| Emotional intelligence | Soft | Reading the room and managing your own reactions under pressure | Throughout |
| Organisation and time management | Soft | Keeping many moving parts under control, including your own diary | Throughout |
| Business acumen | Business | Understanding the business case, benefits and commercial context | Initiation and closure |

### Hard skills: the technical toolkit
Hard skills are the teachable, measurable techniques of project management. They are the easiest to learn from courses and books, and the easiest to test in an exam such as the [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) or CAPM.

#### Scope and requirements management
Scope management means agreeing exactly what the project will deliver and what it will not, then controlling changes to that agreement. In practice you facilitate requirements sessions, write a scope statement, build a work breakdown structure and route every new request through change control.

#### Planning and scheduling
Scheduling turns scope into a timeline. You break deliverables into activities, estimate durations, add dependencies and calculate which chain of work sets the end date. The [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) is the core technique; [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) covers the wider process. For example, on a website relaunch you might find that content sign-off, not development, sets the end date.

#### Budgeting and cost control
You estimate what the work will cost, set a cost baseline and track actual spend and forecasts against it. Strong project managers include contingency for known risks and can show whether the project is ahead of or behind plan in money terms. Start with [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/) if this is new to you.

#### Risk management
Risk management is the habit of looking ahead. You identify what could go wrong (and right), assess likelihood and impact, assign owners and plan responses before the risk turns into an issue.

#### Quality management
Quality means delivering what was agreed to the standard that was agreed. You define acceptance criteria early, plan reviews and tests, and make sure defects are fixed rather than hidden. See project quality management.

#### Resource and capacity management
You match people, skills and equipment to the work, spot overloads before they cause burnout or delay, and negotiate for scarce specialists.

#### Reporting, metrics and data literacy
Good reporting is short, honest and decision-focused. You choose a handful of measures that matter, show trends rather than snapshots, and flag problems early with a clear ask. The [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) guide shows a structure that works for most sponsors.

#### Methods and frameworks
You should understand when a predictive (waterfall) plan fits, when an iterative Agile approach fits better and how to combine them.

#### Project management software
Employers expect you to be fluent in at least one work management platform: building a plan with dependencies, setting up a board, running a workload view and producing a dashboard. Our [project management tools rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) compare the leading options, with Wrike ranked first for teams that need planning, resource management and reporting in one place.

### Soft skills: the people side of projects
Soft skills are how you get work done through other people. PMI now calls these **power skills**, which reflects how much they influence project outcomes. They improve mainly through practice and feedback.

#### Communication
Communication is the skill project managers use most. It covers writing clear updates, running meetings that end with decisions, presenting to executives and listening properly. The practical test is whether each audience gets what it needs: a sponsor wants risks and decisions, a team member wants priorities and blockers. [Project communication management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-communication-management/) explains how to plan it.

#### Leadership and influence
Most project managers lead people who report to someone else. Leadership therefore depends on influence: a clear purpose, consistency, fairness, recognising good work and protecting the team from unnecessary noise. On Agile teams this looks like [servant leadership](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/servant-leadership-in-scrum/), where you remove obstacles rather than direct every task.

#### Stakeholder management
You identify everyone affected by or able to affect the project, understand their interests and influence, and plan how to engage each group. Surprises usually come from stakeholders nobody mapped. Use a power/interest grid and a stakeholder register, as described in [project stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/), and a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) to make decision rights explicit.

#### Negotiation and conflict resolution
Projects run on trade-offs between scope, time, cost and quality. Negotiation means reaching agreements people keep: prepare options in advance, understand what the other party needs, and trade rather than concede, for example offering a phased release to keep a date when a sponsor adds scope. When disagreements arise, bring them into the open early, separate the person from the problem and escalate without blame.

#### Problem solving and decision making
You frame the real problem (not just the symptom), gather enough information, compare options and commit. Good decision makers also record why they chose an option, so the team can learn from it later.

#### Emotional intelligence
Emotional intelligence means noticing your own reactions and other people's, and responding rather than reacting. It shows when you deliver bad news calmly or notice that a quiet team member is overloaded.

#### Organisation and time management
You keep track of many actions, dates, documents and conversations without dropping any, and you protect time for the work that matters. Simple systems, such as a single action log and a weekly planning slot, outperform heroic memory.
Finally, **adaptability**: plans change, and good project managers re-plan without drama and keep the team focused on the outcome.

### Business acumen and strategic skills
Business acumen is what separates a task coordinator from a project manager senior leaders trust. It means understanding why the project exists, how it creates value and how it fits the organisation's strategy.
- **Business case thinking**: you can explain the costs, benefits and options behind the project, and know when the case no longer holds.
- **Benefits focus**: you track whether the project's outputs are producing the expected outcomes, not just whether tasks are done.
- **Commercial awareness**: you understand contracts, suppliers and margins, especially in agencies, construction and professional services.
- **Governance**: you know who decides what and when to escalate.
- **Domain knowledge**: you understand enough of the industry and the work (software, construction, healthcare and so on) to judge risks and estimates credibly.
You build business acumen by asking sponsors why decisions are made, reading the business case of every project you join, and spending time with finance and commercial colleagues.

### How the PMI Talent Triangle groups these skills
The Project Management Institute (PMI) organises the skills of project professionals into the **PMI Talent Triangle**, which has three areas. PMI describes them as follows (checked on pmi.org, October 2026):
| Talent Triangle area | PMI's description (summarised) | Skills from this guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ways of Working | Mastering different ways of getting work done, such as predictive, Agile and design thinking approaches, and choosing the right one for each situation | Scope, scheduling, budgeting, risk, quality, resources, methods and tools |
| Power Skills | Interpersonal skills such as collaborative leadership, communication, an innovative mindset, for-purpose orientation and empathy | Communication, leadership, stakeholder management, negotiation, conflict resolution, emotional intelligence |
| Business Acumen | Understanding the influences on the organisation and industry, domain knowledge and how projects align with strategy | Business case, benefits, commercial awareness, governance, decision making |
The Talent Triangle matters in practice because PMI uses it to classify the education professional development units (PDUs) that certification holders must earn to renew. For the PMP, PMI requires 60 PDUs every three years, with education PDUs spread across all three areas. Our guide to [PDUs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pdu-professional-development-units/) gives the exact minimums for each certification.

### Skills for Agile and hybrid projects
Agile teams still need the skills above, but some become more important and others change shape.
- **Facilitation**: running planning, review and retrospective sessions where the team, not the manager, does the thinking.
- **Backlog and value thinking**: helping the team and product owner order work by value and risk rather than by who shouts loudest.
- **Empirical planning**: using velocity or throughput data to forecast, and updating forecasts as evidence arrives.
- **Hybrid integration**: connecting iterative delivery with fixed milestones, budgets and governance that the wider organisation still needs.
The [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) guide explains how the role differs from a traditional project manager in more detail.

### AI and digital skills for project managers
AI features now appear in most project management platforms, from drafting status updates to summarising comment threads. The useful skills are practical:
- **Writing clear prompts and briefs**, giving the tool context, constraints and the format you want.
- **Checking outputs**: treating AI summaries and estimates as drafts that need your judgement, especially for numbers, dates and commitments.
- **Data hygiene**: AI and dashboards are only as good as the data underneath, so consistent statuses, fields and owners matter more than ever.
- **Governance and confidentiality**: knowing your organisation's rules on what project data may be shared with AI tools.
- **Automation design**: spotting repetitive steps, such as routing requests, that rules or AI can take over.
Our overview of [AI project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/ai-project-management-tools/) shows what current tools can and cannot do. In our view, the biggest benefit is freeing time for the human work: conversations, decisions and leadership.

### Proficiency levels: what good looks like
A vague self-rating of "3 out of 5" is not much use. Describing what each level looks like makes self-assessment more honest and gives you a clear next step. The levels below are our own practical descriptions, not an official standard.
| Skill | Beginner | Practitioner | Expert |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduling | Builds a task list with dates | Builds a dependency-linked schedule, finds the critical path and keeps it updated | Schedules multi-team programmes, models scenarios and coaches others |
| Budgeting | Tracks spend against a given budget | Builds a cost estimate with contingency and reports variance and forecasts | Owns budgets with commercial risk, uses earned value and negotiates funding |
| Risk management | Logs risks when asked | Runs regular risk reviews with owners and responses | Builds risk culture; quantifies key risks and links them to contingency |
| Communication | Sends updates on time | Tailors messages to each audience and runs decision-focused meetings | Handles difficult messages at executive level and shapes the narrative |
| Stakeholder management | Knows the main stakeholders | Maps stakeholders and runs an engagement plan | Anticipates political shifts and builds coalitions for change |
| Leadership | Organises tasks for the team | Motivates a team without formal authority and handles poor performance tactfully | Leads leaders across a programme and develops other project managers |
| Tools | Updates tasks and boards | Sets up projects, views, dashboards and simple automations | Designs workspace structures, templates and reporting for many teams |

### Skills by career stage
The mix of skills you need shifts as you progress. Early roles reward organisation and reliability; senior roles reward judgement, influence and business acumen.
| Role | Skills that matter most | Typical evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project coordinator | Organisation, scheduling support, documentation, tools, clear writing | Accurate plans and logs; well-run meetings and minutes |
| Project manager | Planning, risk, budgeting, communication, stakeholder management, negotiation | Projects delivered against agreed scope, time and cost |
| Senior project manager | Leadership, complex stakeholder management, commercial awareness, coaching | Large or high-risk projects recovered or delivered; people developed |
| Programme or portfolio manager | Strategy, governance, benefits, prioritisation, executive influence | Benefits realised across several projects; sound investment decisions |
Specialist routes add their own requirements. A [technical project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/technical-project-manager/), for example, needs enough engineering knowledge to discuss architecture, estimates and technical debt credibly with developers.

### How to assess your project management skills
A short, structured self-assessment tells you where to focus. It takes about an hour.
1. **List the skills your role needs.** Use the table at the top of this guide, plus any skills named in your job description or the role you want next.
2. **Weight each skill by importance** from 1 (nice to have) to 3 (critical for this role).
3. **Rate your current level** from 1 to 4 (1 = beginner, 2 = developing, 3 = practitioner, 4 = expert) using the proficiency descriptions above. Be strict: rate what you have actually done, not what you understand in theory.
4. **Set a target level** for each skill, based on your role or next role.
5. **Calculate a priority score**: (target − current) × importance. The highest scores are your development priorities.
6. **Check your view with others.** Ask a manager, sponsor or peer to rate you on the same scale, then compare.
7. **Choose no more than two priorities** for the next 90 days.

#### Worked example: a newly promoted project manager
Priya has moved from project coordinator to project manager on a 9-month system implementation. Her self-assessment looks like this:
| Skill | Importance (1–3) | Current (1–4) | Target (1–4) | Priority score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduling | 3 | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| Budgeting | 3 | 1 | 3 | 6 |
| Risk management | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| Stakeholder management | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| Negotiation | 2 | 1 | 3 | 4 |
| Communication | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 |
| Tools | 2 | 3 | 3 | 0 |
Budgeting (6) and negotiation (4) come out on top, even though Priya felt least comfortable with stakeholder management. That is the value of weighting: her new project has a fixed budget and a demanding supplier, so those gaps carry the most risk. She keeps risk and stakeholder management on her list for the following quarter.
To run the same exercise for a whole team, use our free [skills matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/), which rates each person against each skill and calculates team averages.

### How to improve your project management skills: a 90-day plan
Skills improve fastest through practice, feedback and reflection, supported by structured learning. Here is how Priya might turn her two priorities into a 90-day plan.

#### Days 1–30: learn the basics and find the practice
- Take a short course or read a solid guide on each priority skill (for Priya, [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/) and negotiation).
- Agree with your manager one real opportunity to practise each skill, such as owning the monthly budget forecast.
- Find a mentor or experienced colleague who is strong in the skill and book three short sessions.

#### Days 31–60: practise on real work
- Do the work yourself, even if it is slower at first: build the forecast, prepare the negotiation options.
- Ask for specific feedback straight after each attempt: one thing to keep doing, one thing to change.
- Keep a simple learning log: what you tried, what happened, what you will do differently.

#### Days 61–90: consolidate and prove it
- Repeat the skill without support and compare the result with your first attempt.
- Capture the evidence: numbers, outcomes and feedback you can use in reviews and on your CV.
- Re-rate yourself and pick the next one or two priorities.
Structured learning speeds things up. A recognised [project management certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) gives you a shared vocabulary and fills gaps you did not know you had, while on-the-job practice turns that knowledge into skill. A [training plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) helps you schedule both.
Tip
Volunteer for the parts of projects other people avoid: the risk workshop, the budget reforecast, the difficult supplier call. They are the fastest way to build the skills employers value most.

### Transferable skills for career changers
Many people move into project management from other roles, and they usually have more relevant skills than they think. The trick is translating them into project language.
| Previous role | Project management skill you already use | How to describe it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Teacher | Planning, stakeholder management, communication | Planned and delivered a year-long curriculum for 120 students, coordinating with parents, colleagues and leadership |
| Events coordinator | Scheduling, budgeting, supplier management, risk | Delivered 15 events a year against fixed budgets and dates, managing 20+ suppliers and contingency plans |
| Marketing specialist | Campaign planning, deadlines, approvals, reporting | Ran multi-channel campaigns from brief to launch, managing reviews and reporting results to leadership |
Our step-by-step guide on [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/) covers how to turn these skills into your first project role.

### How to show project management skills on a CV and in interviews
Hiring managers see the same list of adjectives on every CV. What stands out is evidence: a specific outcome, a number and the method or tool you used.
| Weak | Strong |
| --- | --- |
| Excellent communication skills | Introduced a weekly one-page status report that cut steering meeting time from 90 to 45 minutes |
| Responsible for project budgets | Managed a £400k budget; forecast monthly and delivered 3% under budget after renegotiating two supplier contracts |
| Good at managing risk | Ran fortnightly risk reviews that identified a data-migration risk early; the mitigation saved an estimated two weeks |
| Experienced with project management tools | Set up Gantt plans, workload views and dashboards for 6 concurrent projects in Wrike |
The numbers above are illustrations; use your own real figures. Group skills on your CV into **methods** (for example Agile, PRINCE2, critical path), **tools** and **leadership skills**, and prove each group in your experience section.

#### Interview stories to prepare
Interviewers test soft skills with behavioural questions, so prepare short stories in the **STAR** format (situation, task, action, result) for each of these:
- A project that went off track and how you recovered it
- A disagreement with a stakeholder or sponsor
- A time you had to negotiate scope, time or budget
- A risk you spotted early and acted on
- A team member who was struggling or underperforming
- A decision you made with incomplete information
Keep each story to about two minutes, and finish with the result and what you learned. Honest lessons are more convincing than a flawless record.

### Common mistakes when building project management skills
- **Collecting certificates without practice.** A certification shows knowledge; employers also want proof you have applied it.
- **Focusing only on hard skills.** Tools and techniques are easier to learn, but most project problems are people problems.
- **Trying to fix everything at once.** Pick two priorities per quarter and finish them.
- **Rating yourself on understanding, not doing.** Knowing what earned value is does not make you practised at it.
- **Learning a tool instead of a method.** Software changes; the underlying skills of planning, prioritising and reporting transfer to any platform.
- **Ignoring business acumen.** If you cannot explain why the project matters in money or strategic terms, it is hard to be trusted with bigger ones.

### Next steps
Pick your two priority skills, book the first practice opportunity and set a date in 90 days to re-rate yourself. If you are building the skills for a career move, map your route with our guide on [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/), and compare credentials in our guide to [project management certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/).
To understand what the job involves day to day, read [project manager roles and responsibilities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-roles-and-responsibilities/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the most important project management skills?**
Communication, planning and scheduling, risk management, stakeholder management and leadership are consistently the most valuable, supported by budgeting and negotiation. The exact mix depends on the type and size of project you run.

**Q: Is project management a hard skill or a soft skill?**
Both. Project management combines hard skills, such as scheduling, budgeting and risk analysis, with soft skills, such as communication, leadership and negotiation. Most project managers find the soft skills take longer to master.

**Q: How can I improve my project management skills quickly?**
Pick one or two skills that matter most in your current role, find a real opportunity to practise them, ask for specific feedback after each attempt and add a short course or guide. Re-rate yourself after about 90 days.

**Q: Can I learn project management skills without experience?**
Yes. Start by managing small projects at work or in volunteering, learn the basics through a course or an entry-level certification such as the CAPM, and translate the transferable skills you already have into project language.

**Q: How do I list project management skills on my CV?**
Group them into methods, tools and leadership skills, then prove each one in your experience section with a specific outcome and number, such as a budget managed, a deadline met or time saved.

**Q: What is the PMI Talent Triangle?**
It is PMI's framework for the skills project professionals need, grouped into Ways of Working, Power Skills and Business Acumen. PMI also uses it to classify education PDUs for certification renewal.

**Q: Do project managers need technical knowledge of the work?**
They need enough domain knowledge to understand the work, judge estimates and spot risks. Some roles, such as technical or IT project manager, need much deeper subject knowledge.

**Q: What AI skills do project managers need?**
Mainly practical ones: writing clear prompts, checking AI outputs before relying on them, keeping project data clean, following data-sharing rules and spotting repetitive work that automation can handle.

**Q: Which tools should I learn to build project management skills?**
Learn a full work management platform that covers Gantt charts, boards, workload and dashboards, such as Wrike, plus whatever your target employers use. See our project management tools rankings for the options.

**Q: How long does it take to build project management skills?**
You can learn the basics in weeks, but becoming a confident practitioner usually takes a few years of running real projects. Focusing on one or two skills per quarter makes steady, visible progress.

# Project Management Software Features: 2026 Checklist

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software-features/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project management software features explained: the essential and advanced features, what good looks like, which plans have them and a scoring checklist.


## Project Management Software Features: 2026 Checklist
The key project management software features are task management, multiple views, scheduling with dependencies, collaboration, dashboards and reporting, with resource management, automation, integrations and AI on top. Which ones you actually need depends on the problems you are trying to solve, the size of your team and how many projects you run at once. This guide explains each feature group, what a good version looks like, which plan tier usually unlocks it, and how to score tools against a checklist of your own.
- Published 4 October 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Separate core features every team needs (tasks, views, collaboration, basic reporting) from organisation-level features (resources, portfolios, advanced reporting, governance) that only some teams need.
- The same feature can be shallow or deep: a timeline is not the same as a Gantt chart with dependencies, a critical path and baselines.
- Check the plan, not just the product. Gantt charts, time tracking, workload, portfolios and single sign-on usually sit on paid or higher-tier plans.
- Turn problems into weighted requirements, score shortlisted tools 0 to 3, and confirm the must-haves in a trial with a real project.
- Wrike ranks first in our review because it combines planning, resource, portfolio, proofing and reporting features in one platform; lighter tools can be a better match for simpler needs.

### What are project management software features?
Project management software features are the capabilities a tool provides to plan, organise, track and report on project work. They range from core features such as tasks, views and comments, through scheduling and reporting, to organisation-level features such as resource management, portfolio roll-ups, automation and security controls. Good features solve a specific problem your team has.
It helps to think in three tiers. Each builds on the one below. Tier 1 features are usually on free plans, tier 2 on entry or mid-priced paid plans, and tier 3 on upper or enterprise plans.
| Tier | Features | Problem it solves | Typical buyer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Core work | Tasks, subtasks, owners, due dates, list and board views, comments, files, mobile apps | "Who is doing what, by when?" | Any team, including freelancers and small teams |
| 2. Team coordination | Gantt charts and dependencies, dashboards, templates, automation, request forms, time tracking, guest access, integrations | "Are we on track, and what happens if something slips?" | Teams of 5 to 50 running several projects |
| 3. Organisation level | Workload and capacity planning, portfolios, budgets, advanced reporting and BI, approvals at scale, single sign-on, audit logs, admin controls | "Do we have the people and money for all of this, and can leaders see it?" | PMOs, agencies, departments and enterprises |
If you are new to the category, start with our guide to [what project management software is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/), which explains the main types of tool. This page focuses on the features themselves: what each one does, what a good version looks like and how to test it.

### Planning and scheduling features
Planning features turn a list of work into a schedule people can follow. They are where the difference between a simple task tool and a project management platform shows most clearly.

#### Task management
Every tool has tasks. What separates them is the structure around each task: one accountable owner, start and due dates, priority, status, subtasks or checklists, attachments, and custom fields for the data your team needs (client, budget code, channel, risk level). Recurring tasks handle routine work such as monthly reports.
**What good looks like:** custom statuses per team, custom fields that can be reported on, bulk editing, and a clear hierarchy (for example space, folder, project, task, subtask) that does not get in the way.

#### Multiple views
Views let different people work with the same data in the way that suits them: a list for the person doing the work, a [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) for the team stand-up, a table for bulk updates, a calendar for deadlines and a Gantt chart or timeline for the project manager.

#### Gantt charts, dependencies and the critical path
A [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) shows tasks as bars against time. The feature becomes genuinely useful when it supports [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/), so that moving one task automatically moves the tasks that depend on it. Look for:
- All four dependency types (finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish, start-to-finish) with lead and lag time.
- Automatic rescheduling when a predecessor moves.
- The [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) highlighted, so you know which delays move the end date.
- Baselines, so you can compare the current plan with the approved [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).
- Milestones and drag-and-drop rescheduling.
Not every "timeline" is a scheduling engine. Our reviews note, for example, that Trello's Timeline view has no dependency links, critical path or baselines, and that Jira's timeline is not a classic Gantt chart with critical path and baselines. Both are excellent for what they are designed to do, just not for tightly sequenced plans. See our [Gantt chart software guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/) for a detailed comparison.

#### Milestones, templates and recurring work
Milestones mark key events such as approvals and go-live dates. Templates start each new project from a proven structure with tasks, durations, dependencies and roles in place. If you are still planning in a spreadsheet, our free [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) uses the same structure.
Tip
Test scheduling with your own plan, not the vendor's demo. Import 30 to 50 real tasks, link them, then push a critical task back by a week and see whether the end date moves the way you expect.

### Collaboration and communication features
Collaboration features keep conversations, files and decisions attached to the work rather than scattered across email and chat. The essentials are comments and @mentions on tasks, file attachments with version history, activity streams and configurable notifications.
Three collaboration features deserve a closer look because they vary a lot between tools:
- **Guest and client access.** Can clients or suppliers see or comment on specific projects, and are guests free or charged as users?
- **Proofing and approvals.** Reviewers comment on assets and record a formal approve or reject decision. Essential for creative teams.
- **Notification control.** Look for per-user settings, digests and a filterable inbox, and agree team habits early.
Collaboration works best when the tool becomes the single source of truth. If people keep discussing work in chat, the history in the tool will be incomplete, however good the feature is.

### Tracking, reporting and dashboards
Reporting features answer the weekly questions: are we on track, what is late, who is overloaded and are we within budget? There are four layers.
| Layer | What it gives you | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dashboards | Widgets for tasks by status, overdue work, progress and workload, updated live | Can each person build their own and share it? |
| Status reports | A summary of progress, risks and decisions for stakeholders | Can you schedule or automatically draft a [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/)? |
| Time and cost tracking | Logged time against estimates, timesheets, budgets and actual cost | Estimate vs actual by task? Timesheet approvals? |
| Advanced reporting and BI | Cross-portfolio analysis of financials, resources and trends | Is it built in, on a higher plan, or via export to Power BI or Tableau? |
Advanced analytics usually costs more: in Wrike, operational dashboards and reports come with paid plans, while advanced reporting and BI sit on the quote-based Pinnacle and Apex plans. If you need [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/), check whether the tool calculates it or whether you will export to a spreadsheet.
Time tracking is a must-have for anyone billing by the hour. Its plan tier varies: our reviews show it included from ClickUp's Unlimited plan, on monday.com's Pro plan and on Asana's Advanced plan.

### Resource, workload and portfolio features
These features move a tool from managing one project to managing many projects with shared people.
- **Workload views** show each person's assigned effort over time, so you can spot overload and rebalance work before deadlines slip. See [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) and [resource leveling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/).
- **Capacity planning** compares demand with available hours, often by role before named people are assigned. See [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/).
- **Portfolio management** rolls many projects up into one view of status, priority, budget and resource use, which is what leaders and a [project management office (PMO)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) need to decide what to start, stop or delay.
- **Budgets and financials** track planned versus actual cost and, in some tools, billable rates and margins.
These features nearly always sit on upper tiers. In our reviews, Asana's portfolios and workload are on Advanced, monday.com's portfolio and resource management are on Enterprise, ClickUp's portfolio-level workload management is on Business, and Wrike's advanced resource and capacity planning and budgeting are on Pinnacle.
Tip
A workload view is only as accurate as the estimates behind it. Without effort estimates it simply counts tasks.

### Automation and request intake features
Automation features remove repetitive coordination. Most tools use simple "when this happens, do that" rules: a trigger (status changes, form submitted, date reached), an optional condition and an action (assign, move, notify, create subtasks). Request forms are the front door: stakeholders submit structured requests that become tasks with the right fields already filled in.
| Trigger | Action | Problem solved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request form submitted with type = Design | Create task in the design project, assign to the design lead, set due date from form | Requests arriving by email with missing information |
| Status changes to In review | Assign the reviewer and notify them | Work sitting unnoticed between steps |
| Due date passes and status is not Done | Notify the owner and the project manager | Late work discovered only at the status meeting |
| Project created from client template | Add standard tasks, dependencies and roles | Inconsistent project set-up |
Check how many automation runs each plan includes. monday.com and Trello, for example, cap automation actions by plan, and ClickUp's Business plan lists 5,000 automations per month. To standardise intake before choosing software, try our free [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/).

### AI features in project management software
Almost every major tool now includes AI. The most common AI features in late 2026 are:
- Summaries of long comment threads, tasks and projects.
- Drafting and rewriting text, such as briefs, status updates and task descriptions.
- Creating automation rules, forms or project structures from a plain-language description.
- Assistants that answer questions about your work data, such as "What is late on the Q3 launch?"
- Configurable AI agents that triage requests, check for missing information, assign work or write reports.
Packaging varies more than for any other feature. Wrike includes AI Essentials (content creation and editing, comment summaries, natural-language form and rule creation) from its Team plan, and adds AI Elite (Copilot, AI dashboard widgets and AI agents) from Business with a monthly allowance of actions. In our top 10 comparison, ClickUp's and Microsoft Planner's most capable AI comes as a paid add-on, and Jira's Rovo AI is measured in credits by plan.
Treat AI as a time-saver for routine work, not a replacement for planning judgement, and test it on your own data. Our guide to [AI project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/ai-project-management-tools/) compares the options.

### Agile and software development features
Agile teams need a different feature set from plan-driven teams. The essentials are a product backlog, sprint planning, boards with work-in-progress limits, [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/) or other estimates, burndown and velocity charts, and integrations with code repositories and CI/CD tools.
Jira is the category leader for software teams in our review, with backlogs, sprints, configurable workflows and deep developer integrations, and a Free plan for up to 10 users. ClickUp also includes sprints, with sprint points and sprint reporting on its Business plan. General work management tools such as Wrike, monday.com and Asana support Agile boards and sprints at a lighter level, which suits mixed teams where marketing, product and engineering share one plan. Wrike Sync, an add-on, can keep Wrike aligned with Jira or GitHub in both directions. Our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) goes further.

### Integrations, administration and security features
These features rarely appear in demos, but they decide whether IT will approve the tool.
| Feature | Why it matters | What to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native integrations | Connect email, calendars, chat, file storage, CRM and development tools | Is the integration two-way? Which plan includes it? |
| Permissions and user types | Control who can see and edit what, including guests | Can you restrict a project to named people? Are view-only users free? |
| Single sign-on (SSO) and provisioning | Central login and automatic user set-up and removal | Which plan includes SAML SSO and SCIM? |
| Certifications and data controls | Evidence of security practice; data residency and encryption options | Which certifications apply to the product you will use? Can you control encryption keys? |
| Mobile and desktop apps | Updates and approvals on the move | Can people do their real daily tasks on mobile, not just read notifications? |
Enterprise identity controls are usually on the top tier. Our reviews show SAML single sign-on and SCIM on monday.com's Enterprise plan and Asana's Enterprise plan, and single sign-on on Wrike's higher tiers, where Wrike Lock is also available as an add-on that lets customers control their encryption keys. Ask each vendor for current certification reports as part of your procurement.

### Which features each type of team needs
The right feature set depends far more on the kind of work you do than on the size of the feature list. Use this table as a starting point for your must-haves.
| Team type | Must-have features | Nice to have | Tools that fit well |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Marketing and creative | Request forms, proofing and approvals, calendar and board views, templates | Workload view, AI drafting | Wrike, monday.com, Asana |
| Agencies and professional services | Time tracking, guest/client access, budgets, workload across clients | Portfolio view, approvals | Wrike, ClickUp, monday.com |
| PMOs and multi-project departments | Gantt with dependencies and baselines, portfolios, resource and capacity planning, dashboards | Advanced BI, SSO | Wrike, Smartsheet, Asana |
| Software and Agile teams | Backlog, sprints, boards, story points, developer integrations | Roadmaps, release planning | Jira, ClickUp |
| Construction and engineering | Gantt with critical path and baselines, milestones, document control, mobile | Cost tracking, EVM export | Wrike, Smartsheet |
| Small teams and start-ups | Tasks, boards, comments, mobile apps, low cost | Simple automation | Trello, ClickUp, Notion, Basecamp |
Microsoft 365 organisations should also look at [Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/), which is included in basic form with Microsoft 365.

#### Where key features start, by plan
Prices are per user per month billed annually, as checked on our review pages in October 2026. Confirm on each vendor's pricing page before you buy.
| Tool | Free plan covers | Gantt / timeline from | Upper-tier features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wrike | Basic task management, board and table views | Team ($10, 2 to 15 users), with shareable dashboards and AI Essentials | Business ($25): AI Elite and templatised workspaces; Pinnacle (quote): advanced resource planning, budgeting, BI |
| monday.com | Up to 2 seats | Standard ($12 per seat) | Pro ($19): time tracking, milestones, critical path; Enterprise: portfolios and resources |
| Asana | Personal plan, up to 2 users | Starter ($10.99) | Advanced ($24.99): portfolios, goals, workload, approvals and proofing, time tracking |
| ClickUp | Free Forever (Gantt as a trial) | Unlimited ($7) | Business ($12): advanced dashboards, sprint reporting, portfolio workload |
| Smartsheet | No free plan (30-day trial) | Every plan, from Pro ($9 per member) | Higher plans and add-ons: resource and workload planning |

Wrike ranks first in our review, with a score of 9.4 out of 10, because it brings the widest set of planning, resource, portfolio, proofing and reporting features together in one platform, a strong match for PMOs, agencies and marketing teams. It takes longer to set up than lighter tools, and its most advanced resource and BI features are on quote-based plans. monday.com (9.1) and Asana (9.0) are easier to roll out, and ClickUp (8.9) gives the most features for the money. See our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) for the full feature breakdown.

### How to build a feature checklist step by step
A feature checklist turns a long list of possibilities into a short list of requirements you can score.
1. **List the problems.** Write down what is going wrong today: missed deadlines, overloaded people, requests lost in email, no view across projects, time not billed.
2. **Translate each problem into features.** Missed deadlines might need dependencies and overdue alerts; overloaded people need a workload view with estimates.
3. **Prioritise with MoSCoW.** Mark each feature must-have, should-have, could-have or won't-need. Keep must-haves to roughly eight or fewer.
4. **Weight the features.** Give must-haves a weight of 3, should-haves 2 and could-haves 1.
5. **Define what "good" means.** For each must-have, write one sentence describing a pass, for example "Moving a task automatically moves its successors."
6. **Check the plan tier.** For each shortlisted tool, find the cheapest plan that includes every must-have and calculate the annual cost for your user count.
7. **Score 0 to 3 in a trial.** 0 = missing, 1 = present but weak, 2 = meets the need, 3 = clearly strong. Multiply by the weight and add up.
8. **Decide and record the reasons.** Any tool scoring 0 on a must-have is out, whatever its total.
The checklist is one part of a wider buying process that also covers IT requirements, vendor questions and rollout. Read our guide to [how to choose project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/).

### Worked example: scoring three tools (illustrative)
This is an illustrative example, not a review of real products. A 25-person marketing agency runs about 30 client projects at a time. Its problems are late deliveries, overloaded designers, client feedback lost in email and unbilled hours. It turns those into seven weighted requirements and scores three tools in a two-week trial.
| Requirement | Weight | Tool A | Tool B | Tool C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gantt with dependencies and baselines | 3 | 3 (9) | 2 (6) | 1 (3) |
| Workload view across all clients | 3 | 3 (9) | 2 (6) | 0 (0) |
| Proofing and client approvals | 3 | 3 (9) | 2 (6) | 2 (6) |
| Time tracking with timesheets | 3 | 2 (6) | 3 (9) | 1 (3) |
| Client request forms | 2 | 3 (6) | 2 (4) | 2 (4) |
| Dashboards for account directors | 2 | 2 (4) | 3 (6) | 2 (4) |
| Ease of use for occasional users | 1 | 2 (2) | 3 (3) | 3 (3) |
| Weighted total (max 51) |  | 45 | 40 | 23 |
Tool C is the easiest to use but scores 0 on a must-have (workload view), so it is out regardless of its total. Tools A and B both meet every must-have, so the agency compares cost next.

#### Check the cost of the plan that includes your must-haves
Headline prices can mislead, because the features you need often sit on a higher plan. Using published prices from our reviews (billed annually, checked October 2026) for 25 users:
| Scenario | Calculation | Annual cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asana Starter (timeline, but no portfolios or workload) | $10.99 x 25 x 12 | $3,297 |
| Asana Advanced (adds portfolios, workload, proofing, time tracking) | $24.99 x 25 x 12 | $7,497 |
| Wrike Team (Gantt and dashboards, but capped at 15 users) | Not available for 25 users | n/a |
| Wrike Business (5 to 200 users) | $25 x 25 x 12 | $7,500 |
In this example the cheapest headline plan does not meet the agency's must-haves, and the realistic cost more than doubles once workload and proofing are required. Compare tools at the plan you will actually need, including add-ons, then let the trial decide.
Tip
Do not award points for features nobody will use. A tool that scores 3 on twenty features you marked "won't need" is not better than one that scores 3 on your eight must-haves.

### How to test features in a free trial
Most vendors offer a free plan or a trial: Wrike's trial is 14 days with no credit card, and Smartsheet offers 30 days, according to our reviews. Run a real project with a test script, not a tour of the interface.
| Feature | Test | Pass if |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduling | Import a real plan of 30 to 50 tasks and link dependencies; delay a critical task by five days | Successors and the end date move correctly and the critical path is visible |
| Request intake | Build a form and submit five realistic requests | Each creates a complete, correctly routed task |
| Workload | Add estimates and assign work to three people across two projects | Overload is visible and can be fixed by dragging work |
| Proofing | Upload a draft asset and ask a colleague acting as client to review it | Comments sit on the asset and approval is recorded |
| Reporting | Build the dashboard your sponsor wants to see weekly | It answers their questions without exporting to a spreadsheet |
| AI | Summarise a long thread and ask the assistant what is at risk | The answer is accurate and saves time |
Log each test and result in our free [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/).

### Common mistakes when comparing features
- **Counting features instead of solving problems.**
- **Comparing products, not plans.** The feature you saw in the demo may only be on the enterprise tier.
- **Ignoring depth.** A timeline without dependencies and a workload view without estimates are not the same as their deeper equivalents.
- **Letting one power user decide.** The tool must work for occasional users and clients too, so include them in the trial.
- **Overlooking limits.** Automation runs, AI allowances, storage, guest rules and user caps (such as Wrike Team's 15-user limit or Trello Free's 10 collaborators) can change your plan choice.
- **Forgetting administration.** Every custom field, status and rule needs an owner.
See our [project management software comparisons](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/) for side-by-side feature tables of the leading tools.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the key features of project management software?**
Task management, multiple views (list, board, calendar, Gantt), scheduling with dependencies, collaboration, dashboards and reporting, integrations and mobile apps. Larger teams add time tracking, automation, workload, portfolios, proofing and AI.

**Q: What are the five most important project management software features?**
For most teams: task management with clear owners and dates, multiple views, collaboration on tasks, dashboards for progress, and integrations with the tools you already use. Add Gantt charts with dependencies if your projects are date-driven.

**Q: Which project management software has the most features?**
Wrike and ClickUp both score 10 out of 10 for feature depth in our review. Wrike ranks first overall for its combination of planning, resource, portfolio, proofing and reporting features; ClickUp offers the most features for the money.

**Q: Is a Gantt chart a must-have feature?**
Yes, if your projects have fixed dates and dependent tasks. Look for dependencies, automatic rescheduling, the critical path and baselines. See our [Gantt chart software guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/).

**Q: What is workload management in project management software?**
A view of how much work each person has across all projects over time, usually based on effort estimates, so you can spot overload and rebalance work before deadlines slip.

**Q: Is time tracking a must-have feature?**
It is a must-have for agencies, consultancies and any team that bills time or needs to compare estimates with actual effort. Check which plan includes it.

**Q: Are AI features in project management software worth paying for?**
They can save time on summaries, drafting and routine triage. Test them in a trial and check the usage limits on each plan.

**Q: Which project management software features matter for Agile teams?**
A backlog, sprint planning, boards with WIP limits, story points, burndown and velocity charts, and integrations with code repositories. Jira is the leading choice for software teams in our review.

**Q: Which project management software features matter for agencies?**
Time tracking and timesheets, guest and client access, proofing and approvals, budgets and a workload view across clients. See our guide to [agency project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/agency-project-management/).

**Q: Do free plans include the essential features?**
Free plans usually cover tasks, boards and basic collaboration, which is enough for individuals and small teams. Gantt charts, dashboards, time tracking, automation limits and admin controls typically need a paid plan, and some free plans cap users.

**Q: What security features should project management software have?**
Granular permissions, two-factor authentication, single sign-on and user provisioning for larger organisations, audit logs, encryption and current independent security certifications. Enterprise controls are usually on the top plan.

**Q: How do I compare project management software features across tools?**
Turn your problems into weighted must-haves, find the cheapest plan in each tool that covers them, score each tool 0 to 3 in a trial and exclude any tool that misses a must-have. Our [comparison pages](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/) help with the shortlist.
