# What Is Project Management Software? Types and Uses

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What project management software is, how it works, the main types, features, benefits, costs and how to set up your first project, with examples.


## What Is Project Management Software? Types and Uses
Project management software is an application that lets a team plan, assign, schedule, track and report on project work in one shared place, instead of across spreadsheets, email threads and meetings. This guide explains how it works, the main types, what it does well and badly, what it costs and how to set up your first project, with worked examples throughout.
- Published 4 October 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project management software turns a project into structured data (tasks, owners, dates, dependencies and statuses) that everyone sees and updates in one place.
- The same data appears in many views: lists, boards, Gantt charts, calendars, workload charts and dashboards.
- Types range from simple task apps to team collaboration tools, full project management, work management platforms and portfolio (PPM) suites.
- The main benefits are one source of truth, earlier warning of slippage and far less time spent chasing updates and building reports; the main costs are licences, set-up and the discipline to keep it current.
- In our independent ranking, Wrike is the strongest all-in-one platform; monday.com, Asana and ClickUp follow, and lighter tools such as Trello and Basecamp suit simpler needs.

### What is project management software?
**Project management software** is a digital tool, usually cloud-based, that helps teams plan projects, break them into tasks, assign owners and due dates, link dependent work, track progress and report status. It keeps the plan, the conversation and the files together, so everyone works from the same current information.
The PMBOK Guide from PMI describes a project as a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. That temporary, one-off nature is what makes projects hard to run from memory: the team, the deadlines and the risks are different every time. Software gives each project a consistent structure and a single home.
You will also see vendors describe their products as **work management** platforms. The difference is mostly one of scope. Project management software focuses on projects with a start, an end and a defined outcome. Work management software also covers ongoing work, such as request queues, recurring operations and approvals. Most leading products now do both.
Software is only one kind of project management tool. Techniques such as the critical path method and documents such as a risk register matter just as much. For the full picture, read our guide to the [types of project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-tools/).

### How project management software works
Under the surface, almost every project management application stores the same kinds of objects. Once you understand them, any tool becomes easier to learn, and you can compare products on a like-for-like basis.

#### The building blocks
| Building block | What it is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace or space | The top-level area for a team, department or client | Marketing team space |
| Project or folder | A container for one project's work, with its own dates and owner | Q1 product webinar |
| Task | A single piece of work with an owner, a due date and a status | Write landing page copy |
| Subtask or checklist | Smaller steps inside a task | Draft, review, final edit |
| Milestone | A zero-duration checkpoint marking an important event | Registration page live |
| Dependency | A link saying one task cannot start or finish until another does | Design cannot start until copy is approved |
| Custom field | Extra data you add to tasks | Priority, budget, channel, effort in hours |
| Status and workflow | The stages a task moves through | To do, In progress, In review, Done |
| View | A way of displaying the same tasks | List, board, Gantt, calendar, workload |
| Dashboard and report | Live charts and summaries built from task data | Overdue tasks by owner, progress by milestone |
A project in software is essentially a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) turned into tasks, with owners, dates and dependencies attached. The software then does the bookkeeping: it recalculates dates when something moves, notifies the people affected and rolls progress up to the project and portfolio level.

#### One plan, many views
The most useful idea to grasp is that views are not separate documents. When a designer drags a card from **In progress** to **In review** on a [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/), the same task updates on the [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), the workload chart and the manager's dashboard. Team members can work in a list or board, the project manager in a Gantt or workload view and stakeholders on a dashboard, without anyone maintaining separate copies.

#### The daily loop
Once a project is set up, the software supports a simple repeating cycle:
1. **Plan:** the project manager creates tasks, dates and dependencies, often from a template.
2. **Assign:** each task gets one accountable owner; the software notifies them.
3. **Update:** owners change status, log comments or time and attach files where the work happens.
4. **Alert:** the tool flags overdue tasks, blocked dependencies and approaching milestones.
5. **Report:** dashboards and status reports refresh automatically from the latest data.

### Worked example: one project from request to close
Here is how a typical project runs through project management software. The team and project are fictional, but the steps reflect how most all-in-one platforms work.
**The scenario:** an eight-person marketing team is asked to run a product webinar in six weeks. It involves a landing page, three emails, social posts, slides, a speaker briefing and follow-up content.
1. **Request.** The product manager fills in a request form in the tool, giving the goal, date, audience and budget. It lands in the team's intake queue, not someone's inbox.
2. **Approval and set-up.** The marketing lead approves the request. One click creates a project from the team's "Webinar" template, with 28 standard tasks, owners by role and relative due dates counted back from the webinar date.
3. **Scheduling.** The project manager checks the Gantt view. Dependencies are already in the template, for example slides cannot be designed until the speaker outline is agreed. The critical path shows the speaker outline is the task most likely to delay everything.
4. **Resourcing.** The workload view shows the designer is booked at 130% in week three because of another campaign. The project manager moves two non-critical social graphics to a freelancer added as a guest user, and the designer drops to 95%.
5. **Execution.** Team members work from the board view and their personal "My work" list.
6. **Review and approval.** Slides and landing page designs go through built-in proofing: reviewers mark up the file and approve it, and the task moves on automatically.
7. **Reporting.** Each Friday the stakeholder dashboard shows tasks completed, overdue items and milestone status. The [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) is generated from live data.
8. **Change.** In week four the webinar date moves forward by two days. The project manager shifts the milestone, dependent tasks move with it and every owner affected is notified of their new date.
9. **Close.** After the webinar the team records lessons learned on the project, archives it and updates the template: two tasks are added and one is removed. The next webinar starts from a better plan.
Tip
You do not need every feature from this example on day one. Many teams start with tasks, owners, dates and a board, then add templates, dependencies, workload views and dashboards as the need appears.

### What project management software does: core capabilities
Products differ in depth, but most cover the same capability areas.
| Capability | What it does | Who relies on it most |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task management | Creates tasks with owners, due dates, priorities and statuses | Everyone on the team |
| Scheduling | Gantt charts, dependencies, milestones, baselines and critical path | Project managers on date-driven projects |
| Collaboration | Comments, mentions, file sharing, guest access and approvals | Teams working with clients or across departments |
| Resource management | Workload charts, capacity, allocations and time off | Managers sharing people across projects |
| Time and budget tracking | Timesheets, billable hours, costs against budget | Agencies, consultancies and internal cost centres |
| Automation | Rules that assign, move, notify or create tasks automatically | Teams with repeatable processes |
| Reporting | Dashboards, charts, status reports and exports | Sponsors, PMOs and senior stakeholders |
| Portfolio management | Roll-up views across many projects, with health and priorities | PMOs and leadership teams |
| AI assistance | Summaries, drafting, task suggestions and risk alerts | Busy project managers and team leads |
Not every team needs every capability. Use our [project management software features checklist](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software-features/) to decide which capabilities are must-haves for you. If scheduling is your main need, our guide to [Gantt chart software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/) goes deeper.

### Types of project management software
Our guide to the [types of project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-tools/) groups software by product category. Here we group it by how much of your work it covers, which method it supports and where it runs.

#### By scope: the software ladder
Think of project management software as a ladder. Each rung covers more of the organisation's work and adds more structure, but also more set-up and cost.
| Rung | What it covers | Typical features | Examples from our reviews |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Task and to-do apps | Personal or small-group task lists | Lists, due dates, simple boards | Trello for simple boards |
| 2. Team collaboration tools | Shared projects with messaging at the centre | To-dos, message boards, schedules, files | Basecamp, Notion |
| 3. Project management software | Planning and tracking individual projects | Gantt charts, dependencies, milestones, reports | Smartsheet, Microsoft Planner (paid plans) |
| 4. Work management platforms | Projects plus requests, operations and cross-team work | Multiple views, automation, workload, dashboards, intake forms | Wrike, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp |
| 5. Portfolio management (PPM) | Many projects, programmes and resources across the organisation | Portfolio dashboards, capacity planning, financials, governance | Higher tiers of Wrike, Smartsheet and similar enterprise platforms |
The rungs overlap (Wrike, for example, spans three to five depending on the plan). Climb only as far as your work requires: a three-person team on rung five will spend more time administering the tool than running projects.

#### By delivery method
- **Predictive (waterfall) software** emphasises Gantt charts, baselines, dependencies and the critical path. It suits projects with a fixed sequence, such as construction and events.
- **Agile software** emphasises backlogs, sprints, story points, boards and burndown charts. Jira is the best-known example; see our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/).
- **Hybrid software** supports both, so a team can plan phases on a Gantt chart and run delivery in sprints. Most work management platforms, including Wrike, monday.com and ClickUp, fall here.

#### By deployment and industry
Most project management software is now cloud software (SaaS) used in a browser or mobile app; desktop and self-hosted options survive for specialist needs such as very large engineering schedules or strict data-residency rules. Industry-focused products add what general platforms lack: issue tracking and releases for software teams, time, billing and profitability for agencies (often called professional services automation, or PSA), drawings and site records for construction, and proofing and request intake for creative teams. A specialist tool is worth it when your workflows cannot be modelled in a general platform without heavy customisation.

### Project management software vs related software
Project management software overlaps with other systems you may already use. Knowing the boundaries helps you avoid paying twice.
| Software | Built for | How it relates to project management software |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spreadsheets (Excel, Google Sheets) | Calculations and flexible lists | Fine for small, simple plans; struggles with dependencies, multiple editors and live reporting |
| Chat and messaging (Slack, Teams) | Real-time conversation | Good for quick questions; decisions and tasks should be captured in the project tool, often via an integration |
| CRM | Customer relationships and sales pipelines | A won deal often triggers a delivery project in the PM tool |
| ERP and finance systems | Accounting, procurement and payroll | Holds the official numbers; PM software tracks project-level budgets and time |
| PSA | Billable services businesses | Combines project management with time, billing and profitability |
| PPM | Portfolio selection, funding and governance | Sits above project management; many work management platforms now include PPM features on higher tiers |
Tip
If your team keeps a spreadsheet next to the project tool to track the same tasks, one of them is redundant. Decide which is the source of truth and retire the other.

### Benefits of project management software
The benefits come from replacing manual coordination with shared, structured data:
- **One source of truth.** Everyone sees the same tasks, dates and owners, so there are no competing versions of the plan.
- **Clear ownership.** Every task has a named owner and a due date.
- **Earlier warning.** Overdue tasks, blocked dependencies and overloaded people show up as they happen, not at the next status meeting.
- **Less reporting effort.** Dashboards and status reports build themselves from live data.
- **Better resource decisions.** Workload views show who has capacity before you commit to new work.
- **Smoother collaboration with outsiders.** Guest access lets clients and suppliers see and approve their part without seeing everything.
- **An audit trail.** Comments, approvals and changes are recorded against each task.

#### Worked example: estimating the time saved
Your own estimate is more convincing to a budget holder than vendor figures. The numbers below are illustrative; replace them with your team's.
| Activity today | Who | Time per week now | Time per week with software | Saved |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chasing updates by email and chat | Project manager | 3 hours | 1 hour | 2 hours |
| Building the weekly status report | Project manager | 2 hours | 0.5 hours | 1.5 hours |
| Status meeting | 8 people | 8 hours (1 hour each) | 4 hours (30 minutes each) | 4 hours |
| Searching for the latest file or decision | 8 people | 4 hours (30 minutes each) | 2 hours | 2 hours |
| Total |  | 17 hours | 7.5 hours | 9.5 hours |
In this example, 9.5 hours a week across the team is roughly 400 hours over a 42-week working year. At almost any internal hourly cost, that outweighs the licence cost for an eight-person team. Keep the estimate conservative and re-measure after 90 days.

### Disadvantages and challenges
| Challenge | Why it happens | How to reduce it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Learning curve | Feature-rich tools have many options and settings | Start with a simple structure; train champions first |
| Set-up effort | Templates, fields, workflows and permissions take time to design | Configure one team's process well before scaling |
| Ongoing cost | Per-user licences grow with the team, and key features may sit on higher tiers | Check which plan holds your must-haves; use guest and viewer licences |
| Admin overhead | Someone must maintain templates, users and standards | Name an owner and give them time for it |
| Data quality depends on discipline | A tool is only current if people update it | Keep tasks meaningful; make the tool the only place status is reported |
| Over-reliance | Green dashboards can hide real problems | Keep talking to the team; use the tool to inform conversations, not replace them |
| Switching cost | History, templates and habits are hard to move | Confirm data export before you commit |
Most of these are adoption problems, not software problems. A modest tool used consistently beats a powerful one used half-heartedly.

### Who uses project management software
| Who | Typical needs | What to prioritise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project managers | Plans, schedules, risks and reporting | Gantt charts, dependencies, dashboards |
| Marketing and creative teams | Campaigns, content calendars, approvals | Request forms, proofing, calendar view |
| Software and IT teams | Backlogs, sprints, bugs, releases | Agile boards, sprint reports, developer integrations |
| Agencies and consultancies | Client projects, time, budgets | Guest access, time tracking, budget tracking |
| PMOs and leadership | Portfolio health and capacity | Portfolio dashboards, resource and capacity planning |
| Small businesses and freelancers | Simple coordination at low cost | Ease of use, free or flat-price plans |
A [project management office (PMO)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) often standardises one platform across the organisation so projects are comparable.

### Do you need project management software? A quick self-assessment
Score one point for each statement that is true for your team today:
1. You run more than two projects at the same time.
2. More than five people contribute to a typical project.
3. Tasks depend on each other, and one delay regularly causes others.
4. The same people work on several projects at once.
5. You spend more than an hour a week chasing updates.
6. Status reports are built by hand from several sources.
7. Files and decisions are hard to find after a few weeks.
8. Clients, suppliers or other departments need visibility of progress.
9. You repeat similar projects and rebuild the plan each time.
10. Leaders ask questions about progress that nobody can answer quickly.
| Score | What it suggests | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 to 2 | A spreadsheet or simple board is probably enough | Use a free [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) or a [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) |
| 3 to 5 | You will gain from a team tool | Try the free plan of a simple, visual tool and add a timeline view when needed |
| 6 to 10 | Manual coordination is costing you real time | Shortlist all-in-one platforms with Gantt charts, workload views and dashboards |
Templates stay useful after you move to software. A [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) or [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) is a good way to sketch the structure before building it in a tool.

### How much does project management software cost?
Prices change often, so check the vendor's pricing page. What changes less is how vendors charge.
| Pricing model | How it works | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free plan | A permanently free tier with limits on users, projects, views or storage | Gantt charts, dashboards and automations are often missing |
| Per user per month | You pay for each licensed user, usually less if billed annually | Minimum seat counts or seat bundles on some plans |
| Tiered plans | Higher tiers add more features and higher limits | Your must-have feature may sit one or two tiers above the headline price |
| Flat price | One price for the team regardless of user count | Limits on projects or storage instead |
| Quote-based enterprise | Custom pricing for large organisations | Contract length, renewal increases and add-ons |
| Licence types | Full users, light collaborators, viewers and guests priced differently | Definitions vary by vendor; check who counts as a paid user |
| Add-ons | Extra charges for AI, integrations or premium support | AI usage limits and credits |
For reference, our review data (checked 5 October 2026) shows paid plans starting at around $5 to $11 per user per month for most leading tools. Wrike, for example, offers a free plan, a Team plan at $10 per user per month and a Business plan at $25 per user per month (billed annually), with Pinnacle and Apex on quotes. Basecamp is one of the few that charges a flat monthly price, and Smartsheet no longer has a free plan.

#### Worked example: per-user vs flat pricing
These illustrative figures show how the models compare for three options:
- **Tool A:** $10 per user per month.
- **Tool B:** $25 per user per month, with more advanced features.
- **Tool C:** a flat $99 per month for any number of users.
| Team size | Tool A per year | Tool B per year | Tool C per year |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 users | $600 | $1,500 | $1,188 |
| 10 users | $1,200 | $3,000 | $1,188 |
| 25 users | $3,000 | $7,500 | $1,188 |
| 50 users | $6,000 | $15,000 | $1,188 |
Flat pricing wins as the team grows, and per-user pricing wins for small teams. But price is only part of it: if Tool B is the only one with the workload view and dashboards you need, the cheaper options may cost more in manual work. Our guide to [choosing project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/) includes a full year-one cost example with set-up, training and admin time.

### How to choose project management software
Choosing well is a project in itself. In short:
1. **Start from problems, not features.** List what is going wrong today, such as missed deadlines, overloaded people or slow reporting.
2. **Decide your rung on the ladder.** Match the type of software to the scope of work it needs to cover.
3. **Turn problems into must-haves.** Keep the list short and check which plan tier includes each one.
4. **Trial two or three tools on real work.** Use a live project for two to four weeks with the people who will use the tool daily.
5. **Compare the full cost.** Include the right tier, guests, training, integrations and admin time.
Compare any two shortlisted platforms in our [side-by-side tool comparisons](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/). For the full process, with a requirements checklist, weighted scoring matrix and trial plan, read our [8-step guide to choosing project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/).

### How to set up your first project, step by step
Whichever tool you choose, the first project sets the pattern for everything after it. These steps work in almost any platform.
1. **Agree the outcome and the end date.** Write one sentence describing what done looks like, plus the deadline and the sponsor.
2. **Break the work down.** List the deliverables, then the tasks needed to produce each. Aim for tasks of roughly half a day to a few days; anything smaller belongs in a checklist.
3. **Create the project structure.** Make one project (or folder) and, if it is large, group tasks by phase or deliverable.
4. **Set statuses.** Keep the workflow short: To do, In progress, In review, Done. Add a Blocked status only if you will act on it.
5. **Add only the custom fields you will report on.** Priority and effort are common; resist adding fields nobody will fill in.
6. **Assign one owner and a due date to every task.** Shared ownership usually means no ownership.
7. **Link dependencies and add milestones.** Connect tasks that genuinely depend on each other, then check the Gantt view for the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).
8. **Check workload.** Use the workload or capacity view to spot people booked over 100% and rebalance before work starts. Our guide to [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) explains how.
9. **Build one dashboard.** Include progress by milestone, overdue tasks and upcoming deadlines. Share it with stakeholders instead of sending reports.
10. **Agree team habits.** Decide when updates happen (for example, before the weekly meeting), where questions go (comments on the task) and what gets escalated.
11. **Save it as a template.** After the project closes, turn the improved plan into a template for next time.
Tip
Keep risks visible too. Some platforms have a built-in risk or issue item type; otherwise, link a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) to the project and review it at the same meeting as the schedule.
Rolling out to a whole department needs more planning: champions, role-based training and a date when the old way stops. A [training plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) helps you organise it.

### Common mistakes when adopting project management software
- **Copying the old spreadsheet column for column.** Software works differently. Rebuild the plan around tasks, owners, dependencies and statuses instead of recreating every column.
- **Over-customising early.** Dozens of statuses, fields and automations make the tool hard to use. Start lean and add only what people ask for.
- **Running two systems in parallel.** If status still lives in a spreadsheet or slide deck, people will update that and ignore the tool.
- **Tasks that are too big or too small.** A task called "Website" tells nobody anything; fifty tasks for one email is noise. Size tasks so progress is visible every few days.
- **Notification overload.** Default settings can bury people in alerts. Show the team how to tune notifications in the first week.
- **No archive policy.** Finished projects clutter searches and dashboards. Archive them on close and keep the template.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project management software?**
Project management software is an application, usually cloud-based, that helps teams plan projects, break them into tasks, assign owners and due dates, link dependencies, track progress and report status in one shared place.

**Q: What is an example of project management software?**
Well-known examples include Wrike, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp, Smartsheet, Jira, Microsoft Planner, Notion, Trello and Basecamp. In our independent ranking, Wrike comes first as the most complete all-in-one platform.

**Q: What are the main types of project management software?**
By scope, the main types are task and to-do apps, team collaboration tools, project management software, work management platforms and portfolio management (PPM) suites. Software can also be grouped by method (Agile, predictive or hybrid), deployment (cloud, desktop or self-hosted) and industry.

**Q: What is the best project management software?**
It depends on your needs. Our ranking places Wrike first for all-in-one depth, followed by monday.com for ease of use, Asana for cross-team coordination and ClickUp for value. Jira suits software teams, and Trello or Basecamp suit simpler needs.

**Q: Is there free project management software?**
Yes. Wrike, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp, Jira, Notion, Trello and Basecamp all have free plans with limits on users, projects or features. Smartsheet offers a free trial instead. Free plans usually lack Gantt dependencies, dashboards and workload views.

**Q: How much does project management software cost?**
Most tools charge per user per month, with paid plans for the leading tools starting at roughly $5 to $11 per user per month in our review data (checked 5 October 2026). Some, such as Basecamp, charge a flat monthly price, and enterprise plans are usually quote-based.

**Q: Can Excel be used as project management software?**
Excel and other spreadsheets work for small, simple projects. They struggle when tasks depend on each other, several people edit the plan or stakeholders want live reporting. That is usually the point to move to dedicated software.

**Q: What is the easiest project management software to use?**
Trello and monday.com are among the easiest to pick up, and Basecamp is simple for communication-centred projects. Feature-rich platforms such as Wrike take longer to learn but cover far more as your needs grow.

**Q: Is Jira project management software?**
Yes. Jira is project management software designed mainly for software development and IT teams, with backlogs, sprints, boards and issue tracking. Other teams can use it, but general-purpose platforms are often easier for non-technical work.

**Q: Do small businesses need project management software?**
Not always. If you run one or two simple projects with a few people, a spreadsheet or free board may be enough. Once you juggle several projects, share people between them or spend hours chasing updates, software usually pays for itself.

**Q: Does project management software include AI?**
Most leading platforms now include AI features such as summaries, drafting, task suggestions and risk alerts. Availability and usage limits depend on the plan, so check what is included and treat AI output as a draft. Our ranking of [AI project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/ai-project-management-tools/) compares what each platform offers.

# Types of Project Management Tools: Techniques and Software

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-tools/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: The main types of project management tools explained: planning, scheduling, tracking, collaboration, risk and reporting tools, with examples and tips.


## Types of Project Management Tools: Techniques and Software
Project management tools are the techniques, documents and software that help you plan, schedule, track and control a project, from a simple RACI matrix to a full work management platform. This guide sorts the main types of project management tools by the job they do, shows which ones you need at each phase and how they fit together, so you can build a toolkit that suits your projects.
- Published 4 October 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project management tools come in three layers: techniques (methods), documents and templates (artifacts) and software (platforms that run them).
- Group tools by the job they do: planning, scheduling, task tracking, collaboration, resources, cost, risk, reporting and portfolio governance.
- Most small projects need only six tools: a scope breakdown, a schedule, a task board, a RACI, a risk log and a status report.
- Pick the technique first, start with a template if the project is small, and move to software when dependencies, people or projects multiply.
- For specific products, use our [ranking of the best project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/), where Wrike ranks first.

### What are project management tools?
**Project management tools** are the methods, documents and software a project team uses to plan work, assign responsibilities, schedule activities, track progress, manage risks and report results. They include techniques such as the critical path method, artifacts such as a risk register or RACI matrix, and software platforms that combine these into one shared workspace.
It helps to think of them in three layers:
- **Techniques** are the methods: how you break down scope, calculate a schedule, estimate costs or assess risks. The [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/), PERT and [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) are techniques.
- **Documents and templates** are the artifacts a technique produces or relies on: a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/), a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) or a [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
- **Software** is the platform that holds those artifacts, keeps them current and shares them with the team: [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) such as Wrike, Asana or Jira.
The term also has a formal history. Earlier, process-based editions of PMI's *PMBOK Guide* listed the "inputs, tools and techniques, and outputs" (ITTOs) of every process, which is why study material often talks about "tools and techniques" as one phrase. The 7th edition replaced that structure with a section on models, methods and artifacts. For day-to-day work, the practical distinction above is the one that matters.

### Tools vs techniques vs software
People often use "tool" for all three layers, which causes confusion when you are choosing what to adopt. The table shows how one need runs through each layer.
| Need | Technique (method) | Document or template | Software feature |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Break down the scope | Decomposition | [Work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) | Task hierarchy with subtasks |
| Set realistic dates | [Critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) | Project schedule | Gantt view with dependencies |
| Show who does what | Responsibility assignment | [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) | Assignees, approvers and permissions |
| Visualise flow | Kanban | [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) | Board view with custom statuses |
| Control risk | Risk assessment | [Risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) | Custom risk fields, forms and dashboards |
| Measure performance | [Earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) | Cost and schedule report, S-curve | Dashboards, baselines and budget tracking |
The order matters. Software cannot tell you how to sequence work or which risks matter; it can only make a good method faster and more visible. If the team does not understand the technique, a more powerful tool usually adds confusion rather than control.
Tip
When someone says "we need a better tool", ask which job is failing: planning, tracking, communicating or reporting. The answer tells you whether you need a new technique, a better template or different software.

### The main types of project management tools
The clearest way to classify project management tools is by the job they do. Most projects need something from each of the first six types; the last three matter more as projects and organisations grow.
| Type | Job it does | Typical examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planning tools | Define the goal, scope and approach | Project charter, WBS, project plan, roadmap |
| Scheduling tools | Sequence work and set dates | Gantt chart, network diagram, CPM, PERT, milestones |
| Task and workflow tools | Assign and track day-to-day work | To-do lists, Kanban and Scrum boards, workflows |
| Collaboration and communication tools | Keep people informed and aligned | RACI, communication plan, comments, shared files |
| Resource and capacity tools | Match work to available people | Resource plan, workload view, levelling, timesheets |
| Cost and budget tools | Estimate, budget and control spend | Cost estimate, budget, earned value, time tracking |
| Risk, issue and change tools | Anticipate and handle problems | Risk register, RAID log, issue log, change requests |
| Reporting and dashboard tools | Show progress and health | Status report, dashboards, burndown, S-curve |
| Portfolio and governance tools | Prioritise and oversee many projects | Portfolio dashboards, stage gates, PMO standards |

#### Planning tools
Planning tools turn an idea into an agreed definition of the work. The project charter authorises the project and names the sponsor, objectives and constraints. A [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) decomposes the scope into deliverables and work packages, and the project management plan records how scope, schedule, cost, risk and communication will be managed. For longer initiatives, a project roadmap shows the big phases on one page. Our free templates for each of these are listed in the [templates library](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/).

#### Scheduling tools
Scheduling tools work out when each activity happens. A [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) shows activities as bars on a timeline; a network diagram shows the logic between them; the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) calculates dates and float; and PERT handles uncertain durations with three-point estimates. Milestones mark the dates stakeholders care about. In software, look for dependency links, automatic rescheduling and baselines; our guide to [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) explains the full process.

#### Task and workflow tools
These tools manage the daily flow of work: who is doing what, by when, and what is blocked. A shared task list or a [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) is often enough for a small team; Agile teams use Scrum boards and backlogs. In software, this is the core of every platform: tasks with owners, due dates, statuses, checklists and comments, plus automations that move work between stages.

#### Collaboration and communication tools
Projects fail more often from misunderstanding than from bad maths. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) makes accountability explicit, a communication plan sets who hears what and how often, and stakeholder management techniques help you prioritise attention. Software adds comments on tasks, @mentions, shared documents, proofing and approvals, and guest access for clients and suppliers, so conversations stay attached to the work instead of scattered across email.

#### Resource and capacity tools
Resource tools answer "who is available, and are they overloaded?". The techniques are [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/), capacity planning and resource levelling. A skills matrix helps you match people to work. In software, look for workload or capacity views that show each person's booked hours against their availability; these are usually on mid-tier or higher plans.

#### Cost and budget tools
Cost tools estimate what the project will cost and track what it actually costs. Techniques include cost estimation, building a [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) and [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) for performance measurement. Many teams start with the budget template or project cost estimate template; software adds time tracking, rates and budget fields that roll up across tasks and projects.

#### Risk, issue and change tools
These tools help you see problems coming and deal with the ones that arrive. The [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) records risks, owners and responses; a [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) adds assumptions, issues and dependencies; an issue log tracks problems that have already happened; and change control stops scope from growing unnoticed. Start with our free [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).

#### Reporting and dashboard tools
Reporting tools tell sponsors and the team whether the project is on track. A weekly [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) is the classic format; dashboards show the same information live. Agile teams add burndown charts and velocity; predictive projects use baselines, schedule variance and S-curves. The aim is to report from the data the team already maintains, not to rebuild figures by hand each week.

#### Portfolio and governance tools
Once an organisation runs many projects, it needs tools to choose between them and oversee them consistently. These include portfolio dashboards, stage-gate reviews, project governance frameworks and standards set by a project management office. Our guide to programme vs project vs portfolio management explains where each level of oversight applies.

### Types of project management software
Software is where most of these tools now live. Vendors describe their products in many ways, but most fall into a handful of categories. The examples below come from the ten platforms in our independent reviews.
| Software type | What it is built for | Examples we review |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All-in-one work management | Projects, resources, portfolios, approvals and reporting in one platform | Wrike, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp |
| Spreadsheet-style planning | Grid-based project plans with Gantt, automation and reporting | Smartsheet |
| Agile and software development | Backlogs, sprints, issue tracking and developer integrations | Jira |
| Office-suite planners | Task and project planning inside a productivity suite | Microsoft Planner |
| Docs-first workspaces | Wikis and databases shaped into project trackers | Notion |
| Visual boards | Simple Kanban boards for small teams and personal work | Trello |
| Communication-centred | Messages, to-dos, schedules and files per project | Basecamp |
Beyond these, you will meet more specialised categories: dedicated scheduling software for large engineering and construction schedules, project portfolio management (PPM) suites for PMOs, time-tracking and invoicing tools, and industry-specific platforms. Many teams pair one main platform with one or two of these rather than buying everything at once.
All-in-one platforms suit teams that want planning, execution and reporting in one place. In our ranking, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) comes first because it combines interactive Gantt charts, boards, workload views, request forms, proofing, dashboards and portfolio reporting, and scales from one team to an enterprise. Lighter tools such as Trello or Basecamp are quicker to adopt and work well for simpler needs.

#### Cloud, desktop and on-premises software
Most project management software today is **cloud-based** (software as a service): you use it in a browser or app, the vendor hosts it and updates arrive automatically. **Desktop** scheduling software installed on one computer is still used for complex schedules, but it is harder to share. **On-premises** or self-managed deployments, where the organisation hosts the software itself, are now less common and mostly chosen for specific security or regulatory reasons. Check what each vendor currently offers, because deployment options change.

### Project management tools for each phase
Different tools carry the load at different points in the [project life cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/). The table shows the typical toolkit for each phase.
| Phase | Main tools | Software helps by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiation | Business case, feasibility study, project charter, stakeholder register | Holding intake requests and approvals in one place |
| Planning | WBS, schedule, Gantt chart, budget, RACI, risk register, communication plan | Building the plan with dependencies, owners and baselines |
| Execution | Task boards, workflows, meeting notes, shared documents, approvals | Assigning work, automating hand-offs, keeping files with tasks |
| Monitoring and controlling | Status reports, dashboards, earned value, issue log, change requests | Live progress, variance against baseline, alerts on slipping work |
| Closing | Acceptance sign-off, lessons learned, closure report | Archiving the project and turning it into a reusable template |
A practical consequence: if your tool is strong in execution but weak in planning (or the reverse), you will end up with side spreadsheets. Check that your main platform covers the phases where your projects struggle most.

### Tools for Agile, predictive and hybrid projects
The delivery approach changes which tools carry most weight.
| Approach | Core tools | What to look for in software |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predictive (Waterfall) | WBS, Gantt chart, critical path, baseline, earned value | Dependencies, critical path highlighting, baselines, resource views |
| Agile (Scrum, Kanban) | Product backlog, user stories, Scrum or Kanban board, burndown, velocity | Backlogs, sprints, story points, WIP limits, Agile reports |
| Hybrid | Milestone plan for governance plus boards for delivery teams | Gantt and boards on the same data, shared milestones |
Agile teams still use planning tools, just at a different level: a product backlog instead of a fixed WBS, sprints instead of a detailed activity network, and release forecasts instead of a single end date. Our guide to [Agile tools and techniques](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-tools-and-techniques/) covers these in depth, including the software features Scrum and Kanban teams rely on.
Hybrid is common. A construction or infrastructure project may run a critical path schedule for physical works and Scrum for the software that supports it. Platforms that show the same tasks as both a Gantt chart and a board, such as Wrike, monday.com, ClickUp or Smartsheet, make this easier than running two separate systems.

### The minimum toolkit for a small project
Long lists of tools can make project management look heavier than it is. For a small project of a few weeks with a handful of people, these six tools cover most of what you need:
1. **A one-page scope statement or charter**: the goal, deliverables, what is out of scope, the sponsor and the deadline.
2. **A simple work breakdown**: the deliverables split into tasks small enough to assign.
3. **A schedule with milestones**: a basic Gantt chart or dated task list showing which tasks depend on which.
4. **A task board**: To do, In progress, Done, with an owner on every card.
5. **A RACI or owner list**: who decides, who does the work and who needs to be kept informed.
6. **A risk and issue log plus a weekly status update**: a short list of what could go wrong and a five-line progress note for stakeholders.
Add cost, resource and portfolio tools only when the project needs them: when there is a budget to control, people shared with other work, or several projects competing for the same team. Our free [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) combines several of these essentials in one spreadsheet.

### Worked example: choosing tools for a website redesign
A marketing team of five is redesigning the company website over ten weeks, with an external developer and a sign-off from the head of marketing. Here is how the project manager builds the toolkit, need by need.
| Need | Technique | Document or template | Software feature used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agree what is in scope | Scope definition | Charter and project scope statement | Project overview page with brief attached |
| Break the work down | Decomposition | WBS: content, design, build, test, launch | Folders or phases with tasks and subtasks |
| Set dates | Dependencies and critical path | Schedule with three milestones | Gantt view with dependencies and a baseline |
| Run the daily work | Kanban | Board: Backlog, In progress, Review, Done | Board view with custom statuses |
| Clarify approvals | Responsibility assignment | RACI for copy, design and launch | Approval step on review tasks |
| Handle the developer | Supplier management | Statement of work | Guest access limited to the build tasks |
| Watch for problems | Risk assessment | Risk register with five risks | Custom fields for probability, impact, owner |
| Report progress | Status reporting | Weekly status note | Dashboard shared with the head of marketing |
Notice that the team needs no resource levelling, earned value or portfolio tools: the project is small and the people are dedicated to it. If the same team later runs five websites at once for different business units, workload views and a portfolio dashboard become worth the extra setup.

### Spreadsheets and templates vs project management software
Templates are a perfectly good project management tool, especially when you are learning a technique or running a small project. A spreadsheet is quick to start, everyone can open it and you can shape it exactly as you like.
Spreadsheets start to struggle when:
- Dates depend on each other and you are recalculating them by hand after every slip.
- Several people need to update the same plan at the same time.
- You have to chase updates by email before every status meeting.
- The same people work across several projects and nobody can see their total workload.
- Stakeholders want live dashboards rather than weekly attachments.
When two or three of these apply, project management software usually pays for itself in saved admin time. Many teams keep using templates for documents such as the charter, business case and lessons learned, and run the schedule, tasks and reporting in software. Browse our [free project management templates](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/), including the [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) and a Kanban board template.

### AI features in project management tools
Most major project management platforms now include AI features, and the range is growing quickly. Common uses include:
- Summarising long comment threads and meeting notes.
- Drafting task descriptions, status updates and project briefs.
- Suggesting subtasks, owners or due dates from a project description.
- Flagging tasks at risk of slipping based on progress data.
- Building automations or reports from a plain-language request.
AI features are usually tied to specific plans or usage allowances, so check what is included before you rely on them. Treat AI output as a draft: the project manager still owns the plan, the estimates and what is reported to stakeholders. Our ranking of [AI project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/ai-project-management-tools/) compares what each platform currently offers.

### How to choose the right project management tools
Choosing tools is easier when you work from needs rather than features.
1. **List the jobs that are failing today**: missed deadlines, unclear ownership, overloaded people, slow reporting.
2. **Pick the technique for each job** from the types above, and agree how the team will use it.
3. **Decide where each tool lives**: a template, your main platform or a specialist add-on.
4. **Shortlist two or three platforms** that cover your phases and approach (predictive, Agile or hybrid).
5. **Trial them on a real project** for two to four weeks with the people who will use them daily.
6. **Check the total cost**: licences for the right plan, guests, training, integrations and admin time.
Our [8-step guide to choosing project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/) goes into detail, and the [software features checklist](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software-features/) helps you score each option. If you manage several projects with shared resources and need Gantt charts, workload views and portfolio reporting together, Wrike is a strong place to start; if ease of adoption matters most, look at monday.com or Asana.

### Common mistakes with project management tools
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Buying software before agreeing the method | The tool mirrors existing confusion | Agree the techniques and workflow first, then configure the tool |
| Running the project in several places | Nobody knows which version is right | Name one source of truth for tasks, dates and owners |
| Tracking every tiny task | Updating the tool becomes a job in itself | Track deliverables and tasks of roughly a day or more |
| Using every feature on day one | People feel overwhelmed and stop updating | Start with a simple structure and add features as needs appear |
| No training or champions | Adoption stalls after the first month | Train a few champions and give them time to support others |
| Ignoring permissions and guest access | Clients see too much, or suppliers see too little | Set roles and guest rights before inviting outsiders |
| Reporting by hand | Status reports go stale and take hours | Report from dashboards built on live data |
Tip
A tool cannot fix an unclear plan. Define scope, owners and dates first, then put them into the software.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are project management tools?**
Project management tools are the techniques, documents and software used to plan, schedule, track and control projects. Examples include Gantt charts, work breakdown structures, Kanban boards, RACI matrices, risk registers, status reports and project management software.

**Q: What are the main types of project management tools?**
By the job they do: planning tools, scheduling tools, task and workflow tools, collaboration and communication tools, resource and capacity tools, cost and budget tools, risk and issue tools, reporting and dashboard tools, and portfolio and governance tools.

**Q: What is the difference between a project management tool and a technique?**
A technique is a method, such as the critical path method or earned value management. A tool is what you use to apply it, such as a Gantt chart, a template or a feature in project management software. Good tools make a sound technique faster and more visible; they cannot replace it.

**Q: What is the most commonly used project management tool?**
The Gantt chart and the task or Kanban board are among the most widely used, because almost every project needs a timeline and a way to track who is doing what. Most project management software offers both views.

**Q: What are the 5 basic project management tools?**
There is no official list, but five tools almost every project uses are a work breakdown structure, a schedule or Gantt chart, a task board, a RACI matrix and a risk register. Add a status report and you have a solid minimum toolkit.

**Q: What are the main types of project management software?**
Common categories are all-in-one work management platforms, spreadsheet-style planners, Agile and software development tools, office-suite planners, docs-first workspaces, visual boards and communication-centred tools. By deployment, software is cloud-based, desktop or on-premises.

**Q: Is Excel a project management tool?**
Yes, for small projects. Spreadsheets work well for task lists, simple schedules, budgets and risk logs. Dedicated software is better once dates depend on each other, several people update the plan or you need live dashboards. Our [templates](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/) are a good starting point.

**Q: Is Jira a project management tool?**
Yes. Jira is project management software designed mainly for software and IT teams running Scrum or Kanban, with backlogs, sprints and issue tracking. See our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/).

**Q: What tools do project managers use every day?**
Typically a work management platform for tasks and schedules, a calendar, email or chat, shared documents and a dashboard or status report. Many also keep a risk or RAID log and a RACI for each project.

**Q: Which project management tools are used in each phase?**
Initiation uses the business case and charter; planning uses the WBS, schedule, budget, RACI and risk register; execution uses task boards and workflows; monitoring uses status reports, dashboards and change control; closing uses acceptance sign-off and lessons learned.

**Q: What tools do Agile teams use?**
Agile teams use product backlogs, user stories, Scrum or Kanban boards, burndown charts and velocity, usually in software that supports sprints and WIP limits. See [Agile tools and techniques](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-tools-and-techniques/).

**Q: Are there free project management tools?**
Yes. Many platforms, including Wrike, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp, Jira, Notion, Trello and Basecamp, offer free plans with limits on users, projects or features. Templates in a spreadsheet are another free option. Our [tools ranking](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) lists each free plan.

**Q: What is the best project management tool?**
It depends on the job. For software, our [independent ranking](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) puts Wrike first as the strongest all-in-one platform, followed by monday.com, Asana and ClickUp. For techniques, the best tool is the one that solves the problem you actually have, such as a critical path schedule for fixed deadlines or a Kanban board for continuous flow.

**Q: Do project management tools use AI?**
Many now do. AI features summarise discussions, draft updates, suggest tasks and flag work at risk, usually on specific plans. See our ranking of [AI project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/ai-project-management-tools/).
