# Project Network Diagram: Types, Examples and How to Draw

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project network diagram explained: AON vs AOA, node notation, dummy activities, a step-by-step method and fully worked examples with the critical path.


## Project Network Diagram: Types, Examples and How to Draw
A project network diagram is a picture of a project's activities and the dependencies between them, drawn as boxes or circles joined by arrows from start to finish. It shows the logical order of the work, and it is the basis for the forward and backward pass, float and the critical path. This guide explains the two types, the notation, how to draw one step by step and three fully worked examples.
- Published 25 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- A network diagram shows the logic of a schedule: which activities depend on which, and which can run in parallel.
- Activity on node (AON), also called the precedence diagramming method, is the modern standard and supports all four dependency types.
- Activity on arrow (AOA) puts activities on the arrows, allows only finish-to-start links and sometimes needs dummy activities.
- Each AON node can show ES, duration and EF on top and LS, total float and LF underneath, so the critical path is visible at a glance.
- Burst points spread work into parallel paths; merge points are where delays combine and deserve the closest watching.
- Check the logic before you trust the dates: one start, one finish, no loops and no activities without a predecessor or successor.

### What is a project network diagram?
A **project network diagram** is a graphical representation of the activities in a project and the logical relationships between them. Activities are shown as nodes or arrows, dependencies as connecting arrows, and the whole diagram flows from a single start to a single finish. It is used to check logic, calculate dates and float, and find the critical path.
You may also see it called an **activity network diagram**, a **logic diagram** or a **precedence diagram**. The PMBOK Guide 6th edition called it the **project schedule network diagram** and made it the main output of sequencing activities. Later editions are organised around principles and performance domains rather than processes, but the technique itself has not changed.

#### Where it fits in planning
A network diagram sits between breaking down the work and setting dates:
1. Break the scope into deliverables with a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/).
2. Turn the lowest-level work packages into [activities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-tasks-and-activities/).
3. Sequence the activities with [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/): this is where the network diagram is drawn.
4. Estimate a duration for each activity.
5. Run the [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) on the network to get dates, [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) and the critical path.
6. Show the result on a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) and save a [baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).
The diagram shows **logic**, not calendar time. A long box does not mean a long activity, and two nodes side by side do not have to happen at the same time. For dates against a calendar, you need the Gantt chart; for the reasons behind those dates, you need the network.
Network diagrams date from the late 1950s, when the critical path method was developed for DuPont and PERT for the US Navy. Both originally drew activities on arrows. The activity-on-node approach, published by John Fondahl in the early 1960s, became the basis for the precedence diagramming method used by almost all scheduling software today.

### Network diagram notation and components
| Component | What it is | How it is drawn (AON) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Activity | A piece of work with a duration | A box (node) with an ID and name |
| Dependency | A logical link between two activities | An arrow from predecessor to successor |
| Start and finish nodes | Single entry and exit points for the network | Zero-duration nodes or milestones at each end |
| Milestone | A significant point with zero duration | A node with duration 0, often a diamond |
| Path | Any continuous chain of activities from start to finish | Follow the arrows |
| Critical path | The longest path; it sets the project duration and has the lowest float | Bold or red arrows and nodes |
| Burst point | An activity with two or more successors | One node with several outgoing arrows |
| Merge point | An activity with two or more predecessors | One node with several incoming arrows |
| Lead or lag | An overlap or delay on a link | A label on the arrow, such as FS+3 or SS-2 |
| Dummy activity | A zero-duration link used only in AOA diagrams | A dashed arrow |
Our guide to [predecessors and successors](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/predecessors-and-successors/) explains the terms used on each side of an arrow, and [project milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) covers how to choose them.

#### The AON node box
On an activity-on-node diagram, each box usually holds seven values once the forward and backward pass are done. A common layout is:
| Position | Left | Centre | Right |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Top row | Early start (ES) | Duration | Early finish (EF) |
| Middle |  | Activity ID and name |  |
| Bottom row | Late start (LS) | Total float (TF) | Late finish (LF) |
For example, activity C in the worked example below reads **ES 3 | 2 | EF 5** on top, **C Book removal firm** in the middle and **LS 7 | TF 4 | LF 9** underneath. Layouts vary between textbooks and tools, so always include a key on the diagram.

### Types of network diagram: AON vs AOA
|  | Activity on node (AON) | Activity on arrow (AOA) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Activities shown as | Boxes (nodes) | Arrows |
| Nodes represent | Activities | Events: the start or end of activities |
| Dependency types | FS, SS, FF and SF, with leads and lags | Finish-to-start only |
| Dummy activities | Never needed | Sometimes needed to show logic correctly |
| Also called | Precedence diagramming method (PDM) | Arrow diagramming method (ADM) |
| Where you see it | All modern scheduling tools; PMP exam questions | Older textbooks, some PERT and university courses |

#### Activity on node (precedence diagramming method)
In AON, every activity is a node and every arrow is a dependency. Because the logic sits on the arrows, you can show all four dependency types and label any lead or lag. Adding an activity or a link never needs extra dummy arrows, which makes AON easier to draw, read and change. This guide uses AON unless it says otherwise.

#### Activity on arrow (arrow diagramming method)
In AOA, each activity is an arrow running between two numbered circles called **events** or nodes. An event is the moment when all arrows entering it are complete and those leaving it can start. Two rules apply: events are numbered so that every arrow runs from a lower to a higher number, and no two activities may share the same start and end event. Event times are usually written in the circles: earliest event time and latest event time.

#### Dummy activities
A dummy is a dashed arrow with zero duration and no resources. It is needed in AOA in two situations: to show a dependency that cannot be drawn with real activities alone, and to stop two activities sharing the same pair of events. **Illustrative example:**
| Activity | Duration (days) | Predecessors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P | 2 | - |
| Q | 3 | - |
| R | 4 | P, Q |
| S | 1 | Q |
R needs both P and Q, but S needs only Q. In AOA, draw P from event 1 to event 2 and Q from event 1 to event 3. R leaves event 2, so it would wait only for P. Add a **dummy from event 3 to event 2**: now event 2 is not reached until Q is also done, so R waits for both, while S leaves event 3 and waits only for Q. R and S both end at event 4. In AON none of this is needed: you simply draw arrows P→R, Q→R and Q→S.

#### Related diagrams
- **PERT chart:** a network diagram, usually AOA in its original form, that uses three-point duration estimates. See our [PERT chart guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/).
- **Time-scaled network diagram:** nodes or arrows placed against a time axis, so the diagram shows both logic and timing. It is close to a Gantt chart with links.

### Showing dependency types and lags on the diagram
In AON, the default arrow means finish-to-start with no lag. Anything else should be labelled on the arrow, and the arrow should leave and enter the side of the box the link refers to (the start is the left edge, the finish the right edge).
| Link | Meaning | How to draw and label | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Finish-to-start (FS) | Successor starts after predecessor finishes | Right edge to left edge; no label needed | Pack boxes, then move |
| FS with lag | Delay after the finish | Right to left, labelled FS+3 | Pour concrete, wait 3 days to cure, then build |
| Start-to-start (SS) | Successor starts after predecessor starts | Left edge to left edge, labelled SS or SS+2 | Start electrics 2 days after partitions start |
| Finish-to-finish (FF) | Successor finishes after predecessor finishes | Right edge to right edge, labelled FF or FF+1 | Finish electrics a day after partitions finish |
| Start-to-finish (SF) | Successor finishes after predecessor starts | Left edge to right edge, labelled SF | Old system runs until the new one starts |
| FS with lead | Overlap before the finish | Right to left, labelled FS-2 | Start testing 2 days before the build ends |
Most networks are almost entirely finish-to-start, and quality checks expect that (see below). Use SS and FF where the work genuinely overlaps, and record why. Our guide to [leads and lags](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/) covers when each is justified, and the [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) guide works through an office fit-out network with SS, FF and lag links.

### How to draw a project network diagram step by step
1. **List the activities.** Take them from the lowest level of the WBS. Each should have an ID, a short verb-noun name and a clear finish. Our [work breakdown structure template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) helps if you are starting from scratch.
2. **Record the predecessors** of each activity in a table. Ask "what must be finished before this can start?" rather than "what comes next?", and note any SS, FF or SF links, leads and lags.
3. **Add a Start node** on the left. Every activity with no predecessor connects to it.
4. **Place activities in columns** from left to right. An activity goes in the column after the latest of its predecessors, so the diagram reads in time order.
5. **Draw an arrow for every dependency**, labelling any link that is not a plain finish-to-start.
6. **Add a Finish node** on the right. Every activity with no successor connects to it.
7. **Check the logic**: one start, one finish, no loops, no dangling activities and no redundant links (if A→B→C exists, a direct A→C arrow adds nothing).
8. **Add durations** to each node.
9. **Run the forward pass** to fill in ES and EF, then the **backward pass** for LS and LF, and calculate total float.
10. **Highlight the critical path**: the chain of activities with zero (or the lowest) total float.
11. **Review the diagram with the team** who will do the work. They will spot missing links and impossible sequences faster than anyone.
Tip
Draw the first version with sticky notes, one per activity. Moving notes is quicker than redrawing, and it gets the team involved in the logic.
Free template: the [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) records activities, durations and predecessors and calculates early and late dates and float, so you can check your diagram against it.

### Worked example 1: a six-activity office move
This illustrative network is the same six-activity network used in our [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) and [float and slack](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) guides, so you can follow the same numbers across all three. Here the activities are named for a small office move. Durations are in working days and all links are finish-to-start.

#### Step 1: activity list
| ID | Activity | Duration (days) | Predecessors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Agree move plan and layout | 3 | - |
| B | Fit out new office | 4 | A |
| C | Book removal firm | 2 | A |
| D | Install IT and network | 5 | B |
| E | Pack and label | 3 | C |
| F | Move and unpack | 2 | D, E |

#### Step 2: place the nodes and draw the arrows
| Column | Nodes | Arrows leaving this column |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Start | Start → A |
| 1 | A | A → B, A → C (A is a burst point) |
| 2 | B, C | B → D, C → E |
| 3 | D, E | D → F, E → F |
| 4 | F (a merge point) | F → Finish |
| 5 | Finish | - |
Put B and D on the top row and C and E on the bottom row, so that the two parallel paths are easy to see and no arrows cross.

#### Step 3: list the paths
For a small network, listing every path from start to finish is a quick way to find the critical path before doing any date calculations:
| Path | Durations | Length | Path float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A-B-D-F | 3 + 4 + 5 + 2 | 14 days | 0 (critical) |
| A-C-E-F | 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 | 10 days | 14 - 10 = 4 |

#### Step 4: fill in the nodes
The forward and backward pass (day-0 convention) give these node values:
| Node | ES | Duration | EF | LS | Total float | LF | Free float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A Agree move plan | 0 | 3 | 3 | 0 | 0 | 3 | 0 |
| B Fit out new office | 3 | 4 | 7 | 3 | 0 | 7 | 0 |
| C Book removal firm | 3 | 2 | 5 | 7 | 4 | 9 | 0 |
| D Install IT and network | 7 | 5 | 12 | 7 | 0 | 12 | 0 |
| E Pack and label | 5 | 3 | 8 | 9 | 4 | 12 | 4 |
| F Move and unpack | 12 | 2 | 14 | 12 | 0 | 14 | 0 |

#### Step 5: read the diagram
- **Critical path: A-B-D-F, 14 days.** Highlight these four nodes and their arrows. Any delay to them delays the move.
- **C and E share 4 days of float.** C has no free float, so a slip in C pushes E later; E has 4 days of free float because F cannot start until day 12.
- **A is a burst point.** A late move plan delays both paths at once.
- **F is a merge point.** It needs both the IT installation and the packing. If either path slips beyond its float, the move slips.

#### Step 6: the same network as activity on arrow
Drawn as AOA, the six activities become arrows between six events. No dummy is needed because no two activities share the same pair of events and every dependency can be drawn directly.
| Arrow | From event | To event | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| B | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| C | 2 | 4 | 2 |
| D | 3 | 5 | 5 |
| E | 4 | 5 | 3 |
| F | 5 | 6 | 2 |
The earliest and latest event times are: event 1, 0 and 0; event 2, 3 and 3; event 3, 7 and 7; event 4, 5 and 9; event 5, 12 and 12; event 6, 14 and 14. Events with equal earliest and latest times lie on the critical path, and the gap of 4 at event 4 is the float on the C-E path. See our [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) guide for every step of the calculation.

### Worked example 2: a nine-activity website relaunch
This illustrative example uses the website relaunch network from our [float and slack](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) guide. It has three parallel paths, two merge points and a near-critical path.
| ID | Activity | Duration | Predecessors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Requirements and kick-off | 4 | - |
| B | Visual design | 6 | A |
| C | Content writing | 7 | A |
| D | Content sign-off | 2 | C |
| E | Front-end build | 8 | B |
| F | Back-end integration | 10 | A |
| G | Content load | 3 | D, E |
| H | Testing | 5 | F, G |
| I | Launch | 1 | H |

#### Drawing it
- **Column 1:** A, a burst point with three successors (B, C and F).
- **Column 2:** B, C and F, stacked so that the design path is on top, content in the middle and back end at the bottom.
- **Column 3:** E (after B) and D (after C). F has no successor until H, so its arrow runs across to column 5.
- **Column 4:** G, a merge point for D and E.
- **Column 5:** H, a merge point for G and F.
- **Column 6:** I, then Finish.

#### Paths and float
| Path | Durations | Length | Path float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A-B-E-G-H-I | 4 + 6 + 8 + 3 + 5 + 1 | 27 days | 0 (critical) |
| A-C-D-G-H-I | 4 + 7 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 1 | 22 days | 5 |
| A-F-H-I | 4 + 10 + 5 + 1 | 20 days | 7 |
The critical path runs through design and front-end build. The content path is **near-critical** with 5 days of float: in the float guide, a 6-day slip in content writing switches the critical path to A-C-D-G-H-I and moves the launch to day 28. Mark it in a second colour on the diagram.
The two merge points, G and H, are where most schedule risk collects. If you want to recover time, the diagram also shows where not to look: shortening back-end integration (F) cannot bring the launch forward, because it has 7 days of float. See [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) for how to choose which critical activities to shorten.

### How to read a network diagram
Once the diagram is drawn and the nodes are filled in, look for five things:
1. **The critical path.** The chain of zero-float activities sets the end date. Focus management attention here.
2. **Near-critical paths.** Paths with only a few days of float can become critical after one bad week. Many teams set a threshold, such as 5 or 10 days, and track these paths as closely as the critical path.
3. **Merge points.** When several paths join, the activity can only start when the latest one finishes. The more paths that merge, the more likely at least one is late, an effect often called merge bias. Consider a buffer or earlier start for the paths that feed big merge points.
4. **Burst points.** A delay in a burst activity hits every path that leaves it. Protect them with clear ownership and early starts.
5. **Parallel work and resources.** Activities side by side in the same column can run at the same time, but only if people are available. If the same person is needed on both, you will have to [level resources](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/), which can change the critical path.
For a schedule with significant uncertainty, a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) on the same network shows how often each path ends up critical, which is a better guide to risk than a single set of float values.

### Network diagram vs Gantt chart, PERT chart and WBS
|  | Network diagram | Gantt chart | PERT chart | WBS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shows | Logic and flow of activities | Activities as bars against a calendar | Logic with three-point time estimates | Hierarchy of deliverables and work |
| Time scale | None (unless time-scaled) | Yes | None | None |
| Dependencies | Central | Shown as links between bars | Central | Not shown |
| Best for | Building and checking logic, finding the critical path | Communicating dates and tracking progress | Estimating duration under uncertainty | Defining scope |
| Weakness | Hard to read with hundreds of activities | Logic is harder to check | More estimating effort | Says nothing about sequence |
In practice you use them together: the WBS defines the work, the network sets the logic and the Gantt chart communicates the dates. Read our guide to [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) to see how the pieces fit together.

### Checking the logic: schedule quality tests
A network diagram is only as good as its logic. Missing or wrong links produce wrong dates and misleading float. Several of the checks in the DCMA 14-point schedule assessment, widely used on US defence and government projects, test the logic directly:
| Check | What it looks for | Threshold |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Logic | Incomplete activities missing a predecessor or successor | No more than 5% |
| Leads | Links with negative lag | None (0%) |
| Lags | Links with positive lag | No more than 5% of links |
| Relationship types | Share of finish-to-start links | At least 90% |
| Hard constraints | Activities with fixed dates instead of logic | No more than 5% |
| High float | Incomplete activities with total float above 44 working days | Flagged for review |
You do not need to work on a government contract to use these checks. They catch the most common problems in any network:
- **Loops:** A depends on B, which depends on A. Scheduling tools reject them, but they appear on hand-drawn diagrams.
- **Dangling activities:** an activity with no successor gets its late dates from the project finish, so its float looks far larger than it really is.
- **Constraints instead of links:** a fixed date overrides the logic and hides the real driver.
- **Too many leads and lags:** each one is an assumption that is easy to forget and hard to update.
Our guide to [float and slack](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) explains how unusually high float usually points to missing logic.

### Network diagrams in software
Most scheduling tools build the network from the dependencies you enter, so you rarely draw a large diagram by hand.
- **Microsoft Project** (desktop) has a dedicated Network Diagram view under View > Network Diagram. Format > Layout controls box arrangement and spacing, Format > Box Styles controls what each box shows, and link labels can display the dependency type and any lead or lag.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, shows dependencies and the critical path on its interactive Gantt charts from the Team plan upwards, with all four dependency types, lead and lag time, float and baselines.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** Gantt charts support all four dependency types and show the critical path and slack time.
- **[Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/)** lets you set dependencies between rows and identify the critical path on its Gantt chart, which suits date-driven projects.
- **[Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/)** premium plans include dependencies, and Plan 3 adds baselines and the critical path.
Many tools show the logic as links on the Gantt chart rather than as a separate network view; filter it to the critical and near-critical paths when checking a new schedule. The [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) is a simple starting point if you work in a spreadsheet.

### Common network diagram mistakes
- **Drawing the sequence you expect rather than the logic.** Only link activities that genuinely depend on each other; everything else can run in parallel.
- **Several start or finish points.** Connect every open start to a Start node and every open end to a Finish node.
- **Missing links.** An activity with no successor shows false float and can hide the real critical path.
- **Redundant links.** If A→B→C exists, a direct A→C arrow clutters the diagram without adding logic.
- **Unlabelled SS, FF or lag links.** Anyone reading the diagram will assume finish-to-start.
- **Mixing AON and AOA** in one diagram, or using dummies on an AON diagram.
- **Activities that are too large.** A three-month activity hides the dependencies inside it. Break it down until links are clear.
- **Using hammocks or summaries as logic.** Link the detailed activities, not summary bars; see our guide to [hammock activities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/hammock-activity/).
- **Not updating the diagram.** When durations, links or deadlines change, recalculate. The critical path can switch.
Read our guide to the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) to see how the network diagram fits into the full scheduling process.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project network diagram?**
A diagram of a project's activities and the dependencies between them, drawn as nodes and arrows from a single start to a single finish. It shows the logical sequence of the work and is used to find the critical path.

**Q: What are the two main types of network diagram?**
Activity on node (AON), also called the precedence diagramming method, and activity on arrow (AOA), also called the arrow diagramming method.

**Q: What is the difference between AON and AOA?**
In AON, activities are boxes and arrows are dependencies, and all four dependency types can be shown. In AOA, activities are arrows, nodes are events, only finish-to-start links are possible and dummy activities are sometimes needed.

**Q: What is the precedence diagramming method?**
Another name for activity-on-node diagramming, in which activities are nodes linked by arrows that can be finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish or start-to-finish, with leads and lags.

**Q: What is a dummy activity?**
A zero-duration arrow used in activity-on-arrow diagrams to show a dependency that real activities cannot show, or to stop two activities sharing the same start and end events. AON diagrams never need them.

**Q: What information goes in a network diagram node?**
At minimum an ID, name and duration. After the forward and backward pass, nodes usually also show early start, early finish, late start, late finish and total float.

**Q: What are merge and burst activities?**
A merge activity has two or more predecessors, such as F in our office move example. A burst activity has two or more successors, such as A. Merge points are where delays combine.

**Q: How do you find the critical path on a network diagram?**
List every path and add up its durations, or run a forward and backward pass. The longest path, whose activities have zero total float, is the critical path.

**Q: Is a PERT chart a network diagram?**
Yes. A PERT chart is a network diagram that uses three-point duration estimates to allow for uncertainty.

**Q: What is the difference between a network diagram and a Gantt chart?**
A network diagram shows the logic and flow of activities; a Gantt chart shows activities as bars against a calendar. Most tools build both from the same data.

**Q: Can you draw a network diagram in Excel?**
Yes, for small networks, using shapes and connectors, and a spreadsheet can calculate the dates and float. For larger projects, a scheduling tool that draws the logic automatically is quicker and less error-prone.

**Q: How do you create a network diagram in Microsoft Project?**
In Project desktop, enter tasks, durations and predecessors, then choose View > Network Diagram. Use Format > Layout and Box Styles to arrange the boxes and choose what they display.

**Q: Do I still need a network diagram if my software draws a Gantt chart?**
You may not need to draw one by hand, but reviewing the network logic, or the Gantt chart filtered to the critical path, is still the best way to catch missing links before you commit to dates.

# Project Objectives: How to Write Them (With Examples)

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-objectives/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project objectives explained: what they are, types, SMART criteria, a step-by-step method and 30+ examples, plus goals vs objectives and common mistakes.


## Project Objectives: How to Write Them (With Examples)
Project objectives are the specific, measurable results a project must achieve by a set date, such as cutting order processing time from 48 to 24 hours by 30 September. They turn a broad goal into targets you can plan, track and judge success against. This guide gives you a simple formula, a step-by-step method, a fully worked example and more than 30 examples you can adapt.
- Published 14 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- A project objective states a measurable result, a baseline, a target and a deadline; a goal states the broad direction.
- Write objectives as outcomes (what changes), not as activities or deliverables (what you do or produce).
- Use SMART as a quality check and a simple formula to draft: verb + metric + baseline + target + date + boundary.
- Three to five objectives is usually enough; more than that dilutes focus and makes trade-offs harder.
- Agree how and when each objective will be measured before work starts, and record it in the project charter.
- Revisit objectives at every stage gate and change them only through formal change control.

### What are project objectives?
**Project objectives** are the specific, measurable results a project is expected to achieve within a defined time frame. They describe what will be different when the project succeeds, for example lower costs, faster service or a new capability in use, and give the team, sponsor and stakeholders a shared basis for planning work and judging success.
A well-written objective usually contains five elements:
- **A result** described as a change, not a task ("reduce", "increase", "launch and adopt").
- **A measure** that everyone agrees on (hours, pounds, percentage, score, number of users).
- **A baseline** showing where you are today.
- **A target** showing where you need to be.
- **A deadline** by which the target must be met.
Objectives sit between the strategic reason for the project and the detailed plan. They usually start life in the business case or [feasibility study](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/feasibility-study/), are confirmed in the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) or project initiation document, and then shape the scope, schedule, budget and quality plans in the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/).

### Why project objectives matter
In our experience, clear objectives are the most useful tool a project manager has for making decisions when time, money or people are short.
- **They guide trade-offs.** When a feature, a deadline and a budget collide, the objectives tell you which matters most. An objective that says "live before the January sales peak" makes it clear that a late but perfect system is a failure.
- **They define scope.** Work that does not contribute to an objective is a candidate for removal, which is your first defence against [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).
- **They align stakeholders.** Writing objectives down brings different ideas of success into the open early, when they are cheap to resolve.
- **They make progress measurable.** Status reports can show movement against targets rather than just tasks completed.
- **They make closure possible.** Without measurable objectives you cannot say objectively whether the project succeeded, and [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) become a matter of opinion.
Studies of project success repeatedly rank a clearly defined goal among the most important conditions.

### Project goals vs objectives
A **goal** is the broad aim the project serves. An **objective** is a specific, measurable step towards it. One goal usually breaks down into several objectives.
|  | Project goal | Project objective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Sets direction and explains why | Defines exactly what must be achieved |
| Level of detail | Broad, often qualitative | Specific and quantified |
| Time frame | Often longer than the project | Within the project or a defined period after it |
| Measurability | Hard to measure directly | Measured against a baseline and target |
| Number | Usually one per project | Typically three to five |
| Example | Make it easier for patients to book appointments | Increase online bookings from 15% to 50% of all appointments by 31 March |
A simple test: if you cannot say whether it has been achieved on a given date, it is a goal, not an objective. Make sure every goal is supported by at least one measurable objective.

### Objectives vs deliverables, scope, milestones and KPIs
Project documents often mix objectives up with other planning terms. The table below uses one running example, a new customer self-service portal, to show the difference.
| Term | What it describes | Example (customer portal) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goal | The broad aim | Improve the customer service experience |
| Objective | The measurable result | Handle 40% of support requests through the portal within six months of launch |
| Deliverable | The output produced | A working portal, a knowledge base of 150 articles, trained support staff |
| Scope | The boundaries of the work | Account, billing and order queries; excludes complaints and sales |
| Milestone | A significant point in time | User acceptance testing signed off |
| Success criteria | How success will be judged at the end | Objective met; satisfaction score at least 4.2 out of 5 |
| KPI | An indicator tracked over time | Weekly share of requests resolved through the portal |

#### Outputs vs outcomes
The most common confusion is between **outputs** (what the project produces) and **outcomes** (the change those outputs cause). "Deliver a new CRM system" is an output. "Reduce the time to produce a customer quote from three days to one" is an outcome. Strong objectives focus on outcomes, because an output can be delivered on time and on budget and still fail to make any difference.
Many organisations use two layers: **delivery objectives** the project team controls (time, cost, quality) and **benefit objectives** the business realises, often after closure. Record both and name an owner for each; the sponsor or a business owner usually owns benefits.

### Types of project objectives
Most projects need objectives from more than one category. Covering several types stops the project optimising one dimension at the expense of another, for example hitting the date by cutting quality.
| Type | What it targets | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time | Delivery dates and durations | Open the new warehouse by 1 September 2027 |
| Cost and financial | Budget, savings, revenue, return | Complete the fit-out within the approved budget of £1.2 million |
| Quality | Standards, defects, compliance with specifications | Fewer than 5 high-severity defects open at go-live |
| Performance | Speed, capacity, reliability | Page load time under 2 seconds for 95% of visits |
| Business and benefit | Changes in the organisation's results | Raise repeat purchases from 22% to 30% of customers within 12 months |
| Regulatory and compliance | Legal, audit or safety requirements | Pass the external data protection audit with no major findings by June |
| People and stakeholder | Adoption, skills, satisfaction | 90% of the 300 field staff using the mobile app weekly by month three |
| Sustainability | Environmental and social impact | Divert at least 80% of construction waste from landfill |
PRINCE2 offers a useful cross-check. PRINCE2 7 defines seven performance targets that every project should set and control: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, risk and sustainability. Even if you do not use PRINCE2, asking whether you have an objective or tolerance for each of these seven helps you spot gaps.

### SMART objectives explained
SMART is the most widely used checklist for writing objectives. Most sources today expand it as Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
| Letter | Meaning | Question to ask | Weak | Stronger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S | Specific | What exactly will change, and for whom? | Improve the website | Reduce checkout abandonment on the UK website |
| M | Measurable | Which metric, what baseline, what target? | Make it faster | Cut average checkout time from 4 minutes to 2 minutes |
| A | Achievable | Is it realistic with our budget, people and skills? | Zero abandonment | Reduce abandonment from 70% to 60% |
| R | Relevant | Does it support the business goal and strategy? | Add a new font | Supports the goal of growing online revenue |
| T | Time-bound | By when will it be achieved and measured? | Soon | By 31 March, measured over April |
The idea is usually credited to George T. Doran, whose short article "There's a S.M.A.R.T. way to write management's goals and objectives" appeared in *Management Review* in November 1981. In Doran's original version, A stood for **assignable** (someone is responsible) and R for **realistic**. Both are still worth checking: an objective with no owner tends to drift.

#### When SMART is not enough
SMART checks how an objective is written, not whether it is the right objective. A SMART objective can still measure the wrong thing, such as training sessions held rather than whether staff can use the new system. Use SMART as a quality check, then ask: **does achieving this actually move us towards the goal?** and **could we hit the target while doing harm elsewhere?**
Tip
Pair speed or cost objectives with a quality objective. "Cut call handling time by 20%" on its own can be achieved by rushing customers off the phone; adding "while keeping first-contact resolution at or above 75%" closes that loophole.

### A simple formula for writing project objectives
SMART tells you what a good objective looks like. A formula helps you write one quickly. We use this structure:
**[Action verb] + [metric] + from [baseline] to [target] + by [date] + [boundary or condition]**
| Element | Purpose | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Action verb | Shows the direction of change | Reduce |
| Metric | What will be measured | average invoice processing time |
| Baseline | Where you are now | from 9 working days |
| Target | Where you need to be | to 3 working days |
| Date | When it must be achieved | by 30 June 2027 |
| Boundary or condition | Scope, quality floor or how it is measured | for all UK supplier invoices, measured over July |
Put together: **"Reduce average invoice processing time from 9 working days to 3 working days by 30 June 2027 for all UK supplier invoices, measured over July."** That is one sentence, it can be checked by anyone with access to the finance system, and it leaves the team free to decide how to achieve it.
Good verbs for outcomes include reduce, increase, achieve, adopt and eliminate. Avoid activity verbs such as support, explore or work on.

### How to write project objectives step by step
This process works for a one-page project brief or a full charter. Allow a workshop of one to two hours with the sponsor and key stakeholders for a medium-sized project.
1. **Start from the business need.** Read the business case, [cost-benefit analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/) or problem statement. Write the project goal in one sentence: why is the organisation spending money on this?
2. **Identify the stakeholders who define success.** List the sponsor, the users, the operations owner and anyone who must approve the result. Our [stakeholder management guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) explains how to map them.
3. **Ask what will be different.** For each stakeholder, ask: "If this project succeeds, what will you see or measure differently six months later?" Capture the answers in their own words.
4. **Turn answers into measurable results.** Choose a metric for each result. If there is no reliable data source, decide now how you will collect it, or choose a different metric.
5. **Collect baselines.** Measure the current position. An objective without a baseline cannot show improvement, and you may discover the problem is smaller (or larger) than assumed.
6. **Set realistic targets and dates.** Check targets against budget, resources, past performance and benchmarks. Involve the people who will do the work; they know what is achievable.
7. **Draft each objective with the formula and test it against SMART.** Keep each one to a single sentence and a single result. Split any objective that contains "and".
8. **Prioritise and limit the list.** Rank the objectives so the team knows which wins when they conflict. Aim for three to five.
9. **Assign an owner and a measurement plan.** For each objective record who owns it, the data source, and when it will be measured (at go-live, at closure or after closure).
10. **Agree and record.** Review the objectives with the sponsor and stakeholders, then record them in the charter or project initiation document. From this point, changes go through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
Tip
If stakeholders disagree on the objectives, resolve it before planning. A disagreement about objectives that is postponed to the delivery phase usually returns as a dispute about scope, budget or acceptance.

### Worked example: from business goal to project objectives
Here is the whole process applied to one project. A group of five medical clinics wants patients to book appointments online. Today most bookings come by phone, reception staff are overloaded and patients complain about waiting on hold.

#### Step 1: the goal
**Goal:** make it quicker and easier for patients to book appointments while reducing pressure on reception teams.

#### Step 2: first drafts from the workshop
- "Launch online booking." (an output, not a result)
- "Improve patient satisfaction." (no metric, baseline or date)
- "Reduce phone calls." (no target)
- "Do it within budget." (no figure)

#### Step 3: baselines collected
The practice manager pulls three months of data: 15% of appointments are booked online through an old form, reception answers about 2,400 calls a week, average time on hold is 6 minutes and the latest patient survey scored booking convenience at 3.1 out of 5. The approved budget is £85,000.

#### Step 4: final objectives
| # | Objective | Type | Owner | Measured |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Launch online booking for all five clinics by 28 February 2027, within the approved budget of £85,000 | Time and cost | Project manager | At go-live |
| 2 | Increase the share of appointments booked online from 15% to 50% by 31 August 2027 | Business and benefit | Operations director | Monthly from March; final in September |
| 3 | Reduce average weekly booking calls from 2,400 to 1,500 and average time on hold from 6 to 2 minutes by 31 August 2027 | Performance | Practice manager | Telephony reports, monthly |
| 4 | Raise the patient survey score for booking convenience from 3.1 to 4.0 out of 5 by the September 2027 survey | Stakeholder | Patient experience lead | September survey |
| 5 | Meet the organisation's data protection and accessibility requirements, with sign-off from the data protection officer before go-live | Compliance | Project manager | Before go-live |
Objective 1 covers what the project team controls. Objectives 2 to 4 describe the outcomes the clinics want and are owned by the people who run the service, because they will be measured after the project team has moved on. Objective 3 bundles two call measures with one owner and data source; you could split them. Objective 5 is a pass/fail compliance condition.
The objectives also made scope decisions easy. Online prescription renewals supported no objective, so they went to a later phase. Text-message reminders supported objective 3, so they were added through change control.

### Project objectives examples by project type
Adapt these examples to your own baselines and dates. Figures are illustrative.

#### IT and software projects
- Migrate all 1,200 user mailboxes to the new email platform by 15 May with no more than 4 hours of unplanned downtime per user.
- Reduce average month-end close time from 8 to 5 working days within two months of the new finance system going live.
- Achieve 99.9% monthly availability for the customer portal in the first quarter after launch.
- Retire the legacy CRM and its £60,000 annual licence by 31 December.

#### Construction projects
- Achieve practical completion of the 48-unit residential block by 30 November 2027.
- Complete the project within the contract sum of £6.4 million plus approved variations.
- Record zero RIDDOR-reportable incidents during the build.
- Achieve the agreed energy performance rating for all units at handover.

#### Marketing projects
- Generate 400 qualified leads from the spring campaign by 30 April at a cost per lead of £45 or less.
- Increase organic search traffic to the product pages from 8,000 to 12,000 visits a month by the end of Q3.
- Launch the rebrand across the website, packaging and all social channels by 1 March.

#### HR and training projects
- Train all 220 customer service staff on the new case-management system by 31 January, with at least 90% passing the competency assessment first time.
- Reduce average time-to-hire for engineering roles from 62 to 40 days by the end of the financial year.
- Roll out the new performance review process to every department before the April review cycle.

#### Nonprofit and public sector
- Provide 5,000 additional free school meals per week across the district from the start of the autumn term.
- Reduce the waiting list for the housing advice service from 10 weeks to 4 weeks within 12 months.
- Cut food waste at the three community kitchens by 30% compared with last year's baseline by December.

### Before and after: rewriting weak objectives
Most weak objectives fail in the same few ways. This table shows the problem and a rewrite.
| Weak objective | Problem | Rewritten objective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Improve customer service | Vague; no metric, baseline or date | Raise the customer satisfaction score from 72 to 80 by 31 December |
| Build a new mobile app | Output, not an outcome | Have 25,000 active monthly app users by the end of Q2, six months after launch |
| Hold six training workshops | Activity, not a result | Have 95% of warehouse staff certified on the new scanners by 1 October |
| Increase sales by 300% next month | Not achievable on the evidence | Increase monthly online sales from £40,000 to £52,000 by 30 June |
| Become the market leader | Outside the project's control and timescale | Win 15 new enterprise accounts from the target list by year end |
| Launch as soon as possible | No deadline | Launch the service in all regions by 1 April |
| Reduce processing time by 50% | No baseline | Reduce average processing time from 10 to 5 days by 31 July |

### Project objectives in Agile projects
Agile teams still need objectives, but they hold scope loosely and the outcome tightly: they fix the result they want and adjust the backlog as they learn.
- **Product goal.** The Scrum Guide (2020) introduced the Product Goal: a long-term objective for the product that the Product Backlog serves. It works much like a project goal.
- **Sprint goals.** Each sprint has a single sprint goal that gives the team focus for that iteration. Read more in [what is a sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/).
- **Outcome-based roadmaps.** Many teams express roadmap items as outcomes ("cut onboarding time in half") rather than features. See our guide to the [Agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/).
- **Release or programme objectives.** In scaled frameworks such as SAFe, teams set objectives for each planning interval and the business assigns them a value.
Measure Agile objectives with outcome metrics, not just velocity. Our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) lists useful options such as lead time, customer satisfaction and adoption.

### Project objectives and OKRs
OKRs (objectives and key results) are a goal-setting method developed at Intel under Andy Grove and later popularised by John Doerr. An OKR pairs a qualitative, inspiring **objective** with two to five measurable **key results**. They are usually set quarterly for teams and organisations rather than for individual projects.
The two work well together. A company OKR might be "Make self-service the easiest way to get help", with the key result "40% of support requests resolved without an agent". The customer portal project then adopts that key result as one of its objectives. Our free [OKR template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/okr-template/) helps you set and score them each quarter.

### How to track and evaluate project objectives
Writing objectives is only useful if you check them. Build the measurement into your normal project controls.

#### During delivery
- Show each objective on the first page of your [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/), with its current forecast (on track, at risk, off track).
- Review objectives at every stage gate or steering meeting.
- Assess every change request against the objectives it affects.

#### At closure
- Measure each delivery objective and record the result against its target.
- Explain any variance and capture what caused it in [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).
- Hand over benefit objectives that will be measured later to a named business owner, with dates. See our guide to [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/).

#### After closure
Many benefit objectives can only be measured months later. Schedule a benefits review in advance, for example six or twelve months after go-live, and compare actual results with the baseline and the business case.

### Common mistakes when setting project objectives
- **Writing activities, not results.** "Hold weekly meetings" or "deploy the software" says what you will do, not what will change.
- **No baseline.** "Reduce errors by 30%" is meaningless if nobody knows the current error rate.
- **Too many objectives.** Ten objectives with equal weight give the team no guidance when they conflict.
- **Bundling several results.** One objective containing three targets is hard to measure and impossible to prioritise.
- **Targets outside your control.** Market share or share price depends on factors the project cannot influence; choose something the project can affect.
- **Unmeasurable words.** Avoid "improve", "optimise", "enhance", "world-class" and "user-friendly" unless they are followed by a number.
- **Changing them informally.** Quietly lowering a target because the project is behind hides the real position. Change objectives openly through change control.

### Project objectives checklist
Use this checklist before the charter is signed. Every answer should be yes.
| Check | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Linked | Does each objective clearly support the project goal and a business priority? |
| Outcome | Does it describe a result, not an activity or deliverable? |
| Single | Does it contain one result (or closely related results with one owner)? |
| Measurable | Is there a named metric, a baseline and a target? |
| Time-bound | Is there a date for achievement and a date for measurement? |
| Achievable | Have the people doing the work confirmed it is realistic? |
| Owned | Is there a named owner? |
| Balanced | Is there a quality or risk safeguard against shortcuts? |
| Agreed | Has the sponsor approved it and is it recorded in the charter? |
When the objectives pass this check, use them to define the [project requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/) and build the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/). Every major work package should trace back to at least one objective.
To record your objectives alongside scope, milestones and budget, start with our free [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) or the shorter [project brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-brief-template/). For the investment case behind them, use the [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are project objectives?**
Project objectives are the specific, measurable results a project must achieve within a set time, such as reducing processing time from 10 to 5 days by 31 July. They define success and guide planning and trade-offs.

**Q: What are the 5 SMART objectives in project management?**
SMART is a checklist rather than five separate objectives. Each objective should be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. In George Doran's original 1981 version, A stood for assignable and R for realistic.

**Q: How many objectives should a project have?**
Three to five is a practical number for most projects. That is enough to cover time, cost, quality and the main business outcome without diluting focus. Very large programmes may have more, grouped under a few goals.

**Q: What is the difference between a project goal and a project objective?**
A goal is the broad aim, such as improving the patient booking experience. An objective is a specific, measurable result that moves you towards the goal, such as increasing online bookings from 15% to 50% by 31 August.

**Q: What is the difference between project objectives and deliverables?**
Deliverables are the outputs the project produces, such as a system, report or building. Objectives are the results those outputs should achieve. Read our guide to [project deliverables](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/).

**Q: What is the difference between objectives and success criteria?**
Objectives state what the project must achieve. Success criteria state how you will judge whether the project succeeded, and often include the objectives plus conditions such as stakeholder satisfaction or quality thresholds.

**Q: Can project objectives change during a project?**
Yes, if the business need changes, but only through formal change control with sponsor approval. Record the reason and update the charter, plan and baselines so that success is judged against the agreed version.

**Q: Who sets project objectives?**
The sponsor owns the objectives and approves them. The project manager usually facilitates and drafts them with input from stakeholders, users and the delivery team.

**Q: Where are project objectives documented?**
In the business case and [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) or project initiation document, and then referenced in the project management plan, status reports and closure report.

**Q: What are the main types of project objectives?**
Common types are time, cost and financial, quality, performance, business and benefit, regulatory and compliance, people and stakeholder, and sustainability objectives. Most projects need a mix.

**Q: How do you measure project objectives?**
Agree the metric, data source, baseline and measurement date when you set each objective. Track leading indicators during delivery, measure delivery objectives at closure and measure benefit objectives at a scheduled review afterwards.

**Q: What is an example of a good project objective?**
"Reduce average invoice processing time from 9 to 3 working days by 30 June 2027 for all UK supplier invoices." It states the result, metric, baseline, target, date and boundary in one sentence.

**Q: Are OKRs the same as project objectives?**
Not quite. OKRs pair a qualitative objective with measurable key results and are usually set quarterly for teams or organisations. Project objectives apply to one project. A project is often the way a key result is achieved.
