# Project Procurement Management: Steps, Contracts, Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project procurement management explained: the 4-stage process, procurement plan, RFP vs RFQ, contract types with worked examples, bid scoring and closure.


## Project Procurement Management: Steps, Contracts, Examples
Project procurement management is the work of buying the goods, services and results a project needs from outside the project team: deciding what to buy, choosing suppliers, agreeing contracts and managing them until the work is accepted and closed. Done well, it protects your budget, schedule and quality; done badly, it is a common source of disputes, delays and overruns. This guide covers the four stages, the procurement management plan, RFI, RFQ and RFP documents, contract types with worked numbers, bid scoring and how to control and close contracts.
- Published 30 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project procurement runs in four stages: plan, conduct (select suppliers), control (manage the contract) and close.
- Start with a make-or-buy analysis over the full life of the asset, not just the upfront cost.
- Contract type decides who carries cost risk: fixed price puts most risk on the seller, cost-reimbursable on the buyer, and incentive contracts share it.
- Agree mandatory requirements, weighted criteria and the price-scoring formula before any bids arrive.
- The PMBOK Guide 8th edition covers procurement in a dedicated appendix, and the July 2026 PMP exam includes the task "Plan and manage procurement".

### What is project procurement management?
Project procurement management is the set of activities used to acquire products, services or results from outside the project team. It covers planning what to buy and how, inviting and evaluating bids, selecting suppliers, agreeing contracts, managing supplier performance and changes, and formally closing each contract once the work has been accepted and paid for.
Most projects procure something: contractors and specialist consultants, software licences, equipment, materials, venues or a complete deliverable such as a building or an IT system. On some projects, such as construction or major IT implementations, most of the budget is spent through contracts, so procurement decisions shape the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/), the schedule and the risk profile.
Project procurement differs from routine purchasing. Purchasing is the transactional step of raising orders and paying invoices for things the organisation buys regularly. Project procurement is tied to one temporary project, often buys something unique, and has to fit the project's scope, schedule and risk plan.

#### Who does what in project procurement
| Role | Typical responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Project manager | Defines the need, contributes to make-or-buy decisions, writes or approves the statement of work, manages supplier delivery against the plan, accepts deliverables |
| Procurement or contracts officer | Owns the formal process, chooses the route to market, issues bid documents, runs the evaluation, holds contract authority and signs |
| Legal | Drafts or reviews terms and conditions, liability, intellectual property and dispute clauses |
| Finance | Confirms budget, payment terms and supplier financial checks; processes invoices |
| Technical evaluators | Score bids against technical criteria and check deliverables meet specifications |
| Sponsor | Approves significant spend and the final supplier choice where governance requires it |
In small organisations the project manager may do most of this alone. In larger and public-sector organisations only an authorised contracts officer can commit the organisation to a contract, so agree responsibilities early, ideally in a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/).

### Procurement in the PMBOK Guide and the PMP exam
PMI's treatment of procurement has changed across editions of the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/), which explains why study materials describe it differently.
| Edition | How procurement is covered |
| --- | --- |
| 5th edition (2013) | Four processes: Plan Procurement Management, Conduct Procurements, Control Procurements, Close Procurements |
| 6th edition (2017) | Three processes: Plan Procurement Management, Conduct Procurements, Control Procurements (closing was folded into Control Procurements) |
| 7th edition (2021) | No processes; procurement is discussed within the performance domains and models, methods and artifacts. The 6th-edition processes moved to PMI's Process Groups: A Practice Guide |
| 8th edition (November 2025) | Six principles, seven performance domains and 40 processes, plus a dedicated appendix, X4 Procurement, covering make-or-buy analysis, procurement strategy, bid documents, source selection, contract types and claims administration |
For exam candidates, the PMP exam content outline in force from July 2026 includes the task "Plan and manage procurement" in the Process domain (41% of the exam). Its enablers include planning procurement, selecting contract types, negotiating agreements, managing suppliers and contracts, and evaluating vendor performance. See our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) for the full exam structure.
In practice, most organisations still run procurement in four recognisable stages, whatever framework they follow. The rest of this guide uses those stages.

### The four stages of project procurement
| Stage | What happens | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Plan procurement | Identify what to buy, carry out make-or-buy analysis, choose the procurement strategy and contract type, write the statement of work and selection criteria | Procurement management plan, make-or-buy decisions, statements of work, bid documents, source selection criteria |
| 2. Conduct procurements | Issue bid documents, answer supplier questions, receive and evaluate bids, negotiate and award | Selected suppliers, signed contracts, updated schedule and risk register |
| 3. Control procurements | Monitor delivery and quality, approve invoices, manage changes and claims, review supplier performance | Accepted deliverables, approved changes, performance records, payments |
| 4. Close procurements | Confirm all work is accepted, settle final payments and claims, release retentions, archive records | Closed contracts, supplier performance evaluation, lessons learned |
The stages overlap with the rest of the project. You may be conducting one procurement while still planning another, and control continues for the whole contract. Procurement also links closely to [project integration management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-integration-management/), because supplier changes go through the same change control as everything else.

### How to run a project procurement step by step
The steps below follow one procurement from need to closure. Scale the formality to the value and risk: a $2,000 purchase might need one quote and a purchase order, while a $2 million contract needs a full tender.
1. **Confirm the need.** Check the requirement against the scope baseline and work breakdown structure, and confirm budget is available.
2. **Decide make or buy.** Compare doing the work in house with buying it, over the full life of the asset (see the worked example below).
3. **Choose the procurement strategy.** Decide the route to market (single quote, competitive quotes, open or restricted tender, framework or existing contract), the contract type and how many suppliers you need.
4. **Write the statement of work.** Describe what the supplier must deliver, to what standard, by when and how it will be accepted. See our [statement of work guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/).
5. **Set the evaluation method before you see bids.** Agree mandatory pass/fail requirements, weighted criteria, the scoring scale and the price formula, and record them in the bid documents.
6. **Issue the bid documents.** Send the RFI, RFQ or RFP with clear deadlines, answer questions in writing and share every answer with all bidders.
7. **Evaluate and select.** Check compliance, score bids independently, moderate the scores, check references and financial stability, and negotiate with the preferred bidder.
8. **Award and mobilise.** Sign the contract, notify unsuccessful bidders, hold a kick-off meeting and add the supplier's milestones to the [project schedule](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/).
9. **Control delivery.** Track milestones, quality, invoices, changes and risks, and hold regular supplier performance reviews.
10. **Close the contract.** Confirm acceptance, settle final payments and claims, release any retentions and record supplier performance and lessons learned.
Tip
Allow for procurement lead time. A competitive tender can take weeks or months from approval to signature, and that time belongs in the schedule as activities with owners, not as a single milestone.

### Make-or-buy analysis: a worked example
This is an illustrative example. A project needs a customer booking system. The team can build it in house or buy a hosted product. The comparison covers three years of use.
| Cost item | Make (build in house) | Buy (hosted product) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial cost | 600 hours x $90 = $54,000 | Setup and configuration $8,000 |
| Annual running cost | Maintenance $12,000 | Subscription $1,500 x 12 = $18,000 |
| Three-year total | $54,000 + 3 x $12,000 = $90,000 | $8,000 + 3 x $18,000 = $62,000 |
Over three years, buying is **$28,000 cheaper**. Building only catches up when $54,000 + $12,000t = $8,000 + $18,000t, which gives t = $46,000 / $6,000 = about 7.7 years. Unless the system will last well beyond that, or needs features no product offers, buying is the better choice on cost.
Cost is only part of the decision. Weigh these factors as well:
| Factor | Favours make | Favours buy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control and customisation | Unique requirements, competitive advantage | Standard needs met by existing products |
| Skills and capacity | Skilled staff available now | Skills missing or team fully committed |
| Time to deliver | No suitable product exists | Product available immediately |
| Risk | Supplier lock-in or insolvency would be serious | Delivery risk better held by a specialist |
| Data and intellectual property | Must own the IP and data fully | Licensed use is acceptable |
For larger decisions, discount the cash flows with [net present value](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/net-present-value/) or set them out in a full [cost-benefit analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/).

### The procurement management plan
The procurement management plan is part of the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/). It explains how the project will buy what it needs and who may do what. On a small project it may be a page; on a major programme it is a controlled document.
| Section | What to include | Example entry (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Items to procure | Each package, with make-or-buy result and estimated value | Office fit-out, about $300,000; removals, about $25,000 |
| Roles and authority | Who can approve, negotiate and sign, with spend limits | PM approves up to $10,000; contracts officer signs above |
| Procurement routes | Quotes, tenders or frameworks by value band | Under $25,000: three written quotes; above: competitive RFP |
| Contract types | Preferred type for each package and why | Fit-out: firm fixed price on a detailed design |
| Timeline | Lead times and key procurement dates | Fit-out tender issued week 4, awarded week 10 |
| Selection criteria | Mandatory and weighted criteria for each package | Quality 60%, price 40% |
| Supplier management | Performance reviews, reporting and KPIs | Fortnightly progress meeting and monthly scorecard |
| Risks and constraints | Supplier risks, insurance, bonds, compliance rules | Performance bond of 10% on the fit-out |
Our free [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) helps you estimate the value of each package before it goes into the plan.

### Procurement documents: RFI, RFQ, RFP and SOW
Bid documents tell suppliers what you need and how you will choose. Use the simplest one that fits.
| Document | Use it when | What suppliers return |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request for information (RFI) | You do not yet know what the market can offer | Capabilities, approaches and rough costs |
| Request for quotation (RFQ) | The item is clearly specified and price is the main differentiator | A price and delivery terms |
| Request for proposal (RFP) | The need is complex and you want suppliers to propose a solution | A technical proposal and a price |
| Invitation to bid or tender (IFB/ITB) | Formal, often public-sector, competitions for defined requirements | A sealed bid on standard terms |
Every procurement also needs a **procurement statement of work (SOW)**: the description of what the supplier must deliver. A good SOW states the objectives, scope and exclusions, deliverables and acceptance criteria, standards, schedule and milestones, reporting, and what the buyer will provide. Ongoing services often add a [service level agreement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/service-level-agreement-sla/) with measurable targets.
Our free [RFQ template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/rfq-template/) includes requirements, quantities, terms, submission instructions and a quote comparison sheet.

### Contract types and who carries the risk
The contract type decides how the supplier is paid and therefore who bears the cost if the work costs more than expected. There are three families: fixed price, cost-reimbursable and time and materials.
| Type | How payment works | Risk mainly with | Best when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Firm fixed price (FFP) | One agreed price for defined scope | Seller | Scope is clear and stable |
| Fixed price incentive fee (FPIF) | Target cost and profit, a share ratio for over- or underruns, and a ceiling price | Shared, mostly seller | Performance targets can be measured |
| Fixed price with economic price adjustment (FP-EPA) | Fixed price adjusted for inflation or commodity indices | Shared | Long contracts with volatile input costs |
| Cost plus fixed fee (CPFF) | Actual allowable costs plus a fixed fee | Buyer | Scope is uncertain |
| Cost plus incentive fee (CPIF) | Costs plus a fee that rises or falls with performance against target cost | Shared, mostly buyer | Uncertain scope but measurable targets |
| Cost plus award fee (CPAF) | Costs plus a fee awarded on the buyer's judgement of performance | Buyer | Performance is hard to measure objectively |
| Time and materials (T&M) | Agreed rates per hour or day plus materials, often with a not-to-exceed cap | Buyer | Small or urgent work, staff augmentation |

#### Worked example: the same overrun under four contract types
This is an illustrative example. A supplier estimates the work at $200,000, with a target profit or fee of $20,000 (a target price of $220,000). The work actually costs the supplier **$240,000**, a $40,000 overrun. For the incentive contracts the share ratio is 80/20 (buyer 80%, seller 20%), and the FPIF contract has a ceiling price of $250,000.
| Contract | Calculation | Buyer pays | Seller profit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FFP at $220,000 | Price is fixed | $220,000 | -$20,000 (a loss) |
| FPIF | Profit = 20,000 - 20% x 40,000 = 12,000; price = 252,000, capped at the 250,000 ceiling | $250,000 | $10,000 |
| CPIF | Fee = 20,000 - 20% x 40,000 = 12,000; price = 240,000 + 12,000 | $252,000 | $12,000 |
| CPFF | Fee stays at 20,000; price = 240,000 + 20,000 | $260,000 | $20,000 |
Under FFP the seller absorbs the whole overrun; under CPFF the buyer does. The incentive contracts share it, which keeps the seller motivated to control cost.
The FPIF contract also has a **point of total assumption (PTA)**: the cost above which the seller bears every extra dollar because the ceiling price has been reached. PTA = (ceiling price - target price) / buyer's share + target cost = (250,000 - 220,000) / 0.8 + 200,000 = **$237,500**. Here actual cost ($240,000) is above the PTA, so the buyer's price is capped at $250,000.

#### How to choose a contract type
- Clear, stable scope and competitive market: firm fixed price.
- Reasonably clear scope but long duration or volatile prices: fixed price with economic price adjustment.
- Scope too uncertain for a sensible fixed price: cost-reimbursable with an incentive fee, plus strong cost reporting.
- Small, urgent or open-ended work: time and materials with a not-to-exceed cap.
Whatever you choose, budget for it: fixed prices include the supplier's risk premium, and cost-reimbursable contracts need [contingency reserves](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) on the buyer's side. See our guide to [project cost management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-cost-management/).

### Evaluating bids and selecting a supplier
A fair, defensible evaluation is set up before bids arrive. It has three layers:
1. **Mandatory requirements (pass/fail):** for example, required insurance, data protection compliance, certifications or minimum experience. Any bid that fails is excluded.
2. **Weighted quality criteria:** such as technical approach, relevant experience, team, delivery plan and risk management, each scored on a defined scale by several evaluators.
3. **Price:** usually scored with a formula. A common one is: price score = (lowest compliant price / bid price) x maximum price points.

#### Worked example: weighted bid evaluation
This is an illustrative example. A project is buying a data migration service. Quality is weighted 70% and price 30%. Quality criteria are scored 0 to 10 and multiplied by their weight factor.
| Criterion (max points) | Supplier A | Supplier B | Supplier C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bid price | $180,000 | $150,000 | $165,000 |
| Price (30): lowest / bid x 30 | 25.0 | 30.0 | 27.3 |
| Technical approach (40): score x 4 | 9 = 36 | 6 = 24 | 8 = 32 |
| Relevant experience (20): score x 2 | 8 = 16 | 7 = 14 | 9 = 18 |
| Financial stability and risk (10): score x 1 | 9 | 6 | 8 |
| Total (100) | **86.0** | 74.0 | 85.3 |
Supplier B is cheapest but scores lowest overall. Suppliers A and C are within one point of each other, so the team checks references, clarifies assumptions in both bids and may invite best and final offers before awarding. Keep the evaluation records: they are your defence if an unsuccessful bidder challenges the decision.
Tip
Have evaluators score independently first, then meet to agree a moderated score with written reasons. It reduces bias and gives you a clear audit trail.

#### Negotiating with the preferred supplier
Negotiation should clarify and improve the deal, not reopen the competition. Prepare by listing the points that matter most to the project, such as payment milestones, acceptance tests, key personnel, liability caps and change rates, and decide in advance what you can trade. Agree outcomes in writing, make sure nothing contradicts what other bidders were told, and check that the final price still matches the scope in the statement of work.

### Controlling procurements and managing suppliers
Once the contract is signed, the project manager's job is to make sure the supplier delivers what was agreed, and that the buyer meets its own obligations, such as providing access, information and timely payment.
| Area | What to monitor | Example KPI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule | Supplier milestones against the integrated plan | Milestones achieved on time (%) |
| Quality | Inspections, tests and acceptance results | Deliverables accepted first time (%) |
| Cost | Invoices against milestones, approved changes, forecast final cost | Forecast final cost vs contract value |
| Changes and claims | Change requests, variations and disputes | Open change requests and average days to decide |
| Service | Responsiveness, reporting and service levels | Service level targets met (%) |
- Route every change to scope, price or dates through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) and record it as a contract variation before the work starts. Our [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) helps.
- Pay against accepted milestones or deliverables, not effort, wherever the contract allows.
- Add supplier risks, such as late delivery, key-person loss or insolvency, to the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) as soon as the contract is signed.
- Hold regular performance reviews and keep minutes; problems raised early are cheaper to fix.
- Handle claims and disputes using the process in the contract, escalating to negotiation, mediation or arbitration only as needed.

#### Common supplier risks and responses
| Risk | Early warning signs | Possible responses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Late delivery | Missed interim milestones, vague progress reports | Milestone payments, schedule float on supplier work, recovery plan clause |
| Poor quality | Rework on early deliverables, failed tests | Clear acceptance criteria, inspections before payment, retention |
| Supplier insolvency | Late payment of subcontractors, staff turnover | Financial checks at selection, performance bond, step-in or escrow rights |
| Key-person loss | Named experts replaced without notice | Key personnel clause requiring approval of replacements |
| Cost escalation | Frequent change requests, rising rates | Fixed rates for changes, FP-EPA indices, strict change control |

### Closing procurements
Each contract is closed when its work is complete, which may be long before the project ends. Closing a contract is not the same as closing the project: the [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/) happens once, at the end, while procurements close one by one.
1. Confirm all deliverables have been formally accepted against the SOW.
2. Resolve open change requests, claims and disputes.
3. Reconcile invoices and make the final payment; release retentions or bonds when the defects period ends.
4. Return or confirm transfer of buyer property, data and access rights.
5. Complete a supplier performance evaluation for future procurements.
6. Archive the contract file, correspondence and evaluation records.
7. Send formal written notice that the contract is complete.
8. Capture [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) about the procurement process itself.

### Procurement in Agile and hybrid projects
Traditional fixed-price contracts assume scope can be defined upfront, which clashes with [Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/), where scope evolves sprint by sprint. Common approaches include:
- **Time and materials with a cap** for a team working through a prioritised backlog, with the buyer's product owner controlling priorities.
- **Fixed price per increment or release,** where each increment has defined goals and acceptance criteria, and the buyer can stop after any increment.
- **Target cost contracts** that share savings and overruns, so both sides are motivated to deliver value within budget.
- **Fixed budget, variable scope:** the budget and dates are fixed, and the backlog is prioritised so the most valuable work is delivered first.
Whichever model you choose, write acceptance into the contract: a shared definition of done, regular reviews of working increments and a clear process for changing priorities without a formal contract variation each time.
Public-sector projects add legal rules. In the UK, for example, the Procurement Act 2023 came into force on 24 February 2025, and US federal agencies follow the Federal Acquisition Regulation. Our guide to [government project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/government-project-management/) covers the wider context.

### Common mistakes in project procurement
- **Vague statements of work.** If acceptance criteria are unclear, disputes and claims follow.
- **Setting criteria after seeing bids.** It makes the process unfair and open to challenge.
- **Choosing on price alone.** The cheapest bid can be the most expensive once rework, delays and changes are added.
- **Ignoring lead times.** Procurement activities missing from the schedule are a common cause of late starts.
- **Wrong contract type.** Fixed price on undefined scope leads to inflated bids or constant variations.
- **Informal changes.** Agreeing extra work in a meeting without a written variation creates unbudgeted cost.
- **Involving legal and finance too late.** Bring them in during planning for anything significant.
- **Forgetting to close.** Unclosed contracts leave retentions, warranties and liabilities untracked.
Read our guide to [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) to plan responses to supplier risks before they occur.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project procurement management?**
The processes for buying goods, services or results from outside the project team, from planning and supplier selection to contract management and closure.

**Q: What are the project procurement management processes in PMBOK?**
The PMBOK Guide 6th edition lists three: Plan Procurement Management, Conduct Procurements and Control Procurements. The 5th edition added Close Procurements as a fourth. The 8th edition (November 2025) covers procurement in a dedicated appendix on make-or-buy, strategy, bid documents, source selection, contract types and claims.

**Q: What are the four stages of procurement management?**
Plan procurement, conduct procurements (select suppliers and award contracts), control procurements (manage delivery, changes and payments) and close procurements.

**Q: What is included in a procurement management plan?**
The items to procure, roles and approval limits, procurement routes, preferred contract types, timeline, selection criteria, supplier management approach, and supplier risks and constraints.

**Q: What is a make-or-buy analysis?**
A comparison of the costs, risks and benefits of producing something in house against buying it from a supplier, ideally over the full life of the asset, used to decide whether to procure.

**Q: What are the main types of contracts in project procurement?**
Fixed-price (FFP, FPIF, FP-EPA), cost-reimbursable (CPFF, CPIF, CPAF) and time and materials. Each shares cost risk differently between buyer and seller.

**Q: Which contract type carries the most risk for the buyer?**
Cost-reimbursable contracts, especially cost plus fixed fee, because the buyer pays the seller's actual allowable costs, which may rise.

**Q: Which contract type carries the most risk for the seller?**
Firm fixed price, because the seller must deliver the agreed scope for the agreed price even if its costs rise.

**Q: What is the point of total assumption?**
In a fixed price incentive fee contract, the cost above which the seller bears all further overruns. PTA = (ceiling price - target price) / buyer's share ratio + target cost.

**Q: What is the difference between an RFI, an RFQ and an RFP?**
An RFI gathers market information before you decide how to buy. An RFQ asks for a price for a clearly specified item. An RFP asks suppliers to propose a solution as well as a price.

**Q: What is a procurement statement of work?**
A description of the work, products or services the supplier must deliver, detailed enough for suppliers to price it and for the buyer to accept it. See our [statement of work guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/).

**Q: Who is responsible for project procurement management?**
The project manager defines the need and manages supplier performance, while a procurement or contracts team usually runs the formal process and holds the authority to sign contracts.

**Q: How is a project procurement closed?**
By confirming all deliverables are accepted, settling final payments and claims, releasing retentions, archiving records, evaluating supplier performance and sending formal notice of completion.

# Project Quality Management: Plan, Assure and Control Quality

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: How project quality management works: planning, assurance and control, cost of quality, quality tools, a quality plan template and a worked example.


## Project Quality Management: Plan, Assure and Control Quality
Project quality management is the set of activities that make sure a project's deliverables meet their requirements and are fit for purpose. It combines planning what 'good' looks like, building quality into the way work is done, and checking outputs against agreed standards.
- Published 1 October 2026
- 4 min read

### Key takeaways
- Quality management covers planning, assurance (process) and control (product).
- Prevention is cheaper than finding and fixing failures.
- Agree measurable acceptance criteria with the customer early.
- Use simple tools such as checklists, Pareto charts and fishbone diagrams.

### The three parts of quality management
| Part | Focus | Typical activities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plan quality | Define standards and how they will be met | Set acceptance criteria, choose metrics, write the quality management plan |
| Manage quality (quality assurance) | The process: are we working in a way that produces quality? | Process audits, reviews, design standards, training, continuous improvement |
| Control quality | The product: does this output meet requirements? | Inspections, testing, measurements, sign-off against [requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/) |
PMBOK-based guidance calls these Plan Quality Management, Manage Quality and Control Quality. The underlying idea is that quality is planned and built in, not inspected in at the end.

### Quality vs grade
**Quality** is how well a deliverable meets its requirements. **Grade** is a category for products with the same use but different features. A basic budget hotel can be high quality (clean, reliable, as advertised) and low grade; a luxury hotel with broken lifts is high grade but low quality. Low quality is always a problem; low grade may be a perfectly sensible choice.

### Cost of quality
| Category | Type | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prevention | Cost of conformance | Training, standards, design reviews, better tools |
| Appraisal | Cost of conformance | Testing, inspection, audits |
| Internal failure | Cost of non-conformance | Rework and scrap found before delivery |
| External failure | Cost of non-conformance | Warranty claims, complaints, lost customers, fixes after release |
Money spent on prevention usually saves much more in failure costs, because defects get more expensive the later they are found.

### Quality management plan template
| Section | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Quality objectives | What quality means for this project and its customers |
| Standards | Regulations, company standards and specifications that apply |
| Acceptance criteria | How each [deliverable](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/) will be judged complete |
| Metrics | Measures and targets, e.g. defects per release, first-pass yield |
| Roles | Who reviews, tests, approves and audits |
| Assurance activities | Audits, peer reviews and process checks, with timing |
| Control activities | Inspections and tests for each deliverable |
| Tools | Checklists, templates and tracking tools |
| Non-conformance handling | How defects are logged, fixed and verified |
| Improvement | How lessons feed back into the process |

### Quality tools
- **Checklists and check sheets** to make inspections consistent and collect data.
- **Pareto charts** to show which few causes create most defects.
- **[Fishbone diagrams](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/)** to explore root causes.
- **Control charts** to show whether a process is stable over time.
- **Histograms and scatter diagrams** to understand variation and relationships.
- **Plan-do-check-act (PDCA)** cycles for continuous improvement, also central to [Lean](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/) and [Six Sigma](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/six-sigma/).

### Worked example
A software project sets a quality metric of no more than 5 high-severity defects found in user acceptance testing. In the first release, UAT finds 14. A Pareto analysis shows 9 come from one integration. The team adds contract tests for that interface (prevention) and an extra integration test stage (appraisal). In the next release UAT finds 4 high-severity defects, and rework time falls from 12 to 5 days. The change is recorded in [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) and the quality plan is updated.

### Common mistakes
- Leaving quality to a test phase at the end.
- Acceptance criteria that are vague or never agreed with the customer.
- Gold plating: adding extras the customer did not ask for, which costs time and adds risk.
- Measuring lots of things but acting on none of them.
- Treating quality as the quality team's job instead of everyone's.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project quality management?**
The processes that make sure a project's deliverables meet requirements: planning quality, managing (assuring) quality and controlling quality.

**Q: What is the difference between quality assurance and quality control in quality management?**
Quality assurance focuses on the processes used to create deliverables; quality control checks the deliverables themselves.

**Q: What is the cost of quality in project quality management?**
The total cost of conformance (prevention and appraisal) plus the cost of non-conformance (internal and external failures).

**Q: What is the difference between quality and grade in quality management?**
Quality is how well something meets requirements; grade is a category of features or specification. Low grade can be acceptable; low quality is not.

**Q: What is a quality management plan?**
The part of the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) that sets out standards, metrics, roles and activities for achieving quality.

**Q: What are the seven basic quality tools in quality management?**
They are commonly listed as cause-and-effect diagrams, check sheets, control charts, histograms, Pareto charts, scatter diagrams, and flowcharts or stratification.

**Q: What is gold plating in project quality management?**
Adding features or quality beyond what was agreed. It increases cost and risk without being requested.

**Q: What is PDCA in quality management?**
Plan-do-check-act, a repeating cycle for testing and embedding improvements.

**Q: Who is responsible for quality management on a project?**
The project manager is accountable for the quality approach, but everyone producing work is responsible for its quality.

**Q: How does Agile handle project quality management?**
Through practices such as a [definition of done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), automated testing, frequent reviews with users and continuous improvement in retrospectives.

**Q: How does ISO 9001 relate to project quality management?**
An international standard for quality management systems. Organisations certified to it must follow defined quality processes, which projects often inherit.

# Project Requirements: Types, Examples and How to Gather Them

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project requirements explained: the main types with examples, how to gather, write, prioritise and trace them, plus a worked example and sign-off checklist.


## Project Requirements: Types, Examples and How to Gather Them
Project requirements are the conditions and capabilities a project's result must meet to satisfy its stakeholders and the business need behind it. They are the foundation for your scope, estimates, tests and acceptance, so getting them clear early saves rework later. This guide explains the main types of requirements with examples, then walks you through gathering, writing, prioritising, tracing and controlling them, using one worked example from start to finish.
- Published 18 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Requirements describe what the result must do and the conditions it must meet, not how the team will build it.
- The main types are business, stakeholder, solution (functional and non-functional), transition and project requirements; high-level requirements in the charter are refined into detailed and technical ones.
- Gather requirements with several techniques, such as interviews, workshops, observation and prototypes, and always ask why a requirement is needed.
- Good requirements are necessary, unambiguous, singular, feasible and verifiable, with an ID, a source, a priority and an acceptance criterion.
- Prioritise with a method such as MoSCoW, trace each requirement to its source, deliverable and test, and change the baseline only through change control.

### What are project requirements?
Project requirements are statements of what a project's product, service or result must do, and the conditions it must satisfy, to meet the business need and stakeholder expectations. Each requirement should be specific enough to design, build and test against, and it should describe the need rather than prescribe a particular solution.
A useful test is **what, not how**. "Customers can pay by card online" is a requirement. "Integrate payment provider X using its hosted checkout" is a design decision. Mixing the two too early closes off options and hides the real need.
Strictly, **product requirements** describe the result (features, performance, quality) and **project requirements** describe conditions on the project (milestone dates, reporting, approvals). Most people use "project requirements" for both, as this guide does.
Requirements appear in several places as a project matures. Broad, high-level requirements go into the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/). Detailed requirements live in a requirements document or business requirements document (BRD), or as user stories in a [product backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/). A traceability matrix then links each one to the work and tests that satisfy it.

### Why project requirements matter
Almost everything else in planning depends on requirements. Your [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) defines the work needed to deliver them, the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) breaks that work down, estimates are based on it, and tests and acceptance criteria check that each requirement has been met. If the requirements are vague, every one of those downstream products inherits the vagueness.
PMI has highlighted this for years. Its Pulse of the Profession in-depth report on requirements management found that nearly half (47 percent) of unsuccessful projects failed to meet their goals because of inaccurate requirements management. The pattern is familiar: a missing requirement is cheap to fix in a workshop and expensive to fix after build or go-live.
- **Shared understanding.** Sponsors, users and the delivery team agree on what success looks like before money is spent.
- **Fewer disputes.** Clear, testable requirements make acceptance objective rather than a matter of opinion.
- **Controlled change.** A baselined set of requirements lets you tell an approved change from [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).

### Types of project requirements
The table below follows the IIBA's BABOK Guide classification (business, stakeholder, solution and transition requirements), with technical and project requirements added.
| Type | What it describes | Usually comes from | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Business | Why the project exists and the outcome the organisation needs | Sponsor, business case | Cut the cost of processing a supplier invoice by a third |
| Stakeholder | What a particular group needs from the result | Users, managers, customers | Accounts payable staff need to see all invoices awaiting approval in one list |
| Functional (solution) | What the solution must do: features, behaviours, rules | Users, business analysts | The system matches each invoice to its purchase order automatically |
| Non-functional (solution) | How well it must do it: performance, security, usability, availability | IT, security, users | Search results appear within two seconds for 95% of searches |
| Technical | Technology conditions and constraints the solution must respect | IT architecture, security | Runs on the organisation's existing cloud platform and uses single sign-on |
| Transition | What is needed to move from the current state to the new one | Operations, HR, IT | Migrate 18 months of open invoices; train 40 users before go-live |
| Project | Conditions on how the project is run | Sponsor, PMO, contracts | Go live before the financial year-end; report status fortnightly |

#### High-level requirements
High-level requirements are broad statements of what the result must achieve, captured at initiation, usually in the business case or charter. They are short and written so a sponsor can approve them without technical knowledge. For example: "Suppliers can submit invoices electronically", "Invoices under the approval threshold are processed without manual keying" and "Finance can report on invoice status at any time." Each high-level requirement is later broken down into several detailed functional, non-functional and technical requirements.

#### Functional vs non-functional requirements
Functional requirements describe behaviour: what happens when a user or system does something. Non-functional requirements describe qualities and limits. A system can meet every functional requirement and still fail if it is slow, insecure or unusable, which is why non-functional requirements are the ones most often forgotten.
| Non-functional category | Question it answers | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Performance | How fast, how many? | Handles 5,000 invoices a day with no loss of response time |
| Availability | When must it be working? | Available 07:00 to 20:00 on working days, with planned maintenance outside those hours |
| Security | Who may do what? | Only approvers can change payment details; all changes are logged |
| Usability and accessibility | Can people use it easily? | A new user can log and code an invoice after a one-hour induction |
| Compliance | Which rules apply? | Keeps invoice records for the period required by tax rules |

#### Technical requirements
Technical requirements state the technology conditions a solution must meet: platforms, integrations, data formats, security standards, infrastructure and support arrangements. They often come from enterprise architecture or IT security rather than from users. Give each one a source and a reason; a technical requirement nobody can justify is often an untested assumption.

#### Transition requirements
Transition requirements are temporary. They cover data migration, training, parallel running, cut-over and support during the change, and they disappear once the new state is stable. They are easy to miss because nobody "owns" them until go-live, so ask operations and support teams about them early.

### Requirements vs scope, objectives and deliverables
These terms are closely linked and often confused. Objectives say what the project must achieve, requirements say what the result must do to achieve it, scope says what work and deliverables are included, and deliverables are the outputs handed over.
| Term | Answers | Example from an invoice project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Project objectives](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-objectives/) | What outcome are we after? | Reduce processing cost per invoice by a third within 12 months of go-live |
| Requirements | What must the result do or be? | The system matches invoices to purchase orders automatically |
| Scope | What work and outputs are in and out? | In: invoice capture and approval. Out: expense claims |
| [Deliverables](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/) | What do we hand over? | Configured system, migrated data, trained users, support guide |
When work is delivered by a supplier, many of these requirements are written into a [statement of work](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/) so that both sides agree what will be accepted. See our [guide to project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) for how requirements become a scope statement and baseline.

### How to gather project requirements: step by step
Requirements gathering (often called elicitation) is a cycle of discovering, analysing, confirming and recording, repeated until the requirements are good enough to plan against. Scale the formality to your project's size and risk.
1. **Confirm the business need and objectives.** Read the business case and charter. If you cannot state the problem in one or two sentences, stop and agree it with the sponsor first. Every requirement should trace back to this need.
2. **Identify stakeholders.** List everyone who will use, pay for, support, approve or be affected by the result. Use your [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) analysis to decide who needs an interview, who joins workshops and who just reviews. A missed stakeholder is a missed requirement.
3. **Plan the approach.** Decide which techniques you will use, who will attend, where requirements will be recorded, how they will be prioritised and who signs them off.
4. **Elicit requirements.** Run interviews, workshops, observation sessions and document reviews. Ask about problems and goals, not just features, and ask "why?" until you reach the real need.
5. **Analyse and model.** Remove duplicates, split compound statements, resolve conflicts and fill gaps. Process maps and prototypes expose gaps that a list of sentences hides.
6. **Document.** Write each requirement in a consistent format with an ID, type, description, source, owner, priority and acceptance criterion.
7. **Prioritise.** Agree what is essential for the first release and what can wait, using a method such as MoSCoW.
8. **Validate and sign off.** Walk the stakeholders through the requirements, confirm they are correct and complete enough, and record formal approval. Sign-off does not make them permanent; it makes later changes visible and controlled.
9. **Baseline and trace.** Freeze the approved set as the requirements baseline and link each requirement to its source, design, deliverable and test in a traceability matrix.
10. **Manage change.** Route new or changed requirements through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/), assess their impact on scope, time, cost and risk, and update the baseline only once approved.
Tip
If stakeholders keep proposing solutions ("we need a dashboard"), ask what decision the solution would help them make. The answer is usually the real requirement, and there may be a simpler way to meet it.

### Requirements gathering techniques
No single technique finds everything: observation shows what people actually do, workshops resolve conflicts and prototypes catch misunderstandings early. Combine at least two or three.
| Technique | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interviews | Senior stakeholders, experts, sensitive topics | Time-consuming; one person's view may not represent the group |
| Facilitated workshops | Agreeing requirements across groups and resolving conflicts quickly | Dominant voices; needs a skilled facilitator and clear agenda |
| Observation (job shadowing) | Understanding current processes and workarounds | People behave differently when watched; takes time |
| Surveys and questionnaires | Large or dispersed user groups, testing how widespread a need is | Shallow answers; poor questions give poor data |
| Document analysis | Existing systems, policies, contracts, regulations | Documents may be out of date |
| Prototyping and wireframes | User interfaces and reports, where people know it when they see it | Stakeholders may mistake a prototype for a near-finished product |
| User stories and story mapping | Agile teams building in increments | Stories without acceptance criteria are too vague to test |
| Process mapping | Finding gaps between the current and future process | Can drift into redesign before the need is agreed |
A [gap analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gap-analysis-template/) is a quick way to structure the current-state versus future-state conversation, and a [feasibility study](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/feasibility-study/) can test whether demanding requirements are realistic before you commit to them.

#### Questions to ask stakeholders
- What problem are you trying to solve, and how do you handle it today?
- What would a good outcome look like in six months?
- What happens if this requirement is not met? Is there a workaround?
- Are there rules, policies or regulations that apply?
- How will you know the requirement has been met?

### How to write good requirements
A requirement that can be read two ways will be built one way and tested the other. The requirements engineering standard ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 lists characteristics of a well-formed individual requirement, including that it is **necessary**, **appropriate**, **unambiguous**, **complete**, **singular** (one requirement per statement), **feasible**, **verifiable**, **correct** and **conforming** to an agreed format. In practice, check every requirement against these questions:
- Is it needed to meet the business need, or is it a nice-to-have dressed up as a must?
- Could two people read it differently? Remove words such as fast, easy, flexible, user-friendly and appropriate.
- Does it state one thing? Split statements joined by "and" or "or".
- Can it be tested or inspected, with a clear pass or fail?
| Vague requirement | Improved requirement |
| --- | --- |
| The system must be fast. | Invoice search returns results within two seconds for 95% of searches with 50 concurrent users. |
| The system should be user-friendly. | A new accounts payable clerk can log and code a standard invoice unaided after a one-hour induction. |
| Managers can approve and reject invoices and add comments. | Split into three: approve an invoice; reject an invoice with a mandatory reason; add a comment visible to the submitter. |
| Use the best available security. | Payment detail changes require approval by a second authorised user, and every change is logged with user, date and time. |
Many teams use a consistent sentence pattern. Traditional specifications use "The system shall..." statements. Agile teams use [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) in the form "As a [role], I want [capability] so that [benefit]", each with acceptance criteria, often written as "Given [context], when [action], then [result]". Whatever format you choose, use it consistently. Our [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) gives you the fields to start with.

### Prioritising requirements with MoSCoW
Almost every project has more requirements than time or money. MoSCoW, which came out of the DSDM agile method, sorts requirements into four groups so that the most important ones are protected:
| Category | Meaning | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Must have | Essential; the release is not viable without it | Would we cancel or delay go-live if this were missing? |
| Should have | Important but not vital; a workaround exists | Painful to leave out, but the solution still works |
| Could have | Desirable; included if time and budget allow | Small impact if left out |
| Won't have this time | Agreed as out of this release | Recorded so it is not lost or reopened informally |
The Agile Business Consortium, which maintains DSDM, advises keeping Must haves to no more than around 60% of the effort so that there is contingency to absorb problems. If every stakeholder insists everything is a Must, ask the cancellation question in the table and look for a workaround. Alternatives include value versus effort scoring and the Kano model.

### Worked example: requirements for an invoice-processing project
This illustrative example follows a mid-sized company replacing paper-based supplier invoice handling with an automated system. The names and numbers are made up to show the method.
**Business need:** accounts payable keys around 2,000 paper and emailed invoices a month by hand, approvals are chased by email and late payments are damaging supplier relationships. **Objective:** cut processing cost per invoice by a third and pay 95% of approved invoices on time within 12 months of go-live.
**High-level requirements (in the charter):** HL1 suppliers can submit invoices electronically; HL2 invoices are matched and routed for approval without manual keying; HL3 finance can see the status of any invoice; HL4 the change is in place before the financial year-end.
After interviews with accounts payable, two workshops with approvers and a review of the payments policy, the business analyst breaks the high-level requirements down. An extract:
| ID | Requirement | Type | Priority | Acceptance criterion | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F-01 | The system extracts supplier, date, amount and PO number from PDF invoices | Functional | Must | 95% of test invoices in the sample set extracted without correction | HL2, AP workshop |
| F-02 | Invoices matching a purchase order within tolerance are approved automatically | Functional | Must | Test invoices within tolerance reach Approved with no manual step | HL2, payments policy |
| F-03 | Approvers can approve or reject from a mobile device | Functional | Should | Approval completed on a supported phone in user testing | Approver workshop |
| N-01 | Status search returns results within two seconds for 95% of searches | Non-functional | Must | Performance test with 50 concurrent users | HL3, finance interview |
| T-01 | Uses the company's single sign-on | Technical | Must | Users log in with existing credentials | IT security standard |
| TR-01 | Open invoices from the old process are migrated before go-live | Transition | Must | Reconciled count and value of migrated invoices signed off by finance | AP interview |
| F-04 | Suppliers can see payment status in a self-service portal | Functional | Won't (this time) | Not applicable; deferred to phase 2 | Procurement interview |
Notice what the example does. Each requirement has a single statement, a type, a priority and an objective test. Each traces back to a high-level requirement or a named source. The supplier portal, a popular idea in the workshops, is recorded as a Won't have so it is not lost, and it is not silently added to scope.
The traceability matrix then links forward from each requirement to the design element, the WBS deliverable and the test case:
| Req ID | Source | Design / configuration | Deliverable (WBS) | Test case | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F-01 | HL2 | Capture module settings | 1.2 Configured invoice capture | UAT-04 | Passed |
| F-02 | HL2 | Matching rules, 2% tolerance | 1.3 Approval workflow | UAT-07, UAT-08 | In test |
| N-01 | HL3 | Search index configuration | 1.4 Reporting | PERF-02 | Not started |
| TR-01 | AP interview | Migration script | 2.1 Data migration | MIG-01 | In progress |
Tip
Trace in both directions. Forward tracing shows that every requirement is built and tested. Backward tracing shows that every piece of work exists because of a requirement, which is how you spot gold-plating.

### The requirements document and traceability matrix

#### What a requirements document contains
Predictive projects usually collect requirements in a business requirements document (BRD) or requirements specification. Keep it as short as the project allows; a requirements document nobody reads protects nobody. A typical structure:
- Purpose, background and business need
- Objectives and success measures
- Scope summary, including what is out of scope
- Stakeholders and user groups
- Assumptions, [constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/) and dependencies
- Requirements by type, each with ID, description, priority, acceptance criterion, source and owner
- Approval and sign-off record, with version history
Our free [business requirements document template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/) includes these sections with prioritised requirements, acceptance criteria and a sign-off page, and the [project scope template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-scope-template/) turns the result into a scope statement.

#### The requirements traceability matrix
A requirements traceability matrix (RTM) is a table that links each requirement to where it came from and where it goes: its source, business objective, design element, WBS deliverable, test cases and current status. It answers three questions at any point in the project: Is every requirement being delivered? Is every requirement being tested? What is affected if this requirement changes? A spreadsheet is enough for small projects.

### Requirements in Agile and hybrid projects
Agile teams still need requirements; they just avoid detailing them all up front. Requirements live in the product backlog, usually as epics broken into user stories, owned and ordered by the product owner. Detail is added through [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) shortly before the work is planned, when the team knows most about it.
| Aspect | Predictive (plan-driven) | Agile (adaptive) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When detail is defined | Mostly before design and build | Just in time, ahead of each iteration |
| Main format | Requirements document with "shall" statements | Product backlog of user stories with acceptance criteria |
| Change | Formal change control against a baseline | Expected; the product owner reorders the backlog |
| Acceptance | Testing against the specification, then sign-off | Acceptance criteria per story plus the team's Definition of Done |
Acceptance criteria are specific to each story, while the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) applies quality standards to every item, so non-functional requirements such as security or accessibility checks often sit there. Many organisations run a hybrid: high-level requirements, constraints and non-functional requirements are agreed up front for governance and contracts, and functional detail emerges through the backlog. The [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) works well for this.

### Managing requirement changes
Requirements will change as the business moves and users see early versions. Change is not the problem; uncontrolled change is. Once requirements are approved, treat them as part of the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).
1. Log the proposed change with its reason and who raised it, using a [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/).
2. Use the traceability matrix to find every design element, deliverable and test affected.
3. Assess the impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk.
4. Take it to whoever holds the authority to decide, often the sponsor or a change control board.
5. If approved, update the requirements, baseline, plan and traceability matrix, and tell the team and stakeholders. If rejected, record the decision.
In Agile projects the product owner can reorder the backlog freely, but changes to agreed release goals, budgets or contracts still go through governance. Read our [guide to scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) for ways to spot and stop unapproved requirement growth.

### Common project requirements mistakes
- **Solutions disguised as requirements.** "We need a new CRM" is a solution. Ask what problem it solves and record that.
- **Talking only to managers.** The people who do the work know the exceptions and workarounds. Observe them.
- **Forgetting non-functional and transition requirements.** Performance, security, data migration and training are the usual late surprises.
- **Vague words.** Fast, easy, robust and flexible cannot be tested. Replace them with numbers or observable behaviour.
- **Everything is a Must.** If nothing can be dropped, nothing is prioritised. Use MoSCoW with the cancellation test.
- **No owner or source.** When nobody can explain why a requirement exists, it cannot be challenged or clarified.
- **No change control.** Requirements added in corridors and emails quietly grow the scope.

### Templates and tools for project requirements
For many projects, a document template and a spreadsheet traceability matrix are enough. Start with the [business requirements document template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/), and use the [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) if you work in Agile.
As projects grow, project management software helps keep requirements linked to the work. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, combines request forms for structured intake, custom fields for requirement attributes such as priority and source, and dashboards to track status, which suits teams that manage many requirements across several projects. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is a strong choice for software teams who hold requirements as epics and stories in a backlog.
Requirements are one input to scope and planning. See our [guide to the project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) for where high-level requirements are first agreed.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are project requirements?**
Project requirements are the conditions and capabilities a project's result must meet to satisfy the business need and stakeholders, such as features, performance levels, rules and deadlines.

**Q: What are the main types of project requirements?**
Business, stakeholder, solution (split into functional and non-functional), transition and project requirements. Technical requirements are often listed separately.

**Q: What is an example of a project requirement?**
"Invoices that match a purchase order within 2% are approved automatically" is a functional requirement. "Search results appear within two seconds for 95% of searches" is non-functional. "Train 40 users before go-live" is a transition requirement.

**Q: What are high-level project requirements?**
Broad statements of what the result must achieve, captured at initiation in the business case or project charter. They are short, written for sponsors, and later broken down into detailed functional, non-functional and technical requirements.

**Q: What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements?**
Functional requirements describe what the solution does, such as approving an invoice. Non-functional requirements describe how well it does it, such as speed, availability, security and usability.

**Q: How do you gather project requirements?**
Confirm the business need, identify stakeholders, plan your approach, then elicit requirements through interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis and prototypes. Analyse, document, prioritise and validate them, then baseline and trace them.

**Q: Who is responsible for project requirements?**
The project manager is accountable for the requirements process. Business analysts or product owners usually elicit and document requirements, the sponsor approves them, and users, experts and IT provide the content.

**Q: What is a requirements traceability matrix?**
A table linking each requirement to its source, design, WBS deliverable, test cases and status. It shows every requirement is delivered and tested.

**Q: What is MoSCoW prioritisation?**
A method from DSDM that sorts requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time, so the essential requirements are protected if time or budget runs short.

**Q: Are project requirements the same as project scope?**
No. Requirements say what the result must do. Scope defines the work and deliverables needed to meet those requirements, including what is out of scope. Requirements feed the scope statement.

**Q: How are project requirements handled in Agile?**
As epics and user stories in a product backlog owned by the product owner, refined just before the work is planned, each with acceptance criteria. Common quality standards sit in the Definition of Done.

**Q: Why do project requirements fail?**
Common causes are missing stakeholders, vague wording, solutions recorded instead of needs, forgotten non-functional or transition requirements, weak prioritisation, and changes that bypass change control.
