# Project Resources: Types, Examples and How to Plan Them

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-resources/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What project resources are, the main types with examples, how to identify, estimate and manage them, an RBS, a resource plan example and common mistakes.


## Project Resources: Types, Examples and How to Plan Them
Project resources are the people, equipment, materials, facilities, services and information a project needs to do its work, paid for from the project budget. Planning them well means knowing what you need, when you need it and where it will come from, before the schedule depends on it.
- Published 30 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 14 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project resources fall into two broad groups: the team (people) and physical resources such as equipment, materials and facilities.
- Identify resources from the work breakdown structure, then estimate type, quantity, skill and timing for each activity.
- A resource breakdown structure and resource calendars make needs and availability visible.
- Check availability across all projects, not just yours, before you commit to dates.
- Use allocation, leveling and smoothing to resolve conflicts, and release resources as soon as their work ends.
- PMBOK 8 treats resources as one of seven performance domains, covering both team and physical resources.

### What are project resources?
**Project resources** are everything a project consumes or uses to produce its deliverables: the people who do the work, and the equipment, materials, facilities, software, services and information they need. They are paid for from the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) and are usually limited, shared with other work and available only at certain times.
PMI's PMBOK Guide groups resources into two broad categories: **team resources** (the people assigned to the project) and **physical resources** (equipment, materials, facilities, infrastructure and supplies). Many articles also list **time** and **money** as resources. In PMI's terms, time and cost are better thought of as [project constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/) that resources are planned against: money buys resources, and time limits when they can be used. This guide covers all of them, but keeps that distinction clear.
Resources are different from tasks. A task is the work to be done; a resource is who or what does it. Linking the two is called [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/).

### Types of project resources
| Type | Examples | Typical planning unit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **People (team resources)** | Project manager, analysts, developers, engineers, designers, contractors, subject matter experts | Hours, days or FTE |
| **Equipment** | Machinery, vehicles, laptops, test devices, scaffolding | Units per day or week |
| **Materials and supplies** | Steel, cabling, components, printed materials, consumables | Quantity (tonnes, metres, items) |
| **Facilities** | Offices, meeting rooms, labs, workshops, warehouse space | Days or weeks of use |
| **Software and infrastructure** | Licences, cloud hosting, test environments, data platforms | Licences, months or usage |
| **Services** | Consultancy, testing, translation, security review, legal advice | Fixed price or rate |
| **Information and knowledge** | Standards, historical data, designs, documentation, specialist know-how | Access and availability |
| **Financial resources** | Approved budget, contingency, funding tranches | Money per period |

#### People
People are usually the most critical and the hardest resource to plan. Skills, experience and availability vary, and the same person is often shared between several projects and business-as-usual work. Plan in terms of **roles and skills first**, then name individuals as early as you can. A [skills matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) helps you see who can do what.

#### Physical resources
Equipment, materials and facilities have their own constraints: lead times, storage, delivery windows, maintenance and safety rules. On construction, engineering and event projects they can drive the whole schedule, so long-lead items need ordering early and tracking like tasks.

#### Services, software and information
Outsourced services and software licences are often forgotten until late. Treat them as resources with a start date, a cost and an owner. Information resources, such as access to existing designs or data, can block work just as effectively as a missing person.

#### Tangible and intangible resources
Some guides divide resources into **tangible** (people, equipment, materials, facilities, money) and **intangible** (knowledge, relationships, reputation, goodwill). Intangible resources are harder to plan but still matter: a sponsor's support or a supplier relationship can decide whether you get the tangible resources you need.

### Why managing project resources matters
Most schedules are built from task logic first and only later checked against who is actually available. When resources are not planned, problems appear as:
- **Over-allocation:** the same person is booked on several tasks at once, so work slips.
- **Idle time:** people or equipment wait for work that is not ready, which costs money.
- **Late delivery of materials or equipment**, holding up dependent tasks.
- **Skill gaps** discovered after work has started.
- **Budget overruns** from last-minute contractors, overtime or expedited delivery.
- **Burnout and turnover**, which make every other problem worse.
Good resource planning turns the schedule into something that can be staffed and supplied. It also gives sponsors and resource managers an early view of what the project will need from them, which makes negotiation easier.

### Project resource management in the PMBOK Guide
PMI's **PMBOK Guide, eighth edition** (published late 2025) organises project management around seven performance domains: governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources and risk. The **Resources** domain covers both the project team and physical resources, and replaces the Team domain of the seventh edition. Its processes are:
1. **Plan resource management:** decide how resources will be estimated, acquired, managed and released.
2. **Estimate resources:** work out the type and quantity of people and physical resources each activity needs.
3. **Acquire resources:** obtain the team, equipment, materials and facilities, internally or externally.
4. **Lead the team:** build, develop and support the team, and resolve issues.
5. **Monitor and control resourcing:** check resources are available and used as planned, and correct deviations.
If you studied the sixth edition, these map closely to its six resource processes: Plan Resource Management, Estimate Activity Resources, Acquire Resources, Develop Team, Manage Team and Control Resources. The ideas have not changed much; the newer edition simply groups them into one domain and combines team development and management under leadership.

### How to plan project resources step by step
1. **Start from the scope.** Use the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) to list every [work package](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/) and activity. You cannot estimate resources for work you have not defined.
2. **Identify the resource types each activity needs.** Ask: which skills, which equipment, which materials, which facilities, which services?
3. **Estimate quantity and duration.** How many people, for how many hours, and how much material? Use the estimating methods below.
4. **Build a resource breakdown structure (RBS).** Group the resources by category so nothing is missed and costs can be rolled up.
5. **Check availability.** Compare needs with resource calendars and with other projects' demands. [Capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) shows whether the organisation can supply what you need.
6. **Decide the source.** Internal team, another department, a contractor, a supplier or a hire company. External resources go through [procurement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/).
7. **Cost the resources.** Multiply quantities by rates to build the bottom-up [cost estimate](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/).
8. **Load the schedule.** Assign resources to activities, check for over-allocation and level where needed.
9. **Agree roles and responsibilities.** A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) makes ownership clear.
10. **Document it in a resource management plan.** Record how resources will be acquired, tracked and released, as part of the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/).

#### Estimating resource requirements
- **Bottom-up estimating:** estimate each activity's needs and add them up. The most accurate, but needs a detailed WBS.
- **Analogous estimating:** base needs on a similar past project. Fast, but only as good as the comparison.
- **Parametric estimating:** use a rate, such as hours per screen or square metres per day, multiplied by quantity.
- **Expert judgment:** ask the people who have done the work before, especially for specialist skills.
- **Historical data:** timesheets and actuals from earlier projects are often the best evidence available.
Express people effort in hours or days first, then convert to [full-time equivalents (FTE)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/full-time-equivalent-fte/) for planning. Our guide to [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/) covers the methods in more detail.
Tip
Plan against realistic availability, not a full working week. After meetings, support work, leave and other projects, a "full-time" team member may have only 60 to 80% of their time for your project. Agree the figure with their line manager.

### Resource breakdown structure (RBS)
A **resource breakdown structure** is a hierarchical list of the resources a project needs, grouped by category and type. It does for resources what the WBS does for scope. A simple example:
- **1. Labour**: 1.1 Project management; 1.2 Business analysis; 1.3 Development (1.3.1 Senior developer, 1.3.2 Developer); 1.4 Testing
- **2. Equipment**: 2.1 Laptops; 2.2 Test devices
- **3. Software and infrastructure**: 3.1 Cloud test environment; 3.2 Licences
- **4. Facilities**: 4.1 Training room
- **5. External services**: 5.1 Penetration testing; 5.2 Accessibility audit
The RBS helps you check that every type of resource has been considered, roll costs up by category, and report demand by skill across projects. It is often cross-referenced with the WBS: each work package lists the RBS items it needs.
|  | Work breakdown structure (WBS) | Resource breakdown structure (RBS) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breaks down | The work and deliverables | The resources that do the work |
| Answers | What has to be done? | Who or what will do it? |
| Lowest level | Work package | Specific resource type or role |
| Used for | Scope, schedule and cost control | Resource estimating, costing and capacity checks |

### Resource calendars and availability
A **resource calendar** shows when each resource is available: working days and hours, shifts, public holidays, planned leave, training and commitments to other work. Equipment and facilities have calendars too, covering bookings, maintenance and hire periods.
Resource calendars matter because a schedule calculated on generic working days can be badly wrong. A specialist who works three days a week, or a lab booked by another team for a fortnight, changes what is possible. Most scheduling tools let you set calendars per resource, and the schedule then calculates dates around them.

### Example: a resource plan
Here is an extract from a resource plan for a six-month customer portal project:
| Resource | Quantity | When | Source | Estimated cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project manager | 0.5 FTE | Months 1-6 | Internal PMO | $33,000 |
| Business analyst | 1.0 FTE | Months 1-3 | Internal | $36,000 |
| Developers | 3.0 FTE | Months 2-6 | Contractor | $162,000 |
| Tester | 1.0 FTE | Months 4-6 | Internal QA team | $27,000 |
| Laptops | 3 | Month 2 | IT equipment pool | $0 (reused) |
| Cloud test environment | 1 | Months 3-6 | Cloud service | $4,800 |
| Penetration test | 1 engagement | Month 5 | External supplier | $8,000 |
| Training room | 2 days | Month 6 | Internal facilities | $0 |
Each line should also have an **owner** (who approves the resource), any **assumptions** (such as the contractor day rate) and the **risk** if it is not available on time. The costs roll up into the project budget. A [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) gives you a ready-made structure for this.

### Acquiring resources
Once you know what you need, you have to get it. The main routes are:
- **Internal assignment:** negotiate with functional or resource managers for named people. Agree the percentage of time, dates and how conflicts will be handled.
- **Pre-assignment:** some people are named in the project charter or contract, for example a key technical lead.
- **External hire:** contractors, consultants and agencies, usually under a [statement of work](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/).
- **Purchase or hire of physical resources:** through procurement, with lead times built into the schedule.
- **Shared pools:** equipment, rooms and environments booked from a central pool.
In a matrix organisation the project manager rarely owns the people. Your influence comes from a clear, early request backed by the schedule, and from a good relationship with the resource managers. A [project management office](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/), where one exists, often arbitrates when several projects want the same people.

### Managing resources during the project

#### Allocate and level
Assign resources to tasks, then check for over-allocation. [Resource leveling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) moves work so no one is overloaded, even if the finish date moves. Resource smoothing evens out demand within available float without moving the end date. Both are explained in our leveling guide.

#### Track usage and availability
Compare planned and actual effort each week or sprint. Watch for people consistently working more than planned, tasks waiting on unavailable resources, and materials or equipment arriving late. Variances in resource usage often show up in cost reports later; catching them early is cheaper.

#### Look after the team
People are not interchangeable units. Clear roles, realistic workloads, recognition and quick resolution of conflicts keep productivity steady. The [project manager's role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-roles-and-responsibilities/) includes protecting the team from constant re-prioritisation.

#### Release resources
When a resource's work is finished, release it formally so it can go to other work and stop costing the project. Return equipment, end licences and contracts, and update resource calendars. This is part of project closure, but it happens throughout the project, not only at the end.

### Resources in Agile projects
Agile teams tend to think about resources differently. Instead of assigning individuals to tasks, they keep **stable, cross-functional teams** and plan how much work the team can take on in each iteration. The question changes from "who is free for this task?" to "what is the team's capacity this sprint?"
Physical resources, licences, environments and specialist support still need planning, and organisations running several Agile teams still need cross-team capacity planning. Resource management becomes more about **funding and protecting stable teams** than about booking people task by task.

### Common resource problems and fixes
| Problem | Likely cause | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Key person over-allocated | Booked on several projects or overlapping tasks | Level the schedule, reprioritise with sponsors, or bring in cover |
| Specialist only available late | Not requested early enough | Request early; resequence work; consider a contractor |
| Materials arrive late | Lead times not in the schedule | Add procurement tasks and lead times; order early |
| People idle waiting for work | Dependencies or approvals not ready | Resequence, or release the resource temporarily |
| Skill gap discovered mid-project | Roles planned generically | Training, mentoring or specialist support; update the skills matrix |
| Resource costs above estimate | Rates, overtime or productivity assumptions wrong | Re-estimate remaining work and update the forecast |
If several projects keep competing for the same people, the issue is usually portfolio-level demand rather than any single plan. See [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) for ways to handle it. Critical chain project management is one scheduling method designed specifically around resource constraints.

### Tools for managing project resources
For a small project, a spreadsheet resource plan and a shared calendar can be enough. As soon as people are shared across projects, a tool that shows **workload by person across all projects** saves a lot of manual checking.
- **Wrike** (our top-ranked tool) offers workload and resource planning with cross-project views; its most advanced resource planning, budgeting and financial tracking sit on the higher, quote-based tiers.
- **Asana** includes workload and resource management on its Advanced plan.
- **monday.com** offers workload views, with advanced resource and portfolio features on its Enterprise plan.
- Spreadsheets remain useful for RBS lists, resource plans and skills matrices, even when scheduling happens in a tool.

### Related guides
Project resources connect to almost every part of planning. Our guides to [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) and [full-time equivalents](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/full-time-equivalent-fte/) help you measure supply, and the [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) and [training plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) help with roles and skills.
The natural next step after identifying your resources is assigning them to work.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are project resources?**
Project resources are the people, equipment, materials, facilities, software, services and information a project needs to produce its deliverables, paid for from the project budget.

**Q: What are the main types of project resources?**
People (team resources), equipment, materials and supplies, facilities, software and infrastructure, services, information and knowledge, and financial resources. PMI groups them into team resources and physical resources.

**Q: What are the 4 types of project resources?**
Many guides list four: human, financial, material and time. It is a useful simplification. In PMI's terms, time and money are constraints and the budget, while resources are split into the team and physical resources.

**Q: Is time a project resource?**
It is often described as one, because it is limited and must be planned. Strictly, time is a constraint: the schedule sets when resources can be used, rather than time being consumed like materials.

**Q: What is the difference between human and physical resources?**
Human (team) resources are the people who do the work. Physical resources are the non-human items they use, such as equipment, materials, facilities and infrastructure.

**Q: What is project resource management?**
The processes used to plan, estimate, acquire, lead and control the people and physical resources a project needs, so the right resources are available at the right time and used efficiently.

**Q: Who is responsible for project resources?**
The project manager plans and manages them, but in most organisations functional or resource managers own the people and equipment. Resources are agreed between them, with a PMO or sponsor arbitrating conflicts.

**Q: What is a resource breakdown structure?**
A hierarchical list of the resources a project needs, grouped by category and type, such as labour, equipment, materials and services. It is used for estimating, costing and checking that nothing is missed.

**Q: What is a resource calendar?**
A calendar that shows when a resource is available, including working hours, shifts, holidays, leave and commitments to other work. Scheduling tools use it to calculate realistic dates.

**Q: How do you estimate resource requirements for a project?**
Break the work down with a WBS, decide which skills, equipment and materials each activity needs, then estimate quantities using bottom-up, analogous or parametric methods, expert judgment and historical data.

**Q: What is the difference between resource allocation and resource leveling?**
Allocation assigns specific resources to tasks. Leveling then adjusts task dates so no resource is over-allocated, even if that moves the finish date.

**Q: What happens if project resources are over-allocated?**
Work slips, quality drops and people burn out. Fix it by leveling or smoothing the schedule, reprioritising, adding capacity or reducing scope.

**Q: What is a resource management plan?**
Part of the project management plan that sets out how resources will be identified, estimated, acquired, managed and released, including roles, training needs and how conflicts are resolved.

**Q: How are resources managed in Agile projects?**
Agile teams usually keep stable, cross-functional teams and plan work against team capacity each iteration, rather than assigning individuals task by task. Physical resources and specialist support still need planning.

# Project Risk Management: Process, Steps and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project risk management step by step: plan, identify, score and respond to risks, with a probability-impact matrix, EMV, a worked example and templates.


## Project Risk Management: Process, Steps and Examples
Project risk management is the ongoing process of planning for, identifying, analysing, responding to and monitoring uncertain events that could affect a project's objectives, for better or worse. This guide walks you through the process step by step, gives you scoring scales you can copy, shows how to size a contingency reserve with expected monetary value, and follows one worked example from first workshop to closure.
- Published 30 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project risk management is a continuous loop, not a one-off workshop: plan, identify, analyse, respond, implement and monitor.
- Define probability and impact scales in real units (days, pounds, % of budget) before anyone scores a risk.
- Every significant risk needs a named owner, a response, a trigger and a review date, or it is just a worry on a list.
- Expected monetary value turns a ranked list into a defensible contingency reserve.
- Manage opportunities as deliberately as threats; they rarely appear by accident.
- Scale the method to the project: a small team needs a short register and a monthly review, not a 40-page plan.

### What is project risk management?
**Project risk management** is the systematic process of identifying, analysing, responding to and monitoring project risks throughout the life of a project. Its aim is not to remove all uncertainty, which is impossible, but to make uncertainty visible early so the team can decide deliberately what to do about it while options are still cheap.
A [project risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk/) is an uncertain event or condition that, if it happens, would have a positive or negative effect on at least one objective such as scope, schedule, cost or quality. PMI uses this definition in the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/). Risk management deals with three related things:
- **Threats:** risks with a negative effect, such as a key supplier delivering three weeks late.
- **Opportunities:** risks with a positive effect, such as a new test tool halving regression testing time.
- **Issues:** risks (or surprises) that have already happened and now need resolving. They move out of the risk register and into the [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/).
In the eighth edition of the PMBOK Guide, published by PMI in November 2025, Risk is one of seven performance domains, alongside Governance, Scope, Schedule, Finance, Stakeholders and Resources. The guide describes its risk processes as a continuous loop that the team adapts to the project rather than a fixed sequence.

### Why project risk management matters
Most project problems were visible as risks before they became issues. Risk management is the habit of saying them out loud, writing them down and acting on them.
- **Cheaper responses.** A risk spotted in planning can often be avoided by changing the plan. The same risk discovered during delivery usually costs rework, overtime or a delay.
- **Realistic estimates and reserves.** Analysing risks tells you how much contingency time and money the plan really needs, instead of adding a flat 10% and hoping.
- **Better decisions by sponsors.** A ranked risk list shows decision-makers what they are accepting when they approve a scope, date or budget, and reporting top risks in every [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) means they hear about trouble early.
- **Captured upside.** Looking for opportunities finds savings and shortcuts that teams focused only on threats miss.

### Key risk management terms
These terms come up throughout the process. Agreeing what they mean on your project avoids confusion in workshops and reports.
| Term | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trigger | A warning sign that a risk is about to occur | The contractor misses an interim milestone |
| Risk owner | The person accountable for monitoring a risk and making sure the response happens | Facilities manager |
| Risk exposure | The combined potential effect of the risks you have identified at a point in time | Total expected cost of open threats: £20,000 |
| Residual risk | The risk that remains after a response is in place | Delay still possible, but now one week rather than three |
| Secondary risk | A new risk created by a response | Splitting the move into two weekends adds a risk of data being out of sync |
| Contingency reserve | Time or money set aside for identified risks, inside the baseline | £15,000 held by the project manager |
| Management reserve | Time or money for unidentified risks, held outside the baseline | 5% held by the sponsor |

### The project risk management process in 7 steps
The steps below follow the risk processes in the PMBOK Guide. On a real project they overlap and repeat: you will identify new risks in month five and re-analyse old ones whenever something changes.

#### Step 1: Plan risk management
Decide how risk will be handled on this project before you start listing risks. Record the answers in the risk section of the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/), or in a separate risk management plan on larger projects.
- Roles: who facilitates, who owns risks, who approves the use of contingency.
- Scales and thresholds: what each score means in days and money, and which scores go to the sponsor.
- Rhythm and tools: how often the register is reviewed, where risks are reported and where they are recorded.

#### Step 2: Identify risks
Find as many relevant risks as you reasonably can, from as many viewpoints as possible. Good sources are the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/), assumptions and [constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/), the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/), [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) from similar projects and specialists' [expert judgment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/expert-judgment/).
Write each risk in cause, event and effect form: **Because of** [a fact that is true now], **there is a risk that** [an uncertain event], **which would lead to** [an effect on an objective]. This stops vague entries such as 'resourcing' and makes the next steps much easier.

#### Step 3: Perform qualitative risk analysis
Score each risk for probability and impact using your agreed scales, multiply them and rank the results in a probability-impact matrix. Qualitative analysis is quick and works on every project. It tells you where to spend your attention first.
Also note **proximity**: a medium risk that could happen next week often needs action before a high risk that cannot happen until the final quarter.

#### Step 4: Perform quantitative risk analysis (where justified)
For larger or high-stakes projects, put numbers on the combined effect of the top risks. Common techniques are expected monetary value, decision trees, [sensitivity analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/sensitivity-analysis/) and [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/). Small projects can usually rely on expected monetary value alone.

#### Step 5: Plan risk responses
For each risk above your threshold, choose a strategy (see the response table below), agree specific actions, assign an owner, set a trigger and decide what the [contingency plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) is if the response does not work. Add the cost and effort of responses to the plan and budget; a response with no time or money behind it will not happen.

#### Step 6: Implement risk responses
Carry out the agreed actions. This is where many projects fail: the register shows a sensible mitigation, yet nobody was given time to do it. Put response actions into the schedule as tasks with owners and dates.

#### Step 7: Monitor risks
Review the register on a fixed rhythm and whenever something significant changes. At each review, re-score open risks, check triggers, confirm actions are on track, close risks that can no longer happen, add new ones and move any that have occurred to the issue log. Report the top risks and the remaining contingency to the sponsor.
Tip
A quick test of whether your process is working: pick any high risk in the register and ask its owner what they did about it in the last two weeks. If the answer is 'nothing', the register is a record, not a management tool.

### How to score risks: probability and impact scales
Scores only mean something if everyone uses the same definitions. Agree scales like these in step 1, adjusted to the size of your project. The examples below are for a project with a budget of £400,000 and a duration of nine months.

#### Probability scale
| Score | Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Rare | Less than 10% chance |
| 2 | Unlikely | 10% to 30% |
| 3 | Possible | 31% to 50% |
| 4 | Likely | 51% to 80% |
| 5 | Almost certain | More than 80% |

#### Impact scale
| Score | Schedule | Cost (budget £400,000) | Quality or scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Very low | Under 3 days | Under £4,000 (below 1%) | Barely noticeable |
| 2 Low | 3 days to 1 week | £4,000 to £12,000 (1% to 3%) | Minor, accepted by users |
| 3 Medium | 1 to 2 weeks | £12,000 to £20,000 (3% to 5%) | Noticeable, needs sponsor agreement |
| 4 High | 2 to 4 weeks | £20,000 to £40,000 (5% to 10%) | Key feature reduced |
| 5 Very high | More than 4 weeks | Over £40,000 (above 10%) | Deliverable unfit for purpose |
Score impact on the objective that would be hit hardest. A risk that would cost £5,000 (impact 2) but delay go-live by three weeks (impact 4) scores 4 for impact.

#### Probability-impact matrix
Multiply probability by impact to get a score from 1 to 25, then use agreed bands to decide what happens next.
| Probability \ Impact | 1 Very low | 2 Low | 3 Medium | 4 High | 5 Very high |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 Almost certain | 5 Medium | 10 High | 15 High | 20 Critical | 25 Critical |
| 4 Likely | 4 Low | 8 Medium | 12 High | 16 Critical | 20 Critical |
| 3 Possible | 3 Low | 6 Medium | 9 Medium | 12 High | 15 High |
| 2 Unlikely | 2 Low | 4 Low | 6 Medium | 8 Medium | 10 High |
| 1 Rare | 1 Low | 2 Low | 3 Low | 4 Low | 5 Medium |
| Band | Score | Typical rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Critical | 16 to 25 | Response agreed within a week; reported to the sponsor; reviewed weekly |
| High | 10 to 15 | Response and owner required; reviewed at every project meeting |
| Medium | 5 to 9 | Owner assigned; response if cost-effective; reviewed monthly |
| Low | 1 to 4 | Accept and watch; reviewed at phase ends |
Tip
Watch for the 'everything is a 3' problem. If most risks score 3 by 3, ask scorers to justify each 3 with a number of days or pounds.

### Expected monetary value and contingency reserve
**Expected monetary value (EMV)** is the probability of a risk multiplied by its financial impact. Threats have negative impacts and opportunities positive ones, but it is simpler to keep threats as costs and opportunities as savings, as below. Adding up the EMVs of your identified risks gives a reasoned starting point for the contingency reserve.
| Risk | Probability | Impact if it occurs | EMV |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 Fit-out finishes late, needing extra time in the old building | 40% | £30,000 cost | £12,000 |
| R2 Network cabling fails certification and must be redone | 20% | £15,000 cost | £3,000 |
| R3 Lease signature delayed by the landlord's lawyers | 25% | £20,000 cost | £5,000 |
| O1 Existing furniture can be reused instead of bought | 50% | £10,000 saving | -£5,000 |
| **Total** |  |  | **£15,000** |
On this basis the project would hold a contingency reserve of about £15,000. You will not spend exactly that: if R1 happens it costs £30,000, and if not, nothing. EMV works because across a set of risks some occur and some do not. On large projects, use [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/), which shows the range of outcomes and lets the sponsor choose a confidence level.
- Use EMV to compare responses: a £4,000 mitigation that cuts R1's probability from 40% to 15% reduces its EMV from £12,000 to £4,500, a saving of £7,500 for a £4,000 spend.
- Keep contingency reserve inside the cost baseline and management reserve outside it, as described in our [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) guide.
- Release contingency as risks close, and report the remaining balance with the top risks.

### Risk response strategies for threats and opportunities
PMI describes five strategies for threats and five for opportunities. The table summarises them with examples.
| Threat strategy | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Avoid | Change the plan so the threat cannot happen or cannot affect the objective | Drop an unproven component and use a tested one |
| Mitigate | Reduce the probability, the impact or both | Run a full-volume rehearsal before a data migration |
| Transfer | Move the financial impact or ownership to a third party | Insurance, a fixed-price contract or a performance bond |
| Accept | Take no action now; actively accept by holding a reserve, or passively by doing nothing | Accept a small risk of rain delaying an outdoor survey |
| Escalate | Refer the risk to someone with the authority to act, when it is outside the project's scope | A company-wide hiring freeze that threatens several projects |
| Opportunity strategy | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exploit | Act to make sure the opportunity happens | Assign your best developer to finish a module early |
| Enhance | Increase its probability or benefit | Ask a supplier for early samples of a cheaper component |
| Share | Partner with a third party better able to capture it | Share a test environment with another project and split the cost |
| Accept | Take advantage if it happens, without acting now | Use a price fall if one occurs |
| Escalate | Refer it to a higher level when the benefit lies outside the project | A tool that would help the whole programme |

#### How to choose a response
1. If the risk is outside the project's authority, escalate it and record who accepted it.
2. Ask whether the plan can change to avoid it cheaply; avoidance is often best during planning.
3. Otherwise compare mitigation and transfer options: does the response cost less than the exposure it removes?
4. Accept what is left, with a contingency plan and trigger for high risks, and log any secondary risks.

### Worked example: risk management on an office relocation
A professional services firm is moving 120 staff to a new office. The project has a £400,000 budget, a nine-month schedule and a fixed move weekend agreed with the landlord of the old building. Here is how the team applies the process.

#### Plan and identify
In week two the project manager runs a 90-minute workshop with facilities, IT, HR, finance and the fit-out contractor, using the scales above. Four of the 22 risks identified are shown here.
| ID | Risk statement | P | I | Score | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | Because the fit-out contractor is also working on two other sites, there is a risk that fit-out finishes 2 to 4 weeks late, which would force us to extend the old lease at about £30,000 | 3 | 4 | 12 High | Facilities manager |
| R2 | Because the building's cabling is new and untested, there is a risk that it fails certification, which would cost about £15,000 and a week to redo | 2 | 3 | 6 Medium | IT lead |
| R3 | Because the landlord's legal team is short-staffed, there is a risk that the lease is signed three weeks late, delaying the start of fit-out | 2 | 4 | 8 Medium | Property director |
| O1 | Because most desks are less than three years old, there is an opportunity to reuse them and save about £10,000 | 3 | 2 | 6 Medium | Project manager |

#### Plan responses
- **R1, mitigate and transfer:** add weekly site inspections, include a 50% completion milestone in the contract with liquidated damages for late handover, and agree in advance a two-week extension option on the old lease. Trigger: the 50% milestone is missed by more than five working days.
- **R2, transfer and mitigate:** the cabling contract requires the installer to fix failed runs at its own cost, and the first floor is tested a month early so problems surface while there is time.
- **R3, escalate:** the landlord relationship sits with the property director, who agrees to chase weekly; the project records the risk and its owner but does not try to manage it directly.
- **O1, enhance:** run a furniture condition survey in month two, not month seven, so reuse can be designed into the floor plan.
The responses cost about £4,000 in extra inspections and earlier testing. The team adds them to the schedule as tasks and to the budget, and sets the contingency reserve at £15,000 using the EMV table above.

#### Monitor and close
| Review | What changed | Register update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Month 3 | Lease signed on time; furniture survey confirms 80% of desks reusable | R3 closed. O1 now likely (P4), saving confirmed into the budget |
| Month 5 | Contractor meets the 50% milestone two days early | R1 probability reduced to 2; score 8 (residual risk). Contingency for R1 partly released |
| Month 7 | First-floor cabling test finds four failed runs; installer fixes them at no cost | R2 closed. A new risk added: move weekend clashes with month-end close (P3, I3) |
| Month 9 | Move completes on the planned weekend | Remaining risks closed; lessons recorded |
The point is the rhythm: specific risks, shared scales, owners, funded responses and monthly reviews.

### How to run a risk identification workshop
Workshops bring different viewpoints together. A good one takes 60 to 120 minutes.
1. **Invite the right people.** Include the core team, a sponsor representative, key suppliers and someone who has run a similar project. Six to ten people is a workable group.
2. **Set the scene (10 minutes).** Restate the objectives, scope, key dates and the scoring scales, so everyone assesses against the same targets.
3. **Generate risks silently first (15 minutes).** Ask each person to write risks on sticky notes or a shared board before discussion. This stops the loudest voice setting the agenda.
4. **Walk the plan (30 minutes).** Go through the WBS, the schedule's key dependencies and the list of assumptions, asking 'what could go wrong or better here?'
5. **Run a pre-mortem (15 minutes).** Imagine it is the end of the project and it has failed, or succeeded beyond expectations. Ask what happened.
6. **Group and rewrite (15 minutes).** Merge duplicates and rewrite each risk in cause, event and effect form.
7. **Score quickly and assign owners (15 minutes).** Agree rough scores and a provisional owner; detailed response planning can follow afterwards.
Prompt categories help coverage: schedule, cost, scope, technical, people, suppliers, regulation and stakeholders. Ask explicitly about opportunities, or you will get none.

### Risk appetite, tolerance and thresholds
These three terms describe how much risk the organisation is prepared to take. They decide which risks the project manager can accept and which must go to the sponsor.
| Term | Level | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Risk appetite | Strategic: the broad attitude to risk | 'We will take moderate technical risk to be first to market, but we have very low appetite for safety or data protection risk.' |
| Risk tolerance | The acceptable variation around an objective | 'The launch may move by up to two weeks; the budget may vary by 5%.' |
| Risk threshold | The measurable trigger for escalation | 'Any single risk with a cost impact over £20,000 goes to the steering group.' |
Ask the sponsor to state these in the planning step; otherwise the project manager has to guess what is acceptable. Clear thresholds are part of good [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/).

### PMI, PRINCE2 and ISO 31000 compared
The main frameworks describe the same cycle with different names. You can combine them without conflict.
|  | PMI (PMBOK Guide 8th edition) | PRINCE2 (7th edition) | ISO 31000:2018 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Set-up | Plan risk management | Risk management approach | Scope, context and criteria |
| Find | Identify risks | Identify | Risk identification |
| Analyse | Perform risk analysis (qualitative and quantitative) | Assess | Risk analysis and risk evaluation |
| Respond | Plan risk responses; implement risk responses | Plan; implement | Risk treatment |
| Track and report | Monitor risks | Communicate | Monitoring and review; recording and reporting; communication and consultation throughout |

### Scaling risk management to your project
The right amount of process depends on size, complexity and how much is at stake. These are our suggestions, not rules from any standard.
| Project type | What you need | Review rhythm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small (a few people, under three months) | A one-page register with 5 to 15 risks, a simple 1 to 5 matrix and named owners | Every fortnight or at each status meeting |
| Medium (one team, several months) | A risk section in the project plan, defined scales, a register, EMV for the top risks and a contingency reserve | Weekly for high risks; full review monthly |
| Large or high-stakes | A separate risk management plan, a risk lead, quantitative analysis, management reserve and steering group reporting | Weekly risk meeting; quarterly deep review |
| Agile teams | Risks raised in refinement, planning and retrospectives; spikes to reduce technical uncertainty; risk items in the backlog | Every sprint |
Short increments and early feedback reduce many risks, but risks outside the team, such as suppliers, funding or regulation, still need an owner.

### Tools and templates for project risk management
A spreadsheet register is enough for most projects. Our free [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) includes the columns used in this guide, and the [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) covers risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies in one workbook.
Project management software helps when several projects share risks or you want risks linked to tasks and dashboards. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, combines custom item types and request forms with dashboards and AI features that can help flag at-risk work, which suits PMOs running a standard risk process across a portfolio.

### Common project risk management mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treating risk as a one-off workshop | The register goes stale within weeks | Put a risk review on every project meeting agenda |
| Vague risks like 'budget' or 'resources' | Nobody can score or act on them | Use cause, event and effect statements |
| Scores without defined scales | Two people score the same risk differently | Define scales in days and money before scoring |
| Responses with no owner, date or budget | Nothing happens until the risk becomes an issue | Schedule response actions as tasks |
| Confusing risks and issues | Current problems crowd out future ones | Move occurred risks to the issue log |
| Hiding uncomfortable risks | Sponsors are surprised later, and trust suffers | Report the top five risks honestly in every status report |
| Never closing risks | The register becomes long and ignored | Close risks whose window has passed and release their contingency |
Changes made in response to risks often affect scope, time or cost, so route them through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/). For the underlying concepts and more risk examples, see our guide to [project risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the steps of project risk management?**
The usual steps are: plan risk management, identify risks, perform qualitative risk analysis, perform quantitative risk analysis where justified, plan risk responses, implement responses and monitor risks. They form a loop that repeats throughout the project rather than a one-time sequence.

**Q: What are the 5 steps of risk management?**
A common five-step version is identify, assess, plan, implement and communicate, which is how PRINCE2 describes its risk management procedure. Other sources use identify, analyse, evaluate, treat and monitor. They cover the same ground as PMI's longer list.

**Q: What is a project risk management plan?**
It describes how risk will be managed on a specific project: roles, scoring scales, thresholds, risk appetite, review frequency, reporting and tools. On small projects it can be a page in the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/); large projects often have a separate document.

**Q: What is the difference between a risk and an issue?**
A risk is uncertain and in the future; an issue has already happened and needs action now. When a risk occurs it becomes an issue and moves from the risk register to the [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/).

**Q: Who is responsible for project risk management?**
The project manager leads the process and keeps the register up to date. Each risk has an owner who monitors it and makes sure the response is carried out. The sponsor sets risk appetite, approves major responses and owns risks escalated beyond the project.

**Q: How do you calculate a risk score?**
Multiply the probability score by the impact score, usually on 1 to 5 scales, to get a number from 1 to 25. A risk that is likely (4) with a high impact (4) scores 16. Compare the score with agreed bands to decide the action needed.

**Q: What are the 4 Ts of risk management?**
The 4 Ts are tolerate, treat, transfer and terminate, a shorthand used in some UK organisations. They map to PMI's accept, mitigate, transfer and avoid. Some versions add a fifth T, take (the opportunity).

**Q: What is the difference between risk appetite and risk tolerance?**
Risk appetite is the broad amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its goals. Risk tolerance is the acceptable variation around a specific objective, such as a budget that may vary by no more than 5%.

**Q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative risk analysis?**
Qualitative analysis ranks risks on simple scales to set priorities. Quantitative analysis puts numbers on the combined effect of risks on cost or schedule, for example with expected monetary value or Monte Carlo simulation.

**Q: Do Agile projects need risk management?**
Yes. Short iterations and frequent feedback reduce many delivery risks, but external risks such as suppliers, funding and regulation still need owners. Many Agile teams discuss risks in planning and retrospectives and use spikes to reduce technical uncertainty.

**Q: What software can I use for project risk management?**
A spreadsheet such as our [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) works for most projects. Project management tools add custom risk fields, links to tasks and dashboards; compare them on our [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) page.

# What Is Project Risk? Types, Examples and Risk Statements

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project risk explained: definition, threats vs opportunities, types of project risk with examples, how to write a risk statement and identify risks early.


## What Is Project Risk? Types, Examples and Risk Statements
A project risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it happens, would have a positive or negative effect on at least one project objective, such as scope, schedule, cost or quality. Negative risks are threats and positive risks are opportunities. This guide explains how to describe risks clearly, the main types with examples, and how to find them before they turn into problems.
- Published 30 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 15 min read

### Key takeaways
- A project risk is uncertain and in the future; once it has happened it is an issue.
- Risks can be threats (negative) or opportunities (positive), and both deserve attention.
- Write every risk as cause, event and effect so the team can analyse it and act on it.
- Group risks by type (schedule, cost, scope, technical, resource, external and more) to spot gaps.
- Identify risks continuously, from the charter onwards, and record them in a risk register with an owner.

### What is project risk?
**Project risk** is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more project objectives. PMI uses this definition in the PMBOK Guide. The key ideas are uncertainty (it may or may not happen), the future (it has not happened yet) and an effect on what the project is trying to achieve.
Those three ideas are a useful test. If something is certain, it is a fact to plan for, not a risk. If it has already happened, it is an [issue](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/). If it would not affect scope, time, cost, quality or the expected benefits, it is not worth tracking as a project risk.
- **Objectives a risk can affect:** scope, schedule, cost, quality, benefits, safety, reputation or stakeholder satisfaction.
- **What a risk is not:** a certainty ('the office move is in March'), a current problem ('the server is down') or a vague worry ('resourcing').
- **Why it matters:** projects are temporary and unique, so they always carry uncertainty. Naming it early gives you time to respond while options are still cheap.
The most recent edition of the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) (the eighth, published in November 2025) keeps risk as one of its performance domains and continues to distinguish risks, which have not yet occurred, from issues, which have.

### Threats and opportunities
Most people hear 'risk' and think of something bad. In project management a risk can go either way.
|  | Threat (negative risk) | Opportunity (positive risk) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Effect if it happens | Harms one or more objectives | Benefits one or more objectives |
| Example | A key supplier may deliver three weeks late | A new test tool may halve regression testing time |
| Typical responses | Avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept, escalate | Exploit, enhance, share, accept, escalate |
| Common mistake | Ignoring threats outside the team's control | Not looking for opportunities at all |
Teams rarely find opportunities by accident. Ask directly in risk workshops: 'What could go better than planned, and how could we make it more likely?' Typical opportunities include reusing work from another project, a price fall, an early approval or a supplier finishing ahead of schedule.

### The three parts of a risk: cause, event and effect
A well-described risk has three parts. Separating them stops teams confusing the reason for a risk with the risk itself, or with its consequence.
| Part | Question it answers | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | What fact or condition exists now? | The supplier has only one production line |
| Event | What uncertain thing might happen? | The line may break down during our order |
| Effect | What would that do to our objectives? | Delivery slips by three weeks and the launch date is missed |
A simple template turns the three parts into one sentence: **Because of** [cause], **there is a risk that** [event], **which would lead to** [effect].
Tip
The cause is certain; the event is uncertain; the effect is what you would measure. If your 'event' is already true, you have written a cause or an issue, not a risk.

### How to write a project risk statement
A risk statement is the sentence you put in the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/). Writing it well makes scoring, ownership and responses much easier.
1. **Start with the cause.** State the fact or condition that creates the uncertainty, such as a constraint, an assumption or a dependency.
2. **Describe one uncertain event.** Use 'may' or 'might'. If you find two events, split them into two risks.
3. **State the effect on an objective.** Make it measurable where you can: days of delay, cost, scope lost or quality affected.
4. **Check it is not an issue or a certainty.** If it has happened or definitely will, handle it differently.
5. **Check someone can act on it.** A good statement suggests who should own it and what a response might look like.
| Poor risk statement | Better risk statement |
| --- | --- |
| Resources | Because the data engineer is also on the finance project, they may be unavailable in May, delaying the data migration by two weeks. |
| Budget overrun | Because hardware is priced in US dollars, a weaker pound may raise equipment costs by up to 8%, exceeding the budget. |
| Requirements might change | Because the sales team has not reviewed the requirements, new features may be requested after sign-off, adding rework and [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/). |
| Weather | Because the roof works are scheduled for November, heavy rain may stop work for several days, delaying the watertight milestone. |

### Types of project risk
Grouping risks by type helps you check that identification has covered every area, and helps you compare risks across projects. There is no single official list; use categories that suit your organisation. The table shows a common set.
| Type | Typical sources | Example risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule | Optimistic estimates, late approvals, [dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) | Planning permission may take longer than eight weeks, delaying the start on site |
| Cost | Price rises, exchange rates, rework, inaccurate estimates | Material prices may rise before orders are placed, increasing costs |
| Scope | Unclear [requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/), changing priorities | Stakeholders may request extra reports after design sign-off |
| Technical | New technology, integration, performance | The new API may not handle peak volumes, causing slow response times |
| Resource | Skills gaps, competing projects, staff turnover | The only specialist may leave, stalling testing |
| Quality | Defects, unclear acceptance criteria | Acceptance criteria may be interpreted differently, causing rejected deliverables |
| Procurement and supplier | Supplier capacity, contract terms, insolvency | A subcontractor may go out of business mid-project |
| Stakeholder and communication | Low engagement, conflicting interests | The sponsor may lose interest after a reorganisation |
| Organisational | Funding cuts, restructuring, competing initiatives | The budget may be cut at the mid-year review |
| External | Regulation, weather, market, political events | New data rules may require extra security controls |
Many organisations turn their categories into a risk breakdown structure (RBS), a hierarchy of risk sources similar to a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/). Walking through it in a workshop is a quick way to find gaps.

#### Individual risk and overall project risk
PMI distinguishes **individual project risks**, the specific events in your register, from **overall project risk**, the effect of all uncertainty on the project as a whole. A project can have no single critical risk and still be very risky overall because of many medium risks, ambitious targets or complexity. Overall risk is usually discussed at sponsor or board level and can be estimated with techniques such as [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/).

#### Known and unknown risks
- **Known risks** have been identified and analysed. You plan responses for them and usually cover their expected cost with a contingency reserve inside the cost [baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).
- **Unknown risks** cannot be identified in advance. Organisations often cover them with a management reserve held outside the baseline and released through governance.
- **Emergent risks** are those that only become visible as the project progresses, which is why identification must continue throughout.

#### Project risk, business risk and operational risk
**Project risk** affects the project's own objectives: delivering the agreed scope on time, on budget and to quality. **Business risk** affects the wider organisation's goals, for example whether a new product sells once it is launched. **Operational risk** sits in day-to-day running of the business after handover, such as a system outage. The three are linked: a project often exists to reduce a business risk, and shortcuts taken during a project can create operational risk later.
Exam guides also separate **speculative risk**, which can lead to a gain or a loss, from **pure risk**, which can only lead to a loss, such as fire or theft. Pure risks are often transferred through insurance.

### Project risk examples by industry
Real risk statements are specific to the project. These examples show what threats and opportunities look like in different settings.
| Industry | Risk statement | Threat or opportunity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IT and software | Because the legacy database has undocumented fields, data may fail validation during migration, delaying go-live. | Threat |
| IT and software | Because the cloud provider offers a managed service for this component, we may be able to drop two weeks of build work. | Opportunity |
| Construction | Because the site has not been surveyed for contamination, ground works may uncover hazardous material, adding cost and delay. | Threat |
| Construction | Because the neighbouring project uses the same crane supplier, we may be able to share mobilisation costs. | Opportunity |
| Events | Because the venue is in a flood zone, heavy rain may close access roads, cancelling the event. | Threat |
| Marketing | Because the brand team is reviewing guidelines, creative may need reworking, delaying the campaign launch. | Threat |
| Product | Because a component supplier is launching a cheaper model, unit costs may fall by around 10%. | Opportunity |
| Public sector | Because the policy is under consultation, reporting requirements may change during delivery. | Threat |

### Common project risks and early warning signs
Some risks appear on almost every project. Knowing their early warning signs, called **triggers**, helps you act before they become issues.
| Common risk | Possible trigger |
| --- | --- |
| Unclear or changing requirements | Stakeholders disagree in reviews; open questions grow week by week |
| Optimistic estimates | Early tasks finish late; the team reports 'nearly done' for several days |
| Key people unavailable | Repeated meeting cancellations; people booked on other projects |
| Supplier delay | A supplier misses an interim milestone or stops replying promptly |
| Scope creep | Small requests bypass [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) |
| Technical uncertainty | Prototype results differ from expectations; performance tests fail |
| Weak sponsor support | Decisions are deferred; the sponsor misses steering meetings |
| Budget pressure | Spend runs ahead of progress; estimates to complete keep rising |
| Low stakeholder engagement | Feedback arrives late or not at all; few people attend demos |
Record the trigger next to each risk so the owner knows what to watch for. Our guide to [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) covers many of the people-related risks in more depth.

### Risk attributes you should record
A risk statement on its own is not enough to manage the risk. Most teams record these attributes for each one.
| Attribute | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| ID and category | A unique reference and the type of risk |
| Probability | How likely the event is, on an agreed scale such as 1 to 5 |
| Impact | How severe the effect would be, on an agreed scale |
| Score | Probability multiplied by impact, used to rank risks |
| Proximity | When the risk could occur, so near-term risks get attention first |
| Owner | The named person who monitors the risk and makes sure the response happens |
| Trigger | The warning sign that the risk is occurring |
| Response | The chosen strategy and actions, with dates |
| Status | Open, monitoring, closed or occurred |
Our free [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) includes the core attributes with an automatic probability x impact score.

### Risk vs issue vs assumption vs constraint
These terms are often mixed up. Each one is handled differently, so it is worth separating them.
| Term | Definition | Example | Where it is tracked |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Risk | An uncertain future event that would affect objectives | The supplier may deliver late | Risk register |
| Issue | Something that has happened and needs action now | The supplier has delivered late | [Issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/) |
| Assumption | Something believed to be true for planning, without proof | The supplier can deliver in six weeks | Assumptions log or RAID log |
| [Constraint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/) | A fixed limit the project must work within | The launch date is 1 March | Charter and plan |
| Dependency | A link where one piece of work relies on another | Installation depends on the delivery | Schedule or RAID log |
Assumptions are one of the best sources of risk. For every assumption, ask what would happen if it proved false. If the answer is serious, log a risk. A [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) keeps risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies together, which suits smaller projects; see our [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/).

### How to identify project risks
Risk identification works best as a team activity that starts during initiation and continues to closure.
1. **Review the project documents.** Read the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/), scope, schedule, budget, assumptions and constraints, asking what could go differently.
2. **Challenge assumptions.** For each one, ask how confident you are and what happens if it is wrong.
3. **Walk through the work.** Go through the work breakdown structure and schedule, especially the critical path and external dependencies.
4. **Run a risk workshop.** Bring together the team, sponsor, users and key suppliers. Brainstorm threats and opportunities by category.
5. **Use past experience.** Check [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) and risk registers from similar projects.
6. **Ask specialists.** Use [expert judgment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/expert-judgment/) for technical, legal, safety or commercial areas.
7. **Use structured techniques.** Checklists, a risk breakdown structure, SWOT analysis and root cause tools such as a [fishbone diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/) help teams think beyond the obvious.
8. **Record and assign.** Write each risk as cause, event and effect, log it in the register and name an owner.
Tip
Interview people individually as well as in workshops. Some people will not raise concerns in front of senior stakeholders.
Identification is the first step of a wider process that includes analysis, response planning and monitoring.

### Related risk terms
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Risk appetite | How much risk an organisation is willing to take in pursuit of its objectives |
| Risk tolerance | The acceptable variation around an objective, such as a schedule slip of no more than two weeks |
| Risk threshold | The point at which a risk needs a response or escalation |
| Risk owner | The person accountable for monitoring a risk and carrying out its response |
| Trigger | A warning sign that a risk is about to occur or has occurred |
| Secondary risk | A new risk created by carrying out a response to another risk |
| [Residual risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/residual-risk/) | The risk that remains after responses have been carried out |
| [Contingency plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) | The actions to take if a risk occurs |
| Contingency reserve | Time or money set aside for identified risks |
| Management reserve | Time or money set aside for unidentified risks, held outside the baseline |
Once responses are in place, re-score each risk to see what is left.

### Project risk in Agile projects
Agile ways of working reduce many risks by design. Short iterations, frequent demos and a prioritised backlog surface problems early and limit how much work is lost if direction changes. Risk still needs attention, though.
- Raise risks in sprint planning, daily stand-ups and retrospectives rather than only in a separate meeting.
- Tackle high technical risks early, for example with a time-boxed spike in an early [sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/).
- Add risk-reducing work to the backlog so it is prioritised alongside features.
- Use a clear [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) to reduce quality risk.
- Keep a lightweight risk list or board for risks that span several sprints or depend on other teams.

### Common mistakes when describing project risks
- **Writing categories instead of risks.** 'Staff risk' cannot be scored or owned; 'the lead developer may leave in Q2' can.
- **Recording issues as risks.** If it is already happening, move it to the issue log and act now.
- **Listing certainties.** A known public holiday is a planning fact, not a risk.
- **Mixing several events in one statement.** Split them so each can be scored and owned.
- **Ignoring opportunities.** A register with only threats misses ways to finish sooner or cheaper.
- **Identifying risks once.** New risks appear at every phase; review the list at each stage gate and when anything significant changes.
- **No owner.** A risk without a named owner is rarely managed.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project risk?**
A project risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, would have a positive or negative effect on at least one project objective such as scope, schedule, cost or quality.

**Q: Can a project risk be positive?**
Yes. Positive risks are called opportunities. Examples include a price falling, a task finishing early or a new tool reducing effort. They are managed with responses such as exploit, enhance and share.

**Q: What is the difference between a project risk and an issue?**
A risk might happen in the future; an issue has already happened and needs action now. When a risk occurs it becomes an issue and is usually moved to the [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/).

**Q: What is a project risk statement?**
A sentence that describes a risk's cause, uncertain event and effect, for example: 'Because of [cause], there is a risk that [event], which would lead to [effect].' It makes the risk specific enough to analyse and act on.

**Q: What are the main types of project risk?**
Common types are schedule, cost, scope, technical, resource, quality, procurement, stakeholder, organisational and external risk. Risks can also be classified as threats or opportunities, known or unknown, and individual or overall.

**Q: What are the most common project risks?**
Unclear or changing requirements, optimistic estimates, key people being unavailable, supplier delays, technical uncertainty, scope creep and weak sponsor support appear on many projects.

**Q: What is a risk trigger?**
A warning sign that a risk is about to occur or has occurred, such as a supplier missing an interim milestone. Recording triggers helps risk owners act early.

**Q: What is overall project risk?**
The effect of uncertainty on the project as a whole. It combines individual risks with other sources of variability such as complexity and ambitious targets.

**Q: What is a secondary risk?**
A new risk that arises directly from carrying out a response to another risk. For example, outsourcing a task to reduce a skills risk can introduce a supplier performance risk.

**Q: What is risk tolerance in project management?**
The acceptable range of variation around an objective, such as a budget overrun of no more than 5%. Risks that could push the project outside its tolerances need a response or escalation.

**Q: Who is responsible for identifying project risks?**
Everyone involved. The project manager facilitates identification, but team members, the sponsor, users and suppliers often see risks the project manager cannot.

**Q: Is an assumption a project risk?**
Not by itself, but an assumption that might prove false is a source of risk. Reviewing assumptions is one of the most effective ways to identify risks.

**Q: What is the difference between project risk and business risk?**
Project risk affects the project's objectives, such as delivering on time and budget. Business risk, in the organisational sense, affects the wider organisation, for example whether the product sells once delivered. The two are linked, and a project can reduce or create business risk.

**Q: Where should project risks be recorded?**
In a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/), or in a RAID log on smaller projects, with an owner, score, response and status for each risk.
