# Project Stakeholder Management: Identify, Analyse, Engage

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Who project stakeholders are, how to identify and analyse them with a power/interest grid, the stakeholder register, and how to engage them effectively.


## Project Stakeholder Management: Identify, Analyse, Engage
Stakeholders are people or groups who affect, or are affected by, a project. Stakeholder management identifies them, understands their needs and influence, and keeps them appropriately engaged.
- Published 20 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Identify stakeholders early and continually.
- Use a power/interest grid to plan engagement.
- Keep a stakeholder register and review it regularly.

### Who stakeholders are
- Sponsor and executives.
- Customers and end users.
- Project team and functional managers.
- Suppliers and partners.
- Regulators and the public.

### The process
1. **Identify** stakeholders early and continually.
2. **Analyse** their interests, influence and attitudes.
3. **Plan engagement** for each group.
4. **Engage** through communication and involvement.
5. **Monitor** and adjust as relationships change.

### Power/interest grid
|  | Low interest | High interest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High power | Keep satisfied | Manage closely |
| Low power | Monitor | Keep informed |

### Stakeholder register
A table listing each stakeholder, their role, interests, influence, current and desired engagement, and the owner of the relationship. Review it at each phase.

### Engagement tips
- Involve key stakeholders in defining objectives.
- Tailor communication to each group; see [communication management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-communication-management/).
- Address concerns early.
- Make trade-offs visible.

### Frequently asked questions

Anyone who affects or is affected by the project.

Assessing stakeholders' interests, influence and attitudes.

**Q: What is a project stakeholder register?**
A document listing stakeholders and how they will be managed.

A tool to classify stakeholders by power and interest to plan engagement.

The project manager, supported by the sponsor.

Engagement emphasises involving stakeholders, not just managing them.

Understand their concerns, involve them, and show how the project addresses their interests.

**Q: Why is stakeholder management important?**
Unmanaged stakeholders can derail projects through resistance or late changes.

# Project Status Report: How to Write One (With Examples)

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: How to write a project status report: what to include, RAG status rules, a step-by-step process, weekly and monthly examples and common mistakes.


## Project Status Report: How to Write One (With Examples)
A project status report is a short, regular update that tells stakeholders how a project is performing against its plan: what has been achieved, what comes next, how schedule, budget and scope are tracking, and which risks, issues and decisions need attention. A good one helps people make decisions; a weak one just lists activity. This guide shows you what to include, how to set RAG ratings, a step-by-step writing process and three worked examples you can copy.
- Published 2 October 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- A status report exists to support decisions, so put the overall status and any decision request at the top.
- Compare progress with the baseline: milestones, budget, scope and forecast, not just tasks completed.
- Agree RAG definitions in advance, tie them to tolerances and always explain each colour in words.
- Update the schedule, budget and RAID log first, then write the summary last.
- Tailor the depth to the audience: one page for sponsors, more detail for the team, a short paragraph for executives.
- Keep the format and send day consistent so readers can see trends from one report to the next.

### What is a project status report?
A **project status report** is a regular, concise document in which the project manager summarises a project's current position against its approved plan. It covers progress since the last report, forecast dates and costs, scope changes, the most important risks and issues, and any decisions or help needed. Its purpose is to let stakeholders act early.
The report is a snapshot taken on a fixed status date. It compares actual performance with the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) for schedule, cost and scope, and adds the project manager's forecast of where the project will end up. Who receives it, how often and in what format should be agreed in the [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/communication-plan/).
Different standards use different names for the same idea. PMI's [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) refers to work performance reports: information compiled from project data to support awareness and decisions. [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) calls the regular report from the project manager to the project board a **highlight report**, with frequency set in the project initiation documentation. Whatever the name, the content is broadly the same.
| A status report is | A status report is not |
| --- | --- |
| A summary of progress against the plan | A list of every task the team touched |
| An honest forecast of time, cost and scope | A sales document for the project |
| A place to ask for decisions and help | A substitute for raising urgent problems straight away |
| Short, with links to detail | The full RAID log, schedule and budget pasted in |

### Why project status reports matter
A good status report earns back the time it takes to write:
- **Early warning.** A forecast that a milestone will slip is far cheaper to act on four weeks out than four days out.
- **Faster decisions.** When a sponsor sees a clear question with options and a deadline, they can answer it without a meeting.
- **Fewer status meetings and messages.** Stakeholders stop chasing the team for updates when they know one arrives every Friday.
- **Trust.** Consistent, honest reporting, including bad news, builds confidence in the project manager and the team.
- **An audit trail.** A dated series of reports records what was known and decided, which supports [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) and audits.
Status reporting is one part of [project communication management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-communication-management/). Never let a serious problem wait for the next scheduled report.

### What to include in a project status report
Most status reports, whatever the template, use the same core sections. The table below shows each one, what to put in it and a typical length.
| Section | What to include | Typical length |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Header | Project name, reporting period and status date, author, sponsor, distribution | One line |
| Overall status | RAG rating, trend arrow and a one-line reason | One line |
| Executive summary | Where the project stands, what changed since last time and what matters most | Two to four sentences |
| Schedule | Key [milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) with baseline date, forecast date and status | Three to eight rows |
| Budget | Budget at completion, actual cost to date, forecast at completion and variance | One small table |
| Scope | Change requests raised, approved or rejected this period; any signs of scope creep | One to three lines |
| Achievements this period | Completed deliverables and milestones, not activity | Three to five bullets |
| Planned next period | The main outcomes the team expects to deliver next | Three to five bullets |
| Top risks and issues | The three to five that matter now, each with owner, action and date | Small table |
| Decisions or help needed | What is needed, from whom and by when, with a recommendation | One to three items |

#### Optional sections
Add these only when they help your audience decide something:
- **Benefits or KPIs:** early indicators that the project will deliver its business case, such as adoption or volume figures.
- **Resources:** vacancies, over-allocation or key leave that affects delivery.
- **Dependencies:** inputs from other projects or suppliers that are late or at risk.
- **Earned value:** schedule variance, [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/) and the CPI for projects that use [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).
- **Recognition:** a short thank-you to people or teams who made a difference.
Tip
If a section has nothing new to say, write "No change" rather than deleting it. Readers then know you checked, and the layout stays consistent.

### RAG status: how to rate red, amber and green
Most organisations rate status with red, amber and green (RAG). Some use yellow instead of amber, and some add blue for complete. The colours only work if everyone means the same thing by them, so define them in writing before the first report, ideally as a share of the agreed tolerance for time, cost and scope.
| Status | Meaning | Example threshold | What the reader should do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Green | On track. Any problems are within the team's control | Forecast uses less than half of the tolerance | Nothing; read for information |
| Amber | At risk. A recovery plan exists or attention is needed soon | Forecast uses between half and all of the tolerance, or a high risk is open without a working response | Watch closely; be ready to help |
| Red | Off track. Outside tolerance, or will be without intervention | Forecast exceeds the tolerance | Decide or intervene now |
For example, if the sponsor has agreed a schedule tolerance of plus two weeks on the go-live date, a forecast slip of three days is green, a slip of eight days is amber, and a slip of three weeks is red.

#### Deciding the overall rating
Rate schedule, budget, scope, risks and quality separately first. Then use a simple rule for the overall status:
1. Start from the worst individual rating.
2. Move it down only if you can explain in one sentence why that area does not threaten the project as a whole, and say so in the report.
3. Never rate the overall status green if any area is red.
4. If you are unsure between two colours, choose the worse one and explain. Early amber is better than late red.

#### Add a trend and a forecast
A colour on its own shows the position today. Add a trend arrow (improving, stable or worsening) and, if useful, the forecast status at the next milestone. "Amber, improving" tells a very different story from "amber, worsening".
Tip
Never use colour alone. Write the status as a word as well as a colour, and give the reason, so readers with colour vision deficiency, or anyone printing in black and white, get the same message.

### Types of project status reports
Status reports vary by frequency and by audience. Many projects use two or three of these at once, built from the same data.
| Type | Typical audience | Typical content | When it fits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Daily update | Team, site manager | Work done, blockers, people on site | Construction, cut-overs, launches, incidents |
| Weekly status report | Team, project manager, sponsor | Full core sections on one page | Most active projects |
| Fortnightly or sprint report | Product owner, stakeholders | Sprint goal, increment, release forecast | Agile teams |
| Monthly report | Sponsor, steering committee | Milestones, budget and forecast, top risks, decisions | Larger or longer projects |
| Quarterly or portfolio report | Executives, PMO, portfolio board | One line per project with RAG and key forecasts | Organisations running many projects |
| Exception report | Sponsor or project board | Cause of a forecast tolerance breach, options and a recommendation | Only when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded |
| End-stage or closure report | Project board, sponsor | Stage or project performance against plan, lessons | At a stage gate or at project closure |

### How to write a project status report step by step
The process below works for a weekly or monthly report. The order matters: update the data first and write the narrative last.
1. **Agree the basics once.** In the communication plan, set the audience, frequency, send day, format and RAG definitions. Get the sponsor to confirm them.
2. **Fix the status date.** Use a clear cut-off, such as close of business Thursday, so that schedule and cost figures relate to the same point in time.
3. **Collect inputs from the team.** Ask work package or workstream leads for progress, forecast dates and new risks by a set time. A short form or a [project tracker](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) makes this quicker than chasing people.
4. **Update the plan and logs.** Update the schedule, actual costs and forecast, the [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) and the [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) log. The report should summarise these sources, not replace them.
5. **Compare with the baseline.** For each milestone, compare forecast with baseline. For the budget, compare forecast at completion with budget at completion. Note the variance and whether it is within tolerance.
6. **Rate each area and the overall status.** Apply the agreed RAG definitions and the overall rule. Decide the trend.
7. **Choose the top risks and issues.** Pick the three to five that could change a decision or a forecast. Each needs an owner, an action and a date.
8. **Write the decision request.** State the decision, the options, your recommendation, the impact of delay and the date you need an answer.
9. **Write the summary last.** In two to four sentences, say where the project stands, what changed and what you need. Read it aloud: if it would not make sense to the sponsor in a corridor, rewrite it.
10. **Check, send and follow up.** Check figures against the source data, send on the agreed day and follow up any decision request personally.
Tip
A simple weekly rhythm works for most teams: team updates due Thursday midday, data and RAG ratings updated Thursday afternoon, report sent Friday midday, then walked through at the next project meeting so that time goes on decisions rather than updates.

### Project status report example (weekly)
Here is a filled-in weekly report for a fictional customer portal project.
**Project:** Customer portal. **Period:** week ending 14 March. **Author:** project manager. **Sponsor:** head of customer service. **Overall status: Amber, stable.** Build is on track, but payment integration testing is blocked by supplier sandbox errors.
**Summary:** Account pages and invoice download are complete and tested. User acceptance testing (UAT) is forecast to start one week late because of a supplier defect in the payment sandbox. The go-live date is still achievable within tolerance if UAT starts by 28 March. **Decision needed:** sponsor to approve moving the UAT start by one week, by 17 March.
| Area | Status | Detail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule | Amber | UAT start forecast 28 March against baseline 21 March; go-live 2 May unchanged (tolerance plus two weeks) |
| Budget | Green | £212k actual to date of £480k budget; forecast at completion £470k |
| Scope | Green | CR-05 (brand colours) approved this week with no cost or schedule impact |
| Quality | Green | Sprint 6 regression tests: 148 of 150 passed; two minor defects scheduled |
| Resources | Green | Full team in place; one developer on leave 24 to 28 March, cover agreed |

#### Milestones
| Milestone | Baseline | Forecast | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design sign-off | 7 February | 7 February (done) | Complete |
| Build complete | 14 March | 14 March (done) | Complete |
| UAT start | 21 March | 28 March | Amber |
| UAT sign-off | 11 April | 17 April | Amber |
| Go-live | 2 May | 2 May | Green |

#### Achievements, next steps, risks and issues
- **Done this week:** account pages complete; invoice download tested; CR-05 approved.
- **Next week:** complete password reset; start performance testing; agree UAT test scripts with customer service.
| Ref | Risk or issue | Rating | Owner | Action and date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I-007 | Issue: payment sandbox returns errors, blocking integration tests | High | Supplier manager | Supplier fix due 18 March; daily call until resolved |
| R-012 | Risk: customer service staff unavailable for UAT during month-end | Medium | Sponsor | Confirm named testers by 20 March |
| R-015 | Risk: performance under peak load not yet proven | Medium | Tech lead | Performance test complete by 25 March |
Notice what the example does: the overall rating has a reason; the decision request is in the summary, not at the bottom; milestones show baseline against forecast; and every risk has an owner and a date.

### Monthly steering committee report example
A monthly report to a steering committee covers a longer period with less operational detail and more forecasting. On projects that use earned value, include the key indicators and say in plain words what they mean.
**Project:** Customer portal. **Period:** March. **Overall status: Amber, worsening.**
| Measure | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Budget at completion (BAC) | £480k | Approved budget |
| Planned value (PV) | £260k | Budgeted cost of the work scheduled by 31 March |
| Earned value (EV) | £240k | Budgeted cost of the work actually completed |
| Actual cost (AC) | £252k | What that work has cost |
| Cost variance (CV = EV - AC) | -£12k (-5%) | Completed work has cost £12k more than budgeted |
| Schedule variance (SV = EV - PV) | -£20k | Slightly behind plan in value terms |
| Cost performance index (CPI = EV / AC) | 0.95 | About 95p of value for every £1 spent |
| Estimate at completion (EAC = BAC / CPI) | £504k | Forecast final cost if current efficiency continues |
| Variance at completion (VAC = BAC - EAC) | -£24k | Uses half of the £48k (10%) cost tolerance: amber |
**Summary for the committee:** The portal is forecast to go live on 2 May as planned, but at £504k against a £480k budget, mainly because the payment integration needed more testing effort than estimated. The forecast is within cost tolerance. We recommend no change to plan; we will review again after UAT. **No decision needed this month.**
The EAC = BAC / CPI formula assumes current cost efficiency continues; if the cause has been fixed, say so and use a bottom-up forecast. Our [cost performance index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/) and [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/) guides explain these formulas in more depth.

### Exception report example
An exception report is not a regular report. You raise it as soon as a forecast shows that a tolerance will be exceeded, rather than waiting for the next scheduled update. In PRINCE2, the project manager sends it to the project board, which decides how to respond.
Suppose the supplier's payment fix fails and the go-live forecast moves to 23 May, three weeks late against a two-week tolerance. A short exception report would cover:
- **Cause:** the supplier's sandbox fix of 18 March failed retesting; the supplier now forecasts a fix on 8 April.
- **Impact:** UAT cannot complete until 5 May; go-live forecast 23 May, one week beyond tolerance. Cost impact about £18k of extended team time.
- **Option A, accept the delay:** go live 23 May; extra cost about £18k; no scope change.
- **Option B, reduce scope:** launch on 2 May with card payments only and add direct debit in a later release; no extra cost; customers using direct debit keep the current process for six weeks.
- **Option C, add effort:** bring in the supplier's senior integration team at about £30k; forecast go-live 9 May, within tolerance, but with a delivery risk.
- **Recommendation:** Option B, because it protects the date that customer communications are built around and costs nothing extra.
- **Decision needed:** by 1 April, to brief customer service in time.
The report gives options with consequences, not just bad news, which makes the board's decision quick.

### How to write a status report for executives
Senior readers want the answer first. Use the "bottom line up front" approach: status, why, what you need.
1. **Status and trend:** "Amber, stable."
2. **Reason in one sentence:** "Go-live is on track, but UAT will start a week late because of a supplier defect."
3. **What you need:** "Please approve the one-week UAT move by Tuesday."
Then give two or three lines of supporting facts and a link to the full report. Keep numbers to the few that drive decisions: the forecast go-live date, the forecast final cost against budget and any benefit at risk. An [executive summary template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/executive-summary-template/) can help you keep this discipline.
If the portfolio uses a standard one-line format for every project, follow it exactly. Your [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) analysis will show which executives want more detail and which want less.

### Writing good status updates: before and after
Most weak status reports are not wrong; they are vague. The table shows common weak lines and stronger rewrites.
| Weak | Stronger | Why it is better |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Testing is progressing well." | "120 of 150 test cases passed; on track to finish by 25 March." | Measurable and tied to a date |
| "Some delays with the supplier." | "Supplier fix is five days late; UAT start moves from 21 to 28 March." | States the impact on a milestone |
| "Worked on the data migration." | "Migrated 3 of 5 customer data sets; remaining 2 due 20 March." | Shows progress, not activity |
| "Budget is fine." | "£212k spent of £480k; forecast £470k, within budget." | Gives actual, forecast and comparison |
| "Risk around resources." | "Risk: no UAT testers confirmed for month-end. Owner: sponsor. Action: name testers by 20 March." | Specific, owned and dated |
| "We may need more money." | "Decision: approve £18k contingency release by 1 April, or go-live slips to 23 May." | A clear ask with a deadline and consequence |

### Status reports on Agile projects
Agile teams still need to tell stakeholders how things are going, but the format changes. Scope is expected to flex, so "percentage complete against a fixed plan" is less meaningful. Instead, report:
- **Sprint or iteration goal:** met, partly met or not met, with the reason.
- **What was delivered:** the increment and any features released to users.
- **Release or roadmap forecast:** a burnup chart showing completed work against total scope, with a forecast date range rather than a single date.
- **Flow measures:** cycle time and throughput for teams using Kanban.
- **Impediments and dependencies** that need help from outside the team.
- **Outcome measures:** usage, customer feedback or other evidence that the product is delivering value.
Treat velocity as a team planning aid, not a productivity score to compare between teams. The [sprint review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) is where stakeholders inspect the increment and adapt the backlog; it is a working session, not a status meeting, so a short written update often accompanies it rather than replacing it.

### Status report vs progress report vs highlight report
These terms are often used interchangeably. Where organisations do draw a distinction, it usually looks like this:
| Report | Purpose | Typical author and audience | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Status report | Snapshot of where the project stands against plan, with forecasts and decisions | Project manager to sponsor and stakeholders | Regular, often weekly or monthly |
| Progress report | What work has been completed over a period; often more detailed and team-focused | Team lead or project manager to project manager or client | Regular |
| Highlight report (PRINCE2) | Regular summary of stage status for the project board | Project manager to project board | As set in the project initiation documentation |
| Checkpoint report (PRINCE2) | Progress of a work package against agreed targets | Team manager to project manager | As set in the work package |
| Exception report | Notice that a tolerance is forecast to be breached, with options | Project manager to sponsor or board | Only when needed |
A dashboard and a status report work well together: the dashboard shows the numbers at any time, and the status report adds the project manager's interpretation, forecast and requests.

### Common mistakes (and how to avoid them)
| Mistake | Why it happens | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Watermelon reporting:** green outside, red inside | Vague RAG definitions, fear of bad news, optimism | Tie RAG to tolerances; praise early warnings; ask "what would make this red?" |
| Listing activity instead of progress | Activity is easier to report | Report against milestones and deliverables |
| Burying the decision request | Templates put it last | Put decisions in the summary at the top |
| Listing every risk | Fear of missing something | Report the top three to five; link to the full risk register |
| Stale data | Report written before logs are updated | Update schedule, costs and RAID log first |
| Changing the format each time | Different authors, or tinkering | Fix a template and keep it for the life of the project |
| Undefined percentage complete | "90% done" for weeks | Use milestones or objective rules such as 0/50/100 |
| No owners or dates on actions | Writing in a hurry | Every risk, issue and action has a named owner and a date |
Watermelon projects are rarely caused by dishonesty; more often a project manager hopes to recover before anyone notices. Sponsors who respond to early amber with help rather than blame get earlier, more honest reports.

### Status report checklist before you send
- The status date and reporting period are stated.
- The overall RAG rating has a trend and a one-line reason.
- The summary is four sentences or fewer and makes sense on its own.
- Every milestone shows baseline and forecast dates.
- Budget shows actual to date, forecast at completion and variance against budget.
- No more than five risks and issues, each with an owner, action and date.
- Any decision request says what, who, by when and what happens if it is late.
- The report fits on one page or one screen, with links to detail.
- Nothing in it will surprise the sponsor: anything red has been discussed in person first.

### Tools and templates for status reporting
You do not need special software to write a good status report. A consistent template and current source data matter more. Free templates that help:
- [Project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) to collect task status, owners and progress.
- [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) and [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) for the risks and issues section.
- [Project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) for milestone dates and forecasts.
- [Communication plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/) to agree who gets which report and when.
- [Executive summary template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/executive-summary-template/) for the senior-audience version.
As a project grows, [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) can save a lot of collection time. Most tools now offer dashboards, project status fields and automated status updates, and some generate draft summaries with AI. Wrike, our top-ranked tool, combines dashboards, custom reports and portfolio views, which suits teams reporting across many projects; see our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/). Whichever tool you use, keep a short written summary from the project manager: software can show the numbers, but it cannot judge which risk matters most or what you need the sponsor to decide.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project status report?**
A regular, concise update from the project manager that summarises progress against the plan, forecast dates and costs, scope changes, top risks and issues, and any decisions needed from stakeholders.

**Q: What should be included in a project status report?**
Overall RAG status with a reason, a short summary, milestones, budget and forecast, scope changes, achievements, next steps, top risks and issues, and decisions needed.

**Q: How do you write a weekly status report?**
Fix a status date, update the schedule, costs and RAID log, rate each area against agreed RAG definitions, write any decision request, write the summary last and send it on the same day each week.

**Q: How often should a project status report be sent?**
Weekly is common for active projects; fortnightly or monthly suits longer, steadier projects or senior audiences. Agree it in the communication plan.

**Q: What does RAG status mean?**
Red, amber, green: a rating of whether the project or an area is off track, at risk or on track. Define each colour in advance and always explain it in words.

**Q: How long should a project status report be?**
Ideally one page or one screen, with links to detail. Executive versions can be three to five lines.

**Q: Who writes the project status report?**
The project manager, using inputs from workstream leads and the project's schedule, cost data and logs.

**Q: What is the difference between a status report and a progress report?**
The terms are often used interchangeably. Where they differ, a progress report records work completed over a period, while a status report gives a snapshot against plan with forecasts and decisions.

**Q: Is a highlight report the same as a status report?**
Broadly, yes. Highlight report is the PRINCE2 name for the project manager's regular summary of stage status to the project board.

**Q: What is an exception report?**
A report raised only when a forecast shows an agreed tolerance will be exceeded. It explains the cause and impact and gives options with a recommendation.

**Q: What is a watermelon project?**
A project reported as green while the reality underneath is red. It usually comes from vague RAG definitions, optimism or reluctance to share bad news.

**Q: How do I write a status report for executives?**
Lead with the status and trend, give the reason in one sentence, then state what you need and by when. Link to the full report.

**Q: How do you report status on an Agile project?**
Report the sprint goal result, what was delivered, a burnup-based release forecast with a date range, impediments and outcome measures, rather than percentage complete against a fixed plan.

**Q: Can project management software create status reports?**
Yes. Many tools offer dashboards and automated or AI-drafted updates, but a short written summary from the project manager is still valuable.

# Project Tasks and Activities: Definitions and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-tasks-and-activities/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project tasks and activities explained: the difference, how they fit with work packages, activity attributes, a worked activity list and sizing tips.


## Project Tasks and Activities: Definitions and Examples
Project tasks and activities are the individual pieces of work you schedule, assign and track to produce a project's deliverables. An activity is a distinct, scheduled unit of work with a duration, resources and a clear output; "task" is often used to mean the same thing, or the smaller steps inside an activity. This guide explains the difference, shows how to define and size activities, and walks through a complete activity list.
- Published 23 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- PMI defines an activity as a distinct, scheduled portion of work; it does not formally define "task". Most tools call every schedule line a task.
- Activities come from work packages, the lowest level of the work breakdown structure. Work packages describe outputs; activities describe the work to produce them.
- Name each activity with a verb and a noun, give it one owner and a completion criterion you can check.
- Size activities so they can be estimated and tracked: a common rule of thumb is 8 to 80 hours of effort, and no longer than one reporting period.
- Effort and duration are different. Convert one into the other using the owner's real availability.
- Record attributes (ID, WBS code, predecessors, duration, resources, constraints) so the activity list can become a schedule.

### What are project activities and tasks?
A **project activity** is a distinct, scheduled piece of work that is needed to produce a project deliverable. It has a clear start and finish, an estimated duration, the resources needed to do it and an output you can check. A **project task** is either another word for an activity or, where teams distinguish them, a smaller step within an activity.
The PMBOK Guide defines an activity as a distinct, scheduled portion of work performed during the course of a project. The word "task" is not a defined PMI term, but it is the word most software uses: Microsoft Project, Wrike, Asana and most other tools call each line in a plan a task. In practice you will meet three conventions.

#### Activity vs task: the short answer
| Convention | How the words are used | Where you see it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interchangeable | Activity and task mean the same: a scheduled unit of work | Most organisations and most scheduling tools |
| Activity contains tasks | An activity is scheduled and tracked; tasks are the steps inside it, often managed by the person doing the work | Larger projects, PMI-style planning, many textbooks |
| Task contains activities | A task is the scheduled item; activities are the things people do to complete it | Some organisations and some software, less common |
None of these is wrong. What matters is that your project uses one convention consistently. In this guide we use the second: **activities** are the scheduled units you estimate, link and report on, and **tasks** are the smaller steps the owner uses to get an activity done. If your team uses the words interchangeably, read "activity" and "task" as the same thing throughout.

### Where activities and tasks fit in the work hierarchy
Activities sit between the scope of the project, described in the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/), and the day-to-day work of the team.
| Level | What it describes | Example | Typically estimated in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project | The whole temporary endeavour | Launch a new staff intranet | Months, total budget |
| Deliverable | An output the project must produce | Working search function | Weeks, cost |
| [Work package](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/) | The lowest level of the WBS, owned by one person or team | Search index and results page | Weeks, cost and effort |
| Activity | Scheduled work needed to produce the work package | Configure search index | Days, hours of effort |
| Task | A smaller step inside an activity | Set up synonym list | Hours |
| [Milestone](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) | A significant point or event, with zero duration | Search approved for launch | A date, no effort |

#### Work package vs activity
A work package is described by its **output** (a noun: "Training materials"). Activities are described by the **work** (a verb: "Write training slides"). The WBS stops at work packages; the activity list starts there. This separation keeps the WBS about scope and the activity list about time and effort.

#### Activity vs milestone
An activity consumes time and effort. A milestone marks a moment, such as an approval or a hand-over, and has no duration. Milestones are useful as checkpoints and for reporting, but they cannot be assigned work. If you find yourself writing "Milestone: build the database", it is an activity.

### Types of activities and tasks
Not all activities behave the same way in a schedule. Knowing the type helps you estimate and track them correctly.
| Type | What it is | Example | How progress is measured |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Discrete effort | Work that produces a specific, measurable output | Write the user guide | By the output: drafted, reviewed, approved |
| Level of effort (LOE) | Supporting work that has no output of its own and lasts as long as other work | Project administration, site supervision | By time passing, not by output |
| Apportioned effort | Work that is a fixed proportion of another discrete activity | Quality inspection at 10 per cent of build effort | In proportion to the activity it supports |
| Milestone | A significant event with zero duration | Design signed off | Achieved or not |
| Summary task | A parent line that groups activities; its dates roll up from them | Phase 2: Build | Rolled up from its children |
| [Hammock activity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/hammock-activity/) | A summary that spans between two unrelated activities | Equipment hire from delivery to removal | Calculated from the activities it spans |
| Recurring task | A task that repeats on a schedule | Weekly status meeting | Each occurrence done or not |
The first three are the effort types used in the PMBOK Guide (6th edition) and in [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/). Most activities on a typical project are discrete effort, and they are the ones worth planning in detail.

### Activity attributes: what to record
**Activity attributes** are the details recorded about each activity. Early on there are only a few; more are added as planning progresses. The PMBOK Guide lists attributes such as these, and most scheduling tools have a field for each:
- **Unique ID** and **WBS code**, so cost and progress roll up to the right work package.
- **Name** (verb plus noun) and **description** of the work.
- **Completion criteria**: how you will know it is finished.
- **Predecessors and successors**, with the link type and any lead or lag; see [predecessors and successors](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/predecessors-and-successors/).
- **Effort and duration estimates**, with the basis of estimate.
- **Resources and owner**: the people, skills, equipment or materials needed, and the one person accountable.
- **Constraints and imposed dates**, such as a supplier delivery date.
- **Assumptions**, such as "subject expert available two days a week".
- **Location** and **activity type** where relevant.

#### Example activity attribute record
| Attribute | Entry |
| --- | --- |
| ID | A3 |
| WBS code | 2.1 Training materials |
| Name | Write slides and handouts |
| Description | Write the slide deck and participant handout for the half-day customer service course, following the approved outline |
| Completion criteria | Draft slides (about 40) and a handout of up to 8 pages saved in the shared folder and sent for review |
| Predecessor | A2 Draft course outline (finish-to-start) |
| Successor | A4 Review materials |
| Effort | 36 hours |
| Duration | 8 working days (owner available about 4.5 hours a day) |
| Basis of estimate | Similar course last year took 34 hours; designer's estimate |
| Owner and resources | Instructional designer; brand slide template |
| Constraints | None |
| Assumptions | Outline approved without major changes |
You do not need this level of detail for every activity on a small project. Record what you need to schedule and track the work, and add detail where the risk is highest.

### How to define activities step by step
In PMBOK terms this is the **Define Activities** process, whose main outputs are the activity list, activity attributes and the milestone list. In plain terms, you are turning each piece of scope into a list of work you can schedule.
1. **Start from the WBS.** Take each work package in turn. If you do not have a WBS yet, build one first; our [work breakdown structure template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) gives you a starting format.
2. **Involve the people who will do the work.** Ask them what steps are needed to produce the work package. They know the hidden work, such as set-up, reviews and rework.
3. **List the activities.** Brainstorm first, then tidy. Include non-build work: reviews, approvals, procurement lead times, training and hand-over.
4. **Name each activity** as verb plus noun, and write a completion criterion for it.
5. **Size each activity** so it can be estimated and tracked (see the sizing rules below). Split activities that are too big; merge ones that are trivially small.
6. **Add milestones** for key events: approvals, hand-overs, external deliveries, phase ends.
7. **Record the attributes** you need now (at least ID, WBS code, name, owner) and leave space for those added during sequencing and estimating.
8. **Review the list** with the work package owners. Check that completing every activity would produce the whole work package, and nothing outside it.
Tip
You do not have to define every activity at the start. **Rolling wave planning**, described in the PMBOK Guide, means planning near-term work in detail and later work at a higher level, then adding detail as you learn more. It is often the honest approach on longer projects.
Once the list exists, the next step is to link the activities in order.

### How to name tasks and activities
A good name tells everyone what the work is and hints at when it is finished. Use a **verb plus a noun**, and be specific enough that two people would not interpret it differently.
| Poor name | Why it is weak | Better name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Testing | No verb; no scope; no end point | Run system tests on payment module |
| Ongoing support | Never finishes | Provide go-live support (weeks 1 to 2) |
| Sarah's work | Names a person, not the work | Draft supplier contract |
| Website | That is a deliverable, not an activity | Build product listing pages |
| Look at budget | Unclear output | Approve phase 2 budget |
| Meeting | Which one, and why? | Hold design sign-off review |
Pair each name with a **completion criterion**: a sentence describing the evidence that it is done, such as "report approved by the sponsor by email". If you cannot write one, the activity is probably too vague or too large.

### How big should a task be?
Activities that are too big cannot be tracked: they show "in progress" for weeks and then either finish or suddenly do not. Activities that are too small create a plan nobody can maintain. These rules of thumb help you find the middle:
- **The 8/80 rule:** an activity should take between 8 and 80 hours of effort. It is a planning heuristic, not a standard, so treat it as a guide.
- **The reporting-period rule:** an activity should be no longer than the interval between progress reports, often one or two weeks, so each report shows real movement.
- **The one-owner rule:** if an activity needs two people to be accountable, it is probably two activities.
- **The estimate rule:** if the person doing it cannot estimate it with reasonable confidence, break it down further.
- **The usefulness rule:** do not schedule work that is only minutes long. Keep that as tasks on the owner's own list.

#### Effort vs duration: a worked calculation
Effort is the number of person-hours of work. Duration is the number of working days from start to finish. They are equal only if someone works on the activity full time, which is rare. Convert effort to duration using the owner's real availability:
| Step | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Effort estimate | Designer estimates the slides and handouts | 36 hours |
| Working day | Standard day | 7.5 hours |
| Availability | Designer is 60 per cent on this project | 7.5 x 0.6 = 4.5 hours a day |
| Duration | 36 / 4.5 | 8 working days |
If you had scheduled the 36 hours as five days (36 / 7.5, rounded up), the plan would be wrong by three days before the work had even started.

#### Split or merge? Examples
| Activity as drafted | Size | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Develop the new website | 600 hours | Split by page type or feature into activities of 20 to 80 hours |
| Email the venue | 15 minutes | Merge into "Book training venues" |
| Write and approve the policy | 30 hours writing plus 2 weeks waiting for the board | Split: "Write policy" (activity) and "Board approves policy" (milestone or short activity with its own duration) |
| Install and configure 40 laptops | 60 hours | Keep as one activity if one technician owns it; use tasks for each batch |
The policy example is worth noticing. Waiting time (approvals, supplier lead times, curing, shipping) needs its own line or a lag, otherwise it hides inside the writer's activity and makes them look late.

### Worked example: from deliverable to activity list
A company is introducing a half-day customer service course for 200 staff. The deliverable is "Training programme ready to deliver". The WBS has three work packages: training materials, trainers, and logistics.

#### Step 1: decompose each work package into activities
| Work package | Activities |
| --- | --- |
| 2.1 Training materials | Agree training objectives; Draft course outline; Write slides and handouts; Review materials; Finalise and print materials |
| 2.2 Trainers | Select trainers; Run train-the-trainer session |
| 2.3 Logistics | Book training venues; Invite participants |

#### Step 2: build the activity list
| ID | Activity | Duration | Predecessors | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | Agree training objectives | 2 days | None | Training lead |
| A2 | Draft course outline | 3 days | A1 | Instructional designer |
| A3 | Write slides and handouts | 8 days | A2 | Instructional designer |
| A4 | Review materials | 3 days | A3 | Subject expert |
| A5 | Finalise and print materials | 2 days | A4 | Training lead |
| B1 | Select trainers | 4 days | A1 | HR partner |
| B2 | Run train-the-trainer session | 2 days | A4, B1 | Instructional designer |
| C1 | Book training venues | 3 days | A1 | Office manager |
| C2 | Invite participants | 2 days | C1 | Training coordinator |
| M1 | Milestone: programme ready to deliver | 0 days | A5, B2, C2 | Training lead |

#### Step 3: work out the dates
With all links finish-to-start, a simple forward pass (each activity starts when its last predecessor finishes) gives these working-day numbers, counted from day 0:
| ID | Start | Finish | Float (days) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | 0 | 2 | 0 |
| A2 | 2 | 5 | 0 |
| A3 | 5 | 13 | 0 |
| A4 | 13 | 16 | 0 |
| A5 | 16 | 18 | 0 |
| B1 | 2 | 6 | 10 |
| B2 | 16 | 18 | 0 |
| C1 | 2 | 5 | 11 |
| C2 | 5 | 7 | 11 |
| M1 | 18 | 18 | 0 |
The programme is ready after **18 working days**. Two paths are critical: A1 to A5, and A1 to A4 then B2, both of which pass through writing and reviewing the materials. Trainer selection has 10 days of float and the logistics chain has 11, so those can slip without moving the milestone. If you want the programme ready sooner, shortening A3 or A4 is the only thing that helps; speeding up venue booking would change nothing.
This is what a good activity list gives you: a realistic duration, a clear view of which work drives the date and where you have room. For the method behind the numbers, read our guide to the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).

#### Step 4: break an activity into tasks
The instructional designer turns A3 into a personal task list. These are not scheduled separately; they help the owner manage the 36 hours:
- Set up slide template and folder structure.
- Write module 1 slides (greeting and listening).
- Write module 2 slides (handling complaints).
- Write module 3 slides (follow-up and escalation).
- Write participant handout.
- Self-check against the outline and send for review.
Our [to-do list template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/to-do-list-template/) works well for task lists like this one, while the activity list itself fits the [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/).

### Project task examples by phase
Activities vary by project, but most projects contain similar work in each phase. Use this as a prompt list when you build your own.
| Phase | Example activities and tasks |
| --- | --- |
| Initiation | Draft project charter; Identify stakeholders; Hold kick-off meeting; Confirm sponsor and budget |
| Planning | Build WBS; Define activities; Estimate effort; Develop schedule; Prepare risk register; Agree communication plan |
| Execution | Design solution; Build components; Procure equipment; Run tests; Train users; Migrate data |
| Monitoring and control | Update schedule weekly; Review issue log; Prepare status report; Assess change requests |
| Closure | Obtain acceptance sign-off; Hand over to operations; Hold lessons learned review; Close contracts; Release team |
Project management work itself, such as reporting and meetings, is usually planned as level-of-effort or recurring tasks rather than detailed activities. Include major reviews and decision meetings that other work depends on as activities or milestones.

### From activity list to schedule
The activity list is the input to the rest of schedule planning. The usual sequence is:
1. **Sequence the activities** by adding dependencies; see [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/).
2. **Estimate durations** from effort and availability.
3. **Assign resources** and check for over-allocation; see [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/).
4. **Develop the schedule**, calculate the critical path and show it on a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/).
5. **Baseline the schedule** once it is approved, so progress can be measured against it; see [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).
For the full process, see our guide to [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/).

### Tasks in Agile projects
Agile teams use a different hierarchy, but the idea is similar. Large pieces of work are **epics**, which are split into **[user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/)** that deliver something of value. During [sprint planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/), the developers often break each story into **tasks**: the technical steps needed to complete it, such as "write API endpoint" or "update help text".
- Stories are sized relative to each other (often in story points); tasks, if estimated at all, are usually in hours.
- Tasks live in the [sprint backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) and are owned by the developers, not assigned by a manager.
- Tasks are created just in time for the sprint, which is rolling wave planning in a very short cycle.
- Completion is judged against the [definition of done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), which plays the role of a completion criterion.

### Managing tasks during the project
Once work starts, the activity list becomes a tracking tool. A few practices keep it honest:
- **Update weekly at least:** record actual start and finish dates and the remaining duration, not just a percentage.
- **Be careful with percentage complete:** "90 per cent done" can stay true for weeks. Many teams use simple conventions instead, such as 0/100 (no credit until finished) for short activities or 50/50 (half credit at start, half at finish).
- **Track against completion criteria:** an activity is finished when its criterion is met, not when the owner stops working on it.
- **Re-plan, do not overwrite:** if an activity is going to take longer, change its remaining duration and let the schedule show the effect, rather than editing dates by hand.
- **Keep ownership clear:** a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) helps where several people contribute to an activity.
A spreadsheet works for small projects; our [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) has owner, status and date columns ready to use. For larger or multi-project work, a tool with dependencies, workload views and dashboards saves a lot of manual effort. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, handles task hierarchies, dependencies and Gantt charts well; compare it with the alternatives in our ranking of [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/).

### Common mistakes with tasks and activities
| Mistake | Effect | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Activities with no clear end | Progress cannot be judged; work drifts | Add a completion criterion or time-box it |
| Mixing effort and duration | Schedule is optimistic from day one | Convert using real availability |
| Activities that are too large | Problems surface only at the end | Split to fit one reporting period |
| Too much detail | Nobody maintains the plan | Schedule activities; keep small steps as personal tasks |
| Forgetting non-build work | Reviews, approvals and lead times appear as surprise delays | Add them as activities, milestones or lags |
| Naming deliverables, not work | Owners are unsure what to do | Verb plus noun |
| Several owners per activity | Everyone assumes someone else is on it | One accountable owner; split if needed |
| Activities outside the WBS | Scope creep enters the plan unnoticed | Every activity maps to a work package |
Tip
If you cannot tell whether an activity is finished, it needs a better completion criterion or splitting into smaller pieces.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between a project task and a project activity?**
Many people use them interchangeably. Where a distinction is made, an activity is the scheduled unit of work you estimate, link and track, and tasks are smaller steps within it. PMI defines "activity" but not "task"; most software calls every schedule line a task.

**Q: What is an activity in project management?**
A distinct, scheduled piece of work needed to produce a deliverable, with a start, a finish, a duration, resources and a checkable output.

**Q: What is an example of a project activity?**
"Write slides and handouts" for a training course, "Run system tests on the payment module" or "Pour the ground-floor slab". Each has a clear output and can be estimated and assigned.

**Q: What is a project activity list?**
A list of all the scheduled activities in the project with their IDs, names and scope descriptions. It is the starting point for sequencing, estimating and building the schedule.

**Q: What are activity attributes?**
The details recorded for each activity, such as ID, WBS code, description, predecessors and successors, duration, resources, constraints, assumptions and owner. They grow as planning progresses.

**Q: How big should a project activity be?**
Small enough to estimate and track reliably. Common rules of thumb are 8 to 80 hours of effort, and no longer than one reporting period.

**Q: What is the difference between a work package and an activity?**
A work package is the lowest level of the WBS and describes an output. Activities are the work needed to produce it. See [work package](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/).

**Q: What is the difference between an activity and a milestone?**
An activity takes time and effort. A milestone marks a significant event, such as an approval, and has zero duration.

**Q: How do you name project tasks?**
Start with a verb and name the result, such as "Approve budget" or "Install servers", and pair the name with a completion criterion.

**Q: What is a summary task?**
A parent task that groups subtasks; its dates, effort and cost roll up from them. A [hammock activity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/hammock-activity/) is a related idea that spans between two unrelated activities.

**Q: What is a level of effort activity?**
Supporting work with no output of its own that lasts as long as the work it supports, such as project administration. Progress is measured by time passing.

**Q: Should meetings be included as project tasks?**
Include major reviews and decision meetings that other work depends on. Routine meetings are usually covered as recurring or level-of-effort tasks.

**Q: How do you break a project into tasks?**
Build a work breakdown structure down to work packages, then ask the people doing the work what activities each package needs. Name, size and sequence them, then break activities into personal tasks where useful.

**Q: Are project tasks the same in Agile?**
Agile teams break [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) into tasks during sprint planning. The tasks are owned by the developers and usually last hours rather than days.
