# Project Time Management: Processes, Techniques and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-time-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Project time management explained: the six processes, estimating and scheduling techniques, a worked critical path example, schedule control and tips.


## Project Time Management: Processes, Techniques and Example
Project time management is the set of processes that make sure a project finishes on time: planning how the schedule will be managed, defining and sequencing activities, estimating durations, building the schedule and controlling it. Recent editions of the PMBOK Guide call this area schedule management. This guide explains each process, the main techniques and tools, and works through a full example from three-point estimates to a mid-project status check.
- Published 26 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project time management (now called schedule management) covers planning, building and controlling the project schedule.
- The classic six processes run from planning the approach to controlling the schedule, and they still give you a practical sequence to follow.
- Three-point estimates and the critical path tell you both the likely finish date and how much confidence to put in it.
- Before reacting to a negative schedule variance, check whether the late work is on the critical path.
- In Agile projects, time is fixed by timeboxes and scope flexes instead.
- Good personal time habits help the project manager keep the schedule current and spot problems early.

### What is project time management?
Project time management is the planning, scheduling and control of the activities needed to finish a project by an agreed date. It covers deciding how the schedule will be managed, breaking the work into activities, ordering them, estimating how long each will take, building a schedule baseline and tracking progress against it so delays are found and fixed early.
The term comes from the PMBOK Guide, which called this knowledge area Project Time Management until its 6th edition renamed it Project Schedule Management. Both names describe the same work, and "project time management" is still widely used in courses, job descriptions and exam preparation.
You will also see the phrase used for something different: how a project manager manages their own working time. That matters too, and this guide covers it in a separate section, but the core of project time management is the project's schedule. It sits alongside scope and cost as one of the three classic [project constraints: change one and the others usually move.

### Why project time management matters
A late finish rarely costs only time. Labour and overhead costs rise, benefits arrive later, other projects waiting for the same people are pushed back, and commitments to customers or regulators may be broken. Because activities depend on each other, a few days lost early on the critical path move every later date. Good time management gives you:
- **A realistic finish date** that is based on the work, not on hope or a date imposed without analysis.
- **Early warning** when the project starts to slip, while there is still float, budget or scope to trade.
- **Credible commitments** to sponsors and customers, backed by estimates and a stated level of confidence.
- **A baseline** to measure performance against and to learn from for future estimates.

### The six project time management processes
The PMBOK Guide 6th edition describes schedule management as six processes. They are a logical sequence rather than a rigid one: on most projects you repeat the middle steps as you learn more.
| Process | What happens | Main output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Plan schedule management | Decide the methods, tools, units, rules and reporting for the schedule | Schedule management plan |
| 2. Define activities | Break work packages from the WBS into schedule activities and milestones | Activity list and milestone list |
| 3. Sequence activities | Identify dependencies, leads and lags between activities | Project schedule network diagram |
| 4. Estimate activity durations | Estimate the working periods each activity needs with the planned resources | Duration estimates and basis of estimates |
| 5. Develop schedule | Calculate dates, find the critical path, fit resources and agree the baseline | Schedule baseline and project schedule |
| 6. Control schedule | Track progress, compare with the baseline, forecast and manage changes | Work performance information, forecasts and change requests |

#### How the name and processes have changed
- **5th edition and earlier:** the knowledge area was called Project Time Management and had seven processes, including Estimate Activity Resources.
- **6th edition (September 2017):** renamed Project Schedule Management. Estimate Activity Resources moved to Project Resource Management, leaving the six processes above.
- **7th edition:** replaced process-based knowledge areas with principles and performance domains; scheduling is covered mainly within planning and delivery.
- **8th edition (November 2025):** has six principles and seven performance domains, one of which is Schedule. According to PMI and published summaries, it brings back non-prescriptive process guidance for planning, developing, and monitoring and controlling the schedule.
The underlying work has not changed, so the six processes remain a practical way to learn scheduling. Our [PMBOK Guide overview](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) explains the editions.

### How to manage project time step by step
The steps below follow the six processes and show what to do at each one. They assume you already have an agreed scope and a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/); without those, any schedule is guesswork.

#### Step 1: Plan schedule management
Agree the rules before you build anything: half a page on a small project, a section of the project management plan on a large one.
| Item in the plan | Example decision |
| --- | --- |
| Scheduling method and tool | Critical path method in the team's project management software |
| Units and calendars | Durations in working days; five-day week; public holidays excluded |
| Level of detail | Activities of 1 to 10 working days; rolling wave for work more than three months away |
| Estimating approach | Three-point estimates for critical and uncertain work; analogous for routine work |
| Update cycle | Progress updated every Friday; forecast issued with the weekly status report |
| Control thresholds | Escalate if a milestone forecast slips by more than five working days or SPI falls below 0.90 |
| Baseline rules | Baseline changes only through approved change requests |

#### Step 2: Define activities
Decompose each work package into activities: actions with a clear start, end, owner and output. "Testing" is a work package; "run user acceptance test scripts for finance users" is an activity. Add milestones for key decisions, approvals and handovers, since they carry no duration but anchor the schedule.

#### Step 3: Sequence activities
Link the activities in the order the work must happen. Most links are finish-to-start (B starts when A finishes), but start-to-start, finish-to-finish and, rarely, start-to-finish also occur. Mark which links are mandatory (physical or legal) and which are discretionary (a team preference), because only discretionary links can be overlapped later. Add leads and lags where work can overlap or must wait. See our guide to [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) for all four types with examples.

#### Step 4: Estimate activity durations
Estimate the working time each activity needs with the resources you expect to have. Separate effort (person-days of work) from duration (calendar time): two people on a four-person-day task may take two days, or more if they have other work. Three techniques cover most needs:
- **Analogous estimating:** use the actual duration of a similar past activity, adjusted for differences. Quick, but only as good as the comparison.
- **Parametric estimating:** multiply a quantity by a rate, such as 300 users ÷ 25 users per training session = 12 sessions at half a day each = 6 days.
- **Three-point estimating:** ask for optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P) durations. The beta (PERT) formula gives an expected duration of (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6 and a standard deviation of (P − O) ÷ 6.
Record the assumptions behind each estimate. Our [effort estimation guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/) covers these and other methods in more depth.

#### Step 5: Develop the schedule
Combine the activities, links and durations into a schedule. Use the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/): a forward pass gives the earliest start and finish of each activity, a backward pass gives the latest, and the difference is [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/). Activities with zero float form the critical path, which sets the project's duration.
Then check the schedule against reality. Are people double-booked? Use resource levelling to resolve conflicts, accepting that it may extend the finish date. Does the finish miss a required date? Consider [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) by crashing or fast tracking. When the schedule is realistic and agreed, save it as the project baseline.

#### Step 6: Control the schedule
Update progress at the agreed interval: actual start and finish dates, remaining duration for work in progress, and any new or changed activities. Recalculate, compare forecast dates with the baseline and check float on critical and near-critical paths. Use [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) to measure progress in a consistent way, and route any change to the baseline through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
See our [project scheduling guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) for a full walk-through of building a schedule.

### Worked example: scheduling an expense system rollout
This illustrative example applies steps 2 to 5 to a small project: rolling out a new expense system to 300 staff. All durations are in working days.

#### Activities, dependencies and three-point estimates
| Activity | Depends on | O | M | P | Expected (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A. Requirements workshops | - | 2 | 3 | 10 | 4 |
| B. Configure the system | A | 8 | 10 | 18 | 11 |
| C. Write training material | A | 4 | 5 | 12 | 6 |
| D. Migrate supplier and cost-centre data | A | 5 | 7 | 15 | 8 |
| E. User acceptance testing | B, D | 3 | 5 | 7 | 5 |
| F. Train staff | C, E, H | 4 | 6 | 8 | 6 |
| G. Go-live and early support | F | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 |
| H. Staff communications | A | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 |
Pessimistic estimates pull expected durations above the most likely ones: requirements workshops (A) are most likely to take 3 days but are expected to take 4, because key finance staff are hard to schedule.

#### Forward and backward pass
| Activity | Duration | Earliest start | Earliest finish | Latest start | Latest finish | Total float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 4 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 4 | 0 |
| B | 11 | 4 | 15 | 4 | 15 | 0 |
| C | 6 | 4 | 10 | 14 | 20 | 10 |
| D | 8 | 4 | 12 | 7 | 15 | 3 |
| E | 5 | 15 | 20 | 15 | 20 | 0 |
| F | 6 | 20 | 26 | 20 | 26 | 0 |
| G | 3 | 26 | 29 | 26 | 29 | 0 |
| H | 3 | 4 | 7 | 17 | 20 | 13 |
The critical path is **A → B → E → F → G**, with a total duration of 4 + 11 + 5 + 6 + 3 = **29 working days**. Data migration (D) is near-critical, with only 3 days of float, so it needs watching too. Training material (C) and communications (H) have plenty of float, so they can absorb delays or be scheduled around people's other work. Our guide to the [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) explains the calculations step by step.

#### How confident is the 29-day date?
Add the variances (standard deviation squared) of the critical activities: A (8 ÷ 6)² = 1.78, B (10 ÷ 6)² = 2.78, E 0.44, F 0.44 and G 0.11, a total of about 5.56. The square root gives a standard deviation for the path of about **2.4 days**.
- 29 days is the expected finish, so there is roughly a 50% chance of finishing on or before it.
- 29 + 2.4 ≈ 31.4 days gives roughly 84% confidence (one standard deviation).
- 29 + 4.7 ≈ 33.7 days gives roughly 98% confidence (two standard deviations).
The project manager commits to **32 working days** (about six and a half weeks) and treats the three days between 29 and 32 as schedule contingency, owned by the project manager rather than spread across activities. This simple PERT calculation ignores near-critical paths such as the one through D, so it slightly overstates confidence; a Monte Carlo simulation handles that properly on larger projects.

#### Status check at day 15
At the end of day 15, C and D are complete on time, but configuration (B) is only about 80% done and is forecast to finish on day 17. Because B is critical, the whole chain moves: testing now runs from day 17 to 22, training from 22 to 28 and go-live support from 28 to 31. The 31-day forecast is inside the 32-day commitment, but two of the three contingency days are gone with half the project left.
The project manager reviews the options: add a second tester to shorten acceptance testing from 5 days to 4 (crashing), or start training a pilot group during the last two days of testing (fast tracking, with some risk of retraining if testing finds problems). The team chooses the extra tester, recovering one day at a known cost. Our [fast tracking vs crashing guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/) compares the two approaches.
Tip
Hold contingency at project level and report how much has been used. A schedule that is still "on time" but has used most of its contingency early is a warning sign.

### Worked example: controlling the schedule with earned value
Earned value gives a consistent, numerical view of schedule performance on larger projects. In this illustrative example, a 20-week project has a budget at completion of $200,000, planned to be spent evenly. At the end of week 8, the planned value (PV) is $80,000 and the earned value (EV), the budgeted value of the work actually completed, is $68,000.
| Measure | Formula | Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule variance (SV) | EV − PV | −$12,000 | Less work done than planned |
| SV% | SV ÷ PV | −15% | 15% of the planned work is not yet done |
| Schedule performance index (SPI) | EV ÷ PV | 0.85 | Progressing at 85% of the planned rate |
| Simple time forecast | Planned duration ÷ SPI | 20 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 23.5 weeks | If performance continues at the same rate |
The naive forecast says the project will finish about three and a half weeks late. But earned value does not know which activities are critical, so the project manager looks at where the shortfall sits:
- **$9,000 of the shortfall** is on documentation and training material, which has four weeks of float. It can catch up without moving the finish date, as long as the float is not used up.
- **$3,000 of the shortfall** is on supplier integration, which is on the critical path and is about one week behind.
The better forecast is therefore about **21 weeks**, not 23.5, unless the critical week is recovered. The actions follow from that: focus recovery effort on supplier integration, agree a catch-up date for documentation inside its float, and keep reporting SPI alongside critical path dates.
Our [schedule variance guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) covers SV, SPI and earned schedule in more detail. Read the guide to [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) for the full set of measures.
Tip
SPI alone can mislead late in a project, because it moves towards 1.0 as the work completes even if the project is late. Check critical path dates too.

### Project time management techniques
These are the techniques you will use most often.
| Technique | What it does | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decomposition | Breaks work packages into activities | Defining activities from the WBS |
| Rolling wave planning | Details near-term work and keeps later work high level | Long projects or uncertain later phases |
| Precedence diagramming | Shows activities and their dependencies as a network | Sequencing activities |
| Analogous and parametric estimating | Estimates from past projects or unit rates | Early estimates and repeatable work |
| Three-point (PERT) estimating | Gives an expected duration and a measure of uncertainty | Critical or uncertain activities |
| Critical path method | Finds the longest path and each activity's float | Every schedule with dependencies |
| Critical chain | Uses aggressive estimates and shared buffers, and accounts for resources | Resource-constrained, multi-project environments |
| Resource levelling and smoothing | Removes resource overloads, with or without moving the finish | When people are over-allocated |
| Crashing and fast tracking | Shortens the critical path with money or overlap | When the finish misses a required date |
| Earned value and earned schedule | Measures progress against the baseline in money and time | Control on medium and large projects |

### Project time management tools
The main tools for recording and showing the schedule are:
- **[Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/):** bars on a timeline showing activities, dependencies, milestones and progress. The most common way to communicate a schedule.
- **Network diagrams:** show the logic of the schedule and make the critical path easy to see.
- **Schedule templates:** a quick start for small projects. Our free [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) and [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) work in Excel and Google Sheets, and the [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) calculates float for you.
- **Scheduling software:** recalculates dates automatically when something changes, which matters once you have more than a few dozen activities.
- **Timesheets and time tracking:** record actual effort, which improves future estimates and supports billing.
Most modern project management tools combine several of these. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, offers Gantt charts with dependencies and the critical path highlighted, plus time tracking with approved timesheets, which suits teams running several date-driven projects. [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) supports all four dependency types, automatic rescheduling, the critical path and baselines on its Gantt charts. [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) is very approachable for mixed teams, with time tracking on its Pro plan. [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) suits teams that like a spreadsheet layout with Gantt charts on top, and Microsoft Planner premium plans add dependencies and, on Plan 3, baselines and the critical path.

### Project time management in Agile projects
Agile approaches manage time differently. Instead of fixing scope and estimating how long it will take, they usually fix time and let scope flex.
- **Timeboxes:** work happens in fixed-length iterations. In Scrum, a Sprint lasts one month or less, and events such as the Daily Scrum have a fixed maximum length.
- **Prioritised scope:** the most valuable work is done first, so if time runs out, what is left is the least valuable.
- **Empirical forecasting:** release dates are forecast from the team's measured pace rather than from activity estimates.
- **Visible progress:** burndown or burnup charts show remaining work against time in each iteration and release.
For example (illustrative), a team with 240 story points in its release backlog and a recent velocity of between 28 and 34 points per two-week sprint can forecast 240 ÷ 34 ≈ 7.1 to 240 ÷ 28 ≈ 8.6, so 8 to 9 sprints, or 16 to 18 weeks. As the backlog changes and velocity settles, the forecast is updated every sprint. See [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) for the method in full.
In hybrid projects, treat each block of sprints as a timeboxed summary activity in the master schedule, alongside predictive work such as procurement and deployment.

### Personal time management for project managers
The second meaning of project time management is how you spend your own week. A schedule that is not updated quickly undoes good planning, and a simple weekly rhythm helps:
| When | Activity | Typical time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday morning | Review critical and near-critical paths; confirm the week's priorities with team leads | 45 to 60 minutes |
| Tuesday | Risk and issue review; update the RAID log | 30 to 45 minutes |
| Wednesday | Stakeholder conversations and decisions needed this week | As needed |
| Thursday | Look ahead two to four weeks: resources, approvals, supplier dates | 30 minutes |
| Friday | Collect progress, update the schedule, issue the status report | 60 to 90 minutes |
- **Prioritise deliberately:** sort tasks by importance and urgency; our [priority list template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/priority-list-template/) does this for you.
- **Block focus time** for planning, analysis and writing, and protect it like a meeting.
- **Keep meetings short** with a clear agenda, decisions and actions.
- **Delegate task-level tracking** to team leads and focus your own attention on the critical path, risks and stakeholders.

### Common causes of project delays and how to prevent them
| Cause | Early warning sign | Prevention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unclear or changing scope | New requests appearing in status meetings | Agree scope early and control [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) through change control |
| Optimistic estimates | Activities finishing late one after another | Use three-point estimates and hold contingency at project level |
| Shared resources pulled away | Named people missing from planned work | Agree resource commitments with line managers; level resources |
| Supplier and approval delays | Unanswered queries; approvals not yet scheduled | Put approvals and deliveries in the schedule as activities with owners |
| Schedule not updated | Status reports with the same dates every week | Fixed update cycle with actual dates and remaining durations |
| Multitasking across projects | Many activities started, few finished | Limit work in progress and sequence priorities |

### Common project time management mistakes
- **Scheduling from a deadline backwards** without checking whether the work fits, then discovering the gap months later.
- **Confusing effort with duration**, so a 10-day task assigned to someone working half-time on the project is shown as 10 days instead of about 20.
- **Leaving out non-work time:** holidays, approvals, procurement lead times and handovers.
- **Hard-coding dates** instead of linking activities, so the schedule cannot recalculate when something slips.
- **Padding every activity** instead of holding visible contingency, which hides the real risk and encourages work to expand.
- **Watching only the critical path** and ignoring near-critical paths that can become critical after a small delay.
- **Changing the baseline informally**, which makes the project look on time while it drifts.

### Project time management checklist
Before you baseline the schedule:
- Every work package in the WBS has at least one activity, and every activity has an owner.
- Estimates have recorded assumptions, and uncertain ones use three points.
- Calendars include holidays and part-time availability.
- The critical path makes sense to the people doing the work.
- Contingency is visible and owned, and the commitment date has a stated confidence level.
At each status update:
- Actual dates and remaining durations are entered for all started activities.
- Critical and near-critical paths have been reviewed after recalculation.
- Variances beyond thresholds are explained, with actions and owners.
- Any baseline change has an approved change request.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project time management?**
It is the set of processes used to plan, schedule and control the timing of a project so it finishes by an agreed date: planning the approach, defining and sequencing activities, estimating durations, developing the schedule and controlling it.

**Q: What are the six processes of project time management?**
Plan schedule management, define activities, sequence activities, estimate activity durations, develop schedule and control schedule. Earlier PMBOK editions also included estimate activity resources, which moved to resource management in the 6th edition.

**Q: What is the difference between project time management and schedule management?**
They describe the same area. The PMBOK Guide 6th edition, released in 2017, renamed Project Time Management to Project Schedule Management. The 8th edition covers it in the Schedule performance domain.

**Q: Why is time management important in project management?**
Delays raise costs, postpone benefits, disrupt other projects and break commitments. Good time management produces a realistic finish date, gives early warning of slippage and shows the team which work drives the end date.

**Q: What tools are used in project time management?**
Gantt charts, network diagrams, schedule templates, scheduling software, earned value reports and timesheets. Tools such as Wrike, ClickUp and Smartsheet combine Gantt charts, dependencies and progress tracking in one place.

**Q: What is a schedule management plan?**
A short document that sets the rules for the schedule: the method and tool, units and calendars, level of detail, estimating approach, update cycle, control thresholds and how the baseline can be changed.

**Q: How do you estimate activity durations?**
Use analogous estimates from similar past work, parametric estimates from unit rates, or three-point estimates. With three points, the expected duration is (optimistic + 4 × most likely + pessimistic) ÷ 6. Record the assumptions behind each estimate.

**Q: What is the critical path in project time management?**
The longest sequence of dependent activities, which sets the shortest possible project duration. Critical activities have zero float, so any delay to them delays the finish. See our [critical path method guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).

**Q: How do you control the schedule?**
Update progress at a fixed interval, recalculate the schedule, compare forecast dates with the baseline, check critical and near-critical paths, use measures such as SPI, and act on variances through change control.

**Q: What is the difference between project time management and personal time management?**
Project time management plans and controls the project's schedule. Personal time management is how individuals, including the project manager, organise their own working time. Both matter, but they use different techniques.

**Q: How does time management work in Agile projects?**
Agile teams fix time with timeboxes such as sprints and let scope flex, delivering the highest-priority work first. Release dates are forecast from measured velocity or throughput and updated every iteration.

**Q: What causes project delays?**
Common causes are unclear or changing scope, optimistic estimates, shared resources being pulled away, supplier and approval delays, hidden dependencies and schedules that are not updated, so problems surface late.

**Q: Is project time management on the PMP exam?**
Yes. Planning and managing the schedule is part of the Process domain, which makes up 41% of the PMP exam from July 2026. See our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

# Project Timeline: How to Create One, With Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-timeline/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Learn what a project timeline is, how to create one step by step, the main types, a worked example with dates, and how to keep it up to date.


## Project Timeline: How to Create One, With Examples
A project timeline is a visual, date-ordered view of a project's phases, milestones and key deliverables, showing stakeholders when the important things will happen. It is drawn from the project schedule, which calculates the dates, and presents them on a single page. This guide shows you what to include, the main types, how to build one in eight steps, and a worked example from activity list to finished timeline.
- Published 27 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- A project timeline communicates dates; the project schedule calculates them. Build the schedule first.
- Include phases, 5 to 15 milestones, a today line, status and the date it was last updated.
- Choose the type of timeline for the audience: milestones for sponsors, phase bars for clients, Gantt-style for the team.
- Dates come from durations and dependencies, so the critical path decides your end date.
- When dates move, show baseline and forecast side by side and say what you are doing about it.

### What is a project timeline?
A **project timeline** is a chronological, visual summary of a project's main phases, milestones and deadlines, usually on one page. It shows when key work starts and finishes and when decisions or deliveries are due, without the detail of every task. Its job is communication: giving sponsors, clients and the team a shared picture of the plan.
A timeline sits on top of the [project schedule](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/). The schedule holds the activities, durations, [dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) and resources, and calculates the dates. The timeline selects the dates that matter to its audience and presents them clearly. If the schedule changes, the timeline changes with it.
- **Created:** during planning, once the scope and a first schedule exist.
- **Owned by:** the project manager, with dates agreed by the people doing the work.
- **Used:** at kick-off, in sponsor and client updates, at phase reviews and whenever dates change.
Tip
A timeline drawn from wishful dates rather than a schedule will be wrong by the first review. Derive every date from durations and dependencies, even if the calculation is a simple spreadsheet.

### Why a project timeline matters
- **One shared picture.** Everyone sees the same phases and dates, which reduces 'I thought it was due in May' conversations.
- **Early warning.** A slipping milestone is visible at a glance, while there is still time to recover.
- **Better decisions.** Showing approval points on the timeline makes it clear when you need decisions from sponsors or clients, and what happens if they are late.
- **Realistic expectations.** A timeline built from real durations helps you push back on an impossible deadline with evidence.
- **Coordination.** Teams, suppliers and other projects can plan their own work around your key dates.

### What to include in a project timeline
Keep a timeline lean. Include what the audience needs to understand the plan and act on it, and leave the rest in the schedule.
| Element | What it shows | Tip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phases or workstreams | The main blocks of work, such as design, build and test | Use the same names as the plan and the status report |
| Milestones | Zero-duration points such as approvals, deliveries and go-live | Usually 5 to 15; see our [project milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) guide |
| Key deliverables | What will be handed over and when | Name them as the client would recognise them |
| Critical dependencies | Hand-offs that drive the end date | Show only those on or near the critical path |
| Decision points | Dates by which you need a decision from the audience | Highlight them; they are often why the timeline is shared |
| Today line and status | Where the project is now, and what is on track or at risk | Use a simple, consistent colour key |
| Baseline and forecast | Original dates against current expected dates | Only needed once something has moved |
| Last updated and owner | How current the view is and who to ask | Put it in a corner of every version |

### Project timeline vs schedule, Gantt chart and roadmap
These terms are often used interchangeably. They overlap, but each has a different job.
|  | Project timeline | Project schedule | [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) | [Project roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-roadmap/) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Communicate key dates | Calculate and control dates | Plan and track activities | Show strategic direction and sequence |
| Detail | Phases and milestones | Every activity, dependency and resource | Every activity as a bar, with links | Themes or initiatives, often by quarter |
| Audience | Sponsors, clients, wider team | Project manager and planners | Project team and managers | Executives, product and portfolio owners |
| Date precision | Firm, from the schedule | Exact | Exact | Often approximate |
| Typical size | One page or slide | A scheduling file | Dozens to hundreds of rows | One page |
A **milestone chart** is a timeline that shows only milestones, and is the most common format for senior stakeholders.

### Types of project timeline
Choose the format by asking who will read it and what they need to decide.
| Type | What it looks like | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Milestone timeline | A single horizontal line with diamonds for key dates | Sponsors and boards who want the headline dates |
| Phase (bar) timeline | One bar per phase across months, with milestones on top | Clients and kick-off meetings |
| Gantt-style timeline | Summary bars for workstreams, often expandable to tasks | The project team and functional managers |
| Swimlane timeline | One lane per team, supplier or workstream | Cross-functional projects with many hand-offs; see [swimlane diagrams](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/swimlane-diagram/) |
| Vertical or list timeline | Dates listed top to bottom with short notes | Small projects, emails and mobile screens |
| Roadmap timeline | Quarters or releases with themes rather than exact dates | Product and multi-year programmes |
| Historical timeline | What actually happened, in date order | Project closure and lessons learned reviews |
Many teams keep two views of the same schedule: a milestone timeline for the sponsor and a Gantt-style timeline for the team.

### How to create a project timeline in 8 steps

#### Step 1: Agree the purpose and audience
Decide who the timeline is for and what they need from it. A sponsor wants five dates and the decisions you need; a delivery team wants every hand-off. This choice drives the level of detail in every later step.

#### Step 2: Confirm the scope and deliverables
List what the project will deliver, using the [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) statement. Break the work down in a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) so nothing is forgotten. Work missing from the WBS will be missing from the timeline.

#### Step 3: List the activities
Turn each work package into the activities needed to produce it. For a timeline you only need enough detail to calculate the dates reliably, which is usually activities of one to four weeks for a project lasting a few months.

#### Step 4: Estimate durations
Ask the people who will do the work. Use past projects where you can, and use three-point estimates (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) for uncertain work, as in a [PERT chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pert-chart/). Estimate effort and then duration, allowing for availability: ten days of effort from someone available half-time takes four weeks. Our [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/) guide covers the techniques.
For example, if the build team says the work will take at best 3 weeks, most likely 4 and at worst 8, the PERT estimate is (3 + 4 x 4 + 8) / 6 = 4.5 weeks. Using 4.5 rather than the optimistic 3 is the difference between a timeline that holds and one that slips in the first month.

#### Step 5: Map dependencies
Record which activities must finish before others can start. Most links are finish-to-start, but some work can overlap. Include external dependencies such as supplier deliveries, approvals and other projects; these are the dates most likely to move.

#### Step 6: Calculate dates and find the critical path
Starting from the project start date, work forward through the dependencies to calculate each activity's earliest start and finish. The longest chain of dependent activities is the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/), and it sets the earliest possible end date. Activities off the critical path have [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/), which tells you where there is room to absorb delays. Use a working calendar that includes public holidays and planned shutdowns.

#### Step 7: Select milestones and choose a format
Pick the phases and milestones that tell the story for your audience: usually phase ends, approvals, key deliveries and go-live. Choose a timeline type from the table above, mark today's date, add a short colour key and the last-updated date.

#### Step 8: Review, baseline and share
Walk the draft through with the team and the main stakeholders, check the dates against known holidays and commitments, and agree it. Save the agreed dates as the [schedule baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) so you can show later changes honestly. Then share it, and update it whenever the schedule changes, at least as often as you report status.

### Worked example: a 19-week website redesign
A marketing team is redesigning its company website. The project starts on Monday 1 February 2027 and the team works five-day weeks. To keep the arithmetic simple, this example ignores public holidays; in a real schedule the Easter bank holidays would move some dates.

#### 1. Activities, durations and dependencies
| ID | Activity | Duration | Depends on | Weeks | Dates | Float |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Discovery and requirements | 3 weeks | None | 1 to 3 | 1 Feb to 19 Feb | 0 |
| B | Content audit | 2 weeks | A | 4 to 5 | 22 Feb to 5 Mar | 4 weeks |
| C | Design (wireframes and visual design) | 4 weeks | A | 4 to 7 | 22 Feb to 19 Mar | 0 |
| D | Content writing | 4 weeks | B | 6 to 9 | 8 Mar to 2 Apr | 4 weeks |
| E | Build | 6 weeks | C | 8 to 13 | 22 Mar to 30 Apr | 0 |
| F | Content load | 2 weeks | D and E | 14 to 15 | 3 May to 14 May | 0 |
| G | User acceptance testing and fixes | 3 weeks | F | 16 to 18 | 17 May to 4 Jun | 0 |
| H | Launch preparation and go-live | 1 week | G | 19 | 7 Jun to 11 Jun | 0 |
There are two paths to activity F. Path A, C, E takes 13 weeks; path A, B, D takes 9 weeks. The longer path is the critical path, so the critical path for the whole project is **A, C, E, F, G, H = 19 weeks**. Content audit and writing have four weeks of float: they can slip by up to four weeks without moving go-live.

#### 2. Choose the milestones
| Milestone | Date | Why the sponsor cares |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M1 Requirements signed off | Fri 19 Feb 2027 | Sponsor approval needed; scope is fixed from here |
| M2 Design approved | Fri 19 Mar 2027 | Sponsor approval needed; build cannot start without it |
| M3 Content ready | Fri 2 Apr 2027 | Not critical: may slip to 30 Apr without delaying launch |
| M4 Build complete | Fri 30 Apr 2027 | Last chance to see the site before content goes in |
| M5 Testing signed off | Fri 4 Jun 2027 | Go or no-go decision |
| M6 Go-live | Fri 11 Jun 2027 | The date the business is planning around |

#### 3. Draw the one-page timeline
For the sponsor, the team shows a phase timeline by month with milestone diamonds. In a slide or spreadsheet it looks like this:
| Phase | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Discovery | ■■ ◆M1 |  |  |  |  |
| Design | ■ | ■■ ◆M2 |  |  |  |
| Content | ■ | ■■ | ◆M3 |  |  |
| Build |  | ■ | ■■ ◆M4 |  |  |
| Content load and testing |  |  |  | ■■ | ◆M5 |
| Launch |  |  |  |  | ■ ◆M6 |
Behind this six-row view sits the eight-activity schedule above, and on a larger project perhaps a few hundred activities. The sponsor sees the two approvals they own, the go-live date and the fact that content has some slack, which is exactly what they need.

### When the timeline slips: updating and recovering
Suppose design approval (M2) takes two weeks longer than planned because the sponsor asks for a second round of changes. Design is on the critical path, so every later critical activity moves by two weeks. Content writing does not move, because it has float.
| Milestone | Baseline | Forecast | Variance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M2 Design approved | 19 Mar | 2 Apr | +2 weeks |
| M3 Content ready | 2 Apr | 2 Apr | None (float absorbs it) |
| M4 Build complete | 30 Apr | 14 May | +2 weeks |
| M5 Testing signed off | 4 Jun | 18 Jun | +2 weeks |
| M6 Go-live | 11 Jun | 25 Jun | +2 weeks |
Show baseline and forecast side by side rather than quietly redrawing the timeline. Then set out the options and their trade-offs, so the sponsor can decide:
- **Fast-track:** start loading content into finished page templates while the rest of the build continues, overlapping E and F. This recovers about a week but adds rework risk.
- **Crash:** add a second developer for the last three weeks of build. This costs money and recovers about a week, if the work can be split.
- **Re-scope:** launch with the main pages on 11 June and add the remaining sections a fortnight later.
- **Accept:** move go-live to 25 June and tell everyone planning around it now.
Our guide to [fast-tracking vs crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/) explains both techniques in more detail, and [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) shows how to measure slippage in earned value terms. Delays that you saw coming should already be in the risk register; see [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/).

### Project timeline examples by project type
The phases and milestones change with the type of project, but the pattern is the same: a few phases, the approvals that unlock each one and a clear end point. These outlines are illustrative starting points; your own durations should come from your schedule.

#### Example: a 300-person conference
| Phase | Typical timing | Key milestones |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concept and budget | Months 1 to 2 | Budget approved; date and format agreed |
| Venue and suppliers | Months 2 to 4 | Venue contract signed; catering and AV booked |
| Programme and speakers | Months 3 to 6 | Speakers confirmed; agenda published |
| Marketing and registration | Months 4 to 8 | Registration opens; early-bird deadline |
| Final preparation | Final month | Final numbers to venue; run-through |
| Event and close | Event week plus 4 weeks | Event day; feedback survey; final accounts |

#### Example: an office refurbishment
| Phase | Typical timing | Key milestones |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brief and design | Weeks 1 to 6 | Design signed off; budget confirmed |
| Approvals and procurement | Weeks 5 to 12 | Permissions granted; contractor appointed |
| Construction and fit-out | Weeks 13 to 24 | Site handed over; first fix complete; practical completion |
| Move and snagging | Weeks 25 to 28 | Move weekend; snagging list closed |

#### Example: a software feature release
| Phase | Typical timing | Key milestones |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discovery | Sprint 0 (2 weeks) | Problem and success measures agreed |
| Build in sprints | Sprints 1 to 4 | Demo at the end of each sprint |
| Beta | Sprint 5 | Beta released to selected users |
| General release | Sprint 6 | Release; support handover; usage review after 30 days |
Notice that the approvals (budget, design, permissions, contract) are usually the milestones the sponsor cares about most. They are also the dates most likely to slip, so give each one its own duration in the schedule rather than assuming it happens overnight.

### How to make a project timeline in Excel or PowerPoint
Spreadsheets and slides are fine for one-off or small-project timelines. The main drawback is that they do not recalculate when a dependency moves, so you must update them by hand.

#### In Excel (or Google Sheets)
1. Create a table with three columns: phase or task name, start date and duration in days.
2. Select the table and insert a **stacked bar** chart.
3. Click the first data series (the start dates) and set its fill to **no fill**. The remaining bars now float at the right dates.
4. Format the vertical axis and tick **categories in reverse order** so the first phase is at the top.
5. Set the horizontal axis minimum to your project start date (and the maximum to the end date) so the bars fill the chart.
6. Add milestones as a separate row with a duration of zero and a marker, or as labelled shapes.
7. Add a vertical line or shape for today's date and a text box with the last-updated date.

#### In PowerPoint
1. Draw a horizontal line or a row of month boxes across the slide.
2. Add a bar per phase using rectangles, and a diamond per milestone with its date underneath.
3. Use one colour per status (for example green, amber and red) and explain it in a small key.
4. Copy the dates from the schedule, never from memory, and note the source and last-updated date on the slide.
If you want a ready-made layout, our free [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) holds tasks, durations, dependencies and milestones, and the [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) turns dates into bars automatically.

### Project timelines in Agile projects
Agile teams plan in short iterations and expect scope to change, so they rarely publish a fixed activity-by-activity timeline. They still need to tell stakeholders when value will arrive.
- **Release timeline:** shows sprints or iterations and the planned release dates, with the main features expected in each. See [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/).
- **Roadmap timeline:** shows themes or outcomes by quarter, with dates becoming firmer as they get closer. Our [product roadmap template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-roadmap-template/) is a starting point.
- **Fixed date, flexible scope:** when a date is fixed, such as a regulatory deadline, the timeline holds the date and the team adjusts what is included in each release.
Hybrid projects often combine both: a firm timeline for hardware, contracts and go-live, and a sprint-based release timeline for the software inside it.

### Tips for presenting a project timeline to stakeholders
- **Lead with the decision you need.** 'We need design approval by 19 March to hold the June launch' is more useful than a list of dates.
- **Use plain language.** Write 'Design approved', not 'WP3.2 complete'.
- **Show uncertainty honestly.** If a date depends on a supplier or an approval, say so, and consider showing a range for later phases.
- **Keep one version.** Generate the timeline from the schedule or a single master file so different decks never show different dates.
- **Pair it with a status update.** Add the timeline to your [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) so movement is explained, not just shown.
- **Use colour sparingly.** Reserve red and amber for real problems; if everything is coloured, nothing stands out.

### Common project timeline mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting from the deadline and working backwards without checking durations | The timeline looks fine but cannot be delivered | Build it forwards from estimates, then compare with the deadline |
| Ignoring dependencies | Activities shown in parallel turn out to be sequential | Map dependencies and find the critical path |
| Forgetting approvals and reviews | Sign-off time is often longer than the work itself | Give each approval its own duration |
| No allowance for holidays or availability | Dates slip as soon as people take leave | Use a working calendar and realistic availability |
| Too much detail | Stakeholders cannot see the key dates | Keep 5 to 15 milestones on the stakeholder view |
| Redrawing without showing what moved | Trust drops when changes are hidden | Show baseline and forecast dates |
| Never updating it | The timeline becomes fiction | Update it at every status cycle |

### Project timeline tools and templates
For small projects, a spreadsheet template is enough. For larger projects, or when several people update the plan, [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) is easier, because its timeline or Gantt view is generated from the live schedule and moves automatically when a dependency changes.
Most leading tools include a timeline or Gantt view. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, offers interactive Gantt charts with dependencies, critical path and baselines on paid plans, along with shareable dashboards, which suits teams that report the same timeline to several audiences.
For the scheduling method behind every good timeline, read our guide to [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project timeline?**
A project timeline is a visual, date-ordered summary of a project's main phases, milestones and deadlines. It shows stakeholders when the key things will happen, without the detail of every task.

**Q: What is the difference between a project timeline and a project schedule?**
The schedule is the detailed model: activities, durations, dependencies and resources, from which dates are calculated. The timeline is a simplified view of the schedule's key dates for communication. Build the schedule first, then draw the timeline from it.

**Q: What is the difference between a project timeline and a Gantt chart?**
A Gantt chart shows every activity as a bar with its dependencies and is used by the team to plan and track work. A timeline shows only phases and milestones and is used to communicate. A summary Gantt chart can serve as a timeline.

**Q: What should a project timeline include?**
Phases or workstreams, key milestones and deliverables, critical dependencies, decision points, a today line, status, baseline and forecast dates once anything has moved, and the date it was last updated.

**Q: Who is responsible for creating the project timeline?**
The project manager usually builds and maintains it, but the dates should come from the people doing the work, and the sponsor or client should agree the key milestones.

**Q: When is a project timeline created?**
During planning, after the scope is agreed and a first schedule exists. A rough timeline may appear earlier in a business case or [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/), but treat those dates as estimates until the schedule is built.

**Q: How many milestones should a project timeline have?**
Usually between five and fifteen. Fewer may hide important approvals; more turns the timeline into a task list. Larger projects can show milestones by phase.

**Q: Are milestones the same as deadlines?**
Not quite. A milestone marks a significant point, such as an approval or delivery, and has no duration. A deadline is a date by which something must be done. Many milestones have deadlines, but not every deadline is a milestone.

**Q: How often should a project timeline be updated?**
Whenever a key date changes, and at least as often as you report status, which is often weekly or fortnightly. Keep the baseline so you can show what has moved.

**Q: How do you estimate a project timeline?**
Break the work into activities, estimate each duration with the people doing it, map the dependencies and calculate the dates forwards from the start. The longest chain of dependent activities, the critical path, gives the earliest end date.

**Q: How long should a project timeline be?**
As long as the schedule says, not as long as the deadline allows. On the page, a stakeholder timeline should fit one slide or sheet. For long projects, show the next three to six months in detail and later phases as summary bars.

**Q: What is the timeline section of a project proposal?**
A short overview of the proposed phases, milestones and end date, so the reader can judge whether the plan is realistic. Mark the dates as estimates that will be confirmed once the detailed schedule is built and the project is approved.

**Q: Can I make a project timeline in Excel?**
Yes. A stacked bar chart with the start-date series hidden creates a simple timeline, or you can use a ready-made template. Excel does not recalculate dates when dependencies change, so update it by hand.

**Q: What does a project timeline look like in Agile?**
Usually a release timeline or roadmap showing sprints, planned releases and the main features or outcomes in each, with near-term dates firm and later ones indicative.

# RACI Matrix (Responsibility Assignment Matrix) With Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a RACI matrix is, what Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed mean, an example, how to build one, and variants like RASCI.


## RACI Matrix (Responsibility Assignment Matrix) With Example
A RACI matrix, a type of responsibility assignment matrix, clarifies who does what for each task or deliverable. It prevents gaps, overlaps and confusion about decision-making.
- Published 20 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- RACI clarifies Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed.
- Only one Accountable per task.
- Use Cs and Is sparingly.

### What RACI means
| Letter | Role | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R | Responsible | Does the work |
| A | Accountable | Owns the outcome and signs off; only one per task |
| C | Consulted | Gives input before decisions (two-way) |
| I | Informed | Kept up to date (one-way) |

### Example
| Deliverable | Sponsor | Project manager | Designer | Developer | Marketing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | A | R | C | C | C |
| Website design | I | A | R | C | C |
| Development | I | A | C | R | I |
| Launch plan | A | R | I | I | C |

### How to build a RACI
1. List deliverables or tasks down the side.
2. List roles or people across the top.
3. Assign one A per row.
4. Assign at least one R per row.
5. Add C and I sparingly.
6. Review with everyone involved.

### Variants
- **RASCI:** adds Supportive.
- **RACI-VS:** adds Verifier and Signatory.
- **DACI:** Driver, Approver, Contributors, Informed, used for decisions.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does RACI stand for?**
Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed.

**Q: Can a task have more than one Accountable in a RACI matrix?**
No. Only one person should be accountable.

**Q: Can someone be both R and A in a RACI matrix?**
Yes, often for smaller tasks.

**Q: What is a responsibility assignment matrix?**
A grid mapping work to roles; RACI is the most common type.

**Q: When should you create a RACI?**
During planning, after the WBS is defined.

**Q: What is the difference between Consulted and Informed in RACI?**
Consulted gives input before decisions; Informed is told afterwards.

**Q: Is RACI used in Agile?**
Less formally, but it can clarify roles outside the team, such as approvals.

**Q: How is RASCI different from RACI?**
RASCI is RACI plus Supportive, for people who help the Responsible person.

**Q: What are common RACI mistakes?**
Too many Cs, no clear A, or one person with too many Rs.

**Q: Where is the RACI kept?**
In the project plan or a shared document everyone can see.
