# RAID Log: Meaning, Example and How to Create One

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: A RAID log tracks project risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies. See what to include, a worked example, the columns, review steps and pitfalls.


## RAID Log: Meaning, Example and How to Create One
A RAID log is a single register in which a project records its **R**isks, **A**ssumptions, **I**ssues and **D**ependencies, each with an owner, an action and a status. It gives the project manager, team and sponsor one place to see everything that could knock the project off course. This guide explains each letter, the columns to use, a full worked example and how to run a RAID review.
- Published 1 October 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- A RAID log tracks risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies together, so one review covers all four.
- Some teams read the A as Actions and the D as Decisions; agree your version at the start.
- Every entry needs a clear description, a rating, a named owner, an action, a date and a status.
- Items move between categories: a false assumption becomes a risk, and a risk that happens becomes an issue.
- Review the log on a fixed rhythm, usually weekly, and report only the top items to the sponsor.
- A short, current log is far more useful than a long one nobody reads.

### What is a RAID log?
A **RAID log** is a project management document that records the risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies affecting a project in one place. Each entry has a description, a rating, an owner, an agreed action, a due date and a status. The log is created during initiation or planning, reviewed regularly and kept up to date until project closure.
Think of it as the project's early-warning system and memory in one. Because all four categories sit side by side, a single review can spot connections, such as a late dependency that is about to turn a risk into an issue.
The RAID log is not a formal product in PMI's PMBOK Guide or in PRINCE2. It is a widely used practice, especially in the UK, in consultancies and in PMOs, that combines several registers those methods describe. That makes it flexible: you can keep it as a light summary on a small project or as the main control log on a medium-sized one.
It works closely with other project controls. The [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) and business case are usually the first sources of risks and assumptions, the [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) summarises the top RAID items, and on larger projects a detailed [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) and [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/) sit behind it.

### What does RAID stand for?
In its most common form, RAID stands for risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies. Each letter answers a different question about the project.
| Letter | Item | Question it answers | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R | Risks | What might go wrong (or better than planned)? | The supplier may deliver the hardware late |
| A | Assumptions | What are we relying on without proof? | Users will be available for testing in May |
| I | Issues | What is going wrong today? | The test server has been down for two days |
| D | Dependencies | What do we need from others, and what do they need from us? | Data migration needs the finance team's new chart of accounts |

#### Common variations
The letters are used in different ways. Asana's guide, for example, reads the D as **decisions**, and the University of Waterloo's IST project office uses **risks, actions, issues and decisions**. Other versions include:
- **RAIDD:** risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies and decisions, so nothing is lost.
- **RAIDO or RAIDOO:** adds opportunities, which some teams prefer to keep apart from threats.
None of these is wrong. What matters is that everyone uses the same version: decide at kick-off and write the definitions at the top of the log. If you need actions and decisions as well, add them as extra tabs.

### Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies explained
Each category needs slightly different information. Here is what to record, with a weak and a strong entry for each.

#### Risks
A [project risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk/) is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, would affect at least one project objective such as scope, time, cost or quality. Write risks in a **cause, event, effect** format so the owner knows what to watch and what to protect.
| Weak entry | Strong entry |
| --- | --- |
| Supplier risk | Because the supplier is also delivering to two larger customers (cause), the server hardware may arrive after 1 March (event), delaying installation and go-live by up to three weeks (effect). |
Rate each risk for probability and impact, then agree a response: avoid, reduce, transfer, accept or, for opportunities, exploit and enhance. What remains after the response is your [residual risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/residual-risk/), and any fallback plan belongs in a [contingency plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/).

#### Assumptions
An assumption is something the plan treats as true without proof, such as a resource being available, a licence covering extra users or a regulation staying the same. Assumptions are dangerous because they are invisible until they fail. Record them so they can be **tested**: give each one a validation owner and a date by which it will be confirmed or disproved.
| Weak entry | Strong entry |
| --- | --- |
| Licences are fine | The current CRM licence covers 50 extra users at no additional cost. Validate with procurement by 15 May; if false, budget impact is about one month of licence fees per user. |
Most assumptions start in the business case and charter, where they are often listed alongside [project constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/). When an assumption is proved false, raise it as a risk or an issue straight away and close the assumption with a note.

#### Issues
An issue is a problem that is happening now or is certain to happen. Unlike a risk, there is no probability to assess; you rate it by **priority or severity** and resolve it. Typical issues are a failed delivery, a defect or a missing team member.
| Weak entry | Strong entry |
| --- | --- |
| Testing problems | Integration tests have failed since 3 June because the security certificates on the test environment expired. Blocks 12 test cases on the critical path. Infrastructure to renew certificates by 7 June. |
Keep the full history of large issues in a dedicated issue log if you have one, and escalate any issue that breaks the agreed tolerances for time, cost or scope. Issues that need a change to the baseline go through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).

#### Dependencies
A dependency is a relationship in which your project relies on something it does not fully control, or something else relies on your project. Inside the schedule these are [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/); in the RAID log you mainly track **external** ones: other projects, suppliers, other departments, regulators and client decisions.
| Weak entry | Strong entry |
| --- | --- |
| Need brand guidelines | Inbound: website build needs final brand guidelines from the marketing rebrand project by 30 April. Provider: marketing PM. If late, page templates slip day for day. Status: at risk, draft due 14 May. |
Record the direction (inbound or outbound), the provider and receiver, the date needed and the impact if it is late. Outbound dependencies, what others need from you, are easy to forget and are often the ones that damage relationships between teams.

### Why use a RAID log?
A RAID log costs little to set up and pays back quickly if kept current. Its main benefits are:
- **One view of project health.** The sponsor and team see threats, problems, assumptions and dependencies together instead of in four documents.
- **Earlier warning.** Regular reviews catch risks and late dependencies before they become issues.
- **Clear accountability.** Every item has a named owner, an action and a date, so it cannot drift.
- **Better decisions and reporting.** Recorded assumptions and decisions explain why the plan looks as it does, and the top items feed straight into the status report.
- **Useful lessons.** At closure the log shows what was foreseen, what was missed and what worked, which feeds [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).
It also has limits, and it helps to be honest about them:
- It takes discipline: a log that is not updated gives false comfort.
- It can become a dumping ground for minor worries, hiding what matters.
- On large or regulated projects it may not hold enough detail, so separate registers sit behind it.
Tip
As a rough guide, if your RAID log has more than about 40 open items on a medium-sized project, it is probably acting as a to-do list. Move routine tasks to the plan or board and keep the log for things that genuinely threaten objectives.

### What to include: RAID log columns
A practical RAID log uses one set of core columns for every entry, plus a few fields that apply to only one type. A single table with a **Type** column is easiest to filter and sort; a workbook with one tab per type gives more room for detail. Both work.
| Column | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| ID | Unique reference, ideally prefixed by type |
| Type | Risk, assumption, issue or dependency |
| Date raised | When the item was logged |
| Raised by | Who identified it |
| Description | Clear statement using the formats above |
| Category or area | Workstream, deliverable or theme |
| Impact | Effect on time, cost, scope, quality or benefits |
| Probability | Risks only (and assumptions, if you rate the chance they are false) |
| Score or RAG | Probability x impact for risks; priority for issues |
| Owner | One named person responsible for the item |
| Action or response | What will be done, by whom |
| Due or review date | When the action is due or the item is next checked |
| Status | Open, in progress, monitoring, closed (or confirmed/false for assumptions) |
| Date closed and notes | When and why it was closed |
| Links | Related items, tasks or change requests |

#### Type-specific fields
| Type | Extra fields worth adding |
| --- | --- |
| Risks | Trigger or early warning sign, response strategy, contingency, residual rating |
| Assumptions | Validation method, validation date, consequence if false |
| Issues | Severity, escalation level, resolution, date resolved |
| Dependencies | Direction (inbound/outbound), provider, receiver, date needed, date committed |

#### A simple scoring scale
Use a scale everyone understands. A common approach is to rate probability and impact from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high) and multiply them. The thresholds below are an example; set your own with the sponsor and record them at the top of the log.
| Score (P x I) | Rating | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15 to 25 | Red | Owner acts now; reported to the sponsor in the next status report |
| 8 to 14 | Amber | Response agreed and tracked at every RAID review |
| 1 to 7 | Green | Monitored; reviewed monthly or at stage gates |
For issues, a three-level priority (high, medium, low) tied to escalation rules is usually enough, for example: high issues that threaten a milestone go to the sponsor within 24 hours. The free [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) has columns for ID, type, description, impact, probability, owner, action, due date and status, with dropdowns for type and ratings, so you can start with the core set and add fields as you need them.

### How to create a RAID log step by step
You can build a working RAID log in an afternoon. The steps below suit most projects; scale the detail to the size and risk of yours.
1. **Agree the scope and letters.** Decide whether D means dependencies or decisions, whether you track actions, and whether the RAID log is the main register or a summary of separate ones.
2. **Choose a format.** A shared spreadsheet is enough for most single projects. Use a project management tool if many owners will update items or you need a programme roll-up.
3. **Set the columns and scales.** Start with the core columns above, define your probability and impact scales and agree the escalation thresholds with the sponsor.
4. **Gather the first items.** Review the charter, business case, [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/), schedule, contracts and lessons from similar projects. Then run a 60 to 90 minute RAID workshop (sometimes called RAID analysis) with the team and key stakeholders.
5. **Write each entry properly.** Use cause-event-effect for risks, testable statements for assumptions, evidence for issues and both parties for dependencies. Remove duplicates.
6. **Assign one owner per item.** The owner is the person best placed to act, not always the project manager. Confirm each owner has accepted the item; a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) helps where ownership is unclear.
7. **Agree actions and dates.** Every open item needs a next action and a date for the next check, even if the action is simply to monitor.
8. **Set the review rhythm.** Put a recurring RAID review in the calendar, decide what goes in the status report and publish the log where everyone can see it.
Involve the people doing the work: they usually know about the risk that will hurt you long before a steering group does. Good [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) also gets easier when people see their concerns recorded and acted on.

### RAID log example
Here is a worked example for a fictional project: a company is replacing its customer relationship management (CRM) system for a 120-person sales team, with go-live planned for 1 September. The log below shows a snapshot from week 10, using a 1 to 5 scale for probability (P) and impact (I).
| ID | Type | Description | P | I | Owner | Action | Due | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 | Risk | Because old CRM data has many duplicates, migration may overrun its 3 weeks, delaying user acceptance testing. | 4 | 4 | Data lead | Run a trial migration on 10% of records; book a cleansing contractor if trial exceeds 3 days | 20 Jun | Open: trial booked |
| R-02 | Risk | Because late June is quarter end, training attendance may be low, reducing adoption. | 3 | 3 | Sales ops manager | Move training to early July; record short videos | 15 Jun | Monitoring |
| A-01 | Assumption | The existing licence agreement allows 30 extra users at no cost during parallel running. |  | 4 | Procurement | Confirm in writing with the vendor | 12 Jun | False: raised as I-02 |
| A-02 | Assumption | The sales director will sign off the new pipeline stages by the end of June. |  | 3 | PM | Agenda item at the steering group on 24 Jun | 24 Jun | Unconfirmed |
| I-01 | Issue | Finance integration fails for invoices over 50 lines, blocking order-to-invoice testing. |  | 4 | Integration developer | Fix pagination in the API call; retest | 14 Jun | In progress |
| I-02 | Issue | Parallel running licences cost an extra amount not in the budget (from A-01). |  | 3 | PM | Request contingency release from sponsor | 18 Jun | Escalated |
| D-01 | Dependency | Inbound: single sign-on depends on the IT security project's identity upgrade, needed by 1 Aug. |  | 5 | PM | Fortnightly check with IT security PM; track their milestone | 1 Aug | On track |
| D-02 | Dependency | Outbound: the marketing automation project needs our final field list by 30 Jun. |  | 3 | Solution architect | Publish field list after design sign-off | 30 Jun | At risk |
Reading the log takes a minute: R-01 scores 16 (red) and goes in the status report; I-01 is on the critical path; A-01 has already been disproved and moved on as I-02; D-02 is an outbound dependency that another team is waiting for. That is the kind of picture a sponsor needs in a single glance.

#### How items move between categories
RAID items change type over time, and keeping them together lets you follow each one.
| What happens | Move | Example from the log |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An assumption is proved false | Assumption becomes a risk or an issue | A-01 licences were not free, so I-02 was raised |
| A risk occurs | Risk becomes an issue; close the risk | If the trial migration overruns, R-01 becomes an issue |
| A dependency is late | Dependency becomes an issue, or a risk if lateness is likely but not certain | D-02 marked at risk; if the field list misses 30 Jun, raise an issue |
| An issue reveals a wider threat | Issue spawns a new risk | I-01 suggests other large transactions may fail, so a new risk is logged |
| A decision resolves an item | Record the decision and close the item | Sponsor releases contingency, I-02 closed |
When you move an item, close the original with a note such as 'Converted to I-02 on 12 Jun' rather than deleting it. The history matters at audits and for lessons learned.

### How to run a RAID review meeting
The log only works if it is reviewed. Most project teams review RAID weekly, often as part of the regular status meeting; fast-moving or high-risk projects may look at red items daily, and steady projects may review fortnightly with a deeper look at each stage gate.
| Time | Agenda item | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 min | New items raised since the last review | Accepted, merged or rejected; owner agreed |
| 10 min | Red risks and high-priority issues | Actions confirmed or escalated |
| 5 min | Assumptions due for validation | Confirmed, or converted to risks/issues |
| 5 min | Dependencies due in the next four weeks | Status checked with the other team |
| 5 min | Items to close and items to escalate | Clean log; escalation list for the sponsor |
A few practices keep the meeting short and useful:
- Ask owners to update their items **before** the meeting, so the review is about decisions rather than data entry.
- Invite the owners of dependencies from other teams when their items are due.
- Finish by agreeing the three to five items that go into the [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
- Record decisions in a decisions tab or the minutes.
At steering group or board level, present a one-page summary: counts by type and rating, the top red items, the trend since last month and any decisions needed. That fits naturally with the escalation routes in your [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) arrangements.

### RAID log vs risk register, issue log and decision log
People often ask whether they need a RAID log as well as other registers. The table shows what each one covers.
|  | RAID log | Risk register | Issue log | Decision log |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Covers | Risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies (or variants) | Risks only, often threats and opportunities | Current problems, concerns and change requests | Decisions, who made them and why |
| Detail per item | Moderate | High: causes, triggers, responses, residual risk, contingency | High: impact analysis, resolution history, escalation | Low to moderate |
| Best for | Small and medium projects; programme summaries | Large, complex or regulated projects | Projects with many issues or formal change control | Projects where decisions must be traceable |
A sensible rule of thumb: on small and medium projects, one RAID log is enough. On large, high-risk or regulated projects, keep a detailed risk register and [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/) and use the RAID log as the summary view across them. Methods such as PRINCE2 describe separate risk and issue records, so teams using those methods often treat RAID as a reporting layer rather than a replacement.
Whichever you choose, avoid keeping the same item in two places with different statuses. If you have separate registers, the RAID summary should pull from them, not duplicate them. A [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) works well behind a RAID summary for larger projects.

### RAID logs in Agile teams and programmes
Agile teams manage much of what a RAID log holds through their normal ways of working. Impediments come up in the [daily scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) and sit on the board, risks are reduced by delivering in small increments, and assumptions are tested with real users each sprint.
A RAID log still earns its place when several teams depend on each other, when work involves suppliers or other departments, or when governance needs a record. Common patterns are:
- **Programme RAID:** in scaled frameworks, cross-team risks and dependencies identified at [PI planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/) are tracked on a programme board and a shared RAID view.
- **Lightweight RAID:** a short list reviewed at sprint planning or the retrospective, holding only items the team cannot resolve on its own board.
- **Decision records:** a decisions tab captures architecture and product choices and the reasoning behind them.
Keep it lean: if an item can live as a card on the board, put it there.

### Common RAID log mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vague one-word entries such as 'resources' | Owners cannot act on them | Use cause-event-effect and add the impact |
| No named owner, or 'the team' as owner | Nobody acts | One person per item, who has agreed to own it |
| Every item rated high | Nothing stands out | Use defined scales and challenge ratings in the review |
| Assumptions recorded but never tested | Hidden risks stay hidden | Give each assumption a validation date |
| Issues logged as risks (or the reverse) | Wrong response and urgency | Ask: has it happened? If yes, it is an issue |
| Only inbound dependencies tracked | Other teams are let down | Log what others need from you too |
| Log updated only before steering meetings | Out of date most of the time | Owners update continuously; weekly review |
| Using it as a task list | Real threats get buried | Move routine tasks to the plan or board |
| Not linked to the plan or budget | Actions never happen | Put responses in the schedule and contingency in the budget |
The most damaging mistake is cultural: punishing people who raise bad news. If raising a risk feels like admitting failure, the log will look calm until the project misses its date.

### Tools for keeping a RAID log
A spreadsheet is the most common RAID tool, and for a single project it is often all you need. Our [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) is ready to use in Google Sheets or Excel.
Move to a project management tool when several owners update items, when items need to link to tasks, or when a PMO wants to roll up RAID across many projects. Features worth looking for:
- Custom fields for type, probability, impact and status, and intake forms so anyone can raise an item.
- Automations that remind owners of due dates and flag red items.
- Dashboards that roll up RAID across projects, with links to the tasks that resolve each item.
Most leading platforms can do this with custom fields and dashboards. Wrike, our top-ranked tool, suits teams that want request forms, cross-project dashboards and configurable workflows in one place; Smartsheet suits teams who prefer a spreadsheet layout; Jira suits software teams who log impediments as issues.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a RAID log in project management?**
A RAID log is a single register for a project's risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies. Each item has an owner, action, date and status, and the log is reviewed regularly so problems are dealt with early.

**Q: What does RAID stand for?**
Most often risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies. Some organisations use actions instead of assumptions, or decisions instead of dependencies, and RAIDD adds decisions as a fifth category.

**Q: What is the purpose of a RAID log?**
To give the project team and sponsor one up-to-date view of what could go wrong, what is going wrong, what the plan relies on and what it depends on, with clear owners and actions for each.

**Q: Who is responsible for the RAID log?**
The project manager, or a project coordinator or PMO analyst on their behalf, maintains the log. Each item has its own owner, who keeps that entry up to date and carries out the action.

**Q: How often should a RAID log be reviewed?**
Weekly is typical, often as part of the status meeting. High-risk projects may review red items daily, and steady projects may review fortnightly plus a fuller review at stage gates.

**Q: What is the difference between a RAID log and a risk register?**
A [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) covers risks only, usually in more detail. A RAID log also covers assumptions, issues and dependencies, giving a broader but less detailed view.

**Q: What is the difference between a risk and an issue?**
A risk is uncertain and might happen in future; an issue is happening now or is certain. When a risk occurs, it becomes an issue.

**Q: What is the difference between an assumption and a risk?**
An assumption is something you treat as true for planning without proof. The possibility that it is false creates a risk, so test assumptions and convert false ones into risks or issues.

**Q: What is a dependency in a RAID log?**
A link where your project relies on something outside its control, such as another project's deliverable, a supplier or a decision, or where another team relies on you. Record the provider, receiver, date needed and impact if late.

**Q: What is a RAIDD log?**
A RAID log that also records decisions: risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies and decisions.

**Q: What is RAID analysis?**
RAID analysis is the exercise of identifying and assessing a project's risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, often in a workshop at the start of the project. Its output is the first version of the RAID log.

**Q: Can I create a RAID log in Excel or Google Sheets?**
Yes. A spreadsheet with one table and a type column, or one tab per category, is the most common format. Our free [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) is available for Google Sheets, Excel and PDF.

**Q: Do Agile teams use RAID logs?**
Some do, mainly for cross-team dependencies, programme risks and decisions. Day-to-day impediments are usually handled on the team board instead.

**Q: What happens to the RAID log at project closure?**
Open items are closed or handed to the operational owner, every item gets a final status, and the log is archived. This is part of [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/), and patterns from the log feed the [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) review.

# Residual Risk in Project Management: Meaning and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/residual-risk/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Residual risk in project management: definition, inherent vs residual vs secondary risk, how to calculate it with examples, and when it is acceptable.


## Residual Risk in Project Management: Meaning and Examples
Residual risk in project management is the risk that remains after you have planned and carried out your risk responses. Few responses remove a risk completely, so most projects carry residual risk that must be measured, accepted by the right person, covered by reserves and monitored. This guide explains how to calculate it, with worked examples, and how to decide whether it is acceptable.
- Published 1 October 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 14 min read

### Key takeaways
- Residual risk is what is left after responses; inherent risk is the level before any response.
- A secondary risk is a new risk created by a response, which is different from residual risk.
- Calculate residual risk by re-scoring probability and impact, or expected monetary value, after responses.
- Compare residual risk with agreed tolerances; if it is too high, add responses or escalate.
- Significant residual risk should be accepted explicitly by the sponsor or board and recorded in the risk register.

### What is residual risk?
**Residual risk** is the level of risk that remains after risk responses have been implemented. PMI's PMBOK Guide describes residual risks as those expected to remain after planned responses have been taken, including risks that have been deliberately accepted. ISO's risk management vocabulary (ISO Guide 73) defines it more briefly as risk remaining after risk treatment.
In plain terms, you start with a [project risk](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk/), decide what to do about it, do it, and then ask: how likely is this now, and how bad would it be? The answer is the residual risk.
- **It is an identified risk.** You know about it, so you can plan for it, unlike unknown risks.
- **It is rarely zero.** Mitigation reduces probability or impact; transfer moves the financial effect; neither usually removes the event entirely.
- **It is a decision point.** Once you know the residual level, someone must decide whether it is acceptable.
- **It is used beyond projects.** Information security, health and safety, internal audit and enterprise risk management all use the same idea.

### Inherent, residual and secondary risk
Four related terms come up in risk management and in PMP and CAPM exam questions. The table shows how they differ, using one data migration risk.
| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inherent risk | The risk before any response or control | Data loss during migration: probability 3 x impact 5 = 15 |
| Residual risk | The risk that remains after responses | After full backups and a rehearsal: probability 1 x impact 4 = 4 |
| Secondary risk | A new risk created directly by carrying out a response | The rehearsal ties up the test environment, delaying other testing |
| Emergent risk | A risk that only becomes visible as the project progresses | A new data regulation is announced during delivery |

#### Residual risk vs secondary risk
The two are easy to confuse because both appear after a response. The difference is where they come from:
- **Residual risk** is the **same risk**, reduced but not removed. The event can still happen.
- **Secondary risk** is a **different risk** that your response has introduced. It needs its own entry in the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/), its own score and owner.
Example: to reduce the risk of a skills shortage, you outsource testing to a specialist firm. Some chance remains that testing still runs late (residual risk). Outsourcing also creates a new chance that the firm misunderstands your requirements (secondary risk).
Tip
An exam shortcut: if the question asks what 'remains', the answer is residual risk; if it asks what 'arises from the response', the answer is secondary risk.

### Why residual risk matters
Planning a response can create false comfort. Measuring residual risk keeps the risk picture honest.
- **Honest reporting.** Sponsors need to know what risk is left after the team's actions, not just what was originally identified.
- **Right-sized reserves.** Contingency reserve is usually sized from the expected cost of residual and accepted risks.
- **Value for money.** Comparing inherent and residual risk shows whether a response is worth what it costs.
- **Clear accountability.** When residual risk is recorded and formally accepted, everyone knows who decided to live with it.
- **Better focus.** Risks with high residual scores stay on the agenda; risks reduced to a low level can move to routine monitoring.

### How each response strategy affects residual risk
The response you choose shapes what is left. These are the threat strategies PMI describes, with their usual effect on residual risk.
| Strategy | What it does | Typical residual risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Avoid | Change the plan so the threat cannot occur, e.g. drop a risky feature | Close to zero for that risk, but check for new risks from the change |
| Mitigate | Reduce probability, impact or both | Lower than inherent; the most common source of residual risk |
| Transfer | Pass the financial impact to a third party, e.g. insurance or a fixed-price contract | Financial impact falls, but schedule and reputation impact may remain, and the third party may fail |
| Accept | Take no action now; perhaps hold a reserve or contingency plan | Equal to inherent risk |
| Escalate | Pass ownership to a higher level because it is outside the project's authority | Leaves the project register, but the organisation still carries it |
For opportunities the logic is reversed: after exploiting, enhancing or sharing, you re-assess how likely the benefit now is and how large it would be.

### How to calculate residual risk
There is no single official formula. Most projects use one of the three methods below. Choose one, use it consistently and define your scales in the risk management plan.

#### Method 1: re-score probability and impact
This is the simplest and most common approach, and it matches the probability x impact matrix most registers use.
1. Score the inherent risk: probability (1-5) x impact (1-5).
2. List the responses and confirm they are realistic, funded and owned.
3. Re-score probability and impact assuming the responses work as planned.
4. Multiply to get the residual score.
For example, an inherent probability of 4 and impact of 4 gives 16. If mitigation reduces probability to 2 and impact stays at 4, the residual score is 8.

#### Method 2: expected monetary value
Where you can estimate costs, express residual risk in money. **Residual expected monetary value = residual probability x residual cost impact.** A 10% chance of a £20,000 overrun gives a residual exposure of £2,000. This is useful for sizing contingency reserve and for comparing responses with their cost. For a whole project, [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) can combine many residual risks into a range of outcomes.

#### Method 3: control effectiveness
Some organisations, especially in security and audit, estimate how effective the controls are and reduce the inherent score accordingly: **residual risk = inherent risk x (1 - control effectiveness)**. An inherent score of 15 with controls judged 60% effective gives 6. Treat this as a rough guide: effectiveness percentages are judgements, and a response that cuts probability does not always cut impact.
Tip
You will often see the shorthand 'residual risk = inherent risk - impact of controls'. It describes the idea, but you still need one of the methods above to turn it into a number.

### Worked example: residual risk on a construction project
A construction project depends on a hired tower crane to erect the steel frame. A breakdown could stop work for up to six weeks while a replacement is found.
| Step | Detail | Score or value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inherent risk | Probability 3 (possible) x impact 5 (very high) | 15 (high) |
| Inherent exposure | 30% chance x £120,000 cost of a six-week delay | £36,000 |
| Response 1 | Weekly inspections by the hire company reduce probability | Probability 2 |
| Response 2 | Standby agreement with a second hire company limits any delay to three days | Impact 2 |
| Residual risk | Probability 2 x impact 2 | 4 (low) |
| Residual exposure | 10% chance x £15,000 cost of a three-day delay | £1,500 |
| Cost of responses | Inspection fees plus standby fee | £5,000 |
| Secondary risk | The standby company may not have a crane free at short notice | Logged separately, score 3 |
The responses cost £5,000 and reduce expected exposure by £34,500, so they are clearly worthwhile. The residual score of 4 is within the project's tolerance of 6, so the project manager records the risk as accepted at its residual level, holds £1,500 in contingency reserve and keeps monitoring the inspection reports.
The figures here are illustrative. On your own project, use your organisation's scales and cost estimates.

### More residual risk examples
| Project | Inherent risk | Response | What remains (residual risk) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IT system migration | Data may be corrupted during cut-over (3 x 5 = 15) | Full-volume rehearsal and verified backups | A small chance of corruption that a rollback could fix within a day (1 x 3 = 3) |
| Outdoor event | Bad weather may reduce attendance (3 x 4 = 12) | Marquee hire and cancellation insurance | Attendance may still fall; reputation impact is not insured (3 x 2 = 6) |
| Software release | A security flaw may be released (2 x 5 = 10) | Code review, automated scanning and a penetration test | Unknown flaws may remain (1 x 5 = 5), so monitoring and an incident plan stay in place |
| Supplier contract | Supplier may deliver late (4 x 3 = 12) | Penalty clause and weekly progress checks | Late delivery is less likely, but penalties do not recover lost time (2 x 3 = 6) |
| Marketing launch | A competitor may launch first (2 x 4 = 8) | Accept and prepare a differentiated message | Unchanged, as the risk was accepted (2 x 4 = 8) |
Notice that transfer and penalty clauses often reduce the financial effect but not the schedule or reputational effect. Record what remains honestly.

### How to assess residual risk step by step
1. **Score the inherent risk** using the agreed probability and impact scales.
2. **Agree the responses**, with an owner, cost and date for each action.
3. **Estimate the planned residual risk**: re-score assuming the responses work. This is your target.
4. **Check for secondary risks** created by the responses and log them separately.
5. **Compare with tolerances** set in the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/).
6. **Decide**: accept, add further responses or escalate.
7. **Record the decision**, including who accepted the residual risk and when.
8. **Re-score once the responses are complete** to get the actual residual risk, and keep monitoring triggers.
Tip
Keep planned and actual residual scores separate. A response that is only planned has not reduced anything yet.

### Is the residual risk acceptable?
Deciding whether residual risk is acceptable is a judgement, but it should follow agreed rules rather than gut feel.
- **Compare it with tolerances.** Your risk management plan should say which scores the project can accept and which need escalation, based on the organisation's risk appetite.
- **Weigh the cost of further reduction.** If another response would cost more than the exposure it removes, accepting the residual risk is often sensible. A [cost-benefit analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/) helps here.
- **Consider non-financial effects.** Safety, legal and reputational risks may need to be reduced further even when the money case is weak.
- **Make the decision visible.** Significant residual risks should be accepted explicitly by the sponsor or project board through the project's [governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) arrangements, not quietly by the team.
An example of agreed rules, using the 1-25 scoring scale:
| Residual score | Band | Typical action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15-25 | High | Not acceptable at project level; add responses or escalate to the sponsor or board |
| 8-14 | Medium | Acceptable only with sponsor agreement, a contingency plan and close monitoring |
| 1-7 | Low | Project manager can accept; monitor at normal review frequency |
These bands are our suggestion, not a standard. Set your own to reflect your organisation's appetite and the project's importance.

### Managing residual risk: contingency reserve and fallback plans
Accepted residual risk still needs a plan. Two tools are commonly used.
| Tool | What it is | When it is used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Contingency plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) | Actions to take if the risk occurs | Triggered when the risk event happens or a trigger is reached |
| Fallback plan | A second set of actions if the contingency plan does not work | For high-impact risks where a single plan is not enough |
| Contingency reserve | Time or money set aside for identified risks, including residual ones | Sized from expected values and drawn down if risks occur |
| Management reserve | Time or money for unknown risks, held outside the baseline | Released through governance for risks nobody identified |
Contingency reserve sits inside the cost [baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) and is part of the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/). Summing the residual expected values of your accepted risks gives a defensible starting point for its size.
If a residual risk does occur, it becomes an issue: move it to the [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/), carry out the contingency plan and, if the budget or schedule changes, go through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).

### Recording residual risk in the risk register
A register that only shows one score hides the effect of your responses. Add columns so the before and after picture is clear.
| Column | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Inherent probability, impact and score | The assessment before any response |
| Response strategy and actions | Avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept or escalate, with dates and owners |
| Planned residual score | The expected score once responses are complete |
| Actual residual score | The re-assessed score after responses have been carried out |
| Residual exposure (optional) | Residual probability x cost impact, used for reserves |
| Accepted by and date | Who accepted the residual risk and when |
| Secondary risks | References to any new risks created by the response |
Our free [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) calculates a probability x impact score automatically; add residual score and acceptance columns beside it to track the after-response position.

### Reporting residual risk to sponsors
Sponsors and boards do not need every risk, but they do need to know what risk the project is carrying.
- Show the top risks with inherent and residual scores side by side, so the effect of responses is visible.
- Highlight any residual risks above tolerance and the decision you need from the sponsor.
- Report the remaining contingency reserve against the residual exposure it is meant to cover.
- Include residual risk in the regular [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) and in stage-gate reviews.
On smaller projects a [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) can hold risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies in one place; see our [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/).

### Common mistakes with residual risk
- **Assuming a response removes the risk.** Unless you have avoided it, something usually remains.
- **Re-scoring too early.** Reducing the score when the response is planned, rather than done, overstates progress.
- **Ignoring secondary risks.** Every response can create new risks; check for them each time.
- **Treating transfer as elimination.** Insurance or contracts move money, not time, reputation or safety.
- **Keeping it from the sponsor.** Residual risk accepted silently by the team is not properly accepted.
- **No reserve.** Accepting residual risk without contingency time or money means any occurrence becomes a budget or schedule problem.
- **Never revisiting it.** Conditions change; review residual scores at every risk review and stage gate.
Residual risk is one part of a wider process of identifying, analysing, responding to and monitoring risks.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is residual risk in project management?**
The risk that remains after risk responses have been planned and carried out. It is the same risk as before, at a reduced (or, if accepted, unchanged) level of probability or impact.

**Q: What is an example of residual risk?**
A team runs a full rehearsal and takes backups before a data migration. Data corruption is now much less likely, but a small chance remains. That remaining chance and its effect are the residual risk.

**Q: How do you calculate residual risk?**
Re-score probability and impact assuming the responses are in place and multiply them, or calculate expected monetary value using the reduced probability and cost impact. Some organisations instead reduce the inherent score by an estimated control effectiveness.

**Q: What is the formula for residual risk?**
A common shorthand is residual risk = inherent risk - the effect of responses or controls. In practice you calculate it as residual probability x residual impact, or as inherent risk x (1 - control effectiveness).

**Q: What is the difference between inherent risk and residual risk?**
Inherent risk is the level of risk before any response or control; residual risk is the level that remains after responses.

**Q: What is the difference between residual risk and secondary risk?**
Residual risk is what remains of the original risk after a response. A secondary risk is a new, different risk that arises directly from carrying out a response.

**Q: Can residual risk be zero?**
Rarely. Only avoiding a risk completely, for example by removing the activity that causes it, brings that risk close to zero, and even then the change may introduce new risks.

**Q: Who accepts residual risk on a project?**
The project manager can usually accept low residual risks. Significant ones should be accepted by the sponsor or project board, in line with the project's governance and tolerances.

**Q: What is an acceptable level of residual risk?**
One that falls within the tolerances agreed in the risk management plan and reflects the organisation's risk appetite. What is acceptable varies by organisation and by the type of impact, especially for safety and legal risks.

**Q: Where is residual risk recorded?**
In the risk register, usually in a residual score column next to the inherent score, with the name of the person who accepted it and the date.

**Q: What do you do if residual risk is too high?**
Add further responses, change the plan to avoid the risk, transfer more of the impact, escalate it to a higher level or, in extreme cases, decide not to proceed.

**Q: How is residual risk covered financially?**
Usually through contingency reserve, which is sized from the expected cost of identified risks including residual and accepted ones. Management reserve covers unknown risks.

**Q: What is a fallback plan?**
A second set of actions to use if the contingency plan for a risk does not work. Fallback plans are often prepared for residual risks with a high impact.

**Q: Is residual risk used outside project management?**
Yes. It is a standard concept in information security, internal audit, health and safety and enterprise risk management, where it is often defined as the risk remaining after risk treatment.

# Resource Allocation in Project Management: Steps & Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Resource allocation in project management explained: how to assign people to tasks, calculate availability and utilisation, a worked example and mistakes.


## Resource Allocation in Project Management: Steps & Example
Resource allocation in project management is the process of assigning the right people, equipment and materials to specific tasks for specific periods, based on what each task needs and what each resource really has available. Done well, it gives every task the skills and time it needs without overloading anyone. This guide walks through the steps, the maths of availability and utilisation, and a full worked example.
- Published 30 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Resource allocation decides who or what does each task, how much of their time it takes and when.
- Allocate against real availability: subtract leave, other commitments and non-project time first.
- Staff critical-path tasks and scarce skills first, then fill in the rest.
- Check each person's load per week; anything over 100% of available time is over-allocation to resolve before you baseline.
- Shared people need agreements with their line or resource managers, not just a name in the plan.
- Review allocations weekly and re-plan when scope, priorities or people change.

### What is resource allocation?
**Resource allocation** is the assignment of available resources, mainly people but also equipment, materials and facilities, to the tasks in a project schedule for defined periods. For each task it answers three questions: **who or what** will do the work, **how much** of their time it needs, and **when**. The aim is to deliver the plan without overloading or idling anyone.
Allocation sits in the middle of resource management. Before it, you identify the [project resources](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-resources/) you need and estimate the effort for each task. After it, you resolve clashes with [resource leveling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/), approve the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) and then track actual use against the plan.
PMI treats this as a core part of project management. The PMBOK Guide's sixth edition placed it in the Project Resource Management knowledge area, with processes including Estimate Activity Resources, Acquire Resources and Control Resources. The eighth edition, published in November 2025, lists **resources** as one of its seven performance domains. Our [PMBOK Guide overview](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) explains how the editions differ.

### Why resource allocation matters
Most project plans fail on people, not on logic. A schedule can be perfectly sequenced and still be impossible if the same specialist is needed in three places at once. Careful allocation gives you:
- **A realistic schedule.** Dates reflect when people can actually do the work, not just when the task logic allows it.
- **Fewer bottlenecks.** Clashes for scarce skills show up in planning, when they are cheap to fix.
- **Controlled cost.** Knowing who works on what, at what rate, lets you build an accurate [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/).
- **Sustainable workloads.** People are not routinely asked for 50-hour weeks, which protects quality and reduces burnout.
- **Better use of skills.** Experts spend their time on work that needs them, and others get development opportunities.
- **Earlier warning.** When something changes, you can see straight away who and what is affected.
Without it, the usual symptoms are familiar: some people overloaded while others wait, tasks stalled for a missing skill, overtime that nobody planned and a schedule that slips week by week.

### Types of resources you allocate
People are usually the hardest resource to allocate, but most projects also need to schedule other resources. Each type has its own constraints.
| Resource type | Examples | What to plan for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| People (human resources) | Team members, specialists, contractors, client staff | Skills, availability, part-time patterns, leave, other projects |
| Equipment | Machinery, test devices, vehicles, servers, environments | Booking slots, maintenance windows, set-up and transport time |
| Materials | Components, concrete, licences, consumables | Lead times, delivery dates, storage, minimum order quantities |
| Facilities | Meeting rooms, labs, workshops, sites | Capacity, booking rules, access and security |
| Budget | Funding for labour, purchases and contingency | When money is released, approval limits, cash flow |
For the rest of this guide we focus on people, because that is where most allocation decisions are made. The same steps apply to equipment and facilities, with a booking calendar in place of a person's availability.

### Resource allocation vs related terms
Several resource terms are used loosely and often interchangeably. The table separates them.
| Term | What it means | Typical horizon |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resource planning | Working out what resources a project or portfolio will need, and how they will be obtained | Months to years |
| [Capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) | Comparing total demand with the total supply of people or skills across teams | Quarters to a year |
| **Resource allocation** | Assigning named resources to specific tasks for specific periods | Weeks to months |
| Project scheduling | Setting task dates from logic, durations and resources | Whole project |
| [Resource leveling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) | Moving task dates to remove over-allocation; may delay the finish | Whole project |
| Resource smoothing | Moving tasks only within float to even out demand; finish date fixed | Whole project |
| Resource utilisation | A measure of how much of a person's available time is allocated or used | Weekly or monthly |
In short: planning and capacity planning ask **do we have enough?**, allocation asks **who does what, when?**, and leveling asks **how do we fix the clashes?**

### Who is responsible for resource allocation?
The project manager plans and maintains the allocation for their project. But in most organisations they do not own the people, so allocation is a negotiation as much as a calculation.
| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Project manager | Defines resource needs, builds the allocation, resolves clashes within the project, tracks use |
| Resource or functional manager | Owns the people, agrees who is released to the project and for how much time |
| PMO or portfolio manager | Sets priorities between projects and sees demand across the portfolio |
| Sponsor | Approves extra budget, contractors or changes in priority when the project cannot be staffed |
| Team members | Give honest estimates and flag clashes with other work early |
In a **matrix organisation**, where people report to a line manager but work on projects, the allocation is only real once the line manager has agreed it. Record who agreed what, and when; a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) helps make those responsibilities explicit. Where many projects share the same people, a [project management office](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) usually runs a regular resource meeting to settle priorities.

### How to allocate resources step by step
The process below works for most projects. On small projects you may do it in one sitting; on larger ones it is repeated each stage.
1. **Confirm the scope and deliverables.** You cannot allocate resources to work that is not defined. Start from the approved scope and the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/).
2. **Estimate effort and skills per task.** Record the hours or days each task needs and the skill required. Effort is not the same as duration; see [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/).
3. **Build the resource pool.** List the people who could do the work, with their skills, cost rates and the share of their time available to your project.
4. **Calculate real availability.** Subtract leave, public holidays, other project commitments and routine non-project time from each person's contracted hours (see the next section).
5. **Allocate critical and scarce work first.** Staff tasks on the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) and tasks that need rare skills before anything else. A [skills matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) shows who can do what.
6. **Fill in the remaining tasks.** Assign the rest by skill, availability and cost, using development opportunities where risk allows.
7. **Check the load per person per period.** Add up allocated hours for each person, week by week, and compare them with availability. Anything over 100% is over-allocation.
8. **Resolve conflicts.** Use [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) to move non-critical work, reassign tasks, split work, add temporary capacity or, if necessary, move dates through resource leveling.
9. **Agree, baseline and monitor.** Confirm allocations with resource managers, publish them, include them in the baseline and review actual against planned at least weekly.

#### What a resource allocation plan contains
The output of these steps is a resource allocation plan. It does not need to be a long document; a well-structured spreadsheet or tool view is enough if it contains:
- Each task or work package with its effort estimate and required skill.
- The named person or resource assigned, and the hours or percentage allocated per week.
- Each person's availability and resulting utilisation per period.
- Cost rates and the total cost per resource, feeding the budget.
- Assumptions, such as part-time patterns or a contractor still to be hired, recorded in the [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/).
- Who agreed each allocation, and when it was last reviewed.
Our [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) is a good place to start: add an assignee column and a weekly hours grid alongside the tasks.

### How to calculate availability and utilisation
Two simple calculations sit at the heart of resource allocation: how much time a person really has, and how much of it you have allocated.

#### Available hours
**Available hours = contracted hours x share of time given to the project - leave and holidays - routine non-project time**
Routine non-project time covers team meetings, email, admin, training and support work that happens every week regardless of the project. Many planners handle it with a **focus factor**: the percentage of the remaining time that can realistically be spent on planned project tasks. Planning at about 70 to 80% is common practice and our own recommendation; it is a planning assumption, not a standard, so adjust it to what your timesheets show.
| Person | Contracted hours/week | Share given to project | Focus factor | Planning capacity/week |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ana (developer) | 40 | 100% | 80% | 32 hours |
| Ben (developer) | 40 | 50% | 80% | 16 hours |
| Chloe (tester) | 40 | 100% | 80% | 32 hours |
| Priya (designer) | 40 | 50% | 80% | 16 hours |
Leave comes off on top. If Chloe is on leave for a whole week, her planning capacity that week is zero, not 32 hours. Converting capacity into [full-time equivalents (FTE)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/full-time-equivalent-fte/) is useful when you compare demand across teams.

#### Utilisation
**Utilisation = allocated hours / available hours x 100**
If Ana is allocated 40 hours in a week where her planning capacity is 32, her utilisation is 40 / 32 x 100 = **125%**: she is over-allocated by 8 hours. Below 100% means spare capacity; exactly 100% means fully loaded against your planning capacity, which already includes the focus-factor buffer.
Tip
Track utilisation against planning capacity, not contracted hours. A person at 100% of planning capacity still has time for meetings and email. A person at 100% of contracted hours does not, and will slip.

### Worked example: allocating a four-week website project
This fictional example uses the four people above to deliver a small website relaunch over four weeks. The tasks and their effort estimates are:
| Task | Skill | Effort (hours) | Timing constraint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| UX design | Designer | 24 | Weeks 1-2 |
| CMS set-up and integration | Developer | 72 | Weeks 1-3; no predecessor |
| Build page templates | Developer | 64 | Weeks 2-3; after UX design starts |
| Bug fixing | Developer | 24 | Week 4 |
| Test planning and test cases | Tester | 24 | Weeks 1-2 |
| System and acceptance testing | Tester | 64 | Weeks 3-4 |
Chloe has booked leave for all of week 3. Go-live is fixed at the end of week 4.

#### Step 1: the first draft allocation
The project manager allocates work in the natural order of the tasks, then adds up each person's hours per week.
| Person (capacity/week) | Week 1 | Week 2 | Week 3 | Week 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ana (32 h) | CMS 16 h | Templates 32 h + CMS 8 h = 40 h | Templates 32 h | Bug fixing 16 h |
| Ben (16 h) | CMS 16 h | CMS 16 h | CMS 16 h | Bug fixing 8 h |
| Chloe (32 h, 0 h in week 3) | Test planning 8 h | Test cases 16 h | Testing 32 h | Testing 32 h |
| Priya (16 h) | UX 16 h | UX 8 h | 0 h | 0 h |

#### Step 2: find the problems
- **Ana, week 2:** 40 hours allocated against 32 available, so 125% utilisation and 8 hours over.
- **Chloe, week 3:** 32 hours of testing allocated in a week when she is on leave, a shortfall of 32 hours.
- **Spare capacity:** Ana has 16 hours free in week 1, Chloe 16 hours in week 2, and Priya 8 hours in week 2 and 16 in weeks 3 and 4.

#### Step 3: consider the options
| Problem | Option | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ana over by 8 h in week 2 | Pull 8 h of CMS work forward into week 1 | Possible: CMS has no predecessor and Ana has 16 h free |
| Ana over by 8 h in week 2 | Ask Ben's line manager for 8 more hours | Possible but uses goodwill; keep as a fallback |
| Chloe away in week 3 | Move all testing to week 4 | Not possible: week 4 would need 64 h from 32 h of capacity |
| Chloe away in week 3 | Start 16 h of testing early in week 2 on the CMS pages already built | Uses Chloe's spare week 2 hours |
| Chloe away in week 3 | Priya reviews designs against the build for 8 h in week 3 | Uses spare designer time for visual acceptance checks |
| Chloe away in week 3 | Contract a tester for the remaining 8 h in week 3 | Adds cost but protects the go-live date |

#### Step 4: the final allocation
| Person | Week 1 | Week 2 | Week 3 | Week 4 | Total / capacity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ana | 24 h (75%) | 32 h (100%) | 32 h (100%) | 16 h (50%) | 104 / 128 h (81%) |
| Ben | 16 h (100%) | 16 h (100%) | 16 h (100%) | 8 h (50%) | 56 / 64 h (88%) |
| Chloe | 8 h (25%) | 32 h (100%) | Leave | 32 h (100%) | 72 / 96 h (75%) |
| Priya | 16 h (100%) | 8 h (50%) | 8 h (50%) | 0 h | 32 / 64 h (50%) |
| Contract tester | - | - | 8 h | - | 8 h |
Every person is now at or below 100% of planning capacity in every week, the go-live date is unchanged and the only extra cost is 8 contractor hours. At an example rate of £50 an hour, that is £400, which the project manager takes to the sponsor for approval from contingency.
Two things are worth noting. First, Ben runs at 100% for three weeks with no slack, so he is the person to watch; any overrun on his tasks will hit the dates. Second, the low utilisation in week 4 for Ana and Ben is deliberate: it is the buffer for bug fixing, which is hard to estimate. If the dates had not been fixed, delaying part of the testing into a fifth week would have been the cheaper option.

### Resource allocation techniques

#### Priority rules for who gets assigned
When several people could do a task, a consistent rule makes decisions faster and easier to explain.
| Rule | How it works | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Skills-first | Assign the person with the best-matching skills | Specialist, high-risk or customer-facing tasks |
| Availability-first | Assign whoever is free soonest | Routine tasks with many capable people |
| Critical-path-first | Staff critical tasks before any others | Date-driven projects |
| Cost-first | Use the lowest-cost capable resource | Fixed-budget projects |
| Development | Pair a less experienced person with an expert | Building capability and reducing single points of failure |
| Pull | Team members take the next priority item when they are free | Agile and Kanban teams |

#### Scheduling techniques that shape allocation
- **Critical path method (CPM):** identifies which tasks drive the finish date so you can staff them first. See [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).
- **Critical chain:** schedules around the most constrained resources and protects the plan with shared buffers rather than padding each task; see [critical chain project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-chain-project-management/).
- **Resource leveling:** moves tasks to remove over-allocation, even if the finish date moves.
- **Resource smoothing:** moves tasks only within float, keeping the finish date fixed.
- **Fast-tracking and crashing:** overlap tasks or add resources to recover time; both affect allocation and cost. See [fast-tracking vs crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/).
In practice most project managers combine them: allocate critical work first, smooth within float, and level only when there is no other way.

### Allocating resources across multiple projects
Allocation gets harder when people work on several projects at once. A **resource allocation matrix**, a grid of people against projects showing the percentage of time committed to each, gives everyone the same picture.
| Person | Website relaunch | Mobile app | Support and business as usual | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ben | 50% | 30% | 20% | 100% |
| Priya | 50% | 40% | 10% | 100% |
| Omar | 0% | 70% | 40% | 110% |
Omar is over-committed before any task is scheduled, so no amount of project-level planning will fix his weeks; the resource managers must change the split. Some practical rules for shared people:
- **Agree priorities at portfolio level.** When two projects need the same person, the PMO or portfolio board decides, not whoever asks loudest.
- **Limit the number of projects per person.** Every switch between projects costs focus time; fewer, larger allocations usually work better than many small ones.
- **Protect scarce specialists.** Track people whose skills are needed on many projects and plan their time first.
- **Book time in blocks.** Two full days a week on a project is usually more productive than 40% of every day.
- **Review demand monthly.** Use [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) to see future demand before it becomes a clash.
Our guide to [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) covers prioritisation and scheduling across a portfolio in more detail.

### Resource allocation in Agile teams
Agile teams usually turn the problem around. Instead of allocating people to tasks, organisations keep **stable, cross-functional teams** and allocate **work to teams**. The team then decides who does what during the sprint or iteration.
- Capacity is planned per team per sprint, based on availability and past [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/).
- In [sprint planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/), the team pulls the highest-priority items it believes it can complete.
- Individuals pick up tasks as they free up, which avoids detailed person-by-person schedules.
- Allocation decisions still happen above the team: which teams work on which products, and whether specialists are shared.
People-level allocation still matters when specialists are shared across teams or when people split time between product work and support.

### Common resource allocation mistakes
| Mistake | What happens | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Allocating people at 100% of contracted hours | No time for meetings, email or the unexpected; tasks slip | Plan against a focus factor of around 70-80% |
| Planning with generic roles only | Real clashes between named people stay hidden | Use placeholders early, then replace them with names |
| Ignoring leave and part-time patterns | Tasks land on people who are not there | Keep a resource calendar for every person |
| Putting one expert on several critical tasks at once | One delay hits the whole schedule | Spread critical work or train a backup |
| Treating effort as duration | A 40-hour task is planned as one week for someone available 16 hours | Convert effort to duration using each person's availability |
| No agreement from line managers | People are pulled back to other work | Get allocations confirmed and recorded |
| Allocating once and never updating | The plan drifts from reality within weeks | Review actual against planned weekly |
| Ignoring non-people resources | Work waits for equipment, environments or rooms | Book key equipment and facilities alongside people |
The most common root cause is optimism: assuming people have more time than they do. Using recent timesheet data to set your focus factor is the simplest correction.

### Resource allocation tools
A spreadsheet works well for a single small team: one row per task, one column per week, and a total per person with conditional formatting to highlight anything over capacity. Pair it with a [skills matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) to see who can do what.
Once several projects share people, dedicated software saves a lot of time. Look for:
- Workload or capacity views that show each person's load per week, with over-allocation highlighted.
- Allocation by hours or percentage, not just by assignee.
- Leave, holidays and part-time calendars per person.
- Cross-project views for resource managers and the PMO.
- Placeholders or job roles for people not yet hired or named.
- Time tracking, so you can compare planned and actual hours.
Wrike, ranked first in our [project management software rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/), offers workload charts that show who is over- or under-allocated, with effort allocation, job roles and capacity planning on its higher tiers; it suits PMOs and services teams managing many projects. Asana, monday.com and ClickUp include workload views on their paid plans, and Microsoft Project and Smartsheet suit teams that prefer scheduling-led or spreadsheet-style planning.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is resource allocation in project management?**
It is assigning specific people, equipment and materials to project tasks for defined periods, based on what each task needs and what each resource has available, so the work can be delivered on time and within budget.

**Q: What are the steps in resource allocation?**
Confirm scope, estimate effort and skills per task, list available resources, calculate real availability, staff critical and scarce-skill tasks first, fill in the rest, check each person's load, resolve conflicts, then agree, baseline and monitor.

**Q: What is an example of resource allocation?**
A project manager assigns a developer 32 hours a week to build page templates, a part-time developer 16 hours a week to CMS work and a tester to testing in weeks 3 and 4, then adjusts when the tester's leave creates a gap.

**Q: Why is resource allocation important?**
It makes the schedule realistic, exposes clashes early, keeps costs under control and stops people being overloaded while others wait for work.

**Q: Who is responsible for resource allocation?**
The project manager plans it, but resource or functional managers must agree to release their people, and a PMO often sets priorities when projects compete for the same staff.

**Q: What is the difference between resource allocation and resource leveling?**
Allocation assigns resources to tasks. [Resource leveling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) then adjusts task dates to remove any over-allocation that results, which can move the finish date.

**Q: What is the difference between resource allocation and capacity planning?**
Capacity planning compares overall demand with supply across teams over months. Allocation assigns named people to specific tasks within that capacity.

**Q: What is over-allocation?**
A resource is over-allocated when the work assigned in a period exceeds its available time, for example 40 hours of tasks against 32 hours of planning capacity, a utilisation of 125%.

**Q: How do you calculate resource utilisation?**
Divide allocated (or actual) hours by available hours and multiply by 100. For example, 28 allocated hours against 32 available is 87.5% utilisation.

**Q: Should you allocate people at 100%?**
Not of their contracted hours. Allocating against a planning capacity of around 70-80% of working time leaves room for meetings, email and support work; that figure is a common rule of thumb, so check it against your own timesheets.

**Q: What is a resource allocation matrix?**
A grid of people against projects or tasks showing how much of each person's time is committed to each. It quickly shows who is over-committed across projects.

**Q: How do you allocate resources across multiple projects?**
Agree priorities at portfolio level, keep a shared view of each person's commitments, limit the number of projects per person, protect scarce specialists and review demand regularly.

**Q: How does resource allocation work in Agile?**
Agile organisations usually keep stable teams and allocate work to teams rather than people to tasks. Each team plans its sprint capacity and pulls the highest-priority work.

**Q: Which tools help with resource allocation?**
Spreadsheets suit small teams. Tools with workload and capacity views, such as Wrike, Asana, monday.com, ClickUp, Smartsheet and Microsoft Project, help when people are shared across projects; see our [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) rankings.
