# S-Curve in Project Management: What It Is and How to Use It

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/s-curve/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What an S-curve is in project management, why cumulative cost forms an S shape, how to build one, and how to read PV, EV and AC curves, with an example.


## S-Curve in Project Management: What It Is and How to Use It
An S-curve is a graph of cumulative cost, effort or progress plotted against time. It usually forms an S shape because spending starts slowly, speeds up in the middle of a project and tails off near the end. Comparing planned and actual S-curves shows at a glance whether a project is on track.
- Published 29 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- An S-curve plots cumulative cost or work over time.
- The baseline PV curve ends at BAC.
- Compare EV with PV for schedule and EV with AC for cost.
- Diverging curves are an early warning sign.

### Why the curve is S-shaped
- **Start:** few people, planning and design work, so cumulative cost rises slowly.
- **Middle:** the full team and most purchases, so the curve is steepest.
- **End:** testing, handover and closure with fewer people, so it flattens out.

### How to build a baseline S-curve
1. Create the schedule and assign a budget to each activity or work package.
2. Total the planned cost for each period (week or month).
3. Calculate the running cumulative total.
4. Plot cumulative planned value against time. The last point equals the [budget at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/budget-at-completion/).
5. Each reporting period, add cumulative earned value (EV) and actual cost (AC) lines.

### Example
| Month | Planned in month | Cumulative PV | Cumulative EV | Cumulative AC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | $10,000 | $10,000 | $8,000 | $10,000 |
| 2 | $15,000 | $25,000 | $22,000 | $27,000 |
| 3 | $25,000 | $50,000 | $45,000 | $55,000 |
| 4 | $30,000 | $80,000 | $70,000 | $85,000 |
| 5 | $40,000 | $120,000 |  |  |
| 6 | $35,000 | $155,000 |  |  |
| 7 | $25,000 | $180,000 |  |  |
| 8 | $20,000 | $200,000 |  |  |
At month four the AC line ($85,000) sits above the EV line ($70,000): the project is over budget. The EV line sits below the PV line ($80,000): it is behind schedule. The gaps are the [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/) (-$15,000) and [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) (-$10,000).

### How to read the three curves
| Pattern | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| EV below PV | Behind schedule |
| EV above PV | Ahead of schedule |
| AC above EV | Over budget for work done |
| AC below EV | Under budget for work done |
| Curves diverging over time | The problem is growing; act now |

### Other uses of S-curves
- Cumulative labour hours for [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/).
- Cash-flow and funding requirements for the finance team.
- Cumulative tasks or deliverables completed.
- Target, early-start and late-start curves to show the range of possible spending profiles.

### Tips
- Plot the lines on the same axes and scale.
- Extend the curve with a forecast line from today to the [EAC](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/).
- Do not judge progress by the AC line alone; spending is not progress.
- Most [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) and spreadsheets can produce S-curves.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an S-curve in project management?**
A graph of cumulative cost, effort or progress against time, which usually has an S shape.

**Q: Why is it called an S-curve?**
Because cumulative spending starts slowly, accelerates mid-project and slows at the end, forming an S.

**Q: What does an S-curve show?**
Planned versus actual progress and cost over time, making cost and schedule variances visible.

**Q: How do you create an S-curve?**
Total the planned cost per period, calculate the running cumulative total and plot it against time.

**Q: What is a baseline S-curve?**
The cumulative planned value curve from the approved cost baseline. It ends at BAC.

**Q: How is an S-curve used in earned value management?**
PV, EV and AC are plotted as three cumulative curves; the gaps show schedule and cost variances.

**Q: What does it mean if the actual S-curve is above the plan?**
If AC is above EV, the project is over budget for the work done. Compare AC with EV, not PV.

**Q: Can an S-curve be made in Excel?**
Yes. Put periods in one column and cumulative values in others, then insert a line chart.

**Q: Does every project follow an S-curve?**
Not always. Projects with large early purchases or a flat staffing profile may produce different shapes.

**Q: What is the end point of the baseline S-curve?**
The budget at completion, the total planned cost of the work.

# Schedule Compression: Techniques, Steps and Worked Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Schedule compression explained: crashing and fast tracking, crash cost slope, a step-by-step method, a worked time-cost example, risks and when to stop.


## Schedule Compression: Techniques, Steps and Worked Example
Schedule compression is a set of techniques for shortening a project schedule without reducing its scope. The two main techniques are crashing, which adds resources to critical activities at extra cost, and fast tracking, which overlaps activities at extra risk. This guide explains both, shows how to choose which activities to compress, and works through a full example with costs, paths and trade-offs.
- Published 25 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 16 min read

### Key takeaways
- Schedule compression shortens the timeline while keeping scope the same.
- Crashing buys time with money; fast tracking buys time with risk.
- Only compress critical activities, cheapest first, one step at a time, and recheck the critical path after each step.
- Compression can lower total cost up to a point, because indirect costs fall as the project gets shorter.
- Stop when you reach the target or when the next day saved costs more than it is worth.

### What is schedule compression?
Schedule compression is the shortening of a project schedule to meet a deadline or recover lost time without reducing the agreed scope. It works by shortening activities on the critical path, either by adding resources (crashing) or by overlapping activities that would normally run in sequence (fast tracking). Both trade time for extra cost or risk.
Compression only works on the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/), the longest chain of dependent activities. Shortening anything else just adds [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) to that activity and leaves the finish date where it was. And because the critical path can move, compression is an iterative process: shorten, recalculate, repeat.
The PMBOK Guide's 6th edition listed schedule compression as a tool and technique of the Develop Schedule process, and crashing and fast tracking remain standard topics in [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) preparation. You will use it in two situations: during planning, when the first schedule misses a required date, and during delivery, when the project has slipped and needs to recover.

### When to compress a schedule
- **An imposed date:** a regulatory deadline, an event, a contract milestone or a market launch window.
- **Negative float:** the calculated finish is later than a required date, so critical activities show negative total float.
- **Schedule slippage:** a negative [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) on critical work, or an earned schedule forecast beyond the deadline.
- **Earlier benefits:** finishing early brings revenue, savings or compliance forward.
- **Penalties or high running costs:** late-delivery damages, site costs or team costs that accrue every day.
- **Resource windows:** a specialist, facility or shutdown period that is only available on certain dates.
During delivery, earned value data often provides the trigger. In the illustrative CRM project in our schedule variance guide, an SV of -$25,000 at month five translated into an earned schedule forecast of about 11 months against a 10-month plan. If go-live were tied to a fixed date, that forecast would be the starting point for a compression analysis: about one month to recover, concentrated in the build and testing work on the critical path.
Compression is often the wrong answer when requirements are still changing (overlap leads to rework), when the team is already working overtime, or when the cost of compressing is greater than the cost of finishing late. In those cases, negotiating the date or the scope through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) is usually better.

### Schedule compression techniques

#### Crashing
Crashing shortens critical activities by adding resources: more people, overtime, extra shifts, faster equipment or premium delivery from suppliers. It increases direct cost, but the time saved is usually more predictable than with fast tracking.
Crashing has limits. Each activity has a crash point beyond which no amount of money makes it shorter, and returns diminish well before that. New people need onboarding and add communication overhead. Fred Brooks put it memorably in The Mythical Man-Month (1975): "adding manpower to a late software project makes it later". Crash work that can genuinely be divided, such as installation, data entry or parallel testing, rather than work that depends on a few people's knowledge.

#### Fast tracking
Fast tracking overlaps activities that would normally run one after another, for example starting build before design is fully signed off. In scheduling terms you change a finish-to-start dependency into one with a lead, or into a start-to-start link. See [leads and lags](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/).
Fast tracking has little direct cost, but it adds risk: if the earlier activity changes, work already done on the later one may need redoing. It only works on discretionary (soft) dependencies, not on mandatory ones such as "concrete must cure before loading". Our guide to [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) explains the difference.

#### Other ways to shorten a schedule
Crashing and fast tracking are the textbook techniques, but recovery plans often start with cheaper options:
- **Remove waiting time:** shorten lags, speed up approvals and procurement, pre-order long-lead items.
- **Rethink the logic:** challenge dependencies that are habits rather than necessities.
- **Move people from float to critical work:** reassign resources from non-critical activities, within their skills.
- **Remove blockers:** missing decisions, access, data or environments.
- **Improve productivity:** fewer interruptions and handoffs, better tools, focused teams.
| Technique | How it saves time | Main trade-off | Typical example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Crashing | More resources on critical activities | Higher cost | Second installation crew; weekend shifts |
| Fast tracking | Overlapping sequential activities | Rework risk | Start build on approved design modules |
| Remove waiting | Shorter lags and approval cycles | Needs stakeholder cooperation | Weekly sign-off meeting instead of email chains |
| Change logic | Remove unnecessary dependencies | May need a new method | Test each module rather than the whole system at the end |
| Reassign from float | Use spare capacity on critical work | Skills match | Analyst with float helps prepare test data |

### What is not schedule compression
Three other responses to a deadline problem are often confused with compression:
| Option | What it does | Why it is different |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reducing scope | Delivers less, or delivers some items later | Compression keeps scope the same. Cutting scope changes the deliverables and needs sponsor approval; see [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) |
| Resource levelling | Resolves over-allocation by delaying activities | It usually lengthens the schedule; see [resource levelling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) |
| Re-baselining | Approves a new finish date | Accepts the delay rather than recovering it |
All three are legitimate options, and a recovery plan often combines them with compression. Just label them correctly, so the sponsor knows whether they are buying time with money, risk or scope.

### Crash cost slope and the time-cost trade-off
To crash efficiently you need to know what each day saved costs. The crash cost slope gives that figure for each activity:
**Crash cost slope = (crash cost - normal cost) / (normal duration - crash duration)**
For example, an activity with a normal duration of 15 days costing $30,000 that can be crashed to 12 days for $32,400 has a slope of 2,400 / 3 = $800 per day. The crash duration (12 days) is its crash point.
Project costs fall into two groups, and they move in opposite directions as you compress:
- **Direct costs** belong to activities: labour, materials, equipment. Crashing increases them.
- **Indirect costs** accrue with time: project management, site or office costs, team overheads, financing, late penalties. Shortening the project reduces them.
As long as the crash cost slope is less than the indirect cost saved per day, compression lowers total cost. The duration where total cost is lowest is the least-cost (or optimum) duration. Beyond it, each day saved costs more than it saves, until you reach the crash limit, where no more time can be saved at any price.
Tip
Many projects never calculate indirect costs per day, so compression always looks like pure extra cost. Ask finance or the PMO for the daily running cost of the team and any penalties. It often changes the decision.

### How to compress a schedule step by step
1. Confirm the target date and how many days must be saved, and whether the date is truly fixed.
2. Update the schedule with current progress and run the [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) to find the critical path and near-critical paths.
3. List options for each critical activity: can it be crashed (by how much, at what cost), can it overlap its predecessor, and can its lags or waiting time shrink?
4. Calculate the crash cost slope for each crashable activity, and assess the rework risk of each fast-tracking option.
5. Start with the cheapest, lowest-risk option on the critical path. Prefer activities shared by several near-critical paths, because one change shortens them all.
6. Shorten one day (or one period) at a time and recalculate. When another path becomes critical, you must shorten both paths together.
7. Stop at the target date, at the least-cost duration if there is no fixed target, or when the next step costs more than the benefit.
8. Record new risks in the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/), update the budget, and check that resources are really available.
9. Approve the revised schedule and costs through change control and update the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).

### Worked example: compressing a website relaunch
This illustrative example is larger than the six-activity network in our [fast tracking vs crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/) guide, so you can see what happens when more than one path becomes critical. A company is relaunching its website. The schedule is 58 working days, but the sponsor needs the site live in 52 days for a product launch. Normal direct cost is $180,000, and indirect costs (project team, agency retainer and environments) run at $1,000 per day.
| Activity | Predecessors | Normal days | Crash days | Max days saved | Crash cost slope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A Requirements | - | 10 | 8 | 2 | $1,200/day |
| B Design | A | 15 | 12 | 3 | $800/day |
| C Content writing | A | 12 | 9 | 3 | $500/day |
| D Front-end build | B | 20 | 16 | 4 | $1,500/day |
| E Integrations build | B | 18 | 15 | 3 | $1,000/day |
| F Content load | C | 6 | 5 | 1 | $600/day |
| G Testing | D, E, F | 10 | 8 | 2 | $2,000/day |
| H Launch | G | 3 | 3 | 0 | Cannot crash |
There are three paths through the network:
- A-B-D-G-H: 10 + 15 + 20 + 10 + 3 = **58 days** (critical).
- A-B-E-G-H: 10 + 15 + 18 + 10 + 3 = **56 days** (near-critical, 2 days of float).
- A-C-F-G-H: 10 + 12 + 6 + 10 + 3 = **41 days**.
C is the cheapest activity to crash, but it is not on the critical path, so crashing it buys nothing.

#### Crashing one day at a time
| Days saved | Action | Cost per day | Path lengths (ABDGH / ABEGH / ACFGH) | Cumulative extra cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Start | - | 58 / 56 / 41 | $0 |
| 1-3 | Crash B by 3 days (on both top paths) | $800 | 55 / 53 / 41 | $2,400 |
| 4-5 | Crash A by 2 days (on all paths) | $1,200 | 53 / 51 / 39 | $4,800 |
| 6 | Crash D by 1 day | $1,500 | 52 / 51 / 39 | $6,300 |
| 7 | Crash D by 1 more day: two paths now critical | $1,500 | 51 / 51 / 39 | $7,800 |
| 8-9 | Crash G by 2 days (shared, cheaper than D + E) | $2,000 | 49 / 49 / 37 | $11,800 |
| 10-11 | Crash D and E together | $2,500 | 47 / 47 / 37 | $16,800 |
The 52-day target is reached after six steps for $6,300. At 51 days both top paths are critical, so every further day must shorten both. The schedule cannot go below 47 days: A, B, D and G are at their crash points and H cannot be crashed.

#### Finding the least-cost duration
| Duration | Direct cost | Indirect cost | Total cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 58 days | $180,000 | $58,000 | $238,000 |
| 55 days | $182,400 | $55,000 | **$237,400** (least cost) |
| 53 days | $184,800 | $53,000 | $237,800 |
| 52 days (target) | $186,300 | $52,000 | $238,300 |
| 49 days | $191,800 | $49,000 | $240,800 |
| 47 days (crash limit) | $196,800 | $47,000 | $243,800 |
Crashing B at $800 per day saves $1,000 per day of indirect cost, so the first three days actually reduce total cost. From there, every activity costs more than $1,000 per day, so total cost rises. Meeting the 52-day target by crashing alone costs only $300 more than the original plan, which is a much easier conversation with the sponsor than "$6,300 extra".

#### Fast tracking the same project
Instead of paying for time, the team could overlap both builds with the end of design, starting each build on design modules already approved. With a 6-day lead on B to D and a 4-day lead on B to E, the two longest paths both become 52 days, at no direct cost. The price is risk: front-end development would start six days before design sign-off, and any late design change means rework. Both paths would also have zero float, so any slip moves the launch date.

#### Comparing the options
A third option combines the two: crash design by three days with a second designer ($2,400), then overlap front-end build with design by 3 days and integrations build by 1 day. Both paths come out at 52 days (10 + 12 - 3 + 20 + 10 + 3 for the front end, and 10 + 12 - 1 + 18 + 10 + 3 for integrations).
| Option | Duration | Extra direct cost | Indirect saving | Net cost change | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Crash only | 52 days | $6,300 | $6,000 | +$300 | Low; needs two extra developers available |
| Fast track only | 52 days | $0 | $6,000 | -$6,000 before any rework | High; builds start 4-6 days before design sign-off |
| Crash and fast track | 52 days | $2,400 | $6,000 | -$3,600 | Moderate; 1-3 days of overlap on stable modules |
In this example the combined option is the most balanced recommendation: it meets the date, saves money overall and keeps overlap short enough to manage. Fast tracking alone looks cheapest on paper, but a single significant design change could wipe out the saving. Whatever the choice, the new risks go into the risk register and the revised schedule goes through change control.

### Choosing between crashing and fast tracking
| Situation | Usually better | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements and design are stable | Fast tracking | Low chance of rework, little direct cost |
| Requirements are still changing | Crashing | Overlap would build on moving foundations |
| Budget is available, date is critical | Crashing | More predictable time savings |
| Budget is fixed, some risk is acceptable | Fast tracking | Little direct cost |
| Work divides easily between people | Crashing | Extra people genuinely add output |
| Work depends on a few experts | Fast tracking or logic changes | Extra people slow the experts down |
| Large gap to close | Both, plus waiting-time reductions | One technique rarely closes a big gap alone |
Our [fast tracking vs crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/) guide compares the two in more detail with a second worked example.

### How to present compression options to a sponsor
Compression is a trade-off between time, cost, risk and sometimes quality, so the decision belongs to the sponsor, not the project manager alone. Present it as a choice between clear options rather than a single request for money.
1. State the problem in time terms: the current forecast finish, the required date and the gap in days.
2. Explain what drives the date: the critical path and any near-critical paths.
3. Show two or three options, each with the new finish date, extra direct cost, indirect savings, net cost and main risks, as in the comparison table above.
4. Include the do-nothing option: the cost and consequences of finishing late, such as penalties, lost revenue or a missed launch.
5. Make a recommendation and explain why.
6. Say what you need: budget, people, decisions or faster approvals, and by when.
Framing compression against the [project constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/) helps sponsors see that time cannot be bought without moving cost, risk or scope. A sponsor who chooses an option knowing its risks is far more likely to support you when one of those risks occurs.

### Risks of schedule compression and how to manage them
| Risk | Why it happens | How to manage it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rework | Later work starts on unfinished inputs | Overlap only stable components; agree change rules; review early |
| Cost overrun | Crashing costs more than estimated | Get firm quotes; track compression costs separately |
| Burnout and quality loss | Long periods of overtime | Time-limit overtime; protect testing and reviews |
| Onboarding drag | New people need time and support | Add people early, to divisible work, with a named mentor |
| More critical paths | Compression consumes float | Monitor near-critical paths weekly; hold a small buffer |
| Coordination overload | More parallel work and handoffs | Short daily coordination; clear interfaces and owners |
The common thread is that a compressed schedule is more fragile. With less float and more parallel work, small delays travel further. Some teams protect the compressed plan with an explicit buffer before the deadline, an idea borrowed from [critical chain project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-chain-project-management/).

### Schedule compression in Agile and hybrid projects
Agile teams rarely compress in the traditional sense. Sprints are fixed time-boxes, so when a release date is at risk the usual response is to reprioritise the [product backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) and deliver the most valuable items by the date, which is a scope decision rather than compression.
Agile does have its own versions of the techniques. [Swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/), where the team works together on the highest-priority item, is a way of shortening the critical work without adding people. Adding people to a team mid-release behaves like crashing and carries the same onboarding cost.
In hybrid projects, classic compression still applies to the predictive parts, such as procurement, infrastructure, data migration and training, while Agile teams manage scope within their time-boxes.

### Common schedule compression mistakes
- Compressing non-critical activities because they are cheap or easy.
- Forgetting to recalculate after each step, and missing a new critical path.
- Fast tracking mandatory dependencies.
- Adding people to work that cannot be divided.
- Ignoring indirect costs, so every option looks more expensive than it is.
- Treating scope cuts as compression without sponsor approval.
- Leaving the extra cost and risk out of the budget and risk register.

### Schedule compression checklist before approval
- The target date and the number of days to save are confirmed and agreed.
- The critical path and near-critical paths have been recalculated with current progress.
- Only critical activities are being compressed.
- Crash cost slopes are based on real quotes or rates, not guesses.
- Extra people or equipment are confirmed as available on the dates needed.
- Every overlap is on a discretionary dependency, with a plan for handling changes.
- Indirect cost savings and any penalties avoided are included in the comparison.
- New risks are in the risk register with owners; our [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) has the fields you need.
- The revised budget, schedule and baseline are approved through change control.
- Near-critical paths will be monitored more often until the deadline.

### Tools and templates for schedule compression
Compression analysis needs a schedule with real dependencies. Our [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) calculates early and late dates and float, the [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) and [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) show the effect of overlaps, and the [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) records the approved trade-off.
On larger projects, scheduling software that recalculates the critical path as you edit durations and dependencies makes one-step-at-a-time compression much faster. Wrike, our top-rated tool, includes interactive Gantt charts with dependencies, the critical path and baselines from its Team plan, so you can compare the compressed plan against the original; see our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).
For the wider context of building and maintaining a realistic schedule, read our guide to [project scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the two main schedule compression techniques?**
Crashing, which adds resources to critical activities at extra cost, and fast tracking, which overlaps activities normally done in sequence at extra risk.

**Q: What is the difference between crashing and fast tracking?**
Crashing shortens activities by adding people, overtime or equipment, so it costs more. Fast tracking runs activities in parallel, so it costs little directly but increases the risk of rework.

**Q: What is an example of schedule compression?**
Adding a second designer to finish design three days sooner (crashing), or starting development on approved design modules before the full design is signed off (fast tracking).

**Q: How do you calculate crash cost per day?**
Use the crash cost slope: (crash cost - normal cost) / (normal duration - crash duration). An activity crashed from 15 to 12 days for an extra $2,400 costs $800 per day saved.

**Q: What is the crash point of an activity?**
The shortest duration an activity can reach however many resources are added. Beyond it, extra money buys no more time.

**Q: Is fast tracking always cheaper than crashing?**
Not always. Fast tracking has little direct cost, but if overlapping work has to be redone, the rework can cost more than crashing would have. Its true cost depends on how stable the earlier work is.

**Q: Why do you only compress critical path activities?**
Only critical activities determine the project finish date. Shortening a non-critical activity adds float to it but does not bring the finish forward.

**Q: Is reducing scope a schedule compression technique?**
Strictly, no. Compression keeps scope the same. Reducing scope is a separate option that changes the deliverables and needs sponsor approval.

**Q: What is the difference between schedule compression and resource levelling?**
Compression shortens the schedule. Resource levelling resolves over-allocation by delaying activities, so it usually lengthens the schedule.

**Q: Can schedule compression reduce total project cost?**
Yes, up to a point. If the cost of crashing a day is less than the indirect cost saved per day, total cost falls. The lowest point is the least-cost duration.

**Q: How far can you compress a schedule?**
Until every critical path is at its crash limit, or until risk or cost outweighs the benefit. In practice, stop at the target date or the least-cost duration.

**Q: Does schedule compression increase risk?**
Yes. Both techniques reduce float and create more critical paths, and fast tracking adds rework risk. Record the new risks in the risk register.

**Q: Can Agile teams compress a schedule?**
Agile teams usually hold the date and adjust scope through the product backlog. Swarming and adding team members are the closest Agile equivalents to compression.

# Schedule Variance (SV): Formula, Examples and Analysis

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Schedule variance (SV) explained: the SV = EV - PV formula, SV% and SPI, worked examples, earned schedule, thresholds and how to fix a negative SV.


## Schedule Variance (SV): Formula, Examples and Analysis
Schedule variance (SV) tells you whether a project has completed more or less work than planned by a given date. It is calculated as SV = EV - PV: a negative result means you are behind schedule, and a positive result means you are ahead. This guide covers the formula, a worked example across five work packages, how to convert SV into time with earned schedule, and what to do when the number turns red.
- Published 29 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- SV = EV - PV. Negative means less work done than planned; positive means more.
- SV% = SV / PV x 100 and SPI = EV / PV let you compare work packages and projects of different sizes.
- SV is measured in money, not time, and drifts back to zero as the project finishes, even if it finishes late.
- A healthy total SV can hide a slipping critical path, so always check critical activities too.
- Earned schedule converts SV into time units (SV(t) and SPI(t)) and gives a forecast finish date.

### What is schedule variance (SV)?
Schedule variance (SV) is the difference between the budgeted value of the work actually completed (earned value, EV) and the budgeted value of the work planned to be completed (planned value, PV) at a given status date. It shows, in money, how far ahead of or behind plan the work is. A negative SV means the project is behind schedule.
SV is one of the core measures in [earned value management (EVM)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/), alongside [cost variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-variance/), the schedule performance index (SPI) and the [cost performance index](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-performance-index/). Both of its inputs come from the time-phased budget: PV is what the [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) says should have been earned by now, and EV is what the team has actually earned by completing work.
Older EVM material and some government contracts use different names for the same inputs:
| Current term | Older term | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Earned value (EV) | BCWP: budgeted cost of work performed | The budget for the work actually done |
| Planned value (PV) | BCWS: budgeted cost of work scheduled | The budget for the work that should have been done by now |
So SV = BCWP - BCWS is exactly the same formula as SV = EV - PV.
Tip
Scheduling tools often show a "variance" column comparing baseline dates with current dates, in days. That is useful, but it is not EVM schedule variance. When someone quotes a schedule variance, check whether they mean days of slippage or EV - PV in money.

### The schedule variance formula
| Formula | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| SV = EV - PV | Schedule variance in money: the value of work ahead of or behind plan |
| SV% = (SV / PV) x 100 | Schedule variance as a percentage of the work planned to date |
| SPI = EV / PV | Schedule performance index: the share of planned work actually achieved |
| EV = % complete x BAC | Earned value for a work package or the project |
BAC is the [budget at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/budget-at-completion/), the total approved budget for the work, excluding management reserve. PV is read from the cumulative baseline budget at the status date.
A quick example: at the end of month four a project has PV = $80,000 and EV = $70,000.
- SV = 70,000 - 80,000 = -$10,000.
- SV% = -10,000 / 80,000 x 100 = -12.5%.
- SPI = 70,000 / 80,000 = 0.875: the team has achieved 87.5% of the work planned by now.

### How to read the result
| Result | SPI | Meaning | Typical response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SV > 0 (positive) | Above 1 | More work done than planned: ahead of schedule | Check progress is reported accurately and whether the extra work is on the critical path |
| SV = 0 | Exactly 1 | Work done matches the plan | Keep monitoring |
| SV < 0 (negative) | Below 1 | Less work done than planned: behind schedule | Find the cause, check the critical path, forecast the finish and agree action |
As with cost variance, negative is unfavourable. SV and SPI always point the same way because they use the same inputs. Note the careful wording: "less work done than planned", not "days late". SV measures the value of missing work, which is not the same as how late the project will finish.

### How to calculate schedule variance step by step
1. Fix the status date. EV and PV must relate to the same cut-off, such as the last working day of the month.
2. Confirm the performance baseline, including approved changes.
3. Read PV for each work package: the cumulative budget scheduled to be complete by the status date.
4. Measure progress using agreed rules, such as 0/100 for short tasks, 50/50, or weighted milestones for longer ones.
5. Calculate EV for each work package (% complete x BAC) and add them up.
6. Calculate SV, SV% and SPI for each work package and the total.
7. Compare with the previous period and with your thresholds.
8. Check whether the work packages behind plan are on the critical path or have float.
9. Forecast the impact on the finish date and report it.
Steps 2 and 4 cause most errors. A baseline not updated for approved changes makes SV mix performance with scope change. Subjective percent complete (the task stuck at 90% for weeks) inflates EV and makes SV look better than it is.

### Worked example: CRM implementation by work package
This is the same illustrative CRM implementation used in our cost variance guide: a budget at completion of $400,000 over a planned ten months. Here is the schedule position at the end of month five.
| Work package | BAC | PV | EV | SV | SV% | SPI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Requirements and design | $60,000 | $60,000 | $60,000 | $0 | 0.0% | 1.00 |
| 2. Configuration and build | $140,000 | $98,000 | $84,000 | -$14,000 | -14.3% | 0.86 |
| 3. Data migration | $70,000 | $21,000 | $28,000 | +$7,000 | +33.3% | 1.33 |
| 4. Testing | $80,000 | $26,000 | $8,000 | -$18,000 | -69.2% | 0.31 |
| 5. Training and go-live | $50,000 | $0 | $0 | $0 | - | - |
| **Project total** | **$400,000** | **$205,000** | **$180,000** | **-$25,000** | **-12.2%** | **0.88** |

#### Calculating the totals
- PV = 60,000 + 98,000 + 21,000 + 26,000 + 0 = $205,000.
- EV = 60,000 + 84,000 + 28,000 + 8,000 + 0 = $180,000, or 45% of the BAC.
- SV = 180,000 - 205,000 = -$25,000, and SV% = -25,000 / 205,000 x 100 = -12.2%.
- SPI = 180,000 / 205,000 = 0.878: the team has completed about 88% of the work planned by now.

#### What the breakdown tells you
- Testing is the biggest problem: -$18,000, SPI 0.31. It was planned to start in month four as build modules were handed over, and because build is late it has barely started.
- Configuration and build is $14,000 behind. This is the root of the testing delay, and the same package drives the cost overrun in the cost variance guide.
- Data migration is $7,000 ahead, but it has float in this plan. Finishing it early does not bring go-live forward.
- The total of -$25,000 is therefore flattered by migration. The critical sequence of build, testing and go-live is $32,000 behind.
This is the key lesson: totals net off. Work done early on non-critical packages can hide slippage on the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/). Look at the breakdown and the critical path before telling a sponsor the project is "only 12% behind".
Tip
Align work packages with your [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) and schedule, so every SV figure can be traced to activities on the Gantt chart. If you cannot see which activities sit behind a variance, you cannot tell whether it matters.

### Cumulative and period schedule variance
Most reports show cumulative SV, from the start of the project to the status date. Period SV looks at one month on its own and shows when a problem started and whether it is getting worse.
| Month | PV this month | EV this month | Period SV | Cumulative PV | Cumulative EV | Cumulative SV | SV% | SPI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | $20,000 | $20,000 | $0 | $20,000 | $20,000 | $0 | 0.0% | 1.00 |
| 2 | $30,000 | $25,000 | -$5,000 | $50,000 | $45,000 | -$5,000 | -10.0% | 0.90 |
| 3 | $45,000 | $40,000 | -$5,000 | $95,000 | $85,000 | -$10,000 | -10.5% | 0.89 |
| 4 | $55,000 | $45,000 | -$10,000 | $150,000 | $130,000 | -$20,000 | -13.3% | 0.87 |
| 5 | $55,000 | $50,000 | -$5,000 | $205,000 | $180,000 | -$25,000 | -12.2% | 0.88 |
Cumulative SV has grown every month since month two, but the period figures add detail. Month four was the worst, when build slipped and testing could not start. In month five the team earned 91% of what was planned for the month (50,000 / 55,000), against 82% in month four, and cumulative SPI ticked up from 0.87 to 0.88.
That is what early recovery looks like: period performance better than the cumulative figure, even though cumulative SV is still negative. If the period figures get worse again, the problem is structural and the forecast should change.
Plot cumulative PV, EV and AC on one chart: the gap between PV and EV is your schedule variance, and the gap between EV and AC is your cost variance. See our guide to the [S-curve](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/s-curve/).

### Schedule variance vs SPI and cost variance
| Measure | Formula | Units | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule variance (SV) | EV - PV | Money, to date | Value of work ahead of or behind plan |
| Schedule performance index (SPI) | EV / PV | Ratio | Efficiency trend; comparing projects; forecasting |
| Cost variance (CV) | EV - AC | Money, to date | Whether completed work cost more or less than budgeted |
| Cost performance index (CPI) | EV / AC | Ratio | Cost efficiency; estimate at completion |
| SV(t), earned schedule | ES - AT | Time | How far behind in time; forecast finish |
SV shows the amount of work at stake in money, which matters to a sponsor. SPI shows efficiency as a ratio, which travels well between projects of different sizes. Report both.
SV compares work done with work planned; CV compares work done with what it cost. Both anchor on EV, which is what separates "are we on time?" from "are we spending efficiently?".

#### Reading schedule variance with cost variance
| SV | CV | What it usually means | Questions to ask |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Positive | Positive | Ahead of schedule and under budget | Is progress reported accurately? Was the plan too cautious? |
| Positive | Negative | Ahead of schedule but over budget | Are we paying for speed with overtime or extra staff? Was that agreed? |
| Negative | Positive | Behind schedule but under budget | Are resources missing? Is work being delayed rather than done cheaply? |
| Negative | Negative | Behind schedule and over budget | What is the root cause? Is a re-plan or change request needed? |
The CRM project is in the bottom row: SV -$25,000 and CV -$17,000. That is the hardest combination, because catching up on time usually costs money. The combined forecast AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) captures the effect; see our guide to the [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/).

### The limitations of schedule variance
- **It is measured in money, not time.** An SV of -$25,000 does not tell you how many days late you are. Earned schedule (below) converts it properly.
- **It returns to zero at the end.** When all work is complete, EV = PV = BAC, so SV = 0 and SPI = 1, even if the project finished months late. In the later stages SV gradually loses its power to show schedule problems.
- **It ignores the critical path.** EV adds up all work equally, so progress on non-critical work can mask critical delays.
- **It depends on progress measurement.** Subjective percent complete inflates EV; front-loaded credit rules flatter SV early.
- **It depends on the baseline.** An unrealistic or out-of-date baseline means every variance is measured against the wrong yardstick.
- **It dilutes with level-of-effort work.** For activities such as project management, EV is usually set equal to PV, so they always show zero SV.
None of this makes SV useless. It is an early, objective signal that the project is earning value more slowly than planned. It just needs to be read with the schedule, not instead of it.
Tip
Use SV and SPI to ask "are we doing the planned amount of work?" and the critical path and [float](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/float-and-slack/) to ask "will we finish on time?". You need both answers.

### Earned schedule: schedule variance in time units
Earned schedule (ES) extends earned value management to measure schedule performance in time rather than money. It was introduced by Walt Lipke in 2003 in the article "Schedule Is Different", published in The Measurable News of PMI's College of Performance Management, and it uses the same PV and EV data you already have.
The idea: find the point at which the current EV should have been earned according to the baseline. If you have earned what the plan expected by month 4.5, but it is now month 5, you are half a month behind.
| Measure | Formula | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Earned schedule (ES) | C + (EV - PV at C) / (PV at C+1 - PV at C) | When the current EV was planned to be earned. C is the last whole period in which cumulative PV was at or below EV. |
| Actual time (AT) | Periods elapsed | How long the project has been running |
| SV(t) | ES - AT | Schedule variance in time; negative means behind |
| SPI(t) | ES / AT | Time-based schedule performance index |
| IEAC(t) | Planned duration / SPI(t) | Forecast total duration if current performance continues |

#### Worked earned schedule example
In the CRM project, EV at month five is $180,000. Cumulative PV was $150,000 at month four and $205,000 at month five.
1. Find C: PV at month 4 ($150,000) is below EV and PV at month 5 ($205,000) is above, so C = 4.
2. ES = 4 + (180,000 - 150,000) / (205,000 - 150,000) = 4 + 0.55 = 4.55 months.
3. AT = 5 months, so SV(t) = 4.55 - 5 = -0.45 months, roughly two working weeks behind.
4. SPI(t) = 4.55 / 5 = 0.91.
5. IEAC(t) = 10 / 0.91 = about 11.0 months: roughly one month late if current performance continues.
That is a far more useful message for a sponsor than "SV is -$25,000".

#### Why earned schedule matters at the end of a project
Suppose the CRM project finishes all its work at the end of month 12, two months late. At that point EV = PV = BAC = $400,000.
| Measure | Calculation | Result | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SV | 400,000 - 400,000 | $0 | On schedule |
| SPI | 400,000 / 400,000 | 1.00 | On schedule |
| SV(t) | ES 10 - AT 12 | -2 months | Two months late |
| SPI(t) | 10 / 12 | 0.83 | 83% of planned schedule efficiency |
Only the time-based measures tell the truth at completion. Earned schedule still adds up all work regardless of the critical path, so use it alongside your schedule.

### Schedule variance thresholds and when to act
Most organisations set variance thresholds in the project management plan: limits beyond which the project manager must explain the variance, forecast its impact and propose action. Thresholds often tighten as the project matures, because there is less time to recover.
There is no universal standard. The right limits depend on the industry, the contract and how firm the deadline is. This table is an example to adapt, not a rule:
| Status | Example threshold (cumulative) | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Green | SV% within plus or minus 5%, and no critical milestone forecast late | Report as normal |
| Amber | SV% between -5% and -10%, or a critical milestone up to two weeks late | Variance explanation and recovery plan in the next report |
| Red | SV% beyond -10%, or a critical milestone more than two weeks late | Escalate to the sponsor; re-forecast the finish; consider compression or a change request |
Combining SV% with a time check on critical milestones avoids flagging small packages that do not matter while missing critical ones that do. Under these example thresholds the CRM project (-12.2%, forecast about a month late) is red. Many teams also set a favourable threshold, such as +10%, because a large positive variance often signals overstated progress.

### Common causes of negative schedule variance
- **Optimistic estimates:** best-case productivity, missing tasks or no allowance for risk.
- **Resource shortages:** people not available when planned, or shared specialists pulled onto other work.
- **Late inputs:** data, approvals, equipment or deliverables from another team, supplier or client.
- **Rework:** defects, unclear requirements or design changes.
- **Unapproved scope:** [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) absorbs effort without changing the baseline.
- **Realised risks:** supplier failure, outages, regulatory change, weather or site conditions.

#### When a positive schedule variance is a warning
- Overstated progress, which inflates EV.
- Easy, non-critical work done first while harder critical work waits.
- Work started out of sequence that may need redoing.
- A cautious baseline with padded durations.
To find the real cause of a significant variance, use a structured technique such as a [fishbone diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/) or five whys with the people doing the work.

### How to fix a negative schedule variance
1. Validate the data: status date, progress measurement and baseline.
2. Locate the variance by drilling down to work packages and activities.
3. Check the critical path. If the late work has enough float, monitor it; if it is critical, act.
4. Find the root cause: resources, dependencies, rework, scope or estimates.
5. Forecast the new finish date with SV(t) and SPI(t) or an updated schedule.
6. Compare recovery options by cost and risk, and agree them with the sponsor.
7. Raise a change request through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) if the baseline is no longer achievable.
8. Watch next period's SV and SPI to check the actions are working.

#### Recovery options
| Option | When it helps | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove blockers (decisions, access, inputs) | Delays caused by waiting rather than effort | Needs sponsor support |
| Re-sequence or reassign work | People on tasks with float can move to critical work | Skills match and new overloads; see [resource levelling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) |
| Fast tracking | Dependencies are discretionary and requirements stable | Rework from overlapping work |
| Crashing | Money is available and extra resources genuinely speed the work | Extra cost; new people are slower at first |
| Reduce or defer scope, with approval | The date is fixed and some features can wait | Benefits may fall |
| Re-baseline with a new date | The original plan is no longer realistic | Needs formal approval |
Fast tracking and crashing are the two classic [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) techniques. See our worked comparison of [fast tracking vs crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/).

#### Example schedule variance explanation
A good explanation states the variance, where it sits, the cause, the impact, the actions and any decision needed. For the CRM project: "The project is $25,000 behind plan (SV% -12.2%, SPI 0.88), about two weeks in time terms. The critical sequence of build and testing is $32,000 behind; data migration is ahead but has float. Build is late because two integration developers joined five weeks after plan. At current performance, go-live moves from the end of month 10 to around the end of month 11. Actions: move one migration analyst to test preparation (PM, from 10 November); overlap testing with the last build sprint for low-risk modules (test lead, plan by 14 November). Decision needed: approve two weeks of contractor support for build, or accept a revised go-live date."

### Schedule variance in Agile projects
EVM was designed for plan-driven projects, but schedule variance can be adapted to Agile delivery at release level:
- Use the release budget as BAC and the story points planned for the release as the scope.
- PV is the share of points the release plan expected to be done by now, multiplied by BAC.
- EV is the share of points actually done (meeting the definition of done), multiplied by BAC.
- Re-baseline planned points when the product owner changes scope, so SV reflects pace rather than scope change.
Illustrative example: a 300-point release has a budget of $300,000 over 12 sprints. After sprint 6 the plan expected 150 points; the team has completed 120. PV = $150,000, EV = $120,000, SV = -$30,000 and SPI = 0.80: the team is delivering about 80% of the planned pace, which a release burn-up chart would also show.
Most Agile teams track this signal directly through burn-ups and [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/), and adjust scope rather than date. Release-level SV is most useful when a PMO needs Agile and predictive projects reported in the same terms. See our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).

### Common schedule variance mistakes
- Treating SV as a number of days.
- Reporting only the project total, so non-critical work hides critical slippage.
- Using subjective percent complete, which inflates EV.
- Measuring against a baseline that excludes approved changes.
- Mixing status dates for progress and planned value.
- Relying on SV and SPI late in the project, when they drift towards zero and one.
- Explaining the variance without forecasting the finish date.

### Tools and templates for tracking schedule variance
For a small project, a spreadsheet with BAC, PV, percent complete, EV, SV, SV% and SPI per work package is enough. Build the schedule in our [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) or [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/), track progress in the [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/), and use the [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) when a variance needs a baseline change.
For larger projects, look for software with saved baselines, dependencies, the critical path and percent complete. Wrike, our top-rated tool, includes Gantt charts with dependencies, the critical path and baselines from its Team plan; see our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/). Check whether a tool calculates earned value directly or whether you will need custom fields or a spreadsheet export.
Schedule variance is one input to a reliable forecast. Read our guide to [project forecasting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the schedule variance formula?**
SV = EV - PV, where EV is earned value (the budget for the work actually completed) and PV is planned value (the budget for the work scheduled to be done by now). As a percentage, SV% = SV / PV x 100.

**Q: What does a negative schedule variance mean?**
Less work has been completed than planned by the status date, so the project is behind schedule in earned value terms. Check the critical path to see whether the finish date is actually at risk.

**Q: Is a positive schedule variance always good?**
No. It can come from overstated progress, easy non-critical work done early, or a cautious baseline, and it can hide a slipping critical path.

**Q: How do you calculate schedule variance percentage?**
Divide SV by PV and multiply by 100. An SV of -$25,000 on PV of $205,000 is -12.2%.

**Q: What is the difference between schedule variance and SPI?**
Both use EV and PV. SV is the difference in money; SPI is the ratio EV / PV. A negative SV always means an SPI below 1.

**Q: What is the difference between schedule variance and cost variance?**
Schedule variance (EV - PV) compares work done with work planned. Cost variance (EV - AC) compares work done with what it cost. Both use earned value as the anchor.

**Q: Why is schedule variance measured in money?**
Earned value measures progress in budget units so that different kinds of work can be added together. Earned schedule converts the result into time.

**Q: Why does schedule variance return to zero at the end of a project?**
When all work is complete, EV and PV both equal the budget at completion, so SV is zero however late the project finished. Earned schedule's SV(t) does not have this problem.

**Q: What is earned schedule?**
An extension of earned value management, introduced by Walt Lipke in 2003, that finds when the current EV was planned to be earned. It gives SV(t) = ES - AT and SPI(t) = ES / AT in time units.

**Q: What is an acceptable schedule variance?**
There is no universal figure. Thresholds are set in the project management plan, often as a percentage band such as plus or minus 5% or 10%, combined with a check on critical milestone dates.

**Q: How often should you calculate schedule variance?**
At every reporting period: usually monthly on larger projects and weekly or fortnightly on short ones. Use one status date for all figures and track the trend.

**Q: Can a project have a positive schedule variance and still be late?**
Yes. If non-critical work is ahead while critical-path work slips, total SV can be positive while the finish date moves out.

# Scope Creep: Causes, Examples and How to Prevent It

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Scope creep explained: what it is, why it happens, warning signs, real examples and a step-by-step way to prevent and control it on any project.


## Scope Creep: Causes, Examples and How to Prevent It
Scope creep is the gradual, uncontrolled growth of a project's scope without matching changes to time, budget or resources. It rarely arrives as one big request; it builds up through small additions that nobody formally approved. This guide explains what causes scope creep, how to spot it early, and a practical process for preventing and controlling it.
- Published 16 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 16 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scope creep is uncontrolled scope growth: work is added but time, cost and resources stay the same.
- Change itself is normal. The problem is change that bypasses assessment and approval.
- Most scope creep starts with vague requirements, missing exclusions and no single route for requests.
- A signed-off scope statement, a WBS and a simple change control process prevent most of it.
- When a new request arrives, show its impact and offer options: defer, swap, fund it or decline.
- In Agile, new ideas go to the Product Backlog for the Product Owner to order, and the Sprint Goal is protected.

### What is scope creep?
**Scope creep** is the uncontrolled expansion of a project's product or project scope without corresponding adjustments to time, cost and resources. It happens when new features, deliverables or tasks are added after scope has been agreed, but nobody assesses their impact, approves them formally or updates the plan to reflect them.
PMI uses almost exactly this framing in its glossary, and it is a useful test: if work has been added and the [scope baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/), schedule and budget have not changed, you have scope creep.
It helps to separate two kinds of scope. **Product scope** is the features and functions of what you are building, such as a website with search and checkout. **Project scope** is the work needed to deliver it: design, build, test, train and launch. Scope creep can affect either one. A client asking for a live chat feature expands the product scope; a sponsor asking the team to also migrate ten years of archive data expands the project scope.
The word "creep" matters. A single large change is usually noticed and discussed. Scope creep is many small changes, each of which seems too minor to formalise: one more report, an extra round of revisions, a quick tweak to the login page. Individually they look harmless; together they can add weeks.
It is also common. PMI's *Pulse of the Profession* 2018 report found that 52% of projects completed in the previous 12 months had experienced scope creep, up from 43% five years earlier.
Our guide to [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) explains how to define scope properly in the first place.

### Scope creep vs scope change, gold plating and feature creep
Not every change to scope is scope creep. Projects learn as they go, and approved changes that add value are part of good project management. The difference is control.
| Term | Who usually causes it | Approved? | Plan updated? | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Approved scope change | Sponsor, client or team via a change request | Yes | Yes: scope, schedule and budget re-baselined | Client requests a payment option; impact assessed; extra two weeks and budget agreed |
| Scope creep | Stakeholders, client or team | No (or informally) | No | Payment option added after a hallway conversation; deadline unchanged |
| Gold plating | The project team | No | No | A developer adds animations nobody asked for because they "look better" |
| Feature creep | Product owners, users, sales | Often informally | Rarely | A product keeps gaining features until it becomes harder to use and later to ship |
**Gold plating** is a form of scope creep that comes from inside the team. It is usually well-meant, but it consumes time and budget, adds risk and can introduce defects in areas the customer never asked for. **Feature creep** is the product-development term for the same pattern, focusing on the product rather than the project.
Tip
Ask one question to tell them apart: "Has this change been assessed and approved by the person who owns the scope, and has the plan been updated?" If the answer is no, treat it as scope creep, however small.

### What causes scope creep?
Scope creep almost always has more than one cause. These are the ones that come up most often.

#### Unclear scope and requirements
If the [scope statement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) is vague ("a modern website", "improved reporting"), almost any request can be argued to be in scope. Missing or loosely written [requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/) and acceptance criteria leave room for interpretation, and that room tends to fill with extra work.

#### No formal change control
Without a defined [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) process, there is no agreed way to say "yes, and here is what it costs". Requests are either accepted quietly or refused awkwardly, and the quiet acceptances become scope creep.

#### Stakeholders going around the project manager
Requests sent straight to a designer or developer by email, chat or in a meeting bypass the project manager. The team member wants to help, does the work, and the plan never hears about it.

#### Gold plating and good intentions
Teams sometimes add features or polish to impress the customer. It feels like good service, but it uses time the plan did not include and can set expectations for future projects.

#### Long projects and shifting business needs
The longer a project runs, the more the business around it changes: new regulations, new competitors, new leadership. Some of those changes are legitimate, but they need to be assessed rather than absorbed.

#### Weak sponsorship and commercial pressure
A sponsor who is not engaged in trade-off decisions leaves the project manager without backing to push back. On client work, a fear of upsetting the client (or a fixed-price contract with a vague [statement of work](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/)) makes it tempting to absorb requests rather than raise them.

### Scope creep examples
These examples show how scope creep looks in different types of project. In each case the original request was reasonable; the problem was that it was never assessed against time and cost.
| Project | Original scope | What crept in | Typical impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Website redesign | 10-page site, contact form, CMS | Blog, multilingual pages, live chat, extra design rounds | Launch slips, developer overtime, budget overrun |
| Software feature | Export a report to CSV | Also PDF, scheduled emails, custom branding | Sprint goal missed, testing squeezed |
| Office move | Move 80 staff to a new floor | New furniture, IT upgrades, meeting-room AV | Extra suppliers, unbudgeted spend, move date at risk |
| Event | Half-day conference for 150 | Evening reception, livestream, printed brochure | Venue and supplier costs rise, team overstretched |
| Internal report | Five charts for the board | Twenty charts after each review adds "just one more" | Analyst time doubles, other work delayed |

#### Worked example: how small requests add up
Imagine a 12-week website project with a fixed launch date. Over six weeks, the client asks for five "small" things, each agreed informally:
- An extra landing page (3 days).
- A newsletter sign-up connected to their email platform (2 days).
- A third round of homepage design revisions (3 days).
- Cookie banner customisation (1 day).
- Importing 40 old blog posts (4 days).
None of these looks significant on its own, but together they add 13 working days, nearly three weeks, to a 12-week plan. Nothing in the schedule or budget has changed, so the team works overtime, testing is cut short and the launch either slips or goes live with defects.
Now run the same requests through change control. Each one is logged, the impact is shown, and the client chooses: the landing page and newsletter sign-up are approved with a one-week extension and extra budget; the blog import moves to a phase 2; the extra design round is swapped for a lower-priority page. The project still grows, but it grows on purpose.

### The impact of scope creep
Scope creep hurts projects because of the [triple constraint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/): scope, time and cost are linked. If scope grows and the other two do not move, something else gives, usually quality or the team.
- **Schedule delays:** extra work pushes out milestones, and the critical path often absorbs it first.
- **Budget overruns:** more effort, more materials and more supplier costs, with no budget to cover them.
- **Lower quality:** testing, reviews and documentation are squeezed to protect the deadline.
- **Team burnout:** people work longer hours on work that does not appear in any plan, which damages morale.
- **Damaged trust:** stakeholders are surprised when dates slip, even though they asked for the additions.
- **Delayed benefits:** the core value of the project reaches users later than it could have.
- **Weaker reporting:** progress percentages become meaningless because the baseline no longer reflects the real work.
On commercial projects there is an extra cost: unbilled work. Agencies and consultancies that absorb scope creep lose margin on every project where it happens.

### Warning signs of scope creep
Scope creep is easiest to deal with when you catch it early. Watch for these signals:
- Tasks appear on the board or in timesheets that are not in the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/).
- Requests arrive by email, chat or in meetings, rather than through the agreed intake route.
- You hear phrases like "while you're at it", "it should only take five minutes" or "we assumed that was included".
- Acceptance criteria are rewritten after work has started.
- The team is working overtime but the schedule shows no change.
- Deliverables stay "almost done" for weeks.
- The scope line on a burn-up chart keeps rising, or the backlog grows faster than the team delivers.
- Actual effort runs well ahead of estimates on tasks that were well understood.
- Stakeholders who were not involved in planning start shaping the solution late in the project.
Tip
Review the WBS against actual tasks and timesheets in your weekly check-in. Anything that does not map to a WBS element is either missing from the plan or creeping in.

### How to prevent scope creep
Prevention is mostly about agreeing scope clearly and agreeing, in advance, how changes will be handled. These steps work on traditional and hybrid projects of any size.
1. **Agree clear objectives.** Write measurable objectives in the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) so every request can be tested against them: does it help achieve the objective?
2. **Collect requirements properly.** Involve the people who will use the result, not only the people who are paying for it, and record [requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/) with priorities.
3. **Write a scope statement with exclusions.** List what is in scope and, just as importantly, what is out of scope. Exclusions prevent the "we assumed that was included" conversation.
4. **Break the work down.** Create a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) and a WBS dictionary so the full scope is visible and every [deliverable](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/) has a definition.
5. **Define acceptance criteria.** For each deliverable, agree how you will know it is done. Moving acceptance criteria is one of the quietest forms of scope creep.
6. **Get sign-off and set a baseline.** Have the sponsor or client approve the scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary. Together they form the scope baseline you will measure changes against.
7. **Set up change control before you need it.** Agree how requests are logged, who assesses them, who approves them and how the plan is updated. Keep it light for small projects.
8. **Create a single intake route.** Ask stakeholders to send all requests to the project manager or through a request form, and ask the team to redirect side-channel requests politely.
9. **Communicate regularly.** Use a steady rhythm of [status reports](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) and reviews so stakeholders see progress and feel heard, which reduces informal requests.
10. **Put change terms in contracts.** On client work, the statement of work should say how changes are requested, priced and approved.
The [project scope template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-scope-template/) covers objectives, deliverables, in scope, out of scope, acceptance criteria, constraints and assumptions, which is most of the groundwork above in one document.
Change control is the single most important control on this list.

### How to manage scope creep when it happens
Even well-planned projects get new requests. The aim is not to refuse change but to make every change visible and deliberate.

#### Step-by-step response to a new request
1. **Pause before agreeing.** Thank the person, and say you will look at the impact. Avoid an on-the-spot yes or no.
2. **Log it.** Record the request in a change log or [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/): what is being asked, by whom, and why.
3. **Check it against the baseline.** Is it genuinely new, or is it already covered by an existing requirement or acceptance criterion?
4. **Assess the impact.** Estimate the effect on schedule, cost, resources, quality and risk. Involve the people who would do the work.
5. **Prepare options.** Present realistic choices rather than a single answer (see the table below).
6. **Get a decision from the right person.** The sponsor, client or change control board decides, not the team member who received the request.
7. **Update the plan.** If approved, update the scope statement, WBS, schedule, budget and risk register, then re-baseline.
8. **Communicate the outcome.** Tell the requester, the team and other stakeholders what was decided and what it changes.

#### How to say no (or "yes, and") to a stakeholder
Saying no outright can damage relationships, especially with clients and senior stakeholders. It usually works better to show the trade-off and let the decision-maker choose:
| Option | What you say | When it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Defer | "We can add this in phase 2 or the next release." | Useful but not urgent; core delivery should not slip |
| Swap | "We can include this if we remove X, which is a similar size." | Fixed deadline or budget; the client values the new item more |
| Approve with more time or budget | "This adds about two weeks and this much cost. Shall I raise a change request?" | The change is valuable and the sponsor can fund it |
| Decline | "This falls outside the project objectives, so we recommend not including it." | The request does not support the agreed objectives |
Keep the conversation about the project's objectives rather than personal preferences, and put the outcome in writing. Our guide to [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) covers how to handle these conversations with different types of stakeholder.
Tip
Record approved, deferred and declined requests. A clear history protects the team when someone later asks why a feature is missing, and it gives you evidence for future estimates.

### Scope creep in Agile projects
Agile approaches expect scope to change. That does not mean Agile teams are immune to scope creep; it means change is handled differently.
In Scrum, all known work lives in the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/), which the [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) orders. According to the Scrum Guide 2020, during a Sprint no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal, and scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned. New ideas therefore go to the backlog, not straight to a developer, and are pulled into a future Sprint at [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) if they are valuable enough.
Time and cost are typically fixed per iteration, and scope is the variable. Scope creep in Agile looks different from a traditional project:
- Stakeholders asking developers to slip work into the current Sprint.
- Sprint Goals repeatedly missed because unplanned work is pulled in mid-Sprint.
- A backlog that grows without being ordered or refined, so nothing is ever deprioritised.
- A release date and a full feature list both treated as fixed.
- "Done" quietly changing because there is no shared [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
A burn-up chart with a separate scope line makes this visible: if the scope line rises as fast as the completed-work line, the release date will not arrive. Velocity tracking helps here too; see our guide to the [Agile velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/).

### Tools and templates that help control scope
You do not need specialist software to control scope, but a few documents make it much easier:
- [Project scope template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-scope-template/): objectives, deliverables, inclusions, exclusions, acceptance criteria, constraints and assumptions.
- [Change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/): a change request form and change log with impact on scope, schedule and cost.
- [WBS template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/): WBS codes, levels, deliverables, owners, effort and cost.
- [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/): risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, including the assumptions that scope depends on.
- [Business requirements document template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/): requirements and priorities agreed before build.
Project management software helps when requests come from many people. Request forms, approval workflows and a visible baseline reduce side-channel work. Our #1-ranked tool, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), is a good fit for teams that want structured request forms and approvals across several projects; other tools handle this well too, as our [project management software rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) explain.

### Common mistakes to avoid
- **Treating all change as bad.** Refusing every request frustrates stakeholders and can leave the project delivering something nobody needs. Control change; do not block it.
- **Accepting verbal approvals.** If it is not written down, it will be remembered differently later.
- **Ignoring small changes.** The worked example above shows how small, unrecorded requests become weeks of work.
- **Leaving out exclusions.** A scope statement without an out-of-scope list invites assumptions.
- **Letting the team gold-plate.** Recognise the intent, but redirect extra ideas into change requests or the backlog.
- **Approving changes without re-baselining.** If the plan is not updated, progress reports become misleading.
- **Making the process too heavy.** A ten-page form for a one-day change encourages people to bypass it. Scale the process to the size of the change.
For the wider picture of how change control differs from organisational change, read [change management vs change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-management-vs-change-control/).
