# Service Level Agreement (SLA): Examples, Template & Metrics

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/service-level-agreement-sla/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a service level agreement (SLA) is, what to include, types, metrics, availability and service credit examples, and how projects agree SLAs.


## Service Level Agreement (SLA): Examples, Template & Metrics
A service level agreement (SLA) is a documented agreement between a service provider and its customer that defines the service, the measurable levels it must meet, how performance is reported and what happens when targets are missed. Projects meet SLAs in two ways: when they buy a service from a supplier, and when they hand a new service over to an operations team. This guide covers what to include, the key metrics, a full illustrative SLA and worked calculations for availability, credits and response clocks.
- Published 2 October 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- An SLA turns "good service" into measurable targets, with agreed reporting and remedies when targets are missed.
- The three common types are customer-based, service-based and multi-level SLAs; internal SLAs between departments follow the same structure.
- Know the related terms: SLIs are the measurements, SLOs are the targets and OLAs are the internal agreements that support the SLA.
- Precise definitions (when the clock starts, which hours count, what is excluded) matter more than ambitious numbers.
- An end-to-end target can never be better than the services it depends on, so check suppliers and OLAs before you promise it.
- Projects that create a service should agree its SLA during design and make SLA readiness a handover criterion.

### What is a service level agreement?
A **service level agreement (SLA)** is a documented agreement between a service provider and a customer that describes the service to be delivered and the level of service the customer can expect. It sets measurable targets, such as availability or resolution times, explains how they are measured and reported, and states the remedies if they are missed.
That definition follows the one used in ITIL 4, the widely used IT service management framework, which describes an SLA as a documented agreement identifying both the services required and the expected level of service. ITIL places SLAs within the **service level management** practice, whose purpose is to set clear, business-based targets so that a service can be assessed, monitored and managed against them.
Every SLA answers five questions:
- **What service?** What is included, what is excluded and who uses it.
- **How good?** The measurable service levels, such as 99.9% availability or a four-hour fix for critical incidents.
- **Measured how?** The data source, the measurement period and the business hours that count.
- **Reported how?** The report, its frequency and the review meeting.
- **What if targets are missed?** Service credits, improvement plans, escalation and, ultimately, termination rights.
SLAs can be **external**, forming part of a contract with a supplier, or **internal**, agreed between departments such as IT and finance. External SLAs are usually legally enforceable through the contract they sit in; internal ones are management commitments rather than contracts.

### Why SLAs matter in projects
SLAs are often seen as an operations topic, but projects create and buy most new services, so project managers shape the SLAs that operations teams live with for years.
- **When a project buys a service.** Hosting, software as a service, support, maintenance and facilities management are bought with SLAs attached. The SLA is part of [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/): it defines what you are paying for after go-live.
- **When a project delivers a service.** A new system, help desk or shared service needs agreed service levels before operations accepts it. The SLA becomes a set of acceptance criteria for the handover.
- **When teams depend on each other.** Internal agreements, such as a procurement team turning purchase requests round in five working days, keep a project's critical activities predictable.
In project terms an SLA is both a procurement tool and a quality standard. It defines what "good" looks like once the service is live, which links it directly to [project quality management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/).

### Where SLAs fit in the project lifecycle
Leaving the SLA until the week before go-live is one of the most common causes of difficult handovers. Service levels affect architecture, staffing and cost, so they belong in planning.
| Project phase | SLA activity |
| --- | --- |
| Initiation and business case | Agree the business need for the service: who relies on it, when and what an outage costs |
| Requirements | Capture service levels as non-functional [project requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/), such as availability, response time and support hours |
| Procurement | Put supplier SLAs, measurement rules and service credits into the tender and the contract |
| Design and build | Design for the target: redundancy, monitoring, backup and support model |
| Testing | Run operational acceptance tests: monitoring, alerting, failover, backup restore and support processes |
| Transition | Agree the SLA and supporting OLAs, train the support team and run a period of early life support |
| Closure | Confirm SLA readiness as a handover criterion during [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/) and record lessons learned |
Tip
Ask early: "What does one hour of downtime cost the business, and when?" The answer tells you whether you need 99% or 99.99%, and the price difference between them can be large.

### Types of SLA
Most sources describe three main types. They differ in who the agreement is written for.
| Type | What it covers | Example | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Customer-based SLA | All services provided to one customer or customer group | An agreement covering email, payroll system and help desk for the finance department | Key customers with a distinct set of needs |
| Service-based SLA | One service, on the same terms for every customer | A standard IT help desk SLA that applies to all staff | Standard services with many users |
| Multi-level SLA | Layers of terms: corporate-wide, customer-specific and service-specific | Company-wide security and hours, plus faster response for the trading floor | Large organisations with varied needs |
You will also hear about **internal SLAs**, between departments in the same organisation, and **supplier** or **vendor SLAs**, which a provider publishes or negotiates for its product. Cloud providers, for example, usually publish standard service-based SLAs with fixed credit terms.

### SLA, SLO, SLI, OLA and related terms
These terms are often mixed up. The distinction matters because each one has a different owner and audience.
| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SLA (service level agreement) | The agreement with the customer, often with consequences | 99.9% monthly availability, with service credits if missed |
| SLO (service level objective) | A specific target, often stricter than the SLA, used to run the service | 99.95% availability as an internal target |
| SLI (service level indicator) | The actual measurement used to judge the target | Percentage of successful requests in the month |
| Error budget | The amount of failure an SLO allows (100% minus the SLO) | 0.05% of the month, about 21.6 minutes |
| OLA (operational level agreement) | An agreement between internal teams that supports the SLA | Database team restores a backup within 2 hours |
| Underpinning contract | A contract with an external supplier that supports the SLA | Hosting provider guarantees 99.95% availability |
| KPI (key performance indicator) | Any important performance measure, not necessarily agreed with a customer | Customer satisfaction score |
SLIs, SLOs and error budgets come from site reliability engineering, a practice popularised by Google. Setting the SLO tighter than the SLA gives the team an early warning before a contractual breach.

#### SLA vs contract, MSA and SOW
In supplier relationships the SLA is usually one schedule within a wider contract. The **master services agreement (MSA)** sets the legal terms, such as liability, confidentiality and termination. A [statement of work (SOW)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/) describes a specific piece of project work with deliverables and dates. The **SLA** describes ongoing service performance after that work is delivered. A typical managed service has all three: an MSA, an SOW for transition and an SLA for the running service.

### What to include in an SLA
These sections cover what most SLAs need. Use them as a checklist when you draft or review one.
| Section | What it contains | What good looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parties, term and review | Who the agreement is between, start date, duration and review date | Named owners on both sides; review at least annually |
| Service description | What the service does, who can use it, what is included and excluded | Specific enough that both sides agree on borderline requests |
| Service hours | When the service is available and when support is provided | Separate the two, e.g. service 24/7, support 08:00 to 18:00 Monday to Friday |
| Service levels | Metrics, targets, measurement period and data source | Each target has an SLI and a formula |
| Priority definitions | What counts as priority 1, 2, 3 and 4 | Defined by business impact and number of users affected |
| Responsibilities | What the provider and the customer each must do | Includes customer duties, such as reporting incidents through the agreed channel |
| Reporting and reviews | Report content, frequency and meetings | Monthly report and service review with agreed attendees |
| Remedies | Service credits, improvement plans, escalation and termination triggers | Credit tiers with a cap, plus a route for repeated failure |
| Exclusions | Planned maintenance, customer-caused faults, events outside the provider's control | Maintenance windows and notice periods stated |
| Escalation and contacts | Names, roles and escalation path | Kept current in an appendix |
| Change process | How the SLA itself is changed | Changes go through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) |
Many SLAs also cover security, data protection, backup and disaster recovery. Two common recovery measures are the **recovery time objective (RTO)**, how quickly a service must be restored after a disaster, and the **recovery point objective (RPO)**, how much data loss is acceptable, expressed as time.

### Common SLA metrics
Choose a small set of metrics that reflect what users experience. Five to eight is plenty for most services.
| Metric | What it measures | Example target | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Availability (uptime) | Percentage of time the service is usable | 99.9% per calendar month | How "usable" is defined and what is excluded |
| Response time | Time from incident logged to acknowledgement and start of work | P1 within 15 minutes | An automatic reply should not count as a response |
| Resolution time | Time from incident logged to fix or workaround | P1 within 4 hours | Whether the clock pauses while waiting for the customer |
| Target compliance | Share of tickets meeting their target | 95% of P3 tickets resolved within target | A single very late ticket can hide inside a good percentage |
| Performance (latency) | Speed of the service for users | 95% of page loads under 2 seconds | Averages hide slow outliers; use percentiles |
| First contact resolution | Share of issues resolved at the first contact | 70% for service desk calls | Can encourage closing tickets too quickly |
| Mean time to restore (MTTR) | Average time to restore service after a failure | Under 1 hour | Averages can be skewed by one long outage |
| Customer satisfaction | User rating after a ticket or survey | 4.2 out of 5 | Low response rates |
Response and resolution measures are close cousins of the flow metrics in Kanban; our guide to [cycle time vs lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/) explains how to measure elapsed time through a process consistently.

### How to write an SLA step by step
Whether you are agreeing an SLA with a supplier or for a service your project is handing over, follow these steps.
1. **Identify the service and its users.** Describe what the service does, who uses it and when. Involve the people who will rely on it, using your [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) plan.
2. **Understand the business impact.** Ask what an outage or slow response costs, and at which times it hurts most. This sets the level of service worth paying for.
3. **Choose the metrics.** Pick measures users care about, such as successful transactions or time to resolve, not only whether a server is switched on.
4. **Define each metric precisely.** State the formula, data source, measurement period, service hours and exclusions. Decide when the clock starts, pauses and stops.
5. **Set targets from evidence.** Use baseline performance, supplier commitments and business need. A target the service has never achieved is a promise, not a plan.
6. **Check the supply chain.** Confirm that OLAs and supplier contracts support every target you promise to the customer.
7. **Agree priorities and responsibilities.** Define priority levels by impact, and write down what the customer must do as well as the provider. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) helps here.
8. **Agree remedies and escalation.** Set service credit tiers, a cap, an improvement-plan trigger and the escalation path.
9. **Set up measurement and reporting before go-live.** Monitoring, ticket categories and report templates should be tested during the project, not built afterwards.
10. **Sign off and schedule reviews.** Get approval from both sides, publish the SLA where users can find it and set the first review date.
Our free [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) is a quick way to record who owns each SLA responsibility on both sides.

### Example SLA for a new service
This example is illustrative. A project is replacing a company's customer portal and handing it to the internal IT operations team, with hosting bought from an external provider.
- **Service:** Customer portal for account management and online payments, used by external customers and the customer service team.
- **Service hours:** Portal available 24/7. Support 08:00 to 18:00 Monday to Friday, excluding public holidays, with on-call cover for priority 1 incidents outside those hours.
- **Availability:** 99.9% per calendar month, measured by synthetic login checks every minute from two locations.
- **Performance:** 95% of page loads under 2 seconds during support hours.
- **Planned maintenance:** Sunday 02:00 to 04:00 with five working days' notice; excluded from availability.
- **Reporting:** Monthly service report by the fifth working day; quarterly service review with the business owner.
| Priority | Definition | Response target | Resolution target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 Critical | Portal unavailable or payments failing for all users | 15 minutes, 24/7 | 4 hours |
| P2 High | Major function unavailable or many users affected | 1 business hour | 8 business hours |
| P3 Medium | Single user or minor function affected; workaround exists | 4 business hours | 3 business days |
| P4 Low | Question, request or cosmetic issue | 1 business day | 10 business days |
Targets like these should reflect business need and what the organisation is willing to pay for, not a template copied from another service.

### Worked examples: calculating SLA performance
SLA disputes often come down to arithmetic and definitions. These illustrative calculations show the common cases.

#### Availability and allowed downtime
Availability = (total minutes - downtime minutes) / total minutes. A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes and a 365-day year has 525,600.
| Availability target | Allowed downtime per 30-day month | Allowed downtime per year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 99% | 432 minutes (7.2 hours) | 87.6 hours |
| 99.5% | 216 minutes (3.6 hours) | 43.8 hours |
| 99.9% | 43.2 minutes | 8.76 hours |
| 99.95% | 21.6 minutes | 4.38 hours |
| 99.99% | About 4.3 minutes | About 53 minutes |
Each extra "nine" cuts the allowance by a factor of ten, and usually adds significant cost in redundancy, monitoring and on-call staff.

#### Availability with exclusions
In a 30-day month the portal had 90 minutes of unplanned outage and 150 minutes of maintenance. If the maintenance happened inside the agreed window, it is excluded: availability = (43,200 - 90) / 43,200 = **99.79%**. If the maintenance overran the window or was not notified, it counts: (43,200 - 240) / 43,200 = **99.44%**. The same month either meets a 99.5% SLA comfortably or misses it, depending on one definition.

#### Service credits
Assume a monthly hosting fee of $20,000 and these illustrative credit tiers, capped at 50% of the monthly fee:
| Monthly availability | Credit |
| --- | --- |
| 99.9% or higher | None |
| 99.5% to below 99.9% | 10% of the monthly fee |
| 99.0% to below 99.5% | 25% of the monthly fee |
| Below 99.0% | 50% of the monthly fee |
At 99.79% the credit is 10%, or $2,000. At 99.44% it is 25%, or $5,000. Notice that the credit is small compared with what a long outage may cost the business. Service credits encourage performance; they rarely compensate for losses, which is why the design of the service matters more than the penalty clause.

#### The business-hours clock
A P2 incident has an 8 business hour resolution target, and support hours are 08:00 to 18:00 Monday to Friday. An incident logged at 16:30 on Friday uses 1.5 hours on Friday, so the remaining 6.5 hours run from 08:00 on Monday: it is due at **14:30 on Monday**. If the SLA lets the clock pause while waiting for the customer, and the team waits two hours for a screenshot on Monday morning, the deadline moves to 16:30.
Compliance is then counted across all tickets. If 226 of 240 P3 incidents in a month were resolved within target, compliance is 94.2%, which misses a 95% target even though most users were well served.

#### End-to-end availability depends on suppliers
When a service depends on several components in series, and any one failing takes the service down, their availabilities multiply. If the hosting is 99.95%, the database service 99.9% and the network 99.99%, the best end-to-end availability you can expect is 0.9995 x 0.999 x 0.9999 = **about 99.84%**, assuming failures are independent. That allows roughly 69 minutes of downtime a month, so promising customers 99.9% would be a promise your suppliers cannot support. Fix it with redundancy, better underpinning contracts or a lower customer target.

#### Error budgets
If the internal SLO is 99.95% per month, the error budget is 0.05%, or 21.6 minutes. If 15 minutes are used by day ten, the team has 6.6 minutes left and might pause risky releases until the month resets. The SLA at 99.9% is still met, which is exactly why the SLO is set tighter.

### Monitoring, reporting and service reviews
An SLA without regular reporting is just a document. Agree the reporting rhythm before go-live.
- **Monthly service report:** performance against each target, trend over the last few months, major incidents and their root causes, credits due, and actions in progress.
- **Service review meeting:** the provider and customer review the report, agree actions, discuss upcoming changes and log issues in an [issue log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/issue-log/) with owners and dates.
- **Annual SLA review:** check whether targets still match business need, retire metrics nobody uses and add ones that matter.
Beware the **watermelon SLA**: green on the outside, red on the inside. Every metric is met but users are unhappy, often because the metrics measure what is easy to count rather than what users experience. ITIL guidance recommends balancing operational metrics with customer satisfaction and feedback. Some organisations add experience measures, sometimes called experience level agreements (XLAs), for the same reason.
For internal services, tools that combine request intake with task tracking make SLAs easier to monitor. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), for example, turns request forms into assigned tasks with statuses and due dates, and its dashboards show overdue work; teams with formal IT service management needs often add a dedicated service desk tool. For a simple start, our [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) logs each request with its priority, due date, owner and status.

### What happens when an SLA is breached
A missed target is a management event, not just a refund. A sound SLA sets out a proportionate sequence:
1. **Verify the data.** Agree the facts, including whether any exclusion applies.
2. **Apply the remedy.** Calculate and issue any service credit as the SLA defines it, usually on the next invoice.
3. **Find the root cause.** For major incidents, require a written incident review with causes and actions.
4. **Agree an improvement plan.** For repeated misses, the provider commits to specific actions and dates.
5. **Escalate.** If the plan fails, use the agreed escalation path to senior management on both sides.
6. **Use contractual rights.** For persistent or severe breaches, the contract may allow termination or other remedies. Take legal advice before relying on them.
On a project, a supplier breach during early life support is also a project risk. Record it in the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) and report it in your [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) so the sponsor sees it before handover.

### Common SLA mistakes
- **Vague definitions.** "Respond promptly" or "high availability" cannot be measured or enforced.
- **Measuring the infrastructure, not the service.** A server can be up while users cannot log in.
- **Promising more than suppliers support.** End-to-end targets must be backed by OLAs and underpinning contracts.
- **Too many metrics.** Thirty targets dilute attention. Focus on the few that matter to users.
- **Targets with no baseline.** Measure current performance before committing to improvements.
- **Forgetting customer responsibilities.** If the customer must report incidents through the service desk, say so.
- **Relying on credits for protection.** Credits are usually capped and small; design resilience into the service instead.
- **Never reviewing the SLA.** Business needs change. Review at least annually and capture issues as [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).

### SLA readiness checklist for project handover
Before operations accepts a new service from your project, check that:
- The SLA is agreed and signed by the service owner and the business owner.
- Supporting OLAs and supplier contracts cover every target.
- Monitoring measures each SLI and alerts the right team.
- Ticket categories and priorities match the SLA definitions.
- The support team is trained, with knowledge articles and an escalation list.
- The first monthly report has been produced from real data during testing or early life support.
- Open defects and known errors are documented and accepted.
If the SLA needs to change after sign-off, raise it formally; our [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) records the impact and approval. Read our guide to [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/) for the wider handover checklist.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a service level agreement?**
A documented agreement between a service provider and a customer that defines the service, the measurable levels it must meet, how performance is reported and what happens if targets are missed.

**Q: What should an SLA include?**
The parties and term, service description, service hours, measurable service levels, priority definitions, responsibilities, reporting, remedies, exclusions, escalation contacts and how the SLA is changed.

**Q: What are the three types of SLA?**
Customer-based SLAs cover all services for one customer, service-based SLAs cover one service for all customers, and multi-level SLAs combine corporate, customer and service-level terms.

**Q: What is the difference between an SLA and an SLO?**
An SLA is the agreement with the customer, often with consequences. An SLO is a specific target, usually stricter, that the provider uses to run the service and stay inside the SLA.

**Q: What is the difference between an SLA and an OLA?**
An SLA sets commitments to the service's customers. An OLA is an operational level agreement between internal teams that supports those commitments, such as a database team's restore time.

**Q: What is the difference between an SLA and a KPI?**
An SLA is an agreement that contains targets. A KPI is any key measure of performance, which may or may not form part of an SLA.

**Q: How much downtime does a 99.9% availability SLA allow?**
About 43 minutes in a 30-day month, or about 8.8 hours over a year, before any agreed exclusions such as planned maintenance.

**Q: What is a service credit in an SLA?**
A discount or refund the provider gives the customer when agreed service levels are missed, usually a percentage of the monthly fee and capped at a maximum.

**Q: What is the difference between response time and resolution time?**
Response time is how quickly the provider acknowledges an incident and starts work. Resolution time is how quickly it is fixed or a workaround is in place.

**Q: Is an SLA legally binding?**
When it forms part of a contract with an external supplier it usually is, through that contract. Internal SLAs between departments are management commitments rather than legal contracts. Take legal advice on contractual terms.

**Q: Who writes an SLA?**
Usually the provider drafts it, but the customer, service owner and often procurement and legal teams shape the targets, definitions and remedies before both sides sign.

**Q: What happens if an SLA is breached?**
Typically the data is verified, any service credit is applied, the root cause is investigated and an improvement plan is agreed. Repeated or severe breaches can trigger escalation or contractual remedies.

**Q: When should a project define the SLA for a new service?**
During requirements and design, because service levels affect architecture, staffing and cost. The SLA should be agreed and tested before handover to operations.

# Six Sigma in Project Management: DMAIC, Belts and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/six-sigma/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Six Sigma explained: what 3.4 DPMO means, DMAIC step by step with a worked example, DMADV, belts, tools and how to calculate sigma level.


## Six Sigma in Project Management: DMAIC, Belts and Tools
Six Sigma is a data-driven method for improving processes by finding and removing the causes of defects and reducing variation, delivered through structured projects that usually follow five phases: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve and Control (DMAIC). For project managers it offers a disciplined way to run improvement projects and a toolkit for quality problems on any project. This guide explains what "six sigma" means, walks through DMAIC with a full worked example, shows how to calculate sigma level and covers belts, tools and limitations.
- Published 11 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Six Sigma reduces defects and variation using data, not opinion. A process at six sigma quality produces about 3.4 defects per million opportunities.
- DMAIC (Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control) improves existing processes; DMADV designs new ones.
- Every Six Sigma project is still a project: it needs a charter, a sponsor, a scope, a schedule and stakeholder management.
- Sigma level comes from DPMO: defects divided by (units x opportunities), multiplied by one million.
- Belts (White, Yellow, Green, Black, Master Black) describe training and role; there is no single official certification body.
- Six Sigma is strongest on repeatable processes with measurable output and weakest on one-off, highly innovative work.

### What is Six Sigma?
Six Sigma is a quality improvement methodology that uses statistical analysis to reduce variation and defects in a process, so that its output consistently meets customer requirements. It works through structured improvement projects, usually following the DMAIC cycle, led by trained practitioners known as Green Belts and Black Belts, with results measured in quality and money.
Six Sigma was introduced at Motorola in 1986 by engineer Bill Smith and became widely known after General Electric, under Jack Welch, made it central to its business strategy from 1995. It builds on earlier quality thinking from Walter Shewhart, W. Edwards Deming and Joseph Juran, and the international standard ISO 13053, first published in 2011, describes the DMAIC methodology and its tools.
Is Six Sigma a project management methodology? Not exactly. It is a quality improvement method that is delivered through projects. A Six Sigma project still needs everything a normal project does, and Six Sigma tools are useful on ordinary projects whenever quality is the problem. It sits alongside the wider [project quality management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/) processes rather than replacing them.

### What does "six sigma" mean?
Sigma (σ) is the statistical symbol for standard deviation, a measure of how much a process varies. The more standard deviations you can fit between the average of a process and the nearest limit the customer will accept, the fewer outputs fall outside that limit. "Six sigma" describes a process so consistent that, by Six Sigma convention, it produces no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities (DPMO).
| Sigma level | Defects per million opportunities (DPMO) | Yield (defect-free) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 308,538 | 69.1% |
| 3 | 66,807 | 93.3% |
| 4 | 6,210 | 99.38% |
| 5 | 233 | 99.977% |
| 6 | 3.4 | 99.99966% |
The gap between levels is not linear. Moving from three to four sigma cuts defects by about 90%; moving from five to six sigma removes most of the rest. In practice few processes need six sigma. The value lies in using data to understand variation and choosing a target that makes commercial sense.

#### The 1.5 sigma shift
The figures above include a convention called the 1.5 sigma shift: they assume a process mean will drift by up to 1.5 standard deviations over time, so a "six sigma" process is treated as performing at 4.5 sigma in the long term. Without the shift, six sigma would mean around two defects per billion. The convention is associated with Mikel Harry and is debated by statisticians, including Donald Wheeler, who regard it as arbitrary. Treat sigma levels as a common reporting language, not a precise law of nature.

### The core principles of Six Sigma
- **Focus on the customer.** Quality is defined by what the customer needs, expressed as critical-to-quality (CTQ) requirements.
- **Use data, not assumptions.** Decisions are based on measurement and analysis, and claims about causes are tested.
- **Understand the process.** Outputs (Y) are a function of inputs and process steps (X); fix the Xs and the Y follows.
- **Reduce variation.** A consistent process is easier to improve and to predict than one that is right on average but erratic.
- **Remove root causes, not symptoms.** Fixes target the few causes that create most of the defects.
- **Sustain the gain.** Every project ends with controls so the process does not drift back.
- **Show the money.** Projects are selected and judged on measurable financial and customer benefits.

### How Six Sigma fits into project management
A Six Sigma improvement effort is a project in the full sense: temporary, with a defined goal, a team, a budget and a finish. Frank T. Anbari's paper for PMI (2002) describes typical Six Sigma projects as lasting three to six months, with larger problems split into several smaller projects.
| Aspect | Typical project | Six Sigma project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goal | Deliver an agreed output | Improve a measurable process metric by a target amount |
| Starting document | [Project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) | Six Sigma charter with problem statement, baseline metric and target |
| Life cycle | Initiation to closure | DMAIC phases with tollgate reviews |
| Success measure | Scope, time, cost, quality | Metric improvement sustained, verified benefits |
| Key roles | Sponsor, project manager, team | Champion, Black or Green Belt, process owner, team |
| Closure | Handover of deliverables | Handover of a controlled process to its owner |
Normal project management disciplines still apply. You will need [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) to win support from process owners, a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) to clarify who decides, and scope discipline to stop a defect-reduction project becoming a redesign of the whole department. Most organisations hold a tollgate review at the end of each DMAIC phase, where the champion confirms the phase deliverables before the team moves on.

#### Using Six Sigma tools on everyday projects
You do not need a formal Six Sigma programme to benefit from its tools. On ordinary projects they help whenever the same problem keeps recurring:
- **Recurring defects in deliverables**, such as failed test cases or rejected documents: count them by type, build a Pareto chart and fix the top one or two causes first.
- **Repeated schedule slippage** on similar tasks: measure actual against estimated durations, look at the spread as well as the average, and ask why the variation is so wide.
- **Stakeholder complaints**: turn vague dissatisfaction into specific CTQ requirements and agree how each will be measured.
- **Handover problems between teams**: map the process with a SIPOC to agree inputs, outputs and owners.
- **Post-project reviews**: use the 5 whys to get beneath symptoms when capturing lessons learned.

### DMAIC: the five phases step by step
DMAIC is the Six Sigma method for improving an existing process. Each phase answers one question and ends with defined deliverables.
| Phase | Key question | Typical tools | Tollgate deliverables |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Define | What is the problem and why does it matter? | Charter, SIPOC, voice of the customer, CTQ tree | Signed charter, scope, CTQs, team |
| Measure | How bad is it today? | Data collection plan, measurement system analysis, process map | Validated baseline and sigma level |
| Analyse | What causes it? | Pareto chart, fishbone diagram, 5 whys, hypothesis tests, regression | Verified root causes |
| Improve | What fixes the causes? | Solution selection, pilots, design of experiments, FMEA | Piloted solution with measured results |
| Control | How do we keep the gain? | Control charts, control plan, standard work | Control plan, handover to process owner, benefits sign-off |

#### 1. Define
1. Write a problem statement: what is wrong, where, when, how big and how you know. Our [problem statement template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/problem-statement-template/) gives the structure.
2. Capture the voice of the customer and translate it into measurable CTQ requirements.
3. Draw a SIPOC (suppliers, inputs, process, outputs, customers) to agree the start and end of the process in scope.
4. Set a measurable goal, such as "reduce the defect rate from 4.8% to below 1% within six months".
5. Name the champion, process owner and team, and get the charter signed.

#### 2. Measure
1. Define each defect and each opportunity precisely, so two people counting the same work get the same answer.
2. Check the measurement system: if the data is unreliable, fix that first.
3. Collect baseline data over a representative period.
4. Map the process as it really runs, including rework loops; a [swimlane diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/swimlane-diagram/) shows handoffs clearly.
5. Calculate the baseline DPMO, yield and sigma level.

#### 3. Analyse
1. Stratify the defects by type, location, shift, supplier or product, and build a Pareto chart.
2. Brainstorm possible causes with a [fishbone diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/) and drill down with the 5 whys.
3. Test the likely causes with data, using hypothesis tests or regression where the volume allows.
4. Agree the verified root causes; record the [root cause analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) and evidence.

#### 4. Improve
1. Generate solutions that address each verified root cause.
2. Select solutions using effort, impact, cost and risk; use FMEA to anticipate how the new process could fail.
3. Pilot on a small scale and measure the result against the baseline.
4. Refine, then plan the full roll-out with an [action plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/action-plan-template/).

#### 5. Control
1. Write a control plan: what is measured, how often, by whom and what happens if it goes out of limits.
2. Introduce control charts, standard work and training so the new method becomes routine.
3. Hand the process formally to its owner and agree how benefits will be tracked.
4. Close the project and capture [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).
Tip
Some organisations add a Recognise step before Define to choose the right problem in the first place, and some add Standardise and Integrate after Control. The core five phases stay the same.

### Worked example: reducing invoice errors with DMAIC
This example is illustrative: the organisation and figures are invented to show the method and the calculations.

#### Define
A shared-services finance team processes 2,000 supplier invoices a month. Suppliers complain about late and incorrect payments, and staff spend hours on rework. The finance director acts as champion and a Green Belt leads a five-person team. The charter sets the goal: cut invoice defects by at least 75% within five months. The team identifies five opportunities for a defect on each invoice: missing or wrong purchase order (PO) number, wrong cost code, wrong amount or duplicate, wrong supplier details, and late approval.

#### Measure
Over one month the team finds 480 defects across 2,000 invoices, with 410 invoices having at least one defect.
| Measure | Calculation | Baseline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opportunities | 2,000 invoices x 5 | 10,000 |
| DPMO | 480 / 10,000 x 1,000,000 | 48,000 |
| Sigma level | From DPMO, with 1.5 shift | About 3.2 |
| First-pass yield | (2,000 - 410) / 2,000 | 79.5% |
| Cost of rework | 480 defects x 25 minutes x £30 per hour | £6,000 a month |

#### Analyse
A Pareto analysis of the 480 defects shows that two defect types cause two-thirds of the problem:
| Defect type | Count | Share | Cumulative |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Missing or wrong PO number | 205 | 42.7% | 42.7% |
| Wrong cost code | 118 | 24.6% | 67.3% |
| Wrong amount or duplicate | 72 | 15.0% | 82.3% |
| Wrong supplier details | 49 | 10.2% | 92.5% |
| Late approval | 36 | 7.5% | 100% |
A fishbone session and the 5 whys trace the PO problem to suppliers who are never told the PO number, because buyers raise some orders by email instead of in the purchasing system. The cost-code errors trace to a free-text field. Data confirms both: 88% of PO defects come from email orders, and cost-code errors fall sharply on invoices from the one department that already uses a drop-down list.

#### Improve
The team pilots three changes for six weeks: a rule that all orders are raised in the purchasing system, an automatic email sending the PO number to the supplier, and a drop-down list of valid cost codes. A duplicate-check rule is added to the finance system at little extra cost.
| Measure | Baseline | After improvement | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Defects per month | 480 | 62 | -87% |
| DPMO | 48,000 | 6,200 | -87% |
| Sigma level | About 3.2 | About 4.0 | +0.8 |
| First-pass yield | 79.5% | 97.1% | +17.6 points |
| Rework cost | £6,000 a month | £775 a month | About £62,700 a year saved |

#### Control
The accounts payable manager takes ownership. A weekly p-chart tracks the proportion of defective invoices, with a rule that two weeks above the upper control limit triggers a review. Procedures and training are updated, and the champion signs off the benefits with the finance controller. The project closes after five months, on target.
The example shows why Six Sigma pairs well with project management: the team needed a clear charter, sponsor support to change purchasing rules across departments, a pilot plan and a formal handover. Without those, the analysis alone would not have changed the process.

### How to calculate DPMO and sigma level
1. **Define a unit**: the thing you produce or process, such as an invoice, a part or a patient admission.
2. **Define the opportunities**: the distinct ways one unit can fail to meet a CTQ requirement. Count only meaningful, measurable ones; inflating opportunities flatters the result.
3. **Count the defects** found in a sample of units.
4. **Calculate DPO**: defects / (units x opportunities per unit).
5. **Calculate DPMO**: DPO x 1,000,000.
6. **Convert to sigma level**: use a sigma table, or in Excel or Google Sheets use =NORM.S.INV(1 - DPMO/1000000) + 1.5.
| Metric | Formula | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DPU (defects per unit) | Defects / units | Simple internal tracking |
| DPMO | Defects / (units x opportunities) x 1,000,000 | Comparing processes of different complexity |
| First-pass yield | Units with no defects / total units | Share of work right first time |
| Sigma level | NORM.S.INV(1 - DPMO/1,000,000) + 1.5 | Common reporting language |

### Process capability: Cp and Cpk
When output is a measurement rather than a pass or fail, such as a delivery time or a dimension, Six Sigma uses process capability indices to compare the spread of the process with the specification limits.
| Index | Formula | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cp | (USL - LSL) / 6σ | Whether the process spread fits within the limits, if it were perfectly centred |
| Cpk | Lower of (USL - mean) / 3σ and (mean - LSL) / 3σ | How capable the process actually is, allowing for an off-centre mean |
Example: a warehouse promises delivery within 48 hours (an upper limit only). Delivery times average 40 hours with a standard deviation of 3 hours. Cpk = (48 - 40) / (3 x 3) = 0.89. A Cpk below 1 means a noticeable share of deliveries will breach the promise, so the team should either reduce variation or move the average down. Many organisations treat a Cpk of 1.33 as a minimum target; a six sigma process corresponds to a short-term Cpk of 2.

### DMADV and Design for Six Sigma
When there is no process to improve, or the existing one is beyond repair, Six Sigma uses DMADV: Define, Measure, Analyse, Design, Verify. It is part of Design for Six Sigma (DFSS), which aims to build quality into a new product, service or process from the start.
|  | DMAIC | DMADV |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Improve an existing process | Design a new process, product or service |
| Phases | Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control | Define, Measure, Analyse, Design, Verify |
| Measure phase focuses on | Current performance and baseline | Customer needs and CTQ targets |
| Analyse phase focuses on | Root causes of defects | Design options and trade-offs |
| Ends with | A controlled, improved process | A verified design handed to production or operations |
| Typical length | Months | Often longer, depending on the design |

### Six Sigma roles and belts
Six Sigma borrows martial-arts belt names to show training level and role. ASQ describes the roles as follows:
| Role | Typical responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Executive leadership | Sets the strategic focus of the Six Sigma programme |
| Champion | Turns goals into a deployment plan, selects projects, secures resources and removes roadblocks |
| Master Black Belt | Trains and coaches Black and Green Belts; acts as an internal consultant |
| Black Belt | Leads complex problem-solving projects, often full time, and coaches teams |
| Green Belt | Leads smaller projects alongside a normal job; supports data collection and analysis for Black Belt projects |
| Yellow Belt | Project team member who understands the basics and reviews improvements |
| White Belt | Awareness of basic concepts; supports local problem-solving teams |
Process owners, who run the process day to day, are not belts but are vital: they own the result after the project ends.

#### Six Sigma certification
No single body owns Six Sigma, so certificates vary in rigour. Well-known options include ASQ (Certified Six Sigma Yellow, Green and Black Belt, and Master Black Belt) and IASSC, alongside many universities and training providers. Some certifications are exam-only; others, such as ASQ's Black Belt, also require evidence of completed projects. Check the current requirements with the certifying body before you enrol.
Most people start with a Yellow Belt for awareness or go straight to a Green Belt if they will lead projects. If your main goal is project leadership rather than process improvement, compare options in our guide to [project management certifications](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/).

### Six Sigma tools by phase
| Tool | Phase | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SIPOC | Define | High-level map of suppliers, inputs, process, outputs and customers |
| CTQ tree | Define | Turns customer needs into measurable requirements |
| Process map | Measure | Shows how the process really runs, including rework |
| Measurement system analysis | Measure | Checks the data is reliable before you trust it |
| Pareto chart | Analyse | Shows the few causes behind most defects |
| Fishbone diagram and 5 whys | Analyse | Explore and drill into possible causes |
| Hypothesis testing and regression | Analyse | Prove or disprove suspected causes with data |
| Design of experiments | Improve | Tests several factors at once to find the best settings |
| FMEA | Improve | Ranks how a process or design could fail and how to prevent it |
| Control chart | Control | Separates normal variation from special causes over time |
| Control plan | Control | Defines ongoing measures, owners and reactions |
FMEA overlaps with [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/): both identify what could go wrong, how likely and severe it is, and what to do first.

### Lean, Lean Six Sigma and Agile
Lean and Six Sigma attack different problems. Lean removes waste so that work flows faster; Six Sigma reduces variation so that results are consistent. Lean Six Sigma combines them, usually inside the DMAIC structure, using Lean tools such as [value stream mapping](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) alongside Six Sigma statistics. Our [Lean vs Six Sigma guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-vs-six-sigma/) compares them side by side, and [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/) covers Lean in more depth.
Six Sigma and [Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) can also work together. Agile teams can use Six Sigma's root-cause tools to tackle recurring defects, and a Six Sigma team can run DMAIC phases in short, time-boxed iterations with frequent stakeholder reviews.

### Benefits and limitations of Six Sigma
| Benefits | Limitations |
| --- | --- |
| Decisions based on evidence rather than opinion | Needs reliable data; weak where data is scarce or hard to measure |
| Tackles root causes, so improvements last | Can feel slow and bureaucratic for simple problems |
| Common language and toolkit across the organisation | Training and certification take time and money |
| Links improvement to measurable customer and financial results | Less suited to one-off projects and radical innovation |
| Control phase protects the gains | Gains fade without process owner commitment |
| Works in manufacturing, healthcare, finance, services and IT | Belt hierarchy can create an expert elite if not managed |
Critics have also pointed out that much of Six Sigma repackages earlier quality methods (Joseph Juran made this point) and that the 1.5 sigma shift is a convention rather than a measured fact. Neither criticism undermines the core idea: define the problem precisely, measure it, find the real causes and keep the fix in place.

### How to choose a good Six Sigma project
- **A repeatable process** with enough volume to produce data, not a one-off event.
- **A clear, measurable problem**, such as an error rate, cycle time or complaint rate, with a known baseline or one you can collect quickly.
- **An unknown cause.** If the solution is already obvious, just implement it.
- **Meaningful benefit** to customers or costs, ideally confirmed by a short [cost-benefit analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/) or a [business case](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/).
- **A scope one team can finish** in roughly three to six months.
- **A committed champion and process owner.**
Industries with high-volume, repeatable processes tend to get the most from Six Sigma; see our guide to [manufacturing project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/manufacturing-project-management/).

### Common Six Sigma mistakes
- **Starting with a solution.** "Implement a new system" is not a Six Sigma problem statement; "reduce invoice defects by 75%" is.
- **Scope too big.** "Improve customer satisfaction" will not finish; pick one process and one metric.
- **Trusting bad data.** Skipping measurement system checks leads to precise analysis of the wrong numbers.
- **Inflating opportunities** to make the sigma level look better.
- **Jumping from Measure to Improve** without verifying root causes.
- **No control plan.** The process quietly drifts back within months.
- **Ignoring change management.** People must adopt the new way of working; plan communication and training, and use [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) for any agreed changes to project scope.

### Software and templates for Six Sigma projects
Statistical analysis usually happens in a spreadsheet or dedicated statistics software, but the project itself needs managing like any other: tasks by DMAIC phase, tollgate approvals, actions from the Improve phase and a visible control plan. Work management tools handle that well. Wrike, our top-rated tool, supports phase-based project templates, approvals and dashboards that suit tollgate reviews; see our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).
Start with a [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) for the Define phase, the [problem statement template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/problem-statement-template/) for a precise problem, and the [root cause analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) for the Analyse phase.
Six Sigma is one part of a wider quality system. Read our guide to [project quality management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is Six Sigma in simple terms?**
A way of improving a process by measuring how often it goes wrong, finding the real causes with data and fixing them so results are consistent. It is usually run as a project following DMAIC.

**Q: What are the five steps of Six Sigma?**
Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve and Control (DMAIC). They take a project from a clear problem statement to a verified, controlled improvement.

**Q: Why is it called Six Sigma?**
Sigma is the symbol for standard deviation. A process with six standard deviations between its average and the nearest specification limit produces about 3.4 defects per million opportunities, using the standard 1.5 sigma shift.

**Q: What does 3.4 defects per million opportunities mean?**
It is the defect rate of a process at six sigma: out of every million chances to make a defect, only 3.4 result in one, a defect-free rate of 99.99966%.

**Q: Is Six Sigma a project management methodology?**
It is a quality improvement methodology delivered through projects. Each Six Sigma project still needs a charter, sponsor, plan and stakeholder management.

**Q: What is the difference between DMAIC and DMADV?**
DMAIC improves an existing process. DMADV (Define, Measure, Analyse, Design, Verify) designs a new process, product or service and is part of Design for Six Sigma.

**Q: What are the Six Sigma belts?**
White Belt (awareness), Yellow Belt (team member), Green Belt (leads smaller projects part time), Black Belt (leads complex projects and coaches) and Master Black Belt (trains, coaches and guides the programme).

**Q: Which Six Sigma belt should I start with?**
Yellow Belt for awareness, or Green Belt if you expect to lead improvement projects. Check each certifying body's requirements, as they vary.

**Q: How do you calculate sigma level?**
Calculate DPMO as defects / (units x opportunities) x 1,000,000, then convert it with a sigma table or the spreadsheet formula =NORM.S.INV(1 - DPMO/1000000) + 1.5.

**Q: How long does a Six Sigma project take?**
Typically three to six months for a DMAIC project. Larger problems are usually split into several smaller projects.

**Q: What is the difference between Lean and Six Sigma?**
Lean removes waste to make work flow faster; Six Sigma reduces variation to make results consistent. Lean Six Sigma combines the two.

**Q: Can Six Sigma be used with Agile?**
Yes. Agile teams can use Six Sigma's root-cause and measurement tools, and Six Sigma teams can run DMAIC in short iterations with frequent reviews.

**Q: Is Six Sigma still relevant?**
Yes, especially in manufacturing, healthcare, finance, logistics and shared services, and often as Lean Six Sigma. Its data-driven problem solving is useful in most industries.

**Q: Who created Six Sigma?**
Engineer Bill Smith introduced it at Motorola in 1986. General Electric popularised it from 1995 under Jack Welch.
