# Statement of Work (SOW): What to Include, With Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a statement of work (SOW) is, what to include, the main types, a full worked example and a step-by-step method for writing one that prevents disputes.


## Statement of Work (SOW): What to Include, With Example
A statement of work (SOW) is a document that describes the work a supplier will perform for a buyer: what will be delivered, by when, to what standard, how it will be accepted and how it will be paid for. It is usually signed alongside, or under, a contract or master service agreement. This guide explains what to include, which type of SOW to use, how to write one step by step, and walks through a complete example.
- Published 18 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 22 min read

### Key takeaways
- An SOW turns a commercial agreement into a precise description of work, deliverables, timing, acceptance and payment.
- The most important parts are usually the scope boundaries (including exclusions), testable acceptance criteria and the buyer's own responsibilities.
- Choose the SOW type to match how well you can define the work: design/detail, level of effort (time and materials) or performance-based.
- Link payments to accepted deliverables or milestones, and make sure the numbers in every table reconcile.
- Once signed, the SOW is a baseline: changes go through a written change request that states the cost and schedule impact.
- For Agile work, fix the budget, time box and ways of working, and let the backlog flex within them.

### What is a statement of work?
A **statement of work (SOW)** is a written description of the work a supplier agrees to perform for a buyer. It defines the purpose, scope, deliverables, schedule, standards, acceptance criteria, responsibilities and payment terms for a specific piece of work. When signed, or incorporated into a contract, it becomes the agreed baseline both parties deliver and measure against.
In simple terms, the contract or master service agreement sets the legal rules of the relationship, and the SOW says exactly what is being bought this time. One supplier relationship can have many SOWs, one for each project or phase.
SOWs are used wherever one party does work for another:
- **Outsourced projects:** agencies, consultancies, IT suppliers, construction subcontractors and freelancers.
- **Professional services:** implementation, training, audits, research and managed services start-up work.
- **Public-sector procurement:** governments describe the work they are buying in an SOW or one of its performance-based variants.
- **Internal services:** some organisations use an internal SOW when one department charges another for work.
In project management, the SOW sits inside [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/). PMI's process-based PMBOK Guide editions describe a *procurement statement of work* that the buyer prepares while planning procurement, so that potential suppliers can decide whether they can deliver and price the work.

### Why a statement of work matters
Most supplier disputes are not about bad faith. They come from two parties reading the same vague sentence in different ways. A good SOW removes that ambiguity before money changes hands. It gives you:
- **A shared definition of done:** both parties know what will be delivered and how it will be judged.
- **A scope baseline:** anything outside the SOW is a change, which protects the buyer from surprise costs and the supplier from unpaid extra work; see [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).
- **A link between money and results:** payments are tied to accepted deliverables or milestones, not just elapsed time.
- **Clear responsibilities:** what the supplier does, what the buyer must provide, and what happens if either side is late.
- **A basis for closure:** at the end you can check every deliverable against the SOW and formally close the work; see [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/).
Tip
Write the SOW for a reader who was not in the room. If a new project manager on either side could pick it up in six months and understand exactly what was agreed, it is specific enough.

### What to include in a statement of work
There is no single mandatory format, but most good SOWs cover the same ground. The table lists the sections, what to write in each, and the mistake to avoid.
| Section | What to write | Common mistake |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Background and purpose | Why the work is needed and the business outcome it supports | Skipping it, so the supplier cannot make sensible judgement calls |
| 2. Objectives | Measurable results the work should achieve | Objectives that cannot be measured, such as 'improve the website' |
| 3. Scope of work | The activities the supplier will perform and the boundaries of the work | Describing activities but not limits (volumes, locations, systems) |
| 4. Exclusions (out of scope) | Work that is explicitly not included | Leaving it out, which invites assumptions |
| 5. Deliverables | Each output, its format and quantity, with an ID | Mixing deliverables with activities ('attend meetings' is not a deliverable) |
| 6. Acceptance criteria and process | How each deliverable is reviewed, tested and signed off; review windows; rework cycles | Subjective criteria such as 'to the client's satisfaction' |
| 7. Schedule and milestones | Start and end dates, milestone dates, period of performance | Dates that ignore the buyer's own review time |
| 8. Location, tools and resources | Where work happens, who provides equipment, systems access and licences | Assuming access to buildings or systems that takes weeks to arrange |
| 9. Standards and requirements | Quality, security, accessibility, regulatory and brand standards that apply | Referring to 'industry standards' without naming them |
| 10. Roles and responsibilities | Key personnel, buyer responsibilities, decision makers and escalation | Listing only the supplier's duties |
| 11. Reporting and governance | Status reports, meetings, risk and issue reporting | No agreed reporting rhythm, so problems surface late |
| 12. Pricing and payment terms | Pricing model, milestone payments, invoicing, expenses | Payment tables that do not add up to the total price |
| 13. Assumptions and dependencies | What both parties are assuming, and what the work depends on | Hidden assumptions that later become disputes |
| 14. Change control | How changes are requested, assessed, approved and priced | No process, so changes are agreed verbally |
| 15. Signatures | Authorised signatories for both parties and the date | Signed by someone without authority to commit budget |

#### Sections that are often missed
Competitor guides and generic templates tend to stop at scope, timeline and cost. In practice, the clauses below cause a large share of real-world disputes, so check that your SOW covers them:
- **Buyer responsibilities:** content, data, approvals, subject-matter experts and access the buyer must provide, with dates. If the buyer is late, the schedule should move.
- **Key personnel:** named or role-based people the supplier commits, and whether they can be replaced without consent.
- **Handover and intellectual property:** what the buyer receives at the end (source files, documentation, credentials, training). Ownership terms usually sit in the main contract, but the SOW should list the handover items.
- **Order of precedence:** which document wins if the SOW, the contract and any attachments conflict. This is usually stated in the master agreement; check it rather than assume it.
- **Warranty or hypercare period:** how long defects are fixed at no extra cost after acceptance.

### Types of statement of work
SOWs are commonly grouped into three types, depending on how much the buyer specifies about the method. Some sources list more (functional, hybrid), but these are variations on the same three ideas.
| Type | What it specifies | Typical pricing | Best when | Risk mainly sits with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design or detail SOW | Exactly how the work must be done: methods, materials, specifications | Fixed price or unit rates | The buyer knows precisely what it wants and how, e.g. construction to drawings | Buyer (if the design is wrong, the supplier still delivered what was specified) |
| Level of effort / time and materials SOW | The time, people or materials to be provided, and the type of work | Day or hourly rates, often with a cap | Scope is uncertain, or the buyer needs skilled capacity, e.g. support or discovery work | Buyer (cost grows with effort unless capped) |
| Performance-based SOW | The results and performance standards required; the supplier chooses the method | Fixed price or outcome-based, sometimes with incentives | The outcome is clear and measurable but suppliers may know better methods | Supplier (must achieve the outcome) |

#### Design or detail SOW
A design SOW describes the method and specification in detail. It suits work where the buyer has the expertise and the design is already fixed, such as building to architect's drawings or manufacturing to a technical specification. The supplier's job is to follow it; acceptance checks conformance to the specification.

#### Level of effort and time-and-materials SOW
A level of effort SOW buys a quantity of time or service, such as 'two senior developers for 12 weeks' or 'up to 40 days of consultancy'. It is flexible and quick to agree, which makes it common for discovery, support and staff augmentation. Protect the buyer with a not-to-exceed cap, regular timesheets and a clear description of the type of work expected.

#### Performance-based SOW, PWS and SOO
A performance-based SOW states what must be achieved and how performance will be measured, then lets the supplier decide how. US federal procurement promotes this approach through two related documents: a **performance work statement (PWS)**, which describes required results with measurable performance standards, and a **statement of objectives (SOO)**, a shorter statement of high-level goals from which bidders propose their own PWS or SOW. Performance standards in these documents often look like service levels; see [service level agreements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/service-level-agreement-sla/).

#### How to choose the right type
- If you can draw it or specify it exactly, and you want it done your way, use a **design SOW**.
- If you cannot yet define the output but know the skills and time you need, use a **level of effort SOW** with a cap and a review point.
- If you can measure the outcome but want suppliers to propose the method, use a **performance-based SOW**.
- If the work has a defined phase followed by an uncertain one, split it: a fixed-price SOW for discovery, then a second SOW once the scope is known.

### Statement of work vs related documents
The SOW is one of several documents that describe a project. The differences matter, because each one is owned, approved and changed differently.
| Document | Purpose | Who usually writes it | Legally binding? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Statement of work | Defines the work, deliverables, schedule, acceptance and payment for one engagement | Buyer, supplier or both | Usually, once signed or incorporated into a contract |
| Master service agreement (MSA) | Sets the general legal terms for a relationship: liability, confidentiality, IP, termination | Both parties' legal teams | Yes |
| Project scope statement | Describes the product and project scope, exclusions, constraints and assumptions | Project manager | No, it is an internal planning document |
| Project charter | Formally authorises a project and the project manager internally | Sponsor with the project manager | No |
| RFP or RFQ | Invites suppliers to propose or quote, often with a draft SOW attached | Buyer | No |
| Proposal | The supplier's offer: approach, team and price | Supplier | Not on its own; it may be incorporated into the contract |
| Service level agreement (SLA) | Defines ongoing service performance standards and remedies | Both parties | Usually, as part of a service contract |

#### SOW vs scope of work
The **scope of work** is one section of the SOW: the description of the activities and boundaries. The **statement of work** is the whole document, which adds deliverables, acceptance, schedule, responsibilities and payment. On an internal project, your [project scope statement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) plays a similar role to the scope section, without the commercial terms.

#### MSA vs SOW
An MSA is signed once and governs every piece of work between two parties. Each new engagement then gets its own SOW, which refers back to the MSA for legal terms. This saves renegotiating liability or confidentiality every time. You can have an SOW without an MSA, but then the SOW (or a short contract around it) must carry the essential legal terms itself. Always take legal advice on the contractual terms; this guide covers the project-management content of the SOW.

### How to write a statement of work step by step
The steps below work whether you are the buyer drafting an SOW for tender or the supplier drafting one for a client to sign. Each step names the planning artefact that feeds it.
1. **Confirm the purpose and objectives.** Write two or three sentences on why the work is needed and how success will be measured. Use your business case or [project objectives](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-objectives/).
2. **Gather requirements.** List what the output must do and the standards it must meet. Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves; see [project requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/).
3. **Break the work down.** Build a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) for the supplier's part of the work. Each lowest-level element should map to a deliverable or [work package](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/) in the SOW.
4. **Define each deliverable.** Give every deliverable an ID, description, format, quantity and owner. Keep activities and deliverables separate.
5. **Write acceptance criteria for every deliverable.** State the test, who performs it, the review window and how many rework cycles are included.
6. **Draw the scope boundary.** List exclusions, volumes and limits (for example 'up to 300 pages', 'two rounds of revisions', 'UK sites only').
7. **Set the schedule and milestones.** Add start and end dates, milestone dates and the buyer's review periods. Check dependencies on the buyer; see [project milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/).
8. **Agree roles, reporting and responsibilities.** Name decision makers, the supplier's key personnel and the buyer's obligations. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) attached to the SOW removes a lot of doubt.
9. **Price the work and set payment terms.** Choose the pricing model, base it on a proper [cost estimate](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/), link payments to accepted milestones and check that every figure reconciles to the total.
10. **Record assumptions, risks and change control.** Write down assumptions and dependencies, note key risks in your [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) and describe how changes will be handled.
11. **Review, test and sign.** Ask someone from each side who did not draft it to read it and list every sentence they could interpret two ways. Fix those, take legal review, then have authorised signatories sign.
Tip
Draft the acceptance criteria before you price the work. Suppliers price risk, and vague acceptance criteria are one of the biggest risks they face. Clear criteria usually mean sharper, more comparable quotes.

### Statement of work example
The example below is a condensed, fictional SOW for a website redesign. The company names are invented. It shows the level of detail that prevents arguments later; a real SOW would add the legal references to the MSA.

#### 1. Purpose and objectives
Northfield Housing Association (the buyer) is replacing its 10-year-old website. The new site must let tenants report repairs and pay rent online, meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA, and cut repair-related phone calls. Brightline Digital Ltd (the supplier) will design, build and launch the site.
- Objective 1: launch the new site by 30 June.
- Objective 2: all page templates pass an independent WCAG 2.2 AA audit with no critical issues.
- Objective 3: online repair reporting live at launch, integrated with the buyer's housing management system.

#### 2. Scope and exclusions
| In scope | Out of scope |
| --- | --- |
| Discovery workshops (up to 4) and sitemap | Writing new content (the buyer provides all copy) |
| Design of up to 8 page templates, with 2 rounds of revisions each | Photography and video production |
| Build on the buyer's chosen content management system | Changes to the housing management system itself |
| Migration of up to 300 existing pages | Migration of pages beyond 300 (available as a change) |
| Repair-reporting form integrated via the existing API | Hosting costs and domain renewals |
| Training for up to 10 staff editors (2 sessions) | Ongoing support after the warranty period (separate SOW) |

#### 3. Deliverables and acceptance criteria
| ID | Deliverable | Acceptance criteria |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | Discovery report and sitemap | Buyer's project lead approves in writing within 5 working days of receipt |
| D2 | Design system and 8 page templates | All templates approved after no more than 2 revision rounds; colour contrast meets WCAG 2.2 AA |
| D3 | Built site on staging | All 42 user acceptance test scripts pass; no open severity 1 or 2 defects |
| D4 | Migrated content | 300 pages migrated; random sample of 30 pages checked with zero broken internal links |
| D5 | Live site | Site live on production domain; repair form creates a job in the housing system in 10 of 10 test submissions |
| D6 | Training and handover pack | 2 training sessions delivered; admin guide, credentials and source files handed over |

#### 4. Milestones and payments
The fixed price is **£48,000** excluding VAT. Each payment is invoiced only after the linked deliverables are accepted.
| Milestone | Linked deliverables | Target date | Payment | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M1 Discovery complete | D1 | 14 February | 15% | £7,200 |
| M2 Design approved | D2 | 28 March | 25% | £12,000 |
| M3 Build ready for testing | D3 | 16 May | 30% | £14,400 |
| M4 Go-live and acceptance | D4, D5, D6 | 30 June | 20% | £9,600 |
| M5 End of 30-day warranty | All defects fixed | 30 July | 10% | £4,800 |
| Total |  |  | 100% | £48,000 |

#### 5. Responsibilities, assumptions and change control
- The buyer provides final copy for all new pages by 2 May, and API credentials for the housing system by 21 March. If either is late, affected milestone dates move by the same number of working days.
- The buyer reviews each deliverable within 5 working days. If no response is received within 10 working days, the supplier may escalate to the buyer's sponsor.
- The supplier provides a named project manager and lead developer, who will not be replaced without the buyer's written agreement.
- Status reports are sent every Friday; a steering meeting is held every four weeks.
- Changes are requested in writing using the change request form. The supplier responds within 5 working days with cost, schedule and risk impact. No change work starts until both parties sign the change.
Notice what makes this example robust: every deliverable has a testable criterion, every payment depends on accepted deliverables, the payment table adds up, and the buyer's obligations have dates and consequences. Use a [project deliverables template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-deliverables-template/) and a [project scope template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-scope-template/) to draft these sections quickly.

### Writing acceptance criteria that work
Acceptance criteria decide whether the supplier gets paid and whether the buyer gets what it needs. The test is simple: could two reasonable people disagree about whether the criterion has been met? If yes, rewrite it.
| Vague | Testable |
| --- | --- |
| The website will be fast | Key pages load within the agreed performance budget, measured with a named tool on a stated connection profile |
| Training to the client's satisfaction | Two 3-hour sessions delivered to up to 10 staff; at least 8 attendees complete the editing exercise unaided |
| Report of high quality | Report covers the 6 sections in Annex A, cites data sources and is approved by the project lead after one revision round |
| System fully tested | All agreed test scripts executed and passed; no open severity 1 or 2 defects; test log delivered |
| Migrate the content | Up to 300 listed pages migrated with formatting preserved; sample of 30 pages has no broken links |
Alongside the criteria, define the **acceptance procedure**:
- who reviews and who signs off;
- the review window (for example 5 working days);
- how defects are classified and which severities block acceptance;
- how many rework cycles are included in the price;
- what happens if the buyer does not respond (escalation, or in some contracts deemed acceptance, which needs careful legal drafting).
Acceptance criteria are part of quality management; see [project quality management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-quality-management/) for how to plan reviews and tests.

### Managing changes to a signed SOW
Once signed, the SOW is a baseline. Changes are normal, but they should never be agreed in a corridor or a chat message. Use a simple, written [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) process:
1. The requester describes the change in writing, using a [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/).
2. The supplier assesses the impact on cost, schedule, quality and risk, and states any assumptions.
3. Both parties review the impact; the buyer's project manager checks it against budget and priorities.
4. Authorised people on both sides approve or reject the change.
5. The approved change is recorded as a numbered SOW amendment, and the plan, budget and payment schedule are updated.

#### Worked example: a change request
In the website example, the buyer discovers 120 more pages that must be migrated. The SOW includes 300, so this is out of scope.
| Item | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Migration effort | 120 pages x 0.3 hours per page | 36 hours |
| Checking and project management | Fixed allowance | 4 hours |
| Total effort | 36 + 4 | 40 hours |
| Cost | 40 hours x £75 per hour (rate card in the MSA) | £3,000 |
| Schedule | Migration capacity of 20 hours per week; one week overlaps user testing | Go-live moves by 1 week |
The buyer now has a clear choice: approve £3,000 and a one-week delay, ask the supplier to migrate the extra pages after launch, or archive the pages instead. Without the 300-page limit in the original SOW, this would have become an argument rather than a decision.

### Writing an SOW for Agile work
Classic SOWs assume scope can be fixed up front. With Agile delivery, the detailed scope is expected to change as the team learns. You can still write a sound SOW by fixing different things:
| Approach | What is fixed | What flexes | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capacity-based (team for a period) | Team size, roles, duration, rate, ways of working | Backlog content and order | Product development where the buyer's product owner sets priorities |
| Fixed budget, flexible scope | Budget and end date; a prioritised initial backlog | Lower-priority items drop if needed | Projects with a hard deadline and a clear minimum viable product |
| Phase-by-phase SOWs | One short SOW per phase or release | Scope of later phases | Uncertain work where trust is still being built |
| Outcome-based | The measurable outcome and a shared definition of done | Method and backlog | Mature relationships with clear, measurable goals |
In an Agile SOW, the acceptance criteria often refer to a shared [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) and to sprint reviews, and the buyer's responsibilities include providing a product owner with authority to make decisions. State how the backlog is changed (usually by the product owner, without a formal change request) and what still needs one (budget, team size, end date).

### SOW quality test: check before you sign
Run this checklist before either party signs. Each 'no' is a likely future dispute.
| Check | Buyer asks | Supplier asks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | Is everything we need in scope, with volumes and limits? | Are exclusions and limits written down? |
| Deliverables | Does every deliverable have an ID and a format? | Are deliverables separate from activities? |
| Acceptance | Can we test every criterion objectively? | Is there a review window and a limit on rework cycles? |
| Schedule | Do the dates meet our deadline? | Do the dates allow for the buyer's review time and dependencies? |
| Responsibilities | Is the supplier's team named or defined? | Are the buyer's obligations dated, with consequences if late? |
| Money | Are payments tied to accepted deliverables? | Do the payment figures add up to the total price? |
| Change | Can we change priorities without renegotiating everything? | Is unapproved extra work clearly not required? |
| Documents | Does the SOW reference the right MSA or contract? | Is the order of precedence clear? |
This check is also a good moment to confirm stakeholders on both sides have seen the SOW; see [project stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/).

### Common statement of work mistakes
- **Vague verbs:** 'support', 'assist' and 'optimise' without a measurable output. Replace them with deliverables and quantities.
- **No exclusions:** if it is not written as out of scope, someone will assume it is in.
- **Subjective acceptance:** 'to the client's satisfaction' gives the supplier no target and the buyer no protection.
- **Forgetting the buyer's obligations:** late content, data or approvals are a common cause of delay; dates and consequences belong in the SOW.
- **Payments not linked to acceptance:** paying by calendar date rewards time spent, not results.
- **Numbers that do not reconcile:** check that milestone payments, cost breakdowns and totals match.
- **Copying a template without editing it:** irrelevant clauses confuse readers and can contradict the contract.
- **Duplicating or contradicting contract terms:** keep legal terms in the MSA or contract and refer to them.
- **No change process:** verbal changes are the start of [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).
- **Ignoring constraints:** budget, regulatory and resource limits should shape the SOW; see [project constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/).
If you are buying from several suppliers, issue the same draft SOW with your request for quotation so quotes are comparable. Our [RFQ template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/rfq-template/) and [project proposal template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-proposal-template/) cover the buyer and supplier sides of that exchange.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a statement of work?**
A statement of work (SOW) is a document that describes the work a supplier will perform for a buyer: the purpose, scope, deliverables, schedule, standards, acceptance criteria, responsibilities and payment terms. Once signed or attached to a contract, it is the baseline both parties deliver and measure against.

**Q: What should a statement of work include?**
At minimum: purpose and objectives, scope of work, exclusions, deliverables, acceptance criteria and process, schedule and milestones, location and resources, standards, roles and responsibilities (including the buyer's), reporting, pricing and payment terms, assumptions, change control and signatures.

**Q: Is a statement of work legally binding?**
Often, yes. An SOW is usually signed by both parties or incorporated into a contract or master service agreement, which makes its terms enforceable. The exact position depends on the wording and the governing law, so take legal advice on important agreements.

**Q: Who writes the statement of work?**
Either party can. Buyers often draft the SOW to include with a request for proposal or quote, while agencies and consultancies often draft it for the client to review. The best SOWs are reviewed and agreed by both sides before signature.

**Q: What is the difference between a statement of work and a scope of work?**
The scope of work is a section within the SOW that describes the activities and boundaries of the work. The statement of work is the full document, which also covers deliverables, acceptance, schedule, responsibilities and payment.

**Q: What is the difference between an MSA and an SOW?**
A master service agreement sets the general legal terms for a relationship and is signed once. Each SOW describes one specific engagement under that MSA: its scope, deliverables, schedule and price. One MSA can have many SOWs.

**Q: Can you have an SOW without an MSA?**
Yes. For one-off work, an SOW can stand alone or sit within a short contract, but it then needs to include essential legal terms such as liability, confidentiality, intellectual property and termination.

**Q: What is the difference between an SOW and a project charter?**
A project charter authorises a project internally and gives the project manager authority to use resources. An SOW defines work that one party will do for another, usually as part of a commercial agreement. A supplier's SOW can be an input to the buyer's charter.

**Q: What are the three types of statement of work?**
The three common types are the design or detail SOW (specifies how the work is done), the level of effort or time-and-materials SOW (buys a quantity of time or service) and the performance-based SOW (specifies outcomes and lets the supplier choose the method).

**Q: What is a performance work statement?**
A performance work statement (PWS) is a performance-based document, used particularly in US government procurement, that describes the required results and measurable performance standards rather than the method of doing the work.

**Q: How long should a statement of work be?**
Long enough to remove ambiguity and no longer. A small freelance job may need two or three pages; a complex IT or construction engagement can run to dozens of pages with annexes for requirements, acceptance tests and pricing.

**Q: How do you change a statement of work after it is signed?**
Through a written change request. The supplier assesses cost, schedule and risk impact, authorised people on both sides approve it, and the change is recorded as a numbered amendment to the SOW.

**Q: Can you use a statement of work for Agile projects?**
Yes. Instead of fixing detailed scope, an Agile SOW usually fixes team capacity, duration, budget and ways of working, refers to a shared Definition of Done, and lets the product owner reprioritise the backlog within those limits.

**Q: Who signs the statement of work?**
Authorised signatories from both parties: people with the authority to commit budget and resources. On the buyer side this is often the sponsor or a procurement lead; on the supplier side an account director or company officer.

# Swimlane Diagram: What It Is, Examples and How to Make One

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/swimlane-diagram/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: A swimlane diagram shows who does each step in a process. Learn the symbols, see worked examples and follow our step-by-step method to make one.


## Swimlane Diagram: What It Is, Examples and How to Make One
A swimlane diagram is a flowchart divided into lanes, one for each person, team or system involved in a process, so every step sits in the lane of whoever performs it. You can see at a glance who does what, in what order, and where work is handed from one party to another. This guide covers the symbols, a step-by-step method, two worked examples and how to use the finished diagram to make a process faster.
- Published 27 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- A swimlane diagram is a flowchart with lanes that show who is responsible for each step.
- Every arrow that crosses a lane boundary is a handoff, and handoffs are where most waiting and miscommunication happen.
- Map the process as it really works today, with the people who do it, before designing an improved version.
- Adding work time and waiting time to each step turns the diagram into a measurement tool, not just a picture.
- Keep to roughly three to seven lanes and one consistent level of detail so the diagram stays readable.
- Use a swimlane diagram for the flow of work, a RACI matrix for detailed accountability and a Gantt chart for timing.

### What is a swimlane diagram?
A **swimlane diagram** is a process flowchart arranged in parallel lanes, where each lane represents one participant: a person, role, team, department or system. Each step is drawn in the lane of the participant who performs it, and arrows show the sequence. The result shows both what happens in a process and who is responsible for each step.
The name comes from the lanes of a swimming pool: each participant stays in their own lane, and you can see when work crosses from one lane to the next. You will also see swimlane diagrams called **cross-functional flowcharts**, **deployment flowcharts**, **Rummler-Brache diagrams** or simply **swimlane process maps**. They all describe the same idea.
Process charts with separate columns for different departments existed long before modern diagramming software. The format became widely known through Geary Rummler and Alan Brache's 1990 book *Improving Performance: How to Manage the White Space on the Organization Chart*, which argued that the biggest problems in organisations often sit in the gaps between departments. That is still the main reason to draw one today: a swimlane diagram makes those gaps visible.
An ordinary flowchart answers "what are the steps?". A swimlane diagram also answers "who does each step?" and "where does work change hands?", which matters because delays usually come from work waiting for the next person, not from slow work.

### Parts of a swimlane diagram
Most swimlane diagrams use a small set of standard flowchart symbols. Keeping to these makes your diagram readable by anyone, whatever tool they use.
| Element | Usual shape | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lane | Horizontal or vertical band with a label | The person, role, team or system responsible for the steps inside it |
| Phase (optional) | Column or row crossing all lanes | A stage of the process, such as Request, Assess, Decide, Deliver |
| Start or end | Rounded rectangle or oval | The trigger that starts the process and the outcome that ends it |
| Activity | Rectangle | A single step, named with a verb and a noun, such as 'Approve invoice' |
| Decision | Diamond | A question with two or more exits, usually labelled Yes and No |
| Document | Rectangle with a wavy base | A form, report or record that is produced or used |
| Data or system | Cylinder or parallelogram | A database, file or system that stores or supplies information |
| Flow arrow | Solid arrow | The order in which steps happen |
| Handoff | Any arrow crossing a lane boundary | Work or information passing to another participant |
Keep activity names short. If a box needs a paragraph to explain it, it is probably several steps, or the detail belongs in a supporting procedure.

#### Pools and lanes in BPMN
Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), the process modelling standard maintained by the Object Management Group, uses the same idea with stricter rules. A **pool** represents a whole participant, usually an organisation such as your company, a customer or a supplier. **Lanes** subdivide a pool into roles or departments. Sequence flows (solid arrows) stay inside a pool, while communication between pools is shown with **message flows** (dashed arrows).
For most project processes a plain swimlane diagram is easier for stakeholders to read. Use BPMN when the process will be automated or your organisation already uses it as a standard.

### Swimlane diagram vs flowchart and other process maps
Swimlane diagrams are one of several ways to describe a process. Each answers a different question, and they work well together.
| Technique | What it shows | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basic flowchart | Steps, decisions and order | Simple processes with one owner, or explaining logic |
| Swimlane diagram | Steps, order and who does each step | Processes that cross teams, with handoffs and approvals |
| BPMN diagram | Steps, events, messages and participants in a formal notation | Processes that will be automated or formally documented |
| [Value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) | Flow of value with lead time, process time and waiting | Finding waste across an end-to-end flow |
| SIPOC | Suppliers, inputs, process, outputs, customers at a high level | Agreeing the boundaries of a process before mapping it |
| [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) | Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed | Detailed accountability, not sequence |
| [Project network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/) | Dependencies between project activities | Scheduling and critical path analysis |
A useful rule of thumb: if the question is "who does what, and in what order?", draw a swimlane diagram. If it is "who is accountable and who must be consulted?", build a RACI matrix. If it is "when will it be finished?", you need a schedule such as a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/).

### When to use a swimlane diagram (and when not to)
Swimlane diagrams earn their place whenever responsibility for a process is spread across more than one person or team. Typical uses include:
- **Approval processes**, such as change requests, purchase approvals or document sign-off.
- **Onboarding and offboarding**, where HR, IT, facilities and line managers all have a part to play.
- **Service and support processes**, such as incident handling or customer complaints.
- **Project handovers**, for example from delivery to operations or from sales to the project team.
- **Designing a new workflow** for a project deliverable before the team starts using it.
- **Training and audits**, where people need a clear picture of their role and controls.
- **Process improvement**, to find delays, duplicate work and unnecessary handoffs.
They are less helpful in some situations:
- **One person does every step.** A checklist or simple flowchart is enough.
- **You need dates and durations across a whole project.** Use a schedule, not a process map.
- **The process is mostly unstructured knowledge work**, such as creative exploration, where the order of steps changes every time.
- **You need to show degrees of responsibility**, such as who must be consulted. Pair the diagram with a RACI matrix.

### Horizontal vs vertical swimlanes
Lanes can run across the page (horizontal) or down it (vertical). Neither is more correct; pick the layout that fits your process and your medium.
| Layout | How it reads | Works best when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Horizontal lanes | Left to right, like a timeline | There are many steps and a moderate number of participants; slides and wide screens |
| Vertical lanes | Top to bottom, like a page of text | There are many participants and fewer steps; printed A4 documents and procedure manuals |
You can also choose what the lanes represent. Be consistent within one diagram.
| Lane type | Example lanes | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roles | Requester, Project manager, Technical lead | Several people in one team share a process |
| Departments | Sales, Finance, Operations | You are looking at cross-department flow |
| Systems | CRM, Finance system, Email | Automated steps matter as much as human ones |
| External parties | Customer, Supplier, Regulator | The process crosses organisational boundaries |
| Phases (as columns) | Request, Assess, Decide, Deliver | You want to show stages as well as owners |

### How to make a swimlane diagram: step by step
The method below works whether you draw on a whiteboard, in a spreadsheet or in a diagramming tool. The most important work happens before you draw anything.
1. **Choose one process and set its boundaries.** Write down the trigger that starts it and the outcome that ends it, for example 'starts when a change request is raised; ends when the requester is told the decision'.
2. **Decide what the lanes will represent.** Roles are usually the most useful for project processes. Systems get a lane only if they perform steps on their own.
3. **List the participants.** Aim for three to seven lanes. If you have more, combine minor participants or split the process into two diagrams.
4. **Get the people who do the work in the room.** Managers often describe how a process should work; the people doing it know how it actually works.
5. **Capture the steps on sticky notes or a list.** Use verb-and-noun names and one level of detail. Ask 'what happens next?' and 'what happens if not?' at every step.
6. **Place each step in the right lane, in sequence.** Steps that happen at the same time sit side by side in their own lanes.
7. **Add decisions and exception paths.** Show the main path first, then the important alternatives, such as rejection, rework or escalation.
8. **Connect the steps with arrows and mark the handoffs.** Every arrow that crosses a lane line is a handoff; highlight or count them.
9. **Add time data.** For each step, note the typical work time and the typical wait before the next step starts.
10. **Validate, then version it.** Walk through the diagram with each lane owner, fix gaps, date it and store it where the team can find it.

#### Setting the scope
Most swimlane diagrams fail because the scope is too big. 'Project delivery' is not one process; 'raising and approving a change request' is. If you cannot describe the start and end in one sentence each, narrow the scope. A high-level SIPOC (suppliers, inputs, process, outputs, customers) can help you agree the boundaries with stakeholders first.

#### Interviewing the people who do the work
Run a short workshop with one representative from each lane, or one-to-one interviews if people are spread out. Ask them to describe the last real case they handled, not the ideal one: what triggered their step, what information they needed, how long it waited before they picked it up, and what usually goes wrong.
When drawing, keep the main flow moving in one direction and reorder lanes so the busiest handoffs sit next to each other, which avoids crossing arrows. If you prefer to work in a spreadsheet, our [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/) records each step with its owner, inputs, outputs, tools, handoffs and time, which gives you the data behind the diagram.

### Worked example: a project change request process
This illustrative example shows how a swimlane diagram turns into a measurement and improvement tool. A project team wants to know why change requests take so long to approve. They map the current (as-is) process with five lanes: Requester, Project manager, Technical lead, Change board and Delivery team. Times assume a 7.5-hour working day.

#### The as-is process
| # | Lane | Step | Work time | Wait before next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Requester | Email change request to project manager | 0.5 h | 2 days (sits in inbox) |
| 2 | Project manager | Log request in change log and check it is complete | 0.5 h | None |
| 3 | Project manager | Ask technical lead for an impact estimate | 0.25 h | 3 days (lead busy with sprint work) |
| 4 | Technical lead | Estimate effort and technical impact | 3 h | 1 day |
| 5 | Project manager | Assess impact on scope, schedule, cost and risk; prepare board paper | 2 h | 5 days on average (fortnightly board) |
| 6 | Change board | Decision: approve the change? | 0.75 h | 1 day |
| 7 | Project manager | Yes: update plan and baseline. No: inform requester | 1.5 h | None (end) |
Drawn as a swimlane diagram, the flow zig-zags between lanes: Requester to Project manager, Project manager to Technical lead, back to the Project manager, up to the Change board, back to the Project manager and finally out to the requester or delivery team. That is **six handoffs** for a seven-step process.

#### Measuring the as-is process
- **Total work time:** 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.25 + 3 + 2 + 0.75 + 1.5 = **8.5 hours** (about 1.1 days).
- **Total waiting time:** 2 + 3 + 1 + 5 + 1 = **12 working days** (90 hours).
- **Elapsed time:** 90 + 8.5 = 98.5 hours, or about **13 working days** from request to decision.
- **Flow efficiency:** work time ÷ elapsed time = 8.5 ÷ 98.5 = **about 9%**.
In other words, a change request spends around 91% of its life waiting. The diagram makes it obvious where: the inbox, the technical lead's queue and the fortnightly board. None of those delays would show up in a task list, because no one is doing anything during them. See [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) for more on this measure.

#### The to-be redesign
The team agrees four changes, each aimed at a specific wait or handoff shown on the diagram:
1. Replace email with a [change request form](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) whose required fields feed the change log directly, removing the separate logging step.
2. Agree a two-day turnaround for impact estimates and reserve capacity for them in each sprint.
3. Delegate **minor changes** to the project manager: under three days of effort, no movement of a milestone and no budget increase.
4. Move the change board from fortnightly meetings to a weekly slot, with urgent items decided asynchronously.
The redesigned diagram has two paths after the impact assessment: minor changes go straight to the delivery team, and major changes still go to the board. Assuming half a day for triage, the two-day estimate turnaround, half a day before the assessment, an average wait of 2.5 days for the weekly board and half a day after it, the numbers compare as follows.
| Measure | As-is | To-be (minor change) | To-be (major change) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Steps | 7 | 5 | 6 |
| Handoffs | 6 | 4 | 6 |
| Work time | 8.5 h | 7.5 h | 8.25 h |
| Waiting time | 12 days | 3 days | 6 days |
| Elapsed time | about 13 days | about 4 days | about 7 days |
| Flow efficiency | about 9% | about 25% | about 15% |
Notice that work time barely changes. The improvement comes almost entirely from removing waiting and one handoff, which is typical of process improvement work. The new design also needs to be written into the project's [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) procedure and communicated to everyone in each lane.
Tip
Mark each handoff with a number on the diagram, then ask the receiving lane: how do you find out that work is waiting for you? If the answer is 'someone chases me', you have found an improvement target.

### Second example: new starter IT access with parallel lanes
The first example was largely sequential. Many processes have steps that happen in parallel, and a swimlane diagram shows that well. In this illustrative example, a new employee must have a laptop, accounts and access to a finance system on their first day.
| Lane | Steps | Typical duration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hiring manager | 1. Confirm start date and role. 6. Welcome new starter on day one | 0.5 day |
| HR | 2. Create employee record and trigger IT request | 0.5 day |
| IT service desk | 3a. Order and configure laptop | 5 working days (supplier delivery) |
| Identity system | 3b. Create email and core accounts automatically from the HR record | Same day |
| Finance system owner | 4. Approve finance system access after 3b | 3 working days |
| IT service desk | 5. Hand over laptop and credentials | 0.5 day |
Steps 3a and 3b start at the same time in different lanes, so they are drawn side by side. The laptop branch takes 5 days; the accounts-plus-approval branch takes about 3.5 days. The longer branch sets the duration, exactly as the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) does in a project schedule. The diagram therefore gives HR a simple rule: trigger the request at least six working days before the start date, or the new starter arrives without a laptop.
It also shows why a system can deserve its own lane. Step 3b involves no person, but if the HR record is incomplete it fails silently. Giving the system a lane prompts the question: who is told when this step fails?

### How to analyse a swimlane diagram for improvements
Once the as-is diagram is validated, look for the patterns below. Each one points to a likely improvement.
| What you see on the diagram | What it usually means | Possible fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Many arrows crossing lanes | Work bounces between people; each handoff adds a wait | Combine steps in one lane; give one person end-to-end ownership |
| Long waits before a step | A queue, meeting cycle or overloaded person | Service-level targets, more frequent decisions, reserved capacity |
| Loops back to earlier steps | Rework caused by missing information or unclear criteria | Better intake forms, checklists, clear acceptance criteria |
| Several approvals in a row | Approval stacking; nobody trusts the previous check | Delegate approval thresholds; approve once at the right level |
| One lane with far more steps | A bottleneck or single point of failure | Redistribute work, cross-train, automate routine steps |
| Steps in no clear lane | Ownership gaps; things fall through the cracks | Assign an owner and record it in a RACI matrix |
| Same information entered twice | Duplicate data entry between systems | Integrate systems or use one shared record |
Ask three questions of every step: does it add value for the customer of the process, does it need to be done by this lane, and does it need to happen in this order? Steps that fail all three are candidates for removal.
If you need to find the root cause of a recurring problem, such as frequent rework at one step, a [fishbone diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/) is a good next tool. For broader waste reduction, swimlane analysis fits naturally with [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/) and [Six Sigma](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/six-sigma/) methods.

### Swimlanes in project management
In projects, swimlane diagrams usually appear in four places:
- **Project processes.** Change control, risk escalation, procurement approvals and reporting cycles can all be documented as swimlanes in the [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/), so everyone knows the route a request will take.
- **Roles and responsibilities.** A swimlane diagram shows sequence; a RACI matrix shows accountability. Draw the swimlane first, then use each step as a row in your [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/).
- **Designing deliverables.** When a project creates a new service or system, the future-state swimlane diagram is often a deliverable in its own right, agreed with stakeholders before the build starts.
- **Operational handover.** At [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/), swimlane diagrams help the operations team understand the processes they are inheriting.
The word 'swimlane' also appears in two other planning tools. On a Kanban board, swimlanes are horizontal rows that separate types of work, teams or priority levels on the same board; see [Kanban swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/). On a Gantt chart, swimlanes group tasks by team or workstream so you can see parallel work at a glance. Both borrow the same idea of lanes, but neither is a process map.
See our [guide to the RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) to turn the lanes on your diagram into clear accountability.

### Common swimlane diagram mistakes
- **Mapping the ideal process instead of the real one.** You cannot improve a process you have not seen as it is. Map the as-is first.
- **Scope too wide.** A diagram of 'everything the PMO does' helps no one. Map one process with a clear start and end.
- **Too many lanes.** Beyond about seven, the diagram becomes hard to follow. Merge minor participants or split the process.
- **Mixed levels of detail.** 'Deliver project' next to 'Click Submit' confuses readers. Keep every step at the same level.
- **Only the happy path.** Rejections, rework and escalations are where the time goes. Show the important exceptions.
- **Unlabelled decisions.** Every diamond needs a question and labelled exits.
- **Lanes named after individuals.** People change roles. Use role names, such as 'Finance approver'.
- **No time data.** Without work and wait times you can describe the process but not improve it.
- **Drawing it alone.** A diagram built without the people in each lane will be wrong and will not be trusted.

### Tools and templates for swimlane diagrams
Sticky notes on a wall are often best for a first workshop because everyone can move them. For a diagram you will share and maintain, you have three broad choices.
| Option | Good for | Things to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spreadsheet | Capturing steps, owners and times in a structured way | Our [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/) holds the data behind the diagram; you can also shade columns as lanes |
| Diagramming and whiteboard tools | Polished diagrams, BPMN, real-time workshops | Most include ready-made swimlane templates and drag-and-drop shapes |
| Project management software | Turning the agreed process into a live workflow | Custom statuses, request forms and automation can enforce the to-be design |
Among the [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) we review, several support this work. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, is a good fit once the diagram is agreed: its custom workflows, request forms and automation rules let you build the to-be process so requests arrive with the right information and move between owners automatically. Wrike Whiteboard is available as an add-on (included in the Apex plan) if you want to draw the diagram in the same place. [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) includes Whiteboards on its plans, with limits on the lower tiers, and [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) supports swimlanes by assignee, epic or priority on its Kanban boards for software and IT teams.
If your process starts with a request from another team, pair the diagram with a [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) so the intake step collects everything the next lane needs.

### Swimlane diagram checklist
Before you share or publish a swimlane diagram, check that:
- The title, start trigger and end outcome are clear.
- There are no more than about seven lanes, named by role, team or system.
- Every step sits in one lane, and every decision has labelled exits.
- Important exceptions, loops and escalations are shown, and handoffs are numbered.
- Work and wait times are noted for the as-is version.
- Each lane owner has agreed it, and it has an owner, version and review date.
Revisit the diagram after each significant process change and as part of your [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) review, so it stays a working document rather than a one-off drawing.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a swimlane diagram?**
A swimlane diagram is a flowchart split into lanes, one for each person, team or system, showing who carries out each step in a process and where work is handed from one participant to another.

**Q: Why is it called a swimlane diagram?**
The lanes resemble the lanes of a swimming pool. Each participant stays in their own lane, and you can see when work crosses into another lane.

**Q: What is another name for a swimlane diagram?**
It is also called a cross-functional flowchart, a deployment flowchart, a Rummler-Brache diagram or a swimlane process map.

**Q: What is the difference between a flowchart and a swimlane diagram?**
A standard flowchart shows the steps and decisions in a process. A swimlane diagram shows the same steps arranged in lanes, so it also shows who performs each step and where handoffs happen.

**Q: What is the difference between a pool and a lane?**
In BPMN, a pool represents a whole participant, usually an organisation, and lanes divide a pool into roles or departments.

**Q: Should swimlanes be horizontal or vertical?**
Either works. Horizontal lanes suit processes with many steps; vertical lanes suit many participants and fewer steps, and fit printed documents better.

**Q: How many lanes should a swimlane diagram have?**
As few as you need. Three to seven lanes is a practical range; with more than that, consider merging minor participants or splitting the process into separate diagrams.

**Q: What symbols are used in a swimlane diagram?**
Standard flowchart symbols: ovals for start and end, rectangles for activities, diamonds for decisions, a document shape for forms and arrows for the flow.

**Q: Can a swimlane diagram show time?**
Yes. Note the work time and waiting time on each step, or add phase columns, so you can calculate elapsed time and flow efficiency.

**Q: How do you show a loop or rework in a swimlane diagram?**
Draw an arrow from the decision or check back to the earlier step that has to be repeated, and label it with the reason, such as 'information missing'. Frequent loops are a sign of an improvement opportunity.

**Q: Can I make a swimlane diagram in Excel?**
Yes. Use shaded rows or columns as lanes and shapes or cells for steps, or record the steps, owners and times in a structured sheet such as our workflow template and draw the diagram from that data.

**Q: What are swimlanes in a Kanban board?**
They are horizontal rows that separate different types of work, teams or priority levels on the same board. They organise the board rather than map a process.

**Q: What are swimlanes in a Gantt chart?**
They are groupings of tasks by team, workstream or owner, used to show parallel streams of work on a project timeline.
