# Task Dependencies: Types, Examples and How to Manage Them

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Task dependencies explained: the four types (FS, SS, FF, SF), mandatory vs discretionary, a worked example, and how to identify and manage them.


## Task Dependencies: Types, Examples and How to Manage Them
Task dependencies are the logical links between activities that decide when one activity can start or finish relative to another. They turn a list of tasks into a schedule that can calculate dates, find the critical path and show how far a delay will spread.
- Published 23 September 2026
- Last updated 14 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- A task dependency links a predecessor to a successor and says which end of one controls which end of the other.
- There are four types: finish-to-start (by far the most common), start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish (rare).
- Dependencies are also classified as mandatory or discretionary, and internal or external; discretionary links are your main lever when you need to shorten a schedule.
- Find dependencies by asking two questions of every activity: what must happen before this, and what is waiting for it?
- Give every external dependency a named owner and review it at each status meeting.
- Let dependencies drive dates. Typing dates in by hand hides the logic and breaks the critical path.

### What is a task dependency?
A **task dependency** is a logical relationship between two activities in which the start or finish of one activity (the **successor**) depends on the start or finish of another (the **predecessor**). Dependencies set the order of work, and once durations are added they allow a schedule to calculate dates, float and the critical path.
The simplest example: you cannot print a brochure until the text has been proofread. "Proofread" is the predecessor, "Print" is the successor, and the link between them is a finish-to-start dependency. If proofreading slips by two days, printing slips by two days too, unless you change the plan.
Dependencies are one of the three building blocks of a schedule, alongside the activity list and the duration estimates. If you have not yet broken the work down, start with the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) and the [activity list](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-tasks-and-activities/), then add the links.

#### Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Predecessor | The activity that comes first and controls the timing of the other |
| Successor | The activity that depends on the predecessor |
| Link type | Which end of the predecessor controls which end of the successor: FS, SS, FF or SF |
| Lag | A deliberate wait added to a link, such as 3 days for concrete to cure |
| Lead | An overlap on a link, written as a negative lag, such as FS-2 days |
| Driving predecessor | When an activity has several predecessors, the one that actually sets its start date |
| Float (slack) | How long an activity can slip without delaying the project end date |
| Critical path | The longest chain of dependent activities, which sets the shortest possible project duration |
The two ends of a link are covered in detail in our guide to [predecessors and successors](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/predecessors-and-successors/).

### Why task dependencies matter
A task list with durations but no dependencies is just a list. Once the links are in place, the schedule starts doing useful work for you:
- **Realistic dates:** start and finish dates are calculated from the logic rather than guessed.
- **A critical path:** tools use the links to run the forward and backward pass and show which activities have zero float.
- **Delay forecasting:** when an activity slips, every affected successor moves, so you see the knock-on effect straight away.
- **Clear hand-offs and risks:** each link is a hand-off between people, and external links (suppliers, approvals) are early warnings of likely delay.
- **What-if analysis:** you can test overlapping activities or removing a preferred sequence before you commit.

### The four types of task dependencies
Every dependency joins one end of the predecessor (its start or its finish) to one end of the successor. That gives four possible combinations, known as the four logical relationships.
| Type | Rule | Example | Notation | How common |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Finish-to-start (FS) | The successor cannot start until the predecessor finishes | Pour the foundations, then build the walls | B: A FS | By far the most common; the default in most tools |
| Start-to-start (SS) | The successor cannot start until the predecessor starts | Start editing chapters once writing has started | B: A SS | Common for overlapping work |
| Finish-to-finish (FF) | The successor cannot finish until the predecessor finishes | Testing cannot finish until development finishes | B: A FF | Common for parallel work that must end together |
| Start-to-finish (SF) | The successor cannot finish until the predecessor starts | The old system keeps running until the new one goes live | B: A SF | Rare; often a sign the logic can be written more simply |

#### Finish-to-start (FS)
The successor waits for the predecessor to be complete. Use FS when the successor genuinely needs the output of the predecessor: you need approved designs before you build, a signed contract before you order materials, and data migration finished before user acceptance testing. Most schedules are made up mainly of FS links, and it is the default when you link tasks in tools such as Microsoft Project, Smartsheet or Wrike.

#### Start-to-start (SS)
The successor can begin once the predecessor has begun, so the two run in parallel. SS links usually carry a lag: "start laying cables two days after trenching starts" is SS+2 days. SS is useful when work can flow in batches, for example when an editor can start on chapter one while the author writes chapter two.

#### Finish-to-finish (FF)
The successor cannot be completed until the predecessor is complete. The two activities may start at different times, but their finishes are tied. A common example is documentation that cannot be finished until the feature it describes is finished. FF links are often paired with an SS link on the same two activities to model overlapping work properly.

#### Start-to-finish (SF)
The successor cannot finish until the predecessor starts. The classic example is a hand-over: the night security shift cannot end until the day shift has started, and an old system cannot be switched off until the new one is live. SF is rare in real schedules. If you find yourself using it, check whether an FS link with the activities the other way round says the same thing more clearly.
Tip
Default to finish-to-start. Use SS and FF only when the work really can overlap, and record why. Overlaps shorten the schedule but add risk, because the successor starts on incomplete information.

### Leads and lags on a dependency
Any of the four link types can carry a timing adjustment:
- **Lag** is a wait between the predecessor and the successor. Plaster must dry for 3 days before painting: Paint depends on Plaster FS+3 days.
- **Lead** is an overlap. Testers can start 2 days before development finishes: Test depends on Develop FS-2 days. Most tools record a lead as a negative lag.
- **SS and FF lags** offset the starts or finishes: Proofread SS+2 days means proofreading starts two days after writing starts.
A lag is waiting time, not work. If someone has to do something during the gap, such as inspect the concrete, make it an activity with an owner rather than hiding it in a lag. Our guide to [leads and lags](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/) has more worked examples.

### Mandatory, discretionary, internal and external dependencies
The four link types describe timing. A second way to classify dependencies describes **why** the link exists and **who controls it**. The PMBOK Guide (Sixth Edition) describes four attributes, which are used in pairs: every dependency is either mandatory or discretionary, and either internal or external.
|  | Internal (within the team's control) | External (outside the project) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mandatory** (hard logic) | You cannot test code that has not been written | You cannot open a building before the fire safety certificate is issued |
| **Discretionary** (soft logic) | The team prefers to finish the design before starting the build | The client prefers to approve each phase before the next starts, though the contract does not require it |
- **Mandatory dependencies** are required by the nature of the work, the law or a contract. They are also called hard logic. You cannot remove them without changing the work itself.
- **Discretionary dependencies** reflect best practice, experience or a preferred sequence. They are also called soft logic or preferential logic. They can be changed, usually at the price of more risk.
- **External dependencies** involve something outside the project: suppliers, regulators, other projects, the client. The project team cannot control them, only monitor and influence them.
- **Internal dependencies** are between activities the project controls.
Discretionary dependencies are the first place to look when you need to shorten the schedule. Overlapping two activities that were in sequence only by preference is called fast tracking; see [fast tracking vs crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/). Document why each discretionary link exists, so you know what risk you take on by changing it.

#### Other labels you will meet
- **Resource dependency:** two activities could run in parallel, but the same person or machine is needed for both, so one has to wait. Many planners handle this through resource levelling rather than a logical link.
- **Cross-team dependency:** one team needs a deliverable from another team, common in Agile programmes and large organisations.
- **Logical dependency:** another name for a mandatory link driven by the nature of the work.
- **Preferential dependency:** another name for a discretionary link.

### Dependencies vs constraints, blockers and risks
These terms are often used interchangeably, but they mean different things and are managed differently.
| Term | What it is | Example | Where to record it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dependency | A logical link between two activities | Install software after hardware set-up | Schedule (predecessor column) |
| Constraint | A limit placed on an activity or the project, such as a fixed date, budget or resource cap | Exhibition opens on 4 May; budget is capped at £50,000 | Schedule date constraint, project charter; see [project constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/) |
| Blocker | Something stopping work right now | The test environment is down | Issue log or board, raised at the stand-up |
| Risk | An uncertain event that may affect the project | The supplier may deliver late | Risk register |
An external dependency often creates a risk (it might be late) and, when it is late, a blocker. Many teams track all of these together in a [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/), which stands for risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies.

### How to identify task dependencies, step by step
Dependencies are easiest to find in a short workshop with the people who will do the work, using sticky notes or a shared whiteboard.
1. **Start from the activity list.** Make sure each activity is a clear piece of work with an owner and a deliverable. Vague activities produce vague links.
2. **Ask the backward question.** For each activity: what must be finished, started or available before this can start? Those are its predecessors.
3. **Ask the forward question.** For each activity: what is waiting for this? Those are its successors. Asking both questions catches links that one question misses.
4. **Choose the link type.** Default to finish-to-start. Use SS or FF only if the work can genuinely overlap, and agree the lag.
5. **Classify the link.** Mark it mandatory or discretionary and internal or external, and note the reason in a comment.
6. **Find the external dependencies.** Walk through suppliers, approvals, other projects, client inputs and shared environments. Add each as a milestone or activity with an owner.
7. **Check the network.** Draw or generate a [network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/). Every activity except the start and finish should have at least one predecessor and one successor, and there should be no loops.
Useful prompts for the workshop:
- What information, approval or material does this activity need?
- Who hands work to you, and who do you hand it to?
- Is this order required, or is it just how we usually do it?
- Does anything outside the team have to happen first?
- Could part of this start before the previous activity is fully complete?

### How to record task dependencies
Record dependencies in a consistent format so they can be checked, reviewed and entered into a tool. A simple dependency table is enough for most projects.
| ID | Activity | Predecessor(s) | Type and lag | Category | Owner (external links) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | Install network cabling | 1 | FS | Mandatory, internal |  | Needs final floor plan |
| 5 | Install furniture | 3 | FS | Mandatory, external | Facilities manager | Supplier delivery |
| 6 | Set up IT equipment | 4; 5 | FS; SS+1d | Mandatory; discretionary |  | Can start once first desks are in |

#### Predecessor notation in scheduling tools
Microsoft Project and several other tools use a compact notation in the Predecessors column: the predecessor's ID, then the link type, then any lag or lead. A bare ID means finish-to-start with no lag.
| Entry | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 3 | Finish-to-start from task 3, no lag |
| 3FS+2d | Finish-to-start from task 3, then wait 2 days |
| 3SS+1d | Start 1 day after task 3 starts |
| 3FF | Finish no earlier than task 3 finishes |
| 3FS-25% | Start when task 3 is 75% through its duration (a lead) |
| 3,5SS | Two predecessors: FS from task 3 and SS from task 5 |

#### Dependency matrix
On programmes with many teams, a dependency matrix gives an overview. List teams or workstreams down the side and across the top, and in each cell note what the row team needs from the column team and by when. It quickly shows which teams are heavily depended on and where to focus coordination.

### Worked example: an office move
A small team is relocating to a new office. The activities, durations and dependencies are below. Durations are in working days, and day 0 is the start of the project.
| ID | Activity | Duration | Predecessors | Category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Confirm floor plan | 3 | None | Start |
| B | Order furniture | 2 | A FS | Mandatory, internal |
| C | Furniture delivery (supplier) | 10 | B FS | Mandatory, external |
| D | Install network cabling | 5 | A FS | Mandatory, internal |
| E | Install furniture | 3 | C FS | Mandatory, internal |
| F | Set up IT equipment | 4 | D FS; E SS+1 | Mandatory; discretionary |
| G | Pack old office | 4 | E SS | Discretionary |
| H | Move day | 1 | E FS; F FS; G FS | Mandatory |
| I | Snagging and handover | 2 | H FS | Mandatory |

#### Step 1: calculate the dates
Work forward through the network. Each activity starts at the latest date allowed by all of its predecessors (its driving predecessor sets the date).
| Activity | Start | Finish | Driving predecessor and why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A Confirm floor plan | 0 | 3 | Project start |
| B Order furniture | 3 | 5 | A finishes on day 3 |
| C Furniture delivery | 5 | 15 | B finishes on day 5 |
| D Network cabling | 3 | 8 | A finishes on day 3 |
| E Install furniture | 15 | 18 | C finishes on day 15 |
| F Set up IT | 16 | 20 | E starts on day 15, plus 1 day lag = 16, which is later than D's finish on day 8 |
| G Pack old office | 15 | 19 | E starts on day 15 |
| H Move day | 20 | 21 | F finishes on day 20, later than E (18) and G (19) |
| I Snagging and handover | 21 | 23 | H finishes on day 21 |
The project takes **23 working days**.

#### Step 2: find the critical path and float
The critical path is A → B → C → E → F → H → I, running through the furniture supplier. These activities have zero float: any delay to them delays the move.
- **D Network cabling** finishes on day 8 but F does not need it until day 16, so D has **8 days of float**. A slip of a few days in cabling does not matter.
- **G Pack old office** finishes on day 19 and the move starts on day 20, so G has **1 day of float**.
- The furniture delivery, an **external** dependency, is on the critical path. That tells the project manager exactly where to spend attention: confirm the order early and chase the supplier.
For the full method, see the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) and [forward and backward pass](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/forward-and-backward-pass/) guides.

#### Step 3: test a delay
The supplier calls on day 8: delivery will take 15 days, not 10. Because the links are in place, the schedule recalculates on its own. C now finishes on day 20, E runs 20 to 23, F runs 21 to 25, G runs 20 to 24, H moves to day 25 and the project finishes on **day 28**, five days late. The 8 days of float on network cabling are unaffected, so the cabling contractor does not need to be rebooked.
The team now looks at its discretionary links. If IT set-up can start on temporary desks as soon as cabling is finished (removing the SS link from E), F runs 8 to 12 and is no longer critical. The move is then driven by packing (finishing on day 24) and the project ends on day 27, recovering one day. This is the kind of what-if analysis that is only possible when dependencies are recorded properly.

#### Step 4: see what the link types saved
If every link had been finish-to-start, IT set-up would have waited for furniture installation to finish (day 18), finishing on day 22, and the project would have ended on day 25. Using SS+1 for IT set-up and SS for packing saves **2 days** on the original plan, at the cost of some overlap risk that the team has accepted.
Tip
When you present a schedule, point out the external dependencies on or near the critical path. They are where a phone call today can save a week later.

### Showing task dependencies on a Gantt chart and network diagram
On a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) a dependency is drawn as an arrow from the predecessor bar to the successor bar. The end of the bar the arrow leaves and the end it enters show the type: from the right end to the left end is FS, left to left is SS, right to right is FF. Most tools also let you highlight the critical path in red and show the driving predecessor of a selected task.
A [project network diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-network-diagram/) shows the same logic without the timescale. Activities are boxes and dependencies are arrows. It is the better view for checking the logic itself: open ends, loops and missing hand-offs are easy to see, while on a busy Gantt chart they are hidden among the bars.
Most project management tools draw dependencies for you once you enter predecessors. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) includes interactive Gantt charts with dependencies, critical path and baselines on paid plans, and [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) combines a spreadsheet grid with dependencies, Gantt view and critical path.

### How to manage task dependencies
Identifying dependencies is half the job. Keeping them under control through delivery is the other half.
1. **Let the logic drive the dates.** Avoid typing start dates into a scheduling tool, because a fixed date overrides the dependencies and the schedule stops reacting to delays. Use a date constraint only for a genuine external date, and record why.
2. **Name an owner for every external dependency.** The owner keeps in touch with the supplier, regulator or other team and reports any change early.
3. **Track external dependencies as milestones.** "Planning permission granted" or "API available in test" as a [milestone](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) makes them visible on the timeline and easy to report.
4. **Review dependencies at every status meeting.** Go through those due in the next two to four weeks and confirm each is still on track. Log them in a [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) so nothing is forgotten.
5. **Watch merge points.** An activity with several predecessors (like move day in the example) starts only when the last of them finishes. These are frequent points of delay; consider a small buffer before them.
6. **Protect the critical path.** Put your best people, earliest confirmations and closest monitoring on critical and near-critical dependencies.
7. **Use discretionary links deliberately.** If the schedule needs to come in, review soft logic first, then consider other [schedule compression](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-compression/) options.
8. **Re-check the logic after changes.** Every approved change request can add, remove or alter dependencies. Re-run the network check before re-baselining the schedule; see [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).
Our free [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) has columns for predecessors, dependency type and dates, and works for small projects without scheduling software.

### Task dependencies in Agile projects
Agile teams use the same idea with different tools. Inside a sprint, the team manages dependencies informally: it orders the sprint backlog so that items others depend on come first, and it swarms on blocked items. Between teams and with the outside world, dependencies need more structure.
- **Link backlog items.** Most Agile tools support links such as "blocks" and "is blocked by" between work items, so a blocked story is visible on the board.
- **Raise dependencies in refinement.** When a story needs something from another team, raise it before sprint planning, not during the sprint.
- **Plan dependencies across teams.** In SAFe, teams map cross-team dependencies on the ART planning board (formerly the program board) during [PI planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/), drawing a red string from the team that provides a dependency to the feature that needs it. Smaller set-ups use a [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/) to coordinate.
- **Design dependencies out.** Cross-functional teams that can deliver a feature end to end have fewer hand-offs. Reducing dependencies is usually more effective than managing them.
On Agile projects with fixed external dates, a high-level timeline that shows epics and external milestones can help.

### Common task dependency mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open ends (activities with no predecessor or no successor) | A delay to that activity does not move anything, so the end date looks safer than it is | Link every activity into the network except the start and finish milestones |
| Hard-coded start dates | The schedule stops reacting to delays and the critical path breaks | Let dependencies set dates; use constraints only for real external dates |
| Redundant links (A to C when A to B to C already exists) | Clutters the diagram and makes changes harder | Link only to immediate predecessors |
| Lags used instead of activities | Hidden work has no owner and is not tracked | Make any work in the gap a real activity |
| Circular logic (A needs B, B needs A) | The schedule cannot be calculated | Split one activity into two parts or rethink the sequence |
| Overusing start-to-finish | Confusing to read and easy to get backwards | Rewrite as FS where possible |
| Linking summary tasks | Hides which detailed activity actually drives the date | Link detailed activities and milestones, not summary rows |
| Missing external dependencies | The plan looks optimistic until the supplier or approver is late | Run a specific check for suppliers, approvals and other projects |
| Treating every link as mandatory | No room to recover when the schedule slips | Label discretionary links so you know what can be changed |
Once the logic is sound, the next step is to calculate and protect the critical path; see our [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) guide.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a task dependency?**
A task dependency is a logical relationship between two activities that controls when one (the successor) can start or finish relative to the other (the predecessor). Dependencies set the order of work and allow a schedule to calculate dates and the critical path.

**Q: What are the four types of task dependencies?**
Finish-to-start (the successor cannot start until the predecessor finishes), start-to-start (it cannot start until the predecessor starts), finish-to-finish (it cannot finish until the predecessor finishes) and start-to-finish (it cannot finish until the predecessor starts).

**Q: Which type of task dependency is most common?**
Finish-to-start. Most links in a typical schedule are FS, and it is the default type when you link tasks in most scheduling tools.

**Q: What is an example of a start-to-finish dependency?**
A hand-over: the night security shift cannot finish until the day shift has started, or an old system cannot be switched off until the new system goes live. Start-to-finish is the least common type.

**Q: What is the difference between mandatory and discretionary dependencies?**
A mandatory dependency (hard logic) is required by the nature of the work, the law or a contract, such as foundations before walls. A discretionary dependency (soft logic) is a preferred order based on best practice, and can be changed if you accept more risk.

**Q: What is an external dependency?**
A dependency on something outside the project team's control, such as a supplier delivery, a regulator's approval, another project's output or a client decision. Give each one an owner and track it as a milestone.

**Q: Can a task have more than one dependency?**
Yes. An activity can have several predecessors and several successors. When it has several predecessors, the one that finishes latest (the driving predecessor) sets its start date.

**Q: What happens when a dependency is delayed?**
Every successor moves by the amount of the delay, minus any float it has. If the delayed activity is on the critical path, the project end date moves too, unless you compress the schedule.

**Q: How do task dependencies affect the critical path?**
The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities, so it is defined by the dependencies. Adding, removing or changing a link can change which activities are critical and how long the project takes.

**Q: What is the difference between a dependency and a constraint?**
A dependency links two activities. A constraint is a limit on an activity or the project, such as a fixed date, a budget cap or limited resources. A constraint can override dependency logic, so use date constraints sparingly.

**Q: How do I show task dependencies on a Gantt chart?**
Enter the predecessors for each task and the tool draws arrows between the bars. The ends of the bars the arrow connects show the type: finish to start, start to start, finish to finish or start to finish.

**Q: What does 3FS+2d mean?**
It is Microsoft Project notation for a finish-to-start dependency on task 3 with a 2-day lag: the task can start 2 days after task 3 finishes. A bare 3 means finish-to-start with no lag.

**Q: What is a dependency matrix?**
A grid listing teams or workstreams on both axes, with each cell showing what one needs from the other and by when. It gives an overview of cross-team dependencies on larger programmes.

**Q: How do Agile teams manage dependencies?**
Within a team, by ordering the backlog and swarming on blocked items. Across teams, by linking work items (blocks / is blocked by), raising dependencies during refinement, mapping them at PI planning or a Scrum of Scrums, and designing teams to need fewer hand-offs.

# Technical Project Manager: Role, Skills and Career Path

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/technical-project-manager/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a technical project manager does, how the role differs from IT PMs and tech leads, the skills and certifications you need, and how to become one.


## Technical Project Manager: Role, Skills and Career Path
A technical project manager is a project manager with enough hands-on technical knowledge, usually in software, infrastructure, data or engineering, to plan and deliver technically complex projects and hold informed conversations with the people building them. This guide explains what the role involves day to day, how it differs from similar titles, the skills and certifications that help, and how to move into it, with two worked examples.
- Published 3 October 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- A technical project manager (TPM) combines delivery leadership with genuine technical understanding.
- Their technical knowledge is used to spot risks, test estimates and translate trade-offs, not to design the solution themselves.
- Agree decision rights with the tech lead early: the TPM owns how and when work is delivered, the tech lead owns how it is built.
- Many TPMs come from development, QA, infrastructure or data roles and add project management skills later.
- Useful credentials include the PMP or CAPM, Agile and Scrum certifications and platform certifications in your field.
- Job titles vary widely, so always judge a role by its description rather than its name.

### What is a technical project manager?
A **technical project manager** is a project manager who leads projects with significant technical complexity, such as software releases, system integrations, cloud migrations or infrastructure upgrades, and who understands the technology well enough to take part in design, estimation and risk discussions. They are accountable for delivering the project on time, within budget and to the agreed scope.
The role sits between the engineering team and the rest of the organisation. Engineers need someone who understands why an integration test environment matters; sponsors need someone who can explain, in business terms, why that environment affects the launch date. The TPM does both.
Watch out for the acronym. **TPM** can mean technical project manager or technical programme manager, and some companies use the titles interchangeably. A programme manager usually coordinates several related projects, so read the job description to see which role is meant. Technical project managers work in software companies, IT departments, digital agencies, telecoms, engineering firms and any organisation running technology change.

### What does a technical project manager do?
The responsibilities follow the project life cycle, with a technical angle at every stage.
| Phase | Core project management work | The technical angle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiation | Clarify objectives, stakeholders and constraints; help shape the business case | Check technical feasibility, dependencies on other systems and vendor constraints |
| Planning | Define scope, build the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/), schedule, budget and resource plan | Break work down by components and interfaces; plan environments, testing and releases; challenge estimates |
| Execution | Coordinate the team, remove blockers, manage suppliers and communicate progress | Follow technical decisions, track integration points and keep non-functional work (security, performance) visible |
| Monitoring and control | Track progress, cost, risks, issues and changes | Read signals from builds, defect trends and test results; assess the technical impact of change requests |
| Closure | Confirm acceptance, hand over and capture lessons | Plan cut-over and rollback, operational handover, runbooks and support arrangements |
In Agile teams some of these duties are shared with the Product Owner and Scrum Master, and the TPM's focus often shifts towards cross-team dependencies, release planning and stakeholder reporting. See our guide to [project manager roles and responsibilities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-roles-and-responsibilities/) for the general duties of the role.

#### A typical week (illustrative)
| Day | Typical activities |
| --- | --- |
| Monday | Review progress and the risk log; join sprint planning or a work-planning session; update the release plan |
| Tuesday | Architecture review on an integration; agree test environment dates with the infrastructure team |
| Wednesday | Supplier call on API changes; resolve a dependency with another product team; refine estimates with the tech lead |
| Thursday | Write the weekly status report; steering group meeting with the sponsor; assess a change request |
| Friday | Release readiness check; sprint review or demo; follow up actions and plan next week |
The balance changes with the project. Early on, more time goes into planning and technical discovery; near a release, most of the week is spent on readiness, risks and communication.

### What makes the role technical
Any project manager can run a schedule. What sets the technical project manager apart is the ability to use technical understanding to make better delivery decisions. In practice that means:
- **Understanding system architecture** well enough to see where the risks are: interfaces, shared databases, third-party services and legacy components.
- **Breaking technical work into a realistic plan**, including the work people forget, such as environments, data migration, test automation and deployment.
- **Challenging [effort estimates](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/)** with informed questions rather than accepting or cutting them blindly.
- **Keeping non-functional requirements visible**: performance, security, accessibility, reliability and compliance.
- **Managing technical debt** as a delivery risk, and making its cost visible to decision-makers.
- **Planning releases**, cut-overs and rollbacks with operations and support teams.
- **Translating technical trade-offs into business language** so sponsors can make informed decisions.
The depth needed depends on the organisation. A TPM in a platform engineering team may be expected to read code and design documents; one in a corporate IT department may need a broader understanding of systems, vendors and infrastructure.

### Technical project manager vs similar roles
Several job titles overlap with the technical project manager. The table shows the typical differences, although every organisation draws the lines a little differently.
| Role | Main focus | Technical depth | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Technical project manager | Delivering technically complex projects | High | Delivery plan, risks, schedule, stakeholder communication |
| Project manager | Delivering projects in any field | Varies | Delivery of the project |
| [IT project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/it-project-manager/) | Delivering technology projects, often infrastructure or business systems | Moderate to high | Delivery of IT change |
| Technical programme manager | Coordinating several related technical projects | High | Programme outcomes and cross-team dependencies |
| Engineering manager | Leading and growing engineers | High | People, hiring and engineering practices |
| Product manager | Deciding what to build and why | Varies | Product strategy, priorities and outcomes |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Helping a Scrum Team work effectively | Varies | Scrum practice and team effectiveness |
| Tech lead or architect | Technical direction and design | Very high | Technical design and quality |
The most common confusion is between project and programme roles. A technical programme manager usually spans several teams or projects contributing to one outcome, such as a platform migration, while a technical project manager usually delivers one project. See [project manager vs program manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-manager-vs-program-manager/) for the wider distinction.

### Who decides what: the TPM and the tech lead
The most frequent source of friction in this role is overlap with the tech lead or architect. A TPM with an engineering background can be tempted to design the solution; a tech lead can be tempted to run the plan. Agreeing decision rights at the start avoids that. The split below is a common starting point.
| Decision | Technical project manager | Tech lead or architect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overall delivery plan and milestones | Decides | Advises |
| Technical design and architecture | Advises on delivery impact | Decides |
| Effort estimates | Challenges and aggregates | Provides with the team |
| Order of work and release scope | Proposes with the Product Owner or sponsor | Advises on technical dependencies |
| Technical risk response | Owns the risk log and escalation | Owns the technical mitigation |
| Tooling and coding standards | Is consulted | Decides |
| Stakeholder and sponsor reporting | Decides content and owns it | Contributes |
Write the agreed split into a [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) and revisit it if the team or project changes shape.
Tip
A useful test: if a question is about how the system is built, the tech lead decides. If it is about when, in what order, at what cost or with what risk the work is delivered, the TPM decides or escalates.

### Technical project manager skills
Successful technical project managers combine three groups of skills. Employers look for evidence in all three.
| Skill group | What it includes | How to show it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Technical | Architecture basics, software development life cycle, cloud and infrastructure concepts, APIs and integration, testing, security basics, data | Past engineering roles, technical certifications, examples of technical risks you spotted early |
| Delivery | [Scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/), [scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/), estimation, [risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/), budgeting, change control, release planning, Agile and hybrid methods | Projects delivered, PM certifications, plans and risk logs you have built |
| People | [Stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/), communication with non-technical audiences, negotiation, facilitation, supplier management | Status reports, steering group experience, conflicts you resolved |
Of the three, communication is the one most often underestimated. A TPM who can explain why a database migration needs a weekend freeze, in two sentences a finance director understands, is far more valuable than one who can only discuss it with engineers. For a broader list, see our guide to [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/).

### Worked example: a payment API integration
This illustrative example shows how technical reading changes a plan. A retailer needs its online shop to connect to a new payment provider within 12 weeks, because the current provider's contract ends.

#### What the technical project manager spots
Reviewing the provider's API documentation in week 1, the TPM notices three things the initial plan missed:
1. Refunds use a different authentication method from payments, so they are not a small extension of the payments work.
2. The provider's sandbox does not simulate partial refunds, which the retailer's returns process relies on.
3. The security team's review, planned for week 9, must sign off the authentication design before it is built, not after.

#### Changes to the plan
The TPM adds a separate refunds work package to the WBS, moves the security review to week 3 and adds a pilot phase where a small share of live traffic uses the new provider before full rollout. To size the refunds work, they run a three-point estimate with the tech lead:
- Optimistic (O): 4 days. Most likely (M): 7 days. Pessimistic (P): 14 days.
- PERT estimate = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6 = (4 + 28 + 14) ÷ 6 = **7.7 days**.
- Standard deviation = (P − O) ÷ 6 = 10 ÷ 6 = **1.7 days**, so planning for about 9.5 days gives a reasonable buffer.
| Weeks | Work |
| --- | --- |
| 1–2 | Discovery, API review, sandbox access, architecture decision |
| 3 | Security review of the authentication design (moved forward from week 9) |
| 3–6 | Build payments integration |
| 5–7 | Build refunds integration (new work package) |
| 8–9 | End-to-end testing with the provider's sandbox and agreed test cases for partial refunds |
| 10 | Performance and failure testing; runbook and rollback plan |
| 11 | Pilot with a small share of live traffic behind a feature flag |
| 12 | Full rollout and early-life support |
The TPM also adds an entry to the [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/): 'Sandbox does not reproduce live refund behaviour, so defects may appear only in production.' The response is to request written test cases from the provider and rely on the pilot to catch issues while exposure is small, with the tech lead owning the technical mitigation.
Without that week-1 reading, refunds and the security review would probably have surfaced in weeks 8 to 9, too late to protect the contract deadline. Our [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) and [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) are useful starting points for this kind of plan.

### Worked example: explaining a technical trade-off to a sponsor
In this second illustrative example, the team discovers mid-project that a reporting module depends on a software library that is reaching end of support. Upgrading it properly will take three weeks. The sponsor does not need the technical detail; they need a decision framed in terms of time, cost and risk.
| Option | Delivery impact | Cost | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A. Release on time with a workaround | Launch date kept | About two sprints of rework later | Security patches stop when support ends; rework competes with new features |
| B. Delay three weeks to upgrade first | Launch moves by three weeks | Three weeks of team cost now | Lowest long-term risk; marketing launch must move |
| C. Phased: launch on time, upgrade in the next release | Launch date kept; upgrade fixed for the following release | Similar to B, spread over two releases | Short exposure window; needs a firm commitment to the second release |
The TPM recommends option C and sets out what the sponsor is agreeing to: the launch date stays, the upgrade is scheduled and protected in the next release, and the short-term risk is recorded and monitored. The engineering discussion about libraries happens separately with the tech lead. See our guide to [technical debt in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/) for more on making this kind of cost visible.

### Agile, waterfall and hybrid delivery
Technical project managers work across delivery approaches, and many projects mix them.
- **Agile and Scrum.** The Product Owner owns the backlog and the Scrum Master supports the team, so the TPM typically focuses on release planning, cross-team dependencies, risks, budgets and stakeholder communication. See [Agile software development](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-software-development/).
- **Kanban.** Common for platform, infrastructure and support teams. The TPM tracks flow, blockers and service commitments rather than sprint goals.
- **Waterfall or stage-gated.** Common for infrastructure, hardware and regulated projects, where design approval, procurement and testing gates are fixed. The TPM runs a more traditional plan with a baseline and formal change control.
- **Hybrid.** Very common in practice: a fixed-date programme plan with Agile teams delivering inside it. The TPM connects the two, turning sprint progress into milestone forecasts.
If you are moving from a traditional to an Agile environment, our guide to the [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) explains how the role changes.

### Tools technical project managers use
Most TPMs work across several tools: one for planning and tracking work, one for documentation, and the engineering team's own tools for code, builds and incidents. The table shows how some of the tools we review are typically used.
| Tool | Our rating | Typical use for a TPM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) | #1, 9.4/10 | Cross-functional projects and portfolios with custom workflows, dashboards and resource planning |
| monday.com | #2, 9.1/10 | Visual project boards and workflows that business stakeholders adopt quickly |
| Asana | #3, 9.0/10 | Cross-team task and goal tracking |
| ClickUp | #4, 8.9/10 | Tasks, docs, sprints and dashboards in one workspace at a lower price point |
| [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) | #6, 8.6/10 | Backlogs, sprints, boards and developer integrations for software teams |
A common pattern is for developers to work in Jira while the TPM and business teams plan and report in a broader work management tool. Wrike is a strong fit for that role: its Wrike Sync add-on can keep items aligned two-way with Jira and GitHub, so the TPM gets one view across engineering and non-engineering work without asking developers to change tools. Our [Wrike vs Jira comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/wrike-vs-jira/) covers the differences in detail.
Beyond work management, TPMs rely on documentation tools for decisions and runbooks, diagramming tools for architecture and process maps, and read-only access to build, deployment and monitoring dashboards so they can see delivery signals without waiting for someone to report them.

### How to become a technical project manager
There are two common routes into the role. Most TPMs start in a technical job and add project management; others start in project management and build technical depth.

#### From a developer, engineer or QA role
1. **Volunteer for coordination work.** Offer to run a release, coordinate a small integration or lead the team's planning for a sprint.
2. **Learn project management fundamentals:** scope, scheduling, estimation, risk, budgets and stakeholder management.
3. **Practise communicating upwards.** Write short status updates for a non-technical audience and ask for feedback.
4. **Get a recognised credential.** The CAPM or a Scrum certification is a good first step; the PMP once you meet its experience requirement.
5. **Build evidence.** Keep a record of projects you coordinated, decisions you influenced and risks you spotted.
6. **Apply for hybrid roles** such as technical lead with delivery duties, release manager or project coordinator in a technical team.

#### From a non-technical project management role
1. **Choose a technical domain** that matches your organisation or target employers, such as cloud, data or software delivery.
2. **Learn the basics properly:** the software development life cycle, how APIs and integrations work, testing types and deployment pipelines.
3. **Take a foundation-level platform certification** to structure your learning and show commitment.
4. **Sit with engineering teams**: attend design reviews and retrospectives and ask questions.
5. **Move into an IT or digital project** where your delivery skills are already valued, then grow technical depth on the job.
Our guide on [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/) covers the general career path in more detail.

### Certifications for technical project managers
No single certification is required, but credentials help, especially when changing career. Most TPMs combine a project management certification with something specific to their technical field.
| Certification | Best for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) | Experienced project managers | Requires three to five years of project leadership within the last 10 years depending on education (two with a GAC-accredited degree), plus 35 hours of training or an active CAPM. The current exam launched in July 2026 |
| [CAPM](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) | Those new to project management | Entry-level PMI credential; no project experience required |
| PMI-ACP | TPMs in Agile environments | PMI's Agile certification, covering several Agile approaches |
| [Scrum certifications](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/) | Working with Scrum Teams | Such as Professional Scrum Master or Certified ScrumMaster |
| CompTIA Project+ | IT professionals starting in project work | Vendor-neutral, entry-level project management certification |
| Cloud or platform certifications | Building technical credibility | From cloud providers and platform vendors relevant to your work |
If you are planning the PMP, note that from 1 December 2026 live instructor-led training only counts towards the 35 hours if it comes from a PMI Authorized Training Partner or an eligible accredited programme. See our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) for the full requirements.

### Technical project manager salary
Pay varies widely by country, industry, seniority and how the role is defined, so treat any single figure as a rough guide. Published US data gives a sense of the range:
- The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median annual wage of **$102,320** for project management specialists, the broad occupation that includes most project managers, in its May 2025 data.
- For **computer and information systems managers**, which covers senior technology management roles, the BLS reports a median of **$175,140** (May 2025), with employment projected to grow 16% from 2025 to 2035.
- Coursera, citing Glassdoor data accessed in July 2026, reports a US median total pay of about **$138,000** for technical project managers, including bonuses.
Outside the US, check national salary surveys and current job adverts for your location. When comparing offers, look at the scope of the role (one team or many), the technical depth expected and whether the role includes people management, as these drive pay more than the job title.

### Technical project manager interview questions
Interviews usually combine project management, technical and behavioural questions. The table shows common questions and what a strong answer demonstrates.
| Question | What a strong answer shows |
| --- | --- |
| Tell us about the most technically complex project you delivered. | You understood the technical risks and explain them clearly, without jargon |
| How do you handle an estimate you think is too optimistic? | You challenge with questions and data, involve the team and do not simply impose a number |
| Describe a time you disagreed with a tech lead. | Respect for decision rights, focus on outcomes, and a clear resolution |
| How would you explain technical debt to a sponsor? | Business framing: cost, risk and options, not code detail |
| How do you plan a release with dependencies on other teams? | Dependency mapping, early agreements, contingency and communication |
| What do you do when a critical issue appears the day before launch? | Calm triage, go or no-go criteria, rollback plan and honest communication |
| How technical are you? | An honest, specific answer with examples of how you used that knowledge |

### Common pitfalls
- **Designing the solution yourself.** Your role is to enable good technical decisions, not to make them all. Contribute, then let the tech lead decide.
- **Getting lost in technical detail** and missing schedule, budget or stakeholder risks.
- **Using jargon with sponsors.** Translate every technical point into impact on time, cost, scope or risk.
- **Under-estimating integration and testing.** These are where technical projects most often slip; plan them explicitly.
- **Ignoring non-functional work** such as security reviews, performance testing and operational readiness until late.
- **Letting technical knowledge go stale.** Set aside time to keep up with the technologies your teams use.
- **Becoming the single point of contact for everything.** Encourage direct conversations between engineers and stakeholders where that is faster.
Tip
Agree with the tech lead, in the first week, where your role stops and theirs begins. Writing it down takes ten minutes and prevents months of friction.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a technical project manager?**
A project manager with strong technical knowledge, usually in software, infrastructure, data or engineering, who leads technically complex projects and can take part in design, estimation and risk discussions while owning delivery.

**Q: What does a technical project manager do day to day?**
Plans and tracks work, manages risks and dependencies, joins technical reviews, coordinates releases and suppliers, and reports progress to stakeholders in business terms.

**Q: Is a technical project manager the same as an IT project manager?**
They overlap a lot. Technical project manager roles usually expect deeper hands-on knowledge of the technology, while IT project manager roles can be broader and more focused on business systems and infrastructure.

**Q: What is the difference between a technical project manager and a technical programme manager?**
A technical programme manager coordinates several related technical projects or teams towards a shared outcome, while a technical project manager usually delivers one project. Some companies use the titles interchangeably.

**Q: Do technical project managers need to code?**
Usually not as part of the job, but many have a development or engineering background. You need to understand how software is built, tested and released well enough to discuss it credibly.

**Q: What background do technical project managers have?**
Often software development, quality assurance, systems administration, infrastructure, data or engineering, followed by project coordination or delivery roles.

**Q: Which certifications help a technical project manager?**
The PMP or CAPM for project management, PMI-ACP or a Scrum certification for Agile work, CompTIA Project+ for IT professionals, and cloud or platform certifications relevant to your field.

**Q: How do I move from developer to technical project manager?**
Volunteer to coordinate releases or small projects, learn project management fundamentals, practise communicating with non-technical stakeholders and consider an entry-level certification such as the CAPM.

**Q: Can a non-technical project manager become a technical project manager?**
Yes. Choose a technical domain, learn its fundamentals, take a foundation-level platform certification and work closely with engineering teams on IT or digital projects to build depth.

**Q: What tools do technical project managers use?**
Jira is common for software teams, with broader work management platforms such as Wrike used for cross-functional planning and reporting, plus documentation, diagramming and build or deployment dashboards.

**Q: How much do technical project managers earn?**
It depends on location, sector and seniority. In the US, the BLS reports a May 2025 median of $102,320 for project management specialists overall; Glassdoor data cited by Coursera puts the median total pay for technical project manager titles at about $138,000.

**Q: Is technical project manager a good career?**
It suits people who enjoy both technology and organising people and work. It offers routes into programme management, delivery leadership and engineering management.

**Q: What is the hardest part of being a technical project manager?**
Balancing technical depth with the wider delivery and stakeholder work, and resisting the urge to solve every technical problem yourself.
