# Waterfall Project Management: Phases, Pros, Cons & Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Waterfall project management explained: the phases, deliverables and gates, a worked example, pros and cons, when to use it and how it compares with Agile.


## Waterfall Project Management: Phases, Pros, Cons & Example
Waterfall project management is a sequential, plan-driven approach in which a project moves through fixed phases, such as requirements, design, build, test and deployment, with each phase finished and approved before the next begins. It works best when requirements are stable and the result only has value once it is complete. This guide covers the phases and their deliverables, how to run a waterfall project step by step, a worked example, the pros and cons and how waterfall compares with Agile.
- Published 7 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Waterfall is a predictive approach: you define scope, schedule and cost up front, baseline them and control the project against that plan.
- Typical phases are requirements, design, implementation, verification, deployment and maintenance, separated by phase gates where sponsors approve the work.
- It suits stable requirements, regulated or contract-driven work, physical builds and teams repeating a familiar type of project.
- Its main weakness is late feedback: users see the result near the end, when changes are most expensive.
- Royce's 1970 paper, usually cited as the origin, actually warned against a single pass and recommended feedback between phases.
- Many organisations now use hybrids: waterfall governance and milestones with iterative delivery inside some phases.

### What is waterfall project management?
**Waterfall project management** is a linear way of running a project in which the work flows through a series of phases in a fixed order: requirements, design, build, test, deploy and support. Each phase produces approved deliverables that become the input to the next. Scope, schedule and budget are planned in detail at the start and changes go through formal change control.
PMI and the PMBOK Guide describe this style as a **predictive** approach, because you predict and commit to the outcome early, then manage the project against a baseline. Agile approaches are described as **adaptive**, and a mix of the two as **hybrid**. Waterfall is the classic, best-known form of predictive delivery.
Three ideas sit at the heart of waterfall:
- **Sequence.** Phases follow one another. You do not start building until the design is approved, and you do not release until testing is complete.
- **Up-front definition.** The project requirements and project scope are agreed and signed off early, so estimates and contracts can be based on them.
- **Control against a plan.** A [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) for scope, time and cost is set before execution, and progress is measured against it.
Waterfall is still widely used in construction, engineering, manufacturing, defence, government, infrastructure and parts of regulated IT, where a design must be approved before money is spent on building it.

### Where the waterfall model came from
The sequential model is usually traced to a 1970 paper by Winston W. Royce, "Managing the Development of Large Software Systems". Royce drew the familiar cascade of phases, but he did not recommend running them in a single pass. He described that version as risky and argued for feedback between phases, early prototyping, heavy documentation and doing the job twice, so that a pilot version informed the final one.
Royce never used the word "waterfall". The label is generally traced to later writers, with a 1976 paper by Bell and Thayer often cited as an early use. The irony is that the paper most often quoted as the source of rigid waterfall was one of its first critics.
Phase-by-phase delivery is older than software, however. Construction and engineering projects have long separated feasibility, design, procurement, construction and commissioning, because changing a design after concrete is poured or steel is fabricated is extremely expensive.

### The phases of waterfall project management
Sources name and count the phases differently, from five to seven. The six below are the most common. Whatever names you use, each phase should have a clear purpose, defined deliverables and exit criteria.
| Phase | Purpose | Key deliverables | Typical exit criteria |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Requirements | Define what the solution must do and the constraints it must meet | Requirements specification, acceptance criteria, scope statement | Requirements signed off by the sponsor and key users |
| 2. Design | Decide how the solution will meet the requirements | High-level and detailed design, specifications, test strategy | Design review passed; traceability to requirements confirmed |
| 3. Implementation | Build, configure, construct or manufacture the solution | Built components, unit-tested code, constructed works | All components complete and unit tested |
| 4. Verification | Prove the solution meets the requirements | Test plans, test results, defect log, user acceptance sign-off | Agreed defect thresholds met; acceptance signed |
| 5. Deployment | Release or hand over the solution to users | Go-live plan, training, handover documents | Go-live checklist complete; operations accept handover |
| 6. Maintenance | Support, fix and improve after release | Support model, warranty fixes, lessons learned | Warranty period ends; project formally closed |

#### 1. Requirements
You gather and document everything the solution must do: functional requirements (features and behaviour), non-functional requirements (performance, security, accessibility) and constraints such as regulation, budget and dates. Interviews, workshops, document analysis and observation are the usual techniques. The output is a requirements specification that is precise enough to design, estimate and test against. Ambiguous requirements are the most common root cause of waterfall failures, so this phase deserves more time than teams usually give it.

#### 2. Design
The team turns requirements into a solution. In software this means architecture, data models, interfaces and screen designs; in construction it means drawings and specifications; in manufacturing it means engineering designs and tooling plans. Many projects split design into a high-level (outline) design and a detailed design, each with its own review. A traceability matrix links every requirement to the design element that satisfies it and, later, the test that proves it.

#### 3. Implementation
This is the build phase, usually the longest and most resource-intensive. Work is organised using the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) into [work packages](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/) with owners, estimates and dates. The project manager tracks progress against the schedule and cost baselines and reports variances.

#### 4. Verification
The solution is tested against the requirements: system testing, integration testing, performance and security testing and, finally, user acceptance testing (UAT). Defects are logged, prioritised and fixed. Because testing comes late, it often gets squeezed when earlier phases overrun, so protect its duration in the schedule.

#### 5. Deployment
The solution goes live or is handed over. Activities include data migration, cutover planning, training, communications and a go/no-go decision. In construction this is commissioning and handover; in manufacturing it is the start of production.

#### 6. Maintenance
After go-live the solution is supported, defects found in live use are fixed and small enhancements are made. Many projects define a warranty or hypercare period after which support transfers to business as usual and the project is formally closed.
Tip
Do not confuse these delivery phases with the project management life cycle (initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, closing). The life cycle wraps around the delivery phases: you initiate and plan before requirements start and close after handover. See our guide to [project management phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/).

### Phase gates and sign-offs
A **phase gate** (also called a stage gate or decision point) is a formal review at the end of a phase where the sponsor or a steering group decides whether the project should continue. Gates are what make waterfall controllable: they stop a project drifting into the next phase on the strength of unfinished or unapproved work.
At each gate the decision-makers typically choose one of four outcomes:
| Decision | Meaning | When it is used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Go | Approve the phase and release funding for the next one | Exit criteria are met and the business case still holds |
| Hold | Pause until a condition is met | A dependency, funding or approval is outstanding |
| Recycle | Rework the current phase | Deliverables are incomplete or quality is not acceptable |
| Stop | Close the project | The business case no longer holds or risk is too high |
A simple gate checklist covers five questions: Are the phase deliverables complete and approved? Does the next phase have an updated plan, budget and resources? Are the top risks and issues understood and owned? Is the business case still valid? Are any open change requests resolved or explicitly carried forward?

### How to run a waterfall project step by step
The steps below follow a typical waterfall project from approval to closure. Scale the documentation to the size and risk of the project: a three-month internal project needs far less than a multi-year contract.
1. **Initiate the project.** Write a [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) that names the sponsor and project manager, states objectives, high-level scope, budget and key dates, and authorises the work.
2. **Gather and sign off requirements.** Run workshops and interviews, document requirements with acceptance criteria and get formal sign-off. Agree how requirements will be changed later.
3. **Define the scope and WBS.** Turn the requirements into a scope statement and a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) that covers 100% of the work, broken down to work packages. Use our [WBS template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/).
4. **Estimate effort, duration and cost.** Estimate each work package bottom up, add contingency for known risks and build the budget.
5. **Build the schedule.** Break work packages into activities, add task dependencies, assign resources and calculate the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/). Show it on a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/).
6. **Set the baselines.** Once the plan is approved, save the scope, schedule and cost baselines. Every later variance is measured against them.
7. **Plan risk, quality and communications.** Start a risk register, define quality checks and testing, and agree who receives which reports and when.
8. **Execute phase by phase.** Deliver each phase's work, hold reviews and pass each phase gate before starting the next. Report progress with a regular project status report.
9. **Control changes formally.** Log every change request, assess its impact on scope, time, cost and risk, and get a decision from the change authority before acting. See [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
10. **Test and accept.** Complete system and user acceptance testing against the signed-off requirements, fix defects and obtain formal acceptance.
11. **Deploy and hand over.** Execute the go-live or handover plan, train users and transfer the solution to operations or the client.
12. **Close the project.** Confirm all deliverables are accepted, release resources, close contracts, archive documents and capture lessons learned. See our guide to [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/).

### Waterfall project management example
The following example is **illustrative**: the organisation, figures and dates are invented to show how the phases, gates and change control fit together.
A 400-person organisation is replacing its payroll system. The new system must be live before the start of the next tax year, the requirements are largely dictated by payroll law and company policy, and the vendor contract is fixed price against an agreed specification. Those three facts (a fixed deadline, stable requirements and a fixed-price contract) make a waterfall approach a sensible choice.
| Phase | Planned duration | Main deliverables | Gate decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | 4 weeks | Requirements specification (180 requirements), data migration scope, acceptance criteria | Gate 1: Go, signed by the HR director and finance director |
| Design | 5 weeks | Configuration design, interface specifications for HR and finance systems, test strategy | Gate 2: Recycle for one week; two interface designs incomplete, then Go |
| Implementation | 10 weeks | Configured system, built interfaces, three trial data migrations | Gate 3: Go |
| Verification | 6 weeks | System test, two parallel payroll runs against the old system, UAT sign-off | Gate 4: Go, with two low-priority defects accepted |
| Deployment | 2 weeks | Final migration, cutover, training for 12 payroll staff, go-live | Go-live approved at a go/no-go meeting |
| Maintenance | 8 weeks hypercare | Defect fixes, first live payroll runs, handover to the support team | Project closure report approved |

#### Handling a change request
During verification, the finance team asks for a new monthly cost-centre report that was not in the signed-off requirements. Under waterfall, the request is not simply added to the build. The project manager logs it and runs an impact assessment:
- **Scope:** one new report, plus changes to two existing interfaces.
- **Schedule:** about 6 days of extra build and testing effort on the critical path, which would push go-live past the tax year deadline.
- **Cost:** a quoted vendor change of £4,800 (illustrative figure).
- **Risk:** retesting interfaces late in the project increases the chance of defects at go-live.
The change control board decides to **defer** the report to a post-go-live enhancement, protecting the fixed deadline. The decision, the reason and the new delivery date are recorded in the change log and communicated to finance. That is waterfall working as intended: change is possible, but it is a deliberate decision with known consequences rather than scope creep.

#### What the example shows
- Gate 2 caught incomplete designs before they turned into build defects. Recycling one phase cost a week; finding the gaps in testing would have cost far more.
- Two parallel payroll runs gave the business evidence, not just assurance, that the new system produced correct results.

### Advantages of waterfall
| Advantage | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Clear structure and milestones | Everyone knows what phase the project is in, what comes next and what "done" means for each phase. |
| Predictable scope, cost and schedule | With stable requirements you can estimate, budget and commit to dates early, which sponsors and finance teams value. |
| Fits contracts and regulation | Fixed-price contracts, public procurement and regulated industries often require approved specifications and sign-offs. |
| Thorough documentation | Requirements, designs and test records support audits, handovers, staff changes and long-term maintenance. |
| Less demand on stakeholders' time | Users and sponsors are heavily involved at the start and at gates, rather than continuously. |
| Easy to understand | New team members and external stakeholders grasp a sequential plan quickly; it maps naturally to a Gantt chart. |
| Good for dependencies on physical work | Where later work physically depends on earlier work (foundations before walls), sequencing is not optional. |

### Disadvantages of waterfall and how to reduce them
| Disadvantage | What happens | How to reduce it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Late feedback | Users see the working solution near the end, when changes are expensive | Use prototypes, mock-ups or a pilot during design; hold design walkthroughs with real users |
| Costly change | A requirement change after design can ripple through build and test | Invest in requirements quality; use formal change control and a contingency reserve |
| Risks found late | Integration problems and misunderstood requirements surface in testing | Test critical integrations early; run a technical spike or proof of concept in design |
| Testing gets squeezed | Overruns in build eat into the test window | Protect test duration on the critical path; set entry criteria for testing |
| No value until the end | Benefits arrive only after deployment | Split large projects into phased releases, each delivering usable value |
| Assumes requirements can be known | For new products or uncertain markets, early specifications are guesses | Choose an Agile or hybrid approach where uncertainty is high |
Most of these weaknesses are not arguments against planning; they are arguments against a single pass with no feedback. That is exactly what Royce warned about in 1970.

### When to use waterfall (and when not to)
Use the checklist below to judge whether a project leans towards waterfall, Agile or a hybrid. A project rarely ticks every box; look at where most of the answers fall.
| Project characteristic | Leans waterfall | Leans Agile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | Stable, known and can be written down | Unclear, likely to change or discovered through use |
| Value | Only useful when complete (a bridge, a payroll system) | Useful in increments (a website, an app) |
| Cost of change late on | Very high (physical, contractual or regulatory) | Low (software that can be released often) |
| Contract | Fixed price against a specification | Time and materials or outcome based |
| Regulation and audit | Formal approvals and documentation required | Lighter documentation is acceptable |
| Stakeholder availability | Limited; available at key points | Available frequently to give feedback |
| Team experience | Has delivered similar projects before | Doing something new |
| Technology | Mature and well understood | New, experimental or fast-changing |
Typical good fits for waterfall include construction and fit-out projects, infrastructure, equipment installation, regulated system validation, data centre moves, office relocations, events with a fixed date and repeatable implementation projects where the method is well proven.
Typical poor fits are new digital products, research and innovation work, marketing experiments and any project where users cannot describe what they need until they see something working. For these, see [what is Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/).

### Waterfall vs Agile
Waterfall and Agile answer the same question (how do we deliver this project?) with different assumptions about uncertainty.
| Aspect | Waterfall | Agile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planning | Detailed plan up front, baselined | High-level plan, detailed planning each iteration |
| Scope | Fixed; time and cost estimated from it | Flexible; time and cost often fixed, scope varies |
| Delivery | One release at the end (or a few large ones) | Frequent small increments |
| Customer involvement | Heavy at start and at gates | Continuous |
| Change | Controlled through formal change requests | Expected; reprioritised in the backlog |
| Testing | A separate phase after build | Built into every iteration |
| Documentation | Comprehensive | Just enough |
| Progress measure | Planned vs actual against baselines, milestones, earned value | Working increments, velocity, burndown |
| Project manager role | Plans, directs and controls against the baseline | Often shared across product owner, Scrum Master and team |
Neither is better in general. The right choice depends on the project characteristics above, and many organisations use both. For a full comparison see our guide to [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).
If you are weighing specific frameworks, we also compare [Scrum vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/), and our overview of [project management methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-methodologies/) covers PRINCE2, Lean, Six Sigma and Critical Chain alongside them.

### Variations of the waterfall model

#### V-model
The V-model bends the waterfall into a V. The left side descends through requirements, system design, architecture and detailed design; the bottom is coding; the right side climbs back up through unit, integration, system and acceptance testing. Each design level is paired with the test level that verifies it, and test plans are written at the same time as the design. It is common in safety-critical and regulated fields such as automotive, medical devices and defence.

#### Waterfall with feedback and overlapping phases
Here phases are allowed to overlap slightly, and the team can return to the previous phase when a problem is found. Design might start on well-understood requirements while others are still being finalised. This is closer to what Royce actually recommended and to how most real waterfall projects run. The risk is rework if early decisions change, so overlaps should be managed deliberately.

#### Phased or incremental waterfall
A large scope is split into several releases, each run as a mini-waterfall. A system might go live for one region first, then others; a building might be handed over floor by floor. This brings value and feedback earlier while keeping predictive control within each release. See [iterative and incremental development](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/iterative-and-incremental-development/).

#### Hybrid approaches
Hybrid models combine waterfall governance (a charter, budget, phase gates and milestone dates) with Agile delivery inside some phases. A common pattern, sometimes nicknamed "water-scrum-fall", runs requirements and funding in a predictive way, builds in Scrum sprints, then uses a formal release and deployment phase. Methods such as [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) also support this: its management stages and stage boundaries give control, while delivery inside a stage can be Agile.

### Common waterfall mistakes
- **Signing off vague requirements.** "The system should be user friendly" cannot be designed or tested. Write requirements with measurable acceptance criteria.
- **Treating sign-off as a formality.** If sponsors approve documents they have not read, problems pass through the gate and resurface in testing.
- **Skipping the baseline.** Without a saved baseline you cannot measure variance, and status reports become opinions.
- **Absorbing changes informally.** Small "while you are at it" additions accumulate into delays. Route every change through change control.
- **Squeezing testing to recover the schedule.** Cutting test time moves defects into live use, where they cost more. Recover time elsewhere or agree a new date.
- **No user involvement between requirements and UAT.** Show designs, prototypes or demonstrations to users during design and build, even in a waterfall project.
- **Using waterfall for an uncertain product.** If nobody can say what good looks like, a predictive plan will be wrong. Choose a hybrid or Agile approach instead.

### Tools and templates for waterfall projects
Waterfall projects lean heavily on scheduling, so the most useful tools are those with strong Gantt charts, dependencies, the critical path and baselines.
- **Templates.** For small projects a spreadsheet is enough. Start with our [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/), [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) and [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/), and use the [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) to log changes.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, includes interactive Gantt charts from the Team plan with all four dependency types, the critical path and baselines for planned-versus-actual tracking, which suits date-driven, multi-phase projects and PMOs running many of them.
- **[Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/)** combines a familiar spreadsheet grid with Gantt charts, dependencies and critical path highlighting, which many construction and enterprise planning teams find natural.
- **[Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/)** premium plans offer timelines and dependencies, with baselines and critical path on Planner and Project Plan 3, which suits organisations already standardised on Microsoft 365.
- **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)** and **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** both offer Gantt views with dependencies and milestones, and suit teams that run waterfall and Agile work side by side.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the phases of waterfall?**
The most common list is requirements, design, implementation, verification (testing), deployment and maintenance. Some sources merge or rename phases, giving five or seven, but the sequence is the same.

**Q: Is waterfall outdated?**
No. It remains a sound choice for stable, regulated, contract-driven or physical projects, such as construction, infrastructure and system validation. It is less suitable for new products where requirements are uncertain.

**Q: Who created the waterfall model?**
The sequence is usually traced to Winston Royce's 1970 paper on managing large software systems. Royce warned that a single pass was risky and recommended feedback and iteration. He did not use the word "waterfall", which was applied by later authors.

**Q: What is the main difference between waterfall and Agile?**
Waterfall fixes scope up front and delivers in one sequence of phases; Agile delivers in short iterations, gathers feedback continuously and lets scope change as the team learns.

**Q: When should you use waterfall?**
When requirements are stable and well understood, the result only has value once complete, late changes are expensive, a contract or regulator requires approved stages, or the team has delivered similar projects before.

**Q: What is an example of a waterfall project?**
Constructing a building, replacing a payroll system to a fixed legal deadline, installing manufacturing equipment or relocating an office. Each has a defined end state and a natural order of phases.

**Q: What is the V-model?**
A variant of waterfall that pairs each design phase with a matching test phase, so acceptance tests are planned against requirements, system tests against the system design and so on. It is common in safety-critical industries.

**Q: Is waterfall the same as predictive project management?**
Broadly, yes. Predictive is the wider term PMI uses for approaches that define scope, schedule and cost early and control against a baseline. Waterfall is its classic form.

**Q: Can waterfall and Agile be combined?**
Yes. Hybrid approaches use waterfall-style governance, budgets and milestones with Agile delivery inside some phases, or run fixed-scope parts of a project predictively and uncertain parts iteratively.

**Q: Can you go back to a previous phase in waterfall?**
In practice, yes, though it should be a controlled decision. A gate can recycle a phase, and a change request can reopen approved requirements or designs, with the impact on time and cost assessed first.

**Q: Do waterfall projects use Gantt charts?**
Yes. Gantt charts are the standard way to show phases, activities, dependencies, milestones and the critical path in a waterfall schedule, and to compare actual progress with the baseline.

**Q: Is PRINCE2 a waterfall method?**
Not exactly. PRINCE2 is a project management method with management stages and stage boundaries that can be used with either predictive or Agile delivery. It is often used to govern waterfall projects, but it does not require them.

**Q: What documents does a waterfall project need?**
Typically a project charter, requirements specification, design documents, project management plan with schedule and budget baselines, risk register, change log, test plans and results, acceptance sign-offs and a closure report with lessons learned. Scale them to the project's size and risk.

# What Is a Project? Definition, Characteristics, Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-a-project/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What is a project? A clear definition, the key characteristics, project vs operations and tasks, types of projects, examples and the project life cycle.


## What Is a Project? Definition, Characteristics, Examples
A project is a temporary piece of work, with a defined start and end, undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. That is the definition used by PMI, and the two words that matter most are temporary and unique. This guide explains what makes something a project, how projects differ from everyday operations, tasks and programmes, and gives examples and a quick checklist you can use on your own work.
- Published 4 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 16 min read

### Key takeaways
- A project is temporary and creates something unique: it ends when its objective is met, or when it is stopped.
- Every project has an objective, a defined scope, deliverables, stakeholders and constraints of time, cost and quality.
- Operations keep the organisation running; projects change it. A project usually hands its result over to operations.
- Related projects can be grouped into a programme, and all of an organisation's change work forms its portfolio.
- Projects move through a life cycle from initiation to closure, using a predictive, adaptive (Agile) or hybrid approach.

### What is a project?
A **project** is a temporary endeavour with a defined beginning and end, undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. It has a specific objective, works within limits of time, budget and resources, and is carried out by a team brought together for the purpose. When the objective is achieved, or the project is stopped, the project ends.
In plain words, a project is a one-off piece of work with a goal and a finish line. Redesigning a website, opening a new office, launching a product or running a conference are all projects. Answering customer emails every day is not, because it never ends and each day looks much like the last.

#### Standard definitions of a project
The main project management standards describe a project in slightly different words, but they agree on the essentials: it is temporary, it delivers something specific and it exists for a purpose.
| Source | Definition (summarised) | What it emphasises |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PMI (PMBOK Guide) | A temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result | Temporary and unique output |
| PRINCE2 | A temporary organisation created to deliver one or more business products according to an agreed business case | The organisation around the work and the business case |
| ISO 21502:2020 | A temporary endeavour to achieve one or more defined objectives | Defined objectives |
If you are studying for an exam, learn the PMI wording for the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) and CAPM/PMP, and the PRINCE2 wording for [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/). In practice, all three point you to the same questions: what are we delivering, why, by when and within what limits?

#### What "temporary" and "unique" really mean
- **Temporary does not mean short.** A project can last two weeks or ten years. Temporary means it has a planned end, not that it is quick.
- **The result can last.** A bridge built by a project may stand for a century. The project is temporary; its output is not.
- **Unique does not mean never done before.** Your company may have moved office three times, but this move, to this building, with these people and this budget, is still unique.
- **The team is usually temporary too.** People join from different departments or suppliers and return to their normal roles when the project closes.

### Key characteristics of a project
Most textbooks list five to seven characteristics. These are the ones that help you recognise a project and plan it well:
1. **Temporary:** it has a defined start and end date, and closes when the objective is met or the project is cancelled.
2. **Unique result:** it creates a new product, service, result or change, even if similar work has been done before.
3. **Specific objective:** there is a clear, agreed goal, ideally written as [SMART project objectives](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-objectives/).
4. **Defined deliverables:** the outputs the project must hand over, such as a building, a system, a report or a trained team. See [project deliverables](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/).
5. **Constraints:** limits on time, cost, scope, quality, resources and risk. Changing one usually affects the others; see [project constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/).
6. **Progressive elaboration:** plans start broad and become more detailed as the team learns more, rather than being complete on day one.
7. **Uncertainty and risk:** because the work is new, projects carry more risk than routine work and need active risk management.
PRINCE2 adds a useful point: projects are usually **cross-functional**. They draw people together from different teams, departments or suppliers, which is why clear roles, a sponsor and good communication matter so much.

### Elements of a project
Whatever its size, every project has the same basic building blocks. Writing each of them down, even briefly, is the quickest way to turn an idea into something you can manage.
| Element | What it is | Where it is usually recorded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Objective | The measurable outcome the project exists to achieve | Business case, [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) |
| Scope | The work and outputs included, and what is excluded | [Project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) statement |
| Deliverables | The tangible or intangible outputs handed over | Scope statement, [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) |
| Sponsor | The senior person who authorises, funds and champions the project | Charter, governance plan |
| Project manager and team | The people who plan and do the work | Charter, RACI matrix |
| Stakeholders | Anyone affected by or able to influence the project | Stakeholder register |
| Schedule and milestones | When the work happens and the key checkpoints | Schedule, [project milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) |
| Budget | The money and resources approved | Budget, cost plan |
| Risks and assumptions | What could go wrong, and what you are taking for granted | Risk register, RAID log |
| Success criteria | How you will judge whether the project worked | Charter, business case |
Small projects can capture all of this on a single page. Our free [project brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-brief-template/) and [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) are built around these elements.

### Project vs operations
The most important distinction in project management is between projects and operations (sometimes called business as usual, or BAU). Operations keep the organisation running. Projects change it.
|  | Project | Operations (business as usual) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Duration | Temporary, with a planned end | Ongoing, no planned end |
| Output | Unique product, service or result | Repeated products or services |
| Goal | Achieve a specific objective, then close | Sustain and improve the business |
| Team | Often temporary and cross-functional | Stable, functional team |
| Risk | Higher: the work is new | Lower: the process is known |
| Funding | A specific budget, approved for the project | Recurring operating budget |
| Example | Implement a new payroll system | Run payroll every month |
The two are closely connected. Most projects end by handing their result over to operations: the new payroll system becomes part of the finance team's monthly routine. Planning that hand-over (training, support, documentation and ownership) is part of the project, not an afterthought.
Tip
Some work sits in between. A continuous improvement team that makes a stream of small changes is usually run as operations or with a Kanban flow, while a larger improvement with its own budget and deadline is worth running as a project.

### Project vs task, programme and portfolio
People often use "project" loosely for anything from a single to-do item to a multi-year change programme. These are the four levels most organisations use:
|  | Task | Project | Programme | Portfolio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A single piece of work, usually done by one person | A temporary effort to create a unique result | A group of related projects managed together for shared benefits | All the projects, programmes and related work an organisation funds to meet its strategy |
| Typical length | Hours to days | Weeks to a few years | Several years | Ongoing |
| Measure of success | Done or not done | Deliverables on time, on budget, to scope and quality | Benefits realised | Strategic value and return |
| Led by | The person assigned | Project manager | Programme manager | Portfolio manager or board |
| Example | Book the venue | Run the annual conference | Customer engagement programme | All of the company's change initiatives |
A project is made up of many [tasks and activities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-tasks-and-activities/). Several projects may belong to a programme, and every project and programme should fit somewhere in the portfolio.

### Why projects are started
Projects do not appear from nowhere. Each one should exist for a reason that matters to the organisation. Common drivers include:
- **Strategy:** delivering a strategic goal, such as entering a new market or modernising systems.
- **Customer or stakeholder requests:** a client contract, a new feature customers have asked for, or a request from another department.
- **Regulation and compliance:** a new law, safety standard or audit finding the organisation must respond to.
- **Problems to fix:** a failing system, a quality issue or a process that no longer copes.
- **Opportunities and new technology:** automating manual work, adopting AI tools or launching a new product.
- **Social and environmental goals:** reducing emissions, improving accessibility or supporting a community.
In a well-run organisation, the reason is written down in a business case, which compares costs, benefits and risks, and the project is formally authorised with a [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/). Our [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) gives you a structure for the first of these.

### Types of projects
There is no single official list of project types. Classifying a project helps you choose the right approach, people and level of control.

#### By industry or field
- **IT and software:** new systems, upgrades, migrations, apps and websites.
- **Construction and engineering:** buildings, infrastructure, fit-outs and plant.
- **Business change:** restructures, new processes, mergers and policy changes.
- **Marketing and creative:** campaigns, rebrands, product launches and content.
- **Research and development:** new products, studies and prototypes.
- **Events:** conferences, launches, festivals and internal events.
- **Public sector and community:** services, programmes funded by grants and civic infrastructure.

#### By delivery approach
| Approach | How it works | Suits projects where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predictive (Waterfall) | Plan most of the work up front, then deliver in phases | Requirements are clear and stable, such as construction |
| Adaptive (Agile) | Deliver in short iterations and adjust based on feedback | Requirements are uncertain or likely to change, such as software |
| Hybrid | Combine a predictive plan with Agile delivery for some parts | Some parts are fixed and others need flexibility |

#### By size and complexity
Small projects (a few people, a few weeks) need a light plan and simple tracking. Medium projects need a schedule, budget, risk log and regular reporting. Large or complex projects, with many stakeholders, suppliers or dependencies, need formal [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) and may be split into stages or grouped into a programme.

#### By sponsor and funding
- **Internal projects** improve the organisation itself, such as a new HR system.
- **External or client projects** are delivered for a customer under a contract or statement of work.
- **Public, private or mixed funding** affects approval rules, reporting and procurement.

### Examples of projects
These examples show how the same definition applies across very different fields:
| Field | Project | Main deliverable | Typical constraint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IT | Migrate company email to a new platform | Working mailboxes for every user, old system retired | Minimal downtime |
| Construction | Build a new primary school | Completed, certified building | Fixed budget and opening date |
| Marketing | Launch a product campaign | Campaign assets, live channels, results report | Launch date |
| Healthcare | Open a new outpatient clinic | Equipped, staffed clinic seeing patients | Regulatory approval |
| HR | Introduce a new performance review process | Policy, forms, trained managers | Annual review cycle |
| Events | Organise a two-day conference | Venue, speakers, delegates, follow-up | Ticket income |
| Software | Release a mobile app | App published in the stores | Scope that fits the release date |
Projects are not only for work. Planning a wedding, renovating a kitchen or writing a dissertation all meet the definition: each is temporary, has a unique result and has limits on time and money.

#### Worked example: an office move
A company of 80 people needs to move to a new office when its lease ends in nine months. Here is how that becomes a project:
1. **Initiation:** the operations director (sponsor) sets the objective: move all staff into the new office by 30 June with no more than one working day of disruption, within the approved budget. A charter names the project manager and key stakeholders.
2. **Planning:** the team defines scope (fit-out, IT, furniture, removals, communications), breaks it into work packages, builds a schedule with milestones and agrees a budget and risk log.
3. **Execution:** suppliers complete the fit-out, IT installs the network, and staff are briefed and packed.
4. **Monitoring and controlling:** the project manager tracks progress against the plan weekly and handles changes, such as a delayed furniture delivery.
5. **Closure:** staff move in, snags are fixed, the old office is handed back, facilities take over day-to-day running and the team records [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).
Once facilities take over, the work becomes operations. The project is finished.

### Is it a project? A quick checklist
Use these questions when someone hands you a piece of work and you need to decide how to run it. If you answer yes to most of them, treat it as a project:
1. Does it have a clear objective and a point at which it will be finished?
2. Will it create something new or change how things work?
3. Does it need people from more than one team, or an external supplier?
4. Will it take more than a few days of effort?
5. Does it need its own budget, or does it compete for shared resources?
6. Are there real risks if it is late, over budget or wrong?
7. Does someone senior need to approve it or be kept informed?
If most answers are no, it is probably a task or routine work, and a simple list will do; our [to-do list template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/to-do-list-template/) is enough. If the answers are yes but the work is small, run it as a light project: a one-page brief, a short task list with owners and dates, and a weekly check-in.
Tip
Many organisations set their own threshold, such as a minimum cost or number of days of effort, above which work must be run as a formal project with a charter and governance. Check whether yours has one.

### The project life cycle
Every project moves through a life cycle from idea to closure. The most widely taught model has five phases, based on the PMI process groups:
| Phase | What happens | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiation | Confirm the need, check feasibility, appoint a sponsor and project manager | Business case, project charter |
| Planning | Define scope, schedule, budget, risks, quality and communication | Project management plan, baseline |
| Execution | Do the work and produce the deliverables | Deliverables, status updates |
| Monitoring and controlling | Track progress, manage changes, risks and issues | Status reports, change log |
| Closure | Hand over, release the team, capture lessons | Acceptance, closure report |
Agile projects follow the same broad journey but repeat planning, delivery and review in short iterations. PMI's current [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) (eighth edition, 2025) organises project work around principles and performance domains rather than a strict sequence of phases, but the life cycle above is still the simplest way to understand how a project runs.

### What makes a project successful
Traditionally, a project was judged on the triple constraint: delivered on time, on budget and to scope. That still matters, but most organisations now also ask whether the project achieved the outcome it was started for. A system delivered on time that nobody uses is not a success.
- **Success criteria** are the measures you use to judge the project, agreed at the start: for example, "all 80 staff working from the new office by 30 June, within budget".
- **Success factors** are the conditions that make success more likely, such as an engaged sponsor, clear objectives, a capable team and good stakeholder communication. See [critical success factors](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-success-factors/).
- **Benefits** are the improvements the organisation gets after the project, such as lower costs or happier customers. They are often measured after the project closes.
A skilled project manager keeps all three in view.

### Common misconceptions about projects
- **"Everything is a project."** Labelling routine work as a project adds paperwork without adding control. Keep projects for work that is temporary and unique.
- **"A project needs a big plan."** The level of planning should match the size and risk. A two-week project needs a page, not a manual.
- **"The project ends when the work is done."** It ends when the deliverables are accepted, handed over and the project is formally closed. Skipping [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/) leaves loose ends.
- **"Agile work has no projects."** Agile product teams often work continuously on a product, but time-bound initiatives within that work, such as a launch or migration, are still projects.
- **"No end date is fine for now."** A project without an end date tends to drift and absorb resources. Set at least a target date and review it.
- **"The project manager owns the outcome alone."** The sponsor owns the business case and benefits; the project manager owns delivery of the project.

### Next steps
Once you can recognise a project, the next step is learning how to manage one: setting objectives, planning the work, leading the team and keeping stakeholders informed. Start with a one-page brief or charter, agree the objective and scope with your sponsor, and build a simple plan. Our [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) gives you a ready-made structure.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a project in simple words?**
A project is a one-off piece of work with a clear goal, a start and an end date, and limits on time, money and people. When the goal is achieved, the project finishes.

**Q: What is the PMI definition of a project?**
PMI defines a project as a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. This definition is used in the PMBOK Guide and in PMI exams such as CAPM and PMP.

**Q: What are the main characteristics of a project?**
A project is temporary, creates a unique result, has a specific objective and defined deliverables, works within constraints of time, cost and quality, is progressively elaborated and carries uncertainty and risk. It usually involves people from more than one team.

**Q: What is the difference between a project and operations?**
A project is temporary and creates something new or changes how things work; operations are ongoing and repeat the same work to keep the organisation running. Implementing a new payroll system is a project; running payroll every month is operations.

**Q: What is the difference between a project and a task?**
A task is a single piece of work, usually done by one person in hours or days. A project is a set of many tasks and activities, often across several people or teams, that together create a unique result.

**Q: What is the difference between a project and a programme?**
A programme is a group of related projects managed together to achieve benefits that none of them could deliver alone. See [project vs programme vs portfolio](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/program-vs-project-vs-portfolio-management/).

**Q: What are the 5 phases of a project?**
Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure. Monitoring and controlling runs alongside execution rather than after it. See the [project management phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/).

**Q: What are some examples of projects?**
Migrating email to a new platform, building a school, launching a marketing campaign, opening a clinic, introducing a new HR process, organising a conference and releasing a mobile app.

**Q: Can a project be ongoing?**
No. By definition a project has a planned end. Work that continues indefinitely is operations, although an ongoing product may be improved through a series of projects or releases.

**Q: How small can a project be?**
Any temporary effort with a unique result can be managed as a project. Very small projects need only light planning: an objective, a task list with owners and dates, and a check-in.

**Q: Why are projects started?**
To deliver a strategic goal, meet a customer request, comply with regulation, fix a problem, take an opportunity or new technology, or meet a social or environmental goal. The reason is usually set out in a business case.

**Q: What is progressive elaboration?**
Adding detail to a project's plans as more information becomes available, rather than trying to know everything at the start. It is why plans are reviewed and refined throughout the project.

**Q: Who is responsible for a project?**
The sponsor authorises and funds the project and owns its business case; the project manager is responsible for planning and delivering it; the team does the work. A [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) usually names these roles.

**Q: What makes a project successful?**
Delivering the agreed deliverables within the agreed time, cost, scope and quality, and achieving the outcome or benefits the project was started for. Agree success criteria at the start so everyone knows how success will be judged.
