# What Is PMI? Project Management Institute Explained

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-pmi/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What is PMI? The Project Management Institute explained: what it does, its 13 certifications, the PMBOK Guide 8th edition, membership and whether to join.


## What Is PMI? Project Management Institute Explained
PMI, the Project Management Institute, is a global not-for-profit professional association that sets standards for project management, awards certifications such as the PMP and CAPM, and runs a worldwide network of members and local chapters. Founded in the United States in 1969, it publishes the PMBOK Guide, now in its eighth edition. This guide explains what PMI does, every current certification and how to earn one, what membership includes, and how to decide whether joining is worth it for you.
- Published 9 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- PMI is a not-for-profit professional body, not a government regulator: its certifications are voluntary, but the PMP is one of the most widely requested project management credentials in job adverts.
- PMI currently lists 13 certifications, from the entry-level CAPM (no experience needed) to the PMP, PgMP and PfMP, plus specialist credentials in Agile, risk, scheduling, business analysis, PMOs, construction, sustainability and AI.
- The PMBOK Guide 8th edition (November 2025) is built on six principles, seven performance domains and five focus areas with 40 processes.
- The PMP exam changed in July 2026, and from 1 December 2026 live instructor-led training only counts towards the 35 hours if it comes from a PMI Authorized Training Partner or an eligible accredited programme.
- Membership is optional. It usually pays for itself if you are about to sit a PMI exam, because members get lower exam fees and a free digital PMBOK Guide.
- Most PMI certifications last three years and are renewed by earning PDUs: 60 for the PMP, 15 for the CAPM.

### What is PMI?
**PMI (the Project Management Institute) is a global, not-for-profit professional association for project, programme and portfolio management.** It develops recognised standards such as the PMBOK Guide, sets and examines certifications including the PMP and CAPM, and supports practitioners through membership, local chapters, research, events and learning. PMI is headquartered in Newtown Square, Pennsylvania, USA.
PMI describes its wider community as more than 800,000 project professionals worldwide, organised in part through over 300 local chapters. It has no legal power to license project managers: nobody needs PMI's permission to manage a project. Its influence comes from the fact that employers, clients and governments in many countries recognise its standards and credentials.
Three terms are often confused, so it helps to separate them early.
| Term | What it is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PMI | The organisation | The body that writes the standard and runs the exam |
| PMBOK Guide | PMI's flagship standard and guide to good practice | The book you study from; see our [PMBOK Guide explainer](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) |
| PMP | A certification awarded by PMI | The credential you add after your name; see [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) |
| PDU | A unit of continuing education used to renew PMI certifications | One hour of learning or giving back; see [PDUs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pdu-professional-development-units/) |
If you are new to the field, start with [what project management is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) and then come back to see where PMI fits.

### What does PMI do?
PMI's work falls into six broad areas. Knowing them helps you decide which parts are relevant to you, because most people use only one or two.
| Area | What PMI provides | Who it helps most |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standards | The PMBOK Guide, The Standard for Project Management, standards for programmes, portfolios, risk and earned value, and practice guides such as the Agile Practice Guide | Practitioners, PMOs and trainers who need a shared vocabulary |
| Certification | 13 credentials, from entry level to portfolio management and specialist areas | Individuals proving competence to employers and clients |
| Membership and community | Discounts, free digital standards, eLearning, the PMI Infinity AI coach, a job board and online communities | Anyone studying for an exam or building a career |
| Chapters | Local branches that run events, mentoring and volunteering | People who want local networking and PDUs |
| Research and thought leadership | The Project Management Journal, research reports and the PMI learning library | Senior practitioners, academics and PMO leads |
| Events and learning | Courses, webinars, PMXPO and the annual Global Summit | Practitioners earning PDUs or keeping up to date |
PMI also supports social-impact work through the PMI Educational Foundation, which promotes project skills in education and charities.

### A short history of PMI
PMI's own history page records that it began with a meeting of five founders at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta in 1969. The milestones below show how a small US association grew into a global standards and certification body.
| Year | Milestone |
| --- | --- |
| 1969 | Founded by James Snyder, Eric Jenett, Gordon Davis, Ned Engman and Susan Gallagher; incorporated in Pennsylvania |
| 1970s | First chapter formed in Houston and the first Seminars and Symposium held in Atlanta |
| 1984 | First PMP exam held; by the end of 1989 PMI had issued 264 PMP certifications |
| 1996 | First edition of A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide) |
| Late 2000s to early 2010s | Certification range expands, including the PgMP for programme managers and the PMI-ACP for Agile practitioners |
| 2021 | PMBOK Guide 7th edition moves from processes to 12 principles and 8 performance domains |
| 2024 | PMI launches its PMI:Next strategy and the PMIxAI initiative |
| November 2025 | PMBOK Guide 8th edition published |
| July 2026 | Updated PMP exam launched, with a much larger Business Environment domain |
The direction of travel is clear: PMI has moved from a single, process-heavy standard towards a broader view of delivering value with predictive, Agile and hybrid approaches, and more recently towards AI and sustainability.

### PMI standards and the PMBOK Guide
The PMBOK Guide is PMI's best-known publication and the main reference behind its exams. It is a **standard and guide to good practice, not a methodology**: it describes what good project management involves, and leaves you to tailor how you do it. Methods such as [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) or Scrum are more prescriptive.

#### What is in the PMBOK Guide 8th edition?
According to PMI, the eighth edition was published in November 2025 and runs to 408 pages, including The Standard for Project Management. It keeps the principle-based approach of the seventh edition but brings back process guidance in a non-prescriptive way.
- **Six principles:** adopt a holistic view, focus on value, embed quality, lead accountably, integrate sustainability, and build empowered teams.
- **Seven performance domains:** governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources and risk.
- **Five focus areas:** initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing, which echo the process groups of older editions.
- **40 processes** organised within those focus areas, presented as guidance rather than mandatory steps.

#### 7th edition vs 8th edition
| Feature | PMBOK Guide 7th edition (2021) | PMBOK Guide 8th edition (2025) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Principles | 12 principles | 6 consolidated principles |
| Performance domains | 8 (stakeholders, team, development approach and life cycle, planning, project work, delivery, measurement, uncertainty) | 7 (governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources, risk) |
| Processes | Removed from the guide | Reintroduced: 40 processes in 5 focus areas |
| Emphasis | Value delivery and tailoring | Value, governance, sustainability and practical how-to guidance |
If you studied an older edition, the core ideas you learned, such as [scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/), [scheduling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) and [risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/), are all still there. The [project management principles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-principles/) and [processes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-processes/) guides explain them in plain English.

#### Other PMI standards and practice guides
- The Standard for Program Management and The Standard for Portfolio Management.
- Standards for risk management and earned value management.
- Practice standards for scheduling, estimating and work breakdown structures.
- Practice guides including the Agile Practice Guide, benefits realisation, requirements management and business analysis.
- A standard and practice guide for sustainability in project management (GPM P5).
Members can read PMI's standards digitally as part of membership, and PMIstandards+ offers searchable online access.

### PMI certifications explained
PMI's certifications page lists 13 credentials, split into five flagship and eight specialised certifications. The experience levels below are taken from that page (checked 25 October 2026); the exact eligibility rules are in each certification's handbook and exam content outline.
| Certification | Type | Experience PMI lists | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **CAPM** (Certified Associate in Project Management) | Flagship | None required | Students, career changers, project coordinators |
| **PMP** (Project Management Professional) | Flagship | 3+ years leading projects (more without a degree) | Practising project managers |
| **PgMP** (Program Management Professional) | Flagship | 4 to 7 years | Programme managers coordinating related projects |
| **PfMP** (Portfolio Management Professional) | Flagship | 8+ years | Portfolio managers and senior PMO leaders |
| **APL** (Advanced Project Leader) | Flagship | Not stated; recognition is peer-based rather than exam-based | Experienced leaders |
| **PMI-ACP** (Agile Certified Practitioner) | Specialised | 2+ years | Agile practitioners using several frameworks |
| **PMI-RMP** (Risk Management Professional) | Specialised | 3 to 5 years | Risk specialists |
| **PMI-SP** (Scheduling Professional) | Specialised | 2 to 3 years | Planners and schedulers |
| **PMI-PBA** (Professional in Business Analysis) | Specialised | 3 to 5 years | Business analysts on projects |
| **PMI-PMOCP** (PMO Certified Professional) | Specialised | 3+ years | People setting up or running a PMO |
| **PMI-CP** (Construction Professional) | Specialised | 3+ years | Construction project managers |
| **CSPP** (Certified Sustainable Project Professional) | Specialised | None required | Anyone leading projects with sustainability goals |
| **PMI-CPMAI** (Certified Professional in Managing AI) | Specialised | None required | People leading AI and data projects |

#### Which PMI certification should you choose?
Pick the credential that matches the job you do now or the next job you want, not the most senior one available. Use this table as a starting point.
| Your situation | Sensible first PMI credential | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Student or career changer with no project experience | CAPM | No experience requirement; shows you know the vocabulary and fundamentals |
| Project coordinator with 1 to 2 years' experience | CAPM now, PMP later | The CAPM also satisfies the PMP's education requirement |
| Project manager with 3+ years leading projects and a degree | PMP | The most widely recognised general credential |
| Scrum Master or Agile team lead | PMI-ACP, or a Scrum certification | Covers several Agile approaches, not only Scrum |
| Planner, scheduler or risk lead | PMI-SP or PMI-RMP | Proves depth in one discipline |
| Programme or portfolio manager | PgMP or PfMP | Designed for work above single projects |
| Leading AI-related projects | PMI-CPMAI | No experience requirement; focuses on managing AI initiatives |
For non-PMI options such as PRINCE2, APM and Scrum credentials, compare them in our [project management certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/).

### How to get a PMI certification step by step
The process is similar for every PMI exam-based credential. These steps follow the PMI Certification Handbook (revised June 2026).
1. **Check eligibility.** Read the certification's exam content outline and handbook on pmi.org. For the PMP, PMI asks for project leadership experience within the last 10 years (five years with secondary education, four with an associate or vocational qualification, three with a bachelor's degree, two with a degree from a PMI GAC-accredited programme) plus 35 hours of project management training or an active CAPM.
2. **Complete the required education.** The PMP needs 35 hours; the CAPM needs 23 hours. Keep certificates, because you will need them if you are audited. See [35 contact hours for the PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/35-contact-hours-pmp/).
3. **Decide whether to join PMI first.** Member exam prices only apply if you are a member before you pay, so join before step 5 if you plan to.
4. **Submit the online application.** Describe each project: your role, the dates, and what you did across the project life cycle. Write in your own words and be specific.
5. **Respond to an audit if selected.** All applications can be audited and a percentage are chosen at random. You are told before payment, and you then have 90 days to send copies of your diploma, signed experience confirmations and course certificates. PMI says the review then takes about five to seven business days.
6. **Pay the exam fee.** PMI emails your eligibility ID once payment is made.
7. **Schedule the exam.** Book with Pearson VUE at a test centre or online. You have one year from approval (or from passing the audit) to take the exam, and up to three attempts in that year.
8. **Pass and maintain.** Your certification cycle starts on the day you pass. Earn and report PDUs over the next three years and pay the renewal fee to keep it active.
Tip
If you plan to meet the PMP's 35 hours through live, instructor-led training, check the date. From 1 December 2026, PMI only accepts live training from a PMI Authorized Training Partner, a China Registered Education Provider or an eligible accredited academic programme. Training completed before that date still counts under the old rules, and self-paced courses can still come from any provider.

#### What the PMP exam looks like now
| Item | Current PMP exam (from 9 July 2026) |
| --- | --- |
| Questions | 180 |
| Time | 240 minutes, with two 10-minute breaks |
| Domains | People 33%, Process 41%, Business Environment 26% |
| Question styles | Multiple choice plus case and scenario questions and graphic-based items (for example dashboards and project artefacts) |
| Delivery | Pearson VUE test centre or online |
PMI says AI and sustainability now appear as part of the project context in scenarios rather than as separate topics. Our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) has a full study plan.

### Worked example: planning a PMP application
To make the rules concrete, here is a fictional candidate working through them.
**Amira** has a bachelor's degree and has worked as a project manager at an engineering firm since March 2022. By November 2026 she has about four years and eight months of project leadership experience, all within the last 10 years. She wants to sit the PMP in early 2027.
| Requirement | What PMI asks for | Amira's position | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Education | Bachelor's degree | Has one | Keep a copy of the certificate for a possible audit |
| Experience | 3 years leading projects (bachelor's route) within 10 years | About 4 years 8 months | Meets it; list 3 to 5 projects that show leadership across the life cycle |
| Training | 35 hours or an active CAPM | None yet | Book a course; if it is live training starting after 1 December 2026, choose a PMI Authorized Training Partner |
| Membership | Optional | Not a member | Join before paying the exam fee to get the member price |
| Exam window | One year from approval, three attempts | Wants to test in about 10 weeks | Apply once training is complete; schedule the exam straight after approval |
Her experience descriptions might read: "Led a 12-person team to deliver a substation upgrade; developed the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) and schedule, managed a risk register, chaired weekly stakeholder reviews and closed the project with a lessons-learned report." Short, specific statements like this, using PMI's vocabulary, are easier to verify in an audit than vague job descriptions.
Tip
Collect evidence while you work. A signed [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/), a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) and a [WBS](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) you produced make it easy to describe your experience accurately.

### Keeping your certification: PDUs and renewal
Most PMI certifications are valid for three years. To renew, you earn Professional Development Units (PDUs), where one PDU equals one hour of learning or giving back to the profession, and then pay a renewal fee, which PMI says is separate from any membership fee.
PMI groups learning under its Talent Triangle: **Ways of Working** (technical project skills), **Power Skills** (leadership and communication) and **Business Acumen** (strategy and the wider organisation). Each certification has a minimum in each area.
| Certification | PDUs per 3 years | Education (minimum) | Giving back (maximum) | Minimum per Talent Triangle area |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CAPM | 15 | 9 | 6 | 2 |
| PMI-ACP, PMI-RMP, PMI-SP, PMI-CP, PMI-CPMAI, CSPP | 30 | 18 | 12 | 4 |
| PMP, PgMP, PfMP, PMI-PBA | 60 | 35 | 25 | 8 |
| PMI-PMOCP | 30 | 20 | 10 | 3 / 7 / 10 (Ways of Working / Power Skills / Business Acumen) |

#### Worked example: a three-year PDU plan for a PMP
Amira passes in March 2027. Rather than rushing to earn 60 PDUs in her final months, she spreads them over the cycle.
| Activity | Talent Triangle area | PDUs | Type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Online course in Agile and hybrid delivery | Ways of Working | 12 | Education |
| Chapter workshops on negotiation and stakeholder communication | Power Skills | 10 | Education |
| Webinars on benefits realisation and finance for project managers | Business Acumen | 8 | Education |
| Reading PMI standards and articles | Mixed | 8 | Education |
| Working as a project manager (counts as giving back) | Not applicable | 8 | Giving back |
| Mentoring two junior colleagues and volunteering at chapter events | Not applicable | 14 | Giving back |
| **Total** |  | **60** | 38 education, 22 giving back |
Her plan meets every rule: at least 35 education PDUs, no more than 25 giving-back PDUs and at least 8 in each Talent Triangle area.

### PMI membership: types, benefits and costs
Membership is optional, and you can hold any PMI certification without it. PMI's membership page (checked 25 October 2026) lists these options.
| Option | What it is | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free PMI.org account | Registration only | Free eLearning, articles and job board browsing |
| 30-day trial membership | Short trial of member benefits | PMI says no credit card is needed and it does not renew automatically |
| Professional membership | Full individual membership | 12 months, then billed annually |
| Student membership | Discounted membership | For full-time college or university students |
| Gift membership | Membership bought for someone else | Useful for managers and mentors |
| Chapter membership | Membership of a local chapter | Being bundled with PMI membership in more countries under PMI's new membership model |

#### What members get
- Member pricing of **up to 30% off** certifications, learning and events.
- Free digital editions of the PMBOK Guide and other PMI standards.
- PMI Infinity, PMI's AI-powered coach for members.
- Free eLearning courses, which can also earn PDUs.
- The Project Management Journal and a business reading centre.
- Early access to job board postings and PMI's salary survey tool.
- Project templates and premium webinars.

#### How much does PMI membership cost?
PMI does not show prices on its public membership page; they appear at checkout and can vary by country. Independent guides updated in 2026 quote individual membership at roughly **US$129 to US$139 a year plus a one-off US$10 application fee**, with lower student rates. Chapter dues are extra in some places and vary by chapter. Treat these figures as indicative and confirm the price in your PMI account before you pay.
Tip
Look out for PMI's new membership model. PMI is bundling chapter membership with global membership country by country; the third phase, covering countries including the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Australia, Singapore, Mexico and Nigeria, went live on 1 February 2026.

### Is PMI membership worth it? A worked example
The honest answer depends on what you will use in the next 12 months. The quickest test is a break-even calculation:
**Membership pays for itself if: (non-member exam fee minus member exam fee) + other savings you will actually use ≥ membership dues + application fee.**
Here is an illustration using round, hypothetical numbers. Replace them with the prices shown in your own PMI checkout, as fees vary by region and change over time.
| Item | Non-member | Member |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Membership dues and application fee | 0 | 140 |
| PMP exam fee (hypothetical) | 650 | 430 |
| Digital PMBOK Guide | Bought separately: 60 | Included: 0 |
| **Total first-year cost** | **710** | **570** |
In this example the member saves 140 in the year they sit the exam, before counting free eLearning, PDUs and events. The saving grows if you also retake an exam, since re-examination fees are also discounted for members.

#### When membership is usually worth it
- You will sit a PMI exam in the next year.
- You need PDUs and will use the free courses and chapter events to earn them.
- You want the PMBOK Guide and other standards for reference at work.
- You are job hunting and will use the job board, salary data and networking.

#### When you can probably skip it
- You have just renewed your certification and will not use member resources until the next cycle.
- Your employer already provides PMIstandards+ or training that covers your PDUs.
- You work mainly with PRINCE2, APM or Scrum and only need occasional PMI content.
Many people join the month before booking an exam and decide later whether to renew. That is a perfectly reasonable approach.

### How to join PMI step by step
1. Create a free account at pmi.org with the name that appears on your ID, because it will be used for certification records.
2. Optionally start the 30-day trial to look at the resources before paying.
3. Choose Professional, Student or Gift membership and complete checkout.
4. Add a local chapter if one is not already bundled in your country.
5. Download the PMBOK Guide and any other standards you need from your member account.
6. Set up PMI Infinity and enrol in free eLearning courses that match your goals.
7. If you are about to apply for an exam, check that your membership shows as active before you pay the exam fee.
Membership runs for 12 months and renews annually. If it lapses, you keep any certifications you hold, as long as you keep meeting their renewal requirements.

### PMI chapters and volunteering
A PMI chapter is a local, volunteer-run branch of PMI for a city, region or country. PMI's history notes that the first chapter formed in Houston in the 1970s; today PMI refers to more than 300 chapters worldwide.
Chapters typically offer:
- Evening talks and workshops, many of which earn PDUs.
- Mentoring schemes and study groups for the PMP and CAPM.
- Networking with local employers and recruiters.
- Volunteering roles, from event organisation to board positions, which count as giving-back PDUs and build leadership experience.
The value varies with how active your local chapter is and whether you can attend. Look at its events calendar for the last six months before deciding how much time to invest. Volunteering on a chapter board is also a good way to practise [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/) such as stakeholder engagement and running a budget.

### PMI compared with other project management bodies
PMI is the largest body in many regions, but it is not the only one. In the UK in particular, APM and PRINCE2 are common in job adverts. The table gives a neutral overview.
| Body | Based | Main standard or method | Main credentials | Strongest in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PMI | USA, global | PMBOK Guide and The Standard for Project Management | CAPM, PMP, PgMP, PfMP, PMI-ACP and others | The Americas, Middle East, Asia and multinationals |
| APM (Association for Project Management) | UK | APM Body of Knowledge | APM PFQ, PMQ, PPQ and Chartered Project Professional | UK public and private sectors |
| PeopleCert | Global | PRINCE2 method | PRINCE2 Foundation and Practitioner | UK, Europe, Australia and government projects |
| IPMA (International Project Management Association) | Switzerland, federation of national associations | IPMA Individual Competence Baseline | IPMA levels A to D | Continental Europe |
| Scrum.org and Scrum Alliance | USA, global | The Scrum Guide | PSM, PSPO, CSM, CSPO | Software and product teams |
These are complementary rather than competing choices. A common UK combination is PRINCE2 for method plus the PMP or an APM qualification for broader competence.

### Common mistakes when dealing with PMI
- **Joining after paying the exam fee.** Member pricing only applies if your membership is active before you pay.
- **Vague experience descriptions.** Copying a job description makes an audit harder. Describe what you did on each project in PMI's terms.
- **Assuming any course counts.** From 1 December 2026, live training for the PMP's 35 hours must come from an approved provider. Check before you book.
- **Studying from an old edition only.** The PMP exam now reflects the 2026 exam content outline. Use current materials alongside the PMBOK Guide.
- **Treating the PMBOK Guide as a methodology.** It is a standard; you still need to tailor an approach, whether [waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/), [Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-methodology/) or hybrid.
- **Leaving PDUs until the last month.** Spread them across the three years and report them as you go.
- **Overlooking cheaper routes.** Student membership and the CAPM are inexpensive ways in if you are early in your career.
If you are still deciding on a career direction, our guide on [how to become a project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-become-a-project-manager/) explains where PMI credentials fit. To choose between PMI and other credentials, see our [certification comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does PMI stand for?**
PMI stands for the Project Management Institute, a global not-for-profit professional association for project management founded in the United States in 1969.

**Q: Is PMI a government body?**
No. PMI is an independent not-for-profit association. Its certifications are voluntary, but many employers and public bodies recognise them.

**Q: What is the difference between PMI and PMP?**
PMI is the organisation; the PMP (Project Management Professional) is one of the certifications it awards. You get PMP certified by PMI.

**Q: Do I need to be a PMI member to take the PMP?**
No. Membership is optional. Members pay a lower exam fee and get a free digital PMBOK Guide, which is why many candidates join before applying.

**Q: How much does PMI membership cost?**
PMI shows prices at checkout and they vary by country. Independent guides updated in 2026 quote about US$129 to US$139 a year plus a one-off US$10 application fee, with lower student rates. Check your PMI account for the current price.

**Q: What is the latest edition of the PMBOK Guide?**
The eighth edition, published in November 2025. It has six principles, seven performance domains and five focus areas containing 40 processes. See [the PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/).

**Q: Is the PMBOK Guide free for PMI members?**
Yes. PMI lists free digital editions of the PMBOK Guide and its other standards among member benefits. Non-members can buy it from PMI's store.

**Q: Which PMI certification should I get first?**
With little or no experience, start with the CAPM. With three or more years leading projects and a degree, go straight for the PMP. Agile practitioners often choose the PMI-ACP.

**Q: How many PDUs do I need to renew?**
60 PDUs every three years for the PMP, PgMP, PfMP and PMI-PBA; 30 for most specialist certifications; and 15 for the CAPM.

**Q: What happens if my PMI application is audited?**
You are told before you pay and have 90 days to send copies of your education certificates, signed confirmation of your experience and your training certificates. PMI says the review takes about five to seven business days once everything is received.

**Q: How long is a PMI exam eligibility period?**
One year from application approval, or from passing the audit. You can attempt the exam up to three times in that year.

**Q: Is PMI recognised in the UK and Europe?**
Yes. The PMP is widely recognised internationally, although in the UK many roles also ask for PRINCE2 or APM qualifications. See [PMBOK vs PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-vs-prince2/).

**Q: Should I choose PMI or APM?**
If you work mainly in the UK public or private sector, APM qualifications are well known. If you work internationally or for a multinational, the PMP usually travels further. Many people hold both.

**Q: What is a PMI chapter and should I join one?**
A chapter is a local, volunteer-run branch of PMI that runs events, mentoring and volunteering. Join if you can attend events regularly; they are a low-cost way to earn PDUs and build a network.

# What Is Project Management? Definition, Process, Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What is project management? A clear definition, the 5 phases, the triple constraint, methods, roles, tools and a worked example to follow step by step.


## What Is Project Management? Definition, Process, Examples
Project management is the discipline of planning, organising and leading work to deliver a specific result within agreed limits of time, cost, scope and quality. It turns an idea, such as a new website, an office move or a product launch, into a plan people can carry out and leaders can track. This guide explains the five phases, the constraints you balance, the main methods and roles, and walks through a worked example from start to finish.
- Published 4 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Project management applies knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to a temporary piece of work so that it delivers an agreed result.
- Every project balances scope, time and cost, with quality at the centre; changing one almost always affects the others.
- Projects move through five phases: initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure.
- You can run a project with a predictive (Waterfall), adaptive (Agile) or hybrid approach, depending on how stable the requirements are.
- The current PMI standard, the PMBOK Guide 8th edition (November 2025), is built on six principles and seven performance domains.
- Start small: a one-page charter, a task list and a weekly status check cover most simple projects.

### What is project management?
**Project management** is the practice of planning, organising, leading and controlling the work of a temporary project so that it delivers a defined result, such as a product, service or change, within agreed limits of time, cost, scope and quality. It covers the whole journey, from agreeing why the project exists to handing over the result and capturing what the team learned.
The professional bodies use similar wording. Each definition stresses something slightly different, which is worth knowing if you plan to sit an exam.
| Source | Definition (summarised) | What it emphasises |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PMI (PMBOK Guide) | The application of knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities to meet project requirements | Meeting requirements |
| APM (UK Association for Project Management) | The application of processes, methods, knowledge, skills and experience to achieve specific objectives for change | Projects as the way organisations deliver change |

#### Project management in plain English
Cooking dinner for six friends is a tiny project, but you hardly need project management: everything is in your head and the risks are small. Moving 120 people to a new office in 14 weeks is different. IT, facilities, HR, a removals firm, the landlord and every department are involved, the budget is fixed and the old lease ends on a set date. Without someone defining the scope, sequencing the work, tracking costs and spotting problems early, things fall through the gaps. Project management is the set of practices that stops that happening.

#### What counts as a project?
A project is a temporary effort, with a defined start and end, undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. Temporary does not mean short: a project can last two weeks or five years. Unique does not mean never done before: your tenth office move is still unique because the building, people and budget differ. Recurring work, such as running payroll every month, is operations.

### Why project management matters
Good project management does not guarantee success, but it makes success more likely and failure less surprising. It gives everyone a shared goal, makes trade-offs deliberate, surfaces risks while they are cheap to deal with, gives each piece of work an owner, and lets sponsors trust the forecast. The table shows the problems that most often appear when projects are run informally, and the practice that prevents each one.
| Symptom | Usual cause | Practice that helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The project keeps growing | Scope was never written down or agreed | A scope statement and change control to prevent [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) |
| Deadlines slip without warning | No schedule, or one that ignores dependencies | A schedule built from the work breakdown, with milestones |
| The budget runs out early | Cost was one guess, not built up from the work | A bottom-up budget and regular cost tracking |
| Work is done twice or not at all | Unclear roles | A RACI matrix naming who is responsible and accountable |
| A problem is found too late to fix cheaply | Risks were never discussed | A [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) reviewed at every status meeting |
| Senior people are unhappy at the end | Expectations were never confirmed | Stakeholder analysis and a communication plan |

### The triple constraint and other project constraints
Every project works within limits. The best-known model is the **triple constraint**, or project management triangle: **scope** (what you deliver), **time** (when) and **cost** (money and effort). Quality sits in the middle, because squeezing one side without adjusting another usually lowers quality. Modern standards treat the triangle as a starting point: most projects also manage risk, resources and benefits.

#### Worked example: a deadline moves forward
Your project to launch a customer portal is planned for 12 weeks with a budget of £80,000. The sales director asks for launch in 9 weeks to coincide with a trade show. Rather than simply agreeing, you set out the options:
| Option | What changes | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reduce scope | Launch core features only; add reporting in a second release | Date met, budget held; some users wait for reporting |
| Add resources | Two contract developers for six weeks | Date likely met; cost rises by an estimated £18,000; onboarding time needed |
| Overlap tasks (fast-tracking) | Start testing before development is complete | Date possibly met; higher risk of rework |
| Keep the plan | Launch in week 12 as agreed | No extra cost or risk; trade-show opportunity missed |
The sponsor makes the final call, because it is a business trade-off. Your job as project manager is to make the trade-off visible with honest numbers.

### The project management process: 5 phases
Most projects move through five phases, often called the project life cycle. PMI's process groups, and the five focus areas in the PMBOK Guide 8th edition, use the same names.
| Phase | Key question | Main activities | Typical outputs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Initiation | Should we do this, and why? | Confirm the need, check feasibility, appoint a sponsor and project manager, identify stakeholders | Business case, [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/), stakeholder register |
| 2. Planning | How will we do it? | Define scope, break down the work, estimate, schedule, budget, plan risk, quality and communication | Scope statement, WBS, schedule, budget, risk register, project management plan |
| 3. Execution | Are we doing the work? | Build the deliverables, lead the team, manage suppliers, engage stakeholders | Deliverables, issue log, change requests |
| 4. Monitoring and controlling | Are we on track? | Compare progress with the baseline, manage changes, risks and issues, report status | Status reports, updated forecasts, approved changes |
| 5. Closure | Did we deliver, and what did we learn? | Formal acceptance, handover to operations, close contracts, release the team, review lessons | Acceptance sign-off, lessons-learned report, archived records |
Two points are often missed. Monitoring and controlling is not a separate stage: it runs alongside execution from the first day of work. And in Agile projects, planning, execution and review repeat in short cycles, while initiation and closure still happen once.

### How to manage a project step by step
If you have just been handed your first project, this ten-step process works for most small and medium projects.
1. **Confirm the purpose.** Write down, in two or three sentences, the problem the project solves and how success will be measured.
2. **Identify stakeholders.** List everyone affected by the project or able to influence it, and what each needs from you.
3. **Write a project charter.** Capture purpose, objectives, high-level scope, milestones, budget, risks and the sponsor's sign-off on one or two pages. Our free [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) gives you the structure.
4. **Define the scope.** List what is included and, just as important, what is excluded.
5. **Break down the work.** Split the deliverables into pieces small enough to estimate and assign: the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) (WBS).
6. **Build the schedule.** Estimate each task, identify dependencies, set milestones and find the critical path, usually on a Gantt chart.
7. **Set the budget.** Add up labour, materials, suppliers and a contingency reserve for known risks.
8. **Plan risks, roles and communication.** Start a [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/), agree who is responsible for what, and decide who gets which update and how often.
9. **Execute, track and adjust.** Hold short regular check-ins, update progress weekly against the plan, and assess every change request for its effect on scope, time and cost.
10. **Close the project.** Get formal acceptance, hand over to the people who will run the result, close contracts, thank the team and hold a lessons-learned review.
Tip
Scale the paperwork to the project. A two-week internal project might need only a one-page charter, a task list and a five-minute weekly check-in. A two-year capital project needs every document above and formal governance. The thinking behind each step matters more than the document.
If you want goals, scope, tasks, owners and milestones in one file, start with our free [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/).

### Worked example: a website redesign from start to finish
To see how the pieces fit together, follow one project through its life cycle. A 60-person professional services firm wants to replace its outdated website. The figures are illustrative.

#### Initiation: the charter
The marketing director sponsors the project and appoints a project manager, who writes a one-page charter:
| Charter item | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose | Replace a website that is hard to update and performs poorly on mobile |
| Objectives | Launch within 12 weeks; double contact-form enquiries within six months; meet accessibility guidelines |
| In scope | Design, build, migration of 40 key pages, contact forms, analytics, staff training |
| Out of scope | Client portal, online payments, translation |
| Budget | £60,000 including a £5,000 contingency reserve |
| Milestones | Design approved (week 4), build complete (week 9), launch (week 12) |
| Main risks | Content late; design approval delayed; agency capacity |

#### Planning: breaking down the work
With the web agency, the project manager builds a WBS and turns it into a schedule.
| WBS element | Main deliverables | Owner | Weeks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Discovery | Requirements, site map, content audit | Project manager and agency | 1 to 2 |
| 2. Design | Wireframes, visual design, approval | Agency designer | 2 to 4 |
| 3. Content | Rewritten copy for 40 pages, images | Marketing team | 3 to 8 |
| 4. Build | Templates, forms, analytics, accessibility checks | Agency developers | 5 to 9 |
| 5. Testing | Functional, browser, accessibility and user acceptance testing | Agency and project team | 9 to 11 |
| 6. Launch and handover | Go-live, redirects, staff training, support handover | Project manager | 11 to 12 |
Content sits on the critical path: if the copy is late, build and testing cannot finish on time. The risk register reflects that:
| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Response | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Copy for 40 pages is late | High | High | Page-by-page content schedule; prioritise the 15 most visited pages; freelance copywriter as a fallback | Marketing manager |
| Partners disagree on the design | Medium | Medium | Show two design routes early; one named decision-maker | Sponsor |
| Agency loses a developer mid-build | Low | High | Contract requires a named back-up; weekly demos | Project manager |

#### Monitoring: a status check in week 6
At the end of week 6 the project manager runs a simple [earned value](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) check. The budget at completion (BAC) is £60,000. The plan said £30,000 of work should be done by now (planned value, PV). The work actually completed is worth £24,000 of the budget (earned value, EV), and £27,000 has been spent (actual cost, AC).
| Measure | Formula | Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule variance (SV) | EV - PV | £24,000 - £30,000 = -£6,000 | Behind schedule |
| Cost variance (CV) | EV - AC | £24,000 - £27,000 = -£3,000 | Over budget for the work done |
| Schedule performance index (SPI) | EV / PV | 0.80 | 80% of the planned work is done |
| Cost performance index (CPI) | EV / AC | 0.89 | 89p of value for every £1 spent |
| Estimate at completion (EAC) | BAC / CPI | £60,000 / 0.89 = about £67,500 | Final cost if nothing changes |
The cause is the content risk coming true: only 12 of 40 pages are ready. The project manager offers the sponsor two options: a freelance copywriter for four weeks (about £4,000, using most of the contingency) or launch with 25 pages and add the rest a month later. The sponsor chooses the copywriter. Because this removes the bottleneck, the project manager forecasts a final cost of about £62,000 rather than £67,500, and the sponsor approves a £2,000 budget increase. The decision goes in the change log and the risk register is updated.

#### Closure: handover and lessons
The site launches in week 12 at a final cost of £61,800, within the revised budget. The sponsor signs acceptance, the agency hands over access and documentation, marketing staff are trained to edit pages and support moves to the agency's maintenance contract. A one-hour review records three lessons: start content first, name a single design approver, and track content weekly from day one.

### Knowledge areas, principles and performance domains
If you study project management formally, you will meet three ways of organising the subject, depending on which edition of PMI's [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) you read. Many courses and job adverts still use the older terms.
|  | PMBOK 6th edition (2017) | PMBOK 7th edition (2021) | PMBOK 8th edition (November 2025) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Organised around | Processes | Principles and outcomes | Principles, domains and non-prescriptive processes |
| Main structure | 10 knowledge areas, 5 process groups | 12 principles, 8 performance domains | 6 principles, 7 performance domains, 5 focus areas |
| Areas or domains | Integration, scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risk, procurement, stakeholders | Stakeholders, team, development approach and life cycle, planning, project work, delivery, measurement, uncertainty | Governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources, risk |
| Processes | 49 defined processes | Process detail largely removed | 40 processes grouped under initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, closing |
According to PMI, the 8th edition simplifies the 7th edition's principles and domains, brings back process guidance in a non-prescriptive form, and expands coverage of AI, project management offices and procurement. Its six principles include adopting a holistic view, focusing on value, embedding quality and integrating sustainability.
[PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/), the other widely used framework, is organised differently: PRINCE2 7 (2023) has seven principles, seven practices and seven processes, with people at the centre.
Tip
Whichever framework you follow, the underlying questions are the same: what are we delivering and why, how will we do it, who is involved, what could go wrong, and how will we know we are on track?

### Project management methodologies and approaches
A methodology is a defined way of running projects. There are three broad approaches: **predictive** (plan in detail up front), **adaptive** (plan and deliver in short iterations) and **hybrid** (a mix of both). Within those sit specific methods.
| Methodology | How it works | Often used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) | Sequential phases, each approved before the next starts | Construction, regulated projects, fixed-price contracts |
| [Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) | Deliver working results in short iterations, gather feedback and adapt | Software, digital products, marketing |
| [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) | Agile framework with fixed-length Sprints, a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and Developers | Product development teams |
| [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) | Visualise work on a board, limit work in progress, improve flow | Support, operations, content teams |
| PRINCE2 | Stage-based method with strong governance and business justification | Government and large organisations |
| Lean and Six Sigma | Remove waste (Lean) and reduce variation using data (Six Sigma) | Process improvement, manufacturing |
| Hybrid | Predictive governance and milestones with Agile delivery inside | Large organisations, product launches with fixed dates |

#### How to choose an approach
There is no single best methodology. Look at your project and lean towards the approach that suits most of its characteristics.
| Characteristic | Leans predictive | Leans adaptive (Agile) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | Clear and stable from the start | Expected to change as you learn |
| Customer involvement | At set approval points | Often, ideally every iteration |
| Cost of late change | High (concrete already poured) | Low (software can be updated) |
| Value of early partial delivery | Little: useful only when complete | High: users benefit from early releases |
| Contracts | Fixed scope and price, formal sign-offs | Flexible scope within a time and budget |
If your answers are mixed, a hybrid approach is usually sensible. Each industry also adds its own vocabulary and risks; see [project management by industry](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/) for construction, IT, marketing, healthcare and more.

### Who is involved: roles in project management
Titles vary between organisations, but these are the roles you will meet most often.
| Role | Main responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Sponsor | Owns the business case, provides funding, makes key decisions and removes obstacles |
| Project manager | Plans and coordinates the work, leads the team, manages risks, stakeholders and budget, reports progress |
| Project team | Specialists who carry out the work and produce the deliverables |
| Stakeholders | Anyone affected by the project or able to influence it: users, customers, suppliers, regulators |
| Product Owner and Scrum Master | In Scrum, the Product Owner maximises product value and the Scrum Master helps the team use Scrum effectively |
| PMO | A project management office that sets standards, supports projects and reports across the portfolio |

#### What a project manager does in a typical week
- Runs short check-ins with the team and clears blockers.
- Updates the schedule, budget and risk register with what actually happened.
- Reviews change requests and takes significant ones to the sponsor.
- Sends a short status report: progress, next steps, risks, decisions needed.
- Looks two to four weeks ahead for resource clashes, approvals and supplier deliveries.
To do this well you need technical skills (scoping, estimating, scheduling, budgeting, risk), people skills (communication, leadership, negotiation, facilitation) and business sense (understanding the case for the project and the value it must deliver).

### Project management tools and techniques
Techniques help you think; tools help you record, share and track. These are the ones you will use most:
| Tool or technique | Question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| Work breakdown structure | What exactly do we have to deliver? |
| Gantt chart and critical path | When does each task happen, and which tasks will delay the whole project if they slip? |
| Kanban board | What is in progress, and where is work getting stuck? |
| RACI matrix | Who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed? |
| Risk register or RAID log | What could go wrong, and what are we doing about it? |
| Status report | What has been done, what is next, and what decisions are needed? |
| Lessons-learned review | What should we repeat or change next time? |
Small projects can run on a spreadsheet and free templates. Once several people or projects are involved, project management software saves time by keeping tasks, timelines, files and conversations in one place. In our independent ranking, Wrike comes first as an all-in-one work management platform, with monday.com, Asana and ClickUp close behind; the right choice depends on your team size, methods and budget.

### Project management vs related disciplines
Project management is often confused with neighbouring roles.
| Discipline | Focus | Time frame | Measure of success |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project management | Deliver a specific result | Temporary | Deliverables on time, on budget, to scope and quality |
| Programme management | Coordinate related projects for shared benefits | Several years | Benefits realised |
| Portfolio management | Choose and balance projects and programmes for the strategy | Ongoing | Strategic value and return |
| Operations management | Run repeatable processes efficiently | Ongoing | Efficiency, service levels, unit cost |
| Product management | Decide what to build and why, across the product's life | Life of the product | Customer value, adoption, revenue |

### A short history of project management
People have managed large projects for thousands of years, but project management as a named discipline is mostly a twentieth-century development.
| When | Development |
| --- | --- |
| 1910s | Henry Gantt popularises the bar chart that carries his name |
| Late 1950s | The critical path method (CPM) is developed in industry, and PERT for the US Navy's Polaris programme |
| 1969 | The Project Management Institute (PMI) is founded |
| 1996 | PMI publishes the first edition of the PMBOK Guide, and PRINCE2 is released in the UK |
| 2001 | The Agile Manifesto is published |
| 2021 to 2023 | PMBOK 7th edition moves to principles and performance domains; PRINCE2 7 is released |
| 2025 to 2026 | PMBOK 8th edition (November 2025); PMI launches an updated PMP exam (July 2026) |

### Common project management mistakes
Most project problems come from a few habits. Spotting them early is half the fix.
| Mistake | What it looks like | How to fix it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting without a clear objective | People describe the project differently | Write a charter and have the sponsor sign it |
| Planning tasks but not scope | Long task lists, no agreement on what is excluded | Write in-scope and out-of-scope lists before scheduling |
| Estimating top-down only | "It should take about three months" | Estimate from the WBS with the people doing the work |
| No contingency | Any problem becomes a crisis | Hold a reserve of time and money linked to known risks |
| Saying yes to every change | Scope grows, the date does not move | Assess each change for impact; let the sponsor decide |
| Reporting only good news | Green status until the week before the deadline | Report early and honestly, and bring options |

### How to get started in project management
Many project managers start "accidentally", by being asked to coordinate something at work. To move into the field deliberately:
1. **Learn the fundamentals:** this guide, the five phases and the core documents (charter, scope, schedule, budget, risk register).
2. **Practise on a small project:** an internal improvement, an event or a system roll-out, using the templates above.
3. **Build your people skills:** run meetings, write clear updates and practise handling disagreement.
4. **Choose a certification that fits your stage** (see the table) and keep a record of the projects you lead.
| Certification | Awarding body | Suits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CAPM | PMI | Beginners without project leadership experience |
| PMP | PMI | Practising project managers; requires 35 hours of project management education plus documented experience |
| PRINCE2 Foundation and Practitioner | PeopleCert | Roles in the UK, Europe and government |
| Scrum certifications | Scrum.org, Scrum Alliance and others | Agile and product teams |
| PMAI | Neural Project Institute (this site) | Using AI in project work; a certificate of completion, not a PMI or PeopleCert credential |

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project management in simple terms?**
Organising a one-off piece of work so that it delivers what was agreed, on time and within budget: deciding what will be done, planning who does what and when, tracking progress and dealing with problems before they grow.

**Q: What are the 5 phases of project management?**
Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure. Monitoring and controlling runs alongside execution rather than after it.

**Q: What is an example of project management?**
Redesigning a company website: the project manager agrees the goal and budget in a charter, breaks the work into design, content, build and testing, schedules it over 12 weeks, tracks progress and cost, manages risks such as late content, and closes with a handover and lessons-learned review.

**Q: What are the three main constraints in project management?**
Scope, time and cost, known as the triple constraint, with quality at the centre. Changing one usually affects at least one of the others.

**Q: What does a project manager actually do?**
Defines goals and scope with the sponsor, builds the plan, coordinates the team, manages risks, budget and stakeholders, reports progress and closes the project. Much of the day-to-day job is communication.

**Q: What are the main types of project management?**
By approach: predictive (Waterfall), adaptive (Agile, including Scrum and Kanban) and hybrid. By industry: construction, IT, software, marketing, healthcare, events and many more.

**Q: What is the difference between project management and operations management?**
Project management delivers a temporary, unique result and then ends; operations management runs ongoing, repeatable work. Implementing a payroll system is a project; running payroll every month is operations.

**Q: What is the difference between project management and product management?**
A project manager delivers a defined result within time, cost and scope. A product manager decides what product to build and why, and owns it for its whole life. The roles work closely together, especially in software.

**Q: What skills do you need for project management?**
Planning, estimating, scheduling and budgeting, plus communication, leadership, negotiation and stakeholder management. Judgement and calm under pressure matter as much as method.

**Q: Is project management a good career?**
Project management skills are used in almost every industry, so the role offers variety and clear progression from coordinator to project, programme and portfolio manager. It suits people who enjoy organising, problem-solving and working with others.

**Q: Can you get into project management with no experience?**
Yes. Many people start by coordinating small projects in their current job, or as a project coordinator or assistant project manager. The CAPM is designed for people without project leadership experience.

**Q: Do I need a certification to work in project management?**
No, but a certification shows employers you know the methods and terminology. Common choices are CAPM for beginners, PMP for experienced project managers, PRINCE2 in the UK and Europe, and Scrum certifications for Agile roles.

**Q: What tools are used in project management?**
Work breakdown structures, Gantt charts, the critical path method, Kanban boards, RACI matrices, risk registers and status reports, usually managed in project management software or, for small projects, spreadsheets and templates.

**Q: What is the PMBOK Guide 8th edition?**
The current edition of PMI's project management standard and guide, published in November 2025. It is built on six principles and seven performance domains (governance, scope, schedule, finance, stakeholders, resources and risk) and includes 40 non-prescriptive processes grouped into five focus areas.
