# Work Breakdown Structure (WBS): Examples and How-To

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: Learn what a work breakdown structure (WBS) is, the 100% rule, levels and work packages, with examples, a WBS dictionary and step-by-step instructions.


## Work Breakdown Structure (WBS): Examples and How-To
A work breakdown structure (WBS) is a hierarchical breakdown of all the work in a project into smaller, manageable deliverables and work packages. It shows what the project will produce, and it becomes the foundation for estimates, schedules, budgets and assignments. This guide covers the rules of a good WBS, worked examples and a step-by-step way to build your own.
- Published 16 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 15 min read

### Key takeaways
- A WBS breaks the total project scope into deliverables and, at the lowest level, work packages.
- The 100% rule: the WBS contains all the scope and nothing else, and each level adds up exactly to its parent.
- Name elements as deliverables (nouns), not activities (verbs); activities belong in the schedule.
- Decompose until each work package can be estimated, owned and tracked, usually three to four levels.
- A WBS dictionary describes each element, and together with the scope statement forms the scope baseline.
- Build the WBS with the people who will do the work, then use it to drive the schedule and budget.

### What is a work breakdown structure (WBS)?
A **work breakdown structure (WBS)** is a hierarchical, deliverable-oriented breakdown of a project's total scope into progressively smaller pieces. The top level is the whole project; each level below divides its parent into components, down to **work packages** that can be estimated, assigned and tracked. A WBS shows *what* will be delivered, not when or how.
PMI's PMBOK Guide defines the WBS as a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work to be carried out by the project team to accomplish the project objectives and create the required deliverables. In PMI's framework, the approved [scope statement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/), the WBS and the WBS dictionary together form the **scope baseline**, which is the reference point for measuring and controlling scope.
The technique has its roots in large US defence and space programmes, and the US Department of Defense still maintains a WBS standard (MIL-STD-881). PMI also publishes a dedicated *Practice Standard for Work Breakdown Structures*. You do not need a defence-sized project to benefit, though: a simple three-level WBS on a whiteboard is often enough for a small team.
A WBS is usually drawn as a tree diagram (like an organisation chart) or written as an indented, numbered outline or table. Both show the same thing: the whole project broken into parts that add up exactly to the whole.

### Why a WBS matters
A WBS takes a few hours to build and pays for itself throughout the project. It helps you:
- **See the complete scope.** Breaking work down exposes deliverables that would otherwise be forgotten, such as training, data migration or documentation.
- **Estimate more accurately.** Small, well-defined work packages are far easier to estimate than a whole project. See our guide to [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/).
- **Assign clear ownership.** Every work package has one owner, which makes accountability visible. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) can map roles to WBS elements.
- **Build the schedule and budget.** Activities, durations and costs are planned per work package and roll up through the WBS.
- **Control scope.** Work that does not fit anywhere in the WBS is a signal of [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).
- **Identify risks.** Walking through each element is a structured way to ask "what could go wrong here?"
- **Communicate.** A one-page WBS diagram gives sponsors and teams a shared picture of what the project includes.
The WBS is a central part of the project management plan: the schedule, cost baseline and resource plan are all organised around it.

### Key rules for a good WBS

#### The 100% rule
The **100% rule** is the most important principle. The WBS includes 100% of the work defined by the project scope, including project management work, and nothing outside it. It applies at every level: the children of any element must add up to exactly 100% of that element's work, no more and no less. If a child element contains work that is not part of its parent, it is out of scope; if the children do not cover all of the parent, something is missing.

#### Deliverables, not activities
Name WBS elements as **nouns** that describe outcomes ("Payment integration", "User guide", "Venue") rather than verbs that describe actions ("Integrate payments", "Write guide", "Book venue"). Deliverable-oriented elements make it easier to check completeness and define acceptance criteria. The activities needed to produce each work package are listed later, in the schedule.

#### Mutually exclusive elements
No piece of work should appear in two places. Overlap leads to double-counted estimates, confused ownership and arguments about who is doing what.

#### Decompose to the right level
Stop decomposing when a work package is small enough to estimate reliably, assign to one owner and track, but not so small that managing it takes more effort than doing it. Common rules of thumb (not formal standards) include:
- **The 8/80 rule:** a work package should take roughly between 8 and 80 hours of effort.
- **The reporting period rule:** a work package should not span more than one or two reporting periods, so progress is visible.
- **The "if it makes sense" rule:** decompose further only if it improves estimating, assignment or control.
Most projects need three or four levels. Large programmes may need more, and small projects may need only two.

#### One owner per work package
Every work package should have a single accountable owner, even if several people contribute. Shared ownership usually means no ownership.
Tip
Include a "Project management" branch at level 2. Planning, reporting, meetings and governance take real effort, and leaving them out breaks the 100% rule and makes estimates too low.

### WBS levels and components
WBS levels are numbered from the top. The exact labels vary between organisations, but a typical structure looks like this:
| Level | What it contains | Example (customer portal) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The project or final deliverable | 1 Customer portal |
| 2 | Major deliverables or phases | 1.3 Design; 1.4 Build; 1.5 Testing |
| 3 | Sub-deliverables | 1.4.1 Front end; 1.4.2 Back end; 1.4.3 Integrations |
| 4 | Work packages (lowest level) | 1.4.3.1 Payment provider integration |
Activities and tasks sit below work packages, but they belong in the [project schedule](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/) rather than in the WBS itself. Our guide to [project tasks and activities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-tasks-and-activities/) explains the difference.
Other components you will come across:
- **WBS codes:** a numbering scheme (1, 1.1, 1.1.1) that gives every element a unique identifier and shows where it sits in the hierarchy. Codes link the WBS to the schedule, budget and timesheets.
- **Work packages:** the lowest level of the WBS, where effort, cost and duration are estimated and work is assigned. See our [work package guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/).
- **Control accounts:** management points above work packages where scope, budget and actual cost are compared, often used with [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).
- **Planning packages:** placeholders for work that is known to be in scope but not yet detailed enough to break into work packages.
- **WBS dictionary:** the companion document that describes each element in detail (covered below).
Work packages are where the plan becomes real work.

### Types of work breakdown structure
The main choice is how to organise level 2. The two most common approaches are deliverable-based and phase-based.
|  | Deliverable-based WBS | Phase-based WBS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level 2 organised by | Major outputs (design, build, training) | Project phases (initiation, planning, execution, closure) |
| Strengths | Makes scope and the 100% rule easy to check; clear ownership of outputs | Matches sequential life cycles and stage-gate approvals; familiar to stakeholders |
| Watch out for | Can hide sequencing; needs the schedule to show order | Deliverables can be split across phases, causing overlap |
| Good for | Most projects, especially product, IT and construction | Waterfall projects with formal phase reviews |
Many teams use a hybrid: phases at level 2 and deliverables at level 3. Whichever you choose, apply it consistently at each level. Other organising options include by location (sites or buildings), by subsystem (engineering) or by organisational unit, although organising by department tends to break the deliverable focus.
You can present the same WBS in several formats:
- **Tree diagram:** best for communicating the top three levels to sponsors and teams.
- **Outline:** an indented, numbered list; quick to create and edit.
- **Table or spreadsheet:** one row per element with code, owner, effort and cost; ideal for detail and roll-ups.
- **In a scheduling tool:** the WBS becomes the summary-task structure of a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/).

### Work breakdown structure examples
These examples show the same principles applied to different types of project. Use them as a starting point and adapt the elements to your own scope.

#### Example 1: customer portal (deliverable-based)
| WBS code | Element | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Customer portal | Level 1: the whole project |
| 1.1 | Project management | Plan, status reports, risk management, closure |
| 1.2 | Requirements | Workshops, signed-off requirements document |
| 1.3 | Design | 1.3.1 UX design; 1.3.2 Visual design; 1.3.3 Technical design |
| 1.4 | Build | 1.4.1 Front end; 1.4.2 Back end; 1.4.3 Integrations |
| 1.5 | Testing | 1.5.1 System testing; 1.5.2 User acceptance testing |
| 1.6 | Training | Guides and sessions for support staff |
| 1.7 | Deployment | Release and post-launch support |
This mirrors the example in our free [WBS template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/), where effort and cost entered for each element roll up to the project total.

#### Example 2: the same project, phase-based
| WBS code | Element |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Customer portal |
| 1.1 | Initiation: business case, charter |
| 1.2 | Planning: requirements, plan, budget |
| 1.3 | Execution: design, build, testing, training |
| 1.4 | Deployment: release, support handover |
| 1.5 | Closure: acceptance, lessons learned |
The phase-based version is easier for stage-gate reviews, but notice that the main deliverables are hidden inside "Execution". You would need a further level to make them visible.

#### Example 3: office relocation
| WBS code | Element |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Office relocation |
| 1.1 | Project management |
| 1.2 | New premises: lease, fit-out, furniture |
| 1.3 | IT and telecoms: network, desks and devices, phones |
| 1.4 | Move logistics: removals, packing, storage |
| 1.5 | People and communications: staff briefings, floor plans, new-site guide |
| 1.6 | Old premises exit: clearance, repairs, handback |
Note the easily forgotten deliverable at 1.6. Exiting the old premises is real work with real cost, and a WBS makes it visible early.

#### Example 4: conference
| WBS code | Element |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Annual conference |
| 1.1 | Project management |
| 1.2 | Venue and catering |
| 1.3 | Programme: speakers, agenda, session materials |
| 1.4 | Marketing and registration |
| 1.5 | Delegate experience: badges, signage, app |
| 1.6 | Audio-visual and livestream |
| 1.7 | Post-event: survey, report, content |

### How to create a work breakdown structure
Follow these steps to build a WBS for any project. For a small project you can do this in a single workshop; larger projects may need several sessions.
1. **Start from the approved scope.** Gather the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/), scope statement, requirements and any contract or statement of work. You cannot break down scope that has not been defined.
2. **Define level 1.** Write the project's final deliverable or name at the top.
3. **Choose how to organise level 2.** Decide between major deliverables and phases (see above), and include a project management branch.
4. **Decompose each element.** Break each level 2 element into its component [deliverables](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/). Ask "what does this consist of?" rather than "what do we need to do?"
5. **Stop at work packages.** Continue until each lowest-level element can be estimated, assigned to one owner and tracked within a reporting period.
6. **Apply the 100% rule.** For each parent, check that its children cover all its work and nothing more. Look for gaps and overlaps.
7. **Number the elements.** Give every element a unique WBS code so it can be referenced in the schedule, budget and reports.
8. **Write the WBS dictionary.** Describe each work package: scope, deliverables, acceptance criteria, owner, assumptions and estimates.
9. **Review with the team and stakeholders.** The people doing the work spot missing elements and unrealistic splits; stakeholders confirm nothing is out of scope.
10. **Baseline and maintain it.** Once approved, the WBS becomes part of the scope baseline. Update it only through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
Tip
Run decomposition as a sticky-note workshop: one note per deliverable, grouped under level 2 headings. It is quicker than typing, everyone can contribute, and gaps become obvious on the wall.

### The WBS dictionary
A **WBS dictionary** is the companion document to the WBS. The WBS shows the structure; the dictionary explains each element so that everyone understands exactly what is included. It is particularly useful for work packages, where it acts as a mini-brief for the owner.
A dictionary entry typically includes:
- WBS code and element name.
- Description of the work and what is included and excluded.
- Deliverables and acceptance criteria.
- Owner (responsible person or organisation).
- Effort, cost and duration estimates.
- Key milestones and dependencies.
- Assumptions, constraints and known risks.
- Resources, quality requirements and references.

#### Example dictionary entry
| Field | Entry |
| --- | --- |
| WBS code | 1.4.3.1 |
| Element | Payment provider integration |
| Description | Connect the portal checkout to the payment provider's API, including card payments and refunds. Excludes direct debit. |
| Acceptance criteria | Test payments and refunds succeed in the sandbox; security review passed |
| Owner | Tech lead |
| Estimate | 10 days effort |
| Dependencies | 1.3.3 Technical design approved; provider account set up |
| Assumptions | Provider sandbox available from week 6 |
For larger work packages you can expand the entry into a full work package description using our [work package template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-package-template/).

### From WBS to schedule and budget
The WBS is not a schedule, but it is the input to one. Once the WBS is agreed:
1. List the activities needed to produce each work package.
2. Identify [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) between activities.
3. Estimate durations and effort; our [effort estimation guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/) explains the main techniques.
4. Build the schedule, find the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) and add [milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/).
5. Estimate cost per work package and roll it up into the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/).
It helps to be clear about which document answers which question:
| Document | Answers | Contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WBS | What will we deliver? | Hierarchy of deliverables and work packages |
| WBS dictionary | What exactly does each element include? | Descriptions, owners, criteria, estimates |
| Schedule | When will it happen, in what order? | Activities, dependencies, durations, dates |
| Gantt chart | How does the schedule look over time? | Bars on a timeline, usually grouped by WBS |
| Product backlog | What is most valuable to build next? | Ordered list of epics, features and stories |
Scheduling is the natural next step after the WBS.

### Using a WBS in Agile projects
The Scrum Guide does not mention a WBS, and Agile teams usually work from an ordered [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) instead. The underlying idea, breaking a large outcome into smaller pieces of value, is still very much part of Agile.
In our experience, a backlog hierarchy of themes, [epics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/), features and user stories plays a similar role to a deliverable-based WBS, with two key differences: it is ordered by value rather than structured for completeness, and it is expected to change as the team learns.
A light, high-level WBS can still help Agile and hybrid projects:
- To agree the overall scope and budget with a sponsor before the first Sprint.
- To show non-software deliverables, such as training, data migration or procurement, that may not appear in a backlog.
- To support rolling-wave planning: near-term work is decomposed in detail while later work stays as planning packages.
- To integrate Agile teams into a wider programme that reports against a WBS.
Tip
If your organisation requires a WBS for an Agile project, keep it to two or three levels of deliverables and let the backlog hold the detail. Avoid duplicating every user story in the WBS.

### Common WBS mistakes
| Mistake | Why it matters | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Listing activities instead of deliverables | The WBS becomes a task list and gaps are hard to spot | Rename elements as nouns; move activities to the schedule |
| Leaving out project management | Breaks the 100% rule; estimates too low | Add a project management branch at level 2 |
| Over-decomposing | Tracking overhead outweighs the work | Stop when a package can be estimated and owned |
| Under-decomposing | Estimates are guesses; progress is invisible | Break large packages down until they fit a reporting period |
| Overlapping elements | Double-counted effort and confused ownership | Check siblings against each other for duplication |
| Including out-of-scope work | Hidden scope creep from day one | Check every element against the scope statement |
| Building it alone | Missed work and low team buy-in | Run a workshop with the people doing the work |
| Never updating it | The plan drifts away from reality | Update it through change control when scope changes |

It includes columns for WBS code, level, deliverable or work package, description, owner, effort (days), cost and status, with effort and cost rolling up to the project total. Pair it with the [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) for detailed costing and the [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) to turn work packages into a schedule.
Most project management software can hold a WBS as nested tasks or summary tasks with automatic numbering, which keeps the WBS and the schedule in sync. Our guide to [Gantt chart software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/) and our [project management software rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) compare the options.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a work breakdown structure in simple terms?**
A work breakdown structure is a family tree of everything a project must deliver: the whole project at the top, broken into smaller and smaller pieces until each piece can be estimated and assigned.

**Q: What are the levels of a WBS?**
Level 1 is the project, level 2 is major deliverables or phases, level 3 is sub-deliverables and the lowest level is work packages. Most projects need three or four levels.

**Q: What is the 100% rule in a WBS?**
The WBS must include all the work in the project scope, including project management, and nothing outside it. At every level, the children must add up to exactly 100% of their parent's work.

**Q: What is the 8/80 rule?**
A rule of thumb that a work package should take between about 8 and 80 hours of effort. It is a guideline for the right level of detail, not a formal standard.

**Q: What is a work package in a WBS?**
A work package is the lowest level of the WBS: a defined piece of work with one owner that can be estimated, scheduled and tracked.

**Q: What is a WBS dictionary?**
A WBS dictionary is a document that describes each WBS element in detail, including scope, deliverables, acceptance criteria, owner, estimates, dependencies and assumptions.

**Q: Should a WBS use nouns or verbs?**
Nouns. WBS elements describe deliverables (what is produced), while verbs describe activities, which belong in the schedule.

**Q: What is the difference between a WBS and a Gantt chart?**
A WBS shows what will be delivered, broken into a hierarchy. A Gantt chart shows when the work happens on a timeline. Gantt charts are often organised using the WBS.

**Q: Is a WBS the same as a project schedule?**
No. The WBS defines the scope; the schedule adds activities, dependencies, durations and dates to deliver it.

**Q: When should you create a WBS?**
During planning, after the scope statement is agreed and before you build the schedule, budget and resource plan.

**Q: Who creates the WBS?**
The project manager leads it, working with the team members and subject matter experts who will do the work.

**Q: How do you number a WBS?**
Use a hierarchical code: 1 for the project, 1.1 and 1.2 for level 2, 1.1.1 for level 3, and so on. Each code is unique and shows the element's position.

**Q: Do Agile projects use a WBS?**
Not usually in the traditional form. A backlog of epics, features and stories serves a similar purpose, though a light, high-level WBS can help with budgeting and hybrid projects.

**Q: Can a WBS change during the project?**
Yes, but once baselined it should only change through formal change control, with the scope statement, schedule and budget updated to match.

# Work Package in Project Management: Examples & How-To

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/
Section: Project management guides
Summary: What a work package in project management is, what to include, the 8/80 rule, work package vs task and activity, a worked example and step-by-step guide.


## Work Package in Project Management: Examples & How-To
A work package in project management is the lowest level of the work breakdown structure (WBS): a defined piece of work, with a clear output, that is small enough to estimate reliably, assign to one owner and track to completion. Work packages are where scope turns into estimates, budgets, schedules and accountability. This guide explains what to include, how to size and create work packages, how they differ from tasks and activities, and walks through a complete worked example.
- Published 17 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- A work package is the lowest level of the WBS, where cost and duration are estimated and managed.
- It describes an output (a noun, such as "quote request form"); the activities and tasks inside it describe the work (verbs).
- Every work package needs one owner, a clear deliverable, acceptance criteria, estimates, dates and dependencies.
- Use the 8/80 rule and the reporting-period rule as guides to size, not as fixed standards.
- Work packages roll up into control accounts and the project budget, and break down into schedule activities.
- In PRINCE2, a work package is also the formal instruction the project manager gives a team manager to deliver specific products.

### What is a work package in project management?
A **work package** is the work defined at the lowest level of a work breakdown structure, for which cost and duration are estimated and managed. It produces a specific, verifiable output, has a single accountable owner and is small enough to plan and control, yet large enough to be worth tracking as a unit.
Think of a work package as a small, self-contained project inside your project. It has its own scope (what it delivers), its own estimates (effort, duration and cost), its own owner and its own definition of done. Once it is approved, the owner and their team can get on with the work, and the project manager tracks it as one line in the plan.
Work packages matter because almost everything in project control is built on them:
- **Estimating.** Bottom-up estimates are made at work package level and added up to the project total.
- **Scheduling.** Each work package is broken into activities, which are sequenced and scheduled.
- **Budgeting.** Work package costs roll up into control accounts and the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/).
- **Accountability.** Each package has one named owner, which removes doubt about who is responsible.
- **Progress tracking.** Status, percent complete and earned value are measured package by package.

### Where work packages sit in the WBS
A [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) breaks the total project scope into progressively smaller deliverables. The bottom of each branch is a work package. Under the **100% rule**, the work packages together must cover all of the project's scope, including project management work, and nothing outside it.
| Level | What it represents | Example (website project) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Project | The total scope | New customer website |
| 2. Major deliverable | A main output or phase | 5 Build |
| 3. Control account (optional) | A management point where scope, budget and schedule are integrated and reported | 5 Build, owned by the development lead |
| 4. Work package | The lowest WBS element, estimated, owned and tracked | 5.3 Quote request form |
| Below the WBS: activities | Scheduled work needed to produce the work package | Build CRM integration |
| Below the WBS: tasks | Smaller personal steps inside an activity | Map form fields to CRM fields |
Each work package has a WBS code (such as 5.3) that ties it to its parent and appears in the schedule, budget, timesheets and reports. The detail for each package is recorded in the **WBS dictionary**, which is essentially a collection of work package descriptions.

#### Control accounts and planning packages
On larger projects, particularly those using earned value, work packages are grouped under **control accounts**. A control account is a management point, usually owned by a control account manager, where scope, budget, actual cost and schedule are integrated and compared. Each work package belongs to exactly one control account.
A **planning package** is a placeholder below a control account for work whose scope is known but not yet detailed. It has a budget but no detailed activities. As the work gets closer, the planning package is converted into one or more work packages. This is the essence of **rolling wave planning**: plan the near term in detail and the far term at a higher level.

### Work package vs task, activity and deliverable
These terms are often used loosely, and project management tools call almost everything a "task". The distinctions are still useful, especially for planning and exams.
| Term | What it is | Named as | Typical size | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deliverable | A product, result or capability the project must produce | Noun | Weeks to months | Website build |
| Work package | The lowest WBS element, with an owner, estimates and acceptance criteria | Noun | Roughly 8 to 80 hours of effort | Quote request form |
| Activity | A scheduled piece of work needed to complete a work package | Verb + noun | Hours to days | Build CRM integration |
| Task | A smaller step within an activity, often personal | Verb + noun | Minutes to hours | Test field validation in Safari |
| Milestone | A significant point or event with zero duration | Event | Zero duration | Form approved for launch |
The simplest rule: **work packages describe what is produced; activities and tasks describe how it is produced.** If a WBS element starts with a verb ("design", "build", "test"), it is probably an activity that belongs inside a work package. For more on the lower levels, see our guide to [project tasks and activities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-tasks-and-activities/).
A work package is not always the same as a deliverable either. A large deliverable may be split into several work packages, while a small deliverable may be a single work package. See our guide to [project deliverables](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/).

### What a work package includes
A work package description (also called a work package statement or WBS dictionary entry) records everything someone needs to understand, estimate, deliver and accept the work. Scale it to the project: a small internal project may need only the first eight fields; a contract or earned value project will need all of them.
| Field | What to write | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ID and name | WBS code and a short noun phrase | Links the package to the WBS, schedule and budget |
| Description and scope | What is included and, just as important, what is excluded | Prevents gaps, overlaps and [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) |
| Deliverable | The specific output | Makes completion visible |
| Acceptance criteria | Measurable conditions for "done" and who accepts | Avoids arguments at the end |
| Owner | One named person | Single point of accountability |
| Resources | People, roles, equipment and materials | Feeds resource planning and costing |
| Effort and duration | Hours of work and elapsed time | Effort drives cost; duration drives the schedule |
| Cost estimate | Labour, materials and other costs | Rolls up to the control account and budget |
| Start and finish dates | Planned dates from the schedule | Sets expectations and supports tracking |
| Dependencies | Predecessors, successors and external inputs | Feeds the network diagram and [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) |
| Assumptions and constraints | What the estimate depends on | Explains variances later |
| Risks | Key risks specific to this package | Feeds the risk register |
| Progress method and reporting | How progress is measured and how often it is reported | Consistent status and earned value |
| Approval | Who approved the package and when | Shows that the work is authorised |
You do not need to build this from scratch. Our free [work package template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-package-template/) includes these fields, and the [WBS template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) holds the structure the packages sit in.

### How big should a work package be?
There is no formal standard for work package size. The right size is the one that lets you estimate accurately, assign clearly and see progress early, without creating more administration than the work is worth. Four rules of thumb help.
| Rule of thumb | What it says | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8/80 rule | Between about 8 and 80 hours of effort | Smaller packages add overhead; larger ones are hard to estimate and hide problems |
| Reporting-period rule | No longer than one or two reporting periods | Problems show up in the next status report, not months later |
| Single-owner rule | One person can be accountable for it | If two managers own it, it is probably two work packages |
| Measurable-output rule | Completion can be verified objectively | "Done" should not be a matter of opinion |
Treat these as guides, not laws. The 8/80 rule comes from practitioner experience rather than from a standards body, and large engineering or construction projects often have much bigger packages that are still well controlled. The real test is: **can you estimate it, assign it and track it?** If yes, stop decomposing.
| Signs a work package is too big | Signs a work package is too small |
| --- | --- |
| Estimates vary wildly between estimators | There are hundreds of packages to track |
| It spans several months or several teams | Reporting takes longer than the work |
| Status stays at "in progress" for many periods | Packages are really individual tasks |
| It has several unrelated outputs | The WBS has been decomposed to the level of to-do lists |

### How to create work packages step by step
1. **Start from an agreed scope.** Work from an approved scope statement and requirements. Work packages cannot be better than the [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) they come from.
2. **Decompose the deliverables.** Break each major deliverable into smaller components until each branch reaches a piece of work that passes the sizing tests above. Name each element as a noun.
3. **Check the 100% rule.** Confirm the children of every element add up to all of its work, with no gaps or overlaps. Include project management, testing, training and handover packages.
4. **Assign an owner to each package.** Choose the person who will be accountable for delivery, and agree it with them and their line manager. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) helps where several roles are involved.
5. **Write the work package description.** Fill in the fields from the table above, starting with the description, exclusions, deliverable and acceptance criteria.
6. **Estimate with the people doing the work.** Ask the owner and team to estimate effort, duration and cost. Bottom-up [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/) at this level is usually the most accurate method. Our [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) turns effort into cost.
7. **Identify activities and dependencies.** Break each package into activities, link them with dependencies and feed them into the [project schedule](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scheduling/).
8. **Review and approve.** Review packages with owners and the sponsor, resolve gaps, then include them in the scope, schedule and cost [baselines](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/).
9. **Authorise and track.** Release each package when it is due to start, then track progress, cost and issues against its baseline.
Tip
Write the exclusions as carefully as the inclusions. "Excludes content writing and translation" in a build work package prevents one of the most common arguments at acceptance.

### Work package example: a website build
This example is **illustrative**: the project, rates and figures are invented to show how one work package is defined, broken down and rolled up.
A company is replacing its customer website. The WBS has six major deliverables: 1 Project management, 2 Discovery, 3 Design, 4 Content, 5 Build and 6 Launch. The development lead owns deliverable 5 Build, which is managed as a control account and broken into four work packages.

#### Step 1: decompose the deliverable
| WBS code | Work package | Owner | Effort | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5.1 | Page templates | Front-end developer | 72 hours | £4,680 |
| 5.2 | CMS configuration | Back-end developer | 40 hours | £2,600 |
| 5.3 | Quote request form | Back-end developer | 56 hours | £3,430 |
| 5.4 | Analytics and tracking | Front-end developer | 20 hours | £1,300 |
| 5 Build (control account) |  | Development lead | 188 hours | £12,010 |
Every package sits within the 8/80 range, each has one owner, and the four packages together cover all of the build work. Content writing is in deliverable 4, so it is excluded here.

#### Step 2: write the work package description
| Field | 5.3 Quote request form |
| --- | --- |
| Description | An online form on the Contact and Product pages that lets visitors request a quote and sends each request to the CRM |
| Excludes | Form copy (supplied by 4 Content), CRM licence changes, email nurture sequences |
| Deliverable | Working form in the live environment, connected to the CRM |
| Acceptance criteria | Submissions create a CRM lead within 1 minute; required-field validation works; form meets the agreed accessibility standard; spam protection blocks automated test submissions; accepted by the sales operations manager |
| Owner | Back-end developer |
| Resources | Business analyst 6 h, back-end developer 40 h, tester 10 h, CRM sandbox account |
| Effort and duration | 56 hours over 10 working days |
| Cost | £3,430 (analyst at £55/h, developer at £65/h, tester at £50/h) |
| Dependencies | Starts after 3.2 Form design is approved and 5.2 CMS configuration is complete; 6.1 Launch testing depends on it |
| Assumptions | CRM API access is available by day 1; field list does not change after activity A1 |
| Risks | CRM API rate limits; late changes to form fields from sales |
| Progress method | Weighted milestones: fields agreed 10%, form built 40%, integration working 70%, tested 90%, accepted 100% |

#### Step 3: break the work package into activities
| ID | Activity | Role | Effort | Predecessor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | Confirm form fields and validation rules | Business analyst | 6 h | None |
| A2 | Build front-end form | Developer | 16 h | A1 |
| A3 | Build CRM integration | Developer | 14 h | A1 |
| A4 | Add spam protection and accessibility fixes | Developer | 6 h | A2 |
| A5 | Test form, integration and accessibility | Tester | 10 h | A3, A4 |
| A6 | Fix defects and obtain acceptance | Developer | 4 h | A5 |
The activities add up to 56 hours: 6 for the analyst, 40 for the developer and 10 for the tester. The cost works out as 6 × £55 + 40 × £65 + 10 × £50 = £330 + £2,600 + £500 = £3,430. These activities, not the work package itself, go into the Gantt chart with their dependencies.

#### Step 4: track progress
At the end of week one, A1 and A2 are complete and A3 is half done. Under the weighted milestone rule, the package has reached "fields agreed" and "form built", so it is reported as 40% complete, giving an earned value of 40% × £3,430 = £1,372. If actual cost to date is £1,600, the package is slightly over budget for the work done, which the owner explains in the weekly [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).

### Work package examples by industry
| Industry | Deliverable | Example work packages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Software | Mobile app release | Login and account screens; payment integration; push notifications; app store submission |
| Construction | Office fit-out | Partition walls, level 2; electrical first fix; data cabling; ceilings and lighting |
| Marketing | Product launch campaign | Launch video; landing page; paid social campaign set-up; press kit |
| Events | Annual conference | Venue contract; speaker programme; registration system; on-site signage |
| Manufacturing | New production line | Equipment specification; conveyor installation; safety validation; operator training |
| Research | Clinical study set-up | Protocol document; ethics submission; site selection; data management plan |
| HR and change | New HR system | Data migration; manager training; policy updates; payroll interface |
Notice that every example is a noun describing an output. Each would then get its own owner, estimates and acceptance criteria.

### Work packages in PRINCE2
In [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/), the term has a slightly different, more formal meaning. A PRINCE2 work package is a set of information and instructions that the project manager uses to hand over responsibility for delivering one or more products to a team manager or team member. It is both a description of the work and an **authorisation** to do it.
The project manager authorises work packages as part of controlling a stage. The team manager accepts, executes and delivers them in the managing product delivery process, then reports progress through checkpoint reports. A PRINCE2 work package typically contains:
- A description of the work and the products to be delivered, with their product descriptions
- Techniques, processes or standards to be used
- Agreed tolerances, such as time, cost and scope
- Constraints, interfaces and dependencies
- Reporting arrangements, such as how often checkpoint reports are produced
- Quality requirements and who carries out quality checks
- The date it was agreed between the project manager and team manager
The two meanings fit together well: a PRINCE2 work package can cover one or several WBS work packages, and in both cases the point is clear, agreed, controllable chunks of work with a named person accountable for delivery.

### Tracking work packages and earned value
Because each work package has its own budget and dates, it is the natural unit for measuring progress. The key is to agree, before work starts, how progress will be credited, so that "percent complete" means something.
| Progress method | How it works | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0/100 | No credit until the package is finished | Very short packages, under one reporting period |
| 50/50 | 50% credit at start, 50% at finish | Packages spanning about two reporting periods |
| Weighted milestones | Credit at defined, verifiable points | Longer packages with clear intermediate outputs |
| Units complete | Credit by quantity delivered (metres laid, pages built) | Repetitive work with countable outputs |
| Physical percent complete | Owner's assessment against defined criteria | Work without natural milestones; needs clear rules |
Rolled up to control accounts, these figures give planned value, earned value and actual cost for the whole project. See our guide to [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) for the formulas and how to read the results.

### Benefits of work packages
- **More accurate estimates.** Small, well-defined pieces of work are easier to estimate than whole deliverables, and errors partly cancel out when added up.
- **Clear accountability.** One owner per package means nobody has to ask who is responsible.
- **Easier delegation.** A good description lets the owner and team work with little supervision.
- **Earlier warning of problems.** Packages that fit a reporting period show slippage within weeks.
- **Better cost control.** Actual costs can be collected and compared package by package.
- **Stronger scope control.** Inclusions and exclusions make it obvious when a request is new scope.
- **Reuse.** Well-written packages become templates for similar future projects.

### Common work package mistakes
| Mistake | Consequence | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Naming packages as activities ("Build form") | The WBS turns into a to-do list and outputs are unclear | Name packages as nouns; put verbs in the activity list |
| Shared or unclear ownership | Work falls between people | Assign one accountable owner per package |
| No acceptance criteria | Disputes over whether the work is done | Write measurable criteria and name who accepts |
| Estimating without the team | Optimistic, unowned estimates | Have the people doing the work estimate it |
| Missing project management, testing or training packages | The budget and schedule are understated | Apply the 100% rule to the whole scope |
| Packages far too large | Problems hide until late | Split by output, phase or location to fit a reporting period |
| Decomposing far-off work too early | Wasted effort and false precision | Use planning packages and rolling wave planning |
| Changing packages without change control | The baseline loses meaning | Route changes through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) |

### Managing work packages in project management software
Most tools do not have a field called "work package", but they all let you represent one. The usual pattern is to make each work package a parent item with its own owner, dates and custom fields, and to add the activities as child tasks.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, maps well to a formal WBS: deliverables as projects or folders, work packages as parent tasks with custom fields for WBS code, budget and acceptance criteria, and activities as subtasks on an interactive Gantt chart with dependencies and baselines.
- **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)** works well when each work package is a group or an item, with subitems for activities and columns for owner, timeline, budget and status.
- **[Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/)** can represent work packages as sections or parent tasks within a project, with subtasks, dependencies and custom fields.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** lets you use lists or parent tasks for work packages, with subtasks, custom fields and Gantt views.
- **[Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/)** uses indented parent rows, so a WBS with work packages and activities looks much like the spreadsheet many planners already use.
Whatever the tool, keep the WBS code in a field so that schedule, cost and status reports can be grouped by work package.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a work package in simple terms?**
A small, clearly defined chunk of project work with one owner, a specific output, estimates and acceptance criteria. It is the lowest level of the work breakdown structure.

**Q: What is an example of a work package?**
"Quote request form" on a website project, "electrical first fix" on an office fit-out or "press kit" on a product launch. Each produces a defined output that can be estimated, owned and accepted.

**Q: What is the difference between a work package and a task?**
A work package describes an output at the lowest level of the WBS. Tasks and activities are the steps needed to produce it. One work package usually contains several activities, and each activity may contain several tasks.

**Q: What is the difference between a work package and an activity?**
Work packages belong to the WBS and are named as nouns; activities belong to the schedule and are named as verbs. Activities are created by breaking down work packages.

**Q: What is the 8/80 rule?**
A rule of thumb that a work package should take between about 8 and 80 hours of effort. It is a guide to the right level of detail, not a formal standard.

**Q: Who is responsible for a work package?**
One named owner is accountable for delivering it, even if several people do the work. On larger projects, the owner reports to a control account manager or the project manager.

**Q: What should a work package include?**
At minimum an ID, name, description and exclusions, deliverable, acceptance criteria, owner, resources, effort, duration, cost, dates and dependencies. Larger projects add assumptions, risks, progress method and approval.

**Q: What is a control account?**
A management point in the WBS where scope, budget, actual cost and schedule are integrated and compared for earned value. Each control account contains one or more work packages, and each work package belongs to exactly one control account.

**Q: What is the difference between a planning package and a work package?**
A planning package is a budgeted placeholder for future work whose scope is known but not yet detailed. It is converted into work packages, with activities and estimates, as the work gets closer.

**Q: What is a work package in PRINCE2?**
A set of information and instructions that the project manager uses to authorise a team manager or team member to deliver one or more products, including tolerances, quality requirements and reporting arrangements.

**Q: How many work packages should a project have?**
As many as needed to cover 100% of the scope at a level you can estimate, assign and track. A small project might have 10 to 20; a large programme can have hundreds.

**Q: Is a work package the same as a deliverable?**
Not always. A work package always produces an output, but a large deliverable may be split into several work packages, and some outputs, such as a test report, exist mainly to support other deliverables.

**Q: What is the difference between a work package and a WBS dictionary?**
The work package is the piece of work itself. The WBS dictionary is the document that describes every WBS element, including each work package's scope, owner, estimates and acceptance criteria.

# Agile Capacity Planning: Formula, Steps and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Agile capacity planning step by step: the sprint capacity formula, focus factor, velocity adjustments, a worked example, release forecasts and mistakes.


## Agile Capacity Planning: Formula, Steps and Example
Agile capacity planning is the practice of working out how much work a team can realistically take on in a sprint, release or quarter, based on who is available and how much the team has delivered before. Done well, it stops overcommitment, protects a sustainable pace and makes forecasts believable. This guide gives you the formulas, a fully worked five-person example, and the adjustments for holidays, part-timers, new joiners and unplanned work.
- Published 19 September 2026
- Last updated 14 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Capacity is the time a team has available; velocity is how much it has historically finished. Use velocity as the baseline and capacity as the adjustment.
- Sprint capacity = available person-days × realistic focus hours, minus Scrum events and an allowance for unplanned work.
- Scale average velocity by this sprint's capacity compared with a normal sprint, and plan to a range rather than a single number.
- Historical velocity already includes past interruptions, so do not subtract an unplanned-work buffer from it a second time.
- Check capacity by skill as well as in total: one overloaded specialist can sink a sprint that looks fine on paper.
- The same logic scales up: releases are forecast as ranges, and portfolios are planned in team-sprints.

### What is Agile capacity planning?
**Agile capacity planning** is the process of estimating how much work an Agile team can complete in a coming time-box, usually a sprint, by combining each person's availability with the team's past delivery rate. Its output is a realistic forecast, in hours or story points, that the team uses to decide how much work to commit to.
It is not a separate ceremony. Capacity planning happens inside events you already run: at the start of [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/), during [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/), in [PI Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/) if you use SAFe, and in quarterly portfolio reviews.
The Scrum Guide (2020, still the current official edition) does not prescribe a capacity formula, but it does say that the more the Developers know about their past performance, their upcoming capacity and their [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), the more confident they will be in their Sprint forecasts. Those three inputs are exactly what this guide works with.
Capacity planning matters for three reasons:
- **Sustainable pace.** One of the twelve principles behind the Agile Manifesto asks teams to maintain a constant pace indefinitely. Planning to real capacity is how you do that.
- **Predictability.** Stakeholders can plan launches, marketing and training around forecasts that hold up sprint after sprint.
- **Trust.** A team that regularly meets its Sprint Goal earns the freedom to manage its own work. A team that regularly misses it attracts micromanagement.
Agile capacity planning is a team-level version of a broader discipline. For organisation-wide resource planning, see our guide to [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/).

### Capacity vs velocity and other key terms
Most capacity mistakes come from mixing up a handful of terms. The table sets them side by side.
| Term | What it measures | Unit | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capacity | The time the team has available for sprint work in a given period | Hours or person-days | 42 person-days this sprint |
| Velocity | The amount of work the team has actually finished per sprint, on average | Story points (or items) per sprint | 31 points per sprint |
| Load (demand) | The work the team is being asked to do | Hours or points | 45 points of candidate backlog items |
| Focus factor | The share of available time that goes on planned sprint work | Percentage or ratio | 0.7 (70%) |
| Utilisation | Hours booked against hours available | Percentage | 85% of hours booked |
| Throughput | Items finished per period, used mainly in Kanban | Items per week | 9 items per week |
The working rule is simple: **velocity tells you what a normal sprint produces; capacity tells you how this sprint differs from normal.** Velocity without capacity ignores the fact that two people are on holiday. Capacity without velocity tells you how many hours you have but not how much work fits into them.
For more on measuring and reading velocity, see our guides to [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) and the [Agile velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/).

### Who plans capacity and when
Capacity planning happens at several levels, with different people and units at each one.
| Level | When | Who is involved | Typical unit | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint | Start of every Sprint Planning (prepare availability the day before) | Developers, facilitated by the Scrum Master; Product Owner brings priorities | Hours, person-days or story points | Sprint Backlog that fits the team |
| Release | Release planning, then refreshed every sprint | Product Owner with the team | Story points per sprint, as a range | Forecast of scope by date, or date for scope |
| Quarter or PI | Quarterly planning or PI Planning | Teams, Product Management, Release Train Engineer in SAFe | Points per iteration | Committed objectives per team |
| Portfolio | Quarterly portfolio review | Portfolio leads, product leaders, PMO | Team-sprints or teams per quarter | Which initiatives are funded now and which wait |
In Scrum, the **Developers** decide how much work they can take on. The Scrum Master helps them use good data and keeps the conversation honest; the Product Owner explains which items matter most but does not set the amount. A manager calculating capacity on the team's behalf and handing it down misses the point.

### The sprint capacity formula
There is no official formula, but four versions are in common use. They are the same idea seen from different angles, and the worked example below shows that they give consistent answers.
| Method | Formula | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hours | Σ (available days × focus hours per day) − Scrum events − unplanned-work allowance | Teams that plan tasks in hours; checking specialist workloads |
| Person-days | Σ (sprint days − absences) × allocation to the team | Quick availability check; the input to every other method |
| Velocity scaling | Average velocity × (available person-days ÷ normal person-days) | Teams that estimate in story points |
| Focus factor | Available person-days × (past velocity ÷ past person-days) | The same as velocity scaling, expressed per person-day |

#### What is a realistic focus factor?
The focus factor is the share of someone's working time that actually goes on planned sprint work, once email, support, meetings outside the team, context switching and breaks are taken out. Practitioner guidance commonly puts it between **0.6 and 0.8** (60–80%), with newer teams and teams with heavy support duties at the lower end. That range is a starting point, not a standard: the most reliable focus factor is the one you measure from your own last few sprints.
Tip
A quick way to find your real focus factor: for two sprints, log roughly how many hours each person spent on Sprint Backlog items. Divide by their available hours. Most teams are surprised by how low the number is.

### How to calculate sprint capacity step by step
Use this sequence before or at the start of Sprint Planning. Steps 1 to 5 give you capacity in hours; steps 6 and 7 turn it into a story-point forecast; step 8 checks it is achievable in practice.
1. **List everyone on the team** and the number of working days in the sprint (10 for a two-week sprint, minus any public holidays).
2. **Subtract absences:** annual leave, training, conferences, planned sick leave, on-call days and other known commitments.
3. **Apply each person's allocation.** Someone split 50/50 with another team has half the days.
4. **Multiply by realistic focus hours per day.** Few people manage more than five or six hours a day of focused sprint work.
5. **Subtract Scrum events and set aside an allowance for unplanned work**, based on what actually arrived in recent sprints.
6. **Compare available person-days with a normal sprint** (one with no unusual absences) to get a capacity ratio.
7. **Scale your average velocity by that ratio** and express the result as a range, using your lowest and highest recent sprints.
8. **Sanity-check by skill and by item.** Make sure no single person or skill is overloaded, and that the items selected can genuinely be finished to the Definition of Done.
Keep the arithmetic in a shared sheet so the team can see it. Our free [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) has a Capacity tab with columns for team member, available days, focus factor, capacity in days and notes, and totals it for you.

### Worked example: a five-person team
Here is the whole method applied to one team. It is a two-week sprint with 10 working days and no public holidays.
| Team member | Role | Absence this sprint | Allocation to team | Available days | Normal days |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Priya | Developer | None | 100% | 10 | 10 |
| Tom | Developer | 2 days annual leave | 100% | 8 | 10 |
| Sara | Developer | None | 50% (shared with another product) | 5 | 5 |
| Luis | Tester | None | 100% | 10 | 10 |
| Mei | Designer | 1 day training | 100% | 9 | 10 |
| **Team total** |  |  |  | **42** | **45** |

#### Method 1: capacity in hours
- Focus hours: the team uses 6 focus hours per day, so 42 days × 6 = **252 hours**.
- Scrum events: Sprint Planning (3 hours), Sprint Review (1.5), Sprint Retrospective (1.5) and backlog refinement (2) come to 8 hours per full-time person, or 4 for Sara. That is 4 × 8 + 4 = **36 hours**.
- Unplanned work: over the last three sprints, about 10% of hours went on production support and urgent requests, so the team reserves 10% of the remaining 216 hours, about **22 hours**.
- **Plannable capacity: 252 − 36 − 22 ≈ 194 hours.**

#### Method 2: scaling velocity
- The last three sprints delivered 33, 29 and 31 points. Average velocity = 93 ÷ 3 = **31 points**.
- Those sprints all had normal availability of 45 person-days. This sprint has 42, so the capacity ratio is 42 ÷ 45 = **0.93**.
- Forecast = 31 × 0.93 ≈ **29 points**. Applying the same ratio to the lowest and highest sprints (29 and 33) gives a range of about **27 to 31 points**.

#### Method 3: focus factor per person-day
Past delivery was 31 points from 45 person-days, or about 0.69 points per person-day. This sprint: 42 × 0.69 ≈ **29 points**. It is the same answer as Method 2 because it is the same calculation written differently, which is a useful check that your inputs are consistent.

#### Cross-check by skill
Luis is the only tester. His 10 days × 6 hours = 60 hours, minus 8 hours of events and a 10% allowance, leaves about 47 hours. When the team breaks down the candidate items, they find 58 hours of testing. Rather than overload Luis, two developers agree to pair on test automation for one story, and the team drops a low-priority item that needed heavy manual testing. Total capacity was fine; skill capacity was not.

#### What the team commits to
The Product Owner's top items are sized 8, 5, 5, 3, 5 and 3 points. The first five total 26 points and are enough to meet the Sprint Goal; the sixth brings the total to 29, at the top of the comfortable range. The team's task breakdown comes to about 180 hours against 194 available, so they take all six, with the Sprint Goal resting on the first five. The next refined item stays at the top of the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) in case capacity frees up.
Tip
Notice that the velocity method did not subtract the 10% unplanned-work allowance. Past velocity already reflects the interruptions that happened in past sprints. Subtracting a buffer from velocity as well would count the same interruptions twice.

### Should you plan in hours or story points?
Both work. Many teams use story points to decide how much to take on, and hours or days only to check availability and specialist load.
|  | Story points and velocity | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it captures | Relative size, complexity and uncertainty | Effort per task |
| Strengths | Quick, accounts for uncertainty, self-corrects through velocity | Intuitive, easy to check against calendars, good for spotting overloaded specialists |
| Weaknesses | Abstract for stakeholders; easy to misuse as a productivity score | Encourages false precision and time-sheet thinking; estimates are often optimistic |
| Good fit | Stable teams with a few sprints of history | New teams, mixed-skill teams, client work billed by the hour |
Our advice: if you have at least three sprints of stable velocity, plan in points and use hours as a sanity check. If the team is new or its membership has just changed, start with hours and switch once velocity settles.

### Planning for unplanned work
Few teams get a sprint free of interruptions. Production incidents, urgent customer requests and questions from other teams all eat into capacity. Ignoring them does not make them go away; it just means the Sprint Goal pays for them.
1. **Measure it.** Tag unplanned items on the board for three or four sprints and record the hours or points they took.
2. **Reserve the average.** If unplanned work takes 10–15% of capacity, reserve that share in the hours method.
3. **Consider a rotation.** One person per sprint handles interruptions, protecting the focus of everyone else. Rotate the role so nobody is stuck with it.
4. **Make it visible.** Show unplanned work as its own swimlane so the team and stakeholders can see what it costs.
5. **Reduce it at source.** Use the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) to tackle the causes, such as fragile code or unclear support routes. Paying down technical debt is often the best long-term fix.
If unplanned work is more than about half of what the team does, and it cannot wait until the next sprint, fixed sprints may be the wrong container. A flow-based approach with explicit [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) often works better; see [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/).

### Special cases that change capacity

#### Part-time members and shared specialists
Count people at their real allocation, and be honest about it. Someone nominally 50% on your team who spends most of the week firefighting elsewhere may give you 30%. Shared specialists such as UX designers, data engineers or security reviewers should be planned explicitly, because their availability often limits what the team can finish. Expressing allocations as [full-time equivalents (FTE)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/full-time-equivalent-fte/) keeps the arithmetic clear.

#### New team members
A new joiner usually reduces capacity for the first sprint or two, because experienced colleagues spend time helping them. Plan the newcomer at a low focus factor at first, for example 0.3 to 0.5, and lower the mentor's slightly too. Fred Brooks observed in The Mythical Man-Month that adding people to a late software project tends to make it later; the same effect applies at sprint scale.

#### Holidays and peak leave periods
Collect planned leave a sprint ahead, and check public holidays in every country where team members work. Around holiday seasons, consider a shorter Sprint Goal rather than a shorter sprint, because changing [sprint length](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/) disrupts your velocity history.

#### Skill bottlenecks
Total capacity hides skill constraints, as the worked example shows. A simple [skills matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) shows where one person is the only one who can do a type of work. Over time, cross-training and pairing widen the team's skills and make capacity more flexible. Swarming, where several people work on one item together, is another way to stop work queuing behind one person.

#### Team changes and velocity resets
When the team's membership changes significantly, old velocity becomes a poor guide. Use the hours method for two or three sprints, then rebuild a velocity baseline from the new team's actual results.

### Capacity planning beyond the sprint

#### Release and quarter forecasts
For a release, multiply the number of sprints by a velocity range, adjusted for known capacity changes. Continuing the example: the team has six sprints in the quarter, and one falls in a holiday period with about 70% of normal capacity. That gives 5.7 sprint-equivalents.
| Scenario | Velocity | Calculation | Forecast for the quarter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pessimistic | 29 | 29 × 5.7 | ≈ 165 points |
| Expected | 31 | 31 × 5.7 | ≈ 177 points |
| Optimistic | 33 | 33 × 5.7 | ≈ 188 points |
The release backlog holds 150 points of Must-have items and 40 points of Should-have items. The Product Owner can tell stakeholders with confidence that all Must-haves will land this quarter, plus somewhere between 15 and 38 points of Should-haves. That is far more useful than a single date that is either padded or wrong. Update the forecast every sprint as real results come in. Our [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) helps you lay this out.

#### SAFe and PI Planning
In the Scaled Agile Framework, each team calculates capacity for every iteration of the Program Increment during [PI Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/). For teams with no velocity history, SAFe describes a starting method using normalised story points: give the team eight points for every full-time member, adjust for part-timers, and subtract one point for each vacation day or holiday. For our example team that is 8 + 8 + 4 + 8 + 8 = 36, minus 3 days of absence, or 33 points. SAFe presents this as a way to start, not a permanent rule; once the team has real velocity, it uses that instead.
SAFe also uses **capacity allocation**: agreeing in advance what share of capacity goes on new features versus enablers, maintenance and technical debt. The split is a policy decision for each Agile Release Train, not a fixed ratio.

#### Portfolio capacity
At portfolio level, the useful unit is usually the **team-sprint**: one stable team for one sprint. Leaders compare roadmap demand with the number of team-sprints available and decide what not to start.
| Item | Team-sprints |
| --- | --- |
| Supply: 4 teams × 6 sprints | 24 |
| Less 20% reserved for maintenance and technical debt | −5 (rounded) |
| **Available for new initiatives** | **19** |
| Demand: Initiative A (8), B (6), C (5), D (4) | 23 |
| Decision | Fund A, B and C now (19); start D next quarter |
Matching work to stable teams, rather than moving people between projects, keeps velocity meaningful and avoids the cost of constant team changes.

#### Kanban and flow-based teams
Kanban teams do not plan sprints, but they still manage capacity, mainly through WIP limits. Instead of velocity they use [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/), the number of items finished per week. To answer "how many items by date X?" or "when will these 30 items be done?", many teams run a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) on their historical throughput, which gives a forecast with a stated probability rather than a single number.

### Tools and templates for capacity planning
A spreadsheet is enough for one team. Our free [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) includes a Capacity tab (team member, available days, focus factor, capacity in days, notes) next to the Sprint Backlog, so you can check one against the other in the same session.
As you add teams, most Agile tools offer capacity or workload views, often on higher-priced plans. Azure DevOps, for example, has a capacity page for each sprint; Jira, Wrike, monday.com, ClickUp and Smartsheet offer workload or resource views that show who is over-allocated. Wrike's workload and resource planning features are a good fit when several teams share specialists and managers need to see allocation across projects. Before you choose, compare options in our [project management tools ranking](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) and check which plan includes the feature you need.
Whatever you use, keep three things visible: each person's availability for the sprint, the team's recent velocity, and how much unplanned work arrived. For organisation-wide planning, our guide to [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) explains how to match people to projects.

### Common capacity planning mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planning at 100% of available hours | No room for meetings, interruptions or problems; the Sprint Goal is missed | Plan with a realistic focus factor and an unplanned-work allowance |
| Ignoring leave and public holidays | Velocity is applied to a sprint that has fewer people in it | Collect availability before every Sprint Planning |
| Double-counting interruptions | Subtracting a buffer from historical velocity under-commits the team | Use the buffer in the hours method only |
| Treating velocity as a target | Teams inflate estimates; forecasts stop meaning anything | Use velocity only for forecasting, never as a performance score |
| Comparing velocity between teams | Story points are relative to each team, so comparisons are meaningless | Compare predictability and outcomes, not points |
| Assuming new people are fully productive | Capacity drops while they learn, and mentors slow down too | Plan newcomers and mentors at a lower focus factor |
| Checking total capacity only | One overloaded specialist blocks several items | Check capacity by skill during planning |
| Managers setting capacity for the team | Commitment without ownership; trust erodes | Developers decide; managers provide data and remove obstacles |
| Single-number forecasts | Stakeholders hear a promise, not a forecast | Give a range and update it every sprint |
If capacity planning keeps failing, look at item size. Large, poorly understood items are the most common reason forecasts slip. Good [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) that splits work into small, well-understood items makes every capacity calculation more accurate.

### Capacity planning checklist
Run through this before your next Sprint Planning:
- Everyone's leave, training, on-call and public holidays for the sprint are recorded.
- Part-time and shared members are counted at their real allocation.
- The focus factor reflects recent sprints, not an ideal week.
- Average velocity and the range from your last three to five sprints are to hand.
- Unplanned work from recent sprints is measured, and an allowance is agreed.
- Candidate items are refined, sized and small enough to finish in the sprint.
- Specialist skills are checked so nobody is overloaded.
- The Sprint Goal can be met even if the last item selected is not finished.
- The forecast is shown as a range, and the method is visible to the whole team.
Capacity planning is one input to a good sprint. For the full event, from the Sprint Goal to the plan for the first day, see our guide to [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is capacity planning in Agile?**
Agile capacity planning is working out how much work a team can realistically take on in a sprint, release or quarter, by combining each person's availability with the team's past delivery rate. It helps the team commit to an achievable amount and give stakeholders believable forecasts.

**Q: How do you calculate sprint capacity?**
List each person's available days after leave and other commitments, apply their allocation to the team, multiply by realistic focus hours per day, then subtract Scrum events and an allowance for unplanned work. To get story points, scale your average velocity by available person-days divided by a normal sprint's person-days.

**Q: What is the difference between capacity and velocity?**
Capacity is the time the team has available in a period. Velocity is the work it has historically finished per sprint. Velocity is the baseline for what a normal sprint produces; capacity shows how this sprint differs from normal.

**Q: What is a focus factor?**
The share of a person's working time that actually goes on planned sprint work after email, support, other meetings and context switching. A focus factor of 0.7 means 70% of available time goes on sprint work.

**Q: What is a good focus factor for a Scrum team?**
Practitioner guidance commonly suggests 0.6 to 0.8, with new teams and teams carrying support work at the lower end. The best value is the one you measure from your own recent sprints.

**Q: Should capacity planning use hours or story points?**
Either works. Many teams use story points and velocity to decide how much to take on, and hours or days only to check availability and specialist workloads. New teams with no velocity history often start in hours.

**Q: How do you adjust velocity for holidays?**
Multiply average velocity by the ratio of available person-days to a normal sprint's person-days. If a team normally has 45 person-days, has 42 this sprint and averages 31 points, plan for about 31 × 42 ÷ 45 ≈ 29 points.

**Q: Should teams plan at 100% capacity?**
No. Leave room for Scrum events, support, unplanned work and the unexpected. Planning at 100% of hours makes missing the Sprint Goal very likely and undermines a sustainable pace.

**Q: How do you handle unplanned work in capacity planning?**
Measure how much arrives over a few sprints, reserve that share of hours, or rotate one person to handle interruptions. Do not also subtract it from historical velocity, which already includes past interruptions.

**Q: Who is responsible for capacity planning in Scrum?**
The Developers decide how much work they can take on. The Scrum Master facilitates and helps them use good data, and the Product Owner explains priorities. Managers can provide information but should not set the team's capacity for it.

**Q: How is capacity calculated in SAFe?**
Teams plan capacity for each iteration during PI Planning. For teams without velocity history, SAFe describes a starting method of eight normalised story points per full-time team member, adjusted for part-timers, minus one point per vacation day or holiday. Real velocity replaces this once available.

**Q: Does Kanban use capacity planning?**
Yes, but differently. Kanban teams limit work in progress rather than planning sprints, and forecast using throughput, often with Monte Carlo simulation, rather than velocity.

**Q: How do new team members affect capacity?**
They usually reduce it at first, because they are learning and colleagues spend time helping them. Plan the newcomer and their mentor at a lower focus factor for the first sprint or two.

**Q: What is portfolio capacity planning?**
Matching roadmap demand with the number of stable teams and sprints available, usually counted in team-sprints, then deciding which initiatives to start now and which to defer. See our [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) guide for the wider discipline.

**Q: Can you change capacity during a sprint?**
Capacity changes when someone falls ill or urgent work arrives. The Developers review progress at the Daily Scrum and, if needed, renegotiate scope with the Product Owner while protecting the Sprint Goal. The sprint length itself does not change.
