# Agile Epics: What They Are, How to Write Them, Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Agile epics explained: what an epic is, how to write one with a template, worked examples, sizing and forecasting, tracking progress and SAFe epics.


## Agile Epics: What They Are, How to Write Them, Examples
Agile epics are large backlog items with a single goal that are too big to finish in one Sprint, so teams split them into smaller user stories and deliver them over several Sprints. Epics connect day-to-day stories to the outcomes on your roadmap and give stakeholders one place to see progress on something that matters. This guide shows how to write a good epic with a template, how to size, forecast, track and close one, and how SAFe uses the term, with worked examples you can adapt.
- Published 5 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- An epic is a large body of work with one goal and a finish line. It spans several Sprints and is split into user stories before the team builds it.
- Write epics around outcomes: a clear title, who benefits and why, one to three success measures, scope boundaries and high-level acceptance criteria.
- Most team-level epics take several Sprints and fit within a quarter. If an epic never ends, it is really a theme.
- Forecast an epic with a velocity range and the share of capacity it actually gets, not the team's full velocity.
- An epic is done when its goal is met, not when every story ever linked to it is finished. Move leftover stories out and close it.
- In SAFe, an epic is much larger: a portfolio-level investment with a hypothesis, an MVP and a Lean business case.

### What is an epic in Agile?
**An epic is a large backlog item that describes one goal and is too big to deliver in a single Sprint.** It is broken down into smaller user stories that the team completes over several Sprints, sometimes across several teams. An epic has a clear outcome and a finish line, and closes once that outcome is achieved.
Epics sit between the strategic level (themes, initiatives or objectives) and the user stories the team pulls into Sprints. An epic says what you want to achieve, such as 'self-service returns'; its stories describe the individual slices that get you there, such as 'as a customer, I want to print a returns label so that I can send an item back without calling'.
Good epics share four characteristics:
- **One goal.** Every story in the epic contributes to the same outcome.
- **Too big for one Sprint.** If it fits in a Sprint, it is a story.
- **Split before it is built.** The team never works on the epic directly, only on its stories.
- **A finish line.** You can tell when it is done. Ongoing areas of work, such as 'site performance', are themes.
Epics are a widely used convention, not part of Scrum. The 2020 Scrum Guide only describes Product Backlog items, and teams decide for themselves how to group them. See our guide to [epics vs stories vs tasks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/) for a side-by-side comparison of the three levels and how tools such as Jira name them.

### Why teams use epics
Epics give a long backlog a structure that people outside the team can follow.
- **They connect strategy to delivery.** Items on the [Agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) become epics, and epics become stories, so everyone can see why a story matters.
- **They make release planning possible.** A Product Owner can order and size a dozen epics long before every story is written; see [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/).
- **They give stakeholders one place to look.** Progress on 'self-service returns' is easier to follow than progress on 14 separate stories.
- **They help control scope.** Boundaries and acceptance criteria at epic level make it obvious when a new request belongs somewhere else.

### Types of epics
Most epics deliver something to users, but not all. Labelling the type helps the Product Owner balance the backlog and explain non-feature work to stakeholders.
| Type | What it delivers | Example (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business (feature) epic | New or improved value for customers or users | Self-service returns for online orders |
| Enabler or technical epic | Architecture, infrastructure or tooling that future features depend on | Move order data to a new event-driven platform |
| Compliance epic | Changes required by law, regulation or policy | Bring the checkout up to WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility |
| Exploration epic | Learning that informs a decision, usually through experiments or prototypes | Test whether customers will pay for same-day delivery |
| Improvement or debt epic | Reduced technical debt, faster delivery or lower running cost | Replace the legacy payment library; see [technical debt](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/) |
Size also varies by context. A **team epic** is owned by one Product Owner and delivered in a few Sprints. A **portfolio epic** in the [Scaled Agile Framework](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) is a much larger investment that may run across several teams for many months; it is covered later in this guide.

### Anatomy of a good epic
An epic needs enough information for the team to split it and for stakeholders to know what success looks like. Use these fields as a template.
| Field | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| Title | A short outcome-focused name (two to five words) |
| Epic statement | Who benefits, what changes for them and why it matters |
| Success measures | One to three measurable outcomes and a time frame |
| In scope | What the epic will deliver |
| Out of scope | What it will not deliver, to prevent scope creep |
| Acceptance criteria | High-level conditions that must be true for the epic to be done |
| Dependencies and risks | Other teams, systems, suppliers or decisions it relies on |
| Rough size | T-shirt size or initial story-point range |
| Links | The roadmap item or objective it supports, and its child stories |

#### Writing the epic statement
Three formats are common. Pick one and use it consistently.
- **Outcome statement:** 'Customers can return items online without contacting support.' Short and easy for stakeholders.
- **Story-style:** 'As an online customer, I want to start a return myself so that I get my refund without waiting on the phone.' Familiar to teams that already write [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/).
- **Hypothesis:** 'We believe that self-service returns for online customers will reduce return-related contacts. We will know we are right when contacts fall below 1,000 a month.' Useful when the benefit is uncertain and you want to test it.

#### Epic acceptance criteria and Definition of Done
Epic acceptance criteria describe the whole outcome, not individual screens: 'customers can start, track and complete a return for any eligible UK order', or 'support staff can see every return started online'. Each story still has its own acceptance criteria and must meet the team's [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/). The epic is done when its acceptance criteria are met and its success measure can be tracked.
Tip
The one-sentence test: if you cannot explain why an epic matters to a user or the business in one sentence, it is probably a bundle of unrelated work. Split it into separate epics with their own goals.

### How to write an epic, step by step
Use this process when a roadmap item is ready to move into the backlog, typically one or two quarters before work starts.
1. **Start from the outcome.** Take the roadmap item or objective and ask what should be different for users or the business when this work is finished.
2. **Name it by outcome.** Write a short title that describes the result, not the technical work. 'Self-service returns', not 'Returns API'.
3. **Write the epic statement.** Use an outcome, story-style or hypothesis format to say who benefits and why.
4. **Define success.** Choose one to three measures with a baseline and a target, such as 'return contacts fall from about 2,400 to under 1,000 a month within three months of launch'.
5. **Set boundaries.** List what is in and out of scope, and anything still undecided.
6. **Add high-level acceptance criteria.** Three to six conditions that describe the finished outcome.
7. **Note dependencies and risks.** Identify other teams, suppliers, data or approvals you need, and plan early stories or spikes to reduce the biggest risk.
8. **Size it roughly.** Ask the team for a T-shirt size or a story-point range. If it looks larger than a quarter, split it into two epics with separate goals.
9. **Split the first slice into stories.** Write the stories for a thin end-to-end slice first and leave later parts rough until you get closer. Our [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) includes an epic sheet.
10. **Order it in the backlog.** Place the epic in the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) by value, risk and dependencies, and review it in [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/). Our [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) keeps the order, value and estimates in one place.
The [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) usually writes the epic, but the best epics are shaped with Developers, designers and stakeholders, who spot risks and simpler options early.

### Worked example: a self-service returns epic
The following example is illustrative. An online retailer handles returns by email and phone, and its support team receives about 2,400 return-related contacts a month. The Product Owner writes an epic to change that.

#### The completed epic
| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Title | Self-service returns |
| Epic statement | As an online customer, I want to start and track a return myself so that I get my refund or exchange without contacting support. |
| Success measures | Return-related contacts below 1,000 a month, and 70% of returns started online, within three months of launch |
| In scope | UK orders, refunds and exchanges, prepaid labels, status tracking, staff view |
| Out of scope | In-store returns, marketplace sellers' items |
| Acceptance criteria | Customers can start, track and complete a return for any eligible UK order; staff can see every online return; refunds are issued automatically when the item is received |
| Dependencies and risks | Carrier label service (risk: integration effort unknown); finance sign-off on automatic refunds |
| Rough size | Medium: about 40 to 50 points |

#### Stories and sizes
| # | User story | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | As a customer, I want to see which of my items can be returned so that I know my options | 5 |
| 2 | As a customer, I want to choose items and a reason so that the retailer knows what is coming back | 5 |
| 3 | As a customer, I want a prepaid returns label so that I can send the parcel without paying | 8 |
| 4 | As a customer, I want to choose a refund or an exchange so that I get what I need | 8 |
| 5 | As a customer, I want to track my return so that I know when my refund is coming | 5 |
| 6 | As a customer, I want email confirmations so that I have a record of my return | 3 |
| 7 | As a support agent, I want to see returns started online so that I can answer questions quickly | 5 |
| 8 | As a customer, I want to see why an item cannot be returned so that I do not need to contact support | 3 |
|  | Total | 42 |
Before story 3, the team runs a time-boxed spike to test the carrier's label service, because that is the biggest unknown.

#### Forecasting the epic
The team's velocity ranges from 30 to 36 points per Sprint, but it also handles bugs and another epic. The Product Owner plans to give this epic about 40% of capacity, so it gets roughly 12 to 15 points a Sprint.
| Case | Points per Sprint on this epic | Calculation | Sprints needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fast | 15 | 42 ÷ 15 = 2.8 | 3 |
| Slow | 12 | 42 ÷ 12 = 3.5 | 4 |
The forecast is three to four two-week Sprints. Using the team's full velocity (42 ÷ 36) would have suggested about one and a half Sprints, a common and avoidable forecasting error. See [Agile estimation and story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/) for how to size stories consistently.

#### Tracking and closing
| Sprint | Points completed | Points added | Points remaining |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Start | - | - | 42 |
| Sprint 1 | 13 (stories 1, 2, 6) | 0 | 29 |
| Sprint 2 | 13 (stories 3, 5) | 5 (international returns) | 21 |
| Sprint 3 | 13 (stories 4, 7) | 0 | 8 |
| Sprint 4 | 3 (story 8) | 0 | 5 |
In Sprint 2 the team discovered that international orders need customs paperwork and added a 5-point story. The core returns flow went live at the end of Sprint 3. In Sprint 4 the Product Owner reviewed the acceptance criteria, which cover UK orders only, and moved the international story out of the epic into its own backlog item, because international orders are a small share of returns and can be prioritised separately. The epic was closed at the end of Sprint 4, within the forecast range. The success measure stays on the roadmap and is reviewed three months after launch.

### More epic examples
Epics work for any team that delivers outcomes in increments, not only software teams. These examples are illustrative.
| Context | Epic | Success measure | Sample stories |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Software product | Two-factor sign-in | 90% of active accounts protected within six months | Set up an authenticator app; receive a backup code; recover access if the phone is lost |
| Marketing | Spring product launch campaign | Target number of qualified leads by the end of the campaign | Landing page; launch email sequence; partner webinar; paid social tests |
| Operations | Barcode scanning in the warehouse | Picking errors halved | Scan on receipt; scan on pick; exception report for mismatches |
| Public sector | Online parking permit renewals | Most renewals completed online without staff | Renew with a reference number; pay online; get a digital permit |

#### Non-software example: new starter onboarding
Illustrative. An HR team wants new employees to be productive faster. Epic: **New starter ready in week one.** Statement: as a new starter, I want everything I need on my first day so that I can start useful work within my first week. Success measure: average time to first independent task falls from about 15 working days to 7. Stories include:
- As a new starter, I want my laptop and accounts working on day one so that I do not lose my first days waiting.
- As a hiring manager, I want a pre-start checklist so that nothing is forgotten.
- As a new starter, I want a named buddy so that I have someone to ask.
- As HR, I want contracts signed electronically before the start date so that onboarding is not delayed by paperwork.
- As a new starter, I want a first-week plan so that I know what is expected of me.
Each story can be delivered and tested with the next intake of new starters, which gives the team feedback long before the whole epic is finished. Our guide [Is Agile only for software?](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-only-for-software/) has more examples outside IT.

### How big should an epic be?
There is no standard size. Vendors' guidance ranges from 'anything that takes weeks or longer' to one to four months. For a single team, a practical rule is that an epic takes several Sprints and fits within a quarter, so it can be planned on the roadmap and finished before priorities shift.
| Signal | What it suggests | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fits in one Sprint | It is a story, not an epic | Treat it as a single backlog item |
| Two to six Sprints, one clear goal | A healthy team epic | Keep it; split stories progressively |
| More than a quarter | Probably several goals bundled together | Split into two or more epics with separate outcomes |
| No end in sight | It is a theme or a product area | Turn it into a theme and create finite epics under it |
| Dozens of stories after refinement | Too broad, or stories are too small | Check the goal; merge tiny stories or split the epic |
The number of stories varies with how finely a team splits work. Many team epics end up with somewhere between about five and fifteen stories; far more than that is a prompt to check whether the epic has one goal.

### The epic lifecycle
Tracking epics through clear states stops half-defined ideas from reaching Sprint Planning and stops finished epics from staying open for months. A typical team-level lifecycle looks like this:
| State | What happens | Ready to move on when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Idea | Captured from the roadmap, stakeholders or the team | Someone owns it and it supports a current objective |
| Shaping | Statement, success measures, boundaries and rough size written | The team understands the goal and the biggest risks |
| Ready | First stories written and refined; epic ordered in the backlog | Enough stories are ready for one or two Sprints |
| In progress | Stories delivered Sprint by Sprint; progress tracked | Epic acceptance criteria are met |
| Done | Outcome delivered; leftover stories moved or removed | The success measure is being tracked |
| Abandoned | Stopped because evidence or priorities changed; a healthy outcome if early releases show a smaller benefit | Decision and reason recorded |

### How to break an epic into user stories
Split epics into **vertical slices**: stories that each deliver something a user can see or use, cutting through every layer needed to make it work. Avoid splitting by technical layer ('database', 'API', 'screen'), because none of those delivers value on its own.
1. **Map the user journey.** Lay out the steps a user takes, left to right, and list options under each step.
2. **Choose a thin end-to-end slice first.** In the returns example, that was 'see returnable items, choose them, get a label'. It proves the whole flow early.
3. **Add rules, variations and exceptions as later stories.** Exchanges, international orders and error messages come after the core path works.
4. **Refine progressively.** Detail the next one or two Sprints' stories and leave the rest as rough placeholders.
For a full table of splitting patterns (workflow steps, business rules, data variations, user roles, happy and unhappy paths, interfaces and spikes), see our guide to [epics vs stories vs tasks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/). Read our guide to [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) for help writing the stories themselves.

### Tracking epic progress
Track an epic on two levels: delivery (how much of the planned work is done) and outcome (whether the goal is being achieved).
- **Epic burndown or burnup.** Shows remaining or completed points Sprint by Sprint, including scope added along the way. A burnup makes scope growth easier to see.
- **Forecast range.** Remaining points divided by the slow and fast rate the epic actually receives, updated each Sprint.
- **Outcome measure.** The success measure from the epic, tracked once the first slice is live.
Warning signs: scope growing faster than work is completed, the epic getting far less capacity than planned, and stories finished but not released. Our guide to the [Agile velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) explains how to read the team's pace.

### When to close an epic
Close an epic when its goal is achieved and its acceptance criteria are met, even if some linked stories remain. Leftover stories are a sign of learning, not failure.
- **Move** stories that still matter but are not needed for this goal into their own backlog items or a new epic.
- **Remove** stories that no longer add value.
- **Record** what was delivered, what was moved and why, in a sentence or two on the epic.
- **Keep tracking** the success measure on the roadmap or in your OKRs; our [OKR template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/okr-template/) can hold it.
If the same area keeps needing work, create a theme and add new, finite epics to it.

### Epics in SAFe: portfolio epics
In the Scaled Agile Framework, an epic is far larger than a team epic. SAFe defines it as a container for a significant solution development initiative, the kind of investment that a portfolio decides to fund. SAFe distinguishes **business epics**, which deliver value directly, from **enabler epics**, which build the architectural runway that future business needs depend on.
- **Epic hypothesis statement:** describes the epic, the expected business outcomes and the leading indicators that will show whether it is working.
- **Minimum viable product (MVP):** an early, minimal version used to prove or disprove the hypothesis with real users.
- **Lean business case:** the result of analysing the epic, which portfolio leaders review to make a go or no-go decision.
- **Epic Owner:** the person responsible for coordinating the epic's analysis and helping split it into features or capabilities for the teams.
- **Portfolio Kanban:** a board where epics move through states from initial idea to approval, implementation and completion.
SAFe states that epics are not simply another word for projects: rather than funding projects, it funds value streams and uses the epic to manage a large investment. Features from an approved epic are then planned in [PI Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/). If you are not using SAFe, you can still borrow the hypothesis and MVP ideas for risky epics. Our guide to [Agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/) covers how organisations decide which large epics to fund.
|  | Team epic | SAFe portfolio epic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scale | One team, several Sprints | Several teams or trains, often many months |
| Splits into | User stories | Features or capabilities, then stories |
| Approved by | Product Owner | Portfolio leaders, via a Lean business case |
| Owned by | Product Owner or product manager | Epic Owner |
| Tracked on | Team backlog or roadmap | Portfolio Kanban |

### Epics in project management tools
Most project management tools support epics directly or through parent items, so check how the tool connects epics to roadmaps and reports before you set it up.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** has epics at the top of its default work item hierarchy, with stories, tasks and bugs below and sub-tasks beneath them. Administrators can add levels above epics, and epic progress appears on boards, timelines and reports.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)** (our #1, 9.4) lets teams model epics as parent items or projects with subtasks, and connect them to Gantt charts, dashboards and portfolio reporting, which suits organisations that need epic progress visible to leadership.
- **monday.com** (9.1), **Asana** (9.0) and **ClickUp** (8.9) can represent epics as parent items, projects or tasks with subtasks, with roadmap, timeline and dashboard views; monday.com also offers a separate product, monday dev, for sprint-based software teams.
Whichever tool you use, agree a simple convention: one epic per goal, a status that matches the lifecycle above, and a link from each epic to the roadmap item it supports. Compare tools side by side on our [project management tools comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/).

### Common mistakes with epics
| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Epics that never end | Open for a year; progress bar never moves | Give each epic a goal and a finish line; use themes for ongoing work |
| Splitting by technical layer | Stories finished but nothing usable for months | Split into vertical slices that users can try |
| Writing every story up front | Detailed stories go stale before they are built | Detail the next slice only; refine the rest later |
| Too many epics in progress | Everything is 60% done and nothing is released | Limit work in progress to one or two epics per team |
| Forecasting with full velocity | Epics always 'nearly done' | Forecast with the share of capacity the epic actually gets |
| No success measure | Nobody knows whether it worked | Add one to three measures with a baseline and target |
See our guide to [the role of the project plan in Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/role-of-the-project-plan-in-agile/) for how epics fit into the wider plan.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an epic in Agile?**
A large backlog item with one goal that is too big for a single Sprint. It is broken down into smaller user stories that the team delivers over several Sprints, and it closes when the goal is achieved.

**Q: What is an example of an epic?**
'Self-service returns' for an online retailer is a typical epic: customers can start, track and complete a return without contacting support. Its stories include viewing returnable items, printing a prepaid label and tracking the refund.

**Q: How do you write a good epic?**
Give it an outcome-focused title, a one-sentence statement of who benefits and why, one to three success measures, in-scope and out-of-scope lists, high-level acceptance criteria, dependencies and a rough size.

**Q: How long should an epic be?**
There is no fixed rule. For a single team, an epic usually takes several Sprints and fits within a quarter. If it is expected to run much longer, split it into epics with separate goals.

**Q: How many user stories should an epic have?**
It depends on how finely the team splits work. Many team epics end up with roughly five to fifteen stories. Far more than that suggests the epic has more than one goal.

**Q: Who writes epics?**
Usually the Product Owner or product manager, with input from the Developers, designers and stakeholders. In SAFe, an Epic Owner coordinates portfolio epics.

**Q: Are epics part of Scrum?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide does not mention epics; it describes Product Backlog items. Epics are a common practice that many Scrum Teams use to organise the backlog.

**Q: Do epics have story points?**
Teams often give epics a rough T-shirt size or a story-point range for roadmap planning, then replace it with the sum of the story estimates once the epic is split.

**Q: Should an epic have acceptance criteria?**
Yes. High-level acceptance criteria describe when the outcome as a whole is achieved. Individual stories still have their own acceptance criteria and must meet the Definition of Done.

**Q: What is the difference between an epic and a user story?**
An epic is a large goal that spans several Sprints; a user story is a small slice of value that fits in one Sprint. Epics are split into stories. See our guide to [epics vs stories vs tasks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/).

**Q: What is the difference between an epic and a feature?**
It depends on the framework. In SAFe, epics are larger and are split into features, which are then split into stories. Many teams outside SAFe use the words loosely or interchangeably.

**Q: What is the difference between an epic, a theme and an initiative?**
A theme or initiative is a broad objective or focus area that can contain several epics and may have no end date. An epic is a specific body of work with a finish line.

# Agile Estimation: Story Points and the Fibonacci Scale

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: How Agile teams estimate with story points, why the Fibonacci scale works, how to run planning poker, and common estimation mistakes to avoid.


## Agile Estimation: Story Points and the Fibonacci Scale
Agile teams rarely estimate in hours. Instead, they compare pieces of work with each other using relative units called story points, often on a Fibonacci-like scale. This guide explains why, and how to do it well.
- Published 14 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Story points measure relative size, combining effort, complexity and uncertainty.
- The Fibonacci scale's growing gaps reflect growing uncertainty.
- The discussion during estimation is more valuable than the number.

### Why relative estimation?
People are poor at predicting exactly how long work will take, but good at comparing: "this is about twice as big as that." Relative estimation uses that strength. Story points combine effort, complexity and uncertainty into one number that is only meaningful within the team.

### The Fibonacci scale
The Fibonacci sequence is 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, where each number is the sum of the two before it. Many teams use a modified version: 0, ½, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100.
The gaps grow as the numbers grow, which reflects reality: the bigger the item, the less precise the estimate can be. It also stops pointless debates between, say, 11 and 12.
Tip
If an item scores 13 or more, it is usually too big to finish in one sprint. Split it before planning.

### How to run planning poker
1. The Product Owner explains a backlog item and answers questions.
2. Each estimator privately picks a card from the scale.
3. Everyone reveals their card at the same time.
4. The highest and lowest estimators explain their reasoning.
5. The team discusses and votes again until estimates converge.
The conversation matters more than the number. Wide differences usually reveal misunderstandings or hidden risks.

### Other estimation techniques
- **T-shirt sizing** (XS, S, M, L, XL) for quick, rough sizing of large backlogs or roadmap items.
- **Affinity estimation:** the team silently places items on a wall from small to large, then groups them.
- **Bucket system:** items are placed into Fibonacci-labelled buckets, good for estimating many items quickly.
- **No estimates:** some teams split all work into similarly sized small items and simply count them.

### Using estimates
Story points combine with [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/), the number of points a team completes per sprint, to forecast how much it can take on and when a release might be ready.

### Common mistakes
- Converting points back into hours.
- Comparing story points or velocity between teams.
- Letting one senior person estimate for everyone.
- Re-estimating finished work to make velocity look better.
- Treating estimates as commitments or deadlines.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Why use story points instead of estimating in hours?**
Hours invite false precision and depend on who does the work. Relative points are faster to agree and become reliable for forecasting once the team's velocity is known.

**Q: Who estimates story points in Agile?**
The people who will do the work. The Product Owner clarifies the item but does not estimate it.

**Q: What are story points in Agile?**
A relative unit of estimation that combines effort, complexity and uncertainty. A 2-point item is roughly twice the size of a 1-point item, but points have no fixed link to hours.

**Q: Why do Agile teams use the Fibonacci sequence for story points?**
The gaps between numbers grow as items get bigger, reflecting that large items are less predictable. It also prevents pointless debates between close numbers like 11 and 12.

**Q: What is planning poker for story points?**
An estimation game in which each person privately chooses a card, everyone reveals at once and the highest and lowest estimators explain their thinking before re-voting.

**Q: How many hours is a story point?**
There is no standard conversion, and fixing one defeats the purpose. Points are only meaningful relative to other items estimated by the same team.

**Q: What is T-shirt sizing compared with story points?**
A rough estimation technique using sizes such as XS, S, M, L and XL. It is useful for large backlogs or roadmap items before detailed estimation.

**Q: How do you choose a reference story for story points?**
Pick a small, well-understood item the team has completed and agree its size, often 2 or 3 points. Compare new items with it.

**Q: Can story points be compared between teams?**
No. Each team calibrates points differently, so comparing them is meaningless and encourages point inflation.

**Q: What if an item is estimated at 13 story points or more?**
It is usually too large to finish in one sprint. Split it into smaller items before planning.

**Q: What is #NoEstimates, and does it replace story points?**
An approach in which teams split work into similarly sized small items and simply count them for forecasting instead of estimating each one.

# Agile for Creative Teams: Kanban, Sprints and Feedback

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-for-creative-teams/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Agile for creative teams explained: choose Kanban or sprints, set up a creative board, tame feedback rounds and track flow, with worked examples.


## Agile for Creative Teams: Kanban, Sprints and Feedback
Agile for creative teams means managing design, content, video and brand work in small, visible pieces, with limits on how much is in progress and short, regular feedback loops. It suits creative work because good ideas already emerge by making something, showing it and refining it. This guide shows how to choose between Kanban and sprints, set up a creative board, control review rounds and measure flow, with two illustrative worked examples.
- Published 24 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile helps creative teams handle a constant stream of requests, shifting priorities and long feedback chains without sacrificing time for good work.
- Kanban is the usual starting point for in-house studios with continuous requests; sprints suit larger, goal-driven work such as a website, campaign or content hub.
- Limit work in progress: fewer jobs in parallel means each one gets real attention and finishes sooner.
- Most creative delay sits in review, so agree reviewers, consolidate feedback through one person and set the number of rounds in the brief.
- Track cycle time, throughput and review rounds per job rather than hours or story points.
- Start with one team, one board and one intake route, then improve the process at a short retrospective every few weeks.

### What is Agile for creative teams?
**Agile for creative teams is the use of Agile values and practices, such as visual boards, limits on work in progress, short iterations and regular reviews, to manage creative work like design, copywriting, video and content.** It replaces long, hidden production cycles with small, visible steps, so stakeholders give feedback early and the team works on the most important jobs first.
Agile did not start in creative work, but it fits well. Concepts, sketches, storyboards and rough cuts are already iterative: you make something, show it and refine it. What creative teams usually lack is not iteration but control over how much arrives, in what order it is done and how feedback flows. That is the part Agile supplies.
This page focuses on the Agile practices themselves. See our guide to [creative project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/creative-project-management/) for the broader discipline, including roles, briefs and careers.

### Why creative teams adopt Agile
Most creative teams turn to Agile because of a handful of recurring problems. Each has a specific Agile practice that helps.
| Common problem | What it looks like | Agile practice that helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Too many requests from too many people | Work arrives by email, chat and corridor conversations | One intake route and a visible backlog |
| Unclear priorities | Everything is urgent; the loudest stakeholder wins | One person orders the backlog; classes of service for genuine urgency |
| Constant context switching | Each designer juggles eight jobs at once | Work-in-progress (WIP) limits |
| Long, conflicting feedback chains | Five reviewers, five sets of contradictory comments | Named reviewers, one consolidator, agreed review rounds |
| Work that is "almost done" for weeks | Jobs stall waiting for sign-off | Visible review columns and WIP age tracking |
| Late surprises | Stakeholders see finished work for the first time and reject the direction | Share rough concepts early in short review slots |
| No time to improve | The same problems repeat every month | A short retrospective every few weeks |

### Translating Agile for creative work
Agile vocabulary comes from software, so translate it into creative terms before you introduce it. The table shows the equivalents most teams use.
| Agile concept | Creative equivalent | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product backlog | Ordered list of creative requests and projects | Spring campaign assets, new sales deck, recruitment video |
| User story | A brief written from the audience's point of view | As a first-time visitor, I want a homepage banner that explains the offer in five seconds |
| Increment | A reviewable piece of work | Three logo routes, a storyboard, a first draft, a rough cut |
| Definition of Done | A shared checklist for "finished" | Proofread, brand-checked, correct sizes exported, files named and archived |
| Sprint Review | A regular show-and-tell with stakeholders | Fortnightly 30-minute review of work in progress |
| Retrospective | A short session on how the team works | Why did the brochure take four rounds? What will we change? |
| WIP limit | A cap on jobs in each stage | No more than four jobs in design at once |
The [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) is particularly useful for creative teams, because many reworks happen after approval when sizes, formats or legal copy turn out to be wrong.

#### What does not translate well
- **Precise estimates for exploratory work.** Concept work is hard to estimate in hours. Use rough sizes and timeboxes instead.
- **Velocity comparisons between people.** Creative jobs vary too much in nature; compare the team with itself over time, never designer against designer.
- **Rigid sprint scope.** Creative teams usually need room for urgent work, so plan a capacity buffer rather than pretending interruptions will not happen.

### Kanban, Scrum, Scrumban or design sprint?
There is no single Agile framework for creative teams. Choose by how work arrives and how much of it is goal-driven.
| Approach | How it works | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) | Continuous flow on a board with WIP limits and explicit policies | In-house studios and content teams with a steady stream of requests of different sizes | Without WIP limits it becomes just a to-do board |
| [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) | Fixed sprints of one month or less with a Sprint Goal, planning, review and retrospective | Larger, goal-driven work: a website, a design system, a content hub, a campaign launch | Urgent requests breaking the sprint; too many meetings for a small team |
| Scrumban | Kanban flow plus a regular planning and review cadence | Teams with both continuous requests and a few larger projects | Drifting back into an unlimited to-do list |
| Design sprint | A five-day process to map a problem, sketch, decide, prototype and test with customers | Answering one big question quickly, such as a new product concept or campaign idea | It is a one-off workshop, not a way to run the team |
Do not confuse a **design sprint** with a Scrum Sprint. The design sprint was developed by Jake Knapp, who ran it at Google from 2010 and brought it to GV in 2012, and it is described in the book *Sprint* (2016). It compresses discovery into five days and ends with customer testing of a prototype. A Scrum Sprint is a repeating cycle for delivering work.
Most in-house creative teams start with Kanban and add a fortnightly review and planning slot, which is effectively Scrumban. Our comparison of [Kanban vs Scrumban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrumban/) explains the difference in more detail.

### How to set up a creative Kanban board, step by step
1. **Map how work really flows today.** Follow three or four recent jobs from request to delivery and list every stage they passed through, including waiting for feedback.
2. **Turn the stages into columns.** Keep it to six to eight columns. Split review into internal and stakeholder review if they are handled by different people.
3. **Write an entry policy for each column**: what must be true before a card can move there. This is what stops half-briefed jobs entering production.
4. **Set WIP limits.** A simple starting point is one to one and a half jobs per person in active stages, then adjust after two or three weeks.
5. **Design the card.** Include requester, deliverable, deadline, size, class of service and a link to the brief and files.
6. **Add an expedite lane** with a limit of one card, for genuinely urgent work.
7. **Agree a short daily check** at the board, focused on blocked and ageing cards rather than a status round.
8. **Review the board every two to four weeks** in a retrospective and adjust columns, policies and limits.

#### Example creative Kanban board
| Column | Entry policy | WIP limit (team of 6) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requests | Request submitted through the intake form | No limit |
| Ready | Brief complete; priority and deadline agreed | 8 |
| Concept | Designer or writer assigned; brief reviewed with requester | 3 |
| Production | Concept direction approved | 5 |
| Internal review | Self-checked against the brief | 3 |
| Stakeholder review | Shared with named reviewers, with a feedback deadline | 5 |
| Final artwork | Feedback consolidated and agreed | 3 |
| Delivered | Definition of Done met; files handed over and archived | No limit |
WIP limits are what make the board Agile rather than decorative. See our guide to [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) for how to set and adjust them.
You can build this in a spreadsheet first with our [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/), and our guide to [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) covers swimlanes and card design.

### Intake, prioritisation and classes of service
A creative team cannot control its flow if work enters through ten different doors. Set up **one intake route**, usually a request form, and make a complete brief the price of entry. A [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) covers the basics for small requests, and the [creative brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/creative-brief-template/) covers larger projects: objective, audience, key message, deliverables, mandatories, deadline and approvers.

#### Who decides the order?
Name one person who orders the backlog, usually the creative director, head of content or studio manager, working from priorities agreed with marketing or business leaders. Stakeholders can argue for their requests, but only one person sets the order, otherwise the team falls back into "loudest wins".

#### Sizing creative work
Rough sizing is enough for creative capacity planning. Many teams use t-shirt sizes, for example **S** (up to a day), **M** (two to three days), **L** (about a week) and **XL** (more than a week, so split it). If you want relative points instead, our guide to [Agile estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/) explains how.

#### Classes of service
Classes of service, a practice from the Kanban Method, give different types of work different rules, so urgency is handled openly rather than by interruption.
| Class | Example | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Expedite | Fixing an error in a live advert | Starts immediately; limit of one at a time; can break WIP limits |
| Fixed date | Event signage, a print deadline, a launch | Pulled early enough to meet the date, based on cycle time |
| Standard | Most requests | First in, first out within the agreed priority order |
| Intangible | Template library, brand guidelines refresh | Reserved share of capacity, such as 10%, so it does progress |
Tip
Agree with stakeholders in writing what qualifies as expedite. If more than one or two jobs a fortnight are expedited, the real problem is planning upstream, and that is worth raising at a leadership level.

### Running creative work in sprints
Sprints work well when a creative team has a clear goal for a few weeks, such as launching a campaign or building a set of templates. Two weeks is the most common length for creative teams; the 2020 Scrum Guide allows up to one month.

#### Write outcome-focused Sprint Goals
- **Weak:** design 12 banners, 3 emails and a landing page.
- **Better:** launch the spring offer across web and email so that customers understand the offer and how to claim it.
An outcome-focused goal lets the team trade one deliverable for another when feedback shows a better route, without breaking the sprint.

#### Adapted events for a two-week creative sprint
| Event | Creative adaptation | Typical length |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Planning | Agree the goal, pick backlog items by size and capacity, confirm briefs are ready | 1 to 2 hours |
| Daily check-in | 15 minutes at the board: what is blocked, what is waiting for feedback | 15 minutes |
| Mid-sprint review slot | Stakeholders see concepts and drafts while change is still cheap | 30 minutes |
| Sprint Review | Show finished and in-progress work against the goal; gather feedback for the backlog | 45 to 60 minutes |
| Retrospective | Discuss what helped and hindered, such as review rounds or unclear briefs | 45 to 60 minutes |
Plan only 70 to 80% of capacity for sprint work and keep the rest for urgent requests and small fixes. Use our [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) to run the retrospective, and see our guide to the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) for formats.

### Managing feedback and review rounds
In many creative teams, more time is spent waiting for or reacting to feedback than making the work. Agile helps by making review visible, early and bounded.

#### A simple review process
1. **Name reviewers in the brief**, including one approver who has the final say.
2. **Share early.** Show rough concepts, wireframes, outlines or storyboards before investing in polish.
3. **Ask for feedback against the brief**: does this meet the objective for this audience? Personal taste comes second.
4. **Set a feedback deadline**, such as two working days, and put the card in a stakeholder review column so the wait is visible.
5. **Consolidate.** One person, usually the requester, resolves conflicting comments before they reach the creative.
6. **Count the round** on the card, and record the reason when a job needs an extra round.
7. **Treat extra rounds beyond the agreed number as change**, to be prioritised against other work.

#### How many review rounds?
Two rounds after the concept stage is a common agreement for standard work, with one more for complex or high-profile pieces. The number matters less than agreeing it in advance and tracking it. Rounds that keep exceeding the agreement usually point to weak briefs or reviewers joining late, both of which you can fix.
Our [Agile workflow](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-workflow/) guide shows how to design review stages and approval steps into the workflow itself.

### Worked example 1: an in-house design studio on Kanban
This example is **illustrative**; the organisation and figures are invented to show the method.
A retail company's in-house studio has six people: four designers, a motion designer and a studio manager. It serves marketing, e-commerce and HR. Requests arrive by email and chat, every designer is juggling seven or eight jobs, and stakeholders complain that small jobs take weeks.

#### What the team changed
1. **Week 1:** mapped five recent jobs and found most of their elapsed time was spent waiting in review or for missing information.
2. **Week 2:** launched one request form, built the eight-column board above and wrote entry policies. Jobs without a complete brief stayed in Requests.
3. **Week 3:** set WIP limits of three in Concept and five in Production, which meant finishing jobs before starting new ones, and added an expedite lane with a limit of one.
4. **Week 4:** introduced a two-day feedback deadline and a single consolidator per request.
5. **Week 6:** held the first retrospective and split Stakeholder review into two lanes, because legal review needed its own policy.

#### Before and after (illustrative)
| Measure | Before | After 8 weeks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jobs in progress at once | 41 | 16 |
| Average cycle time, all jobs | About 19 working days | About 6 working days |
| Average review rounds per job | 3.6 | 2.1 |
| Jobs delivered per week | 11 | 13 |
| Expedited jobs per fortnight | Not tracked | 2 |
The team did not work harder; it worked on fewer things at once and removed waiting. The figures follow Little's Law, which links the three averages: cycle time equals work in progress divided by throughput (41 jobs at 11 a week is about 3.7 weeks; 16 jobs at 13 a week is about 1.2 weeks). Cut WIP without cutting throughput and cycle time falls.

### Worked example 2: a content team on two-week sprints
This example is also **illustrative**. A B2B software company's content team of five (a managing editor acting as product owner, two writers, a designer and an SEO specialist) needs to launch a new pricing resource hub in six weeks.

#### Capacity
Two weeks contain 10 working days, so the team has 50 person-days. After holidays (3 days) and a 20% buffer for urgent requests (about 9 days), it plans around 38 person-days of sprint work.

#### Sprint 1 plan
Sprint Goal: **publish the hub's core page and two cornerstone guides so prospects can compare plans without contacting sales.**
| Backlog item | Size | Person-days |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hub page: structure, copy and design | L | 8 |
| Guide 1: how pricing tiers compare | L | 7 |
| Guide 2: calculating total cost of ownership | L | 7 |
| Comparison table graphic | M | 3 |
| Keyword and internal-link plan for the hub | M | 3 |
| Email announcing the hub | S | 1 |
| Two social cut-downs of the comparison graphic | S | 2 |
| Definition of Done checks (SEO, legal, accessibility) | M | 3 |
| **Total** |  | **34** |
Mid-sprint, the sales director reviews the outline of Guide 2 and asks for a worked cost example. The editor swaps the second social cut-down for the extra work, so the Sprint Goal still holds. At the Sprint Review, sales asks for a calculator; the editor adds it to the backlog for Sprint 2 rather than squeezing it in. The retrospective finds that legal review took four days, so the team books a standing legal slot for Sprint 2.
Plan publishing dates across sprints with the [content calendar template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/content-calendar-template/). Read our guide to [Agile marketing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/) for campaign-focused sprints and a worked campaign example.

### Agile for design, content and video
The principles stay the same across creative disciplines, but the unit of work and the early artefact you share differ.
| Discipline | Typical unit of work | Early artefact to share | Usual framework |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Graphic and brand design | An asset or asset set | Sketches, mood boards, two or three routes | Kanban |
| UX and product design | A user journey or screen set | Wireframes, clickable prototype | Scrum alongside the product team |
| Copy and content | An article, page or email | Outline and headline options | Kanban or Scrumban |
| Video and motion | A video or series of edits | Script, storyboard, animatic, rough cut | Phased plan for the shoot, Kanban or sprints for edits |
| Campaigns | A launch across channels | Key visual and message test | Sprints |
Video shows why hybrids are common: pre-production and shoot days are fixed and need a predictive plan, while editing benefits from short review cycles on rough cuts. Our guide to [video production project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/video-production-project-management/) covers both parts. If you are unsure whether a project needs a fixed plan at all, compare the approaches in [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).

### Agile for agencies and client work
Agencies face an extra constraint: the client. A fixed-scope statement of work that lists every deliverable sits awkwardly with Agile. Three adjustments help:
- **Retainers with a capacity model.** The client buys a team's time each month, and a client-side owner prioritises the backlog with the account lead.
- **Phased scopes.** Fix the scope and price of discovery and concept work, then agree production scope once the direction is approved.
- **Rounds and change in the contract.** State the number of review rounds and how extra rounds or new deliverables are handled.
Invite the client to regular reviews rather than sending finished work for approval. Our guide to [agency project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/agency-project-management/) covers pricing models, scoping and resourcing in detail.

### Roles on an Agile creative team
| Role | Agile equivalent | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Creative director or head of content | Product owner | Owns the creative vision, orders the backlog, makes final quality calls |
| Studio, traffic or creative operations manager | Scrum Master or flow manager | Runs intake, protects WIP limits, removes blockers, facilitates retrospectives |
| Designers, writers, editors, motion designers | Developers (the team) | Plan and do the work, decide how to meet the brief, share work early |
| Requesters and approvers | Stakeholders | Write complete briefs, attend reviews, give consolidated feedback on time |
In small teams one person often combines the product owner and flow manager roles, which works as long as someone still has time to improve the process.

### Metrics for Agile creative teams
Measure the flow of work, not hours or individual output. These measures are easy to collect from a board and lead to useful conversations.
| Metric | How to calculate | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) | Delivery date minus the date work started, per job | How long a job takes once started; use it to promise dates |
| Throughput | Jobs delivered per week or sprint | Team capacity and trend |
| Review rounds per job | Rounds recorded on each card, averaged by job type | Brief quality and review discipline |
| First-time-right rate | Jobs approved at first review divided by all jobs reviewed | Alignment between brief, creative and stakeholders |
| WIP age | Days each open job has been in progress | Stalled work before it becomes late |
| On-time delivery | Jobs delivered by the agreed date divided by all jobs delivered | Reliability as seen by stakeholders |
Review the numbers at retrospectives and look for trends, not targets for individuals. Our guide to [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) explains cumulative flow diagrams and other charts if you want to go further.

### How to introduce Agile to a creative team
1. **Explain the why in creative terms.** Start from the team's frustrations, such as interruptions and endless rounds, not from Agile jargon.
2. **Pick a pilot team** of up to ten people who share work and a manager willing to protect the experiment.
3. **Agree the order-setter** and the single intake route with the stakeholders who send most requests.
4. **Build the board together** from a map of real recent jobs, with entry policies and WIP limits.
5. **Choose a cadence**: daily 15-minute board check, a fortnightly stakeholder review and a retrospective every two to four weeks.
6. **Collect a baseline** of cycle time, throughput and review rounds in the first two weeks.
7. **Run for eight weeks before judging.** Adjust columns, limits and policies at each retrospective.
8. **Share results with stakeholders** and extend to other teams only once the pilot works.
Agile works outside software when the work can be shown in pieces and feedback is available; our guide to [whether Agile is only for software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-only-for-software/) covers other non-software examples.

### Common mistakes when applying Agile to creative work
- **Copying software Scrum wholesale.** Five events, story points and burndown charts can overwhelm a four-person studio. Start with a board, WIP limits and a retrospective.
- **A board without WIP limits.** It shows the overload but does nothing to reduce it.
- **Letting work bypass intake.** One senior exception soon becomes everyone's habit.
- **Sharing work only when polished.** Late feedback on finished work causes the most expensive rework.
- **Unlimited reviewers.** Every additional reviewer adds a round; name them in the brief.
- **Measuring individuals.** Comparing designers' output damages trust and encourages rushing; measure the team's flow.
- **No time for exploration.** Timebox concept work rather than squeezing it out; creative quality depends on it.
- **Skipping retrospectives when busy.** That is when the team most needs to fix the process.

### Tools for Agile creative teams
Creative teams need more than a board: request forms, proofing on the asset, approvals and workload views make the biggest difference.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool (9.4/10), is a strong choice for marketing and creative teams that need structured request forms, proofing and approvals, plus dashboards across many projects. It rewards time spent on setup.
- **[Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/)** (9.0/10) is easy to adopt and offers approvals and proofing on images and creative assets on its Advanced plan.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** (8.9/10) combines forms, content calendars, proofing, docs for briefs and whiteboards at a competitive price.
- **monday.com** (9.1/10) offers highly visual boards that creative teams adopt quickly, and **Trello** suits small teams that want a simple Kanban board.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Does Agile limit creativity?**
Done well, it protects creativity. Limiting work in progress reduces interruptions, clear priorities stop constant re-planning, and early feedback means less effort is wasted on directions that will be rejected. Timebox exploratory work rather than squeezing it out.

**Q: What is the best Agile framework for creative teams?**
Kanban is usually the best start for in-house studios, because creative requests arrive continuously and vary in size. Scrum suits goal-driven projects such as a website or campaign launch. Many teams combine them as Scrumban.

**Q: Is Scrum or Kanban better for designers?**
Kanban suits designers handling a stream of varied requests; Scrum suits designers embedded in a product or campaign team with a shared goal for each sprint. UX designers working with software teams often follow the team's Scrum cadence.

**Q: How long should a creative sprint be?**
Two weeks is the most common length for creative teams. The 2020 Scrum Guide allows up to one month. Shorter sprints give faster feedback but more planning overhead; longer ones risk late surprises.

**Q: Should creative teams estimate their work?**
Rough sizing, such as small, medium and large, is usually enough to plan capacity. Precise hour estimates are rarely worth the effort for exploratory creative work. Use cycle time data to forecast dates instead.

**Q: What is a design sprint?**
A design sprint is a five-day process, developed by Jake Knapp at Google and GV, in which a small team maps a problem, sketches solutions, decides on one, builds a prototype and tests it with customers. It answers one big question quickly and is different from a Scrum Sprint.

**Q: How do you manage feedback in Agile creative teams?**
Name reviewers and one approver in the brief, share rough work early, ask for feedback against the brief's objective, set a feedback deadline and have one person consolidate conflicting comments before they reach the creative.

**Q: How many review rounds should creative work have?**
Two rounds after the concept stage is a common agreement for standard work, with one more for complex pieces. Agree the number in the brief, track rounds on each job and treat extra rounds as change.

**Q: How do Agile creative teams handle urgent requests?**
Use an expedite lane on the board with a limit of one job, agree in writing what qualifies as urgent, and keep 20 to 30% of sprint capacity free for unplanned work.

**Q: Can video production use Agile?**
Yes, usually as a hybrid. Pre-production and shoot days need a fixed plan, while scripting and editing benefit from short review cycles on storyboards, animatics and rough cuts.

**Q: How do agencies use Agile with fixed-scope clients?**
They use phased scopes, retainers based on team capacity, and contracts that state the number of review rounds and how changes are handled. Clients are invited to regular reviews instead of seeing only finished work.

**Q: What columns should a creative Kanban board have?**
A typical board has Requests, Ready, Concept, Production, Internal review, Stakeholder review, Final artwork and Delivered, each with a simple entry policy and WIP limits on the active stages.
