# Agile Gantt Chart: How to Use Gantt Charts in Agile

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-gantt-charts/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: How to use an Agile Gantt chart: what to show, how to build one step by step, a worked release example, how to update it and mistakes to avoid.


## Agile Gantt Chart: How to Use Gantt Charts in Agile
An Agile Gantt chart is a high-level timeline that shows sprints, releases, epics and key milestones against dates, rather than a detailed schedule of every task. Used at that level, and updated after every sprint, a Gantt chart helps Agile teams communicate plans and dependencies to stakeholders without fixing scope in advance.
- Published 6 September 2026
- Last updated 14 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Gantt charts can work in Agile if they show sprints, releases, epics and external milestones, not individual tasks.
- Place epics using a velocity range, and show confidence: committed for the next sprint, forecast for the next few, indicative beyond that.
- Treat the chart as a forecast, not a promise: scope is the variable, and the chart is updated after every sprint review.
- It is most useful for stakeholder communication, cross-team dependencies, fixed external dates and hybrid projects.
- Keep daily work on the task board and the backlog; the Gantt chart should be generated from them, not maintained separately.
- Pair it with a release burnup chart, which shows the real rate of progress behind the bars.

### What is an Agile Gantt chart?
An **Agile Gantt chart** is a timeline view of an Agile plan that shows time-boxes (sprints or iterations), releases, epics or features and key milestones as bars and markers against a calendar. Unlike a traditional [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), it does not schedule individual tasks, and its later bars are forecasts based on the team's measured velocity, not commitments.
Think of it as a picture of the release plan. The detail of what the team is doing this week lives in the sprint backlog and on the task board. The Gantt chart answers different questions: roughly when will each large piece of work land, what depends on what, and are we still on course for the dates that matter?
Its main audiences are stakeholders outside the team (sponsors, senior managers, marketing, operations, clients), other teams that depend on the work, and project managers or PMOs who need to fit Agile delivery into a wider plan.

### Can you use a Gantt chart in Agile?
Yes, with care. Nothing in Agile forbids a timeline. The [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/) values "responding to change over following a plan", while saying there is value in the items on the right, plans included. The Scrum Guide does not mention Gantt charts at all; it neither requires nor bans them, and leaves the choice of planning practices to the team.
The problem is not bars on a calendar. It is a particular style of Gantt chart: every task listed, fixed dates for months ahead, and a baseline used to judge the team. That style assumes the scope is known and stable, which is exactly what Agile does not assume.

#### Why Agile teams are wary of Gantt charts
- **False precision.** A bar for a task in five months' time looks as certain as a bar for tomorrow, even though it is a guess.
- **Fixed scope by stealth.** Once a detailed chart is shared, stakeholders tend to treat every bar as a promise, which undermines the Product Owner's freedom to reorder the backlog.
- **Maintenance effort.** A task-level chart goes out of date within days in a sprint-based team and becomes a second plan that someone has to keep in step with the backlog.
- **Top-down control.** Detailed charts can encourage managers to assign and schedule work, rather than letting the team plan its own sprint.

#### Where a Gantt chart helps Agile teams
- Communicating a release plan to stakeholders who are used to timelines.
- Coordinating several teams whose work depends on each other.
- Showing fixed external dates, such as a regulatory deadline, trade show or contract milestone.
- Hybrid projects where some workstreams (procurement, construction, training) are planned in a predictive way and others iteratively.
- Governance and portfolio reporting, where a PMO needs one view across Agile and non-Agile projects.
The answer is to change the level of detail and the meaning of the bars, not to avoid the format.

### Agile Gantt chart vs traditional Gantt chart
|  | Traditional Gantt chart | Agile Gantt chart |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit of work shown | Tasks and activities | Epics, features and releases |
| Time structure | Calendar days | Sprints or iterations of fixed length |
| How dates are set | Durations and dependencies of each task | Team velocity applied to the size of each epic |
| Certainty | All bars shown as equally firm | Confidence decreases with distance: committed, forecast, indicative |
| What flexes when things change | Dates and cost, often under change control | Scope: lower-priority items move to a later release |
| Dependencies | Between tasks, often hundreds | Between epics, teams and external milestones only |
| Who plans the detail | Project manager, usually up front | The team, sprint by sprint, in the backlog |
| When it is updated | Against a baseline, often weekly | After each sprint review |
| Main purpose | Control the schedule | Communicate the forecast and coordinate |
For the wider differences between the two approaches, see [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).

### When to use an Agile Gantt chart (and when not to)
An Agile Gantt chart earns its place when someone outside the team needs to understand timing. Use one when:
- Stakeholders ask "when will we get it?" and a release burnup on its own does not answer the question in a form they use.
- Two or more teams depend on each other's epics, so sequence matters.
- The release has a fixed external date and you need to show which scope is safe and which is at risk.
- The project mixes Agile delivery with predictive workstreams that are already on a timeline.
- Your PMO or governance board requires a timeline view for every project.
Skip it, or keep it very light, when:
- A single team works on a continuous flow of small items, as in many Kanban teams; a Kanban board and cycle time data serve better.
- There are no external dates and stakeholders are happy with the product backlog and sprint reviews.
- Nobody would read it. A chart produced only because "we always have one" is waste.
Tip
If a stakeholder insists on a task-level Gantt chart, ask which decisions they need it for. Usually the real need is a date for a few key outcomes and early warning of risk, and an epic-level chart meets that need better.

### What to show on an Agile Gantt chart
| Element | How to show it | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sprints or iterations | A row of equal-length blocks across the top, numbered and dated | Gives the time structure; everything else lines up with it |
| Releases | Vertical lines or milestone diamonds at release dates | The dates stakeholders care about most |
| Epics or features | Bars spanning the sprints in which they are expected to be worked on | The main content: what lands roughly when |
| External milestones | Diamonds for fixed dates outside the team's control | Shows constraints such as a supplier or regulatory date |
| Dependencies | Arrows between epics, teams or milestones | Highlights the hand-offs that can delay a release |
| Confidence | Solid bars (committed), shaded bars (forecast), outline or hatched bars (indicative) | Stops later bars being read as promises |
| Team swimlanes | One lane per team on multi-team charts | Shows who delivers what and where teams depend on each other |
| Today line | A vertical line at the current date | Makes progress and slippage obvious at a glance |
Leave out individual user stories, tasks, named people and hours. Those belong in the backlog and on the board. If you need a refresher on the hierarchy, see [epics vs stories vs tasks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/).

#### Three levels of confidence
- **Committed:** the current or next sprint, based on sprint planning. Show as solid bars.
- **Forecast:** roughly the next two to four sprints, based on the velocity range and a refined backlog. Show as shaded bars.
- **Indicative:** anything further out, based on rough epic sizes. Show as outlined or hatched bars, and say so in the legend.

### How to create an Agile Gantt chart step by step
1. **Set the horizon and the time-boxes.** Decide what the chart covers, usually one release or one quarter. Add each sprint as a fixed-length block with its dates, and mark holidays or other known capacity changes.
2. **Mark the fixed dates.** Add release dates and any external [milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/): regulatory deadlines, events, supplier deliveries, contract dates.
3. **Size the epics.** With the Product Owner and team, make sure each epic in the release has a rough size in story points or a similar unit. See our guide to [Agile epics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/).
4. **Work out capacity as a range.** Use the team's recent [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) to give a low, typical and high figure per sprint, adjusted for holidays. A range is more honest than a single number, and it lets you show which scope is safe and which is at risk.
5. **Place the epics in priority order.** Take the epics in [product backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) order and fill each sprint up to typical capacity. Each epic's bar spans the sprints it is expected to use.
6. **Add dependencies between epics and teams only.** Draw links where one epic needs another, or needs an external milestone. Do not link stories or tasks. Our [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) guide covers link types.
7. **Mark confidence.** Make the near-term bars solid and the later ones shaded or hatched, and add a short legend.
8. **Check the forecast against the range.** Compare total scope with low and high capacity. If the release only fits at the high end, decide now which epic is the first to move, and label it.
9. **Agree the update rhythm.** Update the chart after every [sprint review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/), and agree with stakeholders that it is a forecast that will change.
You can build this in a spreadsheet with our free [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/), or plan the release itself with the [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/).

### Worked example: a six-sprint release plan
A team is building the first release of a fitness studio's class booking app. It works in two-week sprints, and its velocity over the last six sprints has ranged from 26 to 34 story points, averaging 30.

#### Inputs
| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Sprint length | Two weeks (10 working days) |
| Sprints in the release | 6, from Monday 11 January 2027 to Friday 2 April 2027 |
| Velocity range | 26 (low), 30 (typical), 34 (high) points per sprint |
| Known capacity change | Sprint 6 contains Good Friday (26 March) and Easter Monday (29 March), so it has 8 working days: about 80% capacity |
| External milestone | Payment provider's sandbox API due at the start of sprint 4 (22 February) |
| Release date | Friday 2 April 2027 |

#### Capacity check
|  | Low | Typical | High |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sprints 1 to 5 (5 sprints) | 130 | 150 | 170 |
| Sprint 6 (80%) | 21 | 24 | 27 |
| Total capacity | 151 | 174 | 197 |

#### Epics in priority order
| Epic | Size (points) | Planned sprints | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Class timetable | 25 | 1 | Starts immediately |
| Booking and cancellation | 40 | 2 to 3 | Needs the timetable |
| Waiting lists | 30 | 3 to 4 | Needs booking |
| Payments | 45 | 4 to 5 | Depends on the provider's sandbox API by 22 February |
| Reminders | 20 | 5 to 6 | Lowest priority; first to move if needed |
| **Total** | **160** |  |  |
Total scope of 160 points fits comfortably at typical capacity (174) and at high capacity (197), but at low capacity (151) it is about 9 points short. The plan therefore labels **Reminders** as the epic most likely to move to the next release. That is the honest message for stakeholders: the release date is fixed and the scope at the bottom of the list is not.

#### The chart
Shown as a simple text grid (■ committed, ▒ forecast, ░ indicative, ◆ milestone):
|  | S1 (11 Jan) | S2 (25 Jan) | S3 (8 Feb) | S4 (22 Feb) | S5 (8 Mar) | S6 (22 Mar) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Milestones |  |  |  | ◆ Payment API |  | ◆ Release 2 Apr |
| Class timetable | ■■■ |  |  |  |  |  |
| Booking and cancellation |  | ■■■ | ▒▒▒ |  |  |  |
| Waiting lists |  |  | ▒▒▒ | ▒▒▒ |  |  |
| Payments |  |  |  | ▒▒▒ | ░░░ |  |
| Reminders |  |  |  |  | ░░░ | ░░░ |
A dependency arrow runs from the Payment API milestone to the start of the Payments bar. The load per sprint is 25, 30, 30, 30, 30 and 15 points, which leaves room in the shorter Easter sprint for hardening and release work.
Tip
Give stakeholders the forecast as a range, not a single date: "At our usual pace all five epics will be in the 2 April release. If we run at our slowest recent pace, Reminders will move to the next release."

### Updating the chart after a sprint review
The value of an Agile Gantt chart comes from keeping it honest. Here is what happens to the example at the end of sprint 2 (5 February).

#### What has changed
- **Progress:** the team completed 27 points in sprint 1 and 31 in sprint 2, a total of 58. The timetable is done and 33 of the 40 booking points are done.
- **New scope:** at the sprint review, the studio owner asked for **class reviews** (15 points), and the Product Owner placed it above Payments.
- **External dependency:** the payment provider now says the sandbox API will be ready on 1 March, a week late, which is the second week of sprint 4.

#### Recalculating
Remaining scope is 160 − 58 + 15 = **117 points**. Remaining capacity (sprints 3 to 5 plus the short sprint 6) is 99 at low velocity, 114 at typical and 129 at high. At typical velocity the plan is about 3 points short; at low velocity it is 18 points short. The Product Owner decides to move **Reminders** (20 points) to the next release, which brings remaining scope to **97 points**: within capacity even at the low end.
| Epic | Original plan | Updated plan | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Class timetable | Sprint 1 | Done in sprint 1 | Complete |
| Booking and cancellation | Sprints 2 to 3 | Finishes early in sprint 3 (7 points left) | On track |
| Waiting lists | Sprints 3 to 4 | Sprints 3 to 4 | Unchanged |
| Class reviews (new) | Not planned | Sprint 4 | Added at sprint review, higher priority than Payments |
| Payments | Sprints 4 to 5 | Late sprint 4 to sprint 6 | Sandbox API now due 1 March |
| Reminders | Sprints 5 to 6 | Next release | Moved to protect the release date |
| Release | 2 April | 2 April | Unchanged, with about 17 points of buffer in sprint 6 at typical velocity |
When you share the updated chart, say what moved and why in two or three lines. Stakeholders accept change much more readily when they can see the reasons and the trade-off, and when the change was flagged as possible from the start.
Pair the chart with a release burnup, which plots completed points against total scope sprint by sprint, so people can see the trend behind the bars.

### Agile Gantt charts for multiple teams
Gantt-style timelines are most valuable when several teams contribute to one release, because the main risk moves from "how fast is the team?" to "will the pieces arrive in the right order?"
- **Use one swimlane per team**, with epics or features in each lane and the shared release dates across the top.
- **Show only cross-team dependencies.** An arrow from team A's API feature to team B's integration feature is exactly what the chart is for.
- **Put the provider's delivery at least one sprint before the consumer needs it.** That gives the consuming team time to integrate.
- **Review it in a joint session**, such as a Scrum of Scrums or a quarterly planning event, not separately with each team.
In the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe), the equivalent is the ART planning board (formerly called the program board), built during [PI planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/). It shows features by team and iteration, with dependencies linked by red string and milestones along the top. An Agile Gantt chart is a calendar-based version of the same idea for organisations that do not use SAFe.

### Using an Agile Gantt chart on hybrid projects
Many projects mix approaches: software built in sprints alongside procurement, construction, legal approvals, training or a marketing launch planned in a predictive way. A Gantt chart is often the one view that can show both.
- Show predictive workstreams at task or phase level, with their normal dependencies.
- Show Agile workstreams at epic or release level, with sprint blocks and confidence styling.
- Join them only at the hand-off points: for example, "training materials can start once the booking epic is in a release candidate".
- Agree which dates are fixed (usually the external ones) and which scope is flexible (usually the lower-priority epics).
This keeps the parts of the plan that should be firm firm, without pretending the Agile work is more certain than it is. Our [Agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) guide covers the strategy level above this.

### Agile Gantt chart vs roadmap, burnup chart and task board
An Agile Gantt chart is one of several planning views. Each answers a different question, and most teams use two or three together.
| View | Shows | Time horizon | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agile Gantt chart | Epics, releases and dependencies on a dated timeline | One release or quarter | Stakeholder communication, cross-team coordination, fixed dates |
| Agile roadmap | Goals, themes and outcomes, often as Now, Next, Later | Several quarters | Strategy and direction |
| Release burnup chart | Work completed versus total scope over time | One release | Forecasting and showing scope change |
| Product backlog | Ordered list of everything that might be built | Ongoing | Prioritisation |
| Sprint or task board | Status of each item in the current sprint | One sprint | Daily coordination inside the team |
For release-level planning, our guide to [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) explains how to set release goals and use velocity to forecast. A [product roadmap template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-roadmap-template/) works well for the level above.

### Tools and templates for Agile Gantt charts
The best set-up is a tool that draws the timeline from the same backlog the team uses, so the chart updates when the backlog does. Most mainstream project management tools now combine boards with timeline or Gantt views:
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)** offers interactive Gantt charts with dependencies, critical path and baselines from its Team plan, alongside board and table views. It suits hybrid projects and PMOs that need Agile and predictive work in one place.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is built around Scrum and Kanban boards and includes a timeline view on all plans, with advanced cross-team planning on Premium. It suits software teams who want the timeline generated from epics in the backlog.
- **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)** offers timeline and Gantt views from its Standard plan, which makes it easy to show the same items as a board and a timeline.
- **[Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/)** includes timeline and Gantt views with dependencies and milestones on paid plans.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** combines sprints, boards and a Gantt view in one workspace.
- **[Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/)** suits teams who like a spreadsheet grid with Gantt and dependencies on top.
For a wider comparison, see our guide to [Gantt chart software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/). If you prefer a spreadsheet, the free [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) can be set up with sprint columns instead of weeks.

### Pros and cons of Gantt charts in Agile

##### Pros
- Familiar format for stakeholders and governance boards
- Makes cross-team and external dependencies visible
- Shows fixed dates and what scope is at risk
- Bridges Agile and predictive workstreams on hybrid projects
- Helps other functions (marketing, support, training) plan around releases

##### Cons
- Easily read as a fixed promise if confidence is not shown
- Extra maintenance if it is not generated from the backlog
- Tempts people to add task-level detail
- Does not show the rate of progress on its own (use a burnup)
- Can encourage top-down scheduling of team work

### Common mistakes and how to avoid them
- **Putting tasks on the chart.** Task-level bars create false precision and constant rework. Stop at epics or features.
- **Showing every bar as equally certain.** Use committed, forecast and indicative styling, and explain it in a legend.
- **Using a single velocity figure.** Plan with a range, and show which scope is at risk at the low end.
- **Keeping the chart separate from the backlog.** Two plans always drift apart. Generate the timeline from the backlog in your tool, or update the chart at every sprint review without fail.
- **Treating changes as failures.** Moving an epic to the next release because something more valuable came up is Agile working as intended. Explain the trade-off rather than apologising for it.
- **Linking everything to everything.** Show only the dependencies between epics, teams and external milestones that could actually delay the release.
- **Updating it daily.** The chart is a release-level view. Daily changes belong on the board; update the chart after each sprint review or when a major forecast changes.
- **Forgetting capacity changes.** Holidays, onboarding and planned absences reduce velocity. In the example, the Easter sprint was planned at 80%.
To see how release planning, velocity and the timeline fit together, see our guide to [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Can you use a Gantt chart in Agile?**
Yes, at a high level. Show sprints, releases, epics and external milestones rather than individual tasks, mark later bars as forecasts, and update the chart after each sprint review.

**Q: What is an Agile Gantt chart?**
A timeline view of an Agile plan that shows sprints, releases, epics or features and key milestones against dates. Later bars are forecasts based on the team's velocity, not fixed commitments.

**Q: Is a Gantt chart Agile or Waterfall?**
The format itself is neutral. It is most associated with Waterfall because traditional Gantt charts schedule every task in advance. What makes a Gantt chart fit Agile is the level of detail (epics, not tasks) and treating it as a forecast that changes.

**Q: Does Scrum use Gantt charts?**
The Scrum Guide does not mention Gantt charts and does not prescribe any planning chart. Some Scrum teams use a high-level timeline for release planning and stakeholder reporting, alongside the product backlog and sprint reviews.

**Q: Why do Agile teams avoid Gantt charts?**
Detailed, task-level Gantt charts imply fixed scope and dates, take effort to keep current and can encourage top-down scheduling. Those are problems with how the chart is used, which an epic-level, forecast-based chart avoids.

**Q: What do Agile teams use instead of Gantt charts?**
Product backlogs, task boards, release burnup or burndown charts and roadmaps. Many teams use these alongside a light Agile Gantt chart rather than instead of it.

**Q: How do you show sprints on a Gantt chart?**
Add each sprint as a fixed-length block along the top of the chart with its dates, then place epics as bars across the sprints in which they are expected to be worked on.

**Q: How detailed should an Agile Gantt chart be?**
Epics or features, releases, external milestones and the dependencies between them. Leave stories, tasks, people and hours in the backlog and on the board.

**Q: How often should an Agile Gantt chart be updated?**
After each sprint review, or sooner if a major forecast changes, such as an external dependency slipping. Daily updates are unnecessary because the chart works at release level.

**Q: Should an Agile Gantt chart show dependencies?**
Yes, but only between epics, teams and external milestones. Avoid task-level dependency chains, which create maintenance work and false precision.

**Q: What is the difference between a Gantt chart and an Agile roadmap?**
A Gantt chart is date-based and shows when work is forecast to happen. A roadmap focuses on goals and outcomes, often using broad horizons such as Now, Next and Later rather than dates.

**Q: Is there a free Agile Gantt chart template?**
You can adapt our free Gantt chart template by using sprint columns instead of weeks and adding epics as rows. It is available for Google Sheets, Excel and PDF.

**Q: Which tools offer Gantt charts for Agile teams?**
Many tools combine boards with timeline or Gantt views, including Wrike, Jira, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp and Smartsheet. Choose one that builds the timeline from the same backlog the team uses.

# Agile Glossary: 120+ Agile Terms Defined A to Z

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-glossary/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Agile glossary: plain-English definitions of Agile, Scrum, Kanban, XP and SAFe terms A to Z, plus commonly confused terms, a worked example and guides.


## Agile Glossary: 120+ Agile Terms Defined A to Z
This Agile glossary defines more than 120 terms from Agile, Scrum, Kanban, Extreme Programming (XP), Lean and scaled Agile, in plain English and A to Z. Where it matters, each definition says where the term comes from, so you can tell official Scrum Guide language from common practice. Find a term in the letter sections, then use the commonly confused terms and the worked Sprint example to see how the vocabulary fits together.
- Published 9 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile vocabulary comes from several sources: the Agile Manifesto, the 2020 Scrum Guide, Kanban, XP, Lean and scaling frameworks such as SAFe.
- Story points, velocity, epics, user stories and the Definition of Ready are widely used practices, not part of the Scrum Guide.
- Several terms have been renamed: "Development Team" is now Developers, "self-organising" is now self-managing, and since SAFe 6.0 PI means Planning Interval.
- The most commonly confused pairs are burndown and burnup, cycle time and lead time, velocity and throughput, and the Definition of Done and acceptance criteria.
- Agree a short team glossary, especially for "done", "ready" and when the clock starts for cycle time.

### What is an Agile glossary?
**An Agile glossary is a reference list of the terms used in Agile ways of working, each with a short, plain definition.** It covers values and principles, frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban, roles, events, artifacts, estimation, flow metrics, engineering practices and scaling, so that everyone on a team uses the same words in the same way.
Shared vocabulary supports transparency: it breaks down quickly when one person's "done" means coded and another's means released. Official Scrum terms below follow the 2020 Scrum Guide, still the current version. For official Scrum vocabulary only, use our [Scrum glossary](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-glossary/). See [what Agile project management is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) for the bigger picture.

### Agile terms A to B

#### A
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Acceptance criteria | Conditions one specific backlog item must meet to be accepted. Unlike the Definition of Done, they differ for each item. See [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/). |
| Acceptance test-driven development (ATDD) | Writing acceptance tests with business representatives before building a feature. |
| Agile | A way of working that delivers in short cycles, seeks frequent feedback and adapts plans, guided by the Agile Manifesto. |
| Agile coach | Someone who helps teams and leaders adopt and improve Agile ways of working through coaching, teaching and facilitation. |
| Agile Manifesto | Four values and twelve principles written by seventeen practitioners at Snowbird, Utah, in February 2001. See the [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/). |
| Agile mindset | The attitudes behind Agile practice: curiosity, learning from feedback, collaboration and comfort with change. |
| Agile Release Train (ART) | In SAFe, a long-lived team of Agile teams, typically 50 to 125 people, that plans and delivers together. |
| Artifact (Scrum) | The Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment. Each has a commitment that gives it focus. |

#### B
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Backlog | An ordered list of work still to be done, usually the Product Backlog. Try our [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/). |
| Backlog refinement | Ongoing work to split, clarify, order and size backlog items for future Sprints. Formerly called grooming. See [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/). |
| Behaviour-driven development (BDD) | Describing behaviour through plain-language examples, often Given–When–Then, that become automated tests. |
| Blocker | Anything that stops a work item progressing, such as a missing decision or another team's dependency. |
| Burndown chart | A chart of work remaining against time, sloping down towards zero as work is finished. |
| Burnup chart | A chart of work completed rising over time, with a separate total-scope line so scope changes stay visible. |

### Agile terms C

#### C
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Cadence | A regular, predictable rhythm of events, such as two-week Sprints. |
| Capacity | How much work a team can realistically take on in a period after leave, support and other commitments. |
| Ceremony | Informal name for a recurring Agile meeting; the Scrum Guide says event. See [Agile meetings and ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-meetings-and-ceremonies/). |
| Class of service | In Kanban, a policy for handling a type of work, such as expedite, fixed date or standard. |
| Commitment (Scrum) | Product Goal for the Product Backlog, Sprint Goal for the Sprint Backlog, Definition of Done for the Increment. |
| Continuous delivery (CD) | Keeping software releasable at all times so any change can go live quickly and safely. |
| Continuous deployment | Automatically releasing every change that passes the pipeline to production. |
| Continuous integration (CI) | Merging code into a shared mainline several times a day, with automated build and tests. |
| Cost of delay | The value lost by delivering something later rather than sooner; used for prioritisation. |
| Cross-functional team | A team with all the skills needed to turn backlog items into finished work without hand-offs. |
| Cumulative flow diagram (CFD) | A stacked area chart of items in each workflow stage over time; widening bands show bottlenecks. See the [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/). |
| Cycle time | Elapsed time from starting work on an item to finishing it. |

### Agile terms D to E

#### D
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Daily Scrum | A 15-minute event in which the Developers inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan. |
| Daily stand-up | General name for a short daily team check-in; Scrum's version is the Daily Scrum. |
| Definition of Done (DoD) | A formal description of the quality the Increment must meet; anything short of it is not Done. See the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/). |
| Definition of Ready (DoR) | An optional checklist for when an item is clear enough to enter a Sprint. Not part of the Scrum Guide. |
| Developers (Scrum) | Scrum Team members who create the usable Increment each Sprint. Replaced "Development Team" in 2020. |
| DevOps | Culture and practices joining development and operations to deliver changes quickly and reliably. |
| Disciplined Agile (DA) | A toolkit for choosing and tailoring your way of working, owned by PMI since 2019. |
| DORA metrics | Five software delivery measures since 2024: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate. |
| DSDM | Dynamic Systems Development Method: an Agile framework that fixes time and cost and varies scope. It popularised MoSCoW. |

#### E
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Empiricism | Deciding based on observation. Scrum's three pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation. |
| Epic | A body of work too big for one Sprint, split into user stories. See [epics vs stories vs tasks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/). |
| Escaped defect | A defect found after work was considered Done, often by users. |
| Estimation | Forecasting the size or effort of work, usually relatively in Agile teams. |
| Extreme Programming (XP) | Kent Beck's Agile method from the late 1990s, known for pair programming, TDD, continuous integration and refactoring. |

### Agile terms F to I

#### F
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Feature | Functionality that delivers value to users. In SAFe, it sits between epic and story and fits in one Planning Interval. |
| Feature toggle | A switch (feature flag) that turns functionality on or off without redeploying. |
| Fibonacci scale | Story point scale such as 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20; widening gaps reflect uncertainty. |
| Flow | The smooth, steady movement of work from start to finish. |
| Flow efficiency | Active work time ÷ total elapsed time × 100. Low values mean items mostly wait. |

#### G to H
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Given–When–Then | Format for acceptance criteria: given a context, when an action happens, then an outcome follows. |
| Goodhart's law | Usually summarised as "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure". |
| Hardening sprint | A Sprint reserved for testing and fixing before release; usually a sign the Definition of Done is too weak. |

#### I
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Impediment | Anything slowing the team. The Scrum Master is accountable for causing impediments to be removed. |
| Increment | A usable stepping stone towards the Product Goal that meets the Definition of Done. A Sprint can produce several. |
| Information radiator | A large, visible display of team information, such as a board or chart. |
| INVEST | Bill Wake's checklist for user stories: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. |
| Iteration | A fixed time-box in which a team builds and reviews working results; a Sprint in Scrum. |
| Iterative and incremental | Improving work through repeated cycles (iterative) and delivering it in usable pieces (incremental). |

### Agile terms K to M

#### K
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Kaizen | Japanese for "change for the better": continuous small improvements, central to Lean. |
| Kanban | A strategy for improving flow by visualising work, limiting WIP and managing flow. David J. Anderson's Kanban Method applies it to evolutionary change. See [what is Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/). |
| Kanban board | A board with a column per workflow stage and a card per item. See [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/). |

#### L
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS) | Framework for two to eight teams on one product with one Product Owner; LeSS Huge covers more. |
| Lead time | Elapsed time from a request being made to its delivery. See [cycle time vs lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/). |
| Lean | Thinking from the Toyota Production System focused on customer value, flow and removing waste. |
| Little's Law | In a stable system, average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput. |

#### M
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Minimum marketable feature (MMF) | The smallest piece of functionality worth releasing to all customers on its own. |
| Minimum viable product (MVP) | The smallest version of a product that tests a key assumption with real users; popularised by Eric Ries's The Lean Startup. |
| Mob programming | The whole team working on one task at one computer; also called ensemble programming. |
| Monte Carlo forecasting | Simulating many futures from past throughput to give probabilistic forecasts, such as "85% likely within 9 weeks". |
| MoSCoW | Prioritisation into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time). |

### Agile terms N to P

#### N to O
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Nexus | Scrum.org's framework for three to nine Scrum Teams on one product, with a Nexus Integration Team. |
| Non-functional requirement | A quality such as performance, security or accessibility, often built into the Definition of Done. |
| OKRs | Objectives and key results: a qualitative objective paired with a few measurable results. |
| Outcome | The change in user behaviour or business results that work produces, as opposed to output. |

#### P
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Pair programming | Two developers working on the same code at one workstation, swapping roles often. An XP practice. |
| Persona | A research-based profile representing a group of users. |
| PI Planning | In SAFe, a cadence-based event, typically two days, in which the whole ART plans the next Planning Interval. See [PI Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/). |
| Planning Interval (PI) | In SAFe, a time-box of typically 8 to 12 weeks. Called Program Increment before SAFe 6.0 (2023). |
| Planning poker | Consensus estimation: everyone reveals a card at once, then the highest and lowest explain their reasoning. |
| Product Backlog | The single ordered list of what is needed to improve the product; its commitment is the Product Goal. |
| Product Goal | The long-term objective for the Scrum Team, added in the 2020 Scrum Guide. |
| Product Owner | The one person accountable for maximising product value, including ordering the Product Backlog. See [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/). |
| Psychological safety | A shared belief that people can raise problems and admit mistakes without fear of punishment. |
| Pull system | New work starts only when there is capacity, rather than being pushed onto the team. |

### Agile terms R to S

#### R
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Refactoring | Improving the internal structure of code without changing its behaviour. |
| Relative estimation | Sizing items by comparing them with each other rather than in hours. |
| Release | Making an Increment available to users, at any point in a Sprint. |
| Release planning | Forecasting which features are likely to be ready for a release and when, as a range. |
| Retrospective | A regular meeting to inspect how the team works and agree improvements. See the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/). |
| Roadmap | A high-level, regularly updated plan of goals and themes over time. |

#### S
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) | A framework for applying Lean and Agile practices across many teams and the enterprise. See [SAFe](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/). |
| Scrum | A lightweight framework in which a Scrum Team delivers value in Sprints of one month or less. See [what is Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/). |
| Scrum Master | Accountable for establishing Scrum and for the Scrum Team's effectiveness. |
| Scrum of Scrums | A coordination meeting for representatives of several Scrum Teams. |
| Scrum Team | One Scrum Master, one Product Owner and Developers; typically 10 or fewer people. |
| Scrum values | Commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. |
| Scrumban | A blend of Scrum and Kanban, often Scrum's events with Kanban's WIP limits and flow metrics. |
| Self-managing team | A team that decides who does what, when and how. Replaced "self-organising" in the 2020 Scrum Guide. |
| Service level expectation (SLE) | In Kanban, a forecast such as "85% of items finish within 8 days". |
| Spike | A time-boxed piece of research to reduce uncertainty before building. Originally an XP term. |
| Sprint | A fixed time-box of one month or less in which a Scrum Team turns ideas into value. |
| Sprint Backlog | The Sprint Goal, the selected Product Backlog items and the Developers' plan. |
| Sprint Goal | The single objective for the Sprint, created in Sprint Planning. |
| Sprint Planning | The event that starts a Sprint: why it is valuable, what can be done and how. |
| Sprint Review | The event in which the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the Sprint's outcome and adapt the plan. |
| Sprint zero | An informal set-up period before the first Sprint; not a Scrum term. |
| Stakeholder | Anyone with an interest in, or affected by, the product. |
| Story mapping | Arranging stories along a user journey to plan releases; associated with Jeff Patton. |
| Story points | Relative units for sizing backlog items. See [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/). |
| Sustainable pace | A rhythm the team can keep up indefinitely; one of the Manifesto principles. |
| Swarming | Several team members working together to finish one item. |
| Swimlane | A horizontal band on a board separating types of work. |

### Agile terms T to Z

#### T
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| T-shaped skills | Deep expertise in one area plus working knowledge of others. |
| T-shirt sizing | Rough relative sizing in XS, S, M, L and XL, useful for epics. |
| Task | A technical step needed to complete a user story. |
| Technical debt | The future cost of shortcuts, a metaphor coined by Ward Cunningham. See [technical debt in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/). |
| Test-driven development (TDD) | Write a failing test, write code to pass it, then refactor. An XP practice. |
| Theme | A broad area of focus that groups several epics. |
| Three Amigos | Business, development and testing perspectives agreeing what a story means before work starts. |
| Three Cs | Ron Jeffries' view of a story: Card, Conversation and Confirmation. |
| Throughput | The number of items finished per period; needs no estimates. |
| Time-box | A fixed maximum duration, such as the 15-minute Daily Scrum. |
| Trunk-based development | Integrating small changes into one main branch at least daily. |

#### U to V
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| User story | A need described from the user's view: "As a [user], I want [goal] so that [benefit]". See our [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/). |
| Value stream | All the steps, including waiting, that deliver value from request to customer. |
| Velocity | Story points finished to the Definition of Done per Sprint, for the team's own forecasting. See the [velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/). |
| Vertical slice | An item that cuts through every layer to deliver a small piece of working functionality. |

#### W to Z
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Waterfall | A sequential, plan-driven approach; also called predictive. |
| Weighted shortest job first (WSJF) | In SAFe, cost of delay ÷ job size, so short, valuable items rise to the top. |
| Work in progress (WIP) | Items started but not finished. |
| WIP limit | A cap on items in a stage or the whole system. See [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/). |
| Work item age | How long an unfinished item has been in progress; a Kanban Guide flow metric. |
| Working agreement | Rules a team agrees for how it works together. |

### Agile terms by category and source
This table regroups the key terms so you can see which are framework rules and which are optional practices.
| Category | Key terms | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Values and principles | Agile, Agile Manifesto, sustainable pace | Agile Manifesto (2001) |
| Scrum accountabilities, events and artifacts | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers; Sprint and its four events; Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment and their commitments | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| Backlog and estimation | User story, epic, acceptance criteria, INVEST, Definition of Ready, story points, velocity, planning poker | Common practice |
| Flow and metrics | WIP, cycle time, lead time, throughput, work item age, SLE, CFD | Kanban and Lean |
| Engineering practices | TDD, pair programming, refactoring, CI, CD, feature toggles | XP and DevOps |
| Scaling | ART, Planning Interval, PI Planning, WSJF, Nexus, LeSS | SAFe, Scrum.org, LeSS |
Tip
If a term is not in the Scrum Guide, your team is free to use, adapt or drop it. Story points and the Definition of Ready help many teams, but nobody is doing Scrum "wrong" without them.

### Equivalent and renamed Agile terms
Different frameworks use different words for similar ideas, and some terms have been renamed.
| You may hear | Current or equivalent term | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Iteration | Sprint | Iteration is used in XP and SAFe. |
| Ceremony | Event | The Scrum Guide uses event. |
| Daily stand-up | Daily Scrum | Scrum's version, for the Developers, time-boxed to 15 minutes. |
| Backlog grooming | Product Backlog refinement | Renamed in the 2013 Scrum Guide. |
| Development Team | Developers | Changed in the 2020 Scrum Guide. |
| Self-organising | Self-managing | Changed in the 2020 Scrum Guide. |
| Program Increment | Planning Interval | Renamed in SAFe 6.0 (2023); still PI. |
| Flow time, flow velocity, flow load | Cycle time, throughput, WIP | SAFe's names for similar flow measures. |
Read [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/) to see how Scrum relates to Agile as a whole.

### Commonly confused Agile terms
These pairs cause the most misunderstandings. The numbers are illustrative.

#### Burndown vs burnup
A release starts at 100 points. After two Sprints, 40 are finished, then 20 points of new scope are added. The burndown jumps from 60 remaining to 80, as if the team went backwards. The burnup shows completed work still at 40 and the scope line stepping up from 100 to 120.

#### Cycle time vs lead time
A request is logged on 1 March, started on 10 March and delivered on 14 March. Lead time is 13 days; cycle time is 4 days. The customer feels the lead time; the team mostly controls the cycle time.

#### Velocity vs throughput
A team finishes six items sized 3, 5, 2, 8, 3 and 5 points. Velocity is 26 points; throughput is 6 items. Both can drive forecasts, but throughput needs no estimating.

#### Done, acceptance criteria and ready
| Term | Applies to | Example | In the Scrum Guide? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Definition of Done | Every item | Code reviewed, tests automated, deployed to staging | Yes |
| Acceptance criteria | One item | A user can cancel up to 24 hours before the appointment | No |
| Definition of Ready | Items before Sprint Planning | Has acceptance criteria and fits in one Sprint | No |

#### Epic vs user story vs task
The epic "Online appointment booking" contains the story "As a patient, I want to cancel my booking online so that I do not have to phone", which contains tasks such as "Add cancel button" and "Send cancellation email".

### Worked example: Agile terms in a two-week Sprint
Follow one illustrative piece of work through a Sprint for a six-person Scrum Team building an appointment booking service.
1. **Goal.** The **roadmap** shows a self-service **theme**; the **Product Owner** sets the **Product Goal**: patients manage their own appointments online.
2. **Refinement.** The **epic** is split into **user stories** that meet **INVEST**, with **acceptance criteria** agreed in a **Three Amigos** conversation.
3. **Estimation.** The Developers use **planning poker**. One story has too many unknowns, so they add a two-day **spike**.
4. **Sprint Planning.** Using a recent **velocity** of about 24 points and reduced **capacity**, the team agrees the **Sprint Goal**, "Patients can cancel a booking online", and forms the **Sprint Backlog**.
5. **During the Sprint.** A **WIP limit** of four applies on the **Kanban board**. At the **Daily Scrum**, one item's **work item age** is unusually high, so two Developers **swarm** on it. The **Scrum Master** helps remove an **impediment**.
6. **Done.** Stories meet the **Definition of Done**, including **TDD** and **continuous integration**, and form a usable **Increment** released behind a **feature toggle**.
7. **Review and Retrospective.** At the **Sprint Review**, stakeholder feedback adds items to the **Product Backlog**. At the **Retrospective**, the team agrees to tackle **technical debt** in the booking module.

### How to create an Agile glossary for your team
1. **Collect the terms people use**, including local jargon and abbreviations from your board and meetings.
2. **Choose sources of truth**, such as the 2020 Scrum Guide and the Kanban Guide, so debates have a reference point.
3. **Agree high-risk definitions first:** what "done" and "ready" mean, and when the clock starts for cycle time.
4. **Mark local terms** so nobody mistakes team conventions for framework rules.
5. **Publish it** beside your working agreement and link it from onboarding notes.
6. **Review it** at a Retrospective every few months, or whenever a misunderstanding causes rework.
Our backlog and story templates use the same terms as this glossary. See the [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) and the [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/).

### Common mistakes with Agile terminology
- **Using retired terms** such as "Development Team", "grooming" or "self-organising".
- **Treating practices as rules.** Story points, velocity and the Definition of Ready are optional.
- **Calling any deadline a sprint.** A Sprint has a goal, a plan and a usable Increment, not just a rush.
- **Comparing velocity between teams.** Points are relative to each team; see [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).
- **Mixing up done and released.** Work can be Done without being released yet.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the basic Agile terms every beginner should know?**
Start with Agile, Sprint, Product Backlog, user story, Definition of Done, Daily Scrum, retrospective, Kanban board, WIP limit and velocity.

**Q: What is the difference between Agile and Scrum?**
Agile is a broad approach defined by the Agile Manifesto. Scrum is one specific framework that applies it, with defined accountabilities, events and artifacts.

**Q: What is a sprint in Agile?**
A fixed time-box of one month or less, often two weeks, in which a Scrum Team works towards a Sprint Goal and produces at least one usable Increment.

**Q: What is the difference between an epic, a user story and a task?**
An epic is a large body of work, a user story is a slice of it finishable in one Sprint, and a task is a technical step towards a story.

**Q: What does WIP mean in Agile?**
Work in progress: items started but not finished. WIP limits reduce multitasking and shorten cycle time.

**Q: What is velocity in Agile?**
The story points a team finishes to the Definition of Done per Sprint. Use it for the team's own forecasts, never to compare teams.

**Q: What is a spike in Agile?**
A short, time-boxed piece of research or prototyping that answers a question before the team commits to building something.

**Q: What is the difference between a burndown and a burnup chart?**
A burndown shows work remaining. A burnup shows work completed against a separate scope line, so scope changes are visible.

**Q: Are story points part of Scrum?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide mentions neither story points nor velocity; they are common practices.

**Q: What is the Definition of Ready?**
An optional checklist for when a backlog item is clear and small enough to enter a Sprint. It is not part of the Scrum Guide.

**Q: What does MVP mean in Agile?**
Minimum viable product: the smallest version of a product that lets you test a key assumption with real users.

**Q: Is "ceremony" an official Scrum term?**
No. The Scrum Guide calls the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective events.

# Is Agile Project Management Applicable to Construction?

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-in-construction/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: How Agile and Lean ideas apply to construction: what works, what does not, the Last Planner System, and a practical hybrid approach.


## Is Agile Project Management Applicable to Construction?
Construction seems like the opposite of Agile: you can't release half a building, and changing the foundations late is enormously expensive. Yet many Agile and Lean ideas fit construction well, especially in design, planning and site coordination.
- Published 25 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- The overall construction project usually remains predictive.
- Agile ideas work well in design, look-ahead planning and site coordination.
- The Last Planner System is the Lean construction equivalent of layered Agile planning.

### What doesn't translate directly
- The final product cannot be delivered in usable increments.
- Late changes to structure are costly and may be unsafe.
- Contracts, permits and regulations require detailed upfront plans.
- Work depends on physical materials, weather and long supply chains.
For these reasons the overall project usually stays predictive, with a baseline schedule and budget. See [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).

### What works well
- **Design phase:** architects and engineers work in iterations with frequent client reviews, using models and visualisations.
- **Short-interval planning:** detailed plans are made a few weeks ahead with the people who will do the work.
- **Daily coordination:** short site huddles to clear blockers.
- **Visual management:** boards showing tasks, constraints and progress.
- **Retrospectives** at the end of each phase or major milestone.
- **Continuous improvement** of site processes.

### Lean construction and the Last Planner System
Lean construction applies Lean principles to building projects. Its best-known tool is the Last Planner System, developed in the 1990s by Glenn Ballard and Greg Howell. It works in layers that mirror Agile planning:
1. **Master schedule:** major milestones.
2. **Phase planning:** the trades plan each phase together, often by working backwards from milestones.
3. **Look-ahead planning:** constraints such as materials, permits and information are identified and removed a few weeks in advance.
4. **Weekly work planning:** the "last planners", foremen and crew leads, commit to work they know they can complete.
5. **Learning:** the team tracks the percentage of planned work completed and analyses why work was missed.

### A practical hybrid
Keep a predictive master plan and contract for governance, and use Agile and Lean practices for design, look-ahead planning and daily site coordination. This combines the certainty owners need with the adaptability crews need.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Can you use Scrum for Agile in construction?**
Pure Scrum rarely fits the build phase, but its ideas (short planning cycles, daily coordination, reviews and retrospectives) are widely used, especially in design and pre-construction.

**Q: What is the Last Planner System for Agile in construction?**
A Lean construction planning method in which the people closest to the work make weekly commitments, constraints are removed in advance, and completion rates are tracked to improve reliability.

**Q: Can Agile in construction really work?**
Partly. The overall build usually stays predictive, but design, pre-construction and site coordination benefit from short planning cycles, daily huddles, visual boards and retrospectives.

**Q: Why doesn't Agile in construction fit directly?**
A building cannot be delivered in usable increments, late structural changes are costly and unsafe, and contracts and permits require detailed upfront plans.

**Q: How does Lean construction relate to Agile in construction?**
The application of Lean principles, such as reducing waste, improving flow and involving workers in planning, to building projects.

**Q: Who created the Last Planner System used for Agile in construction?**
Glenn Ballard and Greg Howell developed it in the 1990s.

**Q: What is look-ahead planning in Agile construction?**
Planning a few weeks ahead to identify and remove constraints such as materials, permits and information before work is due.

**Q: What is percent plan complete (PPC) in Agile construction?**
The share of planned weekly tasks actually completed. It is tracked in the Last Planner System to improve planning reliability.

**Q: What is short-interval planning in Agile construction?**
Detailed planning a few weeks ahead with the people who will do the work, instead of fixing every detail at the start.

**Q: Which parts of a project suit Agile in construction best?**
The design phase, where architects and engineers can iterate with client reviews, and site coordination through daily huddles and visual management.

**Q: Is a hybrid approach used for Agile in construction?**
Yes. A predictive master plan and contract provide governance, while short-cycle planning and Lean methods manage the detailed work. See [construction project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/construction-project-manager/).
