# The Agile Manifesto: 4 Values and 12 Principles Explained

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: The Agile Manifesto explained: the 4 values and 12 principles in plain English, with examples, history, common misreadings and how to apply it today.


## The Agile Manifesto: 4 Values and 12 Principles Explained
The Agile Manifesto is a short statement of four values and twelve principles, written by seventeen software practitioners in February 2001, that defines what it means to work in an Agile way. It values individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change more than processes and tools, comprehensive documentation, contract negotiation and following a plan. This guide explains each value and principle in plain English, with practical examples, the history behind it, common misreadings and a step-by-step way to apply it in your own team.
- Published 10 September 2026
- Last updated 15 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- The Manifesto has four values and twelve principles. The values say what to prioritise; the principles say how to work.
- Each value ranks one thing above another. The items on the right (processes, documentation, contracts, plans) still matter; they come second.
- It is not a method. Scrum, Kanban, XP and other frameworks are ways of putting the Manifesto into practice.
- Agile teams still plan. They plan in layers, in detail only for the near term, and keep every plan easy to change.
- Replace "working software" with "working results" and the Manifesto applies to almost any knowledge work.
- The text has not changed since 2001. It remains the shared reference point for every Agile framework.

### What is the Agile Manifesto?
The **Agile Manifesto**, officially the *Manifesto for Agile Software Development*, is a one-page declaration published in 2001 that sets out four values and twelve supporting principles for developing software in an adaptive, collaborative and customer-focused way. It does not prescribe roles, meetings or tools; instead, it describes the priorities that any Agile method should share.
The Manifesto opens with a short preamble. Its authors say they are uncovering better ways of developing software by doing it and helping others do it, and that through this work they have come to value the four statements that follow. It closes with the line that is most often forgotten: while there is value in the items on the right, they value the items on the left more.
That structure matters. The Manifesto is not a list of rules; it is a set of trade-offs. When two good things pull in different directions, such as following the plan versus responding to new information, it tells you which one to favour. To see how these ideas shape a whole approach to delivery, read our overview of [Agile methodology](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-methodology/).

### The four values of the Agile Manifesto
Each value compares two things that both have value. The Agile preference is for the item on the left.
| We value… | …over | What it means in practice | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Individuals and interactions** | Processes and tools | Talk to each other before reaching for a form or a ticket. Tools should serve the team, not the other way round. | A developer walks over (or starts a call) to clarify a requirement instead of raising a ticket and waiting two days. |
| **Working software** | Comprehensive documentation | Measure progress by results people can use. Write the documentation that is genuinely needed. | The team demonstrates a working checkout page at the end of the sprint instead of presenting a 40-page design specification. |
| **Customer collaboration** | Contract negotiation | Work with the customer throughout, rather than relying on a fixed specification signed at the start. | The client joins each review and reprioritises the backlog, instead of raising change requests against the contract. |
| **Responding to change** | Following a plan | Plans are useful, but when the facts change, the plan should change too. | User testing shows customers ignore a planned feature, so the team drops it and builds what testing revealed people need. |
Tip
A common misreading is that Agile rejects documentation, contracts, processes or plans. It does not. The Manifesto says plainly that the items on the right have value; it ranks them below the things they are meant to support.

#### 1. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Processes and tools exist to help people work together. When they start to replace conversation, for example when every question must go through a ticketing system, they slow teams down and hide misunderstandings. In practice this value leads to small, cross-functional teams, frequent short conversations, and tools chosen by the team to fit how it works. Outside software, a marketing team might replace a weekly email status round-up with a ten-minute stand-up.

#### 2. Working software over comprehensive documentation
Before 2001, many software projects produced extensive requirements and design documents long before anything ran. The Manifesto shifts the measure of progress to something users can actually try. Documentation still has a place: user guides, regulatory evidence, architecture decisions and handover notes are often essential. The question is whether each document helps someone, not whether it completes a template. For teams outside software, read "working software" as "working results": a published campaign, a piloted process or a tested prototype.

#### 3. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
A contract that fixes every requirement at the start assumes the customer knows exactly what they need. Often they do not, and both sides spend energy arguing about scope rather than building the right thing. Agile teams involve the customer (or a product owner representing them) throughout, show work regularly and adjust priorities together. Contracts still exist; Agile-friendly contracts tend to fix the budget and timebox and let scope flex, or pay per increment delivered.

#### 4. Responding to change over following a plan
Plans are made with the best information available at the time, which is usually the least information you will ever have. This value asks teams to treat new information, such as user feedback, market shifts or technical discoveries, as a reason to update the plan rather than as a threat to it. It does not mean having no plan; Agile teams plan often, in short cycles, and keep plans light enough to change cheaply. The section on planning below explains how.

### Which value matters most?
The Manifesto does not rank its four values against each other. Many practitioners point to **individuals and interactions** as the foundation, because the other three depend on it: collaborating with customers, delivering working results and responding to change all require people who communicate well and trust each other. If a team gets that right, the other values become much easier to live by. Our guide to the [Agile mindset](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-mindset/) explores the behaviours behind this value.

### The twelve principles behind the Agile Manifesto
Behind the values sit twelve principles that turn them into practical guidance. The table gives a short form of each principle as published on agilemanifesto.org, with what it means for a team today.
| # | Principle (short form of the official wording) | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Our highest priority is to satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software. | Deliver something useful soon, then keep delivering. Value reaches users in small pieces rather than one big release. |
| 2 | Welcome changing requirements, even late in development. | Treat change as an opportunity to give the customer an advantage, not as a failure of planning. |
| 3 | Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference to the shorter timescale. | Work in short cycles. Many teams now release far more often than every two weeks. |
| 4 | Business people and developers must work together daily throughout the project. | Close, continuous collaboration between the people who know the problem and the people who build the solution. |
| 5 | Build projects around motivated individuals; give them the environment and support they need, and trust them to get the job done. | Hire good people, remove obstacles and avoid micromanagement. |
| 6 | Face-to-face conversation is the most efficient and effective way of conveying information to and within a team. | Prefer direct conversation. For remote teams, a video call usually beats a long message thread. |
| 7 | Working software is the primary measure of progress. | Judge progress by what is done and usable, not by documents produced or hours spent. |
| 8 | Agile processes promote sustainable development; sponsors, developers and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely. | No permanent crunch. A steady pace protects quality, morale and predictability. |
| 9 | Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility. | Quality makes change cheap. Cutting corners builds up debt that slows everything later. |
| 10 | Simplicity, the art of maximising the amount of work not done, is essential. | Build only what is needed. Every feature not built is time saved for something more valuable. |
| 11 | The best architectures, requirements and designs emerge from self-organising teams. | The people closest to the work should decide how to do it. |
| 12 | At regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts its behaviour accordingly. | Hold regular retrospectives and act on what you learn. |
The principles are easier to remember in five themes. The examples below show each theme in a software team and a non-software team.

#### Delivering value (principles 1–3)
These principles shift the goal from finishing a plan to delivering value early and often. A software team that once released twice a year moves to a release at the end of every two-week [sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/). An HR team redesigning onboarding releases a new first-day checklist to one department, gathers feedback and improves it before rolling it out more widely. Both get feedback months earlier than a big-bang launch would allow. Delivering in small pieces is the idea behind [iterative and incremental development](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/iterative-and-incremental-development/).

#### Working together (principles 4–6)
Agile depends on short feedback loops between the people who need something and the people who make it. In Scrum, the product owner fills this role every day; in a marketing team, the campaign owner sits with the designers and copywriters rather than reviewing work only at the end. Trust is central: principle 5 asks leaders to give motivated people what they need and then step back.

#### Measuring and sustaining progress (principles 7–8)
Progress is measured by results, which is why Agile teams agree a [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) and demonstrate finished work at reviews. Sustainable pace means planning to a capacity the team can keep up indefinitely. A team that hits every deadline through weekend work is not succeeding; it is borrowing against future quality and retention.

#### Quality and simplicity (principles 9–10)
Technical excellence keeps the cost of change low. Teams that skip testing and refactoring accumulate [technical debt](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/), and every later change becomes slower and riskier. Simplicity is the partner principle: build the smallest thing that meets the need. Writing work as small, testable [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) helps teams stay focused on what users actually need.

#### Self-organisation and improvement (principles 11–12)
Teams that decide how to do their own work tend to find better solutions and own the results. Regular reflection, usually a [sprint retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/), is how they get better over time. Our free [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) gives you a simple structure to start.

### How the values and principles connect
Each principle supports one or more of the four values. This mapping is our own reading, not part of the Manifesto, but it helps when you want to check whether a practice really serves a value.
| Value | Principles that put it into practice |
| --- | --- |
| Individuals and interactions | 4 (work together daily), 5 (motivated individuals), 6 (face-to-face conversation), 8 (sustainable pace), 11 (self-organising teams), 12 (reflect and adjust) |
| Working software | 1 (early and continuous delivery), 3 (deliver frequently), 7 (working software as the measure), 9 (technical excellence), 10 (simplicity) |
| Customer collaboration | 1 (satisfy the customer), 4 (business and developers together), 2 (welcome change for the customer's advantage) |
| Responding to change | 2 (welcome changing requirements), 3 (short cycles), 9 (good design keeps change cheap), 12 (regular adjustment) |

### Common misreadings of the Manifesto
Because the Manifesto is short, it is easy to quote half of a sentence. These are the misreadings we see most often.
| Misreading | What the Manifesto actually says |
| --- | --- |
| "Agile means no documentation." | Documentation has value; working results come first. Write what is genuinely useful. |
| "Agile means no planning." | Responding to change is preferred over following a plan, not over planning. Agile teams plan frequently. |
| "Agile means no deadlines." | Nothing in the Manifesto rules out dates. Many teams fix the date and let scope flex. |
| "Agile means no process." | Processes and tools have value. They should serve people rather than replace conversation. |
| "Agile means the customer can change anything at any time." | Change is welcomed, but it is managed through collaboration and prioritisation, such as at the start of each iteration. |
| "Agile is Scrum." | Scrum is one framework that applies the Manifesto. Kanban, XP and others do too. |
| "Agile is only for software." | The wording is about software, but the values apply to most knowledge work. See [is Agile only for software?](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-only-for-software/) |

### Who wrote the Agile Manifesto, and why?
According to the official history on agilemanifesto.org, seventeen people met at The Lodge at Snowbird ski resort in Utah on 11–13 February 2001 to talk, ski and look for common ground. They represented a range of so-called lightweight methods, including Extreme Programming (XP), Scrum, DSDM, Adaptive Software Development, Crystal, Feature-Driven Development and Pragmatic Programming, along with others who wanted an alternative to heavyweight, documentation-driven processes.
The seventeen signatories were Kent Beck, Mike Beedle, Arie van Bennekum, Alistair Cockburn, Ward Cunningham, Martin Fowler, James Grenning, Jim Highsmith, Andrew Hunt, Ron Jeffries, Jon Kern, Brian Marick, Robert C. Martin, Steve Mellor, Ken Schwaber, Jeff Sutherland and Dave Thomas. They agreed on the word "Agile" and the four values at the meeting, and the group named itself the Agile Alliance; the twelve principles were refined by the group shortly afterwards.
What united them was frustration with projects that spent months on documents and approvals before delivering anything, then discovered too late that requirements had changed. For the longer story, from 1950s iterative development to today's frameworks, read our [history of Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/history-of-agile/).

### How Agile frameworks put the Manifesto into practice
The Manifesto says what to value; frameworks say what to do. Each one emphasises different values and principles.
| Framework | How it applies the Manifesto | Principles it emphasises most |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) | Short sprints, a product owner who represents the customer, reviews of working increments and a retrospective every sprint | 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 12 |
| [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-principles/) | Visualise work, limit work in progress and improve flow continuously | 1, 8, 10, 12 |
| Extreme Programming (XP) | Pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration and small releases | 3, 6, 9, 10 |
| Lean software development | Eliminate waste, deliver fast and build quality in | 1, 3, 9, 10 |
Scrum adds its own values (commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage), which sit comfortably alongside the Manifesto.

### How the Manifesto addresses planning
"Responding to change over following a plan" is often read as "don't plan". In practice, Agile teams plan more often than traditional teams, just at different levels of detail and over different horizons.
| Level | Horizon | Detail | Typical output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vision | 1–3 years | Very low | Product vision and goals |
| Roadmap | 3–12 months | Low: themes and outcomes | [Agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) |
| Release | 1–6 months | Medium: likely features | [Release plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) |
| Iteration | 1–4 weeks | High: committed work | Sprint goal and backlog |
| Day | 24 hours | Very high | Plan agreed at the daily stand-up |
The principle is to plan in detail only as far ahead as you can see clearly, and to keep every plan easy to change. That is what makes responding to change affordable. For a side-by-side comparison with plan-driven delivery, read [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).

### Applying the Manifesto outside software
Swap "working software" for "working results" and the Manifesto describes how most effective knowledge-work teams operate.
| Team | Working result | Customer collaboration | Responding to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Marketing | A live campaign variant or landing page | Weekly review with the sales team | Shift budget to the channel that converts |
| HR | A piloted onboarding step | Feedback from new starters after week one | Revise the process before rolling it out |
| Research | Interim findings shared with sponsors | Sponsors help reprioritise questions | Drop a line of enquiry that proves unproductive |
| Events | A tested registration journey | Early sessions with key attendees | Change the format when sign-ups show demand |
| Construction design | A reviewed design increment | Client workshops at each design stage | Update the design before it is fixed for build |
Our guides to [Agile marketing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/) and [Agile for creative teams](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-for-creative-teams/) show these ideas in more detail.

### How to apply the Manifesto: a step-by-step team workshop
Reading the Manifesto is easy; living by it is harder. This 90-minute workshop helps a team see where it stands and pick a few concrete improvements.
1. **Read the values and principles together** (10 minutes). Ask each person which statement they find most and least true of the team today.
2. **Score each value** (15 minutes). Everyone privately scores how well the team lives each value, from 1 (rarely) to 5 (consistently). Reveal scores together and note the spread.
3. **Discuss the biggest gaps** (25 minutes). Focus on the lowest-scoring value and the value with the widest disagreement. Ask for specific recent examples.
4. **Map gaps to principles** (15 minutes). Use the mapping table above to find the principles behind each gap.
5. **Agree two or three experiments** (15 minutes). Each should be small, have an owner and be reviewable in the next retrospective.
6. **Review and repeat** (10 minutes now, then quarterly). Re-score in three months to see whether the experiments helped.

#### Worked example
A six-person product team runs the workshop. The average scores and agreed actions look like this:
| Value | Average score (1–5) | Example given | Experiment agreed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Individuals and interactions | 4.2 | Good daily conversation within the team | None needed now |
| Working software | 2.5 | Features sit "done but not released" for weeks | Release to production at least once per sprint |
| Customer collaboration | 2.0 | Stakeholders see work only at quarterly demos | Invite two customer representatives to every sprint review |
| Responding to change | 3.4 | Plan changes are possible but slow to approve | Product owner can reorder the top of the backlog without sign-off |
The lowest score, customer collaboration, links to principles 1 and 4. The team's first experiment addresses it directly. Three months later, the team re-scores and finds customer collaboration has risen, while working software still needs attention, so it adds an experiment on automated testing (principle 9). For a broader roll-out plan, read [how to implement Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-implement-agile/).

### Is the Agile Manifesto still relevant?
Yes. The wording reflects software development in 2001, but the trade-offs it describes still apply wherever work is uncertain and feedback is possible. Every major Agile framework still refers back to it, and many modern practices, such as continuous delivery, DevOps and product discovery, are extensions of its principles, especially early and continuous delivery and technical excellence.

#### Criticisms worth knowing
- **It is software-centric.** The language of developers and working software can feel foreign to other teams, although the ideas translate well.
- **It is easy to misuse.** Teams sometimes cite it to avoid documentation or planning that is genuinely needed, which it does not support.
- **It is silent on scale.** It says little about large organisations, portfolios or regulated environments, which is why frameworks such as SAFe and LeSS emerged.
- **The authors were a narrow group.** Commentators have noted that the seventeen signatories came from similar backgrounds, which shaped its emphasis.

#### Later statements
The Manifesto itself has not been revised. Some practitioners have written their own short statements to restate Agile for today: for example, Joshua Kerievsky's *Modern Agile* and Alistair Cockburn's *Heart of Agile*. These are separate works by individuals, not updates to the Manifesto.

### Where to go next
The Manifesto is the starting point; the next step is seeing how its values shape day-to-day project work.
If you are choosing a framework to put the Manifesto into practice, compare the options in [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Who wrote the Agile Manifesto?**
Seventeen software practitioners, including Kent Beck, Martin Fowler, Ken Schwaber, Jeff Sutherland, Alistair Cockburn, Ward Cunningham and Robert C. Martin. They represented methods such as XP, Scrum, DSDM, Crystal and Feature-Driven Development.

**Q: When and where was the Agile Manifesto written?**
At a meeting held on 11–13 February 2001 at The Lodge at Snowbird ski resort in Utah, USA. See our history of Agile for the background.

**Q: What are the 4 values of the Agile Manifesto?**
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; and responding to change over following a plan.

**Q: How many principles are in the Agile Manifesto?**
Twelve. They cover early and continuous delivery, welcoming change, frequent delivery, daily collaboration, motivated individuals, face-to-face conversation, working software as the measure of progress, sustainable pace, technical excellence, simplicity, self-organising teams and regular reflection.

**Q: Which Agile value is the most important?**
The Manifesto does not rank its values, but many practitioners see individuals and interactions as the foundation, because collaboration, delivery and responding to change all depend on people communicating well.

**Q: What is the most important Agile principle?**
The principles are not ranked either, but the first, satisfying the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable work, is often seen as the purpose that the other eleven serve.

**Q: Does the Agile Manifesto say documentation is bad?**
No. It values working results more than comprehensive documentation and states that the items on the right still have value. Teams should write the documentation that is genuinely useful.

**Q: Is the Agile Manifesto a methodology?**
No. It is a short statement of values and principles. Frameworks such as Scrum, Kanban and XP are the methods that put it into practice.

**Q: What is the difference between the Agile Manifesto and Scrum?**
The Manifesto describes values and principles shared by all Agile approaches. Scrum is one specific framework, with defined accountabilities, events and artefacts, that applies those values.

**Q: Is the Agile Manifesto still relevant?**
Yes. Its wording is software-focused, but its values describe how most successful knowledge-work teams operate, and it remains the shared reference point for every Agile framework.

**Q: Has the Agile Manifesto ever been updated?**
No. The text published in 2001 has not been revised. Later statements such as Modern Agile and Heart of Agile are separate works by individual authors.

**Q: Can I reproduce the Agile Manifesto text?**
The authors allow the Manifesto to be freely copied in any form, but only in its entirety and with their notice. The official text is published at agilemanifesto.org.

**Q: What does sustainable pace mean in the Agile Manifesto?**
Teams, sponsors and users should be able to keep a constant pace indefinitely, without relying on overtime. Constant crunch lowers quality and leads to burnout, which undermines delivery.

**Q: Can non-software teams use the Agile Manifesto?**
Yes. Read "working software" as "working results", such as a live campaign or a piloted process, and the values and principles apply to marketing, HR, research, events and many other teams.

# Agile Marketing: What It Is, Examples and How to Start

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Agile marketing explained: the manifesto's values, Scrum vs Kanban for marketing, a two-week sprint example, team set-up, metrics and steps to get started.


## Agile Marketing: What It Is, Examples and How to Start
Agile marketing is a way of running marketing in short cycles, using small experiments, a single prioritised backlog and frequent reviews of real results to decide what to do next. Instead of betting a quarter's budget on one big campaign, an Agile marketing team launches the smallest useful version, measures it and doubles down on what works. This guide covers the Agile Marketing Manifesto, the main frameworks, team set-up, a worked sprint example, metrics and a step-by-step plan to get started.
- Published 24 September 2026
- Last updated 14 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile marketing applies Agile ways of working to marketing: short cycles, one ordered backlog, cross-functional teams and decisions based on data.
- The current Agile Marketing Manifesto, finalised in 2021, has five values and ten principles, starting with customer value and business outcomes over activity and outputs.
- Scrum suits goal-driven campaigns and launches; Kanban suits continuous request streams such as content, social and design; many teams combine them as Scrumban.
- Good Sprint Goals describe a customer or business outcome, such as more trial sign-ups, not a list of assets.
- Protect the team with a single intake route for requests and a reserved share of capacity for urgent work.
- Start with one pilot team, a visible board and two-week cycles, then improve the process at every retrospective.

### What is Agile marketing?
**Agile marketing** is an approach in which marketing teams plan and deliver work in short cycles, test ideas with small experiments, and use data and customer feedback to decide what to do next. Work is held in one prioritised backlog, delivered by a small cross-functional team, and reviewed with stakeholders every one to two weeks.
The idea comes from Agile software development, which favoured working results, customer collaboration and responding to change over rigid plans. Marketers saw the same problems in their own work: long planning cycles, campaigns launched with no chance to adjust, and teams overloaded with requests from every direction. Our guide to [whether Agile is only for software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-only-for-software/) shows how far these ideas have spread.
In practice, an Agile marketing team does five things differently:
- **Works in short cycles.** Plans one or two weeks at a time, or manages a continuous flow of work with limits on how much is in progress.
- **Tests before scaling.** Launches small versions of ideas to a slice of the audience, measures them, then scales what works.
- **Keeps one backlog.** Collects every campaign idea, request and experiment in one ordered list instead of many inboxes.
- **Works cross-functionally.** Content, design, channel and analytics specialists work on the same goal at the same time.
- **Reviews results often.** Shows stakeholders real outcomes every cycle and changes the plan when the data says so.
Agile marketing does not mean having no plan. Strategy, brand guidelines, budgets and annual goals still matter. What changes is how far ahead you commit to detail: you plan the direction for the year, the priorities for the quarter and the detailed work for the next cycle only.

### Agile marketing vs traditional marketing
The table contrasts a traditional campaign-planning approach with an Agile one. Most teams sit somewhere between the two.
| Aspect | Traditional marketing | Agile marketing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planning horizon | Detailed annual or quarterly plan set in advance | Strategy for the year, detailed plans for the next one to two weeks |
| Campaign approach | A few large campaigns, fully produced before launch | Many small launches and experiments, scaled when they work |
| Decisions based on | Experience, opinion and last year's plan | Test results, customer data and feedback |
| Handling change | Changes need re-approval and often wait for the next plan | Priorities are reordered in the backlog each cycle |
| Team set-up | Specialist silos handing work between them | Small cross-functional team sharing one goal |
| Requests | Arrive by email, chat and meetings; hard to see | One intake route into a visible backlog |
| Success measure | Assets delivered on time, campaign launched | Customer and business outcomes |
| Reporting | End-of-campaign report | Results reviewed every cycle |

### The Agile Marketing Manifesto
The Agile Marketing Manifesto adapts the software [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/) for marketing. According to the manifesto's official history, it developed in three stages:
| Event | Date | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SprintZero | 11 June 2012, San Francisco | About 35 marketers drafted a first version with seven values and ten principles, always intended as a draft |
| SprintOne | 12 May 2017, San Francisco | Focused on helping marketers adopt Agile; its main lasting result was the ICAgile Agility in Marketing certification |
| SprintTwo | 8 and 9 September 2021, virtual | Attendees voted on and finalised five values; the ten principles were finalised in October 2021 |
Many articles still describe only the 2012 draft. The current version is the 2021 one below.

#### The five values
Each value is written as "X over Y": both sides matter, but the left side matters more. The wording below is quoted from the manifesto; the explanations are ours.
| Value (verbatim) | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Focusing on customer value and business outcomes over activity and outputs | Measure leads, revenue and retention, not how many posts or emails went out |
| Delivering value early and often over waiting for perfection | Launch a simple version this week and improve it, rather than a polished one next quarter |
| Learning through experiments and data over opinions and conventions | Settle debates with a test, not with seniority or "we always do it this way" |
| Cross-functional collaboration over silos and hierarchies | Writers, designers and channel experts work on the same goal together |
| Responding to change over following a static plan | Shift budget and effort when results, competitors or the market change |

#### The ten principles
1. Great marketing requires close alignment, transparency, and quality interactions with internal and external customers.
2. Seek out different and diverse points of view.
3. Embrace and respond to change to enhance customer value.
4. Plan only to a level sufficient to ensure effective prioritization and execution.
5. Take chances, and learn from your failures.
6. Organize in small, cross-functional teams where possible.
7. Build marketing programs around motivated individuals and trust them to get the job done.
8. Long-term marketing success benefits from operating at a sustainable pace.
9. Agile marketing isn't enough. Excellence in marketing requires continuous attention to marketing fundamentals as well.
10. Strive for simplicity.
The ninth principle is worth highlighting: Agile is a way of organising the work, not a replacement for marketing skill, positioning or brand discipline. To see where these ideas came from, read the [history of Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/history-of-agile/).

### Benefits and challenges of Agile marketing
Agile marketing brings real advantages, and it also asks teams and leaders to change habits. Knowing both sides helps you set realistic expectations.

#### Benefits
- **Faster learning.** Small launches show what works within days, not at the end of a quarter.
- **Less wasted spend.** Budget moves towards channels and messages that are proving themselves.
- **Clear priorities.** One ordered backlog makes trade-offs visible, so the team stops trying to do everything at once.
- **Better collaboration.** Cross-functional work cuts hand-offs and rework between content, design and channel teams.
- **Transparency for stakeholders.** Sales and leadership can see what is being worked on and why.
- **A sustainable pace.** Work-in-progress limits and capacity planning reduce last-minute fire-fighting.

#### Challenges
- **Stakeholder habits.** Leaders used to fixed annual plans may find a changing plan uncomfortable. Show results every cycle to build trust.
- **Specialist bottlenecks.** A single designer or video editor can limit the whole team. Make the bottleneck visible and plan around it.
- **Agency and approval lead times.** Legal review, print and media buying do not always fit two-week cycles. Plan them earlier and track them as dependencies.
- **Measuring outcomes.** Some outcomes, such as brand awareness, take longer to show. Pair them with faster leading indicators.
- **Process for its own sake.** Copying every Scrum event without adapting it to marketing creates overhead with little benefit.

### Agile marketing frameworks: Scrum, Kanban and Scrumban
Most Agile marketing teams use one of three frameworks, or a blend of them.

#### Scrum for marketing
[Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) organises work into fixed sprints of one month or less, most often two weeks, each with a Sprint Goal. The team holds Sprint Planning, short daily check-ins, a Sprint Review with stakeholders and a retrospective. Scrum works well for campaigns, launches and growth experiments where a clear goal for each cycle helps focus.

#### Kanban for marketing
[Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) visualises work on a board and limits how many items can be in progress at once, so work flows steadily from request to done. There are no fixed sprints; the team pulls new work when capacity frees up. Kanban suits teams that handle a continuous stream of requests, such as content production, social media, design services and marketing operations. Setting good [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) is the key skill.

#### Scrumban
Scrumban combines a Kanban board and WIP limits with some Scrum events, such as regular planning and retrospectives. Many marketing teams settle here because it gives them a planning rhythm without forcing every request into a sprint.
|  | Scrum | Kanban | Scrumban |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Best for | Campaigns, launches, growth experiments | Continuous requests: content, social, design, ops | Mixed planned and unplanned work |
| Cadence | Fixed sprints (usually 2 weeks) | Continuous flow | Continuous flow with regular planning |
| Planning | Sprint Planning each sprint | Replenish the board when needed | Planning on a schedule or when the queue runs low |
| Limits work by | Sprint scope | WIP limits per column | WIP limits |
| Roles | Product Owner, Scrum Master, team | No required roles | Usually a priority owner and a facilitator |
| Handles urgent requests | Usually waits for the next sprint, or uses reserved capacity | An expedite lane | An expedite lane |
Tip
Not sure which to choose? If most of your work is planned campaigns with clear goals, start with Scrum. If most of it arrives as requests from other teams, start with Kanban. You can change once you have a few cycles of data.

### Roles and team structure
Agile marketing works best with small, stable, cross-functional teams of around three to nine people. The roles below borrow from Scrum but can be adapted.
| Role | What they do in Agile marketing | Often filled by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marketing owner (Product Owner) | Owns the backlog and its order, sets goals with stakeholders, accepts finished work | Marketing manager, campaign lead or head of a channel |
| Facilitator (Scrum Master or Agile coach) | Runs the events, removes blockers, coaches the team and protects its focus | Team lead, marketing operations manager or a dedicated coach |
| Team members | Plan, create, launch and measure the work | Content writers, designers, channel and performance specialists, analysts |
| Stakeholders | Bring requests and context, attend reviews, use the results | Sales, product, leadership, regional teams |

#### Common team structures
- **One cross-functional pod.** A single team with every skill needed to launch a campaign end to end. Good for small marketing departments.
- **Pods by customer journey or segment.** For example, an acquisition pod, a customer-retention pod and a partner-marketing pod, each with its own backlog and goal.
- **A service team plus pods.** Shared specialists such as video or brand design run a Kanban service that several pods pull from.

### Building an Agile marketing backlog
The backlog is the single ordered list of everything the team might work on. A good marketing backlog is short at the top, detailed for the next cycle and rough further down.

#### What goes in it
- **Campaign work:** landing pages, emails, ads, events, launch content.
- **Experiments:** tests of new channels, offers, messages or audiences, each with a hypothesis.
- **Requests:** work for sales, product or other teams, arriving through one intake route.
- **Always-on work:** blog posts, social content, SEO updates, newsletters.
- **Improvements:** fixing tracking, updating templates, automating reports.

#### Writing marketing user stories
Many teams write backlog items as [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/), describing who benefits and why. Two examples:
- "As a trial user who has not logged in for a week, I want a short email showing one feature I have not tried, so that I see value before my trial ends."
- "As a sales rep, I want a one-page comparison against our main competitor, so that I can answer the question in first calls."
For experiments, a hypothesis format works better: "We believe that **a shorter sign-up form** for **visitors from paid search** will **increase trial sign-ups**. We will know it worked when **the conversion rate rises by at least 10 per cent** over **two weeks**."

#### Prioritising the backlog
Order items by expected value against effort, with urgency and dependencies as tie-breakers. Simple scoring helps: rate impact and confidence from 1 to 5, divide by an effort estimate, and use the result to start a conversation, not to replace judgement. Spend a short session each week on [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) so the next cycle's items are clear before planning.
Our free [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) gives other teams a consistent way to submit requests.

### How an Agile marketing sprint works
Here is a typical two-week marketing sprint for a team using Scrum or Scrumban. Kanban teams run the same activities without the fixed start and end.
1. **Sprint Planning (up to 2 hours).** The marketing owner explains the priorities, the team agrees one Sprint Goal and selects the items it can finish, allowing for leave, meetings and reserved capacity.
2. **Daily stand-up (15 minutes).** The team checks progress towards the goal, flags blockers such as late approvals, and adjusts the day's plan.
3. **Create and launch.** The team builds the smallest version that can be tested, gets it reviewed and launches it within the sprint wherever possible.
4. **Measure.** Results are tracked against the goal as soon as data arrives, not only at the end.
5. **Refine.** A short mid-sprint session prepares items for the next sprint.
6. **Sprint Review (up to 1 hour).** The team shows stakeholders what launched and what the data shows, and agrees what to keep, change or stop.
7. **Retrospective (up to 1 hour).** The team picks one or two improvements to how it works.
Two weeks is a good default for marketing: long enough to launch and gather some data, short enough to react. Some social and performance teams use one-week cycles. Learn more about how [sprints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/) work.

### Worked example: a two-week campaign sprint
A B2B software company has a five-person growth marketing team: a marketing owner, a content writer, a designer, a performance marketer and a marketing analyst who also facilitates. The figures below are illustrative.

#### Sprint Goal
"Increase free-trial sign-ups from paid search and the pricing page, and learn which message works best for operations managers."

#### Sprint Backlog
| Item | Type | Size (points) | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Two landing-page variants for paid search: "save time" vs "reduce errors" | Experiment | 5 | Writer and designer |
| Shorter sign-up form on the pricing page (5 fields to 3) | Experiment | 3 | Designer and analyst |
| New ad set targeting operations managers | Campaign | 3 | Performance marketer |
| Re-engagement email for inactive trial users | Campaign | 3 | Writer |
| Competitor comparison page for sales | Request | 5 | Writer and designer |
| Fix sign-up tracking on mobile | Improvement | 2 | Analyst |
| Reserved for urgent requests | Buffer | About 15% of capacity | Whole team |
The team's recent average is around 21 points per sprint, so it commits to 21 points of planned work and keeps a small buffer.

#### During the sprint
- Day 2: tracking fix goes live first, because every experiment depends on it.
- Day 4: both landing-page variants and the new ad set launch, splitting paid-search traffic evenly.
- Day 6: sales asks for an urgent webinar invitation; it fits within the buffer, so nothing else moves.
- Day 8: the shorter form launches on the pricing page.
- Day 9: the competitor page is approved by product marketing and published.

#### Sprint Review
The team shows the results. In this example the "reduce errors" variant converts at 3.1 per cent against 2.4 per cent for "save time", and the shorter form is trending upwards but has too little data to call. The stakeholders agree to:
- Move most paid-search budget to the "reduce errors" message and test it in the re-engagement email next sprint.
- Leave the form test running for another week before deciding.
- Add a sales-team request for a second comparison page to the backlog, ordered below the current experiments.

#### Retrospective
The team notices that two items waited two days for legal review. Its improvement action: agree a standing 24-hour review slot with the legal team for campaign copy.

### Handling ad-hoc requests and urgent work
Unplanned requests are the most common reason marketing teams say Agile "doesn't work for us". A few simple rules solve most of the problem:
1. **One front door.** All requests come through one intake form or channel, never direct messages to individual team members.
2. **Triage on a schedule.** The marketing owner reviews new requests once or twice a week and places them in the backlog by value.
3. **Reserve capacity.** Hold back a share of each sprint, often 10 to 20 per cent, for genuine urgent work. Adjust it based on how much you actually use.
4. **Define "urgent".** Agree with stakeholders what qualifies for the expedite lane, for example a legal requirement or a press issue, and limit it to one item at a time.
5. **Make the cost visible.** When an urgent item displaces planned work, show stakeholders what moved out so the trade-off is clear.
Teams with a high share of unplanned work often do better with Kanban than with Scrum. Our guide to [Agile for creative teams](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-for-creative-teams/) covers protecting creative time and managing feedback loops.

### Metrics for Agile marketing
Measure outcomes first, then the health of the process. Track a small set and review it at every Sprint Review.
| Category | Example measures | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outcomes | Qualified leads, trial sign-ups, conversion rate, pipeline or revenue influenced, retention | Shows whether the work is creating customer and business value |
| Experiments | Number of tests run, share that produced a clear learning, time from idea to result | Shows how fast the team is learning |
| Flow | Cycle time from start to launch, throughput per week, work in progress, items blocked | Shows how smoothly work moves and where it gets stuck |
| Predictability | Sprint Goal achieved (yes/no), planned vs completed work | Helps stakeholders trust the plan |
| Team and stakeholders | Team health check, stakeholder satisfaction, unplanned work share | Warns of overload before it hurts results |
Avoid counting outputs, such as number of posts or emails, as success measures on their own. Our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) explains how to calculate flow measures such as [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/).

### How to start Agile marketing: step by step
These steps are our recommended way to introduce Agile marketing with low risk. Expect the first few cycles to feel awkward; that is normal.
1. **Pick a pilot team and goal.** Choose one team of three to nine people and one meaningful goal, such as a product launch or lead-generation target.
2. **Get leadership support.** Agree with your manager that the pilot will run for about three months and that stakeholders will attend reviews.
3. **Map all current work.** List every campaign, request and recurring task the team is doing. Most teams find far more in progress than they expected.
4. **Build one visible board.** Put all the work on a single [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) with simple columns: backlog, ready, doing, review, done.
5. **Name a priority owner.** One person decides the order of the backlog after listening to stakeholders.
6. **Choose a framework.** Two-week Scrum sprints for goal-driven campaigns, Kanban with WIP limits for request-heavy work.
7. **Set up intake.** Create one route for requests and agree triage times and what counts as urgent.
8. **Run the first cycle.** Hold planning, daily stand-ups, a review and a retrospective. Keep the meetings short and practical.
9. **Review results and adjust.** Use each [retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) to change one thing about how you work.
10. **Expand gradually.** After three to six cycles, share what worked with other marketing teams and help them start their own pilots.
Our free [marketing campaign template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/marketing-campaign-template/) covers goal, audience, channels, budget, KPIs and results, and the [content calendar template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/content-calendar-template/) helps you plan always-on content alongside sprints.

### Tools for Agile marketing
You can start Agile marketing with sticky notes on a wall or a shared spreadsheet. As the team grows, a work management tool helps with request intake, approvals and reporting.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)** is a strong fit for marketing and creative departments: request forms, proofing and approvals, Kanban boards and cross-team reporting in one platform. It is our top-rated tool overall.
- **[Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/)** and **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)** are easy for marketing teams to adopt, with boards, timelines and campaign templates.
- **[Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/)** is a simple way to start with Kanban for small teams.

### Common Agile marketing mistakes
- **Renaming the old process.** Calling weekly status meetings "stand-ups" without changing how work is prioritised. Fix: start with one backlog and one priority owner.
- **Output goals.** Sprint Goals such as "publish 10 posts". Fix: write goals as outcomes, such as "increase newsletter sign-ups from the blog".
- **No WIP limits.** Starting everything and finishing little. Fix: limit work in progress and finish before starting.
- **Letting requests bypass the backlog.** Side requests sent to individuals undermine planning. Fix: one front door and reserved capacity.
- **Experiments without hypotheses.** Testing without saying what success looks like. Fix: write the hypothesis and the measure before launch.
- **Skipping the review.** Launching work but never looking at results with stakeholders. Fix: make the Sprint Review the main reporting meeting.
- **Forgetting fundamentals.** Running fast experiments with a weak brand or unclear positioning. Fix: follow the manifesto's ninth principle and keep marketing fundamentals strong.
- **Copying software Scrum exactly.** Adopting every rule without adapting. Fix: keep the principles, adjust the practices, and review them at each retrospective.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is Agile marketing?**
Agile marketing is an approach in which marketing teams work in short cycles, keep one prioritised backlog, test ideas with small experiments and use data and feedback to decide what to do next.

**Q: What are the values of the Agile Marketing Manifesto?**
The 2021 version has five values: customer value and business outcomes over activity and outputs; delivering value early and often over waiting for perfection; learning through experiments and data over opinions and conventions; cross-functional collaboration over silos and hierarchies; and responding to change over following a static plan.

**Q: When was the Agile Marketing Manifesto created?**
A first draft was written at SprintZero in San Francisco on 11 June 2012. The current five values and ten principles were finalised in 2021 after the SprintTwo event.

**Q: What is an example of Agile marketing?**
A growth team sets a two-week goal of increasing trial sign-ups, launches two landing-page variants and a shorter sign-up form, reviews the results with stakeholders at the end of the sprint, and moves budget to the message that performed best.

**Q: How is Agile marketing different from traditional marketing?**
Traditional marketing fixes detailed plans months ahead and launches a few large campaigns. Agile marketing plans detail one cycle at a time, launches many small experiments and adjusts priorities based on results.

**Q: Is Agile marketing the same as Scrum?**
No. Scrum is one framework teams use for Agile marketing. Many marketing teams use Kanban or Scrumban instead, especially when much of their work arrives as requests.

**Q: How long should an Agile marketing sprint be?**
One or two weeks is typical, and two weeks is a good default. The aim is a regular point to review results and re-plan.

**Q: Should Agile marketing teams use Scrum or Kanban?**
Scrum suits campaigns and launches with clear goals; Kanban suits continuous requests such as content, social and design. Many teams combine them as Scrumban.

**Q: Does Agile marketing need a Scrum Master?**
Not necessarily. Many teams start with a team lead or marketing operations manager facilitating. A dedicated coach helps larger teams or those adopting Scrum in full.

**Q: What metrics do Agile marketing teams track?**
Outcome measures such as leads, conversions and revenue influenced, experiment measures such as tests run and learnings, and flow measures such as cycle time, throughput and work in progress.

**Q: How does Agile marketing handle ad-hoc requests?**
Requests arrive through one intake route and are prioritised in the backlog. Teams reserve a share of capacity, often 10 to 20 per cent, for genuinely urgent work, with an agreed definition of urgent.

**Q: Is Agile marketing only for digital marketing?**
It is most common in digital channels, where feedback is fast, but brand, events, content, product marketing and communications teams use it too, sometimes with longer cycles.

**Q: Is there an Agile marketing certification?**
Yes. ICAgile offers the ICAgile Certified Professional in Agility in Marketing (ICP-MKG), which grew out of the 2017 SprintOne event. Training providers run courses leading to it.

**Q: How do you start Agile marketing?**
Pick a pilot team and goal, put all work on one visible board, name a priority owner, set up a single intake route, run two-week cycles or a Kanban flow, and improve the process at every retrospective.
