# Agile Metrics and KPIs: What to Track, Formulas, Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Agile metrics and KPIs explained: flow, delivery, quality, DORA, value and team health measures with formulas, worked examples and how to report at scale.


## Agile Metrics and KPIs: What to Track, Formulas, Examples
Agile metrics and KPIs are the measures teams and leaders use to see whether Agile work is delivering value predictably, at good quality and at a sustainable pace. The best set is small and balanced: a few flow or delivery measures, one or two quality measures, an outcome measure and a team health check, reviewed as trends rather than targets. This guide explains each metric with formulas and worked examples, shows how to measure across several teams and a portfolio, and gives you a step-by-step way to choose your own.
- Published 18 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Cover five areas: delivery and predictability, flow, quality and stability, value and outcomes, and team health. Each area balances the others.
- Flow metrics (WIP, cycle time, throughput, work item age) work in any Agile method and support forecasts without story points.
- DORA now has five software delivery metrics: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate.
- Report outcomes, forecast ranges and quality trends to leaders; keep velocity and story points inside the team.
- At scale, add measures for the whole system, such as flow distribution and predictability, instead of adding up team velocities.
- Metrics are for learning, not for ranking teams or rating individuals. When a measure becomes a target, people optimise the number instead of the result.

### What are Agile metrics and KPIs?
**Agile metrics are quantitative measures that Agile teams and organisations use to make their work visible and improve it.** They show how much work is delivered, how smoothly it flows, how good it is, what value it creates and whether the team can sustain its pace. Agile KPIs are the few metrics an organisation chooses to track progress towards its goals.
The difference matters. A metric can be anything the team finds useful, such as a cumulative flow diagram it looks at in a Retrospective. A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measure leadership has chosen as a critical signal of progress, usually reviewed monthly or quarterly and often with a target. Good KPIs tend to be outcome measures, such as customer satisfaction or lead time, rather than output measures, such as velocity, which are easy to inflate.
Most Agile metrics work in Scrum, Kanban, Scrumban or hybrid teams alike. The table shows where each approach puts its emphasis.
| Approach | Typical metrics | Where to read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum | Sprint Goal success rate, velocity, burndown, burnup | [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/) |
| Kanban | WIP, cycle time, throughput, work item age, service level expectation | [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) |
| XP and DevOps | DORA metrics, test coverage trend, build health | [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/) |
| Scaled Agile | Flow distribution, flow predictability, portfolio outcomes | [SAFe](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) |
Our Scrum guide covers Scrum-specific measures, Evidence-Based Management and metrics for each Scrum event. This page focuses on metrics that apply across methods, flow-based forecasting and measuring several teams. Terms are defined in our [Agile glossary](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-glossary/).

### The five categories of Agile metrics
A balanced set covers five areas. Pick one or two measures per area that answer questions your team or stakeholders actually ask.
| Category | Question it answers | Example metrics | Main level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Delivery and predictability | Do we deliver what we plan, and when will it be ready? | Say/do ratio, Sprint Goal success, velocity, burnup | Team, programme |
| Flow | How smoothly and quickly does work move? | WIP, cycle time, lead time, throughput, work item age, flow efficiency | Team, programme |
| Quality and stability | Is what we deliver reliable? | Escaped defects, change fail rate, deployment rework rate | Team, product |
| Value and outcomes | Are we building the right thing? | Adoption, NPS or CSAT, time to value, OKR progress | Product, portfolio |
| Team health | Can we keep working this way? | Happiness score, unplanned work, retro actions completed | Team |
The categories check each other. Throughput can rise because the team skips testing, which shows up in escaped defects. Cycle time can fall because only easy items are picked, which shows up in outcomes. Never read one category alone.

### Delivery and predictability metrics
These metrics answer the stakeholder question "can we rely on your plans?"

#### Velocity
Velocity is the amount of work, usually in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/), that a team finishes to the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) in an iteration. It is a planning aid for that team only. Because points are relative, velocities cannot be compared across teams, and a velocity target simply encourages inflated estimates. Our [velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) guide shows how to chart it and forecast from it.

#### Burndown and burnup charts
A burndown shows work remaining in an iteration; a burnup shows work completed against a separate scope line, so it reveals scope changes. Use burnups for release and roadmap conversations.

#### Say/do ratio (planned vs completed)
The say/do ratio compares what a team planned with what it finished. It works with points or item counts.
**Formula:** say/do ratio = work completed that was planned ÷ work planned × 100.
**Worked example (illustrative):** over six iterations a team planned 30, 28, 32, 30, 26 and 30 points and completed 24, 27, 22, 28, 25 and 29 of those planned points. Totals: 155 completed ÷ 176 planned = 88%. The one low iteration (22 of 32) followed an over-ambitious plan, so the team now plans at its recent average rather than its best.
Use it to improve planning, not to push the team. Always 100% usually means plans are too cautious; wide swings point to unplanned work or large items. Scrum teams often prefer the Sprint Goal success rate, covered in the Scrum guide.

#### Release forecasts as ranges
Whatever delivery metric you use, forecast with a range from your actual history, such as "6 to 8 iterations", and update it as scope and pace change. Our [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) records the forecast and its assumptions.

### Flow metrics
Flow metrics measure how work moves through your process, regardless of how it was estimated. The Kanban Guide names four: WIP, cycle time, work item age and throughput. Lead time and flow efficiency are widely used additions.
| Metric | Definition | How to calculate | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Work in progress (WIP) | Items started but not finished | Count items in active workflow stages | Overload; high WIP lengthens cycle time |
| Cycle time | Time from start to finish of an item | Finish date − start date; report percentiles | How long items take once started |
| Lead time | Time from request to delivery | Delivery date − request date | How long customers wait |
| Throughput | Items finished per period | Count items done per week or iteration | Delivery rate, without estimates |
| Work item age | Time an unfinished item has been in progress | Today − start date | Items at risk, while you can still act |
| Flow efficiency | Share of elapsed time spent actively working | Active time ÷ total time × 100 | How much time items spend waiting |
For definitions in more depth, read our guides to [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/), [cycle time vs lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/), [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/), [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) and the [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/).

#### Worked example: cycle time percentiles
Cycle times are rarely evenly distributed: most items are quick and a few take much longer. That is why percentiles are more useful than averages. Take ten finished items (illustrative) with cycle times, sorted, of 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 14 days.
1. **Average:** 57 ÷ 10 = 5.7 days. The single 14-day item pulls it up.
2. **Median (50th percentile):** the midpoint between the 5th and 6th values, (4 + 5) ÷ 2 = 4.5 days. Half of items finish within 4.5 days.
3. **85th percentile:** 0.85 × 10 = 8.5, rounded up to the 9th value, which is 9 days. Using this simple nearest-rank method, 85% of items finished within 9 days.
4. **Service level expectation:** the team can tell stakeholders "once we start an item, 85% are done within 9 days" and use 9 days as the alarm level for work item age.
Percentiles become more reliable with more data, so collect 20 to 30 items before publishing a service level expectation.

#### Worked example: Little's Law
Little's Law links the three core flow metrics for a stable system: **average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput**. Suppose a team averages 12 items in progress and finishes 4 items a week. Average cycle time is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 weeks. If the team lowers WIP to 8 items and throughput holds at 4 a week, average cycle time falls to 8 ÷ 4 = 2 weeks, with no one working harder. This is the reasoning behind [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/). Use it to understand your system, not to forecast single items: it assumes a roughly stable system.

#### Worked example: forecasting with throughput
Throughput lets you forecast without estimating every item. Over the last eight weeks a team finished 5, 7, 4, 6, 8, 5, 6 and 7 items: an average of 6 a week, with a low of 4 and a high of 8. With 60 items left in the backlog:
- Likely: 60 ÷ 6 = 10 weeks.
- Cautious: 60 ÷ 4 = 15 weeks.
- Optimistic: 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5, so about 8 weeks.
A **Monte Carlo** forecast improves on this by simulating thousands of possible futures: each simulated week draws a random throughput value from your history until the 60 items are done, and the results are reported as probabilities, such as "85% of simulations finished within N weeks". Our guide to [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) explains the technique. Allow for backlog growth from new and split items.

### Quality and delivery stability metrics
Quality metrics check that faster delivery is not being bought with problems later.
- **Escaped defects:** defects found after work met the Definition of Done, counted per iteration or month. The Scrum guide gives the defect escape rate formula and an example.
- **Definition of Done adherence:** the share of finished items that genuinely met every criterion, checked on a sample.
- **Technical debt trend:** known shortcuts logged in the backlog, test coverage or static analysis trends.

#### DORA software delivery metrics
For software teams, the most widely used delivery measures come from the DORA research programme. Since 2024 there are five, in two groups. Mean time to restore was renamed failed deployment recovery time in 2023, and deployment rework rate was added in 2024, so older articles listing four metrics are out of date.
| Metric | Group | What it measures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change lead time | Throughput | Time from a code change being committed to running in production |
| Deployment frequency | Throughput | How often changes are deployed to production |
| Failed deployment recovery time | Throughput | Time to recover when a deployment causes a failure |
| Change fail rate | Instability | Share of deployments that cause a failure needing immediate fix or rollback |
| Deployment rework rate | Instability | Share of deployments that are unplanned and made to fix a user-facing problem |
**Worked example (illustrative):** a team made 40 production deployments last month. Three needed a rollback or hotfix, so change fail rate = 3 ÷ 40 × 100 = 7.5%. Two further deployments were unplanned fixes for user-reported bugs, so deployment rework rate = 2 ÷ 40 × 100 = 5%. The team tracks both monthly, alongside deployment frequency, so that releasing more often does not quietly increase failures.
DORA metrics rely on [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/) practices such as automated pipelines. Non-software teams can borrow the idea: how often you deliver, how long it takes and how often deliveries need rework.

### Value and outcome metrics
Delivery, flow and quality metrics say how well you build; value metrics say whether you are building the right thing. They are the strongest candidates for KPIs.
| Output (what we produced) | Outcome (what changed) |
| --- | --- |
| Features released | Share of active users who use the new feature |
| Campaign pages launched | Visit-to-sign-up conversion rate |
| Reports automated | Hours saved per user per week |

#### Net Promoter Score (NPS)
NPS asks customers how likely they are to recommend you on a 0 to 10 scale. **NPS = % promoters (9 or 10) − % detractors (0 to 6)**, giving a score from −100 to +100. Example: of 200 responses, 110 are promoters (55%), 50 passives and 40 detractors (20%). NPS = 55 − 20 = +35. Watch the trend after each release, not a single survey.

#### Feature adoption rate
**Adoption rate = users who used the feature in a period ÷ active users in that period × 100.** Example: 1,200 of 8,000 monthly active users used a new booking feature in its first 30 days, an adoption rate of 15%. If the Product Owner expected 30%, that is evidence to investigate discoverability or usefulness before building more on top of it.

#### Time to value and OKRs
Time to value measures how long it takes from starting an initiative, or a user signing up, to the first real benefit. Many organisations frame outcome KPIs as objectives and key results; our [OKR template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/okr-template/) helps you set and score them. Scrum.org's Evidence-Based Management offers a fuller value framework, summarised in our Scrum metrics guide.
Outcome data lags, so review value metrics over several iterations.

### Team health metrics
Sustainable pace is an Agile Manifesto principle. Team health metrics warn you before burnout appears in delivery.
- **Happiness or engagement score:** a quick anonymous 1 to 5 rating at each [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/), with a reason.
- **Unplanned work:** the share of capacity spent on work not in the plan, such as urgent support.
- **Retrospective actions completed:** the share of agreed improvements that were actually done.
Keep these inside the team. Publishing individual scores or ranking teams by happiness destroys the honesty the metric needs.

### Agile metrics at scale
When several teams work on one product, adding up team metrics misleads: summed velocities mean nothing, and every team can look fast while the system waits on integration. Measure the system as well as the teams.
| Level | Typical questions | Useful metrics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Team | Are we improving how we work? | Cycle time, throughput, WIP, escaped defects, happiness |
| Team of teams (programme or ART) | Are we delivering together, predictably? | Feature lead time, cross-team dependencies open, predictability, release frequency |
| Portfolio | Are we investing in the right things? | Outcome KPIs, flow distribution, epic lead time, value delivered per initiative |

#### SAFe flow metrics
SAFe groups its measures into three domains: outcomes, flow and competency. Its six flow metrics apply at team, Agile Release Train and portfolio level:
| SAFe flow metric | Meaning | Closest team-level equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flow distribution | Share of completed work by type, such as features, enablers, defects and risks | Work type mix |
| Flow velocity | Number of backlog items completed per period | Throughput |
| Flow time | Time from an item entering the workflow to release | Lead time |
| Flow load | Total number of items in progress | WIP |
| Flow efficiency | Share of elapsed time items are actively worked on | Flow efficiency |
| Flow predictability | How closely delivered business value matches what was planned | Say/do ratio |
**Flow distribution example (illustrative):** an Agile Release Train completed 40 items in a Planning Interval: 24 features (60%), 8 enablers (20%), 6 defects (15%) and 2 risk items (5%). If leaders expected 30% of capacity for architecture enablers, the 20% figure prompts a capacity conversation at the next PI Planning.
**Predictability example (illustrative):** teams' committed PI objectives were given 50 planned business value points by business owners; at the end of the PI, business owners scored the actual value achieved at 42. Predictability = 42 ÷ 50 × 100 = 84%. SAFe guidance commonly treats 80% to 100% as a predictable range.
See our guide to [Agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/) for how portfolio metrics connect to funding and strategy.

### Measuring an Agile transformation
Leaders often want to know whether a move to Agile is working. Counting teams trained or ceremonies held measures activity, not results. Compare a baseline from before the change with the same measures afterwards.
| Instead of measuring | Measure |
| --- | --- |
| Number of teams "doing Agile" | Lead time from idea to customer, before and after |
| Ceremony attendance | Release frequency and change fail rate |
| Maturity questionnaire scores alone | Customer satisfaction and adoption of what was delivered |
| Velocity across teams | Predictability of commitments and forecasts |
| Training completion | Employee engagement and voluntary attrition in delivery teams |
Maturity assessments can still help a team reflect, but they should not be the headline result. Our [Agile transformation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/) guide covers how to plan the change itself.

### Agile KPIs to report to leadership
Leaders need answers to a few questions, not a wall of charts. Map each question to one KPI and an agreed cadence.
| Leadership question | Suggested KPI | Cadence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When will it be ready? | Forecast range from throughput or velocity, with confidence level | Every iteration or month |
| Are we delivering what we said? | Say/do ratio, Sprint Goal success or PI predictability | Monthly or per PI |
| How quickly do we respond? | Lead time (85th percentile) or change lead time | Monthly |
| Is quality holding up? | Escaped defects trend, change fail rate | Monthly |
| Is it making a difference? | Adoption, NPS or CSAT, OKR key results | Monthly or quarterly |
Share ranges and trends with a short commentary, and keep story points, burndowns and individual data inside the team. A one-page [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) is a good format.

### How to choose and introduce Agile metrics
This step-by-step process, based on the Goal–Question–Metric approach, keeps your set small and useful.
1. **Start with goals.** Write down what the team or programme is trying to achieve this quarter, for example "reduce the time customers wait for fixes".
2. **Ask the questions that goal raises.** For example: how long do customers wait now, where does work wait, and are fixes sticking?
3. **Choose one metric per question.** Lead time, flow efficiency and deployment rework rate answer those three. Aim for four to six metrics in total, across at least three of the five categories.
4. **Define each metric precisely.** Agree when the clock starts and stops, which items count and which percentile you report. Write the definitions into your working agreement.
5. **Automate collection.** Let your tool produce the data, and make sure board states match reality, or the metric will be wrong.
6. **Collect a baseline.** Gather four to six iterations or eight weeks of data before drawing conclusions.
7. **Review at a fixed point.** Look at team metrics in Retrospectives and outcome KPIs in reviews with stakeholders, and ask "what will we do differently?"
8. **Retire metrics nobody uses.** Every quarter, drop any metric that has not changed a decision.
Tip
Pair every speed metric with a quality metric: throughput with escaped defects, deployment frequency with change fail rate. It stops one improving at the expense of the other.

### Worked example: a three-team metrics review
This illustrative example shows three teams working on one customer platform, reviewed at the end of a quarter. Each team uses its own method, so the programme compares flow and outcome measures, not velocity.
| Team | Method | Throughput (items/week) | Cycle time, 85th pct (days) | WIP (avg) | Change fail rate | Happiness (1–5) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Payments | Scrum | 7 | 6 | 8 | 4% | 3.9 |
| Onboarding | Kanban | 9 | 5 | 7 | 6% | 4.1 |
| Mobile app | Scrumban | 5 | 14 | 16 | 15% | 3.0 |
How the programme lead and teams read it together:
1. **Mobile app stands out on flow.** Its 85th percentile cycle time is more than twice the others, and its WIP is twice as high. By Little's Law, high WIP with lower throughput means long waits.
2. **Quality confirms the pattern.** A 15% change fail rate suggests work is rushed at the end to clear the queue.
3. **Health completes the picture.** A happiness score of 3.0 with comments about context switching fits the same story.
4. **Root cause.** The team found it was waiting on another team's API changes, so items sat half-finished while new ones were started.
5. **Actions.** A WIP limit of 8, a weekly dependency check with the Payments team and a shared definition of an API change being done.
Throughput alone would have invited pressure on Mobile app to work harder. Reading flow, quality and health together revealed a system problem that more effort could not fix.

### Common mistakes with Agile metrics
- **Setting velocity or throughput targets.** Teams respond by inflating estimates or splitting items, and the number rises while value does not.
- **Comparing or ranking teams.** Teams differ in context, work type and definitions.
- **Using team metrics in individual reviews.** People stop surfacing problems, which ruins the data.
- **Reporting averages for cycle time.** A few long items distort them; use percentiles.
- **Counting partly finished work.** Only work that meets the Definition of Done should count.
- **Ignoring the system at scale.** Every team can look healthy while the whole programme waits on dependencies.
Most of these come from using metrics as verdicts instead of questions. Read [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/) for the Scrum-specific view.

### Tools for tracking Agile metrics
You can track every metric here in a spreadsheet, but most teams let their work management tool collect the data automatically.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** includes the standard Agile reports: sprint reports, burndown and burnup charts, velocity, cumulative flow diagrams and control charts for cycle time. It is widely used by software teams.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** offers sprint reporting with burndown, burnup, velocity and cumulative flow, plus dashboards and goals.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-ranked tool overall, suits organisations that need configurable dashboards and portfolio reporting across many teams, including Agile and non-software work.
- **monday.com** and **Asana** suit business teams that want easy dashboards and goal tracking alongside their projects.
Whatever you choose, the tool can only report what the board shows, so keep item states current and make sure "done" means the Definition of Done. See our comparison of [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the most important Agile metrics?**
There is no single list, but a strong starter set is cycle time, throughput, WIP, escaped defects or change fail rate, one outcome measure such as adoption or NPS, and a team health measure. Scrum teams often add Sprint Goal success rate.

**Q: What is the difference between Agile metrics and KPIs?**
A metric is any measure a team finds useful for improving. A KPI is one of the few measures leadership chooses as a critical signal of progress towards a goal, usually reviewed monthly or quarterly.

**Q: How do you measure Agile team performance?**
Look at several areas together: flow (cycle time, throughput), predictability (say/do ratio), quality (escaped defects), outcomes (adoption, satisfaction) and team health. Compare each team with its own past, never with other teams.

**Q: Should velocity be used as a KPI?**
No. Velocity is a planning aid for one team. As a KPI it encourages inflated estimates and cannot be compared across teams. Use forecast ranges, lead time or outcome measures instead.

**Q: What is the difference between cycle time and lead time?**
Lead time starts when a request is made; cycle time starts when work begins. Both end at delivery, so lead time is always at least as long as cycle time.

**Q: What are the DORA metrics?**
Five software delivery metrics: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate. The fifth was added in 2024.

**Q: What are flow metrics in Agile?**
Measures of how work moves through a process: WIP, cycle time, work item age and throughput, often with lead time and flow efficiency. They work in any Agile method.

**Q: How many Agile metrics should a team track?**
Usually four to six, covering at least three of the five categories. More than that tends to go unread.

**Q: How do you forecast delivery without story points?**
Use throughput. Divide remaining items by your lowest, average and highest weekly throughput to get a range, or run a Monte Carlo simulation on your throughput history for probability-based forecasts.

**Q: What Agile metrics should executives see?**
Forecast ranges, predictability, lead time, quality trends and outcome KPIs such as adoption or customer satisfaction. Keep story points, burndowns and individual data inside the team.

**Q: How do you measure the success of an Agile transformation?**
Take a baseline before the change and track outcomes after it: lead time, release frequency, change fail rate, customer satisfaction and employee engagement, rather than the number of teams trained.

**Q: What is a good say/do ratio?**
There is no universal standard. A stable ratio that is high but not always 100% suggests realistic planning; a ratio that is always 100% may mean plans are too cautious.

# Agile Mindset: What It Is, Key Traits and How to Develop It

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-mindset/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: What the Agile mindset means, its core traits and behaviours, how it links to the Agile Manifesto, examples at work and practical ways to develop it.


## Agile Mindset: What It Is, Key Traits and How to Develop It
The Agile mindset is a set of attitudes that puts customer value, collaboration, learning and adaptability ahead of rigid plans and processes. It is the thinking behind Agile practices: without it, sprints and stand-ups become rituals; with it, teams keep finding better ways to deliver.
- Published 8 September 2026
- 4 min read

### Key takeaways
- The Agile mindset puts customer value, collaboration, learning and adaptability first.
- It comes from the Agile Manifesto's values and principles.
- It is developed through practice and leadership behaviour, not training alone.
- Without the mindset, Agile practices become empty rituals.

### Where the mindset comes from
The mindset is rooted in the four values and twelve principles of the [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/), published in 2001. The values prefer individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change, while still recognising the value of processes, documentation, contracts and plans. Agile frameworks such as [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) and [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) give structure; the mindset decides how well they work.

### Core traits of an Agile mindset
| Trait | What it looks like in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Customer focus | Judging work by the value it gives users, not by output or effort |
| Embracing change | Treating new information as useful rather than as a threat to the plan |
| Learning by doing | Running small experiments and using the results to decide |
| Collaboration | Solving problems together across roles instead of handing work over |
| Transparency | Making work, progress and problems visible early |
| Ownership | Teams taking responsibility for outcomes and how they work |
| Continuous improvement | Regularly reflecting and making small changes |
| Simplicity | Maximising the amount of work not done, as the Manifesto puts it |

### Fixed vs Agile mindset: examples
| Situation | Fixed, plan-driven response | Agile response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer changes a requirement | "That's out of scope; raise a change request." | "What problem are you trying to solve? Let's see where it fits in the backlog." |
| A sprint goal is missed | Find out who is to blame | Ask what the team learned and adjust |
| A risky new feature | Plan it fully before building anything | Build a small version and test it with users |
| A manager wants a status update | Write a long report | Invite them to the [sprint review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) to see working results |
| A team member is stuck | Wait until the weekly meeting | Raise it at the [daily stand-up](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) and swarm on it |

### How to develop an Agile mindset
1. **Learn the values and principles:** read the Agile Manifesto and discuss what each principle means for your work.
2. **Shorten feedback loops:** deliver something small and get a reaction within days, not months.
3. **Make work visible:** use a board so everyone can see progress and blockers; see [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/).
4. **Run honest retrospectives:** focus on the system, not on blame; try [retrospective games](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective-games/) to keep them fresh.
5. **Treat plans as hypotheses:** state what you expect to happen and check it.
6. **Practise psychological safety:** reward people for raising problems early.
7. **Lead by example:** managers who ask questions, accept uncertainty and admit mistakes make it safe for others to do the same; see [servant leadership](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/servant-leadership-in-scrum/).

### Common misunderstandings
- **"Agile means no planning."** Agile teams plan often, in shorter horizons.
- **"Agile means no documentation."** The Manifesto values working software more, but documentation still has a place.
- **"Agile means faster at any cost."** Sustainable pace and technical quality are Agile principles.
- **"The mindset is only for developers."** Leaders, product owners and support functions need it too, perhaps most of all.
- **"You can install a mindset with training."** Training helps, but mindset changes through practice, experience and leadership behaviour.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the Agile mindset?**
A way of thinking that values customer outcomes, collaboration, learning and adaptability over rigid plans and processes.

**Q: Why is the Agile mindset important?**
Practices alone do not make a team Agile. The mindset determines whether teams use them to learn and improve or simply follow rituals.

**Q: What are the key traits of an Agile mindset?**
Customer focus, embracing change, learning by experiment, collaboration, transparency, ownership, continuous improvement and simplicity.

**Q: Is the Agile mindset the same as a growth mindset?**
They are related. A growth mindset is the belief that abilities can be developed; the Agile mindset applies a similar learning attitude to how teams deliver work.

**Q: How do you develop an Agile mindset?**
Through practice: short feedback loops, visible work, honest retrospectives, small experiments and leaders who model the behaviours.

**Q: Can managers have an Agile mindset?**
Yes, and it is essential. Leaders who empower teams and accept uncertainty enable everyone else; see [how to manage Agile teams](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-manage-agile-teams/).

**Q: What is the opposite of an Agile mindset?**
A fixed, plan-driven mindset that treats change as failure, values following the plan over outcomes and relies on command and control.

**Q: Does an Agile mindset mean no plans?**
No. Agile teams plan regularly; they simply expect plans to change as they learn.

**Q: How does the Agile mindset relate to the Agile Manifesto?**
The Manifesto's four values and twelve principles describe the mindset; frameworks put it into practice.

**Q: Can you have an Agile mindset without using Scrum?**
Yes. Scrum is one framework; Kanban, Extreme Programming and others also support an Agile mindset. See [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/).

**Q: How do you know if a team has an Agile mindset?**
Look for behaviours: frequent delivery, open discussion of problems, decisions based on feedback, and steady improvements from retrospectives.

# Agile in IT Operations: How Ops Teams Apply Agile and DevOps

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-operations-it/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: How IT operations teams apply Agile: handling planned and unplanned work, Kanban for ops, DevOps links, metrics, an example and common mistakes.


## Agile in IT Operations: How Ops Teams Apply Agile and DevOps
Agile in IT operations means applying Agile values and practices, such as visible work, short feedback loops and continuous improvement, to the teams that run infrastructure, networks, service desks and production systems. Because operations work mixes planned projects with unplanned incidents, ops teams often favour Kanban and close collaboration with development through DevOps.
- Published 8 September 2026
- 5 min read

### Key takeaways
- Operations teams apply Agile by making all work visible and planning for interruptions.
- Kanban with classes of service and WIP limits usually fits ops better than strict sprints.
- Reserve capacity for unplanned work and invest steadily in automation.
- Close collaboration with development through DevOps multiplies the benefits.

### Why operations is different
Development teams can usually plan a sprint and protect it. Operations teams face a steady stream of interruptions: incidents, service requests, security patches and urgent changes. A strict sprint commitment often breaks within days. Agile still helps, but the practices need adapting.
| Work type | Example | Typical approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unplanned | Outage, security alert, urgent fix | Handled immediately through an expedite lane |
| Routine requests | New user accounts, access changes | Standardised and automated where possible; flow through a board |
| Planned improvement | Upgrade a database cluster, automate backups | Broken into small items and prioritised in a backlog |
| Maintenance | Patching, certificate renewals | Scheduled as recurring work with capacity reserved |

### Agile practices that work for ops teams
- **Kanban boards with WIP limits:** visualise all work types and limit how much is in progress; see [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/).
- **Classes of service:** an expedite lane for incidents, a fixed-date lane for deadlines and a standard lane for everything else; see [Kanban swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/).
- **Reserved capacity:** keep a share of capacity, for example 30–40%, for unplanned work, based on your own history.
- **Short daily stand-ups at the board:** focus on blocked and ageing items.
- **Regular retrospectives and post-incident reviews:** blameless reviews that lead to concrete improvements.
- **Automation as backlog work:** treat automating repeated tasks as planned improvement items.
- **Shared ownership with development:** joint on-call, shared metrics and infrastructure as code; see [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/).

### How to introduce Agile in an operations team
1. **Make all work visible:** put incidents, requests and projects on one board for two to four weeks without changing anything else.
2. **Measure the mix:** count how much work is unplanned versus planned.
3. **Set classes of service and WIP limits:** agree rules for what can interrupt planned work.
4. **Reserve capacity:** set aside enough for the unplanned work you measured.
5. **Prioritise improvement work:** create a backlog of automation and reliability items with a clear owner.
6. **Add a cadence:** a weekly replenishment meeting and a fortnightly retrospective are a good start; see [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/).
7. **Review metrics monthly:** look at [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/), [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) and incident trends, then adapt.

### Worked example
A six-person infrastructure team tracks four weeks of work and finds that 45% of completed items were unplanned. They reserve about half their capacity for unplanned work, introduce an expedite lane limited to one item at a time and set a WIP limit of eight across the board. Each week they pull the top improvement items from the backlog. After two months the team automates its three most frequent requests (password resets for a legacy system, test environment builds and log-access requests), and the share of unplanned work falls to around a third. Average cycle time for standard requests drops from eight days to four.

### Metrics for Agile operations
| Metric | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Cycle time per class of service | Shows how quickly each type of work is completed |
| Throughput | Shows how many items the team completes per week |
| Planned vs unplanned ratio | Shows whether improvement work is reducing interruptions |
| Mean time to restore service | Shows how quickly the team recovers from incidents |
| Change failure rate | Shows how often changes cause problems |
| Service level performance | Shows whether agreed targets are met; see [service level agreement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/service-level-agreement-sla/) |

### Common mistakes
- Forcing two-week sprint commitments on a team that is mostly interrupt-driven.
- Leaving unplanned work off the board, so the team looks idle when it is busy.
- Never protecting time for improvement, so the same incidents keep happening.
- Treating Agile and IT service management frameworks as enemies; their processes can coexist with Agile ways of working.
- Separating development and operations so tightly that problems are thrown over the wall.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Can IT operations teams use Agile operations practices?**
Yes. They adapt it to handle unplanned work, usually with Kanban, reserved capacity and close collaboration with development.

**Q: Is Scrum or Kanban better for Agile IT operations?**
Kanban usually fits better because it handles a continuous flow of interruptions. Teams with mostly planned project work can use Scrum. See [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/).

**Q: How do Agile ops teams handle incidents?**
Through an expedite lane or class of service that lets urgent work bypass the normal queue, with a strict limit on how many expedited items run at once.

**Q: What is the difference between Agile operations and DevOps?**
Agile operations applies Agile practices inside ops teams; [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/) joins development and operations into a shared way of building, releasing and running software.

**Q: How much capacity should Agile operations teams reserve for unplanned work?**
Base it on your own history. Track several weeks of work, measure the unplanned share and reserve around that amount.

**Q: Can Agile IT operations work with ITIL?**
Yes. ITIL describes service management practices; Agile describes how teams work. Many organisations use both.

**Q: What metrics should an Agile ops team track?**
Cycle time, throughput, planned versus unplanned work, time to restore service, change failure rate and service level performance.

**Q: Do Agile operations teams need a product owner?**
Many benefit from someone who prioritises improvement work and balances requests; some call this a service owner.

**Q: How do Agile ops teams run stand-ups?**
Briefly, at the board, focusing on blocked, ageing and expedited items rather than individual status updates.

**Q: What is a blameless post-incident review in Agile operations?**
A review that looks at how the system and process allowed an incident to happen, rather than who caused it, and agrees improvements.

**Q: Which tools suit Agile IT operations?**
Tools that support Kanban boards, request intake and automation; compare options in our [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) reviews.

# Agile PMO: Roles, Services and How to Build One

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-pmo/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: An Agile PMO enables value delivery instead of policing projects. Learn its services, roles, metrics, governance and how to transform a traditional PMO.


## Agile PMO: Roles, Services and How to Build One
An Agile PMO is a project, programme or portfolio management office that helps Agile teams deliver value by coordinating portfolio decisions, lightweight governance, flow metrics and coaching, rather than by enforcing detailed plans and stage gates. This guide explains how it differs from a traditional PMO, the services and roles inside one, how it works in SAFe, and a step-by-step plan to transform the PMO you already have.
- Published 23 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- An Agile PMO exists to help value flow from strategy to customers; it coordinates and enables rather than polices.
- Its core services are portfolio prioritisation, Lean funding and guardrails, dependency management, flow and outcome metrics, and coaching.
- Stage gates and RAG reports give way to regular reviews of working product, forecasts and outcome data.
- In SAFe the same function is called a value management office (VMO) and facilitates Lean Portfolio Management.
- Transform gradually: agree a new purpose, pilot with a few teams, replace one control at a time and measure the result.
- The biggest mistake is renaming the PMO without changing what it asks teams to do.

### What is an Agile PMO?
An **Agile PMO** is a project, programme or portfolio management office redesigned for organisations that deliver through Agile teams. Instead of approving detailed plans and chasing status reports, it helps leaders choose and fund the right work, keeps governance light, connects teams that depend on each other, and measures flow and outcomes.
You will also see it called an **Agile programme management office (APMO)**, a **Lean PMO**, a **portfolio office** or, in the Scaled Agile Framework, a **value management office (VMO)**. The names differ, but the shift is the same: from controlling projects to enabling the flow of value.
If you are new to PMOs in general, start with our guide to the [project management office (PMO)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/), which covers the supportive, controlling and directive types, PMO levels and how to set one up. The [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) 8th edition, published by PMI in November 2025, has an appendix on PMOs and describes the PMO moving from a process-focused unit towards a partner tailored to strategy, which is close to what an Agile PMO aims to be.

#### What an Agile PMO is not
- **Not a team that runs sprints.** Scrum Teams manage their own work; the Agile PMO works at portfolio and cross-team level.
- **Not a reporting factory.** It does not ask teams to retype data that already lives in their tools.
- **Not a rename.** A PMO that keeps every old template and gate but adds "Agile" to its name has not changed.

### Agile PMO vs traditional PMO
The table below sets out the main differences. Most real PMOs sit somewhere between the two columns, and the direction of travel matters more than the label.
| Aspect | Traditional PMO | Agile PMO |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Control and compliance of projects | Enabling value delivery across the portfolio |
| Unit of work | Temporary projects | Long-lived products, value streams and epics |
| Planning | Detailed plans approved up front | Rolling roadmaps and quarterly planning, detail added just in time |
| Funding | Budget approved per project | Funding for teams or value streams, steered by guardrails |
| Governance | Stage gates and sign-offs | Lightweight guardrails and regular reviews of working results |
| Reporting | Status reports and RAG ratings | Live dashboards, flow metrics, forecasts and outcomes |
| Change | Formal change control to protect the baseline | Reprioritising the backlog is normal and cheap |
| Relationship with teams | Oversight and audit | Service, facilitation and coaching |
| Measure of success | On time, on budget, to scope | Outcomes achieved, flow predictability and customer value |

#### What stays the same
An Agile PMO still answers the same executive questions: are we doing the right work, will it be ready when needed and is money well spent? What changes is **how** the answers are produced: from working product and live data rather than plans and opinions.

### Why an Agile organisation still needs a PMO
Agile frameworks such as Scrum describe how a team works. They say little about how 20 or 200 teams share a budget, agree priorities or coordinate a release. Those gaps appear quickly when an organisation scales Agile but leaves the old PMO untouched:
- **Dual reporting.** Teams update their board for the sprint and then fill in a separate status template for the PMO.
- **Project funding fights team stability.** Each new project needs a business case and a new team, so stable Agile teams are broken up.
- **Invisible dependencies.** Teams plan independently and discover late that they need something from each other.
- **Too much work in progress.** Every request is approved, nothing is stopped, and lead times grow.
An Agile PMO solves these portfolio problems so that teams can stay focused on delivery. It is often the function that makes an [Agile transformation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/) stick beyond the first few pilot teams.

#### When you may not need one
A single product with two or three teams usually manages without a formal PMO: the Product Owner and Scrum Master cover coordination. The case for an Agile PMO grows with the number of teams, shared budgets and regulatory requirements.

### Agile PMO services and responsibilities
An Agile PMO is easiest to design as a short catalogue of services. Pick the ones that solve your current problems; few PMOs offer all of them.
| Service | What the Agile PMO does | What good looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Portfolio flow and prioritisation | Runs intake, maintains the portfolio Kanban, prepares prioritisation data such as cost of delay | New ideas are triaged within weeks; work in progress at portfolio level is limited |
| Funding and guardrails | Supports budgeting for teams or value streams and tracks spend against guardrails | Funding decisions take days, not months, and the spend mix matches strategy |
| Lean governance | Designs lightweight decision points and reviews based on working results | Decisions happen at the lowest sensible level with a clear audit trail |
| Capacity | Keeps a view of team capacity and demand across the portfolio | Leaders can see what the teams can absorb before they commit |
| Dependencies and release calendar | Facilitates cross-team planning and keeps one release and dependency view | Blocking dependencies are spotted at planning, not in the last sprint |
| Metrics and reporting | Publishes flow and outcome metrics generated from team tools | One live dashboard, no retyped reports |
| Capability and coaching | Trains and coaches teams, leaders and PMO staff; runs communities of practice | Practices improve and new teams ramp up quickly |
| Tools and data | Configures shared tools and agrees minimum data standards | Data entered once, consistent fields across teams |
| Risk and compliance | Maps regulatory controls onto Agile practices; keeps a cross-team RAID view | Auditors get evidence from normal work, not extra paperwork |
| Event facilitation | Organises portfolio reviews, quarterly planning and cross-team retrospectives | Events start on time, have clear outputs and decisions are recorded |
Several of these services are covered in more depth in our guides to [Agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/), [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) and the [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/).

### Supportive, controlling and directive PMOs in an Agile setting
The classic PMO types still apply, but each looks different once teams work in an Agile way. Use the table to decide which model you are moving towards.
| PMO type | Traditional version | Agile version | Main risk in an Agile setting |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Supportive | Templates, training, lessons learned | Coaching, communities of practice, shared tool set-up, metrics help | Teams ignore it if the help is not practical |
| Controlling | Mandatory methods, reports and gates | A small set of non-negotiable guardrails, such as Definition of Done, security checks and funding limits | Guardrails grow back into a full stage-gate process |
| Directive | PMO employs and assigns project managers | PMO hosts delivery leads or Release Train Engineers who serve groups of teams | Command and control returns under a new name |
Most Agile PMOs end up as a **supportive PMO with a few firm guardrails**: teams choose how they work, but everyone follows the same minimum rules for funding, quality, security and data. That combination keeps autonomy high without losing the control that regulators and finance teams need.

### Agile PMO structure and roles
Job titles vary widely. The roles below are the building blocks; a small Agile PMO may combine three or four of them in one person.
| Role | Typical responsibilities | Useful background |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head of Agile PMO or VMO lead | Owns the PMO's purpose and services, works with portfolio leaders, champions lean governance | Senior delivery or portfolio leadership, change management |
| Portfolio manager | Runs intake and the portfolio Kanban, prepares prioritisation and funding decisions | Portfolio management, finance, business analysis |
| Portfolio or data analyst | Builds dashboards, maintains data standards, analyses flow metrics | Data skills, Jira or work management tools, reporting |
| Agile coach | Coaches teams and leaders, trains PMO staff, improves practices | Scrum, Kanban, facilitation, coaching |
| Release Train Engineer or delivery lead | Facilitates cross-team planning and events, removes impediments across teams | Scrum Master or programme experience |
| PMO coordinator | Organises events, keeps the calendar, supports onboarding | Organisation and communication; a common entry role |
The [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) and [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) roles sit mainly in or beside the teams, but many people move into Agile PMO roles from both.

#### Where the Agile PMO sits
Smaller portfolios usually have one **central** Agile PMO. Larger organisations prefer **hub and spoke**: a small central team owns guardrails, metrics and tools, while people in each product area or release train apply them. Mature organisations may go further and **embed** most PMO roles in the value streams.
A centre of excellence focuses on methods and coaching, while an Agile PMO also covers portfolio, funding and governance; many organisations combine them under one leader.

### The Agile PMO in SAFe: the value management office
The [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) gives the Agile PMO a specific name and job. SAFe describes the **value management office (VMO)** as the function responsible for facilitating Lean Portfolio Management and fostering operational excellence and lean governance. SAFe notes that VMOs often emerge from existing PMOs, and earlier SAFe material called the same function the Agile PMO or APMO.
SAFe separates two complementary functions: the **Lean-Agile Center of Excellence (LACE)** leads and coaches the transformation as a whole, while the **VMO** focuses on the portfolio activities that connect strategy to delivery.

#### Portfolio events the VMO supports
| Event | Typical frequency | Purpose | VMO contribution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Portfolio Sync | Typically monthly | Review epic progress, flow and dependencies; make portfolio decisions | Keeps the portfolio Kanban and metrics current, tracks actions, filters the agenda |
| Strategic Portfolio Review | Typically quarterly | Check strategy, investment mix and portfolio performance | Prepares data on outcomes, spend and capacity |
| Participatory Budgeting | Typically twice a year | Stakeholders allocate budget across value streams together | Prepares options and the business context, records the result |

#### Lean budget guardrails
SAFe defines Lean budget guardrails as the policies and practices for budgeting, spending and governance for a portfolio. It lists four:
1. **Guiding investments by horizon**, so spending is balanced across current, emerging and future solutions.
2. **Applying capacity allocation**, so new features, maintenance and technical work each get a planned share.
3. **Approving significant initiatives**, so large epics above an agreed threshold get portfolio approval.
4. **Continuous Business Owner engagement**, so business stakeholders stay involved in reviews and planning.
The VMO also supports [Agile release trains](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/) and their [PI planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/) events. You do not need SAFe to use these ideas: guardrails, a portfolio Kanban and a regular portfolio sync work in any scaled Agile setting.

### Lean governance: replacing stage gates
Governance does not disappear in an Agile organisation; it moves closer to the work and relies on evidence from working product. The table translates the controls a traditional PMO runs into their Agile equivalents. Our guide to [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) covers the underlying principles.
| Traditional control | Agile equivalent | What the Agile PMO checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full business case before any work | Lean business case for each epic with a hypothesis and an MVP | The hypothesis is measurable and the MVP is small enough to test quickly |
| Stage gate sign-off | Regular review of working product at sprint or system demos | Increments are reviewed by stakeholders, and decisions to continue, pivot or stop are recorded |
| Baseline and change control | Backlog reprioritisation by the Product Owner within guardrails | Large changes to scope, cost or direction go to the portfolio sync |
| Project budget approval | Funding for teams or value streams, reviewed periodically | Spend stays within guardrails and matches priorities |
| RAG status report | Live flow metrics, forecasts and outcome data | Forecasts are based on actual throughput, not optimism |
| Quality gate at the end | Definition of Done, automated tests and security checks on every increment | The Definition of Done is applied consistently across teams |

#### Satisfying audit and compliance
Regulated organisations often worry that Agile governance will fail an audit. Auditors need evidence that controls exist and operate, not specific documents. List the controls you must meet, map each one to an Agile practice (such as pull request approvals or the Definition of Done), agree what tool evidence will be accepted, and pilot the mapping with one team before scaling it.

### Agile PMO metrics and reporting
An Agile PMO reports on flow, outcomes and quality, using data generated by the teams' tools. Choose a few measures, explain them clearly and show trends rather than single numbers.
| Metric | What it measures | How the Agile PMO uses it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) | Items finished per week or sprint | Forecasting how much the portfolio can deliver |
| [Cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) | Time from start to finish for an item | Spotting slow stages and setting realistic expectations |
| Epic lead time | Time from an epic's approval to its release | Showing how quickly strategy turns into delivered value |
| Portfolio WIP | Number of epics in progress at once | Limiting parallel work so things finish |
| Plan predictability | Planned vs delivered objectives each quarter | Building trust in forecasts without demanding certainty |
| Outcome measures | Progress on OKRs or business results such as adoption or cost | Checking that delivery changes something that matters |
| Quality | Escaped defects, incidents, change failure rate | Making sure speed is not bought with rework |
| Investment mix | Spend by value stream, horizon or work type | Checking that spend follows strategy and guardrails |
Tip
Never compare velocity between teams or use it as a performance target. Story points are relative to each team, so a velocity league table only teaches teams to inflate their estimates.

#### What an Agile portfolio report looks like
A one-page portfolio report, generated from live data, typically contains:
- **Outcomes:** progress on the quarter's objectives or OKRs, with a short commentary.
- **Flow:** throughput and cycle time trends, plus epics in progress against the WIP limit.
- **Forecasts:** for each major epic or release, a date or scope range based on actual throughput.
- **Risks and dependencies:** the top cross-team blockers and who owns them.
- **Decisions needed:** what the portfolio leaders must decide at the next sync.
It replaces, rather than adds to, the traditional [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/). For a wider list of measures, see our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).

### How to transform a traditional PMO into an Agile PMO
Transforming a PMO is itself a change programme, so run it in an Agile way: small steps, visible results, regular feedback.
1. **Agree a new purpose with leadership.** Write one sentence, such as "help the organisation deliver the most valuable work, predictably, with the least overhead", and have the sponsor endorse it.
2. **Map the current PMO.** List every report, template, gate and meeting the PMO runs, who uses each one and how long it takes teams to produce.
3. **Ask the customers.** Interview executives, Product Owners and team members about what helps them and what gets in the way.
4. **Choose a pilot area.** Pick one product area or group of three to five willing teams.
5. **Agree minimum guardrails.** Decide the few non-negotiables: funding limits, Definition of Done, security and data rules.
6. **Replace one control at a time.** For example, swap the monthly status template for a live dashboard built from team tools.
7. **Set up a portfolio Kanban.** Visualise epics from idea to done, add WIP limits and agree how items are prioritised.
8. **Start a portfolio cadence.** Run a monthly portfolio sync and a quarterly planning and review event.
9. **Retrain and redeploy PMO staff.** Train them in Agile, Lean, flow metrics and facilitation; some will become portfolio analysts or coaches.
10. **Agree the governance mapping with audit.** Document how existing controls are met by Agile practices.
11. **Measure and publish results.** Track a few before-and-after measures such as reporting effort, decision time and epic lead time.
12. **Expand in waves.** Add the next group of teams only when the pilot works, and retire old processes as you go.

#### A 90-day plan
| Period | Goals | Outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Days 1-30: understand | Map current services, interview customers, agree purpose and pilot | PMO service inventory, problem list, one-sentence purpose, pilot teams chosen |
| Days 31-60: pilot | Live dashboard, portfolio Kanban, first portfolio sync | Dashboard replacing one report, visible portfolio WIP, first decisions recorded |
| Days 61-90: learn and plan | Review the pilot, agree guardrails with finance and audit, plan the next wave | Guardrail document, governance mapping, results shared with the sponsor |
If the wider organisation is also changing, align this plan with the [how to implement Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-implement-agile/) roadmap rather than running a separate initiative.

### Worked example: an Agile PMO for 12 teams
This example is illustrative. A financial services firm has 12 Scrum Teams building customer and internal products. The PMO is a five-person controlling PMO built for waterfall projects. Teams complain that they spend hours each month on status templates, and executives complain that they still cannot tell what will ship this quarter.

#### Quarter 1: stop the double reporting
- The head of PMO and the CTO agree a new purpose: help the teams deliver the highest-value work with the least overhead.
- The PMO lists 14 recurring reports and templates. Six are used by nobody and are retired at once.
- Four pilot teams move to a live dashboard built from their work management tool; the monthly status template is dropped for them.
- A portfolio Kanban shows 31 epics in progress across the 12 teams, far more than the teams can finish in a quarter.

#### Quarter 2: limit work in progress and plan together
- Portfolio leaders agree a WIP limit of 15 epics. Ten epics are paused and three are stopped.
- The first joint quarterly planning event brings all 12 teams together and surfaces 22 cross-team dependencies.
- Internal audit agrees a mapping of change-control requirements onto pull request approvals and the Definition of Done.

#### Results after two quarters
| Measure | Start | After 6 months |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recurring PMO reports and templates | 14 | 5, all generated from tools |
| Team time spent on status reporting | About 4 hours per team per month | Under 1 hour, mostly review |
| Epics in progress | 31 | 15 (at the WIP limit) |
| Median epic lead time | About 9 months | About 5 months |
| Quarterly objectives delivered as planned | Not measured | About 75% |
The figures are illustrative, but the pattern is common: the quickest gains come from removing unused reports and limiting work in progress, not from new processes. The PMO's influence grew because teams could see it saving them time.

### Common Agile PMO mistakes
| Mistake | What it looks like | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Renaming without changing | The "Agile PMO" still asks for Gantt charts, gates and RAG reports | Retire at least one old control for every new practice |
| Dual reporting | Teams update their board and a separate PMO template | Generate every report from the tools teams already use |
| Velocity league tables | Teams ranked by story points per sprint | Use throughput and cycle time trends for forecasting, never for ranking |
| No limit on portfolio WIP | Everything is approved and nothing finishes | Set a WIP limit for epics and stop work when it is reached |
| Guardrails that grow into gates | Each incident adds a new mandatory check | Review guardrails every quarter and remove the ones that add no value |

### Agile PMO tools and templates
An Agile PMO needs one place where portfolio data lives, ideally the same tool the teams use day to day, so reports are generated rather than assembled. Options from our reviews:
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool (9.4/10), combines boards, request intake, workflows, resource planning and cross-project dashboards, and its top plans add deeper portfolio, financial and resource analysis for PMO-level insight. It suits Agile PMOs that oversee a mix of Agile and non-Agile work across departments.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is the natural choice where software teams already work in it; its Premium and Enterprise plans add Plans (previously Advanced Roadmaps) for cross-team planning, dependencies and capacity.
- **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)** is easy to adopt and offers dashboards across boards, with portfolio and resource management on its higher plans.
- **[Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/)** links projects to portfolios and goals on its Advanced plan, which helps when the PMO reports progress against OKRs.

See all of them side by side on our [tool comparison page](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/). If you are starting without a platform, our [product roadmap template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-roadmap-template/) gives a simple portfolio roadmap and the [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) covers cross-team risks and dependencies.

### Agile PMO skills, careers and certification
Agile PMO work rewards a different mix of skills from traditional PMO work. Templates and compliance checking matter less; data, facilitation and portfolio thinking matter more.
- **Portfolio management:** prioritisation, cost of delay, funding models and investment mix.
- **Data and flow metrics:** throughput, cycle time, forecasting and dashboard design.
- **Facilitation:** running planning events, portfolio reviews and cross-team retrospectives.
- **Stakeholder and change skills:** working with finance, audit and executives to change long-standing processes.
Relevant credentials include PMI's PMO credential (PMI-PMOCP), Agile certifications such as PMI-ACP or Scrum certifications, SAFe's Lean Portfolio Management training for SAFe organisations, and P3O for PMO design. Requirements change, so check each awarding body's site before you apply.
Read our guide on [how to learn Agile and get certified](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/) to compare the main Agile credentials and plan your next step.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an Agile PMO?**
A project, programme or portfolio management office redesigned for Agile delivery. It coordinates portfolio decisions, Lean funding, lightweight governance, flow metrics and coaching rather than enforcing detailed plans and stage gates.

**Q: What is the difference between a PMO and an Agile PMO?**
A traditional PMO controls projects through plans, stage gates and status reports. An Agile PMO enables long-lived teams through roadmaps, guardrails, live dashboards and regular reviews of working product.

**Q: Does Agile need a PMO?**
Not always. A small product with a few teams can coordinate without one. Larger organisations with shared budgets, many teams and regulatory requirements usually benefit from an Agile PMO or similar portfolio function.

**Q: What is the role of the PMO in Scrum?**
Scrum does not define a PMO. In Scrum organisations, the PMO typically supports portfolio prioritisation, funding, cross-team dependencies, metrics and coaching, while Scrum Teams manage their own work.

**Q: What does a value management office (VMO) do?**
In SAFe, the VMO facilitates Lean Portfolio Management and fosters operational excellence and lean governance. It supports portfolio events, keeps the portfolio Kanban and metrics current and often evolves from an existing PMO.

**Q: What is an APMO?**
An Agile programme management office: another name for an Agile PMO. Earlier SAFe material used the term; current SAFe guidance describes the value management office (VMO) instead.

**Q: What metrics should an Agile PMO track?**
Throughput, cycle time, epic lead time, portfolio work in progress, plan predictability, outcome measures such as OKR progress, quality and investment mix. Avoid comparing velocity between teams.

**Q: How do you transform a traditional PMO into an Agile PMO?**
Agree a new purpose, map current reports and gates, pilot with a few willing teams, replace one control at a time with a lighter Agile equivalent, retrain PMO staff, agree the approach with audit and expand in waves.

**Q: What roles are in an Agile PMO?**
Typically a head of Agile PMO or VMO lead, portfolio managers, portfolio or data analysts, Agile coaches, delivery leads or Release Train Engineers, a tools administrator and coordinators.

**Q: What is lean governance?**
Governance that relies on lightweight guardrails, decentralised decisions and evidence from working product, instead of detailed up-front approval and stage gates.

**Q: Is an Agile PMO the same as a centre of excellence?**
Not exactly. A centre of excellence focuses on methods and coaching; an Agile PMO also covers portfolio decisions, funding, governance and reporting. Many organisations combine the two.

**Q: How long does it take to build an Agile PMO?**
A pilot with a live dashboard, portfolio Kanban and portfolio cadence can run within about three months. Changing funding and governance across a whole organisation usually takes a year or more.
