# The Agile Project Manager: Role, Skills and Career Path

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: What an Agile project manager does, how the role differs from a Scrum Master and traditional PM, key skills, certifications and a step-by-step career path.


## The Agile Project Manager: Role, Skills and Career Path
An Agile project manager coordinates the delivery of work done by Agile teams: aligning it with business goals, managing budget, risk and dependencies, and reporting progress to sponsors, while the teams themselves plan and organise their own work. Scrum has no project manager role, yet many organisations still employ Agile project managers, especially where several teams, suppliers or governance requirements are involved. This guide explains what the role involves, how it differs from the Scrum Master and a traditional project manager, and how to move into it, with worked examples.
- Published 20 September 2026
- Last updated 15 October 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- An Agile project manager coordinates delivery around self-managing teams: funding, budget, dependencies, risk, governance and reporting.
- The 2020 Scrum Guide has no project manager. In Scrum, project management work is shared between the Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers, so the role usually sits outside or across Scrum Teams.
- The role is most useful with several teams, external suppliers, fixed budgets or dates, regulation, or hybrid projects that mix predictive and Agile work.
- Agile project managers lead through facilitation and service. They forecast from real team data and report working increments and trends, not percentage complete.
- PMI-ACP, PMP, PRINCE2 Agile and Scrum certifications are all relevant; hands-on experience on an Agile team matters most.

### What is an Agile project manager?
An **Agile project manager** is a project manager who delivers outcomes through Agile teams rather than by directing tasks. They create the conditions for teams to succeed: clear goals, secured funding, managed dependencies and risks, and transparent reporting. They plan in layers, forecast from the team's actual delivery data and adapt the plan as the work reveals new information.
Two things make the role confusing. First, the Scrum Guide does not include it: a [Scrum Team](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) consists of a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and Developers, and the project management work inside the team is shared between them. Second, organisations use the title for quite different jobs, from a delivery lead for one team to a programme manager coordinating many.
PMI's Agile Practice Guide describes the project manager in Agile settings as a servant leader whose emphasis shifts from directing work to coaching, removing obstacles and helping collaboration across the organisation. That is a useful summary of the mindset. In practice, Agile project managers are most common in:
- organisations running several Agile teams that depend on each other;
- projects with a fixed budget, a contractual date or external suppliers;
- regulated sectors such as finance, healthcare and government, where governance and audit evidence are required;
- [hybrid projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) that combine predictive work (procurement, construction, hardware) with Agile software delivery;
- companies part-way through an Agile transformation, where existing project managers take on new responsibilities.

### What does an Agile project manager do?
The responsibilities below are typical. A single-team role will lean towards the first few; a programme role will lean towards funding, governance and cross-team coordination.

#### 1. Align the work with business goals and secure funding
The Agile project manager makes the case for the work, often through a business case or project charter, agrees the objectives with the sponsor and secures funding. In Agile organisations funding is increasingly allocated to long-lived teams or value streams rather than fixed-scope projects, and the project manager helps translate between the two models.

#### 2. Coordinate teams, suppliers and dependencies
When several teams contribute to one release, someone has to make cross-team dependencies visible and resolve conflicts early. Agile project managers run or support dependency boards, [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/) meetings and joint planning, and they manage supplier relationships and contracts.

#### 3. Manage the budget
Agile teams usually have a stable size, so cost per Sprint is predictable. The project manager tracks spend against value delivered, forecasts the cost of remaining work and flags early when budget and scope no longer match.

#### 4. Manage risks, issues and decisions
Team-level impediments belong to the team and the Scrum Master. The Agile project manager handles risks that cross teams or need management attention: supplier delays, regulatory change, funding decisions, organisational blockers. A [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) keeps risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies visible.

#### 5. Forecast and report progress
Instead of percentage complete, the Agile project manager reports working increments, burnup charts, forecast ranges and outcome measures, and explains what they mean for dates and budget.

#### 6. Satisfy governance without slowing teams down
Stage gates, steering committees and audit requirements do not disappear in Agile organisations. A good Agile project manager meets them with evidence the teams already produce, such as Sprint Review outcomes, the Definition of Done and release records, rather than asking teams to create extra documents.

#### 7. Support the team and the Product Owner
They help the Product Owner with stakeholder management, protect the team from disruption and remove organisational obstacles. They do not assign tasks or decide how the work is done.
| Level | Typical scope | Main activities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Team level | One or two Agile teams | Release forecasting, budget, stakeholder updates, supplier coordination, support for the Scrum Master and Product Owner |
| Multi-team level | Three to ten teams on one product or programme | Dependency management, joint planning, integrated release plans, cross-team risks, steering reporting |
| Programme or portfolio level | Several products or value streams | Funding and investment decisions, governance, benefits tracking; often works with an [Agile PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-pmo/) |

### Agile project manager vs Scrum Master, Product Owner and traditional project manager
The four roles overlap, and in small organisations one person may cover more than one. The table separates them by focus and accountability.
|  | Agile project manager | Scrum Master | Product Owner | Traditional project manager |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Defined by | The organisation | The Scrum Guide | The Scrum Guide | The organisation; standards such as PMBOK and PRINCE2 |
| Main focus | Delivery across teams, budget, risk, governance | Team effectiveness and Scrum practice | Product value and the Product Backlog | Delivering agreed scope on time and on budget |
| Authority over the work | Indirect: sets constraints and context | None over the work itself | Orders the backlog | Plans and assigns tasks |
| Planning style | Layered, adaptive, forecast from data | Facilitates team planning | Sets priorities and the Product Goal | Detailed upfront plan and baseline |
| Typical reporting | Burnup, forecasts, outcomes, RAID | Team improvement, impediments | Value delivered, roadmap progress | Milestones, earned value, % complete |
| Leadership style | Servant leadership and facilitation | Servant leadership and coaching | Decisive on value | Often directive |

#### Agile project manager vs traditional project manager
| Area | Traditional project manager | Agile project manager |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | Fixed early; changes go through change control | Flexible; time and cost are often fixed and scope is prioritised |
| Plan | Detailed plan at the start | High-level release plan refined every Sprint |
| Team | Assigns and tracks tasks | Supports a self-managing team |
| Estimates | Effort estimates per task | Team estimates and historical velocity or throughput |
| Progress | Milestones and percentage complete | Working increments and burnup |
| Risk | Identified upfront and reviewed periodically | Reduced continuously through early, frequent delivery |
| Stakeholders | Formal updates at stage gates | Regular Sprint Reviews with working product |

#### Can a Scrum Master be the project manager?
It is possible but usually unwise. The Scrum Master's accountability is the effectiveness of the Scrum Team, and they need the team's trust to coach it. Combining that with budget control and reporting to sponsors can make the Scrum Master look like a supervisor, which discourages openness. If one person must do both, agree clearly which hat they are wearing in each meeting.
| Decision | Agile project manager | Scrum Master | Product Owner | Developers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Overall budget and funding requests | Leads | Informed | Consulted | Informed |
| What to build next | Consulted | Informed | Decides | Consulted |
| How to build it and who does which task | Informed | Informed | Informed | Decide |
| Release date forecast | Leads, using team data | Facilitates | Consulted | Provide estimates |
| Cross-team dependency resolution | Leads | Supports | Consulted | Contribute |
| Process improvements within the team | Informed | Facilitates | Contributes | Decide |
On the product side, see how the [Agile product manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-product-manager/) and the [Scrum Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) divide strategy and backlog ownership.

### When does an organisation need an Agile project manager?
Not every Agile team needs one. A single, stable Scrum Team with an empowered Product Owner and an internal sponsor can usually manage itself. The role earns its place as complexity grows.
| You probably need one if… | You probably do not if… |
| --- | --- |
| Several teams must deliver one integrated release | One team owns the whole product |
| External suppliers or contracts are involved | All work is done in-house |
| The budget or date is fixed by contract or regulation | Funding is stable and dates are flexible |
| Governance requires stage gates or audit evidence | Governance is light and trust-based |
| The project mixes predictive and Agile work | All work suits iterative delivery |
| The Product Owner is overloaded with stakeholder management | The Product Owner has capacity and authority |
Tip
If you are introducing the role, write down what it is accountable for and what it is not. Most conflict with Scrum Masters and Product Owners comes from unclear boundaries, not bad intentions.

### How an Agile project manager plans and forecasts: a worked example
Agile projects still need answers to "when will it be ready?" and "how much will it cost?". The difference is that the answers come from the teams' real delivery data and are updated every Sprint. The example below is illustrative.
**Scenario:** two Scrum Teams of seven people are building a new customer portal. The sponsor needs a release in 12 weeks for a contract renewal and has approved a budget of £450,000. Sprints are two weeks long, so there are six Sprints left.

#### Step-by-step forecasting process
1. **Agree the release goal and order the scope.** With the Product Owner, split the backlog into Must have, Should have and Could have. Here the Must haves total 260 story points and the full backlog is 330 points.
2. **Collect recent velocity.** Combined velocity over the last six Sprints was 52, 61, 48, 57, 55 and 59 points. Use a range, not a single number: lowest 48, highest 61.
3. **Forecast a range.** Multiply by the six Sprints remaining: a pessimistic 6 × 48 = 288 points and an optimistic 6 × 61 = 366 points.
4. **Compare with scope.** All Must haves (260) fit even in the pessimistic case. The full backlog (330) is likely but not certain.
5. **Calculate the cost per Sprint.** 14 people × an assumed blended rate of £500 a day × 10 working days = £70,000 per Sprint. Six Sprints cost £420,000; adding £15,000 for environments and licences gives £435,000, leaving £15,000 of contingency.
6. **Communicate the forecast honestly.** Tell the sponsor that Must haves are expected by the date, Should haves are likely, and Could haves depend on the next few Sprints.
7. **Update every Sprint.** Plot completed work and total scope on a burnup chart and refresh the forecast after each Sprint Review.
| Forecast | Velocity per Sprint | Points in 6 Sprints | Must haves (260) | Full backlog (330) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pessimistic | 48 | 288 | Delivered | Not all delivered |
| Average | 55 | 330 | Delivered | Delivered, no margin |
| Optimistic | 61 | 366 | Delivered | Delivered with margin |
If scope grows during the project, the burnup chart shows the total-scope line rising, which makes the trade-off visible: add time, add budget or move items out. That conversation belongs with the Product Owner and sponsor, supported by the project manager's data.
Learn the underlying techniques in our guides to [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/), the [Agile velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) and [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/).

### Reporting progress the Agile way
Sponsors still want to know whether the project is on track. Agile project managers answer with evidence rather than estimates of percentage complete.
| Instead of… | Report… | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| % complete per task | Increments accepted at the Sprint Review | Working product is the clearest measure of progress |
| A single forecast date | A forecast range with confidence levels | Shows uncertainty honestly |
| Tasks completed | Burnup of scope delivered against total scope | Makes scope change visible |
| Hours spent | Spend against budget and value delivered | Links cost to outcome |
| Red/amber/green opinion | Trends in throughput, cycle time and escaped defects | Data that teams already produce |

#### Example of a one-page status update
- **Sprint 4 of 6 complete.** Increment accepted: customer login and account dashboard.
- **Forecast:** Must haves on track for the release date; two Should haves at risk.
- **Budget:** £280,000 spent of £450,000; on plan.
- **Top risks:** payment provider API change (mitigation agreed); security review booking (escalated to sponsor).
- **Decisions needed:** confirm whether the reporting module can move to the next release.
For measures that work at team and programme level, see [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).

### Running hybrid projects
Many Agile project managers work on hybrid projects, where some parts of the work suit a predictive plan and others suit iterative delivery. The skill is deciding which approach fits each part and integrating them through shared milestones.
**Example:** opening a new customer contact centre.
| Workstream | Approach | Why | How it is managed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Building fit-out | Predictive | Fixed design, contractor dependencies, little benefit from iteration | Gantt chart, contractor milestones, change control |
| Telephony procurement | Predictive | Formal tender and contract | Procurement plan and supplier contract |
| CRM configuration | Agile (Scrum) | Requirements will emerge as agents test the system | Two-week Sprints, Product Owner from operations |
| Staff training | Iterative | Content improves after each pilot group | Short cycles with feedback after each cohort |
The Agile project manager sets integration milestones (for example, "CRM ready for first training cohort") that both the predictive plan and the Agile release plan work towards, and manages the dependencies between them.

### Essential skills for an Agile project manager
| Skill | Type | What it looks like in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agile frameworks | Hard | Understands Scrum, Kanban and at least one scaling approach well enough to work with them, not against them |
| Forecasting with data | Hard | Uses velocity, throughput and burnup to give ranges, not guesses |
| Budgeting and contracts | Hard | Manages team-based costs and Agile-friendly contracts, such as time and materials with capped Sprints |
| Risk and dependency management | Hard | Keeps a live RAID log; spots cross-team dependencies before they block work |
| Facilitation | Soft | Runs workshops, joint planning and steering meetings that end in decisions |
| Stakeholder management | Soft | Keeps sponsors, suppliers and users informed and involved |
| Servant leadership | Soft | Removes obstacles and supports teams instead of directing them |
| Comfort with uncertainty | Soft | Re-plans calmly as new information arrives |
For the leadership side, see [servant leadership in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/servant-leadership-in-scrum/) and [how to manage Agile teams](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-manage-agile-teams/).

### Certifications for Agile project managers
Certification is rarely mandatory, but it helps when changing roles or applying to organisations that screen for it. The details below were checked against the awarding bodies on 15 October 2026; always confirm the current rules before you book.
| Certification | Awarding body | What it shows | Key requirements |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PMI-ACP | PMI | Agile knowledge across Scrum, Kanban, Lean and other approaches | Secondary education; 2 years of Agile experience in the last 5 years (or 1 year plus a GAC-accredited degree or a third-party Agile certification, or an active PMP); 21 hours of Agile training. 120 questions in 180 minutes |
| PMP | PMI | Broad project management across predictive, Agile and hybrid approaches | Project experience and 35 contact hours; the exam updated in July 2026 has about 40% predictive content, with the rest Agile and hybrid |
| PRINCE2 Agile | PeopleCert | Combining PRINCE2 governance with Agile delivery | Foundation and Practitioner levels |
| PSM / CSM | Scrum.org / Scrum Alliance | Understanding of Scrum and the Scrum Master accountability | Assessment (PSM) or course plus assessment (CSM) |
| SAFe certifications | Scaled Agile | Working in SAFe programmes | Course plus exam, by role |
PMI lists the PMI-ACP exam content as Mindset (28%), Leadership (25%), Product (19%) and Delivery (28%). For PMP details, see our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

### How to become an Agile project manager
Most Agile project managers come from one of two directions: traditional project managers learning Agile, or Scrum Masters and team leads taking on broader delivery responsibility.
1. **Learn the foundations of both worlds.** Understand predictive project management (scope, schedule, cost, risk, governance) and Agile values, principles and frameworks.
2. **Work on an Agile team.** Join a Scrum or Kanban team in any role. Nothing replaces seeing how self-managing teams plan, estimate and improve.
3. **Practise facilitation.** Run retrospectives, planning sessions and workshops. Ask for feedback on how you facilitate.
4. **Learn to forecast from data.** Track velocity or throughput and build a burnup forecast for a real release.
5. **Take a recognised certification.** Choose PMI-ACP, PRINCE2 Agile or a Scrum certification depending on your background and local job market.
6. **Take on cross-team work.** Volunteer to coordinate a dependency, a supplier or a multi-team release.
7. **Build a record of outcomes.** Describe projects by the value delivered and how you helped teams achieve it, not by the size of the plan you managed.

#### A 90-day plan for traditional project managers
| Period | Focus | Actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Days 1–30 | Learn and observe | Read the Scrum Guide; attend every Scrum event as an observer; map stakeholders and governance requirements |
| Days 31–60 | Contribute | Set up a RAID log and burnup forecast; agree role boundaries with the Scrum Master and Product Owner; simplify one governance report |
| Days 61–90 | Lead | Facilitate a multi-team planning session; present a forecast range to the sponsor; start a certification |
For a full learning path, read [how to learn Agile and get certified](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/).

### Common mistakes Agile project managers make
| Mistake | Why it hurts | Better approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assigning tasks to Developers | Undermines self-management and ownership | Agree goals and constraints; let the team plan the work |
| Recreating a detailed Gantt chart for Sprint work | Creates false precision and duplicate tracking | Use a release plan and burnup; keep Gantt charts for predictive workstreams |
| Reporting percentage complete | Hides risk until late | Report accepted increments and forecast ranges |
| Acting as a proxy Product Owner | Splits accountability for value | Support the Product Owner; do not decide priorities for them |
| Adding governance on top of Scrum | Slows teams and duplicates evidence | Map governance needs to artefacts teams already produce |
| Treating velocity as a target | Teams inflate estimates and the forecast loses value | Use velocity only for forecasting |

- [Agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/) for milestones, Sprints and releases.
- [Release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) for release goals and forecast scope.
- [Sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) for Sprint Goals and capacity.
- [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) for risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies.
For software, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is a good fit for Agile project managers who coordinate several teams and departments, because it combines Agile boards with Gantt charts, workload views and portfolio reporting in one place, which suits hybrid projects well. Software development teams often prefer [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/), which is built around backlogs, Sprints and developer workflows.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does an Agile project manager do?**
Aligns work with business goals, secures funding, coordinates dependencies between teams and suppliers, manages budget and risk, forecasts and reports progress, meets governance needs and removes organisational obstacles.

**Q: Is there an Agile project manager in Scrum?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide defines the Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers only. Project management work inside a Scrum Team is shared between them, but many organisations still have Agile project managers working across or outside Scrum Teams.

**Q: Is an Agile project manager the same as a Scrum Master?**
No. The Scrum Master is accountable for one Scrum Team's effectiveness and has no authority over the work. An Agile project manager usually coordinates delivery, budget, risk and stakeholders, often across several teams.

**Q: How is an Agile project manager different from a traditional one?**
The Agile project manager facilitates layered, adaptive planning and supports a self-managing team, rather than creating a detailed plan upfront and assigning tasks. Progress is shown through working increments and forecasts instead of percentage complete.

**Q: What skills does an Agile project manager need?**
Knowledge of Agile frameworks, forecasting from data, budgeting and contracts, risk and dependency management, facilitation, stakeholder management, servant leadership and comfort with changing plans.

**Q: Can a traditional project manager become an Agile project manager?**
Yes. Learn the frameworks, work on an Agile team, practise facilitation, learn to forecast from velocity or throughput, and shift from directing tasks to setting goals and removing obstacles.

**Q: What is a hybrid project manager compared with an Agile project manager?**
A hybrid project manager deliberately combines predictive planning for some workstreams with Agile delivery for others. Many Agile project managers work this way, particularly in regulated or large organisations.

**Q: How do Agile project managers report progress?**
With increments accepted at the Sprint Review, burnup charts, forecast ranges, spend against budget, key risks and the decisions needed from sponsors.

**Q: What is PMI-ACP for an Agile project manager?**
PMI's Agile Certified Practitioner credential, covering Scrum, Kanban, Lean and other approaches. PMI requires Agile experience (or an active PMP) and 21 hours of Agile training.

**Q: Does the PMP cover what an Agile project manager needs?**
Partly. PMI's 2026 exam content outline says about 40% of questions represent predictive approaches and the rest Agile and hybrid. See [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

**Q: Do Agile project managers need certification?**
Not always, but PMI-ACP, PRINCE2 Agile or a Scrum certification helps show your knowledge, especially when changing roles.

**Q: Does an Agile project manager manage the team's tasks?**
No. Developers decide how to do the work and who does which task. The Agile project manager works on the conditions around the team: goals, budget, dependencies and risks.

**Q: What is the difference between an Agile project manager and an Agile product manager?**
The product manager decides what to build and why and is measured on customer and business outcomes. The project manager makes sure agreed work is delivered within its constraints. See [Agile product manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-product-manager/).

# Agile Release Planning: Steps, Example and Template

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Agile release planning explained: what a release plan is, how to build one step by step, a worked velocity forecast, burnup charts and a free template.


## Agile Release Planning: Steps, Example and Template
Agile release planning is the practice of forecasting which backlog items a team is likely to deliver in its next one or more releases, and roughly when, using the team's measured pace and updating that forecast every sprint. It answers the question every stakeholder asks, "When will we get it?", with an honest range instead of a single date fixed on day one. This guide explains what a release plan contains, how to build one step by step, and how the forecasting maths works, with two worked examples you can copy.
- Published 16 September 2026
- Last updated 14 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- A release plan groups ordered backlog items into upcoming releases and forecasts when each is likely to be ready, using a range of velocities rather than one number.
- It sits between the product roadmap (strategy, months to years) and the sprint plan (detail, weeks).
- Fix either the date or the scope, never both. Agile teams usually fix the date and let lower-priority scope flex.
- Sort the backlog into "will have", "might have" and "won't have" for the release, so trade-offs are visible from the start.
- The 2020 Scrum Guide has no release planning event, but forecasting with burn-ups, burn-downs or cumulative flow is a common complementary practice.
- A release plan is a living forecast: update it after every Sprint Review and show progress on a release burnup chart.

### What is Agile release planning?
**Agile release planning** is a recurring activity in which the Product Owner, the team and key stakeholders decide which product backlog items should go into an upcoming release, estimate how much work that is, and use the team's measured velocity to forecast when the release is likely to be ready. The result is a release plan: a living forecast that is revised every sprint as real progress becomes known.
A **release** is the point at which a set of finished work is made available to users or customers. Some teams release several times a day; others bundle work into a release every few months because of app-store reviews, customer contracts, hardware, training or regulation. Release planning matters most in the second situation, where stakeholders need to know what is coming and roughly when.
Three ideas separate Agile release planning from a traditional fixed plan:
- **It is a forecast, not a promise.** It is based on how fast the team has actually been working, and it states its uncertainty as a range.
- **It is ordered by value.** The most important items are scheduled first, so if time runs out, what is left out is the least valuable work.
- **It is updated continuously.** Every sprint produces new data (completed work, scope changes), and the plan is adjusted to match.

### Where release planning fits: the levels of Agile planning
Agile teams plan constantly, but at different levels of detail and over different horizons. A common way to picture this is the "planning onion", with strategy on the outside and daily work at the centre. Release planning is the middle layer that turns a roadmap into something the team can deliver.
| Level | Typical horizon | Question it answers | Main output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vision and strategy | 1–3 years | Why does the product exist and where is it going? | Product vision, Product Goal |
| Product roadmap | 3–12 months | Which outcomes and themes come in what order? | [Agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) |
| Release plan | 1–6 months | Which backlog items are likely in each release, and when? | Release plan and burnup chart |
| Sprint (iteration) plan | 1–4 weeks | What will we deliver this sprint, and how? | Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog |
| Daily plan | 24 hours | What will we do today to reach the Sprint Goal? | Updated plan from the Daily Scrum |
Each level is planned in more detail the closer it is in time. That is deliberate: detailed plans for work six months away tend to be wrong, so Agile teams keep the far future coarse and refine it as it approaches.

### Release plan vs product roadmap vs sprint plan
These three documents are often confused. The table shows how they differ in purpose, content and audience.
|  | Product roadmap | Release plan | Sprint plan |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Communicate strategy and priorities | Forecast delivery of specific scope | Organise the next few weeks of work |
| Content | Goals, themes, outcomes | Epics and features, estimates, sprints, dates | Backlog items, tasks, Sprint Goal |
| Unit of time | Quarters or Now / Next / Later | Sprints and release dates | Days within one sprint |
| Owner | Product manager or Product Owner | Product Owner with the team | The Developers, with the Product Owner |
| Audience | Leadership, customers, whole organisation | Stakeholders, support, marketing, sales | The Scrum Team |
A practical rule: the roadmap says **why and in what order**, the release plan says **what and roughly when**, and the sprint plan says **exactly what next and how**. If you need a roadmap first, start with the free [product roadmap template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-roadmap-template/).

### Is release planning part of Scrum?
Not formally. The current Scrum Guide (the 2020 edition, still the official version by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland) defines five events: the Sprint, Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. There is no release planning event.
Instead, the Scrum Guide gives the Product Backlog a long-term objective, the **Product Goal**, and says the Product Owner is accountable for maximising value. On forecasting, it says that "various practices exist to forecast progress, like burn-downs, burn-ups, or cumulative flows", and adds that these do not replace the importance of empiricism. It also allows Increments to be delivered to stakeholders before the end of a sprint, so a release does not have to wait for the Sprint Review.
In practice, many Scrum teams still do release planning as a complementary practice, because their organisations need delivery forecasts. They typically:
- Use the Product Goal and roadmap as the release goal.
- Use [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) to size the items in the release.
- Revisit the forecast during each Sprint Review, where stakeholders discuss progress towards the Product Goal.
- Plan each sprint in [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) with the release forecast in mind.
Release planning has older roots in Extreme Programming (XP), whose "planning game" includes a release planning step, and it is formalised at scale in the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe), where teams plan together in [PI Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/) at the start of each Planning Interval.

### What an Agile release plan includes
A good release plan fits on one page or one screen. It usually contains:
- **Release goal:** one or two sentences on the outcome the release should achieve, for example "customers can manage their own billing without calling support".
- **Target date or target scope:** whichever is fixed (see the next section).
- **Ordered list of features or epics:** taken from the [product backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/), with the most valuable first.
- **Estimates:** in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/), T-shirt sizes or item counts.
- **Velocity range:** the team's slow, average and fast pace, based on recent sprints.
- **Sprint allocation:** which items are expected in which sprint, at least roughly.
- **Capacity adjustments:** holidays, public holidays, training, new joiners, planned support work.
- **Dependencies:** work needed from other teams, suppliers or platforms, with dates.
- **Risks and assumptions:** what could change the forecast, and what you are assuming.
- **Definition of Done and release criteria:** what "ready to release" means, including testing, documentation and approvals. See [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
- **Will / might / won't split:** which items are very likely, possible and unlikely to make the release.

### Fixed date or fixed scope?
Every release is constrained by time, scope, cost (mostly the size of the team) and quality. In Agile, quality is held constant through the Definition of Done, and team size changes slowly, so the real choice is between fixing the date and fixing the scope.
| Approach | What is fixed | What flexes | Typical example | Forecast question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed date | Release date | Scope (lowest-priority items) | Launch at a trade show, regulatory deadline, seasonal campaign | How much can we deliver by this date? |
| Fixed scope | A minimum feature set | Release date | Replacing a legacy system that cannot be switched off until everything works | When will this set of features be ready? |
| Fixed date and scope | Both | Quality, team health (in practice) | Contracts written without Agile in mind | Usually unanswerable without cutting corners |
Agile teams avoid fixing both at once. When both are fixed, the only things left to give are quality and people's evenings, and both create problems later. Our advice: prefer a fixed date with flexible scope where you can. It gives stakeholders certainty about the date and forces healthy prioritisation conversations early.

### How to create an Agile release plan: 9 steps
The steps below work for a single team using Scrum or another sprint-based approach. They take a few hours the first time and much less once the backlog is in good shape.
1. **Agree the release goal.** Start from the roadmap and Product Goal. Write a short statement of the outcome the release must achieve and how you will know it worked. Without a goal, release plans turn into a list of features nobody can prioritise.
2. **Decide what is fixed.** Agree with stakeholders whether the date or the scope is fixed, and record why. If the date is fixed, write it down; if the scope is fixed, write down the minimum set of features.
3. **Select and order the backlog items.** Pull the epics and stories that support the goal from the product backlog and order them by value, risk and dependencies. Use MoSCoW (must, should, could, won't) or a simple ranked list.
4. **Size the work.** Ask the Developers to estimate the items, in story points or T-shirt sizes for anything far away. Split very large items so that each fits comfortably in one sprint. Estimate only as precisely as the decision needs.
5. **Measure velocity as a range.** Take the team's completed points for the last six to eight sprints. Calculate a slow figure (for example, the average of the three worst sprints) and a fast figure (the average of the three best). Our [velocity chart guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) explains how to read the trend.
6. **Adjust for capacity.** Count the sprints available before the date, then reduce for holidays, training, onboarding or planned support work. Our [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) guide shows how.
7. **Forecast.** Multiply the slow and fast velocities by the number of effective sprints to get a scope range (fixed date), or divide the remaining points by each velocity to get a range of sprints (fixed scope). Draw a line in the ordered backlog at each figure.
8. **Check dependencies and risks.** Walk through the plan sprint by sprint with anyone the release depends on: other teams, suppliers, security review, app-store approval. Move items or add buffer where a dependency is uncertain.
9. **Agree, publish and update.** Review the plan with stakeholders, confirm the will / might / won't split, and publish it where everyone can see it. Update it after every Sprint Review using actual velocity and scope changes.
Steps 1 to 8 usually happen in a release planning meeting; step 9 continues until the release ships.

### Worked example: forecasting a fixed-date release
A team building a customer billing portal runs two-week sprints. The business wants a release in time for a sales event on **Friday 22 January 2027**. Sprint 1 starts on Monday 2 November 2026, so there are six sprints before the date.

#### Step A: find the velocity range
Completed story points in the last six sprints were 28, 34, 30, 25, 32 and 31. The average is 30, but one number hides the variation, so the team uses a range:
| Measure | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slow velocity | Average of the three lowest sprints: (25 + 28 + 30) ÷ 3 | 27.7 points |
| Average velocity | (28 + 34 + 30 + 25 + 32 + 31) ÷ 6 | 30.0 points |
| Fast velocity | Average of the three highest sprints: (31 + 32 + 34) ÷ 3 | 32.3 points |

#### Step B: adjust capacity
Two of the six sprints fall over the Christmas and New Year holidays, when about half the team is away for a week. The team counts each of those sprints as three-quarters of a normal sprint, so it has **5.5 effective sprints** instead of six.

#### Step C: forecast the scope range
| Scenario | Calculation | Points the team can expect to finish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slow | 27.7 × 5.5 | About 152 points |
| Fast | 32.3 × 5.5 | About 178 points |

#### Step D: draw the lines in the backlog
The ordered backlog for the release totals 250 points: 140 points of must-have items, 50 of should-have and 60 of could-have. Drawing lines at 152 and 178 points gives this picture:
| Group | Items (in priority order) | Points | Cumulative | Forecast |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Will have | Online invoices, card payments, payment history, email receipts | 140 | 140 | Very likely: fits even at slow velocity (152) |
| Might have | Direct debit set-up, downloadable statements | 38 | 178 | Possible: fits only if the team runs near its fast velocity |
| Won't have (this release) | Multi-currency, accounting export, saved payment methods | 72 | 250 | Unlikely: plan for the next release |
The Product Owner now has a clear message for stakeholders: the must-have features will be ready for the sales event, two extra features might make it, and the rest should be planned for the following release. The 12-point gap between the must-haves (140) and the slow forecast (152) is a small buffer for surprises.

#### Step E: allocate to sprints
| Sprint | Dates | Planned focus | Planned points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 2–13 Nov 2026 | Online invoices | 30 |
| 2 | 16–27 Nov 2026 | Card payments (part 1) | 30 |
| 3 | 30 Nov–11 Dec 2026 | Card payments (part 2), payment history | 30 |
| 4 | 14–25 Dec 2026 | Email receipts, payment history (finish) | 23 (holiday) |
| 5 | 28 Dec 2026–8 Jan 2027 | Hardening, Direct debit set-up (start) | 23 (holiday) |
| 6 | 11–22 Jan 2027 | Downloadable statements, release preparation | 30 |
Planned points use average velocity with the holiday reduction; the forecast range above is what the team communicates. The allocation is a guide only: each Sprint Planning decides the real content of each sprint.

### Worked example: forecasting a fixed-scope release
Now imagine the same team must replace a legacy billing system, and nothing can be switched off until all 250 points of scope are done. Work starts on Monday 1 March 2027, with no holidays in the period.
| Scenario | Calculation | Sprints needed | Forecast finish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fast | 250 ÷ 32.3 = 7.7, rounded up | 8 sprints | Friday 18 June 2027 |
| Slow | 250 ÷ 27.7 = 9.0, rounded up to allow for the remainder | 10 sprints | Friday 16 July 2027 |
The honest forecast is **between mid-June and mid-July 2027**. Round up, because a release cannot ship part-way through the last item. If the business needs certainty sooner, it has three levers: reduce scope (move items to a later release), add capacity early (new people slow a team down at first), or accept the later date.
For larger or riskier releases, a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) of past sprint results can give probabilities such as "85% chance of finishing by 2 July" instead of a simple range.
Tip
No velocity history yet? Run one or two sprints before making a forecast, or ask the team to plan a sample sprint from the backlog and use that as a first, very rough, velocity. Say clearly that the forecast will tighten after three or four sprints.

### Running a release planning meeting
Release planning is often done in a single workshop at the start of a release, then revisited briefly every sprint. For a single team and a release of three to six months, half a day to a day is usually enough.

#### Who attends
- **Product Owner** (leads the meeting and owns the backlog order).
- **Developers** (estimate, flag technical risks and dependencies).
- **Scrum Master or Agile delivery lead** (facilitates and keeps it time-boxed).
- **Key stakeholders** for the parts that affect them: customer support, marketing, sales, operations, security, and any team the release depends on.

#### Sample agenda
| Time | Item | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 20 min | Release goal, context and the roadmap it supports | Agreed release goal |
| 15 min | Fixed date or fixed scope, and why | Agreed constraint |
| 45 min | Walk through the ordered backlog; clarify and split large items | Ordered, understood list |
| 60 min | Estimate items that are not yet sized | Sized backlog for the release |
| 20 min | Velocity range and capacity for the release period | Effective sprints and velocity range |
| 30 min | Forecast; draw will / might / won't lines | Draft release plan |
| 30 min | Dependencies, risks and assumptions | Risk and dependency list with owners |
| 20 min | Confidence check and agreement | Agreed plan, next review date |
End with a quick **confidence vote**: everyone holds up one to five fingers for how confident they are in the plan. Any score of one or two is a signal to talk about the concern before leaving the room.

### Tracking the release with a burnup chart
A **release burnup chart** plots two lines across sprints: the total scope of the release and the cumulative work completed. The release is done when the lines meet. Unlike a burndown, a burnup shows scope changes clearly, which is why many teams prefer it for releases.
| After sprint | Total release scope (points) | Completed (cumulative) | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 250 | 29 | On track for the slow forecast |
| 2 | 250 | 61 | Slightly ahead of average |
| 3 | 262 | 90 | Scope grew by 12 points: discuss what moves out |
| 4 | 262 | 112 | Holiday sprint, as expected |
| 5 | 255 | 135 | Seven points moved to the next release |
| 6 | 255 | 166 | Must-haves done; part of the might-have group delivered |
To forecast from a burnup, extend the completed line at your slow and fast velocities and see where each crosses the scope line. That gives an updated date range every sprint. Our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) covers burnups, burndowns and cumulative flow in more depth.

### Communicating release forecasts to stakeholders
These habits help stakeholders trust the forecast:
- **Give ranges, not single dates.** "Between mid-June and mid-July" is honest. "16 June" sounds like a promise.
- **Show the will / might / won't split.** Stakeholders can see exactly what is at risk and argue about priority, not effort.
- **Share the burnup chart every sprint,** with one sentence on what changed and why.
- **Explain the trade-offs when scope grows.** Adding 20 points to a fixed-date release means 20 points move out, or the date moves.
- **Raise risks early.** A dependency that slips is easier to handle six weeks before the release than six days before.
A sample update: "After sprint 3 we have completed 90 of 262 points. The must-have features remain on track for 22 January. Downloadable statements are now unlikely because 12 points of payment-provider changes were added; we suggest moving them to the March release." For more on keeping stakeholders aligned, see [project stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/).

### Release planning with continuous delivery
Teams that practise [continuous delivery](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/continuous-delivery/) can deploy any finished item to production at any time. For them, the technical act of releasing is cheap, so a big release plan matters less. Release planning still has a role, but it shifts:
- **Plan feature releases, not deployments.** Code ships continuously, often behind feature toggles, and the release plan forecasts when a feature will be switched on for customers.
- **Forecast by throughput.** Teams using Kanban often forecast with item counts and throughput instead of story points.
- **Coordinate the non-technical work.** Marketing, training, documentation and support readiness still need dates.
Kanban teams can therefore do release planning too, using throughput and cycle time instead of sprints.

### Release planning across multiple teams
When several teams contribute to one release, planning separately creates hidden dependencies and late surprises. Common approaches:
- **Joint release planning:** all teams plan together, map dependencies on a shared board and agree the order of work. This is the core of SAFe [PI Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/), held at the start of each Planning Interval, which SAFe describes as a timebox of 8 to 12 weeks.
- **Agile release trains:** in SAFe, a long-lived team of Agile teams plans and delivers together on a shared cadence. See [Agile release train](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/).
- **Shared backlog or coordination meeting:** Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS) keeps one backlog and one Product Owner for many teams, while a Scrum of Scrums brings team representatives together to manage dependencies.
Whatever the framework, the same rules apply: forecast with ranges, make dependencies visible and update the plan every cycle.

### Common release planning mistakes
- **Treating the forecast as a commitment.** The plan is the best estimate today. If leaders treat it as a contract, teams start padding estimates and the forecast loses value.
- **Using one velocity number.** An average hides variation. Always forecast with a slow and a fast figure.
- **Fixing date and scope together.** Something has to flex. If it is not scope, it will be quality.
- **Forgetting the non-development work.** Testing, security review, documentation, training and app-store approval all take time.
- **Comparing velocity across teams.** Story points are relative to each team, so one team's 30 is not another team's 30. See [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/).
- **Never updating the plan.** A release plan that is not revised every sprint becomes fiction within a month.

### Agile release planning tools and templates
You can run release planning in a spreadsheet or in Agile project management software. Start with whatever your team will keep up to date.
- **Spreadsheet:** our free [Agile release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) lists releases, sprints, features, story points, cumulative points and forecast capacity, and flags whether each release is on track. It also works as a simple PI planning worksheet.
- **Supporting templates:** the [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) for ordering and estimating, and the [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) for each sprint.
- **Software:** tools such as [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) and [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) support versions or releases, velocity reports and burnup charts. Compare options in our [project management tools ranking](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/).
Whatever you use, keep one source of truth for the release plan and update it after every Sprint Review.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is release planning in Agile?**
Release planning in Agile is forecasting which product backlog items are likely to be delivered in upcoming releases, and roughly when, based on the team's measured velocity. The plan is updated every sprint as real progress and scope changes become known.

**Q: Who is responsible for release planning in Agile?**
The Product Owner or product manager owns the release plan and the order of the backlog. The Developers provide estimates and velocity, the Scrum Master facilitates, and stakeholders contribute priorities, dependencies and constraints.

**Q: Is release planning part of Scrum?**
Not formally. The 2020 Scrum Guide has no release planning event, but it mentions forecasting practices such as burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flow. Many Scrum teams do release planning as a complementary practice and review the forecast at each Sprint Review.

**Q: How far ahead should an Agile release plan go?**
Usually one to three releases, or roughly three to six months. Beyond that, uncertainty is too high for item-level forecasts, and an outcome-based [Agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) is more useful.

**Q: How often should a release plan be updated?**
After every sprint, ideally straight after the Sprint Review, using the latest velocity and any scope changes. A brief update takes 15 to 30 minutes once the plan exists.

**Q: What is the difference between release planning and sprint planning?**
Release planning forecasts what will be delivered over several sprints and roughly when. [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) decides the Sprint Goal, the items for the next sprint and how the team will deliver them. Release planning is coarser and longer-range; sprint planning is detailed and short-range.

**Q: What is the difference between a release plan and a product roadmap?**
A product roadmap shows strategic direction: goals, themes and outcomes over months or quarters. A release plan shows delivery detail: which features or stories are expected in which release and sprint, based on estimates and velocity.

**Q: How do you forecast a release date in Agile?**
Divide the remaining story points by the team's slow and fast velocities to get a range of sprints, round up, and convert to dates. For example, 250 points at 27.7 to 32.3 points per sprint needs 8 to 10 sprints.

**Q: What happens in a release planning meeting?**
The team and Product Owner agree the release goal and whether date or scope is fixed, review and estimate the ordered backlog, calculate capacity and velocity range, draw will / might / won't lines, and agree dependencies and risks.

**Q: How long is a release in Agile?**
There is no fixed length. Some teams release several times a day, while others release every few weeks or every few months. A release often spans three to six sprints when releases are planned in batches.

**Q: What is a release burnup chart?**
A release burnup chart shows the total scope of a release and the cumulative work completed, sprint by sprint. Where the two lines meet is the forecast finish, and changes in the scope line show scope growth clearly.

**Q: Is release planning the same as PI planning?**
No. PI Planning is the SAFe event in which all teams on an Agile release train plan the next Planning Interval together. It is a form of multi-team release planning with specific roles, agenda and outputs. See [PI Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/).

**Q: Can you do release planning with Kanban?**
Yes. Kanban teams forecast with throughput (items finished per week) and cycle time instead of story points and sprints, often using Monte Carlo simulation to produce probability-based dates.

**Q: What if the team has no velocity history yet?**
Run one to three sprints before forecasting, or ask the team to plan a sample sprint and use that as a provisional velocity. Present early forecasts as wide ranges and narrow them as real data arrives.
