# Agile Release Train (ART): Roles, Events and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: What is an Agile Release Train? Learn ART roles, events, SAFe 6.0 terms, how to launch one step by step, with a worked example and common mistakes.


## Agile Release Train (ART): Roles, Events and Example
An Agile Release Train (ART) is a long-lived team of Agile teams, typically 50 to 125 people, that plans, commits and delivers together on a shared cadence in the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe). This guide explains how an ART is structured, who does what, which events it runs each Planning Interval and how to launch one step by step. It finishes with an illustrative worked example, a comparison with other team structures and the mistakes that most often derail a train.
- Published 22 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- An Agile Release Train is a long-lived team of Agile teams, generally 50 to 125 people, organised around a flow of value and able to define, build, test and release its solution.
- Since SAFe 6.0 (2023), PI means Planning Interval, the program backlog is the ART backlog and the program board is the ART planning board; older names are still common in tools.
- Four roles lead the train: the Release Train Engineer, Product Management, the System Architect and Business Owners, supported by Product Owners and Scrum Masters/Team Coaches in each team.
- Every PI follows the same rhythm: PI planning, synchronised iterations, ART Sync, System Demos and Inspect and Adapt.
- Launch a train deliberately: choose the value stream, define the ART, set the PI calendar, train everyone, prepare the ART backlog, then run the first PI planning.
- Most ART failures come from organising around departments instead of value, overloading the plan and treating SAFe events as status meetings.

### What is an Agile Release Train?
**An Agile Release Train is a long-lived team of Agile teams, usually 50 to 125 people, that plans together every Planning Interval and delivers a shared solution on a common cadence. It contains every skill needed to define, build, test and release that solution, and it is organised around a flow of customer value rather than around departments.**
The ART is the central delivery structure of the [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) and appears in every SAFe configuration. Scaled Agile describes it as "a long-lived team of Agile teams" that builds, delivers and often runs one or more solutions.
You need a train when a solution is too large for one team. A single [Agile team](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-an-agile-team/) of ten or fewer people can manage its own backlog. Once eight teams work on the same product, someone has to align their priorities, dates, dependencies and integration. The ART gives them one backlog, one calendar, one set of events and shared leadership roles, while each team still works internally with SAFe Scrum or SAFe Kanban.

### SAFe 6.0 terminology: Planning Interval and other changes
SAFe 6.0, released by Scaled Agile in 2023, renamed several terms you will meet on any train. Scaled Agile has added articles and competencies since then, but 6.0 remains the current numbered version. Many organisations, job adverts and tools still use the older names, so it helps to know both.
| Older term | Current SAFe 6.0 term | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Program Increment (PI) | Planning Interval (PI) | The fixed timebox, usually 8 to 12 weeks, in which the train plans and delivers |
| Program backlog | ART backlog | The prioritised list of features and enablers for the whole train |
| Program Kanban | ART Kanban | The board that shows how features flow from idea to release |
| Program board | ART planning board | The visual plan of features, milestones and cross-team dependencies by iteration |
| Scrum of Scrums | Coach Sync (part of ART Sync) | The regular cross-team coordination meeting of Scrum Masters/Team Coaches |
| Scrum Master | Scrum Master/Team Coach | The team-level coach and facilitator |
The abbreviation PI did not change, so the event is still called [PI planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/). This guide uses the current names.

### Why it is called a release train
The name comes from a railway timetable. A train leaves at fixed, published times: if your freight is ready, it goes on this train; if not, it waits for the next one, and the timetable does not move for late cargo. On an ART, the dates of PI planning, iterations and demos are fixed in advance, and features that are not ready move to the next PI instead of delaying everyone.
SAFe sums this up as **develop on cadence, release on demand**. Planning, integration and demos follow the shared calendar, but a team can release a feature whenever it is ready and the business wants it, using [continuous delivery](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/continuous-delivery/) practices. The train is about synchronised planning, not about holding work back until the end of a PI.

### Characteristics of an Agile Release Train
Use the table to check whether a group of teams is really working as a train. The warning signs show what you typically see when a characteristic is missing.
| Characteristic | What it means | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Team of Agile teams | Usually 5 to 12 teams, 50 to 125 people in total | Over 150 people and nobody knows who is on the train |
| Long-lived | Work is brought to the train; teams stay together | Teams are re-formed for every new project |
| Organised around value | Built around a value stream, product or customer journey | Teams map to departments such as front end, back end and testing |
| Cross-functional | Can define, build, test and release without hand-offs | Every feature waits for an outside testing or release group |
| Shared cadence | All teams use the same iteration and PI dates | Teams run sprints of different lengths on different days |
| One ART backlog and quality bar | One prioritised feature list and a shared [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) | Features are "done" in each team but fail when combined |

### ART roles and responsibilities
An ART has a small set of train-level roles plus the usual roles inside each team.
| Role | Level | Main responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Release Train Engineer (RTE) | Train | Servant leader and coach of the ART; facilitates ART events, manages risks and impediments, improves flow |
| Product Management | Train | Owns the ART backlog and vision; defines and prioritises features |
| System Architect | Train | Owns the technical vision and architectural runway; guides enablers |
| Business Owners | Train | Senior stakeholders accountable for business outcomes; assign business value to PI objectives |
| Product Owner | Team | Owns the team backlog; turns features into stories; accepts work |
| Scrum Master/Team Coach | Team | Coaches the team, facilitates team events, removes impediments |
| Agile team members | Team | Plan, build, test and deliver stories each iteration |
| System Team and Shared Services | Supporting | Integration and deployment infrastructure; specialists who serve several teams |

#### Release Train Engineer
The RTE is often called the chief Scrum Master of the train. They prepare and facilitate PI planning, ART Sync, System Demos and Inspect and Adapt, track risks and dependencies, escalate impediments and coach leaders. They do not assign work or own scope: Product Management owns the what, and teams own the how. Many RTEs come from project or programme management, but the job is facilitation and coaching rather than command and control.

#### Product Management and the System Architect
Product Management is the content authority. It turns strategy into a vision and roadmap, writes and prioritises features, and works with the [Product Owners](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) who refine those features into team-level [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/). The System Architect defines the technical direction, plans enablers and helps teams resolve technical dependencies, keeping the solution coherent without becoming a design approval gate. On large trains both are often small teams rather than single people.

#### Business Owners
Business Owners are typically a handful of senior people accountable for the value the train delivers, often a business sponsor, a technology leader and someone from operations. They present context at PI planning, score each team's PI objectives for business value, attend System Demos and help resolve risks. Their attendance is one of the clearest signs of whether leadership takes the train seriously.

### How teams are organised on an ART
Deciding which teams sit on the train, and what each owns, is the most important design choice you will make. SAFe recommends organising around value and draws on the four team types from *Team Topologies* by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais.
| Team type | Purpose | Example on an ART |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stream-aligned | Delivers value directly to customers along a flow of work | A team that owns the online quote journey end to end |
| Complicated subsystem | Owns a part of the system that needs deep specialist knowledge | A pricing or risk-calculation engine team |
| Platform | Provides internal services that make other teams faster | A team running shared APIs, data pipelines or test environments |
| Enabling | Helps other teams build new skills for a period | A small group coaching teams on test automation |
Most teams on a healthy train should be stream-aligned. The other types exist to reduce the load on stream-aligned teams, not to become queues that every feature must pass through.

#### Choosing the boundary of the train
1. Map the development value stream: the steps and people needed to turn a customer request into a released solution. Our [value stream mapping guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) shows how.
2. Group people so that most features can be delivered inside one train, ideally inside one team.
3. Check the size. Well above 125 people, split along a natural seam such as customer segment or product line; well below 50, consider joining a neighbouring train or a lighter approach.
4. Name the remaining cross-train dependencies and agree how they will be handled, for example through shared services.
For more team shapes, see [Agile team structures](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-team-structures/).

### The ART calendar: iterations and the Planning Interval
A Planning Interval is a fixed timebox, typically 8 to 12 weeks. With two-week iterations, a common pattern is four development iterations followed by one Innovation and Planning (IP) iteration. Every team on the train uses the same dates.
| Weeks | Iteration | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before week 1 | Previous IP iteration | PI planning for this PI |
| 1–2 | Iteration 1 | Teams start the PI plan; System Demo at the end |
| 3–4 | Iteration 2 | Delivery continues; dependencies tracked at ART Sync |
| 5–6 | Iteration 3 | Mid-PI check against objectives; releases as features are ready |
| 7–8 | Iteration 4 | Final development iteration and System Demo |
| 9–10 | IP iteration | Innovation, learning, final integration, Inspect and Adapt, next PI planning |
The IP iteration is also the PI's main buffer. Fill it with planned features and you lose both the time for improvement and the margin for estimates that prove wrong.
Features come from the **ART backlog**, which Product Management orders using Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF): cost of delay divided by job size. The **ART Kanban** shows each feature's flow from funnel through analysis, implementation and release; [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) on it stop the train starting more than it can finish.

### ART events
SAFe defines train-level events that run on the PI cadence. Team-level events (iteration planning, stand-ups, review and retrospective) continue inside each team. Durations are typical; adjust them to your train.
| Event | When | Who attends | Purpose and output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PI planning | Once per PI, usually two days | Everyone on the train plus Business Owners | Team PI objectives with business value, ART planning board, ROAMed risks, confidence vote |
| ART Sync | Weekly or twice weekly, about 30 to 60 minutes | RTE, Product Management, Product Owners, Scrum Masters/Team Coaches | Progress against objectives, dependencies, impediments, scope adjustments |
| System Demo | End of every iteration | Teams, Product Management, Business Owners, stakeholders | Integrated increment shown working; feedback |
| Inspect and Adapt | End of every PI, in the IP iteration | Whole train plus Business Owners | PI system demo, measures review and a problem-solving workshop |

#### ART Sync: Coach Sync and PO Sync
ART Sync combines two conversations. The **Coach Sync** (formerly Scrum of Scrums) brings the RTE and Scrum Masters/Team Coaches together on progress, dependencies and impediments. The **PO Sync** brings Product Management and Product Owners together on scope and priorities. Small trains often hold one combined meeting; larger trains often run them on different days. Our [Scrum of Scrums guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/) covers the facilitation technique.

#### System Demo and Inspect and Adapt
The System Demo shows the integrated work of all teams, not a series of separate team demos. If teams can only show their own components on their own machines, the train is not yet integrating, and that is the first thing to fix.
Inspect and Adapt is the train's retrospective, scaled up. It has three parts: a PI System Demo of everything delivered, a quantitative and qualitative review of measures such as predictability, and a structured problem-solving workshop in which the train finds root causes of its biggest problems and adds improvement items to the ART backlog.
See our [PI planning guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/) for the full two-day agenda, breakouts and confidence vote.

### How to launch an Agile Release Train step by step
Scaled Agile's implementation roadmap places the ART launch after leaders have been trained and value streams identified. Its preparation activities include defining the ART, setting the launch date and PI calendar, training leaders and roles, forming teams, assessing readiness and preparing the ART backlog. The steps below turn them into a practical sequence.
1. **Choose the value stream.** Pick one with a clear business problem, strong leadership support and people mostly in one organisation. Early wins matter more than a perfect first choice.
2. **Define the ART.** Agree its mission, solution, boundary and rough size. A one-page canvas covering vision, customers, Business Owners and key roles is enough.
3. **Fill the train-level roles.** Appoint the RTE, Product Management, System Architect and Business Owners first; they design the rest of the launch.
4. **Design and form the teams.** Use the value stream map and team types. A [skills matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) shows whether each team has the skills it needs.
5. **Set the launch date and PI calendar.** Publish the dates of the first PI planning and the next three or four PIs, including iterations, System Demos and Inspect and Adapt.
6. **Train everyone.** Leaders first, then each role, then the teams. Scaled Agile recommends training all teams together in one room rather than team by team.
7. **Prepare the ART backlog.** Write and prioritise the top features and enablers for the first PI, with acceptance criteria and rough sizes.
8. **Check readiness.** Roles filled and Business Owners committed, vision and backlog ready, room, tools and remote set-up in place.
9. **Run the first PI planning.** Expect it to feel messy. The goal is a credible plan and shared understanding of dependencies, not perfection.
10. **Coach the first PI closely.** Run ART Sync, System Demos and the first Inspect and Adapt with experienced coaches, and act on what you learn.
Tip
Launch one train well before launching a second. The first ART becomes the reference for everyone else, and its problems are much easier to fix while it is the only one.

### Worked example: a 60-person onboarding ART
This example is **illustrative**: the organisation, teams and figures are invented. A mid-sized insurer wants to cut the time it takes a new customer to buy home insurance online. The work is spread across web, mobile, IT integration, testing and pricing departments, and every release needs four sign-offs.

#### Team design
The insurer maps the onboarding value stream and forms one train of seven teams plus train-level roles.
| Team | Type | People | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quote and Apply | Stream-aligned | 9 | Online quote and application journey |
| Identity and Verification | Stream-aligned | 8 | ID checks, fraud screening, customer records |
| Policy Documents | Stream-aligned | 8 | Policy schedule, emails and document portal |
| Onboarding Mobile | Stream-aligned | 9 | Mobile app onboarding journey |
| Pricing Engine | Complicated subsystem | 7 | Premium calculation and rating rules |
| Onboarding Platform | Platform | 8 | Shared APIs, test data and environments |
| System Team | Supporting | 6 | Build pipeline, integration and end-to-end testing |
| Train-level roles | Train | 5 | RTE, two product managers, System Architect, UX lead |
That gives 60 people. Three Business Owners (the head of personal lines, the IT director and the operations director) are accountable for outcomes but are not counted as train members.

#### PI calendar and capacity
The train uses two-week iterations and a ten-week PI: four development iterations and one IP iteration, with dates published four PIs ahead. Each team estimates its capacity from recent velocity and planned leave, then plans committed work to roughly 80% of it, leaving room for support and surprises. (Planning to about 80% is our own rule of thumb, not a SAFe requirement.)

#### PI objectives and the predictability measure
At PI planning, the Quote and Apply team drafts four objectives, and the Business Owners score each from 1 to 10 for business value. At Inspect and Adapt they score what was actually achieved.
| PI objective | Type | Planned value | Actual value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Launch the new online home quote to 10% of web traffic | Committed | 10 | 9 (reached 5% after a late pricing defect) |
| Cut the application form from 42 to 25 fields | Committed | 7 | 7 |
| Use the new ID verification API (depends on Identity and Verification) | Committed | 8 | 5 (live for new customers only) |
| Pilot save-and-resume for long applications | Uncommitted | 5 | 3 (staff pilot only) |
Planned value counts committed objectives only: 10 + 7 + 8 = **25**. Actual value includes anything achieved, uncommitted objectives too: 9 + 7 + 5 + 3 = **24**. Predictability is 24 / 25 = **96%**. SAFe guidance treats roughly 80% to 100% as predictable. If the seven teams range from 72% to 98% and average 87%, the train is predictable overall, but the lowest team's plan becomes a topic for the problem-solving workshop.
At Inspect and Adapt, the train traces the pricing defect to test data that did not match production rating rules. The improvement item for the next PI is an enabler for the Onboarding Platform team: refresh rating test data automatically every night. That is the cycle working as intended: plan, deliver, measure honestly, fix the system.
You can record a plan like this in our free [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) and track risks in a [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).

### Agile Release Train vs Scrum team, Solution Train and project team
|  | Scrum team | Agile Release Train | Solution Train | Project team |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Size | 10 or fewer people | 50 to 125 people in several teams | Several ARTs and suppliers | Any size |
| Lifespan | Long-lived | Long-lived | Long-lived | Temporary |
| Planning horizon | One sprint | One PI (8 to 12 weeks) | One PI, aligned across ARTs | Whole project |
| Coordinator | Scrum Master | Release Train Engineer | Solution Train Engineer | Project manager |
| Used when | One team can build the product | A solution needs several teams | A solution needs several trains | Work is a one-off with a defined end |
A Solution Train belongs to SAFe's Large Solution configuration, for very large systems that need several ARTs and suppliers to coordinate. For decisions above the train, see [Agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/).

### Measuring ART performance
SAFe 6.0 groups measures into three domains: **outcomes** (is the train delivering the intended business results?), **flow** (how efficiently does value move?) and **competency** (how well are Lean-Agile practices applied?). A new train should start with a handful of measures reviewed at every Inspect and Adapt.
| Measure | What it tells you | How to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predictability | How reliably the train meets its PI objectives | Aim for a stable range rather than 100% |
| Flow velocity | Features completed per PI | Watch the trend, not single PIs |
| Flow time | Time from starting a feature to releasing it | Shorten it by cutting WIP and hand-offs |
| Flow distribution | Mix of features, enablers, defects and risk work | Protect time for enablers and technical debt |
| Business outcomes | Changes in customer or business metrics | Link each feature's benefit hypothesis to a measure |
Avoid comparing teams' velocities or ranking teams by predictability; both encourage gaming. Our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) explains how to calculate and present these measures.

### Common Agile Release Train mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organising the train by department or component | Every feature crosses several teams, creating queues | Re-form around the value stream; make most teams stream-aligned |
| Overloading the PI plan | No buffer; uncommitted objectives disappear; morale drops | Plan below full capacity and protect the IP iteration |
| Renaming the old programme office | Same reporting and approvals with new labels | Give teams real decision rights; the RTE coaches rather than controls |
| Business Owners who never attend | Teams lose context; value scores become guesses | Make PI planning and System Demos fixed diary commitments |
| Turning ART Sync into a status report | Long meetings with little coordination | Focus on dependencies, risks and decisions |
| Constantly reshuffling teams | Velocity and trust reset every PI | Keep teams stable and bring work to them |
If you see three or more of these, the train has probably adopted SAFe's events without changing how decisions, funding and teams are organised. Review the train's design before tuning its meetings.

### Tools and templates for running an ART
You can run a first PI with a wall, sticky notes and spreadsheets. As the train grows, you will want a tool that links features to team stories, shows cross-team dependencies and rolls progress up into dashboards.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is a common choice for software-heavy trains. Every plan has a timeline for epics, and Premium adds Plans for cross-team roadmaps and capacity.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, suits trains that mix software with marketing, operations or other business work, thanks to custom workflows, cross-project dashboards and portfolio views. Compare them in our [Wrike vs Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/wrike-vs-jira/).
- Before a tool is configured, a [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) can hold the ART backlog for the first PI.
See [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) for how release forecasts work across teams.

### Criticisms of ARTs and lighter alternatives
SAFe has critics. Common concerns are that it is heavy and prescriptive, that it lets organisations keep top-down control under Agile labels, and that a synchronised cadence limits team self-organisation. Supporters answer that the ART gives large organisations a practical way to align many teams, and that most problems come from poor implementation.
- Two or three teams on one product rarely need a train; a Scrum of Scrums and a shared backlog are often enough.
- [Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/) keeps one Product Owner and one Product Backlog for up to eight teams, with fewer added roles.
- An ART tends to suit organisations with many teams, real integration complexity, governance needs and leaders who want a well-documented model.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an Agile Release Train in simple terms?**
A large, permanent team made up of several smaller Agile teams, usually 50 to 125 people in total, working on the same product or service. The teams plan together every 8 to 12 weeks, share one calendar and combine their work regularly into one working solution.

**Q: Why is it called an Agile Release Train?**
Like a train timetable, the ART runs on fixed, predictable dates. Features that are ready catch the train; those that are not wait for the next one, and the timetable does not move for late work.

**Q: How many people and teams are in an Agile Release Train?**
Scaled Agile says an ART is generally 50 to 125 people. With teams of ten or fewer, that is typically about 5 to 12 teams plus the train-level roles.

**Q: What does PI stand for in SAFe?**
Since SAFe 6.0 (2023), PI stands for Planning Interval, a fixed timebox of usually 8 to 12 weeks. Older material and many tools still say Program Increment. The abbreviation, and the name PI planning, did not change.

**Q: What does a Release Train Engineer do?**
The RTE is the servant leader and coach of the train. They facilitate PI planning, ART Sync, System Demos and Inspect and Adapt, manage risks and dependencies, escalate impediments and help the train improve its flow.

**Q: Is a Release Train Engineer the same as a project manager?**
No. A project manager often owns scope, schedule and budget for a temporary project. An RTE facilitates a long-lived train, while Product Management owns scope and teams plan their own work. The role relies on coaching rather than direction.

**Q: What is the difference between an Agile Release Train and a Scrum team?**
A Scrum team is one team of ten or fewer people planning one sprint at a time. An ART is several such teams sharing a backlog and planning a whole Planning Interval together. Each team on an ART can still use Scrum or Kanban internally.

**Q: What is ART Sync?**
The regular coordination event during a PI. It combines the Coach Sync, where the RTE and Scrum Masters/Team Coaches review progress, dependencies and impediments, and the PO Sync, where Product Management and Product Owners review scope and priorities.

**Q: Does an Agile Release Train release only at the end of a PI?**
No. SAFe's principle is develop on cadence, release on demand. Planning, demos and integration follow the PI cadence, but teams can release whenever a feature is ready and the business wants it.

**Q: How long does it take to launch an Agile Release Train?**
It depends on the organisation. Before the first PI planning you need to identify the value stream, define the train, fill roles, train everyone and prepare the backlog. Expect the first two or three PIs to be a learning period.

**Q: Can an Agile Release Train be fully remote?**
Yes. Many trains run PI planning, ART Sync and System Demos online with a shared digital planning board. Remote trains need more preparation, firm facilitation and schedules that respect time zones.

**Q: Do you need SAFe certification to work on an ART?**
No certification is required to be a team member. Scaled Agile offers role-based certifications such as SAFe Release Train Engineer and SAFe Scrum Master, and organisations launching a train usually train people in their roles. See our guide to [Agile certifications](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/).

# Agile Roadmap: Formats, Example and How to Build One

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: An Agile roadmap shows the outcomes a team is working towards over time. Learn the main formats, see a worked example and follow 9 steps to build your own.


## Agile Roadmap: Formats, Example and How to Build One
An Agile roadmap is a high-level, regularly updated plan that shows the goals and outcomes a product or team is working towards, ordered by priority over broad time horizons rather than fixed dates. This guide explains how it differs from a traditional plan and a release plan, compares the main formats, walks through a worked example and gives you nine steps to build and maintain your own.
- Published 16 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- An Agile roadmap communicates direction and priorities; the backlog and release plan hold the detail.
- Good roadmaps are built around outcomes and problems to solve, not lists of features with dates.
- Now-Next-Later, outcome-based and theme-based timelines are the most common formats.
- Detail and confidence should fall the further out an item sits; show genuine deadlines, avoid invented ones.
- Roadmap items become epics, epics become user stories, and stories are planned into releases and sprints.
- Review the roadmap on a fixed cadence, usually monthly or quarterly, and after any major learning.

### What is an Agile roadmap?
An **Agile roadmap** is a short, visual plan that shows where a product or team is heading and why. It lists the goals, problems or outcomes the team will work on, in priority order, across broad time horizons such as now, next and later or the coming quarters. It is reviewed and updated as the team learns.
The term usually means an **Agile product roadmap**, owned by a Product Owner or product manager. The same idea is used for Agile project roadmaps in non-software teams, and for **portfolio roadmaps** that combine several products. What makes any of them Agile is the approach: outcomes before outputs, honest uncertainty, and frequent revision.

#### Why use an Agile roadmap?
- **Alignment:** everyone can see how today's work connects to strategy.
- **Better conversations:** stakeholders discuss goals and trade-offs instead of arguing over feature dates.
- **Focus:** a short list of priorities makes it easier to say no to everything else.
- **Honest expectations:** confidence levels show what is committed and what is still being explored.
- **Context for the team:** developers understand why items matter, which leads to better solutions.
Product Owners and [Agile product managers](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-product-manager/) typically spend much of their stakeholder time on these conversations.

#### Is a roadmap part of Scrum?
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide defines three artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment) and does not mention a roadmap. It does introduce the **Product Goal**, a long-term objective that the Product Backlog works towards, and makes the Product Owner accountable for the Product Backlog. Many Scrum Teams use a roadmap to show the sequence of goals between today and that Product Goal. See our guides to the [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) and the [product backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/).

### Agile roadmap vs traditional roadmap
| Aspect | Traditional roadmap or plan | Agile roadmap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | Features, tasks and deliverables | Goals, outcomes and problems to solve |
| Time | Exact dates for everything | Broad horizons; dates only where genuinely fixed |
| Detail | Even across the whole plan | Detailed near term, broad further out |
| Change | Formally re-baselined | Expected and reviewed on a cadence |
| Measure of success | Delivered on the planned date | Outcome achieved, such as higher retention |
| Audience | Mainly the delivery team and sponsor | Leadership, stakeholders, customers and the team |
| Link to delivery | Usually a separate Gantt chart | Items flow into epics, the backlog and releases |
A traditional roadmap is not wrong: it suits projects with fixed scope, contracts and dependencies, which our guide to the [project roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-roadmap/) covers. Many hybrid teams combine both, using fixed milestones for external commitments and an Agile roadmap for everything else. Our guide to the [role of the project plan in Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/role-of-the-project-plan-in-agile/) explains how the two fit together.

### Where the roadmap fits: from vision to sprint
Agile planning works in levels. Each one adds detail over a shorter horizon, and the roadmap sits in the middle, linking strategy to the backlog.
| Level | Question it answers | Typical horizon | Usual owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Product vision | Why does the product exist and who is it for? | Several years | Product leadership |
| Strategy and goals | Which goals, such as OKRs, matter most now? | One year | Product leadership with the Product Owner |
| Agile roadmap | Which outcomes will we pursue, in what order? | Six to eighteen months | Product Owner or product manager |
| Release plan | What will ship in the next few releases? | One to six months | Product Owner with the team |
| Product backlog | What exactly is next, in what order? | Ongoing | Product Owner |
| Sprint backlog | What will we do this sprint? | One to four weeks | Developers |
The roadmap answers "where and why"; the [release plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) answers "what and roughly when"; the backlog and [sprint planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) answer "exactly what next". Keeping these apart is what stops the roadmap turning into a Gantt chart.

### What to include in an Agile roadmap
- **Vision or Product Goal** at the top, so every item can be traced back to it.
- **Goals or outcomes**, each with a measure, such as "increase trial-to-paid conversion".
- **Initiatives or themes**: the problems or opportunities the team will tackle to reach each goal.
- **Time horizons**: now, next and later, or quarters, with detail falling as you go further out.
- **Status or confidence** for each item, so readers know what is committed and what is exploratory.
- **Key dependencies and genuine deadlines**, such as regulatory dates or a trade show.
- **Owner and last-updated date**, so people know whom to ask and whether it is current.

#### What to leave out
Individual user stories, task assignments, story point estimates and exact dates for work more than a release or two away. They belong in the backlog and release plan. A roadmap that tries to hold them becomes out of date within weeks and stops being trusted.

### Types of Agile roadmap
Choose the format that fits your audience and the amount of certainty you have. Many teams keep one underlying roadmap and show it in two formats.
| Format | How it is laid out | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Now-Next-Later | Three columns by priority and certainty, no dates | Products with high uncertainty; teams moving away from date-driven plans | Stakeholders who need dates may push back |
| Outcome-based (goal-oriented) | Each item is a measurable goal with initiatives beneath it | Empowered teams and leadership using OKRs | Goals that are too vague to measure |
| Theme-based timeline | Quarters or months with broad themes | Organisations that need some time structure for budgeting and sales | Themes quietly turning into fixed feature commitments |
| Feature or epic timeline | Epics on a timeline, often in a tool | Near-term delivery coordination for one or a few teams | False precision further out |
| Portfolio roadmap | Several products or teams in swimlanes | Leaders coordinating across teams | Too much detail for an executive audience |

#### Now-Next-Later roadmap
Popularised by Janna Bastow, co-founder of ProdPad, the Now-Next-Later roadmap replaces dates with three columns. **Now** holds work in progress or about to start and is the most detailed. **Next** holds what comes after that, shaped but not yet refined. **Later** holds problems and opportunities you intend to explore, described broadly. Items move left as they become clearer and closer, and can be removed if priorities change.

#### Outcome-based and GO roadmaps
An outcome-based roadmap lists goals such as "reduce time to first value for new customers" instead of features. Teams are then free to find the best solution. A well-known version is Roman Pichler's goal-oriented (GO) product roadmap, which has five elements for each period: date, name, goal, features and metrics. Our [OKR template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/okr-template/) pairs well with this format.

#### Theme-based timeline
A theme-based timeline keeps quarters or months along the top but places broad themes, such as "self-service onboarding", rather than features in each period. It gives finance and sales a sense of timing while leaving the detail open.

### How to create an Agile roadmap in 9 steps
1. **Start from the vision and strategy.** Write the product vision and the Product Goal in a sentence each. If leadership has set OKRs or strategic goals, list them; every roadmap item must support one.
2. **Gather inputs.** Collect customer feedback, analytics, sales and support themes, technical debt, regulatory changes and stakeholder requests. Group them into problems rather than feature requests.
3. **Choose three to five goals for the coming period.** Express each as an outcome with a measure and a target, such as "raise 30-day retention from 40% to 50%".
4. **Identify initiatives for each goal.** For each goal, list the problems or bets that could move the measure. Keep them broad; these are candidate [epics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/), not stories.
5. **Prioritise.** Score the initiatives with a simple method such as RICE or cost of delay (see below), and agree the order with key stakeholders.
6. **Place items on time horizons.** Put the top-priority, best-understood items in Now, the next ones in Next and the rest in Later. Check that Now fits the team's real capacity.
7. **Mark dependencies, deadlines and confidence.** Note any genuine external dates, dependencies on other teams and a confidence level for each item.
8. **Review with the team and stakeholders.** Walk through the draft with developers for feasibility and with stakeholders for value. Record what you decided not to do and why.
9. **Publish, connect and maintain.** Share it in one place, link each Now item to its epic in the backlog, and set a review date.
Tip
Keep the first version small enough to fit on one screen or slide. If it does not fit, you are either including too much detail or trying to do too much at once.

#### Running a roadmap workshop
Steps 3 to 8 are easiest in a single half-day workshop with the Product Owner, two or three developers and the main stakeholders. An illustrative agenda:
| Time | Activity | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 min | Recap vision, strategy and last period's results | Shared context and lessons |
| 45 min | Review grouped inputs and agree three to five goals with measures | Draft goals |
| 45 min | Brainstorm initiatives per goal, then cluster and name them | Candidate initiatives |
| 45 min | Score initiatives and place them on Now, Next and Later | Draft roadmap |
| 30 min | Check capacity, dependencies and deadlines; agree what is out | Reviewed roadmap and a "not doing" list |
| 15 min | Agree owners, how it will be shared and the next review date | Actions and review date |

### Agile roadmap example
This example is illustrative. A team of eight builds a project management app for small agencies. The vision is "help small agencies deliver client work on time without spreadsheets". Leadership's goals for the year are growth in paying customers and lower churn.
| Horizon | Goal and measure | Initiatives | Confidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Now (this quarter) | Improve trial-to-paid conversion from 8% to 11% | Guided onboarding with sample project; import from spreadsheets | High: discovery done, epics refined |
| Now (this quarter) | Reduce support tickets about invoicing by 30% | Redesign invoice set-up; in-app help | High |
| Next (next 3-6 months) | Raise 90-day retention for teams of 5+ users | Client portal for approvals; workload view | Medium: problem validated, solutions open |
| Next (next 3-6 months) | Enter the accounting integration market | Integration with one major accounting tool | Medium: depends on partner API access |
| Later (6-12 months) | Grow average account size | Advanced reporting; resource planning | Low: exploring |
| Later (6-12 months) | Meet enterprise security requirements | Single sign-on; audit log | Low: waiting on customer research |
Notice what the roadmap does not show: individual stories, estimates or sprint dates. It also lists a dependency (partner API access) and is honest that Later items may change.

#### From roadmap item to sprint
Here is how the first Now item flows into delivery:
1. **Roadmap item:** improve trial-to-paid conversion with guided onboarding.
2. **Epic:** "Guided onboarding", with a hypothesis: if new users create a sample project in their first session, more will convert.
3. **User stories:** for example, "As a new trial user, I want a sample client project created for me so I can see how the app works." See our guide to [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/).
4. **Release plan:** the team's forecast shows the minimum version of the epic fitting in the next two sprints, with spreadsheet import following in the release after.
5. **Sprints:** stories are pulled into sprint planning in priority order.
6. **Measure:** after release, the Product Owner checks conversion and updates the roadmap.

#### Example for a non-software team
Agile roadmaps work outside software too. An illustrative Now-Next-Later roadmap for an in-house marketing team:
| Horizon | Goal and measure | Initiatives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Now | Increase qualified leads from the website by 20% | Rewrite three landing pages; launch a comparison guide |
| Next | Shorten the sales cycle for mid-sized clients | Case study series; webinar programme |
| Later | Build awareness in a new region | Local partner events; translated content |
Our guide to [epics vs stories vs tasks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/) explains each level of this breakdown. You can build the same structure in our [product roadmap template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-roadmap-template/) and [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/).

### How to prioritise roadmap items
Prioritisation decides what goes in Now. Use a simple, transparent method so stakeholders can see why one item beats another.
| Method | How it works | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RICE | Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort | Product teams comparing many ideas with some data |
| Cost of delay / WSJF | Value lost by waiting, divided by job size | Portfolios and scaled Agile; time-sensitive work |
| Value vs effort | Plot items on a two-by-two grid | Quick workshops with stakeholders |
| MoSCoW | Must, Should, Could, Won't have | Fixed-date releases with negotiable scope |

#### Worked example: RICE scores
Continuing the illustrative example, the team scores four candidate initiatives. Reach is users affected per quarter, impact is on a scale from 0.25 (minimal) to 3 (massive), confidence is a percentage and effort is in person-months.
| Initiative | Reach | Impact | Confidence | Effort | RICE score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Guided onboarding | 2,000 | 2 | 80% | 2 | 1,600 |
| Spreadsheet import | 1,200 | 1 | 80% | 1 | 960 |
| Client portal | 600 | 2 | 50% | 3 | 200 |
| Advanced reporting | 300 | 1 | 50% | 4 | 38 |
Guided onboarding and spreadsheet import go to Now; the client portal goes to Next while the team raises confidence through discovery. Treat scores as an input to a conversation, not a final answer: strategic or regulatory work may still jump the queue.

### Dates, deadlines and confidence
Stakeholders will ask "when?". An Agile roadmap can answer honestly without committing to dates the team cannot know.
| Horizon | What to show | Confidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Now | A target release or month, based on the team's forecast | High |
| Next | A quarter or a range, such as "Q2-Q3" | Medium |
| Later | No date, or a half-year at most | Low |
- **Show genuine deadlines.** Regulatory dates, contract milestones and events are real constraints. Mark them clearly as [milestones](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/).
- **Forecast from data.** Base near-term dates on the team's actual [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) or velocity, and give a range.
- **Separate forecasts from commitments.** Label which items are committed and which are forecasts; only a few should be commitments.
- **Update dates openly.** When a forecast moves, say so and explain why. Hidden slips destroy trust faster than visible ones.

#### Worked example: forecasting a Now item
Continuing the illustrative example, the guided onboarding epic has been split into 24 stories. Over the last eight two-week sprints, the team finished between 6 and 9 stories per sprint, with roughly half of its capacity going to this epic and half to other work. That gives 3 to 4.5 onboarding stories per sprint, so the epic needs about 6 to 8 sprints, or 12 to 16 weeks. The roadmap therefore shows "Now: target end of Q2, high confidence for the core flow", and the Product Owner agrees with stakeholders which stories form the minimum version if the lower end of the range applies. Our guide to [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) covers this kind of forecast in more detail.

### Presenting the roadmap to different audiences
One roadmap, several views. Keep a single source and tailor the level of detail.
| Audience | What they need | Suggested view |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Executives | Link to strategy, outcomes, investment and risk | Outcome-based, one page, by quarter or Now-Next-Later |
| Sales and customer success | What is coming and roughly when, what to avoid promising | Theme-based, with clear confidence labels |
| Delivery team | Priorities, context and what comes next | Now-Next-Later linked to epics in the backlog |
| Customers or the public | Direction and problems being solved | High-level themes, usually without dates |
| Other teams | Dependencies and timing that affect them | Epic timeline with dependencies marked |
Our guide to [project stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) covers how to map audiences and their interests.

### Keeping the roadmap up to date
An Agile roadmap is only useful if it is current. Agree a cadence and stick to it:
- **Every sprint or fortnight:** the Product Owner checks Now items against progress and moves anything finished.
- **Monthly:** review Next and Later with key stakeholders; add, remove or reorder items.
- **Quarterly:** revisit goals and measures, usually alongside quarterly business or OKR planning.
Also review it whenever something important changes: a major customer insight, a competitor move, a failed experiment or a change in budget. Frequent small updates are a sign of learning; a roadmap that has not changed in six months is a warning sign.

### Agile roadmaps across multiple teams
When several teams work on one product or portfolio, each team keeps its own roadmap and a combined view shows how they connect.
- **Shared goals:** all team roadmaps trace back to the same product or portfolio goals.
- **Dependency view:** a portfolio roadmap shows where one team's Next depends on another team's Now.
- **Joint planning:** teams align roadmaps at a regular event; in SAFe this is [PI planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/).
- **One tool:** linking team epics in one tool lets the combined roadmap update itself.
Portfolio-level roadmaps are usually maintained by portfolio leaders with support from an [Agile PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-pmo/). See our guide to [Agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/) for how priorities and funding are set at that level.

### Agile roadmap checklist
Before you share a roadmap, check that it passes these tests:
- Every item traces back to the vision or a stated goal.
- Each goal has a measure and a target, not just a name.
- Now fits the team's real capacity, including support and maintenance work.
- Detail and confidence fall from Now to Later.
- Genuine deadlines and cross-team dependencies are marked.
- Each Now item links to an epic in the backlog.
- It fits on one page or screen for its main audience.
- It shows an owner, a last-updated date and the next review date.

### Common Agile roadmap mistakes
| Mistake | What it looks like | How to fix it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feature list with dates | Every item is a feature with a delivery date | Rewrite items as outcomes; keep dates for genuine deadlines |
| Too much detail | Stories and tasks on the roadmap | Move detail into the backlog; keep the roadmap to one page |
| Never updated | The roadmap still shows last quarter's plan | Set a monthly review and show a last-updated date |
| Overloaded Now column | Ten things "in progress" for one team | Check Now against capacity and limit work in progress |
| Built alone | The Product Owner presents a finished roadmap | Involve developers and stakeholders before publishing |
| No link to delivery | Roadmap and backlog drift apart | Link every Now item to an epic in the backlog |
| Treated as a promise | Sales commits Later items to customers | Label confidence and agree what can be shared externally |

### Agile roadmap tools and templates
A slide or whiteboard is enough to start. Once the roadmap needs to stay linked to the backlog, a work management tool saves a lot of manual updating. Options from our reviews:
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** includes a timeline view on every plan that shows epics and their child work, which works well as a single-team Agile roadmap. Premium and Enterprise add Plans (previously Advanced Roadmaps) for cross-team roadmaps, dependencies and capacity.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool (9.4/10), combines Gantt and board views, request intake and cross-project dashboards, which suits roadmaps that span product, marketing and operations teams.
- **[Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/)** links projects to goals and portfolios on its Advanced plan, a natural fit for outcome-based roadmaps tied to OKRs.
- **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)** sells monday dev, a separate product for sprints, roadmaps and bug tracking, alongside its work management boards.
- **ClickUp** and **Notion** are flexible options for smaller product teams: ClickUp combines sprints, goals and timelines, and Notion's timeline view is often used as a lightweight product roadmap.
Compare them on our [tool comparison page](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an Agile roadmap?**
A high-level, regularly updated plan showing the goals and outcomes a product or team is working towards, in priority order over broad time horizons rather than exact dates.

**Q: What should an Agile roadmap include?**
The vision or Product Goal, three to five measurable goals, the initiatives that support them, time horizons, confidence levels, genuine deadlines and dependencies, and an owner and last-updated date.

**Q: What is a Now-Next-Later roadmap?**
A format with three columns: what the team is working on now, what comes next and what it plans to explore later. It replaces dates with priority and is honest about uncertainty further out.

**Q: What is an outcome-based roadmap?**
A roadmap where each item is a measurable goal, such as reducing onboarding time, rather than a feature. It leaves the team free to find the best solution.

**Q: What is the difference between a roadmap and a release plan?**
A roadmap shows goals and priorities over six to eighteen months. A release plan forecasts which backlog items will ship in the next few releases, usually one to six months ahead.

**Q: What is the difference between a roadmap and a product backlog?**
The roadmap is a high-level view of goals and initiatives. The product backlog is the detailed, ordered list of items, such as user stories, that the team will work on.

**Q: Is a roadmap part of Scrum?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide has three artifacts and no roadmap, but it includes the Product Goal. Many Scrum Teams use a roadmap to show the steps towards that goal.

**Q: Who owns the Agile roadmap?**
Usually the Product Owner or product manager, with input from leadership, customers, stakeholders and the development team.

**Q: Can an Agile roadmap have dates?**
Yes, for near-term items and genuine external deadlines. Further out, use quarters, ranges or no dates at all, and label the confidence of each item.

**Q: What is a theme in an Agile roadmap?**
A broad area of focus, such as self-service onboarding, that groups related initiatives. Themes give a sense of direction and timing without committing to specific features.

**Q: How far ahead should an Agile roadmap go?**
Commonly six to eighteen months, with detail and confidence decreasing the further out it goes.

**Q: How often should you update an Agile roadmap?**
Check Now items every sprint, review the wider roadmap monthly and revisit goals quarterly, plus after any major learning or change in strategy.

**Q: What is the difference between an Agile roadmap and a project roadmap?**
A project roadmap usually shows phases and milestones for a project with defined scope and end date. An Agile roadmap focuses on outcomes for an ongoing product and changes as the team learns.

**Q: What tools can I use for an Agile roadmap?**
A slide, whiteboard or spreadsheet template is enough to start. Tools such as Jira, Wrike, Asana, monday dev, ClickUp and Notion offer roadmap or timeline views linked to the backlog.

# How Agile Software Development Works: Practices and Best Practices

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-software-development/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: How Agile software development works day to day: user stories, CI/CD, testing, code review and DevOps, plus best practices for high-performing teams.


## How Agile Software Development Works: Practices and Best Practices
Agile software development is where Agile began. Teams deliver working software in short iterations, supported by engineering practices that keep quality high while requirements change.
- Published 25 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile software teams deliver working software in short iterations.
- TDD, CI/CD, code review and refactoring keep quality high under change.
- DevOps extends Agile into release and operations.

### The development cycle
1. The Product Owner orders a backlog of user stories.
2. In [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-meetings-and-ceremonies/), developers pick stories and break them into tasks.
3. Developers write code and automated tests together.
4. Code is reviewed and merged frequently into a shared main branch.
5. Continuous integration builds and tests every change automatically.
6. Finished stories are demonstrated at the Sprint Review and released, sometimes many times a day.
See the [Agile development life cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-development-life-cycle/) for the wider process.

### Core engineering practices
| Practice | What it is | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Test-driven development (TDD) | Write a failing test, then the code to pass it, then refactor | Fewer defects, better design |
| Continuous integration (CI) | Merge and test code at least daily | Integration problems found early |
| Continuous delivery (CD) | Keep software always releasable; automate deployment | Fast, low-risk releases |
| Pair programming | Two developers share one task | Quality and knowledge sharing |
| Code review | Another developer checks each change | Quality and shared ownership |
| Refactoring | Improve code structure without changing behaviour | Keeps code easy to change |
| Trunk-based development | Short-lived branches merged quickly | Avoids painful merges |

### Agile and DevOps
DevOps extends Agile beyond development into operations: teams own their software in production, automate infrastructure, monitor real usage and recover quickly from failures. Widely used DevOps measures include deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service.

### Best practices
- Keep stories small enough to finish in a few days.
- Make the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) include automated tests.
- Pay down technical debt continuously; reserve capacity each sprint.
- Automate builds, tests and deployments.
- Release small changes often, using feature flags to separate deployment from release.
- Involve users early and measure real usage after release.
- Hold blameless reviews after incidents.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between Agile software development and DevOps?**
Agile focuses on how teams plan and build software iteratively; DevOps extends that collaboration and automation into releasing and running the software.

**Q: Does Agile software development still need documentation?**
Yes: enough to help users and future developers, such as clear code, automated tests, API docs and short decision records.

**Q: What is Agile software development?**
Building software in short iterations by small cross-functional teams, with frequent integration, testing and release, and regular feedback from users.

**Q: What is test-driven development in Agile software development?**
Writing a failing automated test first, then the code to pass it, then refactoring. It leads to fewer defects and better design.

**Q: What is continuous integration in Agile software development?**
Merging and testing code changes at least daily, with automated builds and tests, so integration problems are found early.

**Q: In Agile software development, what is the difference between continuous integration and continuous delivery?**
Continuous integration merges and tests changes frequently; continuous delivery keeps the software always releasable, with automated deployment.

**Q: What is pair programming in Agile software development?**
Two developers working on one task at one screen, improving quality and spreading knowledge.

**Q: What is trunk-based development in Agile software development?**
A practice in which developers use short-lived branches and merge into the main branch frequently, avoiding painful merges.

**Q: What is refactoring in Agile software development?**
Improving the structure of code without changing its behaviour, so it stays easy to change.

**Q: What is technical debt in Agile software development?**
The future cost of shortcuts in code or design. Left unmanaged, it slows teams down and can show up as falling velocity.

**Q: How big should a user story be in Agile software development?**
Small enough to finish in a few days, so it can be built, tested and integrated within a sprint. See [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/).

# What Is Agile Swarming? How Teams Finish Work Faster

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: What swarming means in Agile, when to use it, how it reduces work in progress and cycle time, and practical tips for teams starting to swarm.


## What Is Agile Swarming? How Teams Finish Work Faster
Swarming is when several team members work together on the same backlog item until it is done, instead of each person working on a separate item. It is one of the simplest ways to finish work faster and reduce the amount of half-done work.
- Published 17 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Swarming means several people finish one item together.
- It reduces work in progress and speeds up delivery.
- Ask "what can we finish?" rather than "what can we start?"

### Why swarming works
When everyone works on separate items, many items are in progress at once and none are finished until late in the sprint. Swarming reduces work in progress (WIP), which shortens cycle time, exposes blockers sooner and spreads knowledge across the team.

### When to swarm
- A high-priority item is at risk of not finishing in the sprint.
- An item is blocked and needs several skills to unblock it.
- The board shows too many items in progress.
- A new team member needs to learn part of the product.
- A production incident needs urgent attention.

### How to start swarming
1. At the Daily Scrum, ask "What can we finish today?" rather than "What will you start?"
2. Set WIP limits on your board.
3. Break the item into tasks that can be done in parallel.
4. Pair or mob on the hardest parts.
5. Celebrate finished items, not busy people.

### Swarming vs mobbing vs pairing
| Practice | Who | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pairing | Two people | Share one task at one screen |
| Swarming | Several people | Split one item into parallel tasks |
| Mobbing | The whole team | Everyone on one task at one screen |

### Pitfalls
- Too many people on a tiny item, so they get in each other's way.
- Swarming only in emergencies, so it never becomes a habit.
- No shared definition of when the item is done; agree it upfront using the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Does swarming reduce productivity?**
Individual utilisation may drop, but the team finishes more items, sooner, with fewer handoffs and less rework.

**Q: Is swarming only for software teams?**
No. Any team can swarm, for example a marketing team finishing a campaign launch together.

**Q: What is swarming in Agile?**
Several team members working together on the same backlog item to finish it quickly, instead of each working on a separate item.

**Q: What is the difference between swarming and mobbing?**
In swarming, several people split one item into parallel tasks. In mobbing, the whole team works on one task together at a single screen.

**Q: When should a team use swarming?**
When a high-priority item is at risk, an item is blocked and needs several skills, too much work is in progress, or a production incident needs urgent attention.

**Q: How does swarming relate to WIP limits?**
WIP limits encourage swarming: when a column is full, team members help finish existing items instead of starting new ones.

**Q: Is swarming the same as pair programming?**
No. Pairing is two people sharing one task; swarming involves several people working in parallel on parts of one item.

**Q: How many people should be swarming on one item?**
As many as can contribute without getting in each other's way. For most items, two to four people is enough.

**Q: Does swarming work for remote teams?**
Yes, with a shared board, video calls and clear task splits. Remote swarming often uses screen sharing for the hardest parts.

**Q: What are the benefits of swarming?**
Shorter cycle times, earlier detection of blockers, fewer handoffs and wider knowledge across the team.

**Q: How do you encourage swarming?**
Ask "what can we finish today?" at the Daily Scrum, set WIP limits and celebrate finished items rather than busy individuals.

# Agile Team Structures: Types, Roles and How to Choose One

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-team-structures/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: The main Agile team structures compared: generalist, specialist, feature, component and platform teams, plus roles, team size and how to choose.


## Agile Team Structures: Types, Roles and How to Choose One
An Agile team structure is the way people, skills and responsibilities are organised so that a small, cross-functional team can deliver value end to end. Common structures include feature teams, component teams, generalist and specialist mixes, and platform teams, often grouped into larger units as organisations scale.
- Published 7 September 2026
- 5 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile teams are small, cross-functional, self-managing and long-lived.
- Feature teams reduce hand-offs; component and platform teams provide depth and shared services.
- Design structures around the flow of value and minimise dependencies.
- Review structures periodically, but keep teams stable.

### What makes a team Agile
- **Cross-functional:** the team has all the skills needed to turn a backlog item into a finished result.
- **Small and stable:** typically around ten people or fewer; the 2020 Scrum Guide says a Scrum Team is typically 10 or fewer.
- **Self-managing:** the team decides how to do its work.
- **Long-lived:** teams stay together across many projects so that they learn and improve.
- **Focused on one goal or product at a time.**
See [what is an Agile team](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-an-agile-team/) for the basics.

### Common Agile team structures
| Structure | How it works | Strengths | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Feature team | Owns complete customer features across all layers | Fast end-to-end delivery, fewer hand-offs | Needs broad skills; shared code needs good practices |
| Component team | Owns one part of the system, such as payments or search | Deep expertise, consistent architecture | Features need several teams; more dependencies |
| Generalist team | Members can work across many types of task | Flexible, avoids bottlenecks | May lack deep expertise |
| Specialist team | Members each hold a distinct skill | High quality in each discipline | Bottlenecks when one skill is overloaded |
| Hybrid (T-shaped) team | Members have one deep skill and broader secondary skills | Balances depth and flexibility | Takes time and support to build |
| Platform team | Provides shared tools and services to other teams | Reduces duplicated effort | Must treat other teams as customers |
Tip
Most organisations use a mix: mainly feature teams, supported by a small number of platform or component teams for shared services.

### Roles in an Agile team
| Role | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| Product owner | Maximises value; owns and orders the backlog; see [Scrum Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) |
| Scrum Master or Agile coach | Team effectiveness and removing impediments; see [Scrum Master role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) |
| Developers or team members | Build, test and deliver the work; may include engineers, designers, analysts, testers and writers |
| Stakeholders | Provide input and feedback, especially at reviews |
| Agile project manager (in some organisations) | Coordination across teams, budgets and reporting; see [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) |

### How to design your team structure
1. **Start from the value stream:** map how work flows from request to customer; see [value stream mapping](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/).
2. **Choose the team type:** prefer feature teams aligned to customer journeys or products, and add component or platform teams only where expertise or scale demands it.
3. **Size the teams:** aim for around five to nine members, and split larger groups.
4. **Fill skill gaps:** list the skills needed to finish work without hand-offs, then hire, train or pair to cover gaps.
5. **Minimise dependencies:** if a team regularly waits on another, adjust boundaries.
6. **Define how teams coordinate:** use practices such as a [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/) or shared planning.
7. **Review regularly:** check flow, dependencies and morale every few months and adapt.

### Example: from component to feature teams
An online retailer has four component teams (web front end, mobile, checkout services and database) of six people each. A typical feature needs all four, so items wait in queues and a simple change takes six weeks. The company re-forms into three feature teams aligned to customer journeys (browse, buy, account), each with front-end, mobile, back-end and testing skills, plus one small platform team of six for shared infrastructure. With fewer hand-offs, most features are now completed by a single team within one or two sprints.

### Structures at scale
- **Team of teams:** several teams working on one product share a backlog and coordinate; see [Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/).
- **Agile Release Train:** in SAFe, typically 5–12 teams plan and deliver together; see [Agile Release Train](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/).
- **Squads, tribes, chapters and guilds:** a model popularised by Spotify; see [squads, tribes, chapters and guilds](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/squads-tribes-chapters-guilds/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the best Agile team structure?**
There is no single best structure. Feature teams suit most product work, with platform or component teams where specialist depth or shared services are needed.

**Q: How big should an Agile team structure be?**
Small, typically around ten people or fewer. Larger groups should usually split into several teams.

**Q: What is a cross-functional Agile team structure?**
A team that has all the skills needed to deliver a finished result without relying on other teams.

**Q: Which Agile team structure is better: feature teams or component teams?**
A feature team delivers complete customer features across the system; a component team owns one part of the system.

**Q: What is a T-shaped team member in an Agile team structure?**
Someone with deep expertise in one area and working knowledge of several others, which helps the team share work.

**Q: Does an Agile team structure need a project manager?**
Not within Scrum, which has no project manager role. Some organisations keep project managers for cross-team coordination; see [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/).

**Q: Who leads in an Agile team structure?**
Agile teams are self-managing. The product owner sets priorities, the Scrum Master supports effectiveness, and the team decides how to do the work.

**Q: What is a platform team in an Agile team structure?**
A team that builds and runs shared tools or services so that other teams can deliver faster.

**Q: Should an Agile team structure be co-located?**
Co-location helps communication, but many teams work well remotely or in hybrid setups with good tools and agreed working hours.

**Q: How often should an Agile team structure change?**
Teams benefit from stability, so avoid frequent reshuffles. Review structures every few months and change them when dependencies or goals shift.

**Q: How does an Agile team structure coordinate multiple teams?**
Through shared backlogs, joint planning, regular cross-team meetings and scaling frameworks; see [scaled Agile framework](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/).
