# Agile Velocity Chart: How to Read, Build and Use It

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: An Agile velocity chart shows story points committed and completed per sprint. Learn to read it, build one, calculate velocity and forecast releases.


## Agile Velocity Chart: How to Read, Build and Use It
An Agile velocity chart is a bar chart that shows how much work a team planned and actually finished in each recent sprint, usually measured in story points. Read across several sprints, it tells you how much the team can realistically take on next and roughly when a release is likely to be ready. This guide explains how the chart works, how to calculate velocity, how to build and read one, and how to forecast with it, using a worked eight-sprint example you can copy.
- Published 15 September 2026
- Last updated 15 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Velocity is the total estimate of the backlog items that met the Definition of Done in a sprint; partly finished work counts as zero.
- A velocity chart normally shows two bars per sprint, committed and completed, often with a rolling average line.
- Plan the next sprint from the average of the last three to five sprints, adjusted for the team's actual availability.
- Forecast releases as a range (for example 6 to 8 sprints), not a single date, and update the forecast every sprint.
- Look for stability and trends rather than growth. A steady velocity makes forecasting reliable; a rising one is often a sign of estimate inflation.
- Never use velocity to compare teams or judge individuals. It is a planning aid for the team, not a productivity score.

### What is an Agile velocity chart?
An **Agile velocity chart** is a bar chart that plots, for each completed sprint, the amount of work the team committed to at Sprint Planning and the amount it actually completed to its Definition of Done. Teams use the trend across several sprints to plan how much to take on next and to forecast when larger pieces of work will be finished.
**Velocity** itself is the sum of the estimates, most often [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/), of every backlog item that met the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) during a [sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/). An item that is 90% finished counts as zero in that sprint and is counted in full in the sprint in which it is actually done. This all-or-nothing rule keeps the measure honest: it records finished, usable work rather than effort.
The term comes from Extreme Programming (XP). According to the Agile Alliance's practices timeline, "velocity" was added to XP around 2000, replacing an earlier idea called the load factor, and Scrum teams widely adopted it soon afterwards. It is worth knowing that the 2020 Scrum Guide does not mention velocity at all. It says that the more the Developers know about their past performance, upcoming capacity and Definition of Done, the more confident they will be in their Sprint forecasts. Velocity is simply the most common way teams record that past performance. For the Scrum-specific view, see [velocity in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/).

### Anatomy of a velocity chart
Most velocity charts, whether drawn in a spreadsheet or generated by a tool, share the same elements.
| Element | What it shows | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Horizontal axis | Sprints in order (Sprint 1, 2, 3…), usually the last 6 to 10 | Lets you see the trend rather than a single result |
| Vertical axis | Story points (or another unit such as item count) | The unit must stay the same across sprints for the chart to mean anything |
| Committed bar | Points in the Sprint Backlog when the sprint started | Shows what the team forecast it could finish |
| Completed bar | Points for items that met the Definition of Done by the end of the sprint | This is the velocity for that sprint |
| Average line (optional) | Rolling average of completed points, often over the last three sprints | Smooths out noise and is the usual planning figure |
| Range band (optional) | Lowest and highest recent velocities | Supports forecasting with a range instead of one number |
In Jira, for example, the velocity report on a Scrum board shows a commitment bar and a completed bar for each recent sprint, based on the estimation statistic the board uses. Other tools and spreadsheets follow the same idea, even if the labels differ.

### How to calculate velocity

#### The formulas
- **Sprint velocity** = sum of the estimates of all items that met the Definition of Done in the sprint.
- **Average velocity** = total completed points over the last *n* sprints ÷ *n* (most teams use the last three to five sprints).
- **Say/do ratio** (also called commitment reliability) = completed points ÷ committed points × 100%.
For example, if a team completed 25, 26 and 24 points in its last three sprints, its average velocity is (25 + 26 + 24) ÷ 3 = 25 points per sprint.

#### What counts and what does not
Teams get inconsistent charts mainly because they count different things from sprint to sprint. Agree the rules once, write them down and apply them every time.
| Situation | Count it? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Item met the Definition of Done | Yes, at its original estimate | Finished, usable work |
| Item 90% done at sprint end | No (zero this sprint) | Return it to the Product Backlog; count it when it is finished |
| Item added mid-sprint and finished | Yes, in completed (not in committed) | It was delivered, but the gap with commitment shows the disruption |
| Item removed mid-sprint | No | Show it in committed only if your tool records the original commitment |
| Item re-estimated after starting | Use the estimate agreed before work began | Re-estimating after the fact makes velocity self-fulfilling |
| Bugs and technical debt work | Your choice, but be consistent | Many teams estimate and count them; others leave them unestimated and accept a lower velocity |
| Spikes (time-boxed research) | Usually no points | Their output is knowledge, not a working increment |

#### Worked example: an eight-sprint dataset
The table below follows a six-person team running two-week sprints. We use it throughout this guide.
| Sprint | Committed | Completed (velocity) | Rolling 3-sprint average | Say/do ratio | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 30 | 22 | – | 73% | New team, over-committed |
| 2 | 28 | 25 | – | 89% |  |
| 3 | 27 | 24 | 23.7 | 89% |  |
| 4 | 26 | 27 | 25.3 | 104% | Pulled in one extra story |
| 5 | 28 | 18 | 23.0 | 64% | Two people on leave; production incident |
| 6 | 26 | 25 | 23.3 | 96% |  |
| 7 | 27 | 26 | 23.0 | 96% |  |
| 8 | 28 | 24 | 25.0 | 86% |  |
Over eight sprints the team committed 220 points and completed 191, an average velocity of 23.9 and an overall say/do ratio of 87%. The last three sprints average 25. The first sprint shows the usual pattern of a new team learning what it can finish; sprint 5 is a one-off dip with a known cause, so the team notes it rather than treating it as a trend.

### How to build a velocity chart step by step
You do not need special software. A spreadsheet produces a perfectly good velocity chart in about ten minutes, and it is a useful exercise even if your tool draws one automatically, because it forces you to agree what counts.
1. **Agree the counting rules.** Confirm the unit (story points or item count), the Definition of Done and how you treat bugs, spikes and items added mid-sprint.
2. **Set up the columns.** In a sheet, create columns for Sprint, Committed, Completed, Rolling average and Say/do ratio.
3. **Record committed points at Sprint Planning.** Enter the total estimate of the Sprint Backlog as soon as planning ends. Do not change it later, even if items are added or removed.
4. **Record completed points at the end of the sprint.** Add up only the items that met the Definition of Done before the Sprint Review.
5. **Add the formulas.** For the rolling average in row 4, use =AVERAGE(C2:C4) and fill down. For the say/do ratio use =C2/B2 formatted as a percentage.
6. **Insert a clustered column chart** using the Sprint, Committed and Completed columns, so each sprint has two bars side by side.
7. **Add the average as a line.** Add the rolling average column as a second series and change its chart type to a line.
8. **Label it clearly.** Title the chart, label the axes, and add short notes for unusual sprints (holidays, incidents, team changes).
9. **Review it every sprint.** Look at it briefly at Sprint Planning (to set capacity) and at the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) (to discuss trends).
Tip
Keep the chart next to your planning data. Our free [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) gives you a place to record capacity, committed items and completed points sprint by sprint.

### How to read a velocity chart

#### Four questions to ask
1. **Is it stable?** Look at the spread of completed points over the last five or so sprints. A narrow spread means forecasts will be reliable.
2. **Which way is the trend going?** A gradual rise or fall over several sprints matters more than any single bar.
3. **How big is the gap between committed and completed?** A consistent small gap is healthy. A large or growing gap suggests over-commitment, interruptions or poor refinement.
4. **Can we explain the outliers?** Mark known causes (leave, incidents, team changes) so nobody over-reacts to them.

#### Common patterns and what they usually mean
| Pattern | Likely causes | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stable bars within about ±15% of the average | Settled team, consistent estimating, well-refined backlog | Keep going; use the average with confidence |
| Steady rise over many sprints | Genuine learning and better tooling, or estimate inflation | Check whether similar items now get bigger estimates; compare with item counts |
| Steady fall | Growing [technical debt](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/), more support work, unclear requirements, team changes | Raise it at the retrospective; make the hidden work visible |
| Saw-tooth (high, low, high, low) | Large items finishing in alternate sprints, or work carried over | Split stories smaller so most finish within one sprint |
| Completed always well below committed | Over-commitment, optimism, frequent interruptions | Plan to the recent average, protect the sprint from unplanned work |
| Completed often above committed | Under-commitment or work pulled in mid-sprint | Commit a little more, or check that pulled-in work is genuinely priority |
| One sudden dip | Holiday, illness, incident, release freeze | Annotate it and exclude it from range calculations if it is clearly a one-off |
| Completed exactly equals committed every sprint | Scope being trimmed or estimates adjusted to match | Check that the counting rules are being followed honestly |
Applied to our example, the chart shows a team that over-committed early, settled at around 24 to 27 points, and had one explained dip. The say/do ratio has stayed at or above 86% for the last four sprints, which suggests planning is now realistic.

### Using the velocity chart for sprint planning
Velocity tells you what the team has historically finished. [Capacity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) tells you how much time it has available next sprint. Good sprint planning combines the two.
1. **Start with the recent average.** Use the last three sprints (25 points in our example).
2. **Work out normal capacity.** Six people × 10 working days = 60 person-days in a typical sprint.
3. **Subtract known absences.** One person is on leave for 5 days and there is a public holiday for everyone (6 person-days). Available capacity is 60 − 5 − 6 = 49 person-days, or about 82% of normal.
4. **Scale the velocity.** 25 × 0.82 ≈ 20 points.
5. **Select items up to that level.** Take the top items from the ordered Product Backlog until you reach roughly 20 points, and agree a Sprint Goal that those items support.
6. **Sense-check the plan.** Ask the Developers whether it feels achievable. The number is a guide; the team's judgement decides.
Tip
Plan to the recent average, not the best sprint ever. Planning to the peak sets the team up to miss, and repeated misses push people to inflate estimates.

### Forecasting a release with velocity
The most valuable use of a velocity chart is answering the question "When will it be ready?" with evidence. The method is simple, but it only works if you forecast a range.
1. **Size the remaining work.** Make sure everything in scope for the release is in the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) and roughly estimated.
2. **Calculate a slow and a fast velocity.** A common approach is to average the three lowest and the three highest of the last eight or so sprints.
3. **Divide and round up.** Remaining points ÷ each velocity gives a range of sprints.
4. **Allow for scope growth.** If scope has been growing, subtract the average growth per sprint from each velocity before dividing.
5. **Convert to dates.** Multiply by sprint length and map onto the calendar, allowing for holidays.
6. **Update every sprint.** Recalculate after each Sprint Review and show progress on a burnup chart.

#### Worked example
The team has 150 points left in the release. From the eight sprints above, the three lowest velocities are 18, 22 and 24 (average 21.3) and the three highest are 25, 26 and 27 (average 26).
| Scenario | Velocity used | Calculation | Sprints needed | Weeks (2-week sprints) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fast | 26 | 150 ÷ 26 = 5.8 | 6 | 12 |
| Typical | 23.9 (8-sprint average) | 150 ÷ 23.9 = 6.3 | 7 | 14 |
| Slow | 21.3 | 150 ÷ 21.3 = 7.0 | 8 | 16 |
| Typical with 5 points of scope growth per sprint | 23.9 − 5 = 18.9 | 150 ÷ 18.9 = 7.9 | 8 | 16 |
The honest message to stakeholders is: "Most likely in 7 sprints (about 14 weeks), and very probably within 6 to 8 sprints, provided scope stays roughly where it is." If the date is fixed, the same numbers tell you how much scope is realistic: 6 sprints × 21.3 points ≈ 128 points in a pessimistic case, so the lowest-priority 22 or so points are at risk.
For larger portfolios or higher-stakes dates, teams sometimes go further with probabilistic techniques such as [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/), which resample past sprint results thousands of times to give likelihoods for each date.
Tip
Fix either the date or the scope, not both. Velocity forecasting works best when lower-priority scope is allowed to flex.

### Velocity chart vs burndown, burnup and other Agile charts
Velocity is one of several charts Agile teams use. Each answers a different question, and most teams use two or three together.
| Chart | What it shows | Time frame | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Velocity chart | Points committed and completed per sprint | Across many sprints | Planning capacity and long-range forecasts |
| Sprint burndown | Work remaining in the current sprint, day by day | One sprint | Seeing whether the Sprint Goal is on track |
| Release burnup | Completed work and total scope over time | Several sprints | Showing progress when scope changes |
| [Cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) | Items in each workflow state over time | Continuous | Spotting bottlenecks and growing work in progress |
| [Throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) chart | Number of items finished per period | Continuous | Forecasting without story points |
| [Cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) scatterplot | How long each item took from start to finish | Continuous | Predicting how long a single item will take |
A velocity chart tells you how much the team gets done per sprint. A burndown tells you whether this sprint is on track. A burnup tells you whether the release is on track and whether scope is growing.

### Velocity vs capacity
The two terms are often confused, but they look in different directions.
|  | Velocity | Capacity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Looks | Backwards at what was completed | Forwards at time available |
| Unit | Story points (or items) per sprint | Person-days or hours |
| Changes when | The team's way of working, item size or estimating changes | People take leave, join, leave or split their time |
| Used for | Forecasting how much work fits | Adjusting that forecast for the coming sprint |
In practice: velocity × (available capacity ÷ normal capacity) gives a sensible starting point for the next sprint, as in the planning example above.

### How to stabilise and genuinely improve velocity
People often ask how to increase velocity. The honest answer is that you cannot improve it directly without distorting it. What you can do is remove the things that slow the team down, and a steadier, sometimes higher, velocity follows.
- **Split stories smaller.** Items that each fit comfortably in a few days finish within the sprint, which removes the saw-tooth pattern. Our guide to [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) covers splitting techniques.
- **Refine the backlog regularly.** Ongoing [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) means items arrive at planning clear, estimated and ready.
- **Stabilise the Definition of Done.** If "done" means different things in different sprints, velocity will wobble for reasons that have nothing to do with the work.
- **Limit work in progress.** Finishing a few things beats starting many. [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) apply inside a sprint too.
- **Protect the sprint.** Route unplanned requests through the Product Owner, and make support or incident work visible rather than hidden.
- **Pay down technical debt.** Fragile code and manual testing slow every item a little; together they slow the team a lot.
- **Keep the team stable.** Frequent changes of membership reset velocity, because the team's shared sense of what a point means changes.
- **Use the retrospective.** Look at the velocity chart at each retrospective and pick one improvement to try.

### Common velocity chart mistakes
- **Comparing teams.** Each team calibrates story points differently, so 30 points for one team and 30 for another mean different things. Comparisons encourage point inflation.
- **Setting velocity targets.** Goodhart's law, usually paraphrased as "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure", applies directly: targets make estimates grow, not output.
- **Measuring individuals.** Velocity is a team measure. Individual velocity discourages pairing, helping and swarming.
- **Counting partly finished work.** It flatters the current sprint and creates a hidden debt of unfinished work.
- **Re-estimating finished items.** Changing an estimate after the work is known makes the chart self-fulfilling and useless for forecasting.
- **Mixing units.** Switching between hours, points and item counts breaks the trend.
- **Treating the forecast as a promise.** A forecast is a range with uncertainty, and stakeholders should hear it that way.
- **Valuing output over outcomes.** A high velocity on low-value work is not success. Pair velocity with measures of customer value and quality.
- **Over-reacting to one sprint.** One low bar with a known cause is noise, not a trend.

### Velocity charts in project management tools
Most Agile project management tools can draw a velocity chart automatically from sprint data, which saves time and removes counting errors, provided the team closes sprints and records estimates consistently.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** includes a velocity report on Scrum boards showing commitment and completed work for recent sprints, and uses average velocity in its planning features.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** offers sprint features with velocity, burndown and burnup reporting for teams that run sprints.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool overall, suits organisations where Agile teams work alongside marketing, operations or PMO teams and need shared dashboards, boards and cross-project reporting in one place.
- **Spreadsheets** remain a good option for small teams or for agreeing the counting rules before choosing a tool.
Whichever tool you use, the chart is only as good as the data: close sprints on time, keep estimates unchanged once work starts, and record items added mid-sprint.

### Velocity without story points
Story points are not the only option. Some teams find that counting items works just as well, especially once stories are consistently small.
- **Item count velocity.** Count finished backlog items per sprint instead of points. It works when items are of broadly similar size.
- **Throughput in Kanban.** Kanban teams do not usually use sprints or velocity; they track [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) (items finished per week) and cycle time instead, and forecast from those.
- **#NoEstimates.** An approach in which teams split work into small, similar-sized items and forecast by counting them rather than estimating each one.
If you switch units, start a new chart rather than mixing the old and new data. To compare velocity with other forecasting approaches, see our guide to [project forecasting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a velocity chart in Agile?**
A bar chart that shows, for each recent sprint, the story points a team committed to and the points it actually completed to its Definition of Done. Teams use the trend to plan future sprints and forecast releases.

**Q: How do you calculate velocity in Agile?**
Add up the estimates of every item that met the Definition of Done in the sprint. For planning, average the last three to five sprints: for example, 25, 26 and 24 points give an average velocity of 25.

**Q: What is a good velocity for a Scrum team?**
There is no universally good number, because each team sizes story points differently. A good velocity is a stable one, because stability makes forecasts reliable.

**Q: How many sprints does it take for velocity to become reliable?**
Usually three to five sprints with a stable team and consistent counting rules. New teams often over-commit in the first one or two sprints.

**Q: Should velocity increase over time?**
Not necessarily. Velocity may rise a little as a team matures, but a steady rise is often a sign of estimate inflation. Aim for stability and improve the conditions for flow instead.

**Q: Do unfinished stories count towards velocity?**
No. Partly finished items count as zero and go back to the Product Backlog. Their full estimate is counted in the sprint in which they meet the Definition of Done.

**Q: What is the difference between a velocity chart and a burndown chart?**
A velocity chart compares committed and completed work across many sprints for planning. A sprint burndown tracks the work remaining day by day within one sprint.

**Q: Can you compare velocity between teams?**
No. Story points are relative to each team, so the same number means different amounts of work for different teams. Comparing velocities encourages teams to inflate estimates.

**Q: Is velocity part of the Scrum Guide?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide does not mention velocity. It refers to the Developers' past performance and capacity when forecasting. Velocity is a common complementary practice that came from Extreme Programming. See [velocity in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/).

**Q: What should we do when velocity drops suddenly?**
First check for a simple cause such as leave, an incident or a team change. If there is none, raise it at the retrospective and look for growing technical debt, unclear requirements, dependencies or items that are too large.

**Q: Does Kanban use velocity?**
Not usually. Kanban teams work in a continuous flow without sprints, so they track throughput (items finished per period) and cycle time instead.

**Q: Should bugs and technical debt count towards velocity?**
Either approach works if you are consistent. Counting them shows the true workload; leaving them unestimated means velocity reflects only new features. Agree the rule and keep to it.

**Q: What does the gap between committed and completed mean?**
It shows how realistic the team's planning is. A small, steady gap is healthy. A large or growing gap suggests over-commitment, interruptions, poor refinement or items that are too big.

**Q: How do you forecast a release date with velocity?**
Divide the remaining points by a slow and a fast recent velocity to get a range of sprints, allow for any scope growth, and convert the range to dates. Update the forecast after every sprint.

# Agile vs Scrum: Key Differences, Examples and When to Use

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Agile vs Scrum explained: Agile is a mindset, Scrum is a framework. Compare roles, events and planning, see examples and learn when to use each.


## Agile vs Scrum: Key Differences, Examples and When to Use
The difference between Agile and Scrum is that Agile is a set of values and principles for delivering work iteratively, while Scrum is one specific framework, with defined accountabilities, events and artefacts, for putting those principles into practice. All Scrum teams are working in an Agile way, but Agile teams can also use Kanban, XP, Lean or their own hybrid. This guide compares the two side by side, shows the same project run both ways, and gives you a step-by-step process for deciding whether Scrum suits your team.
- Published 12 September 2026
- Last updated 14 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile is the philosophy, set out in the 2001 Agile Manifesto as four values and twelve principles. Scrum is a lightweight framework that applies it.
- Scrum adds structure that Agile does not prescribe: three accountabilities, five events, three artefacts and fixed-length Sprints of one month or less.
- Scrum is older than the Agile Manifesto: it was first presented in 1995, and both Scrum co-creators signed the Manifesto in 2001.
- You can be Agile without Scrum (Kanban, XP, Lean), but running Scrum events without Agile values gives you the meetings without the benefits.
- Choose Scrum for a dedicated team building a product in planned increments; consider Kanban for unpredictable, continuous-flow work.

### Agile vs Scrum: the short answer
**Agile** is a way of thinking about work: deliver in small, usable increments, collaborate closely with customers, and adapt the plan as you learn. **Scrum** is a specific framework that turns that thinking into a working routine, with fixed-length Sprints, a Product Owner, a Scrum Master, Developers and a set of regular events. Agile tells you what to value; Scrum tells you one way to organise a team around those values.
An everyday comparison helps. "Eating healthily" is a set of principles; a specific meal plan is one way to follow them. Some people follow a structured plan, others build their own habits, and both can be healthy. Agile is the principle, and Scrum is one well-tested plan.
|  | Agile | Scrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A mindset: values and principles | A framework within Agile |
| Defined by | Agile Manifesto (2001) | The Scrum Guide (current edition 2020) |
| Tells you | What to value and why | Who does what, and when |
| Relationship | The umbrella | One of the methods under it |

### What is Agile?
Agile is an approach to project and product work that delivers results in short cycles, uses feedback to steer, and treats the plan as something to update rather than defend. It was named in February 2001, when 17 software practitioners met in Snowbird, Utah, and wrote the [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/). The Manifesto sets out four values:
- **Individuals and interactions** over processes and tools.
- **Working software** over comprehensive documentation.
- **Customer collaboration** over contract negotiation.
- **Responding to change** over following a plan.
The authors stress that the items on the right still have value; the items on the left are valued more. Twelve supporting principles add detail, such as delivering working software frequently, welcoming changing requirements, sustainable pace, and regular reflection on how to become more effective.
What Agile does **not** contain is just as important. It prescribes no roles, no meetings, no iteration length and no documents. That is deliberate: it is a set of ideas that teams apply through frameworks and practices. The best known are Scrum, [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/), Extreme Programming (XP), Lean, and scaled frameworks such as SAFe.

### What is Scrum?
The Scrum Guide describes Scrum as a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organisations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. It is maintained by its creators, Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, and the 2020 edition is still the official version. In June 2025 Jeff Sutherland released a Scrum Guide Expansion Pack, but it is an optional supplement and does not replace the 2020 Scrum Guide.
Scrum is built on **empiricism** (knowledge comes from experience and decisions are based on what is observed) and **lean thinking** (reduce waste, focus on essentials). Its three pillars are **transparency, inspection and adaptation**, and its five values are **commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage**.

#### The Scrum framework at a glance
| Element | What the Scrum Guide defines |
| --- | --- |
| Scrum Team | One Product Owner, one Scrum Master and Developers; typically 10 or fewer people, cross-functional and self-managing |
| Accountabilities | Product Owner (maximises value, manages the Product Backlog), Scrum Master (establishes Scrum and the team's effectiveness), Developers (create a usable Increment each Sprint) |
| Events | The Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective |
| Artefacts | Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment |
| Commitments | Product Goal (for the Product Backlog), Sprint Goal (for the Sprint Backlog), Definition of Done (for the Increment) |

#### Scrum time-boxes
| Event | Maximum duration (one-month Sprint) | Usual for a two-week Sprint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint | One month or less | Two weeks |
| Sprint Planning | 8 hours | Up to about 4 hours |
| Daily Scrum | 15 minutes | 15 minutes |
| Sprint Review | 4 hours | Up to about 2 hours |
| Sprint Retrospective | 3 hours | Up to about 1.5 hours |
The Scrum Guide sets the maximums and says the events are usually shorter for shorter Sprints; the two-week figures are common practice, not rules. For more depth, see [what is Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) and the [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/).

### Agile vs Scrum: key differences
The table compares Agile as a whole with Scrum as one framework. Where the Agile column says "not prescribed", individual Agile frameworks may still define something.
| Aspect | Agile | Scrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Philosophy: four values and twelve principles | Framework with explicit rules |
| Source | Agile Manifesto, 2001 | Scrum Guide, first published 2010, current edition 2020 |
| Roles | Not prescribed | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers |
| Cadence | Any iterative rhythm, or continuous flow | Fixed-length Sprints of one month or less, back to back |
| Meetings | Not prescribed; regular reflection is a principle | Five events with time-boxes |
| Planning | Plan in layers and adapt | Sprint Planning each Sprint, towards a Product Goal |
| Change during a cycle | Welcomed, even late | Scope can be clarified and renegotiated; changes that endanger the Sprint Goal are avoided |
| Measure of progress | Working product | A usable Increment that meets the Definition of Done |
| Team size | Not prescribed | Typically 10 or fewer people |
| Leadership | Self-organising teams | Self-managing team; Scrum Master as a true leader who serves |
| Applies to | Any team, product or organisation | Mainly one team (or several on one product) building something complex |
| Flexibility | Very high: you design the practices | Immutable core; you add practices around it |

### How Scrum puts the Agile values into practice
One way to see the relationship is to map each Agile value to the parts of Scrum that make it happen. This is our own mapping, not part of either official document.
| Agile value | How Scrum supports it |
| --- | --- |
| Individuals and interactions over processes and tools | Small, cross-functional, self-managing team; the Daily Scrum is a conversation, not a status report; the Retrospective improves how people work together |
| Working software over comprehensive documentation | Every Sprint must produce at least one usable Increment that meets the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) |
| Customer collaboration over contract negotiation | The Product Owner represents stakeholders daily; the Sprint Review invites stakeholders to inspect the Increment and shape what comes next |
| Responding to change over following a plan | The Product Backlog is reordered continuously; each Sprint is a short planning horizon; the plan is inspected and adapted at every event |
The same exercise works for the principles. "Deliver working software frequently" becomes the Sprint; "at regular intervals, the team reflects" becomes the Sprint Retrospective; "business people and developers must work together daily" becomes the Product Owner's role.

### What Agile and Scrum have in common
Because Scrum is an Agile framework, the two share a lot:
- **Iterative and incremental delivery:** both build the product in small usable slices and refine it with feedback.
- **Customer focus:** value to the customer decides what is built next.
- **Empirical control:** inspect real results, then adapt the plan.
- **Self-organising or self-managing teams:** the people doing the work decide how to do it.
- **Continuous improvement:** regular reflection on the way the team works.
- **Transparency:** visible backlogs, boards and progress so everyone sees the same reality.

### Which came first: Agile or Scrum?
Scrum came first. Many people assume Scrum was created to implement the Agile Manifesto, but the timeline runs the other way.
| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| 1986 | Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka publish "The New New Product Development Game" in Harvard Business Review, using the rugby term "scrum" for fast, team-based product development |
| 1995 | Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland present Scrum as a software development framework at the OOPSLA conference |
| 2001 | 17 practitioners, including Schwaber and Sutherland, write the Agile Manifesto in Snowbird, Utah |
| 2010 | The first Scrum Guide is published |
| 2020 | The current Scrum Guide is released: shorter, less software-specific, adds the Product Goal and the three commitments |
So Scrum was one of the lightweight methods whose shared ideas the Manifesto put into words.

### Scrum vs other Agile approaches
If Agile is the umbrella, it helps to see Scrum next to the other options under it.
| Approach | Core idea | Cadence | Roles defined? | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum | Empirical delivery in fixed Sprints towards a Sprint Goal | Sprints of one month or less | Yes: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers | Product development by a dedicated team |
| Kanban | Visualise work, limit work in progress, improve flow | Continuous flow | No | Support, operations, maintenance, varied requests |
| Extreme Programming (XP) | Engineering practices: pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration | Short iterations, often one to two weeks | Some (customer, developer, coach) | Software teams wanting high technical quality |
| Lean | Maximise customer value, eliminate waste | Flow-based | No | Process improvement across a value stream |
| Scrumban | Scrum structure combined with Kanban flow and WIP limits | Sprints or flow | Optional | Teams moving between Scrum and Kanban, or mixed work |
| SAFe | Scaling Agile across many teams with shared planning | Iterations within Planning Intervals | Yes, at several levels | Large organisations with many teams on one solution |
Many teams combine elements, for example Scrum events with XP engineering practices and a Kanban board.

### Worked example: the same project run two Agile ways
A team of six (a product lead, four developers and a designer) is building online class booking for a chain of fitness studios. The goal is the same either way: members can book, cancel and join waiting lists online. Here is how the work looks under Scrum and under Kanban, both of which are Agile.

#### Option A: Scrum with two-week Sprints
| When | What happens | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Day 1, morning | Sprint Planning: agree the Sprint Goal "Members can book and cancel a class online", select backlog items, plan the first days | Whole Scrum Team |
| Every day, 15 minutes | Daily Scrum: inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adjust the plan | Developers |
| Mid-Sprint | Backlog refinement: split and clarify the waiting-list items for the next Sprint | Product Owner and Developers |
| Day 10, morning | Sprint Review: studio managers try the booking flow; feedback changes the order of the backlog | Scrum Team and stakeholders |
| Day 10, afternoon | Sprint Retrospective: agree one or two improvements, such as earlier testing | Scrum Team |
The product lead acts as Product Owner and one developer, trained in Scrum, acts as Scrum Master. Stakeholders know that new requests go to the Product Owner and are considered at the next Sprint Planning. Progress is forecast from velocity; see [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/).

#### Option B: Kanban with continuous flow
- The team uses a board with columns **Ready, Design, Build, Test, Done**, and a work-in-progress limit of three items in Build.
- A short weekly replenishment meeting picks the next most valuable items for Ready.
- Each item is released as soon as it is done, so "cancel a booking" might go live on a Tuesday and "join a waiting list" the following Thursday.
- The team holds a stand-up at the board and a fortnightly review of flow metrics such as cycle time.

#### What the comparison shows
| Question | Scrum version | Kanban version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When can a stakeholder add a request? | Any time to the Product Backlog; normally taken into the next Sprint | Any time; pulled when there is capacity |
| How is delivery forecast? | Velocity per Sprint | Throughput and cycle time |
| When is work released? | Whenever an Increment is ready; at least one usable Increment per Sprint | Continuously, item by item |
| Who removes obstacles? | The Scrum Master is accountable for this | Whoever the team agrees |
Both are Agile: they deliver in small slices, collaborate with the studios and adapt. Scrum suits this project well because the work is a defined product feature with a dedicated team. If the same team then moved on to supporting the system and fixing urgent issues, Kanban might suit better.

### Roles: Agile team vs Scrum Team
Agile does not define job titles, which is why organisations use many names. Scrum defines three accountabilities, and they are not job titles either: a person can hold one alongside their job title.
| Role | Where it comes from | Focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product Owner | Scrum | Maximises the value of the product; orders the Product Backlog; owns the Product Goal. See [Scrum Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) |
| Scrum Master | Scrum | Accountable for establishing Scrum and the team's effectiveness; coaches, removes impediments. See [Scrum Master role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) |
| Developers | Scrum | Anyone who creates the Increment: engineers, designers, testers, analysts, writers |
| Agile coach | Common Agile practice | Helps teams and leaders adopt Agile, often across several teams and frameworks |
| Project manager | Traditional and hybrid settings | Not a Scrum accountability; in Agile settings often coordinates budgets, governance, dependencies and stakeholders. See [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) |
Tip
A Scrum Master is not a project manager under another name. The Scrum Master does not assign tasks or own the plan; the Developers manage their own work and the Product Owner orders the backlog.

### Advantages and limitations

#### Agile in general
| Advantages | Limitations |
| --- | --- |
| Early and frequent delivery of value | Needs regular involvement from customers or their representatives |
| Feedback reduces the risk of building the wrong thing | Long-term dates and costs are forecasts, which some governance processes find uncomfortable |
| Adapts well to changing requirements | Without discipline, "flexibility" can turn into a lack of direction |
| Works with many frameworks and industries | Requires a culture that trusts teams to self-organise |

#### Scrum specifically
| Advantages | Limitations |
| --- | --- |
| Clear structure that is easy to start with | Needs a dedicated team and a Product Owner with real authority |
| Regular rhythm of planning, review and improvement | The events take time; poorly run, they feel like overhead |
| Sprint Goals give focus and protect the team from constant interruption | Less suited to work that arrives unpredictably and must be handled within hours |
| Transparent progress through the Increment and backlogs | Scaling to many teams needs an additional approach such as Nexus, LeSS or SAFe |
Which limitations matter depends on your work. The next sections help you decide.

### When to use Scrum (and when another Agile approach fits better)
| Situation | Good fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A dedicated team building a new product or major feature | Scrum | Sprints, a Product Goal and regular reviews suit planned, incremental development |
| IT support, help desk or operations with urgent tickets | Kanban | Continuous flow handles unpredictable arrivals better than fixed Sprints |
| A software team struggling with quality and defects | Scrum or Kanban plus XP practices | XP's engineering practices address quality directly |
| A marketing team running campaigns plus ad-hoc requests | Scrumban or Kanban | Mixes planned work with flow |
| Ten or more teams building one product | Scaled framework (SAFe, LeSS, Nexus) | Needs shared planning and dependency management |
| A fixed-scope, regulated project with little room for change | Hybrid or Waterfall | Agile may still help in delivery stages; see [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) |

### How to choose between Scrum and other Agile approaches
Use these steps with your team. They take about an hour in a workshop.
1. **Describe your work.** List the last month of work items. Were most of them planned in advance, or did they arrive unexpectedly and need fast handling?
2. **Check your team set-up.** Is there a stable team of about 10 or fewer people who mainly work on one product? Scrum assumes this; Kanban does not.
3. **Check for a decision-maker.** Is there someone with the authority and time to be Product Owner and order the backlog? Without one, Scrum struggles.
4. **Test the cadence.** Could the team commit to a Sprint Goal for two weeks without frequent urgent interruptions? If not, consider Kanban or Scrumban.
5. **Consider the organisation.** Do stakeholders need regular demos and forecasts? Scrum's Sprint Review and velocity help. Are there many teams? Look at scaling frameworks.
6. **Run an experiment.** Try your chosen approach for three Sprints or six weeks, then review what improved and what did not. Agile applies to your way of working too.
Tip
If the answers are mixed, start with Scrum's events and a Kanban board, then adjust. Many teams settle on a hybrid that keeps the Scrum events and adds WIP limits.

### How to start using Scrum in an Agile team
If you decide Scrum fits, a simple start works better than a big launch:
1. **Read the Scrum Guide together.** It is short. Agree that the core rules are not optional while you learn.
2. **Assign the accountabilities.** Choose a Product Owner and a Scrum Master; everyone else is a Developer.
3. **Build the first Product Backlog.** List and order the work, and refine the top items until they are small and clear. Our [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) helps.
4. **Agree a Definition of Done.** Write down what "done" means for every item.
5. **Pick a Sprint length.** Two weeks suits most teams starting out. See [what is a sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/).
6. **Run the first Sprint Planning.** Set a Sprint Goal and choose a realistic amount of work. Use the free [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/).
7. **Hold every event.** Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective, each within its time-box. The [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) gives you a ready format.
8. **Inspect and adapt after three Sprints.** Review what is working, and improve one thing at a time.
For an organisation-wide roll-out, read [how to implement Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-implement-agile/).

### Common misconceptions and mistakes
- **"Agile and Scrum are the same thing."** Scrum is one Agile framework among several.
- **"We do Scrum, so we are Agile."** Holding the events without empowering the team or acting on feedback is sometimes called "mechanical Scrum". It gives you meetings without the benefits.
- **"Agile means no planning."** Agile teams plan at several levels, from the roadmap to the day. They simply expect the plan to change.
- **"Agile means no documentation."** The Manifesto values working results more than documents, not instead of them. Write the documents people actually use.
- **"The Scrum Master is the team's manager."** The Scrum Master serves the team and the organisation; they do not assign work.
- **"Scrum only works for software."** The 2020 Scrum Guide removed most software-specific language, and Scrum is used in marketing, research, HR and other fields.
- **Changing Scrum's core rules too early.** Dropping the Retrospective or extending Sprints hides the problems Scrum is designed to reveal. Learn the framework first, then adapt around it.

### Agile vs Scrum certifications
The same distinction shows up in certification. Agile certifications cover the broad mindset and several methods; Scrum certifications focus on the Scrum framework and a specific accountability.
- **Agile-wide:** PMI's PMI-ACP covers Agile principles and several frameworks, including Scrum, Kanban, XP and Lean.
- **Scrum-specific:** Scrum.org's Professional Scrum Master (PSM) and Professional Scrum Product Owner (PSPO), and Scrum Alliance's Certified ScrumMaster (CSM) and Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO).
If you work in a Scrum team, a Scrum certification is the more direct choice; if you lead projects across different approaches, an Agile-wide certification is broader. Requirements and fees change, so check the certifying body before you book.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Scrum Agile?**
Yes. Scrum is one of the most widely used Agile frameworks. It applies the Agile values and principles through fixed-length Sprints, three accountabilities, five events and three artefacts.

**Q: What is the main difference between Agile and Scrum?**
Agile is a philosophy: a set of values and principles for iterative delivery. Scrum is a specific framework that puts that philosophy into practice with defined roles, events, artefacts and time-boxes.

**Q: Can you be Agile without Scrum?**
Yes. Teams can be Agile using Kanban, Extreme Programming, Lean, Scrumban or their own tailored practices, as long as they deliver in small increments, seek feedback and adapt.

**Q: Can you use Scrum without being Agile?**
You can hold the Scrum events without following Agile values, but you will not get the benefits. If the team cannot self-manage, the Product Owner cannot make decisions, or feedback is ignored, you are using Scrum's vocabulary without its intent.

**Q: Which came first, Agile or Scrum?**
Scrum. It was presented in 1995 and the Agile Manifesto was written in 2001. Scrum's co-creators, Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, were among the Manifesto's 17 authors.

**Q: Is Scrum a methodology or a framework?**
The Scrum Guide calls Scrum a lightweight framework. It defines a minimal set of rules and deliberately leaves many practices, such as estimation methods or technical practices, for teams to choose.

**Q: Is Kanban Agile or Scrum?**
Kanban is an Agile approach but it is not Scrum. It uses continuous flow and work-in-progress limits instead of Sprints, and it does not prescribe roles. See [Kanban vs Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-agile/).

**Q: Which is better, Agile or Scrum?**
They are not alternatives: Scrum is a way of being Agile. The real choice is between Scrum and other Agile approaches, and the best one depends on your type of work, team set-up and how predictable your requests are.

**Q: What is the difference between a Scrum Master and an Agile coach?**
A Scrum Master is accountable for Scrum's effectiveness in one Scrum Team (sometimes two or three). An Agile coach usually works more broadly, helping several teams and leaders adopt Agile across different frameworks.

**Q: Is Jira Agile or Scrum?**
Neither: [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is software that supports Agile ways of working. It offers both Scrum boards (with Sprints and backlogs) and Kanban boards. Compare options in our [project management tools ranking](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/).

**Q: Can Scrum be used outside software development?**
Yes. The 2020 Scrum Guide uses general language, and Scrum is used for marketing, research, product design, HR and other complex work. It works best where a team can deliver a usable result every Sprint.

**Q: Should I get an Agile or a Scrum certification?**
Choose a Scrum certification (such as PSM or CSM) if you work in or with Scrum teams, and an Agile-wide certification (such as PMI-ACP) if you manage projects using several approaches. See [how to learn Agile and get certified](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/).

**Q: What are the Scrum values?**
The Scrum Guide lists five values: commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. They support Scrum's three pillars of transparency, inspection and adaptation.

**Q: Does Agile mean no planning or documentation?**
No. Agile teams plan continuously, at the roadmap, release, sprint and daily levels, and they keep documentation that people actually use. They simply value working results and adaptation more highly.
