# Agile vs Waterfall: Differences and How to Choose

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Agile vs Waterfall compared: key differences, pros and cons, a suitability check, hybrid models and worked examples to help you choose an approach.


## Agile vs Waterfall: Differences and How to Choose
Agile vs Waterfall is a choice between two ways of running a project: Waterfall plans the whole project up front and delivers in sequential phases, while Agile delivers in short cycles and adapts the plan as the team learns. Neither is better in general; the right choice depends on how uncertain the work is and whether it can be delivered in pieces. This guide compares them side by side, gives you a scoring check for choosing, and shows illustrative worked examples of Agile, Waterfall and hybrid plans.
- Published 11 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Waterfall is a predictive approach: fix the scope, plan it in detail, then design, build and test in sequence. Agile is an adaptive approach: fix the timebox and team, and let scope evolve through feedback.
- Agile is a family of values and frameworks (Scrum, Kanban, XP, Lean), not a single method, so Agile vs Waterfall compares two philosophies rather than two rulebooks.
- Choose Waterfall for stable, regulated or physical work that only has value when complete; choose Agile when what you learn will change what you build and the result can be released in parts.
- A quick suitability check across culture, team and project factors turns the decision into a conversation with evidence rather than a matter of taste.
- Hybrid approaches are common and often the most practical: predictive governance and milestones with Agile delivery inside them.
- The PMBOK Guide 8th edition and the July 2026 PMP exam cover predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches, so practitioners are expected to know all three.

### What is the difference between Agile and Waterfall?
**The main difference between Agile and Waterfall is how they handle uncertainty.** Waterfall assumes requirements can be known at the start, so it plans everything first and completes each phase before the next. Agile assumes you will learn as you go, so it delivers working results in short iterations and re-plans after each one, letting scope change while time and cost stay fixed.
PMI calls these **predictive** and **adaptive** approaches, and a deliberate mix of the two **hybrid**. Waterfall is the classic predictive life cycle. Agile is an umbrella term for adaptive ways of working that share the values of the 2001 Agile Manifesto and are put into practice through frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban.
If you are choosing between Waterfall and a specific framework, our guides to [Scrum vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/) and [Kanban vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-waterfall/) go into that detail. This page stays at the level of approaches: how to choose, and how to combine the two.

### Agile vs Waterfall comparison table
| Aspect | Waterfall (predictive) | Agile (adaptive) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core assumption | Requirements can be known and fixed early | Requirements emerge as people see working results |
| Planning | Comprehensive plan up front, baselined | Rolling plans at several levels: roadmap, release, iteration |
| What is fixed | Scope; time and cost are estimated from it | Time and cost per iteration; scope flexes |
| Requirements | Detailed specification signed off before build | Prioritised backlog that is refined continuously |
| Delivery | One release at the end, or a few large ones | Small usable increments every iteration or continuously |
| Customer involvement | Heavy at the start and at acceptance | Regular, at every review |
| Handling change | Change requests, impact assessment, approval | New items enter the backlog and are re-prioritised |
| Testing | A separate phase after build | Built into every iteration |
| Risk | Reduced by analysis; many risks surface late | Reduced by short feedback loops; risks surface early |
| Documentation | Comprehensive, produced phase by phase | Just enough; working output is the main record |
| Progress measure | Milestones, % complete, earned value | Working increments, burn-up, velocity or throughput |
| Typical fit | Construction, infrastructure, hardware, regulated rollouts | Software, digital services, new products, marketing |

### What is Waterfall?
Waterfall is a sequential, plan-driven approach. A project moves through phases such as requirements, design, build, test and deployment, and each phase produces approved deliverables that feed the next. A gate at the end of each phase decides whether the project continues. Scope, schedule and cost are planned in detail, saved as a [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) and protected through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).

#### Where Waterfall came from
Phased development is older than the name: Herbert Benington described it for the SAGE air-defence system in 1956. Winston Royce's 1970 paper is usually cited as the first detailed diagram of the model, but Royce did not call it Waterfall and warned that a single pass with testing only at the end was risky, recommending feedback between phases. The term "waterfall" may first appear in a 1976 paper by Bell and Thayer, and the US defence standard DOD-STD-2167 (1985) required sequential phases, which helped make the model the default for large projects.
Before you commit to a fully sequential plan, it helps to know where Waterfall projects usually go wrong. Read our guide to [Waterfall project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) for the phases, gates, a worked example and how to reduce its weaknesses.

### What is Agile?
Agile is a set of values and principles for delivering work in small, usable increments with frequent feedback. It was named in the [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/), written by 17 software practitioners in 2001, which values individuals and interactions, working results, customer collaboration and responding to change over their more formal counterparts. Agile drew on earlier iterative methods, so the ideas are older than the label.
Agile is applied through frameworks. The most common are:
| Framework | How it works | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum | Fixed Sprints of one month or less, a Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers, and a usable Increment every Sprint (2020 Scrum Guide) | Complex product work with a clear goal and evolving requirements |
| Kanban | Continuous flow on a visual board with limits on work in progress | Steady streams of requests, support, operations, content |
| Extreme Programming (XP) | Engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development and continuous integration | Software teams that need high technical quality |
| Lean | Eliminate waste, optimise the whole flow of value, deliver fast | Process improvement and product development at any scale |
See [what is Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) for the full picture and [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/) for a deeper comparison of frameworks.

### The spectrum: predictive, iterative, incremental and adaptive
Agile vs Waterfall is not a binary switch. PMI's guidance describes a spectrum of life cycles, and the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) 8th edition (published November 2025) frames the choice as predictive, adaptive or hybrid development approaches. Two ideas sit between the extremes: **iterative** (repeat a cycle to refine the solution) and **incremental** (deliver the solution in usable pieces).
| Life cycle | Requirements | Delivery | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Predictive (Waterfall) | Fixed up front | Once, at the end | Building a warehouse to an approved design |
| Iterative | Refined through prototypes and feedback | Once, at the end, after several refinement loops | A new brand identity developed through rounds of concepts |
| Incremental | Mostly known, split into parts | In usable pieces, frequently | Rolling a new system out to one region at a time |
| Adaptive (Agile) | Emerge and change throughout | Small usable increments, frequently | A new mobile app shaped by user feedback each Sprint |
Agile combines iterative and incremental delivery. Our guide to [iterative and incremental development](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/iterative-and-incremental-development/) explains both ideas. The spectrum gives you a better question than "Agile or Waterfall?": how much of this project is known, and how much can be delivered in parts?

### The key differences explained

#### 1. The triple constraint is turned upside down
In Waterfall, scope is fixed first and time and cost are estimated from it. When estimates prove wrong, time and cost usually give way. Agile reverses this: a stable team and fixed iteration length make time and cost predictable, and scope flexes, with the most valuable items done first. If an Agile project runs out of money, it stops with the most valuable features already delivered; a Waterfall project that runs out may have nothing usable yet.

#### 2. Planning happens at different times
Waterfall front-loads planning: a work breakdown structure, schedule and cost estimate exist before the build starts. Agile still plans, but in layers and as late as is responsible: a roadmap, a release plan and detailed planning only for the next iteration. Our guide to [the role of the project plan in Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/role-of-the-project-plan-in-agile/) shows how those layers fit together.

#### 3. Change costs different amounts
In Waterfall, a change after sign-off may ripple through design, build and test, so it goes through impact assessment and approval. In Agile, the unbuilt part of the plan is kept deliberately light, so most changes are simply new or re-ordered backlog items. Agile does not make change free; it makes change cheaper by delaying detailed decisions until they are needed.

#### 4. Testing and quality
Waterfall tests in a dedicated phase after the build, and that phase is often squeezed when earlier phases overrun. Agile builds testing into every iteration through a [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) and acceptance criteria, so defects and misunderstood requirements are found within weeks.

#### 5. Risk surfaces at different points
Waterfall reduces risk through analysis and contingency, but integration and acceptance problems often appear late, when they are most expensive to fix. Agile exposes technical and product risk early by integrating working output and showing it to users every iteration.

#### 6. Stakeholders, documentation and leadership
Waterfall asks for intensive stakeholder input during requirements and at gates, produces comprehensive documents phase by phase, and usually has a project manager who plans and assigns the work. Agile asks for a little stakeholder time often, keeps documentation to what is needed to build, support and audit the product, and splits leadership: a product owner decides what to build and a cross-functional team decides how. If stakeholders cannot attend regular reviews, Agile loses much of its benefit.

### Pros and cons of Agile and Waterfall
|  | Waterfall | Agile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main advantages | Predictable scope, dates and budget when requirements are stable; clear milestones; thorough documentation; fits fixed-price contracts; lighter demand on stakeholders' time | Early and frequent value; problems found within weeks; change absorbed cheaply; quality built in; motivated, self-managing teams |
| Main disadvantages | Late feedback from users; expensive late change; risks found in testing; no value until the end; assumes requirements can be known early | Less up-front certainty about final scope; needs an empowered product owner and regular stakeholder time; harder to fit fixed-price contracts; relies on stable, dedicated teams |
| Biggest risk | Delivering exactly what was specified, on time, and finding it is not what users need | Delivering a stream of increments without a clear goal, so the product drifts |

### When to use Waterfall
Waterfall, or a predominantly predictive approach, is the better choice when most of these are true:
- **Requirements are clear and stable**, and the customer can describe the result in detail before work starts.
- **The product only has value when complete**, such as a bridge, a factory line or a physical installation.
- **Late change would be very expensive or unsafe**, for example once concrete is poured or hardware is manufactured.
- **Regulation or contracts demand it**: mandatory documentation, formal approvals or a fixed-price contract against a specification.
- **The team has done very similar projects before**, so estimates are reliable.
- **Stakeholders cannot commit regular time** and need to approve the plan once, then see milestones.
Typical examples are construction, civil engineering, infrastructure, office relocations, equipment installation and many compliance-driven system rollouts. Even here, parts of the work, such as interior design or software components, may benefit from an Agile approach.

### When to use Agile
Agile, or a predominantly adaptive approach, is the better choice when most of these are true:
- **The goal is clear but the best solution is not**, and the team will learn what works by building and testing.
- **Users or a product owner can give regular feedback.**
- **The result can be delivered and used in pieces**, so early releases create value or learning.
- **The environment is changing**: technology, competitors, regulation or customer needs are moving during the project.
- **Speed to first value matters** more than delivering everything at once.
- **The team is stable and cross-functional**, or can become so.
Typical examples are software products, websites and apps, digital services, data and analytics products, marketing campaigns, research and new product development. Agile is not limited to software; any work with uncertain requirements and usable increments can benefit.

### How to choose: a suitability check
PMI's Agile Practice Guide (published in 2017 with the Agile Alliance) includes a suitability filter that rates a project on culture, team and project factors and plots the answers on a radar chart: answers near the centre suggest Agile, answers at the edge suggest a predictive approach, and a mix suggests hybrid. The check below is our simplified adaptation for quick use; it is not PMI's exact tool.

#### Step by step
1. **Gather the right people:** the sponsor, a delivery lead and someone who represents users.
2. **Describe the project in two sentences:** the outcome, the deadline and any hard constraints such as regulation or a fixed contract.
3. **Score the nine questions below from 1 to 5.** Discuss each one and agree a score; disagreement is useful information.
4. **Total the scores and read the band**, then look at individual low scores, because one very low answer can matter more than the total.
5. **Decide how to handle the gaps.** A low score is a risk to manage, not automatically a veto. Poor access to users, for example, can be fixed by appointing a product owner.
6. **Record the decision and the reasons** in the project charter, and revisit it at the first major review.
| Area | Question | 1 (points to predictive) | 5 (points to Agile) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Culture | Does the sponsor actively support an adaptive approach? | Wants a fixed plan and sign-off | Actively backs short cycles and changing scope |
| Culture | Do sponsors trust the team to turn feedback into the right product? | Low trust; wants detailed control | High trust |
| Culture | Can the team make day-to-day decisions without escalation? | Most decisions go up the hierarchy | Team decides how to do the work |
| Team | How small and stable is the core team? | Large, part-time or changing | Stable team of about ten or fewer |
| Team | Does the team have experience with the work and the approach? | New to both | Experienced in both |
| Team | Can the team reach a user or business representative easily? | Weeks to get an answer | Daily access |
| Project | How likely are requirements to change? | Very stable | Very likely to change |
| Project | How safe is it to release early, imperfect versions? | Defects could cause serious harm | Low consequence; easy to fix |
| Project | Can the result be delivered and used in parts? | Only useful when complete | Easily split into usable increments |
| Total score | Suggested starting point |
| --- | --- |
| 9–20 | Predominantly predictive (Waterfall), possibly with prototypes or phased releases |
| 21–33 | Hybrid: predictive governance or components, with Agile delivery where uncertainty is highest |
| 34–45 | Predominantly Agile, using a framework such as Scrum or Kanban |
Tip
Ask one question if you have no time for a full check: how likely is it that what we learn during the project will change what we build? The higher that likelihood, the more adaptive your approach should be.

### Worked example: choosing an approach for three projects
The following example is **illustrative**: the organisation, scores and figures are invented to show how the suitability check works. A mid-sized insurance company has three projects starting in the same quarter.
- **Office relocation.** Move 220 staff to a new building by a fixed lease date. Fit-out design is approved; contractors are on fixed-price contracts.
- **Customer claims app.** Let customers submit and track claims on their phones. Nobody knows which features customers will actually use.
- **CRM replacement.** Replace an old customer database with a commercial CRM. Data migration and regulatory reporting are well defined; how sales teams will use the new screens is not.
| Question | Office relocation | Claims app | CRM replacement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sponsor support for adaptive approach | 2 | 5 | 3 |
| Trust in the team | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| Team decision-making | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| Small, stable team | 2 | 5 | 3 |
| Experience | 4 | 4 | 3 |
| Access to users | 2 | 5 | 4 |
| Likelihood of change | 1 | 5 | 3 |
| Safe to release early | 1 | 4 | 2 |
| Can be delivered in parts | 1 | 5 | 4 |
| **Total** | **18** | **41** | **29** |
| **Approach** | **Predictive** | **Agile** | **Hybrid** |

#### What the scores tell the team
- **Office relocation (18): predictive.** The design is fixed, the move cannot be half done and the lease date cannot move. The project manager builds a detailed schedule with a [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/), tracks dependencies and controls changes formally.
- **Claims app (41): Agile.** A cross-functional Scrum team works in two-week Sprints, releases a minimal version to a pilot group of customers early, and lets usage data shape the backlog. A [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) holds the ordered work.
- **CRM replacement (29): hybrid.** The low score on safe early release (regulatory reporting must be right first time) and the high score on delivering in parts point to a mix, shown in the hybrid plan in the next section.
Notice that the decision was made per project. A company can be "Agile" and still run its office move as a Waterfall project.

### Hybrid approaches: combining Agile and Waterfall
A hybrid approach deliberately mixes predictive and adaptive elements. It is common in large organisations, regulated industries and projects that combine physical and digital work. Some people call it "wagile" or "water-scrum-fall", sometimes as a criticism, but a well-designed hybrid is a legitimate approach recognised in the PMBOK Guide.

#### Four common hybrid patterns
| Pattern | How it works | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predictive governance, Agile delivery | A milestone plan, budget and stage gates at the top; teams deliver in Sprints within each stage | Organisations with formal funding and approval processes; see [PRINCE2 vs Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/prince2-vs-agile/) |
| Agile discovery, predictive rollout | Explore and prototype in short iterations, then plan the full rollout in detail once the solution is known | New services that must then be deployed widely, such as a new process across 40 branches |
| Split by component | Stable or physical components run predictively; uncertain components run in Sprints; they synchronise at integration milestones | Hardware plus software, buildings plus digital systems |
| Predictive front end, Agile build | Requirements and architecture agreed up front, then built and tested incrementally | Contracted software where the customer needs a baseline but wants early working releases |

#### Worked example: the CRM replacement as a hybrid plan
Continuing the **illustrative** example, the insurance company has a budget of £600,000 and 36 weeks. The fixed elements (data migration, regulatory reports, go-live date) are planned predictively; the sales screens and workflows are built in two-week Sprints with sales staff reviewing each Increment.
| Stage | Weeks | Approach | Gate or output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Initiation and vendor setup | 1–4 | Predictive | Business case, contract, architecture and data-migration plan approved |
| 2. Core configuration and migration design | 5–12 | Predictive for migration; Sprints 1–4 for sales workflows | Migration rules signed off; first usable sales pipeline screens demonstrated |
| 3. Build and test | 13–28 | Sprints 5–12; migration rehearsals in weeks 18 and 26 | Regulatory reports tested against the old system; sales workflows accepted by pilot team |
| 4. Cut-over and handover | 29–36 | Predictive | Final migration, training, go-live gate, support handover |
The project manager keeps one integrated plan showing milestones, migration tasks and Sprint boundaries, reports progress with a milestone chart and a burn-up of sales features, and agrees with the sponsor that lower-priority sales features may move to a post-launch release if the budget tightens. That agreement is what keeps the hybrid honest: the predictive parts protect the date and compliance, and the Agile parts protect usefulness.
Tip
Decide in advance which changes are routine backlog decisions and which need formal change control. A useful rule: anything that threatens a fixed milestone, compliance or the budget is a change request; everything else is a backlog decision.

### Contracts, budgets and reporting

#### Contracts
Waterfall fits a fixed-price contract against a detailed specification or statement of work: the supplier carries the risk of estimating, and changes are priced separately. Agile fits time-and-materials contracts or a **fixed budget with flexible scope**, where the customer buys a team for a period and the product owner decides what that capacity is spent on. A common middle ground is a fixed price per release, with the scope of later releases agreed as you learn.

#### Budgeting
A Waterfall budget is built bottom-up from the work breakdown structure and controlled against the baseline. An Agile budget is usually built from team capacity: in an illustrative case, a team of seven at a blended £5,000 per person per week costs £35,000 a week, so a 20-week release costs about £700,000. The question becomes how much value that capacity can deliver, and the forecast is refreshed every iteration.

#### Reporting progress
| Question sponsors ask | Waterfall answer | Agile answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Are we on schedule? | Milestones met vs the baseline; schedule variance | Release burn-up: scope completed vs scope planned for the date |
| Are we on budget? | Cost variance and [earned value](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) | Cost per iteration is fixed; forecast scope for the remaining budget |
| Is it any good? | Results of the test phase and acceptance | Working increments reviewed and used by real users |
| What are the risks? | Risk register and contingency | Risk register plus what each review revealed |
For the Agile measures, see our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).

### Moving from Waterfall to Agile
If your organisation mostly runs Waterfall projects, start with one pilot that scores high on the suitability check. Appoint a product owner with real authority, form a stable cross-functional team, turn the requirements into an ordered backlog and agree with governance what the sponsor will see each iteration. Run a few iterations and review honestly before scaling. If you are switching an existing project, do it at a natural boundary such as the start of a phase.
For an organisation-wide plan, use our guide on [how to implement Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-implement-agile/). See [Scrum vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/) for a project run both ways and for mapping Waterfall roles and documents to Scrum.

### Common mistakes when choosing between Agile and Waterfall
- **Treating it as a belief system.** Picking Agile because it is fashionable, or Waterfall because it feels safe, instead of looking at the project.
- **One approach for every project.** Organisations run many kinds of work; choose per project, or per component.
- **Calling no plan "Agile".** Agile teams still have goals, roadmaps, release plans and forecasts.
- **Running Waterfall in two-week chunks.** Sprints that hand designs to builders and builds to testers keep Waterfall's late feedback while adding meetings.
- **Fixing scope, time and cost all at once.** No approach can guarantee all three under uncertainty; decide which one flexes.
- **Over-engineering the hybrid.** Two full sets of controls on one project creates double reporting. Keep the predictive layer focused on what genuinely must be fixed.

### Tools for Agile, Waterfall and hybrid projects
Most modern project management tools support both approaches, but they lean in different directions.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool (9.4/10), suits hybrid work well: Gantt charts with dependencies for the predictive layer, boards and custom workflows for Agile teams, and dashboards that show both. It takes time to set up properly.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is the most complete Agile tool for software teams, with backlogs, Sprints and boards, but it does not offer a classic Gantt chart with critical path and baselines, so it is less suited to plan-driven projects.
- **monday.com, Asana and ClickUp** offer boards plus timeline or Gantt views for mixed portfolios; compare them in our [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) guide.
If you are not ready for software, our [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) covers a predictive plan and the [Agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/) covers releases and iterations. Raise formal changes on a hybrid project with the [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the main difference between Agile and Waterfall?**
Waterfall plans the whole project up front and delivers it in sequential phases, usually once at the end. Agile plans in layers and delivers working increments in short cycles, letting scope change as the team learns while time and cost per cycle stay fixed.

**Q: Which is better, Agile or Waterfall?**
Neither is better in general. Agile suits uncertain work that can be delivered in pieces and where users can give regular feedback. Waterfall suits stable, well-understood, regulated or physical work that only has value once complete. Many projects are best served by a hybrid.

**Q: Is Waterfall outdated?**
No. It remains the right choice for stable, regulated or physical projects such as construction and equipment installation. What has changed is that it is no longer the default for everything, especially software and digital products.

**Q: Is Scrum Agile or Waterfall?**
Scrum is an Agile framework. It delivers work in Sprints of one month or less, with a usable Increment each Sprint, as defined in the 2020 Scrum Guide. See Scrum vs Waterfall for a detailed comparison.

**Q: Can you combine Agile and Waterfall?**
Yes. A hybrid approach might use a Waterfall-style milestone plan, budget and stage gates for governance while teams deliver in Agile iterations, or run physical components predictively and software in Sprints. Decide in advance which changes need formal approval.

**Q: Can you switch from Waterfall to Agile mid-project?**
Yes, but do it at a natural boundary such as the start of a phase. Convert the remaining requirements into an ordered backlog, appoint a product owner, agree with the sponsor how progress will be reported, and start with short iterations.

**Q: What are examples of Waterfall projects?**
Construction, civil engineering, office relocations, equipment installation, hardware manufacturing and heavily regulated system implementations are classic examples, because requirements are fixed and partial results have little value.

**Q: Is Agile or Waterfall cheaper?**
Neither is inherently cheaper. Waterfall can look cheaper on paper because costs are estimated up front, but late changes and building features nobody uses can make it expensive. Agile needs more stakeholder time but reduces wasted work, and its cost per iteration is predictable.

**Q: How is testing different in Agile and Waterfall?**
In Waterfall, testing is usually a separate phase after the build. In Agile, testing happens within every iteration as part of the Definition of Done, so defects and misunderstandings are found sooner and fixed more cheaply.

**Q: Does the PMP exam cover Agile and Waterfall?**
Yes. PMI states that the PMP exam introduced in July 2026 covers predictive and Agile methods and hybrid applications, so candidates need to understand all three. See our [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) guide for the exam details.

# Agile Workflow: Stages, Examples and How to Design One

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-workflow/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: What an Agile workflow is, its stages, Scrum and Kanban examples, and a step-by-step way to design one with column policies, WIP limits and flow metrics.


## Agile Workflow: Stages, Examples and How to Design One
An Agile workflow is the sequence of states a piece of work moves through from idea to done, such as backlog, ready, in progress, review and done, usually shown as columns on a board. Making that path visible, agreeing rules for each step and limiting work in progress turns the board from a status display into a tool for finishing work faster. This guide explains the stages, compares Scrum and Kanban workflows, and walks you through designing your own with an illustrative example.
- Published 18 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- An Agile workflow describes how individual work items flow from start to finish. It is different from the Agile lifecycle (ideation to retirement) and from the cadence of Sprint events.
- Design the workflow from how work really happens today, not from an ideal process. Map the current steps first, then improve them.
- Every column needs an entry policy: a short rule stating what must be true before a card can move in. Policies make quality and readiness explicit.
- Work-in-progress (WIP) limits are what make a board a management tool. When a column is full, the team helps finish work downstream instead of starting more.
- Measure flow with four metrics from the Kanban Guide: WIP, throughput, work item age and cycle time. Review them in retrospectives and change one thing at a time.
- Scrum, Kanban and Scrumban teams all use workflows; they differ in cadence, how the board resets and how WIP is controlled.

### What is an Agile workflow?
**An Agile workflow is the series of states that a unit of work passes through, from the moment a team commits to it to the moment it is finished.** It is usually shown as columns on a board, with explicit rules for moving between states and limits on work in progress, so the team can see and improve flow.
The idea comes from two places. Scrum Teams use a board to make their Sprint Backlog visible. Kanban teams treat the workflow itself as the thing to manage, with the goal of moving work through it smoothly and predictably. Most modern teams borrow from both.
A visible workflow helps in three ways:
- **Transparency.** Everyone can see what is being worked on, what is waiting and what is blocked, without a status meeting.
- **Focus on finishing.** Limiting work in progress shifts attention from starting new items to completing the ones already started.
- **Improvement.** When the workflow is explicit, you can measure it, spot bottlenecks and test changes.
If you are new to boards, start with our guide to [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/), which explains columns, cards and swimlanes.

### Agile workflow vs lifecycle vs process
Search for 'Agile workflow' and you will find pages describing three different things. They all matter, but they answer different questions.
| Level | Question it answers | Typical stages | Time scale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Product or project lifecycle | Where is the whole product in its life? | Ideation, inception, iteration, release, maintenance, retirement | Months to years |
| Delivery cadence | When does the team plan, inspect and adapt? | Backlog refinement, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Retrospective | Days to weeks |
| Work item workflow | Where is this piece of work right now? | Backlog, ready, in progress, review, done | Hours to days |
This guide focuses on the third level, the work item workflow, because it is the one teams configure on a board and change week to week. For the first level, see our guide to the [Agile development life cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-development-life-cycle/). The second level is set by your framework, such as the Scrum events.

### The stages of a typical Agile workflow
Most Agile workflows start from five stages. The entry policies below are examples; write your own to match your team's quality standards.
| Stage | What it means | Example entry policy | Usually pulled by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Backlog | Ideas and requests, ordered by priority | Has a clear title and a requester | Product Owner adds and orders |
| Ready | Refined and ready to start | Acceptance criteria written, estimated, no open blocking questions | Product Owner with the team |
| In progress | Actively being worked on | Someone has capacity and the column is under its WIP limit | Developers or team members |
| Review or test | Being checked against acceptance criteria | All tasks complete; automated tests pass | A different team member or reviewer |
| Done | Meets the Definition of Done | Accepted and, ideally, released or ready to release | Team, confirmed by the Product Owner where needed |
Some teams add **Released** or **Live** after Done to separate 'finished by us' from 'in users' hands'. Others split Backlog into **Options** (not yet committed) and **Committed** so stakeholders can see what is actually planned. The [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) is effectively the exit policy for the whole workflow.
What moves through the workflow? Usually user stories, bugs and other backlog items. Tasks inside a story often go on a separate task board or checklist. Our guide to [epics vs stories vs tasks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/) explains which level belongs where.

### Elements of a well-defined workflow
The Kanban Guide by John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti (edition 2025.5, May 2025) sets out a minimum **Definition of Workflow** that any team, Kanban or not, can use as a checklist. According to the guide, it should state:
1. **The units of value** that move through the workflow, called work items. Decide whether these are stories, tickets, requests or something else.
2. **When work items are started and finished.** Agree the exact points. 'Started' might be when an item enters Ready or In progress; 'finished' might be Done or Released.
3. **One or more defined states** between started and finished, such as development, review and test.
4. **How WIP will be controlled**, for example column limits, a limit for the whole board or a limit per person.
5. **Explicit policies** for how items flow through each state, such as entry rules and who can move a card.
6. **A service level expectation (SLE)**: a forecast of how long an item should take from start to finish, with a probability, for example '85% of items finish within 8 days'.
The guide adds three practices: defining and visualising the workflow, actively managing items in it, and improving it. The rest of this page follows that order.
Tip
Write your Definition of Workflow on one page and pin it to the board. New team members learn the rules in minutes, and arguments about whether a card 'should' move become a quick check against the policy.

### Scrum, Kanban and Scrumban workflows compared
All three approaches use a visible workflow. They differ in how often the board resets and how work in progress is controlled.
|  | Scrum workflow | Kanban workflow | Scrumban workflow |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cadence | Fixed Sprints of one month or less | Continuous flow; cadences chosen by the team | Regular planning and review, continuous flow inside |
| What is on the board | Items in the current Sprint Backlog | All work in the system | Work in the system, often with a planning trigger |
| Board resets? | Usually at the start of each Sprint | No | No; the Ready column is refilled when it falls below a threshold |
| How WIP is limited | Indirectly, through the Sprint forecast | Explicit WIP limits per column or workflow | Explicit WIP limits |
| Adding work mid-cycle | Only if it does not endanger the Sprint Goal | Whenever there is capacity | Whenever there is capacity |
| Typical metrics | Sprint Goal achieved, velocity, burndown | WIP, throughput, cycle time, work item age | Both sets |
A Scrum board and a Kanban board can look almost identical. The difference is how the team uses them. Our guides to [Scrum boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) and [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) cover the trade-offs in more depth.

### How to design an Agile workflow, step by step
Allow 60 to 90 minutes with the whole team for the first version. Use a whiteboard or a blank board in your tool.
1. **Agree the unit of work.** Decide what a card represents (a story, a request, a ticket) and roughly how big it should be. Mixed sizes make metrics hard to read.
2. **Map the current process.** Take three or four recently finished items and trace every step they went through, including hand-offs and waiting. Draw what actually happened, not what the process document says. A quick [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) helps here.
3. **Set the start and finish points.** Mark where the team commits to an item (the start of your cycle time) and where it is truly finished.
4. **Choose the states.** Turn the steps into columns. Combine steps that always happen together and drop any that add nothing. Most teams end up with four to seven columns.
5. **Show waiting explicitly.** Split busy columns into 'doing' and 'done' sub-columns, or add a 'waiting for' column, so queues are visible instead of hidden inside 'In progress'.
6. **Write entry policies.** For each column, write one to three rules a card must meet to enter it. Keep them short enough to fit on the column header.
7. **Set WIP limits.** Start with a limit per active column of roughly the number of people who work in that column, or slightly more, then adjust from experience.
8. **Add swimlanes or classes of service if needed.** An expedite lane with a limit of one handles genuine emergencies; lanes per product area or work type help larger teams. See our guide to [Kanban swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/).
9. **Agree how you will measure.** Record the date each item starts and finishes so you can calculate cycle time and throughput from day one. After a few weeks, use the data to set a service level expectation.
10. **Review and evolve.** Inspect the workflow in every [retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) or monthly review. Change one thing at a time and watch the metrics.
Our free [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/) helps you map the current process with steps, owners, inputs and outputs, and the [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) gives you ready-made columns with WIP limits.

### Worked example: redesigning a product team's board
This illustrative example follows a team of six (four developers, one tester and one designer) building a customer portal.

#### Before
The board has three columns: To do, In progress and Done. In a typical week, about 18 items sit in In progress and the team finishes about 6 items. Stakeholders complain that nothing seems to finish, and the tester is overwhelmed at the end of every fortnight.
A quick calculation shows why. Little's Law says that, in a reasonably stable system, average cycle time equals average WIP divided by average throughput. With 18 items in progress and 6 finished per week, the average item takes about **3 weeks** from start to finish.

#### Mapping the real process
Tracing four recent items shows the real steps: refine, design (for some items), develop, code review, test, Product Owner acceptance, release. Much of the 3 weeks was waiting: for review, for the tester, and for acceptance.

#### After
| Column | Entry policy | WIP limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backlog | Ordered by the Product Owner | None |
| Ready | Acceptance criteria agreed; design attached if needed; estimated | 8 |
| Development: doing | A developer has capacity | 4 |
| Development: done | Code complete, unit tests pass | Shared with the column above |
| Code review | Pull request opened | 2 |
| Test | Review approved, deployed to test environment | 3 |
| Acceptance | All acceptance criteria pass | 2 |
| Done | Meets the Definition of Done; released or in the next release | None |
An expedite swimlane with a limit of one handles urgent production fixes. Developers agree that when Code review or Test is full, they help review or test before starting new work.

#### Result
The active columns now hold at most 11 items. If throughput stays at about 6 items per week, Little's Law suggests an average cycle time of under 2 weeks (11 ÷ 6 ≈ 1.8 weeks), without anyone working harder. In practice, finishing work sooner often raises throughput too, because there is less context switching. After six weeks of recorded data, the team sets a service level expectation from its own cycle times, such as '85% of items finish within 10 working days', and reviews it monthly.
Tip
Little's Law describes averages in a stable system. Use it to understand why too much WIP slows everything down, not as a precise forecast for an individual item.

### Agile workflow examples by team
Agile workflows are not only for software. The stages change, but the principles of visible states, policies and WIP limits stay the same.
| Team | Example workflow | Useful policy or limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Software development | Backlog → Ready → Develop → Code review → Test → Done → Released | Code review limit of 2 so reviews do not pile up |
| Marketing | Ideas → Brief ready → Creating → Review → Scheduled → Live | Nothing enters Creating without an approved brief |
| Customer support | New → Triage → In progress → Waiting on customer → Resolved | Separate lane for urgent tickets with a response-time target |
| Recruitment | Open roles → Sourcing → Screening → Interviewing → Offer → Hired | Limit open roles per recruiter |
| Creative or design | Requests → Briefed → Concept → Internal review → Client review → Final | Two review rounds before escalation |
| IT operations | Requests → Triage → Planned → Implementing → Verifying → Closed | Changes need an approved change record before Implementing |
| PMO or project intake | Submitted → Assessed → Approved → In delivery → Closed | Business case attached before Assessed |
Non-software teams often find the 'waiting' states the most revealing. A marketing team that tracks 'Waiting for legal review' explicitly can show exactly how much time is lost there. See our guide to [Agile marketing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/) for more on running marketing work this way.

### WIP limits in practice
A work-in-progress limit caps how many items can be in a column, a group of columns or the whole workflow at once. Limits create a pull system: work moves forward only when the next step has room, which exposes bottlenecks quickly.

#### Setting the first limits
- Count the people who work in each active column and start with a limit equal to that number or slightly above it.
- For shared steps such as review, start low (two or three) so queues are noticed early.
- Apply a limit to 'doing' and 'done' sub-columns together, so finished work waiting for the next step still counts.
- Do not limit the Backlog or Done columns.

#### When a column is full
1. Stop starting new work in the upstream column.
2. Look right on the board: can you help finish, review or test something already in progress?
3. If an item is blocked, swarm on the blocker or escalate it.
4. If a limit is constantly hit and nobody can help, discuss in the retrospective whether the limit, the policy or the team's skills mix needs to change.
Treat breaking a limit as a signal to discuss, not a crime. Our guide to [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) covers more ways to set and adjust them.

### Measuring and improving your workflow
The Kanban Guide names four flow measures. Together they tell you whether work is flowing smoothly.
| Metric | Definition | What to look for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WIP | Number of items started but not finished | Rising WIP usually means rising cycle times |
| Throughput | Number of items finished per unit of time | Stable or rising throughput shows predictability |
| Work item age | Time since an item started, for items still in progress | Old items are at risk; discuss them in the Daily Scrum |
| Cycle time | Time from start to finish for completed items | Use percentiles (for example the 85th) to set expectations |
[Cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) and [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) look backwards; work item age looks at what is happening now, which makes a [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) one of the most useful daily views. A [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) shows how much work sits in each state over time: a widening band means a queue is growing.
You can also calculate [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/): active working time divided by total cycle time. If an item took 10 days and someone actively worked on it for 2, its flow efficiency is 20%. Low figures are common and point to waiting, not slow people.

#### Questions for your next retrospective
- Where do cards pile up, and why?
- Which items aged far beyond our usual cycle time, and what held them up?
- How often do cards move backwards (for example from Test to Develop)? What would prevent that?
- Are any policies ignored? Should we enforce them or change them?
- What is one change we will try before the next review?
See our guide to [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) for charts and calculations, and [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) for Scrum-specific measures.

### Automating your workflow in tools
A physical board works well for co-located teams, but most teams now run their workflow in software. Whatever tool you use, configure it to match the workflow you designed rather than adopting its default columns.
- **Statuses and columns:** create a status for each state and map statuses to board columns.
- **WIP limits:** many tools let you set column limits; check whether yours blocks moves or only warns.
- **Automation rules:** for example, move a card to Code review when a pull request opens, assign the reviewer, or notify the requester when an item reaches Done.
- **Required fields:** enforce entry policies by requiring fields such as acceptance criteria before a status change.
- **Reporting:** turn on cycle time, throughput or cumulative flow reports, or export dates to a spreadsheet.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, suits organisations that want custom workflows, request forms and cross-project dashboards in one place, and its board view is available even on the Free plan. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is the most complete option for software teams that need Scrum and Kanban boards with configurable workflows. [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) is strong for visual, easy-to-adopt workflows across non-technical teams, and [Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/) is a simple way to start with Kanban boards.
Whichever tool you choose, set up the workflow on paper first. Teams that start from a tool's default template often end up with columns that do not match their work, and then stop trusting the board.

### Who owns and changes the workflow
The workflow belongs to the people who do the work. In Scrum, the Developers own the Sprint Backlog and how they organise it, so they decide the columns, policies and limits. The Scrum Master helps the team see problems in the flow and coaches them to improve it, and the Product Owner influences what enters the workflow through the order of the Product Backlog.
Stakeholders and managers should be able to see the board and its metrics, but they should not add columns or bypass WIP limits without the team. If a stakeholder needs a different view, such as a status summary across several teams, create a report or dashboard rather than changing the team's workflow.
Agree a simple rule for changes: anyone can propose one, the team decides at its next retrospective or review, and the change is written into the policies on the board.

### Agile workflow checklist
Use this checklist when you set up a new board or audit an existing one.
- Everyone can say what one card represents.
- Start and finish points are agreed and recorded with dates.
- Columns reflect real steps, including waiting states.
- Each column has a written entry policy.
- Active columns have WIP limits, and the team knows what to do when one is full.
- Blocked items are marked visibly and discussed daily.
- The Definition of Done is visible and used as the final exit policy.
- Cycle time, throughput, work item age and WIP are tracked.
- A service level expectation is set from the team's own data.
- The workflow is reviewed at least once a month.

### Common Agile workflow mistakes
| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Designing the ideal process instead of the real one | Cards skip columns or sit in the wrong place | Map current work first; improve from there |
| One giant 'In progress' column | Queues and blockers are invisible | Split into real steps and add 'done' sub-columns |
| No WIP limits | Many items started, few finished; long cycle times | Add limits to active columns and stop starting when they are full |
| Too many columns | Cards move every hour; board is hard to read | Merge steps that always happen together |
| Unwritten policies | Arguments about whether work is ready or done | Write entry policies on each column |
| Ignoring blocked items | Cards sit for days unnoticed | Mark blockers visibly and review work item age daily |
| Changing many things at once | No one knows which change helped | Change one thing, then observe for a few weeks |
| Using the board for status reporting only | Board is updated just before meetings | Make the board the place where work is pulled and discussed |
If your workflow keeps growing more complex, step back and ask whether it reflects one team's work or several. Splitting a board by team or value stream is often simpler than adding more columns. For the wider differences between flow-based and phase-based approaches, read our comparison of [Agile vs waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an Agile workflow?**
The series of stages work passes through from commitment to done, such as backlog, ready, in progress, review and done, usually shown as columns on a board with policies and WIP limits.

**Q: What are the stages of an Agile workflow?**
A typical flow is backlog, ready, in progress, review or test, and done. Many teams add released, waiting or acceptance states. Adapt the stages to how your work actually happens.

**Q: What are the phases of the Agile lifecycle?**
Commonly described phases are ideation, inception, iteration, release, maintenance and retirement. The lifecycle covers a whole product, while a workflow describes how individual work items move.

**Q: How do you create an Agile workflow?**
Agree the unit of work, map how work really flows today, set start and finish points, choose states, show waiting, write column policies, set WIP limits, record dates for metrics and review regularly.

**Q: Is an Agile workflow the same as a Kanban board?**
Not quite. The workflow is the set of states and rules; a Kanban board is the most common way to visualise it. Scrum Teams use similar boards for their Sprint Backlog.

**Q: How many columns should an Agile board have?**
As few as possible to show the real stages. Most teams use four to seven columns, plus sub-columns where waiting time matters.

**Q: What is a WIP limit?**
A cap on how many items can be in a workflow stage at once. When a column is full, the team helps finish work downstream instead of starting more.

**Q: What are column policies?**
Short, explicit rules stating what must be true for a card to enter or leave a column, such as having acceptance criteria before moving to Ready.

**Q: What is a service level expectation?**
A forecast of how long a work item should take from start to finish, with a probability, for example '85% of items finish within 8 days'. The Kanban Guide includes it in the Definition of Workflow.

**Q: What is the difference between a Scrum and a Kanban workflow?**
A Scrum board usually shows the current Sprint's items and resets each Sprint, with WIP controlled through the Sprint forecast. A Kanban workflow is continuous and uses explicit WIP limits.

**Q: How do you measure an Agile workflow?**
Track WIP, throughput, work item age and cycle time. A cumulative flow diagram and a WIP aging chart help you spot queues and stuck items.

**Q: How is an Agile workflow different from a waterfall workflow?**
A waterfall workflow moves the whole project through phases in sequence. An Agile workflow moves many small items through short, repeated stages, so value is delivered and feedback gathered continuously.

**Q: Can non-software teams use an Agile workflow?**
Yes. Marketing, support, HR, recruitment, design and operations teams all use boards with stages that reflect their own work.

**Q: What is a swimlane in an Agile workflow?**
A horizontal row that separates types of work, such as an expedite lane for urgent items or a lane per product area.

# Definition of Done in Agile: Meaning, Examples and Checklist

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: What the Definition of Done is in Agile and Scrum, how it differs from acceptance criteria, examples for software and non-software teams.


## Definition of Done in Agile: Meaning, Examples and Checklist
The Definition of Done (DoD) is the shared checklist that every piece of work must meet before a team can call it finished. It stops "done" from meaning different things to different people, and it protects quality sprint after sprint.
- Published 14 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- The Definition of Done is a shared quality checklist for all work.
- Acceptance criteria are specific to one item; the DoD applies to every item.
- Keep it short, visible and improving.

### What the Definition of Done is
In Scrum, the Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality standards required for the product. Work that does not meet it is not done, cannot be released and does not count towards velocity. The Definition of Done is the commitment attached to the Increment.

### Definition of Done vs acceptance criteria
|  | Definition of Done | Acceptance criteria |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Applies to | Every backlog item | One specific item |
| Describes | Quality standards for all work | What this item must do |
| Written by | The team (and organisation standards) | Product Owner with the team |
| Example | Code reviewed, tested, documented | A user can reset their password by email |
An item is complete only when it meets both its acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done.

### Example: software team
- Code written and peer reviewed.
- Automated tests written and passing.
- Integrated into the main branch without breaking the build.
- Meets agreed security and accessibility checks.
- User-facing text reviewed.
- Product Owner has seen it working.

### Example: marketing or content team
- Copy approved by the editor.
- Brand and legal checks completed.
- Links and tracking tested.
- Published or scheduled in the correct channel.
- Results dashboard set up.

### How to create and evolve your Definition of Done
1. Start with your organisation's quality standards, if any.
2. Hold a short workshop with the team: "What must be true before we'd be happy to release this?"
3. Keep it short enough to check every time; a handful of items is usually enough.
4. Make it visible on your board.
5. Review it in retrospectives and tighten it as the team matures.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Who owns the Definition of Done?**
If the organisation has a standard, all teams follow it as a minimum. Otherwise the Scrum Team creates its own.

**Q: Can the Definition of Done change?**
Yes. Teams usually strengthen it over time. Any change applies to future work, and teams should be honest about work that was done to an older standard.

**Q: What is the Definition of Done in Agile?**
A shared checklist of quality standards that every piece of work must meet before it counts as complete. In Scrum it is the commitment attached to the Increment.

**Q: What is the difference between Definition of Done and acceptance criteria?**
The Definition of Done applies to every backlog item and describes general quality standards; acceptance criteria apply to one item and describe what it must do. An item needs both.

**Q: What is the Definition of Ready compared with the Definition of Done?**
An optional checklist some teams use to decide when a backlog item is clear enough to bring into a sprint. Unlike the Definition of Done, it is not part of the Scrum Guide.

**Q: What should be in a Definition of Done?**
Typical items include peer review, testing, integration, documentation where needed, security or accessibility checks and Product Owner review. Keep it short enough to check every time.

**Q: What happens if an item does not meet the Definition of Done?**
It is not done. It cannot be released or counted in velocity and returns to the Product Backlog for re-ordering.

**Q: Is the Definition of Done the same for all teams?**
If several teams work on the same product, they share one Definition of Done. Each can add stricter standards of its own.

**Q: Where should the Definition of Done be displayed?**
Somewhere the team sees it daily, such as on the board or in the team's tool, so it is used during work rather than forgotten.

**Q: Does the Definition of Done apply to non-software teams?**
Yes. A marketing team might require editor approval, brand and legal checks and tested links before a piece counts as done.

**Q: How does the Definition of Done relate to velocity?**
Only items that meet the Definition of Done count towards [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/). Partially finished work counts as zero.
