# Epics vs Stories vs Tasks: Agile Hierarchy With Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Epics vs stories vs tasks explained: definitions, a comparison table, a worked example, how to break epics down, Jira naming and common mistakes.


## Epics vs Stories vs Tasks: Agile Hierarchy With Examples
Epics vs stories vs tasks is a question about size and purpose: an epic is a large goal that spans several Sprints, a user story is a small slice of value for a user that fits in one Sprint, and a task is a technical step the team takes to finish a story. Together they turn a broad objective into work people can pick up today. This guide compares the three levels, shows a full worked example, explains how Jira and other tools name them, and gives you a step-by-step way to break work down.
- Published 6 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Epics hold goals, user stories hold value and tasks hold steps. Only epics and stories describe something a user or customer can benefit from; a task on its own does not.
- Typical sizes: an epic runs for several Sprints, a story fits comfortably inside one Sprint, and a task takes a day or less.
- The Product Owner or product manager shapes epics and stories with the team; the Developers create tasks, usually in Sprint Planning and during the Sprint.
- In Jira, a Task is a peer of a Story, not a child of it. The step inside a story is a Sub-task. Agree which meaning your team uses.
- The hierarchy is a widely used convention, not part of the Scrum Guide. Scrum only defines Product Backlog items, so keep the structure as simple as your work allows.
- Break work down progressively: refine the next few Sprints in detail and leave later epics rough until you know more.

### What are epics, stories and tasks?
**Epics, user stories and tasks are three levels of an Agile backlog.** An epic is a large body of work with one goal, delivered over several Sprints. A user story is a small, user-focused piece of that goal that fits in one Sprint. A task is a technical step, usually a day or less, that completes a story.
The levels exist because no one can start work on something as vague as 'improve onboarding'. Splitting work from big to small lets the Product Owner discuss outcomes with stakeholders while the Developers plan concrete work for the next few days.

#### Epic
An [epic](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/) is a container for related stories that share one goal, such as 'Online class booking' or 'Self-service password reset'. It is too big to finish in one Sprint, so it is split into stories before anyone starts building. Good epics have a clear outcome and a way to tell when they are finished, for example 'members can book, cancel and join waiting lists online, and at least half of bookings are made without staff'.

#### User story
A [user story](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) describes a small piece of functionality from the point of view of the person who benefits. The common format is 'As a [type of user], I want [capability] so that [benefit]', backed by acceptance criteria that define when it works. A story should be small enough that the team can finish several in one Sprint, and valuable enough that a user would notice if it shipped.

#### Task
A task is a unit of work the team does to complete a story: build the screen, add the database field, write the tests, update the help text. Tasks are written by and for the Developers. They make progress visible during the Sprint but do not deliver value on their own: a finished database migration with no working feature on top helps no one yet.
Tip
These terms are conventions, not standards. The 2020 Scrum Guide does not mention epics, stories or tasks; it only describes Product Backlog items and a Sprint Backlog. Many teams find the three-level hierarchy useful, but you are free to name the levels differently as long as everyone agrees.

### The Agile work hierarchy at a glance
Most organisations add one or two levels above epics to connect day-to-day work with strategy. The table shows the common levels from largest to smallest.
| Level | What it is | Typical horizon | Usually written by | Where it appears |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Theme or initiative | A strategic objective or focus area that groups several epics | Several months to a year or more | Leadership, product management | Strategy, OKRs, portfolio roadmap |
| Epic | A large body of work with one goal | Several Sprints, often within a quarter | Product Owner or product manager | Product roadmap, release plan |
| Feature (optional) | A distinct capability, used between epic and story in SAFe and some tools | One to a few Sprints | Product Owner or product manager | Release plan, Program Backlog |
| User story | A small slice of value for a user | A few days; fits in one Sprint | Product Owner with the team | Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog |
| Task (sub-task) | A technical step to complete a story | Hours to one day | The Developers doing the work | Sprint Backlog, task board |
Not every team needs every level; a small team may track tasks as checklists. Large programmes using the [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) define their own levels (epics, features and stories) and give 'epic' a larger meaning than most single teams do, so check which definition people are using before you compare sizes.
The idea resembles a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/), except that an Agile backlog is broken down progressively, a few Sprints ahead, rather than all at once.

### Epics vs stories vs tasks: key differences
The quickest way to tell the levels apart is to ask who benefits, how big it is and how you know it is done.
|  | Epic | User story | Task |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Group related stories under one goal | Deliver value a user can see or use | Complete one step of a story |
| Point of view | Business or user outcome | A specific user | The team or the technology |
| Delivers value on its own? | Yes, once enough stories are done | Yes | No |
| Typical size | Several Sprints | A few days; fits in one Sprint | Hours to one day |
| Estimated in | T-shirt size or the sum of its story points | Story points or similar relative units | Hours, or not estimated at all |
| Written by | Product Owner or product manager | Product Owner with the team and stakeholders | Developers |
| Done when | Its goal is met (not necessarily every story) | Acceptance criteria and Definition of Done are met | The step is complete |
| Lives in | Roadmap and release plan | Product and Sprint Backlogs | Sprint Backlog and task board |

#### Epic vs user story
The difference is mainly size and specificity. An epic says what you want to achieve ('online class booking'); a story says exactly what one type of user will be able to do next ('as a member, I want to cancel a booking so that someone else can take my place'). If the team cannot estimate an item with reasonable confidence or finish it in one Sprint, it is behaving like an epic and needs splitting.

#### User story vs task
The difference is value. Ask: 'If we stopped after this item, would a user notice anything?' If yes, it is a story. If the answer is 'no, but it is a step towards something they will notice', it is a task. 'Add a cancel button and release the place' is a story. 'Create the cancellations table' is a task.
See our guide to [writing user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) for formats, acceptance criteria and examples.

### What 'task' means in Jira and other tools
The word 'task' causes more confusion than any other term on this page, because tools use it in two ways.
- **In the generic Agile hierarchy** (and on this page), a task is a step inside a story. Teams create several per story.
- **In Jira**, the default hierarchy has three levels. Epics sit at the top. Stories, Tasks and Bugs sit together on the middle level as peers. Sub-tasks sit at the bottom and can belong to any of them. A Jira Task is therefore not a child of a Story; it is a piece of work that is not written from a user's point of view, such as renewing a certificate or setting up a test environment. The step inside a story is a Sub-task.
Atlassian's documentation says additional levels above epics, such as initiatives, are available on Jira Premium. Jira now calls issues 'work items'. Our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) covers its hierarchy, boards and pricing in detail.
A simple rule works in most tools: **user value = story; necessary work with no direct user value = task (peer of a story); a step to finish a story = sub-task.**

#### How common tools name the levels
General work management tools do not have built-in epics and stories, so teams map the levels onto their own structure. The mappings below are common choices rather than vendor rules.
| Tool | Native structure | A common way to map epic / story / task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jira | Epic, then Story, Task and Bug as peers, then Sub-task | Epic / Story / Sub-task (Task for non-user work) |
| Wrike | Spaces, folders, projects, tasks and subtasks | Project or parent task / task / subtask, with custom item types and fields |
| Asana | Teams, projects, tasks and subtasks | Project or parent task / task / subtask |
| ClickUp | Spaces, folders, lists, tasks and nested subtasks | List or parent task / task / subtask, with sprint points switched on |
| monday.com | Workspaces, boards, groups, items and subitems | Group or board / item / subitem (monday dev adds dedicated sprint tools) |
If your organisation needs Agile delivery alongside portfolio planning, resource management and request intake in one place, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, handles the hierarchy well through custom item types and cross-project views. Software teams that live in backlogs and story points often prefer [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/), and [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) and [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) both work well for mixed teams. Compare options side by side in our [project management tool comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/).

### Worked example: from initiative to tasks
This illustrative example follows one piece of work for a fictional gym chain from strategy down to the tasks a developer picks up on a Tuesday morning.

#### Initiative
**Increase class attendance through self-service.** Today members book classes by phone or at reception, staff spend hours on bookings, and popular classes have no-shows while others have queues.

#### Epic
**Online class booking.** Goal: members can find, book and cancel classes online, and empty places are refilled from a waiting list. Success measure (set by the Product Owner): most bookings made online within three months of launch. Out of scope for now: paid classes and personal training.

#### User stories in the epic
| # | User story | Estimate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | As a member, I want to see the class timetable with remaining places so that I can choose a class that has space | 3 points |
| 2 | As a member, I want to book a place in a class so that it is reserved for me | 5 points |
| 3 | As a member, I want to cancel a booking so that someone else can take my place | 3 points |
| 4 | As a member, I want to join a waiting list for a full class so that I get a place if one becomes free | 5 points |
| 5 | As a member, I want a reminder two hours before class so that I do not forget | 2 points |
| 6 | As an instructor, I want to see who has booked my class so that I can check people in | 3 points |
The epic totals 21 points. If the team usually completes 20 to 25 points per Sprint and also has other work, the Product Owner can expect the epic to take roughly two Sprints. That forecast belongs in [release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/), not in a promise.

#### Acceptance criteria for story 2
- Given a class has places left, when a member taps Book, then the place is reserved and the remaining count drops by one.
- Given a class is full, when a member views it, then the Book button is replaced by Join waiting list.
- Given a member already has a booking for that class, when they try to book again, then they see a message and no second booking is created.
- The member receives an on-screen and email confirmation.

#### Tasks for story 2
In Sprint Planning, the Developers break story 2 into tasks:
| Task | Estimate |
| --- | --- |
| Build the Book button and confirmation screen | 4 hours |
| Add the booking endpoint with a capacity check | 6 hours |
| Prevent duplicate bookings for the same member and class | 3 hours |
| Send the confirmation email | 2 hours |
| Write automated tests for available, full and duplicate cases | 4 hours |
| Update the timetable to show the new remaining count | 2 hours |
| Accessibility and mobile check | 1 hour |
Notice what changed at each level: the initiative explains why, the epic sets a goal and boundary, each story is usable by a member or instructor, and each task fits in a day. When every task is done, the story is checked against its acceptance criteria and the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/). When enough stories are done to meet the goal, the epic closes, even if story 5 (reminders) is still in the backlog.
Want to set this up for your own team? Our free [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) includes fields for the epic, the story, acceptance criteria, estimate and priority.

### How to break an epic down, step by step
Use this process whenever a new epic reaches the top of the roadmap. It works for software and non-software teams alike.
1. **Start from an outcome.** Take an objective from the [Agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) and state the problem, the users affected and how you will measure success.
2. **Write the epic.** Give it a short name, a one-sentence goal, a success measure and an explicit list of what is out of scope. The boundary stops the epic growing for ever.
3. **Map the user journey.** List the steps users take, left to right (find a class, book, attend, cancel). Under each step, note the things users need. This story map shows the whole epic on one page.
4. **Slice into stories.** Turn each need into a story using the 'As a / I want / so that' format, or a plain sentence if your team prefers. Use the splitting patterns in the next section when a story is too large.
5. **Choose a thin first release.** Pick the smallest set of stories that delivers the goal end to end, even crudely. Everything else becomes a later, lower-priority story.
6. **Refine the top stories.** In [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/), add acceptance criteria, discuss risks and check each story against INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable (a checklist credited to Bill Wake).
7. **Estimate.** Size the stories relatively with [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/) or another unit. Large or uncertain items go back for further splitting.
8. **Order the backlog.** The Product Owner places the ready stories in the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) according to value, risk and dependencies.
9. **Create tasks in Sprint Planning.** The Developers pull stories into the Sprint and break them into tasks of a day or less. This is the plan for how they will deliver the Sprint Goal.
10. **Track and close.** Update tasks daily on the [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/), close each story when it meets its criteria, and close the epic when its goal is met.
Tip
Do not break every epic down on day one. Refine stories for the next two or three Sprints in detail and leave later epics as one-line placeholders. You will know more by the time you reach them.

### Story-splitting patterns with examples
Most teams struggle less with writing stories than with making them small enough. These patterns split a large story while keeping each piece valuable to a user. The examples use the gym booking epic.
| Pattern | Split by | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workflow steps | Each step in the user's journey | Browse timetable / book / cancel / check in |
| Happy path first | The simplest successful route, then the exceptions | Book an available class first; handle full classes and duplicates later |
| Business rules | One rule per story | Limit of three bookings per week; no booking within 30 minutes of start |
| User types | Each kind of user | Members first, then instructors, then reception staff |
| Data or variations | Different types of input or content | Group classes first, then swimming lessons with lane allocation |
| Interfaces or channels | Each device or channel | Mobile web first, then the app, then the kiosk at reception |
| Simple then complex | A basic version, then refinements | Text reminder first; personalised reminders with travel time later |
| Spike | A time-boxed investigation before the real story | Two days to test the payment provider's API before paid classes |
Avoid splitting by technical layer (front end, back end, database). Each piece would be a task disguised as a story, and none of them would be usable alone. If you find yourself writing 'As a developer, I want...', check whether it is really a task.

### Which level is this item? Bugs, spikes and technical work
Real backlogs contain more than tidy user stories. This table shows where common item types usually fit.
| Item | Usually sits at | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New capability for users | Story | The default for most backlog items |
| Bug found after release | Story level (Jira: Bug) | Ordered in the Product Backlog with other work; may link to an epic |
| Bug found during the Sprint in the story being built | Task inside that story | Fix it as part of finishing the story |
| Spike or research | Story level, time-boxed | Output is knowledge or a decision, not a feature |
| Technical debt or upgrades | Story level (Jira: Task) | Explain the benefit, such as faster releases or reduced risk; see [technical debt in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/) |
| Large compliance or platform change | Epic | Split into stories that each deliver a verifiable part |

### Sizing rules of thumb
There are no official sizes for any of these levels. The ranges below are common guidance that works for many teams; adjust them to your Sprint length and context.
| Level | Common guidance | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Epic | Delivers its goal in a few Sprints, often within one quarter | Open for more than a couple of quarters, or has dozens of stories |
| Story | Small enough that several fit in one Sprint | Regularly carried over to the next Sprint |
| Task | One day or less | Sits 'in progress' on the board for several days |
The task guidance has a basis in Scrum itself. The 2020 Scrum Guide says that Developers often plan the Sprint by decomposing Product Backlog items into smaller work items of one day or less. It describes this as common practice, not a rule.
For epics, a clear goal matters more than the number of stories: an epic that has drifted for six months probably needs splitting or redefining. Our guide to [estimation and story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/) explains how to size work relatively.

### Who creates and owns each level
Ownership follows the question each level answers: why and what (Product Owner) versus how (Developers).
| Activity | Product Owner or product manager | Developers | Stakeholders |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Define initiatives and epics | Leads | Advise on feasibility | Contribute goals and constraints |
| Write and order user stories | Accountable | Help write and refine | Provide needs and feedback |
| Write acceptance criteria | Accountable | Contribute test cases and edge cases | Confirm intent |
| Estimate stories | Clarifies questions | Estimate | Not involved |
| Create and update tasks | Not involved | Own entirely | Not involved |
In Scrum, the [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) is accountable for the Product Backlog, which includes epics and stories, but anyone can propose items. The Sprint Backlog, including tasks, belongs to the Developers. Assigning tasks to named people at Sprint Planning works against this: let the team decide who picks up what during the Sprint.

### How the hierarchy fits Scrum events
Each level is worked on at a different point in the cycle.
- **Roadmap and release planning:** initiatives and epics are ordered and given rough sizes.
- **Backlog refinement:** epics are split into stories, and the top stories gain acceptance criteria and estimates.
- **[Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/):** the team picks stories for the Sprint Goal and breaks them into tasks, creating the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/).
- **Daily Scrum:** the team inspects progress on tasks and stories and adjusts the plan.
- **Sprint Review:** completed stories are shown to stakeholders; epic progress is discussed against its goal.
- **Retrospective:** the team reflects on whether stories were the right size and tasks were useful.

### Common mistakes and how to fix them
| Mistake | Why it hurts | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Using tasks for everything | The backlog becomes a to-do list with no visible outcomes | Write stories for anything a user benefits from; keep tasks inside stories |
| Epics that never close | Progress is invisible and the roadmap loses meaning | Give each epic a goal, a success measure and an out-of-scope list; close it when the goal is met |
| Splitting stories by technical layer | No piece is usable on its own, so nothing can be released or reviewed | Split by workflow step, rule or user type instead |
| Adding story points and task hours together | The units measure different things and the total means nothing | Track stories in points and tasks as counts or hours, separately |
| Writing all tasks up front for the whole epic | Wasted effort when plans change | Create tasks only for stories in the current Sprint |
| Too many levels | People cannot find work or agree where it belongs | Use three levels, plus one above epic only if strategy needs it |
| Inconsistent use of 'task' | Reports and boards mix up peer tasks and sub-tasks | Write a one-page working agreement on what each level means |
| Stories with no acceptance criteria | Endless debate about whether something is done | Add criteria during refinement, before the story enters a Sprint |

### How to set up the hierarchy in your team
Agree the hierarchy once, write it down and revisit it at a retrospective after a few Sprints. A short working agreement covers most of it:
1. Name the levels you will use (for example: initiative, epic, story, sub-task) and give one example of each from your own product.
2. Define size guidance for each level and what 'done' means at each level.
3. Decide where bugs, spikes and technical work go.
4. Decide who can create each level and who orders the backlog.
5. Configure your tool to match, and remove item types you will not use.
6. Review the agreement after two or three Sprints and simplify where people are confused.
Our free [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) shows ordered items with epics and estimates, and the [Sprint Planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) gives you a place to record the Sprint Goal, selected stories and tasks. Once the hierarchy is in place, design the board those items move across; see our guide to [designing an Agile workflow](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-workflow/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between an epic, a story and a task?**
An epic is a large goal that takes several Sprints, a user story is a small slice of that goal that delivers value to a user within one Sprint, and a task is a technical step, usually a day or less, needed to finish a story.

**Q: Is a task smaller than a story?**
In the generic Agile hierarchy, yes: tasks are steps inside a story. In Jira, a Task is a peer of a Story on the same level and is not necessarily smaller; the step inside a story is called a Sub-task.

**Q: Do tasks need story points?**
Usually not. Story points are applied to stories so the team can forecast. Tasks are often estimated in hours or simply counted. Do not add task hours to story points.

**Q: What is the difference between a task and a sub-task in Jira?**
A Jira Task sits on the same level as a Story and Bug and represents work without a user-facing outcome. A Sub-task belongs to a parent item (a Story, Task or Bug) and represents one step of it.

**Q: What comes above an epic?**
Many organisations group epics under themes or initiatives that link to strategic objectives or OKRs. In Jira, Atlassian says levels above epic are available on the Premium plan.

**Q: What is the difference between an epic and a feature?**
Where both are used, as in SAFe, a feature is a capability that sits between an epic and stories and can usually be delivered within a planning increment. Many single teams skip features and use only epics and stories.

**Q: How many user stories should an epic have?**
There is no rule. Many epics contain somewhere between a handful and a few dozen stories. If an epic keeps growing and never closes, split it into smaller epics with their own goals.

**Q: Who writes user stories and tasks?**
The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog, but stories are usually written with the Developers and stakeholders. Tasks are created by the Developers, mainly in Sprint Planning.

**Q: Can a story exist without an epic?**
Yes. Small, standalone stories such as a single improvement or bug fix do not need a parent epic.

**Q: Where do bugs fit in the hierarchy?**
Bugs found after release are usually ordered in the Product Backlog at story level, sometimes linked to an epic. Defects found while building a story are fixed as tasks within that story.

**Q: Are epics and user stories part of Scrum?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide describes Product Backlog items and a Sprint Backlog but does not prescribe epics, stories or tasks. They are complementary practices many Scrum Teams use.

**Q: Can non-software teams use epics, stories and tasks?**
Yes. A marketing team might have an epic for a product launch, stories such as 'as a prospect, I want a comparison page so that I can choose a plan', and tasks for copy, design and review.

**Q: Where should I track epics, stories and tasks?**
In any backlog or work management tool that supports parent and child items. See our [project management tool comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/) to shortlist options.

# History of Agile: When Did It Start? Full Timeline

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/history-of-agile/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: The history of Agile, from 1950s iterative development and Lean to the 2001 Agile Manifesto, Scrum, scaling frameworks and today, with a full timeline.


## History of Agile: When Did It Start? Full Timeline
The history of Agile has two starting points: the word "Agile" was adopted in February 2001, when seventeen software practitioners wrote the Manifesto for Agile Software Development at Snowbird, Utah, but the ideas behind it go back to iterative engineering projects of the 1950s and Toyota's production system. This guide tells the story in order, from those early roots through the lightweight methods of the 1990s, the Manifesto itself, and the frameworks, scaling models and standards that followed, with a full timeline you can use for study or training.
- Published 10 September 2026
- Last updated 15 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- The term Agile dates from the Snowbird meeting of 11 to 13 February 2001, but iterative and incremental development was in use on engineering programmes from the late 1950s.
- Winston Royce's 1970 paper is often blamed for Waterfall, yet it warned that a purely sequential process was risky and recommended iteration and feedback.
- Lean manufacturing and Takeuchi and Nonaka's 1986 "rugby" article shaped Agile's focus on flow, waste and self-organising teams.
- Scrum (presented 1995), DSDM (1994), XP (late 1990s), Crystal, FDD and Adaptive Software Development all existed before the Manifesto.
- After 2001, Agile spread through training and certification, then scaled to large organisations with SAFe, LeSS, Disciplined Agile and others.
- Today most organisations mix Agile, Lean and predictive approaches, and standards such as the PMBOK Guide now cover all of them.

### When did Agile start? The short answer
**Agile started, as a named movement, in February 2001**, when seventeen practitioners met at Snowbird, Utah, and wrote the Manifesto for Agile Software Development. The ideas it describes are older: iterative and incremental development dates from the late 1950s, Lean thinking from post-war Toyota, and frameworks such as Scrum and XP from the 1990s.
Both dates matter. The Manifesto gave a shared name and a set of values to methods that had been developing separately for years. Knowing the longer history helps you understand why Agile works the way it does, and why it is not tied to any one framework or tool. For the content of the Manifesto itself, see our guide to the [Agile Manifesto values and principles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/).

### Agile history timeline at a glance
This timeline gathers the key dates in one place. Each era is explained in more detail below.
| Year | Event | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1940s–1970s | Toyota develops what becomes the Toyota Production System | Source of Lean: flow, pull, waste reduction, kanban and continuous improvement |
| 1957 | Incremental development used at IBM's Service Bureau Corporation (cited by Larman and Basili) | One of the earliest recorded uses of incremental software development |
| 1960s | NASA's Project Mercury uses short iterations | Early example of iterative engineering on a complex programme |
| 1970 | Winston Royce publishes "Managing the Development of Large Software Systems" | Later cited as the origin of Waterfall, although it recommended iteration |
| 1977–1980 | IBM Federal Systems Division builds Space Shuttle avionics software in 17 iterations over 31 months | Iteration chosen because requirements kept changing |
| 1986 | Takeuchi and Nonaka publish "The New New Product Development Game" in Harvard Business Review | Introduces the rugby "scrum" metaphor for cross-functional product teams |
| 1986 | Barry Boehm describes the spiral model | Risk-driven, iterative software life cycle |
| 1990 | "The Machine That Changed the World" popularises the term lean production | Brings Toyota's ideas to a wide Western audience |
| 1993 | Jeff Sutherland first uses Scrum at Easel Corporation | Scrum begins as a working practice |
| 1994 | DSDM Consortium founded in the UK | Fixed time and cost, flexible scope, MoSCoW prioritisation |
| 1995 | Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland present Scrum at the OOPSLA conference | Scrum's first public description |
| 1996–1999 | Kent Beck and colleagues develop Extreme Programming; Beck's book follows in 1999 | Engineering practices: pair programming, test-first, continuous integration |
| 1997 | Feature-Driven Development created by Jeff De Luca and Peter Coad | Planning and building by small client-valued features |
| 2000 | XP leaders meet at the Rogue River Lodge, Oregon; Ken Schwaber describes the burndown chart; XP adopts velocity | The groundwork for Snowbird and for today's Agile charts |
| February 2001 | Seventeen practitioners write the Agile Manifesto at Snowbird, Utah | The word Agile is adopted; four values and twelve principles |
| Late 2001 | The Agile Alliance is formed as a non-profit | Promotes Agile methods and runs an annual conference |
| 2002–2005 | Planning Poker, INVEST, user story books and the Declaration of Interdependence | Practical techniques spread widely |
| 2003 | Mary and Tom Poppendieck publish Lean Software Development | Connects Lean thinking directly to software |
| 2007–2010 | Kanban method for knowledge work emerges; David J. Anderson's book published in 2010 | Flow-based alternative to iterations |
| 2009 | First DevOpsDays held in Ghent, Belgium; Scrum.org founded | Agile ideas extended to operations and deployment |
| 2010 | First official Scrum Guide published | A single, free definition of Scrum |
| 2011 | Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) first released; PMI introduces the PMI-ACP | Agile at enterprise scale; PMI formally recognises Agile |
| 2012 | Disciplined Agile created; Spotify's squads and tribes paper published | More approaches to scaling and team structure |
| 2014 | Dave Thomas writes "Agile is Dead (Long Live Agility)" | Backlash against commercialised, rule-bound Agile |
| 2017 | PMI publishes the Agile Practice Guide with the Agile Alliance, packaged with the PMBOK Guide 6th edition | Agile enters mainstream project management standards |
| 2019 | PMI acquires Disciplined Agile (announced August 2019) | Agile becomes part of PMI's own portfolio |
| 2020 | Scrum Guide 2020 released | Simpler, less software-specific, introduces the Product Goal |
| 2021 | PMBOK Guide 7th edition moves to principles and covers predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches | Agile and predictive treated as options, not opposites |
| November 2025 | PMBOK Guide 8th edition published | Continues the tailored, multi-approach view of project delivery |

### Before Agile: iterative and incremental development (1950s–1980s)
Agile is often presented as a rebellion against Waterfall, but iterative development is in fact older than the Waterfall label. In their 2003 article "Iterative and Incremental Development: A Brief History", Craig Larman and Victor Basili traced incremental development back to IBM's Service Bureau Corporation in 1957, and to NASA's Project Mercury in the early 1960s, which used short, time-boxed iterations.
One of the clearest early examples is the Space Shuttle's primary avionics software. Between 1977 and 1980, engineers at IBM's Federal Systems Division, several of whom had worked on Mercury, built it in 17 iterations over 31 months, averaging about eight weeks each. They chose iteration because the shuttle's requirements kept changing. Our guide to [iterative and incremental development](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/iterative-and-incremental-development/) explains the two ideas in more depth.

#### What Winston Royce actually said
In 1970 Winston Royce published "Managing the Development of Large Software Systems". Its early diagram shows requirements, analysis, design, coding, testing and operations flowing one after another, and this sequence later became known as the Waterfall model. The word "waterfall" does not appear in the paper.
What is often forgotten is that Royce described the purely sequential version as risky and inviting failure, because problems are discovered only at testing, when they are most expensive to fix. He went on to recommend feedback between stages, building an early version or prototype, and involving the customer. In other words, the paper usually cited as the origin of Waterfall argued for some of the ideas Agile later championed. Even so, sequential life cycles became the norm in many government and corporate software contracts through the 1970s and 1980s. For how the two approaches compare today, see [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) and our guide to [Waterfall project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/).
In 1986 Barry Boehm described the spiral model: repeated cycles of planning, risk analysis, building and evaluation, each tackling the biggest remaining risk. Its central idea runs straight through modern Agile practice.

### Lean manufacturing and the Toyota Production System
The second root of Agile is manufacturing. From the late 1940s onwards, Taiichi Ohno and colleagues at Toyota developed what became the Toyota Production System. Its core ideas will be familiar to any Agile team:
- **Eliminate waste:** anything that does not add value for the customer, including waiting, rework and unfinished inventory.
- **Just-in-time and pull:** make only what the next step needs, when it needs it, signalled by kanban cards. See [just-in-time (JIT)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/just-in-time-jit/).
- **Stop and fix:** any worker can stop the line to fix a problem at its source, rather than passing defects on.
- **Continuous improvement (kaizen):** small, frequent improvements made by the people doing the work.
- **Respect for people:** front-line teams are trusted to solve problems.
The word "lean" itself was coined by researcher John Krafcik in 1988 and popularised by the 1990 book *The Machine That Changed the World*. In 2003, Mary and Tom Poppendieck's *Lean Software Development* translated these principles explicitly for software, and Lean later shaped the Kanban method.

#### The rugby approach: Takeuchi and Nonaka, 1986
In January 1986 Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka published "The New New Product Development Game" in the Harvard Business Review. Studying companies such as Honda, Canon and Fuji-Xerox, they contrasted a sequential "relay race" approach to product development with a "rugby" approach in which a small, cross-functional, self-organising team works through overlapping phases together. They used the word scrum to describe it, and Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber later named their framework after it.

### The software crisis and heavyweight processes
By the early 1990s, many software organisations followed detailed, document-driven processes designed to bring discipline to large projects. Practitioners increasingly found serious drawbacks:
- **Long cycles.** It could take years from requirements to delivery, by which time the business need had changed.
- **Late discovery of problems.** Integration and testing happened at the end, when fixing mistakes was slow and expensive.
- **Change was treated as failure.** Formal change control made it hard to respond to what users learned once they saw the product.
- **Documents stood in for progress.** Plans and specifications could be complete while no working software existed.
- **Separated roles.** Analysts, designers, developers and testers handed work over rather than collaborating.
The alternatives that appeared in response were, at first, simply called lightweight methods.

### The 1990s: the lightweight methods
During the 1990s several groups, working largely independently, developed methods built on short cycles, close customer involvement and small empowered teams.
| Method | Origin | Key idea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rapid Application Development (RAD) | James Martin, 1991 book | Prototyping, user workshops and time-boxed delivery |
| Scrum | Jeff Sutherland (Easel Corporation, 1993) and Ken Schwaber; presented at OOPSLA in 1995 | Small self-organising teams working in fixed-length sprints from an ordered backlog |
| DSDM | UK consortium of organisations, 1994 | Fixed time and cost, flexible scope, MoSCoW prioritisation, active user involvement |
| Crystal | Alistair Cockburn, 1990s | A family of methods tailored to team size and project criticality |
| Feature-Driven Development (FDD) | Jeff De Luca and Peter Coad, 1997 | Planning and building by small, client-valued features |
| Extreme Programming (XP) | Kent Beck, Ward Cunningham, Ron Jeffries and others, late 1990s | Engineering practices such as pair programming, test-first development and continuous integration |
| Adaptive Software Development (ASD) | Jim Highsmith; book published 2000 | Speculate, collaborate, learn cycles |
| Pragmatic Programming | Andrew Hunt and Dave Thomas; book published 1999 | Practical craftsmanship habits for developers |

#### Scrum
Jeff Sutherland first used Scrum at Easel Corporation in 1993, drawing on Takeuchi and Nonaka's article. He and Ken Schwaber presented it formally at the OOPSLA conference in 1995. The earliest Scrum writings already described sprints, and Schwaber described the daily scrum in the late 1990s. Scrum therefore predates the Agile Manifesto by several years.

#### Extreme Programming
Extreme Programming grew out of Kent Beck's work on a payroll project at Chrysler from 1996. The first public article about it appeared in 1998, and Beck's book *Extreme Programming Explained* followed in 1999. XP contributed many of the engineering and planning practices Agile teams still use, including user stories, short iterations, test-first development, continuous integration and, around 2000, the idea of [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/).

#### DSDM
DSDM was created in 1994 by a consortium of organisations in the UK that wanted a common, vendor-independent framework for rapid application development. Its principle of fixing time and cost while letting scope flex, and its MoSCoW prioritisation, remain widely used. The consortium rebranded as the Agile Business Consortium in 2016.

### 2001: the Snowbird meeting and the Agile Manifesto
The path to the Manifesto began in spring 2000, when Kent Beck invited leaders of the XP community, and some people from other lightweight methods, to a retreat at the Rogue River Lodge in Oregon. They discussed the common ground between their approaches but made no formal decisions.
In September 2000 Robert C. ("Uncle Bob") Martin of Object Mentor proposed a follow-up meeting. After some debate between Chicago, Anguilla and Snowbird, the group chose The Lodge at Snowbird ski resort in Utah. The meeting took place from **11 to 13 February 2001**.

#### The seventeen authors
The people who met at Snowbird represented most of the lightweight methods of the time. All seventeen signed the Manifesto.
| Author | Mainly associated with |
| --- | --- |
| Kent Beck | Extreme Programming |
| Mike Beedle | Scrum |
| Arie van Bennekum | DSDM |
| Alistair Cockburn | Crystal |
| Ward Cunningham | Extreme Programming (and inventor of the wiki) |
| Martin Fowler | Extreme Programming, refactoring |
| James Grenning | Extreme Programming |
| Jim Highsmith | Adaptive Software Development |
| Andrew Hunt | Pragmatic Programming |
| Ron Jeffries | Extreme Programming |
| Jon Kern | Feature-Driven Development |
| Brian Marick | Software testing |
| Robert C. Martin | Object Mentor; organised the meeting |
| Steve Mellor | Model-driven development |
| Ken Schwaber | Scrum |
| Jeff Sutherland | Scrum |
| Dave Thomas | Pragmatic Programming |

#### Why "Agile"?
Until then the methods had been called lightweight, a label many of the group disliked because it sounded insubstantial. According to Martin Fowler's account of the meeting, they considered several names and settled on "agile" because it captured the adaptiveness and response to change at the heart of their approach.

#### What they agreed
The participants disagreed about many details of method, but agreed on four values, each preferring one thing over another while still valuing the second:
- **Individuals and interactions** over processes and tools.
- **Working software** over comprehensive documentation.
- **Customer collaboration** over contract negotiation.
- **Responding to change** over following a plan.
The twelve principles behind the Manifesto were refined in the weeks after the meeting. They cover early and continuous delivery, welcoming change, daily collaboration, motivated teams, face-to-face conversation, working software as the measure of progress, sustainable pace, technical excellence, simplicity, self-organising teams and regular reflection.
Later in 2001, several of the authors formed the **Agile Alliance**, a non-profit organisation to support the community, which still runs an annual conference.

### Where everyday Agile practices came from
Many practices people now think of simply as "Agile" have specific origins. These dates come mainly from the Agile Alliance's practices timeline.
| Practice | Origin | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily stand-up | Jim Coplien's Stand-Up Meeting pattern; daily scrum described by Ken Schwaber | 1993; 1997 |
| Sprints (time-boxed iterations) | Earliest Scrum writings | 1995 |
| Burndown chart | Ken Schwaber, while at Fidelity Investments | 2000 |
| Velocity | Added to XP, replacing the earlier "load factor" | 2000 |
| "As a… I want… so that…" user stories | Team at Connextra in London | 2001 |
| Card, Conversation, Confirmation | Ron Jeffries | 2001 |
| Retrospectives | Norm Kerth's *Project Retrospectives*; endorsed at XP 2001 | 2001 |
| Planning Poker | James Grenning; popularised by Mike Cohn's *Agile Estimating and Planning* (2005) | 2002 |
| INVEST checklist for stories | Bill Wake | 2003 |
| Story mapping | Jeff Patton | 2005 |
| Kanban for software teams | First experience reports; David J. Anderson's book (2010) | 2007 |
Our guide to [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) shows how several of these practices fit together today.

### 2002–2010: Agile spreads
In the decade after Snowbird, Agile moved from a niche of enthusiasts to common practice in software development.
- **Training and certification.** Scrum spread quickly through two-day courses and certifications. Ken Schwaber later founded Scrum.org in 2009. Scrum became the most widely used Agile framework.
- **Books turned ideas into techniques.** Mike Cohn's *User Stories Applied* (2004) and *Agile Estimating and Planning* (2005) gave teams practical methods for planning and estimating.
- **Leadership and project management.** In 2005 a group including Jim Highsmith and Alistair Cockburn published the Declaration of Interdependence, applying Agile values to project and team leadership.
- **Lean and Kanban.** The Poppendiecks linked Lean to software in 2003. From 2007, teams reported using kanban systems with work-in-progress limits instead of iterations, and David J. Anderson's book on the [Kanban method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) followed in 2010.
- **DevOps.** The first DevOpsDays conference in Ghent in 2009 gave a name to extending Agile collaboration to deployment and operations. See our guide to [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/).
- **The Scrum Guide.** In 2010 Schwaber and Sutherland published the first official Scrum Guide, giving Scrum a single, freely available definition.

### The 2010s: scaling Agile and mainstream adoption
As large organisations adopted Agile, they faced a new question: how do dozens or hundreds of teams work together on the same product? Several scaling approaches emerged.
| Framework or model | Origin | Main idea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) | Dean Leffingwell; first released 2011 | Agile release trains of teams aligned through regular PI planning |
| [Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/) | Craig Larman and Bas Vodde, developed from the mid-2000s | Many teams, one Product Owner and one Product Backlog, with minimal extra roles |
| Disciplined Agile | Scott Ambler and Mark Lines, 2012; acquired by PMI in 2019 | A toolkit for choosing a way of working that suits the context |
| [Spotify model](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/squads-tribes-chapters-guilds/) | Henrik Kniberg and Anders Ivarsson's 2012 paper | Squads, tribes, chapters and guilds; a description of one company, not a framework |
| Nexus | Scrum.org, 2015 | A light framework for three to nine Scrum teams |
| PRINCE2 Agile | AXELOS, 2015 | Agile delivery within PRINCE2 governance |
Mainstream project management bodies also embraced Agile. PMI introduced the PMI Agile Certified Practitioner (PMI-ACP) credential in 2011, and in 2017 it published the Agile Practice Guide, developed with the Agile Alliance and packaged with the PMBOK Guide 6th edition.

#### How the Scrum Guide has changed
| Version | Notable changes |
| --- | --- |
| 2010 | First official Scrum Guide |
| 2011 | Sprint Backlog described as a forecast rather than a commitment; Product Backlog "ordered" rather than prioritised |
| 2013 | Clarifications to events and artifacts, including the Daily Scrum as a planning event |
| 2016 | Scrum values (commitment, courage, focus, openness, respect) added |
| 2017 | Uses of Scrum beyond software described; Daily Scrum questions made optional |
| 2020 | Shorter and less prescriptive; Product Goal added; one Scrum Team with Developers instead of a separate Development Team; "self-managing" replaces "self-organising" |

### Agile beyond software
From the 2010s, teams outside software began adopting Agile practices. Marketing teams used backlogs and short campaigns, HR and finance teams used boards and retrospectives, and public-sector organisations such as government digital services adopted Agile delivery for online services. Construction, manufacturing and research projects increasingly used hybrid approaches: predictive plans for physical work and fixed milestones, with Agile cycles for design and stakeholder feedback.
The Scrum Guide's own wording reflects this. Since 2017 it has described Scrum's use beyond software, and the 2020 edition removed much of the remaining software-specific language.

### Criticism and backlash
Agile's success brought criticism, much of it from the Manifesto's own authors. Understanding it helps you avoid the same traps.
- **"Agile is dead (long live agility)".** In 2014 Dave Thomas argued that the word Agile had been turned into a marketing label, and encouraged people to focus on being agile rather than buying Agile.
- **The "Agile industrial complex".** In a 2018 talk, Martin Fowler criticised Agile imposed on teams by management and consultants, contrary to the Manifesto's emphasis on teams choosing their own process.
- **Process over people.** Some organisations adopted ceremonies and tools without changing how decisions are made, which is the opposite of the first Manifesto value.
- **Misuse of metrics.** Velocity and story points, intended as team planning aids, were sometimes turned into performance targets.
None of these critics argued for returning to heavyweight processes. Their message was to return to the values: working results, collaboration, adaptation and respect for the people doing the work.

### Agile in the 2020s
Agile is now a mainstream part of project delivery rather than a movement in opposition to it. Several trends define the current period:
- **Agile and predictive as options.** The PMBOK Guide 7th edition (2021) replaced its process-based structure with principles and performance domains covering predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches. The 8th edition, published in November 2025, continues this tailored view. See our guide to the [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/).
- **Hybrid delivery.** Many organisations use a predictive milestone plan for governance with Agile delivery inside each phase.
- **Business agility.** Attention has shifted from individual teams to whole organisations: funding, portfolio management and leadership.
- **Outcomes and flow.** Teams increasingly pair delivery metrics with measures of customer outcomes and flow metrics such as cycle time.
- **AI-assisted work.** Teams are using AI tools to help draft stories, summarise feedback and analyse delivery data, while the Agile emphasis on human collaboration and judgement remains.
For a closer look at where things may go next, read [is Agile the future of project management?](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-the-future-of-project-management/).

### What the history of Agile teaches you today
The history is more than trivia. It explains why Agile works as it does and how to apply it well.
1. **Agile is a set of values, not a single method.** The Manifesto was written by people from competing methods. Choose the framework that suits your context; our guide to [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/) compares them.
2. **Iteration was always about managing uncertainty.** From Project Mercury to the Space Shuttle, teams iterated because requirements changed. Use Agile where uncertainty is high and consider predictive or hybrid approaches where it is low.
3. **Engineering discipline matters.** XP's practices were part of Agile from the start. Process changes without technical quality rarely last.
4. **Lean thinking complements Agile.** Limiting work in progress and removing waste often improves delivery more than adding meetings.
5. **Metrics are aids, not targets.** Velocity and burndown were invented to help teams plan, and history shows what happens when they are turned into performance measures.
6. **Adoption should be invited, not imposed.** The strongest criticism of modern Agile is about process forced on teams. Involve the team in shaping how it works.
Tip
Starting your own Agile project? Our free [Agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/) sets out releases, sprints and backlog items in one place.
To build your knowledge further, see [how to learn Agile and get certified](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: When did Agile start?**
The term Agile was adopted at the Snowbird meeting on 11 to 13 February 2001, when the Agile Manifesto was written. The ideas behind it are older: iterative development dates from the late 1950s, and Scrum, DSDM and XP were in use during the 1990s.

**Q: Who invented Agile?**
No single person. Agile was defined by the seventeen authors of the Agile Manifesto, building on earlier work in iterative development, Lean manufacturing and the lightweight software methods of the 1990s.

**Q: Who wrote the Agile Manifesto?**
Kent Beck, Mike Beedle, Arie van Bennekum, Alistair Cockburn, Ward Cunningham, Martin Fowler, James Grenning, Jim Highsmith, Andrew Hunt, Ron Jeffries, Jon Kern, Brian Marick, Robert C. Martin, Steve Mellor, Ken Schwaber, Jeff Sutherland and Dave Thomas.

**Q: Where was the Agile Manifesto signed?**
At The Lodge at Snowbird ski resort in the Wasatch mountains of Utah, USA, in February 2001.

**Q: Why was Agile created?**
To offer an alternative to heavyweight, document-driven software processes that were slow, handled change poorly and discovered problems late. The authors wanted to deliver working software frequently, collaborate closely with customers and adapt to change.

**Q: What came before Agile?**
Iterative and incremental development on engineering programmes, Lean manufacturing from Toyota, Rapid Application Development, and 1990s lightweight methods such as Scrum, DSDM, Crystal, XP and Feature-Driven Development.

**Q: Is Scrum older than Agile?**
Yes. Jeff Sutherland first used Scrum in 1993 and presented it with Ken Schwaber in 1995, six years before the Agile Manifesto. Schwaber, Sutherland and Mike Beedle were among the Manifesto's authors. See [what is Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/).

**Q: Did Winston Royce invent the Waterfall model?**
Not in the sense usually claimed. His 1970 paper described a sequential process that later became known as Waterfall, but it warned that a purely sequential approach was risky and recommended iteration, prototyping and customer involvement. The word waterfall does not appear in it.

**Q: How did Lean influence Agile?**
Lean thinking from the Toyota Production System contributed ideas such as eliminating waste, limiting work in progress, pulling work when needed and continuous improvement. Kanban boards come directly from this tradition.

**Q: Why is it called Agile?**
The Snowbird participants wanted to replace the label "lightweight methods", which many disliked. They chose "agile" because it described the adaptiveness and response to change at the heart of their approaches.

**Q: What is the Agile Alliance?**
A non-profit organisation formed by several Manifesto authors in late 2001 to support the Agile community. It runs an annual conference and publishes resources, including a timeline of Agile practices.

**Q: When did Agile spread beyond software?**
Mainly from the 2010s, when marketing, HR, operations and public-sector teams began adopting Agile practices, and frameworks such as SAFe and PRINCE2 Agile brought it into large organisations.

**Q: Is Agile dead?**
No. Critics such as Dave Thomas argued in 2014 that the word had become a marketing label, but their point was to focus on agility rather than branded processes. Agile practices remain widely used and are now part of mainstream standards such as the PMBOK Guide.
