# How to Implement Agile: A 10-Step Plan for Organisations

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-implement-agile/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: How to implement Agile across teams or a whole organisation: a 10-step plan, readiness check, pilot scoring, 90-day example and mistakes to avoid.


## How to Implement Agile: A 10-Step Plan for Organisations
To implement Agile, define the problem it should solve, secure real leadership sponsorship, start with one or two willing pilot teams, change the governance around them, measure against a baseline and then spread the approach team by team. This guide gives you a 10-step plan for adopting Agile across a department or organisation, with a readiness check, a pilot scoring matrix and an illustrative 90-day example. To run a single project the Agile way, use our companion guide instead.
- Published 25 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Implementing Agile is an organisational change, not a training course. The hard part is changing how leaders set priorities, fund work and measure progress.
- Start with a clear problem and a measured baseline so you can tell whether Agile has helped.
- Choose one or two pilot teams with explicit criteria: willing people, an available Product Owner, visible value and few dependencies.
- Start with one framework as written, usually Scrum or Kanban, and adapt it once the team understands why each part exists.
- Adapt governance, funding and reporting around the pilots, or teams will run Agile meetings inside an unchanged system.
- Judge pilots after five or six iterations, then scale in waves, using pilot members as coaches.

### What does it mean to implement Agile?
**Implementing Agile means changing how a team, department or organisation plans, delivers and improves its work so that it follows Agile values and principles in practice.** Teams deliver in short cycles, one person owns priorities, work is visible and decisions move closer to the people doing it. It changes roles, governance and leadership behaviour, not only meetings.
People use the phrase for three different jobs, and mixing them up is a common reason plans go wrong.
|  | Running an Agile project | Implementing Agile (this guide) | Agile transformation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | One project or product | Several teams, a department or the organisation | The whole organisation and its operating model |
| Led by | Product Owner, Scrum Master or Agile project manager | Sponsor, change lead and coaches | Executive team |
| What changes | How this project is planned, delivered and reported | Team practices, roles, training, local governance and metrics | Structure, funding, HR, portfolio management and culture |
| Typical timescale | The life of the project | Months for the first teams, longer to spread | Typically several years |
Most organisations begin with the middle column: get a few teams working well, prove the value, then decide how far to go. Read [how to run an Agile project](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-run-an-agile-project/) if you only need to run one project.
Read [Agile transformation: a practical roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/) if you are planning a whole-organisation change.

### Agile readiness check
Before you commit to a timeline, test how ready the organisation is. Answer each question honestly with the people involved. Warning signs do not mean you should not start; they tell you what to fix first.
| Question | Ready signal | Warning signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can you name the problem Agile should solve? | A specific problem with a measure, such as lead time | "Everyone else is doing it" |
| Will a senior sponsor give time, not just approval? | Sponsor attends reviews and removes blockers | Sponsor delegates everything |
| Can someone own priorities with real authority? | A named person can say yes and no to scope | Every priority goes to a committee |
| Can teams stay stable for six months or more? | People mostly work on one team | People are split across four or five projects |
| Can work be delivered in small pieces? | Increments can be released or demonstrated | Nothing is usable until everything is finished |
| Will governance accept a forecast range? | Stage gates can be adapted for a pilot | Fixed scope, date and cost are non-negotiable |
| Is there budget for training and coaching? | Training and a coach are funded | "Read a book and start on Monday" |
If you have three or more warning signals, spend extra time on steps 2 and 8 before choosing a pilot. A [gap analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gap-analysis-template/) is a simple way to record the current state, the target state and the actions in between.

### The 10-step Agile implementation plan at a glance
The steps overlap in practice, but this order keeps the most common failures, such as starting without a sponsor or judging results too early, out of your way.
| Step | Main output | Typical timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Define the problem and success measures | Problem statement and baseline | Weeks 1–2 |
| 2. Secure sponsorship | Named sponsor and leadership commitments | Weeks 1–3 |
| 3. Choose the pilot teams | One or two pilots chosen with explicit criteria | Weeks 2–4 |
| 4. Choose a starting framework | Scrum, Kanban or Scrumban for each pilot | Week 3 |
| 5. Map roles and form teams | Product Owner, Scrum Master or flow lead, team | Weeks 3–5 |
| 6. Train and coach | Training delivered; coach in place | Weeks 4–6 |
| 7. Set up the team basics | Backlog, board, Definition of Done, cadence | Week 6 |
| 8. Adapt governance, funding and reporting | Agreed exceptions for the pilots | Weeks 4–8 |
| 9. Run, measure and improve | Five or six iterations; 90-day review | Weeks 6–18 |
| 10. Scale team by team | Expansion plan in waves | Month 4 onwards |
Timings are illustrative for a department of 50–100 people; regulated organisations usually need longer for steps 2 and 8.

### Step 1: Define the problem and how you will measure success
Agile is a means, not a goal. Write down the specific problem it should solve and how you will know it has improved. A clear reason guides later decisions, from pilot choice to metrics, and gives sceptics something concrete to test.
- **Weak:** "We want to be more Agile."
- **Better:** "Requests take too long to reach customers."
- **Best:** "The median time from an approved request to release is about three months, and stakeholders only see results at the end. We want to release at least monthly and get feedback every two weeks."
Then capture a baseline before anything changes. The figures below are illustrative; use measures that match your problem.
| Problem | Baseline measure | Illustrative baseline | Target after 6 months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slow delivery | Median lead time from approval to release | 90 days | Under 30 days |
| Infrequent feedback | Times per quarter users see working output | 1 | 6 or more |
| Unclear priorities | Items in progress per team | 14 | 5 or fewer |
| Quality problems | Defects found after release per month | 20 | Under 10 |
A [problem statement template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/problem-statement-template/) helps you agree the wording with leaders.

### Step 2: Secure sponsorship and agree what leaders will change
Agile asks leaders to accept flexible scope, stable teams and decisions made closer to the work. Without that, teams run stand-ups and retrospectives inside a system that still demands fixed plans, moves people between projects and escalates every decision. The sponsor's job is to change that system, starting with the pilot.
Brief leaders on what will change for them, not just for teams, and agree the commitments in writing.
| Today (typical) | What leaders agree to during the pilot |
| --- | --- |
| Approve a detailed plan up front, then track variance | Approve a goal, budget and time window; review working results every iteration |
| Assign people to several projects at once | Keep pilot team members on one team for at least six months |
| Escalate priority decisions to a committee | Give the Product Owner authority to order the backlog |
| Ask for percentage-complete status reports | Attend Sprint Reviews and accept burnup charts and forecast ranges |
| Add urgent work directly to individuals | Route new requests through the Product Owner |
Also name a **change lead** who plans the rollout, arranges training, removes organisational blockers and reports to the sponsor. In a large organisation this is usually a dedicated role supported by coaches.
Tip
Ask the sponsor to attend the first three Sprint Reviews of each pilot team. Nothing signals more clearly that the change is real, and it shows leaders what Agile progress looks like.

### Step 3: Choose the pilot teams
Start with one or two teams, not the whole department. A pilot lets you learn in a contained way, build internal examples and find organisational blockers before they affect everyone.

#### What makes a good pilot
- **Meaningful work** that stakeholders care about, so success is visible.
- **Willing volunteers**, not reluctant conscripts.
- **An available Product Owner** with authority to make priority decisions.
- **Few dependencies** on other teams or suppliers.
- **Not the most critical, highest-pressure project.** An immovable deadline leaves no room to learn.
- **Results visible within about three months.**

#### Worked example: a pilot scoring matrix
Score each candidate from 1 (poor) to 5 (strong) against weighted criteria, multiply and add. The candidates and scores are illustrative.
| Criterion (weight) | A: Customer portal | B: Core platform migration | C: Internal reports | D: Partner onboarding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Visible value (3) | 4 | 5 | 2 | 4 |
| Team willingness (3) | 5 | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| Product Owner availability (3) | 4 | 3 | 2 | 5 |
| Independence from other teams (2) | 4 | 1 | 5 | 3 |
| Deadline flexibility (2) | 4 | 1 | 5 | 4 |
| Results within 3 months (2) | 4 | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| **Weighted total (max 75)** | **63** | **38** | **52** | **56** |
For candidate A: (4×3) + (5×3) + (4×3) + (4×2) + (4×2) + (4×2) = 12 + 15 + 12 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 63.
A and D become the pilots. The core platform migration (B) has the most value but scores badly on willingness, dependencies and deadline pressure, so it waits for a later wave. Internal reports (C) is easy but would convince few people.

### Step 4: Choose a starting framework
Start with one framework as written. Each part of Scrum or Kanban exists for a reason, and teams that customise on day one usually remove the parts that would have exposed their problems. Adapt it through retrospectives once the team understands why each element exists. Our guide to [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/) covers the wider options.
|  | Scrum | Kanban | Scrumban |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Best for | Planned product or project work delivered in increments | Continuous requests, support and operations | Mixed planned and reactive work |
| Cadence | Sprints of one month or less, usually two weeks | Continuous flow with regular replenishment | Planning cadence with flow inside it |
| Roles | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers | None required; many add a flow lead | Usually a Product Owner and facilitator |
| Size of change | Larger: new roles and events | Smaller: improve the current process | Medium |
Choose Scrum when the team builds something new and needs a rhythm of planning and feedback; choose Kanban when work arrives unpredictably or the team wants less disruption. Non-software teams, such as marketing or operations, often start with Kanban. See [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) and [what is Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) for the framework as defined in the 2020 Scrum Guide.

### Step 5: Map roles and form the teams
Agile teams are small, cross-functional and stable. The Scrum Guide describes a Scrum Team of 10 or fewer people with all the skills needed to create value each Sprint. Forming those teams changes some existing roles, and people will want to know early what happens to theirs.
| Existing role | Common Agile destination | What changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project manager | Scrum Master, Product Owner or [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) | From directing tasks to enabling teams and managing stakeholders, budget and cross-team risk |
| Business analyst | Team member supporting the Product Owner | Requirements refined continuously as user stories |
| Product or service manager | [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Owns and orders the backlog; available every Sprint |
| Team leader | Developer on the team, or Scrum Master | The team plans its own work |
| Line manager | People and capability manager | Hiring, development and removing blockers, not daily task allocation |
| Steering committee | Sprint Review attendees and quarterly portfolio review | Decisions based on working results and forecasts |
| PMO | [Agile PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-pmo/) | From enforcing stage gates to supporting cadence, metrics and portfolio flow |

#### The three roles to fill first
- **Product Owner:** the most important appointment. Choose someone with authority over priorities and time to work with the team every week.
- **Scrum Master or flow lead:** coaches the team on the framework and removes impediments. See the [Scrum Master role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/).
- **Team members:** a stable group with the skills to finish work without waiting on others.
Tip
Tell people about role changes before training starts. Uncertainty about their own job is the most common reason capable people resist a rollout.

### Step 6: Train and coach
Train the team, the Product Owner and their managers together where you can, so everyone shares the same vocabulary and expectations. Then support teams with coaching, because most learning happens during the first iterations, not in the classroom.
| Audience | What they need | Format (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sponsor and senior leaders | What changes for them; how to read Agile progress | Half-day workshop |
| Pilot teams | Values, principles, the chosen framework, estimation, the board | Two days, with the Product Owner |
| Product Owners | Backlog ordering, slicing stories, stakeholder management | Two days plus mentoring |
| Scrum Masters or flow leads | Facilitation, coaching, metrics, removing impediments | Two days plus mentoring |
| Line managers and PMO | Their new role and the governance changes | Half-day workshop |
Consider an experienced Scrum Master or Agile coach for the first few months to speed up learning, spot bad habits early and train internal people to take over. Record the plan in a [training plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/).

### Step 7: Set up the team basics
Before the first iteration, each pilot team needs a small set of basics. Keep them simple; the team will improve them through retrospectives.
1. **A single, ordered backlog** owned by the Product Owner.
2. **A visible board** showing work from to-do to done. A [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) is enough to start.
3. **A [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/)** so everyone agrees what finished means.
4. **A fixed cadence** for planning, daily coordination, reviews and retrospectives.
5. **A team working agreement** covering hours, channels and how decisions are made.
6. **A short list of metrics** linked to the problem from step 1.
The day-to-day detail of running the work, including kickoff, the first backlog, release forecasts and the sprint cycle, is covered in our guide to [running an Agile project](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-run-an-agile-project/). This guide stays focused on what the organisation must put in place around the teams.

### Step 8: Adapt governance, funding and reporting
This is the step most implementations skip, and the main reason pilots stall. If the pilot team still has to pass the same stage gates, produce the same documents and report percentage complete, it spends its energy satisfying two systems at once. Agree temporary exceptions for the pilots, then make the successful ones permanent.
| Traditional control | Agile equivalent for the pilot |
| --- | --- |
| Detailed requirements sign-off before work starts | Agreed product vision, initial backlog and Definition of Done |
| Stage-gate approval at each phase | Sprint Review every iteration plus a quarterly continue or stop decision |
| Project budget for fixed scope | Funding for a stable team for a time window, scope ordered by value |
| Change control board for scope changes | Product Owner reorders the backlog; large changes discussed at Sprint Review |
| Percentage-complete status report | Burnup chart, forecast range, demo and top risks |
| Individual utilisation targets | Team-level outcomes and flow measures |
Keep the controls that matter, such as financial approval limits, regulatory requirements and security reviews, but build them into the Definition of Done or the team's cadence rather than adding them at the end. Our guide to [Agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/) shows how funding and prioritisation work once Agile spreads beyond the pilots.

### Step 9: Run, measure and improve
Run at least five or six iterations before judging results. The first two are usually messy as the team learns the framework, estimates poorly and discovers hidden dependencies. Use retrospectives to improve each time, and keep tracking the measures from step 1.
| If the problem was… | Track | Avoid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slow delivery | Lead time, cycle time, release frequency | Comparing velocity between teams |
| Unclear priorities | Work in progress, share of work that was planned | Counting tickets closed |
| Poor quality | Escaped defects, rework | Hours spent testing |
| Low stakeholder confidence | Sprint Goal success rate, forecast accuracy | Ceremony attendance |
See [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) for definitions and calculations.

#### Questions for the 90-day review
- Has the baseline measure moved in the right direction, and by how much?
- Which organisational blockers did the pilot hit, and which were removed?
- Did leaders keep their commitments from step 2?
- Would the pilot team members choose to keep working this way?
- What would we change before the next teams start?

### Step 10: Scale team by team
Once the pilots show results, expand in waves rather than switching everyone at once. Each wave should be small enough for your coaches to support properly.
1. **Share the pilot results openly**, including what did not work. Honest results convince more people than a polished success story.
2. **Plan waves of two to four teams**, starting with teams whose work is similar to the pilots.
3. **Seed pilot team members into new teams** so experience spreads.
4. **Set up a community of practice** where Scrum Masters, Product Owners and team members share problems and solutions.
5. **Fix the shared blockers** every team hits, such as release approvals, procurement and HR policies.
6. **Add a scaling approach only when teams must coordinate closely** on one product, for example a [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/) or the [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/).
When the change starts to involve funding models, organisational structure and HR policy everywhere, you have moved from implementation into transformation, which our [Agile transformation roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/) covers.

### Worked example: a 90-day Agile implementation
This example is illustrative. The organisation, figures and results are invented to show how the steps fit together.
A mid-sized insurer's claims systems department has about 70 people working on 12 projects at once. Approved changes take around 90 days to reach users, releases are quarterly, and stakeholders only see results when it is too late to change them. The head of department wants monthly releases and earlier feedback.
| Weeks | Activity | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–2 | Baseline measured: 90-day median lead time, quarterly releases, 14 items in progress per team | Problem statement and baseline |
| 1–3 | Claims director named as sponsor; leadership commitments agreed | Commitments signed; change lead appointed |
| 2–4 | Four candidates scored; customer portal (63) and partner onboarding (56) chosen | Two pilots |
| 3–5 | Both choose Scrum with two-week Sprints; two project managers become Scrum Masters, two service managers become Product Owners | Teams of 7 and 8 |
| 4–6 | Team training, leaders' workshop, external coach three days a week | Training complete |
| 4–8 | Stage gates replaced by Sprint Reviews and a monthly sponsor review; status reports replaced by burnup charts | Governance exceptions |
| 6–18 | Six Sprints per team; coach steps back from Sprint 4 | Working increments every Sprint |
| 13 | 90-day review with sponsor, teams and stakeholders | Decision to expand |

#### What happened
- Sprints 1 and 2 were rough: both teams over-committed, and the partner onboarding team found a dependency on a supplier's API.
- By Sprint 4 the customer portal team was releasing every two weeks, and median lead time for its changes had fallen to about 25 days.
- The biggest blocker was the monthly change advisory board. The sponsor agreed a standard-change route for low-risk releases.
At day 90 the department agreed a second wave of three teams, each seeded with a pilot team member, and asked the change lead to fix release approvals for every team before wave three. The core platform migration stayed on its existing plan until the organisation had more experience.

### Managing the people side of the change
Most resistance to Agile is reasonable from the person's point of view. Treat it as information about what the plan has missed.
| What you hear | What it often means | What helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "We tried Agile before and it failed." | A previous rollout changed meetings but not the system | Ask what went wrong; show which leadership commitments are different |
| "What happens to my job?" | Role uncertainty | Publish the role mapping early; talk to each affected person |
| "We can't commit without a full plan." | Governance or contract pressure | Show forecast ranges and burnup charts; agree governance exceptions |
| "Our work is too regulated for Agile." | Fear of losing control | Build controls into the Definition of Done; start with a lower-risk pilot |
Communicate the plan, the reasons and the results regularly. A [communication plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/) helps you decide who hears what and when.

### Common mistakes when implementing Agile
- **Mandating Agile without explaining why.** People attend the meetings and keep the old behaviour.
- **Renaming roles without changing them.** A Scrum Master who still assigns tasks changes nothing.
- **Leaving governance untouched.** Teams produce Agile and traditional reporting at the same time.
- **Choosing the most critical project as the pilot.** Pressure removes the room to learn.
- **Customising the framework on day one.** Teams drop the parts that would expose their problems.
- **Splitting people across many projects.** It defeats stable teams and short cycles.
- **Measuring velocity or attendance instead of outcomes.** Measure the problem you set out to solve.
- **Judging after one or two iterations, or scaling before the pilots work.** Both spread problems rather than benefits.

### Tools that support an Agile rollout
Tools do not make an organisation Agile, but the right one makes work visible across teams and saves the change lead from building reports by hand. Start with the simplest tool that gives each team a board and backlog and gives leaders a shared view of progress.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, suits organisations rolling Agile out across mixed teams and portfolios, with boards, request forms, dashboards and cross-project reporting in one place.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** offers mature Scrum and Kanban boards and is a strong choice for software development teams.
- **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)** and Asana are easy for non-technical teams to adopt, which helps when rolling out beyond IT.
Compare options on our [project management tool comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/). Agree a common minimum configuration, such as statuses and dashboard fields, across teams.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the steps to implement Agile?**
Define the problem and success measures, secure sponsorship, choose pilot teams, choose a starting framework, map roles and form teams, train and coach, set up the team basics, adapt governance and reporting, run and measure five or six iterations, then scale team by team.

**Q: How long does it take to implement Agile?**
A pilot team can work well within about three months. Spreading Agile across a department usually takes many months, and changing an organisation's structure, funding and culture typically takes years.

**Q: Do we need an Agile coach to implement Agile?**
Not always, but an experienced coach or Scrum Master speeds up learning and helps avoid common mistakes. Many organisations use a coach for the first few months and train internal people to take over.

**Q: Should we start with Scrum or Kanban?**
Choose Scrum for planned work that can be delivered in increments, and Kanban for continuous requests or teams that want to evolve their current process with less disruption.

**Q: How do you choose a pilot team for Agile?**
Look for meaningful work, willing volunteers, an available Product Owner, few dependencies and results visible within about three months. Avoid the highest-pressure project. A weighted scoring matrix makes the choice transparent.

**Q: What is the biggest obstacle to implementing Agile?**
Usually the organisation around the teams: fixed-scope approvals, people split across many projects, stage gates that do not fit iterative delivery, and leaders who keep decisions away from the team.

**Q: What happens to project managers when an organisation implements Agile?**
Many become Scrum Masters, Product Owners or Agile project managers who coordinate several teams and manage stakeholders, budgets and risks. The role shifts from directing tasks to enabling teams.

**Q: How do you measure whether an Agile implementation is working?**
Compare against the baseline captured at the start, using measures linked to the original problem, such as lead time, release frequency, escaped defects or stakeholder satisfaction.

**Q: What is the difference between implementing Agile and an Agile transformation?**
Implementing Agile usually means adopting Agile practices in a set of teams or a department. A transformation changes the whole organisation's structure, funding, governance and culture.

**Q: Can you implement Agile in a non-software team?**
Yes. Marketing, HR, operations and construction teams use Agile, often starting with Kanban. The steps are the same; what counts as a finished increment changes.

**Q: Can you implement Agile without changing the organisation's structure?**
You can start without restructuring, which is why pilots work. But if governance, funding and reporting never change, teams eventually hit limits, so plan to adapt them as the pilots show what gets in the way.

# How to Learn Agile and Get Certified: Step-by-Step Path

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: How to learn Agile from scratch: what to study, a 90-day plan, how to get experience, and how to choose PSM, CSM, PMI-ACP, SAFe or PRINCE2 Agile.


## How to Learn Agile and Get Certified: Step-by-Step Path
To learn Agile, start with the Agile Manifesto and the Scrum Guide, practise the ideas on real work as soon as you can, and then choose a certification that matches your role and the employers you want to work for. You can understand the basics in a couple of weeks; becoming good at Agile takes months of practice. This guide gives you a syllabus, a 90-day learning plan, ways to get experience, and a side-by-side comparison of the main Agile certifications.
- Published 26 September 2026
- Last updated 14 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Learn the foundations first: the Agile Manifesto and its principles, the Scrum Guide, and the basics of Kanban. All are free.
- Practise early. A personal Kanban board, running a retrospective or volunteering on a sprint-based project teaches more than any course.
- Choose a certification by role and market: PSM I or CSM for Scrum Masters, PSPO or CSPO for Product Owners, PMI-ACP for experienced practitioners, SAFe or PRINCE2 Agile where employers use them.
- Entry-level Scrum certifications need no prior experience; the PMI-ACP requires Agile experience and 21 hours of training.
- Renewal rules differ: PSM I does not expire, CSM renews every two years and SAFe annually, so factor them into the cost.
- Certification opens doors, but employers hire for evidence that you can apply Agile. Build both.

### What does learning Agile involve?
**Learning Agile** means understanding the values and principles behind Agile ways of working, learning at least one framework such as Scrum or Kanban in detail, and building the practical skills to use them: planning in short cycles, working with a backlog, facilitating team events and improving through feedback. Knowledge comes quickly; skill comes from practice.
It helps to separate three layers:
- **Mindset:** the values and principles in the [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/), such as responding to change, collaborating with customers and delivering working results often.
- **Frameworks and methods:** specific ways of applying those ideas, most commonly [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) and [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/), plus scaling frameworks such as SAFe and hybrid approaches such as PRINCE2 Agile.
- **Practices and skills:** user stories, estimation, backlog ordering, facilitation, coaching, stakeholder management and the habit of inspecting and adapting.
A common beginner mistake is to treat Agile and Scrum as the same thing. Scrum is one Agile framework; Agile is the wider set of values it is built on. Our guide to [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/) explains the difference.

### What to learn: the Agile syllabus
Use this table as a checklist. The first six rows are the core every Agile practitioner needs; the rest depend on your role.
| Topic | What you should be able to do | Where to start |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agile values and principles | Explain the four values and twelve principles and give examples of each in practice | [Agile Manifesto guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/) |
| Agile vs predictive approaches | Explain when Agile, Waterfall or a hybrid suits a project | Our hybrid and PRINCE2 comparisons |
| Scrum | Describe the three accountabilities, five events, three artefacts and their commitments | [What is Scrum?](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) |
| Kanban | Visualise work, set WIP limits and read basic flow metrics | [What is Kanban?](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) |
| Backlogs and user stories | Write and split user stories with acceptance criteria | [User stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) |
| Estimation and forecasting | Use story points, velocity and capacity to forecast | Our story points and velocity guides |
| Facilitation and retrospectives | Run a Sprint Retrospective that ends in a few concrete actions | [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) |
| Agile frameworks overview | Know what XP, Lean, DSDM, SAFe and LeSS are for | [Types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/) |
| Scaling (if relevant) | Explain how many teams coordinate on one product | [SAFe guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) |
Do not try to master every row before you start practising. Learn the first four, try them on real work, then return to the rest.

### Step-by-step: how to learn Agile
The path below works whether you are new to project work or an experienced project manager adding Agile to your toolkit.
1. Learn the foundations: values, principles and the main frameworks.
2. Go deeper on Scrum and Kanban, the two frameworks you will meet most often.
3. Practise on real work, even in a small way.
4. Choose and take a certification that fits your role.
5. Specialise in a role: Scrum Master, Product Owner, Agile project manager or coach.
6. Keep learning through communities, mentoring and reflection.

#### Step 1: Learn the foundations
Read the Agile Manifesto and its twelve principles; they take ten minutes to read and much longer to understand. Then read the official Scrum Guide. The current edition is the 2020 version by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland; it is short, free at scrumguides.org and the basis of most Scrum exams. Finish this step by working through our overview of the [Agile methodology](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-methodology/) so you can see how the pieces fit together.

#### Step 2: Go deeper on Scrum and Kanban
Reread the Scrum Guide until you can explain each event and artefact without looking. Learn why each element exists, not just what it is: for example, why the Sprint Goal matters more than the list of items. For Kanban, learn the core practices (visualise, limit work in progress, manage flow, make policies explicit, improve) and the basic metrics such as cycle time and throughput.

#### Step 3: Practise on real work
Practice turns knowledge into skill. Start a [personal Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/personal-kanban/) board for your own tasks, offer to facilitate a retrospective for your team, or run a small project in two-week sprints. Keep notes on what worked and what did not; they become useful evidence in interviews. The section below on getting experience without an Agile job gives more options.

#### Step 4: Choose a certification
Once you understand the basics and have tried them, choose a certification that matches your goal. Taking an exam before you have practised at all tends to produce people who can recite the Scrum Guide but struggle in a real Sprint Planning. The comparison table later in this guide shows the main options.

#### Step 5: Specialise in a role
Agile teams need different skills in different roles. Decide which one you are aiming for and study it specifically: the [Scrum Master role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/), the [Scrum Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/), or the [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/), who often works across Agile and predictive delivery.

#### Step 6: Keep learning
Agile practice keeps evolving. Join a community, find a mentor, teach others, and run retrospectives on your own work. Explaining Agile to someone else is one of the fastest ways to find the gaps in your own understanding.

### A 90-day Agile learning plan
Here is a realistic plan for someone studying part-time, around five hours a week. Adjust the pace to suit you; the order matters more than the dates.
| Weeks | Focus | Activities | Output to keep |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1–2 | Foundations | Read the Manifesto and principles; read the Scrum Guide twice; read our Agile overview | A one-page summary of Agile in your own words |
| 3–4 | Scrum and Kanban | Study each Scrum event, accountability and artefact; learn Kanban practices and flow metrics | A personal Kanban board you use every day |
| 5–6 | Core practices | Write and split user stories; try planning poker; learn velocity and capacity | Ten user stories with acceptance criteria for a real or practice product |
| 7–8 | Practice | Run two short sprints on a real piece of work, or facilitate a retrospective for a team | Sprint notes and retrospective actions |
| 9–10 | Certification preparation | Choose your certification; take free practice assessments; revisit weak areas | Practice test scores above the pass mark, consistently |
| 11–12 | Exam and reflection | Sit the exam or attend the required course; update your CV and profile | Certificate plus two or three real examples to talk about |
| 13 | Next steps | Pick a role to specialise in and a second learning goal | A short development plan for the next six months |
Tracking this in a simple [training plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) keeps you honest about progress. If your employer is funding the training, it also gives them a clear picture of what you are learning and when.

### Free and low-cost ways to learn Agile
You do not need to spend money to learn Agile well. Most of the primary sources are free.

#### Primary sources
- **The Agile Manifesto and its twelve principles** at agilemanifesto.org.
- **The Scrum Guide** (2020) at scrumguides.org, available in many languages.
- **Free Kanban guides** published by Kanban University and by ProKanban.org.
- **The Agile Practice Guide**, published by PMI with Agile Alliance; useful if you come from a PMI background.
- **Free practice assessments** offered by several certification bodies, such as Scrum.org's open assessments.

#### Books worth reading
- *Scrum: The Art of Doing Twice the Work in Half the Time* by Jeff Sutherland, for the story and reasoning behind Scrum.
- *Agile Estimating and Planning* by Mike Cohn, for estimation, velocity and release planning.
- *User Story Mapping* by Jeff Patton, for turning ideas into a backlog that makes sense.
- *Kanban* by David J. Anderson, for the origins of the Kanban Method in knowledge work.
- *The Phoenix Project* by Gene Kim, Kevin Behr and George Spafford, a novel about flow and DevOps that many people find an easy way in.

#### Communities and events
Local and online Agile meetups, Agile Alliance and Scrum Alliance community groups, and conference talks published online are all good ways to hear how other teams solve real problems. Ask questions; practitioners are generally generous with their time.

#### Our free guides and templates
This site's Agile, Scrum and Kanban guides are free and written to be read in order. Pair them with practical templates: a [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) to run your own work and a [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) to facilitate your first retrospective.

### How to get Agile experience without an Agile job
Many entry-level roles ask for experience, which can feel like a catch-22. These options let you build real, discussable experience:
- **Use Agile on your current work.** Even in a traditional role, you can visualise your team's work on a board, hold short planning sessions and run retrospectives at the end of a phase.
- **Volunteer to facilitate.** Offer to run a retrospective or a planning session for a team that does not have a Scrum Master.
- **Run a personal project in sprints.** A home renovation, a course project or a side business all work. Keep a backlog, plan two-week sprints and review results.
- **Help a charity or community group.** Many small organisations welcome someone who can help them organise their work.
- **Shadow an Agile team.** Ask to observe Sprint Reviews or Daily Scrums in another department.
- **Join hackathons or open-source projects**, where short, goal-driven cycles are normal.
When you describe this experience on a CV or in an interview, be specific: what problem the team had, what you did, and what changed. "Facilitated six retrospectives for a five-person marketing team; two actions cut campaign approval time from ten days to four" is far stronger than "familiar with Agile". Agile is used well beyond software, so experience from marketing, HR or operations counts; see [is Agile only for software?](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-only-for-software/)

### Agile certifications compared
The table summarises the most widely recognised Agile certifications. Formats and renewal rules were checked on 14 October 2026 using issuers' websites where available and reputable exam-preparation sources otherwise. They change, so confirm details with the issuer before you register.
| Certification | Issuer | Level | Prerequisites | How you earn it | Renewal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) | Scrum.org | Entry | None; course optional | Online assessment: 80 questions, 60 minutes, 85% to pass | Does not expire |
| Certified ScrumMaster (CSM) | Scrum Alliance | Entry | 16-hour course with a Certified Scrum Trainer | Online test after the course; 74% to pass | Every two years: 20 SEUs and a US$100 fee |
| PSPO I / CSPO | Scrum.org / Scrum Alliance | Entry (Product Owner) | PSPO: none; CSPO: course | PSPO: online assessment; CSPO: course-based | As for PSM / CSM |
| PMI Agile Certified Practitioner (PMI-ACP) | PMI | Intermediate | Agile experience (see below) and 21 hours of Agile training | Exam: 120 questions, 180 minutes | 30 PDUs every three years |
| SAFe Agilist (SA) | Scaled Agile, Inc. | Entry to intermediate (scaled) | Leading SAFe course | Exam: 45 questions, 90 minutes, 35 correct to pass | Annual fee (check Scaled Agile for the current amount) |
| PRINCE2 Agile Foundation | PeopleCert | Entry | None | Exam: 40 questions, 60 minutes, 60% to pass | Check PeopleCert's current rules |
| PRINCE2 Agile Practitioner | PeopleCert | Intermediate | PRINCE2 Agile Foundation | Exam: 50 questions, 150 minutes, open book, 60% to pass | Check PeopleCert's current rules |
| ICAgile Certified Professional (ICP) | ICAgile | Entry | Accredited course | Course-based; no central exam, the trainer assesses learning | Check ICAgile's current rules |
| Kanban Management Professional (KMP) | Kanban University | Intermediate (Kanban) | Accredited classes | Completing the two required classes | Check Kanban University's current rules |
| PMAI | Neural Project Institute | Entry to intermediate | None | Six online courses with assessed chapters and a verifiable certificate, including Sprintcraft: Agile & Scrum Practitioner | See the certification page |

#### PMI-ACP eligibility in detail
PMI's certification page lists a secondary degree, 21 contact hours of Agile training, 12 months of general project experience in the last five years (a current PMP or PgMP satisfies this) and 8 months of Agile project experience in the last three years (checked 4 November 2026). Many people take PSM I or CSM first and the PMI-ACP later.

#### About PRINCE2 Agile and the 2025 update
PeopleCert released version 2 of PRINCE2 Agile in 2025, aligned with PRINCE2 7. Practitioner candidates need PRINCE2 Agile Foundation (either version). If your organisation runs projects under PRINCE2 governance, read our comparison of [PRINCE2 and Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/prince2-vs-agile/).

#### About PMAI
PMAI (Project Management Artificial Intelligence) is this site's own certification. It covers practical project management, Agile and Scrum, and the use of AI in project work across six courses, with assessed chapters and a verifiable certificate. It is currently free for a limited time. It is a newer credential than the established ones above, so treat it as a structured way to learn and evidence your skills alongside them. [See the PMAI certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/).

### Which Agile certification should you choose?
Start from your goal, not from the certificate. The table gives a sensible first choice for common situations.
| Your situation | Sensible first choice | Good next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New to Agile, aiming to be a Scrum Master | PSM I or CSM | PSM II, Advanced CSM or PMI-ACP |
| Moving into a Product Owner or product role | PSPO I or CSPO | Advanced product owner credentials |
| Experienced project manager adding Agile | PMI-ACP if eligible; otherwise PSM I or CSM first | PMI-ACP alongside the PMP |
| Working in a PRINCE2 organisation | PRINCE2 Agile Foundation | PRINCE2 Agile Practitioner |
| Working in an organisation that uses SAFe | SAFe Agilist or the SAFe role certification for your job | SAFe role-specific certifications |
| Team that runs on flow, such as support or operations | Kanban training (for example KMP) | Flow metrics and forecasting |
| Non-software team (marketing, HR, finance) | ICAgile ICP or a Scrum entry certification | Role-specific learning |
| Want broad, practical PM, Agile and AI skills | PMAI | A role-specific Agile certification |

#### PSM I or CSM?
Both are well recognised entry-level Scrum Master certifications. The main differences are format and renewal. PSM I is an exam you can take whenever you are ready, with an 85% pass mark and no expiry. CSM requires a live 16-hour course with a Certified Scrum Trainer, which many people value for the interaction, and renews every two years. If you learn well on your own and want the lowest ongoing cost, PSM I fits; if you want guided training and your employer will pay for the course, CSM fits. Our guide to [Scrum certification and training](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/) compares them in more detail.

#### PMI-ACP or PMP?
They do different jobs. The PMP is PMI's flagship project management certification and its exam covers predictive, Agile and hybrid approaches. The PMI-ACP focuses entirely on Agile and suits practitioners who already work on Agile teams. Many project managers hold both.

#### Should you start with a scaling framework?
Usually not. SAFe and other scaling frameworks build on team-level Scrum and Kanban. Learn those first unless your employer already uses SAFe and expects you to join a train straight away.

### How long it takes and what it costs
These preparation times are our estimates for someone studying part-time who has already covered the foundations. Your time will depend on your background.
| Certification | Typical preparation (our estimate) | Cost structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PSM I | 2–4 weeks of self-study with the Scrum Guide and practice tests | Exam fee only; optional course |
| CSM | The required course (usually spread over two or three days) plus a few hours of revision | Course fee, which includes the test; renewal fee every two years |
| PMI-ACP | 1–3 months, after meeting the experience requirement | 21 hours of training plus the exam fee (lower for PMI members) |
| SAFe Agilist | The Leading SAFe course plus one to two weeks of revision | Course fee, which includes the exam; annual renewal |
| PRINCE2 Agile Foundation | 2–4 weeks of self-study, or a short course | Exam fee, often bundled with a course |
| ICAgile ICP / KMP | Duration of the accredited course(s) | Course fee includes certification |
Prices vary by country, training provider and membership status, and change often, so we do not list them here. When you compare costs, look at the total over three years: an exam with no renewal can be cheaper overall than a course-based credential with annual fees, even if the first payment is higher. For PMI credentials, the [PDU guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pdu-professional-development-units/) explains how to earn the continuing education units you need to renew.

### How to prepare for an Agile certification exam
1. **Read the source material the exam is based on**, such as the Scrum Guide for PSM and CSM, or the official handbook or exam content outline for the PMI-ACP and PRINCE2 Agile.
2. **Read it again, slowly.** Exam questions often turn on exact wording, such as who is accountable for what.
3. **Take a free practice assessment** to find your weak areas before you spend money.
4. **Study the reasoning, not just the rules.** Many questions describe a situation and ask what a Scrum Master or Product Owner should do.
5. **Use a study group or forum** to discuss questions you got wrong.
6. **Keep taking practice tests** until you pass comfortably and consistently, not just once.
7. **Plan the exam day.** Check the time limit, whether the exam is open book, your internet connection for online exams, and the retake policy.
Tip
For PSM I, aim to score well above the 85% pass mark in practice before you book. The time limit (80 questions in 60 minutes) leaves little room for looking things up.

### Is Agile certification worth it?
Certification is worth it when it solves a specific problem for you. It is less useful as a substitute for experience.
| Certification helps most when… | Experience matters more when… |
| --- | --- |
| You are changing career and need to get past CV screening | You are applying for senior Scrum Master, coach or Agile lead roles |
| Employers in your market list a specific certification in job adverts | The hiring manager asks for examples of teams you have improved |
| Your organisation requires it (for example SAFe or PRINCE2 Agile) | You already have a strong track record in Agile delivery |
| You want a structured way to learn with a clear finish line | You are learning mainly to improve your current team's work |
Our view: for most people, one well-recognised entry-level certification plus real practice is the right combination. Collecting many certificates without practice adds little. Before you choose, look at twenty job adverts for the role you want and note which credentials they mention most often.

### Common mistakes when learning Agile
- **Learning the rules without the reasons.** Following Scrum mechanically without understanding why each element exists leads to empty ceremonies.
- **Treating Agile as only Scrum.** Kanban, Lean and hybrid approaches suit many types of work better.
- **Skipping practice.** Reading about facilitation is not the same as running a tense retrospective.
- **Choosing a certification by price or difficulty alone.** Choose by role and by what employers in your market ask for.
- **Starting with scaling.** Scaling frameworks make more sense once you understand team-level Agile.
- **Ignoring traditional project management.** Many roles combine Agile with predictive governance, budgets and milestones. Knowing both makes you more useful.
- **Stopping after the exam.** The certificate is the start of learning, not the end.

### Where Agile skills can take you
Agile skills open several career paths. Most people start in one role and move to others as their experience grows.
| Role | What the role focuses on | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum Master | Helping a team use Scrum well, removing impediments and coaching the organisation | [How to become a Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/how-to-become-a-scrum-master/) |
| Product Owner | Maximising the value of the product and managing the Product Backlog | [Scrum Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) |
| Agile project manager | Delivering projects with Agile or hybrid approaches, often across several teams | [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) |
| Agile coach | Helping teams and leaders adopt Agile across an organisation | [How to implement Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-implement-agile/) |
| Team member in any function | Using Agile practices in marketing, HR, operations or engineering | [Agile beyond software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-only-for-software/) |
Whichever path you choose, the combination that employers value most is a solid grasp of the principles, a recognised credential and specific stories about teams you have helped.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: How do I start learning Agile?**
Read the Agile Manifesto and its twelve principles, then the 2020 Scrum Guide, then the basics of Kanban. Next, apply what you learn on real work, for example with a personal Kanban board or by facilitating a retrospective, before choosing a certification.

**Q: How long does it take to learn Agile?**
You can learn the basics in one to two weeks of part-time study. Becoming confident usually takes a few months of practice on real work, and becoming highly skilled takes years of experience with different teams.

**Q: Can I learn Agile for free?**
Yes. The Agile Manifesto, the Scrum Guide and Kanban guides are free, several certification bodies offer free practice assessments, and free guides such as this one cover the rest. You only need to pay if you want a certification.

**Q: What is the best Agile certification for beginners?**
Entry-level Scrum certifications such as PSM I from Scrum.org or CSM from Scrum Alliance are the most common starting points. PSPO I or CSPO suit aspiring Product Owners, and PRINCE2 Agile Foundation suits PRINCE2 environments.

**Q: Can I get Agile certified without experience?**
Yes. PSM I, CSM, PSPO I, CSPO, PRINCE2 Agile Foundation and ICAgile ICP have no experience requirement. The PMI-ACP does require Agile experience.

**Q: What is the difference between PSM and CSM?**
PSM I from Scrum.org is an online assessment with no required course, an 85% pass mark and no expiry. CSM from Scrum Alliance requires a 16-hour course with a Certified Scrum Trainer, has a 74% pass mark and renews every two years.

**Q: What are the PMI-ACP requirements?**
A secondary degree, 21 contact hours of Agile training, 12 months of general project experience in the last five years (a current PMP or PgMP satisfies this) and 8 months of Agile project experience in the last three years. The exam has 120 questions in 180 minutes.

**Q: Which Agile certification is best for project managers?**
Experienced project managers often choose the PMI-ACP, or PRINCE2 Agile in PRINCE2 organisations. A Scrum certification is a good first step if you are not yet eligible for the PMI-ACP.

**Q: Is Agile certification worth it?**
It is worth it when you need to pass CV screening, your employer requires it, or you want a structured way to learn. It does not replace experience, so combine it with practice.

**Q: Do Agile certifications expire?**
Some do. PSM I does not expire. CSM renews every two years with 20 SEUs and a fee, SAFe certifications renew annually, and the PMI-ACP requires 30 PDUs every three years.

**Q: How much does Agile certification cost?**
It depends on the credential, provider and country. Exam-only credentials such as PSM I usually cost less than course-based ones such as CSM or SAFe. Include renewal fees and check current prices on the issuer's website.

**Q: Is Scrum the same as Agile?**
No. Agile is a set of values and principles; Scrum is one framework for applying them. Kanban, XP and Lean are other Agile approaches.

**Q: Can I learn Agile without working in IT?**
Yes. Agile is used in marketing, HR, finance, education, construction and many other fields. The principles are the same, though practices are adapted to the work.

**Q: Should I learn Agile or traditional project management?**
Ideally both. Many organisations combine predictive governance with Agile delivery, and project managers who can choose and blend approaches are in demand.

**Q: What comes after a first Agile certification?**
Specialise in a role, gain a year or two of practice, then consider an advanced credential such as PSM II, Advanced CSM, PMI-ACP or a role-specific SAFe certification.
