# How to Manage Agile Teams: A Practical Guide for Managers

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-manage-agile-teams/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: How to manage Agile teams: what managers do, delegation levels, a weekly rhythm, measuring performance, conflict, remote teams and worked examples.


## How to Manage Agile Teams: A Practical Guide for Managers
To manage Agile teams well, you set clear goals and decision boundaries, build the team's capability and remove the obstacles it cannot remove alone, while the team plans and manages its own day-to-day work. This guide explains what changes for managers, how to split responsibilities with the Scrum Master and Product Owner, how to delegate using clear levels and how to measure performance fairly. It also gives you a step-by-step process, a weekly rhythm, illustrative worked examples and the mistakes to avoid.
- Published 21 September 2026
- Last updated 8 November 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- Managing an Agile team means shaping the system the team works in (goals, boundaries, people, environment), not assigning tasks or checking hours.
- Agree in writing who decides what: the team owns how the work is done, the Product Owner owns what is built and in which order, and the manager owns people, budget and organisational obstacles.
- Use explicit delegation levels, from tell to delegate, so the team knows exactly how much authority it has for each type of decision.
- Measure team outcomes and trends (value, flow, quality, predictability, health) and never compare velocity between teams.
- Protect focus: route new requests through the Product Owner, keep teams stable and avoid splitting people across many teams.
- Your own role keeps changing as the team matures; review it every quarter and delegate more as trust grows.

### What does it mean to manage an Agile team?
**Managing an Agile team means creating the conditions for a self-managing team to deliver value: a clear purpose, agreed decision boundaries, the right people and skills, and an environment free of avoidable obstacles. The team decides how to do its work; the manager looks after people, direction and the wider organisation.**
In a traditional project team, the manager breaks down the work, assigns tasks, chases progress and solves problems. In an Agile team, most of that moves inside the team. The [2020 Scrum Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) describes Scrum Teams as self-managing, meaning they decide internally who does what, when and how. Kanban teams work in a similar way, pulling work when they have capacity.
That does not make managers unnecessary. Someone still has to hire and develop people, set budgets, agree priorities with senior leaders, fix cross-team problems and create a culture where people can raise bad news early. The difference is where your attention goes: from the work itself to the system that produces the work. If you are new to Agile teams, start with our guide to [what an Agile team is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-an-agile-team/).

### What changes for managers
The table shows the most important shifts. You do not have to make them all at once, but you should know where you are heading.
| From (traditional) | To (Agile) | What it looks like in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assigning tasks | Setting clear goals and context | You explain the outcome and constraints; the team plans the sprint |
| Checking progress | Making progress visible and trusting the team | You read the board and attend the Sprint Review instead of asking for status reports |
| Solving problems for the team | Helping the team solve problems | You ask questions and remove organisational blockers, not technical ones |
| Individual performance targets | Team outcomes and individual growth | Goals are shared; one-to-ones focus on skills and career |
| Approving every decision | Agreeing boundaries, then delegating | A delegation board shows who decides what |
| Maximising utilisation | Maximising flow and focus | People work on one team; work in progress is limited |
| Fixed plans | Plans that adapt to feedback | Forecasts are ranges and are updated every sprint |
Many managers find the hardest change is emotional rather than procedural. Your value used to come from knowing the answer; now it comes from building a team that finds better answers than you would. Our guide to the [Agile mindset](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-mindset/) explores this shift.

### Who does what: manager, Scrum Master and Product Owner
Confusion about roles causes more friction than any other issue in Agile teams. Agree this split with your Scrum Master and Product Owner and write it down, for example in a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/).
| Area | Team (Developers) | Product Owner | Scrum Master | Line manager |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What to build and in which order | Advises | Decides | Coaches the process | Shares strategy and constraints |
| How to build it and who does which task | Decides | Informed | Coaches | Stays out |
| Sprint Goal and sprint scope | Commits with the Product Owner | Proposes | Facilitates | Informed |
| Process and ways of working | Decides in retrospectives | Contributes | Coaches and facilitates | Supports changes beyond the team |
| Hiring and team membership | Interviews and recommends | Contributes | Contributes | Decides |
| Career development and pay | Peer feedback | Feedback | Feedback | Decides |
| Budget and headcount | Informed | Consulted | Informed | Decides or secures |
| Organisational impediments | Raises | Raises | Escalates | Removes |
The [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) is accountable for the team's effectiveness and coaches the organisation on Scrum. The [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) is accountable for maximising the value of the product. The line manager is not a Scrum accountability at all: you sit outside the Scrum Team and support it. See [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) for the full detail.

#### When the manager is also the team lead
In smaller organisations, one person may line-manage the team and also work in it. That can work, but be careful: when the person who writes your appraisal is in the room, people speak less openly. If you hold both positions, make your role explicit in each meeting ("I am speaking as a Developer now"), let others facilitate retrospectives and keep performance conversations strictly in one-to-ones.

#### Managing several Agile teams
If you manage people across several teams, your job is mostly at the system level: keeping teams stable, resolving dependencies, aligning priorities with other managers and growing people across teams. Organise your reports by team where possible so you are not constantly switching context, and rely on each team's Scrum Master for the day-to-day picture. Coordination patterns such as the [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/) help when teams share a product.

### How to manage an Agile team: step by step
Use these ten steps when you take on an Agile team, or to reset an existing one. Steps one to five usually take the first few weeks; steps six to ten become your ongoing routine.
1. **Clarify purpose and outcomes.** Agree with senior stakeholders and the Product Owner what the team exists to achieve this year, expressed as outcomes such as a Product Goal or a few [OKRs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/okr-template/), not a list of features.
2. **Agree roles and responsibilities.** Use the table above as a starting point. Confirm who the Product Owner and Scrum Master are and what you will and will not decide.
3. **Set decision boundaries.** Run a delegation exercise (see the next section) for the 10 to 15 decisions that cause most friction, and publish the result.
4. **Check team design.** Make sure the team is stable, dedicated and cross-functional, with typically ten or fewer people. Use a [skills matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) to find gaps and single points of failure. Our guide to [Agile team structures](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-team-structures/) explains the options.
5. **Make work visible.** Agree one board and one backlog the team uses every day, so you can see progress without asking for status reports.
6. **Set up your rhythm.** Book regular one-to-ones, attend Sprint Reviews as a stakeholder and hold a regular slot with the Scrum Master to review impediments.
7. **Protect focus.** Route all new requests to the Product Owner, keep people on one team and push back on mid-sprint changes that do not support the Sprint Goal.
8. **Remove organisational obstacles.** Keep an impediment list of problems the team cannot solve alone, such as access, approvals, environments or dependencies on other departments, and work through it.
9. **Measure and learn.** Review a small, balanced set of measures each month with the team, and use them to ask questions, not to rank people.
10. **Grow people and step back.** Invest in training and pairing, widen delegation as trust grows and review your own role every quarter.
Tip
Tell the team explicitly what you are changing and why. A manager who silently stops assigning tasks is often read as disengaged rather than empowering.

### Set decision boundaries with delegation levels
"Self-managing" does not mean the team decides everything. It means the boundaries are clear and the team has full authority inside them. A simple way to agree those boundaries is the seven levels of delegation described by Jurgen Appelo in Management 3.0 (often played as a card game called delegation poker).
| Level | Name | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Tell | The manager decides and explains the decision |
| 2 | Sell | The manager decides and tries to win the team's support |
| 3 | Consult | The manager asks for input, then decides |
| 4 | Agree | The manager and team reach consensus together |
| 5 | Advise | The team decides; the manager offers an opinion first |
| 6 | Inquire | The team decides, then explains its decision to the manager |
| 7 | Delegate | The team decides and the manager does not need to be told |

#### How to run a delegation session
1. List 10 to 15 recurring decisions that cause friction or delay.
2. For each one, ask everyone to choose a level privately, then reveal at the same time.
3. Discuss the highest and lowest answers until you agree a level.
4. Record the result on a delegation board visible to everyone.
5. Revisit the board every quarter and move decisions to higher levels as trust and capability grow.

#### Worked example: a delegation board (illustrative)
A manager of a seven-person product team runs the session in a 60-minute workshop. The agreed board looks like this:
| Decision | Agreed level | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Choice of tools and libraries within the approved list | 7 Delegate | Team has the expertise and bears the consequences |
| Sprint length and event times | 6 Inquire | Team decides; manager wants to know for planning with other teams |
| Working hours and core collaboration time | 5 Advise | Team decides within company policy |
| Hiring a new team member | 4 Agree | Team interviews; team and manager must both say yes |
| Spending over the team's training budget | 3 Consult | Manager is accountable for the budget |
| Moving a person to another team | 3 Consult | Affects other teams; manager decides after hearing the team |
| Company-wide security standards | 1 Tell | Set outside the team; not negotiable |
The value is less in the board itself than in the conversation. In the example, the team assumed it could choose any tool, while the manager assumed new tools needed approval. Agreeing "within the approved list" removed a recurring source of tension.

### A weekly rhythm for managers of Agile teams
A predictable rhythm stops you drifting back into status-chasing. This example assumes two-week sprints and a manager with six to eight direct reports on one or two teams.
| Activity | Cadence | Time | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One-to-ones with each report | Every week or two | 30 minutes each | Growth, wellbeing, feedback, career |
| Impediment review with the Scrum Master | Weekly | 30 minutes | Clear organisational blockers the team has raised |
| Product Owner check-in | Weekly | 30 minutes | Priorities, stakeholder pressure, upcoming demand |
| Sprint Review | Every sprint | 60 minutes | See the increment and give feedback as a stakeholder |
| Read the board and metrics | Twice a week | 15 minutes | Spot trends without interrupting the team |
| Peer managers sync | Weekly | 30 to 45 minutes | Dependencies, shared people, cross-team problems |
| Team health and measures review | Monthly | 45 minutes | Discuss trends with the team and agree experiments |
| Delegation and role review | Quarterly | 60 minutes | Widen delegation; adjust your own role |
Notice what is missing: daily status meetings with you, and attendance at the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/). The Daily Scrum is the Developers' planning meeting. Attend only if invited, and if you do, listen rather than ask for updates. Use a consistent [meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/) for your one-to-ones and check-ins so they stay focused.

### Protecting focus and handling stakeholder requests
Teams lose more time to interruptions and context switching than to slow work. Protecting focus is one of the most valuable things you can do, and it often means saying "not now" to people more senior than you.
- **One front door.** All new requests go to the Product Owner, who decides where they sit in the backlog.
- **Stable sprints.** Changes during a sprint should support the Sprint Goal. If something urgent truly cannot wait, the Product Owner makes the trade-off openly.
- **One team per person.** Splitting people across three teams means each team gets less than a third of them, once switching costs are counted.
- **Limits on work in progress.** Fewer items in progress means faster delivery of each one. See our guide to [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/).
- **A buffer for the unplanned.** Teams that support live products often reserve part of their capacity for urgent fixes. Our [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) guide shows how to size it.

#### Worked example: a mid-sprint request (illustrative)
On day four of a ten-day sprint, a sales director asks you to have the team build a custom report for a prospect by Friday. The team's Sprint Goal is to release a new onboarding flow.
1. **Do not accept the work yourself.** Thank the director and explain that requests go to the Product Owner, who owns priorities.
2. **Bring the Product Owner in quickly.** Help the director explain the value: the size of the deal, the deadline and what happens if it slips.
3. **Let the Product Owner make the trade-off.** In this case the report is about 3 days of effort. Adding it would put the Sprint Goal at risk, so the Product Owner offers two options: a simpler export the team can produce in half a day this sprint, or the full report as the top item next sprint.
4. **Back the decision publicly.** The director accepts the export. You confirm the outcome to both sides and note the pattern: if sales requests keep arriving mid-sprint, the Product Owner may agree a small regular slot for them.
Your role was to protect the process and support the Product Owner, not to decide the priority. Our guide to [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) covers how to prepare for these conversations.

### Measuring Agile team performance
Measure the team, not individuals, and use a balanced set so that improving one number does not damage another. Review trends over several sprints rather than reacting to a single data point.
| Dimension | Example measures | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outcomes and value | Progress against OKRs or the Product Goal; customer feedback; usage of released features | Are we building the right things? |
| Flow | Cycle time, throughput, work item age, [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) | How smoothly does work move? |
| Predictability | Sprint Goals met; forecast vs actual over several sprints | Can stakeholders rely on our forecasts? |
| Quality | Escaped defects, incidents, rework, [technical debt](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/) trend | Are we building things right? |
| Team health | Regular health checks or short surveys; retention; sustainable working hours | Can we keep this up? |
Tip
Never compare velocity between teams or use it as a performance target. Story points are relative to each team, so targets simply inflate the estimates. See our guide to [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/).

#### Worked example: reading the signals (illustrative)
Over four sprints, a team's throughput rises from 14 to 19 items per sprint, which looks positive. But escaped defects rise from 2 to 7 per sprint and the health check shows people working late before every review. Instead of praising the speed, the manager brings the three trends to the team's monthly review. The team decides to strengthen its [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) with automated tests and to cap work in progress. Two sprints later throughput settles at 16, defects fall to 3 and late working stops. The balanced view prevented a short-term gain from hiding a long-term cost.
See [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) for definitions, formulas and how to build a team dashboard.

### Feedback, one-to-ones and performance reviews
Team-based work does not remove the need for individual conversations. It changes what they are about. Team-level feedback belongs in the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/); individual feedback belongs in private one-to-ones.

#### A simple one-to-one agenda
1. **Their agenda first.** What is on their mind? What would make their work easier?
2. **Wellbeing and workload.** Are they working at a sustainable pace?
3. **Feedback both ways.** One specific piece of feedback for them, and ask for one for you.
4. **Growth.** Progress on their development goals, such as a new skill or wider responsibility.
5. **Actions.** Agree who will do what before the next meeting.

#### Fair performance reviews in a team system
- Assess contribution to team outcomes, collaboration, skill growth and how the person helps others, not individual output counts such as tickets closed.
- Collect peer feedback from the team, the Product Owner and the Scrum Master, ideally against a few agreed behaviours.
- Avoid forced ranking within a team; it rewards competition over collaboration.
- Keep development goals visible in a simple [training plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) so reviews are not a surprise.

#### Handling underperformance
Teams usually notice performance problems before managers do, and good teams often address them directly. When they cannot, act early and privately: describe specific behaviour and its effect, ask about causes (unclear expectations, skills gaps, personal circumstances or a poor fit with the role), agree clear expectations and support, and set a date to review. Do not use team events or metrics to single people out. If the problem continues, follow your organisation's formal process with HR support.

### Building capability and motivation
Self-managing teams need the skills and confidence to manage themselves. Building them is a core part of your job, not an optional extra.
- **Map skills and spread them.** A skills matrix shows who can do what. Use pairing, rotation and short internal sessions to remove single points of failure.
- **Grow T-shaped people.** Encourage deep expertise in one area and working skills in neighbouring ones, so the team can swarm on bottlenecks. See [Agile swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/).
- **Give time to improve.** Protect time each sprint for learning, tooling and process improvement, not only feature work.
- **Explain the why.** Share business goals, customer feedback and financial context so the team can make good trade-offs.
Daniel Pink's book Drive argues that knowledge workers are motivated by autonomy, mastery and purpose. Agile practices map neatly onto those three: delegation provides autonomy, investment in skills builds mastery and clear outcomes give purpose. Recognition matters too: celebrate learning and useful failed experiments, not only successful releases.
Google's Project Aristotle research on its own teams found that psychological safety, the belief that you can take interpersonal risks without being punished, was the most important of the team dynamics it studied. As a manager, you set the tone: admit your own mistakes, thank people for raising problems and never punish the messenger. Our guide to [servant leadership in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/servant-leadership-in-scrum/) describes this leadership style in more depth.

### Handling conflict in Agile teams
Agile teams work closely and decide things together, so disagreement is normal. Healthy conflict about ideas (task conflict) improves results. Personal conflict (relationship conflict) damages trust and should be addressed early.
1. **Agree how decisions are made in advance.** For example: the person doing the work decides small technical choices; the team decides bigger ones by consent; the Product Owner breaks ties on priority.
2. **Let the team try first.** Many disagreements resolve in a well-run retrospective. The Scrum Master facilitates; you stay out unless asked.
3. **Talk privately when it becomes personal.** Meet each person separately, listen, then bring them together to agree specific behaviours.
4. **Use a neutral facilitator for deeper conflict.** The Scrum Master, an Agile coach or HR can help structure a conversation.
5. **Follow up.** Check in after a sprint or two to see whether the agreed behaviours have stuck.
Conflict models such as Thomas-Kilmann describe five common styles: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating. None is always right; the useful skill is noticing which style you and others default to and choosing deliberately. A [working agreement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-an-agile-team/) agreed by the team also prevents many conflicts by making expectations explicit.

### Managing remote and hybrid Agile teams
Remote and hybrid Agile teams can work very well, but informal communication does not happen by itself. Design it in.
- **Default to written and visible.** Keep decisions, plans and progress on shared boards and documents so nobody depends on overheard conversations.
- **Agree core collaboration hours.** A short daily window when everyone is available makes the Daily Scrum, pairing and quick questions easy.
- **Use video for key events.** Planning, reviews and retrospectives work better on camera, with digital whiteboards.
- **Rotate inconvenient meeting times** fairly when the team spans time zones.
- **Make connection deliberate.** Short social calls, in-person meet-ups for planning or kick-offs, and pairing all build trust.
- **Watch for invisible overwork.** Remote people often work longer without anyone noticing. Ask about workload in one-to-ones.
Our guide to [remote project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/remote-project-management/) covers tools and communication plans for distributed teams in more detail.

### Worked example: a new manager's first 90 days
This illustrative example follows Priya, newly appointed to manage eight people across two Scrum teams in a mid-sized insurance company. Her predecessor assigned tasks daily and asked for a weekly status report.
| Period | What Priya does | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Days 1 to 30: listen | Holds a one-to-one with every report, meets both Scrum Masters and Product Owners, reads past retrospective notes, attends Sprint Reviews | Finds three recurring problems: two people split across both teams, mid-sprint requests from operations, unclear approval rules for tools |
| Days 31 to 60: clarify | Agrees a responsibilities table with the Scrum Masters and Product Owners, runs a delegation session with each team, moves the two shared people to one team each, sets up an intake route for operations requests via the Product Owners | Weekly status report replaced by the boards and Sprint Reviews; fewer mid-sprint changes |
| Days 61 to 90: improve | Introduces a monthly measures and health review, builds a skills matrix with each team, starts a pairing rotation to cover a single point of failure in testing | Teams propose their own improvement experiments; Priya's time shifts from coordination to growth and cross-team issues |
The lesson is sequence: listen before changing, clarify roles and boundaries before chasing metrics, and remove structural problems (shared people, uncontrolled intake) before asking the team to improve its process.

### Attitudes and mistakes that sink Agile teams
Each of these attitudes undermines trust or quality and, over time, turns Agile into a set of rituals without results.
| Mistake or attitude | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "We'll do Agile, but scope and deadline are both fixed." | Removes the team's only levers, so quality is cut silently | Fix the date or the scope, and let the other flex; agree a minimum viable scope |
| "Just tell me who is behind." | Encourages blame and hides problems | Ask what is blocking the team and how you can help |
| "Retrospectives are a waste of time." | Stops the team improving | Protect the retrospective and act on what it raises; try a [retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) to refresh the format |
| "The team can decide, as long as it decides what I want." | Destroys trust in delegation | Agree delegation levels honestly and respect them |
| "We don't have time to fix technical debt." | Slows every future sprint | Reserve regular capacity for quality work |
| "Documentation isn't Agile." | Creates knowledge gaps and risk | Document what is useful to readers, just enough and kept current |
| Comparing velocity between teams | Inflates estimates and damages collaboration | Compare each team with its own past trends |
| Reshuffling teams for every project | Resets teams to the start of their development | Keep teams stable and bring work to them |
| Attending the Daily Scrum to collect status | Turns it into a report to the manager | Read the board instead; attend only if invited |

### Tools that help you manage Agile teams
Tools do not make a team Agile, but the right one makes work visible and saves you from chasing status. Look for boards and backlogs for the team, plus portfolio views and reporting for managers.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated platform, suits managers who look after several teams or need to connect Agile work with wider portfolio planning: it offers Kanban boards, Gantt charts, workload views, request forms and cross-project dashboards.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is the long-standing choice for software teams, with mature Scrum and Kanban boards, configurable workflows and sprint reports.
- **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)** is quick for mixed business teams to adopt, with flexible boards, automations and dashboards.
- **[Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/)** works well for cross-functional teams that want clear goals linked to everyday tasks.
Start with the simplest setup the team will actually use, and let the team own its board. Read our guide to the [Agile project manager role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) if you also coordinate budgets and dependencies across teams.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do Agile teams need managers?**
They need leadership, but not task assignment. Managers remain important for hiring, people development, budgets, setting direction and removing organisational obstacles that the team cannot remove alone.

**Q: What does a manager do in an Agile team?**
A manager sets goals and context, agrees decision boundaries, keeps the team stable and properly skilled, protects its focus, removes organisational obstacles and supports each person's growth through one-to-ones and feedback.

**Q: What is the difference between a manager and a Scrum Master?**
The Scrum Master is accountable for the team's effectiveness and coaches the team and organisation on Scrum. A line manager looks after people, careers, budgets and the wider organisation. The Scrum Master usually has no authority over pay or appraisals.

**Q: Can a manager be the Scrum Master?**
It is possible but risky. When the person who appraises you also facilitates retrospectives, people tend to speak less openly. If it cannot be avoided, separate the roles clearly and let someone else facilitate some events.

**Q: How do you measure an Agile team's performance?**
Use a balanced set of team measures covering outcomes, flow, predictability, quality and team health, and review trends over several sprints. Avoid individual output counts and never compare velocity between teams.

**Q: Should managers attend Scrum events?**
Managers usually attend Sprint Reviews as stakeholders. They should not attend the Daily Scrum or Sprint Retrospective unless invited, because their presence can reduce openness.

**Q: How do you delegate to an Agile team?**
List the decisions that matter, agree a delegation level for each (from tell to delegate), publish the result on a delegation board and widen it as trust grows.

**Q: How do you handle an underperforming team member?**
Act early and privately. Describe specific behaviour and its effect, explore causes, agree clear expectations and support, and review progress on a set date. Never use team events or metrics to single people out.

**Q: How do you handle conflict in an Agile team?**
Agree how decisions are made in advance, let the team try to resolve task conflict in retrospectives, address personal conflict privately and early, and use a neutral facilitator when needed.

**Q: How do you manage remote Agile teams?**
Default to written updates and shared boards, agree a short core collaboration window, use video for key events, rotate meeting times fairly and make informal connection deliberate.

**Q: How do you motivate an Agile team?**
Explain why the work matters, give the team real autonomy within clear boundaries, invest in its skills and celebrate learning as well as results.

**Q: How many Agile teams can one manager look after?**
There is no fixed rule. It depends on the number of direct reports and how mature the teams are. Many organisations aim for a span of roughly six to ten direct reports, ideally organised by team to reduce context switching.

**Q: What mistakes do managers make with Agile teams?**
Fixing scope and deadline together, interrupting sprints, comparing velocity between teams, attending stand-ups to collect status, reshuffling teams often and treating retrospectives as optional.

# How to Run an Agile Project: Step-by-Step With Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-run-an-agile-project/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: How to run an Agile project from kickoff to release: vision, team, backlog, release forecast, sprints, reporting and closure, with a worked example.


## How to Run an Agile Project: Step-by-Step With Example
To run an Agile project, agree a clear vision, form a small cross-functional team with a Product Owner, build and order a backlog, plan a minimum viable product with a forecast range, then deliver in short sprints and review working results with stakeholders every sprint until you release. This guide takes one project from kickoff to closure in 10 steps, with a sprint calendar, a worked release forecast and an illustrative three-month example. If you are introducing Agile across several teams or a whole organisation, see our guide to implementing Agile instead.
- Published 26 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- An Agile project fixes the team, the time window and the budget, and lets scope flex by value. The Product Owner decides what is built next.
- Start with a one-page vision and a short inception phase, not a detailed plan. You need just enough backlog for the first release.
- Aim for a minimum viable product and forecast it as a range, using the team's velocity, then update the forecast every sprint.
- Run a steady cadence of Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Retrospective, and invite stakeholders to every review.
- Report working output, a burnup chart, the forecast range and the top risks rather than percentage complete.
- Release as soon as the increment is valuable, measure real use, then close the project or hand the product to a continuing team.

### What does running an Agile project involve?
**Running an Agile project means delivering a product or outcome in short, fixed-length iterations, with a stable team that plans just enough, builds a usable increment every cycle, shows it to stakeholders and adjusts the plan based on what it learns.** Scope is ordered by value and can change; the team, the cadence and the quality standard stay fixed.
The table shows how this differs from running the same project in a traditional, plan-driven way.
|  | Traditional project | Agile project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planning | Detailed plan up front | Vision and release plan up front; detail planned each sprint |
| Scope | Fixed; changes go through change control | Flexible; the Product Owner reorders the backlog |
| Delivery | One delivery near the end | A usable increment every sprint; releases as soon as valuable |
| Progress measure | Tasks complete against the plan | Working output and a forecast range |
| Stakeholder involvement | Mainly at the start and end | At every Sprint Review |
For a fuller comparison, see [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/). This guide assumes you have the freedom to run one project the Agile way. Read [how to implement Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-implement-agile/) if you are introducing Agile across teams or a department.

### The Agile project lifecycle at a glance
Agile projects still have a beginning, middle and end. The phases below are a practical way to organise them; the sprint phase repeats until the product is ready to release.
| Phase | Purpose | Main outputs | Typical length |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initiate | Confirm the problem, sponsor and fit | Vision, lightweight charter | Days to 2 weeks |
| Inception (Sprint 0) | Align the team, shape the first backlog | Story map, initial backlog, Definition of Done, release forecast | 1–2 weeks |
| Sprints | Deliver and learn in short cycles | Done increments, updated backlog and forecast | Most of the project |
| Release | Put the product in users' hands | Released increment, support plan | Can happen every sprint or at milestones |
| Close or continue | End the project or hand over to a product team | Lessons learned, handover | 1–2 weeks |
Many UK public-sector teams use a similar phased approach called discovery, alpha, beta and live, where discovery tests whether the problem is worth solving and alpha tests possible solutions before building the real service.

### Step 1: Check that Agile fits the project
Agile works best when the outcome is clear but the best way to reach it is not, and when users can give feedback on partial results. Use this quick check before you commit.
| Signal | Points to Agile | Points to a predictive or hybrid approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | Likely to change as people see results | Stable and well understood |
| Delivery | Can be split into usable increments | Only useful when complete, such as a building |
| Users | Available to give regular feedback | Not available until acceptance |
| Team | Can be dedicated and stable | People join for short specialist tasks |
| Constraints | Some flexibility in scope | Scope, date and cost all fixed by contract |
Mixed signals usually suggest a hybrid: a predictive plan for fixed parts, such as procurement or installation, and Agile sprints for the parts where learning matters, such as software or service design.

### Step 2: Write the vision and a lightweight charter
Before anyone writes a user story, agree why the project exists. A short product vision keeps decisions consistent when priorities change. A simple template:
Tip
For [target users] who [need or problem], the [product] is a [category] that [key benefit]. Unlike [current alternative], it [main differentiator].
Add the essentials a sponsor needs to approve the work. Keep it to one or two pages.
- **Goal and success measures:** what will be different, and how you will measure it, such as online bookings or time saved.
- **Constraints:** budget, time window, regulations and fixed dates.
- **Team and roles:** who is the sponsor, Product Owner and team.
- **Assumptions and top risks.**
- **Governance:** how often the sponsor sees progress, usually at Sprint Reviews.
Our [project charter guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) explains each element, and the free [Agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/) includes a lightweight Agile charter alongside the vision, epics and release plan.

### Step 3: Form the team and agree roles
An Agile project team is small, cross-functional and stable. The Scrum Guide describes a Scrum Team of 10 or fewer people, including the Product Owner and Scrum Master, with all the skills needed to create a usable increment each Sprint.
| Role | Accountable for | Time on the project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sponsor | Funding, the business case, removing organisational blockers | Attends Sprint Reviews |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Vision, ordering the backlog, accepting work, stakeholder decisions | Most of their week |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) or Agile lead | The process, coaching, removing impediments | Part- or full-time |
| Developers (all skills) | Building, testing and delivering the increment | Full-time where possible |
| Stakeholders and users | Feedback on increments, domain knowledge | Reviews and workshops |
Where does the project manager fit? On a single Scrum team the project management work is shared out: the Product Owner owns scope and priorities, the team owns delivery and the Scrum Master owns the process. Many organisations keep an [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) to handle budget, contracts, risks, dependencies and reporting, especially on larger or hybrid projects.
Finish by agreeing a team working agreement: core hours, communication channels, how decisions are made and how the team handles urgent requests. See [what is an Agile team](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-an-agile-team/) for more on team design.

### Step 4: Hold a kickoff and an inception phase
A kickoff gets everyone on the same page; a short inception phase, often called Sprint 0 or iteration zero, prepares enough to start delivering. The Scrum Guide does not define a Sprint 0, so treat it as a common practice: keep it short, and if it can produce something usable, even a basic working page, do so.
| Session | Who | Output | Typical time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kickoff: vision, goals, constraints | Sponsor, Product Owner, team, key stakeholders | Shared understanding of why | 2 hours |
| Story-mapping workshop | Product Owner, team, users | Story map and first release slice | Half a day |
| Technical and design spikes | Developers | Approach agreed for the riskiest parts | 1–3 days |
| Definition of Done and working agreement | Team, Product Owner | Agreed quality standard | 1–2 hours |
| Initial estimation | Team | Story points or sizes for the first release | 2–3 hours |
| Board and tools set-up | Scrum Master, team | Board, backlog, dashboards | Half a day |
By the end of inception you should be able to answer: what are we building first, roughly how big is it, what does done mean, and when is the first Sprint Review?

### Step 5: Build the backlog with a story map
A story map lays out the user's journey from left to right and the stories that support each step underneath, most important at the top. A horizontal line then marks what goes into the first release. It stops the backlog becoming a flat list of features with no sense of the whole.

#### Example: a story map for an online class booking service
This example is illustrative.
| Find a class | Book | Pay | Manage booking |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Search by day and centre (MVP) | Book a place (MVP) | Pay by card (MVP) | Cancel a booking (MVP) |
| Filter by class type (MVP) | Join a waiting list (release 2) | Use membership credits (release 2) | Email reminder (MVP) |
| Save favourite classes (release 2) | Book for a friend (later) | Pay by gift voucher (later) | Rate a class (later) |

#### Write stories the team can deliver
Turn each item into a user story with acceptance criteria, for example: "As a member, I want to cancel a booking up to two hours before the class, so that someone else can take my place." Acceptance criteria then state the rules, such as the two-hour cut-off and the confirmation email. See our guide to [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) and the free [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/).
Order the backlog by value, risk and dependencies, put the riskiest learning early, and make sure the top items meet your [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) criteria before you call them finished.

### Step 6: Define the MVP and forecast the release
A minimum viable product (MVP) is the smallest version that delivers value to real users and generates learning. Use MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't this time) to agree the line on the story map with stakeholders, then [estimate](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/) the items above it.

#### Worked example: a release forecast
The numbers are illustrative. The MVP backlog is estimated at 120 story points. After the first sprints, the team's velocity ranges from 18 to 24 points per two-week sprint.
| Scenario | Velocity | Calculation | Sprints needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Optimistic | 24 points | 120 ÷ 24 = 5.0 | 5 sprints (10 weeks) |
| Pessimistic | 18 points | 120 ÷ 18 = 6.7, rounded up | 7 sprints (14 weeks) |
Communicate the forecast as a range: "The MVP is likely to be ready in 10 to 14 weeks." Before the team has any velocity, use a capacity-based estimate and say clearly that the range will narrow after two or three sprints. If stakeholders need a fixed date, fix it and let the scope beneath the MVP line flex instead.
See [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) for release burnup charts and multi-release planning.

### Step 7: Run the sprint cycle
Most of the project happens here. A sprint is a fixed period of one month or less, usually two weeks, in which the team turns backlog items into a Done increment. The 2020 Scrum Guide sets maximum timeboxes for a one-month Sprint (Sprint Planning 8 hours, Sprint Review 4 hours, Sprint Retrospective 3 hours); for shorter Sprints the events are usually shorter. The Daily Scrum is 15 minutes.

#### A typical two-week sprint calendar
| When | Event | Typical length | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Day 1 morning | [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | 2–4 hours | Agree the Sprint Goal and select backlog items |
| Every day | Daily Scrum | 15 minutes | Inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan |
| Around day 6 | Backlog refinement | 1–2 hours | Clarify and size items for the next sprint |
| Day 10 | [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) | 1–2 hours | Show the increment to stakeholders and update the backlog |
| Day 10 | [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | 1–1.5 hours | Agree improvements to how the team works |
Protect the Sprint Goal. If something urgent arrives, the Product Owner decides whether it waits for the next sprint or, in rare cases, whether the Sprint Goal is still worth pursuing. For more on how sprints work, see [what is a sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/).
Tip
Keep the Sprint Review a working session, not a presentation. Let stakeholders use the increment, then discuss what to change in the backlog.

### Step 8: Manage scope, risks and change
In an Agile project, change is expected, but it still needs managing. The rule is simple: the team's capacity is fixed, so adding something means something else moves down or out.
1. **New request arrives.** It goes to the Product Owner, not straight to a team member.
2. **Product Owner assesses value** against what is already in the backlog and the vision.
3. **Team sizes it** during refinement.
4. **Product Owner places it** in the backlog. If it goes above the release line, an item of similar size moves below it.
5. **Forecast is updated** and the trade-off is explained at the next Sprint Review.
Treat risks the same way. Add risk-reducing work, such as a prototype or a load test, to the backlog and order it early. Keep a simple log of risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, for example our [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/), and review the top items at each Sprint Review.
Larger changes that affect the vision, budget or time window go back to the sponsor. That is a governance decision, not a backlog decision.

### Step 9: Report progress to stakeholders
The best report on an Agile project is the working increment at the Sprint Review. Between reviews, a one-page status update is usually enough.
| Include | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Sprint Goal and whether it was met | Shows focus and reliability |
| What was completed, with a link or demo | Evidence of real progress |
| Release burnup chart | Shows completed work against total scope, including scope changes |
| Forecast range for the next release | Answers when it will be ready, honestly |
| Top three risks or blockers and who owns them | Where stakeholders can help |
| Decisions needed | Keeps the sponsor engaged |
Avoid percentage complete: on an Agile project the total scope changes, so the percentage misleads. A burnup chart shows both lines, completed work and total scope, so everyone can see whether the gap is closing. Our guide to the [Agile velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) explains how to read the team's delivery trend.

### Step 10: Release, measure and close
Release as soon as the increment is valuable, rather than waiting for everything. Before each release, check:
- All items meet the Definition of Done, including testing, accessibility and security checks.
- Users, support and operations teams know what is changing.
- There is a way to measure use, such as analytics or feedback forms, linked to the success measures in the charter.
- There is a rollback or fix plan if something goes wrong.
After release, feed real usage data and feedback back into the backlog. Many Agile products then continue with the same team, and the project simply becomes ongoing product development.

#### Closing an Agile project
If the project does end, close it deliberately: hold a final retrospective covering the whole project, hand over to the team that will support the product, close budgets and contracts, archive the backlog and share lessons learned. A [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) keeps this short and useful.

### Worked example: running a three-month Agile project
This example is illustrative. The organisation, figures and events are invented to show how the steps fit together.
A group of leisure centres wants members to book classes online instead of by phone. The sponsor sets a budget for a team of seven for three months: a Product Owner from the membership team, a Scrum Master and five developers covering design, front-end, back-end and testing. Success means at least half of class bookings made online within three months of launch.

#### Inception (week 1)
The kickoff agrees the vision. A half-day story-mapping session with two centre managers and four members produces the map shown in step 5. The MVP, covering search, book, pay by card, cancel and reminders, is estimated at 120 points. The deadline allows six two-week sprints.

#### Sprint by sprint
| Sprint | Velocity | Done so far | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 16 | 16 / 120 | Search and basic booking work end to end; payment provider set-up takes longer than expected |
| 2 | 22 | 38 / 120 | Card payment live in test; forecast after Sprint 2: 4–6 more sprints, so the deadline is at risk |
| 3 | 24 | 62 / 120 | At the review, centre managers ask for a waiting list (13 points) |
| 4 | 23 | 85 / 120 | Waiting list built; scope changes below take the MVP to 112 points |
| 5 | 21 | 106 / 112 | Accessibility review finds issues; fixes added to the backlog |
| 6 | 14 + fixes | 112 / 112, plus class filter | Last MVP items, accessibility fixes and load test; release |

#### How the scope change was handled
After Sprint 3, 58 points remained and three sprints were left. Recent velocity of 16–24 points gave a capacity of roughly 48–72 points. Adding the 13-point waiting list made 71 points, close to the optimistic end. The Product Owner moved "email reminder" (13 points) to release 2 and placed "filter by class type" (8 points) below the line as a stretch item, giving 50 points and a realistic plan. The sponsor agreed the trade-off at the Sprint 4 review. Because Sprints 4 and 5 went well, the team also delivered the class filter in Sprint 6.

#### Outcome
The service launched at the end of week 13. The team stayed together for a further quarter to add email reminders, membership credits and the waiting-list improvements users asked for, so the project closed with a handover to that continuing product team and a project retrospective rather than a disbanded team.

### Running an Agile project with a fixed budget or deadline
Most real projects have at least one fixed constraint. Agile handles this by fixing time and cost and letting scope flex, which is the opposite of the traditional triangle where scope is fixed and time and cost absorb the changes.
| Constraint | What stays fixed | What flexes | How to manage it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed budget | Team size and number of sprints | Scope below the MVP line | Order by value so the most important items are done first |
| Fixed deadline | Release date | Scope below the MVP line | Forecast every sprint; move items early, not in the last week |
| Fixed scope | Must-have features | Date and cost | Use a predictive or hybrid plan; still deliver incrementally |
| Fixed price contract | Price and outcome | Detailed features within an agreed scope | Agree a swap rule: new items replace items of equal size |
Whatever is fixed, make the MVP smaller than the full capacity, so the project has a buffer for surprises.

### Common mistakes when running an Agile project
- **Skipping the vision.** Without it the backlog becomes a list of requests with no way to choose between them.
- **A Product Owner with no time or authority.** Decisions stall and the team guesses.
- **Too long an inception.** Weeks of analysis before any delivery is a waterfall phase with a new name.
- **Promising a single date.** Give a range and narrow it as velocity becomes reliable.
- **Adding work mid-sprint.** It breaks the Sprint Goal and makes velocity meaningless.
- **Reporting percentage complete.** Use burnup charts and working output.
- **Treating the Sprint Review as a demo only.** Its purpose is to decide what to change next.
- **Leaving testing and release tasks to the end.** Build them into the Definition of Done from the start.

### Tools for running an Agile project
For a small co-located team, a physical board and a spreadsheet backlog can be enough. Most teams use a digital tool for the board, backlog, burnup chart and stakeholder visibility.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** has mature Scrum and Kanban boards, backlogs and sprint reports, and is a strong choice for software projects.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, works well for cross-functional Agile projects that combine sprints with request intake, dashboards for sponsors and reporting across several projects.
- **monday.com** and **ClickUp** offer flexible boards and sprint features that non-technical teams find easy to adopt.
Whatever tool you choose, start from the [Agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/) and the [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) to agree the vision, epics and forecast before you configure the tool.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the steps to run an Agile project?**
Check Agile fits, write the vision and a light charter, form the team, hold a kickoff and short inception, build the backlog with a story map, define the MVP and forecast it, run sprints, manage scope and risk through the backlog, report with working output and burnup charts, then release, measure and close or continue.

**Q: How do you start an Agile project with no backlog?**
Run a story-mapping workshop with users and stakeholders. Lay out the user journey, list the stories under each step, draw a line for the first release and write user stories with acceptance criteria for the items above it.

**Q: Who manages an Agile project?**
Management is shared. The Product Owner owns scope and priorities, the team owns delivery and the Scrum Master owns the process. Many organisations also use an Agile project manager for budget, contracts, risks and dependencies.

**Q: What is Sprint 0 in an Agile project?**
A short preparation period, usually one or two weeks, used to align the team, build the first backlog, agree the Definition of Done and set up tools. It is a common practice rather than part of the Scrum Guide.

**Q: How long should sprints be in an Agile project?**
One month or less under the Scrum Guide. Two weeks is the most common choice because it gives frequent feedback without too much planning overhead. Keep the length consistent once chosen.

**Q: How do you forecast how long an Agile project will take?**
Divide the remaining backlog estimate by the team's lowest and highest recent velocity to get a range of sprints, then update it every sprint. See [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/).

**Q: How do you report on an Agile project?**
Show the working increment at Sprint Reviews and share a short update with the Sprint Goal result, a release burnup chart, the forecast range, top risks and decisions needed. Avoid percentage complete.

**Q: Can you run an Agile project with a fixed budget?**
Yes. Fix the team and the number of sprints, order the backlog by value and let lower-priority scope flex so the most valuable features are delivered within the budget.

**Q: How do you handle scope changes in an Agile project?**
New requests go to the Product Owner, who weighs them against the backlog. If a new item goes above the release line, an item of similar size moves below it, and the forecast is updated at the next Sprint Review.

**Q: What documents does an Agile project need?**
Usually a product vision, a lightweight charter, an ordered backlog with user stories, a Definition of Done, a release plan with a forecast range, a risk or RAID log and short status updates. Add whatever your governance or regulations genuinely require.

**Q: How do you close an Agile project?**
Hold a final project retrospective, hand over to the team supporting the product, close budgets and contracts, archive the backlog and share lessons learned. Many Agile products continue with the same team instead.

**Q: Can a non-software project be run with Agile?**
Yes, if the work can be split into increments that people can review, such as marketing campaigns, service designs or process changes. Projects that are only useful when complete often suit a hybrid approach.
