# Is Agile Only for Software? How Agile Works Beyond IT

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-only-for-software/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Is Agile only for software? No. See how marketing, HR, finance, government and hardware teams use Agile, what changes, worked examples and how to start.


## Is Agile Only for Software? How Agile Works Beyond IT
Is Agile only for software? No. Agile was named and popularised by software developers, but its core idea, delivering value in small steps and adjusting based on feedback, works for most knowledge work where the answer is not fully known at the start. This guide explains where the myth comes from, when Agile fits outside software and when it does not, what changes in practice, and how to start, with two worked examples.
- Published 24 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile is not only for software: marketing, HR, finance, government, hardware and construction teams all use Agile practices.
- Agile's roots were never purely software: Scrum drew on studies of copiers, cameras and cars, and Kanban comes from manufacturing.
- Agile fits best where the work is uncertain, can be delivered in usable pieces and feedback is available quickly.
- Outside software, translate the terms: an increment might be a campaign, a policy pilot or a prototype, and the Definition of Done covers checks such as legal or brand approval.
- Kanban is often the easiest starting point for non-software teams; many projects end up with a hybrid of predictive and Agile planning.

### Is Agile only for software? The short answer
No. Agile is a way of working that delivers results in small, usable increments, gets feedback early and adapts the plan as the team learns. It started in software development, but any team facing uncertainty, changing priorities and work that can be split into smaller pieces can use it, from marketing and HR to hardware engineering.
What matters is not the industry but the nature of the work. Agile helps most when you cannot fully specify the result in advance, when customer or stakeholder feedback will change what you build, and when delivering something partial early is better than delivering everything late. It helps least when the work is well understood, cannot be split, or is very expensive to change once started.
Our guide to [Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) explains the approach in general; this guide focuses on using it beyond software.

### Why people think Agile is only for software
The myth has understandable causes:
- **The language.** The Agile Manifesto, written at Snowbird, Utah in February 2001, values "working software over comprehensive documentation" and says "working software is the primary measure of progress". Read literally, it is about software.
- **The authors.** The seventeen people who wrote the Manifesto were mostly software practitioners, and the early frameworks, such as Extreme Programming, include practices that only make sense in code.
- **The tools and job titles.** Agile tools such as Jira grew up in software teams, and roles such as "developer" sound technical.
- **Training and certification.** Much Agile training uses software examples, so people outside IT rarely see their own work reflected.
- **Early success stories.** The most visible Agile transformations happened in technology companies and IT departments.
None of these makes the ideas themselves software-specific. Replace "working software" with "working results" and most of the [Agile Manifesto values and principles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/) apply directly.

### Agile's roots were never purely software
Many of the ideas behind Agile came from outside software:
- **Scrum's inspiration came from hardware.** Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka's 1986 Harvard Business Review article, "The New New Product Development Game", described a "rugby" approach in which a cross-functional team moves forward together. The products they studied included the Fuji-Xerox FX-3500 copier, the Canon PC-10 personal copier and AE-1 camera, the Honda City car and the NEC PC 8000 personal computer.
- **Lean and Kanban came from manufacturing.** Flow, waste reduction, pull systems and visual boards grew out of the Toyota Production System. See our guide to [Lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/).
- **Iterative development predates the Manifesto.** Iterative and incremental approaches were used on engineering programmes from the late 1950s, decades before the word Agile was adopted. Our [history of Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/history-of-agile/) gives the full timeline.
The 2020 Scrum Guide is explicit about this. Its authors write that Scrum is being adopted "in many domains holding essentially complex work, beyond software product development where Scrum has its roots", and that "we use the word 'developers' in Scrum not to exclude, but to simplify. If you get value from Scrum, consider yourself included." The 2020 revision also removed software-specific terminology. Our guide to [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) explains the framework itself.

### Translating the Agile Manifesto for non-software work
The four values and twelve principles translate with small changes of wording. This table shows the parts most often questioned by non-software teams.
| Original wording | General version | Example outside software |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Working software over comprehensive documentation | Working results over comprehensive documentation | A tested campaign landing page rather than a 40-page campaign plan |
| Working software is the primary measure of progress | Usable outcomes are the primary measure of progress | Roles filled, not CVs screened; a policy piloted, not drafted |
| Deliver working software frequently | Deliver usable results frequently | Publish one module of a new course every two weeks for learner feedback |
| Customer collaboration over contract negotiation | Unchanged | Finance business partners reviewing forecast drafts with budget holders |
| Responding to change over following a plan | Unchanged | Moving campaign budget to the channel that is working this month |
| Continuous attention to technical excellence | Continuous attention to craft and quality | Consistent brand, legal and accessibility standards |

### When Agile works outside software, and when it does not
Agile is a tool, not a goal. Use this test to judge whether it suits a piece of work, whatever the industry.
| Question | Points towards Agile | Points towards a predictive plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How well is the result understood? | Requirements will emerge or change | Requirements are known and stable |
| Can the work be split into usable pieces? | Yes, each piece gives value or learning | No, value only exists when everything is finished |
| How quickly can you get feedback? | Days or weeks | Only at the end |
| How expensive is a change after work starts? | Low: content, process, design, prototypes | High: concrete, tooling, regulated submissions |
| Is there a fixed external sequence? | Little mandated sequence | Regulatory or physical steps must happen in order |
| Is the team stable and able to decide? | Dedicated, cross-functional team | Many part-time contributors and sign-off layers |
Most real projects mix both columns. Building a new office is predictive at its core, but the workplace design, move communications and IT set-up can be run iteratively. Launching a regulated product has fixed submission steps, but marketing content and training can be built in sprints. A hybrid plan, with a predictive backbone and Agile delivery inside it, is often the right answer. Our [Agile vs Waterfall guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) compares the two approaches in detail.
Tip
A useful rule: use Agile where learning is the main risk, and predictive planning where coordination and sequence are the main risk.

### Who uses Agile outside software
| Function or sector | How Agile is typically used |
| --- | --- |
| Marketing | Campaigns run as short experiments; content planned in sprints; results reviewed weekly and budgets moved to what works |
| Product and design | Discovery work, prototypes and usability testing in short cycles |
| HR and people teams | Recruitment pipelines on Kanban boards; new policies piloted with one department first; see [HR project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/hr-project-management/) |
| Finance | Rolling forecasts instead of a single fixed annual budget; funding persistent teams rather than individual projects |
| Legal | Contract and matter work on boards with work-in-progress limits; templates improved in iterations |
| Operations | Continuous improvement with Kanban and Lean; process changes tested in small pilots |
| Education | Courses designed in iterations, with student feedback between modules |
| Research and data | Analyses shared as interim findings rather than one final report |
| Government | Digital public services built in increments with real users |
| Hardware and manufacturing | Prototypes in short iterations; Lean and Kanban on the shop floor |
| Construction | Lean construction and short-interval planning such as the Last Planner System |

#### Government
In the UK, the government's Service Standard, which public services are assessed against, includes point 7, "Use agile ways of working", and point 8, "Iterate and improve frequently". In the US, the Digital Services Playbook's fourth play is "Build the service using agile and iterative practices". These standards are written for digital services, but the teams applying them include policy specialists, content designers, user researchers and operations staff, not only developers. Our guide to [government project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/government-project-management/) covers the wider context.

#### Hardware and manufacturing
Physical products have long lead times, so teams iterate on what can change quickly: designs, simulations, prototypes and test plans. One frequently cited example is Saab's Gripen fighter programme. According to the book Doing Agile Right (Rigby, Elk and Berez, 2020), as reported by Acquisition Talk, Saab's aeronautics business created more than 100 Agile teams across software, hardware and fuselage, coordinated through a common rhythm of three-week sprints.

#### Marketing
Marketing is one of the most established non-software uses. The current Agile Marketing Manifesto, finalised in 2021, adapts the Agile values to campaigns, with five values and ten principles. See our guide to [Agile marketing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/) for a two-week sprint example.

#### Construction
Construction cannot iterate on a poured foundation, but it can plan in short, collaborative cycles. The Last Planner System, from Lean construction, makes weekly commitments with the people who do the work and reviews why commitments were missed. Read our guide to [Agile in construction](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-in-construction/).

#### How widespread is Agile outside software?
Digital.ai's annual State of Agile survey asks respondents which parts of their organisation have adopted Agile. Scrum.org, citing those surveys, reports these figures:
| Function | 2019 | 2020 | 2022 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Operations | 12% | 29% | 26% |
| Marketing | 7% | 17% | 19% |
| Human resources | 6% | 16% | 17% |
| Sales and sales operations | 5% | 11% | 12% |
These are survey responses from organisations already interested in Agile, so treat them as a sign of direction rather than a measure of the whole economy.

### What changes when you use Agile outside software
The principles stay the same, but the vocabulary and some practices need translating. This table maps common software terms to non-software equivalents.
| Software term | Non-software equivalent | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Working software / increment | A usable result that can get feedback | A published article, a piloted process, a prototype, interim research findings |
| User story | A need from the customer's point of view | "As a new starter, I want my laptop ready on day one so I can start training" |
| Definition of Done | The quality checks every item must pass | Brand approved, legal reviewed, accessibility checked, published and tracked |
| Developers | The people doing the work | Writers, recruiters, analysts, designers, engineers |
| Release | Making results available to customers | Launching a campaign, rolling out a policy, opening a course |
| Bug | A defect or error in delivered work | A wrong price in a brochure, a broken form, an unclear policy clause |
| Technical debt | Shortcuts that slow future work | Outdated templates, undocumented processes, messy shared drives |
- **Roles may be part-time.** A small marketing or HR team rarely has a full-time Scrum Master; one team member or a shared coach often takes the role. See [the Scrum Master role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/).
- **Cadence follows the work.** Two-week sprints suit campaign or content work; a continuous flow with weekly replenishment suits request-driven teams.
- **Metrics change.** Velocity in story points matters less; lead time, throughput and outcome measures such as conversion, time to hire or forecast accuracy matter more.
- **Some work stays predictive.** Contracts, procurement, regulatory steps and physical lead times still need dates and dependencies.
Our guide to the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) explains how to write one for your kind of work.

### Scrum, Kanban or hybrid: choosing a framework
|  | Kanban | Scrum | Hybrid (predictive plan with Agile delivery) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Best for | Continuous flow of requests: HR, legal, operations, finance services | Project-like work towards a goal: campaigns, course design, product development | Projects with fixed dates or physical steps plus uncertain parts |
| Cadence | Continuous, with regular review meetings | Fixed sprints of one month or less | Milestones plus sprints or a Kanban flow |
| Roles | No new roles required | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers | Project manager plus Agile roles inside teams |
| Change | New work can enter whenever capacity frees up | Changes wait for the next sprint unless urgent | Change control for the backbone; backlog for the rest |
| Starting effort | Low: start with your current process | Medium: new events and roles | Medium to high: two ways of planning to align |
Kanban is usually the easiest start because you begin with the process you already have and improve it. Scrum works well when a team does project-like work with a clear owner who can set priorities. Our [Kanban vs Scrum comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) goes into more depth, and [what is Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) covers the basics if you are new to it.

### Worked example: an HR recruitment team on Kanban
This illustrative example shows how a three-person recruitment team supporting a 400-person organisation might move to Kanban. Before the change, the team had 18 open vacancies, all nominally "in progress", and hiring managers chased individual recruiters for updates.

#### Step 1: Map the workflow onto a board
Each card is one vacancy. The columns follow the real process, with explicit entry criteria so everyone knows when a card can move.
| Column | A card can enter when | WIP limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approved | Budget and headcount are approved | None |
| Role brief agreed | Hiring manager has signed off the job description and selection criteria | 3 |
| Advertising | The advert is live on the agreed channels | 6 |
| Shortlisting | The advert has closed or enough applicants have been received | 4 |
| Interviewing | Interview panel and dates are confirmed | 4 |
| Offer | A preferred candidate has been selected | 3 |
| Hired | Offer accepted and start date agreed | None |

#### Step 2: Limit work in progress
With WIP limits in place, the team stops starting new vacancies when a column is full and helps move existing ones forward instead, for example by chasing interview feedback. Lower-priority vacancies wait in Approved, visibly, so hiring managers can see the queue and the team can agree priorities with them. Our guide to [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) explains how to set them.

#### Step 3: Agree a review rhythm
- **Twice-weekly 15-minute stand-up** at the board, focused on blocked and ageing cards.
- **Fortnightly replenishment** with HR business partners to agree which approved vacancies start next.
- **Monthly retrospective** on the process, such as how to shorten the time between interview and offer.

#### Step 4: Measure flow and outcomes
The team tracks time to hire (from Approved to Hired), how many vacancies are filled each month, and how long cards sit in each column. If cards wait longest in Interviewing, the bottleneck is panel availability, not recruiter effort, and the fix is to book interview slots in advance. These measures replace the old status spreadsheet and give hiring managers a realistic forecast. A free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) is enough to start.

### Worked example: a hybrid plan for a product launch event
This illustrative example shows a hybrid approach for a product launch event 14 weeks away. Some parts are fixed and must be planned predictively; the rest is uncertain and benefits from sprints.

#### The predictive backbone
| Week | Fixed milestone | Why it is fixed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Venue contract signed | Availability and cancellation terms |
| 4 | Registration opens | Announced publicly with the product teaser |
| 6 | Speakers confirmed | Needed for the agenda and travel bookings |
| 11 | Print and signage deadline | Supplier lead time |
| 14 | Event day | Fixed date |

#### Agile delivery inside it
Content, the registration campaign and the attendee experience are run in seven two-week sprints by a small cross-functional team: a marketer, a content writer, a designer and an events coordinator, with the marketing lead as product owner.
- **Sprint 2 goal:** registration page and first email live, with tracking in place to see which messages drive sign-ups.
- **Sprint 3 goal:** double down on the best-performing channel and test two new agenda descriptions.
- **Sprint 5 goal:** final agenda published and the attendee app content ready for review.
Backlog items are written as needs, for example "As a prospective attendee, I want to see who is speaking so I can decide whether to attend". The team's Definition of Done for any public item is: copy proofread, brand approved, accessibility checked, links tested, published and tracked. Each sprint review is held with the sales and product leads, who see real registration data and can redirect effort.
The project manager tracks the five milestones in a simple plan and checks at each sprint review that the Agile work is on course to meet them. If a sprint threatens the print deadline, scope is cut (fewer printed items, more digital) rather than moving the date. Our [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) and [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) support this kind of plan.

### How to start using Agile outside software
1. **Pick one team and one type of work** where uncertainty or frequent change is causing pain. Avoid starting with work that is fixed and well understood.
2. **Make the current work visible** on a simple board with columns that match your real process.
3. **Agree what "done" means** for your work: the checks and approvals every item must pass.
4. **Limit work in progress** so the team finishes before starting more.
5. **Find the smallest useful result** you can deliver in one to two weeks, and show it to the customer or stakeholder.
6. **Set a rhythm:** a short planning meeting, brief check-ins and a regular review with stakeholders.
7. **Hold a retrospective** every two to four weeks and change one thing at a time.
8. **Measure outcomes,** not only activity, and share what you learn with other teams before scaling up.
A six-week pilot might look like this:
| Weeks | Focus | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Map the workflow and build the board | Board with all current work on it |
| 2 | Agree the Definition of Done and WIP limits | Written team policies |
| 3 | First review with stakeholders | Feedback on delivered items |
| 4 | First [sprint retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | One or two process changes |
| 5 | Start measuring lead time and throughput | Baseline flow measures |
| 6 | Pilot review with leadership | Decision to continue, adjust or extend |
See our guide on [how to implement Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-implement-agile/) for a wider roll-out.

### Common mistakes when applying Agile beyond software
- **Copying software practices literally,** such as story points and two-week sprints for a team that handles a continuous stream of requests.
- **Renaming without changing:** calling the weekly meeting a stand-up and the to-do list a backlog, while work is still planned and approved the old way.
- **No real customer feedback,** so increments are reviewed only by the team and the benefit of iteration is lost.
- **Forcing Agile onto fixed work,** such as statutory reporting with set content and dates, where a checklist and a plan work better.
- **Ignoring sign-off layers:** if every item needs three approvals, the approvals are the bottleneck and must be part of the redesign.
- **Starting too big,** with an organisation-wide transformation before one team has shown what works. See [Agile transformation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/).
- **Measuring busyness** (tasks completed) instead of outcomes for the customer.

### Tools for non-software Agile teams
Non-software teams usually need visual boards, simple forms for incoming requests, approvals and reporting more than developer features. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, combines boards, request forms, Gantt charts and dashboards, which suits marketing, operations and PMO teams running hybrid work across departments. [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) has colour-coded boards that non-technical teams adopt quickly. [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) is easy to roll out across departments and supports boards and sprint-style projects. [Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/) is a simple way to start with Kanban.
Jira supports almost every Agile software practice, but for a team whose work is mainly non-technical it is usually more tool than it needs. Whatever you choose, start with a board that matches your process and add features only when the team needs them.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Agile only for software development?**
No. Agile started in software, but marketing, HR, finance, legal, operations, education, government, hardware and construction teams all use Agile practices. It suits any work that is uncertain, can be split into usable pieces and benefits from early feedback.

**Q: Can Scrum be used for non-software projects?**
Yes. The 2020 Scrum Guide says Scrum is used in many domains of complex work beyond software, and that the term developers is meant to include anyone doing the work. It suits project-like work with a clear product owner.

**Q: Which Agile framework is best for non-software teams?**
Kanban is often the easiest to start with, especially for teams handling a continuous flow of requests. Scrum works well for goal-driven project work. Many teams use a hybrid of a predictive plan with Agile delivery.

**Q: What are examples of Agile outside software?**
Marketing campaigns run as experiments, recruitment pipelines on Kanban boards, rolling financial forecasts, government services built with users, hardware prototypes in short iterations and Last Planner weekly planning in construction.

**Q: When should you not use Agile?**
When the work is well understood and stable, cannot be split into usable pieces, is very expensive to change once started, or must follow a fixed regulatory or physical sequence. A predictive or hybrid plan usually fits better there.

**Q: What does an increment look like outside software?**
Anything usable that generates feedback: a published article, a tested campaign, a piloted process, a course module, a prototype or interim research findings.

**Q: How do you adapt the Definition of Done for non-software work?**
Replace software checks with the quality steps your work needs, such as proofreading, legal review, brand approval, accessibility or safety checks. See our [Definition of Done guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).

**Q: Do non-software Agile teams need a Scrum Master?**
Not always. Kanban requires no new roles. Small teams using Scrum often give the Scrum Master accountability to a team member or share a coach across several teams.

**Q: Can HR and finance teams use Agile?**
Yes. HR teams often run recruitment and onboarding on Kanban boards and pilot new policies with one department. Finance teams use rolling forecasts and fund persistent teams rather than individual projects.

**Q: Is Agile used in government?**
Yes. The UK government's Service Standard asks teams to use agile ways of working and iterate frequently, and the US Digital Services Playbook includes building services using agile and iterative practices.

**Q: Can Agile work in manufacturing and hardware development?**
Yes. Teams iterate on designs, simulations and prototypes, while Lean and Kanban are long established on the shop floor. Saab's Gripen programme is a frequently cited example of Agile at scale in hardware.

**Q: What is business agility?**
The ability of a whole organisation, not just its delivery teams, to sense change and respond quickly with new products, services or ways of working, supported by funding, governance and leadership that allow it.

**Q: Do you need special software to use Agile outside software?**
No. Many teams start with a whiteboard, sticky notes or a shared spreadsheet. Project management tools help once work is shared across locations or teams, because they keep the board, requests and reporting in one place.

**Q: Is Agile only for small teams?**
No. Agile teams are usually small (the Scrum Guide suggests 10 or fewer people), but larger organisations coordinate many such teams, as Saab does with a common sprint rhythm. Scaling frameworks exist for this, though most non-software teams should start with one team.

**Q: How long does it take a non-software team to adopt Agile?**
A single team can see whether basic practices help within a six- to eight-week pilot. Changing approvals, funding and culture across an organisation takes much longer and works best when built on early team results.

# Is Agile the Future of Project Management?

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-the-future-of-project-management/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Is Agile the future of project management? The evidence on hybrid, AI, business agility and PMBOK 8, a decision guide and the skills you need next.


## Is Agile the Future of Project Management?
Is Agile the future of project management? Its ideas are: short feedback loops, empowered teams and delivering value early are now standard practice. But the future is not "Agile only". It is adaptive and increasingly hybrid, with each project's approach chosen to fit its risks, and with AI taking over much of the routine administration. This guide looks at the evidence, the "Agile is dead" debate, the trends that matter and what you should do about them.
- Published 26 September 2026
- Last updated 15 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile ideas have won: iteration, visible work and frequent feedback are expected on most projects, including non-software ones.
- Agile as a single, universal method has not. Survey data shows hybrid and customised approaches growing fastest.
- Predictive planning remains the better fit for stable, regulated, fixed-scope and physical work.
- AI is automating reporting, scheduling and analysis, which raises the value of judgement, facilitation and stakeholder leadership.
- PMI's standards and the PMP exam launched in July 2026 cover predictive, Agile and hybrid approaches, with more weight on business outcomes.
- The most future-proof skill is choosing and tailoring the right approach for each piece of work.

### Short answer: is Agile the future of project management?
**Agile is part of the future of project management, but not all of it.** The values and practices behind Agile (small increments, frequent feedback, self-managing teams and openness to change) have become mainstream good practice. What is fading is the idea that one framework suits every project. Most organisations now tailor and combine approaches, and AI is changing how the work is done.
Put simply, the future looks like this:
- **Agile ideas: yes.** Expect iterative delivery and frequent stakeholder feedback on most projects, whatever the industry.
- **Agile-only: no.** Predictive planning, stage gates and fixed baselines remain right for many projects, and most organisations mix the two.
- **Adaptive and hybrid: the direction of travel.** The skill that matters is choosing the right approach, then adjusting it as the project learns.
- **AI-assisted: increasingly.** Routine planning, reporting and forecasting are being automated, so human value shifts to judgement and leadership.
The rest of this guide explains the evidence behind each point and what it means for you.

### What we mean by "Agile"
Much of the argument about Agile's future comes from people using the same word for different things. It helps to separate three meanings:
| Meaning | What it covers | Outlook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agile values and principles | The 2001 Agile Manifesto: individuals and interactions, working results, customer collaboration and responding to change | Strong. These ideas now appear in general project management standards and in most industries. |
| Agile frameworks | Scrum, Kanban, XP, SAFe, LeSS and others, each with defined roles, events and artefacts | Mixed. Lightweight team frameworks remain popular; heavy, prescriptive rollouts face more scrutiny. |
| Agile as a brand or industry | Large transformation programmes, consultancies, certifications and dedicated Agile job titles | Under pressure. Many organisations are cutting dedicated Agile roles and asking for proof of business results. |
When someone says "Agile is dead", they usually mean the third row. When someone says "Agile is the future", they usually mean the first. Both can be true at once.

### The evidence: where Agile stands in 2026
No single survey gives a complete picture, and most Agile surveys over-represent software teams and people who already practise Agile. Read the figures below as signals of direction, not precise market measurements. Each is attributed to its source.
| Source | Finding | What it suggests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PMI, Pulse of the Profession 2024 (15th edition) | Use of hybrid approaches rose from 20% of projects in 2020 to 31.5% in 2023 | Hybrid is the fastest-growing way of working, not pure Agile or pure predictive |
| Digital.ai, 18th State of Agile Report (October 2025) | 74% of respondents use hybrid or customised Agile models | Organisations tailor frameworks rather than adopting them by the book |
| Digital.ai, 18th State of Agile Report | 84% use or plan to use AI in the software delivery life cycle, up from 68% | AI is becoming part of how Agile teams plan and deliver |
| Digital.ai, 18th State of Agile Report | Only 13% say Agile is fully embedded across their business; 76% report growing pressure to prove the return on Agile initiatives | Team-level Agile is common; organisation-wide agility and proof of value are the unfinished work |
| Digital.ai, 17th State of Agile Report (January 2024) | Scrum is used by 63% of Agile teams; small companies reported higher satisfaction with Agile than large ones | Agile works most easily at team scale; scaling is the hard part |
| PMI, PMBOK Guide Eighth Edition (November 2025) | Keeps the principles and performance domains of the 7th edition, reintroduces non-prescriptive process guidance and expands coverage of AI | The main standard supports tailoring across approaches rather than one method |
| Gartner press release (March 2019) | Predicted that 80% of today's project management tasks will be eliminated by 2030 as AI takes over | Routine PM administration is the most exposed part of the job |
Tip
Survey percentages describe the people who answered, not every organisation. The 18th State of Agile Report, for example, drew mainly on Agile coaches and consultants in large organisations. Use the trend, not the exact number.
Taken together, the evidence points the same way: Agile practices are widespread, but organisations adapt and combine them, and they increasingly want proof that the way they work improves business results.

### Is Agile dead? Separating the backlash from the ideas
"Agile is dead" articles and talks have appeared for more than a decade, and the debate grew louder as technology companies cut dedicated Agile roles such as Scrum Master and Agile coach. It is worth being precise about what critics object to.

#### What the critics are reacting to
- **Heavy, framework-first transformations** that added meetings, roles and reporting without improving delivery.
- **"Agile theatre"**: teams holding stand-ups and sprints while plans, budgets and approvals stay fixed and annual.
- **A certification industry** that sometimes taught a single "right way" rather than judgement.
- **Dedicated Agile roles** that organisations struggled to justify when budgets tightened, especially where the role was seen as administrative.
- **Weak links to business outcomes**: velocity and story points reported upwards instead of customer or financial results.

#### What remains intact
- Breaking work into small, valuable increments and delivering them early.
- Short planning horizons with regular re-planning based on real feedback.
- Visible work (boards, backlogs, WIP limits) and frequent inspection.
- Cross-functional teams that own outcomes rather than hand work between silos.
- Retrospectives and continuous improvement.
These practices are not disappearing; they are being absorbed into normal project and product management. The likely future is less "doing Agile" as a separate programme and more working in an adaptive way by default. That is a sign of success rather than decline, though it changes which jobs exist.

### Why hybrid is the most likely future
A **hybrid approach** combines predictive elements (business cases, baselines, stage gates, fixed milestones) with Agile elements (backlogs, iterations, frequent demos) in one project or programme. PMI's 2024 Pulse of the Profession reported hybrid as the approach whose use grew fastest between 2020 and 2023, and most practitioners will recognise it from daily work.
Hybrid is popular because it matches how organisations are actually run. Boards still approve budgets annually, regulators still expect documented controls and suppliers still sign contracts with dates, while delivery teams benefit from iterating. Common patterns include:
| Hybrid pattern | How it works | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predictive governance, Agile delivery | Business case, budget and stage gates are predictive; teams deliver in sprints within each stage | Corporate IT, digital programmes in regulated sectors |
| Agile front end, predictive back end | Discovery and design iterate with users; build and roll-out follow a fixed plan | New services, construction design, product launches |
| Mixed workstreams | Software streams run Agile; hardware, facilities, legal or training streams run predictively under one integrated plan | ERP and CRM roll-outs, office moves, manufacturing changes |
| Agile at team level, rolling-wave at programme level | Teams plan in sprints; the programme plans in detail for the next quarter and at milestone level beyond | Large transformations, scaled Agile programmes |
| "Water-Scrum-Fall" | Upfront requirements and a long test and release phase sandwich Scrum-style development | Often a transitional state; usually worth evolving towards smaller, more frequent releases |
Tip
Hybrid works when the choice is deliberate: each element is there because it manages a real risk. It fails when it is an accident, for example sprints inside a project where requirements are frozen and change requests take months.

### Where predictive approaches will stay
Agile's own principles assume that early feedback is possible and that changing direction is affordable. When those conditions do not hold, predictive planning remains the sensible choice, and that will not change:
- **Physical work with high change costs**, such as construction, civil engineering and plant installation, where you cannot iterate on a poured foundation. See [construction project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/construction-project-management/).
- **Regulated and safety-critical projects** that need documented design approval before build.
- **Fixed-scope, fixed-price contracts** where the client and supplier must agree the deliverables in advance.
- **Repeatable projects** the organisation has delivered many times, where the plan is well understood and surprises are rare.
- **Events and hard deadlines** where the date cannot move and the scope is mostly known.
Even here, Agile ideas creep in: design teams iterate, construction uses lean pull planning and short look-ahead schedules, and events use daily stand-ups in the final weeks.

### Five trends shaping the future of project management

#### 1. AI moves from assistant to team member
AI tools already draft plans, summarise meetings, write status reports, flag risks and forecast completion dates from historical data. The 18th State of Agile Report describes a shift towards "agentic" AI, tools that take actions rather than only make suggestions, and found that only about half of respondents had guardrails in place for this. Expect AI to handle more of the administration of both Agile and predictive projects, with people setting goals, making trade-offs and owning accountability.

#### 2. Business agility and outcomes over outputs
The focus is moving from team-level ceremonies to how quickly a whole organisation can change direction: funding, governance, HR and portfolio decisions included. Organisations increasingly measure success by customer and business outcomes rather than by velocity or on-time delivery of a fixed scope.

#### 3. From projects to products
Many organisations, especially in technology, fund long-lived product teams with a budget per quarter instead of temporary project teams with a budget per project. Projects do not disappear (one-off changes still need them), but more ongoing work is managed as a product with a roadmap and backlog.

#### 4. Scaling with lighter frameworks
Large organisations still need to coordinate many teams. Frameworks such as the [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) remain widely used, but the 18th State of Agile Report found most respondents using hybrid or home-grown models. The trend is towards taking the coordination practices that help (shared cadences, joint planning, visible dependencies) and leaving the rest.

#### 5. Standards that describe a range of approaches
PMI's [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) Eighth Edition (November 2025) keeps the principle-based approach of the 7th edition and adds non-prescriptive process guidance, with expanded coverage of AI, PMOs and procurement. The new [PMP exam](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/), introduced on 9 July 2026, keeps the People, Process and Business Environment domains but raises Business Environment from 8% to 26% of the exam, and continues to test predictive, Agile and hybrid approaches. Professional standards no longer ask "Agile or not?" but "which approach, tailored how?"

### What AI changes for Agile and project managers
Gartner's 2019 prediction that 80% of today's project management tasks would be eliminated by 2030 is often quoted. Whatever the exact figure turns out to be, the direction is clear: the tasks most exposed are the routine, data-handling ones. The table shows our own view of how common project tasks are likely to change.
| Task | Likely future | Human role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status reports and meeting notes | Largely automated from tool data and transcripts | Check accuracy, add context and judgement |
| Schedules and sprint forecasts | Generated and updated automatically from history and progress | Challenge assumptions, set priorities, negotiate dates |
| Risk identification | AI suggests risks from similar projects and live signals | Judge which risks matter and own the responses |
| Backlog writing and refinement | AI drafts user stories, acceptance criteria and splits | Make sure the work reflects real user needs and value |
| Resource and capacity planning | Optimised suggestions across teams | Balance people's skills, wellbeing and development |
| Stakeholder management | AI helps prepare and summarise | Build trust, resolve conflict, influence decisions |
| Choosing the delivery approach | AI can surface patterns from past projects | Decide and take accountability |
For Agile specifically, AI lowers the cost of re-planning, which strengthens the case for adaptive approaches: if updating a plan takes minutes instead of days, there is less reason to freeze it. It also tests teams' discipline, because faster output is only valuable if it is the right output.

### What changes by 2030 and what stays the same
Predictions are uncertain, so treat this as a planning aid rather than a forecast. It reflects the trends above and our own judgement.
| Area | Likely to change | Likely to stay the same |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Methods | More tailoring and hybrid models; fewer by-the-book framework roll-outs | Iterative delivery for uncertain work, predictive planning for stable work |
| Roles | Fewer purely administrative PM and Agile roles; more blended delivery, product and change roles | Need for someone accountable for delivery, risk and stakeholders |
| Tools | AI agents updating plans, boards and reports | Need for a single, trusted view of the work |
| Governance | More frequent, lighter funding and portfolio reviews | Accountability for money, risk and compliance |
| Measures | Outcomes, flow and customer value | Cost, time and quality still matter to sponsors |
| Skills | Data literacy and AI fluency become baseline | Leadership, communication and judgement |

### How to choose the right approach for a project
If the future is adaptive, the core skill is choosing an approach deliberately. Use this five-step process at project start-up and revisit it at each major milestone.
1. **Assess requirements uncertainty.** How well do you and the customer know what is needed? If the answer will only emerge from feedback, lean Agile.
2. **Assess technical uncertainty.** Has your organisation done this kind of work before with this technology? New technology favours short experiments.
3. **Check the cost of change.** If changing course late is cheap (software, content, services), iterate. If it is expensive (concrete, tooling, regulated documents), plan upfront.
4. **Check the constraints.** Contracts, regulators, funding rules and fixed dates may require predictive elements, such as approved baselines or stage gates.
5. **Check customer and team availability.** Agile needs a customer or product owner who can give frequent feedback and a team that can work together closely. Without them, predictive or hybrid is safer.
6. **Decide per workstream, not just per project,** and write down why. Review the choice at each stage gate or quarterly planning point.
A simple scoring grid helps. Score each factor from 1 (favours predictive) to 3 (favours Agile):
| Factor | 1 = predictive | 2 = either | 3 = Agile |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements clarity | Clear, stable and signed off | Partly known | Unclear or expected to change |
| Technology | Proven and familiar | Some new elements | New to the team or the market |
| Cost of late change | High | Moderate | Low |
| Customer involvement | Rare, formal reviews | Monthly | Weekly or more |
| Ability to deliver in increments | Only the whole is useful | Some parts are usable alone | Small slices deliver value |
| External constraints | Fixed contract or heavy regulation | Some controls | Few |
A total of 6–10 suggests predictive, 11–14 hybrid and 15–18 Agile. Use the result to start a conversation, not to replace judgement.

#### Worked example: a CRM roll-out
A 400-person company is replacing its customer relationship management (CRM) system. The team scores the work:
| Workstream | Scores | Total | Approach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Configuring sales and service workflows | Requirements 3, technology 2, change cost 3, customer 3, increments 3, constraints 2 | 16 | Agile: two-week sprints with sales users reviewing each increment |
| Data migration | Requirements 2, technology 2, change cost 1, customer 2, increments 2, constraints 1 (data protection) | 10 | Predictive: mapping, trial loads and a fixed cut-over plan |
| Contract and licensing | Requirements 1, technology 1, change cost 1, customer 1, increments 1, constraints 1 | 6 | Predictive: procurement milestones |
| Training and change | Requirements 2, technology 1, change cost 3, customer 2, increments 3, constraints 2 | 13 | Hybrid: fixed go-live training plan, iterated materials based on pilot feedback |
The overall project is therefore hybrid: a predictive governance layer (budget, go-live date, stage gates) with an Agile configuration stream inside it. The project manager integrates the streams with a milestone plan and a shared risk log, and the configuration team works from a prioritised backlog. You can start from our free [Agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/) or the [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/).

### Skills project managers will need
The skills below appear repeatedly in professional standards, exam outlines and job descriptions. The right-hand column gives practical ways to build each one.
| Skill | Why it matters | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approach selection and tailoring | Hybrid work needs someone who can design the way of working | Practise the scoring method above on past projects; study PMBOK tailoring guidance |
| Agile delivery fluency | Most teams use backlogs, sprints or Kanban somewhere | Run or join a Scrum or Kanban team; learn the Scrum Guide and Kanban basics |
| Predictive planning | Budgets, contracts and dependencies still need baselines | Build a schedule with a critical path and a cost baseline on a real project |
| Facilitation and coaching | Teams increasingly self-manage; leaders guide rather than direct | Facilitate retrospectives, workshops and planning sessions |
| Business and financial acumen | The 2026 PMP exam gives Business Environment 26% of the weighting | Learn to read a business case, benefits plan and value metrics |
| Data literacy and AI fluency | AI tools generate forecasts you must question | Use AI in your tools for drafts and analysis, and check outputs against reality |
| Stakeholder leadership and change | AI cannot build trust or resolve conflict | Own stakeholder mapping and communications on your next project |

### A 12-month plan to future-proof your career
Whether you come from a predictive or an Agile background, this plan builds the blend of skills described above. Adjust the order to fit your role.
1. **Months 1–3: fill your biggest gap.** If you are predictive-trained, learn the Agile Manifesto, the Scrum Guide and Kanban basics, then join an Agile team or run a small pilot. If you are Agile-trained, learn budgeting, contracts and critical path scheduling.
2. **Months 4–6: practise hybrid on a real project.** Apply the approach-selection process, document why you chose each element and review it at a milestone.
3. **Months 7–9: build AI and data fluency.** Use AI features in your project tools to draft reports and forecasts, and compare them with actual results. Learn the basics of the metrics your organisation uses.
4. **Months 10–12: validate and share.** Choose a certification that matches your direction (PMP for broad project management, PMI-ACP or a Scrum certification for Agile roles, or our PMAI certification for AI in project management) and run a lessons-learned session on what you changed.

### What this means for organisations
For PMOs, sponsors and delivery leaders, the practical implications are:
- **Stop asking "Agile or Waterfall?"** Ask which approach each piece of work needs, and make that choice part of project start-up.
- **Fix the system, not just the teams.** Annual budgets, fixed-scope business cases and slow approvals undermine Agile teams. Move to more frequent, lighter funding reviews where you can.
- **Measure outcomes.** Report customer and business results alongside time and cost, and stop using velocity as a performance target.
- **Rethink the PMO.** A modern [Agile PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-pmo/) supports teams with standards, data and coaching instead of only policing gates.
- **Set guardrails for AI.** Decide which decisions AI may automate, how outputs are checked and who is accountable.
- **Develop blended skills.** Train project managers in Agile and Agile practitioners in governance and finance.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Agile dead in 2026?**
No. The core practices, such as iterative delivery, visible work and frequent feedback, are more widespread than ever. What has declined is enthusiasm for heavy, by-the-book transformations and some dedicated Agile roles. Most organisations now tailor Agile and combine it with predictive elements.

**Q: Will Agile replace Waterfall?**
Unlikely. Predictive planning remains the better fit for stable, regulated, fixed-price and physical projects. The trend is towards choosing and combining approaches, often within the same project. See [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).

**Q: Will AI replace project managers?**
AI is automating routine tasks such as reporting, scheduling and forecasting; Gartner predicted in 2019 that 80% of today's project management tasks would be eliminated by 2030. The human work of leading people, managing stakeholders, making trade-offs and taking accountability remains, and becomes a larger share of the role.

**Q: Is hybrid project management the future?**
For most organisations, yes. PMI's Pulse of the Profession 2024 reported hybrid use rising from 20% of projects in 2020 to 31.5% in 2023, and the 18th State of Agile Report found 74% of respondents using hybrid or customised Agile models.

**Q: Is Agile still in demand for jobs?**
Agile skills are in demand, but many employers now expect them as part of broader delivery, product or project management roles rather than as a standalone job. Combining Agile with governance, financial and AI skills makes you more employable.

**Q: What comes after Agile?**
There is no single successor. The main directions are business agility (adaptive organisations, not just teams), outcome-based funding, product operating models and AI-assisted delivery. All of them build on Agile ideas rather than replacing them.

**Q: Should I learn Agile or traditional project management?**
Both. Most roles expect you to understand predictive planning and Agile delivery and to combine them. Start with whichever you know least. See [how to learn Agile and get certified](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/).

**Q: Does PMI see Agile as the future of project management?**
PMI treats Agile as one of several approaches. The PMBOK Guide Eighth Edition supports tailoring across a range of approaches, the PMP exam launched in July 2026 tests predictive, Agile and hybrid methods, and PMI offers the PMI-ACP certification for Agile practitioners.

**Q: Is Agile only for software?**
No. Marketing, HR, operations, education and construction design teams use Agile practices, usually adapted. See [is Agile only for software?](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-only-for-software/).

**Q: What is business agility?**
Business agility is the ability of a whole organisation, including funding, governance and HR, to sense change and respond quickly. Many see it as the next goal beyond team-level Agile.

**Q: How is AI changing Agile?**
AI drafts user stories and acceptance criteria, summarises ceremonies, forecasts delivery and flags risks. Because it makes re-planning cheaper, it strengthens the case for adaptive approaches, but teams still need to check that faster output is the right output.

**Q: Which certification is most future-proof?**
One that matches your direction. PMP covers predictive, Agile and hybrid approaches; PMI-ACP and Scrum certifications suit Agile delivery roles; AI-focused certifications such as PMAI add skills in using AI for project work. Practical experience matters more than any certificate.

**Q: Is the future of project management moving from projects to products?**
Partly. Many technology organisations fund long-lived product teams instead of one-off projects. Projects remain essential for one-off changes such as system roll-outs, construction and organisational change.
