# Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS): Rules, Roles and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS) explained: rules, 10 principles, roles, events, LeSS Huge, a worked example, adoption steps and LeSS vs SAFe and Nexus.


## Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS): Rules, Roles and Examples
Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS) is a framework for applying Scrum to many teams that work together on one product, with one Product Owner, one Product Backlog and one shared Sprint. Created by Craig Larman and Bas Vodde, it adds as little extra structure as possible and asks the organisation to change instead. This guide explains the rules, the ten principles, the roles and events, LeSS Huge, a worked Sprint example and how to adopt it.
- Published 23 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- LeSS is Scrum applied to many teams on one product: one Product Owner, one Product Backlog, one Definition of Done and one Sprint ending in one integrated increment.
- Basic LeSS is for two to eight teams; LeSS Huge, for more than eight, adds requirement areas of four to eight teams, each with an Area Product Owner.
- Teams are long-lived, cross-functional feature teams that deliver whole customer features, not component teams that own one layer.
- LeSS adds only a few events to Scrum: a shared Sprint Planning One, multi-team refinement, one product-level Sprint Review and an Overall Retrospective.
- Compared with SAFe, LeSS has far fewer roles and layers but demands deeper organisational change, such as removing functional reporting lines.
- Adopt it deep and narrow: one product group at a time, with education first and volunteers wherever possible.

### What is Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS)?
**Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS)** is a lightweight framework for scaling Scrum to many teams that build one product together. All teams share one Product Owner, one Product Backlog, one Definition of Done and one Sprint, and deliver one integrated product increment. Instead of adding roles and layers, LeSS changes the organisation around the product.
LeSS grew out of practical work by **Craig Larman and Bas Vodde**, who began collaborating on scaling Scrum in 2005 when clients asked for help with large, multi-site and offshore development. Their ideas are set out in three books: *Scaling Lean & Agile Development* (2008), *Practices for Scaling Lean & Agile Development* (2010) and *Large-Scale Scrum: More with LeSS*, which acts as a primer for the series. The official site, less.works, lists adoptions in organisations such as Ericsson, Nokia Networks, UBS, Cisco and bwin.party, most of them with around five teams in one or two locations.
The central idea is that **large-scale Scrum is still Scrum**. It is not team-level Scrum with a management layer on top. If you know [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/), you already know most of LeSS; the difference lies in how many teams share each element and how the organisation is structured around them.

#### The building blocks of LeSS
LeSS is published as four layers, from firm to optional:
| Layer | What it contains | How binding it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Principles | Ten ideas, such as whole-product focus and systems thinking, used to decide anything the rules do not cover | The foundation for every decision |
| Rules | A short set of rules that define the LeSS and LeSS Huge structures (current version dated November 2024) | Required: this is what makes it LeSS |
| Guides | Practical advice on applying the rules, such as how to run Sprint Planning One or adopt LeSS | Recommended: try them |
| Experiments | Many situational ideas from the books that worked, or failed, somewhere | Optional: use them to learn |

### LeSS rules: the "one of everything" structure
Most of the LeSS rules can be summarised as **one of everything at product level**, with teams doing the work inside that frame. The table compares the main rules with a single-team Scrum setup.
| Element | One-team Scrum | LeSS (2–8 teams) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product | One product | One product, defined broadly and from the customer's point of view |
| Product Owner | One | One, for the whole product |
| Product Backlog | One | One, shared by all teams |
| Definition of Done | One | One common DoD; each team may make it stronger but not weaker |
| Sprint | One | One product-level Sprint; all teams start and end together |
| Increment | One | One integrated, potentially shippable increment |
| Teams | One Scrum Team | Two to eight self-managing, cross-functional, long-lived feature teams |
| Scrum Master | One per team | A dedicated, full-time Scrum Master for one to three teams |
| Sprint Backlog and Daily Scrum | One | One per team |
| Managers | Not defined | Optional; their focus moves to improving the product development system |
LeSS also asks you to set up the **full structure for the product group from the start**, rather than piloting parts of it, and sets a long-term goal of a shippable product every Sprint or more often.

#### One product, defined broadly
The product definition decides who is in the product group and what goes into the single [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/). LeSS recommends a broad, customer-centric definition: "online banking" rather than "the payments API". Narrow, component-based definitions recreate the hand-offs LeSS is designed to remove.

#### One Definition of Done and undone work
All teams work to one [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/). LeSS contrasts it with a **perfect Definition of Done** that covers everything needed to put the product in customers' hands. The gap between the two is planned **undone work**, such as a separate release or performance test. Undone work hides risk and delay, so the aim is to expand the Definition of Done Sprint by Sprint until none is left.

### The 10 LeSS principles
The principles are what you use when the rules are silent. less.works lists ten:
| Principle | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Large-Scale Scrum is Scrum | Keep Scrum's purpose, elements and empiricism at any size; do not invent a new process |
| Empirical process control | Shape the product, the process and the organisation through frequent inspection and adaptation |
| Transparency | Base decisions on done items, short cycles, shared definitions and a culture where problems can be raised safely |
| More with less | Get more learning, ownership and value with fewer roles, artifacts, special groups and processes |
| Whole-product focus | One backlog, one Product Owner, one increment and one Sprint, however many teams there are |
| Customer-centric | Judge value and waste from the paying customer's point of view and shorten the customer's wait |
| Continuous improvement towards perfection | Run small, bold improvement experiments every Sprint towards an ideal of perfect delivery |
| Systems thinking | Optimise the whole flow from concept to cash, not individual teams or people |
| Lean thinking | Managers as teachers who go and see the real work, stop and fix problems, and respect people |
| Queuing theory | Use what is known about queues to manage work in progress, batch size and variability |
Lean thinking and queuing theory explain why LeSS avoids component teams, which create queues between teams, and prefers small items. See [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) for the idea in practice.

### LeSS roles
LeSS has the same three Scrum accountabilities as one-team Scrum. It adds only one role, the Area Product Owner, and only in LeSS Huge.

#### Product Owner
With up to eight teams, the [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) cannot write and explain every item personally. LeSS does not solve this with proxies. Instead, the Product Owner focuses on prioritisation and the overall direction, and the teams **clarify items directly with customers, users and stakeholders**. All prioritisation still goes through the Product Owner, and only the Product Owner gives work to the teams.

#### Teams: feature teams, not component teams
LeSS is built on **feature teams**: stable, cross-functional, cross-component teams that can take a customer-centric item from the backlog and finish it. Most organisations start with component teams or functional groups, so this is usually the biggest structural change.
|  | Feature team | Component team |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owns | Customer features end to end | One technical layer or component |
| Backlog items | Customer-centric features | Technical tasks split from a feature |
| Hand-offs per feature | Few or none | Several teams, with queues between them |
| Coordination | Mostly in code and through shared practices | Mostly through plans, managers and integration phases |
| Learning | Broad, across the product | Deep but narrow |
| Risk | Code quality across components needs active care | Late integration and delayed customer feedback |
Feature teams need enough collective skill to finish items, not individuals who know everything. Our guide to [Agile team structures](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-team-structures/) compares the models.

#### Scrum Master
In LeSS, the [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) is a dedicated, full-time role that serves one to three teams. The focus shifts from a single team towards the whole system: the Product Owner, cross-team coordination, engineering practices and organisational policies that get in the way.

#### Managers
Managers are optional. Where they exist, they stop directing daily work and act as teachers and capability builders who go and see the work and remove systemic impediments. LeSS also recommends **removing project managers from the teams**, because the Product Owner and teams share that work.

### LeSS events step by step
Every LeSS Sprint follows the same pattern. Here is the order of events in one Sprint:
1. **Sprint Planning One (all teams).** The Product Owner and the teams, or representatives of each team, meet together. The Product Owner presents the top items; the teams decide which team takes which items, clear up open questions and agree a Sprint Goal if they use one. A popular format is to lay the item cards on a table and let teams pick.
2. **Sprint Planning Two (per team).** Each team plans how it will deliver its items and creates its own Sprint Backlog. When teams are working on closely related items, they hold a **multi-team Sprint Planning Two** in the same room, each still planning separately but able to discuss shared design and agree who does what.
3. **Daily Scrum (per team).** Each team holds its own [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/). Teams can send an observer to another team's Daily Scrum when their work overlaps.
4. **Coordination during the Sprint.** Teams coordinate directly and informally, mainly through code and conversation, rather than through a central coordinator. See the next section.
5. **Product Backlog Refinement (preferably multi-team).** An optional, short overall refinement identifies which teams will probably build which items; detailed [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) then happens per team or, often better, with two or more teams together.
6. **Sprint Review (one for the product).** The Product Owner, members of all teams and relevant customers, users and stakeholders inspect the integrated increment. LeSS suggests a **bazaar** or science-fair format: each team staffs an area of a large room and stakeholders move between them.
7. **Team Retrospectives.** Each team holds its own [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/).
8. **Overall Retrospective.** After the team retrospectives, the Product Owner, the Scrum Masters, rotating team representatives and any managers meet to improve the whole system. The maximum length is 45 minutes per week of Sprint.
Our guide to [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) covers the single-team version in detail, and the [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) works for each team's Sprint Planning Two.

### How teams coordinate in LeSS
LeSS deliberately avoids coordination roles and status meetings between teams. It prefers decentralised, informal techniques, with teams responsible for coordinating with each other. less.works names several:
- **Just talk.** Developers on different teams talk directly when they need to, in person or in chat, without going through a manager or Scrum Master.
- **Communicate in code.** Teams integrate their work continuously into one shared codebase, so conflicts show up within hours rather than at the end of the Sprint. This depends on solid [continuous integration and delivery](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/continuous-delivery/).
- **Travellers.** An expert in a specialist area joins different teams for a Sprint or two at a time to do real work with them and spread the knowledge.
- **Open Space.** A self-organised meeting where anyone can raise a topic, used for larger cross-team questions.
- **Communities.** Communities of practice around a component, a skill or a topic, such as test automation or user experience, that cut across teams.
- **Multi-team events.** Multi-team refinement and multi-team Sprint Planning Two are themselves major coordination tools.
LeSS does not require a [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/); if your teams find one useful, keep it short and run by the teams themselves.

### Worked example: one Sprint in a five-team LeSS product
This example is **illustrative**: the company, teams and items are invented to show how the rules work in practice. An insurer runs one product, its customer claims platform, with five feature teams (Amber, Birch, Cedar, Delta and Elm), one Product Owner, two Scrum Masters and a two-week Sprint. All teams work in one shared codebase.

#### Step 1: before the Sprint
In the previous Sprint, a short overall refinement suggested which teams would probably take the next items, and Amber and Birch refined the new photo-upload feature together.

#### Step 2: Sprint Planning One
The Product Owner presents the top of the Product Backlog. Using the cards-on-the-table format, the teams agree the following split and a product-level Sprint Goal: "Customers can submit a motor claim with photos from their phone."
| Team | Items taken | Why this team |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amber | Photo upload in the claim form; photo compression | Refined the feature last Sprint |
| Birch | Photo review screen for claim handlers | Same feature as Amber; holds multi-team Sprint Planning Two with Amber |
| Cedar | Claim status notifications by text message | Worked on notifications before |
| Delta | Fix for duplicate claim references; accessibility improvements | Volunteered to learn the reference service |
| Elm | First slice of fraud-check integration | Has the strongest knowledge of the partner API |

#### Step 3: during the Sprint
- Amber and Birch hold a multi-team Sprint Planning Two in one room, agree the shared photo data model and pair across teams on the first day.
- All teams integrate into the main branch several times a day, so a clash between Cedar's notification change and Delta's reference fix shows up on day 3 and is fixed by the two developers involved.

#### Step 4: Sprint Review and retrospectives
The Sprint Review is a bazaar: five stations in one room, with claim handlers, a customer panel and the head of claims moving between them. They try the full photo journey end to end on a phone. The Product Owner then reorders the backlog based on the feedback.
Each team then holds its retrospective. In the Overall Retrospective, the Product Owner, both Scrum Masters, one rotating member from each team and the head of engineering look at a system problem that three teams raised: the separate security review, which sits outside the Definition of Done and delays every release by about a week. They agree an experiment: a security specialist will work as a traveller with two teams next Sprint, with the aim of moving security review into the Definition of Done.
Notice what is not in the example: no team-level Product Owners, no integration team, no release train and no project manager assigning work. That is what "more with less" looks like.

### LeSS Huge: more than eight teams
When a product needs more than eight teams, one Product Owner can no longer keep the whole backlog in view. LeSS Huge solves this by dividing the product into **requirement areas** while keeping one product, one Product Backlog and one Sprint. Eight is an empirical limit, not a magic number, and LeSS Huge adds overhead, so do not use it for smaller groups.
| Element | Basic LeSS | LeSS Huge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Number of teams | Two to eight | More than eight |
| Product Owner | One | One overall Product Owner, plus an Area Product Owner per requirement area |
| Backlog | One Product Backlog | One Product Backlog; each item belongs to exactly one requirement area, viewed through an Area Product Backlog |
| Team grouping | None | Requirement areas of four to eight teams each |
| Sprint | One product-level Sprint | Still one product-level Sprint and one integrated product |
| Product Owner coordination | Not needed | Product Owner and Area Product Owners form a Product Owner Team and synchronise before Sprint Planning and after the Sprint Review |
A **requirement area** groups strongly related customer requirements, such as "payments" or "onboarding", not technical components. Teams specialise in one area for a long time, and the overall Product Owner decides how many teams work in each area, moving teams only when another area offers more value.

#### Worked sizing example
This sizing is **illustrative**. A retail bank's mobile banking product has grown to 20 feature teams. The Product Owner and Area Product Owners group the backlog by customer area:
| Requirement area | Share of backlog value | Teams | Area Product Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Everyday banking (accounts, cards, payments) | About 40% | 8 | One |
| Lending and mortgages | About 35% | 7 | One |
| Onboarding and identity | About 25% | 5 | One |
| Total | 100% | 20 | Three, plus the overall Product Owner |
Every area has between four and eight teams, so the split fits the rules. Teams can move between areas as value shifts, but because they have specialised, each move costs learning time.
LeSS Huge is adopted **incrementally**, often one requirement area at a time, and the less.works rules note that this can take months or years.

### LeSS vs SAFe vs Nexus vs Scrum@Scale
LeSS is one of several ways to scale Scrum. The four best known compare as follows:
|  | LeSS | SAFe | Nexus | Scrum@Scale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Philosophy | Scrum scaled with minimal additions; change the organisation | Comprehensive framework covering team, programme and portfolio | Light exoskeleton around Scrum focused on integration | Modular, scale-free networks of teams |
| Typical size | 2–8 teams; LeSS Huge beyond | Agile Release Trains of typically 50–125 people, up to portfolios | About 3–9 Scrum Teams | Any size, repeated in groups of 4–5 teams |
| Product Owner | One for the product (plus Area POs in LeSS Huge) | Product Owners per team plus Product Management | One Product Owner for the Nexus | Product Owner per team plus Chief Product Owners |
| New roles | Very few | Many (for example Release Train Engineer, Solution and Portfolio roles) | Nexus Integration Team | Scrum of Scrums Master, Executive Action Team, MetaScrum |
| Organisational change | Deep: feature teams, fewer managers, no functional silos | Fits around existing structures | Moderate | Moderate to deep, led by executives |
| Best for | One product, leaders willing to simplify the organisation | Large enterprises that want a detailed blueprint and portfolio governance | Several teams on one product that need integration focus | Organisations scaling Scrum across many products and leadership |

#### How to choose
- **Choose LeSS** if you have one product, your teams already run Scrum well and leaders are willing to restructure around feature teams.
- **Choose SAFe** if you need a documented model for many trains and portfolios, with roles and events that fit around existing governance. See our [SAFe guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) and [Agile Release Train](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/) guide.
- **Choose Nexus** if you have three to nine teams and your biggest problem is integrating their work each Sprint.
- **Choose Scrum@Scale** if you want a modular approach that extends into executive leadership across several products.
Whichever you choose, scale only when one team genuinely cannot deliver the product. See our guide to [Scrum at scale](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-at-scale/) for the Scrum@Scale framework in detail.

### How to adopt LeSS step by step
less.works sets out three principles for adoption:
- **Deep and narrow over broad and shallow.** Make LeSS work well in one product group before spreading it.
- **Top-down and bottom-up.** Leaders change structures and fund education; teams shape the details.
- **Use volunteering.** Let informed people volunteer for the first product and teams.
Combining those principles with the LeSS getting-started guide gives a practical sequence:
1. **Educate everyone.** Give the whole product group several days of Scrum and LeSS training, then coaching. Explain why each rule exists.
2. **Define the product.** Agree a broad, customer-centric definition. This sets the scope of the adoption and which people join.
3. **Define done.** Agree the first common Definition of Done and list the undone work that remains outside it.
4. **Form feature teams.** Let people self-design long-lived, cross-functional teams. People leave their functional departments and stop reporting to their old functional managers.
5. **Make the Product Owner the only source of work.** All requests from managers, sales and other departments go through the Product Owner.
6. **Remove project managers from the teams**, and agree new roles for functional managers as capability builders.
7. **Create one Product Backlog** and run initial refinement with all teams. A [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) helps if you are starting from scattered lists.
8. **Start the first Sprint** with the full LeSS structure: Sprint Planning One, Sprint Planning Two, Daily Scrums, one Sprint Review and an Overall Retrospective.
9. **Inspect and adapt the system.** Use the Overall Retrospective to strengthen the Definition of Done and remove organisational impediments.
LeSS adoption is an organisational change, so it benefits from the same care as any [Agile transformation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/): clear reasons, visible leadership support and patience while productivity dips and recovers.

### Common LeSS mistakes
- **Scaling before Scrum works.** If one team cannot deliver a done increment each Sprint, eight teams will not either.
- **Renaming component teams as feature teams.** If every item still passes through three teams, nothing has changed.
- **Adding a Product Owner per team.** Team-level "Product Owners" who only pass on requirements recreate the proxy layer LeSS removes. Let teams talk to customers directly.
- **Running separate Sprints.** Staggered or different-length Sprints break the single integrated increment.
- **Letting teams weaken the Definition of Done.** Teams may only strengthen it. Undone work should shrink over time, not grow.
- **Creating requirement areas too early.** Requirement areas with one or two teams each are a common novice error; Basic LeSS does not use them at all.
- **Appointing a central coordinator.** A cross-team manager who allocates work undermines team self-management and the Product Owner's role.
- **Skipping the Overall Retrospective.** Without it, system-level problems, such as external sign-offs or tooling, are never tackled.
- **Reviewing slides instead of the product.** The Sprint Review should inspect working, integrated software with real stakeholders.
- **Ignoring engineering practices.** Without continuous integration and test automation, communicating in code does not work.

### Tools for running LeSS
LeSS needs very little tooling: a single Product Backlog that every team can see, a Sprint Backlog per team and a way to integrate code continuously. Co-located teams can simply keep their Sprint Backlogs on physical boards. When you do use software, check that it can show **one product backlog across many teams**, rather than forcing a separate backlog per team.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is the most common choice for software teams. Every plan supports backlogs, sprints and boards, and Premium and Enterprise add Plans for cross-team planning, capacity and dependencies.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, suits LeSS groups that also need portfolio views, dashboards and request intake across departments, for example when non-software teams join the product group.
See our comparison of [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) for more options. The [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) works for both team retrospectives and the Overall Retrospective.

### LeSS training and certification
LeSS certifications are issued by **The LeSS Company B.V.** and delivered by licensed LeSS trainers. Scrum Alliance lists the courses in its catalogue, and attending them counts towards the Scrum Education Units needed to renew Scrum Alliance certifications.
| Course | Typical length | Who it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Certified LeSS Basics (CLB) | One day | Anyone involved in a LeSS adoption who needs an overview |
| Certified LeSS Practitioner (CLP) | Three days in person (a longer online provisional version also exists) | Scrum Masters, Product Owners, managers and team members adopting LeSS |
| Certified LeSS for Executives (CLE) | Several days | Senior leaders and managers supporting a LeSS adoption |
Lengths vary by trainer. No certification is required to use LeSS; the rules and guides are free on less.works.
Read our guide to [Scrum certification and training](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/) to compare LeSS courses with PSM, CSM and other options.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is LeSS in Agile?**
Large-Scale Scrum, a framework for applying Scrum to many teams working on one product, with one Product Owner, one Product Backlog, one Definition of Done and one shared Sprint.

**Q: Who created LeSS?**
Craig Larman and Bas Vodde, who began working together on scaling Scrum in 2005, based on their work with large, multi-site product development groups.

**Q: How many teams can use LeSS?**
Basic LeSS is designed for two to eight teams. Above eight teams, LeSS Huge applies, with requirement areas of four to eight teams each.

**Q: What is LeSS Huge?**
The version of LeSS for more than eight teams. It divides the product into requirement areas, each with an Area Product Owner and four to eight teams, while keeping one Product Backlog and one Sprint.

**Q: Does LeSS have a Scrum Master?**
Yes. Each Scrum Master is a dedicated, full-time role serving one to three teams, with a focus on the whole system as well as the teams.

**Q: What are feature teams in LeSS?**
Long-lived, cross-functional and cross-component teams that deliver complete customer features end to end, rather than component teams that each own one technical layer.

**Q: What is Sprint Planning One and Two in LeSS?**
In Sprint Planning One, the Product Owner and all teams (or their representatives) decide which team takes which items. In Sprint Planning Two, each team, or several related teams together, plans how to do its work.

**Q: What is an Overall Retrospective?**
A retrospective held after the team retrospectives, in which the Product Owner, Scrum Masters, team representatives and any managers improve the whole system. It lasts at most 45 minutes per week of Sprint.

**Q: What is the difference between LeSS and SAFe?**
LeSS adds very few roles and events to Scrum and asks the organisation to restructure around feature teams. SAFe is a comprehensive framework with additional roles, events and portfolio layers that fits around existing structures.

**Q: What is the difference between LeSS and Nexus?**
Both scale Scrum for one product with one Product Owner and Product Backlog. Nexus, for about three to nine teams, adds a Nexus Integration Team; LeSS has no integration team and relies on feature teams and continuous integration.

**Q: Can LeSS work outside software?**
Yes, in principle, for any product built by several teams, and less.works lists adoptions in telecoms, banking and trading as well as software companies. Most published experience comes from software and systems products.

**Q: Is there a LeSS certification?**
Yes. The LeSS Company issues Certified LeSS Basics, Certified LeSS Practitioner and Certified LeSS for Executives, delivered by licensed trainers. Certification is not required to use LeSS.

# PI Planning in SAFe: Agenda, Steps and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: PI planning explained: what happens at SAFe's two-day event, the agenda, roles, PI objectives, ROAM, the confidence vote and a worked team example.


## PI Planning in SAFe: Agenda, Steps and Example
PI planning is the regular, usually two-day event in the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) where every team on an Agile Release Train plans the next Planning Interval together, face to face or online. Over the two days the teams turn the highest-priority features into iteration plans, agree dependencies and risks, and commit to PI objectives that Business Owners have valued. This guide explains the agenda, the roles, how to prepare and what each output looks like, with a worked example of one team's plan.
- Published 22 September 2026
- Last updated 15 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- PI planning is a cadence-based event, typically two days every 8 to 12 weeks, in which the whole Agile Release Train (ART) plans the next Planning Interval together.
- Since SAFe 6.0 (2023), PI stands for Planning Interval; you will still see the older name, Program Increment, in many organisations and tools.
- The main outputs are committed and uncommitted PI objectives with business value, an ART planning board showing features and dependencies, ROAMed risks and a confidence vote.
- Most of the success of the event is decided beforehand: a ready ART backlog, known capacity, briefed Business Owners and good logistics.
- Plan teams below full capacity and keep uncommitted objectives as a buffer, so the plan survives normal surprises.
- PI planning is only the start: the plan is tracked through the PI and scored at Inspect and Adapt using the predictability measure.

### What is PI planning?
**PI planning** is a cadence-based planning event in the Scaled Agile Framework in which all the teams and stakeholders of an Agile Release Train meet, usually for two days, to agree what they will deliver in the next Planning Interval. Teams create their own iteration plans and PI objectives, expose cross-team dependencies and risks, and finish with a confidence vote.
Scaled Agile describes PI planning as "a cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision", typically held over two days every 8 to 12 weeks and facilitated by the Release Train Engineer.

#### What does PI stand for?
In SAFe 6.0, released in 2023, Scaled Agile renamed the **Program Increment** to the **Planning Interval**. The abbreviation PI did not change, so the event is still called PI planning. The new name emphasises the planning cadence rather than a fixed output, and it fits trains that are not organised as formal programmes. You will meet both terms, and older material (and many tools) still says Program Increment.

#### How long is a Planning Interval?
A PI is a fixed timebox, typically 8 to 12 weeks. With two-week iterations, a common pattern is four development iterations followed by one **Innovation and Planning (IP) iteration**. The IP iteration gives room for innovation, learning, final integration and the Inspect and Adapt event, and it is when the next PI planning normally takes place, so planning does not interrupt delivery.
PI planning is the scaled equivalent of [sprint planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/): instead of one team planning one sprint, five to twelve teams plan several iterations together. To understand the team-of-teams structure that takes part, see our guide to the [Agile Release Train](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/).

### Key PI planning terms
SAFe has its own vocabulary, and several terms changed in version 6.0. The table covers the words you will hear during the event.
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Agile Release Train (ART) | A long-lived team of Agile teams, typically 50 to 125 people, that plans, delivers and is funded together |
| Planning Interval (PI) | A fixed timebox of usually 8 to 12 weeks; formerly called Program Increment |
| IP iteration | The final Innovation and Planning iteration of each PI, used for innovation, Inspect and Adapt and the next PI planning |
| Release Train Engineer (RTE) | The servant leader and coach who facilitates the ART's events, including PI planning |
| Business Owners | Senior stakeholders accountable for the business outcomes of the train; they assign business value to objectives |
| Product Management | Owns the ART backlog and presents the vision and the top features |
| System Architect | Presents the architectural vision and enablers; helps teams with technical dependencies |
| PI objectives | A summary, in business terms, of what each team (and the ART) intends to achieve in the PI |
| ART planning board | A visual board of features, milestones and cross-team dependencies by iteration; formerly the program board |
For a broader overview of the framework and its configurations, read our guide to [what SAFe is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/).

### Why PI planning matters
Bringing 100 people together for two days is expensive. Scaled Agile's stated benefits include face-to-face communication, aligning development to business goals, identifying dependencies, matching demand to capacity and fast decisions. In practice, the value comes from four things:
- **Alignment.** Every team hears the same business context and vision at the same time, from the people accountable for it.
- **Dependencies surface early.** A dependency found on day one of planning costs a conversation; the same dependency found in week seven of delivery can cost a feature.
- **Realistic commitments.** Teams plan against their own measured capacity and negotiate scope in the room, rather than receiving a plan from above.
- **Speed of decision.** Business Owners, architects and Product Management are present, so trade-offs that would normally take weeks of email are settled within hours.

### Who attends PI planning
SAFe's guidance is that everyone on the ART attends, along with the key stakeholders who shape or depend on its work. The table shows the main roles and what each does during the event.
| Role | What they do during PI planning |
| --- | --- |
| Release Train Engineer (RTE) | Prepares and facilitates the event, keeps time, runs the draft and final plan reviews, the risk review and the confidence vote |
| Business Owners | Present business context, take part in management review, assign business value to team objectives, help ROAM risks |
| Product Management | Present the vision and the top features of the ART backlog; negotiate scope with teams |
| System Architect | Present the architectural vision, enablers and development practices; advise teams on technical dependencies |
| Product Owners | Clarify features and stories for their team, help set priorities in breakouts, draft team objectives |
| Scrum Masters / Team Coaches | Facilitate their team's breakout, track capacity, load and dependencies, keep the team to time |
| Agile team members | Plan iterations, identify risks and dependencies, vote |
| Shared services and other trains | Agree hand-offs with the teams that depend on them |

### PI planning vs sprint planning vs release planning
PI planning is often confused with other planning events. The main difference is scale: PI planning coordinates many teams over several iterations, while sprint planning is one team planning one sprint.
|  | PI planning | Sprint (iteration) planning | Release planning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Framework | SAFe | Scrum (and SAFe iterations) | Not a defined event in Scrum; common Agile practice |
| Who plans | All teams on the ART plus stakeholders | One Scrum team | Product Owner, team and stakeholders |
| Horizon | One PI (8–12 weeks) | One sprint (up to one month) | One or more releases |
| Timebox | Typically two days | Up to 8 hours for a one-month sprint | Varies |
| Main outputs | PI objectives, ART planning board, ROAMed risks, confidence vote | Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog | Release plan and forecast |
| Facilitator | Release Train Engineer | Usually the Scrum Master | Usually the Product Owner |
If your organisation does not use SAFe but still needs to coordinate a few teams, a lighter approach is often enough.

### How to prepare for PI planning
Experienced RTEs agree that the event is won or lost in preparation. SAFe groups readiness into three dimensions:
- **Organisational readiness:** the scope of the train is clear, Business Owners and Product Management agree on priorities, and the right people are available and invited.
- **Content readiness:** the business context is drafted, the vision and near-term [roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) are ready, the top features of the ART backlog (often derived from portfolio [epics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/)) are defined with acceptance criteria and rough sizes, architectural enablers are known and each team's capacity is calculated.
- **Logistics readiness:** the venue or online space, breakout rooms, boards, video links, tooling, food and agenda are ready, and everyone knows how the event will run.

#### A suggested preparation timeline
SAFe does not prescribe exact lead times. The timeline below is our own suggestion for a train that already has a few PIs behind it; allow more time for your first event.
| When | Activity | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6–8 weeks before | Confirm dates and venue or online tools; send invitations; agree the PI scope | RTE |
| 4–6 weeks before | Prioritise the top ten or so features (many trains use Weighted Shortest Job First); draft benefit hypotheses and acceptance criteria | Product Management, Business Owners |
| 3–4 weeks before | Socialise features with Product Owners and teams; flag known dependencies and enablers | Product Management, System Architect |
| 2–3 weeks before | Readiness check: features refined, capacity known, presenters briefed; fix any gaps | RTE |
| 1–2 weeks before | Teams calculate capacity per iteration; Product Owners pre-split features into candidate stories | Scrum Masters, Product Owners |
| Final week | Dry run of tools and agenda; print or set up boards; confirm working agreements | RTE, Scrum Masters |
Tip
Pre-PI work is about reducing discovery, not pre-making the plan. If teams arrive with a plan already filled in for them, the breakouts become theatre and the confidence vote loses its meaning.

### The two-day PI planning agenda
SAFe publishes a standard agenda that most trains follow, adjusting times to suit. The table shows a typical version for a co-located train; online events are usually spread over more days.
| Time | Day 1 | Day 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 08:00 | Business context (Business Owner or senior leader) | Planning adjustments (RTE presents changes agreed overnight) |
| 09:00 | Product and solution vision (Product Management) | Team breakout 2 |
| 10:30 | Architecture vision and development practices (System Architect) | Team breakout 2 continues; Business Owners circulate to assign business value |
| 11:30 | Planning context and lunch (RTE explains the process) | Final plan review and lunch |
| 13:00 | Team breakout 1 | ART risks reviewed and ROAMed |
| 16:00 | Draft plan review (each team presents) | Confidence vote |
| 17:00 | Management review and problem-solving | Plan rework if necessary, then planning retrospective |

#### Day 1: context, breakouts and draft plans
The morning gives everyone the same picture: why the work matters, what is wanted, how it should be built, and how the next day and a half will run.
In the afternoon, **team breakout 1** is where the real work starts. Teams turn features into iteration plans and draft objectives (see the next section), while Product Management, architects and Business Owners move between teams to answer questions.
At the **draft plan review**, each team presents its draft capacity and load, objectives, risks and dependencies in a few minutes. This is where conflicts become visible: two teams relying on a third in the same iteration, a feature that no longer fits, or a risk that needs a decision.
Day 1 ends with **management review and problem-solving**. Business Owners, Product Management, the RTE and architects decide on adjustments to scope, priority, people or dates. It often runs into the evening.

#### Day 2: adjustments, commitment and close
Day 2 opens with **planning adjustments**: the RTE or Product Management explains what management decided overnight. In **team breakout 2**, teams finalise their plans and objectives, and Business Owners visit each team to assign business value to its objectives.
In the **final plan review**, each team presents its plan and objectives and asks the Business Owners to accept them. The train then reviews the ART-level risks and handles each one using **ROAM**. Next comes the **confidence vote**. If confidence is low, teams rework their plans until it is acceptable. A short **planning retrospective** closes the event.

### What happens in a team breakout
Breakouts are where most of the time is spent. A good Scrum Master or Team Coach keeps the team moving through a predictable sequence:
1. **Confirm capacity.** Write each iteration's capacity on the team board, taking holidays, leave, training and support duties into account.
2. **Review the features assigned to the team.** Ask Product Management and the Product Owner any questions while they are in the room.
3. **Split features into stories** small enough to finish within an iteration. See our guide to [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/).
4. **Estimate the stories,** usually in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/), using the team's normal technique.
5. **Load the iterations.** Place stories in iterations without exceeding capacity; leave headroom for unplanned work and defects.
6. **Identify dependencies** on other teams, suppliers or shared services, agree them in person and record them on the ART planning board.
7. **Draft PI objectives** in business language, separating committed and uncommitted objectives.
8. **List risks** that could stop the team meeting its objectives, ready for the ART risk review.
9. **Prepare the summary** for the draft or final plan review: capacity and load, objectives, risks and dependencies.
Tip
Do not try to plan the IP iteration with feature work. It is there for innovation, learning, integration and planning, and it acts as an estimating buffer. If teams fill it with features, the PI has no slack left.

### Worked example: one team's PI plan
The example follows a fictional team, Payments, on a train with a 10-week PI: four two-week development iterations (I1 to I4) plus an IP iteration. Payments has five developers and testers, a Product Owner and a Scrum Master.

#### Step 1: calculate capacity
Payments is a new team with no stable velocity yet, so it uses SAFe's normalised estimating guidance as a starting point: about 8 story points per full-time developer or tester per two-week iteration, minus 1 point for each person-day of holiday or leave. (Established teams should use their own measured [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) instead.)
| Iteration | People | Base capacity | Days off | Capacity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I1 | 5 | 40 | 0 | 40 |
| I2 | 5 | 40 | 5 (public holiday for everyone) | 35 |
| I3 | 5 | 40 | 5 (one person on leave all week) | 35 |
| I4 | 5 | 40 | 0 | 40 |
| Total |  | 160 | 10 | 150 |

#### Step 2: load the iterations
The team plans committed work to about 80% of capacity, adds a small amount of uncommitted work, and leaves the rest as a buffer for defects, support and surprises. Planning to roughly 80% is our own rule of thumb, not a SAFe requirement.
| Iteration | Capacity | Committed load | Uncommitted load | Unplanned buffer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I1 | 40 | 32 | 0 | 8 |
| I2 | 35 | 28 | 4 | 3 |
| I3 | 35 | 27 | 6 | 2 |
| I4 | 40 | 28 | 10 | 2 |
| Total | 150 | 115 | 20 | 15 |

#### Step 3: write and value the objectives
The Product Owner drafts objectives with the team, and on day 2 the Business Owners assign business value on SAFe's 1 to 10 scale.
| PI objective | Type | Planned business value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customers can save a card and pay with one click at checkout | Committed | 9 |
| Refund API available to the Orders team by the end of I3 | Committed | 7 |
| Payment page loads in under two seconds for 95% of visits | Committed | 5 |
| Prototype a pay-later option and test it with 20 customers | Uncommitted | 6 |
| Automate evidence collection for the annual card-security audit | Uncommitted | 4 |
The Refund API objective is a dependency for another team, so it appears on the ART planning board as a red string from Payments' I3 column to the Orders team's I4 column. The team also lists two risks: a third-party payment provider has not confirmed its sandbox dates, and one developer may be moved to an urgent project.
Payments can now summarise its plan in three minutes at the draft plan review.

### Writing good PI objectives
PI objectives summarise, in business language, what a team intends to achieve. They describe outcomes someone outside the team can recognise, not a list of features or stories.

#### Committed vs uncommitted objectives
- **Committed objectives** are those the team is confident it can deliver within the PI. Business Owners and other teams plan around them.
- **Uncommitted objectives** are planned work that the team is less sure about, usually because of a high unknown or a dependency. They are included in capacity, not a wish list, and give the plan a buffer: if something goes wrong, they are dropped first. They still receive business value, which counts if they are delivered.

#### Business value
Business Owners assign each objective a business value from 1 (lowest) to 10 (highest). The conversation matters as much as the number, because it tells the team what the business cares about most.
Tip
Write each objective so a Business Owner can say "yes, that was done" or "no, it was not" at the end of the PI. Keep the list short (three to five committed objectives per team is typical) and include enabler and improvement work so its value is visible.

### The ART planning board
The **ART planning board** (called the program board before SAFe 6.0) is the train's shared picture of the plan. It is usually a large wall or digital whiteboard with iterations as columns and teams as rows.
- **Features** are placed in the iteration in which the team expects to complete them.
- **Milestones and events** (a trade show, a regulatory deadline, a release, a hardware delivery) are placed in a row at the top.
- **Dependencies** are drawn as lines, traditionally red string, between the card that needs something and the card that provides it.
- **Other trains, suppliers and shared services** get their own rows so their commitments are visible too.
Warning signs include many strings converging on one team in one iteration, a dependency needed before it is delivered, or features clustered in the last iteration. For more on dependency types, see our guide to [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/).

### Managing risks with ROAM
During the final plan review, the train collects the risks teams have raised that could affect the PI objectives. Each risk is discussed in front of the whole train and placed in one of four categories:
| ROAM category | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resolved | The risk has been dealt with and is no longer a concern | Business Owners confirm the developer will not be moved to the other project |
| Owned | Someone takes responsibility for the risk because it cannot be resolved in the room | The RTE will chase the payment provider for sandbox dates by next Friday |
| Accepted | The risk is understood and accepted because nothing practical can be done | A regulator may change a rule mid-PI; the train will adapt if it happens |
| Mitigated | A plan reduces the likelihood or impact of the risk | Payments builds a stub so work continues if the sandbox is late |
ROAMing risks in public prevents risks being quietly ignored and makes ownership explicit. Owned and mitigated risks should be tracked through the PI, for example in a [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raid-log/) or [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/).

### The confidence vote
The confidence vote closes the planning part of the event. Everyone votes at the same time by holding up one to five fingers ("fist of five"), first for their team's objectives and then for the ART's plan as a whole.
In common practice, an average of three or more allows the train to commit. Anyone who votes one or two is invited to explain their concern, because they often know something the rest of the room does not. If confidence is low, teams rework their plans, sometimes with help from management, and vote again.
Tip
Protect the honesty of the vote. If leaders react badly to low scores, people will learn to hold up three fingers whatever they think, and the vote stops telling you anything. Simultaneous voting, and anonymous digital voting for online events, help.

### After PI planning: execution and the predictability measure
After the event, teams enter their stories into their tools and keep the plan alive through iteration planning, SAFe's coach sync and PO sync meetings, system demos and updates to the ART planning board.
At the end of the PI, the **Inspect and Adapt** event has three parts: a PI system demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. During the measurement part, Business Owners score the **actual business value** each team achieved for every objective, committed and uncommitted, on the same 1 to 10 scale.

#### Calculating predictability
The team's predictability is actual business value achieved divided by planned business value, where planned value counts only committed objectives. Continuing the Payments example:
| Objective | Type | Planned BV | Actual BV |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One-click card payments | Committed | 9 | 8 |
| Refund API for Orders team | Committed | 7 | 7 |
| Page loads under two seconds | Committed | 5 | 3 |
| Pay-later prototype | Uncommitted | (6, not counted) | 4 |
| Audit evidence automation | Uncommitted | (4, not counted) | 0 |
| Total |  | 21 | 22 |
Predictability = 22 ÷ 21 = about 105%. Delivering part of an uncommitted objective pushed the team above 100% despite falling short on one committed objective. SAFe guidance treats a range of roughly 80 to 100% as predictable. Far below that suggests over-commitment; consistently far above suggests the team is sandbagging or under-using uncommitted objectives. Use the trend over several PIs to improve planning, not to rank teams. For other measures that help, see our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).

### Remote and distributed PI planning
Many trains now plan online or in a hybrid format. Scaled Agile's guidance for distributed PI planning recommends splitting the agenda across overlapping working hours, often over two and a half to three or more days, rather than asking any location to work through the night.
- **Shorten each day** and spread the agenda over more days so every time zone has reasonable working hours.
- **Schedule synchronisation points** when teams overlap, for the draft plan review, dependency negotiation and business value scoring (short, pre-booked slots with Business Owners work well).
- **Use one shared digital ART planning board** and keep team spaces open for anyone to view.
- **Agree working agreements** upfront: cameras on in breakouts, one conversation at a time, microphones for every speaker, time-boxes respected.
- **Vote simultaneously** using a digital poll, so no group sees others' votes first.

### Common PI planning mistakes
- **Arriving unprepared.** Features that are not defined or sized turn breakouts into requirement workshops.
- **Planning to 100% of capacity.** Any surprise breaks the plan. Leave room, and use uncommitted objectives.
- **Filling the IP iteration with features.** This removes the PI's only buffer and the time for innovation and planning.
- **Handing teams a pre-made plan.** If the plan is decided before the event, commitment and the confidence vote become meaningless.
- **Hidden dependencies.** Make every dependency visible on the board and agreed by both teams.
- **Business Owners who are not present.** Without them, scope decisions wait and business value scores are guesses.
- **Punishing low confidence votes.** People stop telling the truth, and problems surface weeks later.
- **Skipping the retrospective.** Capture improvements for next time while they are fresh.

### PI planning tools and templates
A physical wall, sticky notes and red string still work well for a co-located train. Distributed trains usually use a digital whiteboard for the ART planning board and their work management tool for stories and dependencies.
- **Team planning:** our [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) works for each team's iteration capacity and load.
- **Release view:** the [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) helps map features to iterations and forecast dates.
- **Roadmap input:** use the [product roadmap template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-roadmap-template/) to prepare the vision and near-term roadmap.
- **Risks and dependencies:** track ROAMed risks and dependencies in the [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/).
- **Software:** [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is widely used by software trains for story-level planning, and [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is well suited to cross-team and portfolio visibility when your trains include non-software work. Compare more options in our [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) rankings.
Before your first event, make sure each team has consistent estimation and a known capacity.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does PI stand for in PI planning?**
PI stands for Planning Interval. Before SAFe 6.0 (2023) it stood for Program Increment, and many organisations and tools still use the older name. Both refer to the same fixed timebox, usually 8 to 12 weeks.

**Q: How long is PI planning?**
Typically two days for a co-located train. Distributed trains often spread the agenda over two and a half to three or more shorter days so every time zone works reasonable hours.

**Q: How often does PI planning happen?**
Once per Planning Interval, so typically every 8 to 12 weeks. It is normally held during the Innovation and Planning (IP) iteration at the end of the previous PI.

**Q: Who attends PI planning?**
Ideally everyone on the Agile Release Train, plus Business Owners, Product Management, the System Architect and any shared services or other trains the ART depends on. The Release Train Engineer facilitates.

**Q: What are the outputs of PI planning?**
PI objectives with business value, an ART planning board of features and dependencies, ROAMed risks and a commitment confirmed by the confidence vote.

**Q: What is the difference between committed and uncommitted objectives?**
Committed objectives are those the team is confident it can deliver. Uncommitted objectives are planned but less certain; they act as a buffer and do not count in planned business value.

**Q: Who assigns business value to PI objectives?**
Business Owners, on a scale of 1 to 10, usually during the second breakout on day 2. At the end of the PI they score the actual value achieved.

**Q: What is ROAM in PI planning?**
A way of handling ART-level risks in front of the whole train: each is marked Resolved, Owned, Accepted or Mitigated.

**Q: What happens if the confidence vote is low?**
People who voted one or two explain their concerns and teams rework their plans until confidence is acceptable. In common practice an average of three or more is enough to commit.

**Q: What is the IP iteration?**
The Innovation and Planning iteration ends each PI. It is used for innovation, learning, integration, Inspect and Adapt and the next PI planning, and acts as a buffer.

**Q: Can PI planning be done remotely?**
Yes. Many trains plan online with a shared digital board, video breakouts and an agenda spread over more days to suit time zones.

**Q: Do you need SAFe to run PI planning?**
No. It is a SAFe event, but a regular big-room planning session for several teams can be used without the rest of the framework. Smaller groups may find joint release planning or a Scrum of Scrums enough.
