# PRINCE2 vs Agile: Key Differences and How to Combine Them

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/prince2-vs-agile/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: PRINCE2 vs Agile compared: governance vs delivery, roles, documents and tolerances, plus PRINCE2 Agile, a worked example and how to combine them.


## PRINCE2 vs Agile: Key Differences and How to Combine Them
PRINCE2 vs Agile is less a contest than a comparison of two different jobs: PRINCE2 is a method for governing a project (who decides, when and within what limits), while Agile is a way of delivering the work in short, feedback-driven cycles. Many organisations that use PRINCE2 also run Agile teams, and PRINCE2 Agile is the official guidance for combining them. This guide compares the two side by side, maps roles and documents across, and shows step by step how to run Agile delivery inside PRINCE2 governance, with an illustrative worked example.
- Published 12 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- PRINCE2 is a project governance method; Agile is a family of values and delivery frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban. They work at different levels, so you can use both.
- PRINCE2 is not inherently waterfall: its stages are decision points for the project board, and the work inside a stage can be delivered in sprints.
- PRINCE2 Agile, first published in 2015 and refreshed by PeopleCert in 2025 to align with PRINCE2 7, shows how to combine them.
- The central idea is fix and flex: fix time and cost, let scope and quality criteria flex within agreed limits, and escalate only when a tolerance will be breached.
- Map the roles deliberately: the Product Owner usually works for or alongside the senior user, and the Scrum team delivers inside the team manager's work packages.
- Choose by context: PRINCE2 alone for tightly specified, contract-heavy work; Agile alone for product teams with empowered owners; both when you need accountability and adaptability.

### What is the difference between PRINCE2 and Agile?
**The main difference between PRINCE2 and Agile is that PRINCE2 governs a project while Agile delivers the work.** PRINCE2 defines who authorises what, in management stages, within agreed tolerances. Agile describes how a self-managing team builds and releases value in short iterations, using frequent feedback and a prioritised backlog. Because they operate at different levels, they can be combined.
That is why "PRINCE2 vs Agile" is partly a false choice. PRINCE2 says little about how specialists organise day-to-day work, and Agile frameworks say little about business cases, stage approvals or how a board holds a project to account. PRINCE2 provides the frame; Agile fills it. The real question is how much governance the project needs and how to stop it undermining Agile delivery.

### PRINCE2 vs Agile at a glance
|  | PRINCE2 | Agile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A project management method | A set of values and principles, applied through frameworks such as Scrum, Kanban and XP |
| Owner | PeopleCert (originally UK government) | No single owner; the Agile Manifesto (2001) is the shared reference |
| Main focus | Governance, accountability and control | Delivering value early and adapting to feedback |
| Unit of control | Management stages, approved by a project board | Iterations (sprints) or continuous flow |
| Planning | Project, stage and team plans, refined stage by stage | Product backlog, release plans and sprint plans, refined continuously |
| Handling change | Issues assessed through change control against tolerances | New items enter the backlog and are re-prioritised by the Product Owner |
| Key roles | Project board (executive, senior user, senior supplier), project manager, team manager | Product Owner, Scrum Master or coach, Developers |
| Documentation | Defined management products, tailored to the project | Just enough documentation; working output is the main measure |
| Typical settings | Public sector, regulated industries, multi-supplier and contract-based projects | Software, digital products, marketing and other work with evolving requirements |
Read our [guide to PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) for the full method, and [what is Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) for the Agile side.

### What is PRINCE2?
PRINCE2 (PRojects IN Controlled Environments) is a process-based project management method. It originated with the UK government and is now owned by PeopleCert, which acquired the previous owner, AXELOS, in 2021. The current edition, PRINCE2 7, was published in 2023 and is built from five integrated elements: seven principles, people, seven practices, seven processes and the project context.

#### How PRINCE2 controls a project
- **Three levels of management.** The project board directs, the project manager manages day to day, and team managers deliver the specialist work.
- **Management stages.** The project is split into stages. The board approves each stage plan before the stage starts and reviews progress at each stage boundary.
- **Management by exception.** The board sets tolerances, and the project manager acts freely within them, escalating only when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.
- **Continued business justification.** The business case is reviewed throughout. If the project stops being worth doing, it should stop.
- **Focus on products.** Outputs are defined up front with product descriptions and quality criteria.
In PRINCE2 7, tolerances can be set against seven performance targets: time, cost, quality, scope, benefits, risk and sustainability. Sustainability was added in the seventh edition; older articles list only six. A [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) is a practical starting point for the document that keeps the whole method honest.

### What is Agile?
Agile is an approach to delivering work in small, usable increments, with the people who need the result involved throughout. It traces back to the [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/), written by 17 software practitioners in 2001, which sets out four values and twelve principles, such as welcoming changing requirements and delivering working output frequently.
Agile itself is not a method. Teams apply it through frameworks, the most common being [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) (fixed-length sprints, three accountabilities and five events, as defined in the 2020 Scrum Guide) and [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) (continuous flow with limits on work in progress). Others include Extreme Programming (XP), DSDM and scaling frameworks such as SAFe.
- **Iterative and incremental.** The team delivers something usable every few weeks and learns from it.
- **Empirical.** Plans are adjusted based on what actually happened, not what was predicted months earlier.
- **Value-ordered backlog.** One person, usually a Product Owner, decides what comes next.
- **Self-managing teams.** The people doing the work decide how to do it.
Our overview of [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/) compares the main frameworks.

### Key differences between PRINCE2 and Agile explained

#### 1. Governance versus delivery
PRINCE2 concentrates on directing and managing: business justification, authorisation, tolerances and reporting. Agile concentrates on delivering: how a team plans, builds, tests, demonstrates and improves. Almost every other difference follows from this.

#### 2. Planning horizon
PRINCE2 asks for a project plan at initiation and a detailed plan for the next stage only, so it is less front-loaded than people assume. Agile also plans at several horizons (roadmap, release, sprint) but expects the backlog to change continuously. A stage plan for an Agile project describes the stage goal, sprints and outcomes, not tasks.

#### 3. Handling change
In PRINCE2, a request for change is an issue. The project manager assesses its impact, and the change authority or board decides, which gives a clear audit trail. In Agile, most changes are simply new or re-ordered backlog items, decided by the Product Owner without ceremony. Combining them means agreeing which changes are routine backlog decisions and which are real issues for [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/), for example anything that threatens a Must-have, the budget or the date.

#### 4. Roles and accountability
PRINCE2 makes one person, the executive, accountable for the project, with a hierarchy beneath. Agile spreads decisions: the Product Owner owns value and the team owns how the work is done. They coexist only if the board governs outcomes and tolerances, not tasks.

#### 5. Documentation
PRINCE2 defines management products such as the business case, project initiation documentation, highlight reports and end stage reports. Agile favours working output over comprehensive documentation. PRINCE2 has always expected these products to be tailored, so a highlight report can be a one-page summary of the Sprint Review and the burn-up chart rather than a long narrative.

#### 6. Customer involvement and quality
In PRINCE2 the customer is represented on the board by the senior user, and quality is controlled through product descriptions and quality reviews. In Agile the customer or their proxy sees the product every iteration, and quality is built in through the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) and acceptance criteria. Agile gives faster feedback; PRINCE2 gives a clearer record of who accepted what.

### Is PRINCE2 waterfall?
PRINCE2 is often described as a waterfall method, but that is not accurate. **PRINCE2 management stages are decision points for the board, not technical phases** such as design, build and test. A stage can contain any mix of activities, including several sprints that each design, build and test a slice of the product.
The confusion arises because many organisations have paired PRINCE2 with sequential delivery. That is a choice about delivery approach, not a requirement of the method. PRINCE2 7 explicitly asks you to tailor the method to the project, including its delivery approach.
See [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) for a full comparison of sequential and iterative delivery, and our guide to [Waterfall project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) for when sequential delivery is the better choice.

### Similarities between PRINCE2 and Agile
The two have more in common than the usual comparisons suggest:
- **A focus on value.** PRINCE2's continued business justification and Agile's value-ordered backlog both ask whether the work is still worth doing.
- **Learning from experience.** PRINCE2 has a principle for it; Agile builds it into every [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/).
- **Clear roles.** Both define who is accountable for what, even though the roles differ.
- **Tailoring.** Both expect you to adapt them to the context rather than follow them mechanically.

### What is PRINCE2 Agile?
PRINCE2 Agile is official guidance on running Agile delivery within PRINCE2 governance. It was first published in 2015. In 2025 PeopleCert released a new version that aligns it with PRINCE2 7 and adds material on performance targets, Agile leadership, team empowerment and mindset, tailoring and scaling. It covers frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban and positions PRINCE2 Agile as compatible with scaling approaches such as SAFe.
PRINCE2 Agile does not replace PRINCE2; it explains how to tailor the same principles, practices and processes for Agile work. Its best-known idea is **fix and flex**: rather than fixing scope and letting time and cost slip, you fix time and cost and let the amount of scope delivered vary.
| Aspect | Traditional default | PRINCE2 Agile approach | In practice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time | Often flexes when scope grows | Fixed | Timeboxed sprints and fixed release dates |
| Cost | Often flexes | Fixed | Stable team, so cost per sprint is predictable |
| Scope | Fixed in a specification | Flexes | Lower-priority features can be dropped or deferred |
| Quality criteria | Fixed | Flex within limits | Nice-to-have criteria can flex; essential quality and the Definition of Done do not |
| Benefits | Fixed | Fixed or flex | Agreed per project with the customer |
| Risk | Fixed | Fixed or flex | Agreed per project with the customer |
To make scope flex safely, requirements need a clear priority. MoSCoW (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time), which comes from DSDM, is commonly used: Must-haves are the minimum usable product, and tolerances are expressed as how much of the Should and Could work can be deferred.
Tip
Fix and flex only works if the board genuinely accepts that not every requested feature will be delivered. Agree this explicitly at initiation and record it in the project initiation documentation, or the first deferred feature will be treated as a failure.

### How PRINCE2 and Agile roles map to each other
PRINCE2 Agile keeps the PRINCE2 roles and places Agile roles inside them. A common mapping looks like this; adjust it to your organisation.
| PRINCE2 role | Agile counterpart | How it usually works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Executive | Sponsor (outside the Scrum Team) | Owns the business case and sets tolerances with the board |
| Senior user | Product Owner or the Product Owner's sponsor | Represents users; the Product Owner often reports to or is appointed by the senior user |
| Senior supplier | Delivery lead or head of engineering | Commits the people and skills the teams need |
| Project manager | No direct Scrum equivalent | Manages stages, reporting, risks, dependencies and the board interface; does not assign tasks to the team |
| Team manager | Scrum Master, team lead or the team collectively | Accepts work packages and delivers them as sprints |
| Project assurance | Agile coach or quality lead (partly) | Checks the project is run properly, independently of the project manager |
| Change authority | Product Owner for backlog changes within tolerance | Routine scope decisions are delegated; tolerance-breaking changes go to the board |
The most important design decision is the Product Owner's authority. If the Product Owner has to refer every priority call to the board, the team will stall. Delegate backlog decisions within scope tolerance to the [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/), and keep the [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) focused on the team's effectiveness rather than on PRINCE2 paperwork.

#### Documents and controls mapped
| PRINCE2 product or control | Agile equivalent or input | Tip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business case | Product vision and Product Goal | Keep one business case; link the Product Goal to it |
| Stage plan | Release plan for the stage | State the stage goal, number of sprints and target outcomes |
| Work package | Sprint Goal and selected backlog items | Agree a work package per sprint or per release |
| Product description | User stories with acceptance criteria | Describe Must-haves in detail; leave lower priorities lighter |
| Quality register | Definition of Done and test results | Record that each increment met the Definition of Done |
| Checkpoint report | Daily Scrum, sprint board and burndown | Let the board read the team's own information radiators |
| Highlight report | Sprint Review outcome and burn-up chart | One page per sprint or fortnight |
| Issue register and change control | Product backlog refinement | Only tolerance-affecting changes become formal issues |
| End stage report | Release review | Show what was released, value achieved and the forecast |
A [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) and a [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) cover most of the Agile-side artefacts the board will want to see.

### How to combine PRINCE2 and Agile: step by step
Use these steps when a PRINCE2 organisation wants its teams to deliver in an Agile way.
1. **Confirm the project suits an Agile delivery approach.** Check that requirements are likely to change, work can be released in usable slices and a customer representative is available every sprint.
2. **Write a business case that tolerates flexible scope.** Express benefits in terms of outcomes (for example, applications processed online) rather than a fixed feature list, so that deferring a lower-priority feature does not break the case.
3. **Agree what is fixed and what flexes.** With the board, fix time and cost, define the Must-have scope and set tolerances for quality, benefits, risk and sustainability. Record these in the project initiation documentation.
4. **Map roles and delegate authority.** Name the Product Owner, confirm what they can decide alone and agree how the project manager, team manager and Scrum Master divide their responsibilities.
5. **Align stages with releases.** Make each management stage a whole number of sprints that ends with a usable release. The stage boundary then becomes a review of real output rather than of documents.
6. **Issue work packages as sprint or release goals.** The team manager accepts a goal and a set of prioritised items, and the team plans the detail in Sprint Planning.
7. **Report from the team's own data.** Base highlight reports on the Sprint Review, burn-up chart and Definition of Done results, not separate status documents.
8. **Escalate by exception.** Monitor forecasts against tolerances each sprint. When the forecast shows a Must-have will not fit, or cost or time tolerance will be exceeded, raise an exception report with options for the board.
9. **Close and learn.** Confirm benefits measures, hand over the product and feed retrospective themes into the lessons report.
See our guide to [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) for how to build the release plans that sit inside each stage.

### Worked example: Agile delivery inside PRINCE2 governance
The following example is illustrative. A county council needs to replace a paper permit application with an online service. A change in regulation means the service must be live in 30 weeks. The approved budget is £480,000, which funds one Scrum Team of eight people working two-week sprints.

#### Stages and sprints
| Stage | Weeks | Sprints | Stage goal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Initiation | 1–4 | None | Business case, Must-have scope, tolerances, team and Product Owner agreed |
| 2. Discovery and prototype | 5–12 | Sprints 1–4 | Tested prototype of the application journey with real applicants |
| 3. Build | 13–24 | Sprints 5–10 | Working service handling the main permit types in a test environment |
| 4. Release and handover | 25–30 | Sprints 11–13 | Live service, staff trained, support handed over |

#### Tolerances agreed by the board
| Performance target | Fixed or flex | Tolerance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time | Fixed | Zero: go-live by week 30 |
| Cost | Fixed | ±5% (£24,000) |
| Scope | Flex | All Must-haves delivered; up to 40% of Should and Could items may be deferred |
| Quality | Flex within limits | Definition of Done, including the council's accessibility standard, is not negotiable |
| Benefits | Fixed | Online share of applications reaches an agreed target within six months of launch |
| Risk | Flex | No high-rated risk without an owner and response |
| Sustainability | Fixed | Hosted within the council's existing cloud arrangement |

#### What happens mid-project
At the end of Sprint 7, the team's average velocity is 30 points against the 38 assumed in the stage plan. The remaining Must-have backlog is estimated at 210 points, and six sprints remain (Sprints 8 to 13). At current velocity the team can complete about 6 × 30 = 180 points, leaving roughly 30 points of Must-have work undone. That breaches the scope tolerance, so the project manager raises an exception report rather than quietly asking the team to work faster.
| Option | Effect | Within tolerance? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Add a developer for four sprints | Costs about £36,000 (illustrative) | No: exceeds the £24,000 cost tolerance |
| B. Reclassify card payment as a Should-have and take payments by phone for three months | Removes about 35 points of Must-have work; senior user confirms the service is still usable | Yes, if the board approves the change to Must-have scope |
| C. Add one sprint | Delivers everything two weeks late | No: time is fixed by regulation |
The board chooses option B, approves an exception plan for the rest of the stage and asks the Product Owner to put card payments first after launch. The team never stopped work; the board decided one specific trade-off, which is how management by exception should support Agile delivery.
Tip
Track Must-have scope separately on your burn-up chart. A single line for all scope hides the moment when the minimum usable product is at risk.

### When to use PRINCE2, Agile or both
| Situation | Best fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed specification, regulated output, little expected change (for example, a building refurbishment) | PRINCE2 with sequential delivery | Change is expensive and stage approvals protect the investment |
| Product team with an empowered Product Owner and continuous funding | Agile on its own (for example, Scrum or Kanban) | There is no fixed end point to govern, and heavy stage gates add delay |
| Public-sector digital service with a fixed deadline and budget | PRINCE2 Agile or a similar hybrid | The board needs accountability; the team needs room to learn |
| Multi-supplier programme with contracts and audit requirements | PRINCE2 governance with Agile teams inside suppliers | Clear customer-supplier roles plus iterative delivery |
| Short internal improvement with one team | Lightweight Agile with a simple charter | Full PRINCE2 governance would cost more than the project |
| Organisation new to Agile but committed to PRINCE2 | PRINCE2 Agile pilot on one project | Lets governance and teams learn together |
If you also need to choose between PRINCE2 and PMI's standard, read [PMBOK vs PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-vs-prince2/).

### PRINCE2 and Agile pros and cons
|  | Strengths | Limitations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PRINCE2 | Clear accountability and decision rights; strong business justification; audit trail; works across many suppliers; widely recognised in the UK, Europe and Australia | Can become document-heavy if not tailored; stage approvals can slow delivery; says little about how teams should do the work |
| Agile | Early and frequent delivery; fast feedback; handles changing requirements; motivated, self-managing teams; quality built in each iteration | Needs an available, empowered Product Owner; long-range forecasts are ranges, not dates; light on governance for large funded projects |
| PRINCE2 Agile | Combines accountability with adaptability; gives boards a language for flexible scope | Needs careful role design and real board buy-in; can drift into Agile ceremonies inside an unchanged stage-gate process |

### Common mistakes when combining PRINCE2 and Agile
- **Fixing scope, time and cost all at once.** Something has to give. Decide in advance that it is lower-priority scope.
- **Making stage boundaries document reviews.** End each stage with a release or demonstrable increment and review that instead.
- **Asking the team for duplicate reporting.** Build highlight reports from the sprint board, burn-up chart and Sprint Review.
- **A Product Owner without authority.** If every priority decision goes to the board, the team waits. Delegate scope decisions within tolerance.
- **The project manager acting as task-master.** In an Agile team the Developers plan their own work; the project manager manages the project environment.
- **Ignoring the business case after initiation.** Continued business justification is a PRINCE2 principle; review it at every stage boundary using real release data.
A [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) helps you track the delivery risks that most often trigger exceptions, such as dependency delays or an unavailable Product Owner.

### Which certification: PRINCE2, PRINCE2 Agile or Agile?
| Qualification route | Suits | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PRINCE2 Foundation and Practitioner | Project managers in UK, European, Australian and public-sector roles | Foundation has no prerequisite; Practitioner tests applying and tailoring the method |
| PRINCE2 Agile Foundation and Practitioner | Project managers in PRINCE2 organisations running Agile teams | Check PeopleCert for the current version, prerequisites and exam format |
| Scrum certifications (for example, Scrum Master or Product Owner) | People working in or alongside Scrum Teams | Focus on the Scrum framework rather than project governance |
Many experienced project managers hold one governance qualification and one Agile qualification. Read [how to learn Agile and get certified](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/) to compare the main Agile routes.

### Tools for hybrid PRINCE2 and Agile projects
A hybrid project needs two views of the same work: a stage and milestone view for the board and a backlog and board view for the team. Choose a tool that keeps both in one place so reporting comes from live data.
- [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool, suits hybrid governance well: interactive Gantt charts for stages and milestones, boards for sprint work, request forms and shareable dashboards for highlight reporting.
- [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is the natural home for software teams' backlogs, sprints and Agile reports, and is often paired with a portfolio or reporting layer for the board.
- [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) is easy to adopt and combines timeline and board views with dashboards, which helps when business teams and delivery teams share one plan.
Whichever tool you use, add a field for Must-have items so scope tolerance shows on a dashboard. An [Agile PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-pmo/) can standardise this across projects.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is PRINCE2 agile or waterfall?**
Neither by definition. PRINCE2 is a governance method whose stages are decision points for the board, not technical phases. It is often paired with sequential delivery, but the work inside each stage can be delivered in sprints.

**Q: Can PRINCE2 and Scrum be used together?**
Yes. PRINCE2 provides the governance layer (business case, project board, stages and tolerances) and the Scrum Team delivers inside it, with work packages expressed as sprint or release goals.

**Q: What is PRINCE2 Agile?**
Official guidance from PeopleCert on running Agile delivery within PRINCE2 governance. It was first published in 2015, and a new version aligned with PRINCE2 7 was released in 2025. It covers frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban and how to tailor PRINCE2's principles, practices and processes for Agile work.

**Q: What does fix and flex mean in PRINCE2 Agile?**
It means fixing time and cost and letting scope and some quality criteria flex within agreed tolerances. Benefits and risk can be fixed or flexed depending on the project. In practice, Must-have scope is protected and lower-priority features are deferred if time runs short.

**Q: Does PRINCE2 have a Scrum Master or Product Owner?**
Not as named roles. In PRINCE2 Agile, the Product Owner usually works for or alongside the senior user, and the Scrum Master supports a team that delivers work packages under the team manager role.

**Q: Who owns PRINCE2?**
PRINCE2 originated with the UK government and is now owned by PeopleCert, which acquired AXELOS in 2021. PeopleCert also owns PRINCE2 Agile and runs the certification exams. The current edition of the core method is PRINCE2 7, published in 2023.

**Q: How does management by exception work in an Agile project?**
The board sets tolerances for time, cost, scope and other targets, and the team works freely within them. The project manager forecasts against those tolerances each sprint, usually from velocity and the remaining Must-have backlog, and escalates only when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.

**Q: Is PRINCE2 still relevant?**
Yes, particularly in the UK, Europe, Australia and the public sector. PeopleCert updated the core method in 2023 and PRINCE2 Agile in 2025.

**Q: Which is better for my career, PRINCE2 or an Agile certification?**
It depends on your market. PRINCE2 is widely requested for project manager roles in the UK, Europe and the public sector; Scrum and other Agile certifications are common in product and technology roles. Many project managers hold one of each.

**Q: Do I need PRINCE2 before taking PRINCE2 Agile?**
Not necessarily for the Foundation level, but prerequisites can differ by level and version and PeopleCert sets them. Check PeopleCert's current requirements before you book.

**Q: How do PRINCE2 stages relate to sprints?**
A management stage usually contains several sprints and ends with a release or demonstrable increment. Making each stage a whole number of sprints means the stage boundary review looks at real output and an updated forecast rather than at documents alone.

**Q: What replaces a highlight report in an Agile team?**
Nothing needs replacing; it changes form. A short report built from the Sprint Review outcome, the burn-up chart, forecasts against tolerances and key risks gives the board what it needs without extra paperwork.

# Role of the Project Plan in Agile: Levels and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/role-of-the-project-plan-in-agile/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: The role of the project plan in Agile: the five planning levels, what an Agile plan contains, how to build one step by step, and a worked example.


## Role of the Project Plan in Agile: Levels and Example
The role of the project plan in Agile is to set direction, forecast delivery and make trade-offs visible, not to fix every task in advance. Agile projects do plan, but they replace one large baseline with several smaller plans at different levels of detail, from the product vision down to today's work, and update them as the team learns. This guide explains each planning level, what an Agile project plan contains, who owns it, how to build one step by step, and how it copes with fixed budgets, deadlines and governance boards.
- Published 17 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile projects still have a plan. It is layered (vision, roadmap, release, Sprint, daily) and gets more detailed the closer the work is.
- The plan's job is to align people on the goal, forecast what is likely by when, show the constraints and make every change and trade-off visible.
- In most Agile plans time and cost are held steady and scope flexes. The plan says which outcomes are committed and which are only forecast.
- A useful Agile project plan is short: goal, success measures, scope boundaries, team and cadence, release forecast, milestones, budget, risks and reporting.
- Forecast with a velocity range, not a single number, and re-forecast at the end of every Sprint using what the team has actually finished.
- Governance boards can be satisfied with working increments, burnup charts, a decision log and stage reviews aligned with releases.

### What role does the project plan play in Agile?
**In Agile, the project plan is a living, layered forecast rather than a fixed baseline.** It states the goal, the constraints and the likely path to delivery, then is refined every iteration using real progress. Its role is to align stakeholders, guide prioritisation and make trade-offs visible, while detailed task planning happens just in time.
A common myth says Agile teams do not plan. The Agile Manifesto values 'responding to change over following a plan', but it also says there is value in the items on the right. The point is not to stop planning; it is to stop treating the first plan as the truth. Agile teams usually plan more often than predictive teams, just in smaller pieces.
In practice, an Agile project plan does five jobs:
- **Aligns people on the outcome.** Everyone can see the goal, the success measures and what is out of scope.
- **Forecasts delivery.** It shows what is likely to be ready by when, as a range rather than a promise.
- **States the constraints.** Budget, fixed dates, regulatory milestones and dependencies are written down so priorities respect them.
- **Supports governance.** Sponsors and boards get a clear basis for funding, reviewing and stopping work.
- **Makes trade-offs explicit.** When something changes, the plan shows what moves as a result, so decisions are made deliberately.
The document itself matters less than the planning conversations behind it. A good Agile plan fits on a few pages or a single workspace in your tool, and the team can explain it without reading it out.

### Agile plan vs traditional project plan
Both approaches plan; they differ in what they fix, how much detail they commit to up front and how they handle change. The table compares a typical predictive [project management plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-plan/) with a typical Agile project plan.
| Aspect | Traditional (predictive) plan | Agile plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is fixed | Scope, then time and cost are estimated from it | Usually time and cost; scope is prioritised to fit |
| Detail up front | Full work breakdown and schedule before execution | Detail only for the next one or two Sprints |
| Planning horizon | The whole project | Layered: years, quarters, months, weeks, days |
| How change is handled | Formal change control against a baseline | Expected; reprioritised in the backlog every Sprint |
| Measure of progress | Percentage of planned tasks complete, earned value | Working increments, outcomes and a burnup of completed scope |
| Forecast form | A single date and cost | A range, updated with real velocity or throughput |
| Typical artefacts | Gantt chart, WBS, baseline schedule, plan document | Vision, roadmap, release plan, Sprint Backlog, burnup |
Neither is 'no plan'. Predictive plans suit work where requirements are stable and changes are expensive; Agile plans suit work where you learn by delivering. Many organisations combine both. See our comparison of [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/) for when each approach fits.

### The five levels of Agile planning
Agile planning is often drawn as an onion, a model popularised by Mike Cohn in Agile Estimating and Planning. The outer layers cover long horizons with little detail; the inner layers cover short horizons in fine detail. Authors label the layers slightly differently (some add strategy and portfolio layers), but most teams work with these five:
| Level | Horizon | Question it answers | Usually owned by | Typical artefact | Revisited |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vision | One to several years | Why are we doing this and for whom? | Sponsor, product manager or Product Owner | Vision statement, Product Goal | Rarely; when strategy changes |
| Roadmap | Quarters | Which outcomes come first? | Product Owner or product manager | Agile roadmap (Now-Next-Later or by quarter) | Monthly or quarterly |
| Release | One to six months | What is likely to be ready by when? | Product Owner with the team | Release plan and burnup | Every Sprint |
| Sprint (iteration) | One to four weeks | What will we deliver next, and how? | The Scrum Team | Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog | Every Sprint Planning |
| Daily | Today | What will we do next to reach the Sprint Goal? | The Developers | Plan agreed at the Daily Scrum, task board | Every day |

#### Vision and roadmap
The vision explains the problem and who benefits. In Scrum, the Product Goal describes a future state of the product that the team plans against. The [Agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) turns that goal into an ordered sequence of outcomes, usually expressed as themes or [epics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/), with near-term items more specific than later ones.

#### Release planning
A release plan forecasts which backlog items are likely to be delivered by a date, or when a set of items is likely to be ready. It combines an ordered backlog, rough estimates and the team's velocity range. This is the level most sponsors mean when they ask for 'the plan'. Our guide to [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) covers the forecasting maths in detail.

#### Sprint and daily planning
At the start of each Sprint, [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) sets a Sprint Goal, selects items from the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) and decides how to deliver them. The 2020 Scrum Guide describes the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) as 'a plan by and for the Developers'. The [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) then adjusts that plan every day and produces an actionable plan for the next day of work.
Tip
Detail should increase as the horizon shortens. If your roadmap lists individual tasks for next year, or your Sprint Backlog contains vague goals with no concrete work, the levels have been mixed up.

### What an Agile project plan contains
When a sponsor, PMO or client asks for an Agile project plan, they usually need one short document or workspace that ties the levels together. These are the components most organisations expect.
| Component | What to write | Example (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goal and problem | The outcome in one or two sentences and why it matters | Let policyholders track claims online so that status calls fall |
| Success measures | Two or three measurable outcomes and how they will be tracked | Status calls down 40% within six months of launch |
| Scope boundaries | What is in, what is out, what is undecided | In: claim status and document upload. Out: new claims intake |
| Stakeholders | Who is involved, how and how often | Claims director at every Sprint Review; legal at release gates |
| Team and roles | Who is on the team and who makes which decisions | Product Owner, Scrum Master, five Developers |
| Cadence | Sprint length and the meeting schedule | Two-week Sprints; Review and Retrospective every other Thursday |
| Initial backlog | Epics in priority order with rough sizes | Six epics, about 340 story points in total |
| Release forecast | Likely scope by date, as a range | MVP between Sprint 7 and Sprint 9 |
| Milestones and dependencies | Fixed dates and external inputs | Data protection review before the pilot |
| Budget | Funding, cost per Sprint and runway | £38,000 per Sprint, 12 Sprints funded |
| Risks and assumptions | Top risks, owners and responses | Legacy claims system integration; spike in Sprint 1 |
| Reporting and governance | What is reported, to whom and when | Burnup and forecast to the steering group monthly |
Keep each component brief. Detailed work belongs in the backlog, risks in a living [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) or RAID log, and dates in the release plan. The project plan links to those artefacts instead of copying them.
See our free [Agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/), which covers all of these sections and includes a lightweight Agile project charter.

### Who owns the plan in an Agile project
Ownership is shared, because each planning level has a different owner. Confusion usually comes from expecting one person to write and defend every level.
| Role | Planning responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Sponsor or business owner | Sets the vision and funding, agrees success measures, approves the budget and stage decisions |
| Product Owner | Owns the Product Goal, roadmap and Product Backlog order; makes scope trade-offs; leads release forecasting |
| Project manager (where the role exists) | Owns the overall project plan in hybrid or governed settings: budget, milestones, dependencies, risks, reporting and stakeholder communication |
| Scrum Master | Makes sure planning events happen and are useful; helps the team improve forecasting and remove impediments |
| Developers | Size the work, plan each Sprint, own the Sprint Backlog and the daily plan |
Scrum itself has no project manager accountability, but many organisations keep the role for budgets, contracts and cross-team coordination. Our guide to the [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) explains how the role works alongside a Product Owner and Scrum Master.

### How to create an Agile project plan, step by step
Follow these steps for a new Agile project. Expect the first version to take days, not weeks; you will refine it every Sprint.
1. **Agree the outcome.** Write the problem, who benefits and two or three success measures. If people cannot agree on these, more planning detail will not help.
2. **Set the boundaries and constraints.** Record what is in and out of scope, the budget, any fixed dates, regulatory or contractual milestones and known dependencies.
3. **Form the team and choose the cadence.** Confirm who is on the team, the Sprint length (two weeks is common) and the schedule of Sprint Planning, Reviews and Retrospectives.
4. **Build an initial backlog.** Break the outcome into epics and the first few epics into user stories. Order them by value, risk and dependency. Use MoSCoW or a ranked list to mark what is essential.
5. **Size the work roughly.** Ask the team to estimate epics with T-shirt sizes or [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/). Precision is not the goal; a consistent relative size is.
6. **Estimate a velocity range.** If the team has history, use its slowest, average and fastest recent Sprints. If not, forecast capacity for the first Sprints and replace the guess with real data after two or three Sprints.
7. **Forecast releases.** Divide the remaining work by the velocity range to show earliest and latest likely Sprints for each release. Mark what is committed (usually the minimum viable scope) and what is only forecast.
8. **Calculate cost per Sprint and runway.** Multiply team cost by Sprint length, add other recurring costs, and divide the budget by the result. This tells you how many Sprints are funded.
9. **List risks, assumptions and milestones.** Plan early work to reduce the biggest risks first, for example a technical spike in Sprint 1.
10. **Agree reporting and review points.** Decide what stakeholders will see (Sprint Reviews, a burnup, a monthly forecast) and when the plan is formally reviewed.
11. **Plan the first Sprint in detail.** Hold Sprint Planning for Sprint 1 only. Later Sprints are planned when you reach them.
For the forecasting steps, our [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) and [Sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) do the arithmetic for you.

### Worked example: a plan for a claims portal project
The following example is illustrative. A mid-sized insurer wants policyholders to track the status of their claims online and upload documents, so that fewer customers phone the claims team. The sponsor asks for a plan before approving funding.

#### Team, cadence and budget
| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Team | Product Owner, Scrum Master, five Developers (7 people) |
| Sprint length | Two weeks (10 working days) |
| Blended day rate | £520 per person |
| Team cost per Sprint | 7 × £520 × 10 = £36,400 |
| Tools and hosting per Sprint | £1,600 |
| Total cost per Sprint | £38,000 |
| Approved budget | £456,000 |
| Funded runway | £456,000 ÷ £38,000 = 12 Sprints (24 weeks) |

#### Backlog and forecast
The team sizes six epics at about 340 story points. The Product Owner marks 210 points as the minimum viable product (must-have), 70 as should-have and 60 as could-have. The team has worked together before, so it uses a velocity range of 24 (slow), 28 (average) and 33 (fast) points per Sprint.
| Scope | Points | Fast (33) | Average (28) | Slow (24) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MVP (must-have) | 210 | 7 Sprints | 8 Sprints | 9 Sprints |
| MVP + should-have | 280 | 9 Sprints | 10 Sprints | 12 Sprints |
| Everything | 340 | 11 Sprints | 13 Sprints | 15 Sprints |
Each figure is the points divided by velocity, rounded up to whole Sprints. With 12 Sprints funded, the plan says:
- **Committed:** the MVP, released to all policyholders by the end of Sprint 9 at the latest.
- **Forecast:** should-have items by Sprint 12, likely but not guaranteed.
- **Not promised:** could-have items. They are only reached if the team runs at the fast end of its range.

#### Releases, milestones and risks
| Release or milestone | Target | Contents or condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Technical spike | Sprint 1 | Prove the connection to the legacy claims system (the biggest risk) |
| Data protection review | Before Sprint 5 ends | Required before any customer data is shown in the pilot |
| Release 1: pilot | End of Sprint 5 | Claim status for a pilot group of policyholders |
| Release 2: MVP | End of Sprint 7 to 9 | Status, document upload and notifications for all policyholders |
| Release 3: enhancements | End of Sprint 12 | Should-have items such as live chat hand-off |

#### Re-planning after Sprint 6
After six Sprints the team has completed 165 points, all from the MVP (an average of 27.5 per Sprint). Legal has added 18 points of compliance stories to the MVP. The Product Owner updates the forecast:
| Measure | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remaining MVP | 210 + 18 − 165 | 63 points |
| Sprints to finish MVP | 63 ÷ 33 to 63 ÷ 24 | 2 to 3 Sprints, so Sprint 8 or 9 |
| Remaining must + should | 63 + 70 | 133 points |
| Capacity left in budget | 6 Sprints × 24 to 6 Sprints × 33 | 144 to 198 points |
| Could-have items | 133 + 60 = 193 points | Only reachable at the fast end |
The commitment still holds, the should-have forecast has improved, and the sponsor can see that the extra compliance work was absorbed without new funding. That conversation took ten minutes because the plan already showed what was committed, what was forecast and why.

### Fixed dates, budgets and scope: how the plan handles constraints
Most Agile plans hold time and cost steady and let scope flex. That does not mean scope is vague: the plan names the minimum that must be delivered and orders everything else by value. When a constraint is fixed, the plan shows which other variable absorbs change.
| Situation | What the plan fixes | What flexes | How to plan it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed budget | Cost per Sprint and number of Sprints | Scope beyond the minimum | Fund a stable team for a set runway; forecast scope with a velocity range |
| Fixed deadline | Release date | Scope, ordered by value | Work out how many Sprints fit before the date; commit to what fits at the slow velocity |
| Fixed scope | A defined minimum feature set | Date, within a range | Forecast a date range; review it every Sprint and act early if it slips |
If a stakeholder insists on fixing scope, date and budget together, the honest response is to show the forecast range and ask which constraint gives way if the slow case happens. Writing that agreement into the plan prevents arguments later. Our guide to [project constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/) explains the underlying trade-offs.

### Satisfying governance without a fixed plan
Many organisations need plans for funding approval, audit and oversight. Agile teams can meet these needs without writing a detailed baseline that will be out of date in a month.
| Governance need | Agile answer |
| --- | --- |
| Approve funding | Fund a stable team for a set runway, with a clear outcome and success measures; review continuation at agreed points |
| Know when things will be ready | Release forecast as a range, updated every Sprint |
| See real progress | Working increments at Sprint Reviews, plus a burnup chart of completed scope |
| Control scope | Ordered backlog; any addition shows what moves down or out |
| Manage risk | Short, living risk and decision log; risky work scheduled early |
| Stage gates or phase reviews | Gates aligned with releases (pilot, MVP, full rollout) rather than with design or build phases |
Frameworks such as PRINCE2 Agile combine stage-based governance with Agile delivery: the project and stage plans focus on features and outcomes, while teams plan their own work. Our guides to [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) and [PRINCE2 vs Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/prince2-vs-agile/) explain the options.
Tip
Align stage gates with releases, not with activities. A gate that asks 'is the pilot working for real customers?' tells the board far more than one that asks 'is the design document signed off?'.

### Keeping the plan alive
An Agile plan loses its value as soon as it stops reflecting reality. Build updates into the cadence so they are routine rather than a special exercise.
| What to update | When | Who | Typical trigger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Backlog and daily plan | Every day | Developers | Progress or new information at the Daily Scrum |
| Sprint Goal and Sprint plan | Every Sprint Planning | Scrum Team | Start of each Sprint |
| Release forecast and burnup | End of every Sprint | Product Owner | New velocity data or scope change |
| Risk and decision log | Every Sprint, and when something happens | Project manager or Product Owner | New risk, issue or decision |
| Roadmap | Monthly or quarterly | Product Owner or product manager | Learning from releases, market or strategy change |
| Budget and runway | Monthly | Project manager or sponsor | Spend reports, team changes |
Changes are expected; what matters is that each one is visible. Keep a short change history in the plan (date, change, reason, impact on forecast).

### Tracking progress against an Agile plan
Progress in an Agile project is measured by what is finished and usable, not by how many tasks have started. These measures show whether the plan is on track:
- **Burnup chart:** completed scope against total scope over time. It shows both progress and scope growth on one chart.
- **Velocity range:** points (or items) completed per Sprint. Use the range for forecasts; see our guide to the [Agile velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/).
- **Release forecast:** earliest and latest likely Sprint for each release, recalculated each Sprint.
- **Outcome measures:** the success measures in the plan, such as fewer status calls or faster processing, tracked once releases are live.
The 2020 Scrum Guide notes that practices such as burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flow are useful for forecasting but do not replace empiricism: only what has already happened can be used for forward-looking decisions. In other words, re-forecast with real data rather than defending the original estimate. Our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/) covers more measures and their pitfalls.

### Hybrid plans: when part of the work is predictive
Many projects mix Agile delivery with work that must be planned predictively: hardware lead times, procurement, building works, regulatory submissions or a fixed go-live event. In these cases the project plan often has two layers:
- **A milestone-level schedule** for fixed dates and external dependencies, sometimes shown as a Gantt chart for stakeholders.
- **Agile release and Sprint plans** for the work the team can deliver incrementally, linked to those milestones.
Keep the Gantt chart at milestone or release level; day-to-day work stays in the backlog and on the board. Our guide to [Agile Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-gantt-charts/) shows how to combine the two without creating two competing plans.
See our guide on [how to run an Agile project](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-run-an-agile-project/) for the full delivery cycle once the plan is in place.

### Common mistakes with Agile project plans
| Mistake | Why it hurts | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Having no plan at all | Sponsors lose confidence and impose a predictive plan instead | Write a short layered plan with a goal, forecast, budget and risks |
| Planning every Sprint up front | Detail goes out of date quickly and creates false certainty | Plan only the next one or two Sprints in detail |
| Forecasting with one number | The first slow Sprint looks like failure | Use a velocity range and show earliest and latest dates |
| Committing to everything | No room to absorb change; quality suffers | Commit to the minimum; forecast the rest |
| Hiding scope changes | Dates slip with no visible reason | Show scope growth on a burnup and in the change history |
| Treating the backlog as the whole plan | Budget, risks, stakeholders and milestones go unmanaged | Keep a one-page plan that links to the backlog |
| Never re-forecasting | The plan becomes fiction | Update the forecast at the end of every Sprint |

### Tools for Agile project planning
A spreadsheet works for small projects; a project management tool keeps the planning levels connected.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)** (our #1, 9.4) suits hybrid plans well: Gantt charts, dependencies and milestones sit alongside boards, request intake and portfolio reporting, so governance and team work stay in one place.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is strongest for software Scrum teams: backlogs, epics, story points, Sprints and velocity reports.
- **monday.com** (9.1) is easy to adopt and offers timeline and Gantt views for stakeholder-facing plans.
- **Asana** (9.0) links work to goals and portfolios, which helps when plans roll up to business objectives.
- **ClickUp** (8.9) combines Sprints, Gantt views, docs and dashboards at a modest price.
Compare features and scores side by side on our [project management tools comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What role does the project plan play in Agile development?**
It sets direction and forecasts delivery rather than fixing every task. The plan aligns stakeholders on the goal, states constraints such as budget and fixed dates, forecasts what is likely by when and makes trade-offs visible. Detailed work is planned just in time, Sprint by Sprint.

**Q: Do Agile projects have a project plan?**
Yes. Agile projects plan in layers: a vision, a roadmap, release plans, Sprint plans and a daily plan. Many organisations also keep a short project plan that ties these together with the budget, milestones, risks and reporting.

**Q: What are the five levels of Agile planning?**
Vision, roadmap, release, iteration (Sprint) and daily. Detail increases as the horizon gets shorter. The model is often drawn as a planning onion, and some authors add strategy and portfolio layers outside the vision.

**Q: What should an Agile project plan include?**
The goal, success measures, scope boundaries, stakeholders, team and roles, cadence, initial backlog, release forecast, milestones and dependencies, budget, risks and assumptions, and how progress will be reported.

**Q: Who is responsible for the project plan in Agile?**
Ownership is shared. The sponsor owns the vision and funding, the Product Owner owns the roadmap, backlog order and release forecast, the Developers own Sprint and daily plans, and a project manager, where there is one, often owns the overall plan, budget and reporting.

**Q: Is the product backlog the same as the project plan?**
No. The backlog is the ordered list of work and is a core part of the plan, but a full Agile project plan also covers goals, success measures, stakeholders, cadence, budget, milestones and risks.

**Q: How does an Agile project plan handle a fixed budget?**
Usually by funding a stable team for a set number of Sprints. Divide the budget by the cost per Sprint to find the runway, then forecast how much of the ordered backlog fits, committing to the minimum and forecasting the rest.

**Q: How does Agile handle a fixed deadline?**
Count the Sprints before the date, forecast how much work fits at the slow end of the velocity range and commit only to that. Lower-priority items are delivered if the team runs faster.

**Q: Can you use a Gantt chart in Agile?**
Yes, at milestone or release level, especially for stakeholders and for dependencies on predictive work such as procurement. Day-to-day planning stays in the backlog and on the board.

**Q: How often is an Agile project plan updated?**
The Sprint plan is updated every Sprint and the daily plan every day. Re-forecast releases at the end of every Sprint, review the roadmap monthly or quarterly, and change the vision only when strategy changes.

**Q: What is the difference between a release plan and a project plan in Agile?**
A release plan forecasts which backlog items are likely to be ready by which date. The project plan is broader: it includes the release plan plus goals, budget, team, stakeholders, milestones, risks and governance.

**Q: How do you report Agile progress to a steering committee?**
Show working increments, a burnup chart of completed versus total scope, the latest release forecast as a range, budget burn and the top risks and decisions. Align formal reviews with releases.

# What Is SAFe? The Scaled Agile Framework Explained

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: SAFe explained: core values, configurations, Agile Release Trains, Program Increments, key roles, benefits and criticisms of the Scaled Agile Framework.


## What Is SAFe? The Scaled Agile Framework Explained
The Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) is the most widely adopted framework for applying Agile across large organisations. It provides roles, events and practices to align many Agile teams around shared goals, while keeping the team-level practices of Scrum and Kanban.
- Published 22 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- SAFe aligns many Agile teams through Agile Release Trains and Program Increments.
- PI Planning and Lean Portfolio Management are its signature practices.
- It is powerful at scale but can become heavy if adopted mechanically.

### Where SAFe comes from
SAFe was created by Dean Leffingwell and first released in 2011. It is maintained by Scaled Agile, Inc., which publishes the framework and runs training and certification. It draws on Agile, Lean, systems thinking and DevOps, and it is updated regularly; check the official site for the current version.

### Core values
- **Alignment:** everyone understands and works towards the same goals.
- **Transparency:** progress, problems and decisions are visible.
- **Respect for people:** the people doing the work are trusted and developed.
- **Relentless improvement:** the organisation keeps learning and improving.

### The four configurations
| Configuration | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| Essential SAFe | One or a few Agile Release Trains deliver a product or solution |
| Large Solution SAFe | Very large, complex systems need several trains and suppliers working together |
| Portfolio SAFe | Strategy, funding and governance must be connected to delivery |
| Full SAFe | All of the above in very large enterprises |

### Key building blocks
- **Agile teams** of about ten or fewer people use Scrum, Kanban or both.
- **[Agile Release Train (ART)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/):** a long-lived team of Agile teams, typically 50 to 125 people, that plans and delivers together.
- **Program Increment (PI):** a planning interval, usually 8 to 12 weeks, often four development iterations followed by an Innovation and Planning iteration.
- **[PI Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/):** a regular, usually two-day event in which the whole ART plans the next PI together.
- **[Lean Portfolio Management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/):** connects strategy and funding with execution.

### Key roles
| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Release Train Engineer (RTE) | Servant leader and coach for the ART; facilitates PI Planning |
| Product Management | Owns the ART's backlog and vision |
| System Architect | Guides technical direction across teams |
| Business Owners | Key stakeholders accountable for business outcomes |
| Product Owner and Scrum Master (team coach) | Team-level roles, as in Scrum |

### Benefits and criticisms
**Benefits reported by adopters** include better alignment between strategy and delivery, more predictable releases, fewer dependency surprises and clearer visibility for leaders.
**Criticisms** include that SAFe can feel heavy and prescriptive, that it may preserve hierarchy under new names, and that large planning events can become theatre if teams lack real autonomy. Alternatives such as [LeSS](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/) take a lighter approach.
Tip
Scale only when you need to. If one or two teams can deliver the product, a scaling framework may add more overhead than value.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is SAFe Agile?**
SAFe is built on Agile and Lean principles, and its teams use Scrum and Kanban. Critics argue some implementations become too process-heavy, so how it is adopted matters a lot.

**Q: How big must an organisation be for SAFe?**
SAFe is designed for programmes of roughly 50 or more people working on one solution. Smaller organisations rarely need it.

**Q: What is SAFe in simple terms?**
A framework for coordinating many Agile teams that work on the same large product or solution, with shared planning, cadence and governance.

**Q: Who created SAFe?**
Dean Leffingwell, who first released it in 2011. It is maintained by Scaled Agile, Inc.

**Q: What is a Program Increment in SAFe?**
A planning interval, usually 8 to 12 weeks, often four development iterations followed by an Innovation and Planning iteration. Recent SAFe versions call it a Planning Interval.

**Q: What is an Agile Release Train in SAFe?**
A long-lived team of Agile teams, typically 50 to 125 people, that plans and delivers together. See [Agile Release Train](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/).

**Q: What are the SAFe configurations?**
Essential SAFe, Large Solution SAFe, Portfolio SAFe and Full SAFe, chosen according to size and complexity.

**Q: What is a Release Train Engineer in SAFe?**
The servant leader and coach for an Agile Release Train, who facilitates PI Planning and other ART events and helps remove impediments.

**Q: What are the criticisms of SAFe?**
Critics say it can be prescriptive and process-heavy, and that some implementations rename existing structures without changing how work is done.

**Q: What is the difference between SAFe and LeSS?**
SAFe adds roles, events and layers for large enterprises; [LeSS](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/) keeps Scrum's simplicity and scales it with as little extra structure as possible.

**Q: What certifications does SAFe offer?**
Scaled Agile, Inc. offers role-based certifications such as SAFe Agilist, SAFe Scrum Master and Release Train Engineer. Check its site for current options.
