# What Does a Scrum Master Do? Role and Responsibilities

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: What does a Scrum Master do? Responsibilities per the 2020 Scrum Guide, a typical day, skills, worked examples and Scrum Master vs project manager.


## What Does a Scrum Master Do? Role and Responsibilities
A Scrum Master helps a Scrum Team and its organisation use Scrum well: according to the 2020 Scrum Guide, they are accountable for establishing Scrum and for the Scrum Team's effectiveness. In practice they coach the team in self-management, help the Product Owner manage the backlog, make sure the Scrum events happen and are useful, and cause impediments to be removed, all without any authority over the work itself. This guide explains the role as the Scrum Guide defines it, what it looks like day to day and across a Sprint, and what it is not, with worked examples, tables and step-by-step processes.
- Published 20 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum and for the Scrum Team's effectiveness. It is an accountability, not a rank, and it carries no authority over who does what.
- The 2020 Scrum Guide describes three areas of service: to the Scrum Team, to the Product Owner and to the wider organisation.
- Scrum Masters do not assign tasks, own the Sprint Backlog, run the Daily Scrum for the Developers or cancel Sprints; those belong to the Developers and the Product Owner.
- Most of the work is coaching, facilitation and causing impediments to be removed, plus changing the organisational conditions that slow the team down.
- Judge a Scrum Master by how well the team improves and delivers valuable, Done increments, not by velocity or how busy they look.
- PSM I and CSM are the common entry certifications, but real experience with a team matters more to most employers.

### What is a Scrum Master?
A **Scrum Master** is the member of a Scrum Team who is accountable for establishing Scrum as the Scrum Guide defines it and for the team's effectiveness. They help the team, the Product Owner and the organisation understand Scrum theory and practice, coach the team towards self-management, and make sure obstacles to progress are removed. They lead by serving, not by directing.
The 2020 Scrum Guide, still the current official version in October 2026, describes a [Scrum Team](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) as a small group (typically 10 or fewer people) with three accountabilities: the [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/), the Scrum Master and the Developers. The word 'accountability' matters. The Scrum Master is not a job grade or a manager. It is a set of things someone on the team is answerable for, and in some organisations the person who holds it does other work too.
The guide calls Scrum Masters 'true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organization'. Earlier editions used the term 'servant-leader'; the 2020 wording keeps the idea but stresses that serving is a form of leadership, not a support function. If you are new to the framework itself, start with [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/).
Tip
A useful one-line test: if the Scrum Master went on holiday for a Sprint, would the team still plan, inspect and adapt well? A good Scrum Master is steadily making that answer 'yes'.

### What does a Scrum Master do? The three areas of service
The Scrum Guide groups the Scrum Master's work into service to the Scrum Team, the Product Owner and the organisation. Each table summarises the guide (left) and gives our practical examples (right).

#### Serving the Scrum Team
| Scrum Guide responsibility | What it looks like in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Coaching team members in self-management and cross-functionality | Asking the team to decide who picks up work; encouraging pairing so knowledge spreads; not answering questions the team can answer itself |
| Helping the team focus on high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done | Making the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) visible; challenging 'nearly done' work; helping the team finish before starting |
| Causing the removal of impediments to progress | Keeping an impediment list, deciding with the team who acts, escalating what the team cannot fix |
| Ensuring all Scrum events take place and are positive, productive and kept within the timebox | Booking the events, preparing formats, keeping time, and stepping back once the team can run them alone |

#### Serving the Product Owner
| Scrum Guide responsibility | What it looks like in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management | Introducing story mapping, ordering techniques or a lightweight [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) structure |
| Helping the team understand the need for clear and concise Product Backlog items | Facilitating [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) so items are understood before Sprint Planning |
| Helping establish empirical product planning for a complex environment | Showing how to forecast from actual delivery data instead of fixed upfront estimates |
| Facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed | Designing a Sprint Review where stakeholders try the product and give feedback |

#### Serving the organisation
| Scrum Guide responsibility | What it looks like in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Leading, training and coaching the organisation in its Scrum adoption | Running short Scrum sessions for managers and stakeholders; answering 'why do we work this way?' |
| Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organisation | Advising on team boundaries, release practices and how Scrum fits governance |
| Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work | Explaining [empiricism](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/): decisions based on what is observed, not on the original plan |
| Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams | Replacing status reports with Sprint Reviews; connecting the team directly with users |
Note the verb: the Scrum Master is accountable for **causing** the removal of impediments, not removing each one personally. Ideally the team learns to remove its own, and the Scrum Master focuses on those needing organisational change.

### What a Scrum Master does not do
Job adverts often describe the Scrum Master as an administrator or a renamed project manager. The 2020 Scrum Guide gives several of those duties to other accountabilities.
| Common assumption | What the 2020 Scrum Guide says |
| --- | --- |
| The Scrum Master assigns tasks | Developers are self-managing and decide who does what. They create the plan for the Sprint, the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/). |
| The Scrum Master runs the Daily Scrum | The [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) is a 15-minute event for the Developers. The Scrum Master makes sure it happens and may coach, but the Developers run it. If the Scrum Master is working on Sprint Backlog items, they take part as a Developer. |
| The Scrum Master decides what gets built | The Product Owner is accountable for maximising value and for the Product Backlog. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. |
| The Scrum Master can cancel a Sprint | Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel a Sprint, and only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. |
| The Scrum Master is the team's manager | The role has no line authority. Scrum Masters lead through influence, coaching and facilitation. |
| The Scrum Master writes the status report | Progress is made transparent through the artefacts and the Sprint Review. A Scrum Master may help make information visible but does not report on the team's behalf. |
A Scrum Master may still update a board or book a room; those tasks are simply not the point of the role. If administration fills most of the week, coaching and organisational work are being neglected.

### The Scrum Master across a Sprint
A Sprint lasts one month or less. The Scrum Guide sets maximum timeboxes for a one-month Sprint and notes that events are usually shorter for shorter Sprints. The table shows each event and the Scrum Master's contribution.
| Event or activity | Maximum timebox (one-month Sprint) | What the Scrum Master does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | 8 hours | Checks the Product Owner has a proposed objective and refined items; facilitates so the team agrees a Sprint Goal and a realistic plan; protects the timebox |
| Daily Scrum | 15 minutes | Makes sure it happens and stays focused on progress towards the Sprint Goal; coaches the Developers to run it themselves; notes impediments raised |
| Backlog refinement | Ongoing activity, not an event | Helps the Product Owner and Developers keep enough work ready for the next one or two Sprints |
| [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) | 4 hours | Helps design a working session with stakeholders, not a slide show; keeps attention on the product and the Product Goal |
| [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | 3 hours | Chooses a format that fits the team's current problems, keeps it safe and focused, and makes sure the team leaves with one or two concrete improvements |
For a two-week Sprint, many teams use around half of the one-month timeboxes, for example up to four hours of Sprint Planning. That is a common practice rather than a rule. A [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) and a [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) help new Scrum Masters prepare the first few events.

### A typical day for a Scrum Master
The schedule below is an illustrative day for a Scrum Master supporting one team, on day four of a two-week Sprint.
| Time | Activity | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 08:45 | Check the Sprint board and burndown; review open impediments | Spot work that has stalled before the Daily Scrum |
| 09:30 | Attend the Daily Scrum (15 minutes) and observe | See whether the team is talking about the Sprint Goal or just reporting status |
| 09:50 | Follow up two impediments: a test environment outage and a pending security approval | Keep blocked work moving; agree owners and dates |
| 10:30 | One-to-one coaching with the Product Owner on splitting a large item | Make the next Sprint Planning easier |
| 13:30 | Backlog refinement session (60 minutes) | Keep enough items ready; check acceptance criteria are clear |
| 15:00 | Meeting with the release manager about a slow approval process | Remove an organisational barrier that affects several teams |
| 16:00 | Draft next week's retrospective format | Target the retrospective at a real problem |
| 16:30 | Update the impediment log | Make recurring problems visible |

#### How the week changes across a Sprint
- **Start of the Sprint:** facilitating Sprint Planning and helping the team turn the Sprint Goal into a first plan.
- **Middle of the Sprint:** more observation, coaching, refinement and impediment work; time with stakeholders and other teams.
- **End of the Sprint:** preparing and facilitating the Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective, and checking that last Sprint's improvement actually happened.
- **Throughout:** work with managers and other Scrum Masters on cross-team issues, for example through a [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/).

### How a Scrum Master removes impediments: step by step
An impediment is anything that slows the team's progress towards the Sprint Goal that the team cannot easily resolve by itself. Examples include a broken build pipeline, a missing decision from a stakeholder, a dependency on another team, or a policy that forces work through a slow approval. A simple process keeps impediments visible and stops the Scrum Master becoming a bottleneck.
1. **Make it visible.** Add every impediment to a shared list or a column on the board with the date raised and the item it blocks.
2. **Clarify the impact.** Ask which Sprint Goal or backlog item is affected and what happens if it is not resolved this week.
3. **Decide who can solve it.** Classify it: the team can solve it; the Scrum Master should act; or it needs someone outside the team.
4. **Coach before acting.** If the team can solve it, ask questions that help them do so rather than fixing it for them.
5. **Act or escalate with evidence.** For impediments outside the team, take facts to the person who can decide: what is blocked, for how long, and the cost of waiting.
6. **Follow up daily.** Agree an owner and a next date. Report the status briefly at or after the Daily Scrum.
7. **Prevent recurrence.** Bring repeat impediments to the retrospective and look for the root cause, not just the symptom.

#### Example impediment log
| Raised | Impediment | Blocks | Who can solve | Action and owner | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Day 2 | Test environment down after an upgrade | Two items | Platform team | Scrum Master raises with the platform lead; developer pairs on fix | Resolved day 3 |
| Day 3 | Security approval for a new library has taken 9 days | Sprint Goal | Security manager | Scrum Master presents the delay and options; Product Owner agrees a fallback | Approved day 5 |
| Day 4 | Two developers pulled into support every afternoon | Team capacity | Engineering manager | Raised in retrospective; proposal for a support rota | Open |
For larger programmes the same information often sits in a [RAID log](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) alongside risks, assumptions and dependencies.

### Worked example: coaching a team that keeps missing its Sprint Goal
This example is illustrative, but the pattern is common. It shows the role combining observation, data, facilitation and organisational work.

#### The situation
A team of six Developers works in two-week Sprints. It has missed its Sprint Goal in three Sprints in a row. In each Sprint it pulled in about 12 backlog items and finished 7 or 8. At the end of each Sprint, 4 or 5 items were 'in progress', and the next Sprint started with carry-over. The Product Owner is frustrated and a manager has asked the Scrum Master to 'make the team commit properly'.

#### What the Scrum Master did
1. **Observed before acting.** Over one Sprint they noted that the team regularly had 8 to 10 items in progress at once, and that most items waited several days for review or testing.
2. **Shared the data, not a judgement.** At the retrospective they showed a simple chart of items started versus finished per day and asked the team what they saw.
3. **Let the team choose the experiment.** The team agreed to limit work in progress to 4 items and to swarm on items waiting for review before starting new ones. See our guide to [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/).
4. **Worked with the Product Owner.** They coached the Product Owner to propose one clear Sprint Goal rather than a list of unrelated items, and to split two large items in refinement.
5. **Changed the conversation with the manager.** Instead of 'commit harder', they explained that a Sprint Backlog is a forecast and that the team needed fewer items in parallel, not more pressure.
6. **Inspected the result.** After two Sprints they reviewed the same chart with the team.

#### The outcome
| Measure | Before (average of 3 Sprints) | After (average of next 2 Sprints) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Items planned | 12 | 9 |
| Items Done | 7.5 | 8.5 |
| Items in progress at Sprint end | 4.5 | 1 |
| Sprint Goal met | 0 of 3 | 2 of 2 |
The team delivered more by planning less, and the Sprint Goal became meaningful again. The Scrum Master assigned no work and set no target: they made the problem visible, helped the team design its own fix and handled the outside pressure.

### Coaching, teaching, facilitating and mentoring
Scrum Masters switch between several ways of helping people. Choosing the right one for the moment is a large part of the skill. The four below are widely used in Agile coaching; the advice on when to use each is ours.
| Stance | What it means | Use it when | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Teaching | Explaining Scrum theory or a practice directly | The team or a stakeholder lacks knowledge | Explaining why the Sprint Goal gives the Sprint focus |
| Coaching | Asking questions so people find their own answers | The team has the knowledge but needs to think it through | 'What would need to be true for us to finish this item tomorrow?' |
| Facilitating | Designing and guiding a conversation so a group reaches a decision | A group needs to make a shared decision within a timebox | Running a retrospective with a structured format and a clear end |
| Mentoring | Sharing your own experience as guidance | Someone is learning a role you have done | Helping a new Product Owner prepare their first Sprint Review |
Once a team knows the mechanics of Scrum, shift from teaching to coaching. Our [retrospective games](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective-games/) guide has formats for different situations.

### Key Scrum Master skills
Most of what makes a good Scrum Master is interpersonal. Technical knowledge helps but is rarely the deciding factor.
| Skill | Why it matters | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Facilitation | Events that end in decisions save the team time | Practise timeboxed formats; ask for feedback after each event |
| Coaching and questioning | Builds self-management instead of dependence | Learn open questions; resist giving the answer first |
| Deep knowledge of Scrum and Agile | Credibility and the ability to explain why | Reread the Scrum Guide; study [Scrum values](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-principles-and-values/) and [empiricism](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/) |
| Influence without authority | The role has no power to instruct | Build relationships before you need them; use data and stories |
| Conflict resolution | Healthy disagreement improves decisions; unresolved conflict stalls teams | Name the tension early; separate people from positions |
| Observation | Patterns are often invisible to people inside them | Keep notes on recurring behaviours and share them neutrally |
| Organisational change | Many impediments sit outside the team | Learn how decisions are really made in your organisation; see our [Agile transformation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/) guide |
You do not need a technical background, but understanding how your team's work flows (review, testing, release) helps you ask good questions. Scrum Masters come from development, testing, project coordination, business analysis and teaching.

### Scrum Master vs project manager, Product Owner and Agile coach
These roles are often confused, and in smaller organisations one person may hold more than one. The table compares their focus and authority.
|  | Scrum Master | Project manager | Product Owner | Agile coach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Defined by | The Scrum Guide | The organisation; standards such as PMBOK and PRINCE2 | The Scrum Guide | The organisation |
| Main focus | Team effectiveness and use of Scrum | Delivering agreed scope, time and budget | Maximising product value | Agile ways of working across several teams or the organisation |
| Authority over the work | None | Usually plans and assigns work | Orders the Product Backlog | None; advisory |
| Typical scope | One or a few teams | A project | A product | Several teams, a department or leadership |
| Success looks like | A team that improves and delivers Done increments | Objectives met on time and budget | Valuable outcomes for users and the business | Lasting change in how the organisation works |
The biggest practical difference between a Scrum Master and a project manager is control. A project manager typically creates and maintains the plan; in Scrum, the Developers plan their own work and the Product Owner orders the backlog. Many organisations still employ project managers around Scrum Teams, especially for budgets, suppliers and cross-team coordination.

### How to tell whether a Scrum Master is effective
The best evidence is in the team, not in the Scrum Master's calendar. Useful signals include:
- The team regularly meets its Sprint Goal, and Increments meet the Definition of Done.
- Retrospective actions are completed and visibly change how the team works.
- Impediments are resolved faster over time, and fewer of them recur.
- Events finish within their timebox and produce decisions, and the team runs more of them without help.
- Stakeholders attend the Sprint Review and their feedback reaches the Product Backlog.
- Flow measures such as cycle time and work in progress become more stable.
Avoid using [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) as a target for the team or the Scrum Master. Velocity is a planning aid for the team; when it becomes a target, estimates tend to inflate and the number stops meaning anything. Our guide to [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/) explains which measures help.

### Full-time or part-time? How many teams?
The Scrum Guide does not say whether the Scrum Master must be full-time or how many teams one person can support. The scenarios below are our own guidance, based on how much coaching and organisational work each situation tends to need.
| Situation | Typical arrangement | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New team, or an organisation new to Scrum | Full-time, one team | Most time goes on teaching, facilitation and organisational impediments |
| Established team with a stable way of working | One Scrum Master for two teams | Leaves room for coaching both teams and cross-team work |
| Very mature, self-managing teams | Up to three teams, or a part-time role | Risk: the role shrinks to booking meetings; watch for that |
| Small company with one team | A Developer also holds the Scrum Master accountability | Works if they protect time for the role; can be hard during busy Sprints |
Can the Scrum Master also be the Product Owner? The Scrum Guide does not explicitly forbid it, but we advise against it: the Product Owner pushes for value and scope while the Scrum Master protects the way of working, and combining them removes that balance.

### Common Scrum Master mistakes
Most of these come from slipping back into a manager or administrator role.
| Mistake | What happens | Better approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acting as the team's administrator | No time left for coaching or organisational work | Automate or share admin; protect time for coaching |
| Running the Daily Scrum as a status meeting | Developers report to the Scrum Master instead of planning together | Step back; coach the Developers to focus on the Sprint Goal |
| Solving every impediment personally | The team becomes dependent and the Scrum Master becomes a bottleneck | Coach the team to solve what it can; escalate the rest |
| Avoiding conflict with managers | Organisational impediments persist | Bring evidence and options; frame issues in terms of outcomes |
| Same retrospective format every Sprint | Low energy and repeated, vague actions | Vary formats; follow up on actions at the start of each retrospective |
| Enforcing Scrum rigidly without explaining why | Scrum is seen as bureaucracy | Link each practice to the problem it solves |
| Using velocity to compare or push teams | Inflated estimates and lost trust | Use velocity for forecasting only, inside the team |

### Scrum Master certifications
No certificate is required to work as a Scrum Master, but employers often ask for one. The two most common entry-level options are Professional Scrum Master I from Scrum.org and Certified ScrumMaster from Scrum Alliance.
|  | Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) | Certified ScrumMaster (CSM) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Awarded by | Scrum.org | Scrum Alliance |
| Course required | No (a course is recommended, not required) | Yes: a live course with a Certified Scrum Trainer, 16 hours, usually over two to three days, according to Scrum Alliance |
| Exam | 80 questions, 60 minutes, 85% to pass | 50 questions, 60 minutes, 74% to pass |
| Cost | US$200 per attempt (assessment only) | Included in the course fee, which varies by trainer |
| Renewal | Lifetime; no renewal fee | Every two years: US$100 and 20 Scrum Education Units |
PSM I facts are from Scrum.org (checked 25 October 2026). CSM facts are as published for Scrum Alliance at the time of writing; check its website before you book, as course formats and fees vary. Both organisations offer advanced levels (such as PSM II and Advanced CSM) for experienced Scrum Masters.
Experience counts more than any certificate: facilitating retrospectives or acting as Scrum Master for a team gives you real examples to discuss.
For a side-by-side comparison of courses and certificates, read our guide to [Scrum certification and training](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/).

### Will AI replace the Scrum Master?
AI tools can already summarise meetings, flag stalled work and spot patterns in delivery data. That reduces administration and leaves more time for the parts of the role that depend on trust and judgement: coaching a team through conflict, persuading a manager to change a policy, or noticing that a quiet team member has stopped contributing. In our view, AI changes how Scrum Masters spend their time rather than removing the need for the accountability. Our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) covers boards and assistants that support the role.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What does a Scrum Master do every day?**
A typical day includes observing the Daily Scrum, following up impediments, coaching the Product Owner or Developers, supporting backlog refinement, preparing upcoming events such as the retrospective, and working with managers or other teams to remove organisational blockers.

**Q: Is a Scrum Master a manager?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide describes Scrum Masters as true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the organisation. They have no authority to assign work or decide how it is done; they lead through coaching, facilitation and influence.

**Q: Who does a Scrum Master report to?**
Scrum does not specify a reporting line. In practice, Scrum Masters often report to a head of delivery, an Agile coach, an engineering manager or a PMO.

**Q: Does the Scrum Master run the Daily Scrum?**
No. The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers. The Scrum Master makes sure it takes place and stays useful, and may coach the team, but the Developers run it. If the Scrum Master is also working on Sprint Backlog items, they take part as a Developer.

**Q: Can the Scrum Master also be a Developer or the Product Owner?**
A Scrum Master can also be a Developer, which is common in small teams. The Scrum Guide does not explicitly forbid combining Scrum Master and Product Owner, but we advise against it because the two accountabilities balance each other.

**Q: How many teams can a Scrum Master support?**
Our guidance is one team for a new team, two for established teams and up to three for very mature, self-managing teams.

**Q: Does a Scrum Master need a technical background?**
Not necessarily. Understanding how the team's work flows helps you ask good questions, and many Scrum Masters come from development or testing. Facilitation and coaching skills matter more.

**Q: What is an example of an impediment?**
Anything that slows the team's progress that it cannot easily fix alone: a broken test environment, a decision a stakeholder has not made, a dependency on another team, a slow approval process, or team members repeatedly pulled into other work.

**Q: Does a Scrum Master need a certification?**
Not formally, but employers often ask for one. PSM I from Scrum.org is an assessment with no course requirement and no renewal fee; CSM from Scrum Alliance requires a live course and renewal every two years. Practical experience with a team matters more.

**Q: What is the difference between a Scrum Master and a project manager?**
A Scrum Master is accountable for the team's effectiveness and use of Scrum and has no authority over the work. A project manager typically plans and directs work to deliver agreed scope on time and on budget.

**Q: What does 'true leaders who serve' mean?**
It is the 2020 Scrum Guide's description of Scrum Masters, replacing the earlier term 'servant-leader'. It means the Scrum Master leads by helping others succeed: removing obstacles, coaching and creating the conditions for good work, rather than by giving instructions.

# Squads, Tribes, Chapters and Guilds: The Spotify Model Explained

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/squads-tribes-chapters-guilds/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: The Spotify model explained: squads, tribes, chapters and guilds, how they balance autonomy and alignment, and lessons for organisations copying it.


## Squads, Tribes, Chapters and Guilds: The Spotify Model Explained
Squads, tribes, chapters and guilds are terms from the so-called Spotify model, described in a 2012 paper by Henrik Kniberg and Anders Ivarsson. It shows one way to keep many Agile teams autonomous while still aligned.
- Published 24 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Squads deliver, tribes coordinate, chapters develop skills, guilds share knowledge.
- The model balances team autonomy with organisational alignment.
- Copy the principles, not the labels.

### The building blocks
| Unit | What it is | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Squad | A small, cross-functional, self-organising team with a long-term mission | Deliver a part of the product end to end |
| Tribe | A group of squads working in a related area, kept small enough for people to know each other (the paper suggests under about 100) | Coordinate related squads |
| Chapter | People with the same skill within a tribe, such as testers or designers, led by a chapter lead who is also their line manager | Maintain skills and standards |
| Guild | A voluntary community of interest across the whole organisation | Share knowledge across tribes |

### How it balances autonomy and alignment
Squads decide how to build their part of the product; leaders provide a clear mission and context. Chapters give people a professional home and consistent practices across squads. Guilds spread knowledge informally. The result is a matrix in which delivery is organised by squad and tribe, and people development by chapter.

### Important caveat
The paper described how Spotify worked at one point in time. Spotify has said its organisation kept evolving and that the model was never meant to be copied as a framework. Organisations that adopt the labels without the underlying culture of trust, autonomy and continuous improvement often struggle.
Tip
Borrow the ideas, not the names. The lasting lessons are: small autonomous teams, clear missions, communities of practice and leaders who provide context rather than control.

### When to consider it
- Several product teams need autonomy but must share technology and standards.
- You want people to grow their craft while working in cross-functional teams.
- Leadership is ready to trust teams and decentralise decisions.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is the Spotify model a framework?**
No. It was a description of one company's way of working at one time, not a prescriptive framework.

**Q: In the Spotify model, what is the difference between chapters and guilds?**
A chapter is a formal group of people with the same skill within one tribe, with a chapter lead. A guild is an informal, voluntary community across the whole organisation.

**Q: What is the Spotify model?**
A description, published by Spotify in 2012, of how it organised engineering into squads, tribes, chapters and guilds to balance team autonomy with alignment.

**Q: What are squads in the Spotify model?**
A small, cross-functional, self-organising team with a long-term mission for part of the product, similar to a Scrum team.

**Q: What is a tribe in the Spotify model?**
A group of squads working in a related area, kept small enough for people to know each other; the paper suggested under about 100 people.

**Q: What is a chapter in the Spotify model?**
People with the same skill within a tribe, such as testers, led by a chapter lead who is also their line manager.

**Q: What is a guild in the Spotify model?**
A voluntary community of interest across the whole organisation, used to share knowledge on topics such as testing or web development.

**Q: Does Spotify still use the Spotify model?**
Spotify has said its organisation kept evolving and that the model described one point in time. It was never meant to be copied as a fixed framework.

**Q: Why do companies struggle with the Spotify model?**
Many adopt the labels without the culture of trust, autonomy and continuous improvement that made it work, so little actually changes.

**Q: What is a chapter lead in the Spotify model?**
The line manager for people in a chapter, responsible for their growth and for consistent practices, while usually also working in a squad.

**Q: What can I learn from the Spotify model?**
Small autonomous teams with clear missions, communities of practice and leaders who provide context rather than control. See [Agile team structures](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-team-structures/).

# Types of Agile Methodologies: Scrum, Kanban, XP, Lean and More

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: Compare the main Agile methodologies (Scrum, Kanban, Scrumban, XP, Lean, Crystal, DSDM and FDD) and learn which suits your team and work.


## Types of Agile Methodologies: Scrum, Kanban, XP, Lean and More
"Agile" covers a family of methods that share the same values but differ in structure. Some prescribe roles and ceremonies; others only add a few rules to the way you already work. This guide compares the most common ones and helps you choose.
- Published 13 September 2026
- 4 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum uses sprints and roles; Kanban uses flow and WIP limits; Scrumban mixes both.
- XP adds engineering practices; Lean removes waste across the whole system.
- Choose by the shape of your work, then adapt carefully.

### Scrum
Work happens in fixed-length [Sprints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/) of one month or less. A Product Owner orders the backlog, Developers build an Increment that meets the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), and a Scrum Master helps the team improve. **Best for:** product development by a dedicated team. See [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/).

### Kanban
Kanban visualises work on a board, limits work in progress (WIP) and manages flow continuously. There are no fixed iterations or prescribed roles, so you can start with your current process and improve it. Teams track cycle time and throughput. **Best for:** support, operations and any team that receives a steady stream of requests of varying size.

### Scrumban
Scrumban combines Scrum's planning and review rhythm with Kanban's flow and WIP limits. Teams often keep regular planning and retrospectives but pull work continuously rather than committing to a fixed sprint scope. **Best for:** teams moving from Scrum to Kanban, or teams that mix planned feature work with unplanned requests.

### Extreme Programming (XP)
XP focuses on engineering practices that keep software quality high while requirements change: pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases, refactoring, collective code ownership and a sustainable pace. **Best for:** software teams that want technical excellence; often combined with Scrum.

### Lean
Lean comes from manufacturing. It aims to maximise customer value and eliminate waste, such as waiting, handoffs, rework and unused features. Lean software development, described by Mary and Tom Poppendieck, adapts these ideas to knowledge work. **Best for:** improving end-to-end flow and decision-making across an organisation.

### Crystal, DSDM and FDD
- **Crystal** (Alistair Cockburn) is a family of methods tailored to team size and project criticality, with an emphasis on people and communication.
- **DSDM** (Dynamic Systems Development Method) fixes time, cost and quality and flexes scope using MoSCoW prioritisation: Must, Should, Could, Won't have this time. It suits organisations that need more governance.
- **FDD** (Feature-Driven Development) plans and builds by small, client-valued features, with a short modelling phase up front. It suits larger software teams.

### How to choose
| If your work… | Consider |
| --- | --- |
| Is new product development with a dedicated team | Scrum |
| Arrives continuously and unpredictably | Kanban |
| Mixes planned features and urgent requests | Scrumban |
| Needs high software quality under changing requirements | XP practices with Scrum or Kanban |
| Needs governance with fixed deadlines | DSDM or a hybrid approach |
| Spans many teams | A [scaling framework](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) |
Tip
Start with one framework as written. Adapt it only after a few iterations, when you understand why each part exists.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the most popular Agile methodology?**
Scrum is the most widely used, often combined with Kanban practices.

**Q: Can teams mix Agile methodologies?**
Yes. Many teams run Scrum with XP engineering practices and Kanban boards. The key is that every practice serves the Agile values.

**Q: How many Agile methodologies are there?**
There is no fixed number. The best known are Scrum, Kanban, Scrumban, Extreme Programming, Lean, Crystal, DSDM and Feature-Driven Development, plus scaling frameworks such as SAFe and LeSS.

**Q: What is the difference between the Scrum and Kanban Agile methodologies?**
Scrum works in fixed-length Sprints with defined roles and events; Kanban manages a continuous flow of work with WIP limits and no required roles or iterations.

**Q: What is Extreme Programming (XP) as an Agile methodology?**
An Agile method focused on engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, refactoring and small releases. It is often combined with Scrum.

**Q: What is Lean among Agile methodologies?**
Lean comes from manufacturing and aims to maximise customer value by eliminating waste such as waiting, handoffs and rework. Lean software development applies these ideas to knowledge work.

**Q: What is DSDM as an Agile methodology?**
The Dynamic Systems Development Method, created by a UK consortium in 1994. It fixes time and cost, lets scope flex and uses MoSCoW prioritisation.

**Q: What is Feature-Driven Development as an Agile methodology?**
An Agile method created by Jeff De Luca and Peter Coad in 1997 that plans and builds software as small, client-valued features.

**Q: Which Agile methodology is best for beginners?**
Kanban is the easiest to start because it builds on your current process. Scrum gives more structure, which some new teams find helpful.

**Q: Which Agile methodology is used for large organisations?**
Scaling frameworks such as [SAFe](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/), [LeSS](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/), Scrum@Scale and Disciplined Agile coordinate many teams.

**Q: How do I choose an Agile methodology?**
Look at how work arrives and how it is delivered. Planned product work by a dedicated team suits Scrum; unpredictable requests suit Kanban; software quality problems suggest adding XP practices.

# User Stories: How to Write Them, With Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/
Section: Agile guides
Summary: User stories explained: the template, acceptance criteria, INVEST, splitting techniques and worked examples, with a free user story template.


## User Stories: How to Write Them, With Examples
User stories are short, plain-language descriptions of something a user needs, written from that user's point of view: who they are, what they want and why. Agile teams use them to fill the product backlog and to start conversations about the detail, rather than writing full specifications upfront. This guide covers the template, acceptance criteria, the INVEST checklist, how to split large stories and a complete worked example.
- Published 5 September 2026
- Last updated 15 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- A user story states who needs something, what they need and why: "As a [user], I want [goal] so that [benefit]."
- A story is a placeholder for a conversation. The card, the conversation and the confirmation (acceptance criteria) work together.
- Acceptance criteria make each story testable; the Definition of Done applies to every story.
- Use INVEST to check quality, and split any story too large to finish within a sprint into thin, valuable slices.
- User stories are not required by Scrum, but they are the most popular way to write Product Backlog items.
- The most common mistakes are technical tasks disguised as stories, missing "so that" clauses and vague acceptance criteria.

### What is a user story?
A **user story** is a brief, informal description of a feature or change, told from the perspective of the person who wants it. It names the user, the goal and the benefit, fits on an index card and is detailed through conversation. User stories are the most common way Agile teams express requirements in a product backlog.
User stories began in Extreme Programming (XP) in the late 1990s. The familiar "As a… I want… so that…" wording is usually credited to a team at the UK company Connextra around 2001, and Mike Cohn's book *User Stories Applied* (2004) made the practice widespread. Today they are used well beyond software, by marketing, HR, operations and service design teams.
Note that the [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) Guide does not mention user stories. It talks about **Product Backlog items**, and leaves the format to the team. User stories are simply the most popular way to write those items.
A good story has three qualities:
- **User-centred.** It describes value to a real person, not a technical component.
- **Small.** The team can finish it within one sprint, ideally within a few days.
- **Testable.** Everyone can agree when it is done, thanks to clear acceptance criteria.
Stories usually sit within a larger hierarchy: themes and initiatives at the top, [epics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/) below them, stories below epics, and tasks that the team creates to deliver each story.

### The user story template
The standard format has three parts:
**As a** [type of user], **I want** [some goal] **so that** [some benefit].
| Part | What it captures | Good choice | Weak choice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| As a… | Who needs it: a specific role or persona | "As a returning customer", "As a warehouse picker" | "As a user", "As the system", "As a developer" (unless they really are the user) |
| I want… | What they want to do or achieve, described as a goal | "I want to reorder a previous purchase" | "I want a REST endpoint for orders" (a solution, not a need) |
| So that… | Why it matters: the value or outcome | "so that I can restock my favourite items in under a minute" | "so that I can reorder" (repeats the goal) |
The "so that" clause is the part teams most often drop, and the most valuable. It tells the team what success looks like, lets them suggest simpler solutions and helps the Product Owner judge priority.

#### Alternative formats
- **Job stories:** "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]." Useful when the context matters more than the user's role, for example "When I'm about to miss a delivery, I want to change the delivery slot, so I can still receive my order."
- **Plain sentences:** "Members can join a waiting list for full classes." Perfectly acceptable when the user and value are obvious to everyone.
Tip
The template is a tool, not a rule. If forcing a story into "As a… I want… so that…" makes it harder to understand, write a clear sentence instead and keep the acceptance criteria.
Download our free [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) for Google Sheets, Excel or PDF. It includes columns for the story, acceptance criteria, story points, priority and status, plus an Epics tab.

### The 3 Cs: card, conversation, confirmation
Ron Jeffries, one of the creators of XP, described user stories as having three critical aspects. They explain why a one-line story can be enough.
| C | What it is | In practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Card | The short written story, originally on an index card | One or two sentences in your backlog tool or template; enough to remember the need |
| Conversation | The discussions between the Product Owner, team and users that fill in the detail | Refinement sessions, quick chats, sketches, examples and questions |
| Confirmation | The acceptance criteria and tests that show the story is done | A list of conditions or Given-When-Then scenarios agreed before work starts |
The card is deliberately incomplete. It reminds the team to have the conversation, and the confirmation records what the conversation agreed. Teams that skip the conversation tend to either over-write the card (turning it into a mini specification) or build the wrong thing.

### Acceptance criteria
**Acceptance criteria** are the specific conditions a story must meet to be accepted by the Product Owner. They define the story's boundaries, make it testable and reduce misunderstandings between the people asking for the work and the people doing it.

#### Two common styles
| Style | Example | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Checklist (rule-based) | Booking shows class time and location. Member receives a confirmation email within one minute. Free places count decreases by one. | Simple stories, UI rules, content and non-software work |
| Given-When-Then (scenario-based) | Given a class has free places, when a member taps Book, then a place is reserved and the free places count falls by one. | Behaviour with conditions, edge cases and automated testing |
Given-When-Then comes from behaviour-driven development (BDD). **Given** sets the context, **When** describes the action and **Then** states the expected outcome. Add **And** to chain conditions.

#### How to write good acceptance criteria
1. Write them before the sprint starts, ideally during [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/).
2. Describe outcomes the user can observe, not how the team will build them.
3. Cover the main path first, then important alternative and error paths.
4. Make each one pass or fail, with no room for interpretation: "loads in under two seconds on 4G" rather than "loads quickly".
5. Aim for roughly three to six criteria. Many more usually means the story should be split.
6. Agree them with the Product Owner, developers and testers together.

#### Acceptance criteria vs Definition of Done
|  | Acceptance criteria | Definition of Done |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Applies to | One specific story | Every story and increment |
| Written by | Product Owner with the team | The Scrum Team (or organisation standard) |
| Example | Member sees their position on the waiting list | Code reviewed, tests passing, accessibility checked, deployed to staging |
| Purpose | Confirms the right thing was built | Confirms it was built to the agreed quality |
A story is complete only when it meets both.

### The INVEST checklist
Bill Wake proposed the INVEST acronym in 2003 as a quick check for story quality. Use it during refinement before a story goes into sprint planning.
| Letter | Meaning | Question to ask | If it fails |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | Independent | Can it be delivered without waiting for another story? | Combine tightly coupled stories or reorder them; make remaining dependencies visible |
| N | Negotiable | Is the detail open to discussion rather than fixed? | Remove solution detail; return to the user's goal |
| V | Valuable | Does it deliver value to a user or the business? | Rewrite technical layers as a thin end-to-end slice |
| E | Estimable | Does the team understand it well enough to size it? | Hold a conversation, gather examples or run a spike |
| S | Small | Can it be finished within one sprint? | Split it using the techniques below |
| T | Testable | Are there clear acceptance criteria? | Add measurable criteria or Given-When-Then scenarios |
Not every story will pass every letter perfectly. Independence in particular is a goal rather than an absolute. Treat INVEST as a prompt for discussion, not a gate.

### How to write a user story, step by step
Use this process for each new piece of work. It works whether the Product Owner writes stories alone or the team writes them together in a workshop.
1. **Identify the user.** Use a real role or persona from research, support tickets or interviews. If several users need the same thing in different ways, write separate stories.
2. **Understand their goal and problem.** Ask what they are trying to achieve and what gets in the way today. Note any evidence.
3. **Write the story.** Use the template in one or two sentences. Keep the solution out of it.
4. **State the value.** Write a "so that" that describes an outcome, not a repeat of the goal.
5. **Add acceptance criteria.** Three to six checklist items or Given-When-Then scenarios.
6. **Discuss it with the team.** In refinement, developers and testers ask questions, spot risks and suggest simpler options. Update the story and criteria.
7. **Check INVEST and split if needed.** If it will not fit in a sprint, split it into smaller valuable slices.
8. **Estimate and order it.** The team sizes the story, for example in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/), and the Product Owner orders it in the [product backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) by value, risk and dependencies.
Stories near the top of the backlog should be detailed and ready; stories further down can stay rough until they get closer. Our [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) helps you keep that order visible.

### Worked example: from idea to sprint-ready story
A gym chain is building a mobile booking app. Members complain that popular classes are always full and they miss places freed by cancellations. Here is how a team turns that problem into a sprint-ready story.

#### 1. Persona and epic
**Persona:** Priya, a member who works shifts and books classes on her phone, often at short notice. **Epic:** Waiting lists for full classes. **Goal:** Increase class attendance and reduce empty places after late cancellations.

#### 2. First draft
"As a member, I want a waiting list so that I can get into classes." This is a start, but the value is vague and the scope is open-ended: notifications, priority rules, time limits and admin settings are all hidden inside it.

#### 3. Conversation and improved story
In refinement, the team asks how members will hear about a free place, how long they get to accept it and what happens if they do not. The Product Owner decides to start with the simplest version that delivers value.
**Story:** As a member, I want to join a waiting list when a class is full so that I can get a place if someone cancels.

#### 4. Acceptance criteria
- Given a class is full, when I view it, then I see a "Join waiting list" button instead of "Book".
- Given a class has free places, when I view it, then I do not see the waiting list option.
- Given I join the waiting list, then I see my position (for example "You are 3rd").
- Given I am first on the list, when a place becomes free, then I receive a push notification and email offering the place.
- Given I have been offered a place, when I do not accept within two hours, then the offer passes to the next person.
- Given I am on the waiting list, when I tap Leave, then I am removed and positions behind me move up.

#### 5. INVEST check
| Criterion | Result | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Independent | Pass | Depends only on existing booking and notification features |
| Negotiable | Pass | Notification channel and time limit open to discussion |
| Valuable | Pass | Directly addresses members' main complaint |
| Estimable | Pass | Team has built similar features |
| Small | Fail | First estimate: 13 points, more than half the team's typical sprint capacity |
| Testable | Pass | Six clear criteria |

#### 6. Split
The team splits by workflow step and by rule:
| Story | Acceptance criteria kept | Estimate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| As a member, I want to join a waiting list for a full class so that I can be considered if a place frees up. | Button shown only when full; position displayed; leave the list | 5 |
| As a member on a waiting list, I want to be offered a freed place so that I can attend the class. | Push and email offer to first person; accept to book | 5 |
| As a member, I want an unaccepted offer to pass to the next person after two hours so that places are not wasted. | Two-hour expiry; offer passes on | 3 |
The first two stories go into the next sprint; the third waits for the following one. Each slice is usable and testable on its own, and the team learns from real usage before adding the expiry rule. You can record all three, with their epic, in our free [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/).

### How to split user stories
Large stories are the most common reason sprints fail to finish. Split **vertically**, so that each slice delivers something a user can see and test, rather than horizontally by technical layer (database, API, interface), which delivers nothing usable until every layer is done.
Mike Cohn of Mountain Goat Software summarises five splitting techniques as **SPIDR**: Spike, Paths, Interfaces, Data and Rules. The table adds two other common patterns.
| Technique | How it works | Before | After (first slice) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spike | Split off a time-boxed research task to reduce uncertainty | Pay with a new payment provider | Spike: test the provider's sandbox for two days; then the payment story |
| Paths | Split by alternative routes through the feature | Pay for an order | Pay by card; later stories add PayPal and gift cards |
| Interfaces | Split by device, browser or a simple-then-richer interface | Book a class on any device | Book on the iOS app; Android and web follow |
| Data | Start with a subset of data or data types | Import contacts from any file | Import contacts from CSV; Excel and vCard later |
| Rules | Defer business rules to later stories | Apply discount codes with all restrictions | Apply a single percentage discount code; expiry and limits later |
| Workflow steps | Deliver one step of a process at a time | Manage expense claims | Submit a claim; approval and payment steps follow |
| Happy path first | Deliver the main success path, then errors and edge cases | Reset password | Reset via email link; expired link and lockout handling next |
Tip
After splitting, check each slice still has a user, a goal and a benefit. If a slice delivers no visible value, it is a task, not a story.
When a story is so large that it needs several sprints, treat it as an epic.

### User story examples by team
User stories work for any team that delivers something to a customer, internal or external. These examples show the format across different kinds of work.
| Team | User story | Sample acceptance criterion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Software (SaaS) | As an account admin, I want to invite colleagues by email so that my team can start using the product without contacting support. | Invite email arrives within one minute and the link expires after seven days |
| E-commerce | As a returning customer, I want to reorder a previous order in one tap so that I can restock quickly. | All items available in stock are added to the basket; unavailable items are listed |
| Internal tools | As a finance analyst, I want to export monthly spend by cost centre to Excel so that I can prepare board reports. | Export includes all cost centres and matches the ledger total |
| Marketing | As a prospective customer, I want to compare plans side by side so that I can choose the right one. | Comparison page shows price, limits and key features for every plan |
| HR | As a new starter, I want a checklist of first-week tasks so that I know what to do before my induction. | Checklist is sent three days before the start date and shows completion |
| Events | As a conference attendee, I want to add sessions to a personal agenda so that I do not miss the talks I care about. | Agenda syncs to the attendee's phone calendar |
For more non-software examples, see [Agile marketing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/).

### User stories vs requirements, use cases, epics and tasks
User stories sit alongside other ways of describing work. The differences come down to purpose, level of detail and who they are written for.
| Item | What it is | Detail level | Typical size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| User story | A user need with a benefit, detailed through conversation | Low on the card, high in acceptance criteria | A few days, within one sprint |
| Traditional requirement | A precise statement of what a system must do ("The system shall…") | High, agreed upfront | Varies; often grouped in a specification |
| Use case | A step-by-step description of how an actor interacts with a system, including alternative flows | High; covers main and alternative scenarios | Often equivalent to several stories |
| Epic | A large body of work with a shared goal, broken into stories | Low to medium | Several sprints |
| Task | A technical step the team does to deliver a story | Specific and technical | Hours to a day |
Stories and formal requirements are not mutually exclusive. Many organisations keep a high-level [business requirements document](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/) for scope and compliance, with detail held in stories.

### Who writes user stories and when
Anyone can write a user story: Product Owners, developers, testers, designers, stakeholders or users. The [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) is accountable for the product backlog, so they make sure stories are clear, valuable and in the right order.
Stories move through a typical life cycle:
| Stage | What happens | Who is involved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capture | Idea recorded as a rough story or epic | Anyone; often Product Owner or stakeholders |
| Refinement | Story discussed, clarified, given acceptance criteria, split and estimated | Product Owner and developers |
| Ready | Story meets the team's readiness checks and sits near the top of the backlog | Product Owner |
| Sprint Planning | Story selected for the sprint and broken into tasks | Whole Scrum Team |
| In progress | Team builds and tests, clarifying detail as needed | Developers, with the Product Owner |
| Done and accepted | Meets acceptance criteria and Definition of Done; shown at the Sprint Review | Product Owner and stakeholders |

#### A "ready" checklist
Many teams use a Definition of Ready, a short list of conditions a story should meet before Sprint Planning. It is not part of the Scrum Guide, and should never become a bureaucratic gate, but a light version helps:
- The user, goal and benefit are clear.
- Acceptance criteria are written and agreed.
- The team has estimated it and it fits in a sprint.
- Known dependencies are resolved or visible.
- Designs or examples are attached where needed.
Most teams track this life cycle in a backlog tool such as [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/); many tools can now also draft stories and acceptance criteria with AI, which saves time but never replaces the conversation with the team.

### Estimating and prioritising user stories
Most teams estimate stories with **relative sizing** rather than hours: they compare each story with others they have already done. Common scales are story points on a modified Fibonacci sequence (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13…) and T-shirt sizes (S, M, L, XL). Planning poker is a popular way for the whole team to agree an estimate. Over several sprints, the team's average completed points, its [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/), helps forecast how much fits into future sprints.
To prioritise, Product Owners weigh several factors:
- **Value:** how much the story helps users or the business.
- **Risk and learning:** stories that test a risky assumption early may go first.
- **Dependencies:** some stories unlock others.
- **Cost:** the estimate, compared with the value (a simple value-to-effort ratio).
- **Deadlines:** legal, contractual or market dates.
Techniques such as MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't) help in workshops with stakeholders.

### User story mapping
A flat backlog can hide the big picture. **User story mapping**, popularised by Jeff Patton, arranges stories on a wall or digital board to show the user's journey:
1. Across the top, list the main activities the user performs, in order (for the gym app: find a class, book, attend, review).
2. Under each activity, list the steps and then the stories that support them.
3. Order stories vertically by priority, with the most essential at the top.
4. Draw horizontal lines to mark releases. The top slice across all activities is your first usable release.
Story maps make gaps and dependencies visible and help teams agree a minimum viable release. They work well at the start of a product or a large epic, alongside an [Agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/).

### Common mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Technical tasks disguised as stories ("As a developer, I want a bookings table") | No user value; cannot be demonstrated | Write a thin end-to-end slice; make the table a task |
| No "so that" clause | Hides the real need and makes prioritising harder | Always ask "why?" until you reach an outcome |
| Stories too large to finish in a sprint | Work carries over; velocity becomes unreliable | Split with SPIDR or by workflow step |
| Vague acceptance criteria ("easy to use") | Disagreements at review; rework | Make each criterion measurable or scenario-based |
| Story treated as a contract | Stops conversation and better ideas | Keep the card short; agree detail together |
| Writing the whole backlog in detail upfront | Wasted effort when priorities change | Detail only the stories near the top |
| Forcing every item into the template | Awkward, unclear wording | Use a plain sentence where it is clearer |

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a user story in Agile?**
A short description of a user need, written from the user's point of view, that the team turns into working functionality. It states who needs something, what they need and why.

**Q: What is the user story format?**
As a [type of user], I want [some goal] so that [some benefit]. Teams also use job stories ("When… I want to… so I can…") or plain sentences when they are clearer.

**Q: What are the 3 Cs of user stories?**
Card, Conversation and Confirmation, described by Ron Jeffries: the short written story, the discussion that fills in the detail and the acceptance criteria that confirm it is done.

**Q: Who writes user stories?**
Anyone can, including developers, testers, stakeholders and users. The Product Owner is accountable for the product backlog, so they make sure stories are clear and correctly ordered.

**Q: Are user stories part of Scrum?**
No. The Scrum Guide refers to Product Backlog items and does not prescribe a format. User stories are the most popular way to write them.

**Q: What are acceptance criteria in user stories?**
Specific, testable conditions a story must meet to be accepted, usually written as a checklist or as Given-When-Then scenarios.

**Q: How many acceptance criteria should a user story have?**
There is no fixed rule, but three to six is common. If a story needs many more, it is usually too large and should be split.

**Q: How small should a user story be?**
Small enough to finish within one sprint, and ideally within a few days. Many teams aim for several stories per developer per sprint.

**Q: What does INVEST stand for in user stories?**
Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. Bill Wake proposed it in 2003 as a checklist for good stories.

**Q: What is the difference between a user story and a use case?**
A user story is a short statement of need detailed through conversation; a use case describes the step-by-step interaction between an actor and a system, including alternative flows. One use case often covers several stories.

**Q: What is the difference between a user story and an epic?**
An [epic](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/) is a large body of work that takes several sprints and is broken into stories; a story fits within a single sprint.

**Q: How do you estimate user stories?**
Most teams use relative sizing such as [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/) or T-shirt sizes, agreed together, often through planning poker.

**Q: Can user stories be used outside software?**
Yes. Marketing, HR, events and operations teams write stories such as "As a new starter, I want a first-week checklist so that I know what to do before my induction."

**Q: What is a technical story?**
A backlog item for technical work with no direct user-facing value, such as upgrading a framework. Many teams call these enablers or technical items rather than forcing them into the user story template, and explain the benefit in plain terms.
