# The Scrum Guide: Learn Scrum Step by Step

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: A free, practical Scrum guide: what Scrum is, the 3 accountabilities, 5 events and 3 artifacts, how a Sprint works, and 35 in-depth guides to learn Scrum.


## The Scrum Guide: Learn Scrum Step by Step
This Scrum guide explains how Scrum works in plain English: a small team delivers value in short, fixed-length Sprints, inspecting the result and adapting its plan as it goes. Start with the summary below, follow the reading path for your role, then go deeper with 35 practical guides to the Scrum Team, events, artifacts, estimation and scaling.
- 35 guides
- Last updated 9 October 2026

### Key takeaways
- Scrum is a lightweight framework for complex work, built on empiricism: transparency, inspection and adaptation.
- It has three accountabilities (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers), five events and three artifacts, each with a commitment.
- The official rules are in the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland; the current version dates from November 2020.
- Story points, velocity, user stories and burndown charts are popular complementary practices, not part of the Scrum Guide itself.
- Use the reading paths below to learn Scrum in a sensible order for your role.

### What is Scrum?
**Scrum** is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organisations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems, as the official Scrum Guide puts it. A small, cross-functional Scrum Team works in Sprints of one month or less, produces a usable Increment each Sprint and uses regular events to inspect progress and adapt the plan.
Scrum was created by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, who first presented it publicly in 1995. They published the first Scrum Guide in 2010 and have revised it several times since; the current version is the **2020 Scrum Guide**. That revision made Scrum less software-specific and less prescriptive: it replaced "roles" with accountabilities, merged the Development Team into a single Scrum Team with Developers, and added the Product Goal and the idea of a commitment for each artifact.
In June 2025, Ralph Jocham, John Coleman and Jeff Sutherland published the **Scrum Guide Expansion Pack**, which adds context, theory and examples around the framework. It is a supplement, not a replacement: the 2020 Scrum Guide remains the definition of Scrum.
This hub is our own, independent guide. Where we describe a rule of Scrum, we follow the 2020 Scrum Guide; where we recommend a practice or format, we say it is our advice or common practice.

### Scrum at a glance: the 3-5-3 structure
People often summarise Scrum as **3-5-3**: three accountabilities, five events and three artifacts. The table pulls the essentials from the Scrum Guide into one place. Time-boxes are the maximum for a one-month Sprint and are usually shorter for shorter Sprints.
| Element | What it is | Key rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product Owner | Accountable for maximising the value of the product and for the Product Backlog | One person, not a committee |
| Scrum Master | Accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness and for establishing Scrum | Serves the team, the Product Owner and the organisation |
| Developers | The people who create a usable Increment each Sprint | Own the Sprint Backlog and the plan for the Sprint |
| The Sprint | The container for all other events | Fixed length of one month or less |
| Sprint Planning | Sets why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done and how | Up to 8 hours |
| Daily Scrum | Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt | 15 minutes, every working day |
| Sprint Review | Inspects the outcome with stakeholders and adapts the Product Backlog | Up to 4 hours |
| Sprint Retrospective | Plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness | Up to 3 hours |
| Product Backlog | Ordered list of what is needed to improve the product | Commitment: Product Goal |
| Sprint Backlog | Sprint Goal, selected items and the plan to deliver them | Commitment: Sprint Goal |
| Increment | A usable step toward the Product Goal | Commitment: Definition of Done |
The Scrum Team is typically 10 or fewer people, with no sub-teams or hierarchies. Underneath the structure sit the three pillars of empiricism (**transparency, inspection and adaptation**) and five values (**commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage**).

### How Scrum works: one Sprint step by step
Every Sprint follows the same rhythm. Here is what happens from start to finish.
1. **The Product Owner keeps the Product Backlog ordered** toward a clear Product Goal, and the team refines upcoming items so they are small and clear enough to select.
2. **Sprint Planning** starts the Sprint. The team agrees a Sprint Goal, selects Product Backlog items and plans how to deliver them, creating the Sprint Backlog. See [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/).
3. **The Developers work toward the Sprint Goal**, meeting for the Daily Scrum to inspect progress and adjust the plan.
4. **Work that meets the Definition of Done becomes part of the Increment.** The team can release it to users whenever it is ready, even before the Sprint ends.
5. **The Sprint Review** shows stakeholders what was achieved and gathers feedback, which updates the Product Backlog.
6. **The Sprint Retrospective** closes the Sprint. The team decides on the most helpful improvements to how it works.
7. **The next Sprint starts immediately**, with the improved backlog and ways of working.

### Official Scrum vs common Scrum practices
The Scrum Guide is deliberately short. It defines what Scrum requires and leaves teams to choose their own practices. Many things people associate with Scrum come from those choices, which is why different Scrum teams can look quite different.
| Defined in the Scrum Guide | Common complementary practices |
| --- | --- |
| Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers | Job titles such as "Scrum Master" as a full-time role, Agile coach |
| The Sprint and its four events | The term "Scrum ceremonies", Sprint 0, hardening Sprints |
| Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment | User stories, epics, story mapping |
| Product Goal, Sprint Goal and Definition of Done | Definition of Ready, acceptance criteria templates |
| Refinement as an ongoing activity | A regular backlog refinement meeting |
| Monitoring progress toward goals | Story points, velocity, burndown and burnup charts, planning poker |
| Transparency of the artifacts | Physical or digital Scrum boards and software tools |
Complementary practices are not wrong; many are very useful. The point is to treat them as choices you can change when they stop helping, rather than as rules. Our guide to [Scrum techniques](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-techniques/) covers the most useful ones.

### Scrum compared with Agile, Kanban and Waterfall
| Comparison | The short answer | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum vs Agile | Agile is a set of values and principles; Scrum is one framework for putting them into practice | [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/) |
| Scrum vs Kanban | Scrum works in fixed Sprints with defined accountabilities; Kanban manages continuous flow with WIP limits | [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) |
| Scrum vs Waterfall | Scrum plans and delivers in short cycles; Waterfall plans the whole project up front and delivers in sequence | [Scrum vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/) |
| Scrum vs Lean | Lean focuses on flow and removing waste; Scrum adds a team structure and cadence | [Scrum vs Lean](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-lean/) |
Many teams combine approaches, for example Scrum with Kanban-style WIP limits, or Scrum teams delivering inside a wider predictive programme. The Scrum Guide allows this as long as the Scrum framework itself is kept intact.

### Scrum templates and tools
You can run Scrum with a whiteboard and sticky notes, but templates and software help once the team is distributed or the backlog grows.
- [Sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) to record the Sprint Goal, selected items and capacity.
- [Product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) to order and refine backlog items.
- [User story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) for writing items with acceptance criteria.
- [Sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) to capture improvements and follow them up.
For software, [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is the specialist choice for software teams running Scrum, with backlogs, Sprints and Agile reports. Teams mixing Scrum with Gantt-based planning or work from other departments often prefer an all-in-one platform such as Wrike, which ranks first in our [project management tools ranking](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/).

### Common mistakes when adopting Scrum
- **Renaming old roles and meetings** without changing how decisions are made, for example a project manager assigning tasks under the title of Scrum Master.
- **No clear Sprint Goal**, so the Sprint becomes a list of unrelated tasks and the Daily Scrum turns into a status report.
- **A weak or missing Definition of Done**, which leaves "almost finished" work piling up and makes the Increment unusable.
- **A Product Owner without authority** to order the backlog, or a committee acting as Product Owner.
- **Treating velocity as a target** or comparing it between teams, which encourages inflated estimates.
- **Skipping the Retrospective** when the team is busy, which removes the event that makes every other improvement possible.
Tip
If you change only one thing, make the Sprint Goal real: one clear objective, agreed in Sprint Planning, that the whole team uses to make trade-offs during the Sprint.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the Scrum Guide?**
The Scrum Guide is the official, freely available definition of Scrum, written by Scrum's creators Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. It sets out Scrum theory, values, the Scrum Team, events, artifacts and commitments. This hub is our independent, practical companion to it.

**Q: What is the latest version of the Scrum Guide?**
The current official version is the November 2020 Scrum Guide. The Scrum Guide Expansion Pack, published in June 2025 by Ralph Jocham, John Coleman and Jeff Sutherland, adds context and examples but does not replace it.

**Q: What is the 3-5-3 rule in Scrum?**
It is shorthand for Scrum's structure: three accountabilities (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers), five events (the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective) and three artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment).

**Q: What are the 3 roles in Scrum?**
The 2020 Scrum Guide calls them accountabilities: the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the Developers. Together they form one Scrum Team with no sub-teams or hierarchies. See [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/).

**Q: What are the 5 Scrum events?**
The Sprint, Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. The Sprint contains the other four. See [Scrum ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/).

**Q: What are the 3 Scrum artifacts?**
The Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment. Each has a commitment: the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done. See [Scrum artifacts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-artifacts/).

**Q: What are the pillars and values of Scrum?**
The three pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation. The five values are commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage.

**Q: How long is a Sprint in Scrum?**
One month or less, and the same length each time. Many teams choose one or two weeks. Shorter Sprints mean more frequent feedback and less risk per Sprint.

**Q: How big should a Scrum Team be?**
The Scrum Guide says a Scrum Team is typically 10 or fewer people: small enough to stay nimble, large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint.

**Q: Is Scrum the same as Agile?**
No. Agile is a mindset described by the Agile Manifesto's values and principles. Scrum is one specific framework for working in an Agile way. See [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/).

**Q: Can Scrum be used outside software development?**
Yes. The 2020 Scrum Guide was written to be less software-specific, and teams use Scrum for marketing, product, research, operations and other complex work where requirements change.

**Q: How do I learn Scrum and get certified?**
Read the Scrum Guide and our beginner reading path above, practise on a real team, then consider a certification such as PSM or CSM for Scrum Masters, or PSPO or CSPO for Product Owners. See [Scrum certification and training](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/).

# Advantages of Scrum: Benefits and Limitations

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/advantages-of-scrum/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: The main advantages of the Scrum framework for teams, customers and organisations, the limitations to be aware of, and when Scrum fits best.


## Advantages of Scrum: Benefits and Limitations
Scrum's popularity rests on practical benefits: faster feedback, clearer priorities and more engaged teams. It also has limits, and knowing them helps you decide when to use it.
- Published 6 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum delivers value early and adapts to change.
- It needs an empowered Product Owner and a stable team.
- It suits complex product work more than routine operations.

### Advantages
- **Early, regular value:** a usable Increment every Sprint.
- **Fast feedback:** stakeholders see real progress at every Sprint Review.
- **Clear priorities:** one ordered Product Backlog and one Product Owner.
- **Adaptability:** priorities can change between Sprints without heavy change control.
- **Transparency:** visible backlogs, boards and goals.
- **Continuous improvement:** Retrospectives every Sprint.
- **Team ownership:** self-managing teams decide how to do the work.
- **Predictability over time:** stable teams develop a reliable pace.

### Limitations
- Needs an engaged Product Owner with authority.
- Works best with dedicated, stable, cross-functional teams.
- Can struggle with frequent urgent interruptions; consider [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/).
- Scaling across many teams requires extra coordination; see [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/).
- Easy to adopt the rituals without the values, which produces poor results.

### When Scrum fits best
| Good fit | Poor fit |
| --- | --- |
| New product development | Routine, repetitive operations |
| Changing requirements | Fully specified, fixed-scope contracts |
| Cross-functional team available | Specialists shared across many projects |
| Engaged stakeholders | Stakeholders who won't attend reviews |

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Which advantages of Scrum make teams choose it?**
To get usable results sooner, respond to change, and give teams more ownership of their work.

**Q: What is the biggest risk to the benefits of Scrum?**
Adopting events and roles without the underlying values and empiricism, sometimes called "zombie Scrum".

**Q: What are the main benefits of Scrum?**
Usable results every Sprint, fast stakeholder feedback, clear priorities through one ordered Product Backlog, and built-in continuous improvement. Teams also gain ownership because they decide how to do the work.

**Q: What are the disadvantages of Scrum?**
Scrum needs an engaged Product Owner, a stable cross-functional team and regular stakeholder involvement. It can struggle with frequent urgent interruptions and needs extra coordination when many teams work on one product.

**Q: Is better quality one of the benefits of Scrum?**
It can, because each Increment must meet the Definition of Done and quality must not decrease during a Sprint. The benefit depends on the team keeping a strong Definition of Done rather than cutting corners.

**Q: Do small teams get the benefits of Scrum?**
Yes. Scrum is designed for small teams, typically ten or fewer people. Very small teams sometimes find the events heavy and shorten them in proportion to Sprint length.

**Q: Is lower project risk one of the advantages of Scrum?**
Yes. Scrum reduces the risk of building the wrong thing, because stakeholders inspect working results every Sprint. Short Sprints also limit how much time and money is at risk in any one cycle.

**Q: Why do some teams never see the benefits of Scrum?**
Common causes include a Product Owner without authority, management that undermines self-management, skipped Retrospectives, and Increments that never really meet the Definition of Done. These remove the feedback that makes Scrum work.

**Q: Do the advantages of Scrum apply to fixed-price projects?**
Only partly. Scrum can be used, but fixed scope, time and cost leave little room for adaptation. Contracts that fix time and budget but allow scope to be re-prioritised fit Scrum better.

**Q: When do the disadvantages of Scrum outweigh its benefits?**
When the work is routine and predictable, when requests arrive continuously with constantly changing urgency, or when no one can act as an empowered Product Owner. [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) or a predictive approach may suit better.

**Q: Do the advantages of Scrum make it better than Waterfall?**
Not in every case. Scrum suits complex work with changing requirements; Waterfall suits stable, well-defined work. See [Scrum vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/).

# Backlog Refinement in Scrum: How to Run It, With Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Backlog refinement explained: what the Scrum Guide says, who attends, how long and how often, a step-by-step agenda, splitting techniques and examples.


## Backlog Refinement in Scrum: How to Run It, With Examples
Backlog refinement is the ongoing activity of breaking down Product Backlog items and adding detail, such as a description, order and size, so the top of the backlog is ready for Sprint Planning. In Scrum it is not a formal event, but most teams still give it regular time. This guide explains what the Scrum Guide 2020 says, who takes part, how much time to spend, and how to run refinement step by step, with a timed agenda, splitting techniques, a worked example and the mistakes to avoid.
- Published 20 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not one of the five Scrum events, and the 2020 Scrum Guide sets no time limit for it.
- It breaks large items into smaller, more precise ones and adds a description, order and size, so items can be Done within one Sprint.
- The Product Owner and Developers refine together; the Developers who will do the work size the items.
- Aim to keep roughly one to two Sprints' worth of items ready at the top of the backlog, and leave the rest coarse.
- Good refinement has work before and after the session: prepare items, refine in short focused rounds, then follow up open questions.
- Split items vertically, so every slice is usable on its own, and treat a Definition of Ready as an optional guide, not a gate.

### What is backlog refinement?
**Backlog refinement** (or product backlog refinement) is the ongoing work of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items. The Product Owner and Developers clarify what each item means and why it matters, split anything too large, add acceptance criteria and size the work, so the next Sprints can be planned with confidence.
Refinement turns rough ideas near the top of the [product backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) into work the team understands. Its outputs are usually:
- **Shared understanding** of the problem, the user and the outcome wanted.
- **Smaller items** that can each be Done within one Sprint.
- **Sizes** from the Developers, for example in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/).
- **Acceptance criteria** and notes on dependencies, risks and open questions.
- **An updated order**, because what the team learns often changes what should come first.
| Backlog refinement is | Backlog refinement is not |
| --- | --- |
| Clarifying what an item means and why it matters | Committing to work for the next Sprint |
| Splitting large items into smaller ones that still deliver value | Assigning tasks to individuals |
| Sizing items so they can be ordered and forecast | Detailed technical design of every item |
| Adding acceptance criteria and surfacing risks | A status meeting or progress report |
| Ongoing and collaborative | Something the Product Owner does alone |

### What the Scrum Guide 2020 says about refinement
The Scrum Guide gives refinement only a few sentences. The 2020 edition is still the current official version (checked 25 October 2026). The table summarises what it says and what each point means for your team.
| The Scrum Guide says | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items | Refinement is about precision and size, not about writing long specifications |
| It is an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order and size | It is not one of the five [Scrum events](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/), so it has no official time-box or agenda |
| Attributes often vary with the domain of work | Use the attributes that help your team; user stories and story points are optional |
| The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing | The Product Owner explains and makes trade-offs, but does not set estimates |
| Items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning | This is the only readiness test in Scrum; anything bigger must be split first |
| During the Sprint, the Product Backlog is refined as needed | Refinement happens alongside delivery, inside the Sprint |
| The Scrum Team may refine items during Sprint Planning | Last-minute clarification is allowed, but planning goes faster if most refinement is done earlier |
| The Scrum Master helps find techniques for effective Product Backlog management | The Scrum Master coaches and facilitates; they do not own the backlog |

#### What changed from earlier versions
- **The 10% guideline was removed.** The 2017 Scrum Guide said refinement usually consumed no more than 10% of the Development Team's capacity. The 2020 Guide sets no figure, so the team decides how much time it needs.
- **"Grooming" became "refinement"** in the 2013 Scrum Guide. Backlog grooming and backlog refinement mean the same activity, and refinement is now the standard term.
Tip
The Scrum Guide does not mention a Definition of Ready, refinement meetings, story points or a fixed cadence. These are complementary practices that you can adopt, change or drop.

### Who takes part in backlog refinement?
Refinement works best as a conversation between the people who understand the need and the people who will build the solution. The table shows who usually does what.
| Who | Role in refinement | Attendance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Brings the items, explains the value and context, answers or finds answers to questions, makes trade-offs and updates the order | Normally every session; accountable for the backlog |
| Developers | Ask questions, explore edge cases and risks, suggest simpler options and splits, write or improve acceptance criteria and size the items | Those likely to do the work; many teams invite all Developers |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Coaches the team on techniques, facilitates when needed, keeps the session focused and helps remove obstacles to good refinement | Optional once the team is confident |
| Stakeholders and experts | Users, designers, architects, compliance or support staff who hold knowledge an item needs | Invited for specific items, not every session |
**Who facilitates?** Anyone can. The Product Owner often leads because they bring the items, the Scrum Master often facilitates while the team is learning, and mature teams rotate the role. The facilitator keeps time and makes sure everyone is heard.
**Whole team or a few people?** Involving all Developers builds shared understanding. Larger teams sometimes let two or three Developers refine an item in depth and then walk the others through it. Either works if the whole team agrees with the result before Sprint Planning.

### How long and how often should refinement take?
The 2020 Scrum Guide sets no time limit for refinement. The old 2017 guideline of no more than 10% of capacity is still a useful ceiling for many teams, but treat it as a reference point and inspect and adapt the amount at your [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/).

#### Worked example: how much time is 10%?
Take five Developers in a two-week Sprint of ten working days, each with about six focused hours a day. Their capacity is 5 x 10 x 6 = 300 hours, so 10% is 30 hours. Two one-hour refinement sessions with all five Developers use 10 hours. That leaves around 20 hours for informal refinement work such as spikes, prototypes and conversations with users. In our experience, struggling teams more often spend too little time on refinement than too much.

#### Suggested cadence by Sprint length
This is our own starting suggestion, not a Scrum rule. Adjust it once you see how ready your backlog is at each Sprint Planning.
| Sprint length | Typical refinement pattern | Total per Sprint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 week | One session of 45 to 60 minutes mid-Sprint, plus ad hoc conversations | About 1 hour |
| 2 weeks | Two sessions of about 60 minutes, for example on days 4 and 8 | About 2 hours |
| 3 weeks | Two or three sessions of 60 to 75 minutes | 2 to 3 hours |
| 4 weeks | Weekly sessions of about 60 minutes | 3 to 4 hours |
Short, regular sessions beat one long session the day before [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/): attention drops after an hour, and late questions have no time to be answered.

#### How far ahead to refine
Aim to keep roughly the next one to two Sprints' worth of items refined and sized. Refining much further ahead wastes effort because priorities and understanding change. Refining less makes Sprint Planning slow and uncertain. Items further down the backlog stay as coarse epics until they approach the top.

### How to run backlog refinement, step by step
The session is the visible part of refinement; the preparation before and the follow-up after are what make it work.

#### Before the session
1. **Check the top of the backlog.** The Product Owner reviews the next items against the Product Goal and removes or moves anything no longer relevant.
2. **Pick a short list.** Choose three to six items for a one-hour session, in backlog order, plus one or two spare items in case the team moves quickly.
3. **Add what you already know.** For each item, write the problem, who it is for and why it matters now. Attach designs, data or customer feedback if you have them.
4. **Share the list a day or two ahead** so Developers can arrive with questions, and invite any expert an item needs for that part of the session only.

#### During the session: a 60-minute agenda
| Time | Activity | Led by | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 to 5 min | Context: current Product Goal, what changed since the last session, list of items | Product Owner | Shared focus |
| 5 to 45 min | Work through the items one at a time (about 8 to 10 minutes each): explain the why, ask questions, agree acceptance criteria, split if needed, size | Product Owner and Developers | Refined, sized items or a list of open questions |
| 45 to 52 min | Review the order in the light of what was learned | Product Owner | Updated backlog order |
| 52 to 57 min | Check readiness: which items could be Done within one Sprint? How many Sprints are ready? | Facilitator | Ready backlog depth |
| 57 to 60 min | Confirm follow-ups: who will answer each open question, and by when | Facilitator | Action list |
For each item, a useful rhythm is: the Product Owner explains the need in two minutes; the Developers ask questions; the group writes or adjusts the acceptance criteria; the Developers judge whether it fits in one Sprint and split it if not; then they size it. If an item is still unclear after ten minutes, stop, record the questions and move on.

#### After the session
1. **Update the backlog straight away**: new or split items, acceptance criteria, sizes and the new order.
2. **Chase open questions.** Each question has an owner and a date. Answers go into the item so everyone can see them.
3. **Run spikes where needed.** If uncertainty is too high to size an item, add a short, time-boxed spike to the backlog or the current Sprint.
4. **Inspect the practice.** At the Retrospective, ask whether refinement is giving the team what it needs for Sprint Planning.

### Techniques for refining items
The Scrum Guide leaves technique to the team. These are widely used complementary practices.

#### Splitting large items
Split vertically, so each slice delivers something a user can see or the team can learn from. Splitting horizontally into layers such as database, interface and testing creates items that have no value on their own and cannot be Done in a meaningful sense. Mike Cohn's **SPIDR** approach (Spikes, Paths, Interfaces, Data, Rules) is a popular checklist, and the patterns below cover most situations.
| Pattern | How it splits | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spike | Investigate first, then size the real work | Time-boxed spike: can the courier API handle our volume? |
| Paths or workflow steps | One route or step through the workflow at a time | "Checkout" becomes basket review, delivery details and payment |
| Interfaces | One device, browser or channel first | Mobile web first, the app later |
| Data | One type or subset of data first | Card payments first, then digital wallets |
| Rules | Simplest business rule first, exceptions later | Standard delivery first, express and international delivery later |
| User or role | One group of users first | Customers first, then customer service staff |
| Simple, then better | A basic version first, improvements later | Basic search, then filters, then saved searches |

#### Collaboration techniques
- **Three Amigos.** Business, development and testing perspectives discuss an item together before it is sized. Quick, and useful between full sessions.
- **Example mapping.** Usually credited to Matt Wynne. Write the story, its rules, concrete examples under each rule and open questions on different coloured cards. Many rules or questions suggest the item should be split.
- **User story mapping.** Popularised by Jeff Patton. Arrange user activities left to right and detail top to bottom, then slice across the map to refine a large epic into releasable pieces.

#### Estimating during refinement
Refinement is where most sizing happens. Common techniques include Planning Poker (each Developer reveals an estimate at the same time, then the highest and lowest explain their reasoning), T-shirt sizes for coarse items and affinity estimation for sorting many items quickly. A wide spread of estimates is useful: it usually means people understand the item differently, so talk before re-voting. Our guides to [Agile estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/) and [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) explain how sizes feed forecasts.

#### Writing acceptance criteria
Acceptance criteria describe the conditions a specific item must meet. Many teams use the Given / When / Then format, for example: "Given an order has shipped, when the customer opens their account page, then they see the status Shipped and the date it was sent." Acceptance criteria are different from the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), which is the quality standard that applies to every item in the Increment. Our guide to [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) has more examples.

### When is an item ready? Ready vs Definition of Ready
According to the Scrum Guide, items that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning, and they usually reach that level of transparency through refinement. That is the only readiness rule in Scrum.
Some teams add a **Definition of Ready**: a short checklist an item should meet before it enters Sprint Planning. It is not part of the Scrum Guide. Many teams also use Bill Wake's **INVEST** criteria (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) as a quick check of item quality. A light checklist might be:
- The problem and the user are clear, and the Product Owner can explain why it matters now.
- Acceptance criteria are drafted and understood by the Developers.
- The Developers have sized it and believe it can be Done within one Sprint.
- Known dependencies are visible, and none blocks the start of the work.
- Any design, data or access the team needs is available or planned.
Use it as a guide, not a gate. A long, strict Definition of Ready turns refinement into a hand-off process and delays learning. If an item is nearly ready and important, the Scrum Team can still discuss it in Sprint Planning.

### Worked example: refining "Customers can track their order"
An online shop's Scrum Team usually completes about 25 points a Sprint. Near the top of the backlog is an item from customer service: **"Customers can track their order."** Calls asking "Where is my order?" are the most common reason customers contact the shop.
**Preparation.** Two days before the session the Product Owner adds the context: call volumes from the support team, a screenshot of the current account page and a note that the courier offers a tracking API.
**Discussion.** The Developers ask what customers most need to know, whether all orders use the same courier, how often tracking can be refreshed and what happens when a delivery fails. Their first estimate is about 20 points: too big to fit comfortably in one Sprint alongside other work, and uncertain because nobody knows the API's limits.
**Splitting.** Using the paths and spike patterns, they split the item into four smaller ones:
| Order | New item | Acceptance criteria (summary) | Size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Show order status on the account page | Status shows Placed, Packed, Shipped or Delivered, with the date of each change | 5 |
| 2 | Email the customer when an order ships | Email sent within 10 minutes of dispatch, including the tracking link | 3 |
| 3 | Spike: courier API limits | Answer by the end of the spike: can we request updates every 15 minutes for all open orders? | 2 |
| 4 | Show live courier tracking on the account page | Latest courier event shown; message if tracking is unavailable | 8 |
**Re-ordering.** The total is 18 points, and each item is usable on its own. The Product Owner orders the status page and the shipping email first because together they answer most "Where is my order?" calls. The spike comes next so that live tracking is lower risk by the time it reaches the top. A fifth idea, SMS notifications, is added near the bottom of the backlog as a coarse item.
**Readiness check.** After the session, the ready items at the top of the backlog total 46 points. With an average velocity of about 25, that is just under two Sprints of ready work, which is where the team likes to be. The Product Owner records the open question about failed deliveries against item 4 and asks customer service for the current process before the next session.

### Backlog refinement vs Sprint Planning
Refinement prepares items over time; Sprint Planning turns the best-prepared items into a plan for one Sprint. The better the refinement, the shorter and calmer Sprint Planning becomes.
|  | Backlog refinement | Sprint Planning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Ongoing activity | Scrum event |
| Time-box | None in the Scrum Guide | Up to 8 hours for a one-month Sprint, usually shorter for shorter Sprints |
| When | Throughout the Sprint | At the start of each Sprint |
| Focus | Items for the next one to two Sprints and beyond | The current Sprint: why, what and how |
| Main outputs | Clear, smaller, sized and ordered items | Sprint Goal, selected items and the plan: the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) |
| Commitment | None; it prepares options | The Sprint Goal |
If Sprint Planning keeps running long because the team is discovering what items mean, move that conversation into refinement.

### How to tell whether refinement is working
Refinement is working when Sprint Planning is short and focused and items rarely surprise the team mid-Sprint. These measures are our suggestions, not Scrum rules.
| Measure | How to calculate it | Healthy range (guide only) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ready backlog depth | Points (or items) refined and sized at the top, divided by average velocity (or throughput) | About 1 to 2 Sprints |
| Sprint Planning time | Minutes spent on the "what" part of Sprint Planning | Falling or stable |
| Mid-Sprint surprises | Items whose scope changed significantly after selection | Rare |
| Carry-over | Items selected but not Done at the end of the Sprint | Occasional, not routine |
| Open questions | Questions recorded in refinement and still unanswered at Sprint Planning | Close to zero |
**Worked example.** A team with an average velocity of 30 points has refined items worth 24 points. Its ready depth is 24 / 30 = 0.8 Sprints, so the next Sprint Planning risks stalling. The team adds a second refinement session this Sprint and asks the Product Owner to bring larger items early so they can be split in time. Use these numbers for the team's own improvement, never to compare teams or individuals.

### Remote, asynchronous and multi-team refinement

#### Remote refinement
- Share the item on screen and edit it live, so everyone sees the same acceptance criteria.
- Keep sessions to 45 to 60 minutes and use a digital whiteboard for mapping techniques.
- Use simultaneous estimation, so quieter voices are not anchored by the first number spoken.

#### Asynchronous pre-refinement
Teams spread across time zones often comment on items in the tool before the session: questions, risks and a first-pass estimate. The live session then focuses on items where people disagree. Comments are a good supplement, but they rarely replace the conversation entirely.

#### Refinement with several teams
When several Scrum Teams work on one product, they share one Product Backlog and one Product Owner. Large-scale frameworks add structure: [Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/), for example, describes overall refinement to look across the product and multi-team refinement in which members of several teams refine items together. A simpler approach is to send one or two representatives from each team to a short cross-team session, then refine in detail within each team.

### Common backlog refinement mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Refining only the day before Sprint Planning | No time to answer questions or run spikes | Hold short sessions throughout the Sprint |
| The Product Owner arrives unprepared | Sessions become brainstorming and run long | Pick and annotate items a day or two before |
| The Product Owner or a lead sets the sizes | Estimates lose the Developers' insight and ownership | Developers size; the Product Owner explains trade-offs |
| Splitting by technical layer | No slice is valuable or Done on its own | Split vertically through the workflow |
| Over-specifying items | Detail written early is often wasted and limits better ideas | Capture enough to size and start; talk during the Sprint |
| Ignoring technical work | Technical debt builds up invisibly | Refine and order technical items alongside features |
| Letting discussions run indefinitely | Few items get refined | Time-box each item and move deep questions to a spike |

### Templates and tools for refinement
A shared spreadsheet is enough for one team. Our free [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) has columns for order, item, type, value, estimate, readiness and Sprint, and the [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) adds a consistent format with acceptance criteria. The [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) takes refined items into the Sprint.
For several teams or remote work, a digital tool helps. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) has a backlog view built for Scrum. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool overall, suits teams whose backlog sits alongside portfolio, resourcing and reporting needs.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is backlog refinement in Scrum?**
It is the ongoing activity of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items, adding details such as a description, order and size, so they are ready for Sprint Planning.

**Q: Is backlog refinement a Scrum event?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide describes it as an ongoing activity, not one of the five events. Teams can still schedule regular refinement sessions.

**Q: Is backlog refinement the same as backlog grooming?**
Yes. Grooming is the older term; the Scrum Guide switched to refinement in 2013, and refinement is now the standard name.

**Q: Who attends backlog refinement?**
The Product Owner and the Developers, with the Scrum Master helping where useful. Stakeholders or experts join for items that need their knowledge.

**Q: Who facilitates backlog refinement?**
Anyone the team chooses. The Product Owner often leads because they bring the items, and the Scrum Master often facilitates for new teams. Many mature teams rotate facilitation.

**Q: How long should backlog refinement take?**
The 2020 Scrum Guide sets no limit. The 2017 Guide said it usually took no more than 10% of capacity, which is still a common ceiling. Many two-week teams spend about two hours a Sprint in sessions, plus informal work.

**Q: How often should we refine the backlog?**
Continuously. Most teams hold one or two short sessions per Sprint and handle smaller questions as they arise, rather than one long session before Sprint Planning.

**Q: Who estimates during backlog refinement?**
The Developers who will do the work. The Product Owner explains the items and trade-offs but does not set the estimates.

**Q: What is the difference between backlog refinement and Sprint Planning?**
Refinement prepares items over time and has no time-box. Sprint Planning is a time-boxed event at the start of the Sprint where the Scrum Team sets the Sprint Goal, selects items and plans the work.

**Q: What does ready mean in backlog refinement?**
The Scrum Guide says items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. Some teams add an optional Definition of Ready checklist.

**Q: How far ahead should we refine the backlog?**
Usually enough for the next one or two Sprints. Refining far ahead risks waste because priorities and understanding change.

**Q: Can refinement happen during the Sprint or in Sprint Planning?**
Yes to both. The Scrum Guide says the backlog is refined as needed during the Sprint, and that the Scrum Team may refine items during Sprint Planning.

**Q: What if refinement sessions keep overrunning?**
Prepare items in advance, focus on the top of the backlog, time-box each item to about ten minutes and move deep technical questions to a smaller follow-up or a spike.

# Daily Scrum: Purpose, Format, Rules and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: The Daily Scrum explained: its purpose, 15-minute time-box and who attends, formats compared, how to run one step by step, a worked example and fixes.


## Daily Scrum: Purpose, Format, Rules and Examples
The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of a Scrum Team to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog, held at the same time and place every working day. Many teams call it the daily stand-up. This guide explains what the Scrum Guide 2020 requires, who attends, how to run a Daily Scrum step by step, which formats work best, and how to fix the most common problems, with a worked example from a real-looking Sprint.
- Published 11 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers, held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint.
- Its purpose is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog; its output is an actionable plan for the next day.
- The 2020 Scrum Guide removed the three questions: the Developers choose any structure that keeps the focus on the Sprint Goal.
- The Product Owner and Scrum Master take part as Developers only if they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items.
- Walking the board, closest to Done first, is a simple way to avoid a round of individual status reports.
- Raise impediments in the Daily Scrum, but solve them afterwards with only the people needed.

### What is the Daily Scrum?
The **Daily Scrum** is one of the five [Scrum events](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/). It is a 15-minute event for the Developers, held at the same time and place every working day, to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary. Its output is an actionable plan for the next day of work.
The Daily Scrum takes place inside the Sprint, between [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) at the start and the [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) and [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) at the end. In a two-week Sprint the team holds it roughly eight or nine times. Each one is a small loop of inspection and adaptation: look at where the team is against the Sprint Goal, then decide what to do next.
It is not a status report to a manager, a problem-solving workshop or a backlog refinement session. Those conversations still matter, but they happen elsewhere.

### What the Scrum Guide 2020 says about the Daily Scrum
The 2020 Scrum Guide is still the current official version (checked 25 October 2026). Its Daily Scrum section is short; the table sums up each rule and what it means in practice.
| The Scrum Guide says | What it means for your team |
| --- | --- |
| The purpose is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary | Start from the Sprint Goal, not from individual activity |
| It is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team | 15 minutes at most, whatever the Sprint length; the Developers own it |
| It is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint, to reduce complexity | Nobody has to ask when or where it is |
| If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on Sprint Backlog items, they participate as Developers | Otherwise they are not required to take part |
| The Developers can select whatever structure and techniques they want | The three questions are optional; choose what works |
| It should focus on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produce an actionable plan for the next day | If nobody can say what changes today, the event has not done its job |
| It improves communication, identifies impediments, promotes quick decision-making and removes the need for other meetings | A good Daily Scrum should replace other status meetings, not add to them |
| It is not the only time Developers can adjust their plan | Developers often meet during the day to adapt or re-plan in more detail |

#### What changed from the 2017 Scrum Guide
| Topic | 2017 Scrum Guide | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who it is for | The Development Team | The Developers (there is no separate Development Team) |
| Structure | Three example questions: what I did yesterday, what I will do today, any impediments | No questions; any structure that focuses on the Sprint Goal |
| Scrum Master | Ensures the meeting happens, teaches the 15-minute time-box and keeps others from disrupting it | No specific Daily Scrum duties; the general duty to make sure all events take place, are positive and productive, and stay within the time-box |
| When | Every day of the Sprint | Every working day of the Sprint |
| Focus | Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal | The same, plus self-management and an actionable plan for the next day |
Tip
If your team still uses the three questions, it is not breaking Scrum. They were removed because they became a ritual for many teams, not because they are wrong.

### Purpose and benefits of the Daily Scrum
The Daily Scrum exists because plans made at Sprint Planning go out of date quickly. Work turns out bigger or smaller than expected, someone is ill, a test environment fails. A short daily inspection keeps the gap between the plan and reality small, so the team can adapt while there is still time.
- **Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.** Is the team on course to meet it, and if not, what needs to change?
- **Adapt the Sprint Backlog.** Re-order, add or remove tasks, or swap who pairs with whom. The Sprint Goal stays the same; the plan to reach it can change.
- **Surface impediments early**, while they are still small and cheap to solve.
- **Make quick decisions** without waiting for a weekly meeting.
- **Build self-management.** The Developers plan their own day together, rather than being told what to do.
- **Reduce other meetings.** If the Daily Scrum works, separate status updates are rarely needed.
Because it relies on an up-to-date [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/), the Daily Scrum also supports transparency, one of the three pillars of empiricism in Scrum.

### Who attends the Daily Scrum?
The Daily Scrum is for the Developers. Everyone else is optional, and their role depends on whether they are doing Sprint work.
| Who | Role at the Daily Scrum |
| --- | --- |
| Developers | Required. They run the event, inspect progress and agree the plan for the next day. |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Takes part as a Developer only if working on Sprint Backlog items. Otherwise not required, though many attend with a new team to coach and to make sure the event happens and stays within 15 minutes. |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Takes part as a Developer only if working on Sprint Backlog items. Often useful nearby to answer questions, but should not turn it into a progress report. |
| Managers and stakeholders | Not participants. If the team agrees they can observe, they listen and keep questions for afterwards. |
**Who facilitates?** The Developers. The Scrum Master often facilitates for a new team and then steps back, because the aim is for the Developers to manage their own Daily Scrum. Many teams rotate facilitation daily or weekly. The 2017 Scrum Guide said the Development Team was responsible for conducting the Daily Scrum; the 2020 Guide simply makes it the Developers' event.
A useful test is who people look at while they speak. If they look at the Scrum Master or the Product Owner, the event has drifted into reporting. If they look at the board and each other, it is working. For how the Scrum Master can step back well, see our guide to [servant leadership in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/servant-leadership-in-scrum/).

### Time-box, time and place
The Daily Scrum is time-boxed to **15 minutes**, whether the Sprint is one week or one month. Fifteen minutes is a maximum, not a target: a small team with a clear board may finish in eight.
The Scrum Guide asks for the same time and place every working day, but leaves the choice to the Developers. Things to weigh:
| Choice | Works well when | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Early in the working day | Most people start at similar times; the plan shapes the whole day | Late starters or people with school runs missing it |
| Late morning | Hours vary; people have already looked at overnight results | Half the day has gone before the plan is adapted |
| After lunch or end of day | Teams across time zones need an overlap | Plans are made for tomorrow; urgent issues wait |
| Beside a physical board | Co-located teams | Remote colleagues left out in hybrid teams |
| In a video call with a shared board | Remote or hybrid teams | Cameras, audio and screen sharing slowing the start |
Start on time, even if someone is missing, and finish on time. Some teams use the **"sixteenth minute"**, a phrase used by Mike Cohn and others: once the Daily Scrum ends, the people needed for a specific problem stay behind to solve it while everyone else gets back to work.

### How to run a Daily Scrum, step by step
The Scrum Guide does not prescribe an agenda. The steps below are our recommended starting point; inspect and adapt them at your Retrospective.

#### Before the Daily Scrum
1. **Update the board.** Each Developer moves their items and tasks so the [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) shows the real state of work.
2. **Check the Sprint Goal.** Make sure it is visible at the top of the board or the start of the call.
3. **Note anything blocked**, so it can be raised quickly rather than discovered in the meeting.

#### A 15-minute agenda
| Minutes | What happens | Question to answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 to 1 | Restate the Sprint Goal and the day of the Sprint | Where are we in the Sprint? |
| 1 to 3 | Quick confidence check, for example a show of fingers from 1 to 5 | Do we believe we will meet the Sprint Goal? |
| 3 to 11 | Walk the board from the column nearest Done back to the start | What does each item need to move forward today? |
| 11 to 13 | Impediments and risks | What is blocking us, and who will act on it? |
| 13 to 15 | Agree the plan for today and any follow-up conversations | What will we do differently from yesterday's plan? |

#### After the Daily Scrum
1. **Hold follow-up conversations** with only the people needed: the sixteenth minute.
2. **Update the Sprint Backlog** with any re-planning: new tasks, removed tasks or a changed order.
3. **Act on impediments.** The Scrum Master helps remove those the Developers cannot remove themselves.
4. **Tell the Product Owner** early if the Sprint Goal is at risk, so scope can be negotiated in good time.

### Daily Scrum formats compared
Because the Developers choose their own structure, teams use many formats. These are the most common, with our view of when each works best.
| Format | How it works | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Three questions | Each person says what they did yesterday, what they will do today and any impediments | New teams learning the event | Turns into individual status reports; the Sprint Goal is easily forgotten |
| Walk the board | Go through items from right to left (closest to Done first), asking what each needs to finish | Most teams; focuses on finishing work rather than starting it | Quiet members not speaking if nobody owns their item |
| Sprint Goal first | Start with "Are we on track for the Sprint Goal?" and discuss only what affects it | Mature teams with a clear goal | Needs a real Sprint Goal, not a list of items |
| Blockers first | Discuss blocked and at-risk items before anything else | Teams with many dependencies | Can skip items that are quietly drifting |
| Flow-based | Review work item age and items over the team's usual cycle time, as in the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams | Teams using Kanban practices within Scrum | Needs a board that tracks when work started |
| Traffic lights | Each item is marked green, amber or red, and red items are discussed first | Larger teams or many parallel items | Colours can hide detail; agree what each means |

#### Questions that keep the focus on the Sprint Goal
- What did we learn yesterday that changes our plan?
- Which item is closest to Done, and what does it need to finish today?
- Is anything blocked or waiting? Who can help?
- Is any item older than we expected? What is holding it up?
- Are we still confident we will meet the Sprint Goal? If not, what do we change?
- Who needs to pair or swarm on something today?
[Swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/), where several Developers work together on one item, is often the decision that comes out of a good Daily Scrum. For more on item age, see our guide to the [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/).

### Worked example: day 6 of a two-week Sprint
A team of five Developers is building an online returns service for a retailer. The Sprint Goal is: **"A customer can request a return online and print a prepaid label."** It is day 6 of 10. The board at 9:30 looks like this:
| Item | Status | Age (days in progress) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Return request form | In testing | 4 | Two minor defects found yesterday |
| Generate prepaid label (courier API) | In progress | 4 | Courier test account rejected requests yesterday afternoon |
| Return confirmation email | In progress | 1 | Template drafted |
| Returns list for customer service staff | To do | 0 | Not needed for the Sprint Goal |
| Accessibility fixes on return form | To do | 0 | Needed to meet the Definition of Done |
**Walking the board.** Starting nearest Done, Priya says the form defects are small and she can fix them by midday. Tom explains that the courier API problem is a credentials issue he cannot solve alone. Sam, who planned to start the customer service list, offers to pair with Tom instead.
**Confidence check.** Two people show three fingers, three show four: the team is fairly confident, but the label is the risk. The label is essential to the Sprint Goal; the customer service list is not.
**Adapted plan for today.**
- Priya fixes the two form defects, then starts the accessibility fixes, which are needed for the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
- Tom and Sam pair on the courier API. The Scrum Master contacts the courier's support team about the test credentials straight after the Daily Scrum.
- Ana finishes the confirmation email and reviews Priya's fixes.
- Leo tests the form again after lunch.
- The customer service list stays in To do. If the label work is still blocked tomorrow, the Developers will ask the Product Owner whether to drop it from the Sprint.
**Follow-up.** Tom, Sam and the Scrum Master stay for five minutes to agree what to ask the courier. The whole event took 12 minutes. Nobody gave a list of yesterday's tasks, but everyone left knowing what to do and why.

### Handling impediments raised in the Daily Scrum
An impediment is anything that slows the team down or stops progress that the Developers cannot easily resolve themselves. The Scrum Guide makes the Scrum Master accountable for causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team's progress, but the Developers solve many themselves.
1. **Raise it briefly.** Describe the problem and its effect on the Sprint Goal in one or two sentences.
2. **Decide who acts.** A Developer, a pair, the Scrum Master or the Product Owner takes ownership.
3. **Solve it after the event**, with only the people needed.
4. **Make it visible.** Flag the item on the board, or keep a short impediment list beside it.
5. **Check it the next day.** If it is still open, decide whether to escalate or change the plan.
6. **Look for patterns at the Retrospective.** Repeated impediments usually point to a process or organisational problem.
| Type of impediment | Example | Who usually acts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Technical | A failing build or test environment | Developers, possibly with platform support |
| Knowledge | Nobody understands an old module | Developers pair or ask an expert |
| Requirements | Unclear acceptance criteria | Product Owner |
| External dependency | Waiting for another team or supplier | Scrum Master and Developers together |
| Organisational | Developers pulled onto other work mid-Sprint | Scrum Master with management |

### Daily Scrum vs status meeting vs stand-up
People often use "Daily Scrum" and "daily stand-up" as if they were the same. In practice the stand-up is a general practice used by many Agile and non-Agile teams, while the Daily Scrum is the specific Scrum event with fixed rules.
|  | Daily Scrum | Daily stand-up (general) | Status meeting |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan | Daily coordination; purpose set by the team | Report progress to a manager |
| Owner | Developers | Varies | Manager or project manager |
| Time-box | 15 minutes | Usually about 15 minutes | Often 30 to 60 minutes |
| Focus | The Sprint Goal and the next day | Today's work | What each person has done |
| Standing | Not required | Traditionally yes, to keep it short | No |
| Output | An actionable plan for the next day | Shared awareness | A status update |
Standing up is a habit, not a rule: Scrum Alliance notes the stand-up probably came from Extreme Programming, where standing kept meetings short. Sitting is fine if the time-box holds and it is more inclusive for your team.

### Remote, hybrid and asynchronous Daily Scrums

#### Remote and hybrid
- Share the board on screen and have one person move items as the team talks.
- Join a minute early to sort out audio and screen sharing, so the 15 minutes is used for the plan.
- In hybrid teams, have everyone join from their own laptop so remote colleagues are not left listening to a room.
- Agree on cameras as a team. Cameras help some conversations but are not a Scrum rule, and some people have good reasons to keep them off.
- Use the chat for links and follow-ups, not for side conversations during the event.

#### Across time zones
Choose the time with the best overlap and rotate an inconvenient slot if no time suits everyone. If the overlap is very small, some teams hold the Daily Scrum at the start of one location's day and use a written handover for the rest.

#### Asynchronous check-ins
Some distributed teams replace the live event with written updates in a chat tool. The Scrum Guide describes a 15-minute event, and a thread of updates rarely produces the joint decision-making that adapts the plan. If you use written updates, make them goal-focused ("what changes our plan?") and still meet live on the days when the Sprint Goal is at risk.

### Common Daily Scrum mistakes and how to fix them
| Mistake | Why it hurts | How to fix it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reporting to the Scrum Master or a manager | Developers stop talking to each other and plan nothing | Facilitator stands aside; speak to the board and the team |
| Regularly running past 15 minutes | People dread it and stop paying attention | Move detailed discussions to the sixteenth minute; start on time |
| Nobody mentions the Sprint Goal | The event becomes a list of activities | Open with the Sprint Goal and a confidence check |
| Impediments raised but never resolved | People stop raising them | Give each one an owner and check it the next day |
| Problem-solving in the event | Most people wait while two people debate | Agree who will meet afterwards and move on |
| Refining backlog items | Takes time from today's plan | Note the question and take it to [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) |
| Cancelled when the Scrum Master is away | Shows the team thinks it is someone else's event | Rotate facilitation among Developers |
| Board not updated beforehand | Time is spent finding out the state of work | Update the board before the event starts |
| Skipped because "nothing has changed" | Small problems grow unnoticed | Keep it short instead; a five-minute Daily Scrum is fine |

### Is your Daily Scrum working? A quick health check
Ask the Developers to answer these questions honestly at your next Retrospective. Three or more "no" answers suggest the format needs to change. This checklist is our own suggestion, not part of Scrum.
- Do we finish within 15 minutes on almost every day?
- Does everyone know the Sprint Goal without looking it up?
- Did yesterday's Daily Scrum change what someone did?
- Are impediments raised early and resolved within a day or two?
- Do we talk to each other rather than to the Scrum Master or Product Owner?
- Would the team keep the Daily Scrum if it were optional?
If the answers are mostly "no", try a different format for two Sprints and compare. Changing from three questions to walking the board is often the quickest improvement.

### Templates and tools for the Daily Scrum
The most important tool is a board that shows the real state of the Sprint. A physical wall or our free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) works for a single team. If you want to record follow-ups or decisions, the [meeting notes template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-notes-template/) keeps actions and owners in one place, and the [meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/) helps a new facilitator plan the 15 minutes.
Digital tools help remote and hybrid teams. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) has Scrum boards with Sprint Goals and filters for each Developer. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool overall, works well when the board needs to connect to wider reporting and resource planning.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is the Daily Scrum the same as a stand-up?**
Many teams call it a stand-up. The Daily Scrum is Scrum's specific event: 15 minutes, for the Developers, focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal.

**Q: How long is the Daily Scrum?**
15 minutes at most, regardless of Sprint length. Shorter is fine if the team has agreed its plan for the day.

**Q: Who attends the Daily Scrum?**
The Developers. The Product Owner and Scrum Master take part as Developers only if they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items.

**Q: Does the Scrum Master have to run the Daily Scrum?**
No. It is the Developers' event. The Scrum Master makes sure Scrum events take place and stay within their time-box, and often facilitates for new teams before stepping back.

**Q: Should the Product Owner attend the Daily Scrum?**
Only as a Developer if working on Sprint Backlog items. Many Product Owners stay available afterwards to answer questions without turning the event into a report to them.

**Q: Are the three questions still part of the Daily Scrum?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide removed them. Developers can use any structure that focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces a plan for the next day.

**Q: What time should the Daily Scrum be held?**
At the same time and place every working day, chosen by the Developers. Early in the working day is common, but any consistent time works.

**Q: Can the Daily Scrum be skipped?**
Not in Scrum. If it feels pointless, use the Retrospective to change its format or make it shorter rather than dropping it.

**Q: What if a Developer cannot attend the Daily Scrum?**
The event goes ahead at the usual time. The absent person can share a short note in advance and catch up with a colleague afterwards.

**Q: Can the Daily Scrum be held asynchronously?**
Some distributed teams use written updates, but the Scrum Guide describes a 15-minute event. Asynchronous check-ins risk losing the real-time conversation that adapts the plan.

**Q: What is walking the board in a Daily Scrum?**
A format in which the team reviews items from right to left on the Scrum board, starting with those closest to Done, and asks what each needs to finish.

**Q: What is the output of the Daily Scrum?**
An actionable plan for the next day of work, reflected in an updated Sprint Backlog, plus any impediments with an owner.

**Q: Is the Daily Scrum the only time Developers can adjust the plan?**
No. The Scrum Guide notes that Developers often meet throughout the day for more detailed discussions about adapting or re-planning the rest of the Sprint's work.

**Q: Do we have to stand up?**
No. Standing is a habit that helps keep the meeting short, not a Scrum rule. Sitting or joining remotely is fine if you keep to 15 minutes.
