# Empiricism in Scrum: The 3 Pillars Explained with Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Empiricism in Scrum explained: transparency, inspection and adaptation, what the Scrum Guide says, empirical vs defined processes and worked examples.


## Empiricism in Scrum: The 3 Pillars Explained with Examples
Empiricism in Scrum means making decisions based on what has actually been observed, not on what was predicted, using three pillars: transparency, inspection and adaptation. The 2020 Scrum Guide says Scrum is founded on empiricism and Lean thinking, and every Scrum event exists to inspect and adapt. This guide explains what that means in practice, why complex work needs it, how each pillar works, and how to strengthen empiricism in your own team, with worked examples and a self-assessment.
- Published 5 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed. Scrum is founded on it, together with Lean thinking.
- Its three pillars depend on each other: transparency enables inspection, and inspection enables adaptation. Remove one and the others stop working.
- Empirical process control suits complex work where outcomes cannot be predicted reliably; defined process control suits simple, repeatable work.
- Every Scrum event is a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt, and the Sprint is the container that sets the rhythm.
- The three artifacts and their commitments (Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done) make the work transparent enough to inspect.
- Adaptation is hardest when people are not empowered or self-managing, so empiricism depends on how the organisation treats the team, not just on the events.

### What is empiricism in Scrum?
**Empiricism** in Scrum is the principle that knowledge comes from experience and that decisions should be based on what is observed. Instead of trying to predict everything up front, a Scrum Team makes work visible, inspects real results frequently and adapts its product, plan and process as soon as it learns something new.
Scrum puts this into practice through short, fixed-length Sprints. Each Sprint produces a usable Increment that people can see and use, and each one ends with evidence: what was built, what users and stakeholders think of it, and how well the team worked. That evidence shapes the next Sprint. The Scrum Guide describes this as an iterative, incremental approach used to optimise predictability and to control risk.
A simple analogy is driving at night. You cannot see the whole road, so you do not plan every turn of the steering wheel before you set off. You look at what the headlights show you, check where you are, and correct your course continuously. The destination stays fixed; the route is adjusted to what you see. In Scrum the destination is the Product Goal, the headlights are the events and artifacts, and the corrections are adaptations to the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the way the team works.

### What the Scrum Guide 2020 says about empiricism
The 2020 Scrum Guide, still the current official version (checked 26 October 2026), covers empiricism in its 'Scrum Theory' section. The table sums up each statement and what it means for your team.
| The Scrum Guide says | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Scrum is founded on empiricism and Lean thinking | Two foundations: decide from evidence, and cut waste to focus on the essentials |
| Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed | Trust what has happened more than what was forecast |
| Scrum employs an iterative, incremental approach to optimise predictability and to control risk | Small Increments every Sprint limit how much can go wrong before you find out |
| Four formal events for inspection and adaptation sit within a containing event, the Sprint | Planning, Daily Scrum, Review and Retrospective are the scheduled checkpoints |
| The emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving the work | Transparency is for stakeholders too, not just the team |
| Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful | Inspecting a board that does not reflect reality leads to bad decisions |
| Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless | If nothing changes after an event, the event did not do its job |
| Adaptation becomes more difficult when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing | Teams need authority to change their plan and process |
| A Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection | Do not wait for the next scheduled event if the evidence is clear now |
The Guide also makes a point about forecasting: practices such as burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flow diagrams are useful, but they do not replace the importance of empiricism. In complex environments, only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decisions.

### Why complex work needs empiricism
Some work is predictable. Baking the same cake from the same recipe in the same oven gives the same result every time, so a detailed plan works. Other work, such as building a new product for users whose needs are only partly known, has more unknowns than knowns. Requirements change as people see results, technology behaves unexpectedly and the market moves. A detailed plan made at the start soon goes out of date.

#### Empirical vs defined process control
|  | Defined process control | Empirical process control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suits | Simple, repeatable work with known inputs and outputs | Complex work where inputs, methods and outcomes vary |
| How you control it | Follow a detailed plan and procedure | Inspect results frequently and adjust |
| Where knowledge comes from | Up-front analysis and past repetitions | Experience gained while doing the work |
| Planning horizon | Long and detailed | Short and detailed, long and coarse |
| Response to variance | Treated as an error to be corrected back to plan | Treated as information that may change the plan |
| Examples | Manufacturing a standard part; payroll runs | New product development; research; marketing experiments |

#### Where the idea came from
In his 1995 paper 'SCRUM Development Process', Ken Schwaber drew on industrial process control, which distinguishes processes that are fully defined from those that must be treated as empirical 'black boxes'. He argued that systems development behaves like the second kind and described the Sprint as an empirical process. The idea has stayed at the centre of every edition of the Scrum Guide since 2010.

#### Recognising complex work
Many coaches use Dave Snowden's Cynefin framework to explain when empiricism is needed. In its 'complex' domain, cause and effect can only be understood in hindsight, so the recommended approach is to probe, sense and respond: run small experiments and learn from them. The Scrum Guide does not mention Cynefin, but the logic is the same. If your work is genuinely simple and repeatable, a defined approach may suit it better; see [Scrum vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/).

### The three pillars of empiricism
Scrum implements empiricism through three pillars. They are often listed separately, but each one only works with the others.

#### Transparency
Transparency means the process and the work are visible to everyone who does the work or receives it. In Scrum, important decisions are based on the perceived state of the three artifacts, so the Scrum Guide warns that artifacts with low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.
What needs to be transparent:
- **The Product Backlog and Product Goal**, so stakeholders can see what is planned and why.
- **The Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal**, so the Developers and anyone interested can see the real state of the Sprint.
- **The Increment and the Definition of Done**, so everyone knows what 'Done' means and what was actually delivered.
- **Problems and impediments**, including bad news. Transparency is as much about honesty as about boards and tools.
Signs of low transparency: work that is '90% done' for days, a board updated only before meetings, items marked Done that still need testing, and risks that first appear at the Sprint Review.

#### Inspection
Inspection means the artifacts and progress toward agreed goals are inspected frequently and diligently to detect undesirable variances or problems. Scrum provides a cadence for inspection through its five events, but the team can inspect whenever it needs to.
Inspection is done by the people who do and receive the work: the Developers at the Daily Scrum, the whole Scrum Team and stakeholders at the Sprint Review, and the Scrum Team at the Retrospective. It is not an audit or a reason for managers to check on individuals. Inspecting too often or too intrusively can get in the way of the work, so the events are time-boxed.

#### Adaptation
Adaptation means changing the process or the product when inspection shows something has gone outside acceptable limits. The Scrum Guide says the adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimise further deviation, and that a Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new.
Typical adaptations include re-ordering the Product Backlog, changing the plan in the Sprint Backlog, renegotiating scope with the Product Owner, changing a working practice or strengthening the Definition of Done. Adaptation depends on authority: the Guide notes that it becomes more difficult when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing.
Tip
A quick test after any Scrum event: what is different now because of it? If the honest answer is 'nothing', the team inspected but did not adapt.

### How the pillars depend on each other
The pillars form a chain. If one link is weak, the whole chain fails.
| If this is missing | What happens | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transparency | Inspection is based on a false picture, so it is misleading and wasteful | The Sprint Review shows a feature as finished, but it has not been tested; stakeholders approve the wrong next step |
| Inspection | Problems stay hidden until they are expensive | The team skips Daily Scrums in a busy week and discovers on day 9 that two items are blocked |
| Adaptation | The team learns but nothing improves; inspection becomes pointless | The same impediment is raised in three Retrospectives and nobody acts on it |
This is why Scrum's events, artifacts and accountabilities are designed together. Remove any one of them and you lose part of the feedback loop.

### Lean thinking: the second foundation
The 2020 Scrum Guide added Lean thinking alongside empiricism: an approach that reduces waste and focuses on the essentials. The two support each other. Short Sprints and small items reduce the amount of work at risk, and reducing waste (half-finished work, unused features, waiting and hand-offs) makes the evidence clearer and faster to collect.
In practice, Lean thinking shows up in Scrum as finishing work rather than starting more, keeping the Product Backlog free of items that no longer serve the Product Goal, and building only what is needed to learn the next thing. For a fuller comparison, read our guide to [Scrum vs Lean](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-lean/).

### Empiricism in every Scrum event
The Scrum Guide describes each event as a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt Scrum artifacts. The table shows what each event inspects and adapts.
| Event | What is inspected | What is adapted | How often |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The Sprint | Progress toward the Product Goal, one Sprint at a time | Everything below; the Sprint itself can be cancelled by the Product Owner if its goal becomes obsolete | Continuously; one month or less |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | Product Backlog, latest Increment, capacity and past performance | Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog | Start of each Sprint |
| [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) | Progress toward the Sprint Goal | The Sprint Backlog and the plan for the next day | Every working day |
| [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) | The Increment, progress toward the Product Goal and changes in the environment | The Product Backlog | End of each Sprint |
| [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | Individuals, interactions, processes, tools and the Definition of Done | How the team works; improvements may go into the next Sprint Backlog | End of each Sprint |
[Backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) is not an event, but it is also a form of inspection and adaptation: the team looks at upcoming items, learns more about them and changes them. For the order in which all of this happens, see [the Scrum process step by step](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-process-and-phases/).
Why are the events time-boxed and regular? Because empiricism needs a dependable rhythm. The Scrum Guide says events are used to create regularity and minimise the need for meetings not defined in Scrum. It also notes that when a Sprint's horizon is too long, the Sprint Goal may become invalid, complexity may rise and risk may increase. Shorter Sprints give more learning cycles; our guide to the [Sprint cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-sprint-cycle/) helps you choose a length.

### Artifacts and commitments: the basis for transparency
The Scrum Guide says the artifacts are designed to maximise transparency of key information, so that everyone inspecting them has the same basis for adaptation. Each artifact has a commitment that gives inspection a reference point.
| Artifact | Commitment | What it makes transparent | Inspected at |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) | Product Goal | What the team believes is needed next, in order, and the long-term objective | Sprint Planning, Sprint Review, refinement |
| [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) | Sprint Goal | The single objective of the Sprint and the Developers' current plan | Daily Scrum, throughout the Sprint |
| [Increment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/increment-in-scrum/) | Definition of Done | Exactly what has been finished to the required quality | Sprint Review; whenever it is released |
The **Definition of Done** deserves special mention. Without it, 'Done' means different things to different people, and the Sprint Review inspects an illusion. A strong, shared Definition of Done is one of the most effective ways to improve transparency.

### How the Scrum values make empiricism work
The Scrum Guide links the five values (commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage) directly to empiricism: when they are embodied by the Scrum Team and the people they work with, the pillars of transparency, inspection and adaptation 'come to life', building trust.
- **Openness** makes transparency real: people share bad news, not just good news.
- **Courage** makes adaptation possible: telling a stakeholder that a feature is not ready, or dropping an item that no longer makes sense.
- **Respect** keeps inspection safe: the work is inspected, not the people.
- **Focus** and **commitment** keep inspection pointed at the Sprint Goal and Product Goal rather than at activity.
Our guide to [Scrum principles and values](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-principles-and-values/) covers each value with examples.

### Worked examples of empiricism in Scrum
The examples below are illustrative. Each one shows the three pillars in sequence.

#### Example 1: a product decision at the Sprint Review
| Pillar | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Transparency | The team released a new two-page sign-up flow and added a simple funnel report to the Increment, so everyone could see how many people finished each page |
| Inspection | At the Sprint Review, the report showed that most people who started the sign-up abandoned it on the second page |
| Adaptation | The Product Owner moved 'shorten the second page' to the top of the Product Backlog, above two new features that had been planned for the next Sprint |
The original plan said to build the new features. The evidence said to fix the sign-up first. Empiricism means following the evidence.

#### Example 2: re-planning at the Daily Scrum
| Pillar | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Transparency | On day 6 of a ten-day Sprint, the board showed an integration item still in progress after three days, with a note that the supplier's test system was down |
| Inspection | At the Daily Scrum, the Developers agreed the Sprint Goal was at risk if they waited |
| Adaptation | Two Developers built a temporary stub so testing could continue; the Scrum Master took the supplier issue away to get it resolved; the team agreed with the Product Owner to drop a low-priority item to protect the Sprint Goal |

#### Example 3: a process change at the Retrospective
| Pillar | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Transparency | The team tracked how long items waited for code review; the chart was visible on the board |
| Inspection | At the Retrospective, they saw items waited about two days on average for review, and two items had missed the Sprint because of it |
| Adaptation | They agreed to review before starting new work each morning and added the change to the next Sprint Backlog; at the following Retrospective the waiting time was checked again |
A simple way to keep this loop visible is to record each improvement and its result in a [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/).

#### Example 4: forecasting from actual data
A team was asked when a set of features worth about 120 story points would be ready. Before the first Sprint, a manager had assumed 30 points a Sprint, which suggested four Sprints. After three Sprints, the team had actually completed 18, 22 and 20 points.
| Approach | Assumed rate per Sprint | Forecast for 120 points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original plan | 30 points | 4 Sprints |
| Empirical forecast from the last three Sprints | About 20 points (range 18 to 22) | About 6 Sprints (between 5.5 and 6.7) |
The Product Owner shared the range with stakeholders and re-ordered the backlog so the most valuable features would be in the first release whatever happened. The forecast was updated every Sprint as new data arrived. This is the Scrum Guide's point about forecasting: past performance informs the forecast, but in complex work it is still only a forecast.

### How to strengthen empiricism in your team, step by step
Most teams that struggle with Scrum have the events in their calendar but weak empiricism. The steps below are our recommended way to improve it, one Sprint at a time.
1. **Check the state of transparency.** Walk the [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) with the team. Does it match reality? Is the Definition of Done written down, and does every Done item meet it?
2. **Make the goals visible.** Put the Product Goal and the current Sprint Goal at the top of the board or the start of every event.
3. **Tighten the Definition of Done.** If work regularly needs 'finishing' after a Sprint, add those steps to the Definition of Done.
4. **Shorten feedback loops.** Split items so they finish in a few days, get users or stakeholders to the Sprint Review, and consider shorter Sprints if feedback arrives too late.
5. **End every event with a decision.** Close the Daily Scrum with the plan for the day, the Sprint Review with changes to the Product Backlog and the Retrospective with one or two concrete improvements.
6. **Follow up adaptations.** Track improvements from the Retrospective in the Sprint Backlog and check at the next Retrospective whether they worked.
7. **Remove barriers to adaptation.** Work with managers so the team can change its own plan and practices; the [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) leads this with the wider organisation.

#### Self-assessment: how empirical is your team?
| Question | Healthy answer |
| --- | --- |
| Could a stakeholder understand the state of the Sprint from the board without asking? | Yes, at any time |
| Does every item marked Done meet the Definition of Done? | Yes, without exceptions |
| Did the last Sprint Review change the Product Backlog? | Yes, based on feedback or data |
| Did the team change its plan during the last Sprint because of something it learned? | Yes, when needed, without waiting for permission |
| Can you name a Retrospective improvement that is now normal practice? | Yes, and the team checked whether it helped |
| Do forecasts use the team's actual results? | Yes, and they are updated every Sprint |
If you answer 'no' to two or more, start with transparency: it is the pillar the others depend on.

### Common pitfalls that undermine empiricism
| Pitfall | Pillar weakened | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Updating the board just before meetings | Transparency | Update as work moves; walk the board in the Daily Scrum |
| Calling work Done when testing or review is outstanding | Transparency | Apply the Definition of Done strictly and return unfinished items to the Product Backlog |
| Hiding bad news until the Sprint Review | Transparency | Raise risks as soon as they are known; make it safe to do so |
| Skipping events when the team is busy | Inspection | Keep the events and shorten them; busy times are when feedback matters most |
| Sprint Reviews with no real stakeholders | Inspection | Invite the people who use or pay for the product; show working software, not slides |
| Using inspection to judge individuals | Inspection | Inspect the work and the process; keep the focus on the Sprint Goal |
| Retrospective actions that are never done | Adaptation | Pick one or two improvements and add them to the next Sprint Backlog |
| Plans that cannot change without approval from outside the team | Adaptation | Agree with management what the team can decide for itself |
| Treating the initial release plan as a commitment | Adaptation | Forecast from actual data and update the forecast every Sprint |
Teams that keep Scrum's events but lose its empiricism, and with it the [agile mindset](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-mindset/), are sometimes described as doing 'zombie Scrum' or 'mechanical Scrum': the meetings happen, but nothing changes as a result.

### Empiricism beyond the Scrum Team
Empiricism works best when the wider organisation uses it too. If managers demand fixed scope, dates and budgets agreed a year in advance, the team can inspect all it likes but has little room to adapt.
- **Leaders** can ask for evidence (Increments, user data, actual delivery rates) rather than status reports and percentage-complete estimates.
- **Stakeholders** can attend Sprint Reviews and accept that the Product Backlog will change as a result.
- **Metrics** should measure outcomes and value, not activity. Our guide to [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/) suggests which to use.
- **Funding and governance** can be set per Product Goal or per quarter, with regular reviews, rather than locked to a detailed plan.
Scrum.org's Evidence-Based Management guide applies the same thinking at organisational level, using four key value areas: current value, unrealised value, ability to innovate and time to market. It is a complementary framework, not part of the Scrum Guide.
If you are introducing Scrum in an organisation used to predictive planning, explaining empiricism first often makes the rest of the framework easier to accept.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is empiricism in Scrum?**
The principle that knowledge comes from experience and decisions should be based on what is observed. A Scrum Team makes work transparent, inspects real results frequently and adapts its product, plan and process.

**Q: What are the three pillars of empiricism in Scrum?**
Transparency, inspection and adaptation. Transparency enables inspection, and inspection enables adaptation, so the three only work together.

**Q: Why is Scrum based on empiricism?**
Because Scrum is designed for complex work, where there are more unknowns than knowns and long-range predictions soon become inaccurate. Short cycles of inspecting real results and adapting keep mistakes small and learning fast.

**Q: What is empirical process control?**
A way of controlling work by observing actual results and adjusting, rather than following a detailed plan made in advance. Scrum applies empirical process control through Sprints, events and artifacts.

**Q: What is the difference between empirical and defined process control?**
Defined process control follows a fixed procedure that gives predictable results, which suits simple, repeatable work. Empirical process control relies on frequent inspection and adaptation, which suits complex work where outcomes vary.

**Q: Are the Scrum pillars the same as the Scrum values?**
No. The pillars (transparency, inspection, adaptation) describe how empiricism works. The values (commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage) describe the behaviours that make the pillars work in practice.

**Q: Which Scrum event is not an opportunity for inspection and adaptation?**
None. The Scrum Guide describes every event as a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt, with the Sprint acting as the container for the other four.

**Q: Who inspects in Scrum?**
The people who do and receive the work. The Developers inspect progress at the Daily Scrum, the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the Increment at the Sprint Review, and the Scrum Team inspects its process at the Retrospective.

**Q: What does 'inspection without transparency is misleading' mean?**
If the artifacts do not show the real state of the work, for example items marked Done that are not finished, any inspection is based on a false picture and leads to poor decisions.

**Q: How does the Definition of Done support empiricism?**
It makes the state of the Increment transparent, so everyone knows exactly what Done means. Without it, the Sprint Review inspects work that may not really be finished.

**Q: How does Lean thinking relate to empiricism in the Scrum Guide?**
The 2020 Scrum Guide says Scrum is founded on both. Empiricism bases decisions on observation; Lean thinking reduces waste and focuses on the essentials, which makes feedback faster and clearer.

**Q: Can empiricism work with long Sprints?**
It can, but more slowly. The Scrum Guide warns that when a Sprint's horizon is too long, the Sprint Goal may become invalid, complexity may rise and risk may increase. Shorter Sprints give more learning cycles.

**Q: Is empiricism only for software teams?**
No. Any team doing complex work with uncertain outcomes, such as marketing, research or product design, can use empirical process control. The 2020 Scrum Guide deliberately removed most software-specific language so it applies to any complex work.

# How to Become a Scrum Master: Skills, Steps and Certification

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/how-to-become-a-scrum-master/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: How to become a Scrum Master: the most useful Scrum Master skills, practical experience to gain, certification options, and how to land your first role.


## How to Become a Scrum Master: Skills, Steps and Certification
The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness. It's a role that rewards people skills as much as process knowledge. Here's how to build both and step into the job.
- Published 9 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum Masters need facilitation, coaching and influence.
- Gain hands-on experience before or alongside certification.
- PSM I and CSM are common entry-level certifications.

### What a Scrum Master does
Scrum Masters coach the team, the Product Owner and the organisation in Scrum, remove impediments, and make sure events are productive. See [what a Scrum Master does](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) for full responsibilities.

### The most useful Scrum Master skills
| Skill | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Facilitation | Turns meetings into decisions |
| Coaching | Helps people find their own solutions |
| Active listening | Surfaces hidden problems |
| Conflict resolution | Keeps disagreement productive |
| Teaching | Spreads understanding of Scrum |
| Influence without authority | Changes the system around the team |
| Observation | Spots patterns and impediments |
| Patience | Change takes time |

### Steps to become a Scrum Master
1. **Learn Scrum thoroughly:** read the Scrum Guide several times.
2. **Get hands-on:** join a Scrum Team in any role, or facilitate events for your current team.
3. **Practise facilitation:** run retrospectives and workshops.
4. **Get certified:** PSM I (Scrum.org) or CSM (Scrum Alliance) are common entry points; see [Scrum certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/).
5. **Find a mentor** among experienced Scrum Masters or Agile coaches.
6. **Apply internally first:** many Scrum Masters move into the role within their own organisation.
7. **Keep learning:** coaching, facilitation, Kanban and Lean.

### Interview tips
- Share concrete stories of impediments you removed.
- Explain how you would handle a team that skips retrospectives.
- Show you understand servant leadership; see [servant leadership in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/servant-leadership-in-scrum/).
- Ask about the organisation's support for Scrum.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do you need a technical background to be a Scrum Master?**
No, though understanding the team's work helps. Facilitation and coaching skills matter more.

**Q: Which Scrum Master certification is best?**
PSM I and CSM are the most common. PSM I is an online assessment; CSM requires a live course. Employers in your market may prefer one.

**Q: What does a Scrum Master do day to day?**
Coaches the team in self-management, helps remove impediments, makes sure events happen and are productive, and supports the Product Owner and wider organisation in using Scrum effectively.

**Q: Can I become a Scrum Master with no experience?**
It is possible but difficult. Most people first gain experience on a Scrum Team, facilitating events or leading improvement work, and pair that with a certification such as PSM I or CSM.

**Q: How long does it take to become a Scrum Master?**
You can earn an entry-level certification in a few days of study or a two-day course, but becoming effective in the role usually takes months of hands-on practice.

**Q: Is the Scrum Master a project manager?**
No. A Scrum Master does not assign tasks or own scope and schedule; they are accountable for the team's effectiveness. Some project managers do move into the role and adapt their style.

**Q: Is a Scrum Master certification worth it?**
It is often useful for getting interviews, because many job adverts ask for PSM or CSM. Practical experience and coaching skills matter more once you are in the role.

**Q: What is the difference between the PSM I and CSM Scrum Master certifications?**
PSM I from Scrum.org is an online assessment with optional training. CSM from Scrum Alliance requires attending a course with a certified trainer and then passing a test. See [Scrum certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/).

**Q: Can a Scrum Master work with more than one team?**
Yes. The Scrum Guide does not limit this, and many Scrum Masters support two teams. Supporting too many can leave little time for coaching.

**Q: What career paths follow the Scrum Master role?**
Common next steps include Agile coach, Release Train Engineer in SAFe, delivery manager, Product Owner or a wider leadership role in an [Agile transformation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/).

**Q: What questions are asked in Scrum Master interviews?**
Expect scenarios such as a Daily Scrum running long, a Product Owner who is never available or a team missing its Sprint Goal. Interviewers look for practical examples and a clear grasp of the Scrum Guide.

# What Is an Increment in Scrum? Definition and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/increment-in-scrum/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: What an Increment is in Scrum, how it relates to the Definition of Done, whether you can release several per Sprint, and examples across industries.


## What Is an Increment in Scrum? Definition and Examples
An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment adds to all prior Increments, is thoroughly verified, and must be usable.
- Published 15 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- An Increment is a usable step towards the Product Goal.
- Only work meeting the Definition of Done counts.
- Increments can be released at any time.

### Key rules
- Work becomes part of an Increment only when it meets the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
- Each Increment is additive and works with all previous ones.
- Multiple Increments can be created within a Sprint.
- Increments can be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint.
- The Sprint Review should never be the only gate to releasing value.

### Examples
| Team | Example Increment |
| --- | --- |
| Software | A working checkout flow released to 10% of users |
| Marketing | A tested landing page with analytics live |
| Hardware | A working prototype that passes defined tests |
| Education | A complete course module, reviewed and published |

### Why usable matters
A usable Increment allows real feedback. Partially done work hides risk and delays learning, which undermines empiricism. If work doesn't meet the Definition of Done, it returns to the Product Backlog.

Free product roadmap template with themes, initiatives, quarters, owners and status; also…
Beginner · Advanced · Expert
[Browse all templates](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/)

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Does an Increment have to be released?**
It must be usable, but whether to release it is a business decision.

**Q: Can there be more than one Increment per Sprint?**
Yes. Teams practising continuous delivery may release many Increments in a Sprint.

**Q: What is a product increment?**
In Scrum, an Increment is a concrete, usable step towards the Product Goal. It adds to all previous Increments and is thoroughly verified so they work together.

**Q: When is an Increment created?**
The 2020 Scrum Guide says an Increment is born the moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done.

**Q: What is the commitment for the Increment?**
The Definition of Done, which describes the quality the Increment must meet.

**Q: What happens to work that does not meet the Definition of Done for the Increment?**
It cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review as done. It returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

**Q: Is an Increment the same as a release?**
No. An Increment is usable and could be released; releasing it is a separate business decision. Several Increments can be bundled into one release, or each released immediately.

**Q: What does potentially shippable increment mean?**
A phrase from earlier versions of the Scrum Guide meaning the Increment is in a releasable state. The 2020 Guide uses the word usable instead.

**Q: Does the Increment have to be software?**
No. In non-software work an Increment could be a tested landing page, a published course module or a working prototype that meets agreed quality standards.

**Q: Who creates the Increment?**
The Developers create it. The whole Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.

**Q: How does the Increment relate to the Sprint Review?**
The Sprint Review inspects the Increment with stakeholders and adapts the Product Backlog. See [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/).

# Product Backlog: What It Is and How to Manage It in Scrum

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: The product backlog explained: what it contains, who owns it, how to build, order and refine it step by step, prioritisation techniques and examples.


## Product Backlog: What It Is and How to Manage It in Scrum
The product backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve a product, and the single source of work for the Scrum Team. The Product Owner is accountable for it, and its commitment is the Product Goal. This guide explains what the Scrum Guide says, what goes into a backlog, and how to build, order and refine one step by step, with worked examples, prioritisation techniques and the mistakes to avoid.
- Published 20 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- The product backlog is an emergent, ordered list and the single source of work for the Scrum Team. There is one backlog per product.
- Its commitment is the Product Goal: a future state of the product that the team plans against, one goal at a time.
- The Product Owner is accountable for the content and order; the Developers who will do the work size the items.
- Items near the top are small, clear and ready for Sprint Planning; items lower down stay coarse until they are needed.
- Order by value, risk, dependencies and learning, using techniques such as MoSCoW or WSJF as inputs, not as a replacement for judgement.
- Keep the backlog healthy: refine continuously, delete items that no longer serve the Product Goal and avoid a list that only grows.

### What is a product backlog?
A **product backlog** is an ordered list of everything the Scrum Team currently believes is needed to improve a product: features, fixes, technical work, research and experiments. The 2020 Scrum Guide calls it "an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product" and the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.
The product backlog is one of the three [Scrum artifacts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-artifacts/), alongside the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) and the [Increment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/increment-in-scrum/). Each artifact has a commitment that gives it focus; for the product backlog, that commitment is the Product Goal.
Four characteristics set it apart from an ordinary to-do list:
- **Emergent.** It is never complete. Items are added, changed, split and removed as the team, users and stakeholders learn.
- **Ordered.** Every item has a position relative to every other item, so everyone can see what comes next.
- **The single source of work.** If the Scrum Team is going to work on something, it should be visible in the product backlog, not hidden in emails or side lists.
- **One per product.** Several Scrum Teams working on the same product share one product backlog and one Product Owner.
Tip
The product backlog describes the product, not a project. It lives as long as the product does.

### What the Scrum Guide says about the product backlog
The Scrum Guide is short, and it says less about the product backlog than many people assume. The 2020 edition is still the current official version (checked 25 October 2026). The table summarises its main points and what each one means in practice.
| The Scrum Guide says | What it means for your team |
| --- | --- |
| An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product | Expect constant change, and keep one clear sequence rather than a pile of labels |
| The single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team | Work outside the backlog is invisible; bring it in |
| Its commitment is the Product Goal | Every item should help reach the current Product Goal, or be questioned |
| Refinement breaks items down and adds detail such as a description, order and size | Refinement is an ongoing activity, not a formal Scrum event |
| The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing | The Product Owner can explain trade-offs but should not dictate estimates |
| Items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning | Large items must be split before they are pulled into a Sprint |
| Those wanting to change the backlog do so by trying to convince the Product Owner | Stakeholders influence the order through the Product Owner, not around them |
| Teams on the same product share one Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner | No separate competing backlogs for one product |
Notice what is missing: the Scrum Guide does not require user stories, story points, epics, a Definition of Ready or any prioritisation technique. These are optional complementary practices.

### The Product Goal
The **Product Goal** describes a future state of the product that the Scrum Team plans against. According to the Scrum Guide it is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team, it sits in the product backlog, and the rest of the backlog emerges to define what will fulfil it. The team must fulfil or abandon one Product Goal before taking on the next.
| Artifact | Commitment | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product Backlog | Product Goal | Patients can book, change and pay for appointments online without phoning the clinic |
| Sprint Backlog | Sprint Goal | A patient can book an initial appointment online and receive a confirmation |
| Increment | Definition of Done | Code reviewed, tested on mobile and desktop, accessible and deployed to production |

#### How to write a useful Product Goal
1. Start from the product vision or strategy and the problem you most need to solve next.
2. Describe an outcome for users or the business, not a list of features.
3. Make it reachable within months rather than years, so the team can see progress.
4. Make it testable: you should be able to tell when it has been met.
5. Show it above the backlog and review it at every Sprint Review.
For example, "Improve reporting" is a weak Product Goal; "Finance managers can produce the month-end report without exporting to spreadsheets" is a strong one.

### Who owns the product backlog?
The [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) is accountable for effective product backlog management. Under the 2020 Scrum Guide this includes:
- Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal.
- Creating and clearly communicating product backlog items.
- Ordering product backlog items.
- Ensuring that the product backlog is transparent, visible and understood.
The Product Owner may do this work or delegate it to others, but remains accountable. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee.
| Who | What they do with the product backlog |
| --- | --- |
| Product Owner | Owns the Product Goal, decides the order, makes sure items are understood |
| Developers | Size items, raise technical work and risks, help split and clarify items during refinement |
| Scrum Master | Helps the Product Owner find techniques for Product Goal definition and backlog management |
| Stakeholders and users | Suggest items, give feedback at the Sprint Review, and try to convince the Product Owner when they want the order to change |
In many teams anyone can add an item to the backlog. That is fine, as long as the Product Owner decides where it goes and whether it stays.

### What goes into a product backlog?

#### Types of product backlog items
Product backlog items (PBIs) can describe any work that improves the product. Keeping it all in one list makes honest ordering possible.
| Item type | What it is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feature or user story | New capability or change that users will notice | As a patient, I want to reschedule my appointment online so that I do not have to phone |
| Bug | A defect in something already released | Opening hours show the wrong day on mobile |
| Technical debt | Work that keeps the product maintainable and safe to change | Upgrade the logging framework before support ends |
| Spike or research | Time-boxed investigation to reduce uncertainty | Spike: can the diary system accept bookings via its API? |
| Experiment | A small change to test an assumption with real users | Show prices on the booking page to half of visitors and compare completed bookings |
| Non-functional or compliance work | Quality attributes such as accessibility, security or performance | Fix the issues found in the accessibility audit |
| Epic (coarse item) | A large item that will be split later | Insurance claims handled online |
Many teams write features as [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) and group them under [epics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/). Technical work deserves its own place in the order; our guide to [technical debt in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/) explains why.

#### Product backlog item attributes
The Scrum Guide says attributes vary with the domain of work. Most teams record something like this:
| Attribute | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Description | What is needed and why, often as a user story |
| Order | Its position relative to other items (Product Owner) |
| Size | Relative effort, for example in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/) (Developers) |
| Value | The expected benefit or the outcome it supports |
| Acceptance criteria | Conditions that show the item does what it should |
| Type, links and status | Feature, bug, spike or debt; related epic or designs; progress |

#### How detail changes from top to bottom
A healthy backlog looks like an iceberg: small and detailed at the top, larger and vaguer further down. Detail added months early is often wasted.
| Part of the backlog | Typical horizon | Level of detail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Top | Next one to two Sprints | Small items, sized, with acceptance criteria; can be Done within one Sprint |
| Middle | The following few Sprints | Medium items or small epics, roughly sized, some open questions |
| Bottom | Later | Large epics and ideas, a single line each, not yet sized |

### The DEEP product backlog
A popular checklist for backlog quality is **DEEP**, an acronym usually credited to Roman Pichler and Mike Cohn. It is not part of the Scrum Guide, but it fits it well.
| Letter | Meaning | Quick check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D | Detailed appropriately | Can the team explain the top five items without guessing? |
| E | Estimated | Are the next two Sprints' items sized by the Developers? |
| E | Emergent | Did anything change at the last Sprint Review? |
| P | Prioritised (ordered) | If two items tie, does the Product Owner know which goes first? |
If a check fails, fix it at the next refinement session.

### How to create a product backlog, step by step
Use this process for a new product, or to rebuild a backlog that has become unmanageable.
1. **Agree the Product Goal.** Write one sentence describing the outcome the team will work towards next. Everything else hangs from it.
2. **Collect what you already know.** Gather requests, ideas, known bugs, technical work and stakeholder commitments, without worrying about detail yet.
3. **Remove duplicates and unrelated items,** noting who asked for each one.
4. **Group items into epics or themes** to show the shape of the work and reveal gaps.
5. **Write the top items properly.** For the items most likely to come first, add a clear description, the reason it matters and draft acceptance criteria. A [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) helps keep them consistent.
6. **Ask the Developers to size them.** Use relative estimates such as story points or T-shirt sizes; see [Agile estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/). Split anything too large to finish within one Sprint.
7. **Order the backlog.** Weigh value, risk, dependencies, cost of delay and what you need to learn. Use a technique from the section below if it helps the conversation.
8. **Check readiness and plan the first Sprint.** Make sure roughly one to two Sprints' worth of items at the top are clear and sized, then hold [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/).
After that first pass, the backlog is maintained through ongoing refinement, Sprint Reviews and regular pruning. Our free [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) gives you a ready-made sheet for steps 2 to 8.

### Worked example: building a backlog from scratch
A physiotherapy clinic wants patients to stop phoning reception to book. The Product Owner sets the Product Goal: **"Patients can book, change and pay for appointments online without phoning the clinic."**
**Steps 1 and 2: collect, group and filter.** A workshop with reception staff, physiotherapists and the IT supplier produces 18 raw ideas. The Product Owner groups them into epics (booking, managing bookings, payments, reminders, staff tools) and moves exercise videos and insurance claims to the bottom, because they do not serve the current Product Goal.
**Step 3: write, size and order.** After a refinement session with the Developers, the top of the backlog looks like this:
| Order | Item | Type | Size (points) | Why it is here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Spike: confirm the diary system can accept bookings via its API | Spike | 2 | Online booking depends on it; reduces the biggest risk first |
| 2 | Book an initial appointment online (choose clinician, date and time) | Story | 8 | Core to the Product Goal; nothing else works without it |
| 3 | Fix opening hours shown on the wrong day on mobile | Bug | 1 | Tiny, visible to every patient, and confuses bookings |
| 4 | Email confirmation after booking | Story | 3 | High value, small, reassures patients |
| 5 | Cancel a booking online | Story | 3 | Directly reduces phone calls |
| 6 | Reschedule a booking online | Story | 5 | Directly reduces phone calls |
| 7 | SMS reminder 24 hours before the appointment | Story | 5 | Clinic reports no-shows as a cost |
| 8 | Pay a deposit by card when booking | Story | 8 | Part of the Product Goal; needs a payment provider decision |
| 9 | Fix issues from the accessibility audit | Non-functional | 3 | Clinic has committed to fix these this quarter |
| 10 | Staff view of today's online bookings | Story | 5 | Useful for reception, less urgent while volumes are low |
| Later | Insurance claims online | Epic | Not sized | Next Product Goal, not this one |
| Later | Exercise video library | Epic | Not sized | Possible future goal; may be deleted |
**Step 4: forecast the first Sprint.** The team is new, so it has no velocity yet. In Sprint Planning the Developers look at the top items and judge that items 1 to 4 (14 points) are achievable. The Sprint Goal becomes "A patient can book an initial appointment online and receive a confirmation."
**Step 5: adapt.** Over the next three Sprints the team completes 13, 16 and 14 points, an average of about 14. Items 5 to 10 total 29 points, so the Product Owner forecasts two to three more Sprints for the remaining Product Goal work and updates that forecast after each Sprint Review.

### How to order and prioritise a product backlog
The Scrum Guide uses the word **ordered**, not prioritised. In practice that means every item has a unique position in one sequence. Labels such as high, medium and low still leave you to decide which high item goes first; an ordered list makes that decision explicit.
Order is not only about value. The Product Owner weighs several factors:
| Factor | Question to ask |
| --- | --- |
| Value | How much does this help users or the business reach the Product Goal? |
| Cost of delay | What do we lose for each Sprint we wait? Is there a deadline? |
| Risk | Would doing this early reveal a problem we cannot afford to find late? |
| Dependencies | Does something else need this first? |
| Size | How much effort does it take? Small, valuable items are cheap wins. |
| Learning | Will this give us feedback that changes what we do next? |

#### Prioritisation techniques compared
Techniques give structure to the conversation. None of them replaces the Product Owner's judgement, and none is required by Scrum.
| Technique | How it works | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MoSCoW | Sort items into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time); originated in DSDM | Agreeing scope for a release or Product Goal with stakeholders | Too many Musts; it groups items rather than ordering them |
| Value vs effort | Plot items on a two-by-two grid of value against size | Quick visual sorting in a workshop | Ignores risk and dependencies |
| WSJF (weighted shortest job first) | Cost of delay divided by job size; widely used in SAFe and based on Don Reinertsen's work | Large backlogs where timing matters | Scores can look precise when they are guesses |
| RICE | (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort; popularised by Intercom | Product teams with usage data | Needs reasonable reach estimates |
| Kano model | Classifies features as basic expectations, performance features or delighters | Understanding what users really expect | Needs user research to be reliable |

#### Worked example: scoring and ordering six items
The clinic's Product Owner uses a simple WSJF-style score for six middle-of-the-backlog items. Value, time criticality and risk reduction are each scored from 1 to 10 in a short session with stakeholders; size comes from the Developers. Score = (value + time criticality + risk reduction) / size.
| Item | Value | Time criticality | Risk reduction | Size | Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spike: choose a payment provider | 1 | 3 | 8 | 2 | 6.0 |
| Fix accessibility audit issues | 5 | 8 | 3 | 3 | 5.3 |
| Reschedule a booking online | 8 | 5 | 1 | 5 | 2.8 |
| SMS reminder 24 hours before | 7 | 6 | 1 | 5 | 2.8 |
| Staff view of today's bookings | 6 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 1.8 |
| Pay a deposit by card | 6 | 3 | 2 | 8 | 1.4 |
The scores suggest an order; the Product Owner decides. Here rescheduling goes above reminders because reception gets more calls about changes than about forgotten appointments. Card deposits stay low until the payment spike reports back.

### Refining the product backlog
**Product backlog refinement** is the ongoing activity of breaking down and adding detail to items, such as a description, order and size. It is not one of the five Scrum events; teams fit it in wherever it works, often as one or two short sessions per Sprint plus informal conversations. The 2020 Scrum Guide sets no time limit, so inspect and adapt the amount you spend.
A typical session:
1. The Product Owner brings the next few items and explains the need and the context.
2. The Developers ask questions, raise risks and suggest simpler options.
3. Together they draft or improve acceptance criteria.
4. Items that are too large are split into thin slices that still deliver value.
5. The Developers size the items.
6. The Product Owner adjusts the order if anything new was learned.
**Splitting example.** "Pay a deposit by card when booking" (8 points) is split into "Pay a deposit by debit or credit card" (5), "Receive a deposit receipt by email" (2) and "Refund the deposit when cancelling more than 24 hours ahead" (3). The parts add up to more than the original estimate, which is common: splitting often reveals work nobody had noticed.
For techniques, agendas and timings, see our full guide to [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/).

#### Definition of Ready: optional, not Scrum
Some teams agree a **Definition of Ready**, a checklist an item must meet before it can enter Sprint Planning. The Scrum Guide does not include one; it only says items that can be Done within one Sprint are ready for selection. A light checklist (clear description, drafted acceptance criteria, sized, fits in one Sprint, dependencies visible) can help. Keep it short: a long one becomes a stage gate that delays learning.

### From product backlog to Sprint Planning
Items leave the product backlog when they are selected in Sprint Planning. The Scrum Team agrees a Sprint Goal, and the Developers select the items they forecast they can complete. Those items, the Sprint Goal and the Developers' plan form the Sprint Backlog.
Use recent velocity as a guide to how much to select, adjusted for holidays and other capacity changes. If an item is not Done at the end of the Sprint, it returns to the product backlog for the Product Owner to reorder.
The [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) closes the loop: the team shows what was done, stakeholders give feedback, and the product backlog is adjusted to meet new opportunities. A [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) helps you record capacity, the Sprint Goal and the selected items.

### Product backlog vs sprint backlog
|  | Product backlog | Sprint backlog |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contents | Everything that might improve the product | The Sprint Goal, the selected items and the plan for delivering them |
| Accountable | Product Owner | Developers |
| Commitment | Product Goal | Sprint Goal |
| Time horizon | The life of the product | One Sprint |
| How it changes | Continuously, as the Product Owner reorders, adds and removes items | Updated by the Developers throughout the Sprint as they learn |

### Keeping the product backlog healthy
Backlogs tend to grow faster than teams can deliver. These checks, which are our own suggestions rather than Scrum rules, help you spot problems early.
| Check | Healthy sign | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ready items | About one to two Sprints' worth of refined, sized items at the top | Sprint Planning keeps stalling on unclear items |
| Size of the list | The Product Owner can explain why each item is there | Hundreds of items nobody has read in months |
| Age | Few items older than a year | Many items untouched since they were created |
| Link to the Product Goal | Top items clearly serve the current goal | The top is full of unrelated requests |
| Mix of work | Features, bugs and technical work all appear in the order | Technical debt never rises near the top |

#### How to prune an overgrown backlog
1. Export or list every item with its creation date and last update.
2. Delete duplicates and items that no longer fit the product.
3. Archive items older than an agreed age (for example 12 months) that nobody has championed; good ideas tend to come back.
4. Re-order what remains against the current Product Goal.
5. Tell stakeholders what was removed and how to raise it again if it matters.
Clear ordering against a Product Goal is one of the best defences against [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).

### Common product backlog mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A backlog that only grows | The important items are buried and refinement takes longer each Sprint | Prune regularly and delete items that no longer serve the Product Goal |
| Several backlogs for one product | Teams optimise locally and nobody can order work across the product | One product backlog and one Product Owner, with views or filters per team |
| Everything is high priority | Labels hide the real decisions | Keep one strict order |
| Too much detail too early | Specifications for distant items are rewritten or thrown away | Detail the top; keep the rest coarse |
| The Product Owner works alone | Items are unclear and sizes are guesses | Refine with the Developers and involve stakeholders |
| No Product Goal | The backlog becomes a list of requests rather than a plan for value | Agree and display a Product Goal |
| Technical work kept off the backlog | Debt accumulates invisibly and slows every Sprint | Make technical items visible and order them alongside features |

### Product backlog templates and tools
You do not need special software to start. A spreadsheet or a wall of sticky notes works for a single team. Our free [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) for Google Sheets, Excel and PDF has columns for Order, ID, Item / user story, Type, Value (1-10), Estimate (points), Ready?, Sprint and Status, with dropdowns for item type and readiness.
Move to a tool when several teams share the backlog or stakeholders need a live view. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is the most common choice for software teams and has a dedicated backlog view. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool overall, suits teams that need the backlog to sit alongside wider portfolio, resource and reporting needs.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a product backlog in Scrum?**
It is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product, and the single source of work for the Scrum Team. Its commitment is the Product Goal, and the Product Owner is accountable for it.

**Q: Who owns the product backlog?**
The Product Owner is accountable for it, including the Product Goal, the items and their order. Others can help, but the accountability stays with the Product Owner.

**Q: Who can add items to the product backlog?**
Anyone can suggest items, and in many teams Developers and stakeholders add them directly. The Product Owner decides whether an item stays and where it goes in the order.

**Q: What is the difference between a product backlog and a sprint backlog?**
The product backlog covers everything that might improve the product for its whole life and belongs to the Product Owner. The sprint backlog is the Sprint Goal, the items selected for one Sprint and the Developers' plan, and belongs to the Developers.

**Q: Why does Scrum say ordered rather than prioritised?**
Priority labels such as high, medium and low leave ties. Ordering puts every item in one sequence that can reflect value, risk, dependencies and learning.

**Q: How big should a product backlog be?**
There is no rule. A useful test is whether the Product Owner can explain why each item is there. Keep detailed items to a few Sprints' worth and hold the rest as coarse epics.

**Q: How often should the product backlog be refined?**
Continuously. Most teams hold one or two short refinement sessions per Sprint. The 2020 Scrum Guide sets no time limit; the old guidance of no more than 10% of capacity was removed.

**Q: Do product backlog items have to be user stories?**
No. The Scrum Guide does not prescribe a format. User stories are popular for features, but bugs, technical tasks and spikes are often clearer as plain descriptions.

**Q: Who estimates product backlog items?**
The Developers who will do the work are responsible for sizing. The Product Owner helps them understand items and trade-offs but should not set the estimates.

**Q: When is a product backlog item ready?**
The Scrum Guide says items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. Some teams add a short Definition of Ready, which is optional.

**Q: Can multiple teams share one product backlog?**
Yes. Teams working on the same product share one Product Goal, product backlog and Product Owner.

**Q: Is the product backlog the same as a product roadmap?**
No. A [roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) shows direction and themes over quarters or years. The product backlog lists the specific work needed next, in order, and changes far more often.

**Q: Do bugs and technical debt belong in the product backlog?**
Yes. Putting them in the same list as features lets the Product Owner order all work honestly, and stops important maintenance from being forgotten.
