# Scrum Artifacts: The 3 Artifacts, Commitments and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-artifacts/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum artifacts explained: the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment, their commitments, who owns each, a worked example and common mistakes.


## Scrum Artifacts: The 3 Artifacts, Commitments and Examples
Scrum artifacts are the three things a Scrum Team uses to make work and value visible: the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment. Under the 2020 Scrum Guide each has a commitment (the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done) that gives it focus and a way to measure progress. This guide explains what each artifact is, who owns it and how the three fit together, then follows them through a real-world Sprint with step-by-step setup advice and the mistakes to avoid.
- Published 14 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum has exactly three artifacts: the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment.
- Each artifact has a commitment: the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done. The commitments were added in the 2020 Scrum Guide.
- The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog, the Developers own the Sprint Backlog, and the whole Scrum Team is accountable for a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.
- The purpose of every artifact is transparency: everyone inspecting it should see the same reality, so decisions are based on facts.
- Work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment and returns to the Product Backlog.
- Burndown charts, roadmaps, velocity and Definitions of Ready are useful practices, but they are not Scrum artifacts.

### What are Scrum artifacts?
**Scrum artifacts** are the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment. According to the 2020 Scrum Guide, they represent work or value and are designed to maximise transparency of key information. Each artifact has a **commitment** (the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done) that provides focus and a measure of progress.
The word comes from software development, where an artifact is something produced or used while building a product. Scrum.org describes Scrum's artifacts as the information a Scrum Team and its stakeholders need to understand the product, the work being done and the value delivered.
- The **Product Backlog** shows everything the team currently believes is needed to improve the product.
- The **Sprint Backlog** shows what the Developers plan to do this Sprint, and why.
- The **Increment** is the real, usable product that results.
The artifacts sit alongside Scrum's three accountabilities and five events. If you are new to the framework, start with [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/), then read about the [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) and [Scrum events](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/).

### The three Scrum artifacts and their commitments at a glance
|  | Product Backlog | Sprint Backlog | Increment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product | The Sprint Goal, the items selected for the Sprint and the plan for delivering them | A concrete, usable stepping stone towards the Product Goal |
| Commitment | Product Goal | Sprint Goal | Definition of Done |
| Accountable | Product Owner | Developers | The whole Scrum Team; the Developers create it |
| Time horizon | The life of the product | One Sprint | Permanent: each Increment adds to all prior Increments |
| Changes | Continuously, as the team learns | Throughout the Sprint, as the Developers learn | Grows whenever an item meets the Definition of Done |
| Mainly inspected at | Sprint Planning, Sprint Review, refinement | Daily Scrum | Sprint Review |
Tip
A quick way to remember the pairs: the Product Backlog points to the Product Goal, the Sprint Backlog points to the Sprint Goal, and the Increment must meet the Definition of Done.

### What the Scrum Guide says about artifacts
The Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland is short, so it is worth knowing exactly what it says. The November 2020 edition is still the current official version (checked 26 October 2026).
| The Scrum Guide says | What it means for your team |
| --- | --- |
| Artifacts represent work or value and are designed to maximise transparency | If an artifact is out of date or hidden, it is failing at its main job |
| Each artifact contains a commitment that enhances transparency and focus against which progress can be measured | Every artifact answers "towards what?": the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal or the Definition of Done |
| Decisions are based on the perceived state of the artifacts; low transparency can diminish value and increase risk | Poor artifacts lead to poor decisions, at every level |
| The Product Backlog is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team | Work outside the backlog is invisible and should be brought in |
| The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers | Managers and the Product Owner do not dictate the plan |
| Work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done | "Nearly done" is not done |

#### What changed in the 2020 Scrum Guide
The 2017 Scrum Guide already had the same three artifacts. The 2020 edition added the idea of a commitment for each one, introduced the **Product Goal** as a new concept, and moved the Sprint Goal inside the Sprint Backlog. It also made the Definition of Done the formal commitment for the Increment. Many older articles and exam dumps predate these changes, so check the date of anything you study.
The three artifacts support Scrum's three pillars of [empiricism](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/): transparency makes inspection possible, and inspection makes adaptation possible.

### How the Scrum artifacts fit together
The artifacts are linked through the Scrum events. In one Sprint, the flow looks like this:
1. The Product Owner keeps the **Product Backlog** ordered against the **Product Goal**, with help from the Developers during refinement.
2. In **Sprint Planning**, the Scrum Team agrees a **Sprint Goal**, and the Developers select items from the top of the Product Backlog and plan the work. Together these form the **Sprint Backlog**.
3. Each day, the Developers inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal at the **Daily Scrum** and adapt the Sprint Backlog.
4. Whenever an item meets the **Definition of Done**, it becomes part of the **Increment**. It can be released at any time, even before the Sprint ends.
5. At the **Sprint Review**, the team and stakeholders inspect the Increment and progress towards the Product Goal, and the Product Backlog is adjusted.
6. At the **Sprint Retrospective**, the team looks at how it worked, which can include strengthening the Definition of Done.
7. Items not Done return to the Product Backlog, and the next Sprint begins.
Each artifact feeds the next: no Product Backlog, no Sprint Backlog; no Sprint Backlog, no plan for an Increment; no Increment, nothing real to inspect.

### Product Backlog and the Product Goal
The **Product Backlog** is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product, and the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team. Items at the top are small and clear enough to be Done within one Sprint; items further down stay coarse until they are needed. **Product Backlog refinement** is the ongoing activity of breaking items down and adding detail such as a description, order and size. The Developers who will do the work are responsible for sizing.
The **Product Goal** is its commitment. The Scrum Guide describes it as a future state of the product that serves as a target for the Scrum Team to plan against. The team must fulfil or abandon one Product Goal before taking on the next.
| Weak Product Goal | Stronger Product Goal | Why it is stronger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Improve the website | Members can reserve and renew books online without visiting a branch | Describes an outcome for users that can be tested |
| Build version 2 | Small retailers can set up their online shop in under an hour without help | States who benefits and how you will know |
The [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) is accountable for the Product Backlog, including developing and communicating the Product Goal, creating and ordering items and keeping the backlog transparent. Many teams write items as [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/), but the Scrum Guide does not require any format.
For ordering techniques, a worked example of building a backlog and how to keep it healthy, read our full guide to the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/).

### Sprint Backlog and the Sprint Goal
The **Sprint Backlog** is the Developers' plan for the Sprint. The Scrum Guide describes it as a highly visible, real-time picture of the work the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint to achieve the Sprint Goal. It has three parts:
| Part | Question it answers | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Goal | Why are we doing this Sprint? | Members can renew a loan online and see the new due date |
| Selected Product Backlog items | What will we deliver? | Renew a single loan; show a message when the renewal limit is reached |
| The plan | How will we deliver it? | Tasks such as connect to the library system's renewal API, build the renew button, write automated tests |
The **Sprint Goal** is the single objective for the Sprint. It is created by the whole Scrum Team during Sprint Planning and added to the Sprint Backlog. Although it is a commitment by the Developers, it allows flexibility in the exact work needed to achieve it.
The Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned, and should have enough detail for the Developers to inspect their progress in the Daily Scrum. If the work turns out to be different from what they expected, the Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog without affecting the Sprint Goal.
| Change during the Sprint | Allowed? |
| --- | --- |
| Developers add, split or remove tasks | Yes, at any time; it is their plan |
| Developers and Product Owner swap or drop an item, keeping the Sprint Goal | Yes, by negotiation |
| A stakeholder adds work directly | No; requests go to the Product Owner and the Product Backlog |
| Changes that would endanger the Sprint Goal | No; if the goal becomes obsolete, only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint |

### Increment and the Definition of Done
An **Increment** is a concrete stepping stone towards the Product Goal. According to the Scrum Guide, each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified, so that all Increments work together, and it must be usable in order to provide value.
Four rules from the Scrum Guide are often misunderstood:
- **Several Increments can be created within one Sprint.** The sum of them is presented at the Sprint Review.
- **An Increment can be delivered before the Sprint ends.** The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.
- **Only Done work counts.** The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born.
- **Unfinished work goes back.** An item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review; it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

#### The Definition of Done
The **Definition of Done** is the commitment for the Increment: a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product. It creates transparency by giving everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed.
- If the organisation has a Definition of Done as a standard, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum.
- If not, the Scrum Team must create one appropriate for the product.
- The Developers are required to conform to it.
- Several Scrum Teams working on the same product must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.
A Definition of Done for a web product might read:
- Code peer-reviewed and merged to the main branch.
- Automated tests written and passing; no known critical defects.
- Meets the organisation's accessibility standard.
- Works on current mobile and desktop browsers.
- Help text updated and deployed to production behind a feature switch if needed.

### Artifacts and events: when each is created, inspected and adapted
Every Scrum event inspects or adapts at least one artifact. This table shows the main touchpoints.
| Event | Product Backlog | Sprint Backlog | Increment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | Top items are inspected and selected | Created: Sprint Goal, items and initial plan | Plan for the next Increment is made |
| [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) | Not normally touched | Inspected and adapted by the Developers | Progress towards Done items is checked |
| During the Sprint | Refined; reordered by the Product Owner as needed | Updated as the Developers learn | Grows as items meet the Definition of Done; may be released |
| [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) | Adjusted based on feedback and progress towards the Product Goal | Results inspected against the Sprint Goal | Inspected by the team and stakeholders |
| [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | How the backlog is managed may be improved | How planning works may be improved | The Definition of Done may be strengthened |

### Who owns each Scrum artifact?
Ownership in Scrum means accountability, not exclusive access. Everyone can see every artifact, and several people contribute to each.
| Artifact | Accountable | Contributes | Typical update rhythm |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Product Backlog | Product Owner | Developers size and clarify items; stakeholders suggest items and give feedback; the Scrum Master helps with techniques | Continuously; at least after every Sprint Review |
| Sprint Backlog | Developers | The Product Owner helps clarify items and negotiate scope; the Scrum Master coaches | Daily, or whenever the plan changes |
| Increment | Whole Scrum Team | Developers build it to the Definition of Done; the Product Owner decides with stakeholders when to release, within organisational rules | Every time an item meets the Definition of Done |
For how the three accountabilities divide the rest of the work, see [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/).

### Worked example: the three artifacts through one Sprint
A city library service is building online services for its members. The team has a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and five Developers, and runs two-week Sprints. The library and its people are illustrative.

#### Product Backlog and Product Goal
**Product Goal:** "Members can reserve and renew books online without visiting a branch." Before Sprint 4, the top of the Product Backlog looks like this:
| Order | Item | Size (points) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Renew a single loan online | 5 |
| 2 | Show a clear message when a loan cannot be renewed | 2 |
| 3 | Email confirmation of the new due date | 3 |
| 4 | Fix: due dates shown in the wrong date format | 1 |
| 5 | Renew all loans at once | 5 |
| 6 | Reserve a book that is on loan | 8 |

#### Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal
In Sprint Planning, the Product Owner explains that renewals cause the most phone calls. The Developers' recent average is about 11 points per Sprint, so they select items 1 to 4 (11 points). The Scrum Team agrees the **Sprint Goal**: "Members can renew a loan online and see the new due date." The Developers break the items into tasks:
| Item | Tasks (the plan) |
| --- | --- |
| Renew a single loan online | Connect to the library system's renewal API; build the renew button; update the loans page; automated tests |
| Message when a loan cannot be renewed | List the refusal reasons; write the messages with the content designer; tests |
| Email confirmation | Email template; trigger on renewal; tests |
| Date format fix | Change the date formatting; regression test |

#### During the Sprint
- **Day 3:** the date fix meets the Definition of Done and is released. That is the first Increment of the Sprint.
- **Day 6:** the Developers discover that the library system rejects renewals for books another member has reserved, which needs extra handling. At the Daily Scrum they see that the email confirmation is now at risk. They talk to the Product Owner, who agrees to return the email item to the Product Backlog. The Sprint Goal is unchanged.
- **Day 8:** online renewal and the refusal messages meet the Definition of Done. The Product Owner releases them straight away rather than waiting for the Sprint Review.

#### Sprint Review and the next Sprint
At the Sprint Review, branch staff and a group of members try the Increment. They ask for a way to renew everything at once and point out that the refusal message should say when the book will be free. The Product Owner moves "Renew all loans at once" up, adds a new item for the expected-availability date, and places the email confirmation third. The Sprint Retrospective adds "tested against the library system's test environment" to the Definition of Done, because the reservation problem would have been found earlier.
| Artifact | Start of Sprint 4 | End of Sprint 4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product Backlog | Six top items ordered for the Product Goal | Reordered after feedback; two new items; email confirmation returned |
| Sprint Backlog | Sprint Goal, four items, 12 tasks | Sprint Goal met; three items Done, one returned |
| Increment | Previous Increments: login and loans list | Plus online renewal, refusal messages and the date fix, all released |

### How to set up Scrum artifacts, step by step
Use these steps for a new Scrum Team, or to reset artifacts that have drifted. The order is our recommendation; the rules come from the Scrum Guide.
1. **Write the Product Goal.** The Product Owner drafts one sentence describing the next future state of the product and shares it with the team and stakeholders.
2. **Create the Product Backlog.** Gather known requests, bugs and technical work in one ordered list. Write the top items clearly and keep the rest coarse.
3. **Refine and size the top items.** The Developers ask questions, split large items and size them, until roughly one or two Sprints' worth of work is clear.
4. **Agree the Definition of Done.** Start from any organisational standard, then add what your product needs. Make it visible on the team board.
5. **Plan the first Sprint.** Agree the Sprint Goal, select items and break them into a plan. Record all three parts in one place: the Sprint Backlog.
6. **Make everything visible.** Put the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Definition of Done where the team and stakeholders can see them, on a wall or in a tool.
7. **Update the Sprint Backlog daily.** Use the Daily Scrum to inspect it and adjust the plan.
8. **Inspect the Increment and adapt.** Show only Done work at the Sprint Review, update the Product Backlog with what you learn, and improve the Definition of Done at the Retrospective.
A physical or digital [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) is the simplest way to make the Sprint Backlog visible. Our free [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) and [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) cover steps 2 to 5.

### Keeping Scrum artifacts transparent
Because transparency is the purpose of every artifact, check it regularly. These signs are our own suggestions rather than Scrum rules.
| Artifact | Healthy sign | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product Backlog | Ordered; the Product Owner can explain the top ten items; visible to stakeholders | Hundreds of stale items; everything labelled high priority; side lists in email |
| Product Goal | One clear goal, shown above the backlog and discussed at the Sprint Review | No goal, or several competing goals |
| Sprint Backlog | Shows the Sprint Goal, items and tasks, and reflects today's reality | Not updated for days; work happening that is not on the board |
| Sprint Goal | Developers can state it from memory and use it to make trade-offs | A list of item numbers rather than an objective |
| Increment | Released or releasable; meets the Definition of Done | "Done except testing"; demos of work that is not finished |
| Definition of Done | Written down, visible and strengthened over time | Exists only in people's heads, or is quietly skipped under pressure |

### Official Scrum artifacts vs other useful tools
Some popular articles list five or seven Scrum artifacts. The Scrum Guide defines three. The rest are complementary practices: often valuable, but optional and not part of Scrum itself.
| Item | Scrum artifact? | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment | Yes | The three official artifacts |
| Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done | No: they are commitments attached to the artifacts | Focus and a measure of progress for each artifact |
| Burndown and burnup charts | No | Visualising remaining or completed work over time; see [Scrum metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/) |
| Velocity | No | Forecasting how much work fits in future Sprints; see [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) |
| Product vision | No | Long-term direction, often a source for Product Goals |
| Product roadmap and release plan | No | Communicating direction and timing to stakeholders; see [Agile roadmaps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) |
| Definition of Ready | No | An optional checklist some teams use before Sprint Planning |
| Scrum board | No | A way to display the Sprint Backlog |
| Working agreement | No | How the team agrees to work together |
Tip
If an exam question asks for the Scrum artifacts, the answer is the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment. The Definition of Done is the Increment's commitment, not a fourth artifact.

### Common Scrum artifact mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Several backlogs for one product | Nobody can order work across the product | One Product Backlog per product, with filters or views per team |
| No Product Goal | The backlog becomes a list of requests rather than a plan for value | Agree one Product Goal and review it at every Sprint Review |
| Sprint Goal written as a list of items | Developers lose the flexibility to trade scope and still succeed | Write an objective that explains why the Sprint matters |
| Sprint Backlog owned by a manager | The team stops self-managing and the plan goes stale | The Developers create and update their own plan |
| Calling unfinished work done | Hidden work piles up and forecasts become fiction | Apply the Definition of Done strictly; return unfinished items to the Product Backlog |
| Treating the Sprint Review as a release gate | Value waits needlessly | Release Done Increments when it makes sense |
| Keeping artifacts in private tools or spreadsheets | Stakeholders and other teams cannot inspect them | Make every artifact visible to everyone who needs it |
| Technical work kept off the Product Backlog | Debt grows unseen and slows every Sprint | Order technical items alongside features; see [technical debt in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/) |

### Templates and tools for Scrum artifacts
A wall of sticky notes or a spreadsheet works well for a single co-located team. Our free [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) has columns for order, item, type, value, estimate, readiness, Sprint and status, and the [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) records the Sprint Goal, capacity and the selected items with their tasks.
Once several teams share a backlog or stakeholders need a live view, a tool helps. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is widely used by software teams for backlogs and Sprint boards, and [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool overall, suits organisations that want Scrum artifacts to sit alongside wider portfolio and resource planning.
To go deeper into the first artifact, read our guide to [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the three Scrum artifacts?**
The Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment. The Scrum Guide defines no others.

**Q: What are the commitments in Scrum?**
Each artifact has one: the Product Goal for the Product Backlog, the Sprint Goal for the Sprint Backlog and the Definition of Done for the Increment. They were introduced in the 2020 Scrum Guide to add focus and a way to measure progress.

**Q: Why are they called artifacts?**
The term comes from software development, where an artifact is something produced or used in building a product. In Scrum, the artifacts hold the information the team and stakeholders need to inspect the product and the work.

**Q: Is the Definition of Done a Scrum artifact?**
No. It is the commitment attached to the Increment: the formal description of the quality the Increment must meet.

**Q: Is a burndown chart a Scrum artifact?**
No. Burndown and burnup charts are popular practices for showing progress, but they are not among the Scrum Guide's three artifacts.

**Q: Is a product roadmap or product vision a Scrum artifact?**
No. Many Scrum Teams use them to communicate direction, and a vision often informs the Product Goal, but the Scrum Guide does not define either.

**Q: Who owns the Sprint Backlog?**
The Developers. It is a plan by and for them, and they update it throughout the Sprint.

**Q: Which Scrum artifact does the Product Owner own?**
The Product Backlog. The Product Owner is accountable for its content, order and transparency and for the Product Goal, though others contribute items.

**Q: Which Scrum artifact is the most important?**
They depend on each other, so none works alone. Many practitioners point to the Increment, because it is the only one that delivers value directly to users.

**Q: Can a team create more than one Increment in a Sprint?**
Yes. The Scrum Guide says multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint, and an Increment can be delivered to stakeholders before the Sprint ends.

**Q: What happens to work that does not meet the Definition of Done?**
It is not part of the Increment, cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review, and returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

**Q: Do multiple Scrum Teams share artifacts?**
Teams working on the same product share one Product Backlog, one Product Goal and one Definition of Done. Each team has its own Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal.

**Q: Are there 7 Scrum artifacts?**
No. Lists of five or seven usually add items such as a product vision, burndown chart or Definition of Done. The Scrum Guide defines three artifacts, each with one commitment.

# Scrum@Scale Framework: Roles, Cycles and How to Start

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-at-scale/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum@Scale explained: the two cycles, EAT, MetaScrum and roles, a worked example, steps to implement it and how it compares with SAFe, LeSS and Nexus.


## Scrum@Scale Framework: Roles, Cycles and How to Start
Scrum@Scale is a framework created by Jeff Sutherland, co-creator of Scrum, for scaling Scrum from one team to a whole organisation by linking small teams into networks that work the same way at every level. It adds a Scrum Master cycle for how work gets done, a Product Owner cycle for what gets built, and two leadership forums, the Executive Action Team and the Executive MetaScrum. This guide explains every component, walks through an illustrative example and gives you a step-by-step way to start.
- Published 19 September 2026
- Last updated 3 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum@Scale extends Scrum rather than replacing it. Each team still runs Scrum as the 2020 Scrum Guide describes; Scrum@Scale only adds what is needed to coordinate many teams.
- Its structure is scale-free: teams of about five people, grouped four or five at a time into a Scrum of Scrums, which can be grouped again into a Scrum of Scrum of Scrums.
- Two cycles run in parallel. The Scrum Master cycle covers impediment removal, cross-team coordination and delivery; the Product Owner cycle covers vision, prioritisation, refinement and release planning.
- The Executive Action Team acts as the Scrum Master for the whole organisation, and the Executive MetaScrum acts as its Product Owner, meeting at least once per Sprint.
- Start small: get one team working well, build a reference model of a few teams, then scale out. Scaling poor Scrum only scales the problems.
- Compared with SAFe, Scrum@Scale is lighter and less prescriptive; compared with LeSS and Nexus, it reaches further into executive leadership and organisational change.

### What is Scrum@Scale?
**Scrum@Scale is a framework for scaling Scrum across a team of teams, a department or a whole organisation.** It links small Scrum Teams into networks, coordinates them through a Scrum Master cycle and a Product Owner cycle, and gives leadership two forums to remove impediments and set priorities. It aims to use the least bureaucracy needed to deliver value.
Jeff Sutherland developed Scrum@Scale with Scrum Inc. from fieldwork with organisations of many sizes. Its official definition is The Scrum@Scale Guide, currently version 2.1 (February 2022), which is published free under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence at scrumatscale.com. Like the Scrum Guide, it is short and deliberately incomplete: it tells you which components you need and leaves the detailed practices to you.
The [Scrum Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) describes a single Scrum Team of ten or fewer people. Once a product needs many teams, you need answers Scrum does not give on its own: how teams integrate their work every Sprint, how one set of priorities reaches every team, and who removes impediments above team level. Scrum@Scale answers them with Scrum's own building blocks.
Tip
Scrum@Scale assumes good team-level Scrum. If your teams cannot yet deliver a Done Increment each Sprint, fix that first. Scaling multiplies whatever you already have.

### Scale-free architecture and minimum viable bureaucracy
Two ideas shape everything else in Scrum@Scale.

#### Scale-free architecture
In Scrum@Scale, the same pattern repeats at every level. A small team runs Scrum. A handful of teams form a **Scrum of Scrums (SoS)**, which itself behaves like a Scrum Team, with its own backlog, events and accountabilities. A handful of Scrums of Scrums form a **Scrum of Scrum of Scrums (SoSoS)**, and so on. Because each level works the same way, the organisation can grow without inventing a new type of structure each time, and people moving between levels already understand how things work.

#### Why teams of about five
The guide points to research by J. Richard Hackman suggesting that the average optimal team size is about 4.6 people, and applies the same logic to groups of teams. That is why it recommends four or five teams per Scrum of Scrums. These are guidelines, not rules.

#### Minimum viable bureaucracy
The guide defines minimum viable bureaucracy as the least amount of governing bodies and processes needed to carry out the organisation's functions without slowing the delivery of customer value. In practice it means every meeting, approval and role you add should earn its place. If a steering committee duplicates what the Executive MetaScrum already decides, Scrum@Scale would have you remove the committee rather than keep both.

### Scrum@Scale structure at a glance
The table shows how the levels fit together and who looks after how and what at each level.
| Level | Unit | How (Scrum Master side) | What (Product Owner side) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Team | Scrum Team of about 5 people | Scrum Master | Product Owner |
| Team of teams | Scrum of Scrums (4–5 teams) | Scrum of Scrums Master | Chief Product Owner and a Product Owner Team |
| Larger group | Scrum of Scrum of Scrums (4–5 SoS) | Scrum of Scrum of Scrums Master | Chief Product Owner for the wider group |
| Organisation | Whole agile organisation | Executive Action Team (EAT) | Executive MetaScrum (EMS) |
If you already run a [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/), you have the first building block. Scrum@Scale adds the Product Owner side, the organisation-level forums and the feedback loops that connect them.

### The Scrum Master cycle: how the work gets done
The Scrum Master cycle is about delivery and continuous improvement. It is led by Scrum Masters at team level, the Scrum of Scrums Master at the next level and the Executive Action Team at the top. It has three components.

#### Continuous improvement and impediment removal
Teams surface impediments in their Daily Scrums and Retrospectives. Anything a team cannot fix itself goes up to the Scrum of Scrums, and anything the Scrum of Scrums cannot fix goes to the Executive Action Team. The aim is to remove impediments at the lowest level possible and to spread successful improvements across teams rather than leaving them in one team's notes.

#### Cross-team coordination
Teams working on one product must manage dependencies, share interfaces and avoid blocking each other. The Scrum of Scrums handles this through the Scaled Daily Scrum and through shared practices such as a common [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/). The goal is fewer hand-offs, not more meetings.

#### Delivery
The guide expects the teams in a Scrum of Scrums to produce a fully integrated set of potentially shippable Increments at the end of every Sprint. Delivery is a joint responsibility: one team's Done work is not enough if the integrated product does not work.

### The Product Owner cycle: what gets built and why
The Product Owner cycle sets direction. It is led by Product Owners at team level, a Chief Product Owner and Product Owner Team for each Scrum of Scrums, and the Executive MetaScrum at the top. It has four components.

#### Strategic vision
A clear, shared vision explains why the organisation and its products exist and where they are heading. The guide asks for it to be communicated both internally and externally, and revisited as conditions change. Without it, every team optimises for its own backlog.

#### Backlog prioritisation
Priorities must follow a single path from the executive level down to each team. The Chief Product Owner creates one ordered backlog for the Scrum of Scrums, and team [Product Backlogs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) align with it. A [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) helps you keep the order visible.

#### Backlog decomposition and refinement
Large initiatives are broken into items that individual teams can finish in a Sprint. The Product Owner Team does this together so dependencies are spotted before work starts, using the same habits as team-level [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/).

#### Release planning
Release planning looks further ahead than a single Sprint. It forecasts when valuable groups of features are likely to ship, communicates expectations to stakeholders and shows the likely financial impact. See our guide to [agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) and the [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) for a practical format.

### Where the two cycles meet
The cycles are drawn as two loops that touch at three points. These are where the how and the what must stay in step.
- **Team process.** The first point of contact: each team runs Scrum as the Scrum Guide describes, aiming to maximise the flow of Done work, improve performance over time, work at a sustainable pace and speed up customer feedback.
- **Product and release feedback.** What customers and stakeholders say about released work feeds back into the vision, the backlog and the way teams work.
- **Metrics and transparency.** Everyone can see the same data about progress, value and quality, so decisions are based on evidence rather than status opinions.
The guide suggests a minimum set of four metric categories. The examples in the right-hand column are illustrative; choose measures that fit your product and keep the set small. Our guide to [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/) covers how to calculate the common ones.
| Category | What it tells you | Example measures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Productivity | Is the system delivering more working product? | Change in working product delivered per Sprint; integrated Increments released |
| Value delivery | Is the work worth doing? | Business value per unit of team effort; adoption of new features |
| Quality | Is what we deliver reliable? | Defect rate; service downtime; escaped defects per release |
| Sustainability | Can people keep working this way? | Team happiness or engagement surveys; unplanned overtime |

### Scrum@Scale roles and accountabilities
Scrum@Scale keeps the three Scrum accountabilities at team level and adds a small number of scaled ones. Many organisations fill scaled roles with people who already hold a team-level role, which keeps the structure lean.
| Role or forum | Accountable for | Who usually fills it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum of Scrums Master (SoSM) | Making sure scaled events happen, stay productive and stay within their timeboxes; coordinating delivery with release plans; removing cross-team impediments | One of the teams' Scrum Masters or a dedicated person |
| Chief Product Owner (CPO) | Strategic vision for the group, a single ordered backlog, choice of metrics, assessing feedback and facilitating the MetaScrum | An experienced Product Owner or product leader |
| Product Owner Team | Making sure teams' priorities follow one path; a coordinated roadmap and release plan | The CPO plus each team's Product Owner |
| Executive Action Team (EAT) | The Scrum Master accountabilities for the whole organisation: the agile operating model, funding the Product Owner organisation, measuring Scrum quality, removing organisational impediments | Senior leaders with authority over structure, budget and policy |
| Executive MetaScrum (EMS) | The Product Owner accountabilities for the whole organisation: vision, priorities, budgets and realigning teams | Executives and key stakeholders, facilitated by a Chief Product Owner |
Two points are easy to miss. First, the EAT is not a status committee: it has its own backlog of transformation initiatives and should work it in Sprints. Second, the Executive MetaScrum is where priorities and budgets change. The guide says decisions of that kind should be made in this forum and at no other time during the Sprint, which protects teams from mid-Sprint priority swings.
For the team-level accountabilities, see our guides to [Scrum Team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/), the [Scrum Master role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) and the [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/).

### Scrum@Scale events and forums
Team-level events stay exactly as they are in Scrum. Scrum@Scale adds scaled versions to coordinate across teams. Where the guide does not set a cadence, the table says so: decide it yourself and inspect it in your retrospectives.
| Event or forum | Purpose | Who attends | Timebox or cadence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scaled Daily Scrum | Surface cross-team impediments and dependencies, check progress towards integrated delivery | A representative of each team, facilitated by the SoSM; others as needed | 15 minutes or less, daily |
| Scaled Retrospective | Share experiments and results, spread improvements that worked | The Scrum Masters of each team | Every Sprint |
| MetaScrum / Executive MetaScrum | Align vision and priorities, negotiate trade-offs, change budgets or team alignment | Leaders and stakeholders, each team's Product Owner or a proxy, facilitated by a CPO | At least once per Sprint |
| EAT working sessions | Work the transformation backlog and remove impediments escalated by teams | EAT members, often with the SoSMs | Not fixed by the guide; set your own |
| Scaled refinement and release planning | Decompose large items, spot dependencies, update the release plan | Product Owner Team | Not fixed by the guide; commonly once per Sprint |
Hold the Scaled Daily Scrum shortly after the team Daily Scrums and keep it to cross-team questions: what affects other teams, and what is blocking us that we cannot fix alone. Our guide to the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) covers the team-level version.

### Worked example: scaling from three teams to twelve
The following example is illustrative. The company, numbers and timings are invented to show how the parts fit together.
**Starting point.** A payments company has three Scrum Teams building a merchant app on two-week Sprints. Each team has its own Product Owner and backlog. Releases slip because teams integrate only at the end of each quarter, and the sales director regularly asks individual developers for urgent changes.

#### Months 1–3: build the reference model
- The three teams form a Scrum of Scrums. One Scrum Master becomes the Scrum of Scrums Master alongside her team role.
- The most experienced Product Owner becomes Chief Product Owner. The three Product Owners merge their backlogs into one ordered backlog for the merchant app, with team backlogs drawn from it.
- Teams agree a shared Definition of Done that includes integration testing, so each Sprint ends with one integrated Increment rather than three separate ones.
- A 15-minute Scaled Daily Scrum starts at 9.45, after the team Daily Scrums at 9.15.
- The chief technology officer, head of product, head of sales and HR director form an Executive Action Team with a short backlog: approve continuous integration tooling, move a shared database specialist into a team, and agree how urgent sales requests reach the Chief Product Owner instead of developers.

#### Months 4–6: add the executive forums
- An Executive MetaScrum meets on the first Monday of each Sprint for 60 minutes. Sales requests are now negotiated there and ordered in the single backlog.
- The team measures four things: integrated features released per Sprint, merchant adoption of new features, escaped defects and a monthly team happiness score.
- Integration now happens every Sprint. The first quarterly release under the new model ships on the planned date.

#### Months 7–12: scale out
- Demand grows, and the company adds a consumer app. It forms nine more teams over six months, two at a time, rather than all at once.
- The 12 teams become three Scrums of Scrums of four teams each: merchant, consumer and platform. Each has its own SoSM and Chief Product Owner.
- A Scrum of Scrum of Scrums coordinates the three groups. Its Scaled Daily Scrum has three representatives, one from each SoS.
- The Executive MetaScrum now includes the three Chief Product Owners, who bring a single ordered list of cross-product priorities for leaders to agree.
| Measure | Month 1 | Month 12 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Teams | 3 | 12 |
| Integration frequency | Quarterly | Every Sprint |
| Places where priorities change | Ad hoc, anywhere | Executive MetaScrum only |
| Escalation path for impediments | Unclear | Team → SoS → SoSoS → EAT |
Notice what did not change: each team still runs all five Scrum events. Scrum@Scale only added the coordination each new level needed.

### How to implement Scrum@Scale step by step
The guide recommends incremental, prioritised change rather than a big-bang launch. A practical sequence looks like this.
1. **Check team-level Scrum.** Each team should be able to deliver a Done Increment every Sprint and run all five events well. Use the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) to fix gaps before adding scale.
2. **Form the Executive Action Team.** Choose leaders who can change structure, budget and policy. Give the EAT a transformation backlog, a Product Owner and a Scrum Master of its own, and ask it to work in Sprints.
3. **Pick a reference model.** Choose one product area with four or five teams that need to work together. This becomes your prototype for the rest of the organisation.
4. **Set up the Product Owner side.** Appoint a Chief Product Owner, form a Product Owner Team and create one ordered backlog for the group. Agree a shared vision statement.
5. **Set up the Scrum Master side.** Appoint a Scrum of Scrums Master, start the Scaled Daily Scrum and Scaled Retrospective, and agree a shared Definition of Done that includes integration.
6. **Start the Executive MetaScrum.** Hold it at least once per Sprint. Make it the only place where priorities, budgets and team alignment change mid-stream.
7. **Agree a small set of metrics.** Pick one or two measures for productivity, value delivery, quality and sustainability, and make them visible to everyone.
8. **Inspect the reference model for several Sprints.** Use the EAT and Scaled Retrospective to fix what does not work before you copy it.
9. **Scale out in small steps.** Add new Scrums of Scrums one at a time, using the reference model as the pattern. When you have four or five SoS, add a Scrum of Scrum of Scrums.
10. **Keep removing bureaucracy.** Review existing committees, reports and approvals against the new forums and retire anything that duplicates them.
For the wider organisational change, see our guide to [agile transformation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/).

### Scrum@Scale vs SAFe, LeSS and Nexus
Scrum@Scale is one of several scaling frameworks. None is best for every organisation; the table summarises the main differences so you can choose based on your situation.
|  | Scrum@Scale | SAFe | LeSS | Nexus |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Created by | Jeff Sutherland and Scrum Inc. | Scaled Agile, Inc. | Craig Larman and Bas Vodde | Ken Schwaber and Scrum.org |
| Philosophy | Scale-free networks of Scrum teams, minimum viable bureaucracy | Comprehensive enterprise framework with defined roles, events and portfolio levels | Scrum applied to many teams with as little added as possible | Lightweight exoskeleton for several teams on one product |
| Typical size | Any; repeats in groups of 4–5 | Teams of teams (Agile Release Trains) up to large portfolios | Up to about eight teams; LeSS Huge beyond | About 3–9 Scrum Teams |
| Product ownership | Chief Product Owner, Product Owner Team, Executive MetaScrum | Product Management, Product Owners and portfolio roles | One Product Owner and one Product Backlog | One Product Owner and one Product Backlog |
| Leadership involvement | Explicit: EAT and Executive MetaScrum | Explicit: portfolio and lean governance | Organisational redesign expected, few new roles | Mainly product level |
| Best for | Organisations wanting Scrum at every level, including leadership | Large enterprises that want a detailed, documented structure | Product groups willing to simplify their organisation | A single product with a handful of teams |
In short, choose SAFe if you need a detailed blueprint and portfolio governance, LeSS or Nexus if you have one product and want to stay as close to plain Scrum as possible, and Scrum@Scale if you want a light, modular approach that extends to leadership. Read our guides to [SAFe](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) and [Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/) to compare in more depth.

### Common Scrum@Scale mistakes
- **Scaling before teams are ready.** If teams cannot reliably meet their Sprint Goals, adding scaled events increases overhead without improving delivery.
- **Treating the EAT as a steering committee.** An EAT that only receives reports and does not work a backlog of impediments will not change much.
- **Several backlogs with no single order.** If each Product Owner prioritises independently, teams pull against each other. The Chief Product Owner must own one order.
- **Changing priorities outside the MetaScrum.** Side-channel requests to individual teams undermine the whole Product Owner cycle.
- **Scaled Daily Scrums that become status meetings.** Keep them to cross-team impediments and dependencies, and keep them to 15 minutes.
- **Separate Definitions of Done.** Teams that do not share integration standards cannot produce one integrated Increment.
- **Adding bureaucracy instead of removing it.** Keeping old governance alongside the new forums doubles the overhead.
- **Measuring activity rather than outcomes.** Story points completed across teams say little; track value delivered, quality and sustainability.

### Tools for running Scrum@Scale
Scrum@Scale does not require any particular software, but once you have several teams you need shared visibility of one backlog, cross-team dependencies and the metrics in your transparency layer.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)** (our top-rated tool, 9.4) works well when Scrum@Scale reaches beyond software teams. Its cross-project dashboards, custom workflows and portfolio views help an Executive MetaScrum and EAT see priorities, dependencies and progress in one place.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is widely used by software teams for Scrum boards, backlogs and Sprint reports, and Atlassian offers further tooling for scaled planning.
- **monday.com, Asana and ClickUp** all support Scrum-style boards, shared backlogs and dashboards that suit teams of teams, with different strengths in ease of use and breadth of features.
Whatever you choose, make every team draw from the same ordered backlog. Our roundup of [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) compares the options in more detail, and our guide to [agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/) explains how to connect team work to strategic priorities.

### Scrum@Scale training and certification
Scrum Inc. and its registered trainers run a Scrum@Scale Practitioner course. The credential is usually listed as Registered Scrum@Scale Practitioner (RS@SP), though some providers use slightly different names. Scrum Inc. also runs a programme for people who want to become Scrum@Scale trainers. Course formats, prices and exam rules change, so check the official Scrum@Scale or Scrum Inc. website before you book.
If you are new to Scrum, a foundation Scrum Master or Product Owner certificate is usually the better first step. See our comparison of [Scrum certification and training](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is Scrum@Scale?**
Scrum@Scale is a framework created by Jeff Sutherland for scaling Scrum across an organisation. It links small Scrum Teams into networks, coordinates them through a Scrum Master cycle and a Product Owner cycle, and adds two leadership forums, the Executive Action Team and the Executive MetaScrum.

**Q: Who created Scrum@Scale?**
Jeff Sutherland, co-creator of Scrum, developed Scrum@Scale with Scrum Inc. The official Scrum@Scale Guide is free to read at scrumatscale.com; the current version is 2.1, published in February 2022.

**Q: Is Scrum@Scale the same as Scrum of Scrums?**
No. A Scrum of Scrums is one building block of Scrum@Scale: a group of four or five teams that coordinate their work. Scrum@Scale adds the Product Owner cycle, the Executive Action Team, the Executive MetaScrum and shared metrics around it.

**Q: What are the two cycles in Scrum@Scale?**
The Scrum Master cycle covers how work is delivered: continuous improvement and impediment removal, cross-team coordination and delivery. The Product Owner cycle covers what is built: strategic vision, backlog prioritisation, backlog decomposition and refinement, and release planning.

**Q: What is the Executive Action Team in Scrum@Scale?**
The Executive Action Team (EAT) fulfils the Scrum Master accountabilities for the whole organisation. Its members are leaders who can change structure, budget and policy. It removes impediments teams cannot solve and works a backlog of initiatives for transforming the organisation.

**Q: What is a MetaScrum?**
A MetaScrum is a forum where Product Owners, leaders and stakeholders align vision and priorities across teams. At the top level it is called the Executive MetaScrum. It meets at least once per Sprint and is where priorities, budgets and team alignment should change.

**Q: What does the Chief Product Owner do in Scrum@Scale?**
The Chief Product Owner sets the strategic vision for a group of teams, maintains one ordered backlog, decides which metrics to monitor, assesses customer feedback and facilitates the MetaScrum. They lead a Product Owner Team made up of each team's Product Owner.

**Q: How many teams can be in a Scrum of Scrums?**
The guide recommends four or five teams per Scrum of Scrums, based on research suggesting an optimal team size of about five. When you have more teams, you form additional Scrums of Scrums and coordinate them through a Scrum of Scrum of Scrums.

**Q: How is Scrum@Scale different from SAFe?**
Scrum@Scale is a minimal, modular extension of Scrum that leaves most practices to you. SAFe is a more detailed enterprise framework with many defined roles, events and portfolio structures. Organisations wanting a documented blueprint often prefer SAFe; those wanting a lighter approach often prefer Scrum@Scale.

**Q: How is Scrum@Scale different from LeSS and Nexus?**
LeSS and Nexus both focus on several teams working on one product with a single Product Owner and Product Backlog. Scrum@Scale also uses a single ordered backlog, but adds Chief Product Owners, a Product Owner Team and explicit executive forums, so it reaches further into organisational leadership.

**Q: How long does it take to implement Scrum@Scale?**
There is no fixed timescale. A reference model of four or five teams can usually be set up within a few Sprints, but extending Scrum@Scale across a large organisation is a gradual change that typically continues for many months or longer, depending on size and starting point.

**Q: Is there a Scrum@Scale certification?**
Yes. Scrum Inc. and its registered trainers offer a Scrum@Scale Practitioner course, usually leading to the Registered Scrum@Scale Practitioner credential. Check the official Scrum@Scale or Scrum Inc. website for current formats and requirements.

# Scrum Boards: How to Set Up and Use One

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: How a Scrum board works, typical columns, what goes on a Scrum card, physical vs digital boards, and the differences from a Kanban board.


## Scrum Boards: How to Set Up and Use One
A Scrum board makes the Sprint Backlog visible. It shows every item and task in the current Sprint and where each one is, so the team can coordinate at a glance.
- Published 17 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- A Scrum board visualises the Sprint Backlog.
- Update it daily and show the Sprint Goal.
- It resets each Sprint, unlike a Kanban board.

### Typical columns
| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Sprint Backlog / To do | Selected for the Sprint, not started |
| In progress | Being worked on |
| Review / Test | Being checked |
| Done | Meets the Definition of Done |

### What goes on a Scrum card
- Item title, ideally as a user story.
- Story point estimate.
- Acceptance criteria or a link to them.
- Owner of current tasks.
- Blocker marker when stuck.

### Using the board
- Set it up at Sprint Planning.
- Update it during the Daily Scrum.
- Display the Sprint Goal at the top.
- Add a burndown chart next to it.
- Clear it at the end of the Sprint; unfinished items return to the Product Backlog.

### Scrum board vs Kanban board
|  | Scrum board | Kanban board |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifespan | One Sprint | Persistent |
| Limits | Sprint scope | WIP limits per column |
| Changes | Avoid changes that endanger the Sprint Goal | New items can be pulled any time |
See [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do Scrum teams need a Scrum board?**
The Scrum Guide doesn't require one, but a board is the simplest way to make the Sprint Backlog transparent.

**Q: Can a Scrum board have WIP limits?**
Yes. Many teams add WIP limits to improve flow within the Sprint.

**Q: What is a Scrum board?**
A visual board showing the items and tasks in the current Sprint and their status, making the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) transparent.

**Q: What columns should a Scrum board have?**
A simple board has To do, In progress and Done. Many teams add Review or Test, matching how their work actually flows.

**Q: Who updates the Scrum board?**
The Developers, as they work and during the Daily Scrum.

**Q: Is a Scrum board the same as a Kanban board?**
They look similar, but a Scrum board shows one Sprint and resets each Sprint, while a Kanban board is persistent and uses WIP limits. See [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/).

**Q: Should the Scrum board show the Sprint Goal?**
Yes. Displaying the Sprint Goal keeps the team focused on the objective rather than just a list of tasks.

**Q: Is a task board the same as a Scrum board?**
Yes, task board is another name for a Scrum board, usually one where each Product Backlog item is broken into tasks that move across the columns.

**Q: Should we use a physical or digital Scrum board?**
Physical boards work well for co-located teams and encourage conversation. Digital boards suit remote teams and produce reports automatically.

**Q: Can several Scrum Teams share one Scrum board?**
Teams sharing a product can use a shared view for dependencies, but each team usually needs its own board for its own Sprint Backlog.

**Q: What tools offer Scrum boards?**
Jira, Azure DevOps, ClickUp, Asana, Wrike, monday.com, Trello and many others. See [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) and our [tool comparisons](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/).

# Scrum Ceremonies: The 5 Scrum Events Explained

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: The five Scrum events (Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Retrospective): purpose, attendees, time-boxes and how they fit together.


## Scrum Ceremonies: The 5 Scrum Events Explained
Scrum's events, often called ceremonies or meetings, create a regular rhythm for planning, inspecting and adapting. Each has a clear purpose and a maximum duration, and together they replace most other meetings.
- Published 10 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum has five events: the Sprint plus four inside it.
- Each event has a purpose and a maximum time-box.
- Backlog refinement is ongoing, not a formal event.

### The five events at a glance
| Event | Purpose | Who | Time-box (1-month Sprint) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [The Sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-sprint-cycle/) | Container for all other events | Scrum Team | One month or less |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | Plan the Sprint's goal and work | Scrum Team | Up to 8 hours |
| [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) | Inspect progress and adapt the plan | Developers | 15 minutes |
| [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) | Inspect the outcome and adapt the backlog | Scrum Team and stakeholders | Up to 4 hours |
| [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | Improve quality and effectiveness | Scrum Team | Up to 3 hours |
For shorter Sprints, the events are usually shorter.

### Why time-boxes matter
A time-box is a maximum duration. It keeps events focused, limits waste and creates a predictable rhythm. If an event regularly needs more time, that is a signal to investigate, for example poorly refined backlog items.

### What about backlog refinement?
Product Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not a formal event. Teams typically spend some time each Sprint clarifying, splitting and estimating upcoming items, often in a regular session.

### Making events effective
- Hold them at the same time and place every Sprint.
- Prepare inputs in advance, such as a refined backlog for planning.
- Keep the focus on the event's purpose.
- Respect time-boxes.
- Use outcomes: every event should change something, such as a plan, the backlog or the way of working.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Are Scrum ceremonies mandatory?**
Yes. The Scrum Guide says each event is a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt, and skipping events loses those opportunities.

**Q: Which Scrum event is often mistaken for a status meeting?**
The Daily Scrum. It is actually a planning meeting for the Developers, focused on progress towards the Sprint Goal.

**Q: What are the 5 Scrum ceremonies?**
The Sprint, Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. The Scrum Guide calls them events.

**Q: Is backlog refinement a Scrum ceremony?**
No. The Scrum Guide describes Product Backlog refinement as an ongoing activity, not a formal event. See [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/).

**Q: What is the order of Scrum events?**
Each Sprint starts with Sprint Planning, has a Daily Scrum every working day, and ends with the Sprint Review followed by the Sprint Retrospective.

**Q: How long are Scrum ceremonies in a two-week Sprint?**
The Scrum Guide sets maximums for a one-month Sprint: Planning 8 hours, Review 4 hours, Retrospective 3 hours. Shorter Sprints usually have shorter events, and the Daily Scrum stays at 15 minutes.

**Q: Why does the Scrum Guide say Scrum events rather than Scrum ceremonies?**
The Scrum Guide uses the word events. Ceremonies is an informal term some teams use, though it can suggest empty ritual rather than purposeful inspection and adaptation.

**Q: Who facilitates Scrum events?**
The Scrum Master ensures events take place and are positive, productive and within their time-box, but anyone in the Scrum Team may facilitate.

**Q: Can Scrum events be held remotely?**
Yes. Remote teams use video calls and shared digital boards. Keeping cameras on, using timers and preparing materials in advance helps keep events focused.

**Q: Can two Scrum ceremonies, the Sprint Review and Retrospective, be combined?**
It is best not to. They have different purposes and attendees, and combining them usually reduces the depth of both. See [Sprint Review vs Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review-vs-retrospective/).

**Q: What is the purpose of time-boxing Scrum events?**
Time-boxes set a maximum duration so events stay focused and predictable. Regularly hitting the time-box is a signal to investigate the cause, such as poorly refined backlog items.
