# Scrum Certification: Options, Costs and Training Guide

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum certification compared: PSM, CSM, PSPO, CSPO and SAFe exam facts, fees and renewal, total costs, training formats and a step-by-step way to choose.


## Scrum Certification: Options, Costs and Training Guide
A Scrum certification is a credential from an organisation such as Scrum.org or Scrum Alliance showing that you understand Scrum, earned by passing an assessment, completing a course or both. The most common starting points are Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) and Certified ScrumMaster (CSM) for Scrum Masters, and PSPO I or CSPO for Product Owners. This guide compares the main options, their fees and renewal rules (checked on the issuers' websites on 4 November 2026), and shows you how to choose the right certification and training.
- Published 20 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum.org certifications (PSM, PSPO, PSD and others) are earned by passing an online assessment; a course is optional and the certification never expires.
- Scrum Alliance certifications (CSM, CSPO) require a 16-hour course with an approved trainer and renew every two years with Scrum Education Units and a fee.
- PSM I costs US$200 per attempt: 80 questions, 60 minutes, 85% to pass. CSM: 50 questions, 60 minutes, 74% to pass, with the test included in the course fee.
- SAFe Scrum Master suits organisations that use SAFe; PMI-ACP suits experienced practitioners who want a broader Agile credential.
- Compare total cost over three years, not only the first payment: course fees, retakes and renewals change the picture.
- A certificate gets you interviews; experience on a real Scrum Team gets you the job. Plan both.

### What is a Scrum certification?
**A Scrum certification is a credential that shows you have learned Scrum to a defined standard, usually based on the [2020 Scrum Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/).** Depending on the issuer, you earn it by passing a timed online assessment, by attending a course with an approved trainer, or both. Certifications are role-based: Scrum Master, Product Owner, Developer or leader.
Scrum itself does not require any certificate. The Scrum Guide is free, and anyone can practise the framework. Employers, however, often list a certification in job adverts as a quick signal that a candidate knows the vocabulary and rules, which is why many people take one early in their Scrum career.
It helps to separate two things that are often sold together:
- **Training** is the learning experience: a two-day class, a self-paced course, coaching or self-study.
- **Certification** is the credential: the assessment or course completion recorded by the issuing body, often with a digital badge you can share.
With Scrum.org you can certify without training; with Scrum Alliance the training is part of the certification. That single difference shapes cost, format and renewal, and it runs through every comparison in this guide.

### Scrum certifications at a glance
The table covers the entry-level certifications most people consider first. Fees are in US dollars and exclude taxes; course prices are set by trainers and vary by country and format.
| Certification | Issuer | For | Course required? | How you earn it | Fee | Renewal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) | Scrum.org | Scrum Masters, team members | No (recommended) | Online assessment: 80 questions, 60 minutes, 85% | $200 per attempt | None: lifetime |
| Certified ScrumMaster (CSM) | Scrum Alliance | Scrum Masters | Yes: 16 hours with an approved trainer | Course, then a test: 50 questions, 60 minutes, 74% | Included in course fee | Every 2 years: 20 SEUs + $100 |
| Professional Scrum Product Owner I (PSPO I) | Scrum.org | Product Owners | No (recommended) | Online assessment: 80 questions, 60 minutes, 85% | $200 per attempt | None: lifetime |
| Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO) | Scrum Alliance | Product Owners | Yes: 16 hours | Course completion (no test) | Course fee | Every 2 years: 20 SEUs + $100 |
| Professional Scrum Developer (PSD) | Scrum.org | Developers | No (recommended) | Online assessment: 80 questions, 60 minutes, 85% | $200 per attempt | None: lifetime |
| SAFe Scrum Master | Scaled Agile, Inc. | Scrum Masters in SAFe organisations | No (course or proctored exam) | Exam: 45 questions, 90 minutes, 80% | Course fee, or $495 proctored exam | Annual: $195 + 24 CEUs every two years |
Tip
Fees, exam formats and renewal rules change. Every figure in this guide was checked on the issuer's own website on 4 November 2026; check again before you book.

### Scrum.org certifications
Scrum.org was founded by Scrum co-creator Ken Schwaber and Alex Armstrong, and runs the Professional Scrum certifications. All of them are online assessments with a high pass mark, none requires a course, and none expires. Scrum.org's own count, last updated on 1 November 2026, lists 778,506 PSM I holders, 279,802 PSPO I holders and over 1.2 million Professional Scrum certifications in total.

#### Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I)
PSM I is the most widely held Scrum.org certification and shows a fundamental understanding of Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide.
- **Format:** 80 multiple-choice, multiple-answer and true/false questions in 60 minutes.
- **Pass mark:** 85%.
- **Fee:** US$200 per attempt. Each password is valid for one attempt and does not expire.
- **Languages:** English and Japanese, with Simplified Chinese through Scrum.org's China site.
- **Course:** not required, but recommended. The official two-day Professional Scrum Master class includes one free attempt, and if you take it within 14 days and score below 85% you get a second attempt free.
- **Renewal:** none. The certification is for life and includes a digital badge.
See our guide to the [Scrum Master role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) for how PSM I fits a Scrum Master career.

#### Advanced Scrum Master levels: PSM II and PSM III
| Level | Fee | Questions | Time | Pass mark | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PSM II | $250 | 30 (some with partial credit) | 90 minutes | 85% | Scenario-based; PSM class graduates get 40% off after passing PSM I |
| PSM III | $500 | 24 essay questions | 150 minutes | Expert-graded pass or did not pass | Scrum.org warns that it is very difficult for anyone scoring below 90% on PSM I and II |
Neither level has a formal prerequisite, but each assumes real experience. Most people take PSM II after at least a year as a Scrum Master.

#### Other Scrum.org certifications
| Certification | For | Fee | Questions / time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PSPO I | Product Owners | $200 | 80 / 60 minutes |
| PSPO II | Experienced Product Owners | $250 | 40 / 60 minutes |
| Professional Scrum Developer (PSD) | Developers on Scrum Teams | $200 | 80 / 60 minutes |
| Professional Scrum with Kanban (PSK I) | Teams using Kanban practices with Scrum | $200 | 45 / 60 minutes |
| Professional Agile Leadership (PAL I) | Managers and leaders | $200 | 36 / 60 minutes |
| Scaled Professional Scrum (SPS) | Teams scaling with Nexus | $250 | 40 / 60 minutes |
| PSM-AI Essentials | Scrum Masters using AI in their work | $200 | 40 / 60 minutes |
All of these have an 85% pass mark. Scrum.org also offers PSPO III, PSPO-AI Essentials, AI Fluency, Evidence-Based Management (PAL-EBM), facilitation and backlog management skills credentials, user experience (PSU) and product discovery (PPDV).

### Scrum Alliance certifications
Scrum Alliance certifications are built around live training. You attend a course taught by an approved trainer, complete any required work or test, and maintain the certification with continuing education.

#### Certified ScrumMaster (CSM)
- **Course:** 16 hours of training, usually spread over two or three days, live online or in person.
- **Test:** 50 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes; you need 37 correct (74%).
- **Attempts:** the course fee includes two attempts within 90 days of the course; after that, each attempt costs $25.
- **Cost:** set by the trainer. Scrum Alliance quotes a range of $250 to $2,495 based on public course prices as of October 2023.
- **Languages:** the test is available in 13 languages, including English, Spanish, French, German, Japanese and Simplified Chinese.

#### Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO)
CSPO requires a 16-hour class, live online or in person. Scrum Alliance currently has no test requirement for CSPO: you earn it by completing the course to your trainer's satisfaction. See our guide to the [Product Owner accountability](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) for what the role involves day to day.

#### Advanced and professional levels
| Certification | Prerequisite | Experience (validated) | Course |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Advanced CSM (A-CSM) | CSM, or Scrum.org PSM I or PSM II | 12 months as a Scrum Master in the past five years | At least 16 hours |
| Advanced CSPO (A-CSPO) | CSPO | 12 months as a Product Owner in the past five years | At least 16 hours |
| Certified Scrum Professional – ScrumMaster (CSP-SM) | A-CSM | 24 months as a Scrum Master in the past five years | Approved CSP-SM course |
| Certified Scrum Professional – Product Owner (CSP-PO) | A-CSPO | 24 months as a Product Owner in the past five years | Approved CSP-PO course |
Note the first row: a PSM I holder can join the Scrum Alliance path at A-CSM level without taking the CSM first.

#### Renewing Scrum Alliance certifications
| Level | Examples | Scrum Education Units (SEUs) | Fee every two years |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Foundational | CSM, CSPO, CSD | 20 | $100 |
| Advanced | A-CSM, A-CSPO | 30 | $175 |
| Professional | CSP-SM, CSP-PO | 40 | $250 |
If you hold several, you pay for the highest level only; renewing it also renews lower levels on the same track, and each certification on another track needs half its SEUs and no fee. Earning a new Scrum Alliance certification renews your others. SEUs come from courses, events, reading and volunteering, and cannot be bought.

### SAFe Scrum Master and other options

#### SAFe Scrum Master
Scaled Agile, Inc. offers the SAFe Scrum Master certification, now taught through its AI-Empowered SAFe Scrum Master course. It covers the Scrum Master's role inside a [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) organisation: working on an Agile Release Train, PI Planning and coordinating with other teams.
- **Exam:** 45 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes; pass mark 80%.
- **Routes:** attend the course (two exam attempts included if taken within 60 days), or buy a proctored exam without the course for $495 plus tax, which also includes two attempts within 60 days.
- **Renewal:** annual, at the SAFe Foundational rate of $195 a year plus tax, with 24 continuing education units over each two-year cycle.
Choose it if you work, or want to work, in a SAFe organisation; for lighter ways to scale Scrum, compare [Scrum@Scale](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-at-scale/). Outside SAFe, PSM I or CSM are more widely recognised as Scrum credentials.

#### PMI Agile Certified Practitioner (PMI-ACP)
The PMI-ACP covers several Agile approaches, including Scrum and Kanban, and suits practitioners who already have Agile experience. The exam has 120 questions in 180 minutes, and PMI lists the fee as $435 for members and $495 for non-members. Eligibility requires Agile training and Agile project experience; PMI's certification page lists a secondary degree, 21 contact hours of Agile training, 12 months of general project experience in the last five years (a current PMP or PgMP satisfies this) and 8 months of Agile project experience in the last three years (checked 4 November 2026). Renewal is 30 PDUs every three years. Our [project management certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) compares it with the [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

#### ICAgile and PMAI
ICAgile accredits courses run by training providers rather than setting a central exam: you earn its knowledge-based ICAgile Certified Professional (ICP) certifications by completing an accredited class, and its expert level through demonstrated competence. Our own PMAI certification (Project Management Artificial Intelligence) includes Sprintcraft: Agile & Scrum Practitioner, one of six online courses with assessed chapters. It complements, rather than replaces, a Scrum-specific credential.

### PSM I vs CSM: which should you choose?
These are the two most common first certifications for Scrum Masters. Both are respected; they differ mainly in how you earn and keep them.
|  | Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I) | Certified ScrumMaster (CSM) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Awarded by | Scrum.org | Scrum Alliance |
| Course required | No (a course is recommended, not required) | Yes: 16 hours with an approved trainer |
| Exam | 80 questions, 60 minutes, 85% to pass | 50 questions, 60 minutes, 74% to pass |
| Cost | US$200 per attempt (assessment only) | Included in the course fee, which varies by trainer |
| Renewal | Lifetime; no renewal fee | Every two years: US$100 and 20 SEUs |
| Best for | Self-directed learners; people who want the lowest ongoing cost | People who learn best in a live class, or whose employer pays for training |
Many people find PSM I harder to pass because of its high pass mark and the lack of a required course, while CSM's value lies in the class itself: two or three days of discussion and exercises with an experienced trainer. If your employer will fund a course, CSM gives you structured training and the credential together. If you are paying yourself, PSM I through self-study is the cheapest recognised route. Check job adverts in your market: in some regions and sectors one is mentioned more often than the other.

### What Scrum certification really costs: a worked example
The following example is illustrative. The course fees are assumptions chosen for the calculation; the exam and renewal fees are the issuers' published figures.
**Scenario.** Sam, a business analyst, wants a Scrum Master certification and is comparing four routes over three years. Sam assumes a public PSM course costs $1,000 and a CSM course $800 in their area.
| Route | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 | Three-year total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PSM I by self-study (passes first time) | $200 exam | $0 | $0 | $200 |
| PSM I by self-study (needs a second attempt) | $400 (two exams) | $0 | $0 | $400 |
| PSM class (includes exam attempt) | $1,000 | $0 | $0 | $1,000 |
| CSM course (includes two test attempts) | $800 | $0 | $100 renewal + 20 SEUs | $900 |
| SAFe Scrum Master proctored exam, no course | $495 | $195 renewal | $195 renewal | $885 |
Three points stand out. First, the cheapest route is self-study for PSM I, but only if you prepare well: each failed attempt adds $200. Second, CSM's renewal is small in money but needs 20 SEUs every two years, which take time. Third, SAFe's annual renewal adds up: over five years it would add $780 on top of the exam. None of this makes one option better; it simply means you should compare the full cost, and ask your employer which costs it will cover.
Tip
Many employers pay for certification as part of a [training plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/). Ask before you pay for a course yourself, and ask whether they will also fund renewals.

### Scrum training options
Training and certification can be bought separately, so choose the format that suits how you learn.
| Format | What it is | Good for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Instructor-led class, in person | Two or three days with an approved trainer | Discussion, exercises, networking; required for CSM and CSPO | Highest cost; travel; time away from work |
| Live virtual class | The same course delivered online, often over more, shorter sessions | Remote learners; lower travel cost | Screen fatigue; needs a quiet space |
| Self-paced online course | Recorded lessons and quizzes | Flexible timing; low cost | Quality varies; check content is based on the 2020 Scrum Guide |
| Self-study | The Scrum Guide, books and free practice assessments | PSM I and PSPO I candidates on a budget | Easy to underestimate the exam; no one to ask |
| In-house team training | A private class for your organisation | Whole teams adopting Scrum together; tailored examples | Needs a sponsor and budget |
| Coaching | An experienced Agile coach works alongside the team | Turning knowledge into practice | Does not lead to a certificate by itself |
For managers buying training for a team, an in-house class followed by a few weeks of coaching usually transfers more into daily practice than sending individuals to public courses. Pair it with a short [sprint planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) and retrospective routine so the team applies what it learned straight away.

### How to choose a Scrum certification step by step
1. **Start with your role.** Scrum Master: PSM I or CSM. Product Owner: PSPO I or CSPO. Developer: PSD. Manager or leader: PAL I. If you are unsure of the differences, read our guide to [Scrum Team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) first.
2. **Check your context.** If your organisation uses SAFe, a SAFe role certification may matter more. If it runs a hybrid of Scrum and Kanban (see [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/)), PSK I is worth a look.
3. **Look at real job adverts.** Collect ten adverts for the role you want in your area and note which certifications they name.
4. **Decide how you learn best.** Self-directed learners suit Scrum.org assessments; people who value a live class suit Scrum Alliance courses.
5. **Work out the three-year cost,** including likely retakes, renewals and the time needed to earn SEUs or CEUs.
6. **Choose a trainer or study plan,** checking reviews, the trainer's credentials and that materials follow the 2020 Scrum Guide.
7. **Plan how you will use it.** Book a date, then line up practical experience: facilitating a retrospective, supporting backlog refinement or joining a Scrum Team.

### Scrum certification paths by role
Most people take one entry-level certification, gain experience, then add an advanced or complementary one. The table shows common paths; you do not need every step.
| Role | Start with | Next, after about a year of practice | Advanced |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum Master | PSM I or CSM | PSM II or A-CSM; PSK I if the team uses Kanban | PSM III or CSP-SM |
| Product Owner | PSPO I or CSPO | PSPO II or A-CSPO | PSPO III or CSP-PO |
| Developer | PSD | PSK I or PSM I to understand the wider framework | Technical certifications in your field |
| Manager or leader | PAL I | PAL-EBM | SPS or a scaling framework certification |
| Project manager | PSM I or CSM | PMI-ACP | PMP alongside, for hybrid roles |
| SAFe organisation | SAFe Scrum Master or SAFe Agilist | SAFe Advanced Scrum Master | Release Train Engineer |
Project managers moving into Agile delivery often combine a Scrum credential with the PMI-ACP; our guide to the [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) role explains how the jobs differ. See [how to learn Agile and get certified](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-learn-agile-and-get-certified/) for a fuller learning plan that covers Agile beyond Scrum.

### How to prepare for the PSM I assessment
PSM I questions test whether you understand the Scrum Guide precisely, including its exact wording on accountabilities, events and commitments. This four-week plan is our suggestion for someone new to Scrum studying about five hours a week.
| Week | Focus | Activities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The Scrum Guide | Read the Scrum Guide twice. Summarise the three accountabilities, five events and three artifacts with their commitments in your own words. |
| 2 | Theory and values | Study empiricism, the five values and self-management. Take the free Scrum Open practice assessment and note every wrong answer. |
| 3 | Events and artifacts in depth | Review timeboxes, who attends each event and what happens when a Sprint is cancelled. Retake Scrum Open until you score 100% several times in a row. |
| 4 | Exam readiness | Do timed practice at 45 seconds a question. Re-read the guide once more, then book the assessment while it is fresh. |
- Use the Scrum Guide as your primary source; if a study aid disagrees with it, the guide wins.
- Our guides to [Scrum ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/), [Scrum artifacts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-artifacts/) and [Scrum values](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-principles-and-values/) cover the most-tested areas, and the [Scrum glossary](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-glossary/) defines the terms.
- Read each question carefully for words such as "must", "should" and "best".
- Leave hard questions and come back: 80 questions in 60 minutes leaves little time to linger.

### Getting the most from a CSM or CSPO course
Because the course is the certification, preparation pays off in what you learn rather than in a pass mark.
1. Read the Scrum Guide before day one, so class time goes on discussion rather than definitions.
2. Bring two or three real problems from your workplace to ask the trainer about.
3. Take part fully in exercises; they are where most of the learning happens.
4. Take the CSM test within a few days, while the material is fresh and your two included attempts are still available.
5. Afterwards, try one new practice with your team within a fortnight, such as a better [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) format.

### Is a Scrum certification worth it?
For most people starting out, yes, with limits. A certification is useful when:
- You are moving into a Scrum Master or Product Owner role and need to get past CV screening.
- You want a structured way to learn Scrum properly rather than from second-hand descriptions.
- Your employer funds it, or the role you want names it.
It is less useful on its own. Hiring managers usually ask what you have done with Scrum: how you handled a difficult retrospective, how you helped a team stop carrying work over between Sprints. A certificate cannot answer those questions. See our guide on [how to become a Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/how-to-become-a-scrum-master/) to build that experience alongside a certification.

### Common mistakes when choosing Scrum training
- **Comparing only the first payment.** Renewals, retakes and time spent on SEUs change the total cost.
- **Booking PSM I too early.** At an 85% pass mark, a few weak areas cause a fail. Practise until you score well above it.
- **Collecting certificates instead of experience.** Two entry-level certificates add less than one year on a real team.
- **Choosing a SAFe credential when you do not work with SAFe,** or a pure Scrum credential when your organisation runs SAFe.
- **Using outdated materials.** Make sure courses and practice questions reflect the 2020 Scrum Guide, which replaced the term "Development Team" with "Developers".
- **Letting a Scrum Alliance certification lapse** because the renewal email went unnoticed. Note the renewal date when you pass.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Which Scrum certification is most recognised?**
PSM I from Scrum.org and CSM from Scrum Alliance are the most widely recognised entry-level Scrum Master certifications. Scrum.org's published count shows over 778,000 PSM I holders as of 1 November 2026.

**Q: Which is harder, PSM I or CSM?**
Most people find PSM I harder: it has an 85% pass mark and no required course. The CSM test has a 74% pass mark and follows a 16-hour course that covers the material.

**Q: Can I get Scrum certified without taking a course?**
Yes. All Scrum.org certifications, including PSM I and PSPO I, can be earned by passing the online assessment without a course. Scrum Alliance certifications require a course; the SAFe Scrum Master exam can be bought as a proctored exam without the course.

**Q: Do Scrum certifications expire?**
Scrum.org certifications do not expire and have no renewal fee. Scrum Alliance certifications renew every two years with SEUs and a fee ($100 for CSM or CSPO). SAFe certifications renew annually.

**Q: How much does Scrum certification cost?**
PSM I and PSPO I cost US$200 per attempt. CSM and CSPO are included in a course fee set by the trainer; Scrum Alliance quotes $250 to $2,495 for CSM based on October 2023 prices. The SAFe Scrum Master proctored exam is $495.

**Q: How long does it take to get Scrum certified?**
A CSM or CSPO takes the course length, usually two or three days, plus the CSM test. For PSM I, most people new to Scrum need a few weeks of study; experienced practitioners may need only a few days.

**Q: What is the best Scrum certification for beginners?**
PSM I or CSM for aspiring Scrum Masters, and PSPO I or CSPO for aspiring Product Owners. None requires prior experience. Choose by how you prefer to learn and what employers in your market ask for.

**Q: Can I study for a Scrum certification for free?**
Yes. The Scrum Guide is free, and Scrum.org offers free open practice assessments. You only pay for the PSM I or PSPO I assessment itself.

**Q: Is there a Scrum certification for Developers?**
Yes. Scrum.org's Professional Scrum Developer (PSD) assessment covers Scrum and modern development practices, and Scrum Alliance offers Certified Scrum Developer (CSD) through its courses.

**Q: Is SAFe Scrum Master a worthwhile certification?**
It is useful if you work, or want to work, in an organisation that uses SAFe, because it covers how Scrum Teams operate on an Agile Release Train. Outside SAFe, PSM I or CSM are more widely recognised.

**Q: Is PMI-ACP a Scrum certification?**
Not exclusively. The PMI-ACP covers several Agile approaches, including Scrum, and requires Agile training and experience. Many people take PSM I or CSM first and the PMI-ACP later.

**Q: Can a PSM I holder take Scrum Alliance's advanced certification?**
Yes. Scrum Alliance accepts a Scrum.org PSM I or PSM II in place of the CSM as the prerequisite for the Advanced CSM, alongside 12 months of validated Scrum Master experience in the past five years.

**Q: What comes after an entry-level Scrum certification?**
Real experience first, then an advanced level such as PSM II or A-CSM, or a complementary credential such as PSK I or PSPO I. See our guide on [how to become a Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/how-to-become-a-scrum-master/).

# Scrum Glossary: 120+ Scrum Terms Defined A to Z

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-glossary/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum glossary: plain-English definitions of 120+ Scrum terms A to Z, each marked as Scrum Guide 2020 or common practice, plus retired terms and examples.


## Scrum Glossary: 120+ Scrum Terms Defined A to Z
This Scrum glossary defines more than 120 Scrum terms in plain English, from accountability to working agreement, and marks the source of each one. Official terms follow the 2020 Scrum Guide, which is still the current version, so you can tell Scrum rules from common practices, related frameworks and retired wording. Find a term in the A to Z tables, then use the commonly confused terms and the worked Sprint example to see how the vocabulary fits together.
- Published 21 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- Official Scrum vocabulary comes from the 2020 Scrum Guide: three accountabilities, five events, three artifacts and three commitments, built on three pillars and five values.
- Story points, velocity, user stories, epics, burndown charts and the Definition of Ready are widely used practices, not Scrum Guide rules.
- Several terms have been retired: "Development Team" became Developers, "roles" became accountabilities, "self-organising" became self-managing and "grooming" became refinement.
- The most commonly confused pairs are Sprint Goal and Product Goal, Definition of Done and acceptance criteria, Done and released, and forecast and commitment.
- The 2025 Scrum Guide Expansion Pack is an optional supplement; it does not replace the 2020 Scrum Guide.
- Agree a short team glossary, especially for "Done", "ready" and how you size and forecast work.

### What is a Scrum glossary?
**A Scrum glossary is a reference list of the terms used in Scrum, each with a short, plain definition and its source.** It covers the framework's accountabilities, events, artifacts, commitments, pillars and values, plus the practices teams commonly add, so that everyone on a Scrum Team and its stakeholders use the same words in the same way.
Shared vocabulary matters because Scrum depends on transparency: if one person's "Done" means coded and another's means deployable, every forecast becomes unreliable.
Every table below has a **Source** column:
- **Scrum Guide:** defined or used in the 2020 Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. Scrum Guide terms are usually capitalised, such as Sprint, Product Owner and Increment.
- **Practice:** widely used with Scrum but not required by it. Use, adapt or drop these as your team sees fit.
- **Scrum.org, Kanban, XP or Scaling:** terms from Scrum.org's own glossary, from Kanban or Extreme Programming, or from frameworks for many teams.
- **Retired:** older Scrum wording you will still hear but which the current Scrum Guide no longer uses.
For wider Agile, Kanban, XP and SAFe vocabulary, use our [Agile glossary](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-glossary/). See [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) for how the framework fits together.

### Scrum terms A to B

#### A
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acceptance criteria | Conditions one specific backlog item must meet to be accepted. Unlike the Definition of Done, they differ for each item. | Practice |
| Accountability | The 2020 Scrum Guide's word for the three areas of responsibility in a Scrum Team: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers. See [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/). | Scrum Guide |
| Adaptation | Adjusting the process or the product as soon as possible when inspection shows it has drifted outside acceptable limits. One of the three pillars of empiricism. | Scrum Guide |
| Agile | A way of working based on the 2001 Agile Manifesto: short cycles, frequent feedback, adaptable plans. Scrum is one Agile framework. | Agile Manifesto |
| Artifact | Something that represents work or value. Scrum has three: the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment. See [Scrum artifacts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-artifacts/). | Scrum Guide |

#### B
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backlog grooming | The older name for Product Backlog refinement, replaced in the 2013 Scrum Guide. | Retired |
| Blocker | Anything that stops one item progressing, such as a missing decision. Scrum's wider term is impediment. | Practice |
| Bug (defect) | A flaw in the product, usually added to the Product Backlog and ordered like any other item. | Practice |
| Burndown chart | A chart of work remaining against time, sloping towards zero. The Scrum Guide names burn-downs as one forecasting practice but does not require them. | Practice |
| Burnup chart | A chart of work completed rising over time against a separate total-scope line, so scope changes stay visible. Also named in the Scrum Guide as an optional practice. | Practice |

### Scrum terms C

#### C
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cancellation (Sprint) | Ending a Sprint early because its Sprint Goal has become obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel a Sprint. | Scrum Guide |
| Capacity | How much time the Developers realistically have in a Sprint after leave, holidays, events and support work. | Practice |
| Ceremony | An informal name for a Scrum event. The Scrum Guide says event, not ceremony. See [Scrum ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/). | Practice |
| Chickens and pigs | An old fable separating people committed to the work from those merely involved. No longer part of the Scrum Guide. | Retired |
| Coherence | Product Backlog items that together form a meaningful whole, such as items serving one Sprint Goal. | Scrum.org |
| Commitment (artifact) | The element that gives each artifact focus: the Product Goal for the Product Backlog, the Sprint Goal for the Sprint Backlog and the Definition of Done for the Increment. Added in 2020. | Scrum Guide |
| Commitment (value) | Scrum Team members commit to achieving their goals and to supporting each other. One of the five Scrum values. | Scrum Guide |
| Courage | Doing the right thing and working on tough problems. A Scrum value. | Scrum Guide |
| Cross-functional | Having all the skills needed to create value each Sprint without depending on people outside the team. | Scrum Guide |
| Cumulative flow diagram (CFD) | A stacked chart of items in each workflow state over time; named in the Scrum Guide as an optional forecasting practice. | Kanban |
| Cycle time | Elapsed time from starting work on an item to finishing it. | Kanban |

### Scrum terms D to E

#### D
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily Scrum | A 15-minute event, at the same time and place each working day, in which the Developers inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan. See the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/). | Scrum Guide |
| Daily stand-up | A general name for a short daily team check-in. Scrum's version is the Daily Scrum. | Practice |
| Definition of Done (DoD) | A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product. It is the commitment for the Increment. See the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/). | Scrum Guide |
| Definition of Ready (DoR) | An optional checklist for deciding when an item is clear enough to bring into Sprint Planning. Not part of the Scrum Guide. | Practice |
| Demo | Informal name for showing work at the Sprint Review, which the Scrum Guide says should be a working session, not just a presentation. | Practice |
| Dependency | A relationship where one item or team needs something from another before work can finish. | Practice |
| Developers | Scrum Team members who create any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint, including testers, designers, analysts and writers. | Scrum Guide |
| Development Team | The pre-2020 name for the Developers as a team inside the Scrum Team. Replaced in 2020 by one Scrum Team with Developers. | Retired |
| Done | Meeting the Definition of Done. Work that is not Done cannot be part of an Increment, released or presented at the Sprint Review. | Scrum Guide |

#### E
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Emergence | New facts or requirements becoming visible unexpectedly as work progresses. | Scrum.org |
| Empiricism | Making decisions based on what is known and observed. Scrum's pillars of empiricism are transparency, inspection and adaptation. See [empiricism in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/). | Scrum Guide |
| Epic | A large body of work that is split into smaller Product Backlog items. | Practice |
| Event | A formal opportunity to inspect and adapt. Scrum has five: the Sprint, Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. | Scrum Guide |
| Evidence-Based Management (EBM) | Scrum.org's framework for measuring value across current value, unrealised value, time to market and ability to innovate. | Scrum.org |
| Expansion Pack | The Scrum Guide Expansion Pack, published in June 2025 by Ralph Jocham, John Coleman and Jeff Sutherland as an optional supplement. It does not replace the 2020 Scrum Guide. | Supplement |

### Scrum terms F to O

#### F
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | Concentrating on the work of the Sprint to make the best possible progress towards the goals. A Scrum value. | Scrum Guide |
| Focus factor | Velocity divided by available person-days; a planning aid, never a performance score. | Practice |
| Forecast | The Developers' prediction of what they can get Done in a Sprint. The 2011 Scrum Guide replaced "commit" with "forecast" for selected work; the commitment is the Sprint Goal. | Scrum Guide |

#### H to I
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardening Sprint | A Sprint reserved for testing and fixing before release. Not part of Scrum; it usually signals a weak Definition of Done. | Practice |
| Impediment | Anything slowing the Scrum Team's progress. The Scrum Master is accountable for causing impediments to be removed. | Scrum Guide |
| Increment | A concrete, usable stepping stone towards the Product Goal that meets the Definition of Done. A Sprint can create several. See [Increment in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/increment-in-scrum/). | Scrum Guide |
| Inspection | Frequently and diligently checking artifacts and progress to spot undesirable variances. A pillar of empiricism. | Scrum Guide |
| INVEST | Bill Wake's checklist for good user stories: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. | Practice |
| Iteration | The general Agile word for a fixed, repeated development cycle. In Scrum, the Sprint. | Practice |

#### K to L
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kanban | A strategy for optimising flow by visualising work, limiting work in progress and managing flow. Often combined with Scrum. See [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/). | Kanban |
| Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS) | A framework for two to eight teams working on one product with one Product Owner and one Product Backlog; LeSS Huge covers more. | Scaling |
| Lean thinking | Reducing waste and focusing on the essentials. The Scrum Guide names it, with empiricism, as a foundation of Scrum. | Scrum Guide |

#### M to O
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimum viable product (MVP) | The smallest version of a product that lets a team test a key assumption with real users. | Practice |
| Monte Carlo forecasting | Simulating many futures from past throughput to give a probabilistic forecast. | Practice |
| Nexus | Scrum.org's framework for three to nine Scrum Teams working on a single product, with a Nexus Integration Team. | Scaling |
| Openness | Being open about the work and its challenges. A Scrum value. | Scrum Guide |
| Ordering | Arranging the Product Backlog in sequence. The Scrum Guide says ordered, not prioritised, because value, risk and dependencies all matter. | Scrum Guide |

### Scrum terms P to R

#### P
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pillars | The three pillars of empiricism: transparency, inspection and adaptation. | Scrum Guide |
| Planning Poker | Consensus estimation in which everyone reveals an estimate card at once, then the highest and lowest explain their reasoning. | Practice |
| Product | A vehicle to deliver value, with a clear boundary, known stakeholders and well-defined users or customers. | Scrum Guide |
| Product Backlog | An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product; the single source of work for the Scrum Team. See the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/). | Scrum Guide |
| Product Backlog item (PBI) | A single entry in the Product Backlog, such as a feature, fix, technical improvement or experiment. | Scrum Guide |
| Product Backlog refinement | Breaking down and adding detail, such as description, order and size, to Product Backlog items. An ongoing activity, not an event. See [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/). | Scrum Guide |
| Product Goal | The future state of the product the Scrum Team plans against; the commitment for the Product Backlog. Added in 2020. | Scrum Guide |
| Product Owner | One person, not a committee, accountable for maximising the value of the product and for effective Product Backlog management. See the [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/). | Scrum Guide |
| Product Owner proxy | Someone standing in for an absent Product Owner; it weakens decisions if the proxy cannot actually decide. | Practice |

#### R
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ready | In the Scrum Guide, items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. Stricter checklists are the Definition of Ready. | Scrum Guide |
| Refinement | Short for Product Backlog refinement. | Scrum Guide |
| Release | Making an Increment available to users. It can happen at any time in a Sprint; the Sprint Review is never a gate to releasing value. | Scrum Guide |
| Release plan | A forecast of when groups of features are likely to be ready, usually shown as a range. | Practice |
| Respect | Respecting each other as capable, independent people. A Scrum value. | Scrum Guide |
| Retrospective formats | Structured Retrospective activities, such as Start, Stop, Continue. | Practice |
| Roles | The pre-2020 word for Product Owner, Scrum Master and Development Team. Replaced by accountabilities. | Retired |

### Scrum terms S

#### S
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum | A lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organisations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. | Scrum Guide |
| Scrum Alliance | A membership and certification body that issues the CSM, CSPO and related certifications. | Certification |
| Scrum board | A visual board showing Sprint Backlog items and their status, physical or in a tool. | Practice |
| Scrum Guide | The official definition of Scrum by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, free online. The current version was published in November 2020. | Scrum Guide |
| Scrum Master | Accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide and for the Scrum Team's effectiveness. See the [Scrum Master role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/). | Scrum Guide |
| Scrum of Scrums | A coordination meeting for representatives of several Scrum Teams working on related products. | Scaling |
| Scrum.org | Ken Schwaber's organisation offering Professional Scrum training and assessments such as PSM and PSPO. | Certification |
| Scrum Team | One Scrum Master, one Product Owner and Developers; typically 10 or fewer people, with no sub-teams or hierarchies. | Scrum Guide |
| Scrum values | Commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage; added to the Scrum Guide in 2016. See [Scrum principles and values](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-principles-and-values/). | Scrum Guide |
| Scrum@Scale | Jeff Sutherland's framework for scaling Scrum through networks of Scrum Teams. | Scaling |
| Scrumban | A blend of Scrum and Kanban, often Scrum's events with Kanban's WIP limits and flow metrics. | Practice |
| Self-managing | The Scrum Team decides internally who does what, when and how. Replaced "self-organising" in 2020. | Scrum Guide |
| Self-organising | The pre-2020 description of how the Development Team chose how to do its work. | Retired |
| Servant-leader | The 2017 description of the Scrum Master. The 2020 Scrum Guide says Scrum Masters are true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation. | Retired |
| Spike | A time-boxed piece of research to reduce uncertainty before estimating or building. Originally an XP term. | Practice |
| Sprint | A fixed-length event of one month or less that contains all the other events. A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends. See the [Scrum Sprint cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-sprint-cycle/). | Scrum Guide |
| Sprint Backlog | The Sprint Goal (why), the selected Product Backlog items (what) and an actionable plan (how). A plan by and for the Developers. See the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/). | Scrum Guide |
| Sprint Goal | The single objective for the Sprint, created during Sprint Planning; the commitment for the Sprint Backlog. | Scrum Guide |
| Sprint length | The fixed duration of a Sprint: one month or less, kept consistent. Two weeks is a common choice. | Scrum Guide |
| Sprint Planning | The event that starts the Sprint and addresses why it is valuable, what can be Done and how. See [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/). | Scrum Guide |
| Sprint Retrospective | The event that concludes the Sprint, used to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness. See the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/). | Scrum Guide |
| Sprint Review | The second-to-last event, in which the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome of the Sprint and decide future adaptations. See the [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/). | Scrum Guide |
| Sprint zero | An informal set-up period before the first Sprint. Not a Scrum term. | Practice |
| Stakeholder | Anyone outside the Scrum Team with an interest in the product, such as customers, users, sponsors and managers. | Scrum Guide |
| Story mapping | Arranging user stories along a user journey to plan releases; associated with Jeff Patton. | Practice |
| Story points | Relative units for sizing backlog items. Not mentioned in the Scrum Guide. See [story points in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/). | Practice |
| Swarming | Several team members working together to finish one item before starting another. | Practice |

### Scrum terms T to Z

#### T
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task | A small technical step in the Developers' plan, often a day or less of work. | Practice |
| Technical debt | The future cost of shortcuts in the product, such as untested or poorly structured code. | Practice |
| Test-driven development (TDD) | Write a failing test, write code to pass it, then refactor. Often part of a Definition of Done. | XP |
| Three Amigos | Business, development and testing perspectives agreeing what an item means before work starts. | Practice |
| 3-5-3 | Shorthand for Scrum's three accountabilities, five events and three artifacts. | Practice |
| Three questions | Yesterday, today and blockers: a Daily Scrum format the 2020 Scrum Guide no longer requires. | Retired |
| Throughput | The number of items finished per period. A forecasting input that needs no estimates. | Kanban |
| Time-box | A fixed maximum duration. The Sprint is one month or less; for a one-month Sprint, Sprint Planning is up to 8 hours, the Sprint Review 4 and the Retrospective 3; the Daily Scrum is 15 minutes. | Scrum Guide |
| Transparency | Making the process and the work visible to those doing it and those receiving it. A pillar of empiricism. | Scrum Guide |
| T-shirt sizing | Rough relative sizing in XS, S, M, L and XL, useful for early or large items. | Practice |

#### U to V
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User story | A need described from the user's view: "As a [user], I want [goal] so that [benefit]". A popular way to write Product Backlog items. | Practice |
| Velocity | Story points (or items) finished to the Definition of Done per Sprint, used for the team's own forecasting. See [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/). | Practice |
| Vertical slice | An item that cuts through every layer of the product so it is usable on its own. | Practice |

#### W to Z
| Term | Definition | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WIP limit | A cap on how many items can be in progress at once, borrowed from Kanban. | Kanban |
| Work item age | How long an unfinished item has been in progress; useful at the Daily Scrum to spot stuck work. | Kanban |
| Working agreement | Rules the Scrum Team agrees for how it works together. | Practice |

### The Scrum Guide at a glance
The 2020 Scrum Guide is deliberately short, and most of its vocabulary fits in one table.
| Element | Scrum Guide terms | Commitment or time-box |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Theory | Empiricism and lean thinking; pillars of transparency, inspection and adaptation | — |
| Values | Commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage | — |
| Accountabilities | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers (one Scrum Team, typically 10 or fewer) | — |
| Events | Sprint; Sprint Planning; Daily Scrum; Sprint Review; Sprint Retrospective | One month or less; 8 hours; 15 minutes; 4 hours; 3 hours (maximums for a one-month Sprint) |
| Artifacts | Product Backlog; Sprint Backlog; Increment | Product Goal; Sprint Goal; Definition of Done |
Tip
If a term is not in the Scrum Guide, it is not a Scrum rule. Story points and burndown charts help many teams, but nobody is doing Scrum "wrong" without them.

### Retired and renamed Scrum terms
The Scrum Guide has been revised several times since 2010. Older wording survives in training material, tools and job adverts, so it helps to know what replaced it.
| You may hear | Current term or practice | Changed in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chickens and pigs | Scrum Team and stakeholders | Early revisions; no longer in the Guide |
| The team commits to the selected items | The Developers forecast the selected items; the Sprint Goal is the commitment | 2011 Scrum Guide (forecast); 2020 (commitments) |
| Backlog grooming | Product Backlog refinement | 2013 Scrum Guide |
| (no values) | Five Scrum values added | 2016 update |
| Roles | Accountabilities | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| Development Team | Developers, in one Scrum Team | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| Self-organising | Self-managing | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| Servant-leader | True leaders who serve | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| Three Daily Scrum questions | Any structure that focuses on progress towards the Sprint Goal | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| Ceremony | Event | Never a Scrum Guide term |

### Commonly confused Scrum terms
These pairs cause the most misunderstandings in Scrum Teams. The numbers are illustrative.

#### Sprint Goal vs Product Goal
A team building a patient booking service has the **Product Goal** "Patients can manage all their appointments online by spring". It will take many Sprints. The **Sprint Goal** for one two-week Sprint is narrower: "Patients can cancel a booking online". The Product Goal guides ordering of the Product Backlog; the Sprint Goal guides daily decisions.

#### Definition of Done vs acceptance criteria
| Term | Applies to | Example | In the Scrum Guide? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Definition of Done | Every item and the whole Increment | Code reviewed, automated tests passing, accessibility checked, deployed to staging | Yes |
| Acceptance criteria | One item | Cancellation is blocked within 24 hours of the appointment | No |
| Definition of Ready | Items before Sprint Planning | Has acceptance criteria and fits in one Sprint | No |

#### Done vs released
Done means the work meets the Definition of Done and is usable. Released means users can actually get it. A team may finish five Done items in a Sprint, release two mid-Sprint and hold three behind a feature flag until marketing is ready. All five are part of the Increment.

#### Forecast vs commitment
The Developers forecast that eight items, about 24 story points, fit in the Sprint. They commit to the Sprint Goal. If one item proves bigger than expected, they renegotiate scope with the Product Owner rather than abandoning the goal or cutting quality.

### Worked example: Scrum terms in one Sprint
Follow one illustrative two-week Sprint for a seven-person Scrum Team building that booking service. Every term in bold is in the glossary above.
1. **Product Goal.** The **Product Owner** keeps the **Product Backlog** **ordered** towards the Product Goal: patients manage their appointments online.
2. **Refinement.** Mid-Sprint, the team splits an **epic** into **user stories** that are **vertical slices**, adds **acceptance criteria** in a **Three Amigos** conversation and sizes them with **Planning Poker** in **story points**.
3. **Sprint Planning.** Using recent **velocity** of 22–26 points and reduced **capacity** for a public holiday, the whole **Scrum Team** agrees the **Sprint Goal**. The **Developers** forecast eight items and break them into **tasks**, forming the **Sprint Backlog**.
4. **During the Sprint.** At each 15-minute **Daily Scrum**, the Developers check progress towards the Sprint Goal. One item's **work item age** is unusually high, so two people **swarm** on it. A third-party API change is an **impediment** the **Scrum Master** helps remove.
5. **Done.** Items meet the **Definition of Done**, including **TDD** and code review, and together form a usable **Increment**. Two items are **released** mid-Sprint.
6. **Review and Retrospective.** At the **Sprint Review**, **stakeholders** try the cancellation flow and their feedback reorders the Product Backlog. At the **Sprint Retrospective**, the team adds accessibility checks to the Definition of Done. The next **Sprint** starts immediately.

### How to build a Scrum glossary for your team
A one-page team glossary prevents most terminology arguments. Build it in a 30-minute session, then keep it alive.
1. **List the terms people actually use**, including tool labels, abbreviations and local jargon from your board and events.
2. **Choose a source of truth.** Use the 2020 Scrum Guide for Scrum terms and this glossary or the Agile glossary for practices.
3. **Agree the high-risk definitions first:** your Definition of Done, what "ready" means, how you size work and what counts towards velocity.
4. **Mark local terms** so new joiners do not mistake team conventions for Scrum rules.
5. **Publish it** next to your working agreement and Product Backlog, and link it from onboarding notes.
6. **Review it at a Sprint Retrospective** every few months, or whenever a misunderstanding causes rework.
Our free templates use the same terms. See the [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) and the [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/).

### Common mistakes with Scrum terminology
- **Using retired terms** such as "Development Team", "grooming", "roles" or "self-organising" in new training or tools.
- **Treating practices as rules.** Story points, velocity, user stories and the Definition of Ready are optional.
- **Calling the Sprint Review a demo.** It is a working session about what to do next, not a presentation.
- **Saying "prioritised" instead of "ordered"**, then arguing over which items are "all priority one".
- **Confusing Done with accepted or released**, which hides unfinished work inside the Increment.
- **Comparing velocity between teams.** Story points are relative to each team, so the numbers do not compare.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the most important Scrum terms for beginners?**
Start with Scrum Team, Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers, Sprint, Sprint Goal, Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment, Definition of Done, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.

**Q: What is 3-5-3 in Scrum?**
A shorthand for Scrum's three accountabilities (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers), five events (Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective) and three artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment).

**Q: Where are official Scrum terms defined?**
In the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. The current version was published in November 2020 and is free online.

**Q: What changed in the 2020 Scrum Guide terminology?**
It added the Product Goal and the three commitments, replaced roles with accountabilities and the Development Team with Developers, replaced self-organising with self-managing, and dropped the three Daily Scrum questions.

**Q: Is the Scrum Guide Expansion Pack a new Scrum Guide?**
No. Published in June 2025 by Ralph Jocham, John Coleman and Jeff Sutherland, it is an optional supplement. The 2020 Scrum Guide remains the official definition of Scrum.

**Q: What is a time-box in Scrum?**
A fixed maximum duration for an event. The Sprint is one month or less and the Daily Scrum 15 minutes. For a one-month Sprint, Sprint Planning is up to 8 hours, the Sprint Review 4 and the Retrospective 3; shorter Sprints usually need less.

**Q: What is the difference between the Sprint Goal and the Product Goal?**
The Sprint Goal is the single objective for one Sprint. The Product Goal is the longer-term objective the Scrum Team works towards across many Sprints.

**Q: Are story points and velocity official Scrum terms?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide mentions neither. They are popular practices for sizing and forecasting work.

**Q: Is the Definition of Ready part of Scrum?**
No. The Scrum Guide only says items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection. A Definition of Ready is an optional team checklist.

**Q: What is the difference between a Scrum Master and a project manager?**
A Scrum Master coaches the team and organisation in Scrum and removes impediments; they do not plan or assign the Developers' work. Scrum has no project manager accountability.

**Q: Which Scrum terms matter most for PSM I and CSM exams?**
Both are based on the Scrum Guide, so focus on its terms: accountabilities, events, artifacts, commitments, pillars, values and time-boxes. Practices such as story points are rarely what the questions test.
