# Scrum Metrics and KPIs: What to Track and How

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum metrics and KPIs explained: Sprint Goal success, velocity, burndown, flow, quality and value measures, with formulas, examples and pitfalls.


## Scrum Metrics and KPIs: What to Track and How
Scrum metrics are the measures a Scrum Team uses to inspect its progress, quality, flow and the value it delivers, so it can adapt its plans and ways of working. The 2020 Scrum Guide does not require any metric, but a small, well-chosen set makes empiricism easier. This guide explains which Scrum metrics and KPIs are worth tracking, how to calculate each one with worked examples, which to review at each event and how to avoid the mistakes that turn metrics into targets.
- Published 16 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- The Scrum Guide mandates no metrics; it names burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows as useful forecasting practices that do not replace empiricism.
- Cover six areas with a handful of measures: goals, delivery, flow, quality, value and team health.
- Sprint Goal success rate and a value measure usually tell you more than velocity alone.
- Use velocity and throughput for forecasting ranges, never as targets or to compare teams.
- Evidence-Based Management from Scrum.org gives a value-focused frame: current value, unrealised value, time to market and ability to innovate.
- Review metrics with the team at the Sprint Review and Retrospective, and always look at several together.

### What are Scrum metrics?
**Scrum metrics** are quantitative measures that a Scrum Team uses to make its work transparent and to support inspection and adaptation. They cover whether the team meets its Sprint Goals, how much work it completes, how smoothly work flows, the quality of each Increment, the value delivered to users and the health of the team itself.
People often use "Scrum metrics" and "Scrum KPIs" interchangeably, but there is a useful distinction. A metric is any measure the team finds informative. A **key performance indicator (KPI)** is a measure an organisation has chosen as a critical indicator of progress towards an intended result, usually with a target attached.
|  | Scrum metric | KPI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Help the team inspect and adapt | Show progress towards an organisational result |
| Typical owner | The Scrum Team | Leadership, product or portfolio management |
| Typical examples | Burndown, velocity, cycle time, retro actions completed | Customer satisfaction, adoption, revenue per user, release frequency |
| Review cadence | At least once per Sprint | Monthly, quarterly or per release |
| Target attached? | Usually not; trends matter more | Often yes |
| Risk if misused | Gaming, such as inflated estimates | Local optimisation at the expense of the whole |
The best Scrum KPIs are outcome measures, such as product usage or customer satisfaction, that the team can influence and that link to the Product Goal. Output measures such as velocity make poor KPIs because they are easy to inflate and say nothing about value.

### What the Scrum Guide says about metrics
The [Scrum Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) (2020 edition, still the current official version) does not define any metric. It does not mention velocity, story points or KPIs at all. What it does say is relevant to every metric you choose:
- **Scrum is founded on empiricism and Lean thinking.** Knowledge comes from experience and decisions are based on what is observed. Metrics are one way to observe. See [empiricism in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/).
- **Forecasting practices are optional.** In the Sprint section the Guide says: "Various practices exist to forecast progress, like burn-downs, burn-ups, or cumulative flows. While proven useful, these do not replace the importance of empiricism."
- **Only what has happened can be used for decisions.** The Guide notes that in complex environments what will happen is unknown, so only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making. Every forecast should rest on actual past data.
- **Done work is the evidence.** Work cannot count as part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done. Any metric that counts unfinished work weakens transparency.
- **The Developers forecast their own Sprint.** In Sprint Planning, the Guide says the more the Developers know about their past performance, their upcoming capacity and their Definition of Done, the more confident they will be in their Sprint forecasts.
So metrics are a complementary practice, like story points or user stories. The team chooses them, owns them and changes them when they stop helping. Our guide to [Scrum artifacts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-artifacts/) explains the commitments (Product Goal, Sprint Goal and Definition of Done) that most good metrics are anchored to.

### The six categories of Scrum metrics
A balanced set covers six areas. You do not need every metric below; pick one or two per category that answer questions your team is actually asking.
| Category | Question it answers | Example metrics | Main users |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Goals | Are we achieving what we set out to do? | Sprint Goal success rate, Product Goal progress | Whole Scrum Team, stakeholders |
| Delivery | How much can we complete, and when will it be ready? | Velocity, Sprint burndown, release burnup | Developers, Product Owner |
| Flow | How smoothly and predictably does work move? | Cycle time, throughput, WIP, work item age | Developers, Scrum Master |
| Quality | Is the Increment really done and sustainable? | Escaped defects, Definition of Done adherence, technical debt, change failure rate | Developers |
| Value | Are we building the right thing? | Usage, customer satisfaction, business outcomes | Product Owner, stakeholders |
| Team health | Can we keep working this way? | Happiness or engagement, retrospective actions completed | Scrum Master, whole team |
The categories balance each other. Velocity can rise while quality falls; cycle time can drop because the team only picks easy items; happiness can be high while users are ignored. Looking across categories is what makes the picture trustworthy.

### Goal and delivery metrics
These are the most familiar Scrum metrics. They help the team plan Sprints and answer the stakeholder question "when will it be ready?".

#### Sprint Goal success rate
The **Sprint Goal success rate** is the percentage of Sprints in which the team met its Sprint Goal. Because the Sprint Goal is the single objective for the Sprint, this is the most direct measure of whether the team delivers what it intends.
**Formula:** Sprint Goal success rate = Sprints where the Sprint Goal was met ÷ total Sprints × 100.
Tip
Worked example: over the last ten Sprints, the team met its Sprint Goal in seven. Success rate = 7 ÷ 10 × 100 = 70%. In the Retrospective the team notices that two of the misses came from unplanned production support, so it agrees to reserve some capacity for support in Sprint Planning.
Do not chase 100%. A team that always meets its goal may be setting goals that are too safe. The goal also needs to be outcome-focused ("customers can reset their own password") rather than a list of tickets, or the metric becomes a count of items done.

#### Velocity
**Velocity** is the amount of work, usually in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/), that meets the Definition of Done in a Sprint. Partly finished items count as zero. It is a planning aid for the team, not a productivity score. Our guide to [velocity in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) covers how to calculate, chart and use it in detail.

#### Sprint burndown chart
A **Sprint burndown** plots the work remaining in the Sprint Backlog against the days of the Sprint. The Developers use it, often at the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/), to see whether they are on track for the Sprint Goal. A flat line for several days usually means work is blocked or items are too big to finish in a day or two; a line that jumps up means work was added.

#### Release or Product Goal burnup
A **burnup chart** shows completed work rising over time against a separate line for total scope. Because scope has its own line, it makes scope changes visible, which a burndown hides. It is the most useful chart for longer-range forecasts towards a release or the Product Goal.
Worked example of a burnup forecast:
1. The Product Owner estimates that the remaining work for the next release is 180 points in the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/).
2. Velocity over the last five Sprints was 24, 21, 27, 23 and 25, an average of 24.
3. Middle forecast: 180 ÷ 24 = 7.5, so about 8 Sprints.
4. Pessimistic forecast using the lowest velocity: 180 ÷ 21 ≈ 8.6, so 9 Sprints.
5. Optimistic forecast using the highest velocity: 180 ÷ 27 ≈ 6.7, so 7 Sprints.
6. The forecast is shared as a range: "7 to 9 Sprints, most likely 8, if scope stays as it is". It is updated at every Sprint Review as velocity and scope change.
Giving a range, rather than a single date, is the honest way to reflect uncertainty. Our free [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) has space to record the forecast.

### Flow metrics for Scrum teams
Flow metrics come from Kanban and Lean but work well inside Scrum, especially for teams whose backlog items are small and similar. They measure how work moves rather than how big it was estimated to be.
| Metric | Definition | How to calculate | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cycle time | Time from starting an item to finishing it | Done date minus start date for each item; report the median or 85th percentile | How long a typical item takes; how predictable delivery is |
| Throughput | Number of items finished per period | Count items that meet the Definition of Done each Sprint or week | Delivery rate without needing estimates |
| Work in progress (WIP) | Number of items started but not finished | Count items in active columns on the board | Overload and multitasking; high WIP lengthens cycle time |
| Work item age | How long an unfinished item has been in progress | Today minus start date for each open item | Items at risk of stalling, while there is still time to act |
A practical example: the team's 85th percentile cycle time is six working days. In the middle of a Sprint, one item has been in progress for nine days. Its **age** flags it at the Daily Scrum before it becomes a missed Sprint Goal, and the Developers swarm on it.
Throughput can also replace velocity for forecasting. If the team finishes 10 to 12 items per Sprint and 60 items remain, the forecast is 5 to 6 Sprints, without estimating any item in points.
For definitions, charts and percentile forecasting in more depth, read our guides to [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/), [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) and the [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/), which is one of the forecasting practices the Scrum Guide names.

### Quality metrics
Quality metrics check that "done" really means done. Without them, velocity and throughput can look healthy while problems pile up for later Sprints.
- **Escaped defects.** Defects found after an item met the Definition of Done, often by users in production. Track the count per Sprint and look at the trend.
- **Defect escape rate.** Escaped defects ÷ (escaped defects + defects caught before release) × 100. Example: 4 defects reached production and 36 were caught in the Sprint, so 4 ÷ 40 = 10%.
- **Definition of Done adherence.** The share of completed items that genuinely met every Definition of Done criterion. Some teams check a sample at the Retrospective.
- **Technical debt indicators.** Items such as known shortcuts logged in the backlog, test coverage trends or static analysis warnings. See [technical debt in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/).
- **Change failure rate.** The share of releases or deployments that cause a failure needing a fix or rollback. It is one of the DORA software delivery metrics and appears among the example measures in the Evidence-Based Management Guide.
A rising escaped-defect trend is usually a signal to strengthen the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), for example by adding automated regression tests, rather than a reason to blame individuals.

### Value and outcome metrics
Value metrics answer the question the other categories cannot: are we building the right thing? They are the Product Owner's main evidence for ordering the Product Backlog and the best candidates for KPIs.
| Output measure (what we produced) | Outcome measure (what changed) |
| --- | --- |
| Number of features released | Share of active users who use the new feature |
| Story points completed | Reduction in support tickets about the old process |
| Reports delivered | Time saved per user per week |
| Campaign pages launched | Conversion rate from page visit to sign-up |
Choose outcome measures that the team can influence within a few Sprints and that relate to the Product Goal. Customer satisfaction scores such as CSAT or NPS, product usage, task completion rates and revenue or cost per user are common choices. Review them at the [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/), where stakeholders and the Scrum Team inspect the outcome of the Sprint and decide what to do next.
Outcome data often lags. A feature released this Sprint may only show its effect on usage after a month, so treat value metrics as trends across several Sprints, not as a score for one Sprint.

### Team health metrics
Scrum depends on a self-managing team working at a sustainable pace. Team health metrics give early warning before burnout or disengagement shows up in delivery.
- **Happiness or engagement score.** A quick anonymous rating, such as 1 to 5, collected at each Retrospective, with a short reason.
- **Retrospective actions completed.** The share of improvement actions agreed at the last [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) that were actually done. A low rate suggests the team agrees too many actions or does not add them to the Sprint Backlog.
- **Unplanned work.** The share of capacity spent on work that was not in the Sprint Backlog at Sprint Planning, such as urgent support.
Keep these inside the team. Sharing an individual's happiness score, or ranking teams by it, destroys the honesty the metric depends on.

### Evidence-Based Management
**Evidence-Based Management (EBM)** is a framework from Scrum.org for measuring and improving the value an organisation delivers. The EBM Guide was first released in 2015 and has been updated several times, most recently in 2024. It is not part of the Scrum Guide, but it fits naturally with Scrum's focus on goals and empiricism.
EBM groups measures into four **Key Value Areas**:
| Key Value Area | Question | Example measures named in the EBM Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current Value | How much value does the product deliver today? | Customer satisfaction, employee satisfaction, customer usage index, revenue per employee |
| Unrealised Value | How much more value could the product deliver? | Market share, customer or user satisfaction gap |
| Time to Market | How quickly can we deliver and learn? | Release frequency, lead time, customer cycle time, time to learn, mean time to repair |
| Ability to Innovate | How effectively can we deliver new capabilities? | Innovation rate, defect trends, technical debt, change failure rate, time spent context-switching |
EBM also describes three levels of goals: a long-term **Strategic Goal**, nearer-term **Intermediate Goals**, and **Immediate Tactical Goals** that teams pursue through small experiments. In Scrum terms, the Product Goal often sits at the intermediate level and each Sprint Goal is an immediate tactical step.
For most teams the practical lesson is simple: make sure at least one of your metrics sits in each value area, so you are not measuring speed alone. The [OKR template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/okr-template/) is a convenient way to record goals and the measures you will use to judge them.

### Which metrics to review at each Scrum event
Metrics are only useful if someone looks at them at the moment a decision is made. Scrum's events give natural points to do that.
| Event | Metrics to look at | Decision they support |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Planning | Average velocity or throughput, capacity, Sprint Goal success trend | How much to select and how ambitious the Sprint Goal should be |
| Daily Scrum | Sprint burndown, WIP, work item age | What to swarm on today; what is blocked |
| Sprint Review | Product Goal or release burnup, value and outcome measures, forecast range | What to do next; changes to the Product Backlog and release forecast |
| Sprint Retrospective | Sprint Goal met, escaped defects, cycle time trend, happiness, retro actions completed | Which one or two improvements to make next Sprint |
| Backlog refinement (ongoing) | Item size distribution, age of top backlog items | Which items to split or clarify before Sprint Planning |
Our guide to [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) shows how the forecasting discussion fits into that event.

### Scrum metrics for leadership and stakeholders
Managers often ask for "Scrum KPIs" to report upwards. That is reasonable, but the metrics a team uses to improve are not always the right ones to report.
| Share widely | Keep mostly inside the team |
| --- | --- |
| Product Goal progress and forecast ranges | Velocity in story points |
| Value and outcome measures | Sprint burndown |
| Release frequency and lead time | Individual workload or task counts |
| Escaped defects trend | Happiness scores |
| Sprint Goal success rate | Retrospective details |
Story points are relative to one team, so a stakeholder who sees team A's velocity of 40 and team B's of 20 will draw the wrong conclusion. Forecast ranges, outcomes and quality trends answer the questions leaders actually have: when, what value and how reliably. For metrics across several teams or a whole programme, see our guide to [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).

### How to choose and introduce Scrum metrics
A new metric works best when the team chooses it to answer a real question. This step-by-step process keeps the set small and useful.
1. **Start from questions, not dashboards.** In a Retrospective, ask what the team, Product Owner and stakeholders most need to know. For example: "Will we hit the release?", "Why do items take so long?", "Are users adopting what we ship?"
2. **Pick one measure per question.** Match each question to a metric from the six categories. Aim for four to six metrics in total.
3. **Agree definitions in writing.** Decide exactly what counts: when does an item "start", which defects count as escaped, what is the scale for happiness. Write it in the team's working agreement.
4. **Automate collection where possible.** Most Scrum tools produce burndown, velocity and cycle time automatically if the board reflects reality.
5. **Collect a baseline for three to five Sprints** before drawing conclusions. Single Sprints are noisy.
6. **Review at the right event** using the event table above, and ask "what will we do differently because of this?" each time.
7. **Pair every speed metric with a quality metric.** For example velocity with escaped defects, or throughput with Definition of Done adherence.
8. **Retire metrics that nobody acts on.** Every few months, drop any measure that has not changed a decision.
If you are setting up Sprints for the first time, our free [Sprint Planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) captures the Sprint Goal, capacity and selected items, which gives you the raw data for Sprint Goal success and velocity.

### Worked example: a Scrum team dashboard
Here is a one-page dashboard for a fictional six-person team working in two-week Sprints. It shows six Sprints and one metric from most categories.
| Sprint | Sprint Goal met? | Velocity (points) | Throughput (items) | Cycle time, 85th pct (days) | Escaped defects | Happiness (1–5) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 14 | Yes | 24 | 11 | 6 | 1 | 3.8 |
| 15 | Yes | 26 | 12 | 6 | 0 | 3.9 |
| 16 | No | 22 | 9 | 8 | 2 | 3.4 |
| 17 | No | 27 | 10 | 9 | 4 | 3.1 |
| 18 | Yes | 23 | 11 | 7 | 3 | 3.3 |
| 19 | Yes | 24 | 12 | 6 | 1 | 3.7 |
How the team read it at the Retrospective after Sprint 17:
- **Velocity alone looked good.** Sprint 17 had the highest velocity of the period, 27 points.
- **But the goal was missed twice in a row**, cycle time rose from 6 to 9 days and escaped defects jumped to 4.
- **Happiness fell** from 3.9 to 3.1. Team comments mentioned pressure to finish a large stakeholder request and skipping some testing.
- **Diagnosis:** the team had pulled in more work than usual, started too many items at once and let the Definition of Done slip to show progress.
The team agreed two actions: a WIP limit of four items in progress, and adding automated regression tests to the Definition of Done. By Sprint 19, cycle time and escaped defects were back to normal and both Sprint Goals had been met, at a slightly lower but steadier velocity.
Tip
Look at metrics together and as trends. Any one of the columns above, read on its own, would have told the wrong story about Sprint 17.

### Common mistakes with Scrum metrics
Most metric problems come from how numbers are used, not from the numbers themselves. The idea often summarised as Goodhart's law applies: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
- **Setting velocity targets.** Teams respond by inflating estimates, so velocity rises while real output does not.
- **Comparing or ranking teams.** Story points and even cycle times depend on each team's context and definitions.
- **Using team metrics in individual performance reviews.** People stop reporting problems honestly, which undermines transparency, the first pillar of empiricism.
- **Counting unfinished work.** Giving partial credit for items that do not meet the Definition of Done makes forecasts unreliable.
- **Tracking too many metrics.** A dashboard of twenty charts that nobody discusses adds work and no insight.
- **Measuring activity instead of outcomes.** Hours logged, tickets closed or lines of code say little about value.
- **Optimising one metric at the expense of others,** such as speed over quality or throughput over customer value.
- **Collecting data nobody acts on.** If a metric never changes a decision, drop it.
The [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) can help by coaching the team and stakeholders on what each metric does and does not show, and by keeping the conversation focused on improvement rather than judgement.

### Tools for tracking Scrum metrics
You can track every metric on this page in a spreadsheet, but most teams let their Scrum tool collect the data. Jira Software is widely used by software teams for its Sprint reports, burndown and velocity charts. [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) offers sprint reporting with burndown, burnup, velocity and cumulative flow. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool overall, suits organisations that need configurable dashboards across many teams and projects, including Agile and non-software work.
Whatever you use, the tool can only report what the board shows, so keep item states up to date and make sure "done" on the board means the Definition of Done.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the most important Scrum metrics?**
There is no official list, but a strong starter set is Sprint Goal success rate, velocity or throughput for forecasting, cycle time, escaped defects, one value or outcome measure and a team health measure. Together they cover goals, delivery, flow, quality, value and sustainability.

**Q: Which metrics does the Scrum Guide require?**
None. The 2020 Scrum Guide says various practices exist to forecast progress, such as burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows, and that while proven useful, these do not replace the importance of empiricism. Velocity and story points are not mentioned.

**Q: Is velocity a KPI?**
It should not be. Velocity is a team-specific planning aid based on relative estimates, so it is easy to inflate and cannot be compared between teams. Use it to forecast, and choose outcome measures such as usage or customer satisfaction as KPIs.

**Q: What is the difference between a Scrum metric and a KPI?**
A Scrum metric is any measure the team uses to inspect and adapt, such as a burndown or cycle time. A KPI is a measure an organisation has selected as a key indicator of progress towards a result, usually with a target, such as customer satisfaction or release frequency.

**Q: How do you calculate Sprint Goal success rate?**
Divide the number of Sprints in which the team met its Sprint Goal by the total number of Sprints, then multiply by 100. For example, seven goals met in ten Sprints gives a 70% success rate.

**Q: What is the difference between a burndown and a burnup chart?**
A burndown shows work remaining falling towards zero. A burnup shows completed work rising towards a separate total scope line, so it makes scope changes visible and is better for release and Product Goal forecasts.

**Q: What are escaped defects?**
Escaped defects are defects found after an item was considered done, often by users in production. A rising trend usually means the Definition of Done needs strengthening, for example with more automated testing.

**Q: What metrics should a Scrum Master track?**
Scrum Masters usually focus on metrics that reveal how well Scrum is working: Sprint Goal success, cycle time and work item age, WIP, retrospective actions completed and team happiness. The team, not the Scrum Master alone, should own and interpret them.

**Q: What metrics should a Product Owner track?**
Product Owners need forecast and value measures: release or Product Goal burnup, forecast ranges from velocity or throughput, and outcome measures such as usage, customer satisfaction or the business result the Product Goal targets.

**Q: Can flow metrics be used in Scrum?**
Yes. Cycle time, throughput, WIP and work item age work well alongside Scrum, and cumulative flow is one of the forecasting practices the Scrum Guide names. Some teams forecast from throughput instead of story points.

**Q: Should Scrum metrics be used for performance reviews?**
Generally no. Using team metrics to judge individuals encourages gaming and hiding problems, which undermines transparency and empiricism. Review metrics as a team to decide improvements.

**Q: How does Evidence-Based Management relate to Scrum metrics?**
Evidence-Based Management is a Scrum.org framework that groups value measures into four Key Value Areas: current value, unrealised value, time to market and ability to innovate. It helps teams and leaders balance delivery metrics with measures of value.

**Q: How do you measure the success of a Scrum team?**
Look at whether it reliably meets Sprint Goals, delivers Increments that meet the Definition of Done with few escaped defects, moves measurably towards the Product Goal and creates value users notice, while keeping a sustainable pace.

# Scrum of Scrums: How to Coordinate Multiple Scrum Teams

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: What a Scrum of Scrums is, who attends, how often it meets, a sample agenda, common pitfalls, and how it fits with Scrum@Scale, LeSS and SAFe.


## Scrum of Scrums: How to Coordinate Multiple Scrum Teams
A Scrum of Scrums is a meeting, and a structure, in which representatives of several Scrum Teams coordinate their work. It is the simplest way to scale Scrum when a few teams build one product together.
- Published 19 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- A Scrum of Scrums coordinates several Scrum Teams through representatives.
- It focuses on dependencies, integration and shared impediments.
- It is the basic building block of Scrum@Scale.

### How it works
- Each team sends a representative, often a Developer with the right technical knowledge, sometimes the Scrum Master.
- Representatives meet regularly, from daily to a few times a week, often for about 15 minutes, with time afterwards for problem-solving.
- The focus is integration, dependencies and impediments that affect more than one team.
- Representatives share the outcome with their own teams.

### Sample agenda
1. What has my team done since we last met that affects other teams?
2. What will my team do next that affects other teams?
3. What impediments is my team facing that others could help with?
4. Are we about to put something in another team's way?
5. Problem-solving on the issues raised (after the core time-box).

### Tips
- Keep a shared board of cross-team dependencies and impediments.
- Send the person best placed to discuss current dependencies, which may change over time.
- Align Sprint cadences so teams plan and review together.
- Hold a joint Sprint Review for the integrated product.

### Pitfalls
- Turning it into a status report for managers.
- Representatives who can't make decisions or don't report back.
- Too many teams in one meeting; split into layers if needed.

### How it relates to scaling frameworks
The Scrum of Scrums is a core building block of [Scrum@Scale](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-at-scale/). Similar coordination appears in [LeSS](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/) and in SAFe's ART Sync; see [Agile Release Train](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-train/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: How many teams can a Scrum of Scrums coordinate?**
Typically up to about five to ten teams. Beyond that, organisations add another layer, sometimes called a Scrum of Scrums of Scrums.

**Q: Is the Scrum of Scrums part of the Scrum Guide?**
No. It is a widely used scaling practice, not part of the official Scrum framework.

**Q: What is a Scrum of Scrums?**
A coordination meeting in which representatives from several Scrum Teams discuss dependencies, integration and shared impediments.

**Q: Who attends a Scrum of Scrums?**
One representative per team, often a Developer with relevant technical knowledge or the Scrum Master. The best person can change depending on current dependencies.

**Q: How often does a Scrum of Scrums meet?**
Anywhere from daily to a few times a week, depending on how many dependencies exist. Many keep the core discussion to about 15 minutes.

**Q: Who created the Scrum of Scrums?**
The practice is generally credited to Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber, who used it to coordinate multiple teams in the 1990s.

**Q: What is the difference between a Daily Scrum and a Scrum of Scrums?**
The Daily Scrum is for one team's Developers to plan their day towards the Sprint Goal. A Scrum of Scrums coordinates work between teams.

**Q: What is a Scrum of Scrums Master?**
In Scrum@Scale, the person who facilitates the Scrum of Scrums and helps remove impediments across teams. See [Scrum@Scale](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-at-scale/).

**Q: How does the Scrum of Scrums relate to SAFe?**
SAFe uses similar coordination events, such as the ART Sync, to align teams on an Agile Release Train. See [SAFe](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/).

**Q: What makes a Scrum of Scrums effective?**
Representatives who can make decisions, a shared board of dependencies and impediments, aligned Sprint cadences and a focus on problems rather than status.

**Q: Is the Scrum of Scrums a status meeting?**
It should not be. Its purpose is to surface and resolve cross-team issues, not to report progress to managers.

# Scrum Principles and Values: Pillars, Values and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-principles-and-values/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum principles and values explained: the three pillars and five values from the Scrum Guide, real examples, a team workshop and how to live them.


## Scrum Principles and Values: Pillars, Values and Examples
Scrum principles and values are the three pillars of empiricism (transparency, inspection and adaptation) and the five Scrum values (commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage) set out in the 2020 Scrum Guide. The pillars describe how a Scrum Team learns its way through complex work; the values describe how people need to behave for that learning to work. This guide explains each one, shows what they look like in real teams and gives you a step-by-step way to build them into your own.
- Published 5 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking. Its three pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation; each one depends on the one before it.
- The five Scrum values are commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. They were added to the Scrum Guide in 2016 and remain in the 2020 version.
- The values are what make the pillars work: without openness and courage, information stays hidden and inspection is based on a false picture.
- Commitment in Scrum means commitment to goals and to each other, not a promise to finish every item in the Sprint Backlog.
- Lists of "six Scrum principles" (such as self-organisation and time-boxing) come from training bodies, not from the Scrum Guide itself.
- Values are built through behaviour, not posters: agree what each one looks like, write working agreements and inspect them in the Sprint Retrospective.

### What are Scrum principles and values?
**Scrum principles and values are the theory and behaviours that hold the Scrum framework together.** The principles are the three pillars of empiricism (transparency, inspection and adaptation) that let a team learn from experience. The values are commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage, the behaviours that make those pillars work in a real team.
The [Scrum Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/), written by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland and last updated in November 2020, does not use a heading called "principles". It says Scrum is founded on **empiricism** (knowledge comes from experience and decisions are based on what is observed) and **lean thinking** (reduce waste and focus on the essentials). It then describes three pillars that make empiricism work and five values that people need to live. When people talk about "Scrum principles", they almost always mean those pillars. The table shows which elements are official and which come from elsewhere.
| Element | What it includes | Source | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum theory | Empiricism and lean thinking | 2020 Scrum Guide | Official |
| Three pillars | Transparency, inspection, adaptation | 2020 Scrum Guide | Official |
| Five values | Commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage | Scrum Guide since 2016 | Official |
| Self-managing teams | The team decides who does what, when and how | 2020 Scrum Guide | Official (replaced "self-organising" in 2020) |
| Six Scrum principles | Empirical process control, self-organisation, collaboration, value-based prioritisation, time-boxing, iterative development | SBOK Guide (SCRUMstudy) | Not part of the Scrum Guide, but consistent with it |
| Agile values and principles | Four values and twelve principles | Agile Manifesto (2001) | Wider Agile context, not Scrum-specific |

### How pillars, values and the framework fit together
It helps to think of Scrum in four layers, each resting on the one below:
1. **Values** shape behaviour: whether people speak up, focus and support each other.
2. **Pillars** depend on that behaviour: work is only transparent if people are open.
3. **Events and artifacts** give the pillars structure: the [Scrum events](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/) are the points to inspect and adapt, and the [Scrum artifacts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-artifacts/) make the work visible.
4. **Outcomes** follow: valuable Increments, problems found early and a team that improves every Sprint.
The Scrum Guide says that when the values are embodied by the Scrum Team and the people they work with, the pillars come to life and build trust. Teams that copy the events but skip the values get meetings that change nothing.
Tip
If your Sprint Review never changes the Product Backlog and your Retrospective never changes how you work, the pillars are not working. Look at the values first.

### The three pillars of Scrum
The three pillars are a chain. The Scrum Guide puts it plainly: transparency enables inspection, and inspection enables adaptation. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful; inspection without adaptation is pointless.

#### Transparency
Transparency means the process and the work are visible to the people doing the work and the people receiving it. Important decisions are based on the state of the three artifacts, so if those artifacts are incomplete or misleading, decisions carry more risk. In practice transparency looks like a Product Backlog anyone can read, a [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) and [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) that show the real state of work, and a shared [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) so "done" means the same thing to everyone.
**Warning signs:** items marked done that still need testing, a separate "real" plan kept outside the backlog, or status reports that differ from what the board shows.

#### Inspection
Inspection means frequently and diligently examining the Scrum artifacts and progress towards the agreed goals to spot problems early. It is not an audit by outsiders; the Scrum Team inspects its own work, often together with stakeholders. Scrum's events provide a regular rhythm for it, so inspection does not depend on someone remembering to ask.
**Warning signs:** Daily Scrums that are status reports to one person, Sprint Reviews that are slide shows rather than a look at the working Increment, or retrospectives where nobody mentions the real problem.

#### Adaptation
Adaptation means adjusting the process or the product as soon as possible when inspection shows something has drifted outside acceptable limits. The Scrum Guide notes that adaptation becomes harder when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing, which is why Scrum gives the team authority over how it works.
**Warning signs:** the same retrospective actions every Sprint, a backlog order that never changes after stakeholder feedback, or a plan that cannot change without approval from outside the team.

### Where the pillars appear in Scrum events and artifacts
Every Scrum event is a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt something. The Sprint itself is the container for the other four.
| Event | Inspect | Adapt |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | Product Backlog, Product Goal, past performance and capacity | The Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog |
| [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) | Progress towards the Sprint Goal | The plan for the next working day; the Sprint Backlog |
| [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) | The Increment and the outcome of the Sprint, with stakeholders | The Product Backlog and, if needed, the Product Goal |
| [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | How the Sprint went: people, interactions, processes, tools, Definition of Done | Ways of working; improvements added to the next Sprint |
The three artifacts provide the transparency that inspection depends on, and each has a commitment that gives it a clear focus: the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) has the Product Goal, the Sprint Backlog has the Sprint Goal and the Increment has the Definition of Done. Our [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) and [Sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) keep both visible.
See our guide to [empiricism in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/) for the theory behind the pillars and four more worked examples.

### The five Scrum values explained
The Scrum Guide says that successful use of Scrum depends on people becoming more proficient in living five values. Here is what each one means, what it looks like and how it is commonly misread.

#### Commitment
The Scrum Team commits to achieving its goals and to supporting each other. The goals are the Product Goal and the Sprint Goal, and the Definition of Done is a commitment about quality.
- **In practice:** the team works together towards the Sprint Goal, swarms on blocked items and keeps its working agreements.
- **Example:** a Developer who finishes early helps a colleague test a story that is at risk, rather than pulling new work into the Sprint.
- **Misreading:** treating commitment as a promise to complete every item in the Sprint Backlog regardless of what is learned. The Scrum Guide treats the selected work as a forecast and makes the Sprint Goal the commitment.

#### Focus
The team's primary focus is on the work of the Sprint so that it makes the best possible progress towards its goals.
- **In practice:** limit work in progress, finish before starting, protect the Sprint from unplanned requests and route new ideas to the Product Owner.
- **Example:** a stakeholder asks a Developer directly for a quick change. The Developer thanks them and takes it to the Product Owner, who decides whether it goes into the Product Backlog.
- **Misreading:** focus as tunnel vision, where the team ignores stakeholder feedback or important information until the Sprint ends.

#### Openness
The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges. Openness is the value most directly behind transparency.
- **In practice:** raise risks and blockers as soon as they appear, show unfinished work honestly, say "I don't know" and stay open to other people's ideas.
- **Example:** at the Daily Scrum a Developer says a third-party API is returning errors and the story may not be finished, three days before the Sprint Review rather than during it.
- **Misreading:** openness only within the team. The Guide extends it to stakeholders, so the Sprint Review should show what is genuinely done and what is not.

#### Respect
Scrum Team members respect each other to be capable, independent people, and are respected as such by the people they work with.
- **In practice:** trust Developers to decide how to do the work, assume good intent, listen to different views and respect the Product Owner's decisions about order and value.
- **Example:** a manager who wants a feature sooner talks to the Product Owner rather than reassigning tasks inside the team.
- **Misreading:** respect as avoiding disagreement. Respectful teams disagree openly about ideas while staying respectful of the people.

#### Courage
Scrum Team members have the courage to do the right thing and to work on tough problems.
- **In practice:** say no to work that would break the Definition of Done, challenge unrealistic expectations, admit mistakes and raise uncomfortable topics in the Retrospective.
- **Example:** the Product Owner tells a senior stakeholder that the release date holds but two features will move to the next Sprint, instead of letting the team cut testing.
- **Misreading:** courage as heroics, such as working through the night to hide a problem. That trades the team's sustainability for short-term appearances.

### How the values make the pillars work
Each value supports one or more pillars. When a value is missing, you can usually see which pillar breaks first.
| Value | Main pillar it supports | What breaks without it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Openness | Transparency | Problems stay hidden, so inspection looks at a false picture |
| Courage | Transparency and adaptation | People see the problem but do not raise it or act on it |
| Focus | Inspection | Work is scattered, so there is little finished to inspect |
| Commitment | Adaptation | Changes agreed in events are not followed through |
| Respect | All three | People stop sharing honest information because they expect blame |
The common thread is **trust**: a team that trusts its leaders tells them the truth early; a team that expects blame tells them what they want to hear.

### Scrum values in everyday behaviour
The table turns the values into behaviour you can observe and discuss.
| Value | Looks like | Does not look like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commitment | Working together towards the Sprint Goal | Committing to unrealistic scope to please others |
| Focus | Finishing Sprint work before starting new tasks | Constant context switching between projects |
| Openness | Raising a risk at the Daily Scrum | Hiding a problem until the Sprint Review |
| Respect | Letting Developers decide how to do the work | Assigning tasks over their heads |
| Respect | Disagreeing about ideas, not people | Blaming individuals in the Retrospective |
| Courage | Telling stakeholders a feature is not ready | Releasing work that does not meet the Definition of Done |
| Courage | Admitting a mistake and proposing a fix | Covering up an error to protect your reputation |

### Scrum values by accountability
Everyone in and around the [Scrum Team](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) lives the same five values, but they show up differently depending on the accountability.
| Who | What living the values looks like |
| --- | --- |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Keeps the Product Backlog transparent and ordered; explains the reasons behind priorities (openness); says no to low-value requests (courage); respects the Developers' estimates and choices about how to build |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Models the values rather than enforcing them; makes impediments visible; protects the team's focus; coaches the organisation when behaviour outside the team undermines the values |
| Developers | Commit to the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done; raise risks early; help each other; hold each other accountable as professionals |
| Managers and stakeholders | Respect the team's self-management; bring requests through the Product Owner; respond to bad news with help, not blame; attend the Sprint Review and give honest feedback |
The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness, so fostering the values is part of the role, but that does not mean policing them. A Scrum Master models them and removes the conditions, such as blame or overload, that make them hard to live. Our guide to [servant leadership in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/servant-leadership-in-scrum/) covers this style in more depth.
Tip
Managers have a big influence on openness and courage. If bad news is punished even once, teams learn to hide it. Thank people for raising problems early, especially when the news is unwelcome.

### Worked example: one Sprint with and without the values
The following example is **illustrative**: the team, product and dates are invented to show how the values and pillars affect a real Sprint.
A seven-person team is building a booking feature for a dentists' appointment app. The Sprint is two weeks long and the Sprint Goal is: "Patients can book and cancel an appointment online." On day three, a Developer finds that the practice-management system the app connects to rejects cancellations made less than 24 hours ahead.

#### Version A: the values are weak
- **Day 3:** the Developer assumes they can find a workaround and says nothing at the Daily Scrum (no openness).
- **Days 4 to 8:** two Developers start extra stories to look busy while the problem is unresolved (no focus). A manager asks one of them to fix an unrelated bug, which they do quietly (no respect for the Product Owner's ordering).
- **Day 9:** the workaround fails. To protect the Sprint Review, the team marks cancellation as done without the edge-case tests (no courage, no commitment to the Definition of Done).
- **Sprint Review:** stakeholders see a working demo and approve a release. Two weeks after go-live, patients start receiving cancellation errors.

#### Version B: the values are strong
- **Day 3:** the Developer raises the issue at the Daily Scrum. The team updates the board so the risk is visible (openness, transparency).
- **Day 3, afternoon:** the Product Owner checks with the practice manager and confirms the 24-hour rule is intentional (inspection).
- **Day 4:** the Product Owner and Developers renegotiate the Sprint scope: the app will block late cancellations and show the practice's phone number instead (adaptation, commitment to the goal rather than the original plan).
- **Days 4 to 9:** the team swarms on the remaining work; the manager is asked to raise the unrelated bug with the Product Owner (focus, respect).
- **Sprint Review:** the team shows exactly what is done. Stakeholders ask for clearer wording on the error message, which goes to the top of the backlog (openness, inspection, adaptation).
| Measure | Version A | Version B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When the problem became visible | After release | Day 3 of the Sprint |
| Sprint Goal met | Apparently, but not really | Yes, with an agreed change to scope |
| Definition of Done | Broken | Kept |
| Stakeholder trust after the Sprint | Falls once defects appear | Rises because there were no surprises |
The events and artifacts were identical in both versions; only the behaviour differed.

### How to embed Scrum values in your team, step by step
Values cannot be installed, but they can be made explicit, practised and inspected like anything else in Scrum.
1. **Explain the why.** Link each value to the pillar it supports and to a problem the team has actually had.
2. **Define observable behaviours.** For each value, list two or three things you would see if it were present and absent. The behaviour table above is a starting point.
3. **Turn them into working agreements.** Pick five to eight specific agreements, such as "we raise blockers at the Daily Scrum, even if we think we can solve them" or "nobody marks an item done until it meets the Definition of Done".
4. **Make them visible.** Put the working agreements next to the Scrum board or in the team's shared space. Visibility is transparency applied to the team's own process.
5. **Agree how outsiders interact with the team.** Share with managers and stakeholders how to bring requests (through the Product Owner) and how to respond to bad news. Many value problems start outside the team.
6. **Model them from the top.** The Product Owner, Scrum Master and managers go first: admit their own mistakes, share uncomfortable information and respect the team's decisions.
7. **Inspect them in the Retrospective.** Every few Sprints, use a values exercise (see the self-assessment below) and pick one improvement. Our [Sprint Retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) has space for this, and our list of [retrospective games](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective-games/) offers more formats.
8. **Recognise the behaviour.** When someone raises a risk early or pushes back on a broken Definition of Done, say so publicly. What gets recognised gets repeated.
9. **Adapt the agreements.** Remove agreements that the team now follows naturally and add new ones as the context changes, such as new team members or a new stakeholder group.

### A 90-minute Scrum values workshop
If you want a ready-made session for steps 1 to 4, this agenda works for teams of up to about ten people, in person or remote.
| Time | Activity | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 to 10 min | Check-in: each person names a time a team they were in worked really well, and why | Shared language about good teamwork |
| 10 to 20 min | Short explanation of the pillars and five values and how they connect | Common understanding |
| 20 to 45 min | Small groups take one or two values each and list "looks like" and "does not look like" behaviours from their own work | Behaviour lists for all five values |
| 45 to 60 min | Each group presents; the whole team adds or challenges | Agreed behaviours |
| 60 to 75 min | Dot-vote the behaviours most worth working on and turn the top five to eight into working agreements | Draft working agreements |
| 75 to 85 min | Agree how the agreements will be displayed, shared with stakeholders and reviewed | Visibility and review plan |
| 85 to 90 min | Close: one word each on how they feel about the agreements | Quick read of buy-in |
Keep the output to one page the team will actually use.

### Scrum values self-assessment
Use these questions in a Retrospective. Ask each person to score each value from 1 (rarely true) to 5 (almost always true), anonymously if trust is still low, then discuss the lowest score and the biggest spread of opinion.
| Value | Question | Healthy signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commitment | Do we pursue the Sprint Goal together, even when it means helping outside our speciality? | Items are swarmed; few items sit half-finished at Sprint end |
| Focus | Do we finish what we start before taking on more? | Low work in progress; unplanned requests go through the Product Owner |
| Openness | Would anyone here raise a problem on the day they found it? | Blockers appear on the board within a day |
| Respect | Do we trust each other's judgement and challenge ideas, not people? | Disagreement happens in the open and is resolved |
| Courage | Have we said no to anything this Sprint that would have hurt quality or the goal? | The Definition of Done holds under pressure |
Track the trend over several Sprints, and never use the scores to compare teams or individuals; that would undermine the openness you are trying to build.

### Other principles often taught with Scrum
Because the Scrum Guide is short, training bodies and authors have published their own lists of Scrum principles. The best known is the six principles in the SBOK Guide from SCRUMstudy. They are consistent with the Scrum Guide but are not part of its official text, so exam questions on the Scrum Guide will not use them.
| Principle (SBOK) | Closest Scrum Guide equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| Empirical process control | Empiricism and the three pillars |
| Self-organisation | Self-managing Scrum Teams |
| Collaboration | Cross-functional teams working together and with stakeholders |
| Value-based prioritisation | The Product Owner ordering the Product Backlog to maximise value |
| Time-boxing | Fixed-length Sprints and maximum durations for each event |
| Iterative development | Delivering a usable Increment every Sprint |

#### Self-managing versus self-organising
Earlier versions of the Scrum Guide described Development Teams as self-organising. The 2020 Guide uses **self-managing**, meaning the Scrum Team decides internally who does what, when and how.

#### Lean thinking
The 2020 Guide added lean thinking alongside empiricism: reducing waste and focusing on the essentials. In practice that means small batches, finishing work and removing anything that does not add value. Our comparison of [Scrum vs Lean](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-lean/) explains how the two ideas fit.

#### Scrum values compared with other Agile values
The [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/) has four values and twelve principles that apply to all Agile approaches. Extreme Programming (XP) has its own values: communication, simplicity, feedback, courage and respect, so courage and respect appear in both. The Scrum values are the Scrum-specific expression of the broader [Agile mindset](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-mindset/).

### Common mistakes with Scrum principles and values
- **Values as wall posters.** Printing the five values without agreeing what they mean in behaviour changes nothing. Define observable behaviours.
- **Reading commitment as a scope promise.** Treating the Sprint Backlog as a contract leads to overtime, cut corners and hidden problems. Commit to the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done.
- **Using velocity as a target.** Pressuring teams to raise [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) encourages inflated estimates and destroys transparency.
- **Openness inside the team only.** If the Sprint Review hides unfinished work from stakeholders, transparency fails at the point where it matters most.
- **Confusing respect with politeness.** Avoiding difficult conversations to keep the peace lets problems grow. Respect allows honest disagreement.
- **Blaming people for bad news.** One reaction like this teaches the team to stay quiet. Respond to problems with questions and help.
- **Leaving managers out.** Many value problems, such as interrupting the team or reassigning work, come from outside the Scrum Team. Include managers and stakeholders in the conversation.
- **Mixing up official and unofficial principles.** For a Scrum Guide-based exam, learn the pillars and values from the Guide, not from SBOK-style lists. Our guide to [Scrum certification and training](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/) compares the main options.
Read our [guide to the Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) to see how each accountability supports the values.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the 5 Scrum values?**
Commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. The Scrum Team commits to its goals and to supporting each other, focuses on the work of the Sprint, is open about the work and its challenges, respects each other as capable people and has the courage to do the right thing and work on tough problems.

**Q: What are the three pillars of Scrum?**
Transparency, inspection and adaptation. Together they make empiricism work: the work is made visible, it is inspected frequently, and the product or process is adjusted as soon as something drifts off course.

**Q: What are the principles of Scrum?**
The Scrum Guide says Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking, supported by the three pillars of transparency, inspection and adaptation. Some training bodies, such as SCRUMstudy's SBOK Guide, add a list of six principles, but those are not part of the official Scrum Guide.

**Q: Why are the Scrum values important?**
Because empiricism only works with honest information. Without openness, courage and respect, people hide problems, inspection is based on a false picture and adaptation comes too late. The values build the trust that makes the pillars work.

**Q: When were the Scrum values added to the Scrum Guide?**
The five values were added in an update announced in July 2016 and remain in the current 2020 Scrum Guide. They were discussed in Scrum writing well before that.

**Q: Who is responsible for the Scrum values?**
Everyone on the Scrum Team lives the values, and the Guide extends them to the people the team works with. The Scrum Master helps the team and organisation understand and apply them, mainly by modelling them and removing obstacles, not by enforcing them.

**Q: Which Scrum value is the most important?**
The Scrum Guide does not rank them. In practice, openness and courage often need the most attention because they decide whether problems surface early.

**Q: Is self-organisation a Scrum principle?**
Not in the current Scrum Guide's wording. The 2020 Guide describes Scrum Teams as self-managing, meaning they decide who does what, when and how. Self-organisation appears as a principle in some training frameworks and in earlier versions of the Guide.

**Q: What does commitment mean in Scrum?**
Commitment to achieving the team's goals and to supporting each other. It does not mean promising to finish every Sprint Backlog item; those items are a forecast. Each artifact also has a commitment: the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done.

**Q: How do Scrum values relate to the Agile Manifesto?**
Both put people, collaboration and responding to change at the centre. The Manifesto applies to all Agile approaches; the Scrum values describe the behaviours that make Scrum work.

**Q: How can a team practise the Scrum values?**
Agree what each value looks like in behaviour, turn the most important behaviours into working agreements, make them visible and inspect them in the Sprint Retrospective.

**Q: What happens if a team ignores the Scrum values?**
Events and artifacts become rituals. Information gets hidden, trust drops and problems are discovered late. Teams often keep the meetings but lose the benefits.
