# The Scrum Process: Phases, Steps and the Sprint Cycle

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-process-and-phases/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: The Scrum process step by step: what happens before the first Sprint, each step of the Sprint cycle, phase models compared and a worked example.


## The Scrum Process: Phases, Steps and the Sprint Cycle
The Scrum process is the repeating cycle a Scrum Team follows to turn an ordered Product Backlog into usable Increments: plan a Sprint, build and inspect the work every day, review the result with stakeholders, improve how the team works, then start the next Sprint straight away. The official Scrum Guide does not divide Scrum into phases, but several popular models do. This guide walks through each step in order, shows who does what with which inputs and outputs, compares the phase models with the Scrum Guide 2020, and follows a worked example across three Sprints.
- Published 6 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- The Scrum process is a cycle of back-to-back Sprints, each one month or less, in which a Scrum Team turns Product Backlog items into a usable Increment.
- Inside every Sprint the steps are the same: Sprint Planning, daily work with a Daily Scrum, ongoing backlog refinement, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.
- The 2020 Scrum Guide has no phases. Pregame, game and postgame (Schwaber, 1995) and the five SBOK phases are other models, useful for teaching but not official Scrum.
- Before the first Sprint you need a Product Goal, a first ordered Product Backlog, a Scrum Team, a Definition of Done and a Sprint calendar. Scrum does not define a Sprint Zero.
- The output of each Sprint is the input to the next: a Done Increment, an adapted Product Backlog and at least one improvement to how the team works.
- Releases are not a separate phase. A team can release whenever an Increment is Done, including several times within a Sprint.

### What is the Scrum process?
The **Scrum process** is the sequence of steps a Scrum Team repeats to deliver value: the Product Owner orders the work in a Product Backlog, the team turns a selection of it into a usable Increment during a fixed-length Sprint, the team and stakeholders inspect the result, and the plan is adjusted for the next Sprint. It is a cycle, not a line.
That four-step summary comes almost directly from the 2020 Scrum Guide, which describes Scrum 'in a nutshell' as: a Product Owner orders the work for a complex problem into a Product Backlog; the Scrum Team turns a selection of the work into an Increment of value during a Sprint; the Scrum Team and its stakeholders inspect the results and adjust for the next Sprint; repeat. A Scrum Master fosters the environment in which this happens.
Everything in the process happens inside **Sprints**. The Scrum Guide calls the Sprint 'the heartbeat of Scrum' and treats it as a container for the other four events: [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/), the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/), the [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) and the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/). A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends, so there is no gap, no hand-over phase and no separate testing stage.
This guide follows the 2020 Scrum Guide, still the current official version (checked 26 October 2026). New to the framework? Start with [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/).

### The Scrum process at a glance
The table shows each step of the Scrum process, who leads it, what goes in and what comes out. The time-boxes are the Scrum Guide maximums for a one-month Sprint; shorter Sprints usually use less time.
| Step | Who leads | Main inputs | Main outputs | Time-box |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Set the Product Goal and order the Product Backlog | Product Owner | Vision, stakeholder needs, feedback, data | Product Goal; ordered Product Backlog | Ongoing |
| 2. Sprint Planning | Whole Scrum Team | Ordered Product Backlog, latest Increment, capacity, Definition of Done | Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog | Up to 8 hours |
| 3. Daily work and Daily Scrum | Developers | Sprint Backlog, progress so far | Adapted Sprint Backlog; plan for the next day | 15 minutes a day |
| 4. Backlog refinement | Product Owner and Developers | Upcoming Product Backlog items | Smaller, clearer, sized items | No time-box (ongoing activity) |
| 5. Build a Done Increment | Developers | Sprint Backlog, Definition of Done | One or more usable Increments | Throughout the Sprint |
| 6. Sprint Review | Scrum Team with stakeholders | Increment, progress toward the Product Goal, market changes | Revised Product Backlog | Up to 4 hours |
| 7. Sprint Retrospective | Scrum Team | How the last Sprint went: people, interactions, processes, tools, Definition of Done | Improvements, some added to the next Sprint Backlog | Up to 3 hours |
| 8. Next Sprint begins | Scrum Team | All of the above | A new Sprint Planning, immediately | None: there is no gap |
Steps 2 to 7 repeat in every Sprint. Step 1 never really stops: the Product Owner keeps the Product Backlog ordered as the team learns. The rest of this guide explains each step, then puts them together in a worked example.

### Does Scrum have phases?
Not officially. The 2020 Scrum Guide does not mention phases at all. It describes accountabilities, events, artifacts and commitments, and all product work happens within Sprints that repeat until the product is no longer developed. Each Sprint contains its own planning, building, testing, reviewing and improving, so the activities a Waterfall project would spread across separate phases happen together, in small batches, every few weeks.
Many people still search for the 'phases of Scrum', because training courses, textbooks and older papers use phase models. Two are common.

#### Pregame, game and postgame (Schwaber, 1995)
In his 1995 paper 'SCRUM Development Process', Ken Schwaber described three groups of phases: a **pregame** of planning and high-level architecture, a **game** of development Sprints (each with develop, wrap, review and adjust steps) and a **postgame** of closure, covering final documentation, pre-release testing and release. The paper treated the Sprints as the empirical part and the planning and closure phases as defined processes.
That early model shows where Scrum came from, but the framework has moved on. Today's Scrum Guide has no pregame or postgame: preparation happens as part of normal backlog work and the first Sprint, and release can happen at any time.

#### The five SBOK phases
The SBOK Guide, published by SCRUMstudy, organises Scrum into five phases containing 19 processes (2013 edition): **Initiate**, **Plan and Estimate**, **Implement**, **Review and Retrospect**, and **Release**. Candidates for SCRUMstudy certifications learn this model, and it explains most search results for '5 phases of Scrum'. It is a separate body of knowledge, not part of the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland.

#### How the phase models map to the Scrum Guide
| SBOK phase | Schwaber 1995 | Where it happens in the 2020 Scrum Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiate (vision, team, epics, prioritised backlog, release planning) | Pregame: planning and architecture | Product Goal and Product Backlog, owned by the Product Owner; team formation is outside the Guide; release planning is a complementary practice |
| Plan and Estimate (user stories, estimates, tasks, Sprint Backlog) | Start of each Sprint | Backlog refinement and Sprint Planning |
| Implement (deliverables, daily stand-up, backlog grooming) | Game: develop and wrap | Daily work, the Daily Scrum and refinement during the Sprint |
| Review and Retrospect (Scrum of Scrums, demonstrate and validate, retrospect) | Game: review and adjust | Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective |
| Release (ship deliverables, retrospect project) | Postgame: closure | Not a separate step: Done Increments can be released at any time, even within a Sprint |
Scrum can still sit inside a phased governance model: many organisations wrap Scrum Teams in stage gates or funding milestones, as explained in the Waterfall comparison below.

### Before the first Sprint: getting ready
The Scrum Guide says nothing about what happens before Sprint 1, so teams decide for themselves. In our experience the following steps make the first Sprint far smoother. Most take days, not weeks.
1. **Agree the product and the Product Goal.** Name the product, describe who it serves and write the first Product Goal: a future state the team can plan against, such as 'Patients can book, move and cancel appointments online without phoning'.
2. **Form the Scrum Team.** Confirm one [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/), a [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) and the Developers, with all the skills needed to create a usable Increment. The Scrum Guide says a Scrum Team is typically 10 or fewer people. See [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/).
3. **Build a first Product Backlog.** Collect the ideas you have, write the most important ones as user stories or plain descriptions, and order them. Only the top items need detail; a story-mapping workshop is a quick way to start. Our [product backlog guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) covers this in depth.
4. **Agree a Definition of Done.** Decide the quality standard every Increment must meet, such as tested, reviewed and deployable. If your organisation already has one, use it as the minimum. See [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
5. **Choose a Sprint length and calendar.** Pick a fixed length of one month or less and book the events at the same time and place for the next few Sprints. Our guide to the [Sprint cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-sprint-cycle/) compares lengths.
6. **Refine the top of the backlog.** Hold one refinement session so the first few items are small and clear enough for Sprint Planning. See [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/).
7. **Set up the board and tools.** A physical or digital [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) is enough to start; access to code repositories, environments and test data matters more than fancy software.

#### What about Sprint Zero?
**Sprint Zero** is an informal name for a preparation period before 'real' Sprints start. It is not defined in the Scrum Guide, and Ken Schwaber has publicly criticised the term because it is often used to describe planning that is not a Sprint at all. Every Sprint, including the first, should aim to produce a usable Increment.
Our advice: keep preparation short and give Sprint 1 a modest Sprint Goal. If set-up work such as environments or pipelines is needed, pair it with a thin slice of real functionality that stakeholders can inspect.

#### Readiness checklist for Sprint 1
| Check | Ready when |
| --- | --- |
| Product Goal | Written, visible and understood by the whole team |
| Product Owner | One named person with authority to order the Product Backlog |
| Developers | Have between them the skills to deliver a Done Increment |
| Product Backlog | Ordered; the top items are clear and small enough for one Sprint |
| Definition of Done | Agreed and written down |
| Sprint calendar | Length fixed; Planning, Daily Scrum, Review and Retrospective booked |
| Stakeholders | Know when the first Sprint Review is and have accepted the invitation |
| Board and tools | The team can see all the work and change it themselves |

### The Scrum process step by step
Once the team is ready, the same steps repeat every Sprint. Each step below covers who is involved, what happens and what it produces, with a link to the detailed guide.

#### Step 1: Keep the Product Goal and Product Backlog current
The [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) is the single source of work for the Scrum Team, and its commitment is the Product Goal. The Product Owner is accountable for ordering it, though they may delegate some of the work. The backlog changes constantly as the team learns; the Product Goal stays stable until it is fulfilled or abandoned, and the Scrum Guide says the team must fulfil or abandon one Product Goal before taking on the next.
**Output:** an ordered backlog whose top items are ready for Sprint Planning.

#### Step 2: Sprint Planning
Sprint Planning starts the Sprint. The whole Scrum Team attends, and the Scrum Guide organises it around three topics:
- **Why is this Sprint valuable?** The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value; the team agrees a **Sprint Goal** before Planning ends.
- **What can be Done this Sprint?** The Developers select items from the Product Backlog, using their past performance, upcoming capacity and the Definition of Done.
- **How will the chosen work get done?** The Developers plan the work, often by breaking items into tasks of one day or less.
**Output:** the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/), which is the Sprint Goal (why), the selected items (what) and the plan for delivering them (how). Our [Sprint Planning guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) gives an agenda and examples.

#### Step 3: Daily work and the Daily Scrum
Most of the Sprint is spent building. Every working day, the Developers hold a 15-minute Daily Scrum at the same time and place to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog. Its output is an actionable plan for the next day. The Developers choose the format; the three questions were removed from the Scrum Guide in 2020.
Throughout the Sprint, no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal and quality does not decrease.

#### Step 4: Backlog refinement (ongoing)
Refinement is not an event but an ongoing activity: the Product Owner and Developers break down upcoming Product Backlog items and add detail, such as a description, order and size. The Developers who will do the work are responsible for the sizing. Many teams hold one or two short sessions a Sprint so the next Sprint Planning has enough ready items. The 2020 Scrum Guide sets no time limit for refinement.
**Output:** the next one or two Sprints' worth of items, small and clear enough to plan.

#### Step 5: Build a Done Increment
An **Increment** is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Work only becomes part of an Increment when it meets the Definition of Done; anything that does not is returned to the Product Backlog for future consideration. Several Increments can be created in one Sprint, and an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the Sprint ends.
**Output:** one or more usable, Done Increments.

#### Step 6: Sprint Review
Near the end of the Sprint, the Scrum Team presents the results of its work to key stakeholders and discusses progress toward the Product Goal. The Scrum Guide describes it as a working session rather than a presentation: attendees look at what was achieved and what has changed in the environment, then collaborate on what to do next.
**Output:** a revised Product Backlog that reflects what everyone has learned. The [Sprint Review guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) explains how to run one.

#### Step 7: Sprint Retrospective
The Retrospective concludes the Sprint. The Scrum Team inspects how the last Sprint went with regard to individuals, interactions, processes, tools and its Definition of Done, identifies the most helpful changes and plans how to make them. The most impactful improvements are addressed as soon as possible and may even be added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint.
**Output:** a small number of concrete improvements.

#### Step 8: Start the next Sprint
The next Sprint starts immediately, with Sprint Planning. Its inputs are the outputs of the Sprint just finished: the latest Increment, the revised Product Backlog and the team's improvements. This is how Scrum turns experience into better decisions, an idea explained in our guide to [empiricism in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/).

### Time-boxes for each step
Every Scrum event has a maximum duration. The Scrum Guide sets the maximums for a one-month Sprint and says that for shorter Sprints the events are usually shorter. Many teams scale them in proportion to Sprint length; that is common practice, not a rule.
| Event | Scrum Guide maximum (one-month Sprint) | Common practice for a two-week Sprint | Who attends |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint | One month or less, fixed length | Two weeks | Scrum Team |
| Sprint Planning | 8 hours | Up to 4 hours | Scrum Team; others by invitation for advice |
| Daily Scrum | 15 minutes, every working day | 15 minutes | Developers |
| Sprint Review | 4 hours | Up to 2 hours | Scrum Team and key stakeholders |
| Sprint Retrospective | 3 hours | Up to 1.5 hours | Scrum Team |
| Backlog refinement | No time-box (not an event) | Often 1 to 2 hours a week | Product Owner and Developers |
A time-box is a maximum, not a target. A Sprint Review that achieves its purpose in 45 minutes has done its job. For more on choosing a Sprint length and the rules for changing or cancelling a Sprint, read our guide to [the Scrum Sprint cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-sprint-cycle/).

### How artifacts and commitments flow through the process
Scrum has three artifacts, and the 2020 Scrum Guide gives each one a commitment that tells the team what it is working toward. Following them through the process shows how each step feeds the next.
| Artifact | Commitment | Created or updated in | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Product Backlog | Product Goal | Ongoing ordering and refinement; Sprint Review | Sprint Planning |
| Sprint Backlog | Sprint Goal | Sprint Planning; updated daily by the Developers | Daily Scrum; daily work |
| Increment | Definition of Done | Throughout the Sprint, whenever work meets the Definition of Done | Sprint Review; release to users |
For examples of each artifact see [Scrum artifacts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-artifacts/); for all five events in one place, see [Scrum ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/).

### Worked example: three Sprints of a booking app
This example is illustrative. A team of six (a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and four Developers) is building online booking for a group of physiotherapy clinics. Its Product Goal is: **'Patients can book, move and cancel appointments online without phoning the clinic.'** The team uses two-week Sprints that start on a Wednesday.

#### One Sprint, day by day
| Day | What happens | Step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Day 1 (Wed) | Sprint Planning, 9:30 to 12:30. Sprint Goal agreed; items selected and broken into tasks | 2 |
| Days 1 to 10 | Daily Scrum at 9:30 every working day; design, build and test work | 3 and 5 |
| Day 3 (Fri) | Refinement, 1 hour: split and size items for the next Sprint | 4 |
| Day 6 (Wed) | First Increment of the Sprint deployed to the test environment and checked against the Definition of Done | 5 |
| Day 8 (Fri) | Refinement, 1 hour: confirm the top items for next Sprint Planning | 4 |
| Day 10 (Tue) | Sprint Review, 13:00 to 14:30 with clinic managers and two receptionists; Sprint Retrospective, 15:00 to 16:30 | 6 and 7 |
| Day 11 (Wed) | Next Sprint Planning | 8 |

#### Three Sprints, each feeding the next
|  | Sprint 1 | Sprint 2 | Sprint 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Goal | A patient can book a first appointment at one clinic | Patients can cancel online, and reception can see every online booking | Patients can move an appointment, and the first clinic goes live |
| Increment | Booking flow for one clinic, in the test environment | Cancellation and a reception view, released to staff for trial | Rescheduling; booking live for patients at the pilot clinic |
| What the Sprint Review revealed | Receptionists need to see online bookings or they will double-book | Clinic managers want text reminders before go-live | Patients drop out when asked to create an account first |
| How the Product Backlog changed | Reception view moved to the top | Reminders added and ordered above multi-clinic support | Guest booking moved to the top for Sprint 4 |
| Retrospective improvement | Book a shared test environment to stop waiting | Pair on database changes to cut rework | Add a release checklist to the Definition of Done |
Notice three things. First, every Sprint ended with something real that stakeholders could inspect, even Sprint 1. Second, the Sprint Review changed the order of the backlog each time: the plan was adapted to evidence, not defended. Third, the team released in Sprint 3 as soon as an Increment was ready; it did not wait for a release phase.
Tip
If you run this process with a spreadsheet, our free [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) and [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) match the steps above.

### Releasing in the Scrum process
Scrum has no release phase. Under the 2020 Scrum Guide, an Increment can be delivered to stakeholders as soon as it meets the Definition of Done, and the Sprint Review should never be treated as a gate to releasing value. Some teams release once a Sprint; teams with automated pipelines may release several times a day.
Release decisions still need thought. The Product Owner usually decides when enough value has been built to release to users, with input from stakeholders and the Developers. Many teams also keep a lightweight release plan or product roadmap to forecast which Product Backlog items are likely to be in which release. That is a complementary practice: it should be updated from real progress every Sprint, not fixed at the start.
If your organisation needs a hardening or stabilisation Sprint before every release, treat it as a signal. It usually means the Definition of Done is too weak, because Done work should already be releasable.

### Scrum process vs Waterfall phases
A Waterfall life cycle moves through sequential phases (requirements, design, build, test, deploy) and delivers at the end. The Scrum process repeats every activity in every Sprint, so planning, testing and user feedback happen every few weeks.
|  | Waterfall (phased) | Scrum process |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planning | Mostly up front; changes go through change requests | Continuous: Product Backlog always, Sprint Backlog every Sprint |
| Testing | A late phase | Inside every Sprint, as part of the Definition of Done |
| User feedback | Usually at the end | At every Sprint Review and after each release |
| Risk | Builds up until integration and testing | Limited to one Sprint at a time |
Waterfall suits stable, well-understood work; the Scrum process suits complex work where requirements and solutions emerge.

### Common mistakes in the Scrum process
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Running a long Sprint Zero (or several) | Weeks pass with nothing to inspect; plans are based on assumptions | Keep preparation short and make Sprint 1 deliver a thin, real slice |
| Treating SBOK or pregame/postgame phases as official Scrum | Teams add a separate release or testing phase and lose fast feedback | Use phase models as teaching aids; release Done Increments whenever ready |
| Leaving gaps between Sprints | Momentum drops and 'unofficial' work escapes planning | Start the next Sprint Planning immediately after the Retrospective |
| Skipping refinement | Sprint Planning turns into a long analysis session | Refine a little every week so the top of the backlog stays ready |
| Planning without a Sprint Goal | The Sprint becomes a list of unrelated tasks with no focus for the Daily Scrum | Agree a single objective for the Sprint before Planning ends |
| Calling work Done when it is not | Hidden work piles up and the Sprint Review shows a false picture | Apply the Definition of Done strictly; return unfinished items to the Product Backlog |
| Sprint Review as a demo only | Stakeholders watch but the backlog never changes | End every Review by agreeing changes to the Product Backlog |
| Retrospectives with no follow-through | The same problems repeat every Sprint | Choose one or two improvements and put them in the next Sprint Backlog |
| Changing Sprint length every Sprint | No stable rhythm and no reliable data on what the team can do | Pick a length and keep it unless there is a good reason to change |
Most of these come from treating the process as a schedule rather than a feedback loop. If someone plans a 'testing phase' after several Sprints, the team is drifting back to Waterfall.

### Tools and templates to run the Scrum process
A whiteboard and sticky notes are enough for a co-located team; digital tools help remote teams and teams that share a backlog. A [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) with columns such as To do, In progress, Review and Done makes the Sprint Backlog visible, and our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) compares the main options. If you prefer spreadsheets, use the [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/), [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) and [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/).
Whatever you choose, the test is simple: can everyone on the team, and the stakeholders who need to, see the real state of the work at any time?

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the 5 phases of Scrum?**
The five phases usually quoted are Initiate, Plan and Estimate, Implement, Review and Retrospect, and Release. They come from the SBOK Guide by SCRUMstudy. The official Scrum Guide does not divide Scrum into phases; all work happens within repeating Sprints.

**Q: What are the steps in the Scrum process?**
Order the Product Backlog toward a Product Goal, then run Sprints: Sprint Planning, daily work with a Daily Scrum, ongoing backlog refinement, building a Done Increment, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective. The next Sprint starts immediately.

**Q: Is the Scrum lifecycle the same as the Scrum process?**
Yes. Both terms describe the repeating cycle of Sprints through which a product evolves, Increment by Increment, toward its Product Goal.

**Q: What comes first in the Scrum process?**
A Product Goal and an ordered Product Backlog. Without them there is nothing to plan at the first Sprint Planning. In practice the team also forms and agrees a Definition of Done and a Sprint length.

**Q: Is Sprint Zero part of the Scrum process?**
No. Sprint Zero is an informal term for preparation before the first Sprint. The Scrum Guide does not define it, and every Sprint, including the first, should aim to produce a usable Increment. Keep preparation short.

**Q: What are the three phases of Scrum?**
Pregame, game and postgame. Ken Schwaber described them in his 1995 paper on the SCRUM development process: planning and architecture, development Sprints, and closure. The current Scrum Guide no longer uses them.

**Q: How long is one cycle of the Scrum process?**
One Sprint, which is a fixed length of one month or less. Two weeks is a popular choice. The overall process has no fixed end: Sprints continue for as long as the product is being developed.

**Q: Is there a gap between Sprints?**
No. The Scrum Guide says a new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous one. The Sprint Retrospective ends one Sprint and Sprint Planning begins the next.

**Q: Where does backlog refinement fit in the Scrum process?**
It runs alongside the other steps throughout the Sprint. It is an ongoing activity rather than an event, so the 2020 Scrum Guide sets no time-box for it. See our [backlog refinement guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/).

**Q: When do you release in the Scrum process?**
Whenever an Increment meets the Definition of Done and the Product Owner judges it valuable to release. That can be several times within a Sprint. The Sprint Review is not a release gate.

**Q: Can you skip a step in the Scrum process?**
Not without losing something. Each event is a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt, and the Scrum Guide warns that failing to operate the events as prescribed means lost opportunities to inspect and adapt. Shorten events when the Sprint is short rather than dropping them.

# What Is a Product Owner in Scrum? Role and Must-Have Skills

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: The Scrum Product Owner explained: accountabilities, daily activities, must-have skills, how the role differs from a product manager, and common pitfalls.


## What Is a Product Owner in Scrum? Role and Must-Have Skills
The Product Owner is accountable for maximising the value of the product resulting from the Scrum Team's work. They decide what the team works on next, and why, by managing the Product Backlog.
- Published 8 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- The Product Owner maximises value through the Product Backlog.
- They own the Product Goal and backlog order.
- Decisiveness, empathy and availability are essential.

### Accountabilities
- Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal.
- Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items.
- Ordering Product Backlog items.
- Ensuring the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood.
The Product Owner may delegate some of this work, but remains accountable. Their decisions are visible in the content and order of the Product Backlog and in the Increment.

### A typical week
- Talking with customers and stakeholders.
- Refining backlog items with Developers.
- Taking part in Sprint Planning to propose how the Sprint can increase value.
- Answering questions during the Sprint.
- Leading the conversation about what to do next at the Sprint Review.
- Analysing usage data and business results.

### Must-have skills
- **Decisiveness:** making and owning prioritisation decisions.
- **Customer empathy:** understanding real user needs.
- **Communication:** explaining the why behind priorities.
- **Negotiation:** balancing stakeholder demands and saying no.
- **Analytical thinking:** using data to measure value.
- **Domain knowledge** of the market and product.
- **Availability:** being there for the team.

### Product Owner vs product manager
In many organisations the Product Owner is also the product manager. In larger ones, a product manager may focus on market strategy while Product Owners work closely with teams. See [the Agile product manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-product-manager/).

### Pitfalls
- A proxy Product Owner with no real authority.
- Writing detailed specifications instead of collaborating.
- Treating the backlog as a wish list rather than an ordered plan.
- Being unavailable to the team.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Who does the Product Owner report to?**
Scrum doesn't define reporting lines. What matters is that the organisation respects the Product Owner's decisions.

**Q: Can the Product Owner write user stories?**
Yes, though anyone can add items to the Product Backlog. The Product Owner decides their order.

**Q: What does a Product Owner do?**
The Product Owner maximises the value of the product by developing and communicating the Product Goal, creating and ordering Product Backlog items and keeping the backlog transparent and understood.

**Q: What is the difference between a Product Owner and a product manager?**
Product manager is a job title found in many organisations; Product Owner is a Scrum accountability. Often one person does both, though some organisations split strategy and team-level backlog work.

**Q: Does the Product Owner attend the Daily Scrum?**
The Daily Scrum is for the Developers. The Product Owner attends as a participant only if they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items; otherwise they may be available but should not take it over.

**Q: Can a Product Owner cancel a Sprint?**
Yes. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel a Sprint, which is done if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. See [the Sprint cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-sprint-cycle/).

**Q: Does the Product Owner decide how much work goes into a Sprint?**
No. The Product Owner proposes how the Sprint could increase value, but the Developers select how much they can take on during [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/).

**Q: Can the Product Owner change priorities during a Sprint?**
They can re-order the Product Backlog at any time, but should not make changes that endanger the current Sprint Goal. Scope within the Sprint may be clarified and renegotiated with the Developers.

**Q: How many teams can one Product Owner support?**
When several Scrum Teams work on the same product, the Scrum Guide says they share one Product Owner. How many teams that person can effectively support depends on the product and how much they delegate.

**Q: What makes a good Product Owner?**
Decisiveness, customer understanding, clear communication, negotiation skills and enough availability to work closely with the team. Real authority to make product decisions is essential.

**Q: Is there a Product Owner certification?**
Yes. Common options include Scrum.org's PSPO and Scrum Alliance's CSPO. See [Scrum certification and training](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-certification-and-training/).

# Scrum Software Tools: What to Look For and How to Choose

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum software tools compared: must-have features, the main options and free plans, a step-by-step way to choose and set one up, and mistakes to avoid.


## Scrum Software Tools: What to Look For and How to Choose
Scrum software tools are applications that help a Scrum Team manage its Product Backlog, plan and track Sprints, and make progress visible to everyone. Scrum does not require any software, but most teams, especially remote and multi-team ones, use a tool, and the right one makes Scrum easier while the wrong one adds bureaucracy. This guide explains which features matter, compares the main options using our review data, and gives you a step-by-step way to choose and set up a tool.
- Published 18 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- A Scrum tool needs an ordered Product Backlog, Sprint planning, a Sprint board, estimation fields, burndown or velocity reports and a visible Sprint Goal. Everything else is optional.
- Dedicated Agile trackers such as Jira give the deepest Scrum features; all-in-one platforms such as Wrike, monday.com, Asana and ClickUp suit organisations where Scrum teams work alongside other teams.
- Wrike, our top-rated tool overall (9.4/10), is a strong choice when Scrum teams need cross-team visibility, portfolio views and resource planning; Jira scores highest for pure software Scrum in our reviews.
- Choose by trialling two or three tools on a real Sprint, scoring them against weighted criteria and asking the team which helped most.
- Start with default settings, one Product Backlog per product and as few workflow statuses as possible. Add configuration only when a real problem needs it.
- Tools support transparency but never replace the conversations in Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Retrospective.

### What are Scrum software tools?
**Scrum software tools are applications that hold a Scrum Team's Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and progress in one shared place.** They let teams order work, plan Sprints, track items on a board, estimate effort and see reports such as burndown charts. Good tools make Scrum's artifacts transparent without changing how the team works.
The 2020 Scrum Guide does not mention software at all. A wall, sticky notes and a marker still make a perfectly good [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) for a co-located team. Teams adopt software because it solves practical problems: remote and hybrid team members need to see the same board, stakeholders want access without attending every event, reports are tedious to draw by hand, and work items need to link to code, documents and chat.
The risk runs the other way too. A tool configured with dozens of statuses, mandatory fields and approval steps can quietly replace self-management with process. The best Scrum tool is the simplest one that makes your artifacts transparent.
Tip
Before you compare products, write down the three problems you want a tool to solve. If you cannot name them, a physical board or a free plan may be all you need for now.

### Types of Scrum tools
Scrum tools fall into a few broad groups. Many teams combine one main tool with a couple of supporting ones.
| Type | Examples | Strengths | Trade-offs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dedicated Agile and developer trackers | Jira, Azure DevOps, Linear | Deep backlog, Sprint and reporting features; tight links to code repositories | Built around software work; can feel technical to business teams |
| All-in-one work management platforms | Wrike, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp | One platform for Scrum teams and the rest of the organisation; dashboards, portfolios and automation | Scrum-specific reports vary by tool and plan |
| Microsoft 365 tools | Microsoft Planner premium plans | Lives in Teams and Outlook; backlogs and Sprints on premium plans | Lighter Scrum reporting |
| Docs-first workspaces | Notion | Specs, notes and Sprint boards in one place | You build and maintain much of the system yourself |
| Simple board tools | Trello | Fast to adopt, very visual | Limited backlog management and Sprint reporting |
| Supporting tools | Online whiteboards, planning poker apps, chat and video | Help with Retrospectives, estimation and remote events | Do not hold the backlog; add to your tool count |
| Spreadsheets and physical boards | Excel, Google Sheets, a wall | Free, flexible, no learning curve | No live board for remote teams; manual reports |

### Must-have features mapped to Scrum
The easiest way to judge a Scrum tool is to check whether it supports each part of the framework. The table lists the features that matter and why.
| Scrum element | Feature to look for | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) | One ordered list with drag-and-drop ranking, item types and filters | The Product Owner must be able to order work quickly and show one clear priority |
| Backlog refinement | Item detail with description, acceptance criteria, attachments and comments; parent-child links (epics and stories) | Refinement needs somewhere to capture what the team learns |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | Create a Sprint with dates, drag items into it, see total estimate against capacity | Helps the team forecast realistically |
| Sprint Goal | A visible goal field on the Sprint or board | Keeps the Sprint focused on an outcome, not a list |
| Sprint Backlog and board | A board with a few clear columns, swimlanes and WIP indicators | Supports the Daily Scrum and shows progress at a glance |
| Estimation | Story point or effort field; optional planning poker | Needed for forecasting and velocity; see [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/) |
| Increment and Definition of Done | Checklists or a linked Definition of Done; release or version tracking | Makes the quality bar visible on every item |
| Reports | Burndown or burnup, [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/), cumulative flow | Feeds inspection at the Sprint Review and Retrospective |
| Transparency for stakeholders | Read-only or guest access, shareable dashboards | Stakeholders can see progress without status meetings |
| Integrations | Code repositories, chat, documents, calendars | Keeps the tool current without double entry |

#### Useful extras
- **Automation**, for example moving an item to Done when its pull request merges, or rolling unfinished items back to the backlog.
- **Cross-team views**, such as shared backlogs, dependency links and portfolio dashboards, once you have several teams.
- **Retrospective boards** built into the tool, or an integration with a whiteboard app.
- **Workload and capacity views** that show who is overloaded across teams.
- **AI assistance** for drafting stories, summarising threads or answering questions about progress. Useful, but check which plan includes it.

### The main Scrum tools in brief
Each tool below can support Scrum. The notes focus on how well each one fits Scrum specifically; follow the links for full reviews.

#### Wrike
Wrike is our top-rated project management tool overall (9.4/10). For Scrum, it offers board views on every plan, including Free, plus ready-made Agile Teamwork, Sprint Planning and Sprint Retrospective templates, custom workflows, workload views and dashboards. Its main strength for Scrum is what sits around the team: cross-project dashboards, portfolio views and resource planning that help when several Scrum teams, marketing and operations share one platform, or when you are [scaling Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-at-scale/). Our review rates its Sprint tooling as partial and its Agile score as 8/10: it is less specialised in Scrum reports than Jira. Wrike Sync, an add-on included in Apex, offers two-way sync with Jira and GitHub so developers and business teams can each stay in their preferred tool.

#### Jira
Jira is the most complete Agile tool for software teams that we review, with a 10/10 Agile score. Backlogs, epics, story points, Sprints, Scrum boards, burndown, velocity and cumulative flow reports, and deep links to code are all mature, and the Free plan covers up to 10 users. The trade-offs are a steep learning curve and real administration effort, and non-technical teams often find it heavy. Compare the two leaders in [Wrike vs Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/wrike-vs-jira/).

#### ClickUp
ClickUp is one of the stronger general-purpose tools for Scrum (9/10 for Agile). Sprints are dated Lists, unfinished work can roll over automatically, and the Business plan adds sprint points plus burndown, burnup, velocity and cumulative flow reporting. Docs for specifications sit next to the work. Expect to invest time in setup; reviewers mention a dense interface and occasional lag.

#### monday.com
monday.com is one of the easiest capable platforms to roll out. Work management boards handle simple Sprints, and monday.com sells a separate product, monday dev, for Sprints, roadmaps and bug tracking. It suits organisations where many non-technical teams also need workflows and dashboards.

#### Asana
Asana is approachable and strong at coordinating work across teams and linking it to goals. It supports boards and Sprint-style projects; teams that rely on backlogs, story points and Agile reports will find dedicated tools deeper. Product teams often pair Asana with Jira or GitHub through integrations.

#### Microsoft Planner
Planner's premium plans (Plan 1 and above) add a prioritised backlog and time-boxed Sprints inside Microsoft 365, which suits light Agile work. Microsoft does not document story points, velocity or burndown, so Scrum teams that rely on these should test carefully.

#### Notion
Notion can add Sprints to a task database, with Current sprint, Sprint planning and Backlog views, a choice of what happens to unfinished tasks and optional automated Sprints that start and close on schedule. It is excellent for specs and decision logs next to the work, but lacks packaged velocity and burndown reports.

#### Trello
Trello is the quickest way to get a Sprint board in front of a small team. Custom fields (Standard plan and above) or Power-Ups can hold story points, but there is no native backlog management or Sprint reporting. Jira, from the same company, is the natural next step.

#### Smartsheet and Basecamp
Smartsheet offers a board view on a grid-first platform and suits teams that plan in spreadsheets; its Sprint tooling is limited compared with Jira. Basecamp is designed for calm, communication-centred projects and has no backlogs, Sprints or velocity reports, so Scrum teams usually pair it with, or choose, a dedicated tool.

#### Other options
Outside our reviews, **Azure DevOps** (Azure Boards) is common in Microsoft-centred engineering teams: its Basic plan is free for the first five users, then $6 per user per month, and includes backlogs, Sprint planning and Kanban boards (checked 4 November 2026). **Linear** is popular with product and engineering teams that like a fast, keyboard-driven tracker; it calls Sprints cycles. Check both vendors' current plans directly.

### Which Scrum tool suits your team?
Use this table to build a shortlist of two or three tools. It is a starting point, not a verdict; your trial decides.
| Your situation | Shortlist to trial | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One or a few software teams running Scrum by the book | Jira, ClickUp | Deepest Scrum features and developer integrations |
| Scrum teams inside a larger organisation that needs portfolio, resource and cross-team visibility | Wrike, Jira (with Wrike Sync if teams want different tools) | Wrike's dashboards, portfolios and resource planning; Jira for engineering depth |
| Mixed software and business teams on one platform | Wrike, ClickUp, monday.com | One tool for everyone, with Sprint support of varying depth |
| Non-software teams adopting Scrum (marketing, HR, operations) | Wrike, monday.com, Asana | Easier for non-technical users; flexible workflows |
| Microsoft 365 organisation with light Agile needs | Microsoft Planner (premium), Azure DevOps for engineering | Stays inside Teams and Outlook |
| Small team, tight budget | Jira Free, ClickUp Free Forever, Trello | Usable free plans |
| Docs-heavy product team | Notion, ClickUp | Specs and Sprint boards side by side |

### How to choose a Scrum tool, step by step
A structured selection takes two to four weeks and avoids choosing on demos alone.
1. **List your problems and must-haves.** Start from the feature table above. Mark each feature as must-have, nice-to-have or not needed.
2. **Identify who will use it.** Developers, Product Owners, Scrum Masters, stakeholders and other teams have different needs. Include at least one person from each group in the selection.
3. **Set weighted criteria.** Typical criteria are Scrum features, cross-team visibility, ease of adoption, integrations, scalability and cost. Weights should add up to 100%.
4. **Shortlist two or three tools.** Use the situation table and our [tool reviews](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) to narrow the field.
5. **Trial on a real Sprint.** Set up your actual backlog, run one full Sprint, including all events, in each tool or in parallel teams. Sample data hides friction.
6. **Score each tool.** Ask trial users to score each criterion from 1 to 5, then calculate weighted scores.
7. **Check the total cost.** Include the plan you will really need (for example, story points or dashboards may need a higher tier), add-ons, AI usage and admin time.
8. **Decide and plan the rollout.** Choose, agree conventions, migrate the backlog and review the decision after three or four Sprints.
Our guide on [how to choose project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/) covers vendor questions and contract checks in more detail.

#### Worked example: a weighted scoring matrix
The following example is illustrative. The organisation, weights and scores are invented to show the method; your weights and results will differ.
A 120-person company has three Scrum software teams plus marketing and operations teams. Leadership wants one view of all work and team capacity, and the software teams want solid Sprint support. The selection group shortlists Wrike, Jira and ClickUp, trials each for one Sprint, and scores them from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) for this company's needs.
| Criterion | Weight | Wrike | Jira | ClickUp |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum features (backlog, Sprints, estimation, reports) | 20% | 3 | 5 | 4 |
| Portfolio and resource visibility across teams | 30% | 5 | 3 | 3 |
| Ease of adoption for non-technical teams | 15% | 3 | 2 | 3 |
| Integrations (code, chat, documents) | 15% | 4 | 5 | 4 |
| Scalability and admin controls | 10% | 5 | 4 | 4 |
| Cost | 10% | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| **Weighted score** | 100% | **3.95** | **3.75** | **3.65** |
Wrike wins here because this company puts the most weight on cross-team visibility and resource planning. A company with only software teams that weighted Scrum features at 40% would probably land on Jira or ClickUp instead. That is the point of the method: the weights encode what matters to you, and the trial supplies the scores.

### How to set up a Scrum tool
Whatever you choose, these steps keep the tool working for Scrum rather than against it.
1. **Create one Product Backlog per product.** Several teams on one product should draw from the same backlog, filtered by team if needed.
2. **Keep the workflow short.** Start with To do, In progress and Done, and add a column such as In review only if it shows a real wait state.
3. **Add only the fields you need.** Item type, estimate, Sprint, priority order and acceptance criteria are usually enough.
4. **Set the Sprint length and naming.** Use consistent dates and names so reports line up.
5. **Make the Sprint Goal visible** on the board or Sprint, not buried in a document.
6. **Link the Definition of Done.** Add it as a checklist template or a pinned page so every item shows the quality bar. See our guide to the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
7. **Switch on the core reports**: burndown or burnup, velocity and cumulative flow if available.
8. **Give stakeholders read access** or a shared dashboard so they can follow progress between Sprint Reviews.
9. **Connect integrations** for code, chat and documents so the board stays current without double entry.
10. **Agree conventions** for writing items, using labels and moving cards, and write them down in one short page.
If your team is migrating from a spreadsheet, our [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) shows a clean column structure that imports easily into most tools.

### Running Scrum events in a tool
Tools can make events smoother, but each event's value comes from the conversation. The table shows where to draw the line.
| Event | What the tool helps with | What must stay a conversation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Planning | Showing the ordered backlog, estimates, capacity and the draft Sprint Backlog | Agreeing the Sprint Goal and what can realistically be done |
| Daily Scrum | Showing the board and blocked items | Adapting the plan towards the Sprint Goal |
| Sprint Review | Burnup or release charts, the Increment, updated backlog | Stakeholder feedback and what to do next |
| Sprint Retrospective | Past actions, metrics, a whiteboard for ideas | Honest discussion and choosing improvements |
| Backlog refinement | Item details, splitting, estimating | Shared understanding of what the work means |
Keep [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) actions where the team will see them, for example as items in the next Sprint Backlog. Our [Sprint Retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) works well alongside any tool.

### Free and low-cost Scrum tools
Several tools offer free plans that can run real Sprints. The limits below come from our reviews (checked 7 October 2026).
- **Jira Free:** up to 10 users, with Scrum and Kanban boards, backlogs, the timeline, reports and basic automation. One of the most capable free options for software teams.
- **ClickUp Free Forever:** unlimited members, Board view and Sprints, but 60MB of storage and trial-only Dashboards; sprint points need Business.
- **Wrike Free:** board and table views with basic task and project management; Gantt charts and shareable dashboards start on Team.
- **Trello Free:** up to 10 collaborators per Workspace with simple boards; no native Sprint reports.
- **Notion Free:** task databases with Sprint views, good for small teams that also want docs.
- **Azure DevOps Basic:** free for the first five users.
Free plans are a good way to test whether a tool suits your way of working. Pay when a real problem, such as reporting, more users or integrations, needs a paid feature.

### Can you run Scrum with a spreadsheet or physical board?
Yes, within limits. A physical board is excellent for a co-located team: it is always visible, easy to change and encourages conversation at the Daily Scrum. A spreadsheet can hold an ordered backlog, a Sprint plan and a simple burndown.
The limits appear as soon as people work remotely, stakeholders want live visibility or you run more than one team. Spreadsheets have no live board, weak collaboration on individual items and manual reports. Treat them as a starting point or a stopgap.
If you want to start that way, our free [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) and [Sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) give you a ready-made structure, and the columns map directly onto most Scrum tools when you are ready to move.

### Tips for adopting a Scrum tool
- **Start with default settings** and add fields, statuses and automations only when the team agrees a real need.
- **Keep one Product Backlog per product**, ordered by the Product Owner.
- **Agree conventions** for writing items, labels and estimates, and keep them on one page.
- **Train by doing.** Run Sprint Planning in the tool from day one rather than holding a separate training session.
- **Use the board at the Daily Scrum** so it stays current.
- **Review the tool in a Retrospective** after three or four Sprints. Ask what helps, what gets in the way and what to switch off.
- **Name a tool owner** to handle administration, but keep decisions about the workflow with the team.

### Common mistakes when choosing and using Scrum tools
- **Choosing on a demo.** Demos use perfect sample data. Always trial on a real Sprint.
- **Letting the tool define the process.** If a default workflow does not match how the team works, change the workflow, not the team.
- **Over-configuring.** Ten statuses and fifteen mandatory fields slow everyone down and hide the real state of work.
- **Several backlogs for one product.** Teams pull against each other and the Product Owner loses control of order.
- **Using reports to judge people.** Velocity and burndown are planning aids, not performance targets. See our guide to [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/).
- **Forcing one tool on very different teams** without checking their needs. Shared reporting matters, but so does adoption.
- **Ignoring total cost.** Key Scrum features such as story points, dashboards or AI may sit on higher plans or add-ons.
- **Replacing conversations with comments.** A comment thread is not a Sprint Review.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the best Scrum tool?**
There is no single best tool. In our reviews Jira scores highest for Agile and software teams, while Wrike is our top-rated tool overall and suits Scrum teams that need cross-team visibility and resource planning. ClickUp, monday.com and Asana also support Scrum, with different strengths.

**Q: Do we need a paid Scrum tool?**
No. Many teams start with a physical board or a free plan such as Jira Free or ClickUp Free Forever. Pay for features that solve real problems, such as reporting, more users or integrations.

**Q: Is Jira a Scrum tool?**
Jira is a general work management and issue-tracking tool with very strong Scrum support: backlogs, Sprints, story points, Scrum boards and burndown and velocity reports, all available on its Free plan for up to 10 users.

**Q: Can Wrike be used for Scrum?**
Yes. Wrike offers board views, Agile Teamwork, Sprint Planning and Sprint Retrospective templates, custom workflows, workload views and dashboards. Its strength is visibility across teams and projects; for the deepest Scrum-specific reporting, software teams often use Jira, which Wrike can sync with through its Wrike Sync add-on.

**Q: Can Trello work as a Scrum tool?**
Yes, for simple setups. Lists for each stage and custom fields or Power-Ups for story points can work, but backlog management and Sprint reporting are limited.

**Q: What features should a Scrum tool have?**
An ordered Product Backlog, Sprint planning with capacity, a Sprint board, estimation fields, burndown or velocity reports, a visible Sprint Goal, stakeholder access and integrations with code and chat tools.

**Q: Can Excel be used as a Scrum tool?**
A spreadsheet can hold a backlog, a Sprint plan and a simple burndown, but it lacks a live board and item-level collaboration. It is a sensible stopgap rather than a long-term solution for remote or multi-team work.

**Q: Are there free Scrum tools?**
Yes. Jira Free (up to 10 users), ClickUp Free Forever, Wrike Free, Trello Free, Notion Free and Azure DevOps Basic (first five users) can all support small teams. Check each vendor's current limits.

**Q: What is the difference between Scrum and Kanban tools?**
Scrum tools add time-boxed Sprints, Sprint Goals, estimation and Sprint reports such as burndown and velocity. Kanban tools focus on continuous flow, WIP limits and flow metrics. Most modern tools support both.

**Q: Should all teams use the same Scrum tool?**
It helps for coordination and reporting across teams, but forcing one tool on very different teams can backfire. A common compromise is one platform for planning and reporting, with integrations for teams that need specialised tools.

**Q: Who should own the Scrum tool?**
Anyone can administer it, often a Scrum Master or a tool administrator. What matters is that the team decides how the workflow works and the tool supports that, rather than dictating it.

**Q: How do you choose between Scrum tools?**
List must-have features, set weighted criteria, trial two or three tools on a real Sprint, score them with the people who used them and check the total cost of the plan you really need.

**Q: Do Scrum tools replace Scrum events?**
No. Tools support transparency, but the conversations at Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Retrospective cannot be replaced by software.

**Q: Which Scrum tool is best for non-software teams?**
Teams in marketing, HR or operations usually adopt easier, more visual platforms such as Wrike, monday.com or Asana faster than developer-focused trackers. Choose based on your trial and how much Sprint reporting you need.
