# Scrum Sprint Cycle: Stages, Length, Rules and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-sprint-cycle/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: The Scrum sprint cycle explained: the five events in order, time-boxes for 1–4 week Sprints, the rules, a two-week calendar and worked examples.


## Scrum Sprint Cycle: Stages, Length, Rules and Examples
The Scrum sprint cycle is the repeating loop of Sprint Planning, daily work with a Daily Scrum, a Sprint Review and a Sprint Retrospective, all inside a fixed-length Sprint of one month or less. When one Sprint ends, the next starts immediately, so each cycle builds on what the last one taught you. This guide shows each stage with its inputs and outputs, time-boxes for any Sprint length, the rules, a two-week calendar and worked examples you can copy.
- Published 10 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- A Sprint is a fixed-length event of one month or less that contains Sprint Planning, Daily Scrums, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. Sprints run back to back with no gap.
- Each stage has a clear output: a Sprint Backlog from planning, an updated plan each day, an adapted Product Backlog from the Review and improvements from the Retrospective.
- The Scrum Guide sets maximum time-boxes for a one-month Sprint (8, 4 and 3 hours, plus 15 minutes daily); shorter Sprints usually need proportionally less.
- Sprints are never extended. Scope can be renegotiated with the Product Owner, but changes that endanger the Sprint Goal or lower quality are not made.
- Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and only when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
- Keep the length stable so the cycle becomes a reliable learning loop for forecasts and improvements.

### What is the Scrum sprint cycle?
**The Scrum sprint cycle is the fixed, repeating rhythm in which a Scrum Team plans, builds, inspects and improves its work. Each cycle is one Sprint of one month or less: it starts with Sprint Planning, continues with daily work and Daily Scrums, and ends with a Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.**
The 2020 Scrum Guide, still the current official version, calls Sprints the heartbeat of Scrum, where ideas are turned into value. The Sprint is a container: all the work needed to achieve the Product Goal, including every other Scrum event, happens inside it. The Guide also notes that each Sprint may be considered a short project.
The cycle matters because Scrum is empirical. Every few weeks the team and its stakeholders look at a real, usable Increment and decide what to do next, instead of following a plan made months earlier. The shorter and steadier the cycle, the faster you learn.
See [what a sprint is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/) for the basics, or [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) for the full framework.

### The Scrum sprint cycle at a glance
Each stage of the cycle has a purpose, a set of inputs and a concrete output that feeds the next stage.
| Stage | When | Who | Main input | Output | Maximum time-box (one-month Sprint) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Planning | Start of the Sprint | Whole Scrum Team | Ordered Product Backlog, Product Goal, capacity, past performance, Definition of Done | Sprint Backlog: Sprint Goal, selected items, plan | 8 hours |
| Daily Scrum | Every working day, same time and place | Developers | Sprint Backlog and progress towards the Sprint Goal | Adapted plan for the next day | 15 minutes |
| Sprint work | Throughout the Sprint | Developers | Sprint Backlog | One or more Done Increments | The Sprint length |
| Refinement | Ongoing, as needed | Scrum Team, often with stakeholders | Upcoming Product Backlog items | Smaller, clearer, sized items | No time-box (an activity, not an event) |
| Sprint Review | Near the end, second-to-last event | Scrum Team and key stakeholders | Increment, progress towards the Product Goal, market changes | Adjusted Product Backlog | 4 hours |
| Sprint Retrospective | Last event of the Sprint | Scrum Team | How the Sprint went: people, processes, tools, Definition of Done | Improvements, some added to the next Sprint Backlog | 3 hours |
Read our overview of the [five Scrum events](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/) for how they connect.

### The stages of the Scrum sprint cycle, step by step

#### 1. Sprint Planning: set the goal and the plan
Sprint Planning starts the Sprint. The whole Scrum Team answers three questions: why is this Sprint valuable, what can be Done this Sprint, and how will the chosen work get done.
1. The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value, and the team agrees a **Sprint Goal**.
2. The Developers select Product Backlog items that serve the goal, using past performance and upcoming capacity to judge how much fits.
3. The Developers plan the work, often breaking items into tasks of a day or less.
4. The Sprint Goal is final before the event ends. Goal, items and plan together form the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/).
See our step-by-step guide to [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/).

#### 2. The Sprint work and the Daily Scrum
Most of the cycle is the Developers building the Increment. Each working day they hold a 15-minute [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) to inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan. The Scrum Guide no longer prescribes the three questions; any structure that keeps the focus on the goal works.
- Finish items before starting new ones, so Done work accumulates steadily rather than all at the end.
- Update the Sprint Backlog as you learn; it is a living plan owned by the Developers.
- Raise impediments early. The Scrum Master causes those the team cannot solve to be removed.
- Release whenever it makes sense. An Increment can go to users at any point; the Sprint Review is never a gate to releasing value.

#### 3. Product Backlog refinement: prepare the next cycles
[Backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) is an ongoing activity, not an event, so it has no fixed time-box. The team breaks down upcoming items and adds detail such as description, order and size, so that items for the next one or two Sprints can be Done within a single Sprint. Many teams book one or two short sessions per Sprint.

#### 4. Sprint Review: inspect the product with stakeholders
The [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) is the second-to-last event. The Scrum Team shows what it accomplished, discusses progress towards the Product Goal and agrees with stakeholders what to do next. It is a working session, not a slide presentation, and its output is an adjusted [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/).

#### 5. Sprint Retrospective: improve the way of working
The [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) concludes the Sprint. The team inspects individuals, interactions, processes, tools and its Definition of Done, then picks the most helpful changes. The most impactful improvements can go straight into the next Sprint Backlog so they actually happen.

#### 6. The next Sprint starts immediately
There is no gap, "stabilisation week" or planning pause between Sprints. The next Sprint begins with Sprint Planning as soon as the Retrospective ends, carrying forward the updated Product Backlog, the agreed improvements and fresh data about capacity and pace.

### The rules of the Sprint
The Scrum Guide sets only a few rules for the Sprint itself. Each one protects the cycle as a learning loop.
| Scrum Guide rule | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Sprints are fixed-length events of one month or less | Pick a length and keep it; never stretch a Sprint to finish work. |
| A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends | No gaps or buffer weeks between Sprints. |
| No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal | New requests normally go to the Product Backlog, not into the current Sprint. |
| Quality does not decrease | Never relax the Definition of Done to hit a date. |
| The Product Backlog is refined as needed | Preparation for future Sprints happens during the current one. |
| Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned | If an item proves bigger than expected, agree a smaller slice that still meets the goal. |
| Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete | Cancellation is a rare business decision, not a way to reset a bad Sprint. |
The Guide adds that forecasting practices such as burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows can be useful, but they do not replace empiricism. Inspecting the real Increment matters more than any chart.

### How long is a sprint cycle?
The Scrum Guide's only length rule is one month or less. Within that limit the Scrum Team chooses, and in practice most teams use one to four weeks, with two weeks the most common choice.
| Length | Best for | Benefits | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 week | Fast-changing products, early-stage start-ups, support-heavy teams | Very fast feedback; small risk per Sprint | Events take a larger share of time; large items are hard to finish |
| 2 weeks | Most teams, and a sensible default | Balances feedback speed with event overhead | Items still need splitting to a few days each |
| 3 weeks | Teams with longer test or sign-off steps | More room for complex items | Less common, so harder to align with other teams |
| 4 weeks / one month | Stable environments, hardware or heavily regulated work | Fewer events; bigger Increments | Slow feedback; the Sprint Goal may go stale; more risk per Sprint |

#### How to choose the length
Think of the length as a range with a floor and a ceiling.
- **Floor: can you create a Done Increment?** Team size and skills, your Definition of Done, the technology and the size of typical items set the shortest workable Sprint.
- **Ceiling: how long can feedback wait?** The faster customer needs, the market or the technology change, the shorter the Sprint should be. The Scrum Guide warns that when a Sprint's horizon is too long, the goal may become invalid, complexity may rise and risk may increase.
- **Pick the shortest length that clears the floor**, then hold it for several Sprints before judging.
The Scrum Guide does not say who decides the length. In practice the Scrum Team agrees it together: the Product Owner brings the need for feedback, and the Developers bring what it takes to get work Done.

### Time-boxes for every Sprint length
The Scrum Guide gives maximum time-boxes for a one-month Sprint and says shorter Sprints usually have shorter events. Many teams scale the maximums in proportion to the Sprint length. Only the one-month column and the Daily Scrum are Scrum Guide figures; the rest are a common rule of thumb.
| Event | 1-week Sprint | 2-week Sprint | 3-week Sprint | One-month Sprint (Scrum Guide) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Planning | Up to 2 hours | Up to 4 hours | Up to 6 hours | Up to 8 hours |
| Daily Scrum | 15 minutes | 15 minutes | 15 minutes | 15 minutes |
| Sprint Review | Up to 1 hour | Up to 2 hours | Up to 3 hours | Up to 4 hours |
| Sprint Retrospective | Up to 45 minutes | Up to 1.5 hours | Up to 2.25 hours | Up to 3 hours |
Tip
Time-boxes are maximums, not targets. A team with a well-refined backlog often finishes two-week Sprint Planning in 60 to 90 minutes. If events keep overrunning, look at refinement and item size before adding time.

### Worked example: a two-week sprint cycle calendar
This illustrative calendar is for a six-person Scrum Team with a two-week Sprint that starts on a Wednesday. Mid-week boundaries avoid losing Sprint Planning or the Review to Monday bank holidays and Friday absences, a common practice rather than a rule.
| Day | Date pattern | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Day 1 | Wednesday, week 1 | Sprint Planning 09:30–12:30; work starts after lunch |
| Days 2–5 | Thursday to Tuesday | Daily Scrum 09:30–09:45; build, test and integrate |
| Day 6 | Wednesday, week 2 | Daily Scrum; refinement session 14:00–15:30 for the next Sprint |
| Days 7–9 | Thursday to Monday | Daily Scrum; finish items to Done; release where useful |
| Day 10 | Tuesday, week 2 | Daily Scrum; Sprint Review 13:00–14:30; Sprint Retrospective 15:00–16:30 |
| Day 11 | Wednesday, week 3 | Next Sprint starts with Sprint Planning |

#### Calculating capacity for the cycle
Before Sprint Planning, the team works out how much time it really has. The numbers are illustrative.
1. **Nominal days:** 6 Developers × 10 working days = 60 person-days.
2. **Holidays and leave:** one public holiday for everyone (6 days) and one person on 3 days' leave leaves 51 person-days.
3. **Scrum events and refinement:** about 12 hours each, or roughly 2 days each at 6 focused hours a day, removes 12 person-days, leaving 39.
4. **Support and unplanned work:** the team reserves 10% for production support, leaving about 35 person-days.
5. **Compare with history:** the team's last three Sprints at full strength averaged 24 story points with about 45 available person-days. Scaling by 35 ÷ 45 suggests about 19 points, so the Developers forecast 18 to 20 points and pick a Sprint Goal that fits.
Our [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) has a capacity table built in. See [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) for other methods.

### How the cycle repeats: three feedback loops
The sprint cycle is really three loops running at different speeds:
| Loop | Frequency | Inspects | Adapts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Daily loop | Every working day | Progress towards the Sprint Goal | The Sprint Backlog plan |
| Sprint loop | Every Sprint | The Increment and the way of working | The Product Backlog and team practices |
| Product loop | Over many Sprints | Progress towards the Product Goal and market response | The Product Goal, roadmap and release plans |

#### Worked example: forecasting across cycles
Stable cycles turn history into forecasts. An illustrative team completes 21, 26 and 24 story points in three two-week Sprints, an average of about 24 and a range of 21 to 26. About 120 points of work remain for the next release.
- **Optimistic:** 120 ÷ 26 ≈ 4.6, so 5 Sprints (10 weeks).
- **Cautious:** 120 ÷ 21 ≈ 5.7, so 6 Sprints (12 weeks).
- **Forecast to stakeholders:** "5 to 6 Sprints, so 10 to 12 weeks, assuming scope stays the same." Update it after every Sprint Review.
This only works if the Sprint length and the Definition of Done stay stable; change either and the history no longer compares. See [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) and [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) for more forecasting methods.

### Changing work during a Sprint
The Sprint Goal is fixed; the detailed work is not. Use this table when something changes mid-cycle.
| Situation | Allowed? | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Developers discover extra tasks for a selected item | Yes | Add them to the Sprint Backlog; it is the Developers' plan. |
| An item is much bigger than expected | Yes, by renegotiation | Agree with the Product Owner a smaller slice that still meets the Sprint Goal; return the rest to the Product Backlog. |
| A stakeholder asks for a new feature | Not usually | The Product Owner adds it to the Product Backlog and orders it for a future Sprint. |
| An urgent production defect appears | Yes, if the team decides it must be fixed | Fix it; if this threatens the Sprint Goal, the Product Owner decides what to drop or whether the goal still holds. |
| Someone wants to lower testing to finish on time | No | Quality does not decrease. Finish fewer items to the Definition of Done instead. |
| The Sprint Goal no longer makes sense | Only the Product Owner can act | The Product Owner may cancel the Sprint (see below). |
| Work is unfinished on the last day | The Sprint still ends | Unfinished items return to the Product Backlog to be re-ordered; they are not part of the Increment. |

### Cancelling a Sprint, step by step
A Sprint can be cancelled only if its Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, for example because a merger, a regulatory change or a cancelled contract makes the goal pointless. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel. The 2020 Scrum Guide says nothing more, so the steps below are common practice.
1. **Confirm the goal is truly obsolete.** A difficult Sprint, a late item or a new idea is not a reason to cancel.
2. **The Product Owner decides and tells the Scrum Team and key stakeholders**, explaining why.
3. **Inspect the work already Done.** Done items still form a usable Increment and may be released.
4. **Return unfinished items to the Product Backlog**, where the Product Owner re-orders them in light of the new situation.
5. **Hold a short Retrospective** on what led to the cancellation and whether anything could have been spotted sooner.
6. **Start a new Sprint with Sprint Planning** straight away, usually keeping the normal length so the cadence returns quickly.
Tip
Cancellation consumes resources and unsettles the team, so it should be rare. Frequent cancellations usually mean Sprints are too long for how fast priorities change.

### Sprint cycle vs release cycle
Sprints and releases are separate decisions. Producing a Done Increment every Sprint means you could release; whether and when you do is a business choice.
| Cycle | Typical length | Purpose | Who decides |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint | One month or less, often two weeks | Produce at least one Done Increment and inspect it | Scrum Team |
| Release | From several times a day to every few Sprints | Put Increments in users' hands | Product Owner, with the organisation |
| Product roadmap horizon | Months to quarters | Steer towards the Product Goal | Product Owner with stakeholders |
| Planning Interval (SAFe) | Typically 8 to 12 weeks | Align many teams on shared objectives | Agile Release Train |
Teams with continuous delivery may release many times per Sprint; teams with regulated or hardware products may release after several. Our [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) helps map Sprints to releases.

### Running sprint cycles across several teams
When several Scrum Teams work on one product, the Scrum Guide says they share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner, and must agree the same Definition of Done. Aligning their sprint cycles is the natural next step.
- **Share a cadence:** the same Sprint length and start day, so integration, Reviews and forecasts line up.
- **Integrate continuously**, so the combined Increment is Done every Sprint, not just each team's part.
- **Coordinate across teams** through a Scrum of Scrums or a joint refinement session.
- **Use a scaling framework if you need more structure:** Nexus and LeSS both run teams on a common Sprint. See [Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/large-scale-scrum-less/).

### How to set up a sprint cycle for your team
1. **Agree a Product Goal and an ordered Product Backlog**, with the top items refined small enough to finish in one Sprint.
2. **Write a Definition of Done** that everyone understands; it defines what each cycle must produce. See the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
3. **Choose the Sprint length**, usually two weeks to start, using the floor and ceiling questions above.
4. **Pick start and end days**, often mid-week, and check them against public holidays and other teams' cycles.
5. **Book every event as a recurring series** for the next three months: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, refinement, Sprint Review and Retrospective, with time-boxes scaled to your length.
6. **Set up a visible board** showing the Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog, in a tool or on a wall.
7. **Run three Sprints before changing anything structural**, recording completed work, capacity and Retrospective actions.
8. **Review the cycle at a Retrospective.** If feedback is too slow, shorten the Sprint; if nothing gets Done, split items or strengthen engineering practices before lengthening it.
Use our [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) to capture improvements at the end of each cycle.

### Common sprint cycle problems and how to fix them
| Problem | Typical sign | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overcommitting | Half the items roll over every Sprint | Plan from real capacity and recent history; aim for a goal, not a full list. |
| Mini-waterfall inside the Sprint | Testing piles up in the last two days | Split items smaller; test and integrate continuously; limit work in progress. |
| No real Sprint Goal | The goal is a list of ticket numbers | Write an outcome the Sprint achieves and let items flex around it. |
| Extending Sprints | "Just two more days" to finish | End on time; return unfinished work to the Product Backlog; discuss at the Retrospective. |
| Hardening Sprints | A Sprint reserved for fixing before release | Strengthen the Definition of Done so every Increment is releasable. |
| Changing length often | Velocity jumps around and forecasts mean little | Hold one length for several Sprints; change it only by Retrospective decision. |
| Retrospective actions never happen | The same issues come up every Sprint | Put one improvement into the next Sprint Backlog with an owner. |
For signals to watch over many cycles, see our guide to [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/).

### Tools and templates for the sprint cycle
Any board, physical or digital, can run a sprint cycle. Tools help once you want automatic burndowns, rollover of unfinished work and history across Sprints.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)**, ranked #6 in our reviews and our pick for software and Agile teams, has mature backlogs, Sprints, boards and Sprint reports.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our #1 overall (9.4/10), suits teams whose Sprints sit alongside cross-department projects, dashboards and portfolio reporting; its AI agents can handle Sprint operations such as rolling over work and writing summaries.
- **ClickUp** (8.9/10) includes Sprints even on its Free Forever plan, which suits small teams starting out.
Compare more options in our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/). If your work is continuous rather than cycle-based, read [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/), and use the [Scrum glossary](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-glossary/) for any unfamiliar terms.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a sprint cycle in Scrum?**
The repeating rhythm of a fixed-length Sprint of one month or less: Sprint Planning, daily work with Daily Scrums, a Sprint Review and a Sprint Retrospective. The next Sprint starts immediately afterwards.

**Q: What are the stages of a sprint cycle?**
Sprint Planning, the Sprint work with a Daily Scrum each day, ongoing backlog refinement, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. Then the next Sprint begins.

**Q: How long is a sprint cycle?**
One month or less. Most teams use one to four weeks, and two weeks is the most common choice. Keep the length stable once chosen.

**Q: Who decides the Sprint length?**
The Scrum Guide does not say. In practice the Scrum Team agrees it, balancing the Product Owner's need for feedback with the Developers' ability to finish Done work.

**Q: Can a Sprint be extended?**
No. The Sprint ends on time even if work is unfinished. Incomplete items return to the Product Backlog and the next Sprint starts straight away.

**Q: Is there a break between Sprints?**
No. A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends, beginning with Sprint Planning.

**Q: What happens to unfinished work at the end of a Sprint?**
It returns to the Product Backlog, where the Product Owner re-orders it. It is not part of the Increment and cannot be shown as Done at the Sprint Review.

**Q: Can you add work to a Sprint in progress?**
The Developers can add tasks to their plan, and scope can be renegotiated with the Product Owner, but no change should endanger the Sprint Goal. New requests normally go to the Product Backlog.

**Q: Who can cancel a Sprint?**
Only the Product Owner, and only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

**Q: Is backlog refinement part of the sprint cycle?**
Yes, but as an ongoing activity, not an event. The team refines upcoming items during the current Sprint so future Sprint Planning goes smoothly.

**Q: Can you release before the end of a Sprint?**
Yes. An Increment can be released whenever it is Done and useful. The Sprint Review is never a gate to releasing value.

**Q: Should all teams on one product share the same sprint cycle?**
It is strongly recommended. A shared length and start day make integration, Reviews and forecasting much easier, and frameworks such as Nexus and LeSS use a common Sprint.

**Q: What is the difference between a sprint cycle and a sprint cadence?**
They are often used interchangeably. Cycle usually means the sequence of events in one Sprint; cadence means the regular rhythm of Sprints over time, such as every two weeks from Wednesday.

**Q: What are Sprint zero and hardening Sprints?**
Neither is part of Scrum. Sprint zero is an informal set-up period before the first Sprint; a hardening Sprint is reserved for fixing before release and usually signals a weak Definition of Done.

# Story Points in Scrum: What They Are and How to Estimate

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Story points in Scrum explained: what they measure, how to estimate with reference stories and planning poker, points vs hours, examples and mistakes.


## Story Points in Scrum: What They Are and How to Estimate
Story points in Scrum are relative units that Developers use to size Product Backlog items by the amount of work, complexity and uncertainty involved, rather than by hours. The Scrum Guide does not require them, but they are one of the most popular ways to size work and plan Sprints. This guide explains what story points measure, how to start estimating with them, how they feed velocity and forecasts, and the mistakes to avoid.
- Published 15 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- Story points are relative: an item is sized by comparing it with other items, not by counting hours.
- They combine the amount of work, complexity and uncertainty into one number.
- The Scrum Guide makes the Developers responsible for sizing but does not prescribe story points or any other technique.
- Start with one or two reference stories, a Fibonacci-like scale and a quick estimation session such as planning poker.
- Points completed per Sprint give your velocity, which guides Sprint Planning and release forecasts.
- Never convert points to hours, compare them between teams or use them as a performance target.

### What are story points?
**Story points** are a unit of relative estimation used by Agile and Scrum teams to express how big a Product Backlog item is compared with other items. A story point estimate combines the amount of work, the complexity and the risk or uncertainty involved, so a 5-point item is roughly two and a half times the size of a 2-point item.
The key word is **relative**. People are poor at saying how many hours something will take, but quite good at saying "this is about twice as big as that". Story points use this strength. The numbers have no meaning on their own; they only mean something compared with other items the same team has estimated.
A story point estimate usually reflects three things:
- **Amount of work.** How much there is to do: screens, records, tests, documents, pages.
- **Complexity.** How hard the work is to think through: tricky logic, many integrations, unfamiliar technology.
- **Uncertainty and risk.** How much the team does not yet know: unclear requirements, dependencies on others, untested assumptions.
Story points do **not** measure business value (that is the Product Owner's job when ordering the backlog), and they are not a disguised unit of time. Think of them like sizing furniture for a removal van: you do not need to know exact dimensions to know a wardrobe is about three times the size of a chair.
The name comes from [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/), the short "As a..., I want..., so that..." format many teams use for backlog items, but you can point any Product Backlog item, whether or not it is written as a story.

### Are story points part of Scrum?
No. The Scrum Guide (2020 edition, still the current official version) says that the Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for sizing Product Backlog items, and that the Product Owner may help them understand the trade-offs. It does not say how to size them. Story points, like user stories, are a complementary practice that many Scrum teams choose to add.
Story points grew out of Extreme Programming (XP) in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Ron Jeffries, one of XP's founders, has explained that teams first estimated in "ideal days" (how long a pair would take with no interruptions) and then multiplied by a load factor to get calendar time. Because stakeholders found ideal days confusing, the team started calling them "points". In a 2019 article Jeffries wrote that he may have suggested the name and is "sorry now" about how points are often misused, while also saying teams that find them valuable should carry on.
That history explains both the strengths and the criticisms of story points, which we cover below. For how Scrum fits together as a whole, see [what is Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/).

### Why Scrum teams use story points
Used well, story points help a team in several ways:
- **Faster estimates.** Comparing items is quicker than building up hour-by-hour task lists for work months away.
- **Shared understanding.** Different estimates expose different assumptions. The conversation that follows is often more useful than the number.
- **Uncertainty is built in.** A bigger number for a riskier item signals that it needs splitting or a spike before it is ready.
- **Skill-neutral.** A senior and a junior developer may take very different times, but they can agree that one item is about twice the size of another.
- **Better forecasts.** Points completed per Sprint give a velocity that makes Sprint Planning and release forecasting more realistic.
- **Earlier backlog decisions.** Rough sizes help the Product Owner weigh cost against value when ordering the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/).
Story points work best for teams that are stable, work on similar kinds of items, and plan in Sprints. They add less value for a team that already splits work into small, similar items, which can simply be counted.

### Story points vs hours
|  | Story points | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What they measure | Relative size: work, complexity and uncertainty | Expected elapsed or effort time |
| Who it depends on | The team, not an individual | Usually the person doing the work |
| Precision | Deliberately coarse | Looks precise, but often isn't |
| Effect of uncertainty | Raises the estimate | Often ignored or padded |
| Best used for | Sizing backlog items, velocity, release forecasts | Short tasks within a Sprint, time-and-materials billing |
| Risk if misused | Inflation when treated as a target | Becomes a deadline people are judged against |
Can you convert points to hours? Not reliably. Mike Cohn of Mountain Goat Software, who has written widely on Agile estimation, argues that each point value corresponds to a **range** of hours rather than a fixed number, and that the range differs between people. A 3-point item might take a senior developer half a day and a newcomer two days; both can still agree it is a 3. Fixing "1 point = 4 hours" just turns points back into hours with an extra step.
That does not make time useless. Many teams size backlog items in points and then, during Sprint Planning, break selected items into tasks of a few hours to plan the work. If your organisation needs effort figures for budgets, our guide to [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/) covers hour-based techniques.
Tip
If someone asks "how many hours is a point?", answer with your velocity instead: "We usually finish about 30 points in a two-week Sprint." That gives the time view without corrupting the estimates.

### Story point scales
Most teams use a scale with growing gaps between the numbers. The gaps reflect the fact that bigger items carry more uncertainty, and they stop the team arguing over the difference between a 6 and a 7.
| Scale | Values | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fibonacci | 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 | The classic choice for story points |
| Modified Fibonacci | 0, ½, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100 | Common on planning poker decks; large values flag items that must be split |
| Powers of two | 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 | Simple doubling; some teams find it easier to reason with |
| T-shirt sizes | XS, S, M, L, XL | Rough early sizing of epics or roadmap items; can be mapped to points later |
Planning poker decks often add special cards: **0** for trivial work, **?** for "I can't estimate this yet" and a coffee cup for "let's take a break". A **?** usually means the item needs refinement or a spike before anyone estimates it.

#### Example reference table
Each team's scale is its own, but writing down what the numbers mean to you helps new members and keeps estimates consistent. Here is an example for a web product team:
| Points | What it typically means for this team | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Tiny, well understood, almost no risk | Change a label or fix a typo in an email template |
| 2 | Small, familiar, few unknowns | Add a field to an existing form with validation |
| 3 | Our reference story: moderate, familiar work | Add a filter to an existing list page |
| 5 | Bigger or touches several parts of the system | New settings page that saves user preferences |
| 8 | Large or with real unknowns; consider splitting | Integrate a new payment option using a documented API |
| 13+ | Too big or too uncertain for one Sprint; split or spike first | Rebuild checkout for a new market |

### How to estimate story points, step by step
Here is a practical way to introduce story points to a Scrum team. Steps 1–3 are one-off set-up; steps 4–8 become routine.
1. **Choose a reference story.** Pick a recently completed item that everyone remembers, that was neither tiny nor huge, and that went roughly as expected. Give it a value, often 2 or 3.
2. **Add one or two more anchors.** A clearly smaller item (1) and a clearly larger one (5 or 8) make comparison easier. Together these form your baseline.
3. **Agree the scale and the rules.** Choose a Fibonacci-like scale, decide your largest acceptable size for a Sprint, and agree how you will handle bugs and spikes.
4. **Refine before you estimate.** In [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/), the Product Owner explains each item and the team clarifies acceptance criteria. Estimating unclear items wastes time.
5. **Estimate together.** Each Developer forms a view by comparing the item with the reference stories, then everyone reveals at once, for example with planning poker.
6. **Discuss differences, not averages.** If estimates range from 2 to 8, the highest and lowest explain their reasoning. Often one person knows something the others don't. Re-vote; settle quickly once you are close.
7. **Split anything too big.** If an item lands above your agreed maximum, split it into smaller, still valuable pieces before it enters a Sprint. Our guide to [epics, stories and tasks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/) shows how.
8. **Record and review.** Put the estimate on the item. Every few Sprints, look back in a retrospective: do items you called 5 really feel alike? Adjust your reference examples, not past estimates.
Tip
Keep it quick. If a team spends more than a few minutes on one item, the problem is usually unclear requirements, not the number. Park it and refine it further.

### Planning poker in Scrum
Planning poker is the most common way to agree story points. It is quick, gives everyone a voice and avoids anchoring on the first number spoken.
1. The Product Owner reads the item and answers questions.
2. Each Developer privately picks a card from the scale.
3. Everyone reveals at the same time.
4. If the cards are close, take the most common value or agree a number and move on.
5. If they differ widely, the highest and lowest estimators explain their thinking, then the team votes again.
In Scrum, the **Developers** vote. The Product Owner explains the item and the Scrum Master facilitates, but neither casts a card unless they are also doing the work. Remote teams can use a simple online planning poker tool or the estimation feature in their project management software.
For other techniques such as affinity estimation, bucket systems and T-shirt sizing, see our guide to [Agile estimation and the Fibonacci scale](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/).

### Worked example: estimating a backlog
A team building an online booking system uses **"Customer can cancel a booking from the confirmation email" = 3 points** as its reference story. In refinement it estimates the next items like this:
| Backlog item | Compared with the reference | Estimate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Show booking reference on the confirmation page | Much smaller; one known change | 1 |
| Customer can change the time of an existing booking | Similar logic to cancelling, plus availability check | 5 |
| Send an SMS reminder 24 hours before a booking | New external SMS service; unknown rate limits | 8 |
| Add booking notes field for staff | Slightly smaller than the reference | 2 |
| Customer can pay a deposit when booking | Payments, refunds, security review: too big and uncertain | 13 (split first) |
| Export the day's bookings to CSV | About the same as the reference | 3 |
The 13-point deposit item is too large to finish safely in one Sprint, so the team splits it into "Pay deposit by card (happy path)", "Refund deposit on cancellation" and a short spike on the payment provider's test environment. The SMS item gets an 8 mainly because of uncertainty; once the team has used the SMS service once, similar items will probably shrink.
Notice that the team never mentions hours. Each number is a comparison with the 3-point reference.

### Who estimates story points and when
| Role | Part in estimation |
| --- | --- |
| Developers | Estimate the items, because they will do the work. Everyone who contributes to the Increment, including testers and designers, takes part |
| Product Owner | Explains items, answers questions and uses estimates to make ordering decisions; does not set or negotiate the numbers |
| Scrum Master | Facilitates, keeps sessions short and protects the team from pressure to change estimates |
| Stakeholders | May ask for forecasts, but do not estimate |
Most estimation happens during **backlog refinement**, so that items near the top of the backlog are already sized when [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) starts. The team may re-estimate in planning if its understanding has changed significantly. Once a Sprint has started, most teams leave the estimate alone and learn from any difference in the retrospective.
Only estimate a few Sprints ahead. Items far down the backlog are likely to change, so give them rough T-shirt sizes and point them properly when they come closer.

### From story points to Sprint Planning and forecasts
Story points become useful when you add them up. The total points of items **fully Done** in a Sprint is the team's [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/). Items that are not Done score nothing, however close they are; this is what keeps velocity honest.

#### Using velocity in Sprint Planning
Suppose a team's last three Sprints delivered 28, 33 and 30 points. Its average velocity is about **30 points**. Next Sprint, one of six Developers is on leave for the whole two weeks, so the team expects roughly five-sixths of its usual capacity: about **25 points**. In Sprint Planning it pulls items from the top of the backlog until it reaches around 25 points that fit a coherent Sprint Goal, and stops there.
This is a guide, not a quota. The Developers still decide how much they can take on, and the Sprint Goal matters more than hitting a total. Our guide to [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) explains how to account for holidays and other commitments.

#### Forecasting a release
If 150 points of estimated work remain before a release and velocity has ranged from 25 to 33, the release is likely to take **5 to 6 Sprints** (150 ÷ 33 ≈ 4.5 and 150 ÷ 25 = 6). Always give a range, and update it every Sprint as velocity and the backlog change. A [velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) makes the trend easy to show.

### Bugs, spikes and unfinished work
Teams handle these differently. What matters is choosing a rule and applying it consistently, so velocity stays comparable from Sprint to Sprint.
- **Bugs found in work from the current Sprint** are part of finishing that item. Don't point them separately; the item isn't Done until they are fixed.
- **Bugs from earlier work or production** are new Product Backlog items. Many teams point them like any other item so the effort shows in velocity; others keep a small, unpointed allowance for them. Either works if you are consistent.
- **Spikes** (time-boxed research to reduce uncertainty) are usually time-boxed rather than pointed, or given a small fixed value. Their output is knowledge that lets the team estimate the real item.
- **Technical debt** work can be pointed like features so it competes fairly for space in the backlog. See [technical debt in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/).
- **Unfinished items** return to the Product Backlog. Don't split the points between Sprints; re-estimate the remaining work if it has changed, and count it when it is Done.

### Common story point mistakes
| Mistake | What happens | Better approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Converting points to hours | Points become a slower way of estimating time, and individual speed creeps back in | Use velocity to answer time questions |
| Comparing teams by velocity | Each team's scale differs, so comparisons are meaningless and encourage inflation | Compare each team only with its own past |
| Using points as a performance target | Estimates inflate and velocity rises while output doesn't | Treat velocity as a planning aid owned by the team |
| The Product Owner or a manager sets estimates | Developers lose ownership and estimates lose accuracy | Let the people doing the work estimate |
| Spending too long estimating | Refinement drags and the team avoids it | Time-box each item; park anything that needs more refinement |
| Estimating huge items | Large estimates hide uncertainty and spill over | Split before the item enters a Sprint |
| Giving partial credit | Velocity overstates progress | Count only items that meet the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) |
| Re-estimating finished work | Velocity history becomes unreliable | Leave past estimates alone; adjust reference stories instead |
Velocity is one of several useful measures.

### Criticisms and alternatives to story points
Story points have critics, including some of the people who popularised them. Common concerns are that teams spend too long debating numbers, that managers treat velocity as a productivity score, and that points give a false sense of precision. These are mostly problems of misuse, but they are real.
If story points are not helping your team, consider these alternatives:
- **Counting items.** If the team splits work into small items of broadly similar size, simply counting items finished per Sprint often forecasts as well as points, with no estimation meetings.
- **Throughput and probabilistic forecasting.** Use historical [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) and a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) to produce forecasts with confidence levels, such as "85% likely by 14 March".
- **T-shirt sizing.** Coarse S/M/L sizes are enough for roadmap and epic-level decisions.
- **#NoEstimates.** A movement that questions detailed estimation altogether and focuses on slicing work small and forecasting from flow. See [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/) for how flow-based teams plan.
Whichever method you use, the Scrum Guide's requirement stays the same: the Developers size the work in a way that helps them plan Sprints and helps the Product Owner make decisions.

### Story point templates and tools
- [Sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/): Sprint Goal, capacity, selected items with story points, owners and tasks.
- [User story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/): story, acceptance criteria, epic and estimate in one place.
- [Product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/): an ordered backlog with value and estimate columns.
Most Scrum tools include an estimate field and velocity reports. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) has story point estimation built into its Scrum boards and reports, which is why it is popular with software teams.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a story point in Scrum?**
A story point is a relative unit Developers use to estimate the size of a Product Backlog item, combining the amount of work, complexity and uncertainty. It is compared with other items the team has estimated and is not a measure of hours.

**Q: Are story points required in Scrum?**
No. The Scrum Guide makes the Developers responsible for sizing Product Backlog items but does not prescribe a technique. Story points are a popular, optional practice that came from Extreme Programming.

**Q: Who estimates story points?**
The Developers who will do the work, including everyone who contributes to the Increment such as testers and designers. The Product Owner explains items and the Scrum Master facilitates, but neither sets the estimates.

**Q: How do you calculate story points?**
You don't calculate them from a formula. Pick a reference item, give it a value such as 3, then compare each new item with it and choose the closest number on your scale, usually as a team using planning poker.

**Q: How many hours is one story point?**
There is no fixed conversion. A point represents a range of effort that differs between people and items. If you need a time view, use velocity: the number of points the team usually completes in a Sprint.

**Q: Why are story points based on the Fibonacci sequence?**
The widening gaps between numbers such as 5, 8 and 13 reflect the greater uncertainty of larger items and stop teams debating false precision, such as whether an item is a 6 or a 7.

**Q: What is a good story point size for an item?**
Small enough to finish comfortably within one Sprint, ideally in a few days. Many teams agree a maximum, often 8, and split anything larger before it enters a Sprint.

**Q: How many story points should a team complete per Sprint?**
There is no correct number. It depends on the team's own scale, size and Sprint length. Use your recent average velocity, adjusted for capacity, as a guide for Sprint Planning.

**Q: Can story points be compared between teams?**
No. Each team calibrates points against its own reference items, so a 5 in one team is not a 5 in another. Comparing teams by points or velocity encourages inflation.

**Q: Should bugs be given story points?**
Bugs in work from the current Sprint are part of finishing that item and are not pointed separately. Bugs from earlier work can be pointed like any other backlog item; the key is to be consistent.

**Q: What does a 0 or a question mark card mean in planning poker?**
A 0 means the work is trivial. A question mark means the estimator does not understand the item well enough to size it, which usually means it needs more refinement or a spike.

**Q: What is the difference between story points and T-shirt sizes?**
T-shirt sizes (XS to XL) are a coarser relative scale used for early or roadmap-level sizing. Story points give finer numbers that can be added up for velocity and Sprint Planning.

**Q: Can you change story points after Sprint Planning?**
Most teams leave estimates unchanged once the Sprint starts, so velocity reflects the original plan. If an item turns out much bigger, the team talks to the Product Owner and may split it or return part to the backlog.

**Q: Is #NoEstimates an alternative to story points?**
Yes. #NoEstimates is a movement that questions detailed estimation and instead slices work into small items and forecasts from throughput. It works best when items are consistently small.

# Scrum Team Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum team roles explained: what the Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers do, who decides what, team size, worked examples and common mistakes.


## Scrum Team Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers
The three Scrum team roles are the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the Developers, and the 2020 Scrum Guide calls them accountabilities rather than roles. Together they form one small, self-managing Scrum Team with no sub-teams or hierarchy. This guide explains what each accountability involves, who decides what, how big a team should be and how to set one up, with worked examples, comparison tables and the mistakes to avoid.
- Published 8 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- A Scrum Team has one Product Owner, one Scrum Master and Developers: typically 10 or fewer people, with no sub-teams or hierarchies.
- The Product Owner is accountable for maximising the value of the product; the Scrum Master for establishing Scrum and the team's effectiveness; the Developers for creating a usable Increment each Sprint.
- The 2020 Scrum Guide replaced the Development Team with Developers and speaks of accountabilities, not job titles.
- The team is self-managing: nobody inside it assigns the Developers' daily work, and the whole team is accountable for a valuable Increment every Sprint.
- When a team grows too large, split it into several Scrum Teams that share one Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner.
- Most role problems come from blurred accountabilities: a Product Owner without authority, a Scrum Master acting as task-master, or Developers split into silos.

### What are the Scrum team roles?
**Scrum team roles** are the three accountabilities within a Scrum Team: the **Product Owner**, who maximises the value of the product; the **Scrum Master**, who establishes Scrum and makes the team effective; and the **Developers**, who create a usable Increment every Sprint. The 2020 Scrum Guide calls them accountabilities because they describe responsibilities, not job titles.
People often remember the framework as **3-5-3**: three accountabilities, five events (the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective) and three artifacts.

### What the Scrum Guide says about the Scrum Team
The Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland is the official definition of Scrum. The November 2020 edition is still the current official version (checked 26 October 2026); community add-ons such as the Scrum Guide Expansion Pack are not official revisions. The table summarises what it says about the team and what that means in practice.
| The Scrum Guide says | What it means for your team |
| --- | --- |
| The Scrum Team consists of one Scrum Master, one Product Owner and Developers | Exactly one person in each of the first two accountabilities; as many Developers as the work needs, within the size limit |
| There are no sub-teams or hierarchies | No separate "dev team" and "test team", and no team lead who outranks the others |
| It is a cohesive unit focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal | The team works towards one shared outcome rather than a list of unrelated projects |
| Cross-functional: members have all the skills needed to create value each Sprint | The team should not need to hand work to another department to finish it |
| Self-managing: they internally decide who does what, when and how | Managers set direction and boundaries; the team organises the work |
| Small enough to remain nimble, large enough to complete significant work, typically 10 or fewer people | Count everyone, including the Product Owner and Scrum Master |
| Responsible for all product-related activities, from stakeholder collaboration to maintenance, operation, experimentation and research | Support, operations and discovery work belong to the team too, not just new features |
| The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint | Success and failure are shared; there is no "we did our part" |

### Roles or accountabilities? What changed in 2020
Older guides, many training courses and most top search results still describe a "Development Team" and a "servant leader" Scrum Master. That wording comes from the 2017 Scrum Guide. The 2020 edition changed several things about the team:
| Topic | 2017 Scrum Guide | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name of the group doing the work | Development Team (a team within the Scrum Team) | Developers, one accountability within a single Scrum Team |
| Team description | Self-organising | Self-managing: decides who does what, when and how |
| Size guidance | Development Team of 3 to 9 people | Scrum Team typically 10 or fewer people in total |
| Scrum Master | Described as a servant leader | Accountable for the team's effectiveness; "true leaders who serve" the team and the organisation |
| Language | Roles | Accountabilities |
| Product focus | No Product Goal | Product Goal added as the commitment for the Product Backlog |
Why does the wording matter? A **role** sounds like a job title in an organisation chart. An **accountability** is a set of outcomes someone answers for. A senior engineer, a tester and a technical writer can all hold the Developer accountability; a business analyst might become a Product Owner without changing job title. The 2020 wording also removes the idea of a team within a team, which used to encourage a "them and us" split between the Product Owner and everyone else.

### The Product Owner
The [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) is accountable for maximising the value of the product resulting from the Scrum Team's work. How they do that varies widely between organisations, teams and individuals, but according to the Scrum Guide they are also accountable for effective Product Backlog management, which includes:
- Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal.
- Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items.
- Ordering Product Backlog items.
- Ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood.
The Product Owner may do this work themselves or delegate it, but remains accountable. They are **one person, not a committee**, though they may represent the needs of many stakeholders. The Guide adds that for Product Owners to succeed, the entire organisation must respect their decisions, and that people who want to change the backlog do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.

#### What a Product Owner does in practice
- Talks to customers, users and stakeholders to understand needs and measure outcomes.
- Keeps the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) ordered and the top items clear, often during [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) with the Developers.
- Proposes how the product could increase its value in Sprint Planning and helps shape the Sprint Goal.
- Leads the conversation about what to do next at the Sprint Review and adjusts the backlog afterwards.
- Says no, or not yet, to requests that do not serve the Product Goal.

### The Scrum Master
The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide, by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, both within the Scrum Team and the organisation. They are also accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness. The 2020 Guide describes Scrum Masters as true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation.
The Guide lists three groups the Scrum Master serves:
| Serves | Examples from the Scrum Guide |
| --- | --- |
| The Scrum Team | Coaching members in self-management and cross-functionality; helping them focus on high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done; causing the removal of impediments; ensuring all Scrum events take place and are positive, productive and kept within the timebox |
| The Product Owner | Helping find techniques for Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management; helping the team understand the need for clear, concise backlog items; helping establish empirical product planning; facilitating stakeholder collaboration |
| The organisation | Leading, training and coaching Scrum adoption; planning and advising Scrum implementations; helping people understand an empirical approach; removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams |
A Scrum Master is not a project manager, a team lead or the person who assigns work. Their influence comes from coaching, facilitation and making problems visible. For a full description of the role, a typical day and a step-by-step approach to removing impediments, read our guide to the [Scrum Master role](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/).

### The Developers
In Scrum, **Developers** are the people in the Scrum Team who are committed to creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint. The word is not limited to software developers: designers, testers, analysts, data specialists, writers, engineers and marketers can all be Developers. The Scrum Guide notes that the specific skills needed are often broad and vary with the domain of work.
According to the Guide, the Developers are always accountable for:
1. Creating a plan for the Sprint, the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/).
2. Instilling quality by adhering to a [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
3. Adapting their plan each day towards the Sprint Goal.
4. Holding each other accountable as professionals.

#### What this looks like day to day
- Sizing Product Backlog items and helping split them during refinement.
- Selecting, with the Product Owner, how much work to take into a Sprint, based on their capacity and past performance.
- Running the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/), which is the Developers' event, and updating the Sprint Backlog as they learn.
- Collaborating with the Product Owner to renegotiate scope within the Sprint, without endangering the Sprint Goal, when the work turns out differently from expected.

#### Cross-functional does not mean everyone does everything
The Scrum Guide requires the team as a whole to have the skills it needs. It does not require every person to do every kind of work. In our experience the most resilient teams mix deep specialists with people who can help outside their speciality (often called T-shaped skills), so that one absence does not stop the Sprint. A [skills matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) is a quick way to see where you are thin.

### Scrum team roles compared
The table puts the three accountabilities side by side. The first three rows come from the Scrum Guide; the rest is our practical guidance.
|  | Product Owner | Scrum Master | Developers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Accountable for | Maximising the value of the product | Establishing Scrum and the Scrum Team's effectiveness | Creating a usable Increment each Sprint |
| Artifact most closely linked | Product Backlog | None directly; helps all three stay transparent | Sprint Backlog and Increment |
| Commitment they champion | Product Goal | All three, by coaching the team to use them | Sprint Goal and Definition of Done |
| Main question | What should we build next, and why? | How can we work better together? | How will we build it, to what quality? |
| Number per team | One | One | As many as needed, within about 10 people in total |
| Typical background | Product management, business analysis, a business or customer-facing role | Delivery, coaching, facilitation, project management, team leadership | Engineering, design, testing, analysis, content, data |
| Signs it is working | Stakeholders understand the order; the team rarely waits for decisions | Impediments are cleared quickly; events are short and useful; the team improves each Sprint | Done Increments every Sprint; few surprises; quality stays high |

### Who does what in each Scrum event
Every event involves more than one accountability. This summary is based on the Scrum Guide; the brackets show common practice.
| Event | Product Owner | Scrum Master | Developers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | Proposes how the product could increase its value; ensures attendees are prepared to discuss the most important items | Ensures it happens, is productive and stays within its timebox (often facilitates) | Select items with the Product Owner, size the work and create the plan for the Sprint |
| Daily Scrum | Attends only if actively working on Sprint Backlog items, then as a Developer (often available afterwards for questions) | Ensures it takes place (does not run it as a status meeting) | Own and run it: inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan |
| [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) | Discusses the backlog with stakeholders and adjusts it afterwards | Ensures it is productive and that stakeholders can collaborate | Present the work that is Done and discuss problems and solutions |
| [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | Takes part as a team member | Ensures it takes place (often facilitates, sometimes rotates the role) | Take part and own improvement actions |
| Backlog refinement (ongoing activity, not an event) | Brings items, explains the need, adjusts the order | Helps find techniques, coaches the team | Ask questions, split and size items |

### Who decides what? Decision rights in a Scrum Team
Most friction in Scrum Teams comes from unclear decision rights. The table shows who makes common decisions. Where the Scrum Guide is explicit, it says so; where it is silent, we give the usual practice.
| Decision | Who decides | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The order of the Product Backlog | Product Owner | Scrum Guide |
| The Product Goal | Product Owner develops and communicates it | Scrum Guide |
| The Sprint Goal | The whole Scrum Team, during Sprint Planning | Scrum Guide |
| Which items are selected for the Sprint | Developers, through discussion with the Product Owner | Scrum Guide |
| Size of each item | The Developers who will do the work | Scrum Guide |
| How the work is done and who does which task | Developers (the team is self-managing) | Scrum Guide |
| Changing the Sprint Backlog during the Sprint | Developers; scope is renegotiated with the Product Owner if needed, without endangering the Sprint Goal | Scrum Guide |
| Cancelling the Sprint | Only the Product Owner, when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete | Scrum Guide |
| Definition of Done | The organisation's standard if one exists; otherwise the Scrum Team creates one | Scrum Guide |
| Sprint length | The Scrum Team, within one month or less, ideally with the organisation's agreement | Common practice |
| Releasing an Increment | Usually the Product Owner, within the organisation's release rules; the Sprint Review is not a gate to releasing value | Common practice / Scrum Guide |
If you already use a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/), you can map these decisions into it. Keep Scrum's single points of accountability intact: one Product Owner for the order, the Developers for the plan.

### Scrum team size and structure
The Scrum Guide says a team should be small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint, typically **10 or fewer people**, adding that smaller teams generally communicate better and are more productive. The number includes the Product Owner and Scrum Master.
If a Scrum Team becomes too large, the Guide says it should consider reorganising into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product. Those teams share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner.

#### Worked example: splitting a 14-person team
An online travel company has one 14-person team working on its booking app: a Product Owner, a Scrum Master, five back-end engineers, three front-end engineers, two testers, a designer and a data analyst. Sprint Planning takes most of a day and the Daily Scrum regularly overruns.
1. **Keep one product view.** The Product Owner keeps a single Product Backlog and Product Goal ("Travellers can change their own bookings without calling support").
2. **Split by customer value, not by layer.** Rather than a front-end team and a back-end team, they form two cross-functional teams: Team Search and Book, and Team Manage My Trip.
3. **Spread scarce skills.** Each team gets back-end, front-end and testing skills, ending up with eight people each including the shared Product Owner and Scrum Master. The designer and analyst join one team each and pair across teams when needed.
4. **Decide on the Scrum Master.** The existing Scrum Master serves both teams for now; the organisation plans to add a second Scrum Master within two quarters.
5. **Share one Definition of Done.** Because both teams work on the same product, they must agree and follow the same Definition of Done.
6. **Coordinate lightly.** Teams hold a joint Sprint Review and a short cross-team sync twice a week. Our guide to the [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/) explains this pattern.
For larger products, see [Scrum at scale](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-at-scale/).

### How to set up a Scrum Team, step by step
Use this process when you form a new team or reset one that has drifted. The steps are our recommended sequence; the rules they rely on come from the Scrum Guide.
1. **Define the product.** Agree what the team will own: a product, service or clearly bounded part of one. Without a product, the Product Owner has nothing to maximise.
2. **Appoint one Product Owner with real authority.** Choose someone who understands customers and can make ordering decisions that the organisation will respect. Make their mandate explicit to stakeholders.
3. **Assemble cross-functional Developers.** List the skills needed to turn backlog items into a Done Increment (for example design, build, test, deploy, content) and make sure the team has them, keeping the total around 10 people or fewer.
4. **Appoint a Scrum Master.** Prefer someone with coaching and facilitation skills who is not the line manager of the Developers.
5. **Agree a working agreement.** Core hours, communication channels, how to raise problems and how decisions are made. Keep it to one page.
6. **Create or adopt the Definition of Done.** Start from any organisational standard, then add what the product needs.
7. **Set the Product Goal and seed the backlog.** The Product Owner drafts the goal and the first ordered items; the Developers help refine and size the top of the list.
8. **Run the first Sprint and inspect.** Hold [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/), then use the first Sprint Retrospective to fix whatever was unclear about who does what.
A [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) helps you capture capacity, the Sprint Goal and the selected items for that first Sprint.

### Worked example: forming a Scrum Team for a customer app
A regional energy supplier wants customers to submit meter readings and manage payments in an app instead of phoning the call centre. The head of digital forms a Scrum Team. The names are illustrative.
| Person | Job title | Scrum accountability | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Priya | Senior product manager | Product Owner | Knows the customers, owns the budget for the app and can make ordering decisions |
| Tom | Delivery manager | Scrum Master | Experienced facilitator; not the line manager of any team member |
| Ana and Kofi | Mobile engineers | Developers | Build the iOS and Android app |
| Lena | Back-end engineer | Developer | Integrates with billing and meter systems |
| Sam | Tester | Developer | Builds automated tests and checks accessibility |
| Jo | UX designer | Developer | Researches with customers and designs flows |
| Ravi | Content designer | Developer | Writes in-app text and help content |
**Sprint 1.** The Product Goal is "Customers can submit meter readings and see their balance in the app." In Sprint Planning, Priya explains why meter readings come first: they generate the most calls. The Developers select three items and agree the Sprint Goal "A customer can log in and submit a meter reading." Tom facilitates and keeps the session within its timebox.
**A role problem appears.** Midway through the Sprint, the call-centre manager asks Ana directly to add a reading-history screen. Ana starts on it. At the Daily Scrum the Developers notice the Sprint Goal is at risk. Tom coaches the team to redirect the request to Priya, who adds it to the Product Backlog and explains to the call-centre manager how ordering works.
**Sprint 1 Retrospective.** The team agrees that all requests go through the Product Owner, and that Priya will join refinement every Tuesday. Sam raises that testing piles up at the end of the Sprint; the Developers agree to pair on tests from day one.

### Roles outside the Scrum Team
Scrum defines only three accountabilities, but plenty of other people affect a Scrum Team's work. The Guide refers to them mostly as stakeholders. This table shows how common roles usually fit; it reflects common practice rather than Scrum rules.
| Role | Part of the Scrum Team? | How they usually work with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stakeholders (customers, users, sponsors, other departments) | No | Give feedback at the Sprint Review, collaborate with the Product Owner and influence the backlog through them; see [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) |
| Line or functional managers | No | Hire, develop and support people; set boundaries and remove organisational impediments; do not assign Sprint work |
| Project manager | No accountability in Scrum | Often becomes Product Owner or Scrum Master, or works across teams on budgets, contracts, dependencies and reporting; see the [Agile project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-project-manager/) |
| Architects and specialists (security, data, legal) | Only if they work on the Increment as Developers | Join refinement or pair with Developers; some organisations embed them part-time |
| Executives and sponsors | No | Set strategy and funding; respect the Product Owner's decisions; attend Sprint Reviews where useful |
Tip
Scrum has no project manager accountability, but it does not ban project managers. The question to ask is which accountability, if any, the person holds inside the team, and how their other work supports it.

### Can one person hold more than one Scrum role?
The Scrum Guide does not explicitly forbid combining accountabilities, apart from the requirement for one Product Owner and one Scrum Master per team. Whether it is wise is a different question. The advice column is our view.
| Combination | Allowed by the Scrum Guide? | Our advice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum Master and Developer | Not forbidden. If they work on Sprint Backlog items, they take part in the Daily Scrum as a Developer. | Workable in small or mature teams; watch for coaching being squeezed out by delivery pressure |
| Product Owner and Developer | Not forbidden; same Daily Scrum rule applies | Possible for very small products; risky if the Product Owner stops talking to stakeholders |
| Product Owner and Scrum Master | Not explicitly forbidden | Avoid. The two accountabilities provide a check on each other; one person doing both tends to drop coaching in favour of delivery |
| Line manager as Scrum Master | Not forbidden | Avoid where possible; people are less open about problems with the person who writes their appraisal |

### Common Scrum team role mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A proxy Product Owner with no authority | Every decision waits for someone outside the team; the backlog order keeps changing | Give the Product Owner a real mandate, or make the real decision-maker the Product Owner |
| A Product Owner committee | Conflicting priorities and no single order | One Product Owner who represents many stakeholders |
| The Scrum Master as task-master or project manager | The team stops self-managing and waits to be told what to do | Developers plan and assign their own work; the Scrum Master coaches |
| Sub-teams inside the team ("dev" and "test") | Hand-offs, queues and late defects | One group of Developers sharing the Definition of Done |
| Teams that are too large | Long events, side conversations and diluted ownership | Split into cross-functional teams sharing one Product Backlog |
| Stakeholders bypassing the Product Owner | Hidden work and missed Sprint Goals | Route requests through the Product Owner and make the backlog visible |
| Everyone "part-time" on several teams | Context switching and no real team | Keep most people dedicated to one team |
Many of these problems are easier to spot at the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) if the team regularly asks, "Is it clear who decides what?"

### Templates and tools for Scrum team roles

Software helps once several teams or stakeholders need the same view. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is common among software teams, and [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool overall, suits organisations that need Scrum Teams to work alongside wider portfolio and resource planning.
