### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the three roles in Scrum?**
The Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the Developers. The 2020 Scrum Guide calls them accountabilities rather than roles, to make clear they are responsibilities within one team rather than job titles.

**Q: Who is the leader of a Scrum Team?**
Scrum has no single team leader. The Product Owner leads on product direction, the Scrum Master leads on how Scrum is used and the team's effectiveness, and the Developers lead their own work. The Scrum Guide says there are no hierarchies within the team.

**Q: How many people should be in a Scrum Team?**
Typically 10 or fewer, including the Product Owner and the Scrum Master. The Scrum Guide notes that smaller teams generally communicate better and are more productive.

**Q: What is the difference between a Product Owner and a Scrum Master?**
The Product Owner is accountable for the value of the product and owns the Product Backlog. The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum and the team's effectiveness. One focuses on what to build and why; the other on how the team works.

**Q: Can the Product Owner and Scrum Master be the same person?**
The Scrum Guide does not explicitly forbid it, but it is widely discouraged. The two accountabilities pull in different directions, and combining them removes a useful check on each.

**Q: Can a Scrum Master also be a Developer?**
Yes. The Scrum Guide does not prevent it. If the Scrum Master works on Sprint Backlog items, they take part in the Daily Scrum as a Developer. Make sure coaching does not disappear under delivery pressure.

**Q: Is there a project manager in Scrum?**
Scrum does not define a project manager accountability. Its work is shared between the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the self-managing Developers. Project managers often take one of these accountabilities or work across teams on budgets, contracts and dependencies.

**Q: Who manages the Developers in Scrum?**
Nobody inside the Scrum Team manages their daily work. The Developers are self-managing and decide who does what, when and how. Line managers outside the team still support people's development and careers.

**Q: Is the Development Team still a Scrum role?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide removed the Development Team. There is now one Scrum Team made up of the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the Developers.

**Q: Are testers, designers and analysts Developers in Scrum?**
Yes. Anyone committed to creating any aspect of a usable Increment is a Developer, whatever their job title or speciality.

**Q: Are stakeholders part of the Scrum Team?**
No. Customers, users, managers and sponsors are stakeholders outside the team. They collaborate with it, mainly through the Product Owner and at the Sprint Review.

**Q: What happens when a Scrum Team becomes too large?**
The Scrum Guide suggests reorganising into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams focused on the same product, sharing one Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner. They must also share a Definition of Done.

**Q: Does every Scrum Team need a full-time Scrum Master?**
The Scrum Guide requires a Scrum Master but does not say full-time. Many experienced Scrum Masters serve two or three teams; new teams usually benefit from more of their time.

# Technical Debt in Scrum: How to Spot, Track and Pay It Down

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Technical debt in Scrum explained: types, causes, warning signs, who decides, a step-by-step paydown process, backlog item template and worked example.


## Technical Debt in Scrum: How to Spot, Track and Pay It Down
Technical debt in Scrum is the extra work a team creates for its future Sprints when it chooses a quick solution today instead of a better one that would take longer. Scrum handles it through transparency: you make debt visible in the Product Backlog, stop new debt with a strong Definition of Done, and pay existing debt down a little every Sprint. This guide shows you how to spot it, who decides when to fix it, and a step-by-step process with templates and a worked example.
- Published 17 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Technical debt has a principal (the cost of fixing it) and interest (the extra effort every future change costs until you do). Prioritise debt by its interest, not by how ugly the code looks.
- The 2020 Scrum Guide never uses the term, but its tools cover it: debt items belong in the Product Backlog, and the Definition of Done prevents new debt reaching the Increment.
- The whole Scrum Team owns quality. Developers make the cost of debt visible; the Product Owner orders it against features; the Scrum Master helps the team keep it visible and under control.
- Pay debt down continuously: refactor as part of normal work, reserve some Sprint capacity, and turn larger debt into ordered backlog items. Debt-only Sprints are a last resort.
- Explain debt to stakeholders in business terms, such as slower delivery, incidents and risk, and show progress at the Sprint Review.
- Not all debt is bad. Deliberate, short-term debt taken to learn or hit a real deadline can be wise, as long as it is recorded and repaid.

### What is technical debt in Scrum?
**Technical debt in Scrum is the future rework a Scrum Team takes on when it picks a quick or easy solution instead of a better one.** It shows up as slower changes, more defects and riskier releases. Like financial debt, it has a principal to repay and interest that grows each Sprint until the team repays it.
Ward Cunningham introduced the debt metaphor in 1992 to explain to business colleagues why the team needed time to restructure working code. The idea is simple. Shipping a shortcut is like borrowing: you get something sooner. The **principal** is the effort needed to put the shortcut right. The **interest** is the extra effort every later change costs because the shortcut is still there: the manual test you have to run, the tangled module you have to work around, the one person who has to be consulted.
The [2020 Scrum Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) does not use the term technical debt. It does not need to. Its commitments already cover it: every [Increment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/increment-in-scrum/) must meet the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) is the single source of work, and transparency means everyone can see the real state of the product. Debt that is hidden breaks all three.
Tip
Technical debt is a trade-off, not a moral failing. The goal is not zero debt; it is debt the team chose deliberately, can see clearly and is paying down at a sensible rate.

### Types of technical debt
Debt is not only messy code. Naming the type helps you estimate and explain it.
| Type | What it looks like | Typical symptom |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code debt | Duplicated logic, long methods, unclear names, dead code | Simple changes take longer than they should |
| Design and architecture debt | Tightly coupled modules, a structure that no longer fits the product | A change in one area breaks something unrelated |
| Test debt | Missing or flaky automated tests, reliance on manual regression | Releases need a long manual test phase; defects escape |
| Build, infrastructure and dependency debt | Slow pipelines, manual deployments, outdated libraries and frameworks | Deployments are rare and stressful; security patches are hard to apply |
| Documentation and knowledge debt | Undocumented decisions, knowledge held by one person | Work stalls when that person is away; onboarding is slow |
| Defect debt | Known bugs deferred Sprint after Sprint | Support load grows and workarounds pile up |

#### The technical debt quadrant
Martin Fowler's technical debt quadrant (2009) sorts debt by two questions: was it **deliberate or inadvertent**, and was it **prudent or reckless**? It is useful in a Retrospective because each cell calls for a different response.
|  | Reckless | Prudent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Deliberate** | The team knowingly skips design or tests because it believes it has no time. Response: challenge the trade-off; it is usually a false saving. | The team knowingly ships a simpler solution to meet a real deadline or test an idea, and records the debt. Response: create a backlog item and agree when to repay it. |
| **Inadvertent** | The team does not know good practice, so it creates debt without noticing. Response: training, pairing, code review and a stronger Definition of Done. | The team learns, after building something, how it should have been designed. Response: expected and healthy; refactor as you learn. |

### What causes technical debt in Scrum?
Most debt comes from a small set of causes. Recognising yours tells you whether to fix the debt, the process that created it, or both.
- **Overcommitted Sprints.** When a team pulls in more than it can finish properly, quality is what gives.
- **A weak Definition of Done.** If Done does not include automated tests, code review or documentation, shortcuts become part of every Increment by default.
- **Missing automation.** Without automated tests and deployment, every change carries manual effort and risk, and teams avoid touching fragile areas.
- **Changing requirements.** A design built for last quarter's needs becomes debt when the product moves on. That is normal; it becomes a problem only when nobody refactors.
- **Outdated libraries and infrastructure.** Skipping regular upgrades turns a small job into a large migration.
- **Knowledge held by one person.** Code only one Developer understands is a form of debt, because every change depends on them.
- **No time for refactoring.** If the Product Owner sees every Sprint as feature capacity only, debt accumulates silently.
- **"Nearly Done" work.** Items counted as finished but carrying hidden to-dos create debt that nobody has recorded.

### Warning signs your technical debt is growing
Debt rarely announces itself. Look for these signals, and check them with data rather than impressions.
| Signal | What you notice | How to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simple changes take longer | Estimates for small items keep growing | Compare [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) for similar items over several Sprints |
| Falling or erratic velocity | The team completes less, or wildly different amounts, each Sprint | Look at the [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) trend, not single Sprints |
| More escaped defects | Users report bugs that tests should have caught | Track defects found after release per Sprint |
| No-go areas | Developers avoid certain modules or always ask the same person | Ask in the Retrospective; review who changes which files |
| Slow or fragile pipeline | Builds are slow, tests are flaky, deployments need heroics | Measure build time and failed deployments |
| Growing workaround list | Support and operations keep manual fixes going | Count recurring incidents and manual steps |

### Who is responsible for technical debt in Scrum?
The Scrum Guide makes the whole Scrum Team accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint, so quality is a shared responsibility. Within that, each accountability plays a different part. See our guide to [Scrum Team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) for the full picture.
| Accountability | Role in managing technical debt |
| --- | --- |
| Developers | Instil quality by following the Definition of Done; spot and record debt; explain its principal and interest in plain terms; decide how to do the work, including refactoring inside items; refuse to call work Done when it is not |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Orders the Product Backlog, including debt items, by weighing their cost against features; makes sure stakeholders understand the trade-off |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Helps the team keep debt transparent, coaches on technical practices and the Definition of Done, and removes impediments such as pressure to skip quality |
| Stakeholders and managers | Respect the Product Owner's ordering and the Definition of Done; avoid pushing for scope that forces shortcuts |

### How Scrum events and artifacts help you manage debt
You do not need extra meetings for technical debt. Each part of Scrum already has a job to do.
| Event or artifact | What to do about technical debt |
| --- | --- |
| Product Backlog | Record debt as ordered items with a clear description of cost, so it competes openly with features |
| [Backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) | Break large debt into Sprint-sized items, estimate them and note the interest each one costs |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | Agree how much capacity goes to debt and whether a debt item supports the Sprint Goal |
| [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) | Include the refactoring tasks needed to finish selected items properly |
| Daily Scrum | Raise newly discovered debt that threatens the Sprint Goal |
| Increment and Definition of Done | Stop new debt reaching the product; anything that does not meet Done goes back to the Product Backlog |
| [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) | Show stakeholders what debt is costing and what repaying it has achieved |
| [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | Find the causes of new debt and strengthen the Definition of Done |

### How to manage technical debt in Scrum, step by step
This nine-step process works for a single team and can be repeated every few Sprints.
1. **Take an inventory.** With the Developers, list the debt everyone knows about: where changes are slow, what breaks often and what people avoid. Start with what hurts.
2. **Write each piece of debt as a backlog item.** Describe the problem, the impact today and the proposed fix. Use the format in the next section.
3. **Estimate the principal.** Size the fix the same way you size other items, for example in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/) or days.
4. **Estimate the interest.** Ask how often the team touches the area and how much extra effort, risk or support each change costs. A rough figure per Sprint is enough.
5. **Order the debt with the Product Owner.** Put high-interest, low-principal items near the top. Leave debt in code nobody changes near the bottom; its interest is close to zero.
6. **Choose a paydown strategy.** Combine continuous refactoring with a share of capacity or specific backlog items (see the strategies table below).
7. **Plan it into Sprints.** At Sprint Planning, include debt items or capacity explicitly. Where possible, link debt work to the Sprint Goal, for example by refactoring the module the next feature depends on.
8. **Close the tap.** Strengthen the Definition of Done so the same type of debt is not created again.
9. **Inspect and adapt.** Show progress at the Sprint Review, check the signals in the Retrospective, and revisit the inventory every few Sprints.
If you also track project risks, add any debt that could cause a serious outage or security issue to your [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) so it is visible beyond the team.

### How to write a technical debt backlog item
A debt item is easiest to prioritise when it reads like any other item: who benefits, what changes and how you will know it is finished.
| Field | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| Title | A short, specific name, such as "Add automated tests to invoice calculation" |
| Problem | What the debt is and where it sits |
| Interest (cost today) | Extra effort, defects, incidents or risk it causes, with rough numbers |
| Proposed fix (principal) | What the team will do and an estimate |
| Benefit | What gets faster, safer or cheaper once it is fixed |
| Acceptance criteria | How the team and Product Owner will know it is done |
| Type and label | For example test debt, label tech-debt, so it can be filtered and reported |

#### Example: a filled-in debt item
The following example is illustrative.
- **Title:** Add automated regression tests to invoice calculation.
- **Problem:** The invoice calculation module has no automated tests. Every change needs about a day of manual regression testing.
- **Interest:** The team changes this module three or four times a Sprint, so roughly three to four Developer-days of manual testing per Sprint. Two of the last five releases had invoicing defects.
- **Proposed fix:** Write characterisation tests covering the current behaviour, then add them to the pipeline. Estimate: 8 story points (about 8 Developer-days).
- **Benefit:** Manual regression testing for this module falls to near zero; invoicing defects should be caught before release.
- **Acceptance criteria:** Tests cover all current tax and discount rules; tests run on every commit; the pipeline fails if they fail; the manual test script is retired.
You can also write it as a [user story](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/): "As a Developer changing invoice rules, I want automated regression tests so that I can release changes without a day of manual testing." Our free [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) and [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) both have room for a type or label column.

### Strategies for paying down technical debt
There is no single right strategy. Most mature teams combine the first two and use the third for larger debt.
| Strategy | How it works | Strengths | Watch out for | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Continuous refactoring | Improve code you touch as part of each item (the "leave it better than you found it" habit) | No negotiation needed; debt shrinks where work happens | Can make estimates uneven; does not reach areas nobody touches | Always, as a baseline |
| Capacity allocation | Reserve a share of each Sprint for debt and improvement work | Predictable; easy for stakeholders to understand | The share can become a ritual rather than a decision | Debt is steady and spread across the product |
| Dedicated backlog items | Turn larger debt into ordered Product Backlog items | Fully transparent; competes on value | Items can be postponed for ever if interest is not explained | Debt needs focused work of a day or more |
| Debt-only Sprints | Spend a whole Sprint on clean-up | Fast progress on a backlog of debt | Delivers little visible value; can signal debt is "someone else's problem" the rest of the time | Rarely; after a crisis or before a major change |
| Rewrite or replace | Rebuild a component from scratch | Removes deep architectural debt | High risk and cost; the old system still needs support meanwhile | Only when incremental change is clearly impossible |

#### How much Sprint capacity should go on technical debt?
There is no rule in the Scrum Guide and no agreed industry standard. Many teams start by reserving a modest share of capacity, often somewhere between 10% and 20%, and adjust it based on the trend in their warning signs. If cycle time and defects are improving, the share is working. If they are getting worse, raise it for a few Sprints, or move a specific high-interest item up the backlog. Make the decision at Sprint Planning with the Product Owner, using [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) so the debt work is visible rather than hidden inside feature estimates.
Tip
Avoid "hardening" Sprints that exist only to fix what earlier Sprints left undone. If you need them regularly, your Definition of Done is not being met, and the Increments were never really Done.

### Worked example: paying down debt over six Sprints
The following example is illustrative. The team, numbers and timings are invented to show how principal and interest guide decisions.
**Starting point.** A team of six Developers runs two-week Sprints on a subscription billing product, with about 60 Developer-days of capacity per Sprint. The invoice module has no automated tests and is tightly coupled to tax rules. The team touches it about four times a Sprint, and each change costs roughly three extra Developer-days in manual testing and untangling. That is about **12 Developer-days of interest per Sprint**, or a fifth of capacity.

#### Sizing the decision
- **Principal:** characterisation tests (about 8 days), extracting invoice calculation into its own module (about 9 days) and separating tax rules (about 5 days): **22 Developer-days** in total.
- **Interest after the fix:** the team expects each change to cost well under a day extra, so about **3 Developer-days per Sprint**.
- **Saving:** about 9 Developer-days per Sprint. The fix pays for itself in roughly **two and a half Sprints** (22 ÷ 9), and every Sprint after that is a gain.
Faced with those numbers, the Product Owner moves the three debt items above two lower-value features and agrees to spend around 15% of capacity on them for three Sprints, rather than stopping feature work.

#### Sprint by Sprint
| Sprint | Debt work completed | Interest on invoice changes (Developer-days) | Feature points completed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before | None | 12 | 30 (typical) |
| 1 | Characterisation tests added and running in the pipeline | 12 | 26 |
| 2 | Invoice calculation extracted into its own module | 9 | 26 |
| 3 | Tax rules separated; dead code removed | 6 | 29 |
| 4 | Continuous refactoring only | 4 | 32 |
| 5 | Continuous refactoring only | 3 | 34 |
| 6 | Continuous refactoring only | 3 | 34 |
**What changed.** Feature output dipped for two Sprints, then rose above the old level as interest fell. Invoicing defects stopped appearing in releases. The team also added "automated tests updated for changed behaviour" to its Definition of Done so the module does not slide back. Points here are only a planning signal for this team; do not compare them across teams or use them as a target, as our guide to [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/) explains.

### How to measure technical debt
There is no single number for technical debt. Use a small set of indicators, watch their trend and pair them with the team's judgement.
| Measure | What it tells you | Caution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cycle time for similar items | Whether everyday changes are getting slower | Compare like with like |
| Escaped defects per Sprint or release | Whether quality problems reach users | Depends on how defects are recorded |
| Build and deployment time; failed deployments | Health of the pipeline and infrastructure | One-off incidents can skew it |
| Automated test coverage trend | Whether test debt is shrinking | High coverage does not prove good tests |
| Static analysis findings | Code smells, duplication and complexity | Tools find code issues, not design or knowledge debt |
| Debt items in the backlog: count, age and estimated interest | Whether known debt is being repaid | Only covers debt someone has recorded |
| Team perception | Where Developers feel slowed down | Subjective, but often the earliest signal |
Static analysis tools can estimate remediation effort for code issues. Treat such figures as a guide, because they cannot see architectural, test or knowledge debt.

### How to explain technical debt to stakeholders
Stakeholders rarely care about code structure. They care about speed, reliability, risk and cost. Translate debt into those terms.
- **Talk about interest, not code.** "Changes to invoicing take three times longer than elsewhere and caused two of our last five production incidents."
- **Show the payback.** "About three weeks of focused work would recover roughly nine Developer-days every Sprint after that."
- **Offer options.** "We can repay it over three Sprints alongside features, or do nothing and accept slower delivery in this area."
- **Connect it to goals.** "The new pricing plans on the roadmap all change invoicing. Fixing this first makes them cheaper and safer."
The Sprint Review is the natural place for this conversation: show the trend in one or two measures, what debt work was completed and what it changed. Over time, stakeholders come to see debt paydown as part of delivering value. See our guide to [the Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) for how to run that conversation well.

### Preventing new debt with the Definition of Done
Paying down old debt is pointless if every Sprint adds more. The Definition of Done is Scrum's main defence: it is the quality standard every Increment must meet, and anything that does not meet it returns to the Product Backlog rather than being released.
A Definition of Done aimed at preventing debt might include the following. Treat it as an example to adapt, not a standard.
- Code reviewed by at least one other Developer.
- Automated tests written or updated for new and changed behaviour, and all tests passing.
- No new static analysis issues above an agreed severity.
- Integrated into the main branch and deployed to a test environment through the pipeline.
- Dependencies added or upgraded are on supported versions.
- Significant design decisions recorded where the team will find them.
- Product Owner has checked the acceptance criteria.
Strengthen the Definition of Done gradually. Each Retrospective, ask which debt appeared this Sprint and what one addition to Done would have prevented it. Our [Sprint Retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) has space to record that action. See our full guide to the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).

### Common technical debt mistakes in Scrum
- **Hiding debt.** Keeping debt in Developers' heads or a private list means the Product Owner cannot weigh it. Put it in the Product Backlog.
- **Describing debt in technical terms only.** "Refactor the service layer" will lose to almost any feature. Describe the interest in time, defects and risk.
- **Repaying debt nobody pays interest on.** Cleaning up stable code that never changes feels good but returns little.
- **Treating a weak Definition of Done as normal.** If Done regularly means "done apart from tests", the team is creating debt by design.
- **Inflating feature estimates to sneak in clean-up.** It hides the real cost from the Product Owner. Be explicit instead.
- **Relying on debt-only Sprints.** They treat the symptom and suggest debt is acceptable the rest of the time.
- **Big-bang rewrites.** Rebuilding from scratch is rarely the fastest route; incremental refactoring keeps delivering value and lowers risk.
- **Blaming individuals.** Most debt is a rational response to pressure or a result of learning. Fix the system, not the person.

### Tools for tracking technical debt
You do not need a special tool. Debt should live in the same backlog as everything else, where it can be filtered and reported.
- **In your backlog tool**, use a label, issue type or custom field (for example tech-debt) plus a field for estimated interest. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) supports custom issue types, labels and filters that many software teams use for this. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated project management tool, lets you add custom fields and build dashboards, which helps when debt needs to be visible to managers and stakeholders outside the team.
- **In your codebase**, static analysis tools flag code smells, duplication and complexity, and many integrate with the pipeline so new issues fail the build.
Whichever tool you use, avoid a separate "debt backlog" that nobody orders. Read our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) to compare options.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is technical debt in Scrum?**
It is the future rework a team creates when it chooses a quick solution instead of a better one. It slows later Sprints through extra effort, defects and risk until the team repays it.

**Q: Who coined the term technical debt?**
Ward Cunningham introduced the debt metaphor in 1992 to explain to business stakeholders why refactoring working code was worth the time.

**Q: Who decides when to pay down technical debt?**
The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog, so they decide when debt items are worked on, informed by Developers who explain the cost of the debt. Developers decide how to do their work, including refactoring inside the items they build. The best decisions come from the two working together.

**Q: Should technical debt go on the Product Backlog?**
Yes. Recording debt as Product Backlog items makes it transparent and lets the Product Owner weigh it against features. Small clean-ups done while working on an item do not need their own backlog item.

**Q: How much time should a Scrum Team spend on technical debt?**
There is no rule. Many teams reserve a modest share of each Sprint, often somewhere around 10% to 20%, and adjust it based on whether cycle time, defects and other warning signs are improving. High-interest debt may justify more for a few Sprints.

**Q: Should we have a technical debt Sprint?**
Usually not. Debt-only Sprints deliver little visible value and suggest debt is acceptable the rest of the time. Paying debt down continuously works better, though an occasional focused clean-up can make sense before a major change.

**Q: Should technical debt items be estimated in story points?**
Many teams estimate debt items the same way as other items so they can be planned in Sprint Planning. Estimate the principal like any other work, and describe the interest separately in time, defects or risk so the Product Owner can prioritise.

**Q: Is all technical debt bad?**
No. Deliberate, short-term debt taken to learn quickly or meet a genuine deadline can be a sensible business decision, as long as it is recorded and repaid. Debt becomes a problem when it is hidden, unplanned or never repaid.

**Q: How do you measure technical debt?**
There is no single measure. Teams watch the trend in indicators such as cycle time, escaped defects, build times, test coverage, static analysis findings and the number and age of debt items in the backlog.

**Q: How does the Definition of Done prevent technical debt?**
The Definition of Done sets the quality standard every Increment must meet. If it includes automated tests, code review, integration and documentation, shortcuts cannot become part of the released product. Work that does not meet it returns to the Product Backlog.

**Q: What is the difference between technical debt and a bug?**
A bug is behaviour that does not work as intended. Technical debt is a weakness in how the product is built that makes future work slower or riskier, even if everything currently works. Debt often causes bugs, and deferred bugs are sometimes called defect debt.

**Q: How does refactoring reduce technical debt?**
Refactoring improves the internal structure of code without changing its behaviour. Doing it as part of every item keeps code easy to change; automated tests make it safe.

**Q: Is technical debt only a software problem?**
The term comes from software, but similar debt exists elsewhere: outdated processes, undocumented knowledge, quick fixes in data or content, and manual workarounds in operations. The same approach applies: make it visible, estimate its cost and repay the expensive parts first.

**Q: How do you convince stakeholders to pay down technical debt?**
Explain it in business terms, such as slower changes, incidents and risk, show the payback period and connect the work to upcoming goals. Report progress at the Sprint Review.

# Scrum Techniques: 20 Practices, Examples and How to Use Them

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-techniques/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum techniques explained: 20 practices teams add to Scrum, from user stories and planning poker to swarming and Five Whys, with steps, examples and tips.


## Scrum Techniques: 20 Practices, Examples and How to Use Them
Scrum techniques are the practices teams add to the Scrum framework to carry out the work it defines, such as user stories, planning poker, burndown charts, swarming and the Five Whys. The 2020 Scrum Guide is purposefully incomplete: it sets out the events, artifacts and accountabilities, and leaves the techniques to you. This guide explains 20 widely used Scrum techniques, which problem each one solves, how to use it step by step and how to choose the right ones for your team.
- Published 18 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum defines events, artifacts, commitments and accountabilities. Techniques such as user stories, story points and burndown charts are optional complementary practices.
- Good techniques solve a specific problem. Start from the problem your team has, not from a list of popular practices.
- Backlog techniques (user stories, acceptance criteria, INVEST, splitting, story mapping) make Product Backlog items clear and small enough to finish in a Sprint.
- Estimation and tracking techniques (planning poker, capacity planning, burndowns, burn-ups) support forecasting, but the Scrum Guide says they do not replace empiricism.
- Delivery and improvement techniques (swarming, WIP limits, pairing, test-driven development, Five Whys) help teams finish work and get better each Sprint.
- Introduce one technique at a time as an experiment, inspect it in the Sprint Retrospective, and keep it only if it helps.

### What are Scrum techniques?
**Scrum techniques are optional practices that a Scrum Team uses inside the Scrum framework to carry out the work Scrum describes. Examples include user stories for Product Backlog items, planning poker for sizing, burndown charts for tracking progress and the Five Whys for solving problems. The Scrum Guide does not require any of them.**
The 2020 Scrum Guide describes the framework as purposefully incomplete, defining only the parts needed to implement Scrum theory, and says that various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within it. That is deliberate. Scrum tells you that the Developers must size their work, for example, but not how. One team may use story points and planning poker; another may simply split items until they are all roughly the same size.
This flexibility is a strength, but it causes confusion. Many people believe user stories, velocity or a Definition of Ready are part of Scrum. They are not. Knowing the difference helps you keep the parts of Scrum that make it work and change the techniques freely when they stop helping. For the framework itself, start with our guide to [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/).

### What Scrum defines and what it leaves to you
The table shows each part of Scrum, what the Scrum Guide actually requires, and the techniques teams commonly use to meet that requirement.
| Scrum element | What the Scrum Guide requires | Common complementary techniques |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) | An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product, refined into smaller, more precise items | User stories, acceptance criteria, INVEST, story splitting, story mapping |
| Sizing | Developers who will do the work are responsible for sizing | Story points, planning poker, T-shirt sizes, affinity estimation |
| Sprint Planning | A Sprint Goal, selected items and a plan for delivering them | Capacity planning, Definition of Ready, task breakdown |
| Monitoring progress | Progress towards goals is inspected; forecasting practices are allowed | Burndown and burn-up charts, velocity, cumulative flow diagrams |
| Sprint Backlog | Visible, real-time picture of the Developers' work | Physical or digital Scrum boards, WIP limits |
| Increment and Definition of Done | A usable Increment meeting the Definition of Done | Test-driven development, continuous integration, pair and mob programming, swarming |
| Daily Scrum | 15 minutes for the Developers to inspect progress and adapt the plan | Walking the board, focusing on the Sprint Goal |
| Sprint Retrospective | Plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness | Retrospective formats, Five Whys, fishbone diagrams, working agreements |
Our guides to the Scrum artifacts and [Scrum events](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/) explain each element in detail.

### Product Backlog techniques
These techniques help the Product Owner and Developers turn ideas into clear, ordered items that can be finished within a Sprint. Most of the work happens during [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/).

#### User stories and the Three Cs
A user story describes a need from the point of view of the person who has it, usually in the form: As a [type of user], I want [goal] so that [benefit]. Ron Jeffries proposed in 2001 that a story has three parts, the Three Cs: the **card** (a short written reminder), the **conversation** (the discussion that fills in the detail) and the **confirmation** (the tests that show it works). The card is a placeholder for a conversation, not a specification. Our guide to [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) covers writing them in depth, and our free [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) gives you a ready-made format.

#### Acceptance criteria and Given-When-Then
Acceptance criteria are the conditions a specific item must meet to be accepted. Many teams write them in the Given-When-Then format, which comes from behaviour-driven development: **Given** a starting situation, **When** something happens, **Then** this result should follow. For example: Given a member has two active reservations, When they reserve a third book, Then they see a message that the limit is two. Acceptance criteria are specific to one item; the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) applies to every item.

#### The INVEST checklist
INVEST, attributed to Bill Wake, is a checklist for good backlog items: **Independent** (can be built in any order), **Negotiable** (details are open to discussion), **Valuable** (delivers something a user or customer cares about), **Estimable** (the team can size it), **Small** (fits comfortably in a Sprint) and **Testable** (you can tell when it works). Use it as a quick quality check during refinement, not as a scoring system.

#### Story splitting patterns
Large items should be split vertically, so each slice still delivers something usable from end to end, rather than horizontally into layers such as database, interface and testing. The worked example below is illustrative.
**Original item:** As a library member, I want to reserve books online so that I can collect them when they are ready.
| Splitting pattern | Resulting smaller item |
| --- | --- |
| Workflow step | Member can reserve an available book; notification and collection come later |
| Business rule | Enforce the limit of two active reservations |
| Simple then complex | Reserve from one branch first; choosing a collection branch comes later |
| Data variation | Reserve printed books first; audiobooks and DVDs as separate items |
| Interface | Reserve on the website first; the mobile app as a separate item |
| Happy path then exceptions | Successful reservation first; handling of books lost or withdrawn later |
Each split item is still valuable on its own and can be ordered separately. See [epics vs stories vs tasks](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/epics-vs-stories-vs-tasks/) for how splitting fits the wider backlog hierarchy.

#### User story mapping
Story mapping, described by Jeff Patton in his book User Story Mapping (2014), lays out the user's journey as a row of activities from left to right, with stories for each activity stacked beneath in priority order. Drawing a horizontal line across the map shows the smallest set of stories that delivers a complete journey, which is often a good first release. It helps teams avoid building one feature in depth while leaving the rest of the journey unusable.

#### Spikes
A spike is a timeboxed piece of research or experimentation to reduce uncertainty, for example testing whether a payment provider's interface supports refunds. The output is knowledge, not a feature: enough understanding to split or size the real item. Keep spikes short and give them a clear question to answer.

### Estimation and Sprint Planning techniques
Scrum says the Developers who will do the work are responsible for sizing it. These techniques help them do it quickly and consistently.

#### Story points and planning poker
Story points are a relative measure of the effort, complexity and uncertainty of an item compared with others. Planning poker is a technique for agreeing them. It was named by James Grenning in 2002 and popularised by Mike Cohn. Each Developer has cards with values from a scale such as 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20.
1. The Product Owner reads the item and answers questions about it.
2. Each Developer privately chooses a card that reflects their estimate.
3. Everyone reveals their card at the same time, which avoids anchoring on the first voice.
4. The people with the highest and lowest estimates explain their reasoning.
5. The team discusses briefly, then votes again.
6. Repeat until the estimates converge, or agree on the higher value and move on. If an item is very large, split it instead.
Our guide to [story points in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/) covers scales, reference stories and common pitfalls.

#### T-shirt sizing and affinity estimation
When you have dozens of items to size, planning poker is slow. T-shirt sizing (XS, S, M, L, XL) gives quick rough sizes for roadmap and release discussions. Affinity estimation goes further: the team silently places item cards on a wall from smallest to largest, then discusses only the items that people keep moving. Both are useful early on, before items are refined in detail.

#### Capacity planning
Capacity planning checks how much time the Developers actually have in the coming Sprint, allowing for holidays, training, support duties and meetings, before they select work. A team that usually completes around 30 points but has a quarter of its time away might plan for closer to 22. See our guide to [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) for a full method.

#### Definition of Ready
A Definition of Ready is an optional checklist an item should meet before the team selects it, for example: acceptance criteria written, dependencies known, sized by the Developers, small enough for one Sprint. It is not part of the Scrum Guide. Used lightly, it improves Sprint Planning. Used as a strict gate, it can recreate hand-offs and delay valuable work, so treat it as a guide for refinement rather than a rule. Our free [Sprint Planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) includes a capacity calculation and a space for the Sprint Goal.

### Tracking and transparency techniques
Scrum requires transparency and regular inspection, but not any particular chart. The 2020 Scrum Guide mentions burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows as practices for forecasting progress and notes that, while proven useful, they do not replace the importance of empiricism. In other words, charts support decisions; they do not make them.

#### Scrum boards
A [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) shows the Sprint Backlog as columns such as To do, In progress and Done. It makes blockers and unfinished work visible at a glance and gives the Daily Scrum a shared focus.

#### Burndown and burn-up charts
A Sprint burndown chart plots the work remaining each day against an ideal straight line to zero. A burn-up chart plots work completed against total scope, which makes scope changes visible, so it is often better for release forecasts. Here is an illustrative burndown for a ten-day Sprint with 40 points of selected work. Points only count as burned when an item meets the Definition of Done.
| End of day | Ideal remaining | Actual remaining | What it suggests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 40 | 40 | Sprint starts |
| 2 | 32 | 37 | Many items started, few finished |
| 4 | 24 | 33 | Too much work in progress; team agrees to swarm |
| 6 | 16 | 22 | Items now finishing |
| 8 | 8 | 13 | Recovering, but behind |
| 10 | 0 | 3 | One item not Done; it returns to the Product Backlog |
The flat start is a classic sign of too much work in progress rather than slow work. That points to techniques such as swarming and WIP limits rather than longer hours.

#### Velocity
Velocity is the amount of work, often in story points, that a team completes per Sprint. Averaged over several Sprints, it helps with Sprint Planning and release forecasts. It is a planning aid for one team, not a performance target, and it cannot be compared between teams. See our guide to [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/).

### Delivery and quality techniques
These techniques help the Developers finish work to the Definition of Done and produce a usable Increment every Sprint.

#### Pair and mob programming
In pair programming, two people work on one task at one computer: one types while the other reviews and thinks ahead, and they swap regularly. In mob programming, also called ensemble programming, the whole team works on the same task together, rotating who types. Both spread knowledge, catch defects early and reduce hand-offs. They work for non-coding tasks too, such as writing a policy or designing a campaign together.

#### Test-driven development and continuous integration
Test-driven development (TDD) means writing a small automated test first, writing just enough code to make it pass, then improving the code while keeping tests green. Continuous integration (CI) means merging everyone's work into a shared codebase frequently, with automated builds and tests on every change. Together they make a demanding Definition of Done achievable within a Sprint, because problems surface within minutes rather than at the end.

#### Swarming
[Swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/) means several Developers working together on the highest-priority item to finish it, instead of each starting a separate item. It shortens the time each item spends in progress and reduces the risk of ending the Sprint with many items almost finished and none Done.

#### WIP limits within the Sprint
A [work-in-progress limit](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) caps the number of items allowed in a column of the Scrum board at once, for example no more than three items In progress for a team of six. When the limit is reached, people help finish existing work before starting anything new. WIP limits come from Kanban but fit naturally inside a Sprint.

### Improvement and facilitation techniques
The Sprint Retrospective is where the team plans how to increase quality and effectiveness. These techniques help it find the real causes of problems and turn them into action.

#### Retrospective formats
Changing the format keeps Retrospectives fresh and helps quieter people contribute. Common formats include Start, Stop, Continue; Mad, Sad, Glad; the Sailboat; and the 4Ls (Liked, Learned, Lacked, Longed for). Our guide to [Sprint Retrospective games](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective-games/) explains when to use each, and the [Sprint Retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) gives you a ready-made board.

#### Five Whys
The Five Whys technique, which comes from the Toyota Production System, asks why a problem happened, then asks why again of each answer until you reach a cause you can act on. Five is a guideline, not a rule. An illustrative example:
1. **Problem:** two items failed the Definition of Done on the last day of the Sprint. **Why?** Regression tests failed.
2. **Why were failures found so late?** The full regression suite only runs at the end of the Sprint.
3. **Why only then?** It takes four hours and is run by hand by one tester.
4. **Why is it run by hand?** It was never added to the continuous integration pipeline.
5. **Why not?** The automation work was never visible on the Product Backlog, so it was never ordered against features.
**Action:** the Developers explain the cost to the Product Owner, who adds an item to automate the regression suite near the top of the Product Backlog. The 2020 Scrum Guide notes that the most impactful improvements may even be added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint. When a problem probably has several causes rather than one chain, a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, which groups causes under headings such as people, process and tools, works better. A free [root cause analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) helps you record either.

#### Working agreements
Working agreements are a short list of rules the team writes for itself, such as core collaboration hours, how to raise a blocker, or that nobody starts new work while a review request is waiting. Review them every few Sprints and change them when they stop reflecting how the team wants to work.

#### Walking the board at the Daily Scrum
Instead of each person reporting in turn, the team walks the Scrum board from right to left, starting with the items closest to Done, and asks what it will take to finish each one. It keeps the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) focused on the Sprint Goal rather than on individual status updates.

### How to choose and introduce a Scrum technique, step by step
Teams that adopt many techniques at once often end up with more process and no clear improvement. Treat each technique as an experiment.
1. **Name the problem.** Write it in one sentence, with evidence. For example: in the last three Sprints, 30 to 40 per cent of selected items were not Done.
2. **Choose one technique that targets it.** Use the at-a-glance table above. For unfinished work, WIP limits or swarming are good candidates.
3. **State a hypothesis.** We believe that limiting work in progress to three items will mean at most one item is left unfinished per Sprint.
4. **Agree how you will measure it.** Pick one simple measure you already have, such as items not Done or the shape of the burndown.
5. **Run it for two or three Sprints.** One Sprint is rarely enough to judge a new habit.
6. **Inspect it in the Retrospective.** Did the measure move? What did people notice? Was there a cost?
7. **Keep, adapt or drop it.** Write down the decision, so the team does not reopen it every Sprint without new evidence.
Tip
If no one can name the problem a technique solves, it is probably ceremony. Drop it and see whether anyone misses it.

### Worked example: choosing techniques for a struggling team
This example is illustrative. The team, numbers and outcomes are invented to show the process.
**Context.** A team of six works in two-week Sprints on an internal finance application. In the Retrospective, the team lists three problems: items regularly spill into the next Sprint, the Daily Scrum has become a 25-minute status report to the Product Owner, and the same complaint about late testing appears in every Retrospective.
| Problem | Evidence | Technique chosen | Measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Items spill over | Four of eleven items not Done in each of the last three Sprints | WIP limit of three items, plus swarming on the top item | Items not Done per Sprint |
| Daily Scrum is a status report | Averages 25 minutes; Developers address the Product Owner | Walk the board, right to left, focused on the Sprint Goal | Duration; team rating out of 5 |
| Late testing keeps recurring | Mentioned in five consecutive Retrospectives | Five Whys, then one improvement item ordered in the Product Backlog | Defects found after the Sprint |
**After three Sprints.** Items not Done fall from four to one per Sprint. The Daily Scrum settles at about 12 minutes and the team rates it 4 out of 5, up from 2. The Five Whys exercise leads to automating the slowest manual tests; defects found after the Sprint fall, but the team agrees it needs more Sprints to be sure. The team keeps all three techniques, adds them to its working agreements and decides that its next experiment will be pairing on complex items.
Notice what the team did not do: it did not introduce story mapping, a Definition of Ready and a new estimation scale at the same time. Each change answered a problem the team could measure.

### Common mistakes with Scrum techniques
- **Treating techniques as Scrum rules.** Insisting that every item must be a user story or that velocity must rise each Sprint confuses the framework with optional practices.
- **Adopting too many at once.** The team cannot tell which change helped, and the process becomes heavier than the work.
- **Using velocity as a performance target.** Teams inflate estimates, and the number stops being useful for forecasting.
- **Comparing story points between teams.** Points are relative to each team and mean nothing across teams.
- **Turning the Definition of Ready into a gate.** Valuable work waits for paperwork, and refinement becomes a hand-off.
- **Splitting horizontally.** Items split into layers deliver nothing usable until the last layer is finished.
- **Running the same retrospective format forever.** Conversations become predictable and people disengage.
- **Keeping techniques nobody can justify.** Review your practices regularly and remove those that no longer solve a problem.
See our guide to the [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) for how techniques such as hands-on demonstrations and backlog walk-throughs make that event more useful.

Most techniques need nothing more than a whiteboard, sticky notes and a shared document. Free templates help you get started:
- [User story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/) for stories and acceptance criteria.
- [Product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) to order and size items.
- [Sprint Planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) for capacity and the Sprint Goal.
- [Sprint Retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) for formats and actions.
As your team grows, project management software saves time on boards, charts and reports. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated platform, suits teams that need custom workflows, dashboards and visibility across several teams or departments. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is built around backlogs, sprints, story points and agile reports, which makes it a common choice for software teams. monday.com, ClickUp and Asana also support boards and sprint-style work. Compare them in our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Are Scrum techniques part of the Scrum framework?**
No. Scrum defines the accountabilities, events, artifacts and commitments. The 2020 Scrum Guide says the framework is purposefully incomplete and that various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within it. Techniques are the optional practices you choose.

**Q: Is planning poker part of Scrum?**
No. Scrum only says that the Developers who will do the work are responsible for sizing it. Planning poker is one popular way to do that, alongside T-shirt sizing, affinity estimation and simply splitting items to a similar size.

**Q: Are user stories required in Scrum?**
No. Scrum requires Product Backlog items, not a particular format. User stories are a popular way to write them because they keep the focus on who needs something and why.

**Q: What is the INVEST checklist?**
A checklist for good backlog items, attributed to Bill Wake: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. Teams use it during refinement to check that items are ready to be discussed in Sprint Planning.

**Q: What is a Definition of Ready?**
An optional checklist that a backlog item should meet before the team selects it, such as having acceptance criteria and a size. It is not in the Scrum Guide and works best as a guide rather than a strict gate.

**Q: What is the difference between acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done?**
Acceptance criteria are specific to one item and describe what it must do. The Definition of Done is a quality standard that applies to every item in the Increment, such as being tested, reviewed and documented.

**Q: What is a spike in Scrum?**
A timeboxed piece of research or prototyping that reduces uncertainty, so the team can split or size a backlog item. Its output is knowledge rather than a usable feature, and it should answer a specific question.

**Q: What is swarming in Scrum?**
Several Developers working together on the highest-priority item to finish it quickly, instead of each starting a separate item. It reduces work in progress and the risk of ending the Sprint with many items almost done.

**Q: What is the difference between pair and mob programming?**
Pair programming is two people working on one task at one computer. Mob, or ensemble, programming involves the whole team working on the same task together, rotating who types. Both spread knowledge and reduce hand-offs.

**Q: Is a burndown chart required in Scrum?**
No. The Scrum Guide mentions burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows as useful forecasting practices but says they do not replace the importance of empiricism. Many teams use one, but it is optional.

**Q: What techniques does a Scrum Master use?**
Mostly facilitation and coaching techniques: retrospective formats, Five Whys and fishbone diagrams, working agreements, and coaching the team on practices such as WIP limits, swarming and walking the board at the Daily Scrum.

**Q: How many techniques should a new Scrum team adopt?**
As few as possible at first. Get the Scrum events and artifacts working, then add one technique at a time to solve a problem you can name, and review it in the Retrospective after two or three Sprints.

**Q: Can non-software teams use Scrum techniques?**
Yes. User stories, acceptance criteria, splitting, swarming, pairing, Scrum boards and Five Whys all work for marketing, HR, operations and other teams. Only a few, such as test-driven development, are specific to software.
