# Scrum Velocity: How to Calculate and Use It, With Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum velocity explained: the formula, a worked example, using it in Sprint Planning and release forecasts, what affects it and how to avoid misuse.


## Scrum Velocity: How to Calculate and Use It, With Examples
Scrum velocity is the amount of work a Scrum Team completes to its Definition of Done in one Sprint, usually measured in story points. The Scrum Guide does not mention it, but it is the most common way teams record the past performance that Sprint Planning relies on. This guide shows how to calculate velocity step by step, how to use it in each Scrum event and for release forecasts, what changes it, and how to avoid the misuse that makes it worthless.
- Published 16 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Velocity is the total estimate of the Product Backlog items that met the Definition of Done in a Sprint. Partly finished items count as zero.
- The 2020 Scrum Guide does not mention velocity. It is a complementary practice from Extreme Programming that records the past performance the Guide refers to.
- Plan from the average of the last three to five Sprints, scaled for this Sprint's availability, and keep the Sprint Goal more important than the number.
- Forecast releases as a range from slower and faster recent Sprints, and update the forecast after every Sprint Review.
- Velocity belongs to the Developers. It is specific to one team, so never compare teams, add it up across teams without care, or turn it into a target.
- You improve velocity by removing what slows the team down, not by pushing for bigger numbers.

### What is velocity in Scrum?
**Velocity** in Scrum is the sum of the estimates of all Product Backlog items that a Scrum Team completes to its Definition of Done during a Sprint. It is usually measured in [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/). Averaged over several Sprints, it tells the team roughly how much it can take on next and helps forecast when larger pieces of work may be finished.
A simple illustration: if a team finishes items estimated at 8, 5, 5 and 3 points in a Sprint, its velocity for that Sprint is 21. An item that was 90% complete at the end of the Sprint adds nothing.
Velocity measures **output in the team's own units**, not value, quality or effort. Two teams can both have a velocity of 30 and be doing very different amounts of work, because each team sizes its points differently. That is why velocity is a planning aid for the team that produces it, and almost useless outside it.

### Is velocity part of Scrum?
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide, still the current version (checked 26 October 2026), does not use the word velocity. What it does say, in the Sprint Planning section, is that the more the Developers know about their **past performance, their upcoming capacity and their Definition of Done**, the more confident they will be in their Sprint forecasts. Velocity is simply the most widely used way to record that past performance.
The Guide also notes that various practices exist to forecast progress, such as burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows, and that while proven useful, these do not replace the importance of empiricism. Velocity sits in the same category: helpful, optional and subordinate to what the team actually learns each Sprint.
The term came from Extreme Programming (XP), and Scrum teams adopted it widely. Many teams use velocity alongside other measures, and some use none at all, forecasting instead from item counts or flow metrics. All of these are compatible with Scrum.

### How to calculate Scrum velocity, step by step
1. **Agree the unit and the rules.** Usually story points; decide once how you treat bugs, spikes and items added mid-Sprint, and write it down.
2. **Record the forecast at Sprint Planning.** Note the total estimate of the items selected. This is the committed figure, useful for comparison later.
3. **At the end of the Sprint, list the items that meet the Definition of Done.** Do this before the [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/), using the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) strictly.
4. **Add up their original estimates.** Use the estimate agreed before work began, not one revised afterwards.
5. **Give unfinished items zero.** Return them to the Product Backlog; they count in full in the Sprint in which they are Done.
6. **Record the result and repeat.** After three to five Sprints you have a meaningful average and range.

#### The formulas
- **Sprint velocity** = sum of the estimates of items Done in the Sprint.
- **Average velocity** = total points Done over the last *n* Sprints ÷ *n* (most teams use three to five).
- **Velocity range** = the lowest and highest velocities over the same Sprints.
- **Say/do ratio** = points Done ÷ points forecast at Sprint Planning × 100%.

#### What counts toward velocity
| Situation | Counts? | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Item meets the Definition of Done | Yes, at its original estimate | The only thing that counts |
| Item nearly finished | No | Zero this Sprint; full estimate when Done |
| Item added mid-Sprint and Done | Yes | Shows in completed but not in the original forecast |
| Bugs and technical work | If estimated, yes | Either approach works if applied consistently |
| Spikes | Usually not | Their output is knowledge rather than a usable Increment |
Our [Agile velocity chart guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) has a fuller counting table and shows how to turn these numbers into a chart.

### Worked example: six Sprints of velocity
A Scrum Team of five Developers is building a lettings website and runs two-week Sprints. Here is how it calculated velocity for its fourth Sprint.
| Product Backlog item | Estimate | Done at Sprint end? | Counts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Search properties by postcode | 8 | Yes | 8 |
| Filter results by price and bedrooms | 5 | Yes | 5 |
| Save favourite properties | 5 | Yes | 5 |
| Fix map pins on mobile | 3 | Yes | 3 |
| Accessibility labels on search form | 3 | Yes | 3 |
| Email alerts for new listings | 5 | No: about 80% complete, not yet tested | 0 |
| **Total** | **29 forecast** |  | **24 velocity** |
The email alerts item goes back to the Product Backlog. The Product Owner places it at the top again, and its 5 points will count in Sprint 5 if it is Done then. Over six Sprints the team's record looks like this:
| Sprint | Forecast | Velocity (Done) | Say/do ratio | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 26 | 18 | 69% | First Sprint as a new team |
| 2 | 25 | 24 | 96% |  |
| 3 | 24 | 22 | 92% | One Developer ill for 3 days |
| 4 | 29 | 24 | 83% | Email alerts not finished |
| 5 | 25 | 23 | 92% |  |
| 6 | 26 | 25 | 96% |  |
- **Average of the last three Sprints:** (24 + 23 + 25) ÷ 3 = **24 points**.
- **Average of the last five Sprints:** (24 + 22 + 24 + 23 + 25) ÷ 5 = **23.6 points**.
- **Range over the last five Sprints:** 22 to 25 points.
- **Overall say/do ratio:** 136 Done ÷ 155 forecast ≈ 88%, and 92% or more in four of the last five Sprints.
Sprint 1 is left out of the averages because a new team's first Sprint is rarely representative. The team now has a stable velocity of about 24, with a narrow range, which makes both Sprint Planning and release forecasts much more reliable.

### How velocity is used across the Scrum events
Velocity is not discussed in every event, but it informs several of them. The table shows where it typically appears in practice.
| Event or activity | How velocity helps | What to avoid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) | Shows how much refined work the team needs at the top of the backlog: about one to two Sprints' worth | Refining far more than velocity suggests the team can use |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | A starting point for how much the Developers forecast they can complete | Treating the average as a quota |
| [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) | Not normally used; the focus is progress toward the Sprint Goal, often with a Sprint burndown | Tracking points per day or per person |
| Sprint Review | Updates release forecasts for stakeholders: what is likely to be ready, and when | Presenting velocity as a performance score |
| [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | The trend and the gap between forecast and Done prompt questions about flow, quality and interruptions | Blaming individuals for a low Sprint |
In each case velocity starts a conversation; it does not settle one. The Sprint Goal and what the team learned in the Sprint matter more than the number.

### Using velocity in Sprint Planning
Continuing the example, the team prepares for Sprint 7. A public holiday falls in the Sprint, so each of the five Developers has 9 working days instead of 10.
1. **Start with the recent average:** 24 points (last three Sprints).
2. **Work out availability:** 5 × 9 = 45 person-days against a normal 50, a ratio of 0.9.
3. **Scale the average and the range:** 24 × 0.9 ≈ 22 points; the range 22 to 25 becomes about 20 to 23.
4. **Agree the Sprint Goal first**, then select items from the top of the Product Backlog that support it, stopping at about 20 to 23 points.
5. **Plan the how and sense-check.** If the task plan shows one skill overloaded, swap or drop an item, whatever the points say.
6. **Keep the next refined item ready** in case the team finishes early.
Tip
Do not subtract an extra allowance for interruptions from velocity. Past velocity already reflects the support work and surprises of past Sprints, so a further buffer would count them twice. Only adjust for what is genuinely different this Sprint, such as holidays.
Velocity is one input among several. The Scrum Guide puts past performance alongside upcoming capacity and the Definition of Done, and many teams cross-check the points with a task plan in hours or days. Our guide to [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) explains the capacity side in detail, and our [Sprint Planning guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) shows the whole event with a worked example.

### Forecasting with velocity
Beyond the next Sprint, velocity answers two questions stakeholders ask most: **when will it be ready**, and **how much will we get by a date**. Always answer with a range, because a single figure suggests more certainty than any team has.

#### Fixed scope: how many Sprints?
The lettings team has 110 points of estimated work left for a tenant portal release. Using the last five Sprints:
| Scenario | Velocity | Calculation | Sprints needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Faster | 25 | 110 ÷ 25 = 4.4 | 5 |
| Typical | 23.6 | 110 ÷ 23.6 = 4.7 | 5 |
| Slower | 22 | 110 ÷ 22 = 5.0 | 5 |
| Slower, with 3 points of new scope per Sprint | 22 − 3 = 19 | 110 ÷ 19 = 5.8 | 6 |
The honest message is: "Five Sprints, about ten weeks, if scope stays steady; six if requests keep arriving at the current rate."

#### Fixed date: how much scope?
A trade show is four Sprints away. At 22 to 25 points per Sprint, the team can expect to finish **88 to 100 points** of work. In the ordered Product Backlog, the top 88 points are likely, the next 12 are possible, and anything beyond 100 points is unlikely. This gives the Product Owner a clear basis for deciding what matters most before the date.
Update both forecasts after every Sprint Review as velocity and the backlog change. For larger or higher-stakes forecasts, techniques such as [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) use past Sprint results to give probabilities rather than ranges.

### Velocity vs capacity vs throughput vs Sprint Goal success
Velocity is often confused with other measures. Each answers a different question, and healthy teams look at more than one.
| Measure | Question it answers | Unit | Looks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Velocity | How much estimated work did we finish per Sprint? | Story points per Sprint | Backwards |
| Capacity | How much time do we have available next Sprint? | Person-days or hours | Forwards |
| [Throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) | How many items did we finish per Sprint or week? | Items per period | Backwards |
| Sprint Goal success | Did we achieve what the Sprint was for? | Goals met ÷ Sprints | Backwards |
| Say/do ratio | How realistic was our forecast? | Percentage | Backwards |
A team can have a steady velocity and still miss its Sprint Goal every time, which usually means it is finishing items that do not add up to the goal, or that the goal was never clear. Equally, a team can meet every Sprint Goal with a modest, steady velocity, which is a far better result.

### What affects velocity
Velocity moves for many reasons, and most have nothing to do with how hard people work. The table lists the common ones and what to do about each.
| Factor | Effect on velocity | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Holidays, illness, training | Temporary drop | Scale the forecast for availability; do not treat as a trend |
| Team membership changes | Drop for several Sprints while people learn and the team re-forms | Keep teams stable where possible; expect a dip |
| Large or unclear items | Saw-tooth pattern as items finish in alternate Sprints | Split [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) smaller in refinement |
| Unplanned work and interruptions | Lower and less predictable | Make it visible; route requests through the Product Owner |
| [Technical debt](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/) | Gradual decline as every change takes longer | Pay it down steadily as part of each Sprint |
| Dependencies on other teams | Items stall and carry over | Surface dependencies in refinement and Sprint Planning |
| A stronger Definition of Done | Drop, because each item now includes more work | Expected and healthy; start a new baseline |
| Estimate drift or inflation | Rise without more value delivered | Re-anchor estimates to reference items; remove targets |
| Better tools, skills and automation | Gradual genuine rise | Note what changed so the trend makes sense |

### Velocity when things change

#### A new team with no history
A new team has no past performance to draw on. Our advice: for the first Sprint, plan by capacity instead, breaking items into tasks and stopping when the available time is used, and treat the result as a learning exercise. Use the actual velocity from Sprints 2 to 4 as your first baseline. SAFe describes a starting method for new teams of about 8 points per full-time developer or tester per two-week iteration, minus one point for each day of leave or public holiday, but even SAFe intends this only until measured velocity is available.

#### Someone joins or leaves
Expect a dip for a few Sprints. A new member needs time to learn the product, and existing members spend time helping them. Avoid simply scaling velocity by headcount; watch the next two or three Sprints and re-baseline.

#### Changing Sprint length
Velocity is per Sprint, so a change from two to three weeks breaks the series. Scaling by working days gives a rough first estimate, but the shorter or longer cycle changes how work flows, so treat the next few Sprints as a new baseline.

#### Changing the Definition of Done
Adding automated testing or security review to the Definition of Done usually lowers velocity because each item now includes more work. That is a sign of higher quality, not lower performance. Mark the change on your chart and compare only with Sprints after it.

#### Changing the estimation scale
If the team re-calibrates its story points, or switches to counting items, start a new series rather than mixing old and new numbers.

### Velocity in Scrum vs flow metrics in Kanban
Velocity depends on fixed-length Sprints, so it fits Scrum naturally. Kanban teams work in a continuous flow and usually measure flow instead. Many Scrum Teams now use both: velocity for Sprint-level planning, and flow metrics to see where work gets stuck inside the Sprint.
|  | Velocity (common in Scrum) | Flow metrics (common in Kanban) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Measures | Estimated work Done per Sprint | Throughput, cycle time, work item age and work in progress |
| Needs estimates? | Yes, usually story points | No; items are counted and timed |
| Time frame | Per Sprint | Continuous, often per week |
| Best at | Deciding how much to take into the next Sprint | Spotting bottlenecks and forecasting single items |
| Forecasting method | Remaining points ÷ velocity range | Throughput history, often with Monte Carlo simulation |
If your items are small and similar in size, counting them may give forecasts as good as points with less estimation effort.

### Velocity with multiple Scrum Teams
When several Scrum Teams work on one product, it is tempting to add their velocities together or rank them. Both cause problems, because each team's points mean something different.
- **Do not compare teams.** A team with a velocity of 40 is not twice as productive as one with 20; it may simply use bigger numbers.
- **Forecast per team, then combine dates, not points.** Ask each team when its part is likely to be Done, then look at the combined picture and the dependencies.
- **Normalise only if you must.** The [Scaled Agile Framework](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) describes optionally aligning teams' story points to a shared reference so that estimates can be added at Agile Release Train level. It helps aggregate forecasting, but it does not make velocities a fair performance comparison.
- **Count items as a cross-check.** If all teams split work to similar small sizes, item counts can be compared more safely than points.
Whatever the scale, the Scrum Guide's position holds: forecasts come from each team's own past performance and capacity.

### Who owns velocity?
| Who | Relationship with velocity |
| --- | --- |
| Developers | Own their estimates and their velocity; use it to decide how much to take on in Sprint Planning |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Uses it to forecast releases and order the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/); does not set it or push for a higher number |
| Scrum Master | Coaches the team and the organisation to use velocity for planning, not judgement; helps remove the impediments that lower it |
| Managers and stakeholders | Receive forecasts as ranges; should not use velocity to compare teams or rate individuals |
Velocity is always a **team** measure. Tracking points per person discourages pairing and helping colleagues, which are exactly the behaviours that help a team meet its Sprint Goal.

### How to improve velocity the right way
You cannot improve velocity directly without distorting it: ask for more points and estimates grow. What you can do is improve the conditions that let the team finish work, and a steadier, sometimes higher velocity follows.
- **Split items smaller** so most finish well within the Sprint.
- **Refine regularly** so items arrive at Sprint Planning clear and sized.
- **Limit work in progress** inside the Sprint: finish before starting.
- **Protect the Sprint** from unplanned requests, and make the ones you accept visible.
- **Invest in automation and technical debt reduction**, which speeds every future item.
- **Keep the team stable** and give it time to learn together.
- **Use each Retrospective** to pick one improvement and check its effect over the next few Sprints.
Our [velocity chart guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) explains how to read trends and patterns before deciding what to change.

### Velocity anti-patterns and how to avoid them
Goodhart's law, usually paraphrased as "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure", explains most velocity problems. These are the patterns we see most often.
| Anti-pattern | What happens | Better approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Velocity targets ("get to 40 points") | Estimates inflate; velocity rises while value does not | Track Sprint Goal success and outcomes instead |
| Comparing teams | Teams game their scales; trust drops | Compare each team only with its own past |
| Individual velocity | People stop helping each other | Measure the team only |
| Partial credit for unfinished items | Velocity looks better than reality; hidden unfinished work builds up | Count only items that meet the Definition of Done |
| Re-estimating after the work is known | Velocity becomes self-fulfilling and useless for forecasting | Keep the estimate agreed before work began |
| Weakening the Definition of Done to finish more | Quality falls and defects return later | Treat the Definition of Done as fixed within a Sprint |
| Planning at the best-ever velocity | Repeated misses and pressure to inflate | Plan to the recent average |
| Single-date forecasts | Stakeholders hear a promise | Give a range and update it every Sprint |

### Velocity templates and tools
A spreadsheet is enough to track velocity for one team. Our free [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) totals the story points of selected items and includes a capacity calculator, and the [Agile release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) compares cumulative points against a forecast built from your average velocity.
Most Scrum tools calculate velocity automatically from closed Sprints. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) has a velocity report on Scrum boards showing commitment and completed work per Sprint. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool overall, suits organisations that want Agile teams' delivery data in the same dashboards as other projects. Whatever you use, the numbers are only as good as the counting rules.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is velocity in Scrum?**
The total estimate, usually in story points, of the Product Backlog items a Scrum Team completes to its Definition of Done in a Sprint. Teams use the average over several Sprints for planning and forecasting.

**Q: How do you calculate velocity in Scrum?**
Add up the original estimates of every item that met the Definition of Done in the Sprint, giving unfinished items zero. For planning, average the last three to five Sprints.

**Q: Is velocity part of the Scrum Guide?**
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide does not mention velocity. It refers to the Developers' past performance, upcoming capacity and Definition of Done; velocity is a common way to record past performance.

**Q: What is a good velocity?**
There is no good number, because each team sizes points differently. A good velocity is a stable one, because stability makes forecasts reliable.

**Q: Should velocity increase over time?**
Not necessarily. It may rise a little as a team matures, but a steady rise often signals estimate inflation. Aim for stability and better conditions for finishing work.

**Q: Do incomplete stories count toward velocity?**
No. They count as zero and return to the Product Backlog. Their full estimate counts in the Sprint in which they meet the Definition of Done.

**Q: What is the difference between velocity and capacity?**
Velocity looks back at how much the team finished; capacity looks forward at how much time it has next Sprint. Teams scale velocity by capacity when planning.

**Q: How do you estimate velocity for a new team?**
Plan the first Sprint by capacity, breaking items into tasks until the available time is used, then use actual velocity from the next few Sprints as the baseline.

**Q: How many Sprints before velocity is reliable?**
Usually three to five Sprints with a stable team, a consistent Definition of Done and consistent counting rules.

**Q: Can you compare velocity between teams?**
No. Story points are relative to each team, so the same number means different amounts of work. Comparisons encourage teams to inflate estimates.

**Q: Why does velocity drop?**
Common causes are leave, team changes, unplanned work, technical debt, large or unclear items and a stronger Definition of Done. Look for a simple cause first, then discuss sustained drops at the Retrospective.

**Q: Is velocity a measure of productivity?**
No. It measures output in team-specific units, not value or outcomes. Using it to judge productivity leads to inflated estimates rather than better results.

**Q: Who is responsible for velocity?**
The Developers own their estimates and velocity. The Product Owner uses it to forecast, and the Scrum Master coaches everyone to use it for planning rather than judgement.

**Q: Can you use velocity without story points?**
Yes. Some teams count finished items per Sprint instead, which works well when items are consistently small. Kanban teams usually track throughput and cycle time instead.

# Scrum vs Lean: Key Differences and How to Combine Them

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-lean/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum vs Lean compared: origins, principles, roles, cadence and metrics, how the Scrum Guide uses Lean thinking, and how to combine both with examples.


## Scrum vs Lean: Key Differences and How to Combine Them
Scrum vs Lean is not a straight contest: Lean is a broad management philosophy for maximising customer value and removing waste across a whole value stream, while Scrum is a lightweight framework for teams doing complex product work in fixed-length Sprints. The two overlap heavily, and the 2020 Scrum Guide says Scrum is founded on empiricism and Lean thinking. This guide compares them side by side, explains where each fits and shows, step by step and with a worked example, how to use Lean thinking to get more from Scrum.
- Published 7 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Lean is a philosophy and management system from the Toyota Production System; Scrum is a team-level framework first presented in 1995.
- The Scrum Guide says Scrum is founded on empiricism and Lean thinking, which "reduces waste and focuses on the essentials".
- Scrum prescribes accountabilities, events, artifacts and a Sprint cadence; Lean prescribes no team structure or iterations.
- Both value customer focus, small batches, visible work, continuous improvement and respect for people.
- Use Scrum inside product teams and Lean tools such as value stream mapping and WIP limits to improve the wider system around them.
- Many teams find their biggest delays sit outside the Sprint, which only a Lean view of the whole value stream reveals.

### Scrum vs Lean at a glance
**The main difference between Scrum and Lean** is scope. Lean is a way of thinking about an entire organisation's value stream, focused on flow and eliminating waste. Scrum is a specific framework that tells one small, cross-functional team how to organise its work into Sprints with defined accountabilities, events and artifacts. Lean answers "how should the whole system work?"; Scrum answers "how should this team deliver and learn?".
|  | Lean | Scrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A philosophy, set of principles and toolkit | A lightweight framework defined in the Scrum Guide |
| Origin | Toyota Production System, developed from the late 1940s | Software and product development; presented by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland in 1995 |
| Scope | The whole value stream, from request to delivery, often across departments | One Scrum Team and its product |
| Core aim | Maximise customer value by improving flow and removing waste | Deliver valuable, usable Increments and learn through empiricism |
| Structure | No fixed roles, events or iterations | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers; five events; three artifacts |
| Cadence | Continuous flow; work is pulled when there is capacity | Fixed-length Sprints of one month or less |
| Handling change | Any time; decide as late as responsibly possible | New work is usually added to the Product Backlog; the Sprint Goal stays fixed during the Sprint |
| Typical metrics | Lead time, cycle time, throughput, flow efficiency | Sprint Goal success, velocity, burndown and burnup (none mandated) |
| Improvement | Continuous (kaizen), anywhere in the system | Built in through the Sprint Retrospective each Sprint |
| Best suited to | Repeatable or flow-based work and whole-organisation improvement | Complex product work with high uncertainty |
Because Scrum already uses Lean thinking, most organisations do not choose one or the other. They use Scrum inside product teams and Lean principles to improve how work reaches and leaves those teams.

### What is Lean?
**Lean** is a management approach that aims to deliver the most value to customers with the least waste, by making work flow smoothly and improving continuously. It grew out of the Toyota Production System, developed from the late 1940s by Taiichi Ohno, Eiji Toyoda and colleagues, when Toyota needed to build cars efficiently in small volumes. The word "lean" itself was coined by researcher John Krafcik in 1988 and popularised by *The Machine That Changed the World* (1990) by Womack, Jones and Roos.

#### The five Lean principles
In *Lean Thinking* (1996), James Womack and Daniel Jones summarised Lean as five steps, which the Lean Enterprise Institute still teaches:
1. **Specify value** from the end customer's point of view.
2. **Identify the value stream**: every step needed to deliver that value, and remove the steps that add none.
3. **Make value flow** through the remaining steps without interruptions, queues or rework.
4. **Let the customer pull** work, so nothing is produced before it is needed.
5. **Pursue perfection** by repeating the cycle, steadily removing more waste.

#### The seven wastes
Ohno identified seven forms of waste (in Japanese, *muda*): transport, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, over-processing and defects. Many practitioners add an eighth: unused talent. Toyota later summarised its philosophy, in *The Toyota Way 2001*, as two pillars: **continuous improvement** and **respect for people**.
Lean also brought tools that are now common in project work: kanban systems, Just-in-Time production, value stream mapping, 5S, root cause analysis with the Five Whys, and kaizen events. For the manufacturing roots, see our guide to [Lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/); for applying Lean to projects, read [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/).

### Lean in software and knowledge work
In 2003, Mary and Tom Poppendieck's *Lean Software Development: An Agile Toolkit* translated Lean for software. They described seven principles:
- Eliminate waste.
- Amplify learning.
- Decide as late as possible.
- Deliver as fast as possible.
- Empower the team.
- Build integrity in.
- Optimise the whole.
Physical waste is easy to see on a factory floor. In knowledge work it hides in backlogs, queues and inboxes. The table maps Ohno's manufacturing wastes to their common knowledge-work equivalents, following the approach the Poppendiecks popularised.
| Manufacturing waste | Knowledge-work equivalent | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory | Partially done work | Code written but not tested or released; designs waiting for approval |
| Overproduction | Extra features | Building options nobody asked for or uses |
| Over-processing | Extra processes | Duplicate sign-offs, reports nobody reads |
| Transport | Handoffs | Work passed from analysts to developers to testers to operations |
| Motion | Task switching | People split across several projects at once |
| Waiting | Waiting / delays | Waiting for decisions, environments or another team |
| Defects | Defects | Bugs found late, rework after release |
Lean ideas also shaped the [Kanban Method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-kanban/) for knowledge work, the [theory of constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/) mindset many teams use and the [pull system](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/) that underpins both Kanban and Scrum's Sprint Planning.

### What is Scrum?
**Scrum** is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organisations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. A small Scrum Team, made up of a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and Developers, works in Sprints of one month or less. Each Sprint contains Sprint Planning, Daily Scrums, a Sprint Review and a Sprint Retrospective, and produces at least one usable Increment that meets the Definition of Done.
Scrum is defined in the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. The current version dates from November 2020. Scrum was first presented publicly in 1995 and took its name from Takeuchi and Nonaka's 1986 Harvard Business Review article "The New New Product Development Game", which compared high-performing product teams, many of them at Japanese manufacturers, to a rugby scrum.
For the full framework, see [what is Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) and [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/). For how it compares with Agile more broadly, read [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/).

### How the Scrum Guide uses Lean thinking
The 2020 Scrum Guide opens its theory section with: "Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking. Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed. Lean thinking reduces waste and focuses on the essentials." The Guide does not go further, but many Scrum rules are easy to read as Lean ideas in practice.
| Scrum element | Lean idea it reflects |
| --- | --- |
| Short Sprints with a usable Increment each time | Small batches and fast feedback; less partially done work |
| Definition of Done | Build quality in; avoid defects and hidden rework |
| Ordered Product Backlog and a Product Goal | Specify value; focus on the essentials |
| Developers select work in Sprint Planning | Pull rather than push |
| Cross-functional, self-managing team | Fewer handoffs; respect for people |
| Sprint Retrospective | Continuous improvement (kaizen) |
| Time-boxed events | Reduce waiting and over-processing in meetings |
| Transparent artifacts | Visual management; make problems visible |
The other foundation, empiricism, has three pillars: transparency, inspection and adaptation. Our guides to [empiricism in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/) and [Scrum principles and values](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-principles-and-values/) explain them in detail.

### Key differences between Scrum and Lean

#### Scope: system versus team
Lean looks at the whole value stream: how a customer request travels through sales, design, development, approval, release and support. Scrum focuses on a single team and its product. A Scrum Team can be very efficient within the Sprint while most of the delay happens before work reaches it or after it leaves. Lean is the lens that finds those delays.

#### Structure and cadence
Scrum is prescriptive about a few things: three accountabilities, five events, three artifacts and their commitments, and a fixed Sprint length. Lean prescribes no roles, meetings or iterations. Lean-based systems such as Kanban usually work in continuous flow, releasing whenever an item is ready, with planning and review happening on their own cadences.

#### Roles
Scrum defines who is accountable for what: the Product Owner for maximising value and managing the Product Backlog, the Scrum Master for the team's effectiveness, and the Developers for creating a usable Increment each Sprint. Lean organisations often have value stream owners or improvement leaders, but Lean itself does not require any team roles.

#### Planning and change
Scrum plans in Sprint-sized chunks around a Sprint Goal. The plan can change during the Sprint, but nothing should endanger the Sprint Goal, so most new requests wait for the next Sprint Planning. Lean favours deciding as late as responsibly possible and pulling the next most valuable item whenever capacity frees up.

#### Measures
Scrum teams commonly track Sprint Goal success, velocity and burndowns, although the Scrum Guide mandates none of them. Lean emphasises end-to-end flow: lead time, cycle time, throughput and [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/).

#### Improvement
Scrum guarantees an improvement conversation at least once per Sprint through the Retrospective. Lean expects improvement to happen continuously and anywhere, from small daily changes to structured kaizen events, often using root cause analysis.

### What Scrum and Lean have in common
- **Customer value as the goal.** Lean starts by specifying value; Scrum orders the Product Backlog by value and inspects outcomes at the Sprint Review.
- **Small batches and fast feedback.** Lean reduces batch size to improve flow; Scrum delivers Increments every Sprint.
- **Built-in quality.** Lean stops to fix problems at the source; Scrum will not release work that fails the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
- **Continuous improvement.** Kaizen in Lean; the Sprint Retrospective in Scrum.
- **Respect for people.** Lean treats it as a pillar; Scrum's values include respect, and teams are self-managing.
- **Visible work.** Lean uses visual management; Scrum requires transparent artifacts, often on a board.
- **Pull.** Lean lets demand pull work; Scrum Developers pull items into the Sprint rather than having work assigned.
These shared roots explain why Scrum and Lean tools mix so easily, and why the Agile Manifesto drew on both Lean manufacturing and 1990s methods such as Scrum.

### When to use Scrum, Lean or both
The question is rarely "Scrum or Lean?" but "where does a fixed Sprint cadence help, and where would continuous flow serve better?". This is our guidance, not a rule from either body of knowledge.
| Situation | Better fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New product with uncertain requirements | Scrum | Sprints, Sprint Goals and Reviews create regular learning loops |
| Team needs structure, clear accountability and a shared rhythm | Scrum | Defined events and accountabilities give a simple starting point |
| Steady stream of small, unpredictable requests (support, operations) | Lean / Kanban | Continuous flow avoids waiting for the next Sprint |
| Delays come mostly from handoffs between departments | Lean | Value stream mapping covers the whole system, not one team |
| Repeatable process with known steps | Lean | Standard work and waste removal improve predictable processes |
| Several Scrum teams with long end-to-end lead times | Both | Scrum in the teams, Lean across the value stream |
| Scrum team with good velocity but slow delivery to users | Both | Lean exposes the waiting before and after the Sprint |
If you are deciding between Scrum and a Lean-based flow method for one team, our comparison of [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) goes into the team-level trade-offs, and [Kanban vs Scrumban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrumban/) covers the hybrid.

### Five questions to choose your approach
If you are setting up a new team or rethinking how an existing one works, answer these questions in order. They are our own checklist, drawn from the differences above.
1. **How uncertain is the work?** If the team is discovering what to build and expects requirements to change as it learns, Scrum's Sprint Goals and Sprint Reviews give structured feedback. If the work is well understood and repeatable, Lean flow and standard work are usually enough.
2. **How do requests arrive?** Work that can be planned in batches every week or two suits Sprints. Work that arrives unpredictably and must start within hours, such as incidents or service requests, suits continuous flow with WIP limits.
3. **Where does the delay happen?** Measure lead time from request to delivery and compare it with your Sprint length. If most of the time is spent outside the team, start with a Lean value stream view before changing anything inside the team.
4. **Does the team need structure or freedom?** A new or struggling team often benefits from Scrum's clear accountabilities and events. A mature team with good flow may prefer the lighter structure of a Lean or Kanban system.
5. **Who needs to be involved?** Scrum changes how one team works. Lean improvements often need people from several departments, so they need sponsorship from someone who can change the wider system.
Two short examples show how the answers play out:
- **A product team building a new customer portal** faces high uncertainty, plans work every two weeks and needs a regular rhythm with stakeholders. Scrum is the natural core, with WIP limits and cycle time added once the basics are stable.
- **An IT operations team handling access requests and incidents** receives unpredictable, small items that need fast turnaround. A Lean, Kanban-style flow system fits better, with a regular improvement meeting borrowed from the Scrum Retrospective.
Many organisations end up with both patterns side by side, sharing the same Lean improvement practices across teams.

### How to combine Lean and Scrum step by step
This process adds Lean thinking to an existing Scrum Team without changing the Scrum framework itself.
1. **Define value with the Product Owner.** Make sure the Product Goal and the top of the Product Backlog describe customer outcomes, not just features. Remove backlog items nobody can explain the value of.
2. **Map the end-to-end value stream.** With the team and people from upstream and downstream, walk one typical item from request to use. Record each step, who does it, active work time and waiting time. Our guide to [value stream mapping](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) shows how.
3. **Measure lead time and flow efficiency.** Lead time is request to delivery; flow efficiency is active time ÷ lead time × 100. Compare lead time with Sprint length to see how much of the delay sits outside the Sprint.
4. **Pick the biggest queue, not the easiest fix.** Use the map to find the longest wait or the most rework. That is your first improvement target.
5. **Limit work in progress inside the Sprint.** Agree a [WIP limit](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) on the Sprint board so Developers finish items before starting new ones. This cuts partially done work and shortens cycle time.
6. **Bring work into the team to reduce handoffs.** Where a separate team tests, reviews or releases, aim to include those skills in the Scrum Team and in the Definition of Done.
7. **Use the Retrospective for waste hunting.** Every few Sprints, review the seven wastes as a checklist and pick one to reduce. Our [Sprint Retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) has space for this.
8. **Find root causes.** For recurring problems, use the Five Whys or a fishbone diagram before agreeing an action. The [root cause analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) helps structure it.
9. **Track flow metrics alongside Scrum metrics.** Add cycle time and lead time next to Sprint Goal success and velocity, and review them at the Sprint Review and Retrospective.
10. **Repeat.** Re-map the value stream every few months, as Lean's fifth principle suggests.
Tip
Keep the Scrum framework intact while you add Lean practices. WIP limits, flow metrics and value stream maps are complementary practices; they do not replace Sprints, the Sprint Goal or any Scrum event.

### Worked example: finding waste around a Scrum team
The figures below are an illustrative example, not data from a real organisation. A Scrum Team in a mid-sized company works in two-week Sprints (10 working days) and has a stable velocity. Stakeholders still complain that requested changes take "months". The team maps one typical feature from approval to use.
| Step | Active work (days) | Waiting (days) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approved request waits in the Product Backlog | 0 | 30 |
| Refinement with the Product Owner | 0.5 | 0 |
| Waits for the next Sprint Planning | 0 | 5 |
| Built during the Sprint | 4 | 6 |
| Separate test team checks it | 1 | 4 |
| Waits for the monthly release window | 0.5 | 9 |
| **Total** | **6** | **54** |
Lead time is 6 + 54 = 60 working days. Flow efficiency is 6 ÷ 60 × 100 = **10%**. The Sprint itself accounts for only 10 of the 60 days, so improving velocity alone could never fix the stakeholders' complaint.
The team agreed four changes over the next few Sprints:
- **Shorter backlog queue.** The Product Owner removed low-value items and refined only the next few Sprints' worth of work in detail, cutting the backlog wait.
- **Testing inside the team.** A tester joined the Scrum Team and automated regression tests were added to the Definition of Done, removing the separate test handoff.
- **WIP limit of three items** on the Sprint board, reducing waiting inside the Sprint.
- **Release when done.** The team worked with operations to automate deployment, so items release when they meet the Definition of Done rather than waiting for a monthly window.
| Measure | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lead time (working days) | 60 | 25 |
| Active work (days) | 6 | 6 |
| Waiting (days) | 54 | 19 |
| Flow efficiency | 10% | 24% |
Nothing about Scrum changed: the team still ran Sprints, Sprint Goals and every event. Lean thinking simply showed where the waste was. For other ways to visualise the result, see the [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/).

### Lean wastes as Scrum anti-patterns
The seven wastes make a practical checklist for a Retrospective. Each has a typical symptom in Scrum teams and a countermeasure from Scrum, Lean or both.
| Waste | How it shows up in Scrum | Countermeasure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Partially done work | Many items in progress at Sprint end; work carried over | WIP limits; smaller items; swarming |
| Extra features | Features built without evidence of need | Product Goal focus; validate at Sprint Review |
| Extra processes | Status reports duplicating the Sprint Review; extra approvals | Use Scrum events instead of parallel meetings |
| Handoffs | Separate design, test or release teams | Cross-functional team; stronger Definition of Done |
| Task switching | Developers split across several teams or projects | Dedicated team members; fewer parallel goals |
| Waiting | Blocked items, slow decisions, external dependencies | Scrum Master removes impediments; map the value stream |
| Defects | Escaped defects and rework next Sprint | Automated testing; Definition of Done; root cause analysis |
Bring this table to your next [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) and ask which waste cost the team most in the last Sprint.

### Scrum, Lean, Kanban and Lean Six Sigma: where each fits
Searchers often meet these terms together. They work at different levels.
| Approach | What it is | Main focus | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lean | Philosophy and management system | Value, flow, waste removal | Whole organisations and value streams |
| Scrum | Team framework | Empiricism and Increments in Sprints | Complex product development |
| Kanban | Flow method built on Lean | Visualising work, limiting WIP, managing flow | Service, support and continuous delivery work; also used with Scrum |
| Six Sigma | Data-driven quality method | Reducing variation and defects | Repeatable processes |
| Lean Six Sigma | Combination of Lean and Six Sigma | Waste and variation together | Process improvement programmes |
| Lean-Agile | General term for combining Lean and Agile | Flow plus adaptive delivery | Often used by scaling frameworks such as SAFe |
Scaling frameworks such as the [Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) describe themselves in Lean-Agile terms and combine Scrum-style teams with Lean portfolio and flow practices. For the quality side, read [Lean vs Six Sigma](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-vs-six-sigma/).

### Common mistakes when comparing or combining Scrum and Lean
- **Treating them as rivals.** Scrum already rests on Lean thinking; forcing a choice usually means losing useful tools from one side.
- **Calling Scrum "Lean" while ignoring waste outside the team.** A fast Sprint inside a slow value stream still gives slow delivery.
- **Copying tools without the thinking.** WIP limits or value stream maps without respect for people and genuine improvement become another layer of process.
- **Abandoning Scrum events in the name of flow.** Dropping the Retrospective or Sprint Review removes the inspection points empiricism depends on.
- **Using Lean to cut people rather than waste.** Lean's respect-for-people pillar is about improving the system, not headcount.
- **Measuring only velocity.** Without lead time and flow efficiency, teams cannot see most of the delay customers experience.
- **Over-processing the combination.** Adding every Lean tool at once creates the very waste Lean warns against. Start with one queue.
If you are also weighing Scrum against plan-driven methods, our guide to [Scrum vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/) covers that comparison.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the main difference between Scrum and Lean?**
Lean is a broad philosophy for maximising customer value and eliminating waste across a whole value stream. Scrum is a specific team framework with Sprints, accountabilities, events and artifacts for complex product work.

**Q: Is Scrum Lean or Agile?**
Scrum is usually classed as an Agile framework, and both of its creators signed the Agile Manifesto. The Scrum Guide also says Scrum is founded on empiricism and Lean thinking, so it is Agile with Lean foundations rather than one of the classic Lean methods.

**Q: Does the Scrum Guide mention Lean?**
Yes. The 2020 Scrum Guide says Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking, and that lean thinking reduces waste and focuses on the essentials. It does not prescribe specific Lean tools.

**Q: Can you use Lean and Scrum together?**
Yes, and most organisations do. A common pattern is Scrum inside product teams, with Lean practices such as value stream mapping, WIP limits and flow metrics used to improve how work reaches and leaves those teams.

**Q: Which came first, Lean or Scrum?**
Lean. It comes from the Toyota Production System, developed from the late 1940s, and the term "lean" dates from 1988. Scrum was first presented in 1995.

**Q: Is Kanban Lean or Scrum?**
Kanban comes from Lean. It is a flow-based method rather than part of Scrum, though many Scrum teams borrow Kanban practices such as WIP limits and flow metrics.

**Q: Which is better, Lean or Scrum?**
Neither is better in general. Scrum suits complex product work that benefits from a regular cadence of delivery and learning. Lean suits improving flow across a whole system or repeatable processes. Many organisations use both.

**Q: What are the five Lean principles?**
As set out by Womack and Jones in Lean Thinking: specify value, identify the value stream, make value flow, let the customer pull, and pursue perfection.

**Q: What are the seven wastes in software development?**
Following Mary and Tom Poppendieck: partially done work, extra processes, extra features, task switching, waiting, handoffs (motion) and defects.

**Q: Do Lean and Scrum define the same roles?**
No. Scrum defines three accountabilities: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers. Lean does not prescribe team roles, although Lean organisations often have value stream owners or improvement leaders.

**Q: What is Lean Agile?**
Lean Agile is a general term for combining Lean principles, such as flow and waste reduction, with Agile values and frameworks such as Scrum. Scaling frameworks such as SAFe describe themselves in Lean-Agile terms.

**Q: Is Lean Six Sigma the same as Scrum?**
No. Lean Six Sigma is a process improvement method that combines waste reduction with statistical quality control. Scrum is a framework for delivering complex products in Sprints. They can coexist but solve different problems.

**Q: Which is faster, Lean or Scrum?**
Neither is inherently faster. Lean shortens lead time across the whole system, while Scrum gives a regular cadence of delivery. Combining them usually gives the biggest gain, because many delays sit outside the Sprint.
