# Scrum vs Waterfall: Differences, Examples and How to Choose

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Scrum vs Waterfall compared: planning, roles, change, testing and risk, the same project run both ways, a scoring tool for choosing and hybrid options.


## Scrum vs Waterfall: Differences, Examples and How to Choose
Scrum vs Waterfall comes down to when you plan and when you deliver: Waterfall plans the whole project up front and delivers the result at the end, while Scrum plans in short Sprints and delivers a usable Increment every Sprint. Neither is better in general; each fits a different kind of work. This guide compares them point by point, runs the same project both ways and gives you a simple way to choose, combine or switch.
- Published 7 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Waterfall is a predictive approach: fix the scope, plan it in detail, then build and test in sequence. Scrum is an adaptive framework: fix the Sprint length and team, and let scope evolve through feedback.
- In Waterfall, users usually see the working result near the end. In Scrum, stakeholders inspect a usable Increment at every Sprint Review.
- Waterfall handles change through formal change requests; Scrum handles it by re-ordering the Product Backlog between Sprints.
- Waterfall suits stable requirements, physical or contract-driven work and heavy regulation. Scrum suits uncertain, complex work where early feedback is valuable.
- Hybrids are common: Waterfall-style governance and milestones with Scrum teams delivering inside them.
- When moving from Waterfall to Scrum, turn the remaining requirements into a Product Backlog and map existing roles to the three Scrum accountabilities.

### Scrum vs Waterfall: what is the difference?
**The difference between Scrum and Waterfall is how they deal with uncertainty.** Waterfall assumes the requirements can be known up front, so it plans everything first and completes each phase in sequence. Scrum assumes you will learn as you go, so it delivers in Sprints of one month or less and adapts the plan after each one.
PMI describes these as **predictive** and **adaptive** approaches, and a mix of the two as **hybrid**. Waterfall is the classic predictive life cycle. Scrum is the most widely used adaptive framework, defined by the 2020 Scrum Guide. Strictly, you are comparing a life cycle model with a framework, but in practice both answer the same question: how should this project be planned and delivered?

### Waterfall in brief
In Waterfall, a project moves through fixed phases, typically requirements, design, implementation, verification, deployment and maintenance. Each phase produces approved deliverables that feed the next, and a phase gate at the end of each one decides whether the project continues. Scope, schedule and cost are planned in detail, saved as a [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/) and controlled through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
A project manager usually plans and directs the work, specialists hand work from one phase to the next, and progress is shown on a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) against the baseline.
See our full guide to [Waterfall project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) for the phases, gates, a worked example and its pros and cons.

### Scrum in brief
Scrum is a lightweight framework in which a small, cross-functional Scrum Team, typically ten or fewer people, delivers value in fixed-length Sprints of one month or less. It has three accountabilities (Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers), five events (the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective) and three artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment).
The Product Owner orders the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) to maximise value. Each Sprint, the team selects work towards a Sprint Goal, builds a usable Increment that meets the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), shows it to stakeholders at the [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) and improves its own way of working at the Retrospective. Our guide to [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) covers each element in detail.

### Scrum vs Waterfall comparison table
| Aspect | Waterfall | Scrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approach | Predictive, sequential | Adaptive, iterative and incremental |
| Planning | Detailed plan up front, baselined | Product Goal plus detailed planning each Sprint |
| What is fixed | Scope; time and cost are estimated from it | Sprint length and team; scope varies |
| Requirements | Specification signed off early | Product Backlog that evolves |
| Delivery | One release at the end, or a few large ones | A usable Increment every Sprint |
| Roles | Project manager, analysts, designers, developers, testers | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers |
| Decision-making | Project manager and sponsor, through gates | Product Owner decides what; Developers decide how |
| Change | Formal change requests and impact assessment | Re-order the Product Backlog; applies from the next Sprint |
| Testing | A separate phase after build | Within every Sprint, to meet the Definition of Done |
| Risk | Many risks surface late, in integration and testing | Surfaces early through frequent integration and feedback |
| Stakeholder involvement | Heavy at the start and at gates | At every Sprint Review and through the Product Owner |
| Documentation | Comprehensive, created phase by phase | Just enough; backlog and Increments are the main record |
| Progress measure | Planned vs actual, milestones, earned value | Working Increments, Sprint Goals, burndown and velocity |
| Typical contract | Fixed price against a specification | Time and materials, or fixed budget with flexible scope |
| Typical fit | Construction, infrastructure, regulated rollouts | Software, digital products, new services |

### Pros and cons of Scrum and Waterfall
Each approach's strengths are the mirror image of the other's weaknesses.
|  | Waterfall | Scrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main advantages | Predictable scope, dates and budget when requirements are stable; clear phases and milestones; thorough documentation for audits and handovers; fits fixed-price contracts; less demand on stakeholders' time | Early and frequent delivery of value; problems and misunderstandings found within weeks; change absorbed cheaply; quality built in every Sprint; motivated, self-managing teams |
| Main disadvantages | Late feedback from users; costly change after sign-off; risks found late in testing; no value until the end; assumes requirements can be known early | Less up-front certainty about final scope and date; needs an empowered Product Owner and regular stakeholder time; harder to fit fixed-price contracts; relies on a dedicated, cross-functional team |
| Biggest risk | Delivering exactly what was specified, on time, and finding it is not what users need | Delivering a stream of Increments without a clear Product Goal, so the product drifts |
| How to reduce it | Prototypes, design walkthroughs with users, phased releases | A clear Product Goal, an ordered backlog and real stakeholders at every Sprint Review |
Many of Waterfall's weaknesses come from running a single pass with no feedback, and many of Scrum's come from adopting the events without the discipline behind them. Both work well when they are applied to the kind of work they were designed for.

### The key differences explained

#### Planning
Waterfall front-loads planning. Before the build starts you have a work breakdown structure, a schedule with dependencies and a cost estimate. Scrum spreads planning across the project: a long-term Product Goal, an ordered backlog refined continuously, and detailed planning only for the next Sprint. Scrum still plans; it just plans at the last responsible moment. See our guide to [the role of the project plan in Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/role-of-the-project-plan-in-agile/).

#### Scope, time and cost
Waterfall fixes scope and estimates time and cost from it. Scrum turns this around: the team and Sprint length fix the cost and cadence, and scope is what flexes, with the most valuable items done first. If the money or time runs out, a Scrum project stops with the most valuable features already delivered; a Waterfall project that runs out may have nothing usable yet.

#### Delivery and value
Waterfall delivers value once, at the end. Scrum requires a usable Increment every Sprint, which can be released early to some or all users. Early releases bring earlier benefits and real feedback, but only if the product can be used in parts.

#### Roles and decision-making
Waterfall usually has a project manager who plans, assigns and controls work, with specialists working phase by phase. The Scrum Guide has no project manager role. The [three Scrum accountabilities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) split that job: the Product Owner decides what to build and in what order, the Developers decide how and manage their own work, and the Scrum Master improves the team's effectiveness.

#### Handling change
In Waterfall, a change after sign-off goes through a change request, an impact assessment and a decision by the change authority, because it may ripple through design, build and test. In Scrum, new ideas go into the Product Backlog and the Product Owner re-orders it; the change takes effect from the next Sprint. Scrum does not make change free. It makes it cheaper by keeping the unbuilt part of the plan light.

#### Testing and quality
Waterfall tests in a dedicated phase after the build, so defects and misunderstood requirements are often found late. In Scrum, work is not done until it meets the Definition of Done, which normally includes testing, so quality is built in every Sprint. Waterfall testing time is also the first thing squeezed when earlier phases overrun.

#### Risk
Waterfall reduces risk through analysis, design reviews and contingency. Scrum reduces it through short feedback loops: technical risks surface when the team integrates working software every Sprint, and product risks surface when stakeholders inspect the Increment.

#### Documentation and reporting
Waterfall produces requirements specifications, design documents, test plans and status reports at each phase. Scrum favours just enough documentation, with the Product Backlog, Increment and Sprint Review as the main sources of truth. Regulated Scrum teams still produce the documents auditors need, often as part of the Definition of Done.

### Scrum vs Agile vs Waterfall
These three terms are often compared as if they were equals, but they are not the same kind of thing.
- **Agile** is a mindset and set of values and principles, set out in the 2001 Agile Manifesto.
- **Scrum** is one specific framework for working in an Agile way. Kanban, Extreme Programming and others are alternatives.
- **Waterfall** is a predictive life cycle, the opposite end of the spectrum from Agile.
So Scrum vs Waterfall compares a specific Agile framework with a predictive approach. For the broader comparison see [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/); for how Scrum relates to Agile, see [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/); and if you are considering a flow-based option, our Kanban guides compare it with both.

### Worked example: the same project run both ways
The following example is **illustrative**: the organisation, durations and figures are invented to show how the two approaches behave on the same project.
A housing association with 8,000 tenants wants an online portal where tenants can report repairs, pay rent and update their details. The budget allows a team of seven for about six months. Tenants have never had online services before, so nobody is sure which features they will use most.

#### Run as Waterfall
| Phase | Weeks | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | 1 to 5 | Workshops with housing officers; 140 requirements signed off |
| Design | 6 to 9 | Screen designs, integration design for the housing and payments systems |
| Build | 10 to 19 | All three features built in parallel |
| Test | 20 to 23 | System testing, then user acceptance testing with 20 tenants |
| Deploy | 24 to 26 | Launch to all tenants |
In week 16, housing officers ask for tenants to be able to upload photos with repair reports, because contractors keep arriving without the right parts. The project manager raises a change request. The impact assessment shows changes to the signed-off design, the build and the test scripts, adding about three weeks. The change board approves it and moves the launch to week 29. In UAT, tenants find the rent payment journey confusing; fixing it adds another two weeks.

#### Run as Scrum
| Sprints (2 weeks each) | Sprint Goal | What is released |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 to 3 | Tenants can report a repair online | Repairs reporting, released to a pilot of 300 tenants after Sprint 3 |
| 4 to 6 | Tenants can pay rent online | Rent payment, released to the pilot; feedback reshapes the journey in Sprint 6 |
| 7 to 8 | Repair reports include photos | Photo upload, added to the backlog after pilot feedback and ordered first |
| 9 to 11 | All tenants can use the portal | Wider release, accessibility fixes, update-details feature |
| 12 | Improve based on live use | Highest-value fixes from live data |
The photo request arrives in Sprint 6 from pilot users and housing officers. The Product Owner orders it above "update your details", which tenants have rarely asked for. Nothing already built has to change. At the end of six months, update-details is simpler than first planned, which the sponsor accepts because repairs and rent were working months earlier.

#### Comparing the outcomes
| Measure | Waterfall | Scrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First tenant use | Week 26 (moved to week 31 after changes) | Week 7 (pilot) |
| Photo upload change | Change request, three-week delay | Re-ordered in the backlog, no rework |
| Usability problems found | In UAT, near the end | In the pilot, Sprint 5 |
| What flexed | Time and cost | Scope of a low-value feature |
| Up-front certainty | High: dates and scope agreed early | Lower: scope agreed Sprint by Sprint |
Scrum fits this project because the value is uncertain and the portal is useful in parts. Change the facts, though, and the answer changes: a fixed-price contract with a regulator-approved specification, or an office move with a hard lease date, would favour Waterfall.

### When Waterfall is the better choice
- **Requirements are stable and well understood**, for example a payroll system dictated by legislation.
- **The output only has value when complete**: a bridge, a data centre move or an office relocation.
- **Late change is very expensive**, because work is physical or manufacturing tooling is involved.
- **Contracts or regulation require approved stages**, such as fixed-price public procurement or validated systems.
- **The team has delivered similar projects many times** and the method is proven.
- **Stakeholders are only available at key points**, not every few weeks.

### When Scrum is the better choice
- **The solution is uncertain** and needs discovery, such as a new digital product or service.
- **The product is useful in increments**, so early releases bring early value and feedback.
- **Users and stakeholders can give regular feedback** at Sprint Reviews.
- **Speed to market matters** more than delivering everything at once.
- **Technology is new or changing**, so technical risk is best reduced by building and integrating early.
- **A small, cross-functional, stable team** can be dedicated to the work.

### How to choose between Scrum and Waterfall
Use these steps for a new project, or at a phase boundary on an existing one.
1. **Describe the end result.** Write one paragraph on what will exist when the project is finished and who will use it.
2. **List the fixed constraints.** Note hard dates, fixed budgets, contracts, regulatory approvals and physical dependencies.
3. **Score the project.** Rate each factor in the table below from 1 to 5.
4. **Look for splits.** Different parts of the project may score differently, for example hardware versus software.
5. **Check the organisation.** Can you provide a Product Owner with authority, a dedicated team and stakeholders for Sprint Reviews? If not, Scrum will struggle until you can.
6. **Decide and record why.** Note the approach and reasons in the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) so it can be revisited.
| Factor | 1 (leans Waterfall) | 5 (leans Scrum) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement clarity | Fully known and stable | Unclear or likely to change |
| Value in parts | Only useful when complete | Useful in small increments |
| Cost of late change | Very high | Low |
| Contract | Fixed price, fixed specification | Time and materials or flexible scope |
| Regulation | Formal stage approvals required | Lighter documentation acceptable |
| Stakeholder availability | Only at milestones | Every few weeks |
| Technology | Mature and well understood | New or experimental |
| Team set-up | Specialists shared across projects | Dedicated, cross-functional team |
Add up the eight scores. As a rule of thumb, **8 to 18** points to Waterfall, **19 to 29** to a hybrid and **30 to 40** to Scrum. These bands are a starting point for discussion, not a formula. The tenant portal above scored 5, 5, 4, 3, 3, 4, 3 and 4, a total of 31, which supports using Scrum. A fixed-date office move might score 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1 and 2, a total of 12.

### Hybrid approaches: combining Scrum and Waterfall
Many organisations combine the two rather than choose. The most common patterns are:
| Pattern | How it works | Works well when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scrum inside phase gates | Funding, milestones and gates are predictive; delivery between gates runs in Sprints | Governance needs gates but the solution needs feedback |
| Water-scrum-fall | Requirements and funding up front, build in Sprints, then a formal release and deployment phase | Release processes or operations teams are not yet Agile |
| Split by workstream | Hardware, construction or procurement run as Waterfall; software runs as Scrum | Some parts are physical and some are digital |
| Predictive programme, Scrum projects | The programme plan sets major dates; each team uses Scrum | Large change programmes with several teams |
To make a hybrid work, agree where the boundary sits, which dates are fixed and which scope can flex, and how Sprint progress rolls up into milestone reporting. Use [release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) to connect Sprints to milestones. The risk is getting the worst of both: heavy up-front specifications that remove Scrum's flexibility, plus Sprints that never release. Methods such as [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) explicitly support Agile delivery within management stages.

### How to move from Waterfall to Scrum, step by step
You can switch at any point, but a phase boundary, often after design, is the easiest place.
1. **Agree why you are switching.** Name the problem Scrum should solve, such as late feedback or frequent change.
2. **Appoint a Product Owner.** Choose one person with the authority to order the work and access to stakeholders, often the business lead or senior analyst.
3. **Form the Scrum Team.** Bring designers, developers and testers into one team of ten or fewer, and choose a Scrum Master.
4. **Convert remaining requirements into a Product Backlog.** Rewrite open requirements as backlog items with acceptance criteria. Our [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) helps.
5. **Order the backlog by value and risk.** Put high-value and high-risk items first.
6. **Write a Definition of Done.** Include testing, documentation and any regulatory evidence previously produced in later phases.
7. **Agree Sprint length and run the first Sprint.** Two weeks is common. Keep the Sprint Review open to the sponsors who used to attend gates.
8. **Reconnect governance.** Agree with the sponsor how Sprint Reviews and release plans replace or feed phase-gate reporting.
9. **Inspect and adapt the transition.** Use the first few Retrospectives to fix what is not working.
Tip
Do not convert a signed-off specification into a backlog and treat it as fixed. The point of switching is that the Product Owner can re-order, split and drop items as you learn.
Read our guide on [how to implement Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-implement-agile/) for the wider organisational changes.

### Mapping Waterfall roles and documents to Scrum
The Scrum Guide does not say what happens to existing job titles; organisations decide. These mappings are common starting points, not rules.
| Waterfall role | Common move in Scrum |
| --- | --- |
| Project manager | Product Owner, Scrum Master, or a delivery or programme role outside the team handling budgets, contracts and reporting |
| Business analyst | Developer focused on refinement, or supports the Product Owner |
| Designers, developers, testers | Developers in one cross-functional Scrum Team |
| Test manager | Developer with a quality focus; shapes the Definition of Done |
| Sponsor and steering group | Key stakeholders at Sprint Reviews; set the Product Goal and budget |
| Waterfall document | Scrum equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| Requirements specification | Product Backlog with acceptance criteria |
| Project plan and Gantt chart | Product Goal, release plan and Sprint Backlog |
| Change request | New or re-ordered Product Backlog item |
| Status report | Sprint Review, burndown and release forecast |
| Test plan and sign-off | Definition of Done and acceptance criteria |
| Lessons learned | Sprint Retrospective, every Sprint |

### Common mistakes when comparing or switching
- **Choosing by fashion.** Picking Scrum because it is popular, or Waterfall because it is familiar, ignores the project's actual characteristics.
- **Assuming Scrum means no planning.** Scrum plans continuously; teams without a Product Goal or ordered backlog are just busy.
- **Assuming Waterfall means no feedback.** Prototypes, design walkthroughs and phased releases bring feedback into predictive projects.
- **Mini-waterfalls inside Sprints.** Design in Sprint 1, build in Sprint 2, test in Sprint 3 is not Scrum. Each Sprint must produce a done Increment.
- **No real Product Owner.** A committee or a proxy without authority slows every decision.
- **Fixing scope, time and cost in a Scrum project.** If everything is fixed, Scrum loses its main lever. Agree what can flex.
- **Letting scope creep into Waterfall.** Informal additions accumulate into delays; route every change through change control.
- **Keeping both sets of paperwork.** Teams that produce Waterfall reports and Scrum artifacts get the overhead of both. Agree which reports Scrum artifacts replace.

### Tools for Scrum, Waterfall and hybrid projects
Waterfall projects need strong Gantt charts, dependencies and baselines; Scrum teams need backlogs, boards and Sprint planning. Hybrid teams need both in one place.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, includes interactive Gantt charts with dependencies, the critical path and baselines from the Team plan, plus Kanban boards on every plan, so a phase plan and team boards can sit together. That makes it a strong option for hybrid portfolios and PMOs.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is the most complete Agile tool for software teams that we review, with backlogs, sprints, story points and boards. It has no classic Gantt chart with critical path and baselines, so pair it with a planning tool for Waterfall work.
- **[Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/)** combines a spreadsheet grid with Gantt charts and dependencies, which suits plan-driven teams.
- **[monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/)**, **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** and **Asana** all offer timeline or Gantt views alongside boards, and suit teams running both kinds of work.
- **Templates.** Start with our [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) for Waterfall work and our [Sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) for Scrum.
See our comparison of [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) for more options.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the main difference between Scrum and Waterfall?**
Waterfall completes requirements, design, build and test in sequence and delivers at the end. Scrum delivers a usable Increment every Sprint and adapts the plan based on feedback.

**Q: Which is better, Scrum or Waterfall?**
It depends on the work. Scrum suits uncertain, changing requirements and products that are useful in parts; Waterfall suits stable, well-understood work, physical builds and regulated projects needing staged approvals.

**Q: Which is faster, Scrum or Waterfall?**
Scrum usually delivers usable results much sooner because it releases in increments. Total duration depends on scope and team, and Scrum often finishes by trimming low-value scope rather than building everything.

**Q: Which is cheaper, Scrum or Waterfall?**
Neither automatically. Scrum can reduce waste by stopping low-value work early and finding problems sooner; Waterfall can be efficient when requirements are stable. Total cost depends on scope, team and context.

**Q: Is Scrum the same as Agile?**
No. Agile is a set of values and principles; Scrum is one framework for applying them. Kanban and Extreme Programming are other Agile approaches.

**Q: What is the difference between a Sprint and a Waterfall phase?**
A Sprint is a fixed time-box of one month or less that produces a usable Increment and includes all the work needed, from refinement to testing. A Waterfall phase covers one type of work, such as design, and ends when its deliverables are approved.

**Q: Is there a project manager in Scrum?**
The Scrum Guide has no project manager role. Its responsibilities are shared between the Product Owner, Developers and Scrum Master. Many organisations keep a delivery or programme role outside the team for budgets, contracts and reporting.

**Q: How is testing different in Scrum and Waterfall?**
In Waterfall, testing is usually a separate late phase. In Scrum, testing happens within every Sprint so each Increment meets the Definition of Done.

**Q: How does documentation differ in Scrum and Waterfall?**
Waterfall relies on detailed documents created phase by phase. Scrum favours just enough documentation, with the Product Backlog and working Increments as the main sources of truth.

**Q: How are changes handled in Scrum vs Waterfall?**
Waterfall handles changes through formal change requests and impact assessment. Scrum handles them by re-ordering the Product Backlog, so changes take effect from the next Sprint.

**Q: Can Scrum and Waterfall be combined?**
Yes. Common hybrids use predictive governance, budgets and milestones with Scrum teams delivering inside them, or run hardware and construction as Waterfall and software as Scrum.

**Q: Can a project switch from Waterfall to Scrum midway?**
Yes. It works best at a phase boundary: appoint a Product Owner, form a cross-functional team, turn the remaining requirements into a Product Backlog and agree how Sprint Reviews feed governance.

**Q: Is Scrum or Waterfall better for construction projects?**
Physical construction usually follows a predictive approach because the build sequence is fixed and late change is expensive. Scrum ideas can still help in design, fit-out planning and internal work.

# Servant Leadership in Scrum: What It Means in Practice

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/servant-leadership-in-scrum/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: What servant leadership means in Scrum, its origins, how Scrum Masters and managers practise it, and the difference between serving and pleasing.


## Servant Leadership in Scrum: What It Means in Practice
The Scrum Guide describes Scrum Masters as true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation. Servant leadership means leading by helping others succeed rather than by directing them.
- Published 9 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Servant leaders lead by helping others succeed.
- Remove obstacles, coach, protect focus and grow people.
- Serving the team sometimes means challenging it.

### Origins
Robert K. Greenleaf introduced the idea of servant leadership in a 1970 essay, The Servant as Leader. His test was whether those served grow as persons and become healthier, wiser, freer and more autonomous.

### Servant leadership in practice
| Behaviour | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Removing obstacles | Getting a test environment fixed so the team can finish its work |
| Coaching, not telling | Asking "what options do you see?" instead of giving the answer |
| Protecting focus | Redirecting mid-Sprint requests to the Product Owner |
| Growing people | Encouraging team members to facilitate events themselves |
| Listening | Holding one-to-ones to understand concerns |
| Building trust | Admitting mistakes openly |

### Serving is not pleasing
Servant leaders serve the team's long-term effectiveness, not every short-term wish. That sometimes means challenging the team, holding it to the Definition of Done, or telling stakeholders uncomfortable truths. Courage is one of the [Scrum values](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-principles-and-values/).

### Managers as servant leaders
Managers of Scrum Teams also practise servant leadership: setting clear goals, removing organisational barriers, and investing in people's growth, while leaving day-to-day decisions to the team. See [how to manage Agile teams](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/how-to-manage-agile-teams/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is servant leadership weak leadership?**
No. It requires strong conviction, courage and the ability to influence without formal authority.

**Q: Who practises servant leadership in Scrum?**
Above all the Scrum Master, but also Product Owners and managers who support Scrum Teams.

**Q: What is servant leadership?**
A leadership approach in which the leader's main aim is to help others grow and succeed. The term was coined by Robert K. Greenleaf in his 1970 essay The Servant as Leader.

**Q: Does the 2020 Scrum Guide still call the Scrum Master a servant leader?**
The 2020 Scrum Guide replaced the phrase servant-leader with a description of Scrum Masters as true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation. The idea of leading by serving remains.

**Q: What are examples of servant leadership in Scrum?**
Removing an impediment the team cannot fix, coaching people to solve problems themselves, protecting the team from mid-Sprint interruptions and helping stakeholders understand Scrum.

**Q: How does servant leadership differ from traditional leadership?**
Traditional leadership often relies on authority and direction. Servant leadership relies on influence, coaching and creating conditions in which the team can make its own decisions.

**Q: Can a Scrum Master practising servant leadership tell the team what to do?**
A Scrum Master may teach Scrum and challenge the team, but does not direct its day-to-day work. The Developers are self-managing and decide how to deliver the Sprint Backlog.

**Q: How does a Scrum Master show servant leadership towards the Product Owner?**
By helping find techniques for defining the Product Goal and managing the Product Backlog, helping the team understand the need for clear backlog items and facilitating stakeholder collaboration.

**Q: How does a Scrum Master show servant leadership towards the organisation?**
By leading, training and coaching the organisation in its Scrum adoption, helping people understand an empirical approach and removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

**Q: What skills does a servant leader need?**
Listening, empathy, coaching, facilitation, persuasion and the courage to raise difficult issues. See [how to become a Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/how-to-become-a-scrum-master/).

**Q: Is servant leadership only for Scrum Masters?**
No. Product Owners, line managers and executives can all lead by supporting teams, setting clear goals and removing organisational obstacles.

# Sprint Backlog: What It Is, How to Create It, Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: The sprint backlog explained: its three parts, who owns it, how to create and update it in Scrum, what can change mid-Sprint, plus worked examples.


## Sprint Backlog: What It Is, How to Create It, Examples
The sprint backlog is the Developers' plan for the Sprint: the Sprint Goal, the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint and an actionable plan for delivering them. It is created in Sprint Planning and updated every day as the team learns. This guide explains what the 2020 Scrum Guide says, who owns the sprint backlog, how to build and update one step by step, what can and cannot change during a Sprint, and the mistakes to avoid, with a full worked example.
- Published 14 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- The sprint backlog has three parts: the Sprint Goal (why), the selected Product Backlog items (what) and the Developers' plan (how).
- It is a plan by and for the Developers. They create it in Sprint Planning and own it for the whole Sprint.
- Its commitment is the Sprint Goal. The goal stays fixed; the items and the plan can change as the team learns.
- If the work turns out different from expected, the Developers renegotiate scope with the Product Owner without endangering the Sprint Goal.
- Update it at least daily so progress can be inspected at the Daily Scrum. Tasks, hours and burndown charts are optional practices, not Scrum rules.
- At the end of the Sprint, Done items join the Increment and unfinished items go back to the Product Backlog.

### What is a sprint backlog?
A **sprint backlog** is the Developers' plan for one Sprint. It contains the Sprint Goal, the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint and an actionable plan for turning them into a usable Increment. The 2020 Scrum Guide describes it as a highly visible, real-time picture of the work the Developers plan to accomplish to achieve the Sprint Goal.
The sprint backlog is one of the three [Scrum artifacts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-artifacts/), alongside the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) and the [Increment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/increment-in-scrum/). Each artifact has a commitment that gives it focus. For the sprint backlog, that commitment is the **Sprint Goal**.
Four features set it apart from an ordinary task list:
- **It has a purpose.** The Sprint Goal explains why the Sprint is worth doing, so the team can make sensible trade-offs.
- **It belongs to the Developers.** Nobody outside the Developers decides how the work is done or who does which task.
- **It is live.** It changes throughout the Sprint as the team learns, not only at the start.
- **It lasts one Sprint.** A new sprint backlog is created at every Sprint Planning.

### What the Scrum Guide 2020 says about the sprint backlog
The 2020 Scrum Guide is still the current official version (checked 26 October 2026). The Scrum Guide Expansion Pack published in June 2025 by Ralph Jocham, John Coleman and Jeff Sutherland adds context and examples, but it is a supplement and does not change the rules. The table summarises what the Scrum Guide says about the sprint backlog and what each point means for your team.
| The Scrum Guide says | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| The sprint backlog is composed of the Sprint Goal (why), the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint (what) and an actionable plan for delivering the Increment (how) | A list of tickets without a goal or a plan is not a complete sprint backlog |
| It is a plan by and for the Developers | The Developers create it, own it and change it; managers do not assign its tasks |
| It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work | Keep it where everyone can see it and keep it current |
| It is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned | The plan is expected to change; that is not a failure |
| It should have enough detail that the Developers can inspect their progress in the Daily Scrum | If you cannot tell at the Daily Scrum whether the Sprint Goal is on track, add detail |
| The Sprint Goal is the commitment; it is created in Sprint Planning and added to the sprint backlog | Write the goal at the top of the board, not in a separate document |
| If the work turns out different from expected, the Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the sprint backlog without affecting the Sprint Goal | Items can be added, removed or changed mid-Sprint; the goal is what you protect |
| Planning is often done by decomposing items into smaller work items of one day or less; how is at the sole discretion of the Developers | Tasks of a day or less are common, but the format is the team's choice |
| The most impactful improvements from the Sprint Retrospective may be added to the sprint backlog for the next Sprint | Make improvement work visible next to product work |
Notice what is missing. The Scrum Guide does not require tasks, hour estimates, story points, assignees, due dates or a burndown chart. These are complementary practices that many teams find useful. Treat them as choices you can change, not as rules.

### The three parts of a sprint backlog

#### Why: the Sprint Goal
The **Sprint Goal** is the single objective for the Sprint. The whole Scrum Team agrees it during Sprint Planning, starting from the Product Owner's proposal of how the Sprint could increase the product's value. It gives the Developers focus and flexibility: if one item turns out harder than expected, they can find another way to meet the goal.
| Weak Sprint Goal | Why it is weak | Stronger Sprint Goal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complete stories 101 to 108 | A list of items, not an objective; gives no room to adapt | Customers can choose a delivery slot at checkout |
| Work on the reporting module | Not testable; nobody can tell when it is met | Finance managers can export the monthly sales report without manual edits |
| Deliver as much as possible | Encourages overloading the Sprint | New users can sign up and verify their email address on mobile |
A good Sprint Goal is short, describes an outcome, can be checked at the Sprint Review and moves the team toward the Product Goal.

#### What: the selected Product Backlog items
The Developers select Product Backlog items from the top of the ordered Product Backlog, in discussion with the Product Owner, to form the forecast for the Sprint. Most items should directly support the Sprint Goal. It is common to include a small amount of other work, such as an urgent bug or an improvement action, as long as everyone can still see what the goal is.
Items should be small enough to be Done within the Sprint. That is the job of [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) before Sprint Planning, not of the first days of the Sprint.

#### How: the plan
The plan describes how the Developers will turn the selected items into a usable Increment that meets the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/). Many teams break each item into tasks of a day or less, because small tasks make progress visible at the Daily Scrum. Others plan only the first few days in detail and add tasks as they go. Both are valid; the plan only needs to be actionable and inspectable.
Good plans include everything needed to meet the Definition of Done, such as testing, documentation and deployment steps, not just the build work.

### Who owns the sprint backlog?
The **Developers** own the sprint backlog. The Scrum Guide makes them accountable for creating a plan for the Sprint, and describes the sprint backlog as a plan by and for the Developers. In practice, that means:
| Who | Their part in the sprint backlog |
| --- | --- |
| Developers | Select items with the Product Owner, create the plan, choose who does what, update it daily, raise risks to the Sprint Goal |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Proposes how the Sprint could add value, clarifies items, agrees the Sprint Goal, negotiates scope when the work changes, decides where unfinished items go |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Helps the team plan well, coaches self-management, makes sure impediments are removed; does not assign tasks |
| Stakeholders and managers | Can see the sprint backlog for transparency; raise new requests with the Product Owner rather than adding them directly |
The Product Owner and Scrum Master take part as Developers only when they are actively working on sprint backlog items. For the full picture of who does what, see our guide to [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/).

### When and how the sprint backlog is created
The sprint backlog is created in [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/), the event that starts every Sprint. Sprint Planning addresses three topics, and each one produces one part of the sprint backlog.
| Sprint Planning topic | Question | Part of the sprint backlog it creates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Topic one | Why is this Sprint valuable? | The Sprint Goal |
| Topic two | What can be Done this Sprint? | The selected Product Backlog items |
| Topic three | How will the chosen work get done? | The plan |
Sprint Planning is time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint and is usually shorter for shorter Sprints. Its main inputs are the ordered Product Backlog, the latest Increment, the Developers' projected capacity and their past performance.

### How to create a sprint backlog, step by step
Use these steps in Sprint Planning. Steps 1 and 2 can be prepared beforehand so the event stays focused.
1. **Check the top of the Product Backlog.** Make sure roughly one to two Sprints' worth of items are clear, sized and small enough to be Done within a Sprint. If not, the team will spend Sprint Planning refining instead of planning.
2. **Work out capacity.** List each Developer's available days, subtracting leave, training, support duties and public holidays. See [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) for methods.
3. **Agree the Sprint Goal.** The Product Owner proposes how this Sprint could add value; the whole Scrum Team shapes it into one clear objective.
4. **Select items.** Starting at the top of the Product Backlog, the Developers pull in items that serve the goal until they judge the forecast is realistic. Use recent [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) as a guide, adjusted for capacity, not as a target.
5. **Plan the work.** For each item, the Developers decide how they will build, test and finish it. Break items into tasks of a day or less where that helps. Plan the first few days in the most detail.
6. **Add an improvement action.** Bring in one of the most important actions from the last [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) so it is planned, not forgotten.
7. **Sense-check against the Definition of Done.** Ask: if we finish these tasks, will every item meet the Definition of Done? Add missing testing, review or release work.
8. **Make it visible.** Put the Sprint Goal at the top of the board, the items in order and the tasks underneath. Do not pre-assign every task; let people pull work as they become free.
Tip
If the team finishes Sprint Planning and cannot explain in one sentence what success looks like, the Sprint Goal needs more work before anyone writes code.

### Worked example: building a two-week sprint backlog
A team of five Developers builds the online shop for a garden centre. Sprints last two weeks (ten working days). The current Product Goal is **"Customers can order plants for home delivery on a day that suits them."**
**Step 1: capacity.** Before Sprint Planning, the Developers list their availability.
| Developer | Available days | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Priya | 10 |  |
| Tom | 8 | Two days' leave |
| Aisha | 10 |  |
| Marek | 9 | One training day |
| Lena | 10 | Also on the support rota |
| Total | 47 of 50 | About 94% of normal capacity |
**Step 2: forecast.** The team completed 26, 30 and 28 points in its last three Sprints, an average of 28. At 94% capacity that suggests about 26 points. Because Lena is on support, the Developers decide to aim a little lower, at around 23.
**Step 3: Sprint Goal.** The Product Owner explains that customers are abandoning orders because they cannot choose a delivery day. The Scrum Team agrees the Sprint Goal: **"Customers can choose a delivery slot at checkout."**
**Step 4: selected items.**
| Order | Product Backlog item | Size (points) | Supports the Sprint Goal? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Show available delivery slots for the customer's postcode | 5 | Yes |
| 2 | Choose and reserve a delivery slot at checkout | 8 | Yes |
| 3 | Show the chosen slot in the order confirmation email | 3 | Yes |
| 4 | Release a reserved slot if checkout is abandoned after 15 minutes | 5 | Yes |
| 5 | Bug: basket total rounds incorrectly when two discounts apply | 2 | No, but customers are being overcharged |
| 6 | Improvement: automate the checkout regression tests (from last Retrospective) | Not sized | Indirectly; protects quality |
|  | Total forecast | 23 |  |
**Step 5: the plan.** The Developers break each item into tasks of a day or less. Here is the plan for item 2:
| Task | Size | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add slot picker to the checkout page | 1 day | Use existing date component |
| API endpoint to reserve a slot with the delivery partner | 1 day | Partner API documented |
| Save the reserved slot against the order | Half a day |  |
| Error messages when a slot is taken | Half a day | Agree wording with the Product Owner |
| Accessibility check of the picker (keyboard and screen reader) | Half a day | Required by the Definition of Done |
| Automated tests and code review | 1 day | Required by the Definition of Done |
Only items 1 and 2 are broken down in full on day one. Items 3 to 6 get a few starter tasks and are planned in detail when the team reaches them. Nobody is assigned to item 4 yet; whoever finishes first will pull it.
The result is a sprint backlog with a clear goal, a realistic forecast and a plan detailed enough to inspect at tomorrow's [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/).

### Updating the sprint backlog during the Sprint
The sprint backlog should always show the current plan. Most teams update it continuously as tasks move, then check it together at the Daily Scrum. The Daily Scrum's job is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the sprint backlog as necessary.
Not everything in the sprint backlog is equally open to change. This table shows what usually changes and who decides.
| Element | Can it change during the Sprint? | Who decides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Goal | No. If it becomes obsolete, the Product Owner may cancel the Sprint | Product Owner (cancellation only) |
| Selected items | Yes, scope can be clarified and renegotiated as long as the Sprint Goal is not endangered | Developers with the Product Owner |
| The plan and tasks | Yes, at any time | Developers |
| Order of work | Yes | Developers |
| Who does what | Yes | Developers |
| Quality standards | No. Quality does not decrease during a Sprint | Nobody |

#### Worked example: renegotiating scope on day 6
On day 6 of the garden centre Sprint, Marek finds that the delivery partner's API does not support releasing a reserved slot automatically. Item 4 ("Release a reserved slot if checkout is abandoned") now looks like 13 points instead of 5, because the team would need a scheduled job and a manual fallback.
1. At the Daily Scrum, Marek raises the risk. The Developers agree that items 1 to 3 are still on track and that the Sprint Goal does not depend on item 4.
2. Straight after the Daily Scrum, two Developers meet the Product Owner and explain the options.
3. The Product Owner agrees to remove item 4 from the Sprint. It returns to the Product Backlog with a note about the API limit and will be re-refined.
4. The Developers update the board, and the freed capacity goes into finishing item 2 and the regression tests.
5. The Sprint Goal is unchanged and is met by the end of the Sprint.
This is Scrum working as intended: the plan changed, the commitment did not.

#### Handling unplanned work and urgent bugs
Urgent work will arrive. Deal with it openly rather than hiding it:
- **Make it visible.** Add the item to the sprint backlog, marked as unplanned, so the team can see its effect.
- **Check the Sprint Goal.** If the new work threatens the goal, the Developers and the Product Owner decide together what comes out.
- **Route requests through the Product Owner.** Stakeholders should not add items directly; the Product Owner decides whether something is urgent enough to interrupt the Sprint.
- **Discuss patterns in the Retrospective.** If interruptions happen every Sprint, keep some capacity free or rotate a support role.
If the Sprint Goal itself becomes obsolete, for example because the business changes direction, only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint.

### How to track sprint backlog progress
Most teams show the sprint backlog on a [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/), physical or digital. A simple board has the Sprint Goal at the top, one row per selected item and columns such as **To do, In progress, Review and Done**. Our suggestions, which go beyond the Scrum Guide:
- **Keep columns about state, not job titles.** Columns such as Analysis, Development and Testing encourage hand-offs and mini-waterfalls inside the Sprint.
- **Limit work in progress.** Finishing two items is better than having five half-done. Many teams borrow [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) from Kanban or swarm on the top item.
- **Show blocked work clearly,** for example with a red marker and the date it became blocked.
- **Track items, not hours.** An item is either Done or not. Counting hours spent says little about whether the Sprint Goal will be met.
The Scrum Guide mentions burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flow as practices for forecasting progress, but does not require any of them. A **sprint burndown chart** plots the work remaining each day against an ideal straight line.

#### Worked example: a burndown in numbers
The garden centre team tracks remaining story points at the end of each day. A point only burns down when its whole item meets the Definition of Done.
| Day | Ideal remaining | Actual remaining | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 23 | 23 | Sprint Planning |
| 1 | 20.7 | 23 | Work started on items 1, 2 and the bug |
| 2 | 18.4 | 23 |  |
| 3 | 16.1 | 21 | Bug fix Done (2 points) |
| 4 | 13.8 | 21 |  |
| 5 | 11.5 | 16 | Item 1 Done (5 points) |
| 6 | 9.2 | 11 | Item 4 (5 points) returned to the Product Backlog |
| 7 | 6.9 | 11 |  |
| 8 | 4.6 | 3 | Item 2 Done (8 points) |
| 9 | 2.3 | 0 | Item 3 Done (3 points); Sprint Goal met |
| 10 | 0 | 0 | Regression tests finished; Sprint Review |
The flat line on days 1 and 2 is normal for teams that finish items rather than spread effort thinly. A flat line for four or five days in the middle of a Sprint is the warning sign worth discussing.

### What happens to the sprint backlog at the end of the Sprint
A sprint backlog lasts exactly one Sprint. When the Sprint ends:
1. **Done items** become part of the Increment. They may already have been released during the Sprint.
2. **The Sprint Review** inspects the Increment and progress toward the Product Goal with stakeholders, and the Product Backlog is adjusted. It reviews the outcome, not the task list. See [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/).
3. **Unfinished items** go back to the Product Backlog. They do not roll over automatically; the Product Owner re-orders them like any other item.
4. **The Sprint Retrospective** uses what happened in the sprint backlog (interruptions, blocked items, scope changes) as evidence for improvements.
5. **A new sprint backlog** is created at the next Sprint Planning, which starts straight away.
Tip
Never mark an item as partly Done to keep a velocity number looking good. Undone work is not part of the Increment and its points do not count.

### Sprint backlog vs product backlog
|  | Product backlog | Sprint backlog |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it contains | Everything currently believed to be needed to improve the product | The Sprint Goal, the items selected for this Sprint and the plan to deliver them |
| Accountable | Product Owner | Developers |
| Commitment | Product Goal | Sprint Goal |
| Time horizon | The life of the product | One Sprint |
| Level of detail | Detailed at the top, coarse lower down | Detailed enough to inspect progress daily |
| How it changes | Re-ordered, added to and pruned continuously by the Product Owner | Updated by the Developers throughout the Sprint; scope renegotiated with the Product Owner |

### Common sprint backlog mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No Sprint Goal, just a list of tickets | The team cannot make trade-offs and every item feels equally urgent | Agree one clear Sprint Goal and show it at the top of the board |
| Filling the Sprint to 100% of capacity | No room for surprises, so the Sprint Goal is missed | Forecast from recent velocity adjusted for capacity, and leave some slack |
| Treating the sprint backlog as fixed | The team follows an outdated plan instead of learning | Update it daily; renegotiate scope with the Product Owner when needed |
| Managers or stakeholders adding work directly | Undermines the Developers' ownership and the Sprint Goal | Send new requests to the Product Owner |
| Pre-assigning every task in Sprint Planning | Creates bottlenecks and discourages collaboration | Let Developers pull the next task when they are free |
| Starting everything at once | Many items are 90% done at the end and none is usable | Limit work in progress and finish items in order |
| Tasks that only cover building | Testing and release work appear late and push items past the Sprint | Plan every step needed to meet the Definition of Done |
| Board not updated | The Daily Scrum becomes guesswork | Move cards as work happens; check the board at every Daily Scrum |
| Hidden work | Support, meetings and side requests eat capacity invisibly | Put all significant work on the board, marked as unplanned if necessary |
| Using the sprint backlog as a management report | People optimise for looking busy rather than for the goal | Report progress toward goals at the Sprint Review instead |
Scope that keeps growing inside a Sprint is a form of [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/). The Sprint Goal is your best defence.

### Sprint backlog templates and tools
A whiteboard and sticky notes are enough for a co-located team. A spreadsheet works for small remote teams. Our free [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) for Google Sheets, Excel and PDF has a Sprint plan tab with columns for Backlog item, User story / description, Story points, Owner, Tasks, Acceptance criteria and Status, a space for the Sprint Goal, and a Capacity tab that calculates each person's available days with a focus factor. For a visual board, try the [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) with your own columns.
Use a digital tool when the team is remote or when the sprint backlog needs to link to code, tests and releases. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) has dedicated sprint, backlog and burndown features and is the most common choice for software teams. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool overall, suits teams that run Sprints alongside wider portfolio, resource and reporting needs.
Compare options in our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/). For writing clear items, see [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) and [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a sprint backlog in Scrum?**
It is the Developers' plan for the Sprint: the Sprint Goal (why), the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint (what) and an actionable plan for delivering the Increment (how). Its commitment is the Sprint Goal.

**Q: Who owns the sprint backlog?**
The Developers. The Scrum Guide describes it as a plan by and for the Developers, and they are accountable for creating it and keeping it up to date.

**Q: When is the sprint backlog created?**
In Sprint Planning at the start of each Sprint. It is then updated throughout the Sprint as the Developers learn more.

**Q: What are the three parts of the sprint backlog?**
The Sprint Goal, the selected Product Backlog items and the Developers' plan for delivering them.

**Q: Can the sprint backlog change during the Sprint?**
Yes. The plan and tasks change as the Developers learn, and scope can be renegotiated with the Product Owner. The Sprint Goal stays fixed and quality does not decrease.

**Q: Can the Product Owner change the sprint backlog?**
Not directly. The Product Owner can clarify items and negotiate scope with the Developers, but the Developers own the sprint backlog. If the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint.

**Q: What is the difference between the sprint backlog and the product backlog?**
The product backlog lists everything that might improve the product, belongs to the Product Owner and lasts as long as the product. The sprint backlog covers one Sprint, belongs to the Developers and is committed to the Sprint Goal.

**Q: Should the sprint backlog include tasks?**
It is optional. The Scrum Guide only requires an actionable plan. Many teams break items into tasks of a day or less so progress is easy to inspect at the Daily Scrum.

**Q: How many items should be in a sprint backlog?**
There is no fixed number. Select as many items as the Developers forecast they can finish, using recent velocity and capacity as a guide. Many teams find several smaller items work better than one or two large ones.

**Q: How often should the sprint backlog be updated?**
Continuously, and at least once a day. It should be current enough to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal at every Daily Scrum.

**Q: What happens to unfinished sprint backlog items?**
They return to the Product Backlog, where the Product Owner re-orders them. They do not carry over to the next Sprint automatically, and their points do not count toward velocity.

**Q: Do retrospective improvements go in the sprint backlog?**
They can. The Scrum Guide says the most impactful improvements may be added to the sprint backlog for the next Sprint.

**Q: Is a sprint burndown chart required?**
No. The Scrum Guide mentions burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flow as possible practices but requires none of them. Use one if it helps the team see whether the Sprint Goal is on track.
