# Sprint Planning in Scrum: Agenda, Steps and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Sprint Planning explained: the three topics, time-box, who attends, a step-by-step agenda, Sprint Goal examples, capacity checks and a worked example.


## Sprint Planning in Scrum: Agenda, Steps and Examples
Sprint Planning is the Scrum event that starts every Sprint: the whole Scrum Team agrees why the Sprint is valuable, what can be Done in it and how the work will get done. It is time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint and produces the Sprint Backlog. This guide explains what the Scrum Guide 2020 requires, how to prepare, a step-by-step agenda, how to write a Sprint Goal and decide how much to take on, with a fully worked two-week example.
- Published 11 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Sprint Planning starts the Sprint and answers three questions: why is this Sprint valuable, what can be Done, and how will the chosen work get done.
- The whole Scrum Team attends. The Product Owner brings the most important items; the Developers decide how much they can take on and how to do it.
- The time-box is up to eight hours for a one-month Sprint; shorter Sprints usually need proportionally less.
- The output is the Sprint Backlog: the Sprint Goal, the selected Product Backlog items and the Developers' plan. The Sprint Goal is the commitment.
- Use past performance, upcoming capacity and the Definition of Done to forecast how much fits, and leave some slack for the unexpected.
- Good refinement before the event is the single biggest factor in short, calm Sprint Planning.

### What is Sprint Planning?
**Sprint Planning** is the first event of every Sprint in Scrum. The whole Scrum Team collaborates to agree a Sprint Goal that explains why the Sprint is valuable, the Product Backlog items the Developers forecast they can complete, and a plan for delivering them. Together these form the Sprint Backlog. It is time-boxed to eight hours for a one-month Sprint.
Sprint Planning is one of the five [Scrum events](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/). It happens at the very start of the [Sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/), immediately after the previous Sprint ends, and it is followed by the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) every working day, then the [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) and [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) at the end.
It is where the long-term view in the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) becomes a concrete plan for the next few weeks.

### What the Scrum Guide 2020 says about Sprint Planning
The 2020 Scrum Guide is still the current official version (checked 26 October 2026). Its Sprint Planning section is short, so most of what teams do in the event is practice built around a few rules. The table summarises those rules and what they mean in practice.
| The Scrum Guide says | What it means for your team |
| --- | --- |
| Sprint Planning initiates the Sprint by laying out the work to be performed | It happens first; no Sprint work starts before it |
| The plan is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team | Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers all take part |
| It addresses three topics: why, what and how | Cover all three; skipping the "why" leaves you with a list of items, not a goal |
| The Sprint Goal must be finalised before the end of Sprint Planning | Do not leave the event without one |
| The more the Developers know about their past performance, upcoming capacity and Definition of Done, the more confident their Sprint forecasts | Bring data on recent Sprints and availability |
| How the work is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers | Nobody outside the Developers tells them how to build the Increment |
| Time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint; usually shorter for shorter Sprints | A maximum, not a target |

#### What changed from the 2017 Scrum Guide
| Topic | 2017 Scrum Guide | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Topics | Two: what can be done, and how will the chosen work get done | Three: a new first topic, why is this Sprint valuable, followed by what and how |
| Sprint Goal | Crafted during planning as part of the "what" | Created by the whole Scrum Team and must be finalised before the end of the event; it is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog |
| Who selects items | The Development Team | The Developers, through discussion with the Product Owner |
| Team model | A Development Team inside the Scrum Team, described as self-organising | One Scrum Team with three accountabilities, described as self-managing |

### The three topics of Sprint Planning

#### Topic one: why is this Sprint valuable?
The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint. The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a **Sprint Goal** that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders. Start here: the goal tells the Developers which items matter most and gives them room to adjust the detail later.

#### Topic two: what can be Done this Sprint?
Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select items from the Product Backlog to include in the Sprint. The Scrum Guide notes the Scrum Team may refine these items during this process, which increases understanding and confidence. Selecting how much to take on is the hardest part of the event; we cover it in detail below.

#### Topic three: how will the chosen work get done?
For each selected item, the Developers plan the work needed to create an Increment that meets the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/). They often break items into tasks of a day or less. How they do this is entirely their decision.
| Topic | Led by | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Why | Product Owner proposes; whole Scrum Team agrees | The Sprint Goal |
| What | Developers select, in discussion with the Product Owner | The selected Product Backlog items (a forecast) |
| How | Developers | A plan, often tasks of a day or less |
The topics are not strictly sequential; teams often go back and forth. The firm rule is that all three are covered and the Sprint Goal is final before the event ends.

### Who attends Sprint Planning and what each role does
Sprint Planning is for the whole [Scrum Team](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/). Each accountability brings something different.
| Who | Role in Sprint Planning | Decides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Brings the ordered, refined Product Backlog; explains the Product Goal and the value of top items; proposes the Sprint's objective; answers questions | The order of the Product Backlog |
| Developers | Ask questions, size and refine items, select how much they can take on, plan how to do it | How much to take on and how to do the work |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Makes sure the event happens, stays within the time-box and is positive and productive; coaches the team on Sprint Goals and self-management | Nothing about scope; the Scrum Master facilitates, not directs |
| Invited experts | Give advice on specific items, such as security, legal or data | Nothing; they advise |
| Managers and stakeholders | Not participants by default; their input belongs in the Sprint Review and refinement | Nothing in this event |
**Who decides how much goes into the Sprint?** The Developers. The Product Owner can negotiate on value but cannot make them take on more than they believe they can complete.

### How long should Sprint Planning take?
The Scrum Guide sets a maximum of **eight hours for a one-month Sprint** and says the event is usually shorter for shorter Sprints. It does not give figures for other Sprint lengths. Many teams scale the maximum in proportion, as in the table, and aim well below it.
| Sprint length | Proportional maximum (common practice) | Typical well-run team |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 week | 2 hours | 45 to 90 minutes |
| 2 weeks | 4 hours | 1.5 to 3 hours |
| 3 weeks | 6 hours | 2 to 4 hours |
| 4 weeks / 1 month | 8 hours (Scrum Guide maximum) | 3 to 6 hours |
Rules of thumb vary. Atlassian suggests up to two hours per week of Sprint, while Mike Cohn of Mountain Goat Software suggests aiming for about 45 minutes per week of Sprint length and calls the eight-hour maximum far longer than most teams need.
**Signs the event is running too long:** the team is discovering what items mean for the first time, estimating everything from scratch, or trying to list every task for the whole Sprint. The fix for the first two is regular [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/); the fix for the third is planning the first few days in detail and the rest in outline.

### Inputs and outputs of Sprint Planning

#### Inputs
| Input | Why it matters | Who brings it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordered, refined Product Backlog | Items that can be Done within one Sprint are ready for selection | Product Owner, with the Developers through refinement |
| Product Goal | Shows which direction the Sprint should move the product | Product Owner |
| Latest Increment and Sprint Review feedback | What exists now and what stakeholders said about it | Whole Scrum Team |
| Past performance | Recent [velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) or throughput, and how much carried over | Developers |
| Upcoming capacity | Leave, public holidays, support duties, part-time members | Developers, often collected by the Scrum Master |
| Definition of Done | Sets how much work each item really involves | Scrum Team (or the organisation) |
| Retrospective improvements | The Scrum Guide says the most impactful improvements may be added to the next Sprint Backlog | Whole Scrum Team |

#### Outputs
- **A Sprint Goal**: the single objective for the Sprint and the Developers' commitment.
- **The selected Product Backlog items**: the Developers' forecast of what they will complete.
- **A plan for delivering them**: often tasks for the first days, with the rest outlined.
- Together these are the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/).

### How to prepare for Sprint Planning
Most problems in Sprint Planning start before the event. These checklists are our own suggestions for the few days beforehand.
| Role | Before Sprint Planning |
| --- | --- |
| Product Owner | Order the top of the Product Backlog; make sure roughly one to two Sprints' worth of items are refined and sized; draft a candidate Sprint objective; gather feedback from the Sprint Review and stakeholders |
| Developers | Take part in refinement; flag items that still look too big or unclear; check their own availability; note technical work or debt that needs space |
| Scrum Master | Book the room or call and the time-box; collect availability; bring last Sprints' completed work and carry-over; remind the team of agreed retrospective actions |
| Whole Scrum Team | Review the Definition of Done and any changes to it; check known dependencies on other teams |
Tip
A useful test from our [backlog refinement guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/): divide the points already refined at the top of the backlog by the team's average velocity. Below about one Sprint's worth, the next Sprint Planning is likely to stall.

### How to run Sprint Planning, step by step
The Scrum Guide does not prescribe an agenda. The steps below are our recommended starting point for most teams; inspect and adapt them at your Retrospective.
1. **Open and set the frame.** Restate the time-box, the Product Goal and what happened at the last Sprint Review.
2. **Confirm capacity and past performance.** Share who is available, for how many days, and what the team completed in recent Sprints.
3. **Product Owner proposes the objective.** Explain which outcome would add most value now and which items support it.
4. **Draft a Sprint Goal together.** Write a short, outcome-focused sentence. Treat it as a draft until the end of the event.
5. **Select items.** Developers pull items from the top of the backlog that serve the goal, asking questions and refining as needed, until they reach a realistic forecast.
6. **Check for dependencies and risks.** Anything needing another team, a supplier or a specialist should be visible now.
7. **Plan the how.** Break the first items into tasks of a day or less; outline the rest. Consider the order of work so testing starts early.
8. **Check the plan against capacity.** If the tasks clearly exceed available time, or one skill is overloaded, remove or swap an item.
9. **Finalise the Sprint Goal.** Reword it if selection has changed what is realistic.
10. **Confidence check and close.** Ask each Developer how confident they are; agree what to do if it is low; update the Scrum board.

#### Sample agenda for a two-week Sprint (about 2 hours 45 minutes)
| Time | Step | Lead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0:00 to 0:10 | Open: purpose, time-box, Product Goal, Sprint Review highlights | Scrum Master and Product Owner |
| 0:10 to 0:20 | Capacity and recent performance | Developers |
| 0:20 to 0:35 | Product Owner proposes the Sprint's objective | Product Owner |
| 0:35 to 0:50 | Draft the Sprint Goal | Whole Scrum Team |
| 0:50 to 1:35 | Select and clarify items | Developers with the Product Owner |
| 1:35 to 1:45 | Break |  |
| 1:45 to 2:30 | Plan the how: tasks, order of work, risks | Developers |
| 2:30 to 2:45 | Finalise the Sprint Goal, confidence check, close | Whole Scrum Team |
For a one-week Sprint, halve most blocks; for a four-week Sprint, consider two sessions rather than one long meeting.

### How to write a good Sprint Goal
The Scrum Guide calls the Sprint Goal **the single objective for the Sprint**. It is a commitment by the Developers but gives them flexibility over the exact work needed to achieve it, and it encourages the Scrum Team to work together rather than on separate initiatives.

#### What makes a good Sprint Goal
- **Outcome-focused**: describes a change for users or the business, not a list of tasks.
- **Single and coherent**: one objective the selected items all support.
- **Achievable in one Sprint**: the team believes it can meet it with some room to spare.
- **Negotiable in detail**: several sets of items could achieve it, so scope can flex.
- **Understandable to stakeholders**: someone outside the team can tell whether it was met.
- **Connected to the Product Goal**: a step towards the larger objective.
| Weak Sprint Goal | Why it is weak | Stronger version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complete stories PB-112 to PB-119 | A list of items; no reason or flexibility | New customers can sign up and verify their email without contacting support |
| Work on the reporting module | Activity, not outcome; no way to tell when it is met | Finance managers can export the monthly sales report to Excel |
| Fix bugs, update the API and start the redesign | Three unrelated goals | Pick the most valuable one, and treat the others as other items in the Sprint Backlog |
A simple template some teams use: **"By the end of this Sprint, [who] can [do what], so that [why]."** Use it as a prompt, not a rule.

#### When the Sprint Goal is at risk
If the work turns out to be different from what was expected, the Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to renegotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog without affecting the Sprint Goal. If the goal itself becomes obsolete, for example because a market change makes it pointless, only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint. The Daily Scrum is where most teams first spot the risk.

### Deciding how much work to take on
The Scrum Guide does not prescribe a method. It says the Developers' forecasts improve the more they know about their past performance, upcoming capacity and Definition of Done. In practice teams use one of three approaches, often in combination.
| Approach | How it works | Strengths | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Velocity-based | Take items from the top of the backlog until their [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/) reach the recent average velocity, adjusted for availability | Quick; uses real past results | A single Sprint's velocity varies; ignores who is available for which skills |
| Capacity-based (commitment-driven) | Break each item into tasks, estimate them in hours and stop when the team's available hours are used up | Reflects this Sprint's real availability and skills | Slower; hour estimates can become a target |
| Throughput-based | Count how many items of roughly similar size the team usually finishes per Sprint | Simple; no points needed | Works only if items are consistently small |
**Our recommended approach** for most teams combines the first two: use velocity to set a rough range, then let the task plan and the Developers' judgement confirm it. Our guide to [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) gives the formulas and a detailed example.
1. Take the average velocity of the last three to five Sprints.
2. Scale it by this Sprint's availability: available person-days divided by normal person-days.
3. Use the lowest and highest recent Sprints to give a range rather than a single number.
4. Select items up to the lower half of that range, so there is slack for the unexpected.
5. Check the task plan and skills; adjust if one person or specialism is overloaded.
6. Keep the next refined item ready at the top of the Product Backlog in case the team finishes early.
Tip
Plan to the recent average, never to your best Sprint ever. Planning at 100% of capacity leaves no room for support work, illness or learning, and repeated misses push teams to inflate estimates.

### Worked example: planning a two-week Sprint
A Scrum Team is building a mobile app for a chain of fitness studios. It has a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and five Developers, and runs two-week Sprints of 10 working days. The Product Goal is: **"Members can manage all their class bookings in the app without calling the front desk."**

#### Step 1: inputs
- **Past performance:** the last three Sprints delivered 28, 33 and 30 points, an average of about 30.
- **Capacity:** normally 5 Developers × 10 days = 50 person-days. This Sprint one Developer is on leave for 4 days, so 46 person-days are available, a ratio of 0.92.
- **Forecast range:** 30 × 0.92 ≈ 28 points as a central figure; 28 × 0.92 ≈ 26 to 33 × 0.92 ≈ 30 as a range.
- **Sprint Review feedback:** members are frustrated that full classes simply show "Full" with no way to get a place.
- **Retrospective action:** add automated tests around the booking service, after two booking bugs reached production.

#### Step 2: the Sprint Goal
The Product Owner proposes tackling full classes. After discussion, the Scrum Team agrees the goal: **"Members can join a waiting list for a full class and are offered a place automatically when one opens."**

#### Step 3: selecting items
| Order | Product Backlog item | Points | Supports the goal? | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Join a waiting list for a full class | 8 | Yes, essential | Selected |
| 2 | Offer the first person on the list a place, held for 30 minutes | 5 | Yes, essential | Selected |
| 3 | Push notification when a place is offered | 5 | Yes, essential | Selected |
| 4 | Leave a waiting list | 2 | Yes | Selected |
| 5 | Automated tests for the booking service (retrospective action) | 3 | Indirectly; protects quality | Selected |
| 6 | Show the member's position on the waiting list | 3 | Yes, nice to have | Selected; first to drop if needed |
| 7 | Rate a class after attending | 5 | No | Left at the top of the backlog |
Items 1 to 6 total **26 points**, at the bottom of the forecast range. The Developers deliberately stop there because nobody on the team has used the push notification service before, and they want slack for that uncertainty.

#### Step 4: planning the how
The Developers break the first two items into tasks of a day or less, such as the waiting-list API (1 day), the "Join waiting list" button (half a day) and the job that expires unaccepted offers (1 day). Later items are outlined for now. They start the push notification work on day 2, so problems with the new service appear early.

#### Step 5: final check
Planned tasks come to about 41 person-days against 46 available, and two Developers will write the automated tests so the tester is not overloaded. In a fist-of-five confidence check four Developers show four fingers and one shows three, citing the notification service. If notifications slip, item 6 is dropped and the Sprint Goal stays intact. The event took 2 hours 20 minutes.

### Sprint Planning vs backlog refinement vs PI planning
These three are often confused because each involves choosing and preparing work. They operate at different levels.
|  | Sprint Planning | Backlog refinement | PI planning (SAFe) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Scrum event | Ongoing activity in Scrum, not an event | Event in the Scaled Agile Framework, not Scrum |
| Horizon | One Sprint | The next one to two Sprints and beyond | A Program Increment, typically 8 to 12 weeks |
| Who | One Scrum Team | Product Owner and Developers, plus experts as needed | All teams on an Agile Release Train and stakeholders |
| Main output | Sprint Backlog with a Sprint Goal | Clear, sized, ordered Product Backlog items | Team and program objectives and a program board of dependencies |
| Time-box | Up to 8 hours for a one-month Sprint | None in the Scrum Guide | Usually two days |
Refinement prepares options; Sprint Planning turns the best of them into a plan. If you work at scale, see our guide to [PI planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/pi-planning/), and for the bigger picture of when releases will land, [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/).

### Remote and hybrid Sprint Planning
- **Share one board.** Plan directly in the tool the team will use during the Sprint, so the plan does not need to be copied afterwards.
- **Split long sessions.** Two shorter calls (why and what, then how) work better online than one three-hour call. Keep both on the first day of the Sprint.
- **Prepare asynchronously.** Share candidate items, the draft objective and availability a day ahead.
- **Mind time zones.** Choose an overlap that works for everyone, and rotate inconvenient slots.

### Common Sprint Planning mistakes and how to fix them
| Mistake | Why it hurts | How to fix it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Items arrive unrefined | The event turns into hours of discovery and guessing | Refine regularly; keep one to two Sprints of ready items at the top |
| No Sprint Goal, or a goal that is a list of items | No focus, no flexibility and nothing to tell stakeholders | Start with the why; use the good vs weak examples above |
| Planning to 100% of capacity | No room for support, illness or surprises; regular carry-over | Plan to the recent average and leave slack |
| The Product Owner or a manager decides how much | Developers stop owning the forecast; quality suffers | Developers select; the Product Owner negotiates on value |
| Skipping the how | Problems and dependencies appear mid-Sprint | Break down at least the first few days of work |
| Ignoring technical debt and retrospective actions | Quality erodes and the same problems repeat | Make space for one improvement each Sprint; see [technical debt in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/) |
| Last-minute changes by the Product Owner | The team plans work it has never seen | Bring new items to refinement first, unless urgent |
| Carry-over accepted as normal | Velocity becomes unreliable; Sprint Goals are missed | Split items smaller and take on less until carry-over is rare |

### Sprint Planning templates and tools
A shared sheet or board is enough for a single team. Pair it with the [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) and the [user story template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/user-story-template/), and use the [meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/) to share the agenda in advance.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What happens in Sprint Planning?**
The Scrum Team agrees a Sprint Goal, the Developers select the items they forecast they can complete and plan how to do the work. The result is the Sprint Backlog.

**Q: How long is Sprint Planning for a two-week Sprint?**
The Scrum Guide only sets a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint. Scaling in proportion gives up to four hours for two weeks, but most well-prepared teams need 1.5 to 3 hours.

**Q: Who attends Sprint Planning?**
The whole Scrum Team: the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the Developers. Other people may be invited to give advice.

**Q: Who decides how much work goes into the Sprint?**
The Developers, through discussion with the Product Owner. The Product Owner can explain priorities but cannot make the Developers take on more than they believe they can complete.

**Q: Who creates the Sprint Goal?**
The Product Owner proposes how the Sprint could increase value, and the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define the Sprint Goal. It must be finalised before Sprint Planning ends.

**Q: Can the Sprint Goal change during the Sprint?**
No changes should be made that endanger the Sprint Goal. The scope of the Sprint Backlog can be renegotiated with the Product Owner. If the goal becomes obsolete, only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint.

**Q: What are the inputs to Sprint Planning?**
A refined, ordered Product Backlog, the Product Goal, the latest Increment, past performance, upcoming capacity and the Definition of Done.

**Q: What is the output of Sprint Planning?**
The Sprint Backlog: the Sprint Goal, the selected Product Backlog items and the plan for delivering them.

**Q: Should we estimate tasks in hours?**
Scrum does not require it. Some teams use hours to check capacity; many simply break items into tasks of a day or less.

**Q: Should tasks be assigned to people in Sprint Planning?**
It is not required. Many teams leave most tasks unassigned so Developers can pull them during the Sprint, which encourages shared ownership of the Sprint Goal.

**Q: What happens to unfinished items from the last Sprint?**
They return to the Product Backlog. The Product Owner reorders them, and they are considered again in Sprint Planning like any other item, re-estimated if the remaining work has changed.

**Q: What is the Scrum Master's role in Sprint Planning?**
To make sure the event takes place, is productive and stays within the time-box, and to coach the team. The Scrum Master does not decide scope.

**Q: Can stakeholders attend Sprint Planning?**
Only if the Scrum Team invites them to give advice. Stakeholder feedback normally comes through the Sprint Review and refinement.

**Q: What if the team cannot agree on a Sprint Goal?**
Go back to the Product Goal and ask the Product Owner which outcome matters most now. Persistent difficulty usually means the top of the backlog holds unrelated items and needs reordering in refinement.

# Sprint Retrospective Games: 10 Formats That Work

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective-games/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Ten proven Sprint Retrospective games and formats, including Start Stop Continue, Sailboat, 4Ls, Starfish and Timeline, with when to use each.


## Sprint Retrospective Games: 10 Formats That Work
Changing the retrospective format keeps the conversation fresh and surfaces different insights. Here are ten formats teams use, with what each is best for.
- Published 13 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Varying formats keeps retrospectives productive.
- Pick a format that matches the team's mood and problems.
- Every format should end with concrete actions.

### Ten formats
| Format | How it works | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start, Stop, Continue | List what to start doing, stop doing and keep doing | Quick, action-focused retros |
| Mad, Sad, Glad | Sort notes by emotion | Surfacing feelings and morale |
| 4Ls | Liked, Learned, Lacked, Longed for | Balanced reflection |
| Sailboat (Speedboat) | Wind pushes us, anchors slow us, rocks are risks, the island is our goal | Visual teams; risks and goals |
| Starfish | Keep doing, less of, more of, stop, start | Fine-tuning practices |
| Timeline | Plot events across the Sprint and mark highs and lows | Long or eventful Sprints |
| Lean Coffee | Participants propose topics, vote, and discuss in time-boxed rounds | Open, democratic discussion |
| Five Whys | Ask "why?" repeatedly about one problem | Finding root causes |
| Hot air balloon | What lifts us up, what weighs us down | Simple visual alternative |
| Appreciation round | Each person thanks someone specifically | Ending on a positive note |

### Check-in ideas
- **One word:** describe the Sprint in one word.
- **Weather report:** sunny, cloudy or stormy?
- **ESVP:** are you here as an Explorer, Shopper, Vacationer or Prisoner? Useful for gauging engagement.

### Choosing a format
- After a difficult Sprint: Timeline or Mad, Sad, Glad.
- When actions keep repeating: Five Whys.
- When energy is low: Sailboat or an appreciation round.
- When short on time: Start, Stop, Continue.

### Remote retrospectives
Use a shared digital whiteboard, timed silent brainstorming and dot voting. Keep cameras on where possible and split large groups into breakout rooms for discussion.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: How often should we change the retrospective format?**
Every few Sprints, or whenever discussions feel stale.

**Q: Do retrospective games make the Sprint Retrospective less serious?**
No. Good formats structure the conversation; the outcome should still be concrete improvement actions.

**Q: How does the Start, Stop, Continue retrospective game work?**
The team lists practices to start, stop and continue, then picks one or two actions. It is quick and works well when time is short.

**Q: What is the Sailboat retrospective game?**
The team draws a boat heading for an island (the goal), with wind (what helps), anchors (what slows it) and rocks (risks). It is visual and good for discussing goals and risks.

**Q: What is the 4Ls retrospective format?**
Team members write what they Liked, Learned, Lacked and Longed for during the Sprint, then group and discuss the notes.

**Q: What is the Mad, Sad, Glad retrospective game?**
Participants sort their observations by emotion. It helps surface feelings and morale, especially after a difficult Sprint.

**Q: What is the Starfish retrospective format?**
A five-part format: keep doing, more of, less of, stop doing and start doing. It allows finer adjustments than Start, Stop, Continue.

**Q: Can Lean Coffee be used as a retrospective format?**
Yes. Lean Coffee is a structured but agenda-free meeting format: participants propose topics, vote, and discuss them in short time-boxed rounds, deciding together whether to continue each topic.

**Q: What are good retrospective games for remote teams?**
Any format works with a shared digital whiteboard. Use silent writing, dot voting, breakout rooms and timers to keep everyone involved.

**Q: Which retrospective games make good icebreakers?**
Simple check-ins such as one word for the Sprint, a weather report, or ESVP (Explorer, Shopper, Vacationer, Prisoner) get everyone speaking early.

**Q: Where do retrospective games come from?**
Many come from the Agile community and books such as Agile Retrospectives by Esther Derby and Diana Larsen. See [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) for the five-step structure they fit into.

# Sprint Retrospective: Agenda, Steps, Questions and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: How to run a Sprint Retrospective: what the 2020 Scrum Guide says, who attends, timebox, a 5-stage agenda, questions, worked example and action items.


## Sprint Retrospective: Agenda, Steps, Questions and Example
A Sprint Retrospective is the Scrum event in which the Scrum Team inspects how the last Sprint went and plans ways to increase quality and effectiveness. It concludes the Sprint, it is timeboxed to a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint, and its result is a small number of improvements the team acts on straight away. This guide covers what the 2020 Scrum Guide requires, a timed agenda built on the five stages of a retrospective, questions to ask, an illustrative worked example and the mistakes that make retros feel pointless.
- Published 12 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- The purpose of the Sprint Retrospective is to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness. It is about how the team works, not about the product.
- The whole Scrum Team attends: Developers, Product Owner and Scrum Master. Other people join only if the team invites them.
- The maximum is three hours for a one-month Sprint. Many teams with two-week Sprints need 60 to 90 minutes.
- The five stages (set the stage, gather data, generate insights, decide what to do, close) give every retro a reliable shape.
- Aim for one to three specific actions with an owner and a way to check the result. The most impactful can go straight into the next Sprint Backlog.
- Start each retro by checking last Sprint's actions. Retros feel repetitive when actions are never finished.

### What is a Sprint Retrospective?
**A Sprint Retrospective is the last event of a Scrum Sprint, in which the Scrum Team reviews how it worked during that Sprint (its people, interactions, processes, tools and Definition of Done), agrees what to keep and what to change, and commits to a few concrete improvements for the next Sprint.**
It follows the [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) and comes just before the next [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/). It is one of the five [Scrum events](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/), alongside the Sprint itself, Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum and the Sprint Review.
The Sprint Review asks whether the team is building the right product. The Retrospective asks whether the team is building it in the right way. Both rest on [empiricism](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/): inspect what really happened, then adapt. Teams can improve at any time, but the Retrospective gives that work a protected slot every Sprint so delivery pressure does not crowd it out.

### What the Scrum Guide 2020 says about the Sprint Retrospective
The 2020 Scrum Guide describes the Sprint Retrospective in one short paragraph. In summary:
- **Purpose:** plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness.
- **What is inspected:** how the last Sprint went with regard to individuals, interactions, processes, tools and the team's [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
- **What is discussed:** what went well, what problems arose and how those problems were, or were not, solved.
- **Assumptions:** the team identifies the assumptions that led it astray and explores where they came from.
- **Outcome:** the team identifies the most helpful changes to improve its effectiveness. The most impactful are addressed as soon as possible and may even be added to the [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) for the next Sprint.
- **Timing:** it concludes the Sprint and is timeboxed to a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint, usually shorter for shorter Sprints.
The guide also makes the Scrum Master accountable for ensuring that all Scrum events take place and are positive, productive and kept within the timebox. It does not say who must facilitate, which format to use or how many actions to choose. Those are team decisions.

#### What changed from the 2017 Scrum Guide
- The 2017 guide said the Sprint Backlog must include at least one high-priority process improvement from the previous Retrospective. The 2020 guide softened this: the most impactful improvements **may** be added to the Sprint Backlog.
- The 2020 guide names the **Definition of Done** as something to inspect and adds the idea of examining **assumptions that led the team astray**.
- The 2017 guide described the Scrum Master as participating as a peer team member. The 2020 version is shorter and less prescriptive throughout.
Tip
Scrum does not prescribe a format such as Start, Stop, Continue. Any technique that helps the team inspect and adapt honestly is valid, which is why it pays to vary formats.

### Inputs and outputs of the Sprint Retrospective
Knowing what to bring and what should come out keeps the session focused. If nothing in the right-hand column exists at the end, the team had a conversation, not a Retrospective.
| Inputs | Outputs |
| --- | --- |
| Actions agreed at the previous Retrospective and their status | One to three improvement actions, each with an owner and a check |
| The Sprint Goal and whether it was met | Improvement items added to the next Sprint Backlog where they need capacity |
| Observations from the Sprint Review | Updates to working agreements or the Definition of Done |
| Delivery data: burndown, velocity, [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/), defects, interruptions | Impediments to escalate beyond the team, with a named person to raise them |
| Team members' experiences and feelings | A shared understanding of what to keep doing |

### Who attends the Sprint Retrospective and who facilitates
The Sprint Retrospective is an event for the Scrum Team: one Scrum Master, one Product Owner and the Developers. See our guide to [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) for how the accountabilities fit together.
| Attendee | Typical role in the Retrospective |
| --- | --- |
| Developers | Share observations, analyse causes, propose and own most actions |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Takes part as a full team member; backlog clarity and stakeholder access are often the topics that matter most |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Makes sure the event happens and is positive, productive and timeboxed; often facilitates; also contributes views on how the team works |
| Guest facilitator (optional) | Another team's Scrum Master or a coach, useful when the Scrum Master wants to participate fully |
| Managers and stakeholders | Not attendees by default; join only if the team invites them for a specific topic |
Some articles say the Product Owner attends only sometimes. That is not Scrum: the Product Owner is part of the Scrum Team, and excluding them tends to split the team into 'us' and 'them'. Rotating the facilitator among team members is a good habit: it spreads skills, brings fresh formats and lets the Scrum Master take part as a participant.

### How long should a Sprint Retrospective be?
The only rule is the maximum: three hours for a one-month Sprint, usually shorter for shorter Sprints. The typical durations below are common practice, not Scrum Guide rules. If the team keeps running out of time to decide on actions, the retro is too short.
| Sprint length | Scrum Guide maximum | Typical in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One week | Shorter than three hours | 30 to 45 minutes |
| Two weeks | Shorter than three hours | 60 to 90 minutes |
| Three weeks | Shorter than three hours | 90 minutes to 2 hours |
| One month | Three hours | 2 to 3 hours |
Hold it at the same time and place each Sprint where you can, usually on the last day after the Sprint Review. For more on Sprint lengths, see [what a Sprint is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/).

### The five stages of a retrospective
The most widely used structure comes from Esther Derby and Diana Larsen's book *Agile Retrospectives: Making Good Teams Great* (2006; a second edition with David Horowitz followed in 2024). Each stage has a job, and skipping one usually causes a predictable problem.
| Stage | Purpose | Example activities | Share of time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Set the stage | Get everyone talking early, state the focus and set a safe tone | One-word check-in, read the prime directive, review last Sprint's actions | About 10% |
| 2. Gather data | Build a shared picture of what actually happened, facts and feelings | Sprint timeline, metrics, silent writing on cards, Mad/Sad/Glad | About 25% |
| 3. Generate insights | Understand why things happened and spot patterns | Group cards into themes, dot vote, five whys, [fishbone diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fishbone-diagram/) | About 30% |
| 4. Decide what to do | Choose a few experiments the team will actually run | Impact/effort grid, draft actions, agree owners and checks | About 25% |
| 5. Close | Confirm commitments, appreciate each other and improve the retro itself | Read back actions, appreciations, quick feedback vote | About 10% |
The commonest failure is skipping stage three. Teams list problems and jump straight to fixes, so they treat symptoms. A few minutes asking 'why did that happen?' usually produces better actions than another round of sticky notes.

### Sprint Retrospective agenda
This 60-minute agenda suits a two-week Sprint and maps to the five stages. Scale each slot proportionally for other Sprint lengths.
| Time | Stage | What happens | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0:00–0:05 | Set the stage | Welcome, state the focus, one-word check-in from everyone | Everyone has spoken once |
| 0:05–0:10 | Set the stage | Review last Retrospective's actions: done, not done, did it help? | Keep, adapt or drop each one |
| 0:10–0:25 | Gather data | Show key Sprint data, five minutes of silent writing, then read out cards | A wall of observations |
| 0:25–0:40 | Generate insights | Group into themes, dot vote, five whys on the top one or two themes | Root causes |
| 0:40–0:52 | Decide what to do | Brainstorm options, choose one to three actions, agree owners and checks | Action list |
| 0:52–1:00 | Close | Read back actions, decide which go into the Sprint Backlog, appreciations, feedback on the retro | Commitments confirmed |
Share the agenda in advance with our free [meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/), or use the [Sprint Retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/), which has sections for what went well, what to improve, ideas and owned action items.

### How to prepare for a Sprint Retrospective
Preparation takes the facilitator 20 to 30 minutes and makes a large difference. The day before:
1. **Collect last Sprint's actions** and check their status with the owners.
2. **Pull two or three pieces of data:** whether the Sprint Goal was met, the burndown shape, unplanned work, cycle time or escaped defects. Our guide to [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/) explains which are useful.
3. **Note anything from the Sprint Review** that points to a process issue rather than a product issue.
4. **Choose a focus and a format.** If the last three retros used the same format, change it.
5. **Prepare the space:** a private room with wall space, or an online whiteboard with columns set up and the prime directive at the top.
6. **Decide where actions will live**, ideally the same tool as the Sprint Backlog.

### How to run a Sprint Retrospective, step by step
Follow these steps with the agenda above. They work in person, remotely and in hybrid rooms.
1. **Open and set the tone.** State the purpose and timebox, and read the prime directive if the team uses it.
2. **Check in.** Ask everyone for one word or a number from 1 to 5 that sums up the Sprint. People who speak early are more likely to speak later.
3. **Review previous actions.** Did we do it, and did it help? Keep, adapt or drop each one before raising anything new.
4. **Show the data.** Facts anchor the conversation and reduce arguments about what happened.
5. **Write silently, then share.** One idea per card, written before anyone speaks, so the loudest voices do not set the agenda.
6. **Group and vote.** Cluster cards into named themes and give everyone three votes.
7. **Dig into causes.** For the top theme, ask 'why?' until you reach something the team can influence.
8. **Choose actions.** Brainstorm options, then pick one to three that are specific, small and owned by a named person.
9. **Agree how you will check** whether each action helped, and when.
10. **Close.** Read back the actions, add those needing capacity to the Sprint Backlog, offer appreciations and ask for feedback on the retro.
Tip
Keep the facilitator out of the content. If the Scrum Master has strong views on a topic, ask a team member or another Scrum Master to facilitate that part.

### Sprint Retrospective questions
The three classic questions are: what went well, what did not go well, and what will we do differently? They are a fine start. The questions below go further; pick two or three per stage.

#### Set the stage
- In one word, how was this Sprint for you?
- From 1 to 5, how freely do you feel you can speak today?

#### Gather data
- What happened this Sprint that we did not expect?
- When were you most productive, and when were you most blocked?
- Where did work wait the longest?
- Did anything nearly slip past our Definition of Done?

#### Generate insights
- Why did that happen? And why did that happen?
- Is this a one-off or a pattern we have seen before?
- Which assumption turned out to be wrong?
- What is within our control, and what needs help from outside the team?

#### Decide and close
- What is the smallest change that would make a noticeable difference?
- Who will own it, and how will we know if it worked?
- What will we stop doing to make room for it?
- Was this retro worth the time? What would improve the next one?

### Worked example: a Sprint Retrospective for a two-week Sprint
The following example is illustrative. The team, people and numbers are invented to show how the stages fit together.
**Context.** A seven-person Scrum Team builds an online booking app for a chain of physiotherapy clinics. Its Sprint Goal was **patients can reschedule an appointment without phoning the clinic**. The goal was partly met: rescheduling works, but the confirmation text message did not meet the Definition of Done. One of the Developers facilitates a 60-minute retro.

#### Set the stage and previous actions
Check-in words were mostly 'rushed', 'blocked' and 'OK'. Last retro's action, 'pair on every pull request over 300 lines', was done on four of five large changes and caught two defects early. The team kept it.

#### Gather data
The facilitator showed three facts: the burndown was flat for six days and then dropped steeply; three unplanned production fixes took about four person-days; and pull requests waited a median of 1.5 days for review. Silent writing produced 23 cards.

#### Generate insights
The dot vote put **'stories not ready at Sprint Planning'** first and **'interruptions from production issues'** second. Five whys on the first theme:
1. Why was the burndown flat for six days? The two biggest stories were waiting for answers.
2. Why? The message wording and cancellation rules had not been agreed.
3. Why? The clinic operations lead, who decides them, had not seen the stories before Sprint Planning.
4. Why? [Backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) only involved the Developers and the Product Owner.
5. Why? No one asked which stakeholder decisions each upcoming story depended on.

#### Decide what to do
| Action | Owner | How we will check | When |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Add a 'decisions needed from' field to stories; get those decisions before a story enters Sprint Planning | Product Owner | Stories waiting more than one day for a business decision (target: zero) | Next retro |
| One Developer per day is the production support contact on a rota; others stay on the Sprint Goal | Scrum Master organises the rota | Person-days of unplanned work by people not on rota | Next retro |
| (Parked) Reduce pull request wait time | Not assigned | Revisit if the median wait stays above one day | Next retro |
The rota needed capacity, so it went into the next Sprint Backlog. The new field was a working agreement and took ten minutes to set up.

#### What happened at the next retro
The team opened with the actions. One story still waited two days for a decision, so the first action was tightened: the Product Owner now books a 15-minute slot with the operations lead before each refinement session. The rota cut unplanned work for everyone else to under one person-day, so it became a permanent working agreement.
What made this retro useful: real data, one theme explored properly, actions small enough to finish and a check at the next retro. For deeper problems, a [root cause analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) gives the analysis more structure.

### How to write retrospective action items that actually happen
Most retros generate good ideas; far fewer turn them into change. The difference is usually in how the action is written.
| Weak action | Why it fails | Stronger version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Communicate better | No one knows what to do differently | Post a two-line update in the team channel when a story is blocked for more than half a day |
| Improve testing | Too big for one Sprint and no owner | Sam writes automated tests for the three most-used booking endpoints this Sprint |
| Management should stop interrupting us | Outside the team's control as written | Scrum Master agrees an interruption route with the operations manager by Friday |
| Everyone reviews code faster | Owned by everyone, so by no one | Review requests older than four hours are picked up first after each Daily Scrum; Priya tracks wait time |
A good action is **specific** (anyone knows what will change), **owned** by one named person, **small** enough for one Sprint, **checkable** with agreed evidence and **visible** on the team board or in the Sprint Backlog. Treat actions as experiments: if one does not work, drop it at the next retro rather than carrying it forward out of guilt.

### Popular Sprint Retrospective formats
Changing the format every few Sprints keeps people engaged and surfaces different kinds of issue. Each of these fits mainly into the gather data stage.
| Format | Prompts | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start, Stop, Continue | What should we start, stop and keep doing? | New teams and quick retros |
| 4Ls | Liked, Learned, Lacked, Longed for | Balanced reflection after an eventful Sprint |
| Sailboat | Wind, anchors, rocks and the island (goal) | Linking team issues to a goal or release |
| Mad, Sad, Glad | What made you mad, sad and glad? | Surfacing feelings and morale |
| Timeline | Plot events and highs and lows across the Sprint | Long or eventful Sprints |
See our guide to [Sprint Retrospective games](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective-games/) for ten formats with step-by-step instructions and check-in ideas.

### Psychological safety and the prime directive
A retrospective only works if people say what they really think. That depends on psychological safety: confidence that you can raise a problem or admit a mistake without being punished or embarrassed.
Many teams open with the **Retrospective Prime Directive**, written by Norm Kerth in *Project Retrospectives: A Handbook for Team Reviews* (2001). In short, it asks everyone to believe that, whatever the team discovers, each person did the best job they could, given what they knew at the time, their skills and abilities, the resources available and the situation at hand. It moves the conversation from who to blame towards what in the system to change.
- **Agree a confidentiality rule:** details stay in the room; only agreed actions are shared.
- **Run an anonymous safety check** from 1 to 5. If the average is low, talk about that first.
- **Discuss systems, not individuals:** 'Alex broke the build' becomes 'one change can break our build; why?'.
- **Model it:** facilitators and senior team members go first in admitting their own mistakes.
These habits reflect the [Scrum values](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-principles-and-values/) of openness, respect and courage.

### Remote and hybrid Sprint Retrospectives
- Set up an online whiteboard with columns, timer and voting before the session starts.
- In hybrid sessions, ask everyone to join from their own device so the room does not dominate.
- Use a round-robin speaking order, and collect cards asynchronously the day before if time zones are tight.
- Keep it slightly shorter than in person, and paste actions into the team's tool before the call ends.

### When the same problems keep coming back
Repetition is the most common complaint about retros. It usually has one of four causes.
| Cause | What it looks like | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Actions are never finished | The same theme every Sprint with similar actions | Open with last Sprint's actions; fewer, smaller actions in the Sprint Backlog |
| The cause is outside the team | Complaints about other teams, environments or approvals | Name an owner, usually the Scrum Master, to escalate it as an impediment and report back |
| Symptoms, not causes | Actions such as 'try harder' or 'be more careful' | Spend longer on insights; use five whys or a fishbone diagram |
| The format has gone stale | Low energy, the same people talking | Change format or facilitator, or run a retro on your retros |

### Common Sprint Retrospective mistakes and how to fix them
| Mistake | Why it hurts | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Skipping the retro when the Sprint went well | Lessons about what to repeat are lost and the habit weakens | Keep it, shorten it, and focus on what made the Sprint work |
| Too many actions | Nothing gets finished | Limit to one to three; park the rest on a visible list |
| No owners or checks | Actions drift and are forgotten | One owner and one piece of evidence per action |
| Blaming individuals | People stop speaking openly | Discuss the system; keep performance conversations elsewhere |
| Uninvited managers or stakeholders | The team self-censors | Keep it to the Scrum Team; share actions, not discussion |
| Turning it into a product review | Mixes up review and retrospective | Send product feedback to the Product Backlog |
| Skipping the insights stage | Fixes treat symptoms | Protect about a quarter of the time for understanding why |

### Sprint Retrospective vs Sprint Review
The two events are held back to back and are often confused, but they inspect different things.
|  | Sprint Review | Sprint Retrospective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | The product and what to do next | How the team works |
| Who attends | Scrum Team and key stakeholders | The Scrum Team |
| Main output | A revised Product Backlog | Improvements, some added to the next Sprint Backlog |
| Order in the Sprint | Second to last event | Last event; concludes the Sprint |
| Maximum for a one-month Sprint | Four hours | Three hours |
Read our full comparison of the [Sprint Review vs the Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review-vs-retrospective/).

### Sprint Retrospective templates and tools
A retro needs very little: a space to write, a way to vote and a place where actions stay visible. Start with the [Sprint Retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/). At the end of a release or project, run a wider [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) review with the [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/).
Keep actions in the same tool as the Sprint Backlog so they are not forgotten. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated platform, suits teams that want retro actions, sprint boards and cross-team dashboards in one place, which helps when impediments need escalating. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is a natural home for many software teams, with sprint reports that feed the gather data stage. monday.com, ClickUp and Asana also support sprint boards and recurring retro tasks. See our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) for a full comparison.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the five steps of a Sprint Retrospective?**
Set the stage, gather data, generate insights, decide what to do, and close. The structure comes from Esther Derby and Diana Larsen's book Agile Retrospectives. It is not part of the Scrum Guide, but it is the most widely used way to organise the event.

**Q: What are the three Sprint Retrospective questions?**
What went well, what did not go well, and what will we do differently next Sprint? Adding 'why did that happen?' before choosing actions usually produces better results.

**Q: Who attends the Sprint Retrospective?**
The Scrum Team: the Developers, the Product Owner and the Scrum Master. Other people attend only if the team invites them for a specific reason.

**Q: Should the Product Owner attend the Sprint Retrospective?**
Yes. The Product Owner is a member of the Scrum Team, and many process issues involve the backlog, stakeholders or the Sprint Goal. If the team cannot speak openly with the Product Owner present, treat that as an issue to resolve.

**Q: Who facilitates the Sprint Retrospective?**
Often the Scrum Master, but the Scrum Guide does not require it. Any team member or a guest facilitator can lead it, and rotating the role builds skills.

**Q: How long is a Sprint Retrospective for a two-week Sprint?**
The Scrum Guide sets a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint, usually shorter for shorter Sprints. Many two-week teams use 60 to 90 minutes, which is common practice rather than a rule.

**Q: What is the output of a Sprint Retrospective?**
A small number of improvements to act on as soon as possible. The most impactful may be added to the next Sprint Backlog. Updated working agreements or a revised Definition of Done are also common outputs.

**Q: How many action items should a retrospective produce?**
Usually one to three. A few actions that are finished and checked are worth far more than a long list that is forgotten.

**Q: Can we skip the retrospective if the Sprint went well?**
No. It is a Scrum event, and good Sprints hold lessons about what to repeat. Keep it short if there is little to discuss, but keep the habit.

**Q: Should managers attend the Sprint Retrospective?**
Not by default. Managers in the room can reduce openness. The team can invite a manager for a specific topic and share its actions afterwards.

**Q: What is the retrospective prime directive?**
A statement by Norm Kerth, from his 2001 book Project Retrospectives, asking participants to believe that everyone did the best job they could given what they knew, their skills, the resources available and the situation. Many teams read it to set a blame-free tone.

**Q: What if retrospectives feel repetitive?**
Check whether actions are being finished, whether the real cause sits outside the team, and whether you are treating symptoms. Then change the format, theme or facilitator.

# Sprint Review vs Sprint Retrospective: What's the Difference?

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review-vs-retrospective/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: Sprint Review vs Retrospective compared: purpose, focus, attendees, outputs and order, so each Scrum event does its own job.


## Sprint Review vs Sprint Retrospective: What's the Difference?
The Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective both happen at the end of a Sprint, which is why they are often confused. The short version: the Review is about the product; the Retrospective is about the process.
- Published 13 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Review: product and stakeholders; Retrospective: process and team.
- The Review updates the backlog; the Retrospective creates improvement actions.
- Keep them separate.

### Side by side
|  | Sprint Review | Sprint Retrospective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | The product: what was built | The team: how it worked |
| Question | What should we do next? | How can we work better? |
| Attendees | Scrum Team and stakeholders | Scrum Team only |
| Output | Updated Product Backlog | Improvement actions |
| Time-box (1-month Sprint) | Up to 4 hours | Up to 3 hours |
| Order | First | After the Review; concludes the Sprint |

### Why both are needed
Without the Review, the team may build the wrong thing efficiently. Without the Retrospective, it may build the right thing inefficiently, and never improve. Together, they apply empiricism to both the product and the process.

### Common mix-ups
- Discussing team problems in front of stakeholders at the Review.
- Turning the Retrospective into a product-feedback session.
- Combining both into one meeting and losing depth in each.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Which comes first, the Sprint Review or Retrospective?**
The Sprint Review comes first; the Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint.

**Q: Can stakeholders attend both the Sprint Review and Retrospective?**
Stakeholders are key attendees at the Sprint Review. The Retrospective is for the Scrum Team; inviting others can reduce openness, though teams sometimes invite guests for specific topics.

**Q: Sprint Review vs Sprint Retrospective: what is the main difference?**
The Review inspects the product and adapts the Product Backlog with stakeholders. The Retrospective inspects how the Scrum Team worked and plans improvements.

**Q: How long are the Sprint Review and Retrospective?**
For a one-month Sprint, the Review is time-boxed to four hours and the Retrospective to three hours. Both are usually shorter for shorter Sprints.

**Q: Can the Sprint Review and Retrospective be on the same day?**
Yes. Many teams hold the Review and then the Retrospective on the last day of the Sprint, often with a break between them.

**Q: What are the outputs of the Sprint Review and Retrospective?**
The Sprint Review produces an adapted Product Backlog. The Sprint Retrospective produces improvement actions, some of which may be added to the next Sprint Backlog.

**Q: Are the Sprint Review and Retrospective just a demo and a lessons learned?**
Broadly, though the Review is more than a demo because it discusses what to do next. The Retrospective is a regular, short-cycle version of [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).

**Q: Does the Product Owner attend the Sprint Review and Retrospective?**
Yes. The Product Owner is a member of the Scrum Team and takes part in both events.

**Q: Which is more important, the Sprint Review or Retrospective?**
Neither. The Review ensures the team builds the right thing; the Retrospective ensures it works well. Skipping either weakens empiricism.

**Q: Does product feedback belong in the Sprint Review or Retrospective?**
In the Sprint Review. If product feedback comes up in a Retrospective, pass it to the Product Owner, who can consider it for the Product Backlog. The Retrospective itself should stay focused on how the team works.

**Q: How do the Sprint Review and Retrospective differ from Sprint Planning?**
The Review and Retrospective look back, at the Increment and at how the team worked; Sprint Planning looks forward and selects work for the next Sprint. Both feed into Planning: the Review through the adapted Product Backlog and the Retrospective through improvement actions.
