# Sprint Review in Scrum: Agenda, Steps and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: How to run a Sprint Review: what the 2020 Scrum Guide says, who attends, timebox, a timed agenda, prep checklist, worked example, questions and mistakes.


## Sprint Review in Scrum: Agenda, Steps and Examples
A Sprint Review is the Scrum event where the Scrum Team and key stakeholders inspect the outcome of the Sprint and agree what to do next, usually by adjusting the Product Backlog. It is a working session rather than a presentation, it is the second to last event of the Sprint, and it lasts no more than four hours for a one-month Sprint. This guide covers what the Scrum Guide requires, a timed agenda, a preparation checklist, an illustrative worked example and the mistakes that turn reviews into slide shows.
- Published 12 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- The Sprint Review inspects the outcome of the Sprint and determines future adaptations. Its main output is a revised Product Backlog, not a sign-off.
- It is a working session with stakeholders. The 2020 Scrum Guide tells teams to avoid limiting it to a presentation.
- Only work that meets the Definition of Done can be presented. Unfinished items go back to the Product Backlog.
- The timebox is a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint. Many teams with two-week Sprints need 60 to 90 minutes.
- The Sprint Review is never a gate to releasing value. A Done Increment can be released at any point in the Sprint.
- Good reviews are prepared: the right stakeholders, a realistic environment, a clear agenda and specific questions you want answered.

### What is a Sprint Review?
**A Sprint Review is a Scrum event held near the end of each Sprint in which the Scrum Team shows key stakeholders what it achieved, discusses progress towards the Product Goal and what has changed in the wider environment, and agrees together what to do next. Its main result is an updated Product Backlog.**
The Sprint Review comes after the Developers have finished the Sprint's work and before the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/), which closes the Sprint. It is one of the five [Scrum events](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/), alongside the Sprint itself, [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) and the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/).
It matters because it is the main scheduled feedback loop between the people building the product and the people who use, pay for or depend on it. Scrum is founded on [empiricism](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/empiricism-in-scrum/): decisions based on what is observed rather than what was planned. The Sprint Review is where the team and stakeholders observe the real Increment together and use what they learn to steer the next Sprint.

### What the Scrum Guide 2020 says about the Sprint Review
The Scrum Guide's Sprint Review section is short. In summary, it says:
- **Purpose:** inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations.
- **Content:** the Scrum Team presents the results of its work to key stakeholders, and progress towards the Product Goal is discussed.
- **Inspection:** the Scrum Team and stakeholders review what was accomplished in the Sprint and what has changed in their environment.
- **Adaptation:** based on that information, attendees collaborate on what to do next, and the Product Backlog may be adjusted to meet new opportunities.
- **Format:** it is a working session, and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation.
- **Timing:** it is the second to last event of the Sprint and is timeboxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, it is usually shorter.
Two other rules in the guide shape the event. The section on the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) says that an item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review; it returns to the Product Backlog instead. And the section on the [Increment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/increment-in-scrum/) says an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint, and that the Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.

#### What changed from the 2017 Scrum Guide
Much of the advice online still follows the 2017 Scrum Guide, which listed specific elements: the Product Owner explaining what was and was not Done, the Development Team discussing what went well and demonstrating the work, the Product Owner projecting likely delivery dates, and a review of timeline, budget, capabilities and the marketplace. The 2020 version replaced that list with the shorter description above, added the Product Goal, and no longer states that the Product Owner invites the stakeholders. The old elements are still useful as an agenda, which is how this guide uses them, but they are no longer rules.
Tip
Scrum does not say who must chair the Sprint Review or who must demonstrate. Decide it as a team, and keep the focus on stakeholders using and discussing the product rather than on who holds the clicker.

### Inputs and outputs of the Sprint Review
Knowing what goes in and what should come out keeps the event focused. If nothing in the right-hand column changes, the review was probably a presentation.
| Inputs | Outputs |
| --- | --- |
| The Increment: all work that meets the Definition of Done | A revised [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/): new, removed, re-ordered or reworded items |
| The Sprint Goal and whether it was met | A shared understanding of progress towards the Product Goal |
| The current Product Backlog and Product Goal | An updated release or delivery forecast, where the team uses one |
| Progress data such as burn-up charts or velocity | Decisions and agreed next steps, including candidate items for the next Sprint Goal |
| Changes in the environment: market, users, budget, regulation, timeline, dependencies | Stakeholder feedback captured as backlog items rather than lost in meeting notes |
The Sprint Review does not produce an approval, a sign-off or a list of accepted stories. The Product Owner can review work with Developers at any point during the Sprint, and the Definition of Done is what makes work complete.

### Who attends the Sprint Review and what each person does
The Scrum Guide names the Scrum Team and key stakeholders. In practice the Product Owner usually decides who the key stakeholders are and sends the invitations, because the Product Owner is accountable for maximising the value of the product and for managing the Product Backlog.
| Attendee | Typical role in the Sprint Review |
| --- | --- |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Hosts the session, restates the Sprint Goal, leads the discussion of the Product Backlog and forecast, and decides how feedback changes the order of work |
| Developers | Show and explain the Done work, answer questions, describe problems they met and how they solved them, and hear feedback first-hand |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Makes sure the event takes place, is positive and productive, and stays within its timebox; facilitates if the team wants help |
| Customers and users | Try the Increment, describe how they would use it and say what is missing or confusing |
| Sponsors and business owners | Share changes in budget, strategy or priorities, and discuss trade-offs in the forecast |
| Other teams and specialists | Spot dependencies, integration issues and compliance, security or support needs |
Keep the list to people who will give useful feedback or make decisions. Our guide to [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) can help you map who matters most for each product area.

### How long should a Sprint Review be?
The only rule is the maximum: four hours for a one-month Sprint, and usually shorter for shorter Sprints. A common rule of thumb, not found in the Scrum Guide, is about one hour per week of Sprint. Treat it as a starting point and inspect it in your Retrospectives.
| Sprint length | Scrum Guide maximum | Typical in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One week | Shorter than four hours | 30 to 60 minutes |
| Two weeks | Shorter than four hours | 60 to 90 minutes |
| Three weeks | Shorter than four hours | 90 minutes to 2.5 hours |
| One month | Four hours | 2 to 4 hours |
The timebox is a maximum, not a target. A tightly prepared 60-minute review with real discussion beats a three-hour tour of every ticket. For more on Sprint lengths and timeboxes, see our guide to [what a Sprint is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/).

### Sprint Review agenda
This agenda suits a two-week Sprint with a 75-minute review. It keeps the most time for hands-on inspection and backlog discussion. Scale each slot up or down for other Sprint lengths.
| Time | Item | Led by | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0:00–0:05 | Welcome and purpose | Product Owner | Introductions if needed; remind everyone that this is a working session and feedback is the goal |
| 0:05–0:10 | Sprint Goal and outcome | Product Owner | Restate the Sprint Goal, say whether it was met and list what is Done and what is not |
| 0:10–0:35 | Inspect the Increment | Developers | Live demonstration, ideally with stakeholders trying it themselves; questions as you go |
| 0:35–0:45 | What has changed | Product Owner and stakeholders | Market, users, budget, timeline, regulation, dependencies, new risks or opportunities |
| 0:45–1:05 | Product Backlog and forecast | Product Owner | Walk through the top of the backlog, discuss re-ordering, review the release forecast or progress towards the Product Goal |
| 1:05–1:12 | Agree next steps | Whole group | Confirm backlog changes, likely focus of the next Sprint and any follow-up owners |
| 1:12–1:15 | Close | Product Owner | Thank attendees, recognise contributions, confirm the date of the next review |
Share the agenda and a one-paragraph summary of the Sprint Goal a day or two before. Our free [meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/) has timed items, owners and outcomes ready to adapt.

### How to prepare for a Sprint Review
Most weak Sprint Reviews fail before they start. Preparation is light but it has to happen at the right times.

#### Preparation timeline
| When | What to do | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sprint Planning | Book the review for the whole year or quarter at a fixed time; note which stakeholders care about this Sprint Goal | Product Owner, Scrum Master |
| Mid-Sprint | Confirm attendance of key stakeholders; ask what they most want to see or decide | Product Owner |
| Two to three days before | Agree which items will meet the Definition of Done; choose who shows what; prepare a stable demo environment and realistic data | Developers |
| Day before | Send the agenda, the Sprint Goal and links to try the Increment; update the backlog and forecast chart | Product Owner |
| On the day | Test the demo, the video link and access for remote attendees 15 minutes before | Developers, Scrum Master |

#### Preparation checklist
1. Key stakeholders invited, with at least one real user or customer representative where possible.
2. Only items that meet the Definition of Done selected for inspection.
3. A realistic environment and test data that let people try the product, not just watch it.
4. A short list of what is not Done, and why, ready to share openly.
5. The top of the Product Backlog ordered and visible, with any forecast chart up to date.
6. Two to four specific questions you want stakeholders to answer.
7. A way to capture feedback straight into the backlog, such as a shared board or a shared notes page.
8. A facilitator and timekeeper agreed, so the Product Owner can focus on the conversation.
Avoid rehearsing a polished show. Fifteen minutes of preparation by the presenters is usually enough; anything longer is time taken from the Sprint Goal.

### How to run a Sprint Review, step by step
Use these steps with the agenda above. They work in person, remotely or in a hybrid room.
1. **Open with purpose.** The Product Owner explains that the aim is to inspect the product and decide what to do next, and invites honest feedback.
2. **Restate the Sprint Goal.** Say plainly whether it was met. Transparency here sets the tone for the rest of the session.
3. **Separate Done from not Done.** List the items that meet the Definition of Done and briefly mention the ones that do not. Do not demonstrate unfinished work.
4. **Let stakeholders use the Increment.** Hand over the keyboard, share a test link or walk a real scenario. Ask them to think aloud.
5. **Capture feedback as it comes.** A scribe writes each point on the shared board as a candidate backlog item, not as a note to remember later.
6. **Discuss what has changed.** Ask stakeholders about market, budget, timeline and priorities. A change here can matter more than any feature shown.
7. **Review the Product Backlog together.** The Product Owner shows the top items, explains the current order and discusses changes the group suggests.
8. **Update the forecast.** If you use a release plan or burn-up chart, show how today's progress and feedback change it.
9. **Agree and record next steps.** Summarise the backlog changes and decisions, name owners for follow-ups and close on time.
Tip
Let the Developers hear feedback directly. When it reaches them second-hand through the Product Owner, much of the context is lost.

### Worked example: a Sprint Review for a two-week Sprint
The following example is illustrative. The organisation, people and numbers are invented to show how the parts fit together.
**Context.** A housing association's digital team is building an online repairs service for tenants. It works in two-week Sprints. The Sprint Goal was: **Tenants can report a leaking tap online and receive a booking confirmation.** The 75-minute review is attended by the Scrum Team, the head of repairs, two call-centre advisers, a tenant panel member and the IT security lead.

#### What was shown
- **Done:** the repair report form for kitchen and bathroom taps, photo upload, and an automatic confirmation email with a reference number.
- **Not Done:** the slot-booking step. Integration with the contractor's scheduling system was blocked by an access issue and did not meet the Definition of Done, so it was not shown. The Sprint Goal was therefore only partly met.
- The tenant panel member reported a repair on a phone using test data while the group watched on screen.

#### What the group learned
- The tenant could not tell whether the leak counted as an emergency. The call-centre advisers said about a third of their tap calls are emergencies that need a same-day response.
- The head of repairs shared a change in the environment: a new contractor framework starts in two months, with a different scheduling system.
- The security lead asked how long uploaded photos are kept, which no one could answer.

#### Resulting Product Backlog changes
| Change | Backlog item | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New | Ask an emergency triage question before the form and route emergencies to the phone line | Ordered first; candidate for the next Sprint Goal |
| New | Agree and apply a retention period for uploaded photos | Ordered second; security lead to supply the policy |
| Re-ordered | Slot booking with the current contractor's system | Moved down; building it for a system being replaced in two months is poor value |
| New | Slot booking with the new contractor's scheduling system | Added; needs refinement once the API documentation arrives |
| Removed | Printable PDF of the repair report | Removed; no stakeholder needed it |
**Forecast.** The Product Owner updated the release burn-up to show the first public release moving two Sprints later than the earlier forecast, because emergency triage and the new booking integration were added. The head of repairs accepted the change because it avoids rework. The review ended with clear next steps and a next Sprint Goal that was already half-formed: safe triage of emergency repairs.
Notice what made this a working session: stakeholders used the product, the team was open about the missed part of the goal, a change in the environment re-ordered the backlog, and every piece of feedback became a backlog decision. You can record the same structure in our [meeting notes template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-notes-template/) and keep the backlog itself in a [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/).

### Questions to ask stakeholders in a Sprint Review
Polite applause is not feedback. Prepare a few open questions that invite people to share what they actually think. Pick two to four per review rather than asking them all.

#### About the Increment
- What would you do next if you were using this for real?
- What surprised or confused you?
- What is missing before you would use or release this?

#### About value and priorities
- Which of the next five backlog items matters most to you, and why?
- If we could only do one more thing before release, what should it be?
- Is there anything on the backlog you no longer need?

#### About the environment
- Has anything changed in your area since the last review: customers, budget, deadlines, rules?
- Are there risks or dependencies we have not seen?
- Is the current release forecast still acceptable? What would change if it moved?

### What if the Sprint Goal was not met?
Hold the Sprint Review anyway. A missed goal is exactly the kind of information stakeholders need, and hiding it only delays decisions.
- Say early and plainly that the goal was not met, what was achieved and what blocked the rest.
- Show only the items that meet the Definition of Done. Unfinished items return to the Product Backlog; the Product Owner decides where they go.
- Discuss the impact on the forecast and the Product Goal rather than dwelling on blame.
- Leave the question of how the team works for the Retrospective. The review is about the product, the Retrospective is about the process.
If the same problem appears in review after review, the Sprint Goal or the forecast may be too ambitious. Our guide to [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/) explains how to use past performance to set more realistic expectations.

### Sprint Review vs demo vs Sprint Retrospective
These three are often confused. A demo is part of many Sprint Reviews, but a Sprint Review is more than a demo, and it is a different event from the Retrospective.
|  | Sprint Review | Demo | Sprint Retrospective |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | The product and what to do next | Showing features | How the team works |
| Purpose | Inspect the outcome and adapt the Product Backlog | Inform or impress an audience | Plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness |
| Who attends | Scrum Team and key stakeholders | Anyone the presenter invites | The Scrum Team only |
| Typical output | Revised Product Backlog and forecast | Reactions and questions | Improvements, some of which may go into the next Sprint Backlog |
| Part of Scrum? | Yes, a Scrum event | No, a technique often used inside the review | Yes, a Scrum event |
| Maximum length (one-month Sprint) | Four hours | None defined | Three hours |
Read our full comparison of the [Sprint Review vs the Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review-vs-retrospective/).

### Remote, hybrid and multi-team Sprint Reviews

#### Remote and hybrid reviews
- Send a test link in advance so stakeholders can try the Increment before or during the session.
- Use a shared online board for feedback, with one column per backlog decision: add, change, remove, park.
- Give everyone the same experience in hybrid sessions: if anyone is remote, everyone joins from their own device.
- Keep the session shorter and add a five-minute break if it runs over an hour.
- Record the demonstration for people who cannot attend, but do not let recordings replace the live conversation.

#### Several teams on one product
When several Scrum Teams work on one product, hold a single joint Sprint Review of the integrated Increment rather than a series of separate team demos. Stakeholders see the whole product, and integration problems surface early. The Nexus framework, for example, replaces individual team reviews with one Nexus Sprint Review. A popular format is a review bazaar or market: each team runs a station, stakeholders move between them, and everyone regroups for the backlog discussion. See our guide to the [Scrum of Scrums](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-of-scrums/) for coordinating teams between reviews.

### Sprint Reviews for non-software teams
The Sprint Review works wherever a team delivers something usable each Sprint. What changes is what the Increment looks like and who the stakeholders are.
| Team | What stakeholders inspect | Typical backlog adaptation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marketing | Live campaign assets, landing pages, early results | Shift budget to the best-performing channel, add a new audience segment |
| HR or internal change | A new onboarding pack tried by two recent starters | Remove steps that confused new starters, add a manager checklist |
| Construction design | Updated models or drawings walked through with the client | Re-order design packages after a planning condition changes |
| Research or policy | Draft findings and a short briefing note | Drop a line of enquiry, add interviews with an overlooked group |
The principle is the same: inspect real output with the people who will use it, then adapt what comes next.

### Common Sprint Review mistakes and how to fix them
| Mistake | Why it hurts | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A slide show instead of the product | Stakeholders react to descriptions, not to the real thing | Show the working Increment and let people use it |
| Demonstrating unfinished work | Creates false expectations and breaks the Definition of Done | Show only Done items; mention the rest briefly |
| No real stakeholders | The team talks to itself and learns nothing new | Invite users and decision-makers; ask them what they want to see |
| Feedback recorded but never acted on | Stakeholders stop attending | Turn feedback into backlog items during the session and show the changes next time |
| Treating it as an approval gate | Delays value and contradicts the Scrum Guide | Release Done work when it is ready; use the review to inspect and adapt |
| A status report of tickets and hours | Focuses on activity rather than outcomes | Talk about the Sprint Goal, value and what was learned |
| Skipping the backlog and forecast discussion | Loses the adaptation half of the event | Protect at least a quarter of the time for the backlog and forecast |
| Hiding a missed Sprint Goal | Erodes trust and delays decisions | State it early and discuss the impact openly |
| Turning it into a process post-mortem | Mixes up review and retrospective | Keep team process issues for the Retrospective |

### Sprint Review templates and tools
A Sprint Review needs very little tooling: the Increment itself, a visible Product Backlog and a place to capture feedback. These free templates cover the rest:
- [Meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/) for a timed agenda with owners.
- [Meeting notes template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-notes-template/) to record decisions and follow-ups.
- [Product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) to keep the order visible during the discussion.
- [Release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) to update the forecast with stakeholders; our guide to [agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) explains how.
If your backlog lives in project management software, show it there rather than copying it into slides. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated platform, works well when a review spans several teams or departments, thanks to its shareable dashboards and cross-project views. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is the natural home for many software teams, with sprint boards and built-in agile reports. monday.com, ClickUp and Asana also support sprint-style work and dashboards. See our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) for a full comparison.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the main purpose of a Sprint Review?**
To inspect the outcome of the Sprint and decide what to do next. The Scrum Team and stakeholders look at the Increment, discuss progress towards the Product Goal and changes in the environment, and adapt the Product Backlog.

**Q: Who runs the Sprint Review?**
The Scrum Guide does not name a chair. In most teams the Product Owner hosts and leads the backlog discussion, the Developers show the work, and the Scrum Master makes sure the event happens, stays productive and keeps to its timebox.

**Q: How long is a Sprint Review for a two-week Sprint?**
The guide sets a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint and says shorter Sprints usually have shorter reviews. Many two-week teams use 60 to 90 minutes, based on the common rule of thumb of about an hour per Sprint week.

**Q: Is a Sprint Review the same as a demo?**
No. A demo shows features. A Sprint Review also discusses feedback, changes in the environment, the Product Backlog and the forecast, and ends with decisions about what to do next. A demo is often one part of it.

**Q: Can you show unfinished work in a Sprint Review?**
No. The Scrum Guide says an item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. You can mention it when explaining what was and was not completed; it returns to the Product Backlog.

**Q: Is the Sprint Review mandatory?**
Yes, if you are using Scrum. It is one of the five Scrum events, and the Scrum Guide says that each element serves a specific purpose. Skipping it removes the main feedback loop with stakeholders.

**Q: Do stakeholders have to attend the Sprint Review?**
They are not obliged to, but without them the event loses most of its value. If stakeholders stop coming, ask why, adjust the timing or format, and show them how their earlier feedback changed the backlog.

**Q: What is the output of a Sprint Review?**
A revised Product Backlog that reflects what was learned, plus a shared view of progress towards the Product Goal and often an updated release forecast. It does not produce a formal sign-off.

**Q: Can the team release before the Sprint Review?**
Yes. The 2020 Scrum Guide says an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint and that the Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.

**Q: Does the Product Owner accept or reject work in the Sprint Review?**
Not as a formal step. Work is complete when it meets the Definition of Done. The Product Owner can review items with the Developers at any time during the Sprint, so nothing should be a surprise at the review.

**Q: What comes first, the Sprint Review or the Retrospective?**
The Sprint Review. It is the second to last event of the Sprint, and the Sprint Retrospective concludes it. Holding the review first means the team can reflect on stakeholder feedback in the Retrospective.

**Q: Can a Sprint Review be held remotely?**
Yes. Share a test link so stakeholders can try the Increment themselves, use a shared online board to capture feedback as backlog items, and keep the session slightly shorter than you would in person.

**Q: What should you do if no stakeholders turn up?**
Still inspect the Increment and the backlog as a team, then find out why stakeholders stayed away. Common fixes are a better time slot, a shorter agenda, inviting different people and showing how their feedback has changed priorities.

# What Is Scrum? How the Scrum Framework Works, With Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/
Section: Scrum guides
Summary: What is Scrum? A clear guide to the Scrum framework: team, events, artifacts, pillars and values, a worked Sprint example, and when to use Scrum.


## What Is Scrum? How the Scrum Framework Works, With Examples
Scrum is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organisations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. A small team works in fixed-length Sprints of one month or less, delivers a usable Increment each Sprint, then inspects the result with stakeholders and adapts its plan. This guide explains how the Scrum framework fits together according to the 2020 Scrum Guide, walks through a real-looking Sprint, and shows when Scrum fits and how to start.
- Published 4 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Scrum is a lightweight framework, not a full methodology. It defines a small set of accountabilities, events, artifacts and rules, and leaves the detailed practices to the team.
- It is built on empiricism (transparency, inspection and adaptation) and lean thinking, supported by five values: commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage.
- The structure is often summarised as 3-5-3: three accountabilities, five events and three artifacts, each artifact with its own commitment.
- Work happens in Sprints of one month or less. Each Sprint has a Sprint Goal and should produce a usable Increment that meets the Definition of Done.
- Scrum suits complex work where the solution is uncertain and feedback matters. For continuous, unpredictable request work, Kanban is often a better fit.
- The 2020 Scrum Guide is still the official definition (checked 26 October 2026). Story points, user stories and burndown charts are optional practices, not Scrum rules.

### What is Scrum?
**Scrum** is a lightweight framework for developing and sustaining complex products. A small, self-managing Scrum Team works in short, fixed-length cycles called Sprints, delivers a usable piece of the product every Sprint, and uses regular events to inspect the result and adapt both the product and the plan. Its official definition is the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland.
The 2020 Scrum Guide summarises Scrum in four steps. In our words:
1. A Product Owner orders the work for a complex problem into a Product Backlog.
2. The Scrum Team turns a selection of that work into an Increment of value during a Sprint.
3. The Scrum Team and its stakeholders inspect the results and adjust for the next Sprint.
4. Repeat.
A Scrum Master fosters the environment that makes this possible.

#### Framework, not methodology
People often call Scrum a methodology, but the Scrum Guide deliberately calls it a framework and describes it as purposefully incomplete. It tells you which accountabilities, events and artifacts you need and the rules that bind them together. It does not tell you how to write requirements, estimate, test or design. Teams add their own practices inside the framework, which is why two Scrum Teams can look quite different.
The Scrum Guide also says that Scrum exists only in its entirety. You can use parts of it, but if you drop an event or an accountability, the result is not Scrum, and you usually lose the feedback loop that makes it work.
Tip
Scrum in one sentence: a small team builds something usable in short cycles, shows it to the people who care, and uses what it learns to decide what to do next.

### Scrum in simple terms: an everyday example
Imagine a small team asked to rebuild a museum's website. A traditional plan would specify every page up front and launch everything after six months. With Scrum, the team agrees a goal for the first two weeks, such as "Visitors can see opening times and buy a ticket online." At the end of those two weeks there is a working page to show the museum's staff. The staff point out that most visitors are on phones and that school groups need a separate booking route. The team adjusts the plan, and the next two weeks start from what everyone has learned rather than from the original guess.
That is the core of Scrum: short cycles, a clear goal for each one, something real to inspect at the end and permission to change direction based on evidence.

### The theory behind Scrum: empiricism and lean thinking
According to the Scrum Guide, Scrum is founded on **empiricism** and **lean thinking**. Empiricism means knowledge comes from experience and decisions are based on what is observed. Lean thinking means reducing waste and focusing on the essentials. Scrum applies them through an iterative, incremental approach to improve predictability and control risk.

#### The three pillars
| Pillar | What it means | What it looks like in Scrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transparency | The work and the process are visible to those doing the work and those receiving it | A visible Product Backlog and Sprint Backlog; an honest Definition of Done |
| Inspection | Artifacts and progress toward goals are inspected frequently to spot problems | Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective |
| Adaptation | If something deviates outside acceptable limits, adjust as soon as possible | Re-plan the Sprint, re-order the Product Backlog, change how the team works |

#### The five Scrum values
| Value | What it means | In practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commitment | The team commits to its goals and to supporting each other | Working together to reach the Sprint Goal rather than finishing individual tasks |
| Focus | Attention on the work of the Sprint and progress toward the goals | Finishing items before starting new ones |
| Openness | Being open about the work and the challenges | Raising a risk at the Daily Scrum instead of hiding it until the Review |
| Respect | Respecting each other as capable, independent people | Letting the Developers decide how to do the work |
| Courage | Doing the right thing and working on tough problems | Telling stakeholders that a feature is not Done yet |
The pillars only work when people feel safe to share honest information, which is why the values matter.

### The Scrum framework at a glance: 3-5-3
A popular memory aid summarises Scrum as **3-5-3**: three accountabilities, five events and three artifacts. Add the three commitments and you have every formal element of the framework.
| Element | Parts | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 accountabilities | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers | Make clear who is accountable for value, effectiveness and the Increment |
| 5 events | The Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective | Create regular points to inspect and adapt |
| 3 artifacts | Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment | Make the work and its progress transparent |
| 3 commitments | Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done | Give each artifact a focus to measure progress against |

### The Scrum Team and its three accountabilities
The **Scrum Team** is a small team of one Product Owner, one Scrum Master and Developers. The Scrum Guide describes it as cross-functional (between them, members have all the skills needed to create value each Sprint) and self-managing (they decide internally who does what, when and how). It is typically 10 or fewer people and has no sub-teams or hierarchies. If a team grows too large, it should split into several cohesive Scrum Teams that share one Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner.
| Accountability | Accountable for | Typical work | Does not |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Product Owner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-product-owner/) | Maximising the value of the product resulting from the Scrum Team's work | Sets the Product Goal, orders the Product Backlog, works with stakeholders, decides what to release | Tell the Developers how to do the work |
| [Scrum Master](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scrum-master-role/) | Establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide and the Scrum Team's effectiveness | Coaches, facilitates, causes impediments to be removed, helps the organisation adopt Scrum | Assign tasks or act as the team's manager |
| Developers | Creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint | Plan the Sprint, build and test the work, meet the Definition of Done, adapt their plan daily | Work from tasks handed down by others |
The 2020 Scrum Guide uses the word **accountabilities** rather than roles, and "Developers" covers anyone doing the work, whether they are engineers, designers, writers or analysts. Scrum does not define a project manager; project management work is shared between the three accountabilities.

### The five Scrum events
Scrum uses five events. Each is a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt, and holding them at regular times reduces the need for other meetings. Time-boxes below are maximums for a one-month Sprint; shorter Sprints usually have shorter events.
| Event | Purpose | Time-box | Main output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The Sprint | Container for all other events; where ideas are turned into value | One month or less, fixed length | A usable Increment |
| [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) | Decide why the Sprint is valuable, what can be Done and how | Up to 8 hours | Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog |
| [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/) | Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan | 15 minutes, every working day | An actionable plan for the next day |
| [Sprint Review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-review/) | Inspect the outcome with stakeholders and decide what to do next | Up to 4 hours | A revised Product Backlog |
| [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) | Inspect how the last Sprint went and plan improvements | Up to 3 hours | Improvements, the most important often added to the next Sprint Backlog |
Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not a sixth event. Many people call the events "Scrum ceremonies"; the Scrum Guide does not use that term.

### The three Scrum artifacts and their commitments
Scrum's artifacts represent work or value, and are designed to make key information transparent. Since 2020, each artifact has a commitment that gives it focus.
| Artifact | What it is | Accountable | Commitment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) | An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product; the single source of work | Product Owner | Product Goal: the long-term objective the team plans against |
| [Sprint Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-backlog/) | The Sprint Goal, the items selected for the Sprint and the Developers' plan | Developers | Sprint Goal: the single objective for the Sprint |
| [Increment](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/increment-in-scrum/) | A concrete, usable stepping stone toward the Product Goal | Developers create it | [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/): the quality standard the Increment must meet |
Work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment and is not shown at the Sprint Review as finished. Several Increments can be created and released within one Sprint.

### How Scrum works: a Sprint step by step
Every Sprint follows the same rhythm, and the next Sprint starts as soon as the previous one ends.
1. **Prepare the Product Backlog.** The Product Owner keeps it ordered toward the Product Goal, and the team refines the top items until they are small and clear enough to be Done within a Sprint.
2. **Plan the Sprint.** In Sprint Planning the Scrum Team agrees a Sprint Goal, the Developers select items they forecast they can finish, and they plan the work. Output: the Sprint Backlog.
3. **Build and inspect daily.** The Developers work toward the Sprint Goal and hold a 15-minute Daily Scrum each working day to inspect progress and adapt their plan.
4. **Finish to the Definition of Done.** Each item becomes part of the Increment only when it meets the Definition of Done. It can be released to users as soon as it is ready.
5. **Review the outcome.** At the Sprint Review the Scrum Team shows stakeholders what was achieved, discusses what changed in the market or organisation, and updates the Product Backlog.
6. **Improve the way of working.** In the Sprint Retrospective the team decides on the most helpful changes to its process, tools, relationships or Definition of Done.
7. **Start the next Sprint** straight away, from the updated backlog.
For timings across a whole Sprint, see the worked example below.

### Worked example: one Sprint in a real-looking team
A regional chain of gyms has a Scrum Team building its class-booking app: a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and five Developers (three engineers, a designer and a tester). Sprints last two weeks. The Product Goal is **"Members can book, cancel and join waiting lists for classes from their phone."**
**Sprint Planning (day 1, about two hours).** Popular classes fill up within minutes, and members phone the front desk to ask about cancellations. The Product Owner proposes tackling this. The team agrees the Sprint Goal **"Members can join a waiting list for a full class and are told when a place becomes free."** Based on recent Sprints and one Developer's leave, the Developers select four items and plan the first few days in detail.
| Day | What happened | Scrum in action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Sprint Planning; work starts on "Join a waiting list" | Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog created |
| 3 | "Join a waiting list" meets the Definition of Done | First part of the Increment finished |
| 5 | Developers find that push notifications need an app store review that will take longer than the Sprint | Raised at the Daily Scrum |
| 5 | Developers and Product Owner agree to notify members by email this Sprint and move push notifications back to the Product Backlog | Scope renegotiated; Sprint Goal unchanged |
| 8 | Waiting lists released to one pilot gym | Increment released before the Sprint ends |
| 10 | Sprint Review with two gym managers and the membership lead | Feedback: cap waiting lists at ten people; add "leave the waiting list" |
| 10 | Sprint Retrospective | Action: automate the release checklist that caused a late-night fix on day 8 |
**Result.** The Sprint Goal was met, members at the pilot gym can join waiting lists, and the Product Backlog now has two new items near the top and push notifications re-ordered. The team did not deliver everything it originally selected, but it delivered what mattered and learned something that changed the plan. That is a successful Sprint.

### What Scrum requires and what it leaves to you
Much of what people associate with Scrum is not in the Scrum Guide. These complementary practices can be very useful, but they are choices you can change, not rules.
| Defined by the Scrum Guide | Common complementary practices |
| --- | --- |
| Product Backlog items | User stories, epics, acceptance criteria |
| Sizing by the Developers | Story points, planning poker, T-shirt sizes |
| Monitoring progress toward goals | Velocity, burndown and burnup charts |
| Transparency of the Sprint Backlog | Physical or digital Scrum boards |
| Daily Scrum focused on the Sprint Goal | The three stand-up questions, walking the board |
| Items ready for selection when they can be Done within one Sprint | A Definition of Ready |
Use the Retrospective to decide which ones earn their place in your team.

#### What changed in the 2020 Scrum Guide
If you learned Scrum from older material, these are the main differences.
| Before 2020 | 2020 Scrum Guide |
| --- | --- |
| A Development Team inside the Scrum Team | One Scrum Team; "Developers" is an accountability |
| Roles | Accountabilities |
| Self-organising team | Self-managing team |
| Development Team of 3 to 9 people | Scrum Team typically 10 or fewer people |
| No Product Goal | Product Goal added as the commitment of the Product Backlog |
| Sprint Planning: what and how | Sprint Planning: why, what and how |
| Three suggested Daily Scrum questions | Questions removed; Developers choose any structure |
| More software-specific language | Simpler language for any kind of complex work |

### A short history of Scrum
| Year | Milestone |
| --- | --- |
| 1986 | Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka publish "The New New Product Development Game" in Harvard Business Review, comparing high-performing product teams to a rugby scrum |
| Early 1990s | Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber apply similar ideas to software in their own organisations |
| 1995 | Schwaber and Sutherland present Scrum together at the OOPSLA conference in Austin, Texas |
| 2001 | Both sign the Manifesto for Agile Software Development; Schwaber and Mike Beedle publish the first Scrum book |
| 2002 | The Scrum Alliance is founded and launches its Certified ScrumMaster programme |
| 2009 | Schwaber leaves the Scrum Alliance and founds Scrum.org |
| 2010 | The first Scrum Guide is published |
| 2016 | The five Scrum values are added to the Scrum Guide |
| November 2020 | The current Scrum Guide is published |
| June 2025 | Ralph Jocham, John Coleman and Jeff Sutherland publish the Scrum Guide Expansion Pack, a supplement that adds context and examples without changing the 2020 rules |
The name comes from rugby, where the whole team packs together to move the ball forward.

### Benefits and limitations of Scrum
Scrum's benefits come from short feedback loops and clear accountability. Its limitations usually appear when an organisation adopts the events without the conditions Scrum needs.
| Benefits | Limitations and challenges |
| --- | --- |
| Usable results every Sprint, so value and risk are visible early | Needs a Product Owner with real authority and time to order the backlog |
| Regular stakeholder feedback reduces the risk of building the wrong thing | Needs a stable, dedicated team; part-time members weaken focus |
| Short planning horizons make change cheaper | Fixed-date, fixed-scope contracts sit uneasily with emergent scope |
| Clear accountabilities and a visible backlog improve transparency | Events can feel like overhead if they are run as status meetings |
| Retrospectives build continuous improvement into the work | Says little about scaling, budgeting or architecture; you must add practices |
| Self-managing teams often report higher ownership | Exposes organisational problems quickly, which can be uncomfortable |

### When to use Scrum (and when another approach fits better)
Scrum was designed for complex work, where more is unknown than known and the best solution emerges through experiment. Use the table as a quick fit check. These are our suggestions, not rules from the Scrum Guide.
| Situation | Scrum fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New product or major feature with uncertain requirements | Strong | Short cycles and reviews let you learn what users really need |
| Digital, marketing or research work that can be delivered in usable pieces | Strong | Each Sprint produces something to test or release |
| A dedicated, cross-functional team of up to about 10 people | Strong | Matches the Scrum Team design |
| Support or operations work with unpredictable incoming requests | Weak | Sprint commitments are disrupted daily; Kanban usually fits better |
| Repeatable work with a known solution | Weak | Little to learn each Sprint; a simple plan or checklist is enough |
| Construction or manufacturing with fixed sequences and long lead times | Mixed | Use Scrum for design and planning work, a predictive plan for physical delivery |
| Very large programmes with many teams | Possible | Needs a scaling approach and one Product Backlog per product |

### Scrum vs Agile, Kanban and Waterfall
Scrum is often confused with Agile and compared with Kanban and Waterfall. The short version:
|  | Scrum | Agile | Kanban | Waterfall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A lightweight framework | A set of values and principles (2001 Manifesto) | A method for managing flow | A sequential, plan-driven approach |
| Cadence | Fixed Sprints of one month or less | Not prescribed | Continuous flow | Phases, one after another |
| Roles | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers | Not prescribed | None required | Typically a project manager and functional teams |
| Change | Welcomed between Sprints; scope negotiable within a Sprint | Welcomed | Any time, as capacity frees up | Through formal change control |
| Key measure | A Done Increment toward the Product Goal | Working software or outcomes | Cycle time, throughput, WIP | Progress against the baseline plan |
Scrum is one way to be Agile: both Scrum co-creators signed the Agile Manifesto. For detail, see [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/), [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) and [Scrum vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/).

### How to start using Scrum, step by step
A practical sequence for a team adopting Scrum for the first time:
1. **Read the Scrum Guide together.** It is free and short. Agree that you will try Scrum as written before changing it.
2. **Fill the three accountabilities.** Choose one Product Owner with authority over the backlog, one Scrum Master and a dedicated group of Developers with the skills to finish the work.
3. **Agree a Product Goal** that describes the outcome you are working toward next.
4. **Build an initial Product Backlog,** ordered, with the top items small enough to finish within a Sprint. Our [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) helps.
5. **Write a first Definition of Done.** Keep it realistic: what must be true for work to be usable?
6. **Choose a Sprint length.** Two weeks is a common starting point. Keep it consistent.
7. **Schedule the events** for the first few Sprints so they become a habit: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.
8. **Run the first Sprint** and expect it to be imperfect. Invite real stakeholders to the Sprint Review.
9. **Use Retrospectives to improve,** one or two changes at a time. Add complementary practices only when they solve a problem you have seen.
Tip
Start with one team and one product. Scaling Scrum before a single team can deliver a Done Increment every Sprint usually multiplies the problems.

### Common Scrum myths and mistakes
| Myth or mistake | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| Scrum is a project management methodology | It is a framework for developing products; it leaves most practices to the team |
| The Scrum Master is the team's manager | The Scrum Master serves the team and organisation and has no authority to assign work |
| Scrum means no planning | Planning happens at every level: Product Goal, Sprint Planning and every Daily Scrum |
| Scrum means no documentation | Write what is needed for the Increment to be usable; include it in the Definition of Done |
| The Daily Scrum is a status report to the manager | It is the Developers' planning event, focused on the Sprint Goal |
| Story points and velocity are part of Scrum | They are optional practices; the Scrum Guide does not mention them |
| A Sprint can be extended to finish the work | Sprints have a fixed length; unfinished work returns to the Product Backlog |
| Scrum is only for software | It is used for marketing, research, product design, education and more |

### Scaling Scrum and getting certified
When several teams work on one product, they share one Product Backlog, one Product Goal and one Product Owner, and coordinate through practices such as a Scrum of Scrums or frameworks like Nexus, LeSS, Scrum@Scale and SAFe. Start with our guide to [Scrum at scale](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-at-scale/).
Certification is not required to use Scrum, but it can help in a job search. The most common entry certificates are Professional Scrum Master (PSM I) from Scrum.org and Certified ScrumMaster (CSM) from the Scrum Alliance, with equivalents for Product Owners.

### Scrum templates and tools
You can run Scrum with a whiteboard and sticky notes. Free templates make the first Sprints easier: the [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) records the Sprint Goal, capacity and selected items, and the sprint retrospective template captures what went well, what to improve and action items with owners.
For remote or multi-team work, a digital tool keeps the backlogs visible. [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) is the most common choice for software teams, with dedicated Scrum boards, backlogs and sprint reports. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-rated tool overall, suits organisations that run Scrum alongside wider portfolio, resource and reporting needs.
To continue learning, see our [complete Scrum guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/) with reading paths for every role.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is Scrum in simple terms?**
Scrum is a way for a small team to tackle complex work in short, fixed-length cycles called Sprints. Each Sprint the team delivers something usable, gets feedback and uses what it learned to plan the next Sprint.

**Q: Is Scrum a methodology or a framework?**
The Scrum Guide calls it a framework. It is deliberately incomplete: it defines the accountabilities, events, artifacts and rules, and leaves the detailed practices to the team.

**Q: What are the 3-5-3 of Scrum?**
A memory aid for three accountabilities (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers), five events (the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective) and three artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment).

**Q: What are the three pillars of Scrum?**
Transparency, inspection and adaptation. Together they put empiricism into practice.

**Q: What are the five Scrum values?**
Commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage.

**Q: Who created Scrum?**
Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. They presented Scrum together in 1995 and co-author the official Scrum Guide.

**Q: Why is it called Scrum?**
The name comes from the scrum in rugby, where the whole team works together to move the ball forward. Takeuchi and Nonaka used the analogy in their 1986 Harvard Business Review article on product development.

**Q: How long is a Sprint?**
One month or less, and the length stays consistent. Two weeks is a common choice.

**Q: How big is a Scrum Team?**
The Scrum Guide says typically 10 or fewer people, including the Product Owner and Scrum Master. Larger groups should split into several Scrum Teams working on the same product.

**Q: Is Scrum only for software?**
No. Scrum was designed for complex product work and is used in marketing, research, education, hardware and public services as well as software.

**Q: Does Scrum have a project manager?**
Scrum does not define a project manager. Project management work is shared between the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the self-managing Developers.

**Q: What is the difference between Agile and Scrum?**
Agile is a set of values and principles for working adaptively. Scrum is one specific framework for putting them into practice, with defined accountabilities, events and artifacts.

**Q: Is there a newer Scrum Guide than 2020?**
No. The November 2020 Scrum Guide is still the official version (checked 26 October 2026). The Scrum Guide Expansion Pack published in June 2025 is a supplement and does not replace it.

**Q: What are the disadvantages of Scrum?**
It needs a committed Product Owner and a stable, dedicated team, it can feel heavy if events become status meetings, and it fits poorly with unpredictable support work or fixed-scope contracts.
