# Blocker Clustering: How to Find and Fix Recurring Delays

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Blocker clustering groups blocked Kanban work by cause and cost in blocked days. Learn the steps, a worked example, the priority matrix and common fixes.


## Blocker Clustering: How to Find and Fix Recurring Delays
Blocker clustering is a Kanban improvement technique in which a team records every blocked work item, groups the blockers by cause and adds up the days each group cost, so it can fix the causes that delay delivery most. Instead of arguing from memory about what slows you down, you end up with a ranked, evidence-based list of problems. This guide explains what counts as a blocker, how to capture the data, how to run the clustering session, and how to prioritise and fix the results, using a full worked example you can copy.
- Published 14 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- Blocker clustering turns individual blocked cards into data: reason, start date, end date and whether the cause was internal or external.
- Group similar blockers, then rank the clusters by total blocked days, not by how often they occurred.
- A few clusters usually account for most of the lost time, so fixing the top two or three gives the biggest gain.
- Prioritise with three rules: fix what is cost-effective, fix blockers at the constraint first, and weigh impact against ease of solving.
- Use 5 Whys or a fishbone diagram to find the root cause of a cluster, then run a small, measurable experiment.
- Clusters also feed risk reviews and forecasts: they tell you how likely an item is to be blocked and for how long.

### What is blocker clustering?
**Blocker clustering** is a structured way of analysing blocked work. Each time a work item cannot progress, the team records why and for how long. After several weeks, the team groups the blocker records into clusters of similar causes, totals the blocked days per cluster, and targets the clusters that cost the most time with improvement experiments.
The technique was developed by Klaus Leopold and popularised with Troy Magennis, who presented it at the Lean Kanban Central Europe conference in 2014 and described it in a 2015 InfoQ article on blockers and defects. Their central observation, reported by InfoQ, is that blockers are not isolated events: they have systemic causes, and they keep coming back until those causes are dealt with.
The output of blocker clustering is simple: a short table of causes ranked by blocked days, with a decision about which one or two to tackle next. That table is far more persuasive in a conversation with another team or a manager than a general complaint that things are slow.
It fits the Kanban practice of improving collaboratively and evolving experimentally; see [Kanban principles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-principles/).

### Why blocked work matters more than it looks
A blocked card looks harmless on a board. It sits in its column with a red marker and nobody is working on it. In practice, blocked work damages flow in four ways.
- **It adds straight to cycle time.** Every day an item is blocked is a day added to the time the customer waits. If your typical item takes eight days and spends two of them blocked, a quarter of your [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) is blocker delay.
- **It lowers flow efficiency.** Blocked time is pure waiting time, so it lowers the share of elapsed time spent actively working. See [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) for how to calculate it.
- **It still uses work in progress.** A blocked item usually counts against the column's [WIP limit](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/). Teams then either stall or start new work to stay busy, which increases WIP and, by Little's Law, lengthens average cycle time further.
- **It costs more at the constraint.** A blocker at the stage that limits the whole system's output delays everything behind it. A blocker at a stage with spare capacity may cost almost nothing. See the [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/).
There is also a human factor: once a blocker is cleared, people forget it. Retrospectives recall the latest or most dramatic blocker, not the one that quietly cost two days on a dozen items. Blocker clustering replaces memory with a record.

### What counts as a blocker?
Before you collect anything, agree what you will record. The most common confusion is between work that is blocked and work that is simply waiting in a queue.
| State | What it means | Record as a blocker? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blocked | Someone wants to work on the item now but cannot, because of something outside their control: missing information, a broken environment, an approval, another team | Yes |
| Waiting in a queue | The item is finished at one stage and waiting for the next stage to pull it, for example in a 'Ready for test' column | No, this is queue time; make it visible with a waiting column instead |
| Not started | The item is in the backlog or options column | No |
| Paused by choice | The team deliberately set the item aside to work on something more urgent | Usually no, but track it if it happens often, because it may point to an expedite or prioritisation problem |
| Defect found | Rework is needed before the item can move on | Optional. Leopold and Magennis treat defects as blockers too, because they tie up people and delay flow |
A simple test: if someone could and would work on the item today but something stops them, it is blocked.

#### Internal and external blockers
The first split in any blocker clustering exercise is between causes the team controls and causes it does not.
- **Internal blockers** are caused within the team and can be solved by the team alone: unclear acceptance criteria written by the team, a skill held by only one person, a broken local build, or work started before it was ready.
- **External blockers** come from outside the team: another team's dependency, a customer sign-off, a shared test environment, a supplier, a legal or security approval.
Internal clusters can usually be improved at the next retrospective. External clusters need data and a conversation with whoever owns the cause, which is exactly where the blocked-day totals earn their keep.
Tip
Write your definition down as a one-line blocker policy, such as 'An item is blocked when the person working on it cannot continue for more than half a day because of something they cannot resolve themselves.' Put it on the board so everyone records blockers the same way.

### How to record blockers on your board
The data collection must be quick, or people will stop doing it. The original approach is deliberately low-tech: put a red sticky note on the blocked card with a short reason, add a tick mark for every day it stays blocked during the daily meeting, and when the blocker is cleared, move the note to a separate 'blocker parking' area instead of throwing it away. Our guide to [Kanban cards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-cards/) shows common ways to mark blocked cards.
Digital boards work the same way. Most tools let you flag a card as blocked and add a comment; some record the blocked period automatically. Whatever you use, make sure you can get these fields out at the end of the collection period.
| Field | Example | Why you need it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Item ID and title | PAY-214 Refund email template | To look up the item later |
| Stage when blocked | Testing | Shows where blockers occur and whether they hit the constraint |
| Blocked date | 3 March | Start of the delay |
| Unblocked date | 7 March | End of the delay |
| Blocked days | 4 | The cost measure you will total |
| Reason (free text) | No test data for refunds in staging | Raw material for clustering; write enough to remember the cause in a month |
| Internal or external | External | First level of grouping |
| Cluster | Test environment / data | Filled in during the clustering session, not at the time |
| Escalated? | Yes, to platform team on day 2 | Shows whether your escalation policy is working |
Agree up front whether you count calendar days or working days and stick to it. Working days are fairer for teams that do not work weekends; calendar days match how the customer experiences the delay. Either is fine if you are consistent.
A free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) is a good starting point if you want to track blocked items in a spreadsheet alongside your board.

### How to run blocker clustering, step by step
Here is the full cycle, from agreeing the rules to checking whether your fix worked.
1. **Agree the definition.** Write the blocker policy and decide on calendar or working days.
2. **Mark blockers as they happen.** Flag the card as soon as it is blocked, with a short reason and the date.
3. **Track duration daily.** At the daily meeting, add a tick or confirm the blocked status. Clear the flag and note the date when the blocker is removed.
4. **Keep every record.** Never discard a resolved blocker note. Move it to the parking area or make sure the tool keeps the history.
5. **Collect for long enough.** Four to six weeks is a common first period. Low-volume teams may need longer to gather enough records to see patterns.
6. **Cluster the records.** In a short workshop, split the records into internal and external, then group similar reasons together and give each cluster a clear name.
7. **Total and rank.** For each cluster, count the blockers and add up the blocked days. Rank by blocked days.
8. **Prioritise and analyse.** Apply the prioritisation rules below, choose one or two clusters, and find their root cause.
9. **Run an experiment and review.** Agree a change, a measure and a review date. Keep collecting blocker data so you can see whether the cluster shrinks.

#### Running the clustering workshop
The clustering session itself rarely needs more than 90 minutes. A simple agenda:
| Time | Activity | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10 min | Recap the purpose and the blocker policy; show the period covered and number of items finished | Shared context |
| 15 min | Lay out all blocker records (cards on a wall or rows on a shared screen) and split them into internal and external | Two groups |
| 20 min | Silently group similar reasons, then discuss and name each cluster | Named clusters |
| 10 min | Count blockers and total blocked days per cluster | Ranked table |
| 20 min | Place the top clusters on the solvability matrix and choose one or two | Agreed focus |
| 15 min | Start the root cause discussion and agree who will design the experiment | Owner and next step |
Many teams run this session as part of a retrospective or a monthly service delivery review; see [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/) for where it fits.

### Worked example: one quarter of blocker data
The numbers below are illustrative, but the method is exactly what you would do with your own data. A product team of six tracked blockers for 12 weeks. In that period it finished 60 work items and recorded 23 blockers totalling 162 working days.
After the clustering workshop, the table looked like this:
| Cluster | Type | Blockers | Blocked days | Average days per blocker | Share of blocked days | Cumulative share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test environment or test data unavailable | External | 7 | 46 | 6.6 | 28% | 28% |
| Waiting for customer sign-off | External | 5 | 41 | 8.2 | 25% | 54% |
| Waiting for another team's API change | External | 3 | 27 | 9.0 | 17% | 70% |
| Unclear acceptance criteria | Internal | 4 | 22 | 5.5 | 14% | 84% |
| Defect found in review | Internal | 3 | 15 | 5.0 | 9% | 93% |
| Database specialist unavailable | Internal | 1 | 11 | 11.0 | 7% | 100% |
| **Total** |  | **23** | **162** | **7.0** | **100%** |  |

#### How to read the results
- **Three clusters cause 70% of the delay.** This Pareto pattern is common: a few causes account for most blocked time. The team does not need to fix everything.
- **Frequency and cost differ.** Unclear acceptance criteria happened almost as often as customer sign-off delays but cost about half as many days. Ranking by count alone would have pointed the team at the wrong problem.
- **External causes dominate.** Three-quarters of blocked days came from outside the team. That is a signal to take the data to the platform team and the customer, not to work harder.
- **One-off outliers need judgement.** The single 11-day database blocker is expensive, but one record is not a pattern. Note it, and watch whether it recurs.
- **Blocker cost per item.** 162 blocked days across 60 finished items is an average of 2.7 days of blocker delay per item. If the team's typical cycle time is around ten days, roughly a quarter of it is blocker delay.
You can also express each cluster as a risk. Seven of the 60 items, about 12%, hit a test environment blocker, and when they did, they lost about 6.6 days. That framing is useful in forecasting and in conversations about service levels, covered further below.
Tip
Draw the clusters as a bar chart sorted from largest to smallest blocked days, with the cumulative share as a line. Teams and stakeholders understand a Pareto chart at a glance.

### How to prioritise blocker clusters
The biggest cluster is not automatically the one to fix first. In their InfoQ article, Leopold and Magennis offer three quick rules.
1. **Only fix what is cost-effective.** Some blockers cost more to eliminate than the delay they cause. If removing a rare blocker would need a new environment that costs more than the time lost, live with it.
2. **Fix blockers at the constraint first.** A blocker at the bottleneck delays the whole system; a blocker at a stage with spare capacity may not change delivery dates at all.
3. **Weigh impact against how easy it is to solve.** Use a simple matrix to compare clusters on both dimensions.
A solvability matrix places each cluster by its impact (blocked days) and by how easy it is to solve. Read it from the top-left: high impact and easy to solve is where you start.
| Ease of solving | High impact | Medium impact | Low impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Easy | **Do now** (quick win) | Do soon | Do when convenient |
| Medium | Plan and do next | Consider | Probably leave |
| Hard | Escalate or make a business case | Monitor | Accept |
Applied to the worked example:
| Cluster | Impact | Ease | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test environment or test data | High | Medium: the platform team already provisions environments for others | Plan and do next; testing is also the team's constraint, so it moves to first place |
| Customer sign-off | High | Hard: depends on the client's own approval process | Make the case with data; propose an agreed turnaround time |
| Another team's API change | Medium | Medium | Consider; raise in the cross-team planning meeting |
| Unclear acceptance criteria | Medium | Easy: fully within the team's control | Do soon as a quick win |
So the team chose two actions: an internal quick win on acceptance criteria, and a data-backed request to the platform team about test environments.

#### When to use simulation
For larger systems with many stages, intuition about which blocker matters most can be wrong, because the effects interact. Leopold and Magennis describe running a Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis: reduce each blocker type by a fixed percentage in a simulation model, one at a time, and see which change saves the most delivery time. They suggest using simulation only when the simple heuristics do not give a clear answer. Our guide to [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) explains the general approach.

### Find the root cause of a cluster
A cluster name such as 'unclear acceptance criteria' describes a symptom. Before you change anything, ask why it keeps happening. The 5 Whys technique is usually enough for a well-defined cluster:
1. **Why were items blocked on unclear acceptance criteria?** Developers found missing edge cases halfway through the work.
2. **Why were edge cases missing?** The criteria were written by one person shortly before the item was pulled.
3. **Why only one person?** Refinement had been reduced to save meeting time.
4. **Why did that matter?** Testers no longer saw items before they were started, so their questions came late.
5. **Why was there no other check?** The team had no explicit policy for when an item is ready to pull.
The root cause here is a missing replenishment policy, not careless writing. A fix might be a short three-person review (product, development, testing) before an item can enter 'In progress'.
For broad clusters with many contributing factors, such as 'test environment unavailable', a cause-and-effect diagram works better than a single chain of whys.

### Turn clusters into improvement experiments
Treat each fix as an experiment with a clear hypothesis, a measure and a review date. That makes it easy to see whether the change worked and to drop it if it did not.
| Element | Example: acceptance criteria | Example: test environments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hypothesis | If product, development and testing review each item before it is pulled, blockers from unclear criteria will fall | If the platform team provides on-request test environments within one working day, environment blockers will fall |
| Change | Add a 15-minute 'three amigos' check as an explicit pull policy | Agree a request process and turnaround time with the platform team |
| Measure | Blocked days in this cluster per month | Blocked days in this cluster per month; cycle time 85th percentile |
| Target | Below 3 blocked days per month | Below 6 blocked days per month |
| Review | Next monthly blocker review | After eight weeks |
Keep collecting blocker data during the experiment. If the target cluster shrinks but another grows, you may have moved the problem rather than solved it.
Record what you learned, including experiments that did not work. A short entry in your [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) log stops the next team from repeating the same test.

### Using blocker clusters for risk and forecasting
Blocker data is also risk data. Each cluster tells you two things: how likely an item is to be hit, and how much delay it causes when it is. In the worked example, about 8% of items waited for customer sign-off and lost an average of 8.2 days. That is a known, quantified risk to every new item.
David J Anderson's writing on the Kanban Method describes blocker clustering as a key input to the **Risk Review**, one of the Kanban Method's feedback cadences, where the probability and impact of each blocker type inform how the service is planned and protected. You can use the same numbers in several ways:
- **Service level expectations.** If one cluster regularly pushes items beyond your target cycle time, either fix it or reflect it honestly in the service level you agree. See [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/) and our guide to [service level agreements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/service-level-agreement-sla/).
- **Forecasts.** Probabilistic forecasting methods already include past blocker delay, because it is part of historical cycle time. Clustering explains where that spread comes from and what could narrow it.
- **Risk registers.** Large external clusters belong in the project [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) with an owner and a response, especially when they depend on suppliers or clients.
- **Early warning.** A sudden rise in one blocker type, such as items waiting for review, often shows a new queue forming. Spot it on a [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) before it hits delivery dates.

### Common blocker clusters and countermeasures
Every team's clusters are different, but some appear again and again in knowledge work. Use this table as a starting point for ideas, not as a list of answers; the right fix depends on your root cause.
| Cluster | Usually | Possible countermeasures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Waiting for another team | External | Make dependencies visible earlier, agree turnaround times, invite the other team to planning, or reduce the dependency by changing team boundaries |
| Approvals and sign-off | External | Agree approval service levels, delegate approval limits, approve smaller batches, or approve the policy instead of each item |
| Test environments or data | External or internal | Automate environment set-up, share booking visibility, create reusable test data sets |
| Unclear or changing requirements | Internal | Explicit ready-to-pull policy, joint refinement, clearer acceptance criteria |
| Specialist or single-person skills | Internal | Pairing, a skills matrix, cross-training, swarming on specialist work |
| Defects and rework | Internal | Stronger [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/), earlier testing, automated checks |
| Missing access or tools | External | Onboarding checklist, standard access bundles, a named contact in IT |
| Supplier or vendor delays | External | Clear contractual turnaround times, earlier requests, escalation route |
| Customer information missing | External | Intake form that captures what you need before work starts |
If you are not sure where the delays sit in your end-to-end process, a [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) will show the hand-offs where blockers tend to gather.

### Blocker clustering in Scrum
Scrum teams usually say impediment rather than blocker, but the technique works on any board where blocked items are visible.
- Raise and mark impediments during the [Daily Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/daily-scrum/), recording the reason and start date.
- Keep resolved impediments in a log instead of deleting them.
- Every few sprints, use part of the [Sprint Retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/) to cluster the log and pick one improvement for the next sprint.
- The Scrum Master can take data on external impediments to the people who can remove them; the Scrum Guide lists causing the removal of impediments among the Scrum Master's services to the team.

### Tools for blocker clustering
You do not need special software. A wall of red sticky notes is how the technique started and remains the easiest way to engage a team.
- **Spreadsheet.** A simple table with the fields listed earlier, plus a pivot table summarising blocked days by cluster, is enough for most teams.
- **Jira and similar developer tools.** You can flag an issue as blocked on a board and add a reason in a comment or custom field. Export the data for clustering. See our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/).
- **Kanban analytics tools.** Some Kanban platforms provide a dedicated chart; Businessmap, for example, offers a blocker clustering chart that groups blocked time by blocker type.
- **Work management platforms.** Tools such as [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), which we rank first overall, let you add custom statuses and fields for blocked reasons and report on them across projects. That is useful when blockers span several teams.
Check that your tool keeps the history of blocked periods after the flag is removed; if not, add date fields. Our [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) rankings compare the main options.

### Metrics to track after blocker clustering
To see whether your improvements are working, track a handful of measures over time. Most can be calculated from the same blocker log.
| Metric | How to calculate it | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total blocked days per month | Sum of blocked days for all items | Overall cost of blockers |
| Blocked days per cluster | Sum of blocked days for each cluster | Whether a targeted fix is working |
| Share of items blocked | Items blocked at least once ÷ items finished | How widespread blocking is |
| Average blocker duration | Total blocked days ÷ number of blockers | How quickly blockers are cleared; tests your escalation policy |
| Blocked days at the constraint | Blocked days recorded at the bottleneck stage | The blockers that matter most to delivery |
| Cycle time (85th percentile) | From your cycle time data | Whether customers feel the improvement |
| Flow efficiency | Active time ÷ total elapsed time | Whether waiting time is falling overall |
These sit naturally alongside your other [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/). A [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) will also show whether bands that used to widen around a blocked stage are becoming steadier.
To understand how blocked time affects the active and waiting split, see our guide to [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/).

### Common mistakes to avoid
- **Throwing away resolved blockers.** The whole technique depends on keeping the records.
- **Recording queues as blockers.** Waiting for the next stage to pull an item is queue time. Mixing the two hides both problems.
- **Ranking by count, not by days.** A frequent, short blocker may matter less than a rare, long one.
- **Blaming people.** If marking a blocker feels like admitting failure, people stop marking them. Keep it blame-free and focus on the system.
- **Clustering too early.** A week of data rarely shows a reliable pattern. Collect for at least several weeks.
- **Trying to fix every cluster.** Pick one or two, run an experiment, and come back. Some blockers are not worth solving.
- **Ignoring the constraint.** Fixing a cluster at a stage with spare capacity can feel productive but change nothing for the customer.
- **Stopping after one round.** Systems change. New clusters appear as old ones shrink, so make blocker review a regular cadence, monthly for most teams.
To see how blocker delay shows up in your delivery times, read our guide to [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is blocker clustering?**
Blocker clustering is a Kanban technique for recording every blocked work item with its reason and duration, grouping the records by similar cause and ranking the groups by total blocked days. The team then fixes the clusters that cost the most delivery time.

**Q: Who created blocker clustering?**
The technique was developed by Klaus Leopold and popularised with Troy Magennis. They presented it at Lean Kanban Central Europe in 2014 and described it in a 2015 InfoQ article on blockers and defects.

**Q: What is the difference between blocked and waiting work?**
Blocked work is an item someone wants to work on now but cannot, because of something outside their control. Waiting work is finished at one stage and sitting in a queue until the next stage pulls it. Record blockers; show queues with waiting columns.

**Q: How long should we collect blocker data before clustering?**
Four to six weeks is a common first period. Teams that finish only a few items a week may need longer to gather enough records. Keep collecting afterwards so you can measure the effect of your improvements.

**Q: Who should attend a blocker clustering session?**
The whole team, plus a representative of any team or function that appears often in the external clusters. Their presence turns the session into joint problem-solving rather than a list of complaints.

**Q: How do you measure the cost of a blocker?**
The standard measure is blocked days: the number of days between the item becoming blocked and being unblocked. Add them up per cluster. You can translate days into money or missed dates for a business case, but days are usually persuasive enough.

**Q: What should we do about external blockers we cannot control?**
Take the data to the people who own the cause. A table showing that waiting for one team cost 40 days last quarter supports a request for an agreed turnaround time, earlier involvement or a change in team boundaries.

**Q: Can Scrum teams use blocker clustering?**
Yes. Scrum teams usually call blockers impediments. Record them during the Daily Scrum, keep a log, and cluster it during a Sprint Retrospective every few sprints.

**Q: How do you do blocker clustering in Jira or another digital tool?**
Flag blocked issues and record the reason in a comment or custom field, then export the issues with their blocked dates. Cluster the reasons in a spreadsheet or on a virtual whiteboard. Some Kanban analytics tools provide a ready-made blocker clustering chart.

**Q: How does blocker clustering relate to a Kanban risk review?**
In the Kanban Method, blocker clustering is a key input to the Risk Review cadence. Each cluster gives a probability of an item being blocked and an average delay, which helps the team plan and protect its service.

**Q: Are defects blockers?**
They can be. Leopold and Magennis recommend treating defects as blockers because they tie up people and stop items progressing. Many teams record them as a separate cluster so rework is visible alongside other delays.

**Q: Is blocker clustering the same as root cause analysis?**
No. Blocker clustering identifies and ranks the problems. Root cause analysis, using 5 Whys or a fishbone diagram, then explains why the top clusters happen so you can design a fix.

# Continuous Delivery: Pipeline, Principles and Kanban Flow

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/continuous-delivery/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Continuous delivery keeps software always releasable. Learn how it differs from CI and continuous deployment, the pipeline, DORA metrics and Kanban flow.


## Continuous Delivery: Pipeline, Principles and Kanban Flow
Continuous delivery is a software development practice in which every change is kept in a releasable state, so the team can put it into production safely, quickly and at any time. When to release becomes a business decision rather than a technical event. This guide explains how continuous delivery differs from continuous integration and continuous deployment, how a deployment pipeline works, how to measure it, and what it changes for Kanban flow, release planning and governance.
- Published 19 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Continuous delivery means any version that passes the deployment pipeline could be released to users at the push of a button.
- Continuous integration is the foundation; continuous deployment goes one step further and releases every passing change automatically.
- A deployment pipeline automates build, test and deployment so every change gets fast, reliable feedback.
- Fixed release windows add waiting time: with a monthly release, a finished item waits about 15 days on average before reaching users.
- DORA's five delivery metrics measure throughput and instability; pair them with Kanban flow metrics such as cycle time and throughput.
- For project and product managers, release planning shifts from dates and big launches to small, frequent, low-risk changes.

### What is continuous delivery?
**Continuous delivery** (often abbreviated to CD) is the ability to get changes of all kinds, such as new features, configuration changes, bug fixes and experiments, into production or into the hands of users safely, quickly and sustainably. The code is kept deployable at all times, so releasing becomes a routine, low-risk activity that can happen whenever the business chooses.
Martin Fowler's widely quoted description gives four practical tests. You are doing continuous delivery when:
1. Your software is deployable throughout its lifecycle.
2. Your team prioritises keeping the software deployable over working on new features.
3. Anybody can get fast, automated feedback on the production readiness of their systems whenever someone makes a change.
4. You can perform push-button deployments of any version of the software to any environment on demand.
The second test is the one teams most often miss. Continuous delivery is not just tooling; it is a commitment that a broken build or a failing test is fixed before anyone adds more work, in the same way that a Kanban team stops starting and starts finishing.
In Kanban terms, continuous delivery removes the batch-release step at the end of the process. Each item can flow to the customer as soon as it is done, which is why this guide sits in our Kanban section next to [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/) and [value stream mapping](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/).

### Where continuous delivery came from
The idea is older than the name. The first principle behind the Agile Manifesto (2001) reads: 'Our highest priority is to satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.' See our guide to the [Agile Manifesto values and principles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/).
The practice was set out in detail by Jez Humble and David Farley in their 2010 book *Continuous Delivery: Reliable Software Releases through Build, Test, and Deployment Automation*. It built on continuous integration from Extreme Programming and on Lean manufacturing ideas: small batches, building quality in rather than inspecting it in afterwards, and stopping the line when something goes wrong. Our [Lean Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-kanban/) guide covers those roots.
Later research by the DORA programme (DevOps Research and Assessment), summarised in the 2018 book *Accelerate* by Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim, linked continuous delivery practices with higher software delivery performance. DORA continues to publish annual research on the topic.

### Continuous integration vs continuous delivery vs continuous deployment
The three terms are related, and the abbreviation CI/CD is used loosely for all of them. The key difference is how far automation goes and where a person makes a decision.
|  | Continuous integration (CI) | Continuous delivery (CD) | Continuous deployment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What happens | Developers merge small changes into the main branch frequently; each merge triggers an automated build and tests | Every change that passes CI moves through further automated tests and deployment to test environments, producing a release candidate | Every change that passes the whole pipeline is released to production automatically |
| Path to production | Not covered; releases may still be manual and infrequent | One-click or one-command release, whenever the business decides | Automatic; no human step |
| Human decision | Whether a merge is ready | When to release | None for routine changes; people act on failures |
| Main prerequisites | Version control, automated build, fast tests, merging at least daily | CI plus deployment automation, broad test coverage and feature flags | Continuous delivery plus very high confidence in tests and monitoring |
| Typical fit | Any software team | Most teams, including those with regulated or scheduled releases | Web services and products where frequent releases are welcome |
Fowler sums up the relationship: continuous deployment means every change goes through the pipeline and automatically into production; continuous delivery means you are able to do that, but may choose not to, usually for business reasons. You cannot do continuous deployment without first doing continuous delivery.
Tip
When someone says 'we do CI/CD', ask what the last step is. If a human presses the release button, that is continuous delivery. If nothing stops a passing change from going live, that is continuous deployment.

### The five principles of continuous delivery
Jez Humble's site continuousdelivery.com sets out five principles. The middle column summarises each; the right-hand column is our interpretation for people who manage the work rather than write the code.
| Principle | What it means | What it means for project and delivery managers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build quality in | Find and fix defects as early as possible, ideally with automated tests, rather than relying on inspection at the end | Budget for test automation as part of each item, not as a separate phase |
| Work in small batches | Move each change towards release in small increments for faster feedback and easier fixes | Split work into thin, independently releasable slices; keep WIP low |
| Computers perform repetitive tasks, people solve problems | Automate builds, regression tests and deployments so people focus on higher-value work | Treat manual release checklists as automation candidates |
| Relentlessly pursue continuous improvement | Improvement is part of everyday work, not a one-off project | Hold regular reviews of pipeline delays and failures, as you would for blockers |
| Everyone is responsible | Quality and delivery outcomes are shared, not someone else's job | Avoid hand-off structures where development 'throws work over the wall' to test or operations |
Each of these mirrors a Kanban idea: limiting WIP, making policies explicit and improving collaboratively. Continuous delivery is effectively the engineering side of a pull system.

### How a deployment pipeline works
The **deployment pipeline** is the automated path every change follows from a developer's commit to a production release. Its job is to give fast, reliable feedback: if a change would break something, the team should find out in minutes, not weeks. Pipelines differ, but most contain these stages.
| Stage | What happens | Feedback it gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Commit stage | Code is compiled or packaged and fast unit tests and static checks run on every commit | Does the change work in isolation? Usually within minutes |
| 2. Automated acceptance tests | The build is deployed to a production-like test environment and functional and integration tests run | Does the system still do what users need? |
| 3. Further testing | Performance, security and other non-functional checks, plus any manual exploratory or user acceptance testing | Is it fast, secure and usable enough? |
| 4. Staging or pre-production | The same build is deployed using the same scripts that will be used in production | Will the deployment itself work? |
| 5. Production release | The release candidate is deployed, often gradually or behind feature flags | Does it work for real users? |
| 6. Monitoring and feedback | Errors, performance and usage are monitored; the team can roll back or roll forward quickly | Did the change achieve its purpose without harm? |

#### Rules for a healthy pipeline
- **Build once, deploy many times.** The same artefact moves through every stage, so what you tested is what you release.
- **Fast feedback first.** Put the quickest tests early, so most problems are caught in minutes.
- **Stop the line.** If the pipeline fails, fixing it takes priority over new work. A pipeline that is often red stops being trusted.
- **Everything in version control.** Application code, tests, configuration, infrastructure definitions and database changes should all be versioned. See our guide to [configuration management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/configuration-management/).
- **Same process for every environment.** Use the same deployment method for test, staging and production to remove last-minute surprises.
- **Make it visible.** Display pipeline status where the team can see it, just like a Kanban board.

### Core technical practices behind continuous delivery
You do not need to be an engineer to manage a team that practises continuous delivery, but it helps to recognise the practices that make it possible and to protect time for them.
- **Trunk-based development.** Developers integrate into a single main branch at least daily, keeping branches short-lived. Long-lived branches create large, risky merges.
- **Test automation.** A broad suite of fast automated tests replaces most manual regression testing. Without it, every release needs a long test phase and small releases are impractical.
- **Deployment automation.** Releasing is a scripted, repeatable action rather than a manual runbook.
- **Infrastructure as code.** Servers, networks and environments are defined in code, so test environments can be created on demand and match production.
- **Database change management.** Database changes are scripted, versioned and backwards-compatible, so the application can be released without a long maintenance window.
- **Loosely coupled architecture.** Teams can test and release their part of the system without coordinating with many others.
- **Monitoring and observability.** The team can see how a change behaves in production and detect problems quickly.
When these practices are missing, the gap usually shows up as [technical debt](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/) and long release cycles. Paying it down is part of the investment in continuous delivery.

### Release strategies that make delivery safe
Continuous delivery separates **deploying** code (putting it into production) from **releasing** a feature (making it available to users). These techniques make that separation practical.
| Technique | How it works | Why teams use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feature flags (toggles) | A setting in the code switches a feature on or off without redeploying | Ship unfinished work safely; release to selected users; turn off a faulty feature instantly |
| Dark launch | New code runs in production but its results are hidden from users | Test performance and behaviour under real load before users see it |
| Canary release | A new version goes to a small share of users or servers first, then gradually to everyone | Limit the impact of a problem and compare behaviour with the old version |
| Blue-green deployment | Two identical production environments; traffic switches from the old (blue) to the new (green) | Near-zero downtime releases and an instant switch back if needed |
| Roll back or roll forward | Revert to the previous version, or quickly deploy a fix | Recover fast when something goes wrong |
For product managers, feature flags are particularly useful. They let marketing, support and sales choose the launch moment for a feature that has been safely in production for weeks.

### Continuous delivery and Kanban
Kanban and continuous delivery solve two halves of the same problem. Kanban manages the flow of work through the team; continuous delivery removes the technical barriers that stop finished work reaching users. Together they let each item flow to customers in small batches.
- **Extend the board to the customer.** Add columns for 'Ready to release' and 'Live' or 'Validated', so the board shows the full journey. See [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) for design tips.
- **Redefine done.** An item is done when it is in production and working, not when development hands it to test. Update your [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) accordingly.
- **Limit WIP on the release queue.** If 'Ready to release' fills up, that is a visible signal that releases are too infrequent. Apply a [WIP limit](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) there too.
- **Measure end-to-end.** Track [lead time and cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/) all the way to production, so release delays are not hidden.
- **Treat pipeline failures as blockers.** Record them and analyse them with [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/), just like any other delay.

#### Worked example: what a monthly release window costs
This example is illustrative, but the arithmetic applies to any team. Suppose a team finishes work steadily through the month and releases once a month. An item finished on the first day waits about 30 days for the release; one finished the day before waits one day. On average, a finished item waits about **half the release interval**.
| Release interval | Average wait for release (finished work) | Items waiting at any time if the team finishes 10 a month |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quarterly (about 90 days) | About 45 days | About 15 |
| Monthly (about 30 days) | About 15 days | About 5 |
| Fortnightly (14 days) | About 7 days | About 2 to 3 |
| Weekly (7 days) | About 3.5 days | About 1 to 2 |
| On demand (continuous delivery) | Hours | Close to zero |
The third column follows from Little's Law: average items waiting equals the rate at which items arrive multiplied by the average time they wait. Those waiting items are finished but unused work, which Lean thinking treats as inventory.
Now look at one typical item before and after the team adopted continuous delivery:
| Stage | Before: monthly release | After: continuous delivery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Development | 3 days | 3 days |
| Waiting for code review | 1 day | 0.5 days |
| Testing | 2 days (mostly manual) | 1 day (mostly automated) |
| Waiting for the release window | 15 days on average | 0.5 days |
| Release hardening and regression testing | 3 days | None; the pipeline does it on every change |
| **Total lead time from start** | **24 days** | **5 days** |
| Flow efficiency (active ÷ total) | About 33% (8 of 24 days) | 80% (4 of 5 days) |
Development took the same time in both cases. Almost all of the improvement came from removing the release batch and the manual phase it required. That is why teams often find continuous delivery shortens lead time more than any change to how they write code.

### How to measure continuous delivery
The best-known measures come from DORA. Since 2024 DORA has used five software delivery metrics, grouped into throughput and instability. In 2023 it renamed mean time to restore as failed deployment recovery time and narrowed it to failures caused by a change, and in 2024 it added deployment rework rate.
| DORA metric | Group | What it measures | Closest Kanban measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Change lead time | Throughput | Time from a code commit to that change running successfully in production | Lead time or cycle time, measured from start to live |
| Deployment frequency | Throughput | How often changes are deployed to production | [Throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) of released items |
| Failed deployment recovery time | Throughput | How long it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and needs immediate attention | Cycle time of expedited fixes |
| Change fail rate | Instability | Share of deployments that cause a failure in production needing immediate action | Share of items that return as defects |
| Deployment rework rate | Instability | Share of deployments that are unplanned, made to fix a problem in production | Share of failure demand in your throughput |
DORA's research has consistently found that speed and stability move together rather than trading off: teams that deploy more often tend to have lower failure rates, not higher ones.
Use these metrics to guide improvement, not as targets for individuals or comparisons between teams. A team told to raise deployment frequency can do it by splitting deployments artificially without delivering anything faster. Combine them with your [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) and customer outcomes.

### How to implement continuous delivery, step by step
Continuous delivery is adopted gradually. A sensible sequence for an existing product looks like this.
1. **Map the current path to production.** Run a [value stream mapping](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) session from commit to live and record process time and waiting time at each step.
2. **Agree the goal and the measures.** Pick two or three measures, such as change lead time and change fail rate, and record a baseline.
3. **Get continuous integration working.** Everyone merges to the main branch at least daily, every merge is built and tested automatically, and broken builds are fixed immediately.
4. **Automate the slowest manual test work first.** Use the value stream map to find the biggest test delays and automate those regression checks.
5. **Script the deployment.** Make deployment one repeatable command, then use it for every environment.
6. **Make environments reproducible.** Define test environments in code so they can be created on demand and match production.
7. **Introduce feature flags.** Let unfinished features be merged and deployed safely while switched off.
8. **Shrink the work.** Split backlog items into small, independently releasable slices.
9. **Increase release frequency in steps.** Move from monthly to fortnightly to weekly to on demand, fixing what hurts at each step.
10. **Review and improve regularly.** Look at pipeline failures, delays and DORA measures in a regular review, and decide whether continuous deployment would add value.
Humble's site sums up the attitude: if something hurts, do it more often and bring the pain forward. Each increase in release frequency exposes the next manual or fragile step to fix.

### What changes for project and product managers
Continuous delivery is often treated as an engineering topic, but it changes how work is planned, governed and communicated.

#### Release planning
Release planning moves from fixing a date and cramming scope into it towards a steady flow of small changes, with launches managed through feature flags. Roadmaps describe outcomes and sequences rather than release trains of features. Our guide to [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) explains how to plan when releases are frequent, and the free [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) works for both scheduled and on-demand releases.

#### Governance and change approval
Many organisations route every production change through a change advisory board. In *Accelerate*, the authors report that approval by an external body was associated with slower delivery and was not associated with fewer failures. That does not mean removing control: it means building it into the pipeline with peer review, automated tests, audit trails and clear policies for higher-risk changes. Our guide to [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) explains how to make approval proportionate.

#### Risk and stakeholders
Small releases are individually less risky and easier to reverse, which changes the risk conversation from 'will the big launch go well?' to 'how quickly can we detect and recover?'. Record residual risks such as dependency on a single environment in your [risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) process, and agree with stakeholders how they will hear about changes when there is no big release event.
If you work in Scrum, continuous delivery fits well: the Scrum Guide says an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint, and the Sprint Review should not be seen as a release gate.

### Benefits of continuous delivery
The benefits below are those most often reported by practitioners and supported by DORA's research. How much you gain depends on your starting point.
- **Lower-risk releases.** Small changes are easier to test, understand and reverse than large batches.
- **Shorter lead time.** Finished work reaches users in hours or days instead of waiting for a release window.
- **Faster feedback.** You learn sooner whether a feature is used and valued, and can stop building what is not.
- **Higher quality.** Automated tests on every change catch regressions early, when they are cheapest to fix.
- **Less stressful release days.** Releasing becomes routine rather than a late-night, all-hands event.
- **More reliable forecasts.** Without a release batch, cycle times are shorter and less variable, which makes flow-based forecasting more accurate.
- **Business control over timing.** The business decides when users see a feature, independently of when the code was finished.

### Challenges and when continuous delivery is harder
Continuous delivery applies widely, but some contexts need adaptation. The goal is always the same: keep the software releasable, even if you release less often.
| Situation | Challenge | How teams adapt |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regulated industries | Audit, validation and approval requirements | Automate evidence collection in the pipeline; keep every change traceable; make releases small so validation is quicker |
| Mobile apps | App store review and users choosing when to update | Keep the code releasable continuously; use feature flags and server-side configuration to control what users see |
| Embedded or hardware products | Physical devices and long certification cycles | Use simulators and hardware-in-the-loop testing; deliver continuously to internal or test devices |
| Large legacy systems | Slow builds, few automated tests, tightly coupled components | Start with the parts that change most often; add tests around them; gradually decouple |
| Shared environments | Teams queue for the same test environment | Infrastructure as code to create environments on demand |
| Organisational habits | Hand-offs between development, test and operations; fear of change | Cross-functional teams, shared goals and visible metrics; see [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/) |
The upfront investment in automation is real, and benefits usually arrive gradually. Plan it as a series of small improvements with measurable effects rather than a single transformation project.

### Continuous delivery tools
No single product delivers continuous delivery; it comes from combining tools with disciplined practices. Most pipelines include tools from these categories.
| Category | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Version control | Stores code, tests, configuration and infrastructure definitions with full history |
| CI/CD server or service | Runs the pipeline: builds, tests and deployments on every change |
| Test frameworks | Automate unit, integration, acceptance, performance and security tests |
| Artefact repository | Stores the built packages that move through the pipeline |
| Infrastructure as code and containers | Create consistent environments on demand |
| Feature flag management | Control which users see which features |
| Monitoring and observability | Show how changes behave in production and alert on problems |
| Work tracking | Links work items to commits, builds and deployments so you can see flow end to end |
For work tracking, developer-focused tools such as [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) can show builds and deployments against each work item when connected to development tools. Cross-functional teams that also manage marketing, launches and operations work may prefer a broader platform; our [project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) rankings compare the main options. A simple [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) is enough to start visualising the path to live.

### Common continuous delivery mistakes
- **Treating it as a tooling project.** Buying a CI/CD service without changing batch size, testing or team habits rarely shortens lead time.
- **Tolerating a red pipeline.** If failed builds are left for days, nobody trusts the pipeline and people bypass it.
- **Keeping long-lived branches.** Weeks of isolated work produce the same risky merge that continuous delivery is meant to remove.
- **Automating the deployment but not the tests.** Fast deployment of untested code moves risk rather than reducing it.
- **Measuring only speed.** Deployment frequency without change fail rate and recovery time encourages careless releases.
- **Stopping the board at 'done in development'.** If your board ends before production, release delays stay invisible.
- **Big-bang adoption.** Trying to change everything at once usually stalls. Improve one bottleneck at a time; the [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/) helps you choose.
- **Leaving operations and security out.** Continuous delivery works best when the people who run and secure the system help design the pipeline.
For the cultural side of continuous delivery and how development and operations work together, see our guide to [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is continuous delivery in simple terms?**
Continuous delivery means your software is always in a state where it could be released to users. Every change is built and tested automatically, and releasing is a quick, routine step the business can take whenever it chooses.

**Q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?**
In continuous delivery, every change that passes the pipeline is ready to release, but a person decides when to release it. In continuous deployment, every change that passes the pipeline is released to production automatically.

**Q: What is the difference between continuous integration and continuous delivery?**
Continuous integration means merging small code changes into the main branch frequently and building and testing each one automatically. Continuous delivery builds on it, so integrated code is also deployable to production at any time.

**Q: Is CI/CD the same as DevOps?**
No. CI/CD describes specific practices for integrating, testing and releasing software. DevOps is the broader culture and set of practices that bring development and operations together, and CI/CD is one of its core technical practices.

**Q: What are the stages of a continuous delivery pipeline?**
A typical pipeline has a commit stage with fast tests, automated acceptance tests, further testing such as performance and security, deployment to staging, the production release and monitoring. The details vary by team and product.

**Q: What are the principles of continuous delivery?**
Jez Humble's continuousdelivery.com lists five: build quality in; work in small batches; computers perform repetitive tasks, people solve problems; relentlessly pursue continuous improvement; and everyone is responsible.

**Q: Who wrote the book Continuous Delivery?**
Jez Humble and David Farley, in 2010. The full title is Continuous Delivery: Reliable Software Releases through Build, Test, and Deployment Automation.

**Q: Is continuous delivery only for software?**
The practice comes from software. The underlying ideas of small batches, building quality in and keeping work always ready to release can be applied to websites, content, documentation and other digital products.

**Q: Can you do continuous delivery with Scrum sprints?**
Yes. The Scrum Guide allows Increments to be delivered before the end of a Sprint, and the Sprint Review is not meant to be a release gate. Many Scrum teams release several times a sprint.

**Q: What is a feature flag?**
A feature flag, or feature toggle, is a setting that switches a feature on or off without redeploying the code. It lets teams deploy unfinished work safely and release features to selected users when the business is ready.

**Q: What is trunk-based development?**
A way of working in which developers integrate their changes into a single main branch at least once a day, rather than working on long-lived branches. It keeps merges small and is a key enabler of continuous delivery.

**Q: What are the DORA metrics?**
DORA's five software delivery metrics are change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate. The first three measure throughput and the last two measure instability.

**Q: How long does it take to adopt continuous delivery?**
It depends on the starting point. A new product can be set up for continuous delivery from the start; an existing system with few automated tests usually improves step by step over months, with benefits arriving at each step.

**Q: Can regulated organisations use continuous delivery?**
Yes. Many regulated organisations practise it by building approvals, audit trails and validation evidence into the pipeline, so every change is traceable. They may release less often, but the software stays releasable.
