# Cumulative Flow Diagram: How to Read and Use a CFD

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: A cumulative flow diagram (CFD) shows work in each stage over time. Learn to read bands, spot bottlenecks, estimate cycle time and build one step by step.


## Cumulative Flow Diagram: How to Read and Use a CFD
A cumulative flow diagram (CFD) is a stacked area chart that shows how many work items have reached each stage of your workflow, day by day or week by week. In one picture it tells you how much work is in progress, where it is piling up and how quickly it is being finished. This guide explains how a CFD is built, how to read work in progress, cycle time and throughput from it, what the common patterns mean and how to build your own, using an eight-week worked example.
- Published 13 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- A CFD has one band per workflow stage. Each line counts every item that has reached that stage or any later one, which is why the lines never fall.
- The vertical distance between two lines is the work in progress between those stages on that date.
- The horizontal distance between the line where work starts and the Done line is an approximate average cycle time.
- The slope of the Done line is your delivery rate (throughput); the slope of the top line is your arrival rate.
- A band that keeps getting wider is the clearest sign of a bottleneck. Look for the first widening band, working up from Done.
- Read the CFD for trends over several weeks, and pair it with a cycle time scatterplot and a WIP aging chart for item-level detail.

### What is a cumulative flow diagram?
A **cumulative flow diagram** is a stacked area chart that plots, over time, the total number of work items that have reached each stage of a workflow. Each coloured band represents one stage. The thickness of a band shows how much work is in that stage, and the slope of the lines shows how fast work is arriving and leaving.
The chart comes from queueing theory, where it is sometimes called a cumulative input-output diagram, and it is used in traffic engineering and manufacturing as well as in knowledge work. Agile and Kanban teams adopted it because it shows the health of a whole process at once, not just the result at the end. The PMBOK Guide (7th edition) also describes it, as a chart showing features completed over time alongside features in other states and those in the backlog.
A CFD answers three practical questions:
- **How much work is in progress?** Read the vertical gap between the lines.
- **Where is work waiting?** Look for the band that is getting wider.
- **How fast is work being finished, compared with how fast it arrives?** Compare the slope of the Done line with the slope of the top line.
It is one of the core charts of the [Kanban method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/), alongside the cycle time scatterplot, the throughput run chart and the WIP aging chart. For how they fit together, see our guide to [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/).

### Anatomy of a cumulative flow diagram
Whether your CFD comes from Jira, Azure DevOps or a spreadsheet, it is built from the same parts.
| Element | What it shows | What to look for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Horizontal axis | Time: days or weeks | A long enough range to show a trend, usually 4 to 12 weeks |
| Vertical axis | Cumulative count of work items | Items, not story points or hours, in most Kanban practice |
| Bands | One stage of the workflow each, in board order | Done at the bottom, the earliest stage at the top |
| Top line (arrivals) | Everything that has entered the system so far | Its slope is the arrival rate |
| Bottom line (departures) | Everything that has reached Done so far | Its slope is the delivery rate, or throughput |
| Band thickness | Items currently in that stage | Steady thickness means stable WIP in that stage |
| Horizontal gap | Time between an item entering one stage and leaving another | An approximation of average time in process |
Tip
Most tools use the same colour order as your board columns. If the chart looks upside down, check whether the tool stacks Done at the top; the reading rules are the same, only mirrored.

### How a CFD is built: the counting rule

#### Count everything that has reached a stage or beyond
The single idea that makes a CFD readable is its counting rule. Each line does not show the items sitting in a stage today; it shows **every item that has ever reached that stage or any stage after it**. So the In progress line counts items in progress, plus items in review, plus items done. The Done line counts everything delivered since the chart started.
Plot those cumulative totals as lines, shade the space between neighbouring lines, and each shaded band is exactly the number of items in one stage on that date. That is why the gap between two lines equals work in progress.

#### Why the lines never go down
Because each line is a running total of arrivals into a stage, it can rise or stay flat but it cannot fall in normal use. A line only drops if items are deleted, moved backwards on the board, or filtered out of the report. If you see a dip, check for board clean-ups, items reopened or a change to the report filter before reading anything into it.

#### Which stages to include
Include every column between your **commitment point** (where the team agrees to do the work) and your **delivery point**. Adding the backlog or an options column above the commitment point is optional. It shows demand, but a large backlog can dwarf the rest of the chart. Many teams show the backlog on a separate chart or leave it out and keep a short, replenished Ready column instead. If your board has split columns such as Review: doing and Review: done, keep both, because the done half is a queue and the CFD will show it filling up. For board design, see [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/).

### Worked example: eight weeks of one team's board
A five-person team runs a Kanban board with four stages: Ready, In progress, Review and Done. Every Friday it records how many items have reached each stage so far. These are the cumulative counts, the numbers you plot.
| Week | Arrived (entered Ready) | Started (entered In progress) | Entered Review | Done |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 10 | 8 | 5 | 3 |
| 2 | 16 | 14 | 11 | 8 |
| 3 | 22 | 20 | 16 | 13 |
| 4 | 28 | 26 | 22 | 18 |
| 5 | 34 | 31 | 27 | 21 |
| 6 | 40 | 36 | 32 | 23 |
| 7 | 46 | 40 | 36 | 26 |
| 8 | 51 | 43 | 40 | 33 |
Subtracting neighbouring columns gives the number of items in each stage, which is what the band thickness shows on the chart. Subtracting each week's Done figure from the previous week's gives the weekly throughput.
| Week | In Ready | In progress | In Review | Total WIP (started, not done) | Finished this week | Started this week |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 8 |
| 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 6 | 5 | 6 |
| 3 | 2 | 4 | 3 | 7 | 5 | 6 |
| 4 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 8 | 5 | 6 |
| 5 | 3 | 4 | 6 | 10 | 3 | 5 |
| 6 | 4 | 4 | 9 | 13 | 2 | 5 |
| 7 | 6 | 4 | 10 | 14 | 3 | 4 |
| 8 | 8 | 3 | 7 | 10 | 7 | 3 |
**Weeks 1 to 4: steady flow.** The bands rise roughly in parallel. The team starts about six items a week and finishes about five, and total WIP creeps up only slightly, from 5 to 8.
**Weeks 5 to 7: a bottleneck in Review.** The one person who does most reviews is pulled onto a customer escalation. The Review band swells from 4 items to 10 while the Done line flattens to two or three items a week. Notice what the team does upstream: it keeps starting four or five items a week, so total WIP climbs to 14. This is the classic shape of a bottleneck. Work keeps flowing in, but it cannot get out.
**Week 8: recovery.** At the retrospective in week 7 the team sets a [WIP limit](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) of four on Review, agrees that developers pair on reviews before pulling new work, and stops starting new items until Review is below its limit. Within a week the Review band shrinks to 7, throughput jumps to 7 items and total WIP falls to 10. The Ready band grows, because the team deliberately started less, which is the right trade-off while the queue clears.
Tip
Notice that the bottleneck was visible on the CFD from week 5, two weeks before anyone raised it. That early warning is the main reason to look at the chart every week rather than only at the end of a project.

### How to read WIP, cycle time and throughput from a CFD

#### Vertical distance: work in progress
Draw a vertical line at any date. The distance between two lines along it is the number of items between those stages on that date. In the example, at week 4 the Started line is at 26 and the Done line at 18, so 8 items are in progress. At week 7 the gap is 40 − 26 = 14 items: WIP has almost doubled in three weeks.

#### Horizontal distance: approximate average cycle time
Draw a horizontal line at any count. The distance along it between the Started line and the Done line is roughly how long items took to get from starting to finishing. It is an approximation of the average, not the cycle time of any particular item, because items do not necessarily finish in the order they started.
- **At week 4:** the Done line reaches 18. The Started line reached 18 about two-thirds of the way through week 3 (it went from 14 to 20 that week). The horizontal gap is about **1.3 weeks**.
- **At week 7:** the Done line reaches 26. The Started line was at 26 at the end of week 4, so the gap is about **3 weeks**.
- **At week 8:** the Done line reaches 33, which the Started line passed during week 6 (it was 31 at week 5 and 36 at week 6). The gap is about **2.6 weeks** and starting to close.
The approximate cycle time more than doubled during the bottleneck. Measure the gap between the top line and the Done line instead and you get an approximate lead time, which includes waiting in Ready. For item-level detail and percentiles, use a [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) scatterplot; for the difference between the two measures, see [cycle time vs lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/).

#### Slope: throughput and arrival rate
The steepness of the Done line is your delivery rate. In weeks 2 to 4 it rises by 5 items a week; in weeks 5 to 7 by fewer than 3. The steepness of the top line is the rate at which new work arrives: about 6 items a week throughout. When the top line is persistently steeper than the bottom line, WIP is growing and cycle time will follow. Healthy systems have arrival and departure lines that are, over a few weeks, roughly parallel. For more on measuring and forecasting with delivery rate, see [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/).

### Cumulative flow diagram patterns and what they mean
The table below is a pattern library you can use in reviews. The causes are the ones teams most often find; always confirm with the board and the people doing the work before acting.
| Pattern on the chart | What it means | Likely causes | What to try |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bands rising in parallel, steady thickness | Stable, predictable flow | WIP limits respected; arrivals match capacity | Keep going; consider gently lowering WIP limits |
| One band steadily widening | Items enter the stage faster than they leave: a bottleneck | Too few people or skills in that stage; external dependency; large items | Limit WIP upstream, swarm on the stage, look at its capacity |
| Band narrowing to nothing | The stage is starved of work | Upstream bottleneck; nothing ready to pull | Look upstream; check that the Ready column is replenished |
| Flat Done line | Nothing is being delivered | Blocked release, holiday, waiting for a batch deployment | Find and remove the blocker; release smaller batches |
| Stair steps on the Done line | Work is delivered in batches | Release trains, sprint-end acceptance, weekly sign-offs | Fine if intended; otherwise move towards smaller, more frequent releases |
| Top line much steeper than the Done line | Demand exceeds capacity; WIP and lead time are growing | Too much accepted work; weak replenishment policies | Say no or not yet; tighten replenishment; agree priorities with stakeholders |
| All bands widening together | The team keeps starting more than it finishes | No WIP limits, or limits ignored | Introduce or enforce WIP limits; stop starting, start finishing |
| Bulge in a band that then collapses | A queue formed, then cleared in a rush | Review or test backlog cleared at a deadline | Fine if rare; if regular, smooth the work with WIP limits |
| Sudden drop in a line | Items removed or moved backwards | Board clean-up, reopened items, changed filter | Check the data before interpreting |
| Backlog band ballooning above the commitment point | Ideas arriving faster than they are considered | Everyone can add to the backlog; no pruning | Prune regularly; separate options from commitments |
Tip
Find the first widening band, working up from Done. Bands above a bottleneck tend to widen as a knock-on effect, so the lowest widening band is usually closest to the real constraint. The [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/) explains what to do once you have found it.

### How to create a cumulative flow diagram step by step
Most Kanban tools draw a CFD automatically, but building one in a spreadsheet takes about 20 minutes and is worth doing once: it makes the counting rule obvious and works for physical boards too.
1. **List your stages in board order**, from the commitment point to Done. Decide whether to include the backlog.
2. **Choose a snapshot frequency.** Daily gives the most detail; weekly is fine for teams that finish a handful of items a week. Pick a fixed time, such as 5 pm or Friday afternoon.
3. **Record the count in each column** at every snapshot, one row per date and one column per stage. On a physical board, one person counts cards; in a tool, use a filtered list. For Done, record the running total of everything finished since the chart began, even if you archive done cards.
4. **Check the cumulative totals.** Add a helper column for each line: Started = In progress + Review + Done, Entered review = Review + Done, and so on. Every helper column should rise or stay flat from row to row; a fall means a counting error or an item moved backwards.
5. **Order the stage columns so Done comes first** in the data range. Spreadsheet tools stack series in data order, so Done becomes the bottom band.
6. **Insert a stacked area chart of the stage counts** (not the helper columns). Stacking does the cumulative adding for you, so the top edge of each band lands exactly on the helper totals. Plotting the helper columns as a stacked chart would double-count.
7. **Format for reading:** use the same colours as your board, label the axes, start the vertical axis at zero, and add a short note at any date when a policy changed.
8. **Update it at every snapshot and look at it weekly.** The value comes from the trend, not from any single day.
If you are setting up a board from scratch, a template saves time: ours includes To Do, In Progress, Review and Done columns, WIP limits and card details, and you can add a snapshot tab with one row per date beside it.

### Using a CFD with Little's Law
Little's Law, published by John Little in 1961, links the three measures a CFD displays. In flow terms:
**Average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput.**
In weeks 2 to 4 of the example, average WIP was (6 + 7 + 8) ÷ 3 = 7 items and throughput was 5 items a week. Little's Law gives 7 ÷ 5 = 1.4 weeks, which agrees closely with the 1.3 weeks read horizontally off the chart.
Now try weeks 5 to 7. Average WIP was (10 + 13 + 14) ÷ 3 ≈ 12.3 and average throughput was (3 + 2 + 3) ÷ 3 ≈ 2.7, giving about 4.6 weeks, well above the 2.3 to 3 weeks the chart showed. The numbers disagree because the law only holds when its assumptions are met, and in those weeks they were not. Daniel Vacanti, who has written extensively on applying the law to knowledge work, sets out conditions along these lines:
- Average arrival rate roughly equals average departure rate over the period.
- Work that is started is eventually finished, rather than abandoned in the system.
- WIP is roughly the same at the start and end of the period.
- The average age of work in progress is neither growing nor shrinking.
- WIP, cycle time and throughput are measured in consistent units and over the same boundaries.
So use the CFD in two ways: as a picture that tells you whether the system is stable, and, when it is, as a source for Little's Law estimates. When the bands are diverging, treat any calculation as a warning, not a forecast. The practical lesson is the one Kanban teams act on every day: with throughput steady, reducing WIP shortens cycle time.

### How to use a CFD in reviews and meetings
A CFD is most useful as a regular conversation starter, not as a report for managers. A simple weekly or fortnightly routine works well, for example at a service delivery review or a retrospective (see [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/)).
1. **Look at the last four to eight weeks**, not the whole history. Long ranges flatten recent problems.
2. **Compare the top and bottom slopes.** Is work arriving faster than it leaves?
3. **Scan for widening bands**, starting from Done. Name the first one.
4. **Check WIP against your limits.** If a band is thicker than its column limit allows, the limit is being ignored; ask why.
5. **Estimate the horizontal gap** now and a month ago. Is time in process growing?
6. **Agree one experiment**, such as lowering a WIP limit, pairing on reviews or splitting large items, and mark the date on the chart.
7. **Review the effect** at the next meeting by comparing the bands before and after the marker.
Day to day, a [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) is the better tool, because it shows which individual items are stuck now. The CFD tells you where the system is struggling; the aging chart tells you which card to help with this morning. When a band widens because items are blocked, record why and look for patterns with [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/).

### CFD vs burnup, burndown and other flow charts
| Chart | What it shows | Best for | Blind spot |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cumulative flow diagram | Items per workflow stage over time | Seeing WIP, bottlenecks and arrival vs delivery rate | Averages only; no item-level detail |
| Burnup chart | Completed work against total scope | Tracking progress to a fixed scope or release | Shows nothing about stages in between |
| Burndown chart | Remaining work over a sprint or release | Sprint progress at a glance | Hides scope changes and where work is stuck |
| Cycle time scatterplot | Each finished item's cycle time | Percentiles and service level expectations | Only shows finished work, so it lags |
| WIP aging chart | Age of each item still in progress | Spotting stuck work today | No history or trend |
| Throughput run chart | Items finished per period | Forecasting how many items by a date | Says nothing about where work waits |
| Velocity chart | Story points completed per sprint | Sprint planning in Scrum | Depends on estimates; no stage view |
A burnup chart is sometimes described as a simplified CFD with only two lines: total scope and done. The CFD adds a line for every stage in between, which is what lets you see where work is accumulating. For the Scrum equivalent, see our [Agile velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) guide, and for a wider view of measures, [Agile metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-metrics-and-kpis/).

### Can Scrum teams use a cumulative flow diagram?
Yes. A CFD works for any team that moves work through visible stages, whether or not it uses Kanban. Scrum teams can use it in two ways:
- **Within a sprint:** a CFD starting on day one of the sprint shows whether items are moving into Review and Done steadily or all at once on the last day. A Done band that only rises at the end is a sign of large items or too much work started in parallel.
- **Across sprints:** a rolling CFD over several sprints shows trends in WIP and delivery that a burndown resets every two weeks.
The chart complements rather than replaces Scrum's own measures. For the metrics Scrum teams commonly track, see [Scrum metrics and KPIs](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-metrics-and-kpis/), and for how the two frameworks compare, [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/).

### Cumulative flow diagrams in project management tools
Most Agile tools generate a CFD from your board's status history, so the main job is keeping card statuses up to date. A few notes from vendor documentation (checked 25 October 2026):
- **Jira** offers a cumulative flow diagram report for boards, showing how many work items are in each column over time, and a separate control chart for time in status. See our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/).
- **Azure DevOps** provides a cumulative flow report and dashboard widget. Microsoft's documentation describes rolling periods of 14 to 180 days for continuous flow, or a fixed start date for sprint-style work.
- **ClickUp** dashboards include cycle time cards, and its help centre also documents a sprint cumulative flow card (now marked as legacy). See our [ClickUp review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/).
- **Wrike**, our top-ranked tool overall, describes a work progress chart in its analytics as a way to get a similar view of work by status over time, which suits teams managing several projects and stakeholders. See our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).
- **Spreadsheets** work well for physical boards and small teams, using the step-by-step method above.
Whichever tool you use, check three settings before trusting the chart: which statuses are mapped to which bands, whether filters or swimlanes are excluding work, and the date range.

### Common mistakes when using a CFD
- **Reading a single day.** A CFD is a trend chart. One thick day means little; a band widening for two weeks means a lot.
- **Including a huge backlog.** It flattens every other band. Leave it out or chart it separately.
- **Mixing units.** Count items. Switching to story points or hours partway through breaks the chart.
- **Forgetting that statuses drive the chart.** If people move cards late, the CFD shows false bottlenecks and false jumps.
- **Treating horizontal distance as exact.** It approximates average time in process; use item-level cycle times for percentiles and service level expectations.
- **Applying Little's Law to an unstable system.** When bands are diverging, calculations based on averages mislead.
- **Blaming the stage with the thick band.** The constraint is often a policy, a dependency or a hand-off, not the people in that column.
- **Changing the workflow without a note.** Adding or merging columns changes the bands; mark the date so later readers are not confused.
- **Using the CFD to compare teams.** Workflows, item sizes and policies differ. Use it to improve your own system.
Swarming on the stage that is struggling is often the fastest fix; see [Agile swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/). And because much of the delay a CFD reveals is waiting rather than working, it pairs naturally with [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) analysis.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a cumulative flow diagram in simple terms?**
It is a chart with one coloured band for each stage of your workflow. The bands stack up over time, so you can see how much work is in each stage, where it is piling up and how fast it is getting to Done.

**Q: How do you read a cumulative flow diagram?**
Read vertically for work in progress (the gap between two lines), horizontally for approximate average time in process (the gap between the start line and the Done line), and look at slopes for rates: the top line is arrivals and the bottom line is throughput. Then look for any band that keeps getting wider.

**Q: What does a widening band mean on a CFD?**
Work is entering that stage faster than it is leaving, so a queue or bottleneck is forming. If several bands widen, start with the lowest one, nearest to Done, because problems upstream are often knock-on effects.

**Q: What does a healthy cumulative flow diagram look like?**
Bands that rise smoothly and roughly in parallel, with fairly constant thickness, and a top line and Done line with similar slopes over a few weeks. That shows stable WIP, steady delivery and arrivals that match capacity.

**Q: What does a flat line on a CFD mean?**
Nothing crossed into that stage during the period. A flat Done line means nothing was delivered, which might be a holiday, a batch release or a blocker. A flat top line means no new work was accepted.

**Q: How do you calculate cycle time from a CFD?**
Pick a point on the Done line and measure horizontally back to the line where work starts, such as In progress. That distance is an approximate average cycle time for items finishing around then. For individual items and percentiles, use a [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) scatterplot.

**Q: What is the difference between a CFD and a burnup chart?**
A burnup chart shows two things: total scope and completed work. A CFD shows every stage in between as well, so it reveals where work is accumulating and how much is in progress, not just how much is done.

**Q: Why does the bottom band of a CFD never go down?**
Because each line is a running total of items that have reached that stage or beyond. Finished items stay counted. A line only falls if items are deleted, moved backwards or filtered out of the report.

**Q: Should the backlog be included in a CFD?**
It is optional. Including it shows demand, but a large backlog can dwarf every other band. Many teams start the chart at the commitment point, such as a Ready column, and track the wider backlog separately.

**Q: How often should a team review its CFD?**
Weekly or fortnightly is common, for example at a service delivery review or retrospective. Use a WIP aging chart for daily attention to individual items.

**Q: Can you make a cumulative flow diagram in Excel or Google Sheets?**
Yes. Record the number of items in each column at a fixed time each day or week, put Done first in the data range, and insert a stacked area chart of the stage counts. The step-by-step method above takes about 20 minutes to set up.

**Q: Is the cumulative flow diagram in the PMBOK Guide or the PMI-ACP exam?**
The PMBOK Guide (7th edition) describes the cumulative flow diagram, and it is a standard Agile chart that exam preparation materials for PMI-ACP commonly cover. Check PMI's current exam content outline for the latest scope.

# Cycle Time vs Lead Time: Differences, Formulas, Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Cycle time vs lead time explained: where each starts and stops, how to calculate both, worked Kanban examples, Little's Law and which one to report.


## Cycle Time vs Lead Time: Differences, Formulas, Examples
The difference between cycle time and lead time is where the clock starts: lead time runs from the moment a customer asks for something until they receive it, while cycle time runs only from when the team starts work until the work is finished. Cycle time sits inside lead time, so lead time shows what your customers experience and cycle time shows how quickly your process moves once work begins. This guide shows where each clock starts and stops on a Kanban board, how to calculate both from the same card dates, two worked examples, what the gap between them tells you and how to shorten each one.
- Published 12 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Lead time = request to delivery (the customer's wait). Cycle time = start to finish (the team's process). Lead time = waiting before work starts + cycle time + any wait before delivery.
- Definitions vary between sources. The Kanban Guide defines cycle time but not lead time; Kanban University, DORA and tools such as Azure DevOps each draw the lead time boundary differently. Write down your own start and stop points.
- Calculate both from card dates with the same convention, for example finish date − start date + 1 in calendar days, and report medians and 85th percentiles rather than averages.
- A short cycle time with a long lead time means work is waiting in the queue, not that the team is slow. Fix it by shortening the queue and deciding faster, not by working harder.
- Little's Law applies to both: average lead time ≈ items in the whole system ÷ throughput; average cycle time ≈ items in progress ÷ throughput.
- Show lead time to customers and stakeholders; use cycle time and work item age inside the team to improve the process.

### What is the difference between cycle time and lead time?
**Lead time** is the elapsed time from when a request is made to when it is delivered to the customer. **Cycle time** is the elapsed time from when the team starts work on an item to when it is finished. Lead time includes the wait before work starts, so cycle time is always part of lead time.
Put simply, lead time is measured from the customer's point of view and cycle time from the team's. A customer who asks for a report on Monday and receives it three weeks later experiences three weeks, even if the report was only in progress for four days. The relationship is:
**Lead time = waiting before work starts + cycle time + any waiting between finishing and delivery**
|  | Lead time | Cycle time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clock starts | When the request is made or logged | When the team starts work on the item |
| Clock stops | When the customer receives it | When the work is finished |
| Includes queue waiting | Yes | No |
| Whose experience it reflects | The customer's or requester's | The team's working process |
| Question it answers | How long will I wait if I ask now? | Once you start, how long until it is done? |
| Mainly influenced by | Queue length, prioritisation, release schedule, plus cycle time | WIP, item size, handoffs, reviews and blockers |
| Typical use | Customer forecasts, service levels, stakeholder reporting | Process improvement and daily flow management |
Both are elapsed time and both include waiting. Neither is the hours someone spent actively working, which is touch time. See our guide to [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) for how to measure active versus waiting time.

### Where the clock starts and stops on a Kanban board
Most confusion disappears once you mark the points on your [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) where each clock starts and stops. Five points matter:
1. **Request logged:** the item is added to the backlog or arrives through a request form.
2. **Commitment point:** the team agrees to deliver it, usually by pulling it into a Ready column. Before this, it is only an option.
3. **Work started:** the item enters the first in-progress column.
4. **Work finished:** the item reaches Done.
5. **Delivered:** the customer can use it, for example after a scheduled release.
| Measure | From | To | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lead time (customer view) | 1. Request logged | 5. Delivered | The customer's total wait |
| Lead time from commitment | 2. Commitment point | 5. Delivered | How long the team takes once it has said yes |
| Cycle time | 3. Work started | 4. Work finished | How long work takes once started |
| Wait after finish | 4. Work finished | 5. Delivered | Release batching and handover delays |
On many teams commitment and start are the same column, and finish and delivery happen together, so the only difference between the two measures is the backlog wait. Where they are separate, the extra segments often hide the largest waits.

#### Why definitions differ between sources
If three articles gave you three definitions, you are not imagining it. Different communities draw the boundaries in different places:
| Source | Lead time | Cycle time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The Kanban Guide (v2025.5) | Not defined; the guide uses cycle time only | Elapsed time from when a work item started to when it finished |
| Kanban University (2023) | Customer lead time: from receiving the request to delivering it. System lead time: from the commitment point to the first column with no WIP limit | Not a core glossary term |
| DORA metrics | Change lead time: from a code commit to successful deployment in production | Not one of the four DORA metrics |
| Azure DevOps | From when a work item is created until it is completed | From when it first enters In Progress until it is completed |
| Manufacturing | Order to delivery, including queues and transport | Often the time to complete one unit at a process step |
Kanban University changed its definition of customer lead time in 2023: it used to start at the commitment point and now starts when the request is received. That is why older articles start lead time at commitment and newer ones at the request. Both measure something real; they just measure different spans.

#### Write your definitions down as a policy
The label matters much less than the boundary. Agree the start and stop points as an explicit board policy and use them on every report:
Tip
Example policy: 'Lead time runs from the date a request is logged to the date it is released to users. Cycle time runs from the date a card first enters In Progress to the date it enters Done. Both are counted in calendar days as end date − start date + 1. Items that move backwards keep their original start date.'

### How to calculate lead time and cycle time
Both are simple date arithmetic on finished items. Using the same convention as our [cycle time guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/):
- **Lead time = delivery date − request date + 1** (calendar days)
- **Cycle time = finish date − start date + 1** (calendar days)
The + 1 is a counting convention: an item requested, started and finished on the same day counts as 1 day rather than 0. Some tools count elapsed hours instead. Either works if you are consistent and say which you use. Calendar days suit lead time in particular, because customers wait through weekends too.
1. **Agree the boundaries** for both measures and write them down.
2. **Record the dates on every card:** requested, started, finished and, if different, delivered. Digital tools log these from status changes; on a physical board, write them on the card, as shown in our [Kanban cards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-cards/) guide.
3. **Calculate per item once it is finished**, with a third column for queue time before start (start date − request date). For unfinished items, track work item age instead.
4. **Summarise the distribution** with the median and 85th percentile for each measure.
5. **Compare the two medians.** The gap is the typical waiting time outside the process, and it tells you where to look first.
6. **Review trends regularly**, over several weeks rather than single values.
A spreadsheet with columns for item, type, requested, started, finished, delivered, queue time, cycle time and lead time is enough for most teams. Our free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) already has started, finished and cycle time columns that you can extend with a requested date.

#### Averages, medians and percentiles
Lead and cycle time data are usually skewed: most items finish quickly and a few take much longer, pulling the average up. Report the **median** (half of items finished within this time) and the **85th percentile** (85% finished within this time). The cycle time guide shows the nearest-rank method for calculating percentiles by hand.

### Worked example: one request from start to finish
This illustrative example follows one request through a digital team's board. The team releases to users every Tuesday, so finished work waits for the next release.
| Point | Date | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request logged | Mon 14 Sep | A sales manager asks for a new filter on the customer report |
| Commitment point | Mon 21 Sep | Pulled into Ready at the weekly replenishment meeting |
| Work started | Mon 28 Sep | A developer picks it up |
| Work finished | Fri 2 Oct | Built, reviewed and tested; card moves to Done |
| Delivered | Tue 6 Oct | Released in the Tuesday release |
1. **Cycle time** = 2 Oct − 28 Sep + 1 = **5 days**.
2. **Lead time** = 6 Oct − 14 Sep + 1 = **23 days**.
3. **Lead time from commitment** = 6 Oct − 21 Sep + 1 = **16 days**.
4. **Break the lead time down:** 7 days before commitment, 7 days committed but not started, 5 days of cycle time and 4 days waiting for the release. 7 + 7 + 5 + 4 = 23.
The sales manager waited 23 days for something the team took 5 days to build. Asking the developer to work faster could save a day or two at most; replenishing twice a week and releasing as soon as work is done could save up to 11 days without anyone working harder.
Tip
If your team only reports cycle time, this request looks excellent. If your stakeholders only see lead time, it looks slow. Seeing both side by side shows where the time actually went.

### Worked example: ten finished items
Now take ten requests an internal IT team (illustrative) finished in September and October. Here commitment and start happen together and items are delivered as soon as they are finished, so lead time = queue time before start + cycle time.
| Item | Requested | Started | Finished | Queue time (days) | Cycle time (days) | Lead time (days) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 | Tue 1 Sep | Thu 3 Sep | Fri 4 Sep | 2 | 2 | 4 |
| R-02 | Tue 1 Sep | Tue 15 Sep | Wed 16 Sep | 14 | 2 | 16 |
| R-03 | Thu 3 Sep | Thu 3 Sep | Thu 3 Sep | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| R-04 | Fri 4 Sep | Thu 24 Sep | Mon 28 Sep | 20 | 5 | 25 |
| R-05 | Mon 7 Sep | Wed 16 Sep | Tue 22 Sep | 9 | 7 | 16 |
| R-06 | Tue 8 Sep | Wed 7 Oct | Fri 9 Oct | 29 | 3 | 32 |
| R-07 | Thu 10 Sep | Tue 15 Sep | Fri 18 Sep | 5 | 4 | 9 |
| R-08 | Fri 11 Sep | Tue 29 Sep | Tue 6 Oct | 18 | 8 | 26 |
| R-09 | Mon 14 Sep | Fri 25 Sep | Tue 29 Sep | 11 | 5 | 16 |
| R-10 | Tue 15 Sep | Fri 9 Oct | Tue 20 Oct | 24 | 12 | 36 |
| **Total** |  |  |  | **132** | **49** | **181** |
Sorted, the cycle times are 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 7, 8, 12 and the lead times are 1, 4, 9, 16, 16, 16, 25, 26, 32, 36. With ten items, the median is the average of the 5th and 6th values, and the nearest-rank 85th percentile is the 9th value (10 × 0.85 = 8.5, rounded up).
| Statistic | Cycle time | Lead time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Average | 4.9 days | 18.1 days |
| Median | 4.5 days | 16 days |
| 85th percentile | 8 days | 32 days |
- **Waiting dominates.** Of 181 days of lead time, 132 (about 73%) were spent in the queue. The process is reasonably quick; the queue is not.
- **Lead time is much less predictable.** Queue time ranges from 0 to 29 days depending on prioritisation, so the 85th percentile lead time is four times the cycle time figure.
- **Expedites have a cost.** R-03 went straight in, which is right for a genuine emergency, but every jump lengthens the wait for everything behind it.
- **Customer promises should use lead time.** 'We usually finish in about 5 days' is true of cycle time and misleading about the requester's experience. '85% of requests are delivered within 32 days' is honest and gives the team a clear target to improve.

### What the gap between lead time and cycle time tells you
Comparing the two medians is one of the quickest diagnostics you can run on a board:
| Pattern | Likely cause | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Short cycle time, short lead time | Small queue, quick decisions, healthy WIP | Protect WIP limits and replenish little and often |
| Short cycle time, long lead time | Long backlog, slow prioritisation, release batching | Shorten the queue, decide faster, release more often |
| Long cycle time, lead time slightly longer | Too much WIP, large items, internal waits for reviews | Lower WIP limits, split work, speed up reviews |
| Both long and highly variable | Overloaded system: starting and committing to too much | Stop starting and start finishing: cut WIP and the queue together |
Watch the trend too. If lead time is rising while cycle time is flat, demand is outrunning [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) and the queue is growing. A [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) shows this as a widening backlog band.

### Lead time, cycle time and Little's Law
Little's Law, published by John Little in 1961, links average time in a system with the number of items in it and the rate at which they leave. It works for either boundary, as long as you count WIP and throughput over the same one:
- **Average cycle time ≈ average items in progress ÷ average throughput**
- **Average lead time ≈ average items in the whole system (committed queue + in progress) ÷ average throughput**

#### Worked example: halving lead time without working faster
An illustrative team finishes about 4 items a week, with 6 items in progress and 20 committed items waiting in Ready.
|  | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Items in progress | 6 | 6 |
| Committed items waiting | 20 | 8 |
| Throughput | 4 a week | 4 a week |
| Average cycle time (6 ÷ 4) | 1.5 weeks | 1.5 weeks |
| Average lead time | 26 ÷ 4 = 6.5 weeks | 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5 weeks |
The team caps Ready at 8 items, holds the rest as uncommitted options and replenishes weekly. Nobody works faster and throughput is unchanged, yet average lead time falls by almost half. Lowering [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) inside the process would shorten cycle time in the same way.
Two cautions. Little's Law describes averages in a reasonably stable system, so use it to understand cause and effect, not to forecast a single item. And an uncommitted backlog of ideas is not a queue: many options will be discarded, so apply the law from the commitment point, or from the request only if every request will be done.

### Cycle time vs lead time vs other flow measures
This table shows how lead time and cycle time sit among the other common flow measures.
| Measure | What it is | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lead time | Request to delivery, per finished item | How long does the customer wait? |
| Cycle time | Start to finish, per finished item | Once started, how long does work take? |
| Work item age | Time since an unfinished item started | Which items in progress are at risk now? |
| Throughput | Items finished per period | How much do we deliver? |
| Takt time | Available time ÷ customer demand | How often must we finish an item to keep up? |
| Change lead time (DORA) | Code commit to production deployment | How quickly can a code change reach users? |
Two similar-sounding terms are different. In manufacturing, cycle time often means the time to produce one unit at a workstation; see [lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/). In scheduling, a **lead** is an overlap that lets a successor start before its predecessor finishes, explained in [leads and lags](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/leads-and-lags/).
For items still on the board, a [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) compares each item's age with your historical cycle times, so you can act before it becomes a long lead time. Read our guide to [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) for the full set.

### Which one should you report, and to whom?
| Audience | Main measure | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customers and requesters | Lead time, as a probability | It is the wait they actually experience |
| Stakeholders and sponsors | Lead time and throughput | When things will arrive and how much will be delivered |
| The delivery team | Cycle time, work item age and WIP | What the team controls day to day |
| Service desks with an SLA | Lead time against the agreed target | Contracts usually start the clock when the ticket is raised |
To give customers an honest forecast from lead time data:
1. Collect lead times for at least 15–20 recent finished items of a similar type.
2. Find the 85th percentile, as in the ten-item example.
3. Phrase it as a probability: '85% of requests like this are delivered within 32 days.'
4. Offer a limited expedite route for genuine emergencies.
5. Recalculate monthly and publish the improved figure as queue time falls.
The Kanban Guide's **service level expectation** applies the same idea to cycle time. A contractual commitment belongs in a [service level agreement (SLA)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/service-level-agreement-sla/). To forecast many items at once, combine throughput history with a [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/), as explained in [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/).

### How to reduce lead time
Because most lead time is usually waiting, the biggest gains come from managing the queue and the decisions around it.

#### Shorten and prune the queue
A long committed backlog is a promise you cannot keep quickly. Cap committed items, move the rest back to options and remove requests that are no longer needed. Regular [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) keeps the queue small and current.

#### Replenish little and often
If you pull new work once a month, a request that arrives the day after replenishment waits a month before it is even considered. Weekly or on-demand replenishment cuts that wait. This is the core of a [pull system](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/): work enters when there is capacity.

#### Decide faster, and say not yet sooner
Requests often wait for someone to decide whether they will be done at all. Agree who decides, how often and on what criteria. A clear 'not yet' lets the requester find another route.

#### Remove waits after done
If finished work waits for a monthly release, lead time includes that wait. More frequent releases, or [continuous delivery](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/continuous-delivery/) in software, close the gap. Elsewhere, hand work over as soon as it is ready.

#### Use expedite lanes sparingly
Every expedited item delays everything behind it, so limit expedites to one at a time. To find the longest waits across the whole flow, including outside your team, use [value stream mapping](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/).

### How to reduce cycle time
- **Limit work in progress.** Fewer items in progress means each finishes sooner.
- **Split large items** into smaller useful pieces; techniques for splitting [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) apply to most work.
- **Shrink internal waits** for review, testing and approval.
- **Remove recurring blockers** and swarm on items older than your 85th percentile.
- **Automate** repetitive steps such as testing and deployment.
Cutting cycle time also cuts lead time, because cycle time is part of it; a shorter queue, though, leaves cycle time unchanged. See our full guide to [measuring and reducing cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/).

### Measuring lead time and cycle time in project management tools
Most digital boards calculate both from status history, but each draws the boundaries its own way, so check them against your policy.
- **Wrike**, our top-rated tool, combines request intake forms with custom workflow statuses and dashboards. Logging requests through a form records when each one arrived, giving a clean start point for lead time. See our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).
- **Jira** includes cumulative flow diagrams and a control chart for cycle time in which you choose the statuses that count. See our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/).
- **Azure DevOps** has separate Lead Time and Cycle Time widgets, using the Microsoft definitions in the table above.
- **ClickUp** offers cycle time cards for dashboards and cumulative flow in sprint reporting. See our [ClickUp review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/).
- **A spreadsheet** works with any board: record the dates, apply the formulas and use percentile functions.
Whatever the tool, lead time is only accurate if requests are logged when they arrive. A simple [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) or intake form solves that.

### Common mistakes when comparing cycle time and lead time
- **Using the terms interchangeably** without defining where each starts and stops.
- **Reporting cycle time to customers.** It understates their wait.
- **Measuring only active time** and calling it cycle time.
- **Relying on averages** instead of medians and 85th percentiles.
- **Starting the lead time clock late**, when a request is typed in weeks after it arrived by email.
- **Ignoring the wait after done** when delivery happens later than finish.
- **Mixing very different work types** in one figure.
- **Turning either number into a target for individuals**, which leads to gaming.
Review lead time, cycle time and the other flow measures together at a regular [Kanban review meeting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/), and change one thing at a time.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between cycle time and lead time?**
Lead time runs from when a customer requests an item to when it is delivered. Cycle time runs from when the team starts work on it to when it is finished, so cycle time is part of lead time.

**Q: Is lead time always longer than cycle time?**
It is never shorter when both are measured on the same item, because cycle time sits inside it. It is usually longer, because items wait before work starts and sometimes after it finishes. The two are equal only when work starts the moment it is requested and is delivered the moment it is finished.

**Q: How do you calculate lead time and cycle time?**
Lead time = delivery date − request date + 1, and cycle time = finish date − start date + 1, in calendar days. Calculate them for finished items and summarise with medians and 85th percentiles.

**Q: What is lead time in Kanban?**
It depends on the source. Kanban University defines customer lead time as the time from receiving a request to delivering it. The Kanban Guide does not define lead time and uses cycle time instead.

**Q: What is the commitment point?**
The point where the team decides it will deliver an item, usually when it is pulled into a Ready or Committed column. Before that, items are options that may be discarded. Some definitions of lead time start here.

**Q: Which is more important, lead time or cycle time?**
Neither on its own. Lead time matters most to customers because it is their wait; cycle time matters most to the team because it is what they improve directly. Tracking both shows whether delays come from the queue or the process.

**Q: What is the difference between lead time, cycle time and takt time?**
Lead time and cycle time measure how long items take. Takt time is a target rate: available working time divided by customer demand, telling you how often you must finish an item to keep up.

**Q: Is DORA lead time for changes the same as cycle time?**
No. DORA's change lead time runs from a code commit to successful deployment in production, so it covers the delivery pipeline only. Cycle time usually starts earlier, when work on the item begins.

**Q: How do lead time and cycle time relate to throughput?**
Lead time and cycle time measure how long each item takes; throughput counts items finished per period. Little's Law links them: average time in a system ≈ average items in it ÷ throughput.

**Q: Should I use calendar days or working days?**
Calendar days are usually better, especially for lead time, because customers wait through weekends. Whichever you choose, use it for both measures and say so on reports.

**Q: Does a 'lead' in project scheduling relate to lead time?**
No. A lead is a scheduling overlap that lets a successor activity start before its predecessor finishes. Lead time is a flow measure of how long a request takes to be delivered.

**Q: What is the difference between lead time and work item age?**
Lead time is measured on finished items. Work item age is how long an unfinished item has been in progress so far, so you can act on it before it turns into a long lead time.

# Cycle Time in Kanban: Formula, Examples and How to Reduce It

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Cycle time in Kanban is how long an item takes from start to finish. Learn the formula, percentiles, scatterplots and SLEs, with worked examples.


## Cycle Time in Kanban: Formula, Examples and How to Reduce It
Cycle time in Kanban is the elapsed time a work item takes from the moment the team starts it to the moment it is finished. It answers the question customers and stakeholders ask most often: once you have started, how long until it is done? This guide covers where to start and stop the clock, how to calculate cycle time, how to analyse it with percentiles and scatterplots, how to turn it into a service level expectation and how to reduce it, using a worked dataset of 20 finished items.
- Published 11 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Cycle time is elapsed time from start to finish for one item, measured between two points on your board that the team agrees and writes down.
- A common convention is finish date − start date + 1, in calendar days, so an item started and finished on the same day has a cycle time of 1 day.
- Cycle time data is usually skewed by a few long items, so percentiles (50th, 85th) describe it better than the average.
- The 85th percentile is a popular basis for a service level expectation, such as 85% of items finish within 11 days.
- Watch work item age every day: it is the live version of cycle time and warns you before an item finishes late.
- The biggest levers for reducing cycle time are lower WIP, smaller items, less waiting and faster handling of blockers.

### What is cycle time in Kanban?
**Cycle time** is the amount of elapsed time a work item spends in progress: from the point where the team starts it to the point where it is finished. It is measured per item, in calendar time, and includes all the waiting, reviewing and rework in between, not just the hours someone was actively working on it.
The Kanban Guide, written by Daniel Vacanti and John Coleman, names cycle time as one of four flow measures every Kanban system should track, alongside work in progress (WIP), [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) and work item age. Together they describe how work flows through a system. Cycle time is the one that speaks most directly to the customer, because it tells them how long they can expect to wait once their request is under way.
Two cautions on terminology:
- **Manufacturing** often uses cycle time to mean the time to complete one unit at a single process step, which is a different measure. In knowledge work it usually means the whole start-to-finish time of an item. See [lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/) for the factory meaning.
- **Kanban communities differ.** Some Kanban Method material, for example, calls the time from the commitment point to delivery lead time. The label matters less than the definition: write down where your clock starts and stops.
For the difference between the two most commonly confused measures, see [cycle time vs lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/).

### Where cycle time starts and stops
Cycle time is only meaningful when everyone agrees on the start and finish points. These are policies the team chooses and records on its board, usually as the commitment point and the delivery point.
| Start point | Finish point | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Card enters In progress | Card enters Done | Team's working process | The most common definition |
| Card enters Ready (committed) | Card is released to users | Commitment to delivery, including release | Teams with a separate deployment step |
| Card enters Development | Card enters Review | Time in one part of the process | Diagnosing a specific stage |
| Request is logged | Customer receives it | The customer's full wait (lead time) | Service levels for internal customers |
- **Pick one primary definition** and use it on every report, so trends are comparable.
- **You can track more than one cycle time**, such as one for the whole process and one for Review, as long as each is labelled.
- **Record the dates automatically if you can.** Digital tools log status changes; on a physical board, write the start and finish dates on the card. Our [Kanban cards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-cards/) guide shows a simple layout.
- **Decide what happens with items that move backwards.** Most teams keep the original start date, so rework counts as part of the item's cycle time.

### How to calculate cycle time

#### The formula
**Cycle time = finish date − start date + 1** (in days)
The + 1 is a convention, not a law. Without it, an item started and finished on the same day would have a cycle time of zero, which understates the time it took. Practitioners such as John Coleman, co-author of the Kanban Guide, recommend counting this way so that the minimum cycle time is one day. Some tools count elapsed time in hours or fractions of a day instead. Either is fine if you use it consistently and say which one you use.
**Average cycle time** = sum of the cycle times of finished items ÷ number of finished items. It is easy to calculate but, as the worked example below shows, often misleading on its own.

#### Calendar days or working days?
|  | Calendar days | Working days |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Counts weekends and holidays | Yes | No |
| Matches the customer's experience | Yes: they wait through weekends | Less so |
| Stable across holidays and part-time staff | Yes: no calendar needed | Needs a shared working calendar |
| Example: Fri 11 Sep to Tue 15 Sep | 5 days | 3 days |
| Recommended by | Most flow practitioners, for simplicity and honesty | Some teams with strict office-hours SLAs |
Our advice: use calendar days unless you have a strong reason not to. It is simpler, it is what your customers experience, and it avoids debates about which days counted.

#### Worked example: six items
Here is how the formula applies to six finished items from a product team's board, using calendar days and the + 1 convention.
| Item | Type | Started | Finished | Calculation | Cycle time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C-101 | Feature | Mon 7 Sep | Wed 9 Sep | 2 days elapsed + 1 | 3 days |
| C-102 | Bug | Thu 10 Sep | Thu 10 Sep | 0 days elapsed + 1 | 1 day |
| C-103 | Feature | Fri 11 Sep | Tue 15 Sep | 4 days elapsed + 1 | 5 days |
| C-104 | Feature | Mon 14 Sep | Mon 21 Sep | 7 days elapsed + 1 | 8 days |
| C-105 | Bug | Tue 15 Sep | Wed 16 Sep | 1 day elapsed + 1 | 2 days |
| C-106 | Feature | Thu 3 Sep | Tue 29 Sep | 26 days elapsed + 1 | 27 days |
In a spreadsheet, put start and finish dates in two columns and use a formula such as finish − start + 1 in a third. Our [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) already has Started, Finished and Cycle time (days) columns on its Cards tab.

### Cycle time vs lead time, work item age, throughput and takt time
Cycle time is easiest to use when you are clear about how it differs from its neighbours.
| Measure | What it is | Unit | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cycle time | Elapsed time from start to finish of one finished item | Days per item | Once started, how long does work take? |
| Lead time | Elapsed time from request to delivery | Days per item | How long does the customer wait in total? |
| Work item age | Elapsed time since an unfinished item started | Days per item | Which items in progress are at risk now? |
| Throughput | Number of items finished per period | Items per week | How much do we deliver? |
| WIP | Number of items started but not finished | Items | How much are we juggling? |
| Takt time | Available time ÷ customer demand | Time per item | How often must we finish an item to keep up with demand? |
Cycle time looks backwards at finished work; work item age looks at work still in progress; throughput counts rather than times.

### Worked example: analysing 20 finished items
Over five weeks in September and early October, the same team finished 20 items, including the six above. Sorted from shortest to longest, their cycle times in days were:
**1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 18, 27**
The total is 141 days, so the **average cycle time is 7.05 days**. But the middle value, the median, is only **5 days**, and 14 of the 20 items finished in 7 days or less. Two long items (18 and 27 days) pull the average up; remove the 27-day item and the average drops to 6 days. This right-skewed shape, many short items and a long tail of a few slow ones, is typical of knowledge work, and it is why flow practitioners prefer percentiles to averages.

#### Calculating percentiles step by step
A percentile tells you the cycle time within which a given share of items finished. A simple, transparent way to calculate one is the nearest-rank method:
1. Sort the cycle times from shortest to longest.
2. Multiply the number of items (n) by the percentile. For the 85th percentile with 20 items: 20 × 0.85 = 17.
3. Round up to the next whole number if the result is not whole. Here 17 is already whole.
4. Count along the sorted list to that position. The 17th value is **11 days**.
5. State it plainly: 85% of items finished in 11 days or less.
| Percentile | Position (20 items) | Cycle time | Plain-English reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 50th (median) | 10th | 5 days | Half of items finished within 5 days |
| 70th | 14th | 7 days | Seven in ten finished within a week |
| 85th | 17th | 11 days | Most items, but not the slow tail, finished within 11 days |
| 95th | 19th | 18 days | Nearly all finished within 18 days |
Spreadsheet functions such as PERCENTILE.INC interpolate between values, so they can give slightly different answers (for example 11.3 instead of 11). Either is acceptable; use the same method every time.

#### Seeing the shape with a histogram
Grouping the same data into ranges shows the distribution at a glance.
| Cycle time | Items | Share | Cumulative share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1–2 days | 3 | 15% | 15% |
| 3–4 days | 6 | 30% | 45% |
| 5–7 days | 5 | 25% | 70% |
| 8–14 days | 4 | 20% | 90% |
| 15+ days | 2 | 10% | 100% |
The peak is at 3 to 4 days, with a tail stretching to 27. When the team looked at the two items in the tail, one had waited 12 days for a decision from another department and the other had been far larger than a typical item. Both are classic causes of long cycle times, and both suggest specific fixes: escalation rules for external decisions and splitting large work before it starts.

#### Splitting by work type
| Work type | Items | Median | 85th percentile |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Features | 14 | 6 to 7 days | 13 days |
| Bugs | 6 | 2 to 3 days | 4 days |
| All items | 20 | 5 days | 11 days |
Bugs move much faster than features, so a single blended figure would mislead both. Where work types differ greatly, report cycle time separately for each, or use [swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/) for the types. With only six bugs, treat their figures as provisional until more data builds up.

### How to read a cycle time scatterplot
A cycle time scatterplot is the standard chart for this data. Each dot is one finished item: its finish date on the horizontal axis and its cycle time on the vertical axis. Horizontal lines mark percentiles, typically the 50th, 85th and 95th.
In our example, a scatterplot would show most dots clustered between 1 and 7 days, an 85th percentile line at 11 days, and two dots well above it, at 18 and 27 days. Those two are the first items to discuss at the next review.
| What you see | What it suggests | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dots clustered tightly, low on the chart | Predictable, short cycle times | Keep current policies; consider lowering WIP limits |
| A few dots far above the 85th percentile line | Outliers with a special cause | Investigate each: blockers, size, dependencies |
| Dots drifting upwards over time | Cycle times getting longer | Check whether WIP is rising; look at the cumulative flow diagram |
| Two distinct bands of dots | Two kinds of work mixed together | Split the chart by work type or class of service |
| Gaps with no dots, then many at once | Batch delivery | Release smaller batches more often |
| Wide vertical spread everywhere | Low predictability | Right-size items and limit WIP before forecasting |
| Dots creeping down after a policy change | The change is working | Mark the date on the chart and keep monitoring |
Some tools draw a rolling average and standard deviation band instead of percentiles. Jira's control chart and Azure DevOps's cycle time widget both work this way. These are useful for trends, but because cycle time data is skewed, percentiles are usually easier to use for forecasts. To see where time is going inside the process, pair the scatterplot with a [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/).

### Setting a service level expectation from cycle time
A **service level expectation (SLE)** is a forecast of how long an item should take once started, made of two parts: a period of elapsed time and a probability. The Kanban Guide describes it as based on historical cycle time and recommends making it visible as part of the team's definition of workflow.
1. **Collect at least 10 to 20 finished items** of similar type, using one consistent definition of start and finish. With less data, use a best guess and say so.
2. **Calculate the 85th percentile** (some teams use the 70th or 90th). In the example it is 11 days.
3. **Write the SLE in plain words:** 85% of items are finished within 11 days of starting.
4. **Set separate SLEs for very different work types**, for example 4 days for bugs and 13 days for features.
5. **Make it visible** on the board, for example on the column header after your commitment point.
6. **Use it every day** to spot items at risk (see work item age below), and **when someone asks when an item will be done**: once started, there is roughly an 85% chance it will be finished within 11 days.
7. **Review it every month or quarter**, or after a major process change. Use a rolling window such as the last 30 to 50 items so it reflects the current process.
Tip
An SLE is a forecast, not a promise or a target. If people are pressured to hit it, they start gaming start dates or avoiding hard items, and the data stops meaning anything.
For forecasting batches of work, such as when 40 items will be done, use throughput and Monte Carlo methods.

### Using cycle time every day: work item age
Cycle time only exists once an item is finished, so it is a lagging measure. **Work item age**, the elapsed time since an unfinished item started, is its leading counterpart and is calculated the same way: today − start date + 1.
Suppose it is Wednesday 14 October and the team has three items in progress, with an SLE of 85% within 11 days and a 70th percentile of 7 days.
| Item | Started | Age today | Against the SLE | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C-131 | Mon 5 Oct | 10 days | One day from the 85th percentile | Discuss first at the daily meeting; swarm or remove the blocker |
| C-132 | Thu 8 Oct | 7 days | At the 70th percentile | Check it is moving; ask what it needs |
| C-133 | Tue 13 Oct | 2 days | Well within | No action needed |
Reviewing age every day, oldest item first, is how teams stop a 10-day item becoming a 27-day one. A [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) shows this visually, with every in-progress item plotted by stage and age against the percentile lines. Helping finish an old item rather than starting a new one is the heart of [Agile swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/).

### Cycle time and Little's Law
Little's Law, published by John Little in 1961, links the three main flow measures:
**Average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput**
In the example, the team finished 20 items in about five weeks, roughly 4 items a week. If the board held about 4 items in progress on average, Little's Law gives an average cycle time of about 1 week, or 7 days, which agrees with the 7.05 days measured. The equation also explains why WIP limits work: if throughput stays the same and WIP halves, average cycle time roughly halves too.
The law describes averages over a period in which the system is stable: work arrives at about the rate it leaves, items that start eventually finish, and WIP is roughly the same at the start and end. Use it to understand cause and effect and to sense-check your numbers, not to forecast an individual item. For the visual version, see how to read cycle time from a [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/).

### How to reduce cycle time
Most of an item's cycle time is usually spent waiting, not being worked on. Measuring [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/), active time as a share of total time, often shows that waiting accounts for most of it. That is good news: reducing queues is usually easier than making anyone work faster.

#### Limit work in progress
Lower [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) gradually, one column at a time, and agree that when a column is full people help finish work downstream instead of starting more. Of all the levers, this one has the most direct link to cycle time through Little's Law.

#### Right-size items before they start
Large items dominate the tail of the distribution. Before committing to an item, ask whether it is likely to finish within your SLE; if not, split it into smaller pieces that each deliver something useful. Techniques for splitting [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) apply to any kind of work item.

#### Cut waiting and hand-offs
Make queues visible with split columns such as Review: waiting and Review: doing, then agree turnaround policies for them. Fewer hand-offs between people and teams mean fewer queues. A [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) of the whole process often reveals waits that nobody on the team controls.

#### Deal with blockers and ageing items quickly
Flag blocked items the moment they stop, escalate external dependencies early, and keep a record of every blocker. Over a few months, [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/) shows which causes cost the most days, so you can fix the system rather than individual cases.
| Symptom in the data | Likely cause | Action to try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long tail of very slow items | Oversized work or external dependencies | Right-size before starting; escalation policy for dependencies |
| Cycle time rising month on month | WIP creeping up | Lower WIP limits; stop starting, start finishing |
| Most time spent in one column | Bottleneck stage | Swarm, cross-train, apply the [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/) |
| Items wait days for review or approval | Queue between stages | Review-first policies; shared ownership of reviews |
| Wide spread for similar items | Inconsistent process or frequent interruptions | Explicit policies; protect focus time; classes of service |
| Items bounce back from testing | Quality issues found late | Build quality in earlier; clear Definition of Done |
Avoid the tempting shortcuts that only make the number look better: starting the clock later, closing items before they are really done, or splitting items into pieces that deliver nothing on their own.

### Measuring cycle time in project management tools
Most digital boards calculate cycle time from status history. A few notes from vendor documentation (checked 25 October 2026):
- **Jira**'s control chart plots the time each work item spent in the statuses you select, with average, rolling average and standard deviation. Choose the statuses that match your agreed start and finish points. See our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/).
- **Azure DevOps** has cycle time and lead time widgets. Microsoft defines cycle time as the time from when an item first enters an In Progress state to when it reaches Completed, and notes that reopened items keep their original start, so rework is included.
- **ClickUp** offers cycle time cards for its dashboards. See our [ClickUp review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/).
- **Spreadsheets** work for any board: record start and finish dates, calculate finish − start + 1, and use percentile functions and a scatter chart.
Whatever the tool, check that its start and finish statuses match your written policy, and whether it counts working or calendar days.

### Common cycle time mistakes
- **Relying on the average.** A few long items distort it. Report the median and 85th percentile.
- **Changing the start or finish point** without resetting the history, which makes trends meaningless.
- **Mixing very different work types** in one figure, such as bugs and large features.
- **Measuring only active time.** Cycle time is elapsed time; waiting is part of what customers experience and where most improvement lies.
- **Turning it into a target.** Pressure to hit a number leads to gaming rather than improvement.
- **Using it to compare individuals or teams.** It describes the system, not anyone's performance.
- **Looking only backwards.** Watch work item age daily so you act before items finish late.
- **Ignoring items that never finish.** Abandoned or long-stuck items disappear from cycle time statistics; review them separately.
Cycle time also feeds wider [project forecasting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/), and it is one of the topics covered in our review meetings guide for [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/).
