### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a good cycle time?**
There is no universal figure, because it depends on the size and type of work. What matters is that cycle time is short enough for your customers, predictable (a narrow spread) and stable or improving over time. Compare your own trend, not other teams.

**Q: Is cycle time the same as lead time?**
No. Lead time usually starts when the request is made, while cycle time starts when work begins, so cycle time is part of lead time. Some communities use the terms differently, so always define the start and finish points. See [cycle time vs lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/).

**Q: How do you calculate average cycle time?**
Add the cycle times of all finished items in a period and divide by the number of items. For example, 20 items totalling 141 days give an average of 7.05 days. Report the median and 85th percentile alongside it, because averages are skewed by a few long items.

**Q: Why do some teams add one day to cycle time?**
So that an item started and finished on the same day counts as 1 day rather than 0. It is a counting convention recommended by several flow practitioners; whichever you choose, apply it consistently.

**Q: Should weekends count in cycle time?**
Most flow practitioners recommend calendar days, including weekends, because that is what customers experience and it avoids maintaining a working calendar. Working days are acceptable if you apply them consistently and say so.

**Q: What is the 85th percentile cycle time?**
It is the cycle time within which 85% of past items finished. With 20 items sorted from shortest to longest, it is the 17th value. Teams often use it as a [service level expectation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/).

**Q: Why use percentiles rather than the average?**
Cycle time data usually has a long tail of slow items, so the average sits above what most items actually take. Percentiles give a plain-English statement, such as 85% within 11 days, that people can plan with.

**Q: How many items do you need before cycle time data is useful?**
You can start learning from about 10 items, and 20 to 30 give a reasonably stable picture. Keep using a rolling window of recent items so the figures reflect your current process.

**Q: What is the difference between cycle time and takt time?**
Cycle time is how long items actually take. Takt time is the pace needed to meet demand: available time divided by the number of items customers need. It comes from [lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/).

**Q: Does blocked time count in cycle time?**
Yes. Cycle time is elapsed time from start to finish, so time spent blocked or waiting is included. That is deliberate: blocked time is one of the main things teams can reduce.

**Q: What happens to cycle time when an item moves backwards?**
Most teams and tools keep the original start date, so the rework counts towards the item's cycle time. Azure DevOps, for example, documents this behaviour for reactivated items.

**Q: Should cycle time be used to measure individual performance?**
No. Cycle time reflects the whole system, including queues, dependencies and policies that individuals do not control. Using it to judge people encourages gaming and hides problems.

**Q: Can Scrum teams use cycle time?**
Yes. Many Scrum teams track cycle time for backlog items within and across sprints, and Scrum.org publishes the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams for exactly this. It helps reveal items that are too large to finish comfortably within a sprint.

**Q: How do you show cycle time on a Kanban board?**
Write the start date on each card and the finish date when it reaches Done, or let your tool record status changes. Show the SLE on the board and highlight cards whose age is approaching it. See [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/).

# What Is DevOps? Culture, Practices and Metrics

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: DevOps explained: its origins, the CALMS model, the Three Ways, key practices, DORA metrics, and how DevOps connects to Lean, Agile and Kanban.


## What Is DevOps? Culture, Practices and Metrics
DevOps is a set of cultural values, practices and tools that bring software development and IT operations together, so teams can deliver changes quickly and reliably. It extends Agile and Lean thinking across the whole path from code to customer.
- Published 19 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- DevOps unites development and operations around shared goals.
- CALMS and the Three Ways summarise its principles.
- Measure it with deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore.

### Origins
The term DevOps emerged around 2009, when Patrick Debois organised the first DevOpsDays conference in Ghent, Belgium. It grew from frustration with the wall between developers, who wanted change, and operations, who wanted stability.

### The CALMS model
| Element | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Culture | Shared responsibility and collaboration between development and operations |
| Automation | Automate builds, tests, infrastructure and deployments |
| Lean | Small batches, limited WIP, focus on flow |
| Measurement | Measure flow, quality and user outcomes |
| Sharing | Share knowledge, tools and lessons learned |

### The Three Ways
Popularised by The Phoenix Project and The DevOps Handbook:
1. **Flow:** speed up the flow of work from development to operations to the customer.
2. **Feedback:** create fast feedback from operations and users back to development.
3. **Continual learning and experimentation:** build a culture that learns from failure and improves.

### Key practices
- [Continuous integration and continuous delivery](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/continuous-delivery/).
- Infrastructure as code.
- Automated testing and monitoring.
- Small, frequent releases with feature flags.
- Teams that build and run their own services.
- Blameless post-incident reviews.

### Measuring DevOps performance
The DORA research programme popularised four key measures of software delivery:
- **Deployment frequency:** how often you release.
- **Lead time for changes:** from commit to production.
- **Change failure rate:** share of releases causing problems.
- **Time to restore service:** how quickly you recover from failure.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is DevOps a role or a culture?**
Primarily a culture and set of practices. Many organisations also have "DevOps engineer" roles focused on automation and tooling.

**Q: How does DevOps relate to Kanban?**
Both focus on flow, small batches and visibility. Many operations and platform teams use Kanban to manage their work.

**Q: What is DevOps in simple terms?**
DevOps is a way of working that brings software development and IT operations together, so teams can build, release and run software faster and more reliably.

**Q: When did DevOps start?**
The term emerged around 2009, when Patrick Debois organised the first DevOpsDays conference in Ghent, Belgium.

**Q: What does CALMS stand for in DevOps?**
Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement and Sharing: a model summarising the main elements of DevOps.

**Q: What are the four DORA metrics in DevOps?**
Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. They measure both speed and stability of software delivery.

**Q: What are the Three Ways of DevOps?**
Flow from development to operations, fast feedback in both directions, and a culture of continual learning and experimentation.

**Q: Is DevOps part of Agile?**
DevOps extends Agile ideas beyond development into release and operations. Agile speeds up building software; DevOps speeds up getting it safely to users.

**Q: What is the difference between DevOps and continuous delivery?**
Continuous delivery is a specific technical practice for keeping software releasable. DevOps is the broader culture and set of practices, of which continuous delivery is a key part; see [continuous delivery](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/continuous-delivery/).

**Q: What does a DevOps engineer do?**
A DevOps engineer usually builds and maintains deployment pipelines, infrastructure automation and monitoring, helping development and operations teams work together.

**Q: What is a blameless post-incident review in DevOps?**
A review after an outage that focuses on what in the system allowed the problem to happen, rather than who to blame, so people share information openly and the team learns.

# Flow Efficiency: Formula, Examples and How to Improve It

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Flow efficiency explained: the formula, worked examples, how to measure active and wait time on a Kanban board, what a good figure is and how to improve it.


## Flow Efficiency: Formula, Examples and How to Improve It
Flow efficiency is the percentage of an item's total time in your process that is spent actively working on it, rather than waiting in queues, for approvals or behind blockers. When teams measure it for the first time, they usually find that most of the delay comes from waiting, not from slow work, which means the quickest gains come from managing queues rather than asking people to work harder. This guide gives you the formula, two worked calculations, a step-by-step way to measure it on a Kanban board and the practical levers that raise it.
- Published 13 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Flow efficiency = active work time ÷ total time in process × 100%. If an item takes 20 days and someone works on it for 6 of them, flow efficiency is 30%.
- It measures how continuously work moves, not how busy people are. Pushing resource utilisation towards 100% usually lowers flow efficiency because queues grow.
- To measure it, split your board into active and waiting columns, agree what counts as active, track blocked time and calculate it from card timestamps.
- There is no validated industry benchmark. Commonly quoted ranges are anecdotal, so set your own baseline and track the trend and the spread.
- The biggest levers are lower WIP limits, faster pick-up of reviews and approvals, fewer handoffs, smaller items and removing recurring blockers.
- Use flow efficiency to find where work waits and improve the system, never to rate individuals or compare unlike teams.

### What is flow efficiency?
**Flow efficiency** is a flow metric that compares the time a work item is actively being worked on with the total time it spends in the process from start to finish. It is expressed as a percentage. A low figure means items spend most of their life waiting in queues, for decisions or behind blockers rather than being progressed.
Picture it by watching the work item, not the people. Follow one feature, contract or design request from start to done and note when anyone is actually touching it. Everything else is waiting.
The idea comes from Lean thinking, where the same ratio is often called the value-added ratio or, in Lean Six Sigma, **process cycle efficiency**. Niklas Modig and Pär Åhlström's book *This Is Lean: Resolving the Efficiency Paradox* (2012) made the contrast between flow efficiency and resource efficiency widely known, and Kanban practitioners adopted flow efficiency as a way to show how much time work spends in queues.
In Kanban it is a supporting metric rather than a core one. The Kanban Guide (2025 edition) names four measures every Kanban system should track: work in progress, throughput, work item age and [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/). Flow efficiency sits alongside them, as our guide to [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) explains, and is most useful for diagnosing where time is lost.

### The flow efficiency formula
The calculation is simple:
**Flow efficiency = active work time ÷ total time in process × 100%**
Total time in process is the sum of active time and everything that is not active: waiting time and blocked time. So you can also write it as active time ÷ (active time + wait time + blocked time).
| Term | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Active time (touch time) | Someone is working on the item | Writing, designing, coding, testing, reviewing |
| Wait time | Expected time in a queue | Ready for review, awaiting a scheduled release |
| Blocked time | Unexpected time the item cannot progress | Waiting for client content or an absent approver |
| Total time in process | Elapsed time from agreed start to agreed end | Usually cycle time; sometimes lead time |

#### Cycle time or lead time as the denominator?
Most Kanban teams use **cycle time** (start to finish), the part of the process the team controls. Value stream analyses often use **lead time** (request to delivery), which adds backlog waiting, so the result is lower and closer to the customer's experience. Both are valid; choose one and stay consistent. Our guide to [cycle time vs lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/) explains where each one starts and stops.

#### Item-level vs aggregate flow efficiency
You can calculate flow efficiency for a single item, or for a set of items completed in a period. For a set, there are two methods:
- **Aggregate:** add up all the active time and divide by all the total time. This weights long-running items more heavily, which reflects where most of the elapsed time actually went.
- **Average of percentages:** calculate each item's percentage and take the mean. This treats every item equally, so a few long, slow items have less influence.
The two can differ noticeably, as the team example below shows. The aggregate is generally the better guide to the system; whichever you choose, use it every time.

### Worked example: calculating flow efficiency for one item
This illustrative example follows one card, a landing page update, across a marketing team's board. The request sat in the backlog for 5 working days before anyone started it. The table shows how the next 20 working days were spent.
| Stage on the board | Working days | Type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analyse: in progress | 1 | Active |
| Analysed, waiting for design | 2 | Wait |
| Design: in progress | 2 | Active |
| Design: blocked, waiting for brand assets | 3 | Blocked |
| Designed, waiting for build | 2 | Wait |
| Build: in progress | 2 | Active |
| Ready for review | 4 | Wait |
| Review: in progress | 1 | Active |
| Approved, waiting for scheduled release | 3 | Wait |
| **Total** | **20** | **6 active, 11 waiting, 3 blocked** |
Work through the calculation step by step:
1. Add up the active days: 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = **6 days**.
2. Add up all days from start to finish to get the cycle time: **20 days**.
3. Divide active time by cycle time: 6 ÷ 20 = 0.30, so flow efficiency is **30%** on a cycle-time basis.
4. For lead time, add the 5 days the request waited in the backlog: 5 + 20 = 25 days. Flow efficiency on a lead-time basis is 6 ÷ 25 = **24%**.
5. Rank the waits from longest to shortest: Ready for review (4 days), Design blocked (3), waiting for release (3), then two 2-day handoffs.
Step 5 matters more than the percentage. If everyone worked twice as fast, the item would still take 17 days (3 active plus 14 waiting or blocked). Cutting the review queue to one day and the release wait to zero would bring cycle time to 13 days with no extra effort, lifting flow efficiency to about 46%.
Tip
Working days or calendar days? Either works, as long as you use the same unit for active and total time. Working days are easier for teams to reason about; calendar days match what customers experience.

### Worked example: flow efficiency for a team
Now take five items the same team finished in a month (illustrative figures, cycle-time basis):
| Item | Active days | Cycle time (days) | Item flow efficiency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 2 | 10 | 20% |
| B | 6 | 12 | 50% |
| C | 1 | 20 | 5% |
| D | 3 | 8 | 37.5% |
| E | 4 | 30 | 13.3% |
| **Total** | **16** | **80** |  |
- **Aggregate flow efficiency:** 16 ÷ 80 = **20%**.
- **Average of item percentages:** (20 + 50 + 5 + 37.5 + 13.3) ÷ 5 = **25.2%**.
The aggregate is lower because items C and E took 50 of the 80 days and were mostly waiting. That is the discussion to have: why did C, one day of work, take four weeks? Usually the answer is a long queue, a dependency on another team or a blocker nobody owned. The spread of individual values, not one summary number, is what turns flow efficiency into action.

### Flow efficiency vs resource efficiency
**Resource efficiency** (often called utilisation) measures how much of the available time people or machines are busy. **Flow efficiency** measures how much of the work item's time is spent being progressed. The two pull in opposite directions. If every person must be busy all the time, work has to queue in front of them so that nobody runs out of something to do, and queued work is waiting work.
Modig and Åhlström describe this as the efficiency paradox and summarise the trade-off in an efficiency matrix:
| State | Resource efficiency | Flow efficiency | What it looks like |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Efficient islands | High | Low | Every team is busy, but items wait between them and take a long time overall |
| Efficient ocean | Lower | High | Some spare capacity is kept so work moves quickly when it arrives |
| Wasteland | Low | Low | People are not busy and work still waits, often because of poor coordination |
| Perfect state | High | High | Only reachable with highly predictable demand and work, so rarely achievable in practice |
Queueing theory explains why. In a simple single-server queueing model with random arrivals and work times, the average time an item spends waiting relative to the time it takes to do grows sharply as utilisation rises. The table below uses that simplified model to show the effect at one step:
| Utilisation of the person or step | Average wait as a multiple of work time | Flow efficiency at that step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 50% | 1× | 50% |
| 70% | About 2.3× | 30% |
| 80% | 4× | 20% |
| 90% | 9× | 10% |
| 95% | 19× | 5% |
Real processes are messier, but the shape holds. That is why the [theory of constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/) deliberately keeps spare capacity at non-bottleneck steps, and why a [pull system](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/) with WIP limits usually beats pushing work in as fast as it arrives. If you plan team workloads, our guide to [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) explains how to leave room for flow.

### Flow efficiency vs cycle time, lead time and other metrics
Flow efficiency explains other flow metrics rather than replacing them. Use it alongside them:
| Metric | Question it answers | Link to flow efficiency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cycle time | How long does an item take once started? | Usually the denominator |
| Lead time | How long does the customer wait? | Alternative denominator, including backlog waiting |
| Throughput | How much do we deliver? | Better flow usually shortens cycle time rather than raising throughput |
| Work in progress (WIP) | Are we overloaded? | Too much WIP is the most common cause of low flow efficiency |
| Work item age | What is stuck right now? | The live warning; flow efficiency is the after-the-fact view |
The link to cycle time comes through Little's Law: average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput. If WIP falls while throughput holds, cycle time falls, and because the active time per item has not changed, flow efficiency rises. Our guides to [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) and the [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) show how to read the related measures.

### What is a good flow efficiency?
There is no validated industry benchmark, so be wary of any article that gives one as fact. Figures are widely quoted in the Kanban community, such as single-digit percentages being common in knowledge work and around 40% being very good, but these are usually attributed to practitioners' experience (often to Kanban Method pioneer David J. Anderson) rather than to published studies.
One of the few published data sets comes from an Agile coach at the online retailer ASOS, who reported in 2023 that across 63 teams in his organisation, team-level flow efficiency averaged 35%, with values from 9% to 68%. That is one organisation measured one way, not a benchmark, but it shows how widely results vary with how you define active and waiting states.
In practice, a useful target has three parts:
1. **A baseline**, measured over a few weeks of completed items with a clearly written definition of active time.
2. **A direction**, such as raising aggregate flow efficiency by cutting the two longest waits, rather than a fixed percentage.
3. **A check on the spread**, so the slowest items, not just the average, are getting better.
Tip
If your first measurement comes out above 60% or 70%, check your board before celebrating. A process with few or no waiting columns will look highly efficient simply because waiting is hidden inside active columns.

### How to measure flow efficiency step by step
You can measure flow efficiency with a digital board or a physical one. These steps work for both:
1. **Agree the boundaries.** Decide where the clock starts (usually the first in-progress column) and stops (done or delivered), and whether you use cycle time or lead time.
2. **Split each stage into doing and done.** A "done" or "ready for next" column makes finished-but-waiting work visible as waiting.
3. **Write a policy for what counts as active**, for example "someone is working on it today", and put it on the board.
4. **Track blocked time separately** with a blocker flag. Blocked time is non-active even if the card sits in a doing column.
5. **Capture timestamps.** Digital tools record column moves; on a physical board, date the card each time it moves.
6. **Calculate per item, then for the period**, using the aggregate method.
7. **Find the longest waits.** List the stages with the most waiting time and pick one to improve.
8. **Review regularly**, every few weeks, alongside cycle time and throughput.

#### Designing a board that shows waiting
Here is an illustrative board layout with each column labelled for measurement purposes:
| Column | Counts as | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backlog / Options | Outside cycle time | Counts only if you measure lead time |
| Ready to start | Wait | A small committed queue; limit it |
| Build: doing | Active | WIP-limited |
| Build: done | Wait | Finished but not yet pulled by review |
| Review: doing | Active | WIP-limited |
| Ready for release | Wait | Often a long queue if releases are batched |
| Done | Clock stops | End of cycle time |
Our guide to [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) covers board design in more detail, and the free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) gives you columns and WIP limits you can adapt to this structure.

#### Measuring without a digital tool
If your tool cannot calculate flow efficiency, sample instead. Take 15 to 30 recently finished items, reconstruct their dates from cards, comments or emails, and ask the people involved roughly how many days of hands-on work each needed. Approximate figures are enough to find the biggest queues. A lighter option is to add a dot to a card at the end of each day it was actively worked on: dots ÷ days in progress gives a quick figure.

#### Flow efficiency in a value stream map
A [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) records process time and wait time for every step from request to delivery, so total process time ÷ total lead time gives flow efficiency across teams and departments. You can sketch the steps first with our free [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/).

### Why flow efficiency is often low
Low flow efficiency is normal in knowledge work, and the causes are usually structural rather than individual. The table lists the common ones:
| Cause | What you see on the board | Typical fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Too much work in progress | Many cards in every column; people switching between items | Lower WIP limits; stop starting, start finishing |
| Queues before reviews and approvals | "Ready for review" or "Awaiting sign-off" columns full | Review pick-up policies; more reviewers; smaller review batches |
| Handoffs between specialists | Cards wait in a done column for the next person | Cross-skilling; pairing; fewer stages |
| Dependencies on other teams | Cards blocked waiting for another team's work | Agree service levels with the other team; restructure ownership |
| Batched releases | Finished items pile up before a scheduled release | Release more often; automate deployment |
| Recurring blockers | Same blocker reasons appear again and again | Analyse and remove root causes |
Most of these are policy choices, and changing them is usually cheaper than hiring or asking people to work faster.

### How to improve flow efficiency
Start with the longest waits you found when measuring, then work through these levers in roughly this order.

#### 1. Limit work in progress
With fewer items in the system, each spends less time queued behind others. Lower [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) a step at a time and watch cycle time and blocked items.

#### 2. Shrink the queues before reviews and approvals
These are often the largest waits. Agree explicit policies, such as "pick up reviews before starting new work" or "approvals within one working day", give the queue its own WIP limit, and delegate approval of low-risk items.

#### 3. Reduce handoffs and dependencies
Every handoff creates a queue. Bring the needed skills into the team, pair specialists and merge stages one person could carry through. For other teams, agree turnaround times and track breaches as blockers.

#### 4. Make work items smaller
Small items move faster, get reviewed sooner and are blocked less often. Split work into slices that can each be finished on their own; our guide to [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) shows how to slice work for software and non-software teams.

#### 5. Remove recurring blockers
Record why items are blocked, group the reasons and tackle the most frequent or most costly cause first. [Blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/) is a simple workshop technique for this, and a [root cause analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) helps you dig into the biggest cluster.

#### 6. Swarm on the oldest items
When an item is ageing or blocked, have people with spare capacity help finish it rather than start something new. [Swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/) trades some individual utilisation for much faster flow, which is exactly the trade flow efficiency rewards.

#### 7. Pace intake to the bottleneck
Work always queues in front of the slowest stage, so release new work at the pace it can absorb and improve it first. The [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) shows this as a band that keeps widening.
See our guide to [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) for how to set and adjust the limits that drive most of these gains.

### Worked example: improving a team's flow efficiency
This illustrative example follows a six-person product team that finishes about 6 items a week. When they start measuring, there are about 24 items in progress and each item needs around 3 days of active work.
1. **Baseline.** Using Little's Law, average cycle time = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 weeks, or 20 working days. Flow efficiency = 3 ÷ 20 = **15%**.
2. **Diagnosis.** Measuring waiting by column shows the longest queue is "Ready for review" (about 6 days on average), followed by items blocked waiting for another team's data feed.
3. **Change 1: WIP limits.** The team sets WIP limits that bring total WIP down to about 12 items over three weeks, by finishing work before pulling more.
4. **Change 2: review policy.** Developers agree to pick up review requests before starting anything new, and the review column gets a WIP limit of 3.
5. **Change 3: dependency.** The team agrees a two-day turnaround with the data team and flags anything older as blocked in the daily meeting.
6. **Result.** Throughput stays at about 6 items a week, so cycle time = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 weeks, or 10 working days. Active time is still about 3 days, so flow efficiency = 3 ÷ 10 = **30%**.
| Measure | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work in progress | About 24 items | About 12 items |
| Throughput | About 6 items/week | About 6 items/week |
| Average cycle time | 4 weeks (20 working days) | 2 weeks (10 working days) |
| Active time per item | About 3 days | About 3 days |
| Flow efficiency | 15% | 30% |
Nobody worked faster. The team started less, so items waited less and customers got their work in half the time.

### Limitations of flow efficiency
Flow efficiency is a useful diagnostic, but it has real weaknesses that you should be honest about when you report it:
- **It depends on your board.** A workflow with no waiting columns always shows 100%. The figure measures how you model the process as much as the process itself.
- **Active time is fuzzy**, and items often sit blocked in a doing column, inflating active time unless blockers are flagged.
- **Averages hide the story.** A single percentage can mask the handful of very slow items that matter most.
- **It does not compare well across teams.** Different definitions, work types and board designs make cross-team comparisons misleading.
- **It can be gamed.** Removing waiting columns, moving cards late or splitting items artificially can all raise the number without improving delivery.
Treat flow efficiency as a conversation starter about where work waits, confirm with cycle time and blocker data, and never make it an individual target.

### Common flow efficiency mistakes
- **Treating it as a productivity measure for people.** It measures the system. Using it to judge individuals encourages people to look busy, which lowers flow.
- **Chasing utilisation at the same time.** You cannot keep everyone 100% busy and have work flow quickly. Accept some slack.
- **Changing definitions mid-stream**, which breaks the trend.
- **Fixing the work instead of the waits.** Training people to work faster rarely helps when most of the time is queueing.
- **Comparing teams on a league table.** Use each team's own trend instead.

### Tools and templates for tracking flow efficiency
Any board that records when cards change column can supply the data. Look for separate active and waiting stages, blocker flags and time-in-status reporting.
- **Wrike** (our top-rated tool) builds boards on custom statuses, so you can create separate doing and waiting stages for each step, and its dashboards show where work is piling up across projects. See our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).
- **Jira** is popular with software teams and includes cumulative flow diagrams and control charts for cycle time, which help you spot the stages where items wait. See our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/).
- **Dedicated Kanban analytics tools**, such as Businessmap, include ready-made flow efficiency charts if you want the calculation done for you.
If you are starting on paper or in a spreadsheet, the free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) gives you a board with WIP limits, and the [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/) helps you map each step, owner and handoff before you decide which columns count as waiting.
For the wider Lean context, see [Lean Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-kanban/) and [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/).
Read our guide to [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) to see how flow efficiency fits with WIP, cycle time, throughput and work item age.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is flow efficiency?**
Flow efficiency is the share of an item's total time in process that is spent actively working on it, rather than waiting in queues, for approvals or behind blockers. It is expressed as a percentage.

**Q: How do you calculate flow efficiency?**
Divide active work time by total time in process and multiply by 100. For example, 6 active days in a 20-day cycle time gives 6 ÷ 20 = 30%.

**Q: What is a good flow efficiency?**
There is no validated benchmark. Figures such as 40% being very good are widely quoted but anecdotal. Measure your own baseline, then aim to improve the trend and reduce the slowest items.

**Q: Is flow efficiency the same as resource utilisation?**
No. Utilisation measures how busy people are; flow efficiency measures how continuously work moves. Pushing utilisation close to 100% usually lowers flow efficiency because queues grow.

**Q: What is the difference between flow efficiency and cycle time?**
Cycle time is the total elapsed time to finish an item once started. Flow efficiency shows what proportion of that time was active work, so it explains why cycle time is long.

**Q: Should blocked time count as active time?**
No. Blocked time is time the item cannot progress, so count it as non-active, even if the card sits in a doing column, and record the blocker's cause.

**Q: Is flow efficiency an official Kanban metric?**
It is widely used by Kanban practitioners, but the Kanban Guide's four required measures are WIP, throughput, work item age and cycle time. Flow efficiency is a supporting, diagnostic metric.

**Q: What is the difference between flow efficiency and process cycle efficiency?**
They measure the same ratio of value-adding or active time to total time. Process cycle efficiency is the Lean Six Sigma name; flow efficiency is the term most Kanban teams use.

**Q: How do you improve flow efficiency?**
Lower WIP, shrink review and approval queues, reduce handoffs and dependencies, split work into smaller items, remove recurring blockers and swarm on ageing items. Start with the longest wait.

**Q: Can you compare flow efficiency between teams?**
Not reliably. Teams define active and waiting states differently and do different work. Compare each team with its own baseline instead.

**Q: Does value stream mapping measure flow efficiency?**
Yes. A value stream map records process time and wait time at each step, and total process time divided by total lead time gives flow efficiency across the whole value stream.

# Just-in-Time (JIT): How It Works, Examples, Pros and Cons

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/just-in-time-jit/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Just-in-Time (JIT) explained: how pull, takt time and kanban work, a worked cost example, pros and cons, JIT vs just-in-case and JIT in projects.


## Just-in-Time (JIT): How It Works, Examples, Pros and Cons
Just-in-Time (JIT) is a way of running operations so that each process makes or receives only what is needed, when it is needed and in the amount needed. Toyota uses those words to describe it, and it is one of the two pillars of the Toyota Production System. This guide explains how JIT works, works through takt time and delivery-cost examples, sets out the benefits and risks, and shows how JIT thinking applies to projects.
- Published 16 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- JIT means making or delivering only what the next step needs, when it needs it and in the amount it needs, so production is triggered by real demand rather than forecasts.
- It rests on pull, takt time, continuous flow and level scheduling, held together by kanban signals, small batches, quick changeovers and built-in quality.
- Ordering more often without making each delivery cheaper usually costs more. JIT works as a whole system, not as a purchasing policy.
- The main risk is fragility: with little buffer, a supplier failure or demand spike stops the line. Most firms now keep targeted buffers for critical, hard-to-source items.
- Start with stability (quality, reliable equipment and suppliers, levelled demand), then reduce inventory step by step.
- In projects, JIT becomes just-in-time planning, backlog refinement just before work starts, WIP limits and material deliveries timed to the programme.

### What is Just-in-Time (JIT)?
**Just-in-Time (JIT)** is an operations approach in which materials, parts and products are made or delivered only when the next process or the customer needs them, in exactly the quantity needed. Production is pulled by actual demand rather than pushed by forecasts. This keeps inventory low, exposes problems quickly and shortens the time from order to delivery.
The term covers three closely related ideas, and it helps to keep them apart:
- **JIT production (or manufacturing):** each process makes only what the downstream process has used. This is the original Toyota meaning.
- **JIT inventory:** a stock policy that keeps raw materials, work in progress and finished goods to a minimum, replenished as they are consumed.
- **JIT delivery:** suppliers deliver small quantities frequently, sometimes in the exact sequence the line will use them.
Two misunderstandings are common. JIT does **not** mean zero inventory: a JIT plant holds small, deliberate stocks (in supermarkets, kanban containers and buffers) sized to the time it takes to replenish them. And JIT is **not** simply ordering more often. Without the supporting practices described below, more frequent ordering usually raises costs, as the worked example later in this guide shows.

### Where JIT came from
JIT grew out of Toyota's search for a way to build cars efficiently in small volumes in post-war Japan, when the company could not afford the large inventories of American mass production. Toyota's own account credits these people:
| Who or what | Contribution | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sakichi Toyoda (1867–1930) | Invented automatic looms that stopped when a thread broke, the origin of jidoka ("automation with a human touch") | Weft-breakage stopping device 1896; Type-G automatic loom 1924 |
| Kiichiro Toyoda (1894–1952) | Advocated Just-in-Time and introduced flow production with a chain conveyor; the approach was applied to body assembly at the Koromo (now Honsha) Plant | Plant completed 1938 |
| Taiichi Ohno | Turned JIT and jidoka into a working production system through years of trial and error, later documented as the Toyota Production System | Late 1940s onwards |
| The "supermarket method" | Inspired by how supermarkets restock only what customers take; it evolved into the kanban system once a production instruction was added | Introduced 1954 |
| Roll-out | Whole Honsha Plant in the late 1950s, all Toyota plants from 1960, Toyota Group suppliers from the late 1960s | 1950s–1980s |
Western manufacturers studied the approach from the 1970s and 1980s, and researchers later used the term **Lean** to describe it. Today JIT is treated as one part of [Lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/), alongside jidoka, standard work and kaizen.
Tip
Toyota describes the Toyota Production System as resting on two pillars: Just-in-Time and jidoka. JIT without jidoka (stopping to fix problems at source) tends to fail, because low stock leaves no room for defects.

### The building blocks of JIT
The Lean Enterprise Institute describes JIT as built on heijunka (level scheduling), with three operating elements: the pull system, takt time and continuous flow. In practice several supporting practices make those elements possible.
| Element | What it means | Practical example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pull | A process makes or moves something only when the next process has used it | An empty container returning to the paint shop authorises it to paint 20 more panels |
| Takt time | The pace of customer demand: available time divided by units demanded | A takt of 60 seconds means one finished unit should leave the line every minute |
| Continuous flow | Items move one (or a few) at a time between steps without waiting in piles | Machining, washing and inspection placed side by side in a cell |
| Heijunka (levelling) | Smooth the mix and volume of production over time instead of building in large runs | Build A-B-A-C-A-B each hour rather than all As on Monday |
| Kanban | Cards, bins or electronic signals that carry the pull instruction | A two-bin system for fasteners at each workstation |
| Small lots and quick changeovers | Reduce set-up times so small batches are economical | Cutting a die change from 60 minutes to 9 minutes |
| Jidoka and quality at source | Stop and fix defects immediately so bad parts do not flow on | An operator pulls an andon cord when a fault appears |
| Supplier partnership | Few, reliable, often nearby suppliers delivering small quantities frequently | Daily deliveries timed to shift patterns |
| Standard work and kaizen | A documented best way to do each job, improved continuously | Weekly improvement on the biggest source of waiting |

#### Takt time, with a worked example
Takt time sets the heartbeat of a JIT system. The formula is: **takt time = available working time ÷ customer demand in the same period.**
1. Work out available time. A plant runs two 8-hour shifts (480 minutes each). Each shift has a 30-minute meal break and two 10-minute breaks, leaving 430 minutes. Two shifts give 860 minutes, or 51,600 seconds, a day.
2. Work out demand. Customers order an average of 860 units a day.
3. Divide: 51,600 ÷ 860 = **60 seconds**. The line should complete one unit every minute, no faster and no slower.
4. Balance the work. If the total work content per unit is 6 minutes, you need about 6 operators (6 minutes ÷ 1-minute takt), each with roughly 60 seconds of work.
5. Recalculate when demand changes. If demand falls to 645 units a day, takt rises to 80 seconds (51,600 ÷ 645) and you rebalance the line with fewer people, instead of building stock nobody has ordered.
Producing faster than takt creates overproduction, which Ohno counted as the worst of the seven wastes because it hides all the others. Producing slower than takt means you will miss demand.

#### Pull and kanban signals
Pull is what makes JIT self-regulating. A downstream step uses parts, and the empty container or card goes back upstream as an instruction to replace exactly what was used. No card, no production. Our guides to [pull vs push systems](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/) and [kanban inventory management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-inventory-management/) explain the mechanics and show how to calculate the number of kanbans.

#### Small batches and quick changeovers
Large batches are economical only when changing over is slow. If a press takes an hour to change dies, you run thousands of parts between changes and store them. Reduce the changeover to a few minutes (the approach known as SMED, single-minute exchange of die) and small batches become affordable. Inventory then falls without any loss of capacity. This is why JIT programmes usually start on the shop floor, not in the purchasing department.

### How a JIT system works, step by step
Here is one customer order travelling through a simple JIT system, from the order back to the supplier:
1. **A customer order arrives** and joins a levelled production schedule (heijunka). Only the final assembly line receives a schedule; no other process is scheduled centrally.
2. **Final assembly builds at takt**, taking parts from small containers at each station.
3. **A container empties.** Its withdrawal kanban goes to the parts supermarket, the small controlled store that feeds the line.
4. **A material handler collects a full container** from the supermarket on a fixed route and delivers it to the line. The production kanban from that container is placed in the producing cell's queue.
5. **The upstream cell makes exactly one container's worth**, in the order the kanbans arrived, and puts it back in the supermarket.
6. **That cell's own parts are consumed**, sending kanbans further upstream, and eventually supplier kanbans go to external suppliers.
7. **Suppliers deliver small quantities frequently**, often on a milk run (one truck collecting from several suppliers on a fixed loop).
8. **Problems stop the flow visibly.** A defect, a breakdown or a missing part shows up within minutes, because there is little stock to cover it, and the team fixes the root cause.
The key point is that information flows upstream in small, frequent signals, and material flows downstream in small, frequent movements. A [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) is the standard way to draw both flows and see where JIT is breaking down.

### Worked example: the true cost of more frequent deliveries
Many organisations try to "go JIT" by asking suppliers to deliver more often. The numbers show why that alone rarely works. The figures below are illustrative.
A part costs £5. Annual usage is 48,000 units (4,000 a month). Holding inventory costs 25% of its value a year (capital, space, insurance, handling, obsolescence). Each delivery costs £60 to arrange, ship and receive. Average stock is roughly half the delivery quantity.
| Scenario | Delivery size | Average stock (value) | Annual holding cost | Deliveries a year × cost | Total annual cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A. Monthly deliveries | 4,000 | 2,000 units (£10,000) | £2,500 | 12 × £60 = £720 | **£3,220** |
| B. Weekly deliveries, same delivery cost | about 923 | about 462 units (£2,308) | £577 | 52 × £60 = £3,120 | **£3,697** |
| C. Weekly milk run shared with other suppliers | about 923 | about 462 units (£2,308) | £577 | 52 × £20 = £1,040 | **£1,617** |
- **Scenario B is more expensive than A.** Inventory fell by 77%, but delivery costs more than quadrupled. This is the classic economic order quantity trade-off.
- **Scenario C cuts the total by about half** because the cost of each delivery fell. That is what JIT practices do: milk runs, standard containers, simple call-offs, supplier agreements and quicker receiving.
- **The hidden benefits are not in the table.** Less stock also frees floor space, reduces damage and obsolescence, and exposes quality problems sooner. These are real but harder to price.
Tip
Before asking for more frequent deliveries, cut the cost of each one. Combine suppliers into milk runs, standardise containers and simplify the call-off. The same logic applies inside the plant: reduce set-up time before you reduce batch size.

### Benefits of Just-in-Time
| Benefit | Why it happens |
| --- | --- |
| Lower inventory and carrying costs | Less raw material, work in progress and finished stock tied up in cash, space and insurance |
| Less waste and obsolescence | Fewer parts expire, get damaged or become redundant after a design change |
| Problems surface quickly | With little buffer, defects and breakdowns stop flow and must be fixed at the root |
| Shorter lead times | Small batches move through the process faster; see [cycle time vs lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/) |
| Better responsiveness | The schedule follows real demand, so product mix changes are absorbed faster |
| Higher quality | Small lots mean fewer bad parts made before a problem is spotted |
| More usable floor space | Space once used for storage can host new lines or cells |
| Stronger supplier relationships | Long-term partnerships replace transactional, price-only buying |
Lean practitioners often describe inventory as water in a river and problems as rocks. A high water level hides the rocks. Lowering the water (inventory) reveals them so they can be removed. This is why JIT is an improvement system as much as an inventory policy: each reduction in stock exposes the next problem to solve.

### Disadvantages and risks of JIT
The same low buffers that expose problems also leave the system with little protection when something goes wrong.
| Risk | What happens | How to reduce it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Supplier failure | A single late or failed delivery can stop production within hours | Dual sourcing for critical parts, supplier development, strategic buffers |
| Demand spikes | Stock-outs and missed orders when demand jumps beyond buffer capacity | Levelled scheduling, finished-goods buffer for volatile lines, capacity flex |
| Transport disruption | Weather, strikes, port congestion or border delays break frequent delivery schedules | Nearer suppliers, alternative routes, buffer sized to the disruption you choose to cover |
| Quality failures | With no spare stock, a defective batch halts the line | Jidoka, supplier quality audits, poka-yoke (error-proofing) |
| Higher transaction costs | More orders, deliveries and handling | Milk runs, e-kanban, standard containers (see the worked example) |
| Supplier dependence and power | Few suppliers means less leverage and more exposure | Long-term contracts, shared improvement, visibility of sub-tier suppliers |
| Implementation effort | Takes years of process improvement and culture change | Pilot one value stream, train teams, measure and expand |

#### What real disruptions have shown
- **The 1997 Aisin fire.** A fire at Aisin Seiki, which made about 99% of Toyota's brake proportioning valves, threatened weeks of lost output. Published accounts describe suppliers improvising production of the valves, with Toyota losing about five days. It is often cited both as JIT's fragility and as the strength of its supplier network.
- **Semiconductors after 2011.** Reuters reported in 2021 that after the 2011 earthquake Toyota adopted a business continuity plan requiring suppliers to hold two to six months of chip stock, depending on lead time. A Toyota spokesperson called it "a classic lean solution". The lesson is that JIT allows deliberate buffers where the risk justifies them.
For project and programme teams, these risks belong in the risk register. Our guides to [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/) and [contingency plans](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) show how to record and plan for them.

### JIT vs just-in-case (and finding the balance)
Just-in-case (JIC) holds extra inventory to protect against uncertainty. JIT holds the minimum and relies on fast, reliable replenishment. Few organisations use either in pure form.
|  | Just-in-Time | Just-in-case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory level | Minimal, sized to replenishment time | High, sized to worst-case scenarios |
| Triggered by | Actual consumption (pull) | Forecasts and safety targets (push) |
| Cost focus | Carrying cost, waste, lead time | Cost of stock-outs and lost sales |
| Strength | Efficiency, quality, cash | Resilience against disruption |
| Weakness | Fragile when supply fails | Ties up cash and space, hides problems |
| Best for | Stable demand, reliable nearby supply, short lead times | Volatile demand, long or risky supply, critical items |

#### A simple matrix to set your buffer policy
Classify each item by how likely its supply is to be disrupted and how serious a stock-out would be. Then apply a different policy to each group. This is our recommended working approach, not a formal standard.
|  | Low impact of a stock-out | High impact of a stock-out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Low supply risk** | Pure JIT: kanban or two-bin, minimal safety stock | JIT with a modest safety stock; monitor supplier performance |
| **High supply risk** | JIT with a second source or quick substitute | Strategic buffer (weeks or months), dual sourcing, visibility of sub-tier suppliers |
Review the matrix at least yearly and after any major disruption. Items move between quadrants as suppliers, markets and designs change.

### JIT vs Lean, Kanban, MRP and EOQ
JIT is often confused with the tools and approaches around it. This table sets out how they relate.
| Concept | What it is | Relationship to JIT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/) | A whole management philosophy focused on value and removing waste | JIT is one of Lean's core pillars, with jidoka |
| [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) | The signalling system (cards, bins or electronic signals) | Kanban is how JIT is controlled day to day; JIT is the goal |
| MRP (material requirements planning) | Calculates material needs from a master schedule and forecasts, then pushes orders | Push-based; many firms use MRP for long-term planning and kanban (JIT) for execution |
| EOQ (economic order quantity) | A formula that balances ordering cost against holding cost | JIT attacks the ordering and set-up cost so the economic quantity becomes small |
| [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/) | Focuses improvement on the bottleneck; uses drum-buffer-rope | Complementary: TOC places buffers deliberately in front of the constraint |
| [Six Sigma](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-vs-six-sigma/) | Statistical reduction of variation and defects | Lower variation makes JIT more reliable |

### Real-world examples of JIT
- **Toyota car assembly.** The reference case: a levelled final assembly schedule, kanban-controlled supermarkets, frequent supplier deliveries and jidoka on every line, as documented in Toyota's own history.
- **Sequenced supply in vehicle assembly.** Large, variant-specific parts such as seats are commonly delivered in the exact build sequence, shortly before they are fitted, so the plant holds hours rather than weeks of them.
- **Made-to-order food.** Fast-food kitchens that assemble items when ordered, keeping only a small, timed buffer of components, are a widely used everyday illustration of pull.
- **Hospital consumables.** Many hospitals restock wards with two-bin systems: when the front bin empties, it triggers replenishment while the back bin covers demand.
- **Construction sites.** Contractors on congested city sites often schedule deliveries of steel, precast units or facade panels for specific days or hours because there is no space to store them.
- **Retail replenishment.** Point-of-sale data triggers store replenishment from distribution centres, so shelves are refilled to match what was sold.
Notice that every example combines short, reliable replenishment with a deliberately small buffer. None of them runs at literally zero stock.

### Is your organisation ready for JIT?
Cutting stock before the process is stable is the fastest way to discredit JIT. Score yourself honestly against these conditions before you start reducing inventory.
| Condition | Ready | Not ready yet |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Demand | Steady or can be levelled; mix is predictable | Large unpredictable spikes, highly seasonal, mostly one-off orders |
| Quality | Low, stable defect rates; problems stopped at source | Frequent rework; defects found late |
| Equipment | Reliable, with planned maintenance | Frequent unplanned breakdowns |
| Changeovers | Minutes, or reducing | Hours, with no improvement plan |
| Suppliers | Reliable, nearby or with dependable logistics; willing to partner | Long lead times, poor on-time delivery, adversarial relationships |
| People | Trained, empowered to stop the line and suggest improvements | Blamed for stopping; no time for improvement |
| Information | Accurate stock records and simple signals | Records unreliable; replenishment done by guesswork |
Tip
If you have three or more "not ready yet" answers, start with stability work (quality, maintenance, set-up reduction and supplier performance) and treat inventory reduction as the result, not the starting point.

### How to implement JIT in 8 steps
1. **Pick one value stream.** Choose a product family with steady demand and a willing team. Map its current state with a [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/), recording inventory, lead time and process time.
2. **Calculate takt time** for that family and compare it with the cycle time of each step to find imbalances and the bottleneck.
3. **Stabilise the process.** Fix the main quality problems, introduce standard work and planned maintenance, and make problems visible with [visual management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/visual-management/).
4. **Reduce changeover times** on the equipment that forces large batches, so smaller lots become economical.
5. **Create flow** by moving steps together into cells where possible and removing waiting between them.
6. **Introduce pull** where flow is not possible: set up supermarkets and kanban loops, sized with the kanban formula, and level the final schedule.
7. **Bring suppliers in.** Agree delivery frequency, container sizes, quality standards and call-off signals; consider milk runs. Our guide to [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) covers supplier agreements.
8. **Lower the water level gradually.** Remove kanbans or reduce buffers one step at a time, fix each problem that appears, measure lead time, inventory turns and on-time delivery, then extend to the next value stream.
Treat the roll-out itself as a project, with a sponsor, milestones and a risk log. Our guide to [manufacturing project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/manufacturing-project-management/) covers running improvement projects on a live production floor.

### Just-in-Time thinking in project management
JIT was designed for repetitive production, but its central idea, doing work only when it is needed and in small amounts, transfers well to projects. This is part of [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/).

#### Just-in-time planning and backlog refinement
Detailed plans made months ahead become inventory: they age, need rework when circumstances change and hide the fact that nobody knows the answer yet. Agile teams plan at several levels, and detail is added only as work approaches.
- Keep the long-range plan at the level of themes and milestones; see [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/).
- Refine backlog items just before they are needed, typically one or two iterations ahead; see [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/).
- Make irreversible decisions at the **last responsible moment**: the latest point at which you can still decide without losing options or causing delay.
- Keep a short, ordered queue of ready work rather than a large pile of detailed specifications. A [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) helps keep it tidy.

#### JIT deliveries on construction and engineering projects
On constrained sites, materials are often called off to match the programme. The example below is illustrative and shows how a planner might set delivery windows and buffers for one floor of a building.
| Material | Needed on site | Supplier lead time | Delivery window | Buffer held |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Precast stair units | Week 12, day 2 | 6 weeks | Week 12, day 1, 07:00–09:00 (crane booked) | None on site; next floor's units ready at the factory |
| Plasterboard | Weeks 14–16 | 1 week | Weekly, Monday morning | About 2 days' usage on the floor |
| Facade panels | Weeks 15–18 | 10 weeks | Daily, sequenced by elevation | 1 day's panels; factory holds 1 week |
| Fixings and consumables | Throughout | 2 days | Two-bin replenishment from site store | Second bin |
- **Long-lead items** still need early procurement: JIT is about the timing of *delivery*, not the timing of *ordering*.
- **Book logistics resources** (cranes, hoists, loading bays) with the delivery, or the material will wait on the lorry.
- **Keep buffers where the risk is high**, as the matrix above suggests: one day of facade panels protects the critical path from a single late lorry.
- Our guide to [construction project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/construction-project-management/) covers logistics planning in more depth.

#### Pull and WIP limits in knowledge work
Kanban brought JIT's pull idea to knowledge work. Teams limit work in progress, start new items only when capacity frees up and measure how long work takes to flow through. [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) play the same role as a fixed number of kanban cards, and [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) shows how much of an item's lead time is spent waiting. A [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) is an easy way to start.

### Common JIT mistakes
- **Cutting inventory first.** Removing stock before fixing quality, breakdowns and set-ups simply causes stock-outs, and JIT gets the blame.
- **Pushing inventory onto suppliers.** If suppliers simply hold the stock you no longer hold, total cost in the supply chain does not fall, and the price you pay eventually rises.
- **Ignoring transaction costs.** More deliveries without cheaper deliveries raise total cost (see the worked example).
- **Treating JIT as a software feature.** A system can generate signals, but flow, levelling and problem-solving happen on the floor.
- **One policy for every item.** Critical, long-lead or single-source items need different buffers from cheap, local, fast-moving ones.
- **No levelling.** Kanban loops sized for average demand break down when the final schedule swings wildly from day to day.
- **Not stopping to fix problems.** Without jidoka, teams work around problems, and the low buffers make every workaround more painful.
- **Copying Toyota's tools without its culture.** Kanban cards and takt boards do little without managers who support improvement and people who are trusted to stop the line.
JIT is one half of a larger system. To see how it fits with jidoka, standard work and kaizen, read [Lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is Just-in-Time in simple terms?**
Just-in-Time means making or buying only what you need, when you need it and in the amount you need. Instead of building stock to a forecast, each step replaces only what the next step has used.

**Q: Who invented Just-in-Time?**
JIT was developed at Toyota. Kiichiro Toyoda advocated the idea in the 1930s, and Taiichi Ohno built it into the Toyota Production System from the late 1940s onwards.

**Q: What are the main elements of JIT?**
The Lean Enterprise Institute names three operating elements: the pull system, takt time and continuous flow, all built on level scheduling (heijunka). Kanban, small lots, quick changeovers, built-in quality and reliable suppliers make them work.

**Q: What is the difference between JIT and Kanban?**
JIT is the goal: produce only what is needed when it is needed. Kanban is the signalling method, using cards, bins or electronic messages, that tells each process what to make or move. See [kanban inventory management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-inventory-management/).

**Q: Is JIT the same as Lean?**
No. Lean is the broader philosophy of maximising value and removing waste. JIT is one of its two core pillars, alongside jidoka (building quality in).

**Q: What is the difference between JIT and just-in-case?**
Just-in-case holds extra stock to protect against uncertainty. JIT holds the minimum and relies on fast, reliable replenishment. Most organisations blend the two, using JIT for most items and buffers for critical ones.

**Q: What is the difference between JIT inventory and JIT manufacturing?**
JIT manufacturing is the production approach in which each process makes only what the next has used. JIT inventory is the resulting stock policy: minimal raw material, work in progress and finished goods, replenished as consumed.

**Q: What are the biggest disadvantages of JIT?**
Vulnerability to supplier failure, transport disruption and demand spikes, higher ordering and transport costs if deliveries are not made cheaper, dependence on a few suppliers, and the long effort needed to implement it properly.

**Q: Which businesses should not use JIT?**
Pure JIT suits organisations poorly when demand is highly unpredictable, supply lead times are long or unreliable, items are critical and single-sourced, or quality is unstable. Such businesses can still apply JIT to the items where conditions are right.

**Q: Is JIT still used after recent supply chain disruptions?**
Yes. Many companies have kept JIT for most items and added strategic buffers for critical or hard-to-source parts. Toyota itself, according to Reuters, asked suppliers to hold several months of chip stock after the 2011 earthquake.

**Q: Does JIT mean zero inventory?**
No. JIT keeps small, deliberate stocks sized to the replenishment time, such as kanban containers and supermarkets. The aim is the minimum inventory needed for smooth flow, not none at all.

**Q: How do you calculate takt time?**
Divide available working time by customer demand for the same period. For example, 51,600 seconds of working time a day ÷ 860 units demanded = a takt time of 60 seconds per unit.

**Q: Is Just-in-Time a pull system?**
Yes. Production and delivery are triggered by actual downstream consumption rather than by a forecast. See [pull vs push systems](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/).

**Q: How does JIT apply to project management?**
Project teams apply JIT by planning in detail only just before work starts, refining backlog items one or two iterations ahead, deciding at the last responsible moment, limiting work in progress and timing material deliveries to the programme.
