# Kanban Board: What It Is, Examples and How to Build One

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: What is a Kanban board? Learn its parts, see examples for software, marketing and IT, and build your own step by step with WIP limits and policies.


## Kanban Board: What It Is, Examples and How to Build One
A Kanban board is a visual display of your workflow, with columns for each stage, cards for each work item and limits on how much work can be in progress at once. It shows at a glance what is being worked on, where work is waiting and where it is stuck. This guide explains every part of a board, gives examples for different teams and walks you through designing your own, with a fully worked example.
- Published 5 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- A Kanban board makes your real workflow visible: columns for stages, cards for work items, WIP limits, commitment and delivery points, and explicit policies.
- The Kanban Guide calls the board the visualisation of your Definition of Workflow and sets no required layout, so design it from how work actually flows, including waiting stages.
- WIP limits are what turn a board into a flow-management system: work is pulled when there is capacity rather than pushed onto people.
- A board gives you four flow measures for free: work in progress, throughput, work item age and cycle time.
- Run the board daily by walking it from right to left and focusing on blocked and ageing items, and review its design regularly.
- Any good tool can host a board; Wrike, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp, Jira, Trello and Microsoft Planner all offer board views, or start with our free template.

### What is a Kanban board?
A **Kanban board** is a visual tool for managing the flow of work. Each column represents a stage in your process, each card represents one work item, and limits on work in progress (WIP) stop any stage taking on more than it can finish. The board makes progress, queues, bottlenecks and blockers visible to everyone.
The word kanban is Japanese for a signboard or visual signal. The idea grew out of the Toyota Production System under industrial engineer Taiichi Ohno, where cards signalled when to replenish parts. In the 2000s, David J. Anderson adapted it to knowledge work, first with a software team at Microsoft and later at Corbis. Our guide to [what Kanban is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) covers the history and the wider method.
The Kanban Guide (edition 2025.5, by John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti) describes the board as the visualisation of a team's **Definition of Workflow**: the shared agreement about what work items are, where they start and finish, the states in between, how WIP is controlled, the policies that apply and the service level the team expects. It deliberately sets no required layout. That is good news: your board should look like your process, not like someone else's template.

### Parts of a Kanban board
David J. Anderson's widely quoted list has five components: visual signals (cards), columns, WIP limits, a commitment point and a delivery point. Most working boards add policies, swimlanes and blocker markers.
| Element | What it is | Practical tip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Cards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-cards/) | One card per work item, showing title, owner, type and key dates | Keep items small enough to move every few days |
| Columns | The stages work passes through, left to right | Model the real process, including queues and hand-offs |
| [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) | The maximum number of items allowed in a column or group of columns | Write the number in the column header where everyone can see it |
| Backlog or options | Requests and ideas not yet committed to | Keep it short and ordered; it is not a to-do list |
| Commitment point | The line where the team agrees to do an item and the clock starts | Usually between Ready and the first active column |
| Delivery point | Where the item reaches the customer and the clock stops | Define it as value delivered, not just work finished |
| Policies | Short rules for entering and leaving each column | Write them on the board, beneath the column names |
| [Swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/) | Optional horizontal rows for classes of service or work types | Add only if they change how people act |
| Blocker markers | A sticker, flag or tag showing an item cannot progress | Record why and since when, so you can analyse patterns later |
| Done | Finished work, kept briefly for review | Clear it at a regular interval so the board stays readable |

#### Upstream and downstream
Many boards have two zones. **Upstream**, to the left of the commitment point, holds options: ideas and requests the team might do, which can still be dropped. **Downstream**, to the right, holds commitments the team will finish, governed by WIP limits. Separating the two stops the board turning into a wish list and makes delivery times measurable. See [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/) for how replenishment moves work across the line.

#### Doing and done sub-columns
A column such as Develop can be split into **doing** and **done**. Items in done are finished at that stage and waiting to be pulled by the next one. This shows queues that would otherwise be invisible, and queues are often where most of the delay hides.

### How a Kanban board works
Kanban is a **pull system**. Instead of a manager pushing tasks onto people, team members pull the next item when they have capacity, and WIP limits make that capacity explicit. Our guide to [pull vs push systems](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/) explains why this reduces overload and multitasking.
Here is one card's journey across a simple software board with the columns Options, Ready, Develop, Review, Test and Done:
1. A stakeholder adds a request to **Options**. It is a possibility, not a promise.
2. At the weekly replenishment meeting the team selects it and moves it to **Ready**, which has a limit of 5. It is now ordered and fully described.
3. When a developer finishes an item and Develop drops below its limit of 4, they pull the top card from Ready. This is the **commitment point**, and the cycle-time clock starts.
4. When coding is finished, the card moves to **Develop: done**, signalling it is ready for review.
5. A reviewer with capacity pulls it into **Review**. A question for the product owner blocks it for a day, so the card gets a red blocker marker with the reason.
6. Once unblocked and reviewed, it is pulled into **Test**, then into **Done** when it is released. That is the **delivery point**, and the clock stops.
At no point did anyone assign the work. The board, the order of Ready and the limits did the coordinating.

### Types of Kanban boards
| Type | Typical columns | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simple three-column board | To do, Doing, Done | Getting started, small teams, personal Kanban |
| Team workflow board | Options, Ready, several active stages with doing and done, Done | Most delivery teams |
| Upstream or discovery board | Ideas, Researching, Shaping, Ready for delivery | Product and design teams deciding what to build |
| Portfolio or project board | Proposed, Approved, In delivery, Releasing, Benefits review | PMOs and leaders tracking projects or epics, not tasks |
| Service desk board | New, Triage, In progress, Waiting on customer, Resolved | IT support, HR and facilities requests |

#### Physical vs digital boards
|  | Physical board | Digital board |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best for | Co-located teams | Remote, hybrid or multi-site teams |
| Strengths | Highly visible, quick to change, encourages conversation | Automatic history, flow metrics, integrations and remote access |
| Weaknesses | No automatic data; hard to share across sites | Easy to ignore if nobody displays it; tool limits can shape the process |
| Tip | Photograph it weekly to keep a record | Show it on a screen at the daily meeting |
Many teams start on a whiteboard to experiment with the design, then move to software once the columns and policies have settled. Kanban boards are part of the wider practice of visual management.

### Kanban board examples
These are starting points to adapt, not prescriptions. WIP limits depend on team size; the figures assume a team of about five and are illustrative.
| Team | Columns | Starting WIP ideas | Example policy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Software | Options, Ready, Develop (doing / done), Review, Test, Deploy, Done | Ready 5, Develop 4, Review 2, Test 3 | Nothing enters Review without passing automated tests |
| Marketing | Requests, Brief, Create (doing / done), Review, Scheduled, Live | Brief 3, Create 6, Review 3 | No brief without audience, channel and deadline |
| IT support | New, Triage, In progress, Waiting on customer, Resolved | In progress 2 per person | Triage within 4 working hours |
| HR recruitment | Role approved, Sourcing, Screening, Interviews, Offer, Hired | Interviews 6 roles | Hiring manager feedback within 2 days of interview |
| Product discovery | Ideas, Researching, Testing, Decided, Ready for delivery | Researching 3, Testing 2 | Each idea has a hypothesis before research starts |
| Construction design approvals | Drafting, Internal check, Client review, Revisions, Approved | Client review 5 | Chase client after 5 working days |
| Legal | Intake, Assessment, Drafting, Negotiation, Signed | Drafting 2 per lawyer | Urgent matters use the expedite lane, limit 1 |
| Personal | To do, Doing, Done | Doing 3 | Finish before starting something new |
Our free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) gives you a ready-made board with columns, WIP limits and card details in Google Sheets, Excel and PDF.

### How to create a Kanban board, step by step
This process works for a whiteboard or a tool. Involve the whole team: a board designed by one person rarely reflects how work really flows.
1. **Define your work items.** Agree what a card represents, such as a feature, a campaign asset or a support ticket, and roughly how large it should be.
2. **Trace real work.** Take two or three recently finished items and walk through how each actually moved from request to delivery, including every wait and hand-off. A value stream map helps on complex processes.
3. **Turn stages into columns.** Create one column per real stage, including waiting stages such as "Ready for test" or "Waiting on client". Merge stages that never hold work for long.
4. **Split busy stages into doing and done** so queues between stages become visible.
5. **Mark the commitment and delivery points.** Decide where the clock starts and stops.
6. **Put current work on the board.** Add a card for everything genuinely in progress today. The count is often a surprise.
7. **Set WIP limits.** Start a little below today's WIP in each active stage, or around one to one and a half items per person working that stage.
8. **Write policies.** One or two lines per column on what must be true for a card to enter or leave it. A [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/) helps you document them.
9. **Add swimlanes only if needed**, for example an expedite lane with a limit of one.
10. **Agree how you will run it:** a short daily meeting, a replenishment rhythm and a monthly review of the board design itself.
Tip
Resist designing the ideal process. Map how work flows today, then improve it in small steps. Kanban starts with what you do now.

### Kanban board policies with examples
Policies are the rules of the board. The Kanban Guide lists them as part of the minimum Definition of Workflow, and Kanban University's general practices include making policies explicit. Without them, people interpret column names differently and the board stops meaning the same thing to everyone. Keep each policy to a line or two, write it on the board and change it only by team agreement.
| Policy type | Example | Why it helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry criteria | A card enters Ready only with a description, an owner for questions and acceptance criteria | Stops half-understood work being started |
| Exit criteria | A card leaves Develop only when code is merged and unit tests pass | Makes done at each stage unambiguous |
| Pull order | Pull the oldest item in the column to the left unless an expedite item is waiting | Prevents favourites jumping the queue |
| WIP breach | If a limit must be exceeded, say so at the next daily meeting and record why | Keeps exceptions visible and rare |
| Blockers | Mark a blocked card within an hour; escalate if blocked for more than 2 days | Turns hidden waits into visible problems |
| Expedite | Only the service owner can add an expedite card; maximum one at a time | Protects the system from everything becoming urgent |
| Service level expectation | 85% of items finish within 10 days of the commitment point | Gives stakeholders a realistic answer to when will it be done |
The service level expectation is a forecast, not a promise: the Kanban Guide describes it as a time period plus a probability, based on historical cycle times once you have them.

### Worked example: designing a marketing team's board
This illustrative example uses an invented team and figures to show the design process and the arithmetic.
A six-person in-house marketing team produces campaign assets: emails, landing pages, social posts and short videos. Stakeholders complain that nothing arrives on time, yet everyone feels overloaded. The team lead traces five recent assets and finds that most of their elapsed time was spent waiting: for briefs to be clarified, for reviewers and for sign-off.

#### Step 1: count today's work
| Stage | Items in progress today | People who work this stage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brief | 4 | 1 (team lead) |
| Create | 12 | 4 (writers and designers) |
| Waiting for review | 7 | None: a queue |
| Review | 4 | 2 (team lead and brand manager) |
| **Total committed WIP** | **27** |  |
Over the last eight weeks the team finished an average of 9 items a week. Little's Law (average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput) gives 27 ÷ 9, an average of about **3 weeks** from commitment to approval.

#### Step 2: design the board
| Column | WIP limit | Policy to enter or leave |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requests (options) | None | Anyone can add; reviewed weekly |
| Ready | 5 | Brief template complete: audience, channel, deadline, assets |
| Brief | 3 | Commitment point: the card enters here only when the team lead pulls it |
| Create: doing | 7 | Owner named on the card; swarm rather than start a new item when blocked |
| Create: done | 4 | Self-checked against the brand checklist |
| Review | 6 | Reviewer responds within 1 working day |
| Scheduled | None | Delivery point: approved and booked into the content calendar |
| Live | None | Cleared every Friday |
The new limits cap committed WIP at 3 + 7 + 4 + 6 = **20 items**, a cut of about a quarter. The team deliberately avoided halving WIP overnight, which tends to stall work and lose goodwill. If throughput holds at about 9 a week, average cycle time should move towards 20 ÷ 9, or a little over **2 weeks**.

#### Step 3: run it and review
- When Review is full, writers stop starting new work and help clear review, for example by peer-checking against the brand checklist.
- Blocked cards get a red marker with the reason and date; the team reviews blocker patterns monthly using blocker clustering.
- After four weeks, the team compares cycle time and throughput with the baseline and decides whether to tighten limits further.
Little's Law describes averages in a reasonably stable system, so treat the forecast as a direction of travel rather than a promise. Our [content calendar template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/content-calendar-template/) pairs well with the Scheduled column.

### Kanban board metrics
A well-run board produces flow data as a by-product. The Kanban Guide names four measures every Kanban system should track.
| Measure | Definition | How the board shows it | Our guide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Work in progress | Items started but not finished | Count of cards between the commitment and delivery points | [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) |
| Throughput | Items finished per unit of time | Cards reaching the delivery point each week | [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) |
| Work item age | Time since an unfinished item started | Days since each in-progress card crossed the commitment point | [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) |
| Cycle time | Time from start to finish for completed items | Days from commitment point to delivery point | [Cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) |
Two charts make these measures easy to read. A [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) shows the number of items in each column over time; widening bands reveal growing queues. An aging chart plots each in-progress item by column and age, so you can rescue items before they become late. For the full set, see our guide to [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/).

### Running your Kanban board day to day
A board only works if it reflects reality and people act on it. Most teams settle on a small set of routines, which our guide to [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/) covers in detail.
- **Daily Kanban meeting (about 15 minutes):** walk the board from right to left, starting with items closest to delivery. Ask what is blocked, what is ageing and what can be finished today, rather than going round each person.
- **Update as work happens:** move a card when its state changes, not just before the meeting.
- **Handle blockers visibly:** mark them, name an owner for the unblocking action and escalate if one is older than an agreed threshold.
- **Replenish on a rhythm:** refill Ready weekly or when it falls below a trigger level, ordered by value and urgency.
- **Review the board design monthly:** are columns, limits and policies still right? Change one thing at a time and watch the effect.
The team that does the work owns the board. Anyone can view it, but changes to columns, limits or policies should be agreed together.

### Kanban board vs Scrum board and other tools
|  | Kanban board | Scrum board |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timebox | Continuous flow, no sprints | Reset each sprint |
| What it holds | All work in the system, from options to delivery | Only the Sprint Backlog |
| How work is limited | WIP limits per column or stage | The amount forecast at sprint planning |
| Changes mid-cycle | New items can enter whenever capacity frees up | Sprint scope is protected; the Sprint Goal should not change |
| Main measures | Cycle time, throughput, work item age | Velocity, sprint burndown |
| Roles | None required | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers |
Many Scrum teams add WIP limits and flow measures to their sprint board. See [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) and our guide to [Scrum boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) for more.

#### Kanban board vs to-do list and Gantt chart
A to-do list records tasks but says nothing about stages, queues or capacity. A Kanban board adds the flow: where each item is, where work waits and how much is in progress. A [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) answers a different question: when planned activities should happen and how they depend on each other. Projects with fixed dates and dependencies often use both: a Gantt chart for the plan and a board for the day-to-day flow of tasks.

### Kanban board software and templates
Every major project management tool now offers a board view. The differences are in WIP limits, swimlanes, flow metrics and how the board connects to the rest of your work. Check current plan details before you buy.

### Common Kanban board mistakes
- **Designing the ideal process instead of the real one.** The board then hides the waits and hand-offs you most need to see.
- **No WIP limits.** Without them, a Kanban board is a to-do list with columns.
- **Too many columns.** If people cannot read the board in a few seconds, merge stages. Most boards need between four and eight active columns.
- **Cards that are too big.** Items that sit in one column for weeks hide progress; split them.
- **No commitment point.** Without one, you cannot measure cycle time or protect the team from overload.
- **Ignoring blocked and ageing items.** The oldest card on the board is usually the most important one to discuss.
- **A stale board.** If the board is not updated, nobody trusts it, and people go back to asking for status.
- **Using swimlanes per person.** They encourage silos and discourage helping each other; show owners on cards instead.
Read our [guide to WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) next to set limits that change how your board behaves.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a Kanban board?**
A Kanban board is a visual display of work, with columns for each stage of the workflow, cards for each work item and limits on work in progress. It shows what is in progress, where work is waiting and where it is stuck.

**Q: What are the parts of a Kanban board?**
Cards, columns, WIP limits, a commitment point and a delivery point are the core. Most boards also have written policies for each column, blocker markers and sometimes swimlanes.

**Q: What are the basic columns on a Kanban board?**
The simplest board has To do, Doing and Done. Most teams expand this to match their real process, for example Options, Ready, Develop, Review, Test and Done.

**Q: How many columns should a Kanban board have?**
As few as needed to show the real stages, usually four to eight. Add a column when work genuinely waits or changes hands there; merge columns that never hold work for long.

**Q: What is the difference between a Kanban board and a Scrum board?**
A Scrum board holds only the Sprint Backlog and is reset each sprint. A Kanban board shows continuous flow, has no sprints and uses WIP limits per column to control how much work is in progress.

**Q: How do you set WIP limits on a Kanban board?**
Count today's work in each active stage and set limits a little below it, or around one to one and a half items per person in that stage. Write them in the column headers and adjust after a few weeks.

**Q: Should I add waiting columns to a Kanban board?**
Yes. Queue columns such as Ready for test, or doing and done sub-columns, show where work is waiting, which is often where most delay hides.

**Q: Physical or digital Kanban board: which is better?**
Physical boards are quick to start and very visible for co-located teams. Digital boards suit remote and hybrid teams and collect flow metrics automatically. Many teams prototype on a whiteboard, then move to a tool.

**Q: Can you make a Kanban board in Excel or Google Sheets?**
Yes, for small teams or to try the idea. Our free Kanban board template works in Google Sheets and Excel, with columns, WIP limits and card details. Dedicated tools are easier once you want metrics or automation.

**Q: Who owns the Kanban board?**
The team that does the work owns it and keeps it up to date. Anyone can view it, and changes to its design or policies should be agreed together.

**Q: How often should you update a Kanban board?**
As work happens, so the board always shows the true state. At the least, the team checks and corrects it at the daily Kanban meeting.

**Q: Do Kanban boards work for remote teams?**
Yes. A digital board becomes the shared view of work for a distributed team. Keep policies on the board, update cards in real time and walk the board together on a video call each day.

**Q: What tools can you use for a Kanban board?**
A whiteboard and sticky notes work well. Digital options include Wrike, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp, Jira, Trello and Microsoft Planner, all of which offer board views, some on free plans.

# Kanban Cards: What to Put on Them and Why

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-cards/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: What a Kanban card is, the information each card should show, how to size work items, blocker markers, and examples of well-designed cards.


## Kanban Cards: What to Put on Them and Why
Each card on a Kanban board represents one work item. Well-designed cards let anyone understand an item's purpose, status and urgency at a glance.
- Published 6 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- One card represents one valuable work item.
- Show title, owner, type, dates and blockers.
- Keep items small so they flow.

### What a card should show
- **A short, clear title** that describes the outcome.
- **Owner** or owners currently working on it.
- **Type or class of service**, often shown by colour.
- **Due date**, only for genuinely fixed-date items.
- **Start date**, to see how long it has been in progress.
- **Blocker marker** when the item cannot progress.
- **Link** to details in a ticket or document.

### Sizing work items
Cards should be small enough to move through the board in days rather than weeks. Large items hide problems and make [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) unpredictable. Split big work into smaller valuable pieces, or use a parent card with child cards.

### Using colour and markers
| Visual | Typical meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Card colour | Work type: feature, defect, request, improvement |
| Red tag | Blocked; see [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/) |
| Avatar or initials | Who is working on it |
| Dots per day | How many days the card has been in its column |
Keep the legend simple and display it on the board.

### Card examples
- "Customer can export invoices as PDF" · feature · owner: Ana · started 3 Mar
- "Fix login error on Android 14" · defect · expedite · owner: Raj
- "Q3 webinar landing page" · fixed date 15 Jul · owner: Kim

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Should every task have a Kanban card?**
Track work items that deliver value to a customer. Very small sub-tasks can live as checklists on the parent card.

**Q: What is a blocked Kanban card?**
A card that cannot progress because of an external dependency or problem. Mark it clearly so the team can help resolve it.

**Q: What is a Kanban card?**
A Kanban card represents one work item on a Kanban board. It shows what the work is and moves across the columns as the item progresses.

**Q: What information should be on a Kanban card?**
A clear title, the owner, the work type, the start date and any due date, plus a visible blocker marker when it is stuck. Digital cards can link to fuller details.

**Q: How big should a Kanban card be?**
Small enough to finish in days rather than weeks, so work flows and problems show up quickly. Split large items into smaller pieces that still deliver value.

**Q: Why put a start date on a Kanban card?**
A start date lets the team see each item's age and calculate [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/). Ageing items are an early warning that work is stuck.

**Q: Can Kanban cards be colour-coded?**
Yes. Colours often show work type, such as feature, defect or maintenance, or class of service. Keep a visible key so everyone reads them the same way.

**Q: Should Kanban cards show estimates?**
They can, but many Kanban teams skip detailed estimates and instead keep items similar in size. Forecasting then uses [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) and cycle time data.

**Q: How many people should be assigned to a Kanban card?**
Usually one person is shown as the owner who drives it to completion, even if others help. Some teams use small avatars to show who is working on each card.

**Q: What happens to a Kanban card when it is done?**
It moves to the Done column and, after a review or release, is archived. Keeping its start and finish dates lets you track metrics over time.

**Q: What is the difference between a Kanban card and a user story?**
A user story describes a need from the user's point of view; a Kanban card is the visual token tracking any work item, which may be a user story, a bug or a task. See [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/).

# Kanban Meetings and Cadences: Which Ones You Need

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: The Kanban cadences explained: daily Kanban meeting, replenishment, delivery planning, service delivery review, operations, risk and strategy reviews.


## Kanban Meetings and Cadences: Which Ones You Need
Kanban does not prescribe Scrum-style ceremonies, but it does recommend regular feedback loops called cadences. Teams pick the ones they need, at a frequency that suits their work.
- Published 7 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Kanban uses cadences: regular feedback loops at different levels.
- Start with a daily meeting and a replenishment meeting.
- Walk the board right to left, focusing on finishing.

### The seven Kanban cadences
The Kanban Method describes seven cadences, from daily team meetings to quarterly strategy reviews:
| Cadence | Typical frequency | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kanban meeting (daily stand-up) | Daily, 15 minutes | Coordinate and remove blockers |
| Replenishment meeting | Weekly or as needed | Select new work to commit to |
| Delivery planning meeting | Per delivery | Plan handover to customers |
| Service delivery review | Every two weeks | Review service performance against customer expectations |
| Operations review | Monthly | Review interactions between services |
| Risk review | Monthly | Understand and respond to delivery risks |
| Strategy review | Quarterly | Align services with strategy |

### The daily Kanban meeting
The daily meeting focuses on the work, not the people. Instead of each person giving an update, the team walks the board from right to left, closest to done first, asking what is needed to move each item forward. Blocked and old items get attention first. See [WIP aging](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/).

### Replenishment
In a replenishment meeting, stakeholders and the team decide which items to pull from the backlog into the Ready column, based on capacity and priority. It replaces sprint planning, and it can be held as often as needed.

### Starting small
Most teams begin with just two cadences: a daily Kanban meeting and a weekly replenishment. Add a service delivery review or retrospective once the board is stable, and the higher-level reviews when several teams or services interact.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Do Kanban meetings include retrospectives?**
The Kanban Method uses service delivery and operations reviews for improvement, but many teams also hold regular retrospectives.

**Q: Is sprint planning one of the Kanban meetings?**
No. Work is pulled continuously; replenishment meetings decide what to make ready next.

**Q: What are the main Kanban meetings?**
Kanban describes seven cadences: the daily Kanban meeting, replenishment, delivery planning, service delivery review, operations review, risk review and strategy review. Teams adopt only those they need.

**Q: What is a Kanban cadence?**
A cadence is a regular feedback loop, such as a meeting held at a set frequency, used to review work, flow or strategy. Kanban uses cadences instead of fixed Scrum-style ceremonies.

**Q: What is a daily Kanban meeting?**
A short daily meeting, often 15 minutes, held at the board. The team walks the board from right to left, focusing on items closest to done, blockers and ageing work rather than individual status updates.

**Q: How is the daily Kanban meeting different from a Daily Scrum?**
A Kanban standup reviews the flow of work across the board, often from right to left, while the Daily Scrum inspects progress towards the Sprint Goal. See [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/).

**Q: Which Kanban meeting decides what to work on next?**
The replenishment meeting. The team and stakeholders choose which items to move from the backlog into the Ready column, based on priority and capacity. It is held weekly or as needed.

**Q: Which Kanban cadence reviews how well the team serves its customers?**
The service delivery review: a regular review, often every two weeks, of how well the team is meeting customer expectations, using measures such as [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/), throughput and blockers.

**Q: Which Kanban meeting plans releases to customers?**
The delivery planning meeting. It plans and coordinates releases of finished work to customers, and its frequency follows the team's delivery rhythm.

**Q: Are Kanban meetings mandatory?**
No. The Kanban Method recommends feedback loops but lets teams choose which cadences to hold and how often. Most start with a daily meeting and replenishment.

**Q: Who attends the strategy review, the least frequent Kanban cadence?**
Senior leaders and service owners, usually quarterly, to review direction and decide which services and types of work the organisation should focus on.

# Kanban Inventory Management: Two-Bin System and Formula

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-inventory-management/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Kanban inventory management explained: two-bin and card systems, the kanban formula with worked examples, card design, setup steps, pros and cons.


## Kanban Inventory Management: Two-Bin System and Formula
Kanban inventory management is a replenishment method in which a signal (a card, an empty bin or an electronic message) triggers restocking only when stock has actually been used. It keeps inventory low and matched to real demand without complex forecasting. This guide explains two-bin and card systems, works through the kanban formula step by step and shows you how to set up, run and improve a kanban loop.
- Published 17 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Kanban inventory replaces exactly what was used: a fixed quantity is reordered whenever a container empties, so timing varies with demand while quantities stay the same.
- The two-bin system is the simplest form. Size each bin to cover demand during the replenishment lead time plus a safety allowance.
- Number of kanbans = daily demand × lead time (days) × (1 + safety factor) ÷ container quantity, rounded up.
- Replenishment lead time includes waiting for the card to be collected, ordering, making or supplying, transport and put-away. Underestimating it is the most common sizing error.
- Kanban suits items with steady, repeating demand. Test variability (an XYZ check) before you convert an item.
- Shorter lead times reduce inventory far more than smaller containers. Review card counts regularly and remove cards to drive improvement.

### What is kanban inventory management?
**Kanban inventory management** is a pull-based way of controlling stock in which each container of parts or materials carries a signal. When the container is emptied, the signal goes back to the supplier or producing process as an authorisation to replace that container, and nothing more. Inventory is therefore driven by actual consumption rather than forecasts, and stays within a fixed, visible maximum.
"Kanban" is Japanese for signboard or visual card. The method comes from the Toyota Production System, where it is the day-to-day control mechanism for [Just-in-Time (JIT)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/just-in-time-jit/) production. Toyota's history records that it introduced a "supermarket method" in 1954, modelled on the way supermarkets restock only what customers take; once a production instruction was added, this became the kanban system.
The same ideas, visual signals and a fixed limit on the amount of work in the system, were later adapted to knowledge work as [Kanban for projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/). This guide covers the original, physical-inventory version.

### How a kanban replenishment loop works
Every kanban system is made up of loops. A loop links one consuming point (a workstation, a ward, a shelf) with one supplying point (a store, an upstream process, an external supplier) through a fixed number of containers, each with its own signal.
1. **Containers are filled to a fixed quantity** and each carries a kanban card or label.
2. **The consuming point uses parts** from one container at a time.
3. **When a container is empty**, its card is removed and placed in a collection post, or the empty bin itself is returned, or a barcode is scanned.
4. **The signal reaches the supplying point** on a regular collection route or electronically.
5. **The supplier makes or picks exactly one container's quantity**, attaches the card and sends it back.
6. **The full container returns** to its location before the consuming point runs out.
The defining feature is **fixed quantity, variable timing**. The quantity per container never changes between reviews; what changes is how often containers come back. When demand rises, cards cycle faster; when it falls, they cycle slower, and the system adjusts without anyone re-planning.

#### Toyota's rules for kanban
Toyota's rules for using kanban are widely quoted, usually in a form close to this:
1. The downstream process withdraws only the items and quantities shown on the kanban.
2. The upstream process produces only the items, quantities and sequence shown on the kanban.
3. Nothing is made or moved without a kanban.
4. A kanban always stays attached to its goods.
5. Defective items are never sent to the next process.
6. Reducing the number of kanbans, carefully, exposes problems and drives improvement.
Rules 3 and 4 are the ones most often broken in practice. If people order "a few extra" without a card, or cards are separated from their containers, the loop's inventory limit stops meaning anything.

### The two-bin system
The two-bin system is the simplest kanban, and often the best place to start. Each item is held in two containers, usually one in front of the other or one on top of the other.
1. Use stock from the front (or top) bin only.
2. When it is empty, move the empty bin, or its card, to the reorder point: a shelf, a box, a board or a scanner.
3. Pull the back bin forward and keep working from it.
4. The empty bin is refilled to its fixed quantity and returned behind the one in use.
5. If the second bin empties before the first returns, that is a signal that the bin size, lead time or demand has changed and the loop needs review.

#### Sizing a two-bin system: worked example
A hospital ward uses an average of **12 boxes of examination gloves a day**. The materials team collects empty bins once a day and delivers refills the following day, so the worst-case time from "bin empty" to "bin back on the shelf" is **2 days**. The ward manager wants **1 extra day** of cover for busy periods.
- **Bin quantity = daily usage × (replenishment lead time + safety days)**
- Bin quantity = 12 × (2 + 1) = **36 boxes per bin**.
- Check: when the first bin empties, the second holds 36 boxes. In the worst case, 2 days pass before the refill returns, using 24 boxes and leaving 12, which is the 1-day safety allowance.
- Maximum on the shelf is 72 boxes (both bins full); typical stock is well below that.
Two-bin systems work best for low-cost, high-use items with short lead times: fasteners, consumables, packaging, office and cleaning supplies, and medical consumables. Many hospitals and workshops use them because they need almost no training and no software.

### Types of kanban signals
Larger operations use several kinds of signal, depending on what is being authorised and where.
| Type | What it authorises | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Withdrawal (conveyance) kanban | Moving a container from a store or supermarket to the point of use | Line-side replenishment from a parts supermarket |
| Production kanban | Making one container's worth of a part | An upstream machining cell that feeds assembly |
| Supplier kanban | An external supplier delivering a container | Bought-in parts on a regular delivery or milk run |
| Signal (triangle) kanban | Starting a batch when stock falls to a set level | Processes with long changeovers, such as presses or moulding |
| Express or emergency kanban | A one-off, temporary replenishment outside the normal loop | Recovering from a defect, breakdown or demand spike; removed afterwards |
| Two-bin | Reordering when one of two bins empties | Consumables and small parts |
| Three-bin | A cycle of one bin at the point of use, one in the store and one at the supplier | Bought-in parts where the supplier holds the third bin |
| Kanban square or space | Producing when a marked floor or shelf space is empty | Large items, pallets or finished goods between adjacent processes |
| E-kanban | Any of the above sent electronically, usually by scanning | Multi-site operations, external suppliers, ERP-linked replenishment |
Tip
Track express kanbans. If you need them often, the loop is undersized or the process is unstable, and the root cause should go onto your improvement list.

### What goes on a kanban card
A good inventory kanban card answers every question the person refilling the container might have, so nobody has to look anything up. A typical card includes:
| Field | Example | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Part number and description | BLT-M8-30, M8 × 30 hex bolt, zinc | Removes ambiguity between similar items |
| Quantity per container | 200 | The fixed quantity that is always replenished |
| Container type | Blue bin, size 3 | Standard containers make counting and handling easy |
| Point of use | Line 2, station 4, shelf B | Where the full container must be delivered |
| Supplying location | Main stores, aisle 6 / Supplier: Fastco | Where the signal goes |
| Replenishment lead time | 1 day | Helps spot late returns |
| Card number | Card 3 of 6 | Shows the loop size and reveals lost cards |
| Barcode or QR code | Scannable code | Enables e-kanban and accurate records |
| Colour code | Green = bought-in, yellow = made in-house | Lets people see the signal type at a glance |
Laminated cards or durable labels survive best. Number every card ("3 of 6") so you can audit the loop: if only five cards can be found, one is lost or a container is hiding somewhere. For the project-board equivalent, see our guide to [Kanban cards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-cards/).

### How to calculate the number of kanbans
The number of kanbans in a loop sets the maximum inventory the loop can hold. Too few and you run out; too many and you carry stock you do not need.

#### The kanban formula
A widely used formula, associated with Toyota and found in most operations textbooks, is:
**N = (D × L × (1 + α)) ÷ C**
- **N** = number of kanbans (cards or containers) in the loop, rounded up.
- **D** = average demand per period, for example units per day.
- **L** = replenishment lead time in the same period, for example days.
- **α (alpha)** = safety factor, as a decimal: 0.1 means 10% extra.
- **C** = quantity per container.
Some organisations express safety as days of cover instead: N = D × (L + safety days) ÷ C. Both are equivalent ways of adding a buffer. More detailed methods, such as the one set out by AllAboutLean, add extra kanbans for lot-size formation, batch orders and demand peaks. Whichever you use, treat the answer as a starting estimate to be adjusted by observation.

#### Break down the replenishment lead time
L is not the supplier's quoted lead time. It is the full time from the moment a container empties to the moment it is back, full, at the point of use. In this example, an assembly line runs a 16-hour day and is supplied by a machining cell.
| Lead time element | Hours | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Waiting for the card to be collected | 2.0 | Cards are collected every 2 hours, so allow the worst case |
| Queue at the machining cell | 3.0 | Other kanbans ahead of it in the queue |
| Production of one container (40 parts at 90 seconds each) | 1.0 | Including a short set-up |
| Transport to the supermarket and put-away | 1.0 | Fixed material-handling route |
| **Total replenishment lead time** | **7.0** | 7 ÷ 16 = **0.4375 days** |

#### Worked example
1. **Demand (D):** assembly uses 480 parts a day.
2. **Lead time (L):** 0.4375 days, from the table above.
3. **Safety factor (α):** 20% (0.2), because the cell's queue time varies.
4. **Container quantity (C):** 40 parts.
5. **Calculate:** N = (480 × 0.4375 × 1.2) ÷ 40 = 252 ÷ 40 = 6.3.
6. **Round up:** use **7 kanbans**. The loop can never hold more than 7 × 40 = 280 parts.

#### What really drives the number of cards
Using the same demand and safety factor, here is how the number of kanbans (N) and the maximum loop inventory (N × C) change with lead time and container size.
| Lead time | Container 20 | Container 40 | Container 80 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.25 days (4 hours) | 8 cards, max 160 parts | 4 cards, max 160 parts | 2 cards, max 160 parts |
| 0.4375 days (7 hours) | 13 cards, max 260 parts | 7 cards, max 280 parts | 4 cards, max 320 parts |
| 1 day (16 hours) | 29 cards, max 580 parts | 15 cards, max 600 parts | 8 cards, max 640 parts |
- **Lead time dominates.** Cutting lead time from 1 day to 4 hours reduces maximum inventory by roughly 70 to 75%, whatever the container size.
- **Container size mainly affects rounding.** Smaller containers trim the maximum a little and smooth the flow, but they also mean more cards, trips and handling.
- **So attack lead time first:** collect cards more often, cut queue time with [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/), reduce set-ups and shorten transport routes. Our guide to [cycle time vs lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/) explains how to measure each.
Tip
Always round up, never down, and use at least two kanbans per loop: one being used, one being replenished. Record why you chose your safety factor so the next review can challenge it.

### Which items suit kanban? (with a worked XYZ check)
Kanban works best for items with steady, repeating demand. A quick way to test that is an **XYZ analysis**, which classifies items by how variable their demand is, using the **coefficient of variation (CV) = standard deviation ÷ average**. It is often combined with ABC analysis, which classifies items by annual value.
Here are five weeks of demand for three items. In practice, use at least 12 weeks of data; five weeks are used here only to keep the arithmetic short.
| Item | Weekly demand (5 weeks) | Average | Standard deviation | CV | Class |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M8 bolts | 100, 96, 104, 102, 98 | 100 | 2.8 | 3% | X (steady) |
| Shipping cartons | 80, 40, 120, 60, 100 | 80 | 28.3 | 35% | Y (variable) |
| Spare motor | 0, 40, 5, 120, 10 | 35 | 44.7 | 128% | Z (erratic) |
Thresholds vary between organisations. In this guide we use X below 25%, Y from 25% to 75% and Z above 75%. Then match the policy to the class:
| Class | Suggested policy |
| --- | --- |
| X: steady demand | Kanban or two-bin; small safety factor |
| Y: variable demand | Kanban with a larger safety factor, more frequent card-count reviews, or a seasonal card adjustment |
| Z: erratic or one-off demand | Order to requirement (MRP or make-to-order), or a minimal stock with a manual review; not usually kanban |
Also exclude, or treat separately, items with very long or unreliable supply lead times, short shelf lives, very high unit costs or upcoming design changes. For those, decide the buffer deliberately; our [JIT guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/just-in-time-jit/) includes a supply-risk matrix for this.

### Kanban vs reorder point, min-max and MRP
Kanban is one of several replenishment methods. They often sit side by side in the same organisation.
| Method | What triggers an order | Order quantity | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kanban / two-bin | A container empties (physical or scanned signal) | Fixed: one container | Steady, repeating items; visual control at the point of use | Lost cards, unofficial extra orders, demand changes not reflected in card counts |
| Reorder point (ROP) | Recorded stock falls to a set level | Fixed (often EOQ) | Stocked items managed in an inventory system | Depends on accurate stock records |
| Min-max | Stock falls to or below the minimum | Variable: up to the maximum | Retail, spares and maintenance stores | Periodic reviews can miss fast consumption |
| MRP | Planned requirements from a master schedule and bill of materials | Calculated per requirement | Complex, variable or one-off demand; long lead times | Forecast errors; frequent re-planning ("nervousness") |
A two-bin system is effectively a reorder point system in which the reorder point is physical: the second bin is the reorder level. That is why it works without accurate stock records. Many manufacturers use MRP for planning and long-lead purchases and kanban for day-to-day replenishment, which is a practical blend of [push and pull](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/).

### How to set up kanban inventory in 10 steps
1. **Choose a pilot area** with a manageable number of steady items, such as one production line, ward or store room.
2. **Map the flow** of materials and information from supplier to point of use; a simple [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) is ideal.
3. **Select items** using ABC and XYZ analysis; start with high-use, low-variability, low-cost items.
4. **Collect data**: average daily usage, its variability and every element of replenishment lead time.
5. **Choose containers** and standard quantities that suit handling, space and supplier pack sizes.
6. **Calculate the number of kanbans** for each item with the formula, rounding up.
7. **Design and print cards or labels**, number them, and mark locations clearly using [visual management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/visual-management/) (labels, colours, shelf markings).
8. **Agree the rules with suppliers and the team**: collection times, response times, what to do if a bin runs out and how express kanbans work. Put external supplier commitments in writing, for example in a [service level agreement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/service-level-agreement-sla/) or contract; an [RFQ template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/rfq-template/) helps when you go out to suppliers.
9. **Train everyone and go live**, keeping the old method available as a fallback for the first few weeks.
10. **Review and improve**: monitor stock-outs, express kanbans and maximum stock; recalculate card counts monthly or when demand changes; remove a card when the loop is consistently over-supplied.
Treat the pilot as a small project with a clear owner, a start and end date and success measures, then roll out in waves. Our guide to [manufacturing project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/manufacturing-project-management/) covers running improvement projects on a live site.

### Running a kanban inventory board
A board makes the replenishment pipeline visible, which is especially useful for bought-in items where a card disappears to purchasing for days. A simple purchasing board has these columns:
| Column | What it means | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Signal received | Cards or scans waiting to be processed | Purchasing |
| Ordered | Order placed with the supplier | Purchasing |
| In transit | Supplier has confirmed dispatch | Supplier / logistics |
| Received | Goods booked in, awaiting put-away | Stores |
| Back in use | Container returned to its location (cards then recycle) | Stores |
- Add a **swimlane** per supplier or item category so a single late supplier stands out; see [Kanban swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/).
- Flag cards that exceed their expected lead time, for example with a red dot, and review them daily.
- Track a few simple measures: stock-outs, express kanbans used, average replenishment time and on-time supplier delivery. Our guide to [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) explains how lead time and throughput are measured on a board.
You can run the board on a whiteboard, in a spreadsheet or with our free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/).

### E-kanban and software
Electronic kanban (e-kanban) keeps the same logic but sends signals digitally. Typically, someone scans the barcode or QR code on an empty container, and the system raises a replenishment request, notifies the supplier or creates a purchase order, often through an ERP system.
- **Benefits:** no lost cards, instant signals to distant suppliers, accurate data on lead time and usage, and easier recalculation of card counts.
- **Costs:** scanners, software and integration effort, plus the risk that people trust the screen and stop looking at the shelf.
- **Good fit:** multi-site operations, many external suppliers, regulated environments that need traceability, and loops with long physical distances.
Options range from kanban modules inside ERP and inventory systems, through specialist e-kanban platforms, to general work-management tools used as a purchasing board. Tools such as [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) or [Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/) can host a clear replenishment board with columns, owners and due dates, while scanning, stock levels and automatic purchase orders are better handled by inventory or ERP software. Many small operations simply start with cards and a board, and add scanning once the loops are stable.

### Kanban inventory examples by industry
| Setting | How kanban is used | Typical signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car and component manufacturing | Line-side parts replenished from a supermarket; upstream cells produce to production kanbans | Withdrawal and production cards, e-kanban to suppliers |
| Hospitals and clinics | Ward and theatre consumables restocked by materials teams; see [healthcare project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/healthcare-project-management/) | Two-bin with scannable labels |
| Restaurants and kitchens | Prepared ingredients and packaging topped up to fixed par levels | Two-bin or marked shelf spaces |
| Small workshops and e-commerce | Fasteners, packaging and fast-selling components reordered from a box of cards; see [small business project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/small-business-project-management/) | Two-bin with cards |
| Construction site stores | Fixings, consumables and PPE replenished from a site store or supplier | Two-bin, weekly supplier call-off |
| Offices and facilities | Stationery, printer supplies and cleaning products | Two-bin or reorder card inside the last pack |
Notice that the method scales from a single shelf of bins to a supplier network. The principles stay the same: fixed containers, a clear signal, a known lead time and a disciplined loop.

### Benefits and limitations of kanban inventory
| Benefits | Limitations |
| --- | --- |
| Lower inventory and carrying costs, with a hard maximum per item | Needs reasonably steady, repeating demand |
| Fewer stock-outs on fast-moving items | Relies on reliable suppliers and predictable lead times |
| Simple and visual: anyone can see what needs replenishing | Poorly suited to one-off, highly seasonal or erratic items |
| Little or no forecasting needed for covered items | Card counts go stale if demand changes and nobody recalculates |
| Less time spent counting stock and chasing orders | Lost cards or unofficial orders break the inventory limit |
| Exposes problems (late suppliers, long queues) so they can be fixed | Physical cards are slow over long distances unless you move to e-kanban |
| Cleaner, better-organised storage areas | Requires discipline and training to sustain |

### Common kanban inventory mistakes to avoid
- **Using the supplier's quoted lead time** instead of the full replenishment time, including waiting for cards to be collected.
- **Setting card counts once and never revisiting them.** Demand, suppliers and container sizes change.
- **Including unsuitable items** (erratic, long-lead or expensive) and then blaming kanban for stock-outs.
- **Allowing "just in case" orders** outside the loop, which quietly inflates inventory.
- **Not numbering cards**, so lost cards go unnoticed until a stock-out.
- **No rule for empty bins.** Decide in advance who acts and how quickly when a second bin starts to run low.
- **Over-engineering the first pilot** with software before the physical loop works.
- **Ignoring the bottleneck.** If an upstream process simply cannot keep up, no number of cards will fix it; see the [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/).

### From inventory kanban to project Kanban
Project and software teams borrowed kanban's core ideas. A Kanban board's columns are the stages of a replenishment loop, its cards are the signals, and its [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) play the same role as a fixed number of kanbans: nothing new starts until something finishes. Individuals use the same principle in [personal Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/personal-kanban/).
If you manage the procurement side of a project, kanban can also run your site or workshop stores, while your [procurement plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) handles long-lead and one-off purchases.
To understand the production philosophy kanban was designed to support, read [Just-in-Time (JIT)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/just-in-time-jit/).
For the wider system of waste reduction it belongs to, see [Lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is kanban inventory management?**
Kanban inventory management uses signals, such as cards, empty bins or barcode scans, to trigger replenishment only when stock has been used. A fixed quantity is replaced each time, keeping inventory low and matched to real demand.

**Q: How does a two-bin kanban system work?**
Stock is split into two bins. You use the first; when it is empty it becomes the reorder signal, and the second bin covers demand until the refilled first bin returns. Each bin should cover demand during the replenishment lead time plus a safety allowance.

**Q: How do you calculate the number of kanbans?**
Number of kanbans = daily demand × replenishment lead time in days × (1 + safety factor) ÷ container quantity, rounded up. For example, (480 × 0.4375 × 1.2) ÷ 40 = 6.3, so use 7 kanbans.

**Q: What information goes on a kanban card?**
Part number and description, quantity per container, container type, point of use, supplying location or supplier, lead time, a card number such as "3 of 6", and usually a barcode or QR code.

**Q: Is kanban inventory the same as Just-in-Time?**
Not quite. Just-in-Time is the goal of producing and delivering only what is needed when it is needed; kanban is the signalling method that makes JIT inventory work day to day. See [Just-in-Time (JIT)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/just-in-time-jit/).

**Q: What is the difference between a production kanban and a withdrawal kanban?**
A production kanban authorises a process to make a container of parts. A withdrawal, or conveyance, kanban authorises moving a container from a store or supermarket to the point of use.

**Q: What is e-kanban?**
Electronic kanban sends replenishment signals digitally, usually when someone scans a barcode or QR code on an empty container, often creating a request or purchase order in an ERP or inventory system.

**Q: What is a three-bin kanban system?**
A loop with three containers: one at the point of use, one in the store and one at the supplier being refilled. It is common for bought-in parts where the supplier takes part in the loop.

**Q: Which items should not be managed with kanban?**
Items with erratic or one-off demand, very long or unreliable lead times, short shelf lives, very high unit costs or imminent design changes are usually better ordered to requirement or given a deliberate buffer.

**Q: What is the difference between kanban and a reorder point?**
Both reorder when stock reaches a set level. A reorder point relies on recorded stock figures in a system; kanban makes the trigger physical or scanned at the point of use, so it works without accurate stock records.

**Q: How often should you review the number of kanbans?**
Review monthly for most items, and whenever demand, lead time, supplier or container size changes. Recalculate the card count, and remove cards when a loop is consistently over-supplied.

**Q: Can small businesses use kanban inventory?**
Yes. A two-bin system with simple cards is cheap and effective for consumables, packaging, spare parts and fast-selling stock, and it needs no software.

**Q: What are the main disadvantages of kanban inventory?**
It needs steady demand and reliable suppliers, card counts go stale without regular review, lost cards or unofficial orders undermine it, and it suits one-off or erratic items poorly.

**Q: How is inventory kanban related to Kanban for projects?**
Both use visual signals and pull. Project [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) adapted the idea to knowledge work, with WIP limits playing the role of a fixed number of kanban cards.

# Kanban Metrics: The Flow Measures That Matter

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: The essential Kanban metrics: WIP, cycle time, lead time, throughput, work item age and flow efficiency, plus the charts that show them.


## Kanban Metrics: The Flow Measures That Matter
Kanban teams improve by measuring how work flows. A small set of flow metrics, collected automatically from the board, tells you how fast work moves, how much gets done and where it gets stuck.
- Published 11 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- The core flow metrics are WIP, cycle time, throughput and work item age.
- Use percentiles and trends rather than averages and single points.
- Metrics improve the system; they should not judge people.

### The four core flow metrics
| Metric | Definition | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work in progress (WIP) | Items started but not finished | Are we overloaded? |
| [Cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) | Time from start to finish for one item | How long will this take? |
| [Throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) | Items finished per unit of time | How much do we deliver? |
| Work item age | Time an unfinished item has been in progress | What is stuck right now? |

### Supporting metrics
- **[Lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/):** from request to delivery, including time waiting in the backlog.
- **[Flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/):** the share of time items are actively worked on.
- **Blocked time** and blocker causes; see [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/).
- **Service level expectation:** for example, 85% of items finish within 8 days.

### Key Kanban charts
| Chart | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| [Cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) | WIP per stage over time; bottlenecks |
| Cycle time scatterplot | Each item's cycle time, with percentile lines |
| [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) | Age of each in-progress item by stage |
| Throughput run chart | Items finished per week |

### Using metrics well
- Look at trends and distributions, not single values.
- Use percentiles (50th, 85th) rather than averages for cycle time; cycle times are rarely normally distributed.
- Review metrics in service delivery reviews or retrospectives.
- Use metrics to improve the system, never to rank individuals.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the most important Kanban metric?**
Cycle time is often the most useful for customers, but it should be read alongside WIP, throughput and work item age.

**Q: Is velocity one of the Kanban metrics?**
Rarely. Kanban teams usually measure throughput (items per week) instead of story points per sprint.

**Q: What are the main Kanban metrics?**
The core flow metrics are work in progress, [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/), [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) and work item age. Many teams also use lead time, flow efficiency and a cumulative flow diagram.

**Q: What is work item age as a Kanban metric?**
Work item age is how long an unfinished item has been in progress. It warns you about stuck work before it becomes late; see the [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/).

**Q: Why use percentiles instead of averages for Kanban metrics?**
Cycle times are rarely normally distributed and often have a long tail. Percentiles such as the 50th and 85th give a more honest picture of what customers can expect.

**Q: Which Kanban metrics belong on a dashboard?**
A small set of charts: a cycle time scatterplot, a throughput run chart, a [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) and a WIP aging chart. Review it at service delivery reviews.

**Q: Which Kanban metrics measure team performance?**
Look at flow and predictability: how quickly and reliably items are delivered, how much WIP is in the system and whether blockers are falling. Avoid using metrics to compare individuals.

**Q: Which tools track Kanban metrics?**
Many digital boards, such as [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/), produce cycle time and cumulative flow reports. Teams on physical boards can track start and finish dates in a spreadsheet.

**Q: Which Kanban metric does a cycle time scatterplot show?**
Cycle time. The chart has one dot per finished item, plotted by finish date and cycle time, with percentile lines showing how long most items take.

**Q: How often should Kanban metrics be reviewed?**
Glance at work item age daily and review the full set every week or two, typically at a service delivery review or retrospective.

**Q: Can Kanban metrics be used for forecasting?**
Yes. Throughput and cycle time history support date forecasts and service level expectations, including Monte Carlo forecasts. See [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/).
