# Kanban Planning: How to Plan and Forecast Without Sprints

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Kanban planning explained: replenishment, commitment points, service level expectations and throughput forecasting, with worked examples and steps.


## Kanban Planning: How to Plan and Forecast Without Sprints
Kanban planning is the continuous process a Kanban team uses to decide what to start next and to forecast when work will be finished, using its own flow data instead of sprint commitments. Kanban has no sprints, but it is far from unplanned: teams replenish their queue regularly, commit to work at a clear point, and answer "when will it be done?" with probabilities. This guide walks through each planning layer, with worked examples of a service level expectation, a throughput forecast and a Monte Carlo simulation.
- Published 8 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- Kanban plans continuously at several levels: strategy and portfolio reviews set direction, replenishment decides what starts next, and delivery planning decides what ships when.
- The commitment point separates options, which can be dropped, from work the team has committed to finish.
- Most Kanban teams count right-sized items instead of estimating effort, then forecast from their own cycle time and throughput history.
- A service level expectation, such as "85% of items finish within 11 days", answers when a single item will be done.
- For many items, Monte Carlo simulation on past weekly throughput gives a date range with a confidence level for each date.

### What is Kanban planning?
Kanban planning is the ongoing practice of choosing which work to start next, committing to it only when the team has capacity, and forecasting delivery from historical flow data. Instead of planning a fixed batch of work for a sprint, a Kanban team replenishes a small queue regularly and uses cycle time and throughput to give probabilistic dates.
It answers two questions that every stakeholder asks. **What will you work on next?** is answered by the backlog, replenishment and classes of service. **When will it be done?** is answered by service level expectations for single items and throughput forecasts for groups of items.
Kanban planning in knowledge work builds on the [Kanban Method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) and the Kanban Guide. In manufacturing and ERP systems, "Kanban planning" usually means something different: calculating card quantities and replenishment signals for parts and materials. If that is what you need, see our guide to [Kanban inventory management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-inventory-management/).

### Kanban planning vs sprint planning
Scrum and Kanban both plan, but they plan at different moments and with different units. Scrum teams plan a sprint at a fixed point; Kanban teams plan whenever capacity frees up and the queue needs refilling.
| Aspect | Scrum sprint planning | Kanban planning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When it happens | At the start of each sprint | Continuously, with a regular replenishment meeting |
| What is committed | A Sprint Goal and a forecast of backlog items for the sprint | Each item individually, when it crosses the commitment point |
| How much is taken on | Based on capacity and past performance | Limited by WIP limits and the size of the Ready column |
| Estimation | Commonly story points (not required by the Scrum Guide) | Often none; items are right-sized and counted |
| Answering "when?" | Velocity and release planning | Service level expectations, throughput and Monte Carlo forecasts |
| Changing priorities | New work normally waits for the next sprint | New work can be pulled in at the next replenishment, or expedited |
Neither approach is better in general. Kanban planning suits work that arrives unpredictably, such as support, operations and marketing requests, and teams that want to release continuously. See [sprint planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) for the Scrum event, and [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) for a full comparison.

### The layers of Kanban planning
Kanban planning happens at several levels, each with its own regular meeting, called a cadence. Kanban University describes seven cadences; most teams start with the daily meeting and replenishment, then add the others as they need them.
| Layer | Cadence | Question it answers | Typical starting frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strategy | Strategy review | Which services and outcomes should we focus on? | Quarterly |
| Portfolio and capacity | Operations review; risk review | How should capacity be shared across teams and work types? What could hurt delivery? | Monthly |
| Service performance | Service delivery review | Are we meeting customers' expectations? What should change? | Every one to two weeks |
| What starts next | Replenishment (commitment) meeting | Which options should we commit to next? | Weekly |
| What ships when | Delivery planning meeting | What goes into the next release, and who needs to know? | For each release |
| Today's flow | Daily Kanban meeting | What is blocked or ageing, and how do we finish it? | Daily, 15 minutes |
Treat the frequencies as starting points rather than rules. A team that receives requests daily may replenish twice a week; a small team with stable work may combine the service delivery review with replenishment. See [Kanban meetings and cadences](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/).
Kanban University separates replenishment from delivery planning deliberately. Committing to start a piece of work is a different promise from committing to a release date, and keeping them apart helps you only make promises you can keep.

### Backlog, options and the commitment point
A Kanban board has two zones. **Upstream** of the commitment point, items are options: ideas and requests that the team might do. **Downstream**, items are commitments that the team will finish.
- **Backlog (options):** a pool of possible work. The Open Guide to Kanban treats a backlog as optional and emergent; it does not need to be a long, fully ordered list. Discarding options here is normal and healthy.
- **Ready (replenishment queue):** the small set of options selected at replenishment, waiting to be pulled. Give it a WIP limit so it does not become a second backlog.
- **Commitment point:** Kanban University defines it as the point at which the decision is made to start activities to deliver a work item. On most boards it is the line between Ready and the first active column.
- **Delivery point:** where the item reaches the customer or is released.
The clock for cycle time usually starts at the commitment point. Everything before it is planning; everything after it is delivery, governed by [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/). Our free [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) helps you keep options tidy, and a [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) gives stakeholders a consistent way to submit new ones.

### How to run a replenishment meeting
Replenishment is the heart of day-to-day Kanban planning. It is short, regular, and decides which options the team commits to next.

#### Who attends and what to bring
- **Attendees:** the people who decide priorities (product owner, service manager or key stakeholders) and a few team members who understand the work.
- **Inputs:** the current board, the number of free slots in Ready, the team's service level expectation, any fixed-date items, and the shortlist of options.

#### Agenda
1. **Check capacity.** Count free slots in the Ready column (its WIP limit minus items already there). This is the maximum number of items you can select.
2. **Review what is coming due.** List any fixed-date items whose latest start date falls before the next replenishment.
3. **Shortlist options.** Stakeholders bring their top candidates. Discard anything that no longer matters.
4. **Prioritise.** Order the shortlist using cost of delay and class of service, described below.
5. **Check size.** For each candidate, ask whether it can finish within the SLE. Split anything that cannot.
6. **Confirm readiness.** Make sure each selected item has enough information to start.
7. **Commit and communicate.** Move the selected items into Ready and tell stakeholders what was chosen and what was not.
Keep it to 30 minutes or less; if it runs longer, the shortlist is too long or items are arriving unprepared. The outputs are a refilled Ready column and a clear record of what was deferred.

#### Worked example: one replenishment meeting
**Illustrative example.** A marketing operations team has a Ready limit of 8 and three items already waiting, so there are five free slots. Its SLE is 11 days, and it replenishes every Monday.
| Option | Class of service | Fits the SLE? | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Landing page for a product launch on the 30th | Fixed date | Yes | Selected first: latest start is the 19th, before the next replenishment |
| Fix broken sign-up form tracking | Standard (high cost of delay) | Yes | Selected |
| Quarterly newsletter | Standard | Yes | Selected |
| Rebuild the whole resources section | Standard | No | Split; the first slice (new navigation) selected |
| Two blog post requests | Standard | Yes | One selected, one deferred |
| Upgrade the email template library | Intangible | Yes | Deferred; the improvement slot is already in use |
| Social campaign idea with no brief | Standard | Unknown | Returned to the requester for a brief |
Five items enter Ready, one large request is split, and the requesters of the deferred items hear why the same day.

#### Prioritising with cost of delay and classes of service
Cost of delay is the value lost by doing something later rather than sooner. Kanban groups work into classes of service according to the shape of that cost, and each class gets its own policy. Kanban University describes four archetypes:
| Class of service | Impact of delay | Planning policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Expedite | High and immediate | Pulled straight away, outside replenishment; limit of one at a time |
| Fixed date | Occurs at a specific date | Start by a latest start date worked out from the SLE |
| Standard | Typical of current conditions | Selected in order at replenishment |
| Intangible | Unknown or not yet felt | Kept flowing in a small share of capacity, such as upgrades and improvements |
Classes of service are often shown as [Kanban swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/) so everyone can see how capacity is split.

### Right-sizing instead of estimating
Many Kanban teams skip effort estimation. Instead of asking "how many points is this?", they ask a simpler question at replenishment: **is this item small enough to finish within our SLE?** If yes, it goes into Ready. If not, the team splits it.
This works because, once items are right-sized, counting them gives forecasts that are usually as useful as summing estimates, and it costs far less meeting time. Items will still vary in size, but that variation is already captured in the team's cycle time and throughput history.
- Split by user outcome or workflow step rather than by technical layer, so each piece delivers something usable.
- Watch out for items that are much bigger than the rest; they distort forecasts and age badly on the board.
- Track how often large items split, because that tells you how much scope grows after commitment.
Story points can still help if your organisation needs them, or if items vary greatly in size. See [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/) for how they work.

### Service level expectations: planning single items
A service level expectation (SLE) tells stakeholders how long a single item is likely to take once started. The Kanban Guide describes it as having two parts, a period of elapsed time and a probability, based on historical [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/).

#### How to calculate an SLE
1. Collect the cycle times of your most recent finished items, from the commitment point to the finish point. Twenty to thirty items is a reasonable sample.
2. Sort them from shortest to longest.
3. Pick a confidence level. The 85th percentile is a popular choice because it covers most items without being stretched by rare outliers.
4. Find the value at that percentile. That is your SLE.
5. Show it on the board and recalculate every month or so.

#### Worked example
**Illustrative data.** A team's last 20 finished items took these numbers of days: 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15 and 21. The average is about 7.6 days, but the average hides the long tail, so the team uses percentiles instead.
| Percentile | Cycle time | How to say it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 50th | 6 days | Half our items finish within 6 days |
| 70th | 8 days | Seven in ten finish within 8 days |
| 85th | 11 days | 85% of items finish within 11 days (our SLE) |
| 95th | 15 days | Almost all items finish within 15 days |
The team now tells stakeholders: "Once we start an item, 85% of the time it is done within 11 days."

#### Using the SLE day to day
The SLE is also a daily planning tool. Compare each in-progress item's age with it: an item at day 8 is approaching the SLE and needs attention before it becomes late. A [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) shows this at a glance.

### Forecasting many items with throughput
When a stakeholder asks "when will these 40 items be done?", the SLE is not enough, because items flow in parallel. Use [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/), the number of items finished per week.
**Illustrative data.** Over the last 10 weeks a team finished 6, 9, 7, 4, 8, 10, 7, 5, 8 and 6 items, an average of 7 a week. The remaining scope is 40 items.

#### Method 1: average and range
| Method | Calculation | Forecast |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Average | 40 ÷ 7 items per week | About 5.7 weeks, so 6 weeks |
| Optimistic | 40 ÷ 10 (best week) | 4 weeks |
| Pessimistic | 40 ÷ 4 (worst week) | 10 weeks |
The average gives roughly a 50/50 date, which is not a promise you want to make. The range is honest but very wide, because it assumes every week is as good or as bad as the extreme.

#### Method 2: Monte Carlo simulation
A [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) produces something more useful: a probability for each possible date. The steps are:
1. Take your recent weekly throughput history (here, the 10 weeks above).
2. Simulate a future week by picking one of those weekly values at random. Repeat week by week, adding up the items, until the total reaches 40.
3. Record how many weeks that took.
4. Repeat the whole simulation thousands of times (we ran 10,000).
5. Count how often each outcome occurred and turn the counts into cumulative percentages.
| Finished within | Probability (40 items) | Probability (48 items, allowing 20% growth) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 weeks | About 12% | Close to 0% |
| 6 weeks | About 72% | About 10% |
| 7 weeks | About 98% | About 62% |
| 8 weeks | Almost 100% | About 96% |
The team can now say: "We are about 72% likely to finish all 40 items within 6 weeks and very likely within 7." The third column shows why you should allow for scope growth. If past items have tended to split or attract extra work, a forecast on the original count will be optimistic.

#### Method 3: how many items by a date
Monte Carlo can answer the opposite question too. Simulating six weeks of throughput 10,000 times, the same team finished at least 42 items in half the runs, at least 38 items in 85% of runs and at least 35 items in 95% of runs. So for a deadline six weeks away, the team can commit with high confidence to the 35 to 38 most important items and treat the rest as stretch.
Tip
Give forecasts as a date and a confidence level, such as "85% likely by week 7", and update them every week as new throughput data arrives. A forecast that changes with evidence is a feature, not a failure.
Two cautions. Forecasts are only as reliable as the system is stable: if WIP is rising or the work mix has changed, the past is a weaker guide. And you need some history; ProKanban.org suggests you can begin with about ten completed items, accepting that early forecasts will be wide. For wider forecasting techniques, see our guide to [project forecasting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-forecasting/).

### Planning around fixed deadlines
Kanban handles deadlines well, provided you plan backwards from them.
1. **Classify the item as fixed date.** Mark it clearly on the board so it is visible at every daily meeting.
2. **Work out a latest start date.** Subtract your SLE from the deadline. With an 85th-percentile SLE of 11 days, an item due on the 30th should start by the 19th; to be 95% confident, use the 95th percentile (15 days) and start by the 15th.
3. **For a group of items, forecast the scope.** Use Monte Carlo to see how many items you can finish by the date, as in the example above.
4. **If the forecast misses, change something now.** Reduce or reorder scope, protect capacity by pausing standard work, or agree a later date. Making the trade-off early is the point of forecasting.
5. **Track item age against the latest start and finish dates.** Escalate at the daily meeting as soon as an item looks likely to miss.
Do not turn every item into a fixed-date item. If most work carries a deadline, the deadlines lose meaning and the team loses the ability to protect the genuinely time-critical ones.

### Long-term planning: roadmaps and capacity allocation
Kanban does not replace roadmaps. Roadmaps sit above the board as themes, goals or large initiatives, reviewed at strategy and operations reviews. The board then shows how the pieces of those initiatives flow through delivery.

#### Capacity allocation
A practical way to connect strategy to the board is to split WIP across work types. **Illustrative example:** a team with a total WIP limit of 10 agrees the following allocation at its quarterly strategy review.
| Work type | Share of capacity | WIP slots |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roadmap features | 60% | 6 |
| Defects and support | 20% | 2 |
| Improvements and technical work | 10% | 1 |
| Expedite | 10% | 1 |
Changing the allocation is a strategic decision: shifting one slot from features to improvements is visible, deliberate and easy to reverse. Throughput per work type then tells you how fast each roadmap theme is likely to move.

#### Portfolio Kanban
At portfolio level, the same ideas apply to larger items: initiatives flow through stages such as Proposed, Analysing, Approved, In progress and Done, with WIP limits on how many run at once. Our guides to the [agile roadmap](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-roadmap/) and [agile portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/) cover this level, and the [product roadmap template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-roadmap-template/) gives you a starting structure. If several teams share a portfolio, a work management tool with cross-project dashboards and request forms, such as [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), makes the link between roadmap items and team boards easier to see.

### Setting up Kanban planning step by step
If your team is new to Kanban planning, introduce it in this order:
1. **Map your workflow** and mark the commitment point and the finish point on the board.
2. **Add a Ready column with a WIP limit**, sized to roughly one replenishment interval of throughput.
3. **Set WIP limits** on active columns so work is pulled, not pushed.
4. **Start recording dates**: when each item crosses the commitment point and when it finishes.
5. **Hold a weekly replenishment meeting** with the people who set priorities.
6. **Agree classes of service** and a policy for expedite and fixed-date work.
7. **After 20 or more finished items, calculate an SLE** and show it on the board.
8. **Start forecasting with throughput** and review forecasts every week at the daily or service delivery meeting.
Our free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) includes a Ready column and WIP limit fields, so you can try this in a spreadsheet before configuring a tool. To read the resulting data, see [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/).

### Common Kanban planning mistakes
- **Treating "no sprints" as "no planning".** Without replenishment and forecasting, Kanban becomes a to-do list and stakeholders lose trust.
- **Letting Ready become a second backlog.** An unlimited Ready column hides priorities; limit it.
- **Committing too early.** Pulling items past the commitment point before there is capacity inflates WIP and lengthens cycle time.
- **Promising single dates.** An average-based date is a coin toss. Give a date with a confidence level.
- **Forecasting an unstable system.** If WIP is climbing, fix flow first; a [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) shows whether it is stable.
- **Ignoring scope growth.** Allow for items splitting after commitment, as in the 48-item forecast above.
- **Making everything urgent.** Too many expedite and fixed-date items destroy predictability for all other work.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: How does Kanban planning work without sprints?**
The team replenishes a small Ready column at regular meetings, commits to each item when it crosses the commitment point, and limits WIP so work is pulled as capacity frees up. Dates come from historical cycle time and throughput rather than a sprint commitment.

**Q: Does Kanban have sprint planning?**
No. Kanban has no sprints, so there is no sprint planning. Its closest equivalents are the replenishment meeting, which decides what starts next, and the delivery planning meeting, which decides what ships in each release.

**Q: What is a replenishment meeting in Kanban?**
A short, regular meeting where the people who set priorities and the team choose which options to move into the Ready column, based on free capacity, cost of delay and class of service.

**Q: How often should a Kanban team replenish?**
Weekly is a common starting point. Replenish often enough that the Ready column never runs dry but not so often that the meeting becomes a distraction; teams with fast-moving demand may replenish twice a week.

**Q: What is a commitment point in Kanban?**
The point on the board at which the team decides to start delivering an item, usually the line between Ready and the first active column. Before it, items are options that can be dropped; after it, the team commits to finishing them.

**Q: Does Kanban planning involve estimating?**
Often not in effort. Many teams right-size items so each can finish within the service level expectation, then count items and forecast from throughput. Some teams still estimate when items vary greatly in size.

**Q: Are story points used in Kanban?**
They are optional. Kanban does not require them, and many teams find counting right-sized items simpler and just as useful for forecasting.

**Q: What is a service level expectation in Kanban?**
A forecast of how long a single item should take once started, made of a time period and a probability, such as "85% of items finish within 11 days". It is calculated from historical cycle times.

**Q: How do you forecast delivery dates in Kanban?**
Use the SLE for single items. For many items, divide the remaining count by average weekly throughput for a rough figure, or run a Monte Carlo simulation on past weekly throughput to get a probability for each date.

**Q: What is Monte Carlo forecasting in Kanban?**
A simulation that randomly samples your past weekly throughput thousands of times to model possible futures. It gives answers such as "72% likely within 6 weeks, 98% likely within 7".

**Q: How much data do you need to forecast in Kanban?**
You can start with about ten finished items, accepting wide ranges. Forecasts improve as you collect more weeks of throughput, as long as the workflow stays reasonably stable.

**Q: Can Kanban handle fixed deadlines?**
Yes. Use a fixed-date class of service, work out a latest start date by subtracting your SLE from the deadline, and use throughput forecasts to check that a larger scope can fit before the date.

**Q: What is the difference between the backlog and the Ready column?**
The backlog holds options that may or may not be done. The Ready column holds the small, limited set selected at replenishment, waiting to be pulled when capacity frees up.

**Q: How does Kanban planning handle long-term roadmaps?**
Roadmap themes and initiatives sit above the board and are reviewed at strategy and operations reviews. Capacity allocation across work types links them to day-to-day flow, and throughput shows how fast each theme is moving.

# Kanban Principles and Practices: A Practical Guide

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-principles/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Kanban principles and practices explained: the four foundational principles, service delivery principles and six practices, with worked examples.


## Kanban Principles and Practices: A Practical Guide
Kanban principles are the guiding rules of the Kanban Method: start with what you do now, agree to pursue evolutionary change, respect current roles and titles, and encourage leadership at every level. Alongside them sit three service delivery principles and six general practices that turn those ideas into daily habits. This guide explains each one, shows how the lists differ between Kanban University and the Kanban Guide, and walks through worked examples you can copy.
- Published 5 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Kanban University's principles page lists four foundational principles; its newer Official Guide groups three change management principles with three service delivery principles.
- The six general practices are visualise, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, and improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally.
- The Kanban Guide (2025.5) condenses Kanban into three practices and says improvements need not be small or incremental, a real difference from the Kanban Method.
- Principles explain why you change gently; practices are what you actually do at the board each day.
- WIP limits and explicit policies do most of the work: they expose bottlenecks and make improvement a matter of evidence, not opinion.
- STATIK gives a step-by-step way to apply the principles when you introduce Kanban to a team.

### What are Kanban principles?
**Kanban principles** are the beliefs that shape how the Kanban Method introduces and evolves change. They say you begin with your current process, improve it through small agreed steps, keep existing roles and titles, and let anyone lead an improvement. The six **Kanban practices** are the concrete activities, such as limiting work in progress, that put those principles into action.
The principles are the constitution; the practices are the working rules. A team can follow the practices mechanically and still fail if it ignores the principles, for example by forcing a new board on people who were never asked.
Here is the whole picture on one table. Each item is explained in detail below.
| Group | Items | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foundational (change management) principles | Start with what you do now; agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change; respect the current process, roles, responsibilities and titles; encourage acts of leadership at all levels | Kanban University principles page |
| Service delivery principles | Understand and focus on customer needs and expectations; manage the work, let people self-organise around it; regularly review the network of services and its policies | Kanban University Official Guide to the Kanban Method |
| General practices | Visualise; limit WIP; manage flow; make policies explicit; implement feedback loops; improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally | Kanban University |
| Agendas | Sustainability; service orientation; survivability | Kanban Method literature (Mike Burrows, David J. Anderson) |
| Kanban Guide practices | Defining and visualising a workflow; actively managing items in a workflow; improving a workflow | The Kanban Guide 2025.5 (kanbanguides.org) |
If you are new to Kanban itself, start with our overview of [what Kanban is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/), which covers its history, the board and the core flow metrics. This page goes deeper into the principles and practices.

### Which list is right? 4 principles, 6 principles or 3 practices
Different websites quote different numbers, and each is correct for the source it follows.
| Source | Principles | Practices | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kanban University principles page (first published 2014) | 4 foundational principles | 6 general practices | The list most search results and quiz questions use |
| David J. Anderson, "Revisiting the Principles and General Practices" (2021) and the Official Guide to the Kanban Method (2022) | 3 change management + 3 service delivery | 6 general practices | Respect for roles and titles is folded into "start with what you do now" |
| The Kanban Guide 2025.5 (Coleman and Vacanti, May 2025) | No numbered principles | 3 practices plus a Definition of Workflow and 4 flow metrics | A minimal, flow-focused definition maintained separately from Kanban University |
Small wording differences also appear. The 2014 page says "agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change", while the Official Guide says "agree to pursue improvement through evolutionary change". The meaning is the same: the team agrees, in advance, to change gradually rather than through a big redesign.
Tip
Studying for an exam? Check which body of knowledge it follows. Kanban University courses use the change management and service delivery principles with six general practices; ProKanban.org's courses use the Kanban Guide's three practices. Our own advice in this guide draws on both.

### The four foundational Kanban principles
These principles describe how Kanban changes an organisation: from the inside, with consent, one step at a time. Kanban University's principles page lists them in this order.

#### 1. Start with what you do now
Kanban is applied to the process you already have, not to an ideal process drawn on a whiteboard. You map how work really flows today, including the awkward parts such as waiting for sign-off, and put it on a board. The method does not prescribe a process of its own.
- **How to apply it:** interview the people doing the work, follow three or four recent items from request to delivery, and draw the states they actually passed through.
- **Example:** a finance team believes invoices go Received, Approved, Paid. Tracing ten invoices shows a hidden "Waiting for purchase order" state where most of them sat for days. That state becomes a column.
- **Warning sign:** the board has columns nobody recognises, or people keep a private list because the board does not match reality.

#### 2. Agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change
Everyone affected agrees up front that the process will improve through a series of small changes, each kept or reversed on the evidence. Agreement matters because Kanban relies on the team owning the change; without it, the initiative has no support when the first WIP limit feels uncomfortable.
- **How to apply it:** say explicitly at kick-off that nothing is final, that each change will be reviewed, and that any change can be rolled back.
- **Example:** instead of reorganising a support desk into tiers, the team first adds a single policy, "blocked tickets are raised at the daily meeting", and reviews the effect after a month.
- **Warning sign:** a manager announces a new workflow, new tool and new roles in the same week.

#### 3. Respect the current process, roles, responsibilities and titles
Kanban does not start by changing who does what. Keeping existing roles reduces fear, which Kanban University describes as a way to build broader support for change. If roles do need to change later, the evidence from the board will show why, and the team can agree it.
- **How to apply it:** keep job titles, reporting lines and approval responsibilities as they are on day one; put them on the board as states or policies if they affect flow.
- **Example:** a legal reviewer is a bottleneck. Rather than removing the review, the team limits how much reaches it at once and agrees which contract types genuinely need it.
- **Warning sign:** the first conversation about Kanban is about new roles.

#### 4. Encourage acts of leadership at all levels
Improvement ideas often come from the people closest to the work. Kanban asks for an environment where anyone, from a new starter to a director, can spot a problem and propose a well-reasoned change.
- **How to apply it:** keep a visible improvement column or list, and let whoever raises an idea run the experiment with the team's agreement.
- **Example:** a junior developer notices that most blocked cards wait on one shared test environment, gathers a month of blocker data and proposes a booking policy.
- **Warning sign:** only the team lead changes the board or its policies.
These four principles explain why Kanban meets less resistance than many transformations. For how they fit a wider organisational change, read our guide to [Agile transformation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-transformation/).

### The service delivery principles
Kanban University adds three principles that treat a team's output as a service delivered to customers.

#### Understand and focus on customer needs and expectations
A service is judged by its customers. David J. Anderson describes this as being "fit for purpose" in the customer's eyes, and suggests using customers' own criteria, such as how quickly and how predictably they get what they asked for, as the measures you improve.
**Example:** an internal IT team discovers that requesters care less about the average fix time than about knowing when a fix will arrive. The team starts publishing a [service level expectation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/), such as 85% of standard requests within five working days.

#### Manage the work; let people self-organise around it
Work items can be counted, sized, limited and tracked; people's time and effort are much harder to predict in knowledge work. Kanban therefore manages the flow of work and trusts the team to organise itself around it. Managers ask "what is blocked?" rather than "what is everyone doing?".
**Example:** the daily meeting walks the board from right to left, card by card, instead of going round the room for individual status updates. Our guide to [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/) gives an agenda.

#### Regularly review the network of services and its policies
Most teams depend on others, and others depend on them. Policies, such as classes of service and WIP limits, determine how the whole network behaves, so they should be reviewed regularly and improved to get better outcomes for customers and the business.
**Example:** a product team and a data team find that every release waits on the same data migration step. A joint monthly review agrees a shared policy for scheduling migrations and an explicit limit on how many can run at once.

### The three Kanban agendas and nine values
Kanban Method writers also describe three agendas, the purposes an organisation might adopt Kanban for, each linked to three values. Mike Burrows set these out in a 2014 series of InfoQ articles, and they appear in Kanban University training. They are useful for explaining why a team is adopting Kanban, but they are less often quoted than the principles and practices.
| Agenda | What it is about | Associated values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sustainability | Relieving overburdened individuals and teams by balancing demand with capability | Transparency, balance, collaboration |
| Service orientation | Looking outward at customers and the flow of services that meet their needs | Customer focus, flow, leadership |
| Survivability | Building an adaptable organisation that can keep evolving as its environment changes | Understanding, agreement, respect |
Most teams begin on the sustainability agenda ("we are overloaded") and move to service orientation as they publish expectations to customers.

### The six general practices of the Kanban Method
The practices are where principles become habits. They are listed in roughly the order teams adopt them, but they reinforce each other: visualisation shows where to limit WIP, WIP limits make flow problems visible, and explicit policies make improvement possible.

#### 1. Visualise the work, workflow and business risks
Make invisible work visible. Every item is a card, every state is a column, and risks are shown with colours, markers or swimlanes. Kanban University's wording includes **business risks**, which many teams forget: a card's type, due date or cost of delay should be visible at a glance.
1. List every type of work the team does, including unplanned and internal work.
2. Draw the states from your traced items as columns, splitting busy states into "doing" and "done" where work waits.
3. Put every current item on a [Kanban card](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-cards/) with its start date.
4. Add risk markers and use [swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/) only where they help a decision, such as an expedite lane.

#### 2. Limit work in progress
A WIP limit caps how many items can be in a state, a group of states or the whole system. It creates a pull system: new work starts only when capacity frees up. Kanban University calls the limits more important than the exact mechanism you use to pull.
**Worked example: setting first WIP limits.** A six-person software team has one analyst, four developers and one tester. Today the board shows 3 items in Analysis, 9 in Development and 6 waiting for test.
| State | People | Items now | Starting WIP limit | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analysis | 1 | 3 | 2 | One active plus one ready to hand over |
| Development | 4 | 9 | 5 | About one item per developer plus one for pairing or a blocked item |
| Ready for test (queue) | - | 6 | 3 | A small buffer in front of the constraint |
| Test | 1 | - | 2 | The tester is the constraint; protect their focus |
With Ready for test full, developers stop starting new items and help test or automate checks. This is the Theory of Constraints idea of subordinating everything to the bottleneck; see our guide to the [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/).
**Why it works, in numbers.** Little's Law says average cycle time is roughly average WIP divided by average throughput in a stable system. If the team finishes 3 items a week and holds 15 in progress, the average item takes about 15 ÷ 3 = 5 weeks. Holding 8 in progress at the same throughput points to about 8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.7 weeks. Nobody works harder; items simply wait less.

#### 3. Manage flow
Managing flow means watching how work moves and acting when it does not: clearing blockers, finishing ageing items and smoothing queues. The aim, in Kanban University's words, is work that flows fast, smoothly and predictably.
1. Each day, look for the oldest items in progress and the items marked blocked.
2. Ask what it would take to move each one, starting from the right of the board.
3. Swarm on items close to breaching your expectation; see [Agile swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/).
4. Record start and finish dates so you can measure [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) and [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/).
5. Watch a [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) and a [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) for growing queues.
**Example:** a card has been in Review for six days while most items clear Review in two. At the daily meeting the team learns the reviewer is waiting for a test account. One person requests it immediately; the card is done the next day, and a policy is added for requesting accounts at the commitment point.

#### 4. Make policies explicit
Policies are the rules the team works by. Written down and visible, they make discussions about improvement rational and evidence-based instead of emotional and anecdotal, which is how Kanban University puts it. The Official Guide gives pull criteria, WIP limits and classes of service as typical examples.
| Policy | Example wording | Why it helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry to Ready (commitment point) | Has a named requester, acceptance criteria and a size of small or medium | Stops vague work entering the system |
| Blocked items | Tag red, add the reason and date; raise at the next daily meeting | Makes blockers visible and measurable |
| Expedite class of service | One card at a time; may exceed WIP limits; used only for production incidents | Lets urgent work through without wrecking flow |
| Exit from Done | Meets the [definition of done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) and the requester has been told | Agrees what finished means |
Keep policies short, put them on the board next to the column they govern, and change them only by agreement. Classes of service and replenishment rules are covered in our guide to [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/).

#### 5. Implement feedback loops
Feedback loops are regular meetings and reviews, often called cadences, where the team compares what it expected with what happened and adjusts. The Official Guide to the Kanban Method suggests these team-level cadences as a starting point:
| Cadence | Suggested frequency | Practice it mainly serves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Team Kanban meeting | Daily | Manage flow: blockers, ageing items, what can we finish today? |
| Internal team replenishment meeting | Weekly or as needed | Limit WIP and make policies explicit: what enters Ready, and why |
| Team retrospective | Every two weeks or monthly | Improve collaboratively: review data and agree experiments |
Service-oriented cadences, such as service delivery, operations, risk and strategy reviews, are added when several teams or services are involved. Reuse meetings you already hold where you can; that respects the current process.

#### 6. Improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally
Change is made together and treated as an experiment. Kanban University suggests using models, such as the Theory of Constraints, the Theory of Profound Knowledge and the Lean Economic Model, to predict the effect of a change, then comparing the prediction with what actually happens. Run safe-to-fail experiments, one at a time.
**Example experiment card:**
- **Observation:** the 85th percentile cycle time is 12 days, and cards wait an average of three days in Ready for review.
- **Hypothesis:** if we limit Review to 2 and pair on reviews, the 85th percentile will fall to about 9 days within six weeks, with throughput unchanged.
- **Measure:** cycle time percentiles and weekly throughput from the board.
- **Review date and rollback:** retrospective in six weeks; if throughput drops by more than one item a week, revert.
Data from [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/) and [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) are good sources of experiments.

### The Kanban Guide's three practices compared
The Kanban Guide, written by John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti, is a separate, shorter definition. Its 2025.5 edition (May 2025) defines Kanban as a strategy for optimising the flow of value through a process and describes three practices: defining and visualising a workflow, actively managing items in a workflow, and improving a workflow. Each team records the first in a **Definition of Workflow**, which must cover work items, start and finish points, states, how WIP is controlled, explicit policies and a service level expectation.
| Kanban Guide practice | Closest Kanban Method practices | What the Kanban Guide adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Defining and visualising a workflow | Visualise; make policies explicit | A written Definition of Workflow with an SLE |
| Actively managing items in a workflow | Limit WIP; manage flow | Explicit focus on controlling WIP, preventing unnecessary ageing and unblocking work |
| Improving a workflow | Implement feedback loops; improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally | Improvement can happen just-in-time, with no required meetings |
Two differences are worth knowing. First, the Kanban Guide has no change management principles and no required roles or meetings. Second, it says improvements need not be small or incremental, whereas the Kanban Method asks teams to agree to evolutionary change. In our experience, small changes are still the safer default, but the Kanban Guide's view is a fair reminder that an obviously broken policy can be fixed immediately.
The Kanban Guide also requires four flow metrics: WIP, throughput, work item age and cycle time. Our [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) guide shows how to calculate and chart them.

### How to apply Kanban principles step by step with STATIK
Kanban University recommends STATIK, the Systems Thinking Approach to Introducing Kanban, for designing a Kanban system that respects the principles. Its Official Guide lists six steps. Do them with the team, not for it: the guide specifically advises against a project manager, team lead or coach doing STATIK alone.
1. **Identify sources of dissatisfaction.** Ask the team and its customers what frustrates them, such as late delivery, overload or unpredictability. Output: a short list of problems in their words.
2. **Analyse demand.** List the types of work that arrive, where they come from and roughly how often. Output: work item types with arrival rates.
3. **Analyse system capabilities.** Look at how much the team delivers and how long items take today. Output: baseline throughput and cycle time, even if rough.
4. **Model the workflow.** Map the states each work type passes through, including queues. Output: the board's columns and the commitment and delivery points.
5. **Identify classes of service.** Agree how different kinds of urgency are treated, for example expedite, fixed date, standard and intangible. Output: classes of service with policies.
6. **Design the Kanban system.** Set WIP limits, policies, cadences, the board layout and the metrics you will track. Output: a working board and a calendar of meetings.
Steps 1 to 3 are where "start with what you do now" happens in practice. Steps 4 to 6 produce the practices. To map flow in more detail before step 4, a [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) helps, and our free [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/) gives you a place to record states and owners.

### Worked example: an HR recruitment team
A five-person recruitment team supports hiring managers across a company. Hiring managers complain that they never know when a role will be filled, and recruiters feel overloaded. Here is how the team applied the principles and practices over twelve weeks.
| Weeks | Principle or practice | What the team did | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Start with what you do now | Traced eight recent hires and mapped Requested, Job ad, Sourcing, Screening, Interviews, Offer, Accepted | Found a hidden wait for interview panel availability |
| 2 | Visualise; respect current roles | Built a board with every open role; kept recruiter and coordinator roles unchanged; showed panel scheduling as its own state | 27 roles open, 11 of them waiting on panels |
| 3 | Limit WIP | Agreed a limit of 4 active roles per recruiter in Sourcing and Screening, and 6 roles in Interviews across the team | Two new requests waited in Requested for a week instead of starting |
| 4 | Make policies explicit | Wrote entry criteria for Job ad (approved budget and job description) and a 48-hour panel-booking policy agreed with hiring managers | Fewer roles stalled after starting |
| 5–8 | Manage flow; feedback loops | Daily 15-minute board walk; weekly replenishment with HR business partners; flagged any role in Interviews for more than ten working days | Panel waits became the main blocker discussed |
| 9–12 | Improve collaboratively; focus on customers | Ran one experiment: pooled interviewers for common roles. Published an expectation to hiring managers based on recent cycle times | Hiring managers received a realistic time to offer for standard roles |
Tip
The numbers in this example are illustrative, not data from a real company. The pattern is what matters: trace, visualise, limit, write policies, manage flow, then improve one thing at a time.
Notice what the team did not do. It did not rename roles, buy a new applicant tracking system or redesign the hiring process. The board and its data showed the problem, and the team agreed the fix.

### Common mistakes when applying Kanban principles
| Mistake | Principle it breaks | Better approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Designing the ideal board before looking at real work | Start with what you do now | Trace recent items and map what actually happened |
| Announcing Kanban with new roles and a new tool at once | Evolutionary change; respect current roles | Change one thing, review it, then decide the next step |
| A board with no WIP limits | Limit WIP | Set generous limits first, then lower them as flow improves |
| Policies that live in someone's head | Make policies explicit | Write short rules on the board beside each column |
| Changing several things at once | Evolve experimentally | One experiment at a time, with a measure and a review date |
| Measuring averages only | Manage flow; focus on customers | Use cycle time percentiles to set expectations |

If requests reach your team informally, a [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) gives you a consistent intake before the commitment point.
Once the board is running, the most valuable next step is getting WIP limits right.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are the 4 principles of Kanban?**
Kanban University's principles page lists: start with what you do now; agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change; respect the current process, roles, responsibilities and titles; and encourage acts of leadership at all levels.

**Q: What are the 6 practices of Kanban?**
Visualise; limit work in progress; manage flow; make policies explicit; implement feedback loops; and improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally.

**Q: Why do some sources list six Kanban principles?**
Kanban University's Official Guide groups three change management principles (start with what you do now, agree to pursue improvement through evolutionary change, encourage leadership at all levels) with three service delivery principles. Respect for current roles is folded into the first.

**Q: What are the Kanban service delivery principles?**
Understand and focus on customer needs and expectations; manage the work and let people self-organise around it; and regularly review the network of services and its policies to improve outcomes.

**Q: What is the most important Kanban principle?**
Kanban University gives no ranking. In practice, starting with what you do now is the foundation, and limiting WIP is the practice that usually makes the biggest difference to flow.

**Q: What does "start with what you do now" mean in Kanban?**
It means applying Kanban to your existing process. You map how work really flows today and improve it step by step, rather than designing a new process first.

**Q: What are feedback loops in Kanban?**
Regular meetings and reviews where the team compares expected and actual results and adjusts. Kanban University suggests a daily Kanban meeting, replenishment weekly or as needed, and a retrospective every two weeks or monthly.

**Q: What are the Kanban Guide's three practices?**
The Kanban Guide 2025.5 lists defining and visualising a workflow, actively managing items in a workflow, and improving a workflow.

**Q: What are the three agendas of Kanban?**
Sustainability, service orientation and survivability. Each is linked to three values: transparency, balance and collaboration; customer focus, flow and leadership; understanding, agreement and respect.

**Q: How are Kanban principles different from Scrum values?**
Scrum's five values describe how a Scrum Team behaves inside a defined framework. Kanban principles describe how to evolve an existing process gradually without imposing a new one. See [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/).

# Kanban Swimlanes: Types, Examples and How to Use Them

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Kanban swimlanes explained: the main types, classes of service, WIP limits per lane, a worked board example and step-by-step setup, plus common mistakes.


## Kanban Swimlanes: Types, Examples and How to Use Them
Kanban swimlanes are horizontal rows across a Kanban board that group cards by category, such as urgency, work type, team or customer, while the columns still show the stages of the workflow. Used well, they make priorities and policies visible at a glance and help you protect capacity for different kinds of work. This guide covers the main types of swimlanes, classes of service, WIP limits per lane, a worked board design and a step-by-step setup.
- Published 6 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Columns show where work is in the process; swimlanes show what kind of work it is. Sequential steps belong in columns, parallel streams in lanes.
- Common lane types are class of service, work type, team or person, customer or project, and epic or feature. Pick one dimension per board.
- An expedite lane needs a strict limit, usually one item, or it quickly becomes the normal way to get work done.
- WIP limits can apply per lane as well as per column; lane limits are a simple way to reserve capacity, for example for improvement work.
- Keep lanes few (two to four is typical), write an explicit policy for each, and measure cycle time and throughput by lane to check they help.

### What is a Kanban swimlane?
A Kanban swimlane is a horizontal row that runs across every column of a Kanban board and holds one category of work. Cards still move left to right through the workflow stages, but they stay in their own lane, so you can see the flow of each category separately and apply different policies, priorities or WIP limits to it.
Picture a board with the columns Ready, In progress, Review and Done. Add three rows labelled Expedite, Standard and Improvement, and you have a grid. Every card sits in one cell: its column says how far along it is, and its lane says what kind of work it is and which rules apply. Most digital boards start with a single default lane; you add lanes only when you need them.
Swimlanes are an optional part of [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/). Kanban University's Official Kanban Guide notes that some boards use horizontal swimlanes to make policies, types of work or classes of service more visible. Nothing in Kanban requires them; they are a visual tool to use when they change how the team acts.

### Swimlanes vs columns
Columns and swimlanes are often confused, especially when people try to show two teams that hand work to each other. The rule of thumb: if work moves from one to the other in sequence, it is a column; if the categories run in parallel, they are lanes.
|  | Columns | Swimlanes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Represent | Stages of the workflow (Ready, Build, Test, Done) | Categories of work (Expedite, Feature, Defect, Client A) |
| Card movement | Cards move through them from left to right | A card normally stays in the same lane |
| WIP limits | The usual place for WIP limits | Optional limits per lane or per lane and column |
| Question answered | How far along is this work? | What kind of work is this, and which rules apply? |
| Wrong use | A column per category of work | A lane per stage, such as separate Development and Testing lanes |
If Development hands items to Testing, they are stages, so make them columns. If Team London and Team New York each work through the same stages in parallel, they can be lanes. See our [guide to Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) for how to design the columns first.

### Why use swimlanes (and when not to)
A single-lane board treats every card the same. Swimlanes help when different kinds of work need different treatment or when you need to see a balance between them.
- **Make priorities explicit.** An expedite lane at the top shows everyone what must be pulled first.
- **Protect capacity.** A lane with its own limit guarantees some time for maintenance, improvement or [technical debt](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/), even when feature demand is high.
- **See the mix of work.** Lanes by work type show at a glance whether defects are crowding out new work.
- **Spot where work piles up.** Lanes by team, client or epic show which stream is stuck.
- **Apply different policies.** Fixed-date items, for example, can be started earlier than standard work.
- **Share one board.** Several small groups can use one board without losing sight of their own work.
You may not need lanes at all. Skip them when all work is treated the same way, the board has only a few cards, or one person works the board, as in [personal Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/personal-kanban/). Every lane adds visual noise, so add one only when it would change a decision.

### Types of Kanban swimlanes
Most boards use one of the types below. Choose one dimension per board; mixing, say, team lanes and priority lanes on the same board makes it unclear where a card belongs. Other categories can be shown with card colours, tags or avatars instead.
| Lane type | Example lanes | Best when | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Class of service | Expedite, Fixed date, Standard, Intangible | Work has different urgency and cost of delay | Expedite becoming the default route |
| Work type | Features, Defects, Maintenance, Improvement | You need a balanced mix of work | Too many fine-grained types |
| Team or person | Design, Content, Development; or one lane per person | Several groups share a board | Silos and individual utilisation over flow |
| Customer or project | Client A, Client B, Internal | Agencies and shared services serving several customers | Lanes multiplying as clients are added |
| Epic or feature | Checkout redesign, Mobile app, Reporting | Large teams building several features in parallel | Long-lived lanes for finished epics |
| Priority | High, Normal, Low | Simple boards without formal classes of service | Everything drifting into High |

#### Swimlanes by class of service
The most powerful lane type, because each lane carries a different policy for how work is selected and handled. It is covered in detail in the next section.

#### Swimlanes by work type
Lanes for features, defects and maintenance make the balance of demand visible. A service team might use Incidents, Requests and Changes. Work-type lanes pair well with lane WIP limits, for example no more than two maintenance items in progress at once.

#### Swimlanes by team or person
Team lanes help when several groups share a board and the same workflow. A lane per person shows who is overloaded, but it can push people towards "my lane" thinking and discourage swarming on blocked work. Many teams show assignees as avatars on the [Kanban cards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-cards/) instead, and keep lanes for something that affects how work is treated.

#### Swimlanes by customer or project
Agencies, consultancies and internal shared services often give each major customer or project its own lane, plus an Internal lane. This makes it easy to show a client their work and to see if one customer is taking more than their share. If you have more than four or five active customers, use card tags and filters instead.

#### Swimlanes by epic or feature
Product teams sometimes give each epic in flight its own lane. You can see which feature is stalled, and lanes can be removed as epics are finished. Keep the number of epics in progress low, and the number of lanes stays low too.

### Classes of service and the expedite lane
A class of service is a set of policies for how a type of work item is treated, based on what happens if it is delayed. Classes of service were popularised by David J. Anderson's Kanban Method, and Kanban University's glossary defines four common archetypes by the impact of delay: **expedite** (high and immediate), **fixed date** (the impact arrives at a specific date), **standard** (typical of current conditions) and **intangible** (unknown, or not felt yet).
| Class | Cost of delay | Typical pull policy | Typical WIP rule | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expedite | High and immediate | Pulled at once, ahead of everything; may interrupt other work | Limit of one across the board | Payment system outage; security breach |
| Fixed date | Low until a date, then high | Started early enough to finish before the date, based on cycle time data | Small limit; reviewed at replenishment | Regulatory change due on a set date; event materials |
| Standard | Steady; rises the longer it waits | Pulled in priority order, first in first out within priority | Most of the board's capacity | New features, routine requests |
| Intangible | Low or unclear now, may rise sharply later | Pulled when there is reserved capacity | Fixed share, such as one or two items | Technical debt, upgrades, process improvements |
Lanes are the clearest way to show classes of service, but not the only one. Some teams use card colours instead, and some flow practitioners prefer no permanent expedite lane at all: urgent items simply breach the WIP limit by explicit, recorded exception. Choose whichever your team will follow consistently.

#### Rules for an expedite lane
1. Define what qualifies in writing, for example "a production outage affecting customers" or "a legal deadline within 48 hours".
2. Name who can authorise an expedite, such as the service owner, rather than anyone who shouts loudest.
3. Limit the lane to one item. A second expedite request waits or is escalated.
4. Let the expedite item break column WIP limits, and agree who drops what to swarm on it.
5. Track how often the lane is used. If it is busy every week, the real problem is in planning or quality, not prioritisation.

#### Fixed-date and intangible lanes
Fixed-date items fail when they are started too late. Use your [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) data to decide when to start: if 85% of similar items finish within 10 working days, start at least 10 working days before the deadline, plus a margin. Intangible work fails the opposite way: it never starts. A lane with a fixed allocation, such as one or two items at all times, keeps it moving without letting it take over.

### WIP limits and swimlanes
Swimlanes give you three ways to limit [work in progress](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/), and you can combine them:
- **Column limits** across all lanes, such as a maximum of six items In progress. This is the standard Kanban approach.
- **Lane limits** across the whole board, such as no more than one Expedite item and two Intangible items anywhere.
- **Cell limits** for a lane within a column, such as a maximum of three Standard items In progress.
Lane limits are also a simple form of capacity allocation. A team that wants roughly 70% of its effort on standard work, 20% on improvement and 10% kept free for urgent work can express that as lane limits that add up to the column limit.
**Worked example (illustrative).** A team of six has an In progress limit of 6. It sets cell limits of 4 for Standard, 1 for Intangible and 1 for Fixed date, with the Expedite lane normally empty. On Tuesday the In progress column holds 4 Standard, 1 Intangible and 1 Fixed date item: the column is full. An outage arrives and is pulled into Expedite. The column now shows 7, one over the limit, which the expedite policy allows. Two developers swarm on the outage; the Standard items they leave stay where they are rather than being replaced. When the outage is fixed, the column drops back to 6 and normal pull resumes. Nobody starts new work while the column is over its limit.
Tip
Lane and cell limits should add up to no more than the column limit, otherwise the column limit stops doing anything. Start with your current average WIP per lane and lower it gradually.

### Worked example: redesigning a team's board with swimlanes
This illustrative example follows a seven-person digital team that builds and runs a customer website. The details are made up to show the method.
**The problem.** The team used a single-lane board with the columns Backlog, Ready, In progress, Review and Done. Urgent fixes kept jumping the queue without anyone seeing it, a fixed-date compliance change was nearly missed, and planned upgrades had not moved in months. In the [replenishment meeting](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/), every conversation turned into an argument about priority.
**The design.** The team chose class of service as its single lane dimension and agreed this layout:
| Lane | Ready | In progress (limit 6) | Review (limit 3) | Policy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expedite | None held | Max 1, may exceed column limit | Reviewed first | Live site down or data at risk; authorised by product lead |
| Fixed date | Max 2 | Max 1 | Shared | Start when the deadline is within the 85th percentile cycle time plus 5 days |
| Standard | Max 6 | Max 4 | Shared | Pulled top to bottom in the order agreed at replenishment |
| Improvement | Max 2 | Max 1 | Shared | Always one item in progress; chosen at the monthly service delivery review |
**What the team watched.** For the next eight weeks the team tracked how often the expedite lane was used, the cycle time of each lane and the age of the oldest improvement item. In this example the expedite lane was used three times, each time for a genuine outage, and the first improvement item, an overdue framework upgrade, was finished within a month. The board also revealed that most "urgent" requests were simply standard work with an impatient requester, which the team handled by publishing a cycle time forecast for standard items.
**What changed later.** After two months the team noticed the Fixed date lane was empty most of the time and merged those items into Standard with a red date flag. Lanes should be reviewed and simplified like any other policy.

### How to set up Kanban swimlanes: step by step
1. **Start with the problem.** Write down what you want swimlanes to fix: urgent work invisible, improvement never done, one client crowding out others. If you cannot name a problem, do not add lanes.
2. **Get the columns right first.** Map your workflow stages as columns. Lanes cannot fix a board whose columns do not match the real process.
3. **Choose one lane dimension.** Pick the category that changes how work is treated, usually class of service or work type. Show other attributes with colours or tags.
4. **Keep it to two to four lanes.** Fewer lanes keep the board readable. Put the most urgent lane at the top, since people scan from the top.
5. **Write a policy for each lane.** State what qualifies, who decides, how items are pulled and any limits. Make the policy visible on the board.
6. **Set lane or cell WIP limits.** Base them on current WIP, make sure they fit within the column limits, and decide how the expedite lane interacts with them.
7. **Move existing cards into lanes.** Do this as a team, so everyone applies the policies the same way.
8. **Measure by lane.** Track cycle time, throughput and item age for each lane from day one.
9. **Review after four to six weeks.** In a retrospective or service delivery review, ask whether each lane changed behaviour. Merge or remove lanes that are empty or ignored.
A free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) is enough to test a lane design on paper or in a spreadsheet before you change your software. If you need to map the process first, start with the [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/).

### Writing swimlane policies
Making policies explicit is one of the core [Kanban practices](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-principles/), and lanes are only useful if everyone knows their rules. Keep each policy to a few lines and display it on the board, next to the lane name. Examples:
- **Expedite:** "Customer-facing outage or security incident only. Authorised by the on-call lead. One item maximum. Anyone may be asked to help."
- **Fixed date:** "Items with a contractual, legal or event date. Card shows the date. Pulled when the date is within our 85th percentile cycle time plus five working days."
- **Standard:** "Pulled from the top of Ready. Order agreed at the weekly replenishment meeting."
- **Improvement:** "At least one and at most two items in progress at all times. Chosen at the monthly review."
- **Client lanes:** "Each client lane has a WIP limit agreed in the contract. New requests beyond the limit wait in Ready."
Review policies when the lane is not behaving as intended. A policy that is broken every week is either wrong or not understood.

### Kanban swimlane examples by team
| Team | Columns | Lanes | Why it works |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Software product team | Ready, Build, Code review, Test, Done | Expedite, Features, Defects, Tech debt | Shows the balance of work and protects debt reduction |
| IT service desk | New, Triage, In progress, Waiting on user, Resolved | Incidents, Service requests, Changes | Each type has different targets and handling |
| Marketing team | Briefed, Drafting, Review, Approved, Published | Campaign A, Campaign B, Always-on content | Shows each campaign's progress against its launch date |
| Agency or consultancy | Requested, In progress, Client review, Delivered | Client lanes plus Internal | Makes each client's queue and share of capacity visible |
| HR or operations | To do, In progress, Waiting, Done | Fixed date (payroll, compliance), Standard, Improvement | Protects deadline work without starving improvement |
For more board layouts, see our [Kanban boards guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/), which includes example boards for different teams.

### Measuring flow by swimlane
The only way to know whether lanes help is to measure them. Most [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) become more useful when you split them by lane:
- **Cycle time by lane.** Expedite items should be fast; if standard items are slowing down, expedites may be interrupting too often.
- **[Throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) mix.** Count finished items per lane each week. This shows whether your intended allocation, such as 20% improvement, is really happening.
- **Item age.** A [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) split by lane shows intangible work quietly stalling.
- **Cumulative flow.** A [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) per lane shows whether one stream is building a queue.
- **Service level expectations.** Publish a forecast per class, such as "85% of standard items finish within 12 days", much like an internal [service level agreement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/service-level-agreement-sla/).
Blockers are worth tracking by lane too. If one client lane or work type collects most blockers, [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/) will show you why.

### Common swimlane mistakes
- **Too many lanes.** Eight lanes on a small board hide the flow. Merge until each lane changes behaviour.
- **Lanes for workflow stages.** Development and Testing are steps, so they belong in columns.
- **Mixing dimensions.** Team lanes and priority lanes on one board leave nobody sure where a card goes.
- **An unlimited expedite lane.** If anything can be expedited, everything will be, and standard work stalls.
- **Lanes without policies.** A lane name alone does not tell people how to treat the work.
- **Lane per person by default.** It shows workload but discourages collaboration. Use avatars unless individual lanes solve a real problem.
- **Never removing lanes.** Empty lanes for finished epics or former clients add clutter. Review lanes regularly.
- **Ignoring total WIP.** Lane limits that add up to more than the column limit quietly raise work in progress.

### Swimlanes in Kanban software
Most Kanban tools now support swimlanes, though the options differ. Check the current documentation for your plan before you design around a feature.
| Tool | Swimlane support |
| --- | --- |
| [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) | Board view works as a Kanban board on every plan and can group horizontal swimlanes and columns by single- or multi-select custom fields, so you can create lanes for class of service, work type or client (check which custom field options your plan includes) |
| [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) | Board swimlanes by assignee, epic or priority, alongside column WIP limits and quick filters |
| [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) | Swimlanes on Board view since July 2025 on paid plans, grouped by sections, assignees or single-select custom fields |
| [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) | Swimlanes on Board view to group tasks by category or team, plus WIP limits per column |
| [Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/) | No native swimlanes on the base board; teams use labels, separate lists or Power-Ups |
| Azure Boards | Named swimlanes (up to 50 per board) and swimlane rules that route items into lanes automatically |
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is a good fit for teams that want class-of-service or client lanes driven by custom fields across several projects, with dashboards on top. Jira suits software teams already working in epics, and Trello suits small teams happy to use labels rather than lanes. Compare the options in our [project management tools comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/compare/).

### Kanban swimlanes vs swimlane diagrams
The word swimlane also appears in process mapping. A [swimlane diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/swimlane-diagram/) is a flowchart divided into lanes by role or department, showing who does each step of a process and where hand-offs happen. A Kanban swimlane is a row on a live board that tracks real work items as they move. The diagram describes a process; the board manages the work flowing through it. Mapping the process with a swimlane diagram first is often a good way to choose your Kanban columns.
Read our [guide to WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) next to set the column limits your swimlanes will sit within.
