### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a Kanban swimlane?**
A horizontal row across a Kanban board that groups cards of one category, such as urgent work, a work type, a team or a client. Cards move left to right through the columns but stay in their lane.

**Q: What are the common types of Kanban swimlanes?**
Lanes by class of service (expedite, fixed date, standard, intangible), by work type, by team or person, by customer or project, by epic or feature, and by priority.

**Q: What is the difference between a Kanban swimlane and a column?**
Columns show the stages of the workflow, so cards move through them. Swimlanes group cards by category, so a card normally stays in the same lane.

**Q: How many swimlanes should a Kanban board have?**
As few as possible, usually two to four. Add a lane only if it changes how the team treats the work, and remove lanes that stay empty.

**Q: What is an expedite swimlane?**
A lane for urgent items with a high and immediate cost of delay, such as an outage. Items are pulled ahead of everything else, and the lane is usually limited to one item.

**Q: What are classes of service in Kanban?**
Sets of policies for how different work is treated, based on the impact of delay. Common archetypes are expedite, fixed date, standard and intangible, and many teams give each its own lane.

**Q: Should Kanban swimlanes have WIP limits?**
They can. Lane or cell limits reserve capacity for certain work, such as improvement items, but they should add up to no more than the column limit.

**Q: Should I use a swimlane for each team member?**
Lanes per person show who is overloaded but can create silos and discourage swarming. Most teams prefer avatars on cards and lanes by work type or class of service.

**Q: Why give intangible work its own swimlane?**
Intangible items, such as technical debt or upgrades, have no deadline, so they tend never to start. A lane with a fixed allocation keeps some capacity on them.

**Q: Does Trello or Jira have swimlanes?**
Jira boards support swimlanes by assignee, epic or priority. Trello has no native swimlanes on the base board, so teams use labels, separate lists or Power-Ups.

**Q: Can a card move from one swimlane to another?**
Yes, if its category changes, for example when a standard item becomes urgent and is formally expedited. Record the reason, as frequent lane changes suggest unclear policies.

**Q: When should you not use Kanban swimlanes?**
When all work is treated the same way, the board is small, or one person works it. Lanes add visual noise, so add them only when they change decisions.

**Q: Is a Kanban swimlane the same as a swimlane diagram?**
No. A swimlane diagram is a process flowchart split into lanes by role. A Kanban swimlane is a row on a board that tracks live work items.

# Kanban vs Agile: Differences, Overlap and When to Use Each

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-agile/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Kanban vs Agile explained: Agile is a mindset, Kanban is a flow method that applies it. Compare principles, boards and metrics, with a worked example.


## Kanban vs Agile: Differences, Overlap and When to Use Each
Kanban vs Agile is not a choice between two rival methods: Agile is a set of values and principles for delivering work in small increments and adapting to change, while Kanban is a flow-based method that many teams use to work in an Agile way. The real decision is between Kanban's continuous flow and time-boxed Agile frameworks such as Scrum. This guide explains how the two relate, compares boards, planning and metrics, works through a real-world style example and gives you a step-by-step process for choosing.
- Published 9 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agile is a philosophy set out in the 2001 Agile Manifesto; Kanban is a method for managing and improving the flow of work. They sit at different levels, so they are not alternatives.
- Kanban comes from Lean and the Toyota Production System, not from the Agile software movement, but it fits the Manifesto's values closely and is widely counted as an Agile approach.
- There are two main definitions of Kanban today: the Kanban Method (Kanban University) and The Kanban Guide (Vacanti and Coleman, edition 2025.5). Both centre on visualising work, limiting work in progress and improving flow.
- The practical comparison is flow vs time-box: Kanban has no sprints or prescribed roles and measures cycle time and throughput, while Scrum uses fixed Sprints, three accountabilities and Sprint Goals.
- Kanban suits work that arrives unpredictably or continuously; time-boxed frameworks suit a dedicated team building a product towards planned goals. Many teams combine the two.

### Kanban vs Agile: the short answer
**Agile** is a mindset for delivering value in small, frequent increments, collaborating closely with customers and adapting the plan as you learn. **Kanban** is a method for visualising work, limiting how much is in progress and improving the flow of items from request to delivery. Agile tells you what to value; Kanban gives you one practical way to act on those values.
|  | Agile | Kanban |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A set of values and principles | A method for managing and improving flow |
| Defined by | The Agile Manifesto (2001): 4 values, 12 principles | The Kanban Method (Kanban University) and The Kanban Guide (edition 2025.5) |
| Roots | Lightweight software development methods of the 1990s | Lean thinking and the Toyota Production System |
| Tells you | What to value and why | How to see, limit and improve the work in your system |
| Relationship | The umbrella | One of the approaches used under it |
So the real question is not Agile or Kanban, but continuous flow, fixed Sprints, or a mix.

### What is Agile?
Agile is an approach to product and project work that delivers in short cycles, uses feedback to steer and treats the plan as something to update rather than defend. It was named in February 2001, when 17 software practitioners wrote the [Agile Manifesto](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-manifesto-values-and-principles/). The Manifesto values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan.
Twelve principles add detail. Among them: satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery; welcome changing requirements, even late in development; deliver working software frequently, preferring shorter timescales; maintain a sustainable pace indefinitely; and, at regular intervals, reflect on how to become more effective and adjust.
Just as important is what Agile does **not** contain. It prescribes no roles, meetings, iteration length, board or metric. Those come from the frameworks and methods that put Agile into practice, including Scrum, Kanban, Extreme Programming (XP), Lean software development, Scrumban and scaled frameworks such as SAFe.

### What is Kanban?
"Kanban" is Japanese for signboard or visual signal. At Toyota, from the late 1940s onwards, cards travelled with parts and signalled when an upstream process should make more, so that production followed real consumption rather than a forecast. That is the origin of the **pull system**, explained in our guide to [pull vs push systems](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/).
Applied to knowledge work, Kanban grew from David J. Anderson's work with software teams, starting with a project at Microsoft in 2004 and continuing at Corbis, and was described in his 2010 book *Kanban: Successful Evolutionary Change for Your Technology Business*. Today two well-known sources define it.

#### The Kanban Method (Kanban University)
Kanban University's official guide describes Kanban as a method for defining, managing and improving services that deliver knowledge work. It sets out three **change management principles** (start with what you do now; agree to pursue improvement through evolutionary change; encourage acts of leadership at all levels), three **service delivery principles** (understand and focus on customer needs and expectations; manage the work and let people self-organise around it; regularly review the network of services and its policies) and **six general practices**:
1. Visualise the work and the workflow.
2. Limit work in progress (WIP).
3. Manage flow.
4. Make policies explicit.
5. Implement feedback loops, such as a daily team Kanban meeting and regular replenishment and retrospectives.
6. Improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally.

#### The Kanban Guide (Vacanti and Coleman)
The Kanban Guide, written by Daniel Vacanti and John Coleman (current edition 2025.5, May 2025), defines Kanban as a strategy for optimising the flow of value through a process. It has three practices: defining and visualising a workflow, actively managing items in a workflow, and improving a workflow. It requires four flow measures: **WIP** (items started but not finished), **throughput** (items finished per unit of time), **work item age** (time since an unfinished item started) and **cycle time** (time from start to finish).
The two differ in emphasis but agree on the core: make work visible, limit WIP so that work is pulled rather than pushed, and use data to improve. Neither prescribes roles, Sprints or estimation. For the principles in more detail, see [Kanban principles and practices](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-principles/), or start with [what is Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/).

### Is Kanban Agile?
In practice, yes: Kanban is almost always listed among Agile approaches, and most Agile teams use a Kanban board at some level. The nuance is that Kanban was not created from the Agile Manifesto. Its roots are Lean manufacturing, and The Kanban Guide does not mention Agile at all; it draws on Lean principles, systems thinking and the Toyota Production System. The Kanban Method describes itself as a way to manage any professional service, Agile or not.
It is accurate to say Kanban is a Lean method that is fully compatible with, and widely used for, Agile ways of working.
|  | Lean | Agile | Kanban |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Origin | Toyota Production System; named "Lean" in the late 1980s | Agile Manifesto, 2001 | Toyota kanban cards; adapted for knowledge work in the 2000s |
| Core idea | Maximise customer value, remove waste, create flow | Deliver small increments, collaborate, adapt to change | Visualise work, limit WIP, manage and improve flow |
| Unit of improvement | The whole value stream | The team and its product | The workflow (service) the team runs |

### How Kanban puts the 12 Agile principles into practice
A useful way to judge whether a method is Agile is to check it against the twelve principles. The table below is our own mapping, not part of either official document. The third column shows where Kanban says little and you need to add a practice of your own.
| Agile principle (summarised) | How Kanban supports it | What you may need to add |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Early and continuous delivery of value | Items flow to Done one at a time; nothing waits for the end of a cycle | A clear Definition of Done so "done" means usable |
| 2. Welcome changing requirements | Anything not yet past the commitment point can be reordered at the next replenishment | A product owner or service manager who decides order |
| 3. Deliver frequently, shorter timescales preferred | Cycle time is measured and reduced; small items are encouraged | Technical ability to release often (see continuous delivery) |
| 4. Business and developers work together daily | Daily Kanban meeting at the board; stakeholders can see the board | An explicit invitation for stakeholders to attend reviews |
| 5. Build projects around motivated individuals | "Manage the work, let people self-organise around it" | Little beyond this; it is close to the Manifesto |
| 6. Face-to-face conversation | Not addressed directly | Team norms for conversation, especially for remote teams |
| 7. Working software is the measure of progress | Throughput counts finished items, not effort | Avoid counting partly done work as progress |
| 8. Sustainable pace | WIP limits stop overload and constant task switching | Respect the limits under pressure |
| 9. Technical excellence and good design | Not addressed directly | Engineering practices such as testing and refactoring (XP) |
| 10. Simplicity: maximise work not done | Explicit policies and a visible backlog make low-value work easy to drop | Regular backlog pruning |
| 11. Self-organising teams | People pull work; no one assigns tasks to full queues | Agreement on how the team handles expedites |
| 12. Regular reflection and adjustment | Feedback loops and "evolve experimentally" | A fixed retrospective cadence so improvement is not skipped |
Tip
Two principles, face-to-face conversation and technical excellence, are where Kanban teams most often fall short. Kanban is a flow method, not an engineering method, so software teams usually pair it with practices such as automated testing and continuous integration.

### Kanban vs time-boxed Agile frameworks: key differences
Because Agile itself prescribes no practices, the meaningful comparison is between Kanban and the time-boxed frameworks people usually mean by "Agile", most often Scrum. The Scrum column below follows the 2020 Scrum Guide.
| Aspect | Kanban | Time-boxed Agile (e.g. Scrum) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cadence | Continuous flow; meetings on a cadence the team chooses | Fixed-length Sprints of one month or less, back to back |
| Planning | Replenishment as often as needed; just-in-time | Sprint Planning at the start of each Sprint |
| Commitment | Per item, at the commitment point | To a Sprint Goal for the whole Sprint |
| Roles | None prescribed; keep your current roles | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers |
| Change during a cycle | New items can enter whenever capacity frees up | Scope can be renegotiated, but changes that endanger the Sprint Goal are avoided |
| Limiting work | Explicit WIP limits per column or per system | Indirectly, by what fits in the Sprint |
| Estimation | Optional; many teams use item counts and right-sizing | Common (story points), though not required by the Scrum Guide |
| Core metrics | WIP, throughput, cycle time, work item age | Velocity, Sprint burndown, Sprint Goal success |
| Board | Persistent; reflects the real workflow | Often reset each Sprint |
| Release | Whenever an item is done | At least one usable Increment per Sprint; can release more often |
| Starting point | Your current process, changed gradually | Adopt the framework's roles and events |
| Best-fit work | Unpredictable arrivals, support, operations, mixed requests | New product or feature development by a dedicated team |
For a full side-by-side, including ceremonies and boards, read [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/).

### Agile (Scrum) board vs Kanban board
Both boards show cards moving left to right, which is why they are often confused. The difference is in the rules, not the columns.
- **Lifespan:** a Scrum board usually holds the current Sprint Backlog and is cleared at the end of each Sprint. A Kanban board is persistent: items stay until they are done, however long that takes.
- **WIP limits:** a Kanban board shows a limit on columns or on the whole system. A Scrum board normally has none, because the Sprint itself caps the work.
- **Commitment point:** a Kanban board marks the point where an option becomes a commitment (often between "Options" and "Ready"). On a Scrum board the commitment happens at Sprint Planning.
- **Explicit policies:** Kanban boards often show entry and exit criteria for each column, such as "Ready = acceptance criteria agreed".
- **Classes of service:** Kanban teams may add an expedite lane or colour code for fixed-date items. See [Kanban swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/).

#### Example layout
| Options | Ready (limit 4) | In progress (limit 3) | Review (limit 2) | Done |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ideas and requests not yet committed | Agreed and prioritised; pulled from here | Being worked on | Waiting for check or sign-off | Delivered to the customer |
Learn more in our guides to [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) and [Scrum boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/), or set one up quickly with the free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/).

### Agile metrics vs Kanban metrics
Time-boxed teams tend to measure how much they finish per Sprint; Kanban teams measure how long items take and how many finish per week. Both are useful, and many teams track both.
| Metric | Typical in | What it tells you | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Velocity | Scrum | Story points completed per Sprint, used for forecasting | Not comparable between teams; easy to inflate |
| Sprint burndown | Scrum | Work remaining in the Sprint | Says nothing about flow after the Sprint |
| WIP | Kanban | How many items are started but not finished | Count items, not people |
| Throughput | Kanban | Items finished per week | Needs items of broadly similar size |
| Cycle time | Kanban | Time from start to finish for each item | Use percentiles, not only the average |
| Work item age | Kanban | How long unfinished items have been in progress | Old items are your early warning |

#### Worked example: Little's Law
Little's Law, first proved by John Little in 1961, links three of the Kanban measures: **average cycle time = average WIP / average throughput**. Suppose your team usually has 12 items in progress and finishes 4 a week. On average an item takes 12 / 4 = **3 weeks** from start to finish. If you cap WIP at 6 and throughput stays at 4 a week, average cycle time falls to 6 / 4 = **1.5 weeks**. Nobody worked faster; items simply spent less time waiting.
The law holds over the long run only when the system is stable (roughly as many items start as finish, and items are not abandoned), so use it to understand your system rather than to promise dates. Compare with the [Agile velocity chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/) and [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/).

### Worked example: one team, two Agile ways
The following example is illustrative: the team and figures are invented to show the mechanics, not taken from a study.
A five-person internal digital team at a regional housing association looks after the tenant website and portal. Its work is a mix: about 60% planned improvements (a new repairs-booking journey, accessibility fixes) and about 40% unplanned requests (content changes, urgent bugs, requests from the call centre).

#### Version A: two-week Sprints
- Sprint Planning every other Monday picks enough planned work to fill about 80% of capacity, leaving a buffer for urgent requests.
- Urgent bugs interrupt the Sprint two or three times a week. The team often misses its Sprint Goal and the buffer is either too big or too small.
- Content requests from the call centre wait up to two weeks for the next Sprint unless someone treats them as urgent.
- The repairs-booking journey gets focused attention, and the Sprint Review gives tenants' representatives a regular slot to see progress.

#### Version B: Kanban
- Board columns: Options, Ready (limit 5), Build (limit 3), Test (limit 2), Done.
- Two classes of service: **Expedite** (one item at a time, may exceed limits) for portal outages, and **Standard** for everything else.
- Cadences: 15-minute daily meeting at the board; weekly replenishment with the service manager to choose what moves into Ready; monthly service delivery review with call-centre and housing leads; monthly retrospective.
- Planned and unplanned work share one board, so the trade-off between them is visible and decided at replenishment rather than in the middle of a Sprint.

#### What six weeks of data showed
| Measure | Sprints (weeks 1 to 6) | Kanban (weeks 7 to 12) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Average WIP | 11 items | 6 items |
| Throughput | 5 items a week | 5.5 items a week |
| Average cycle time | about 2.2 weeks | about 1.1 weeks |
| Content requests: typical wait | up to 2 weeks | 2 to 4 days |
| Repairs-booking journey | steady progress, visible each Sprint | progress slowed in week 8 until the team reserved 2 of the 3 Build slots for planned work |
The lesson is not that Kanban "won". Kanban suited this team's mixed, interrupt-driven work, but it needed an explicit policy (reserving Build capacity) to protect the planned project, something Sprints had provided for free. A team whose work was almost all planned product development would probably have kept Sprints. Plan replenishment and reviews using our guide to [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/).

### When to use Kanban (and when a time-boxed framework fits better)
| Situation | Usually a good fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IT support, service desk or operations | Kanban | Work arrives continuously and urgently; flow handles it without breaking a Sprint |
| A dedicated team building a new product | Scrum or another time-boxed framework | Sprint Goals and regular reviews give focus and a predictable feedback rhythm |
| Marketing, HR or finance teams new to Agile | Kanban | Starts from the current process; no new roles to introduce |
| A Scrum team constantly interrupted by urgent work | Scrumban or Kanban | Keeps some structure but adds WIP limits and flow |
| Maintenance of a mature product with frequent small releases | Kanban | Items are small and independent; continuous delivery fits |
| Many teams working on one large solution | A scaled framework, often with Kanban at portfolio level | Needs shared planning across teams; SAFe, for example, uses a Portfolio Kanban |
None of these is a rule, which is why the next section gives you a process rather than a verdict.

### How to choose: a step-by-step decision process
1. **Describe your work.** Mark the last 30 items your team finished as planned or unplanned, and note how urgent each was on arrival.
2. **Check how predictable arrivals are.** If more than about a third were unplanned and needed doing within days, Sprints will be interrupted often.
3. **Check whether you need a shared goal per cycle.** One product heading for a release benefits from a Sprint Goal; a team serving many requesters often does not.
4. **Look at your stakeholders.** Do they want regular review dates or quick turnaround on individual requests?
5. **Consider how much change you can absorb.** Scrum adds new accountabilities and events; Kanban starts with what you do now.
6. **Score the options** below, choose, and agree a date (say, eight weeks out) to review the data and adjust.

#### Decision scorecard
Score each statement from 1 (disagree) to 5 (agree). A higher left-hand total points to Kanban, a higher right-hand total to a time-boxed framework; close scores suggest Scrumban.
| Points towards Kanban | Score | Points towards time-boxed Agile | Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Work arrives unpredictably | 1 to 5 | Work is mostly planned weeks ahead | 1 to 5 |
| Items are small and independent | 1 to 5 | Items combine into a larger product increment | 1 to 5 |
| We serve many requesters | 1 to 5 | We serve one product and one product owner | 1 to 5 |
| We want to change our process gradually | 1 to 5 | We are ready to adopt new roles and events | 1 to 5 |
| Fast turnaround matters more than a fixed cadence | 1 to 5 | A fixed rhythm of review and planning matters most | 1 to 5 |
If you choose time-boxing, our [what is a Sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/) guide and free [Sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) will help you start.

### How to introduce Kanban in an Agile team
1. **Map your current workflow.** Write down the real stages work goes through today, including waiting stages such as "awaiting approval".
2. **Build the board.** One column per stage, plus Options and Done. Put every item currently in progress on it, including the ones nobody likes to admit to.
3. **Agree the commitment point and Definition of Done.** Decide where an idea becomes a commitment and what "done" means for your customers.
4. **Set initial WIP limits.** A common starting point is around the number of people working in a stage, or slightly lower. Treat the first limits as an experiment.
5. **Make policies explicit.** Write entry and exit criteria for columns, how to handle expedites, and how blocked items are shown.
6. **Start the cadences.** A short daily meeting at the board, a replenishment meeting, and a regular review and retrospective.
7. **Measure from day one.** Record start and finish dates for every item so that WIP, throughput, cycle time and work item age are available after a few weeks.
8. **Improve one thing at a time.** Use the data to find the biggest queue or most frequent blocker, change one policy, and check the effect.
Track ageing items with a [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/).

### Combining Kanban with other Agile frameworks
Kanban is designed to be applied to an existing process, so it combines readily with other approaches.
- **Scrum with Kanban practices:** a Scrum team keeps its Sprints, roles and events but adds WIP limits, flow metrics and explicit policies to the Sprint Backlog. This is permitted by the Scrum Guide, which leaves the team free to choose its own practices.
- **Scrumban:** a hybrid that started as a way to move from Scrum to Kanban (described by Corey Ladas in 2008) and is now often used as a lasting mix of planning cadence and flow. See [Kanban vs Scrumban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrumban/).
- **Scaled frameworks:** SAFe uses Kanban systems to manage the flow of epics at portfolio level, alongside time-boxed iterations for teams. See [SAFe](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/).
For the full family of approaches, read [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/), and for the Scrum side specifically, [Agile vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-scrum/).

### Common misconceptions and mistakes
- **"We have a board, so we do Kanban."** A board without WIP limits, explicit policies and flow measurement is a visual to-do list. Useful, but not Kanban.
- **"Kanban means no planning."** Kanban plans continuously through replenishment and uses throughput data to forecast. It simply does not tie planning to a fixed time-box.
- **"Kanban means no deadlines."** Fixed-date work is handled as a class of service and prioritised so that it finishes in time.
- **Setting WIP limits and then ignoring them.** If the limit is always exceeded, either change it deliberately or treat the breach as a signal to swarm on blocked work.
- **Measuring people instead of flow.** Cycle time and throughput describe the system. Using them to rank individuals encourages gaming and hides problems.
- **Dropping reflection.** Without Sprints forcing a retrospective, some Kanban teams stop improving. Put a retrospective in the calendar.

### Advantages and limitations of Kanban as an Agile approach
| Advantages | Limitations |
| --- | --- |
| Starts from your current process, so it is easy to adopt | Gives little guidance on roles; unclear ownership of priorities can cause problems |
| Handles unpredictable and urgent work without breaking a cycle | Without a Sprint Goal, a team can lose focus on a larger objective |
| WIP limits reduce overload and shorten cycle time | Requires discipline to respect limits under pressure |
| Flow metrics give realistic forecasts based on real data | Forecasts need several weeks of data before they are reliable |
| Works for any type of knowledge work, not only software | Silent on engineering quality; software teams need to add practices |
If you are weighing Kanban against a traditional plan-driven approach instead, read [Kanban vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-waterfall/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Kanban Agile?**
Yes, in practice. Kanban is usually listed among Agile approaches because it delivers value continuously, welcomes changing priorities and builds in regular reflection. Strictly, it comes from Lean manufacturing rather than the Agile Manifesto, so it is best described as a Lean method that fits Agile values.

**Q: What is the difference between Kanban, Agile and Scrum?**
Agile is the philosophy: four values and twelve principles. Scrum and Kanban are two ways to apply it. Scrum uses fixed-length Sprints, three accountabilities and five events; Kanban uses continuous flow, WIP limits and flow metrics, without prescribed roles or Sprints.

**Q: Does Kanban have sprints?**
No. Kanban uses continuous flow: items are pulled when there is capacity and released when they are done. Teams still hold regular meetings, such as replenishment and reviews, but they are not tied to a delivery time-box. If you want Sprints with Kanban practices, look at Scrumban.

**Q: Which is better, Agile or Kanban?**
Neither, because they are not alternatives. Kanban is one way of being Agile. The useful question is whether continuous flow (Kanban) or fixed time-boxes (such as Scrum) suit your work better; the decision process above helps you answer it.

**Q: Is Kanban Agile or Lean?**
Both. Kanban's origins are in the Toyota Production System and Lean thinking, and The Kanban Guide does not mention Agile. Because it shares Agile's focus on customer value, feedback and improvement, it is widely used and taught as an Agile approach too.

**Q: Is Kanban a methodology or a framework?**
It is usually called a method: the Kanban Method. It provides principles and practices that you apply to your existing process, rather than a complete framework of roles and events. The Kanban Guide calls it a strategy for optimising the flow of value.

**Q: Does Kanban have roles?**
Neither the Kanban Method nor The Kanban Guide requires roles. Some teams use optional roles such as a service request manager (who orders incoming work) and a service delivery manager (who looks after flow), but you can keep your existing job titles.

**Q: Can you use Kanban without Scrum?**
Yes. Many teams practise Agile using Kanban alone. Kanban needs a visual workflow, WIP limits, explicit policies and feedback loops, none of which depends on Scrum.

**Q: Is a Kanban board in Jira or Trello automatically Agile?**
No. A tool's board view is a way of displaying work. It becomes Kanban when you add WIP limits, explicit policies and flow measurement, and it supports Agile when the team uses it to deliver small increments and adapt based on feedback.

**Q: Is Kanban iterative?**
Kanban is incremental and continuous rather than iterative in fixed cycles. Each item is delivered when finished, and the process is improved through regular feedback loops.

**Q: Can non-software teams use Kanban as their Agile approach?**
Yes. Marketing, HR, finance, legal, operations and construction teams often use Kanban as their entry point to Agile because it starts with their current process and needs no new roles or Sprints.

# Kanban vs Scrum: Key Differences, Examples and How to Choose

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Kanban vs Scrum compared: cadence, roles, planning, WIP limits and metrics, the same team run both ways, a scoring checklist and how to switch.


## Kanban vs Scrum: Key Differences, Examples and How to Choose
Kanban vs Scrum is a choice between continuous flow and fixed Sprints: Kanban manages a steady stream of work by visualising it and limiting work in progress, while Scrum delivers in Sprints of one month or less with three defined accountabilities and five events. Neither is better in general. This guide compares them point by point, runs the same team both ways with real numbers, and gives you a checklist for choosing and step-by-step guidance for switching.
- Published 8 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Kanban is a flow strategy: visualise the workflow, limit work in progress (WIP) and improve flow. Scrum is a framework of fixed-length Sprints with a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and Developers.
- Scrum commits to a Sprint Goal and protects it during the Sprint. Kanban makes no batch commitment, so the team can re-prioritise anything not yet started at any time.
- Scrum limits work through the Sprint Backlog; Kanban limits it with explicit WIP limits on each column or on the whole board.
- Scrum teams often track velocity and burndown; Kanban teams track throughput, cycle time, work item age and cumulative flow.
- Choose Kanban for unpredictable, mixed-size or service work; choose Scrum for a dedicated team building a product under uncertainty.
- You can combine them: many Scrum teams add WIP limits and flow metrics, and the hybrid known as Scrumban sits between the two.

### Kanban vs Scrum: what is the difference?
**The main difference between Kanban and Scrum is how they organise time.** Scrum divides work into fixed-length Sprints, each with a goal, planning, a review and a retrospective, and defines three accountabilities. Kanban has no Sprints and no required roles: work flows continuously across a board, and WIP limits control how much is in progress.
Both are Agile in spirit, draw on Lean thinking and rely on transparency and frequent inspection, which is why teams often mix them. The differences matter most when work is interrupted, when priorities change daily, or when stakeholders want a fixed rhythm of reviews.

### Kanban at a glance
Kanban began in Toyota's production system and was adapted for knowledge work in the 2000s. Two sources define it today:
- **The Kanban Guide (Edition 2025.5)** describes Kanban as a strategy for optimising the flow of value. It has three practices (define and visualise the workflow, actively manage items in the workflow, improve the workflow) and four flow measures: WIP, throughput, work item age and cycle time.
- **The Kanban Method from Kanban University** starts with what you do now, respects current roles and adds six general practices, such as making policies explicit and implementing feedback loops, plus a set of optional meetings called cadences.
Neither requires new job titles or iterations. Our guides to [what Kanban is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) and the [Kanban principles and practices](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-principles/) cover each element.

### Scrum at a glance
Scrum is defined by the 2020 Scrum Guide, which is still the current version. A Scrum Team of typically ten or fewer people delivers a usable Increment in each Sprint of one month or less. The framework has:
- **Three accountabilities:** the Product Owner, who maximises value and orders the Product Backlog; the Scrum Master, who establishes Scrum and helps the team improve; and the Developers, who create the Increment.
- **Five events:** the Sprint, Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective.
- **Three artifacts, each with a commitment:** the Product Backlog (Product Goal), the Sprint Backlog (Sprint Goal) and the Increment (Definition of Done).
Story points, velocity and burndown charts are common Scrum practices, but the Scrum Guide does not require them. See [what Scrum is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) and [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) for the detail.

### Kanban vs Scrum comparison table
| Aspect | Kanban | Scrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Flow strategy or method applied to your existing process | Framework with defined events, accountabilities and artifacts |
| Defining guide | Kanban Guide (2025.5); Kanban Method from Kanban University | Scrum Guide (2020) |
| Cadence | Continuous flow; meetings on a cadence that suits the team | Fixed-length Sprints of one month or less |
| Roles | None required; some organisations add a Service Request Manager and Service Delivery Manager | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers |
| Planning | Replenishment when capacity frees up or on a regular schedule | Sprint Planning at the start of every Sprint |
| Commitment | Service level expectation for each item; no batch commitment | Sprint Goal for the Sprint |
| Change | Anything not yet started can be re-prioritised at any time | Sprint Goal is protected; scope can be renegotiated with the Product Owner |
| Limiting WIP | Explicit WIP limits per column, lane or board | Implicit, through the size of the Sprint Backlog |
| Estimation | Optional; many teams right-size items instead | Optional, though many teams use story points |
| Board | Persistent; items flow across it indefinitely | Usually reset or re-scoped each Sprint |
| Typical metrics | Throughput, cycle time, work item age, WIP, cumulative flow | Velocity, Sprint burndown or burnup, Sprint Goal success |
| Forecasting | From throughput and cycle time history, often with Monte Carlo | From average velocity across recent Sprints |
| Delivery | Whenever an item is ready | At least one usable Increment per Sprint; release can happen any time |
| Team | Can be shared specialists or a whole service | Dedicated, cross-functional, self-managing |
| Best for | Support, operations, maintenance, marketing and other variable work | New product development under uncertainty |

### What Kanban and Scrum have in common
The two approaches share more than many comparisons suggest. Both:
- **Make work visible**, usually on a board, so problems surface early.
- **Use pull**: people take new work when they have capacity.
- **Limit work in progress**, explicitly in Kanban and through the Sprint Backlog in Scrum.
- **Rely on empiricism**: decisions follow what the team observes, not a detailed long-range plan.
- **Build in improvement** through retrospectives, reviews and feedback loops.
- **Favour small batches and frequent delivery** to reduce risk and speed up feedback.

### The key differences explained

#### Cadence: Sprints versus continuous flow
Scrum's Sprint is a container for all other events, commonly one or two weeks long, so the team plans, reviews and improves on a predictable rhythm. Kanban has no container: items enter and leave one at a time, and the team sets separate rhythms for replenishing, reviewing and improving.

#### Roles and accountabilities
Scrum establishes three accountabilities from day one, which usually means appointing a Product Owner and a Scrum Master. Kanban keeps existing roles. Some mature Kanban systems name a Service Request Manager and a Service Delivery Manager, but neither is required.

#### Planning and commitment
In [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/), the Scrum Team agrees a Sprint Goal and selects items from the [Product Backlog](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/product-backlog/) that it forecasts it can complete. Kanban replaces this with replenishment: when the Ready column runs low, the team or its requesters choose the next items. The commitment is per item, often expressed as a service level expectation such as 85% of items finished within eight working days.

#### How each handles change
During a Scrum Sprint, no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal, although scope can be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as the team learns. New ideas go into the Product Backlog for a future Sprint. In Kanban, anything not yet started can be re-ordered at any time, and an urgent item can enter an expedite lane straight away.

#### How work in progress is limited
Scrum limits work by limiting what goes into the Sprint. Within the Sprint, nothing stops five Developers starting eight items. Kanban sets explicit [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/), for example a maximum of three items in Testing. When a column is full, people help finish existing work instead of starting more.

#### Meetings and cadences
Kanban is sometimes described as having no meetings. That is not accurate: the Kanban Method describes seven cadences, but none is mandatory and their frequency is up to you.
| Purpose | Scrum event | Kanban cadence (Kanban Method) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily coordination | Daily Scrum, 15 minutes | Kanban meeting, daily, about 15 minutes |
| Choosing work | Sprint Planning, up to 8 hours for a one-month Sprint | Replenishment meeting, often weekly or when Ready runs low |
| Reviewing results | Sprint Review, up to 4 hours for a one-month Sprint | Service delivery review and delivery planning meeting |
| Improving the process | Sprint Retrospective, up to 3 hours for a one-month Sprint | Operations review, risk review and team retrospectives |
| Direction | Product Goal, managed by the Product Owner | Strategy review, often quarterly |
Our guides to [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/) and [Scrum ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-ceremonies/) give agendas and timings.

### Kanban board vs Scrum board
Both boards show cards in columns, so they can look identical. The rules behind them differ:
| Feature | Kanban board | Scrum board |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | All work flowing through the team's process | The Sprint Backlog for the current Sprint |
| Lifespan | Persistent | Cleared or re-scoped at the end of each Sprint |
| Columns | Every real step, such as Ready, Build, Review, Test, Done | Often simpler: To do, In progress, Done |
| WIP limits | Shown on each column or lane | Uncommon, though allowed |
| Swimlanes | Often used for classes of service, such as Expedite | Often used per user story |
| Ownership | The team, with explicit policies | The Developers |
Our guides to [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) and [Scrum boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) show more layouts, and the free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) gives you WIP limits ready to edit.

### Worked example: one team, run both ways
To see the differences in practice, follow one team through both approaches. **This example is illustrative; the team and figures are invented to show the mechanics.**
A seven-person team builds and supports a customer billing portal. It has a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and five Developers. Most work is planned feature development, but customers also raise urgent production issues, on average three or four every two weeks.

#### The Scrum version
The team runs two-week Sprints (ten working days). Its velocity over the last four Sprints was 27, 31, 24 and 30 points, an average of 28. Here is Sprint 14:
| Day | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Sprint Planning: Sprint Goal is "Customers can update their billing details online". The team selects 10 items totalling 29 points. |
| 3 | Urgent production issue 1 arrives. Two Developers spend most of a day fixing it. |
| 6 | Urgent issue 2 arrives and takes another developer-day and a half. |
| 7 | The Developers and Product Owner renegotiate scope: two items (6 points) not needed for the Sprint Goal go back to the Product Backlog. |
| 8 | Urgent issue 3 arrives and is fixed the same day. |
| 10 | Sprint Review: 8 items (23 points) are Done and the Sprint Goal is met. At the Retrospective, the team agrees to reserve capacity for unplanned work. |
Scrum worked as designed: the goal was protected and scope flexed. The cost is noise: velocity swings with interruptions, forecasts get less reliable and the team renegotiates every Sprint.

#### The Kanban version
The same team drops Sprints and sets up a board with WIP limits: Ready (6), Build (4), Review (2), Test (3) and Done, plus an Expedite lane limited to one item. It holds a daily Kanban meeting, a weekly replenishment meeting with the product lead, and a service delivery review and retrospective every two weeks.
Urgent issues go straight into the Expedite lane and are pulled by the next free Developer. Planned work continues; nobody has to renegotiate a batch. Over eight weeks, the team finishes 4, 6, 5, 3, 5, 7, 4 and 6 planned items per week (an average throughput of 5), plus the urgent fixes. Planned items take 5 working days on average from start to finish, and 85% finish within 8 working days, which becomes the team's service level expectation.

#### What the comparison shows
- **Delivery speed is similar**: about ten planned items every two weeks either way. Neither approach makes a team faster by itself.
- **Kanban absorbs interruptions with less overhead**, because there is no Sprint commitment to protect.
- **Scrum gives a clearer goal and a fixed review rhythm**, which stakeholders of a new feature often value.
- **The work decides.** If interruptions grew to half the team's capacity, Kanban would fit better; if they disappeared, Scrum would lose little.

### Kanban vs Scrum metrics compared
Scrum and Kanban answer the same questions with different measures:
| Question | Typical Scrum measure | Typical Kanban measure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How much do we finish? | Velocity (points per Sprint) | Throughput (items per week) |
| How long does an item take? | Rarely measured directly | Cycle time and its percentiles |
| Is anything stuck? | Sprint burndown flattening | Work item age and a WIP aging chart |
| Is work piling up? | Unfinished items at Sprint end | Widening bands on a cumulative flow diagram |
| What can we promise? | Sprint Goal | Service level expectation |
Read more in our guides to [Scrum velocity](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-velocity/), [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/), [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) and the [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/).

#### Forecasting the same backlog both ways
Using the illustrative team above, suppose 30 planned items remain for the billing release, estimated at 84 story points.
1. **Scrum forecast.** Divide the points by average velocity: 84 / 28 = 3 Sprints, or about six weeks. Using the slowest and fastest recent Sprints (24 and 31 points) gives a range of 2.7 to 3.5 Sprints, so plan for three to four Sprints.
2. **Kanban forecast.** Divide the items by average weekly throughput: 30 / 5 = 6 weeks. If every week were as slow as the slowest week (3 items), it would take 10 weeks; as fast as the fastest (7 items), just over 4 weeks.
3. **Narrow the range.** Instead of best and worst cases, Kanban teams usually run a Monte Carlo simulation that samples past weekly throughput thousands of times and reports a date for each confidence level, such as 85%. Our [Kanban planning guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/) walks through it.
4. **Communicate a range, not a date**, and update it every week or Sprint as new data arrives.

#### Little's Law: the link between WIP and speed
Little's Law says that, in a stable system, average cycle time equals average WIP divided by average throughput. The Kanban team above finishes about one planned item per working day with about five in progress, so items take about five working days. If WIP drifted up to ten without any faster finishing, cycle time would double to about ten days. That is why Kanban limits WIP, and why Scrum teams that add WIP limits often see items finish sooner. Our [Kanban metrics guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) covers the other measures.

### When to choose Kanban
Kanban tends to fit when:
- Work arrives unpredictably and often needs starting within days, as in IT support, operations or maintenance.
- Priorities change daily and a two-week commitment would be broken repeatedly.
- Items vary greatly in size, from an hour to several weeks.
- The team is made up of shared specialists who also serve other teams.
- You want to improve an existing process gradually without new roles or a reorganisation.
- Customers care about how quickly a request will be finished, which a service level expectation answers directly.

### When to choose Scrum
Scrum tends to fit when:
- A dedicated, cross-functional team is building a new product or major feature.
- There is real uncertainty about what to build, so regular inspection with stakeholders is valuable.
- Most work can be planned a week or two ahead without constant interruption.
- Someone can act as Product Owner and make ordering decisions.
- The team and stakeholders benefit from a fixed rhythm of planning, review and reflection.
- The organisation wants a common, well-documented framework with widely recognised training.

### How to choose: an eight-question checklist
Answer each question honestly, based on how work really arrives, and note which approach each answer points to.
| Question | Points to Kanban if | Points to Scrum if |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Does more than about a quarter of your work arrive unplanned and need starting within days? | Yes | No |
| 2. Can one person act as Product Owner and order all the work? | No | Yes |
| 3. Is the team dedicated and cross-functional? | No, shared specialists | Yes |
| 4. Do stakeholders want a fixed rhythm of reviews of working results? | No | Yes |
| 5. Do items vary widely in size, from hours to weeks? | Yes | No |
| 6. Do you want to change the current process gradually, without new roles? | Yes | No |
| 7. Is the work new product development with high uncertainty? | No | Yes |
| 8. Do customers expect a service level, such as fixes within five days? | Yes | No |
**Reading your score:** six or more answers on one side give a clear choice. A five-three split is a lean, so start with that approach and borrow the practices you need from the other. A four-four split usually means a hybrid will serve you well.
**Worked scores (illustrative).** An IT service desk answers every question on the Kanban side: eight to Kanban, a clear choice. A mobile app team answers on the Scrum side for everything except question 5, because its items vary a lot: seven to Scrum, so it starts with Scrum and adds rules for splitting large items.
Tip
Re-run the checklist every six months: after a first release, product work often shifts towards support.

### Kanban vs Scrum by type of team
| Team | Usual starting point | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Software product team | Scrum | Uncertain requirements and stakeholders who want to inspect working software each Sprint |
| Platform, DevOps or SRE team | Kanban | High share of unplanned requests and incidents |
| IT service desk | Kanban | Continuous flow of tickets with service levels |
| Marketing team | Either | Kanban for always-on content; Scrum for campaign launches with a fixed review rhythm |
| Creative or design agency | Kanban | Mixed client requests of very different sizes |
| Operations, finance or HR | Kanban | Recurring processes that improve gradually |
| Individual or very small team | Kanban | Lightweight, with no roles to fill |

### How to switch from Scrum to Kanban
Teams usually switch when unplanned work keeps breaking Sprint commitments. Change in steps:
1. **Agree why you are switching.** Name the problem at a Retrospective, such as "we miss most Sprint Goals because of urgent work", so you can check later whether Kanban fixed it.
2. **Map your real workflow.** Replace To do, In progress and Done with the steps work actually goes through, such as Ready, Build, Review, Test and Done.
3. **Set starting WIP limits**, roughly the number of people working in each column, and add an Expedite lane limited to one item.
4. **Replace Sprint Planning with replenishment.** Decide when Ready is refilled (weekly, or when it falls below a set number) and who chooses.
5. **Keep a review and a retrospective** with stakeholders and the team every two to four weeks.
6. **Start measuring flow.** Record start and finish dates on each card to track throughput, cycle time and work item age.
7. **Agree what happens to Scrum roles.** The Product Owner often keeps ordering work and the Scrum Master often coaches flow; nobody needs a new title.
8. **Review after six to eight weeks**, comparing cycle time, throughput and interruptions with your Sprint data.
If you would rather keep Sprints while you test Kanban practices, a staged hybrid such as Scrumban is a gentler route, covered under using Kanban and Scrum together below.

### How to move from Kanban to Scrum
Teams move the other way when they start a new product, need clearer goals, or want a regular demo for stakeholders.
1. **Confirm the team can be dedicated.** Scrum works best when most members spend most of their time on one product.
2. **Name the accountabilities.** Choose a Product Owner who can order the backlog and a Scrum Master who will help the team adopt Scrum.
3. **Turn the board backlog into a Product Backlog** with a Product Goal, and refine the top items until they are small enough for a Sprint.
4. **Choose a Sprint length**, usually one or two weeks for a first attempt, and agree a Definition of Done.
5. **Run the first Sprint Planning**, using your Kanban throughput to forecast how many items to select.
6. **Keep useful Kanban habits**, such as WIP limits and an Expedite lane, as long as they support the Sprint Goal.
7. **Inspect after three Sprints** at the Retrospective and adjust the Sprint length or practices.
Our free [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) and [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) help you set up the first Sprint.

### Using Kanban and Scrum together
You do not have to choose one exclusively. There are two common ways to combine them:
- **Scrum with Kanban practices.** Scrum.org's Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (2021 edition) adds flow practices such as WIP limits, work item age and service level expectations to Scrum without changing any Scrum rules. The team keeps Sprints, accountabilities and events.
- **Scrumban.** A hybrid that keeps some of Scrum's structure, such as regular planning and retrospectives, but replaces the fixed Sprint commitment with Kanban's continuous pull and WIP limits. It was originally described as a way for Scrum teams to move towards Kanban.
The first is still Scrum; the second is a different way of working. Read our guide to [Kanban vs Scrumban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrumban/) for how the hybrid works and how to set it up.

### Tools for Kanban and Scrum teams
Most work management tools support both approaches. The question is how far each goes:
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool (9.4/10), gives every plan a board view built on custom statuses, so you can model a Kanban workflow quickly, alongside Gantt charts, dashboards and request forms. It suits organisations running Kanban and Scrum-style work across several departments.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** has the deepest dedicated Scrum and Kanban support for software teams, including backlogs, Sprints, WIP limits, cumulative flow diagrams and control charts. Its free plan covers up to 10 users.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** combines Sprints, sprint points and burndown with per-column WIP limits on its board view, which suits teams mixing both approaches on a budget.
Whatever the tool, agree the workflow and policies first, then configure the software to match.

### Common mistakes when choosing between Kanban and Scrum
- **Choosing Kanban to avoid discipline.** Kanban without WIP limits, explicit policies and regular reviews is just a to-do list on a wall.
- **Choosing Scrum for a support queue.** If most work is unplanned, Sprint Goals will be broken repeatedly and the team will lose faith in planning.
- **Dropping retrospectives when moving to Kanban.** Improvement is a core Kanban practice; keep a regular cadence for it.
- **Comparing velocity with throughput.** Points and item counts measure different things, so you cannot compare a Scrum team's velocity with a Kanban team's throughput.
- **Switching without a baseline.** Record cycle time, throughput or Sprint Goal success before you change, or you will not know whether the change helped.
- **Treating the choice as permanent.** Teams and work change. Revisit the decision when the mix of planned and unplanned work shifts.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the main difference between Kanban and Scrum?**
Scrum organises work into fixed-length Sprints of one month or less, with a Sprint Goal, three accountabilities and five events. Kanban manages a continuous flow of work with WIP limits, no required roles and no iterations.

**Q: Which is better, Kanban or Scrum?**
Neither is better in general. Kanban suits continuous, unpredictable or mixed-size work such as support and operations. Scrum suits a dedicated team building a product where regular inspection with stakeholders adds value. Use the checklist above to decide for your team.

**Q: Is Kanban agile?**
Yes. Kanban is widely used as an Agile approach because it delivers in small batches, responds to change and improves continuously. It also draws heavily on Lean thinking.

**Q: Does Kanban have sprints?**
No. Kanban has no Sprints or other fixed iterations. Work is pulled continuously, and planning, review and improvement meetings run on whatever cadence the team chooses.

**Q: Does Kanban need a Scrum Master or Product Owner?**
No. Kanban requires no new roles. Some organisations add a Service Request Manager to order incoming work and a Service Delivery Manager to look after flow, and teams moving from Scrum often keep their Product Owner in a similar ordering role.

**Q: Is Kanban easier to learn than Scrum?**
Kanban is usually easier to start because it begins with your current process and adds no roles, though doing it well still takes discipline. Scrum asks for more change on day one but gives a clearer structure.

**Q: Can a Scrum team use a Kanban board?**
Yes. Many Scrum teams show their Sprint Backlog on a board with Kanban-style columns and WIP limits. As long as the team keeps its Sprints, accountabilities and events, it is still doing Scrum.

**Q: What does Kanban use instead of velocity?**
Kanban teams measure throughput (items finished per week), cycle time, work item age and WIP, and use a cumulative flow diagram to spot bottlenecks. Throughput history also supports forecasting.

**Q: Do Kanban teams estimate work?**
Estimation is optional. Many Kanban teams skip story points, split work into items of roughly similar size and forecast from throughput and cycle time.

**Q: Can you change priorities mid-Sprint in Scrum?**
The Product Backlog can be re-ordered at any time, but changes to the current Sprint should not endanger the Sprint Goal. Scope can be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner. If the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint.

**Q: Is Jira Kanban or Scrum?**
Jira supports both. You can create a Scrum board with a backlog and Sprints, or a Kanban board with continuous flow and WIP limits, and its reports cover velocity and burndown as well as cumulative flow and cycle time.

**Q: Which is better for small teams?**
Both can work. Individuals and very small teams often prefer Kanban because it needs no roles or fixed events. A small dedicated product team can run Scrum well if one person can act as Product Owner.

**Q: How long does it take to switch from Scrum to Kanban?**
A team can set up a Kanban board and WIP limits in a day, but give the new system six to eight weeks, long enough to collect flow data and tune the WIP limits, before judging it.
