# Kanban vs Scrumban: Differences, Examples and When to Use Each

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrumban/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Kanban vs Scrumban explained: what Scrumban takes from Scrum, how its planning trigger and board work, a worked example, and when to choose each.


## Kanban vs Scrumban: Differences, Examples and When to Use Each
Kanban vs Scrumban comes down to how much structure you add to flow: Kanban improves your existing process with a visual board and WIP limits, and needs no roles or iterations, while Scrumban is a hybrid that keeps parts of Scrum, such as regular planning, reviews and retrospectives, on top of Kanban's continuous pull. Scrumban is most useful for Scrum teams whose Sprints keep being disrupted by unplanned work. This guide explains how Scrumban works, how to set it up step by step, and how to choose.
- Published 9 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Kanban is a flow method you apply to your current process. Scrumban is a hybrid that adds Scrum-style planning, reviews, retrospectives and often Scrum roles to Kanban flow.
- Scrumban replaces the fixed Sprint commitment with planning on demand: the team plans when the Ready column falls to a set trigger point.
- Both use WIP limits, pull and flow metrics. The difference is whether Scrum's structure stays in place.
- Scrumban was popularised by Corey Ladas in 2009 as a way for Scrum teams to move towards Kanban. It has no official guide.
- Choose Scrumban when a Scrum team faces mixed planned and unplanned work; choose Kanban if you do not use Scrum today or your work is almost entirely unplanned.

### Kanban vs Scrumban: what is the difference?
**The difference between Kanban and Scrumban is where you start and what you keep.** Kanban starts with your current process and adds a visual board, WIP limits and flow metrics, with no required roles or iterations. Scrumban usually starts with Scrum and swaps the Sprint commitment for Kanban's continuous pull, while keeping regular planning, reviews and retrospectives.
In practice, the two can look alike: both use a board with WIP limits and both pull work as capacity frees up. What sets Scrumban apart is the Scrum scaffolding it keeps. If your team has a Product Owner, a Scrum Master, a fortnightly review and a planning trigger, it is running Scrumban. If it has none of those and simply manages flow, it is running Kanban.

### What is Scrumban?
Scrumban is a hybrid Agile approach that combines Scrum's structure with Kanban's flow. The name was popularised by Corey Ladas, whose 2009 book *Scrumban: Essays on Kanban Systems for Lean Software Development* described it as a way for Scrum teams to evolve towards a Kanban system step by step.
Many teams now treat Scrumban as a destination rather than a stepping stone. They like Scrum's rhythm of planning and reflection but find fixed Sprint commitments a poor fit for work that arrives unpredictably.
There is no official Scrumban guide in the way the [Scrum Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) defines Scrum or the Kanban Guide defines [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/). Some consultancies and tool vendors publish their own Scrumban guides, but each team shapes its own version. That flexibility is useful, but it also means you need to write down your rules so everyone knows which parts of Scrum still apply.

### What Scrumban takes from Scrum and from Kanban
| Element | From Scrum | From Kanban | Typical Scrumban practice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Work selection | Planning meeting | Pull when capacity frees up | Plan on demand when Ready hits a trigger point |
| Time box | Sprint | None | Optional iteration used for rhythm, not commitment |
| Limiting work | Sprint Backlog size | Explicit WIP limits | WIP limits per column |
| Board | Sprint board | Persistent board with policies | Persistent board; not reset each iteration |
| Roles | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers | None required | Often kept, especially the Product Owner |
| Daily coordination | Daily Scrum | Kanban meeting | Daily stand-up focused on the board |
| Improvement | Sprint Retrospective | Feedback loops and reviews | Regular retrospective, often every two weeks |
| Stakeholder feedback | Sprint Review | Service delivery review | Regular review of finished work |
| Metrics | Velocity, burndown | Throughput, cycle time, work item age | Mostly flow metrics |
| Estimation | Often story points | Optional; right-sizing | Often reduced or dropped over time |

### Kanban vs Scrumban comparison table
| Aspect | Kanban | Scrumban |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting point | Your current process, whatever it is | Usually an existing Scrum team |
| Defining source | Kanban Guide (2025.5) and Kanban University's Kanban Method | No official guide; Ladas (2009) and team practice |
| Iterations | None | Optional, for planning and review rhythm |
| Commitment | Per item, often a service level expectation | No Sprint commitment; per-item expectations |
| Planning | Replenishment as capacity frees up or on a schedule | Planning on demand, triggered by the Ready column |
| Roles | None required; optional Service Request Manager and Service Delivery Manager | Often keeps the Product Owner and Scrum Master |
| Meetings | Optional cadences chosen by the team | Usually keeps stand-up, planning, review and retrospective |
| WIP limits | Core practice | Core practice |
| Board | Persistent | Persistent |
| Estimation | Optional | Often keeps story points at first, then drops them |
| Metrics | Throughput, cycle time, work item age, WIP | The same, sometimes alongside velocity during transition |
| Change | Anything not started can be re-prioritised | Anything not started can be re-prioritised |
| Learning curve | Low to start; discipline needed to sustain | Moderate; the team must agree which Scrum rules remain |
| Best for | Service, support, operations and any team improving its current process | Scrum teams with a mix of planned and unplanned work |
The rows that differ are the ones about structure: starting point, iterations, roles, meetings and planning. The rows about flow are identical, because Scrumban takes its flow mechanics directly from Kanban.

### Scrum vs Kanban vs Scrumban at a glance
If you are also considering plain Scrum, this summary places all three side by side:
|  | Scrum | Scrumban | Kanban |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cadence | Fixed Sprints of one month or less | Optional iterations; continuous flow | Continuous flow |
| Commitment | Sprint Goal | None per batch | None per batch |
| Planning | Every Sprint | On demand | Replenishment |
| Roles | Three accountabilities | Usually kept | None required |
| WIP limits | Not required | Yes | Yes |
| Main metrics | Velocity, burndown | Flow metrics | Flow metrics |
See our guide to [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) for a full comparison of the two parent approaches, with the same team run both ways and a checklist for choosing.

### How Scrumban works

#### The board and WIP limits
A Scrumban board is persistent: items move across it continuously and the board is never cleared at the end of an iteration. Each in-progress column has a [WIP limit](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/), and many teams add [swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/) to separate planned work, unplanned requests and genuine emergencies.

#### Planning on demand
Instead of planning a fixed batch at the start of each Sprint, the team keeps a Ready column with a minimum level, the planning trigger. When Ready drops to that level, the Product Owner and team hold a short planning session to refill it. Planning happens as often as the team consumes work, not on a fixed calendar. This is the main mechanism that turns a Scrum team into a [pull system](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/).

#### Iterations: optional, for rhythm not commitment
Some Scrumban teams keep two-week iterations so that reviews, retrospectives and reporting happen on a familiar schedule. The difference from Scrum is that nobody commits to finishing a batch by the end of the iteration, and unfinished work simply continues. Other teams drop iterations entirely and schedule each meeting on its own cadence.

#### Meetings
Most Scrumban teams keep four meetings: a daily stand-up that walks the board from right to left, an on-demand planning session, a regular review with stakeholders and a regular [retrospective](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-retrospective/). Many also hold [backlog refinement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/backlog-refinement/) so items reaching Ready are small and clear.

#### Roles
Scrumban does not mandate roles. Teams moving from Scrum usually keep a Product Owner to order the backlog and decide what enters Ready. The Scrum Master often becomes a flow coach, watching WIP limits, blockers and ageing items. Over time, some teams drop the titles and share these responsibilities.

#### Long-range planning: buckets, feature freeze and triage
Because there is no Sprint plan, Scrumban teams need another way to see further ahead. Three practices appear in many Scrumban descriptions, though none is formally required:
- **Bucket planning:** ideas sit in time-horizon buckets, such as one year, six months and three months, and move closer as they become concrete enough to plan.
- **Feature freeze:** close to a fixed deadline, the team stops adding new features to the release and only finishes what is in progress.
- **Triage:** straight after a feature freeze, the team decides which unfinished items will make the deadline and which go back to the backlog.

### How to calculate a Scrumban planning trigger
The planning trigger, sometimes called the order point, is the number of items left in Ready that prompts the next planning session. Set it too low and the team runs out of work; set it too high and you are back to planning large batches.
1. **Measure throughput.** Count how many items the team finishes per working day on average over the last six to eight weeks. See our guide to [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/).
2. **Measure planning lead time.** Note how many working days it takes, from deciding to plan, to get new items refined and agreed, including finding time with the Product Owner.
3. **Multiply the two.** Throughput per day times planning lead time gives the number of items the team will consume while planning is being arranged.
4. **Add a small safety margin** of one or two items to cover busy weeks.
5. **Set the Ready limit** above the trigger, so each planning session adds a sensible batch, often about a week's work.
6. **Write the policy on the board**, for example "When Ready falls to 4, the Product Owner books planning within two days".
7. **Review the trigger monthly.** If Ready empties often, raise it; if planning feels too frequent, raise the Ready limit instead.

#### Worked example
**Illustrative figures.** A team finishes 10 items every two weeks, which is 1 item per working day. Arranging and holding a planning session takes up to 2 working days. Adding a safety margin of 2 gives a trigger of (1 x 2) + 2 = **4 items**. The team sets the Ready limit at **8**, so each planning session adds about four items, roughly every four working days.
| Input | Value | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Throughput | 1 item per working day |  |
| Planning lead time | 2 working days | 2 items consumed while waiting |
| Safety margin | 2 items |  |
| Planning trigger |  | 4 items in Ready |
| Ready limit |  | 8 items |
| Planning frequency |  | About every 4 working days, adding about 4 items |
See our [Kanban planning guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/) for forecasting further ahead, such as when a whole feature will be finished.

### Example Scrumban board
Here is an illustrative board for a seven-person team that builds features and handles support requests:
| Column | WIP limit | Policy for moving in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backlog | None | Ordered by the Product Owner; large items split during refinement |
| Ready | 8 (plan at 4) | Small enough to finish within 7 working days; acceptance criteria agreed |
| In progress | 5 | A person has capacity and nothing is waiting in Review |
| Review | 2 | Code complete, tests written, ready for a peer |
| Test | 3 | Peer review passed |
| Done | None | Meets the Definition of Done |
The team also splits the In progress limit across swimlanes to protect planned work:
- **Expedite lane (limit 1):** production incidents only. Any free person pulls it immediately.
- **Requests lane (limit 2):** unplanned support and small changes, about 40% of capacity.
- **Features lane (limit 3):** planned backlog items, about 60% of capacity.
Each column's policy works like a mini [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/). Our free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) has WIP limits and columns you can adapt to this layout, and the [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/) helps you map the steps first.

### Worked example: moving a Scrum team to Scrumban
**This example is illustrative; the team and figures are invented to show a typical transition.**
A seven-person platform team runs two-week Sprints. About 40% of the items it finishes are unplanned: bug fixes, access requests and small changes from other teams. It has missed the Sprint Goal in four of its last six Sprints, and Sprint Planning has become a negotiation about how much capacity to hold back. The team decides to move to Scrumban in three stages, reviewing each at a retrospective.
| Stage | What changes | What stays from Scrum | What to watch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Weeks 1 to 4 | Map the real workflow on the board; add WIP limits and an Expedite lane | Sprints, Sprint Goal, all events, story points | Blocked items and columns that hit their limit |
| 2. Weeks 5 to 10 | Replace the Sprint commitment with a planning trigger (plan at 4, Ready limit 8); add Requests and Features lanes | Two-week review and retrospective; Product Owner and Scrum Master | Whether Ready ever runs empty; how often planning happens |
| 3. Week 11 onwards | Drop story points; forecast from throughput; publish a service level expectation | Review, retrospective, daily stand-up | Cycle time percentiles and work item age |
By stage 3, the team has a clear picture of its flow. Planned items take a median of four working days and 85% finish within seven, so the team publishes "85% of items within seven working days" as its service level expectation. Planning sessions are shorter because they cover a few items at a time, and urgent work no longer breaks a commitment.
The team keeps the fortnightly review and retrospective because stakeholders value the rhythm. If it later decided to drop the Scrum roles and fixed meetings too, it would effectively be running Kanban.
Tip
Change one thing per stage and keep it for at least two weeks before judging it. Changing WIP limits, planning and estimation all at once makes it impossible to tell what helped.

### Scrumban beyond software: a marketing example
Scrumban is not limited to development teams. **This example is illustrative.**
A five-person content marketing team plans campaign content a quarter ahead but also receives a steady stream of requests from sales, such as case studies, slide updates and event copy. Under two-week Sprints, sales requests either waited up to a fortnight or broke the Sprint plan.
The team moves to Scrumban. The head of content keeps the Product Owner role and orders both campaign work and sales requests in one backlog. The board runs Ready (limit 6, plan at 3), Drafting (3), Design (2), Approval (2) and Published. The team finishes about six pieces a week, a little over one per working day, and planning takes a day to arrange, so a trigger of 3 leaves a safety margin of almost two items.
Within a few weeks, the Approval column is often full while writers wait. The WIP limit has exposed the real bottleneck. At the retrospective, the team and its approvers agree a policy of reviewing within two working days, and flow improves. The team keeps a fortnightly review with sales and a monthly retrospective, the Scrum rhythm it valued, without the batch commitment. Our guide to [Agile marketing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/) covers more patterns for marketing teams.

### How to set up Scrumban step by step
1. **Agree the problem you want to solve**, such as missed Sprint Goals or too much time spent planning, so you can measure whether Scrumban helps.
2. **Map your actual workflow** as columns, from Backlog through Ready and each working step to Done.
3. **Write a policy for each column** describing what must be true before an item moves in.
4. **Set starting WIP limits**, roughly the number of people who work in each column, and tune them after two or three weeks.
5. **Add swimlanes** for urgent and unplanned work, and decide how much capacity each lane gets.
6. **Calculate a planning trigger and Ready limit** using your throughput and planning lead time.
7. **Choose your meeting cadence**: daily stand-up, on-demand planning, and a review and retrospective every two to four weeks.
8. **Decide which Scrum roles stay** and write down who orders the backlog and who looks after flow.
9. **Track flow from day one**: record start and finish dates for throughput, [cycle time and lead time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time-vs-lead-time/), and use a [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) to spot stuck items.
10. **Inspect and adapt at each retrospective**, changing one policy at a time.
Our [sprint retrospective template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-retrospective-template/) works just as well for Scrumban retrospectives.

### Is it Kanban or Scrumban? A quick test
The line between the two is blurry, partly because Kanban is not meeting-free: Kanban University's Kanban Method describes seven cadences, from a daily meeting to a quarterly strategy review (see [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/)). So a Kanban team that holds a fortnightly review is still doing Kanban. Use this test instead:
| If your team... | It is probably running |
| --- | --- |
| Started from its existing process with no Scrum in place | Kanban |
| Started from Scrum and kept a Product Owner and Scrum Master | Scrumban |
| Keeps iterations, even without a Sprint commitment | Scrumban |
| Plans when Ready hits a trigger and uses Scrum names for its meetings | Scrumban |
| Has a Sprint Goal and commits to a batch each Sprint | Scrum, perhaps with Kanban practices |
| Has no WIP limits | Neither, yet; add WIP limits first |
The label matters less than clarity. Write down your rules so new team members and stakeholders know how work enters, flows and is reviewed.

### Kanban vs Scrumban: which should you choose?
| Your situation | Usual choice | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| You run Scrum and unplanned work keeps breaking Sprint Goals | Scrumban | Keeps the rhythm the team knows while removing the batch commitment |
| You run Scrum and want to move to Kanban without a big-bang change | Scrumban, then Kanban | Scrumban was designed as this stepping stone |
| You do not use Scrum today | Kanban | Start with your current process; no need to adopt Scrum first |
| Almost all work is unplanned, such as a service desk | Kanban | There is little planned work for Scrum structure to organise |
| Stakeholders want a fixed review rhythm but work is mixed | Scrumban | Regular reviews with continuous flow |
| You want minimal process change and no new titles | Kanban | Kanban respects current roles |
| A Kanban team lacks focus and planning discipline | Scrumban, or add Kanban cadences | A regular planning and review rhythm adds structure |
IT operations and platform teams often sit on the boundary. Our guide to [Agile in IT operations](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-operations-it/) covers how such teams balance planned and unplanned work.

### Pros and cons of Kanban and Scrumban
|  | Kanban | Scrumban |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pros | Starts immediately with the current process; no new roles; handles unpredictable work well; strong flow metrics | Familiar to Scrum teams; keeps a regular review and reflection rhythm; absorbs unplanned work better than Sprints; a gradual route to flow |
| Cons | Can drift without discipline; no built-in planning rhythm unless you add cadences; less guidance on product goals | No official guide, so rules vary; risk of keeping Scrum's overhead without its focus; harder to explain to stakeholders used to Sprint commitments |
| Watch out for | Boards without WIP limits or policies | A hybrid that is really Scrum with broken commitments |

### Moving on from Scrumban to Kanban
Because Scrumban began as a bridge, some teams eventually move on to pure Kanban. Signs you are ready include stable WIP limits, a reliable service level expectation and meetings that would happen anyway without Scrum names. To complete the move:
1. Drop any remaining iterations and schedule each meeting on its own cadence.
2. Replace the Product Owner's planning role with replenishment, ordered by whoever owns demand.
3. Turn the Scrum Master role into shared responsibility for flow, or a Service Delivery Manager if your organisation uses one.
4. Keep the retrospective and stakeholder review; improvement and feedback remain core Kanban practices.
Read our guide to [Kanban principles and practices](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-principles/) for what your team will rely on once the Scrum scaffolding is gone.

### Tools that support Scrumban
Scrumban needs a board with WIP limits, swimlanes and, ideally, flow reports. Most mainstream tools handle it:
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool (9.4/10), builds boards from custom statuses on every plan, and adds dashboards, request forms for unplanned work and automation, which suits Scrumban teams that take requests from several departments.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** offers both Scrum and Kanban boards with WIP limits, swimlanes, cumulative flow diagrams and control charts, so software teams can move from one to the other in the same tool.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/)** combines Sprints with per-column WIP limits on its board view, useful for teams keeping optional iterations alongside flow.

### Common Scrumban mistakes
- **Dropping WIP limits.** Without them, Scrumban is just Scrum without commitments.
- **Keeping every Scrum meeting at full length.** On-demand planning should be short; if planning still takes half a day, the trigger or Ready limit is wrong.
- **Never writing the rules down.** With no official guide, unwritten rules cause confusion about what still applies.
- **Letting the Expedite lane fill up.** If everything is urgent, nothing is. Keep its limit at one and define what qualifies.
- **Measuring only velocity.** Once there is no Sprint commitment, velocity loses meaning; switch to throughput and cycle time.
- **Changing too much at once.** Move in stages, as in the worked example, so you can see what helps.
- **Using Scrumban to avoid hard conversations.** If a team keeps missing goals because of poor refinement, a new label will not fix it.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between Kanban and Scrumban?**
Kanban is a flow method applied to your existing process, with WIP limits and no required roles or iterations. Scrumban is a hybrid that keeps parts of Scrum, such as roles, regular planning, reviews and retrospectives, while replacing the Sprint commitment with Kanban's continuous pull and WIP limits.

**Q: Is Scrumban better than Kanban?**
Neither is better in general. Scrumban suits Scrum teams that want a gradual move to flow or need a regular review rhythm with mixed work. Kanban suits teams that do not use Scrum, or whose work is almost entirely unplanned.

**Q: Who created Scrumban?**
The term was popularised by Corey Ladas, whose 2009 book Scrumban: Essays on Kanban Systems for Lean Software Development described it as a way for Scrum teams to move towards Kanban.

**Q: Does Scrumban have sprints?**
Not in the Scrum sense. Some Scrumban teams keep fixed iterations to time their reviews and retrospectives, but they do not commit to finishing a batch of work by the end of each one. Others drop iterations entirely.

**Q: Does Scrumban have roles?**
Scrumban does not require any roles. Teams moving from Scrum often keep a Product Owner to order the backlog and a Scrum Master to coach flow, while others share these responsibilities across the team.

**Q: What meetings does Scrumban use?**
Most Scrumban teams hold a daily stand-up, planning on demand when the Ready column hits its trigger, a regular review with stakeholders and a regular retrospective. Many also run backlog refinement.

**Q: Does Scrumban use story points?**
It can, but many teams drop them over time. Once work is pulled continuously, throughput and cycle time give more useful forecasts, and teams split items to a similar size instead of estimating each one. See our guide to [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/).

**Q: Is there an official Scrumban guide?**
No. Scrum has the Scrum Guide and Kanban has the Kanban Guide and Kanban University's materials, but Scrumban has no single official definition. Some consultancies and vendors publish their own guides.

**Q: How do you plan work in Scrumban?**
Scrumban uses planning on demand. The team sets a minimum number of items for the Ready column, and when Ready falls to that trigger, the Product Owner and team hold a short session to refill it.

**Q: Is Scrumban agile?**
Yes. Scrumban combines two widely used Agile approaches and keeps their emphasis on small batches, frequent feedback and continuous improvement.

**Q: Can a Kanban team move to Scrumban?**
It can, but it rarely needs to. A Kanban team that wants more structure can usually add Kanban cadences, such as a replenishment meeting and a service delivery review, without adopting Scrum roles.

**Q: Does Scrumban use WIP limits?**
Yes. WIP limits are one of the main elements Scrumban takes from Kanban, and without them it is not really Scrumban.

**Q: How long does it take to move from Scrum to Scrumban?**
A staged move usually takes two to three months: a few weeks to add WIP limits while keeping Sprints, a few more to switch to planning on demand, and then time to collect enough flow data to drop estimation and set a service level expectation.

**Q: Which teams use Scrumban?**
Scrumban is common in software maintenance, platform and DevOps teams, and in marketing or product teams that combine planned projects with a steady stream of requests.

# Kanban vs Waterfall: Key Differences and When to Use Each

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-waterfall/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Kanban vs Waterfall compared: planning, change, delivery and metrics, a scored decision check, a worked example and how to combine them in a hybrid project.


## Kanban vs Waterfall: Key Differences and When to Use Each
Kanban vs Waterfall is a choice between planning a whole project up front and moving through fixed phases in sequence (Waterfall), or managing a continuous flow of work items that you reprioritise and deliver one at a time (Kanban). Neither is better in general: Waterfall suits stable, well-defined projects that only have value when complete, while Kanban suits ongoing or changing work that can be delivered in pieces. This guide compares them side by side, gives you a scored decision check and a worked example, and shows how to combine them.
- Published 10 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Waterfall is a predictive project life cycle: define scope, baseline the plan, then run requirements, design, build, test and deploy in order.
- Kanban is a method for managing flow: visualise the work, limit work in progress and improve continuously, delivering each item when it is ready.
- They are not strictly alternatives. Kanban can run on top of any process, including the phases of a Waterfall project.
- Choose Waterfall for fixed requirements, physical or regulated work and fixed-price commitments; choose Kanban for continuous requests, changing priorities and work that can be released in parts.
- Waterfall measures progress against a baseline schedule and budget; Kanban uses flow metrics such as cycle time and throughput to forecast.
- Hybrids are common: Waterfall governance, milestones and a Gantt chart at the top, with Kanban boards for day-to-day execution.

### What is the difference between Kanban and Waterfall?
**The main difference between Kanban and Waterfall is how they plan and deliver work.** Waterfall plans the entire project at the start and completes each phase before the next, delivering the result at the end. Kanban plans continuously, pulls work items through a visual board as capacity frees up and delivers each item as soon as it is finished.
They also sit at different levels. [Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) is a project life cycle: a way of structuring a project from start to finish. [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) is a method for managing the flow of work through whatever process you already have. That is why the comparison is partly a false choice, and why many teams use a Kanban board inside a Waterfall project.
In PMI terms, Waterfall is the classic **predictive** approach and Kanban is an **adaptive** one; a deliberate mix is a **hybrid** approach. The PMBOK Guide 8th edition and the current PMP exam expect project managers to understand all three, so knowing when each fits is a core skill, not a matter of preference.

### Kanban vs Waterfall comparison table
|  | Waterfall | Kanban |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A sequential project life cycle | A method for managing and improving flow |
| Planning | Detailed, up front, then baselined | Continuous; the backlog is replenished as capacity frees up |
| Structure | Phases in a fixed order with gates | Work items flow through board columns one by one |
| Scope | Fixed early and controlled | Flexible; anything not started can change |
| Handling change | Formal change control | Reprioritise at the next replenishment |
| Delivery | Usually once, at the end | Continuously, whenever an item is ready |
| Cadence | Phase-based milestones | No required timeboxes; regular reviews by choice |
| Roles | Project manager plus functional specialists | No prescribed roles; keeps existing roles |
| Progress measures | Schedule and budget against baseline, % complete, earned value | WIP, cycle time, throughput, work item age |
| Forecasting | Estimates of every task, rolled up | Probabilistic forecasts from past throughput |
| Documentation | Extensive; each phase produces approved documents | Light; explicit policies on the board |
| Customer involvement | Mainly at the start and at acceptance | Ongoing, as items are delivered |
| Typical tools | Gantt chart, WBS, baseline schedule | Kanban board, WIP limits, cumulative flow diagram |
| Best for | Stable, well-defined, often physical or regulated projects | Continuous, variable or fast-changing work |

### What is Waterfall?
Waterfall runs a project through a fixed series of phases, typically requirements, design, build, test, deployment and maintenance. Each phase produces approved deliverables that feed the next, and a phase gate lets sponsors check the work before money is committed to the next stage.
Scope, schedule and budget are planned in detail at the start and fixed in a [project baseline](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-baseline/). Progress is tracked against that baseline, usually with a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) and milestones, and changes go through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).
The model is usually traced to Winston Royce's 1970 paper, which actually warned against a single pass and recommended feedback between phases. In practice, Waterfall's strength is predictability: everyone knows what will be built, when and for how much. Its weakness is late feedback, because users often see the result only near the end, when change is most expensive.

### What is Kanban?
Kanban began on Toyota's factory floors as a pull system that replenished parts only when they were used. In the 2000s, David J. Anderson adapted it to knowledge work, and his 2010 book set out what became known as the Kanban Method.
A Kanban system makes work visible on a board, limits how many items can be in progress at each stage and manages the flow of items from request to delivery. Teams pull new work only when there is capacity, and they improve the process step by step using data.
Two reference sources describe it slightly differently:
- **The Kanban Method (Kanban University)** starts with change-management principles: start with what you do now, agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change, respect the current process, roles and titles, and encourage leadership at all levels. Its general practices are to visualise, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops and improve collaboratively.
- **The Kanban Guide (2025 edition)** describes three practices: defining and visualising the workflow, actively managing items in the workflow, and improving the workflow. It requires four flow measures: WIP, throughput, work item age and cycle time.
The principle "start with what you do now" matters for this comparison. Kanban does not ask you to abandon Waterfall; it asks you to make your current process visible and improve it. Our guide to [Kanban principles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-principles/) covers them in more detail.

### Key differences explained

#### Planning and commitment
Waterfall commits early: you plan all the work, estimate it and agree a date and budget before execution starts. Kanban commits late and in small pieces: the team commits to an item only when it pulls it into progress, and [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/) happens continuously through replenishment meetings. Waterfall gives you a full plan on day one; Kanban gives you the flexibility to change direction without re-planning everything.

#### How work moves
In Waterfall, the whole project passes through each phase once: all design is done before any building starts. In Kanban, each item moves through the stages on its own. On any given day, one item may be in testing while another is still being analysed. A Kanban board's columns may look like Waterfall phases, but the batch size is one item, not the whole project.

#### Handling change
Waterfall treats change as an exception: a change request is assessed for impact on scope, time and cost, approved or rejected, and the baseline is updated. Kanban treats change as normal: anything not yet started can be reprioritised at the next replenishment at no cost, while work already in progress is usually finished first.

#### When value is delivered
Waterfall usually delivers once, at the end. That is fine when the result only has value as a whole, such as a building or a regulatory submission. Kanban delivers each item when it is finished, so customers start getting value, and giving feedback, much earlier.

#### Roles and responsibilities
Waterfall projects are typically led by a project manager who plans, assigns and controls the work, with specialists contributing in their phase. Kanban prescribes no roles and asks you to keep the ones you have; some organisations add a service delivery manager or a service request manager, but this is optional.

#### Measuring progress and forecasting
Waterfall measures progress against the baseline: percentage complete, milestones hit, and often [earned value](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/). Kanban measures flow: [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/), [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/), WIP and work item age. Instead of estimating every task, Kanban teams forecast from historical throughput, for example "85% of items finish within 8 days" or "we finish 4 to 6 items a week".

#### Documentation and governance
Waterfall relies on documents approved at each gate: requirements specifications, design documents and test plans. Kanban relies on explicit policies on the board, such as WIP limits and a definition of done for each column. Kanban can still produce documents when they are needed; it just does not use them to control progress.

#### Risk
Waterfall reduces risk through up-front analysis and planning, but risks that only show up when users see the product surface late. Kanban reduces risk by delivering small pieces and getting feedback early, but without a plan it can drift if nobody owns priorities or the bigger picture.

### Pros and cons of Kanban and Waterfall
|  | Waterfall | Kanban |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pros | Clear plan, budget and date from the start; easy to contract and govern; strong documentation; suits fixed-price and regulated work; familiar to most stakeholders | Early and continuous delivery; easy to change priorities; low disruption to adopt; exposes bottlenecks; works for ongoing services as well as projects |
| Cons | Late feedback; change is slow and costly; problems found late in testing; risk of building the wrong thing when requirements were uncertain | No built-in long-range plan or fixed end date; needs discipline on WIP limits; can lose sight of the overall goal; less familiar to some sponsors and contracts |
Most of the cons can be reduced. Waterfall teams can add early prototypes and interim reviews; Kanban teams can add a roadmap, milestones and regular service delivery reviews. The real question is which weaknesses your project can tolerate.

### When to use Waterfall
Waterfall is usually the better choice when most of these are true:
- Requirements are stable, well understood and unlikely to change.
- The result only has value when it is complete, such as a building, a factory line or a data-centre move.
- Regulation, safety or a contract requires documented, approved phases.
- Late change is physically or financially very costly.
- The customer needs a fixed scope, price and date before work starts.
- The team has delivered similar projects before and can estimate accurately.
| Example | Why Waterfall fits |
| --- | --- |
| Constructing an office building | Physical dependencies; design must be approved before building starts |
| Implementing a regulated system validation | Each phase must be documented and signed off |
| Relocating a data centre | Fixed cut-over date; tightly sequenced steps |
| Fixed-price client project with a clear specification | Contract defines scope, price and date up front |

### When to use Kanban
Kanban is usually the better choice when most of these are true:
- Work arrives as a continuous stream of requests rather than one defined project.
- Priorities change often, sometimes weekly or daily.
- Items can be delivered and used independently.
- You want to improve an existing process without reorganising teams or roles.
- Timeboxed sprints do not suit the work, for example because urgent requests cannot wait for the next sprint.
- You want to see and remove bottlenecks using data.
| Example | Why Kanban fits |
| --- | --- |
| IT service desk and support | Continuous requests with different urgencies |
| Software maintenance and DevOps | Small changes released as soon as they are ready |
| Marketing content production | Steady flow of requests; priorities shift with campaigns |
| HR, legal or finance request queues | Repeatable work types with clear stages |

### How to choose: a step-by-step decision check
Use this check with your sponsor and team at the start of a project or when setting up a new workstream:
1. **Describe the work.** Is it a one-off project with a defined end, or an ongoing stream? Write one sentence for each major part.
2. **Score each part** against the eight questions below, from 1 (strongly Waterfall) to 5 (strongly Kanban).
3. **Add up the scores** and read the result from the bands.
4. **Look for mixed scores.** A few very low answers, such as a fixed contract or a regulatory gate, usually mean a hybrid: keep those controls and use Kanban inside them.
5. **Agree and record the approach** in your project management plan, including how you will report progress.
6. **Review after the first month** and adjust.
| Question | Score 1 (Waterfall) | Score 5 (Kanban) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How stable are the requirements? | Fixed and signed off | Expected to change often |
| Can the result be used in parts? | Only when complete | Each item is useful on its own |
| How does the work arrive? | One defined project | Continuous stream of requests |
| How much formal phase sign-off is required? | Mandatory, documented gates | Little or none |
| How costly is late change? | Very costly (physical work) | Cheap (digital work) |
| How often can stakeholders give feedback? | Rarely | Weekly or more |
| Do you need a fixed date and price up front? | Yes, contractually | No; a forecast is enough |
| How many tightly sequenced dependencies? | Many | Few |
| Total score | Suggested approach |
| --- | --- |
| 8–18 | Waterfall, possibly with Kanban boards to manage tasks within phases |
| 19–29 | Hybrid: Waterfall governance and milestones, Kanban for execution |
| 30–40 | Kanban, or another adaptive approach such as Scrum |
Tip
Score parts of a project separately. A product launch might score Waterfall for the manufacturing and regulatory work and Kanban for the marketing content and website changes, and you can run each part accordingly.
For a wider comparison of adaptive and predictive approaches, see our guide to [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/), which includes a broader suitability check.

### Worked example: the same work run both ways
This illustrative example follows a five-person digital team asked to deliver 12 improvements to an online booking process, each of similar size.

#### Run as Waterfall
The team gathers requirements for all 12 improvements (weeks 1 to 2), designs them (weeks 3 to 4), builds them (weeks 5 to 10), tests them together (weeks 11 to 12) and releases everything in week 13. The sponsor gets a fixed date and a clear plan on day one. Customers see nothing until week 13.

#### Run as Kanban
The team orders the 12 items by value, sets a WIP limit of 3 and pulls the top items. Each item takes about three weeks from start to release, and after the first few the team finishes about one a week. The first improvement goes live in week 3.
| End of week | Waterfall: items live | Kanban: items live |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 0 | 2 |
| 8 | 0 | 6 |
| 12 | 0 | 10 |
| 13 | 12 | 11 |
| 14 | 12 | 12 |
In this illustration Kanban finishes the full set a week later, because each release carries its own testing and deployment overhead. But 10 of the 12 improvements were in customers' hands by week 12, and the team learned from each release as it went.

#### A change in week 6
In week 6, booking data shows many customers abandon at the payment step, and the sponsor wants a simpler payment page as the top priority.
- **Waterfall:** the team raises a change request (see our [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/)). Design must be reopened, the build plan reworked and testing extended. In this illustration the change is approved and the release moves to week 15, with 13 items.
- **Kanban:** the new item goes to the top of the backlog at the next replenishment, is started in week 7 and goes live around week 9. The lowest-value original item slips to the end or is dropped.

#### Forecasting the remaining work
At the end of week 8, the Waterfall team reports progress against the baseline (for example, build 60% complete, on schedule). The Kanban team uses its throughput, about 0.8 to 1.2 items a week, to forecast that the remaining six items will take roughly five to eight weeks. The first answer sounds more precise; the second is based on what the team has actually delivered.

### Combining Kanban and Waterfall (hybrid)
Many organisations need Waterfall's governance (business cases, budgets, phase gates, milestones) but want Kanban's visibility and flow for day-to-day work. A hybrid gives you both.

#### Kanban inside Waterfall phases: step by step
1. **Keep the phase plan and milestones.** Leave your Gantt chart, milestones and gate reviews in place for sponsors.
2. **Turn work packages into cards.** Break each phase's work into items that take days rather than weeks, and put them in the phase backlog.
3. **Design the board.** Create columns for how work actually flows within the phase, and use swimlanes for phases or workstreams if several run at once.
4. **Set WIP limits** on in-progress and review columns so the team finishes work before starting more.
5. **Make the gate a column.** Add an "Awaiting approval" column and agree a [definition of done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) that matches the gate criteria.
6. **Hold a short daily board walk** from right to left, focusing on blocked and ageing items.
7. **Report both views.** Give sponsors milestone status from the Gantt chart and flow measures from the board.
| Column | Purpose | Example WIP limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phase backlog | Work packages from the plan, in priority order | None |
| Ready | Items agreed and ready to start | 5 |
| In progress | Being worked on | 3 |
| Review | Peer or specialist review | 2 |
| Awaiting approval | Ready for sign-off at the gate | None, but monitored |
| Done | Meets the definition of done | None |

#### What to report to sponsors
Sponsors used to Waterfall reports want to know whether the project is on time and on budget. Keep giving them milestone dates and budget status, and add three flow measures: throughput (items finished per week), WIP and the oldest items in progress. A [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) is often the easiest single chart to explain.

#### Moving from Waterfall to Kanban
If your team wants to move further towards Kanban, follow the Kanban Method's advice to start with what you do now:
1. Map your current process, phases and handoffs as board columns, without changing anything.
2. Put all current work on the board and watch it for two to four weeks.
3. Introduce WIP limits where work piles up.
4. Make policies explicit, such as entry and exit criteria for each column.
5. Start delivering smaller items as soon as they are ready, where the business can use them.
6. Replace some status reports with flow metrics once stakeholders trust them.
See our guide to [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) for how to design columns and swimlanes for your first board.

### Kanban vs Waterfall vs Scrum
Scrum is often the third option on the table. It is adaptive like Kanban, but organises work into fixed-length sprints with defined accountabilities and events, as described in the 2020 Scrum Guide.
|  | Waterfall | Scrum | Kanban |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Approach | Predictive | Adaptive, iterative | Adaptive, flow-based |
| Cadence | Phases | Sprints of one month or less | Continuous |
| Roles | Project manager and specialists | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers | No prescribed roles |
| Change | Change control | Between sprints, via the Product Backlog | Any time before work starts |
| Main measure | Progress against baseline | Sprint Goal and increments delivered | Cycle time and throughput |
For the detail, read our comparisons of [Kanban vs Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) and [Scrum vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-vs-waterfall/).

### Common mistakes when comparing or combining them
- **Treating board columns as phases.** If the whole project moves through each column together, you have a Waterfall plan drawn as a board. Let items flow individually.
- **Choosing by fashion.** Pick the approach that fits the work and constraints, not the one that sounds modern.
- **Using Kanban without WIP limits.** A board without limits is a to-do list; you lose most of Kanban's benefits.
- **Dropping the plan entirely.** Kanban teams still need a goal, priorities and, for projects, milestones stakeholders can rely on.
- **Forcing Waterfall on uncertain work.** If requirements will change, a fixed plan becomes a series of change requests.
- **Reporting only one view in a hybrid.** Sponsors need milestone status; teams need flow data. Give both.
- **Changing everything at once.** Kanban works best as incremental change from your current process.
- **Ignoring contracts.** Fixed-price contracts often need Waterfall-style scope control, even if delivery uses Kanban.

### Tools and templates for Kanban, Waterfall and hybrid work
Hybrid teams need a tool that shows the same work as both a board and a schedule. Most leading tools now do both:
- **Wrike** (our top-rated tool) includes a board view even on its Free plan, and its interactive Gantt charts, from the Team plan upwards, support dependencies, the critical path and baselines, which makes it a strong fit for hybrid projects. See our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).
- **monday.com** shows the same board as a Kanban, table, timeline or Gantt view, which suits teams that want visual workflows with milestones; see our [monday.com review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/).
- **Smartsheet** combines a spreadsheet-style plan and Gantt chart with a board view, which suits plan-driven teams that want to add Kanban; see our [Smartsheet review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/).
- **Jira** is strong for software Kanban, with WIP limits, cumulative flow diagrams and control charts, though it does not offer a classic Gantt chart with critical path and baselines; see our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/).
- **Trello** is a simple, quick way to start with Kanban boards for small teams.
If you want to start on paper or in a spreadsheet, use our free [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) for the phase plan and milestones and our [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) for day-to-day work.
Read our guide to [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) before you set up your first board, because they are what turn a board into a Kanban system.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between Kanban and Waterfall?**
Waterfall plans the whole project up front and runs it in sequential phases, delivering at the end. Kanban manages a continuous flow of work items, limits work in progress and delivers each item when it is ready.

**Q: Is Kanban agile or waterfall?**
Kanban is generally classed as an Agile, adaptive approach. It can, however, be applied to any process, including the tasks inside a Waterfall project.

**Q: Is Kanban better than Waterfall?**
Neither is better in general. Kanban suits continuous, changing work that can be delivered in parts; Waterfall suits stable, well-defined projects that only have value when complete.

**Q: Can a Waterfall project use a Kanban board?**
Yes. Keep the phase plan, milestones and gates, and use a Kanban board with WIP limits to manage the tasks within each phase.

**Q: Which delivers faster, Kanban or Waterfall?**
Kanban usually delivers individual items much sooner, because each is released when ready. Total completion time for a fixed set of work may be similar.

**Q: When is Waterfall the better choice?**
When requirements are stable, late change is costly, regulation or contracts require approved phases, or the result only has value when complete, as in many construction projects.

**Q: When is Kanban the better choice?**
When work arrives continuously, priorities change often and items can be used independently, as in support, maintenance, DevOps and content production.

**Q: Do Kanban teams use Gantt charts?**
Not usually. Kanban relies on the board and flow metrics, though hybrid teams often keep a Gantt chart for milestones and dependencies.

**Q: How is progress measured in Kanban vs Waterfall?**
Waterfall measures progress against a baseline schedule and budget, for example with earned value. Kanban tracks flow measures such as cycle time, throughput, WIP and work item age.

**Q: How does change control differ in Kanban and Waterfall?**
Waterfall routes scope changes through formal change control and updates the baseline. In Kanban, anything not yet started can be reprioritised at the next replenishment.

**Q: Does Kanban have deadlines?**
Kanban has no built-in deadlines, but teams can manage fixed-date items with classes of service and forecast delivery dates from past throughput.

**Q: Which is cheaper, Kanban or Waterfall?**
Neither is inherently cheaper. Kanban can reduce the cost of building the wrong thing, while Waterfall can be efficient when requirements are truly fixed.

**Q: How do you move from Waterfall to Kanban?**
Start with what you do now: map your current process on a board, add WIP limits where work piles up, make policies explicit and deliver smaller items as soon as they are ready.

**Q: Can Kanban be used in construction projects?**
Yes, for managing tasks, snagging lists and design requests within phases, while the overall project usually keeps a Waterfall plan because of physical dependencies.

# Lean Kanban: How Lean Thinking Shapes the Kanban Method

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-kanban/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: How Lean principles underpin Kanban: value, flow, pull and continuous improvement, the history of Lean Kanban, and how to apply both together.


## Lean Kanban: How Lean Thinking Shapes the Kanban Method
Kanban for knowledge work grew directly out of Lean thinking. Understanding the Lean ideas behind it explains why Kanban focuses so much on flow, waste and pull, and helps teams use it well.
- Published 15 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Kanban for knowledge work is built on Lean principles.
- Value, value stream, flow, pull and perfection guide Kanban practices.
- Pull, flow and continuous improvement are the shared core.

### Lean in brief
Lean thinking comes from the Toyota Production System. In their 1996 book Lean Thinking, James Womack and Daniel Jones summarised it in five principles:
1. **Value:** define value from the customer's point of view.
2. **Value stream:** map every step that delivers that value; see [value stream mapping](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/).
3. **Flow:** make the remaining steps flow smoothly without interruption.
4. **Pull:** produce only what the customer needs, when they need it; see [pull vs push](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/).
5. **Perfection:** keep improving continuously.

### How Kanban applies Lean
| Lean idea | Kanban practice |
| --- | --- |
| Pull | Start work only when there is capacity; [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) |
| Flow | Manage and measure flow with [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) and [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) |
| Eliminate waste | Expose waiting, handoffs and rework on the board |
| Visual management | The [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) |
| Kaizen (continuous improvement) | Regular reviews and evolutionary change |
| Respect for people | Start with what you do now; leadership at every level |

### Lean Kanban in the knowledge-work community
In the late 2000s, practitioners including David J. Anderson adapted these ideas for software and IT, creating the Kanban Method. Kanban University continues to develop and teach it, and Lean Kanban remains a common name for this approach.

### Applying Lean Kanban
- Define who your customers are and what they value.
- Map your value stream before designing your board.
- Limit WIP to create pull.
- Measure flow and focus on removing waiting.
- Hold regular reviews to make small, continuous improvements.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Are Lean and Kanban the same thing?**
No. Lean is a broad management philosophy; Kanban is a method that applies Lean principles to managing work.

**Q: What are the seven wastes behind Lean Kanban?**
Transport, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, over-processing and defects. Many add an eighth: unused talent. See [Lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/).

**Q: What is Lean Kanban?**
Lean Kanban is a common name for the Kanban Method applied to knowledge work, emphasising its roots in Lean thinking: delivering customer value, reducing waste and improving flow.

**Q: What is the difference between Lean and Kanban?**
Lean is a broad philosophy for maximising customer value and eliminating waste. Kanban is a specific method, originating in Lean, for visualising work and limiting WIP.

**Q: Which five Lean principles underpin Lean Kanban?**
As described by Womack and Jones: define value, map the value stream, create flow, establish pull, and pursue perfection through continuous improvement.

**Q: What is kaizen in Lean Kanban?**
Kaizen means continuous, incremental improvement. In Kanban it appears as the practice of improving collaboratively and evolving the process experimentally.

**Q: In Lean Kanban, what does waste look like in knowledge work?**
Examples include partly done work, waiting for approvals, hand-offs, task switching, unnecessary features, rework from defects and searching for information.

**Q: Is Lean Kanban only for software teams?**
No. It started in software and IT but is now used in marketing, HR, finance, healthcare administration and other service work.

**Q: What is Lean Kanban University?**
Lean Kanban University, now called Kanban University, is the organisation that continues to develop and teach the Kanban Method and offers accredited Kanban training.

**Q: How do Lean and Kanban improve flow?**
Both limit work in progress, make queues visible and pull work only when capacity is available, so items move steadily rather than piling up. See [pull vs push systems](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/).

**Q: Can you use Lean Kanban with Scrum?**
Yes. Scrum teams often adopt Lean Kanban practices such as WIP limits and flow metrics, and the mix is often called [Scrumban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrumban/).

# Lean Manufacturing: Principles, Wastes and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Lean manufacturing explained: Toyota origins, the seven wastes, key tools such as 5S, kanban, JIT and kaizen, and lessons for project teams.


## Lean Manufacturing: Principles, Wastes and Tools
Lean manufacturing is a way of producing goods that maximises customer value while minimising waste. Developed at Toyota and later studied worldwide, it underpins Kanban, Agile and much of modern operations management.
- Published 15 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Lean began at Toyota and focuses on value and waste.
- The seven wastes apply to knowledge work as well as factories.
- JIT, kanban, jidoka, 5S and kaizen are core Lean tools.

### Origins
Lean grew out of the Toyota Production System, developed from the late 1940s by Taiichi Ohno, Eiji Toyoda and colleagues. The term "lean" was coined by researcher John Krafcik in 1988 and popularised by The Machine That Changed the World (1990), a study of the global car industry by Womack, Jones and Roos.

### The seven wastes (muda)
| Waste | Manufacturing example | Knowledge-work example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transport | Moving parts between distant areas | Handing work between many teams |
| Inventory | Stockpiles of parts | Large backlogs; half-finished work |
| Motion | Workers walking to fetch tools | Searching for files and information |
| Waiting | Machines idle for parts | Waiting for approvals or reviews |
| Overproduction | Making more than ordered | Building features nobody uses |
| Over-processing | Unneeded precision | Excessive documentation or gold-plating |
| Defects | Scrap and rework | Bugs and errors needing rework |
Many practitioners add an eighth waste: unused talent.

### Key Lean tools
- **[Just-in-Time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/just-in-time-jit/):** produce only what is needed, when needed.
- **Kanban:** signals that pull production; see [what is Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/).
- **Jidoka:** build quality in; stop the line when a problem occurs.
- **5S:** sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain; see [visual management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/visual-management/).
- **Kaizen:** continuous, incremental improvement by everyone.
- **Value stream mapping:** see the whole flow; see [VSM](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/).
- **Heijunka:** level the production schedule.
- **Poka-yoke:** mistake-proofing.

### Lessons for project teams
- Focus on customer value and stop doing work that doesn't add it.
- Limit work in progress and make work flow.
- Make problems visible and fix their causes.
- Let the people doing the work improve it.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the main goal of Lean manufacturing?**
To deliver maximum customer value with minimum waste, through continuous improvement.

**Q: Is Lean manufacturing only for factories?**
No. Although Lean manufacturing began in factories, Lean principles are used in healthcare, software, services, construction and project management.

**Q: What is Lean manufacturing?**
Lean manufacturing is an approach to production that maximises customer value by systematically removing waste and improving flow. It grew out of the Toyota Production System.

**Q: Where did Lean manufacturing come from?**
It came from the Toyota Production System, developed from the late 1940s by Taiichi Ohno, Eiji Toyoda and colleagues. The term "lean" was coined by John Krafcik in 1988.

**Q: What is muda in Lean manufacturing?**
Muda is the Japanese word for waste: any activity that uses resources without adding value for the customer. Lean also targets mura (unevenness) and muri (overburden).

**Q: What is 5S in Lean manufacturing?**
5S is a workplace organisation method: sort, set in order, shine, standardise and sustain. See [visual management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/visual-management/).

**Q: What is jidoka in Lean manufacturing?**
Jidoka, sometimes called automation with a human touch, means machines or people stop the process as soon as a defect is detected, so problems are fixed at the source.

**Q: What are the main Lean manufacturing tools?**
Common tools include [Just-in-Time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/just-in-time-jit/), kanban, jidoka, 5S, kaizen, [value stream mapping](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) and standard work.

**Q: What is the difference between Lean manufacturing and Six Sigma?**
Lean focuses on removing waste and improving flow, while Six Sigma focuses on reducing variation and defects with statistical methods. Many organisations combine them as Lean Six Sigma.

**Q: How do project managers use Lean manufacturing ideas?**
Project teams apply Lean by cutting waiting and hand-offs, limiting work in progress, visualising work and running regular improvement reviews.

**Q: How does the Toyota Production System relate to Lean manufacturing?**
The Toyota Production System is Toyota's approach to manufacturing, built on Just-in-Time and jidoka. It is the foundation of Lean manufacturing and of kanban.

# Personal Kanban: Manage Your Own Work With Two Simple Rules

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/personal-kanban/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: How to use personal Kanban to manage your own tasks: the two rules, a simple board setup, WIP limits for individuals, and tips that make it stick.


## Personal Kanban: Manage Your Own Work With Two Simple Rules
Personal Kanban applies Kanban to an individual's work. It was popularised by Jim Benson and Tonianne DeMaria Barry, whose 2011 book reduced it to two rules: visualise your work, and limit your work in progress.
- Published 7 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Personal Kanban has two rules: visualise work and limit WIP.
- Start with Ready, Doing and Done.
- Review weekly and finish before starting.

### The two rules
- **Visualise your work:** put every task on a board so you can see your real workload.
- **Limit your work in progress:** decide how many things you will work on at once, and finish before starting more.

### Setting up a personal board
1. Use a whiteboard, sticky notes on a wall, or a simple app.
2. Create three columns: **Ready**, **Doing**, **Done**.
3. Write each task on its own card.
4. Set a WIP limit on Doing, typically two or three.
5. Each morning, pull the most important card into Doing.

### Useful additions
- A **Backlog** column for everything you might do, with Ready holding only this week's priorities.
- A **Waiting** column for items blocked on other people.
- A **Today** column for daily focus.
- Colours for work, personal and learning tasks.

### Why it works
- Seeing all your work reduces anxiety and forgotten commitments.
- Limiting WIP reduces task switching, which costs focus.
- The Done column shows real progress.
- Weekly reviews help you notice patterns, such as tasks that keep stalling.

### Making it stick
- Keep the board where you see it every day.
- Review it weekly and clear the Done column.
- Say no, or not yet, when Doing is full.
- Keep tasks small enough to finish in a day or two.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a good WIP limit for personal Kanban?**
Two or three active tasks is common. Start low and adjust after a week or two.

**Q: Can families use personal Kanban?**
Yes. Many households use a shared board for chores, errands and plans.

**Q: What is personal Kanban?**
Personal Kanban applies Kanban to one person's work, using a simple board to see everything you need to do and limit how much you work on at once.

**Q: What are the two rules of personal Kanban?**
Visualise your work and limit your work in progress. The approach was popularised by Jim Benson and Tonianne DeMaria Barry in their book Personal Kanban.

**Q: What columns should a personal Kanban board have?**
Start with Backlog, Doing and Done. Many people add a Today or Ready column, and a Waiting column for items blocked on someone else.

**Q: What is the best app for personal Kanban?**
Any simple board tool works, such as [Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/) or a Kanban view in [Notion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/notion/). A sticky-note board on a wall or notebook works just as well.

**Q: How is personal Kanban different from a to-do list?**
A to-do list shows what needs doing, while a personal Kanban board also shows what is in progress, what is waiting and limits how much you start. That makes overload visible.

**Q: Can students use personal Kanban?**
Yes. Students often use it to manage assignments, revision and deadlines, keeping a small WIP limit so they finish one task before starting the next.

**Q: How do you handle recurring tasks on a personal Kanban board?**
Keep a reusable card for each recurring task and move it back to the backlog when done, or keep routine chores in a separate small lane so they do not crowd out project work.

**Q: How often should you review a personal Kanban board?**
Glance at it daily to choose what to pull next, and do a short weekly review to clear Done, reprioritise the backlog and reflect on what slowed you down.

**Q: Does personal Kanban help with procrastination?**
It can, because a small WIP limit and a visible next step make it easier to start and finish one thing. Seeing the Done column grow is also motivating.
