# Pull System vs Push System: Differences and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: Pull system vs push system explained: what triggers work, how WIP limits define pull, worked examples, Little's Law and how to move from push to pull.


## Pull System vs Push System: Differences and Examples
The difference between a pull system and a push system is what starts the work: a push system releases work according to a forecast, plan or schedule, whether or not the next step is ready, while a pull system starts work only when there is real demand and free capacity downstream. The clearest test is whether the amount of work in progress is explicitly capped. Kanban is a pull system. This guide compares the two with tables, a manufacturing and a knowledge-work worked example, and a step-by-step route from push to pull.
- Published 17 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Push releases work from forecasts and schedules; pull releases work when a downstream signal shows demand and spare capacity.
- A widely cited definition from Hopp and Spearman (2004) says a pull system is one that explicitly limits work in process. If nothing caps WIP, it is push, even if you build to order.
- Capping WIP shortens lead times: by Little's Law, average cycle time equals average WIP divided by throughput.
- Push still makes sense for stable demand, long supply lead times and work that benefits from batching. Most organisations use a hybrid with a push-pull boundary.
- In knowledge work, pull means people take the next item when they finish one, controlled by WIP limits on a Kanban board, instead of a manager assigning work to full queues.

### Pull system vs push system: the short answer
A **push system** starts work because a plan says so: a forecast, a production schedule or a manager's allocation pushes items into the process. A **pull system** starts work only when a downstream step or customer signals that it needs more and capacity is free, so the amount of work in progress stays capped. Push optimises for keeping everyone busy; pull optimises for finishing work quickly.
|  | Push system | Pull system |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What starts work | Forecast, schedule or plan | A signal of real demand and free capacity |
| Work in progress | Not explicitly limited; tends to grow | Explicitly capped |
| Information flows | Top down, ahead of demand | Upstream, from the point of consumption |
| Typical tools | MRP, master production schedules, task assignment | Kanban cards, WIP limits, two-bin systems, CONWIP |
| Main risk | Overproduction, overload, long queues | Shortages or delays if demand spikes or processes are unreliable |

### What is a push system?
In a push system, work is released into a process based on what is expected to be needed. A planning step (often software such as material requirements planning, MRP) turns a demand forecast into a schedule, and each stage produces its quota and passes the output on. Nothing in the system stops a stage producing more because the next one is already full.

#### Examples of push
- A clothing manufacturer produces its autumn range in spring to a sales forecast and stores it until the season starts.
- A bakery bakes 200 loaves every morning based on last month's average sales.
- A factory releases work orders every Monday from the master schedule, regardless of how much is already on the shop floor.
- A manager splits a project plan into tasks and assigns five to each person on Monday, whatever they are already working on.
- A marketing department commissions next quarter's content in one batch at the planning meeting.
Push is not a mistake in itself. It works well when demand is stable and predictable, when supply lead times are longer than customers are willing to wait, or when large batches bring real economies of scale. Its weakness is that forecasts are always wrong to some degree, and the error shows up as excess stock, queues and overloaded people.

### What is a pull system?
In a pull system, work is triggered by consumption. When a customer takes a product, or a downstream step finishes an item and has room for another, a signal goes upstream to replace or supply it. Kanban University's glossary defines a pull system as one for delivering work only when both demand exists and delivery capacity is available.
The idea came from Taiichi Ohno at Toyota. According to the Lean Enterprise Institute, he based the **supermarket** concept on American stores, where shelves are restocked as customers take goods, and Toyota installed its first supermarket in 1953. Cards called kanban (Japanese for signboard) travelled with parts and authorised production of exactly what had been used.

#### Examples of pull
- A supermarket restocks a shelf when the gap appears, and the store reorders from the warehouse based on what was sold.
- A two-bin system on a workbench: when the first bin of screws is empty, it is sent to stores for refilling while the second bin is used.
- An assembly line where each station has a fixed number of kanban cards, so it can only build what the next station has used.
- A café that makes each coffee when it is ordered, with a limit on how many orders the barista accepts at once.
- A software team whose board allows three items in Build; a developer pulls a new item from Ready only when one leaves Build.
In knowledge work, the cards are usually virtual: a WIP limit on a board column is the pull signal. The Kanban Guide makes the link directly, noting that an effect of controlling WIP is that it should create a pull system. Learn more in [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) and [what is Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/).

### The WIP-cap test: a clearer way to tell push from pull
Many articles say push is "forecast-driven" and pull is "demand-driven". That is a useful rule of thumb, but it breaks down quickly. Wallace Hopp and Mark Spearman, in their 2004 paper "To Pull or Not to Pull: What Is the Question?" (*Manufacturing & Service Operations Management*), proposed a sharper definition: a pull production system is one that **explicitly limits the amount of work in process** that can be in the system. A push system has no such limit.
This test clears up three common misconceptions:
- **"Make-to-order is pull."** Not necessarily. A tailor who only makes suits to order but accepts and starts every order immediately has no WIP cap, so queues and lead times grow without limit. That behaves like push.
- **"Make-to-stock is push."** Not necessarily. Toyota builds some cars without a specific customer order, but within a system of capped buffers and kanban, which is pull.
- **"MRP is push and kanban is pull."** Usually true, but Hopp and Spearman note that MRP with a WIP constraint becomes a pull system. The planning tool matters less than whether releases are capped.
Pull systems still use forecasts. You need an estimate of demand to size buffers and WIP limits. The difference is that the forecast sets the capacity of the system, while actual consumption decides what happens day to day.

#### Push or pull? Nine scenarios
| Scenario | Push or pull? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bakery bakes 200 loaves each morning from last month's average | Push | Output is set by forecast; no link to what was sold today |
| Supermarket restocks a shelf when it empties | Pull | Consumption triggers replenishment; shelf space caps stock |
| Two-bin system for screws | Pull | An empty bin is the signal; two bins cap inventory |
| Tailor starts every order the day it arrives, however many are open | Push | Built to order, but nothing limits WIP |
| Car plant builds to dealer stock using a fixed number of kanban cards | Pull | Make-to-stock, but WIP is capped by the cards |
| Manager assigns five tickets to each person every Monday | Push | Work is allocated regardless of what is finished |
| Team takes the next item from Ready when an In progress slot frees up | Pull | Column WIP limit is the signal |
| Scrum team selects items at Sprint Planning based on its capacity | Pull at Sprint level | The team pulls what it can complete; the Sprint bounds the work |
| MRP releases work orders only when shop-floor WIP is below a cap | Pull | Hopp and Spearman class MRP with a WIP constraint as pull |

### Push vs pull: key differences
| Aspect | Push | Pull |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trigger | Plan, forecast or schedule | Consumption or a free capacity slot |
| Control variable | Throughput (how much to release) | WIP (how much is allowed in the system) |
| WIP and inventory | Can grow without limit | Capped by cards, bins or limits |
| Lead time | Long and variable as queues grow | Shorter and more predictable |
| Response to a change in demand | Slow; the plan must be revised and existing stock used up | Fast; the next signal reflects the new demand |
| Problem visibility | Hidden by buffers of stock or work | Exposed quickly because there is little slack |
| Utilisation | Aims to keep every resource busy | Accepts some idle time to keep flow |
| Prioritisation | Fixed when the plan is made | Deferred until the moment work starts |
| Cash tied up | Higher (stock and part-finished work) | Lower |
| Dependence on forecasts | High | Lower, though still used to size the system |
| Dependence on reliable processes | Lower; buffers absorb problems | High; breakdowns stop the flow |
| Typical failure mode | Overproduction, obsolete stock, overloaded teams | Stock-outs or waiting when demand spikes |

### Types of pull system
"Pull" covers several mechanisms. The right one depends on how many variants you produce and whether you hold stock.
| Type | How it works | Best suited to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Replenishment (supermarket) pull | A set stock of each item is held; each item used is replaced, triggered by a card or empty container | Standard, frequently used parts or products |
| Sequential pull | Items are made to order in sequence and flow first-in, first-out through capped lanes | Many variants or custom items that cannot all be stocked |
| Two-bin system | Two containers per item; an empty bin is the reorder signal | Consumables and low-cost parts |
| CONWIP (constant WIP) | A fixed number of cards circulates for the whole line; a card returning to the start releases the next most urgent job, whatever its type | Make-to-order or mixed products; described by Spearman, Woodruff and Hopp in 1990 |
| Drum-buffer-rope | Release is tied to the pace of the bottleneck (the drum), with a time buffer protecting it | Systems with a clear constraint; from the Theory of Constraints |
| Virtual kanban (knowledge work) | WIP limits on board columns or the whole board; a free slot is the pull signal | Teams handling requests, projects or product work |

### Worked example: sizing a kanban pull loop in a workshop
The figures in this example are illustrative. A metal workshop makes a bracket used by its own assembly cell. Assembly uses about **120 brackets a day**. It takes the bracket line **1.5 days** to replenish a container once it is signalled (including queueing, machining and moving). Brackets travel in containers of **30**, and the team adds a **20% safety factor** for variation.
A commonly used formula for the number of kanban cards is:
**Number of cards = (daily demand x replenishment lead time x (1 + safety factor)) / container quantity**
1. Demand during the lead time: 120 x 1.5 = 180 brackets.
2. Add the safety factor: 180 x 1.2 = 216 brackets.
3. Divide by the container size: 216 / 30 = 7.2.
4. Round up to **8 cards**. The most brackets that can ever be in the loop is 8 x 30 = 240.

#### What the same workshop looks like under push
Under its old push schedule, the bracket line produced 700 a week (140 a day) because that was the forecast. Real demand was 600 a week. In four weeks the workshop built up 400 surplus brackets, which took up floor space and cash, and when the design changed in week five, 400 brackets had to be reworked or scrapped. With the pull loop, at most 240 brackets existed at any time and the design change affected only those.
Tip
Review the number of cards whenever demand or lead time changes noticeably. Many pull systems slowly turn back into push because the cards were sized once and never revisited; Toyota's practice of steadily reducing cards to expose problems is the opposite habit.

### Worked example: from assigning work to pulling it in a design team
This example is also illustrative. A four-person in-house design team receives requests from marketing, product and sales.

#### Before: push
- Every Monday the team lead assigns new requests so that each designer has about four on the go.
- Average WIP is 16 items. The team finishes about 8 a week.
- By Little's Law, average cycle time is 16 / 8 = **2 weeks**, even though most requests take less than a day of actual design effort.
- Designers switch between jobs all day, requesters chase constantly, and urgent items jump the queue by escalation.

#### After: pull
1. The team maps its workflow onto a board: Requests, Ready (limit 4), Designing (limit 4), Review (limit 3), Done.
2. The lead stops assigning. Instead, she runs a 20-minute replenishment twice a week with the requesting teams to agree which requests move into Ready.
3. A designer who finishes an item pulls the top card from Ready. If Review is full, they help clear Review first.
4. A policy allows one expedite item at a time, agreed by the lead.
5. The team records start and finish dates for every card.

#### Results after six weeks
| Measure | Push (before) | Pull (after) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Average WIP | 16 items | 7 items |
| Throughput | 8 items a week | 9 items a week |
| Average cycle time (WIP / throughput) | 2 weeks | about 0.8 weeks (4 working days) |
| Escalations from requesters | several a week | rare; requesters see the queue at replenishment |
The gain comes mostly from less waiting and less task switching, not from people working harder. You can follow the same steps with our free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) and gather requests consistently with the [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/).

### Why limiting WIP shortens lead time (Little's Law)
Little's Law, first proved by John Little in 1961, states that in a stable system **average cycle time = average WIP / average throughput**. If you keep throughput the same and halve the amount of work in progress, the average time each item spends in the system halves too.
Push systems tend to increase WIP, because work is released whether or not it can be processed, so cycle time grows. Pull systems cap WIP, so cycle time is bounded. Pull often raises throughput a little as well, because fewer items compete for attention and problems are fixed sooner.
The law describes long-run averages and assumes a stable system, where roughly as many items start as finish and items are not abandoned part-way. Use it to understand and explain your system, not to promise a date for a single item. For forecasting individual items, use the distribution of past [cycle times](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) and [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/).

### Advantages and disadvantages of push and pull

#### Push system
| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Stock is ready when demand is predictable or seasonal | Forecast errors become surplus stock or shortages |
| Supports long supply lead times and large batches | WIP and queues grow, lengthening lead times |
| Easy to plan resources and purchasing in advance | Problems are hidden behind buffers |
| Resources stay highly utilised | People and machines are overloaded; quality can suffer |
| Familiar to most organisations and planning software | Slow to respond to changes in demand or priority |

#### Pull system
| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Less overproduction, stock and part-finished work | Needs reliable processes and suppliers; a breakdown stops flow |
| Shorter, more predictable lead times | Can struggle with sudden spikes in demand |
| Priorities stay flexible until work starts | Requires discipline to respect limits under pressure |
| Problems surface quickly and get fixed | Some idle time is accepted, which can feel uncomfortable |
| Less multitasking and overload in teams | Buffers and limits must be sized and reviewed regularly |

### When push is the better choice
Pull is not always superior. Push, or a push-heavy hybrid, often makes more sense when:
- **Demand is stable and well understood**, so forecasts are accurate and stock rarely goes to waste.
- **Supply lead times are long**, such as components shipped from overseas, and customers will not wait that long.
- **Demand is seasonal**, so capacity must be used in quiet months to build stock for the peak.
- **Batching brings real savings**, for example a long, expensive machine set-up or a bulk purchase discount.
- **Work must be committed far ahead**, such as a fixed event date, a regulatory deadline or a construction sequence that needs materials on site in advance.
- **Processes are not yet reliable**, so removing buffers would expose customers to every breakdown. Stabilise first, then move towards pull.

### Push-pull hybrids and the push-pull boundary
Most real systems combine both. The **push-pull boundary** (sometimes called the decoupling point) is the place in the chain where work stops being driven by forecast and starts being driven by actual demand. Upstream of it you push; downstream you pull.
| Setting | Pushed (to forecast) | Pulled (to demand) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build-to-order computers | Components bought and stocked to a forecast | Final assembly once a customer orders |
| Bespoke furniture | Common frames and materials prepared in advance | Upholstery and finishing for each order |
| Restaurant | Ingredients bought and prepared to expected covers | Dishes cooked when ordered |
| Project portfolio | Annual plan and budget allocate funding to initiatives | Teams pull the next item when they have capacity |
| Kanban team | Options are gathered and refined in the backlog | Items cross the commitment point and are pulled into delivery |
In Kanban the boundary has a name: the **commitment point**. Before it, items are options that can be reordered or dropped. After it, the team has committed and pulls work at the pace its WIP limits allow. Moving the boundary further upstream increases responsiveness but needs a more reliable process; moving it downstream reduces lead time for the customer but needs more stock or more preparation. Plan replenishment in [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/).

### How to move from push to pull: step by step
1. **Map the flow.** Draw the steps that work goes through and where it waits. A [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) shows queues and stock between steps.
2. **Measure current WIP and lead time.** Count items in progress at each step and how long items take end to end. This is your baseline.
3. **Stabilise the process.** Fix the most frequent breakdowns, rework loops and missing information first. Pull exposes instability; it does not cure it.
4. **Choose the pull mechanism.** Replenishment cards for standard items, sequential or CONWIP for made-to-order work, column WIP limits for teams.
5. **Size the limits.** Use the card formula for stock, or start knowledge-work limits around the number of people in a stage. Make them slightly tight so queues become visible.
6. **Stop releasing work by schedule.** This is the hard step. Planners and managers must hold new work until a signal says there is room.
7. **Agree what happens when a limit is hit.** People swarm on the blocked step, help downstream, or improve the process; they do not start something new.
8. **Review and adjust.** Track WIP, throughput and cycle time weekly, reduce limits gradually, and resize buffers when demand changes.
The concept behind these steps is covered in depth in our [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) guide.

### Pull systems in Agile and project work
Pull is the core idea behind Kanban and appears throughout Agile practice.
- **Kanban:** WIP limits on the board turn every free slot into a pull signal. Replenishment meetings decide what is ready to be pulled; the team decides when. See [Kanban vs Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-agile/) for how this fits Agile values.
- **Scrum:** the team pulls work into the Sprint during [Sprint Planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/), choosing how much it can complete towards the Sprint Goal. Within the Sprint, Developers typically pull tasks rather than having them assigned.
- **Resource management:** a push-style approach assigns people to several projects at once to keep utilisation high. A pull-style approach limits the number of active projects and starts a new one only when capacity frees up, which shortens delivery across the portfolio. See [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/), [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) and [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/).
- **Flow measurement:** a [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/) shows whether work is being pushed in faster than it leaves, and [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) shows how much of the lead time is waiting.
For the broader Lean thinking behind this, read our guide to [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/).

### Common mistakes when introducing pull
- **Setting WIP limits but still releasing work on a schedule.** The board shows limits, but new work keeps arriving in people's queues by email. Pull has to apply at the point where work is released.
- **Removing buffers before the process is stable.** Breakdowns that buffers used to hide now stop customers being served, and pull gets the blame.
- **Treating idle time as waste.** Someone waiting for a slot should help clear a bottleneck or improve the process, not start a new item.
- **Sizing cards or limits once.** Demand, lead times and team size change; the limits must change with them.
- **Expediting everything.** If most items are "urgent", the expedite lane becomes a push channel. Limit it to one item at a time.
- **Ignoring the upstream side.** Pull at team level does not help if the portfolio keeps approving more projects than teams can start.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the main difference between a push system and a pull system?**
What starts the work. A push system releases work according to a forecast or schedule; a pull system releases work only when a downstream signal shows demand and spare capacity. As a result, pull systems cap work in progress and push systems do not.

**Q: Is Kanban a push or pull system?**
Kanban is a pull system. A fixed number of cards, or a WIP limit on a board column, means new work can only start when an item has been used or finished. Kanban University defines a pull system as delivering work only when demand exists and capacity is available.

**Q: Is MRP push or pull?**
Traditional MRP is a push system: it releases orders from a master schedule regardless of how much work is already in the system. Hopp and Spearman point out that MRP combined with an explicit WIP limit behaves as a pull system.

**Q: What is an example of a pull system?**
A supermarket restocking a shelf when it empties, a two-bin system for workshop consumables, or a team that pulls the next request from a Ready column only when an In progress slot is free.

**Q: What is an example of a push system?**
A clothing brand producing a whole season's stock to a sales forecast, a factory releasing work orders every week from a fixed schedule, or a manager assigning tasks to people regardless of their current workload.

**Q: Which is better, push or pull?**
Neither in every case. Pull usually gives shorter lead times, less stock and less overload, especially when demand is uncertain. Push can be better for stable or seasonal demand, long supply lead times and work that benefits from large batches. Most organisations combine both.

**Q: Is make-to-order the same as a pull system?**
No. Make-to-order describes when production starts relative to the customer order. Pull describes whether work in progress is capped. A make-to-order business that starts every order at once, with no limit, has the queue problems of a push system.

**Q: What is a push-pull system?**
A hybrid in which earlier stages are pushed to a forecast and later stages are pulled by actual demand. The point where one changes to the other is the push-pull boundary, or decoupling point. Build-to-order assembly from stocked components is a common example.

**Q: Is Scrum a push or pull system?**
Scrum is a pull system at Sprint level: the team pulls the amount of work it can complete into the Sprint at Sprint Planning. Within the Sprint, Developers usually pull tasks themselves rather than having them assigned.

**Q: What are the disadvantages of a pull system?**
It needs reliable processes and suppliers, can struggle with sudden demand spikes, requires discipline to respect limits, and its buffers and limits must be sized and reviewed regularly.

**Q: What is CONWIP?**
CONWIP (constant work in progress) is a pull system in which a fixed number of cards circulates for a whole production line rather than for each part. When a job finishes, its card returns and releases the next most urgent job. It suits make-to-order and mixed products.

**Q: How do WIP limits create a pull system?**
When a column or stage is at its limit, nothing new can enter until an item leaves. The free slot acts as the signal to pull the next item, so work is released by downstream capacity rather than pushed in by a plan.

**Q: How do you calculate the number of kanban cards?**
A common formula is daily demand multiplied by replenishment lead time and by (1 plus a safety factor), divided by the container quantity, rounded up. Review the result whenever demand or lead time changes.

# Theory of Constraints (TOC): Five Focusing Steps Explained

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: The theory of constraints explained: the five focusing steps, drum-buffer-rope, throughput accounting and how to apply TOC in Kanban, with worked examples.


## Theory of Constraints (TOC): Five Focusing Steps Explained
The theory of constraints (TOC) is a management approach which holds that every system has at least one constraint limiting its output, so the fastest way to improve the whole system is to find that constraint and manage everything around it. It gives you a simple, repeatable cycle, the five focusing steps, that works on a factory floor, a Kanban board or a portfolio of projects. This guide walks through the five steps with a worked Kanban example and covers drum-buffer-rope, throughput accounting and TOC in projects.
- Published 16 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Every system has a constraint, the one resource, policy or market limit that caps its output. Improving anything else barely changes the result.
- The five focusing steps are identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate and repeat. Always exploit and subordinate before you spend money elevating.
- On a Kanban board the constraint is usually the stage with the biggest queue in front of it and idle or blocked stages after it.
- Drum-buffer-rope paces the system to the constraint; in Kanban, WIP limits act as the rope and a small ready queue acts as the buffer.
- Non-constraint resources should have spare capacity. Keeping everyone 100% busy simply builds queues and lengthens cycle time.

### What is the theory of constraints?
The theory of constraints is a way of improving any system with a goal, such as a business, a production line or a delivery team, by focusing on the single factor that most limits its performance. Improving other parts of the system produces little or no overall gain.
Think of a chain: it is only as strong as its weakest link. If testers can check six pieces of work a week, the team delivers about six a week, however fast the developers write code.
TOC was developed by Israeli physicist Eliyahu M. Goldratt (1947 to 2011). He introduced it to a mass audience in **The Goal** (1984, written with Jeff Cox), a business novel about a plant manager who rescues his failing factory by finding and managing its bottlenecks. Goldratt set out the five focusing steps in What is this Thing Called Theory of Constraints (1990), launched the TOC thinking processes in 1991 and popularised them in It's Not Luck (1994), and applied the theory to projects in Critical Chain (1997).
TOC began in manufacturing but is now used in supply chains, healthcare, software and projects. It sits alongside [Lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/) and [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/), which share its focus on flow.

### The core ideas behind TOC
TOC rests on a few ideas that often run against normal management instinct. Start by agreeing the goal and how you measure it, such as items delivered per week: you cannot find the constraint until you know what it is constraining. Then think in systems, not departments. An hour the constraint loses to idle time or rework is lost to the whole system, while an hour saved at a non-constraint usually just makes work arrive sooner at the queue in front of the constraint.
| Common belief | TOC view |
| --- | --- |
| Every team should be fully utilised | Only the constraint must be fully utilised; other resources need slack |
| Improve every process a little | Improve the constraint a lot; leave the rest alone until it becomes the constraint |
| Start work as early as possible | Release work at the pace the constraint can absorb |
| Add people where the work is late | Add capacity only at the constraint, and only after exploiting it |

### Constraint vs bottleneck: types of constraints
The two words are often used interchangeably. Strictly, a **bottleneck** is any resource whose capacity is lower than the demand placed on it. A **constraint** is broader: it is whatever limits the system's performance against its goal, which may be a bottleneck, but may also be a policy, a supplier or the market itself. Every system has a constraint; not every system has a bottleneck. If you can produce more than customers want to buy, demand is the constraint.
Constraints are often grouped as **internal** (inside your control, such as capacity, skills or rules) and **external** (outside it, such as market demand, regulation or a supplier's lead time).
| Type | Operations example | Project or knowledge-work example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physical capacity | One machine slower than the rest of the line | Two testers serving six developers |
| Skills or people | Only one certified welder | One architect who must review every design |
| Policy | Minimum batch size of 500 units | All changes wait for a fortnightly approval board |
| Material or supplier | Late component deliveries | Client content arrives late; a vendor's API is not ready |
| Market | Demand lower than capacity | Not enough approved projects to keep the team supplied |
In knowledge work, policy constraints are common and cheap to fix: an approval step, a batching habit or a rule about who may do what. Look for these before concluding that a team needs more people.
TOC constraints are not the same as the scope, time and cost limits a project works within. Our guide to [project constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-constraints/) covers the triple constraint.

### The five focusing steps
The five focusing steps are TOC's ongoing improvement cycle. Many practitioners add a "step zero": agree the system's goal and how you measure it.
| Step | Key question | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Identify | What limits our output? | Low |
| 2. Exploit | How do we get more from the constraint as it is? | Low |
| 3. Subordinate | How does everything else support the constraint? | Low |
| 4. Elevate | How do we add capacity to the constraint? | Medium to high |
| 5. Repeat | Has the constraint moved? | Low |

#### Step 1: Identify the constraint
Find the part of the system that limits output. In a physical process it is usually where inventory piles up; in a team it is the stage with the largest queue in front of it, or the people everyone waits for. Do not wait for perfect data: a wrong first guess is quickly corrected.

#### Step 2: Exploit the constraint
Exploiting means squeezing the most output from the constraint with the resources you already have. It costs little or nothing. Typical actions:
- Make sure the constraint never sits idle waiting for work; keep a small queue of ready items in front of it.
- Remove tasks that others can do, such as administration, environment set-up or reporting.
- Stop defective input reaching the constraint, so it does not waste time on work that will come back.
- Protect focus time and cut task switching; let the constraint finish one item before starting the next.

#### Step 3: Subordinate everything else
Subordinating means adjusting everything else to support the constraint, even if that leaves other resources partly idle. Release new work only at the pace the constraint can handle, keep a buffer in front of it, and let people with spare capacity help it rather than start new work. Culturally this is the hardest step, because managers must accept visible slack.

#### Step 4: Elevate the constraint
If the constraint still limits output, add capacity: hire or train people, automate, buy equipment or outsource part of the work. Elevating costs money and time, which is why it comes fourth; teams that jump straight to hiring often bury the extra capacity under waste the earlier steps would have removed.

#### Step 5: Repeat, and do not let inertia become the constraint
Once the constraint is broken, another part of the system becomes the limit, so go back to step 1. Goldratt warned that rules introduced for the old constraint can become the new one, so review them each time it moves. Over time, many organisations decide where they want the constraint to sit, often an expensive resource, and keep it there deliberately.
Tip
If you remember one rule, make it this: exploit and subordinate before you elevate. Cheap changes at the constraint usually come before expensive ones.

### Worked example: applying TOC to a Kanban board
This illustrative example follows a software team using a four-stage Kanban board. About nine new items are started each week. Average capacity per stage:
| Stage | People | Capacity (items/week) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analyse | 1 analyst | 12 |
| Build | 5 developers | 10 |
| Test | 3 testers | 6 |
| Release | Automated pipeline, 1 engineer | 15 |

#### Step 1: identify
Nine items a week enter, but only six a week leave Test, so the queue in front of Test grows by three items every week. Release is often idle. Test is the constraint. After a couple of months there are about 42 items in progress. Using Little's Law (average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput), the average item takes 42 ÷ 6 = 7 weeks to get through the system.

#### Step 2: exploit
Looking at how testers spend their week reveals two problems:
- Each tester spends roughly a day a week setting up test environments and writing status reports. A developer scripts the environment set-up and the board replaces the written report. Capacity rises from 6 to 7 items a week.
- About one item in four fails basic checks and has to be retested. The team adds a "ready for test" checklist that developers complete, including unit tests. Fewer retests lift capacity to 8 items a week.
Throughput rises to 8 with no new spending. But nine items are still entering each week, so the queue keeps growing by one a week and cycle time stays around five weeks.

#### Step 3: subordinate
- **The rope:** the team agrees to pull only eight new items a week into Analyse, matching the constraint, and sets WIP limits on Analyse and Build.
- **The buffer:** a "Ready for test" column with a WIP limit of four keeps testers supplied without letting a large queue build up.
- **Helping the constraint:** when Build reaches its WIP limit, developers pair with testers or write automated tests instead of starting new items.
Over the next five weeks the excess work drains away. WIP settles at about 16 items while throughput stays at eight, so average cycle time falls to 16 ÷ 8 = 2 weeks. Developers now have some slack, which is intended.

#### Step 4: elevate
Demand is growing, so the team invests in automated regression tests. Test capacity rises to about 12 items a week and the release rate to 10.

#### Step 5: repeat
With Test at 12, Build (10) is now the slowest stage and becomes the constraint. The team returns to step 1, and also reviews the rule that developers must help Test whenever Build is full, because that rule would now starve the new constraint.
| Measure | Start | After exploit | After subordinate | After elevate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test capacity (items/week) | 6 | 8 | 8 | 12 |
| Items started per week | 9 | 9 | 8 | 10 |
| Throughput (items/week) | 6 | 8 | 8 | 10 |
| Work in progress | 42 and growing | 42 and growing | 16 | About 20 |
| Average cycle time | 7 weeks | About 5 weeks | 2 weeks | 2 weeks |
| Constraint | Test | Test | Test | Build |
The biggest gain in speed came from subordination, not new capacity: it cut cycle time from about five weeks to two by no longer starting work faster than it could be finished. That is why TOC and [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) work so well together.

### How to find the constraint in your workflow
Use this sequence on any board or process:
1. **Map the workflow** from request to delivery, including waiting states and handoffs. A [value stream map](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) or our [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/) helps.
2. **Count throughput by stage** over the last four to eight weeks: how many items each stage finished per week.
3. **Look for the queue.** The constraint usually has the most work waiting in front of it and the oldest items in its queue.
4. **Look downstream.** Stages after the constraint are often idle or starved; stages before it are often blocked or told to slow down.
5. **Check the cumulative flow diagram.** On a [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/), the band that keeps widening is the queue building in front of the constraint.
6. **Check item age.** A [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) shows where items stall for longest.
7. **Look at blockers and ask the team.** [Blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/) often reveals a policy or external constraint, and people usually know who they wait for.
8. **Confirm** by asking: if this stage had 20% more capacity, would the whole team deliver more? If not, keep looking.
Be wary of false constraints. Large batch releases, expedited work that jumps the queue and holidays can all make a stage look like the bottleneck for a week or two. Look at several weeks of data, and remember that low [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) usually means work is waiting, which points to a queue somewhere upstream.

### Drum-buffer-rope
Drum-buffer-rope (DBR) is TOC's method for scheduling a system around its constraint. In The Goal, Goldratt illustrated it with a scout hike where the slowest walker sets the pace.
| DBR element | Purpose | Kanban equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drum | The constraint sets the pace for the whole system | Throughput of the constraint stage sets the replenishment rate |
| Buffer | Protect the constraint so it never starves | A "Ready for" column in front of the constraint with its own WIP limit |
| Rope | Release new work only as fast as the constraint consumes it | WIP limits and a replenishment meeting that pulls only when there is room |
| Buffer management | Spot threats to the constraint early | Item age in the buffer, WIP aging chart, blocker review |

#### Buffer management
TOC tracks buffers in three zones of equal size. If the buffer is mostly full, the constraint is safe; as it empties, risk rises.
| Zone | Meaning | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Green (top third) | The constraint is well protected | No action needed |
| Yellow (middle third) | Upstream is slowing down | Check what is coming and plan a response |
| Red (bottom third) | The constraint is about to starve | Expedite work into the buffer; swarm on upstream blockers |
Size the buffer to cover normal variation upstream: start with a few days of the constraint's work and adjust depending on how often it runs into red or overflows.

### TOC and Kanban
Kanban came from the Toyota Production System and TOC from Goldratt, but they meet in Kanban for knowledge work. David J. Anderson, who later shaped the Kanban Method, first wrote Agile Management for Software Engineering: Applying the Theory of Constraints for Business Results (2003).
- **WIP limits are the rope.** They stop teams starting work faster than the constraint can finish it.
- **Swarming exploits the constraint.** When the constraint stage is full, people elsewhere help clear it rather than start new work; see [agile swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/).
- **Little's Law links the two.** Less WIP at the same [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) means shorter [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/), which is exactly what subordination delivers.
The difference is emphasis. Kanban limits WIP at every stage and improves flow everywhere; TOC focuses improvement on one point and accepts slack elsewhere. Use Kanban's WIP limits and metrics to run the system, and the five steps to decide where to improve next.
Read our guide to [Lean Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-kanban/) to see how flow, waste and constraints fit together.

### Theory of constraints in project management
Projects have constraints too, and they are usually people: a specialist shared across several projects, a sponsor who must approve every decision, or a test environment everyone needs. TOC thinking changes how you plan around them.
In TOC terms, you identify the resource most projects wait for, exploit it by protecting its time and making sure its inputs are complete, subordinate by scheduling other work around its availability, and elevate by training a second person or changing who may approve.

#### Multitasking and staggering projects
When a shared specialist splits time across five projects, every project waits for them and all five finish late. TOC's answer is to start fewer projects at once and stagger them according to the constraint resource's capacity. This multi-project form of drum-buffer-rope can shorten delivery of every project without adding people. Our guide to [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) covers the practical side, and [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) helps you see the constraint before it bites.

#### Critical chain
Goldratt's Critical Chain (1997) applied TOC to scheduling: plan the longest chain of dependent tasks allowing for resource availability, pool safety time into shared buffers instead of padding each task, and track how fast the buffers are consumed. See our guide to [critical chain project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-chain-project-management/) and how it compares with the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-chain-vs-critical-path/).

### Throughput accounting
TOC comes with its own management accounting, designed to support decisions about the constraint. It uses three measures:
- **Throughput (T):** the rate at which the system generates money through sales, calculated as revenue minus truly variable costs (usually materials).
- **Investment or inventory (I):** money tied up in things the system intends to sell, plus equipment and other assets.
- **Operating expense (OE):** money spent turning inventory into throughput, such as wages, rent and overheads.
Net profit is T minus OE, and return on investment is (T minus OE) divided by I. The aim is to raise throughput rather than chase cost cuts that do not affect the constraint.

#### Worked example: prioritising by throughput per constraint hour
In this illustrative example, a small workshop makes two products. Both pass through a cutting machine that is available 40 hours a week and is the constraint.
| Product | Price | Materials | Throughput per unit | Cutter time per unit | Throughput per cutter hour | Weekly demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | $50 | $20 | $30 | 30 minutes | $60 | 60 units |
| B | $40 | $25 | $15 | 10 minutes | $90 | 120 units |
Meeting all demand would need 50 cutter hours (30 for A, 20 for B), but only 40 are available. Product A earns more per unit, so instinct says make A first. TOC says rank by throughput per hour of the constraint instead:
- **A first:** 60 units of A use 30 hours, leaving 10 hours for 60 units of B. Throughput = (60 × $30) + (60 × $15) = $2,700 a week.
- **B first:** 120 units of B use 20 hours, leaving 20 hours for 40 units of A. Throughput = (120 × $15) + (40 × $30) = $3,000 a week.
Prioritising B earns $300 more a week from the same constraint. The same logic applies to a team: when the constraint is a scarce specialist, give them the work that delivers the most value per hour of their time.

### The thinking processes
Many constraints are policies, assumptions or conflicts rather than machines or people. Goldratt's thinking processes are logic tools for these, answering three questions: what to change, what to change to, and how to cause the change. They include the current reality tree (traces symptoms to root causes), the evaporating cloud (resolves a conflict by exposing its assumptions), the future reality tree, the prerequisite tree and the transition tree. For simpler problems, a 5 whys analysis with our [root cause analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/) is often enough.

### TOC vs Lean vs Six Sigma
The three improvement approaches overlap and are often combined.
|  | Theory of constraints | Lean | Six Sigma |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main focus | The constraint that limits system output | Waste and flow across the value stream | Variation and defects |
| Key question | Where is the system limited? | Where is there waste? | Why is the output inconsistent? |
| Main measure | Throughput | Lead time, flow efficiency | Defects per million opportunities |
| Best at | Deciding where to improve first | Making work flow with less waste | Making a process consistent |
A common combination is to use TOC to pick the target, then Lean to remove waste at the constraint and [Six Sigma](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/six-sigma/) to reduce variation in its inputs. See [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/) and [Lean vs Six Sigma](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-vs-six-sigma/) for more.

### Benefits and limitations of TOC
TOC's main benefit is focus: it shows where to improve first, and early gains usually come from changing habits and rules, not investment. Its limitations:
- **Constraints move in knowledge work.** A changing work mix can shift the bottleneck, so look at trends over several weeks.
- **Idle time is uncomfortable.** Subordination clashes with utilisation targets.
- **Evidence is mixed.** Critics note that TOC borrows from earlier operations research and that rigorous studies of its results are limited.
- **The people side matters.** Labelling a team "the constraint" can feel like blame; frame it as the system's limit.

### Common mistakes when applying TOC
- **Elevating first.** Hiring or buying before exploiting and subordinating, which hides waste and adds cost.
- **Improving non-constraints.** Speeding up a stage that is not the constraint only moves the queue.
- **Keeping everyone busy.** Letting non-constraint stages start new work whenever they are free, which floods the constraint.
- **Starving the constraint.** Not keeping a buffer in front of it, so it waits for work after every upstream hiccup.
- **Ignoring policy constraints.** Looking only for slow people or machines when an approval rule or batching habit is the real limit.
- **Treating TOC as a one-off, or chasing every fluctuation.** Repeat the cycle, but decide where the constraint should sit rather than reacting to every weekly change.
- **Leaving old rules in place.** Policies built for the old constraint become the new constraint, which is exactly the inertia step 5 warns about.

### Tools and templates for managing constraints
Software makes queues, WIP and trends easier to see. Look for boards with WIP limits, cumulative flow diagrams and workload views.
- **Wrike** (our top-rated tool) offers boards built on custom statuses plus dashboards showing workload across projects, so you can see where work piles up. See our [Wrike review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/).
- **Jira** supports WIP limits on boards and includes cumulative flow diagrams and control charts for cycle time; see our [Jira review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/).
- **ClickUp** supports WIP limits per column and includes cumulative flow reporting.
To start on paper or in a spreadsheet, use our [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) to set up columns, WIP limits and a buffer column, and the workflow template to map stages, owners and handoffs before you look for the constraint.
See our guide to [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) for how to set the limits that act as your rope.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the theory of constraints in simple terms?**
Every system has one part that limits how much it can produce, like the weakest link in a chain. Find it, get the most out of it and organise everything else around it.

**Q: Who developed the theory of constraints?**
Eliyahu M. Goldratt, an Israeli physicist, who introduced it in the 1984 business novel The Goal, written with Jeff Cox.

**Q: What are the five focusing steps?**
Identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it, and repeat when it moves, without letting inertia become the new constraint.

**Q: What is the difference between a constraint and a bottleneck?**
A bottleneck is a resource whose capacity is below demand. A constraint is anything limiting the system's performance, including policies, suppliers and market demand.

**Q: What are some examples of constraints?**
A slow machine, too few testers, one expert who reviews all work, a fortnightly approval board, late supplier deliveries or too little customer demand.

**Q: What does it mean to exploit the constraint?**
Getting the most from it with existing resources: no idle time, no work others could do, no defective input and protected focus time.

**Q: What does subordinate mean in TOC?**
Aligning everything else to the constraint's pace, such as releasing work only as fast as it can process it, even if other resources are partly idle.

**Q: What is drum-buffer-rope?**
A TOC scheduling method: the constraint sets the pace (drum), a buffer protects it, and the rope releases new work only as fast as the constraint consumes it.

**Q: How do you identify the constraint on a Kanban board?**
Look for the largest, oldest queue, idle columns after it and a widening band on the cumulative flow diagram, then confirm with throughput by stage.

**Q: How does the theory of constraints relate to Kanban?**
WIP limits act as TOC's rope, the board makes the constraint visible and swarming exploits it. TOC tells a Kanban team where to focus improvement first.

**Q: What is throughput accounting?**
TOC's management accounting, using throughput (revenue minus truly variable costs), investment and operating expense, and ranking work by throughput per unit of constraint time.

**Q: How is TOC used in project management?**
Through critical chain scheduling with shared buffers, and by staggering projects around the scarcest shared resource to reduce multitasking.

**Q: What is the difference between TOC and Lean?**
Lean removes waste across the whole value stream; TOC focuses on the one constraint that limits output. TOC is often used to decide where to apply Lean first.

# Throughput in Kanban: How to Measure and Use It

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: What throughput means in Kanban, how to measure it, how to forecast delivery dates with throughput and Monte Carlo simulation, and how to improve it.


## Throughput in Kanban: How to Measure and Use It
Throughput is the number of work items a team finishes in a given period, such as a week. It is simple to measure and, combined with cycle time, is the basis of Kanban forecasting.
- Published 12 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Throughput is items finished per period.
- It powers simple and Monte Carlo forecasts.
- Raise it by removing bottlenecks and rework, not by starting more.

### Measuring throughput
Count the items that crossed your delivery point in each period. Plot the counts as a run chart, week by week, to see variation and trends. Unlike velocity, throughput counts items, not story points, so no estimation is needed.

### Throughput and Little's Law
**Average throughput = average WIP ÷ average cycle time.** For example, a team with 12 items in progress and an average cycle time of 3 weeks finishes about 4 items a week. Adding more WIP does not raise throughput once the team is at capacity; it only lengthens cycle time.

### Forecasting with throughput
- **Simple:** 60 items remaining ÷ about 6 per week ≈ 10 weeks.
- **Range:** use the slowest and fastest recent weeks for a pessimistic and optimistic forecast.
- **Monte Carlo:** randomly sample past weekly throughput thousands of times to get probabilities, such as "85% chance of finishing by 30 May".
Tip
Forecasts are more reliable when items are similar in size. Split very large items before counting them.

### Improving throughput
- Remove bottlenecks; see [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/).
- Reduce rework by improving quality early.
- Cut time spent blocked; see [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/).
- Automate repetitive steps.
- Keep WIP limited so work finishes rather than piling up.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between throughput and velocity?**
Throughput counts finished items per period; velocity sums story points per sprint. Throughput needs no estimation.

**Q: Should throughput keep going up?**
Not necessarily. Stable, predictable throughput with short cycle times is usually more valuable than a rising number.

**Q: What is throughput in Kanban?**
Throughput is the number of work items finished in a period, such as items per week.

**Q: How do you calculate throughput?**
Count the items that reached Done in each period. For example, 6, 8 and 7 items over three weeks gives an average throughput of 7 per week.

**Q: How is throughput used for forecasting?**
Divide remaining items by typical throughput for a rough date, or run a Monte Carlo simulation on past weekly throughput for a probability-based forecast. See [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/).

**Q: How does throughput relate to cycle time?**
By Little's Law, average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput. At steady throughput, reducing WIP shortens cycle time.

**Q: Should all items count equally in throughput?**
Many teams count items regardless of size, which works well if items are split to a similar size. Track throughput by work type if items differ greatly.

**Q: What is a throughput run chart?**
A chart showing throughput per period over time, helping you spot trends, seasonality and the effect of process changes.

**Q: How can a team increase throughput?**
Relieve the bottleneck, reduce blockers and rework, and limit WIP so effort goes into finishing. See [Theory of Constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/).

**Q: Why does throughput vary week to week?**
Items differ in size, holidays and absences change capacity, and blockers come and go. Use ranges and percentiles rather than a single number.

**Q: Is throughput a productivity measure?**
It measures delivery rate, not individual productivity. Use it to understand and forecast the system, not to compare people or teams.

# Value Stream Mapping: How to Map and Improve Your Process

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: A step-by-step guide to value stream mapping: current and future state maps, key metrics like process time and lead time, and how to find waste.


## Value Stream Mapping: How to Map and Improve Your Process
Value stream mapping (VSM) is a Lean technique for visualising every step needed to deliver a product or service to a customer, including the waiting between steps. It shows where time and effort are wasted, so you can design a better process.
- Published 18 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- VSM maps every step and wait from request to delivery.
- It measures process time, wait time and flow efficiency.
- Design a future state that removes the biggest waste.

### Origins
VSM comes from Toyota's material and information flow diagrams and was popularised by Mike Rother and John Shook's 1998 book Learning to See. It is now used in software, services, healthcare and offices as well as manufacturing.

### Key metrics on a value stream map
| Metric | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Process time | Time spent actively working on a step |
| Wait time | Time between steps |
| Lead time | Total time from request to delivery |
| % complete and accurate | How often a step receives work it can use without rework |
| [Flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) | Total process time ÷ total lead time |

### How to create a value stream map
1. **Choose the value stream:** one product, service or request type.
2. **Define start and end:** from customer request to customer receipt.
3. **Walk the process** with the people who do the work.
4. **Map each step** with its process time, wait time and quality.
5. **Add information flows:** how work is triggered and communicated.
6. **Calculate totals:** lead time, process time, flow efficiency.
7. **Identify waste:** long waits, rework loops, handoffs, unnecessary steps.
8. **Design a future state map** that removes the biggest waste.
9. **Plan and run improvements**, then map again.

### Example: software change request
A team maps a change request from customer to release. Active work totals about 3 days, but total lead time is about 30 days, a flow efficiency near 10%. Most time is spent waiting for approval and for a monthly release window. The future state introduces weekly releases and a delegated approval, aiming to cut lead time by more than half. Illustrative example.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the difference between a process map and a value stream map?**
A process map shows the steps; a value stream map adds time, waiting, quality and information flow, focusing on the customer's end-to-end experience.

**Q: How long does a VSM workshop take?**
Often half a day to two days, depending on the complexity of the process.

**Q: What is value stream mapping?**
Value stream mapping (VSM) is a Lean technique for drawing every step, hand-off and wait involved in delivering a product or service, so you can see and remove waste.

**Q: Who created value stream mapping?**
It comes from Toyota's material and information flow diagrams and was popularised by Mike Rother and John Shook's 1998 book Learning to See.

**Q: What are the steps of value stream mapping?**
Choose a product or service, walk the process, map the current state with process and wait times, identify waste, design a future state and create an improvement plan.

**Q: What is a current state value stream map?**
A map showing how the process works today, including each step, its process time, waiting time between steps and information flows.

**Q: What is a future state value stream map?**
A map of the improved process the team aims to reach, with waste removed and flow improved, used to plan specific changes.

**Q: What data do you collect for a value stream map?**
For each step: process time, waiting time, rework or defect rates, number of people involved and hand-offs. Totals give lead time and [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/).

**Q: What symbols are used in value stream mapping?**
Standard icons include process boxes, inventory triangles, push arrows, supermarkets, kanban signals and a timeline along the bottom. Simple boxes and arrows are fine for knowledge work.

**Q: Can value stream mapping be used in software development?**
Yes. Software teams map the path from idea to production to find delays in approvals, testing and deployment, often feeding [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/) improvements.

**Q: How does a value stream map help design a Kanban board?**
It shows the real stages and queues in your process, which become the board's columns and waiting stages. See [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/).

# Visual Management: Make Work and Problems Visible

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/visual-management/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: What visual management is, its Lean roots, tools such as boards, andon and 5S, examples for project teams, and tips for effective visual displays.


## Visual Management: Make Work and Problems Visible
Visual management means arranging information so that anyone can understand the state of work at a glance, without asking or reading reports. It is a cornerstone of Lean and the reason Kanban uses boards.
- Published 18 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- Visual management makes work and problems obvious at a glance.
- Boards, andon and 5S are classic tools.
- Display only information that leads to action.

### Why it works
- Problems become visible immediately, so they get fixed sooner.
- Everyone shares the same picture, which reduces status meetings.
- Standards and expectations are clear.
- Teams can manage themselves with less supervision.

### Common visual management tools
| Tool | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) | Work items and their stage |
| Andon | A signal that a problem has occurred and help is needed |
| 5S workplace organisation | Everything has a visible place |
| Performance boards | Key metrics against targets |
| Shadow boards | Where each tool belongs; missing tools are obvious |
| Colour coding | Status, priority or type |

### 5S
1. **Sort:** remove what isn't needed.
2. **Set in order:** a place for everything.
3. **Shine:** clean and inspect.
4. **Standardise:** make good practice the norm.
5. **Sustain:** keep it up through habits and audits.
In digital work, 5S applies to shared drives, boards and tools as much as physical spaces.

### Visual management for project teams
- A team board with WIP limits and blockers.
- A milestone timeline on the wall or dashboard.
- A visible risk list with owners.
- Simple charts: [burnup](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-velocity-chart/), [cumulative flow](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/).
- Red, amber and green indicators only where they trigger action.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is an andon in visual management?**
A signal, originally a cord or light on a production line, that any worker can use to flag a problem and call for help.

**Q: Does visual management work for remote teams?**
Yes, through shared digital boards and dashboards that everyone sees daily.

**Q: What is visual management?**
Visual management is the practice of making work, standards and problems visible at a glance, so anyone can see the current state and act quickly.

**Q: What are examples of visual management?**
Kanban boards, andon lights, 5S floor markings, shadow boards for tools, performance charts and colour-coded status indicators.

**Q: What are the benefits of visual management?**
Faster problem detection, shared understanding, less time spent in status meetings and clearer standards that make deviations obvious.

**Q: What is a visual management board?**
A board displaying key information for a team or area, such as work status, targets, issues and actions. A [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) is one common type.

**Q: What is a shadow board in visual management?**
A board with the outline of each tool painted or drawn on it, so it is immediately clear where each tool belongs and which are missing.

**Q: How is visual management used in project management?**
Project teams use Kanban boards, [Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), RAG status indicators, burnup charts and risk heat maps to make progress and problems visible.

**Q: What is the difference between visual management and visual controls?**
Visual controls are the individual tools, such as signs and markings. Visual management is the wider system of using them to run and improve work.

**Q: What makes a good visual management display?**
It is simple, current, visible where the work happens, and shows clearly what is normal and what is not, so it prompts action.

**Q: How is RAG status used in visual management?**
Red, amber, green status is a simple visual signal of whether something is on track, at risk or off track. Define each colour clearly so it is used consistently; see [project status reports](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
