# What Is Kanban? Definition, Principles and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: What is Kanban? Learn the Kanban method's meaning, principles, practices, board, WIP limits and flow metrics, with worked examples and step-by-step setup.


## What Is Kanban? Definition, Principles and Examples
Kanban is a method for managing work by making it visible on a board, limiting how much is in progress at once and continuously improving how smoothly work flows from request to delivery. It began on Toyota's factory floors and is now used by software, IT, marketing, HR and operations teams. This guide explains what Kanban means, how a Kanban system works, its principles, practices and metrics, and how to set one up step by step, with worked examples throughout.
- Published 4 September 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Kanban is a pull-based way of managing work: you visualise it, limit work in progress (WIP) and improve flow in small, evidence-based steps.
- The Kanban Guide (2025.5 edition) defines Kanban as a strategy for optimising the flow of value through a process, built on three practices and four flow metrics.
- The Kanban Method from Kanban University adds four principles and six general practices, starting with what you do now.
- WIP limits are what turn a task board into a Kanban system: they stop the team starting too much and shorten the time each item takes.
- Measure WIP, throughput, cycle time and work item age, and use percentiles of past cycle times to set a service level expectation.
- You can start in a day with a whiteboard or a free template; no new roles, sprints or reorganisation are required.

### What is Kanban?
**Kanban** is a method for managing and improving work that flows through a process. The team shows every work item as a card on a board, divides the board into the stages the work passes through, limits how many items can be in progress at once, and pulls new work only when capacity frees up. The aim is faster, more predictable delivery.
The Kanban Guide, the short official guide written by John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti, puts it more briefly: Kanban is a strategy for optimising the flow of value through a process. Its latest edition (2025.5, May 2025) describes three practices that work together, defining and visualising the workflow, actively managing items in the workflow and improving the workflow, and calls their combined use a **Kanban system**.
In simple terms, Kanban answers three everyday questions for a team:
- **What are we working on, and where is it?** The board shows every item and its stage.
- **Should we start something new?** Only if the WIP limit for that stage leaves room.
- **How do we get faster and more reliable?** Watch where work waits, change one thing, and check the data.
Kanban does not prescribe sprints, roles or fixed meetings. You apply it to the process you already have, which makes it one of the easiest Agile approaches to start with. For how it sits among other approaches, see our overview of [types of Agile methodologies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/types-of-agile-methodologies/).

### What does Kanban mean? Origins and history
**Kanban** (看板) is Japanese for signboard or visual card. In manufacturing, a kanban was a physical card attached to a container of parts. When a downstream process used the parts, the card went back upstream as a signal to make or deliver more. Nothing was produced without a card, so production was pulled by actual demand rather than pushed by forecasts.
The system grew out of the Toyota Production System under industrial engineer Taiichi Ohno. Toyota studied how supermarkets restock shelves, replacing only what customers have taken, from the late 1940s, and applied the idea in its main plant machine shop in 1953. Kanban became a core tool of [Just-in-Time production](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/just-in-time-jit/) and the wider Lean movement.
In the 2000s, David J. Anderson adapted these ideas to knowledge work, first with a software maintenance team at Microsoft and later at Corbis. His 2010 book, *Kanban: Successful Evolutionary Change for Your Technology Business*, set out what became known as the Kanban Method. Kanban University now maintains that body of knowledge, while the separate Kanban Guide, first published in 2020, offers a minimal, flow-focused definition.
| Period | Milestone | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Late 1940s | Toyota studies supermarket restocking | Origin of the pull idea: replace only what has been used |
| 1953 | Kanban used in Toyota's main plant machine shop | Cards become the signal that authorises production |
| Mid-2000s | Anderson applies kanban to software teams at Microsoft and Corbis | Virtual kanban systems for knowledge work |
| 2010 | Anderson publishes the Kanban book | The Kanban Method is formalised |
| May 2025 | Kanban Guide 2025.5 edition | Flow Metrics renamed, SLE moved into the Definition of Workflow |
The core idea has never changed: work is pulled by demand, and limiting what is in progress makes problems visible. For the manufacturing roots, read our guide to [pull vs push systems](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/).

### Three meanings of Kanban
The word Kanban refers to three related but different things. Knowing which one a book, course or colleague means avoids a lot of confusion.
|  | Manufacturing kanban | The Kanban Method | The Kanban Guide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Source | Toyota Production System | David J. Anderson and Kanban University | Daniel Vacanti and John Coleman (kanbanguides.org) |
| Focus | Inventory and production signals | Evolutionary change and service delivery | Optimising the flow of value |
| Core elements | Physical cards, bins, pull signals | 4 principles, 6 general practices, cadences | 3 practices, Definition of Workflow, 4 flow metrics |
| Typical users | Factories, warehouses, supply chains | Knowledge-work teams and whole organisations | Any team that wants a minimal flow-based approach |
| What it asks you to change | How materials are replenished | Little at first: start with what you do now | Little at first: define your workflow and manage flow |
The Kanban Method and the Kanban Guide agree on the essentials, so most knowledge-work teams borrow from both.

### How Kanban works
A Kanban system has a handful of moving parts.

#### A pull system
In a push system, work is assigned as soon as it arrives. In a pull system, people take the next item only when they have finished something and the next stage has room, which keeps the amount of work in the system under control.

#### The Kanban board
The [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) is a visual model of your workflow. Columns represent stages (for example Ready, In progress, Review, Done) and horizontal [swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/) can separate types of work or classes of service.

#### Kanban cards
Each work item is a [Kanban card](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-cards/) showing at least a title, an owner and the date it started. Many teams add a type, due date, blocker flag and class of service. Cards move left to right as work progresses.

#### WIP limits
A [WIP limit](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) caps how many cards can sit in a column, a group of columns or the whole board. When a column is full, the team stops starting and helps finish. WIP limits are the feature that turns a task board into a Kanban system.

#### Commitment and delivery points
The **commitment point** is where the team agrees to do an item; the clock for cycle time usually starts here. The **delivery point** is where the item is finished or handed to the customer. The Kanban Guide asks every team to define these start and finish points explicitly.

#### Explicit policies
Policies are the team's agreed rules: what must be true before a card can enter a column, who can pull from Ready, how blocked items are handled, how urgent work jumps the queue. Writing them down makes improvement easier, because you can change a rule and see the effect.
Here is an example board for a small IT support team, showing WIP limits and policies on one screen:
| Column | WIP limit | Entry policy (example) | Cards now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Backlog | None | Any request logged with a requester and summary | 14 |
| Ready (commitment point) | 6 | Triaged, sized as small or medium, priority agreed at replenishment | 5 |
| In progress | 4 | One person owns it; started date written on the card | 4 (full) |
| Waiting on customer | 3 | Question sent; follow up after 2 working days | 2 |
| Review | 2 | Fix tested by someone other than the owner | 1 |
| Done (delivery point) | None | Requester confirms or ticket auto-closes after 3 days | 23 this month |
In progress is at its limit, so nobody starts a new ticket. Instead, the free person helps the reviewer or chases the oldest item waiting on a customer. Repeated daily, that decision is how Kanban improves flow.

### Kanban principles and practices
The Kanban Method describes four principles and six general practices. They guide how to introduce Kanban without disrupting the team.

#### The four Kanban principles
Kanban University lists these principles:
1. **Start with what you do now.** Map the current process as it is, rather than redesigning it first.
2. **Agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change.** Make small, safe changes and keep the ones that work.
3. **Respect the current process, roles, responsibilities and titles.** Avoid a reorganisation that creates fear and resistance.
4. **Encourage acts of leadership at all levels.** Anyone who sees a problem can propose an improvement.

#### The six general practices
| Practice | What it means | How it looks in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visualise | Make the work, the workflow and business risks visible | Every item on the board, blocked work flagged in red |
| Limit WIP | Cap work started but not finished | Column limits; stop starting, start finishing |
| Manage flow | Watch and smooth how work moves | Review cycle time, throughput and ageing items |
| Make policies explicit | Agree and display the rules | Entry and exit criteria for each column |
| Implement feedback loops | Review regularly at several levels | Daily Kanban meeting, service delivery review |
| Improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally | Use models and data to guide change | Run one experiment at a time and compare the metrics |

#### The Kanban Guide's three practices
The Kanban Guide condenses this into three practices: **defining and visualising the workflow**, **actively managing items in the workflow** (controlling WIP, preventing items ageing unnecessarily and unblocking work) and **improving the workflow** continuously rather than on a fixed schedule. It asks each team to write a **Definition of Workflow** covering, at minimum:
- the work items that flow through the process;
- where items start and finish;
- the states between start and finish;
- how WIP is controlled;
- explicit policies for moving items through the states;
- a service level expectation (SLE).

### Kanban metrics: measuring flow
Kanban relies on a few simple measures rather than estimates and velocity. The Kanban Guide names four required flow metrics:
| Metric | Definition (Kanban Guide) | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work in progress (WIP) | The number of items started but not finished | How much are we juggling right now? |
| Throughput | The number of items finished per unit of time | How much do we deliver each week? |
| Work item age | Elapsed time from start to now, for unfinished items | Which items are at risk of being late? |
| Cycle time | Elapsed time from start to finish | How long does an item usually take? |
Teams often visualise these with a [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/), a cycle time scatterplot and a [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/). Our [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) guide explains each chart.

#### Worked example: ten finished items
A five-person content team finished 10 items over the last two weeks (14 calendar days). Their [cycle times](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/), in calendar days and sorted from shortest to longest, were: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 8, 9, 14.
| Measure | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Throughput | 10 items ÷ 2 weeks | 5 items per week (about 0.71 per day) |
| Average cycle time | 59 days ÷ 10 items | 5.9 days |
| 50th percentile (median) | 5th of 10 sorted values | 5 days |
| 85th percentile | 0.85 × 10 = 8.5, round up to the 9th value | 9 days |
| Average WIP implied by Little's Law | 0.71 items per day × 5.9 days | About 4 items |
Notice that one 14-day item pulls the average above the median. Cycle time data is usually skewed like this, which is why Kanban practitioners prefer percentiles to averages.
**Little's Law** links the three measures: average cycle time ≈ average WIP ÷ average throughput, as long as the system is reasonably stable. Suppose the board actually holds 8 items in progress while throughput stays at about 0.71 per day. Then average cycle time will drift towards 8 ÷ 0.71 ≈ 11 days. Halving WIP to 4 points back towards 5 to 6 days, with no one working harder. This is the arithmetic behind WIP limits.

#### Service level expectation and work item age
A **service level expectation (SLE)** has two parts, an elapsed time and a probability, such as 85% of items finish within 9 days. The Kanban Guide says it should be based on historical cycle time; with no history, a best guess is acceptable until data builds up. With only 10 data points, the content team treats its SLE as provisional and revisits it monthly.
The SLE becomes useful day to day when you compare it with **work item age**. If a card has been in progress for 7 days and the SLE is 9 days, it is close to becoming an outlier, so the team swarms on it, splits it or removes the blocker. Watching age prevents late items instead of reporting them afterwards.

### A worked example: Kanban for a marketing team
**Before Kanban.** The team kept a shared task list. Requests arrived by email and chat, each writer had six to eight pieces on the go, and nobody could say when a new request would be done.
**Week 1: visualise.** The team mapped its real process: Requested, Ready, Drafting, Editing, Design, Approval, Published. Every open piece became a card. The board showed 31 items started and only 2 in Approval, which made the problem obvious: too much started, too little finished.
**Week 2: limit WIP and set policies.** They agreed limits of 5 for Drafting, 3 for Editing, 2 for Design and 3 for Approval, and two policies: no new draft starts while Editing is full, and any card blocked for more than two days is raised at the daily meeting. A weekly replenishment meeting with the head of marketing replaced ad hoc requests.
**Weeks 3–6: manage flow.** Cards piled up in Approval, so the team agreed a 48-hour approval policy with stakeholders and added an Expedite swimlane limited to one card for genuine emergencies. They started recording start and finish dates to measure cycle time and throughput.
**Week 8: improve.** With two months of data, they set an SLE and could answer the question stakeholders cared about most: if we commit to your article today, it will usually be live within a known number of days.
Tip
The numbers in this example are illustrative. Your own data will differ; the point is the sequence: visualise, limit, manage flow, measure, then improve one thing at a time.

### How to implement Kanban step by step
These steps follow the Kanban principle of starting with what you do now.
1. **Choose the scope.** Pick one team or one service with a clear group of customers, such as IT support requests or the content pipeline.
2. **Map the current workflow.** List the stages work really goes through today, including waiting states such as Waiting for approval.
3. **Define your work items.** Agree what a card represents (a request, a feature, a deliverable) and roughly how big it should be.
4. **Build the board and load it.** Create one column per stage, mark the commitment and delivery points, and put every current item on a card with its start date.
5. **Set initial WIP limits.** A common starting point is about one to one and a half items per person in each active stage, or simply the current count minus one. Expect to adjust them.
6. **Write explicit policies.** Add entry criteria for each column, a rule for blocked items and a rule for urgent work.
7. **Start a daily Kanban meeting.** Fifteen minutes at the board, walking it right to left: what is blocked, what is ageing, what can we finish today?
8. **Agree replenishment.** Decide how and how often new items enter Ready, and who prioritises them.
9. **Measure and review.** Track WIP, throughput, cycle time and work item age. After two to four weeks, hold a review, pick one bottleneck and run one experiment.
A realistic first month looks like this:
| Week | Focus | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Map and visualise | Board with every current item, commitment and delivery points marked |
| 2 | Limit WIP and agree policies | WIP limits on active columns, written entry criteria, daily meeting running |
| 3 | Manage flow | Blockers flagged and cleared daily, start and finish dates recorded |
| 4 | First review | Baseline cycle time and throughput, one improvement experiment chosen |

### Kanban meetings and cadences
The Kanban Guide does not mandate any meetings; it asks you to manage and improve the workflow regularly. The Kanban Method suggests a set of feedback loops, often called cadences, that teams adopt as they need them. Typical frequencies are a starting point, not a rule.
| Cadence | Purpose | Typical frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kanban meeting (stand-up) | Review the board, unblock work, focus on finishing | Daily, about 15 minutes |
| Replenishment meeting | Select and commit to the next items for Ready | Weekly, or when Ready runs low |
| Delivery planning meeting | Plan and coordinate releases to customers | Per delivery |
| Service delivery review | Compare delivery against customer expectations and SLEs | Every two weeks |
| Operations review | Look across services for shared bottlenecks | Monthly |
| Risk review | Analyse blockers and recurring risks | Monthly |
| Strategy review | Check services still match business direction | Quarterly |
Most teams begin with the daily meeting and replenishment, then add a monthly review using [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/). Our [Kanban ceremonies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/) guide gives agendas for each.

### Benefits of Kanban
- **Visibility.** Everyone sees what is in progress, what is waiting and what is blocked, without status meetings.
- **Shorter, more predictable delivery.** Limiting WIP reduces cycle time, and percentile-based SLEs give honest forecasts.
- **Flexibility.** Priorities in the backlog can change at any time; you only commit when an item is pulled into Ready.
- **Less overload and context switching.** People finish work before starting more, at a sustainable pace.
- **Easy adoption.** No new roles, sprints or reorganisation; you start from the current process.
- **Continuous improvement.** Data and visible bottlenecks show where to improve next.
- **Works beyond software.** Any process with stages, from recruitment to legal review, can use a board.

### Limitations of Kanban and how to handle them
Kanban's lightness is also its weakness if a team is not disciplined.
| Limitation | Why it happens | How to handle it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No built-in time boxes | Work flows continuously, so deadlines can feel vague | Use SLEs, fixed-date classes of service and a regular delivery cadence |
| Boards can become cluttered | Every item is visible, including stale ones | Archive Done weekly; review cards older than your SLE |
| Easy to skip WIP limits | Limits feel restrictive when demand is high | Make limits a written policy and discuss every breach |
| Less guidance than Scrum | Few prescribed events or roles | Adopt the cadences you need and write them down |
| Long-range planning is not built in | The focus is on flow, not release plans | Use throughput data for forecasts and a simple roadmap |

### When to use Kanban
Kanban fits best where work arrives continuously and priorities change often.
| Situation | Kanban fit | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IT support, operations, maintenance | Strong | Unpredictable arrivals; SLEs map naturally to service levels |
| Marketing, content and design teams | Strong | Many small deliverables, frequent reprioritisation |
| Software teams releasing continuously | Strong | Pairs well with continuous delivery |
| New product with a fixed release goal | Good with care | Consider Scrum or Scrumban for a time-boxed rhythm |
| Large fixed-scope project with a contract | Partial | Use Kanban for task flow inside a phase-based plan |
| Personal productivity | Strong | A three-column board with a small WIP limit works well |

### Kanban vs Scrum and other approaches
Both Kanban and Scrum are Agile, but they organise work differently.
| Aspect | Kanban | Scrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cadence | Continuous flow | Fixed-length Sprints of one month or less |
| Roles | None required | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers |
| Commitment | Item by item, when pulled into Ready | A Sprint Goal and selected items each Sprint |
| Changing priorities | Any time, for work not yet started | Sprint scope is protected; the backlog can change |
| Limiting work | Explicit WIP limits | Limited by the Sprint and the team's capacity |
| Key metrics | WIP, throughput, cycle time, work item age | Commonly Sprint progress and velocity, though not required |
| Board | Persistent board, never reset | Typically reset each Sprint |
Many teams combine them. Scrum teams often add WIP limits and flow metrics, and Scrumban blends Scrum's events with Kanban's pull system.

### Common Kanban mistakes
| Mistake | Why it hurts | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Using a board without WIP limits | It becomes a to-do list; work piles up and cycle time grows | Set limits on active columns, even generous ones, and lower them over time |
| Designing an ideal process first | The board does not match reality, so people stop updating it | Map how work really flows today |
| Hiding waiting states | Waiting time is invisible, yet it is often most of cycle time | Add queue columns such as Ready for review; see [flow efficiency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/flow-efficiency/) |
| Cards that are too big | Items sit in one column for weeks and hide progress | Split work into items that finish within your SLE |
| Ignoring blocked cards | Blockers age quietly until a deadline is missed | Flag blockers visibly and discuss them first every day |
| Reporting averages only | Outliers distort the average and forecasts | Use percentiles of cycle time |
| Changing many things at once | You cannot tell which change helped | Run one experiment at a time and compare the data |

### Kanban tools: physical boards and software
A whiteboard and sticky notes are enough to start. Digital tools help when the team is remote, when you want automatic flow charts, or when several teams need to see each other's work.
- **[Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/)** is a simple, approachable board tool, popular for small teams and personal Kanban.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** offers Kanban boards with column constraints and flow reports, well suited to software teams.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)**, our top-rated tool, combines board views with workflows, dashboards and cross-team reporting, a good fit when Kanban spans several departments.
Before choosing, check that the tool supports WIP limits, custom columns, blocked flags and start and finish dates.

If you want to try Kanban today, download the free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/). It includes a board with WIP-limited columns and a cards tab that records start and finish dates and calculates cycle time, in Google Sheets, Excel and PDF.
Once your board is running, the most valuable next skill is setting and respecting limits.
To design columns, swimlanes and card layouts that match your workflow, see our guide to [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is Kanban in simple terms?**
Kanban is a way of managing work by putting every item on a visual board, limiting how much is in progress at once and steadily improving how work flows to completion.

**Q: What does Kanban mean in Japanese?**
Kanban (看板) means signboard or visual card. At Toyota, kanban cards signalled when a process needed more parts.

**Q: Is Kanban Agile or Lean?**
Both. Kanban comes from Lean manufacturing and is widely used as an Agile approach for knowledge work, focused on flow and continuous improvement rather than fixed iterations.

**Q: What are the 4 principles of Kanban?**
Kanban University lists: start with what you do now; agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change; respect the current process, roles, responsibilities and titles; and encourage acts of leadership at all levels.

**Q: What are the 6 practices of Kanban?**
Visualise, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, and improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally. The Kanban Guide condenses these into three practices.

**Q: Is Kanban a methodology or a framework?**
The Kanban Guide calls Kanban a strategy for optimising flow, and Kanban University calls it a method. It is lighter than Scrum, with no required roles or events.

**Q: Does Kanban use sprints?**
No. Kanban manages a continuous flow of work, pulling items in as capacity frees up. Teams that want a time-boxed rhythm often use Scrumban.

**Q: Does Kanban have roles?**
No roles are required. Some organisations add a Service Request Manager and a Service Delivery Manager as their Kanban practice matures.

**Q: What is a WIP limit in Kanban?**
A WIP limit caps how many items can be in a stage or on the board at one time. It stops the team starting too much and shortens cycle time.

**Q: What are the main Kanban metrics?**
The Kanban Guide requires four flow metrics: work in progress, throughput, work item age and cycle time.

**Q: What is an example of Kanban?**
A support team puts every ticket on a board with columns Ready, In progress, Review and Done, limits In progress to four tickets, and pulls a new ticket only when one is finished.

**Q: What are the disadvantages of Kanban?**
Without time boxes, deadlines can feel vague, boards can become cluttered and teams may skip WIP limits. SLEs, explicit policies and regular reviews address these.

**Q: Do you need software to use Kanban?**
No. A whiteboard and sticky notes are enough to start. Software helps remote teams and calculates flow metrics automatically.

**Q: Who created the Kanban Method?**
David J. Anderson developed the Kanban Method for knowledge work in the 2000s, building on the kanban system of the Toyota Production System led by Taiichi Ohno.

**Q: How long does it take to implement Kanban?**
You can set up a board in a day. Expect two to four weeks before you have enough data to tune WIP limits, and a few months before an SLE is reliable.

# WIP Aging Chart: Spot Stuck Work Before It's Late

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: What a WIP aging chart is, how to read it with cycle time percentiles, and how to use work item age in daily Kanban meetings to prevent delays.


## WIP Aging Chart: Spot Stuck Work Before It's Late
Cycle time tells you about items you have already finished. Work item age tells you about items still in progress. A WIP aging chart puts every unfinished item on one chart, so you can act before an item becomes late.
- Published 14 September 2026
- 3 min read

### Key takeaways
- A WIP aging chart plots unfinished items by stage and age.
- Compare ages with historical cycle time percentiles.
- Act on old items first in the daily meeting.

### What the chart shows
The horizontal axis lists the workflow stages; the vertical axis shows age in days. Each in-progress item is a dot in its current stage, at the height of its age. Background bands show historical [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) percentiles, for example the 50th and 85th.

### How to read it
- **Dots below the 50th percentile:** on track.
- **Dots approaching the 85th percentile:** at risk; discuss today.
- **Dots above the 85th percentile:** already slower than most past items; act now.
- **Old dots in early stages:** items that started and stalled.

### Using it in the daily meeting
1. Start with the oldest items, especially those nearing your service level expectation.
2. Ask what is needed to move each one forward.
3. Swarm, unblock or split items where needed.
4. Avoid starting new work while old items are at risk.

### Why work item age matters
Age is a leading indicator: it warns you while there is still time to act. Combined with a [service level expectation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/), it turns Kanban from reporting what happened into managing what is happening.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is work item age on a WIP aging chart?**
The time since an unfinished item started, measured from the same start point used for cycle time.

**Q: How is a WIP aging chart different from a cycle time scatterplot?**
The scatterplot shows finished items; the aging chart shows unfinished ones.

**Q: What is a WIP aging chart?**
A WIP aging chart shows every item currently in progress as a dot, placed in its workflow stage and plotted by how long it has been in progress.

**Q: How do you read a WIP aging chart?**
Look for dots approaching or above your 85th percentile cycle time line, and for old dots stuck in early stages. Those items need attention first.

**Q: Why is a WIP aging chart a leading indicator?**
Because it plots work item age, which warns you about items at risk while they are still in progress, before they finish late. Cycle time only tells you after the item is done.

**Q: How is work item age calculated for a WIP aging chart?**
Age = today's date − start date for each unfinished item, using the same start point as for [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/).

**Q: What should a team do when the WIP aging chart shows an ageing item?**
Discuss it at the daily meeting, swarm on it, remove the blocker or split it. Starting new work should wait until it moves.

**Q: What are the percentile lines on a WIP aging chart?**
They show historical cycle time percentiles, such as the 50th and 85th, so you can see whether an item is already taking longer than most past items.

**Q: Which tools produce a WIP aging chart?**
Several Kanban tools and analytics add-ons produce one, and you can build a simple version in a spreadsheet from start dates and stages.

**Q: How often should the WIP aging chart be reviewed?**
Daily, ideally at the daily Kanban meeting, because its value is in catching stuck work early.

**Q: How does a WIP aging chart relate to service level expectations?**
The service level expectation acts as a threshold: items nearing it are at risk of missing it. See [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/).

# WIP Limits in Kanban: How to Set Them, With Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/
Section: Kanban guides
Summary: WIP limits explained: what they are, why they work (Little's Law), how to set your first limits step by step, worked board examples and common mistakes.


## WIP Limits in Kanban: How to Set Them, With Examples
WIP limits cap how many work items can sit in a stage of your workflow, or in the whole workflow, at the same time, so the team finishes work before starting more. They are the practice that turns a Kanban board from a picture of work into a pull system, and they are the most direct way to shorten delivery times and expose bottlenecks. This guide explains why WIP limits work, how to set your first numbers step by step, and how to tune them, using worked examples throughout.
- Published 10 September 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- A WIP limit is an agreed maximum number of items in a column, swimlane, person's queue or whole workflow. When it is reached, the team finishes or unblocks work instead of starting new items.
- Little's Law explains why it works: average cycle time equals average WIP divided by average throughput, so less WIP at the same throughput means faster delivery.
- Start a little below today's actual WIP, or around one to one and a half items per person in each active stage, and make the numbers visible on the board.
- When a column is full, look right to left: help finish, review or unblock downstream work before pulling anything new.
- Treat limits as experiments. Review them every few weeks using cycle time, throughput and blocked-item data, and change one limit at a time.

### What is a WIP limit?
A WIP limit is the maximum number of work items allowed in a defined part of a workflow at one time, such as a board column, a swimlane or the whole system. Once the limit is reached, nobody pulls new work into that part until an item moves on, so the team finishes work before it starts more.
WIP stands for work in progress. The Kanban Guide (edition 2025.5, by John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti) defines it as the number of work items started but not finished, and requires Kanban teams to explicitly control it between their agreed start and finish points. Kanban University's glossary describes a WIP limit as a policy that constrains the amount of work allowed in a given part of the system. In other words, a limit is a team agreement that only works if everyone treats it as binding.
On a board, the limit usually appears in the column header, for example **Test (3)**. A gap below the limit is a **pull signal**: someone in that stage has capacity and may take the next item from the column to the left. That is what separates a [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) from a shared to-do list: work is pulled in when there is room rather than pushed in whenever someone asks. Our guide to [pull vs push systems](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/pull-system-vs-push-system/) explains the wider idea.
Limiting WIP is one of the core practices of the Kanban Method, alongside visualising work and managing flow. See [what is Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) for how the practices fit together.

### Why WIP limits work
Limiting work feels counter-intuitive, but it speeds delivery for three reasons: queueing, task switching and hidden bottlenecks.

#### Little's Law
Little's Law is a result from queueing theory, proved by John D. C. Little in the journal Operations Research in 1961. Applied to a team's workflow it reads:
**Average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput**
Here [cycle time](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cycle-time/) is how long an item takes from start to finish, and [throughput](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/throughput/) is how many items the team finishes per week. The formula shows that, if throughput stays roughly the same, the only way to make each item faster is to have fewer items in progress.
**Illustrative example.** A team has 24 items in progress and finishes about 6 items a week. Average cycle time is 24 ÷ 6 = 4 weeks. If the team lowers WIP to 12 and keeps finishing 6 a week, average cycle time falls to 12 ÷ 6 = 2 weeks. Nobody worked harder; the team simply stopped letting work queue.
Little's Law describes averages over a period and holds when the system is reasonably stable. Keep these conditions in mind before relying on it:
| Condition | What it means for your board |
| --- | --- |
| Consistent units | Measure WIP in items, throughput in items per week and cycle time in weeks (or all in days). |
| Stable system | Roughly as many items finish as start over the period; WIP is not steadily climbing. |
| Items finish | Items that are abandoned or left in progress indefinitely distort the averages; close or remove them explicitly. |
| Same boundaries | Count WIP, cycle time and throughput between the same start and finish points on the board. |

#### Less task switching
Every extra item a person holds adds context switching. Even ignoring that overhead, parallel work delays everything.
**Illustrative example.** You have three jobs, A, B and C, each needing five days of focused work. Working on them one after another, A is done on day 5, B on day 10 and C on day 15, an average of 10 days. Rotating a day at a time between them, A is done on day 13, B on day 14 and C on day 15, an average of 14 days, before you add any switching cost. Same effort, same finish date for the last job, but every customer waits longer.
| Approach | A finishes | B finishes | C finishes | Average wait |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One at a time (WIP 1) | Day 5 | Day 10 | Day 15 | 10 days |
| All three in parallel (WIP 3) | Day 13 | Day 14 | Day 15 | 14 days |

#### Bottlenecks become visible
When every stage has a limit, a slow stage fills up and the stages before it stop being able to push work into it. Instead of a growing pile of half-finished items, you see a full column and idle hands upstream. That is uncomfortable, and useful: it shows exactly where to improve. The [theory of constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/) gives you a method for what to do next.

#### Other benefits
- **Quality:** people finishing one item at a time make fewer mistakes and get feedback sooner, so defects are found while the work is still fresh.
- **Predictability:** stable WIP gives a stable cycle time, which makes forecasting much easier; see [Kanban planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-planning/).
- **Sustainable pace:** limits give people a legitimate reason to say "not yet".
- **Software delivery performance:** the DORA research programme lists WIP limits among the capabilities that help drive improvements in software delivery performance, particularly when combined with visual displays and feedback from monitoring.
Tip
"Stop starting, start finishing" is the Kanban slogan for this. A WIP limit turns the slogan into a rule the whole team can see.

### Types of WIP limits
You can limit WIP at several levels. Most teams start with column limits and add others only to solve a specific problem.
| Type | Example | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per column (stage) | Develop: max 6 | The default. Controls flow through each step and shows where work piles up. |
| Per column group | Develop + Review combined: max 8 | When two stages are done by the same people and you want flexibility between them. |
| Per person | Max 2 items each | When individuals are overloaded or juggling requests from several managers. |
| Per swimlane or class of service | Expedite lane: max 1 | To protect capacity for urgent work and stop everything becoming urgent; see [Kanban swimlanes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-swimlanes/). |
| Per work type | Bugs: max 3 in progress | To keep a balanced mix of features, defects and maintenance. |
| Whole system (CONWIP) | Max 15 items between Ready and Done | A simple first step for small teams, or for workflows where stages change often. |
| Upstream (Ready) limit | Ready: max 8 | To stop the Ready column becoming a second backlog and to make replenishment meaningful. |
**CONWIP** stands for constant work in progress. Instead of limiting each stage, you limit the total number of items in the system: a new item can start only when one finishes. It is easy to introduce, but it will not show you which stage is the bottleneck, so most teams move to column limits once they are comfortable.
The Done column has no limit. It is the end of the flow, and limiting it would only stop work from finishing. Waiting states inside the flow, such as **Ready for test** or **Develop: done**, do need to be counted, because that is where most delay usually hides.

### How to set WIP limits step by step
There is no formula that gives the perfect number. The aim is a sensible starting point that is low enough to change behaviour, then adjustment based on data. Follow these steps.
1. **Agree your start and finish points.** Decide where work counts as started (often when it leaves Ready) and finished (often Done or Released). WIP is everything in between.
2. **Count today's WIP.** For each column, count the items currently in it, including blocked and waiting items. If you can, take the average over the last two to four weeks rather than a single day.
3. **Note who works in each stage.** Write down how many people actually do the work in each column. A column staffed by one specialist needs a much lower limit than one staffed by four people.
4. **Choose starting limits.** A common starting point is a little below today's average WIP, or roughly one to one and a half items per person in each active stage. Avoid halving WIP overnight; a cut of 20 to 30% is usually enough to change behaviour without stalling the team.
5. **Agree the policies.** Decide in advance whether blocked items count (we recommend yes), how expedite items are handled, and what happens if someone wants to break a limit.
6. **Make it visible.** Put each limit in the column header, highlight columns that are at or over their limit, and write the policies on or beside the board.
7. **Run for two to four weeks, then review.** Track cycle time, throughput, blocked items and every limit breach. Adjust one or two limits at your next retrospective or operations review.
Tip
Set limits as a team. Limits imposed by a manager tend to be quietly ignored; limits the team chose are defended by the team.
Our free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) has WIP limit fields in each column header, and the [workflow template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/) helps you map stages first.

### Worked example: setting limits on a team board
**This example is illustrative.** A six-person product team (one analyst, four developers and one tester) uses a board with the columns Ready, Analysis, Develop (split into Doing and Done), Test, Release and Done. They finish about 7 items a week. Today the board looks like this:
| Column | People | Items today | Starting limit | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ready | n/a | 15 | 8 | About one week of throughput plus a small buffer; refilled at weekly replenishment |
| Analysis | 1 | 4 | 2 | One analyst; two items allows one to wait on a stakeholder reply |
| Develop: Doing | 4 | 11 | Shared limit of 8 | About 1.5 per developer, shared with Develop: Done |
| Develop: Done | n/a | 6 | (within the 8) | A waiting state; counting it stops finished code piling up untested |
| Test | 1 | 5 | 3 | One tester; three allows a small buffer so testing never runs dry |
| Release | Shared | 2 | 3 | Releases go out twice a week, so a few items can wait |
| Done | n/a | n/a | No limit | End of the flow |
Between Analysis and Release the team currently has 4 + 11 + 6 + 5 + 2 = 28 items in progress. By Little's Law, 28 ÷ 7 gives an average cycle time of about 4 weeks. The new limits allow at most 2 + 8 + 3 + 3 = 16 items. If throughput holds at 7 a week, average cycle time should fall towards 16 ÷ 7, or a little over 2 weeks.
The team does not throw away the extra work. They stop starting new items until each column drops below its limit, and move back to Ready anything nobody is actively working on.

#### Why Doing and Done sub-columns share a limit
Splitting Develop into Doing and Done shows which finished items are waiting for the next stage. With separate limits, developers could keep finishing work into Done while Test is overwhelmed. A shared limit means that when Develop: Done fills up, developers must help clear it, usually by helping the tester, before starting anything new.

#### What happened over four weeks
The team tracked a few numbers each week (illustrative figures):
| Week | Average WIP | Throughput (items) | WIP ÷ throughput (weeks) | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before | 28 | 7 | 4.0 | Long queues in Develop: Done and Test |
| 1 | 24 | 6 | 4.0 | Throughput dipped while developers learned to test |
| 2 | 20 | 7 | 2.9 | Test at its limit every day; developers paired with the tester |
| 3 | 17 | 7 | 2.4 | Two blockers waiting on another team escalated at the daily meeting |
| 4 | 16 | 8 | 2.0 | Automated regression checks freed tester time |
Three lessons came out of the review. Test was the bottleneck, which nobody had seen while work sat in Develop: Done. Throughput dipped in the first week before recovering, which is common and worth warning stakeholders about. And the Analysis limit was never reached, so the team left it alone rather than changing it without evidence.
To see this kind of change over time, use a [cumulative flow diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/cumulative-flow-diagram/): bands that stop widening are the visible sign that WIP limits are working.

### What to do when a column hits its limit
A full column is not a failure; it tells you where to put your effort. Work from the right of the board to the left:
1. **Do not pull new work into the full column.** Leave the gap for an item to move on first.
2. **Look downstream.** Is there anything in the next stage you can help finish, review or release? Moving work out of later columns creates space all the way back.
3. **Unblock before you start.** Check every blocked item in or after the full column and ask who can remove the blocker today.
4. **Swarm or pair.** Join a colleague on the oldest item in the full column. Our guide to [agile swarming](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-swarming/) explains how.
5. **Use spare time to improve the system.** If you truly cannot help, work on automation, documentation, test data or fixing a recurring cause of blocked work.
6. **Raise it at the daily meeting.** If the same column is full day after day, discuss it at the next review rather than quietly raising the limit.

#### Blocked items
Count blocked items towards the limit. If you do not, a column can fill with blocked work while new items keep arriving, and the limit stops doing its job. Counting them creates healthy pressure to resolve blockers. Mark blocked cards clearly, note the reason and date, and review patterns regularly; [blocker clustering](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/blocker-clustering/) is a simple way to find the causes that recur.

#### Urgent work and breaching a limit
Rather than breaking limits ad hoc, give urgent work an expedite lane with a limit of one and agree who may use it. If a limit must be breached, make it visible (many teams turn the column header red), record the reason and discuss it at the next review. Frequent breaches mean the limit or the process needs to change.

### Tuning WIP limits over time
Your first limits are a hypothesis. Review them every two to four weeks using board data rather than how busy people feel, changing one or two at a time.
| What you see | What it probably means | What to try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A column never reaches its limit | The limit is too high to influence behaviour | Lower it by one and watch for a few weeks |
| A column is always full and the one before it is idle | That stage is the bottleneck | Swarm on it, cut work entering it, then consider more capacity; do not just raise its limit |
| People are often idle waiting for others | Limits may be too tight for current variability, or the work is blocked by other teams | Look at blocker causes first; raise a limit by one only if idleness is structural |
| Cycle time keeps rising | WIP is creeping up or items are getting bigger | Check total WIP against limits; split large items |
| Many breaches each week | Limits do not match reality, or urgent work is unmanaged | Add an expedite lane with its own limit; revisit intake |
| Items age quietly in waiting columns | Waiting states are not limited or not counted | Add waiting columns to the limit; watch the [WIP aging chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-aging-chart/) |
Lower limits gradually where queues form. Raise one only when people are idle for structural reasons, such as a stage gaining a person. If the team changes size, revisit every limit.
Three charts help you judge whether limits are working: the cumulative flow diagram (are the bands stable?), the cycle time scatterplot (is the spread shrinking?) and the WIP aging chart (which items are getting old right now?). See [Kanban metrics](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-metrics/) for how to read them together.

### Introducing WIP limits to a team and stakeholders
The mechanics are simple; the change in habits is not. Resistance usually comes from team members who worry about looking idle and stakeholders who feel their requests are being refused.

#### With the team
- Frame limits as an experiment for a fixed period, such as four weeks, with an agreed review at the end.
- Explain that the aim is to keep work moving, not every person busy; some slack outside the bottleneck is healthy.
- Agree what people do when they cannot pull work: help downstream, review, pair or improve tooling.

#### With stakeholders
- Show them the Little's Law arithmetic with your own numbers.
- Give them a predictable way in: a regular replenishment meeting where they help choose what enters Ready; see [Kanban meetings and cadences](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-ceremonies/).
- Explain the expedite policy so they know genuinely urgent work has a route.

### WIP limits in Scrum, Scrumban and personal Kanban
WIP limits are not only for Kanban teams.

#### Scrum
The 2020 Scrum Guide does not mention WIP limits, but a [sprint](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-a-sprint/) is itself a form of limit: the team commits to a forecast amount of work for a fixed period. Inside the sprint, though, teams often start too many items and finish several on the last day. Column limits on the sprint board, such as three items in progress for five developers, help finish items earlier and reduce carry-over.

#### Scrumban
Scrumban teams keep some Scrum events but replace the sprint commitment with continuous pull governed by WIP limits. See [Kanban vs Scrumban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-vs-scrumban/) for how the hybrid works.

#### Personal Kanban
Jim Benson and Tonianne DeMaria Barry's Personal Kanban reduces the method to two rules: visualise your work and limit your work in progress. A personal limit of two or three items in Doing is a common starting point. Our [personal Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/personal-kanban/) guide shows how to set one up.

### Setting WIP limits in project management tools
Most digital boards can display WIP limits, but they differ in how strictly they enforce them. Whatever the tool, a limit only works if the team treats it as a rule, so write the policy down too.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/):** Kanban board columns support minimum and maximum constraints, and the board highlights a column that breaks its constraint.
- **Azure Boards:** each Kanban column can be given a WIP limit, and columns can be split into Doing and Done.
- **[ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/):** Board view supports WIP limits per column and flags a column when it is full.
- **[Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/):** the base board has no built-in WIP limits, so teams rely on conventions or Power-Ups.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), monday.com and Asana:** all offer board views with custom status columns. Where a limit is not enforced natively, put the number in the column name and track counts by status on a dashboard. Wrike, our top-rated tool, is a good fit when many teams share work, because request forms, custom workflows and cross-project dashboards make WIP visible across teams.

### Common WIP limit mistakes
- **Limits so high they never bite.** If no column ever reaches its limit, nothing changes. Lower them until the board starts prompting conversations.
- **Cutting too far, too fast.** Halving WIP overnight can stall the team. Reduce in steps.
- **Raising a limit whenever it is hit.** A full column is information about a bottleneck. Fix the flow before touching the number.
- **Not counting waiting or blocked items.** Queues and blocked work are where delay hides; leaving them out makes limits meaningless.
- **The same limit for every column.** Stages with one specialist and stages with four people need different numbers.
- **Breaking limits without discussion.** Occasional, visible, recorded breaches are fine. Silent ones teach everyone that the limits are optional.
- **Ignoring work outside the board.** Support tickets and "quick favours" consume capacity. Put them on the board or set lower limits to allow for them.
- **Using WIP limits to judge individuals.** Limits manage the system, not people.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a good WIP limit?**
There is no universal number. A practical starting point is slightly below your current average WIP, or about one to one and a half items per person in each active stage, then adjust based on cycle time and where work queues.

**Q: How do you calculate a WIP limit?**
There is no exact formula. Count your current WIP per column, note how many people work in each stage, and set the limit a little below today's level. Little's Law (average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput) helps you estimate the effect: if you finish 8 items a week and want an average cycle time of 2 weeks, aim for roughly 16 items in progress across the system.

**Q: What does WIP stand for?**
WIP stands for work in progress (sometimes work in process): items that have been started but not yet finished.

**Q: What happens when a WIP limit is reached?**
Nobody pulls new items into that stage. Team members help finish, review or unblock existing work, starting with the items furthest to the right of the board, until there is space.

**Q: Can a team break a WIP limit?**
Occasionally, for a genuine emergency, but the breach should be visible, recorded and discussed at the next review. A better approach is an expedite lane with its own limit of one. Frequent breaches mean the limit or the process needs to change.

**Q: Should blocked items count towards the WIP limit?**
Yes, in most cases. Counting blocked items creates pressure to resolve blockers and stops a column filling up with stuck work while new items keep arriving.

**Q: Should the Done column have a WIP limit?**
No. Done is the end of the flow, so limiting it would only stop work finishing. Waiting columns inside the workflow, such as Develop: Done or Ready for test, should be counted.

**Q: Do WIP limits slow teams down?**
They can feel slower for the first week or two while people adjust, and throughput may dip briefly. After that, each item usually finishes sooner and delivery becomes more predictable, because work is completed rather than left half-done.

**Q: What is CONWIP?**
CONWIP means constant work in progress. Instead of limiting each column, you cap the total number of items in the whole workflow, starting a new item only when one finishes. It is a simple way to start, but column limits show bottlenecks more clearly.

**Q: Can you set WIP limits per person?**
Yes. A personal limit, such as no more than two items each, helps when individuals are overloaded or take requests from several people. Column limits usually reflect team flow better, so many teams use both.

**Q: Does Scrum use WIP limits?**
The Scrum Guide does not require them, but the sprint itself limits how much work the team takes on. Many Scrum teams add column limits to their sprint board to finish items earlier and reduce carry-over.

**Q: What is the difference between a WIP limit and capacity?**
Capacity is how much work a team can do in a period, often in hours or items per week. A WIP limit is how many items may be in progress at once. Capacity planning asks how much fits; WIP limits control how much is started. See [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/).

**Q: How often should you change WIP limits?**
Review them every two to four weeks, or when the team changes size. Change one or two limits at a time, by one item, so you can see the effect of each change.

# Project Management by Industry

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Project management by industry: how construction, IT, marketing, healthcare, government and 25 other sectors plan projects, with methods, KPIs and tools.


## Project Management by Industry
Project management by industry means applying the same core discipline (scope, schedule, budget, risk and people) under the rules, contracts and pace of a particular sector. A construction programme, a software release and a hospital system rollout all need a plan and an owner, but they differ in regulation, life cycle, documents, KPIs and tools. Below are 30 free guides grouped into seven sector families, plus comparison tables to help you adapt your approach.
- 30 guides
- Last updated 9 October 2026

### Key takeaways
- The fundamentals of project management are the same in every industry; what changes is the context they are applied in.
- Regulation, contract and funding models, life cycle gates, pace of change and who the customer is drive most of the differences.
- Construction, engineering and regulated sectors lean towards predictive, stage-gated plans; software and digital teams lean towards Agile.
- Many organisations run hybrids: a fixed governance frame with iterative delivery inside it.
- Pick tools for the work you actually do: resource planning, client access, approvals, sprints or Microsoft 365 integration.
- Your transferable skills move with you between industries; learn the sector's vocabulary, regulation and contracts first.

### What is industry-specific project management?
**Industry-specific project management** is the practice of adapting general project management methods to the constraints of one sector, such as building regulations in construction, clinical safety in healthcare or release cadence in software. The core processes stay the same; the life cycle, documents, approvals, metrics and tools are tailored to how that industry funds, governs and delivers work.
PMI describes a project as a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result, and that definition holds whether you are fitting out an office or launching a campaign. If you are new to the discipline, start with [what project management is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) and what counts as a project, then come back to the guide for your sector.

### What stays the same in every industry
Whatever your sector, the same building blocks turn an idea into a delivered outcome. If you can do these well, you can manage projects anywhere:
- **A clear scope** that says what is in and out, written down in a [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) statement and broken into a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/).
- **A realistic schedule** built from tasks, durations and dependencies; see project scheduling.
- **A budget** with contingency and regular cost tracking; see project budget.
- **Active risk management**, from identification to response and review; see [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/).
- **Stakeholder engagement and communication**, because most projects fail on people rather than plans; see [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/).
- **Clear ownership**, usually captured in a [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) and a RACI matrix.
- **A deliberate close**, with handover, acceptance and lessons learned; see project closure.
These are the parts you take with you when you change sectors. The industry guides show how each one is adapted, for example how a construction schedule is driven by site sequencing and long-lead procurement, while a software schedule is driven by sprints and release trains.

### What changes from one industry to another
In our experience, seven factors explain most of the differences between industries. When you start in a new sector, ask about each of them before you plan.
| Factor | What varies | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regulation and compliance | How much the law, a regulator or a standard dictates the process | Building regulations and health and safety in construction; GxP in pharmaceuticals; public procurement rules in government; data protection in HR and healthcare |
| Contract and funding model | How the work is paid for and what the contract fixes | Fixed-price or design-and-build contracts; time-and-materials client work; annual public budgets; research grants and donor funding |
| Life cycle and gates | The named stages and the approvals between them | RIBA or AIA stages in architecture; stage-gates in manufacturing and energy; sprints and releases in software; clinical trial phases in pharma |
| Pace of change | How stable requirements are once work starts | Stable designs on infrastructure; evolving requirements in software, games and marketing |
| Who the customer is | Internal sponsor, paying client, citizen, donor or patient | Agencies and consultancies manage client expectations and scope changes commercially; internal IT manages business users and adoption |
| Physical or digital output | How expensive it is to change something once built | Rework on a building is slow and costly; a software change can be released the same day |
| Safety and consequence of failure | What happens if something goes wrong | Patient safety, site safety and critical infrastructure need formal risk controls and sign-offs |
Tip
Before you pick a method, find out which approvals are legally or contractually required. Those gates are fixed; almost everything else about how you run the work can be adapted.
Scale matters too. A small business may run a project with one owner and a shared board, while an enterprise runs portfolios through a PMO with standard methods and reporting. The [small business](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/small-business-project-management/) and [enterprise project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/enterprise-project-management/) guides cover both ends.

### Methods, documents and KPIs by industry
The table summarises the typical approach in each sector family. It describes common practice, not a rule: individual organisations vary, and many combine methods.
| Sector family | Typical approach | Key documents | Example KPIs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Construction, engineering and property | Predictive, stage-based delivery with formal design reviews and change control | Contracts, drawings and specifications, programme, cost plan, RFIs, change orders, snag lists | Schedule and cost variance, change order value, safety incidents, defects at handover |
| IT, software and digital | Agile (Scrum or Kanban) for delivery, often inside a stage-gated programme for larger IT changes | Product backlog, release plan, architecture and test plans, cutover plan | Velocity or throughput, cycle time, deployment frequency, defect escape rate, user adoption |
| Marketing, creative and events | Kanban or Agile marketing for ongoing work; fixed-date plans for launches and events | Creative brief, campaign plan, content calendar, run of show | On-time delivery, revision rounds, campaign results, budget variance, attendee numbers |
| Professional services | Engagement life cycle governed by a statement of work, with Agile or phased delivery inside it | Proposal, statement of work, workplan, status reports, change requests | Utilisation, realisation, project margin, client satisfaction |
| Healthcare, public sector and research | Stage-gated governance with strong assurance; Agile increasingly used for digital services | Business case, project initiation document, risk and issue logs, ethics or clinical safety approvals | Benefits realised, milestone delivery, compliance findings, spend against funding |
| Industry and operations | Stage-gate product development, Lean and Six Sigma improvement, regulated validation in pharma | Stage-gate deliverables, FMEA, validation protocols, HSE plans | Time to market, first-pass yield, cost per unit, safety and environmental incidents |
| Business and enterprise | Portfolio governance with a mix of predictive and Agile projects | Business case, portfolio roadmap, benefits register, status dashboards | Strategic alignment, benefits delivered, portfolio on-time rate, resource utilisation |

#### Predictive, Agile or hybrid?
Use a predictive (Waterfall) plan when requirements are stable, the output is expensive to change and approvals must happen in sequence. Use Agile when requirements will evolve and you can deliver and learn in small increments. Many teams in every industry now use a hybrid: the governance, budget and major milestones are planned up front, while design or delivery work runs in iterations.
Agile is not only for software. Our guides to [Agile in construction](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-in-construction/) and [Agile marketing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/) show how sectors outside IT borrow iterative practices.

### Project management tools by industry
General project management platforms work in almost every sector; what differs is the feature you cannot live without. Some industries also use specialist software (for example construction platforms for drawings and site records, or professional services automation tools for billing). The table maps common needs to tools from our independent [ranking of the top 10 project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/).
| Sector family | What to look for | Tools from our ranking that fit well |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Construction, engineering and property | Gantt charts with dependencies, resource and workload views, document control, external access for contractors | [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) |
| IT, software and digital | Backlogs, sprints, issue tracking, developer integrations | [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/), [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) |
| Marketing, creative and agencies | Visual boards, content calendars, proofing and approvals, client guest access | [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/), [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) |
| Professional services and consulting | Resource planning, time tracking, client collaboration, portfolio reporting | [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), [Basecamp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/basecamp/) for simpler client communication |
| Public sector, healthcare and education | Security, permissions, Microsoft 365 integration, audit trails | [Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/), [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/), [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) |

| Enterprises and PMOs | Portfolio management, cross-project resource planning, governance and reporting at scale | [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/), [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) |
Wrike appears in several rows because it combines Gantt planning, resource management, portfolio views and proofing in one platform, which suits mixed teams such as agencies, PMOs and engineering organisations. Smaller teams that do not need that depth are often happier with a simpler tool. Our guide on [how to choose project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/) walks through the decision step by step.

### Templates that work in any industry
Most project documents travel well between sectors. These free templates are a good starting kit, whatever you deliver:
- [Project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) to agree purpose, scope, sponsor and success criteria.
- [Project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) for the schedule, milestones and budget.
- [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) for risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies.
- [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) to make ownership clear across teams and suppliers.

### How to use these guides
If you are starting a project in a sector that is new to you, this sequence works well:
1. **Open the guide for your sector** from the list above and read the phases section first. It tells you the vocabulary and the gates you will be measured against.
2. **List the mandatory approvals and regulations** that apply: permits, safety files, procurement rules, ethics or clinical sign-offs.
3. **Copy the key documents list** into your plan and start the charter and RAID log early.
4. **Choose a delivery approach** (predictive, Agile or hybrid) that fits the gates and how stable your requirements are.
5. **Adapt the KPIs** to what your sponsor cares about, keeping a small set you can measure every week.
6. **Set up your tool** around the views your team needs most, and invite clients or suppliers only where it helps.

### Where project managers work
Project management is used in almost every sector, but some are more project-oriented than others. PMI's 2017 Talent Gap report identified manufacturing and construction, information services and publishing, finance and insurance, management and professional services, utilities, and oil and gas as the sectors with the largest expected demand for project-oriented roles.
Job titles vary by sector: construction has project and site managers, IT has delivery managers and Scrum Masters, agencies have account and project managers, and pharma has clinical project managers.

### Moving into a new industry
Planning, stakeholder management, risk control, communication and leadership transfer between sectors. What does not transfer automatically is domain knowledge: the regulations, the contract forms, the technical vocabulary and the unwritten norms of how work gets approved.
- Learn the sector's life cycle and gate names before your first steering meeting.
- Ask a subject-matter expert to review your first plan and risk register.
- Find out which documents are legally required and who signs them.
- Spend time with the people doing the work, whether that is on site, in a lab or in a sprint review.
- Consider a recognised certification to show your general skills; our [project management certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) compares the main options.
Experience in a regulated industry is often valued in others, because it shows you can work with formal controls. Explain that experience in terms of outcomes rather than sector jargon.

### Common mistakes when applying project management across industries
- **Copying a method without its context**: running two-week sprints on a project where every deliverable needs a regulator's sign-off creates friction rather than speed.
- **Ignoring fixed gates**: permits, procurement windows, academic calendars and payroll cut-offs do not move, so put them in the schedule first.
- **Under-planning adoption**: in IT, HR and healthcare projects, success depends on people using the new system or process, not just on go-live.
- **Choosing tools by popularity**: a tool that suits a software team may frustrate a construction or events team, and the other way round.
- **Measuring the wrong things**: utilisation means a lot in an agency and little in a research lab; pick KPIs your sponsor actually uses.
- **Treating the industry guide as a checklist**: use it to ask better questions, then tailor the plan to your organisation.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is project management by industry?**
It is the practice of applying general project management methods within the rules and conditions of a specific sector. The core processes (scope, schedule, budget, risk and stakeholders) stay the same, while the life cycle, documents, approvals, KPIs and tools are adapted to that industry.

**Q: Which industries use project management the most?**
Project management is used almost everywhere. PMI's 2017 Talent Gap report highlighted manufacturing and construction, information services and publishing, finance and insurance, management and professional services, utilities, and oil and gas as the most project-oriented sectors. IT, healthcare and government also run large project portfolios.

**Q: Is project management the same in every industry?**
The fundamentals are the same, but the context is not. Regulation, contract and funding models, approval gates, the pace of change and the cost of rework all differ, so the way you plan, document and report work changes from sector to sector.

**Q: Which project management methodology is used in construction?**
Construction mostly uses predictive, stage-based delivery with formal design stages, contracts and change control, often supported by the critical path method for scheduling. Lean construction techniques and some Agile practices are used for design and coordination. See our construction project management guide for detail.

**Q: Which methodology do software teams use?**
Most software teams use Agile frameworks such as Scrum or Kanban, often with DevOps practices for frequent releases. Larger programmes may wrap Agile delivery in a stage-gated governance model or use a scaling framework such as SAFe.

**Q: What is the best project management software for my industry?**
It depends on the work. Software teams usually prefer Jira or ClickUp; marketing and creative teams value visual boards and proofing in tools such as Wrike, monday.com or Asana; construction and enterprise teams need Gantt charts and resource planning in tools such as Wrike or Smartsheet. Our top 10 ranking compares them in detail.

**Q: Can a project manager switch industries?**
Yes. Planning, risk management, stakeholder management and leadership are transferable. Expect to learn the new sector's regulations, contracts and vocabulary, and lean on subject-matter experts while you do.

**Q: Do I need industry experience to become a project manager?**
Not always, but it helps. Technical sectors such as construction, engineering and pharma often prefer domain experience, while marketing, operations and many business roles value general project skills and a certification more.

**Q: Which project management certification is best for a specific industry?**
General certifications such as PMP, CAPM and PRINCE2 are recognised across industries. Some sectors add their own: Agile certifications in software, and sector-specific qualifications in construction or healthcare. Our certification guide compares the main options.

**Q: What are the main types of project management?**
Project management is often grouped by industry (construction, IT, marketing and so on), by methodology (Waterfall, Agile, Scrum, Kanban, Lean, PRINCE2) and by scale (project, programme and portfolio management). This hub covers the industry view.

**Q: How is project management different in the public sector?**
Public sector projects face stronger accountability: public procurement rules, fixed funding cycles, formal business cases and assurance reviews, and scrutiny of how money is spent. Our government project management guide explains the phases and controls.

**Q: Are these industry guides free?**
Yes. All 30 industry guides and the linked templates are free to read and download.
