# Agency Project Management: Process, KPIs and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/agency-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Agency project management explained: the process from pitch to invoice, roles, estimating and utilisation worked examples, KPIs, scope control and tools.


## Agency Project Management: Process, KPIs and Examples
Agency project management is how creative, digital, marketing and media agencies plan, deliver and control client work while protecting profit. It combines ordinary project control with commercial disciplines that in-house teams rarely need: estimating and quoting, tracking time against fees, managing scope against a contract and sharing one team across many clients. This guide walks through the process from pitch to invoice, with worked examples for estimating, capacity, budget burn and retainers.
- Published 28 August 2026
- Last updated 16 October 2026
- 17 min read

### Key takeaways
- Agency project management adds commercial control (estimates, time tracking, margin) to ordinary delivery.
- The statement of work's assumptions and exclusions are your main defence against scope creep.
- Estimate from your own past hours, price at both cost and billable rates, and tie contingency to named risks.
- Plan capacity on real available hours, not headcount multiplied by a full working week.
- Compare budget spent with work accepted every week; the gap is your earliest warning of an overrun.
- Match the delivery method to the contract: fixed fee, time and materials and retainers each need a different approach.

### What is agency project management?
**Agency project management** is the planning, delivery and commercial control of client work inside an agency. It covers scoping and estimating, booking people across accounts, running delivery, managing client feedback and change, tracking time and budget against the agreed fee, and invoicing. Success means a happy client and a profitable project, not just on-time delivery.
Agencies are a type of professional services firm, so many of the same measures apply. The table shows how agency work differs from an in-house project.
| Aspect | Agency project | In-house project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who pays | An external client, under a contract | An internal budget holder |
| What is sold | Time and expertise, often as a fixed fee | Nothing; the organisation funds its own work |
| Scope | Defined by a statement of work or retainer agreement | Defined by an internal brief or charter |
| Team | Shared across several clients at once | Usually dedicated to the organisation's priorities |
| Change | Extra work is a commercial event that needs pricing | Extra work is a priority or capacity decision |
| Success measure | Client satisfaction plus margin | Benefits delivered within budget |
For the wider services view, see [professional services project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/professional-services-project-management/).

### What makes agency project management different
- **Time is the product.** Profit depends on how many hours the work actually takes compared with what the client pays.
- **Contracts define scope.** A [statement of work](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/) (SOW) or retainer agreement sets what is included; anything else is a change.
- **Many clients, one team.** The same designers and developers serve several accounts, so resourcing is a daily negotiation.
- **The client relationship.** Project managers balance delivery against keeping the client happy and the account growing.
- **Client dependencies.** Content, feedback and approvals from the client often sit on the critical path.
- **Pitching.** Some work starts before a contract exists, so new-business effort must be planned and capped.

### The agency project process from pitch to invoice
Most agency projects follow the stages below. The right-hand column is what makes it agency project management: a commercial check at every stage.
| Stage | What happens | Key output | Commercial checkpoint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Pitch or proposal | Respond to a brief or tender with an approach and price | Proposal and estimate | Is the price based on past actuals? Is pitch effort capped? |
| 2. Scoping and contract | Agree deliverables, assumptions, rounds of amends, timeline and fee | SOW or retainer agreement | Are exclusions and client responsibilities written down? |
| 3. Kick-off | Internal and client kick-offs; roles, ways of working and approvals agreed | Kick-off notes and plan | Is the estimate turned into an hours budget per role? |
| 4. Discovery and strategy | Research, audits, workshops and strategy | Strategy or insight deck | Does discovery change the scope? If so, re-estimate now |
| 5. Creative or build | Concepts, design, content or development | Draft deliverables | Weekly budget burn against accepted work |
| 6. Client review | Presentations and feedback rounds | Approved deliverables | Are extra rounds logged as changes? |
| 7. Launch or delivery | Go-live or handover of files | Live work and handover pack | Is all time logged and all change approved? |
| 8. Reporting and close | Results reporting, final invoice and project review | Report, invoice, lessons learned | Estimate against actual, recorded for next time |

#### The handoffs that break most projects
Two handoffs cause most trouble. The first is **sales to delivery**: the person who sold the work knows what was promised, but the delivery team only sees the SOW. Hold an internal handover meeting where the account lead walks through promises, risks and the client's personality. The second is **delivery to invoice**: work is finished but time is missing, changes are unbilled or acceptance was never confirmed. Close timesheets and confirm sign-off before the invoice goes out.
Tip
Write the assumptions into the SOW: number of concepts, rounds of amends, what the client must supply and by when. These are what you will point to when scope starts to drift.

### Roles in an agency project
| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Account director or account manager | Owns the client relationship, commercial growth and strategy |
| Project manager or producer | Plans and runs delivery: timelines, budgets, risks and day-to-day client updates on the work |
| Resource or traffic manager | Books people across all projects and resolves clashes |
| Creative director or technical lead | Owns the quality of the creative or technical output |
| Strategists, designers, developers, writers | Deliver the work and log their time |
| Finance | Invoicing, revenue recognition and profitability reporting |
| Client sponsor and approvers | Approve the brief, deliverables and changes |

#### Account manager vs project manager
The split between account management and project management is a common source of friction. As a rule of thumb, the account manager owns **why and what** (the relationship, the client's goals, upselling and renewals) and the project manager owns **how and when** (plan, budget, resources and delivery). Both should agree changes before they reach the team. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) agreed at the start of each account avoids gaps and double handling.

#### Producers and traffic managers
In creative and production agencies the project manager is often called a **producer**, especially where the work includes shoots, video or third-party suppliers. A **traffic manager** schedules work through the studio across all accounts. In smaller agencies one person often does all three jobs.

### Pricing models and how they shape delivery
How the work is sold decides who carries the risk of overruns, and therefore how tightly you must control scope.
| Pricing model | How it works | Who carries overrun risk | Delivery approach that fits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed fee | One price for defined deliverables | Agency | Phased plan, tight SOW, formal change requests |
| Time and materials | Client pays for hours used at agreed rates | Client | Agile sprints or Kanban, with regular budget reports |
| Retainer | Monthly fee for a set amount of hours or deliverables | Shared; agency if over-servicing is absorbed | Kanban with a monthly cap and rollover rules |
| Value-based | Price linked to the value or result for the client | Agency, with upside if results are strong | Clear success measures and a controlled scope |
The commercial model and the delivery method must match. Selling a fixed price and then running open-ended sprints is a common way agencies lose money.

### How to scope an agency project
Before you price anything, make the scope concrete enough that two people would read it the same way. A good SOW covers:
- **Deliverables with quantities**, for example "five page templates" rather than "a website".
- **Acceptance criteria**: what "done" means for each deliverable.
- **Assumptions**: number of concepts, rounds of amends, browsers and devices supported, and what the client supplies (copy, images, access, brand guidelines) and by when.
- **Exclusions**: what is not included, stated in the main document, not hidden in an appendix.
- **Client responsibilities and review times**, for example "feedback within three working days".
- **Change process**: how new requests are priced and approved.
- **Timeline and payment milestones**.
Examples of exclusions that hold up: "Copywriting is excluded; the client will supply final copy for all pages by week 3" and "Two rounds of amends are included per design stage; further rounds are charged at the rates in schedule 2."
Agree the SOW with the people who will deliver the work, not only the person who sold it. Designers and developers spot unrealistic assumptions quickly.

### How to estimate an agency project: worked example
This example estimates a five-page marketing website. All figures are illustrative. Cost rates are what each hour costs the agency (salary plus overheads); billable rates are what the client is charged.
1. **List the deliverables** from the draft SOW: discovery workshop, sitemap and wireframes, visual design for five templates, copy editing, build, testing and launch.
2. **Estimate hours per role from past projects**, not from the client's budget. Look up the actual hours on your last two similar websites.
3. **Add project management time.** Many agencies use a percentage of delivery hours; this example uses 15%.
4. **Price at both cost and billable rates** so you can see the margin.
5. **Add contingency tied to named risks**, not a blanket uplift.
6. **Sense-check** against a comparable past project and investigate any large difference.
| Role | Hours | Cost rate | Cost | Billable rate | Fee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strategist | 12 | £50 | £600 | £120 | £1,440 |
| UX designer | 20 | £40 | £800 | £100 | £2,000 |
| Visual designer | 30 | £40 | £1,200 | £100 | £3,000 |
| Copywriter (editing) | 15 | £35 | £525 | £90 | £1,350 |
| Developer | 60 | £45 | £2,700 | £110 | £6,600 |
| QA tester | 10 | £30 | £300 | £80 | £800 |
| Project manager (15% of 147 h) | 22 | £45 | £990 | £100 | £2,200 |
| Subtotal | 169 |  | £7,115 |  | £17,390 |
| Contingency: extra design round (risk: new stakeholder joins reviews) | 8 | £40 | £320 | £100 | £800 |
| Contingency: CRM form integration (risk: unknown API) | 6 | £45 | £270 | £110 | £660 |
| Total | 183 |  | £7,705 |  | £18,850 |
The quote is £18,850 for 183 hours, with a gross margin on time of about 59% ((18,850 − 7,705) ÷ 18,850). If the comparable project took 230 hours, stop and find out why before sending the price: either this scope is genuinely smaller or the estimate is optimistic.

### How to run an agency project kick-off
A good kick-off turns the signed SOW into shared expectations. Hold two meetings: an internal one first, then one with the client.

#### Internal kick-off
- The account lead walks through what was sold, the client's goals, known sensitivities and any promises made in the pitch.
- The project manager presents the hours budget per role, the draft timeline and the main risks.
- The team challenges the estimate and assumptions before the client sees the plan.
- Agree who may talk to the client about what, so feedback and requests reach the project manager.

#### Client kick-off
- Confirm objectives, deliverables, success measures and the people who will approve work.
- Walk through the timeline, highlighting the dates when the client must supply content or give feedback.
- Explain the change process and how many rounds of amends are included, in plain language.
- Agree the status update format, frequency and channel.
Send short written notes the same day. They become the reference point if expectations drift later.

### Capacity planning and resourcing
Most agency schedules fail because they assume everyone has a full week to give. Start with real available hours.

#### Worked example: available hours and utilisation
| Item | Hours per week |
| --- | --- |
| Contracted hours | 37.5 |
| Less: holiday and leave (averaged) | −3.0 |
| Less: internal meetings and training | −3.5 |
| Less: admin and email | −2.0 |
| Less: new business support | −1.0 |
| Available for client work | 28.0 |
If this designer logs 23 billable hours, billable utilisation is 23 ÷ 28 = 82% of available hours, or 23 ÷ 37.5 = 61% of contracted hours. Both definitions are used in practice, so pick one, write it down and use it consistently. Schedule client work against the 28 hours, not the 37.5.

#### How to book people
1. Convert each project's estimate into hours per role per week.
2. Book named people against named deliverables, not just roles.
3. Hold one resource plan for the whole agency, reviewed at a short meeting early each week for this week and next.
4. Add tentative bookings for likely wins, with a date to confirm or release them.
5. Leave some unbooked capacity for small client requests and amends, so they do not push planned work back.

### Running the work week to week
A steady weekly rhythm catches most problems while they are still small.
| When | What | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday | Resourcing check for this week and next; resolve clashes | Project managers and resource manager |
| Daily | Short stand-up or board review; everyone logs time for the day | Delivery team |
| Midweek | Budget burn against accepted work for each live project | Project manager |
| Thursday or Friday | Client status update: progress, decisions needed, risks, budget | Project manager and account manager |
| Friday | Timesheets closed; change log and risk log reviewed | Everyone; project manager reviews |
Keep one source of truth for status: each piece of work shows its stage, owner, next action and any risk to the date. A short weekly [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) with budget burn keeps the client and the account manager informed without extra meetings.

### Managing change requests and scope creep
Scope creep in agencies rarely arrives as a formal request. It comes as "one quick tweak" in a review call or an extra page mentioned in an email. Use a friendly but consistent process:
1. **Log every new request**, however small, in a change log.
2. **Check it against the SOW.** If it is in scope, schedule it. If not, it is a change.
3. **Set a threshold.** For example, anything that takes more than two hours is quoted before work starts; smaller items are logged and reviewed monthly.
4. **Price it at the original rates** and state the effect on the timeline.
5. **Get written approval** from the authorised client contact before starting.
6. **Update the plan, budget and invoice schedule.**
A [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) makes this quick. Our guides to [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) and [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) cover the wider process.

### Retainer project management
Retainers suit always-on work such as content, social, SEO and website support. They are usually run as a Kanban flow with a monthly cap on hours or deliverables. The main risk is over-servicing: doing more than the fee covers because each request seems small. Track it monthly.
| Month | Retainer hours | Hours worked | Over or under | Effective rate (fee £3,600) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Month 1 | 40 | 38 | −2 | £94.74 |
| Month 2 | 40 | 44 | +4 | £81.82 |
| Month 3 | 40 | 51 | +11 | £70.59 |
| Month 4 | 40 | 48 | +8 | £75.00 |
In this illustrative example the agency's planned blended rate is £90 an hour, but the effective rate has fallen to £70 to £75 because 23 extra hours went unbilled. The fix is a conversation, not a complaint: show the client the trend, agree which requests to drop or move, or propose a larger retainer. Also agree rollover rules for unused hours at the start.
Retainer work flows well on a Kanban board.

### KPIs for agency project management
| KPI | How to calculate it | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billable utilisation | Billable hours ÷ available (or contracted) hours | Team productivity and hiring needs |
| Budget burn | Hours or fees used ÷ hours or fees budgeted | How fast the budget is being spent |
| Burn vs progress | Budget burn compared with % of work accepted by the client | Early warning of an overrun |
| Write-offs (over-servicing) | Hours worked that cannot be billed | Margin leaking on fixed fees and retainers |
| Project margin | (Fee − cost of time − third-party costs) ÷ fee | Profitability by project and client |
| Estimate accuracy | Actual hours ÷ estimated hours | Whether pricing is reliable |
| On-time delivery | Milestones delivered on the agreed date ÷ total milestones | Client confidence |
| Client health | Satisfaction scores, renewals, number of feedback rounds | Account risk and growth potential |

#### Worked example: a budget-burn check
The website above has a budget of 183 hours. Halfway through the schedule, 120 hours have been logged (66% of budget), but the client has accepted only the discovery output and wireframes, which you weight as 50% of the work. A simple forecast is hours used ÷ share complete: 120 ÷ 0.50 = 240 hours, which is 57 hours (31%) over budget.
What to do next: find the cause (extra design rounds, slow approvals or an underestimate), stop any unapproved work, raise change requests for out-of-scope items, and tell the account manager this week rather than at the end. This is a simplified form of [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).

### Methodologies agencies use
| Approach | When it fits |
| --- | --- |
| Waterfall with phased fees | Fixed-price projects with clear deliverables, such as a brand identity or campaign |
| Scrum | Digital product and web builds, often sold as a fixed team for a number of sprints |
| Kanban | Retainers and always-on content or social support, with a monthly hours or deliverables cap |
| Hybrid | Fixed milestones for the client with Agile delivery inside each phase |
If your agency is adopting sprints, start with [what is Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/). Creative teams adapting Agile ideas should read [creative project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/creative-project-management/).

### Common challenges and how to handle them
| Challenge | How to handle it |
| --- | --- |
| Scope creep | Clear SOW assumptions and a friendly but firm change request process |
| Late client feedback | Put client review dates in the plan and state that missed dates move the launch |
| Resource clashes | One resource plan for the whole agency, reviewed weekly |
| Retainer over-servicing | Track hours against the retainer monthly and discuss trends with the client early |
| Poor estimates | Compare actuals with estimates on every project and use the data next time |
| Unbilled work | Make timesheets a daily habit and reconcile them weekly |
| Too many tools | Keep plans, approvals, time and files in one system wherever possible |
| Pitch overload | Cap pitch hours and book them in the resource plan like client work |

### Essential documents and templates
- Proposal: [project proposal template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-proposal-template/).
- Estimate: [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/), built from roles, hours and rates.
- Brief: [creative brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/creative-brief-template/).
- Schedule: [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/).
- Risks and issues: [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/).
- Close: [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/), plus a review of estimate against actual.
Run a short lessons learned review after every project and feed the actual hours back into your estimating data.

### Agency project management software
Agencies need project plans, resource scheduling, time tracking, budgets against estimates, client-facing proofing and approvals, and reporting. Tools fall into three broad groups:
- **Work management platforms** for planning, resourcing, proofing and reporting across many clients.
- **Simple client collaboration tools** for small agencies that mainly need organised communication with clients.
- **Agency management or PSA (professional services automation) systems** for quoting, time, invoicing and financial reporting, sometimes used alongside a work management platform.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is a strong all-in-one option for agencies that want proofing and approvals, workload and resource management, time tracking and client collaboration in one place, and it ranks first in our [project management software rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/). [Basecamp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/basecamp/) suits small agencies that want calm client communication with flat pricing. [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) and [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) are popular for visual workflows and cross-team task tracking, and [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) offers a wide feature set at lower prices.
Whatever you choose, test it with one real project: can you go from estimate to resource plan to time logged to budget report without exporting to a spreadsheet?

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is agency project management?**
It is how agencies plan, deliver and control client projects while tracking time, budget and scope against the client contract to protect profit.

**Q: What does a project manager do in an agency?**
They scope and estimate work, plan timelines, book resources, manage client feedback and approvals, track budget burn, handle change requests and make sure time is logged and invoiced.

**Q: How is agency project management different from in-house project management?**
Agencies sell time, so estimates, timesheets, contracts and margin matter much more. One team also serves many clients, so resourcing and prioritisation are constant.

**Q: What is the difference between an account manager and a project manager in an agency?**
Account managers own the relationship, the client's goals and commercial growth. Project managers own delivery: plan, budget, resources and timelines on specific pieces of work.

**Q: What is a producer in an agency?**
A producer is the agency equivalent of a project manager, a title common in creative, video and production work. They manage budgets, schedules, suppliers and the team from brief to delivery.

**Q: How do you calculate utilisation in an agency?**
Divide billable hours by available hours (contracted hours minus leave and agreed non-client time) or by contracted hours. For example, 23 billable hours out of 28 available is 82%. Use one definition consistently.

**Q: What is over-servicing?**
Over-servicing is work delivered beyond what the client pays for, usually on retainers and fixed fees. It shows up as write-offs and a falling effective hourly rate.

**Q: How do you handle scope creep in agency project management?**
Write clear assumptions and exclusions into the SOW, log every new request, price changes before starting work and get written approval from the client.

**Q: What KPIs matter in agency project management?**
Billable utilisation, budget burn against work accepted, write-offs, project margin, estimate accuracy, on-time delivery and client health.

**Q: How does retainer work fit agency project management?**
Retainers suit Kanban-style flow with a monthly cap on hours or deliverables, tracked monthly against the fee, with agreed rules for unused or extra hours.

**Q: Which methodology is best for agency project management?**
Match it to the contract: phased Waterfall for fixed-price deliverables, Scrum for team-based digital builds, Kanban for retainers and hybrid for fixed milestones with Agile delivery inside.

**Q: What templates help with agency project management?**
A proposal, cost estimate, creative brief, Gantt chart, change request, RAID log and lessons learned template cover the full life cycle.

**Q: What software is used for agency project management?**
A work management platform such as Wrike for planning, proofing and resourcing, often paired with an agency management or finance system. Small agencies may prefer simpler tools such as Basecamp.

**Q: Why do agencies lose money on projects?**
Mostly through optimistic estimates, unbilled extra rounds of amends, over-servicing retainers, unlogged time and work that slips because of late client feedback.

# Architecture Project Management: Stages, Fees and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/architecture-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Architecture project management explained: RIBA and AIA stages, fee and resource control, roles, worked examples, KPIs, templates and software.


## Architecture Project Management: Stages, Fees and Tools
Architecture project management is how an architectural practice plans, resources and controls a design commission, from the client brief through the design stages, approvals and construction-phase services, so that the design is delivered well and the practice earns a fair return on its fee. It means running two projects at once: the client's building and the practice's own time and money. This guide covers the stages, a step-by-step process, worked fee and resourcing examples, roles, KPIs and tools.
- Published 29 August 2026
- Last updated 17 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Architecture project management serves two goals: delivering the client's design and protecting the practice's fee.
- Structure the programme, fee and sign-offs around the RIBA Plan of Work or AIA phases.
- Turn the fee into hour budgets by stage and check hours against progress every week, not at invoice time.
- Treat every client change after sign-off as a potential additional service, and agree it in writing before doing the work.
- Approvals such as planning and, for higher-risk buildings in England, Gateway 2 belong on the critical path.
- Use BIM tools for design and a work management platform such as Wrike for programmes, resources and approvals.

### What is architecture project management?
**Architecture project management** is the planning, coordination and control of an architectural commission. It covers the design programme, the client's decisions and approvals, coordination with consultants and the contractor, and the practice's fee, hours and resources, so that the building is designed to quality and the commission is profitable.
It differs from construction project management, which controls the building works, and from the client-side project management of the whole development. The architect's project manager looks after the design team's part of the project and the practice's commercial position within it.
|  | The client's project | The practice's project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Objective | A well-designed building that meets the brief, budget and programme | Deliver the appointment to quality within the agreed fee |
| Budget | Construction cost and the client's wider budget | The fee, converted into hours and costs by stage |
| Key decisions | Brief, design options, stage sign-offs, approvals | Staffing, hours, additional services, risk and invoicing |
| Typical measures | Design quality, construction cost, approvals obtained, programme | Fee earned vs fee spent, utilisation, profit by stage |
In small studios the project architect usually does all of this. Larger practices add dedicated project managers, practice managers or resourcing leads. If your work is mainly fit-out, see our guide to [interior design project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/interior-design-project-management/).

### What makes architecture projects different
- **The fee is the budget.** Practices are paid a fixed fee, a percentage of construction cost or hourly rates, and every hour spent beyond the fee comes out of profit.
- **Design is iterative.** Clients need to see options and respond, so work loops back before it moves forward.
- **Approvals shape the programme.** Planning or zoning, building regulations or code review, heritage consents and client sign-offs gate each stage, and their timing is often outside your control.
- **Coordination with consultants.** Structural, building services and other engineers, cost consultants and specialists must work to a shared information programme.
- **Professional liability.** Drawings and specifications carry legal responsibility, so quality checking and document control are essential.
- **Long, uneven timelines.** Projects can pause for funding, planning or client decisions, which makes resourcing across several commissions difficult.
Tip
Write your fee proposal stage by stage, and close each stage with a written client sign-off. It is the single most effective way to make extra work visible and chargeable when the client changes direction.

### Architecture project stages: RIBA and AIA
Practices in the UK usually work to the **RIBA Plan of Work 2020**, which organises a building project into eight stages from 0 to 7. In the US, the AIA's standard owner–architect agreement (B101–2017) defines five phases of basic services. The table maps them roughly; they are not exact equivalents.
| RIBA stage | Roughly equivalent AIA phase | Main architect activities | Typical sign-off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 Strategic Definition | Pre-design (often an additional service) | Help define the client's need and whether a building is the answer | Client confirms the business case and requirements |
| 1 Preparation and Briefing | Pre-design / programming | Develop the brief, site appraisal, feasibility, appointment and fee | Project brief agreed |
| 2 Concept Design | Schematic design | Design options, massing, concept proposals, early cost advice | Concept design approved |
| 3 Spatial Coordination | Design development | Coordinated design with engineers; planning application in the UK | Coordinated design approved; planning submitted |
| 4 Technical Design | Construction documents | Detailed drawings and specifications for building and tender | Technical design and tender package issued |
| 5 Manufacturing and Construction | Procurement and construction | Answer queries, review submittals, inspect, certify where appointed | Practical completion |
| 6 Handover | Construction phase closeout | Snagging, as-built information, defects period | End of defects period |
| 7 Use | Post-occupancy (often an additional service) | Post-occupancy evaluation and feedback | Lessons captured |

#### Stage boundaries and approvals
According to RIBA guidance, Stages 0 to 4 generally run in sequence, while Stages 4 and 5 overlap on most projects because the contractor or specialists complete parts of the technical design. RIBA also says planning applications are generally submitted at the end of Stage 3, and recommends earlier submission only when enough information exists and the client is experienced enough to manage the risk. Building planning periods into the programme at the right point, with time for pre-application discussions and conditions, is one of the project manager's main jobs.

#### Higher-risk buildings in England: Gateway 2
Under the Building Safety Act 2022, higher-risk buildings in England (broadly, residential and some other buildings at least 18 metres or seven storeys tall) must pass building control approval from the Building Safety Regulator, known as **Gateway 2**, before construction starts. The statutory period is 12 weeks for new buildings and 8 weeks for work to existing ones, but reported waits in 2025 were far longer. The regulator became a standalone body sponsored by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government in January 2026 and has set a target of deciding non-complex Gateway 2 applications within 18 weeks by March 2027. Because applications need construction-ready design, usually RIBA Stage 4, plan Gateway 2 as a critical-path activity and check current guidance when you programme the work.

#### AIA phases in the US
AIA B101–2017 lists five phases of basic services: schematic design, design development, construction documents, procurement and construction. Pre-design programming and post-occupancy work are usually added as additional services. The AIA does not prescribe how the fee should be split across phases, so each practice sets its own split from its project history.

### How to manage an architecture project step by step
The steps below run from first enquiry to post-occupancy. They apply whether you are a five-person studio or a large practice; only the formality changes.
1. **Qualify the enquiry.** Check the client, the budget, the site and your capacity before you spend time on a proposal.
2. **Agree the brief.** Capture the client's requirements, budget, programme and constraints in a [project brief](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-brief-template/).
3. **Define your scope of services.** List exactly which stages and services are included and which are not (surveys, interiors, Stage 7, extra planning submissions).
4. **Build the fee from the bottom up.** Estimate hours by stage and role, apply cost rates, add risk allowance and profit, then compare with what the market or the client expects.
5. **Sign the appointment.** Make sure the scope, fee, payment stages and process for additional services are written into the appointment before work begins.
6. **Set up the project.** Create stage budgets in hours, the design programme, a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) for the design team and a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).
7. **Agree an information programme with consultants.** Set dates for each consultant's information so coordination reviews happen on time.
8. **Run each stage to a sign-off.** Present options, record client decisions and close the stage with written approval of the stage report.
9. **Track hours and progress weekly.** Compare hours spent with the stage budget and with the deliverables actually complete (see the examples below).
10. **Control change.** Log every client change, assess its effect on fee and programme, and agree any additional service before doing the work using a [change request](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/).
11. **Manage approvals.** Plan pre-application meetings, submissions and determination periods, and track conditions.
12. **Support construction.** Respond to queries and submittals within agreed turnaround times and record site visits and instructions.
13. **Close out and learn.** Agree final fees, archive the project and hold a [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) review that feeds actual hours back into future fee proposals.

### Fees, hours and resourcing: worked examples
The fee is the practice's budget, so fee control is the heart of architecture project management. The examples below use illustrative figures for a mid-sized commission.

#### Common fee bases
| Fee basis | How it works | Main risk for the practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Percentage of construction cost | Fee is a percentage of the construction budget or final cost | Fee may not reflect effort if cost falls or design work increases |
| Lump sum (fixed fee) | Fixed fee for a defined scope, often split by stage | Overruns come straight out of profit unless changes are charged |
| Time charge (hourly) | Hours charged at agreed rates, sometimes capped | Clients may resist open-ended costs; caps turn it into a fixed fee |
| Hybrid | Fixed fee for early stages, time charge for construction-phase services | Needs clear boundaries between the parts |

#### Example 1: turn the fee into stage hour budgets
A practice agrees a lump-sum fee of **£180,000** for RIBA Stages 1 to 6. It splits the fee by stage using its own project history, targets a 15% profit margin (so 85% of the fee is available for cost) and uses an average cost rate of £60 per hour (salary plus overheads).
| Stage | Share of fee | Stage fee | Cost budget (85%) | Hour budget at £60/hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Preparation and Briefing | 5% | £9,000 | £7,650 | 128 |
| 2 Concept Design | 15% | £27,000 | £22,950 | 383 |
| 3 Spatial Coordination | 20% | £36,000 | £30,600 | 510 |
| 4 Technical Design | 30% | £54,000 | £45,900 | 765 |
| 5 Manufacturing and Construction | 25% | £45,000 | £38,250 | 638 |
| 6 Handover | 5% | £9,000 | £7,650 | 128 |
| **Total** | **100%** | **£180,000** | **£153,000** | **2,552** |
The hour budgets are what the team actually manages. Split each one further by role (director, project architect, architect, technologist) so the resourcing plan and timesheets use the same structure.

#### Example 2: check a stage half-way through
Six weeks into Stage 3, the team has booked **360 hours** against the 510-hour budget. Looking at the deliverables (coordinated plans, sections, elevations, the planning package), the project architect judges the stage to be about **50% complete**. So the work done is worth 50% × 510 = **255 budgeted hours**, but it has taken 360.
| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Hour budget for the stage | 510 hours |
| Hours spent | 360 hours |
| Earned hours (50% × 510) | 255 hours |
| Efficiency (earned ÷ spent) | 0.71 |
| Forecast hours at completion (510 ÷ 0.71) | 720 hours |
| Forecast overrun | 210 hours ≈ £12,600 at £60/hour |
At the current rate the stage will cost about £43,200 against a stage fee of £36,000, so it will lose money rather than make £5,400. The causes turn out to be two rounds of layout changes requested by the client and late structural information. The project manager logs the client changes as a claim for additional services, agrees new dates with the engineer and resets the remaining hour budget. This is earned value applied to hours; see our guide to [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/).

#### Example 3: check studio resourcing and utilisation
A six-person studio has 6 × 37.5 = **225 hours** a week available. The practice sets itself a target of 75% chargeable time, leaving room for practice work, CPD and bids, so it aims for about **169 chargeable hours** a week. Planned demand for the next four weeks is:
| Commitment | Hours per week |
| --- | --- |
| Project A (Stage 4) | 80 |
| Project B (Stage 3, planning deadline) | 60 |
| Project C (Stage 5, site queries) | 25 |
| Competition entry (non-chargeable) | 30 |
| **Total demand** | **195** |
Demand exceeds the target by about 26 hours a week. The options are to move the competition to after the planning submission, agree a revised date for part of Project A's information, bring in a freelance technologist for four weeks, or accept overtime for a short period. Seeing this four weeks ahead, rather than in the week itself, is the point of a resource plan. Our guides to [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) and [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) cover the techniques.

#### Example 4: price a client change as an additional service
After Stage 3 sign-off, the client asks to add a roof terrace. Before redesigning, the project manager assesses the impact:
| Item | Impact |
| --- | --- |
| Architect's time | About 70 hours to redesign, coordinate and re-issue drawings; at a charge rate of £95/hour, about £6,650 |
| Consultants | Structural and services engineers each need to review loads, drainage and access; they will quote separately |
| Approvals | The approved planning drawings change, so a planning amendment or new application may be needed |
| Programme | About four weeks added to Stage 4 plus any planning determination period |
| Construction cost | Cost consultant to update the cost plan before the client decides |
The practice sends the client a short additional services letter with the fee, the programme effect and the decision needed, and starts work only once it is approved.

### Example design programme for Concept Design
A design programme shows the client and consultants when information is needed and when decisions are due. Here is an illustrative eight-week programme for RIBA Stage 2 on a mid-sized commission.
| Week | Architect | Consultants | Client decision or milestone |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Review brief and site information; set up model | Receive brief and survey | Kick-off workshop |
| 2–3 | Develop three massing options | Structural and services engineers comment on strategies | Options review meeting (end of week 3) |
| 4 | Develop the preferred option | Cost consultant prepares outline cost plan | Client chooses preferred option |
| 5–6 | Plans, sections and design narrative | Engineers produce outline strategies | Design review with client (end of week 6) |
| 7 | Incorporate comments; compile Stage 2 report | Cost plan update | Pre-application meeting with the planning authority |
| 8 | Issue Stage 2 report | Strategies issued | Client signs off Stage 2 |
A [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) or [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) is enough to build programmes like this, with the critical decisions shown as milestones.

### Key roles in an architecture project
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Partner or director in charge | Client relationship, fee agreement, design quality and commercial oversight |
| Project architect or project lead | Day-to-day lead for design and documentation; coordinates consultants |
| Project manager (in larger practices) | Programme, resourcing, fee tracking, risk, change and client reporting |
| Architects and architectural assistants | Produce designs, drawings and models |
| Architectural technologists | Technical detailing and construction information |
| BIM coordinator or information manager | Model standards, federation, clash checks and the common data environment |
| Consultants | Structural, building services, cost, fire, planning and other specialist advice |
| Client and client's project manager | Decisions, approvals, funding and overall project control |

#### Project architect vs project manager
The **project architect** leads the design and the technical information: what is drawn, how it is detailed and whether it is coordinated. A **project manager** in a practice leads the programme, the hours, the fee and the client's commercial relationship. In smaller practices one person holds both roles; in larger ones they work as a pair, and the project manager may also cover several projects at once.

### Methodologies that fit
| Approach | Use in architecture |
| --- | --- |
| Stage-gated plan | Follows the RIBA or AIA stages with sign-off at each, as in [waterfall project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) |
| Iterative design cycles | Short cycles of options, review and refinement in concept and developed design; see [iterative and incremental development](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/iterative-and-incremental-development/) |
| Kanban for production | A [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) to manage drawing production, queries and submittal reviews |
| Lean and BIM collaboration | Integrated design workflows with consultants and contractors to cut rework |
Many practices find a hybrid works best: a fixed stage plan for the client and the fee, with short iterative loops inside each design stage and a simple board for production and construction-phase queries.

### Essential documents and templates
| Document | Purpose | Template |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project brief | Client requirements, budget and constraints | [Project brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-brief-template/) |
| Fee proposal and resource plan | Hours and cost by stage and role | [Project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/), [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) |
| Design programme | Stages, information deadlines and approvals | [Project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) |
| Responsibility matrix | Who designs what across the design team | [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) |
| Deliverables schedule | Drawings and reports due at each stage | [Project deliverables template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-deliverables-template/) |
| Change log and additional services | Client changes, fee and programme impact, approval | [Change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) |
| Risk register | Design, approval, programme and commercial risks | [Risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) |
| Lessons learned | Actual hours and feedback for future fee proposals | [Lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) |
Add a drawing register and issue sheet, stage reports, design review records and meeting minutes as practice-standard documents.

### KPIs for architecture project management
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fee earned vs fee spent | Value of completed work against hours costed | Stage profitability |
| Hours to complete vs fee remaining | Forecast of remaining effort against remaining fee | Early warning of overruns |
| Utilisation rate | Chargeable hours as a share of available hours | Resourcing and practice health |
| Stage sign-offs on time | Stages closed with client approval by the planned date | Programme reliability |
| Drawing issues on time | Information issued by the programme date | Reliability to consultants and contractor |
| Additional services recovered | Fees agreed for out-of-scope work against changes logged | Commercial discipline |
| Debtor days | How long clients take to pay invoices | Cash flow |
| Design changes per stage | Client-driven revisions after sign-off | Brief stability |

### Common challenges and how to fix them
| Challenge | Why it happens | How to manage it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope creep through small design changes | Clients see each change as minor | Log every change and agree additional services before doing the work |
| Fee overruns in early stages | Option studies expand to fill the time | Cap the number of options in the appointment and track hours weekly |
| Waiting for consultant information | Consultants work to their own priorities | Publish an information required schedule with dates and owners |
| Approval delays | Planning, heritage and building safety reviews take longer than expected | Hold pre-application talks and build realistic determination periods into the programme |
| Too many projects per person | Pipeline peaks and pauses | A practice-wide resource plan reviewed weekly |
| Late client decisions | Unclear decision points | Show decision dates as milestones and explain the cost of delay |
For engaging clients, planners and neighbours, see our guide to [project stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/).

### Common mistakes in architecture project management
- **Starting work before the appointment is signed.** Unsigned scope is the root of most fee disputes.
- **Tracking fees only at invoice time.** By then the hours are spent; check weekly.
- **Skipping stage sign-offs.** Without them, every later change looks like part of the original service.
- **Not feeding actual hours back into proposals.** Fee estimates stay optimistic unless they use real project data.
- **Letting one person hold all project knowledge.** Keep decisions, drawings and actions in shared systems so others can step in.

### Software for architecture project management
Architects rely on several kinds of software. The project management platform ties them together rather than replacing them.
| Tool type | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| BIM and CAD authoring | Designing and documenting the building |
| Common data environment | Sharing and controlling models and drawings with the design team |
| Practice management or ERP | Timesheets, fee tracking, invoicing and financial reporting |
| Work and project management platform | Stage programmes, tasks, resourcing across projects, client approvals and reporting |
For the project layer, look for timeline and Gantt views, workload or resource management, time tracking, approval and proofing workflows, and secure client or consultant access. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) covers these well, including proofing for drawings and visuals, and is the top all-in-one pick in [our tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/). Smaller studios that only need simple programmes and task lists may prefer one of the lighter tools from the same list.

### Skills and qualifications
- **Design and technical knowledge,** so you can judge how long design and coordination will really take.
- **Commercial skills:** fee estimating, appointments, additional services and invoicing.
- **Planning and resourcing** across several projects at once.
- **Communication and negotiation** with clients, consultants, planners and contractors.
- **Regulatory awareness,** including planning, building regulations or codes, and building safety duties.
Professional practice is part of architectural registration in most countries. In the UK, registration with the Architects Registration Board follows a professional practice qualification, often known as Part 3. In the US, the Architect Registration Examination run by NCARB includes Practice Management and Project Management divisions. Many architects add a general project management qualification such as the [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is architecture project management?**
It is how an architectural practice plans, resources and controls a design commission from brief to construction-phase services, delivering the design to quality while protecting its fee.

**Q: What does an architectural project manager do?**
They run the programme, resourcing, fee tracking, risk, change and client reporting for a commission, working alongside the project architect who leads the design and technical information.

**Q: What is the difference between a project architect and a project manager?**
The project architect leads the design and its technical coordination. The project manager leads the programme, hours, fee and commercial relationship. In small practices one person often does both.

**Q: What are the RIBA Plan of Work stages?**
Stage 0 Strategic Definition, 1 Preparation and Briefing, 2 Concept Design, 3 Spatial Coordination, 4 Technical Design, 5 Manufacturing and Construction, 6 Handover and 7 Use.

**Q: What are the AIA phases of design?**
AIA B101–2017 defines five phases of basic services: schematic design, design development, construction documents, procurement and construction. Pre-design and post-occupancy work are usually additional services.

**Q: How should an architect split the fee across stages?**
There is no fixed rule; the AIA does not prescribe a split. Use your own project history, giving the largest shares to technical design or construction documents and to construction-phase services, and review the split after each project.

**Q: How do architects track fees on a project?**
Convert the fee into hour budgets by stage and role, record time weekly, estimate how complete each stage is from its deliverables, and compare earned hours with hours spent to forecast the final position.

**Q: What is a good utilisation rate for an architecture practice?**
It depends on the practice's size, roles and business model, so set your own target. Leave room for practice management, CPD and bids, and track actual utilisation against that target each week.

**Q: How do architects handle scope creep?**
By defining the scope of services in the appointment, closing each stage with a sign-off, logging every client change and agreeing additional services in writing before doing the work.

**Q: When is a planning application submitted in the RIBA Plan of Work?**
RIBA guidance says planning applications are generally submitted at the end of Stage 3 (Spatial Coordination), with earlier submission only when enough information exists and the client can manage the risk.

**Q: What is Gateway 2 under the Building Safety Act?**
It is the building control approval that higher-risk buildings in England need from the Building Safety Regulator before construction starts. Applications need construction-ready design, so it should be planned as a critical-path activity.

**Q: What methodology suits architecture projects?**
Most practices use a hybrid: a stage-gated plan based on RIBA or AIA stages for the client and fee, with iterative design cycles inside each stage and a Kanban board for drawing production and queries.

**Q: What software do architects use for project management?**
BIM and CAD tools for design, a common data environment for sharing information, practice management software for timesheets and invoicing, and a work management platform such as Wrike for programmes, resourcing and approvals.
