# Energy Project Management: Phases, Roles, Controls and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/energy-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Energy project management for renewables, power and oil and gas: stage-gates, FEED, EPC contracts, controls, HSE KPIs, worked examples and templates.


## Energy Project Management: Phases, Roles, Controls and Tools
Energy project management is the planning, control and delivery of projects that produce, transmit or store energy, from wind, solar and battery storage to power stations, grid connections, pipelines and oil and gas facilities. These projects are capital-intensive, long-lived, high-hazard and heavily regulated, so success depends on disciplined front-end planning, formal investment gates, strong contracts and rigorous safety management. This guide explains the life cycle, contracting, project controls, HSE, permitting, commissioning and tools, with worked examples.
- Published 28 August 2026
- Last updated 17 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Energy project management runs on stage-gates: each gate is an investment decision, and the final investment decision (FID) commits most of the capital.
- Time and money spent on front-end definition (FEED or development) is the strongest protection against cost and schedule overruns in construction.
- Permits, grid connection dates and long-lead equipment such as transformers often decide the schedule more than construction itself.
- Safety performance is reported first on almost every energy project; measure it with rates per hours worked, not raw counts.
- Earned value, probabilistic (P50/P90) estimates and a live risk register give owners and lenders an honest forecast.
- Specialist scheduling, cost and HSE systems sit alongside a work management platform such as Wrike for the owner's team and development portfolio.

### What is energy project management?
**Energy project management** is the discipline of taking an energy asset from idea to safe, reliable operation: proving the business case, securing land, permits and grid access, defining the design, contracting and building it, and commissioning it into service. It applies standard project methods with added focus on investment gates, safety, regulation and long-term asset performance.
The term covers very different project types. A 20 MW rooftop solar programme and a multi-billion offshore development share the same principles but differ hugely in scale, risk and governance.
| Project type | Examples | What usually drives the schedule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onshore renewables | Solar farms, onshore wind, agrivoltaics | Land, planning consent and grid connection date |
| Offshore renewables | Offshore wind farms, export cables | Seabed leases, consents, vessel availability and weather windows |
| Energy storage | Battery energy storage systems (BESS), pumped hydro | Grid connection, equipment supply and fire safety approvals |
| Thermal and nuclear generation | Gas turbines, combined heat and power, nuclear | Engineering complexity, licensing and long-lead equipment |
| Networks | Substations, transmission lines, interconnectors | Outages on the existing network, consents and land access |
| Oil and gas | Upstream wells and platforms, pipelines, processing plants | Subsurface uncertainty, engineering, fabrication and permits |
| Low-carbon fuels and capture | Hydrogen, biomethane, carbon capture and storage | First-of-a-kind technology, funding and offtake agreements |
| Energy efficiency | Building retrofits, heat pumps, LED and controls upgrades | Site access, occupied buildings and procurement |

### What makes energy projects different

#### Large capital, long life
Assets may operate for decades, and decisions made in the first few percent of spending fix most of the lifetime cost. Owners therefore invest heavily in feasibility, design and estimating before committing to build. Business cases are usually tested with discounted cash flow measures such as [net present value](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/net-present-value/).

#### Permits and consents
Planning permission, environmental impact assessment, marine or water licences, land rights and conditions attached to consents can take longer than construction. Depending on project size and country, consent may come from a local authority or a national process.

#### Grid connection
Most power projects cannot earn revenue until the network operator connects them. Connection dates, reinforcement works and technical compliance tests often sit on the critical path.

#### High-hazard work
Electrical, lifting, working at height, confined space, marine and process hazards mean permit-to-work systems, safety cases and strict contractor management.

#### Financing and lenders
Many projects, particularly renewables, are project-financed. Lenders and their technical advisers review the schedule, contracts, estimates and risks before financial close and monitor progress during construction.

#### Supply chain, sites and weather
Transformers, turbines, switchgear and specialist vessels can have long lead times. Offshore, remote or mountainous sites add logistics and seasonal weather windows.

### The energy project life cycle
Large oil, gas and power companies commonly use a stage-gate model with names such as Appraise, Select, Define, Execute and Operate. Renewable developers usually follow a development-led sequence. The two map onto each other closely.
| Capital project stage-gate | Renewables development sequence | Main work | Gate decision or milestone |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Appraise | Site origination and feasibility | Identify opportunity, screening studies, early land and grid checks | Is the opportunity worth funding further? |
| Select | Development | Compare concepts, land agreements, surveys, consent application, grid offer | Preferred concept selected; consent and grid secured |
| Define (FEED) | Pre-construction and financing | Front-end engineering design, procurement strategy, tenders, financing | Final investment decision (FID) or financial close |
| Execute | Construction | Detailed design, procurement, construction and installation | Mechanical completion |
| Commission | Commissioning and energisation | Testing, energisation, performance tests | Commercial operation date (COD) and takeover |
| Operate | Operations and maintenance | O&M, warranty period, performance monitoring | Business case benefits realised |
| Decommission | Repowering or decommissioning | Remove or replace the asset and restore the site | Site restored or repowered |
The early stages are often called **front-end loading (FEL)**, usually split into FEL 1 (Appraise), FEL 2 (Select) and FEL 3 (Define). A [feasibility study](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/feasibility-study/) supports the first gate; the business case is refreshed at every gate.
Tip
Protect the front end. Rushing FEED or development to hit an investment date usually moves the problems into construction, where changes cost far more and contractors price the uncertainty.

### Front-end loading, FEED and cost estimate classes
**Front-end engineering design (FEED)** defines the facility well enough to produce a reliable estimate and schedule, tender the main contracts and support the final investment decision. Typical FEED outputs include the design basis, layouts, single-line diagrams, equipment lists, long-lead item specifications, the execution plan, the control estimate and the risk register.
As definition improves, the estimate becomes more accurate. AACE International's estimate classification for the process industries (recommended practice 18R-97) is widely used to describe this. The ranges below are AACE's indicative figures; actual accuracy depends on the project's risk.
| AACE class | Project definition | Typical use | Indicative accuracy range | Typical gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Class 5 | 0% to 2% | Screening, concept | Low −20% to −50%; high +30% to +100% | Appraise |
| Class 4 | 1% to 15% | Study or feasibility | Low −15% to −30%; high +20% to +50% | Select |
| Class 3 | 10% to 40% | Budget authorisation | Low −10% to −20%; high +10% to +30% | FID |
| Class 2 | 30% to 75% | Control or bid | Low −5% to −15%; high +5% to +20% | Execute (control baseline) |
| Class 1 | 65% to 100% | Check estimate or bid | Low −3% to −10%; high +3% to +15% | Execute (lump-sum tenders, changes) |
The practical lesson: an estimate prepared at Appraise is not a budget. Present early numbers as ranges, state the estimate class and move to a single control budget only at FID. Build estimates with a [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) structured by your work breakdown structure so each class refines the same lines.

### Step by step: delivering a utility-scale renewables project
The sequence below reflects how a typical onshore solar, wind or battery storage project moves from site to operation. Timings vary widely by country, size and grid conditions; development commonly takes longer than construction.
1. **Originate the site.** Screen land for resource (sun or wind), grid capacity nearby, environmental constraints and access. Agree options or leases with landowners.
2. **Apply for grid connection.** Submit the application early; the offer sets your connection date, capacity and cost of reinforcement works.
3. **Run surveys and design for consent.** Ecology, landscape, heritage, noise, flood and ground surveys feed the layout and the environmental assessment.
4. **Engage stakeholders and submit the consent application.** Consult the community and statutory bodies before submission, then manage questions and conditions.
5. **Prepare the business case and financing.** Model revenue (power purchase agreement, merchant or support scheme), costs and returns. Use a [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) and confirm the financing route.
6. **Develop the design and procurement strategy.** Choose EPC or multi-contract, prepare specifications and issue tenders using an [RFQ template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/rfq-template/). Order long-lead items such as transformers early if needed.
7. **Reach FID or financial close.** Lenders' technical advisers review contracts, schedule, estimates and risks. Baseline the schedule and budget.
8. **Discharge pre-construction consent conditions.** Many consents require approved plans (traffic, environment, drainage) before work starts.
9. **Construct.** Civil works, foundations or piling, installation of panels, turbines or battery containers, cabling and substation works. Manage HSE, progress, quality and change weekly.
10. **Commission and connect.** Test systems, energise with the grid operator, complete compliance tests and reach the commercial operation date.
11. **Hand over to operations.** Close out punch lists, deliver the handover dossier and as-built drawings and start the warranty and O&M period.
Large oil and gas or thermal projects follow the same logic with far longer engineering, fabrication and commissioning phases. For the construction phase in more depth, see our guide to [construction project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/construction-project-management/).

### Contracting strategies: EPC, EPCM and multi-contract
The contracting strategy decides who carries design, interface and cost risk. It is chosen during Select or development and shapes the owner's team, the controls you need and the financing terms.
| Strategy | How it works | Who carries most risk | Owner's team needed | Often used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EPC (lump-sum turnkey) | One contractor designs, procures and builds for a fixed price and date | Contractor (priced into the contract) | Smaller; focused on assurance | Project-financed renewables, smaller plants |
| EPCM | A firm manages engineering, procurement and construction on the owner's behalf; the owner holds the trade contracts | Owner | Medium; strong controls | Large oil, gas, mining and process projects |
| Multi-contract | Owner contracts separately for main packages (e.g. turbines, balance of plant, grid) | Owner, especially interfaces | Larger; interface management | Wind farms and experienced developers |
| Reimbursable (cost-plus) | Contractor paid actual cost plus fee | Owner | Medium; cost control | Uncertain scope, early works, brownfield |
| Alliance or collaborative | Owner and contractors share pain and gain against targets | Shared | Integrated team | Complex projects with high uncertainty |

#### How to choose
- **Choose EPC** when lenders want price and date certainty, the technology is mature and you have limited in-house engineering capacity. Expect a higher price for the risk transfer.
- **Choose multi-contract** when you have an experienced owner's team and can manage interfaces; it can lower cost but you carry the gaps between packages.
- **Choose EPCM or reimbursable** when scope is still evolving or the project is too large for any contractor to price at fixed cost.
- **Whatever you choose,** write an interface register that lists every physical and contractual interface between packages, with an owner for each.

### Key roles on an energy project
| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Owner or developer | Funds the project, owns the business case and makes gate decisions |
| Project director or owner's project manager | Leads the owner's team; manages contractors against cost, schedule, quality and HSE targets |
| Owner's engineer | Independent technical adviser reviewing designs and contractor work |
| EPC, EPCM or package contractors | Engineering, procurement and construction, or management of these for the owner |
| Project controls team | Planning, scheduling, cost control, earned value, change and reporting |
| HSE manager | Safety management system, permits to work, environmental compliance and incident investigation |
| Permitting and stakeholder lead | Consents, conditions, landowners, communities and regulators |
| Grid and commercial lead | Connection agreement, power purchase agreements and revenue contracts |
| Commissioning manager | Test plans, energisation and handover to operations |
| Grid operator and regulators | Connection works and terms, licences and compliance |
| Lenders and technical advisers | Due diligence before financial close and monitoring during construction |

### Project controls: schedule, cost and earned value

#### The integrated schedule
Energy schedules are built with the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) and usually have several levels: a level 1 milestone summary for the board and lenders, a level 2 or 3 schedule by area and discipline, and detailed contractor schedules. Permits, grid dates and long-lead equipment should appear as logic-linked activities, not just notes. A [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) is fine for an early development plan; large projects move to enterprise scheduling tools.

#### Worked example: earned value on a battery storage project
A battery storage project has a construction budget at completion (BAC) of £40 million over 14 months. At the end of month 8 the controls team reports the figures below. The numbers are illustrative.
| Measure | Value | Calculation | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Planned value (PV) | £18.0m | Budgeted cost of work scheduled to date | What should be done by now |
| Earned value (EV) | £16.0m | Budgeted cost of work actually done | What is done, valued at budget |
| Actual cost (AC) | £17.5m | Cost incurred to date | What it cost |
| Cost performance index (CPI) | 0.91 | EV ÷ AC = 16.0 ÷ 17.5 | £0.91 of work for every £1 spent |
| Schedule performance index (SPI) | 0.89 | EV ÷ PV = 16.0 ÷ 18.0 | Behind plan |
| Estimate at completion (EAC) | £43.75m | BAC ÷ CPI = 40 ÷ 0.914 | Forecast final cost if performance continues |
| Variance at completion (VAC) | −£3.75m | BAC − EAC | Forecast overrun |
The next steps are to find the cause (in this example, slower cabling than planned and a late delivery of power conversion units), check whether the variance is on the critical path, decide on recovery actions and compare the overrun with the remaining contingency. Our guide to [estimate at completion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/estimate-at-completion/) explains which EAC formula to use when the cause is a one-off rather than a trend.
Tip
SPI drifts towards 1.0 as a project nears its end even if it is late, because all planned work is eventually earned. On energy projects always check the critical path and key milestone dates alongside SPI.

#### P50 and P90: probabilistic estimates
Owners and lenders rarely accept a single-point estimate. A [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) runs the schedule or cost model thousands of times with ranges for uncertain items and produces confidence levels.
- **For cost and schedule,** P50 is the value with a 50% chance of not being exceeded and P90 the value with a 90% chance of not being exceeded. Many owners set the budget near P50 and hold contingency up to a higher confidence level.
- **For energy yield,** the language is reversed: a P90 annual output is the level expected to be exceeded in 90% of years. Lenders commonly size debt on conservative yield cases such as P90.
- **Example:** a wind farm's cost model gives P50 £118m and P90 £131m. The board approves a budget of £118m plus £13m of contingency held by the owner, released only through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).

### Health, safety and environment
On energy projects, safety is usually the first item in every report and meeting. A robust HSE system typically includes:
- **Safety management system** covering hazard identification, risk assessment, method statements, training and competence.
- **Permit to work** for hazardous activities such as electrical isolation, hot work, confined spaces and lifting, with clear isolation and handback procedures.
- **Safety case or equivalent** where regulation requires it, for example on major hazard sites.
- **Contractor HSE management:** prequalification, site inductions, supervision ratios and joint inspections.
- **Environmental controls:** ecology protection, pollution prevention, waste and the conditions attached to consents.
- **Legal duties by jurisdiction.** In Great Britain, for example, the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 place duties on clients, designers and contractors on construction projects, including energy construction.

#### Worked example: TRIR and LTIF
Safety performance is compared using rates per hours worked so that projects of different sizes can be compared. Two common measures are the total recordable incident rate (TRIR), usually calculated per 200,000 hours (roughly 100 full-time workers for a year), and the lost time injury frequency (LTIF), usually calculated per 1,000,000 hours. Check which basis your organisation and clients use.
| Input or measure | Value | Calculation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hours worked to date | 1,200,000 | From contractor timesheets |
| Recordable incidents | 3 | Incident log |
| Lost time injuries | 1 | Incident log |
| TRIR | 0.50 | 3 × 200,000 ÷ 1,200,000 |
| LTIF | 0.83 | 1 × 1,000,000 ÷ 1,200,000 |
Lagging rates show what has already happened. Balance them with leading indicators such as safety observations, inspections completed, near misses reported and permit-to-work audits.

### Permits, grid connection and stakeholders
Treat consents and grid works as deliverables with owners and dates, tracked on the critical path. A consents register is the simplest control.
| Consent or agreement | Authority or counterparty | Status | Critical date | Owner | Linked conditions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Planning consent | Planning authority | Granted with conditions | Before construction start | Permitting lead | Traffic plan, ecology plan, drainage |
| Grid connection agreement | Network operator | Signed | Energisation date | Grid lead | Reinforcement works, compliance tests |
| Environmental permit or licence | Environmental regulator | Application submitted | Before relevant works | HSE manager | Monitoring and reporting |
| Land and access rights | Landowners | Options exercised | Before mobilisation | Land manager | Reinstatement obligations |
| Highway approvals | Highway authority | In discussion | Abnormal load deliveries | Construction manager | Delivery windows |
Community and stakeholder engagement starts in development and continues through construction. Map stakeholders by interest and influence, keep a commitments register (promises made in consultation) and assign each commitment an owner.

### Energy project risk management
Maintain one live [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) for the owner, with contractor risks visible, and review it at every gate and monthly in execution. The rows below are typical examples rather than a complete list; a [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) gives you the columns.
| Risk | Cause | Effect | Response | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Grid connection later than plan | Network reinforcement works delayed | Revenue delayed; liquidated damages exposure | Early engagement, monthly interface meetings, schedule float before COD | Grid lead |
| Transformer delivery late | Long manufacturing lead times | Energisation slips | Order early, factory progress inspections, expediting | Procurement lead |
| Unexpected ground conditions | Limited site investigation | Piling or foundation redesign; cost increase | Adequate ground investigation in FEED; allowance in contingency | Engineering manager |
| Weather downtime | Wind or sea state beyond lifting limits | Installation delay | Seasonal planning, weather allowances in schedule | Construction manager |
| Consent conditions not discharged | Late submissions to the authority | Works cannot start | Conditions tracker with submission dates | Permitting lead |
| Interface gaps between packages | Multi-contract scope boundaries unclear | Disputes, rework and delay | Interface register; clear scope splits | Project director |
| Revenue or price change | Market or offtake terms move before FID | Business case weakens | Sensitivity analysis; hedging or PPA strategy | Commercial lead |

### Commissioning and handover
Commissioning proves the asset works safely and as designed. Plan it from FEED, not from the end of construction.
1. **Mechanical completion.** Systems are installed and checked against drawings; walkdowns produce a punch list split by priority.
2. **Pre-commissioning.** Inspections and tests without energy or process fluids: cable tests, insulation resistance, loop checks.
3. **Commissioning.** Systems are energised or started one by one under permit-to-work control and tested against design.
4. **Grid energisation and compliance testing.** Coordinated with the network operator to show the plant meets connection requirements.
5. **Performance and reliability tests.** Output, efficiency or availability is measured against contract guarantees.
6. **Commercial operation date (COD) and takeover.** The owner accepts the asset; warranties and the defects period start.
7. **Handover and close-out.** As-built drawings, operating manuals, spares, training records and the handover dossier go to operations; lessons are captured as part of [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/).
Tip
Track commissioning by system, not by area. A system completion dashboard (systems mechanically complete, pre-commissioned, commissioned and handed over) shows readiness far better than percentage of construction complete.

### Methodologies that fit
| Approach | Use in energy |
| --- | --- |
| Stage-gate | Investment decisions at each gate; standard for capital projects |
| Waterfall and critical path scheduling | Engineering, procurement and construction with long-lead equipment |
| Earned value management | Cost and schedule control on large contracts |
| Lean construction and workface planning | Field productivity and reducing waiting time |
| Monte Carlo risk analysis | Schedule and cost confidence levels for investment decisions |
| Agile | Digital, software, trading, metering and smart-grid projects rather than physical construction |

### Essential documents and templates
- **Business case and feasibility:** [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/).
- **Project charter or execution plan:** [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/), expanded into a project execution plan for large projects.
- **Scope and WBS:** [work breakdown structure template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/).
- **Schedule:** Gantt chart and critical path schedules; large projects use specialist scheduling tools.
- **Cost estimate and budget:** [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/), stating the estimate class.
- **Risk register:** [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) covering technical, permitting, market and HSE risks.
- **Procurement:** [RFQ template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/rfq-template/) for equipment and services.
- **Changes:** [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) for formal management of change.
- **Industry-specific documents:** consents register, interface register, safety case or HSE plan, commissioning plan and handover dossier.

### KPIs for energy project management
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TRIR and LTIF | Safety performance per hours worked | First item on most project reports |
| Leading HSE indicators | Observations, inspections, near misses reported | Preventing incidents before they happen |
| Cost performance index (CPI) | Value of work done against cost | Cost control |
| Schedule performance and critical path float | Progress against baseline and remaining float | Forecasting key dates such as COD |
| Estimate at completion and contingency drawdown | Forecast final cost and contingency used | Board and lender reporting |
| Consents and conditions status | Consents and conditions discharged against plan | Development and pre-construction control |
| Commissioning progress by system | Systems tested and handed over | Readiness for operation |
| Availability and capacity factor | Asset performance once operating | Proving the business case |

### Common mistakes and how to avoid them
| Mistake | What happens | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sanctioning before the front end is complete | Scope grows in construction; overruns | Hold FID until FEED deliverables meet the gate criteria |
| Treating early estimates as budgets | Credibility lost when costs rise | State the estimate class and present ranges until FID |
| Permits and grid managed outside the schedule | Surprise delays to start or energisation | Logic-link consents, conditions and grid works into the critical path |
| Ordering long-lead equipment too late | Energisation slips by months | Identify long-lead items in FEED; consider early orders |
| Weak interface management | Disputes and rework between packages | Interface register with owners and regular interface meetings |
| Reporting progress by percentage built | Late discovery that systems are not ready | System-based commissioning tracking from mid-construction |
| Relying on lagging safety data | Problems found after someone is hurt | Track leading indicators and act on near misses |

### Software for energy projects
Energy projects run on a stack of tools rather than one system.
| Need | Typical tool type |
| --- | --- |
| Large critical-path schedules | Enterprise scheduling software |
| Cost control, earned value and change | Project controls or cost management systems |
| Engineering documents and drawings | Document control and engineering data management |
| Permits, incidents and inspections | HSE management systems |
| Owner's team coordination, development portfolio, permitting workflows | Work management platform |
A work management platform such as [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, fits well for the owner's team: tracking a portfolio of development sites, consents and conditions workflows, document reviews, cross-functional tasks and dashboards for leadership, alongside the specialist engineering and scheduling tools. Spreadsheet-style platforms such as Smartsheet are also popular with developers and contractors for trackers and registers.

### Skills and certifications
Energy project managers need a blend of commercial and contract knowledge, enough engineering understanding to challenge designs, strong HSE leadership and project controls skills. Many come from engineering, construction or project controls backgrounds; our guides to [engineering project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/engineering-project-management/) and [infrastructure project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/infrastructure-project-management/) cover adjacent sectors.
- **Project management:** the [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) is widely recognised by owners and contractors.
- **Cost and controls:** AACE International offers certifications such as the Certified Cost Professional (CCP) and Certified Estimating Professional (CEP).
- **Safety:** industry or national safety qualifications and site-specific training are commonly expected, for example offshore survival and electrical safety training where relevant.
- **Sector knowledge:** grid codes, consenting processes and the technology you are delivering matter as much as general methods.
Start with the method, then add sector depth: master stage-gates, estimating classes, earned value and commissioning, and the rest of the energy toolkit builds on them.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is energy project management?**
It is planning and delivering projects that generate, transmit or store energy, from wind, solar and battery storage to power plants, grid infrastructure and oil and gas facilities, through investment gates, construction and commissioning.

**Q: What does an energy project manager do?**
They lead the project through its gates: coordinating development or design, contracts, budget, schedule, HSE, permits and stakeholders, and reporting progress and forecasts to the owner, board and lenders.

**Q: What are the phases of an energy project?**
Commonly Appraise, Select, Define, Execute, Commission and Operate. Renewable developers describe them as origination, development, financing, construction, commissioning and operation.

**Q: What is FEED in energy project management?**
Front-end engineering design: early engineering that defines the facility well enough to produce a reliable estimate and schedule, tender the main contracts and support the investment decision.

**Q: What is FID?**
The final investment decision: the gate at which the owner, and lenders for project-financed projects, commit the capital to build. It usually follows FEED or development.

**Q: What is the difference between EPC and EPCM?**
Under EPC one contractor designs, procures and builds, usually for a fixed price, and carries most delivery risk. Under EPCM a firm manages the work for the owner, who holds the contracts and most of the risk.

**Q: What is commissioning?**
The staged testing that proves an energy asset is installed correctly and works safely as designed, from pre-commissioning checks to energisation and performance tests, before takeover and commercial operation.

**Q: What do P50 and P90 mean?**
For cost or schedule, P90 is the value with a 90% chance of not being exceeded. For energy yield, P90 is the annual output expected to be exceeded in 90% of years.

**Q: How long does a renewable energy project take?**
It varies by country, size and grid conditions. Development (land, permits, grid and financing) commonly takes longer than construction, so plan development as carefully as the build.

**Q: How does renewable energy project management differ from oil and gas?**
Renewables projects are usually smaller and quicker to build and are often driven by permitting, grid connection and financing. Oil and gas projects are larger, more engineering-heavy and carry subsurface uncertainty.

**Q: Which KPIs matter in energy project management?**
Safety rates such as TRIR and LTIF, leading HSE indicators, CPI, schedule float, estimate at completion, consents status, commissioning progress and, once operating, availability.

**Q: Is Agile used in energy project management?**
Mainly for digital, software, trading and smart-grid work. Physical construction uses stage-gates, critical path scheduling and earned value, sometimes with Lean practices on site.

**Q: What certifications help in energy project management?**
The PMP is widely recognised, AACE certifications such as CCP suit cost and controls roles, and industry safety training is commonly expected.

# Engineering Project Management: Phases, Roles and Methods

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/engineering-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Engineering project management explained: phases and design reviews, roles, methods, a step-by-step process, worked examples, KPIs and software.


## Engineering Project Management: Phases, Roles and Methods
Engineering project management is the planning and control of projects whose main output is an engineered product, system or facility, taking it from requirements through design, build, verification and handover. It combines ordinary project control of scope, time, cost and risk with technical control: requirements traceability, design reviews, configuration and change control, and testing. This guide explains the phases and gates, a step-by-step process, worked examples, roles, methods, KPIs and tools.
- Published 29 August 2026
- Last updated 17 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Engineering project management pairs project control (scope, schedule, cost, risk) with technical control (requirements, design reviews, configuration and verification).
- Design reviews and gates are the main decision points; change becomes much more expensive after design freeze.
- Trace every requirement to a design element and a test, so you always know what is proven and what is not.
- Plan for test failures and long-lead parts explicitly; they decide the end date more often than design tasks do.
- Hybrid approaches work best: iterate on software and early prototypes inside a gated plan for hardware.
- Keep design data in CAD and PLM, and use a work management platform such as Wrike for schedules, resources and approvals.

### What is engineering project management?
**Engineering project management** is the discipline of planning, organising and controlling a project that designs and delivers an engineered output, such as a machine, a product, a control system or a plant. It covers the usual project concerns of scope, schedule, cost, risk and people, plus the technical controls that prove the design works: requirements, design reviews, configuration management and verification.
The work is usually led by a project manager working alongside a chief or lead engineer. The project manager owns the plan, budget and commitments; the lead engineer owns the technical solution.

#### Types of engineering projects
| Project type | Typical output | What usually drives the plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New product development | A product ready for manufacture | Prototype cycles, tooling lead times, certification |
| Machinery and automation | A special-purpose machine, test rig or production line | Long-lead components, factory and site acceptance tests |
| Aerospace and defence systems | A system or subsystem meeting a specification | Formal design reviews, qualification testing, configuration control |
| Process plant and capital projects | A plant, skid or facility upgrade | Engineering deliverables, procurement, construction and commissioning |
| Civil and structural engineering | Bridges, structures, foundations | Design checks, approvals and site constraints |
Manufacturing-led projects such as line changes and new product introduction are covered in our guide to [manufacturing project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/manufacturing-project-management/).

### Engineering project management vs engineering management
The two terms are often confused. Engineering management is the ongoing leadership of an engineering function; engineering project management is the delivery of a specific, time-bound project.
|  | Engineering project management | Engineering management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | Deliver one project to scope, time, cost and quality | Run and develop an engineering team or department |
| Time horizon | Defined start and end | Ongoing |
| Typical decisions | Plan, budget, risks, suppliers, change, acceptance | Hiring, skills, standards, tools, capacity across projects |
| Success measured by | Project objectives met and the output accepted | Team capability, quality and throughput over time |
| Typical title | Engineering project manager, technical project manager | Engineering manager, head of engineering |
In smaller firms one person often does both. If you are making that move from a technical role, our guide to the [technical project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/technical-project-manager/) role covers the skills involved.

### What makes engineering projects different
In engineering projects the hardest risks are usually technical. A design that cannot be manufactured, a component that fails qualification or a misunderstood requirement can cost far more than a late task. That changes how you plan and control the work.
- **Requirements must be traceable.** Every requirement should link to a design element and to a test that proves it.
- **Change is expensive late.** Prototypes, tooling, certification and procurement commitments make late design changes costly, so design freezes matter.
- **Safety and standards.** Many products must meet regulatory or industry standards for areas such as pressure equipment, machinery safety, aerospace, automotive or medical devices.
- **Multiple disciplines.** Mechanical, electrical, software, civil and process engineers must integrate their work through clearly defined interfaces.
- **Technology maturity.** New technology carries uncertainty that no amount of scheduling removes.
- **Long-lead procurement.** Castings, motors, specialist electronics and certified materials can take months to arrive and often sit on the critical path.
- **Test and rework cycles.** New designs rarely pass every test first time, and retest loops are real work that needs to be in the plan.

#### Technology readiness levels (TRLs)
Many engineering organisations use **technology readiness levels**, a nine-point scale developed by NASA, to judge how mature a technology is. NASA describes TRL 1 as basic research, TRL 6 as a fully functional prototype or representative model, and TRL 9 as technology proven in operation. You can use the scale to decide how much schedule and cost risk to carry:
| TRL band | What it means | Planning implication (our advice) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TRL 1–3 | Principles and proof of concept | Treat as research; fund in short, capped stages rather than a fixed delivery plan |
| TRL 4–6 | Components and prototypes tested in increasingly realistic conditions | Plan explicit prototype and test iterations with go/no-go points |
| TRL 7–9 | Demonstrated, qualified and proven in operation | Suitable for a committed delivery schedule with normal contingency |
Tip
If a project needs a technology below about TRL 6 to meet its specification, raise it as a top risk at the first gate and agree a fallback design. Committing to a fixed delivery date on immature technology is one of the most common causes of engineering overruns.

### Engineering project phases and design reviews
Life cycle names vary by sector, but most engineering projects follow the same logic: decide, define, design, build, prove and hand over. Each phase ends with a review where the sponsor and technical authority decide whether the project is ready to move on.
| Phase | What happens | Typical gate or review |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Concept and feasibility | Define the need, explore options, assess technical and commercial feasibility | Concept review / gate 1 |
| 2. Requirements definition | Capture stakeholder needs and turn them into verifiable system requirements | System requirements review (SRR) |
| 3. Preliminary design | System architecture, major trade-offs, early analysis, long-lead item identification | Preliminary design review (PDR) |
| 4. Detailed design | Full models, drawings, calculations, software design and specifications | Critical design review (CDR) and design freeze |
| 5. Build or fabrication | Procure parts, manufacture prototypes or construct the facility | Test readiness or production readiness review |
| 6. Integration, verification and validation | Test subsystems and the whole system against requirements and user needs | Factory or site acceptance tests, qualification |
| 7. Handover and support | Documentation, training, commissioning and transfer to operations or production | Final acceptance and project closure |
The international standard ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 (current edition 2023) describes system life cycle processes in more detail and is a useful reference if your organisation is formalising its own life cycle.

#### PDR, CDR and design freeze
The **preliminary design review (PDR)** checks that the chosen architecture can meet the requirements within cost and schedule, and that the risks are understood. The **critical design review (CDR)** checks that the detailed design is complete enough to build and test. Passing CDR usually triggers a **design freeze**: from then on, every change goes through formal engineering change control because it can affect parts already ordered, tooling and test plans.

#### The V-model
The V-model, widely used in systems engineering, pairs each level of design on the left of the V with a matching level of testing on the right. It is a simple way to make sure verification is planned at the same time as design, not afterwards.
| Left side: define and design | Right side: matching verification |
| --- | --- |
| User needs and concept of operations | Validation and user acceptance |
| System requirements | System verification tests |
| Subsystem design | Subsystem integration tests |
| Component design | Component and unit tests |

### How to manage an engineering project step by step
The steps below follow a typical engineering project from need to closure. Scale the formality to the size and risk of the project.
1. **Clarify the need and success criteria.** Agree the problem, the performance targets, the budget envelope and the date the output is needed. Record them in a [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/).
2. **Appoint the project manager and technical authority.** Name one person accountable for delivery and one for the technical solution, and agree how they make joint decisions.
3. **Assess feasibility and technology maturity.** Compare options, check TRLs and identify the riskiest assumptions to test first.
4. **Write verifiable requirements.** Each requirement should be measurable and have a verification method (test, analysis, inspection or demonstration). A [business requirements document template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/) is a good starting structure; see our guide to [project requirements](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-requirements/).
5. **Build the product-based work breakdown structure.** Break the system into subsystems and deliverables, then add the work to design, buy, build and test each one using a [WBS template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/).
6. **Identify long-lead items and interfaces.** List every part with a long lead time and every interface between disciplines or suppliers, each with an owner.
7. **Estimate with ranges.** Estimate effort by discipline and add allowances for prototype iterations and retests; record assumptions in a [project cost estimate](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/).
8. **Build an integrated schedule.** Link design, procurement, build and test activities, find the critical path and set a baseline. A [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) or [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) works for smaller projects.
9. **Set up risk, change and configuration control.** Open a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/), agree a change board and decide how drawings and part numbers are released and versioned.
10. **Run design reviews as real gates.** Circulate review packs in advance, record actions, and only pass the gate when the entry criteria are met.
11. **Control delivery each period.** Track progress with earned value or milestone completion, review risks, and process engineering changes through the [change request](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) route.
12. **Verify, validate and hand over.** Run the test plan, close non-conformances, complete documentation and training, and obtain formal acceptance.
13. **Close and learn.** Archive the configuration baseline, release the team and capture [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) for the next project.

### Worked example: an automated test rig project
To make the techniques concrete, follow a single example. An engineering firm is designing and building an automated test rig for a customer's electric motors. It has a budget at completion of **£600,000**, a 12-month schedule, and mechanical, electrical and software workstreams. All figures are illustrative.

#### Step 1: build a requirements traceability matrix
The team writes each requirement so it can be verified, then links it to the design element that satisfies it and the test that proves it. An extract:
| Req ID | Requirement | Design element | Verification | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-001 | Rig shall test motors up to 50 kg | Frame drawing TR-100; lifting fixture TR-140 | Load test VT-07 | Passed |
| R-002 | Rig shall measure torque to ±0.5% | Torque transducer spec E-220; calibration procedure | Calibration test VT-12 | Open |
| R-003 | Guarding shall prevent access while the motor runs | Interlocked guard TR-300; safety PLC logic SW-40 | Interlock test VT-15 | Failed, retest planned |
| R-004 | Test cycle shall complete in under 6 minutes | Test sequence software SW-10 | Timed demonstration VT-20 | Not started |
At any review, the matrix shows how many requirements are proven, which are at risk and which have no test yet. A requirement with no verification method is a gap you want to find at PDR, not at acceptance.

#### Step 2: measure progress with earned value
At the end of month 6, the plan said half the work would be done. The project controls figures are:
| Measure | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Budget at completion (BAC) | £600,000 | Total approved budget |
| Planned value (PV) | £300,000 | Budgeted cost of the work scheduled to date |
| Earned value (EV) | £255,000 | Budgeted cost of the work actually completed |
| Actual cost (AC) | £290,000 | What the completed work actually cost |
| Cost variance (EV − AC) | −£35,000 | Over budget for the work done |
| Schedule variance (EV − PV) | −£45,000 | Behind plan |
| Cost performance index (EV ÷ AC) | 0.88 | £0.88 of planned work for every £1 spent |
| Schedule performance index (EV ÷ PV) | 0.85 | Progressing at 85% of the planned rate |
If cost performance stays at this level, the **estimate at completion** is BAC ÷ CPI = £600,000 ÷ 0.879 ≈ **£682,000**. If both cost and schedule pressure persist, a more cautious forecast is AC + (BAC − EV) ÷ (CPI × SPI) = £290,000 + £345,000 ÷ 0.747 ≈ **£752,000**. To finish on the original budget, the **to-complete performance index** would need to be (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) = £345,000 ÷ £310,000 ≈ **1.11**, meaning every remaining pound must buy £1.11 of work. That is unlikely without changing scope or approach, so the project manager takes the forecast to the sponsor now rather than hoping to recover.

#### Step 3: assess an engineering change
After the critical design review, the customer asks for the rig to handle motors up to 65 kg instead of 50 kg. Before anyone agrees, the team assesses the impact across every discipline:
| Area | Impact | Extra cost | Schedule effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanical | Stiffen frame, redesign lifting fixture, re-issue 9 drawings | £14,000 | +3 weeks of design |
| Electrical | Larger drive and cabling; drive is a long-lead item | £9,500 | +6 weeks lead time (critical path) |
| Software | Update load limits, safety logic and test sequences | £4,000 | +1 week, runs in parallel |
| Verification | Repeat load and interlock tests at the new rating | £3,500 | +1 week |
| Documentation | Update risk assessment, manuals and traceability matrix | £1,500 | Runs in parallel |
| **Total** |  | **£32,500** | **About +7 weeks to completion** |
The change board presents three options to the customer: accept the change with the extra cost and date; defer it to a later upgrade; or approve an early order for the larger drive while the design work is confirmed, which cuts about three weeks of the delay for a small cost at risk. The decision, whichever it is, is recorded and the baseline updated.

#### Step 4: plan for test failures and retests
The verification plan has 40 tests. Based on its previous rigs, the team assumes about four in five will pass first time, so it expects around 8 failures. Each failure typically needs about 3 days of diagnosis and rework and 1 day of retest on the rig. Rework can run in parallel with other tests, but rig time cannot, so the plan adds roughly 8 days of rig time plus a small buffer at the end of the test phase instead of assuming every test passes. Tracking the actual first-time pass rate as testing proceeds shows quickly whether that allowance is enough.

### Key roles in an engineering project
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Project sponsor | Owns the business case, approves gate decisions and resolves escalations |
| Engineering project manager | Plans and controls scope, schedule, cost, risk, suppliers and reporting |
| Chief or lead engineer (technical authority) | Owns the technical solution and design decisions |
| Systems engineer | Manages requirements, interfaces and the verification approach across disciplines |
| Discipline engineers | Design and analyse in mechanical, electrical, software, civil or process areas |
| Quality and test engineers | Plan inspections and tests, manage non-conformances and test records |
| Procurement and supply chain | Source components, expedite long-lead items, manage supplier quality |
| Configuration manager | Controls drawings, part numbers, released versions and change records |
| Customer or end user | Agrees requirements and witnesses acceptance tests |
Day to day, the engineering project manager maintains the schedule and forecasts, chairs progress, risk and change meetings, balances engineers' time across projects, chases long-lead suppliers and keeps the customer informed, trading off performance, cost and time with the lead engineer when problems arise.

### Methodologies for engineering projects
There is no single best method. Choose based on how well the requirements are understood, how mature the technology is and how much of the product is software.
| Approach | Best for | How it works in engineering |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage-gate | Product development and capital projects | Go, hold or stop decisions at each gate control investment and risk |
| V-model and systems engineering | Complex and safety-critical systems | Each design level has a matching test level, planned together |
| Waterfall | Facilities and well-understood designs | Sequential phases with formal sign-offs |
| Agile and hybrid | Software-heavy products and early prototyping | Short iterations inside a gated plan; see [iterative and incremental development](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/iterative-and-incremental-development/) |
| [Critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) | Any project with many dependencies | Finds the longest chain of dependent work and the float on everything else |
| Critical chain | Multi-project environments with shared specialists | Buffers protect the end date rather than each task |

#### Combining Agile with gates for hardware
Agile works well for software and early concept work, where feedback is fast and changes are cheap. Hardware still needs gates for long-lead parts, tooling and certification. A practical hybrid is to keep the stage-gate plan and design reviews for the system, run the software team in sprints, and align a few integration points where each hardware build meets a defined software release. Plan both rhythms explicitly rather than letting one team wait on the other.

### Essential documents and templates
| Document | Purpose | Template |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project charter | Authorises the project and names the sponsor, objectives and constraints | [Project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) |
| Requirements specification | Defines what the system must do and how each requirement will be verified | [Business requirements document template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/) |
| Work breakdown structure | Breaks the system into deliverables and work packages | [Work breakdown structure template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) |
| Integrated schedule | Design, procurement, build and test activities with dependencies | [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/), [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) |
| Risk register | Technical, supply and schedule risks with owners and actions | [Risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) |
| Engineering change requests | Proposes, assesses and approves design changes | [Change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) |
| Cost estimate | Labour, materials, tooling and test costs | [Project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) |
| Roles and responsibilities | Who designs, reviews and approves each deliverable | [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) |
Engineering teams also keep a requirements traceability matrix, an interface control document, design review minutes, failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) records, test plans and reports, and a drawing or document register. These usually live in engineering systems rather than the project plan, so link to them rather than copying them.

### KPIs for engineering project management
Pick a small set that covers both project and technical health, and review them every period.
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cost and schedule performance indices | Value of work done against cost and plan | Forecasting outturn cost and completion date |
| Milestones achieved on time | Gate reviews and key deliverables hit on the baseline date | Sponsor reporting |
| Requirements verified | Share of requirements with passed verification | Readiness for acceptance |
| Engineering change rate | Change requests raised after design freeze | Design stability |
| Open design review actions | Actions still unresolved from PDR or CDR | Gate readiness |
| Drawings released on time | Drawings and specifications issued by the planned date | Design progress and supplier readiness |
| First-time test pass rate | Tests passed at the first attempt | Design maturity and retest planning |
| Non-conformances | Parts or work that failed inspection | Supplier and build quality |

### Common challenges and how to fix them
| Challenge | Why it happens | How to manage it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements creep | Customers refine needs as they see the design | Baseline requirements at SRR and route every change through a change board |
| Interfaces between disciplines | Mechanical, electrical and software teams work to different assumptions | Interface control document, named interface owners and regular integration meetings |
| Optimistic test schedules | Plans assume every test passes first time | Plan explicit retest allowance based on past first-time pass rates |
| Long-lead and sole-source parts | Specialist components with long or uncertain lead times | Identify them at PDR, order early where safe, and log them in the risk register |
| Engineers pulled across projects | Specialists shared by several projects | Agree priorities at portfolio level and use [resource levelling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) |
| Immature technology | Committing to a design that has not been proven | Check TRLs at the first gate and keep a fallback option |

### Common mistakes in engineering project management
- **Treating design reviews as presentations.** A review that never says no is not a gate. Set entry criteria and record actions.
- **Writing requirements that cannot be tested.** Words such as 'robust' or 'user-friendly' need measurable criteria.
- **Freezing the design on paper only.** If changes after CDR do not go through change control, the freeze means nothing.
- **Leaving procurement until the design is complete.** Long-lead items need to be identified and, where possible, ordered earlier.
- **Reporting percent complete by feel.** Use measurable progress such as drawings released, tests passed or earned value.

### Software for engineering project management
Engineering organisations run several systems, each holding part of the picture. The project management platform should coordinate work and decisions, not duplicate engineering data.
| Tool type | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| CAD and simulation | Creating and analysing the design |
| Product lifecycle management (PLM) | Parts, bills of materials, released drawings and engineering change records |
| Requirements management | Requirements, traceability and verification status on complex systems |
| Enterprise resource planning (ERP) | Purchasing, inventory and manufacturing orders |
| Work and project management platform | Integrated schedules, resources across projects, approvals, risks, dashboards and reporting |
When choosing the project platform, look for dependencies and critical path, baselines, workload and resource management across projects, approval workflows, custom fields for items such as part or drawing numbers, and dashboards for sponsors. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) fits this coordination role well and leads [our tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/), with Gantt charts, workload views and cross-project portfolio reporting. Keep design data in your PLM system and link to it from tasks rather than duplicating it.

### Skills, qualifications and career path
Most engineering project managers start as engineers and move into project roles by leading work packages, then whole projects. The skills that matter most are a mix of technical and management ability.
- **Technical credibility** in at least one discipline, so you can follow design trade-offs and challenge estimates.
- **Planning and project controls:** scheduling, estimating, earned value and risk analysis.
- **Commercial awareness:** contracts, supplier management and change pricing.
- **Communication and negotiation** with customers, suppliers and engineers.
- **Quality and safety awareness** relevant to your sector's standards.

#### Useful qualifications
- Professional engineering registration, such as Chartered Engineer (CEng) through the Engineering Council in the UK or a Professional Engineer (PE) licence in the US.
- Systems engineering certification from INCOSE, which offers an entry-level ASEP, the CSEP for experienced practitioners and the ESEP at expert level.
- Project management certification such as the [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) or PRINCE2.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is engineering project management?**
Engineering project management is the planning and control of projects that design and deliver an engineered product, system or facility. It combines scope, schedule, cost and risk control with technical control of requirements, design reviews, configuration and testing.

**Q: What does an engineering project manager do?**
They plan and control the project: building the schedule and budget, managing risks, suppliers and change, running progress and design review meetings, balancing engineers' time and reporting to the sponsor and customer, working closely with the lead engineer who owns the technical solution.

**Q: What is the difference between engineering management and engineering project management?**
Engineering management is the ongoing leadership of an engineering team or function. Engineering project management delivers a specific, time-bound project to agreed scope, time, cost and quality.

**Q: Do you need an engineering degree to be an engineering project manager?**
Not always, but on technically complex projects most employers expect an engineering degree or equivalent experience, because the role involves judging design trade-offs and technical risk.

**Q: What are the phases of an engineering project?**
Typically concept and feasibility, requirements definition, preliminary design, detailed design, build or fabrication, integration and verification, and handover. Each ends with a review or gate.

**Q: What methodology is best for engineering projects?**
It depends on the project. Stage-gate and the V-model suit hardware and safety-critical systems, Waterfall suits well-understood designs, and Agile suits software and early prototyping. Many teams use a hybrid of gates for hardware and sprints for software.

**Q: What is a design freeze?**
A design freeze is the point, usually after the critical design review, after which the design is baselined and any change must go through formal engineering change control because it can affect parts, tooling and tests.

**Q: What is the difference between PDR and CDR?**
A preliminary design review (PDR) checks that the chosen architecture can meet the requirements and that the risks are understood. A critical design review (CDR) checks that the detailed design is complete enough to build and test.

**Q: What is a requirements traceability matrix?**
It is a table linking each requirement to the design elements that satisfy it and the tests that verify it, with the current status. It shows what has been proven and highlights requirements without a test.

**Q: What are technology readiness levels?**
Technology readiness levels are a nine-point scale, developed by NASA, for judging how mature a technology is, from basic research at TRL 1 to proven operation at TRL 9. Low TRLs signal high schedule and cost risk.

**Q: What KPIs should engineering project managers track?**
Useful KPIs include cost and schedule performance indices, milestones on time, requirements verified, engineering change rate after design freeze, open design review actions, drawings released on time, first-time test pass rate and non-conformances.

**Q: What software do engineering project managers use?**
CAD and simulation tools for design, PLM for parts and change records, requirements tools on complex systems, ERP for purchasing, and a work management platform such as Wrike for schedules, resources, approvals and reporting.
