# Enterprise Project Management (EPM): Guide and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/enterprise-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Enterprise project management (EPM) explained: EPMO vs PMO, the portfolio life cycle, prioritisation and capacity examples, governance, KPIs and software.


## Enterprise Project Management (EPM): Guide and Examples
Enterprise project management (EPM) is the practice of managing all of an organisation's projects as one coordinated system, with shared governance, standard methods, common tools and a single view of the portfolio and the people who deliver it. It moves the question from "is this project on track?" to "are we running the right projects, and do we have the capacity to finish them?" This guide explains how EPM works, how it differs from a PMO and portfolio management, and how to prioritise, resource, govern and measure projects at enterprise scale, with worked examples.
- Published 27 August 2026
- Last updated 16 October 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Enterprise project management treats every project as part of one portfolio with shared governance, standards, data and tools.
- An enterprise PMO (EPMO) is strategic and organisation-wide; a departmental PMO is mainly tactical and supports delivery.
- Prioritise with a transparent scoring model, then check capacity before approving anything: capacity is the real constraint.
- Tier your governance so small projects stay light and large, risky investments get stage gates and assurance.
- Start simple (inventory, intake, standard status), use one platform as the source of truth, and add resource and benefits management in stages.

### What is enterprise project management?
**Enterprise project management (EPM)** is an organisation-wide approach that selects, prioritises, resources, governs and reports on all projects and programmes as one system. It combines portfolio decisions, standard project methods, enterprise resource management and consistent reporting so that leaders can fund the work that best supports strategy and stop work that no longer does.
Ordinary [project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) asks how to deliver one project well. EPM sits a level above and answers three questions continuously:
1. **Are we doing the right projects?** Every proposal is judged against strategy, value and risk using the same criteria.
2. **Can we deliver them?** Demand for people, skills and money is compared with real capacity before work starts.
3. **Are they delivering value?** Health, spend and benefits are reported the same way across the portfolio, so problems surface early.
EPM overlaps with portfolio and programme management. For how the three levels fit together, see our guide to [program vs project vs portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/program-vs-project-vs-portfolio-management/).

### EPM vs traditional project management vs portfolio management
The terms are often used loosely. This comparison shows where each one focuses.
|  | Project management | Project portfolio management (PPM) | Enterprise project management (EPM) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | One project | A set of projects and programmes | All projects, programmes and portfolios across the organisation |
| Main question | Are we delivering this project on time, on budget and to scope? | Which projects should we fund and in what order? | How do we select, resource, govern and deliver all projects consistently? |
| Time horizon | The project's life | Planning cycles (quarterly or annual) | Continuous |
| Typical owner | Project manager | Portfolio manager or portfolio board | Enterprise PMO and executive team |
| Key outputs | Deliverables, status reports | Prioritised portfolio, funding decisions | Standards, governance, enterprise resource view, portfolio reporting, benefits tracking |
In practice, EPM includes portfolio management and adds the standards, tools, resource management and capability building that make portfolio decisions possible. Many organisations use "EPM" and "PPM" interchangeably; what matters is that someone owns both the decisions and the system behind them.

### EPMO vs PMO: what is the difference?
Enterprise project management is usually run by an **enterprise project management office (EPMO)**. A departmental [project management office (PMO)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) often already exists in IT, engineering or change functions. The two work together, but their remit differs.
|  | Departmental PMO | Enterprise PMO (EPMO) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | One business unit or function | The whole organisation |
| Focus | Tactical: delivery support, methods, reporting | Strategic: portfolio selection, capacity, governance, benefits |
| Reports to | Head of the function (for example the CIO) | Executive team, COO, CFO or a transformation director |
| Typical services | Templates, schedules, status reports, project support | Intake and prioritisation, portfolio board, enterprise resource view, standards, capability building |
| Success looks like | Projects in the function delivered well | The organisation funds the right work and finishes it |
Smaller organisations often have one PMO doing both jobs. As the number of projects and departments grows, the strategic role usually separates into an EPMO, with departmental PMOs or Agile PMOs reporting into it.

### Core elements of an EPM system
Different sources list the components differently; some, for example, describe seven elements drawn from a PMI paper (risk analysis, structured estimating, project reviews, coaching, escalated issue management, time accounting and an information system). In our experience a working EPM system needs the following nine building blocks.
| Element | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Governance | Who approves what, at which thresholds, and how decisions are escalated; see [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) |
| Standard life cycle | Common phases and stage gates so projects can be compared |
| Demand intake | One front door for new ideas and requests, with a standard form and rough sizing |
| Prioritisation | A transparent scoring model and a regular portfolio decision forum |
| Enterprise resource management | A view of demand and capacity by role and skill; see [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) |
| Standard reporting | The same health indicators and definitions everywhere, rolled up automatically |
| Risk and issue escalation | Shared risk scales and escalation routes, including cross-project dependencies |
| Benefits management | Named benefit owners and measurement after delivery |
| Capability and tools | Training, coaching, templates and one platform that acts as the source of truth |

### The enterprise project management life cycle
EPM adds a portfolio life cycle around the life cycle of each individual project. The portfolio cycle repeats, usually quarterly, while each project moves through its own phases.
| Phase | What happens | Who decides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Strategy and planning | Strategic objectives and investment themes set; annual or quarterly budget envelopes agreed | Executive team |
| 2. Demand intake | Ideas and requests captured through a standard form with rough sizing | PMO triage |
| 3. Evaluation and prioritisation | Business cases scored on value, risk, alignment and resource need | Portfolio board or investment committee |
| 4. Approval and resourcing | Selected projects funded and staffed; capacity checked against other commitments | Portfolio board, resource managers |
| 5. Delivery and stage gates | Projects run with their chosen method and report through standard dashboards; gates check continued viability | Project boards and EPMO |
| 6. Portfolio monitoring and rebalancing | Regular reviews of health, spend and capacity; projects accelerated, paused or stopped | Portfolio board |
| 7. Closure and benefits tracking | Projects closed, benefits measured, lessons fed back into standards | Benefit owners and EPMO |

#### How the portfolio cycle connects to each project
Phases 2 to 4 happen before a project formally starts: they produce the approved project charter and the resources to deliver it. Phase 5 is where the project's own life cycle runs, whether that is a Waterfall plan, Scrum sprints or a hybrid. Stage gates link the two: at each gate the project reports in a standard format and the portfolio board decides whether to continue, change or stop. Phase 7 closes the loop, because benefits are often realised months after the project team has disbanded.
Agile organisations run a similar cycle with lean portfolio practices, funding value streams rather than individual projects.

### How to prioritise projects across the enterprise
Prioritisation is the most valuable decision in EPM, and the one most often made by whoever argues loudest. A simple, published scoring model makes it fairer and faster.
1. **Separate mandatory work.** Regulatory, legal and safety projects are not optional; ring-fence their capacity first.
2. **Agree four to six criteria** linked to strategy, such as strategic alignment, financial value, risk reduction, delivery risk and urgency.
3. **Weight the criteria** so they add up to 100%. Get the executive team to agree the weights, not the PMO.
4. **Define each score.** Write what a 1, 3 and 5 look like for each criterion so different assessors score consistently.
5. **Score every proposal** using the business case. Use financial measures such as net present value or return on investment for the value criterion where you can.
6. **Rank, then check capacity.** A ranked list is only a wish list until you compare it with the people available.
7. **Decide and publish.** Record what was approved, deferred or rejected and why, then revisit each quarter.

#### Worked example: scoring five project proposals
Imagine a mid-sized financial services firm with five proposals for next quarter. The portfolio board agreed these weights: strategic alignment 30%, financial value 25%, risk reduction or compliance 20%, delivery risk 15% (5 = low risk) and urgency 10%. Each proposal is scored from 1 to 5.
| Proposal | Alignment (30%) | Value (25%) | Risk reduction (20%) | Delivery risk (15%) | Urgency (10%) | Weighted score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E. Customer self-service app | 5 | 5 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 3.70 |
| A. CRM replacement | 5 | 4 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3.50 |
| B. Regulatory reporting upgrade | 3 | 2 | 5 | 4 | 5 | 3.50 (mandatory) |
| C. Data platform modernisation | 4 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 3.30 |
| D. Office relocation system changes | 2 | 3 | 1 | 4 | 4 | 2.55 |
The weighted score is the sum of each score multiplied by its weight. For proposal E: (5 × 0.30) + (5 × 0.25) + (1 × 0.20) + (3 × 0.15) + (3 × 0.10) = 1.50 + 1.25 + 0.20 + 0.45 + 0.30 = 3.70. Proposal B scores lower on value but is mandatory, so it goes to the top of the queue regardless.

#### Worked example: checking capacity before you approve
The scarcest skill for these projects is data engineering. The team has 12 people, but about 30% of their time goes to business-as-usual support, leaving roughly 8.4 full-time equivalents (FTE) for projects next quarter.
| Order | Proposal | Data engineering FTE needed | Cumulative FTE | Fits within 8.4 FTE? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | B. Regulatory reporting (mandatory) | 2.0 | 2.0 | Yes |
| 2 | E. Customer self-service app | 3.5 | 5.5 | Yes |
| 3 | A. CRM replacement | 2.5 | 8.0 | Yes |
| 4 | C. Data platform modernisation | 4.0 | 12.0 | No: defer or re-sequence |
The board approves B, E and A, and defers C to the following quarter, or approves only its discovery phase, which needs far fewer people. Without this check, all four would have started, each would have been understaffed and all four would probably have slipped. Starting fewer projects usually finishes more. For more on balancing demand, see our guide to [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/).
Tip
Do the capacity check by role or skill, not by headcount. An organisation can have plenty of people overall and still be blocked by three architects or one security specialist.

### Governance tiers: right-sizing control
One of the fastest ways to make EPM unpopular is to apply the same heavy process to every project. Tiering sets lighter or heavier governance according to size and risk. The thresholds below are illustrative; set your own based on your budget authority levels and risk appetite.
| Tier | Typical criteria | Approval | Required documents | Reporting |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tier 3: small | Low cost, under three months, one department, low risk | Department head | One-page brief, entry in the portfolio tracker | Monthly status field update |
| Tier 2: medium | Moderate cost or cross-department, some dependencies | Portfolio board | Charter, light business case, RAID log, schedule | Fortnightly standard status report |
| Tier 1: major | High cost, strategic, regulatory or high risk | Investment committee or executive team | Full business case, plan, stage gates, benefits plan, independent assurance | Fortnightly or weekly status, monthly board review |
Write the tier criteria down and let the EPMO assign the tier at intake. Allow projects to move tiers if their risk or size changes.

### Key roles in enterprise project management
| Role | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Executive team or portfolio board | Sets strategy, approves investments and makes portfolio trade-offs |
| Enterprise PMO (EPMO) director | Owns the EPM framework, portfolio reporting and governance |
| Portfolio managers | Manage a portfolio for a business unit or investment theme |
| Programme managers | Coordinate related projects to deliver shared benefits |
| Project managers | Deliver individual projects within the enterprise standards |
| Resource managers | Allocate people across projects and balance demand with capacity |
| Finance partners | Track capital and operating spend across the portfolio |
| Benefit owners | Business leaders accountable for realising benefits after delivery |

#### What does an enterprise project manager do?
"Enterprise project manager" is used in two ways. Sometimes it means a senior project manager who runs large, cross-functional projects under enterprise standards. More often it describes a portfolio or EPMO role. Typical responsibilities include:
- Running intake, prioritisation and the portfolio board cycle.
- Maintaining the portfolio view: health, spend, milestones, risks and dependencies.
- Working with resource managers to match demand with capacity.
- Setting and improving standards, templates and tool configuration.
- Coaching project managers and sponsors.
- Reporting to executives in plain language, with clear decisions needed.
The role needs strong stakeholder management, financial literacy and the confidence to recommend stopping a project.

### Methodologies and frameworks that fit
There is no single EPM method. Most organisations combine a governance framework with project-level methods suited to each type of work.
| Approach | Best for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage-gate governance | Enterprise-wide control of investment | Standard gates with defined criteria across all projects |
| [PMBOK Guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) or PRINCE2 as the base method | Consistent project-level practice | Tailor to project size; avoid forcing heavy process on small projects |
| Portfolio management standards | Portfolio selection and balancing | PMI publishes The Standard for Portfolio Management (currently the fourth edition); AXELOS publishes Management of Portfolios (MoP) |
| [SAFe](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/scaled-agile-framework-safe/) or other scaled Agile | Large technology and product organisations | Lean portfolio management with funding by value stream |
| Hybrid tiering | Organisations with mixed project types | Tier projects by size and risk, and let each team keep a delivery method that suits its work |
Our advice: standardise what the portfolio needs to compare (gates, health definitions, a small set of mandatory fields) and leave teams free on how they deliver. An Agile team and a construction project can both report progress, forecast, risks and benefits in the same format.

### How to implement enterprise project management step by step
1. **Secure an executive sponsor.** EPM changes who decides what gets funded. Without a senior sponsor it becomes a reporting exercise.
2. **Build a portfolio inventory.** List every active project with its owner, budget, stage, end date and health. Many organisations find far more projects than they expected.
3. **Define a minimal standard.** Agree a simple life cycle, health definitions (what red, amber and green mean) and five to ten mandatory fields.
4. **Open one front door.** Introduce a single intake form for new work and route all requests through it.
5. **Set up the portfolio forum.** Hold a regular portfolio board with a published scoring model and decision log.
6. **Choose one platform.** Move the inventory, intake and status reporting into one tool so reports are generated, not collected.
7. **Add resource management.** Start with the scarcest roles, then widen.
8. **Introduce governance tiers and stage gates.** Apply them to new projects first rather than retrofitting everything.
9. **Track benefits.** Assign benefit owners and review benefits after closure.
10. **Review and improve.** Each quarter, remove steps that do not change decisions and add what is missing.

#### A 12-month EPM roadmap
| Period | Focus | Outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Months 0–3 | Visibility | Sponsor and charter for the EPMO, portfolio inventory, health definitions, intake form, first portfolio board |
| Months 3–6 | Control | Scoring model, governance tiers, standard status report, one platform live for all Tier 1 and 2 projects |
| Months 6–12 | Optimisation | Capacity planning for key roles, stage gates, benefits tracking, lessons learned library, first annual review of the framework |
Tip
Show value early. Within the first quarter, use the inventory to surface duplicate projects or a capacity clash and get a decision made. That earns the EPMO credibility for the harder changes.

### EPM maturity levels
This simple four-level model, our own rather than a formal standard, helps you see where you are and what to work on next.
| Level | What it looks like | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Ad hoc | Projects start through informal routes; no single list; status collected in spreadsheets | Build the inventory and intake form |
| 2. Standardised | Common templates and health definitions; one list of projects | Introduce prioritisation and a portfolio board |
| 3. Managed portfolio | Scored prioritisation, capacity checks and tiered governance; one platform | Add benefits tracking and forecasting |
| 4. Optimised | Portfolio rebalanced regularly on data; benefits measured; lessons change standards | Keep simplifying and automating |

### Essential EPM documents and templates
- **EPM framework or playbook:** life cycle, gates, roles, tiers and reporting standards.
- **Intake form:** a standard [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) for new demand.
- **Business case:** use our [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) so investments can be compared like for like.
- **Project charter:** the [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) authorises approved projects.
- **Standard status report:** consistent health indicators across the portfolio; see [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
- **RAID log:** the [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/) gives a shared format for risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, including cross-project ones.
- **Portfolio tracker:** the [project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/) lists projects, owners, stage and health.
- **Roadmap:** a product roadmap shows the sequence of approved initiatives over time.
- **Skills matrix:** the [skills matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/) supports enterprise resource planning.
- **Lessons learned:** a central library built with the [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/).

### KPIs for enterprise project management
Pick a handful of portfolio measures and define them precisely so every project reports the same way.
| KPI | How to calculate it | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strategic alignment | Spend on projects linked to a strategic objective ÷ total project spend | Whether investment follows strategy |
| Portfolio health | Share of projects rated green, amber and red | Where executive attention is needed |
| Benefits realisation | Benefits realised ÷ benefits planned, for closed projects | Whether projects deliver value, not just outputs |
| Capacity load | Demand for a role ÷ available capacity for that role | Over-allocation before it causes delays |
| Schedule and cost performance | Aggregate earned value indices (SPI and CPI) or milestone and budget variance | Delivery control across the portfolio |
| Time to decision | Days from intake submission to approval or rejection | Whether governance is slowing the organisation down |
| Projects stopped at a gate | Projects cancelled or re-scoped at gates when no longer viable | A healthy sign that governance works |
Avoid measuring the EPMO by the number of templates completed. Measure the decisions it enables and the value the portfolio delivers.

### Benefits of enterprise project management
- **Better investment decisions.** Projects are compared on the same criteria, so money flows to the work that matters most.
- **Realistic commitments.** Capacity checks stop the organisation starting more than it can finish.
- **Earlier warning.** Standard health reporting surfaces failing projects while there is still time to act.
- **Visible dependencies.** Cross-project risks and handovers are tracked rather than discovered late.
- **Consistent delivery.** Shared methods, templates and coaching raise the baseline for every project manager.
- **Proven value.** Benefits tracking shows what the portfolio actually achieved.

### Common challenges and how to handle them
| Challenge | How to handle it |
| --- | --- |
| Too many projects | Make capacity a hard constraint in prioritisation and publish what was deferred |
| Bureaucracy | Tier governance and remove steps that do not change decisions |
| Inconsistent data | Standardise a small set of mandatory fields and automate reporting from one tool |
| Hidden dependencies | Record cross-project dependencies explicitly and review them at the portfolio board |
| Agile and traditional teams in one portfolio | Report on outcomes, forecasts and risks in one format; let teams keep their delivery method |
| Projects that never stop | Define kill criteria at each gate and celebrate good stop decisions |
| EPMO seen as overhead | Show value through faster decisions, better resource visibility and avoided duplication |

### Enterprise project management software
EPM depends on a single source of truth. Spreadsheet portfolios rarely scale beyond a few dozen projects, because data goes stale and reports have to be assembled by hand. When you compare tools, look for:
- Portfolio and programme hierarchies with roll-up reporting and dashboards.
- Enterprise resource management with capacity and demand views by role.
- Configurable intake forms, approval workflows and stage gates.
- Support for both Agile boards and Gantt-based plans in the same system.
- Custom fields and item types so every project reports the same data.
- Enterprise security: single sign-on, granular permissions, audit logs and data residency options.
- Integrations with finance, HR, IT service management and development tools.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, is one of the strongest all-in-one options for EPM. It combines cross-project portfolio views, workload and resource planning, request forms, approvals, custom item types and enterprise security in one platform; advanced resource planning, budgeting and BI sit on its higher, quote-based tiers. [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) suits organisations that prefer spreadsheet-style portfolio planning, and Jira is a natural fit for the software teams within an enterprise portfolio.
If you are moving off an older system, note that Microsoft retired Project Online on 30 September 2026, so many PMOs are currently migrating their portfolios. Treat the migration as a chance to simplify fields and workflows rather than copy them across unchanged.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is enterprise project management?**
Enterprise project management (EPM) is managing all of an organisation's projects as one coordinated system, with shared governance, standard methods, common tools, enterprise resource management and a single portfolio view.

**Q: What is the difference between EPM and project portfolio management?**
Portfolio management focuses on selecting, prioritising and balancing projects. EPM is broader: it includes portfolio decisions and adds the standards, tools, resource management, governance and capability building used across every project.

**Q: What is the difference between a PMO and an EPMO?**
A PMO usually supports delivery in one department and is mainly tactical. An enterprise PMO works across the whole organisation, reports to the executive team and focuses on strategy alignment, prioritisation, capacity and governance.

**Q: What does an enterprise project manager do?**
They run intake and prioritisation, maintain the portfolio view, balance demand with capacity, set standards, coach project managers and report to executives with clear decisions needed.

**Q: What are the elements of enterprise project management?**
Governance, a standard life cycle, demand intake, prioritisation, enterprise resource management, standard reporting, risk and issue escalation, benefits management, and capability and tools.

**Q: What are the phases of enterprise project management?**
Strategy and planning, demand intake, evaluation and prioritisation, approval and resourcing, delivery with stage gates, portfolio monitoring and rebalancing, and closure with benefits tracking.

**Q: How do you implement enterprise project management?**
Secure an executive sponsor, build a portfolio inventory, agree minimal standards, open one intake route, start a portfolio board, move to one platform, then add resource management, tiered governance and benefits tracking in stages.

**Q: What is an example of enterprise project management?**
A firm scores all project proposals against agreed weighted criteria, checks the result against the capacity of its scarcest skills, approves only what it can staff and tracks every approved project through the same gates and dashboards.

**Q: Which methodology is used in enterprise project management?**
Usually a stage-gate governance framework with PMBOK or PRINCE2 practice at project level, portfolio standards such as PMI's Standard for Portfolio Management, and scaled Agile approaches such as SAFe for product teams.

**Q: How does Agile fit into enterprise project management?**
Agile teams keep their delivery methods while the portfolio funds products or value streams and tracks outcomes, forecasts and risks in a common format.

**Q: What KPIs are used in enterprise project management?**
Strategic alignment of spend, portfolio health, benefits realisation, capacity load by role, schedule and cost performance, time to decision and projects stopped at gates.

**Q: What is enterprise project management software?**
Software that provides portfolio views, resource and capacity management, intake and approval workflows and enterprise reporting across all projects. Wrike is a strong all-in-one example.

**Q: Is enterprise project management only for large companies?**
The full model suits larger organisations, but the core ideas (one project list, one intake route, a scoring model and a capacity check) help any business running several projects at once. See [small business project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/small-business-project-management/).

# Event Project Management: Phases, Timeline, Budget and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/event-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Event project management explained: the event life cycle, a backwards timeline, budget and run of show examples, roles, risk, KPIs, templates and software.


## Event Project Management: Phases, Timeline, Budget and Tools
Event project management is the planning and delivery of conferences, trade shows, product launches, festivals and corporate events as projects, with a fixed date, a budget, a target audience and measurable goals. Its defining feature is the immovable deadline: the event happens on the day whether or not everything is ready, so planning backwards, controlling suppliers and managing risk matter far more than late recovery. This guide walks through the life cycle, a step-by-step process, a worked timeline and budget, the run of show, roles, risk, KPIs and tools.
- Published 28 August 2026
- Last updated 16 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Event project management treats an event as a project with a fixed date, budget, audience and success measures.
- Plan backwards from the event date and identify the critical path early: venue, programme lock, print and shipping deadlines.
- Read venue and catering contracts closely: attrition, minimum spend and cancellation clauses are among the biggest financial risks.
- Track registrations weekly against a target curve so you can act while there is still time.
- Run the day from a minute-by-minute run of show with a clear chain of command, then close with a budget reconciliation and lessons learned.

### What is event project management?
**Event project management** is the application of project management methods to plan, coordinate and deliver an event. It covers objectives, scope, schedule, budget, suppliers, marketing, risk and on-the-day operations, from the first idea to the post-event review. The event project manager owns the plan and makes sure every workstream is ready by a date that cannot move.
Every event is a [project](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-a-project/): it is temporary, produces a unique outcome and has a defined start and end. "Event management" is the wider profession, including creative design, hospitality and production. "Event project management" is the planning and control discipline inside it: the schedule, budget, dependencies, risks and decisions that turn an idea into a well-run day.

### What makes event projects different
- **A date that cannot move:** venues and speakers are booked months ahead, so every slip is absorbed by scope, cost or quality rather than time.
- **Heavy supplier dependence:** venue, catering, AV, staging, security, transport and accommodation are mostly outsourced.
- **Live delivery:** the event itself is a short, intense operation where decisions are made in minutes.
- **Safety and licensing:** crowd management, fire safety, food hygiene, accessibility and local licences all apply.
- **Revenue as well as cost:** ticket sales and sponsorship often fund the event, so registrations are a live risk.
- **One chance to get it right:** unlike most projects, there is no second release. Rehearsals and contingency plans replace testing in production.

### Types of events and what drives each plan
The core process is the same, but the main driver and the biggest risk change with the type of event.
| Event type | Main planning driver | Typical lead time | Biggest risk to plan for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Conference or summit | Programme and speakers | Long: often many months to a year or more | Registrations below target |
| Trade show stand | Organiser deadlines and stand build | Set by the show organiser's manual | Missed freight and order deadlines |
| Product launch | Launch date and marketing plan | Medium to long | Product or message changes late in the plan |
| Internal company event | Business objectives and attendance | Medium | Low engagement and last-minute agenda changes |
| Festival or public outdoor event | Licensing, safety and site build | Long | Weather, crowd safety and licence conditions |
| Virtual or hybrid event | Platform and production | Short to medium | Technical failure and remote audience drop-off |
| Workshop or small meeting | Venue availability and agenda | Short: often weeks | Key people unavailable |
For launch events that are part of a wider campaign, see also [marketing project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/marketing-project-management/).

### The event project life cycle
Most events move through seven phases. The timing depends on size, but the order rarely changes.
| Phase | Typical timing | Key activities | Main output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Concept and objectives | Earliest | Purpose, audience, format, success measures, outline budget | Event brief |
| 2. Planning and venue | Many months out | Venue search and contract, date, budget, programme outline | Signed venue contract and baseline budget |
| 3. Suppliers and programme | Months out | Contract AV, catering and production; confirm speakers and sponsors | Supplier contracts and draft agenda |
| 4. Marketing and registration | Ongoing to the event | Launch registration, promote, manage attendee communications | Registrations against target |
| 5. Final logistics | Final weeks | Run of show, floor plans, staffing, briefings, risk assessment, rehearsals | Event operations pack |
| 6. Event delivery | Event days | Build, live operation, incident management, breakdown | The event |
| 7. Evaluation and close | Weeks after | Surveys, budget reconciliation, sponsor reports, lessons learned | Close report |
Tip
Read venue and supplier contracts for attrition and cancellation clauses before you sign. Room-block minimums and catering guarantees are among the biggest financial risks in an event budget.

### How to plan an event step by step
1. **Set objectives.** Write two to four measurable [project objectives](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-objectives/), such as "400 attendees, 80% satisfaction and 150 qualified sales leads".
2. **Define the audience and format.** In person, virtual or hybrid; one day or several; keynote-led or workshop-led.
3. **Agree a sponsor and decision rights.** Name who approves the budget, programme and major changes.
4. **Build an outline budget.** Include income (tickets, sponsorship) as well as costs, and hold a contingency line.
5. **Choose the date and venue.** Check capacity, accessibility, transport, clashes with other events and contract terms.
6. **Break the work down.** Create a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) by workstream: venue, programme, marketing, registration, production, catering, sponsorship, staffing and safety.
7. **Plan backwards from the event date.** Set milestones and supplier deadlines, and identify the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).
8. **Contract suppliers.** Get comparable quotes, confirm everything in writing and record delivery and arrival times.
9. **Launch marketing and registration.** Track sign-ups weekly against a target curve.
10. **Assess risks and plan for safety.** Complete the risk assessment and emergency plan, and agree the chain of command.
11. **Finalise logistics.** Lock the programme, produce the run of show, brief staff and speakers, and rehearse.
12. **Deliver, then close.** Run the event, reconcile the budget, report to sponsors and hold a lessons learned review.

### Building a backwards event timeline
Event schedules are planned in reverse. Start with the event date, then work back through each deadline that must be met for it to happen. Supplier lead times, print and shipping dates and the point at which you must give final numbers to the venue are the fixed points.

#### Worked example: timeline for a 400-person conference
This illustrative plan is for a one-day industry conference with a keynote, breakout sessions, a small exhibition and lunch. "E" is the event date.
| When | Milestone | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E minus 12 to 9 months | Objectives, outline budget, venue shortlist, site visits, venue contract signed | Event project manager, sponsor |
| E minus 8 months | Date announced, save-the-date sent, sponsorship prospectus issued | Marketing lead, sponsorship manager |
| E minus 6 months | Keynotes confirmed, AV and production supplier contracted, early-bird registration opens | Programme manager, event project manager |
| E minus 4 months | Full agenda published, caterer and menu chosen, hotel room block agreed | Programme manager, logistics coordinator |
| E minus 3 months | Sponsor deliverables agreed, main marketing campaign running | Sponsorship manager, marketing lead |
| E minus 6 weeks | Programme locked for print and event app; signage and badge artwork approved | Programme manager |
| E minus 4 weeks | Floor plan, staffing rota, risk assessment and emergency plan complete | Logistics coordinator, safety lead |
| E minus 2 weeks | Speaker briefings, slide deadline, supplier reconfirmation | Programme manager, event project manager |
| E minus 7 days | Final numbers to venue and caterer, run of show final, staff briefing pack issued | Event project manager |
| E minus 1 day | Build, AV installation and technical rehearsal | Production supplier |
| E | Event delivery | Whole team |
| E plus 1 to 4 weeks | Attendee survey, budget reconciliation, sponsor reports, lessons learned | Event project manager |
In this plan the critical path usually runs through the venue contract, keynote confirmation, programme lock, print and badge production, and the final-numbers deadline. Anything on that chain slipping puts the date at risk, so track it weekly. Lay the plan out visually with the [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/).
Tip
Build at least one week of float before every print and shipping deadline. Late speaker changes almost always arrive after the programme lock.

### Event budgeting and contract risk
An event budget has two sides: income and costs. Build both, hold a contingency line and know your break-even point before you commit to large contracts. Our [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) guide covers the general method; the example below shows how it applies to an event.

#### Worked example: conference budget
The same 400-person conference: 350 paid tickets at £295, 50 complimentary places for speakers, press and staff, and four sponsors at £7,500 each. The figures are illustrative.
| Line | Calculation | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ticket income | 350 × £295 | £103,250 |
| Sponsorship income | 4 × £7,500 | £30,000 |
| **Total income** |  | **£133,250** |
| Venue hire | Day rate including rooms | £18,000 |
| Catering | 400 × £65 per head | £26,000 |
| AV and production | Quote | £22,000 |
| Speakers (travel and fees) | Estimate | £9,000 |
| Marketing | Campaign budget | £10,000 |
| Registration platform and badges | Quote | £4,500 |
| Staffing and security | Rota × rates | £6,500 |
| Print, signage and branding | Quote | £4,000 |
| Insurance | Quote | £1,500 |
| Subtotal |  | £101,500 |
| Contingency | 10% of subtotal | £10,150 |
| **Total costs** |  | **£111,650** |
| **Forecast surplus** | £133,250 − £111,650 | **£21,600** |
**Break-even check.** Catering is the main cost that varies with paid attendance (£65 a head). The other costs, plus catering for the 50 complimentary places (£3,250), are about £88,900. Each paid ticket contributes £295 − £65 = £230. After sponsorship, you need (£88,900 − £30,000) ÷ £230 ≈ 256.1, so **257 paid tickets** to break even. That number becomes your minimum registration target and helps you decide whether to go ahead at each review point.
How much contingency to hold is a judgement call. Many planners use around 10% for a familiar event and more for a first-time event, a new venue or an outdoor site. Approve every draw on contingency through one person and record it; see [contingency planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/).

#### Attrition and minimum spend clauses
Venues and hotels often require you to guarantee minimum numbers. An **attrition clause** lets your numbers fall by an agreed amount without penalty, but charges you for shortfalls beyond it.
- **Catering guarantee:** you contract a minimum of 380 covers at £65. If only 300 people attend, you still pay 380 × £65 = £24,700 rather than £19,500, so the shortfall costs £5,200.
- **Hotel room block:** you reserve 120 room-nights at £160 with an 80% pick-up requirement, so you must fill 96. If attendees book only 70, you may be charged for 26 room-nights, up to £4,160, depending on the contract terms.
- **Cancellation scale:** charges usually rise as the event approaches. Know each date at which the cancellation charge steps up and put those dates in your plan as decision points.
Negotiate realistic minimums, review terms with whoever handles contracts in your organisation, and set your final-numbers date in the schedule. Supplier contracting is covered in more depth in our guide to [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/).

### The run of show
The **run of show** (also called a running order or show flow) is the minute-by-minute script for the event. It lists every session, transition, cue and responsible person, and it is the single document everyone works from on the day: stage manager, AV crew, speakers, hosts and venue staff.
A good run of show includes:
- Start time and duration of every item, including changeovers and walk-ons.
- Location (main stage, breakout room, foyer).
- Who is on stage and who is responsible backstage.
- AV and technical cues: slides, video, microphones, lighting and music.
- Notes such as speaker arrival times, accessibility needs or sponsor mentions.
Here is a short illustrative extract:
| Time | Duration | Item | Location | Lead | AV and cues |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 08:00 | 60 min | Registration and coffee | Foyer | Registration lead | Background music; holding slide on screens |
| 09:00 | 5 min | Welcome from host | Main stage | Host | Walk-on music; host mic 1; title slide |
| 09:05 | 40 min | Opening keynote | Main stage | Programme manager | Lapel mic 2; speaker slides; clicker check at 08:45 |
| 09:45 | 15 min | Panel: industry outlook | Main stage | Moderator | Four handheld mics; panel stools set during keynote Q&A |
| 10:00 | 30 min | Break and exhibition | Exhibition hall | Logistics coordinator | Sponsor loop video; doors to breakouts open at 10:20 |
Issue the run of show with version numbers. After the final version is issued, route every change through one person, usually the producer or stage manager, and announce it on the radio channel or team chat.

### Key roles in an event project
| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Event manager or event project manager | Owns the plan, budget, suppliers and on-the-day decisions |
| Event sponsor or owner | Sets objectives and approves budget and major decisions |
| Producer or programme manager | Content, speakers and the run of show |
| Logistics and venue coordinator | Venue relationship, floor plans, deliveries and accommodation |
| Marketing and registration lead | Promotion, ticketing and attendee communications |
| Sponsorship or exhibitor manager | Sells and services sponsor packages |
| Health and safety lead | Risk assessments, crowd and emergency planning, compliance |
| Suppliers | Venue, AV, catering, security, staging and transport teams |
Make on-the-day decision rights explicit with a [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/): who can approve a programme change, call a delay or evacuate a room.

#### What does an event project manager do?
- Turns the event brief into a plan with milestones, budget and owners.
- Negotiates and manages supplier contracts.
- Tracks registrations, spend and risks, and reports to the sponsor.
- Coordinates marketing, programme, logistics and sponsorship workstreams.
- Leads the operation on the day and makes fast decisions when things change.
- Closes the project: reconciliation, reports and lessons learned.
The most useful skills are planning, budgeting, negotiation, [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/), risk awareness and calm decision-making under pressure.

### Managing suppliers
Most of an event is delivered by other organisations, so supplier management is where many events succeed or fail.
1. **Write a clear specification** for each supplier: what, when, where, quantities and standards.
2. **Get at least two comparable quotes** for significant spend.
3. **Check credentials:** insurance, relevant certifications, references and, for structures, safety documentation.
4. **Contract in writing** with delivery times, payment milestones, cancellation terms and named contacts.
5. **Keep a supplier tracker** with contact details, arrival and departure times, access needs and status.
6. **Reconfirm everything in the final week** and share the run of show with suppliers who need it.
7. **Hold a short supplier briefing** on site before doors open.
Agencies that run events for clients will recognise the same pattern; see [agency project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/agency-project-management/).

### Event risk, safety and compliance
Record risks in a [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) from the start and review them at every planning meeting. Typical event risks and responses:
| Risk | Likelihood and impact | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registrations below break-even | Medium likelihood, high impact | Weekly tracking against a curve; extra promotion triggers; go/no-go dates linked to cancellation terms |
| Keynote speaker cancels | Low to medium, high impact | Back-up speaker or format; contract terms on cancellation |
| AV or power failure | Low, high impact | Technical rehearsal, spare equipment, backup laptop with all slides |
| Supplier no-show | Low, high impact | Written confirmation, backup contacts, reconfirmation in the final week |
| Bad weather (outdoor) | Varies, high impact | Written wet-weather plan with a decision deadline |
| Medical emergency or crowd incident | Low, very high impact | First aid provision, emergency plan, staff briefing, clear chain of command |
| Overspend | Medium, medium impact | Contingency line with single approver and weekly budget review |
Safety and legal duties depend on where the event takes place, its size and the venue. Agree with the venue who is responsible for what, and take professional advice where needed. Some UK examples of what to check:
- **Health and safety:** the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) states that the CDM 2015 regulations apply to construction work in the entertainment industry, including building and dismantling temporary structures for live events.
- **Outdoor events:** the Purple Guide is widely used industry guidance for planning outdoor events safely.
- **Security:** the Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act 2025, known as Martyn's Law, received Royal Assent on 3 April 2025 with an implementation period of at least two years. Once in force, it introduces duties for qualifying premises and for qualifying public events with 800 or more people. Check current government guidance for dates and requirements.
- **Licensing, food hygiene, accessibility and data protection** for attendee data also apply; check local authority and venue requirements early.
For the general method, see our guide to [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/).

### Methodologies for events
- **Waterfall and milestones:** the backbone of most events, planned backwards from the event date with clear supplier deadlines.
- **Critical path:** venue contract, programme confirmation, print and shipping deadlines usually form the path to the event.
- **[Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/):** useful for the stream of tasks in the final weeks, from badge printing to signage.
- **Agile sprints:** some teams plan marketing and content for large events in short cycles, adjusting to registration data.
- **Incident command on the day:** a clear chain of command and radio channels for decisions during the live event.

### Essential documents and templates
- **Event plan:** start with our [event planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/event-planning-template/).
- **Budget:** income and cost lines with contingency in the [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/).
- **Timeline:** a Gantt chart planned back from the event date.
- **Agenda:** publish sessions and timings with the [meeting agenda template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-agenda-template/), which also works for workshops and smaller events.
- **Run of show:** minute-by-minute timings, cues, speakers and responsibilities for each session.
- **Supplier tracker and contracts:** who to call, when they arrive and what they deliver.
- **Risk assessment and emergency plan:** plus the project risk register.
- **Responsibilities:** a RACI matrix for on-the-day decisions.
- **Debrief:** the [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/).

### KPIs for event project management
| KPI | How to calculate it | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registrations against target | Cumulative registrations ÷ target for that week | Early warning on attendance and revenue |
| Attendance rate | Attendees ÷ registrations | Planning catering and future no-show allowances |
| Budget variance | Actual − planned, for costs and income | Financial control |
| Cost per attendee | Total cost ÷ attendees | Comparing events and formats |
| Sponsor revenue and renewal | Sponsor income; share of sponsors who return | Commercial success |
| Attendee satisfaction or NPS | Post-event survey scores | Quality of the experience |
| Leads or meetings generated | Qualified leads or meetings booked | Proving return on the event |
In the worked example, if 380 people attend and total costs end at £110,000, cost per attendee is £110,000 ÷ 380 ≈ £289.

#### Tracking registrations against a curve
Registrations rarely arrive evenly. Set a target curve based on past events or a sensible assumption, then compare actuals every week. This example uses the target of 350 paid tickets.
| Weeks before event | Target cumulative (%) | Target tickets | Actual | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12 | 20% | 70 | 74 | On track |
| 8 | 40% | 140 | 110 | Behind (79% of plan): trigger extra promotion |
| 4 | 70% | 245 | 238 | Close to plan after campaign |
| 2 | 85% | 298 |  |  |
| 0 | 100% | 350 |  |  |
Agree in advance what happens when you fall behind: extra campaign spend, partner promotion, a price change or, in the worst case, a smaller room before a cancellation charge increases.

### Common challenges and how to handle them
| Challenge | How to handle it |
| --- | --- |
| Low registrations | Track weekly against a curve, trigger extra promotion early, and know your cancellation deadlines |
| Supplier failure | Confirm details in writing, hold backup contacts and reconfirm in the final week |
| Programme changes | Lock the programme by a fixed date for print and apps; handle later changes through one owner |
| Overspend | Hold a contingency line and approve every variation against it |
| Too many decision-makers | Name one sponsor and record decision rights in a RACI |
| Safety incidents | Do a proper risk assessment, brief all staff and run the event with a clear chain of command |
| Weather for outdoor events | Have a written wet-weather plan and decision deadline |
| No learning between events | Hold a debrief within two weeks and update your event template with what changed |

### Event project management software
Event teams usually combine two kinds of tool: a project management platform for tasks, timelines, approvals and supplier coordination, and specialist event software for registration, ticketing, badging, attendee apps and floor plans. Look for reusable event templates, timeline or Gantt views, workload views across several events, approvals for creative assets and integrations with your registration platform.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, is a strong all-in-one choice for corporate event and marketing teams that run several events a year. It offers reusable templates, interactive Gantt charts, request forms, proofing and approvals for collateral, and workload views across events. [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) is easy to set up and very visual, and [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) works well for cross-team task coordination.

### Skills and certifications
Event project managers need supplier negotiation, budgeting, risk and safety awareness, and calm decision-making under pressure.
The **Certified Meeting Professional (CMP)**, awarded by the Events Industry Council, is a widely recognised event industry credential. Eligibility combines industry experience (typically 36 months of full-time work in meetings, events or hospitality, reduced for graduates of relevant degrees) with at least 25 hours of continuing education in meeting management within the past five years, followed by an exam. Check the Events Industry Council's current requirements before you apply.
General project management credentials strengthen the planning side.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is event project management?**
It is managing an event as a project with a fixed date, budget, audience and objectives, from concept and venue booking through suppliers, marketing and delivery to evaluation.

**Q: What does an event project manager do?**
They own the plan and budget, contract and coordinate suppliers, track registrations and risks, lead the team on the day and close the project with a budget reconciliation and lessons learned.

**Q: What are the phases of event project management?**
Concept and objectives, planning and venue, suppliers and programme, marketing and registration, final logistics, event delivery, and evaluation and close.

**Q: What are the steps to plan an event?**
Set objectives, define the audience and format, agree a sponsor, build a budget, book the venue, break down the work, plan backwards, contract suppliers, launch registration, assess risks, finalise logistics, then deliver and review.

**Q: How far ahead should you start planning an event?**
It depends on size and type. Small meetings may need a few weeks, while large conferences often start a year or more ahead because popular venues and speakers book early.

**Q: What is a run of show?**
A minute-by-minute running order listing every session, transition, technical cue, location and responsible person. It is the single script the whole team works from on the day.

**Q: How much contingency should an event budget have?**
Many planners hold around 10% for a familiar event and more for a first-time event, new venue or outdoor site. Control it through one approver.

**Q: What is an attrition clause in an event contract?**
A clause that lets your guaranteed numbers, such as catering covers or hotel rooms, fall by an agreed amount without penalty, and charges you for shortfalls beyond that amount.

**Q: How do you manage risk at an event?**
Keep a risk register from the start, carry out a risk assessment and emergency plan, check contract cancellation terms, hold contingency budget, plan for weather and brief staff on the chain of command.

**Q: Which KPIs measure event success?**
Registrations against target, attendance rate, budget variance, cost per attendee, sponsor revenue and renewal, attendee satisfaction or NPS, and leads or meetings generated.

**Q: Which templates are used in event project management?**
An event plan, budget, Gantt timeline, agenda, run of show, supplier tracker, risk register, RACI matrix and lessons learned template.

**Q: What software is used for event project management?**
A project management platform such as Wrike for planning, approvals and coordination, plus specialist tools for registration, ticketing, badging and floor plans.

**Q: Is there a certification for event project management?**
The Certified Meeting Professional (CMP) from the Events Industry Council is a recognised event credential; general project management certifications help with planning skills.
