# Game Development Project Management: A Producer's Guide

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/game-development-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Game development project management explained: phases, milestones, producer roles, Agile, scheduling, budgets, crunch control, KPIs and tools.


## Game Development Project Management: A Producer's Guide
Game development project management is the planning, scheduling, budgeting and coordination of a game from the first pitch through pre-production, production, testing, platform certification and launch to live operations. It combines software delivery with creative production, and its defining challenge is that the fun has to be found through prototyping and playtesting rather than written down in advance. This guide covers phases and milestones, producer roles, Agile in studios, a worked schedule and budget, scope control, crunch prevention, KPIs and tools.
- Published 29 August 2026
- Last updated 17 October 2026
- 21 min read

### Key takeaways
- Game projects run on a hybrid model: a milestone plan agreed with the publisher or funder on the outside, Scrum for feature teams and Kanban for content pipelines and bug fixing on the inside.
- Write down exit criteria for every milestone (first playable, vertical slice, alpha, beta, gold) so everyone agrees what 'done' means before the date arrives.
- Use the vertical slice to measure the real cost of content, then rebuild the production schedule from those numbers rather than from the pitch.
- Keep a visible, prioritised cut list from day one; cutting early is the main defence against feature creep and crunch.
- Plan QA, localisation and platform certification as scheduled work with their own lead times, not as a final step.
- In most studios the project manager is called a producer; the job is to protect the team's ability to make a good game on time and within budget.

### What is game development project management?
**Game development project management** is the discipline of planning, resourcing, scheduling and controlling the work needed to make a video game, from concept to launch and post-launch updates. It coordinates design, engineering, art, animation, audio, writing, QA and marketing so that a playable, fun and stable game ships on the agreed platforms, by the agreed date and within budget.
In most studios the person doing this work is called a **producer** rather than a project manager. The principles are the same as general [project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/): define scope, plan, track, manage risk and communicate. What changes is the type of uncertainty, the number of disciplines and the external gates set by publishers and platform holders.
|  | General software project | Game development project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What defines success | Working features that meet requirements | A game players find fun, stable and worth buying or playing |
| Requirements | Mostly known after discovery | Discovered through prototypes and playtests; some ideas are thrown away |
| Work types | Mainly code, design and testing | Code, design, art, animation, audio, writing, cinematics, localisation and QA |
| Volume of content | Moderate | Often thousands of assets moving through repeatable pipelines |
| External gates | Client sign-off, release approvals | Publisher milestones, funding payments, platform certification and store review |
| Release date | Often flexible | Usually tied to marketing campaigns, events and seasonal windows |
| After release | Maintenance | Patches, live events, seasons and downloadable content |
Two features shape everything else: the fun has to be found through prototypes and playtests, and the content has to be produced at scale through pipelines whose throughput, not headcount, limits what you can make. If you already manage software, our guide to [software project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/software-project-management/) covers the engineering side in more depth; this guide focuses on what is specific to games.

### The phases of game development
Studios use slightly different names, but most games move through the same phases. Smaller games compress them; large productions add formal gates between each.
| Phase | Goal | Main activities | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Concept | Decide whether the idea is worth funding | Pitch, target audience and platforms, business model, competitor review, rough scope and budget | Pitch deck, concept art, high-level budget |
| Pre-production | Find the fun and prove the pipeline | Prototypes, art style, technical foundations, tools, pipeline set-up, vertical slice, production plan | First playable, vertical slice, game design document, production schedule |
| Production | Build the game at scale | Feature development in sprints, content creation through pipelines, regular playtests and builds | Feature-complete and content-complete builds |
| Alpha | Make the game playable end to end | Finish remaining features, fill content gaps, fix major issues, start full test passes | Alpha build |
| Beta | Polish and stabilise | Bug fixing, balancing, performance, optimisation, localisation testing, external playtests | Beta build, playtest data |
| Release candidate and certification | Pass platform and store requirements | Compliance testing, submission builds, fixes for failures, launch day patch planning | Release candidate, gold master or approved release build |
| Launch and live operations | Support players and extend the game | Patches, events, seasons, new content, community management and analytics | Update roadmap, live metrics |
Mapped to the standard [project management phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/), concept is initiation, pre-production is planning with real experimentation, production to beta is execution with heavy monitoring, and launch is closure for the development project and the start of an operational phase.
Tip
Do not shorten pre-production to protect the launch date. Problems found in pre-production cost days; the same problems found in production cost months, because by then content has been built on top of them.

### Game development milestones explained
Milestones are the backbone of a game schedule and, for many studios, the basis of publisher payments. Definitions vary between studios and publishers, so the table below shows common usage. The most useful habit is to agree written exit criteria for each one.
| Milestone | What it means | Typical exit criteria to agree |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prototype | Rough, often throwaway build that tests one mechanic or idea | Question answered (for example 'is traversal fun?'), decision recorded |
| First playable | Core loop playable with placeholder art | Core loop can be played for a set time; key controls and camera working |
| Vertical slice | Short section of the game at near-final quality | Representative gameplay, art, audio and UI at target quality; cost per unit of content measured |
| Alpha | Feature complete; playable start to finish | All planned features implemented; placeholder content allowed; no feature work after this point without approval |
| Beta | Content complete; focus on polish and stability | All content in; no known critical bugs blocking progress; performance targets close to met |
| Release candidate | Build the team believes can ship | Bug thresholds met; all compliance checks passed internally |
| Gold or release build | Approved build for release | Platform and store approval received; build archived |
A **vertical slice** deserves special attention. It proves three things at once: that the creative vision works, that the pipeline can produce content at final quality, and how long that content really takes. Treat it as a measurement exercise as well as a showcase, and rebuild your production estimates from what it tells you.
Tip
Write each milestone definition into the project plan and, where there is one, the publisher agreement. Include features, content counts, bug thresholds by severity and performance targets. Ambiguous milestone definitions are a common cause of disputes and late payments.

### Who manages a game project: producers and project managers
Game studios borrow their job titles from film. The producer usually owns delivery; the creative director owns the vision. Large studios add layers, while small teams combine roles.
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Executive producer | Overall responsibility for the game or portfolio, budget, studio and publisher relationships |
| Producer | Plans and runs production: schedule, priorities, risks, dependencies, communication and milestone delivery |
| Associate or assistant producer | Supports the producer, often for one discipline or feature team; runs boards, meetings and tracking |
| Line producer or development manager | Focuses on schedule, staffing and cost across the project |
| Game director or creative director | Owns the creative vision and the player experience; makes final design calls |
| Discipline leads (design, engineering, art, animation, audio, QA) | Estimate and review work in their area, set quality standards and mentor the team |
| QA testers and QA lead | Plan test passes, find and verify bugs, check compliance requirements |
| External or publisher producer | Represents the publisher, reviews milestones, coordinates marketing, localisation and platform relations |

#### Game producer vs project manager
In most studios they are the same job under different names. Where both exist, the producer usually owns scope and priority trade-offs with the creative director, while project managers run detailed scheduling, tracking and coordination for a team or discipline. Some studios also use the title **development manager** for this second role. The skills overlap with any project manager's role: planning, risk, communication and negotiation, plus a working understanding of how games are built.
Tip
A good producer protects the team's time. That means shielding developers from unplanned requests, making trade-offs visible early and saying no to scope that the schedule cannot hold.

### Agile, Scrum and Kanban in game development
Most studios run a hybrid. The outer plan is milestone-based because funding, marketing and platform gates are fixed. Inside each milestone, teams use iterative methods so they can respond to what playtests reveal.
| Approach | Where it fits in a game project | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Milestone or stage-gate plan | The whole project; publisher and funding gates | Gives funders and marketing predictable checkpoints |
| Rapid prototyping | Concept and pre-production | Cheap experiments to find the fun before investing in content |
| Scrum | Feature and gameplay teams during production | Short sprints with a playable build reviewed at each sprint review |
| Kanban | Art, animation and audio pipelines; bug fixing in beta; live ops | Work arrives continuously in many small items; WIP limits keep flow steady |

#### How sprints map to milestones
A milestone of eight to twelve weeks typically contains four to six two-week sprints. Each sprint should end with a playable build and a sprint goal that contributes to the milestone's exit criteria. Use [Agile release planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-release-planning/) to lay out which features and content each sprint targets, then adjust after every review. A shared definition of done for features (for example 'in the build, tested, no critical bugs, audio hooked up') stops half-finished work piling up.
For the basics of the methods themselves, see [what is Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) and our guide to [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/).

### How to manage a game project step by step
The process below works for an indie game or a large production; scale the documentation and the number of gates to the size of the project.
1. **Agree the vision and constraints.** Write a one-page pitch: player fantasy, genre, platforms, audience, business model, target release window and budget ceiling. Get sign-off from the funder or studio leadership.
2. **Time-box prototyping.** Give the team a fixed number of weeks to test the riskiest mechanics. End each prototype with a decision: keep, change or drop.
3. **Set up the foundations.** Choose the engine, version control for large binary assets, build pipeline, bug tracker and task tool. Define naming conventions and folder structures before content production starts.
4. **Build the vertical slice and measure it.** Track how long each asset type and each level or mission took to reach final quality. These numbers become your production rates.
5. **Create the production plan.** Break the game into features and content (a work breakdown structure works well), estimate using vertical slice data, and build a milestone schedule with dependencies between disciplines.
6. **Prioritise and set up the cut list.** Rank every feature and content block by importance to the player experience. Mark what you would cut first if time runs short and agree the list with the creative director.
7. **Plan capacity by discipline.** Compare required effort per discipline with available people per month. Fill gaps with hiring, outsourcing or scope changes before production starts. See [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/).
8. **Run production in sprints and pipelines.** Feature teams work in sprints; content flows through Kanban boards with WIP limits. Hold regular playtests and review a playable build every sprint.
9. **Track milestones and risks weekly.** Compare completed features and content against plan, update the risk register and escalate trade-offs early.
10. **Lock features at alpha and content at beta.** After each lock, changes go through formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) with an impact assessment.
11. **Plan certification and launch.** Book submission slots, run internal compliance passes, prepare store pages and age ratings, and plan a day-one patch if needed.
12. **Run a post-mortem and hand over to live ops.** Capture lessons learned, archive builds and source, and set the post-launch update roadmap.

### Worked example: planning an 18-month game
This example shows how a small studio might plan a single-player action game for PC and two consoles, with a publisher funding development against milestones. The figures are illustrative: replace them with your own rates and estimates.

#### Step 1: lay out the phases and team
| Phase | Months | Average team size | Person-months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Concept | 1 | 3 | 3 |
| Pre-production (to vertical slice) | 4 | 6 | 24 |
| Production (to alpha) | 9 | 14 | 126 |
| Alpha to beta and release candidate | 3 | 14 | 42 |
| Certification and launch | 1 | 10 | 10 |
| Total | 18 |  | 205 |

#### Step 2: turn effort into a budget
Assume a fully loaded cost (salary, taxes, benefits, equipment and overheads) of £6,500 per person per month. Staff cost is 205 × £6,500 = **£1,332,500**. Add outsourced art and audio of £150,000, software licences and tools of £40,000 and external QA and localisation testing of £60,000, giving a subtotal of £1,582,500. A 15% contingency adds £237,375, for a total budget of **£1,819,875**.
The monthly **burn rate** in production is 14 × £6,500 = £91,000 in staff costs alone. Tracking burn rate against plan each month is one of the simplest ways to spot trouble: if the team is growing faster than planned or a phase is running long, the burn rate tells you before the budget does. Our guide to [project budgets](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) explains contingency and cost baselines in more detail.

#### Step 3: check content throughput against the schedule
The vertical slice included one level, which took a level team of four people five weeks, or 20 person-weeks. The game needs 12 more levels. Teams usually get faster after the first level, so the producer assumes 20% fewer hours per level: 16 person-weeks each, or 192 person-weeks in total.
Production lasts about 39 weeks. A level team of five gives 195 person-weeks, which only just covers 192. There is almost no buffer, so the producer agrees three options with the creative director in advance: outsource set dressing for four levels, merge two smaller levels into one, or move one level to post-launch content. These sit at the top of the cut list.

#### Step 4: set milestone dates and payments
| Milestone | Month | Exit criteria summary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Signed concept | 1 | Pitch approved, budget ceiling and platforms agreed |
| First playable | 3 | Core combat and traversal playable with placeholder art |
| Vertical slice | 5 | One level at target quality; production rates measured |
| Production milestones 1 to 3 | 8, 11, 14 | Agreed feature and level counts in the build |
| Alpha | 14 | All features implemented; game playable start to finish |
| Beta | 16 | All content in; performance targets close to met |
| Release candidate and submission | 17 | Bug thresholds met; internal compliance pass complete |
| Launch | 18 | Approved builds released on all platforms |
Tip
Leave a buffer between your internal release candidate date and the date marketing has announced. Certification failures and resubmissions are common, and you need room to fix and resubmit without moving launch.

### Scope control: cut lists and feature creep
Feature creep is the steady addition of 'small' ideas that together overwhelm the schedule. In games it is especially tempting because new ideas often do make the game better. The answer is not to forbid ideas, but to make every addition visible and paid for.

#### Use MoSCoW to rank features and content
| Priority | Meaning in a game | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Must have | The game does not work or is not the pitched game without it | Core combat, save system, first ten levels |
| Should have | Important to quality; painful but possible to cut | Photo mode, two optional boss fights |
| Could have | Nice additions if time allows | Extra cosmetic outfits, bonus challenge mode |
| Won't have (this release) | Agreed out of scope; may come later | Online co-op, level editor |

#### Run the cut list like a budget
- Keep the cut list in the same tool as the backlog, ordered from first to cut to last to cut.
- Review it at every milestone and whenever a new feature is proposed.
- When something new is added, ask what moves down or out to make room.
- Cut early and cleanly: removing a feature before content is built for it is far cheaper than cutting after.
- Record cuts and their reasons so the team understands what happened and can bring ideas back for post-launch updates.

### How to prevent crunch
Crunch is a prolonged period of excessive overtime to hit a deadline. It harms people's health, increases mistakes and bugs, and often leads to staff leaving after launch. Most crunch is caused by planning decisions made months earlier, so prevention is a project management responsibility.
1. **Measure before you commit.** Build production schedules from vertical slice data, not from the pitch.
2. **Plan to around 80% capacity.** Leave room for meetings, illness, reviews and the unexpected, and put holidays in the schedule.
3. **Keep the cut list live.** Make scope the first lever you pull, not hours.
4. **Protect lock dates.** Feature lock at alpha and content lock at beta stop late additions creating late bugs.
5. **Watch leading indicators.** Rising bug counts, falling sprint completion, growing WIP and overtime warn you weeks ahead.
6. **Buffer external dates and escalate early.** Tell funders about schedule risk while there are still choices.
Tip
If the team is regularly working evenings and weekends, the plan is wrong. Re-plan scope and dates with the creative director and funder instead of asking for more effort.

### Content pipelines and asset tracking
A pipeline is the sequence of steps each asset type goes through. Visualising pipelines on Kanban boards shows where work is waiting, which is usually where schedules slip.
| Asset type | Typical pipeline steps | Common bottleneck |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Character | Concept, approval, model, texture, rig, animation, implementation, review | Rigging and animation, which depend on approved models |
| Environment or level | Layout and greybox, playtest, art pass, lighting, set dressing, performance pass, review | Playtest feedback forcing layout changes after the art pass |
| Audio and dialogue | Spec or script, creation or recording, implementation, mix, review | Waiting for final animation timing or late script changes |
- Set [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) per step so work flows instead of piling up in front of busy specialists.
- Measure throughput (assets finished per week) per pipeline, not just per person.
- Find the constraint and plan around it, as described in the [theory of constraints](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/theory-of-constraints/): if rigging is the bottleneck, adding concept artists only makes the queue longer.
- Approve concepts and greyboxes before expensive final art starts, so late feedback does not discard finished work.

### QA, bug management and certification
Testing in games is continuous, but it peaks between alpha and launch. Agree severity levels early and use them to define milestone bug thresholds.
| Severity | Typical definition | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Critical (or A) | Crash, data loss, progression blocker or certification failure | Game crashes when loading chapter 3 |
| Major (or B) | Serious issue with a workaround or that badly affects experience | Quest marker points to the wrong place |
| Minor (or C) | Noticeable but does not affect play | Texture flicker on a distant building |
| Trivial | Cosmetic or very rare | Typo in credits |

#### Plan certification as a project in its own right
Console platform holders publish technical requirements that games must meet before release: PlayStation uses its Technical Requirements Checklist (TRC), Xbox uses the Xbox Requirements (XRs) and Nintendo runs Lotcheck. The documents are confidential and available to registered developers, so read them early, assign an owner and build compliance checks into regular test passes. PC and mobile stores have their own review processes too.
- Book submission dates with the platform or publisher well ahead of launch.
- Run a full internal compliance pass before the release candidate.
- Allow time for at least one failure and resubmission.
- Track age ratings, store assets and legal text as tasks with owners.

### Live operations and post-launch
For games with ongoing updates, launch marks a change of operating model. Work becomes a continuous stream of patches, events and new content, so most live teams switch from milestone plans to a regular release cadence with Kanban for fixes and sprints for larger content drops.
- Set a predictable update rhythm (for example a hotfix lane, monthly patches and seasonal content) and publish a player-facing roadmap only for what is committed.
- Separate urgent fixes from planned content with swimlanes so incidents do not silently consume the roadmap.
- Use player data, such as retention, to decide what to build next, and keep paying down technical debt left from launch.

### Essential documents and templates
Keep documentation light and living: the goal is shared understanding, not paperwork. These documents cover most game projects.
| Document | Purpose | Template |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pitch and game design document (GDD) | Living description of vision, mechanics, systems and content | [Business requirements document template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/) adapted as a GDD |
| Production backlog | Every feature and content block, ordered by priority | [Product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/) |
| Roadmap | Milestones and major features over time | Product roadmap template |
| Milestone schedule | Phases, milestones, dependencies and key dates | [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) |
| Release plan | What ships in each milestone or update | Release plan template |
| Sprint plans | Sprint goals, capacity and selected work | [Sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) |
| Content pipeline board | Assets moving through each production step | [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) |
| Budget | Staff, outsourcing, licences, QA and contingency | [Budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) |
| Risk register | Technical, creative, staffing, platform and schedule risks | [Risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) |
| Post-mortem | What went well, what did not, what to change | [Lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) |

### KPIs for game development project management
Track a small set of measures that tell you whether the game is converging on release. Review them weekly in production and daily near launch.
| KPI | What it measures | How to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Milestone acceptance | Milestones accepted on first submission | Delivery reliability and publisher confidence |
| Feature and content completion | Planned features and assets finished against plan | Forecast whether alpha and beta dates are realistic |
| Pipeline throughput | Assets completed per week by pipeline | Spot bottlenecks and test the schedule |
| Burn rate vs plan | Monthly spend against budget | Early warning of overruns |
| Open bugs by severity | Count and trend of critical, major and minor bugs | Readiness for beta, release candidate and certification |
| Bug find vs fix rate | Bugs opened against bugs closed per week | Shows whether the team is converging |
| Performance targets | Frame rate, load times and memory on each platform | Technical quality against agreed targets |
| Crash rate | Crashes per session or hour played | Stability before and after launch |
| Overtime hours | Hours worked beyond contract per person | Leading indicator of crunch and burnout |
| Player retention (live games) | Share of players returning after 1, 7 and 30 days | Guides live ops content priorities |

### Common mistakes in game production
- **Rushing pre-production.** Production starts before the fun or the pipeline is proven, so content is rebuilt later.
- **Scheduling from the pitch.** Replace early guesses with vertical slice data.
- **Vague milestone definitions.** 'Alpha' means different things to different people unless it is written down.
- **Treating QA as the last phase.** Late bugs are slower to fix and eat into certification time.
- **Ignoring cross-discipline dependencies.** Animation waiting on rigs, or audio on final timing, creates hidden queues.
- **Underestimating localisation and certification.** Both have lead times that cannot be compressed at the end.

### Software for game development project management
Studios combine development tools with a production management tool. A typical stack includes:
- **Game engine and build pipeline**, with automated builds so a playable version is always available.
- **Version control that handles large binary files**, such as art and audio, alongside code.
- **A bug tracker** with severity, platform and build fields.
- **A production management tool** for backlogs, sprints, milestone timelines, pipeline boards and dashboards across disciplines.
- **Review and approval tools** for concept art, cinematics, trailers and store assets.
- **Documentation space** for the GDD, pipelines and onboarding.
Many engineering-led studios use [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) for backlogs, sprints and bug tracking. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), the top tool in our rankings, suits studios and publishers that want milestone timelines, Kanban pipeline boards, workload views and proofing for art, video and marketing assets in one platform, which helps when development, marketing and localisation need to share one plan.
Small indie teams often start with a simple board and a shared spreadsheet, then move to a dedicated tool once several disciplines and an external partner are involved. Large studios add multi-team release planning and dependency maps; for indie teams, ruthless scope control matters most.
Game teams share many habits with other creative fields, especially around feedback and approvals.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is game development project management?**
It is the planning, scheduling, budgeting and coordination of a game from concept and pre-production through production, testing, certification and launch to live operations. It combines software delivery with creative content production and relies on playtesting to find what is fun.

**Q: What are the phases of game development?**
The usual phases are concept, pre-production, production, alpha, beta, release candidate and certification, and launch with live operations. Studios name and split them differently, so agree definitions for your own project.

**Q: What is the difference between a game producer and a project manager?**
In most studios they are the same job. Where both exist, the producer owns scope, priorities and trade-offs with the creative director, while project managers or development managers run detailed scheduling, tracking and coordination for a team or discipline.

**Q: What is a vertical slice in game development?**
A short, playable section of the game at near-final quality in gameplay, art, audio and UI. It proves the vision and the pipeline and shows how long content really takes, so it is used to rebuild production estimates and often to secure funding.

**Q: What is the difference between alpha and beta in game development?**
Alpha usually means feature complete and playable from start to finish, possibly with placeholder content. Beta usually means content complete, with the focus on bug fixing, polish, balancing and performance. Definitions vary, so write them down with your publisher.

**Q: Is Scrum used in game development?**
Yes. Many studios run feature teams in Scrum sprints during production, with a playable build at each sprint review. They usually combine it with a milestone plan for publisher gates and Kanban for art pipelines, bug fixing and live ops.

**Q: How do you avoid crunch in game development?**
Schedule from vertical slice data, plan to around 80% capacity, keep a live cut list, protect feature and content lock dates, buffer external dates and escalate schedule risk early. Treat regular overtime as a sign the plan needs to change.

**Q: What is a cut list?**
A prioritised list of features and content that the team has agreed to remove first if time or money runs short. Keeping it visible from the start makes scope cuts a planned decision rather than a late crisis.

**Q: What is a game design document?**
A GDD is a living document describing the game's vision, mechanics, systems, content and technical constraints. Modern teams keep it short and update it as playtests change the design, often in a wiki linked to the backlog.

**Q: How long does it take to make a game?**
It depends on scope, team size and platforms. Small games can take months, while large productions often take several years. The reliable way to estimate is to measure content costs in a vertical slice and build the schedule from those rates.

**Q: How do you budget a game?**
Estimate person-months per phase and multiply by a fully loaded monthly cost, then add outsourcing, licences, QA, localisation, marketing assets and a contingency. Track monthly burn rate against plan to catch overruns early.

**Q: What software do game studios use for project management?**
Studios combine an engine, version control for large files, a bug tracker and a production tool. Jira is common in engineering-led studios; Wrike suits studios and publishers that want timelines, pipeline boards and asset approvals in one place. Compare tools in our [rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/).

# Government Project Management: Phases, Roles & Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/government-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Government project management explained: the gated life cycle, business cases, procurement, funding years, roles, methods, KPIs and worked examples.


## Government Project Management: Phases, Roles & Examples
Government project management is the planning and delivery of publicly funded projects, from a council's new online service to national infrastructure, under rules for accountability, procurement, spending control and value for money. The core methods are the same as anywhere else, but business case approvals, procurement law, financial years, independent assurance and public scrutiny shape every plan. This guide covers the gated life cycle, the rules that apply, a step-by-step process, two worked examples, roles, methods, KPIs, tools and certifications.
- Published 27 August 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Government projects are judged on public value and accountability, not profit, so decisions, options and assumptions must be recorded and defensible.
- Most public projects follow a gated life cycle tied to the business case; in the UK that means a strategic outline, outline and full business case under the Green Book five case model.
- Treat procurement, approvals and assurance reviews as scheduled tasks on the critical path, not background admin.
- Plan spend by financial year as well as in total: a slipped contract award can leave money unspent and create pressure in the following year.
- Agile delivery works well in government when funding, procurement and assurance are set up for iterative work from the start.

### What is government project management?
**Government project management** is the application of project management to temporary initiatives funded and owned by public bodies. It covers defining the need, appraising options, securing approval and funding, buying goods and services under procurement law, delivering the change and proving the benefits, while staying accountable to ministers or elected members, auditors and the public.
It happens in central and federal government departments, state and regional governments, local councils and municipalities, and in agencies and arm's-length bodies such as regulators, health bodies and transport authorities. Projects range from a six-month process improvement in one team to programmes lasting a decade.
| Project type | Example | Main risk to plan for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Infrastructure and capital | Roads, flood defences, schools, hospitals, depots | Cost and schedule overruns, planning consents, supplier capacity |
| Digital public services | Online applications, payments, case management, a new citizen portal | Legacy systems, data migration, accessibility and take-up |
| Policy implementation | A new benefit, grant scheme, licensing regime or regulation | Fixed legal start dates and changing policy detail |
| Back-office and IT | Finance or HR system replacement, cloud migration | Business disruption and procurement lead times |
| Estates and facilities | Office consolidation, net zero retrofits | Funding across financial years and building constraints |
| Service redesign | Merging contact centres, reducing permit backlogs | Staff consultation and maintaining service during change |
Larger projects are often grouped into programmes and portfolios; see [programme vs project vs portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/program-vs-project-vs-portfolio-management/).

### Government vs private sector project management
Planning, scheduling, risk and stakeholder techniques transfer directly between sectors. What changes is the environment around the project: who decides, how money flows, how suppliers are chosen and how success is judged.
| Factor | Private sector | Government |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Measure of success | Profit, market share, customer growth | Public value, policy outcomes, value for money, service quality |
| Funding | Allocated by the business, can be moved quickly | Approved through budget or spending processes, often by financial year, with limits on moving money between budget lines |
| Decision-making | Executives and boards | Ministers, elected members, accounting officers and formal approval boards |
| Buying from suppliers | Company policy; free to negotiate | Public procurement law, published tenders, equal treatment of bidders |
| Transparency | Mostly internal | Audit, parliamentary or council scrutiny, freedom of information requests, published performance data |
| Users | Chosen target market | Everyone entitled to the service, including people with disabilities and low digital skills |
| Risk appetite | Varies; failure can be absorbed as a business loss | Usually low; failures become public and political |
The result is more documentation, more approvals and longer lead times. Plan for them, make the approval path visible early and keep paperwork proportionate to risk.

### Rules and frameworks that shape public projects
Rules differ by country and level of government, so check the guidance that applies to you. The examples below come mainly from the UK and US federal government.

#### Business cases and appraisal
In the UK, HM Treasury's **Green Book** sets out how central government appraises options. The 2026 edition, first published in March 2026, keeps the **five case model**: the strategic case (why change is needed), the economic case (which option gives best public value), the commercial case (whether a viable deal can be struck), the financial case (whether it is affordable) and the management case (whether it can be delivered). A project business case is usually developed in three stages: a strategic outline case (SOC), an outline business case (OBC) and a full business case (FBC) after procurement. The Green Book also tells appraisers to adjust explicitly for **optimism bias**, the proven tendency to underestimate costs and durations and overestimate benefits. Our [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) can be adapted to this structure.

#### Procurement law
Public bodies must buy goods, works and services through regulated, competitive processes. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland the Procurement Act 2023 has applied since 24 February 2025. US federal agencies follow the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), and EU member states apply national rules based on the EU procurement directives. Whatever the regime, procurement adds weeks or months and limits how freely you can change a supplier or contract later, so involve commercial colleagues before the business case is final. Our guide to [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) covers the process, contract types and bid evaluation in detail.

#### Assurance and portfolio oversight
Large public projects face independent assurance at key decision points. In the UK, the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (NISTA) was formed on 1 April 2025 by merging the Infrastructure and Projects Authority with the National Infrastructure Commission. It oversees the Government Major Projects Portfolio (GMPP) and publishes an annual report in which each project carries a **delivery confidence assessment** (DCA) of red, amber or green: an assessment of the likelihood of the project delivering its objectives to time and cost. The SRO provides the rating each quarter. Departments are expected to follow the Government Project Delivery Functional Standard.
In the US, the Program Management Improvement and Accountability Act (PMIAA) of December 2016 requires the 24 CFO Act agencies to designate a Program Management Improvement Officer, and OMB memo M-18-19 (June 2018) added portfolio reviews and workforce development.

#### Accessibility and digital standards
Public services must work for everyone. UK public sector websites and apps must meet WCAG 2.2 at level AA and publish an accessibility statement. In the US, the Department of Justice's ADA Title II rule requires state and local government web content and apps to meet WCAG 2.1 level AA; in April 2026 the compliance dates were extended by one year, to April 2027 for larger entities and April 2028 for smaller ones. Federal agencies also apply Section 508. Digital services in the UK follow the GOV.UK Service Standard and are assessed as they move between phases.
Tip
Build a one-page "rules register" at the start of every public project: which appraisal guidance, procurement regime, spending controls, assurance reviews, accessibility rules and data protection requirements apply, and who in your organisation owns each. It saves weeks of rework later.

### The government project life cycle
Phase names vary by country and agency, but most public projects follow a gated life cycle in which each phase ends with an approval tied to the business case. The table shows a typical sequence using UK terms.
| Phase | What happens | Gate or approval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Mandate | Problem, policy objective or legal duty defined; SRO appointed | Mandate from minister, council, cabinet or agency head |
| 2. Strategic outline | Case for change, SMART objectives, long list and short list of options including do minimum | Strategic outline case (SOC) approved |
| 3. Outline business case | Short-listed options appraised in detail; preferred option, procurement route and funding identified | Outline business case (OBC) approved; spending approval to procure |
| 4. Procurement | Specification, tender, evaluation, negotiation and contract award under procurement rules | Full business case (FBC) approved; contract signed |
| 5. Delivery | Build, configure or construct; board reporting, change control and assurance reviews | Stage boundary reviews |
| 6. Transition to live | Handover to operations, training, public communications, decommissioning old systems | Readiness (go-live) review |
| 7. Benefits and closure | Benefits tracked against the business case; lessons shared | Post-implementation or benefits review |
Digital services often run an Agile life cycle inside delivery. The UK Government Digital Service model uses **discovery** (understand users and the problem), **alpha** (test ideas with prototypes), **beta** (build the real service, private then public) and **live**, with service assessments before public beta and before live.
Gates are not a reason to stop work. Prepare the next phase while approvals run, and show each approval as a dated task in your [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/).

### How to run a government project step by step
These steps follow a medium-sized public project from mandate to benefits review. Scale the formality to size and risk.
1. **Confirm the mandate and appoint the SRO.** Record the policy objective or legal duty, who commissioned the work and the SRO who will own the benefits.
2. **Build the rules register.** List the appraisal guidance, spending approvals, procurement regime, assurance reviews, accessibility and data protection requirements that apply, with an owner for each.
3. **Define outcomes and benefits.** Write measurable objectives and a benefits map: what will change for citizens, staff or the public purse, how you will measure it and who will report it after the project closes.
4. **Appraise options honestly.** Include a do-minimum option, compare costs and benefits over the whole life of each option and adjust for optimism bias. A [cost-benefit analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-benefit-analysis/) structure works for smaller cases.
5. **Plan procurement early.** Agree the route to market with commercial colleagues, check whether an existing framework agreement can be used and put realistic tender durations into the schedule.
6. **Set up governance.** Create a project board with clear terms of reference, tolerances for time, cost and scope, and an escalation route. Our guide to [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) shows how to size it.
7. **Baseline the plan by financial year.** Build the schedule, then profile costs by month and financial year so finance can see in-year spend, not just the total.
8. **Deliver in stages with regular reporting.** Use stage boundaries or sprint reviews to show working outputs, update the risk register and RAID log, and report delivery confidence honestly to the board.
9. **Prepare the live service.** Train staff, update processes, plan assisted routes for people who cannot use digital channels and agree who owns the service after handover.
10. **Close and prove the benefits.** Hold a closure review, record [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) where other teams can find them and hand benefits tracking to the business owner with dates for follow-up reviews.

### Worked example: replacing a council's parking permit service
This illustrative example follows a local council replacing a paper-based residents' parking permit process with an online service and a new back-office system bought through a compliant procurement.
| Phase | Duration (illustrative) | Key outputs | Gate or decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mandate and SOC | 4 weeks | Problem statement, options long list, SRO named (head of parking services) | Cabinet member approves SOC |
| Discovery | 8 weeks | User research with residents and staff, map of current process, data on permit volumes | Board agrees to proceed to alpha |
| Alpha and OBC | 10 weeks | Prototype journey tested with residents, preferred option (buy a configurable system), cost estimate with optimism bias | OBC approved; budget released to procure |
| Procurement | 14 weeks | Specification, evaluation criteria, call-off from a framework, clarification questions, award | FBC approved; contract signed |
| Private beta | 12 weeks | System configured, data migrated for one permit zone, accessibility audit, staff trained | Service assessment before public beta |
| Public beta | 8 weeks | All zones live online; paper route kept as an assisted option | Readiness review |
| Live and closure | Ongoing; review at 6 months | Old system decommissioned, benefits tracked (processing time, online take-up, staff hours) | Benefits review |
Three lessons come out of planning it this way:
- **Procurement is the longest single phase** before delivery starts. Putting it in the plan as a 14-week block, with its own tasks and owner, stops it being treated as something that happens in the background.
- **Discovery changes the scope.** In this example, research shows many residents renew permits for visitors, so visitor permits move into the first release. Recording why scope changed protects the team when auditors ask later.
- **The assisted route is a requirement.** Keeping a phone and paper option for residents who cannot use the online service is part of the design, budget and staffing plan, not an afterthought.

### Worked example: optimism bias and in-year spend
Two calculations catch many public project managers out. Both examples use illustrative figures, not official uplift percentages.

#### Adjusting an estimate for optimism bias
A team estimates its new case management system at **£2.0 million** and **18 months**. The Green Book requires appraisers to adjust for optimism bias, and HM Treasury's supplementary guidance gives ranges by project type. Suppose the organisation applies an uplift of 25% to capital cost and 20% to duration for this kind of project.
| Item | Base estimate | Illustrative uplift | Adjusted figure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capital cost | £2,000,000 | 25% | £2,500,000 |
| Duration | 18 months | 20% | 21.6 months (about 22) |
The adjusted figures go into the appraisal so options are compared fairly. As risks are identified and priced, the uplift is reduced and replaced by specific risk allowances. Contingency is different: it is money held against known risks, while optimism bias corrects a systematic tendency to underestimate. See our [contingency plan guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) for how to size and release contingency.

#### Profiling spend across financial years
A council project has **£600,000** of capital budget available in the current financial year (April to March). The plan assumes the contract is awarded on 1 October, so most spend falls in the second half of the year.
| Quarter | Planned spend | What happens | Actual or forecast |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q1 (Apr to Jun) | £40,000 | Discovery team | £40,000 actual |
| Q2 (Jul to Sep) | £60,000 | Alpha and procurement | £60,000 actual |
| Q3 (Oct to Dec) | £200,000 | Contract mobilisation and first payments | £90,000 actual (award slipped to 1 December) |
| Q4 (Jan to Mar) | £300,000 | Build and configuration milestones | £360,000 forecast (supplier can absorb some catch-up) |
| Total | £600,000 |  | £550,000 forecast |
A two-month slip in contract award leaves a forecast **£50,000 underspend** (about 8% of the year's budget). Depending on local finance rules, the money may not carry forward automatically, and next year's budget may already be committed. The project manager's options include:
- Tell finance early, in the month the slip happens, so the money can be re-profiled or released for other priorities rather than lost.
- Request a carry-forward or re-profiling through the formal process, with a clear explanation of the cause.
- Bring forward spend that was always planned and is genuinely ready, such as hardware or licences, without paying for work before it is delivered.
- Record the slip in the [schedule variance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/schedule-variance/) reporting and in the risk register for next year's profile.
Tip
Never rush spending into the last month of the financial year just to avoid an underspend. Auditors look for exactly this pattern, and paying in advance for undelivered work breaks most public finance rules.

### Key roles in a government project
| Role | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Senior responsible owner (SRO) or executive sponsor | Personally accountable for the project meeting its objectives and delivering its benefits; chairs or leads the board; reports delivery confidence |
| Project board or steering committee | Approves stages, tolerances and major changes; resolves escalated issues |
| Project or programme manager | Day-to-day planning, control, reporting, risk management and supplier coordination |
| Commercial and procurement lead | Chooses the route to market, runs compliant procurement and manages the contract |
| Finance business partner | Tracks budget against spending controls, profiles and financial year limits |
| Policy lead | Makes sure the project still serves the policy intent as details change |
| Service owner or product owner | Owns the live service and makes product decisions in digital projects |
| Assurance reviewers and auditors | Independent checks on readiness, value for money and governance |
Public projects often span several organisations. Map them early, agree who decides what and keep a decision log. Our guide to [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) covers mapping and engagement techniques.

### Methodologies that fit government projects
| Approach | Best for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PRINCE2 | UK and many Commonwealth and European public bodies | Developed for UK government; the business case, project board, stages and tolerances map neatly onto public governance |
| PMBOK-based stage-gate | Agencies in the US and elsewhere; capital projects | Formal baselines and gate reviews suit audit requirements |
| Earned value management | Large defence, space and infrastructure contracts | US FAR 34.201 requires an earned value management system for major development acquisitions, following OMB Circular A-11 and the EIA-748 standard |
| Agile | Digital services and internal software | Standard for government digital work; needs procurement and funding that allow iterative delivery |
| Hybrid | Programmes mixing policy, procurement and digital delivery | Gated business case approvals outside, Agile delivery teams inside |
| Lean | Casework, permits, licensing and back-office services | Good for reducing backlogs and processing times |
Most departments do not pick one method for everything. A typical pattern is [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) or a [PMBOK-based](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmbok-guide/) stage-gate approach for governance and funding, with Agile teams delivering the digital parts. If your delivery team works in sprints but funding is approved in stages, agree with finance and assurance early how progress will be reported: working features and outcomes, not percentage complete.
See our guide to [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) for the calculations used on large government contracts.

### Essential documents and templates
Keep documents proportionate, but expect to produce these on most public projects:
- **Business case:** SOC, OBC and FBC, or your government's equivalent. Start from the [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/).
- **Mandate and project charter or PID:** authority, objectives, scope, tolerances and SRO. A [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) covers the essentials.
- **Requirements and [statement of work](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/):** outcome-based specifications, so bidders propose how to meet user needs.
- **Quotations:** an [RFQ template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/rfq-template/) for lower-value purchases within your procurement thresholds.
- **Cost estimate and budget:** split by financial year, funding source and capital versus revenue.
- **RAID log:** risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies reviewed at every board. Use our [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/).
- **Schedule:** with procurement lead times, approvals and assurance reviews shown as real tasks.
- **Change requests:** a formal record of every scope, cost or time change; see the [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/).
- **Benefits realisation plan:** baseline measures, targets, owners and review dates.
- **Lessons learned:** many bodies require lessons to be shared across departments.

### KPIs for government projects
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delivery confidence assessment | Likelihood of delivering objectives to time and cost, rated red, amber or green | Board, assurance and portfolio reporting |
| Schedule and cost variance | Progress and spend against the baseline | Monthly board reports; earned value on large contracts |
| In-year spend vs profile | Actual and forecast spend against the financial year profile | Avoiding underspend or overspend |
| Benefits realised | Cash and non-cash benefits against the business case | Benefits and post-implementation reviews |
| Service performance | Processing times, digital take-up, completion rates, user satisfaction | Digital and operational services |
| Accessibility conformance | Conformance with WCAG and assisted digital support | Service assessments and accessibility statements |
| Procurement cycle time | Time from approved requirement to contract award | Planning future projects |
Report delivery confidence as an honest judgement. NISTA stresses that a red rating does not mean a project will fail; it means significant issues need urgent attention. Boards that punish early red ratings get late ones instead.

### Common challenges and how to handle them
- **Long procurement lead times.** Put procurement on the critical path from day one, check existing frameworks and engage commercial colleagues before the business case is final.
- **Optimism bias.** Adjust early estimates, use reference data from similar projects and replace the uplift with priced risks as the design matures.
- **Changing political priorities.** Tie the project to outcomes and record decisions, so a new minister or administration can see why choices were made and what stopping would cost.
- **Legacy systems and data.** Plan discovery work on old systems and data quality before committing to go-live dates.
- **Portfolio overload.** A departmental [PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) with a clear portfolio view stops too many projects competing for the same specialists.
See our guide to [infrastructure project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/infrastructure-project-management/) for capital-heavy public projects such as roads, rail and utilities.

### Software for government project management
Public bodies need tools that satisfy security, data residency and accessibility requirements as well as project needs. Look for:
- Gantt charts with baselines, dependencies and critical path.
- Portfolio dashboards for departmental PMOs and boards.
- Audit trails, role-based permissions and single sign-on.
- Data residency options and the security certifications your organisation requires, such as FedRAMP for US federal cloud services; always confirm the vendor's current status directly.
- Availability on your government's procurement frameworks, which can shorten buying time considerably.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), our top-ranked tool, is a strong all-in-one option for public sector PMOs that need portfolio reporting, Gantt planning, request intake and custom workflows in one place. It offers granular permissions and Wrike Lock for customer-controlled encryption keys; confirm its current certifications against your accreditation requirements. [Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/) is available in Microsoft's government clouds, which simplifies buying for organisations already on Microsoft 365. [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/) lists FedRAMP among the certifications in its trust centre and suits spreadsheet-minded PMOs. Specialist earned value and case management tools often sit alongside them.
Compare all ten tools in our [project management tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/).

### Certifications for government project managers
No single certificate is required everywhere, but several are widely recognised in the public sector:
| Certification | Where it is valued | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PMP (PMI) | Worldwide, including many US agencies and contractors | Requires 3, 4 or 5 years of project experience in the last 10 years depending on education (2 with a GAC-accredited degree) plus 35 contact hours or CAPM; exam updated July 2026 |
| PRINCE2 | UK, Europe, Australia and other Commonwealth governments | Method closely aligned with UK public governance |
| FAC-P/PM | US federal civilian agencies | Federal Acquisition Certification for Program and Project Managers, with entry, mid and senior levels |
| Government-run accreditation | Varies by country | Some governments run their own project delivery profession accreditation and leadership programmes |
See our [PMP certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) for the full exam structure and the July 2026 changes.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is government project management?**
It is the planning and delivery of publicly funded projects under rules for accountability, procurement, spending control and value for money, from local council services to national infrastructure and digital public services.

**Q: How is government project management different from private sector project management?**
Government projects are judged on public value rather than profit, are funded through formal budget processes tied to financial years, must follow procurement law, face public scrutiny and must serve every eligible citizen.

**Q: What are the phases of a government project?**
A typical sequence is mandate, strategic outline case, outline business case, procurement and full business case, delivery, transition to live service, and benefits realisation and closure. Digital services add discovery, alpha, beta and live phases inside delivery.

**Q: What is a senior responsible owner?**
The SRO is the individual personally accountable for a project or programme meeting its objectives and delivering its benefits. In UK central government, SROs also provide the quarterly delivery confidence rating for major projects.

**Q: What is the five case model?**
It is the UK structure for business cases set out in HM Treasury guidance and the Green Book. It covers the strategic, economic, commercial, financial and management cases, and is developed in stages as a strategic outline, outline and full business case.

**Q: What is optimism bias in a business case?**
It is the tendency for appraisals to underestimate costs and durations and overestimate benefits. The Green Book asks appraisers to adjust for it explicitly, with uplifts reduced as risks are identified and priced.

**Q: Which project management methodology does government use?**
PRINCE2 is common in the UK and Europe, PMBOK-based stage-gate approaches elsewhere, earned value management on major US development acquisitions and Agile for digital services. Many programmes are hybrid.

**Q: Can Agile work in government?**
Yes. Government digital teams routinely deliver in short iterations through discovery, alpha, beta and live phases. It works best when funding and assurance accept working software as evidence of progress.

**Q: Why do government projects fail?**
Common causes include unclear objectives, optimistic estimates, procurement delays, changing political priorities, weak senior ownership, legacy systems and too many projects competing for the same people.

**Q: What is a delivery confidence assessment?**
It is a rating of how likely a project is to deliver its objectives to time and cost. UK major projects are rated red, amber or green in NISTA's annual report; a red rating signals significant issues needing urgent attention, not certain failure.

**Q: What certifications help in government project management?**
PMP and PRINCE2 are widely recognised. US federal civilian program and project managers use the FAC-P/PM certification, and some governments run their own project delivery accreditation.

**Q: What KPIs are used for government projects?**
Delivery confidence, schedule and cost variance, in-year spend against profile, benefits realised, service performance such as processing times and digital take-up, accessibility conformance and procurement cycle time.

**Q: What software do government agencies use for project management?**
Agencies use work management platforms such as Wrike, Microsoft Planner and Smartsheet, provided they meet security and data residency requirements, alongside specialist earned value, contract and case management systems.
