# Healthcare Project Management: Phases, Roles and Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/healthcare-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Healthcare project management explained: clinical safety, phases, roles, methods, a worked EHR go-live example, KPIs, templates and software.


## Healthcare Project Management: Phases, Roles and Examples
Healthcare project management is the planning and delivery of change in hospitals, clinics and health systems, such as electronic health record (EHR) rollouts, new clinical pathways, facility upgrades and quality improvement work. It uses the same core methods as any project, but patient safety, health data regulation, services that run around the clock and scarce clinician time change the priorities. This guide covers the life cycle, clinical safety, roles, methods, two worked examples, KPIs, templates and software.
- Published 27 August 2026
- Last updated 16 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Healthcare project management puts patient safety, clinical governance and data protection at the centre of planning.
- Keep a project risk register and a clinical hazard log, cross-referenced, and make clinical safety sign-off a formal gate.
- Most large programmes are stage-gated overall, with Lean, PDSA or Agile cycles used inside workstreams.
- Clinician engagement, training readiness and a controlled go-live decide success more than the plan itself.
- Plan training and backfill as real costs: releasing staff from wards is often the biggest hidden effort.
- Keep patient-identifiable data out of project tools unless the vendor's compliance position has been confirmed.

### What is healthcare project management?
**Healthcare project management** is the application of [project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) methods to temporary initiatives in health and care organisations, with patient safety, clinical governance and health data protection built into every stage. A healthcare project manager coordinates clinical, operational, IT, estates and supplier teams to deliver change without disrupting care.
It happens in acute hospitals, health systems and NHS trusts, primary care networks, community and mental health services, public health bodies and the suppliers that build health technology. Projects range from a single-ward improvement to multi-year, multi-site programmes.
| Project type | Example | Main risk to plan for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clinical systems and digital | EHR or electronic prescribing rollout, patient portal, lab system replacement | Clinical safety, data migration and downtime |
| Clinical pathway redesign | Same-day emergency care, a new stroke pathway, virtual wards | Clinician buy-in and unintended effects on other services |
| Quality improvement | Reducing falls, improving discharge times, cutting medication errors | Measurement and sustaining the change |
| Capital and estates | New theatre suite, ward refurbishment, imaging equipment installation | Infection control, decanting patients, keeping services running |
| Regulatory and compliance | Preparing for an inspection, accreditation or a new reporting requirement | Fixed deadlines and evidence of compliance |
| Service mergers and reconfiguration | Merging two departments or moving services between sites | Staff consultation, patient access and public engagement |
| Workforce and training | Rolling out a new competency framework or role | Releasing staff from clinical duties |

### What makes healthcare projects different
A late office move is an inconvenience; a badly planned change to a medication workflow can harm patients. That one difference shifts the emphasis towards clinical risk, testing, training and controlled go-lives.

#### Patient safety and clinical risk
Changes to clinical systems or pathways can introduce new hazards, such as a wrong default dose or a missed alert. They need a structured clinical risk assessment and sign-off by an appropriately qualified clinician.

#### Health data is heavily regulated
Health records are among the most sensitive data an organisation holds. Privacy law, information governance rules and supplier contracts shape what systems you can use and how data moves during the project.

#### Services cannot stop
Wards, emergency departments and many clinics run 24 hours a day, every day. Cutovers, downtime and training must fit around rotas, bank holidays and seasonal peaks such as winter.

#### Clinician time is scarce
Doctors, nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals are the essential subject matter experts, but they can only be released from clinical duties with notice and backfill.

#### Many stakeholders hold a veto
Clinical leads, nursing and medical directors, information governance, IT, estates, infection prevention, finance, staff side representatives and sometimes patients and the public all need to be engaged. Our guide to [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) covers the techniques.

#### Inspection and accreditation
Regulators and accrediting bodies, such as the Care Quality Commission (CQC) in England or The Joint Commission in the US, expect organisations to show that changes were governed and safe. Good project records double as evidence.

### Clinical safety and information governance
This is the part of healthcare project management with no real equivalent in most other sectors. Treat it as a workstream with its own owner, plan and gates, not as a checklist at the end.

#### Project risks vs clinical hazards
A **project risk** threatens the project's objectives, such as a late go-live or a budget overrun. A **clinical hazard** is a potential source of harm to a patient, such as a drug interaction alert that fails to fire. Keep them in separate logs, owned by different people, but cross-reference them: a delayed test cycle (project risk) may leave a hazard unmitigated.
|  | Project risk register | Clinical hazard log |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concerned with | Scope, time, cost, quality, benefits | Potential harm to patients |
| Owned by | Project manager | Clinical safety lead or Clinical Safety Officer |
| Scored by | Probability and impact on the project | Likelihood and severity of harm |
| Closed when | The risk passes or is managed | The hazard is mitigated to an acceptable level and signed off |
| Template | [Risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) | Organisation's clinical safety format |
An example hazard log entry for an electronic prescribing project might read: **Hazard:** a prescriber selects the wrong patient from a similar-name list. **Cause:** patient search shows names without date of birth. **Effect:** a medicine is prescribed to the wrong patient. **Controls:** show date of birth and hospital number in search results, wristband scanning at administration, training on patient identification. **Residual risk:** assessed and accepted by the Clinical Safety Officer before go-live.

#### Standards and rules to know
- **England:** health IT is governed by the clinical risk management standards DCB0129 (for manufacturers) and DCB0160 (for organisations deploying and using systems), each requiring a named Clinical Safety Officer. NHS England ran a consultation on revisions to both standards from June to September 2026, so check the current versions before you plan.
- **England, buying digital tools:** NHS organisations use the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC) to assess digital health technologies. NHS England published an updated DTAC form and guidance in March 2026.
- **UK and EU data protection:** health data is special category data under UK GDPR and GDPR, so new systems or new uses of patient data normally need a data protection impact assessment (DPIA).
- **United States:** HIPAA governs protected health information (PHI). A vendor that creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI on your behalf is a business associate and needs a business associate agreement (BAA).
- **Medical device software:** some clinical software is regulated as a medical device (by the MHRA in the UK or the FDA in the US), which adds manufacturer obligations. Confirm the classification with the supplier.
Tip
Rules change and vary by country and setting. Ask your clinical safety and information governance leads which standards apply before the plan is baselined, and put their approvals in the schedule as gates.

### Healthcare project life cycle
Most healthcare organisations use a staged, governance-heavy life cycle, even when individual workstreams use Agile methods. A typical clinical system project runs through seven phases.
| Phase | What happens | Typical gate or output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Case for change | Problem defined with clinical and operational data; options appraised; funding sought | Approved business case |
| 2. Initiation | Sponsor, clinical lead and governance confirmed; scope, budget and benefits agreed | [Project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) or project initiation document |
| 3. Clinical design | Current and future workflows mapped with clinicians; configuration specified | Signed-off workflows; initial hazard assessment |
| 4. Build and test | Configuration, integrations (lab, pharmacy, imaging), data migration; system, integration and user acceptance testing | Test exit report; hazard log updated |
| 5. Training and readiness | Role-based training, super users, cutover rehearsals, go/no-go criteria agreed | Go/no-go decision; clinical safety sign-off |
| 6. Go-live and stabilisation | Cutover, command centre, at-the-elbow support, rapid issue triage | Stabilisation exit criteria met |
| 7. Optimisation and closure | Fixes and enhancements, benefits tracking, handover to business as usual, lessons learned | Closure report; benefits review |

#### How this maps to the standard project phases
If you know the classic phases of initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing, phases 1 and 2 are initiation, phase 3 is detailed planning and design, phases 4 to 6 are execution, and phase 7 is closure. The healthcare version makes clinical design, safety sign-off and stabilisation visible as their own stages. Smaller quality improvement projects use a much lighter cycle, covered in the second worked example below.

### How to run a healthcare project step by step
Use these steps for any healthcare project and scale the governance to its size and clinical risk.
1. **Define the problem with data.** Describe the clinical or operational problem and its current measures, for example average time from discharge decision to departure.
2. **Secure an executive sponsor and a clinical lead.** The sponsor owns benefits and funding; the clinical lead owns clinical decisions and brings peers with them.
3. **Agree governance early.** Confirm the project board, clinical safety lead, information governance contact and how decisions are escalated.
4. **Write the charter.** Purpose, scope, out of scope, benefits, budget (including backfill), milestones and gates. Our [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) covers the essentials.
5. **Map stakeholders and staff groups.** List every role affected, how they will be engaged and when they need training.
6. **Plan around the clinical calendar.** Add rota changes, resident doctor rotation dates, bank holidays and winter pressures before scheduling go-lives.
7. **Design with clinicians, not for them.** Run short, focused design sessions and let clinical leads present decisions to their peers.
8. **Run safety and governance alongside delivery.** Keep the hazard log, DPIA and test evidence up to date as the design changes.
9. **Decide go-live on evidence.** Use pre-agreed go/no-go criteria, and rehearse cutover and rollback.
10. **Support, stabilise, then close.** Provide at-the-elbow support, triage issues daily, measure benefits and capture [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) before the next site goes live.

### Worked example: rolling out electronic prescribing across a hospital
A 600-bed hospital is replacing paper drug charts with an electronic prescribing and medicines administration (EPMA) system across 30 inpatient wards. The chief nurse is the sponsor, a consultant physician is the clinical lead, a pharmacist is the Clinical Safety Officer and a project manager coordinates the programme. The figures below are illustrative.

#### Choosing the rollout approach
A single big-bang go-live would demand training every staff group at once and leave no room to learn. The project board chooses a phased rollout: two pilot wards first, then waves of seven wards every three weeks. The trade-off is a period where patients moving between wards switch between paper and electronic charts, which is logged as a clinical hazard with specific controls for transfers.

#### Sizing training and backfill
| Staff group | Headcount | Training hours each | Total hours |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nurses and midwives | 900 | 3 | 2,700 |
| Doctors | 280 | 2 | 560 |
| Pharmacists and pharmacy technicians | 60 | 4 | 240 |
| Allied health professionals and others | 120 | 1.5 | 180 |
| Total | 1,360 |  | 3,680 |
At 7.5-hour shifts, 3,680 hours is about 490 shifts of staff time. Most of it needs backfill from bank or agency staff, so the project manager costs it into the budget and agrees release dates with ward managers ward by ward. Super users (two per ward per shift pattern) receive extra training and are rostered as supernumerary during their ward's first week live. A [training plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) keeps the sessions, attendance and completion by ward in one place.

#### Go/no-go criteria for each wave
| Criterion | Threshold agreed by the project board | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staff trained | At least 90% of each ward's rostered staff trained, and every shift covered by a trained super user | Training lead |
| Clinical hazards | No open hazards rated high; all medium hazards have controls in place | Clinical Safety Officer |
| Testing | All critical and high defects fixed and retested | Test lead |
| Devices and infrastructure | Bedside devices, scanners and Wi-Fi tested on every bay | IT lead |
| Downtime procedures | Paper backup charts and downtime process available and briefed | Ward managers |
| Support | Command centre and at-the-elbow rota confirmed for the first two weeks | Project manager |
| Operational pressure | Hospital not at its highest escalation level on the planned date | Site operations |

#### Go-live and stabilisation
1. Pharmacists transcribe current paper charts into the system for each ward the day before go-live, with a second check.
2. The ward goes live at a planned time agreed with the ward manager, avoiding medicine rounds.
3. A command centre runs daily huddles, logs issues and tracks themes; urgent clinical issues go straight to the Clinical Safety Officer.
4. Super users and floor walkers provide at-the-elbow support on every shift for the first week.
5. The project board reviews stabilisation exit criteria (for example, issue volumes falling and no unresolved safety incidents) before releasing support and starting the next wave.
Lessons from the pilot wards, such as needing more devices on drug rounds, are fed into the next wave's plan. This is the main advantage of phasing: each wave is safer than the last.

### Worked example: a quality improvement project with PDSA cycles
Not every healthcare project is a large programme. Ward-level improvements usually use the Model for Improvement, which asks three questions (what are we trying to accomplish, how will we know a change is an improvement, what changes can we make) and then tests changes in small Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles.
**Illustrative aim:** increase the share of patients discharged before noon on one medical ward over six months. **Measures:** an outcome measure (percentage of discharges before noon), a process measure (percentage of patients with a planned discharge date set within 24 hours of admission) and a balancing measure (readmissions within 30 days), all plotted weekly on a run chart.
| Cycle | Change tested | What was learned | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PDSA 1 | Next-day discharges identified at the afternoon board round for one consultant team for one week | Worked well, but medicines to take home were still late | Adapt: involve pharmacy |
| PDSA 2 | Pharmacy prepares medicines the evening before for identified patients | Fewer morning delays; transport bookings now the bottleneck | Adapt: add transport |
| PDSA 3 | Transport booked the day before for identified patients | Most planned patients left before noon | Adopt for this team |
| PDSA 4 | Process extended to all consultant teams on the ward | Some teams' board rounds are later in the day | Adapt timing, then spread |
The project management is light: a one-page charter, a simple action log, a run chart and a short weekly huddle. The discipline is in measuring, testing small and only spreading what works. For the wider toolkit behind this kind of work, see our guide to [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/).

### Key roles in a healthcare project
| Role | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Executive sponsor or senior responsible owner | Owns the business case and benefits, chairs the project board, removes organisational blockers |
| Clinical lead or chief clinical information officer | Champions the change with clinicians, leads clinical design and resolves clinical disagreements |
| Clinical Safety Officer (or clinical safety lead) | Assesses clinical hazards, maintains the hazard log and safety case, signs off clinical safety |
| Project manager | Plans and controls scope, schedule, budget, risks and reporting; coordinates workstreams; runs go-live planning |
| Information governance or privacy lead | DPIA, data sharing agreements, access controls |
| Clinical and operational subject matter experts | Describe current workflows, validate future ones and test the system |
| Super users | Front-line staff trained early to support colleagues at go-live |
| IT, integration and supplier teams | Build, configure, integrate and support the system |
| Estates and facilities | Lead building, equipment and space work |
A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) is especially useful in healthcare because clinical, technical and governance responsibilities overlap. Be explicit about who approves each clinical workflow and who signs off safety.

#### What does a healthcare project manager do?
A healthcare project manager turns a clinical or operational objective into a governed plan and keeps it moving. Typical duties include building the schedule and budget, coordinating clinical, IT, estates and supplier teams, running the project board, managing risks and issues alongside the clinical hazard log, planning training and backfill, leading go-live readiness and command centre arrangements, and reporting benefits.

#### Skills, qualifications and how to get into the role
- **Project skills:** planning, risk management, stakeholder management and clear reporting.
- **Healthcare knowledge:** how clinical teams work, clinical governance, patient flow and information governance.
- **Credibility with clinicians:** listening, translating between clinical and technical language, and respecting clinical time.
- **Certification:** many employers ask for a recognised qualification such as the [PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) or PRINCE2; see our [project management certification guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) for options.
- **Routes in:** clinicians often move in through improvement or digital roles; project managers from other sectors often start as project officers or in health IT, learning the clinical context on the job.

### Methodologies that fit healthcare projects
Choose the method by the type of change. Many programmes combine them.
| Approach | Best for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage-gate or Waterfall | Capital builds, major system procurements, regulated go-lives | Clear gates suit boards and auditors; plan safety and testing gates explicitly |
| [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) | Public health systems such as the NHS | Widely used in UK public healthcare; project boards and management by exception fit trust governance |
| Lean | Patient flow, waiting times, theatre utilisation | Value stream mapping and waste removal are well established in hospitals |
| PDSA and the Model for Improvement | Ward-level changes, pathways, clinical audit actions | Small tests of change measured on run charts |
| [Six Sigma](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/six-sigma/) | Reducing variation, for example in lab turnaround or medication errors | Often combined with Lean |
| [Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) or Scrum | Digital health apps, patient portals, in-house software | Build clinical safety review into the [definition of done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/) |
| Hybrid | EHR and EPMA programmes | Stage-gated overall, with iterative configuration and test cycles inside the build phase |
Tip
Whatever method you choose, make clinical safety sign-off and information governance approval explicit gates in the plan, not tasks someone remembers at the end.

### Essential documents and templates
Scale the document set to the project. A ward-level improvement might need a charter and a run chart; an EHR programme needs everything below.
- **Business case and [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/):** the problem, clinical and financial benefits, scope and sponsor.
- **[Work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/):** clinical design, build, integration, data migration, training, go-live and support workstreams.
- **Schedule:** planned around rotas, holidays and seasonal peaks, with gates shown as milestones.
- **[Risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) and clinical hazard log:** separate but cross-referenced.
- **DPIA and data sharing agreements:** owned by information governance.
- **[Communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/):** tailored messages for consultants, nurses, administrative staff and patients.
- **Training plan:** role-based training, super user schedule and completion tracking.
- **Go/no-go checklist and cutover plan:** including rollback and downtime procedures.
- **[Change request](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) log:** formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) once clinical design is signed off.
- **Closure report and benefits review:** what was delivered, lessons learned and who owns benefits from here.

### KPIs for healthcare projects
Track delivery measures during the project and outcome measures afterwards. Take a baseline before you start so you can show the change.
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gate adherence | Whether design sign-off, test exit and go/no-go happen on schedule | Board reporting |
| Budget variance | Actual vs planned spend, including backfill and overtime | Financial control |
| Training completion | Percentage of staff trained before go-live, by role and ward | Go/no-go readiness |
| Open clinical hazards | Number and severity of unresolved hazards | Clinical safety sign-off |
| Post go-live issues and incidents | Support tickets and patient safety incidents linked to the change | Stabilisation |
| Adoption | Share of activity recorded in the new system or pathway | Embedding the change |
| Clinical and flow outcomes | For example length of stay, waiting times, turnaround times, medication errors | Benefits review |
| Staff and patient feedback | Surveys or structured feedback | Optimisation priorities |

### Common challenges and how to handle them
- **Clinician engagement.** Involve clinicians from the start, fund backfill, keep sessions short and let clinical leads present decisions to peers.
- **Local variation.** Every ward wants its own workflow. Agree a design principle (standardise unless there is a safety reason not to) and route requests through change control.
- **Fixed go-live dates.** Contract or legacy system end dates often fix the deadline. Protect it with go/no-go criteria and a rehearsed rollback plan, not by cutting testing.
- **Data migration quality.** Start data cleansing early and run several trial loads with clinical validation.
- **Operational pressure.** Avoid go-lives in known peak periods and agree what escalation level would trigger a postponement.
- **Change fatigue.** Coordinate with other programmes through the [PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) so wards are not hit by several changes at once.
- **Declaring success at go-live.** Keep measuring adoption and outcomes for months, and budget for optimisation.

### Software for healthcare project management
Healthcare teams typically use a general work management platform for planning alongside specialist systems: EHR suppliers' implementation and testing tools, IT service management for post go-live tickets, and incident reporting systems for patient safety events. When choosing a project tool, look for:
- Gantt charts, dependencies and baselines for gated plans.
- Portfolio dashboards so a PMO can see every project and shared clinical resources.
- Request forms for intake of improvement ideas and change requests.
- Strong access controls, audit trails and single sign-on.
- A clear data position: keep patient-identifiable data out of the project tool, and if it could ever be stored there, confirm the vendor's compliance commitments (for example a HIPAA BAA in the US, or a DPIA in the UK) before you buy.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is a strong all-round option for health system PMOs because it combines Gantt planning, portfolio views, request forms and enterprise security controls in one platform.
Many healthcare projects are clinical IT projects at heart, and drug development has its own regulated life cycle.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is healthcare project management?**
Healthcare project management is the planning and delivery of projects such as EHR rollouts, clinical pathway changes, facility upgrades and quality improvement work, with patient safety, clinical governance and health data protection built into every stage.

**Q: What does a healthcare project manager do?**
They plan and control scope, schedule, budget and risk, coordinate clinical, IT, estates and supplier teams, run governance gates, plan training and backfill, lead go-live readiness and support, and report benefits.

**Q: What qualifications do you need for healthcare project management?**
Most roles ask for project management experience plus a recognised qualification such as PMP, CAPM or PRINCE2. A clinical, health IT or healthcare operations background is a strong advantage but not always required.

**Q: Can you become a healthcare project manager without a clinical background?**
Yes. Many healthcare project managers come from IT, operations or other sectors. Strong clinical leads on the project provide the clinical expertise, and you learn the context through the work. Respect for clinical time and governance matters more than a clinical qualification.

**Q: What are examples of healthcare projects?**
EHR and electronic prescribing rollouts, patient portals, new clinical pathways, virtual wards, theatre and ward refurbishments, quality improvement projects such as reducing falls, service mergers and preparation for inspections.

**Q: What are the phases of healthcare project management?**
A typical life cycle is case for change, initiation, clinical design, build and test, training and readiness, go-live and stabilisation, then optimisation and closure.

**Q: Which methodology is best for healthcare projects?**
Large system and building projects usually use stage-gate or PRINCE2, improvement work uses Lean or PDSA cycles, and digital products often use Agile. Many programmes combine them.

**Q: How is healthcare project management different from other project management?**
It adds clinical safety assessment, clinician-led design, 24/7 service continuity, health data regulation and inspection readiness to the usual concerns of scope, time and cost.

**Q: What is a Clinical Safety Officer?**
In England, a Clinical Safety Officer is a suitably qualified and registered clinician who is responsible for clinical risk management of a health IT system under the DCB0129 and DCB0160 standards, including the hazard log and safety case.

**Q: Is Agile used in healthcare?**
Yes, especially for digital health products and in-house software. Clinical safety review and governance approvals still need to be built into each release, for example through the definition of done.

**Q: What KPIs are used in healthcare projects?**
Gate adherence, budget variance, training completion, open clinical hazards, post go-live incidents, adoption, and clinical or flow outcomes such as length of stay and waiting times.

**Q: Is project management software HIPAA compliant?**
It depends on the vendor, plan and contract. If protected health information could be stored in the tool, confirm the vendor will sign a business associate agreement and configure the required controls. The safest approach is to keep patient data out of project tools.

# HR Project Management: Examples, Phases, Roles and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/hr-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: HR project management explained: examples of HR projects, a phase-by-phase plan, roles, change management, KPIs, templates and software for HR teams.


## HR Project Management: Examples, Phases, Roles and Tools
HR project management is the use of project management methods to plan and deliver people-related change, such as a new HR system, a redesigned onboarding process or a restructure. It differs from other project work because the outcome is a change in how employees are hired, paid, developed and managed, so employment law, confidentiality and adoption matter as much as the schedule. This guide covers examples, phases, roles, documents, KPIs and tools.
- Published 27 August 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- 16 min read

### Key takeaways
- HR project management applies scope, schedules, roles and risk control to people-related change.
- Typical HR projects include HRIS rollouts, onboarding redesigns, performance processes, restructures and learning programmes.
- Consultation periods, payroll cut-offs and data protection rules shape the schedule, so put them in the plan from day one.
- Adoption is the real deliverable: plan communication, manager briefings and training as workstreams with owners.
- Keep sensitive projects in restricted spaces and measure success with adoption, accuracy and employee outcomes.

### What is HR project management?
**HR project management** is the planning, coordination and control of temporary HR initiatives that change how an organisation attracts, pays, develops or manages its people. It uses the same building blocks as any [project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) discipline (a defined scope, schedule, budget, roles and risks) but adds employment law, sensitive data and employee change adoption.
It helps to separate HR projects from HR operations. Running recruitment, payroll and employee relations every month is business as usual. Redesigning the recruitment process, replacing the payroll system or introducing a new performance review is a project: it has a start, an end and a specific outcome. HR teams usually do both at once, which is one reason project discipline helps.
|  | HR operations (business as usual) | HR project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Keep people processes running | Change or improve a people process, policy or system |
| Time frame | Ongoing | Fixed start and end |
| Example | Processing monthly payroll | Moving payroll to a new provider |
| Success measure | Service levels and accuracy | Benefits delivered and change adopted |

### Examples of HR projects
Most HR projects fall into a handful of recurring types. The table shows common examples and the risk that usually needs the most attention.
| Project type | Example | Main risk to plan for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HR system (HRIS) or payroll implementation | Replacing spreadsheets and an old payroll package with a cloud HRIS | Data migration errors and payroll accuracy |
| Onboarding redesign | A structured first 90 days with pre-boarding, buddies and check-ins | Managers not following the new process |
| Performance management change | Moving from annual appraisals to quarterly check-ins | Manager capability and employee scepticism |
| Restructure or reorganisation | Merging two departments and changing reporting lines | Legal consultation duties and confidentiality |
| Policy introduction | A hybrid working or flexible working policy | Inconsistent application across teams |
| Learning and development programme | A leadership programme for first-time managers | Low attendance and no change in behaviour |
| Recruitment and employer brand | A new careers page and applicant tracking workflow | Integration with existing systems and hiring managers' time |
| Reward and pay review | A new grading structure or pay transparency exercise | Cost, fairness and equal pay risk |
| Engagement action plan | Acting on employee survey results | Actions fading after the first month |
| Mergers and acquisitions people integration | Harmonising terms, policies and systems after an acquisition | Contract changes and transfer rules |
Smaller HR teams often treat these as "just another task". Once a change touches several departments, has a deadline and involves employee data, it deserves at least a light [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) and a named owner.

### Why project management matters in HR
HR change often fails for ordinary reasons: unclear scope, no protected time, late communication and no measure of whether the change worked. A simple project approach addresses each of these.
- **Clear outcomes.** A defined [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) stops an onboarding redesign from turning into a full HR transformation.
- **Visible progress.** Leaders see milestones and decisions rather than a stream of updates, which builds trust in HR's ability to deliver.
- **Protected capacity.** Planning shows how much time the project needs from HR, payroll, IT and managers, so it can be agreed rather than squeezed in.
- **Fewer surprises.** Risks such as consultation timescales and pay run dates are identified early, not discovered in the final week.
- **Better adoption.** Communication and training are planned as work with owners and deadlines.
- **Learning for next time.** Closing the project with a review gives the team a record of what to repeat and what to avoid.

### What makes HR projects different
HR projects share the mechanics of other projects, but six features change how you plan them.

#### Employment law and consultation
Restructures, redundancies, contract changes and some policy changes can trigger legal duties to inform and consult employees or their representatives, with minimum timescales. For example, UK law sets minimum collective consultation periods when 20 or more redundancies are proposed at one establishment, and the US WARN Act generally requires 60 days' notice of plant closings and mass layoffs at covered employers. Rules vary by country and change over time, so take legal advice and build the required periods into the critical path.

#### Confidential and sensitive data
HR projects handle salary, performance, health and disciplinary information. Restrict project membership, keep personal data out of task comments, and check whether a data protection impact assessment is needed for new systems or data uses. Involve your data protection officer early.

#### Every employee is a stakeholder
A change to pay, hours, reviews or reporting lines affects people's livelihoods. That makes [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) and message timing more important than in most internal projects.

#### Payroll and annual cycles
Payroll cut-offs, tax year-end, annual pay reviews, benefits renewal windows and the performance cycle create fixed dates. Plan go-lives and data migrations around them.

#### HR runs operations at the same time
Recruitment, payroll queries and employee relations cases do not pause for a project. Agree protected time and a visible backlog; a shared view of all HR work makes trade-offs easier to agree.

#### Adoption is the deliverable
A performance system that managers ignore has failed, however well it was configured. Measure use and behaviour, not just go-live.

### HR project life cycle: 8 phases
Most HR projects follow a phased life cycle with extra weight on consultation, communication and adoption. A typical HRIS or process change project runs like this:
| Phase | What happens | Key output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Need and business case | Problem defined, for example manual onboarding or poor HR data; options and costs assessed | Approved business case |
| 2. Discovery and requirements | Current process mapped; requirements gathered from HR, managers, employees, payroll and IT | [Requirements document](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/) |
| 3. Design and selection | Future process designed; vendor selected if needed; policy drafted; legal review | Approved design and policy drafts |
| 4. Consultation (if required) | Information and consultation with employees, unions or employee forums | Consultation record and final decisions |
| 5. Build and test | System configured, data migrated and validated, parallel payroll runs, user testing | Test sign-off |
| 6. Communication and training | Manager briefings, employee guides, training sessions, FAQs | Training completion |
| 7. Launch and embed | Go-live, support, adoption tracking, follow-up with low-adoption teams | Adoption report |
| 8. Review and close | Benefits measured, lessons learned captured, handover to HR operations | Closure report |

#### How the phases map to the standard project phases
If you know the five classic [project management phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/) (initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, closing), phases 1 and 2 are initiation, 3 and 4 are planning and design, 5 to 7 are execution with continuous monitoring, and 8 is closure. The HR version simply makes consultation and adoption visible as their own stages.

### How to run an HR project step by step
Use these steps for any HR project, scaling the paperwork to the size and risk of the change.
1. **Define the problem and the outcome.** Write one sentence on what is wrong today and one on what success looks like, for example "new starters are productive within 30 days".
2. **Secure a sponsor.** An HR director or business leader who owns the outcome, approves scope changes and resolves escalations.
3. **Write a short charter.** Purpose, scope, out of scope, budget, milestones and success measures. Our [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) covers the essentials.
4. **Map stakeholders.** Employees affected, managers, payroll, IT, finance, legal, unions or employee forums. Note what each group needs to know and when.
5. **Build the schedule around fixed dates.** Add consultation periods, notice periods, payroll cut-offs and holiday peaks first, then plan tasks around them.
6. **Agree responsibilities.** A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) avoids confusion between HR, managers, IT and payroll.
7. **Log risks early.** Legal, data, payroll, employee relations and adoption risks belong in a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) with owners.
8. **Plan communication and training.** Create a [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/communication-plan/) that says what each group hears, from whom and when. Brief managers before employees.
9. **Build, test and pilot.** Test with a small group, fix issues and adjust guidance before a full launch.
10. **Launch with support.** Provide FAQs, drop-in sessions and a clear route for questions in the first weeks.
11. **Measure adoption and benefits.** Track usage, accuracy and the outcome you defined in step 1.
12. **Close and hand over.** Capture lessons learned, transfer ownership to HR operations and confirm who maintains the process.
Tip
Brief line managers at least a few days before employees hear about a change. Managers who are surprised by an announcement cannot answer their team's questions, and trust drops quickly.

### Worked example: implementing a new HRIS
A 600-person company runs HR on spreadsheets and a separate payroll package. Leaders want reliable headcount data, self-service for employees and fewer payroll errors. The HR operations manager is asked to lead the project, with the chief people officer as sponsor.
| Milestone | Main activities | Watch-outs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business case approved | Problems and benefits defined; three vendors shortlisted; costs compared | Agree what is in scope: core HR and payroll only, or recruitment and learning too |
| Vendor selected and contract signed | Demos scripted around real scenarios; references checked; data protection terms reviewed | Check data residency, access controls and exit terms |
| Design complete | Org structure, approval workflows and permissions designed; policies updated | Keep configuration simple for phase one |
| Data migrated and validated | Employee records cleansed; owners sign off each data set | Poor source data is the most common cause of delay |
| Parallel payroll runs passed | Two pay runs processed in both systems and compared | Schedule around payroll cut-offs and year-end |
| Managers and employees trained | Manager briefings, short videos, quick-reference guides | Train managers first; they approve requests in the new system |
| Go-live and hypercare | Launch, daily issue triage for the first weeks | Keep a visible issue log and daily stand-up |
| Closure | Adoption and accuracy measured; lessons captured; handover to HR operations | Confirm who owns ongoing configuration |
The project manager uses a phased plan with a Gantt chart for the system work, and a separate communication and training workstream with its own owner. Success is measured by data accuracy, payroll accuracy in the first live runs and the share of employees using self-service.

### Key roles in an HR project
| Role | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Sponsor (HR director or chief people officer) | Owns the objectives, secures executive support and resolves escalations |
| HR project manager | Plans, coordinates and reports; manages risks, vendors and timelines |
| HR business partners | Represent business units, gather requirements and lead manager engagement |
| Subject matter experts | Specialists in reward, payroll, recruitment, learning or employee relations |
| Employment lawyer or legal adviser | Advises on consultation duties, contracts and policy wording |
| IT and HRIS administrators | Configure, integrate and secure systems |
| Data protection officer | Advises on employee data handling and impact assessments |
| Employee representatives or unions | Consulted on changes that affect terms and conditions |
| Change champions | Managers and employees who promote and support adoption locally |

#### What does an HR project manager do?
An HR project manager turns a people objective into a plan and keeps it moving. Typical responsibilities include scoping the project with the sponsor, building the schedule and budget, coordinating HR specialists, IT, payroll and vendors, managing risks and issues, leading communication and training, reporting progress and closing the project with a benefits review.
Useful skills combine core [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/) (planning, stakeholder management, risk management, reporting) with HR knowledge: employment law awareness, HR data, change management and the ability to handle confidential matters with discretion. In smaller organisations this role is often an HR manager or HR business partner rather than a dedicated project manager.

### Methodologies and change management for HR
No single method suits every HR project. Choose by the type of change and its constraints.
| Approach | Best for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) or phased | HRIS and payroll implementations, restructures | Legal timescales, payroll cut-offs and data migration need sequential control |
| Change management models (for example ADKAR or Kotter's eight steps) | Culture, performance and ways-of-working changes | Structure the people side of change alongside the project plan |
| [Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) (often called Agile HR) | Employee experience, onboarding redesign, learning content | Test changes with small groups and improve based on feedback |
| Kanban | Ongoing HR improvement and request backlogs | Visualise and limit work in progress for a busy HR team |
| Lean | Recruitment and onboarding process improvement | Remove delays and handoffs, for example in time to hire |
Many HR projects are hybrids: a phased plan for the system and legal steps, with iterative pilots for the employee-facing parts. Whatever you choose, keep two kinds of change apart: organisational change management (helping people adopt the change) and project change control (managing changes to scope, time and cost). Our guide to [change management vs change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-management-vs-change-control/) explains the difference.
Tip
Treat communication and training as workstreams with their own owners, tasks and deadlines, not as a last-week activity.

### Essential HR project documents and templates
You do not need every document for every project. A policy update might need a charter, a communication plan and a risk log; an HRIS implementation needs all of them.
- **[Project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/):** purpose, scope, sponsor and success measures.
- **[Business requirements document](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/):** what the new process or system must do.
- **Gap analysis:** current vs future state of processes, skills or systems.
- **Project schedule:** include consultation periods, pay run dates and notice periods.
- **[RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/):** clarify HR, managers, IT, legal and payroll responsibilities.
- **[Communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/):** what each employee group hears, when and from whom.
- **[Training plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) and [skills matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/):** for learning and capability projects.
- **[Risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/):** legal, data, payroll, employee relations and adoption risks.
- **Work request template:** to capture incoming HR improvement requests.
- **Lessons learned log:** to record what to repeat on the next HR project.

### KPIs for HR projects
Pick a small set of measures that match the project's purpose, and take a baseline before you start so you can show the change.
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adoption rate | Share of managers and employees using the new process or system | Embedding the change |
| Data accuracy | Error rate in migrated or new HR data | HRIS go-live readiness |
| Payroll accuracy | Errors in parallel or live pay runs | Payroll and HRIS projects |
| Time to hire / time to productivity | Speed of recruitment and onboarding | Recruitment and onboarding projects |
| Training completion | Percentage of target staff trained | Readiness |
| Early turnover | Leavers within the first months of employment | Onboarding projects |
| Employee engagement or satisfaction | Survey results before and after the change | Culture and experience projects |
| Schedule and budget variance | Delivery against plan | Sponsor reporting |

### Common challenges and mistakes
- **Resistance to change.** Explain why the change is happening, involve managers early and listen to concerns through consultation channels.
- **Confidentiality leaks.** Limit project membership for sensitive projects such as restructures and use restricted folders and code names.
- **Poor data quality.** Cleanse employee data before migration and assign data owners.
- **Legal timing ignored.** Map statutory consultation and notice periods into the schedule before committing to a launch date.
- **Competing HR priorities.** Agree protected project time and use a visible backlog so the team can say no to new requests.
- **Manager capability.** Many HR changes rely on line managers; train and support them before launch.
- **Declaring success at go-live.** Keep measuring adoption for several weeks and follow up with teams that lag behind.
- **Scope creep.** Park extra requests in a phase two list rather than adding them mid-project.

### HR project management software
HR teams already use an HRIS, payroll, applicant tracking and learning systems. Those systems run HR processes; they are not built to plan and coordinate a project. For the project itself, look for a work management tool that offers:
- Strict permissions and private spaces for confidential projects.
- Request forms for intake of HR improvement work.
- Templates for repeatable projects such as onboarding, annual reviews and policy updates.
- Timelines, dependencies and milestones for system implementations.
- Dashboards for sponsor reporting.
- Integrations with your HRIS and collaboration tools.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is a strong all-round option for HR teams that need confidential spaces, intake forms, templates and Gantt planning in one place, and it ranks first in our [project management software rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/). [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) is popular with HR operations teams for visual boards and automations, and [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) suits teams that want straightforward task and timeline management.
Small HR teams starting out can run a project well with a shared spreadsheet plan, a RACI and a communication plan, then move to software as the number of projects grows.

### Building HR project skills
If you lead HR projects regularly, a short grounding in project management pays off quickly. Learn the basics of scope, scheduling, risk and stakeholder management, then practise on a contained project such as an onboarding refresh before taking on an HRIS or restructure. A [project management certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) is optional for HR roles but can help if project delivery is becoming a larger part of your job.
For the wider context of running change inside an organisation, read [business project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/business-project-management/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is HR project management?**
HR project management is the planning and delivery of temporary HR initiatives, such as HRIS rollouts, onboarding redesigns, restructures and policy launches, using defined scope, schedules, roles and risk control, with particular attention to employment law, confidential data and employee adoption.

**Q: What are examples of HR projects?**
Common examples include implementing an HRIS or payroll system, redesigning onboarding, introducing a new performance process, running a restructure, launching a learning programme, rolling out a hybrid working policy, reviewing pay and grading, and acting on employee survey results.

**Q: What does an HR project manager do?**
An HR project manager scopes HR change with a sponsor, builds the plan and budget, coordinates HR specialists, IT, payroll and vendors, manages risks, leads communication and training, reports progress and closes the project with a review of benefits and lessons learned.

**Q: What skills does an HR project manager need?**
Planning, stakeholder management, risk management and clear communication, plus HR knowledge such as employment law awareness, HR data handling, change management and discretion with confidential information. See [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/).

**Q: What are the phases of an HR project?**
A practical HR life cycle is: need and business case, discovery and requirements, design and selection, consultation where required, build and test, communication and training, launch and embed, and review and close.

**Q: Why is project management important in HR?**
It gives HR change a clear scope, protected time, visible progress and early warning of risks such as consultation timescales and payroll dates. It also makes communication, training and adoption planned work rather than an afterthought.

**Q: Is Agile used in HR?**
Yes. Many HR teams use Agile practices, often called Agile HR, for employee experience, onboarding and learning projects, testing changes with small groups and improving them based on feedback. System implementations and restructures usually still need phased control for legal and payroll steps.

**Q: How long does an HRIS implementation take?**
It depends on organisation size, scope, data quality and the number of integrations. Small, standard implementations can take a few months, while large multi-country projects take much longer. Data cleansing and parallel payroll runs are the usual sources of delay.

**Q: How do you keep HR projects confidential?**
Restrict project membership, use private workspaces and code names for sensitive projects such as restructures, keep personal data out of task comments, and follow data protection rules, including impact assessments where required.

**Q: What KPIs measure HR project success?**
Adoption rate, data and payroll accuracy, time to hire or time to productivity, training completion, early turnover, employee engagement and schedule and budget variance. Choose the few that match the project's purpose.

**Q: Which software is best for HR project management?**
Use your HRIS for HR processes and a work management tool for the project. Wrike is a strong all-round choice for confidential spaces, intake forms and Gantt planning; monday.com and Asana are also popular with HR teams. Compare options in our [tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/).

**Q: Do HR professionals need a project management certification?**
No, but a grounding in project management helps if you lead HR change often. Entry-level options suit HR professionals with little formal project experience; see [project management certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/).

# Infrastructure Project Management: Phases, Roles and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/infrastructure-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Infrastructure project management explained: life cycle, roles, delivery models, contracts, cost and schedule control with worked examples, KPIs and tools.


## Infrastructure Project Management: Phases, Roles and Tools
Infrastructure project management is the management of large, long-lived public or regulated assets such as roads, railways, bridges, water, energy and telecoms networks, from the strategic case and consents through design, construction and handover to the operator. It shares tools with construction project management but works at greater scale, over longer timescales, on or next to live networks and under much closer public scrutiny. This guide covers the life cycle, governance, delivery models, project controls with worked examples, KPIs and software.
- Published 29 August 2026
- Last updated 16 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Infrastructure project management delivers long-lived public assets under formal business case approval and independent assurance.
- Consents, land, utilities, access to live networks and communities shape the programme as much as construction does.
- Choose the delivery model and contract deliberately: they decide who carries which risk and how change is priced.
- Use risk-based estimates (P50 and P80) and earned value to keep cost and schedule forecasts honest.
- Pair specialist scheduling, cost, GIS and BIM systems with a collaborative platform such as Wrike for people, actions and approvals.

### What is infrastructure project management?
**Infrastructure project management** is the planning, coordination and control of projects that create, renew or expand the physical networks a society depends on, such as transport, water, energy and telecoms. It covers the whole path from identifying a need and proving the business case to handing a working asset to the organisation that will operate and maintain it, often for many decades.
Most infrastructure is paid for by government, regulated customers or long-term private investors, so the work is shaped by formal approvals, public accountability and the need to keep existing services running while new ones are built.
|  | Building construction project | Infrastructure project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical client | Developer, business or public body | Government department, agency, regulated utility or concessionaire |
| Scale | One building or site | Linear routes or networks crossing many sites and landowners |
| Timescale | Months to a few years | Several years to more than a decade, including development and consents |
| Working conditions | Usually a closed site | Often on or next to live roads, railways, pipes and cables |
| Approvals | Planning permission and building control | Business case approvals, development consent, environmental assessment, land powers |
| Success measures | Time, cost, quality, sale or occupation | Time, cost, safety, service performance and long-term public benefits |
If you manage buildings rather than networks, see our guide to [construction project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/construction-project-management/).

#### Types of infrastructure projects
| Sector | Examples | Constraint that usually drives the programme |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roads and highways | New bypass, junction upgrade, bridge replacement, smart motorway | Traffic management and lane closures |
| Rail and transit | New line, station rebuild, signalling renewal, electrification | Possessions (track access windows) and systems integration |
| Water and wastewater | Treatment works upgrade, trunk main, storm overflow reduction | Continuity of supply and environmental permits |
| Energy | Grid reinforcement, substations, interconnectors, generation | Outages and grid connection dates; see [energy project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/energy-project-management/) |
| Telecoms and digital | Fibre roll-out, mobile masts, data centres | Wayleaves, street works permits and volume of sites |
| Ports and airports | New terminal, runway resurfacing, berth extension | Operational continuity and security |
| Social infrastructure | Hospitals, schools, prisons, flood defences | Public funding cycles and service user needs |

### What makes infrastructure projects different
- **Public money and accountability.** Business cases, audits, spending controls and published reports mean decisions must be documented and defensible.
- **Long timescales.** Development and consent can take years before construction starts, and the finished asset may operate for a century.
- **Consents and environment.** Environmental assessment, land acquisition and planning or development consent are major workstreams in their own right, and some surveys can only be done in certain seasons.
- **Live networks.** Work often happens on or next to a railway, road or utility that must keep running, so access windows (possessions, lane closures, outages) control the programme.
- **Utilities and third parties.** Diverting gas, water, power and telecoms apparatus depends on other organisations' resources and is a frequent cause of delay.
- **Communities.** Neighbours, local authorities and campaign groups can shape or stop a scheme, so engagement is continuous rather than a one-off consultation.
- **Interfaces.** Large schemes are split into several contracts, and most problems appear where one contract meets another.
Tip
Treat consents, land, utility diversions and access windows as critical-path work from day one. On many schemes they decide the completion date long before the main contractor arrives.

### Phases of an infrastructure project
Life cycle models vary by country and sector, but most infrastructure projects pass through seven phases, each closed by a funding or approval decision.
| Phase | What happens | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Strategic definition | Identify the need and the long list of options; build the strategic case | Strategic outline business case, options appraisal |
| 2. Development and consents | Surveys, outline design, environmental assessment, consultation, land and consent applications | Outline business case, environmental statement, consent decision |
| 3. Procurement | Choose a delivery model and contract and appoint designers and contractors | Contract award, full business case |
| 4. Detailed design | Detailed design, utility diversion design, temporary works and access planning | Approved design, construction programme, access plan |
| 5. Construction | Enabling works, utility diversions, main works, systems installation | Progress and cost reports, early warnings, compensation events |
| 6. Testing, commissioning and handover | System testing, trial operations, asset data and handover to the operator | Asset information, acceptance certificates |
| 7. Operation and benefits realisation | The operator runs the asset; benefits are measured against the business case | Post-project evaluation, lessons learned |

#### Business case stages and the five case model
In the UK, publicly funded schemes normally build their business case in three steps (strategic outline case, outline business case and full business case) using HM Treasury's five case model: the strategic, economic, commercial, financial and management cases. The Green Book, which sets the appraisal rules, was revised in early 2026 after a 2025 review; the revised guidance stresses that value for money is a balanced judgement and that benefit-cost ratios are aids to decision-making, not decision rules. Other countries use similar staged approvals, so the principle travels: funding is released step by step as the case is proven.

#### Independent assurance gate reviews
UK government major projects also go through independent assurance reviews, now run by the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (NISTA), which incorporates the former Infrastructure and Projects Authority. Its gate reviews run from Gate 0 (strategic assessment) through Gate 1 (business justification), Gate 2 (delivery strategy), Gate 3 (investment decision) and Gate 4 (readiness for service) to Gate 5 (operations review and benefits realisation). Even if you work outside government, a similar set of independent reviews at the same points is good practice; our guide to [project governance](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-governance/) explains how to set one up.

### How to plan and deliver an infrastructure project step by step
The steps below follow the life cycle from the client's point of view. Scale them to the size of the scheme.
1. **Define the need and the outcomes.** State the problem (congestion, capacity, resilience, condition) and the measurable benefits you expect, such as journey time savings or reduced leakage.
2. **Appoint a senior responsible owner (SRO).** One accountable person who owns the benefits and chairs the project board.
3. **Appraise options.** Compare a long list of options, including doing the minimum, using cost-benefit analysis and a [business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/).
4. **Set up governance and a charter.** Agree the board, decision rights, tolerances and assurance points in a [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/).
5. **Map stakeholders and consents.** List every consent, landowner, statutory body, utility and community group, with lead times. Plan engagement in a [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/).
6. **Start long-lead surveys early.** Ecology, ground investigation, traffic counts and utility searches feed design and consents; some are seasonal.
7. **Estimate with risk.** Build a base cost estimate, add quantified risk and report P50 and P80 values; see [cost estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/cost-estimation/).
8. **Choose the delivery model and contract.** Decide who designs, who builds, who carries which risks and how change is priced (see the next section).
9. **Build an integrated programme.** One schedule covering consents, land, utilities, design, access windows, construction, testing and handover, with the critical path clear. A [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) is a good starting point for smaller schemes.
10. **Plan access and traffic management.** Book possessions, lane closures and outages early; they are often agreed months or years ahead.
11. **Control delivery.** Use earned value, risk reviews, early warnings and formal [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) every period.
12. **Plan handover from the start.** Agree asset information requirements, testing, training and acceptance criteria with the operator before design is complete.
13. **Measure benefits and capture lessons.** Evaluate outcomes against the business case after opening and share [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) across the portfolio.

### Delivery models and contracts
The delivery model decides who designs and builds the asset and who carries which risks. Choosing it is one of the most important decisions a client makes, because it is very hard to change later.
| Delivery model | How it works | Strengths | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design-bid-build (traditional) | Client completes the design, then tenders construction | Client control of design, competitive prices on a full design | Slower overall; design risk stays with the client |
| Design and build | One contractor designs and builds to the client's requirements | Single point of responsibility, can overlap design and construction | Less client control of detail; requirements must be clear |
| Early contractor involvement / two-stage | Contractor joins during design to advise on buildability and price | Better buildability and risk understanding before price is fixed | Needs strong cost scrutiny in the second stage |
| Alliance or enterprise model | Client, designers and contractors share a collaborative agreement and incentives | Joint planning, shared risk, better at managing interfaces | Requires mature governance and culture |
| Public-private partnership (PPP) or concession | A private partner designs, builds, finances and often operates the asset | Private finance and whole-life responsibility | Complex procurement and long-term contract management |

#### Common contract forms
In the UK and many other markets, the **NEC4** suite is widely used for infrastructure. Its Engineering and Construction Contract offers main options from priced contracts with activity schedules or bills of quantities to target cost and cost-reimbursable options, and relies on project management mechanisms such as **early warnings** (raising risks early so they can be reduced) and **compensation events** (the process for assessing changes to price and time). Internationally, the **FIDIC** suite is common, with different books for employer-designed works and contractor-designed works. US public owners often use their own standard contracts or industry forms for design-bid-build, design-build and construction manager at risk.
Whatever the form, the project manager's job is to run the contract's procedures on time: missed notification periods are a common source of disputes. Our guide to [project procurement management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-procurement-management/) covers tendering and contract selection more broadly.

### Roles in infrastructure project management
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Senior responsible owner (SRO) | Accountable for the project meeting its objectives and delivering its benefits |
| Client body or asset owner | Sets requirements, funds the project and will own the asset |
| Programme and project managers | Plan and control delivery across workstreams and contracts |
| Project controls team | Scheduling, cost control, risk analysis, earned value and reporting |
| Commercial and contract managers | Procurement, contract administration, change and payment |
| Designers and engineers | Civil, structural, systems, environmental and geotechnical design |
| Contractors and supply chain | Build the works, often under framework or alliance agreements |
| Consents and stakeholder managers | Consultation, landowner and community relations, and consent compliance |
| Operator and maintainer | Defines operational requirements and accepts the asset |

#### What an infrastructure project manager does
Day to day, an infrastructure project manager keeps the scheme's many workstreams moving together: chairing progress and risk meetings, maintaining the integrated programme, running contract procedures such as early warnings and change, reporting to the project board, coordinating with utilities and statutory bodies, and making sure safety, environmental and consent obligations are met. On large schemes the role is split between a programme director, several project managers and a project controls team, usually organised as a programme; see [program vs project vs portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/program-vs-project-vs-portfolio-management/).

#### Skills and qualifications
- **Technical understanding** of the asset type, often from a civil, electrical or mechanical engineering background.
- **Project controls:** scheduling, cost management, risk analysis and earned value.
- **Commercial and contract skills,** especially the contract forms your client uses.
- **Stakeholder and political awareness,** because public projects attract scrutiny from many directions.
- **Safety leadership** on sites that sit next to live traffic, trains or high-voltage equipment.
- **Recognised qualifications** such as chartered engineering status, a project management certification or contract-specific accreditation help, depending on the employer and country.

### Project controls: worked examples
Project controls turn progress into numbers that can be compared and forecast. The three examples below use illustrative, rounded figures; they are not benchmarks.

#### Example 1: earned value on a road scheme
A road improvement contract has a **budget at completion (BAC)** of £120 million. At month 18 the project controls team reports:
| Measure | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planned value (PV) | £48m | Budgeted cost of work scheduled to date |
| Earned value (EV) | £42m | Budgeted cost of work actually completed |
| Actual cost (AC) | £46m | What the completed work actually cost |
| Cost variance (EV − AC) | −£4m | Over budget for the work done |
| Schedule variance (EV − PV) | −£6m | Behind plan |
| Cost performance index (EV ÷ AC) | 0.91 | £0.91 of work for every £1 spent |
| Schedule performance index (EV ÷ PV) | 0.88 | Progressing at 88% of the planned rate |
If cost performance continues at the current rate, the **estimate at completion** is BAC ÷ CPI = £120m ÷ 0.913 ≈ **£131.4m**, an overrun of about £11.4m. If both cost and schedule pressure persist, a more cautious forecast is AC + (BAC − EV) ÷ (CPI × SPI) = £46m + £78m ÷ 0.80 ≈ **£143.6m**. To finish on the original budget, the remaining work would need a to-complete performance index of (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) = £78m ÷ £74m ≈ 1.05, meaning every remaining £1 must buy £1.05 of work. That is a signal to re-plan, not to hope.

#### Example 2: P50 and P80 cost estimates
Single-figure estimates hide uncertainty, and early infrastructure estimates are prone to optimism bias. Many public clients therefore report estimates as confidence levels produced by quantitative risk analysis. Suppose a bridge replacement has a base cost (no risk) of £100m. A [Monte Carlo simulation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/monte-carlo-simulation/) of the risk register produces this range:
| Confidence level | Estimate | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base cost | £100m | Cost if no risks occur; unlikely to be achieved |
| P50 | £112m | 50% chance the final cost is at or below this |
| P80 | £121m | 80% chance the final cost is at or below this |
| P95 | £130m | Very cautious figure, used to test affordability |
A common approach is to give the project team a budget at P50 and hold the difference up to P80 as a sponsor-controlled contingency, released only through governance. The figures are re-run at each stage as design matures and risks are retired.

#### Example 3: access window utilisation
A rail renewal team books a 52-hour weekend possession. After allowing for taking possession, isolations and testing before handback, 36 hours are planned for productive work. Plant breakdowns and a late start mean 30 hours of productive work are achieved. Utilisation is 30 ÷ 36 = **83%**. Tracking this every possession shows whether problems are planning, logistics or productivity, and helps you avoid booking more possessions than the team can use well.

### Consents, environment and stakeholders
Consenting rules depend on the country and the size of the scheme, so always take specialist advice. Two examples show why consents belong on the critical path.
- **England and Wales:** the largest schemes (nationally significant infrastructure projects) need a development consent order under the Planning Act 2008. The Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025, which received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, removes the statutory pre-application consultation requirement and allows some projects to switch to the ordinary planning route, with commencement dates set by later regulations. Check which provisions are in force when you plan.
- **United States:** federal involvement in a project triggers review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Amendments in the Fiscal Responsibility Act 2023 set deadlines of two years for an environmental impact statement and one year for an environmental assessment, with page limits of 150 and 75 pages respectively (excluding appendices, and with exceptions for extraordinarily complex actions).
Stakeholder work on infrastructure is continuous. Keep a stakeholder map that covers landowners, residents, businesses, local authorities, statutory bodies and utilities, and log every commitment made to them so it is built into the design and the contract. Our guide to [project stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) covers mapping and engagement techniques.

### Methodologies and frameworks
| Approach | When it fits | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage-gate with business case approvals | Publicly funded schemes | Funding is released phase by phase as the case is proven |
| PRINCE2 and PMBOK practices | Governance and control across the programme | Defined roles, tolerances and stage boundaries |
| [Critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) and schedule risk analysis | Programmes with high uncertainty | Supports realistic completion dates and float management |
| Earned value management | Large contracts | Objective progress and cost performance measurement |
| Lean and collaborative contracting | Alliances and frameworks | Shared incentives, joint planning and continuous improvement |
| Agile practices | Digital systems, signalling software and asset data | Short iterations inside a gated overall plan |
Most infrastructure programmes are hybrid: predictive and gated at the top, with collaborative planning (such as last planner style weekly planning) at the workface.
