### KPIs for infrastructure projects
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cost performance index (CPI) | Value of work done per unit of cost | Forecasting outturn cost |
| Schedule performance index (SPI) | Progress against plan | Programme health |
| Risk-adjusted cost forecast (P50 / P80) | Probable final cost at different confidence levels | Funding and contingency decisions |
| Contingency drawdown vs risk retired | Whether contingency is being used faster than risks are closing | Early warning of under-estimated risk |
| Access window utilisation | Planned work completed in each possession or closure | Productivity on live networks |
| Consent and environmental compliance | Breaches or incidents against consent conditions | Regulatory assurance |
| Safety rates | Accidents and near misses per hours worked | Workforce and public safety |
| Benefits realised | Actual versus forecast benefits after opening | Post-project evaluation |

### Common challenges and how to manage them
| Challenge | Why it happens | How to manage it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Optimism bias in early estimates | Pressure to secure funding, immature design, unknown ground and utilities | Reference class data, risk-based ranges, independent estimate reviews |
| Consent delays | Seasonal surveys, objections, complex legal processes | Start surveys early, engage statutory bodies before applying, keep float |
| Utility diversions | Third-party resources and records of buried apparatus | Engage utilities at design stage, survey early, treat diversions as critical path |
| Interface risk between contracts | Several contractors working on connected scope | Interface register with a single owner for each interface |
| Political and funding change | Spending reviews, elections, changing policy | Keep the business case current and the scheme phased so it can flex |
| Late discovery of operator requirements | Operators involved too late | Involve the operator from options stage; agree acceptance criteria early |
| Supply chain capacity | Many schemes competing for the same skills and plant | Market engagement, frameworks, realistic programmes |
Log each challenge with an owner in a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) and review it at every board.

### Common mistakes in infrastructure project management
- **Committing to a single-figure cost too early.** Announce ranges until the design and risk picture justify a firm number.
- **Leaving utilities and land to the contractor.** They usually need client-side action years before construction.
- **Separate programmes for each contract.** Without an integrated programme, interfaces and access windows clash.
- **Treating handover as the last step.** Asset information, testing and operator training need planning from design onwards.
- **Running contract procedures late.** Missed early warnings and late change assessments turn small issues into disputes.
- **Measuring outputs, not outcomes.** A finished road is an output; reduced journey times and fewer accidents are the outcomes the business case promised.

### Software for infrastructure project management
Infrastructure programmes rely on several specialist systems, each holding part of the picture.
| Tool type | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| Enterprise scheduling | Large critical path programmes with thousands of activities |
| Risk analysis | Quantitative cost and schedule risk analysis (P50, P80) |
| Cost control and earned value | Budgets, commitments, forecasts and performance indices |
| GIS and BIM / common data environment | Spatial data, 3D models, drawings and asset information |
| Collaborative work management | Workstream plans, stakeholder actions, approvals, requests and reporting across teams |
For that collaborative layer, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is the strongest all-in-one choice in [our tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/), with portfolio dashboards, request forms and workload views that suit multi-team programmes. Use it to coordinate people and decisions while the specialist systems hold the detailed schedule, cost and asset data.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is infrastructure project management?**
Infrastructure project management is the planning and control of projects that create or renew roads, railways, bridges, water, energy and telecoms networks, from the business case and consents through design and construction to handover and benefits realisation.

**Q: What does an infrastructure project manager do?**
They plan and control delivery across design, consents, procurement and construction: maintaining the integrated programme, running contract procedures, managing risks and stakeholders, reporting to the project board and preparing the asset for handover to the operator.

**Q: What are the phases of an infrastructure project?**
Strategic definition, development and consents, procurement, detailed design, construction, testing and commissioning with handover, and operation with benefits realisation.

**Q: What are the main types of infrastructure projects?**
Roads and highways, rail and transit, water and wastewater, energy, telecoms and digital, ports and airports, and social infrastructure such as hospitals, schools and flood defences.

**Q: How is infrastructure project management different from construction project management?**
Infrastructure projects are usually larger, linear or networked, publicly funded and built next to live services, so business case approvals, consents, land, utilities and access windows weigh more heavily than on a typical building project.

**Q: Why do infrastructure projects go over budget?**
Common causes include optimism bias in early estimates, immature design, unknown ground conditions and utilities, consent delays, scope change and interface problems between contracts. Risk-based estimates and strong change control reduce the effect.

**Q: What is a P50 and P80 estimate?**
They are cost or schedule figures from quantitative risk analysis. A P50 estimate has a 50% chance of not being exceeded; a P80 estimate has an 80% chance. Many clients budget at P50 and hold the difference to P80 as contingency.

**Q: What contracts are used for infrastructure projects?**
Common forms include the NEC4 suite (widely used in the UK), the FIDIC suite internationally, and public owners' own standard contracts in the US, used within delivery models such as design-bid-build, design and build, alliances and PPPs.

**Q: What is the five case model?**
It is HM Treasury's structure for UK public sector business cases, covering the strategic, economic, commercial, financial and management cases.

**Q: How long do infrastructure projects take?**
Small renewals can take months, but major schemes often spend several years in development and consent before construction, and construction itself can take many years. Build the consent timeline into the programme from the start.

**Q: What qualifications do infrastructure project managers need?**
There is no single requirement. Many hold engineering degrees or chartered status, plus a project management certification and experience with the contract forms their clients use.

**Q: What software is used for infrastructure project management?**
Enterprise scheduling, risk analysis, cost control, GIS and BIM tools for the technical data, and a collaborative work management platform such as Wrike for workstream plans, actions, approvals and reporting.

# Interior Design Project Management: Phases, FF&E and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/interior-design-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Interior design project management for studios: phases from brief to install, FF&E procurement, roles, documents, KPIs, challenges and software to use.


## Interior Design Project Management: Phases, FF&E and Tools
Interior design project management is how a designer or studio runs a project from the client brief through concept, design, documentation, procurement and installation to the final reveal. Its defining challenge is managing hundreds of individual items, from furniture and lighting to fabrics and finishes, each with its own approval, price, lead time and delivery, while keeping the client happy and the studio profitable.
- Published 29 August 2026
- 6 min read

### Key takeaways
- Interior design project management is shaped by hundreds of individual products, each with an approval, price and lead time.
- Work backwards from the install date to set must-order dates for every item.
- Clear sign-offs and a change log protect the budget and the studio's fee.
- Use specialist FF&E tools for product data and a platform such as Wrike when you need a multi-project view.

### What makes interior design project management different
- **Product-heavy scope.** A single project can involve hundreds of furniture, fixtures and equipment (FF&E) items, each needing selection, approval, ordering, tracking and installation.
- **Lead times set the date.** Bespoke joinery, upholstery and imported items can take many weeks, so ordering dates drive the programme.
- **Taste is subjective.** Approvals depend on client preference, so clear sign-off of samples and boards is essential.
- **Money flows through the studio.** Many studios buy on the client's behalf, handle deposits and markups, and carry the risk of mistakes.
- **Coordination with trades.** Contractors, joiners, electricians, decorators and installers must work in the right order, often in an occupied home or a live workplace.
- **Regulation.** Fire ratings for fabrics and finishes, accessibility and building rules apply, especially in commercial and hospitality projects.

### Phases of an interior design project
| Phase | What happens | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Discovery and brief | Client meeting, site survey, needs, style and budget | Brief, measured survey, fee proposal and agreement |
| 2. Concept design | Mood boards, space planning options, initial palette | Concept presentation, approved layout |
| 3. Design development | Detailed layouts, lighting, joinery, finishes and FF&E selections with costs | Sample boards, FF&E schedule, budget estimate |
| 4. Documentation | Drawings and specifications for contractors and suppliers | Drawing package, specifications, tender or quote requests |
| 5. Procurement | Quotes, client approvals, deposits, purchase orders, order tracking | Purchase orders, delivery schedule |
| 6. Construction and installation | Site works by trades, deliveries, installation and styling | Site reports, snag list |
| 7. Handover and reveal | Final snagging, care guides, photography, final invoice | Completed space, close-out pack |
In UK office projects you will also hear 'Cat A' (a landlord's base fit-out) and 'Cat B' (the tenant's fit-out to suit its needs); interior designers usually lead Cat B design.

### Key roles
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Principal or lead designer | Client relationship, design direction and final approvals |
| Project designer / project manager | Day-to-day delivery, programme, budget and coordination |
| Junior designer / design assistant | Drawings, sample sourcing, boards and schedules |
| FF&E or procurement coordinator | Quotes, orders, deposits, tracking and deliveries |
| Contractor and trades | Building works, joinery, decoration and installation |
| Architect or engineers | Structural or services changes on larger projects |
| Client | Brief, budget, decisions and payments |

### Methodologies that fit
| Approach | Use in interior design |
| --- | --- |
| Phased (stage-gate) plan | Clear client sign-off at concept, design development and procurement; see [project management phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/) |
| Kanban | Track every FF&E item through quote, approved, ordered, shipped, delivered and installed; see [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) |
| Critical path planning | Work backwards from install date using lead times; see [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) |
| Iterative design reviews | Short cycles of present, feedback and refine; see [Agile for creative teams](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-for-creative-teams/) |
Tip
Give every FF&E item a 'must order by' date calculated from its lead time and the install date. Sort the schedule by that date each week.

### Essential documents and templates
| Document | Purpose | Template |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Design brief | Client goals, style, budget and constraints | [Creative brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/creative-brief-template/), [project brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-brief-template/) |
| Fee proposal and budget | Studio fee plus FF&E and works budgets | [Budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/), [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) |
| Project schedule | Design phases, ordering deadlines, works and install | [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/), [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) |
| FF&E tracker | Every item with status, cost and dates | [Project tracker template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/), [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) |
| Change log | Client changes and their cost and time impact | [Change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) |
| Supplier quote requests | Prices and lead times from suppliers and trades | [RFQ template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/rfq-template/) |
| Close-out review | What went well and what to change | [Lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) |

### KPIs for interior design projects
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Budget variance | FF&E and works spend against approved budget | Client trust and change control |
| Hours vs fee | Studio time spent against fee by phase | Studio profitability |
| Items ordered on time | FF&E ordered by the must-order date | Install date protection |
| Approval turnaround | Days from presentation to client decision | Programme risk |
| Delivery issues | Damaged, wrong or late items | Supplier performance |
| Snags at handover | Defects outstanding at reveal | Quality of installation |

### Common challenges
- **Slow client decisions.** Present a limited number of options and set approval deadlines tied to order dates.
- **Discontinued or delayed items.** Hold approved alternatives for critical pieces and track shipments weekly.
- **Budget creep from upgrades.** Show the cost of every change before it is approved; see [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).
- **Trade sequencing in occupied spaces.** Agree working hours, protection and access in advance and share a simple weekly plan.
- **Cash flow.** Collect deposits before placing orders and agree payment terms in the contract.

### Software for interior design project management
Many studios use specialist interior design software for product libraries, FF&E specifications, client approvals, purchase orders and invoicing, alongside CAD or 3D tools for drawings and visuals. A general project management platform is useful when the studio runs many projects at once, needs resourcing across designers, or works on commercial fit-outs with larger teams.
Look for timeline views, custom fields for item data, approval workflows and client-friendly sharing. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is the strongest all-in-one option in [our tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) for studios that need that portfolio view; smaller residential studios may find a specialist interior design tool covers most of their needs.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is interior design project management?**
Interior design project management is how a designer or studio runs a project from brief and concept to procurement, installation and handover, while controlling budget, schedule and client approvals.

**Q: What are the phases of interior design project management?**
Discovery and brief, concept design, design development, documentation, procurement, construction and installation, and handover.

**Q: What is FF&E in interior design project management?**
FF&E stands for furniture, fixtures and equipment: the movable and installed items specified, ordered and installed by the design team.

**Q: How do you manage lead times in interior design project management?**
Calculate a must-order-by date for each item from its lead time and the install date, then track orders weekly against those dates.

**Q: What documents are used in interior design project management?**
A design brief, fee proposal and budget, project schedule, FF&E schedule and tracker, drawings and specifications, change log and close-out pack.

**Q: What KPIs matter in interior design project management?**
Budget variance, hours against fee, items ordered on time, approval turnaround, delivery issues and snags at handover.

**Q: What software is used for interior design project management?**
Specialist interior design tools for FF&E and purchasing, CAD and 3D tools, and a project platform such as Wrike for multi-project planning and resourcing.

**Q: Who handles interior design project management in a studio?**
A project designer or project manager, supported by a procurement coordinator and overseen by the principal designer.

**Q: How do you handle client changes in interior design project management?**
Record the change, show its cost and time impact, get written approval and update the budget and FF&E schedule.

**Q: What is the difference between Cat A and Cat B in interior design project management?**
Cat A is a landlord's base fit-out of an office; Cat B is the tenant's fit-out designed around its own needs, often led by the interior designer.

**Q: Can Kanban help with interior design project management?**
Yes. A Kanban board is an easy way to see every item move from quote to approval, order, delivery and installation.

# IT Project Management: Phases, Roles, Methods and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/it-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: IT project management explained: phases from initiation to hypercare, roles, Agile, Waterfall and ITIL, key documents, KPIs, challenges and software.


## IT Project Management: Phases, Roles, Methods and Tools
IT project management is the planning, delivery and control of technology changes inside an organisation, such as system implementations, cloud migrations, infrastructure upgrades, cybersecurity programmes and service rollouts. What sets it apart is that the work has to land safely in a live environment: users, data, security and day-to-day IT operations must all keep working while the change goes in.
- Published 29 August 2026
- 6 min read

### Key takeaways
- IT project management delivers technology change into live environments, so cutover, rollback and handover are central.
- Choose Waterfall, Agile, Kanban or hybrid by the type of work, and use ITIL practices to release changes safely.
- Data migration, integration and user adoption are the most common sources of trouble.
- Combine ITSM and developer tools with a portfolio platform such as Wrike for planning and reporting.

### What makes IT project management different
- **Live systems.** Most IT projects change something people already depend on, so cutover, rollback and downtime planning are central.
- **Integration and data.** New systems must exchange data with existing ones, and data migration is often the riskiest workstream.
- **Security and compliance.** Data protection law, security standards and audit requirements shape design and testing.
- **Vendors and licences.** Much of the work is delivered by suppliers or through software-as-a-service products, so contract and vendor management matter.
- **Handover to operations.** The project must hand a supportable service to the service desk and operations teams, not just a working system.
- **People change.** Training and adoption decide whether the benefits arrive.
For the role itself (responsibilities, skills and career path) see our [IT project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/it-project-manager/) guide.

### Phases of an IT project
| Phase | What happens | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiation | Define the problem, benefits, options and high-level cost | Business case, [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) |
| Requirements and design | Capture business and technical requirements; solution and security architecture | Requirements document, solution design, data migration approach |
| Build and configure | Configure software, develop integrations, build environments | Configured system, integration code, test environments |
| Test | System, integration, performance, security and user acceptance testing | Test reports, defect log, UAT sign-off |
| Deploy and cut over | Training, data migration, go-live and rollback plan | Cutover plan, go/no-go decision, live service |
| Hypercare and handover | Enhanced support after go-live, transfer to business-as-usual support | Support model, known issues list, operational acceptance |
| Closure | Benefits tracking, lessons learned and contract closure | Closure report, [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) |
Tip
Plan the cutover weekend as its own mini-project, with an hour-by-hour runbook, named owners, go/no-go checkpoints and a rehearsed rollback.

### Key roles
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Executive sponsor | Owns the business case, removes blockers, makes major decisions |
| IT project manager | Plans and controls scope, schedule, budget, risks, vendors and communication |
| Business analyst | Elicits and documents requirements and processes |
| Solution or enterprise architect | Designs how the solution fits the wider technology landscape |
| Engineers and developers | Build infrastructure, configuration and integrations |
| Test lead | Plans and runs testing and manages defects |
| Information security | Reviews risks, controls and compliance |
| Service owner and operations | Accept and run the service after go-live |
| Vendor or partner | Delivers contracted products and services |

### Methodologies for IT projects
| Approach | When it fits | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) | Infrastructure, data centre moves and fixed-scope vendor implementations | Clear phases and sign-offs suit predictable work |
| [Agile](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) / [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) | Application development and evolving requirements | Deliver value in increments and adapt based on feedback |
| [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) | Infrastructure, support and continuous improvement work | Visualise flow and limit work in progress |
| Hybrid | ERP and large business system programmes | Phased plan with iterative build and test cycles |
| ITIL | Releasing changes into live services | Change enablement, release and service transition practices |
| [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/) | Governance-heavy public and corporate environments | Stages, tolerances and project board decisions |
See [Agile operations in IT](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-operations-it/) and [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/) for how delivery and operations teams work together.

### Essential documents and templates
| Document | Purpose | Template |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business case and charter | Why the project exists and who owns it | [Business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/), [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) |
| Requirements | What the solution must do | [Business requirements document template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-requirements-document-template/) |

### KPIs for IT project management
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule and budget variance | Delivery against baseline | Sponsor and steering group reporting |
| Defects by severity at go-live | Open critical and high defects | Go/no-go decisions |
| Change success rate | Changes deployed without incident or rollback | Release quality |
| Incidents after go-live | Service desk tickets linked to the change | Hypercare effectiveness |
| User adoption | Active users or transactions on the new system | Benefits realisation |
| Service availability | Uptime against the agreed [service level agreement](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/service-level-agreement-sla/) | Operational stability |
| Benefits achieved | Cost savings or performance gains against the business case | Post-project review |

### Common challenges
- **Unclear requirements.** Involve real users early, prototype where possible and keep a prioritised backlog.
- **Data migration surprises.** Profile and cleanse data early and run several trial migrations.
- **Vendor dependency.** Define deliverables, acceptance criteria and service levels in the contract and hold regular performance reviews.
- **Resistance to change.** Plan communication and training from the start; see [change management vs change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-management-vs-change-control/).
- **Competing priorities with operations.** Agree resource commitments with operational managers and protect them in a [capacity plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/).

### Software for IT project management
IT teams typically use an IT service management (ITSM) platform for incidents, requests and change records, a developer tool for code and issue tracking, and a project or portfolio platform to plan projects, manage resources and report to leadership.
Look for portfolio dashboards, request intake forms, Gantt and Agile board views in one place, resource management and integrations with ITSM and developer tools. [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is the strongest all-in-one option in [our tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) for this, while engineering-heavy teams may also use [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) for development work.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is IT project management?**
IT project management is planning, delivering and controlling technology changes such as system implementations, migrations and infrastructure upgrades so that they land safely in live environments.

**Q: What are the phases of IT project management?**
Initiation, requirements and design, build and configure, test, deploy and cut over, hypercare and handover, and closure.

**Q: Is Agile or Waterfall better for IT project management?**
It depends on the work. Waterfall suits fixed-scope infrastructure and vendor rollouts; Agile suits application development with changing requirements. Many IT projects are hybrid.

**Q: How does ITIL relate to IT project management?**
ITIL covers how IT services are run and changed. Projects use ITIL practices such as change enablement and release management to move their output safely into live service.

**Q: What does an IT project management plan include?**
Scope, requirements, schedule, budget, RAID log, test strategy, cutover and rollback plans, communication and training plans, and the support model.

**Q: What KPIs are used in IT project management?**
Schedule and budget variance, defects at go-live, change success rate, incidents after go-live, user adoption, availability and benefits achieved.

**Q: What software is used for IT project management?**
An ITSM platform for service records, developer tools for code and issues, and a project platform such as Wrike for planning, resources and reporting.

**Q: What is hypercare in IT project management?**
A period of enhanced support immediately after go-live, during which the project team fixes issues quickly before handing over to normal support.

**Q: What certifications help with IT project management?**
Common options are the PMP, PRINCE2, Scrum and Agile certifications and ITIL 4 Foundation.

**Q: What are the biggest risks in IT project management?**
Unclear requirements, data migration problems, integration failures, vendor delays, security issues and poor user adoption.

**Q: What is the difference between IT project management and software project management?**
IT project management covers all technology change in an organisation, including infrastructure and purchased systems; software project management focuses on building software products.

# Legal Project Management: Process, Roles, Tools and Tips

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/legal-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Legal project management explained: matter phases for litigation and transactions, roles, budgeting and fee models, templates, KPIs and LPM software.


## Legal Project Management: Process, Roles, Tools and Tips
Legal project management (LPM) is the application of project management discipline to legal matters, such as litigation, transactions, regulatory work and investigations, so that they are scoped, staffed, budgeted and delivered predictably. Law firms and in-house legal teams use it mainly to give clients cost certainty, support fixed and capped fees, and reduce wasted effort, while lawyers keep full control of legal judgement.
- Published 28 August 2026
- 6 min read

### Key takeaways
- Legal project management brings scope, budgets and planning to legal matters without replacing legal judgement.
- Define phases and written assumptions at instruction; they underpin every budget conversation.
- Consistent phase and task coding is what makes future estimates accurate.
- Report spend against budget often so clients are never surprised.

### What makes legal project management different
- **Uncertain path:** the other side, the court or a regulator can change the course of a matter at any time.
- **Deadlines set by others:** court timetables, limitation periods and completion dates are often fixed externally.
- **Professional duties:** confidentiality, privilege, conflicts and regulatory rules sit above any efficiency goal.
- **Billing culture:** many matters are still billed by the hour, but clients increasingly ask for budgets, caps and fixed fees.
- **Leverage:** work is spread across partners, associates, paralegals and support staff, so delegating each task to the right level drives both cost and quality.

### Matter phases
Each matter type has its own recognisable phases. Defining them up front is the foundation of LPM because budgets, staffing and reporting all follow the phases.
| Litigation (typical) | Transaction (typical) |
| --- | --- |
| Case assessment and strategy | Instruction, scoping and term sheet |
| Pleadings | Due diligence |
| Disclosure (discovery) | Drafting and negotiation of documents |
| Witness and expert evidence | Regulatory approvals and conditions |
| Trial preparation | Signing |
| Trial or hearing | Completion (closing) |
| Post-trial, appeal or settlement | Post-completion tasks |
Standard coding schemes such as the UTBMS (Uniform Task-Based Management System) litigation code set let firms record time by phase and task, which makes budgets and comparisons possible.
Tip
Agree scope assumptions with the client at instruction: for example the number of witnesses, the volume of documents for review or the number of drafting rounds. When reality differs, the assumption is your basis for a fair budget conversation.

### Key roles
| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Responsible partner or lead lawyer | Owns legal strategy, the client relationship and the matter budget |
| Legal project manager | Builds the plan and budget, tracks progress and spend, and reports to the client |
| Associates, paralegals and trainees | Carry out legal work at the appropriate level |
| Pricing manager | Prices matters and designs alternative fee arrangements |
| Knowledge and legal technology teams | Templates, precedents, e-discovery and automation |
| In-house counsel or legal operations | Client-side owner who sets expectations, manages panels and approves budgets |

### Methods that fit legal work
- **Phased planning:** define phases and tasks, estimate each and track against it; this is LPM's core and works for both litigation and transactions.
- **Scope and assumptions management:** written assumptions and [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) when the matter moves beyond them.
- **Checklists and process maps:** for repeatable work such as due diligence or contract review; see [Lean project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/) for removing waste from routine work.
- **[Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/):** in-house teams use boards to manage the flow of contract requests and advice queries.
- **Agile:** occasionally used for legal technology and large regulatory remediation programmes.

### Budgets and fee arrangements
| Fee model | What LPM must provide |
| --- | --- |
| Hourly with estimate | A phased budget and regular reports of spend against it |
| Capped fee | Close tracking against the cap and early warning when assumptions break |
| Fixed fee | Tight scope, efficient staffing and process reuse |
| Phased fixed fees | A fixed price per phase, re-scoped at each phase boundary |
| Success or blended arrangements | Clear definitions of outcomes and how fees are calculated |

### Essential documents and templates
- **Matter plan and scope statement:** adapt the [project scope template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-scope-template/) and [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/).
- **Budget by phase:** use the [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) and [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/).
- **Matter timeline:** court or deal milestones in a [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/).
- **Task allocation:** a [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) for who drafts, reviews and signs off.
- **Risk and issues:** the [RAID log template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raid-log-template/).
- **Intake for in-house teams:** a [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/).
- **Matter review:** the [lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/).

### KPIs for legal project management
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Budget variance by phase | Actual fees against budget per phase | Client reporting and early warning |
| Realisation | Fees billed and collected against time recorded | Matter profitability for firms |
| Leverage | Mix of hours by seniority | Checking work is delegated correctly |
| Deadline compliance | Court and contractual deadlines met | Risk control |
| Cycle time | Days to turn round contracts or advice requests | In-house team service levels |
| Matter outcomes | Results against the objectives set at the start | Value delivered to the client |
| Client satisfaction | Feedback at matter close | Relationship and panel reviews |

### Common challenges and fixes
- **Lawyer resistance:** present LPM as support for the lead lawyer, keep tools light and show clients' demand for cost predictability.
- **Unpredictable matters:** budget by phase, re-estimate at each phase boundary and report assumptions alongside numbers.
- **Poor time data:** consistent phase and task codes make future estimates far better.
- **Surprise bills:** report spend against budget monthly or more often, and raise overruns before they happen.
- **Repeated work:** capture precedents and checklists in a knowledge system.

### Software for legal project management
Legal teams usually rely on a practice or matter management system, document management, e-billing and, for litigation, e-discovery platforms. A work management platform adds plans, task tracking, intake and dashboards that these systems often lack. Compare options in [our tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/). [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) can serve as the all-in-one planning and intake layer, especially for in-house legal teams handling request queues, with time and budget data from the legal systems alongside it. Check confidentiality, data residency and security requirements before choosing any tool.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is legal project management?**
Legal project management applies project management methods to legal matters so they are scoped, staffed, budgeted and delivered predictably.

**Q: Why is legal project management important?**
Clients expect cost certainty and alternative fees, and legal project management makes budgets reliable and work more efficient.

**Q: What does a legal project manager do in legal project management?**
They build matter plans and budgets, track progress and spend, manage scope assumptions and report to the lead lawyer and client.

**Q: What are the phases in legal project management for litigation?**
Typically case assessment, pleadings, disclosure, evidence, trial preparation, trial and post-trial or settlement.

**Q: How does legal project management work for transactions?**
Deals are planned through instruction and scoping, due diligence, drafting and negotiation, approvals, signing and completion.

**Q: How does legal project management support fixed fees?**
By defining scope and assumptions, staffing efficiently, tracking time by phase and flagging when the matter moves beyond the agreed scope.

**Q: What KPIs are used in legal project management?**
Budget variance by phase, realisation, leverage, deadline compliance, cycle time, matter outcomes and client satisfaction.

**Q: What are UTBMS codes in legal project management?**
Standard phase and task codes, such as the litigation code set, used to record legal time consistently for budgeting and billing.

**Q: Do in-house teams use legal project management?**
Yes. In-house and legal operations teams use it to manage request intake, outside counsel budgets and contract turnaround.

**Q: What software supports legal project management?**
Matter management, document management, e-billing and e-discovery systems, often with a work platform such as Wrike for planning and intake.

**Q: Do lawyers need training in legal project management?**
Basic LPM training helps lawyers scope, budget and delegate; a general [project management certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) suits dedicated legal project managers.

# Manufacturing Project Management: NPI, Phases and KPIs

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/manufacturing-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Manufacturing project management explained: NPI and APQP phases, line installations, roles, Lean and Six Sigma, worked examples, KPIs and software.


## Manufacturing Project Management: NPI, Phases and KPIs
Manufacturing project management is the planning and control of projects that create or change how products are made: new product introductions (NPI), new production lines, equipment installations, plant expansions and improvement programmes. The project is only finished when the factory can make the product reliably at the target rate, quality and cost, not when the machine is switched on. This guide covers the NPI and capital project life cycles, roles, methods, three worked examples, KPIs, templates and software.
- Published 28 August 2026
- Last updated 17 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Manufacturing project management ends at a stable, capable process running at rate, so plan ramp-up and handover as part of the project.
- New products usually follow stage-gate or APQP phases ending in production part approval; capital projects follow specification, FAT, installation, SAT, commissioning and ramp-up.
- Long-lead tooling and equipment set the critical path, so freeze the design before tooling release and track suppliers weekly.
- Keep FMEAs for product and process risks and a project risk register for schedule, supply and cost risks, and cross-reference them.
- Agree measurable exit criteria (OEE, first pass yield, rate) with the plant manager at the start, not at the end.
- Keep product and production data in PLM, ERP and MES, and coordinate the cross-functional project work in a platform such as Wrike.

### What is manufacturing project management?
**Manufacturing project management** is the application of [project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) methods to temporary initiatives that introduce or change products, processes, equipment or facilities in a manufacturing business. A manufacturing project manager coordinates design, manufacturing engineering, quality, procurement, suppliers and production so that the change reaches stable, approved, at-rate production on time and within budget.
It is different from running the factory day to day. Production management repeats the same process every shift; a project has a defined start, end and unique outcome. The two meet at handover, where the project is judged.
| Project type | Example | What usually sets the critical path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New product introduction (NPI) | A new model, variant or component launched into an existing plant | Design freeze, tooling lead times and customer approval |
| Capital equipment and new lines | A new assembly line, CNC cell, moulding press or packaging line | Equipment build, shutdown windows and acceptance tests |
| Plant expansion or new facility | A new building, hall extension or greenfield site | Permits, construction, utilities and equipment install |
| Process improvement | Reducing scrap, cutting changeover time, improving flow | Data collection and trial runs on a live line |
| Automation and digital | Robots, vision inspection, MES rollout, connected sensors | Integration, software testing and operator training |
| Product or line transfer | Moving production between plants or to a contract manufacturer | Build-ahead stock, requalification and customer approval |

### What makes manufacturing projects different
The standard toolkit still applies: a charter, a work breakdown structure, a schedule and a risk register. What changes is the set of constraints you plan around.

#### The factory keeps running
Many projects happen inside a live plant. Installation work has to fit planned shutdowns, weekends or holiday periods, and every hour of unplanned downtime costs output. Customers still expect deliveries, so build-ahead stock and temporary routings become part of the plan.

#### Physical long-lead items
Moulds, dies, fixtures, special machines and some components can take many weeks or months to make. Once tooling is cut, design changes become expensive. That makes design freeze and tooling release the most important decisions in many NPI schedules.

#### Quality systems and customer approval
Quality management standards such as ISO 9001, sector standards such as IATF 16949 (automotive), AS9100 (aerospace) and ISO 13485 (medical devices), and good manufacturing practice in food and pharmaceuticals require documented, controlled processes. Automotive customers usually require formal production part approval before shipments start. These approvals are milestones on the critical path, not paperwork at the end.

#### Success is measured after go-live
A line that is installed on time but takes six months to reach its target rate has not delivered its business case. Ramp-up, capability and handover criteria belong in the project scope.

#### Many functions must sign off
Design, manufacturing engineering, quality, purchasing, logistics, maintenance, health and safety, finance and production all hold part of the outcome. The project manager's main job is to keep them working to one integrated plan.

### The NPI life cycle: stage-gate and APQP
New product introduction in many companies follows a stage-gate process: work is divided into phases and a gate review decides whether the project has earned the next tranche of investment. In automotive and related supply chains, the AIAG Advanced Product Quality Planning (APQP) framework provides the structure and ends with Production Part Approval Process (PPAP) submission. AIAG published the third edition of the APQP manual in 2024 with a standalone Control Plan manual; the third edition adds a gated management section with suggested checklists for each gate.
| APQP phase | What happens | Key outputs | Typical gate question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Plan and define the programme | Capture customer requirements, targets, volumes and constraints | Design goals, quality targets, preliminary bill of materials and process flow, special characteristics | Is the scope clear enough to fund design? |
| 2. Product design and development | Detailed design, design FMEA, prototypes and design verification | Drawings, DFMEA, prototype build, verification results, design freeze | Is the design frozen enough to release tooling? |
| 3. Process design and development | Design the process, layout, tooling, fixtures, gauges and controls | Process flow diagram, process FMEA, pre-launch control plan, layout, work instructions | Are tools, equipment and suppliers on track for trials? |
| 4. Product and process validation | Trial runs at rate, measurement system analysis, capability studies | Production run results, MSA, capability data, production control plan, PPAP | Is the process capable and approved for shipment? |
| 5. Feedback, assessment and corrective action | Run at rate, reduce variation, close actions | Improvement actions, delivery and quality performance, lessons learned | Can the project close and hand over? |

#### What goes into a PPAP submission
PPAP is the customer's evidence that your process can consistently make parts that meet every requirement. The AIAG PPAP manual lists 18 elements, including design records, engineering change documents, the DFMEA and PFMEA, process flow diagram, control plan, measurement system analysis, dimensional results, material and performance test results, initial process studies, appearance approval, sample parts and the Part Submission Warrant. The customer chooses one of five submission levels, which sets how much evidence you send and how much you retain.
Tip
Outside automotive the names change but the logic is the same: aerospace suppliers complete a first article inspection, medical device makers complete design transfer and process validation, and food and pharmaceutical plants qualify equipment and validate processes before release.

### The capital project life cycle: from specification to ramp-up
Installing a new line, cell or major machine follows a parallel path. It looks more like a [Waterfall project](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/waterfall-project-management/) with a hard sequence of acceptance tests.
| Stage | What happens | Key output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Business case and concept | Define capacity, product mix, cycle time and budget; compare options | Approved capital request and [business case](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) |
| 2. User requirements specification (URS) | What the equipment must do: rate, tolerances, changeovers, safety, utilities, data | Signed URS used for quotations and acceptance tests |
| 3. Supplier selection | Request for quotation, technical comparison, negotiation | Purchase order, functional specification and payment milestones |
| 4. Design review | Review layouts, guarding, controls and maintenance access with the supplier | Approved design and FAT protocol |
| 5. Factory acceptance test (FAT) | Run the equipment at the supplier with your parts and criteria before shipping | Signed FAT report and punch list |
| 6. Delivery and installation | Site preparation, utilities, rigging, mechanical and electrical installation | Installed equipment, safety checks completed |
| 7. Site acceptance test (SAT) and commissioning | Prove performance in your plant with your utilities, materials and operators | Signed SAT report, open points list |
| 8. Ramp-up and handover | Staged increase to target rate; training; spares; maintenance plan | Exit criteria met and formal handover |
In regulated sectors such as pharmaceuticals and food, installation, operational and performance qualification (IQ, OQ, PQ) are added before the equipment can make saleable product.

### How to run a manufacturing project step by step
This sequence works for both NPI and capital projects. Scale the documentation to the size of the project.
1. **Define the outcome and exit criteria.** Write the [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) with product, volume, rate, quality target, budget and start-of-production (SOP) date. Agree measurable handover criteria with the plant manager now.
2. **Form the cross-functional team.** Name owners from design, manufacturing engineering, quality, purchasing, logistics, maintenance, safety and production, and set out decision rights in a RACI matrix.
3. **Break down the work.** Build a [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) covering product, process, tooling, equipment, facility, people and documentation.
4. **Identify long-lead items first.** List tooling, equipment and components with quoted lead times and order as early as design maturity allows.
5. **Schedule backwards from SOP.** Work back through approval, trials, tooling and design freeze to find the latest start for each item and the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).
6. **Assess risk twice.** Run DFMEA and PFMEA for product and process risks, and keep a project risk register for schedule, supplier, cost and resource risks.
7. **Set the gate reviews.** Define what must be complete at each gate, who decides and what happens if criteria are not met.
8. **Control changes.** Route every engineering and process change through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) with tooling, validation, cost and schedule impact assessed.
9. **Prove the process.** Run FAT and SAT, trial runs, measurement system analysis and capability studies, and fix problems with structured [root cause analysis](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/root-cause-analysis-template/).
10. **Prepare people.** Write work instructions and train operators and maintenance staff before SOP; set up spares and preventive maintenance.
11. **Ramp up in stages.** Increase rate against a plan, track daily against exit criteria and keep the project team in place until they are met.
12. **Hand over and close.** Sign the handover, transfer open actions to production owners, close the budget and run a [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) review that feeds the next launch.

### Worked example 1: backward scheduling an NPI launch
A supplier must launch a new injection-moulded housing for a customer whose SOP is week 40. The figures are illustrative planning assumptions, not industry standards; use your own supplier quotes.
| Milestone | Planned week | Duration logic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kick-off and customer requirements review | 1 | Project start |
| Design freeze | 8 | Prototypes and design verification complete |
| Tool kick-off (purchase order to toolmaker) | 9 | Needs frozen design data |
| First tool trial (T1) samples | 25 | Quoted 16-week tool build |
| Tool corrections after T1 | 25 to 29 | One round of corrections allowed |
| Second tool trial (T2) and dimensional layout | 30 | Confirms corrections |
| Production run, MSA and capability studies | 32 to 35 | Run at rate with production operators |
| PPAP submission | 35 | Evidence pack complete |
| PPAP approval | 37 | Customer review assumed at two weeks |
| SOP | 40 | Three weeks of buffer |
The critical path runs through design freeze, tool build, trials, the production run and approval. Packaging design, operator training and label approval all have float.

#### What happens when the design changes late
In week 20 the customer requests a change to a clip feature. The toolmaker quotes four extra weeks of tool work. The buffer was three weeks, so SOP is now at risk by one week. The options:
- **Crash the tool work:** pay for overtime or a second shift at the toolmaker to recover one to two weeks. See [fast-tracking vs crashing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/fast-tracking-vs-crashing/).
- **Fast-track validation:** start measurement system analysis on the gauges while tool corrections are underway, accepting some rework risk.
- **Defer the change:** agree with the customer to launch on the frozen design and introduce the clip change after SOP.
- **Re-baseline:** if none of these work, agree a new SOP date formally rather than letting the date slip silently.
Whatever the decision, record it as a change request with its cost and schedule impact and update the baseline. Our [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) and [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) are set up for this kind of plan.

### Worked example 2: installing a line in a shutdown window
A plant will replace an ageing assembly line during a two-week summer shutdown (10 working days). The customer keeps calling off 2,000 units a day, five days a week, throughout. The new line should reach full rate three weeks after the shutdown.

#### Step 1: calculate the build-ahead stock
| Source of lost output | Calculation | Units |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shutdown (line not running) | 10 days x 2,000 | 20,000 |
| Ramp-up week 1 at 40% of rate | 5 days x 2,000 x 60% shortfall | 6,000 |
| Ramp-up week 2 at 70% of rate | 5 days x 2,000 x 30% shortfall | 3,000 |
| Ramp-up week 3 at 90% of rate | 5 days x 2,000 x 10% shortfall | 1,000 |
| Safety stock for start-up problems | 3 days x 2,000 | 6,000 |
| Total build-ahead required |  | 36,000 |
Spread over the 40 working days before the shutdown, the old line must make 900 extra units a day. If that is beyond its capacity, the plan needs to change: a longer build-ahead period, a temporary extra shift or a staged changeover. Check warehouse space and shelf life too.

#### Step 2: plan the shutdown day by day
| Days | Work | Acceptance point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before shutdown | FAT passed, site prepared, utilities run, permits and method statements approved | Readiness review: go or no-go to remove the old line |
| 1 to 2 | Isolate and remove the old line, floor preparation | Area handed over clean and safe |
| 3 to 5 | Position, level and fix the new line; mechanical and electrical connection | Installation checks complete |
| 6 to 7 | Power-up, safety system and guarding checks, dry cycling | Safety validation signed off |
| 8 to 9 | SAT with production parts and operators | SAT criteria met or punch list agreed |
| 10 | Trial production, first-off approval | Go for production or activate the contingency plan |
Rehearse the critical tasks, name an owner for every shift of the plan and agree in advance what triggers the fallback, for example keeping the old line in storage until the new one passes SAT.

#### Step 3: define ramp-up exit criteria
| Week after shutdown | Target rate | Criteria to move to the next stage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 40% | No open safety actions; first pass yield at least 90% |
| 2 | 70% | OEE trend improving; top downtime causes not repeating |
| 3 | 90% | First pass yield at target for five consecutive days |
| 4 onwards | 100% | Rate, OEE and yield sustained for two weeks; handover signed |
These targets are examples. Set yours from the business case and the supplier's guaranteed performance.

### Worked example 3: calculating OEE at handover
Overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) is the most common handover measure for new lines. It multiplies availability, performance and quality.
| Factor | Data for one shift | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Availability | Planned time 450 minutes; 45 minutes of stops | (450 - 45) / 450 | 90.0% |
| Performance | Ideal cycle 1.0 minute; 380 parts in 405 minutes of run time | (380 x 1.0) / 405 | 93.8% |
| Quality | 365 good parts out of 380 | 365 / 380 | 96.1% |
| OEE |  | 90.0% x 93.8% x 96.1% | 81.1% |
If the agreed handover target is 80%, this shift passes. Judge the trend over several weeks rather than one shift, and use the loss breakdown to direct improvement: here the 45 minutes of stops are the biggest loss. Agree how planned stops, changeovers and trials are counted before you start, or the project team and the plant will report different numbers.

### Key roles in a manufacturing project
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Project sponsor | Owns the business case, approves budget and resolves cross-functional conflicts |
| Programme or NPI project manager | Integrated plan, gate reviews, risks, budget, change control and reporting |
| Design or product engineer | Product design, design verification and design changes |
| Manufacturing or process engineer | Process design, tooling, fixtures, line layout and work instructions |
| Quality engineer | FMEAs, control plans, measurement studies, capability and approval submissions |
| Purchasing and supplier quality | Sourcing parts and tooling, supplier approvals and supplier PPAPs |
| Plant or production manager | Accepts the process into production and owns ramp-up |
| Maintenance and facilities | Utilities, installation support, spares and preventive maintenance |
| Health, safety and environment | Machinery safety, risk assessments, permits and consents |
| Logistics and planning | Build-ahead stock, packaging, material flow and customer call-offs |

#### Skills and certifications
Useful credentials combine project control with manufacturing knowledge: the [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) or PRINCE2 for project management, Lean and [Six Sigma](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/six-sigma/) belts for improvement work, and training in the automotive core tools (APQP, PPAP, FMEA, MSA, SPC) or the quality standard your sector uses.

### Methodologies that fit manufacturing projects
| Approach | When it fits | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage-gate / APQP | New product introduction | Gates control investment and launch readiness |
| Waterfall with critical path | Line installations, plant expansions, transfers | Fixed sequence with shutdown windows and acceptance tests |
| Critical chain | Plants running many projects through shared engineers | Protects the project with buffers rather than padding every task |
| [Lean manufacturing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/lean-manufacturing/) | New line design and process improvement | Design for flow; use [value stream mapping](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/) |
| Six Sigma DMAIC | Quality and variation problems | Define, measure, analyse, improve, control |
| Agile and hybrid | Automation software, MES rollouts, early product concepts | Iterate on software and prototypes inside the gated plan |
Most manufacturers run a hybrid: a gated plan for the hardware with iterative sprints for controls software, vision systems or data dashboards.

### Managing risk: FMEA and the project risk register
Manufacturing projects need two complementary risk tools.
|  | FMEA (design and process) | Project risk register |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | How the product or process could fail and the effect on the customer | What could stop the project meeting time, cost or scope |
| Owner | Design and quality engineers | Project manager with workstream leads |
| Examples | Weld undersize; wrong part fitted; label misprint | Toolmaker capacity; late customer data; budget overrun |
| Method | Severity, occurrence and detection ratings; the AIAG and VDA FMEA handbook ranks actions by action priority (high, medium, low) | Probability and impact scoring, owners, responses and triggers |
| Output | Design and process changes, controls in the control plan | Mitigation actions, contingency and reserve |
Cross-reference the two: a high-priority failure mode with a late corrective action is also a schedule risk. Example register entry: **Risk:** the toolmaker has three other tools due at the same time. **Effect:** T1 slips two to four weeks, consuming all schedule buffer. **Response:** agree a capacity commitment in the purchase order, hold fortnightly progress visits and line up a second toolmaker for corrections. **Owner:** supplier quality engineer.
Use our [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/) for project risks.

### Quality standards and regulations to plan for
Standards and laws differ by sector and country, so confirm what applies with your quality and safety teams. These are the ones that most often appear as milestones.
- **ISO 9001.** ISO 9001:2026 was published on 16 September 2026, replacing the 2015 edition, with a transition period of about three years for certified organisations. Its changes include stronger expectations on quality culture, risk and opportunity, and planned change, so certified plants may run a transition project alongside their launches.
- **Sector standards.** IATF 16949 for automotive, AS9100 for aerospace and defence, ISO 13485 for medical devices, and good manufacturing practice for pharmaceuticals and food. Each adds specific approval and validation steps.
- **Machinery safety.** In the EU, the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies to machinery placed on the market from 20 January 2027, replacing the Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC. Equipment delivered around that date may fall under the new rules, so state the conformity requirements in the purchase order. Great Britain and the US have their own regimes.

| Document | Purpose | Template |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project charter | Objectives, scope, sponsor, SOP date and exit criteria | [Project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) |
| Business case and capital request | Justifies development or capital investment | [Business case template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/business-case-template/) |

You will also need a RACI matrix, change requests, a training plan and a lessons learned log, all of which are in our free template library. Engineering and quality own the technical documents: DFMEA and PFMEA, process flow diagrams, control plans, work instructions, measurement and capability studies, URS and acceptance test protocols.

### KPIs for manufacturing project management
Track two sets of measures: whether the project is being delivered well, and whether the result performs.
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Milestones on time | Gate and key milestones achieved against baseline | Schedule health |
| Capital spend vs budget | Committed and actual spend against approved amount | Investment control |
| Gate readiness | Share of deliverables complete at each gate | Programme health |
| Open engineering changes | Number and age of changes awaiting decision | Design stability |
| Time to market | Project start to first customer shipment | NPI performance |
| Ramp-up time | SOP to sustained target rate and quality | Launch success |
| Overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) | Availability x performance x quality | Line performance at handover |
| First pass yield | Units right first time without rework | Process capability |
| Process capability (Cpk) | Ability to meet tolerances on key characteristics | Approval and control plan |

### Common challenges and mistakes
- **Tooling and equipment delays.** Track long-lead items weekly, visit suppliers and make FAT a real test with your parts rather than a demonstration.
- **Late design changes.** Freeze the design before tooling release and assess every change for tooling, validation, cost and schedule impact before approving it.
- **Planning only to installation.** A plan that ends at SAT hides the ramp-up. Include ramp-up stages and exit criteria in the baseline.
- **Untrained operators at SOP.** Train operators and maintenance staff on the real equipment before start of production.
- **Shared engineers overloaded.** Plants running several launches depend on the same few engineers. Prioritise at portfolio level; see [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/).
- **Unclear handover.** Agree acceptance criteria with the plant manager at the start and keep the project open until they are met.

### Software for manufacturing project management
Manufacturers rely on specialist systems for operational data: ERP for materials, purchasing and costs; PLM for product data, bills of materials and engineering changes; MES for shop floor execution; and a quality management system for non-conformances and corrective actions. These systems are not designed to coordinate a cross-functional launch, which is where a project management platform helps.
Look for Gantt charts with dependencies and baselines, stage-gate templates, approval workflows, workload views across projects, portfolio dashboards and integrations with your ERP and file storage. Keep detailed product and production data in PLM, ERP and MES, and link to it from the project rather than copying it.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is the strongest all-in-one choice in [our tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) for this coordination role, with Gantt, workload and dashboard features that suit multi-project NPI and capital portfolios. Spreadsheet-minded engineering teams also get on well with Smartsheet.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is manufacturing project management?**
Manufacturing project management is planning and controlling projects that create or change how products are made, such as new product introductions, new lines, equipment installations, plant expansions and improvement programmes. It ends when the factory can make the product reliably at the target rate, quality and cost.

**Q: What are the phases of manufacturing project management?**
For new products, many firms use stage-gate or APQP phases: plan and define, product design and development, process design and development, product and process validation, and feedback and corrective action. Capital projects run from business case and specification through FAT, installation, SAT, commissioning and ramp-up.

**Q: What is APQP in manufacturing project management?**
Advanced Product Quality Planning is a framework published by AIAG and widely used in automotive supply chains. It plans product and process development so parts meet customer requirements, and ends with PPAP approval. The third edition, published in 2024, adds gated management checklists.

**Q: What is NPI in manufacturing project management?**
New product introduction is the process of taking a new product from design into reliable volume production, including tooling, process development, validation, customer approval and ramp-up.

**Q: What is the difference between FAT and SAT in manufacturing project management?**
A factory acceptance test checks equipment at the supplier before it ships. A site acceptance test checks it after installation in your plant, with your utilities, materials and operators.

**Q: How is manufacturing project management different from production management?**
Production management runs the factory every day to make current products to plan. Manufacturing project management delivers a one-off change, such as a new product or line, and hands it over to production when agreed exit criteria are met.

**Q: What KPIs are used in manufacturing project management?**
Project KPIs include milestones on time, capital spend against budget, gate readiness and open engineering changes. Result KPIs include time to market, ramp-up time, OEE, first pass yield and process capability.

**Q: How do you calculate OEE for a manufacturing project handover?**
Multiply availability by performance by quality. For example, 90% availability, 93.8% performance and 96.1% quality give an OEE of about 81%. Agree how planned stops and trials are counted before you measure.

**Q: What documents are used in manufacturing project management?**
A charter, business case, WBS, schedule, cost estimate, RACI, risk register and change requests, plus engineering documents such as FMEAs, process flow diagrams, control plans, work instructions, specifications and acceptance test protocols.

**Q: How do you manage risk in manufacturing project management?**
Use design and process FMEAs for failure risks, a project risk register for schedule, supply and cost risks, and gate reviews to confirm readiness before major commitments such as tooling release.

**Q: Which methodology is best for manufacturing project management?**
Stage-gate or APQP suits new products, Waterfall with critical path suits installations and expansions, Lean and Six Sigma suit improvement projects, and Agile works for automation software inside a gated plan. Most plants use a hybrid.

**Q: What software is used for manufacturing project management?**
ERP, PLM, MES and quality systems hold operational data, and a project platform such as Wrike coordinates schedules, gates, approvals, resources and reporting across launches and capital projects.
