# Marketing Project Management: Process, Roles and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/marketing-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Marketing project management explained: the campaign life cycle, roles, backwards planning, a worked launch example, KPIs, templates and software.


## Marketing Project Management: Process, Roles and Tools
Marketing project management is the planning, coordination and control of marketing work, from a single asset to a multi-channel campaign, so that it launches on time, on brand, within budget and against a measurable goal. It differs from most project work because launch dates are usually fixed before scope is known, many people review the same assets and the work never really stops: one campaign launches while the next is being briefed. This guide covers the campaign life cycle, backwards planning, a worked example, intake, approvals, roles, KPIs and tools.
- Published 28 August 2026
- Last updated 16 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Marketing project management runs many overlapping campaigns with fixed dates, shared specialists and heavy review cycles.
- A signed brief, one intake queue and capped, consolidated review rounds solve most delivery problems.
- Plan backwards from the launch date and cut deliverables early rather than squeezing review time.
- Score incoming requests against goals, deadline and effort so priorities are agreed, not shouted.
- Track delivery KPIs (on-time launch rate, cycle time, review rounds) separately from campaign results.
- Most teams use a hybrid: a milestone plan for launches with Kanban or sprints for production.

### What is marketing project management?
**Marketing project management** is the use of project management methods to plan, schedule, resource and track marketing work, such as campaigns, product launches, content programmes, events and website projects, so it is delivered on time, within budget and against a clear business objective. It applies standard [project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) practice to the realities of marketing: fixed dates, many reviewers and shared creative capacity.
Marketing strategy decides what to do and why: the audience, positioning and channels. Marketing project management decides how the work gets done: who does what, by when, with which approvals. Both matter, and a good marketing project manager connects them by making sure every plan traces back to a goal in the brief.
|  | General project management | Marketing project management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical portfolio | A few large projects | Dozens of small, overlapping projects and requests |
| Fixed constraint | Varies: scope, cost or date | Usually the launch date |
| Main bottleneck | Dependencies, suppliers, technical work | Approvals and shared creative capacity |
| End point | Handover of a deliverable | Launch, then optimisation and reporting |
| Success measure | On time, on budget, to scope | On time and budget, plus campaign results such as leads or revenue |

### Why marketing teams need project management
Marketing teams rarely fail for lack of ideas. They struggle with volume, interruptions and approvals. A light project management approach helps in practical ways:
- **Visibility.** Everyone can see what is in flight, who owns it and when it launches, which cuts status meetings and chasing.
- **Fewer missed launches.** Plans built backwards from fixed dates expose problems while there is still time to cut scope.
- **Faster approvals.** Named approvers and scheduled review windows replace open-ended email threads.
- **Balanced workloads.** Capacity views show when designers, writers or developers are overloaded before quality drops.
- **Clear priorities.** One intake queue and a scoring model replace whoever shouts loudest.
- **Better results over time.** Retrospectives and results reports feed the next brief, so the team learns from each campaign.

### What makes marketing projects different
Marketing projects use the same building blocks as other projects, but six features change how you plan them.

#### Launch dates are fixed
Product launches, trade shows, seasonal sales and press moments set the date before the scope is known. That makes scope and the number of deliverables the main things that can flex.

#### Many reviewers
Brand, legal, product, sales, regional teams and senior leaders may all want to approve the same assets. Review rounds are where most marketing schedules slip.

#### Shared specialists
Designers, copywriters, video editors, web developers and marketing operations staff are split across many campaigns at once, so capacity, not budget, is often the binding constraint.

#### Compliance and claims
Regulated sectors such as financial services, healthcare, alcohol and gambling need claims checked and approvals recorded before anything goes live. Privacy and consent rules also affect email, tracking and data capture.

#### The project continues after launch
A campaign is optimised while live: budgets shift between channels, creative is refreshed and results are reported. Plan this phase, its owners and its reporting dates as part of the project.

#### Continuous volume
Alongside big campaigns there is a steady stream of small requests: social posts, sales collateral, event materials and web updates. Without an intake process, small requests quietly consume the capacity that planned campaigns need.

### Types of marketing projects
Different marketing projects need different amounts of planning. The table shows common types and the risk that usually needs most attention.
| Project type | Example | Main risk to plan for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Integrated campaign | A quarter-long brand campaign across paid social, video, email and out-of-home | Many assets and reviewers converging on one date |
| Product launch | Launch of a new product or feature with a [go-to-market plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/go-to-market-plan-template/) | Late changes to product details, pricing or messaging |
| Content programme | A monthly blog, newsletter and social calendar | Continuous volume and subject-matter expert availability |
| Website project | A redesign or new landing pages | Dependencies on developers, content and SEO migration |
| Event or trade show | A stand, sessions and follow-up campaign | Supplier lead times and fixed event dates |
| Rebrand | New visual identity rolled out across every touchpoint | Scope across hundreds of assets and suppliers |
| Demand generation programme | Webinars, gated content and nurture emails | Tracking, data and sales follow-up processes |
| Small requests | Sales one-pager, social graphic, email update | Volume crowding out planned work |
Smaller teams often treat these as routine tasks. Once work touches several specialists, has a fixed date and needs approvals, give it at least a short brief and a named owner.

### The marketing campaign life cycle: 7 phases
Most marketing projects follow the same seven phases. Small requests compress them into a day or two; a major launch may take months.
| Phase | What happens | Main output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Request and intake | A stakeholder asks for work; the team checks fit, priority and capacity | Accepted, prioritised request |
| 2. Brief | Objective, audience, message, channels, budget, mandatory items, approvers and success measures agreed | Signed campaign or creative brief |
| 3. Planning | Deliverables listed, tasks and owners assigned, review steps and dates set back from the launch date | Campaign plan, schedule and budget |
| 4. Creative development | Concepts, copy, design, video and landing pages produced | Draft assets |
| 5. Review and approval | Feedback rounds from stakeholders, brand, legal and compliance | Approved assets |
| 6. Launch | Assets trafficked to channels, tracking tested, campaign goes live | Live campaign |
| 7. Optimise, report and close | Performance monitored, budget shifted between channels, results and lessons reported | Results report and lessons learned |
If you know the five standard project management phases, phases 1 and 2 are initiation, phase 3 is planning, phases 4 to 6 are execution with monitoring, and phase 7 is monitoring and closure.

### How to plan a marketing campaign step by step
Use these ten steps for any campaign, scaling the documentation to its size.
1. **Confirm the business goal.** Write the objective in measurable terms, such as 400 qualified leads or 2,000 event registrations, and agree how it will be measured.
2. **Write and sign the brief.** Audience, key message, channels, deliverables, budget, mandatory items, launch date, approvers and the number of review rounds. Start from our [creative brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/creative-brief-template/).
3. **List every deliverable.** Each asset, size, language and channel. This is your scope; anything added later is a change.
4. **Break the work down.** Turn deliverables into tasks with owners, from copy and design to tracking links and QA. A simple work breakdown structure helps on large campaigns.
5. **Map dependencies.** Copy before design, landing page before paid media, tracking before launch. See [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/).
6. **Schedule backwards from the launch date.** Place final approval, review rounds, production and briefing dates working back from go-live.
7. **Check capacity.** Compare the plan with your specialists' availability across all campaigns; book freelancers or cut scope early if it does not fit.
8. **Agree the budget.** Separate media spend from production costs and set a contingency.
9. **Run production and reviews to plan.** Hold short weekly check-ins, keep status visible and handle changes through a change request.
10. **Launch, optimise and report.** Test tracking before go-live, monitor results, report against the goal and run a short retrospective.

### Planning backwards from the launch date
Because the launch date is fixed, marketing schedules work best when built backwards. Start at launch and place each milestone before it, including review time and buffers. If the first task lands in the past, you know immediately that scope must shrink or more capacity is needed.
1. Fix the launch date and the final approval date (allow a few working days between them for trafficking and QA).
2. Work back through each review round, adding reviewer turnaround time.
3. Work back through production for each deliverable, using the longest chain of dependencies.
4. Add concept and brief dates.
5. Compare the first date with today. If it has passed, cut or phase deliverables now.
Here is a backwards plan for an illustrative email and paid social campaign launching on a Monday, counted in working days before launch:
| Working days before launch | Milestone | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| -20 | Brief signed | Approvers and two review rounds named |
| -17 | Concepts and key message approved | One route chosen |
| -12 | First drafts of all assets | Copy and design together |
| -10 | Round 1 consolidated feedback due | Two working days for reviewers |
| -7 | Round 2 drafts; legal and brand check | Compliance runs in parallel |
| -5 | Final approval | Recorded in the tool |
| -4 to -2 | Build emails, upload ads, test tracking links | QA checklist |
| -1 | Buffer | For last fixes only |
| 0 | Launch | Monitoring starts |
Tip
If the dates do not fit, cut deliverables early rather than squeezing review time. A smaller campaign that launches well beats a full one with rushed, unchecked assets.
The same logic underpins the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/): find the longest chain of dependent tasks, because that chain sets the earliest possible launch.

### Worked example: a product launch campaign
A B2B software company is launching a new reporting feature. The launch date is set for six weeks away to align with a customer conference. The marketing team has one marketing project manager, a product marketer, a content writer, a designer shared with two other teams, a marketing operations specialist and a paid media agency. This is an illustrative example, not a real company.

#### Brief summary
- **Objective:** 300 demo requests from existing customers and prospects within six weeks of launch.
- **Audience:** operations and finance leads in mid-sized companies; existing customers on older plans.
- **Key message:** reports that used to take a day now take minutes.
- **Approvers:** head of product marketing (messaging), brand lead (visuals), legal (customer claims). Two review rounds included.

#### Deliverables and owners
| Deliverable | Owner | Depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Messaging and positioning document | Product marketer | Product briefing |
| Launch blog post | Content writer | Messaging |
| Landing page with demo form | Designer and marketing operations | Messaging, blog draft |
| Customer email (two sends) | Content writer, marketing operations | Landing page |
| Paid social ads (six variants) | Designer, paid media agency | Key visual, landing page |
| Sales one-pager and slides | Product marketer, designer | Messaging |
| Conference stand screen loop | Designer | Key visual |
| Tracking and reporting dashboard | Marketing operations | Landing page, UTM plan |

#### Budget
| Line | Planned | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paid social media spend | $12,000 | Split across two platforms |
| Agency fees | $3,000 | Ad build and optimisation |
| Freelance video editing | $1,500 | Short product clip |
| Contingency (about 10%) | $1,650 | Held by the project manager |
| Total | $18,150 |  |

#### What happened
Two weeks before launch, the product team renamed one feature. Because the brief named the product marketer as messaging owner, the change went through a quick change request: the copy was updated in round 2 rather than after approval, and the stand loop was finalised last because it was the least time-critical item. The shared designer was overbooked in week four, so the project manager agreed with the head of marketing to delay a lower-priority brochure for another team by a week rather than cut launch assets.
After launch, the team moved a share of paid budget from the weaker platform to the stronger one in week two. The retrospective recorded three lessons: get product naming frozen at brief sign-off, book shared design time at the planning stage, and test tracking a day earlier. Results were reported against the 300-demo objective, separately from delivery measures such as on-time launch and review rounds.

### Request intake and prioritisation
Uncontrolled requests are the biggest threat to planned campaigns. Put every request through one intake route, usually a form, and review the queue at a fixed time each week.

#### What the intake form should capture
- Requester, team and business goal the request supports.
- What is needed: deliverables, formats and channels.
- Audience and key message.
- Deadline and the reason for it (a real event or a preference).
- Budget, if any, and approvers.
- Links to existing assets, brand guidelines and data.
Our [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) includes an intake form and request log you can adapt.

#### A simple prioritisation score
Score each request from 1 to 5 on three criteria, weight them and compare totals. Agree the weights with the marketing leader once, then apply them consistently.
| Request | Goal impact (x3) | Deadline urgency (x2) | Effort, inverted (x1) | Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Launch landing page | 5 (15) | 5 (10) | 3 (3) | 28 |
| Partner webinar promotion | 4 (12) | 3 (6) | 4 (4) | 22 |
| Refresh of old brochure | 2 (6) | 1 (2) | 2 (2) | 10 |
Requests with the highest scores go first; low scorers are scheduled later, simplified or declined with a reason. For the wider discipline of juggling competing work, see [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/).

### Approval workflows that do not stall
Approvals cause more marketing delays than production. These practices keep them moving:
1. **Name approvers in the brief.** Separate who approves (one person per area: messaging, brand, legal) from who is consulted or informed. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) makes this explicit.
2. **Cap and schedule rounds.** Agree the number of rounds and put each review window in reviewers' calendars when the plan is approved.
3. **Consolidate feedback.** One person per stakeholder group collects comments and resolves contradictions before they reach the creative team.
4. **Review on the asset.** Use proofing so comments are pinned to the image, page or video, with versions tracked.
5. **Run compliance in parallel.** Where possible, legal and brand review the same round as stakeholders rather than adding a round at the end.
6. **Record approval.** Note who approved which version and when, especially in regulated sectors.
7. **Treat late changes as changes.** Anything that alters the brief after sign-off goes through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) with an impact on time and cost.
Unmanaged additions after the brief is signed are a classic form of scope creep, so log every one, even when it looks small.

### Key roles in marketing projects
| Role | What they do |
| --- | --- |
| Marketing project manager or campaign manager | Owns the plan, timeline, status and flow of work between specialists |
| Requester or business owner | Product, sales or regional lead who needs the campaign and signs off the brief |
| Marketing leader (CMO or head of marketing) | Sets priorities across campaigns and resolves conflicts over capacity |
| Product marketer | Owns positioning and messaging for product-related work |
| Content and copy | Writes copy, articles, emails and scripts |
| Design and video | Produces visual and motion assets |
| Channel specialists | Paid media, email, social, SEO and web teams who launch and optimise |
| Marketing operations | Runs the martech stack, tracking, data, workflow tooling and reporting |
| Brand, legal and compliance reviewers | Approve claims, trademarks, disclaimers and brand use |

#### What does a marketing project manager do?
A marketing project manager turns briefs into plans and keeps campaigns moving. Day to day that means running intake and prioritisation, building schedules and budgets, booking specialist time, running review rounds, tracking status, managing risks and changes, coordinating launch, and reporting results with lessons learned. In smaller teams, marketing managers or marketing operations staff often do this alongside their main role.

#### Marketing project manager vs marketing manager
A **marketing manager** owns strategy and results: which audiences, messages and channels to use, and whether the campaign hit its goal. A **marketing project manager** owns delivery: the plan, schedule, resources, approvals and launch. The roles work as partners, and in small teams one person often does both, which is why separating strategic and delivery decisions in the brief helps.

### Methodologies that fit marketing
Choose a method by how work arrives and how fixed the dates are.
| Approach | When to use it | How it looks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kanban | Ongoing, request-driven work such as content, social and design support | Board with Intake, Brief, In progress, Review, Approved, Live; WIP limits per stage |
| Scrum or Agile sprints | Growth, digital and content teams that can plan in two-week cycles and test and learn | Backlog, sprint planning, review and retrospective; see [Agile marketing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/) |
| Waterfall | Large, fixed-date launches with long lead-time items such as print, events or TV | Phased plan with dependencies and a Gantt chart |
| Hybrid | Most marketing teams | A milestone plan for the launch with Kanban or sprints for the creative work inside it |
Whatever the method, make work visible on one board or plan, set clear intake rules and agree review rounds up front. [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) stop the team starting more than it can finish.

### Managing many campaigns at once
Most marketing teams run a portfolio rather than a single project. Four habits keep it under control:
- **One marketing calendar.** Show every campaign launch, major content piece and event on a single shared calendar so clashes are visible early.
- **A capacity view across campaigns.** Plan specialist time across all work, not campaign by campaign. See [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/) for the method.
- **A weekly prioritisation meeting.** Short and regular, with the marketing leader deciding trade-offs using the agreed scoring model.
- **Templates for repeat work.** Webinar promotions, product updates and newsletters follow the same steps each time; save them as templates with tasks, owners and relative dates.
Tip
Keep a small reserve of capacity, for example part of each specialist's week, for genuinely urgent requests. It is easier to protect planned campaigns when there is an agreed place for the unexpected.

### Documents and templates for marketing projects
These documents cover most needs. The linked ones are free templates in Google Sheets, Excel and PDF.
- **[Creative brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/creative-brief-template/):** the single most important document for any campaign or asset.
- **[Marketing campaign template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/marketing-campaign-template/):** goal, audience, channels, tactics, budget, timeline and KPIs.
- **[Marketing plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/marketing-plan-template/):** the wider plan that campaigns roll up to.
- **[Content calendar template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/content-calendar-template/):** what publishes where and when.
- **[Work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/):** one intake form and request log.
- **Gantt chart:** for launches with dependencies.
- **Budget tracker:** media and production spend against plan.
- **[Go-to-market plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/go-to-market-plan-template/):** for product launches.
- **[Lessons learned template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/):** capture what to change next time.

### KPIs for marketing project management
Separate **delivery KPIs** (how well the team runs projects) from **campaign KPIs** (how well the campaign performed). A campaign can launch perfectly and still miss its goal, or succeed despite a chaotic process; you need both views to improve.

#### Delivery KPIs
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On-time launch rate | Share of campaigns or assets delivered by the agreed date | Headline delivery health |
| Review rounds per asset | Feedback cycles before approval | Finding approval bottlenecks |
| Cycle time | Days from approved brief to live asset | Realistic timelines and service levels |
| Throughput | Assets or campaigns completed per week or month | Capacity planning |
| Work in progress | Items started but not finished | Spotting overloaded teams |
| Budget variance | Actual spend against plan | Media and production cost control |

#### Campaign KPIs
| KPI | What it measures |
| --- | --- |
| Leads, sign-ups or registrations | Volume against the objective in the brief |
| Cost per lead or acquisition | Efficiency of spend |
| Conversion rate | Share of visitors or recipients who act |
| Pipeline or revenue influenced | Commercial impact, where tracking allows |
| Return on investment | Return against total campaign cost |

### Common challenges and how to handle them
| Challenge | How to handle it |
| --- | --- |
| Requests arrive from everywhere | One intake form and one queue; triage weekly against agreed priorities |
| Endless feedback rounds | Name approvers in the brief, consolidate feedback, cap the rounds |
| Last-minute changes | Freeze key facts (product names, prices) at brief sign-off; use change requests after that |
| Too much work in progress | Set WIP limits and say no or later when the team is full |
| Unclear goals | Do not start without a signed brief that includes a measurable objective |
| Shared specialists overbooked | Plan capacity across all campaigns and agree trade-offs with the marketing leader |
| Tracking broken at launch | Add tracking set-up and testing as tasks with owners and dates |
| No time to learn | Hold a 30-minute retrospective after each major campaign and act on one change |

### Using AI in marketing project management
Many project management and marketing platforms now include AI features. Used sensibly, they save administrative time. Practical uses include:
- Drafting a first version of a brief or task list from meeting notes, for the team to edit.
- Summarising long comment threads and status updates for stakeholders.
- Suggesting subtasks and dates from a campaign template.
- Flagging tasks at risk of missing deadlines based on progress data.
- Producing first drafts of copy variants for testing, with human review.
Keep people in charge of decisions, claims and brand judgement. Check AI-generated copy for accuracy and compliance, and follow your organisation's rules on what data can be shared with AI tools.

### Marketing project management software
Look for a tool that offers:
- **Request forms** with required fields and automatic routing.
- **Calendar and timeline views** to see every launch in one place.
- **Proofing and approvals** with comments on the asset and recorded sign-off.
- **Workload views** across campaigns.
- **Templates** for repeat campaigns with relative dates.
- **Dashboards** for status and delivery KPIs.
- **Integrations** with design tools, file storage or a DAM, marketing automation and chat.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is a strong all-in-one choice for marketing teams because it combines request forms, built-in proofing and approvals, workload management, dashboards and reusable campaign templates in one platform, and it ranks first in our [project management software rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/). [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) is popular with marketing teams for its visual boards and easy automations, and [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) suits teams that want straightforward task, timeline and goal tracking. Most teams also run specialist tools alongside: a marketing automation platform, analytics and often a digital asset management (DAM) system.
Small teams can start with a shared calendar, a campaign plan template and a request form, then move to a dedicated platform when the number of campaigns and reviewers grows.

### Skills and career path
Marketing project managers combine core [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/), such as planning, scheduling, risk and [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/), with marketing knowledge: channels, creative production, tracking and how campaigns are measured. Calm negotiation matters, because you will often balance senior requests against limited capacity.
Many people move into the role from marketing coordination, account management or marketing operations. Certification is not required; practical experience counts most. A general project management certification or Agile training can help as campaigns get larger.
Much marketing work is creative production, which has its own workflow and revision challenges.
If you deliver marketing for clients, our guide to [agency project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/agency-project-management/) covers retainers, statements of work and utilisation.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is marketing project management?**
Marketing project management is the planning, scheduling, resourcing and tracking of marketing work, from single assets to multi-channel campaigns, so it launches on time, within budget and against a measurable business goal.

**Q: What does a marketing project manager do?**
They run intake and prioritisation, turn briefs into plans and budgets, book specialist time, run review and approval rounds, track status, manage changes and risks, coordinate the launch and report results with lessons learned.

**Q: What is the difference between a marketing manager and a marketing project manager?**
A marketing manager owns strategy and results: audiences, messages, channels and whether the goal was met. A marketing project manager owns delivery: the plan, schedule, resources, approvals and launch. In small teams one person often does both.

**Q: What are the phases of a marketing project?**
Request and intake, brief, planning, creative development, review and approval, launch, and optimise, report and close.

**Q: What is an example of a marketing project?**
A product launch campaign is a typical example: a brief with a measurable goal, a landing page, emails, paid social ads, sales materials and tracking, all planned backwards from a fixed launch date and reported against the goal afterwards.

**Q: How far ahead should you plan a marketing campaign?**
It depends on scope and lead times. Build the plan backwards from the launch date, including review rounds and buffers. If the first task already falls in the past, reduce or phase the deliverables. Print, events and video usually need the longest lead times.

**Q: Is Agile good for marketing project management?**
Yes, especially for request-driven and test-and-learn work. Many teams use Kanban or sprints for production and keep a milestone plan for big launches. See [Agile marketing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-marketing/).

**Q: How do you prioritise marketing requests?**
Send every request through one intake form, score it against agreed criteria such as goal impact, deadline urgency and effort, and review the queue weekly with the marketing leader. Low scorers are scheduled later, simplified or declined with a reason.

**Q: How do you reduce approval delays?**
Name approvers in the brief, schedule review windows in their calendars, consolidate feedback through one person per group, cap the number of rounds, run legal and brand checks in parallel and use proofing so comments sit on the asset.

**Q: Which KPIs matter in marketing project management?**
Track delivery KPIs such as on-time launch rate, review rounds per asset, cycle time, throughput and budget variance, and separately track campaign KPIs such as leads, cost per lead, conversion rate and ROI.

**Q: How do you manage several marketing campaigns at once?**
Use one shared marketing calendar, plan specialist capacity across all campaigns, hold a short weekly prioritisation meeting and save repeat campaigns as templates. See [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/).

**Q: What is the best software for marketing project management?**
Choose a tool that combines request forms, proofing, calendars, workload views and templates. Wrike is a strong all-in-one option, with monday.com and Asana also popular. Compare them in our [tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/).

**Q: Do you need a certification for marketing project management?**
No. Practical experience matters most. A general project management certification or Agile training can help as you take on larger campaigns; see [project management certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/).

# Nonprofit Project Management: Process, Examples and Tools

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/nonprofit-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Nonprofit project management explained: a step-by-step process, logframe and budget examples, funder reporting, volunteers, KPIs, templates and tools.


## Nonprofit Project Management: Process, Examples and Tools
Nonprofit project management is the planning and delivery of time-limited projects in charities, NGOs, foundations and community organisations, from service programmes and fundraising campaigns to advocacy and capital appeals. It uses the same core discipline as any project, but success is measured in impact rather than profit, money is often restricted to agreed purposes, and much of the work depends on volunteers, partners and funder approval. This guide gives you a seven-phase process, a fully worked grant-funded example, budget and reporting methods, KPIs, templates and tool advice.
- Published 27 August 2026
- Last updated 17 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Nonprofit project management applies scope, schedule, budget and risk control to mission-driven work, with impact as the measure of success.
- A logframe or theory of change links activities to outputs, outcomes and impact, and most institutional funders expect one.
- Budget by funder and by restricted and unrestricted money, and track burn rate monthly so you neither return unspent grant nor overspend a budget line.
- Keep one master set of indicators and one reporting calendar, then map each funder's format to it instead of running separate systems.
- Choose methods and tools light enough for volunteers and partners to use; Project DPro (formerly PMD Pro) is the sector's own project management standard.

### What is nonprofit project management?
**Nonprofit project management** is the process of planning, delivering and evaluating temporary pieces of work in a charity, NGO or community organisation so that they achieve a defined social outcome within an agreed budget and timescale. It combines standard [project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) practice with impact measurement, restricted funding rules, funder reporting and the coordination of volunteers and partners.
Most nonprofits run three kinds of work side by side. Separating them helps you decide where project discipline is needed and where it would only add paperwork.
| Type of work | What it is | Charity example | Management approach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ongoing service | Continuous delivery with no planned end | A weekly food bank or helpline | Operational management, service standards, KPIs |
| Project | Temporary work with a defined outcome, budget and end date | A two-year grant to pilot a mentoring scheme | Project plan, budget, risk register, funder reporting |
| Programme | A group of related projects managed together for a wider goal | A youth employment programme with mentoring, training and employer projects | Programme management, shared indicators, portfolio view |
Funders usually pay for projects, so plan from day one how a successful pilot will become a service or be handed over when the grant ends.

### How nonprofit projects differ from commercial projects
The mechanics of planning are the same, but the context changes almost every decision. The table summarises the main differences.
| Factor | Commercial project | Nonprofit project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Measure of success | Profit, revenue, cost savings, market share | Outcomes for beneficiaries and progress on the mission |
| Source of money | Internal budget from expected returns | Grants, donations, contracts and appeals, often restricted to a purpose |
| Who you report to | Sponsor and executive team | Trustees or board, several funders, beneficiaries, regulators and the public |
| Workforce | Employees and contractors | Small paid teams plus volunteers and partner organisations |
| Changing scope | Agreed internally through change control | May need written approval from the funder |
| Overheads | Usually built into the business case | Often squeezed; core costs must be negotiated into budgets |
| Safeguarding | Rarely a project requirement | Central when working with children, older people or people in crisis |
Two differences shape most day-to-day decisions. First, grants are usually given for a specific purpose, budget and period, so moving money between lines or changing activities can need the funder's written permission, and unspent money may have to be returned. Second, much of the delivery is done by volunteers and partner organisations you do not employ, so tasks must be small, clear and easy to pick up. Safeguarding, consent and personal data handling are project requirements with owners and deadlines, not admin to finish later.

### Outputs, outcomes and impact
Funders and evaluators use three words that are easy to confuse. Getting them right is the foundation of every proposal, logframe and report.
| Level | Meaning | Example (digital skills project) | How you measure it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Activities | What the project does | Run weekly group sessions; train volunteer buddies | Work plan and attendance records |
| Outputs | The direct, countable products of activities | 48 sessions delivered; 150 people enrolled | Registers and logs |
| Outcomes | Changes for participants that the outputs cause | 70% of completers can use online services unaided | Skills checks, surveys, follow-up interviews |
| Impact | The long-term change the project contributes to | Fewer older residents are digitally excluded | Wider data and evaluation; usually contribution, not proof |
Decide at design stage how you will collect outcome evidence, and collect a **baseline** before activities begin.

### The nonprofit project life cycle: 7 phases
Many development and humanitarian organisations follow a project cycle similar to the one below; smaller charities use a lighter version of the same steps. It maps closely onto the generic [project management phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/), with extra emphasis on needs assessment, funding and evaluation.
| Phase | Key question | Main outputs | Usually led by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Needs assessment | What problem are we solving, for whom, and is anyone else already addressing it? | Needs analysis, beneficiary and stakeholder input | Programme lead |
| 2. Design | What will we do, and why should it lead to change? | Theory of change, logframe, draft budget, risk list | Programme lead with MEL officer |
| 3. Funding | Who will pay for it and on what terms? | Proposal, grant agreement, match funding | Fundraising or grants manager |
| 4. Planning and mobilisation | How exactly will we deliver, measure and report? | Work plan, M&E plan, reporting calendar, recruitment, partner agreements, baseline data | Project manager |
| 5. Implementation | Are we delivering as planned, within budget and safely? | Activities, monthly budget tracking, issue and change logs | Project manager |
| 6. Monitoring, evaluation and learning | Is it working, and what should we change? | Indicator data, mid-term review, final evaluation | MEL officer |
| 7. Close-out | Have we met our obligations and secured what comes next? | Final narrative and financial reports, asset handover, sustainability or exit plan, lessons learned | Project manager and finance |
Two points in the cycle deserve extra care. Collect **baseline data** during mobilisation, before the first activity, or you will not be able to show change. And when scope, timing or budget lines need to change materially during implementation, use [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) and get the funder's agreement in writing before acting.

### Step by step: planning a grant-funded project
Once a grant is confirmed, use these steps to move from proposal to a plan you can run. They suit a project of six months to three years with one or more funders.
1. **Re-read the grant agreement and proposal.** List every commitment: outputs, outcomes, budget lines, reporting dates, permitted variances, branding and asset rules.
2. **Write a one-page project charter.** Capture purpose, beneficiaries, scope, partners, sponsor and key dates, and get it signed off internally. A [project charter template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/) speeds this up.
3. **Break the work down.** Turn each output into deliverables and tasks, with an owner for each. Volunteers need tasks that are small, clear and self-contained.
4. **Build the schedule backwards from fixed dates.** Funder reports, school terms, seasonal demand, board meetings and the grant end date are fixed; plan activities around them.
5. **Set up the budget by funder and by line.** Mirror the funder's approved budget exactly, then add a column for actual spend and a monthly forecast.
6. **Write the monitoring and evaluation plan.** For each indicator, record the baseline, target, data source, collection method, frequency and who collects it.
7. **Create a single reporting calendar.** Put every funder, trustee and partner reporting date in one place, with draft deadlines two weeks earlier.
8. **Identify risks and controls.** Include funding, safeguarding, partner, volunteer, data protection and reputational risks, each with an owner.
9. **Agree roles with a RACI chart.** In small teams one person holds several roles; a [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) shows who decides, who does the work and who must be told.
10. **Collect the baseline and hold a kick-off.** Brief staff, volunteers and partners on the plan, reporting needs and safeguarding rules before the first activity.
Tip
Draft each report two weeks before it is due and share it internally. Late reports are one of the most common reasons funders lose confidence, and a two-week buffer absorbs a sick day or missing data.

### Worked example: a community digital skills project
The example below is illustrative: a small community charity has a 12-month project to help older residents use online services such as booking appointments and video calls. It shows how the documents fit together. Figures are invented for the example.

#### Funding and scope
- **Funder A (a community foundation):** £30,000 restricted to staffing, training delivery, evaluation and a share of overheads.
- **Funder B (the local council):** £12,000 restricted to devices, venue hire and volunteer costs.
- **The charity's unrestricted funds:** £6,000 for management time and contingency.
- **Commitments:** 48 weekly group sessions, 150 people enrolled, 120 completing the course, 20 volunteer "digital buddies" trained, and a lending library of 20 devices.

#### Simplified logframe
| Level | Narrative | Indicator and target | Means of verification | Assumptions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Goal | Fewer older residents in the area are digitally excluded | Contribution described in final evaluation | Evaluation report | Public services keep moving online |
| Outcome | Participants aged 65+ use online services independently | 70% of completers complete 3 set online tasks unaided at 3-month follow-up (baseline 0% at intake) | Follow-up skills check | Participants have home internet or library access |
| Output 1 | Group sessions delivered | 48 sessions; average attendance of 10 or more | Session registers | Venue remains available |
| Output 2 | Participants enrolled and completing | 150 enrolled; 120 complete 6 or more sessions | Enrolment and attendance records | Referral partners promote the course |
| Output 3 | Volunteer buddies trained | 20 trained; 8 or more active each month | Training log, rota | Volunteers can be recruited locally |
| Activities | Recruit via GP surgeries and community centres; train volunteers; run sessions; lend devices | Budget and work plan | Monthly reports | Background checks completed on time |

#### Budget split by funder
| Budget line | Calculation | Amount | Funded by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project coordinator (0.6 FTE) | 12 months | £19,800 | Funder A |
| Trainer sessions | 48 × £150 | £7,200 | Funder A |
| Independent evaluation | Follow-up checks and report | £1,500 | Funder A |
| Share of overheads | Agreed with funder | £1,500 | Funder A |
| Devices for lending library | 20 × £300 | £6,000 | Funder B |
| Venue hire | 48 × £75 | £3,600 | Funder B |
| Volunteer expenses, checks and training | Travel, refreshments, training day | £2,400 | Funder B |
| Management and finance time | Director and finance officer | £4,000 | Unrestricted |
| Contingency | About 4% of total | £2,000 | Unrestricted |
| **Total** |  | **£48,000** | A £30,000; B £12,000; unrestricted £6,000 |
Keeping the budget lines identical to each funder's approved budget means every report can be produced by filtering one sheet. Our [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) has planned, actual and variance columns you can extend with a funder column.

#### Month 6 review: spotting an underspend
At the end of month 6, half the project period has passed. The project manager compares spend on Funder A's lines with the plan:
| Measure | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planned spend to date (Funder A) | £30,000 × 6 / 12 | £15,000 |
| Actual spend to date | From the accounts | £11,400 |
| Burn rate | £11,400 ÷ £30,000 | 38% of budget at 50% of time |
| Forecast at current run rate | £11,400 + (£1,900 × 6 months) | £22,800 |
| Forecast underspend | £30,000 − £22,800 | £7,200 |
The cause is clear from the work plan: trainer sessions started in month 3 instead of month 1 because volunteer background checks took longer than expected. Left alone, the charity would have to return about £7,200 and would miss its target of 48 sessions.
The project manager prepares a short change request with three options: add catch-up sessions in months 7 to 12, extend the project by two months at no extra cost, or move part of the underspend to a second evaluation visit. The funder agrees a no-cost extension in writing; the schedule, reporting calendar and risk register are updated the same week.

#### Reporting calendar
| Month | Report | Audience | Content |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | Quarterly board report | Trustees | Progress, spend, risks, safeguarding |
| 4 | Expenditure return | Funder B | Spend on devices, venue and volunteers |
| 7 | Interim report | Funder A | Narrative, outputs, early outcomes, finance, change request |
| 7 and 10 | Expenditure returns | Funder B | Quarterly spend |
| 13 | Final expenditure return | Funder B | Final spend and asset register |
| 14 (after extension) | Final report and evaluation | Funder A | Outcomes against baseline, finance, lessons, sustainability plan |

#### Results and cost per beneficiary
If 120 people complete the course, the cost per completer is £48,000 ÷ 120 = **£400**, or £320 per person enrolled. Report both figures with context, such as the value of volunteer time and the devices that remain available to the community after the project.

### Theory of change vs logframe
Both tools describe how a project should create change, and many funders ask for one or both. They work best together: the theory of change explains the reasoning, and the logframe turns it into a plan you can monitor.
|  | Theory of change | Logical framework (logframe) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Explains why and how activities should lead to long-term change | Sets out what will be delivered and how progress will be measured |
| Format | Diagram or narrative showing pathways and preconditions | A matrix of goal, outcomes, outputs and activities against indicators, verification and assumptions |
| Strength | Surfaces assumptions and the wider context | Clear targets that are easy to monitor and report |
| Weakness | Can be vague about targets and responsibility | Can look linear and rigid if used alone |
| When to use | Programme design, strategy, evaluation planning | Grant proposals, monitoring plans, funder reporting |
Start with a simple theory of change on one page, test it with staff, beneficiaries and partners, then build the logframe from it.

### Managing restricted budgets and funder reporting
Money is where nonprofit projects most often get into trouble, usually through late tracking rather than overspending. These practices keep you in control. For the general method, see our guide to building a [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/).
1. **Budget by funder, line and month.** Track every grant against its own approved lines, keep restricted and unrestricted funds separate, and review actuals against plan monthly, not only when a report is due.
2. **Watch burn rate, not just totals.** Divide spend to date by total budget and compare it with the share of time elapsed. A large gap either way is an early warning.
3. **Recover the full cost.** Include project management, finance, monitoring and evaluation, and a fair share of overheads where the funder allows it. In the US, recipients of federal awards with no negotiated indirect cost rate can generally use a de minimis rate of up to 15% of modified total direct costs for awards made on or after 1 October 2024 (2 CFR 200.414(f)). Other funders set their own rules.
4. **Keep one master indicator set.** Collect data once, then map each funder's questions to it. This avoids double counting and inconsistent figures.
5. **Ask early, in writing.** Most funders are flexible when asked before a change, much less so afterwards. Keep a log of requests and approvals with the grant file.

### Managing volunteers and partners
Volunteers and partners extend what a small charity can deliver, but they need planning like any other resource.

#### Design volunteer roles like work packages
- Give each role a short description, a time commitment, the training needed and a named contact.
- Break work into tasks that can be finished in a single session, so absence does not stall the project.
- Complete checks, induction and safeguarding training before the first shift, and recognise contributions publicly.

#### Worked example: how many volunteers do you need?
In the digital skills project, each weekly session needs 3 buddies, so 4 sessions a month need 12 volunteer slots. If each volunteer can give 2 sessions a month, you need 6 people available. Allowing for 80% reliability, 6 ÷ 0.8 = 7.5, so you need 8 active volunteers each month. Because some people leave during a year, the plan targets 20 trained volunteers to keep 8 to 10 active. The same calculation works for events, helplines and distribution projects.

#### Partner agreements
Put responsibilities, money, data sharing, safeguarding, branding and reporting into a written partnership agreement, and share one project tracker so everyone sees the same status. Good [stakeholder management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-stakeholder-management/) matters even more when partners have their own boards and funders.

### Key roles on a nonprofit project
| Role | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Board of trustees or directors | Approves strategy and significant projects; holds legal and financial accountability |
| Chief executive or director | Sponsors key projects, signs grant agreements and maintains funder relationships |
| Programme or project manager | Plans and delivers activities, budget and reporting; coordinates staff, volunteers and partners |
| Fundraising or grants manager | Writes proposals, manages funder relationships and tracks reporting deadlines |
| Monitoring, evaluation, accountability and learning (MEAL) officer | Designs indicators, collects data and leads evaluation |
| Finance officer | Tracks restricted and unrestricted funds against grant budgets and prepares financial returns |
| Volunteer coordinator | Recruits, checks, trains, schedules and supports volunteers |
| Safeguarding lead | Makes sure policies, checks, training and reporting routes are in place |
| Implementing partners | Deliver parts of the project under a partnership agreement |
In a small charity one person may hold several of these roles. Write them down anyway, so gaps are obvious.

### Methodologies that suit nonprofits
No single method fits every nonprofit project. Choose by the funding model and how stable the scope is.
| Approach | Best for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Logical framework approach | Grant-funded and international development projects | Expected by many institutional funders; pairs with a theory of change |
| Phased (waterfall) | Capital appeals, building works, fixed-scope grants | Fits fixed budgets and funder milestones |
| Kanban | Small teams juggling campaigns, events and service improvements | Visual and easy for volunteers to follow; see [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) |
| Agile | Digital services, advocacy campaigns and pilots | Test and adapt quickly; agree flexibility with funders up front |
| Project DPro (PMD Pro) | Development and humanitarian project managers | A sector-specific guide and certification from PM4NGOs |
Many organisations combine approaches: a logframe and phased plan to satisfy the funder, with a Kanban board for day-to-day delivery.

### Essential documents and templates
You do not need every document on every project. A small charity project can run on a proposal, a budget, a schedule, a risk register and a reporting calendar. Larger or multi-funder projects need the full set.
- **Project proposal:** start from our [project proposal template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-proposal-template/) and adapt it to each funder's form.
- **Project charter:** objectives, beneficiaries, scope, partners and sponsor for internal sign-off.
- **Logframe and M&E plan:** indicators, baselines, targets, sources and who collects data.
- **Budget:** split by funder and by restricted and unrestricted funds, with monthly actuals.
- **Risk register:** funding, safeguarding, partner, data and reputational risks; use our [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).
- **Communication plan:** funders, trustees, beneficiaries, volunteers and the public; try the [communication plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/).
- **Event plan:** for fundraising and community events; see our guide to [event project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/event-project-management/).

### KPIs for nonprofit projects
Track a small set of indicators that serve both management and funder reporting. The table shows common KPIs and how to calculate them.
| KPI | How to calculate | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Output delivery rate | Outputs delivered ÷ outputs planned to date | Early sign of slippage against funder commitments |
| Outcome achievement | Participants achieving the outcome ÷ participants assessed | The core evidence of impact |
| Budget burn rate | Spend to date ÷ total budget, compared with % of time elapsed | Avoids returning grant or overspending a line |
| Budget variance | Planned spend to date − actual spend to date, per line | Shows where to move money or ask the funder |
| Cost per beneficiary | Total project cost ÷ people served or completing | Value for money and future bids |
| Reporting compliance | Reports submitted on time ÷ reports due | Funder trust and renewal chances |
| Volunteer hours and retention | Hours logged; active volunteers at end ÷ at start | Capacity planning and recognition |
| Funds raised against target | Income secured ÷ target | For fundraising campaigns and match funding |
Put these on a one-page [project status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/) for trustees each quarter, with a sentence on what you are doing about anything off track.

### Common mistakes and how to avoid them
| Mistake | What happens | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No baseline data | You cannot show change at the end | Collect baseline data before the first activity |
| Promising too much in the proposal | Targets are missed and trust suffers | Base targets on past delivery and realistic volunteer capacity |
| Tracking spend only at report time | Underspends and overspends surface too late | Review burn rate monthly by funder and line |
| Leaving project management costs out | Staff are stretched and quality drops | Budget for coordination, finance and MEL time |
| Too many projects for too few people | Burnout and late reports | Keep a single view of all projects; see [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) |

### Choosing software for a nonprofit
Most nonprofits use three systems side by side: a donor or supporter CRM, accounting software and a project or work management tool. The project tool should make delivery and reporting easier for staff, volunteers and partners, not add another place to update.
- **Guest or low-cost access** for volunteers and partners.
- **Simple boards, lists and timelines** that people learn in an hour.
- **Templates** for recurring work such as campaigns, events and grant reports.
- **Dashboards** that roll up progress for trustees and funders.
- **Request forms** so colleagues can submit work in a consistent way.
- **Permissions** to keep safeguarding and personal data restricted.
- **Nonprofit pricing:** several vendors offer it; for example, Asana offers a 50% discount to eligible nonprofits in participating countries (checked 17 October 2026). Ask any vendor you shortlist.
| Organisation size | Typical need | Tools to consider |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Volunteer-led or very small | Shared task lists and boards | [Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/), Basecamp, or Microsoft Planner if you already use Microsoft 365 |
| Small to mid-sized charity | Several projects, simple timelines and dashboards | [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/), monday.com, ClickUp |
| Growing or multi-site organisation | Portfolio view, grant timelines, request forms, approvals and resource planning | [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), Smartsheet |
Wrike, our top-ranked tool, suits nonprofits that run many projects across teams and need grant timelines, request forms, approvals and trustee dashboards in one place. Smaller teams are often well served by the free plans of simpler tools.

### Certification and skills for nonprofit project managers
The best-known sector-specific credential is **Project DPro**, the second edition of the PMD Pro guide, published by the US nonprofit PM4NGOs in 2020. PM4NGOs also maintains related guides in its DPro suite, including Program DPro, MEAL DPro and Finance DPro. These are designed for development and humanitarian work and use sector language such as logframes and MEAL.
General certifications are recognised across sectors and are useful if you may move between charity and commercial roles: the [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) for experienced project managers, the [CAPM](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) for those starting out, and [PRINCE2](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/prince2/), which is widely used in UK public-sector settings.
Beyond certificates, the skills that matter most are clear writing for proposals and reports, budget control, stakeholder and volunteer management, and the judgement to keep processes light. If you also work with public bodies, our guide to [government project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/government-project-management/) covers procurement and accountability rules you are likely to meet.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is nonprofit project management?**
Nonprofit project management is the planning, delivery and evaluation of time-limited projects in charities, NGOs and community organisations so they achieve a defined social outcome within an agreed budget and timescale, usually with restricted funding, funder reporting and volunteer involvement.

**Q: How is nonprofit project management different from business project management?**
Nonprofit projects measure success in outcomes for beneficiaries rather than profit, depend on restricted grants, donations and volunteers, and must report to trustees and several funders. Scope changes may need funder approval.

**Q: What are the phases of nonprofit project management?**
A common cycle is needs assessment, design, funding, planning and mobilisation, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, and close-out. Smaller charities often combine design and funding into one step.

**Q: Do nonprofits need a dedicated project manager?**
Not always. Many small charities give project management to a programme lead or coordinator. What matters is that someone owns the plan, budget, risks and reporting, and that the time is included in grant budgets where funders allow it.

**Q: What is a logframe?**
A logical framework is a table that links a project's goal, outcomes, outputs and activities to indicators, means of verification and assumptions. Many institutional funders require one in proposals and use it for reporting.

**Q: What is the difference between a logframe and a theory of change?**
A theory of change explains why and how activities should lead to long-term change, including assumptions. A logframe sets out what will be delivered and how it will be measured. Use the theory of change to design and the logframe to monitor.

**Q: What is restricted funding and how does it affect a project?**
Restricted funding can only be spent on the purpose the donor or funder specified. You must track it separately, keep to approved budget lines, ask permission for significant changes and possibly return what is unspent.

**Q: How do you measure the impact of a nonprofit project?**
Define outcome indicators at design stage, collect baseline data before activities start, measure the same indicators during and after the project, and use an evaluation to judge how far the project contributed to the change.

**Q: How do you manage volunteers on a project?**
Treat volunteers as a workforce: define roles and time commitments, calculate how many you need with an allowance for absence and turnover, complete checks and training first, give each person a named contact and recognise their work.

**Q: What is the best certification for nonprofit project management?**
Project DPro (formerly PMD Pro) from PM4NGOs is designed for the development and humanitarian sector. PMP, CAPM and PRINCE2 are recognised more widely across sectors.

**Q: What software do nonprofits use for project management?**
Small teams often use free or low-cost tools such as Trello, Asana or Basecamp. Growing organisations with many projects often choose a platform such as Wrike for grant timelines, request forms and dashboards, alongside their CRM and accounting system.

**Q: How much of a grant can be spent on project management?**
It depends on the funder. Many allow coordination, finance and evaluation costs plus a share of overheads if they are justified. For US federal awards, organisations without a negotiated rate can generally claim indirect costs at a de minimis rate of up to 15% of modified total direct costs.
