# Research Project Management: Steps, Roles and Example

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/research-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Research project management explained: life cycle, PI and PM roles, work packages, milestones, grant budgets, ethics, data plans, an example and tools.


## Research Project Management: Steps, Roles and Example
Research project management is the planning and control of research work, such as a funded grant, a multi-partner consortium or a corporate R&D programme, so that it meets funder rules, budgets and deadlines while leaving room for results nobody can predict. This guide covers how research projects differ, who does what, the life cycle, a 12-step process and a worked grant example with milestones, budget and a mid-project review.
- Published 27 August 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Research project management controls time, money, compliance and reporting around work whose results are uncertain; it does not try to plan the findings.
- The principal investigator leads the science and is accountable to the funder; a research project manager runs the plan, budget, partners, risks and reports.
- Structure grants as work packages with deliverables and milestones, and write milestones as decisions or completed activities, never as expected results.
- Ethics approval, recruitment, seasonal or academic-year windows and equipment lead times drive most research schedules, so plan them first.
- Track spend against the funder's profile every month. Underspend is as risky as overspend because unspent grant money is often lost.
- Use work packages for grants, stage-gates and TRLs for corporate R&D, and light Agile or Kanban for day-to-day lab and computational work.

### What is research project management?
**Research project management is the discipline of planning, coordinating and controlling a research project, including its funding, budget, people, partners, ethics and data obligations, milestones and reporting, so that the research can be carried out on the funder's terms and on time, even though its outcome is uncertain.** It manages the conditions for good research, not the research question itself.
In a university the work is shared. The principal investigator (PI) leads the science, the research office helps with funding and costing, post-award finance looks after the grant account and, on larger grants, a research project manager runs the plan day to day. In corporate R&D, a project or programme manager does the same job with commercial gates in place of funder reports.
The tools are familiar, such as a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), risk register and budget, but each needs adapting: milestones that survive negative results, budgets that follow funder rules and schedules built around approvals and seasons.

#### Types of research projects
| Type | Typical example | What dominates the management work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-investigator grant | A three-year study funded by a research council or foundation | Recruiting staff, spend profile, annual reports, publications |
| Consortium grant | Several universities and companies in a multi-country programme | Partner coordination, governance, IP, joint reporting |
| Clinical and health research | A trial or cohort study involving patients | Ethics and regulatory approval, recruitment, data protection |
| Corporate R&D | Developing a new material, product or process | Stage-gate decisions and the cost of continuing vs stopping |
| Doctoral research | A PhD thesis project | Self-management, supervisor meetings, a fixed submission date |

### How research projects differ from other projects
Most project management assumes you know what you are building. Research starts with a question, so some usual assumptions do not hold.
| Aspect | Typical business project | Typical research project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outcome | Defined deliverable, such as a system or building | Knowledge whose content is unknown in advance; negative results are valid |
| Funding | Internal budget approved by a sponsor | External grant with a fixed period, approved budget and rules on eligible costs |
| Schedule drivers | Business deadlines and dependencies | Ethics approval, recruitment, seasons, academic year, equipment lead times, reporting dates |
| Approvals | Internal sign-offs | Ethics committees or institutional review boards (IRBs), regulators, data protection |
| Team | Staff allocated from departments | Academics with several commitments, fixed-term staff, students, external partners |
| Success measure | Benefits delivered on time and budget | Milestones met, outputs published and shared, compliance maintained, impact achieved |
The answer is not to drop project management but to apply it with a light touch: plan the predictable parts (approvals, recruitment, procurement, reporting) tightly, and plan the uncertain science in short stages with decision points.

### Principal investigator vs research project manager
The most common source of confusion on research projects is who decides what. The PI is accountable to the funder for the research and its budget; the research project manager runs the machinery of the project on the PI's behalf. On small grants the PI does both jobs.
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Principal investigator (PI) | Scientific lead; accountable to the funder for the research, budget and conduct of the project |
| Co-investigators and partner leads | Lead work packages or a partner's contribution; report progress and spend |
| Research project manager | Maintains the plan; tracks milestones, deliverables, spend and risks; coordinates partners; prepares reports; runs change control |
| Research office (pre-award) | Finds calls, checks eligibility, costs and submits the proposal |
| Post-award finance | Runs the grant account, checks eligible costs, produces financial statements, handles audits |
| Ethics committee or IRB | Approves research involving people, personal data or other sensitive areas before it starts |
| Data steward | Writes and implements the data management plan |
Record who decides what in a RACI matrix at kick-off, especially for decisions that cross partners, such as moving budget between work packages. Our [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) is a quick start.

### The research project life cycle
Research administrators describe the grant life cycle in three stages: **pre-award** (finding funding and preparing the proposal), **award** (contracting and set-up) and **post-award** (running, reporting and closing the funded project). Expanded into phases:
| Phase | What happens | Key output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Idea and funding search | Research question defined; suitable calls identified; eligibility checked | Concept note |
| 2. Proposal development (pre-award) | Work packages, milestones, budget, partners, impact and data management plan written and costed | Submitted proposal |
| 3. Award and set-up | Grant and collaboration agreements signed, accounts opened, staff recruited, ethics approval obtained | Kick-off and baselined plan |
| 4. Research execution (post-award) | Experiments, fieldwork and analysis; partner meetings; progress, spend and risk tracking | Deliverables and milestone reports |
| 5. Reporting and dissemination | Interim and final reports, publications, conferences, data deposit | Reports, papers, data sets |
| 6. Close-out | Final financial statement, data archiving, staff contracts ended or extended | Closure report |
| 7. Impact and follow-on | Exploitation, technology transfer, policy engagement, follow-on funding | Impact case, next proposal |
Phases 4 and 5 overlap, because most funders expect interim reports and outputs throughout. See our guide to [project closure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-closure/) for the last phase.

### How to manage a research project step by step
The steps follow a funded project from call to close-out. On a small grant one person may do them all; on a consortium each is a task in the management work package.
1. **Read the call and funder rules first.** Note the maximum budget, eligible costs, required documents, reporting dates and rules on changes and extensions.
2. **Define the research question and objectives.** Write two to four objectives that can be checked at the end, whatever the findings.
3. **Break the work into work packages.** Four to eight [work packages](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/), each with a lead, months, tasks and deliverables, including management and dissemination.
4. **Find the fixed dates and long lead times.** Ethics review, recruitment, equipment delivery, fieldwork seasons and academic terms go on the timeline first. Then find the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/).
5. **Set milestones as decisions.** Add go/no-go points where the next stage depends on a result, and write each [milestone](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-milestones/) so it can be met whatever the data show.
6. **Cost the project with the research office.** Build the budget by work package and funder cost category.
7. **Write the risk register, data management plan and ethics plan.** Cover technical, recruitment, staffing, partner, data and regulatory risks, each with an owner.
8. **Agree governance and IP before the start.** Sign the consortium agreement and set decision, dispute and publication rules.
9. **Kick off and baseline the plan.** Confirm the plan and spend profile with every partner in the first month.
10. **Monitor monthly.** Review milestones, spend against profile, recruitment and risks in a short status note.
11. **Report on a calendar.** Put every report, financial statement, deliverable and conference deadline in one calendar with owners.
12. **Close out and archive.** Submit final reports, deposit data, close the account and record lessons for the next proposal.
Our free [project proposal template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-proposal-template/) and [work package template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-package-template/) cover steps 2 to 5.

### Worked example: a three-partner research grant
This example is **illustrative**: the project, partners and figures are invented. It is a 36-month grant to develop low-cost air quality sensors and measure pollution exposure in 20 primary schools. University A leads and runs engineering and fieldwork, University C does the statistics and modelling, and Company B, a small sensor maker, contributes staff time in kind.

#### Work packages and deliverables
| Work package | Lead | Months | Main deliverables |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WP1 Management | University A | 1–36 | D1.1 Project handbook (M2); annual and final reports |
| WP2 Sensor development | University A, with Company B | 1–9 | D2.1 Sensor design and calibration report (M8) |
| WP3 School deployment and data collection | University A | 4–30 | D3.1 Deployment report (M12); D3.2 Data collection report (M30) |
| WP4 Analysis and modelling | University C | 10–34 | D4.1 Interim analysis (M18); D4.2 Exposure model report (M33) |
| WP5 Data and dissemination | University C | 1–36 | D5.1 Data management plan (M6); D5.2 Open data set (M34); D5.3 Guidance for schools (M35) |

#### Milestones and go/no-go points
| Milestone | Month | Verified by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MS1 Consortium agreement signed; ethics application submitted | 3 | Signed agreement; submission receipt |
| MS2 Lab calibration complete; go/no-go on in-house sensor or commercial fallback | 6 | Calibration report and steering group decision |
| MS3 Sensors installed and transmitting in 20 schools | 10 | Deployment log |
| MS4 First winter data quality-checked; decision on year 2 sensor placement | 16 | Data quality report |
| MS5 Exposure model validated, or alternative approach agreed | 28 | Validation report |
| MS6 Final data set deposited in a public repository | 34 | Repository record |
MS2 and MS5 can be met whatever the results. If the in-house sensor fails calibration, the decision is still made and the project continues with the fallback.

#### Budget
Some funders pay a share of the full economic cost (fEC) of research. UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), for example, normally pays 80% of fEC and the host institution covers the rest (EPSRC guidance updated 12 March 2026). The illustrative budget uses that model:
| Cost category | What it covers | Full economic cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staff | PI time, two postdocs for 30 months, technician at 50% | £620,000 |
| Equipment | 60 sensor units and a calibration chamber | £90,000 |
| Consumables and fieldwork | Parts, mobile data, school visits | £60,000 |
| Travel and meetings | Partner meetings, advisory board, two conferences | £45,000 |
| Other direct costs | Open access fees, data storage, translation | £35,000 |
| Indirect and estates costs | Overheads under the funder's method | £400,000 |
| **Total fEC** |  | **£1,250,000** |
| Funder contribution at 80% | £1,250,000 × 0.8 | £1,000,000 |
| Institutions' contribution | £1,250,000 − £1,000,000 | £250,000 |
Direct costs (everything except indirect and estates) total £850,000. That is the figure the project manager tracks monthly by partner and work package, using the same lines as the funder's budget.

#### Month 9 review: ethics delay and underspend
| Measure | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time elapsed | 9 ÷ 36 months | 25% |
| Planned direct spend to date | From the baselined spend profile | £215,000 |
| Actual direct spend to date | From the grant account | £148,000 |
| Spend against profile | £148,000 ÷ £215,000 | 69% |
The first postdoc started in month 4 instead of month 1, and ethics review took 14 weeks instead of the 8 assumed, so school recruitment started late. The bigger problem is the schedule: MS3 is now forecast for month 13, but the study needs a full winter heating season, which in this example runs from month 10 to month 15. Installing in month 13 would lose half of the first winter.
| Option | Effect | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Install in the 10 schools already recruited by month 11; the rest before the second winter | One full winter for half the sample, two winters for the rest | Smaller first-year data set; interim analysis uses 10 schools |
| B. Request a 6-month no-cost extension and study the second and third winters | Full sample in both winters | Needs funder approval; extension staff costs must come from underspend |

#### The decision and what changed
The steering group chooses option A and keeps B as a fallback. The project manager then:
- Splits MS3 into MS3a (10 schools, month 11) and MS3b (20 schools, month 22) and updates the Gantt chart.
- Re-forecasts the spend profile so the staff underspend is visible and planned for.
- Raises a [change request](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) and informs the funder's programme officer, because a reported milestone has moved. Check whether your funder needs notification or prior approval.
- Adds a risk for second-winter school recruitment, owned by the WP3 lead, with earlier outreach as the response.
- Records the lesson: assume at least 14 weeks for ethics review here, and recruit staff before the start date where the funder allows.
Tip
Keep your tracker's budget lines, partner split and work packages identical to the funder's. Every report then comes from filtering one sheet, and variances show up in the month they happen.

### Writing milestones when results are uncertain
A milestone that depends on a particular result is missed whenever the science goes a different way, so the project looks late when it is not. Write milestones as **completed activities or decisions**.
| Weak milestone (depends on the result) | Better milestone (verifiable whatever happens) |
| --- | --- |
| Sensor shown to be accurate | Lab calibration complete; go/no-go on sensor design |
| New catalyst discovered | 200 candidate compounds screened; top 10 selected or criteria revised |
| Intervention reduces symptoms | Main analysis complete and reported to the steering group |
| Paper published in a leading journal | Manuscript submitted (publication timing is outside your control) |
| Participants recruited | 150 participants consented, or recruitment plan revised at the month 12 review |
- Give every milestone a month, an owner and a means of verification.
- Put a go/no-go decision before any expensive stage, such as a main trial after a pilot.
- Agree the fallback in advance so a 'no' does not stall the project.
- Keep milestones few: five to ten across a three-year grant is usually enough.

### Stage-gates and TRLs in corporate R&D
In company R&D the question at each stage is commercial: is the next stage worth paying for? In a stage-gate process, a review board decides at each gate to continue, change course or stop.
Technology readiness levels (TRLs) describe maturity on a scale from 1 to 9. The scale was developed at NASA and is now used by many funders, including the European Commission, which gives gate reviews a shared language.
| TRL band | Meaning | Typical gate question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TRL 1–3 | Principles observed, concept formulated, proof of concept shown | Is the idea feasible enough to fund lab validation? |
| TRL 4–5 | Validated in the lab, then in a relevant environment | Does performance justify a prototype? |
| TRL 6–7 | Prototype demonstrated in a relevant, then operational, environment | Is there a credible product and customer case? |
| TRL 8–9 | System complete and qualified, then proven in operation | Hand over to product development or manufacturing? |
Stopping a weak idea at TRL 4 frees money for stronger ones, so record why each project stopped. See our guides to [engineering project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/engineering-project-management/) and [pharmaceutical project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/pharmaceutical-project-management/) for stage-gates in regulated product development.

### Grant budgets and funder rules
Grant money comes with conditions, and breaking them can mean repaying costs. Finance staff are the experts, but the project manager needs to spot problems early.
- **Eligible costs.** Funders list what they will pay for, often with special rules for equipment, overheads and partners. For example, UKRI funds equipment at 80% of fEC and raised its capital equipment threshold from £10,000 to £25,000 from 1 April 2025.
- **Spend profile.** Compare actual spend with the expected profile monthly, by category and partner.
- **Budget changes.** Moving money between categories or partners often needs approval above a threshold. Ask before you spend.
- **Underspend.** Money not spent by the end date is usually lost. Late recruitment is the most common cause.
- **No-cost extensions.** Many funders allow extra time without extra money. Under US National Institutes of Health (NIH) rules, grantees can usually make one extension of up to 12 months, subject to conditions; further extensions need prior approval.
For budgeting methods, see our guide to the [project budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/). The free [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) has planned, actual and variance columns you can split by funder category.

### Ethics approval and research data management

#### Ethics and regulatory approval
Research involving people, personal data, human tissue, animals or hazardous materials needs approval from an ethics committee, IRB or regulator before that part of the work starts. Review times vary, so treat approval as a critical-path task with its own buffer, and remember that later changes usually need an approved amendment.

#### Data management plans
A data management plan (DMP) explains how research data will be collected, documented, stored, shared and preserved. Many funders require one:
- **Horizon Europe** requires a DMP for projects that generate or reuse research data, with the full plan due by month 6 and updates during longer projects.
- **NIH** has required a Data Management and Sharing Plan for applicable research since 25 January 2023.
- Other funders and universities have their own rules, so check the call and your institution's policy.
A DMP is not a project plan: it covers the data, while the project plan covers who does what and when. Turn DMP actions, such as anonymisation and repository deposit, into scheduled tasks with owners.

### Managing research teams and consortia
Research teams rarely share a line manager. Academics balance teaching and other grants, postdocs are often on fixed-term contracts and partners answer to their own organisations, so management works through agreement and transparency.
- **Governance.** A steering group with one representative per partner, a meeting rhythm and clear decision rules.
- **Consortium agreement.** Ownership and use of results, background IP, publication review periods, confidentiality and disputes, agreed before work starts.
- **Rhythm.** A monthly work package leads call, quarterly steering group and annual all-hands meeting is a common pattern.
- **Turnover.** Document methods, code and data as you go so work continues when someone leaves.
PIs often run several grants at once, each with its own reporting calendar. A portfolio view of milestones helps; see [how to manage multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/).

### Methodologies that suit research
Most teams combine a structured outer plan, which the funder sees, with a lighter way of organising daily work.
| Approach | Best for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work packages and milestones | Funded grants and consortia | The standard structure for many funders, including EU framework programmes |
| Stage-gate | Corporate R&D | Go/kill decisions control investment in uncertain work |
| Agile or Kanban | Lab, software and computational teams | Short cycles and visual boards suit exploratory work; see [what Kanban is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) |
| Waterfall | Clinical trials, facility builds, procurement | Regulated or sequential work needs a fixed plan |
A practical hybrid: keep the work package plan for the funder, and run each work package with a simple board and a fortnightly check-in.

### Essential documents and templates
- **Proposal or charter:** research question, objectives, scope and partners.
- **Work packages and work breakdown:** tasks and deliverables for each package.
- **Timeline:** the grant Gantt chart with milestones and reporting dates; start from our [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/).
- **Budget and spend profile:** by partner, work package and funder category.
- **[Risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/):** technical, recruitment, ethics, partner, staffing and data risks.
- **Data management plan and ethics approvals:** with renewal and amendment dates tracked.
- **Consortium agreement:** IP, publication and governance rules.
- **Reporting calendar and lessons learned:** every deadline in one place, and what to do differently next time.
The free [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) brings goals, tasks, owners, dates and milestones together.

### KPIs for research projects
| KPI | What it measures | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Milestones and deliverables on time | Delivery against the grant schedule | Monthly tracking and funder reports |
| Spend against profile | Actual vs planned spend by category and partner | Avoiding underspend and ineligible costs |
| Recruitment progress | Participants, sites or staff recruited against target | Studies, trials and fieldwork |
| Publications and data | Papers, data sets and software released and deposited | Annual and final reports |
| Impact indicators | Patents, licences, policy citations, follow-on funding | Long-term value and future bids |

### Common mistakes in research project management
| Mistake | What happens | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Milestones written as expected results | Project looks late or failed when results differ | Write activities or decisions with go/no-go points |
| Ignoring ethics review time | Fieldwork starts months late | Submit early; plan review time from past experience |
| Recruiting staff after the start date | Underspend and a squeezed final year | Recruit as soon as the award is confirmed, where allowed |
| Tracking spend only at report time | Problems found too late | Review spend against profile monthly |
| No consortium agreement at the start | Disputes over IP and publications | Sign it before work begins |
| Changing deliverables without telling the funder | Costs disallowed or deliverables rejected | Use change control and ask the programme officer early |

### Software for research project management
Research teams already use lab notebooks, reference managers, data repositories and institutional finance systems. A project tool sits alongside them for tasks, timelines, partners and reporting; keep research data in approved repositories. Look for:
- Gantt or timeline views with milestones for grant schedules.
- Guest access for partners in other institutions and companies.
- Portfolio views for PIs and research offices tracking many grants.
| Team or setting | Typical needs | Tools to consider |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PhD student or small lab | Task lists, boards, shared notes | Trello, Notion, [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) |
| Single grant with a few partners | Timeline, milestones, partner access, reporting calendar | Asana, [Smartsheet](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/smartsheet/), Wrike |
| Consortium or research office | Portfolio dashboards, request intake, approvals, resource views | [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), Smartsheet |
Wrike, our top-ranked tool, suits research offices and consortia that need grant timelines, external collaborators, request forms and portfolio dashboards in one place. Smaller labs are often well served by simpler tools or free plans. Check security options against your institution's policy before storing anything sensitive.
See our [project management tool rankings](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-tools/) to compare options.

### Skills, qualifications and career path
Research project managers are either researchers who move into management or project professionals who move into research. Both need planning, budgeting, clear writing and enough grasp of the science to ask good questions.
- **Research administration credentials.** In the US, the Research Administrators Certification Council (RACC) offers the Certified Research Administrator (CRA), Certified Pre-Award Research Administrator (CPRA) and Certified Financial Research Administrator (CFRA).
- **[PMP certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/).** Requires three, four or five years of project experience in the last ten years depending on education (two with a GAC-accredited degree), plus 35 contact hours or the CAPM. From 1 December 2026, live training must come from a PMI Authorized Training Partner.
- **PMAI.** Our free PMAI certification covers project management foundations, including planning, risk and stakeholders.
Health research has its own rules; see [healthcare project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/healthcare-project-management/). For foundation and charity grants, see [nonprofit project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/nonprofit-project-management/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is research project management?**
It is the planning, coordination and control of research work, including funding, budgets, ethics approvals, partners, milestones, deliverables and reporting, while allowing for results that cannot be predicted.

**Q: What does a research project manager do?**
They support the principal investigator by maintaining the plan, tracking milestones, spend and risks, coordinating partners, running change control and preparing funder reports.

**Q: What is the difference between a principal investigator and a research project manager?**
The PI leads the science and is accountable to the funder. The research project manager runs the plan, budget tracking, partners and reporting. On small grants the PI often does both.

**Q: What are the phases of a research project?**
Idea and funding search, proposal development, award and set-up, research execution, reporting and dissemination, close-out, and impact and follow-on, grouped by research offices as pre-award, award and post-award.

**Q: What is the difference between pre-award and post-award?**
Pre-award covers finding funding and costing, writing and submitting the proposal. Post-award covers running the funded project: spending, compliance, changes, reporting and close-out.

**Q: How do you write milestones when research results are uncertain?**
Write them as completed activities or decisions, such as 'pilot analysed; go/no-go on main study', not expected findings. Give each a month, owner and means of verification.

**Q: What is a work package in a research grant?**
A group of related tasks with a lead, start and end months and deliverables. Grants usually have four to eight, including management and dissemination.

**Q: Can you use Agile for research projects?**
Yes, for day-to-day work. Most teams keep a work package plan with milestones for the funder and run each work package with short cycles and a visual board.

**Q: Is a data management plan the same as a project plan?**
No. A DMP covers how data are collected, stored, shared and preserved; a project plan covers tasks, owners, dates, budget and risks. Put DMP actions into the project plan.

**Q: What is a no-cost extension?**
Extra time on a grant without extra money. Rules vary: the NIH generally allows one extension of up to 12 months, with further extensions needing prior approval.

**Q: What qualifications does a research project manager need?**
There is no single requirement. RACC credentials (CRA, CPRA, CFRA) are recognised in the US, and the PMP and CAPM are valued everywhere. Research experience helps.

**Q: How should a PhD student manage their research project?**
Work back from the submission date, split the thesis into studies or chapters with milestones, allow time for ethics and data collection, and keep a simple board or Gantt chart up to date.

# Small Business Project Management: Steps, Tools & Examples

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/small-business-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Small business project management made simple: an 8-step process, worked examples, cash flow and priority checks, templates, KPIs and the best tools.


## Small Business Project Management: Steps, Tools & Examples
Small business project management is the use of simple, lightweight planning and tracking to deliver projects in a small company, such as a new website, a second location, a software switch or a batch of client jobs. The aim is just enough structure to hit deadlines, protect cash and stop important work slipping while everyone is busy running the business. This guide gives you an 8-step process, two worked examples, a way to prioritise competing projects, templates, KPIs and a fair comparison of tools.
- Published 27 August 2026
- Last updated 4 November 2026
- 18 min read

### Key takeaways
- Small business projects need just enough structure: a written goal, one owner per task, dates, a budget and a weekly 15-minute check-in.
- Check cash flow month by month, not just the total budget; a project that is affordable overall can still empty the bank in one month.
- Limit how many projects run at once and finish them before starting more; a simple score of value, urgency and effort makes the choice easier.
- One shared board showing every project is usually the highest-value first step.
- Turn repeat projects into templates so quality does not depend on one person's memory.

### What is small business project management?
**Small business project management** is the practice of planning, organising and tracking one-off pieces of work in a small company using light, practical methods. It means agreeing what done looks like, who does what, by when and for how much, then checking progress weekly, usually with no dedicated project manager and alongside day-to-day operations.
There is no single definition of a small business. The European Union treats a small enterprise as one with fewer than 50 staff and turnover or a balance sheet of no more than EUR 10 million, while the US Small Business Administration sets size standards that vary by industry. This guide is written for businesses from a handful of people up to about 50, where the owner is still close to most decisions.
| Project type | Example | Main risk to plan for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marketing and sales | New website, rebrand, product launch, trade show | Content and approvals taking longer than expected |
| Growth | Second location, new service line, first sales hire | Cash flow and the owner's time |
| Systems and admin | Switching accounting software, new booking system, moving to the cloud | Data migration and disruption to daily work |
| Premises and equipment | Shop fit-out, office move, new vehicles or machinery | Supplier lead times and deposits |
| Client work | Kitchen installs, design projects, consulting engagements | Underquoting and scope creep |
| Compliance | Health and safety review, data protection update, certification | Fixed deadlines and missing evidence |

### What makes small business projects different
Large companies have project managers, PMOs and approval boards. Small businesses have the owner, a few busy people and the next customer at the door. The basics of project management still apply, but the constraints are different.
| Factor | Large organisation | Small business |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who runs the project | A dedicated project manager | The owner, an operations or office manager, or the most relevant team member |
| Team time | People assigned to the project | People fit project tasks around customers and daily work |
| Money | Annual project budgets | Cash in the bank this month; one large payment can cause a squeeze |
| Decisions | Committees and sign-offs | Fast, often one person; changes need communicating, not approving |
| Specialists | In-house teams | Freelancers, agencies and suppliers |
| Documentation | Templates required by process | Only what saves time or prevents mistakes |
| Tools | Enterprise platforms | Free or low-cost tools that people will actually open |
Speed is the big advantage. A small business can decide on Monday and start on Tuesday. The risks are that nothing is written down, everything depends on the owner and project work always loses to the urgent customer issue.

### How much process does your project need?
Not every piece of work is a project, and not every project needs a plan document. Match the effort to the size and risk of the work.
| Size | Examples | What to write down | Check-in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quick job (under 2 weeks, one person) | Update price list, order new signage | A task with an owner and a due date | In the normal weekly meeting |
| Standard project (2 to 12 weeks, a few people) | Website refresh, new booking system, trade show | One-page brief, task list with owners and dates, budget, top 5 risks | 15 minutes weekly |
| Big bet (over 3 months or a large share of cash) | Second location, major hire, new product line | Brief, project plan with timeline, monthly cash forecast, risk list, change log | Weekly, plus a monthly review with whoever shares the financial risk |
The one-page brief is your lightweight [project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/): what the project is, why it matters, what done looks like, the deadline, the budget and who owns it. If you cannot fill that page in, you are not ready to start.

### How to manage a project in a small business: 8 steps
These steps work for any standard project or big bet. They take a few hours to set up and about 15 minutes a week to run.
1. **Define the project on one page.** Write the goal, why it matters, what done looks like in measurable terms, the deadline, the budget and the owner. Also note what is out of scope, so it does not quietly creep in later.
2. **Break the work down.** List the main deliverables, then the tasks needed for each. For larger jobs a simple [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) helps you spot missing work, such as testing, training or telling customers.
3. **Give every task one owner and a date.** One name, not "the team". Note dependencies, especially on suppliers and freelancers, and confirm their dates in writing.
4. **Check cash and capacity.** Map payments to months against the cash you expect to have, and add up the hours each person needs against the hours they really have after normal work. Adjust the plan if either is too tight.
5. **List the top risks.** Five is enough: what could go wrong, how likely it is, what you will do about it and who watches it. Supplier delays, key people being unavailable and costs rising are the usual suspects.
6. **Run a weekly check-in.** Fifteen minutes on what is done, what is next, what is blocked and whether the dates still hold. Update the board in the meeting, not afterwards.
7. **Deliver and hand over.** Launch, train staff, update any processes and tell customers what has changed.
8. **Review and save the template.** Spend 30 minutes on what to repeat and what to avoid, compare actual cost and hours with the estimate, and save the task list as a template for next time.
Client-facing businesses such as trades, studios and consultancies repeat the same project type many times, so steps 2 and 3 become a reusable template that saves the most time. Our [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) gives you a starting structure.

### Worked example: relaunching a trade business website
This illustrative example follows a 12-person plumbing and heating firm replacing an outdated website. The goal is a mobile-friendly site with online booking requests, live in 10 weeks, for a budget of $9,000: $6,500 web designer, $1,200 copywriter, $800 photographer and $500 contingency.
| Task | Owner | Weeks | Depends on | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Write the one-page brief | Owner | 1 | None | Brief agreed with the office manager |
| 2. Get three quotes and choose a designer | Office manager | 1 to 2 | 1 | Contract signed, 50% deposit paid |
| 3. Gather content: services, areas, prices, reviews | Office manager | 2 to 4 | 1 | Content document complete |
| 4. Photograph team, vans and jobs | Photographer | 4 | 2 | 30 edited photos delivered |
| 5. Write page copy | Copywriter | 4 to 6 | 3 | Copy approved by owner |
| 6. Design and build | Web designer | 3 to 7 | 2, 3 | Staging site ready |
| 7. Test forms, booking and mobile layout | Two engineers and office manager | 8 | 4, 5, 6 | Test checklist passed |
| 8. Launch and redirect old pages | Web designer | 9 | 7 | Site live, old addresses redirected |
| 9. Review results | Owner | 10, then month 3 | 8 | Enquiries compared with the previous quarter |

#### Cash and capacity check
The designer takes a 50% deposit in week 2 ($3,250) and the balance at launch in week 9 ($3,250); the copywriter and photographer are paid on delivery in weeks 4 to 6. That spreads $8,500 of planned spend over two months, with $500 held back.
Internal effort is the harder constraint. The plan needs about 60 hours from the office manager and 10 from the owner. The office manager can protect 8 hours a week for the project, so 60 hours takes about 8 weeks; that fits the 10-week plan only if content gathering starts in week 2, not after the designer begins. Spotting this at the start is the whole point of the capacity check.

#### What made it work
- **A clear definition of done:** "Site live with booking requests working on mobile", not "new website".
- **Content owned internally from week 2.** Late content is the most common reason small business websites slip.
- **A written scope.** When the owner asks for a blog in week 6, it goes on a list for phase 2 with a separate price, rather than delaying launch.

### Worked example: checking cash flow before a big project
In this illustrative example, a cafe plans a second site with a project budget of $60,000: fit-out $35,000 (40% deposit, 60% on completion), equipment $12,000, permits $1,000, hiring and training $5,000, launch marketing $3,000 and $4,000 contingency. The business has $25,000 of spare cash today, generates about $8,000 a month of surplus from the existing cafe, and the owner wants never to drop below a $5,000 buffer.
| Month | Opening cash | Surplus in | Project spend out | Closing cash |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | $25,000 | $8,000 | $14,000 (fit-out deposit) | $19,000 |
| 2 | $19,000 | $8,000 | $1,000 (permits) | $26,000 |
| 3 | $26,000 | $8,000 | $33,000 (fit-out balance and equipment) | $1,000 (below buffer) |
| 4 | $1,000 | $8,000 | $8,000 (hiring, training, marketing) | $1,000 (below buffer) |
The project is affordable in total, but month 3 takes cash to $1,000, well below the buffer, and leaves nothing for an unexpected bill. The owner negotiates with the equipment supplier to pay half on delivery in month 3 and half in month 5.
| Month | Opening cash | Surplus in | Project spend out | Closing cash |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | $26,000 | $8,000 | $27,000 | $7,000 |
| 4 | $7,000 | $8,000 | $8,000 | $7,000 |
| 5 | $7,000 | $8,000 | $6,000 (equipment balance) | $9,000 |
Every month now stays above the $5,000 buffer, before counting any income from the new site. The $4,000 contingency is still not covered by spare cash in months 3 and 4, so the owner also arranges an overdraft facility as a backstop. Other common fixes are staged client or landlord payments, leasing equipment and moving non-essential spend such as launch marketing later.
Add a month-by-month cash view to your [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) for every big bet. See our [project budget guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-budget/) for how to build and control the numbers.

### How to prioritise projects when everything is urgent
Most small businesses have more ideas than people. Starting them all means finishing none. A quick score helps you choose which to run now and which to park.
Score each project from 1 to 5 for **value** (impact on revenue, cost, customers or risk), **urgency** (cost of waiting) and **effort** (time and money needed). Then calculate **value x urgency / effort**.
| Project | Value | Urgency | Effort | Score | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Customer onboarding checklist | 3 | 3 | 1 | 9.0 | Start now |
| Switch accounting software | 3 | 4 | 2 | 6.0 | Start now |
| New website | 4 | 3 | 3 | 4.0 | Next, when a slot frees up |
| Trade show stand | 2 | 4 | 3 | 2.7 | Decide by the booking deadline |
| Second location | 5 | 2 | 5 | 2.0 | Plan properly; schedule deliberately |
With capacity for two active projects, the onboarding checklist and the accounting switch start now and the website follows. The score is a conversation starter, not a verdict: the second location scores low because it is big, but it may still be the most important strategic move, so it gets a planned start date rather than being squeezed in.
Tip
Set a work-in-progress limit for projects, for example no more than two or three active at once, and only start a new one when another finishes. It is the same idea as [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) in Kanban, applied to the whole business.
Use our [priority list template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/priority-list-template/) to score and rank work. See our guide to [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) for keeping several projects moving once they start.

### Who does what in a small business
| Role | Usually held by | Responsibilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sponsor and decision-maker | Owner or managing director | Sets priorities, approves spend, makes final calls |
| Project lead | Owner, office or operations manager, or the most relevant team member | Keeps the plan, chases tasks, runs check-ins, flags problems |
| Team members | Staff who also do day-to-day work | Complete assigned tasks and raise blockers early |
| Freelancers and suppliers | Designers, developers, contractors, accountants | Deliver specialist work to agreed specifications and dates |
| Customer | For client projects | Provides input, approvals and feedback on time |
The owner often holds two or three of these roles at once. That is fine, but write down who owns each decision. Even in a team of five, the most common problem is everyone assuming someone else is handling it. A one-page [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) settles it in ten minutes.

### Working with freelancers and suppliers
Small businesses buy in much of their specialist work, so a lot of project risk sits outside the team. A few habits prevent most problems:
1. **Write a short brief for every external piece of work.** What you need, the deadline, the budget, how you will review it and what done looks like. Two paragraphs agreed by email is far better than a phone call.
2. **Agree dates and payment stages in writing.** Link payments to delivered outputs, such as a deposit on signing and the balance on approval, rather than paying everything up front.
3. **Ask for their lead times early.** Equipment, fit-out trades and printers often need weeks of notice; put those lead times into your plan as tasks.
4. **Give them access to the work, not your whole business.** Use guest access in your project tool so freelancers see their tasks, files and comments without seeing everything else.
5. **Check progress midway.** A quick review at the halfway point catches misunderstandings while they are cheap to fix.
6. **Keep a contact and contract list.** Who supplies what, on what terms and who to call if they go quiet.
Treat repeat suppliers as part of the team: invite them to the check-in when their work is on the critical path, and share the plan so they can see how their dates affect everyone else.

### Methods that fit small businesses
| Approach | Best for | Why it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kanban board | Most small teams and ongoing work | Easy to start, visible to everyone, works with To do, Doing and Done columns |
| Simple Gantt timeline | Projects with fixed deadlines and supplier dependencies, such as a fit-out or event | Shows what must happen first and what a delay will knock on to |
| Light Agile | Websites, apps and digital marketing | Weekly or fortnightly cycles with quick feedback |
| Checklists and templates | Repeat client work and routine projects | Captures know-how so quality does not depend on one person |
| Lean thinking | Improving a core process such as order fulfilment | Focuses on removing waste and delays |
Start with one board for all projects. A single view of everything in flight is what most small businesses are missing, and it shows straight away when too much is being attempted. Our guide to [Kanban boards](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) explains how to set one up, and a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) is worth adding when dates and dependencies matter. If your team builds digital products, [Agile project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-agile-project-management/) adds short cycles and regular feedback.

### Running a 15-minute weekly check-in
The weekly check-in is the habit that keeps small business projects moving. Keep it short, standing if possible, at the same time every week.
1. **Done since last week** (3 minutes): move cards on the board as people speak.
2. **Next this week** (4 minutes): each owner names the tasks they will finish, not just work on.
3. **Blocked** (5 minutes): anything waiting on a decision, a supplier or another person. Agree who unblocks it and by when.
4. **Dates and money** (3 minutes): is the deadline still realistic, and is spend in line with the plan? If not, decide now what changes.
Write decisions on the board or in a shared note. If a topic needs more than two minutes, take it offline with the people involved.

### Templates that save time
- [Project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/): a short plan for standard projects and big bets.
- [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/): everyday tracking for all projects on one board.
- [Project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/): for quoting client work and checking internal projects.
- [Project proposal template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-proposal-template/): to win and scope client projects.
- [Risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/): a short list of the five things most likely to go wrong.
- [Change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/): to price extra client requests instead of absorbing them.

### KPIs worth tracking
Keep the list short. Three or four numbers reviewed weekly beat a dashboard nobody opens.
| KPI | What it measures | How to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On-time completion | Milestones or projects finished by the due date | Weekly check-in; spot slipping projects early |
| Budget vs actual | Spend against the plan | Monthly; catch overruns while they are small |
| Cash position by month | Project spend and income against cash available | Monthly; avoid cash shortfalls |
| Project profitability | Revenue minus all costs, including staff time, for client projects | After each job; price future work |
| Hours actual vs estimated | Accuracy of time estimates | After each project; better quotes and schedules |
| Customer satisfaction | Feedback, reviews or repeat business after delivery | Client projects |

### Common mistakes and how to avoid them
- **Too many projects at once.** Limit active projects to what the team can genuinely handle and finish them before starting more.
- **Projects lose to daily work.** Block regular time for project tasks in calendars and protect it like a customer appointment.
- **Everything lives in the owner's head.** Put tasks and decisions in one shared place so work does not stop when the owner is busy.
- **Underquoting client work.** Track actual hours against estimates and use the data for the next quote.
- **Trusting supplier dates.** Confirm dates in writing, build in buffer and check progress before the deadline, not on it.
- **Letting scope grow for free.** Agree scope in writing and price changes separately; our guide to [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/) shows how.
- **Skipping the review.** Thirty minutes at the end turns one project's lessons into a better template for the next one.

### Software for small business project management
The best tool is the one your team will open every day. Before you compare features, decide what you need: one board for everything, a timeline for deadline-driven work, guest access for clients and freelancers, a mobile app for people on site, and integrations with email, file storage and accounting.
| Tool | Published price (from our reviews) | Good fit for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wrike (our #1, 9.4/10) | Free plan; Team $10 and Business $25 per user/month, billed annually | Growing businesses running several projects, client requests and deadline-driven plans |
| monday.com (9.1/10) | Free for up to 2 seats; Basic $9, Standard $12, Pro $19 per seat/month, billed annually, minimum 3 seats | Visual boards that non-technical staff pick up quickly |
| Asana (9.0/10) | Free Personal plan (2 users); Starter $10.99 and Advanced $24.99 per user/month, billed annually | Teams coordinating tasks across functions |
| ClickUp (8.9/10) | Free Forever; Unlimited $7 and Business $12 per user/month, billed annually | Feature-rich setups on a tight budget |
| Trello (7.8/10) | Free for up to 10 collaborators per Workspace; Standard $5, Premium $10 per user/month, billed annually | Simple Kanban boards for very small teams |
| Microsoft Planner (8.1/10) | Basic Planner included in Microsoft 365; Planner Plan 1 $10 per user/month, paid yearly | Businesses already working in Microsoft 365 and Teams |
| Basecamp (7.6/10) | Free (1 project); flat monthly plans from $25 with no per-user fees | Communication-centred client projects with predictable costs |
Prices change, so check the vendor's site before you buy. For very small teams with simple needs, [Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/) and [Basecamp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/basecamp/) are quick to adopt and inexpensive, and [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) offers a lot for the price. As the business grows and runs more projects, clients and staff in parallel, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is a strong all-in-one option: Gantt charts with dependencies, workload views, request forms and client collaboration in one place, with a free plan to try it. [monday.com](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/) suits teams that want highly visual boards, and if you already pay for Microsoft 365, try [Microsoft Planner](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/) before buying anything new.

#### Spreadsheet or project management software?
A spreadsheet is fine while one person runs a few projects and everyone knows where it lives. Move to a tool when several people update the same plan, when you need reminders and comments on tasks, when clients or freelancers need access, or when you cannot see all your projects in one place.
See our guide to [choosing project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/how-to-choose-project-management-software/) for a step-by-step selection process and trial checklist.

### When to hire a project manager
Most small businesses do not need a full-time project manager, but there are clear signals that someone needs to own coordination as a real part of their job:
- Projects regularly miss deadlines even though the work itself is not hard.
- The owner spends more time chasing tasks than running the business.
- You run several client projects at once and profitability varies widely between them.
- Suppliers and freelancers are coordinated by whoever happens to be free.
Options include giving an operations or office manager formal project responsibility and protected time, hiring a project coordinator, or bringing in a freelance project manager for a big bet such as a second site. Whoever takes the role, give them the authority to chase people and the one-page brief to work from.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is small business project management?**
It is the use of simple, lightweight planning, task tracking and review practices to deliver projects in a small company, without heavy process or a dedicated project manager.

**Q: Do small businesses need project management?**
Yes, in a light form. Any project involving several people, suppliers or a meaningful amount of cash benefits from a written goal, owners, dates, a budget and a weekly check-in.

**Q: Does a small business need a project manager?**
Usually not a full-time one. The owner or an operations lead typically runs projects, but each project needs one clearly named owner with time set aside to coordinate it.

**Q: What are the steps of project management for a small business?**
Define the project on one page, break down the work, give every task an owner and date, check cash and capacity, list the top risks, run weekly check-ins, deliver and hand over, then review and save the plan as a template.

**Q: What is the best project management software for a small business?**
It depends on size and needs. Trello, Basecamp and ClickUp suit very small teams on a budget; Wrike, our top-ranked tool, suits growing businesses that need Gantt charts, workload views, request forms and client access.

**Q: Are free project management tools enough?**
Often, for a small team. Free plans from Wrike, Trello, ClickUp, monday.com and Asana cover basic boards and tasks, but check user limits and which features are trial-only before relying on them.

**Q: Should I use a spreadsheet or project management software?**
A spreadsheet works while one person runs a few projects. Switch when several people update the plan, clients or freelancers need access, or you can no longer see every project in one place.

**Q: How do I manage several projects at once?**
Keep all projects on one board, score them on value, urgency and effort, cap how many run at once and finish current projects before starting new ones.

**Q: How should a small business budget for a project?**
List every cost, add contingency, then map payments to the months they fall in against your expected cash. Negotiate staged payments if any month drops below your minimum buffer.

**Q: What should a small business project plan include?**
The goal and definition of done, deliverables and tasks, owners and dates, dependencies on suppliers, a budget with monthly cash view, the top risks and how progress will be checked.

**Q: Which KPIs should a small business track for projects?**
On-time completion, budget against actual, monthly cash position, project profitability for client work, hours against estimate and customer satisfaction.

**Q: Can Agile work in a small business?**
Yes. Weekly planning, short delivery cycles and quick feedback suit small teams that can change direction fast, especially for websites, apps and marketing.
