# Software Project Management: Process, Methods and KPIs

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/software-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Software project management explained: the SDLC, a step-by-step process, Agile methods, roles, estimation with worked examples, DORA metrics and tools.


## Software Project Management: Process, Methods and KPIs
Software project management is the planning, coordination and control of work that produces or changes software, from discovery and requirements through design, development, testing and release to ongoing improvement. Because requirements change and estimates are uncertain, most software teams deliver in short iterations and measure progress by working software rather than by documents. This guide covers the life cycle, methods, roles, a step-by-step process, estimation and metrics with worked examples, common mistakes and tools.
- Published 29 August 2026
- Last updated 18 October 2026
- 19 min read

### Key takeaways
- Software project management balances people, process and product: who builds it, how the work flows and what gets released.
- Most teams use Scrum or Kanban, supported by DevOps practices; plan-driven or hybrid approaches still suit fixed-scope contracts and regulated software.
- Forecast with ranges based on past throughput, not single-point dates, and fix the date while flexing scope where you can.
- Track delivery with the five DORA metrics and flow metrics, and judge success with outcome metrics such as adoption.
- Make technical debt, dependencies and risks visible early; they cause more late releases than coding speed does.
- Use a developer issue tracker such as Jira for code-level work and a platform such as Wrike when software must be planned with other departments.

### What is software project management?
**Software project management** is the discipline of planning, organising and controlling the people, work and resources needed to deliver a software product, feature or system. It covers scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk, adapted to the realities of software: evolving requirements, uncertain estimates and frequent releases. Its goal is valuable working software delivered predictably.
A useful way to remember the scope of the job is the **three Ps**:
- **People:** forming the team, clarifying roles, managing stakeholders and keeping communication flowing between engineers and the business.
- **Process:** choosing and running a delivery approach (Scrum, Kanban, a plan-driven model or a hybrid), plus estimation, risk and release management.
- **Product:** making sure the right thing is built, to the agreed quality, with requirements, acceptance criteria and testing that prove it works.

#### Types of software projects
| Project type | Example | What usually drives the plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New product build | A first version of a customer mobile app | Discovery, a minimum viable product and early user feedback |
| Feature release | Adding subscriptions to an existing platform | Backlog priority, release date and dependencies on other teams |
| Integration | Connecting an e-commerce site to a new payment provider | Third-party APIs, test environments and vendor timelines |
| Migration or re-platforming | Moving a monolith to cloud services | Data migration, parallel running and cutover risk |
| Maintenance and support | Fixing defects and upgrading libraries | Continuous flow, service levels and capacity |
| Contracted build | An agency building a portal for a client | Statement of work, fixed budget, change control and acceptance |
If your work is mainly about rolling out purchased systems and infrastructure, our guide to [IT project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/it-project-management/) covers that side.

### How software projects differ from other projects
The core project management ideas of scope, time, cost and risk still apply, but software changes how you apply them.
- **Requirements evolve.** Users often only know what they want once they see something working, so plans must expect change.
- **Estimation is uncertain.** Much of the work is new problem-solving. Forecasts based on ranges and historical data beat precise guesses.
- **Delivery can be continuous.** With automated testing and deployment pipelines, teams can release many times a week instead of once at the end.
- **The product is invisible.** Progress is hard to see without demos, working builds and clear definitions of done.
- **Technical debt accumulates.** Shortcuts taken to hit a date slow future work unless they are repaid. See [technical debt in Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-technical-debt/).
- **Quality is built in.** Code review, automated tests and monitoring replace a single large test phase at the end.
- **Projects sit inside products.** Many software teams are long-lived product teams, so the project is often a release, a feature set or a new product line rather than a one-off effort.

### Software project management vs product and IT project management
These roles overlap, and in small companies one person may do all three. The table shows the usual split.
|  | Software project management | Product management | IT project management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main question | How and when will this be delivered? | What should we build and why? | How do we deliver this technology change into the organisation? |
| Typical scope | Building or changing software | A product's strategy, roadmap and outcomes | Infrastructure, purchased systems, upgrades and software builds |
| Typical owner | Software project manager, delivery lead or technical project manager | Product manager or product owner | IT project manager |
| Success measured by | Predictable, quality releases and objectives met | Adoption, retention, revenue and customer value | Change delivered safely with service continuity and adoption |
| Time horizon | A release, programme or contract | Ongoing for the life of the product | A project with a go-live and handover |
The [technical project manager](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/technical-project-manager/) role sits between engineering and delivery, and an IT project manager does a similar job for infrastructure and purchased systems.

### The software development life cycle (SDLC)
The **software development life cycle** is the sequence of activities that takes software from idea to operation. Names and numbers of phases vary between sources; this seven-phase version maps well to both plan-driven and Agile teams.
| Phase | What happens | Key outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Discovery | Understand users, problems and goals; test ideas with research and prototypes | Problem statement, product vision, early prototypes |
| 2. Planning | Shape scope, order the backlog, plan releases, capacity and budget | Product backlog, release plan, roadmap |
| 3. Design | User experience, architecture and technical approach | Designs, architecture decisions, acceptance criteria |
| 4. Development | Write code in small increments with peer review and automated tests | Working, tested increments |
| 5. Testing and quality assurance | Automated, exploratory, performance, accessibility and security testing | Test results, resolved defects |
| 6. Release and deployment | Deploy to production, often through a continuous delivery pipeline | Released feature, release notes |
| 7. Operate and improve | Monitor, support users, measure outcomes and feed learning back into the backlog | Metrics, incident reviews, new backlog items |
In a plan-driven project these phases run broadly in sequence with gates between them. In Agile teams they happen continuously inside every iteration: each sprint includes a little design, build, test and release. Our guide to the [Agile development life cycle](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-development-life-cycle/) shows how that works in practice.

### Software project management methodologies
| Approach | When it fits | How work is organised |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Scrum](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/) | Product teams building new features with regular stakeholder feedback | Sprints of one month or less, with sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review and retrospective (per the Scrum Guide 2020) |
| [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/) | Maintenance, platform and support teams with continuous incoming work | Visual board, WIP limits and flow metrics instead of fixed sprints |
| Extreme Programming (XP) | Teams that want strong engineering discipline | Pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases |
| [DevOps](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/devops/) | Teams that build and run their own services | Automated build, test and deployment, with shared responsibility for operations |
| Waterfall or V-model | Fixed-scope contracts and regulated or safety-critical software | Sequential phases, formal documentation and verification against requirements |
| Hybrid | Agile build inside a fixed budget, contract or regulatory gate | Plan-driven milestones and governance with iterative delivery between them |
| Scaled frameworks such as SAFe | Many teams working on one product | Shared cadence, joint planning and visible cross-team dependencies |

#### How to choose an approach
- **Requirements likely to change and users available for feedback:** Scrum or another iterative approach.
- **Unpredictable, interrupt-driven work such as support:** Kanban.
- **The team runs what it builds in production:** add DevOps practices whatever the framework.
- **Fixed scope, external approval or safety certification:** plan-driven or hybrid, with strong change control and traceability.
- **Several teams on one release:** a scaled approach with shared planning and visible dependencies.
For a side-by-side comparison, read [Agile vs Waterfall](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-vs-waterfall/).

### Roles and responsibilities
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Product owner or product manager | Owns the product goal and orders the backlog by value |
| Software project manager or delivery lead | Plans releases, coordinates dependencies, manages risks, budget and stakeholder reporting |
| Scrum master | Coaches the team in Scrum and removes impediments |
| Engineering manager | Leads engineers, hiring, growth and engineering practices |
| Tech lead or architect | Owns technical direction, design quality and technical risk |
| Developers | Design, build and test the software (the Scrum Guide calls everyone doing this work Developers) |
| QA or test engineers | Test strategy, automation and exploratory testing |
| UX and product designers | User research, journeys and interface design |
| DevOps or site reliability engineers | Pipelines, infrastructure, monitoring and reliability |

#### What a software project manager does day to day
- Keeps the release plan and forecast current, and explains changes to stakeholders in plain language.
- Tracks cross-team dependencies, third-party deliveries and environment availability.
- Runs or supports planning, refinement and review sessions with the product owner and team.
- Maintains the risk register and escalates blockers the team cannot remove itself.
- Reports progress using working software, flow data and outcome measures rather than percentage-complete guesses.
- Manages budget, contracts and change requests where the work is funded as a project.

### Step-by-step process for managing a software project
This process works for a new product, a major feature or a contracted build. Adjust the formality to the size and risk of the work.
1. **Define the outcome.** Agree the problem, the users affected and how success will be measured (for example, "reduce checkout abandonment from 40% to 30%"). Record it in a short charter or project brief.
2. **Identify stakeholders and constraints.** List decision-makers, users, dependent teams, budget, deadlines, compliance needs and technical constraints.
3. **Choose the delivery approach.** Pick Scrum, Kanban, plan-driven or hybrid using the criteria above, and agree the cadence of planning and review.
4. **Build and refine the backlog.** Break the scope into epics and [user stories](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/user-stories/) with acceptance criteria. Order them by value and risk.
5. **Agree a definition of done.** Write down what "done" means: code reviewed, tests passing, documentation updated, deployed to a test environment. See [definition of done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
6. **Estimate and forecast.** Size the backlog with story points or item counts and forecast a date range from historical throughput (worked examples below).
7. **Plan the release.** Group stories into a release plan with milestones, dependencies and a minimum releasable scope.
8. **Deliver in iterations.** Run sprints or a Kanban flow. Demo working software to stakeholders at least every few weeks and update the forecast.
9. **Control risk, change and quality.** Review risks weekly, route scope changes through the product owner (or formal change control for contracts), and watch defect and stability metrics.
10. **Release and review.** Deploy, monitor, and hold a retrospective and a post-release review that compares outcomes with the goal set in step 1.
Tip
Release the smallest useful version first. A thin slice that reaches real users early tests your assumptions and your deployment pipeline at the same time.

### Estimating and forecasting software work
Software estimates are uncertain because much of the work has not been done before. Good practice is to estimate relatively, measure what the team actually completes, and forecast as a range.
- **Story points** compare items by effort, complexity and uncertainty. See [Agile estimation and story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-estimation-story-points/).
- **Velocity** is the number of points a Scrum team completes per sprint.
- **Throughput** is the number of items finished per week, which works without points if items are of similar size.
- **Cycle time** is how long one item takes from start to done, useful for service-level forecasts.
- **Probabilistic forecasting** such as Monte Carlo simulation turns historical data into dates with a confidence level.

#### Worked example: release forecast from throughput
A team has 96 stories left in its release backlog. Over the last eight weeks it finished between 8 and 12 stories a week, averaging 10.
| Scenario | Throughput per week | Calculation | Weeks to finish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Optimistic | 12 | 96 ÷ 12 | 8 weeks |
| Likely | 10 | 96 ÷ 10 | 9.6, so about 10 weeks |
| Pessimistic | 8 | 96 ÷ 8 | 12 weeks |
Teams usually discover extra work as they go. If past releases grew by about 15%, plan for roughly 110 stories, which moves the likely forecast to 11 weeks. You would then tell stakeholders: "Most likely 10 to 11 weeks, and very unlikely to be more than 14 weeks. If the date is fixed at 10 weeks, we will need to drop about 10 to 15 lower-priority stories."

#### Worked example: sprint capacity
A team of five developers runs two-week sprints (10 working days). One person is on leave for three days, and the team keeps 20% of its time for meetings, support and technical debt.
| Step | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Available person-days | (5 × 10) − 3 | 47 days |
| Less 20% reserved time | 47 × 0.8 | About 37.6 focus days |
| Capacity compared with normal | 37.6 ÷ 40 (a full sprint at 80%) | About 94% |
| Points to plan (average velocity 40) | 40 × 0.94 | About 37 points |
Planning about 37 points rather than the usual 40 keeps the sprint realistic. Our [sprint planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/sprint-planning/) guide covers how to turn capacity into a sprint goal.
Tip
When a deadline is fixed, fix the date and flex the scope. Agree a minimum releasable scope early, so cutting lower-priority items is a planned decision rather than a crisis.

### Risk, change and technical debt
Most late software releases are caused by things outside the coding itself: unclear requirements, dependencies, environments and quality problems found late. Track them in a [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/risk-register/) and review it every week or every sprint.
| Common risk | Early warning sign | Typical response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unclear or changing requirements | Stories keep returning from testing; frequent rework | Shorter feedback loops, prototypes, clearer acceptance criteria |
| Cross-team or vendor dependencies | Waiting time on the board; API not ready | Map dependencies, agree interface contracts, use mocks and stubs |
| Unrealistic deadline | Forecast range ends after the committed date | Re-plan scope, add a release phase, or escalate early |
| Technical debt | Cycle time rising; more defects in old code | Reserve capacity each sprint for refactoring |
| Security and compliance gaps | Findings from scans or reviews late in the release | Shift testing left; build checks into the pipeline |
| Key-person dependency | One developer reviews or deploys everything | Pairing, documentation, shared ownership |

#### Managing change
In product teams, change is normal: the product owner reorders the backlog and the forecast is updated. In contracted or regulated work, scope changes usually need formal approval because they affect price, dates or validation. Use a [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/) process with a change request template, and keep versions of code, requirements and releases under configuration management.

#### Managing technical debt
- Record debt items in the backlog with a short note on their cost (slower changes, risk of incidents).
- Agree a standing allowance, for example 10% to 20% of each sprint, with the product owner.
- Pay down debt in the areas you are about to change, where the benefit is felt soonest.
- Track trends such as cycle time and defect rates to show whether debt is growing.

### Software project management metrics and KPIs
Use a small, balanced set of measures: how fast and how reliably you deliver, how well work flows, and whether the software achieves its goal. Avoid using any single metric, especially velocity, to compare teams.

#### DORA software delivery metrics
The DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) programme defines five software delivery performance metrics, grouped into throughput and instability. According to dora.dev, the fifth metric, deployment rework rate, was added in 2024, and the older "time to restore service" was redefined as failed deployment recovery time in 2023.
| Metric | What it measures | Group |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change lead time | Time from a code commit to a successful production deployment | Throughput |
| Deployment frequency | How often changes are deployed to production | Throughput |
| Failed deployment recovery time | Time taken to recover from a deployment that fails | Throughput |
| Change fail rate | Share of deployments that cause a failure in production | Instability |
| Deployment rework rate | Share of deployments that are unplanned, to fix problems in production | Instability |

#### Worked example: calculating DORA metrics for one month
In October a team made 40 production deployments. Four caused a failure needing a fix, recovery took 30, 50, 90 and 70 minutes, and six of the 40 deployments were unplanned hotfixes.
| Metric | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deployment frequency | 40 deployments in about 22 working days | About 2 per working day |
| Change fail rate | 4 ÷ 40 | 10% |
| Failed deployment recovery time | (30 + 50 + 90 + 70) ÷ 4 | 60 minutes on average |
| Deployment rework rate | 6 ÷ 40 | 15% |
On their own these numbers mean little. Track them month by month and look for direction: more frequent, smaller releases with a stable or falling failure rate are a healthy sign.

#### Other useful measures
| Measure | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Cycle time and throughput | Flow speed and forecasting data |
| Work in progress | Whether the team is starting more than it finishes |
| Escaped defects | Bugs found after release, a check on testing effectiveness |
| Forecast accuracy | How well release forecasts matched reality |
| Outcome metrics | Adoption, conversion, retention or task success: whether the software delivers value |
| Budget variance | For funded projects, spend against plan |

### Example: planning a mobile app release
A retailer wants to add click-and-collect to its mobile app before the holiday season, 14 weeks away. Here is how the process above plays out.
1. **Outcome:** 10% of online orders using click-and-collect within two months of launch.
2. **Constraints:** app store review time, a new stock API from the warehouse team, and payment provider changes.
3. **Approach:** Scrum with two-week sprints for the app team; the warehouse API team uses Kanban, so the delivery lead holds a short weekly dependency check.
4. **Backlog:** 70 stories across four epics (store selection, stock check, payment, notifications).
5. **Forecast:** past throughput of 6 to 8 stories a week gives 9 to 12 weeks, inside the 14-week window but with little slack.
6. **Release plan:** a minimum releasable scope of 50 stories, with notifications and loyalty points as "nice to have".
7. **Risk:** the stock API slips by three weeks. The team builds against a mock API, and the delivery lead escalates the dependency in the sprint review.
8. **Result:** the minimum scope ships in week 12 after a beta with staff, and notifications follow in a later release.
The value came from making the dependency visible early and agreeing the minimum scope before pressure built up.

### Essential documents and templates
| Document | Purpose | Who usually owns it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product backlog | Ordered list of everything the product may need | Product owner |
| User stories | Requirements written from the user's point of view, with acceptance criteria | Product owner with the team |
| Sprint plan | Sprint goal and selected work | Development team |
| Release plan | What ships when, and the minimum releasable scope | Product owner and delivery lead |
| Product roadmap | High-level direction over quarters | Product manager |
| Requirements document | Agreed scope for fixed or contracted work | Business analyst or project manager |
| Risk register or RAID log | Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, with owners and responses | Project manager or delivery lead |
| Retrospective notes | Improvements the team has agreed | Scrum master or team |
Many teams also keep architecture decision records and a definition of done alongside these. Keep documents light and current; a short living document beats a long one nobody updates. To start quickly, use our free [product backlog template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/product-backlog-template/), [release plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/release-plan-template/) and [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).

### Common software project management mistakes
- **Committing to a single date too early.** Give a range, explain the assumptions and narrow it as you learn.
- **Fixing scope, date and budget at once.** Something has to flex; agree which one before the project starts.
- **Measuring output instead of outcomes.** Story points delivered say nothing about whether users benefit.
- **Too much work in progress.** Starting many items at once slows everything down. Limit WIP and finish work before starting more.
- **Leaving testing and security to the end.** Build quality checks into every iteration and into the pipeline.
- **Hiding dependencies.** Map them on a shared board and review them every week.
- **Ignoring technical debt.** Without a regular allowance, delivery slows release after release.
- **Process for its own sake.** Ceremonies and documents should help the team deliver; drop or change those that do not.

### Tools for software project management
Software teams usually need two kinds of tool. Developers need an issue tracker that links to code repositories and CI/CD pipelines, with backlogs, boards and sprint reports. Project and delivery managers also need roadmaps, cross-team dependency views, resource planning and reports that non-engineers can read.
- **[Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/)** is widely used by engineering teams for issue tracking, Scrum and Kanban boards and developer integrations, and it has a free plan for up to 10 users.
- **[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/)** is our top-ranked platform overall and a strong fit when software work has to be planned alongside marketing, support, design or client teams. It combines boards, interactive Gantt charts (on paid plans), dashboards, workload views and request forms in one place.
- Many organisations use both: developers work in an issue tracker, and portfolio planning and reporting happen in a work management platform connected to it.
When choosing, check integrations with your code host, support for your framework, cross-project reporting, permissions and total cost per user.

### Skills and career path
Software project managers need enough technical understanding to follow engineering conversations and spot risks, combined with planning, communication and stakeholder skills.
- Understanding of the SDLC, version control, testing and deployment pipelines.
- Agile practices: backlog management, iteration planning, flow and retrospectives.
- Data-based forecasting and clear reporting of uncertainty.
- Risk, dependency and vendor management.
- Facilitation and negotiation with both technical and business stakeholders.
Common routes in are from development, testing, business analysis or project coordination. Useful credentials include the [PMP](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/pmp-certification/) for experienced project managers, the [CAPM](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capm-certification/) for those starting out, and Scrum certifications for Agile roles.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is software project management?**
Software project management is the planning, coordination and control of the people, work and resources needed to deliver software, from discovery and requirements through development, testing and release to ongoing improvement.

**Q: What are the phases of software project management?**
A common version of the software development life cycle has seven phases: discovery, planning, design, development, testing, release and operate-and-improve. Plan-driven projects run them in sequence; Agile teams repeat them in every iteration. Some sources use five project phases instead: initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and controlling, and closure.

**Q: What does a software project manager do?**
They plan releases, forecast dates, coordinate dependencies, manage risks, budgets and change, and keep stakeholders informed, working closely with the product owner, tech lead and development team.

**Q: What are the three Ps of software project management?**
People (the team and stakeholders), process (how the work is planned and delivered) and product (what is built and to what quality).

**Q: Which methodology is best for software projects?**
There is no single best method. Scrum suits feature teams that need regular feedback, Kanban suits continuous support and maintenance work, DevOps practices suit teams that run their own services, and plan-driven or hybrid approaches suit fixed-scope contracts and regulated software.

**Q: How do you estimate a software project?**
Break the work into small items, size them with story points or count them, then forecast a date range from the team's historical velocity or throughput. Add an allowance for scope growth and update the forecast as work is completed.

**Q: What are DORA metrics?**
Five software delivery measures defined by the DORA research programme: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate.

**Q: What is the difference between software project management and product management?**
Product management decides what to build and why, and owns outcomes such as adoption. Software project management focuses on how and when the work is delivered, including planning, risk and coordination.

**Q: What is the difference between IT project management and software project management?**
IT project management covers all technology change in an organisation, including infrastructure, purchased systems and upgrades. Software project management focuses on building or changing software products.

**Q: What tools are used for software project management?**
Issue trackers such as Jira connected to code repositories and pipelines, plus a work management platform such as Wrike when software work needs to be planned and reported alongside other departments.

**Q: How do you manage technical debt in a software project?**
Make it visible in the backlog, agree a regular share of capacity to pay it down, prioritise debt in areas you are about to change, and track cycle time and defect trends to show its effect.

**Q: What documents are used in software project management?**
A product backlog, user stories, sprint and release plans, a roadmap, a definition of done, a risk register or RAID log and, for contracted work, a requirements document and change requests.

**Q: What skills does a software project manager need?**
A working knowledge of the development process, Agile practices, forecasting with data, risk and dependency management, and clear communication with technical and business stakeholders.

**Q: Which certifications help in software project management?**
The PMP for experienced project managers, the CAPM for beginners, Scrum certifications such as CSM or PSM for Agile teams, and the PMI-ACP for experienced Agile practitioners.

# Video Production Project Management: Complete Guide

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/video-production-project-management/
Section: Industry guides
Summary: Video production project management explained: phases, roles, budgets, schedules, call sheets, review rounds, delivery specs, KPIs and tools.


## Video Production Project Management: Complete Guide
Video production project management is the planning and control of a video from the first brief through pre-production, the shoot and post-production to final delivery, so that it meets the brief on time and on budget. Because shoot days are expensive and hard to repeat, most of the work happens before the camera rolls, and most overruns happen in post-production when review rounds are not controlled. This guide gives you a five-phase workflow, roles, a step-by-step process, a worked budget and schedule, a pre-production checklist, delivery specs, KPIs and tools.
- Published 28 August 2026
- Last updated 17 October 2026
- 20 min read

### Key takeaways
- Put most of your planning effort into pre-production: problems solved on paper are cheap, problems solved on set are not.
- Gate the project at treatment, script, rough cut and picture lock, with one named approver at each gate.
- Build the budget line by line, split above-the-line and below-the-line costs and hold a contingency.
- Agree the number of review rounds per cut in the contract and treat extra rounds and late changes after picture lock as change requests.
- Releases, licences, insurance, risk assessments and data backups are project management tasks, not afterthoughts.
- Write the deliverables list (formats, aspect ratios, captions, loudness) at the start, because it drives how you shoot and edit.

### What is video production project management?
**Video production project management** is the process of planning, budgeting, scheduling, resourcing and controlling a video project, from concept and pre-production through filming and post-production to delivery and archiving. It coordinates creative people, crew, talent, equipment, locations and client approvals so that the finished video meets the brief, on time and within budget.
It applies to brand films, adverts, corporate and training videos, documentaries, music videos, event coverage and the steady stream of short-form social video that in-house teams produce. Whether one person or a team of 40 is involved, the same disciplines apply, scaled to the size and risk of the job.
|  | General project | Video production project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Biggest cost driver | People's time over weeks or months | A small number of expensive shoot days with crew, kit, talent and locations |
| Can work be redone? | Usually, at some cost | Reshoots are costly and sometimes impossible (events, locations, talent) |
| Legal and rights | Contracts and data protection | Talent, location and music releases, licences and usage terms |
| Acceptance | Meets requirements | Approved by named people at each cut, against the brief |
| Technical delivery | Varies | Specific formats, aspect ratios, captions and loudness for each platform |
| Typical method | Phased or Agile | Phased with approval gates; Kanban for in-house content teams |

### What makes video projects different
Video shares a lot with other [creative project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/creative-project-management/), but five features change how you plan it.
- **Fixed, expensive shoot days.** Crew, kit, talent and locations are booked for specific days. A lost day is a large, often unrecoverable cost, so everything before the shoot is about removing risk from it.
- **Physical logistics.** Locations, permits, travel, catering, insurance, parking, power and weather all need planning, which makes a shoot closer to an [event project](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/event-project-management/) than to office work.
- **Rights and releases.** Contributors, locations, music, stock footage and archive material need signed releases or licences before the video can be used, and the usage terms (media, territory, duration) must match how the client will publish it.
- **Iterative post-production.** Edits go through several cuts with feedback at each. The number of rounds, and how late changes arrive, drives most post-production overruns.
- **Technical delivery.** Each channel needs its own formats, aspect ratios, captions and audio levels, so the deliverables list affects how you shoot, not just how you export.

### The five phases of video production
Most video projects move through five phases. Small social videos compress them into days; broadcast and brand work adds formal gates and more paperwork.
| Phase | Key activities | Main outputs | Gate and approver |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Development | Brief, objectives, audience, concept, treatment, initial budget and timeline | Signed brief, treatment, budget estimate | Treatment and budget approved by the client or commissioner |
| 2. Pre-production | Script, storyboard, shot list, casting, recces, permits, crew and kit booking, insurance, risk assessment, schedule | Approved script, shooting schedule, call sheets, releases ready | Script and storyboard approved; green light to shoot |
| 3. Production | Shoot days, directing, sound, data management, daily progress reports | Rushes backed up, production reports, signed releases | Producer confirms all required shots and paperwork captured |
| 4. Post-production | Logging, assembly, rough cut, fine cut, picture lock, grade, sound mix, graphics, captions | Approved master | Rough cut, fine cut and picture lock approved; master signed off |
| 5. Delivery and archive | Versions and cut-downs, quality checks, delivery, archiving, rights log, wash-up | Deliverables, archive, rights log, lessons learned | Client confirms receipt and acceptance |
If you know the standard [project management phases](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-phases/), development is initiation, pre-production is planning, production and post-production are execution with tight monitoring, and delivery is closure.
Tip
Never book crew or locations before the treatment, script and budget are approved. Every change after booking costs money in cancellation fees, rebooking or wasted preparation.

### Who does what: roles in a video production
Video teams use film and television titles. On small projects one person may cover several roles, but each responsibility still needs a named owner.
| Role | Main responsibilities |
| --- | --- |
| Producer | Owns the project end to end: budget, schedule, client relationship, hiring and final delivery |
| Line producer or production manager | Runs the budget and logistics day to day: crew, kit, locations, schedule, cost reports |
| Production coordinator | Issues call sheets, books travel and accommodation, manages paperwork and releases |
| Director | Leads the creative vision, works with talent and crew, shapes the edit |
| Director of photography (DoP) | Camera, lighting and the visual look |
| Sound recordist | Clean location sound and wild tracks |
| Data wrangler or digital imaging technician | Copies, verifies and backs up footage during the shoot |
| Editor, colourist, sound mixer, motion designer | Post-production specialists |
| Post-production supervisor | Plans the post schedule, manages versions and delivery specs |
| Client, commissioner or brand lead | Approves the treatment, script, cuts and final master |

#### Producer vs line producer
The **producer** decides what the project is and makes the big trade-offs: creative scope, budget level, key hires and client expectations. The **line producer** (often called production manager on smaller jobs) turns that into a workable plan and keeps it on budget: every day of crew, every kit hire and every location fee. In-house teams often have a single video producer or project manager doing both, with a coordinator on larger shoots.

### How to manage a video production project step by step
Use this process for any video, scaling the paperwork to the size of the job.
1. **Capture the brief.** Agree objective, audience, key message, tone, length, channels, deliverables, budget, deadline and the named approver. A [creative brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/creative-brief-template/) keeps every request consistent.
2. **Develop and approve the treatment.** Describe the creative approach, style, references and structure. Approve it with a first budget estimate before writing the script.
3. **Build the budget line by line.** Separate above-the-line and below-the-line costs, add post-production and licences, and hold a contingency. A [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) helps.
4. **Write and approve the script and storyboard.** Lock what will be filmed and said. Changes after this point affect bookings and cost.
5. **Break down the script into a shot list.** List every shot or setup with location, cast, kit and special requirements.
6. **Schedule backwards from delivery.** Place final delivery, then the master approval, picture lock, review rounds, edit time and shoot days. Find the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) to the first shoot day, which usually runs through permits, casting and key crew availability.
7. **Book people, kit and locations.** Confirm in writing with dates, rates, cancellation terms and overtime rules.
8. **Complete the legal and safety work.** Risk assessment, insurance, permits, release forms and music licences, with owners and due dates.
9. **Issue call sheets and run the shoot.** Track progress against the shot list every few hours, back up footage at each card change and collect releases on the day.
10. **Run post-production in controlled rounds.** Rough cut, fine cut and picture lock, each with one consolidated set of notes from one contact by an agreed date.
11. **Finish, version and quality-check.** Grade, mix, graphics and captions, then produce every version on the deliverables list and check each against the spec.
12. **Deliver, archive and review.** Deliver files, log rights and usage terms, archive project files and rushes, and hold a short wash-up to capture [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/).

### Worked example: a two-day corporate shoot
A company commissions a two-minute brand film plus three 30-second social cut-downs, with two actors and two locations, to be delivered in eight weeks. The rates below are illustrative only; use current local rates and quotes from your suppliers.

#### The budget
| Line | Calculation | Cost (£) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Director | 6 days × £600 | 3,600 |
| Producer | 10 days × £450 | 4,500 |
| Talent | 2 actors × 2 days × £400 | 1,600 |
| Talent usage buyout | Online and social, 12 months | 1,200 |
| Above-the-line subtotal |  | 10,900 |
| Shoot crew (DoP, camera assistant, gaffer, sound, make-up, runner) | £2,300 per day × 2 days | 4,600 |
| Camera, lighting and sound kit | £1,500 per day × 2 days | 3,000 |
| Locations | £1,000 per day × 2 days | 2,000 |
| Catering | 15 people × £25 × 2 days | 750 |
| Production insurance | Quote | 400 |
| Editor | 8 days × £450 | 3,600 |
| Colour grade | 1 day | 700 |
| Sound mix | 1 day | 600 |
| Motion graphics | 3 days × £450 | 1,350 |
| Music licence | Library track, agreed usage | 500 |
| Captions and versioning | Quote | 400 |
| Below-the-line subtotal |  | 17,900 |
| Total before contingency |  | 28,800 |
| Contingency (10%) | £28,800 × 10% | 2,880 |
| Total budget |  | 31,680 |
Production companies usually add a production fee or margin on top; in-house teams may not charge one but should still track the full cost so they can show what each video costs.

#### The eight-week schedule
| Week | Work | Approval at end of week |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Brief, treatment, budget estimate | Treatment and budget |
| 2 | Script and first storyboard | Script |
| 3 | Storyboard, casting, location recces, permits requested | Storyboard, cast and locations |
| 4 | Crew and kit confirmed, risk assessment, call sheets; shoot on days 4 and 5 | Shoot complete, footage backed up |
| 5 | Logging and assembly; rough cut | Rough cut notes (round 1) |
| 6 | Fine cut with graphics in progress | Fine cut notes (round 2) |
| 7 | Picture lock, grade, mix, final graphics, captions | Picture lock and master |
| 8 | Cut-downs, versions, quality checks, delivery and archive | Delivery accepted |

#### What an extra review round costs
In this example each additional edit round takes about one editor day (£450) plus half a producer day (£225), so £675 before any grade, mix or graphics rework. A change after picture lock can cost several times that, because the grade, mix, graphics and captions may all need to be redone. Showing this calculation to the client before the edit starts is one of the most effective ways to keep feedback consolidated and on time.

### Budgeting a video production
A video budget is built bottom-up from the script and schedule, not top-down from a guess.
| Budget area | Typical lines | Control tip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Above the line | Producer, director, writer, lead talent, usage buyouts | Agree usage terms early; extending usage later costs more |
| Production (below the line) | Crew, kit, locations, permits, travel, catering, insurance, art department | Check overtime rules and cancellation terms in every booking |
| Post-production | Edit, grade, sound, graphics, VFX, captions, versioning | Tie the number of rounds to the budget |
| Licences and assets | Music, stock footage, fonts, archive | Log licence terms in a rights register |
| Contingency | Weather, overruns, reshoots, unexpected costs | Release it through the producer, not line by line |
- Hold a [contingency](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/contingency-plan/) of around 10% as a starting point, more for outdoor shoots, complex logistics or untested formats.
- Update a cost report after every shoot day and at each post-production gate, comparing actuals with the approved budget line by line.
- Price changes before agreeing them. Every client request after script approval should come back with a time and cost impact.

### Scheduling the shoot
The shooting schedule groups scenes by location, cast and setup rather than by script order, to reduce moves and talent days.
1. **List every setup.** A setup is a camera and lighting position; several shots may come from one setup.
2. **Estimate time per setup.** Simple interviews or pick-ups may take 15 to 20 minutes; lit dialogue scenes or moving shots can take an hour or more. Use your DoP's estimates.
3. **Group by location and lighting.** Shoot everything in one place and one direction before moving.
4. **Schedule talent efficiently.** Group each actor's scenes to reduce paid days.
5. **Protect the hardest shots.** Put the most important or complex setups early in the day, when the crew is fresh and light is predictable.
6. **Add moves, meals and margin.** Include company moves between locations, meal breaks and a buffer for the unexpected.
7. **Plan weather cover.** For exterior work, keep an interior cover set or a contingency day available.
For example, a ten-hour day with a one-hour lunch and two 30-minute company moves leaves eight hours of shooting. At an average of 40 minutes per setup that is 12 setups. If the shot list has 30 setups across two days, you are six short: you either simplify setups, combine shots or add a half-day before anyone arrives on set.
Use a [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) or a [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) for the overall plan and a separate shooting schedule for the shoot days.

### Pre-production checklist
Use this checklist before you confirm the shoot. Anything not complete is a risk to the shoot day.
| Area | Check | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Creative | Treatment, script, storyboard and shot list approved | Producer and director |
| Budget | Approved budget, contingency held, POs raised | Producer or line producer |
| People | Crew and talent confirmed in writing with rates and terms | Line producer |
| Locations | Recce done, location agreements signed, permits granted, access, parking and power confirmed | Production coordinator |
| Equipment | Kit list agreed with DoP and sound; hires confirmed; spares and media | Line producer and DoP |
| Legal | Talent, contributor and location releases ready; music and stock licensed | Producer |
| Safety | Risk assessment completed and shared; insurance in place; first aid and emergency contacts | Producer |
| Data | Media management plan: backups, naming, storage and who wrangles | Post-production supervisor |
| Logistics | Travel, accommodation, catering, call times | Production coordinator |
| Deliverables | Formats, aspect ratios and versions agreed so framing suits every output | Producer |
Track wider project risks, such as late approvals or a key person becoming unavailable, in a [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).

### Managing shoot days

#### The call sheet
A call sheet is sent the day before each shoot day. It typically includes the date, call times for each person, location addresses and maps, parking, contacts, the day's schedule and scenes, cast, key kit, weather, sunrise and sunset, nearest hospital and safety notes.

#### Track progress during the day
- Check progress against the shot list at agreed points, for example mid-morning, lunch and mid-afternoon.
- If you are behind, decide early with the director what to simplify, combine or drop, rather than running into overtime.
- Record what was shot, any issues and overtime in a short daily production report.

#### Protect the footage
Footage is the only output of an expensive day, so data management is a project control, not just a technical task. A common rule of thumb is to keep at least two verified copies on separate drives before a camera card is formatted, with a third copy off site as soon as practical. Use a consistent folder and file naming convention agreed with the editor.

### Post-production: controlling cuts and review rounds
Post-production is where most video budgets are lost, usually through extra review rounds, conflicting feedback and changes after picture lock.
| Cut | Purpose | What feedback is appropriate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assembly | All usable takes in script order (often internal only) | Structure and missing material |
| Rough cut | Story, structure and pacing | Story, order, length, messaging |
| Fine cut | Refined edit with temporary graphics and music | Detail of shots, timing, graphics content |
| Picture lock | Edit fixed; no more changes to timing | Approval only |
| Online and finishing | Grade, sound mix, final graphics, captions | Technical and brand checks |
| Master and versions | Final files and cut-downs | Quality control against the spec |
- Agree the number of review rounds per cut in the contract or [statement of work](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/statement-of-work/), for example two rounds at rough cut and one at fine cut.
- Name one contact who consolidates all notes into a single document with timecodes.
- Set turnaround dates for feedback and show what happens to the delivery date if they slip.
- Use a review tool that lets reviewers comment on specific frames, so notes are precise.
- Treat changes after picture lock as change requests with a cost and time impact, using a [change request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/).
Tip
Write picture lock into the schedule as a milestone with a named approver and date. Changes after lock ripple into the grade, mix, graphics and captions, and are where post budgets usually overrun.

### Delivery specs and versioning
Write the deliverables list at the start of the project, because it affects how you frame shots and plan the edit. Each item should be a line with a file name, specification and approval status. The [project deliverables template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-deliverables-template/) works well for this.
| Specification | What to agree | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Versions | Main film, cut-downs, lengths, languages | Each version needs time to edit, check and approve |
| Aspect ratios | For example 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1 | Frame wide enough on set to allow vertical and square crops |
| Codec, resolution and frame rate | Master and distribution files | Check each platform's current upload specifications |
| Captions and subtitles | Burned-in or separate caption files; languages | Captions help accessibility and silent autoplay viewing |
| Loudness | Target loudness per destination | Broadcast standards include EBU R128 (-23 LUFS) and ATSC A/85 (-24 LKFS); online platforms set their own targets |
| Graphics and legal | Logos, end frames, legal text, music credits | Confirm against brand guidelines |
| Archive | Project files, rushes and masters to keep | Agree who stores them and for how long |

### Managing in-house video content teams with Kanban
In-house teams that produce a steady stream of social, product and internal videos rarely run one large project at a time. A [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) suits this flow better than a phased plan for each video.
| Column | What it means | Exit rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requests | New video requests from the business | Brief complete and prioritised |
| Pre-production | Script, shot list, bookings | Script approved, shoot booked |
| Shooting | Being filmed or recorded | Footage backed up and logged |
| Editing | In edit | Cut ready for review |
| In review | With the approver | Notes received or approved |
| Finishing | Grade, mix, captions, versions | Quality checked against spec |
| Published | Live on the channel | Performance data captured |
- Limit work in progress in the editing and review columns, which are usually the bottlenecks.
- Batch shoots: film several videos in one day to use crew and kit efficiently.
- Plan publishing dates with a [content calendar template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/content-calendar-template/) and feed the board from it.
- Use templates for repeat formats so each video does not start from scratch.
For more on running creative teams with Agile ideas, see [Agile for creative teams](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-for-creative-teams/).

### Essential documents and templates
| Document | Purpose | Template |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Creative brief | Objective, audience, message, deliverables, approvers | [Creative brief template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/creative-brief-template/) |
| Treatment | Creative approach, style and structure | Written by the director or producer |
| Budget and cost report | Line-by-line costs and actuals | [Budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) |
| Production schedule | Phases, gates and key dates | Project schedule or Gantt chart template |
| Script, storyboard and shot list | What will be filmed and how | Scriptwriting or storyboard tools |
| Call sheet | Daily shoot information | Issued by the production coordinator |
| Risk assessment | Shoot safety hazards and controls | Your organisation's format |
| Releases and licences | Permission to use people, places, music and footage | Legal templates; a rights log |
| Deliverables list | Every final file and version | Project deliverables template |

### KPIs for video production project management
| KPI | What it measures | How to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Budget variance | Actual cost against approved budget by line | Cost control, especially on shoot and post |
| Shoot days against plan | Days used versus scheduled | Production efficiency and estimate accuracy |
| Setups completed per day | Shot list progress during the shoot | Decide early what to simplify or drop |
| Review rounds per cut | Number of feedback cycles | Post-production cost control |
| Feedback turnaround | Days the client took to return notes | Shows where delays come from |
| On-time delivery | Masters delivered by the deadline | Client reliability |
| Brief-to-delivery time | Days from brief to final delivery | Planning repeat formats in content teams |
| Video performance | Views, completion rate, conversions against the objective | Whether the video achieved its purpose |

### Common video production mistakes
- **Booking before approval.** Crew and locations booked before the script is signed off lead to cancellation fees or rushed shoots.
- **An over-full shot list.** Too many setups per day leads to overtime, rushed performances and missed shots.
- **No weather or illness cover.** Exterior shoots need an interior cover set or a contingency day.
- **Missing releases.** Collect signatures on the day; chasing them afterwards is slow and sometimes impossible.
- **Single copy of footage.** Back up before cards are reused.
- **Too many reviewers.** Uncoordinated notes from several people create conflicting changes and extra rounds.
- **Deliverables agreed at the end.** Late requests for vertical or square versions may need reframing that the footage cannot support.
- **Uncontrolled [scope creep](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scope-creep/).** Extra versions and late changes added without a cost conversation erode the budget.

### Software for video production project management
Video teams usually combine a project management platform with specialist production tools. In the project management platform, look for:
- Timeline and calendar views for production schedules and shoot days.
- Request forms so every video starts with a complete brief.
- Resource and workload views for crew, editors and kit.
- Proofing with frame-accurate comments on video, plus version history and recorded approvals.
- Budget or cost tracking, or an easy link to the budget spreadsheet.
- Templates for repeat formats and checklists for pre-production and delivery.
[Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/), the top tool in our rankings, is a strong fit for in-house video teams that sit within marketing, because request forms, schedules, workload views and video proofing and approvals sit in one platform. Production companies also rely on specialist software for script breakdown and scheduling, production budgeting, editing and dedicated video review.
Video projects often sit inside wider campaigns, so it helps to understand how those are planned.
If you produce video for clients, our guide to [agency project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/agency-project-management/) covers retainers, estimates and utilisation.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is video production project management?**
It is the planning, budgeting, scheduling and control of a video project from concept through pre-production, the shoot and post-production to final delivery, so that the video meets the brief on time and on budget.

**Q: What are the stages of video production?**
The usual stages are development, pre-production, production (the shoot), post-production, and delivery and archive. Each ends with an approval gate, such as treatment, script, picture lock and master sign-off.

**Q: What does a video producer do?**
A producer owns the project: budget, schedule, hiring, client relationship and delivery. On larger shoots a line producer or production manager runs the budget and logistics day to day, supported by a production coordinator.

**Q: What is the difference between a producer and a line producer?**
The producer decides what the project is and makes the major creative and budget trade-offs. The line producer turns that into a workable plan and keeps every day of crew, kit and location on budget.

**Q: How do you budget for a video production?**
Build it line by line from the script and schedule: above-the-line costs (producer, director, talent, usage), below-the-line costs (crew, kit, locations, insurance), post-production and licences, plus a contingency of around 10% as a starting point.

**Q: How long does a video production take?**
It depends on length, complexity and approvals. A simple social video can take days; a two-minute brand film with a two-day shoot often takes six to ten weeks from brief to delivery, with approvals usually the biggest variable.

**Q: What is a call sheet?**
A document sent before each shoot day with call times, locations, contacts, schedule, scenes, cast, weather, sunrise and sunset, and safety information such as the nearest hospital.

**Q: What is picture lock?**
Picture lock is the point at which the edit is approved and no further timing changes are made. Grading, sound mixing, final graphics and captions are completed after lock, so later changes are expensive.

**Q: How many revision rounds should a video include?**
There is no standard number. A common approach is two rounds at rough cut and one at fine cut, agreed in the contract. Extra rounds and changes after picture lock should be priced as change requests.

**Q: What should a video deliverables list include?**
Every version and cut-down, aspect ratios, codec, resolution and frame rate, captions and subtitles, loudness targets, graphics and legal text, and which files will be archived.

**Q: What is the difference between above-the-line and below-the-line costs?**
Above-the-line costs cover the key creative people and talent, such as producer, director, writer and lead cast. Below-the-line costs cover crew, equipment, locations, logistics and post-production.

**Q: Is Agile useful in video production?**
Partly. Individual productions are phased because shoot days are fixed, but post-production works in short review cycles, and in-house content teams often run Kanban boards from request to published.

**Q: What software is used for video production project management?**
Teams combine a project management platform for schedules, requests and approvals, such as Wrike, with specialist tools for script breakdown, scheduling, budgeting, editing and video review.

### What is a project management template?
A **project management template** is a ready-made, pre-structured document, such as a spreadsheet or form, that you copy and fill in to plan, track or report on a project. It gives you the right headings, columns and formulas in advance, so you spend your time on the content of the project rather than on designing the document, and every project records the same information in the same way.
Templates do not replace project management judgement. A risk register template will not identify your risks, and a Gantt chart template will not tell you how long tasks take. What they do is make sure you ask the right questions, keep information in one consistent place and can show stakeholders a familiar format. For the method behind each document, our [project management guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/what-is-project-management/) explains the processes the templates support.

### Choose your version: beginner, advanced or expert
Every template on this site comes in three versions, so you can match the document to the size of the project and the experience of the people filling it in.
| Version | What you get | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Beginner | The essential columns on a single tab. Quick to fill in, with nothing to configure. | Small projects, one-off tasks, people new to the document |
| Advanced | The full template with every tab, dropdown list and formula. | Most projects and teams; the version we recommend by default |
| Expert | Everything in Advanced, plus an instructions tab, an auto-summarising dashboard, status colours and a revision history. | Larger projects, PMOs and documents that are reported to sponsors |
All three versions are available as a Google Sheet, an Excel file and a print-ready PDF. Choose the spreadsheet formats when the document will change during the project, and the PDF when you want to fill it in by hand in a workshop or attach a fixed copy to a report.
Tip
If you are unsure, start with the Advanced version. You can always hide the tabs you do not need, but adding missing columns and formulas later takes longer.

### Templates for each phase of a project
Most project management frameworks, including PMI's process groups and PRINCE2's stages, describe a project moving from initiation through planning, execution and control to closure. This table shows which of our templates you will typically use in each phase.
| Phase | What you need to decide or record | Templates to use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiating | Why the project exists, whether it is worth doing and who authorises it | Business case, project proposal, problem statement, project charter, project brief |
| Planning | Scope, deliverables, schedule, cost, roles, risks and communication | Project plan, project scope statement, work breakdown structure, project schedule, Gantt chart, project cost estimate, RACI matrix, communication plan, risk register |
| Executing | Who is doing what this week, and what was agreed in meetings | Project tracker, action plan, meeting agenda, meeting notes, work request form |
| Monitoring and controlling | Progress against plan, new risks and issues, and requested changes | RAID log, change request, budget, critical path |
| Closing | Whether every deliverable was accepted and what the team learned | Project deliverables, lessons learned |
Agile teams use a different rhythm: a product backlog and product roadmap for direction, then a sprint planning template, a Kanban board and a sprint retrospective template in every Sprint.

### The essential starter kit
You do not need all 55 templates on one project. For a typical project, these five documents cover most of what sponsors, team members and auditors expect to see:
1. **[Project charter](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-charter-template/)**: authorises the project and records its purpose, objectives, high-level scope, milestones, budget and sponsor. Read our [project charter guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-charter/) for what to include.
2. **[Project plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/)** or **[project schedule](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/)**: the plan sets out goals, scope, deliverables, owners and dates; the schedule focuses on tasks, durations and dependencies. Smaller projects can use one; larger projects usually need both.
3. **[RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/)**: makes it clear who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each deliverable or decision, which prevents gaps and duplicated effort.
4. **[Risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/)**: lists each risk with its probability, impact, owner and response, so risks are managed rather than discovered.
5. **[Project tracker](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-tracker-template/)**: the working list of tasks, owners, deadlines, priority and status that the team updates every week.
Add a [communication plan](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/), a [budget](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) and a [change request](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/change-request-template/) form as the project grows, and finish with a [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) review.

### Templates for common situations
If you are looking for a template for a specific job, start here:
- **Planning a schedule with dependencies:** the [Gantt chart template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gantt-chart-template/) for a visual week-by-week timeline, and the [critical path template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/critical-path-template/) to calculate early and late dates and find the activities that drive the end date.
- **Breaking down the work:** the [work breakdown structure template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/) for the hierarchy of deliverables, then the work package template to define each package's scope, effort and cost.
- **Estimating and controlling cost:** the [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) to build the estimate by work package, and the [budget template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/budget-template/) to track planned against actual spend each month.
- **Running Scrum:** the user story template, [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/), agile release plan and agile project plan.

- **Strategy and goals:** the OKR template, 5-year plan, business plan and competitor analysis.

- **Analysing a problem:** the root cause analysis (5 Whys) template, gap analysis template and business requirements document.

### How to use a project management template
A template saves time only if it is set up and kept up to date. This is the process we recommend:
1. **Pick the right document for the decision.** Ask what question the document must answer ("Who approves this?", "What could go wrong?", "When will we finish?") and choose the template that answers it.
2. **Choose the version and format.** Beginner for a quick one-off, Advanced for most projects, Expert when you report to a sponsor or PMO. Use Google Sheets when several people will edit it, Excel if your organisation works in Microsoft 365, and PDF for printing.
3. **Make your own copy first.** Use the Google Sheets button to copy the template into your Drive, or download the .xlsx file. Keep the original untouched so you can reuse it.
4. **Tailor it before you fill it in.** Rename columns to your organisation's terms, delete what you will not use and edit the dropdown lists, such as status values or risk categories, so everyone uses the same options.
5. **Fill it in with the people who do the work.** A schedule or risk register written alone by the project manager is usually wrong. Run a short workshop and complete the document together.
6. **Agree an owner and an update rhythm.** Decide who updates each document and how often: a tracker weekly, a risk register at every status meeting, a RAID log whenever something changes.
7. **Save the finished version as your organisation's template.** After the project, add what you learned, so the next project starts from a better document.

### Common mistakes with project templates
- **Filling in every field because it is there.** Templates are a checklist, not a test. Leave out sections that do not apply to a small project.
- **Creating the document and never updating it.** A risk register or tracker that is three weeks out of date is worse than none, because people trust it.
- **Using different templates on every project.** Standard templates let a PMO compare projects and let people move between teams without relearning the paperwork.
- **Confusing similar documents.** A project charter authorises the project; a project plan explains how it will be delivered; a project brief is a short summary for stakeholders. A RAID log covers risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies together, while a risk register covers risks in more depth.
- **Keeping the spreadsheet when it no longer fits.** If several people are overwriting each other's changes or you are copying data between files every week, it is time to move to software.

### Templates or project management software?
Spreadsheet templates are ideal for small and medium projects, for one-off documents such as a charter or business case, and for teams that already work in Excel or Google Sheets. They are free, flexible and easy to share.
Project management software becomes the better choice when many people need to update the same plan at once, when you run several projects that share people, or when you need automatic dependencies, workload views, approvals and dashboards that update themselves. In our independent ranking, [Wrike](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/) is our top pick for teams that want projects, resources, portfolios, approvals and reporting in one platform, while [Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/) and [Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/) are easy first steps up from a spreadsheet. Many tools also let you import a spreadsheet, so a well-structured template makes the move easier.

### How we build our templates
Each template is written by the Neural Project Institute editorial team and follows widely used project management practice, for example the RACI roles, the RAID categories and the critical path calculation of early and late dates. Each template page explains the document, shows a live preview of the first tab, lists every tab and column, and gives a worked example and tips. Templates are free to edit and use in your own work, including commercial projects; please do not resell the templates themselves.

## Free Action Plan Template (Google Sheets, Excel, PDF)
This free action plan template turns one goal into a short list of specific actions, each with an owner, start and due dates, the resources it needs, a measure of success, a priority and a status. Download it for Google Sheets, Excel or as a printable PDF, in a beginner, advanced or expert version.

- Google Sheets · Excel · PDF

### Key takeaways
- An action plan answers four questions for every step: what, who, by when and how you will know it is done.
- Start with one measurable goal; every action in the plan should move you towards it.
- Give each action one owner and a due date, even when several people help.
- Priority and status dropdowns make the plan easy to sort, filter and review in a weekly meeting.
- Choose beginner for a quick six-column plan, advanced for the full plan with dropdowns, or expert for a dashboard and overdue highlighting.

### What is an action plan template?
An **action plan template** is a ready-made table for turning a goal into the specific actions needed to reach it. Each row lists one action with an owner, start and due dates, the resources required, a success measure, a priority and a status, so everyone can see what happens next, who is responsible and whether the plan is on track.
Action plans are lighter than a full project plan. They suit situations where the goal is clear and the work is a few weeks or months of focused effort, for example:
- Follow-up actions from a review, audit, [lessons learned session](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/lessons-learned-template/) or retrospective.
- A small improvement project, such as raising customer satisfaction or reducing a backlog.
- A corrective plan after an incident, missed target or failed inspection.
- A team, department or personal goal for the next quarter.
- Actions agreed in a meeting that need tracking beyond the [meeting notes](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-notes-template/).
If the work needs a detailed scope, budget, schedule and governance, use a [project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-plan-template/) instead, or alongside this one.
