# Free Skills Matrix Template (Excel, Google Sheets, PDF)

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/skills-matrix-template/
Section: Free templates
Summary: Free skills matrix template for Excel, Google Sheets and PDF: rate skills 0-4, see team averages, spot single points of failure and plan training.


## Free Skills Matrix Template (Excel, Google Sheets, PDF)
This free skills matrix template maps the skills your team needs against each person's proficiency on a simple 0 to 4 scale, so you can see strengths, gaps and single points of failure at a glance. Download it in Google Sheets, Excel or PDF at beginner, advanced or expert level, with no sign-up, then overwrite the four sample team members with your own.
- Published 31 August 2026
- Last updated 25 October 2026
- Google Sheets · Excel · PDF

### Key takeaways
- A skills matrix is a grid of people against skills, with a proficiency rating in every cell, that shows who can do what and how well.
- Agree what each rating means before anyone scores themselves: the template's 0-4 scale runs from none to can teach others.
- Read the matrix by column as well as by row: low team averages show weak skills, and skills only one person rates 3 or 4 are a key-person risk.
- Combine self-assessment with a manager or peer calibration conversation so ratings are consistent across the team.
- Turn every finding into an action (training, pairing, hiring or a staffing change) and refresh the matrix about twice a year.

### What is a skills matrix?
A **skills matrix** is a grid that lists team members down one side and the skills the team needs across the top, with a proficiency rating in every cell. It shows at a glance who can do what and how well, where the team is strong, which skills are thin, and who depends on a single expert, so managers can plan training, staffing and hiring.
You will also see it called a **skill matrix**, a **competency grid** or a **cross-training matrix**. Whatever the name, it replaces gut feel about who is good at what with a shared picture the team has agreed on.
Project managers use a skills matrix to staff projects and spot delivery risks; team leads use it for cross-training and cover; HR and learning teams use it to target training budgets. Our guide to [project management skills](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-skills/) lists the hard and soft skills that often become columns in a PM team's matrix.

### What is in this skills matrix template
The template has one data tab, **Skills matrix**, with four sample team members (Ana, Ben, Chen and Dana) rated against six project management skills. A note at the top of the sheet explains the rating scale. Here is a live preview of the advanced version:
Skills matrix
| Team member | Role | Scheduling | Risk management | Stakeholder mgmt | Agile / Scrum | Budgeting | Data / reporting | Average |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ana | PM | 4 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 |
| Ben | PM | 3 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 2.83 |
| Chen | Analyst | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 4 | 2.33 |
| Dana | Coordinator | 3 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 2.17 |
| Team average |  | 3 | 2 | 2.75 | 2.75 | 2 | 3 |  |
Sample rows are examples: replace them with your own.
- **Skills matrix**: Team member, Role, Scheduling, Risk management, Stakeholder mgmt, Agile / Scrum, Budgeting, Data / reporting, Average

#### The columns explained
- **Team member**: one row per person.
- **Role**: the person's job title or project role, such as PM, Analyst or Coordinator.
- **Six skill columns**: Scheduling, Risk management, Stakeholder mgmt, Agile / Scrum, Budgeting and Data / reporting. These are examples for a project team: rename them to the skills your own team needs.
- **Average**: each person's mean rating across the six skills, calculated with an AVERAGE formula.
- **Team average row**: the last sample row averages each skill column across the team.

#### The 0 to 4 rating scale
Every skill cell takes a number from 0 to 4. Agree the descriptions below, or your own version, with the team before anyone rates themselves.
| Rating | Label | What it looks like in practice | Typical action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | None | Has not done this and does not yet know how | Train only if the role or project needs it |
| 1 | Learning | Understands the basics or is in training; needs close guidance | Formal training plus a mentor |
| 2 | Can do with help | Can do routine work but checks in on anything unusual | Stretch assignments with review |
| 3 | Independent | Does the work reliably without supervision, including most exceptions | Use on projects; ready to deputise |
| 4 | Can teach others | Recognised go-to person; can coach, review and improve the method | Mentor others; share knowledge |
Some organisations rate 1 to 5 or 0 to 3 instead. Any scale works if a 3 means the same thing for every person and every skill.

#### Beginner, advanced and expert versions
| Version | What you get | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Beginner | One tab with six columns (Team member, Role, Scheduling, Risk management, Stakeholder mgmt, Agile / Scrum) and the Team average row | A first, quick matrix for a small team |
| Advanced | The full Skills matrix tab with all six skill columns, a personal Average for each person and the Team average row | Most teams and projects |
| Expert | The advanced tab plus an Instructions tab with steps and tips, and a Revision history tab to log each update | Matrices that are reviewed regularly or shared with HR or a PMO |
Every spreadsheet version has a frozen header row and filters, so you can sort by any skill or filter by role. The PDF is a print-ready copy for workshops.

### How to create a skills matrix step by step
For a small team you can fill in the template in an hour. Most of the effort, and most of the value, is in agreeing the skills and the rating definitions.
1. **Decide what the matrix is for.** Staffing a project, planning training and reducing key-person risk need different skill lists. Write the purpose in one sentence and set the scope: one team, one project or a department.
2. **Choose six to twelve skills.** Start from the work, not job titles: your project plan, role descriptions and upcoming projects. Keep skills specific enough to rate ("Budget forecasting" rather than "Finance") and rename the template's six skill columns to match. Insert extra columns before Average if you need more.
3. **Agree the rating definitions.** Use the 0 to 4 scale above and, for important skills, add one example of what a 3 looks like, such as "builds and maintains a resource-loaded schedule without help".
4. **Ask each person to self-assess.** Ask them to note one piece of evidence for any 3 or 4 rating.
5. **Calibrate the ratings.** The manager reviews each person's scores in a short conversation and, where useful, asks a peer who has worked with them. The aim is consistency across the team, not marking people down.
6. **Enter the agreed ratings.** Replace the sample rows with your team. The personal Average and the Team average row calculate automatically for the sample rows; see the spreadsheet tips below when you add more people.
7. **Analyse the results.** Look at team averages for weak skills, count how many people rate 3 or more in each skill to find single points of failure, and note who rates 4 and could coach others. The worked example below shows how.
8. **Act and record the actions.** Turn each finding into a named action with an owner and a date: training, pairing, a staffing change or a hiring decision. Record training in a [training plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/training-plan-template/) and wider improvements in an [action plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/action-plan-template/).

#### Spreadsheet tips
- **Adding more people:** the Team average formulas cover the four sample rows (for example =AVERAGE(C6:C9)). Insert new rows between the first and last sample rows so the ranges expand automatically, or edit the ranges to include every person.
- **Copy the Average formula down:** the empty rows below the sample do not contain the personal Average formula, so copy it from a sample row into each new row.
- **Add a coverage count:** under the Team average row, add a row called "People at 3+" with a formula such as =COUNTIF(C6:C9,">=3") in each skill column. Any skill showing 0 or 1 needs attention.
- **Make a heatmap:** select the rating cells and apply a colour scale (Format > Conditional formatting > Colour scale in Google Sheets; Home > Conditional Formatting > Color Scales in Excel). Red-to-green makes gaps jump out.
- **Keep blanks and zeros distinct:** a blank means not yet rated; a 0 means no skill. AVERAGE ignores blanks but counts zeros, so fill in every cell before you read the averages.

### Skills matrix example: reading the sample data
The sample data describes a four-person project team: two project managers (Ana and Ben), an analyst (Chen) and a coordinator (Dana). Here is what the matrix shows when you read it column by column:
| Skill | Team average | People rated 3 or 4 | Rated 4 (can teach) | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduling | 3.00 | 3 (Ana, Ben, Dana) | Ana | A strength with good cover |
| Risk management | 2.00 | 1 (Ana) | Nobody | Weak skill and a single point of failure |
| Stakeholder mgmt | 2.75 | 2 (Ana, Ben) | Ana | Adequate, but only the two PMs can do it alone |
| Agile / Scrum | 2.75 | 2 (Ben, Chen) | Ben | Adequate, with an internal coach available |
| Budgeting | 2.00 | 1 (Ana) | Nobody | Weak skill and a single point of failure |
| Data / reporting | 3.00 | 3 (Ben, Chen, Dana) | Chen | A strength with good cover |

#### What the example shows
- **Two key-person risks.** Only Ana can do risk management and budgeting independently. If she is away or moves on, the team loses both at once. That is a delivery risk worth recording in the project's [risk register](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).
- **Two clear strengths.** Scheduling and data and reporting have three capable people each, so the team can absorb absence there.
- **Internal coaches.** Ana (scheduling, stakeholder management), Ben (Agile / Scrum) and Chen (data and reporting) all rate 4, so much of the development can happen through pairing rather than paid courses.
- **Personal averages need context.** Ana averages 3.00, Ben 2.83, Chen 2.33 and Dana 2.17. That does not make Dana the weakest team member: a coordinator is not expected to match a PM on budgeting. Compare people with the needs of their role, not with each other.

#### Actions from the example
| Finding | Action | Owner | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Risk management depends on Ana | Ben co-runs the next two risk reviews with Ana; Dana (rated 1) takes a short risk management course | Ana and the team lead | Ben to 3 and Dana to 2 by the next review |
| Budgeting depends on Ana | Ben shadows Ana on the monthly forecast; Chen (rated 1) learns the cost-tracking basics | Ana | Ben to 3 within six months |
| Agile / Scrum is uneven | Ben runs a short internal workshop for Ana and Dana | Ben | Ana and Dana to 3 |
| Data and reporting is strong | Chen documents the reporting process so others can step in | Chen | Written guide in place |
Tip
A skill that only one person can do is often a bigger problem than a skill everybody is mediocre at. Before you look at averages, scan each column for a single 3 or 4.

### How to use a skills matrix in project management
A skills matrix is most useful when you connect it to decisions you already make about people, risk and time.

#### Staffing projects and allocating resources
When you assign work, match the skills each work package needs with the people who rate 3 or 4, and deliberately pair a 4 with a 1 or 2 where you have time for development. Our guide to [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) explains how to assign people across tasks and projects, and [project resources](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-resources/) covers the wider mix of people, equipment and budget.

#### Capacity planning
A skills matrix tells you who can do the work; capacity planning tells you whether they have the hours. A team with spare hours can still be blocked if the one person who can do budgeting is fully booked. Read [capacity planning in project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/), or [Agile capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-capacity-planning/) if you plan in sprints. If a key person is overloaded, [resource leveling](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-leveling/) can rebalance the schedule.

#### Managing key-person risk
Single points of failure are project risks like any other. Record them with a cause, an owner and a response such as cross-training, documentation or a backup supplier.

#### Building cross-functional Agile teams
Agile teams aim to hold every skill needed to deliver, and many encourage T-shaped people with depth in one area and working knowledge of others. A skills matrix shows who should learn what next. Our guides to [what an Agile team is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/what-is-an-agile-team/) and [Scrum team roles](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-team-roles/) explain the structures.

#### Planning training and hiring
Gaps that pairing cannot close become training or recruitment needs. Prioritise by the distance between the rating a person has and the rating the role needs. For project managers, our [project management certification](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-certification/) guide covers formal routes to raise a rating.

### Skills matrix vs competency matrix vs RACI matrix
These documents are easy to confuse because several of them are grids of people against something. Each answers a different question:
| Document | Question it answers | Rows and columns | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Skills matrix | Who can do what, and how well? | People against skills, with proficiency ratings | Staffing, cross-training, key-person risk |
| Competency matrix | Does each person meet the expected standard for their role? | Roles or people against competencies (skills, knowledge and behaviours) and expected levels | Career frameworks, performance and promotion |
| RACI matrix | Who is responsible for what on this project? | Tasks or deliverables against people or roles, marked R, A, C or I | Clarifying ownership and decisions |
| Training plan | Who will learn what, how, by when and at what cost? | Learners against training activities, dates and costs | Acting on the gaps a skills matrix finds |
A common sequence is: build the skills matrix, staff the project, then record who does what in a [RACI matrix template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/). Our [RACI matrix guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/raci-matrix/) explains responsibility assignment in detail. For broader capability gaps across processes or tools, a [gap analysis template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/gap-analysis-template/) is the better fit.

### Common skills matrix mistakes
- **Too many skills.** Forty columns produce a matrix nobody updates. Keep to the skills that affect delivery and split the team into several matrices if needed.
- **Vague skills.** "Communication" is hard to rate consistently; "Running steering group meetings" is easy.
- **No agreed definitions.** Without them, confident people rate high and modest people rate low, and the matrix measures personality rather than skill.
- **Using it as a performance score.** If ratings feed directly into pay or appraisals, people will inflate them. Say up front that the matrix is a planning tool.
- **Building it once.** Skills change after every project and course. A matrix that is a year old is a guess.
- **No actions.** A matrix without a training plan, staffing change or hiring decision attached is just a chart.

### Tips for keeping ratings accurate and fair
- **Ask for evidence.** For any 3 or 4, ask for a recent example: a schedule they built, a risk review they ran, a report they own.
- **Consider an interest column.** Some teams add a simple yes or no for whether the person wants to develop a skill. It helps you pick who to train; it is an optional addition, not part of the template.
- **Mind privacy.** Ratings are personal information. Share the full matrix only with people who need it and keep the team view to averages and coverage if that suits your culture. Check your organisation's HR policy.
- **Refresh it twice a year,** and after major training, a reorganisation, or a project's [lessons learned](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lessons-learned/) review. The expert version's Revision history tab is there to log each update.
If you run people-related projects such as onboarding or a reorganisation, our guide to [HR project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/hr-project-management/) shows how a skills matrix fits alongside the rest of the plan.

### Related templates and guides
A skills matrix is usually the first step in a short chain of documents: the matrix finds the gaps, a training plan closes them, and the project plan and RACI matrix put the right people on the right work. ### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a skills matrix template?**
A skills matrix template is a ready-made grid of team members against the skills your team needs, with a proficiency rating in each cell. This one uses a 0 to 4 scale and calculates each person's average and a team average for every skill.

**Q: Is this skills matrix template free?**
Yes. The skills matrix template is free to download in Google Sheets, Excel and PDF, at beginner, advanced and expert level, with no sign-up.

**Q: How do I create a skills matrix in Excel or Google Sheets?**
List team members in the first column and skills across the top, agree a rating scale, enter a rating for every person and skill, then add AVERAGE formulas for each person and each skill. The template already has this structure, so you only need to rename the skills and enter your team.

**Q: What rating scale should a skills matrix use?**
Use four or five clearly defined levels. This template uses 0 = none, 1 = learning, 2 = can do with help, 3 = independent and 4 = can teach others. The exact scale matters less than everyone using the same definitions.

**Q: What is the difference between a skills matrix and a competency matrix?**
A skills matrix records how well people can perform specific skills. A competency matrix is usually broader, covering skills, knowledge and behaviours against the level expected for each role.

**Q: What is a skills gap matrix?**
A skills gap matrix compares the rating each person or role needs with the rating they have today. You can use this template that way by adding a target rating for each skill and comparing it with the actual ratings.

**Q: Who should fill in the skills matrix?**
Team members self-assess first, then their manager reviews the ratings with them, ideally with input from a peer.

**Q: How often should a skills matrix be updated?**
About every six months, and after major training, a team change or the end of a large project.

**Q: How do I find single points of failure in a skills matrix?**
Count how many people rate 3 or 4 in each skill column, for example with a COUNTIF formula. Any skill where only one person (or nobody) is independent is a key-person risk that needs cross-training or a backup.

**Q: Can I use the skills matrix template for project staffing?**
Yes. Match the skills each task needs with the people rated 3 or 4, and check availability with [resource allocation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/resource-allocation/) and capacity planning.

**Q: Is a skills matrix the same as a RACI matrix?**
No. A skills matrix shows capability: who can do the work. A [RACI matrix](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/raci-matrix-template/) shows responsibility: who does the work, who is accountable, and who is consulted or informed.

**Q: What is the difference between the beginner, advanced and expert skills matrix template?**
The beginner version has one tab with four skill columns and a team average row. The advanced version has all six skills plus personal and team averages. The expert version adds an Instructions tab and a Revision history tab.

Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable: a checklist for good user stories.

**Q: Who writes stories in the user story template?**
Usually the Product Owner, collaborating with the team and stakeholders.

**Q: How big should a story in the user story template be?**
Small enough to finish within one Sprint; split larger stories.

**Q: Can I use the user story template in Jira?**
Yes. Copy the format into Jira issues, or import the user stories from the spreadsheet.

**Q: What is the difference between a user story template and a use case template?**
A user story is a short statement of need; a use case describes detailed interaction steps.

### How to use the work breakdown structure template

2. Break it into major deliverables or phases at level 2, then into work packages at level 3.
3. Give each element a unique WBS code, a short description and a single owner.
4. Estimate effort and cost for each work package; the top row totals them.
5. Check the **100% rule**: the children of each element add up to all of its work, and nothing more.

# Free Work Package Template with Example (Excel, Sheets, PDF)

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-package-template/
Section: Free templates
Summary: Free work package template for Excel, Google Sheets and PDF: scope, deliverables, tasks, owner, effort, cost, dates, dependencies and acceptance criteria.


## Free Work Package Template with Example (Excel, Sheets, PDF)
This free work package template describes one piece of project work on a single page: its WBS code, scope, deliverables, tasks, owner, effort and cost estimates, dates, dependencies, risks, acceptance criteria and sign-off. Download it in Google Sheets, Excel or PDF at beginner, advanced or expert level, with a worked example and no sign-up.
- Published 2 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- Google Sheets · Excel · PDF

### Key takeaways
- A work package is the lowest level of the work breakdown structure: a chunk of work small enough to assign to one owner, estimate, schedule and accept.
- The template has 13 fields, from WBS code and scope to acceptance criteria and approval, on one tab with a filled-in example.
- Use one tab per work package and copy the WBS code and name straight from your WBS so everything traces back.
- A common rule of thumb is 8 to 80 hours of effort, or no longer than one reporting period.
- Testable acceptance criteria and a named approver make progress objective and stop arguments at hand-over.

### What is a work package?
A **work package** is the work at the lowest level of a [work breakdown structure (WBS)](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/). PMI's PMBOK Guide defines it as the work defined at the lowest level of the WBS for which cost and duration are estimated and managed. In practice it is a clearly bounded piece of work with one owner, a defined output and an agreed way to check that it is finished.
The WBS shows the whole hierarchy of deliverables. The work package description, which is what this template produces, zooms in on one box of that hierarchy and records everything the person doing the work needs to know: what is in scope, what they must deliver, roughly how long it will take and cost, what it depends on and how it will be accepted.
The work package owner (often a team lead, team manager or supplier) is accountable for delivering it. The project manager agrees and authorises the package, and an approver signs it off. On larger projects, work package descriptions are often collected into a **WBS dictionary**, which holds the detail for every element of the WBS.
For the concept in more depth, read our guide to [what a work package is](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-package/).

### What is in this work package template
The template has one tab, **Work package**, laid out as a simple form with two columns: **Field** and **Details**. It comes with a worked example (a customer login feature) that you overwrite with your own work. Here is a live preview:
Work package
| Field | Details |
| --- | --- |
| WBS code | 1.4.2 |
| Work package name | Customer login and password reset |
| Owner | Tech lead |
| Description / scope | Build login, logout and password reset using single sign-on. |
| Deliverables | Working feature in test environment; unit tests; release notes. |
| Tasks | Design screens; build API; integrate SSO; write tests. |
Sample rows are examples: replace them with your own.
- **Work package**: Field, Details

#### The 13 fields
- **WBS code**: the reference from your WBS, for example 1.4.2, so the package traces back to its parent deliverable.
- **Work package name**: a short noun phrase that matches the WBS entry.
- **Owner**: the one person accountable for delivering the package.
- **Description / scope**: what the work covers, and where useful what it does not cover.
- **Deliverables**: the outputs that will exist when the package is finished.
- **Tasks**: the main activities needed to produce the deliverables.
- **Effort estimate (days)**: the total working days of effort, not elapsed time.
- **Cost estimate ($)**: labour plus any materials, equipment or services. Change the currency label if you work in another currency.
- **Start / finish**: the planned dates from your schedule.
- **Dependencies**: other packages, projects, suppliers or decisions this work relies on.
- **Acceptance criteria**: the testable conditions the output must meet to be accepted.
- **Risks**: the main threats to the package; record them in full in your risk register.
- **Approved by / date**: who signed the package off and when.
Blank rows sit under the fields so you can add your own, such as budget code, tolerances or reporting frequency.

#### Beginner, advanced and expert versions
| Version | What you get | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Beginner | The one-tab work package form with all 13 fields, the worked example and extra blank rows | Quick, informal hand-overs |
| Advanced | The same one-tab, 13-field form: the standard version | Most projects |
| Expert | The work package form plus an Instructions tab (steps and tips) and a Revision history tab for version, date, author, changes and approver | Projects with formal sign-off, audits or a PMO |
Because the work package is a two-column form, the beginner and advanced versions contain the same fields. The template has no status column, so the expert version does not include a dashboard; track the status of all your packages in your WBS or [project schedule template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-schedule-template/) instead. The PDF is a print-ready copy for kick-off meetings and sign-off.

### How to fill in the work package template
1. **Start from the WBS.** Copy the WBS code and name from your [work breakdown structure template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-breakdown-structure-template/). Write one work package description for each lowest-level element that needs one.
2. **Agree the owner.** Name one person, not a team. Talk to them before you write the rest; they know the work better than you do.
3. **Describe the scope.** Say what is included and, if there is room for doubt, what is excluded. Check it against your [project scope](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-scope/) statement.
4. **List the deliverables**, then the **tasks** that produce them. Keep tasks at a level the owner recognises; the detailed task list can live in their own plan.
5. **Estimate effort and cost** with the owner, using past data or [effort estimation](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/effort-estimation/) techniques such as analogous or three-point estimates.
6. **Add dates and dependencies** from your schedule, and record anything outside the owner's control that the package relies on.
7. **Write acceptance criteria and risks.** Make every criterion testable, and copy the significant risks to your [risk register template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/risk-register-template/).
8. **Agree and approve.** Walk through the package with the owner and approver, then record the approval and date before work starts. After that, changes go through [change control](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/change-control/).

#### Spreadsheet tips
- **Duplicate the tab for each package** and rename it with the WBS code (1.4.2, 1.4.3) so the tabs sort in WBS order.
- **Use the same units everywhere.** If effort is in days on one package, do not switch to hours on the next; the totals will not add up.
- **Roll the numbers up.** Copy each package's effort and cost into your [project cost estimate template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/project-cost-estimate-template/) so the project budget is built from the bottom up.
- **Keep it to one page.** If it runs longer, the package is probably too big.

### Work package example
The template's sample package is a software feature, but the same structure works for a construction stage, a marketing campaign asset or a training course. Here is the example with a note on why each entry works:
| Field | Example entry | Why it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WBS code / name | 1.4.2 Customer login and password reset | Traces directly to the WBS |
| Owner | Tech lead | One accountable role (use a named person in your own file) |
| Description / scope | Build login, logout and password reset using single sign-on | Short and specific about what is in scope |
| Deliverables | Working feature in test environment; unit tests; release notes | Outputs you can see and check |
| Tasks | Design screens; build API; integrate SSO; write tests | Enough to estimate, not a full task list |
| Effort / cost | 12 days; 9,600 | Estimated by the person doing the work |
| Start / finish | 2 Mar 2026 / 17 Mar 2026 | About two weeks: easy to track |
| Dependencies | SSO service (IT security project) | Names an outside dependency to watch |
| Acceptance criteria | All login test cases pass; security review approved | Objective pass or fail tests |
| Risks | SSO delay | Linked to the dependency; add it to the risk register |
The approval field is blank in the example: fill it in only when the owner and approver have agreed the package.

### How big should a work package be?
There is no fixed standard, but two rules of thumb are widely used:
- **The 8/80 rule:** a package should take at least 8 hours and no more than 80 hours of effort. Smaller than that and you are managing tasks, not packages; larger and it becomes hard to estimate and track.
- **The reporting period rule:** a package should be no longer than one reporting period (often two weeks or a month), so every status report shows it as either started, finished or clearly late.
Treat these as guides rather than limits; a large engineering project may hand a contractor packages of several hundred hours.

#### Signs you should split or merge a package
- **Split it** if it has more than one owner, several unrelated deliverables, an estimate nobody is confident about or a duration longer than your reporting cycle.
- **Merge it** if it is only a few hours of work, has no separate deliverable or would be tracked by the same person alongside its neighbour anyway.
Tip
If you cannot write clear acceptance criteria for a package, it is usually a sign that its scope is not yet defined well enough to start.

### Writing good acceptance criteria
Acceptance criteria turn "done" into something you can check. Write them so that the owner and approver would reach the same answer independently:
| Weak criterion | Stronger criterion |
| --- | --- |
| Login works well | All 24 login test cases pass in the test environment |
| Secure | Security review completed and approved by the IT security lead |
| Documentation provided | Release notes published to the team wiki and reviewed by support |
| Wall built to standard | Wall inspected and signed off against drawing A-104 by the site engineer |
Criteria can cover functionality, quality standards, documentation and approvals. For quality-critical work, link the criteria to your quality plan, and see our guide to [project deliverables](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-deliverables/) for how deliverables are accepted at project level.

### Work packages in PRINCE2
In PRINCE2 a work package is a formal management product. Under the Controlling a Stage process, the project manager authorises a work package; under Managing Product Delivery, the team manager accepts it, agreeing that it is understood and achievable, and then delivers it. The team manager reports progress through **checkpoint reports** at the frequency set in the work package.
Our template covers the core of a work package description. To use it as a PRINCE2 work package, add rows for:
- **Product descriptions** for the products to be delivered, including quality criteria
- **Tolerances** for time and cost (and scope, risk or quality if you use them)
- **Reporting arrangements**, including checkpoint frequency
- **Constraints** and **techniques or quality methods** to be used
- **Problem handling and escalation**: how issues and risks are raised to the project manager
Your organisation may have its own PRINCE2 format; if so, follow it.

### Work packages in Agile projects
Agile teams rarely use the term work package, but the idea still applies. An [epic](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-epics/) or feature plays a similar role: a bounded chunk of value, broken down into smaller items and accepted against agreed criteria and the [Definition of Done](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/definition-of-done/).
Where Agile and traditional teams work together, for example when a supplier delivers a fixed piece of work into an Agile programme, a one-page work package is a useful contract between them. For planning the Agile side, use our [agile project plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/agile-project-plan-template/).

### Work package vs task vs WBS
| Term | What it is | Typical size | Owned by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WBS | The full hierarchy of project deliverables | The whole project | Project manager |
| Control account | A management point that groups work packages for cost and schedule control, used in earned value management | Several packages | Control account manager |
| Planning package | A WBS element with known scope but not yet detailed into work packages | Varies | Project manager |
| Work package | The lowest WBS level, estimated, scheduled and accepted as a unit | Days to a few weeks | Work package owner |
| Task or activity | A step needed to complete a work package | Hours to days | Team member |
Work packages describe **what** is delivered; tasks describe **how** it gets done. Tasks are what you sequence and resource in the schedule. Our guide to [project tasks and activities](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-tasks-and-activities/) explains the difference in more detail, and [earned value management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/earned-value-management/) shows how control accounts and work packages are used to measure performance.

### Common work package mistakes
- **No single owner.** "Development team" is not an owner; name one person.
- **Scope that overlaps another package.** Every piece of work should belong to exactly one package, or it gets done twice or not at all.
- **Estimates made without the owner.** People commit to estimates they helped make.
- **Vague acceptance criteria.** "To the client's satisfaction" invites disputes.
- **Hidden dependencies.** If the package relies on another team, supplier or decision, write it down and track it in the schedule. See [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/).
- **Starting before approval.** Without sign-off you have no agreed baseline to measure against.
- **Never updating it.** If scope, dates or estimates change, record the change and a new version rather than editing silently.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a work package template?**
A work package template is a ready-made form for describing one work package: its WBS code, scope, deliverables, tasks, owner, effort and cost estimates, dates, dependencies, risks, acceptance criteria and approval.

**Q: Is this work package template free?**
Yes. The work package template is free to download in Google Sheets, Excel and PDF, at beginner, advanced and expert level, with no sign-up.

**Q: What should a work package include?**
At minimum: a WBS code and name, an owner, a description of scope, deliverables, effort and cost estimates, start and finish dates, dependencies and acceptance criteria. Many organisations add risks, tolerances, reporting arrangements and an approval record.

**Q: How big should a work package be?**
A common rule of thumb is 8 to 80 hours of effort, or no longer than one reporting period. Larger projects sometimes use bigger packages; the test is whether one owner can estimate, track and deliver it.

**Q: What is the difference between a work package and a task?**
A work package defines a deliverable-focused chunk of work at the lowest level of the WBS. Tasks or activities are the steps needed to complete it, and are what you schedule in detail.

**Q: What is the difference between a work package and a WBS?**
The [WBS](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) is the whole hierarchy of project deliverables. A work package is one element at the bottom of that hierarchy, described in detail.

**Q: Who owns a work package?**
One named work package owner, such as a team lead, team manager or supplier, is accountable for delivering it. The project manager agrees and authorises it.

**Q: Can I use this template as a PRINCE2 work package?**
Yes, as a starting point. Add rows for product descriptions, tolerances, reporting arrangements, constraints, quality methods and problem handling, or follow your organisation's PRINCE2 format.

**Q: Is a work package the same as a WBS dictionary entry?**
They are closely related. A WBS dictionary holds the detailed description of every WBS element; a work package description like this one is the entry for one lowest-level element, often with extra detail for authorising the work.

**Q: Can I use work packages in Agile projects?**
Yes. Epics or features play a similar role, and a work package is useful when a supplier or traditional team delivers a defined piece of work into an Agile project.

**Q: How do I manage several work packages in one file?**
Duplicate the Work package tab for each package and name each tab with its WBS code. Track the status of all packages in your WBS or project schedule.

**Q: What goes in the acceptance criteria of a work package?**
Clear, testable conditions the output must meet, such as tests passed, standards met, documents delivered and approvals obtained.

**Q: What is the difference between the beginner, advanced and expert work package template?**
All three contain the same one-tab, 13-field work package form with a worked example. The expert version adds an Instructions tab with steps and tips and a Revision history tab for recording versions and approvals.

# Free Workflow Template for Business Processes (Sheets, Excel, PDF)

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/workflow-template/
Section: Free templates
Summary: Free workflow template to map business process steps, owners, inputs, outputs, tools, handoffs and time. Download for Google Sheets, Excel or PDF.


## Free Workflow Template for Business Processes (Sheets, Excel, PDF)
A workflow template maps a business process step by step: who does what, with which inputs and tools, what they hand over and how long it takes. It is the first step to standardising or improving a process.
- Published 2 September 2026
- Google Sheets · Excel · PDF

### Workflow Template preview
Workflow
| Step | Activity | Owner / role | Input | Output | Tool | Hand off to | Time (hours) | Approval needed? | Pain points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Receive request | Coordinator | Request form | Logged request | Wrike | Team lead | 0.25 | No |  |
| 2 | Assess and prioritise | Team lead | Logged request | Priority and owner | Wrike | Specialist | 0.50 | No | Requests missing details |
| 3 | Do the work | Specialist | Brief | Draft | Design tools | Reviewer | 6 | No |  |
| 4 | Review | Reviewer | Draft | Feedback or approval | Proofing tool | Specialist / requester | 1 | Yes | Feedback scattered across email |
| 5 | Deliver and close | Coordinator | Approved output | Delivered output | Wrike | Requester | 0.25 | No |  |
Sample rows are examples: replace them with your own.

### What's included
- Step-by-step workflow with owners, inputs, outputs, tools, handoffs, time, approvals and pain points
- **Workflow**: Step, Activity, Owner / role, Input, Output, Tool, Hand off to, Time (hours), Approval needed?, Pain points

### How to use the workflow template
1. Pick one process and define where it starts and ends.
2. List each step in order with its owner, inputs and outputs.
3. Record tools, handoffs, time and approvals.
4. Note pain points, delays and rework.
5. Redesign the workflow: remove steps, automate handoffs, and agree the new process with the team.

### Tips for getting the most from it
- Map the process as it really works, not as documented.
- Count handoffs: each one adds delay.
- Use a [swimlane diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/swimlane-diagram/) to visualise roles.
- Automate repeatable steps in your work management tool.

- [Swimlane Diagram: What It Is, Examples and How to Make One](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/swimlane-diagram/)
- [Value Stream Mapping: How to Map and Improve Your Process](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/value-stream-mapping/)
- [Lean Project Management: Principles and Practices](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/lean-project-management/)

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is a workflow template?**
A workflow template is a table or diagram that maps the steps, owners, inputs, outputs and handoffs of a repeatable process.

**Q: Is this workflow template free?**
Yes. The workflow template is free in Google Sheets, Excel and PDF.

**Q: How do I create a workflow with the workflow template?**
Define the start and end, list each step with its owner, inputs and outputs, then record handoffs, time and approvals.

**Q: Can I use the workflow template for business process management?**
Yes. It is a simple business process management template for documenting and improving processes.

**Q: What is the difference between a workflow template and a swimlane diagram?**
A workflow template lists steps in a table; a [swimlane diagram](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/swimlane-diagram/) shows the same flow visually by role.

**Q: Can I use the workflow template for a project management workflow?**
Yes. Map how requests become projects, how work is reviewed and how it is delivered.

**Q: How do I find bottlenecks with a workflow template?**
Look for steps with long waiting times, many handoffs or frequent rework.

**Q: Can a workflow template be automated?**
Yes. Once mapped, many steps can be automated in tools such as Wrike or monday.com.

**Q: What is a good level of detail for a workflow template?**
Five to fifteen steps is usually enough; break larger processes into sub-processes.

**Q: Can I download the workflow template as a PDF?**
Yes. Use the PDF button for a printable workflow template.

**Q: What is the difference between the beginner, advanced and expert workflow template?**
The beginner workflow template keeps only the essential columns on one tab; the advanced version is the full template with every tab, dropdown and formula; the expert version adds a live dashboard, instructions and revision history.

### What is project management software?
**Project management software** is an application that helps a team plan, organise and track the work needed to deliver a project. It typically combines task lists, schedules such as Gantt charts or timelines, Kanban boards, file sharing, comments, automation and reports, so everyone works from one shared, up-to-date plan instead of separate spreadsheets and email threads.
Modern tools range from simple Kanban boards to full work management platforms that also cover resource planning, request intake, approvals, portfolios and business intelligence. Most now include AI features as well. Our guide to [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software/) explains the categories and core features in more detail.

### Why Wrike ranks first
Wrike scores 10 out of 10 in three of our seven categories: feature depth, planning and resource management, and scalability. No other tool in the review matches that combination. In one platform it brings together interactive Gantt charts with dependencies, board, table and calendar views, dashboards, workload and resource planning, cross-project portfolio views, request forms, automation, built-in proofing and approvals, and AI. That makes it a strong fit for PMOs, marketing and creative teams, professional services firms and any organisation that wants a single system of record rather than separate task, resource, proofing and reporting tools.
The trade-offs are the ones you would expect from a deep platform. Wrike takes longer to set up and learn than Trello or monday.com, and its most advanced resource, budgeting and BI features sit on the quote-based Pinnacle and Apex plans. On Wrike's pricing page (checked 7 October 2026), the Free plan covers basic task management with board and table views, Team costs $10 per user per month billed annually for 2 to 15 users and adds interactive Gantt charts, shareable dashboards and AI, and Business costs $25 per user per month for 5 to 200 users. A 14-day free trial is available with no credit card.

| Jira | Free for up to 10 users | Standard about $7.91 | Premium about $14.54 | Monthly small-team rates; per-user price falls as teams grow |
| Microsoft Planner | Basic Planner included in Microsoft 365 | Plan 1 $10 | Planner and Project Plan 3 $30 | Microsoft 365 Copilot is a $30 add-on |
| Notion | Free plan | Plus $10 per member | Business $20 per member | Notion AI included from Business |
| Trello | Free for up to 10 collaborators per Workspace | Standard $5 | Premium $10 | Enterprise $17.50 for 50+ seats |
| Basecamp | Free for 1 project | Freelancer $25/month flat | Studio $59, Pro $99/month flat | Unlimited $299/month billed annually; no per-user fees |
Look beyond the headline price. Seat minimums, the plan you will need in 12 months, paid add-ons such as AI, and whether guests and viewers are free can change the total cost a great deal. Basecamp's flat pricing, for example, is often the cheapest option for a large team with a handful of projects, while per-user tools are usually cheaper for very small teams.

### Best tools for your team

#### Best for small teams and start-ups
Small teams usually value speed of setup and price. [Trello](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/) is the simplest place to start, [ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/) gives the most features for the money, [Basecamp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/basecamp/) suits client-facing teams that want flat pricing, and [Notion](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/notion/) works well when documentation matters as much as tasks. If you expect to need Gantt charts and dashboards soon, Wrike's Team plan (2 to 15 users) gives you room to grow into a full platform.

#### Best for mid-sized organisations and enterprises
Wrike and Smartsheet score highest for scalability and enterprise readiness, with monday.com and Asana close behind. Choose Wrike if you want resource management, portfolios, request intake and approvals in one platform; Smartsheet if your organisation thinks in spreadsheets; and monday.com or Asana if fast adoption across many departments is the priority.

#### Best for Agile and software teams
Jira leads our Agile category, with backlogs, sprints, issue tracking and deep developer integrations; it is free for up to 10 users. ClickUp is a strong second for teams that want sprints alongside docs and dashboards, and Wrike supports Agile boards for organisations running Agile and traditional projects side by side. Our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/) covers sprint tooling in more depth.

#### Best for marketing and creative teams
Wrike's built-in proofing, request forms and approvals make it a natural fit for marketing and creative teams that handle many requests and review cycles. monday.com and Asana are good alternatives when ease of adoption matters most; Asana includes approvals and proofing on its Advanced plan.

#### Best for Microsoft 365 organisations
Microsoft Planner is included in many Microsoft 365 subscriptions and works inside Teams and Outlook. Since Microsoft folded Project for the web into Planner in 2025, its premium plans add Gantt timelines, dependencies, sprints and goals. Teams that need deeper resource, portfolio or approval features often pair Microsoft 365 with a specialist platform such as Wrike or Smartsheet.

### Best free project management tools
Nine of the ten tools in our review offer a free plan or include a free tier, but the limits vary (checked 7 October 2026):
- **Jira:** free for up to 10 users, with Scrum and Kanban boards, backlogs and basic automation. One of the most capable free plans for software teams.
- **ClickUp Free Forever:** unlimited members and tasks with limited storage and automations; Gantt charts and dashboards are available as trials.
- **Trello Free:** up to 10 collaborators and 10 boards per Workspace, with unlimited cards. Ideal for simple Kanban.
- **Wrike Free:** basic task and project management with board and table views, plus web, desktop and mobile apps; a good starting point if you expect to grow into Wrike's paid plans.
- **Notion Free:** aimed at individuals; block limits apply once a workspace has two or more members.
- **Asana Personal:** unlimited tasks and projects for one or two people.
- **monday.com Free:** up to 2 seats and 3 boards.
- **Basecamp Free:** one project with 1 GB of storage.
- **Microsoft Planner (basic):** no stand-alone free plan, but included with many Microsoft 365 business subscriptions.
Smartsheet has no free plan but offers a 30-day trial. Free plans are best for trying a tool or running small projects; most teams that run several projects at once move to a paid plan within months.

### How to choose a project management tool
Rankings narrow the field; a short, structured evaluation makes the decision. This is the process we recommend:
1. **Describe the work.** List your project types, team size, methods (Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban or hybrid) and who outside the team needs access, such as clients or executives.
2. **Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves.** For example: Gantt charts with dependencies, resource and workload planning, sprints, proofing, request forms, time tracking or Microsoft 365 integration. Our guide to [project management software features](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-software-features/) explains each one.
3. **Match the tool to your method.** Predictive projects need schedules, dependencies and baselines; Agile teams need backlogs and sprints; continuous work needs Kanban boards and WIP limits. Read about [Gantt chart software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart-software/) if scheduling is central.
4. **Decide how much you want in one place.** If you need projects, resources, portfolios and approvals together, an all-in-one platform such as Wrike avoids stitching several tools together. If you only need task boards, a simpler tool will be adopted faster.
5. **Check security and administration with IT.** Single sign-on, permissions, audit logs, data residency and the integrations you already rely on.
6. **Work out the total cost for a year,** including seat minimums, guests, add-ons such as AI, and the plan you are likely to need as you grow.
7. **Trial two or three tools on a real project** for two weeks, with the people who will use them daily, and agree who will own templates, training and adoption.

### AI in project management tools
All ten tools now offer AI features, from summarising comment threads and drafting updates to creating automations in plain language and running AI agents. How AI is sold differs: Wrike, monday.com, Asana, Jira and Trello include AI allowances in paid plans; Notion includes Notion AI from its Business plan; ClickUp sells its AI as a paid add-on; and Microsoft 365 Copilot is a separate add-on that also works in Planner. Check the allowance on the plan you are considering, as several vendors meter AI with monthly credits.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What is the best project management tool in 2026?**
Our top pick is Wrike (9.4/10) for growing teams and enterprises, because it combines projects, resources, portfolios, approvals and reporting in one platform. monday.com (9.1) is best for ease of use, Asana (9.0) for cross-team coordination, ClickUp (8.9) for value and Jira for software teams.

**Q: What is the best free project management tool?**
It depends on your team. Trello is the simplest free option, ClickUp's Free Forever plan includes the most features, Jira is free for up to 10 users and suits software teams, and Wrike's Free plan is a good start if you expect to grow into a full work management platform.

**Q: What is the cheapest project management software?**
Among per-user tools, Trello Standard ($5 per user/month billed annually) and ClickUp Unlimited ($7) are the cheapest paid plans in our review. Basecamp's flat pricing, from $25 a month for the whole account, can be cheapest for larger teams with few projects.

**Q: Which project management tool is easiest to use?**
Trello scores highest for ease of use in our review (10/10), followed by monday.com, Asana and Basecamp (9/10).

**Q: Which project management tool is best for small teams?**
Trello, ClickUp, Basecamp and Notion suit small teams. Wrike's Team plan, for 2 to 15 users, is a good choice if the team needs Gantt charts and dashboards.

**Q: Which project management tool is best for enterprises?**
Wrike and Smartsheet score highest for scalability and enterprise readiness (10/10), with monday.com, Asana and Jira close behind. Wrike is particularly strong for PMOs that need portfolio and resource management.

**Q: Which project management tool is best for Agile and Scrum?**
Jira is the standard for software teams and leads our Agile category. ClickUp also supports sprints with sprint points and reporting, and Wrike supports Agile boards alongside traditional project plans; see our [Scrum guide](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/what-is-scrum/).

**Q: What features should project management software have?**
Most teams need task management with owners and due dates, at least two views (such as Kanban and Gantt or timeline), file sharing and comments, notifications, basic automation and reporting. Growing teams add resource and workload management, portfolios, request forms, approvals, time tracking and single sign-on.

**Q: Do I need Gantt charts in a project management tool?**
If your projects have dependencies and fixed dates, yes. Wrike, monday.com, Asana, ClickUp, Smartsheet and Microsoft Planner's premium plans include Gantt or timeline views, usually on paid plans. See our guide to the [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/).

**Q: Is Microsoft Project still available?**
Microsoft retired Project for the web in 2025 and moved its scheduling features into Microsoft Planner's premium plans. Microsoft's pricing pages also stated that Project Online would be retired on 30 September 2026. The Project desktop app remains available with Planner and Project Plan 3. See our [Microsoft Planner review](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/microsoft-planner/).

**Q: Can I use a spreadsheet instead of project management software?**
For small projects, yes: our free [project management templates](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/) cover plans, schedules, RACI matrices and risk registers. Software becomes worthwhile when several people need to update the same plan in real time or you run many projects at once.

**Q: Can project management software use AI?**
Yes. All ten tools offer AI features, from summaries and writing help to automation and AI agents. Some include AI allowances in their plans; ClickUp and Microsoft 365 Copilot sell AI as add-ons.

### What AI does in project management
- **Summaries and status updates:** condense tasks, comments and meetings into updates for stakeholders; see [project status reports](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
- **Intake and triage:** read requests, fill in fields, set priority and route work to the right team.
- **Planning help:** break goals into tasks, suggest schedules and draft [work breakdown structures](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/).
- **Risk spotting:** flag overdue, blocked or at-risk work early; see [project risk management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-risk-management/).
- **Agents:** carry out multi-step processes such as assigning, chasing and updating work, with people approving key actions.
- **Search and Q&A:** answer questions across projects, docs and connected apps.

### How to choose an AI project management tool
1. Start from the jobs you want AI to do (summaries, triage, scheduling, reporting, agents).
2. Check which plan includes those features and how credits or actions are counted.
3. Confirm security: data residency, training use, retention and admin controls.
4. Pilot with one team on real projects for a month and measure time saved.
5. Keep people in charge of decisions; let AI propose and automate the routine.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are AI project management tools?**
AI project management tools are platforms that use artificial intelligence to plan, summarise, prioritise and automate project work, from drafting status updates to running agents that triage requests or flag risks.

**Q: What is the best AI project management tool in 2026?**
Our top pick is **Wrike**, because its agents and Copilot work on full project, resource and portfolio data. monday.com is easiest for AI agents, ClickUp offers the widest choice of AI models, and Jira is best for software teams.

**Q: Are AI project management tools free?**
Some AI features are free or included: Smartsheet and Jira include AI in paid plans, Wrike includes AI Essentials from its Team plan, and monday.com gives accounts a monthly credit allowance. Advanced agents usually cost extra.

**Q: How much do AI project management tools cost?**
Pricing varies: some include AI in the plan, others charge per user (ClickUp's AI add-on starts around $9/user/month) or by credits and actions. Always check credit limits, because heavy agent use can raise costs.

**Q: Can AI project management tools replace project managers?**
No. AI project management tools automate coordination such as summaries, triage and reminders, but people still set goals, make trade-offs, manage stakeholders and own decisions. See our guide to the [future of project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/is-agile-the-future-of-project-management/).

**Q: What can AI agents do in AI project management tools?**
Agents in AI project management tools can triage requests, assign work, draft status reports, summarise meetings, flag risks and update fields, usually with a person approving important actions.

**Q: Are AI project management tools secure?**
Leading AI project management tools offer enterprise controls, but check where data is processed, whether it is used for training, data retention and admin controls before enabling AI for sensitive projects.

**Q: Which AI project management tool is best for small teams?**
For small teams, ClickUp, monday.com or Motion are good AI project management tools; Wrike's Team plan includes AI Essentials if you expect to grow.

**Q: Which AI project management tool is best for enterprises?**
Wrike, Smartsheet, Asana, monday.com and Jira all offer enterprise-grade AI project management tools with admin and security controls; Wrike and Smartsheet are strongest for PMOs.

**Q: What is MCP in AI project management tools?**
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets external AI assistants securely read and act on data in AI project management tools; Wrike, monday.com and Smartsheet offer MCP servers.

**Q: How do I choose between AI project management tools?**
List the jobs you want AI to do, check which plan includes them, test with real projects, compare credit limits and confirm security requirements before rolling AI project management tools out widely.

# Asana Review 2026: Is It Worth It?

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/

## Asana Review 2026: Is It Worth It?
Asana is a work management platform for planning, tracking and coordinating work across teams, and for connecting that work to company goals. Its biggest strengths are a clean, approachable interface and dependable cross-team task management; the main trade-offs are that portfolios, goals, workload and approvals sit on the higher-priced Advanced plan, and that its resource and financial controls are lighter than those of more PMO-oriented tools. This review covers pricing, project views, goals and portfolios, automation, AI, integrations, ease of use, reporting, security and overall value.
- Published 5 September 2026
- Last updated 7 October 2026
- Pricing and Capterra rating checked 7 October 2026

### Asana review: quick verdict
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Best for | Organisations coordinating work across many teams that want easy-to-adopt task management connected to goals and portfolios |
| Less suitable for | Teams that need detailed budgeting, financial tracking or complex resource planning, and very small teams wanting advanced features for free |
| Our overall score | **9.0/10**, ranked #3 in our [top 10 project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) |

| Capterra rating | 4.5/5 from 13,731 reviews (checked 7 October 2026) |
| G2 rating | 4.4/5 from 14,008 reviews (checked 5 October 2026) |
Asana is a polished, reliable work management tool that is at its best when many teams need to coordinate work and see how it ladders up to goals. It is one of the easier platforms in its class to roll out. The trade-offs: the free plan is now limited to two users, the features that make Asana distinctive (goals, portfolios, workload, approvals) start on Advanced, AI usage is metered, and reviewers regularly complain about notification volume and occasional performance problems.
