### What Is Asana?
Asana is cloud-based work management software. It combines task and project management (lists, boards, timelines, dependencies) with the layers organisations need above individual projects: portfolios that group related projects, goals that track objectives, workload views that show who has capacity, and automation and AI that move work along.
Organisations typically use it for:
- **Cross-team projects**, such as product launches that involve marketing, product, sales and support
- **Campaign and content planning**, with calendars, timelines and approvals
- **Request intake**, using forms that turn each submission into a task
- **Goals and OKRs**, linking company objectives to the projects that deliver them
- **Portfolio reporting**, giving leaders a status view across many projects
- **Repeatable operational workflows**, run with templates, rules and AI workflows
Asana runs in the browser, as desktop apps for Mac and Windows, and as mobile apps for iOS and Android. Underneath, Asana describes its data model as the **Work Graph**: tasks, projects, portfolios and goals are connected, so a task completed in one project can update progress on a portfolio or goal. That connection, rather than any single view, is what separates Asana from a simple to-do list app.

### Who Owns Asana?
Asana, Inc. was founded in 2008 by Dustin Moskovitz, a Facebook co-founder, and Justin Rosenstein, and is based in San Francisco. It listed on the New York Stock Exchange (ticker ASAN) through a direct listing in September 2020. Dan Rogers became chief executive in July 2025, succeeding Moskovitz.
For buyers, the practical point is that Asana is a mature, publicly listed company that publishes its financial results, rather than an early-stage start-up.

### How Does Asana Work?
Asana organises work in a hierarchy that is easy to grasp:
- **Organisation (or workspace)** is the company-wide account.
- **Teams** group people, such as Marketing, IT or a client team.
- **Projects** hold the work for an initiative or an ongoing process, split into **sections** (for example Backlog, This week, Done).
- **Tasks and subtasks** are the individual pieces of work. Each task has one **assignee**, a **due date**, optional **collaborators**, **custom fields** and **dependencies**.
- **Portfolios** group projects so managers can monitor them together, and **goals** sit above portfolios and projects to show what the work is for.
- **My Tasks**, **Inbox** and **dashboards** give each person and manager their own view of what matters.
A distinctive detail is that one task can live in several projects at once, so a legal review task can sit in both a launch project and the legal team's intake project without being duplicated.
A typical workflow looks like this:
**Request submitted via form → task created in the right project → rule assigns an owner → work tracked in list, board or timeline → status update posted → portfolio and goal progress update**
For example, a regional sales team submits a request for a customer case study. Asana creates a task in the content team's project, a rule assigns it to the content lead and sets a due date, the writer moves it across the board from Drafting to In review, and the marketing director sees it reflected in the quarterly campaign portfolio without asking for an update.

### Asana Key Features

#### Tasks, Subtasks and My Tasks
Tasks are the core building block. Each one can have subtasks, a single assignee, start and due dates, dependencies, custom fields, attachments, comments and collaborators who follow the task. Recurring tasks handle routine work, and **My Tasks** gathers everything assigned to a person across all projects into one prioritised list.
Asana's one-assignee-per-task rule is deliberate: every piece of work has exactly one owner. This is a real advantage once several teams contribute to the same project, because it removes the "I thought you were doing that" problem. Teams used to shared ownership sometimes find it restrictive, and work around it with subtasks or collaborators.

#### Project Views: List, Board and Calendar
Every project can be switched between views. **List view** groups tasks into sections and can sum, average or count numeric columns. **Board view** works as a [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/): tasks are cards that you drag between columns such as New, In progress and Complete, with due dates, assignees and subtasks visible on each card. **Calendar view** shows tasks by day, and dragging a task to a new day changes its due date.
All three views are available on the free Personal plan, so they are a reasonable way to try Asana. If you are not ready for software, our [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) follows the same idea.

#### Timeline and Gantt Views
Timeline and [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) views are included from the Starter plan. The timeline shows where work starts, ends and overlaps, lets you mark tasks that cannot start until another finishes, and updates dates when you drag tasks. The Gantt view gives a high-level picture of ongoing and upcoming work, shows [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) as chains, and lets you set a target schedule and compare progress against it.
For campaign plans, launches and most cross-team projects this is more than enough. Asana's product pages do not describe critical path analysis, so teams running heavily date-driven schedules where the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/) matters should test this carefully in the trial, or look at a more scheduling-focused tool.

#### Custom Fields and Templates
Custom fields (from Starter) add the data your team needs to every task, such as priority, channel, budget, effort or client. They power filtering, sorting, rules and dashboards, so a consistent set of fields is what turns a collection of projects into something you can report on. Custom project and task templates, plus workflow bundles that package fields, rules and sections together, help larger organisations keep projects consistent.

#### Forms
Forms (from Starter) give stakeholders a structured way to request work. You choose question types such as text, numbers, dates and drop-downs, can require attachments like a brief or PDF, and each submission creates a task in the connected project. Forms can be kept internal, shared publicly by link or embedded on a website. On Advanced, **forms branching** shows different follow-up questions depending on earlier answers.
For example, a creative team can use one form to collect design requests, including deadline, channel, campaign and brief, with a rule that assigns each request to the right designer. Our [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) shows the information worth collecting.

#### Rules and Automation
Rules pair a trigger with an action: when a form is submitted, a task is added to a project, a due date approaches or a task is unblocked, Asana can reassign work, move the task, request an approval, send a reminder, post to Slack or create a Jira issue. All paid plans include unlimited automations, and Asana provides a library of ready-made rules.
Rules are quick to set up, which is one of Asana's advantages over more configurable tools. For multi-step or judgement-based workflows, Asana points teams to AI Studio, covered below.

#### Goals
Goals (on Advanced) are one of Asana's most distinctive features. You can set company, team and individual goals, label them as objectives or key results, break them into sub-goals, and choose quarter, half-year, annual or custom timeframes. Progress can be updated manually or automatically from connected projects and sub-goals, or from data in Salesforce, and owners mark goals as on track, at risk or off track.
For organisations that manage by OKRs, this closes the gap between strategy documents and day-to-day work: people can see which goal a project supports. It only works if teams keep projects up to date, so the value depends on discipline as much as the software. Our [OKR template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/okr-template/) is a useful starting point for defining goals before you build them in Asana.

#### Portfolios
Portfolios (unlimited on Advanced) group related projects so leaders can see the health of every initiative on one screen, drill into details, track metrics such as time and budget, and publish status updates to stakeholders. They are the main way Asana supports [managing multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) and [portfolio management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/agile/agile-portfolio-management/), and they are the reason many mid-sized organisations move from Starter to Advanced.

#### Approvals and Proofing
On Advanced, approval tasks let reviewers approve, request changes or reject work, and proofing lets them comment directly on images and creative assets inside Asana. For marketing and creative teams this keeps feedback attached to the asset rather than scattered across email, although specialist review tools still go further for video and complex proofing.

### Asana AI Features
AI is now central to how Asana positions itself; it describes its approach as "agentic work management", with people and AI agents working from the same plan. There are three main components, all available on paid plans but not on Personal.

#### AI Teammates
AI Teammates are prebuilt AI agents that work inside Asana projects. Asana says there are more than 30, for areas such as marketing, PMO and strategic operations, IT, and industry teams, and you can build custom ones by defining the role, giving guidance, adding skills and granting access. Examples on Asana's site include a content writer that drafts a launch brief from a project, an insights analyst that pulls a monthly portfolio status report, and a capacity planner that shows who would be overloaded by a new initiative.
Teammates follow existing permissions: they only see projects and work the account allows, and admins control who can create and change them. They are best understood as configurable assistants working on structured data, not autonomous employees; someone still needs to own the process and check the output.

#### Asana Dash
Asana describes Dash as an AI "chief of staff" that produces briefs such as a morning summary of priorities, surfaces next steps from meetings, Slack and email, and routes work to the right AI Teammate.

#### AI Studio
AI Studio is Asana's no-code builder for AI-powered workflows. You choose a trigger, such as a new task or form submission, and describe in plain language what should happen; Asana generates a workflow that can include AI steps, branches, human input and approvals. Typical uses are intake and triage, classification and routing, checking requests for missing information, and drafting content or reports.

#### AI Allowances and Data
AI use is metered. According to Asana's pricing comparison, AI Teammates and Dash include 5 requests per user per month, capped at 50 requests per account on Starter and Advanced and 250 on Enterprise, and AI Studio includes a monthly credit allowance per billing account that rises by plan (50,000, 75,000 and 200,000 credits). Extra usage is available as prepaid packs at $0.50 per request or pay-as-you-go at $0.60 per request, with a monthly spend cap. Heavy AI users should model these costs before committing.
Asana also offers AI connectors, including MCP support, so tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Microsoft Copilot can work with Asana data. Asana states that its AI partners do not use customer data to train their models.

### Asana Collaboration Features
Collaboration happens on the work itself: comments and @mentions on tasks, collaborators who follow a task, file attachments, project messages, status updates and an Inbox that collects updates on everything you follow. Paid plans include unlimited free guests, which makes it straightforward to work with clients, agencies and freelancers in the same projects.
This is where Asana is strongest. Third-party reviewers consistently praise how easy it is to see who is doing what across teams. The downside is notification volume: on Capterra, "overwhelming and excessive notifications" is one of the most discussed topics, with 51% of the 712 reviews mentioning it negative. Agree notification settings, @mention habits and when to use status updates early in a rollout. Our guide to [project communication management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-communication-management/) covers the principles.

### Asana Reporting and Dashboards
Reporting works at two levels. **Project and team dashboards**, from Starter, use chart templates to show tasks by status, overdue work, completion trends and custom-field totals such as cost or revenue, and you can click any chart to see the underlying tasks. **Portfolio and goal reporting**, on Advanced, rolls status, progress, time and budget up across many projects, with a status update builder for written [project status reports](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
Advanced also adds Tableau and Power BI integrations for organisations that want Asana data in their BI tools. Capterra reviewers rate Asana's visibility highly: comprehensive real-time project tracking is one of the most discussed topics, with 93% of 1,976 mentions positive. Asana's reporting is easy to use but less configurable than dedicated BI or PMO tools, so teams with complex financial reporting may still export data.

### Workload, Capacity and Time Tracking
Workload (on Advanced) shows each person's assigned effort across projects in a portfolio, using task counts, hours or points, against a weekly limit you set. Managers can drag tasks to reassign or reschedule them and filter by person or project. Advanced also adds time tracking that compares estimated with actual effort.
Enterprise extends this to **universal resource management**, balancing workloads across the whole organisation, and **capacity planning**, where managers allocate people to workstreams by percentage or hours, filter by skills and titles, and view utilisation by person or project. A **Timesheets & Budgets** add-on is available for Starter, Advanced and Enterprise.
This is solid for most teams, but it is lighter than tools built around resource and financial control, which is the main reason our rankings place Wrike ahead for PMOs and professional services firms.

### Asana Integrations
Asana says even its free plan includes more than 100 free integrations. Its directory includes **Slack**, **Microsoft Teams**, **Outlook**, **Google Workspace** (Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Sheets), **Zoom**, **HubSpot**, **Jira**, **GitHub**, **GitLab**, **Azure DevOps**, **Figma**, **Canva**, **Dropbox**, **Box**, **Zapier** and **Make**. **Salesforce**, **Tableau** and **Power BI** integrations are listed as Advanced features.
The Jira and GitHub integrations let developers stay in their tools while other teams follow the same work in Asana, and a public API supports custom integrations. The main constraint is that some of the most useful business integrations, such as Salesforce, require Advanced.

### Asana Ease of Use

#### Initial Setup
A small team can create a project from a template, invite colleagues and be working the same day. Setting Asana up for a whole organisation takes more thought: agreeing team and project structures, standard custom fields, templates, forms, rules, portfolios and goals. Without that, teams build projects in different ways and reporting becomes unreliable.

#### Learning Curve
Basic task management is easy to learn, and Asana's ease-of-use score on Capterra (4.4/5) reflects that. Reviewers frequently describe the interface as clean and intuitive. Advanced features, such as portfolios, goals, workload, rules and AI Studio, take more training, mainly because they depend on consistent habits across teams rather than on technical complexity.

#### Interface
The interface is uncluttered and consistent, with a clear separation between personal views (Home, My Tasks, Inbox) and shared project spaces. On the other side, very large projects can feel slow, and some reviewers report loading delays and glitches, especially in the desktop app: Capterra's "performance and reliability concerns" topic is 60% negative across 490 reviews. Asana is one of the easier tools in its class, but it is not effortless at scale.

### Asana Mobile and Desktop Apps
The iOS and Android apps let you capture tasks by voice, photograph notes and turn them into text, triage your inbox by archiving or creating follow-up tasks, receive push notifications, and comment, attach files and @mention colleagues. The Mac and Windows desktop apps add quick access to priority tasks from the menu bar or system tray and a focus timer that pauses notifications.
The mobile apps are frequently praised in Capterra reviews, though planning, portfolio setup and reporting are better done on a larger screen.

### Asana Pricing
Asana's published plans are below. Prices are per user per month in US dollars; the annual price is the monthly equivalent billed annually, and Asana says annual billing saves up to 18%.
| Plan | Billed annually | Billed monthly | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Personal | $0 | $0 | One or two people managing personal projects |
| Starter | $10.99/user/month | $13.49/user/month | Teams that need timelines, dashboards, forms and automation |
| Advanced | $24.99/user/month | $30.49/user/month | Organisations needing goals, portfolios, workload and approvals |
| Enterprise | Contact sales | Contact sales | Large organisations needing SAML, SCIM and capacity planning |
| Enterprise+ | Contact sales | Contact sales | Regulated organisations needing advanced compliance and governance |
Add-ons include **Timesheets & Budgets** (Starter, Advanced and Enterprise), **Compliance management** and **Permissions management** (Enterprise only), and extra AI usage. Pricing checked on Asana's pricing page on 7 October 2026; always confirm before buying, as prices may vary by region.

#### Asana Personal (Free) Plan
Personal costs $0 and includes unlimited tasks and projects, list, board and calendar views, status updates, time tracking through integrations and more than 100 free integrations. It is now limited to **2 seats per project and team**, so it suits individuals, freelancers and pairs rather than teams. Timelines, dashboards, forms, rules and AI all require a paid plan.

#### Asana Starter Plan
At $10.99 per user/month billed annually ($13.49 monthly), Starter adds timeline and Gantt views, reporting dashboards, unlimited automations, forms, custom fields and templates, unlimited free guests, AI Teammates, Dash and AI Studio. Asana states there are no user seat limits on paid plans. This is the right starting point for most small and mid-sized teams that run projects together.

#### Asana Advanced Plan
At $24.99 per user/month billed annually ($30.49 monthly), Advanced adds unlimited portfolios, goals, resource management (workload within a portfolio), approvals and proofing, forms branching, time tracking with estimated versus actual effort, scaled security, and Salesforce, Tableau and Power BI integrations. Because these are the features that set Asana apart, many organisations that choose Asana for strategic alignment will need Advanced.

#### Asana Enterprise and Enterprise+
Enterprise is quote-based and adds SAML single sign-on, SCIM user provisioning, universal resource management, capacity planning, service accounts, view-only licences, guest invitation permissions and project admin controls. Enterprise+ adds security, compliance and governance features such as SIEM integrations, data residency, audit logs and managed workspaces. These plans are aimed at large and regulated organisations, not small businesses.

#### Asana Free Trial
Asana's help centre says you can start a free Advanced trial from the pricing page, with no credit card required and no commitment to pay. The pricing page does not state the trial length; Asana's referral page describes a 30-day trial. Use the trial to rebuild one real cross-team project, ideally with a portfolio and a goal attached, so you can judge whether Advanced is worth the step up from Starter.

### Asana Pros and Cons

##### Pros
- Clean, intuitive interface that most people learn quickly
- Excellent cross-team task coordination and clear ownership
- Goals connect daily work to company objectives
- Portfolios give leaders a status view across projects
- Unlimited free guests on paid plans
- Unlimited automations and forms from Starter
- Mature integrations, including Slack, Teams, Jira and Salesforce
- Capable AI Teammates and AI Studio included on paid plans
- Strong security credentials and enterprise controls

##### Cons
- Free plan now limited to 2 seats per project and team
- Goals, portfolios, workload and approvals require Advanced
- Lighter resource and financial management than Wrike
- Notification volume can be high without careful settings
- Some reviewers report slow loading and glitches
- AI usage is metered, with paid top-ups
- Permissions not granular enough for some large or sensitive projects
- One assignee per task can feel restrictive
- No critical path analysis described for its Gantt view
This matches what users report: people value Asana's clarity, visibility and ease of adoption, while notifications, performance and the cost of unlocking its higher-level features are the most common drawbacks.

Ratings and review themes as published on G2 and Capterra on 5 October 2026; summarised in our own words. Visit the links above for full, verified user reviews.
On **Capterra**, Asana is rated **4.5/5 from 13,731 reviews**, with sub-scores of **4.4 for ease of use**, **4.4 for features**, **4.4 for value for money** and **4.3 for customer service** (checked 7 October 2026). On **G2**, it is rated **4.4/5 from 14,008 reviews** (checked 5 October 2026). The themes below summarise these third-party reviews in our own words, not Asana's testimonials.
**Positive themes.** Reviewers most often praise real-time visibility into projects and workloads, clear organisation of tasks and priorities, easy deadline tracking, the clean interface and the mobile apps. In Capterra's topic summaries, comprehensive real-time project tracking (93% positive), versatile work organisation (92% positive) and effective deadline management (91% positive) stand out.
**Negative themes.** The most common complaints are excessive notifications, especially by email (51% negative), performance and reliability problems such as slow loading and occasional crashes (60% negative), permissions that are not granular enough for sensitive projects, useful features limited to paid plans, and the need for external tools for accounting and invoicing.
Many recent reviews on Capterra are labelled as vendor-referred with an incentive offered. Both Capterra and G2 label these, and filtering for non-incentivised reviews from companies of your size gives a more cautious picture than the headline score.

### Asana Customer Support
Asana provides a help centre with guides and troubleshooting articles, the Asana Academy for courses and webinars, and an active community forum. Larger and Enterprise customers can get more hands-on onboarding and customer success support, and Asana works with partners for complex rollouts.
Support experience in third-party reviews is generally positive but not outstanding: Capterra's customer service sub-score of 4.3/5 is Asana's lowest sub-score. For an organisation-wide rollout, ask during the sales process exactly what onboarding and support response times your plan includes.

### Asana Security
Asana's trust centre lists SOC 2 Type 2 and SOC 3 reports, ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701 certifications, CSA STAR Level 1, and support for HIPAA (opt-in) and GDPR compliance. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest, and Enterprise Key Management lets customers use their own encryption key. Data residency options include data centres in Europe, Australia and Japan.
Identity and admin controls scale by plan: SAML single sign-on and SCIM provisioning are Enterprise features, and Enterprise+ adds SIEM integrations, audit logs and managed workspaces, with Compliance and Permissions management sold as Enterprise add-ons. Note that a minority of Capterra reviewers criticise permissions controls as too coarse, so test your sharing model in the trial. Confirm current certifications and their scope in Asana's trust documentation as part of procurement.

### Asana for Different Types of Teams

#### Asana for Marketing and Creative Teams
Marketing is one of Asana's strongest fits: campaign timelines and calendars, forms for creative requests, approvals and proofing on Advanced, and portfolios for a campaign programme. AI Teammates for briefs and content add further value.

#### Asana for Operations Teams and PMOs
Operations teams benefit from forms, rules, templates and AI Studio for repeatable processes. A [PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) gets portfolios, goals and status updates on Advanced, and capacity planning on Enterprise. PMOs that need detailed budgets, baselines and financial tracking may find Asana lighter than they need.

#### Asana for Agencies
Agencies can run each client in its own team or project, invite clients as free guests, and track delivery in portfolios. Time tracking and budgets need Advanced or the Timesheets & Budgets add-on, and invoicing still requires separate tools.

#### Asana for Software and Product Teams
Product managers often use Asana for roadmaps, launches and cross-functional coordination, with the Jira or GitHub integrations linking to engineering work. Asana supports boards and sprint-style projects, but teams that need backlogs, story points and Agile reporting will find dedicated tools stronger; see our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/).

#### Asana for Small Businesses
Asana is easy for a small business to adopt, and Starter is reasonably priced for a team that needs timelines, forms and automation. The free plan's two-seat limit means most teams will pay from the start, and the most distinctive features require Advanced.

#### Asana for Enterprises
Large organisations benefit from goals, portfolios, unlimited guests, enterprise identity controls, data residency and strong security credentials. Asana's ease of use helps adoption across non-technical departments, which is often the hardest part of [enterprise project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/enterprise-project-management/).

- Teams needing detailed budgeting and financial tracking
- Very small teams on a tight budget needing advanced features

### Is Asana Worth It?
Asana is likely worth it if you:
- Coordinate work across several teams or departments.
- Want a tool most people can learn quickly, including non-technical staff.
- Manage by goals or OKRs and want work linked to them.
- Need portfolio-level status reporting for leaders.
- Work with many clients, freelancers or partners who can join as free guests.
- Want built-in AI agents and AI workflows inside your project tool.
It may not be worth it if:
- You need detailed budgeting, financial tracking or advanced resource planning.
- You rely on critical path scheduling for complex, date-driven projects.
- You are a small team that wants advanced features on a free plan.
- You only need simple boards for a handful of projects.
- Your organisation needs dedicated Agile tooling for software development.
Our verdict: Asana's strength is making cross-team work clear and easy to follow, and its goals and portfolios connect that work to strategy better than most tools. Its limitations are the price of unlocking those features on Advanced and lighter resource and financial control than PMO-focused platforms. That balance is why it ranks third in our [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) review.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Asana good project management software?**
Yes, for the right team. Asana offers clean, dependable task and project management, strong cross-team visibility, and goals and portfolios that link work to strategy, and it rates 4.5/5 on Capterra. The trade-offs are that key features require the Advanced plan and its resource and financial tools are lighter than PMO-focused platforms.

**Q: Is Asana free?**
Yes. Asana's Personal plan costs $0 and includes unlimited tasks and projects, list, board and calendar views, and more than 100 integrations. It is limited to 2 seats per project and team, and timelines, dashboards, forms, rules and AI require a paid plan.

**Q: How much does Asana cost?**
Asana costs $0 on Personal, $10.99 per user/month on Starter and $24.99 per user/month on Advanced when billed annually, or $13.49 and $30.49 billed monthly. Enterprise and Enterprise+ are priced on request (checked 7 October 2026).

**Q: Does Asana have a free trial?**
Yes. Asana lets you start a free Advanced trial from its pricing page, and its help centre states that no credit card is required. Use the trial to run a real cross-team project with a portfolio and goal attached.

**Q: Is Asana easy to use?**
Mostly. Asana is one of the easier work management tools to learn, with a 4.4/5 ease-of-use score on Capterra. Basic task management is quick to pick up; portfolios, goals, workload, rules and AI Studio need more planning and consistent habits across teams.

**Q: What is Asana best used for?**
Asana is best for coordinating cross-team projects, marketing and creative workflows, request intake, goal and OKR tracking, portfolio status reporting and repeatable operational processes.

**Q: Is Asana better than monday.com?**
Neither is universally better. Asana suits teams that want structured task management linked to goals and portfolios; monday.com suits teams that want a more visual, highly customisable interface. See our [Asana vs monday.com comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/monday-vs-asana/).

**Q: Is Asana better than ClickUp?**
It depends on priorities. Asana is cleaner and easier to adopt across non-technical teams; ClickUp offers more features, including docs and whiteboards, at lower prices but with more complexity. See our [Asana vs ClickUp comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/asana-vs-clickup/).

**Q: Does Asana have Gantt charts?**
Yes. Timeline and Gantt views are included from the Starter plan. They show dependencies, let you drag tasks to reschedule, and allow you to compare progress against a target schedule.

**Q: Does Asana have Kanban boards?**
Yes. Asana's board view works as a Kanban board, with tasks as cards that move between columns, and it is available on every plan, including the free Personal plan.

**Q: Does Asana have AI?**
Yes. Paid plans include AI Teammates (prebuilt and custom AI agents), Asana Dash (AI briefs and next steps) and AI Studio (no-code AI workflows). Usage is metered by plan, with extra requests available as prepaid packs or pay-as-you-go.

**Q: Can Asana track goals and OKRs?**
Yes. Goals on the Advanced plan let you set company, team and individual goals, break them into sub-goals, and update progress automatically from connected projects or Salesforce data.

**Q: What are the main disadvantages of Asana?**
The main disadvantages are that goals, portfolios, workload and approvals require Advanced, the free plan is limited to two seats, notifications can be excessive, some users report performance issues, and its resource and financial management is lighter than PMO-focused tools.

**Q: Does Asana integrate with Slack and Microsoft Teams?**
Yes. Asana integrates with Slack and Microsoft Teams, along with Outlook, Google Workspace, Zoom, Jira, GitHub, Figma and Zapier. Salesforce, Tableau and Power BI integrations are listed on the Advanced plan.

**Q: Is Asana suitable for small businesses?**
Yes, especially on Starter, which adds timelines, forms, dashboards and automation at a moderate price. The free plan's two-seat limit means most small teams will pay from the start, and the most distinctive features require Advanced.

Prices were checked on vendors' pricing pages and ratings on G2 and Capterra on 5 October 2026; both change often, so confirm on the vendor's site before buying. # Basecamp Review 2026: Is It Worth It?

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/basecamp/
Section: Project management software reviews
Summary: Our Basecamp review covers features, flat pricing, Hill Charts, Card Table, AI agents, pros and cons, and whether Basecamp is worth it in 2026.


## Basecamp Review 2026: Is It Worth It?
Basecamp is 37signals' project management and team communication tool. Each project gets one page that brings together a message board, to-do lists, a Kanban-style Card Table, a schedule, group chat, automatic check-ins, and docs and files. Its biggest strengths are simplicity, calm communication, easy client access and flat pricing with no per-user fees. The trade-off is deliberate: it leaves out Gantt dependencies, resource management and deep reporting. This review covers pricing, project organisation, collaboration, client work, AI, integrations, ease of use, reporting, security and overall value.
- Published 9 September 2026
- Last updated 7 October 2026
- Pricing and Capterra rating checked 7 October 2026

### Basecamp review: quick verdict
|  |  |
| --- | --- |

Basecamp is one of the easiest project tools to adopt, and it is very good at one thing: keeping a project's discussions, tasks, files and decisions in one calm, well-organised place that clients can join. Flat pricing makes it unusually economical for larger teams and agencies. The trade-offs are real: project controls and reporting are limited, most plans cap the number of active projects, reviewers regularly complain about notification volume, and there are no built-in AI features yet, only access for AI agents you run yourself.

### What Is Basecamp?
Basecamp is web-based project management and team communication software. Instead of organising work around tasks and views, it organises everything around **projects**: each project has a single page, and the tools on that page replace the email threads, chat apps and shared drives that projects usually spill into.
Teams typically use it for:
- **Client projects**, with clients invited into the same space and shown only what they should see
- **Internal projects**, from a website redesign to an office move
- **Team and company announcements**, using a company-wide HQ and team spaces
- **Recurring check-ins** that replace routine status meetings
- **File and document sharing**, kept next to the discussions about them
- **Simple Kanban workflows**, such as support requests or content production
Basecamp runs in the browser and as apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, and people can reply to many notifications by email. The current version, which 37signals presents as "Basecamp 5 is all new for 2026", added a new home screen, faster search with live filtering, My Bar, subtasks, account-wide Everything pages, voice notes and an editor with tables and Markdown.
Basecamp is not a portfolio or resource management platform, and it does not try to be one: its premise is that most teams need clearer communication more than more project controls.

### Who Owns Basecamp?
Basecamp is made by 37signals, a privately held company based in Chicago. 37signals was founded in 1999 by Jason Fried, Carlos Segura and Ernest Kim, and launched Basecamp in 2004 as its first commercial product. The company renamed itself Basecamp in 2014 and returned to the 37signals name in 2022. Jeff Bezos has held a minority stake through Bezos Expeditions since 2006. 37signals also makes the HEY email service.
For buyers, the practical point is that Basecamp is a mature, independent product with more than two decades of history, not a start-up that may change direction after its next funding round.

### How Does Basecamp Work?
Basecamp has a deliberately flat structure:
- **Account**: your company's Basecamp, with a company **HQ** for organisation-wide announcements and optional **team** spaces.
- **Projects**: one per client job, initiative or ongoing process. Each has its own people and its own page.
- **Tools on the project page**: Message Board, To-dos, Card Table, Docs & Files, Campfire chat, Schedule and Automatic Check-ins. You switch on only the tools a project needs.
- **To-do lists and to-dos**: each to-do can have assignees, a due date, notes, files and, since Basecamp 5, subtasks. To-do lists can be tracked on a **Hill Chart**.
- **Cross-project views**: Home, My Bar, Everything pages, the Lineup timeline, the global calendar, Activity and Reports show what is happening across all projects.
A typical workflow for an agency client project looks like this:
**Kick-off message → to-do lists for each phase → client invited and given selected updates → Hill Chart shows progress → files and approvals discussed in comments → project archived**
For example, a design agency opens a project for a new client website, posts a kick-off message with the brief, creates to-do lists for discovery, design and build, and invites the client. Internal discussions stay hidden, while the client sees milestone updates and the designs they need to approve. Each Friday an automatic check-in asks the team what they worked on, and the account manager reads the Hill Chart rather than calling a status meeting.

### Basecamp Key Features

#### Message Boards
The Message Board is where announcements, proposals and longer discussions live. Each message has its own threaded comments, messages can be organised by category, and people can "boost" a post with a short reaction instead of adding another comment. The aim is to replace internal email: decisions are recorded on the project, where anyone joining later can find them.
It is especially valuable for teams that work asynchronously, encouraging fewer, more considered updates instead of a stream of chat.

#### To-dos and Subtasks
To-do lists hold the actual work. Each to-do can have one or more assignees, a due date, notes, files and comments, and lists can be grouped and reordered. Basecamp 5 added **subtasks** on to-dos and **loose to-dos** that are not tied to a list.
This is enough for most client and internal projects, but it is intentionally simple. There are no task dependencies, no custom fields, no priorities beyond the order of the list, and only one level of subtasks. On Capterra, limited advanced features, including subtasks and customisation, are a recurring complaint from teams that have outgrown Basecamp. If you need a lightweight starting point outside software, our [to-do list template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/to-do-list-template/) follows the same idea.

#### Card Table (Kanban)
The Card Table is Basecamp's version of a [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/), which 37signals says is designed for reactive work. New ideas, requests and bugs arrive in a **Triage** section; approved cards are dragged into workflow columns that you name, colour and reorder for each project; a **Not Now** column keeps ideas you do not want to lose; an optional **On Hold** section within a column holds blocked cards; and finished cards go to **Done**. You can watch particular columns, so an editor is notified only when something reaches Editing.
It works well for request intake, bug triage, content pipelines and simple support queues, and each card has its own page for discussion and files. 37signals does not describe WIP limits, swimlanes or flow metrics, so teams practising Kanban more formally will find it basic.

#### Hill Charts
Hill Charts are Basecamp's most distinctive feature. Every piece of work is treated as having two phases: going **uphill**, while the team is still figuring out the approach and resolving unknowns, and going **downhill**, once the approach is clear and it is a matter of execution. You switch on Hill Chart tracking for a to-do list, and a dot for that list appears on the hill.
Dots are moved by hand: someone clicks Update and drags each dot to where they judge the work to be. Basecamp is explicit that this status is human judgement, not something calculated from completed tasks. Every update is saved as a snapshot in the project history, can carry commentary, and can be commented on, so managers can see what is moving and what is stuck without asking. A dot that never leaves the uphill side is often a sign that the work needs to be broken down differently.
Hill Charts are useful for creative and software work where "80% of tasks done" says little about real progress, but they depend on honest updates and do not replace a schedule.

#### Schedule, Calendar and the Lineup
Each project has a schedule for deadlines and events, and Basecamp 5 adds full-screen global and project calendars that can be subscribed to from other calendar apps. The **Lineup** shows every project as a bar on a timeline by its start and end dates, giving a simple overview of what is running when.
What Basecamp does not offer is a real [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/): there are no [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/), no [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/), no baselines and no automatic rescheduling. Third-party integrations such as Ganttify and Le Gantt can add Gantt views, but teams whose projects depend on detailed scheduling should treat this as a core limitation rather than a missing extra.

#### Campfire Chat and Pings
Every project has a **Campfire**, a real-time group chat for quick questions and casual conversation, with file sharing and image previews. **Pings** are private one-to-one or small-group messages. Notifications and pings appear in the "New For You" sidebar alongside your work, and **Bubble Up** lets you snooze an item so it resurfaces later.
For many small teams, this replaces a separate chat tool; organisations that live in Slack or Microsoft Teams will find no native connection to either.

#### Automatic Check-ins
Automatic Check-ins ask a recurring question on a schedule, such as "What did you work on this week?" every Friday or "What are you planning today?" each morning, and collect everyone's answers in one place. They replace routine status meetings, and the history becomes a record of how a project unfolded.

#### Docs & Files
Docs & Files holds documents written in Basecamp, uploaded files and links to cloud files such as Google Docs, Figma or Dropbox, organised in folders. Basecamp 5 merged its two layouts into one with better previews and filtering, and the new editor supports basic tables, Markdown and colour-coded code blocks. Each item has its own comment thread, so feedback stays with the file.
This is convenient, but it is not a full document management system. On Capterra, "fragmented updates and version challenges" is a frequent topic, with 41% of the 547 reviews mentioning it negative, so agree early where final versions live.

#### My Bar, Everything Views and Search
**My Bar** gives each person instant access to their assignments, upcoming events, bookmarks and private notes from any screen. **Everything** pages gather all messages, documents, comments or files from across every project, and the **Activity** view shows what happened, grouped by topic and filterable by project or person. Basecamp 5 also brought faster search with live filtering on most screens, a universal menu for jumping anywhere, and keyboard shortcuts revealed by pressing Shift.
These address a long-standing criticism: in Capterra reviews, navigation and finding older items are recurring frustrations. Test search on a realistic amount of data during the trial.

### Basecamp AI Features
Basecamp has taken a different route on AI from most of its competitors. As of October 2026, it has **no built-in AI features** such as AI summaries, writing assistance or AI-generated tasks. In a March 2026 post, 37signals co-owner David Heinemeier Hansson wrote that the company had experimented with many AI features but did not ship them because it is "not that easy to make something that's actually good", and that the team keeps working on native AI features.
Instead, Basecamp has made itself **agent-accessible**. 37signals launched a revamped API, a new command-line interface (CLI) and a skill that teaches AI agents how to use them. Its agents page lists official SDKs for Go, Ruby, TypeScript, Swift and Kotlin, names agents such as Claude, Codex, OpenCode and Cursor, and states that "your agents can do anything in Basecamp you can do". The pricing page lists "Bring your own AI agents", CLI access and skills, and ChatGPT and Claude AI connectors on its plans, with full MCP support marked as coming soon.
In practice, this means technical teams can automate Basecamp work with the AI tools they already use: an agent could create to-dos from meeting notes, summarise a week of messages or move cards on a Card Table. Non-technical buyers who want AI built into the interface should look elsewhere for now. 37signals publishes little detail on permission scoping for agents, which appear to act with the access of the person who connects them, so decide who may connect agents before rolling this out. Our guide to [AI project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/ai-project-management-tools/) shows how other tools approach AI.

### Basecamp Collaboration and Client Features
Collaboration is Basecamp's core purpose. Messages, comments, chat, check-ins, files and to-dos all live on the project they belong to, and every item has its own discussion thread, so context is not lost in email. Basecamp's own approach is to notify only the people who need to know, and you choose who is notified when you post.
Client work is where Basecamp stands out. You can invite clients into a project and decide which messages, to-dos, files and events they can see, keeping internal discussion separate. Because paid plans have no per-user fees (Freelancer allows up to 20 users), adding clients does not increase the bill. For agencies and consultancies this is often the deciding factor. Our [communication plan template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/communication-plan-template/) can help agree what clients see and when.
The downside, according to users, is notification volume. On Capterra, "overwhelming and inconsistent notifications" is one of the most discussed topics, with 48% of the 664 reviews mentioning it negative. Agree notification settings and when to use messages, chat and pings early in a rollout.

### Basecamp Reporting and Visibility
Basecamp's **Reports** give high-level overviews such as what is overdue, what is assigned to whom and what is coming up, across projects. Combined with the **Activity** feed, **Hill Chart** history, the **Lineup** and **Everything** views, a manager can usually see what is happening without asking for a [status report](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-status-report/).
This is operational visibility, not analytics. There are no custom dashboards, charts, budget tracking, time-based utilisation reports or portfolio rollups. Capterra reviewers cite limited reporting as a recurring drawback, and third-party tools such as Bridge24 and ClicData exist largely to fill that gap. Teams that need to report formally on many projects, or to [manage multiple projects](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/managing-multiple-projects/) against budgets and capacity, will find Basecamp too light.

### Basecamp Integrations
Basecamp's integrations directory lists 93 third-party integrations in nine categories (checked 7 October 2026). They include time tracking and invoicing tools such as **Harvest**, **Toggl**, **Clockify** and **Everhour**; reporting and planning tools such as **Ganttify**, **Le Gantt** and **Bridge24**; automation platforms such as **Zapier**, **Zoho Flow** and **Unito**; plus customer support, software development and mobile tools. These are built by third parties, not by 37signals, so check each one's quality and pricing separately.
Basecamp lists basic **time tracking** on every plan, the revamped API and SDKs support custom integrations, and the CLI and agent skills open Basecamp to AI tools. What is missing compared with mainstream rivals is a native integration with **Slack** or **Microsoft Teams**; 37signals positions Campfire and pings as the replacement, and third-party connectors exist if you need them.

### Basecamp Ease of Use

#### Initial Setup
Setup takes minutes rather than days: create a project, pick the tools it needs, invite people and start posting. There are no custom fields to design and no workflow engine to build, which is exactly why many teams choose it.

#### Learning Curve
Basecamp is one of the easiest project tools to learn, and Capterra's ease-of-use sub-score of 4.3/5 reflects that. Reviewers repeatedly describe the interface as simple and say it reduces email and meetings. Non-technical staff and clients usually need little or no training, which matters when you are inviting people from outside the organisation.

#### Interface
The interface is calm and consistent: every project looks the same, and every item has the same comment and notification controls. The downsides are the flip side of that simplicity. Some teams want more structure than to-do lists offer, finding older items can be cumbersome, and Capterra's "occasional glitches and slowdowns" topic is 51% negative across 384 reviews. Accounts with many active projects benefit most from Basecamp 5's improved search, My Bar and Everything views.

### Basecamp Mobile and Desktop Apps
Basecamp has apps for iOS and Android and desktop apps for Mac and Windows, and the Card Table and other project tools are available in the mobile apps. You can also reply to many notifications by email, which makes it easy for occasional participants, including clients, to take part without logging in.
Reviewers generally find the mobile apps practical for keeping up with messages, chat and to-dos. 37signals does not advertise offline working, so treat mobile as a companion for staying in touch rather than a full replacement for the web app.

### Basecamp Pricing
Basecamp charges a flat monthly price per account rather than per user, with plans differing mainly by the number of active projects and storage. Archived or deleted projects do not count towards the active-project limit.
| Plan | Price | Active projects | Users | Storage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | 1 | 5 max | 1 GB |
| Freelancer | $25/month | Up to 3 | Up to 20 | 5 GB |
| Studio | $59/month | Up to 10 | Unlimited | 25 GB |
| Pro | $99/month | Up to 25 | Unlimited | 100 GB |
| Unlimited | $299/month, billed annually | Unlimited | Unlimited | 1,000 GB |
Freelancer, Studio and Pro list annual billing as an option but do not show a separate annual price, so confirm the billing period at checkout. Paid plans include 24/7/365 support, and 37signals offers 10% off for registered US 501(c)(3) non-profits and free accounts for K-12 schools and universities for class work. You can cancel any time without a contract, but you cannot downgrade from a paid plan to Free. Pricing checked on Basecamp's pricing page on 7 October 2026; always confirm before buying.

#### Basecamp Free Plan
The Free plan costs $0 and allows one project, up to five users and 1 GB of storage, with no time limit and no credit card. It is enough to try Basecamp properly on a single real project, or for a very small team running one ongoing workstream. It is not a long-term option for a business running several projects at once.

#### Basecamp Freelancer Plan
At $25 per month, Freelancer allows three active projects, 20 users and 5 GB, and adds 24/7/365 support. It suits freelancers and very small studios with a handful of clients.

#### Basecamp Studio Plan
At $59 per month, Studio allows 10 active projects, unlimited users, 25 GB and unlimited tools per project. For a small agency or business, this is likely the best-value starting point, because the price does not change as you add staff or clients.

#### Basecamp Pro Plan
At $99 per month, Pro allows 25 active projects, unlimited users and 100 GB. It suits growing agencies and mid-sized businesses whose main constraint is the number of concurrent projects.

#### Basecamp Unlimited Plan
At $299 per month billed annually, Unlimited removes the project cap and includes 1,000 GB of storage, priority 24/7/365 support, personalised onboarding with a Basecamp expert, enhanced admin features and the option to pay annually by cheque, ACH, wire or card. The pricing page also mentions buying additional storage, though its figures for this are inconsistent, so check with 37signals if storage matters.

#### Basecamp Free Trial
Basecamp offers a 30-day free trial on Freelancer, Studio and Pro, and a 45-day trial on Unlimited. No credit card is required, and nothing is charged automatically when the trial ends. Use the trial to run one or two real projects, including a client if you work with them, so you can judge notifications, client visibility and search with real data.

#### How Flat Pricing Compares with Per-User Pricing
Flat pricing is Basecamp's biggest commercial advantage. A 30-person company on Studio pays $59 a month in total, whatever the number of users. The same team on a per-user tool priced at $10 per user per month would pay $300 a month, and more if clients need paid seats. The calculation reverses for very small teams with many projects: three people running 30 active projects would need Unlimited at $299 a month, which is more than many per-user tools would cost. Count your active projects, not just your people, before choosing a plan.

### Basecamp Pros and Cons

##### Pros
- Very simple and calm to use; minimal training needed
- Flat pricing with no per-user fees
- Excellent client access with control over what clients see
- Messages, tasks, chat, files and schedules in one place
- Hill Charts show real progress, not just task counts
- Automatic check-ins replace routine status meetings
- Fast setup with very few configuration choices
- Long free trials with no credit card
- Open API, CLI and SDKs for AI agents and integrations

##### Cons
- No task dependencies, critical path or real Gantt chart
- No resource, capacity or budget management
- Limited reporting and no custom dashboards
- Active-project caps on all plans except Unlimited
- Notification volume is a common complaint
- No built-in AI features yet
- Little customisation: no custom fields or workflow rules
- Not designed for Agile or Scrum teams
- No native Slack or Microsoft Teams integration
This matches what users report: people value Basecamp's simplicity and the way it centralises communication, while limited advanced features, notifications and occasional performance issues are the most common drawbacks.

Ratings and review themes as published on G2 and Capterra on 5 October 2026; summarised in our own words. Visit the links above for full, verified user reviews.
On **Capterra**, Basecamp is rated **4.4/5 from 14,449 reviews**, with sub-scores of **4.3 for ease of use**, **4.2 for features**, **4.2 for value for money** and **4.3 for customer service** (checked 7 October 2026). On **G2**, it is rated **4.1/5 from 5,489 reviews** (checked 5 October 2026). The themes below summarise these third-party reviews in our own words, not 37signals' testimonials.
**Positive themes.** Reviewers most often praise having messages, tasks, files and schedules in one place, less email and fewer meetings, the simple interface, straightforward file sharing and easy collaboration with remote colleagues and clients. In Capterra's topic summaries, unified team communication (94% positive across 1,767 reviews), team collaboration (96% positive) and centralised file sharing (95% positive) stand out.
**Negative themes.** The most common complaints are excessive or hard-to-manage notifications (48% negative), version and update fragmentation in documents (41% negative), occasional glitches and slowdowns (51% negative), limited advanced features such as reporting, customisation and invoicing, pricing that some smaller users feel is high for the functionality, and cumbersome navigation and search.
When reading reviews yourself, check whether a review was invited or incentivised by the vendor; both Capterra and G2 label these. Many of Basecamp's reviews refer to older versions, so give more weight to recent reviews that mention Basecamp 5.

### Basecamp Customer Support
Paid plans include 24/7/365 support, according to Basecamp's pricing page, and Unlimited adds priority support that jumps the queue plus personalised onboarding with a Basecamp expert. The pricing page does not list a support tier for the Free plan. 37signals also publishes help guides for each feature.
Support is well regarded in third-party reviews, with a Capterra customer service sub-score of 4.3/5. Because the product is simple, most teams need less support than they would with a heavily configurable platform.

### Basecamp Security
According to 37signals' security policy, data in transit is encrypted using HTTPS, uploaded files are encrypted at rest, and database backups are encrypted with AES-256, taken daily and stored in multiple locations. The policy also states plainly that application databases are "generally not encrypted at rest", relying instead on the same protection and monitoring as the rest of its systems. Basecamp is hosted with the colocation provider Summit, which publishes a SOC 3 report and makes its SOC 2 Type II report available under NDA.
37signals publishes a completed CAIQ v4.1 self-assessment and a HECVAT for higher-education reviews, and card payments are handled under a PCI DSS SAQ A self-assessment. Basecamp supports two-factor authentication with standard authenticator apps and backup codes. We could not find SAML single sign-on, SCIM provisioning or a SOC 2 report for 37signals itself advertised, so organisations with formal identity or compliance requirements should confirm these directly with 37signals before buying.

### Basecamp for Different Types of Teams

#### Basecamp for Agencies and Client Services
This is Basecamp's strongest fit. Each client gets a project, clients see only what you share, adding them costs nothing on paid plans, and the message board keeps approvals and decisions on record. Time tracking and invoicing need third-party tools such as Harvest.

#### Basecamp for Small Businesses
Small businesses benefit from fast setup, a predictable monthly bill and a tool that non-technical staff will actually use. The main question is how many projects you run at once, since that decides the plan.

#### Basecamp for Remote Teams
Message boards, automatic check-ins and Hill Charts support asynchronous work across time zones, reducing the need for status meetings. Teams that rely heavily on real-time chat may still prefer a dedicated chat tool alongside it. Our [meeting notes template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/meeting-notes-template/) helps when meetings are still needed.

#### Basecamp for Marketing and Creative Teams
Card Tables work well for content pipelines and creative requests, and files with comment threads keep feedback in one place. Teams that need formal proofing, campaign calendars with dependencies or performance reporting will find Basecamp light.

#### Basecamp for Software Teams
37signals builds its own software in Basecamp, and Card Tables and Hill Charts suit small product teams. But there are no backlogs, sprints, story points or velocity reports, so teams following Scrum should look at dedicated tools; see our guide to [Scrum software tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-software-tools/).

#### Basecamp for Non-profits and Education
The 10% non-profit discount, free classroom accounts and the low learning curve make Basecamp a practical choice for volunteer-heavy organisations and schools.

#### Basecamp for Larger Organisations
Flat pricing scales well on Unlimited, but organisations needing portfolio reporting, resource planning or SAML SSO will usually need a more structured platform for [enterprise project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/enterprise-project-management/).

### Who Should Use Basecamp?

##### Great for
- Agencies and consultancies working with clients
- Small businesses wanting simple project communication

##### Look elsewhere if
- Teams needing scheduling, resource or portfolio controls
- Software teams running sprints

### Basecamp Alternatives and Comparisons
Basecamp fits teams of almost any size, from freelancers with a few clients to companies with hundreds of people on one flat-priced account. It is easy to adopt, even for beginners: new users can start with a single project page, a message board and a to-do list, then add Card Tables, Hill Charts and check-ins as they need them. If you would like to see how it stacks up, we compare Basecamp with Asana, monday.com, ClickUp, Trello, Wrike and others on pricing, features and use cases on dedicated pages:

### Is Basecamp Worth It?
Basecamp is likely worth it if you:
- Want project communication, tasks and files in one calm place instead of email and chat.
- Work with clients and want to control what they see without paying for their seats.
- Have a growing team and want a predictable monthly price.
- Value fast adoption by non-technical staff over configurability.
- Work asynchronously or remotely and want fewer status meetings.
- Run a moderate number of projects at the same time.
It may not be worth it if:
- Your projects depend on dependencies, critical path or detailed scheduling.
- You need resource, capacity or budget management.
- Leadership expects dashboards and portfolio reporting.
- Your development teams run Scrum with backlogs and sprints.
- You want AI built into the interface today.
- You are a very small team running many projects at once.
Our verdict: Basecamp's simplicity is both its biggest advantage and its biggest limitation. For agencies, small businesses and remote teams whose main problem is scattered communication, it is easy to recommend, and flat pricing makes it good value as teams grow. For organisations that need structured planning, reporting and resource control, it is too light, which is why it ranks tenth in our [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) review despite strong user satisfaction.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Basecamp good project management software?**
Yes, for communication-centred projects. Basecamp keeps messages, to-dos, files, schedules and chat in one place, is very easy to learn and rates 4.4/5 on Capterra. It deliberately leaves out dependencies, resource management and detailed reporting, so it suits agencies and small teams more than organisations running complex, date-driven projects.

**Q: Is Basecamp free?**
Yes. Basecamp's Free plan costs $0 and includes one project, up to five users and 1 GB of storage, with no time limit and no credit card required. Teams running more than one project at a time need a paid plan, starting with Freelancer at $25 per month.

**Q: How much does Basecamp cost?**
Basecamp costs $0 on Free, $25 per month on Freelancer, $59 on Studio and $99 on Pro, and $299 per month billed annually on Unlimited. Prices are flat per account, not per user; plans differ mainly by active projects and storage (checked 7 October 2026).

**Q: Does Basecamp have a free trial?**
Yes. Basecamp offers a 30-day free trial on Freelancer, Studio and Pro and a 45-day trial on Unlimited. No credit card is required, and nothing is charged automatically when the trial ends.

**Q: Does Basecamp charge per user?**
No. All Basecamp plans have a flat monthly price with no per-user fees. Studio, Pro and Unlimited allow unlimited users, Freelancer allows up to 20 and Free up to five. The main limit on most plans is the number of active projects.

**Q: Does Basecamp have Gantt charts?**
No. Basecamp has project schedules, calendars and the Lineup timeline of all projects, but no Gantt chart with task dependencies, critical path or baselines. Third-party integrations such as Ganttify and Le Gantt can add Gantt views.

**Q: Does Basecamp have Kanban boards?**
Yes. The Card Table is Basecamp's Kanban-style board, with a Triage section for new requests, custom coloured columns, a Not Now column, On Hold sections and a Done column. Each card has its own page for discussion and files.

**Q: Does Basecamp have AI?**
Not built in, as of October 2026. Instead, Basecamp is agent-accessible: a revamped API, a CLI, skills and SDKs let AI agents such as Claude, Codex and Cursor work in Basecamp, and the pricing page lists ChatGPT and Claude connectors. 37signals says it is still working on native AI features.

**Q: What are Basecamp Hill Charts?**
Hill Charts show progress on to-do lists as dots on a hill. Uphill means the team is still figuring out the approach; downhill means it is executing. Dots are moved manually, every update is saved as a snapshot, and stuck work becomes easy to spot.

**Q: Is Basecamp easy to use?**
Yes. Basecamp is one of the easiest project management tools to learn, with a 4.3/5 ease-of-use score on Capterra. Setup takes minutes, and clients and non-technical staff usually need little training. Some reviewers find navigation and search cumbersome in accounts with many projects.

**Q: What is Basecamp best used for?**
Basecamp is best for client projects, agency and consultancy work, small-business projects, remote teams that work asynchronously, team announcements and simple Kanban workflows such as request intake or content production.

**Q: Is Basecamp better than Asana?**
It depends on what you need. Basecamp is simpler, centred on communication and priced per account; Asana offers more structured task management, timelines, goals and portfolios, priced per user. See our [Basecamp vs Asana comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/asana-vs-basecamp/).

**Q: Is Basecamp better than Trello?**
They suit different needs. Trello focuses on visual Kanban boards; Basecamp combines a Kanban-style Card Table with messages, to-dos, chat, check-ins and files for each project. See our [Basecamp vs Trello comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/trello/trello-vs-basecamp/).

**Q: Does Basecamp integrate with Slack and Microsoft Teams?**
Not natively. 37signals positions Basecamp's Campfire chat and pings as the alternative, but third-party integrations listed in its directory can connect Slack and Microsoft Teams. Zapier, Zoho Flow and Unito can also link Basecamp to other apps.

**Q: What are the main disadvantages of Basecamp?**
The main disadvantages are no task dependencies or Gantt charts, no resource or budget management, limited reporting, active-project caps on most plans, notification volume, little customisation and no built-in AI features.
How we review.
Rankings and scores are the editorial opinion of the Neural Project Institute, based on features, pricing, ease of use, scalability and published user ratings. Prices were checked on vendors' pricing pages and ratings on G2 and Capterra on 5 October 2026; both change often, so confirm on the vendor's site before buying. We are independent and do not receive payment for rankings.

# ClickUp Review 2026: Is It Worth It?

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/
Section: Project management software reviews
Summary: Our ClickUp review covers features, pricing, ClickUp Brain AI, the hierarchy, pros and cons, integrations and whether ClickUp is worth it in 2026.


## ClickUp Review 2026: Is It Worth It?
ClickUp is an all-in-one work platform that puts tasks, projects, Docs, Whiteboards, Chat, Forms, Goals, Sprints, time tracking and Dashboards into a single workspace, with an AI layer called ClickUp Brain on top. Its biggest strength is the sheer breadth of what you get for a low per-user price; the trade-offs are the effort needed to configure it, a dense interface, recurring complaints about lag, and AI features that are priced separately. This review covers pricing, project management, collaboration, automation, AI, integrations, ease of use, reporting and overall value.

- Pricing and Capterra rating checked 7 October 2026

### ClickUp review: quick verdict
|  |  |

ClickUp offers more features per pound or dollar than almost any mainstream project management tool, and it is genuinely capable for Agile teams, agencies and growing businesses that want to replace several apps with one. The costs are real, though: a good setup takes deliberate design, the interface can overwhelm new users, performance and bugs are the most common complaints in third-party reviews, and the most useful AI features add $9 to $28 per user per month on top of the plan.
