### What Is Trello?
Trello is cloud-based, visual work management software based on [Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/what-is-kanban/). Work is organised on boards, each board is split into lists (usually stages such as To do, Doing and Done), and every piece of work is a card that moves from list to list as it progresses.
People and teams use Trello to manage:
- **Personal and team to-do lists**, from household jobs to weekly priorities
- **Simple projects**, such as a website refresh, an office move or a product launch checklist
- **Content and editorial calendars**, with one card per article, post or video
- **Pipelines**, such as recruiting, sales leads or customer onboarding
- **Sprint and Kanban boards** for small software and product teams
- **Request intake**, where colleagues add cards for work they need done
It runs in the browser, as desktop apps and as iOS and Android apps. Trello is deliberately simple: it does not try to be a full project portfolio management suite, and its appeal comes from that restraint. Additional capability arrives through paid plans, built-in automation and Power-Ups (add-ons and integrations), which is both its flexibility and, as we explain below, a source of hidden complexity.

### Who Owns Trello?
Trello was created by Fog Creek Software, the company founded by Joel Spolsky and Michael Pryor, and launched in September 2011. It was spun off as a separate company in 2014, and Atlassian announced its acquisition in January 2017 for $425 million.
For buyers, the practical point is that Trello is part of the Atlassian portfolio. It uses Atlassian accounts, Enterprise security runs through Atlassian Guard, and it connects closely with [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/) and Confluence. It is a mature product with a long track record rather than an early-stage start-up.

### How Does Trello Work?
Trello has a short, flat hierarchy, which is a large part of why it is so easy to learn:
- **Workspaces** hold a team's boards and members. Free Workspaces are limited to 10 collaborators and 10 boards.
- **Boards** represent a project, a team or a workflow.
- **Lists** are the columns on a board, usually stages of work, but they can be anything: weeks, owners, categories.
- **Cards** are the individual tasks or items. Each card can have members, labels, start and due dates, checklists, attachments, comments and (from Standard) custom fields.
- **The board menu** controls permissions, Power-Ups, automation and the activity log.
- **Inbox and Planner** are a personal layer above the boards for capturing to-dos and planning your own time.
A typical workflow looks like this:
**Idea or request captured (card or Inbox) → card added to a board → assigned and dated → moved across lists → automation handles routine steps → team comments on the card → card moved to Done**
For example, a content team keeps a board with lists for Ideas, Writing, Editing, Scheduled and Published. A writer picks up a card, adds the draft link, and drags it to Editing; an automation rule adds the editor and a review checklist; when the post goes live, the card moves to Published and the due date is marked complete. Everyone can see the state of every piece at a glance, without a status meeting.

### Trello Key Features

#### Boards, Lists and Cards
The board is the heart of Trello and is available on every plan, including Free, with unlimited cards. Cards are dragged between lists, colour labels mark type or priority, and checklists break a card into steps. Board and card templates save repeating the same setup.
This is the purest implementation of a digital [Kanban board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/kanban-boards/) among mainstream tools, and it is excellent for making work visible. What it does not do natively is enforce Kanban discipline: there are no built-in [WIP limits](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/wip-limits/) or swimlanes on the base board, so teams that want them rely on conventions or Power-Ups. If you want to practise first, our free [Kanban board template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/kanban-board-template/) follows the same structure.

#### Card Details and Custom Fields
Opening a card shows its full detail: description, members, dates, checklists, attachments, comments and activity. The Standard plan adds **custom fields** (for data such as priority, client, budget or story points), **advanced checklists** (assigning and dating individual checklist items), **card mirroring** (showing one card on several boards) and saved searches.
These additions turn a card into a lightweight record, which is enough for many small teams. They do not add task dependencies between cards, so you cannot say "this card cannot start until that one is finished" and have Trello reschedule the knock-on effects. For work where [task dependencies](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/task-dependencies/) matter, that is the main gap.

#### Trello Views
Board view is available to everyone. Trello's other views require Premium or Enterprise:
- **Timeline:** cards laid out across dates, with drag-to-adjust start and due dates.
- **Table:** a sortable, filterable spreadsheet-style list of a board's cards.
- **Calendar:** cards on a calendar by due date, with third-party calendar sync.
- **Dashboard:** charts of cards per list, per member, per label and by due date.
- **Map:** location-based cards on an interactive map.
- **Workspace views:** Table and Calendar views across multiple boards.
Timeline is the closest Trello gets to a [Gantt chart](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/), and it is useful for seeing when work lands. It is not a scheduling engine: there are no dependency links, critical path or baselines. Workspace-level Table view is the feature that makes Trello workable for a manager overseeing several boards, so teams that need cross-board visibility should budget for Premium from the start.

#### Inbox and Planner
**Inbox** is a personal capture area. Trello says you can send items into it from email and from messaging apps including Slack and Microsoft Teams, then drag them onto the right board later or mark them done in place. Inbox is listed on the Free plan.
**Planner** syncs with your calendar and lets you block focus time for cards; the pricing page lists it among the Standard plan's features. Together they shift Trello slightly towards personal productivity, which is useful for individuals and team members juggling several boards, though they are not a substitute for team-level planning.

#### Butler Automation
Trello's built-in, no-code automation, long known as **Butler**, is included on every board. It offers:
- **Rules** that run actions when a trigger occurs, such as adding a checklist when a card enters a list.
- **Card buttons and board buttons** that run several actions in one click.
- **Calendar commands** that run on a daily, weekly, monthly or yearly schedule.
- **Due date commands** that run as a due date approaches, arrives or passes.
- **Email, Slack and Jira actions**, such as sending an email or creating a Jira issue from a card.
Trello also suggests automations when it notices repeated actions. Usage is metered in Workspace **command runs**: 250 per month on Free, 1,000 on Standard and unlimited on Premium and Enterprise. For small teams, Butler removes a surprising amount of manual card shuffling. Busy boards on Free or Standard can hit the monthly limit, so check usage before relying on automation for anything important.

#### Power-Ups
Power-Ups are add-ons that bring extra features or integrations to a board, and every plan, including Free, allows unlimited Power-Ups per board. Trello's guide says its directory has more than 200. Atlassian-built Power-Ups include Jira, Confluence and Google Drive; others come from third parties and cover time tracking, Gantt charts, voting, card ageing, reporting and more.
This is how Trello stays simple while still letting teams add what they need. It is also a trade-off: capabilities that are built in elsewhere (dependencies, time tracking, advanced reporting) depend on third-party add-ons in Trello, some with their own subscription fees, data access and support. A board with a dozen Power-Ups is no longer a simple tool, so weigh the full cost and admin effort, not just the Trello plan price.

#### Templates
Trello's public template gallery covers project management, content calendars, sprint boards, onboarding, CRM pipelines and much more, and Premium adds Workspace-level templates so teams can standardise their own. Templates make it quick to start, but they are only a starting point; most teams adapt the lists and labels within a week of use. Our [content calendar template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/content-calendar-template/) and [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) translate directly into Trello boards.

### Trello AI Features
Trello's AI features are available on the Standard, Premium and Enterprise plans, on web and desktop, and can be switched on or off by Workspace admins (Enterprise admins manage them from the Enterprise Dashboard). According to Atlassian's documentation, they include:
- **Create a board with AI:** describe a goal and Trello generates a board with lists and cards.
- **Merge cards:** drag one card onto another to combine titles, descriptions, attachments, custom fields and labels; the originals are archived and the merge can be undone.
- **AI-generated checklists:** one click produces a checklist of steps from the card's title and description.
- **AI-recommended focus time:** with a calendar connected, Trello suggests focus blocks for upcoming cards.
- **Due dates from card titles:** natural-language dates such as "this Thursday" in a new card's title set the due date (English only).
- **AI-generated images** for board backgrounds and card covers.
- **Rovo writing tools** to generate, rewrite and summarise card descriptions and comments.
Atlassian announced most of these on 30 July 2026, along with AI-generated widget cards planned for Trello Labs. Separately, the **Trello MCP server**, available on every plan, lets external AI assistants read and act on Trello data.
Our assessment: these are practical conveniences that save minutes, especially board creation, checklists and summaries of long comment threads. They are not project intelligence. Trello's AI does not forecast delivery dates, flag resource conflicts or analyse risk across a portfolio, because Trello does not hold that kind of data. Teams that want AI for planning and reporting should look at our guide to [AI project management tools](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/ai-project-management-tools/).

### Trello Collaboration Features
Collaboration happens on the card: comments, @mentions, attachments, checklists, due dates and a full activity log. Members can watch cards, lists or boards to get notified about changes. The Standard plan adds single-board guests, Premium adds Observers (people who can view and comment without full edit rights), and Enterprise adds multi-board guests, who are billed at the same rate as members.
Because the board is so visual, Trello is good at replacing status meetings and update emails for small teams: everyone sees the same picture. The common downside is notification noise. In Capterra's topic summaries, about 41% of reviews discussing notifications describe them as overwhelming or inconsistent. Agree early on who watches what, and use @mentions deliberately. For distributed teams, see our guide to [remote project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/industries/remote-project-management/).

### Trello Reporting and Tracking
Reporting is one of Trello's thinner areas. On Premium and Enterprise, the **Dashboard view** charts cards per list, per member, per label and by due date status, and **Workspace views** show cards from several boards in one table or calendar. Premium also includes simple data export.
That is enough to answer "what is overdue and who is overloaded with cards?" on a handful of boards. It is not enough for portfolio reporting, time and budget tracking, or [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/), and Trello has no native resource management. Teams that need those either add reporting Power-Ups or export to a spreadsheet or BI tool, and at that point a fuller project management platform is often simpler. Capterra reviewers make the same point: weaker support for large or complex projects, including reporting and resource management, is a recurring criticism.

### Trello Integrations
Integrations come through Power-Ups, automation actions and the API. Commonly used connections include:
- **Slack** and **Microsoft Teams**, for creating cards and capturing messages
- **Jira** and **Confluence**, for linking business boards to engineering issues and documentation
- **Google Drive**, plus Dropbox, OneDrive and other storage via Power-Ups
- **Gmail and Outlook**, for turning emails into cards
- **Calendars**, for Planner and calendar sync
- **Automation platforms** such as Zapier, and Trello's own REST API and MCP server
The Atlassian connections are a real advantage for organisations that already run Jira: a marketing or support team can work in Trello while engineering stays in Jira, with issues linked on the card. Integration quality varies with third-party Power-Ups, so check who maintains any add-on you plan to depend on.

### Trello Ease of Use

#### Initial Setup
Setup is minimal. Create a Workspace, create a board (or pick a template), add lists, invite people and start adding cards. Most small teams are running within an hour. The design decisions that take more thought are naming lists consistently, agreeing what labels mean, and deciding which Power-Ups and automations are worth adding.

#### Learning Curve
Trello has one of the shortest learning curves of any project management tool. Capterra users rate its ease of use 4.5/5, and quick onboarding with little training is one of the most consistent positive themes in reviews. Butler automation and some Power-Ups take more effort to learn, but none of it is required to get value from the product.

#### Interface
The interface is clean, visual and familiar: a board with columns and cards. The weakness shows at scale. Boards with hundreds of cards become long and cluttered, information spreads across many boards, and the lack of hierarchy above the board (beyond Workspaces and Collections on Premium) makes it harder to see how work connects. Capterra reviewers mention cluttered boards as projects grow. Trello is genuinely easy to use; it is less easy to keep organised as the amount of work increases.

### Trello Mobile and Desktop Apps
Trello's iOS and Android apps are included on every plan and cover the core experience well: viewing boards, moving cards, commenting, adding checklists and attachments, and receiving notifications. Because Trello's model is so simple, it translates to a phone better than most project management tools. Desktop apps are also available, and AI features work on web and desktop.
Mobile is good for keeping up to date and capturing work on the move. Setting up automation, Power-Ups and Premium views is better done on a larger screen.

### Trello Pricing
Trello's published plans are below (checked on Trello's pricing page on 7 October 2026). Prices are per user per month in US dollars.
| Plan | Annual billing | Monthly billing | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | $0 | Individuals and small teams (up to 10 collaborators per Workspace) |
| Standard | $5/user/month | $6/user/month | Small teams that need unlimited boards and more structure |
| Premium | $10/user/month | $12.50/user/month | Teams up to 100 tracking multiple projects with extra views |
| Enterprise | $17.50/user/month ($210/user/year) | Not offered | Organisations of 50+ seats needing central administration |
Workspace members and admins are billable, and multi-board guests are billed at the same rate. Non-profit and education discounts are available. Atlassian Guard, for SSO and user provisioning, is sold separately from $4 per user/month for Standard and Premium, while Enterprise includes Atlassian Guard Standard.

#### Trello Free Plan
The Free plan costs $0 and includes up to 10 collaborators and 10 boards per Workspace, unlimited cards, Inbox, unlimited Power-Ups per board, assignees and due dates, an unlimited activity log, the mobile apps, two-factor authentication, 250 automation command runs per month and a 10MB limit per file. It is genuinely useful for individuals, [personal Kanban](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/kanban/personal-kanban/) and small teams. The 10-collaborator cap is the limit that most often forces an upgrade, followed by the 10-board limit and the lack of custom fields and extra views.

#### Trello Standard Plan
At $5 per user/month billed annually ($6 monthly), Standard adds unlimited boards, AI features, Planner, advanced checklists, card mirroring, custom fields, collapsible lists, single-board guests, saved searches, 1,000 command runs per month and a 250MB file limit. It suits small teams that have outgrown Free but still work mainly on boards.

#### Trello Premium Plan
At $10 per user/month billed annually ($12.50 monthly), Premium adds the Timeline, Table, Calendar, Dashboard and Map views, Workspace-level Table and Calendar views, unlimited command runs, admin and security features, Workspace templates, Collections, Observers and simple data export. Trello describes it as best for teams of up to 100 tracking multiple projects. For a team that wants Trello as its main project tool, this is the plan to evaluate.

#### Trello Enterprise Plan
Enterprise costs $17.50 per user/month, billed annually only. Trello's Enterprise page says it is for businesses with 50 seats or more and mentions a $10k minimum spend. It adds unlimited Workspaces, organisation-wide permissions, organisation-visible boards, public board management, multi-board guests, attachment permissions, Power-Up administration, Atlassian Guard Standard (including SSO and user provisioning) and 24/7 Enterprise Admin support. It is aimed at organisations standardising on Trello across many teams, not at small businesses.

#### Trello Free Trial
Trello offers a 14-day free trial of Premium, and its trial page says no credit card is required. If no payment details are added, the Workspace returns to the Free plan when the trial ends. Use the trial to run a real workflow with Premium's views and automation, and decide whether you would actually miss them on Standard or Free.

### Trello Pros and Cons

##### Pros
- Very easy to learn and adopt
- Useful free plan with unlimited cards and Power-Ups
- Low price for paid plans
- Clear, visual Kanban boards
- Built-in no-code automation on every plan
- Large Power-Up and integration ecosystem
- Strong links with Jira and Confluence
- Good mobile apps
- Practical AI features from Standard

##### Cons
- No task dependencies or critical path scheduling
- Free plan capped at 10 collaborators and 10 boards per Workspace
- Timeline, table, calendar and dashboard views need Premium
- No native resource, capacity or portfolio management
- Automation runs are capped on Free and Standard
- Key gaps rely on third-party Power-Ups, which add cost and complexity
- Boards become cluttered as work grows
- Basic reporting; notifications can be noisy
- Granular access controls mostly on higher tiers
This matches what users report: Trello's simplicity, flexibility and visual approach are consistently praised, while its limits for large or complex projects are the most common reason people outgrow it.

Ratings and review themes as published on G2 and Capterra on 5 October 2026; summarised in our own words. Visit the links above for full, verified user reviews.
On **Capterra**, Trello is rated **4.5/5 from 23,628 reviews**, with sub-scores of **4.5 for ease of use**, **4.5 for value for money**, **4.3 for features** and **4.3 for customer service** (checked 7 October 2026). On **G2**, it is rated **4.4/5 from 14,063 reviews** (checked 5 October 2026). The themes below summarise these third-party reviews in our own words, not Trello's testimonials.
**Positive themes.** Reviewers most often praise the intuitive boards, lists and cards, real-time collaboration and centralised communication, flexibility across personal and team use, quick onboarding with little training, and useful automation and integrations. In Capterra's topic summaries, real-time team collaboration (about 97% positive) and flexible visual task management (about 96% positive) stand out.
**Negative themes.** The most common complaints are notifications that are excessive, delayed or hard to customise, basic or unclear access controls (about 41% of reviews on that topic are negative), weaker support for large or complex projects, boards becoming cluttered as projects grow, advanced features needing Power-Ups or higher plans, and occasional slow support responses.
Capterra labels each review as incentivised or non-incentivised, and G2 does something similar. Filtering for non-incentivised reviews, and reading critical reviews from teams of your size, gives a more realistic picture than the headline score.

### Trello Customer Support
Trello support is provided through Atlassian: a help centre with documentation, the Trello guide, webinars and the Atlassian Community forum, with direct support options that vary by plan. Enterprise includes 24/7 Enterprise Admin support.
Third-party feedback is reasonably positive, with a Capterra customer service sub-score of 4.3/5, though some reviewers report slow responses. Because Trello is so widely used, community answers and tutorials are easy to find, which matters more for most small teams than formal support.

### Trello Security
All plans include two-factor authentication and board-level permissions (private, Workspace-visible or public boards). Premium adds admin and security features, and Enterprise adds organisation-wide permissions, control over who can create public boards, attachment permissions, Power-Up administration (approving which Power-Ups staff can use) and SAML single sign-on and user provisioning through Atlassian Guard.
Trello's Enterprise guide lists SOC 2 and SOC 3 reports, ISO/IEC 27001 and 27018, and GDPR compliance among its security credentials, and points to the Atlassian Trust Center for current reports. Confirm current certifications and their scope there as part of procurement. Note that Capterra reviewers who discuss access controls are often critical of how granular they are, so test permissions against your own requirements, particularly if you work with clients or external guests.

### Trello for Different Types of Teams

#### Trello for Small Businesses
Small businesses are Trello's natural market: cheap, quick to adopt and flexible enough for sales pipelines, client work and operations. The Free plan's 10-collaborator cap means a growing business will soon pay for Standard or Premium, but even then costs stay low.

#### Trello for Marketing and Content Teams
Editorial calendars, campaign checklists and creative request boards fit Trello well, and Calendar view (Premium) makes publishing schedules easy to see. Teams that need formal approvals, proofing or campaign budgets will find it limited.

#### Trello for Software and Agile Teams
Small product and development teams can run a simple [Scrum board](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-boards/) or Kanban flow in Trello, and some use Power-Ups for story points. Once a team needs backlogs, sprint reports, velocity or release tracking, [Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/jira/), from the same company, is the more natural fit.

#### Trello for Personal Productivity
Inbox, Planner and the Free plan make Trello a strong personal task manager, particularly for people who think visually. Our [to-do list template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/to-do-list-template/) offers a paper-based alternative.

#### Trello for Larger Organisations
Enterprise gives large organisations central administration, SSO and Power-Up control, and many companies use Trello for team-level boards. As the main project management system for a department running many interdependent projects, it is usually too light: there is no portfolio management, dependency scheduling or resource planning.

### Who Should Use Trello?

##### Great for
- Individuals and small teams
- Simple workflows such as content calendars or recruiting pipelines

##### Look elsewhere if
- Teams managing complex schedules, budgets or many projects

Trello fits teams of almost any size and is one of the easiest project management tools for beginners: you can create a board, add cards and start working in minutes, then add Power-Ups, automation and extra views as your projects grow. If you would like to see how it stacks up, we compare Trello with Asana, monday.com, ClickUp, Wrike and others on pricing, features and use cases on dedicated pages:

### Is Trello Worth It?
Trello is likely worth it if you:
- Want a visual board that everyone understands immediately.
- Are an individual or a small team with fairly simple workflows.
- Need a capable free plan or a low per-user price.
- Run pipelines, content calendars or Kanban-style flows rather than date-driven project plans.
- Already use Jira or Confluence and want a lighter tool for business teams.
- Prefer adding features through Power-Ups to adopting a heavy platform.
It may not be worth it if:
- Your projects depend on task dependencies, critical paths or detailed [project timelines](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-timeline/).
- You need resource, capacity, time or budget management.
- Managers need portfolio reporting across many projects.
- You would need many paid Power-Ups to fill the gaps.
- Your Workspace has more than 10 people and you were counting on the free plan.
Our verdict: Trello's simplicity is both its biggest advantage and its main limit. For individuals and small teams, it is one of the quickest, most affordable ways to make work visible, which is why it remains popular. For complex, multi-project work, it ranks ninth in our [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) review because the depth is not there. Use the 14-day Premium trial on a real workflow before deciding which plan, if any, you need.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Trello good project management software?**
Yes, for simple and moderately complex work. Trello is very easy to learn, affordable and rated 4.5/5 on Capterra. It lacks native task dependencies, resource management and portfolio reporting, so it suits individuals and small teams with board-shaped workflows more than organisations running many interdependent projects.

**Q: Is Trello free?**
Yes. Trello's Free plan costs $0 and includes unlimited cards, Inbox, unlimited Power-Ups per board, mobile apps and 250 automation runs a month. It is limited to 10 collaborators and 10 boards per Workspace, and extra views, custom fields and AI require a paid plan.

**Q: How much does Trello cost?**
Trello costs $0 on Free, $5 per user/month on Standard ($6 billed monthly), $10 per user/month on Premium ($12.50 billed monthly) and $17.50 per user/month on Enterprise, billed annually only. Enterprise is aimed at 50 seats or more (checked 7 October 2026).

**Q: Does Trello have a free trial?**
Yes. Trello offers a 14-day free trial of Premium, and its trial page says no credit card is required. If you do not add payment details, the Workspace returns to the Free plan when the trial ends.

**Q: Is Trello easy to use?**
Yes. Trello is one of the easiest project management tools to learn, and Capterra users rate its ease of use 4.5/5. Boards, lists and cards are intuitive. Automation and Power-Ups take a little more effort, and very large boards can become cluttered.

**Q: What is Trello best used for?**
Trello is best for Kanban-style task tracking, small team projects, content calendars, recruiting and sales pipelines, personal to-do lists, request intake and simple sprint boards: work that moves through stages on a board.

**Q: Is Trello better than Asana?**
Neither is universally better. Trello is simpler and cheaper for board-based work; Asana adds more structure, dependencies, goals and portfolio features. See our [Trello vs Asana comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/asana-vs-trello/).

**Q: Is Trello better than monday.com?**
It depends on your needs. Trello is simpler and less expensive; monday.com offers more views, automation and reporting for teams that need a more customisable platform. See our [Trello vs monday.com comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/monday/monday-vs-trello/).

**Q: Does Trello have Gantt charts?**
Not natively. Premium and Enterprise include a Timeline view that shows cards across dates, but it has no dependency links, critical path or baselines. Some teams add third-party Gantt Power-Ups for that.

**Q: What are Trello Power-Ups?**
Power-Ups are add-ons that bring extra features and integrations to a Trello board, such as Jira, Confluence, Google Drive, time tracking or voting. Every plan, including Free, allows unlimited Power-Ups per board, though some third-party Power-Ups charge separately.

**Q: What is Trello Butler?**
Butler is the name long used for Trello's built-in, no-code automation. It covers rules, card and board buttons, scheduled commands and due date commands. Free includes 250 command runs a month, Standard 1,000 and Premium and Enterprise unlimited.

**Q: Does Trello have AI?**
Yes. On Standard, Premium and Enterprise, Trello AI can create boards from a description, merge cards, generate checklists, recommend focus time, set due dates from card titles, generate images and help write or summarise content. The Trello MCP server is available on every plan.

**Q: Who owns Trello?**
Trello is owned by Atlassian, the company behind Jira and Confluence. Atlassian announced the acquisition in January 2017. Trello was originally created by Fog Creek Software and launched in 2011.

**Q: What are the main disadvantages of Trello?**
The main disadvantages are the lack of task dependencies, resource management and portfolio reporting, the 10-collaborator cap on the Free plan, advanced views needing Premium, reliance on Power-Ups for missing features, cluttered boards at scale and noisy notifications.

**Q: Is Trello suitable for small businesses?**
Yes. Trello is a strong fit for small businesses that want a simple, low-cost way to organise work. Once a business has more than 10 people in a Workspace or needs extra views, it will need Standard or Premium, which are still inexpensive.
How we review.
Rankings and scores are the editorial opinion of the Neural Project Institute, based on features, pricing, ease of use, scalability and published user ratings. Prices were checked on vendors' pricing pages and ratings on G2 and Capterra on 5 October 2026; both change often, so confirm on the vendor's site before buying. We are independent and do not receive payment for rankings.
Product screenshots are © Atlassian Corporation and shown for the purpose of review, with links to their source pages.

# Wrike Review 2026: Is It Worth It?

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/

## Wrike Review 2026: Is It Worth It?
Wrike is a work and project management platform that brings tasks, projects, request intake, workflows, collaboration, reporting and resource planning into one place, for teams ranging from a handful of people to large enterprises. Its biggest strength is the depth of its workflow customisation and cross-project visibility; that same depth is why it takes longer to set up and learn than simpler tools. This review covers pricing, project management, collaboration, automation, AI, integrations, ease of use, reporting and overall value.

Wrike is a powerful, highly configurable work management platform, and it is at its best for teams running many projects and complex, multi-step workflows. The trade-offs are real: initial setup takes time, the advanced functionality can feel overwhelming at first, several of the most valuable capabilities sit on higher-priced plans or add-ons, and small teams may never use most of what they pay for.

### What Is Wrike?
Wrike is cloud-based project and work management software. It combines classic project management (plans, dependencies, Gantt charts, milestones) with broader work management: handling incoming requests, running repeatable workflows, tracking resources and reporting across a whole portfolio of work.
Organisations use it to manage:
- **Tasks and projects**, from one-off jobs to multi-month programmes
- **Requests**, collected through structured forms instead of email and chat
- **Campaigns and creative workflows**, including reviews and approvals
- **Resource planning**, showing who is working on what and who has capacity
- **Reporting and portfolio management**, through dashboards and cross-project views
- **Workflow automation**, using rules and AI agents to move work along
Instead of forcing one project style, Wrike lets teams look at the same work through different views, such as a list, a board, a table, a Gantt chart or a dashboard. It runs in the browser and as desktop and mobile apps, and it works for both traditional, plan-driven [project management](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/) and more flexible, continuous operational work. It is not simply a to-do list app: its value comes from structure, shared data and visibility across teams.

### Who Owns Wrike?
Wrike was founded in 2006 by Andrew Filev. It was acquired by Citrix in 2021, separated from Citrix in 2022 after Citrix was taken private, and has been owned by private equity firm Symphony Technology Group (STG) since 2023. Wrike says it is used by more than 20,000 organisations worldwide.
For buyers, the practical point is that Wrike is a mature, independently operated product with a long track record rather than an early-stage startup.

### How Does Wrike Work?
Wrike organises work in a simple hierarchy that scales up as your needs grow:
- **Spaces** are the top-level areas, usually one per team, department or major client.
- **Folders** group related work inside a space, such as "Q4 campaigns" or "Client A".
- **Projects** are folders with a start date, end date, owner and status.
- **Tasks and subtasks** are the individual pieces of work, each with **assignees**, **due dates** and a **status**.
- **Custom fields** add the data your team needs, such as budget, channel, priority or client.
- **Views** show the same items as a list, board, table, Gantt chart or calendar, and **dashboards** summarise work across projects.
A typical workflow looks like this:
**Request comes in → task or project created → work assigned → status tracked → team collaborates → progress reported → project completed**
For example, a sales team submits a request form for a new product brochure. Wrike creates a task in the marketing space, assigns it to a designer, and moves it through statuses such as In design, In review and Approved. Comments and files stay on the task, and the marketing manager sees progress on a dashboard without chasing anyone for an update.

### Wrike Key Features

#### Task Management
Tasks are the core building block. Each task can have subtasks, one or more assignees, start and due dates, dependencies, priorities, attachments, comments and a custom status. Recurring tasks handle routine work such as monthly reports, and every task has a clear owner, which makes accountability visible.
This matters most when many people or departments touch the same work. In a small team, a shared list is often enough. Once marketing, design, legal and sales all contribute to a launch, knowing exactly who owns each step, and what it is waiting on, is what keeps the work moving.

#### Project Management
Wrike supports full project planning: milestones, dependencies, timelines, project status and project-level custom fields such as budget, client or risk level. Because projects share the same structure and fields, managers can track many projects at once and roll them up into portfolio views and dashboards.
This is where Wrike separates itself from lighter tools. Teams juggling dozens of simultaneous projects can see deadlines, status and workload across all of them, rather than opening each project individually.

#### Gantt Charts
Wrike's interactive [Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) are included from the Team plan upwards. They support all four dependency types with lead and lag time, automatic rescheduling when a predecessor moves, milestones, the [critical path](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/), float, baselines for planned-versus-actual tracking, and drag-and-drop rescheduling.
For complex, date-driven projects such as product launches, events or construction-style schedules, this is genuinely useful: you can see what a delay will knock on to before it happens. For simple task tracking, the Gantt chart is more than most teams need, and a board or table will usually be quicker.

#### Kanban Boards
The board view shows tasks as cards in columns based on their status, and you drag a card to move it along. Columns reflect your custom statuses, so a creative team's board might run Requested, In design, In review, Approved. This gives a fast visual picture of where work is piling up.
Board view is available even on Wrike's Free plan, which makes it a reasonable way to try the product.

#### Table View
Table view presents work like a spreadsheet, with sorting, filtering, custom-field columns and bulk editing. It is the quickest way to manage hundreds of tasks or requests at once, and it is often what convinces spreadsheet-heavy teams to move into Wrike: the layout feels familiar, but the data is live and connected to the rest of the work.

#### Dashboards
Dashboards pull tasks, statuses, workload and metrics from across projects onto one screen. Typical widgets show tasks by status, overdue work, team workload and project progress, and each person can build views that suit them. Shareable dashboards are included from the Team plan.
Dashboards are most valuable for managers and stakeholders who need the big picture without opening every project. A department head can see which projects are late and who is overloaded in a few seconds.

#### Custom Workflows
Wrike lets each team define its own statuses and workflow stages, so marketing, IT and client services can each work their own way inside one platform. A few examples:
- **Marketing:** Brief → Planning → In production → Review → Scheduled → Live.
- **Creative requests:** Requested → Accepted → In design → Client review → Approved.
- **IT:** New → Triage → In progress → Testing → Resolved.
- **Operations:** Submitted → Approved → Scheduled → Done.
- **Client projects:** Scoping → Delivery → Client sign-off → Invoiced.
Combined with automation, tasks can move through these stages and notify the right people automatically. Customisation is one of Wrike's major strengths, but it also drives the learning curve: every extra status, field and rule is something an administrator has to design and every user has to understand.

#### Request Forms
Request forms give stakeholders a structured way to ask for work. Each answer maps to a field on the task or project it creates, conditional logic shows follow-up questions, and rules can assign the work, set its status and file it in the right place. External forms let clients or non-Wrike users submit requests through a link.
For example, a marketing team can use one form to collect design requests, including the deadline, channel, campaign, brief and attachments. Instead of requests arriving by email or chat with half the information missing, every request lands in Wrike complete and already routed. If you are not ready for software, our free [work request template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/work-request-template/) follows the same idea.

#### Wrike Automation
Wrike's automation engine uses rule-based actions: when something happens (a status changes, a form is submitted, a date passes), Wrike does something (assigns a person, changes a status, sends a notification, creates a subtask). Automated assignment and request routing remove much of the repetitive coordination work.
For teams handling large volumes of requests, such as creative services, marketing operations or IT, this is practical and saves real time. Not every capability is on every plan, though: the more advanced automation, AI agents, and cross-tool automation through Wrike Integrate sit on higher tiers or add-ons.

### Wrike AI Features
AI is now a substantial part of Wrike, not a minor add-on. Wrike splits it into two tiers. According to its help centre, **AI Essentials** covers content creation and editing, comment summaries, natural-language creation of forms and automation rules, AI highlights, Board AI and mobile inbox prioritisation. **AI Elite** covers Wrike Copilot, AI-generated dashboard widgets, AI agents and the Whiteboard assistant.
Wrike's pricing page includes AI Essentials from the Team plan, and Team stays on Essentials only. From the Business plan, accounts also get a pooled monthly allowance of AI Elite "actions", which grows on Pinnacle and Apex, and extra action packs can be bought. Agents consume actions for each step they run, so heavy automation needs planning.

#### AI Writing and Editing
Wrike AI can draft and rewrite text inside tasks: turning rough notes into a project brief, tightening a status update, or producing a first draft of documentation. It is most useful for the routine writing that surrounds project work, not as a replacement for a dedicated writing tool.

#### AI Summaries
Long comment threads can be summarised in one click, which helps managers and new team members catch up on a task without reading dozens of messages. On busy projects, this saves real time.

#### Wrike Copilot
Copilot is an AI assistant that answers questions about your work data in plain language, such as "What's the status of our Q3 launch?" or "What changed this week?". Wrike says it can also surface risks and dependencies, show who is overloaded or has capacity, and generate charts and action items. It is part of AI Elite, so it is available from the Business plan's allowance upwards.

#### Wrike AI Agents
AI agents are configurable automations that can take actions inside Wrike. Wrike describes agents for request validation (sending back incomplete requests), task triage and routing, compliance and risk checks, sprint and project operations (rolling over work, updating statuses, writing summaries), auto-assignment at scale and portfolio reporting. Agents are set up through a conversational builder, with testing before deployment, admin controls and an audit trail of what they did.
These are best understood as smart workflow automation, not autonomous employees. They follow the instructions and permissions you give them, they use up your AI action allowance on every run, and someone still needs to own the process they support. Availability and volume depend on your plan.

### Wrike Collaboration Features
Collaboration happens on the work itself: comments and @mentions on tasks, file attachments, shared tasks, activity streams, notifications and formal approvals with named approvers. Keeping conversations attached to the task means decisions are recorded where the work lives, rather than scattered across email and chat.
Collaboration is strongest when Wrike becomes the single source of truth, so different departments see the same status and history. The downside is noise: on Capterra, notifications are one of the more frequent complaints, with reviewers describing them as excessive and hard to tune. Agree notification settings and @mention habits early, or people will start ignoring them.

### Wrike Reporting and Analytics
Wrike's reporting works at two levels. **Operational dashboards and reports**, available on paid plans, show project status, workload, overdue tasks and trends, and are what most teams use day to day. **Advanced reporting and BI**, on Pinnacle and Apex, adds deeper analysis across portfolios, financials and resources for organisations that need executive and PMO-level insight.
Users on Capterra generally rate Wrike's visibility highly: in the topic summaries Capterra publishes, around 96% of reviews mentioning project visibility, dashboards and progress tracking are positive. Some reviewers mention a learning curve in configuring reports, so budget time for an administrator to set up the first set of dashboards properly.

### Resource and Capacity Management
Wrike shows team workload and capacity: who is assigned to what, how much effort is allocated, and who is overloaded. Managers can rebalance work, account for working hours, non-working days and holidays, and use time tracking with approved timesheets.
Advanced resource and capacity planning, including role-based planning and budgeting, is listed among Wrike's Pinnacle capabilities. It is aimed at mature organisations such as PMOs and professional services firms rather than small task-management teams.

### Wrike Integrations
Wrike's integration directory lists around 60 integrations covering CRM, messaging, BI, file storage, Microsoft, Google and software development tools. Examples include **Microsoft Teams** and **Slack**, **Salesforce**, **Google Sheets**, **Power BI**, **Tableau**, **Miro**, and connections for **ChatGPT** and **Microsoft Copilot**. HubSpot is supported through Wrike Sync, and developers can use Wrike's open API.

#### Wrike Integrate
Wrike Integrate automates workflows across third-party software, including cloud and on-premises systems, using ready-made "recipes" and no-code builders. It is an additional capability: it is included in the Apex plan and sold as an add-on for other plans, so do not assume it comes with every subscription.

#### Wrike Sync
Wrike Sync, powered by Unito, keeps work aligned through two-way synchronisation between Wrike and other tools. Wrike says it supports 22 systems, including Jira, GitHub, Salesforce, HubSpot, Airtable, Excel and Zendesk. A common use is connecting engineering and business teams: developers stay in Jira or GitHub while marketing and product track the same items in Wrike. Like Integrate, Sync is included in Apex and otherwise an add-on.

### Wrike Ease of Use

#### Initial Setup
Setting Wrike up well means designing spaces, project structures, workflows, custom fields, dashboards, request forms and permissions. Wrike provides templates, but because almost everything is configurable, setup takes longer than with simpler tools. A small team can be running in a day; a department-wide rollout with custom workflows and reporting is a project in itself.

#### Learning Curve
Basic task management is relatively straightforward, and most people can create, assign and update tasks within minutes. Advanced workflows, automations and reporting take more training, and complex organisations benefit from formal onboarding. New team members can initially find the number of options overwhelming. This is one of the most consistent themes in current Capterra feedback: reviewers value Wrike's flexibility and capabilities but repeatedly mention setup complexity and the effort of onboarding.

#### Interface
The interface is detailed and flexible, offers many views, and puts a lot of information within reach. The same density cuts the other way: it can feel crowded, deeply nested project structures can become hard to navigate, and the amount of information on screen can make finding things less intuitive. Wrike is easy to use for simple things and demanding for complex ones, so it is not fair to call it "easy to use" without that qualification.

### Wrike Mobile App
Wrike's iOS and Android apps let you check and update tasks, respond to comments and @mentions, receive notifications, see progress and handle quick updates while away from your desk. AI Essentials includes mobile inbox prioritisation to surface what needs attention first.
Some recent Capterra reviewers describe the mobile experience as less capable or less polished than desktop. That is a recurring concern rather than a verdict that the app is poor; treat mobile as a companion for keeping up to date, and do planning, configuration and reporting on desktop.

### Wrike Pricing
Wrike's published plans for new purchases are below. Paid prices are monthly equivalents billed annually per user, and Wrike states this packaging applies to new purchases from January 21, 2026. Business and higher plans are annual subscriptions only.
| Plan | Published price | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | Basic task and project management |
| Team | $10/user/month | Small teams needing stronger project management |
| Business | $25/user/month | Teams needing customisable workflows |
| Pinnacle | Contact sales | Complex project, resource, financial and reporting needs |
| Apex | Contact sales | Enterprise workflows with extensive AI and automation |
Some capabilities are add-ons: Wrike Whiteboard is $15 per user/month, and Wrike Integrate, Wrike Sync, Wrike Lock, Datahub and extra AI Elite action packs are priced on request (Apex includes Integrate, Sync and unlimited whiteboards). Pricing checked on Wrike's pricing page on 7 October 2026; always confirm before buying.

#### Wrike Free Plan
The Free plan costs $0 and includes web, desktop and mobile apps, basic project and task management, and board and table views. It is realistic for individuals, freelancers or a very small team trying Wrike out or managing simple work. It is not equivalent to the paid platform: Gantt charts, shareable dashboards and most of the workflow, reporting and resource features that make Wrike worth choosing start on paid plans.

#### Wrike Team Plan
At $10 per user/month billed annually, Team is for 2 to 15 users and adds AI Essentials, shareable dashboards and interactive Gantt charts. It suits small teams that need real project planning and visibility, but its 15-user cap means growing teams will soon need Business.

#### Wrike Business Plan
At $25 per user/month billed annually, Business supports 5 to 200 users and adds templatised workspaces, standard integrations, more customisable workflows and an AI Elite starter allowance (which unlocks Copilot and agents). This is the plan most departments and multi-team organisations should evaluate first.

#### Wrike Pinnacle
Pinnacle is quote-based and adds advanced resource and capacity planning, budgeting and financial tracking, advanced reporting and BI, and three times the AI Elite actions of Business. It is aimed at mature project-management organisations, such as PMOs, agencies and professional services firms, that need resource and financial control across many projects.

#### Wrike Apex
Apex is also quote-based and is Wrike's enterprise plan for human- and AI-led workflows at scale. It adds ten times the AI Elite actions of Business, unlimited whiteboards, Wrike Integrate and Wrike Sync. It is not a small-business plan: it is designed for large organisations automating work across many teams and systems.

#### Wrike Free Trial
Wrike offers a 14-day free trial, and its pricing page says no credit card is required. Use the trial to rebuild one real workflow, such as your actual request process or a live project, with the people who will use it. Clicking around the interface will not tell you whether Wrike fits; running real work through it will.

### Wrike Pros and Cons

##### Pros
- Highly customisable workflows, statuses and fields
- Strong visibility across projects and teams
- Detailed task and project management
- Useful, shareable dashboards
- Gantt charts and Kanban boards in one tool
- Good cross-team collaboration and approvals
- Strong reporting options, with BI on top tiers
- Advanced resource and capacity management
- Extensive integrations, plus Integrate and Sync
- Increasingly capable AI and automation
- Well suited to complex, multi-project environments

##### Cons
- Noticeable learning curve, especially for advanced features
- Initial configuration takes time to do well
- Interface can feel complex or crowded
- Advanced features become expensive
- Key capabilities need higher tiers or add-ons
- More than very small teams need
- Mobile experience less complete than desktop
- Reports and automation can require training to configure
This balance matches what users report: people value Wrike's depth, visibility and customisation, while complexity and onboarding are consistently its main drawbacks.

Some long-time users also mention frustration when features change or are retired.
When reading reviews yourself, check whether a review was invited or incentivised by the vendor. Both Capterra and G2 label these, and filtering for non-incentivised reviews gives a more cautious picture. Read the critical reviews from companies similar in size to yours, not just the five-star ones.

### Wrike Customer Support
Wrike provides a Help Center with feature guides, interactive training through Wrike Discover, webinars, and a user community. Higher plans and enterprise agreements add more hands-on onboarding and support options, and professional services are available for complex rollouts.
Support experience is mixed in third-party reviews: Capterra's customer service sub-score is a solid 4.3/5, but individual experiences vary. For large rollouts, ask during the sales process exactly which onboarding and support are included in your plan.

### Wrike Security
Wrike offers granular access permissions, customisable user types (full, collaborator and read-only), account administration controls, locked spaces, and enterprise identity features such as single sign-on on higher tiers. Its website displays AICPA, BSI and CSA STAR compliance badges; confirm current certifications and their scope in Wrike's trust documentation as part of procurement.
Wrike Lock, an add-on, lets organisations control the encryption keys that protect their data in Wrike, so access can be revoked by the customer. It is a strong control for regulated industries, but it is one layer of security rather than a guarantee on its own: permissions, user management and good governance still matter.

### Wrike for Different Types of Teams

#### Wrike for Marketing Teams
Marketing is one of Wrike's strongest fits: campaign management across channels, request forms for incoming work, creative workflows with approvals, deadline tracking and dashboards for campaign status.

#### Wrike for Creative Teams
Creative teams benefit from structured requests, asset review, approvals with feedback on files, and production workflows that involve many stakeholders. Keeping feedback on the asset instead of in email threads is a real time-saver.

#### Wrike for Agencies
Agencies can run multiple clients in separate spaces, track campaigns and deliverables against deadlines, see resource availability across clients and report on delivery. Time tracking and budgeting on higher tiers support billing.

#### Wrike for Project Management Teams and PMOs
This is arguably Wrike's strongest use case: Gantt charts with critical path and baselines, portfolio views, resource planning, advanced reporting, risk visibility and standardised workflows across many projects. A [PMO](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/project-management-office-pmo/) that wants consistent data across the portfolio will find few tools as complete.

#### Wrike for Small Businesses
Wrike can work for small businesses, particularly those that need structured workflows, client request intake or real project planning. But simple teams that mainly need a shared task list will usually get more value, and faster adoption, from lighter tools.

### Who Should Use Wrike?

- Marketing and creative teams that need proofing and request intake
- Organisations replacing several point tools with one platform

##### Look elsewhere if
- Very small teams that only need a simple to-do board
- Teams unwilling to invest time in setup and training

### Is Wrike Worth It?
Wrike is likely worth it if you:
- Manage many projects at the same time.
- Need clear ownership and status visibility across the organisation.
- Have several departments collaborating on the same work.
- Need custom workflows and structured request intake.
- Rely on dashboards and reporting for decisions.
- Need more advanced resource and capacity planning.
- Are willing to invest time in setup and training.
It may not be worth it if:
- Your team only needs a shared to-do list.
- You want almost zero setup.
- You manage only a handful of basic projects.
- Budget is the overriding priority.
- Your users are unlikely to adopt a complex platform.
Our verdict: Wrike's depth is both its biggest advantage and its biggest drawback. For organisations that will use its workflows, visibility, reporting and resource management, it is one of the most complete platforms available, which is why it ranks first in our [project management software](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/) review. For small teams with simple needs, the same depth adds cost and complexity they do not need. Try it on a real workflow during the free trial before committing.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is Wrike good project management software?**
Yes, for the right team. Wrike offers deep project and work management, strong customisation, cross-project visibility and solid reporting, and it rates 4.4/5 on Capterra. The trade-off is a steeper learning curve than simpler tools, so it suits teams with complex, multi-project work more than those needing a basic task list.

**Q: Is Wrike free?**
Yes. Wrike has a Free plan at $0 per user/month with web, desktop and mobile apps, basic task and project management, and board and table views. Features such as Gantt charts, shareable dashboards and advanced workflows require a paid plan.

**Q: How much does Wrike cost?**
Wrike costs $0 on the Free plan, $10 per user/month on Team and $25 per user/month on Business, with Pinnacle and Apex priced on request. Paid prices are monthly equivalents billed annually per user, and Business and higher plans are annual only (checked 7 October 2026).

**Q: Does Wrike have a free trial?**
Yes. Wrike offers a 14-day free trial, and its pricing page states that no credit card is required. Use it to test a real workflow with your team.

**Q: Is Wrike easy to use?**
Partly. Basic task and project management is accessible and quick to learn, but advanced configuration, such as custom workflows, automation and reporting, creates a steeper learning curve than simpler project management tools. Most organisations benefit from some onboarding.

**Q: What is Wrike best used for?**
Wrike is best for project management across many projects, cross-functional work, marketing and creative workflows, PMO operations, resource planning, structured request management and reporting.

**Q: Is Wrike better than Asana?**
Neither is universally better. Wrike suits teams that need deeper workflow customisation, reporting and resource management; Asana suits teams that prioritise simpler, faster adoption. See our [Wrike vs Asana comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/wrike-vs-asana/).

**Q: Is Wrike better than monday.com?**
It depends on the use case. Wrike offers more project management depth and resource control for complex, multi-project work; monday.com is usually easier to adopt and more visual. See our [Wrike vs monday.com comparison](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/wrike-vs-monday/).

**Q: Does Wrike have Gantt charts?**
Yes. Interactive Gantt charts with dependencies, critical path and baselines are included from the Team plan.

**Q: Does Wrike have Kanban boards?**
Yes. Wrike's board view works as a Kanban board with custom statuses, and it is available on every plan, including Free.

**Q: Does Wrike have AI?**
Yes. AI Essentials (content creation and editing, comment summaries, natural-language form and rule creation, AI highlights, mobile inbox prioritisation) is included from the Team plan. AI Elite (Copilot, AI dashboard widgets, customisable AI agents and the Whiteboard assistant) starts on Business, with usage allowances that grow on Pinnacle and Apex.

**Q: What companies is Wrike best for?**
Wrike is particularly well suited to mid-sized and enterprise organisations, agencies, marketing and creative teams, professional services firms and PMOs that manage complex workflows across many projects.

**Q: What are the main disadvantages of Wrike?**
The main disadvantages are the learning curve, the effort needed to set it up well, a dense interface, the cost of advanced features on higher tiers or add-ons, and more functionality than very small teams need.

**Q: Does Wrike integrate with Slack and Microsoft Teams?**
Yes. Wrike integrates with both Slack and Microsoft Teams, alongside around 60 other integrations including Salesforce, Google Sheets, Power BI, Tableau and Miro.

**Q: Is Wrike suitable for small businesses?**
It can be, especially for small businesses that need structured workflows or client request intake. But small teams that only need basic task management may find simpler, cheaper tools a better fit.

# Asana vs ClickUp (2026): Which Should You Choose?

URL: https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/asana-vs-clickup/
Section: Tool comparisons
Summary: Asana vs ClickUp compared: pricing, AI add-on costs, ease of use, Gantt, sprints, docs, automation limits, ratings and which to choose in 2026.

vs

## Asana vs ClickUp (2026): Which Should You Choose?
Asana vs ClickUp comes down to clarity versus breadth: Asana scores 9.0/10 in our review and ClickUp 8.9/10. Choose Asana if you want polished, easy-to-adopt task management that many teams can share, linked to goals and portfolios; choose ClickUp if you want tasks, docs, chat, sprints and time tracking in one workspace at a lower per-user price, and are willing to invest in setup. Below we compare current pricing (including ClickUp's AI add-ons), ease of use, planning, Agile support, automation, AI and user ratings.
- Published 22 September 2026
- Last updated 9 October 2026
- Prices and ratings checked 5 October 2026

### Key takeaways
- Overall: Asana 9.0/10 vs ClickUp 8.9/10. Asana wins ease of use, collaboration and enterprise readiness; ClickUp wins feature depth, Agile support and value for money.
- Price: ClickUp Unlimited is $7 and Business $12 per user/month billed annually; Asana Starter is $10.99 and Advanced $24.99 (checked 7 October 2026).
- AI: Asana's AI Teammates, Dash and AI Studio are included on paid plans with monthly allowances; ClickUp's full AI is an add-on at $9 or $28 per user/month.
- ClickUp includes Gantt charts, goals, portfolios and time tracking from its $7 plan; Asana needs Advanced for goals, portfolios and time tracking, but includes unlimited automation rules from Starter.
- If you need deeper resource, portfolio and approval management than either offers, look at Wrike, our #1-ranked tool.

### Quick verdict
Asana and ClickUp are both capable, well-rated work management platforms, but they are built on different ideas. **Asana** is deliberately focused: a clean structure of projects and tasks, one owner per task, and goals and portfolios that show leaders how work connects to strategy. **ClickUp** aims to replace several apps at once: tasks, Docs, Whiteboards, Chat, Forms, sprints, time tracking and dashboards in one highly configurable workspace.
- **Pick Asana** if you are rolling a tool out across many non-technical teams, want people productive quickly, and manage by goals or OKRs.
- **Pick ClickUp** if you want the most features for the money, run sprints, want docs next to tasks, and have someone willing to design the setup.
- **Consider Wrike** if resource planning, portfolio control and creative approvals at scale are the deciding factors; it is our highest-rated tool overall.
Read our [Wrike vs Asana](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/wrike-vs-asana/) and [Wrike vs ClickUp](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/wrike/wrike-vs-clickup/) comparisons if resource management is on your list.

### What is Asana?
Asana is a work management platform founded in 2008 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It organises work into teams, projects (split into sections) and tasks, each with exactly one assignee. Above projects sit **portfolios**, which group related projects for status reporting, and **goals**, which can update automatically as connected work progresses.
Asana's strengths are a clean, consistent interface, dependable cross-team coordination and unlimited free guests on paid plans. Its trade-offs are that goals, portfolios, workload and time tracking start on the Advanced plan, AI use is metered, and its resource and financial controls are lighter than PMO-focused tools.

### What is ClickUp?
ClickUp is an all-in-one work platform launched in 2017. Everything sits in a hierarchy of Workspace, Spaces, Folders and Lists, and the same tasks can be shown in more than 15 views, including list, board, table, calendar, Gantt, timeline, workload and mind map. Alongside tasks, ClickUp includes Docs and wikis, Whiteboards, Chat, Forms, Goals, sprints, native time tracking and Dashboards, with an AI layer called ClickUp Brain.
ClickUp's strengths are the breadth of what you get and its low per-user price. Its trade-offs are the effort needed to configure it, a dense interface, recurring complaints about lag in busy Workspaces, and AI features that cost extra.

### Pricing compared
|  | Asana | ClickUp |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plans | **Personal:** $0 **Starter:** $10.99/user/month annual ($13.49 monthly) **Advanced:** $24.99/user/month annual ($30.49 monthly) **Enterprise:** Contact sales | **Free Forever:** $0 **Unlimited:** $7/user/month annual ($10 monthly) **Business:** $12/user/month annual ($19 monthly) **Enterprise:** Contact sales **AI add-ons:** $9 or $28/user/month |
Checked on vendors' pricing pages on 5 October 2026. Read the full [Asana pricing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/asana/#pricing) and [ClickUp pricing](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/#pricing) breakdowns.
ClickUp is cheaper at every tier: $7 (Unlimited) and $12 (Business) per user/month billed annually, or $10 and $19 billed monthly, against Asana's $10.99 (Starter) and $24.99 (Advanced) billed annually, or $13.49 and $30.49 monthly. ClickUp requires upgrades to apply to the whole Workspace rather than to selected users.

#### Plan for plan: which tiers match?
The tiers bundle features differently, so compare the plan you would actually need:
- **ClickUp Unlimited ($7)** already includes unlimited Gantt charts, custom fields, native time tracking, goals and portfolios. In Asana, goals, portfolios and time tracking need Advanced ($24.99). But Unlimited keeps Dashboards as a trial and limits automation executions.
- **Asana Starter ($10.99)** includes timeline and Gantt views, dashboards, forms, custom fields, unlimited automation rules and AI (with allowances). It is the closest match to ClickUp Business for teams that live in dashboards.
- **ClickUp Business ($12)** adds unlimited Dashboards, 5,000 automations a month, sprint points and sprint reporting, portfolio workload, mind maps, proofing and Google SSO.
- **Asana Advanced ($24.99)** adds goals, portfolios, workload, approvals and proofing, time tracking, forms branching and Salesforce, Tableau and Power BI integrations.

#### The cost of AI
This is the most important caveat in the price comparison. Asana's AI Teammates, Dash and AI Studio are included on paid plans, with monthly allowances (5 AI Teammates and Dash requests per user, capped at 50 per account on Starter and Advanced, plus AI Studio credits), and paid top-ups at $0.50 to $0.60 per request. ClickUp's Free plan includes only limited AI trial use; full AI is a per-user add-on: **Brain AI at $9** or **Everything AI at $28** per user/month, with extra AI Super Credits at $10 per 10,000. ClickUp says yearly AI billing is discounted by up to 20%.

#### What a team actually pays
Monthly cost at three team sizes, using annual prices checked on 7 October 2026. Taxes, other add-ons and negotiated discounts are excluded, so treat these as indicative.
| Team size | ClickUp Unlimited | ClickUp Business | ClickUp Business + Brain AI | Asana Starter | Asana Advanced |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 users | $35 | $60 | $105 | $54.95 | $124.95 |
| 10 users | $70 | $120 | $210 | $109.90 | $249.90 |
| 25 users | $175 | $300 | $525 | $274.75 | $624.75 |
Without AI, ClickUp is clearly cheaper. With Brain AI for every user, ClickUp Business costs more than Asana Starter, and with Everything AI ($40 per user/month on Business) it costs more than Asana Advanced. Many teams buy AI for a subset of users only, which keeps ClickUp's price advantage.

#### Free plans and trials
ClickUp's Free Forever plan is the more generous for small teams: unlimited members and tasks, Docs, Board, Calendar and Sprints, one Form, three Whiteboards, up to five Spaces and 100 automation executions, but only 60MB of storage, and Gantt, Dashboards and time tracking only as trials. Asana Personal includes unlimited tasks and projects with list, board and calendar views, but is limited to 2 seats per project and team, with no timelines, dashboards, forms, rules or AI.
For trials, Asana offers a self-serve Advanced trial with no credit card (its pricing page does not state the length). ClickUp does not advertise a fixed-length trial; instead, Free Forever includes trial access to paid features, and the pricing page advertises a money-back guarantee, so check the refund terms before paying.

### Ease of use and setup
This is Asana's clearest win: 9/10 for ease of use against ClickUp's 7/10 in our review. Capterra users score the two closer (Asana 4.4/5, ClickUp 4.3/5 for ease of use), but the difference shows up in rollout.
**Asana** is opinionated. Teams, projects, sections and single-owner tasks give everyone the same mental model, so a new team can be productive on day one and projects look consistent across departments. The harder parts (portfolios, goals, workload, AI Studio) depend on discipline rather than technical setup.
**ClickUp** is configurable. Spaces, Folders, Lists, custom statuses, ClickApps and dozens of views mean there are many ways to model the same work, and reviewers often describe it as overwhelming at first. Teams that invest in a deliberate setup, and hide the features they do not need, get a lot back. Our guide to the [work breakdown structure](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/work-breakdown-structure/) is a good way to decide how to split work into Spaces, Folders and Lists.
Both tools attract some complaints about performance. In Capterra's topic summaries, about 78% of ClickUp reviews that mention lag are negative, and about 60% of Asana reviews that mention performance and reliability are negative. Test either with a realistic volume of tasks during your trial.
Tip
If you choose ClickUp, start with one Space, a handful of Lists and three or four views. Add Docs, Whiteboards, Chat and sprints only when a team asks for them. Most failed ClickUp rollouts are over-built, not under-built.

### Task management, views and Gantt charts
Both tools handle tasks, subtasks, dependencies, custom fields, recurring tasks and templates well. Two differences matter day to day. Asana allows **one assignee per task**, which makes ownership unambiguous; ClickUp allows **multiple assignees**, which suits shared work but needs clear conventions. Asana lets one task live in several projects; ClickUp offers custom task types and subtasks nested up to seven levels.
For scheduling, ClickUp goes further. Its Gantt view supports all four dependency types, automatic rescheduling, the critical path, slack time, milestones and baselines, and is unlimited from the $7 plan. Asana's timeline and Gantt views (from Starter) show dependency chains and let you compare progress against a target schedule, but its product pages do not describe critical path analysis. Both score 8/10 for planning and resource management in our review.
If date-driven scheduling matters, read our guides to [Gantt charts](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/gantt-chart/) and the [critical path method](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/critical-path-method/), then test your real schedule in both tools.

### Docs, whiteboards and chat
This is where ClickUp's all-in-one approach is most visible. ClickUp Docs support nested pages, real-time co-editing, inline comments that become tasks, version history and wikis; Whiteboards turn sticky notes into tasks; and ClickUp Chat adds channels, direct messages and calls next to the work (Chat is included from Unlimited).
Asana is task-first. It has project overviews, messages, status updates and comments, but no full docs-and-wiki workspace or whiteboard, so most Asana teams link documents from Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or a separate wiki through integrations. That is a reasonable choice if you already have those tools; ClickUp's advantage is consolidation, but only if your team actually moves its documents and conversations into it.

### Agile and sprint support
ClickUp scores 9/10 for Agile and software teams in our review, against Asana's 7/10. ClickUp creates sprints as dated Lists, rolls unfinished work into the next sprint automatically, supports sprint points on Business, and reports burndown, burnup, velocity and cumulative flow. GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket integrations link commits and pull requests to tasks.
Asana supports board-based and sprint-style projects, and many product managers use it for roadmaps and launches, linking to engineering work in Jira or GitHub. Teams that need backlogs, story points and Agile reporting inside the tool will find ClickUp stronger. Large engineering organisations should also compare [ClickUp vs Jira](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management-tools/clickup/clickup-vs-jira/). Our free [sprint planning template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/sprint-planning-template/) and guide to [story points](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/scrum/scrum-story-points/) help you set up either tool.

### Automation and forms
Asana includes **unlimited automation rules on every paid plan**. Rules pair a trigger (a form submission, a section change, an approaching due date) with an action (reassign, move, request approval, post to Slack, create a Jira issue), and AI Studio handles multi-step or judgement-based workflows.
ClickUp's automation builder is larger and includes an AI builder that drafts rules from plain language, but executions are capped: 100 on Free Forever, 1,000 on Unlimited, 5,000 a month on Business and 250,000 a month on Enterprise. Busy teams on Unlimited can reach the cap, so check your expected volume.
Both tools turn form submissions into tasks. ClickUp Forms support conditional logic and external submitters, with one Form on the free plan and unlimited from Unlimited. Asana forms start on Starter, with branching on Advanced.

### AI features
**Asana** includes AI Teammates (more than 30 prebuilt AI agents for areas such as marketing, PMO and IT, plus custom ones), Asana Dash (AI briefs such as a morning summary of priorities) and AI Studio (a no-code builder for AI workflows) on paid plans, within the monthly allowances described above.
**ClickUp Brain** answers questions about your tasks, Docs and Chat, writes and summarises, and runs enterprise search across connected apps; the Brain AI add-on also includes AI chat with a choice of models, which ClickUp lists as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. Super Agents can be @mentioned and assigned tasks. The Everything AI tier adds the AI Notetaker, AI Fields, AI automations and dashboards, and more agent usage.
Both vendors state that customer data is not used to train third-party models, and both run agents within existing permissions. The practical difference is cost: Asana's AI is bundled but metered, while ClickUp's is a separate per-user purchase.

### Goals, portfolios, reporting and workload
**Asana** is strongest at the strategic layer. On Advanced, portfolios show the health of many projects on one screen, goals can be broken into sub-goals and updated automatically from projects or Salesforce data, and workload shows each person's effort across a portfolio. Dashboards start on Starter, and Advanced adds Tableau and Power BI integrations. Enterprise adds capacity planning.
**ClickUp** includes Goals, Portfolios and a workload view from Unlimited, and portfolio-level workload on Business. Its Dashboards are actionable (you can update tasks from a card) and can be shared with clients, but unlimited Dashboards with advanced cards need Business. ClickUp connects to Tableau for deeper analysis.
For OKR-driven organisations, Asana's goals are more mature; our free [OKR template](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/templates/okr-template/) helps you define them before you build anything. For small teams wanting capacity views cheaply, ClickUp offers more at a lower tier. PMOs needing formal [capacity planning](https://neuralprojectinstitute.com/project-management/capacity-planning/), budgets and financial tracking may find both lighter than Wrike.
